review_text:
Y ou know you're onto a good thing when the Front of House people are friendly.  Leaving Jane Russell and her team of kindly hippies adorning the foyer, I settled in for Banbridge Musi- cal Society's production of Sweet Char- ity.  Played by Lorraine Jackson Brown, this Charity was exceptionally good. This show hinges on a good Charity.  If you don't like her, you're not going to sit com- fortably for the rest of the night.  I loved her from first sight - she was dressed in a black, almost Mary Quant style dress and this and her dark hair and expressive face and voice had her standing out against everyone else.  I don't mean to say that everyone else was blending into the back- ground, rather that everyone did what they should be doing at that moment; this was the introduction of Charity, our chance to give her the once over to see if we liked her. Banbridge have a talented cast - many people showed they could act, and the chorus was great both in group numbers and in the individual roles they appeared in throughout the show. Director, Choreographer and leading man (phew!) Declan Moore, obviously has boundless energy.  It was reflected in his direction, his cast and in his own portrayal of Oscar.  It was clear that both he and Musical Director Colin Loughead are a good team.  In fact the overall impression of this group is one of great unity of pur- pose.  They presented themselves as a united front, bonded and focused on their objective - to entertain their appreciative audience.

The theatre space is normally a cinema at the Iveagh Movie Studios, with comfort- able tiered seating and a decent stage.  I was warned that the acoustics weren't great, and it was occasionally a problem for the band but Colin Loughead's musi- cal direction was faultless - the orches- tra (who appeared above the action on stage) was tight and played well.  Singers could always be heard above the music so that is very much a plus, even though at times it was difficult to hear all the instruments.  This was my first show as an AIMS adjudicator and now that I had arrived, on time, not having gotten lost once, I relaxed to the Overture, realizing I was in good hands.  All musical numbers were good, Charity sang every song with gusto and a strong voice, but I particularly liked How It All Began and If My Friends Could See Me Now - the band and Jack- son-Brown were in fine fettle.

Andrea Price and Emma Woods as Nickie and Helene respectively, along with the Dance Hall Girls did a super job on Hey Big Spender, and it was clear that there was good interaction between all the girls here and also with Charity.  The girls were also great in There's Gotta Be Something Better Than This, and Andrea Price in particular shone.

When you go to see Sweet Charity, you want to know how they'll handle Rhythm of Life.  This is where the men are separated from the boys (although in this case, it's got to be women from the girls as they very much have the major- ity).  It was a spectacular number, musi- cally bang on and visually exciting.  Very hard not to join in, especially when you're an AIMS adjudicator.  The outrageous costumes and wigs enhanced the fun and Ian Davidson's Daddy Brubeck was having a ball, though this didn't affect his performance.  Denise Bryson was chorus mistress and she had good control of her charges, they never let her down.  Other notable chorus numbers were I'm a Brass Band and I love To Cry At Weddings with a strong performance from James Daly's Herman.

The show worked well on a visual level too, with costumes and make up that caught the essence of the 60's (more Mary Quant style from the younger danc- ers in the Pompeii club and the Rhythm of Life scene for example) along with Rod- ney Ellis' suitable lighting design. Russell Caughey's set allowed for the large en- semble and there were some really clever scenes, I loved the lift scene and the free standing big wheel carriage - all of these built by Stage Manager Anthony Fairley. The Banbridge group is to be envied for its ability to fly the set in from the wings. Declan Moore's direction was creative and he handles large groups really well.  I particularly enjoyed the lift scene, where his character Oscar is introduced - this was wonderfully comedic.  Other notable performances came from Eddie Orr as Vittorio Vidal, though his wig must get some credit too! Vittorio and Ursula played by Adele Kelly worked best when they were fighting, their 'love-making' scene being a little awkward. Pamela McCullough as Carmen gave a gutsy performance and Emma McAvoy played a suitably sweet Rosie, as yet unsullied by the bad influence of those Dance Hall Girls.  Paul Brown deserves praise for taking a butler and making him funny. The choreography worked for this group for the most part - there not being many actual dancers - it was simple and clever and everyone could do it.  However, I would have liked to have seen those who could dance being highlighted more - Charity included.  It didn't affect the show so much, just that one might expect more dancing from dance hall girls!

Overall, the show ran smoothly; musi- cians, singers and technicians got their cues right, the cast shone and there was palpable enthusiasm from the audience. Presumably the production team is very proud of itself.

F or anyone who lived through the 1980's (and there are a few of us!), The Wedding Singer  is a musical filled with nostalgia for a life measured in wedding celebrations, bad boyfriends, big hair and heartfelt songs. In July, Green- hills Variety Group invited everyone to their party and showed us all a very good time.  In many ways, there's a  clue in the title of this show, and the Wedding Singer is musically almost non-stop. The band, under the direction of Sarah Lynch Bar- rett, picked up the style of the music and played with flair and control. Balance was occasionally problematic, but not chroni- cally so, and the versatility of the instru- mentalists was impressive. The singing of the principals was especially strong, and the chorus likewise rose to the different challenges the show presents.  The com- pany is strong on combining movement and music, and the choreography was appropriate to the times portrayed and the abilities of the cast. In fact, the choreog- raphy was like a character in itself, and there were more than a few nods to the styles of Michael Jackson, Madonna and Saturday Night Fever.

all played important roles in creating the atmosphere of the excellent eighties. The level of detail especially in costume, makeup and hair was impressive and occasionally cringeworthy, as we were reminded of the many fashion and hair mistakes that made up that colourful era. The purple bridesmaid dresses in the opening scene set a tone that was both nostalgic and uncomfortable, but in a good way. I also spotted a jumpsuit that would have elicited a guilty chuckle from many an audience member. Frequent nods to trends and actual characters (Boy George, Tina Turner, President Reagan) were managed with forensic attention. This was a complicated and detailed show for those responsible for costume, and the resulting effect was well worth the effort and the nostalgic touches just kept coming.

The set for Wedding Singer was clev- erly constructed and worked best when the atmosphere of a wedding venue was needed. Different scenes were suggested in ingenious ways including a row of sinks in a ladies room, a DeLorean-type car and a dumpster, as well as the ubiquitous sparkly ball. Other details, such as post- ers for the Bangles and Flock of Seagulls were great finishing touches. Stage management was top-class, with scenes changing in an instant with little or no fuss. There was an 80's-style efficiency to the way things moved that really added to the tone of the show, and the pace of the action never had to slow to accommodate shifting scenery or movement of the large cast. Sound and lighting effects were also used to suggest changes of scene and at- mosphere, and again the 80's mood was the guiding force in what was a colourful and well-balanced look.

Across this production of The Wed- ding Singer, the Stage Direction bal- anced music, which was plentiful and plot, which was admittedly thin.  This was a very successful job of story telling, due in great part to the clear path of the principle characters through the show. Individual performers were allowed to re- ally "go for" their characterisations, and it meant that elements of music, dance and drama were fluidly exchanged and allowed the narrative to remain in front. Lovely touches included a 'granny double' cartwheel, a traditional wedding bouquet throwing and Tina Turner and Ronald Reagan impressions. The opening se- quence set a great tone for the show and the various character 'types' came to the fore.  In large scenes there was a sense of everyone engaged with the ac- tion, knowing what they were meant to be doing and when, and these scenes were interesting in terms of the drama as well as music and dance. Smaller scenes which rested less on choreography or music were well realised, and there was real intelligence in the use of the stage. Actors were encouraged to put them- selves fully into their roles and take risks. Uses of moments of 'freeze' were very effective, and the discipline and engage- ment of the ensemble cast was impres- sive.  American accents throughout were very good, consistent and fluent. Alan McHale as Robbie Hart was at- tractive and energetic in the role, and convincing as a wedding singer. At times Robbie was in danger of becoming a cari- cature of himself, which in the context of the show was no bad thing. 'Somebody Kill Me' set a very high bar for the rest of the show's musical numbers. Tracey Armstrong as Julia Sullivan was believ- able as a well-meaning girl trying to do the right thing. Her singing was impres- sive in its dynamic range - she had the sense to vary the volume and 'sell' the lyrics in a way that really helped to ad- vance her character. 'Come Out of the Dumpster', in addition to being the odd- est song title ever, was full of sincerity. David Latham as Sammy exhibited strong acting ability and added solid support to ensemble numbers.  John Conroy  really "went for it" as band member George, a true comedian.  His fraught pathos in 'George's Prayer' and later work made him a real focus in ensemble numbers, and he walked an interesting line in terms of his character's journey in the show. Thomas Creighton as Glen Guglia gave a confident performance and was in good voice on the night.  His characterisation of arrogance and duplicity was spot-on. Amanda Cunningham as Holly has a wonderful voice and provided good sup- port in a strong cast.  'Right in Front of Your Eyes' was a wonderful number, very well sung.  Ciara Murphy as Linda ap- peared to have the most fun of anyone on stage much of the time.  Her numbers 'Note From Linda' and 'Let Me Come Home' were among the most watchable moments in the show.  Her character was over the top in a well judged way and made a strong impression.

The chorus and minor characters in The Wedding Singer worked hard and no one pulled back from channelling their inner 70's popstar, geek or dancin' queen into the action. The tone was set from the very beginning and energy and wit was sustained to the end.

Greenhills Variety Group are clearly a talented and ambitious company. Their choice of The Wedding Singer was in- spired given the enthusiasm of the team and the resources available. The show was well cast and the production struck a balance between the musical, comic and dramatic elements. There were individual standout performances and very strong ensemble work.

I t's hard to believe that Rodgers and Hammerstein's Carousel is 65 years old this year. The themes considered in the show resonate in today's world as much as, if not more than when it was first produced in 1945. This is serious stuff, and any production worth its spin on the carousel needs to balance heart- felt emotion and dramatic tension with the gentle humour that also inhabits this show. Newry Musical and Orchestra Soci- ety managed this with flair and pace. Carousel has a fine, long overture and MD Gerry Doherty and his small band of mostly woodwind and brass players gave the famous waltz a nice swing. Director David Cunningham thoroughly understood the importance of the open- ing section, and the busy bustle of the carnival came across with plenty of ac- tion, including acrobats, red Indians and a dancing bear.  The two freezes - one just before the famous waltz starts and again when Julie Jordan and Billy Bigelow meet on the Carousel, were well-executed and provided way-points in this scene setting segment.

Ciara Bell as Julie Jordan had a won- derful speaking voice and is a solid singer too, and Anthony Fitzpatrick had the right mixture of swagger and occasional uncertainty that kept us interested in this character's journey. Ciara Lavery as Car- rie is a fine actress who picked up on the comic potential of her suitor's name "Eeeee-noch"!, and made her transition to matronly snob later in the show with some flair. Fergal White as Enoch was a strong vocal presence and his deadpan approach gave him the biggest laughs at comic points. "Where's the fire?" stands out as a classic. Unfortunately, Julie and Carrie wore nearly identical black wigs, which threatened to overwhelm their pretty faces and took away from their otherwise natural pres- ence on stage. Sets were cleverly de- signed, moved easily and worked well throughout.

Changes were calm and ef- ficient.  Sound quality was clear, and bal- ance favoured singers at all times. Gently falling leaves during "If I Loved You" were a poignant reminder of how things change as time passes. Lighting was simple but very effective. Costumes were colour- ful and well made, with good detail and everything fit very well indeed. The fluo- rescent carousel itself was not particularly to my taste, with  imaginative lighting making it glow luridly at various points.  I wondered if this crucial element might have been at odds with an otherwise very traditional approach to design.

The chorus work in the show was focussed and lively. Occasionally the men retreated into diagonal lines, but there was good interaction on stage and the women's chorus was animated and sympathetic to the scenes. The singing was strong and part work sure-footed. Also sure-footed were the small team of dancers directed by choreographer Jillian Liggett. They played quite a few roles in the course of this production, with lively combinations of ballet and theatrical movement for numbers like June is Bus- tin' Out All Over and the Waltz segments, as well as portraying carousel horses in the dream sequence. This was an espe- cially effective use of movement, and the costumes were beautiful.

Carousel is a piece populated with great characters, and Newry's produc- tion was bustin' out all over with excellent performances in these roles. Eithne Bell as Mrs Mullins, the owner of the Carousel was wonderfully nasty, yet we still saw the heart of gold underneath. Siobhan McGivern, as Nettie Fowler, though not the operatic singer sometimes placed in this role, was warm and consistent and made the role work in her own way. Damian Lavery played Jigger as a pirate with a difference, spreading his accent across several thousand miles of Atlantic seaboard, ("you're the only goil for me!"), and was among the most watch-able performers, drawing Billy into his net of crime. Mr Bascombe, the intended victim of that crime, was played by Jim McGuigan, who dispatched his assailants with portly ease.

Most interesting and effective was the portray of the Heavenly Friend by Colin McCalmont, who gloried in a slightly camp, impatient take on the role - Gok Wan meets Gordon Gekko, in a bright white suit and severe specs. He was the perfect foil to a suave Lowry Hodgett, who as the Star Keeper guided Billy Bigelow to the edge of heaven to see his troubled teenage daughter Louise, now 15 years old.  Her portrayal, by the excellent Louis Hale, was perfectly balanced - literally, as she's a lovely dancer, and figuratively, as she negotiates for us the angst of grow- ing up in a close, judgemental community with the stigma of her father's untimely death. The snobby Snow children were perfectly captured by a young disciplined and very consistent line of future stars. And speaking of stars, the scene in which Louise meets her father, who gives her a star to keep from heaven is a difficult one to pull off, but I felt this worked well, owing to the set-p in which we see Julie and Carrie as older, wiser women. By this time, we've witnessed Billy's coming of age too, and his yearning to do the right thing by his daughter.

This is a long show, with pockets of implausibility just waiting to trip up an unsuspecting company.  However, David Cunningham guided his cast through the very human and then somewhat super- natural worlds that Rodgers and Ham- merstein have left behind. Rodgers wrote that Oscar Hammerstein "never wrote more meaningful or more moving lyrics", and felt his own music was among his most personally satisfying. Newry held our attention across this production and it didn't seem like a long evening at all.  It was a real nice clambake, and this young company deserves full credit for taking on such a big beautiful show and making it their own.

I didn't know much about Spring Awak- ening before seeing the Irish Premiere and début production of NYMT in the Helix Theatre last September.  My re- search told me it was all about sex; this musical adaptation of the 1891 play by Frank Wedekind which was banned in Germany for almost one hundred years for dealing with the shocking issue of teenage sexual awakening.  Yep, it's all in there: masturbation, homosexuality, child abuse, suicide, rape and bondage.  Oh dear, I thought.  I prepared to be as bro- adminded as possible and at least enjoy the music, written by Duncan Sheik.  My guest was a twenty year old who assured me it was a great show.  Humph!  But I'm no prude, mind!

Now, fast forward to the part where there is an amazing ensemble tableau (similar to the Tonight Ensemble in West Side Story, but not the same, oh no, not the same at all…) Centre stage a boy masturbates (albeit under a long white nightgown); down stage right, another has sexual fantasies about his piano teacher; dotted around are people feeling the pangs of all this frustration.  And me? I was mesmerised, actually delighted that I could enjoy this without a single tinge of embarrassment or shock or anything other than sheer entertainment accompanied by a kind of inner voice, a lesson if you will; Here! This show says. Here - this is what we think about.  This is what happens behind closed bedroom doors and in the darkness of our con- fused minds.  Here - look at it.  This is the truth.  Through fantastic music, brave direction and unbelievable performances this production of Spring Awakening was, well, a wake-up call.  I have an almost eleven year old who keeps asking awk- ward questions.  Now I'm more inclined to answer them and be honest with her so that I don't help create a taboo where one should not exist.  That is the essence of this show I think.

I gather (though I'm not certain) that there is a format that companies per- forming the show need to adhere to. For example, that the action take place on a central podium space (thrust stage) rather than your standard proscenium, and that performers sing into hand held microphones, as this really is a concert and show rolled into one.  There may be other provisos, and  I really don't know how much of the show was up to the per- sonal creativity of the production team, however there was immense effort put in by everyone involved; the floor had a hand painted forest effect, and the back and side walls of the set were amazing - austere looking portraits in gothic style frames along with neon lights and dozens of various coloured light bulbs in individ- ual boxes randomly positioned upon the brick effect wall, all separately wired (the company needed to hire the theatre three days before the show in order to prepare the set). Though simple, it was a visual feast, different to the extreme, striking, thought provoking and at times breath- taking in how it enhanced the story. The attention to detail was above and beyond the expectation of any amateur show. John Donnelly (Director) and John Can- non (Production Manager) were credited with set design so perhaps some of this was indeed a variation from the original. The set was constructed by them and a team of fifteen. On both sides of the stage - another proviso - were wooden chairs upon which some of the cast sat and also some members of the audience. There was a pleasant continuity to this, without awkward entering and exiting the stage area while some luckier spectators really got embroiled into the drama.

Of the music I can only say good things. The nine piece band, under the masterful control of MD Kevin Walsh, were positioned at the back of the stage behind the acting area.  I loved Touch Me, sung beautifully by the boys and girls and accompanied by strings and guitar. The singers were overpowered at times during The Dark I Know Well, particularly by bass guitar though this might have been a sound balance problem. The song Totally F***ed by Melchior and the Com- pany was funny in the sense that anyone who's ever been there knows "there's a moment you know you're f***ed". Oh, how difficult it was not to run out on stage and join in the head-banging - everything here reflected the frustration of the teens and went a long way to explaining some of the crazy exploits on the dance floor, nay even the evolution of the disco! Lighting by Solar Sound Systems, was exceptional, I thought the colours used were quite experimental; purples to reflect a dangerous unstable mood; turquoise and violet with dry ice as we headed into the love making scene. It could be subtle when required and always on cue.

Wendla, the female protagonist, played by Yasmine Missaoui, was just perfect in the role, after a slightly weak start at the beginning of Mama Who Bore Me.  In her performance was a balance of the mix between innocence and the coming of age, very tenderly portrayed.  Her singing strengthened hugely as the show pro- gressed. She cried throughout Whisper- ing without singing off key.  The energy of Vickey Howell as her mother, Frau Berg- man, contrasted effectively and here we had the hub of the story immediately: re- pressive adult, wool pulling over eyes sort of thing - no good can come from this. Ms Howell's comic timing was super yet she could switch from this to the difficul- ties presented to her, and she could sing too.  The girls, Wendla's friends, were in a word, fabulous.  Chill down spine stuff.  Emily Carroll (Ilse), Fiona Carty (Martha), Megan O'Riordan (Thea) and Niamh Maher (Anna) could all easily hold down a lead role.  In particular Fiona's voice had a velvety quality to it; The Dark I Know Well with Ilse was sung with soul by both. Later on Ilse's Blue Wind was very moving. All the girls worked together beautifully and their movement was really graceful. Vocally, everyone was strong. The same could be said of the boys Denis Grindel (Hanschen), Rob Walsh (Ernst), Barry Cannon (Georg) and Der- mot Malone (Otto).

Ruairi O'Connor played a very convinc- ing leading man as Melchior, his strength in his acting over his singing.  I wasn't initially aware of much chemistry between Melchior and Wendla although The Word of your Body was quite beautiful; there was a delayed reaction from the audi- ence, as we were totally mesmerised. A scene where Wendla asks Melchior to beat her was stunning.  This could have gone so horribly wrong yet it was handled with feeling by both actors while adhering to the techniques employed by director John Donnelly.  Later, Melchior sang Left Behind at Moritz's funeral with sincerity and gentleness. When he found Wendla's grave, I felt it in the pit of my stomach. Jonny Holden's Moritz sounded almost exactly like the Broadway actor John Gallagher Jnr though he brought his own very animated energy to it.  The chemistry of friendship between him and Melchior was convincing and he really caught the tortured soul of the character well.  The scene between Moritz and Ilse as they stood face out to the audience speaking directly into microphones was very natu- rally performed.  We had to agree that things really had gotten messy and their desire to be children again was terribly Back to that thing I mentioned already. You remember, don't pretend you don't; the one with the masturbation and stuff in it? This scene was held together by Denis Grindel as Hanschen, who as a sort of Draco Malfoy lookalike pulled things off with absolute confidence. Here again was the comic timing which made this bizarre tableau so entertaining. I may be risking my reputation, so I will say: you had to be there, honestly. That was what was so exceptional about the direction and performance of this and many other mo- ments in the show. Hanschen's seduction of Ernst, played with confidence by Rob Walsh was delightfully funny. Grindel re- ally played with the audience and both actors excelled here.

The 'adults' were presented mostly as cruel and self protecting, living in a repressive village where everyone was faint hearted and easily shocked. Head- master Knochenbruch was portrayed with very convincing authority by John Furlong. His articulation was admirable. Philippa Alford as Fraulein Knuppledick (got to love those names) was an equally hardened teacher, crisp and clear, these two really came across as the baddies. Melchior's mother Frau Gabor was suit- able portrayed by Jennifer McGann as one of the more understanding adults. Adam Lawlor's sternness as Moritz's Fa- ther explained a lot as to why his son was the way he was. Bob O'Mhurcu as the Doctor performed well - there was a poi- gnant scene between him and Wendla's mother.  Ed Leamy played Schmidt, the abortionist and ultimately Wendla's killer - it was deeply disturbing as he carried the screaming Wendla away.

Direction by John Donnelly was superb. There were so many scenes that should not have worked. Clearly this cast were primed and guided. There was a con- stant smooth jump from comic moments to poignant touching scenes. The love making scene on the swing with Melchior and Wendla was well worth the effort it must have taken to get it right. Along with tender singing from the chorus who held onto the swing while the scene unfolded, the mood was perfectly portrayed. Ruairi O'Connor and Yasmine Missaoui are to be greatly admired for their performances during I Believe and full marks for delicate direction. Moritz's suicide by gunshot was powerful because there was no sound, only sudden blackness replaced by a simple bouquet of flowers. The whole fu- neral scene gave me goose bumps; boys sang falsetto while Moritz's father cried inconsolably before a white light blinded the audience. Staging generally was ut- terly beautiful - the gathering of the cast on stage at the final song was simple and moving, they were completely lost in the moment.

Choreographer Thomas Creighton, while respecting the original show, really understood the mood of each number and with the help of Dance Captain Colm O'Leary, oversaw a very tight perfor- mance from every cast member. The boys' sexual frustration and torment was beautifully portrayed in The Bitch of Liv- ing during which the Headmaster held impressively long freeze frames.

The Mirror-Blue Night where Mel- chior is raised on a swing like section of the stage had creative move- ment; physical ex- pressions of the feelings of the repressed teens. The apparently random dancing for Totally F***ed was visually really strong and worked on so many levels.

Costumes, while ordinary everyday at- tire (of a mish mash of eras) looked great on everyone, from the boys' uniforms to the girls' pretty dresses - Wendla's sim- ple blue shift and her thigh length black stockings had you thinking: sexy - oh no, she's too young and innocent what a thought - but wait, it is still sexy… and so on. Everyone else was dressed in shades of browns and faded tones, though Ilse's purple shawl over her green dress at the end was very striking. Costumes were hired from Pat McGann Theatre Hire or sourced by the group.

Jenny Houlihan did hair and make-up. Hair in particular, the boy's hairstyles de- serve mention. They were quite entertain- ing all by themselves.

The sound was good, though balance was straining at times, particularly during The Bitch of Living and annoyingly during the otherwise beautiful The Dark I Know Well.  Voices were almost drowned out during Ilse's song Blue Wind.

All performers in this show were super - from the principals mentioned to the choral parts (swings) and other smaller roles. This is an important show that par- ents of teens in particular should make a point of going to see - the bonus would be if it were anywhere near as good as the efforts of NYMT.

O n more than one occasion dur- ing the Real Theatre Company's début performance of Les Mi- sérables, I put down my pencil and won- dered if I would be given anything I could actually criticise. This is a dream realised for Lucy O'Byrne, Artistic director and founder along with fellow founder and dreamer Andrew Linnie, (above right) who is also the show's Musical Director. And both perform hefty roles (Eponine and En- jolras).  Given that this is the school edi- tion, it means they both have to be aged nineteen or younger.

Out of breath yet? You would have been had you seen it. Director Rachel O'Byrne is still in college studying drama and theatre studies in Trinity, and with a background in dance she also choreo- graphed the show. Apart from some minor clumsiness which will fade away with experience, this is one naturally gifted director. Had I taken a camera with me and snapped at any time, almost every picture would have had perfect composi- tion. Visually this show was breath tak- ing, but the cast clearly understood and shared the vision of the director, given that they executed everything so well. Everyone had a good understanding of the pace and mood, and movement of the group numbers generally was always fluid, although the scene around the top- pling cart in act one was a little weak as was the movement/fight between Javert and Valjean by Fantine's bedside - surely Javert should have been harder to knock down? Though there wasn't much danc- ing the director put time and effort into the movement of each scene, enjoying the visual impact instead. Simple but impor- tant aspects of production were adhered to, such as choreographed entrances and exits of crowds.

The sense of danger and the fear behind the barricade was very palpable.

The shooting and firing was utterly convinc- ing, leading to that wonderful but harrowing final tableau of dead bodies.

The slow motion movement of the dying rebels was exquisite. Choral work was generally executed very well and direc- tion taken. Lighting, music, colours and slow non distracting movement and at other times, stillness, worked very well here. The slow motion memory of Marius' friends during Empty Chairs was an en- lightened piece of choreography, with their ghosts re-creating the rebellion with chairs. Andrew Linnie set up his orches- tra, chorus and principals with remarkable proficiency before handing over to Con- ductor Dave McGauran, who really did a powerful job. Balance was good.  Brass were great.  The musicans were sensitive and powerful without becoming over pow- ering. Strings seemed to be under some strain during A Heart Full of Love, though the number was absolute class from sing- ers and orchestra. One Day More was rousing, I once more put my pencil down, all the more to wallow in the moment. Where to start with this cast? From the beginning they proved themselves to be well worth the effort that was put into finding them; auditions took place far and wide and the results were nothing short of magnificent.  Stephen Perry's kindly Bishop of Digne sang with sincerity and maturity, one of the first of many beauti- ful voices, his was strong and tender at the same time. The chorus quickly es- tablished themselves as excellent for At the End of the Day before the convincing friction between the Factory Girl Caroline Nicholson who sang beautifully against the mellow tones of Leah Penston's Fantine.  A good performance also from understudy Andrew Duane as the Fac- tory Foreman. Fantine's unbearably sad I Dreamed A Dream was sung with con- fidence.  Bamatabois played his part well as the cad who bothers Fantine. Chris Currid brought great stage presence to police captain Javert and a convincing portrayal of the man with principals so rig- idly held to. His voice was strong in Stars and his dilemma on the bridge before jumping to his death was assured. Young Cosette sang Castle on a Cloud with strength yet vulnerability too. Laura Lam- bert's Madame Thénardier was the rough and tough Inn Keeper's wife and brought out some wonderful comic moments with daughter Eponine and particularly hus- band Thénardier, played by understudy James O'Connor. Young Cosette and Eponine were played over the run by Lao- ise McHugh, Sined McMullen and Alison Conroy. All this welcome comedy was en- hanced by very convincing drunks for the colourful number Master of the House, really an excellent chorus input here. Gavroche, played by either Ben Mahon or Jac Mordaunt, was wonderful as the confident little boy of the streets and the duo between him and Lucy O'Byrne's Ep- onine had a natural chemistry. Whichever of the actors I saw portray Gavroche, I did note he was one to watch - such comfort on stage was impressive. Gavroche's death was a pin drop moment, the anger and injustice of it was clearly felt. Lucy O'Byrne's voice was a pleasure and she played the tragic and sad Eponine fright- eningly well. I was heartbroken for her; it was a beautiful portrayal, never becom- ing indulgent. On My Own was sung with absolute sincerity and her dying evoked a tearful response. The cast were still and the audience silent after A Little Fall of Rain, speak- ing louder than any applause.

The rebel- lious students were strong, vocally and in performance.

All could move gracefully and this was used to advantage.

This is where we saw Andrew Linnie perform as the passionate Enjol- ras, proving himself to be some kind of a - dare I say it? - yes I shall - a wunder- kind. This is not meant to patronise; I was genuinely taken aback by his age and achievement when we met.

The female chorus was excellent, voices handling all the choral numbers well and individual singers were strong. Cosette played by Rebecca Murphy sang beautifully and portrayed the character so suitably.  Her relationship with Marius, played by Donal Brennan was convinc- ing.  Marius, yet another talented singer, understood his role and in particular the tragic circumstances of his relationship with Eponine.

And what of Valjean?  Now this was a performance, and from such a young actor. Andrew Gavin (above) played an older man so convincingly and his scenes with Fantine, and later, with Cosette were tender and sincere.  Bring Him Home was utterly beautiful.  Andrew Gavin has a voice like a warm blanket.  He was note perfect here and sent a chill down my spine.  I was totally convinced of the age gap between him Marius and Cosette. He was truly worthy of the meaty role. Light changes were subtle and the design by Caroline Norris and Ali Hayes- Brady really added to the production. Chorus, costumes and lighting worked together beautifully, especially for Lovely Ladies. Lighting on the set for Castle on a Cloud was warm and suggestive of hope perhaps. Sound was for the most part good, balance going off occasionally for the louder orchestral numbers and some voices getting drowned out, though it was not a major complaint.  Sound effects were bang on (pardon the pun: many of these were guns going off).  The echo of the sewers and the subtle water dripping against a strong shaft of light was very ef- fective.  Props were authentic; guns, clay tumblers and flasks.

LA Make-up Academy was responsible for hair and make-up which was very good, aging people being their main em- ployment here. Valjean's initial aging as the Mayor was not convincing, though you are never going to make young faces old, it was a good attempt. Later aging was better. Costumes, hired in from The- atrical Costume Hire and looked after by Joanne Keeling, were very effective. The girl in red for the rousing Red and Black was a nice touch.

Eamonn Crowe as production manager and Gerry McCann as stage manager oversaw an almost flawless show - I liked the way new scenes seemed to 'tumble' gracefully onto the stage.  The set, which was hired in from The Border Studio, worked very well for them - the free standing gate gave no trouble and I enjoyed how the scene change here was incorporated into the action on stage. The barricade was simple and effective (one of the three sections on wheels was constructed by the company themselves and looked as convincing as the rest), also study and strong.  A good marriage with lighting enhanced things.

So, welcome aboard Real Theatre Company! This is a group with talent and vision. Les Misérables is always so very sad, but their production was not harrow- ing for all of that.  I felt completely drawn into the story and I wondered as I left that night, what could this same group do in

T he front page of the programme for this production of All Shook Up said it all: "Inspired by and featuring the songs of Elvis Presley". I found this pro- duction full of inspiration and chock full of all kinds of features that made it a memo- rable night at the theatre.

The opening number, Jailhouse Rock, featured Chad, a soon-to-be-released convict hell bent on introducing the world to his own personal brand of charisma, located conveniently in the region of his swivelling hips and (dare I say) agile pel- vis.

The play moves on to Chad's first destination post-prison, which is an un- named 1950's middle American village in which one can imagine absolutely noth- ing of note happening for years on end. This boredom is conveyed in Heartbreak Hotel, with a great selection of voices tak- ing solo lines.

The arrival of Chad was another great moment involving a great prop, a real live motorcycle, and plenty of crowd reaction. In general, the crowd scenes were well balanced and sensibly populated. We were drawn into the feeling of a town in transition and absorbed with hero wor- ship in a big way: Henry Hill (Music Man) meets The Fonz (Happy Days).

The tone of the production was not overly serious, the performances suitably tongue-in-cheek and over-the-top. A lot of attention was paid to all manner of detail, the look and feel of the era evoked with great 'period' touches such as adverts for Popsicles, Cocoa-cola and Budweiser for 15 cents (American). These were the perfect foil to references in the script to Mamie Eisenhower, Be Bop and the pitch-perfect American accents on stage. Although its structure is Shakespearian, "All Shook Up" is all about the songs, and without the musical element, this would be a very short play. MD John Roe was in command of a very good band, with some starry individuals playing for him, notably on saxes. The entra'cte after the interval was a great example of the band letting loose and playing for fun. Roe is stylisti- cally very good and enough of a musician to give his singers and players freedom to be expressive and develop their charac- ters. Balance was occasionally a problem, but this at times rested with sound design rather than musical direction. When the chorus joined in on 'I Can't Help Fall- ing in Love With You', and other songs, dynamic range tended to disappear into earnest choral singing. Still, the demands of this great music were amply met, and to mix metaphors wildly, the singing in this show was sure-footed and vividly coloured.

Michelle Glynn as Natalie Haller was a perfect casting choice. She's a fine singer, capable of nuance in her voice and her transformation to 'Ed' was ee- rily believable. Part of Natalie's success as a character was due to the object of her affections, Chad, the self-absorbed 'Roustabot' whose appearance leaves ev- eryone All Shook Up. Kenneth Kennedy clearly enjoyed his time on stage, but he was also able to 'dial it down' a bit, as in scenes when he begins to fall for 'Ed' and talks to the audience about it. Kennedy isn't the dancer one might expect in this role, but his open confidence as Chad draws us into the conceit of him as Jimmy Dean writ large.

Blathín Walsh as Lorraine is a good comedienne, unafraid of really inhabiting her role. She's a strong performer with a clear, if somewhat edgy voice, and great rhythmic sensibility. Lorraine's mother Sylvia was played by Denise O'Regan. This is a great character, made believ- able by O'Regan's ability to portray a strong person in an occasionally poignant context Another character caught in the crosshairs of a potentially sad situation is Dennis, played with polished nerdiness by Richard Bell. His myopic devotion to Natalie yielded one of the show's best lines: "Shall I compare thee to a thum- mer's day?" He has this part nailed, placing it in danger of becoming what the Americans call a "schtick". Miss Sandra, whose affections turn to Dennis and his knowledge of Shakespeare, was played by Louise Colohan. She looked every inch the vamp in librarian's clothing as the museum curator with a hidden passionate soul.

Tara O'Carroll was another very con- sistent performer in her role as Mayor Matilda Hyde. Although not a large role, she made this memorable with her deliv- ery of such lines as "you and your music and your pelvis" and the unforgettable "Eaarrlll!" Liam Brennan as Natalie's dad Jim Haller gave a solid performance, as did Eddie Sheahan as Dean Hyde and Bartley Joyce as Sheriff Earl. The All Shook Up chorus, who sang and danced like it was 1955 and never stopped look- ing like they loved every minute. There was a consistency to the collective pres- ence of this chorus which made indi- viduals stand out as members of a very classy and committed ensemble.

Choreography was realistic and origi- nal, within reach of the chorus and not overly cluttered. There was a nice organic feel to the movement, and the cast had a nice sense of the style of the music and dance of the time.

Sets and costume were a key element in the overall success of this show. The stage was impressive, from the big gui- tars that framed the back of the stage, to the beautiful jukebox that glowed and helped define the era of the play. Blue tennis shoes were an ingenious and prac- tical way to evoke the necessary Blue Suede Shoes, and the costumes of the Mayoress and Sandra were especially detailed and apt, adding to the already detailed look of everyone on stage. The show in its look and feel ticked many 1950's boxes. Make-up and hair were well in keeping, and while that 'look' bor- dered on caricature, there was an overall balance to colour and style that worked extremely well on stage.

There was a nice clarity to the way in which the often detailed and heavily pop- ulated set was lit. Smaller scenes were given correspondingly intimate treatment, and comic moments (One Night With You) had the instant focus they needed. Sound in this complicated show was oc- casionally problematic on the night. That said, it was clear and well regulated in its differential between speech and singing. Stage management was top class in All Shook Up. The crew, and the designer, artist, builders, painters who came first were definitely not at "all shook up" when faced with this daunting task. There was much to see, it looked finished on stage and polished in action.

The success of Galway Musical Soci- ety's All Shook Up was due in no small part to director Brian Power, who brought spark, passion and good fun to this show. There was a Gilbert and Sullivan-esque sense of gentle parody to the progress of these characters, locked into a completely implausible situation. It was feel-good and outward-looking, and every person who stood on stage knew what he or she was there for. This is a great achievement for a company, because it allows them and by extension, us in the audience to enjoy it all the more.

C ongratulating myself on no longer getting hopelessly lost (thanks to Michael O'Donoghue for advising a sat nav), I arrived at the St Vincent de Paul Theatre for Kells Musical & Dramatic Society 76's production of Jesus Christ Superstar. Musically, this Lloyd Webber show is tougher than one might think - here modern instruments get to shine as guitars did in the overture, followed by solid brass and woodwind. Musical Direc- tor Paul Byrne achieved a sound that was like listening to a good recording in my sitting room.

Brian O'Neill's lighting design was foretelling of the moods to follow, slowly rising from the back of director John Grant's set, gradually reddening against a rough hewn brick wall effect, the ex- tensions and pillars setting us firming in BC Jerusalem. The opening scene was dramatic, culminating in JC centre, back- lit against a cross (having descended a tad shakily from above) and a women's chorus. Sean Carey playing Jesus had good stage presence from the outset and understood the importance of exuding it: slow, deliberate delivery both vocally and physically helped achieve this. Against this was Brian Gallagher's portrayal of Judas - clothed in jeans, a red t-shirt and black leather jacket. I didn't much care for the jacket; it limited the actor's movement and he looked round shouldered, giving him an apologetic almost stooped over gait. Not so Mr Gallagher's performance however. Vocally he sang really well. Heaven on Their Minds, while he took a while to let go, ended up really powerful. Mary Magdalene (Andrea Fitzpatrick) in a red dress also sang with power. Red was the colour of the show it seems with a gospel style choir on one extension in red robes. This nice touch enhanced any singing on stage.

Sean Carey as Jesus really exhibited a classy voice with a strong chorus for What's the Buzz - the energy here was high. Lisa Tyrrell's choreography - really a series of movements at this stage - kept the mood alive, and the Apostles estab- lished themselves well.

The balance of band and singers was (for the most part) good, though the tempo got a little too quick- there was no chance to calm Jesus before jumping into a too fast Everything's Alright for exam- ple. All the same it was a great number; Judas was suitably angry, trying to keep in control against the sweetness of Mary and a lovely women's chorus. Vocals weren't always audible there did seem to be a sound balance issue, very notice- able towards the end of Judas and Jesus' argument around the Last Supper - and The Priests' entrance on the dais was quite striking - black costumes against red and orange lighting - and where oh where did this group get the perfect Caiaphas?! Jay Rice, How low can you go! Against this lovely deep bass was Ronan Walsh's Annas - a great tenor and the remaining priests, Barry Murray, Brian Dunne and Peter Rogers, all of whom could sing, complementing things wonderfully - though not everyone was properly miked.

I was really impressed with singing in general - top class work from Chorus Mistress Carmel McGivney. This group was in the enviable position of not having any weak singers at all! From a stag- ing point of view, Director John Grant was conscious of moving things fluently and groupings were picturesque. I re- ally loved the tableau for Could We Start Again Please; it was beautiful, along with effective lighting and Mary and Peter harmonising sadly. Overall however, the pace of the show generally was just too fast. Jesus brought up through the audi- ence on the shoulders of worshippers for Hosanna was great but it was over almost before it started - he wasn't that heavy, was he?! Pamphlets raining down on stage from above was a really effective addition to this number. The whole thing was a musical treat, a real marriage of voices and instruments and even at that, some of the higher notes were a struggle but it didn't take from the number. I did question Jesus singing while still balanc- ing on shoulders - this did look a bit awkward. Elsewhere I loved the reporters, all of whom could sing used here instead of a large crowd - this was dramatically very strong, their backs against Mary Magdalene highlighted her frustration. A black clad chorus shining torches on Jesus as he was questioned was very sinister especially against a strong white light - I even got a bit of a chill down my spine. Peter, played by James Reilly gave a sensitive performance especially during his denial. Also very convincing was Judas' hanging in act 2, but it lacked drama because again, it seemed to be rushed. The flogging scene, where Jesus had his hands in shackles from above, used the chorus to individually strike him from the front - it was very different to any way I've seen this done before and very disturbing: what a brilliant way to suggest that everyone was at fault. Also great crowd control from Mr Grant as the mob press Pilate - a simply powerful per- formance from Jim Walsh here. Musically brass continued to excel and drums were controlled but effective.

Simon Zealotes played by Ronan Walsh (you may remember him from pre- vious roles in this show, namely Annas) had the perfect voice for his song accom- panied by really crisp brass. He brought huge energy to the number though I was really looking for some dancing at this stage. However, execution of the move- ment employed was simple and everyone managed it well. Physically Mr Walsh was really comfortable and could easily have done more dancing. Psychedelic back lighting was used well here. Again, Jesus not looking relaxed on shoulders but Poor Jerusalem was sung with sensitivity as the lighting switched to dusky blue. Here at last, the pace slowed down somewhat. Jim Walsh's Pilate sang with crisp clear diction, and was musically very controlled with genuine sensitivity. He was seen first in traditional Roman costume but later the decision to put him in a Nazi uniform didn't seem to make any solid point: foot soldiers were dressed more combat style for example. As is traditional with this show, costumes were modern (though a little too casual). Jesus in simple white, looked fabulous under good lighting - giv- ing that lovely Persil white glow to him, really obvious during the Last Supper against a rustic table and really solid per- formances from all the apostles. This led into an almost flawless musical argument between Judas and Jesus, Mr Carey bringing out the anger in the song well, with some great high notes. Gethsemane was a standalone performance from him, full of passion and yet controlled when needed, though some movement here might have enhanced things further. Conductor and MD Paul Byrne was at his best here, all musicians and percussion in particular respectful of the mood.

The temple scene was visually won- derful - great lighting as silks dropped in from above, golds, blues, even a pole dancer! Some traditional costumes here giving more colour to the set and every- thing was suitably seedy. Jesus was a little unsure with some of the high notes but he went for it hell for leather. With so much going on on stage, it was a good reflection of the backstage workings of stage manager Gerry McGovern. Won- derful stuff but again, all over a bit sud- denly and the subtle change in lighting to pinkish purple for My Time brought with it the lepers: ominous green hues against very effective costumes, but it was just too dim and things weren't quite as vis- ible as they might have been. Here again the pace of the music almost got carried away, preventing us from taking in the mood. I Don't Know How to Love Him was one of the few times I couldn't enjoy lighting: turquoises and pinky purples seemed too repetitive of darker moods and not reflective of this calmer moment. Mary sang well enough, but it did seem a little low for her natural register at times. The flute was fantastic for Damned for All Time. Judas, after being quite violent with Mary Magdalene performed well but there was not enough action on stage here and lights seemed to be doing all the work - this effect became tiresome; the red lights on Judas as he takes the blood money might have been very effective but I had had enough of red lights at this stage. Musically though, Blood Money was amazing, Judas was strong and des- perate and the simple movement of Judas and the Priests worked well. Again, vo- cally the Priests excelled and Judas per- formed his heart out. Joined by a chorus of dark hooded judges, act one ends with the sound of Judas' tears.

Herod, played by multi tasking director John Grant gave a one hundred per cent full on performance against his name spelled in neon behind him. This colourful and animated portrayal was almost Elvis like - bringing out comedy in an otherwise tragic story. Mr Grant was aided here by a fantastic women's chorus - finally a dance! - I wondered why with such competence there wasn't more of the same.  Their trilby hats and gold hot pants looked great and matched the gold attire of Herod. Another great dance moment was Jesus Christ Superstar, where Judas fluidly caught the girls as they leaped in air and danced with each while angels in the background did a bit of funky freaking out. This was brave and dramatic chore- ography which paid off and I only wished these dancers hadn't been otherwise so underused. For the Crucifixion, lighting was toned down to a dusty muted gold, barely back lit as the soldiers worked. A little slow to get to the hammering, but the cross was very effective, ending on silence, broken only by tears and last gasps.

Powerful and punchy is the way I would describe this production - the group were full of energy and while respectful of the story, clearly also having as much fun as possible. I also got to meet President of the group Brian O'Neill in a lively front of house area with plenty of really good photos of the show, and also Tina from Show Times! In the flesh; the actual real person behind the patient emails. Like the rest of the audience, she too enjoyed a great show from this diversely talented Kells group.

G reasepaint Productions staged Calamity Jane in St Mary's Hall in Buncrana - in, it has to be said, a limited playing space, devoid of any decent backstage or wing area. How the production team managed the large cast and all that scenery is a mystery, but it is No space in front of house meant no room for a theme or any photos, but a friendly Elaine Grant looked after us well. The five piece band, under the baton of Musical Director Noel Thompson (also on piano), opened with a very short overture leading to an adaptation by the director to include Deadwood's children, who welcomed us (in very convincing accents) and advised us to keep an eye on exit signs in case of any unexpected 'injun' attacks. There was a good lively sound from the band, particularly during large choral numbers. The company in general sang well - Black Hills of Dakota was strong although soft as a lullaby and Windy City was rousing. Louise Crossan was the vocal coach.

The small stage was fully used - pos- sibly too much at times; while it was ad- mirable to see so many people included wherever possible, sometimes this did impinge on the fluidity of the show. Scene one has plenty of songs and most of the company stayed on stage throughout. The downside of this is that it wasn't al- ways clear who was speaking and when. The exception to this consistently was Donal Chambers, as saloon owner Henry Miller. He showed an understanding of stage technique in his movement and style and was clearly audible throughout. His inclusion of the real audience was a nice touch.

No time was wasted getting straight into the well known and loved The Dead- wood Stage (Whip Crack Away - hard not to sing along!). Costumes, hired from Utopia Costume Hire and managed by Michael Doherty, really added to the performances, particularly the pastels of the girls' outfits against Calamity Jane as she made her animated entrance on stage. I was at a loss as to why Wild Bill was dressed so 'dapper-like' throughout; we saw him in his recognisable cowboy suedes only once and briefly at that. The Doctor too had an unconvincing costume; Doc Pierce, while performed very well by Brendan Fletcher might at least have been given a jacket, and a hat that fit him. Modern looking spectacles and loose hair jarred a little in an otherwise picturesque scene in The Black Hills of Dakota - cos- tumes here were wonderful, and attention to detail was noticeable. My biggest gripe was the constant use of Bill's cowboy hat - even when he wore tails during the ball scene, but more annoyingly, during his love scene with Calamity - it masked his face almost completely and lighting didn't help here either.

Calamity, played by Mary Ruddy, was in fine voice, though I couldn't always hear her as the volume of her micro- phone seemed very low. Added to this, were occasional dips in the energy of her performance- whereas the movements of Calamity Jane were very good and convincing and she could really bring the humour of the character out in a familiar way, stories were sometimes lost in the telling through low pace and energy. This wasn't always the fault of Ms Ruddy however, as she was at times positioned at the back of the stage during some of her tall tales. However, this changed completely for the song Men, which was performed with gusto and proved Mary Ruddy to be a strong performer. More of this was seen particularly when she tried to run Katie out of town, and later quite comical as she striped off and sang the reprise of Men/Girls with Bill.

Another problem with having too many people on stage is that there isn't enough for the performers to do - in this case, the Cowboys played cards and played cards and then, played cards some more. It was clear that director Donall Hender- son was sensitive to the overall picture and was conscious of how chorus acted in the background; however in crowding the stage he may have jeopardised the flow and clarity of the production a little. Much stronger direction was evident for example during the scene between Ca- lamity, Katie, Bill and Danny in Calamity's house and who was going to take who to the Ball. All the actors were comfortable with this scene and it was funny. Wild Bill Hickok, played by Michael Fisher, was capable of bringing the energy back up when it was needed, and his rendi- tion of Adelaide was enjoyable, though I wondered if musically, the tempo was a bit slow. Direction for Bill in the opening scenes seemed dependent on a lot of solo card playing too; I would have liked to have seen a more amused reaction during Calamity's songs and rantings for example, to perhaps give an inkling of the future relationship. We did see some sparks between the two for the very enjoyable I Can Do Without You, the band here also in good form. There was a lovely tender performance from Mr. Fisher for Bill and Calamity's kiss, leading into Secret Love. However, Calamity was somewhat let down by the Musical Direc- tor here who seemed to be no help to her during the beginning of the song. Mary Ruddy found her feet admirably after a shaky start.

Francis Fryer played by Emile Rainey and Susan, played by Niamh Gaffney worked off each other very well. Their song Everyone Complains About the Weather was a real punch of energy and Ms Gaffney's dance in particular was very well executed, while Mr. Fryer's perfor- mance was humorous. Adelaide Adams played by Majella McLaughlin and looking striking in a black dress worked very well with the male chorus (the 'boys'!) in tails and top hats for Harry, although space again, so very limited in front of curtain. Roxanna Farren's Katie was immediately convincing as the naïve and sweet girl next to Adelaide. Her voice was wonder- ful, a sort of smooth silky sound, both spoken and when singing. This performer brought out a nice chemistry between herself and Calamity; their friendship was convincing. She sang nervously very well (to well performed gradually louder heck- ling from the group) but I was not comfort- able with the choice of a white costume here. Keep It Under Your Hat set Katie (and Ms Farren) apart as deserving of a lead role. A Woman's Touch with Calam- ity was great. Danny Gilmartin played by Philip Doherty was convincing as the Lieutenant, the build-up of the relation- ship with Katie was enjoyable. Love You Dearly was really well done, however sound levels were poor, especially on Danny, who sang well.

Cowboys as mentioned did keep up some kind of background action and their indi- vidual performances were good too (I en- joyed the threatening "…but you better git her!"). Lee Magee had seen it all before as Joe the Bartender, there were good performances from William McCarter as Rattlesnake and Terry Tedstone as Colo- nel Stark (though he did look more like General Custer!) The Saloon Girls were a welcome distraction from the card play- ing. This group danced well although I'm not sure how authentic a choice it was to have the other (decent God fearing) women in the chorus cheer at the end of their numbers. Having said that, as al- ways there was an imbalance in the ratio of men to women and I imagine the aim here was to keep things lively. Vocally the chorus was confident; Louise Crossan got a lot out of her singers, and Noel Thomp- son's small orchestra was adequate - in that the sound filled the theatre well. The musicians (keyboards, percussion, lead and bass guitar as well as piano) played tunefully and kept things tight - although some numbers did seem to employ a slower pace.

Choreography, by Elizabeth O'Donnell, was confined by the lack of space and there were some imaginative sequences, rather than dances, which accommodated the numbers on stage. Ms O'Donnell is clearly capable of teaching dance as most numbers were executed well, and I would have liked to have seen perhaps a series of smaller groups and more dancing. The tap-dance (such as it was on a carpeted floor) between Calamity, Francis and one of the Cowboys was an example of how this worked really well for the group. There was an opportunity for some more dancing during the Ball scene but this was never fully appreciated.

Evidence of the whole production team working in tandem with each other was seen with the smooth change of scene before the Ball and a nice link into the company front of curtain for The Black Hills of Dakota.  This was also one of the strongest musical numbers, the chorus of couples here sang well and the move- ment on and off stage was quite flawless. The set designed by Caitriona Brad- ley, was light and bright, I imagine aim- ing to create the illusion of more space, and the costume colours were strong against it. Calamity's house in particular was inspired, with a centre free standing flat complete with windows and flower boxes. Props by Geraldine Bradley were authentic, the lamp and broom in Calam- ity's house especially and other touches - flowers outside the window for example. Adelaide's dressing table was a tad rick- ety and I was nervous for it front of curtain - also the mirror was just too small and Adelaide had to stoop to look into it. Inclu- sion of the Ladies' dance-cards during the Ball was a nice touch. Paddy Doherty provided lighting, which, while basic dur- ing act I, really added to the mood of later songs. However, I did feel lighting was under used somewhat, including the spot light. Sound (Emmett McNamee) was variable, at times the balance was poor but overall the sound from the stage was generally good. Hair and makeup by Ciara Barber, Denise Bradley and team was convincing - hair was generally au- thentically pinned up, and Calamity's tran- sition into a beautiful woman was great. Greasepaint Productions, under the helm of a very dedicated Director/Pro- ducer Donall Henderson, are clear about one thing; they seek to be creative, inclusive and respectful of their com- munity. Against genuine difficulties this group strove to overcome each problem, whether one of space or funding, and worked through each with a positive at- titude. The group I met in Buncrana were enthusiastic and hardworking, and cer- tainly enjoying the ride.

A s anyone who has ever seen a Hot Mikado will know, the clue to this show's success is in the title. Hot must be the order of the day, and hot is most definitely what was on offer when the Pioneer Musical and Dramatic Society took to the stage in Blanchardstown dur- ing October.

There was a certain amount of decep- tion too, however, in that there were ele- ments of the show that stepped back into the inherent reserve of imperial Japan and also the wry, observant humour of Gilbert and Sullivan's original creation. The opening tableaux, for example was pure kabuki theatre: a travel-poster image of Japanese fans in a circle, skilfully and colourfully realised. This attention-getting device was not so much scene setting as reverently traditional. It was a tanta- lising glimpse at the old world as seen from the threshold of the new. When the male chorus came on to sing about being Gentlemen of Japan, the heat suddenly rose, and this Mikado began to sizzle. Karate jumps combined with angular 'scat singing' voices and movements that re- warded the audience with their complexity and speed. The set retained throughout a serene sense of otherness, with a plain white screen beautifully lit with varying co- lours, and simple imperial shapes evoca- tive of generic oriental splendour. John Furlong was a commanding Pooh-Bah and Conor Cronin was a likeable Nanki- Poo. The costumes in this show were composites of traditional kimono fabrics in contemporary shapes, oriental zoot-suits for the jazz age. Colour and texture com- bined in unexpected ways and detail was layered upon detail with shoes, hair and props conspiring to generate an opulent whole.

loves, Yum-Yum, and discovers that she's engaged to her guardian Ko-Ko, the Lord High Executioner. Ko-Ko was played with Bilko-esque aplomb by Brendan Farrell as a freckle-faced, gap- toothed wheeler-dealer, an angst-fuelled Groucho, wielding a sabre he doesn't want to use. 'I've Got a Little List' took pot-shot at various local politicians, Bertie Ahern and Jedward, and resulted at one point in the comic shooting of the hap- less pianist. The band, by the way, were top class under the direction of MD David McGauran. The original Mikado score is a major challenge; one can only marvel at the additional challenges of this heated up version. The arrival of the Ladies of Japan and the Three Little Maids was accomplished with much musical skill and choreographic wit. The ladies cho- rus were expert fan-wielders, and Karla Moloney, Carole O'Toole and Hannah Masterson as Yum-Yum, Pitti-Sing and Peep-Bo came across and fun-loving and ready for anything. The musical numbers come thick and fast, and the agility of the cast in moving from one aspect of the increasingly complex plot to another was highly entertaining. One musical high- light was 'I Am So Proud', sung between Pooh-Bah, Ko-Ko and Pish-Tush, played by John Conroy. This number was very effective: well acted and nicely balanced, with the faster and faster tempo proving no particular problem for the singers (and players) concerned. The ensemble work on 'Let the Throng Our Joy Advance' was also very tight, with tight choreography and articulated singing.

At this point, the National Kabuki The- atre of Japan met the Los Angeles House of Blues, with the entrance of Katisha, played with imperial malevolence by Emma Jane Reilly. This was a 'wow' moment, as a combination of stage pres- ence, costume, hair, make-up, and a voice to be reckoned with joined in scary convergence. Act one left us with the con- viction that 'He's Gonna Marry Yum-Yum', led by an effervescent Pitti-Sing, and the finale was full of all-out choreography and coordinated singing, leaving us all in need of refreshment and dying to see what Act II would bring.

The opening scene of the second half presented a beautifully stylised Japanese screen behind which was silhouetted Yum-Yum and her attendants preparing for her wedding to Nanki-Poo. Another visually lovely scene was created during 'The Sun and I', and in this Karla Mo- loney showed her versatility as a singer with beautifully modulated tones. The lively numbers 'Swing a Merry Madrigal' and 'Here's a Howdy-Do' were agile and rhythmic, with tempos that were made to thrill and challenge. The arrival of the Mikado, wonderfully sung by Eddie Brady, throws light on the fact that Nanki Poo must be executed and Yum-Yum buried alive. There was a running joke in the show about whether the (Japanese) pop- ulation of Titipu ought to be able to read Japanese, and a nice bit when the chorus all hit the floor at the word "punishment". Comic moments like these were given time to register, which was a necessary element in such a fast-paced and musi- cally busy show. Katisha's 'Alone and yet Alive' was an intense soul-fuelled media- tion on the state of things, and Ko-Ko's 'Tit Willow' was an illustrated exercise in pandemonium, complete with excellent props, including an actual singing bird. Katisha and Ko-Ko then combined forces in 'Beauty in the Bellow', and somehow all ends well.

At many points in this Hot Mikado, the intricacy of the music and exuberance of the cast meant that plot seemed almost superfluous. However, a balance was struck within the players themselves, and each had their part in telling the story. While there were certainly star turns in the course of the evening, there was a consistent strength in ensemble playing, especially in the men's chorus which can be the weak link in shows and companies. I was apprehensive about how Gilbert and Sullivan would come out at the end of Hot Mikado but needn't have worried. Great attention was paid to the essential elements of humour, timing and character - those things that G & S themselves val- ued so highly. This was a beautiful look- ing show, all credit to set, props, lighting, wardrobe, wigs, makeup and all behind the scenes. It was a good sounding show, so kudos to the MD and the surprisingly small but very hot band. It was also a show with a strong sense of pace and a carefully balanced feel for contemporary references and traditional values. Direc- tor Damien Douglas and Choreographer Siobhan McQuillan must be thanked for seeing to it that everyone performed at their best, and that the music and story came alive so vividly.

T he town of Wexford is all abuzz in the middle of October for all kinds of reasons, one of which undoubt- edly was the run of Oyster Lane Theatre Group's production of Sweet Charity in the Dun Mhuire Theatre. The programme promised Fun, Laughs, Good Times and this was certainly the order of the night. There was a great buzz in this wonderful Tardis of a hall, with so much more to it than meets the eye from the street. The Overture set the scene, with the brassy confidence of Charity herself writ large, like the skyline of New York shown in sil- houette on stage. An opening crossover likewise took us to Central Park, with ice cream and balloon sellers, couples in love and a watchful policemen among the crowd. Alison Doyle as Charity drew us into the scene, with a true voice and an ability to sing and move convincingly so essential to this role. Her song 'You Should See Yourself' ended with an un- fortunate and unexpected dip in the lake, minus her handbag, which was spirited away by an unscrupulous boyfriend, the sinister Charlie. She emerged more sur- prised than outraged, and more dishev- elled than soaking - an interesting nod to a girl whose troubles seem to roll like water off a duck's back. It is this quality in Charity that draws us in, and sustains the show.

The Fandango Ballroom is populated by somewhat more jaded characters, girls whose aim in life is to meet a Big Spender. This number had the requisite look and fizz, right down to the seams in the girls' stockings, and balance be- tween voices and orchestra improved as it went on. The Oyster Lane Orchestra is a versatile ensemble, kept in good order by Musical Director Patrick Clancy. The musical demands of this show are con- siderable, with a lot of music happening under dialogue and vamping a required element. Charity's Soliloquy was well staged, with movement suited to the point of the piece, not too strenuous but very effective. She meets Vittorio, a well-cast Neal O'Leary, and his hard-work girlfriend Ursula, a spot-on characterisation by Julie Freeman.

The scene in the Pompeii club was visually engaging, with great costume touches in the shiny dresses and sparkly jackets the gals and guys. Their expres- sionless and languid approach to the 'Rich Man's Frug' chimed with the dark bob wigs and polished movements. Back in Vittorio's apartment, elements of near- slapstick combine to create the necessary comic tension as Charity attempts to get to know him better and Vittorio still pines for his Ursula. Signature number 'If My Friends Could See Me Now' played to Charity's strengths as a persistent op- timist, and the athletic demands of the dancing and her exuberant jumping on furniture (with props!) made this memo- rable. The set worked well for this scene, and Charity's time in the closet was comi- cally realised. Vittorio's song 'Too Many Tomorrows' is a difficult one to pull off, but O'Leary met the challenge with a con- sistent accent and movie idol charm. The production's use of subtitles in lights run across the top of the stage ("a new day") was an effective device and created a showbiz style focus.

Back in the Fandango Club, Char- ity shares her good fortune with friends Nickie and Helene and all three embark on a journey in song, dreaming of some- thing 'Better Than This'. Possibly a shade under tempo, this number nevertheless gave these three voices a workout, with a nice chemistry between the girls. Char- ity's decision to better herself brings her to the local YMCA to take a class of some kind. She first encounters the receptionist, a study in comic disdain, a brilliant cameo from Caroline O'Connell. On her way to class Charity meets Oscar in the lift, which gets stuck, throwing them together for an angst-ridden while. James McDer- mott as Oscar is a study in neuroses, with a fear of confined spaces conveyed with pitch-perfect timing. Charity shares her secret for survival, in the song 'I'm the Bravest Individual', and a romance buds. Charity and Oscar's adventures take them to a hippy church where The Rhythm of Life is the order of the day. A transformed Neal O'Leary leads his flock with languid cool-daddy zeal, and the psy- chedelic costume colours of the peacenik chorus created a genuine blast from the past. Things between Charity and Oscar move forward (subtitle: "the first kiss") and her Fandango friends Nickie and Helene exhibit great vocal harmonies on 'Baby Dream Your Dream'. After Charity asks herself 'Where am I Going?', her life takes an upward turn in the Chile Hacienda, as Oscar pops the question. This was an especially nicely set scene, with some gentle comic moments and the chem- istry between these two hesitant lovers made us root for them. 'I'm a Brass Band' was another great chorus number with beautiful costumes and plenty of energy. The miming of musical instruments and precision marching (including a pinwheel formation!) made this scene visually very special. This was followed by an equally engaging version of 'I Love to Cry at Weddings', with Robbie Duggan as Her- mann, suitably blustery and sentimental as the manager of the Fandango Ball- room, leading the celebrations. The joy is short lived, however, and Charity and Oscar part company in a genuinely sad scene in which he tells her he can't marry her. This was especially skilfully realised, with Charity's disappointment turning to hope again in a way that was believable and touching.

There was much to admire in this pro- duction of Sweet Charity, and Oyster Lane is a company that pays attention to detail, with great production values and an enthusiastic, able cast. Director Paul Walsh has a great eye for spectacle and creates nice balanced scenes. Pat- rick Clancy as MD presided over a very good band and steered them through the demands of music under speech and vamping sections with a sure hand. Choreographer Suzanne O'Leary created movements that were both stylistically apt for this piece and realistically tailored to the abilities of a talented cast. Charity is a more complex show in its parts than its lightness of tone would suggest, and the elements of set, lighting, sound and stage management all combined to create a seamless and very entertaining produc- tion.

Dunamaise Theatre In the programme of Portlaoise Musical Society's Beauty and the Beast, there is a list of all the shows this company has performed in their 12-year history. The year 2011 is followed by a long line of question marks, which, judging by the success of this production, indicates only that a show has not been chosen yet, not that there won't be one! This was a tremendous night's entertainment and all concerned are to be congratulated for a job well done and a bright continued future for this company.

The all-important opening sequence began with a female dancer, joined by two others, which helped focus the attention of an audience that was inevitably a mixture of all ages and attention spans. The voice over telling the story was well articulated and amplified with clarity and well-judged volume. Indeed, the sound quality in this complicated production was impressive throughout. The transformation of the Prince into the Beast was done in a way that really did look like magic, and another strength of this show, that of technical production, was established. The curtain opened on to a beautiful street scene, with buildings to the left and right and a painted back cloth that created all-important perspective and sense of depth. This theatre, while comfortable in many respects, is small in terms of stage frontage and back-to- front dimensions, more suited to intimate straight theatre than Disney musical. That said, the space was very well used and the chorus well-drilled with choreographic movement that tended towards the precise and contained, rather than broad or expansive.

We were quickly introduced to the people of the village, notably Belle, played with focused restraint by a perfectly cast Sarah Vaughan, and Gaston, played with a marvellous lack of restraint by lantern-jawed Damien Halpin. He had an extensive repertoire of conceited mannerisms, hip-twirling being the most prevalent, and a strong true voice that fully justified the very entertaining adoration of the (very) silly girls, played by Jayne-Louis Kelly, Claire Carroll and Sarah O'Sullivan. Their grasp of physical comedy was impressive, and this was another overall strength of the show. In a later scene, for the song Me, Halpin lifts and carries Vaughan in various ways, both of them singing all the while. LeFou, played by John McEvoy was convincing and gently comic as a long-suffering sidekick, with good voice characterization and physical manner.
