Belle's father Maurice, played by Colm O'Toole, was softly spoken and fatherly, and he carried this quality into his singing. No Matter What was a touching and affecting song, important to establish the relationship between Belle and Maurice. Maurice encounters a pack of well-choreographed wolves in the forest, whose movements had menace and a kind of scary grace. Lost, he finds his way to a mysterious castle in the woods.

The show moved between scenes in the village and on the castle, necessitating swift and complete changes of set. One of these changes later in the show took place in the space of twelve bars of music or less. This too was one of the show's strengths, with the two main structures on either side of the stage turning to reveal the castle interiors. This created at least four performance spaces, with two 'rooms' above as well as the spaces below, connected by stairs that really added to the feel of a castle, despite (again) the stage's compact dimensions. The first castle scene introduced us to the Beast's servants, former humans who have been turned via a magic spell into objects representing their former occupations. Former maître d' Lumière was played with a flawless fake French accent and fantastically fussy optimism by John Coss.  In contrast, Eoghan Fingleton as Cogsworth was a study in fastidious pessimism, his 'Hooray Henry' accent pitch perfect. Mrs. Potts was Joan White, resplendent in a teapot costume that must certainly have challenged both her and fellow cast members when moving around backstage. Chip, her son, played on alternate evenings by Kurt and George, was a star in the making, delivering lines with perfect clarity and natural comic timing.

Belle comes to the castle looking for her father, who is released by the Beast, in exchange for Belle. She makes the acquaintance of her fellow inhabitants of the castle, including Madame de la Grande Bouche - the Wardrobe, played with regal voice and bearing by Yvonne Murphy.

Back in the village, Gaston is celebrated in song by himself (of course) and the villagers, with a nicely choreographed number in which the clinking of tin drinking mugs played an important part. The coordination of these small details and compact movements created a polished feel to chorus work. Gaston and LeFou's reprise ended comically offstage with the sound of glass breaking.

As time passes and the castle inhabitants become ever more entrenched in their new roles as household items, their desperation for a way out of their predicament leads to ever more comic interaction. Lumiere, the candelabra is ever more allergic to Babette (Aoife Fingelton), the feather duster, and Cogsworth acquires another bit of clockwork machinery. The signature number Be Our Guest was a 'knock your socks off' procession of living silverware, an 'Ooh La La' chorus piece of objects with plenty of personality and coordination. Act I ends with the Beast angry with Belle for entering the forbidden west wing of the castle, and her fleeing for her life.

Act II proceeds with Belle caught in the woods by the wolves, the scene set with an entr'acte played by a relatively small but well-drilled pit orchestra made to sound like a full symphony by way of clever sound design. The choreography of the wolves who turned on the Beast when he arrived to save Belle was extremely well done, a study in physical theatre that takes risks and aims high of the mark. Back at the castle, the relationship between Belle and the Beast blossoms, underscored by lovely moments such as the simple act of the Beast looking in wonder at his own hand which has just been held by Belle, flexing his fingers in happiness. The Objects (among them a corkscrew, toast rack and egg timer) and staff of the castle sing about their hopes of being Human Again, with tight choreography and great smiling enthusiasm.

Back in the village, Gaston, LeFou and a Fagin-esque Monsieur D'Arque (Alex Cathcart) set a nicely sinister tone with their plans to put Belle's father in an asylum, with their number Maison des Lunes.

In the castle, the title song, Beauty and the Beast serenaded the dancing Belle and Beast, finally understanding one another.

Belle returns to the village to help her Father, discovering Gaston and the townspeople's intention to take Maurice to the asylum. To save him, Belle proves that the Beast does exist, which sends them off in a frenzy to find him.

The battle for the Beast joins the townspeople and the castle inhabitants onstage in a frenzy of closely choreographed fighting and crossovers. The scene change to the castle happened behind the mob while still onstage - a well-organised shift. Ultimately, Gaston mortally wounds the Beast, but dies in the process. Belle declares her love to the Beast in the end, and he is transformed back to human form. This was managed with some fairly complicated stage and set work, and a healthy helping of real theatrical magic. Beauty and the Beast is a 'tale as old as time' and in the case of this Portlaoise production, one very well told indeed.

White Memorial Theatre When Koko, the Lord High Executioner announced the arrival of the "Mick Adoo" to the town of Titipu in St. Mary's Choral Society's production of The Mikado, there was a wonderful beat or two of quizzical silence before the audience erupted into laughter. He did correct himself ("Ah. The Mikado") but most of us were already there a split second before. Those split seconds and quizzical beats of silence before the joke hits its mark are among many things that I admired in this production, a fun and knowing version of Mikado that fully exploited the musical and theatrical talents of a fine cast.

A martial arts expert set the scene for us during the overture with a display of oriental footwork and weaponry that contrasted nicely with the stillness of three geishas in a tableau that followed. The gentlemen of Japan, attired in pleasing browns and blues, assembled for the opening number, and their singing sound was strong and impressive.

The delightful White Memorial Theatre has a small stage, so in chorus scenes it was fully and colourfully populated. The St. Mary's cast and choreographer managed movement very well, with small, meaningful gestures such as coordinated fan opening and closing, the miming of clockwork figures for the line "Japanese marionette", and later, a pinwheel formation for "yo, heave ho". John Murphy as Nanki-Poo arrived carrying something along the lines of a Japanese banjo, and his Wandering Minstrel was beautifully sung.

Keith Greene as Pish-Tush has a pleasant voice and a regal presence. Dairmuid Bolger as Pooh-Bah made full use of a deep speaking and singing voice and a relentlessly imperious manner. Despite his bubble-blowing entrance, this character seemed indeed to have been "born sneering". A lesser mortal might not have managed to carry off Pooh-Bah's headdress, a fabulous gold concoction replete with curling antennae. Costumes were rich in detail throughout, as were accessories such as fans and small props. It is obviously a huge job to dress and make up the cast of Mikado, and overall, the Ladies and Gentlemen of Japan looked very well indedd.

Ko-Ko, the Lord High Executioner, was played with gentle but deadly comic aim by Dairmuid Vaughn. The tone was set with his first entrance, carrying a grandly oversized executioner's axe. His "Little List" was thoroughly up-to-date, with references to computer games, the X Factor, chewing gum and an impromptu mobile phone call for "Mr Cowan".

The arrival of the female chorus was a fluttering cacophony of colour, with strong part-singing and tuneful delivery. The Three Little Maids were the animated centre of a vividly coloured, wonderfully coiffed human flower garden.

Nanki-Poo's return to the stage elicited a demure fluttering of fans and mad giggles - a wonderful comic business. Peep-Bo (Siobhan Dempsy) and Pitti- Sing (Clodagh O'Donnell) were able allies of Yum-Yum, played by Jennifer Davis. The chemistry between Yum-Yum and Nanki-Poo was very good, and Davis' singing voice, a rich mezzo, was well suited to the role. Indeed, there was great singing and movement all 'round to take us to the interval, with nifty fan- wielding and a good sense of confusion at the end of the trio "I Am So Proud". Katisha, played by a high-heeled, fabulously-wigged Schira Lane, made a grand entrance, with her two kabuki/ samurai attendants, played with frightening menace and consistency by Sheena Fennessy and Emma Weymouth. The act finished with Katisha attempting to expose Nanki-Poo's true identity, drowned out by general merriment. Act II begins with preparations for the wedding of Nanki-Poo and Yum- Yum, with a nice rendition of Braid the Raven Hair. The Sun Whose Rays was beautifully sung and staged, and the singing of Brightly Dawns Our Wedding Day was lovely. Here's a Howdy-Do had real wit and sparkle, with plenty of comic touches from Ko-Ko, digging a grave with his axe and swinging onto the stage on a rope previously seen as a noose for Nanki-Poo's execution, which will take place as condition of his marrying Yum Yum. The plot thickens, and the Mikado's arrival served to heighten the drama. Derek Ryan as the Mikado has a lush singing voice and great presence There was some beautiful detail in the set at this point, including a wonderful, dragon-festooned throne and a lovely little Japanese hump-backed bridge. The music and mayhem carried on as Ko-Ko and Co. describe the 'execution' of Nanki-Poo, before realising the mistake he's made in 'killing' the heir to the throne. The comedic potential of the musical numbers in this act was very fully realised, with The Flowers that Bloom in the Spring and a very comical Tit Willow aiding and abetting the progression. Ko-Ko's wooing of Katisha (and the audience) is complete, and we realise that there really is Beauty in the Bellow of the Blast. It was hard by the end of it all to decide who on stage was happiest, but there was no doubting the happiness of the Clonmel audience, who left with many songs ringing in their ears, and plenty of colour, spectacle Gilbert

University Concert Hall Opening night for the Cecilian Musical Society in University Concert Hall, Limerick was a journey of discovery. Signs in the foyer showed the way: "This way to Dorothy", "Mind the poppies", "Beware of the Witch". Upon ascending the increasingly enchanted staircase, the Yellow Brick Road snaked away to the auditorium doors. Along the way, several beautiful representations of the emerald City in miniature were displayed; the artistic results of a schools competition. We were definitely NOT in Kansas now, Toto!

The Wiz is a show which, like its predecessor, The Wizard of Oz, relies on certain elements: a tornado, a Scarecrow, Tinman and Lion, Dorothy and her dog and above all, no small quantity of magic. In this production, much of the magic was supplied by a first-class band and MD, wonderful dancing, well- cast principals and seemingly hundreds of great costumes. This is a non-stop show with a lot of "wow" factor built in, but it takes the right company and good direction onstage and musically to make it soar as the Cecilians did.

The overture gave the hard-working band a good chance to exercise their lips and fingers. Coordination between the pit and the offstage chorus was very good, facilitated by a camera contact. The set was detailed and atmospheric, with farm buildings across its length and a projection screen to the back. The Yellow Brick road wrapped around the pit, creating a walkway to the front which was put to great use later in the show. Jean McGlynn as Aunt 'Em has a strong singing voice and her number, The Feeling We Once Had established a poignant relationship with Dorothy that is more ambiguous than in the original musical/film.

The Tornado Ballet was a stunning piece of theatre in which dancers in tornado- grey gauzy costumes whirl and sweep, lifting and twirling farm implements as they went. Most spectacularly, Dorothy herself was lifted and swept away as were parts of the house, literally blown apart by the fury of this human whirlwind. The music for this segment was hard- hitting and stunning.

Dorothy wakes up in Munchkin Land, in this incarnation a place where wheels rule. The Munchkins themselves rolled about on office chairs concealed by voluminous dresses that reached the floor and concealed the bases of the chairs. The result was comic and effective - a simple device that hit the mark. All celebrated the demise of the Wicked Witch of the West, and we met Gráinne Hartnett as Addaperle, Good Witch of the North, struggling a bit on roller skates that aptly continue the wheeled theme.  Her strong Belfast accent underscored just how far north she hailed from. When confronted with Dorothy, she expresses her reservations about helping her, with "transportin' a minor across state borders? I don't want to get inta that sit-ee-ation!" Her suggestion that Dorothy finds the Wiz and asks for help was aided by the Munchkins and six glittery blue chorus girls on roller skates proving their skill at moving well and in concert despite the adverse condition of wheels under their feet.

Dorothy, a petite and pretty Kim Burke, sang Soon As I Get Home, a waltz-time ballad that established her credentials as a singer of skill and nuance.

As Dorothy sang, the set onstage changed behind her to reveal the Scarecrow in his field of corn. Brian Henry played this character in need of a sense of direction as a large, utterly watch-able, loose-limbed dude. There was more than a hint of Motown in his singing of I was Born on the Day Before Yesterday, and he was very ably assisted by the corn, sunflowers and especially the funky crows that populated this scene.

Ease on Down the Road is the signature song of this show, and it was played out on the front apron of the set, with German-accented yellow bricks (Jamie Purcell, Rebecca Kenihan and Alison O'Dwyer) who served to comment on and guide Dorothy and her friends' journey. We were introduced to Jamie Sheehan as the Tin Man next, who came to life when his new friends Slide Some Oil to him. Sheehan has a fresh young voice and an agility which was necessary to negotiate the confines of a rather complicated costume. His moon walking and tap dancing with the Bricks was to be admired, and they all Eased on Down the Road again with some very tasty footwork.

Next up was the Mean Ole Lion, played by Mikey O'Gorman with a strong voice edged with a good growl and an aura of comedic confusion fitting with his psychiatric explorations with an unseen Owl therapist.

Another reprise of Ease on Down the Road introduced ever more precise and funky choreographic moves, with head thrusts and generally strong movement from all concerned.

As the travellers reach Kalidah Country they are faced with crawling skeletons backed up by a scary projection on the back wall. The poppy field was a fashionable revelation, with catwalk models in wonderful poppy hats who lead the Lion astray. He was rescued by the Mice Squad, which in the event could also have been known collectively as Miami Mice. These colourful, witty and stylish details just kept coming, creating a parallel universe that confounded and exceeded our expectations at every turn. At the gates of the Emerald City, a decidedly unimpressed gatekeeper clad in bathrobe and curlers sullenly 'welcomed' Dorothy and her companions, who were then ushered into the fabulous world of Oz. The Emerald City Ballet evolved into a cross between Lambada and Salsa, and the Wiz himself (Tony Fahy) was a smooth operator, Sinatra-esque, with an agenda. In Act II, the bad witch Evillene was played with menacing relish by Anita Croke, flanked by a wonderful array of servants and lackeys. The dance sequence of No Bad News finished with a great, gravity defying lift. Also gravity- defying was the performance of Jamie Purcell as Lord High Underling, a brilliant character, powerless when Evillene cast a spell on him. His body-popping movement and the moment when he seemed to fly was satisfyingly well done. Another 'wow' moment.

Dorothy 'loses her cool' with the Wicked Witch, and douses her with water, Evillene disappearing into a cloud of dry ice. A dance sequence of her minions, transformed and radiant in white prom dresses was a triumph of chorus and choreography, beautiful looking and sounding.

On return to the emerald City, the friends were confronted with the essential fraud of the Wiz, his existence as an opportunistic evangelical figure on a power trip. The songs Who Do You Think You Are? and If You Believe brought us to the conclusion we were already aware of - that the friends already have what they need. This production got to that point with humour and some clever props: a box of 'All Brain' for the Scarecrow, a velcro-attached heart for the Tin Man and courage in a can for the Lion.

Dorothy's hope of going home is momentarily foiled by a runaway hot air balloon, but good old Addaperle and Glinda save the day. Emma Culhane as Glinda 'wowed' in the typical Glinda costume with added lights and a singing voice reminiscent of Mariah Carey. When Dorothy realises that the power to go home was always with her, she clicks her heels and hey presto! she's there. The Wiz is in itself a new take on a familiar story, and The Cecilian Musical Society took that newness to heart and added many fine touches, resulting in a glittering production, that made this a night to remember.

Grand Opera House, Belfast The joint: Belfast's Grand Opera House; The occasion: UOC's show Guys & Dolls; The reception: warm, in the shape of a very nice broad, Olive Melville…oh I love Runyan-speak. Enough already! I'll get on with the review… Having seen UOC in June, I was looking forward to seeing them again and I wasn't disappointed. The overture was played with animation and it seemed to encourage the audience; where normally the overture is a cue to hush up, this audience took it as a cue to speak up and the sense of excitement and anticipation of good entertainment was palpable.  The orchestra, under the baton of Wilson Shields was part of this buzz, with brass in particular sounding confident. Opening onto a strong set with neon lights and great dancers in vibrant costumes, this cast already had our attention. Immediately it was clear that this chorus was going to shine; they were lively and comical, and choreography by Ditanya Martin was strong - in places even acrobatic.

Fugue for Tinhorns (or Can Do) highlighted strong performances from Nicely (Gerry McBrien), Benny (Greg Fox) and Rusty (Simon Cunningham). The style was relaxed, natural and confident and harmonies were excellent; musically everyone was in very capable hands here. This comfortable style was prevalent throughout director Peter Kennedy's show; the stage was used well from the outset and all performers were convincing, with gangsters sounding delightfully polite; accents are important in this show, and the 'speak' is crucial - jokes would be lost otherwise. Jon-Paul Bruce playing Lt. Brannigan certainly understood the use of the language, as did Nathan Detroit - more on him later. Costumes also enhanced things. Sourced from within the group and Theatrical Costume Hire in Newry, I loved the suits; the men looked so dapper in a variety of colours; Nicely in red, Harry the Horse in purple - even the trilby hats came in a number of shades and it helped identify the characters well. Prostitutes looked the part, even if one or two kept hoiking their short skirts down. The contrast of the Salvation Army was obvious then, and Sarah Brown played by Mary Frances Loughran was vocally clear from this first appearance.

The set, hired from Scenic Projects Ltd and lighting by Paul Hinchcliffe combined to give a neon lit effect with some clever back lighting. Scene changes were managed well by Clare Donnelly and her crew (and there were plenty of them), the set moved fluidly - so much so that there was something appealing about watching a street appear or gradually blend into someplace else. The Salvation Army headquarters in particular was authentic. I enjoyed some funny little touches in the set changes, such as the Salvation Army leading the stage crew across. The sewers were quite striking in a cartoonish way and the dripping water sound was very effective. Lighting choices suited the numbers well and were subtly changed throughout.

Kerry Rooney played Nathan Detroit, and immediately identified as a leading man. This was a fluent, dare I say - faultless performance. He simply was Nathan Detroit, and with confident movement and a total understanding of the stage he, along with Nicely, Benny and the Guys delivered a super rendition of The Oldest Established, accompanied by a band in fine fettle. The male chorus of Guys was great; all shady and animated, but without upstaging, and while Mr Rooney stood out, it didn't take from each man's individual performance. This was really impressive group work here, from a directional and choreographed point of view and the interaction between principals and chorus was naturally achieved. Sky Masterson, played by Graeme Hassard was vocally strong from his first song and his sense of timing and comfortable pacing gave a nice impression of the character. However, although individual performances from both he and Ms Loughran were good, there was little chemistry between the two. I'll Know was a wonderful number and confidently sung by both, with Sarah Brown's soprano voice in magnificent control. The orchestra was great here too, subtle in their accompaniment, especially strings and trombone and lighting highlighted the city in the background - everything set up for pent up feelings and chemical excitement, but even the kiss was not convincing. Both actors were true to their characters however and while Sky brought humour and an easy going personality out, Sarah was the ever the austere bible reading do gooder.

Adelaide, played by Angela Harding Montgomery was a convincing main attraction at the Hot Box night club. She carried a presence and owned her space during her performance, whether singing, dancing or acting off someone. In particular, her relationship with Nathan was warm and comfortable and very natural - these two just enhanced each other's performances as the show progressed. In the second act, Sue Me was actually a little moving, such was the connection between these two. Adelaide's Lament was really entertaining; well sung and animated, Ms Harding Montgomery really connected with the audience here and filled the stage with her performance, though she wasn't very well lit. Mimi played Karen Hawthorne brought out humour with a good accent and confident movement. Michelle Harkin's Agatha contrasted wonderfully as a wide eyed innocent. Benny and Nicely worked very well off each other and performances were solid. Guys and Dolls sung by both men was great and the dance full of energy.  Harry the Horse, comically played by Neil Keery had a good accent and language was confident, not to mention some class horsy sounds! Drew Reid's Big Jule, with a bit of a mad eye on him was fun, using his voice well and bringing humour out effectively. General Cartwright (Gabrielle McLarnon) was the polar opposite here and her character was convincing. Chorus was consistently strong and individual roles very enjoyable; Joey on the phone was comical and sounded like he actually was on a very old phone. The MC at the Hot Box night club really enjoyed himself too. The Hot Box dancers were entertaining along with Adelaide. They could sing, they could tap and they looked…well great, though the farmerette costumes were more 7 Brides than brassy chicks. Costumes generally were vibrant but Sarah and Sky wore quite pale colours in Havana and it meant they could blend into the crowd during the dance - taking a little from some otherwise comical moments. Everyone danced with gusto here - it was good choreography and everyone could manage it and as Sarah became more and more tipsy, this got funnier. Ms Loughran showed here that she could dance as well as sing and play a really good drunk too! If I Were a Bell was a lot of fun and I enjoyed both actors a lot more from here on.

Take Back Your Mink in the second act with the girls in long slinky dresses was well sung but with very little dancing - though the girls gave it socks, choreography of this number didn't seem to challenge these performers. However, for Luck Be a Lady (both an instrumental and sung version), the Guys (and a few gals) were certainly put through their paces, with this big choral dance number; it was athletic and it appeared everyone was a strong dancer in this. Sky sang well in the second version (though it seemed a little too fast), the whole thing was rousing. Arvide Abernathy, he of the Salvation Army (well, with a name like that…) played with sincerity by Michael McDowell sang More I Cannot Wish You to foster daughter Sarah Brown. It was a lovely rendition though at times the direction on this was more suitable to a love scene.

Timing of the dialogue during the crap game with Nathan and Big Jule in particular was excellent; I loved the interaction between the guys here, and movement around this scene was very fluid, never distracting from the main action but filling the stage nicely.  Back at the Salvation Army headquarters the company gathered to save their filthy souls and there built up a good atmosphere - if acting did become a little enthusiastic from some choral quarters! Benny and Harry the Horse were enjoyable here, with Big Jule in good humour. Nicely's song Sit Down You're Rocking the Boat was powerful; with simple but effective choreography, this was a big band number yet musicians never took over the song. Vocally this group was so strong and it was fun to watch them show off. Yes, this number was a show stopper with so many people shining. Sarah and Adelaide followed with Marry the Man Today, which was lovely and their own very different voices married together well. Choreography here was nice with flowing movement which both performers managed with ease. The cameos of Nathan dressed as a farmer and Sky with the baby were hilarious and worth the costume change. What a show; each member of this group was a strong performer in their own right. I recognised some faces from their last show and I enjoyed seeing them in more principal roles. Peter Kennedy's direction was worthy of the fabulous Grand Opera House stage, as indeed were the rest of the production team; energy, comedy, fun and great big choral numbers. What more could a doll ask for?

St Jarlath's Hall, Tuam Let's face it; when you go to see 'Titanic' you enter in a sort of arms folded kind of way, expecting to be impressed by, at the very least, attempts made on the ship.  I enjoy when I mention to friends that I am off to see this show or that show and they marvel as to how an amateur group can manage to, in this case, come up with a convincing ship, one that sinks no less.  And there are some key points here; in my day (fadó, fadó) we really did beg, borrow and steal - quite literally.  My poor mother got used to seeking out items of her own furniture when the curtains rose, items she was never actually asked permission for, in case she said no.  I love low budget ingenuity and there was some creative fun had with the set designers of Marian Choral Society's show; Eugene Finnegan and team opted for cardboard flats, both wing and free standing variety.  Yes, I kid you not; cardboard. And it actually worked.  Sure, the free standing SOS office might have been a tad shaky but not hugely so.  Paintwork by Orlaith Kelly and her team was clever too, impressively hand painted, if a little animated, with attention to detail.

But back to first impressions; there was a great front of house area: we entered the theatre through a marquee with photos and old fashioned suitcases setting the mood nicely.  Everything here was beautifully presented, including the front of house staff; House manager Liam Kelly and his staff looked well, the men wore black tie and the women were glamorous.

Musically Maury Yeston's score is very grand; the overture, indicative of what was to come, delivered a big sound, full and melodic, and conductor and MD Shane Farrell was not holding back.  Is it just me, or are Ireland's musical directors getting younger?  What's going on? Is it something in the water? Shane Farrell is only 20.  Come on!!  In some countries he wouldn't be served a beer.  Yet here, he was clearly competently in charge of a strong orchestra.  Singing generally was very strong from this ensemble and individual voices too, particularly Shane Kelly as steam room worker Frederick Barrett, who stood out from early on as having stage presence.  The cast, divided into first, second and third class passengers,  entered from various parts of the hall, through the audience and this worked very well as they portrayed their characters from here, everyone agog at the mighty Titanic.  However things were a little static with so many people on stage - perhaps a little more hubbub or slight movement might have animated things more.  That said, there were nice directorial touches with maids in the background on the gang plank. Costumes, looked after by Rita Courtney and sourced professionally were fantastic and the overall picture was really authentic - although except for the Captain, the hats of the sailors looked more like Greek fishermen's caps, not being hard and flat across their head - this may seem a small thing but it did jar. Make up too was mixed, as if there was no continuity amongst artists - and some people had definitely been tamangoed! Elsewhere some unfortunate members of third class were given some strange sideburns and moustaches, though generally it was fine.

Sound balance started off well, though some voices did end up getting lost in the music, and occasionally some dialogue was difficult to hear.  Musically however, the players were subtle under singing. Sound effects were good, the hooting of the ship for example. Lighting was a little dull initially but there was a lovely touch - and here's the 'ship effect' - with the railing going up as the cast moved forward, giving the impression of the ship moving - first class passengers of course were much too important to move themselves so the platform moved instead - all in all a very classy opening scene and chorally a strong beginning.  So too was the mood; everyone portrayed their excitement so convincingly that I found it quite moving, knowing the final outcome.  (It was also difficult not to wave back!).

The bridge was presented well from a design point of view, along with some occasional flashes of light adding to the authenticity, however a moving spot was a little distracting.  Although the performances of the captain and crew were good, occasionally timing seemed off during the bridge scenes - not helped by the setting up of the boiler room in the middle of one scene (could this not have been set up initially and lit when necessary?) But there did seem to be delays in between, long enough to knock the overall pace of the show.  Shane Kelly as Barrett sang really well, though with little direction during his song; as a stoker his boiler fire was really effective, with dry ice and a red and white flickering light, but Mr Kelly was forced to play with only one token piece of coal, which, after all the effort that went into the boiler itself seemed unfair on the performer. Other performances of note were Louis Brennan as Thomas Andrews, the ship's designer - he sang gently and played the part sincerely; John Mulrooney as haughty and vain ship owner Bruce Ismay; Kevin O'Dwyer as Captain E.J. Smith, used his voice well and gave the character a familiar Bird's Eye Cap'n look; Sarah Griffin as the second class gossip Alice Beane brought great energy and humour to the role with constant twitterings to patient husband John Duggan. Her singing too was strong; Another second class couple, Charles Clarke (Rory Kitt) and Caroline Neville(Amy Byrne)  acted off each other very well too. This was a huge cast and many of them with roles to play, so I hope the society will forgive me if I don't mention everyone.  Suffice to say it was a mammoth task for director Enda Burke and he really brought out the best in this talented cast, particularly in terms of mood and emotion.  Sometimes though, I felt individuals might have benefitted from more guidance in their movement, especially during songs.

Choreography was going to be a challenge with these numbers (forty plus) but Aoife McClafferty managed this well.  Dancers backlit behind a black net curtain was a lovely introduction to the dance of the maids and waiters, a sort of black and white chorus who moved really well in a parlour dance with trays, leading into the first class passengers; women in some fabulous dresses and dapper looking gents.  Chorally this was really strong, though there appeared not to be much room on stage.  This number ended perfectly with everyone seated at a long table.  Special mention here of the Major played by Rory O'Connor, who added a lot of humour to the dinner and brought the eye to him well - given that there were so many at the table I was impressed by his technique.  Everyone had a couple of long freezes here while the Captain grappled with his ego, which they managed very well.  This was a well performed scene overall if space moving off was a little tight.  First Officer William Murdoch was a nice role for Ray McGrath; this is the man who does things by the book, who needs to be sure and the contrast between him and the vanity of the Captain was evident. The song here was well performed but I was a little distracted as the bridge set kept moving!  Perhaps a little uncertainly backstage, though elsewhere (non bridge) scene changes were good. However, setting up of scenes at times while another scene was running just didn't work and distracted from the story.  Stage Manager Aaron Tyler had his work cut out for him with so many large items to continuously re-set and a little tweaking of the script might have made things easier here.  I do think amateur producers have this right over big budget professional productions. Into the bowels of the ship, and an ugly blue white light found us in third class, where the cast performed the part but were given costumes that were nearly too nice for the likes of them.  The three Kates were played here by Emer Kelly, Demelza Hannon and Tara Killilea. Already having proved themselves strong performers, they sang well for Lady's Maid, though tended to block each other at times.  Later, the three girls along with their beaus brought good drama to the tragic scenes. Simple but effective movement for a march like number led into a ceilí, where much needed energy brought life back to the show; I felt the pace had begun to slow down a little. The execution of the dance was good and choreography worked well with the given space, highlighting some very nice Irish dancers and included cartwheels and spirals - great stuff!  Everyone danced their way off stage and into a smooth scene change.   Though the bridge was slow to reassemble, the pace definitely picked up and all the performers seemed to feel it.  Ronan Rooney as radioman Harold Bride was responsible for what may have been my favourite scene; along with Frederick Barrett there was a wonderful raport between these two actors and the song was a breath of fresh air.  While Frederick sang with feeling to the photo of his love, there was a lovely smooth quality from Mr Rooney's voice, and he was expressive throughout the song, although it was sung in its entirety from his chair.

Added to the welcome liveliness was a well managed 1920's dance, Doing the Latest Rag, after a great choral performance for the church service.  The chorus was consistently good, whether they were card playing brandy swigging gents or third class unfortunates.  Ida and Isidor Strauss played by Helen O'Donoghue and Declan Carroll deserve mention as they really acted well off each other and sang well.  There was an ominous sense towards the end of act one, as everyone went about their business, leading to a dramatic moment when the iceberg is hit and the bell is rung.  The orchestra rounded things up powerfully.

Set Builders (Eugene Finnegan and a different team!) did a lot of work for this show, managing not just a ship, gangplank, lookout mast and bridge, but a baby grand piano too. A row of four doors used for first class passengers and then changed to second class passengers' cabins was clever if a little clunky to move around.  Wake up! Wake up! was a good number musically and although I initially felt the cast seemed a little unsure of their movement and appeared aimless, I think this was intentional, as third class passengers moved well and managed the chaos better; it was as if the first class passengers simply couldn't fend for themselves. As the panic ensued, technical crew, music and cast worked very well together to build up the drama, this clearly been a strong point of Enda Burke's direction.

Musically this show was in good hands with MD and orchestra; there were times I wasn't altogether sure that it was a really good studio recording of the music and voices!  The Blame sung by Ismay, Andrews and the Captain had great drama and was sung and performed with wonderful expression. As the argument grew, percussion built up subtly.  To the Lifeboats with so many singers was sad and the chaos here well directed.  At this, almost climactic point, there was so much going on musically and the group's singing was super. Interspersed between were strong individual performances, and this scene ended with a chilling tableau where everyone was visible.  Good lighting on stage, and to enhance the tragedy, lights were shone into the audience as everyone accepted the horror of the situation.  Lighting picked out soloists from the huge tableau well, with slow movement as the women leave.

The water rising effect was convincing as a net curtain slowly rose along with moving gobos while Andrews desperately looked at very realistic blue prints of the ship.  Voiceovers of what must have been real quotes were poignant, though delivered a little fast. Sound managed a great echo effect for the dead and survivors.  The final tableau of the dead was an imaginative creative picture of people's hopes and expectations.  The company finished with a rousing reprise of Titanic.

It seemed everyone I spoke to backstage attributed  the success of their part in the show to another; all efforts were appreciated and there was an air of unity amongst the cast and crew.  While they clearly enjoyed the show, at the same time they were respectful of the tragedy of the story, and in particular the fate of local man, 23 year old Andy Keane, a third class passenger who never made it to his final destination, but who was remembered  by all in Marian Choral Society.

St. Joseph's Hall, Boyle For one's first visit to the lovely village of Boyle, I can think of no better way to get a sense of the place than to attend a show by the Boyle Musical Society. There was a great buzz of excitement in the venue, the large and versatile St. Joseph's Hall. It was fun to see pictures of the cast projected in the Front of House area, giving a flavour of the faces and fun to come. The orchestra were busy playing bits and pieces from the show as the audience filed in, MD Ann Kielty conducting from the piano, running her musicians through some last-minute notes and tricky corners that must be turned in this show.

The show began bang on time, with a few announcements and a welcome to all and sundry. The evening's show was summarised by a sign carried on by girls in black, announcing "The Adventures of Charity", and we were on our way. The opening scene between Charity and her fiancée was well-paced and there was a nice feel of the buzz of Central Park created by crossovers of various New York 'types', including a dog walker and various courting couples. Charity's effervescent optimism, charmingly played by Natasha Fitzpatrick, carries her to the brink of the boating pond, and the bad boyfriend obligingly pushes her in.

Charity emerges from the pond, wringing out her dress, ever the optimist, and the scene is set for the rest of her adventures. Indeed, it was the set of this production that was, quite literally, the point upon which the show revolved. Boyle's design team excelled themselves with a revolving stage mechanism that allowed for quick scene changes and more or less seamless shift of location and mood. Efficient and effective, as well as very practical under the circumstances, the crew are to be commended for their efficient operation of this sophisticated bit of kit.

When we next meet Charity, she's with her co-workers at the Fandango Ballroom, a splendidly dressed bunch of beauties who positively sizzled in their number Big Spender. These were 'broads' with attitude led by Lizi Hannon as Nicki and Lynda Morgan as Helene, two good singers whose rapport with each other and Charity made for a believable friendship. Charity's Soliloquy was a real cry from the heart, with great vocal modulation and a really effective combination of music and movement. There was always a sense in this performance that something was just about to happen, and the pace of the show came into its own as the cast settled into Act 1.

The scenes outside and in the Pompeii Club had a good buzz to them, with the stage well-populated and the minimalist choreography interesting and suggestive of the languid wealth of the party class. Egyptian moves were also incorporated, which carried the theme well. The set was classy and imposing, with two stairways curving down to the main stage level. The black and white theme of the costumes was an inspired choice, and there was a general feel of 'cool' in the scene which contrasted nicely with the slightly chaotic interaction of Vittorio, Ursula and Charity. Damien Wallace as Vittorio Vidal, the famous movie star, did not entirely look the part but certainly acted with star quality, and managed to create a sympathetic character. The scene in his apartment with Charity sparkled, the signature number If My Friends Could See Me Now providing Natasha Fitzpatrick with a chance to prove herself as a song and dance lady of some skill. The return of Ursula, played with wonderful judgement by Grainne Caldbeck, created several long and deliciously uncomfortable moments for Charity and us in the audience, as she and Vittorio 'make up' on his movie star bed.

Once again the revolving stage came into its own for the change back to the Fandango, to a scene with another iconic song, Something Better Than This. Again, the chemistry between the three girls, Charity, Nikki and Helene, made this an entertaining number, with a great look cemented by the poodle skirts worn by the girls.

When Charity decides to 'better herself' by taking a class, she comes across a splendidly disinterested woman in the information booth of the local technical college. Soon she meets Oscar, played with neurotic energy by Ivan Moran. The scene stuck in a lift was very funny and established a good relationship between the two characters.

After the interval, a wonderfully spaced- out chorus threw themselves with psychedelic languor into The Rhythm of Life, led by Paddy Fennelly as Daddy Brubeck. There was much to see in this cast of characters, and a consistency of approach that made the scene really work as an ensemble piece. This was colourful direction that pulled its own weight in terms of grabbing the audience and taking charge following the interval.

The following scene, under the (Brooklyn?) bridge, was beautifully conveyed in the set, a wonderful bit of perspective in scene painting. Back with Nikki and Helene, Charity expressed her feelings about Oscar, and in the song Baby Dream Your Dream, they tried to giver her a sense of perspective. Both actresses are very good singers, and this number had a particular resonance - a song that was very well 'sold' on the night. Dialogue between the Fandango girls, old and new, was witty and fresh.

Charity's song 'Where Am I Going?' was a way of trying to figure out her future, a scene that was particularly important in terms of the direction the plot takes at this point. When Charity and Oscar meet in a café to talk over their options, the set and staging served to deliver laughs and pathos in equal measure, and it is a credit to this cast that the audience were so completely rooting for the relationship between Charity and Oscar to 'go the distance'. In the event, the following number, I'm a Brass Band, cemented Charity's place in our hearts, even if Oscar is determined to let her down. Costumes and movement in this song were wonderful, as is the following party scene. I Love to Cry at Weddings was a great chorus number, colourful and well- paced. Hermann (Adrian King) proved himself to be an impressive singer, and the chorus struck just the right note with their celebrations, including the very supportive Pit Chorus.

When Charity returns to Central Park for the final scene, we join her in anticipation of a happy ending, but instead, Oscar dumps her. This was a poignantly realised scene, Charity and Oscar both hitting the mark where emotional impact is concerned. Charity ends up in the pool, almost exactly where we found her. The intervening couple of hours seemed to fly by and Charity's optimism sent us all out into the Roscommon night with smiles on our faces and more than one song rattling 'round in our heads. Well done, Boyle!

St. Michael's Theatre St Michael's theatre is an impressive space and the stage was used well, including two side extensions. The orchestra may have been in the pit, but most definitely were not 'the pits' (look, I'm behind on my reviews, what with the snow and all and if I make the odd bad joke to keep my pecker up, what of it?) under Musical Director Philip Kennedy. In good control of a tight band, Mr Kennedy also conducted and trained the singers. From here on in, I'm going to become familiar and refer to Mr Kennedy as Philip because his brother, the other Mr Kennedy (or Kevin) directed the show. Kevin also assisted as chorus master and played in the band - percussion, which featured nicely throughout. Brass and woodwind had plenty to do during the overture and occasionally felt the strain, though piano was solid.

The use of the extensions in the prologue, with Beast (Keith Flanagan) on one side and the Enchantress, nicely mimed by Mary Kirwin on the other, got our attention well, to wonderful narration from Brendan Redmond. However, as it was difficult to give the extension a total blackout, the audience could see Beast having to set himself up - or rather, turn himself from a prince into a beast and this was a little awkward, though not the fault of the actor. The main set was really impressive, with large pavement bricks on the floor setting up the village scene nicely. Claire O'Connor was a lovely Belle, though when we first encountered her, she seemed to need direction and walked a little aimlessly across the stage. When the villagers appeared, they seemed crammed into one section of the stage - I would have loved to have seen some choreographed movement of Belle moving through the crowd. However, things settled down for the song Provincial Life (I'm guessing at the titles as they are not listed in the programme), and the replacement of children where the film had goats for story time was a nice touch. Ms O'Connor also proved to have beautiful voice. Gaston, played by Brendan Redmond was marvellous as the vain villain - he used his voice to full effect and his eyebrows even more. Along with sidekick Lefou, played by Nigel O'Neill these two were a lot of fun.

The three 'Silly Girls' played by Linda Hynes, Carrie McCracken and Grace O'Connor were cartoonish and funny, playing really well off Gaston, and all were strong singers and nice movers. Animated movement did feature in this production - quite literally it was as if the cast were trying to imitate the movements of the original animated characters and I liked this touch; it gave the characters more definition, especially because it worked, and particularly between Belle and Gaston as he moved toward her and she politely kept her distance.

David 'Stoney' Burke's entrance as Belle's father, 'Crazy Old' Maurice got the audience going -this actor had his own style presenting Maurice as - well, crazy, but in a doting father kind of way. The song No Matter What was nicely delivered and there was chemistry between the two, indeed the actor brought a very convincing fatherly touch to the role.

Costumes, looked after, sourced and in some cases, made by Therese Canavan were really good and everyone looked exactly as you would expect. Phil Kennedy and Rosemary Burke are credited with the making of human sized cutlery, delph and other enchanted things - these costumes really enhanced things, especially during Be Our Guest and later on, when the villagers attack. After an unsure start Be Our Guest turned into a cracking number, with strong singing, though the dance was not very challenging given that there were some nice dancers involved; Babette in particular moved well. However for choreographer Lorraine Cooper, the overall impact of this huge number was impressive none the less and it seemed half of New Ross filled the stage, albeit dressed (literally) for dinner!

The Wolves looked great too but I really thought a little more direction/ choreography would have helped - there seemed to be a lot of pushing and shoving rather than attacking and musically this really should have been a dance. Dry ice might have been preferable here too as the machine emitted a noisy single jet and spoiled the eerie 'enchantment' somewhat.

Lighting began to get interesting once we entered the Beast's castle, casting dark ominous shapes. It built up Beast's entrance with huge shadows, though the smoke machine was again a bit obvious and obscured both Maurice and Beast completely; for such a good build up it seemed a pity. Beast, played by Keith Flanagan, looked super in his costume, though it was difficult at times for the actor to portray his emotions, given that the wig, beard and make-up took up so much of his face. He was more comfortable with the tender scenes than with wild beast anger (an echo enhanced some growling but could have been increased a little), though some nice comical moments were realized before he and Belle finally bonded. Cogsworth, played by Peter O'Connor gave a strong performance both vocally and visually, with more of that animated movement. Lumiere, played by Denis Lennon spoke well with a French accent and humour was brought out between him and Cogsworth. Therese Canavan was a convincing Mrs Potts, with a lovely soft singing voice, and aged herself subtly, though up close she is much younger. The children involved in this production were really great and in particular, Jamie Cooper, who played Chip, cleverly transported around with his body hidden in a trolley, so all acting was facial and vocal only - well done to this six year old! Babette, played by Jan Kennedy was suitably sexy and French, though her costume was too human against some of the others. Of note also was the performance of Margaret Dunne as Madame de la Grand Bouche (or, the Wardrobe) - full of comedy, she used her excellent costume well and had a great big grand bouche type laugh.

Sound balance started off great, with everyone clearly audible over a great big sound from a competent orchestra. Later however, the sound from the band drowned out voices. Terry Brennan's set was impressive with some great effects. Scene changes could be a little awkward to set and strike and were at times distracting while a scene was still playing. However, the tavern was set up smoothly and the chorus excelled here for the beer tankard song Like Gaston. Singing and form was good and high in energy and Lefou gave everything to the number, backed up by the Silly Girls. Choreography was good here, almost Morris dance-like, and it was well executed, incorporating beer swilling neatly. Brass really came up to the mark too. Mr Redmond continued to impress whether bringing out the humour in his role or when things turned darker later on with Monsieur D'arque, played nice and evilly by Sean O'Brien. The song and dance number here with Gaston and Lefou worked very well.

Director Kevin Kennedy managed this challenging show well, though pace was an issue occasionally with scenes needing to be tied together tighter. Elsewhere some nice work on the principal characters was appreciated, especially the buildup of chemistry between Beast and Belle. A highlight of the show was without doubt Tale as Old as Time; Belle's entrance under soft lighting, Mrs Potts singing beautifully and the orchestra top notch - especially woodwind, which played tenderly. The Waltz which followed was lovely, and both Beast and Belle were well rehearsed in the dance. It seemed most of the performers came into their own from here on in; No Spell Has Been Broken was Beast's best song, while Belle was at her most comfortable during Change in Me. Lighting too, excelled while the mob attacked the castle; the shadows that were cast added to the drama and the deep coloured hues were magnificent. The chorus played the mob with convincing gusto, and choreography and movement was complex. With Gaston very much in control the scene developed nicely with music, lighting and strong direction. Wonderful chaos - clearly there was collaboration between choreographer and director. A choreographed fight between Beast and Gaston was convincing (though the plastic dagger was not!) and Belle performed well for Stay with Me. But, ah, that dratted smoke machine; spoiling things with its distracting hiss! There were great costume transformations and the company gave a rousing performance for the final number. Wonderful stuff from what was clearly a community effort with so many children included.

Headford Musical Society's production of Calamity Jane brought me through snow and ice, on a train that continuously stopped so the track could be cleared. Yes…the snow. Like the Spanish Inquisition, nobody expected it so early and by 2nd December, myself and the gang in Headford were fed up with it. It affected bums on seats - you might say those that did turn up were numb-bums on seats, such was the cold. But there was reward for anyone venturing out that week, and well done to the cast who performed with such energy to a relatively small audience.

Things started promisingly with the overture, under Musical Director Ita Cunningham, who also conducted from the piano stool - a nice player too and her orchestra were in good hands. A sudden opening into the Deadwood Stage with imaginative choreography and a lively cast; there was definitely fun being had up there and individuals with smaller roles were very comfortable too, which I took as a good reflection on the company in general. Movement and choreography continued to impress and allowed for any acting that was necessary to build characters and relationships. Background acting was subtle and didn't distract. The orchestra was in great form for Careless With the Truth, sounding like an old time western band and Ronan Lardner's choreography included many of the large cast and had dramatic shape. Direction was solid and John McHugh got a lot out of his people, with a natural style of joviality which was refreshing.

Calamity Jane, played by Fiona Flanagan, sang with a bigger sound than you might expect and her interaction with others in the chorus was good. An energetic performance - it was hard to believe the actress was also seven months pregnant! What did she do with her bump? She sang with gusto, though was reaching for some of the notes. Ms Flanagan could certainly hold our attention well- I found her quite engaging and almost believed some of her stories! Kevin Walsh as Wild Bill stood out and the interaction between him and Calamity was comfortable. An easy laid back style and a crooner type voice, he performed well with support from the men. Francis Fryer appeared to the audience's delight and in a great pair of specs and although he and Susan performed well for Everyone Complains About The Weather, the pace of the show seemed to slow here for a while. These two were good acting off each other however and were quite funny. Susan was a very likeable, sane character. A dramatic entrance from Liam Brennan as Lieutenant Danny Gilmartin was followed by solid acting from Simon Smith's Doc Pierce. A lively performance too from Gabriel Monaghan as Henry Miller and all the familiar numbers continued to please. Men was one of Calamity's stronger numbers and both she and Bill did justice to I Can Do Without You, along with great support from the band.

Adelaide's dressing room was set up front of curtain by the cast and a little clumsily. Adelaide Adams played with relish by Anita Joyce was super - she really made the most of this small role, though her dress was far too Victorian and not at all suitable. Ms Joyce got good support from the 'boys' who were very funny; I liked that each of them were featured and the song was a highlight. It's a small thing but I thought the hair colour of Katie (blonde) and Adelaide (brunette) should have been more similar, but perhaps folk round Deadwood Way 'aint too quick…either way, Katie Brown, performed by Ruth O'Malley played the nervous 'Adelaide' well with good support from her MD. Like Les Dawson's piano playing, you need to be good to sing 'off' well. Calamity got angry and Katie got confident; there was great energy here and it inspired the whole cast to get up and dance, filling the stage nicely with a well put together number - though I wondered if this took the focus off Katie.

Sound was varied. Often I couldn't hear vocals over the orchestra and levels soared during chaotic moments, with gunshots and screaming sounding distorted. It wasn't always the fault of the sound department though, as at times the noise coming from the stage, including ad-libbing could get too loud.

The set was artistically painted by someone with talent and looked authentic. A Woman's Touch in Calamity's gingham clad house had quite a fast pace and I thought the girls should have been moving quicker to match it; they didn't seem to have enough to do and needed guidance here though in the song their voices complimented each other well. Liam Brennan as Danny had a super voice though the chemistry between him and Katie took some time to build and was never totally convincing. Bill and Calamity hit it off finally, though their romantic moment could have had more directorial support.

The chorus under chorus mistress Margaret Flanagan sounded great, very strong in places and excelled for Black Hills of Dakota; men and women were equally strong, the orchestra was supportive and shone as much as the singers - piano and woodwind in particular. Nicely lit and with some authentic looking lamps this was presented simply as a choral number which worked fine. The reprises for the final scene were sung with energy and both the male and female groups were highlighted here.

Costumes were authentic though not standing out in particular. I liked Bill's outfit and Calamity looked the part (but where did she put her bump?!) Costumes were supplied by Pat McGann productions and overseen by Neasa Cosgrove and team. Make-up and hair was a bit modern, apart from a few individuals who made more of an effort. The ladies of the chorus weren't in ball gowns for the ball; while Katie entered in a fabulous dress, everyone else paled just that bit too much. Calamity's dress, when she finally reveals herself as a beauty, while nice, was not striking enough though the men's reactions were good. She wore it again as her wedding dress and I was disappointed with this; so too with Katie in her ball gown. Susan alone had a proper wedding dress and though this was probably more historically accurate I wanted to see three brides in a row! However it didn't take from the buzz on stage and the show ended very much on a high, the audience glowing in appreciation and Saint Fursa no doubt giving his blessing.

'Tis a silly show, really, and perfect for a young cast like that from UCD Musical Society. Silly it may be, but it's funny too, so long as you're not looking for any depth from this spoofy story. None of it would work of course without the great music of Alan Menkin (with humorous lyrics by Howard Ashman) and it helped that the band, under Musical Director Colin Sweetman were in good form throughout; all musical numbers were well handled, including a nice tempo change during opening number Skid Row (Downtown). Indeed it seemed the mood of each number was well understood by Mr Sweetman, particularly Somewhere That's Green which has some poignancy - percussion and piano were nice here though strings struggled a little in places. Pace was good throughout, with Mushnik and Son being especially fast, but it worked as this was a very comical number - that Chorus Master Denis Kilty had trained everyone well was evident in numbers like these and I felt that singers were in good hands. Mr Kilty also played drums and both percussion and guitar were in top form and really funky throughout. The band's greatest moment might have been during Feed Me with two great singers, Seymour and Audrey II - everyone had fun during this.

The energetic chorus had really warmed up by second song Skid Row and confidence was high (with a very convincing drunken bum!) Choreography by Jane Eyre and Lauren Quinn was very imaginative (dancing with sweeping brushes was a nice touch and brought more dancers in), even if all could not manage it fluently, I enjoyed the creativity. There was plenty of simple but very effective dancing going on and for the most part it was well executed. The stage was used well and I laughed heartily at Mushnik and Son. Don't Feed the Plants at the show's end was really inspired work, with the group moving as one. Individual roles were very well performed by everyone. The Meek Shall Inherit worked really well not least because of the performances.

This production had two directors; could you imagine that working out in most societies around the country? I doubt it! But it seemed to work here - ah, youth… and possibly because Mark O'Brien also managed the mechanics of the plant, so it might have kept him out of Zoe Reynold's way…I'm joking of course - these two managed a cast that enjoyed itself immensely and confidence grew as the show progressed, really adding to the entertainment value. The pace of the show was great and individuals were given good guidance. Comic timing was well understood too. Incidentally, the chorus sat in the seats next to the audience rather than wait backstage and this really kept the energy of the show up.

The problem with a spoof is that the story gets just too silly for its own good and there are things at the end of the show that not only don't sit right, but are confusing because of it. I found myself wondering if Audrey was dying or recovering; if this was an alternate ending - but this has happened to me before at this show. Better death effects and a little more gore perhaps? Seymour's demise too, was over a little too fast with no drama and strangely no sound effects to enhance the moment. However, the story was well told and the entertainment was high.

Ailish McCarthy playing Audrey had a really lovely voice, especially in the lower register, but was possibly miscast; she never convinced me of her trashiness and she also came across as just too intelligent. I don't mean this to reflect on Ms McCarthy as a performer however, she worked well with Seymour and some of her songs were great - Suddenly Seymour in particular.

Seymour, played by Garrett Rodgers was excellent in character and vocally. Da Doo with the Rhonnettes got a great reaction from the audience and Grow for Me was good but the entire thing was sung turned away from us. Good acting off other characters too, Mr Rodgers is a giving actor; he allowed the comedians to be funnier by playing his part completely straight - there can be a tendency to over-do Seymour's social awkwardness, but not so here.

The three girls, Chrystal, Chiffon and Rhonnette (whom I always knew as 'the Rhonnettes' collectively) were switched on from the beginning and all managed to narrate the show with ease. Molly O'Mahony in particular had a great voice; blue and soulful and a little bit black and sexy too. All three brought chemistry and energy to each person they performed with.

Mr Mushnik was played by a vocally excellent and confident Stuart Pollock; this actor created chemistry with whomever he performed off and his accent was bang on - really authentically New York Jewish old guy - though the way he moved and carried himself was just a little too young healthy UCD student! He could sing too and Mushnik and Son with Seymour had excellent comic timing - really good fun and a little camp too!

Orin was played by Diarmuid Browne and he brought great humour to the character. Though Mr Browne was not vocally that strong, he had an excellent manic laugh and gave one hundred percent to his performance; the audience loved him. Scenes with Seymour were really funny though he didn't seem to scare Audrey enough - perhaps he could have been played a tad darker for these moments? The voice of Audrey II came from Garvan Lawler - starting strong and staying that way, building in energy. A really excellent voice, Mr Lawler's sang with great timing and really played up the soulful and evil side of his character. The movement of the plant by co-director Mark O'Brien was well achieved and very coordinated under difficult circumstances.

Multi tasking Mark O'Brien's set design, with a city sky line as an upper backdrop looked good against some green lighting on opening, giving a suitably skid row dark night scene effect. Distressed paint gave the flower shop an old and battered look, and props at this stage were sparse and practical - though I would have liked more of a change (and a lot more flowers) when business got better. There was a good marriage with lighting throughout. The dentist's set could have been more convincing - a more dentist-like chair even? Some of the tools were a little too odd (what was he going to do with that wallpaper scraper?!) though the rusty "antique" was excellent. The gas machine was very home-made looking and it wasn't entirely convincing that Orin could not get it off.

Sally Lennon as stage manager did well - the scene change to bring in the larger plant was achieved with plenty of crew and lively music and there was good audience anticipation before seeing Audrey II. Lighting was very imaginative against the set with plenty of colour and moonlit effects. I liked how boundaries were created to split the stage or for Seymour's asides. Sinister moods were well achieved - especially at the dentist's.

This was a very young cast and aging with make-up wasn't bad. I loved the Rhonnettes' hair and whole look. Costumes were fine generally, though I was disappointed with Audrey's; she simply didn't look cheap and trashy enough and she didn't change costume often enough either; there are so many jokes in the script alluding to her attire and these jokes were lost a lot of the time. She might have been given a coat and a handbag.

Sound was great; I loved the radio which was very authentic with crackly vocals. Balance between vocalists and the orchestra was good (though it took a song or two to get completely right). Sound effects were great fun, especially as people were getting chomped by Audrey II.

I had fun at this production of Little Shop - it really cheered up a rainy evening. Well done to Producer Mike Gallagher for pulling it all together, and indeed to all involved.

Civic Theatre Tallaght I have just re read my notes for Harold's Cross Tallaght's recent show, Me and My Girl, and I smiled all the way through. I may even have chuckled to myself at some of the memories. If the show was still running I would go again and bring a gang. Why? Because it got so much right; this company encompassed all the right ingredients, and everything came together at the right time.

We were transported immediately into the times with a solid overture and energetic conducting from Musical Director Dermot O'Callaghan. The pace changed suitably with muted brass sounding very authentic and percussion adding greatly - already the audience were roused and there was no doubt we would enjoy ourselves from here on in. I don't think I am going too far when I say that I couldn't find fault musically; all musicians were strong players and Mr O'Callaghan ran a very tight ship. The ensemble of 'rich people' in wonderful costumes and their 'help' sang well (MD also responsible). They did seem a little cramped together but everyone managed to get into the car which sat front of curtain and was disassembled by the maids and other staff at the end of the scene. The technique employed by director Pat McElwain with the hired in set was to incorporate the waiting staff into the show where normally backstage crew would be used. This meant that scene setting and striking was as much part of the entertainment as the rest and allowed this excellent chorus to feature as much as possible. Hence the pace of the show never suffered and the comedy enjoyed so much by the audience was never put on hold. Stage crew were credited but not noticed, which is a great reflection on them and stage manager Marie Cusack. Collaboration with all members of the production team meant that every scene was engaging visually and vocally; the maids waiting inside the house looked striking in black and white, in how they assembled and because of the effort that had been put into their simply standing there. Hair and make-up (Martina Foreman) too was authentic. Inside the Hareford home was impressive with its marbled arches and pillars (though upstairs was a little shaky), and a wonderful suit of armour - that it began to walk around four or five songs later was even more impressive and full marks to the actor for capturing the art of stillness so well.

This Stephen Fry revival of the 1930's show is delightful, funny and cheeky but it is super dependent on a strong leading man, one Bill Snibson, who as a sort of male Eliza Doolittle character, gets swept up in the lives of the aristocracy and his inheritance of the title Earl of Hereford. Colin Hughes was such a man; his performance was electric. He swept into the show with charisma and energy. He was completely Cockney in his accent, his physical movement and indeed in his mannerisms - it was quite remarkable. Other characters did not pale in comparison either; Kelly-Marie Davy as Lady Jacqueline, or Jaquie, was hilarious though she never over-played (in as much as can be expected in a farcical show like this). The timing and energy from Jaquie and Bill during You Would If You Could, while she tried to seduce him brought tears of laughter from the audience. (I considered secretly recording the sound and selling it as canned laughter for a high price). Mark Keegan as Gerald Bolingbroke was wonderfully silly and both he and Jaquie worked great together. With comical antics from Mr Keegan, Thinking of No-One But Me set us up really well for a great show.

Direction was exceptional. Technically everyone and everything was positioned correctly and people had been rehearsed to within an inch of their lives - this included any stage crew and chorus who flawlessly changed the scenes in such an engaging way. Timing and comedy was spot on. Yet this wasn't just a hilarious slap stick comedy. Bill's character has some substance and throughout he remains loyal to his Cockney girlfriend Sally, played by Kathryn McKiernan. There was warmth to the relationship between these two and she was instantly likeable, breezy and bright and fun loving. Me and My Girl was a lovely little number (I say 'lovely' and 'little' as Sally and Bill were so sweet together). Ms McKiernan could certainly sing, as could Mr Hughes. His voice was particularly well suited to the number Hold My Hand. Sally's song Once You Lose Your Heart was lovely, though sad - highlighting perhaps the essence of the show and how committed the couple are to each other.

Herbert Parchester played by Frank Beadle was fun to watch; here was the role of the pompous but nervous family solicitor, but presented quite naturally. Again, nobody crossed the line into out and out panto comedy, yet there was plenty to laugh at. The song, The Family Solicitor was funny, but Mr Beadle could sing well too. Sir John Tremayne played by William Lacey was a consistently engaging character; he came across as funny, kind, a bit dim and a bit wise all at the same time. I loved the chemistry between Sir John and Lady H, or the Duchess of Dean played by Rosaleen Nolan. She brought weight to the character and her accent was exquisite. She had a convincing if unlikely regard for Bill too which warmed us to her. Robert Coventry as Sir Jasper, the deaf and doting uncle in the corner played it very well - though this role might occasionally be given to a weaker actor as there isn't much dialogue, this was not the case. His laughter sounded genuine and we knew he knew more than he was letting on. Sally's rendition of Take It On the Chin, acting off Sir Jasper was quite heartwarming - Ms McKiernan really was very comfortable on the stage.

Lighting too was nice and subtle, almost taken for granted, but it added warmth to the mood throughout. Colours against the black and white and greens of the cooking staff in the kitchen looked super. Here too were authentic props such as baking bowls and rough scrubbed tables. Sound was blissfully balanced, everyone could be heard clearly throughout.

All accents were great, whether upper class or Cockney - it's difficult to see any amateur cast so punctilious; were these people in fear for their lives? Did Mr McElwain carry a whip, perchance? Not so, I imagine, as there was genuine regard for him and the rest of the production team backstage. I do love to meet the cast after the show; the united energy coming from everyone is palpable and can at times overwhelm. This cast in particular almost blew me away and if my voice shook, I wasn't nervous (that emotion is removed from our brains on taking this job), it was because I was, if you like, walking against their energy flow, not being involved in any way. However, I will be in trouble for digressing; my reviews are long enough I know…Back in Hareford House, I enjoyed too the subtle nuances of each actor, giving a naturalness to the characters, and this was achieved not just by principals but chorus too. Ushers kept their faces dead pan during the obvious but funny jokes and Robbie Keogh as the Butler matched the pace set before him very well - leading into another smooth scene change. Elsewhere the men in the pub were subtle in their background chatting, and leaving the stage with part of the set mid song worked because they paced themselves with the music.

Dancing from choreographer Joe Conlan was always good; whether little dances brought into songs - steps that everyone could manage well, or larger choral numbers like An English Gentleman with Butler Charles and the other staff; simple movement yes, but every single person did it perfectly. Full attention was given over to the performances of dances such as Me and My Girl with Bill and Sally allowing the personalities of the characters to shine. You Would If You Could with Bill and Jaquie had similar chemistry, and the choreography was highly imaginative. There was nice choral work for Hold My Hand, highlighting some good dancers. Meeting guests at the ball did seem a little awkward (after a bit of trouble with the curtain); perhaps we are meant to feel that on Bill's behalf - however the scene with Lord and Lady Battersby and her fruit laden hat was quite funny. The Pearly King and Queen of Lambeth brought life and colour and a striking set of black and white costumed dancers. Hired in costumes enhanced this production throughout and were looked after by Trish Mooney. Musically the Lambeth Walk was wonderfully familiar and well choreographed - although at times thing were a little tight on stage, work had been put in to ensure easy movement of the cast and no one's input could be faulted; it was great to see so much dancing, and brought so close to the audience too - I would say everyone gave 110% - a great ending to Act 1.

Act 2 continued to entertain; The Sun has got his Hat On proved to be a lovely gay number - with absolutely super performances from especially Gerald, but also Jaquie and the ensemble - and well done to the hair department for changing maids to gentry so convincingly. This was a big tap dance number well executed and a great bit of fun. I also enjoyed the library scene (everything hired in from Proscenium Theatre Hire) where Bill's ancestors held really impressive freezes in picture frames - this was very disciplined, especially as Bill was let run wild as the clownish comedian here - fun had with a cloak, a sword, a tiger skin rug…possibly too much fun…? The Ancestor's Dance to Song of Hareford with Duchess and Bill was a combination of effort put in by costumes, music, choreography, effects and overall performance. Sir John reminded me of TV's The Fast Show sketch when he got vereh vereh drunk - however the actor remained audible throughout and he was vereh vereh funny too. The drunken song Love Makes the World Go Round with Bill and Sir John was very well executed. Jackie Lee gave a great performance as protective Mrs Brown, funny but she got her point across, and I must mention the (very educated) Policeman too who played his part to the full. Although he was so enjoyable throughout, it was for Leaning on a Lamppost that I could fully appreciate the casting of Bill's character. Whereas the other scenes required clownish antics, here it's simple; an apparently effortless performance still carried the same power of personality. A really well choreographed dance with four Sallys and an umbrella (and some fancy whistling) added to the moment.

Thanks to President Jack Gregory for looking after us so well in the Civic Theatre. I am sure he and the rest of the group are delighted with their wonderful show; there was clearly huge support for the strong production team and their efforts were greatly appreciated.

When one has travelled from Dublin to Cork the day before and one get's one's sense of time wrong; when one has a minor heart attack upon reading the satellite navigation system's predicted ETA; when one drives like the clappers from Cork to Claremorris (and makes it in time for the show), one does not expect to find the interval upon them so quickly: such was the entertainment value of Claremorris Musical Society's show Oliver!. Producer and founder June Allison must be proud of the team she has surrounded herself with and their service to the community with a huge cast involved including eighty children (Yes; eighty! Eight. O.)

Director and choreographer Hazel McLynn has a golden touch, and managed her cast really well. Two levels on David Keane's set and a good understanding of movement meant hoards of children marched and danced around the space without bumping into or over-crowding each other.
