Deirdre Lee's band of four gave a good sound considering and although I wanted more of a punch from the sound, they were none the less impressive musicians. Ms Lee on keyboards was a steady support for singers and everyone had been put through their paces. Consider Yourself from the Workhouse Children's chorus was full of energy and the interpretation of Pick a Pocket was good. Oom Pah Pah was a bright colourful number, well handled by Nancy (Vivienne Lee) while Gearoid Clesham's Bill Sykes brought a darkness to his song My Name with intimidating gruffness, if a little low in volume at times.

Joe Kelly shared the part of Oliver with Liam Foody - as Liam was in the chorus on the night I attended I could tell he would have been great in the role. Joe Kelly carried that wonderful innocent presence quite naturally and along with a gorgeous voice and super accent, he really gave life to the part. The relationship with the Artful Dodger (also a shared part with Ethan Jordon on his night off when I attended; courteously looking after audience members front of house, I have no doubt Mr Jordon was wonderful.) Conor Mooney had a good handle on the confident young cockney and his interaction with Oliver, Fagin and the other boys (and girls) in the den was convincing. I'd Do Anything with Nancy, Oliver and Bet (Eleanor Roe) was delightful with strong support from the chorus. Ciaran Kiely's Mr Bumble was highly entertaining along with comical scenes with the Widow Corney (Christina Jordan). Mr Kiely sang very well and spoke with punchy articulation. More nice characterization from Ger McLoughlin as Mr Sowerberry, whose slow deliberation tones were nicely balanced by the animated grumblings of Mrs Sowerberry played by Angela Prenty.

Fagin's den was visually comforting, with its warm looking fire and coloured hankies, and more of those children (they were simply everywhere!) looking suitably raggedy in costumes from Nomac Productions. Speaking of those costumes, I fancied myself in Nancy's gorgeous red dress, but then I would have paled in comparison - she had the golden curls to match. Back to Fagin's Den and the man himself was played by Michael Goulding, who although young for the role, was suitably aged with a wig and beard, and the actor moved convincingly too. The charismatic character was given full attention here and his sense of deep down decency was obvious. Reviewing the Situation was popular with the audience though the reprise of it lost value later as Fagin shared the stage with the dead bodies of Nancy and Bill.

Though I wasn't entirely satisfied with the relationship between Nancy and Oliver (and this is a fault in the script to my mind; it really needs to be highlighted in the production), Vivienne Lee brought drama to the character of Nancy and her personal journey was obvious. Fine Life for example was really well performed, but too much attention was given to the audience rather than building up relationships on stage. The seedy and dangerous relationship with Bill Sykes was clear however and the desperation of her character well realized. Hazel McLynn's solid direction ensured every scene moved and looked well and individuals were given the necessary guidance. Possibly in deference to the children both in the cast and in the audience, the killing of Nancy was tame and lacked drama, but she is beaten to death; it's in the story and it needs to be disturbing. There are worse things happening in DS games I'm sure.

That Hazel McLynn was also the choreographer meant that scenes flowed into each other nicely (bar one or two places where the otherwise smooth scene changes held things up), and the dancing was good; clearly a lot of rehearsal time and consideration given to the children and adult's chorus alike. The dance numbers had drama and imagination. Everyone managed Food Glorious Food well and I smiled throughout Be Back Soon, but it was Who Will Buy that gave me the goosebumps; Laura Beston, Mary Dempsey, Andrea Flatley and Eleanor Roe (who also played a pleasant Bet) really treated us to a standalone piece of musical theatre along with Joe Kelly's Oliver. Annemarie Moore as Mrs Bedwin gave us a lovely reprise of Where Is Love (after Oliver's rendition of this song in Act 1, I didn't think it could be topped!) and Steve Wilson played the gentle Mr Brownlow convincingly. Kevin Murphy as a suitably mean Noah also appeared throughout the chorus as did Grace Treston's Charlotte, played very naturally. Kate Hughes' played the dying Old Sally with dignity and Doctor Grimwig was handled well by Helena Brady. The chorus in this group is to be congratulated for its support and singing and dancing numbers were strong; so too was background acting and crossover scenes. Overall this was a lively, well prepared and highly entertaining production and I'm sure the people of Claremorris are delighted with its musical society.

St Jarlath's Hall, Tuam Let's face it; when you go to see 'Titanic' you enter in a sort of arms folded kind of way, expecting to be impressed by, at the very least, attempts made on the ship. I enjoy when I mention to friends that I am off to see this show or that show and they marvel as to how an amateur group can manage to, in this case, come up with a convincing ship, one that sinks no less. And there are some key points here; in my day (fadó, fadó) we really did beg, borrow and steal - quite literally. My poor mother got used to seeking out items of her own furniture when the curtains rose, items she was never actually asked permission for, in case she said no. I love low budget ingenuity and there was some creative fun had with the set designers of Marian Choral Society's show; Eugene Finnegan and team opted for cardboard flats, both wing and free standing variety. Yes, I kid you not; cardboard. And it actually worked. Sure, the free standing SOS office might have been a tad shaky but not hugely so. Paintwork by Orlaith Kelly and her team was clever too, impressively hand painted, if a little animated, with attention to detail. But back to first impressions; there was a great front of house area: we entered the theatre through a marquee with photos and old fashioned suitcases setting the mood nicely. Everything here was beautifully presented, including the front of house staff; House manager Liam Kelly and his staff looked well, the men wore black tie and the women were glamorous. Musically Maury Yeston's score is very grand; the overture, indicative of what was to come, delivered a big sound, full and melodic, and conductor and MD Shane Farrell was not holding back. Is it just me, or are Ireland's musical directors getting younger? What's going on? Is it something in the water? Shane Farrell is only 20. Come on!! In some countries he wouldn't be served a beer. Yet here, he was clearly competently in charge of a strong orchestra. Singing generally was very strong from this ensemble and individual voices too, particularly Shane Kelly as steam room worker Frederick Barrett, who stood out from early on as having stage presence. The cast, divided into first, second and third class passengers, entered from various parts of the hall, through the audience and this worked very well as they portrayed their characters from here, everyone agog at the mighty Titanic. However things were a little static with so many people on stage - perhaps a little more hubbub or slight movement might have animated things more. That said, there were nice directorial touches with maids in the background on the gang plank. Costumes, looked after by Rita Courtney and sourced professionally were fantastic and the overall picture was really authentic - although except for the Captain, the hats of the sailors looked more like Greek fishermen's caps, not being hard and flat across their head - this may seem a small thing but it did jar. Make up too was mixed, as if there was no continuity amongst artists - and some people had definitely been tamangoed! Elsewhere some unfortunate members of third class were given some strange sideburns and moustaches, though generally it was fine.

Sound balance started off well, though some voices did end up getting lost in the music, and occasionally some dialogue was difficult to hear. Musically however, the players were subtle under singing. Sound effects were good, the hooting of the ship for example. Lighting was a little dull initially but there was a lovely touch - and here's the 'ship effect' - with the railing going up as the cast moved forward, giving the impression of the ship moving - first class passengers of course were much too important to move themselves so the platform moved instead - all in all a very classy opening scene and chorally a strong beginning. So too was the mood; everyone portrayed their excitement so convincingly that I found it quite moving, knowing the final outcome. (It was also difficult not to wave back!).

The bridge was presented well from a design point of view, along with some occasional flashes of light adding to the authenticity, however a moving spot was a little distracting. Although the performances of the captain and crew were good, occasionally timing seemed off during the bridge scenes - not helped by the setting up of the boiler room in the middle of one scene (could this not have been set up initially and lit when necessary?) But there did seem to be delays in between, long enough to knock the overall pace of the show. Shane Kelly as Barrett sang really well, though with little direction during his song; as a stoker his boiler fire was really effective, with dry ice and a red and white flickering light, but Mr Kelly was forced to play with only one token piece of coal, which, after all the effort that went into the boiler itself seemed unfair on the performer.

Other performances of note were Louis Brennan as Thomas Andrews, the ship's designer - he sang gently and played the part sincerely; John Mulrooney as haughty and vain ship owner Bruce Ismay; Kevin O'Dwyer as Captain E.J. Smith, used his voice well and gave the character a familiar Bird's Eye Cap'n look; Sarah Griffin as the second class gossip Alice Beane brought great energy and humour to the role with constant twitterings to patient husband John Duggan. Her singing too was strong; Another second class couple, Charles Clarke (Rory Kitt) and Caroline Neville(Amy Byrne) acted off each other very well too. This was a huge cast and many of them with roles to play, so I hope the society will forgive me if I don't mention everyone. Suffice to say it was a mammoth task for director Enda Burke and he really brought out the best in this talented cast, particularly in terms of mood and emotion. Sometimes though, I felt individuals might have benefitted from more guidance in their movement, especially during songs. Choreography was going to be a challenge with these numbers (forty plus) but Aoife McClafferty managed this well. Dancers backlit behind a black net curtain was a lovely introduction to the dance of the maids and waiters, a sort of black and white chorus who moved really well in a parlour dance with trays, leading into the first class passengers; women in some fabulous dresses and dapper looking gents. Chorally this was really strong, though there appeared not to be much room on stage. This number ended perfectly with everyone seated at a long table.

Special mention here of the Major played by Rory O'Connor, who added a lot of humour to the dinner and brought the eye to him well - given that there were so many at the table I was impressed by his technique. Everyone had a couple of long freezes here while the Captain grappled with his ego, which they managed very well. This was a well performed scene overall if space moving off was a little tight. First Officer William Murdoch was a nice role for Ray McGrath; this is the man who does things by the book, who needs to be sure and the contrast between him and the vanity of the Captain was evident. The song here was well performed but I was a little distracted as the bridge set kept moving! Perhaps a little uncertainly backstage, though elsewhere (non bridge) scene changes were good. However, setting up of scenes at times while another scene was running just didn't work and distracted from the story.

Stage Manager Aaron Tyler had his work cut out for him with so many large items to continuously re-set and a little tweaking of the script might have made things easier here. I do think amateur producers have this right over big budget professional productions.

Into the bowels of the ship, and an ugly blue white light found us in third class, where the cast performed the part but were given costumes that were nearly too nice for the likes of them. The three Kates were played here by Emer Kelly, Demelza Hannon and Tara Killilea. Already having proved themselves strong performers, they sang well for Lady's Maid, though tended to block each other at times. Later, the three girls along with their beaus brought good drama to the tragic scenes. Simple but effective movement for a march like number led into a ceilí, where much needed energy brought life back to the show; I felt the pace had begun to slow down a little. The execution of the dance was good and choreography worked well with the given space, highlighting some very nice Irish dancers and included cartwheels and spirals - great stuff! Everyone danced their way off stage and into a smooth scene change. Though the bridge was slow to reassemble, the pace definitely picked up and all the performers seemed to feel it. Ronan Rooney as radioman Harold Bride was responsible for what may have been my favourite scene; along with Frederick Barrett there was a wonderful raport between these two actors and the song was a breath of fresh air. While Frederick sang with feeling to the photo of his love, there was a lovely smooth quality from Mr Rooney's voice, and he was expressive throughout the song, although it was sung in its entirety from his chair.

Added to the welcome liveliness was a well managed 1920's dance, Doing the Latest Rag, after a great choral performance for the church service. The chorus was consistently good, whether they were card playing brandy swigging gents or third class unfortunates. Ida and Isidor Strauss played by Helen O'Donoghue and Declan Carroll deserve mention as they really acted well off each other and sang well. There was an ominous sense towards the end of act one, as everyone went about their business, leading to a dramatic moment when the iceberg is hit and the bell is rung. The orchestra rounded things up powerfully.

Set Builders (Eugene Finnegan and a different team!) did a lot of work for this show, managing not just a ship, gangplank, lookout mast and bridge, but a baby grand piano too. A row of four doors used for first class passengers and then changed to second class passengers' cabins was clever if a little clunky to move around. Wake up! Wake up! was a good number musically and although I initially felt the cast seemed a little unsure of their movement and appeared aimless, I think this was intentional, as third class passengers moved well and managed the chaos better; it was as if the first class passengers simply couldn't fend for themselves. As the panic ensued, technical crew, music and cast worked very well together to build up the drama, this clearly been a strong point of Enda Burke's direction.

Musically this show was in good hands with MD and orchestra; there were times I wasn't altogether sure that it was a really good studio recording of the music and voices! The Blame sung by Ismay, Andrews and the Captain had great drama and was sung and performed with wonderful expression. As the argument grew, percussion built up subtly. To the Lifeboats with so many singers was sad and the chaos here well directed. At this, almost climactic point, there was so much going on musically and the group's singing was super. Interspersed between were strong individual performances, and this scene ended with a chilling tableau where everyone was visible. Good lighting on stage, and to enhance the tragedy, lights were shone into the audience as everyone accepted the horror of the situation. Lighting picked out soloists from the huge tableau well, with slow movement as the women leave.

The water rising effect was convincing as a net curtain slowly rose along with moving gobos while Andrews desperately looked at very realistic blue prints of the ship. Voiceovers of what must have been real quotes were poignant, though delivered a little fast. Sound managed a great echo effect for the dead and survivors. The final tableau of the dead was an imaginative creative picture of people's hopes and expectations. The company finished with a rousing reprise of Titanic.

It seemed everyone I spoke to backstage attributed the success of their part in the show to another; all efforts were appreciated and there was an air of unity amongst the cast and crew. While they clearly enjoyed the show, at the same time they were respectful of the tragedy of the story, and in particular the fate of local man, 23 year old Andy Keane, a third class passenger who never made it to his final destination, but who was remembered by all in Marian Choral Society.

"Oh dear Lord, let her be good," was my silent prayer upon realizing that Mary Heaney was the stage manager for Castlerea's production of Thoroughly Modern Millie. Would I be forced, I wondered, to criticize the President of AIMS?  Could you imagine? And yet, to not stay true to the task would have been wrong. Hence, the prayer: just let her be good at her job; even mediocre. I'll settle for just not bad. Well, as many of you no doubt already know (what stone have I been hiding under?) Mary Heaney is good at her job; darned good. In fact, if you got the backstage tour, you might say just as well, as I'm still not sure how the set moved so smoothly back and forth in the very limited space.  The venue, River Island, is a night club and Castlerea Musical Society transformed it into a theatre for their week long run. Though my guest and I had possibly the best seats in the house (next to the lighting man, who kindly gave me a little light), others complained of blasts of cold air from above, though possibly the worst problem for this group was the organization of so many people in a difficult venue.  Full marks to Connie Gannon and her team; there were plenty of ushers, dressed in black tie and armed with torches, and they all seemed to know what they were doing.

The specifically constructed stage worked well enough - it was cleverly framed by a colourful backdrop - a sort of skyline I imagine, though it was a little oriental for New York City.  However, Niall and Kevin Heaney's set was impressive; secretaries wheeled themselves in for an office set up, where they sat, sang and danced, all from authentic looking workstations - this show being set in the 1920's. A free-standing flat served very well as a more convincing city backdrop and The Pricilla Hotel, where Millie and the other girls stay, was achieved by the set up of five doors, all of which opened and closed smoothly.  There was a laundry room, a night club and a dressing room too…many of these were cumbersome bulky pieces and while they really enhanced the show, especially given there was no curtain or other frame work here, things might have gone horribly wrong in the hands of a less competent stage manager, because there really was very little room backstage.  However, there was clearly some clever choreography going on back there and plenty of stage crew, all of whom seemed on top of things. First time director Niall Heaney paced the show extremely well, and there were some really comical moments, given strong direction; 'Ah Sweet Mystery of Life'- this scene and song between Miss Dorothy (Michelle Donnellan) and Mr Graydon (David Cooke) still makes me chuckle.  David Cooke was a delightful ham; and he had to be for this character to work; the sillier the better in fact.  Chin Ho and Bun Foo, two abused Chinese workers played by Daniel Doherty and Ivan Moran also impressed; there was great discipline involved in getting their Chinese lingo so convincing - I'm still not sure if they were speaking Chinese or something that just sounded like it, but they seemed to know what they were talking about and I found this highly entertaining even before sub- titles were pointed out to me - on a TV screen possibly a little too far stage right.  Mrs Meers, the villain of the show, was dramatically portrayed by Miriam Conroy.  As she's only pretending to be Chinese herself, (it's part of her cunning plan), the actor used movement and voice to great effect as she stole across the stage looking suspicious all the while.  Julie Connolly was a delightful Millie - she brought out the sense of wonder and innocence in her character along with wonderful facial expression and singing was strong and confident. Stand out numbers were 'Jimmy', with strong support from MD Dr Joseph Ryan, and 'Gimme Gimme', which could have entertained as a standalone piece. There was a nice build up of chemistry between Millie and Jimmy, played by Anthony Flanagan and their relationship developed well.  A self assured performer, each of Mr Flanagan's songs were engaging, in particular 'What do I need with Love' and 'I Turned a Corner', from the ledge of Millie's office window.  Caroline Madigan as Muzzy the night club singer gave an energetic and breezy performance, with strong singing numbers and some comic moments too.  Frances Cooke as Miss Flannery was also funny, and played the no nonsense part well. 'Forget about the Boy' was a great number with good back up from a strong female chorus, though not everyone as well rehearsed as they might have been.  This also occurred to me a couple of times with some of the principals too, as delivery was a little unfocused in places.  Choreographer Patricia McDermott understood the style well, and dances were imaginative while still keeping things 1920's. 'The Speed Test' was a fine number, and introduced some competent tap dancers. The Pricilla Girls had good energy and performed well off each other.  Director Niall Heaney allowed this strong chorus to shine during a scene in the police station where everyone got to be a joker, though he was also able to bring out a fine romance between Millie and Jimmy too. Chorus Mistress Heather Shine oversaw a strong group and I particularly enjoyed the girls for 'Forget about the Boy'. Dr Ryan was a thoroughly supportive MD and principals managed difficult numbers confidently. The orchestra played well, The 'Speed Test' being particularly impressive. Overall sound was well balanced, though there were times when some singers were drowned out.

While the set looked great, it was greatly enhanced by very convincing props and I was impressed by Liam Walsh's attention to little details. Lighting was bright and cheery; lots of pinks and lilacs and everything on cue for the most part - some trouble with gobos and spots on the night I attended. Costumes, hired from Pat McGann and sourced within the group complimented the set well - principals generally clad in browns and beiges against more colourful costumes for the chorus, although when Millie needed to stand out, boy did she stand out (I want that gorgeous red 1920's sequenced number!) as did Miss Dorothy.  Costume and makeup for Mrs Meers worked well also.

When I see how groups manage against difficult circumstances; unsuitable venues, limited space or budget restraints, it always serves as a reminder that this is what it's all about after all - the coming together of creative people; the journey along the way; the up's and the down's; the laughing and the sweating of blood…why do we do it to ourselves? Well, I think everyone reading this already knows the answer to that, and I am very sure that the people in Castlerea are rightly proud of their musical society.

Black Box Theatre I like to dance at weddings, though my style has been described as "outrageously Caucasian". While I'm not quite sure how to take that, there was plenty of dancing - both outrageous and impressive in Galway University Musical Society's production of 'The Wedding Singer' last month. And the outrageous kind was directed to be that way - every stereotype was included here but so too was a development of character and plot that that made the evening so thoroughly enjoyable.

If you don't know the show, it is pretty close to the film with Adam Sandler and Drew Barrymore and the casting reflected this, in terms of the chemistry build up between the characters and indeed in some of the mannerisms of the two leads, especially Ruth Darcy as Barrymore's character. I mean this as a compliment, in much the same way we enjoy seeing John Travolta and Olivia Newton John as Danny and Sandy in Grease.  It's a love story of course with all the usual suspects; Wedding Singer Robbie Hart first becomes friends with waitress Julia before having his heart broken at the altar by his fiancée Linda, who returns to seduce him later, causing complications as Julia realizes she no longer cares for her fiancée Glen but has fallen for Robbie. It's oh so frustrating but a lot of fun along the way with an exceptional cast and some very solid work from a talented production team. High on the entertainment list are Eddie Mullarkey as Sammy and Michael Flanagan as George - Robbie's band mates who are as diverse as they are funny; Sammy is all man and spends much of his time chasing Julia's sexy cousin Holly - also a welcome talent, while George, gay as the day and singing it proudly from the rafters had the audience in stitches, sometimes with just a change in expression, such was his connection with us. Michael Flanagan was also the choreographer for this show, and the dancing was consistently a breath of fresh air. Though I've seen many musicals this year, I aint seen much dancin' and everyone in this young dynamic cast was well used. There was a lot of colour, fun and movement across the stage but above all, there were some really good dancers (including the bride and groom at one wedding, while others were…well, like me I guess - that is, intentionally dancing like old Aunty Emer when she's been exposed to the chardonnay and some 80's music).

Oisin Tierney as Robbie always had us on his side; he played the part with perfect balance - the guy who needs pushing but who is all the more lovable for his insecurities. The relationship between Robbie and Julia was delightful and some of their scenes together were sigh inducing, while others were so enjoyable: 'Get Out of the Dumpster' in particular, and Ruth Darcy's Julia was just a dote: I so wanted these two to get it together! Diarmuid Scahill played Glen, Julia's cad of a boyfriend; only interested in money (and other girls, the scoundrel) he played the part to a tee. 'All About the Green' was a highlight and revealed the fact that Glen can dance -and how! Laura Donnelly aged herself well as Grandma Rosie with a good New York old gal voice though make-up never convinces in turning young skin old - she was funny, with an impressive sense of comic timing. Linda was all the funnier for playing things straight and Orna Ni Bhroin shone here, especially when she sang. Her scene of seduction was brave and her performance super, again highlighting a strong experienced voice. Holly, played by Aine Glynn played the part so well; 'Party Like 1986'/'Saturday Night' showed a great voice and this number in particular was hilarious with really strong chorus backup. Angie, Julia's snobbish mum, was played with controlled humour by Sophie Connoly, in line with her character's traits.

Unfortunately, as is so often the case, there was a noticeable shortage of men and while female wedding guests did their best, it affected the balance of some otherwise great scenes. At times I felt the players themselves were aware of this and felt awkward for it. Generally though the chorus was a great support and anyone given roles to play were really good without exception, in fact too many to mention…BUT I must mention the guys in the bar in Act 2 because this scene was so very funny; even before the song (during which the bar man, heretofore a chorus member, raps like a pro) the sense of fun and energy was palpable. That was the tenor of this show.

Musical Director and Chorus Mistress Eva-Marie Costello was also in charge of a competent set of musicians, if a little loud at times - sound was an occasional issue.

The orchestra were supportive of singers however and some of the songs were excellent - in fact one had to remember that this was a live band; Robbie's hilarious 'You Don't Know How Much I Need You' (a tearful song to a plastic bride on a vibrating bed bought by his Granny kind of sums it all up) was impressive as was 'Casualty of Love' - also an engaging scene. However, perhaps change of scene music might have been tighter - it stopped abruptly during some scene changes leaving awkward silences though changes themselves were smooth for the most part and I found the crew to be funky and fast with it! Well done Stage Manager Alison McGreevy.

Collaboration between director Rory Kitt and choreographer was obvious and the pace of the show was good. This director managed to cast well and all the scenes were played out with excellent timing. The stage was used well and scenes flowed in and out of musical numbers flawlessly. George's Hebrew version of 'I Know This Much is Love' will stay in the memory banks for a while, though it never actually distracted from the conversation taking place downstage - impressive work from Mr Kitt. While humour was handled well, so too was the romance between the principals; it was convincing and the kiss scene was well lit and sort of magical. (Sigh).

Eoin Ryan's set, simple and stark at times, worked very well, with enhancement from lighting; funky colours on stage and backlighting well positioned movable cubes was clever and suited the style of the show.

Costumes were suitably eighties, at times obnoxiously so (what an unfortunate era for those of us who spent our twenties in them) and care had been taken to reflect personalities through their clothing. And hair. Sammy; I think you know I'm talking about you. Not to mention the man with the bad haircut and the lady with the sideburns.

I really enjoyed this group - front of house were friendly, the cast were fun and the production team had done their homework; there was great support for performers from choreographer, MD and director and no one was left fending alone, least of all the appreciative audience.

Coleraine Riverside Theatre There was a great buzz in the Riverside Theatre in January and early February during the long run of Ballywillan Drama Group's Beauty and the Beast. This popular show attracted an audience of all ages and entertained them with extensive sets, costumes, and of course the popular music of this piece.

The scene-setting prologue was accomplished with the aid of images projected onto a screen that lowered from the flies. The narrative voice used for this was strong and melodious, with the correct air of mystery, grabbing our attention.

The projection disappeared quite literally in a flash, and the action was transported to the Little Town. Belle, played by Fiona Flynn, had a great look for this role and an expressive vocal quality. The slow middle section of the song was used to showcase some nice dancing by cast members, one very young lady in particular - a charming addition to the number. A raise area to the right of the well-populated and balanced set was the booksellers, beautifully painted and giving the scene a sense of the scope and scale of a real village.

Ben Crawford, had the right arrogance and swagger for the role of Gaston, and a voice to back this up. Colin McClarty as Lefou brought a manic and comic energy to this sidekick role, completed with a look that squared with a comic- book portrayal of the (almost) loveable buffoon. He's also a good singer and able to turn cartwheels at will!

David McClarty as Maurice brought a nice quality of bumble to the part, and he and Belle had the essential lovely relationship of devoted father and daughter. His wood-chopping invention was a character in itself and admirably functional. On his arrival in the castle, his fascination with Cogsworth as an intriguing piece of engineering was endearingly in character.

Harry Stinson as Cogsworth had the requisite fussiness, David Ferguson as Lumiere brought a suitably French saucy disdain to the role. Ashling Reynolds was excellent as Babette, the coquette with the heart of gold and hands of feathers! Mrs. Potts was a brisk and motherly Helen Wilkinson, with a very consistent accent. Her Chip on the night was Abagail Doherty, a wise and very cute performer with a strong singing voice. Alan McClarty's Beast was a growling, prowling study in menace.

Back in the village, the Silly Girls (Una Culkin, Laura Fisher and Evie Ferguson) did their best to make themselves a nuisance generally and seemed to have a great deal of fun in the process. The village scenes were distinguished by beautifully detailed costumes and props, with a focussed chorus that settled into their various roles very well.

Changes of scene from village to castle were very quickly and efficiently done, with lights only occasionally lagging behind the swift shifts of location. The abundance of minor roles in Beauty and the Beast of course gives cast members ample scope for different portrayals of everything from spoon to wolf, and the designations for one cast member (Shepherd Boy, Villager, Gargoyle, Rolling Pin) read like a sliding scale of personal re-invention. Again, detail figured in so many ways. The winged Gargoyles were particularly scary, as were the wolves.

The tavern scene was well-paced and full of great physical comedy and madcap humour.

Seeds were well sown in this scene for the mob's later pursuit of the Beast and invasion of the castle, and again, the chorus gave individually very strong performances. Their strengths were further demonstrated with a lively, smiling and rhythmic Be Our Guest. 'Spectacle' always applies to this number, and BDG fully lived up to expectations. The Can- Can girls were the piece de resistance, and dual flame fountains added sparkle to an already brilliant scene. Before this and after, the Beast's songs (How Long Must this Go On and If I Can't Love Her) were delivered with intelligent intensity by McClarty whose singing voice is resonant and well pitched. He kept something in reserve for the key changes in the finale to Act 1 and held our attention with a stillness eloquently suggestive of the Beast's essential sorrow and emerging humanness.

The opening scene of Act 2 added the element of sinister trees to the fight with the wolves - nice device that fills the stage and makes for an exciting transformation. The Castle reappeared around them, and another kind of transformation continues with Something There. The Beast's library was revealed as if by magic, and he and Belle embarked on their new-found friendship with a touching bit of dialogue and story reading.

Human Again was another show- stopping number for principals and chorus, with individual voices coming nicely out of the texture for certain lines, including Chip whose playing of this scene was utterly charming. There was great use of the full stage for this, including steps up to side entrances. The exeunt was characteristically swift and smiling. The scene to change to Maison de Lune was also quick and total. Paul Loan as Monsieur D'Arque has great concentration as a performer and a persuasive singing voice. Another great scene and set followed, with Belle and the Beast's dinner. This was beautifully lit and the table setting and other details were lovely.

There was a touching uncertainty between Belle and her Beast, resolved in the course of their dancing, to Mrs. Pott's rendition of the title song.

The Mob Song which follows Belle's homecoming had all of the same energy of earlier chorus number and more, with Gaston's malice in pursuit quite frightening.

Pyrotechnics and clever choreographic effort cover the Beast's transformation to the Prince, and the show rushes headlong to a well-deserved happy ending.

The staff of the castle are Human Again, and reunited with themselves in song and celebration, and audience reaction confirmed that this was a magic night's entertainment by any measure.

Tullamore Court Hotel It was a cold night in Tullamore when the cast of Hot Mikado assembled for their penultimate performance, but the Gentlemen and Ladies of Japan soon warmed things up for a very appreciative audience. The opening tableau with brass instruments set a nice tone, as did an accomplished orchestra under the able direction of MD Enda O'Connor. The look of this opening sequence with brocaded satin zoot suits and choreography that mixed body-popping with hot 40s dance moves established a continuing theme of unpredictability and anachronism. The set, by John O'Donoghue magnified this idea with perspective-challenging side panels showing abstract towers rising from the ground and away from us. There was beauty and symmetry in the way this fit together. The stage in the Tullamore Court Hotel is wide, and chorus placement in big, busy numbers was good and made great use of the space. Michael Bermingham as Nanki-Poo was a study in trends in a satin polka- dot bomber jacket, velvet jeans and red tennis shoes. His voice gained a more centred sound as it warmed up, and he had a pleasant, likeable manner as Yum- Yum's suitor.

Nigel Sammon as Pooh Bah had a wonderful speaking voice and terrific, ornamental eyebrows. The face-painting skill of someone behind the scenes had quite a lot to do in this show, all to good effect. The makeup for Katisha elaborated on the theme of decoration, with swirls and flowers in an adapted oriental motif.

Ultan Keena as Pish Tush brought a kinetic, antsy energy to this somewhat neurotic role, and his dancing skills added sparkle to chorus numbers. The chorus entered into choreographed numbers with gusto, and witty moves like the miming of a noose or guillotine on the words "Lord High Executioner" were accomplished rhythmically and with a knowing verve. The entrance of the aforementioned executioner was heralded by motorcycle noises offstage, appropriate to his mode of transport, a Segway scooter. Ko-Ko was played with apparent enjoyment by Graham Finnerty, and his skill on the scooter was impressive. His characterisation reminded me of American comic Jack Benny, in voice and mannerisms. His look was suitably eccentric, with top hat, striped trousers and tail coat. His Little List was entirely crafted of contemporary references, taking swipes at teenagers, political personalities, the television license man and RTE programmers, among others. His scroll wrapped around Pish Tush as it unravelled, and the pit band's pianist played lovely delicate fills between verses.

A rolling desk and chair combination was to Pooh-Bah what the Segway was to Ko-Ko in the scene where he offers looks at Ko Ko's problem from the point of view of the various roles and offices he occupies. Sammon proved himself to be an able mimic here.

The appearance of the Three Little Maids was a high-octane nod to the Andrews Sisters, with great vocal energy. The maids were in multicoloured bobbed wigs and babydoll dresses that paid very subtle homage to oriental fashion influences.

There was some nice interaction between Nanki-Poo and the band, when he asked them whether he should he should tell Yum-Yum about his past with Katisha. MD O'Connor answered the question, much to the audience's delight.

Sarah Vaughn as Yum-Yum brought a warm soprano voice and natural charm to her role, as well as facility with different musical styles.

There were great comic moments in this production, integrated well and seamlessly with other elements of choreography, music and drama. This was vividly apparent in numbers like Pooh-Bah's I Am So Proud, the celebratory Let the Throng Our Joy Advance and the jive-y He's Gonna Marry Yum-Yum. The mix of styles of dress, setting and choreography continued to mirror the eclectic mix of music that makes up this piece.

The arrival of Katisha (Karen Martin) was calculated to thrill, as was every detail of her appearance, from a stunning black and red costume extravagant gravity- defying hair style and fabulous tattoo makeup detail to the two fit young male attendants replete with chains and collars who accompanied her. Martin made the most of the presence this character inevitably has, and expanded on the potential of stillness and disdain to heighten her menace, as well as the comic possibilities of Katisha's predicament. Hour of Gladness revealed a voice suited to blues and pop, with occasional warm resonance on lower notes.

The plot thickens inevitably in the second act, with greater potential for individual moments in the spotlight which this cast exploited to full effect. The traditional geisha girl look of the chorus in the opening - makeup and costume - was meticulously done. Yum-Yum's signature song The Sun and I was approached with good timing on the humorous set-up lines, and sung with a nice grasp of contemporary ornamentation. This song was beautifully lit as well and directed with a simplicity that chimes with this point in the story. There were good comic bits with Pitti-Sing (Sinead Handy) and Peep-Bo (Audrey O'Meara) and the ladies chorus as they 'sympathised' with Nanki-Poo and the small matter of his imminent beheading.

Swing a Merry Madrigal began a cappella with great rhythmic precision and grand harmonic balance.

The Mikado was played (with a nice, logical masterstroke of casting) by Aoife Fitzsimons, who made 'his' memorable entrance seated on a dragon throne. The Mikado Song made a big impression, with cane twirling, tap dancing and a chorus line of sorts. The costume, hair and general styling of this character was calculated to make a great impact. So great was the Mikado's power over the good people of Titti-Poo that they were compelled to join him in laughter, and stop laughing exactly on cue, an apt demonstration of comic control. Katisha returned to the stage in an even more extravagant costume, and sang Alone and Yet Alive with a sense of drama that was sustained and overcame the difficulty presented to her by the low range of this piece.

The comedy heightened when Ko-Ko began to woo Katisha, and Tit Willow, though performed without the numerous props that occasionally illustrate this number, was a study in physical and vocal comedy, as these two characters warmed to each other. Ko-Ko brought a hip flask for 'Dutch courage' and Katisha's face was framed in total disgust at the beginning, but by the end, they were singing from the same hymn sheet. The mood continued through Beauty in the Bellow, with the two reformed lovers simmering with barely concealed lust. The finale continued the momentum and the company proved themselves to have the stamina to carry the rhythm and colour of their performances all the way to the end.

Simon Ryan Theatre For the town of Tipperary during one week in normally dull mid-February, it was just a short step from Musical Society to High Society in this elegant production of a Cole Porter classic. The beautiful Simon Ryan Theatre in the Excel Centre was a very appropriate venue for a show that pits good manners and social expectation against sparkling wit and human nature.

This show is not often performed, which is a mystery because it has a nice range of principal cast members, good scope for chorus and great songs, some of which are very well known. More than anything, it is an acting show that requires confidence, flexibility and good timing, all of which this society has in abundance.

Front of house included displays of memorabilia from this society's 30- year history, as well as the results of a children's colouring competition.

The band under MD Danny Carroll set the scene with the Prologue, and the curtains opened on to a beautifully decorated set which functioned across the show as various locations outside the mansion of the Lord family.

Tracy, played with an attractive and appropriate confidence by Cathy Keane, made her entrance during the opening chorus number, High Society. She was well cast as the fun-loving but upper class girl who's been around a bit and has ambitions to secure her place in high society by marrying successful but somewhat boring industrialist George, played by Derek Ryan. Ryan's big voice and presence on stage suited this role very well. Tracy's sister is also a confident and utterly precocious lassie called Dinah. She was played with marvellous cheekiness by Emer Carew, a talented newcomer with more than one string to her bow. It is through Dinah's unguarded observations that we learn some of the back-story of this not uncomplicated plot. We also meet Tracy's mother, the imaginatively titled Mother Lord, portrayed with grace and polish by Jane Green.

Another addition to the family unit came in the form of embarrassingly lascivious Uncle Willie, portrayed with a knowing comic flair by Willie Ryan. As the story unfolds, he is called upon to pretend to be the supposedly errant head of the household, Seth Lord, who was really played by Liam Carey, a dignified and believable presence on stage. Lord is about to be the subject of a newspaper expose, courtesy of two reporters, Liz Imbrie and Mike Connor, played by Lynda Kelly and Diarmuid Vaughan. Kelly is a gorgeous girl-Friday type with impeccable comic timing and strong vocal presence. Vaughn is likewise a compelling singer and strong actor. The somewhat complicated plot is advanced by comparatively long stretches of Cole Porter's snappy dialogue, punctuated by equally pithy songs. Indeed, the challenge of the show is integrate the songs into the dialogue in a way that doesn't pit the play against the musical. This is something that this production did well and quite naturally.

MD Carroll brought musical cues in on time and rarely did an actor have to wait to begin a song. Balance was also good, and the busy chorus were well drilled in their music, some of which was simply fragments and reprises of musical numbers from other areas of the show. Most impressive was the fact that so often, entrances and exits of the chorus were combined with set changes, movement of furniture and props and stage business connected with their roles as maids and butlers. This was accomplished with everyone remaining in character, in time, on cue and with smiles (where appropriate) on their faces. Another aspect of the chorus' work was occasional tap dancing, which fit into the tone and type of this show very well. Tracy's ex-husband Dexter was played with unpretentious wit by Cathal O'Donoghue, whose singing voice and manner reminded of Frank Sinatra. His relationship with Tracy and her husband- to-be is strained, whereas Dinah and the rest of the household seem fond of him. There were musical delights in this show in the form of songs that you'd never realise were from a musical. A case in point is I Love Paris, eccentrically sung by Tracy and Dinah as a way to put reporters Mike and Liz off the scent of their father's indiscretions. Four members of the men's chorus dressed in berets and garlic garlands hammed it up, with one miming brilliantly the playing of an accordion. Later, Liz and Mike sing Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? a song as perennial as grass in these hard economic times, and at the end of Act 1, Tracy and Dexter sing the luminous and sad True Love. Another well staged musical number was She's Got That Thing, in which the chorus showed themselves to be very clued into the action, and able to dance and sing while holding silver trays, eventually using them to mime what I took to be the feathers of the dancing girl Seth Lord is supposed to have had a dalliance with. Quite an elegant use of a simple prop. Apart from the attractive songs and clever dialogue, this show has grand scope for chic and elegant costumes, and in this respect Tipperary MS were also persuasive. The clothes of Tracy and Liz especially were covetable, and the dress sense of the gentleman harkened back to an enviable era of elegance. Cole Porter's dialogue has a matching elegance, and a number of the speaking voices on stage, notably those of Liz and Dexter, were beautifully modulated and paced. It was important - essential, in fact, in a show which relies on longer stretches of dialogue than average, that the acting was of such high quality. Act two presses on with the wedding ball going slightly awry as Tracy re-thinks her commitment to George, aided by a bottle of champagne. Let's Misbehave is a big number for the whole cast, developing into a great Charleston routine. Uncle Willie shows himself to be a bit of a Louis Armstrong impersonator vocally and a great time is had by all. The exeunt on this occasion took the form of a conga line. Indeed the chorus added marvellous touches across many of the musical numbers in their role as household staff, looking after empty bottles and wielding them in good visual gags. Other comic business that worked to good effect was Liz's fending off the amorous advances of Uncle Willie and Tracy getting more and more drunk, noticed inevitably by the all-seeing Dinah.

The play ended with the wedding we were promised at the start and we in the audience became wedding guests. Tracy explained her change of plan to us with Dexter's prompting and he became the groom. This was a happy ending, especially as we've know for some time that he really is her True Love.

St. Patrick's Comprehensive School, Shannon Everything about St.

Patrick's Comprehensive School during one week at the end of February said "welcome to the wedding!" In fact, the occasion was not one, but several weddings, courtesy of The Wedding Singer, a show that sparkles and fizzes like a champagne bucket in a limousine.

The 'welcome' and 'emergency exit' announcements began with the sound of a knife clinking on a wine glass and delivered as if a wedding speech. If we didn't already know it, the opening number, It's Your Wedding Day, said it all. Shannon is a company that thinks things through, and there was a lot of appropriate detail in their staging of this fun show. High-octane dancing was on the menu at the first wedding we got to look in on, and the choreography was closely tied to the text of the song, with aunts and mothers coming forward as the words dictated.

The band consisted of likeable master of ceremonies Robbie (Pa Hayes), outlandish and possibly confused George (Chris Willets) and big talkin' New Joisey dude Sammy (Eoin Sheedy). They had a good rapport together in the way that guys in bands do, close but not too close, a little more concerned about gigs and girls (or boys!) than each other.  Their interaction was entertaining and each established a clear separate identity. This was important as the various strands of the plot unfolded. Julia Sullivan (Lauren Dunne) was likeable and persuasive, well cast as the waitress with a heart of gold and yearnings to be on the receiving end of a wedding, like the bridal parties she serves. Her singing voice and delivery were solid and very well in tune. Julia's friend and cousin Holly, played by Joanne O'Sullivan, was a great no-nonsense character, a pragmatic foil to Julia's dreamer.

Much of the appeal of The Wedding Singer as a show rests on how convincing the title character is as an actual part of a wedding band. In this production, all the band members were bona fide musicians, most particularly Hayes, who plays guitar for himself and of course sings. Sheedy as Sam played a bit of sax, and of course, Willetts (George) on keyboard (or not?). There was also the appeal of the character Robbie himself, sympathetic and earnest, believably torn between his feelings for Julia and commitment to his fiancée Julia. In contrast Glenn Guglia, a seedy and opportunistic businessman, was played with well-dressed, oily charm by Eoghan Rice.

Another great character was Grandma Rosie, played by Kathy Hurley - an initially restrained performance that allowed for the flashes of un-granny-like behaviour to surprise and amuse, as in Grandmother's Note, where she sums up Linda's character in pithy language calculated to shock. The heedless, remorseless yet strangely moral Linda was played by Rachel McIntyre. Her amazing punk wedding dress was just one aspect of Note From Linda that was eye-popping and very funny. Anna Maria Barrett as Julia's Mom Angie was another brilliant character, with a strong grasp of her American accent and the embarrassing demeanour of a mother intent on upstaging her daughter at social events. The scene in the ladies loo was very wittily conceived, and the surprise appearance of George in one of the stalls was a great moment.

The chain of events in the aftermath of Robbie's being left at the altar by Linda was well-paced and realised with a lot of wry, humorous touches. Somebody Kill Me was full-on and out of control, with Hayes' guitar playing giving the song a flexibility and contrast that drew all possible pathos and humour from it. The scene change to the next wedding was covered by the dancing of the guests as their venue materialised around them, a nice touch. Casualty of Love showcased Hayes' singing talent, and also some wonderfully geeky choreography from the assorted wedding guest misfits. The unfolding Robbie/Julia relationship was given room to breathe in the Come Out of the Dumpster number, played for a nice balance of laughs and sympathy with the help of a real dumpster. Dunne and Hayes were well cast in their roles, with natural presence and compatibility onstage, which developed across the next sections and scenes, including Not That Kind of Thing.

George rose to the occasion admirably when called upon to sing a Jewish blessing for a bar mitzvah, which followed the very tongue-in-cheek number, Today You Are a Man. George, like Glen, sported some very fine footwear during the show.

Act 1 finished with a full-on and surprising version of Saturday Night in the City, with the principal characters joined by the chorus, all in a variety of black 80's clubbing gear. Choreography was energetic and emphasised dance moves of the era, with a terrific nod to an iconic Flashdance moment at the end as Holly pulled a cord and activated a shower of water over her as she sat in a chair.

By way of contrast, grey office workers for whom its all About the Green opened Act II. This represented a complete shift in tone as well as look, and most of the 'workers' were straight-faced and serious. Seamed tights and severe dresses and shirt/tie combinations, as well as boas made of dollar bills continued the theme. Movements were tightly synchronised and arm movements were especially precise. Glen Guglia's jacket was lined with money, and paper money was flying around like wedding confetti.

Right in Front of Your Eyes from Holly was nicely sung and furthered this character's development as a sounding board for Julia and point of contact between her and Robbie. Fleeting comic touches kept the tone light as well, such as the 'I'm with Stupid' and 'Stupid' tee-shirts and the sequence of Grandma Rosie exercising. The bar scene for Single was populated with great characters, witty dialogue and good dancing. We met Julia's mother again, a small character who made a big impression, with a great walk and unexpectedly modern attitude. Linda's re-appearance re-enforced her stature as a woman completely in her own world, for whom the term 'clueless' might have been coined. This was a brilliantly consistent and funny performance. Another very funny cameo came from the airline agent on the flight to Las Vegas, which set the scene for the various celebrity 'walk-ons' that populated the next segment: Tina Turner, Cyndi Lauper, Mr. T, Billy Idol, Ronald Regan, Imelda Marcos.

Move That Thang was a real crowd- pleasing, toe tapping showstopper, and audience reaction said it all. There was an unstoppable momentum to The Wedding Singer at this point, and across Act II, things like Grandma's cartwheel, the airplane on a stick visual gag and general feel-good carrying on created a sense of the party gradually moving outwards from the stage and drawing us all in. It began to feel like something along the lines of a real wedding, in fact, when you find yourself absorbed and carried along with the momentum of the day. This show, courtesy of Shannon Musical Society supplied a raft of brilliant characters, full-on singing and dancing and the happy ending we were all hoping for.

The complex history of Northern Ireland has as an inevitable focus the period known as The Troubles. At one time the most photographed place on earth, it is now the subject of scrutiny as a place of residual political strife and a testing ground of various approaches to conflict resolution. Few would claim to know the place fully, with all the roots and branches that influence its politics and people. However, artistic expression is one way to approach difficult subjects, and while musical theatre is not perhaps an obvious medium through which to explore Northern Ireland's Troubles, Ballinrobe Musical Society's production of Come the Dawn went some ways towards finding a way through some very challenging territory.

Writer and Composer Peter Kennedy's vision has been a long time coming to this talented society, but the detail and unflinching momentum of the production testified to the fact that they embraced the challenge wholeheartedly.

The story of Come the Dawn reaches backwards and forwards in time, with characters whose lives are entwined, like it or not, with plot points that put them in the kind of impossible positions that were common currency at the height of the Troubles.

Although a work of fiction, the very real backdrop of Belfast's interior and exterior spaces meant that the scenic aspects of this production had the importance of a character in their own right. To that end, scenic artist Karen Forde took obvious care with her designs to portray Belfast as the simultaneously frightening and hopeful place she saw through her artist's eyes on trips to research the setting. This aspect of the production, along with notes on the writing, composing and orchestration of the piece, were explained in the programme and there was also a show synopsis which sketched the story without revealing any of the plot's unseen and ultimately shocking twists.

The musical, while not completely through-composed has a high music- to-speech ratio, with songs used to further the plot as well as to underscore important points and allow for much- needed breathing space as the story advances. This relative complexity placed demands on all concerned, but principal characters and an impressive chorus negotiated the potential difficulties with focus and energy.

The show opened with an unfortunately familiar scenario from this troubled era: a police barricade dealing with a brewing riot. On this occasion it was an Orange march with an associated Loyalist protest. The look of this scene, and so many across the show, while grim and intense, was also very detailed. The RUC uniforms, for example, though not actual Government Issue, were carefully reproduced. Perspex riot shields, truncheons and heavy boots contributed to the look, but in this production what leant the most authentic 'feel' were the actors themselves, in this case, creating a fierce and protracted riot that set a tone which was both disturbing and apt. One constant as well was the movement of the story between chorus groups (essentially Protestant or Catholic) and the interaction of individuals. While the chorus numbers were often fuelled with the emotion of the mob, individual songs and ensembles had the nuance of more subtle conflict; internal rather than tribal. RUC Constable John Thompson was the central, pivotal focus of a story involving his attempt to help a young woman from the Catholic community, Carmel, who turns out to be involved in the IRA. Alan Greaney played John with a sympathy and sensitivity that did not allow for doubt of his commitment to his responsibilities, even as he was placed in a difficult and doubtful situation. His fiancée Lisa was played with measured intensity by Lisa Wilson, who managed to negotiate the difficult task of portraying a woman looking for humanity in inhuman situations. Her one blind spot in this is Davy Saunders, a superior officer in the RUC who had attempted a relationship with Lisa's mother before she became the mistaken victim of a bomb meant for Lisa's father. Saunders was played by Michael Coen as a man who, while clearly twisted and corrupt, is motivated by things that resonate uncomfortably as a clutch of "there but for the grace of God" elements. Lisa's father Robert Wilson was Richard Crumlish, who expressed the humanity of the Protestant tradition in his approach to this role and especially in the ballad In This Empire Great.

On the republican side, Paula O'Neill played Carmel Gallagher, the young woman involved in the IRA. O'Neill's confidence as a performer set the right tone for this character who has little to lose and is fuelled with personal devotion to Seamus Farrell, the Sinn Fein representative. He was played with rational fervour by Niall Conway who gave this key role passion and restraint, with a fine, solid singing voice. Likewise, IRA commander Bernard Gallagher (Seamus Cafferkey), though somewhat less convinced of the possibility of a political solution to the conflict, is also involved in negotiations with a government representative. In contrast, IRA extremist Danny Quinn (John Murphy) was the archetypal 'loose cannon', twitchy and unable to see any wisdom in negotiation. His girlfriend Catriona (Sinead Heneghan) was an example of a young woman in the all-too-familiar situation of just wanting to get on with her life. Her song with Danny, What?, provided one of the lighter moments in the show, in which negotiations about the progress of a night out are the focus. There were other light moments as well, some provided by Sadie and Lily (Siobhan Campbell and Ann Kirrane), two Protestant women who, while fiercely loyal to their own community, still manage to nip across the border for great holidays in Donegal (Donegal). This song takes place in the impressive set of a Protestant pub, the Bull Ring.

Certainly, the stage and set for Come the Dawn was versatile, detailed and designed for ease of movement and quick changes. The Pub opened, literally, across the full width of the stage, complete with upper level and stairs leading to the gents and ladies toilets. The earlier scene between Catriona and Danny took place in a room of their home, built on an upper level at the right of the stage. A gantry across the back and above the stage was well used for various crossovers. A central structure turned to provide several aspects for rooms and streets, including a Titanic mural depicting the ship and its doomed captain.

As Act I established relationships and characters, Act II set into motion a string of events that pulled together some threads of the story and quite literally blew others apart. It began with a helicopter landing to bring a government negotiator, Reginald Dodson-Meade (Enda Gill) to speak with representatives from the Loyalist and Republican sides. As a feat of theatrical engineering, this certainly packed a punch. The use of recorded sound heightened the impact, as did the presence of a line of police guards holding on to their hats ostensibly against the rotor draught. It landed for a moment and then took off, leaving the protagonists to their Talks About Talks. This was a surreal song and dance number with a Latin feel, with two groups of tango dancers delineated by green or orange detail in their costumes. The dance, like much of the dancing in the show had the strong purpose of expressing the situations and attitudes of the two communities. Where this dance was mannered and incongruous, earlier choreographed segments used the fierce stamping of set dancing to express the rage and impotence of opposing views caught in the stalemate that characterised so much of the conflict. Numbers like Nationalist People, They've Built a Bloody Barricade and Our Day Will Come packed a fierce punch and this chorus mustered a fervour which when distilled onto a single stage was vivid and arresting.

The rage of the chorus spilled into the actions of principal characters at times, notably when Davy Saunders, the corrupt cop, attacks Carmel Gallagher, accusing her of throwing a petrol bomb at a riot. John Thompson's intervention costs him dearly, and this scene marked the point when the intertwined actions of the characters begin their inevitable spiral into the violence of the remainder of the play. Michael Coen played Saunders with menace tinged with glimpses of a rational, feeling man. In contrast, John Murphy as Danny Quinn portrayed a young man totally in thrall to a cause, to the point of destroying what was nearest and dearest to him.

The scene of the negotiations with Dodson-Meade took place in a sparsely furnished office with a painted portrait of Queen Elizabeth. This was a fascinating glimpse at the process of negotiation as it might have been, juxtaposed with the characters we have come to know in this play. The song From a Unionist Perspective was a snapshot of personal and political stances brought out into the open.

The plot's essential secrets were revealed across Act II, including the fact that Sanders is actually Lisa's father and was responsible for the bomb that mistakenly killed her mother. Her grief in this and later scenes was heartbreaking, and the murders of John and her father compounded the sense of relentless violence. Some of the gunshots elicited nervous laughter from the audience, caught off guard as the death toll mounted. The deaths were convincing, the trajectory and timing of shots and the victims falling shockingly realistic.

The concentration necessary to carry off the escalating violence and death is not to be underestimated, and the cast's steely and unflinching portrayal of the horrendous events in this plot was impressive. Also impressive was the set, which presented us with a wide range of scenes, from individual rooms that projected claustrophobic intimacy to the pub set which occupied the full width of the stage. There were also well-presented cityscapes and neighbourhood atmospheres for exterior scenes.

The helicopter has already been mentioned, an unnecessary luxury in terms of the plot but very effective, providing a memorable theatrical moment. Perhaps the most memorable moment of shock comes at the end, however, when Carmel Gallagher and Davy Sanders, head into the Bullring pub as a prelude to what we know to be a world-weary pact between them. In an instant, the pub is blown apart, with doors and windows shattered and flames leaping inside the visible interior. As the fire burns, a motionless and dispassionate chorus sings a final reprise of the signature anthem Come the Dawn. Their lack of anger at this point is part of the message of this piece, and we are reminded of the dead who appear on the gantry above as a stark calculation of the price of this kind of conflict.

Hawk's Well Theatre Every show a musical society produces is in many ways really a celebration of all the years of that society's existence. For some, that might mean a quarter or half a century or more of hard work and dedication. For Sligo Musical Society, just twelve years separates their most recent show from their first. To undertake Beauty and the Beast, then, represented for them an admirably met challenge to fulfil the technical and theatrical demands of a show that is more than a little dependant on elements of magic to make it work.

Indeed, there were many things that worked well in this production, beginning with the Prolugue, a balletic sequence in which dancers in red and silver circled the old woman with a rose whose ugly appearance is rejected by the Prince. The transformation revealed her as a beautiful small girl. The Prince's transformation into the Beast was equally well done. The Little Town we saw next was busy and well-populated with all sorts of characters: a baker, a hat seller, ladies with parasols, a woman with a baby carriage. Olwen Parslow as Belle was oblivious to it all, reading continuously as she walked or sat. The song Belle was brisk in tempo and carried on the busy tone. Gaston (Liam Cunningham) made his presence known with the relentless bravado we expect from this character. His sidekick Lefou was a round, freckled and red-haired buffoon played to brilliant comic effect by Micki Murray.

Belle's father Maurice was an endearing eccentric whose relationship with his daughter was as touching as his mechanical enthusiasms were worrying. The town set consisted of built houses and shops to the sides and a beautiful back cloth illustrating a road out of town. The scene change to the woods was quickly accomplished and atmospheric. The wolves were, like the opening fairytale sequence, balletic in their movements, infused with the quick intensity of clever choreography. Maurice fled to the gates of the Beast's castle, with guards stationed outside who chased the wolves away. His "hello" once inside the castle echoed as if in a very large space.

Paul Quinn as Lumiere was marvellously, relentlessly French in manner and accent as was Babette (Emily Tansey), a very saucy servant indeed. The other castle inmates were equally well-cast and capable in their roles. Paul Sinclair was a dignified Cogsworth, with a gift for delivering unintentionally humorous lines with a keen sense of who this character was and is. Mrs. Potts (Pam Lindey) was knowing and busy, a nice mix of fluff and flint. Her Chip (Dylan Fox) was endearing and poised, able to convey a larger presence onstage than just a face on the trolley.

Scene changes were accomplished swiftly - a must in this show with its constant shifting back and forth between town and castle. The castle was beautifully detailed with stone blocks, doors, banisters and many angles and facets. Belle's first meeting with the Beast was characterised by her recoiling in fear - a realistic touch that immediately established their initial relationship. Also frightening, in a very different way, was Madame de la Grande Bouche, played with relentlessly showy single-mindedness by Caroline Hynes. There was a nice bit during her dialogue with Belle, in which Mrs Potts mouths Madame's speech behind her back, in a very "I've heard this all before" manner, which is later repeated. Belle's singing of Home was affecting and emotion- filled. Olwen Parslow was a Belle with a difference, very pretty, but not conventionally so, with an independent strength balanced by palpable emotion. In the village, characters continued to emerge and form into recognisable 'types'. The silly girls (Sarah Burns, Emma Claalghan, Laura Keown) exhibited a knack for being really very silly, in concerted unison; truly annoying and dead funny. They were especially adept and slapstick moments such as tripping one other up as they ran after Gaston. Gaston's speaking voice with an Elvis-y edge to it, was another facet of his pompous character and a nice contrast to Lefou's comedic lisp.

The Gaston chorus number had some nice sections in it, with different groups getting in on the dancing, including the men's chorus, the Silly Girls and some dancing couples. Another nifty sequence of mug-tapping worked really well. Gaston sported a ridiculously short, wide-barrelled gun, reminiscent of Elmer Fudd in "kill the wabbit" mode. Some harmony singing between Gaston and Lefou was missing on the night, but the finish of this number was satisfying and strong. The act finishes in the castle, with the continued transformation of it's convincingly expressed with well-paced dialogue that got all the potential laughs of this segment. Cogsworth's winding key was very large and gold, matching his hat and the clock hands on his face. He, Lumiere and Mrs Potts interacted very well as they witnessed the Beast's attempts to cajole Belle to dinner. Later, Babette got a very good laugh with her throw-away line "I've been burned by you before", and in general, the humorous lines hit their mark.

Be Our Guest was elegant and not over-populated, with movement and choreography tied closely to references in the text. Musical references were also acknowledged, as when the character of accompaniment became Spanish, Italian or French in character. Individual chorus members also had a chance to shine and there were wonderful acrobatic moments from some very flexible and accomplished dancers.

The Beast's discovery of Belle in the West Wing prompted her departure, and John Larkin's singing of if I Can't Love Her packed an emotional punch.

Belle's return to the castle with the injured Beast marked the beginning of his transformation, though he was still infused with interesting 'beastly' characteristics. His growling, lack of table etiquette as they share a bowl of soup, scratching and leaping were all part of a very complete characterisation. His tentative approach to Belle in the scene in which he shares his library with her was affecting. Indeed, all the principal characters were very consistently in character at all times, speaking, moving and singing. Chip's plaintive question "will I ever get to be a boy again?" was met with an appreciative audience sigh. The title song Beauty and the Beast was well sung and beautifully staged, with Belle gently showing the Beast how to dance with her. Their relationship grows in front of our eyes, and the song ended with an exquisite and tender moment as the Beast put his arms around Belle, both facing the audience but literally wrapped up in their own new world.

The end of the scene, and the Beast's very emotional If I Can't Love Her carried on the logical curve of this part of the story. In the village, we met the very slim and sinister Monsieur D'Arque, played with pointed intensity by Eamonn Redden. He and Lefou caught up in Gaston's scheming, sang Maison des Lunes with chilling menace, a shift in their characters from the jolly but harmless to potentially evil.

The movement of this production through the chorus being persuaded to 'Kill the Beast' was accomplished with good intensity, and the sound quality was fine throughout this, with individual microphone turned off or down in the interest of a more natural balance. There were moments of freeze for the mob which were very well done. The little touches of comic chaos in the castle were well realised, for example a human pepper shaker accosting a villager with inevitably funny results. Gaston's fall from the castle walls and the Beast's death and transformation were accomplished with good emotion on the night, and Belle's recognition of the Prince as her Beast was a great moment. Indeed there were many great moments as well as ordinary but unique moments in this thoroughly thought-through production of Beauty and the Beast. It was a pleasure to be surprised again and again by Sligo's magical retelling of this 'Tale as Old as Time'.

St. Michael's Theatre It isn't every day that a musical society gets to present an Irish premiere, but audiences in New Ross were treated to just that during late February and early March. New Ross's 43rd successive production marked the first ever Irish premiere in the history of the society, and indeed in New Ross itself. The show, The Drowsy Chaperone is a delightful pastiche of musical theatre of a certain era, and in their production, New Ross mined the rich seams of gags, music, dance and general nostalgia that the show presents.

Despite the somewhat unpromising title, this show has a bit of everything in it, all presented by and seen through the eyes of The Man in Chair, played with engagingly camp fervour by Derek Shannon. Man in Chair is a fan of musical theatre and to raise his spirits every so often he plays an LP of his favourite musical: The Drowsy Chaperone. He speaks to the audience throughout the show, introducing the action, providing insightful asides and generally giving vent to his enthusiasm for the actors and characters that act out the plot in front of us as the LP spins.

Characters initially emerged from his refrigerator, beginning with the opening chorus, Fancy Dress, during which everyone was introduced and the plot outlined. Basically, Janet Van de Graff (Thérèse Canavan) is a showgirl who is about to give up the limelight in order to marry oil tycoon Robert Martin (Brendan Redmond). Producer and impresario Feldzieg (Milo Walsh) is distraught as he envisions his theatre losing its big star, despite the efforts of star struck wannabe Kitty (Mary Kirwin) to fill Janet's shoes.

The first characters to invade the living room are Mrs. Tottendale, an "absent- minded dowager" played with balanced disdain by Peggy Hussey and the aptly named, deliciously unflappable butler Underling (Ken Moroney). Mrs Tottendale is supposed to host Janet and Robert's wedding, but this looks increasingly unlikely as Feldzig is pressurised by two thugs sent by their sinister 'boss', one of the show's main funders, to stop the wedding. He enlists the services of a Latin Lothario called Adolpho to seduce the bride. Adolpho, a relentlessly conceited Don Juan utterly dedicated to the craft of seduction, was played with terrific comic consistency by Tobie Hickey. He makes a major mistake, however, and   turns his attention to the titular Drowsy Chaperone (Teresa Buckley), who is supposed to be looking after the interests of Janet. Far from drowsy, however, she is mainly tipsy, delightfully irresponsible and utterly taken by Adolpho's charms. Also involved in the increasingly complex and delightfully implausible plot are George (Peter O'Connor) the long suffering Best Man of the planned wedding, and Kitty, a show girl who longs to take Janet's part in the Feldzeig Follies when Janet leaves to get married. Mary Kirwin was very funny in this role - an ingénue with a heart of gold and very little brain. Another comic element came in the shape of the two gangsters disguised as pastry chefs 1 and 2, played by Sean O'Brien and Thomas Crowdie. This pair had a great deal of fun as they bumbled and punned their way through the show, never quite mustering the menace they're meant to. A typical exchange went some thing like this: "You ever spent time in a coma?" "No, but I have a cousin in Seattle!"

The songs in this show are not well- known, but are catchy and of a type that resonate with musicals of a certain era. In this, the chorus played a key part. In the opening number, the chorus were very musical maids and waiters and they also added great colour to later numbers, notably the finale of Act I, Toledo Surprise, in which the dancing resembled a rousing Charleston. However, reminding us that we were watching a performance based on Man in Chair's record player, the dancing fell into a repeated jerky loop of moves when the record 'stuck', the turntable needing a bump to get it going again. At the start of Act II, we were treated to the puzzling spectacle of an oriental number reminiscent of "Small House of Uncle Thomas", because the wrong LP was mistakenly put on the turntable.
