These surreal details were all part of the fabric of this show, a kind of love song to one man's obsession with musical theatre, which I suspect resonated with many audience members and certainly with this reviewer.

The set for Drowsy Chaperone was cleverly constructed to accommodate both the sparse living room of the Man in Chair, and the larger realm of his imagination. In Bride's Lament, for example, sung by Janet and the entire company, the set became a nightime wonderland with a curtain of stars and a beautifully projected moon. Costumes were evocative of the times and settings required, including the mistaken scene from the oriental musical. The well-cast principals looked and sounded well, singing in character and moving well too. Much of the show evoked vaudeville, and these experienced players knew how to draw out the comic atmospheres and utilise timing and expression to great effect. The Chaperone herself was a comic force to be reckoned with, able supported, aided and abetted by the attentions of Adolpho. She wasn't the sort of person you'd really trust to chaperone anyone, but it certainly was a delight to spend an evening in her company, courtesy of the Man in Chair, whose obsession with this particular musical is was so easy to embrace.

Town Hall Theatre "I wish I could tell you about the South Pacific…" were the words projected across the stage in letters and words as if on a typewriter, at the start of Ballinasloe Musical Society's production of South Pacific. This prologue, during the Overture underscored the fact that this entertaining musical has at its heart a serious work of fiction that exposed in its time both the heroic and shameful aspects of war in the Pacific.

The opening scene on the terrace of de Becque's home had a beautiful feel of the islands about it, and the children's singing of Dites-Moi was charming from Jack Delaney and Blaithnaid Fenton. Seamus Feerick was a strong presence as Emile de Becque, consistent in his French accent and secure and resonant in his singing. He projected the required dignity of this role, as well as his urgent affection for Nellie, but was able to suspend that, as when DeBecque mimic's Nellie's dancing.  Louis Colohan's Nellie was girly and giggly when necessary, but able to be pensive too, and also angry and conflicted when she thinks she can't marry De Becque because of his Polynesian children. The Twin Soliloquies, as well as Some Enchanted Evening established a powerful connection between these very different characters so necessary for the central plot to truly work.

Another essential element of any production of south Pacific is a strong male chorus, and Ballinasloe had this for sure. Bloody Mary was a rousing means of establishing the energy and enterprise of the sailors when off-duty. Patrick Byrne as Luther Billis was a convincing wheeler-dealer, swaggeringly sure of himself, but capable of devotion to Nellie and humorous throughout. Other sailors (Stew-pot, the Professor, etc.) created a nice mix of characters, related through circumstance and making the most of their time in the South Pacific.

Fiona O'Leary as Bloody Mary was a dynamic and contradictory presence, larger than life and a great mover - understandably so, as O'Leary was also this production's choreographer. Her Bloody Mary was hard to like and impossible to dislike. Seamus Carroll as Joe Cable projected the right mix of the sure-footed professional soldier and an ordinary man confronted with something that he is almost afraid to understand. His scenes with Liat (Caomihe White) were carefully choreographed and beautifully lit, the lovers at one point in shadow with Bloody Mary walking in silhouette behind the scene. Cable's Younger than Springtime and You've Got to be Carefully Taught, numbers at opposite ends of the emotional spectrum, were effectively sung - the one a heartfelt love song and the other a vehement statement of disillusionment.

As well as managing the dramatic elements of this story, Ballinasloe MS embraced fully the humorous moments that South Pacific demands. The ladies chorus was a very cohesive unit, clearly enjoying their time on stage and making the most of numbers like I'm Gonna Wash That Man Right Out of My Hair and I'm in Love with a Wonderful Guy. Their male counterparts threw themselves into Bloody Mary and Nothing Like a Dame, which are deservedly iconic and actually quite tricky numbers. One enterprising sailor made what might be thought of as a kind of ultimate sacrifice and bared his bottom during the scene involving Luther's shower. The Thanksgiving celebration (including the obligatory coconut brassiere) was very well managed, balancing the light hearted show-within-a-show aspect of the scene with the progress of the more serious drama.

Further on in Act II was the scene in the control room with De Becque and Cable on the radio and Commanders Brackett and Harbisson (Barry Lally and Mike O'Reilly) listening with increasing concern. The large maps of the area used in this scene created a powerful focus of attention, showing us the dangers of the soldiers' position and placing the little world of the Island into a larger context. The reality of war was further established with a busy and highly convincing crossover scene in which chorus members (nurses and sailors) went about their business in the context of the high alert caused by the advance of battle. Musical cues for scene changes and those that suggested the atmosphere of the action onstage were well managed and underscored the shift of emphasis across the show from light-hearted to more tense. Apart from correct-looking military uniforms and off-duty clothes, the simple but well-judged settings did much to support the feel of an era familiar to us through film and television, heightened by the 'live' nature of the play onstage.

By the final scene, South Pacific's essential messages had been well presented by this company, who clearly approached their task with attention to detail of all kinds and also a spirit of fun and an appreciation for the glorious score.

The play ended as it began, on De Becque's terrace. Nellie's singing with the children had an easy, warm feel. When De Becque's voice joined the song, her back was turned to him and her face registered an entire world of emotion, before he sat down across from her and their hands met under the table. This is a show in which such meetings are not only possible but essential, and Ballinasloe's production also met South Pacific's many challenges with a Cockeyed Optimism that made for a very Enchanted Evening.

The Mill Theatre, Dundrum society yes, but with really young people running the show. We didn't put ourselves up for adjudication and we thrived on low budgets. Well, that was then; the warning signs began when we had to take the Y out of our name because all the founders were hitting their thirties. There was a constitutional vote. It was all very grown-up for me; fresh faced and innocent as driven snow. I didn't think I'd see the day that SMCO would allow an adjudicator in the door. I never imagined that adjudicator would be me. Rebel indeed! Fast forward to another time, nay, a different millennium, and SMCO still have their rebels, albeit in the form of the Footloose cast; an entire new posse under the guidance of Chairman and director Emmet McCarthy. This eighties show opened with a blast of energy from really good dancers, though singers sounded a little strained in places. This was to be no reflection on the remainder of the show however with strong choral input and excellent musical direction from Dermot O'Callaghan in command of a very tight band - the clarinet player who also played flute was particularly impressive, as was saxophone…okay, they were all great, and Mr O'Callaghan was a consistent solid support to the cast and production in general. Choreographer Sonya Dunne had put thought into her work and dances were engaging, allowing the essence of the show to come through with contrasts between the stuck up townsfolk against the sensual movement of the girls flirting. Singing was strong with this group and I especially enjoyed Ariel (played by Amy Penston) and her friends - Alison Vard Miller as Rusty, Rachel Flynn as Urleen and Aisling Larkin as Wendy-Jo (got to love those names) They were really good together both from a singing and acting point of view and their energy was infectious. Jenny McCabe and Jen Dalton as Vi (the Rev's wife) and Ethel (Ren's mom) sang a beautiful duet - the combination of two good voices with solid support from the MD was really well handled, down to the closing hum. Vi's character was well fleshed out for a relatively secondary role- her despair with her husband was clear, as was her love for him and a later song Find It in Your Heart was sung with sincerity. When Ren McCormick and his mom leave Chicago city to live in the town of Bomont, you kind of know Ren's not overjoyed at the prospect. But worse, the local pastor Reverend Shaw Moore has banned dancing - what?! How can we have a musical without dancing? Actually there was plenty of action on stage, but this is Ren's show; he's the guy who wins the coolest girl in town, befriends a social outcast and shows the Reverend the error of his ways. Simon Murphy held the role with confidence and singing was always good, though you'd want to see him dance; vital to the character, not many lead men could manage that massive 'footloose-style' jump off a gym horse and the actor nicely got his radio mike back in place without anyone noticing (of course I did, but I have been given bionic x-ray implants for this job.) I did feel Mr Murphy worked very hard with not always enough directorial guidance. Crossing the Line was one of his best numbers and the cast felt it; this number was probably the hub of the show and no one failed here. Niall Dempsey played the Reverend with a solid accent and strong voice and he was totally convincing in the role. He was not entirely in a comfortable register for the song Heaven Help Me, though this is not to take from a good voice. There was an excellent scene with Ren towards the show's end, with great timing and genuine drama. Reluctant hero Willard (Eoghan Fitzpatrick) had good comic timing and his character continued to grow on the audience. The relationship with Willard and Ren had chemistry and was always enjoyable. Eoghan McNeill played a suitable mean Chuck, the guy who would make Ren's life difficult, and Girl Gets Around (I think: songs not listed in programme) was really raw, well sung with husky tones that suited the character. In act 2, Cowboy Bob (Paul Stenson) sang well, though his position on stage meant he was obscured a lot of the time. I loved the line dancing number in this scene, it was executed well by the chorus and Let's Hear it for the Boy was a number well interpreted by choreographer Sonya Dunne.

Director Emmet McCarthy handled his troupe confidently, with movement around the stage nice and natural for the most part and large groups of people handled well. Set struck by the cast was smooth and scene changes generally were slick. Edyta Fleszar's set worked well with the simple inclusion of key pieces, e.g. tyres and a really cool authentic old petrol pump created a dusty old gas station in a two horse town. Back screen projection was used well also, especially at the beginning with a moving train as the curtains opened, but there might have been a technical hitch for the otherwise impressive diner set: giant burgers and people on wheels. There were some cumbersome pieces which stage crew handled well. But please oh please; who sanctioned the excessive use of the smoke machine? It was used almost constantly throughout the show and I could never see a need for it. Plus, you can't do that to contact lens wearers! This was Emmet McCarthy's first time directing however and there were plenty of strong moments; the gym scene unfolded nicely from set up through to people jumping over the horse, but at times distracted from the conversation on stage.  There was good drama when Chuck and Ariel argued and he hit her, the cad. Someone in my row laughed at this, inexplicably, but Ms Penston didn't let it affect the otherwise beautiful song Promises. This was an emotionally charged performance by a gal with a fantastic voice. Mr Emmet seemed to elicit some great performances from his people.

Highlights were I Need a Hero with four male dancers making like Village People and some ham acting from diner lady Betty Blast (Olwyn Boyle on skates) and later, the gorgeous love scene between Ren and Ariel on the bridge. The bridge was cleverly build over the orchestra and more than once Ariel was obliged to scream directly over the heads of the singularly unimpressed band members. (I know it's wrong of me, but I found that funny). Simon Murphy and Amy Penston are both high calibre performers and the chemistry between them on stage was wonderful - I had to stop myself from sighing out loud during moments of high romance. It wasn't all hugs and kisses for Ren however, as Chuck and his cronies beat the daylights out of him - excellent choreography here and well acted by all, with the atmosphere enhanced by the band, especially clarinet and guitar. Let's Hear it for the Boy sung by Alison Vard Miller as Rusty with the girls chorus was really well sung and verified Ms Vard Miller as a very strong performer - another super dancer here. The chorus was strong throughout and I loved the boys in the diner for Willard's song Mamma Says - the guys and especially Ren acted well off him - it was very funny and well choreographed. The reprise was even funnier.

Costumes, sourced within the group by Edward O'Grady Walshe were authentically 80's and added to the pictures on stage. Soundwise, it took some time for there to be good balance between orchestra and singers, with singers straining over the opening numbers and at times actually shouting their lines. Lighting, though designed well, consistently came in off cue and at times key people were not properly lit. Yet there were places where colour changing was subtle and really enhanced the mood.

Footloose, the final number, was a super ensemble effort; the girls looked great, the energy was palpable and the choreography was excellent; lots of really good dancers were well used, while others were well rehearsed and competent. A wonderful end to a highly entertaining evening.

It was midterm break.  I didn't have to teach.  So, naturally, as a self-employed person, that was the week that I could afford to be ill.  And I was really very unwell, though it was nothing contagious (in case I alarm members of Malahide Musical Society) - I literally dragged myself from my bed, threw on something dowdy and tried to walk with dignity.  I no more wanted to be there.  And then: magic.  What a show.  What a tonic!  How I laughed.  And though I climbed back into bed for three more days, I had the memories of that funny show to lift my spirits.  This Essegee Entertainment update of the classic Pirates of Penzance manages to appeal to the modern audience without, I think, offending any Gilbert and Sullivan purists.  The musical numbers stay more or less the same, though there is at times a funkier style for some of the choral songs.  It is irreverand, boisterous and downright hilarious.  This was the Irish premiere of the show, and I imagine we can expect to experience it again and again.

The cast was so good across the board, but I hope they forgive me for very quickly singling out David Latham as the Pirate King.  He was incessant in demanding laughs from us and he got them, every time.  He took every opportunity to flash his chest, in much the same way Eric Morcambe might have twiddled his glasses at his audience.  (Not to compare them physically; Mr Latham is far more attractive!) But all that is nothing if you can't deliver a charismatic character and be able to sing a number or two; from the first number Pour, O Pour the Pirate Sherry we were presented with confident pirates during a lively opening number.  The drama unfolded nicely, with strong acting, able performers (including chorus) who were vocally articulate and handled the language well.  There was a very natural style employed even in background acting, which blended into the action.  Jean Bennett as Ruth sang well enough, but her skill at storytelling brought us forward smoothly.  Kevin Fagin played Frederic and his character developed nicely as he easily enjoyed good banter and fun with the pirates. We were only two songs in and already I adored these fellows; I was impressed even before they did tricks with swords. Yes, they were show-offs and as the biggest show-off of all, Mr Latham's Pirate King flirted with the audience, fought with the conductor (MD Graham Walsh, nice performance!) and impressed mightily with a strong voice. Oh, Better Far to Live and Die had energy and full on comedy.

Director Lynda O'Neill also designed the set, which was well employed, and had been preset and lit with moving water gobos on the side walls, giving the effect of ship in harbour, with sailor type music playing from the PA.  When Musical Director Graham Walsh's orchestra did start up, the sound was good, with a funky overture letting us know what we'd be in for.  There was a big sound from the relatively small band. Singers were well supported by a very competent MD. Monica Fitzsimons was responsible for the excellent costumes, authentic and striking, particularly when several daughters, of a variety of ages entered through the audience for Climbing Over Rocky Mountains; they looked fabulous and care had been taken with hair and make-up.  This female chorus sang well too and when things turned 'rocky', handled the change.  Denise Donohoe's choreography was apt; she kept things in line with the period but somehow managed funky - there was some head banging (I can see G & S lovers shaking their own heads in disbelief here, but honestly, it worked).  Again, the band, especially drums were in fine form here. The three daughters - or the Fabulettes: Hilary Harnett, Tracy Peacock and Emma-Jane Reilly presented in an almost 'Pricilla: Queen of the Dessert' kind of way, and were very funny.  I enjoyed Frederic with the daughters here; he was integrated into the female chorus smoothly and O Is There Not One Maiden Breast was a brave, full on performance; because he was fun to watch, the singing was almost an after thought but Mr Fagin has a good voice and he had fun holding some of those notes.  Mabel, when she appeared for Poor Wandering One, sang sweetly with a competent soprano voice, which hit all the notes with ease; Anne Marie Ireland continued to warm into her character. The beautifully singing daughters all donned heart shaped sunglasses for How Beautifully Blue the Sky, allowing them to use them to great effect during Mabel's solo.  The simple choreography - pacing the stage with gesture - worked so well and was managed perfectly by all, allowing comedy as the Fabulettes built up the fun.  With the arrival of the Pirates, the stage was busy, but also well employed; everyone was seen clearly and the whole effect was visually impressive.  Director Lynda O'Neill could not have directed this show without loving Gilbert and Sullivan, but she must also have really loved her cast as she continued to present them in such good light throughout the show.  There was a line too, that everyone understood not to cross or this show would have become out and out panto.  And then, along came the Major General, who delighted us with his lack of regard for such rules; Barry Kavanagh may have appeared to adlib with impunity but there is a discipline that needs to be employed in order to appear so dotty. There was solid support from MD and band for A Modern Major-General, which had additional lyrics and some banter to an appreciative audience.  Later on in Act two, Mr Kavanagh presented a standalone piece of comedy as he grappled with his conscience and fear. Robert MacWilliams as second Pirate in command Samuel, absolutely shone along with the Pirate King and in fact - everyone on stage for Hold, Monsters! You can't imagine the fun we had; all choral numbers continued to impress through a combination of imaginative colourful choreography, solid direction, super performances and general enhancement from lighting.  Musically, all numbers were highly impressive. As mentioned, lighting was good, with colours introduced to enhance moods and add to the drama.  The sound balance between singers and orchestra was perfect too.

The pirates efficiently cleared the set, making things easier for Stage Manager Therese Farrell.  The Act two set - stone clad pillars and dry ice, back lit with dark blue gave an effective night scene and the daughters' entrance once again through the audience worked well in white nightgowns, nightcaps and little lanterns - this uniformity worked really well, and the Fabulettes more so, almost like vestal virgins in theirs.  Were we done with the laughs?  We were not; as Vincent Oliver's excellent Sergeant and his band of policemen brought us When the Foeman Bares his Steel.  Here I really appreciated the modern version of the show and it's presentation by this production team; with white faces and rouged cheeks there was a Buster Keaton touch to the movement, where good female dancers took the front row and well prepped males managed perfectly well (for the most part!) behind them. The movement of the Fabulettes against this only highlighted the comedy while there was some silliness from Frederic, Mabel and the Major at the side.  By this time, Frederic had a sort of Orlando Bloom type confidence while working as the straight man off Ruth and the Pirate King - the silly dance for When You Had Left Our Pirate Fold was given full effort from all involved, so it worked a treat; the scene that followed was just as silly and just as funny.  Did I mention I was ill this particular night?  Lynda O'Neill's slick, tight direction was very impressive and each scene had been given ample rehearsal time to realize what must have been wonderful visualizations.  Speaking of which, Mabel was simply a vision in her amazing white dressing gown; it was like a quilted debs dress and it helped that she performed so beautifully, along with Frederic for Stay, Frederic, Stay! Even through the humour, it was a lovely duet, and both singers shone here.  The band was equally good here for a softer number as they had been for the more rousing pieces.

The police returned with When a Felon's Not Engaged and all acted really well, keeping up the fearful facial expression and knocking knees.  They were clearly told there was no limit to how frightened they could look and the more it was hammed up the funnier it got. Yes, I felt this director and choreographer collaborated very well and I think the pinnacle of this may have been A Rollicking Band of Pirates We; all the pirates were great, none hiding behind any of the principal actors. The three encores of the number got funnier each time, though I think the players may have worn themselves out a tad!  Hush Hush! Not a Word was a great follow up to the mood as the pirates tried to act as trees. And why did I leave Graham Walsh out of the earlier talk of collaborative efforts? None of this would have worked without the immense effort put in by this MD. The show ended with a Megamix Finale with a good deal of dancing and a nod to the original show.  It ended with the best bowing sequence I ever saw.  What a fabulous show for a lucky chorus - the challenges and interaction for them was a treat.  The principals were without exception strong solid performers and all of them understood how to get a laugh. And laugh we did.  Nay, guffaw we did. It proved the age -old adage: Laughter really is the best medicine. Thanks Malahide.

There was a time when I only had to walk two doors away if I wanted to see a Kilmacud show; now I have to heft myself an entire mile to the Mill Theatre in Dundrum - a first for this group who since 1982 have been staging their musicals in St. Benildus College (where, incidentally, as I write with the window open I can hear the director of a local school's production of 'The Wedding Singer' in rehearsals and he's not happy, not happy at all…) The cast of KMS seemed very happy however during their staging of 'Oklahoma!' - a second time round for them, but with, it seemed to me, a large injection of new blood, and a lot of it young. Great too though, to see some of the familiar faces of bygone days who continue to entertain audiences, albeit in a new venue.

My children are now at the age where I embarrass them, and never more so than when I tried to explain to them what a wonderful show Oklahoma! is; I might have had some chance had I not attempted to sing 'Oh What A Beautiful Morning' (there's a reason I chose direction as my forte). Why oh why, I wondered, had I not brought them with me to KMS's show, where they could be educated and entertained all at the same time? Against a back screen projection of a golden corn field and a big blue sky, Curly sauntered on, in the shape of Niall MacCarthy, and had my children heard him sing they would finally have understood. Although sound levels took some time to adjust, this was a confident performance, very comfortable in the lower register. Mr MacCarthy's relationship with Laurie was good and the chemistry built up very well. Laurie, played by Amy Byrne, also sang well (especially 'Many A New Day') and her portrayal of the character was convincing, with subtle nuances and pretending she cared not a jot for Curly. 'The Surrey with the Fringe on Top' allowed the relationship to develop nicely along to good solid accompaniment from the band, under the baton of musical director David 'Doc' O'Connor. The sound had balanced out at this stage and strings in particular were enjoyable. Yes, I appreciated this band, but their position possibly took up too much space centrally and at times this was a distraction to the action on stage.

I liked Marion Holohan's Aunt Eller - she played the part with conviction and comic timing was bang on, but I would have preferred if the make up people had dowdied her down a bit. Will Parker, played by Kevin Fagan enjoyed some comedic moments with Aunt Eller and a strong male chorus of cowboys - Mr Fagan's super voice was confident and controlled for 'Kansas City' and indeed all his musical numbers.

While groupings on stage were good and visually kept interesting, I did consider the chorus to be somewhat underused, with large groups of people sitting or standing around watching the ongoing action. Understandably there is more for the men to do in this show than for the women, but the female chorus was strong for all of that and there were plenty of capable individuals who might happily have shone if allowed. That said, director Justin Parkes did get a lot out of his principals, and characters such as Ado Annie, played with relish by Kim Bolger really got every bit of humour out of the dialogue. Solid guidance was given to all characters, with Eamonn Murphy's Jud Fry dark as the night, and Ali Hakim (Alan Davoren) delightfully inappropriate at every turn. Many of the actors delivered their lines almost directly to the audience rather than focusing on those they conversed with, and it did affect the energy at times. However, very much the exception to this were Will and Ado Annie, who were funny and good together, precisely because they left us (the audience) out of it. I don't mean to suggest that actors shouldn't connect with the audience, rather that they shouldn't allow our presence to un- focus them - it's a fine line and makes you appreciate the art all the more. Ian Tighe played a grumpy Pa Carnes and had fun with the part. Jennifer Fahy had a good horsie laugh for Gertie but this was also an energetic performance, which heightened the developing chemistry between Laurie and Curly. 'People Will Say We're In Love' had good movement, dependent upon both actors' performances, which didn't disappoint. However, an otherwise tender moment was lost because the stage crew rushed on before the scene had been fully played out. I could see no reason for the panic; with no set changes up to this, we would have been patient for the change into Jud's shack - which was very effective as it happened, with excellent props and Jud silently a-whittling. Eamonn Murphy understood the misunderstood Jud well, and gave the character dignity. 'Poor Jud is Daid' was very well sung here and the band, including muted brass and strings continued to impress. But once again, before the powerful moment had quite finished, out came those busy stage crew people.

Choreography from Nicole McDonald was simple but well executed during 'Kansas City', with Will Parker showing off some impressive footwork; a female chorus and a skipping rope added energy to the dance. The band continued to be strong and brass in particular were in good form during the very enjoyable 'I Cain't Say No', with Ms Bolger's Ado Annie colourfully expressing herself.  'It's A Scandal' was one of the band's best numbers with solid support for Ali Hakim from the MD. All instruments shone, as did Mr Davoren and the chorus brought extra fun to the song.

Mary Lou Hartford was responsible for costumes, which were authentic throughout. The women's change of costume in Act 2 looked good. Although Laurie's dress for the dream sequence was beautiful, it was very much a ballet dress, which didn't tie into the style and was confusing for anyone not familiar with the show. The choreography here has strong imagery, reflecting Laurie's state of mind; her being in love with Curly but also her unwillingness to be an object of desire and her fear of Jud and his lecherous ways.  It was ambitious but for the most part, it did work - although no one was a trained dancer, Ms McDonald's guidance was obvious and Laurie and Curly's sequences were well managed.

Bass guitar was crisp and clean for the opening of Act 2, and dancing was good with everyone managing the well choreographed 'Farmer and the Cowman'. Aunt Eller and Andrew Carnes were in control for this song and there was solid humour with support from all on stage. What with thigh slapping and girls lifted at every opportunity, the audience loved it. With a highly energized chorus, there was room for some fun with bidding during the auction scene and members of this talented cast were able to show off their acting skills. The drama that built during tense bidding between Curly and Jud was balanced nicely by Aunt Eller's lightness. There followed an engaging scene with Ado Annie and Will and their excellent song 'All Er Nuthin' had colour and a sense of fun. The band's support was a delightful enhancement. The proposal between Laurie and Curly was sweet and the love scene comfortable, followed by comical antics from Ali, Will and Ado Annie. 'Oklahoma' was a wonderful choral number from this group, with fine voices full of energy, though it was crying out for some movement. The fight between Jud and Curly had been well choreographed, and the drama was good. The finale reprises of 'Oh What a Beautiful Morning' and 'People Will Say We're in Love' were rousing and Kilmacud Musical Society did what their loyal audiences have come to expect after thirty years; sent us home all a buzzin' and forcing our children to watch You Tube clips of the show.

Because the programme clearly listed a web address for Ennis Musical Society, I logged on (during a moment of painful writer's cramp), and was impressed with the organization of the group as regards the 73 children involved; information on which group was needed when, parents supervision lists and photos of costumes was there along with latest news.  This sense of order came across on stage also and the children were a credit to the society.  They had certainly been well rehearsed but more than that, each child was totally 'switched on' throughout the show; not one of them had an unfocused moment.  Who said never work with children or animals?

The set was impressive too, apparent once lights came up to reveal the workhouse with a familiar London skyline just visible over the backdrop.  This was quite a big stage and the space was well filled in, floor to ceiling, with a high level towards the back.  The children brought immediate energy with Barbara Meany's clever and interesting choreography for 'Food Glorious Food'; the dance was quite different and totally entertaining. Des Henn's direction was solid too and the movement of the children had drama. Tony Murray as Mr Bumble sang well, as did Emer O'Flaherty as the Widow Corney, though a little more connection between their characters would have enhanced the humour.

Musically, the tempo of 'Food Glorious Food' was impressive with nice playing from the members of MD Martin Maloney's orchestra.  The pace might have been a little slow during 'That's Your Funeral', though this was well sung, and Cormac O'Sullivan and Kate Corrigan as Mr and Mrs Sowerberry brought energy to it.  'Where is Love' was really beautiful and Nathan Bluett was a truly wonderful Oliver who knew the song well, confident that he was in good hands with his MD; the band played gently under this and the balance was great, especially where there was a fuller sound.  Strings in particular stood out.  Choreography of the fight between Noah (Bernard Moran) and Oliver was good, while Anne O'Donnell's Charlotte and Mrs Sowerberry added panic to the scene. For young Oliver, it was out of the coffin and into the hands of The Artful Dodger, where Daniel Lynch looked the part in his baggy and raggy rigout, but he also had a super voice and after 'Consider Yourself', he had the audience in the palm of his hand.  Flanked by a strong boys & girls chorus, the street scene filled up well and the dance was great as the children travelled across the stage perfectly in sync with each other. Scene changes weren't always tight, but I loved how the boys blocked the stage while Fagin's Den was being set up.  Brian Henry was a very charismatic Fagin from the outset, full of expression both physically and facially and with a wonderfully familiar Jewish accent.  His movement mirrored that of the children's in 'You've Got to Pick A Pocket or Two' and this really enhanced the whole number.  Choreographer Barbara Meany continued to think outside the box and the band were in fine form.  Mr Henry introduced a little bit of panto humour when his high falsetto notes morphed into 'I Dreamed a Dream' and his performance was strong enough to make that acceptable.  And funny.  There was more playing around with the script and the audience enjoyed it.  (There was also some hamming up with the violin soloist in Act two.) Charlie played by Jack Wall O'Reilly stood out.

Andrea Doolan brought depth to the character of Nancy, and her developing fondness for Oliver was obvious, aided by both director and choreographer. Musically she suited the character well, with a very melodic voice and a strong accent. Bet, played by Zoe Halpin made an impression too, and singing here was also strong, along with Fagin's Boys for an engaging 'I'd Do Anything'.  There was a moment during these scenes where you could really sense the security these children felt with Nancy and Bet, and with Fagin, in an otherwise cruel world. 'Be Back Soon' with marching lines was almost perfectly executed.  Now, I teach children; been working with 'em a long time and I'm baffled - how did so many move so perfectly in sync?  Did you start rehearsing before Christmas?  The chorus sang well and everyone moved ever so smoothly off stage. Delightful! Act two brought us more rich tones from Nancy with her well known and loved song 'Oom Pah Pah': a colourful, rogue-ish rough and tumble dance with tankards and cast iron mugs, and some nice touches from the female chorus. By this time I had glanced through my programme and read that the director and choreographer were a team.  In fact, they were married to each other. That explained a lot as there was collaboration throughout the show, with many dances having dramatic shape and many scenes having smooth flowing movement.  While I'm not suggesting all director/choreographer teams need to bond quite so closely, it does highlight the importance of marrying their skills. Act two also brought us Bill Sykes, with his leather coat and intimidating sideburns, and Kieran McAteer was convincing in the role.  Mr McAteer was well supported by the band during 'My Name', but his strength was in his character portrayal.  Nancy was clearly in awe of Bill while everyone else was afraid.  The drama created when he hit her led into an emotionally charged 'As Long As He Needs Me' which was beautiful against the subtle lighting and colours of a London skyline.  It was sung with control and no gesture.

Oliver's scene for the reprise 'Where is Love' with Mrs Bedwin (Marina Mulqueen) was tender, while Neil Haran's Dr Grimwig brought humour out during scenes with Derek Crosbie's kind Mr Brownlow.  'Who Will Buy' presented as a static picture was very well sung by an able chorus of men and women with Oliver.  The entire adult chorus joined in for the speedier part of this song, looking fabulous in their costumes.  Four tiny boys along with four slightly older girls were incorporated into this dance and they were super.  Accents were solid and anybody with individual lines did well.  Scene changes were smoother in the second half though Fagin's Den was devoid of hankies.  While we could see Nancy and even Fagin battle with their consciences, there was no hope for Bill's dirty soul; indeed their change of heart only highlighted his lack of remorse. Mr Henry's Fagin continued to own the stage and indeed he owned his song too for 'Reviewing the Situation' and this kind of energy was important; the show has some darkness and people's lives are so very bleak that we need to know it's okay to laugh too.  With a new script developing through the actor ("What the dickens?" for example) there was an injection of new life given to this show and it was welcome.  "Who will change the scene for me?" he sang as the crew carried him off. Mr Bumble and the Widow Corney had a funny scene following this, a little OTT but acceptable. Old Sally (Geraldine Westwood) performed well, though I questioned the director here for trying to get humour out of a woman dying.  It's not funny and this is what makes the reprise of 'Oliver' so sinister.  Yes the show takes a definite darker route from here on and Ms Doolan understood that perfectly with an utterly convincing reprise of 'As Long as He Needs Me' referring clearly to Oliver this time.  The following scene built up dramatically from the bridge with help from the band.  In fact the use of music, lighting and thunder really enhanced the dreadful beating to death of Nancy - it absolutely had to be disturbing.  The band levels remained loud - too loud over the following dialogue however and some of the movement was confusing; where Oliver was standing meant he was in the line of gunfire for example.  All the same, the scene had huge dramatic impact and I appreciated that Bet was left the last person on stage with Nancy's dead body.  I also appreciated that Fagin's return and reprise of 'Reviewing the Situation' was without humour.  Yes, he was affected by all that happened; he took Bill's ring, and he didn't sing.  It was a deeply respectful ending to what had been a downright entertaining show. Well done to all involved.

The Strand Theatre It hardly seems possible that 40 years have passed since the first New York run of Godspell, one of the handful of 70's musicals based on Biblical themes. One of the great challenges of this show is its non-stop nature and almost relentless changes of focus and reliance on text more than plot. Carrick-on-Suir struck a good balance in their production, which tackled these demands with great energy and attention to detail.

The show opened with a projected cityscape across the back of the stage, and the sights and sounds of urban life. The stage was soon populated with all sorts of characters, from fruit sellers to policemen. The set itself carried forward the urban theme, with an amalgam of broken walls, brick, and graffiti. A booming voiced announced "my name is God" and a pink horn provided the sound of a shofar, the Jewish 'call to worship' in a sense, bringing the chorus together and creating a focus for Prepare Ye, sung initially by Ray Nolan as Judas, and then taken up by the whole cast. Nolan is a strong vocal presence, and the chorus made a powerful sound, well co-ordinated with the hidden orchestra. Another nicely co-ordinated segment came when Jesus, played by Michael O'Dwyer, accompanied himself on guitar for God Save the People. O'Dwyer is a multi-talented performer whose obvious youth did not get in the way of his being an effective and affectionate leader of the colourful troupe of 'disciples' that form around him. He had a nice quality of friendly other-worldliness that worked very well in this obviously important.

The choreography was a nice mixture of free-style dancing and more formalised and coordinated movements.

This is a show that thrives on individuality, and there was a nice freedom and youthfulness in the essential elements of costume, hair, makeup and movement. Another technical feature was the projection of text above and behind the action; uncited Biblical passages, mostly, that related to the action or song, or simply were thought-provoking in context. The fast pace of dialogue and changes of mood, scene, context, etc. in Godspell makes it easy to lose sight of the solid story behind the parables, so these projections were a clever way of creating focus. Sound effects were also used to underscore movement and help illustrate stories created with minimal props and set pieces.

Carrick-on-Suir MS really looked for opportunities to emphasise the inherent wit of this show by incorporating all kinds of irreverent and anachronistic references to the parables. A pantomime cow appeared as part of the story of the Good Samaritan, along with a Frank Sinatra "start spreading the news" reference, and a bit later, a kazoo accompaniment to a line or so from "All You Need is Love". A reference to Charlie's Angels accompanied the angels who carry away the Poor Man when he dies, and the humming of couple of bars of Grieg's Peer Gynt Suite (Morning) evoked heaven.

There was a core group of fourteen players onstage for much of the show, and they were joined by the full chorus for some numbers. There was a thought- through logic to the places where this occurred, and there were also pit singers. Occasionally the action was pared down to smaller numbers, as a means of creating real focus. One such number was All for the Best, a highlight of the first act. Jesus and Judas were portrayed as puppets, each manipulated by two people, one for face and feet, another for arms and hands. This combined with two differing strands of choreography for the two characters, and the 'real' Jesus and Judas singing with a cane and ukulele respectively, made for a very stylish and funny piece of theatre.

The following song, All Good Gifts, was beautifully sung by Audie Murphy as Lamar, joined by the chorus, whose part- singing was very good. This led into the central parable of the Prodigal Son, again peppered with contemporary references and bits of relevant songs (Big Spender, Celebrate). The number that closed the first half, Light of the World, was a kind of techno-mix version played on a boom box - a big and bright 21st century take on this upbeat number with a nice retro disco feel.

Carrick-on-Suir's excellent band continued to shine in the second half, especially in the opening tune, Turn Back, Oh Man. The soloist in this was Louise Mulcahy as Sonia, and there were four backing dancers in black with Jesus miming the piano part. Across this half, the mood became edgier, and Jesus himself was more and more agitated. The Gospel essentially overtakes the jollity, and in Alas For You, on the line "blind fools", some of the disciples held him back from advancing on the others. The back wall projection read "There may be trouble ahead". In keeping with the shift in mood, By My Side was sung with wonderful warm intensity by Catherine Hogan as Peggy, with harmonies by Jacquie Ahern Slater as Jasmine.

Across this show, the chorus showed great concentration and engagement in the main action, with good facial expressions and a collective feel for the essential narrative arc. The main disciples likewise conveyed the change to the more serious songs with a good feel for how the emotional pace speeds up as the physical pace slows. The stillness of the Last Supper scene (accomplished in a completely deadpan manner with the passing around of bread and cans of coke) was impressive, and the lighting in this was especially effective, illuminating Jesus and creating a feel of a halo around him.

The journey of the show came full circle during On the Willows, when each of the main chorus took leave of Jesus by sharing with him a signature movement which we had seen at the very beginning. This was touching without being mawkish. Elements of the temptation of Christ, his betrayal and the crucifixion were conveyed with a strong sense of dramatic tension, and simple devices (black hoods, red streamers pinned to Jesus' suspenders to indicate flowing blood) helped to underscore the action. Many technical elements of the production, from echo on the chorus voices to strobe and spot lighting and dry ice were brought into play to depict the death and resurrection, and the reprise of Prepare Ye, We Beseech Thee and God Save the People served to ensure that there was a happy ending, and a message for the audience to take with them. Indeed, this was a production in which the message was well balanced with music, dance, humour and familiar points of references that would have resonated with everyone in the hall. This was the Godspel According to Carrick- on-Suir Musical Society, a great tale worth telling which they made their very own in many entertaining ways.

Dean Crowe Theatre Although West Side Story is an iconic, important and demanding show, the story at its heart is simple and perennial. Athlone Musical Society's 95th production managed to bring some new ideas to the stage while retaining the required clarity of the Romeo and Juliet narrative set into a backdrop of feuding 'families'. The set worked well on the not-expansive stage of the Dean Crowe Theatre, with a New York cityscape as backdrop, pieces of scaffolding, chain link fence and of course, the balcony. Minimal set pieces were used to suggest other locations such as the wedding shop, Doc's drug store or Maria's bedroom.

The opening scene established very well the confusion and tension of gang life, with Jets and Sharks entering and leaving the stage with increasing speed, the fight scene materialising and blending in and out of dance moves. The athleticism of cast members was used to very good effect, with lighter, swifter actors (and actress!) leaping like gazelles through sections of scaffold and a 'no-holds- barred' look to fight choreography.

Gradually, individual gang members became known to us through dialogue that was well-varied in pace and tone, naturalistic yet clear. Jared Madden as Riff had an edgy authority and strong vocal presence. Carlos Fidalgo-Romo as Bernardo had an apt Latin intensity and a handsome halo of decorum to his manner and movement which proved crucial to his playing of the role. Colin Fahy as Chino had a lovely approach, manifested with a suggestion of hesitance and sense of not so much wishing for violence as being swept into it. Paul Donnelly as Action gradually emerged as a strong 'player' in the gang, and Joe McCaul as Baby John was like a coiled spring, ready for anything but not quite in control of his own impulses within the gang. As a group, the Jets projected an edginess that bled into their dialogue, with lines coming on top of one another and a nice variation of pace and delivery. The Jet Song had good energy and managed to be rhythmic without losing the gang-like, spontaneous feel. MD Dr. Joe Ryan had the courage of convictions in this and other musical numbers, conducting in a pacey one to a bar. Throughout, tempi were brisk and flowing, a combination that suited most of the singers and staging and certainly posed little problem for his very able band. Tony was played by Mark Adamson, who conveyed a good sense of equivocation and transition in his scene with Riff. His was a likeable Tony, and his relationship with Riff was solid and believable. Adamson is an able singer, with a grand sense and sound of the voice opening up on long notes, and a nice way of singing in the American accent, with the right emphasis and modulation.

Jets and Sharks were distinguished from one another by subtle, plausible costume differences. Sharks were more colourful, Jets more conformist. The dance in the gym emphasised the differences in culture and gave the chorus a chance to establish themselves as members of their respective communities.

The meeting of Tony and Maria was nicely managed, and their later meeting introduced us to the singing voice of Fiona McManus as Maria. Apart from wonderful diction, she has beautiful tone and tuning. The blend and ensemble between Tony and Maria was excellent, and they sang Tonight with a solid feeling for the blooming and fading of long notes across the arc of a phrase.

The lively numbers America for the Sharks and Gee Officer Krupke for the Jets were cheeky and fun, with lots of fine detail and strong singing. The difference between minor tensions within the two groups and the major difficulty of the two communities was very well portrayed in this production. The way the Jets elaborately gave the Sharks a wide berth when meeting them was apt and edgy. Lieutenant Shrank, played by Alfie Kilduff was nervy and prowling, while Colin Kelly as Krupke had a lighter touch. Mick Dillon's Doc was watchful and later angry, observing as the youngsters destroy themselves, powerless to stop them. The dialogue in his scenes was always well-paced.

The contrast between the scene in the dressmaker's (One Hand, One Heart) and The Rumble is always extreme, and Athlone's production emphasised the stillness of the one and the sense of the building tension of the other. Both songs had strong, forward-moving tempos and good vocal balance.

The fight scene that opened Act II was well-staged and had the same intensity and impact as other fight segments in this production. I Feel Pretty followed, another juxtaposition that demanded a complete contrast in mood. The dream sequence that followed Tony's telling Maria that her brother is dead included a miming of the fight scene itself, and then dissolved into Maria's room again. Linda Murray as Anita brought two very contrasting approaches to the role, with feisty humour in the first part of the show, and then the bitterness of A Boy Like That. The scene in which the boys at Doc's molest her was truly frightening, and her transformation afterwards was powerful, prompting the lie about Maria's death that sends Tony out to meet his own. His agony was palpable, and for a moment after Chino's shot rang out it was impossible to tell who had been hit. After Maria's lines ("How many bullets are left, Chino?") the scene arrived at a tableaux, with her cradling Tony's body and the chorus ranged behind. They froze and then lifted their faces and looked straight into the audience - a gaze that spoke volumes and asked many questions all at once. This was a fine production, emotionally rich and musically satisfying. Athlone are clearly a society committed to worthwhile goals and setting high standards. This production grabbed me from the start and it didn't let go until the very last note.

The Moat Theatre, Naas Any watery associations one might have with the name of the Moat Theatre were augmented five fold at least during the run of Naas Musical Society's Pirates of Penzance. The scene was set from the moment one arrived, with a pirate's chest of treasure and other memorabilia in the foyer. Once inside, the world of the famous eponymous pirates was conveyed by means of an impressionistic and expansive painted backdrop with rocks and the shore surrounding a green and white sea. The drama to come was hinted by a skull and crossbones projected onto the floor of the stage, and the Overture of course also hinted at 'coming attractions'. The famous Pirates made their entrance roaring and tumbling, singing in a strong unison and establishing their credentials as hearty mates, swinging on ropes and generally 'strutting their stuff'.  Frederick's splendid uniform, replete with gold braid set Peter Fay apart as a pirate with a difference, and Mona Conroy as Ruth filled us in on the details of his beginnings. Willy Bermingham as the Pirate King was channelling the spirit of Jack Sparrow for his 'look' and much of his demeanour, and clearly enjoyed every moment of his kingship. Frederick underscored his 'otherness' with a rich and deliberate speaking voice, a posh accent and wonderful resonant vowels. He's also nicely good looking. The pirates in generally were a great looking lot, with costumes consisting of a jumble of military-style jackets, some with tails, long waistcoats, boots and colourful sashes. Collective they had a great grasp of the comic potentials of each situation, as when they try to send Ruth away with Frederick, instead of keeping her with them.

Frederick's singing voice really came into it's own upon realising Ruth's deception (Oh! False One) and his ease with the idiom of recitative as well as aria was an asset to this role. The arrival of the maidens was a feast for the eyes and ears, as they were a sea of shrieking, swirling girlhood, with multi-coloured costumes, flounces, hats, parasols and fans. They were also beautifully coiffed, and accompanied by a number of rather fearsome chaperones, who set on Frederick with hilarious ferocity when he informed them that he was a pirate. One of the girls fainted dead away at this point, and there was plenty of swooning and running back and forth after him when he asked 'is there not one maiden breast?'. Eilish Hayden as Edith and Lisa Kelly as Kate had attractive voices and brought out the requisite comic elements of their characters. Tina O'Kelly is an especially able comedienne, and her Josephine was a constant source of amusement. The arrival of Mabel was a pleasingly big moment, and the girls showed their displeasure very amusingly indeed. They were, however, also capable of impressively graceful movement in their big dresses and hats.

The return of the Pirates was inevitably occasion for much mayhem and some funny work with a rope and wielding of maidenly weapons. The Major General (Liam Quinlivan) arrived in Victorian fishing shorts carrying a long fishing pole. While singing about the ways in which he was the very model of a modern major general, her changed into more suitable clothes for his exalted role, completing the task by the song's end - a marvellous device for this number, and very well executed. The finale was a headlong dash through some delightful music and great interaction between chorus and principals. In I'm telling a terrible story, the chorus and Major General froze alternately during their verses, which was a well-executed and clever way to create focus in this. Hail Poetry was of course a great moment, with so many fine voices and a real sense of the creation of a Big Moment. Choreography was well suited to the numbers on stage, and gave individuals in the chorus a chance to establish themselves as individuals too.

At the beginning of Act II the wide, not very deep stage of the Moat Theatre came into its own, and a setting of an ivy-covered cloistered walkway across the raised back platform was beautifully executed. Mabel and the girls, and then after a bit, the policemen, populated these opening numbers with great style. The policemen's entrance had them march across the stage and right off the other side, but the wait for their return was well worth it. They were light-footed and musical and proved in many ways to be their worst enemies, all to brilliant comic effect. Their Policeman's Lot was delightfully staged, with plenty of loose-limbed movement, and their re-appearance during Cat Like Tread (popping up at the sides and back of the stage) was another hilarious treat. The paradox, when it came to light was explained with the help of an abacus, a useful and quite funny tool. Away away was preceded by a joke about going and 'fetching the band', which MD David McGauran 'mistook' for a reference to the pit orchestra. The orchestra had a good sound, with some lovely sonorous playing as well as a nice agility when needed. There was some very well set chorus work across this act as well - one segment with the ladies divided into three groups, in circles, fans fluttering, singing about the breeze, and eventually joined in the ballet by those inevitable policemen. The choral sound of Yield in Queen Victoria's Name was very good.

Indeed, this production made the most of big moments and allowed individual performances to shine as well. There were very good voices on stage and an exceptionally well-drilled and focussed chorus of Pirates and Ladies, young and not so young. Care had obviously been taken to ensure that everything looked

Town Hall Theatre, Galway I would imagine that it isn't every day in the week that the curtain of the Town Hall Theatre, Galway opens on a cast with their backs turned to the audience. However, Patrician Musical Society took this imaginative approach to the opening of their production of Fiddler on the Roof, beginning for them what was clearly a labour of love, an affectionate and affecting re-telling of the story of Tevye the milkman and his family. Indeed, 'extended family' might be more apt, because Tradition, the opening chorus, introduced us to the entire village of Anatevka, and not least to the Fiddler on the Roof himself, Vincent Hurley, an actual fiddler perched on an actual roof, another nice touch.

Peter Kennedy as Tevye has the requisite world-weary look, ostensibly because his horse is lame but also possibly because he was also the director of this production! The papas, the mamas, sons and daughters were duly joined by other villagers as well as soldiers, Russians, the rabbi and the priest. The stage was busy with activity and the song was set with appropriate movement that allowed this number of performers to remain rhythmic and project a sense of the order of life in this corner of the Ukraine.

Denise O'Regan as Golde established a nice, if fractious relationship with Tevye. We sensed a bit of the love behind the scolding, thankfully, and that's as it should be. Katie Creaven was Tzeitel, a very good actress who brought real life and believability to her scenes across the show. Ailbhe Slevin was a busy and comic Yente, with a consistent characterisation that incorporated the way she looked, moved and spoke. The sisters Hodel (Iona le Gros) and Chava (Michelle Glynn) joined Tzeitel for a rousing Matchmaker, a really well staged and choreographed number. This was a strong trio in terms of singing and acting, on top of which they seemed to have great fun.

Another inevitably attractive number was If I were a Rich Man, performed with understated fervour by Kennedy, a confident performer who steered clear of imitation or caricature in his interpretation. The scenes in which we met confident Perchik (Joe Joyce) and Shane O'Grady as nervy and anxious Motel were well- paced, with the dialogue hitting its mark and quickly establishing relationships. The Sabbath Prayer was beautifully staged, with the chorus processing up the dark side aisles, humming and singing, and the family group on stage, lighting candles. This was a very beautiful moment of theatre.

The misunderstanding between Tevye and Lazar Wolf (Andrew Gallagher) about whether a cow or Tzeitel is being discussed was very well managed. Gallagher had the right 'look' for the well-meaning butcher, and was consistently good in his role as a jilted (albeit at one remove) suitor.

To Life was a very entertaining and convincing scene, with the Russian soldiers projecting real camaraderie and energy in their dance and interaction. This was the sort of scene for which the word "revelry" must have been invented. Musically, the stylish Patrician pit orchestra approached a genuine Klezmer sound.

Full marks especially to Bertrand Huvé on clarinet and Marie Zichova on accordion. Outside the pub, the Fiddler appeared again and played the If I Were a Rich Man reprise live.

The following scene with Tevye's daughters and potential suitors Motel and Perchik was a nice contrast to the near- mayhem of the preceding one. Perchik and Hodel's dance was charmingly done, and Tzeitel's grief at learning that she is to marry Lazar Wolf was palpable. A nice touch was her recoiling from Tevye's drink- soaked breath, and also Motel's persistent timidity and gratefulness. Tevye's asides (They gave each other a pledge) further cemented the relationship he built with the audience, an essential part of the viewing of this play, during which we must identify with Tevye as an everyman faced with small and large life-changing events not of his own doing.

The pairing of Motel and Tzeitel was lovely; persuasive and touching. Tevye's Dream which convinces Golde that they were meant to be together was a great scene involving a ghostly chorus in shredded sheets and a demonic denouement. Grandma Tzeitel was Margaret Martin, and the terrifying Fruma Sarah was Emer Barrett, who had a great grasp of the moment and the weird drama of the scene. She's also got a grand voice, deployed to stunning effect in this role.

The wedding celebration was also a strong segment, notably the Bottle Dance, which began with a stunning moment of silence, and Mordcha's speech, delivered with a keen sense of timing and the ironies of the moment. Richard Bell's Mordcha was a strong character across the show, a consistent, watch-able presence. The argument between Teve and Lazar which he prompts was very well conceived, and the chorus participation was excellent. Across Act II of Fiddler the transformation of Tevye's family and the situation of the town Anatevka accelerates. In this production likewise, changes came swiftly and more smoothly. Golde and Tevye's already engaging relationship deepened in Do You Love Me, offset by a sparkling Rumour Song, sometimes left out of productions, but nicely done in Galway, a great slice of village life. Hodel's growing maturity manifested itself very well indeed in Iona le Gro's singing of Far From the Home I Love, in a beautifully set scene, complete with the sound of a bleak Russian wind at the train halt.

Little Bird was also a strong, emotional song, and the ballet that set it was very well designed and danced. Lighting created the effect of distance with pronounced shadows and a tableau of the past, and Chava walked towards Tevye and rejoined the 'real' scene, an effect also achieved through great lighting. Anatevka had a great spoken prologue, and the musical intro was well-paced.

At the final leaving scene, the strength of this cast as actors was demonstrated yet again, and Yenta, Chava, and Fyedka all delivered their lines with particular effect. When Chava placed her hand on her father's back, he flinched with a strong own emotional reaction and the electricity of that parting gesture raced through the audience too. The slow steps of the family and chorus to the final music spoke volumes about the historic context into which this story was set and the Fiddler stood onstage until Tevye beckoned him to follow, another gesture laden with love and meaning beyond words.

INEC Killarney Although My Fair Lady is a big show, it's focus on language and the use of language can make any production seem like quite an intimate theatre piece at times. Killarney Musical society's production, though performed in one of the country's biggest venues, managed to draw the audience in to the play and make us complicit in the central plot to turn Eliza Doolittle into a lady.

The set for the opening scene was pleasingly evocative of the square outside of Covent Garden, with a portico and arches, pillars and a general feel of space and post-performance bustle. Gabriel Butler as Henry Higgins had an effortlessly firm grasp on the essential tone and tenor of the role. Indeed, he has a fine tenor voice and a distinguishing and refreshing feature of his performance was that he sang rather than spoke the songs. Don Rohan as Colonel Pickering had the requisite warm bluster and decorum, and his relationship with Higgins throughout worked well. Why Can't the English established Higgins and to a lesser extent, Pickering, as characters. Their inauspicious meeting with Eliza (Molly Lynch) was well managed, and her vocal punctuation (eeeaooow!) was as annoyingly memorable as it needed to be. Lynch is a pretty and expressive actress, an engaging presence for this role with a strong, well-modulated voice for singing and speaking. Wouldn't it be Loverly was charming, with some very nice choreographic touches.

Alfred P Doolittle was played by Gerry Adams with an infectious glint in his eye and a lateral lisp that worked well for the character. He inhabited the role with an easy rhythmic confidence that was supported by an MD with a keen grasp of the way the music in My Fair Lady often emerges out of speech, and a very alert band. The set for With a Little Bit of Luck was beautiful, with a painted backdrop of what looked like St. Paul's Cathedral and an atmospheric feel for the city of London. There were problems on the night with the mechanism for raising and lowering backdrops, but the sets themselves were 'loverly'. Likewise, the variety of costumes one expects in this show was well in evidence. Doolittle's sidekicks on this occasion had plaid suits, and the three men were well matched for their engagement in the scene's music and movement.

The Higgins house provided a great backdrop later on for Doolittle's unselfconscious yet knowing presence. His scratching caused Higgins to begin scratching too, and his open-mouthed persuasiveness was oddly plausible. The set for Higgins's house was impressive and functional, and his housekeeper Mr's Pierce (Orna Cleary O'Shea) spoke beautifully and had a dignified, rather than fussy, manner. The scene after Eliza's arrival was nicely done, pitting her rough edges against Higgins's, in contrast to the overt civilisation of Pickering and Mrs. Pierce. Great use was made of the balcony of the set, and Eliza's concern at the plans being made for her was portrayed with nice comic timing. Higgins was laconic and manic by turn in I'm an ordinary man. It was easy to warm to the teacher/pupil relationship forged by Higgins and Eliza, and the 'bit' with the pebbles and the candle, etc. got nice laughs.

By the time Just You Wait came around, we felt Eliza's frustration, and her delivery of this song was compact of anger and triumph, very watch-able and fully engaging. The Rain in Spain was everything it needed to be, a palpable weariness on the part of everyone giving way to exuberance and madcap triumph. I Could Have Danced All Night had lovely long lines and a terrific sense of forward momentum. Interjections by the maids were excellently placed, and the maid and butler characters were very sure- footed and a strong feature of the Higgins household.

A beautiful garden scene with a splendid- looking Mrs. Higgins (Nanette O'Leary) gave way to Ascot, with a backdrop of arches and stylised trees. The chorus looked marvellous, with Beeton-esque black and white costumes and impeccable, mannered movements. Eliza's 'new' speaking voice is comically modulated, rounded and full of delicious rolled 'R' sounds. The "bloomin' arse" moment was extremely successful, and the reactions that followed, different depending on the character, were priceless.

Killian Buckley was Freddy Eynsford Hill, who we met at Ascot. On the Street Where You Live was played to the front of the stage, sung with an attractive voice and easy, relaxed manner.

The embassy ball followed, with the unwelcome appearance of Zoltan Karpathy, a great character skilfully played by a suitably heavy-accented Des Furlong. This was an attractive-looking scene, with plenty of dancing and Eliza's costume, hair and general demeanour rising to the occasion. The return to Higgins's house in Act II was a very well-paced scene, with the general sense of excitement contrasting well with Eliza's growing despondency. Her angry scene with Higgins was full of real emotion and bite.  Freddy's reprise of On the Street… was slightly despondent this time, and Show Me was more spoken than sung, an interesting approach that worked well in context.

Doolittle's re-appearance as a 'changed man' had the right pathos and humour, with appropriate vocal mannerisms and a sense of the two worlds he now straddled. I'm Getting Married in the Morning had a beautifully sung prologue (there's just a few more hours…) and a terrific dance sequence, with some of the general choreography resembling sign language. In particular the women's dance line in this was very strong. The freeze at the end was perfectly executed, and Doolittle being carried off as if a corpse was a nice touch. The humorous mood continued back at the Higgins house, with his completely perplexed, utterly self-centred manner during Hymn to Him, and a very funny one-sided phone call between Pickering and a sceptical police officer.

The transformation and softening of Higgins was very well conveyed in the scene at his mother's house, and Eliza's segue into Without You was perfectly timed and pitched. Her dismissal of him is complete, and we believe her. It was with some relief, then that we witnessed her return to him, following a very moving singing of I've Grown Accustomed to her Face. The general consensus in Killarney was that we had also grown accustomed to that face, and to the entire company, and it was with some sadness that this My Fair Lady came to and end.

Trim Town Hall It was quite appropriate for Trim Musical Society to choose Crazy for You for their 25th Anniversary year. The show is itself a celebration of musical theatre, with all the elements of song, dance, great characters and romance rolled into one great evening's entertainment.

The Overture gave us a whirlwind tour of some of the great musical numbers in the show, and when the curtain opened, we found ourselves onstage looking out from behind the curtain at the Zangler Follies, an exciting perspective. Craig Regan as Bobby McCann was an immediately sympathetic character with his love of show biz and his failed audition. Regan, clean cut, handsome and adept at his American accent is also a good dancer and singer. Niall Dempsy was Bela Zangler, all business and no heart - a good nemesis for Bobby's earnestness. Another formidable thorn in Bobby's side was his fiancé Irene, played with confident intelligence by Jenny Seery. Bobby's mother was played by the elegantly dressed Gwen Bagnall. Between them, these two great characters pile enough angst onto poor Bobby to bury him. Their exit just before I Can't Be Bothered Now was accomplished with imagination, leaving the stage to Bobby and the Follies Girls, figments of his imagination in matching pink bob wigs, tap shoes and sparkles. The choreography of this number set a great standard for what was to come.

Bobby's arrival in Deadrock revealed a cast of cowboys Bidin' Their Time with a difference; one of them reading the show-biz magazine Variety, and all of them involved in periodic re-enactments of famous gunfights. Bobby's exhaustion and thirst was quite comic: he asked for water and promptly landed face-down in the street with fatigue. This carried on into the number Things are Looking Up. There were lots of details in the scene in the saloon, including a funny bit during which the bartender slides a drink across the bar to Bobby and he misses it twice. Louise Cassidy was at ease in brown dungarees and ginger pigtails as Polly Baker, and Cormac O'Reilly was Everett Baker, Polly's father and a great character with the same enthusiasm as his daughter for theatrical endeavour. Shall We Dance, a nice soft shoe number, established Polly's credentials as a dancer, and also the chemistry between her and Bobby. We also met Lank Hawkins, (Frank O'Reilly), in love with Polly and hoping the buy the Gaiety Theatre, which became a character almost in it's own right in this production, given that it becomes the centre of much action and attention as Crazy for You progresses.

The arrival of the Zangler Follies Girls was an exciting moment reminiscent of every old movie in which brisk and good looking city slickers turn up in a remote place. The girl's costumes were beautifully colourful and accessorised, with hats, gloves, bags and shoes which all coordinated. Hair and wigs were also very much part of the overall look of these ladies, and they winked and smiled at the cowboys as if there was no tomorrow. One cowboy by the name of "Moose" was a great cameo for an unnamed actor. Bobby disguised as Zangler was comically business-like and a walking, talking caricature of the real Bela. Polly's Someone to Watch Over Me was nicely sung in front of the curtain.

The chaos involved in teaching cowboys to sing and dance for the show that is going to save the theatre was very well conveyed. Each member of the chorus seemed to know what they needed to be doing (or not doing) at any given time. A double bass on stage provided the solution to the problem, and the aforementioned 'Moose' was given a chance to prove himself in a number called Slap That Bass. Miming to the bass player in the pit, the number began with pizzicato and gradually turned into a great, classy song and dance number for full chorus.

The unexpected arrival of Irene set a very canny cat among the pigeons and the strength of this character was in the balance Jenny Seery struck between her being a tyrant and being quite a likeable, smart and strong woman. She checked into the hotel and began to be quite a thorn in Bobby's side. This scene was punctuated with one of the many sight gags that populated this production. Hotel owner Lank, exasperated with Bobby tells him he's 'close to an idiot', whereupon Bobby took a large step away from Lank. These kinds of jokes, corny as they are, always it their mark and got a laugh. There was also a very comic scene with Polly singing EmbraceableYou to Bobby disguised as Zangler, him trying to resist her, because he wants her to fall for Bobby (himself). Somehow, the complications of the plot mattered less than the general feeling that the show must go on. The arrival of gormless tourists Eugene and Patricia Fodor (Richard Harrahill and Edel Murray) provided more comic interest, and it didn't seem to matter that they hadn't actually come for the show.

The real American Folk Song started off Act II, after a grand Entr'acte played by a very accomplished band. The choreography emphasised elbows and arms and again caught the character of the music very well. 'Moose' was consistently loose-limbed and mobile of expression. The arrival in Deadrock of the real Zangler had gone unnoticed, but in this act his laconic presence began to cause confusion, compared to Bobby's more productive version of the producer. Their drunken scene made great use of a mirror image set-up, with the two of them each with a bottle and a sandwich. Both were adept at every mannerism of the classic theatrical drunk, and then some, and also both good movers. The original Bela reacted in character at this point to a cell phone going off in the audience, a great ad lib that got a good reaction. The point in the show when Irene and Lank 'connect' was very funny, sealed with a saucy and clever rendition of Naughty Baby. A scene in which the townspeople meet to discuss the future of the theatre relied very much on the ability of the chorus to engage in the action in a believable way, and various voices from the crowd were convincing in this. Stiff Upper Lip, followed, in which Eugene and Patricia (dressed like boy scouts) joined Bobby and Polly. This number featured some great unison dancing.

Two classic numbers, They Can't Take That Away From Me and But Not For Me, were nicely sung by Bobby and Polly, the latter song proving Polly/Louise Cassidy's ability to hold an audience's attention on her own. She also conveyed in this her transition from believing herself better off without Bobby to realising that she misses him.

The plot's return to New York reunited Bobby and the Follies Girls for a great looking number, Nice work if you can get it, their pink and sparkly entrances nicely done, each one entering to a note in the introduction. The vocal quality on this was softer and well-modulated, and the harmonies were well done. Bobby's reflective soft-shoe dancing spoke volumes about where his heart really was, and his next move took him back to Deadrock, at the same point that Polly decided to go to New York to find him. The comic tension in this scene was well sustained, and while we pretty much knew there would be a happy ending, it was good fun actually having to wait a bit for it. A number of loose ends got tied up as well, and the inevitable big production number that closed the show was a lively pastiche of lovely show-biz elements.

Waterfront Studio Musical Society's production of Crazy for You was the sound of a great live big band coming from somewhere behind the scenes. This is an attractive overture and it helped to establish straight away the kind of larger-than -life approach this company were to take to the show.

This feast for the ears was closely followed by a feast for the eyes, as the "Crazy for You" curtain was swept aside to reveal a stylised Art deco scene with lights, stairs and railings of a theatre. Zangler girls on their way to work with feathers in their hair joined Vijay Sharma as Bobby Child, who, in addition to being beautifully dressed, had also the keen intensity needed for this role of someone desperate to be involved in showbiz. An accomplished dancer, his audition for the electric blue-coated Zangler did not have the desired effect, and we began to sense his frustration. More frustration arrives, in the form of his mother, played by Audrey Neill, and fiancée, Claire McGonagle. Their relationship, one of less-than- amiable rivalry, was well played, in a brief, bitchy scene during which we got all the information we needed to explain Bobby's willingness to decamp to Deadrock. Rebecca Fleming was a sweet-faced Tess, with a well-modulated speaking voice who later proved herself a very able dancer too. Tim Cush as Zangler had an enjoyable disdain in his manner which suited the role very well and worked to overcome his open, youthful appearance. For the number Can't be Bothered Now, the Zangler Follies girls squeeze through a rip in the back curtain, an interesting entrance and an interesting backdrop, with black and white images of signs indicative of the big city: 'Eat', 'Apollo', etc. Their costumes (black and white polkadot dresses with pink fluffy petticoats) were elaborate and evocative of the glamorous and extravagant vaudeville era.
