Sliver shoes and blonde curly wigs completed the ensemble. The choreography was a great mix of nice formations and shapes, with good arm and leg combinations. The Deadrock street scene was nicely atmospheric and provided a great backdrop for our first encounter with the citizens of this remote place. The cowboys really did convey a sense of bidin' their time, and we met Ciara Power as Polly Baker, the femininely-dressed but tough talking daughter of Everett Baker (Drew Reid), a sympathetic character whose enthusiasm for the Gaiety Theatre came across, but was clearly rooted in nostalgia for the theatre's past.

In the saloon, the 'sham fight', cowboy style was quite funny, even if the shooting of the cuckoo clock didn't quite go as planned. Could You Use Me? captured the energy of the earlier Things are looking up, and the dance sequence conveyed nicely the sense of Bobby making a reluctant Polly dance. When they began to dance 'properly' they were well-matched and elegant with smooth and nicely connected movement.

The arrival of the Zangler follies girls in Deadwood was a bright and bustling moment, and Entrance to Nevada established the 'east meets west' aspect of the show. Polly's Someone to Watch Over Me was well delivered, with a lovely musical approach to rhythm that was not slavishly attached to the beat. Slap That Bass was a big production number with quite a few different sections to the dance and changing elements of choreography. Almost filmic in approach, this was evocative of the Gershwin musicals from which these musical numbers are taken. There was a really nice bit in which white ribbons turned the girls into double basses themselves.

Embraceable You was given the care in staging it deserved, with Bobby-as- Zangler trying not to react to Polly's advances. There was a nice bit of harmony on the last line, and a nice comedy approach to their kiss. The arrival of the tourists Patricia and Eugene Fodor (Emma Phoenix Kelly and Michael Blair) made for some very nice funny business - their mannerisms (his speech impediment and her snorting laugh) singled them out as every bit as 'otherworldly' and out of place as the Zangler girls. However, the strong chorus numbers that finish the act serve to pull everyone together. I Got Rhythm was accompanied at one point by some very well played 'found percussion' instruments (washboard, shovel and hammer) and the front tap line was in great form.

The innovation of the Act I finale carried over into Act II's Great American Folk Song, with some interesting use of tin dishes in the choreography. Likewise, the scene with the two drunken Zanglers was well-paced and very funny, and Polly's realisation that there are two of them was very well done and got a great reaction. Irene's love song to Lank (Naughty Baby) was also very funny, and well sung. These two characters really came into their own in this, with good focus and timing. Claire McGonagle is also a very good singer, and made the most of the song's comic potential, with able assistance from Eamonn Connolly as Lank Hawkins, the saloon owner, whose transition from being interested in Polly to being captivated by Irene was very well played.

The town meeting that became the song Stiff Upper Lip was a nice scene for chorus and individuals in the cast as well. They Can't Take That Away From Me was a gentle contrast to this, and again showed the good chemistry between these two principals, Bobby and Polly. Polly's moment in the spotlight for But Not For Me' did not disappoint, with a more emphatic reprise to follow. Bobby's return to New York provided another opportunity for a full-on dance number, Nice Work if You Can Get it, with yet more beautiful costumes and chorus-line choreography. Bobby's return to Deadrock, though not inevitable by this point, is very welcome, as it reunites the whole cast for a big finish. This musical is a great contest between day-to-day life and the magic of theatre, and in Fortwilliam's production of Crazy for You, the theatre won, hands down.

Millbank Theatre If there was any doubt what sort of a journey Rush Musical Society was going to take us on during their production of Anything Goes, the presence of sailors, pursers and assorted passengers in the Millbank Theatre gave the game away pretty quickly. This was a cruise with a difference, however, as we discovered as soon as embarking on the good ship American.

We actually began the journey in a bar with Billy Crocker (Damien Hurley) and Mags Carrick as Reno Sweeney, whose association is lighthearted but potentially complicated. She sang I Get a Kick Out of You to the audience, dressed beautifully and, one sensed, ready for mischief. Billy, however, was earnest in his pursuit of Hope Harcourt played by Niamh Kavanagh, an accomplished actress with just the right 'look' for a Cole Porter love interest. Her mother, played by Helen Kavanagh looked as though she really could be Hope's mother. Could the clue be in the name?

Another undoubted star of the show was the set, which was a splendidly art deco evocation of an ocean liner, a glorious design with plenty of detail. Clever elements like the fold down bar/bed at stage right and left made for instant scene changes and the use of different levels made it possible to accommodate a large cast when required. Another element of this production that was worth noting was the beautiful costumes, especially for the leading ladies. Again, the right 'look' was very much in evidence. Make-up also was very much in keeping with the style of movies of this era, strong colours against pale skins and a good unity across the cast.

The scene in which the full cast join the ship (Bon Voyage) was a busy and well- populated one during which the audience were faced with many names and faces, and the beginning of what was a typically complicated plot, set lightly in true Cole Porter fashion. Indeed, there was nothing heavy-handed in the direction in evidence here, which meant that every nuance of humour was attended to.  Donal Collins was Eli Whitney, who brought a moneyed, myopic disdain to this role, and was quite comic as the victim of Billy's deception. Hope's fiancée, Lord Evelyn Oakleigh was played with frenzied foppishness by Will Fitzpatrick. The clergyman Rev Henry T Dobson was Charlie Monaghan, in a short- lived but pivotal role. His two Chinese converts, Luke and John were the hilarious and very un-PC Richard Cullen and Mark Flynn, two absolute masters of clichéd Chinese mannerisms. Gangster Moonface Martin was Ciaran Canavan, a formidable presence and very believable in this role of a crook with his eye on keeping himself a step or so ahead of the 'Feds'. His sidekick was the very funny Tara Harrison as Erma, with a consistent American accent and great sense of comic and musical timing. I suppose that another star of this show, like most musicals, was the music itself. This Cole Porter score is top class and shot through with familiar melodies and the rhythms and rhymes of a bygone era. Rush's band and MD Sarah Lynch-Barrett were certainly up to the challenge, and one nice touch at the beginning of the show was seeing them 'board the ship' before it sailed, a house band for a house that travels across the Atlantic.

You're the Top was one of the well-known numbers, sung by Reno, whose stylish voice and knowing manner suited this material very well, and Billy. Damien Hurley has a great voice and an ability to sing in character that matched Mags Carrick's facility for this. The choreography for this used the whole stage and the movement was rhythmic and suited these two very good movers.

Singing voices generally had the right quality of sound for the songs, and the singers themselves knew how to get the best from their voices. Chorus numbers were not plentiful, but well prepared and presented with an ease that overtook the fact that sometimes the songs had more to do with entertainment than furthering the plot. The unlikely trio of Reno, Billy and Moon had great fun with the number Friendship, and Reno graciously decides to seduce Lord Oakleigh as a way of helping with Billy with his plan to prevent him marrying Hope. That seduction scene was very funny, with Oakleigh also continuously getting Americanisms wrong and missing many points completely. It's De-Lovely marked a nice point when the romance between Billy and Hope began to take off.

The title song Anything Goes was given star treatment and was the finale of Act I. Reno's entrance was suitably spotlighted and the freeze at the top of the ship's stairs promised something big to come. The formidable combination of the salon girls and Reno's 'angels' were appropriately coiffed (blonde and curly or brown bob) and direction and dance made full use of the set at all levels, even adding another level as the sailors lifted Reno in the air for a big finish.

The full company were again literally on deck for two numbers opening Act II, some of the cast as guests on the cruise for Public Enemy No. 1 and then a full-on shipboard revival meeting led by Moonface Martin disguised rather unnervingly well as a clergyman. Reno and her Angels are inevitably there too cheeky as ever in Blow Gabriel, Blow.  The ladies chorus in general were costumed "to the nines", with fully coordinated wigs/hair, headdresses, jewellery and shoes. The choreography picked up on the ecstatic arm movements of full-on tent revivals, and the entire cast were swept along in the number.

The continued plot involving Reno's plan to break up Lord Oakleigh and Hope took a further step and a subtly-drunk Reno was subject to his advances in The Gypsy in Me. This very funny scene with two OTT characters who have nothing to hide flowed into a cleverly designed set piece with Moonface and Billy in jail, with Moonface singing to try and keep their spirits up. The Chinese 'converts' became involved in a game of strip poker, re-enforcing the impression that there is more to them than meets the eye. Deckside, Irma had a chance to warn the sailors that have fallen in love with her that all might not be as it seem with her either. Her Buddy Beware showed a good voice with real warmth in the lower register especially. Tara Harrison also moves well, and the sailors with her provided a good accompaniment with their own moves. The final deception in this delightful but complicated plot involved a Plum- Blossom of a love-child and the realisation that true love will win out in the end. The Finale proved that while they got no kick from champagne, Rush Musical Society certainly enjoyed themselves onstage and created a most entertaining evening's cruising on the good ship American.

Siamsa Tíre Theatre When writer/composer Bryan Flynn set out to create a musical drama with an Irish voice, the life and times of Michael Collins became his compelling subject. His way in to the story centres on a production of Cathleen Ni Houlihan at the Abbey theatre due to take place the evening on which the Easter Rising began.

Michael Collins, a musical drama begins with a mythical prologue evocative of the play, with a central woman's figure in a circle of dancers. The Abbey Theatre itself is in evidence, the theatre entrance and interior. These were suggested, as many of scenes throughout were, by a well- designed structure of scaffolding which turned and split to create the scenic parameters of the play at various points. Audience members for the Abbey play arranged themselves on further stairs and scaffold that came out from the sides of the stage and ran along the walls of the Siamsa Tíre Theatre. They watched that evening's performance until it is stopped when a man rushes in with news of the Rising. From then, the narrative of Collins' life takes over, punctuated by returns to the play. It is essentially a play-within- a-play, the Cathleen Ni Houlihan story providing a mythical contextual wall against which the Collins story echoes. A brief look at his childhood establishes the Cathleen legend as significant to Collins personally, and that association also returns later, with flashbacks of Collins reading the story. The Players (Jackie O'Mahony, Bryan Carr, Kathryn Smith, Mike Lynch and Sharon Walsh) were the linking device and conduit through which the action flowed, moving between their roles in the Abbey play to their role as narrators of the Collins story. They captioned the history from their vantage points as observers of the action.

The battle scene depicting the Easter Rising was powerful, involving the chorus in slow motion action and sound effects that were many-layered. The mythic dancers from the opening scene re-appeared, and in fact return again and again, underscoring the links and threading together the legend and fact which are central to this story.

The scaffolding 'tower' of the set, and also use of the sides of the theatre as playing space allowed for the sense of expansiveness needed to tell such a big story with the added complication of the play-within-a-play structure. This moved easily and quickly and allowed for actors at times to be at different levels, the gantry also suggesting doorways and interiors without the need for extensive scenery. It created smaller, more detailed and intimate spaces as well, depending on placement and the use of smaller pieces of furniture and props. One face of the structure had the outline of arched and square windows, evocative of a street exterior.

The plain clothes of the Players enabled them to move easily between their various roles, and also provided an almost contemporary resonance, a third element of history which is essentially as present- day observers and commentators, stepping into scenes from Collins' life and putting events into context. They were strong singers, adept at part singing and able to create a dramatic focus even when standing still. They were also ever-present, focussed and observant and as such, their singing when it happened, carried great weight.

A scene in a prison followed, through which the dancers wove and then retreated. An interior setting was evoked with a spot lighting effect through a frame of prison bars. Muiris Crowley as Michael Collins had the right height and bearing for this central figure. His West Cork accent was apt and despite the occasional gravity of scenes and situations, he was able to convey a spirit of humour as well. Jack- Patrick Healy was Joe Emmet, a strong though slight physical presence with a well-modulated singing voice that also had good power, as illustrated by the number Joe Emmett Interrogation.

Fly the Flag of Freedom was an anthem that set some of the tone for the larger moments in this show.

As the Collins Story gathers momentum, so does Collins as a character, joined by the other well-know players of the action. Tim Moran was an almost uncanny De Valera, giving the role an understated power not reliant on caricature. The Letter was a beautifully staged segment that gave real insight into the personal stories behind the central characters of the Rising and its aftermath.  Harry Boland was played by Alan Teahan, a fine actor who negotiated his pivotal role with Collins and Kitty Kiernan with sure-footed emotional resonance, creating a chemistry between himself and them that both heightened and softened the tensions of the plot. Luralee Murphy as Kitty had a warm singing voice and attractive presence on stage.

Historical events dominate this show, and scenes of mustering and battle are key, relying on the strength of the Tralee MS male chorus and also inevitably detailed direction which makes apparently random fighting scenes work well. In Survival of the Fittest, the new recruits looked convincingly unsure of the weapons they were issued and Dublin Killings which follows on from that was augmented by impressively integrated technical devices such as newspaper headlines projected above the action and scenes of killing and assassination silhouetted behind what had appeared to be solid brick walls at the sides of the set. Projections were used at other points too, to convey a London skyline, a docklands scene or the image of a harp, for example where appropriate to the scene.

Alongside the political history portrayed in Michael Collins are of course the personal narratives of the characters. Much of this centred on Kitty and her conflicted feelings for Collins and her fiancé Harry. These more intimate scenes presented the challenge of breaking away from big set pieces and strong music into scenes of a more focussed and intimate sort.

Various historical aspects of the story were staged with powerful resonant performance from the actors, notably scenes of growing conflict between Dev and Collins. The Customs House attack was also effectively conveyed, with dry ice conveying the atmosphere of the aftermath and this, in turn facilitating a return to the Abbey stage and the play. Every Heart Awaken was the anthem that ended Act I, and the Abbey play returned for the beginning of Act II, both orchestra a stage lit for the Entr'acte.

The character of Collins inevitably develops most consistently throughout the play, and his mannerisms and the rhythm, resonance and modulation of his speaking voice became ever more important.  They in effect set down a marker for who the man was and gave the text weight. Physical mannerisms likewise helped to fix this character in history and on stage, and Crowley also sang in the Collins accent. Alan Teahan also proved his singing credentials in I'm Not The Man, an almost narrative song, with heroic, angry lines and strong emphatic musical arc. The vocal range required in this was large, and the last note almost impossibly long. Segments of the show dealing with the Anglo-Irish treaty were well staged, the character of Collins voluble and De Valera more physically and vocally restrained. Treaty Debates featured a well-engaged chorus as opposing sides, a powerfully resonant scene staged with a focussed sense of people with a stake in the proceedings. Collins' Treaty Song brought a new timbre to his singing voice, and the attention of all on stage and in the theatre was riveted on him.

The play returned one last time to the Kitty and Collins story, with their Duet, beautifully sung with close harmonies and beautiful, matched phrasing. Treaty Campaigns ended with The Players holding newspapers that indicate 'conflict ahead' and this was a twofold prophecy, the conflict between Collins and Harry over Kitty, and the conflict of over Ireland herself. This point was well made, without mawkishness or cliché. The Civil War Sequence and Revolution brought the Dancers back into this most incongruous setting, their weaving in and out of the chaos effectively mixing this battle with the myth and legend of a far larger history.

Grand Opera House, Belfast The overture to Calamity Jane is a rousing pastiche of numbers from the show, and in the Grand Opera House, Belfast Musical Society's audience were humming along from the start. Clearly ready for a treat, they were not disappointed by this traditional and very well-resourced production. The Deadwood Stage established itself as a star of the show from the opening, behind a scrim with Calamity riding high. Once the stage opened up, Deadwood and its environs were revealed in the form of a lovely painted backdrop and some of the buildings of the town.

The Deadwood Stage introduced Alice Johnston as Calamity Jane. She brought great energy to the role and took a strong physical approach to this tomboyish and engaging frontier woman. The chorus were well-drilled vocally and in their choreography which took its cue from many of the lines of the song. The scene was populated by townspeople and the girls from the Golden Garter saloon, as well as a row of children who were captivated by 'Clam's' song.

Inside the Golden Garter, Careless With the Truth further established the character of Calamity and her 'exploits' and introduced Wild Bill Hickock (Iain Mercer). Mercer was well cast as the no-nonsense celebrity cowboy with a wardrobe to match. His solid and handsome presence was backed up by a creditable singing voice and well-projected and resonant speaking voice.  The set-up dialogue for Adelaide was well done, showing Belfast Operatic's male chorus to be clued in theatrically and also adept at their singing, with harmonies in place on this well-paced number. The bar room pianist at the back of the scene was a nice touch.

Francis Fryer was played by Gary McAlorum, to all appearances a genuine song and dance man. His theatrical credentials included producing a bouquet of flowers from nowhere and some very nifty hat and umbrella twirling. Danny Gilmartin was Paul Masterson, also well cast and a capable comedian too, very funny in a scene in which both Calamity and Doc Pierce (Jon-Paul Bruce) tend roughly to his wounds.

The Golden Garter Dancers, having been part of the show from the beginning finally get their chance to Can-Can and really proved that they could-could.

Fryer's return as 'Frances' was eerily convincing, and his progression from being thoroughly ill at ease to really quite enjoying it (check out his shimmy!) was convincing too. Saloon owner Henry Miller (Colin Boyd) was a convincingly anxious proprietor of the Golden Garter and his daughter Susan (Oprah Devitt) had a pleasing singing voice and quite a comic take on her attraction to Frances. I Can Do Without You gave us another glimpse of Calamity's fraught relationship with Bill, and it was quite funny when she angrily threw herself at him and he remained utterly solid and unfazed. Following her vow to bring Adelaide Adams to Deadwood, the curtain closed and we found ourselves in the audience of the Bijou Theatre in Chicago, Ill., waiting for the much talked about Ms Adams to appear. Laura Kerr as Adelaide projected the necessary confidence and singing skill onstage, as well as the two-faced arrogance required for her backstage persona. Both sets for these scenes were very beautiful and detailed. There was a nicely surprising moment when Calamity raced up onstage to follow Adelaide behind the curtain after the show.

Katie Brown was played by Kristen Magee, a good actress and singer with the right look for the role - not overly glamorous but pretty enough to be mistaken for a 'star'. The dressing room scene between her and Calamity was very well staged, and we were drawn into the fiction of her going to Deadwood and knocking them dead. As it happens, her first appearance is less than convincing: Magee's 'bad singing' is comically bad indeed, but of course picks up when she's given a chance to perform in her own right. The purple satin stage costumes for Katie and the Golden Garter girls were lovely in this.

And transformations continued as Katie and Calamity fixed up her cabin with A Woman's Touch, including a suddenly anachronistic touch of a button which turned a plain table into one set for tea, complete with crockery and cake. Bill and Danny's scene of rivalry for Katie's attention was nicely done, funny and well paced. The Black Hills of Dakota was impressively populated by officers and their ladies, beautifully dressed and coiffed.

The dance scene was attractive and spread across the stage, front to back, with a nice busy scene of non-dancers involved in the action of the party. Love You Dearly was very well done and our first chance to hear Paul Masterson sing, a strong and pleasing voice. The harmonies in this were clear and well-balanced. Calamity's fury at seeing Danny and Katie together made for brilliant theatre; it was both frightening and funny to witness her reaction. As she stripped down to her bloomers to rid herself of her feminine trappings, she sang a reprise of Men and at one point addressed it to the Opera House boxes, as if to gain sympathy. Her very real and physical anger does not dissipate until Bill realises that he loves her. His characterisation up to this point has been that of a relatively unemotional man, but his sudden realisation came across as real and telling. Secret Love contained some of the best singing of the show, a song well suited to both of these voices. All that remained was a tying up of loose ends and the small matter of a triple wedding, no big deal to Belfast Operatic, who seem to specialise in big moments. The finale saw a reappearance of the Deadwood Stage, again with Rattlesnake at the reins, a great character in his own right. Various reprises of songs and more attractive choreography left us HigherThan a Hawk, and once again, the audience were happily humming along.

The Abbey, Clane Despite being situated backstage, the orchestra for Clane Musical society's Hello Dolly were totally 'up front' when it came to a bright and punchy brass sound for the overture of this popular show. The Hello Dolly theme is one of the most iconic show tunes in the repertoire and a huge, unrestrained brass sound is the way to approach it. MD Dave McGauran clearly let the band have fun and the sound they returned was worth every note.

The cast came onto the stage in darkness as the overture ended and lights up revealed a great range of actors onstage in costumes of all colours and fabrics. This was the bustle of New York, near to Grand Central Station as a sign onstage indicated. The requisite busy atmosphere isn't hard to achieve on the small Abbey stage, but this opening scene was well staged and the urge to Call on Dolly was irresistible. Fiona White as Dolly Levi was very well cast and carried the responsibility of this role with a sure-footed sense of confidence balanced by a degree of warmth. She was nicely distracted on her entrance and a walking definition of multi-tasking. Her 'conversation' with late husband Ephram was touching and brought a nice sense of shade into an otherwise sunny characterisation. In I Put My Hand In, Dolly sang to the audience, demonstrating her talent for "arranging things" with various combinations of couples. There were dance sequences for two couples in a basic quickstep, with some changing of partners.

Martin Fahy was Horace Vandergelder, played with a strong voice and great grasp of the New Joisey accent. His niece Ermengarde was Pamela Killick, adept at crying and with a good grasp of the style of comedy required in this show. Cornelius (Garrett Cummins) and Barnaby (Colin Hughes) emerged from a trap door in the stage, ostensibly the cellar of Vandergelder's feed store. These two had a great rapport and clarity of purpose in their roles. They paced their dialogue well, and used their voices effectively with good modulation. The difference in the ages of their characters came across well, alongside their unity of purpose where finding adventure in New York is concerned. It takes a Woman was nicely choreographed and involved the men's chorus in some simple but very effective movement. Dolly's arrival onstage at any point across this show had the effect of shifting focus and setting things in motion that usually changed the direction of a scene. Her rapid-fire delivery of lines would slow at just the right moments the pace of dialogue never flagged. Put on Your Sunday Clothes picked up on the energy established in this scene, the vocal beginning with Cornelius. This cast by and large had the ability to sing in character, without losing track of accents or the particular vocal nuances that set each role apart. The children's chorus looked cute and had lovely sweet voices.  This number developed into a full-on chorus piece with singers and instrumentalists vying for our attention. The train journey to New York was portrayed with individuals carrying individual train cars, themselves framed as passengers in the windows.

In New York, Minnie (Alison Brady) addressed her lines while standing in front of Mrs. Molloy's Hat Shop to the audience, a short but telling segment that serves to draw us into the action of this part of the plot. The hat shop itself is nicely conveyed with a few well chosen set pieces including wall lamps, a table and of course, hats on stands. Mrs Irene Molloy was played by Helen Spring, a well-dressed, sweet- voiced actress whose understated approach was just right for this elegant character. Minnie, in contrast, has a high pitched, colourful voice with a hesitant yet nosey manner. Their scene with Cornelius and Barnaby pretending to be there to buy hats was very funny. Also bordering on slapstick were their attempts to use the 'Motherhood March' to escape the shop once Vandergelder arrived. The Dancing scene was underscored with some very nice clarinet music, and the coming and going of various pairs of dancers once Dolly has done her teaching. The changing of the scene around them was very nicely managed and the flow of action into Before the Parade and the Finale was pleasing and seamless. By the time the parade actually arrives onstage, the chorus had established itself as a strong singing unit, managing the juicy harmony of some of the text with flair.

The characters of Mrs. Molloy, Minnie, Cornelius and Barnaby were very well matched in this and had a great rapport. Their choreography in Elegance was smart and precise. That precision carried across to the iconic scene in the Harmonia Gardens with the waiters and Dolly. It was a stroke of genius to cast some women (complete with moustaches) as waiters, and their strict choreography and impassive faces were just the thing to make this number work. There were some very funny cameos by women 'connected' with Horace Vandergelder: a woman in an orange dress during a 'Sweet Rosie O'Grady' crossover, and his date for dinner, the coarse Ms. Money. There was a lovely red white and blue finale to the waiter's number. Hello Dolly was impressive as always expected for this number.

The dance competition was the kind of scene for which the phrase "confusion reigned" was coined, and after the small matter of mixed-up wallets, it metamorphosed nicely into the courtroom, complete with judge, court reporter, policeman, podium and American flag. It Only Takes a Moment created a more intimate atmosphere, spotlighting the emotional core of the story with nice singing from Irene, Cornelius and the chorus. An energetic So Long Dearie plus an amazingly quick change brought us back to Vandergelder's shop, nicely dressed with containers and goods, and an effective soliloquy from Dolly about the nature of money. The finale did, as finales do, bring the story to a happy end, with Dolly and Horace and the other couples joined in a pastiche of numbers from the show. There was a grand atmosphere of joy onstage, a spirit of connection between cast and audience, and above all, a strong sense of just how much of a "wonderful woman" this Dolly turned out to be.

Riverside Theatre standing there, with only one set of eyelashes and sensible heels, I often consider the fact that show folk simply love dressing up.  And let me say, the gang from Portrush really dressed up.  It was 42nd Street, after all.  Set in 1933, the musical is based on Bradford Ropes novel about notorious director Julian Marsh, and his efforts to stage a musical extravaganza during the height of the Great Depression. Well, here we are at the height of a Great Recession, so why not? Back then, the Broadway audience cheered at the sight of the glitz and the glam, so why not the people of Portrush?  Beginning with a competently executed tap number against an impressive set, we meet the writers of the show 'Pretty Lady', Maggie and Bert (Elaine Morrison and Donal Macauley), and the choreographer Andy (Gerald McQuilken).  There was a good buzz achieved and directors John McDowell and Kerry Dunn had some nice touches to enhance the mood, though at times the background action was a little too busy. Enter Peggy Sawyer (Elizabeth Lane), fresh from her small hometown to make it big in New York, but she's too late to audition, and though she attracts the attention of lead man Billy (Leroy Dempster) he can't help her.  'Young and Healthy' was a good number and these two worked well off each other.  The appearance of director Julian Marsh (Paul Loan) sets everyone in a tizzy and there was good opportunity for the chorus to perform here.  Maggie was extremely expressive and a performer with welcome energy, and although she has a super voice, her first song 'In Four: Shadow Waltz' was played for laughs. The star of 'Pretty Lady' is Dorothy Brock, a little past her sell by date, but necessary to draw the crowds.  Una Culkin had the charisma to carry this role and she brought humour and many indignant expressions to it.  Dorothy sings 'Shadow Waltz', unhappy that she must audition for the part - incidentally Aaron Loughrey as Oscar accompanying on the piano was an integral part of this production, though we only ever got to see the back of him; playing was accomplished and singers were well supported throughout. There was solid support too from Musical Director Derek Collins with some fine musicians, in particular brass and woodwind, who are so vital to the music in this show.  A beautifully costumed female chorus join Dorothy for a reprise of the number but she's no dancer and there was some humour here, while choreographer Ditanya Martin had fun with the dance in order to highlight this.  Singing from the group was great.  Director Kerry Dunn was also responsible for the set, which had two levels, used constantly and to good effect. There was room here for Dorothy's dressing room to be left set up on stage right, while the cast would disappear through doors and under the higher level of the set; later, these doors were opened out to become a restaurant, where Peggy, Maggie and the girls, poor as church mice, shared a cup of coffee. First though, they tap danced their way there and back and lo, they realize Peggy's talent.  The banter between the girls was natural and delivered with snappy New York accents - Maggie's particularly proficient.  Julian happens to see Peggy dance and offers her a part in the chorus.  Here we see the early sparks of Julian's feelings for Peggy and although it could never be an acceptable alliance, I thought it was given sensitive direction.  Julian's main focus however is the show and he handled this well.  The choreography of the dance numbers as they are rehearsed was well thought out, and the space was used to maximum effect; strong dancers were usefully employed but everyone had been drilled and I imagine Ms Martin was kept busy teaching untrained dancers to tap so assiduously.  Peggy could dance of course, and her singing too was lovely. Maisie, the diligent company secretary, was played with energy (and a great accent) by Brenda Tosh, and her deference to Julian was always funny.  Dorothy's 'sugar daddy' - or financial backer of the show Abner Dillon, was well portrayed by Robert Blair, while he was oblivious to Dorothy's love for Pat Denning, competently played by William Thompson. 'You're Getting to be a Habit with Me' highlighted Ms Culkin's voice well.  Dorothy could sing, but her dancing and acting left a lot to be desired (the character you understand, not the actress!).  When Peggy fainted during a rehearsal, some members of the audience genuinely got a fright and she was gallantly cared for by Pat, hiding out in Dorothy's dressing room.  Oh, the plot continued to thicken, while stage crew, well managed by stage manager Sean Magee smoothly changed the set.  However, scene changes while a scene is running don't always work and can distract from the mood; the orchestra were underused here and might have covered the changing time nicely - though this remains the director's decision.  That said, I enjoyed 'Getting Out of Town' with Maggie, Bert, Pat and the chorus, and the set was well employed here, with light changes subtly leading into a new scene.  Authentic props enhanced the look also, with old- fashioned suitcases, hatboxes and even a birdcage being carried.  The band, though playing well, was too loud over the dialogue and I really appreciated Maggie's shout of "Quiet!" at this point!  'Dames' with Billy and the men's chorus was nicely put together. Incidentally, there were very few men in this group but by golly, they were put to good use.  No one escaped Ditanya Martin's grilling! Meanwhile, the women came from all corners in fabulous frilly numbers and this built into a visually spectacular scene.  There was a nice moment between Julian and Peggy; he the voice of pessimism against her optimism. 'I Know Now' was beautifully handled by Dorothy in a black glitter dress with silvery lace though not everyone in the chorus was freezing when they should have been and it caused some confusion for me.  A four-part Andrews Sisters style of 'We're in the Money' with Annie, Phyllis, Lorraine (Cathy McColgan, Liz Bottomley, Claire Tannahill) and Peggy along with Billy and the chorus was a great number though there was some difficulty getting on and off stage in places. The band was in great form for this number too.  The act finished with Dorothy singing solo (42nd Street), beautifully lit and gorgeous, it was one of her best numbers.  Catastrophe strikes however, and Peggy bumps into Dorothy, breaking her ankle.

Act two opened with a confident band and depressed company as 'Pretty Lady' would have to be cancelled.  After Annie and the chorus sing 'There's a Sunny Side to Ev'ry Situation' from behind their make up mirrors; an impressive scene with no doubt a lot for Sean Magee (also set construction) and his team to do. Each singer had control over their own lights and switched them on during their solo line; I appreciated the rehearsal time it must have taken to get this right and it was nice to hear some really strong singing from individuals in the chorus. The make up mirror bulbs were the only lights here and I'm not sure it was enough. Cathy McColgan's character Anytime Annie comes into her own from here and Julian is sent off by her to bring Peggy back from the train station, offering her Dorothy's part (and to eat some humble pie, having previously sacked her).  Broad Street Station looked convincing and there was another nice moment between the two while Julian ably sings 'Lullaby of Broadway', with Billy, Annie and chorus joining in. Clarinet really enhanced the mood well here too. It was a lively number and in particular I thought Maggie really added a New York showbiz touch here; she oozed it in her voice and whole demeanor. Some of the main dancers shone here too, and indeed it was one of the finest chorus numbers in the show.  The sequence that followed Peggy rehearsing hard (25 pages, 6 songs & 10 dance numbers in 36 hours) had good drama, though I questioned Peggy doing the lot in her travelling suit. Julian and Peggy's rehearsal kiss was comical and both actors got fun out of the scene.  Dorothy enters in a wheelchair to give some kindly advice to Peggy and 'About a Quarter to Nine' was a beautiful number with solid harmony.  The show begins and 'Shuffle Off to Buffalo' with Annie and Bert as a married couple had energy and humour.  The curtains opened to reveal a train of 'babes' all lined up in their various honeymoon suites.  This train was a bulky piece and had been cleverly concealed under the upper level of the set all along.  Maggie's input with the female chorus here was a good support. Meanwhile, Peggy's opening night nerves were felt by us, as we saw her from the other side of the curtain; '42nd Street' was a super number and Peggy was very comfortable with it.  Army chicks and women in cocktail dresses joined her while Billy brought chemistry to the number. But I had forgotten that Billy gets shot; the gunshot was too loud and it nearly gave me a heart attack (I wasn't the only person to jump either!) I know it's a story within a story but I do think the moment might have had drama if Billy hadn't been carted off in a comical fashion.  Either way, Peggy quickly gets over him and dances on.  The final scene with Julian and Peggy had some chemistry and Julian, happy that the show is a success, but suffering a little unrequited love, ends the show with a fine reprise of 42nd Street, along with a beautifully turned out and vocally strong ensemble.  As a first time director, Kerry Dunne brought a lot to this production, along with the experience of John McDowell and I wish this team well in future endeavors.

Backstage Theatre As I sit here alone in my room, I think I hear the music play; I remember the Cabaret, old chums, I remember the Cabaret… even though it was a month ago now, St. Mel's Musical Society made a bit of a lasting impression with their production of Cabaret. From the glamorously dressed front of house staff to the dancing gorilla in a tutu, there was everything in between. Set in Berlin at the beginning of the 1930's, the story follows American writer Cliff Bradshaw and the time he spends with Sally Bowles, a young English singer at the decadent Kit Kat Club. He befriends Ernst, a German apparently in the smuggling game, who gets him a room in Fraulein Schneider's boarding house. Sally moves in with Cliff, Cliff tries to find inspiration for his novel and the Nazi party gains power.The politics and changing times are reflected in the performances from the Master of Ceremonies (Emcee) at the Kit Kat Club, along with Sally and the Kit Kat Girls. It's a little bit cheeky, a little bit naughty and very well portrayed by Doug Fox Roberts as Emcee; Oozing with charisma, Emcee sings 'Willkommen', full of double entendres and suggestions. Though the audience was a little tentative, they were eventually coerced into seedy nightclub life, where Sally sings 'Don't Tell Mama' - a number that confirms she's no convent girl. Sally, played with confidence by Miriam O'Reilly sang well and carried this role with panache. It helped that Musical Director Fintan Farrelly was in good control of a strong orchestra, albeit positioned above and behind the stage and completely out of sight of the audience. Though I imagine it can't have been easy for either the MD or the singers (there was a small monitor on stage), the sound was great and all singers had been clearly well prepared by Mr. Farrelly, whose support for them was evident. Jim Davey played Cliff, a man who is probably not Sally's normal type; he is naive and sweet, falling for Sally and offering to look after her when she falls pregnant with what could be anyone's child. And that's not all; even Ernst pulls the wool over Cliff's eyes, paying him handsomely for a bit of innocent smuggling, which turns out to be on behalf of the ever strengthening Nazi party. Mr Davey portrayed Cliff convincingly and with an easy natural style, and while there were dramatic moments between Sally and Cliff, there was little chemistry. It didn't take from either performance however, and 'Perfectly Marvellous' was a good number, well sung by both. I also have a feeling they may have actually drunk raw eggs on stage. (The things people will do for art.

Meanwhile, Cliff's landlady Fraulein Schneider (Maureen Dunne) becomes engaged to Herr Schultz (Tony Wadd), an elderly Jewish fruit seller who also rents a room in her house. (The things people will do to pay cheap rent.) There is a lovely relationship between these two and both had aged themselves well, Mr. Wadd in particular aging his character with slow deliberate speech and movement, not to mention excellent make up. The comparison of their various ailments was funny and both duets 'It Couldn't Please me More' and 'Married' were entertaining and well sung.

It turned out, Ernst Ludwig was a rotten sod, a stalwart of the Nazi Party and Jim Maher played him well, at first as an amiable sort of guy, and later as an angry bigot. Fraulein Schneider's sad song 'What Would You Do?' after she has broken off her engagement with Herr Schultz was moving; her fear of the Nazi's causes heartbreak for her and Herr Schultz is forced to move elsewhere. Fraulein Kost, a prostitute and another boarder in the house has a similar transition as Ernst; played by Michelle Kelly Conlon, at first she is quite funny, what with all those sailors she keeps smuggling in and out of her room, and later, she becomes a devoted Nazi herself, singing Tomorrow Belongs to Me', a song with innocent lyrics and sinister undertones.

Through all of this, director and choreographer Leonard Anderson oversaw the convincing portrayal of the progression of darkness that descended on Germany at the close of the 1920's. The easy banter with which characters shared in Act 1, was replaced with fanaticism and fear in Act 2, while things crumbled around everyone. With the ominous presence of the Nazi party and the sense that they're creeping in, there were symbolic touches throughout, particularly in the set design (also Mr Anderson); Cliff's room in the boarding house has lovely red trims here and there - a cushion, the quilt, the edge of his writing table, the trim on Fraulein Schneider's housecoat. By the end of Act 1, anything red came to represent the Nazi party so clearly that from here on in, it became disturbing to see red anywhere; particularly in Fraulein Schneider's kitchen - suggesting that while she considers breaking up with Herr Schultz she is inadvertently supporting the Nazi party. I loved this symbolism, and it made the final moments under a dirty great big swastika all the more sinister. The set itself was clever in design, with some great ideas: many cumbersome items were set out on trolleys, which were easily wheeled in and out by competent stage crew (under the management of SM Eddie Kiernan). The large back wall of the bedroom was filled in beautifully with projection of a repeated pattern, which very convincingly looked like wallpaper; it was a wonderful effect, easy to achieve and I imagine, pretty cheap to produce. Lighting also did much to enhance such scenes. Props were given a lot of attention to detail, especially working lamps and an old style telephone on each table in the nightclub. Costumes were sourced within the group and Veronica Naughton and Joyce Jones produced an overall look that very much suited the tone and mood of the show; the Kit Kat Girls looked great- they were dressed uniformly and with identical black bobbed wigs. Elsewhere costumes were authentically 1920/30's with great attention given to Sally's style. Emcee had some dandy outfits too, appearing in tails, drag, as a Nazi and finally in a striped concentration camp uniform, and his make up was given the clown-without- a-wig look. I really enjoyed Emcee, Mr Fox Roberts was a wonderfully impressive theatrical performer and he played the character with absolute discipline. At times looking on at the antics of others - the protagonists, the Nazi's, the Jews; at times directly involved in some fun and games; at times singing with a gorilla ('If You Could See Her'), at times terribly serious ('I Don't Care'), at times squeezing fun out of high moral standards ('Money Money'). He had great support from the Kit Kat Girls, and in particular from Two Ladies (Laura Walsh and Grainne Fox). Ms O'Reilly as Sally continued to impress and her songs became more engaging. 'Cabaret' really showed her to be a performer of some calibre while 'Maybe This Time' with in red coat tails and a red bowler hat was sensitively treated and emotionally charged.

The second act is very different from the first, and things turn dark and nasty. Cliff is beaten up, Sally has an abortion and won't leave Germany to be with him and the Nazi's move in. The final moments were chilling, with Emcee and the Kit Kat Girls (dressed in striped pajamas) slowly dying, surrounded by smoke and a chorus dressed in red and black. Under the Nazi flag, the final number is sung from a strong chorus.

Sound was great; the balance between orchestra and singers was, dare I say, perfect and sound effects well achieved. Between them, every member of St. Mel's Musical Society produced a show that was respectful, moving, entertaining and thoroughly enjoyable.

Colaiste Brid School I've heard there are strange folk who don't like the show Fiddler on the Roof, but I don't believe they exist.  What's not to like? It has a story some with depth; it has great music; it's got a few decent roles for women…and there are some men who would kill to play Tevye.  It's one of those roles men wait for years to be ripe enough to play. Can you imagine Teddy Quinn's horror then, as a week before the show opened, he completely lost his voice? Not that I would have been aware of that if I hadn't been told.  Mr Quinn was very much in fine voice, though he may have been minding it at times, this being the opening night.  Opening night? What kind of adjudicator attends opening night?! Unfortunately, with half the country's musical societies staging shows in the same month, somewhere along the line, someone was going to get me on opening night.  I was all set to forgive any teething problems, but I have to say director Alan Corcoran and his team had a pretty tight running show.

Mark Redmond and Martin Kirwan's set was striking and very well lit from the opening, with James Dobbs playing the Fiddler atop. Both talented artists, the street scene was realistic and allowed plenty of room for dancing and movement. Teddy Quinn had presence as Tevye, and was soon joined by the rest of the cast in a wonderful traditional dance ('Tradition'). Choreographer Anne Marie Stafford understood the pace and mood of the piece and it was respectfully treated. Everyone was focused and vocally this number was a great mix of diversely sounding voices; a blending of men, women and children along with Tevye and other individual characters.

Rooms were set up on side stage extensions and the rustic touches were really authentic.  The kitchen of the house was expanded onto the stage by the use of some free-standing pieces; a partial wall with a window, and another with a door. These pieces were sturdy and visually impressive.  The side extension had a white washed effect on the wall, with exposed beams and truly authentic props; enamel jugs and pots; silver candlesticks and an oil lamp; baskets of vegetables and a black stove with chopped wood. Bustling around here was Golda, played with natural energy by Teresa Buckley and her five daughters. The youngest Shprinteze was a shared role between Niamh Buttle and Rebecca Morrissey and Bielke was played by Caoimhe Kennedy Ryan.  These children, along with the younger chorus members were highly impressive and adhered to direction really well.  Eldest sister Tzeitel was played with energy by Linda Hynes and 'Matchmaker' along with Hodel (Sinead Doyle) and Chava (Dearbhail Murphy) was delightful, gracefully moved with mops as they did their household chores.  Musical Director Kevin Kennedy's orchestra was in good form, and watched him like a hawk throughout, though I found the pace a little fast and the singers seemed to have trouble keeping up.  However, the pace of the show was good and change of scenes under stage manager Jennifer Daly, were snappy.  Tevye had a good connection with the audience but at times I would have preferred more energy.  That said, 'If I were a Rich Man' was great, sung with control and understanding.  Alan Corcoran employed some nice techniques that worked well and use of lighting enhanced some of the more tender moments. 'The Sabbath Prayer' was reverendly sung with tableaux around the stage, each one with the matriarch leading the proceedings and children kneeling.  Musically it was well handled too and the whole effect was utterly beautiful.  As Lazar Wolf John Crosbie played the older man well and had fun with the lines, getting a lot of personality out of the character. The conversation between Lazar and Tevye was well directed and it had plenty of humour, while in the background, though not distracting, the Russian soldiers were clearly different from the locals; in their mannerisms, in what they drank (vodka of course) and in their guardedness.  'To Life' was jovial, and an easy mix of men celebrating together.  Choreographer Ann Marie Cooney had some lovely ideas, and dancing here was impressive, the mix of cultures appreciated.  A full moon gobo and lanterns hanging outside every house gave a good nighttime effect and the drunken men were funny.  Alan Maher's Constable was suitably authoritative and his relationship with Tevye convincingly warm.  But what of the relationship between Tevye and his wife Golde? Teresa Buckley brought much needed energy to these scenes and she enjoyed a kind of respect from everyone, whether on or off stage. The build up of chemistry between Hodel and the student Perchick (Brendan Redmond) was evident through their argument. I found Mr Redmond to be a consistently giving actor and people reacted well off him.  Tzeitel and the tailor Motel were good together too, and Michael Flynn played the timid and easily shook Motel with good humour; Tevye acted well off this and the children in the audience in particular enjoyed his portrayal. 'Miracle of Miracles' had drama and a sense of fun and good MD support. Costumes were not overly bright, yet they weren't depressingly dull either and the girls were given some nicely patterned outfits. Several departments had fun for the Dream Scene; Tevye and Golde in bed under a shaft of light, were soon joined by a creeping chorus covered in cobwebs, like something out of Corpse Bride.  Make up and costume and a solid performance from Liz Armstrong made Grandma Tzeitel so very enjoyable but most impressive was Fruma Sarah, appearing as if out of nowhere, suspended from above while she swooped dramatically across the stage. 'This is an amateur show!' I reminded myself as Una Murphy, fantastically made up, sang as confidently as if she were on terra firma.  She genuinely looked about ten feet tall and the effect worked; Golde agrees to let Tzeitel marry Motel and Tevye's face, having got his way, was priceless. The relationship between Fyedka and Chava was sweet, and had some chemistry. 'Sunrise Sunset' after an unsure start was beautiful, and as with the earlier ensemble, the mix of voices evoked a little emotion me. Golde sang with control and Tzeitel and Motel reacted tenderly to each other.  The wedding party had a good sense of fun and the Bottle Dance was mightily impressive, while the chorus reactions were genuinely felt, bringing energy to the moment. Rabbi Jim Kealey didn't have much to say, but when he did, he spoke with absolute purpose. His son Mordcha, played by Lorcan Dunne, played the part well and very much stamped a personality to the role.  At Perchik's emotionally charged suggestion, the men and women come together and after a tense moment, the dance of the couples warmed up nicely. The drama when the Russians entered to break up the party was possibly a little high, though Tevye's response was moving.

Act 2 brings a change in mood; things are becoming more serious and the opening set with a (properly used) smoke machine gave an authentic fogginess to the village street scene, while the Entr'acte highlighted each musician's skill.  Tevye's relationship with God was delightfully comfortable, and his "on the other hand" monologues had humour, however I felt that this line in particular wasn't given its full worth; it's a sort of Tevye-ism, and shouldn't be thrown away. As the weather gets colder and the costumes reflect this, Tevye and Golde's song 'Do You Love Me?' was beautifully handled by both actors; he keeps it tender and she is coaxed to do likewise, so that the final moment was really quite sweet. The company showed their ability during the buzz and gossip song 'The Rumour' and matchmaker Yente (Jennifer Byrne) continued her strong role here.

Hodel's beautiful song 'Far from the Home I Love' started a little shakily, though it developed into a lovely little scene between father and daughter.  Tevye's anger was deeply felt when Chava asks for his blessing and both performed well here.  'Little Bird' was beautiful and all three sisters danced with grace while Golde looked fondly on.  The dance with Fyedka brought drama and Chava reflected the awful moment of her father's rejection with sincerity. The wonderful optimism of the villagers was appreciated even when they were forced to leave their homes and this was reflected well in the simple moving pictures that lead the procession.  'Anatevka', was well lit and the presentation of the song was treated with respect.  With one tear-jerker after the next, I was moved when Tevye said 'God be with you' to Chava.  The slow dignified march during 'The Leave Taking' was quite sensitively handled and the final moments, leaving only Tevye and the Fiddler was the only way to end this wonderful production.  Sniff.

Nenagh Arts Centre With the horrors of the Japanese earthquake and tsunami still so fresh and raw, the members of Nenagh Choral Society began their production of Hot Mikado with a moment's silence; the curtains opened enough to show a single candle burning and the announcement that preceded it allowed us enjoy our evening's entertainment once the moment had passed. It was emotional and dignified, yet the moment did pass and there followed a truly engaging show that had the audience laughing and whooping for more.

The set by director Greg Browne worked beautifully - Japanese sliding doors that opened and closed with ease and allowed space on stage as we were treated to a blast of jiving colour during the opening number; some really good dancers were used well, especially the girls, with Stephanie Browne playing Yum Yum's sister Peep Bo standing out. Turned out she was assistant choreographer and that made sense; she carried herself with confidence yet because the cast had clearly been put through their paces, there was a balance on the stage too. Director and choreographer of the show was Stephanie's dad Greg Browne, who also played a terribly camp Koko. Choreography was very creative and between the two Brownes, dances had been very well taught. Direction too was very confident, with everyone adhering to instruction. The grouping of people was always visually good and background acting was natural.

The men's chorus sounded good too in their colourful array of zoot suits and make-up (the female dancers were clad in black suits and took on the more challenging dance steps) and this number really got the audience going. I noticed a varying degree of ages, shapes and sizes of men, and all were well presented. Nanki Poo, played by Paul Shesgreen, proved he had a super voice from the outset, with "A Wandering Minstrel" backed up by a dedicated chorus. Four girls helped established his character well; Nanki Poo was a babe, basically. Pooh Bah, Lord High Everything Else, played by Chairperson Ger McCarthy got off to a good start with "And the Drums Will Crash" which was sung well. The band was an excellent support and Musical Director Laura Kearney was in control of a good set of attentive musicians. The tempo was bang on and brass and woodwind in particular were solid. The men's chorus really played up the campness of Koko's entrance dance for "Behold the Lord high Executioner" and this only enhanced his being in touch with his feminine side. For "I've Got a Little List" Browne went off script to poke some fun at the Kilkenny hurling team, the sports world in general, pretty much all politicians, even Jedward didn't escape. Though this banter is expected, I'm not quite sure how ready the audience was for some of the cheekier jokes, and this was possibly a little offensive to some.

Pish Tush was played with animation by Michael Collins, and there were many humorous numbers between him, Koko and Pooh Bah, and indeed a sort of chemistry that was engaging.

"Three Little Maids" brought us three confident and able performers in the shape of Stephanie Browne (Peep Bo), Alison Sheary (Pitti Sing) and Emily Sheary as Yum Yum. (There were families all over this production; there was another Sheary sister somewhere and as well as the Brownes, there were the Cormacks, the Collins and the McCarthys! Who babysat?! Or perhaps that didn't apply…) Back to the maids; in true Andrew Sisters style, they were diverse vocally and their harmonies were strong- all three sang with animation and danced well. Brass and bass were super for this number. However, there was little convincing chemistry between Nanki Poo and Yum Yum, though Emily Sheary worked hard. Lighting enhanced the mood and "This is What I'll Never Do" was sung well by both performers, with Ms Sheary really bringing jazz and passion to the song.

Pish Tush, Koko and Pooh Bah returned with "I am So Proud" which was supported really well by the band; indeed this number really showed Ms Kearney to be an MD/chorus mistress of some worth; all singers showed an understanding of the shape of the song. Greg Browne's Koko continued to be so very watchable; I was always on the verge of saying "Enough! Too much!" but it never quite got to that point and instead veered off into very funny moments, showing good director's understanding of just how far one can go. The chorus was completely OTT too, but with purpose; it was that kind of show. "Let the Throng Our Joy Advance" (why do these songs have such long titles?) was vibrant and energetic though the chorus was a bit squashed at the back, and there was more than enough room for principals downstage. This great dance number was dramatically interrupted by the entrance of Katisha, a woman scorned (Nanki Poo was supposed to marry her) and her accompanying Elvira type girls; wigs, costumes and make-up really stood out here, but Erica Flanagan as Katisha was outstanding. She used her face so well, all open eyed and scary; she crept in movement, yet she held herself well and sang with one fabulous set of lungs. It was at times like a tennis match; look this way- here's someone with a super voice; look the other way - here's another… Alison Sheary as Pitti Sing did not hold back for "He's Gonna Marry Yum Yum"; a greatly controlled voice with excellent choral support. But, oh! How that wonderful band must have loved accompanying Erica Flanagan; "Hour of Gladness" was simply magic; what an accomplished voice- soft and strong, higher and lower register; it didn't matter. If I drove to Nenagh and heard only this song, I'd go home happy. But there was the enhancement of the background ensemble too, and the slow motion movement of hugging couples. With theatre staff no doubt checking that the roof was still attached, we were at the interval.

Sound was well balanced and the set nicely backlit, highlighting the colours of the Japanese panels. The change in mood with Katisha's entrance was achieved with blue muted tones. In the second act the opaque screens were used well, first silhouetting female shapes, then parting to reveal Yum Yum. The form was equally good here, with dancing continuing to impress; numbers had dramatic shape and dancers were expressive.

"Sun and I" a beautiful song, sung with feeling by Yum Yum was another stand alone number and the actress was comfortable in her skin and in her movement; possibly though, lighting could have gotten involved as she seemed all alone on a big open stage. "Swing a Merry Madrigal" was an ensemble number with four great voices and very little music; the diverse mix of sounds was lovely, before the chorus entered to jazz things up and the sisters left to dress Yum Yum behind the screen; a beautiful image of a bride preparing herself, it was smoothly managed. A tap number - nay, an Irish jig - no, Lord of the Dance…whatever it was, it was fun and it preceded the Mikado's entrance well. Gerry Scanlon as the Mikado handled this song well while the male chorus holding banners adorned the set and an all female chorus brought a full and proper tap dance number to life. I loved the dance and I loved that everyone was so well rehearsed. The Mikado, speaking with a strange mix of Asian and New York - a sort of Japanese Don I guess - was funny, yet he had the air of authority he needed too. Katisha's song "Alone and yet Alive" must have been brilliant; I didn't write, other than to make a note that I was too mesmerized…that voice…those scary eyes…that cool band…Back to the silliness with a bang then, when Pooh Bah, dressed as a giant chicken danced some simple steps to Koko's "Tit Willow". But of course, what woman could resist this kind of attention? Katisha and Koko become an unlikely though very entertaining couple and during "Beauty in the Bellow", to tears of laughter from the audience, Koko strips down to his Superman rigout. The song itself had huge energy, and I tried to take my duties seriously, honest.

The final moments of the show were a little weak in comparison with what had gone before, though the talented cast were all highlighted well; there was perhaps too much going on here dance-wise, given there were a lot of soloists to feature. However, that in no way detracted from what really was a fun and engaging evening, with a full on performance from a dedicated cast.

Island Hall Theatre, Lisburn As I come close to the end of my first year as adjudicator with AIMS, I am reminded again and again of one very simple fact: most people are nice people. At a time when so many are worried or angry, wondering how they got into this mess, and whose fault it is, there is a certain section of the population who just get on with it; who understand the importance of give and take; of realizing dreams; of using musicals as a therapy. Who are these wise and wonderful people? Why, show folk of course. They say the best pop bands are formed during recessions because there is no work and people are compelled to sing about it. What about the unsung heroes of your local musical society? For a measly few bob, you can go see a show and forget your troubles for one night. And that's what the good people of Lisburn did last month (though as with everywhere at the moment, there could always be a few more). In the beautiful Island Hall Theatre, where the group celebrates ten years performing there, I was well looked after by charming Vice Presidents Tom Ekin and Mervyn Algie.

Musical Director Ian Milford's orchestra was very tight and there was a good balance between instruments; percussion was impressive as were strings. In fact all the musicians excelled and the Overture left me in no doubt that singers were in good hands here. The opening number was striking with a full ensemble in purples and mauves, and with great attention to detail; ladies' hair was authentically pinned up, they had jewels over gloves, fans and dance books. Alan Marshall's set gave a look of some opulence and the Baron Zeta (Michael Blair) quickly established his character as the worried Ambassador. 'Pontevedro in Paree' with the diplomat Cascada (Colin Gregg) and the chorus was sung well. Set in the Pontevedrian Embassy in Paris, the Ambassador explains that their country is almost bankrupt and the solution is to ensure that a rich widow - the beautiful Anna Glavari, does not marry a foreigner, but rather keep her money in Pontevedro. A suitor is chosen: the free spirited Danilo who knows nothing of it - though he and Anna are former lovers; allowing the plot to thicken. Distracted with his task, Baron Zeta is blind to his wife Valencienne's flirtations with French officer Camille. Though Danilo and Anna are very much in love, pride and money keep them apart, while there is some comedy and confusion around secret liasons, dangerous flirtations, ladies fans and oblivious husbands.

The easy and humorous banter between Baron Zeta and his secretary Njegus (Roy McIlwrath) was engaging, while Valencienne makes a half-hearted attempt to ward off Camille with the song 'Highly Respectable Wife'. Gareth Brown as Camille has a really great voice, and sang confidently with great control. Claire Campbell as Valencienne also sang well, though was stretched a little in the higher register. It didn't affect the performance however, and these two worked well off each other, highlighting comedic moments from Zeta and Njegus. While the band continued to impress, they were too loud for the Widow's entrance and dialogue was lost. Vivian Shepherd as Anna was striking looking in her black gown, and sang beautifully, though I was a little disappointed that she was not more comfortable in the higher register. 'So Many Men' was enjoyable however and the chorus of male suitors was a good support. Director Wilfie Pyper had a good eye and the groupings of people had shape; particularly given that the men and Anna were dressed in black, each person could be seen clearly. The buzz of excited suitors was palpable and the sense of fun that Anna brought with her was infectious. Mirroring this was the bustle of gleeful women around the flirtatious Danilo, freshly arrived from his favourite haunt Maxims, the rogue. 'You'll Find Me at Maxim's' was confidently sung by Andy Scott playing Danilo, a strong voice well supported by the female chorus. Angela Montgomery's choreography had some nice touches here. The French diplomats (and would be suitors) Cascada and St. Brioche (Tim Pentland) worked well as a comical duo and they had fun while Danilo slept his wild evening off on a nearby sofa. While I appreciate Mr Pyper's use of stylized movement here, there were times when characters connected more with the audience than with each other and I felt the opportunity to build up chemistry was made more difficult for Anna and Danilo because of this. Having said that, 'It Goes to Show' was a delightful number.

The Baron was a consistently funny character, and Mr Blair's comedic timing was excellent, although he was perhaps a little unfocused with lines in places. The Finale ('Ladies Choice') was without doubt Anna's best song; she was confident in her performance and the entire company was in good form; the pace and tempo of the song was difficult and this was well managed by MD Ian Milford and his support here was clear. Choreography suited the mood, with everyone participating and dancing girls used very well. The simple waltz steps were gracefully achieved by the dancing couples and the act finished with us in no doubt that there were in fact, sparks flying between Anna and Danilo.

The second act brought an impressive change of costumes and everyone appeared in traditional Pontevedrian costume, Baltic and peasant in style. There was a bit of a set up for stage manager Andrew Bell and team (also set construction). The scene takes place in the garden of Anna's residence, and 'Vilia' sung by Anna and the ensemble was really beautiful, with some graceful dancing. The music flowed easily and the sound was subtle under the singers. Lighting achieved a soft evening glow amongst the white trellis and greenery. Several small subplots with flirting wives and angry husbands added to the fun and Olga, Sylvia and Praskovia did well pressing all the right buttons (Elaine English, Sharon McGee, Louise Lemon). This led nicely into 'Women! Women! Women!' and the men sang really well here, even when the dance steps did not go quite in sync! Having said that, the choreography was well thought out and a bit of fun with chairs worked really well. A diverse group of eight men, ranging in age and dance ability: I thought it was marvellous - even down to the older gentlemen being carted off in stretchers. Things were getting serious between Camille and Valencienne and Gareth Brown shone during 'Romance'; his voice was so well suited to the music. Wilfie Pyper's direction of the farcical humour in and out of and around the summerhouse was very well achieved; who was in there and with whom? The reaction of everyone was good, given that there was so much deception going on. There were no less than five finale numbers at the end of act 2 and although musically people came in on time, there was some distraction and confusion around the action, not least because lighting was a little hit and miss, missing key reactions.

For Act 3, Anna has her garden turned into an exact replica of Maxim's to fool Danilo, though the biggest change here was in costume and the Grisette's Song with Valencienne and the Dancing Girls had attitude: wonderful dancing; these women had 'can can' personalities and they very much went for it, with no shrinking violets to be seen. Their can can was so much better than the men's and it brought plenty of energy to the final scenes. The 'Merry Widow Waltz' was beautifully paced and gentle and the moment was tender between Anna and Danilo. The final Finale had comedy and plenty of input from a full ensemble. Everyone was focused and, now that Danilo and Anna could marry and all the Pontevedrians were happy it was time to go off into the night, delighted to have experienced a highly respectable group.

Oxmantown Hall placed my faith utterly in old Sat Nav and arrived, calm and collected at the lovely Birr Theatre and Arts Centre, parked right outside the door and received a warm welcome from secretary Fred Boulton. So far; so good. If there were complaints that night about a woman consulting her programme with a bright torch, I'd like to take this opportunity to say it wasn't me; I have evolved into a creature that can write in the dark, nay - write without taking my eyes off the stage. Just as well really, as Birr Stage Guild's performance of Oklahoma! was so very watchable. John O'Donoghue's set was quaint, almost animated in style with exaggerated perspective, which suited the stage space well; it was difficult to tell if the space was small or large until the cast appeared. Space was limited, but well managed with clever choreography and solid direction. Some subtle lighting behind a very rustic fence with wheat (or corn or some such) growing behind it added that authenticity, while bales of hay and other nice touches (an old hand drum washer) filled in the picture well.

The band, under Musical Director Enda O'Connor started off energetically with good tempo and brass in particular sounding good. There were also nice touches by director Paul Norton from the beginning to establish characters. And the characters were so very engaging. Curly, played with confidence by Shane Broderick sang with a strong voice and "Oh What a Beautiful Morning" was indicative of a supportive MD. Barbara Hanamy was convincing as a much older woman in Aunt Eller (though make-up was not) and the onstage relationship between these two set up the tone of the show well. Great vocally, both speaking and in song, I heard every word and the story unfolded well through Ms Hanamy. Laurie, played by Audrey O'Meara, was delightful, appearing in her blonde curls and pretty dress, with a rich and tuneful voice that added much to the scene. Ms O'Meara injected so much personality into the character of Laurie, without overplaying; she was sweetly innocent as she tried to play tough in front of Curly and there was chemistry between the two from the beginning. But again, these magic touches from director Paul Norton did much to enhance the moments; "The Surrey with the Fringe on Top" with Aunt Eller was entertaining in its own right and collaboration with choreographer Julianne McNamara was evident. The appearance of the men's chorus along with Will Parker was entertaining and it was clear that everyone had been given solid guidance. Darragh Molloy was an agreeable Will Parker and sang well during "Kansas City" with solid support from the men. This was a confident chorus, and there was some fancy footwork from Will and the boys - it was refreshing to see men-folk dance so well! Against this backdrop of fun and lightness skulked Jud Fry (Adrian Sheils) and for sure he meant trouble. Man, he was dangerous and Laurie's fear of him was palpable; her soliloquy here was proof that Ms O'Meara's acting skills were as assured as her singing ability; there was genuine presence here. Aileen Quade's hilarious Ado Annie brought trickles of delighted laughter from the audience, sometimes just by her appearance on stage, such was the anticipation of what she might say, and how she might say it. "I Can't Say No" was charming in how it had been guided by director and choreographer; Ado Annie sang and moved with animation, while Laurie, clearly her polar opposite enjoyed the differences between them both. The result was the build up of a lovely atmosphere and further development of the two characters. Ali Hakim (Darren Franks) in a great costume was funny and delivered his great lines with confidence.

The chorus of women and cowboys waltzed comfortably onto the farm and the transition here was smoothly managed. The grouping of the women had visual impact and "Many a New Day" further exposed Laurie's personality while the choral input was great - all capable voices involved. The tempo of the piece was well handled and choreography incorporated all the women with some lovely touches. Later on, "Out of My Dreams" was another example of a fine chorus given plenty of guidance. Michael Donegan played Ado Annie's Pa, Andrew Carnes, showing excellent characterization while having fun with each word, literally, and the facial expression to match. He might have upstaged others, except everyone was able for him and I couldn't help but enjoy this charismatic portrayal. Laurie and Curly continued to delight the audience (I had a little sneak peak around me during "People Will Say We're in Love" and everyone was smiling like a Cheshire cat, myself included.)

Costumes had been given attention too, and everyone looked the part. I loved Laurie's frocks and Ado Annie was suitably decked out in an orange outfit, which entirely suited her personality. I appreciated that stage crew also dressed as cowboys; this brought a continuity to the scenes, which were smoothly struck and re-set, with clever multi use of the opening set to recreate other spaces. Jud Fry's shack was impressive in it's authentic shabbiness and I'm still unsure as to whether the sound of a lone dog barking was outside the theatre or part of the production; either way it really suited the mood as stage crew set up! Jud's character is complex and his history only hinted at. Adrian Shiel's presented his character with layers, so it wasn't just a simple case of disliking Jud; his character evoked some sympathy, while Curly was downright nasty during the scene that preceded "Poor Jud is Dead", which was really well sung by both men, and with strong support from the excellent band; strings in particular really holding the piece together. Sound too was well balanced for the most part and the timing of the gunshots here on cue, while the muffled sound of concerned voices from far off was naturally achieved. Jud, the miserable wretch, squeezed himself further for "Lonely Room", which, while drowned out in places by the band, was sung with great control and emotional charge.

Noisy smoke machines aside, I did get chills from the beginning of the Dream Sequence; dancers, none of whom would look at Laurie gave an eerie presence but were on top form and all done with sultry dead pan faces. The performances of the people involved in this scene were exceptional and I got quite emotional as Laurie was lead off. It was, without doubt superbly executed.

Sarah Jane Cleary was a wonderful Gertie and her laugh unrestrained. Slim, Ike and Cord Elam all performed well, especially later on in Act 2, when there was an opportunity for them to shine. Indeed, the movement and grouping of the entire cast during these scenes had great shape and the reactions were very natural.
