More collaboration between director and choreographer: "The Farmer and the Cowman" had some funny and animated moments and Mel Kennedy as Ike Skidmore sang well along with Donegan's Andrew Carnes. This was a cast that integrated well; the girls' dance mid song was well executed, while the men's part was simpler, cleverly choreographed to ensure everyone looked good. Each person in the cast was highlighted at some point and everyone gave one hundred per cent. No one simply hovering in the background here; this was a very capable, switched on cast. Aunt Eller was in good command of the auction scene and there was a good build up of drama, with some great input from individuals. Comedic timing was well understood by all.

Musically, everyone remained in the steady hands of MD Enda O'Connor, and this allowed wonderful chemistry to build up between Will and Ado Annie. Their scenes were funny, but things had turned darker for Curly and Laurie, though their relationship had intensified, there was still the small matter of Jud Fry to attend to. When Laurie finds herself alone with him, I almost died a death for both of them; she was convincingly terrified while he was cringingly fully forceful - and she really did slap him; I totally appreciated this (though Adrian Shiels may not have!). The drama was all the more disturbing because of the involvement of the actors here. Yet the next scene had humour, (With Will) and chemistry (with Curly) and I thought the balance of moods was really well handled by director Mr Norton. The joy of the new couple as they got engaged after the awfulness of Jud's inappropriate behaviour led neatly into a very funny goodbye between Ado Annie and Ali, with Ms Quade's twitching foot in a starring role here.

The ensemble presentation of "Oklahoma" was fantastic with men twirling girls in the air and solo lines being shared around amongst the chorus. This was Mr Broderick's best number and the band continued in the same strong vein as they had started, full of energy. With beautiful harmonies from the female chorus and with a totally focused cast, this was a wonderful interpretation by both choreographer and MD. The choreographed fight between Curly and Jud was convincing and the scene had drama (though it may have been difficult with one or two members of the audience laughing; I reckon they might have known some of the cast and just couldn't believe it, because there was nothing funny here; the scene was well handled and the reactions of all were good. Tommy Lyndon's Cord Elam performed very well here and helped smooth things out for the young lovers. All's well that ends well, and after a welcome and rousing reprise of "Oklahoma" we were sent out into the night, a hummin' and a buzzin' all the way home. Well done to all involved in this wonderful production, and to Paul Norton, who had, wherever possible, plenty of magic touches.

Belfast Waterfront Studio Thorough : (thuhr-oh) executed without negligence…perfect; thorough enjoyment…extremely attentive to accuracy and detail; having full command or mastery of an art: a thorough actress… Yes…my musings through the dictionary hit the nail pretty much on the head. St Agnes' Musical Society's production of Thoroughly Modern Millie could well be described as having been thoroughly enjoyable with attention to detail. Against the set hired in from Castlerea's recent production, this group very much put their own stamp on the show. The opening number was wonderful, with Jolene O'Hara very much standing out as Millie Dillmount; what a voice! What energy - this performer could fill the stage, even when she was the only one on it. 'Not for the Life of Me' was a fun filled lively number with very much the 1920's touch supported by a strong chorus. Singing was impressive and Chorus Mistress Jacqui Vance had clearly got the best out of her people. Musical Director Mark Dougherty was in command of a good set of musicians, with brass and woodwind standing out, though a little too loud in places.

Costumes were put together well, with the girls in general looking super; each of Millie's friends from the Pricilla Hotel had their own style going on, which helped to distinguish them, while the men looked dapper and well groomed, in a 1920's sort of way. Millie had the pick of the frocks, and as I mentioned the cast backstage, I really think it would be a nice gesture to give one of these to the Adjudicator when she visits…no? Well, if you don't ask… David Thompson played Jimmy Smith, the man about town who eventually falls for Millie, and boy could he sing! The villain of the show, Mrs. Meers, was played with malice by Ditanya Martin, whom I know from her other life as a choreographer and didn't recognize as she was heavily made up to fool everyone into thinking she was a traditional Asian lady. Wonderful make up and comically stylish movement gave Mrs. Meers her villainous look and instant appeal. Millie befriends Miss Dorothy, played by Emma Lundy also dressed most tastefully with matching shoes and gloves for every outfit. Their duet 'How the Other Half Lives' was well sung by both performers and I enjoyed the diversity of the two characters; Millie so innocently thinking she is savvy, a little bit tough and a little bit sassy, while Miss Dorothy was delightfully twee and sweet as candy. Declan Moore's direction was solid and he really got the humour out of the dialogue. As choreographer too, there was a smooth link between scenes and dances, particularly Millie and Miss Dorothy tap dancing on the spot in the lift while the numbers climbed upwards on a screen above (though it was a tad tight in there). Scene changes were smooth, and there was a lot for Clare Donnolly and her team to do, with large pieces to set. The Laundry had a lot of fiddly bits to fix but it was assembled in good time. This is where two unfortunate Chinese brothers, Ching Ho and Bun Foo are kept slave labouring for mean Mrs. Meers, actually a New Yorker when she spoke in her own villainous voice (great accent) and Jon-Paul Bruce and Ruaidhri Maguire performed this comical duo well, with what I considered to be excellent Chinese, though I'm a little rusty so I appreciated the translations on the screen above. Incidentally, Mrs. Meers' evil plan is to find young orphaned women and sell them as slaves.

Millie gets herself a job at Sincere Trust Insurance Company, where she sets her sights on her boss Trevor Graydon; she's not interested in him per se, it's a wealthy husband she's after - part of her cunning plan, as she is such a thoroughly modern girl (well, it was written in the 60's…). The office scenes were highly entertaining with identical secretaries wheeling in at their desks and on the phone; dressed in orange and black, with super wigs and Harry Potter specs, it was a good look. Miss Flannery was played by Nicola Cunningham (who had already played the part of Ethel, an unfortunate victim of Mrs. Meers') and she was wonderfully stereotypical as the staid and grumpy stuck up personal assistant, getting a lot of comedy out of the role. Glenn Branney played Mr. Graydon as a laid back, none too bright but extremely focused on the company type of guy and he did it marvelously; 'The Speed Test' with Millie, Miss Flannery and the girls was a tribute to the performers, MD, band, chorus mistress and director, even before the dance began. Starting slowly and gaining speed this developed into quite the impressive number with tap dancing, orange and black flying bodies and Harry Potter glasses everywhere. All the while Mr. Graydon kept in control and packed his pipe. Wonderful! Back at the Pricilla Hotel, Chung Ho and Bun Foo grapple with their consciences as they are being blackmailed to assist Mrs. Meers in her evil ways in order to bring they poor old mum over from Hong Kong. There followed some comedy with a poisonous apple and Mrs. Meers sang 'They Don't Know' really well, with drama and energy. Lighting here was perfectly sinister too and added to the mood.

The Pricilla Girls, including Millie and Miss Dorothy find themselves in the company of Jimmy and end up in the Speakeasy, wherein we find some really good dancers. The girls were great here, dancing nervously or getting drunk, the scene had drama and was very well pulled together by director Declan Moore, especially given the numbers on stage. Millie kept falling, which was really funny and everyone ended up in the police station after the nightclub is busted. There was a lost opportunity to have members of the chorus shine here, as lighting was off cue and individuals getting their photos taken was not properly highlighted; Jimmy wasn't entirely focused either, possibly distracted by the close proximity of the audience. However, Mr. Thompson was in a different place altogether when he began to sing and 'What do I need with Love' was excellent, with great support from the band - violin and brass in particular standing out.

Muzzy Van Hossmere, classy nightclub singer, invites Jimmy, Millie and Miss Dorothy to a party at her place. Clever direction kept the party lively while not distracting from any conversation that kept us up with the plot so far: basically, Jimmy is falling for Millie, but he's a man about town, and secretly the wealthy step son of Muzzy. Millie is falling for Jimmy, but thinking he's poor, insists on pursuing her boss. Muzzy, played with class by Fiona Keegan, and looking stunning in a fabulous dress, sang 'Only in New York' exceptionally well. She really owned the song and the stage was hers - though the party folk swaying behind her enhanced the scene. Others at the party did well, Dorothy Parker and the Gershwins, although everyone had been given guidance and the style was naturally achieved. Millie finished the act with a most impressive rendition of 'Jimmy' following a great build up of chemistry and a kiss. The band, MD and Millie shone like gold here. In Act 2, Millie is down trodden, and her mood - while appearing to be low, never affected the energy of the scene. 'Forget about the Boy' with Miss Flannery and a super female chorus and nicely synced movement brought all the life back and built up into a rousing number. There was so much going on, what with evil plans and sub plots, and I forgot to mention that Jolene O'Hara was quite the comedienne too, with Millie falling through her desk and in particular acting off Glenn Branney's Mr. Graydon. Time for some really silly stuff and 'Ah! Sweet Mystery of Life' was really well done as Graydon falls for Miss Dorothy while Millie, devastated, looks on. Silhouettes on the back wall and serious coarse acting, the singers were stretched a little for this number, but who cared? It was really very funny. 'I Turned a Corner' sung by Jimmy - from the window ledge, was a difficult song sensitively treated. The humour continued with 'Muqin' a hilarious Chinese version of Al Jolson's 'Mammy' with Mrs. Meers, Ching Ho and Bun Foo.

What a treat it was to have so many hugely talented singers all in one show; Fiona Keegan's richly developed voice impressed me hugely, and 'Long as I'm here with You' was sung with intensity and character. Though at times, Muzzy connected more with the audience than with Millie, her performance was emotional when talking about her deceased husband. Later, she played the part of a young country gal with a fabulously over done accent. 'Gimme Gimme' really allowed Jolene O'Hara to build up into a powerful performance; starting slowly with the tempo gradually getting faster, Millie and the band were a great combination here - this performer really gave her heart and soul to the song.

Finally Mrs. Meers is found out - Miss Dorothy (who had been kidnapped) is rescued by her real true love, Ching Ho, Jimmy and Millie kiss and make up, and poor Mr. Graydon is left out in the cold. There were some fun moments had at the end here but I would really like to know how Miss Dorothy fit into that tiny basket! A huge big Broadway style finale with the full company shining brightly rounded things up nicely. Chinese mum even made an appearance. What fun! St Agnes' Thoroughly Modern Millie = a thoroughly enjoyable experience.

St Mary's College, Arklow "Ooh, look at the ducks!" cooed my friend and guest as we made our way into the theatre at St Mary's College for Avonmore Musical Society's production of The Wedding Singer.  Sure enough, there was a family of ceramic ducks, all lined up between large outdoor lanterns with lighting candles.  "How lovely," I agreed, and wandered into the venue.  It was only as I walked under the arch of flowers that I realized the place was all dickied up for a wedding.  Here and there in the foyer, were such touches and front of house gentlemen in black tie ushered people to their seats, where a large screen played news clips from the 80's.  The band, under Musical Director Mairead McKenna, and in full view above and behind the action on stage was in good form, though the opening song took a while to warm up. When it did however, 'It's Your Wedding Day' developed into a really good number with the chorus displaying those dance steps that make my generation cringe - dear God! Did we really dance that way? Did we actually wear those clothes?!  I myself actually wore the exact same bridesmaid's dress at my sister's wedding, only in a lovely shade of cerise instead of peachy pink.  However this wedding party was only poking fun at the dodgy dance steps and the number worked because it was so perfectly in sync, with a nice solo from the Bride and Groom.  Robbie Hart is lead singer with the wedding band "Simply Wed" along with George, (a Boy George lookalike) and Sammy, (a guitar player with really suspect hair).  Conor Cronin as Robbie handled the role well, speaking to the wedding party with confidence and controlling the drunken Best Man.  Singing was good and he managed the leading man comfortably; at times vulnerable, at times funny, but always likable. This is the show to do if you have a lot of eager and talented people, who want a shot at some very funny cameo roles.  Such was the case with the Avonmore group and the cast was well used: the chorus played a variety of roles (Loser Guy; Cyndi Lauper; Sideburns Lady; Bad Haircut Guy - you get the idea).  Also working at the reception hall is Julia, a sweet and naïve waitress who befriends Robbie and eventually falls in love with him.  But first, Robbie has to get over Linda, a rock n roll chick who dumps him at the altar and plunges him into wonderfully over the top dispair.  Julia is engaged also, to Glen: a scoundrel with an eye for other women, a businessman with a serious money obsession. There was a real half car that was silently and smoothly cruised on and off stage too, which I'm sure was not as easy as it looked for stage manager Barry Ryan.   Julia was sweetly portrayed by Danielle Armstrong and there were some nice moments from early on, especially during the comical song 'Awesome' with Robbie.  Rosie, as Robbie's Grandma was delightfully eccentric, played with total conviction by Naoimh Penston.  Make up deserves a mention here as Naoimh was completely transformed from young woman to elderly New York Gran, complete with a tight grey permanent.  As there were three Penston girls in this production, I'm sure they will forgive me for using their first names.  I loved Grandma Rosie's birds and bees talk with Robbie, full of expression and concentration as she struggled to remember how many men she had slept with in her life.  I loved the comedy in this show, it was brought out well by director Bill Stafford and guidance was given to the performers.

The set was simple and lighting helped achieve other looks, such as a window gobo for the Church - as Robbie waits for Linda, played by Leah Penston.  With crimped hair and a fabulous voice (not to mention some great head banging) I loved this portrayal of 'A Note from Linda', and it bothered me that the audience weren't laughing as much as me; it was a super performance and we all know mid week audiences are far more timid than weekend ones.  Funny yes, but I really want to acknowledge Leah's vocal control here too.

'Pop!' was a fun number too, well sung from the Ladies' toilets by Julia, her mum Angie (Elaine Sweeney) and Holly, Julia's sexy cousin played by Amy Penston.  A strong female chorus and some hairspray also featured in this number.  As expected, this Miss Penston was another strong singer and the differences between Julia and Holly were clear.

'Somebody Kill Me' - Robbie's (ahem) lament from his vibrating bed and whilst holding onto a tiny plastic bride was exactly the sort of jig up this audience needed and the energy that Mr Cronin gave here was super.  George, played by Patrick Bracken was hilarious and really enjoyed his lines, not to mention his moves and camp walk. Jonny Holden's Sammy, also a humorous character was generous in his support of George - someone has to be the butt of the jokes and he played the oblivious friend well.   Robbie's down trodden mood is well reflected during the next wedding we see him play at - remember Sideburns Lady and co?  This scene ended in an excellent Thriller style dance with all the so called 'mutants' at table 9; Choreographer Martina Lynch had good ideas and her dances really poked fun at the 80's; however, in order to have fun, her cast needed first to be able to dance well and this group had been put through their paces, with everyone managing the steps well, and trained dancers highlighted where possible. Bill Stafford directed with a sure hand and there were good on stage relationships between the characters; Robbie and Julia built up some chemistry, though I wasn't always convinced of their closeness.  While Holly spent much of the show rejecting the advances of Sammy, there was fun had between these two and when they finally paired up there was the sense that all was well with the world.  In the meantime, Julia goes ahead with her wedding plans, while Glen gets more and more despicable.  Robbie and his band decide to do Bahmitzva's and the Jewish traditional dance here was really well executed, with excellent input from the band. George's Hebrew version of 'This Much is Love' was like something out of the Eurovision (or possibly the Eurovision of the 1980's…) though he did not try to upstage - it was a good balance and very funny, and a pleasant surprise that Mr Bracken could sing so well too.  Musical accompaniment was consistently good, though too loud at times and voices could be drowned out - as during 'Not that Kind of Thing' with Robbie, Julia and the individual and choral voices of the company.  This was a good number however, it had dramatic shape and was no doubt a collaboration between director and choreographer. This led into a beautiful tender moment between Julia and Robbie and their kiss was beautifully lit.  The first act ended with a super ensemble number led by Holly and 'Saturday Night in the City' had everything going for it, not least of which was the great voice of Amy Penston, with a heavy metal twist. Dancers were excellent too and dressed in some really great 80's gear. The band was on top form and lighting was having fun too.  I loved the clever choreography here, where the chorus as a sort of moving clump in the background kept the energy of the scene going, but didn't distract from any dialogue.  In between, it built up into a frenzy of steamy moments - your typical Saturday night in the disco sort of thing (I imagine).  Holly was very central to this number, not just as a singer, but also perhaps as the person getting most worked up - though why this number always ends with Holly dousing herself in a bucket of water is beyond me: yes I know it's meant to be sexy in a Flashdance sort of way but really, how necessary is it after everything she's already done in this number? Maybe I'm getting old. However, the technique worked well enough, though it did mean the actress came out with wet hair for Act 2. (Bah, humbug!).  Some surprises in Act 2 were that Sammy can dance; he leapt in the air and still looked graceful.  The scene in the bar is funny and 'Single' with Sammy, Robbie, George, Ricky the barman and a bar bum was great.  The dance here was really good; Sammy clearly established himself as a dancer, as did the barman. The Bum, not so much…but take heart Robert Donnelly (chairperson and Bum) the performance was super; everyone sang, rapped, danced and excelled in this hilarious number. Scene changes were smoothly done for the most part (I enjoyed the barman wheeling his own bar off the stage).  Things get worse before they get better for the confused couple and a lovely duet between Robbie and Julia ('If I Told You') was followed by fisticuffs between Glen and Robbie - a convincing punch from Sean Hendley playing Glen - the best I've seen yet this year.  Linda returned to put another spanner in the works and her seductive song 'Let Me Come Home' was an exceptional piece of singing. Movement was nice though a little too graceful for a hussy!  Grandma Rosie's rap and dance with George was a class act - while Robbie ran off to get his girl, with the help of fake Billie Idol, fake President Regan, fake Tina Turner and fake Cindi Lauper.  'Grow Old with You' was a lovely number, really well sung and played, and the moment was tender.  The finale (It's Your Wedding Day) was full of life and colour and the band were in fine fettle. The opening dance was repeated but with more energy (if that were possible) as things ended with Robbie and Julia's own wedding.  Julia looked lovely, though I wasn't so sure about Robbie's peach suit. That's right: peach - good work costumes people!  And well done everyone involved in this very enjoyable production.

St Mary's Secondary School Oz, it is wise to get the Stage Manager on your side; some plamaus them with compliments and pints after the show, while others tip toe silently around them. Nina O'Keeffe however married her SM, which I think is a bit extreme. Granted, they were already married, and by all accounts James O'Keeffe was already devoted to Baldoyle Musical Society (oh, and Nina of course), but I've always been a little scared of stage managers. In fact, they are the only people to whom I would add on "If you don't mind" to the end of a request. They're a rare breed of human, these stage managers; they don't want the limelight and they don't hug; they silently watch the show as it finally comes together and nod silently at you, or stare through you as they contemplate the stupidity of what you are asking. (Perhaps that was just my experience?). Either way, they work hard and according to his wife, James O'Keeffe is among the best in the land! Having designed and built the set as well, I would say many in the Baldoyle group agree. This can't have been an easy show to stage, given the very limited room on stage, and Nina O'Keeffe took extra space from the hall wherever possible, bringing Dorothy up through the audience at the opening and employing this several times throughout. Nicola Pollard played Dorothy and brought energy and vitality to the role. The set, suitably grey against a painted backdrop had some nice touches; the hencoop and water tower, giving an authentic Kansas farmstead look. Aunty Em, played by President of the group (and wardrobe mistress) Maura Worthington was too busy for Dorothy's nonsense while Fergal Sweeney's Uncle Henry was more laid back, with nicely paced dry humour. The three farmhands gave a good indication of their future characters, especially Hunk/Scarecrow in his easy movement. Lighting and gobos were well used and the rainbow was effective. 'Over the Rainbow' after an unsure start developed into a beautiful strong rendition. The band was good, though not always watching Musical Director Dave McGauran, however the sound was tight and change of scene music was lively. Miss Gultch (Bernie Owens) was very intimidating when she appeared, costumed in black and looking spinsterish and downright mean. Toto (Coco) was used very well, considering he was not trained for theatre, and he remained calm and obedient when on stage. Professor Marvel sat cooking outside an impressive caravan before the storm appeared; Dave McGauran's band created a great effect and Catherine McCourt's choreography was quite inspired, with black faceless dancers moving about with giant black pompoms, which was effective; the dance here created well the illusion of a storm, while others brought 'broken' bits of the set across the stage; some had ultra violet colours and as Dorothy was carried across it occurred to me that all of this would have been far more effective if the stage crew had not been on stage and working during it all, though I appreciate the need to set up Munchkinland, which was deliciously bright and colourful. Though no one was credited in the programme with makeup, I am going to wax lyrical about it: make-up was stunning; it was all glitter, colour, false eyelashes and glamour. Costumes were wonderful too; Glinda and her entourage were pink, pink, PINK! With some stylized movement and an expressive face, Lesley Cosgrave's Glinda shone. Dorothy's dress, which had been black and white gingham in the opening scene, was now blue and white and the Munchkins looked fantastic; make up, wigs and brightly coloured outfits, but the real wow was their performances. These children were wonderful; smiling and expressive and extremely articulate. The dance was well executed - these were simple steps but required focus and energy and they had both. Individual lines were very well sung and there was good support from the MD, though it was clear the children had been very well rehearsed. The choreography included everyone and it was heart warming to see the joy these children were getting out of their own input in the show. Isn't this what it's all about? Though Nina O'Keeffe took on an ambitious project with this show, the glint in her eye told me she agrees. Budget and venue constraints meant this production couldn't have dramatic special effects, but then people's creativity was challenged in other ways, and performances were strong because of it. Bernie Owens was a super Wicked Witch, entering dramatically, performing with her whole body; even her hands were expressive. She used her face, she used her voice and she had a mean old laugh. 'If I Only Had a Brain' with Dorothy, Scarecrow and the crows was a good number with strong singing though things could have been louder. The dance was fun and the three crows scene at the end had humour. Stephen Byrne was a comfortable scarecrow, and crucially, his movement was excellent, and while expressive vocally, he tended to speak a little fast, losing some dialogue. While some trees with attitude performed well, I liked also the touch of having some human 'ivy' draped around Tin Man; the ivy girls were disciplined in their stillness while the trees supported Tin Man well for 'If I Only had a Heart'. Anthony Ennis played Tin Man and the dance here was well executed. The trio's anxious walk through the forest was accentuated by sound effects of birds and bats, along with some music, though it was a little loud over dialogue. Along came Lion (Shane Byrne) with a full on performance, accent and sense of fun. 'If I Only Had the Nerve' may have had some shaky moments musically, though the dance was tightly executed. Free standing cut outs of poppies were joined by black clad faceless dancers once more, this time holding giant poppies though the lighting here washed out the effect a little. Singing was super however and the falling snow looked good but was a little noisy. The dancing snowflakes looked gorgeous with their white wigs and blue lips.

There was a great big Hollywood sound for the entr'acte and the gate into the Emerald City looked ornate, if a little unstable. Karl Hoffman as the Gate Keeper was funny; he performed with energy and used his voice well and this lead nicely into 'Merry Old Land of Oz'. As expected at this stage, costumes and make up were stunning and between the band and the dancing there was a great 'Oz-ness' about the place. Stage manager James O'Keeffe donned a green coat tails to adjust a set, which was a nice touch. Aunt Em and Uncle Henry, in their alter egos as a welcoming committee were a pleasant surprise, while the Gate Keeper continued to keep the energy up and hold his own for this lively number, and the chorus and band were absolutely brilliant. 'King of the Forest' was sung well by Lion, with good support from his friends, though the pace may have been rushed here. While the main Emerald City set was quite clever and imposing given the actual space involved, the Wizard's quarters were disappointing; though some reverb over the Wizard's voice sounded great, visually there was nothing imposing other than a shiny green curtain and the cast seemed unsure as to where they were meant to focus. Michael Hurly as the Wizard spoke in an intimidating tone however. The Winkies wore green expressionless masks (except for Winkie General Paul Davitt, as he had lines to say), which was an interesting touch. Shauna McCourt as Nikko, the leader of the monkeys gave a good performance, though she had no actual dialogue. 'The Jitterbug' was an ensemble effort, with Dorothy singing well and the orchestra in fine form; keyboards were solid and clarinet excellent, with a nice mellow sound from bass. Very 'bug' looking Jitterbugs moved brilliantly while drums and brass took this number up a notch - great work from Dave McGauran.

I'm not a fan of crew on stage during a scene; I know it works sometimes, but very often a good moment can be lost, no matter how gently the crew set up. While Dorothy cried tears of fear and regret, this genuinely emotional scene was compromised because of stage crew right next to her. However, the drama continued when Dorothy threw a bucket of 'water' (glitter - and a sufficient amount for it to be effective), and the witch melted into the floor.

Later the Emerald curtain was giving trouble and pressure of the stage crew took from the drama somewhat - though this may well have been a problem only on the night I attended. However, it would have helped if the change of scene music continued to play until things were ready. While the Wizard brought some comfortable humour to the role and the jolly old people of Oz flooded onto the stage I was impressed with the group's chairman Alan Whyte's juggling skills! While the journey home had less drama, Dorothy got there in the end. What a huge undertaking and thoroughly enjoyable show this was. Well done to all the enthusiastic cast, young and old, and to the dedicated production team.

Millennium Forum If I do nothing else this summer after a year of musicals, I'm going to buy me a pair of sparkly red shoes. I've seen some glamour over the past twelve months and I reckon I deserve it. After all, there was a little girl who came to Londonderry Musical Society's production of the Wizard of Oz dressed as Dorothy; she had sparkly red shoes, and she wasn't even going on stage (though she was acknowledged by the MC, which was nice of them). If she can get away with it, I don't see why I can't. This is possibly the effect the show has on an otherwise balanced person; it's so darned colourful and bright and sparkly. And this Londerderry group was going for the Hollywood Technicolor look, big time. Musical Director Maurice Kelly started things well, with a good full sound from his band and at a steady pace; musicians all seemed in good form, though volume sounded a little low and the audience were slow to settle during the Overture. However, the curtain slowly rose to reveal a striking set of pale wooden fencing against backscreen photos. Dorothy, played by 16 year old Laura Brown had fantastic energy from the outset and Toto (alias Denver) was simply wonderful, though I believe he's a bit of a pro, having done this sort of thing a few times. 'Over the Rainbow' was delightful, and the moment was well lit, with Dorothy on the veranda against the greys of a cloudy sky. Miss Gultch, played by Maxine McAleenon was suitably grumpy, but played the part with physicality too; first time director Deigh Reid created drama around this scene and with so much emotion on stage I was mightily impressed with Toto's calmness. While we all know that Miss Gultch also plays the Witch of the West, in this production, Aunt Em (Susan Keown) also played Glinda, the good witch, while Uncle Henry (David Thomas) played the Emerald City Guard. This kind of casting was clever and didn't waste the talents of the two actors, who would otherwise appear only at the top and tail of the show. Professor Marvel played by Geoff Coke impressed with his strong vocal ability. This scene with Dorothy was sensitively handled, though the storm came on a bit suddenly (or is that the way with twisters?) The storm itself was really a series of images taken directly from the film, with some wind blowing hay about the stage: the music was not nearly loud enough here to build up the drama necessary while the sound levels on Dorothy's mike were too loud - as she was screaming and shouting the high volume was unnecessary and unbalanced; in fact the scene had drama only because of the energy and performance of the actress. Scene changes were smooth and the audience was mightily impressed with the colourful set. Glinda looked and sounded the part, and her song 'Munchkinland' was beautifully handled, to the well controlled end note. Mr. Reid handled the large numbers here very well and the children took great direction. Where do these children get their confidence? This group of munchkins looked great and sang superbly - a very tight sound and full marks to MD Maurice Kelly. Vanessa Chapman's choreography with marching and twisting lines showed off all the children well. Individuals such as the Mayor and the Coroner sang confidently with real acting skill. Every child knew exactly what to do and all got a chance to dance. I was particularly impressed with the four girls from the Lullaby League, who, as ballerinas, all danced on points. But all the children were super; The Lollipop Guild, the Braggart, the barrister and all the citizens. Make up, costumes, wigs and headgear were given a lot of attention too. Maxine McAleenon as the Wicked Witch was convincing with her movement and voice and her look was pretty scary too! The sparkler effect as she entered and exited was a good touch. Scene changes continued to be snappily set up, though the slow choice of music for the changes meant there was a dip in the energy and this did affect the pace of the show. Scarecrow (earlier farmhand Hunk) played by David Keown moved well and the choreography here was good, allowing some cavorting and incorporating Dorothy well. Three crows, played by children mimed movements to adult voices (recorded) and this was a little confusing, though the children did well and flapped their wings for a considerably long time! Before rescuing Tin Man, Dorothy and Scarecrow encountered four grumpy trees, played by Addis Blair, Julie Faulkner, Karen Love and Judith O'Hare. I loved their look: long fitted dresses (brown, like a trunk) with huge green bonnets (leafy tops), while they held their red apples aloft in their hands. These women must have had amazing biceps by the end of the run, and they accompanied Dylan Reid's Tin Man well for 'If I Only Had a Heart'. Mr. Reid, at 15 years was one of the youngest Tin Men I've seen, but it was an assured performance; movement was really good and singing super. The band here had very much warmed up and things were good and tight, though I still wanted more volume.

Back screen images, smoke and tree stumps created the forest, while the loud sound of a lion's roar delighted the children in the audience. Kieran Connor as Lion had all the clownish antics and energy this character needed, down to the cowardly laugh. I wondered if this group had employed the services of the Dog Whisperer: Toto (Denver) was central to high drama and was he bovvered? Not at all. 'If I Only Had the Nerve' was fun and I felt Dorothy was far more comfortable during these reprises. Off they went, the four of them to see the wizard, while the audience happily clapped along.

The screen was possibly overused, though it did have innovative moments; the extreme close up of the Wicked Witch's face as she made her 'poppies' spell was a novel idea before the image of a gorgeous poppy field became a backdrop to some equally gorgeous poppy children. Glinda entered with some snowdrop children while snow fell; this was a lovely effect, though the execution of the dance was not quite so tight.

Act 2 brought us to the Emerald City, and it was a festival of green, between freestanding pieces and back screen pictures. David Thomas as the Guard was funny and sang well. 'Merry Old Land of Oz' was a lively number and the choreography tied in with the story well. I enjoyed the drama that Mr. Reid elicited from his cast and the sense of panic when the Wicked Witch flew overhead was convincing. 'King of the Forest' was a full on performance from Mr. Connor's Lion, with solid support from Dorothy, Scarecrow and Tin Man, while the music accompaniment was really strong. The individual performances of the four heroes were great; Lion was very expressive - facially too, even through all the hair and make up. While he was hugely animated in his antics (as is expected), Scarecrow and Tin Man had a natural style and the relationship between all of them was comfortable. Another extreme close up gave a sense of drama and fear for the Wizard of Oz and Geoff Coke did well as I think the vocals might have been separately recorded, or possibly were being spoken live along to pre-recorded film - or indeed the whole thing could have been shot live backstage: it was hard to tell as there was that strong sense of drama that live theatre creates. Either way, it was an expressive delivery and the slight movement behind the wizard's green curtain (from whence he would later be 'discovered') was a nice touch.

Nikko (Andrea McCandless) and her Monkeys moved really well and I loved that they 'flew' off at the witch's command: three or four monkeys jumped up into the arms of the others, who carried them off in flying position - I really appreciate this kind of creative invention, which is totally convincing and costs nothing. Lovely work Vanessa Chapman! Likewise the Spooks; completely clad in black (faces too) they moved gracefully through the forest lifting and dancing with the Jitterbugs and creating the illusion of invisibility. The dance as well as the music really impressed. The Winkies looked good and marching was solid, but the movement in the witch's castle was a little unsure, though the witch melted convincingly into the floor. The final scenes of this wonderful show were not as comfortable as earlier ones and the actors seemed to be under some pressure - particularly I imagine Tin Man, Lion and Scarecrow, who had a super quick costume change to re- appear as farmhands Hickory, Hunk and Zeke. However this was an exceptionally ambitious show for any director, not least a first timer, and this production team should be proud of what was fun, glamour and drama at its very best.

St Joseph's Hall I spent my twenties holidaying in Greece, island hopping and socializing with the locals. I loved the place and would often declare: "I'm a Greek woman, trapped inside the body of an Irish girl!" I know well the whitewashed walls and narrow cobbled streets, the perfection of the blue sky and especially how the sunlight gives a hue that is so very different to home. So it was comforting to see Philippa Alford's set reflecting this; it was all there, down to the paint peeling off the doors. Liam Fitzgerald's lighting design really did seem to take that island sunshine into account and the overall effect was all so very Greek to me. As an added touch, the interior of St Joseph's Hall itself had a similar look, so the audience was cozily enveloped into the story even before the show started. Philippa Alford also directed and used the small stage very well, with at no time any sense of crowding, even when the whole company was on stage; there was shape to the grouping and everyone seemed to stand comfortably and with presence. The ease with which the chorus portrayed babbling villagers too was entertaining, and 'Life Is' with the Leader - a beautiful woman in a hooded red dress (Sharon Murphy), who as a sort of Greek conscience reminded everyone what life is. Gifted vocally, she sang expressively and with strength, while the chorus broke into dance - suddenly lines formed out of apparently random groupings. Brass was strong here as the tempo of the music got faster and the villagers responded in a well executed dance.

The musical Zorba is not done very often, but it should be. It's a show with everything: great music, interesting characters and though the story is simple enough, there are scenes with intense depth, things that actors can really get their teeth stuck into. Paul Laycock played the title role and he was so very comfortable in his own skin, like a Greek man having fun inside the body of a very talented Irish actor. Zorba cannot be tied down and travels around free spirited and easy humoured. He befriends Nico, a young American who has inherited an old mime in Crete, which he plans to reopen. Nico is Zorba's polar opposite, and the actor Peter O'Reilly was happy to play him straight to Mr. Laycock's Zorba; this was a very natural portrayal with comfortable gestures and mannerisms to highlight his spirit. In 'The First Time' Zorba explains his love for life, with solid support from the band, while a male dancer added to the mood. Mr. Laycock really got the best out of his voice; it was completely expressive and full of personality. Once again, the chorus as villagers performed admirably and the story unfolded well through individuals here. 'Top of the Hill' beautifully sung by Leader, Alexis and Loukas (Carmel Voelkin and Lorraine Murphy), three gorgeous voices blending well to entice Zorba towards the house on the hill. With the help of Mimiko (solid performance from James Parkes), Nico and Zorba find lodgings with French woman Hortense, played with almost childlike innocence by Marie Kelly. The chemistry between Zorba and Hortense was immediate and the three-way conversation with Nico was funny. Hortense sings about her glory days as a young beauty and 'No Boom Boom' was full of life and humour. The four Admirals that help illustrate the story of Hortense's having saved Crete from being bombarded added much to the scene and the dance steps were handled well, though not always in sync. Zorba and Hortense retire to her bedroom, while the Admirals sing, Barber Shop style as the scene is set behind them. 'Broken Record' was a celebration of what happens when everyone is at their best; while Zorba seduces Hortense the Admirals stand around the gramophone, as a sort of reminder to Hortense of her former beauty and attractiveness. They provide the music for the gramophone, which slows down and is wound up again; the needle gets stuck and eventually, is broken by Zorba so he can get on with the task in hand. Excellent work from director, MD and Admirals; the rehearsals were definitely worth it and it really enhanced the romance in the room! Meanwhile, Nico has his eye on a young widow, but he's not sure if this liaison would be a good idea. There is chemistry between them too, but the widow is constantly intimidated by the villagers, especially the Mavrodani (Robbie Kennedy) father of Pavli (Philip Darragh), a young mentally unstable boy who is infatuated with her.  'The Butterfly' sung by Nico, the widow, Leader, Alexis and Loukas was most beautifully treated; Peter O'Reilly as Nico sang with feeling and character - indeed all five voices blended together to give a spine chilling moment while the band played subtly behind them. The presence of Leader was strongly felt during this number. Nico sends Zorba away to buy supplies needed to open the mine and before he goes Hortense begs Zorba not to forget her in 'Goodbye Canavaro'. The comic timing here was excellent and sung well by both. Zorba immediately spends all the money on a belly dancer. Choreographer Julie Donnelly got good results out of her dancers here, though their look was more in line with the late 1960's (the show is set in the 1920's). Of course, Crete wouldn't have been at the height of fashion back then, and the background characters looked the part in their fishermen's caps and rough clothes. This was a very talented group and acting - whether featured or in the background was naturally portrayed. Zorba really made his presence felt during 'Grandpapa', and Musical Director Dermot O'Callaghan got a very authentically folkish sound from keyboards and plucking strings and the whole scene was convincing of taverna life (which I would know just a little of.) Scene changes were smooth and quick and it was back to the main street scene where Nico convinced Hortense that Zorba would arrive back with an engagement ring. He said nothing of the sort, but Nico is not able for large shows of emotion and rather than upset Hortense, he tells her what she wants to hear. Hortense was a delightful character, if needy and 'Only Love' was beautifully sung by Ms Kelly with sensitivity and control. Leader returned to sing 'Bend in the Road' while Nico is welcomed into the widow's house. It was a sensitively treated moment, and was witnessed by the unfortunate Pavli, who unable to cope with a broken heart, kills himself.

In Act 2, an excellent choral number confidently led by Nico ('Yassou') celebrates Hortense and Zorba's (forced) engagement. It was a wonderful united sound and everyone was very focused, while there were humorous moments between Zorba and Hortense. It was a scene with plenty of people and lots going on and both director and choreographer did well here. Against a beautiful sunset, Zorba sings 'Woman' and later Leader sang with Nico and the widow for 'Why Can't I Speak'; gorgeous voices, strong and controlled, yet tuneful and tender with the MD in absolute control. All the performers here had presence and though they were the width of the stage away, the chemistry between Nico and the widow(played by Sinead Usher) was palpable.

With the villagers assembled before the mine opening, the hubbub was natural and Zorba's voice was subtly audible before we saw him. The group burst into a spontaneous dance where the stage once again was well used. In the midst of this moment the widow appeared, wearing red. It could only mean trouble and the drama that followed was intense. All actions and fighting were convincing and tragically the widow was stabbed by Mavrodani as retribution for Pavli's death. The actual stabbing was a bit lost here which was a pity following such high emotions. There followed some drama between Zorba and Manolakas before the Priest (Niall Dempsey) calmed things. I really enjoyed this company for their performance skills; time and again this came through from individuals and as a chorus.

Hortense became dangerously ill and her dying scene was intensely dramatic; it could so easily have gone wrong in less able hands. The song here was 'The Crow', sung by Leader, four crows and the whole company. Where do I start with this wonderfully theatrical experience? Hortense lay dying on her bed, in Zorba's arms while four black clad women (crows: Linda Connolly, Maeve Cunningham, Claire Nolan and Linda Tapley) like portenders of death circled her, crying out what each of them would take once Hortense was gone. The villagers sat around the room keeping up a chant throughout the drama; their detached faces only highlighted Zorba's pained expression as he appealed to the crows to wait at least until she was gone. Hortense was frightened and her aggitation was most disturbing. Mr. O'Callaghan's wonderful musicians echoed the chant all the while. Just as it was almost too much to bear Hortense sat up and sang: a song that reminded her of her youth -'Happy Birthday' - it was almost like something from 'Cabaret', though it worked as the Admirals stood motionless at the back. Everyone was extremely focused and it was a fine piece of directing with solid musical direction; Hortense's song was emotionally charged and desperate. A moment after she died, there was frenzied screaming from the ensemble as they removed everything she ever owned from her house; her shoes, her clothes, even her bedspread. Zorba was genuinely heartbroken and Nico was appalled. Out of the intense moment we realize the set has effectively been cleared and Hortense has gone. "Don't judge them", Zorba tells Nico, "the dead have no feelings." In essence though, this is Zorba: he doesn't judge anyone and every moment is experienced as if it were the first time, including the death of Hortense. 'I am Free' said it all; the various moods of the show swinging from humour to sorrow, from high drama to peaceful acceptance. Zorba looks around him, as always at peace, full of presence before he leaves for another adventure.

If your group is looking for something special to stage and you have a highly talented cast you'd like to show off, consider this wonderful show. Kilcock did.

University Concert Hall Limerick University One of the joys of Gilbert and Sullivan shows is undoubtedly that you can 'do' a lot with them. Limerick Musical Society, in their production of The Pirates of Penzance, took this fully to heart, and in the process enjoyed themselves immensely.

An exciting reading of the overture put us all in the right frame of mind to meet the pirates, and they did not disappoint. The band, dressed as pirates, were part of the action, whether they liked it or not, and the clear sense was that they did like it quite a lot. We caught a glimpse of a ship (a clever cutout on a stick) in the middle distance sailing across the expanse of moving water that occupied the middle of the set, and the next thing we knew, the bow of the pirate's vessel appeared at the edge of the 'water'. No matter that there was a momentary malfunction of the landing procedure, the pirates jumped ship and were ready for business.

In addition to a range of pirate 'types' including a wonderful Scottish pirate in a kilt, who later proved himself a great character in his own right across the Pirate scenes. Frederic was a genteel-looking young pirate played by Nigel Dugdale. His popstar-blonde good looks and nice manners offset the rather more earthy charms of his 'old' nursemaid Ruth, a mobile-faced Judy O'Connor. Her ability to tread a line between speech and song, especially when explaining Frederic's pi- rate origins was an asset to this role and allowed for much expressive comedy and general mugging. The Pirate King was Martin McNelis, whose 'been there, done that' demeanour was a nice take on a role which can sometimes be a one- dimensional pirate caricature.

The chorus of girls made their entrance with comically little grace and much commotion. There was a great deal to see in terms of their individual approaches to costume: attired for a day out at the seaside, they were a cacophony of anachronism. Each had a small backpack from a decidedly 20th or 21st century source, with decoration along the lines of Barbie, Hello Kitty and Bob the Builder. Foot wear was similarly amazing, with high-heeled high top sneakers and lace up hiking boots the favoured mode. In keeping with their lines about "homely face and bad complexion" there were freckles and spots galore, and a generally wild demeanour and fashion sense worthy of Princesses Eugenie and Beatrice. Oh Is there not one maiden breast?" was the cause of much swooning and general palpitations on the part of the ladies, especially at Frederick's Elvis impersonation 'cadenza' at the end, complete with curling lip, nervous leg and circling hips. Mabel was played by Jean Wallace, an accomplished singer with a very poised stage presence. Poor Wandering One was beautifully sung, and a cadenza moment with the orchestral flute was a great moment. How beautifully blue..." featured some of the quickest choreography ever, and the return of the Pirates was greeted with general hysteria and much umbrella-wielding.

The Major General Stanley was played by Paul F. Monaghan, who made his entrance in pith helmeted, knee-breech wearing , pink parasol holding, purple-sashed white- uniformed splendour. His upright carriage and clear diction did indeed indicate the person of a modern major general, and his singing about it was great entertainment. Once placed in the position of pleading for his daughter's release from the pirates, he becomes very "Oirish" and he further boosted his argument by revealing his true identity as an "Arfen Boye".

Hail Poetry was a suitably big moment and Act I finished with a clear sense of much more to come.

The Gothic chapel ruin that provided the setting for the beginning of Act II also gave the Major General his sleeping place, in the form of the altar. The sound of owls hooting and other evening noises provided another kind of backdrop to this scene. The Policemen, led by a rhythmically gifted and vocally precise Conor J. Ryan provided a suitably chaotic interlude as they 'went off' to battle the Pirates, though the Major General pointed out that they actually weren't leaving, his exasperation growing. Eventually, "no, but you don't go" became "but dammit, you're still here!". Their eventual return underscored the terrific comic timing of Ryan and the earnestness with which the rest of the police sought to follow him. The paradox discovered by Ruth and the Pirate King made for a very funny three- sided patter song along with Frederic, as did their delight in deciding that it really didn't matter. This was a strong comedic trio, who had tremendous fun with this. With Cat-Like Tread was very funny, and three encores later, it was still quite amusing. The Major-General sang Sighing softly to the river to his teddy bear in a fine tenor voice while remaining in character. The entire finale was boldly staged to maximise the humour in this score, and there were nice anachronistic touches, as when, for the lines about yielding in Queen Victoria's name, a poster of the old Queen herself surrounded by marquee lights was brought in on a stick. The return of Poor wandering one expanded on a bit of funny business that had been in evidence the first time around, the daughters (and now everyone) bouncing as if the ground shook on the extended line "take heart" (ha-ha-ha -ha etc.) As much as anything, the chorus and cast (and crew!) remained strong and characterful through this, secure in individual characterisation and choreography. The final mass nuptials were heralded by Pirates in top hats and girls with bouquets, and such was the good atmosphere in Limerick on the night, I do believe each and every one of us would have stayed on to see the weddings as well.

Pavilion Theatre It's hard to believe that Jesus Christ Superstar is 40 years old this year, but it's true, and Dún Laoghaire Musical Society's production paid tribute to the show's origins with a look that referenced the time of that first performance for costumes, makeup and hair styles.

Twelve cast members were onstage as the audience filed in, creating a feel of the story integrating with those of us about to watch it. The set consisted of a variety of box units painted to resemble a cityscape, piled together in the centre. These were versatile pieces that moved about easily to suggest other places.   As the overture reached the Superstar theme, spotlights turned full to the audience, and the actors left the stage, apart from Judas, Shane Willoughby. Willoughby had the right vocal quality and flexibility for this, and also a physical intensity suggestive of the growing anxiety in the Judas role. Denis Grindel as Jesus Christ had an agile voice and a broad range settled mainly in the tenor. His presence in the role was understated and thoughtful, a human approach that projected a feeling of close connection with other characters; the disciples and Mary Magdalene. She was played by Emily Carroll, a strong actress believable in this role and consistent in her characterisation of Mary Magdalene as a watchful, fearful yet faithful disciple. Caiaphas and the High Priests stood on a section of the central cityscape pyramid that separated and was rolled to the side. Their demeanour and stillness in the scene spoke of their position, and the voices were solid, with clear diction and good intonation. Philip Emmet as Caiaphas projected his rough, gravelly notes quite well and managed to keep the text to the fore. When singing in this range became problematic, he adopted a kind of 'sprechstimme' approach, speaking in rhythm and approximating rather than projecting pitch. Derek Scott as Annas had a tremendous voice and presence in this important segment of the work which established the machinations of the state in the story. Hugh Beckett, Barry Dignam and Denis Sherlock as the Priests added muscle and gravitas to this gathering, and the scene was held tightly together by MD Dermot O'Callaghan. His assembled band were well-drilled and coped with the relentless nature of this score admirably. There was some nice ornamentation, especially from lead guitar, and the presence of a violin brought some nice colour to the sound generally.

The tempo of Hosanna was fine, and the quality of choral singing good generally. There was a confidence and enthusiasm to the sound, and tuning stayed centred. Some chorus entered from the back of the theatre and a group of children were presented to Christ, at this point. The changing mood of the crowd was well- portrayed, the text words 'fight' and 'die' given special emphasis.

Movement and dance on this was nicely in unison and an unsettling mood was created by the entrance of troops who were seen off by the crowd, and the way in which Jesus and Mary Magdalene became gradually more ill at ease in their reaction to the crowd.

Simon Zealotes (Eoin Salley) carried the mood forward with a strong, expressive voice, nonetheless rebuked by Jesus whose falsetto at this point came into full play. My Poor Jerusalem was set with atmospheric lights and dry ice effects. Pilate's Dream introduced Paul Healy, a rich-voiced Pilate with a great presence. His acting of this song was compelling and a strong dramatic moment in the show. Both The Temple and The Lepers were strongly staged chorus numbers, the set divided into three pyramids. There was a great contrast between the bacchanalian aspects of the first scene and the ghoulish momentum of the second.

Mary Magdalene's I Don't Know How to Love Him was wonderfully acted and sung, leading towards an equally compelling series of scenes and ultmately Judas' betrayal of Jesus. His uncertainty and reluctance came across strongly, and the relatively static presence of the priests and chorus helped to frame his obvious agony of indecision.

The Last Supper began organically as the opening of this production had, with the apostles already onstage as the audience re-assembled after the interval. Their denial when asked by Jesus who would betray him was emphatic and genuine, but Judas, whose voice by this time was all but worn away in some quarters of his range, was angry and utterly conflicted. Gethsemane was sung with terrific intensity by Denis Grindel as a Jesus in a scene that was powerful vocally and supported by nice technical detail. The lighting was atmospheric and apt, shining through a slight fog of dry ice, with spotlights turned on the audience as Jesus sings "see how I die". There was extra reverb applied to that word "die" and also the final word "mind".

The shift in mood in the following scenes was total and the pace quickened accordingly as Jesus was arrested, Peter denied him and he's taken before Pilate. Peter was played by Keith Kearns who projected a believable and remorseful disciple, caught as they all were in events that no one could have predicted. As the Hosanna reprise turned vicious by the crowd died down, Herod's dancers took their places.

King Herod's Song had the look of a particularly ingenious pantomime, and Herod himself (Paul Laycock) popped out of the tallest of the boxes that had been indicating a skyline and other platforms in the set. The lid of this was lined with quilted satin, and he was flanked by dancing girls with great facial expressions, all tap dancers. The combination of attractive dance moves and Herod's jack- in-the-box appearance was both cute and quite horrifying - an unnerving number that had great impact.

The scene of Judas' utter devastation at what he's done was powerfully sung, parts of this in a thrilling falsetto voice. He took his tie off, wrapped around his neck and as the chorus assembled in front, jumped from a platform at the back.

The Mob scene took shape and Pilate counted out the 39 lashes to Christ, each one administered by the crowd, some of them smearing him with 'blood'. Judas' 'return' to taunt Jesus with the title song was accompanied by the women's chorus, whose unison singing had a riveting purity of sound.

The scene of the crucifixion had Jesus fixed to a stylised cross that resembled a stained glass window, its fragmented panes lit blood red from behind. The last words from the cross were delivered to a tableau of mourners at his feet. This powerful symbol, the fragmented cross, remained centre stage after Jesus' body had been taken away, still lit, but drained of colour as the band played out with one more reprise of the Superstar theme.

White Memorial Theatre The idea of a 'traditional' interpretation of Jesus Christ Superstar is a rather impossible one, given the contemporary language of the libretto and the very concept of creating a rock opera from this story, of all stories. However, Clonmel Musical Society managed to create an historical 'look' for this show with a very detailed set and costumes based on the type of clothing worn in the time of Jesus Christ.

The story began with the overture, with a cross projected on a scrim and then what appeared to be a book projected there as well. This turned out to be an actual large book behind the scrim, quite probably the New Testament, a page of which turned by itself as we watched, revealing a picture of the crucifixion. The arrangement of flat areas, raised levels, doorways, windows, columns, steps palm trees and arches on stage was augmented by two arms of well-trimmed scaffold walkways reaching along the walls of the White Memorial Theatre, and it was from one of these that Judas, played by Diarmuid Vaughn sang his opening number Heaven on Their Minds. During this, we saw what appeared to be a re- construction of the story of Jesus (Ian Purcell) raising Lazarus. Afterwards, a tableau of Jesus surrounded by children and other followers underscored the biblically-driven visual interpretations of this production.

Vaughn's Judas was relentlessly intense, an archetypal outsider seemingly hell-bent on self destruction. Purcell brought an otherworldly quality to his Jesus, a Christ who viewed his destiny with fatalistic serenity.

Caiaphas was sung by Derek Ryan, whose voice was seemingly made for this role, accompanied by Annas, played by Dairmuid Bolger, singing this an octave lower than the traditional high tenor. Both actors conveyed the kind of absolute certainty in their own power and position required for these roles. Their robes and tall headdresses added to the illusion of grandeur established already by fine voices and regal bearing. The other priests (George Barry, Eoin Morissey and Keith Greene) brought a nice balance of stillness on stage and later by dynamic singing. The chorus likewise had good energy when singing, even at points when there was limited movement, as when they were ranged along the scaffolding areas to the side.

Mary Magdalene was played by Aine Hennessy, a quiet presence onstage with a distinctive, agile voice. The singing voice of Jesus was shot through with blues inflections and emotional edginess.

Direction of this show continued to reference specific biblical elements, as the use of palm branches for Hosanna. Another consistent element was the creation of pictures onstage, as the earlier vision of Jesus and the children and an effective tableau of the High Priests at the end of This Jesus Must Die.

Despite the traditional dress of this production, choreography was contemporary to the music, with movements for dancers reminiscent of the 70's and freestyle dancing for the remainder of the chorus for numbers like Simon Zealotes.

Simon Zealotes was Patrick Morrisey whose singing voice was strong, a contrast to the occasionally half-whispered Poor Jerusalem, which also made use of Purcell's flexible falsetto. Another strong vocal presence was David Hughes as Pontius Pilate. His quiet and focussed telling of the Dream was a very compelling point in the story.

Jesus' clearing of The Temple was observed by the Priests, and was a powerful scene, as for very different reasons was the scene that followed, with lepers and other afflicted figures in ragged robes. In both scenes the chorus players brought a great deal of intensity to the stage, negotiating the very different emotional atmospheres, which in turn were reflected in magnified form by Jesus. I Don't Know How to Love Him was a moment of a different sort of intensity, sung by Aine Hennessy as Mary Magdalene. Her voice has a decorative edge to it like that of a traditional singer, and her interpretation captured fully the fear described in the lyric.

The end of Act I focussed on the intractability of Caiaphas, Annas and the Priests and the unexpected vulnerability of Judas which is the signature surprise of Superstar. This production spent time on this moment, and the musical balance and dramatic intensity of the impassive Priests and Judas, who is beyond all hope now, made for powerful theatre.

In the Last Supper, this production stressed the confusion of the disciples as Jesus expresses the meal in terms of his body and blood. The flow of the scene worked very well, with the disciples nearest Jesus listening and intent, and those further away simply enjoying the occasion. The age spread of these actors was contrary to our preconceptions of the disciples all as young men, but in fact this was probably a more accurate reflection. Gethsemane, the great turning point of Superstar, placed Purcell as Jesus centre stage, and his delivery of this anguished movement was passionate. The sneering of the crowd had a changed vocal quality that underscored the change that has taken place in their role in the story. Peter and his denial was sung with great emotional intensity by Gerry Cunningham. Keith Greene as King Herod in a zoot suit and bowler hat was ensconced in an office with seven saucy secretaries and their typewriters. Their swivel chairs were put to amazingly good use and the cheek of this scene was mesmerising. We seemed to be in some kind of foreign exchange bureau, with men at the back, stripped to the waist, also in bowler hats and holding up score cards. A clever cameo was provided by a jump-suited window cleaner at the back. The mayhem was short lived, and Herod ended the scene with a black hood on his head, aiming two hand guns at Jesus.

The return to 'reality' carried the story closer to its conclusion with detail that emphasised points of the story with subtlety and power. Could we start again was staged with candle light spread from the disciples to the chorus, a powerful evocation of Pentecost. The death of Judas was performed with the sung preamble delivered in such a way that this character's despair could have only one conclusion, and the staging of his hanging, grisly and inevitable, was followed by the sound of the creaking of the rope as it swung.

The staging of scenes became inevitably more busy, with the Priests, Pilate and the trial scene ever louder and more rhythmic. The whipping of Jesus was divided by a freeze after nine strokes by a guard, and resumed at 31 of the 39 strokes. Superstar with Judas and the angels in white togas was a busy scene and visually anachronistic with the funky dancing a strange contrast to the formality of the Greek look of the costumes.

The carrying of the cross and the nailing of Jesus to it was punctuated by an evocation of the Veronica's veil story and the contrast between his grief-stricken followers and the taunting, jeering crowd. The chorus, as the crowd, has undergone a complete transformation and are now a bloodthirsty mob. As the scene progresses (and again time was taken here to allow the drama to breathe) the rabble gradually turn away, affected by Christ's words from the cross. Some begin to weep, most leave the stage. Gradually, only the sound of Jesus' rasping breath and the sobs of the few at his feet were left. Following his death, Mary his mother kissed his feet and was led away, the audience left 'alone' with the crucified Christ. John 19:41, played as a kind of postlude and a text was voiced by Jesus with the words "I came not to judge the world, but to save the world".

Watergate Theatre Kilkenny Musical Society's production was distinguished by a stylish set and good technical design. The opening song, The Song of a Hired Man, was set against a dramatic sky, and introduced the set, a gentle hill running left to right across the stage which served throughout the show to indicate aspect of every scene. It created good interest and enabled the kind of simple but dramatic gestures that distinguished chorus movement in this song. The first group of singers entered stage right and walked up the slope - a basic movement which nonetheless was powerful in context. This is the kind of expansive scene - scenes with depth and resonance - that Kilkenny's staging of this show managed particularly well.

John Tallentire was played by Kevin Reade, whose singing voice was expressive and clear. His steady presence as the hired man who does whatever it takes to feed his family was consistent throughout the show and provided an anchor against which other plot activity pulled. Pennington, the man who hires John, was Fergus Heffernan. John's brothers Issac and Seth were Fergal Miller and Ciaran Dunphy, respectively. They were well cast as two differing characters who nonetheless are tied to the action and provide alternative stories against which John's situation is set. Jackson Pennington, the son of the hiring farmer was played by Matt Berry. He is another confident performer, well cast and with the right look and voice for this pivotal part. Emily Tallentine was Rebecca Murphy, a good actress with a pleasant singing voice.

The fatal moment of Emily and Jackson's conversation following the wrestling match was well done - understated but with a feel to it of much to come. Her conversation with Sally (Nicola Brennan) was well- acted and hinted at both her confusion and attraction. His visit to her house put a seal on their future relationship in an understated way that accommodates both her reluctance and a feel for the inevitable course of events.

One strength of the cast of The Hired Man was their facility for accents and the consistency of this aspect of the production. There were also some very nicely modulated speaking voices (Issac, Emily) and solid singing also. Music was especially well integrated into the play by good use of lighting, as when in Get Up and Go Lad, the lighting changed on the last note.

In more intimate scenes, a focussed atmosphere was created and as emotions heighten, so does the musical content. Emily and Jackson's relationship and John's uncertainty in the face of this betrayal were well conveyed, as was the communities condemnation of Emily, but there were lighter moments too, such as the scene in the pub the night before Jackson leaves.

Kevina Cody was May Tallentine, another very good actress with a good grasp of her role at this point of a carefree child far removed from the pain and conflict of 16 years ago. John Treacy played her brother John, another pivotal role into which he grew as this act progressed.

Significant moments in this act were well staged and in particular the conflict and tension of the Union Meeting in which we see that Seth has come into his own in his role as union representative The War scene was another very powerfully staged portrayal of the real horrors of this other type of conflict, and the sloping hill became an effective battle ground with the addition of sections of barriers and barbed wire and excellent sound and lighting effects.

The moment of Harry's death was chilling and sudden, and his song 'from the grave' is haunting and wreathed in smoke.

John and Emily's relationship was beautifully conveyed throughout this play, especially in the later scenes, when they have come to terms with their history. The scene of the mine collapse was imaginatively staged, especially in terms of the way the set was able to convey the confined space in which the miners, including John, were trapped. Emily's death, as John is rescued, was played quietly and May's stillness in this scene conveyed a world of emotion.

The closing chorus with a complicated ostinato-like structure was well sung and held together. Kilkenny Musical Society took great care with this powerful story, and were rewarded with a production that balanced emotional power with historical

GAA Social Centre, Clara With a title like "Curtains" Clara Musical Society's recent offering might have been mistaken for a show about window treatments. As it happens, this was 'whodunnit' with a difference, mixing music with crime drama and coming up with a good evening's nostalgic entertainment.

The show's overture had a great Big Band sound, and we in the audience had a few moments to settle in our seats before realising that we were witnessing the finale (Wide Open Spaces) of another show called "Robbin' Hood, a musical of the Wild West". Our viewpoint was from backstage, a clever perspective that allowed us to see the conductor of Robbin' Hood and the audience behind him.  This was clearly a kitschy show in which the Maid Marion character was played by a Very Bad Actress called Jessica Cranshaw. Her sudden death by poisoning is the shocking event that is the catalyst for the "real" show Curtains. The comedy of Curtains lies in its irreverent take on just about everything that happens, so the death of Jessica Cranshaw, extravagantly played as tone deaf and clueless by Niamh Sammon, is viewed by the Robbin' Hood company as not necessarily a bad thing. The show's composer Aaron Fox (Eoghan Fingleton), lyricist Georgia Hendricks (Sandra Mulvehill) co-producer (Carmen Bernstein) Amanda Cunningham and financial backer Oscar Shapiro (Wayne Handy) were all strong characters, with a nice feel for ensemble and deadpan comic delivery. They looked in vain for good reviews of the show in the papers, and also for any reason that someone would become a critic in What Kind of Man. The twist came when they spotted a good review, and the song became a hymn in praise of critics. Christopher Belling, an outrageously light- on-his-feet theatre director, was played by James Paradise. His constantly busy, fussy demeanour was comic in itself, and his every appearance was an example to 'luvvies' everywhere.

Nigel Sammon and Johnny Harmon the stage manager was terrifically deadpan throughout, his 'New Joisey' accent consistent and his movements laconic. The decision to replace Jessica with Georgia has repercussions among cast members for whom the pecking order of understudy to understudy is important. Niki Harris, understudy to Jessica was played by Sinead Handy, whose good consistent American accent and strong singing voice made her leading lady material for sure. Another woman waiting in the wings was Bambi Bernet, played by Karen Minnock, an able singer and dancer who was engaging as someone who also has her eyes on the bright lights of stardom.

Among the thespians was also Stephen Rabbette as Bobby Pepper, choreographer and actor, and new love interest of Georgia. Rabbette was handsome and believable in this role of a song-and-dance man with an eye for the ladies.

Thinking of Him caused Georgia, Bobby and Aaron to think about their relationships and The Woman's Dead was an opportunity for individual voices from the cast to come out of the choral texture. The show's central character was detective Lieutenant Frank Cioffi, the policeman investigating the murder, played by Malcolm Whelan. His understated approach was engaging, and he had a facility for mixing speech and song. Show People was a nice big number that summed up one of the overarching philosophies of this musical, the idea that this special breed of folks involved in the theatre are different from the rest of the world, and as such, have to stay with the show. In this, Amanda Cunningham proved that she was not only perfectly cast as the tough-talking and funny Carmen Bernstein but she has a strong belt-y voice and is a great mover.

Sid Bernstein was Tommy Scanlon, whose tenure in this short role established him as an able character actor.

The Clara chorus were adept at conveying the predicament of the Robbin' Hood cast, sequestered by Cioffi until he finds the murderer. They are engaged in rehearsals for dance numbers in the Robbin Hood show, and also join in with songs (like Show People) that are part of the 'real' murder plot. The distinction between the two was subtle, but needed to be in place. This "show within a show" dynamic made strong technical demands as well, with props and sets corresponding to the show being rehearsed and also the plot of Curtains itself. Scene changes were instantaneous, and shifts of location and mood conveyed by lighting, subtle for backstage scenes and more focussed for scenes from the show, such as the various versions of the 'new' song In the Same Boat. These were wittily staged and costumed, and the boat props were ingenious.

Simon Cannon as Daryl Grady, the critic, had the right kind of hard-bitten attitude and sure-footed accent for this role, and made the most of his time on stage. Aaron's song I Miss the Music was staged with some nice miming of him playing the piano.

Thataway!, set in a saloon, was 'rehearsed' by the company and provided a rousing end to Act I. There was some attractive movement involving chairs and the choreography generally in this was witty and suggestive, and nicely within reach of the lively Clara dancers. The only thing to mar their mood was the unexpected sight of Sid Bernstein hanging at the back of the stage.

The Man is Dead featured an ingenious lift for Clara's MD and Director Alan Recks, a device that certainly got the audience's full attention. He Did It involved the cast in late-night speculation about the identity of the murderer. Again, this gave chorus members scope to develop their roles in the show, and the triple 'bedroom' setting was comical and worked very well. The singing of the three chorus groups in canon at speed was agile and quite clever. The set-up for It's a Business was well done, with Bambi's pleading to be given a number for her and Bobby and Carmen reacting in a predictably hard-nosed way. The costumes for this were particularly nice, with a great dress for Carmen and brown and black for the male chorus who join her. The Chorography was classic, stylish and very effective.
