Kansasland reached for another extreme, a lively number with colourful costumes from the Wild West, great hairstyles and dance elements including pinwheel formations and other square-dance moves.

Karen Minnock and Stephen Rabbette as Bambi and Bobby are good movers and this number had great momentum.

The growing relationship between Frank and Nicki developed nicely, as did the rekindled romance between Aaron and Georgia. There was a good sense of chemistry between these characters, and the other 'romance' in this story, that of Cioffi's love for the theatre was also nicely and gradually explored. It finally burst into the fantasy sequence A Tough Act to Follow, which was beautifully staged with a curtain of light and two Hollywood- style staircases, complete with chorus in sparkling outfits. The choreography for this was smooth and evocative.

The twists and turns of this plot continued to surprise, including the shooting of Bobby, the murder of stage manager John and the discovery of the identity of the killer. Each of these 'reveals' was well done and supported by good technical production. The scene in which Ciofi's investigation takes him high above the stage was cleverly put together. Another very well-resourced number was the final version of In the same Boat, featuring moving water conveyed by cutouts, two boats, mermaids, river boat gamblers and a paddle steamer.

Complications of the plot not withstanding, this detailed and witty show for all its lightness and melodrama was no small undertaking, and Clara rose to the occasion with a bright and colourful production that conveyed exactly what Show People are all about.

The Solstice Theatre "Thank you for coming to our little fundraiser" was the message from the group (Gaggle? Flock?) of nuns that circulated in the audience of the Solstice Arts Centre, Navan, before St. Mary's Musical Society's production of Nunsense. Indeed, the show really started in the foyer, as various cast members (sister this and sister that) circulated and greeted patrons.

After a "Mount St. Helen's cheer" for the Mother Superior in the theatre (for Nunsense essentially takes the form of a fundraising concert for Mount St. Helen's School), a thoroughly warmed up audience settled in for we knew not what.

The opening number, Nunsense is Habit Forming, helped to establish the decidedly irreverent yet unfailingly affectionate tone of this show that is essentially about all aspects of religious life as seen through the eyes of the Little Sisters of Hoboken, clearly an order with a difference. The purpose of the fundraiser is to help pay for the burials of some of the sisters of the order who were accidentally poisoned by Sister Julia Child of God. They've been put in the convent's freezer until the necessary money can be raised. That explains the title of one of the songs: We've Got to Clean Out the Freezer. Other songs, such as Turn Up the Spotlight, I Just Want to be a Star, and I Could Have Gone to Nashville, speak to the fact that this is a talented and at times frustrated gathering, longing to share their desire to perform with the wider world. Most of the numbers, however, are about the lighter side of religious life. Morning at the Convent, Tackle That Temptation With a Time-Step and Holier Than Thou are examples of this.

One of the secrets of the success of Nunsense is the fact that there really is something inherently funny about nuns doing anything remotely un-nun-like. Straight away, then, the audience, though initially discomfited in the presence of so many 'sisters', were bound to smile, giggle, laugh and finally guffaw loudly at the outrageousness of these holy misfits. Another secret weapon that Navan gleefully deployed was a well-cast community of individuals who clearly relished the chance to misbehave a little, cloaked by the powerful, almost mesmerising effect that a traditional habit has: stealth nuns in all but name.

Sister Mary Regina was Rhona Walsh whose somewhat masculine appearance may or might not have linked 'her' in another life to the actor formerly known as Ronan Walsh. As Mother Superior to the Little Sisters of Hoboken, it fell to 'her' to shepherd that funny little flock, and fend off the petty jealousies that arise inevitably due to 'her' exalted position. Walsh clearly relished this opportunity to test his vocation, and negotiate the vagaries of leadership. Sister MR's finest moment had to be when 'she' confiscated a contraband bottle of 'Rush' (a drug, not the Musical Society), sniffed it and went on a 'trip' while under the influence. As well as laughing uncontrollably, there were passing references to Free Willy and Michelle de Bruin. (Don't ask).

Sister Hubert, mistress of novices was Catríonna Mongey. Her singing voice was a strong asset to the show, with a strong blues edge to Holier than Thou and good rhythmic spirit in Tackle That Temptation With a Time Step.

Sister Robert Anne was a tough-talking Brooklyn nun from a disadvantaged background. Played by Jane Wardick, she was a brilliant character, a stand- out in this admittedly eclectic bunch. Her Playing Second Fiddle, a patter song about being 'second-in-command' in the convent, established her frustrations, and I Just want to be a Star confirmed her ambitions.

Sister Amnesia was the nun with no memory, found by the Sisters and taken in until the day that she remembers who she is. Carol O'Toole played this role with a serene vacant-ness, as enthusiastic about her vocation as a nun could be, she warmed up the crowd with terrible nun jokes and an inane quiz peppered with funny ad libs and wicked religious references. One Quiz prize was a magnetic St. Francis of "a sissy" medal, and the winner was instructed to "stick it anywhere you like". One of her finest moments came with So You Want to Be a Nun, performed a decidedly ventriloquist puppet, in a 'good nun, bad nun' routine. This also referenced music such as Gershwin's Summertime and the 'Queen of the Night' aria from Magic Flute.

Sister Leo was Janet McElroy, a beautiful nun with an ambition to be a ballerina that was somewhat at odds with her vocation. She's a sweet singer and a good dancer, with a serene demeanour onstage that was uncannily nun-like.

Sister Julia, Child of God was the convent's cook, whose 'mistake' cost so mant sisters their lives, necessitating the Nunsense fundraiser. Sister Julia's Cooking Class was exactly what you'd expect from a cook who approaches pressed duck with an ironing board and iron. This was a funny scene between sisters Julia, Amnesia, Hubert and Wilhelm, a bit of slapstick centred around the cookbook 'Baking with the BVM' and also a recipe for Barbeque Ribs St. Joan. The height of hilarity was achieved just before this, with a 'Come Dancing' spoof that transfigured itself into a wildly entertaining bit of Irish dancing. Again, what could possibly be funnier than a hornpipe in a habit?

The set for Nunsense was done up as for a production of Grease by the pupils of Mount St. Helen's School as the 'nuns' were only borrowing it for their show. The band were also nuns (or were they only dressed as nuns?), and were onstage for the show, towards the back of the stage. The Musical Director was Jacqui McGowan, or should I say Sister Jacqui McGowan?

The beauty of this particular show for the average society is that it accommodates the fact that it can be difficult to coax men into a musical society. St. Mary's, however, did have a number of men involved , including Fr. Virgil (David Monaghan) and a number of brothers, all of whom added a sobering presence and no doubt kept the nuns from getting too wild.

The finale of the show was another chorus of Nunsense Is Habit Forming and by this point in the evening, there was absolutely no argument to that.

O'Reilly Theatre My Fair Lady tends to appear near the middle of most books that chronicle the history of musical theatre, and it hardly seems possible that it is 55 years since it's first performances. Teacher's Musical Society's production took on board the significance of the piece and the reasons behind the show's long popularity, which lie in music that appeals and resonates, sparkling dialogue and great characters. Setting was also strong element in this production, and the opening scene in Covent Garden was beautifully portrayed. Eliza Doolittle was Aisling McCormick, an understated cockney with an open attractive voice and look for this role. Rory Robinson as Higgins had an actor's agility with text and combined this and singing with the requisite ease. Justin Parkes was a vigorous and funny Pickering. The chorus scenes throughout this MFL always had interest and pace, and a sense of individuals onstage, harking back to the theatre piece on which it is based.

There was an easy appropriateness in the choreography, a rhythmic sensibility that worked very well. The choral sound was pleasant and well amplified. Doolittle was Paul Mescal, and his interpretation negotiated the inherent complexity of Doolittle with some flair. His first appearance with two mates involved a nice bit of theatre as the pub landlord refuses them entry until he sees the money that Eliza has given him. His portrayal of a man that has had a little too much to drink was measured and colourful.

The scene change to Higgins' house was very swiftly done and the appearance of his room was very complete and detailed. Higgins and Pickering both looked the part, comfortable and gentlemanly. Mrs Pierce was played with marvellous imperiousness by Helen Killeen: a match for Higgins by any measure. This characterisation let us know clearly who really ran that unorthodox household, and made much of what is so often a very minor role. Eliza arrived in what was clearly her best outfit, ready to take on the world and the transition across the scene in which she is drawn into the Higgins/Pickering 'experiment' was very well done.

There was a nice bit of non-verbal communication between Higgins and Pickering when he recorded Eliza's speech, a 'nod and wink' that explains for us later why he has her voice on a cylinder, even though he already indicated that he has enough of the Lissom Grove dialect. Higgins' Let a Woman in Your Life was nicely paced as he became more agitated as the song went on.

Doolittle's Little Bit of Luck was rhythmic and note-perfect, supported by a well- drilled chorus and witty choreography closely tied to the text of the song. There was great projection of character from the chorus and good connection between them and the action of principals. Doolittle carried the energy of his portrayal to Higgins' house, with well-paced dialogue and sense of timing.

Eliza's trials came across well, as did the servants' indulgence of Poor Professor Higgins. The 'moment of revelation' that precedes The Rain in Spain was sensitively and believably done, Higgin's taking Eliza's hand as he explains the purpose of all their hard work and she is transfixed. Her beautifully modulated speaking voice was finally released and that excitement carried through I Could Have Danced All Night.

Eliza's progress into society continued with a wonderful looking Ascot scene, with all the expected glamour in costumes and the mannered discourse of the race- attenders. Mrs Higgins was played by Deirdre Kennedy, and Mrs. Eynsford-Hill was Bairbre Murphy. Both were good characters, with a gloss of upper-class manners tempered by genuine warmth. Freddy was Stuart Pollock, well-cast as the love-struck suitor, with a pleasant, strong singing voice and adept at the non-verbal reactions to Eliza needed for this role. The chorus, beautifully dressed, were also very good at conveying the atmosphere of the race meeting, with plenty of movement and characterisation in the background. The exterior scene at 27A (On the Street where You Live) was nicely peopled by a bobby on the beat, a crossover by two ascot-attired ladies (People stop and stare) and a flower seller. The scene inside the Higgins house just before the Embassy Ball was telling for they way each character reacted to the situation: the excitement of the servants, Pickering's nerves, Eliza's serenity and then Higgins, who was confident and placid until he sees Eliza, and then found he needed a quick glass of port to steady himself. There was a hint of something passing between them as they departed, possibly the beginnings of a different kind of relationship.

The wonderfully po-faced butler at the top of the stairs at the Ball was a briefly scene-stealing and very funny character. Ciarán Murphy was Zoltan Karpathy, in an interesting, understated portrayal with an English accent, almost reptilian in focus. The dancing choreography was detailed and had a sweep and coordination that made it really come alive.

Back at the Higgins house (another very efficient scene change) the scene had a nice company feel, with servants (who had stayed up to wait for their return) hung on every word of Higgins and his triumph was conveyed with good bravado. Their laughter when he suggested that Eliza had been taken for a princess caused her face to fall. His cigar smoking added a touch of elegant self-satisfaction. The arc of the scene carried through to her anger and his baffled concern. There was a more of Shaw in the justifiable disillusionment of Eliza in this scene, a balanced emotion between Higgins and Eliza that finds no common ground.

The scene of Eliza's return to Covent Garden was well-managed, with an accomplished voice from the chorus singing a reprise of Loverly, and Eliza buying a flower from her 'old self', as it were. She leaves the flowers behind at the end of the scene, having met her father, another victim of Higgins' influence. I'm Getting married in the Morning was another lively, character-ful piece of choreography with precise movements and a great sense of engagement between the chorus and Alfred and his cronies. Higgins' indignation at Eliza's sudden departure was palpable, and Mrs Pierce's manner expressed a sense of "I told you so" writ large. Why Can't a Woman and also Pickering's one-sided phone conversation were very funny, and the scene with Mrs. Higgins was equally telling. His musing about the future in I've Grown Accustomed to Her Face completed a dramatic circle in a way that seemed logical, and is a credit to Robinson that his expression of nostalgia was so well balanced by other elements in this character. It is a surprise, but a pleasant one, when Eliza returns to him. Robinson's subdued reaction, a catch of breath as he donned his hat, spoke volumes of the connection forged between these two characters in the course of a very

Gorey Little Theatre The Merry Widow is one of the grand old operetta works of the early 20th century. It's always wonderful to see how this tale of the power of money versus the power of love resonates in a 21st century world. Gorey's production certainly had the look of a classic romance, and good casting was also part of the secret of the show's success.

Anna Glavari was soprano Joanne McCabe, an accomplished singer with the right confidence for this role. Gary Masterson as Count Danilovitsch had the languid good looks and smooth vocal technique to explain Anna's continued attraction to him. Baron Zeta (Mark Ivory) projected the right sort of busy authority to be an ambassador, and Maria Hughes as his wife Valencienne along with having a lovely voice was also an able actress. Her love interest, Camille, was Pádraig D'Arcy, another good actor who projected a nice sense of endless patience with Valencienne's flightiness. Malcolm Byrne was a marvellously- moustachioed Njegus whose watchful assistance created a kind of double act between him and Zeta. Brendan Mackay was a consistently watch-able Cascada, reacting to events and supportive in his scenes. Various attachés and their wives, and other embassy guests were also attentive to the action in their scenes, and chorus numbers were well-populated and colourful throughout.

The set though grand, was versatile and it's arrangement of a large staircase and other raised areas provided different performing levels and any possibilities for chorus and cast placement. The use of a projected chandelier in the first Act was a clever and effective way to suggest this part of the embassy salon location.

Pontevedro in Paree did a good job of establishing the scene and tone of the show, as well a giving characters a chance to make themselves and their interests known. A Highly Respectable Wife and So Many Men Admire Me were well paced and nicely sung, the main singers having both the range and power of voices to carry these rich songs off. Danilo's style of singing, though different from the more operatic voices, was attractive and effective in You'll Find Me At Maxim's, ably assisted by some lady friends and some relevant choreography.

Anna and Danilo had a nice rapport onstage, each a little wary and clearly drawn to each other at the same time. Their singing voices were well-matched for it Goes to Show and ensemble was good. The story of Valencienne and Camille's romance developed very well, adding humour and some tension to the proceedings, and acted well.

The folk dancers at Anna's party were very beautifully dressed and their dance was characteristic and nicely rhythmic. The set was beautifully decorated for this, down to a change of banister spindles in the grand staircase, and a lot of greenery to suggest the garden, including some impressive topiary. Vilia was beautifully sung, and had the requisite lush orchestral and choral atmosphere.

Later in the scene, there was some nice confusion and dialogue surrounding "that fan" and other matters with Olga (Joan Duignan) and Sylvia (Lynette Beechey). Praskovia, played by Julie Kinsella, was a very funny cameo, completely persuaded that Danilo was in love with her, and determined to act on that. By this stage, the general consternation and confusion results in the song Women! Women! Women!, a nicely energetic number that approached the quality and character of close harmony barbershop singing, as well as nice individual singing.

The famous Waltz Scene gave Anna and Danilow, who dance beautifully together, a chance to smooth over their difficulties. This chorus scene was beautifully costumed, and there was some graceful choreography for the cast.

The scene with the summer house was very well done, complete with a lovely gazebo and some very well timed stage-work and swapping of Valencienne and Anna. Music and misunderstandings continued, and we arrived at Madame Glawari's version of Maxim's. The lovely Grisettes were beautifully dressed and enthusiastically choreographed. Throughout this section, Njegus made an impression with his laconic and correct manner. As the various misunderstandings are unpicked and mended, the show comes to a fine musical climax, and the Merry Widow finishes up still merry and also very happy indeed.

St. Mary's Hall The story behind how Leixlip Musical & Variety Group chose to do Our House is a simple one and has undoubtedly been repeated over the years with other societies and other shows. It began ten years ago when some of them bought tickets to a show they didn't know in London and decided that this was one they ought to do. Their production of Our House proved that all things are possible, and Our House is now a show that they know very well indeed.

It begins with three school boys engaged in the serious business of acquiring a condom for the 16th birthday date of one of them, Joe Casey. Because of schoolboy bravado and also genuine pride in who he is, he brings his girl to a building site above his home in Casey Street, to show her the place his family helped build. When the police arrive unexpectedly, he has to decide in a split second whether to run and leave his girlfriend to get into trouble that may ruin her chance to follow the career she wants, or to stay and face the consequences himself. The term "split second" is very relevant, because the rest of the play shows us what would have happened in both of those cases. It quite literally splits Joe in two: Good Joe who eventually makes a dishonest fortune, and Bad Joe, who ends up serving time. Both outcomes of the story are explored, both Joes played by the one actor.

Joe Casey was played by Ian Tighe, impressive in this double role - his Bad Joe had the careless swagger and mean-spirited deception of bad boys everywhere, and his Good Joe projected the dogged virtue of every victim of circumstance. Like everyone in the cast, he sang and danced very well too.

Sarah, Joe's girlfriend, was played by Karla Moloney. She has a clear singing voice and was able to negotiate believably this role which interacts convincingly and in sympathy with both Joe characters. Throughout the play, two consistent adult characters are Joe's father and mother. Joe's Mum Kath Casey was Jenny McCabe, who played the role with a Northern Irish accent and tenaciousness in the face of almost unbearable odds. Her singing voice was emotional and warm, and she related especially well to Good Joe, whose troubles impacted hugely on her as well. John Sweeney played Joe's father, a character ironically ever-present in the play, because he is absent from Joe's life in reality. He functioned as a kind of solo Greek Chorus, observing and commenting on the action, visible only to Joe, sharing insights and also giving us a glimpse into Joe's thoughts. Sweeny is a strong presence on stage, with a good singing voice. He was able to quietly enter a scene almost without notice, and step out again with the same quality of stillness. Emmo and Lewis, Joe's closest friends, were played by Brian Phillips and Ross Murray, two strong comic, vocal and dance performers who were part of what was essentially an extended family against which the lives and decisions of both Joes play out. Billie and Angie were also part of that close community, played by Lynn Brennan and Ella Fitzpatrick. These were committed characterisations by skilled performers who brought a great deal of energy and consistency to their roles. Michael Kiersey was Reecey, the bad influence and petty crook who leads Joe astray. There was a nervous, unpredictable energy in Kiersey's performance, a 'bad guy' characterisation that was without cliché or mannerism. Paul Purcell as Mr. Pressman projected a believable take on a businessman who doesn't get his hands soiled, preferring to delegate the dirty work to others.

The entire cast and chorus brought a great deal of energy to the production, sustained, bright movement and consistently strong singing that gave the story momentum. The wit of the songwriting of Madness and the surrounding story and script melded together well and this cast stepped lightly in and out of the dramatic and purely musical segments of the show. The theatrical sleight-of-hand necessary to have one actor play two parts was exceptionally well-managed, creating moments when we thought we were watching Bad or Good Joe in one part of the stage, and suddenly the 'other Joe' would appear and carry on with another scene.

The choreography was witty and inventive, and relentlessly fast-paced, almost as if watching a series of music videos. Iconic "Madness moves" were incorporated into the dancing, and other dance references (to Swan Lake or Singing in the Rain) also made an appearance.

There is more than a whiff of Blood Brothers in Our House, with possibly less emotional baggage to it but fully as much heart. This cast wore it's collective heart on it's sleeve as well as meeting the musical, choreographic and comic demands of the piece. The tour de force of one actor playing the same character in two different plots simultaneously was a unique challenge, one that didn't happen without a great deal of impressive support, onstage and off. This is only a good choice of show if all its demands can be met, and Leixlip Musical and Variety Group took Our House and made it Their House.

The Grand Opera House, Belfast New Lyric Operatic Company's production of that most urban musical West Side Story began with the sound of a train or subway, an iconic New York noise that helped set the scene for this dramatic and colourful production. The opening fight between Jets and Sharks set a scene as well, and a standard, for choreography that underscored the way in which this show tells its story with movement as well as words and music.

A few of the gang members in this scene emerged as distinct characters, and more became known as the plot developed. Riff (David McCrossan) was a compact and nervy presence, with the kind of energy that identified him as a leader, with a strong tenor voice. His relationship with Tony (Mark Adamson) was strong, despite Tony's loss of interest in the gang. Adamson is a strong presence onstage, able to convey the sense of being caught between two worlds that this role requires. The scene in the dress shop served to characterise life in the Puerto Rican community. Clare McCrory as Maria was a mixture of innocence and a kind of youthful impatience, contrasted by Anita, played by Karen Hawthorne, a strong presence onstage and an outstanding dancer. The dance in the gymnasium materialised behind Maria as she spun around in her new white party dress. This was a great looking scene, with fast and furious dancing and a clear sense of the two sides of the community, separated in style of dress and dance. The slow sequence in which Tony and Maria meet was beautifully framed onstage, and the song Maria introduced with offstage voices in the prologue to it singing her name. Another beautiful moment was created later on when, after a lovely duet on Tonight, Maria tentatively tries out Tony's full name with the line "Te adoro, anton". The versatile and well- textured set, including various segments of fencing and scaffold, provided a very atmospheric background to moments like this throughout the show.

America was a powerful ensemble piece, with the Puerto Rican chorus demonstrating their dancing abilities with characteristic moves, including leaps, stamping and clapping. Cool established the 'American' gang as every bit as accomplished, with choreography that suggested a general anxiety and wariness among the youngsters. The war Council at Doc's brought two of the adult characters into focus, Lieutenant Shrank, whose overt racism was a shocking element, brought to the scene with a knowing, laconic delivery by Gerry McBrien. Doc (Tony Finnegan) was more connected to the action and undercurrents than is sometimes the case, and this enabled this character to function as a kind of moral pivot point, commenting from the centre of the action but not part of it. Bernardo was Jonathan Moreland, well cast and handsome, a good mover and a dignified leader of the Sharks.

The relative calm of the dressmaking shop was well fitted out with mannequins and a sewing machines, etc. The relationship between Maria and Tony had a sense of inevitability to it, conveyed by the actors with urgency and consistency. One Hand, One Heart was beautifully staged, and was followed by the music and then actual scene of the Rumble, again realistically portrayed with nicely balanced fight choreography and the strong presence of the gangs whose characters by this point were well established. The orchestra were agile, rhythmic and colourful in this, with a good grasp of style throughout. The deaths of Bernardo and Riff were expectedly shocking, and the chain link fence that surrounded their bodies was symbolic of the kind of division that both locked in and kept out both sides of this fight. The sound of a train which marked the beginning of the play also signalled the end of Act I.

I Feel Pretty was nicely set, with choreography that related to the text and a nice feel of the relationship of the girls in what is unknowingly their last light moments together. Chino was played by Caolan Keaveney as a timid suitor for Maria, who can hardly bring himself to tell her of her brother's death. His transformation when he realises that she loves Tony was very effectively portrayed, he became unhinged and almost as if not recognising himself, sets out to kill Tony. The Dream Sequence in which the Puerto Rican characters danced with the opposing side was beautifully illustrated with the voice of Joseph Zubier, an accomplished boy soprano who sang There's a Place for Us. The movement suggested reconciliation, but then became more conflicted and gradually the scene disspolved and Tony and Maria were together in her room. The iconic Krupke song was imaginative and funny in its staging, with all the various characters in the song brought to life by this agile Jets chorus. Ande Gray as Action was a great comic presence, and there was some fine singing too, not least when all of the 'boys' sang about having a 'social disease' in extremely high falsetto voices.

The drama of A Boy Like That was followed by a powerful and harrowing scene in which Anita is set upon by the Jets, manhandled and held down on a table.

Her quiet rage resonated across the rest of this play, the silence of her rising from the table and crossing the stage was simply terrifying. Doc's unconcealed emotion as he rages against Tony for having hope in the face of barbarism was also telling, and Tony's resultant despair, believing that Maria is dead completed this triangle of grief.

The scene of Tony's death was also harrowing, with Chino collapsing as soon as he fired the shot, and Maria's angry sorrow as she picked up the gun and asked how many bullets were left. The boy who sang in the dream sequence led the cortege as Tony was lifted and carried off, Doc placing his hand on the body and weeping as it passed him. As one of the Jets placed a shawl around Maria's shoulders, another lifted Chino to his feet. Anita and Maria, left alone, stood in a circle of overhead light, and the stage went black.

The Premier Hall The 60th Anniversary production of Thurles Musical Society was a show that originally appeared nearly three quarters of a century ago and still resonates as a comedy of class and manners, full of memorable characters, sparkling comedy and grand music.

The iconic street lamp was in evidence from the start, and a street scene which welcomed a chorus of travellers getting ready for a Weekend at Hareford. Their cases formed the outline of a car in which they all piled for the journey. Their destination - a grand house in Hereford, appeared first as an impressive exterior and then unfolded to a grand interior, a well populated stage with maids and butlers and some of the residents of Hareford. Lady Jacqueline was Cathy Keane, who played this gold-digging opportunist with a physically intense feel for the inherent comedy in the situation. The Hon Gerald Bolinbroke was John Butler, whose tidy and well-dressed appearance squared with his precise, engagingly uptight approach to this role. The executers of the will of the recently deceased Earl of Hareford were Maria McElgunn as the Duchess of Dene and Sir John Tremayne, played by Brendan Bailey. These two had the requisite upper crust accents and manner to carry forward their plan to make the unexpected heir to the Hareford estate 'suitable' for his position. McElgunn was formidable and quietly persuasive, while Bailey had a good natured flexibility in his approach. The object of their attentions was Jonathan Gleeson as Bill Snibson, a very 'cheeky chappy', likeable and physically agile in the role, with a consistent cockney accent and irrepressible open enthusiasm. The Family Solicitor was Geraint Fyler as Herbert Parchester, who led his eponymous number with a keen rhythmic sensibility and the knowing mannerisms of a keen family servant. The chorus in this number had some tidy moves, reminiscent of the mannered minuets of a bygone era. Lord and Lady Battersby were the very amusing pairing of Pat Hayes and Breda Byrne, providing upper class atmosphere and clearly not themselves amused at the antics of Bill. Another very amusing presence throughout this show was Lord Jasper Tring, played with some flair by Brendan Bailey. This character appealed as only a deaf, and very old upper class gentleman can.

Bill's gal Sally was Michelle O'Connell, whose warm stage presence carried into her singing voice and made for a very likeable character. Her relationship with Bill was believable, they are well- matched, and their singing of Me and My Girl sparkled.

An English Gentleman was sung in the great setting of a kitchen, with a wonderful array of servants engaged in a variety of pursuits: cooking, polishing, shining shoes, etc.  An imperious and tall Barry Derby led the way in the person of Butler Charles Hethersett, and their disapproval of Bill was expressed in chorus.

The rather more intimate situation of Bill and Lady Jacqueline together in the beautifully evoked rose drawing room was a hilarious take on her vigorous seduction of him. You Would if You Could was played for laughs with blatant disregard for life and limb, as he tried to get away and she clung to his leg while lying on the floor, or leapt on to his back. More physical comedy came in the nicely predictable business of Bill trying to put his coat on with the help of Charles, and getting hopelessly caught up in it.

The end of Act I pulled the whole cast together for the Lambeth Walk, a defiant gesture from Sally who brings Bill's mates from London up to Hareford to crash the party. This iconic number, complete with Pearly Kings and Queens gradually drew in the upper-class inhabitants of the house, and then the audience too, who clapped and sang along as the number moved into the aisles. The addition of spoon playing to the general rhythm of the piece was nicely done.

The Sun Has Got His Hat On was another attractively set piece, with a wonderfully eccentric costume (Gerald) and an ensemble of dancers with were elegantly dressed and carried on that theme with nicely precise movements which had a larger overall sweep and momentum. Maria and Sally, in a nice, quite funny exchange, agree that she ought to leave Bill, and Sally's Take it on the Chin was her response to that decision.

Another impressive theatrical sequence came in the form of the Song of Hareford in which portraits of Bill's ancestors came to life and illustrated his Heritage. This was visually fascinating, and the actors concerned were able to be marvellously motionless when necessary. The portraits involved themselves later on in their singing in the chorus of Bill and Sir John's Love Makes the World Go Round, both of them in a delightfully sozzled state.

A scene back in Lambeth had some wonderful cameos for an "educated policeman" and "Anastasia Brown", a very amusing Hilda Ogden-esque character. Leaning on a Lamppost was cleverly set with four Sally look-alikes in a dream sequence ballet.

From then, the die is cast for Bill's return to Lambeth for good, foiled by Sally's success at proving she can be as posh as anyone, and the realisation by all at Hareford Hall that she and Bill were meant to be together, along with Lady Jaqueline and Gerald (afterall!) and Duchess Maria and Sir John. Like most happy endings, it was the journey that counted, and with Thurles MS as tour guides, we all enjoyed our trip down Lambeth Way enormously.

The game of chess is not all that easy to learn and takes patience, concentration and discipline - qualities that S.O.N.G. applied in large amounts to their production of Chess in April.

The set on which all of the action took place was simple in an ingenious way. A set of stairs, lit from inside, led to a platform on top of which the game was played, and which had folding extensions that could represent other spaces and rooms. The prologue, The Story of Chess established a rhythmic precision in the music that remained a constant throughout. The main chorus were dressed in black - quite severe suits that echoed the attire of the chess tournament officials. Younger chorus members were in black and white and they represented chess pieces, ranged on the steps of the set, as if on a tilted chess board. This is a complicated and wordy chorus that featured individual voices from the choir, strong singers with character in their voices and good focus. Kylan Ross was The Arbiter, a strong actor with a voice to match, a voice of reason in the charged world of chess tournaments. Nik Parks was Freddie, an angry young man, unguarded in his opinions, portrayed with intensity and sure-footed conviction. His opponent Anatoly was Brendan Cleary, an appropriately more guarded presence on stage, with a well-modulated singing voice. Florence was Sinéad O'Callaghan, a strong vocal force with great range and clarity in her voice. Molokov, a political 'minder', was an intense Andrew Browne, as inscrutable as Anatoly, but edgier with it. By the time American and Russian flags were lowered from above the players heads, the atmosphere in the Tain Theatre had assumed some of the electricity of an actual chess tournament.

The chorus in this production assumed different roles with minimal changes in costume or use of props. As reporters, diplomats and merchandisers, the chorus in various combinations sang with tremendous rhythmic precision and concentration, conveying much with facial expressions and often minimal movements. A group of female ensemble singers was especially focussed, often observing the action from the sides of the stage, ever-present and watchful.

A team of dancers were stylish and stylised in their movements where necessary to convey the mannered and precise world of chess and its players. The Arbiter was set with angular, almost militaristic movement. Later on, the dancers would also convey the inane enthusiasm of American cheerleaders and then the richly coloured decadence of Bangkok, all with a similar flair.

Dean Garland played Walter, the nervy and snake-like television presenter who functions as a kind of 'devil's advocate' throughout the show, shrewd and persuasive. Garland is a strong singer and believable in his role.

Svetlana was sung by Leanna Carragher with a rich and expressive voice and powerful stillness onstage. As the last principal character to be introduced, she had less time to make an impression, which she did straight away with someone Else's Story. And a similar stillness surrounded Anatoly in his singing of Anthem, in which he was joined by the powerful and well- balanced singing of the full company. Golden Bangkok and One Night in Bangkok were colourful and atmospheric numbers that re-created the sights and sense of Thailand and the chess tournament there. This production relied very much on carefully prepared and performed music with a strong cast and chorus, and well- chosen, carefully staged movement. The precision of the female ensemble singers both vocally and in terms of their intense focus on the action was key as well.

The iconic I Know Him So Well was another reflective point, simply staged and sung by the two women, Florence with a literal reading of the piece and Svetlana a more improvised approach.

Endgame brought all of the various performers and elements of this show together in a beautifully sung and well- choreographed number. The eight dancers in black began their movement in a balletic style which became more angular as the music quickened, weaving in and out of other performers.

The key game was suggested rather than reproduced by the young chorus in black and white, resembling chess pieces. The various threads of the personal and public stories told in Chess pulled towards the conclusion, with a reprise of You and I and Anthem signifying those two elements. This was a visually interesting and musically polished performance by a very committed cast of young people whose engagement with the difficult musical and dramatic material of the piece was impressive.

Wexford Opera House The inhabitants of Titipu were never so well-accommodated as they were for Wexford Light Opera Society's production of Mikado, in the well-appointed and lovely Opera House. The apt metaphor of a fan was used in the set, and a kind of prologue was performed during the Overture by a dancer en pointe, dressed as a geisha and setting the scene gracefully.

The Gentleman of Japan came on armed with sticks reminiscent of Samauri swords, in black and white costumes that were tidy and forbidding. Nanki Poo was George Lawlor, his "shreds and patches" in evidence and a fine singing voice too. Pish-Tush, in bright blue brocade, was Tony Brennan, an engaging character who looked splendid as a Noble Lord. Pooh Bah was played by the rich-voiced Owen Brady, regal in both singing and speaking mode. The dialogue in this early part of Mikado was nicely melodramatic, a tone that, once set, was largely maintained. Young Man Despair was peppered with contemporary Irish and European references (Angela Merkel, a mysterious Brown Envelope), and this was of course the form for Ko-Ko's Little List a little later. James McDermott, a natural, dryly witty comic actor was a youthful and good- looking Ko-Ko, somewhat unusual for this role. Another very funny turn was Pooh- Bah's dialogue with Ko-Ko during which he assumed the many roles he occupies in Titipu, transformations he achieved with little more than turning around and adopting a slight change of inflection in his voice.

The entrance of the ladies chorus was like a festival of flowers, with multi coloured kimonos, parasols and fans. The Three Little Maids wore school uniforms with straw boater hats - a completely non- Japanese design that worked well in context. Orange lollipops completed the look.

So Please You, Sir was comical, with a decidedly uncomfortable Pooh-Bah most un-inclined to fraternise with the little girls. Chorus movement in this was especially good, coordinated and precise. Yum-Yum was Clare Kavanagh, whose strong and centered singing voice was an asset to this role. Her cohorts Pitti-Sing (Maggs Jacob) and Peep-Bo (Rebecca Hadrill) brought lively voices and youthful looks and enthusiasm to these roles, and as a group they were well matched and appeared to have a lot of fun! Yum-Yum and Nanki-Poo's attachment to each other was revealed and the plot eventually arrived at the conclusion that he must be executed. There was a nice moment when a short and solemn few bars of 'Boolavogue' helped illustrate the way in which his death would be marked. Other amusing bits were more predictable, as when every mention of The Mikado elicited a collective "Ah! Mikado", or "Ah so! Mikado!" accompanied by a bow. Closely connected to the Mikado was Katisha, played with dramatic disdain by Siobhan Fawsitt.

Her costume was a fantastic mix of Japanese metaphors, complete with dragon headdress and a mix of black and gold kimono and overmantel. Her strong singing voice had an uncompromising edge to it and was a big part of the momentum of the Finale to Act I, during which the chorus and full cast were very focussed on the action and melodramatic tension.

Act II finds the trio of girls Braiding the Raven Hair, silhouetted behind a traditional screen during Yum-Yum's wedding preparations. The Sun Whose Rays was beautifully set with sun and moon projected onto the back cloth, and Brightly Dawns was equally beautifully sung by the quartet, at a decidedly mournful tempo that belied the cheery words (ding dong). This and other reflective scenes were beautifully lit, making full use of the possibilities represented by such a fine venue. In contrast, Here's a Howdy Do! had a cheerfulness that of course did not correspond to the seriousness of the text. During this, Ko-Ko left the stage and returned dressed as a bridegroom, left again and returned with a shovel, and then wheeling a coffin on a trolley! This was very well received, and the audience were also treated to some inane humour about Ko-Ko practising his execution skills on a guinea pig and then working his way up the animal kingdom to a Second Trombone, and an "impromptu" few bars of the Mikado biscuit theme when The Mikado in human form arrived, played by Dea Whelan. His substantial costume, padded and quilted, corresponded with a fine arrangement of hair and headdress and marvellous makeup. Like Katisha, he also sported fantastically long fingernails. His singing voice matched his appearance, formidable, memorable and suited to the role. The 'discovery' that his son has been beheaded, (even though he hasn't been) was very funny, the dialogue between all the characters clear and given time to resonate. The Flowers that Bloom in the Spring… was also amusingly done, with Ko-Ko attempting and failing to keep everyone on stage, so he doesn't have to face Katisha. That meeting, (Katisha's entrance heralded by the 'Jaws' theme) of course results in them coming to an understanding, with a little help from a Tit Willow glove puppet. The finale came with a flourish and all was well in Titipu, unless you happened to be sentenced to life with Katisha, though judging by the verdict of

Newbridge College Theatre Jesus Christ Superstar is a show that tends to either look as if set in the 70's when it was first performed, or it takes on the look of the time of Christ, or rather how we imagine it to have been. Newbridge Musical Society's production of the show straddled those two worlds and in the process created a new dynamic that supported the story and the characters that inhabit it.

The traditional-looking set had many levels, doors, archways and a feeling of depth, all of which provided a versatile canvas on which the play sat with ease, moving in and out of it's various frames. During the prelude the cast made their way onto the stage from the back of the theatre, a cross section of people, greeting one another and caught up in daily life. Following a freeze, Jesus walked to the front of the stage, which fell silent, after which the chorus and cast filed off, Jesus and Mary Magdalene last.

Judas was sung by Jim Walsh whose tightly-wound presence had great energy, even when not singing, though it was his agile voice and able singing technique that expressed the character most. Jesus was Mark Trundle, a very 'present' Christ, human in his interaction with the cast, but also expressive of a sense of separation from others. Jenna Laming sang Mary Magdalene, her singing voice just one element of a performance that was focussed across many aspects of the role; a portrayal that was watchful and consistently supportive of the drama. The chorus were simply and comfortably dressed in styles reminiscent of the 70's, but not overtly so. Their singing was very well balanced and full of nuance that is normally not within reach of a group unless in a static concert setting. In Everything's Alright, they provided background and a kind of sung punctuation to Mary Magdalene's song. The slide on the 'oooh' line in this was very well executed. On Hosanna, the chorus, including children entered again from the back with signs and placards: "I (heart) Jesus", etc. Their interaction with each other and their participation in the scene was impressive. Caiaphas was Rory Dunne, a singer with the particular range and vocal presence to portray this role. Annas (Padraigh Munnelly) sang with a kind of sly relish as well as accuracy and a strong tone. Hosanna elicited an uneasy exchange of looks between Jesus and Mary Magdalene as the chorus sang about Jesus fighting or dying for them. James Donohoe was Simon Zealotes, a strong singer with a good grasp of the stylistic demands of the music. Pilate was played by Martin Hennessy, whose well articulated, resonant singing gave the role a good clarity and focus on Pilate's Dream.

The Temple scene was busy and raucous, with dollar bills changing hands and tee shirts for sale, dancing and commotion. Jesus' anger cleared the stage with vocal pyrotechnics and the exeunt was swift. The lepers entered via crawl spaces at floor level and other archways and doorways. Individual voices in this were well amplified, clear and emotive. As ever, this is a frightening, unsettling scene, given great poignancy by the singing voices which were very good, in tune and cloying. They crawled off when Jesus told them to "heal yourselves" and as they went, he reached for them, almost in apology, as they went.

I Don't Know How to Love Him was taken at a fairly brisk pace, sung emotionally, at times at the level of a whisper, by Mary Magdalene whose claim to be "running every show" was believable, as was the fear and confusion she feels at that moment.

The scene between Judas and the High Priests was a dramatic contrast to the black-robed chorus that comment on his betrayal, dispassionate and anonymous. The Last Supper is often a segment of Jesus Christ Superstar that is hard to sing in tune, but Newbridge managed to be on pitch and nicely modulated, the final repeat was performed almost sotto voce. Gethsemane began with a beautiful brass obbligato, and lighting that framed the scene and drew attention to Jesus, approaching Calvary alone, despite the presence of the (sleeping) disciples. With a thrilling falsetto quality in his voice, he sang first to a point at the back of the hall, and then turned to the audience, demanding "see how I die". The final phrase, "before I change my mind" was pitch-perfect and emotionally resonant on the night. The arrival of police carrying truncheons effected a change of atmosphere in the piece, and also revealed a changed chorus, now a baying mob.

Peter was sung by Conor Kilduff and his denial had the tension and dramatic import of an operatic scene.

Herods Song was set with a booming- voiced Herod (John Conroy), his name quite literally in lights, flanked by bunny girls and a glamorous chorus line. The mocking tone and sneering intensity built up across this number and ended with Herod in a searing, roaring rage.

The death of Judas was preceded by his almost slow-motion but unstoppable lifting of a rope, climbing to the top level of the set, standing on a box, fastening the rope above his head, putting it around his neck and jumping.

The scene of the scourging of Jesus was presided over by a Pilate gradually more and more unnerved by his prisoner. Initially, in response to Pilate's words "Look at me, Jesus Christ", Jesus stood, turned and faced Pilate, who recoiled in fear, before pronouncing him mad. As a tethered Jesus was whipped, Pilate became increasingly horrified, essentially disabled by what happens and at the 39th stroke Jesus fell into his arms and he and Pilate formed an image of the Pieta at the front of the stage. As the crowd continued to shout for crucifixion, Pilate lifted the crown of thorns and placed it on the head of Jesus.

Superstar introduced a surreal combination of Angels in white and in black and Soul Girls in red bodices, baseball caps and sunglasses. Judas, more relaxed but still somewhat edgy, was the focus of attention in this tongue- in-cheek but demonic number.

Jesus carried his cross down the centre aisle of the theatre, followed by laughing soldiers - an uncomfortable, evocative moment that seemed to implicate the audience in the scene by virtue of proximity. His body when taken down from the cross was touched by each disciple in turn as they walked off. Mary Magdalene was left, cradling the body of Jesus, watched by Judas and of course, the audience, still in the shadow of the cross. I found in this Superstar little hope of resurrection but more of the human aspect of the story, a kind of redemption in itself, moving and memorable.

Portmarnock Community School Hall The term 'blank canvas' is not easily or often applied to musical theatre, but Portmarnock's Jesus Christ Superstar was set against a quite plain set and backdrop. They populated this, however, with a colourful production full of movement and meaning.

The overture was set with whirling coloured lights until the Jesus Christ Superstar theme was played and bright lights were turned to the audience. Jesus and Judas mimed conversation, eventually arguing and leading into Heaven on their Minds. Jesus was played by Christopher Currid, a performer with a great command of the stage and the courage and control to occasionally sing at just above a whisper, often a very powerful sound. Judas was David Latham, whose rhythmic, focussed singing was well-projected and clear, and who also had an ability to access a softer quality when needed. The chorus were dressed in a great variety of outfits, some in combat trousers, some in robes or shawls, and a group of dancers in elaborate tights and bodices. Dance moves were of the period of this show's composition and well-coordinated. Caiaphas was Vincent Oliver, a serene character with a strong voice. Annas was sung by Karl Sheridan, a somewhat sinister character who conveyed the malice with which the Priests approached Jesus. Hosanna was set with very rhythmic and precise choreography and a strong chorus presence.

Simon Zealotes was Daniel Murphy, a gifted dancer and fine singer. There was lovely control in his singing of this, and Poor Jerusalem was a lovely still moment. Pilate was sung by Donal Cantwell with a strong voice and a nice quality of sustain. By way of contrast, the Temple scene was very busy and spread across the wide stage. There were pillars to the sides of this set which suited this scene particularly well. The Lepers were a terrifying concept, well realised and impressive in their transformation. It was well-populated and designed scenes like this that worked best against the relatively plain background. Mary Magdalene was Orla Jennings, a fine singer with a good core to her voice. This was sung to Jesus as he slept, but he wokes slightly, as if having a nightmare, during the instrumental chorus, and Mary comforted him.

The Last Supper had good theatrical power, with the disciples vigorously denying that they will betray Jesus, a very human and plausible scene. The spread of ages among the followers of Jesus was an important and impressive feature of this production.

Gethsemane was a very powerful number, compellingly sung and emotionally sustained. The role of Peter was sung by Damien Hurley, in a scene in which the questioners were journalists pumping him for information. His sense of conflict and remorse was very effective.

Herod's Song was set as an old-fashioned dance number with black tie and a cane. He was joined by five glamour girls and 8 dancers in fedora hats, reminiscent of Liza Minelli and Cabaret. The style of dance in this resembled the work of Bob Fosse. The following Could We Start Again? was very well sung and simply staged, with offstage chorus as if an echo. Judas' final scene with Caiphas and the High Priests was very effective, sinister and scary. His death was simply and quickly portrayed, without dwelling on the manner of it.

The scourging scene was frenzied, the chorus whipping Jesus dressed all in black, aligned with the traditional image of an executioner. Pilate's resistance to the crowd created dramatic tension, and Jesus cried out as the crown of thorns was placed on his head.

Judas reappeared, transformed in a jewelled tee shirt and red leather waistcoat. For Superstar he was flanked by go-go girls.

The scene of the crucifixion was punctuated by the sound of nails being pounded into the cross, and the last words were spoken to a grouping of people at the foot of the cross including Peter, Mary his mother and a family from the chorus, and effective tableau that effectively framed this moving moment. When his body was removed and taken away, a cloth was draped on the cross and it was left there, centre stage. Across this energetic production there was a good sense of pace and dramatic momentum, and at the end, the stillness of that empty cross was a theatrical and emotional moment of great power.

Abbey Hall, Roscrea This was to be my second last show of the year, and as I made my way to Roscrea for their show The Wedding Singer, it occurred to me that I should probably repeat my Leaving Cert Geography and get that honour. Yes, I know the country a lot better than I did this time last year and Ireland's roads really have improved since I was a gal.  I'd swear there's more talent too and I am still flabbergasted at the efforts of musical societies around the country; they are the lifeblood of each community and the dedication and commitment of show folk is quite humbling.

I'm getting to know some of the newer shows as well, and The Wedding Singer is one of them.  It's a great show for a willing chorus and there are very funny cameo roles, with plenty for everyone to do.  Musical Director Mary Rose McNally set the mood well with a great band, above and behind the action on stage. The music, written by Matthew Skiar is nostalgically 80's and there are some great numbers, as well as a good few nods to the likes of Boy George, Spandau Ballet, and Michael Jackson - though you have the costume department to thank for that: one of THE best entrances ever would have to be Sammy in 'Thriller' rigout, accompanied by George, pretty in pink. Oh but none of this makes sense unless you know the show.  It's a simple story about a boy called Robbie who meets a girl called Julia.  He plays in a wedding band and she's a waitress.  Sure, they like each other but he's about to get married to wild rock chick Linda and Julia is working on getting engaged to money mad philanderer Glen.  Robbie is jilted at the altar by Linda, who later returns to try to seduce him while everyone is on to Glen, except Julia.  Tadhg Maher played an extremely enthusiastic Robbie Hart, and had the charisma and personality to carry this central role, though I did want him to tone down his energy by ten percent. Don't get me wrong; energy is good.  Give me energy over apathy any day.  But there were clowns a plenty in this show and Robbie needed to be the romantic guy. After all, Julia, delightfully played by Rachel McMahon was a quiet girl, decent and sweet, and while opposites attract, there has to be a meeting place somewhere in the middle.  However, there was chemistry between these two and director Peter Kennedy (we seem to be following each other around Ireland) got good stuff from his actors.  I loved the humour in this show, everyone got poked at; Robbie's band mates George (beautifully played by John Coss) and Sammy (equally enjoyable Wayne Handy) were very funny, especially because Sammy was so sweetly dim, and talked to George about being one of the boys and 'grabbing a few beers', while George, gay and CAMP! in the PROUDEST! way, has some great lines at Sammy's expense.  Sammy is crazy about Julia's cousin Holly, played by Louise Handy - wait a minute!  Another Handy? Are married couples allowed to flirt with each other on stage? I once had to do a love scene with my husband and I couldn't take him seriously at all.  These two were great together but not before Holly pushed Sammy away so many times he threatened not to come back.  Glen, a devout libertine, was played with suitable sleaze by Paul Spencer.  Julia's mum Angie, played by Holly Hastings loved her daughter but for an easy life, wanted her married off to a rich guy. Grandma Rose (Fionnuala Doyle) was a wonderfully eccentric character that rapped and danced and talked opening about 'special time' with Grandpa.  Linda, the 'skanky whore' - Grandma's words, not mine - was played by Fiona Russell and what a voice she has; The seduction song 'Let Me Come Home' was powerful and the performance was full on, breaking the bed and momentarily halting the progress of the stage crew.  The bed featured quite a lot in this show; first seen as a wedding gift from Grandma, she demonstrated its ability to vibrate.  Robbie spent quite some time in it after his jilting and the number 'Somebody Kill Me' was really very funny. This was a lively production, with well interpreted choreography (also Peter Kennedy); the opening number 'It's Your Wedding Day' had echoes from the dance floor of the 80's, while 'Casualty of Love' - after Robbie has been jilted and is in a poor state of mind - had some great 'Thriller' moments with a capable chorus of 'mutants'.  The chorus was a good support and 'Saturday Night' really set the mood well, while Holly, very much in the mood, showed off a great voice. Ms McNally was a consistent support to singers and her attentive band was strong. Group scenes had shape and everyone had received guidance.  Mr Kennedy designed the set too, and it allowed for plenty of dancing room and crowded wedding scenes.  There were some clever ideas, such as the bed folding up into the wall (though it was very much a single bed, and not a Queen-size as Grandma Rosie intended).  An office wall folded back into Julia's house and the interior of an airplane was created using a row of seats borrowed from a coach, which was very effective. Cameo roles in this show are fun and hats off to Mr Kennedy for the guidance given to individuals here; to pick out one or two, the couples who get engaged all around Julia and Glen, including two male waiters were funny and the air hostess and captain had good input towards the end. I must single out however the excellent rendition of 'Single' sung in the bar by Sammy (in said 'Thriller' gear), George, Robbie, Barman Ricky (John McEvoy) and Bar Bum (Andrew Walsh).  They sang well, their dancing was good and they were funny, very funny.  The costumes took me back and I sincerely hope they were wigs and not real hairstyles.  Stage Manager Ian Hanrahan oversaw a smooth run and the pace of the show was never compromised. With a friendly front of house team and a charming hostess in president Eileen Maloney, this was a wonderful round up of what has been a great year.

The Mill Theatre, Dundrum What was my least favourite show to direct, ever? The Pajama Game. I didn't care for the story, I didn't like the music.  So, why is it that I can't stop singing the songs since seeing Glencullen's production more than a couple of weeks ago?  Songs that I considered to be so complex there was no point in a (mediocre) singer like myself even trying to hum them.  I find I am blasting the numbers out as I go about my day.  'The…pajama game is…the game I'm in.' I tell my bemused students. 'Huh?' Pajamas?' 'Dum dee dah dee dum dee dah…' It actually puts me in a good mood - which is an excellent reflection on the show staged in the Mill Theatre by a relatively small troupe.  I blame Musical Director Gerry Connolly; his musicians were excellent, really solid players.  There were moments when singers delivered songs right next to the orchestra, in a soft spotlight and it worked very well. It's a weak story and shouldn't hold my attention but Shane Morgan and Mary Beth Jennings were good, and I wanted them to work it out; Sid Sorokin (Morgan) is new at the Sleep Tight pajama factory as a diligent and hardworking manager.  Babe Williams is one of the workers and also part of the tough grievance committee, so their initial meeting has chemistry.

He likes her, considers her to be a spunky lady.  She likes him.  So what could go wrong?  Well nothing much for a while, but there are rumblings, bubbling under the surface of the otherwise happy factory life, concerning a certain seven and a half per cent pay rise.  Old Man Hasler (Michael Cahill) the boss, isn't for turning and so there's trouble a brewing, which comes to a head when Babe, being a feisty one, jams up the production line.  Sure, what choice had Sid? He had to fire her, girlfriend or not and that's about all the weight the characters get.  I notice from director Liam Corrigan's biog that he's a bit of an actor himself, having been twice nominated for AIMS best actor award and winning first place when the group did My Fair Lady. It was clear to me he is an actor's director and in particular I was impressed with the treatment of the dated language. With cringe worthy lines for both Babe and Sid in particular, I thought these were delivered really well, and with confidence. There are plenty of other characters too with their own little sub plots going on; Peter O'Brien played Vernon Hines, or Hynsie to his friends, a likeable lad, though fond of the bottle and demonstrating his skills as a knife thrower, (unfortunately at the same time) against a board with a woman in the centre. The technique of this during a company picnic was well done and convinced. His girlfriend Gladys (Katie Doyle) is an outrageous flirt, and Vernon is prone to jealousy.  Secretary Mabel (Ruth Fitzsimons) and Vernon sang a really good rendition of 'I Would Trust Her' (another one stuck in my head); the melody is difficult and it was really well handled by both, with solid support from MD.  Ruth Fitzgerald's Mabel got something out of every line, and where she didn't have a quip, she managed to convey something all the same, and I loved her natural but humorous style.  Shane Morgan too was a solid performer who brought presence to the role of 'lover boy' Sid.  Gifted with a great singing voice, he also has a developed speaking voice and his drama studies at De Montfort were a credit to him; this is so often overlooked and it makes such a difference, particularly with a central role. Both he and Mary Beth Jennings (Babe) were convincing and their scenes together were engaging. 'There Once Was a Man' was given the energy it needed and even the yodelling part seemed perfectly acceptable - but you do see what I mean about the show; yodelling, in a love song.  Babe's scenes with the girls had life and there were solid performances from Aoife Fingleton as Brenda, Laura Monks as Poopsie and Ruth Lalor as Mae, along with a strong female chorus of busy factory workers. 'I'm not at all in Love' was well interpreted by choreographer Helen McCann while 'Steam Heat' with Mae confidently leading a chorus of smoldering women was well executed by everyone here, hats and all. Ruth Lalor had good comic moments with Prez, played by Tom Ronayne, a married man with a roving eye - and because it's set in the 1950's it's perfectly acceptable, especially because it's just a bit of fun for him, the cad.

While the plot thickens, Sid brings Gladys to Hernando's Hideaway, but only to get to the bottom of what Old Man Hassler's up to - and to steal the key of the accounts book, of which she is guardian.  Katie Doyle used her voice well as the flirtatious New York gal, and her drunken scene was hilarious.  Technique was good here too; she slurred but every word was crystal clear, and I would pay to watch her cross the stage again in that classic walk; I can't even explain it properly but she wore heels and walked on the sides of them, while trying not to spill her drink.

Other characters of note were Pop (George Ward), Joe (John McGouran), Charlie (Garrett Grimes) and Max (Daragh O'Duffy). The chorus of only eleven was well used and added to the scenes and dances and got a good sound out of the numbers.  'Once a Year Day' in particular had plenty of life. A couple of silly numbers were well interpreted by all involved and Tom Ronayne's Prez impressed with 'Her Is', along with Gladys first, and later Mae, and I think Brenda didn't escape either. Michael Cahill as the penny-pinching boss was suitably grumpy and his speech at the picnic was delivered with humour.  Both Prez and Vernon Hines had to interact with the audience and this was done confidently and with plenty of energy - it was a pity for the group that the theatre wasn't fuller on the night I attended, but unfortunately that is the situation everywhere these days.  Apart from a couple of unfocused moments from some actors with lines being lost, this was a competent and well- prepared group.

The set, designed by Tom Ronayne and director Liam Corrigan worked for the most part and was let down only by a couple of eye-sores such as modern looking school desks.  However Michelle Kennedy managed to get some very authentic looking props and most of the furniture was quite retro.  Costumes too looked great, with people standing out as necessary - Babe had a good few costume changes and dressed for the occasion.  Lighting enhanced the moods well and sound was well balanced, with impressive work during 'Hey There' where Sid sings a duet with his recorded voice. Scenes were efficiently changed though I would have preferred more energy from Stage Manager Helena Murphy and her team as it differed to the pace of the show. Pam O'Connor and her team had everyone looking authentically 1950's and house management was well organized.  Liam Ryan was his usual charming self and both my guest and myself agreed it was an all round enjoyable and entertaining evening from an impressive group.  My last show of the year: will I ever be able to get these songs out of my head?!

Theatre Royal Waterford At the end of the day, Les Misérables is quite an undertaking, but as pointed out by Colm Wilkinson in his message to the cast in the show's printed programme, "the rewards are big also". The South Eastern Youth Theatre Group is a new company, and their choice of "the world's favourite musical" as their first production was potentially risky and ultimately inspired, given that there was an obvious wealth of talent available in the Waterford and south East area.  Key cast members included Glenn Murphy whose heartfelt portrayal convincingly captured Jean Valjean, the wronged man determined to rise above persecution. Vocally he was everything the role required and the signature song Bring Him Home was deservedly very well received. His nemesis was Ause Braike as Javert, who brought an almost manic intensity to the role, balanced by a finely focussed stage presence. Lauren Cardiff was Fantine, expressive and almost ethereal in her approach to this brief but pivotal role. Kerill Kelley brought a palpable sense of enjoyment and an unrestrained gift for comedy to his Thenardier, while Hayley O'Brien as 'his missus' was delightfully irreverent. Both of these performers saved a little something for their re-appearance post-revolution and effectively brought the house down. Marius was David Farah, an engaging and sincere actor, vocally agile, with great colour in his singing. Julie Power was earnest and entirely consistent as Cosette, a believable actor with a beautiful voice, warm, flexible and able for this demanding role. Eponine was Mimi Lane, another powerful singer, superbly well-cast and intense, her death scene an emotional segment of great power. Nathan Carey was everything you could want in a Gavroche, and the young Cosette and Eponine were likewise fully formed characterisations within the scope of these brief roles. There are, of course, a host of characters in 'Les Mis' and this cast, especially the young men, did double and in some cases triple duty across the show. Of particular note were The Bishop, Enjolras, Marcel and Lesgles. Overall, performances were focussed and heartfelt - on occasion possibly too heartfelt - but forgivably so, given the swift pace of the production and the fantastic youthfulness of this cast, none of whom were more than 19, with a good number well below that upper age limit.    Another particularly impressive 'performance' came from the set, portions of which were required to move on cue (the gate, the barricade) and do so in a manner that while separate from the plot, are nevertheless essential to the action. These elements, along with some wonderfully atmospheric lighting did much to convey the passage of time and various changes in perspective that are the balancing point on which this story turns. Visually the show had the multi-layered sweep and depth of field needed to convey the time, place and the conditions into which the characters fit in their believable tableau. There were some very effective touches of costume detail and makeup at key points. Musically, the show also inevitably packed a punch, with a good band in the deep (and dangerously beckoning) pit, under the direction of Wayne Brown. Like all of the production values in this well-equipped theatre, sound design and realisation were everything one would expect, with good clarity whether we were listening to one performer or the entire cast. Indeed, this was very much a team effort, a labour of love onstage which was clearly fully supported backstage and across the community, whose standing ovation I'm certain was repeated during the all-too short run of this production. It is always a good sign in theatre when we are all left wishing for One Day More.

Island Hall, Lisburn It bodes well for a show, when you peer into the orchestra pit and see the recipient of this year's AIMS Best Musical Director award sitting behind the keyboard. Wilson Shields was just one of the very competent musicians under the baton of Ian Milford, himself an award winner including this year's AIMS best Director. I say it's just showing off, but Mr. Milford managed both mammoth tasks of director and musical director for this production of 'Chess' - apparently he does it all the time.

The young cast of Fusion Theatre seem to like it that way and their energy and enthusiasm was obvious. He was well in control of both band and cast, and everyone could manage the musical numbers with ease - in particular the principals who had some fairly difficult numbers.

The set was simple and stark; a chessboard floor with three video screens. What impressed most was the use of the video footage; this can be annoying sometimes, with images not so much enhancing the onstage action as filling in gaps. However, Sean Walsh, Jack Walsh and Michael Ford on visuals, under the direction of Mr. Milford (who knew exactly what he wanted), married film and theatre extremely well. While not an original concept, it was handled by people who understood film, and the video clips were captivating in their own right. News clips were convincing too, and Walter de Courcey (Caolan Keaveney), gave charisma to the TV reporter, though he tended to get distracted at times. Stage lighting was not always enough, with characters just too obscured in darkness, while in other places lighting could be striking.

Elsewhere direction was solid, with strong performances from a confident cast. Gareth Brown was convincing as Freddie and the arc of his personal journey was treated sensitively, particularly 'Pity the Child', while he had fun with the character at other times. Against this, Raymond Walsh's Anatoly was a more somber soul, and the chemistry with Florence was subtly felt. While both leading men certainly impressed, Orla McCormack as Florence sent shivers down the spine. Several times. A super voice with excellent control, she also seemed to have the X Factor. For a young man, Louis Patterson played Molokov with surprising maturity and really brought out the sinister dishonesty of the KGB agent.

Rebecca Leonard's choreography was lively and fully embraced by the cast, though many numbers required a synchronous effect and some of the performers may have benefitted from more rehearsal time. However, it impressed me that the entire chorus appeared to be able to dance and none of this talent was wasted. While the earlier numbers of the Arbiter (Jack Walsh) were a little confusing dance wise - there was a lot going on, and I felt he didn't stand out enough - the opposite was true by the middle of the first act, with both the character and the chorus excelling. A highlight was the recurring 'Hymn to Chess' with outstanding singing and visually exciting choreography with some really strong dancers. In the second act 'Endgame III' was quite fabulous, with incredible input from everyone involved on and off stage. Time and again I was impressed by the calibre of the musicians, though things did get too loud as the second act progressed, with singers straining to be heard.

Though not appearing until the second act, the abandoned wife of Anatoly, Svetlana, beautifully played by Hannah Conlon, made an impact. 'I Know Him So Well' was eagerly anticipated by the audience and both Ms Conlon and Ms McCormack shone brightly here.

Little touches added to the buzz in the beautiful Island Hall theatre, in particular the KGB agent spies keeping watch in the auditorium. Props were given detailed attention and I loved the old fashioned adverts. Costumes were good, with the black and white theme clear. Backstage, under Anne McCleary ran smoothly enough; a difficult task I imagine with a cast of around seventy young people. Sound was really well balanced for the most part, though from a clarity point of view, I felt some of the singers could have had sharper diction; with a fairly complicated plot, the story was not always clear to the audience. However, the main point was clearly made; everyone is a pawn really, the American TV guy is as bad as the Russian spy - two countries, same morals. Florence, perhaps, is the conscience they lack; the epitome of innocence, pulled in several directions. I wonder if Ian Milford sleeps, or is he one of those creatures that pour themselves into every living moment of the day? How else was this accomplished? Hard work, and certainly dedication to the group, I think he can safely say it was worth the effort. He probably makes rotten tea though…

A wet, windy Wednesday in October; not a good night for filling a theatre. Yet, I wasn't aware that I had been sitting amongst paltry numbers until I returned to my seat after the interval, such was the buzz created by Greenhill's' production of Seussical the Musical.

I'd seen the cartoon seussical style set before at a previous production by Mullingar. It was used differently, yet effectively to suit the stage space. The production was low on extra effects however, and relied solely on the performances of its rather talented cast. Musical Director Sarah Lynch-Barrett also conducted - and she so very pregnant too. It helped that she had gathered about her some fine musicians who did her proud. High calibre players and a focused MD made for some great sounds and there was little to fault here music wise, apart from a slightly unsure start for the first number. Sound was variable, with high notes of both singers and musicians at times just too loud producing winces from the otherwise appreciative audience. One expects to be bombarded with colour and powerful voices for this show and one was not disappointed. The hired costumes, looked after by Loretta McDonagh and Angela O'Flynn were vibrant, and enhanced greatly by make-up (I recognized Ali Murphy's style), subtle enough on chorus members and truly artistic on the likes of Cat and the Wickersham monkey brothers. I did question the dullness of Horton and Gertrude against the gloss of other costumes; true, they are meant to stand alone as unadorned and egoless and the contrast was clear. I simply wondered whether they were just a bit too ordinary. No ordinary performances however, and it was a real joy to experience John Furlong as Horton; how versatile this actor is, and he delivered with genuine sincerity. Suddenly the costume mattered not a jot. Likewise Sarah Carpenter as Gertrude McFuzz was a sheer delight; she managed to bring this gorgeous character to life. A super voice and expressive face, a performance which was innocently portrayed and refreshingly comedic. Wonderful casting from director Damien Douglas, who I would say considered himself blessed to have found a marvellous Jo-Jo in the shape of Georgia Barry, an extremely talented 12 year old that we haven't heard the last of.  It didn't stop there, what with Damien Hurley as a comfortable comedian playing Cat in the Hat; he brought physicality and fun to the part and got his laughs out of the small crowd - really very admiral work.
