Amanda Cunningham was a deliciously selfish Mayzie La Bird, and numbers were belted out with relish. As for Caithriona Mongey playing Sour Kangaroo: I wondered why she wore an afro wig but with her Aretha voice, it soon became clear. What a set of lungs and what soul. Bird Girls Tracy Armstrong, Aisling Toher and Joanne Moran worked beautifully together, their voices blended so well while they really worked as one group. The Wickershams (John Conroy, Gary Lanigan & Sean Flanagan) likewise worked as a unit and there was evidence of solid support and input from Choreographer Laura Martin. Some dance numbers were wonderfully creative, especially McElliogot's Pool, where Jo-Jo 'swam' around. Really good dancers were very well used and everyone very well rehearsed.

Other performances of note were Matthew Carpenter as the Grinch - a great voice possibly underused here, but then this group were blessed with oodles of capable vocalists; Conor Cronin as Mr Mayor and Valerie Andrews as Mrs. Mayor did more than sing; they brought conviction to Jo-Jo's caring family too. Mark Keegan brought energy to General Genghis Khan and the small children were marvellous. All that and a confident chorus too. Stage Manager Wayne Handy ran a smooth show and Damien O'Connor's lighting design was warm and colourful, genuinely adding weight to this thrilling and fun filled show.

Solstice Arts Centre, Navan Meath Youth Musical Society established a forceful and unflinching approach to their production of Rent from the very start of every performance during their run in the Solstice Arts Centre. This is a show that pushes at the boundaries of established musical theatre, and Meath YMT were not afraid of stepping across those boundaries and dancing on top of them. Kevin P Fagan as Mark, the intrepid and nearly omni-present film maker brought strong singing and acting abilities to this pivotal and at times conflicted role. His moment of ambivalence when "selling out" to the film company was especially effective. Roger was Kevin E Fagan, a strong singer and confident actor, with a range of expression in this part from anger to acquiescence. His relationship with Mimi, which was confused and conflicted, was well portrayed. Mimi was Danielle Williamson, an attractive and well-cast actress, a good dancer and singer, occasionally more focussed on movement than music. At its best, her voice was poignant and memorable. Emma Bracken portrayed the outgoing, extrovert Maureen and created a strong impression of this rather "loose canon" with good comic sensibility. Her portrayal was nicely balanced by the sensible Joanne, played by Emma Stowe. She's a very solid, consistent performer with an excellent singing voice and a strong rhythmic delivery. Although their pairing was convincing in the context of the play, rather more emotional resonance was found in the characters of Angel (Adam O'Brien) and Tom (Sean Keany). O'Brien relished his role as the transvestite with a heart of gold, and Keany was restrained but unflinching in his devotion to their partnership. The underlying theme of HIV/Aids that shadows this show was most tellingly played out in these roles, and Angel's death was an unflinching yet luminous snapshot of the ravages of the syndrome: the other meaning of the word "Rent" so vividly portrayed. There was great humour as well in aspects of the Angel/Tom pairing, and their singing voices met the musical challenges of these roles with some style. Benny was played by Craig Regan, well-cast as the sometime bad guy who nonetheless makes a transition that brings him into the disjointed community formed by the main characters. One very strong aspects of this show was the way that the chorus moved easily and convincingly in and out of scenes, becoming street people, party-goers, support group members and other characters as needed. Cameo roles were well-cast and performed effectively and with great grasp of 'type' and tone. Aisling Reid was notable as Mrs Cohen, Mark's ever-present mother, always on the phone. Chorus singing was especially strong, and the choreographic elements were well suited to the overall sense of the episodic nature of the show, less synchronised than possibly intended. The set was minimalist and very functional, a mix of urban and industrial elements that created a sense of the city that is so much key to the story. Lighting was a fairly stark mix of bright and shadowy areas, with an emphasis on full stage illumination. Sound posed an inevitable challenge, with so many voices and the fairly constant musical content. The small band was accomplished; nicely adept at the styles of writing in the show, quick to pick up musical cues and rhythmically solid. The overall look of the production was very successful indeed, with costumes that chimed with the gauntlet thrown down by the original opera's Bohemian theme. There was a pleasing sense of room for individual expression in this, both in the case of principal cast and the impressive chorus who managed to convey the necessary free spirited approach to life while being theatrically disciplined and effective onstage. Overall, there was a good balance achieved between difficult themes and fun times in this production of Rent with confident performances and a sense of great cohesion and sympathy in this talented company.

It's a children's story, right? A fairytale. Not real. Then why did I find such depth in Oyster Lane Theatre Group's production of Beauty and the Beast? Like a Jungian scholar I found something meaningful in the simplest of scenes. "This is ridiculous," I thought, as I fought back the tears during the prison scene, when Belle pleaded with Beast to at least let her say goodbye to her father. "What am I like?" I wondered, when Beast showed mercy to Gaston and I got a tingle down my spine. It may be a children's story but the creative team behind this production celebrated in style the age-old moral of good overcoming evil.  And what a team; Musical Director Patrick Clancy was in good control of a fine orchestra playing the wonderfully familiar Disney soundtrack; the accuracy and pace of the playing was greatly appreciated by an enthusiastic audience. A first time director (who showed no sign of this) had given a strong chorus great guidance; Suzanne O'Leary clearly drew from her skills as an experienced choreographer and her direction was focused and sure. Indeed, there did seem to be a vision here that the entire production team shared, what with Mark Redmond's set design which cleverly dealt with limited space. Listen up, all you space-frustrated societies: three back flats sat, side by side, each on a rotating plinth - one set us in the castle, the other side in the village - the transformation was instant and smooth, and along with the ability to fly in some scenery from above and a few well thought out touches (a warm 'lit' fire, a working contraption for Maurice) we moved seamlessly from forest to tavern, from drawing room to the castle turret. This free standing turret was impressive too, giving the sense of height - enough to convince that Gaston fell far to his death, while a quick rotation allowed for Beast to magically transform back into a prince. Along with Mr Redmond's suitable lighting design and excellent sound from Star Systems, this show ran well from a technical point of view (Good work too from Stage Manager Greg O'Leary). But it was to be a visual feast too, with no expense spared it seemed, on the hired costumes - from Lumiere actually lighting up to Belle's gigantic, and I mean gigantic yellow ball gown.

Emma Shore was a delightful Belle; her movement, as with all the cast, had been directed to mimic the animated film characters and the overall effect was very storybook like - safe in the hands of choreographer director Suzanne O'Leary. Ms Shore's singing was assured and strong and many emotional numbers were sung with great control. (Did I mention I shed a tear?) Comical moments too from this actress, especially with Neal O'Leary's Gaston, a rogue of the highest order whose dark side highlighted the actor's versatility. Le Fou (Dylan Walsh) remained the clown throughout and the tavern number 'Gaston' was performed with super energy along with imaginative choreography and a well-rehearsed chorus. The three silly girls (Niamh Cullen, April Dowdall and Gemma Hore) were wonderfully expressive, really playing up the animated side of their characters. Beast was played by Declan Taylor with the right balance of troubled sulkiness and charm; while not the tallest Beast I've ever seen, he certainly was one of the most convincing in every other way; I wanted him to see the error of his g r u m p y s e l f i s h ways; I e n j o y e d his journey with Belle and his final self discovery of the goodness inside - he could be a funny Beast too, especially when with Cogsworth (Paul Walsh) and Lumiere (Kevin Reade). They made a good comical duo and their characters were very well developed. 'Be Our Guest' with Mr Reade singing was a super number, with a respectful nod to not just the original film version, but all old Hollywood musical numbers - great work from everyone here. 'Human Again' was equally enjoyable. Caroline O'Connell was a kind and motherly Mrs Potts and singing was tender, especially for the beautiful 'Tale as Old as Time.' Feargal Miller aged well as Maurice, and scenes with Belle were tenderly performed, while his eccentricity was amusing.

Other performances of note were Maria Gore as Babette, the sexy French mop/ maid and Kellie Ann Maguire as Mme de la Grande Bouche. Andrew Smith was a dark and sinister D'Arque. Tiana Smith and Caitlin Carty shared the role of Chip - Ms Smith was simply delightful on the night I attended and I heard nothing but good reports of Ms Carty's performance too. The only glitch of the night was when Mr Taylor's microphone refused to come on during his first song (ah, live theatre), though the quality of his voice could still be appreciated. Mr Taylor's voice, especially for all other numbers was wonderful; sensitive yet powerful.

Chairperson Jackie Fitzhenry and her team are no doubt extremely proud of their show this year and I'm sure we have not seen the last of Ms O'Leary's directorial skills.

The downside to this job is to remain calm and composed no matter what. Betimes, I might indulge myself in the odd silent tear, but to do so at the end of Ulster Operatic Company's production of JC Superstar this year, would have been detrimental to my reputation, for the floodgates might have opened. "Keep it together," I told myself, "you can bawl your eyes out on the way home." Would that the cast and production team might have done the same! Tear stained elated faces everywhere in the green room; a people who had been touched by the show under the guidance of a director who, in his own words sniffled, "I should never have read the book…" Interestingly, probably the most composed person in the room was the remarkable Jeff Anderson, the actor who played JC. The twenty one year old carried himself like Jesus the man; thirty three and with literally the weight of the world on his shoulders. He did not indulge himself however; rather there was a sort of comfort in watching him develop the character. He looked the part and was charismatic, but blessing of blessings, the man can sing like JC. And how. Hitting his peak with the powerful 'Gethsemane' Mr Anderson was magnificent. If you missed this show, I am sorry for you. Let this not put the rest of the cast in the shade though, as Director Tony Finnegan fluently guided a very able and talented group. David Latham brought dignity to the troubled Judas, his simmering anger and fears bubbling away underneath; singing was very good, though possibly at times just a little out of Mr. Latham's comfort zone. Karen Hawthorne as Mary Magdalene pulled at the heartstrings, especially as she warmed into the part; 'I Don't Know How to Love Him' was sensitively sung - Ms Hawthorne has a really beautiful voice. 'Could We Start Again Please?' with Simon Cunningham as Peter was a tear jerker, but the reprise while Jesus struggled with the cross, through the auditorium (the side and not the centre aisle) was almost too much to bare. Here was evidence of Tony Finnegan's respect for the story; it took so long to get that cross onto the stage, it felt wrong to sit there and watch without helping. I know some directors like to point an accusational finger at the audience for this show, but here we were rewarded in the end for our endurance, for feeling, my God, why has everyone forsaken him? After a crucifixion where the music was slowed right down and the whole painful ordeal given an horrific reality, and people actually crying on stage - a lone boy child, perfectly cast with a beautiful face and dressed all in black came from nowhere and hugged the empty cross. I thought I'd die from sheer emotion until JC appeared once more and beckoned the boy, whose face opened into a smile and lit up the theatre, ran and embraced Jesus. Was this black clad child representative of Judas, also dressed head to toe in black? (I wondered whether this was too polar opposite to JC dressed in white) Was he representing us; was the black costume hinting at the sins we might carry? Was the child reminding us that we are still learning and doing our best? I'm not sure, but it was a mighty hopeful ending, and a balance to the earlier 'Jesus Christ Superstar' which while a great performance (show stopper standard), saw Judas in a red cape with devil girls: was Mr. Finnegan suggesting Judas was in hell?! Surely not, when the essence of the show is to see things from his point of view… Musical Director Wilson Shields and his orchestra delivered exceptional music, I could not fault it. Choreographer Ditanya McKinty was respectful of the original 1970's musical and dancers were more than capable. Paul Masterson sang really well as Simon and his dance number was well interpreted (Soooo difficult not to get up and join in!)

The apostles were a solid group. They played guitars and tin whistles on stage, which was a nice touch. The women's chorus/apostles' wives were given a nice role - even Judas had a wife who tried to comfort him and highlight his angst. The High Priests were stunning as a group - the mix of voices was solid and harmonious. Mark McGuire as Annas and Samuel Moore as Caiaphas really stood out, though all priests were excellent. Karl McGuckin was a charismatic if somewhat camp Pilate and singing was superb. With a show this emotional, one needs a pick-me-up and the humourous scene with Herod was certainly different and a lot of fun: Matthew Cavan's Freddy Mercury ('Queen Herod') was a class touch - it worked because he did it so well, seamlessly moving in and out of Queen numbers. Stage Manager Clare Donnelly did fantastic work with the impressive set from Scenic Projects (lots of hydraulics and such). Paul Hinchcliffe's lighting design made a genuine impact. Costumes from Triple C and sourced within the group were classier than your average peasant might wear, but then it's show business and should make a visual impression. Norma Spiers on props didn't disappoint for the dramatic market in the temple scene.

The pace of the show was good, but I felt we needed a breather between some of the highly emotional scenes - even a few seconds - we're only human after all. The chorus was mighty strong throughout and the use of children only enhanced the energy already on stage. A wonderful production - this group poured their heart and souls into it. I hope the memories stay with them a long time.

Every thing about Dundalk Musical Society's performance of Oliver! invited us to consider ourselves at home with their detailed and beautiful looking production in the An Táin Theatre. From the workhouse boys and their devotion to Food Glorious Food, to the terrifying Bill Sykes and his evil ways, there were many compelling chorus and individual performances against a truly atmospheric backdrop. Indeed, it was 'set, glorious set' from the start, with a mixture of elegant and down-at-heel details, which carried over into costumes, which had an authentic sensibility and colourful blend. Adam McArdle (above) was a golden- voiced, copper-haired Oliver for whom it was easy to root as his trials and tribulations unfolded.

Along the way, Craig M c H u g h was a bright and persuasive A r t f u l D o d g e r , and Tim A h e r n m o s t definitely e n j o y e d his time in Fagin's long coat.

Lorriane Quigley was a feisty and full- voiced Nancy, treading a fine line between her compassion for Oliver and loyalty to Bill. Gerry O'Hara was a terrifying and gravely-voiced Sykes, while Paudie Breen gave us a young and rather shifty Bumble. The object of his affections, Widow Corney was a shrill and very funny Patricia Savage and together she and Bumble explored the darker side of mayhem. The two Sowerberrys were Ciaran Callan and Aisling McCormack, a skeletal and dour pair who made a strong, if funereal impression in their time on stage. Aideen Ahern and Brian Halpin as Charlotte and Noah were also opposite sides of a fairly unpalatable coin, as they set out to make young Oliver's life a misery.  Bet (Ciara Quigley), an able side-kick to Nancy, had a strong, clear singing voice, as did Mrs Bedwin, Roma Mullen, whose affection for Mr Brownlow, a dignified Dominic Keating, was apparent. Indeed there were very strong performances from across the cast, not least from chorus. There was a nice company feel and focus across the stage. The characterisations in this Oliver followed a fairly well-worn path, with the players putting their stamp on a strong, traditional reading of the show. MD Mary McCague was in charge of a solid pit orchestra with nice individual performances that gave interest and colour. The violin obbligato in Reviewing the Situation was particularly elegant, and a strong brass lead set Oom Pah Pah in motion. This number had great energy and plenty of chorus interaction, busy and bawdy as required. The boys' chorus certainly looked and sounded every inch the urchin band, with a lot of individual appeal and a professional approach, relishing a chance to show off their thieving skills at they Picked a Pocket or Two. Likewise, the chorus enjoyed themselves and larger numbers such as Who Will Buy were enhanced by some very strong solo voices on singing lines. Street scenes were especially well managed, and the plot had a sense of pace and line that brought a well-worn story to life. challenges were mostly well-met, with some lovely lighting effects suggesting both the gloom of London at night and brighter days for young Oliver Twist as he made his way from the workhouse, to Fagin's boys and on to his new family, in a production that traced that journey with clarity, an array of fine voices and strong theatrical presentation.

Mercy Secondary School Marian choral Society's choice of the Tim Rice/Elton John musical version of Aida was a bold and intuitive stroke of theatrical magic which made use of a versatile and committed cast and strong production team. The story of the show is largely that of the Verdi opera of the same name, a tale of love across the boundaries of class, time and duty. The musical content is inevitably different from the opera and gave this company a chance to shine their own particular light on a slice of Egyptian history.

The title character was played by Bróna Culkeen, whose singing had a bluesy depth and expressiveness that made her a good choice for this role. She was also able as an actress to portray a strong character, a princess in disguise who thinks of her country first. Radames was Shane Kelly, who brought a very good voice to this role and much of the music suited his approach to singing and stylistic sensibility very well. His sense of uncertainty about his engagement to Amneris was well-played, as was his restraint upon realising that he loves Aida. Louis Brennaa was Zoser, father of Radames, another good voice and strong stage presence. The role of Amneris was played by Katie St. John, a very strong actress, charged with the task of beginning the play as a bit of a self-absorbed bubble-head but ending up a strong, sadder-but-wiser woman who adheres to duty with impressive effect. She was able to sing in character and also move well. Ronan Rooney was Mereb, solid and quite compelling in the role of a faithful servant who kept secrets and placed loyalty above everything. John Mulrooney was the Pharaoh, who we meet at the end of his life. Mulrooney's skill and consistency in playing a very ill ruler was a strong and pivotal aspect of the show. Kevin O'Dwyer was Aida's father Amonasro, another well- cast actor with a great look for this role. The chorus was divided largely between women as captured slaves or acolytes of Amneris, and soldiers and servants of the royal house. Their singing and facility in choreography was important in a show in which music dominates. MD Shane Farrell saw to it that the technical demands of the colourful and varied music were met, and choreographer Aoife McClafferty found moves and shapes that bridged the gap between a contemporary score and ancient setting. The staging of the show was impressive, with very effective and well-realised set that evoked an Egyptian temple and pyramidal structure. Aida the musical is bookended with scenes in a museum of antiquities, and there were some stunning set-pieces evocative of Egyptian treasures and iconic objects. Indeed, the hall in which the Marian Society perform, though a gymnasium in another life, was transformed by a splendid gold sphinx at the back, a reminder of past splendours of the life and times of the Pharaohs. Well done to all the gods and goddesses in the Marian Society, for taking on an Irish premiere and making it sing to a new and very appreciative audience. Directors Enda Burke and Aofe McClafferty clearly shared their vision with a willing and able cast and crew and brought a timeless story to vibrant life in Tuam.

I travelled to Belfast alone for New Lyric Operatic Company's production of Beauty and the Beast, but I did have assistance throughout the show in the form of enthusiastic comments from some of the younger members of the audience. When Belle appeared in her gigantic lemon coloured meringue dress, an awe struck child behind me gasped, "Aw, she's beautiful!" In your best Belfast accent, imagine, if you will, as Beast let Belle go: "Och, it's really sad, now that he's nice." Emotional turmoil aside, this show really had some eye popping effects, from the most splendiferous of costumes to the magical transformation of Beast. From the beginning director Vivian Coates made the most of a generous budget with a super set from Festival Productions, at times imposing but always impressive. Along with the talents of lighting designer Alastair Kerr, everything looked fairytale book like, from the beautiful Enchantress gracefully flying across the stage to the gargoyle like bats in the dungeon. Attention to little details from choreographer Mary MacDonagh gave the chorus a distinct animated look and I appreciated some moments of depth from Mr Coates' interpretation of the characters; Belle sadly clutched her locket during the lovely duet with Maurice and for the first time in this story I really took in the tenderness of the moment, the memory of her mother. Simple yet beautifully directed. Later, Beast with his new improved personality, shone with joy as he gave Belle his entire book collection - the library was impressive but there was a palpable sense of hope during the scene. All performers were strong indeed and most importantly, I was eager for Belle to see through Beast's faults and fall in love with him. Clare McCrory was a truly convincing Belle; with an openly expressive face that make up artist Lisa Cunningham-Black enhanced to give a real Disney look, she moved gracefully too; this was fun to watch with Gaston during 'The Proposal Song' where she was flung about in real cartoon style by the strapping lad. There was chemistry with Beast too and 'Change in Me' was Ms McCrory's best song, though singing was super throughout. Beast (Mark Adamson) was a suitable bully, who softened gradually and became quite the vulnerable decent lad.

Singing was excellent - 'No Beauty' was sung with controlled emotion, and movement as the tormented creature was convincing.

When he died I wondered if he slumped a little awkwardly, but if he did, it was worth it, for Mr Adamson was hooked to that high wire and there followed a magical transformation of beast into man. I dropped my pencil, sat more upright, realized my mouth was wide open; ten times he must have spun in the air (and he had to instigate this himself) as Wilson Shields' excellent orchestra played the familiar music of one of the most thrilling pieces of animation of modern times - dare I say that this live performance was better? Back on terra firma, he was somehow no longer a beast, but a man - and although usually people would rather Belle married Beast, the theatrics allowed us to love this prince as much. The music of course, very much made the show, with a large orchestra of high calibre musicians giving a full sound. Some moments were played with wild abandon, which was rousing, but a tad loud over dialogue however not a major issue.

Sound balance was good especially as principals were also clearly heard above the chorus. Individuals were in good hands with their MD, and everyone appeared to have a good voice; it was a pleasant surprise to have a vocally strong Maurice in Gerry McBrien, and the father daughter relationship here was tenderly treated. Characterisation was given attention by Mr Coates, particularly the curve of Gaston from likeable cocky guy to dark and dangerous man. Singing was very good; Ian Whyte has lovely mellow tones and lovely muscular arms (!), while Gregory Fox brought a breath of freshness to LeFou with a Cockney accent and clownish antics. Peter Burke gave Cogsworth life with excellent comic timing and class statements delivered with the right degree of pompousness - just enough for us to still warm to him. Gary McAlorum's Lumiere was charming throughout, and an outrageous flirt, though in all fairness, he needed to inject some testosterone into the character to balance the terribly effeminate (and a little futuristic) costume - it was the only jarring thing in both Mr McAlorum's performance and indeed the costume department. Mrs Potts seemed elderly and kindly until I realised it was Fiona Keegan, last seen belting out numbers in sexy sequenced dresses - a lovely portrayal here and 'Tale as Old as Time' was tear jerking, though I may have had something in my eye… I certainly did sniffle a tiny bit during 'Human Again' with wonderful performances from all involved, not least the young Chip who sang out really well and darn near broke my heart when he finally appeared as a real boy. Nathan Johnston played the part on the night I attended and I have it on good authority that Rhys Devlin was equally good on the alternate nights. Other performances of note were Oprah Devitt as a rather sexy Babette, Ciara Mackey as a delightfully funny Madame de la Grande Bouche and Karen Hawthrone, Kati Hall and Gemma McMeel as the three Silly Girls, all of whom seemed to move as one. Ross Chambers moved like the Child Catcher from Chitty Chitty Bang Bang for Monsieur D'Arque, which was really scary. The Children's Chorus impressed throughout. Mary MacDonagh's choreography was lively and dances were interpreted well - 'Gaston' was a lot of fun and good dancers were well used. While 'Be Our Guest' was good it didn't have a huge impact visually apart from the costumes (and a Chandelier Girl descending from above). Technically, Stage Manager Clare Donnelly had a good show and I imagine was kept rather busy. Director Vivian Coates got much out of his actors and apart from some awkwardness in the dungeon scene, used the set very well.

Production Manager David McIlwrath pulled everything together extremely well - and there was a lot to pull! This was a thoroughly engaging show, no doubt New Lyric are still buzzing from the joy of it all.

'All Shook Up' is a sort of 'Footloose' story about a town that has had the spirit sucked out of it by an oppressive female mayor. It's a nice simple story, though the plot does thicken here and there, and possibly some 'Midsummer Night's Dream' influences, with everyone fancying the wrong person and the heroine disguising herself to cause even more confusion. The show was clearly written in order to tie Elvis Presley songs together and show off some nice voices - and that's ok. But it must have substance in order to hold our attention for the evening. And indeed it did; MD Vincent Lynch and his excellent orchestra did justice to every number and singers were well supported. Highlights were the title song 'All Shook Up', and 'A Little Less Conversation' accompanying the wonderful voice of Georgina Cathcart. Chorus Mistress Jane Lynch was in command of a highly musical group; 'Can't Help Falling in Love' was a super presentation of their capabilities and perfect going into the interval. Director Alan Kinsella's interpretation of the script was great - 'tis a silly show, but funny if you can get humour out of the lines and I more than once admired this director's ability to do just that; a long goodbye between would-be lovers at a bus stop, for example, was squeezed for plenty of laughs, with a slow motion sequence and the most anticipated kiss ever. The bus itself was constructed from with the group, under Keith Mason's set design and it looked great, freestanding and convincing along with properly balanced sound effects from Vinnie Osborne. By the time people's heads popped up in the bus windows, comically in time with the song, the audience was rolling in the aisles. Damien Halpin played Chad, a cool stranger who rides into town (motorbike and all) and has all the girls swooning. Mr. Halpin was a very much tongue-in- cheek kind of heartthrob, but easy in the role. Singing was great, with 'Follow that Dream' and 'I Don't Want To' impressing most. Georgina Cathcart was a skilled performer, having to play Natalie, the tomboy girl who falls for Chad, and then disguises herself as Ed, so she can be his sidekick. But oops; Chad - who was such a big hit with the chicks - falls for Ed and confused, questions his sexuality. There were more than one or two cringe moments - purposely directed so that we would squirm in our seats - with Sandra, the curator of the local museum (Aoife Fingleton) also falling for Ed, who is really Natalie. ('Let Yourself Go' was really excellent from Ms Fingleton).The actors in these scenes were given really solid guidance and the confusion was crystal clear, as it were. A sub plot involved the characters of Dean (Pat Cullen) and Lorraine (Sarah O'Sullivan), whose sweet attempts to become an item are thwarted time and again by Dean's power-crazed mother, who happens to be the local mayor. There was chemistry between the forlorn lovers and Ms O'Sullivan really impressed with a quality voice. Gary MacKessy Sheppard was really funny as Dennis the nerd, and quite endearing too. John McEvoy played the part of widower Jim, as in his search for love he tried to dress and act like Chad. Good humour achieved here, but there was chemistry too between Jim and Sylvia, played with great comedic timing by Gillian Haslam. 'There's Always Me' was confidently performed. Joan White had fun playing the big bad mayor ('Devil in Disguise' was highly entertaining) but it turned out she was just putty on the inside after all; the comedy duo between the bully mayor and her sidekick, the mild mannered Sheriff Earl (who often opened his mouth to speak but was shot down before he could make a sound) was engaging and there were celebrations when he finally tells her what he thinks of her at the show's end, before declaring his love; great timing from Richard Finnegan and nice underplaying. Choreography by Grace McGrath was authentically 1950's and dancers were good. Numbers were consistently tight and slick and well rehearsed, and though there was a huge female majority amongst the chorus, there was balance visually. Lighting genuinely added to the mood and costumes, hair and make up suitably 1950's. A great night's entertainment, members of the audience left their seats either tittering at the memory of a joke or humming an Elvis tune. Well done Portlaoise Musical Society for get us well and truly 'shook up'!

Okay, name the show: it's got Darth Vader sharing a room with some sheep, Yul Brynner practicing his golf swing with a samurai sword, a keyboard player who gets shot, punk gentlemen, La La Loopsey dolls, the Village People, angels, a woman scorned, the Bee Gees, Jedward, Countdown, Baby Jane and a pot of boiling oil? You've guessed it: Harold Cross Tallaght's production of 'Hot Mikado', with Pat McElwain at the helm. Was it the Jedward reference that gave it away? Gilbert and Sullivan's original 1885 show 'The Mikado' has roused the creative brilliance of many, what with Mike Todd's 1939 jazz version 'The Hot Mikado', with an entirely African American cast, and then in turn David H Bell's 1980's version, 'Hot Mikado' - still set in Japan, but styled in 1940's America; the zoot suits, the Runyon type language and Rob Bowman's excellent score, full of jazz and swing. Try as I might, I could see no link to the punk era, but it was there in costumes and make up terms at least, for this production. While I appreciate the desire to bring something fresh to the show, it was perhaps confusing for those unfamiliar with any version of the story. Hired from the Costume Room, there was a very conscious move away from the Guys and Dolls look, with the Gentlemen of Japan dressed - uncomfortably, it seemed to me - in shoulder pads and oversized cummerbunds. It was distracting because I was wondering what point was being made, but also they looked so very bizarre. Out of context some of the costumes looked fantastic, particularly during the large ensemble number 'Let the Throng our Joy Advance', where colour and life simply burst onto the stage, with every conceivable shade and style and the impressive makeup and wig design of Ali Murphy. Yum Yum looked stunning in a simple white slip and gown, and a pair of white ballet shoes as she sang 'Sun and I' - the look enhanced greatly by Darren Keane's lighting design. It's possible that there was in fact, no rhyme nor reason to the outrageous rigouts (though I did enjoy the La La Loospey/punk look of the three little maids,) and that it was all just a bit of fun. Pat McElwain paid tribute to many great comedic styles during this production - from Buster Keaton to Monty Python, and once you got used to it, it worked.  The audience may have been a little reticent at the beginning while Koko (Colin Hughes) made his way on stage, heard before seen, and with running sound effects from sound designer Vinny Osborne (whereupon he encountered Darth Vader and the sheep). When he appeared - I thought he was a ringer for Elton John during his 'I'm Still Standing' days - Mr Hughes was funny. It was through sheer hard work; like the first time I sat through a Jim Carey movie, I swore it couldn't make me laugh. But, by God, he works hard, and he wears you down, and laugh I did.

This show may have had a lot of silliness, but it also had some inspired moments of comic genius: Using the music from the TV programme 'Countdown', while an anagram of 'Mikado U Rock!' spelled out some insults was just one of these. Whatever your humour preferences, there is no doubt that the production team were very much on top of things; Laura Martin's choreography had a modern twist that suited both the production and the cast, adapting for stage space where necessary and allowing for clownish antics elsewhere. Much of the dancing was excellent and everyone was well instructed. I was impressed to see Mikado himself (William Lacey in top form) tap dance so competently. Dermot O'Callaghan's excellent orchestra played brilliantly - rousing here, tender and gentle there, and as always Mr O'Callaghan's guidance was evident. Andrew Linnie brought focus to what had been a somewhat distracted men's chorus for 'Wand'ring Minstrel', and his voice continued to impress during 'What I'll Never Do'; both Mr Linnie and Shona Henneberry, playing Yum Yum, managed to get humour out of their scenes, while still convincing us of the chemistry between them. Ms Henneberry was delightful in the part, confident in voice and sincere in portrayal. Amy Penston as Pitti Sing and Tracy Armstrong as Peep Bo brought a lovely mix of voices for 'Three Little Maids'. 'Swing a Merry Madrigal' was pure joy, as were all numbers by Mary-Beth Jennings as Katisha. And she was a very funny drunk. Paul Laycock brought personality to Pooh Bah. Many personalities; his portrayal of his various offices was brilliantly performed. Along with Mark Keegan as Pish Tush and Koko, the problems of the town of Titipu were never going to be in safe hands! Damien Douglas was the soloist in 'Braid the Raven Hair' and his voice was rightly used wherever else was possible. This was a super cast - they even had amongst them a Special Olympic silver medalist, Mary Gavin. Direction was excellent and there were no apologies from Pat McElwain; he knew what he wanted and how he wanted it done, and he got it from his talented cast. Everyone on stage embraced the vision, and the audience got a great night's entertainment. At the end of the day, isn't that what we all want?

A car crash blocked the road into Carnew. I didn't know of an alternate route and it was pushing on for 7.45pm. I had been sitting in my car for maybe twenty minutes and I was beginning to panic. To cut the story a little, the keyboard player, who was parked just behind me, was my saviour. The guitar player was behind him. Another route was found and we arrived just in the nick of time. Problem if the adjudicator doesn't make it, but half the band? That's right: JC Superstar, four in the band - if you don't count MD Lar Duffy who also played keyboards. Naturally a brass section would have been preferable, but if you're limited by your budget, keyboards can be effective. And indeed they were. The music was really good and players were top class; strong percussion, crunchy guitar solos and crucially, keyboards that could handle anything from the flute solo in 'Damned for all Time' to the violins in 'John 19:41', not to mention the effects in between. It wasn't the same as having the real instruments there, and certainly some numbers suffered for it, but it could have been a whole lot worse. Singing was excellent, with a really well trained and talented chorus backing up some very impressive soloists. JC was played by Padraig D'Arcy who performed the part humbly, and with sincerity. Singing was a treat; well-controlled falsetto added to the sadness of 'Poor Jerusalem'; 'Gethsemane' was utterly beautiful; the sparks that flew between JC and Judas during 'What's the Buzz' set up the story well. Indeed the drama between these two was exceptionally well handled by director Michael Dunbar. The gutsy raw sound of David Cox's Judas more than highlighted the torment of the character; his desperation in temple was clear and his suicide - so very demanding of an actor - was given full energy. 'Superstar' was a highlight, with what was in effect, a wicked rock concert! Choreographer Julie Kinsella interpreted both the music and the director's vision very well. 'Superstar' had so much going on and excellent dancing from some fairy-like angels. While 'Simon's Song' was fun, it could have been groovier, though the undercurrent of an angry oppressed people was clearly felt. 'Hosanna' was jubilant and 'Herod's Song' with Charleston style dancing really worked. Director Michael Dunbar played Herod with full on comedic energy. The beautiful sound of Therese Canavan's Mary Magdalene brought tenderness and balanced the raw emotion between Judas and JC, while the Apostles were a strong backup. Brian O'Gorman's Simon was rebellious and volatile and singing was really good. Paul Doran was solid as Peter. 'Could We Start Again Please', a duet with Mary Magdalene was sung with sincerity. Pilate's character was given a lot of weight by Brendan Fitzpatrick; his sense of pending doom was subtly expressed and with the musical competence of both Pilate and JC, the trial was an emotional ride for all. The Priests delivered a super combination of versatile voices and range of personalities - time and again Mr. Dunbar's work as an 'actor's director' was evident. Though not in his natural range, Brian Kelly managed the part of Caiaphas with great control, while John Young's strong voice really suited the part of Annas. Tony Barry's impressive set suggested at once: a desert, a Jewish village, the pillars of the temple, the lofty heights of Pilate's quarters. Along with the intuitive lighting design of Kevin McEvoy, the visual imagery of this production was consistently exciting and authentic. A bright blue sky in one scene became a steely grey background to hooded figures surrounding Judas; Pilate was given purple background hues and the lepers were doused in green. The final picture, with a beautifully lit cross, dissolved into sepia tones. Props, costumes and hair were authentic and while the chorus didn't come across as over colourful, there was life. Mary Magdalene's rusty red dress made her less of a harlot and more of a woman. Michael Dunbar was in no doubt as to the range of emotions he wished to bring his audience through; Judas' frustration was intensely felt and scenes with Jesus were treated as more than black and white arguments. Oh! The year is young and so many musical societies will have me a blubbering wreck by the end of it. But it is so very worth it. The road out of Carnew, now cleared of the crash, was paved with good intentions.

Like Harry Potter discovering Diagon Alley, there magically appeared a Dickensian London street, in a theatre somewhere down Gordon Street way, in the heart of Clonmel town. Against an authentically London backdrop, it looked like a purpose built street, not a stage at all. It worked perfectly for the show too: centrally positioned steps, a bridge that led on both sides to apparently tall buildings with leaded windows and warm fires glowing inside. It came apart and re-hinged itself effortlessly to form Mr. Brownlow's sitting room; a freestanding chimney breast, a swinging candelabra and a washing line - and it was Fagin's Den. This was a set that was designed by someone who knew the stage, really understood what was required - the nitty gritty of the smooth running of a show. So it made sense when I discovered the designer was Diarmuid Vaughan, who had already impressed me on stage as Fagin. Mr. Vaughan was a knowledgeable performer who had learned a thing or two; how to convey a thought subtly, how to squeeze humour out of every bit of dialogue, how to interact naturally, how to move with conviction. While 'Pick a Pocket' was fun, 'Reviewing the Situation' saw him connect fully with the audience (and the band) - it must be a bizarre sensation to hold an audience in the palm of your hand. He wasn't the only engaging performer however; St. Mary's Choral Society have oodles of talent it seems, not least the children who played principal roles. Oliver was shared by Harry Lane and Henry Buttimer - I had the pleasure of experiencing Mr. Buttimer's take on the character, and he was really talented. 'Where is Love' was delightful and MD Danny Carroll was a solid support, along with a seven-piece orchestra, that produced a great sound. I missed Richie Crowe play Dodger, but did get to see Bill Fitzgerald on the night I attended. He had worked hard, and challenging things for a young lad, like a Cockney accent and dance steps, were impressive. I have it on good authority that both Harry Lane and Richie Crowe were equally entertaining. Sheena Fennessy brought colour and life to Nancy and singing was strong and tuneful. 'Oom Pah Pah!' was full of cheeky joy while 'As Long As He Needs Me' was beautifully sincere. Nancy and Bill were a stormy couple and Tim Landers was dark and dangerous as Sykes. 'My Name' was scary! It's all well and good having a strong cast, but they need guidance, and director Maureen Walsh provided that by the bucketful. Here and there, seemingly little touches built up to give this production an authentic Dickensian feel; someone could get a shave on the street; children watched a Punch and Judy show; the Sowerberrys were drunks, and funny with it. Along with strobe lighting, their comical scenes were given a sort of old black and white movie touch during 'That's Your Funeral', which, once it became clear what the intention was, worked well enough (though possibly a little too much strobe.) There were a lot of brilliant children in this show and they all got a chance to shine. Choreographer Gillian Hewitt Fitzgerald interpreted the music well and used the layout on the stage to advantage. No matter the number involved, everyone was incorporated where possible, and everywhere there was bustle and life. 'Oom Pah Pah!' started in slow motion before speeding up into real time, highlighting the bawdiness in the tavern. Chorus Mistress Laura Cotter got a lot out of her people, children and adults alike, with 'Food Glorious Food' as engaging as 'Who Will Buy'. Ian Purcell was a rather nasty Mr. Bumble, who brought the fear of God to the workhouse, when he wasn't dealing with the Widow Corney. Bernie Lonnergan could be mean spirited too, but comically flirtatious with it. 'I Shall Scream' revealed a quality voice. St. Mary's chairperson George Barry got a lot of humour out of Dr. Grimwig's lines. Ause Braike's Noah was a full on bully and Emma Sunderland played Charlotte with a good sense of fun. Bet's character was padded out properly by Lisa O'Brien and Grainne Vaughan brought a quiet grace to Mrs. Bedwin, while Timmy O'Dwyer was a dignified Mr. Brownlow. The show ran smoothly enough under Stage Manager George Barry and against the set, props and costumes were authentic. Some great sound effects added to this - horses on cobblestones and dogs barking, and lighting enhanced the mood well. With the creative collaboration of a really good team, St. Mary's Choral Society really did produce a little bit of magic.

It is probably fairly well known amongst show folk, that the musical 'Sweet Charity' is based on writer director Federico Fillini's 1957 movie 'Nights of Cabiria', the story of a naïve prostitute searching for love but finding only heartbreak. The 1966 Broadway musical, (and later film with Shirley MacLaine) which sees the character Charity as the misguided but hopeful heroine, only ever hints at the seedy side of her life, and instead presents her as a dance hall hostess, or taxi dancer - perhaps so that audiences might be more comfortable with the idea that we could become so attached to a girl who sells herself. Director Arthur McGauran's production for Coolmine Musical Society made no apologies for the chosen profession of Charity. In fact, the point was clearly made: this 'aint no job for a sweet girl, with a strong and quite disturbing presentation of the hostess girls outside the Fandango Ballroom, lined up and roped off while men assessed who they wanted to dance with. And while they did, the girls touted their wares shamelessly (except for Charity, who was always distracted by her own thoughts). I wondered about this blatant disregard for the rose-coloured version of the 60's, and then I accepted Mr McGauran's interpretation; it was a dirty business, women were abused - let's not gloss over that fact. Otherwise, why would Charity, lovely thing, want to get out so badly? So it was against this background - with superb performances by the hostess girls, in particular Claire MacNamee as Helene and Kirstin Smith as Nickie - that Jennifer McGann built her character; with a subtle but decent New York accent and excellent comic timing, it was very easy to warm to this Charity. She was bright, bubbly and optimistic throughout, and her heartbreak was truly emotional. Rory Robinson as Oscar, brought hope to the story just in time for Charity; his performance was energetic and engaging and his comical style was easy. I loved them together and with solid direction from Mr McGauran, there were many lovely moments, particularly in Barney's diner as they (back-to-back) professed their love. Musical Director Caitriona Ni Threasaigh guided extremely well from upstage, with her back to the action most of the time. Numbers were played well, and apart from being a little timid during changes of scene, the sound was great. Eoghan Connolly as chorus master had trained his charge well; 'I'm a Brass Band' was full of energy and 'I love to Cry at Weddings' was a rousing number - both shone over 'Rhythm of Life', which while highlighting a talented chorus, never really got 'big', though Daddy Brubeck (Paul Holloway) impressed. Jennifer MacGann's strong voice handled all numbers with comfort. Rory Robinson sang well, solid and easy. Frank Beadle as Vittorio blew us away with 'Too Many Tomorrows'. What with the accent and all, I might have been listening to the likes of Jose Carreras. 'Something Better' really highlighted the talents of Kirstin Smith (Nickie) and Claire MacNamee (Helene) and that number, with Charity, once again hit home the rotten life of the 'hostess'. The chorus in 'Big Spender' got very involved and gave the number all the steam and dirt it needed to work. Carmen (Alison Dennan) and Rosie (Niamh Flynn) also stood out. Choreographer Brian Keogh's interpretation was very authentic; we were sent to the 1950's good and proper, every time. 'Rich Man's Frug' was a well-moved number, with good dancers well instructed; the whole number had strong visual impact, as did 'Rhythm of Life'. 'Big Spender' was as seedy as it was sexy. 'Something Better' had plenty to keep it interesting, with an almost 'I Feel Pretty' influence. Arthur MacGauran designed the set too, and this was effective, built from within the group, which is always impressive. Costumes and makeup were authentic as were props. Other performances of note were Robbie Kennedy as Hermann; rough on the outside, soft on the inside, he really made 'Cry at Weddings' a fun number. Laura Aspil looked every inch like Ursula and brought humour to the role too. Steve Cowie and Justin Parkes were strong as the NY policemen, and their scene was entertaining. Indeed, it was a strong cast, and every opportunity was taken to highlight this, with individuals taking on minor roles throughout. All in all, it was a thought provoking and highly entertaining evening.

show_raw: most definitely FOUND their feet in the
review_text: beautiful Siamse Tire theatre, with a vivid and emotional reading of West Side Story at the end of November. In addition to a strong cast of principal players and very committed chorus, this production boasted excellent choreography and well- trained voices. Aidan O'Carroll did double duty as Director and Musical Director, and there was much to admire in the fruits of his labours. Colette Maguire Jensen and Aisling O'Carroll were responsible for choreography and this was a strong and binding thread running through this show. This is an ambitious show, and it was good to see that so many of its challenges were being met by an obviously dedicated backstage force. Onstage, Aisling O'Carroll as Maria was one of the most accomplished voices in the cast, and a strong actor and dancer as well. Eric Heaslip as Tony brought wonderfully sustained singing to the mean streets of New York, and his buddy Riff (Darren Mullery) was a born leader, with a consistent and commanding stage presence. Aki O'Rourke as Action was an edgy sidekick and fellow member of the Jets, the gang whose Office Krupke was compact of comedy and camp. Bernardo was Sean Binder, a cool and aloof character, in contrast to fiery Anita whose emotional journey was brought to vivid life by Ann Flood. Chino was played by Timmy Dow, and he along with the other Sharks made a strong and coherent bid for equality in the city which was so effectively portrayed by a series of large projections of streetscapes on the back wall of the set. This device was just one aspect of a very detailed and technically ambitious show. While this West Side Story rested firmly on the shoulders of a largely very young cast and chorus, there was a great deal of experience in evidence onstage, not least from the adult characters, including Niall Fitzgerald as a world-weary, sympathetic Doc, Pierce Heaslip as Schrank, oily and gruff, Tom Bailey as a long-suffering Officer Krupke, and Noel King as an enthusiastically dapper and ultimately ignored Glad Hand. One interesting aspect of this production was the fact that Jets and Sharks were not always easily or obviously possible to tell apart, and this might have been part of a message about the essential fact that underneath it all, we are much the same. The setting of the Dream Sequence, compelling and often very beautiful, was part of this message. Another strong message which resonated in a contemporary sense, was the essential frustration of being young in a divided and pressurised society. This was splendidly brought out in LOST's interpretation of the song Cool, which was compact of edgy choreography and the kind of keen focus that only very young, very talented players can give to a show. This was, I believe, LOST's first production, and I'm very certain that it won't - and shouldn't be - their last.

It was a case of Into the Woods and Onto the Stage for Stagebratz Musical Society in November.

This was the company's first time in the lovely Mermaid Theatre, and with a simple, versatile set they brought the world of fairy tales to life in new and surprising ways as only this big, challenging show can.

It takes lots of characters to populate those Woods, and the company took a vigorous and lively approach, combined with consistent and colourful characterisations. Our guide through the Woods was narrator Gary Finnegan, who brought a great rhythmic vitality to his observations and interjections. He introduced us to a well- cast large assemblage of characters, all of whom had to portray two sides of fairytale life; the one we know from the stories, and the clear-eyed, cockeyed look this show takes at the truth beyond the Woods. Kerry Smith as Cinderella brought an attractive singing voice and expressive stage presence to the role. Mark Flynn as Jack was very funny, slow of voice and wide-eyed at the twists of fate in his story. Grainne Donnelly was his long-suffering mother, a performance that captured the impatience and also indulgence of this character.

Rory Dunne and Joanne Keeling were the Baker and his Wife. Both were strong singers, able to put tremendous emotion into sung as well as spoken lines. They portrayed a strong relationship which was tested on many levels very well indeed. Patrice Brady, Niamh Kavanagh and Kethleen Lyons were Cinderella's Stepmother and step sisters Lucinda and Florinda respectively.

All were really enjoyable to watch and enjoyed these wicked roles. Lucinda and Florinda were an especially comic pairing, as were Julian Capolei and Andrew Carstairs as Raspunzel's Prince and Cinderella's Prince. They really brought the concept of "Agony" to life for us, and got well-deserved laughs for their pains. Andrew Carstairs was also a terrifically dapper and smooth-talking wolf, who met his match in Bronagh McLoughlin as a silvery-voiced Red Riding Hood, a very strongly skilled actress and singer. Naomh Penston was Witch, a feisty portrayal rooted by a great Bronx accent and wonderfully rich and many-layered singing voice.

Mary Doyle was compelling as Cinderella's Mother, Dereck Hamilton was a gruff- voiced and very intriguing Mysterious Man. Caoimhe Cashin was a beautifully voiced and terrifically off-the-wall (out of the tower?) Rapunzel, a gleeful study in neuroses if ever there was one. Theresa Sheekey was Granny and also the Giant, Denis Healey was Cinderella's Father, Dylan Kelly was the Steward, Ciara Kennedy was Snow White and Holly Fitzmaurice was Sleeping Beauty, smaller roles that nonetheless were keenly portrayed and wonderfully costumed. Indeed, the costumes across the show were apt and evocative, as was the set which served many functions across the show and provided an effective backdrop to the magic action.

Sondheim's music is intricate and wordy, essentially through-composed and the company were very well drilled by MD Antonio Cafolla and Producer/director Barry Kavanagh.

The direction brought out the wit and inter- connectedness of the stories, and a very accomplished band provided a colourful and concise canvas for the music. There were some especially lovely moments provided by a cast of Stagebratz children, who on occasion were a flock of birds, among other things and who lent very solid singing support to the adult cast. I'm fairly convinced that anyone who went Into the Woods with Stagebratz in Bray came out the other side lighter of step and heart, believing in magic just a little more for having seen this energetic and multi- faceted jewel of a production.

I've heard of dancers marrying stage managers. I heard of crew members marrying leading ladies. I've many times heard of choreographers marrying directors… but a choreographer marrying a director on the set of the show, in the theatre, two weeks before opening night? That's dedication!

There is no doubt that director Brian Logan was in a romantic frame of mind for Ballywillan Drama Group's production of The Sound of Music. The chemistry between stuffy old Captain Von Trapp (Alan McClarty) and Maria (Laura Douglas) was mind blowing; a wonderfully heated argument; a series of does he-doesn't he moments; a woman scorned and an innocent feisty nun desperately deluding herself she's not in love.

Ah. The Sound of Music…what's not to love? I smiled like a fool throughout some of the numbers. I was totally taken in by the children. Dotes. Their rendition of 'The Sound of Music' was utterly beautiful; Ashling Reynolds' voice as eldest sibling Liesl blended perfectly with her sister Louisa's (Amy Rankin). All of the children could sing, and there was no compromise on cuteness either; Gretl (Anna McGinley) evoked many a tear when she sang us 'Goodbye' at the end of a tiring party. Marta (Niamh Cunning) was equally talented as were the boys Sam Magilton and Jack Ferguson playing Friedrich and Kurt, while Annie Levy as perceptive Brigitta delivered her lines with confidence.

The children worked really well together and choreographer Sharon Logan ('the missus') had an eye for drama; starting with 'Do Re Mi' appearing as if it were in the schoolhouse, to a delightful rendition of 'Lonely Goatherd' with a full family of puppets created by props mistress Karen Hunter and cleverly incorporated into the action. Ms Reynolds' Liesl was certainly cast well as the girl on the cusp of womanhood; 'Sixteen Going on Seventeen' with Adam Goudy's Rolf had just the right balance of innocence and daring, with sweet flirtations and a stolen kiss. Ms Reynolds' singing was wonderful too and highlighted wherever possible by MD Eric Boyd, whose band well supported a strong chorus of mostly women, doubling as nuns and lovely ladies - giving the make up department a run for their money.

While I questioned the overuse of entrances and exits through the auditorium by Mr Logan, I did enjoy his style and interpretation. The Captain's grief was given attention, particularly through his unlikely relationship with Elsa, charmingly played by Maxine McAleenon; he is more at ease with her and the clownish Max (David Ferguson), but there is an obvious underlying desperation to be distracted by anything other than face his demons. It's a pity in a way that the show doesn't go deeper into this grief, especially in this production, as Mr McClarty played the part so naturally. Laura Douglas openly portrayed the unwelcome emotions experienced by Maria, and the blossoming relationship had real credibility.

(Spontaneous applause when they finally kissed.) This would have delighted Sr. Margaretta, played with subtle humour by Evie Ferguson - indeed all the nuns worked well together and 'Maria' was an enjoyable highlight along with cranky Sister Berthe (Louise McClarty) and Sr Sophia (Margaret Brownlow). The Mother Abbess? Practically beatified: 'Climb Every Mountain' exceeded expectations; Olive Hemphill's beautiful voice rang out brilliantly to a rousing audience reaction. It couldn't all be sweetness and light of course, and just when Georg and Maria thought it was safe to settle down, along came the Nazis (now here was a good place to have them traipsing through the aisles, unsettling the audience). Harry Stinson played the nasty villain Herr Zeller with zeal, and I suspect pompous butler Franz (Tom Waddell) was not far behind him. A solid performance too from Audrey Branagh as Frau Schmidt.

Brian Logan was also responsible for the set and lighting design, which not only looked impressive but allowed for smooth scene changes under the management of SM David Wray. The Abbey was resplendent with arches and wrought iron gates, stonework and large looming windows. The Von Trapp house was grand, with lighting announcing whether it was day or night, stormy or fine.

What a team - and I believe there was a second group of talented Von Trapps who played alternate nights (Leon Woods, Hannah McAleenon, Jasmine Gardiner and Erin Wilson). Word is, they were just as good! Collaborative efforts? Between Mr and Mrs Logan and the rest of the production team, they are to be congratulated on a fine production. Oh,

Beauty and the Beast is the show of the day it seems, with many of Ireland's musical societies opting for the timeless musical this year. You might think an adjudicator would get bored after a time, but that is not the case. I once had to adjudicate a group of 56 children, all reciting the poem 'Sir Winter'. That, was difficult. 'Beauty and the Beast' is an altogether different story. For a start, I haven't seen the same set of costumes yet - where are these fantastic garments coming from? What fun the set and lighting designers are having in societies around the country; what challenges for production teams; what budgetary nightmares for committees! More than ever in these hard times I am amazed with what can be done, and none more so than Boyle's production of this show. Ann Kielty was limited in the numbers of her orchestra, and while initially I wondered if the sound would be enough, I soon changed my mind; excellent musicians in good hands brought the Disney score to life and really enhanced the drama and mood of this lovely show. Highlights for me from a vocally strong chorus were 'Gaston' and 'Be Our Guest'. Vivienne Caldbeck Moran's choreography was imaginative and visually exciting and she managed with the limited stage space very well. For the most part, dances were well executed, especially the dance of the tankards in 'Gaston' and of course those great numbers 'Be Our Guest' and 'Human Again'. 'Kill the Beast' was dramatic and the musical interpretation really highlighted the change in mood here. Director Frank O'Mahoney's set design allowed for the numbers of the large cast on a small stage, with nicely painted backdrops and good lighting, bringing scenes to life. Costumes were hired from Clara Musical Society and looked great, though Belle's peasant dress was a little too Wizard of Oz like for me. The first time too, that I've seen costume muscles on Gaston, played with delightful cockiness by Danny Doherty. This performer consistently brought energy and confidence to every scene. Natasha Fitzpatrick was charming as Belle, with 'Is this Home' her best number, tugging at the heartstrings a little. Sean McGuire's Beast, while more comfortable with the more well mannered side of his personality, played well against Belle and there was nice chemistry between the two. Frank O'Mahoney's direction was solid and there were some lovely touches; freeze frames in the village highlighted a good chorus; dramatic moments in the enchanted forest when the wolves attacked Belle; the fading rose as the focus of Belle's attention while Beast transformed into the Prince. The trio of Cogsworth (Ivan Moran), Lumiere (Ronan Smith) and Mrs Potts (Bernadine Casserley) were given good guidance and they worked very well as a comedy trio against an increasingly perplexed Beast (women, eh?). There was plenty of comedy, with Lumiere getting a lot of laughs, though not always for the scripted lines! Paul Kielty was a super little Chip, he really brought personality to the character and singing was excellent. Ms Casserley as Mrs Potts sang a simply beautiful 'Tale as Old as Time' while Elaine McCarthy kept things light and funny as Mme de la Grande Bouche. Other performances of note were Stephen Tighe as the eccentric Maurice and Oriel Regan, sexy as the French maid, who did an excellent job in enticing Lumiere. Gavin Ward was clownish and funny as LeFou while the Silly Girls - four of them, had a combination of good voices and unity of purpose necessary to bring out the comedy here. On the night I attended - with no less than five enthusiastic children (not all mine), the buzz in the air was palpable. Boyle expected a good show and they were not disappointed.

Castlerea Enterprise Hub The lovely town of Castlerea was All Shook Up in February, and Castlerea Musical Society was the source of that disturbance. Performing in a new venue and featuring some players new to the stage altogether, it was Roustabouts to the ready as this lively and very witty production worked its Blue Suede magic. Daniel Doherty was the hip-swivellin' Chad, by all appearances an experienced rocker who relished his role as the heartthrob who never stands still. Of the many hearts he captured, none was more determined than Natalie as played by Julie Connolly, a clear-voiced and likeable actress whose transformation into the ever-so-slightly dodgy Ed was uncanny to say the least. Her amazing ability to drop her voice by at least an octave may have been what captivated Miss Sandra, played with confident allure by Katy Sheridan. Another voice to look out for in future came from Tricia Collins, who played Lorraine with innocent enthusiasm, capturing the heart of the initially uptight Dean, played with growing confidence by a winsome Niall Tully. No-nonsense Sylvia was Jacqueline Kenny, whose flexible and blues-tinged voice was perfect for this role, to which she also brought a flair for comedy. And comedy was definitely to the fore in David Cooke's interpretation of Jim Haller, a physical and emotional portrayal that was compact of subtlety and an almost frightening flair for bad-boy moves. Robert Reid was an unfailingly nerdy Dennis, a portrayal that balanced heart and soul on a knife edge of youthful angst. There was no larger cheer than for the moment when he wins the affections of sexy Sandra. And there was no louder laugh in a production full of them, than for the line "Zip it, Roustabout", part of an unfailingly comic portrayal of Mayor Matilda by Clare Kelly. The actress had only to appear onstage for the giggles to begin, and her performance of Devil in Disguise, aided by a game chorus in over-the-top angel and devil outfits, was a high point. I'm sure that Earl, played by a strong and mostly silent John Callaghan, knew exactly what he was getting when his patience was rewarded in the end. His declaration of love when it finally came was worth the wait.  All Shook Up was supported by an exuberant orchestra presided over with good precision by Shane Farrell. Director Niall Heaney certainly exploited his able cast's strengths, and a succession of comic crossovers when various chorus groups fall (literally) victim to Chad's hip-swivelling reflex, became an increasingly outlandish leit-motif. The stage of the Hub is broad and deep and the cast made full use of this, with choreography appropriately rooted in the 50's and some very effective and detailed set pieces, especially for those scenes set in the abandoned fair ground. Certainly, the was nothing in the way of detail or polish abandoned in this production, and this well-supported show gave us all One Night in which the Heartbreak Hotel gave way to an evening for everyone from Hound Dogs to Teddy Bears to enjoy.

Clever people, those Cecilians; in the foyer of the theatre, on display for all to see, was a vast array of hats - pink hats, white hats, large hats, dainty hats, hats with feathers, hats with lace… and all of them handmade by local school children. This venture, along with some art competitions, got the community talking about 'Hello Dolly' and hopefully ensured full houses for the society - because they well deserved it. Musical Director Noel Lennon oversaw an excellent orchestra. 'Put On Your Sunday Clothes' was just the start of the great big show numbers, which highlighted a strong able chorus. Brian Henry as Cornelius and Mikey O'Gorman as Barnaby were very solid here too, with impressive dancing and singing, not to mention energetic humour. Grainne Harnett was confident as the beautiful widow Irene Molloy and her performance, especially in comic scenes was excellent. Along with sweet Minnie (Kim Burke) there was a nice balance of personalities and all situations these four found themselves in was consistently engaging. Jean McGlynn's Dolly was outstanding; was it the actress or the character that was a charismatic engaging woman? I couldn't tell, but well done Director Des Henn on super casting; Dolly was delightful and funny, but when she sang 'Parade Passes By' in a simple spotlight I was totally drawn into the moment; she begged to be free of her grief, yet there was no self indulgence here. 'Hello Dolly' was striking - costumes were magnificent - and a big highlight was the preamble to this, the 'Waiters Gallop'. What super interpretation by choreographer Barbara Meaney. A really strong dancing troupe was very well employed and we had trolleys and chickens flying around, people somersaulting, break dancing and jumping in perfect harmony - great fun for an appreciative audience! Martin McNeilis warmed his way into our hearts as Horace, hard and grumpy on the outside but oh so soft on the inside. Dolly played him like a fiddle and the chemistry between these two was part of the fun. Ms. McGlynn's voice was class. Des Henn also designed the set, which included a well employed apron and highlighted strong directing skills too - the chaos after the Polka Dance competition into a prison cell was handled smoothly; a comical, animated piece of theatre that travelled well while the crew calmly changed the set behind. Back screen projections enhanced the set, though weren't always necessary. Mike Finneran's lighting design was special; he seemed to have the ability to hone right in on the mood and tone of the scene. Other performances of note were the couple Ambrose (Steven O'Brien) and Ermengarde (Sarah Allen), delightful in their admiration of each other - Ermengarde's crying was always funny, no matter how often she did it. Olivia Parkinson brought good humour to the brassy Ernestina - and a great accent! Rob O'Leary carried the role of the Judge with grounded authority. Individual roles taken on by this chorus were handled with confidence. Indeed, time and again I was impressed by the attention given by Mr. Henn to his cast and collaboration with both the choreographer and the MD was clear. Time and effort was put into sourcing the properly authentic props and costumes, while hair and make up was spot on. What glamour! What fun! What will they do next?

There was a lot to admire in the Claremorris Musical Society production of Calamity Jane. Well-cast, this production gave scope for strong performers to put their stamp on their roles, while keeping to a very traditional interpretation of this classic tale of the course of true love in Deadwood, South Dakota. Vivienne Lee as Calamity certainly looked the part, resembling Doris Day with blonde hair and a strong rhythmic approach to song and movement. Ciaran Kiely as Bill Hickock began the show with the requisite sarcastic disdain for 'Clam', warming well by the end and bringing a fine singing voice to his romantic interests. The other romantic pairing, Michael Goulding and Mary Dempsey as Danny and Katie had a nice chemistry onstage and negotiated their romance with sure-footed acting and harmonious singing. Gearoid Clesham as Francis Fryer exhibited a keen comic talent and a very good pair of legs. His sense of timing and nuance was spot-on. Sarah Farragher as Susan was engaging and her brief singing appearance revealed a strong theatrical voice. James Coen was a much put-upon Henry Miller, and his amusing angst and bluster added colour to the saloon scenes. Liam Newton as Rattlesnake was another source of colour and laconic humour, and Richard Henigan as 'Doc' Pierce is also an able comic and solid performer. The male chorus did very competent double and triple duty as soldiers, cowboys and stage door Johnnies, and the object of their affections was an entertaining, if somewhat jaded Adelaide Adams played by Angela Prenty. The Golden Garter Girls who would have cause to emulate Adelaide were part of an enthusiastic chorus, whose singing was a very strong component of this production. The cast were well supported and surrounded by a well-designed set, the movements of which made for swift scene changes. Sound and lighting also contributed to a nicely complete and put-together 'look'. The set pieces were well-painted, with strong texture and colour. One or two anachronisms in small props might have worried a very picky observer, but overall there was both ease and detail of presentation. Two areas to the side of the stage were also used, and this provided variety and interest. This is a relatively small stage, and a fairly big cast, and movement on and off the stage for chorus numbers was often en masse, which was managed well, if somewhat lacking in realism. There was a delightful young chorus, and the children were very well-used for specific scenes, with logic to their presence onstage and a tremendous sense of professionalism and commitment. Choreography was designed for the available forces and augmented the musical strength of the show, ably presided over by MD Deirdre Lee. As much as anything, this production conveyed a good feel for the Deadwood community and also care taken with the main elements of strong characters, comic energy and musical lift. There was an impressive sense of company in this production, with everyone onstage engaged and engaging, committed to telling a great story with wonderful music and having a marvellous time doing it. I was transported to the Wild West in all it's quirky glory, and wouldn't be at all surprised if there is somewhere in the nether regions of America a place called Claremorris, South Dakota!

society_raw: St. Brendan's Choral and Dramatic Society
review_text: St. Brendan's Choral and Dramatic Society decided to be utterly Footloose this year, and their efforts paid off handsomely. A strong cast that mixed young and less young was the key to their success, along with innovative choreography and well- drilled dancers. The society was founded in 1945 and are clearly enjoying an influx of talent as well as having built a strong sense of a creative community in lovely Loughrea. Leading the charge in the non-dancing town of Bomont was Conor Hanley as Ren McCormack. He had the requisite twinkle toes, and a versatile voice with range and agility. Louise Colohan was very effective as the wild child Ariel, and a strong ensemble singer and dancer as well. Her relationship with her father, the reverend Shaw Moore, was deftly played. He was John Kelly, a strong actor possessed of an equally strong voice. Also in very good voice was Madeline Fleming as his wife Vi, a sympathetic portrayal from an equally adept actress. Ren's mother Ethel was Siobhán Murphy, who forged a really good onstage relationship with her troubled son and acquitted herself well as a singer too. Jonathan Hopper was Willard, awkwardly endearing and very funny as the suitor of Rusty, played by a strong-voiced Helen O'Donoghue. Her comic sensibility was spot-on, and she was ably assisted by girlfriends Urleen and Wendy Jo, strong singers as well, played by Niamh Mahoney and Joanne Kelly. This trio enjoyed themselves immensely and were pitch-perfect in their characterisation of American High School girls. The 'baddie' of the piece was Daire Curley as Chuck Cranston, handsome but not very nice to Ariel. This was a strong performance, and scenes with the other boys in town were very well done. For these he was joined by Daniel Walsh as Lyle and Padraig Larkin as Travis. Their singing and dancing was impressive, as was their sense of comedy in ensemble. Another strong comic turn was enacted by Niamh O'Brien as Betty Blast, the roller-skating owner of the local burger joint. Other roles included Karen Gale as Eleanor Dunbar, wife of Coach Roger Dunbar, played by Michael Holohan, and Wes and Lulu Warnicker, who were Andrew Gallagher and Caroline McCrank. Gallagher was also Cowboy Bob, a very strong cameo with a great grasp of that grand genre, cowboy music. David Byrne was the Sheriff, and Sean Gately was Principal Harry Clarke, both somewhat long-suffering and yet supportive of the efforts of the community to come to terms with the tragedy that prompted the dancing ban that forms the core of this plot. These players were joined by a very strong chorus of able singers and dancers, shepherded with precision and a keen grasp of style by Musical Director Shane Farrell and Choreographers Elaine and Ally O'Hanlon. Brian and Sean Power directed, and the production was supported by a very able (and also possibly footloose?) crew of technical and practical supporters. There was plenty of visual interest in this show to match the dramatic and musical elements, and all in all, this was a grand night's entertainment.

The St. Michael's Theatre Musical Society of New Ross took a walk on the wild side this year and embraced the ducks, drakes, geese, and other creatures that make up the cast of Honk! This was a colourful production which made great use of the comic and musical talents of a company who explored every angle of this classic Hans Christian Anderson fairy tale as seen through the lens of musical theatre.  Keith Flanagan had the dubious honour of being Ugly - the character, not the description - and captured the frustrations of this swan in duck's clothing with gawky grace. Through his adventures, he managed to retain the sympathy of the audience and also capitalise on the humour inherent in this role. Sinéad Goggin as his mother Ida brought strong singing and acting credentials to the role, and her portrayal of the dogged (or should that be 'duck-ed') determination of a mother to always look for the best in her offspring, was thoroughly touching. Seán O'Brien was Cat, and he took obvious pleasure in his performance as this sneaky and self- absorbed feline. His agility and facility with cat-like mannerisms both physical and vocal made for a very complete portrayal.
