James Dobbs was an hysterical Turkey, having mastered a walk and style of speech that spoke uncannily of the real thing. Grace O'Connor was busybody Henrietta, whose consistent, duck-like nosiness was a nice foil to her pondmates Ida and Maureen. Claire Buckley was Maureen, splendidly stuck-up and ever-anxious about appearances; a funny and consistent characterisation. Catherine French was Grace, also quite a grand character with a keen sense of self-importance. Peter O'Connor and Margaret Dunne were Greylag and Dot, respectively, an enormously funny pair whose relentlessly "chocks away" manner and wicked parody of upper-class twit- ness was a delight. Their squadron was equally amusing and chaotic, played with comic flair by Rinnell Mendoza, Jane Ryder and Una Hayden as Barnacles, Snowy and Pinkfoot. Another terrific comic pairing were the deliciously unrestrained Lowbutt and Queenie (Teresa Buckley and Nancy Rochford Flynn). Their madcap appearance was a good match for the marvellously off-kilter set that suggested the odd angles and exaggerated style of their house and furniture. David "Stoney" Burke was a scene-stealing Bullfrog, proving that attractiveness really is a state of mind, and acquitting himself as an accomplished song-and-dance man in the process. His Froglets were a thoroughly engaging group of youngsters with impressive singing and dancing skills. Warts and All was a show-stopping number of the first order. Maggie Pie was Linda Hynes, who found a good American accent and an appropriately pushy reporter's manner to match. Melanie Cleary was Penny, whose calm, swan-like appearance and gentle gracefulness were a lovely antidote to the extremes of other characters encountered by Ugly across the show. Her equally serene parents were Margaret Dunne and John Dwyer, whose diction in speaking was a thing of beauty. The Ducklings were Caoimhe Kenney Ryan, Jamie Cooper, Niamh Ling, Amy Hogan, Stephanie Kinsella, Fionn Murphy, Jack Ryan and Aoibhín Dolan, and a very funny, accomplished little flock they were too. Their interactions with Ugly were especially amusing, and their matter-of- fact duckling bustle and sense of theatrical pace was impressive from start to finish. Their Dad, "Drake" Kevin Kennedy was also Producer/Director for this show, and Lorraine Kennedy Cooper was Assistant Director and Choreographer, with assistant Choreographer Sinéad Furlong. This Honk! spoke clearly of their judgement not only in casting, but also a sense of a light touch that allowed a lot of individual expression and, one imagines, experimentation on the part of some clearly experienced performers. They were musically supported by a strong band under the direction of Philip Kennedy. There were lovely colours in the musical ensemble, and sound and light worked well to frame this colourful story. One can only imagine the backstage crew working furiously throughout, in the way a swan's wildly paddling legs under water enable the outwardly calm progress of it's serene swimming. I hope that cast and crew really enjoyed their travels through this well-known and well-told fairy tale, because I and my fellow audience members certainly did.

Tullamore Court Hotel Can a girl's head be turned by charming men? Why, yes of course it can! Say what you like, it's nice to be appreciated. I'm not just talking about myself; the people of Tullamore who attended Beauty and the Beast were treated well and their support was acknowledged. Front of House manager Frank Nicholson and his team of dashing gentlemen dressed in black tie and personally escorted people to their seats. What they were saying was, 'thank you for coming to our show.' When Frank and President Joan Crehan took the time to sit with me during the interval and ply me with coffee and warm scones, what they were saying was 'our involvement with AIMS is important to us.' (And probably also, 'man, this girl likes her coffee.') After fifty seven years, I guess you learn a thing or two - certainly the 'older' groups tend to know what works and what doesn't and I applaud all those of you who have survived countless recessions and continue to bring a little bit of magic to your community. There was certainly magic in the air with Tullamore Musical Society's production of this increasingly popular show. John O'Donoghue's set design gave the stage a wonderful sense of perspective, and the castle was convincingly large and imposing with pillars and stonework adornments, stained glass windows and impressive scenic painting. Enhancing this was the inclusion of mute Grecian style stone statues - as enchanted as the rest of the cast, but used only to change scenery; the make up department ensured they blended in with the set and some very disciplined freeze frames and passive expressions from the individuals added to the already smooth set changes, under the management of Wayne Handy. With no major interruptions between scenes, the pace of the show was good and director Christine Scarry got good results from her cast. Audrey O'Meara was delightful as Belle, and while she took a scene or two to warm into the role, she evoked quite an emotional response while trying to make some sense out of Beast's nastiness - initially; of course he saw the error of his ways and Eoghan Fingleton, playing a very volatile Beast calmed down to convincingly have Belle fall in love with him. There was good chemistry between these two - comfortable in their humorous scenes as much as their love scenes and the final kiss was breath-takingly romantic. Both were accomplished singers and highlights were the songs delivered with controlled emotional anguish; 'Home' brought a few sniffs, while 'How Long' was also sung with sincerity. Musical Director Enda O'Connor and his excellent orchestra were superb; the music consistently echoed the big Disney sound and singers were well supported. Indeed this chorus showed off a few times and 'Gaston' was a particularly enjoyable number, with choreography from Julie Donnelly making good use of her women. While 'Be Our Guest' and 'Human Again' might have had more movement, the visual impact (and not just of the wonderful costumes) was strong. Ah, Gaston; what fun to play the rogue, and nobody had more fun than Stephen Rabbitte, who, though afflicted with strange eyebrows, exuded egotistical confidence. Singing was good and delivery - of both the comical antics with Le Fou (humorously portrayed by Ultan Keena) and his darker side was excellent. Director Christine Scarry got wonderful results from crowd scenes; the chaos in the castle was confidently handled and things were genuinely funny. Guidance given to individuals was sporadic however; Martin Crowe cut a sympathetic character as Maurice for example, especially when pleading for help. Yet at other times, actors seemed unsure of both their movement and their motivation. It is possible that better collaboration was needed between the director and choreographer here. Aoife Fitzsimons brought out her maternal side for Mrs. Potts and I enjoyed her character, whether with son Chip (a talented Kenny Heffernan) or with the comedy duo Cogsworth and Lumiere. Singing was utterly beautiful, especially during the heart-warming 'Tale as Old as Time.' I fell for Nigel Sammon's speaking voice and he used it to great effect for the pompous Cogsworth, whose lack of humour was what made him funny. This against the energy of John Coss's Lumiere, wearing the only eyesore in terms of costumes (you took one for the team there, Mr. Coss) - these two were a solid combination and 'Be Our Guest' was full on fun. Lumiere could have fun with anyone however, and chase scenes with Jayne Louise Kelly's terribly sexy Babette were entertaining, if not entirely convincing. Niamh Sammon was an audience favourite with her portrayal of Madame de la Grande Bouche; her infectious laugh was delightful and it was always good to see her on stage. Similarly the Silly Girls were clownish and comical and Natalie Kelly, Fiona Goulding and Marguerite McDonnell worked really well together - and indeed with Gaston. Make up was excellent and little touches made all the difference - especially the use of odd looking contact lenses for Monsieur D'Arque - Michael Bermingham was solid in this role, reveling in the nastiness. Lighting design by Gerry Taylor reflected the moods well, and in many ways enhanced the action on stage - the enchanted forest was particularly eerie. Sound balance was good and effects were played at just the right level - slight reverb gave Beast that enchanted but strangely attractive sound. Visually things looked stunning against a great set and props (Nathalie Watts) were authentic and deliciously opulent. Sue Coady was costumes mistress and oversaw a wonderful collection of colours and textures from Triple C Costumes. Ultan Keena (aka Le Fou) oversaw hair and Kay Joyce and team were responsible for make up. A little bit of magic for the people of Tullamore to be sure. And me? Charmed, I'm sure.

A gal gets to notice a thing or two on her nationwide tour of the country; whilst last year many societies struggled to fill houses, what with all the doom and gloom (and snow) around, this year things are different. Perhaps people are working harder on selling the show - indeed there have been some wonderful community incentives. But I think that along with that, Ireland's musical societies want to lift spirits. To quote chairman Pat McGovern, Ballinrobe wanted to give people something 'bright, colourful and happy.' And while the lighting could have been a little brighter (well, it is a fairytale with a dark edge), this production of Beauty and the Beast certainly was colourful and happy. Costumes, for a start, were wonderful, with magical creatures looking enchanting, if one or two outfits may have caused headaches for cast members. I imagine the advice to any society thinking of doing this show might be, think of the size of some of the rigouts before you design your set! The set, designed by director Peter Kennedy and team, worked really well for this show: village buildings constructed on wheels, turned smoothly to become the interior of the castle, giving actors an expanse of corridors and staircases to walk along. I enjoyed Niall Conway as Beast, lurking around these corridors, trying to remember his manners. With a beautiful voice too, Mr. Conway sang with honest sincerity. Physically he managed the awkward movements of the beast, yet brought a sort of grace to his transformation into a man. At the magical moment, while a delightful Belle (Sinead Heneghan) sang emotionally, down came a large dome from above which encased Beast while the actor rid himself of hair and lumpy bits, partially concealed by smoke. The magic was enhanced in no small way by a strong orchestra, under the very able baton of MD John Roe. Sound was in very good hands too with Derek Recks - the many sound effects came in bang on cue and mercifully the balance between music and singers was excellent. Martha O'Toole's chorus were well prepped and they consistently got a great big Disney sound out of such numbers as 'Be Our Guest' and 'Human Again', and even 'Gaston', which was a lot of fun and a particularly enjoyable dance number (Peter Kennedy multi tasking again, with Aoife McClafferty) with swirly girls and men who could dance! As director, Peter Kennedy got much out of his talented cast, though I felt energy was a little low at times for the type of show. The chemistry between Belle and Beast built up nicely however, with encouragement from a strong trio in Lumiere (Mike Ansbro), Cogsworth (Ger Mahon) and Mrs Potts, played by Grainne McConnell, whose beautiful voice was highlighted throughout the show, but in particular for the really lovely 'Tale as Old as Time'. A special mention for David Moran and PJ Feerick who shared the role of Chip and stole the hearts of the audience. Ah. Gaston, the cad, was played with cockiness and confidence by James Conway, an actor with presence and a great voice. His sidekick Le Fou was comically played by Brendan Duignan and his song 'Gaston' as mentioned, was great fun. Seamus Cafferkey brought nice energy to the role of Maurice, with the song 'No Matter What' tenderly treated. Siobhan Campbell was bubbly and bright as Babbette and Madame de la Grande Bouche (Catherine Conway) was always a welcome sight with her sense of enchantment. Padraic Costello was suitably dark as Monsieur D'Arque, while the Silly Girls (Laura Gill, Sadbh Langan and Mariea Sheridan) were a solid trio - here was more of that colour, with their clownish performances full of fun and energy. John Hyland and team saw to it that the set was filled in nicely with some excellent props - rustic in the village (stags' heads and all) and opulent in the castle. In fact some of this opulence spilled out into the foyer, with rich looking candelabras and flowers at every turn. The show moved well, and scene changes were snappy. Bright and colourful indeed. But were the people of Ballinrobe happy? I'll say - there was a buzz in the air and a real sense of appreciation for the fun. Ballinrobe Musical Society: an excellent team, and a job well done.

When Galway University Musical Society set out to produce Spring Awakening, their choice must have brought with it a sense of the challenge this show presents and also the rewards of producing it well. It is a property that pivots on a number of axes, balancing issues raised in the 120 year-old play on which it is based with the contemporary relevance of what are difficult issues in any era. GUMS approached this issue-led drama with a strong cast and a single-minded, concentrated approach to chorus numbers which brought an almost heedless energy to the stage of the Town Hall Theatre. Hazel Doyle was Wendla, sweet-voiced and persistently questioning. She maintained an other-worldly quality that held interest; a confident yet understated presence. Oisin Tierney as Melchoir also presented a calm and balanced persona, increasing the intensity of his performance as events begin to bear down. Diarmuid Scahill was Moritz Stiefel and also this show's choreographer. This was a strong performance that spoke volumes about commitment to character development along personal lines. Scahill's was an individual and ultimately highly sympathetic performance. Emma Van Der Putten was Martha, a singer with a lot of contemporary nuance in her voice and a strong dramatic presence. Ilsa was Mary Conroy, another edgy and interesting performer with wonderful colour in her singing. . Emmet Byrne as Hanschen was a strong actor and flexible singer. Martin Kenny as Ernst is also a good theatrical singer and also brought a strong comic sense to his role. Both actors were also effective in more serious scenes. The relationship between Ernst and Hanschen was played on a surprising knife edge between humour and pathos and was very effective. Thea (Eve-Marie Costello) was a committed player and musically adept. Aoife Kilbane as Anna was also an effective company member and a good dancer. Caoimhin Higgins as Georg was very funny in his portrayal of this character's obsession with Frau Grossenbusterhalter, played with witty abandon by Elizabeth Moon. Adam Keegan was Otto, another performer who moved easily across various roles in scenes across the show. Bart Lever was an imperious Herr Sonnenstich and Hannah O'Reilly as Frau Gabor was sympathetic and effective, her moment of transition in deciding to allow Melchoir to be sent away very well judged. Ryan McCarthy was Herr Gabor, well played, and a strong presence in other segments of the show. David Holland and Aisling Gaffney were a consistent and darkly funny pair of teachers whose brief appearances added to both the humour and the tension of the play. Russell Stewart Browne was both Herr Stiefel and Schmidt with a good stage presence and a grand singing voice. Chris Moran was Father Kaulbeck and Doctor Van Brauspulver, bringing a great vocal presence and sense of pace to this work. As the Doctor, he was especially funny. Music and dance were vivid and varied elements across this production, and the very able musical ensemble was directed by Megan Lohan. The choreography had an almost fierce rhythmic drive, suited to the often angry, subversive context of the musical numbers. The set had a variety of levels and a framed window to the back of the stage used to project elements key to scene setting, from Latin text to images of headstones. Costumes were in keeping with time and place, but this production took its cue mainly from a directorial approach that did not draw back either from bawdy humour or stark grief, landing rather more firmly on the former, but sculpting memorable moments out of the latter.

If I could time travel, I would go back to the mid seventies, so long as it was any Sunday afternoon, in the back seat of our family car as we travelled to Jonesboro in South Armagh. And when an 18 year old British soldier would ask my dad (the father of the four children in the car) where he was going and what his business was, and for the umpteenth time, he would tell them he was going to his home town to visit his mother, I would tell him that in 2012, the Troubles would be so long over that actors dressed as British soldiers would make people giggle walking into a Lisburn theatre by asking to look into their handbags; that adults of a certain age would turn to each other and say "Do you remember that?"; that the soldiers would be used to change the set of a musical version of the trouble in Northern Ireland, a show called 'The Boys in the Photograph'. The musical, which in fact had its premiere in Island Hall theatre last month was a reworking of 'The Beautiful Game', the story of a football team throughout 'The Troubles' in Belfast, and was written by Ben Elton and Andrew Lloyd Webber. Fusion Theatre's show has it all - the beatings, the bombings, the maimings and the anger, the senseless killing, the horror and the empty sorrow. I would be interested to see what reaction it might evoke elsewhere in Ireland because director Ian Milford's production was very much in your face theatre: Gregory, an innocent boy in the wrong place at the wrong time is beaten to death. The entire cast attended his funeral, which was given time and detailed respect. The coffin was actually lowered into the ground (a grave sized hole cut out of a grass carpet, placed over an unused section of the orchestra pit). It was unsettling in its realism. It could not be lost on anyone who has ever put a loved one in the ground. If you didn't take much notice then, Irish Republic, you certainly will with this production, which I very much hope comes back for a second run. There was balance however, with some really funny lines very well delivered; I understand Ian Milford was in communication with Ben Elton to authenticate the language and the Northern humour came very comfortably to this superb cast. 'I Don't Like You' is a funny flirting song between Mary and John, and it was performed excellently well by Connor Carson and Hannah Conlon, who got to sing such class lines as "do your fly up sonny, cos your brain's hanging out." (I should explain: he was in the changing room after football). When things got dark, there was still comedy to be found. Extreme tension was broken when Thomas (brilliantly played by Dave McCrossan), after some IRA activity asked John to help him find his glasses. John declared, "You've got a gun but no glasses!" Milford magic gave us the comfort of a quick belly laugh, before plunging us back into the depths of the dangerous times. Gavin Murphy played Del, the only protestant amongst the main characters, who considered himself an Atheist and therefore a man of peace. Everyone was deaf to this however, except Christine (Victoria Sanders) and their tryst under a burnt out car after a scene of utter chaos and high emotions was hilarious. The chaos was due to an Orange Order band marching through a Catholic street. It was in fact, an actual real live Orange Order marching band, which marched through the auditorium and onto the stage; they were allowed to get so loud as to deafen us to the angry cries of the residents - and the sense of rightfulness and frustrated intolerance was palpable. The genuinely sweet treatment of Gregory and Bernadette's first kiss only brought the horror of his violent death closer to home. Amongst these terrified, confused and angry kids was the local priest, known as 'Father', whose passion for football probably far outweighed his piousness, and it was confidently and humorously played by Brian Trainor.

Mr. Milford was also Musical Director and in command of a fine orchestra - all numbers were played very well and the support for singers was evident. There were many musical highlights with a strong singing company; "God's Own Country" was sung with soul. Football matches were engaging and convincing and Rebecca Leonard's choreography brought life and energy to these moments; 'The Final' had both shape and drama and lots of boys who could dance! As it was set in the seventies, Anne McCleary and her team had fun dressing the set, which was also designed by Ian Milford, along with Maria Mallon. There was graffiti on the back wall and side positioned buildings turned easily on wheels to become internal rooms - Mary's kitchen had a Formica work top and a sacred heart picture complete with red light. The wedding night bedroom included genuine props from the Europa Hotel - lovely touches including a trouser press, which was involved in one of the funniest stage moments I've enjoyed this year. It is an exciting time for Fusion Theatre. Ben Elton and Andrew Lloyd Webber took notice of them. 'The Boys in the Photograph' has begun its proper journey and this team has a lot to be proud of.

why it could be applied to so many of our public figures today. I chuckled, as I did in many places during this wonderful production of Man of La Mancha by Tipperary Musical Society. But mostly, I enjoyed the drama; this is a show for theatre lovers. There's depth to the story, and the story within the story. If you have a strong group of talented individuals, if you are throwing your hands in the air with despair because you can't give everyone a lead role, yet there are so many that are deserving, then this is the show for your group. At the interval, someone said, this is a show you either love or hate, but I think that depends on the production you have seen. There was much to love here, with attention to minute details from director and choreographer David Hennessy, leaving no stone unturned and working in collaboration with set designer Mike Leahy. Apparently random pieces of muslin rags, broken wooden boxes or pieces of cast iron were gracefully blended together to form Don Quixote's horse; Sancho's donkey; the confessional box; the inn. People moved gracefully in and out of characters with conviction, and guidance from Mr Hennessy was always evident. Gerry Taylor's lighting was also inspired work, setting the tone whether it was ominous or warm. Indeed lighting in collaboration with the set could change things in the darker second act - some remarkable work for example during Aldonza's rape, when light is reflected through the billowing white folds of her dress. Deirdre Ryan was perfect as Aldonza, tough and sassy, funny and uncomplicated, singing with sincerity and power, but thankfully never indulging herself in the music - it was a key element of this production for me - and it must be tempting to whip highly dramatic scenes into a frenzy, but Mr Hennessy did not let that happen. Nor did MD Danny Carroll, with a superb band. Guidance from all quarters ensured this strong cast towed the line.

Chorus Mistress Helen Colbert stood over such strong numbers as 'The Impossible Dream' and 'Golden Helmet' and her singers shone. What of the two heroes? William (Bun) Ryan played Sancho Panza with the right balance of comedy and respect for his master - clownish but no buffoonery, nothing was over the top but it was still funny. Cathal O'Donoghue's magnificent performance as both Cervantes and Don Quixote was almost mesmerising, dare I say. For a start I liked his voice. He spoke with conviction; he spoke with clarity. It sounds obvious, but speech is not always given so much attention. Cervantes was a lover of words and there was poetry in Mr O'Donoghue's delivery. Don Quixote was enchanting: dramatic and engaging, his delusions were delightful. The transition from one to the other was subtly treated, yet by the time the old man died in the arms of Aldonza, or should I say, Dulcinea, and his faithful servant, I was deeply moved by the sincerity of the performance and the treatment of the scenes. Everyone shone in this production - chorus members easily transformed into characters within Cervantes' tale. Liam Carey performed with ease the diverse characters of the Governor and the Innkeeper. Joe Franklin was perfect as the gentle Padre and his tenor voice handled all numbers with ease. Dr Curasco (Anthony Flynn) played with pompous comedy, and the beautiful number 'I'm Only Thinking of Him' was beautifully delivered between Jean Lohan as the Housekeeper, the Padre and Schira Lane as Antonia. Phyllis Hickey looking after costumes had the same overall vision of the director, with muted tones and just enough colour to be interesting. Wigs and makeup enhanced the look. Props were wonderfully authentic. Certainly everything came together well for this production team and it was a truly great reflection on the society. Tipperary Musical Society, thanks for the reminder: that it's okay to dream the impossible dream. Perhaps there is a little Don Quixote in us all.

St. Patrick's High School The Pajama Game is a terrific and possibly under-rated show which deserves to be produced more often. Shannon Musical Society has certainly recognised this and pulled together a production that explored and creatively solved a number of technical challenges and spared no effort in bringing their Pajama Game to life. Carmel Griffen presided over a strong orchestra which played stylishly and kept the time-conscious factory workers on their toes. A good variety of choreographic styles directed by Karen Barrett evoked everything from Come Dancing to Cabaret at various points. Above all, however, this show depended on keen comic timing to resolve the controversy over seven and a half cents that is the crux of the crisis in the Sleep Tite factory. In this, Shannon were well supplied with a gaggle of accomplished funny men and women to provide industrial strength laughs and split-second feats of theatrical magic. Although not burdened with too much of the funny stuff, love interests Sid and Babe (Gary Keane and Hilary Orpen) had a nice rapport and a good grasp of the different styles of music they use to express the progress of their relationship. This is old-fashioned romance, and this pair understood how to project that on stage. On another end of the scale, Aodán Fox as Hines and Clare McNelis as Gladys share a rather different relationship, and both were clearly capable of sustaining a level of mayhem to their courtship that carried right across the show. Anna Maria Barrett as Mabel provided a laconic and very funny voice of reason, setting her own pace for dialogue and expertly placing a host of understated punch lines. Lauren Dunne as Mae sizzled under the influence of Steam Heat and found a likeable comic centre to this character as well. Martin McNelis was a busy and bustling Hasler, caught up in the business of business. Eoghan Rice was a persistent yet unlikely Lothario, revelling in an over-the-top performance that capitalised on his ability to be a two-faced yet loveable liar. Jennifer Quinn-O'Connell and Rachel McIntyre as Brenda and Poopsie added comic colour to the factory floor, and Norrie Green as babe's father Pop was a wise counterpoint to the drama of Babe's romance and union involvement.

There was a lot to admire in the set of this Pajama Game, providing as it did a sense of location from the inside looking out and wonderful details such as a "working" elevator, a brace of sewing machines, a "test your strength" carnival game and the illusion of knife throwing that needed to be seen to be believed. Shannon also provided their usual detailed and fulsome front of house display, which extended to the tape measures around the necks of front of house staff, looking ready to measure patrons for their own customised and personal pair of pajamas. Pajama Game, with its undertones of worker's revolt and central thread of industrial justice and corporate fair play has a valid contemporary resonance that came across in this production by virtue of the care taken to tell a well-crafted story with great music and clever characters. From the front door to the factory floor, this was great fun and marvellous vehicle for this talented society.

Sligo's FUN Company certainly did have a lot of fun with their production of All Shook Up. This was a well-cast and brightly paced production, with strong choreography and a marvellous visual approach. While clearly relishing its Elvis-indebted approach to music, dance and dialogue, this production and all concerned also managed to provide moments of individual expression and a somewhat contemporary, filmic vibe. Ken Kennedy enjoyed playing Chad and drew a lot of humour from this role, never taking himself too seriously and setting a high bar in terms of finding aspects of the character to emphasise and personalise. Kelsea Mulcahy as Natalie/Ed was prettier than the average tomboy, but brought her own sort of self-deprecating charm to the role. Arron McDonagh's Dennis was a very detailed characterisation, complete with nervous, nerdy mannerisms and a nicely eccentric whine in both his speaking ad singing voice. Angela McGuire as Sylvia covered her ground musically with a number of vocal styles and the bitterness of her characterisation softened winningly by the end. The object of her affection was Ian Howard as Jim Haller, whose performance had a hint of mid-life crisis about it, and his temporary double-act with Chad was very funny indeed. Michelle Feeney as Miss Sandra sang in a well-supported and musically intelligent way, with a lyrical and mobile voice. Her utter disdain for Chad and subsequent attraction to Denis were equal and opposite sides of a very comical coin. Niamh Casey as Lorraine brought balanced elements of acting, singing and dance to the theatrical table, and Luke Devaney as Dean Hyde was a strong pairing for her. Their relationship was touching and entertaining. Mayor Matilda was Maureen Howley, another performer who developed an entire set of mannerisms and vocal characterisation to support a small but consistently very funny role. At one point she came in from the back of the theatre and managed to heckle a number of patrons on her way to the stage. Robert Fitzpatrick as the long- suffering Sheriff was convincing both as a much put-upon law enforcer and a secretly besotted and (almost always) quiet man. This colourful cast played on a stylish and effective set, with many necessary details and other decorative elements well presented. Costumes were a grand mix of style and colour, all very much in keeping with the era this show so lovingly evokes. The chorus as a theatrical force were very well directed and came across as spontaneous and clued-in, and their dancing was of a very high standard, with a choreographic approach that often took its lead from the play's text, as well as dances current at the time. There was vitality in every aspect of this production and an affectionate tongue- in-cheek sensibility to the way in which the songs, jokes and dances advanced this admittedly corny plot. Sligo's FUN company's work on this production pulled together a lot of serious resources and created a professionally paced and hugely entertaining night of fun!

There is something inescapably optimistic about the musical Annie, and in a well- resourced production like that of St. Agnes Choral Society, there's a bit of old- fashioned glamour too. Topping it all off, of course is the mop-haired namesake of the show, a demanding role which left young Annie and her orphanage chums undaunted and having a great old time. St. Agnes' double cast the girls' chorus and principals, and on the evening I saw the show, Annie was played by Marie-Claire O'Connor, a confident and engaging lassie whose verve and sure-footed theatrical enthusiasm soared in the very grand Opera House. She was most engaging in her scenes with Daddy Warbucks (Michael McDowell), with whom she forged a solid and believable relationship. McDowell had enough bluster and equivocation about bringing an orphan girl into his life to make his transition to doting guardian all the more compelling. This was engineered by Emma Lundy as Grace Farrell, who had a steely way with Miss Hannigan, played by the non-stop and drunkenly funny Fiona Keegan. Chalk and cheese wouldn't have a look in, as prim Farrell faced grim Hannigan, and eventually triumphed. John McMichael was an exuberant Rooster, a song-and-dance man of the old style and a villain in the faux-sinister tradition of many a comic strip. His sidekick Lily was played with tremendous timing and physical ease by Megan McArthur, whose transformation into Shirley Mudge in Act II was comic tour-de-force. Indeed, these three 'baddies' formed a very entertaining 'trio do force' in Easy Street, their anthem to greed and ill-gotten gains.

There was a strong and colourful cast of supporting players, including Brian Trainor as a larger-than-life Bert Healy, aided and abetted by the fabulous Boylan Sisters, Helen Scullion, Michelle Hannaway and Nicola Cunningham. Ruaidhri Maguire was Bundles, the easily-seduced laundry man and David Graham was Lt. Ward. Back at the Warbucks' mansion, a very dry yet secretly cuddly Drake was Sean Allen, and Mrs Greer was Andrea McGrath. An amiable Mrs Pugh was Dympna O'Hare. The Warbucks' circle of influence extends to the White House, and this production produced an uncanny cabinet, headed by Pat Smith as President Roosevelt and including a very strong ensemble cast. However, the strongest ensemble credit must go to the Orphans, whose singing and dancing combined into a powerful theatrical impression. Their choreography challenged them to dance with buckets on their feet, perform acrobatic tricks and look adorable at all times. Did they succeed? Gee whiz, did they ever! From the tall to the small, this was an ensemble to be reckoned with, as poor Miss Hannigan found out to her cost. The Opera House is a big venue and this cast, young to old, filled it with energy to spare with stylish performances that projected to the back wall, kept the pace and the "ahhh" moments coming. Two canine stars also acquitted themselves well, and added to the fulsome tapestry of this production. In terms of detail and scale, the set was a star in its own right, from the faded grandeur of Miss Hannigan's institution to the chic excesses of the Warbucks pad and right to the Oval office. Many of these locations were arrived at in a splendid onstage car, complete with chauffeur.

Offstage resources were impressive as well, with a lively band presided over by Wilson Shields and an undoubtedly busy stage crew. There was a lovely sense that all concerned had a splendid time, and that communicated itself across the footlights, giving us a grand glimpse of some very accomplished stars of tomorrow.

Busy time of year. Took in two shows that day; arrived in Ballinasloe for the evening performance, thinking I might have a gentle time of it before completing the road trip back to Dublin. Gentle time? With Alan Recks' orchestra delivering a great big Disney sound? With all the drama and high jinks? Gentle? Not a bit of it. This production was designed to keep the audience alert with a strong opening number and an excellent chorus supporting a truly talented Niamh Kelly playing Belle. Singing was really wonderful with Home' and 'Change in Me' as highlights. Eoin Croffy's Gaston was as funny as he was cocky, if at times a little too cheeky. Sidekick Le Fou (Declan Finn) delighted us in getting bashed about the place and 'Gaston' was a fun number, a good performance with an animated feel. Indeed movement of characters had been given plenty of guidance in this respect with Belle in particular moving like the cartoon original. Majella Flanagan's direction was solid, with some nice touches, taking every opportunity to get humour out of the lines. Yet Belle and Beast's relationship was taken seriously and it developed sweetly - Kevin Griffin portraying a gentler Beast than I'm used to, but again with a strong emphasis on humour. Lumiere (Enda McGrath) and Cogsworth (Patrick Byrne) were good together and flanked Beast in this respect, with the trio getting laughs, while Sarah Corcoran played an altogether delightful Mrs. Potts. Singing was superb too, and 'Tale as Old as Time' was an absolute highlight. Costumes got to dress a lot of the set in this show, with an opportunity for striking numbers, such as 'Be Our Guest' (Mr. McGrath strong in his singing role here, but also with great energy), and 'Human Again' and there was great colour and authenticity to everyone's look. Maurice's stripy stockings and buckle shoes were very fairytale like, and Brian Derrane played the father role with sincerity - 'No Matter What' was a lovely number, tenderly treated by both singers. MD Alan Recks was very supportive throughout and musicians of a high calibre indeed. Sound balance was good for the most part; some numbers do tend to get unreasonably loud in this show, but there was control here. Pascal Cough's lighting design reflected the mood well and execution mostly tight. Lighting was the main feature of the eagerly anticipated transformation of Beast into Prince, with four strong spots turning and shining on the audience - though not too blindingly - just enough to give Beast time for a quick shave and to ditch the padding. It worked really well in fact, especially after the high drama that preceded it, with Belle's tearful but controlled singing and before that, a well choreographed fight scene that saw Gaston fall to his death. Madame de la Grande Bouche (Catherine Madden) could be counted on to bring humour back each time, and she performed with confidence. The role of Chip was shared by Taylar Higgins and Jack Delaney, the latter playing on the night I attended. He was something else, great acting and singing, and I believe Miss Higgins was just as good. Where do these marvellous children come from? Helen O'Donoghue struck just the right tone for the sexy Babette, while Niall Callaghan was mean and nasty as Monsieur D'Arque. The chorus was properly used throughout and could be dark and threatening when called upon; 'Kill the Beast' was a strong number, well led by Eoin Croffy's Gaston and the chaos in the castle that followed was well directed.

Other performances of note were the Silly Girls (Megan Lawlor, Kate Croffy and Meadbh Egan) while even the carpet (Eamon Warde) got to shine in this show. I also enjoyed the Wolves who moved gracefully and had been well choreographed; this early scene with Maurice had real drama. The set was striking for its specifically painted backdrops by scenic artist Grainne Moore, and scene changes were smooth - indeed each new scene brought applause. The two level set was clever and worked well and Stage Manager Pat McGovern and team were for the most part, unimposing. Props, hair and makeup were authentic. The rose impressed me; it could drop petals on cue. This show had it all; drama, love and humour; edge of the seat stuff. No gentle rest for me, but we did sing all the way home.

Great Hall, Downshire Estate It could be said that part of musical theatre's appeal is that it takes us to places that are often worlds apart from our own lives. While most societies do a great deal to ensure that they re-create a show's setting as carefully as possible, St. Patrick's Choral Society in Downpatrick went a bit further for their production of Fiddler on the Roof and shared village life in Anatevka with the audience before the show actually began. Inhabitants of the town went about their business onstage while the rest of us were taking our seats and having a look through the programme. The milkman's eldest daughter chatted with that young tailor, the matchmaker had a few words with the butcher, and that crazy fiddler took his violin up on to a roof. All became clear as the show progressed, but by the time MD Denise Kelly raised her baton on the Prologue, we were already becoming familiar with the men women and children in that remote place, along with their Traditions. Eugene Armstrong was Tevye, faithful, long suffering and prone to one-sided dialogues with God. Armstrong's fine voice and poised comic timing gave this milkman a presence ideally suited to this central role. Lorna Maguire was Golde, long-suffering in her own way, and very affecting in her reactions to events in the daughters' lives. Yente the Matchmaker was Audrey Neill, who clearly relished this character role. Diarmuid Taggart was Lazar Wolf, a strong actor with an easy manner onstage, consistently connected to each scene he appeared in. Charlotte Burke as Tzeitel was another strong actor, especially affecting and effective when begging Tevye not to make her marry Lazar Wolf. Hodel was Rebecca McKee, a lovely singer and confident actress. Courtney Burns as Chava also brought out the poignancy of her role. Brian McElroy as Motel was very convincing as the somewhat timid but ultimately courageous tailor. Matthew Campbell as Perchik was very strong, slight of stature but a big presence onstage, with the necessary dignity and humour for this role. Michael Sims was a convincing and consistent Mordcha, making the most of a small but colourful role. Mark McMullan as Fyedka likewise made a memorable impression. Aoife Barnes and Oorlagh Carson were Shprinze and Bielke, nicely cast as daughters in what came across as a realistic family group. There was much to admire in chorus scenes, both in terms of music and also a sense of community. There was good detail in both set and interpretation, with a sense of affection and respect for the Jewish traditions so lovingly scripted and composed. Choreography was one area of strong detail, and the wedding scene and bottle dance was especially fine. The dream sequence was full-on in concept, with an especially frightening Frumah Sarah who almost succeeded in carrying Tevye away with her to the afterlife, with a little help from a length of wire - just one example of the handiwork of an extremely busy and skilled backstage crew. In the same way that the evening's opening sequence showed us village life, at the show's end this production gave an eerie glimpse of the aftermath of this story. Instead of a celebratory curtain call, as each group or individual stepped forward, they quietly left something of themselves at the edge of the stage - kerchiefs, books, domestic items and finally, Tevye's milk can. The show finished with this collection of personal, everyday objects - a little bit of this, a little bit of that - for us to remember them by, and by extension, a remembrance of a wider and terrible history. This was theatre at its emotional, heartfelt best.

Glór, Ennis Ennis Musical Society saw to it that the hills were very much alive with The Sound of Music in the Glór theatre. And music was very much to the fore in a production that emphasised the often neglected choral portions of the work, assigned to the nun's chorus, all 23 of whom (to the sharp-eyed among the audience) were called 'Sister Mary' in the programme. Another notable aspect of this production came from a very well-chosen cast of Von Trapp Children. These were led by Leisl, played by Madeline Arkins, a fine actress and very good singer. Her brothers and sisters were Conor Coughlan, Elaine Brennan, Nathan Bluett, Emma Purcell, Sinéad Coughlan and Rhona Kearney as Friedrich, Louisa, Kurt, Brigitta, Marta and Gretl, respectively. Inevitably, the role of young Gretl brings tons of the 'ahhh' factor to the show, and Rhona was no exception, with a lovely true singing voice and poised manner onstage. Another lovely voice came from Zoe Halpin as Maria, a quietly enthusiastic governess who nonetheless made her points about child-rearing clear in no uncertain terms to the Captain, played with dignity and a few softer edges by Morgan Lahiffe. There was more dignity and great warmth too in the Mother Abbess as played by Deirdre Browne, who was joined by Sisters Margaretta, Berthe and Sophia, played by Kate Corrigan, Marian McQueen and Marie Griffen. They never did quite figure out how to Solve a Problem Like Maria, but they approached this riddle with good humour and strong harmony nonetheless. Perhaps the most humour came from Max Detweiler, that jovial but effective houseguest who was brought to good- natured life by Ken O'Shaughnessy. His often opposite number was the elegant Elsa Shraeder, a woman on a mission so innocently thwarted by the unwitting Maria. Edel Heaney gave Elsa a beautifully modulated voice, both speaking and singing, and a slightly brittle but genuine affection for Georg and his money. Heaney and O'Shaugnessy brought two of this show's lesser-known songs to vivid life in their spirited and pitch-perfect versions of How Can Love Survive and No Way to Stop it.

One of this production's best musical moments came in the form of the children's So Long, Farewell. Much of the choreography was directly influenced by the film, and this number was no exception, but these young performers in their musical and theatrical precision were up to the challenge of re-creating a well- known and iconic moment. The set, which gave us the stairway and balcony upon which the children sing their goodbyes, was an aspect of this production that also lived up to filmic standards. It contained a superfluous Austrian street scene too, but the interiors of the convent and the Von Trapp house were carefully dressed and a fine match for an equally well-dressed cast. Costumes were definitely a strong aspect of this Sound of Music, as was sound reproduction, executed with an approach that did nicely restrained justice to the many good voices on stage. MD Martin Moloney presided over a large and very well-balanced orchestra which bloomed and grew across the length of the show, in much the same way as that bright Edelweiss. Well done, Ennis, who Climbed Every Mountain in their pursuit of excellence and delivered a lovely evening's entertainment.

Gorey Little Theatre Godspell, when it appeared more than 40 years ago must have surprised audiences with its eclectic music and free use of sacred texts. Gorey Musical Society's production began with the now- iconic Prepare Ye the way of the Lord, sung with the conviction of a rock god by John the Baptist as played by David Cox. Not even the somewhat over-the- top amplification in the hall could muddy the optimistic fervour of this opening number. Cox was joined by the faithful, a colourful and energetic number that fluctuated across the show, depending on whether the central cast or the whole company were involved. The whole company numbers had a busy joyfulness to them that chimed well with this show's central message of gathering, teaching and sharing. The subject of their devotion was Jesus, played by Jonny Holden, whose approach to the role matched the cast's general youthful mayhem 'step by step and inch by inch'. They played on a cleverly designed set which allowed for different levels and changes of focus. In the printed programme, the scenes were identified in this way: Setting - You Decide! Time - Tonight. In so many ways, this company followed through with this directive, with a musical approach that brought these songs to life in terms of contemporary and stylish singing and clever choreography. Kathleen Holden sang Day by Day with great sincerity and set a high standard of delivery that carried across the show. Jessica Doyle sang Learn Your Lessons Well, bringing a strong, blues-tinged sense of conviction to this. Mags Jacob likewise had a strong affinity with a jazz/blues style and was an unfailingly focussed and funny performer. John Egan performed All God Gifts with understated sincerity, proving that this production wasn't all about mayhem, fun and games. Likewise, a song such as By My Side, with Kathleen again and also Ciara Herron, had a sense of weight and unease to it that made the text all the more potent; two very good voices supported by a strong choral sound. Tanya Tighe led an altogether more saucy number to begin Act II: her Turn Back, O Man was a feast for ear and eye. Colin Doran was part of the On the Willows ensemble, and his performance throughout was sincere and exhibited an ability to move from serious to seriously funny at will. Karol Howell was also a versatile player and strong vocal presence. Key moments musically were David Cox leading an exuberant Light of the World at the end of Act I, and Jonny/ Jesus with an exquisite performance of Beautiful City. He went on to a simple but powerful representation of crucifixion, less graphic than some but powerful in context. During Long Live God, Judas/ John the Baptist carried Jesus down from the upper level of the stage, stepping forward and up on his reprise of Prepare Ye, still carrying Jesus - a strong dramatic moment, followed by Jesus leaping down and joining the company - a resurrection in all but name and a powerful and hopeful message to complete an overwhelmingly happy performance.

The cast were supported by a skilled and stylistically-aware band, directed by Lar Duffy, who allowed the individuals onstage to drive their performance. The momentum and the message were clear, and this take on Godspell was fresh and relevant, as though composed for the 21st century. 'Twas All for the Best, and we Learned Our Lessons Well, taught by a very talented cast in a thoughtful, thought- provoking production.

The Mill Theatre, Dundrum Although Fiddler on the Roof is generally acknowledged to be a big show, not every society performs in a big theatre. Kilmacaud Musical Society is an example of one of these, but they managed to stage an excellent Fiddler in the rather confined performing space of the otherwise lovely Mill Theatre, Dundrum. One of the biggest aspects of this production was the stunningly good choral sound they produced, with a well-drilled chorus who sang rhythmically and were supported by a strong band which included a very fine accordion player, an excellent violinist and a small assortment of other players, all of whom added colour and texture. The added jewel in their musical crown was superb sound design and execution that gave us what we needed, no more no less. As ever, much of this show's success rested on the person of Tevye. Eamonn Murphy is an able actor/singer who brought a wonderfully modulated voice and broad, gently comic confidence to the role. Golde was an excellent mixture of shrew and saint, a strong character who bore the privations and uncertainties of village life with good humour. Yenta was Caroline Rowan, who played this with a strong and consistent accent and a look that emphasised the shamanic aspects of this character. Kim Bolger was Tzeitel, another good actress who rather amusingly was definitely Golde and Tevye's daughter, with mannerisms and an approach that mirrored and combined aspects of their characters. Hodel was Amy Byrne, who warmed to this role across the show and gave a well-paced account of her blossoming romance with Perchik, Conor Cronin. His was a strong and stand-offish interpretation, consistent in tone and a good singer too; these two were very well-matched. Helen Cusack was a luminous Chava, a genuine 'little bird' who balanced her performance beautifully between love of family and Fyedka, played by Chris O'Connor, who was another strong presence onstage, owning the role and making a lasting impression. Motel was Kevin Fagan, a very likeable character from beginning to end, timid and put-upon but strong when it counted - a lovely performer and excellent theatrical singer. Lazar Wolf was Ian Tighe, clearly relishing this role, giving a light-hearted performance that also had an amount of nuance.

These central characters were joined across the production by a very able cast of supporting characters, including a dignified rabbi with clear gravitas, ably assisted by the rabbi's son, another good and consistent actor, an affable but slightly sinister constable, and the inhabitants of Tevye's dream, including a Grandma Tzeitel who momentarily lost her way, and a very present Fruma-Sarah, complete with a voice to wake the dead. This is a big cast, who found their way on and off stage with apparent ease, and inhabited a simple but very detailed and functional set. There was obviously a lot going on backstage, and a sense of a company that thought things through. Part of the thought process included an unusual postlude in which we heard snatches of Tevye's opening monologue, mixed with the sound of the Fiddler's opening tune, played as a ghostly counterpoint to Tevye, standing still on stage. We heard a voice taunt the Fiddler, insisting that "you won't need your fiddle where you're going", followed by the sound of a violin breaking, and the Fiddler's cry. The message that history tried and possibly succeeded in breaking down Jewish tradition was a clear and stark reminder of how the story continued. This was a bleak ending to a powerful story, carefully and skilfully told by Kilmacaud Musical Society.

Millennium Forum Fifty years is a long time for most things - a golden anniversary no matter what the partnership. It's customary to throw a big party, but Londonderry Musical Society went a good many steps farther and produced an elaborate and very beautiful re-creation of the Kingdom of Siam.

From the big dresses of Missus Anna to the Small House of Uncle Thomas, this King and I had it all.

David Keown was the eponymous King, as eccentric and infuriating as you'd expect, especially to surprisingly feisty Anna Leonowens, played by Susan Keown. Neither actor based their interpretation of their roles slavishly on the well-known film performances, but there was enough of the essence of these familiar characterisations to flavour what they brought to the stage. David's King had fewer mannerisms and was possibly less sure of himself than the Yul Brenner caricature, an approach that made him a rather more sympathetic character. Susan Keown's Anna had a slightly contemporary edge, less prim and more indignant than one might remember. The warmth of her singing held the stage whether she was in the company of many children and ladies, or entirely alone. Of the ladies, Patricia O'Donnell as Lady Thiang brought a knowing dignity to her role, emphasising the old Siam, even as the new Siam formed around her. Geoff Cook as The Kralahome was excellent as another exponent of tradition and class distinction. He was deliciously disdainful of the new patterns of though the Teacher brought to this ever less remote kingdom. Tuptim, a clear victim of the conflict of old and new, was luminously played and sung by Rionach McGlinchy, whose musical speaking voice was also used to good effect in the Small House of Uncle Thomas sequence. This was outstanding, a spectacle in every sense, with wonderfully detailed masks and costumes matched by beautifully executed choreography. Lun Tha was James Kelly, a strong singer and subtle actor. Among the children, Mark Gallagher as Louis Leonowens was terrific, a great mix of proper English schoolboy and precocious child rather too apt to speak his mind. His counterpoint, Jordan Henry as Prince Chululongkorn was equally strong and capable of expressing an opinion. Their rapport was delightful - an aspect that so easily could have been a weak link in a show so dependent on these kinds of connections. Smaller roles were equally well-filled. Michael Poole was Sir Edward Ramsey, who managed to convey strong hints of his feelings for Anna in just a few brief lines. Likewise, David Thomas as Captain Orton created a fully-formed character out of very short appearances. The children arrived in waves and took to the stage like so many wee ducks to water. They looked delightful, subtly different from one another in costume, as their mothers were, dressed in a variety of colours and textures, beautifully draped. The children's singing was solid and clear, and they were wonderfully able to combine music and movement. The choreography of scenes like Getting to Know You and movement generally in chorus scenes was very well managed. The set on which this action took place was truly Something Wonderful, and a series of imaginative crossovers allowed scene changes to take place in front of the curtain without any sense of a pause in the action. From top to bottom and side to side, the Kingdom of Siam was lovingly, lavishly created for a Londonderry audience by a cast and crew who filled their theatre with a truly grand production of a very great musical. The palace had levels and layers of detail, along with clever and elaborate ways of creating more intimate scenes. With such a hard-working and talented company, it was most definitely not A Puzzlement that the audience loved every minute of The King and I in Londonderry.

Malahide Community School There's a lot of talk in our house at the moment about censorship; how 'The Hunger Games', for example, is okay because it's a 12A rating, although the content might be…questionable. My girls understood too, that they couldn't accompany me to Sweeney Todd because they know the Johnny Depp film version is 18's.

As it turned out, I could have brought them to Malahide Musical Society's production because, although the horror was there, it was so tastefully done. They would not have been the youngest in the audience either, since someone brought a baby along on the night I attended. Quite well behaved too, the child's timing was impeccable, waiting until Anthony and Johanna had finally kissed before crying. Ah, Anthony and Johanna, how lovely they were too; Fiona McManus was delightful as the vulnerable creature, and singing was assured. Sean McMahon was solid as her gentle hero; 'Johanna' was really beautifully sung. All this talk of delightful gentle things is misleading however, because golly this was a dark show. Jane Lynch and Anna Szczepan's makeup skills were hugely impressive, and the presentation of the company, all Tim Burton like under the bright glare of Cathal Donohoe's excellent lighting design was a real treat. Wouldn't want to meet any of them in a dark alleyway mind you. Scariest of all was Sweeney Todd himself performed with complete involvement by Ciaran Mooney. Dark, moody and dangerous, I wasn't entirely comfortable during his rendition of 'My Friends', I don't care how tenderly he sang about his darling murder weapons. Emma Jane Reilly's portrayal of Mrs. Lovett was a balance to this darkness; funny, very funny, but unsettling too, as she sang 'Epiphany' and 'A Little Priest' along with Mooney. Her interpretation of both dialogue and music was impressive and I loved the development of her relationship with Toby, who might have been her son if things weren't so doomed, what with her going around cooking people that Sweeny Todd had slaughtered. Did I say it would be okay to bring my children? Yes, somehow, because in the sure hands of director Lynda Thomspon, all bases were covered and everyone had really solid guidance. Daniel Murphy is only seventeen, but he fully brought life to Tobias Ragg; this was really impressive character work, convincing from the outset. I would have forgiven him a lot more, especially upon hearing him sing. Paul Laycock was thoroughly convincing as the despicable Judge Turpin, condemning children to hang (nice performance from Tom Bennett), raping Todd's wife and later, forcing himself on her delicate daughter. Grace Kinirons' portrayal of the Beggar Woman/Lucy was engaging and put one on an emotional rollercoaster; she was a funny, dirty old bird and later a desperate tragic heroine, and crossing the line from one to the other was never obvious. Oh my spine, how it tingled! But all the while, Lynda Thompson kept to her vision and her cast followed faithfully. Choreographer Michelle O'Hara understood the director's intention and her work reflected the mood exactly. The masked dance during 'Poor Thing' was disturbing, while movement of a competent chorus during the Pirelli scenes had drama and comedy. 'Parlour Songs' into 'Fogg's Asylum' was inventive work, the group excelled as a slow moving backdrop to the horror unfolding. Musical Director Andrew Linnie oversaw an excellent orchestra and high calibre musicians really got to shine, though it was unfortunate that the music drowned out singing considerably. (Sound was otherwise fine, with effects enhancing things well). Don't get me wrong; this was a super company musically, and the overall sound was powerful, but lyrics were lost in the competition between players and singers too many times. That said, there was solid support from Mr. Linnie throughout and both principals and chorus still impressed. Robert McWilliams as Beadle Bamford managed a difficult number in 'Kiss Me Part II' with comfort for example. Indeed, his portrayal of this nasty piece of work was presented with easy conviction. David Latham as Adolfo Pirelli was refreshingly funny - this confident humour so very necessary in a tale such as this. Jonas Fogg was suitably portrayed by Ray Hoare and Sandra Murphy brought character to the role of the Birdseller. But you might pick any one of this company out as exceptional; indeed, a strong chorus properly led. Costumes looked just right too, dark and drab for sure, but just a bit of colour here and there lifting things sufficiently. Lynda Thompson's set worked perfectly well, with exposed scaffolding and brickwork setting the tone, while the centrally raised barbershop was positioned right in the eye line upstage centre. Sweeney Todd is certainly a challenge: you've got to be sure your entire group is up to it. Isn't it wonderful when a company realises its worth?

Aula Maxima, St. Patrick's College There's something about the name "Aula Maxima" that is intriguing, as if a venue with a Latin title influences what happens there. As it happens, Maynooth Musical Society's production of Rent was at odds with its somewhat genteel surroundings, a full-on, uncompromising take on this non-stop all singing, all-dancing show. This was very well-cast, with great voices and strong actors who knew what they were aiming for and pursued that goal with all their hearts. From the beginning, character and musical individuality were well-established onstage, each named character projecting their material with unfettered energy and confidence. The chorus likewise provided an amount of colour and support that was rhythmic, musical and focussed.

Mark Cohen was Sean McMahon, an able performer in a pivotal role. He blended singing and dialogue well, keeping the thread of relationship with other characters firmly connected. Roger Davis was powerfully voiced by Dan Frawley, an edgy performance poised between emotional engagement and reticence. The object of his affections, Mimi, was Yasmine Missaoui, an attractive and polished performer who combined vulnerability with just enough craziness to keep us guessing. She managed the difficult near-death scene with a nice sense of proportion. David Moore was Angel, an absolutely compelling performance that held little back in terms of charm and openness to everything life throws at him. His other half, Tom, was played by Karl Sheridan who gave an attractive and nuanced performance and was especially affecting during angel's illness and death. Emma Stack was Maureen, very well cast as this more than slightly off-the- wall performance artist. She abandoned herself to the role and took everyone with her, right Over the Moon and back again. Her partner Joanne was Maria Hallinan who matched Emma in terms of stunning vocal agility and she presented a strong and consistent character in relation to both Maureen and her ex Mark. These were skilful performances. Benny was played by Damian Sweeney, who managed to be likeable despite the demands of his role as Rent collector. This was a formidable assemblage of named characters, and only a very skilful and committed chorus was going to match the tone they set and hope to hit a bar set so high. Fortunately, Maynooth has youth on their side, as well as buckets of talent and a clear and potent love of what they do as performers. They were supported and at times engulfed by a classy and powerful band. The hall provided too much echo for the level of amplification used, but the beauty of individual and choral voices won through, and the instrumentalists played so well, it was possible to forgive occasional strain on one's ear drums.

The set was gritty and imaginative, with a variety of levels and suggestions of separate spaces, with clever use of projection and effects of recorded sound. Costumes were eclectic and colourful, with a strong thread of individual taste and details that spoke volumes about each character. Even though Rent is definitely not a family-oriented show, this production spoke volumes about the theatrical family formed by this company, from backstage to onstage and front of house. They didn't flinch from difficult issues, edgy performance requirements or choreographic and musical demands. A young company in every sense, this standard of production speaks volumes and bodes well for the future.

St. Michael's Theatre With a husband and wife team as director and choreographer, there was another guy and doll element to New Ross Musical Society's production, along with Nick Cooney as MD, in command of a strong orchestra playing nicely nicely. Bill Stafford and Anne-Marie Stafford work well together, as one might expect, and such numbers as 'Luck Be a Lady' and 'Sit Down, You're Rockin the Boat' were no doubt collaborative efforts, with a strong dramatic tone and a well-used chorus. There was a good dynamic between the likes of Nicely Nicely (Martyn Gladney), Benny (Thomas Crowdle) and Rusty (Peter O'Connor) starting off, with 'Fugue for Tinhorns' well managed, if pitch was an issue at times. Mr. Gladney was the most competent musically, though it didn't take from the fun of the scenes and interaction with the other gangsters and crapshooters had plenty of comedy. Sean O'Brien was quite the softy as Nathan Detroit, with this take on the character endearingly comedic at times, if never quite convincing of his gangster ways. While the pace of the show did dip here and there, music brought the energy up in such numbers as 'Guys and Dolls' and chorus master John Kissane had certainly worked his people for the likes of 'The Oldest Established' and 'The Happy Ending', as well as the already mentioned choral numbers. The relationship between Joanne McCabe as Sarah Browne and her Uncle Arvide, a very strong Lorcan Dunne, was convincingly tender - 'More I Cannot Wish You' was beautiful - but it took a while to find chemistry between Sarah and Sky Masterson; Brendan Redmond was strong in the role here, and worked hard to achieve warmth with Ms McCabe but direction had them facing away from each other too much of the time, as indeed was the situation with Nathan and Adelaide - with Therese Canavan as Adelaide doing everything right but appealing to the back of Nathan's head a lot of the time. This was a strong cast and they did achieve their love stories, but I felt the intimacy might have come sooner. Mr Stafford's strength lay with humour in this case, and Tom Reddy as Harry the Horse was very funny, with a great accent and sense of timing. Likewise David 'Stoney' Burke had been well guided to get every ounce out of Big Jule's lines, and full marks to this performer for exploring his lower vocal register here. Even General Cartwright was allowed to be funny and Margaret Dunne gave it socks. Vocally, Ms McCabe impressed with all her numbers as did Ms Canavan, and in particular 'Marry the Man Today' was an engaging duet. Eamon O'Connor's suspicious Lieutenant Brannigan was a good balance to all the funny stuff. But where was the Runyonese? Not that many of the gangsters attempted it. For those that did, the dialogue was greatly enhanced. Sound was good and lighting adequately reflected each mood, while Paul Barry's set design was a strong point; all dead end streets and hard times, it was a comfort to see the welcoming doorway of the Salvation Army, and this free standing building turned comfortably to bring us into its interior. Havana was impressive as was the backdrop to the crap game, though the Hot Box set didn't quite achieve the right tone. Stage manager Lucy Goggin ran a tight ship and her crew was snappy and efficient. Costumes, makeup, hair and props were all authentic and tied in well with the overall look - if some of the suits were, well, a tad loud! A strong choral effort too; dancing and singing was in good hands, with notable performances from Ken Moroney as Joey on the phone, Claire Buckley as Mimi and Mary Crowdle as Agatha. A talented bunch of guys and dolls indeed.

The Millbank Theatre There's something truly fascinating about seeing a real person, someone you know about, immortalised in film, television or on stage. I discovered that this fascination increases, ironically, when the subject is not flesh and blood, but a well-loved, two dimensional pen-and-ink rendition of a cheeky chappie called Andy. Rush Musical Society took the aforementioned Mr. Capp, along with his friends and family, and breathed into them a surplus of wit, warmth and good-natured bawdiness. However, the pen-and-ink original was not set aside, because Rush's set was a very clever black and white world in which just about everything, from the sofa in Flo and Andy's living room to the pints in the pub, were made as if cut-outs from the original comic strip. Settings changed with the turn of a page of a giant newspaper to the back of Rush's small but perfectly formed Millbank Theatre, and even an onstage piano folded up neatly, like this mornings paper, ready to be re-opened when needed. John O'Donoghue's design and painting was a character in its own right, and anchored the show firmly into its newspaper origins.

The far-from-two-dimensional cast was led by Gary Finegan as Andy, who made hard drinking and gentle womanising look easy, even as he underscored for us across the show's rather thin plot his lifelong devotion to the long-suffering Flo, played with equal measures of warmth and steel by Helen Kavanagh. What story there was in this character-driven production came from the impending nuptials of Raquel (Niamh Kavanagh) and Elvis (Damien Hurley). These two had an off-beat appeal and their love story, in the hands of two strong but understated actors, was funny and touching in equal measure, a mirror of sorts held up to Andy and Flo. "Understated" is not a word one could apply to Mags Carrick as Mrs Scrimmett, however, whose message to Raquel about "O Gawd, Men…Beasts" was eye-wateringly funny; a table-top tour-de-force. The long-suffering "beast" known as Mr. Scrmmett was Peter O'Brien, in a comic turn of a different sort. His eventual release from long-suffering silence revealed not so much a beast, but rather the epitome of all proud fathers of the bride, utterly focused on spending the family fortune.

The pub and the play were populated by a colourful cast of characters more than happy to help spend some of the Scrimmett millions, including Andy's friend Chalkie (Barry Kavanagh) and his wife Ruby (Noreen Fynes). Kavanagh gave a nicely modulated interpretation of this quintessential best friend and partner- in-crime role, with an engaging rapport with Finegan's Andy. Their Good Old Legs had the audience laughing our own legs off! For her part, Fynes joined the two Kavanagh's Helen and Niamh in their hymn to shopping Spend Spend Spend, in which the spoils of a shopping expedition; dresses and hats; were represented by the aforementioned newspaper cutouts - charming and very well managed.

The rest of the cast were very much flesh- and-blood inhabitants of their northern town, with the occasionally alarming dress sense you'd expect from the time and place. Andy's flat cap and some of the wedding gear were examples of extreme fashion which brought this well- resourced production to life. Musically, all was held together through the miracle of closed-circuit communication from a backstage band led by MD Sarah Lynch- Barrett. Chorus Master Kevin Walsh clearly inspired strong singing and sound was well-managed by Jody Trehy. Musical theatre is all about lifting words and music off the page and giving them life on stage. With Andy Capp, Rush Musical Society went one better and lifted a much-loved and iconic cast of characters from our daily newspapers and breathed life into them fully with spirit and gumption worthy of syndication.

Hawk's Well Theatre "There's no place like home." So say the proud people of Sligo; dash all the depression and hopelessness in the air, that's not the thinking of Sligo Musical Society, who looked at their own home grown talent: their costume designer Ray Lowbridge; graphic artist Wayne O'Connor; construction crew and makeup artists; even a film production house, Sligeach Films…put them altogether and what have you got? Quite an inspired and dramatic production of The Wizard of Oz, that's what. Director Sarah Burns knew what she wanted and I envy the support she got from Producer Jean McConnell, not to mention the rest of the team. Between the graphic artist, the local film production house and her imagination the impressive visual images abounded. The witch flew in the air, Glinda floated down in a bubble, Oz's disembodied head flashed threateningly out from amongst angry flames of fire. Along with the efforts of lighting designer Nick McCaul and sound effects from Alan Dunne, this was like hell - hell I tell you! Though the children were impressed, they weren't afraid - it was a good balance; they could tell it was scary, but there was enough distance to make it safe. Dave McEvoy's orchestra was small for this show, with just eight players, though apart from the storm scene, which was well played but needed more noise, the sound didn't suffer for it. Highlights were 'Jitterbug' (sung by Wicked Witch Denise Burns) and 'Ding Dong the Witch is Dead' with a well guided Munchkin group of children and adults. Indeed, all singers had solid support from Mr. McEvoy and Dorothy in particular was delightful, singing with controlled emotion and sincerity. It was easy to like her and the dynamic between the four heroes was great, all actors enhancing each other's performances. Robert Butler as Scarecrow and John Larkin as Tin Man, both competent singers and movers brought balance to the four way relationship and generously played straight men to Micki Murray's very funny portrayal of Lion. Special effects abounded and Denise Burns as the Wicked Witch brought fire and fear, along with a super performance, vocally and physically. Emily Tansey's appearance as Glinda was really magical, and she delighted as a gushing feminine thing with plenty of humour thrown in. The Wizard was all the stronger for Columb McBride's powerful and articulate voice, though as Professor Marvel he was a kind and considerate uncle type. Uncle Henry (Eamon Reddin) was a steady balance to the motherly sternness of Aunt Em (Caroline Hynes). Eoin O'Suileabhain brought charisma to the role of the Gatekeeper and special mention must be made of Dylan Fox, who played the Mayor and head monkey Nicki, though this was a strong choral group too, and anyone with individual roles did very well. It helped that there was a strong hand guiding everyone, and really, as a first time director, here is a name to watch out for; Sarah Burns must have been a director in a past life. Pace, timing, individual and group guidance, humour, poignancy…it was all covered. Collaboration within this strong group was evident everywhere in fact. The hugely impressive artwork of Wayne O'Connor filled in the background of scenes, giving a sense of the surreal, but yet adding a realistic touch too. The film work was a wonderful addition and all the magic of the show was enhanced by it. Melody Urquhart's choreography tied in beautifully with everything too, and her dances had shape and drama, and made the most of the talent on stage. 'Jitterbug' with its tableaux and lifts made a strong impression, though really there were many vibrant numbers highlighting this group's dance skills. There was a lot for Meg Leahy to do as stage manager, what with houses travelling across the stage, snow falling and fires going off left right and centre. The crew was on top of things and changes for the most part were swift and smooth. Hair and makeup and excellent lighting added much to the magic in this show, while costumes were really something special. Cast member Ray Lowbridge was responsible, with classically beautiful pieces that together had a striking theatrical effect; forty shades of green and as many styles gave the Emerald citizens an original look, while the cast presented themselves as busy New Yorkers; Poppies with upturned heads; Munchkins as colourful as candy. Amongst all this talent was Pippin, who although not a trained actor as such, played Toto so convincingly, it hardly showed, and clever work with sausages, bones and other doggie treats worked very well! A magical production indeed, Sligo MS; now just click your heels three times for the next one - you have the power inside your own town after all.

Come on everybody; follow that dream. Let yourself go; that's all right. It's now or never… Do you get the idea Elvis was an encouraging sort of fellow? Everywhere I go in Ireland these days, are groups of people who just want to jig this country up, shake it back into the happy times. And none more so than Carrick on Suir Musical Society, who with their show All Shook Up, brought laughter and fun to audiences last month. (Okay, two months ago…it's a busy time for those of us writing reviews.) It is a simple story, loosely based around Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, strung together to the music of The King. Musical Director Fergal Carroll did homage here, and his band was really excellent; such numbers as 'C'mon Everybody' and 'Devil in Disguise' had me reaching for the dictionary once again to check that 'stonking' is a word, but 'stonking' was the only way to describe it. There was balance to this wonderful music too, with Chorus Master Eamon O'Malley getting a magnificent sound out of a talented bunch; 'Can't Help Falling in Love' blew us clean into the interval, while the women sang like a gospel choir for 'If I Can Dream'. Director, Liam Butler, went for our jugular (in the comical sense) and really played this show for laughs, though in some cases a little reining in might have been required of the odd individual. Michael Raggett played cool guy Chad with animation, and while he sent himself up a lot, this actor had some lovely moments, such as dealing with rejection or thinking he was gay, while still getting humour out of the lines.
