A great entrance too, sliding down a pole into Chris Hennessy's set during 'Jailhouse Rock', good singing and dancing, supported by a strong female chorus behind hand held jailhouse bars. Louise Mulcahy played Natalie sweetly and Ed bravely; While 'A Little Less Conversation' was powerfully sung, this scene with Chad was delightfully cringe for everyone except the besotted gal. Along with Siobhan Grace as Miss Sandra, 'Let Yourself Go' was hilariously freaky; both women really putting full effort into the bizarre situation, along with some moving statues - great singers, who really enhanced the mood here. (Full marks to the makeup department too; it was hard to tell the real statues from the 'human' ones until they moved. Really.) Dennis the nerd evoked a lot of sympathy, though his finest hour was his solo number 'It Hurts Me' - Ray Nolan really comfortable in this song. Nikki Ahearn really impressed as Lorraine - here was a high calibre singer and scenes with James Dooley, solid and amusing as Dean, highlighted the sweetness of this couple. Sub plot number two involved Jim (Seamus Power) and Sylvia (Catherine Hogan) finally getting around to realising they would be better off together. Mr. Power convinced as the still grieving widower and scenes with Natalie were tender, while there was some fun had learning to gyrate with Chad - Liam Butler's inclusion of two girls in a shoe shop added to the humour. Ms. Hogan's quality voice was appreciated, particularly during the beautiful number 'There's Always Me.' Jenny Hogan was funny as Mayor Matilda and Fergus Power got the audience rowdy as a far-more-vocal- than-he-should-have-been Sheriff Earl - both able comedians, I would have preferred more spotlight on the Mayor. However she was let shine during the wonderful number 'Devil in Disguise' and she was truly hilarious; the face off with Chad saw two electric guitars descend from the ceiling and there was no way Chad was going to win against Matilda in this one. Great stuff, and another fun touch from Mr Butler. Plenty of dancing in this show too, and Sandra Power's choreography really had us tapping our toes and wishing we could join in the fun; 'C'mon Everybody' was a vibrant number with a strong chorus properly used, while 'Let Yourself Go' had great shape and drama, with statues joining in and adding to the surreal mood. Great care had been taken with authenticity and indeed the overall look, and set designer Chris Hennessy also kept in mind the space needed for dancing and motorbikes and what have you. Props enhanced this set - lovely touches everywhere, from sugar dispensers to posters, while costumes had just the right balance of colour. Stage manager Michael O'Hara and his crew were very efficient and things moved smoothly. Lighting suited the mood; colour and fun, if a little confusing during the more complicated part of the story. But I say to myself, don't be cruel; I'm no hound dog, I'm not the devil in disguise; after a fun night in Carrick on Suir, I felt nothing but burning love.

Have they always had so many men in their society, or was it the title 'Guys and Dolls' that attracted half of Naas' male population to sign up for this show? And one way or another, what did choreographer Evelyn Donnelly do to them to get them all dancing so darn well? Really, how did she do that? This is indeed a well-guided group, and director Arthur McGauran left nothing to chance; characters came to life and a wonderful fun story unfolded naturally. Musical Director Michael Fay oversaw an excellent orchestra and numbers such as 'Luck be a Lady' and 'Rockin the Boat' highlighted this. Singing was great too, and choral work impressed throughout. While members of the Salvation Army were visibly worried about their future (Tina O'Kelly looked so cute in that bonnet!), the Hot Box girls reveled in their roles, flanking Miss Adelaide with confidence. 'Take Back Your Mink' is always fun, and the girls here enjoyed the flirt. The Guys had been worked hard too; there must have been thirteen or fourteen of them dancing during the crap game and all of them looked good. Even the nameless amongst them were engaging and it seemed to me everyone had personality; accents, mannerisms and banter was so naturally achieved and Mr. McGauran had ensured that Runyonese was understood and properly delivered - diction was crisp too, and Vinny Osbourne on sound ensured the balance was perfect; in particular during 'Adelaide's Lament', when Julie Donnelly's powerful voice and some super brass players shared the number. Ms. Donnelly was delightful as Adelaide, she was as funny and sweet as she was a willing pushover, though I thought the otherwise great costume department had her dressed far too conservatively. Brendan Farrell's Nathan Detroit was a charming rogue, and 'Sue Me' was well sung by both. I loved these two together, and indeed Nathan's interaction with the Guys was always funny - this actor really got his worth out of the lines. Sky Masterson was well played by Andrew Docherty, who understood the troubled soul of his character. Interaction with Sarah Brown (Helen Spring) was good too and chemistry built up nicely - she gave him a fair whack across the kisser too after he took liberties with her. Another really lovely voice, Ms. Spring's treatment of 'If I Were a Bell' was great, and indeed 'Marry the Man' with Adelaide was strong too. Peter Fay as Nicely was a solid Guy, and humour came easily along with the varying but equally engaging personalities of Benny (the ever versatile Gary Lanigan) and Rusty (Martin Fahy). 'Sit Down You're Rockin the Boat' was a showstopper. The Guys were great, as I think I mentioned, and no principal could afford to sit back on their laurels; they all worked hard, yet the overall mood was one of great ease and coolness. Harry the Horse (Sean O'Keeffe) had a bit of an edge to him, while Big Jule (Conor Byrne), delivering his lines with comedy, convinced as a dangerous bully. The scene going into 'Rockin the Boat' was beautifully directed; each Guy found something interesting (Nicely admiring the ceiling plasterwork) in the room or indeed the sea of red clad Salvation women (did I mention Tina O'Kelly in a really charming bonnet?) caused some excitement. The polar extremes here caused Lt. Brannigan some confusion and the character was played with just the right balance by David Walsh. John Dooley made a lovely Uncle Arvide with a really beautiful voice, rich and melodic and he did great justice to 'More I Cannot Wish'.  Nobody in this chorus was ever going to say: "I just never know what to do with my hands…" Everyone, every corner of every nook and cranny, every sideways glance, every bit of interaction had been expertly guided by director Arthur McGauran; I think he liked the show (understatement), but I guess he liked his people more. Mr. McGauran also designed the set, which worked really well for his impressive crossovers - a delightful surprise when the crap game guys disappeared into a manhole, which was used at the end of the scene again with the guys climbing out of it again - a lot of fun seeing Big Jule and Harry the Horse manage this.  Stage manager (and set builder) Bob O'Kelly and his efficient crew managed things smoothly, and scene changes were always snappy. Lighting by Darren Kellegher enhanced things well. Hair and makeup was authentic, with possibly Adelaide once again given conservative treatment. Nothing conservative about the show however, especially where laughs were concerned; I loved the easy humour as much as I did the visual imagery of Evelyn Donnelly's choreography, and Michael Fay's music consistently adding to the overall enjoyment of this fine production. What have the men folk of Naas been doing with themselves since?

My first task as a newly married woman was to banish my husband's jumpers to the bin; sad, leftover from the eighties, they just wanted to rest in peace with dignity somewhere, but alas, even the charity shop wouldn't take them. I was reminded of this early memory when actor Stephen O'Riain appeared in one of them during Limerick Musical Society's production of Big, The Musical. Nice to know it ended up being useful, and berets off to the costume department here, who really managed to capture the unfortunate fashion styles of that era, and put some amazing children into bright happy colours too; two choruses, teens and younger, gleefully danced the night away to Niamh Twomey's choreography, which reflected both the times and the mood. 'Cross the Line' was typical of this, with plenty of life and energy, while 'The Nightmare' really reflected the crazy goings on in Josh's mind. It's always great to see plenty of dancing in a musical and particularly when the troupe has been so well trained. The music was difficult enough and MD Marie Keary-Scanlon had her hands full with a large cast, but they had been put through their paces and the likes of 'Say Good Morning to Mom' highlighted solid support. It's an Irish premiere, so I'll remind you briefly; this is the musical version of the film where 13 year old Josh Baskin makes a wish and overnight grows into Tom Hanks, or in this case, Stephen O'Riain, who brought just the right balance of childlike innocence to the role - enough to be engaged and not squirm when Hilary Burke, playing Susan repeatedly tried to seduce him. She had some success it must be said, and there was tenderness as well as humour between these two. 'We're Gonna be Fine' was sensitively sung by both competent performers, and 'Little Susan Lawrence' really brought an extra layer to Susan's character. Mostly there were funky eighties style moments however, and director Richie Ryan was a dab hand at these large brightly presented scenes, like the carnival and the toyshop (put me in mind of the Late Late toy show), and the large cast was given plenty of guidance.  'Fun' in the toyshop saw Josh and his future boss, George MacMillan (played by Mr Ryan) dance on a giant keyboard - impressive work here from the set builders, director, choreographer and MD, not to mention the stage crew who managed to put it together mid scene without disturbing anyone. Stage Manager Cathal O'Donovan had a hundred crew I'd say and they worked super efficiently - the director's set design was certainly 'modern' in that 80's sense; bedrooms were trendy and messy and care was taken to leave plenty of space for dancing. Young Josh was played by Christopher Young, and boy could he dance! His pal Billy - an excellent Jared Nadin, kept the continuity of the friendship with Adult Josh too and singing, dancing and acting was great. The villain of the show was Paul Seymour, mean and ambitious and played with relish by Shane Barriscale. Emma Culhane played Mrs Baskin, Josh's heartbroken mother, and 'Stop, Time' was a really beautiful moment. Carol Murphy brought gentle humour to secretary Mrs Watson, and Susan's four friends Paul Noonan, Dermot Winston, Helena Twomey and Vivienne O'Brien really highlighted the dividing line between childhood abandon and serious old grown ups.  Many individual roles were more than capably managed by the strong adult chorus. Somewhat let down by sound on the night I attended - it was difficult to decipher words and lyrics - though sound effects were good. Lighting design was good but execution was a little hit and miss, though the overall images created by people and costumes on a great set more than made up. Props, hair and makeup were authentic too and everywhere one looked were reminders: you wore that, you really did; your hair was once that way, it really was. (Still would be without the blessings of modern technology.) A trip down memory lane, an evening with a talented and diverse group, and a lot of innocent fun: Limerick Musical Society sure did make a Big impression.

Oliver! I'm not sure what the exclamation mark in the title is for, but in Fortwilliam Musical Society's production it was justified as the show highlighted some amazing children having plenty of fun. Humour was a strong point too, and director Siobhan Mullin got a lot out of her cast, with actors playing naturally, yet finding the jokes along the way. Drew Reid and Siobhan Farrell had just the right balance of bawdy humour together as Mr. Bumble and the Widow Corney and their flirting scene had us laughing, while singing was still strong; 'I Shall Scream' was sung with pretend shock by Ms Farrell, and her mimed bossing of the stage crew as they changed the set was a lovely touch, keeping the pace of things flowing nicely. Oliver himself, confidently played by Sean Monaghan, could not only sing, but had an extraordinarily strong musical ear for his age; 'Where is Love' was beautiful, and while Mr Monaghan could give Oliver a sweet edge, he had a more realistic, impish quality too. Indeed, the show abounded with impish behaviour and Ms Mullin and team clearly enjoyed the children's input. The workhouse children had been very well guided; they looked weak and hungry and some of them were teenie tiny - yet all managed to dance and sing marvellously; 'Food Glorious Food' had shape and drama, while another young chorus supported Terry McCann as the Artful Dodger in a very lively 'Consider Yourself'. Dodger was all confidence and charisma and interacted well with Fagin - a surprisingly well aged Vijay Sharma, who convinced as the miser, with physical traits and a great accent; Fagin worked very well off his lost boys (and girls), and 'Pick a Pocket' introduced a great group of naturally interacting children, with Katie Lynn as Charlie standing out. 'Be Back Soon' was a high energy number going into the interval. Before we got to that though, we met Nancy, beautifully played by Dawn Patton, who on one hand showed a maternal side when singing the likes of 'I'd Do Anything' but could play the tough girl too, and with the costume department giving her a shorter than usual red dress and a fancy pair of bloomers, she was able to be uncouth without losing her feminine charms. Bet's character was given plenty of direction and Fiona Donnelly's interpretation was as a sort of hopeful character, all seeing and all caring, but would she go down the same seedy road as Nancy? We all know Bill Sykes is a nasty piece of work, and Barry O'Kelly seemed intent on making sure we didn't forget it. 'My Name' was powerfully delivered and the audience seemed unsure whether to applaud or not (you know, in case it got him going again). Angry and bull headed, it was difficult to see what Nancy saw in him, though 'As Long as He Needs Me' was sincerely sung and a fine orchestra, under the strong baton of William Cairns impressed throughout the show, with numbers such as 'Oom Pah Pah' (a strong choral number) and 'Reviewing the Situation' standing out - violin especially here, along with the confident tones of Mr Sharma's voice. Indeed, Angela Harding's choreography time and again interpreted the music so well and everyone had been well prepped. The Sowerberry couple were polar opposites, with Michael Blair giving Mister S quite the nervous disposition while his wife Joanne Corrigan bossed everyone about. Noah and Charlotte's characters were given extra life by a little bit of harmless flirting too. 'That's Your Funeral' was played slower than I'm used to, but Ms Harding brought a sort of surreal edge to it, with the Sowerberrys acting quite eerie. The set, designed by Border Studios and the director, really allowed for plenty of movement and dancing, yet it cleverly allowed crew easy access with a central arch upstage, under the bridge, which when curtained off with black drapes gave a sort of dark tunnel depth, but with a few lace curtains instead, became the backdrop to Mr. Brownlow's house. Stage Manager Gerard Kelly had things running tightly. Lighting was effective and enhanced many a lovely moment and collaboration was evident everywhere with this production team. Sound was an issue here and there; although balance seemed fine between players and singers, it was not always easy to decipher lyrics. Props were authentic as were hair and makeup, though Mr. Brownlow was quite a young grandfather and might have been made older looking. Performance wise Simon Cunningham had a gentle touch however and convinced as the kindly gent, while Mrs. Bedwin (Katherine Ringland) reflected this, and the reprise of 'Where is Love' was well sung. Kevin McReynolds as Doctor Grimwig got something out of each line and everywhere were lovely touches from the director - a maid catching the messenger boy and boxing his ears; Fagin chewing his nails while everyone else quivered during 'My Name'; Old Sally putting the fear of God in people every time she coughed. I loved the guidance given to all, and characters developed naturally and convincingly. There was real drama during the awful murder scene, though it was all over a bit quick, even for a gentle soul like me. While Fagin sang over the corpses, I was thankful there was no humour in the reprise of 'Reviewing the Situation'. Indeed, it ended darkly, with little hope, though I had the feeling Bet might try to change things for the better. Perhaps that is the intention in the exclamation mark!

The roles of Oliver, Dodger and Fagin were shared with Owen McKavanagh, Niall McDowell and Tony Young respectively. Pity I didn't get to see them all, but I have no doubt they also shone in this wonderful production.

It's been a while since I'd seen 'Show Boat' and I hadn't remembered it being so darned funny; hats off to director Peter Kennedy, he does have a magic sense of humour and the 'play within the play' scenes in particular were very entertaining. Plenty of comic talent too across the board, particularly Michelle Glynn, physical and funny as Ellie, and James Harris equally so as her sidekick Frank, though the prize in this scene must go to Fr Michael Byrne as a desperate Captain Andy, trying to save the show. Margaret Martin as Parthay had a wonderful sense of timing to enhance this, and her bossiness towards everyone was almost comforting. Musical Director John Roe was in charge of some great musicians and his orchestra was a solid support throughout. 'Ol Man River' was a particular highlight. Indeed, Cormac O'Corcorain playing Joe was hugely impressive, with just the right balance of accent, mannerism and low energy physicality to bring this character to life, not to mention that voice! The men, many of them quite young, enhanced the sound. Chorus Mistress Martha O'Toole had trained her chorus well, with finale numbers especially, both into the interval and end of show really sounding big and dramatic. Iona Le Gros was delightful as Magnolia, and her voice utterly beautiful; 'Only Make Believe' proved that, but the same could be said of all Ms. Le Gros' numbers. Chemistry with Ravenal, sincerely played by Ronan Rooney, was convincing, starting even before he had clapped eyes on the girl, during a confident performance of 'Where's the Mate for Me', though again, any of Mr. Rooney's numbers impressed. Aoife Flannery, looking striking - the wardrobe department ensured an authentic look - sang 'Can't Help Lovin' Dat Man' with controlled sincerity with a lovely women's chorus and Ailbhe Slevin was convincing as Queenie; I did appreciate Mr. Kennedy's direction here - speech, mannerisms and attitude built up the characters and skin colour was left alone. Good casting and solid direction was evident throughout, with Mr. Kennedy choreographing the show too. While steps were simple, there were competently performed by all, with a female chorus provided more action when necessary - as indeed did a few cart wheeling men. Steve was admirably played by Joe Joyce before abandoning Julie to the drink and a suitably mean spirited Tim (Karl O'Doherty). Frank and Ellie were a consistently entertaining duo, whether he was delighting us as a very convincing drunk or she was being thrown around like a Barbie doll. Ms Glynn impressed particularly and while she was funny, she also brought depth to her character. Smaller roles were well performed too, and Windy (Colm Heery) was as solid as he was stern, with Pete (Gary Browne) bringing good drama to things early on. Rubberface (Francis Conneely) was funny, especially during those rehearsal scenes, while the Back Wood men (Jack Keane and Robert Brown) added fuel for further humour. Ruth O'Malley as the Irish Landlady gave a confident if short performance. Scene changes were smoothly managed by stage manager Marion Heery, with the hired set working very well for this production, though lighting - which was otherwise great - might have warmed things down a bit in the kitchen. It's not the shortest show in the world, and waiting till the very end to appear was Alix Slattery as the most charming little Miss Kim you ever came across; she spoke clearly, with an accent and with genuine personality. What a find! What a future! I wonder what Michael D Higgins thought of it all, since he had attended the show during the week - word is, he and Sabina had a ball, and were amongst the last to leave the theatre. The Patrician Musical Society had it all: laughs, sniffs and a final happy ending.

Back in my pre-children days, I read. A lot. "I've nothing left to read!" was something I often complained of, as I would scan bookshelves. "What about 'A Tale of Two Cities'?" My husband suggested. "It's a great story. A really great story." I grudgingly picked it up but it wasn't what I was in the mood for. When I finished it, I thanked him from my heart. It was truly one of the most beautiful tales I ever read, and Sydney Carton remains in my mind as a glorious hero. "Was it good then?" he asked. "I never actually read it myself. I just heard it was a great story." Jill Santoriello certainly thought so; she wrote the script, lyrics and music and the show, which, for anyone looking for a possible alternative to Les Mis, is a little bit special. For one thing, Ms Santoriello managed to inject more humour into the story than I remembered from the book. Sydney Carton is a cad to be sure, but he was funny, and Alan Greaney played him with such foppish charm it was impossible not to warm to him. Interaction with characters such as Jerry Cruncher (a confidently comical Richard Bell) and the underhanded spy John Barsad (Sean Hosty) were highly entertaining, and along with a strong chorus, such numbers as 'No Honest Way' in the tavern were quite the treat. Visually, this show had a very strong impact too, with co-directing brothers Brian and Sean Power delivering drama, passion and deeply felt sorrow all over the place (hence the need for humour peppered throughout the show). It was beautiful work, and there were many scenes that frankly looked like moving art. Choreographer Mary MacDonagh wasn't given music that could be danced to as such, but the visual imagery created with a willing chorus was magnificent; 'Round and Round' made great use of people. It was a long enough show, but the pace was good and stage manager Leonard Power saw to it that things stayed snappy with seamless set changes, incorporating the cast for continuity. Brendan Savage's set of rough brickwork and broken buildings was authentic and levels, steps and arches were well employed. Props were impressively authentic. Jim Faullkner's lighting design complemented the set, and indeed enhanced many a beautiful moment, from Sydney Carton singing in a pool of light under light snowfall to his final moments; as characters walked with dignity towards their death, a shaft of bright light was suddenly cut off against the sound of the guillotine and a distant mob cheering. Technically things might have been a little tighter in both the sound and lighting departments, but overall the music was super, with MD Shane Farrell in command of a strong orchestra. There are many memorable tunes in this show, with things gradually getting more powerful, and along with quality soloists and a well-trained chorus, no one could have disappointed in the music. Chorus Master Paddy Daly can be proud. Care and attention had been taken with costumes and the hints of red here and there suggestive of the pending revolution.

My only bone of contention with the twin directors was that they made me cry. Yes, my steely composure crumbled more than once; beginning when Dr Manette, after seventeen years in prison was reunited with daughter Lucie. Never mind the excellent skills of the hair and makeup department; Stephen Macken as the wronged doctor almost broke my heart as he tried to put together the broken pieces of his mind - 'You'll Never Be Alone' highlighted sheer quality voices in both Mr Macken and Blaithin Walsh playing Lucie. Her good nature and sweet manner attracted many and she was easy to love. Miss Pross (beautifully played by Ursula Owens) was devoted to her and softhearted Charles Darnay was besotted - Diarmuid Scahill really came to life through music, and 'The Promise' with Dr Manette was beautifully performed. Darnay was light to his Uncle's darkness, and Jim Dillon played the Marquis St Evremonde with cold calculation, though here was yet another singer of great quality. Sean Hosty gave the spy John Barsad credibility, taking him beyond stereotype and adding levels to the character. Jonathan Hopper, as a rather young Mr. Lorry was a sort of strain of sense through the story, and this was a lovely gentle performance. Katie Creaven was passionate and bitter as Madame Defarge and singing was altogether powerful. 'The Tale' was a real highlight, and when she had finished, no mob in the world would have forgiven Darnay; his doom was well and truly sealed. Or was it? Did I say I love Sydney Carton's character? Alan Greaney brought such sincere tenderness to the role that I must thank him for his portrayal; he suffered unrequited love with quiet dignity and he went to his death a true hero, completely redeemed of his former ways - an image that will stay with me a long time indeed. There were wonderful performances all round, and rich pickings for the production team; Liam Brennan as Ernest Defarge, Mikey Walsh as Gaspard, Gavin Sweeney as the Young Man: all beautiful singers, emotional and sincere; Haughty Stryver (Michael Flanagan), petrified Gabelle (Oisin Tierney); the rioters, the scoundrels, those unfortunates sent to a violent death; the little boy in the prison, Little Gaspard trampled to death and, one to watch in the future, Emily Macken as Little Lucie, a delightful creature who could sing and act as good as any of them (being Stephen Macken's daughter in real life, it would be hard to avoid it). Special mention must be made of Louise Colohan as the Seamstress; a small but memorable role as the final recipient of Carton's selflessness, her fear was palpable but not indulgent, and singing was beautiful. Great justice done to the tale; I might just re-read it.

The streets of Arklow were almost literally paved with gold when Avonmore Musical Society took to the stage with their production of the Wizard of Oz. It was a no-brainer, really (apologies to the Scarecrow!) with the perfect casting choice of Amy Penston on hand as Dorothy. Lloyd-Webber and Co. missed a glorious opportunity when they let this one go. The buzz around town was that this Wizard was a treat, and the performance I saw did not disappoint. On the surface, the St. Mary's College Hall is neither the most promising nor magical of spaces to perform in, but Avonmore took over and made Oz their own, with an imaginative set, detailed costumes, amusing hairstyles and one or two injections of hydraulic wizardry to make their show fly - just about literally as it turned out. James Kearon as Uncle Henry and Paula McLoughlin were a feisty and surprisingly funny duo as they defended Dorothy and her little dog Toto, admirably and effortlessly played by Penny. Their opponent was the rather scary Fiona Walker as Miss Gulch, but as it turned out, we hadn't seen nothin' yet, as her transformation into the Wicked Witch was achieved with comprehensive zeal. Kearon did double duty as doorkeeper to the Emerald City, a very amusing take that made terrific use of his wonderful speaking voice. Ken Moroney was all bustle and bumble as the Professor, and he carried that forward to his turn as the Wizard, making us wonder if the aura of confusion was entirely an act. This was an endearing performance, but Moroney had competition in the shape of the equally endearing Tomás Byrne, Seán Hendley and Patrick Bracken as Scarecrow, Tinman and The Cowardly Lion respectively. These performances inevitably channelled the film to some extent, but there were telling differences, with Scarecrow somewhat more worldly, Tinman a bit less sentimental and the Lion quite roaringly larger than life. Was than an Irish dancing wig on his head, or was he just scared to see us? Their journey with Dorothy took them further than one would have imagined possible in the hall, but the centre aisle became that yellow brick road and was used to good effect. And good effects were the order of the evening, as various clever devices allowed Miss Gulch on her bicycle and the Wicked Witch to fly across the stage, caused a beautiful but colourless Kansas to transform into the Technicolor splendour of Oz and sent the Wizard off in his balloon, sans Dorothy. And the splendour didn't end there, for this talented cast must have been somewhat of a choreographer's dream, and Martina Lynch made ample use of them, especially in a glorious Jitterbug that saw the three intrepid followers of the Yellow Brick Road dancing in spite of themselves, as if possessed. The element of this show that really possessed all of us though, was the measured and melodic performance of Penston as Dorothy, a team player who nonetheless shone at key moments, such as a pitch- perfect Over the Rainbow and her ability to convey real emotion, even as the magic around her glowed and sparkled. Children of all ages in the audience and cast must surely have loved the glimpse she gave them of what really is possible beyond the Rainbow.

Coláiste Bride Although there were slightly fewer than seventy-six trombones in the pit for Enniscorthy Musical Society's production of Music Man, that did not stop this enterprising company from making the most of a wonderful show's musical and theatrical possibilities. The musical requirements of Music Man are many, ranging from performers who can manage everything from patter songs to patriotism, ballads to barbershop. This was seemingly no bother to MD Kevin Kennedy, who took to his duties like a duck to water. The assembled band was terrifically well-balanced and played with the requisite style and punch.

So much for the pit, onstage it was similar story, with each of the variety of 'types' in this story catered for. Harold Hill, the consummate conman on whom the narrative turns, was Brendan Redmond, an experienced player whose interpretation was understated but quietly effective, a man caught out by his unexpected attraction to the "gal with a touch of sin", Marian, played by Joanne McCabe. She has a beautifully strong voice and balanced her interpretation between the somewhat brittle librarian's exterior and a warmer-hearted hometown girl. Her mother, the ever-so-'oirish' Mrs. Paroo, was a pitch-perfect Caroline O'Connell, whose comic and musical timing chimed beautifully. Another comic turn was provided by Liz Armstrong as the gloriously named Eulalie Mackecknie Shinn, an eccentric and easily led woman who presided over a nicely prim gaggle of Pick-a-Little ladies. Mayor Shinn was Lorcan Dunne, whose often-thwarted authority was nicely presented. The family was completed by Dearbháil Murphy as "ye Gods" Zaneeta Shinn, a nicely angst-ridden teenager, who also happened to be a very good dancer. Other notable young performers were Bronagh Hogan as Amarylis and Daithi Medcalf as Winthrop, two strong singer/ actors already at ease onstage and making a good impression. Speaking of ease on stage, Graham Finnerty was a nicely nervy Marcellus Washburn, whose leading of the Shipoopi number allowed his inner song and dance man to emerge fully. There was some good movement across this show, with the setting of a dream-like Marian the Librarian a rhythmic gem and the aforementioned Shipoopi gamely athletic. An element of ballet added to the mix, in the way a well-coordinated and detailed approach to costume filled in the frame. Niall Kavanagh was Tommy Djilas, a neatly packaged performance of the boyfriend every father dreads for his daughter. Strolling in and out of many scenes was the Quartet of Pat Bolger, James Dobbs, Robert Rowe and James O'Connor who were musically sound and nicely pleased with themselves as characters who didn't know they could sing. Ice Cream indeed! There are so many distinct aspects of this show for a company to get their teeth into, and Enniscorthy grabbed onto this from the very start with the Rock Island number on the train very solidly set. All in all, this production had the look and feel of the time and place required, a stubborn Iowa that positively glowed with the small-town concerns and basic connections that provide the story's platform. There may have been Trouble in River City, but there was pure entertainment in Enniscorthy when this Musical Society took to the stage.

It was very much a case of "Once Upon a Time" in Tipperary when Nenagh Choral Society took to the stage with Beauty and the Beast. The prologue to the musical took the form of an actual story telling session that involved a charming small group of children gathered around archetypal storyteller Michael McCormack. This clarity of purpose carried through the production, which was strong on presenting distinct, well-directed characters who worked very well in relation to one another. There was a nice sense of busy-ness in the background of scenes that helped to underscore the story as it unfolded. Niamh Chadwick as Belle brought a sweetly resonant voice to this role, and the progression of Belle's relationship with the Beast was very well realised in this interpretation. Andrew Whelan as The Beast paced his performance in such a way as to make this crucial transformation believable and ultimately quite emotionally resonant. In his castle, Ger McCarthy was a nicely magisterial Cogsworth, petulantly keeping tabs on everything and everybody. Lumiere was fussy and flamboyant in the in the hands of Patrick Rohan Jr., a contrast to Erica Flanagan Walsh's Mrs. Potts, who's calm demeanour and warm voice provided a serene centre to the enchanted inmates. Zelda Dillon was a spectacular Madame de la Grand Bouche, whose frustrated Diva-ish exterior held a heart of gold (somewhere amid all those drawers!) Karen Prout was Babette, whose very witty approach ably defined this character as a chamber maid with more than just feather dusting on her mind. Shane Slattery was Chip, for once not confined in a tea trolley and all the more engaging for it. His singing voice was a treasure. Back in the village another voice to treasure was that of Paul Brown as Gaston. This young actor covered many bases in his performance, which was very funny and also musically resonant. His sidekick, Alan O'Brien as Lefou presented an interpretation that extended to a delightfully whiny voice and deliciously annoying manner. Competing with him for "most annoying in the village" were the superb Silly Girls, Caoimhe Geaney, Emily Sheary and Louise Cormack. Their antics were worth a whole show on their own: Silly Girls, The Musical. Musically, this was well-resourced with a band that drew on a variety of players who occasionally fell foul of some if this demanding score's intricate harmonic meanderings. That said, this was an enthusiastic and rhythmic reading, conducted by MD Laura Kearney. The enthusiasm in the pit extended to the stage as well, and chorus singing was focussed and also rhythmically keen. The set was inevitably a game of two halves, with the village perfectly apt and fit for purpose, but the castle really very fine indeed. There were some terrific painted accents that used tromp l'oeil to add detail and depth. Sound management was very nicely done, and lighting was detailed also, with the 'Kill the Beast' scene in the Castle especially well managed. Costumes were as expected, and a rather mixed bag, some of the most beautifully detailed costumes revealed briefly at the end, when the castle's inmates are finally "human again". Indeed, this was a production infused with a very human touch, giving the audience a story that was most definitely a real page-turner

2012 can quite rightly be described as the year of Titanic, and April, with the 100th anniversary of the sinking, was Titanic month. Portrush Music Society quite rightly took on the task of presenting Titanic the Musical, with a production embellished by a great deal of information and insight, some of which contributed to their front of house displays. There was a grand sense of occasion in the Riverside Theatre, Coleraine and from the very beginning our journey with Titanic's passengers was supported by a very fine orchestra under the able leadership of MD Richard Campbell. The almost through- composed music leaves little time for a musical director to catch breath, much less sit down, and it is the score that was the pulsing engine under the prow of this production. Titanic requires a large cast and chorus, and Portrush's assembled forces made for a substantial passenger list, which meant that the choral sound was solid. Occasionally over-zealous amplification meant that some nuance was lost in the course of our journey, but there was evidence of careful preparation and clarity of purpose on the part of the cast. It was the smaller moments that gave the best glimpse through the window of history that this tragedy occupies. To that end, the singing of Harry Stinson as Harold Bride, radioman, was quite compelling, with a precise, warm simplicity. Paired with him in some scenes was David McDowell as stoker Frederick Barrett, who gave an emotional account of his songs and created real focus. In the third class, the "Three Kates" were led by Elaine Morrison as Kate McGowan, whose persuasive singing and acting was the pivot point of an important sub-plot. Kate Mullins was played by Liz Bottomley and Cathy Colgan was Kate Murphy. Between them, these three were the focus of an iconic scene in which genuine traditional musicians entertained passengers below decks. Occupying Second Class were Helen Wilkinson and William Thompson as Alice and Edgar Beane. He was a gentle and patient 'straight man' to her flamboyant take on this social climber; a very funny performance that provided areas of light in what becomes, inevitably, a rather dark story. The characters of Charles Clark and Caroline Neville also provided a story that added colour to the main narrative, nicely played and sung by Paul Loan and Una Culkin. In First Class, Isador and Ida Strauss were played by Carlton Mullineux and Maxine McAleenon, whose relationship was tenderly and effectively portrayed. Likewise, the family unit of John B., Marion and Jack Thayer were nicely fleshed out by by William Baxter, Addis Blair and Adam Jackson. Other First and Third Class passengers populated the decks in scenes of embarkation, and of course the iconic lifeboats scene. Rory Sheehan was J. Bruce Ismay, a somewhat overwrought portrayal that pulled no punches in terms of placing blame for the ship's demise on this unfortunate passenger. At the helm, Captain E. J. Smith was Paul Sleet, one of the most sure-footed portrayals of the night. Thomas Andrews was played by Peter Olphert with the kind of omniscient fervour expected from this role, functioning as narrator in both prologue and postlude. In these sections, model versions of Titanic herself played a key role in providing focus and setting the scene. They were examples of an approach to production that went far to provide detail and a deliciously complete approach to props that included a hand-painted dinner service with the White Star logo, and replica tickets for the passage. Portrush Music Society certainly put heart and soul into this show, and while the result was uneven at times, the journey was very much worth embarking on

As I write this, I know I am already in trouble with many societies, waiting for their reviews. The backlog is not so much a Sword of Damocles as a chorus of little old ladies, thirty or more of them, dressed identically, wielding handbags and Zimmer frames. They're coming for me! Oh no, it was only a dream; a bizarre mad dream, formed from the memories of Clara Musical Society's hilarious production of The Producers. Director (and Musical Director) Alan Recks clearly put his heart and soul into this production and crucially, he got the humour. It's not everyone's cup of tea - or so they say - the woman sitting behind me nearly had a coronary attack from laughter, and the above mentioned Zimmer frame scene nearly finished her off. She wasn't the only one; everyone had fun. Central, and so vital, was Max Bialystock, played by a perfectly cast Paul Norton; his soliloquy in the prison cell was stand alone theatre and hilarious, but interaction with a solid cast was great and characters such as Ulla (Natalee Kelly), she of the 'If You've Got It, Flaunt It' kind of confidence and Touch Me Hold Me (Aoife Fitzsimons), that randy old lady, was always going to be funny. Max's partner in crime Leo Bloom was another talented performer and Malcolm Whelan brought not just humour, but strong singing talent to the role. Wearing his MD hat, Mr Recks was fortunate enough to have under his solid control not just a super band, but a consistently strong chorus, from 'The King of Broadway' at the top of the show, to a good old Broadway style finale. Did I mention it was funny? Ah, laughter is so good for the soul, and my soul soared when from somewhere on a New York rooftop, Franz Liebkind tended his pigeons and taught Max and Leo the 'Der Gutan Tag Hop Clop'. Seamus Carroll brought everything necessary to this role in order to squeeze maximum comedy from it, and Alan Recks ensured things never crossed the line to become offensive - a lovely balance. I must also mention Mr Carroll's great knees, as he donned traditional costume, and while I'm at it, I must congratulate a strong wardrobe team on excellent work, though I know they had fun; who couldn't enjoy dressing Roger DeBris and his delightfully camp mates - Wayne Handy looked magnificent in a long glittery ball gown, and I'm sure the knowledge of this fact alone provided many bums on seats. Fabulous darlings. John Coss was perfect as his assistant Carmen Ghia. There was plenty of opportunity for this cast to show off in various individual roles, but I must mention Nigel Sammon as Mr Marks - he was simply a brute in the office. Sarah Griffin's choreography really interpreted not just the music well, but the humour came across in the dancing just as much as it did in the acting. She had her work cut out for her certainly during the impressive 'I Wanna Be a Producer', and Tommy Scanlon (and team)'s clever set design worked perfectly here, with accountants dreaming by their movable desks and showgirls appearing out of the filing cabinets. As mentioned, 'Der Gutan Tag Hop Clop' was funny; belly laugh stuff, and the three actors involved rehearsed to within an inch of their lives, I'd say. 'Little Old Lady Land' was given similar treatment. 'Springtime for Hitler' was superb; it ridiculed the entire Nazi regime in the best possible style. Some lovely collaborative touches between director and stage crew, with scene changes being entertaining in their own right. Stage Manager Simon Cannon managed plenty of crew and changes were efficient and snappy. Let me get my bugbear out: I couldn't see the need for the smoke machine at any time in this otherwise excellent production. Sound balance was fine most of the time and lighting reflected the mood well, with a highlight during the prison scene. Clara people are so funny; who knew?

INEC It was opening night of Killarney Musical Society's production of Titanic, and the punters decided to dress up as first class passengers. It was a long drive from Dublin and I decided to dress comfortably - that is, like a third class passenger, so I guess, in a way, I did fit in. Not that chairperson Pam Brosnan was anything less than charming. The last time I had been in the INEC, I looked a little more glam, along with 1000 others, last June. I was impressed by the projection design by John Hurley during the overture; latitudes and longitudes, dimensions and moving images of various locations dissolved beautifully into each other, while the wreck of the Titanic was just about visible; it was quite mesmerising and I wondered, if this was just the beginning, what was yet to come? A singer in a soft spotlight while blueprints dissolved on the screen behind him; characters suddenly appearing while others melted away. What exceptional work from John Hurley, brother of director/ choreographer, Oliver Hurley - more on him in a moment - and presumably both related to one Brian Hurley, who was standing in for the character Murdock that night. Musical Director John O'Brien was exceptional at the helm of a fine orchestra, and the music in this powerful show was consistently impressive, from the flawless beat under everything to the magnificent and heart wrenching ending. Chorus work was rousing too, under Chorus Mistress Aine Nic Ghabhann; this was not easy music and everyone sang well with focused emotion. There is a huge cast in this show, and while many guests are given attention, no one person ever fully develops as fully as they do in your average musical. Director Oliver Hurley stood by his characters loyally and allowed each person to bring all they could to the production; Captain E.J.'s ego is ever being tested and Gabriel Butler brought good balance to the man, who, on his final voyage on the world's largest ever ship could have been forgiven for his pride. Prodding him onwards was Bruce Ismay, arrogant and at times obnoxious, but Gerry Adams never allowed him to become a stereotypical villain. Somewhere between these two, Mr Andrews wavered, and 'The Blame' in particular was a beautifully directed piece highlighting these three men and all they stood for. Indeed, Derek O'Leary, playing the ship's designer, Thomas Andrews, brought the show to its tragic conclusion as he realised in 'Mr Andrew's Vision' his design flaw and the simplicity with which he might have fixed it. Against his impassioned singing on an angled bridge, passengers tried in vain to climb to the top of a sinking ship; movement here was beautifully directed, and great care had been taken in what each individual brought to it as well as the overall desperate image. Boiler room man Frederick Barrett (Reggie McCrohan) and Marconi man Harold Bride (Rory Ward) had a really lovely scene together and both songs in the radio room were well performed. Butler Henry Etches was performed with dignity and steady timing by Conor O'Leary, and Jack Patrick Healy gave Band Leader Wallace Hartley a touch of the times, with an authentically engaging performance of 'Doing the Latest Rag'. In Titanic, there are snippets of people's lives; the three Kates, played with delightful energy by Clarie Doyle, Ciara O'Donoghue and Amano Miura, and along with Jim (Michael Mills) Ms. Doyle played out a lovely romantic scene; Nannette O'Leary and Eddie Phillips played Ida and Isidor Straus beautifully; they were hopelessly in love; Charles and Caroline (Ben Quinlan and Andrea Thornton) intrigued me with the possibilities of their story; the Major (Trevor Edwards) was charming in his dottiness and Mrs Cardoza (Niamh Burns) was the likable modern American woman. Possibly Alice Beane had the most depth to her character and Orna Cleary O'Shea brought both humour and frustrated passion to her, while husband Edgar (Tim Buckley) bore it all with quiet patience. Ms Cleary O'Shea's singing was wonderful too, and she could pick notes out of the air with confidence. This show was a celebration of what can be done through dedicated collaboration from a number of creative people; Oliver Hurley's vision brought rawness to the story, and a sincere desire to reproduce the tragedy as closely as possible; Lighting and technical designer John Hurley enhanced this with great attention to little details and a great understanding of what is visually possible. Along with Oliver Hurley's solid choreography, the music was the heartbeat of this fine show. There was plenty for stage manager Frank Ashe to cope with and the hired set worked very well. Costumes, hair and makeup were wonderful; second-class passengers looked so good I waited in eager anticipation to see what first-class would be wearing, and I wasn't disappointed. Most of all, I was impressed by the chilling reality of the drowning sequence; after the horror of seeing passengers fall back into the water we were plunged into darkness - the only sounds, those of frightened weeping, people shocked by the cold of the water, breathing heavy with terror. But it was gently done, in a 'less is more' manner, and when at last, this powerful chorus sang the final number; there was no doubt in my mind that the entire company had come through their own emotional journey. The possible stories of those who perished lives on.

White Memorial Theatre Long ago, when I was a gal, and everything was in black and white, chess was just a game you played because there was only one TV station. Nobody harboured any grudges if you stole their queen; it didn't make any of us more attractive; no one took it too seriously. Things could get pretty darned serious in St. Mary's Choral Society's production of Chess however, and the tension was palpable at times. If you were lucky enough to catch it, you'll expect me to waste no time mentioning one of the most striking elements - the choreography of the chess game dances. While this is always a strong visual feature in Chess, choreographer Majella Louise Fitzgerald must have started work long ago on her interpretation, because it was flawless in its execution. The dancers were exquisite creatures, gorgeous and graceful as they reflected the game in a series of disciplined moves. It was like moments of moving art dissolving into each other, and while it was utterly engaging, director Michael O'Donoghue still managed to elicit nail-biting tension from the scene surrounding it. There was a strong dynamic between the two challengers throughout the show and Emmet Donlan as Freddie Trumper quickly established his egotistic character with a confident approach. Singing of these difficult numbers was managed with ease, and 'Pity the Child' in particular was treated with great sensitivity, clearly showing Freddie's vulnerable side. 'The Interview' was a passionate affair too, and this number with Anatoly (a highly focused Diarmuid Vaughan) had a lot of drama. I was relieved when they finally made peace and dealt with issues more important than who got the girl; Florence was personably played by Aine Hennessy, and interaction with demanding Freddie was as comfortable as with deep thinking Anatoly. I did enjoy the contrast of Mr. Vaughan as a sophisticated figure against all the locals in the tavern. Under soft moonlight (lovely lighting work by Dick Beauman) how could a girl resist? Musical Director Laura Cotter did exceptional work with a strong orchestra and a powerful chorus. Showoff's, the lot of them, especially during the likes of 'Hymn to Chess'; this is not easy music for anyone, but it didn't seem to bother them. There were some sound issues however, which affected people's pitch here and there, though things improved greatly the in the second act, and I could fully appreciate Ms Hennessy's beautiful voice. 'You and I' was a gorgeous duet with Anatoly, and 'I Know Him So Well' was as beautiful as anticipated, having already experienced the wonderful sound of Michelle Moloney's voice as Svetlana during 'Someone Else's Story'. The Arbiter was played with total impartiality by Sheena Fennessy; considering the last time I saw her she was dancing on tables and showing her bloomers, there was discipline in this - a character who never develops one way or another, and who still carries all the weight of authority. There was evidence everywhere of a very sure hand directing things, particularly in the visual shape of scenes and in movement. Character's motives could be read, though not obviously, and I appreciated the guidance given to actors in the subtleties of body language, or the timing of a look. There was no doubting Molokov's motives and Keith Greene played him with the confidence of a man unbothered by morals. Molokov was matched in his dastardliness by Walter de Courcy, and though David Hughes gave him a more pleasant manner, I wasn't fooled for a moment. Both men were strong singers, and Molokov even managed a little humour during a highly entertaining 'Soviet Machine' with a solid if somewhat drunken men's chorus. Gillian Hewitt Fitzgerald (Majella Louise's proud mammy) choreographed all other numbers and highlighted the talents of the group. 'Soviet Machine' was full of aggression and testosterone with a Russian flair and lots of humour. In scenes with a lot going on, such as the busy 'Merchandisers' dances had shape and drama within. Three children were gainfully used and added that extra smile factor, especially Sarah O'Keeffe who lit up the theatre, and certainly Richie Crowe and Bill Fitzgerald were just as engaging. Diarmuid Vaughan might have been a powerful singer, but he also designed the set, and took full advantage of the space, playing with the black and white theme and making good use of lighting, mirrors and excellent photography. Set changes were smooth and snappy for the most part. Hundreds of props were made within the group and made for vibrant scenes on the streets of Bangkok and amongst the merchandisers of Merano. Costumes were authentic and the overall look was super, especially in the above-mentioned scenes and also in the Buddhist temple (there were a lot of costume changes for this chorus!). Makeup was attentive to the many different looks required for this show. With charming hosts in Patsy and James Butler, the whole affair was impressive from start to finish. Who knew such a fuss could be made about chess?

Pavilion Theatre, Dun Laoghaire So, the audition process for Shona Henneberry must have gone something like this: Can you dance? Can you sing? Can you change key easily? Can you change costume quickly? Can you charm snakes? Can you skip rope? Cartwheel? Play musical glasses? I'm sure there was more going on in the hilarious number 'Show Off' but I was laughing so much I didn't record it. Flanked by an excellent chorus her one-dimensional character Janet really excelled in this hilarious number. But there were many delightful one-dimensional characters in this show; to put it in further perspective, in case you don't know the show, George (highly talented Alec Ward) sends Robert (highly talented Brian Gilligan) off on a pair of roller skates, to calm his pre marriage jitters but also blindfolds him so he doesn't see his bride to be before the big day. It's a very funny, if very silly show, and I chuckle at the memories, but if you're thinking of doing it, you need your cast to be not just talented, but multi- talented. There are many demands made of them. If you can't cartwheel you might be asked to have water spat in your face several times, at close range. You get the idea. It was funny throughout, but it was funny because of the rehearsal time put in by director Pat McElwain, who also played the principal role of Man in Chair. Hard slog = successful show. From the moment the fluent and engaging voice of Man in Chair cut into the darkness, we knew we were in the very sure hands of both director and central character. Timing and delivery were exceptional, not just of Man, but of all the delightful characters that swanned on and off John O'Donoghue's great set; a New York studio apartment, covered in posters of musicals, with a fridge which doubled as doors from whence all the stars appeared. Clever lighting design by Darren Kelleher ensured the mood was properly reflected and costumes were very accurate, with stereotypical characters dressed appropriately.

Excellent props saw that the set was dressed authentically too, with the crucial prop - a turntable - properly working. Musical Director Dermot O'Callaghan's orchestra smoothly took over from the playing record (nice work from sound man Vinny Osborne, here and throughout), and we were treated to number after number which highlighted not just a tight and enthusiastic band, but immensely talented singers. Where are you all coming from, you fabulous singers? Jennifer McGann played the Drowsy Chaperone, which basically meant she was constantly drunk, and darned funny with it. She allowed herself to be ravaged by Adolpho (expressively played by Eoin Salley.) I particularly enjoyed the performance of Justin Parkes as Producer Feldzieg, he gruffly owned his space and likely would have sold his granny if necessary, or at least, poor Kitty, delightfully played by Joanne Keeling who was as sweet as she was dim. I've long since hankered a belief that Pat McElwain has an arrangement with his family, where they agree not to see him for the duration of rehearsals, in return for…well, seeing him again at the end of it. 'That could be said of me!' I hear you say. Ah yes, but do you carry a whip? I'm not saying Mr McElwain does, but how else did he get Mark Keegan and Dylan Kelly to so accurately play Gangster 1 and Gangster 2? They had to be brilliant in order to make sense of their lines, and they had to do it in tandem with each other. Perfectly! Preparation is a trait I admire and this company certainly did prepare. Did choreographer Deirdre Nolan click her heels with joy when she found Brian Gilligan and Alec Ward? Their tap dancing skills were exquisite and the crux of the humour in 'Cold Feets'. 'Toledo Surprise' was a massive company all singing all dancing bells and whistles number going into the so-called interval, and Mr McElwain's stand up comic style analysis of things so far, whilst eating a power bar, only warmed us to Man all the more. Peppered throughout the show were appearances by vaudeville pair, Mrs Tottendale and Underling; utter joyous nonsense, and perfectly pitched by both Jayme Lyon and Tom Delahunty. And I should mention that they were the ones doing the spitting, but it's okay, it was iced water. Or vodka…it was easy to get confused with the ridiculous plot but things certainly got funnier and funnier. When, after total chaos and drama, the company sang and danced around an impressive cutout plane with a working propeller, (and the eventual appearance of Jen Dalton as Trix the Aviatrix), we were plunged back into darkness, as Man in Chair pleaded with us not to switch off but to stay with him until he got rid of the apartment super-intendant (Cian O'Sullivan was a super Super indeed). What sort of conditions were they for Stage Manager Mathew Lyons and his crew to work in? What I came to call Man in Chair's 'cane-dropping' monologue moved fluidly in mood from something hilarious to something very moving and sad. The Super had ruined the moment you see, and Man was distraught. Funny, but distraught, and we felt it. Just before my lip fully turned downward in pity, the characters began to sing, the mood began to turn and Man in Chair sat instead, on the wings of the plane, enveloped by his beloved characters. After many lonely and possibly drowsy years, there was no doubt his soul was finally soaring. After so many belly laughs, it was strange to find myself shedding a little tear.

Temperance Hall, Loughrea So, I thought I was going to circus in a way; I expected to laugh - and I did, heartily. The clown act here was very much Mr. and Mrs. Coleridge, a sort of Captain Andy and Parthay of old London town, confidently played by Peter Kennedy and Katie Creaven. As a double act, they were priceless, with excellent delivery and timing, while singing was always strong, particularly within vibrant group numbers with high energy - and there were plenty of these; 'Roll Up, Roll Up' and 'Who Got the Blame' in act one for example. Peter Kennedy wrote the story and the music, directed, choreographed and played Mr. Coleridge. Oh, and designed the set. And painted the scenery. Encore Theatre Company seems to be proud of him and if one thing struck me about this young vibrant group, it is the sense of enjoyment in what they were doing. Whatever was thrown at them, they took it on with top notch enthusiasm.

'Do a cart wheel!' Mr. Kennedy demanded. 'Easy!' they retorted.

'Throw that woman in the air!' he called out.

'Done!' they said.

'Climb to the top of a human pyramid!' 'I'm already there!' Choreography of large group numbers really celebrated this attitude and with so much going on, one would never expect there was tragedy on the way. This is the story after all, of Clown; a simple man with a complicated life, who finds love in his Sally, after years of unrequited love, only to have his hopes and dreams violently taken from him. Michael Flanagan (above) played Clown with total sincerity; vulnerable, shy and lacking in confidence, he actually gets very little humour to play out (though the spotlight scene was funny, and an excellent piece of comic writing by Mr. Kennedy). Clown is loved by people though, and has good friends, in Mr. and Mrs. Coleridge, in Jennifer, in Arthur and Kitty (Robert Brown and Aoife Kilbane) - a delightful double act, full of energy and that enthusiastic spirit I was mentioning earlier. And then, Sally, loving him for the longest time, Sinead Heneghan was sweet yet strong, a solid backbone in his life. Singing was really beautiful and 'Waiting Here for You' was so sincere, as indeed was everything about this lovely actress. Plenty of strong female characters in this show, and Jennifer was confidently played by Iona Le Gros, another gal with a fabulous voice, which she used throughout, but which almost broke hearts in 'When I Close My Eyes'. The object of her affection was Philip, a cad and a brute, and she couldn't help herself. Niall Conway was indeed engaging and carried great presence, not to mention a super singing voice. He could have had his way with many women, which apparently he did. Andrea Doolan played Elsie, a sassy lady with little sense of decency, who swept him off his feet in the Dog and Duck and there were echoes of 'Oom Pah Pah!' in the super number 'Every Night's a Party'. Musical director Carl Hession also arranged the music, and even with a small enough orchestra, created quite a sound. There was excellent guidance too, particularly for the delightful little Miss Alix Slattery, playing the child Laura and 'Something Known as Love' was wonderful, with a brave performance from young Sean Deely. There was solid performance work too from Kevin Griffin playing Bill and Andrew Gallagher playing Mr. Squires. Chorally this was an excellent group too, and although there were some sound issues, we came to expect brilliance when they grouped on stage. 'God Knows Where We'll Be Tomorrow' followed a more somber monologue from Mr. Coleridge, which started simply and built in power, with impressive harmonies. Lighting carried the mood, no matter which way it turned. Philip returned to cause mayhem, upset and Sally's death in a tragic twist; forget about laughing from this point on; things only got more intensely sad and a tad disturbing (Elsie returned to blame Philip for her awful life and problematic abortion, which was hard to take in a musical, though Ms. Doolan certainly gave a powerful performance). Philip got his comeuppance and Clown, who was destined for tragedy, took his own life, but not before removing the makeup he wore throughout the show. It wasn't a circus, but it was certainly a roller coaster ride.

Watergate Theatre If you say 'Kilkenny' to me, I think: 'last witch in Ireland to be burned at the stake.' Though in fact, t'internet informs me that Kilkenny was the home county to the first woman in Ireland to be accused of witchcraft - apparently she was fond of dismembering animals at crossroads at the midnight hour. Hmmm…so when I heard Kilkenny Musical Society were staging 'Little Shop of Horrors' I wasn't all that surprised, and just a little bit wary walking to the car afterwards. I joke, it wasn't all that scary, though it did have its moments, like when Seymour dismembered Orin and fed him to a plant at midnight…hey, wait a minute… Okay, let's say I prefer to remember the funny parts, of which there were plenty. Director Liam Heffernan understood the humour in this show very well and along with his strong cast, enhanced this with the inclusion of a black and white film clip which made me laugh; it was our introduction to Orin, that funny old sadist, who walked the streets of Kilkenny tormenting homeless unfortunates, little old ladies and blind priests, all hilariously played by Brendan Corcoran who also played a confident New York Mr Mushnik. Appearing amongst an unreasonable amount of smoke but on John O'Donoghue's wonderful set, Mr Corcoran squeezed humour out of almost every line. In the dingy old shop, admirably dressed by an impressive props department, Mr Mushnik bullied Seymour, generously played by Kevin Reade, who was a nerd, yes, but I liked him, and while he was a little hesitant in his speech (well, he was a nerd), singing was strong and I enjoyed the development of his character. There was convincing chemistry with Audrey, delightfully played to a tee by Kevina Hayes and here was a quality voice indeed; I possibly became more engaged that necessary during 'Somewhere That's Green', but it was so terribly sweet and so sensitively sung. Why, oh why did she have to die? I was genuinely sorry to see her go. This scene can be confusing, what with her taking so long to actually pass on and requesting to be fed to the plant, and hats off to Mr Heffernan for excellent direction here. Michael Fay oversaw a strong band and confident chorus and many rousing numbers were impressively delivered, though there was that sense of sweetness too, as mentioned, from Audrey certainly, but also at times from the storytellers, Ronette, Crystal and Chiffon (Delia Lowery, Rebecca Murphy and Sarah Brennan) who not only sang beautifully with easy harmony but enhanced the mood in each scene admirably. The plant, Audrey II, was sung with soul by Greg Porter and well managed by puppeteer David Brydone; what a combination - I was looking out for flaws in synchronicity but darned if I could spot one. Along with a chorus solid as a rock, this was an impressive group indeed and Musical Director Michael Fay was more than supportive. The band was pretty funky too and there was a great sense of enjoyment between singers and players, whether principal or otherwise. Individual roles were played with confidence and group work was well directed. Choreographer Sandra Kavanagh interpreted the music well and brought out the humour in numbers such as 'Mushnik and Son'. Stage Manager and technical director Seamus Reade had work to do backstage and his crew worked quietly, quickly and efficiently. Sound balance was good and sound effects added a lot to scenes, while Gerry Taylor's lighting design not only reflected the mood well, but had fun bouncing off the wonderful images on the set; Marie Cusack should be mentioned here as set construction as should David Brydone and Rebecca Murphy for the in- house creation of all but the largest plant; a nice fresh looking and solidly working couple of plants if anyone looking to do this show next year. But maybe check inside before using. There's a history in Kilkenny…

Island Arts Centre, Lisburn As we come closer to the 50th anniversary of the film of The Sound of Music, somehow the movie seems much more dated than the musical appears. Familiarity is not always a good thing when staging musical theatre, but Lisnagarvey Operatic Society managed to turn in into a virtue, surprising us along the way with strong characterisations and a fresh look.

Atmosphere was the order of the evening where the musical content was concerned, beginning with a lovely and well-balanced chorus of nuns whose a cappella singing hit many a chord literally and figuratively. This set a musical standard that did not waver across the production. The other significant singing group, the children, were another tuneful and focussed element, all under the watchful eyes and ears of MD Ian Milford. The Island Arts Centre in Lisburn is a lovely venue in many respects, but with a full house in attendance, it can be a bit dry and bloom-free. However, technical resources came into play and this cast's careful preparation also contrived to overcome these potential pitfalls. Scenery is one element at which the film inevitably excels, but Lisnagarvey's set had its own charms, and we were almost, almost transported over those mountains.

Certainly, the voice and personality that went a long way towards taking us there belonged to Gillian McQuade as Maria. Burdened initially with a very proper Julie Andrews-esque accent, she warmed up wonderfully, and her enthusiasm for all things to do with music and children won the day. Mind you, the children, headed by Jane McKibben as an initially sullen but ultimately very smiley Liesl, were easy to warm to. Conor Richardson as Friederic negotiated his role very professionally, his fine tenor voice a good anchor for the singing of the rest of the children. Jack Cambell was winning as Kurt (whose singing voice was also very beautiful), Sarah McComb was a lovely and precocious Marta, Demi Lea Weir was a properly cheeky Brigitta, Carlie Rosbotham, another strong singer/actress was Louisa and Rosie Bell was the perfect Gretl, sore finger and all.

Among the adults, Heather Campbell brought a beautifully modulated speaking voice and gentle gravitas to the role of Mother Superior. She was often framed by Liz Johnston, Vivian Shepherd and Clare Manson as Sisters Berthe, Margaretta and Sofia, respectively. These three were supremely well-cast, with different kinds of voices and nicely individualistic approaches to their dialogue and music. Tim Pentland was Captain Von Trapp, dignified and nicely buttoned-up across the show, warming significantly in the presence of Maria and able to play the guitar for real - just one more detail so effortlessly yet skilfully attended to in this production directed by Wilfie Pyper. He must have had great chemistry with this cast, because they had so much chemistry between themselves. Another somewhat buttoned-up character was Elsa (Clare Cranston), whose beautiful clothes and upright bearing set her apart from Maria in just the right ways. Max was an effervescent Simon Pyper, a bundle of kinetic charm with "Hooray Henry" writ large in his DNA. Or would that be "Hooray Heinrich? Either way, a very funny antidote to the plot as it becomes serious. And this as much as anything was the secret of this production: it did funny, sad, slapstick and serious equally well and made them fit into the show's seemingly timeless context. I don't think I agree with the substitution of Something Good for Ordinary Couple, and while I Have Confidence is a good song, the film's interpretation is so imprinted for audiences, nothing on a stage can match Julie Andrews's bus ride through Salzburg or her arrival at the Von Trapp mansion. ("Oh help"). Lonely Goatherd is another number in the musical that never quite meets the film's standard, set by the wonderful Bill Baird Marionettes. However, Lisnagarvey went several hundred extra miles above and beyond the call and had a craftsman re-create those very marionettes, and Act II opened with the aforementioned Goatherd, the little girl in the pale pink coat-herd, her mama (with the gleaming gloat-herd) et al. What can I say? Lay-ee, oh dah lay-ee, oh dah lay, Bra-vo!

Backstage Theatre I have always had a soft spot in my heart for the musical Carousel, a show with its roots planted firmly in the soil and sand of the upper east coast of the USA. St. Mel's Musical Society showed a similar affection for the show in their well-resourced production, which took care in its portrayal of the interface between land and sea and heaven and earth on which Carousel rests. There was good detail in elements of costume and set, and a cast who were well fit for the considerable musical demands of this classic score. MD Fintan Farrelly was instrumental in making the Carousel Waltz spin at the requisite speed, and an opening carnival sequence was nicely populated with a range of performers both human and less so. As the story unfolded, the full personality of the show opened up and all of its attractive ambiguities came to light in good order. Kevin Gormley as Billy Bigelow gave a gruff but ultimately passionate performance underpinned by a fine voice which, though somewhat of a work in progress, shows a great deal of promise. His Soliloquy was powerful. Deirdre McCabe (Julie Jordan) is a fully- fledged, well-trained singer whose voice was beautiful to listen to, even though her delivery and especially pronunciation, was rather more refined than the voices around her. What set her performance apart, however, was a fine actor's grasp of the essential tension in this role; Julie's way of making the best of a bad situation. McCabe's stillness onstage and wonderfully nuanced speaking voice completed the picture and created some fine moments of theatre.

Surrounding these two central characters was a very fine cast, including Deirdre Leavy as Carrie Pipperidge who gave Enoch (Tony Wadd) plenty to think about with a performance that was compact of steel and fluff. Her Mr Snow had a way of melting in her presence, even as he stood his ground on some points, taking things at his own pace. David Flaherty as Jigger managed to be just about thoroughly dastardly, in the grand tradition of many a musical theatre villain. He also had a very good singing voice and rhythmic consistency that made for a lively and very sure-footed portrayal. Nettie Fowler was Aideen Mulligan, who gave a larger- than-life performance and delivered a beautiful interpretation of "that song", You'll Never Walk Alone. Liz Leavey's Mrs. Mullin caught the complexities of this role very well, whereas Benny O'Brien's Starkeeper was equally accomplished but in a delightfully straightforward manner; a major reason for the success of the second act of this production. Heather Moore as Louise was another example of excellence in a smaller role, and she was joined by Jim McDonald, Luke Casserly, Roy Davis and John Kelly as Dr. Seldon, Enoch Snow Jr., Mr Bascombe and the Heavenly Friend respectively. These well-cast players were joined by a strong singing chorus, an especially effective male chorus, and clear evidence of plenty of backstage activity. It was a pleasure to see a production that aimed so high in terms of musical and technical accomplishment, and took such care with this endearing and enduring masterpiece.

Newbridge College Theatre I imagine, once a society have decided to do Beauty and the Beast (and quite a few did this year), the news needs to be broken gently to the treasurer, who couldn't possibly have been around during the process. There must be a point however, when during say, 'Be Our Guest', this person will say, 'Ok, I concede; it was worth it.' At least, I'd say that's what happened in Newbridge Musical Society's production this year, because that number was the very epitome of the show: enchantment, magic, opulence… as the words of the song suggest course after course gets more impressive, so too did each section of this number. It helped that this was one fine chorus, focused and expressive; solo numbers with salt and pepper; a cart wheeling carpet; can-can cutlery; they came up the aisles, and out of unseen crevices - all razzmatazz and magical energy. Wonderful stuff from Choreographer Julianne McNamara, who along with sister and Director  Sharon McNamara and MD Owen C. Lynch really highlighted the good results that can be gotten from a united front. Music really was excellent; Mr. Lynch's orchestra played magnificently and Noel Ryan on sound ensured there was balance between some very rousing powerful numbers and the singers. Crystal clear these performers were, whether singing or speaking and there was a natural style to things too. Director Sharon McNamara clearly enjoyed her cast; while principals were strong, there were no shrinking violets amongst the chorus and I imagine the only problems this production team had was in being spoiled for choice. Possibly that is why there were no less than six Silly Girls who were as funny as they were tightly choreographed. Amongst this animated and vibrant chorus, Lucy Phibbs stood out as Belle, a worthy heroine who could play it light with Gaston or passionate with Beast. 'Change in Me' was her best number by far as we really got to hear this quality voice in full form. Martin Hennessy stuck a good balance as Beast, in that he was just scary enough at the beginning; a tyrant sure, but not a monster. Having said that, he did look the part and had been given great attention by an excellent makeup department. Faces stood out; they looked animated and individuals such as Beast and nasty old M. D'Arque (Conor Kilduff strong here) had well and truly been worked on. Choreographer Julianne McNamara had really worked on movement, especially in the opening numbers such as 'Belle' and 'Me'; there was a definite nod to the animated movie. Mark Trundle's Gaston might have taken this movement a little far in places though it worked really well during musical numbers - 'Gaston' was a super number, with both Mr. Trundle and Phil MacSheoinin as Le Fou shining against a strong chorus of villagers. Ms J McNamara's choreography had shape and at all times she was mindful of the overall visual impact and Mark Trundle's powerful voice stood out as much during these early numbers as it did in act two for the darker 'Kill the Beast'. How could Belle ever love him? Beast was much nicer, and his journey towards selflessness was well developed by Mr. Hennessy. The transformation by the way, was nicely done, with graceful movement, a secret way of removing makeup and prosthetics quickly and just a dab of smoke. Philip Emmett was engaging and a bit roguish as Lumiere, and what's more, I was convinced of his heterosexuality, what with all those shenanigans with Babette, sexily portrayed by Louise O'Reilly. Lumiere was funny too, as was Padraigh Munnelly as Cogsworth - these two were opposites alright but there was always humour in it and I was impressed by how much Mr Munnelly got out of his dialogue. Gill O'Brien was just lovely as Mrs. Potts; she naturally portrayed her motherliness and I had trouble keeping my composure when mother and son (Kyle Dunne wonderful as Chip) had moments. There were tender father daughter moments too between Belle and Michael F. Malone as Crazy Old Maurice, and 'No Matter What' was beautifully treated. Deirdre Maloney knew she had to send herself up as Madame de la Grande Bouche, but it's hard to keep a good voice down, and this performer managed to be funny as well as musically impressive.
