Costumes were fab of course, and well coordinated by Andrew Reddy, while the hired set worked very well for both stage and production and Liam Fitzgerald's excellent lighting design really enhanced many a scene. Stage Manager Tom Kavanagh and his crew worked efficiently; indeed some of the changes were entertaining in their own right, and there was no doubt but that this man was in control. Tony Bird and Jim Donoghue are to be congratulated for the attention to detail in props and the opulence they created, particularly in the castle. Talk about pulling a great team together; by the finale I considered these guys were just showing off. Wonderful stuff.

Annesley Hall, Newcastle Calamity Jane dressed up as man, so why shouldn't the women of Newcastle Glees Musical Society? After all, there was a decided lack of testosterone in the group (no offence to Bill, Danny, Doc and the boys - you guys were very manly), and with the talents of makeup person Lesley Craig, it made perfect sense. Women were convincingly given hairy faces or four o'clock shadows; and along with the odd blackened tooth and some uncouth mannerisms - voila: men! It worked; it actually worked. Director Antoinette Morelli was able to adapt both cast and stage to suit the show and the result was a highly enjoyable theatrical experience. While I'm not a fan of being bothered in my seat, there was something inclusive about bringing Deadwood folk up through the aisles, all excited to be home and off that dang deadwood stagecoach; it made me feel part of things in a comfortable way, and it helped that the cast were all so thoroughly focused. Carol-Anne McKay's set design really made use of a limited playing space and the Golden Garter saloon had three levels, with Musical Director Manus O'Boyle's orchestra situated over the action. Playing was tight and the music was excellent, while Chorus Mistress Careen Starkey could proudly stand over any number ('Black Hills' was gorgeous with confident harmonies, while 'Careless with the Truth' was lively and fun). It was unfortunate however, that due to difficulties with space the company declined to use microphones; there was a balance issue without a doubt, and though Mr O'Boyle was sensitive to this where he could be, numbers like 'Windy City' needed to be rousing and singers were drowned out. The company is to be congratulated however, for excellent diction and projection generally, and dialogue was crystal clear. What about Calam herself? Claire Killough was great; full of mischief and wonderment, she was as innocent as she was funny and it was easy to see how Deadwood folk loved her for her antics and exaggerated stories. Gal could sing too, and held the attention of one and all during any of her numbers. Interaction was great with Bill, Danny and Katie and goshamighty but if I couldn't see the trouble a-brewin' clear as can be. Brian Devlin was a confident no messing around kind of Bill Hickok and scenes with Calamity brewed chemistry like coffee (I'm kind of getting carried away with the terminology here, but blame them!). After a highly volatile argument, and tears, the love scene was romantically charged. Emma Nugent and John Carville made a good couple too, as Katie Brown and Danny Gilmartin. At only seventeen, Mr. Carville's voice is one to watch, and 'Love You Dearly' was a beautiful duet. Ms. Nugent was expressive and likeable as Katie, even before she got to Deadwood, and a slightly cruel, but smoldering Adelaide Adams (last seen designing the set, Carol-Anne McKay) tried to put her in her place. Not sure why Ms Morelli chose to cast the Back Stage Johnnies from principals John Carville and Ross Hoey (also Frances Fryer) as it confused some of the audience, but they were funny all the same, and Ms McKay's singing was appreciated. As Frances, I initially thought Mr Hoey would play him rather sombrely, but after hilarious scenes in a dress, heels and a wig it took some time for him to miss, I changed my mind. He was grounded by Susan, naturally played by Clare Murnin, and abused by Henry Miller, solidly played by Seamus Boden. Choreographer Jennifer Rooney didn't let a small stage space stop her from some great dancing, and there was drama and shape for numbers like 'Careless with the Truth' and 'Windy City', though couples were given good guidance too. The Golden Garter Girls could dance, and cartwheel too, though everyone was given a chance to shine. No doubt Ms Rooney's philosophy was the same as the director's: she liked this group, she saw their focus and dedication and she made sure the audience would too. With excellent and authentic props and costumes adding to the overall look, things in the beautiful Annesley Hall were in mighty good hands.

Venue Theatre, Ratoath Never mind about Tomorrow, the sun was definitely coming out on a nightly basis in Ratoath during the run of their production of Annie. This was a well-resourced production on a scale that just about fit into the cosy confines of the Venue Theatre in the town. There was nothing small about the performances however, and all concerned, from canine to children, were well fit to meet the challenges even the hardest of Hard Knock Life might throw at them. Tegan Rodden (below) was Annie, confident without losing her sense of being an ensemble player. Her singing had a lot of expression in it and she was adept at acting through singing. The rest of the orphans were a strong and feisty bunch who also had a nice feel for the sense of coordination and cooperation that goes into their scenes. They made a nice singing sound right across the range of their music, and like Tegan, did not overact. 'Loving' supervision came from Miss Hannigan, played with devastating comic sensibility by Monica Hannigan (yes, Hannigan). She trod a difficult and consistent line between parody and pathos; a drunk with a heart of, if not gold, perhaps tin, admitting her defeat in the face of those Little Girls, and looking for ways out of her situation. She was at her most subtly funny in moments of delusion; presenting herself to Warbucks (and others) as a sort of down-at-heel femme fatale. David Duff was a gruff but pliable Warbucks. His bluster gave way believably to his affection for Annie and there was a sense of a skilled progression through this role. Maria Brannigan was Grace Farrell, a pretty and rather delicate performance that was understated and very suited to this small theatre. Rooster Hannigan was played by Liam Carroll, whose instinct for this small-time huckster was subtle but compelling. He was especially convincing as Annie's 'distraught father'. A less nuanced performance came from Marie Cantwell as Lily St. Regis, who was nonetheless very funny as a tart without much heart. Joe Murphy as President Roosevelt not only looked the part but mustered the kind of amiable authority one imagines the original had. He is one example of a host of smaller roles that were very well filled by a versatile cast of players who got into the spirit of this show and populated it with colour and very polished singing and dancing. The musical content was presided over by MD Jane Lynch, whose instrumentalists were of a very high calibre indeed. Their prominent, front- of-stage position (dictated by the lack of a pit in the theatre) made them a very visible element of the production. This is a company that encourages and supports young performers especially well, as evidenced by the orphans of course, but also the teenage actors who played the roles of Grace Farrell, Drake, Bert Healey and a number of chorus members. The Hooverville scene further underscored the company feel that Ratoath has, and there were some very nicely chosen costumes, consistently evocative of the period of 1930's depression-era America, on both sides of the economic divide of the period. Behind the scenes there was evidence of some very busy company members, making a big and needfully lavish show fit into this venue. A lot was done with a few well-chosen set pieces. There was a collective professionalism about it all which was in no way diluted by the feeling of great fun which was also so much a part of this production.

St. Mary's Secondary School It seems to have been a year of getting All Shook Up in the musical theatrical sense, and much of what makes this show popular rests on the way the music furthers the story, even as the story gives the music a new context. When Baldoyle Musical Society took to the stage for their production, there was no question that the story came first, and the talented actors in this company made the songs do their bidding. Baldoyle's audience were more than ready for their ride on the back of Chad's bike and from the outset, success was pretty much assured. Kathryn Gibbons was an understated Natalie/Ed, able to act at times with facial expressions alone and possessed of brilliant comic timing. Her voice was also wonderfully clear and full of character. Vying with her for comic kudos was Anthony Ennis as Dennis, the hero in geek's clothing. This was an effortlessly honed performance, full of physical and vocal mannerisms that added up to a character who had to do very little to get a laugh. As Chad, Damien Hurley had only to swivel those hips to get a reaction, but there was much more to his interpretation, and his was another very funny performance. His singing was also terrific, the starting point of which is a voice with a good range and a solid, tuneful centre. Rachel Ryan was also a very solid, theatrical singer, and her 'partner in crime', Ben O'Keefe as Dean, is also a very fine singer-in-the-making, in addition to being what Midwesterners would call 'cute as a bug's ear'.  Both are very good actors, as is Sarah Carroll who was Sylvia. She struck the right note in terms of sardonic wit and gentle persuasion where Jim Haller was concerned, played with some enthusiasm by Karl Hoffman. His 'turn' as the Chad-like, Elvis-channelling suitor to Miss Sandra was musically satisfying and also very funny. For her part, Nicola Pollard as the aforementioned Sandra, was a powerhouse of a singer and wickedly funny as she lusted after poor Ed. All of these principal folk were plagued by a persistently amusing Collette O'Beirne as Mayor Matilda Hyde, in a performance that was so solidly based on reason, she seemed almost plausible. Sheriff Earl (Alan White) made her see the light, and his eventual subduing of the feisty Mayor was as plausible as her impenetrable morality. A well-matched pair! All of these principals went about their business in a beautifully designed and detailed set, the fairground being especially stylishly evoked with lighting and a nicely abstract skyline concept. There was a tunnel of love car that rivalled the real thing; another example of how this production did nostalgia especially well. Some clever direction and choreography made the (by now) familiar story pop up and thrill, most notably the Devil in Disguise which pitted angel grannies against devil dancers. The grannies won, but the real winners were in the audience, as we screamed with laughter. MD Ronan Dooney looked after a very clued-in and enthusiastic band, who were a pleasure to listen to, if occasionally a little too vigorous in sound. Choreographer Karen McCourt laced the show with some characteristic authentic movement and contemporary touches, and there was a good company feel to chorus singing and dancing.

The Helix, Dublin Anyone involved in the weird and wonderful world of musical theatre knows that while all shows are wonderful in their own way, some definitely are weirder than others. A case in point is Little Shop of Horrors, the plot of which gets stranger and stranger as the show progresses. DCU Drama is a company that acknowledged and embraced that fact whole-heartedly in their recent production, and in the process delivered a cracking night's entertainment. A good deal of tongue-in-cheek fun was also the order of the evening, and Lisa Hopper, Gemma Burke and Jean O'Connor were among the first to plant those seeds as Crystal, Chiffon and Ronnette. Their "in your face" attitude permeated their musical and dramatic performances, and they clearly enjoyed every minute of their time in the spotlight as a functioning Greek chorus; commenting on and guiding us through the tale of Audrey II and how she grew. Audrey I was Lorna Dennehy, a singer/ actor in the grand tradition of performers who immerse themselves in a role, give a starry performance and still manage to retain a strong sense of ensemble. Her singing was among the best I heard this year, a voice of terrific clarity and musical nuance. One of her leading men was Dallan Shovlin as Seymour Krelborn, a performance that walked the requisite line between nerd and hero. Audrey's other love interest was Cormac O'Brion as the Dentist, a delightfully off-the-wall performance in which O'Brion seemed to exist in a bizarre world of his own, bringing a fantastic comedic focus and fine tenor voice to the dentist's chair. Nick Sheridan was Mr Mushnik, a very good actor who set aside his youth and transformed himself into the world-weary flower shop owner. The most sinister inhabitant of that shop was expertly 'played' by Eoin O'Dubhghaill, who, as The Plant grew into the role even as Audrey II took over and began to devour more than her fair share of the local population. All was not gruesome, however, and the last few moments before Audrey I was devoured was wonderfully and atmospherically lit, a moment of tension and oddly beautiful sound and lighting. Her final descent to Somewhere That's Green was accomplished with some grace, and spoke volumes of this company's attention to detail and an ability to identify those dramatic/comedic/musical moments that can be extended for good theatrical effect. Director Emma Jane Reilly certainly knows how to populate a stage and producer Emma Wall obviously makes things happen for DCU. Kevin Walsh was MD and his leadership of the band from the keyboard was skilful. There was plenty of volume - occasionally at the expense of pit-to-stage balance, but fine voices and solid acting won through. Choreography by Katie O'Connor spoke loudly of an understanding of the kind of camp, retro movement that works in this show, and there were also plenty of modern elements for an up-to-date vibe. The Helix is a great venue and this company did very well in choosing this show. Their casting was superb, this was well-resourced and I for one will not be visiting a florist's shop or a dentist's office any time soon!

Kilcornan Hall, Clarinbridge The first thing you are treated to when seeing a show in Kilcornan Hall, Clarinbridge, is the journey: a beautiful approach to the hall through a lovely park. The cluster of buildings you eventually arrive at serves a number of purposes, though the actual theatre that Maree Musical Society performs in is not entirely without its challenges. This did not, however, stop (or even slow down) a company which clearly has great ideas, tremendous commitment from its members and imagination and skill in equal measure. One element that sticks in my mind as an outstanding and innovative feature of this production was the use of video projections at the sides of the stage to fill in some detail of the story, including an insanely funny evocation of the Chad/ Ed love story. The specially made short films that punctuated the show filled in gaps and contextualised some of the action in a way that was skilfully done and fit surprisingly well into the context of live theatre. Another memorable moment was Chad's entrance from the back of the hall on a motorbike that he rode up on to the stage via a ramp specially built to accommodate this rather classy bit of action. Stage hands with crowd tape covered the safety aspects of the stunt (I assume), and this was also an unexpected bit o' business that worked very well indeed. The aforementioned Chad was Ronan Rooney, Elvis-like in many mannerisms, and possessed of a fine voice that also echoed the King. He was persuasive as a roustabout heartthrob and this performer also worked the audience well. Amy Byrne as Natalie/Ed brought a true and in tune voice to the role, as well as a good acting approach. Denis was Louis Bourke, who gave a really well projected performance which, combined with some clever staging (multiple Denises!) allowed for him to reveal a many-faceted performer. He chose a few 'nerdy' mannerisms and perfected them. Antoinette Van Ravestijn was a terrifically melodramatic Ms Sandra, as well as occasionally sardonic and sexy; a winning combination. Sylvia was played by Brona Culkeen, also very funny, in a more down- to-earth way. Her blues-tinged voice had a lot of character, and her acting was very persuasive. Jim was Gary Caulfield, whose understated performance was actually quite sympathetic and an antidote at times to the mayhem around him. Yvonne Spelman played Lorraine, using a very fine voice and singing technique to great effect as a means of getting this character across. Ian Folan as Dean Hyde was less accomplished vocally but was very, very funny in this, with a terrific sense of comic timing and overall pace. Tess Fogarty played Mayor Matilda with focus and flair, a very strong and confident performance in which she was aided and abetted by Willie Moriarty as Sheriff Earl, the other half of this formidable comic duo. There was a well-cast supporting band of characters and a very able chorus providing a good feel of ease and familiarity between everyone onstage. This company is full of strong actors who were really effectively deployed across this stage, side to side and front to back. There's a splendid sense of ambition in this musical society, as well as plenty of fresh ideas. Special kudos to the band, which consisted of two players who were able through the miracle of technology (and no little skill) to evoke an entire range of sounds. This was a thoroughly creative approach to every aspect of musical theatre from a company to watch (I hope!) for many years to come.

Solstice Centre, Navan There's a film to be made in Navan that begins with the line "of all the flower shops in all the cities in all the world, she had to walk into mine". I say this because, when St. Mary's Musical Society took to the stage for their Little Shop of Horrors, they treated their audiences to a show calculated to stick in the mind for a good long while, just like (what was her name?) the love interest in Casablanca. Admittedly, Audrey II didn't exactly walk into Mushnik's Flower Shop, but her influence grew and grew, even as she herself thrived on Seymour's increasingly fraught methods of providing nutrition, and this production's attention to detail and host of strong performances emerged. The hidden band under the leadership of MD Paul Byrne set the tone of confidence for the opening night I saw in the Solstice Centre. They had the right mix of instruments to play the score and the right balance of sound between themselves and St. Marys' singing voices, the technical side of which was presided over by sound supervisor Noel Ryan. Another aspect of this company's technical prowess came from the set, which depicted Mushnik's emporium in a kind of cutaway format, as if we were eavesdropping on the strange happenings within. This clever perspective didn't stop at walls and floor, extending to a basement (!), the windows of which were visible at street level and glowed with sinister empathy whenever Audrey II really started to get out of control. Inevitably, Big Audrey's personality was entrusted to a human accomplice, or on this occasion two humans: Jacqui McGovern who presided over the precocious plant's body, and Jay Rice who provided the voice. On occasion, there was a slight lack of absolute synchronisation between these two elements (did I mention it was opening night?) but the combined vitality of Audrey II's movement, speech and singing was greater than the sum of her parts (and ultimately, the sum of other people's parts as they were fed into her increasingly demanding, jaggedly smiling mouth). But enough about the Plant. It all began with the dazzling trio of gals individually known as Chiffon, Crystal and Ronnette. They had a slightly bumpy start vocally and almost immediately morphed into a formidable ensemble that rivalled the famous Andrew Sisters or Bette Midler's Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy in terms of harmonic balance and vocal style. Eimear Donnolly, Caithriona Mongey and Tina Price took their music by the throat and, pitch-perfect and rhythmically seamless, gave us the glue that holds this show together. Their phrasing was flawless (shoop dah doo indeed!). Add to that a dazzling collection of ever more camp costumes and witty, knowing choreography, and they were a package very hard to beat. Never have 'shing-a-ling' and 'shang-a-lang' foreshadowed such an accomplished musical package. Pit singers added a solid choral halo, again aided and abetted by a very clued-in sound mix. Colin Flynn as Seymour was a gently tentative nerd, using his youth and fresh singing voice in combination with a great grasp of a Midwestern accent tinged with New York vowels. However, the award for best accent and paint-strippingly edgy vocal tone goes to Louise Cassidy as Audrey, who never wavered in her Bronx twang and earnest tripping about in impossibly tight skirts. Her singing voice carried this across, and coupled with solid, nuanced, knowing acting, we totally 'got' where this Audrey was coming from. Mushnik, on the other hand, came from somewhere else in the Bronx, and his accent was Yiddish to the core. Ray Hoare had fun with this and delivered it all in a terrifically gruff voice that gave his performance dramatic as well as comic weight. When he sang, however, he really sang, with a lovely musical freedom and confidence. Ronan Walsh as Orin Scrivello also had fun (a lot of fun) with his role, played as a kind of Elvis figure caught in a Rocky Horror time warp. This very strong core ensemble was joined at various points by an equally off- the-wall yet focussed chorus of characters that brought the New York setting to life on a set that was a gritty frame to the odd goings-on. Little Shop, big entertainment, what's not to love? Bravo.

Abbey Hall, Roscrea All Shook Up is a show that has plenty of atmosphere, much of it created by the music; songs so closely associated with Elvis that it is easy to imagine that this musical could be based on one of the movies he made in the 50's. Roscrea Musical Society's production emphasised and expanded on the Elvis theme both with their front of house presentation and a production which faithfully re-created the hometown feel we associate with the best years of the boy from Tupelo. There was some beautiful set design in this production, which channelled Edward Hopper's iconic "Nighthawks" painting; the one depicting Marilyn Monroe, James Dean and Elvis in a corner diner. The small-town feel was fleshed out by the presence of beautifully rendered painted trees, the presence of a poodle skirt among the excellent costumes, and Sylvia's red and white chequered floor. Roscrea's venue, the Abbey Hall, is not without its own unique atmosphere, so all in all there was a feel for history lovingly preserved. The stage area itself is somewhat small, but those limitations were worked 'round rather well. Jailhouse Rock and Heartbreak Hotel confirmed this company's musical credentials with strong individual voices and a 'grab em' by the throat' approach to song and dance. This was energetic preparation for Chad's motorbike entrance, complete with dry ice and plenty of Harley-esque sound. Prionnsias Loughnane used his leading man confidence to good effect in this role, which relied on some uncanny and amusing tricks you might expect to find in an Elvis impersonator's repertoire. Louise Handy as Natalie was a convincing tomboy, and her earnestness was winning. Her singing was beautifully produced, with a great core tone and terrific control. John Coss was Dennis, whose full-on performance was comically well-judged as well as sympathetic. He took an amusing high-pitched approach to Dennis's speaking voice, but his singing, in a 'normal' vocal range, was possibly too well-produced for the character. Aileen Quaid as Miss Sandra gave a deliciously over-the-top take on this role, perhaps a shade too close to caricature for comfort, but wonderfully watch-able. Rachel McMahon was Lorriane, whose crystal-clear singing voice had all the right pop overtones to carry off the music of this very well. Her love interest, Dean, was played by Tadhg Maher, a confident performer who brought an old-before-his- time wariness to the part. Siobhán Bowe was Mayor Matilda, another confident performer who took a pleasingly eccentric line with this and acted and sang with her whole body. Heather Colohan was Sylvia, a measured, sadder-but-wiser interpretation that had good emotional nuance. Likewise Paul Spencer as Jim Haller was warm and engaging, his midlife crisis gently amusing and his singing voice full of interesting colour. Another attractive singing turn came from Colin Williams as Sheriff Earl, whose acting was all the more funny for being understated. Likewise, Gillian Wallace as Henrietta brought a big personality to this small role. One thing about this production that stood out for me was the strong sense I got of hearing some of the lines for the first time - unusual, because I've seen a lot of All Shook Ups (A lot of All Shook Ups). That freshness carried over to the lively band, led by MD Mary Rose McNally and choreography by director Peter Kennedy. As much as anything, this was presented in a great spirit of fun, and even when wisps of raggedness or uncertainty crept in to what was a relatively early night in this run, the "wow" moments carried the evening. As Chad and Natalie (looking not unlike Olivia Newton-John at the end of Grease) ended up not riding off into the sunset, it was nevertheless clear that Roscrea had been well and truly Shook Up by this accomplished society.

show_raw: Joseph And The Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat
review_text: The Tain Theatre, Dundlak This job can get to you; I was at a First Communion on Saturday and I found myself inadvertently judging the school choir. I think the average age was nine. People were appalled when I mentioned that I thought they might have been a little tighter during the Our Father. Like I said, the job can get to you. Mind you, the average age of the chorus in S.O.N.G.'s production of Joseph was pretty similar and chorus mistress Liz McConnon got a great sound out of them, with energy and life during the likes of  'Jacob and Sons' and 'Coat of Many Colours', while 'Close Every Door' was utterly beautiful; Kylan Ross played Joseph with quiet confidence and singing was strong. Interaction with the Narrator was comfortable and humorous too; Claire O'Brien was hugely impressive in this central role, holding things together with the ease of a seasoned pro. Singing was expressive too; in fact I was particularly impressed with the clarity of diction from this very young cast - it helped that Vinnie Osborne had sound well balanced but there is no doubt that director/choreographer Terese Dunne had rehearsed these kids to within an inch of their little lives - and you know what? The children didn't seem to have minded. The sense of fun and life coming from the stage was palpable, and if anything, this show seemed to be not quite enough of a challenge for them. While the singing chorus was strong, there were plenty of gifted soloists in the mix too. Choreography had shape and took into account the variation of young ages, and there was imagination put into the overall look; steps themselves were simple enough but well managed by all. Musical director Patrick Dunne made do with a keyboard (played by himself), one guitar and a set of drums, but the sound was excellent - possibly only ever an issue during the final number, given the strong sound from the entire ensemble. The Brothers, played by both boys and girls, were a force to be reckoned with; they were very cool for a start, and funny too. Personalities quickly established themselves during some of the fun numbers. Kerill Kelly was highly amusing as Potiphor, and along with a deadpan dance chorus, the dynamic between him and his Wife (Lola Farrell) was really very funny. Daire Stanley was a cool and smooth Pharaoh, similarly flanked by a well-rehearsed dancing troupe. Both Mr Kelly and Mr Stanley took on the roles of the Butler and the Baker respectively, and I appreciated the use of good talent here. David McGahey as dad Jacob was possibly a little older than the rest (though not by much) and he added weight to singing numbers with a rich quality voice. The costume team was highly imaginative, with only Joseph's coat being hired in. The Butler and Baker for example, were delightfully presented in a stereotypical manner but with inspired touches - spotty stocking for one, stripy for the other. Joseph was dashing as Vizier and Potipher's costume reflected not just the humour of the character but of the whole scene. 'Go Go Go Joseph' was a great big splash of life and colour. Hair and make up was authentic, especially in Egypt and props (Kathryn Dunne) consistently added something more to scenes. Stage Manager Moya Hodgers ran things smoothly and it helped that Ultan Hodgers and Liam Murphy had designed a clever set of simple pyramids. Cathal Donohue's lighting design was vibrant and refreshing, and moods well interpreted - the prison scene was beautifully lit. Yes, there was much to be impressed by with this young group. I can't wait to see what's next.

Premier Hall, Thurles Society returned to a more traditional show than they've been used to though I have no doubt their production of Calamity Jane continued to delight audiences. I know I sang all the way home, with some really rousing numbers from an impressive chorus under the solid guidance of MD Mary Rose McNally. I'm always impressed by men in a musical, having grown up in my society with a decided lack of them, but these lads could really sing. 'Careless with the Truth' had character and highlighted personalities out of otherwise minor roles, and 'Adelaide' was so beautiful I nearly fell in love with her myself. Accompaniment was excellent and while the orchestra was strong, it helped that Ms McNally padded out the string section with some very competent musical students. Cathy Keane was an engaging and animated Calamity, with fun filled performances during 'Windy City' and 'Careless with the Truth', the reprise of this saw her being strung up by a rope, which was a bit of fun going into the interval. Wild Bill Hickok was confidently played by Jonathan Gleeson and there was good chemistry between these two, with a heated argument naturally leading into the sweetest of love scenes. Director David Heffernan guided well, and characters developed easily. Indeed as mentioned, those in smaller roles made an impact and there was a natural style to chorus reactions amid any unfolding drama. There was plenty of humour too, and while some of the scenes were turned on their head (Adelaide Adams was a little fond of a tipple) I guess you can't blame a guy for injecting something new into the show. Maria McElgunn's lovely voice was at times compromised because of this but only in places, and presumably at the request of the director. The Stage Door Johnnies flanking her were funny, possibly influenced by the voices of the German Pigs in Shrek. John Butler brought easy humour to the role of Henry Miller and I particularly enjoyed the banter between him and Brendan Bailey as Francis Fryer; sweet with Susan (a solid Fiona McCullagh), Mr. Bailey delighted us as Frances, mortified in his wig and heels, though he got quite into the whole thing as 'Honeybee' went on. Michelle O'Connell brought glamour and charm to the role of Katie, and the developing love affair with Danny (Frank Tuohy) was convincing, with a delightful duet in 'Love You Dearly'. Debbie Kiernan's choreography allowed for plenty of good dancing wherever possible and her chorus was well used, particularly in 'Windy City'. Principals were well guided in their numbers; 'I Can Do Without You' was a charged but fun number with Calamity and Bill, and the Golden Garter Girls were properly employed during their numbers - though 'Keep it Under Your Hat' with Katie was particularly strong number. David Heffernan and Tommy Sweeney designed the clever set, which got as much into the Golden Garter as the space would allow, but still left room for dancing and such; wooden panels opened out into wallpapered rooms and Calamity was able to take buns out of a lit stove. Tommy Sweeney stage-managed also, and scenes changed efficiently, nay impressively, and the pace of things was never compromised. The inclusion of a stage director (Rita Loughnane) ensured any potential bumps were smoothed over. Props were authentic and were managed well and costumes had just the right balance of colour and tone; Katie stood out when she needed to, as did Calamity in Fort Scully, and makeup and hair was given suitable attention. Gerry Taylor's lighting design made full use of the set, with sunshine beaming in Calamity's windows and starlight and gobos adding ambience to the Black Hills. Sound (Star Systems) was blissfully balanced. Indeed, I was blissfully balanced driving home, finding solace during this busy season and reminding myself what it's all about anyway: higher than a hawk indeed.

Scoil Mhuire You don't get many shows darker than Sweeney Todd, so a quick flick through the biogs of the cast was odd, as Trim Musical Society wished each other luck and smiled out from their photos. How can such nice people combine to become so dark and dangerous? The makeup department had a lot to do with it, but don't blame them alone; Director Alan Kinsella brought the worst out of his cast - if you know what I mean; I could almost smell the Victorian air - and these, actually very decent people! There was something terrible wrong with the goings on in Judge Turpin's filthy mind, though as Chris Ramsey whipped himself before our eyes, I was quite happy to sit there and watch him. This was a full on brave performance from Mr Ramsey. Philip Scott as Beadle Bamford was almost as despicable, siding with the Judge and his sordid affairs, though he sounded like quite an affable chap in the programme and singing was impressive too. Graham Walsh musically directed this difficult score and oversaw a solid orchestra; though sound effects were great, balance was variable and I also wondered how well singers could hear themselves, as there were some fine voices in there, yet pitch was an occasional issue for many, though certainly not for most of the principals. The switch from comedy to horror was neatly managed by Mr Kinsella, also well reflected in the relationship between Todd and Mrs. Lovett. Ray O'Hare slid further into madness in a rather distracted way, which worked against the comical twitterings of Gwen Bagnall. She made me laugh, even when it felt wrong, and 'A Little Priest' was guilty pleasure indeed. 'By the Sea' was sung as Sweeney Todd sat deliberating future murders next to a meat grinder - wonderful work from the props department, it even had stringy bits. Craig Regan portrayed Anthony as Sweeney Todd's polar opposite - now he was a likable person, as was Johanna, delightfully played by Danielle Williamson, if energy was a little high in places. Their duets were romantic and her rescue was dramatic - the chorus incidentally had been well guided by both Mr Kinsella and choreographer Grace McGrath, and there was plenty to highlight the talent within, from a solid barbershop number, to black clad personifications of Sweeney's demons. The asylum scene is not an easy one for anyone, and direction was solid here, with the odd escaped patient adding to the horror of the hunt for Toby. Kevin Fagan excelled as Tobias Ragg, in so many senses; physically and deep within, but especially vocally. Here was a quality singer; pitch was never an issue, not while he was around. Helen McHugh played the tragic character of the beggar woman with absolute conviction and Ronan Walsh's short but satisfying portrayal of Pirelli stuck a great balance of humour with tension. The set, designed by Scenemaker with scenic artists Janet Bolger and Sean Whelan was a convincing dirty London street and the pie shop/barber shop was well positioned upstage centre, high enough to clearly see the horror above while things apparently went on as normal below. There were some great touches from lighting designer Colm Eton, and while the mood was properly reflected, things were never depressing. There was a haziness in the air when the oven door opened which I loved. Music, choreography and solid direction combined to bring many a poor unfortunate into it, and bodies died and rolled into the cellar gracefully. Stage Manager Bobby White managed an organised and unobtrusive crew - in as much as they could be - there were some questionable changes during tender poignant moments, but I won't blame Mr White for that. Dark stuff indeed, I was tentative going backstage afterwards, but I needn't have worried. Like so many societies, the people I met were personable, decent creative souls, and as I approach the end of my days as adjudicator, it is humbling to be reminded time and again that the country is full of people like that. Sniff.

Wexford Opera House I'm Still Here.  Everyone's out sunning themselves on a rare hot day, but I'm here (typing away)… My children are hungry, my friends have given up on me, but I'm here (yes, still writing reviews)… I got through all of last year, Lord knows at least I was there, and I'm STILL here (a lonely little figure and her laptop)… Has the adjudicator finally lost it? Not at all, I'm just remembering the words of Carlotta Champion's number in Wexford Light Opera's production of Follies. By golly, was Jackie Olohan Curran very much there and engaging her audience, supported by an excellent orchestra under the baton of musical director Gay Kirwan. The music in Stephen Sondheim's score is not easy and there is no hiding in it for anyone. Just as well then, that there were so many competent singers (guess it's called Wexford Light Opera Society for a reason), amongst a bevy of beauties in their present and former glory. Apart from a super ensemble, Catherine Walsh sang with an animated sense of fun as Hattie Walker for 'Broadway Baby'; As Stella Deems, Elizabeth Rose Brown fronted the Weismann Girls for 'Who's That Woman', a really impressive fun number and Edel Quinlan's clever choreography highlighted a strong group who could handle the steps beautifully, before their younger selves joined them for a further bit of showing off. Nicola Roche brought character and energy to 'Ah Paris!' as the sexy Solange La Fitte while both Heidi and her younger self sang sincerely during a beautiful rendition of 'One More Kiss' (Mary Roche and Miriam Mulhall). There were men in there too, and George Lawlor really did justice to 'Beautiful Girls' as MC Roscoe; indeed it was a beautiful moment as the women gracefully presented themselves, flanked by their former showgirl selves. There is much going on, with all these women and memories all over the place, and director Christine Scary really showed the hand of experience in managing to keep everything so clear; to take just one example, there was a remarkable scene with married couple Sally and Buddy, married couple Phyllis and Ben - and their younger selves, where they all argue with each other; ghostly timelines were crossed resulting in what could have been a noisy mess, but instead things were surprisingly clear. Naoimh Penston, played Sally, a desperately sad, slightly unhinged character in love with another man. Ms Penston's beautiful voice highlighted much of this pain, and 'In Buddy's Eyes' was a stand out number. Buddy is her husband by the way, not the one she loves, though he was no angel and Brian O'Gorman's complex character developed naturally, revealing nothing until the vaudeville style Loveland Follies, where his clownish antics with Margie and Sally 2 (Aisling Riordan and Niamh Cullen) were disturbingly honest. In the old days, Sally was Ben's bit on the side, and Paul Monaghan brought real personality and charisma to the ladies' man. 'Too Many Mornings' was beautifully delivered with sincere emotion, while looking back at the love story that was Young Ben and Young Sally. This scene was beautifully lit and Gerry Taylor's lighting design consistently worked hand in hand with the overall perception of Ms Scary's direction; lighting genuinely reflected the depth of the mood, the range of emotions, the past and the present, the virtues and the follies. Siobhan Meyler Fawsitt played Phyllis, Ben's wife, but sure, they were all at it, and she was no exception, seducing the unsuspecting (but willing) waiter, Kevin in front of her husband's eyes. There certainly was chemistry between Phyllis and Ben and they stayed together for a reason, though their relationship was vicious. Ms Meyler Fawsitt's fabulous voice was full of passion and power, and 'Could I Leave You?' was sung with great control. The young versions of Ben, Phyllis, Buddy and Sally were gently played by James McDermott, Renae Von Meding, Eric Hayes and Sarah Vaughan, not getting in the way of the present, but a beautiful reminder of the past. Each could sing well, and their numbers during The Folly of Youth were great across the board. I want to mention everyone, but Tina says there's a word limit, so I daren't (Joanne Flood and Pat Lawlor had a great number in 'Listen to the Rain on the Roof'; Tony Brennan was still very much in control of things as Dmitri Weismann). Like the director, choreographer Edel Quinlan had a knack for dipping in and out of memories and all four dancers in 'Bolero D'Amoure' moved really well to the strong end tableau - there was a sense of being aged, but still beautiful. Backstage, Colin Murphy managed things smoothly and crew was never noticed on the set, which was the magical work of John O'Donoghue; with a balcony upstage facilitating moments of nostalgia, the staircase was convincingly used to flash back to the theatre's former glory, the rough brickwork of the walls were a continuous reminder that the building, like the stars, would not regain those days. Anne Reck and her team presented their women with total glamour, whether they were gorgeous young showgirls or formidable women ageing gracefully, while in makeup, Pauline Roche and Tricia Murphy made sure everyone looked good. Yes, indeed, things looked and sounded good (Star Systems) in the beautiful Wexford Opera House and along with my charming host, Fr. John O'Brien I enjoyed a wonderful evening. In some ways, I wish I were still there. But, I'm not. I'm still here…

Hawk's Well Theatre A wet Sunday afternoon, a long drive to Sligo and a difficult show being performed by a youth group. "This could be hard work", I thought to myself as I hit the M4. Oh how wrong I was! First big lesson of my tenure learned…NEVER underestimate! Director/choreographer Mary McDonagh gave us a real theatrical gem from start to finish. Direction was exciting, controlled, original and intelligent. There was attention to detail lavished on all aspects of this wonderful production. Every single individual on the stage knew exactly what was expected of them, how to act and interact, how to create tension when and where necessary, how to enunciate and project their voices to maximum effect. CATS presents great challenges with regard to clarity as the narrative, such as it is, can easily be lost due to poor diction or poor understanding of the material. These potential pitfalls were offset through Ms. McDonagh`s excellent vision for the show. The hallmark of a great show is attention to detail and there was no stone left unturned in this regard. The feline authenticity of movement of the ensemble as well as their incredible diction were indicative of such attention.

Music was in the very capable hands of Niamh Crowley (above) who presided over a first rate band from her keyboard. Excellent playing from all with some fine, appropriately sombre work on cello heralding the arrival of the faded glamour cat Grizabella. There was a fine stage/ pit balance throughout. A difficult task in a show with such a broad dynamic range. Choral singing in this show was quite simply awesome at times. Excellent harmonies were realised along with superb diction and Ms. Crowley deserves full credit for eliciting such a full choral sound from her charges.

This was an a b s o l u t e l y s t u n n i n g e n s e m b l e .

There was an overwhelming sense of cohesion and togetherness and a very united sense of purpose with every individual knowing exactly what he or she was required to do in order to make the magic happen. This menagerie of furry felines slid and pounced and purred their way through the show with such focused energy and grace. The spoken` Naming of Cats` set the tone for what was to come. Apart from the utterly splendid diction and enunciation of this piece there was something rather overwhelming about the way this appropriately animated ensemble eyeballed the audience and addressed us directly, almost sixty voices of varying tones blending together and building furiously, every last syllable given its rightful, pointed emphasis. Hairs on the back of the neck stuff indeed.

Emer Shannon gave a heartfelt and poignant interpretation of the shunned Grizabella who is ultimately chosen to ascend to the `Heaviside Layer` where she will be re-born. There was a wonderful depth and sincerity to her performance that was most engaging. There was a remarkable physicality to her playing that made her entirely credible as the aged Grizabella. Her rendition of `Memory` was a musical highlight pitched at just the right emotional intensity.

Eoin Colleary showed great presence as the patriarchal Deuteronomy presiding over his jellicle tribe. He possessed a warmth of spirit which was most engaging whilst at the same time commanding the respect and devotion of the tribe. Vocally, Mr. Colleary was very strong with a fine tone and an impressive range.

Killian Filan enjoyed himself no end as Rum Tum Tugger. I loved his Bon Jovi mane, biker jacket and leather leg- warmers! He exuded confidence and attitude throughout and there was a real sense of narcissistic fun in everything he did.

Munkustrap was brilliantly played by Luke Devaney. As the character charged with the unenviable task of effectively narrating and pulling together what is, at best, a rather tenuous storyline, it takes a very special performer to keep things on track. Mr. Devaney exuded confidence and his delivery was so compelling and so intelligent, displaying a real understanding of the show and his own context within it. Seán O`Carroll gave a masterful, stylised performance as the magical Mr. Mistoffelees and his various tricks were carried off with aplomb. Of course his climactic revelation of Old Deuteronomy took us all by surprise! This was pure theatricality and showmanship from Mr. O`Carroll.

I was most impressed with Shane Egan`s moving performance as the ancient theatre cat, Gus. He projected such an air of melancholy, inhabiting his song and feeling every moment.

Colin Gilligan and Evanne Kilgannon were a delightful pair of feline rascals who hit the stage running as the vaudvillesque double-act of Mungojerrie and Rumpleteazer. Singing suffered slightly in their number from their physical exertions but they made amends with their energetic and quirky characterisations.

Arron McDonagh shone in his role as Skimbleshanks. A lovely, rich vocal tone and what a fine dancer he was too. Wonderful stage presence throughout from Mr. McDonagh.

Eoin Lawless had the necessary gluttonous pomposity as the overfed Bustopher Jones. Macavity was played with the required sinister touch by Jack Keane and I was very taken by Darren Kerr`s presence as the Rumpus Cat. Amy Gilligan was a bundle of energy and fun, giving a very quirky portrayal of Jennyanydots. Aisling Forde as Jemima sang beautifully in the `Memory` reprise with Grizabella. Sarah Keating as Jellylorum, Niamh Casey as Bombalurina and Laura Keown as Demeter all combined well with strong harmonies and exquisite dancing although the `Andrews Sisters` trio in `The Old Gumbie Cat` could have been a little better balanced.

One couldn`t but be gushing about the dancing in this production.  Ms. McDonagh choreographed, ably assisted by Steffen Jorgensen. There seemed to be no end to the imaginative, original, exciting and excellently performed routines which kept on coming one after the other. The tap routine complete with toilet brush `canes` was inspired and the `Jellicle Ball` was as fine a dance routine as I have seen in any show.

What struck me most was not just the superbly executed dancing but the energy and level of performance coming from the cast. Exhilarating.

John O`Donoghue`s stunning junkyard set, complete with clever feline references, was the perfect backdrop for this production. A good sense of collaboration and co- operation with Ms. McDonagh here as the set tied in with so many of the wonderful staging ideas. It was beautifully lit by Nick McCall with good choice of gels and gobos and some excellent effects created throughout.

Stage manager Frances McGowan and crew ran a tight ship and, although there were no scene changes as such, I`m pretty sure they were kept on their toes backstage.

Kate McDonagh is credited with the costume design and artistry and what a wonderful job she did too. I was delighted to see that the cast were so involved in the creation of their own costumes. Every character was an individual and this was complemented superbly by Ali Murphy`s stunning make-up design.

Some aspects of sound were very satisfactory such as the stage/pit balance and the well-chosen and timed effects. However, we did have a few missed cues too many and a mic left on backstage which shouldn`t really happen so far into a run.

This was an excellently crafted show with each and every element receiving due care and attention. There were so many fine flourishes and innovative touches with excellent theatrical values realised. Forget the fact that it was a youth production. About ten seconds into the opening number the `youth` thing went out the proverbial window and the Sligo Fun Company came of age, ascending to their very own theatrical Heaviside Layer!

Island Hall There is no escaping the fact that `Evita` deals with some pretty heavy issues including political ambition, power, manipulation and corruption. Popular opinion remains divided on the titular character. Was Eva a corrupt social climber who used her womanly charms to further her ascension to the top of Argentinian society or was she, in fact, the saint-like charitable first lady that many painted her as?

Whatever your take on it, the complexities of the plot and the challenging score mean that Evita will always be a difficult show for any group to pitch, not least a youth group.

Fusion Theatre took on this most ambitious show with a cast of over eighty young performers between the ages of ten and twenty one. There were some outstanding moments both musically and dramatically throughout with director/ MD Ian Milford at the helm. Mr. Milford is the driving force behind this vibrant and talented group. To direct a show of this scale is a big ask in itself. To musically direct on top of everything else is nothing short of mind boggling and I salute such an enormous endeavour. Direction was of a high standard with a good pace and an effort to keep transitions between scenes as fluid as possible. Mr. Milford`s familiarity with the show was clear to see and his vision for this production was clear and assured. His work on characterisation with the principal players was superb. A real strength shown here in eliciting such mature performances. He managed the huge ensemble well although we did have quite a few traffic issues as large numbers attempted to exit the upper walkway of the split level stage. Mr. Milford`s fourteen-piece orchestra was an absolute delight and he conducted with considerable aplomb as we were treated to an eclectic mix of musical styles from the classical nuances of `Requiem for Evita` to the rhythmic Latin feel of `Buenos Aires`. Some exquisite playing in particular from the accordionist who doubled on keyboard. The muted trumpet during `On the Balcony of the Casa Rosada` was superb. Chorally this was a magnificent show. The ensemble was more than up to the challenge of the complex vocal harmonies. `The Art of the Possible` was excellent from the seventeen gentlemen on stage, as was the `Montage` from the full ensemble. The ensemble was very strong with the more experienced performers leading by example. Energy levels on stage were through the roof at times and the more poignant moments were so well handled. Occasionally there was a lack of focus in freezes. Costume adjustments and the occasional itchy nose relieved were distracting. The milling mob with chants of `Peron! Peron!` was so powerful as it built in its intensity and ferocity. Excellent work from all.

Seventeen year old Aisling Quinn played Eva Peron as we followed her humble beginnings to her rise to fame and her tragic early demise. What an outstanding performance from someone so young in her first leading role! Ms. Quinn showed a maturity beyond her years in her acting and, in particular, in her singing. `Don`t Cry for Me Argentina` was just captivating. `You Must Love Me` which was penned for the 1996 film version was possibly the highlight of the show for me. Stunning vocals, acting and beautifully sympathetic playing from the pit combined to create an incredibly memorable and emotional performance.

Gareth Brown turned in a first class performance as Che. His singing was excellent and his diction was crisp and clear. `High Flying Adored` was a real tour de force from this very talented performer whose exceptional rapport with the audience and distinctive delivery were hallmarks of his wonderfully intelligent portrayal. He was dynamic, engaging and sympathetic when necessary. Excellently cast, he was the glue that held the production together.

Having been `discovered` in Fusion`s chorus, Nathan Graham took on his first role playing the part of Peron. This really was a performance of great maturity and understanding. Mr. Graham had a fine, rich baritone voice and a commanding presence befitting of a military leader. `Dice are Rolling` showed his strength as an actor. It was excellently performed and so emotionally engaging.

Connor Carson had fun as Magaldi, Eva`s one way ticket to Buenos Aires. He sang well and had an appealing presence in spite of the unfortunate choice of joke- shop moustache and chest hair.

Jordan Mackin, as Peron`s mistress gave a beautifully melodic rendition of `Another Suitcase in Another Hall`. It was heartfelt and emotional and she combined so well with the exceptional men`s chorus as the number progressed.

Visually there were some elements which needed more attention to bring things up to the very high standards which had been achieved elsewhere. The split-level set worked really well allowing for some excellent movement and staging ideas. However it was the black curtain upstage of the raised walkway/balconies which was the offending article. There were occasions, particularly during the scenes involving the aristocracy, where many people on stage were dressed completely in black. Black costumes against a black backdrop do not work visually unless your lighting design is akin to the Broadway production. In what should be a lighting designer`s dream of a show I felt that the cast deserved better for their efforts. To be fair, the design was hampered somewhat by the backdrop and there may have been more possibilities available with a white cyclorama upstage in its place.

Stage manager Neil McGarry ensured that everything ran relatively smoothly. Using cast to perform scene changes worked really well to keep things flowing. A bed truck got caught in the set but these things happen. However, when it continued to happen in subsequent scenes I had to ask "why?", especially given that it was so late into the run.

Sound, designed and operated by Jody Trehy, was pretty much flawless. There was a wonderful balance between stage and pit. No cues were missed. An admirable feat given that there were over twenty radio mics in use.

Choreography by Rebecca Leonard was, for the most part, effective. Some stunning work in `And the Money Kept Rolling In`, `A New Argentina` and `Rainbow Tour` which were huge numbers full of unrelenting energy, passion and excellent movement from a very committed ensemble. Not everything was this successful though. `Peron`s Latest Flame` depends largely on the ability of the officers to move with some degree of military precision. It has to be sharp to work. On this occasion it did not work. The tango couples were not sharp enough either with some timing issues in evidence. `The Art of the Possible` was given the musical chairs treatment of the original London production, injecting some humour and representing the rise to political power of Peron. It was superbly executed.

Props were authentic to the era and appropriate to their context. Prop microphones and Eva`s wheelchair looked very well, as did the functioning `On Air` sign. Newspapers in `Rainbow Tour` appeared to be too modern in their layout. This kind of detail is important.

Costumes were, in general, well-chosen with most being appropriate to the era. There was, however, a lack of attention to detail at times, particularly with regard to the officers who, by definition, should have a uniformity about them. Some had no gloves, one hat was so ill-fitting that it was almost comical and at one stage we had a lone marcher in black trousers whilst everyone else was in white. These were unfortunate oversights in what was otherwise a strong costume plot.

Fusion Theatre has to be one of the busiest, hardest working groups in the country. In the space of a few months they have performed THREE huge productions from Lisburn to Waterford to Yorkshire. `Evita` is not a show to be trifled with. However, this young group with their stunning choral sound, excellent principal line-up, hard work and dedication showed that they relished the challenge. It was a show where perfomances set very high standards which weren`t always matched by some of the visual or technical elements.

Many thanks to Anne and her team for their lovely hospitality.

Grand Opera House, Belfast When Oklahoma! opened on Broadway in 1943, just months after the horrors of Pearl Harbour, it filled a deep need amongst an American theatre-going public still reeling and desperately seeking anything which offered hope, optimism and escape. All three were in abundance throughout Tony Finnegan`s vibrant production for the Ulster Operatic Company almost seventy years on. It was a production which dispersed with what many consider to be the dated nature of the original, giving us a fresh take on this timeless classic which was both invigorating and thought- provoking in equal measure.

There were so many directorial flourishes in this production. We were treated to superb staging, a wealth of comic business, a beautifully developed love story and an exceptionally realised smoke- house scene. The latter was a stand- alone brilliant piece of theatre, masterfully performed and excellently crafted. The `funeral`, which could have fallen into the dangerous trap of `over-production`, was perfectly judged in its timing and staging and never once distracted from Curly and Jud`s powerful performances.

Community is at the very core of `Oklahoma!` and this ensemble reflected that central theme, giving the impression of being a very tight-knit community indeed. There was a real sense of togetherness and cohesion throughout and an infectious energy and vivacity which swept us along from start to finish.

Wilson Shields was at the musical helm and what a fine job he did too. He presided over an exceptional fifteen- piece orchestra which hit us between the eyes for the rousing title number and had hairs standing on the backs of our necks during the haunting `Lonely Room`. Choral singing was so strong with an excellent stage/pit balance for the most part. The `Dream Ballet` was a tour de force from the orchestra. Superb playing here and some interesting tempi choices combined with excellent onstage action and marvellous lighting to give us a brilliant realisation of this number.

Wendy Mairs is deserved of the reputation which goes before her. Choreography throughout was fresh, energetic and so well performed. The `tap` sequence in `Kansas City`, with over twenty guys on stage, was a joy. Excellent work in the `Dream Ballet`. I was particularly taken with the work of Kyle Dick and Olivia Reid as the young Curly and Laurey. Two very talented children! `The Farmer and the Cowman` was a huge number with over fifty people a-whoopin` and a-hollerin`, giving their all in a hoedown which was breathtaking at times such was the precision, energy, commitment and sheer abandon which radiated from the stage. Kieran Griffiths gave a most assured and polished performance as Curly. After a few pacing issues in his opening exchanges, he grew in confidence and likeability. His playfulness in `The Surrey with the Fringe on Top` drew the audience in and from that point on we were on his side, willing him to `get it on` with Laurey with whom he had a wonderful chemistry. His contribution to the brilliant smokehouse scene was immense. He had a clear, often effortless, singing voice which was full and large when required and soothing and subtle when called for.

Núala Ní Mhainnín was simply stunning in the role of Laurey. It was an inspirational performance from a most intelligent actress. Ms. Ní Mhainnín captured Laurey`s gentle naivety but left us in no doubt that there was a fiery stubbornness underneath. There was a depth to the character that is all too often missing and her beautiful vocal work was just the icing on the cake. She had the most wonderful, crystal-clear voice with an incredible upper register which was nicely shown- off at the end of the reprise of `People Will Say We`re in Love`.

Karl McGuckin gave a compelling portrayal of Jud Fry which balanced a tormented and angry soul with an underlying sadness and despondency. Mr. McGuckin`s Jud was more troubled than villainous and he displayed a vulnerability which was balanced with a deeply disturbed edge. What a magnificent voice he possessed into the bargain! He combined wonderfully with Mr. Griffiths in `Poor Jud is Dead` and his `Lonely Room` was one of the many musical highlights of the evening.

Alison McCalister as Aunt Eller was a dominant character throughout. She was feisty, funny and warm and her love for Laurey was so palpable. Ms. McCalister single-handedly held the auction scene together, orchestrating and ensuring a cracking pace. Her timing in this scene was impeccable. A remarkably strong performance in what can sometimes be a throwaway role.

What comedienne wouldn`t love a shot at playing the overly-amorous Ado Annie? Karen Hawthorne was obviously relishing the role and hit the stage running with unbridled enthusiasm and energy. At times I felt that she was trying a little too hard and that she could have pulled back a little. However, one thing is for certain - the audience was carried along by her infectious energy and enjoyed her antics no end!

Timothy Bell as Will Parker sang and danced up a storm. His dancing in `Kansas City` along with the large male ensemble was simply exhilarating and he displayed a fine tone to his voice particularly in `All Er Nuthin`. Comedy was very well handled for the most part although on occasion pace dropped and we lost momentum. Michael McDowell as Andrew Carnes had a few diction issues in his opening `rabbits` scene, possibly due to forcing his southern drawl just a little. This soon settled though and we were treated to a very fine performance. His work in the auction with Ali was excellent, giving rise to much hilarity.

Ross Chambers was an Ali Hakim (Hak- eem!) like I had never seen before. He was an excellent physical comedian and I couldn`t help seeing him as a rather strange mixture of John Cleese and Borat! His timing was impeccable and he certainly knew how to nail a one- liner. The omission of `It`s a Scandal` was disappointing as I`m sure Mr. Chambers and the very strong male ensemble would have had great fun with the number. Mark McGuire as a self-righteous Cord Elam sang his solo lines with gusto in the title number and he showed great comic reaction to Aunt Eller`s `accusation` of infidelity. Charlotte Elliott`s smug Gertie Cummings was perfectly judged and her laugh managed to elicit the required groans from the audience every time. Shane McCaffery was a strong Ike Skidmore and Jamie Ewing showed great presence throughout whilst being a standout member of the ensemble as required.

A superbly designed set from Scenic Projects was managed with considerable efficiency by Clare Donnelly and her excellent crew. Changes were perfectly choreographed using cast and crew, with plenty of background cheers and business adding to the continuity.

Costumes from Triple C were of a very high standard and thankfully we were spared from wall-to-wall gingham. Ali`s suit was suitably OTT and his hat, (revealing a fez underneath which must have been super-glued to his head!), was a riot. Great choice of costumes for the dream ballet, especially for the showgirls whose costumes looked most appealing indeed!

Props were very well chosen by Norma Spiers and were appropriate to the period. I was very impressed by the sound design and operation by MK Design. Great work here with no cues missed and a very fine stage/pit balance. There were perhaps some missed opportunities for sound effects but this is a minor point in what was an excellent job all evening.

Paul Hinchcliffe must be in great demand as a lighting designer. If not, he should be! It was quite clear that he understood the show and that he knew just how to complement the dramatic possibilities through his design. Lighting was subtle when necessary with perfectly judged timing of cues fading in and out. The `Dream Ballet` was suitably atmospheric with some striking pictures, marvellous timing by the operator and excellent use of the cyc. Soft focus follow spots were used to great effect throughout.

Hair and make-up by Dawn Sutton and her team were well looked after with good attention to detail.

Rodgers and Hammerstein`s first collaboration will celebrate its seventieth birthday next year. In spite of its OAP status, The Ulster breathed new life into this iconic piece of musical theatre. They have set themselves high standards in recent years and Oklahoma was yet another triumph for the company. Thanks to all for a wonderful night`s entertainment.

Yes, `Annie` is often dismissed as a saccharine-sweet, fairytale, rags-to- riches, good conquers evil, schmaltzfest. However, when it`s done as incredibly well as the production by the Oyster Lane Theatre Group one has to reassess this view. Indeed, one could only embrace the exuberance and exhilaration that leapt off the stage of the Dún Mhuire Theatre on a very wet Sunday in October as the huge cast proclaimed, without a hint of irony, that hope and financial security are just around the corner through such memorable numbers as `Tomorrow` and `A New Deal For Christmas`.

Alan Corcoran`s direction was generally slick and controlled and it was quite clear that a huge amount of work had been done to bring his vision to the stage. His staging was wonderful, creating many visually exciting pictures. His work with the orphans, in particular, was just outstanding.

Patrick Clancy was at the musical helm and did a very fine job. Apart from a slight hiccup at the top of the overture, his ten- strong orchestra played to a high standard and provided wonderful support for a cast of over eighty. Whilst the choral work in `Annie` is not overly challenging, it was clear that good work had been done here. Diction was crisp and clear and harmonies were very secure.

Suzanne O`Leary`s considerable experience was stamped all over the choreography in this production. The eighty-five strong cast had been rehearsed to within an inch of their lives and boy did it pay off! Dancing was slick and sharp. There was excellent work with the orphans in `Hard Knock Life` which was a standout number for me.

The `adult` ensemble was excellent. There was a great cohesion and sense of purpose about this group. They were well-rehearsed and there was great use of props to suggest that these were `real` people going about their daily lives and not just a `chorus`. Their work as the servants was exemplary in its disciplined precision. In fact `discipline` was the hallmark of this excellently prepared ensemble with astoundingly slick entrances, exits and even scene changes in constant evidence. I have seen `Annie` on many occasions over the years, both amateur and professional, but I have NEVER witnessed a group of orphans as strong as I did in this production. I find myself running out of superlatives to describe the incredible energy, focus, commitment and talent which this group of seven girls displayed. These talented powerhouses gave a masterclass in ensemble acting which would leave most adults in the shade. Thirteen-year-old Emma Morris took on the titular role radiating confidence, charm and a remarkable maturity in her acting as she cleverly balanced the comic moments with the more poignant ones. This was a performance of some depth from Emma whose fantastic presence was so engaging. As if her acting skills weren`t enough, her singing was top drawer also. She possessed a strong belt voice which was beautifully pure and melodic. `Maybe` tugged at the heartstrings and `The Sun Will Come Out Tomorrow` was full of optimism and hope.

Ted Quinn as Oliver Warbucks looked every inch the hard-nosed, billionaire businessman. However, his considerable physical presence did not always exude the necessary confidence and bluster that we expect of a guy who has fought his way up from Hell`s Kitchen to rubbing shoulders with the U.S. president. His beautiful, deep, baritone voice enriched every song and he was clearly at his most comfortable whilst singing.

Miss Hannigan is a gem of a role for any comedienne and Oyster Lane had a gem of an actress playing this constantly inebriated, morally bankrupt, orphanage supervisor. Adrienne Meyler was simply wonderful. Every single line and every single movement had been thought about carefully, finely tuned and delivered with pinpoint accuracy and timing. Her programme biog suggests that musicals are somewhat `foreign territory` for Ms Meyler. I, for one, hope that her visa is good for a few more visits! Her exasperated delivery of `Little Girls` was a joy and what a fine belt of a voice she displayed in `Easy Street`.

Joanne McCabe did a great job as Oliver Warbucks` warm-hearted aide Grace Farrell. She had a most pleasant presence and showed genuine compassion for Annie. Ms McCabe had a crystal-clear soprano voice which was most impressive during `I Think I`m Gonna Like It Here` and `NYC`.

Rooster Hannigan was played with such marvellous skill by Neal O`Leary. This was comic acting of a very high standard with impeccable timing of delivery and a remarkable physicality which allowed Mr O`Leary to completely inhabit this sleazeball of a character. It would have been very easy for any actress playing Lily St Regis to have been outshone by Mr O`Neal. Nobody told seventeen-year-old Aisling Reardon this...and a good job too as she was excellent as Rooster`s `bimbo` girlfriend. Together they were a delightfully shady duo.

Lorcan Dunne was a fine Franklin D. Roosevelt with a commanding presence befitting of his presidential status and he wholeheartedly embraced Annie`s optimism with his `New Deal`. His cabinet of Robbie Duggan, Marion O`Leary, Andy Fanning, Yvette Walsh and Andrew Smith were very funny indeed in their transition from stuffy governmental-types to all- singing, jazz-hand waving optimists. All other cameo roles were played very well and I was especially taken with Michael Doyle as a highly efficient Drake and Caroline O`Connell and Siobhán Murphy as Mrs Greer and Mrs Pugh respectively. Michael Carroll had a nice comic touch as Bundles. Andrew Smith also impressed as a cheesy Bert Healy, singing `You`re Never Fully Dressed Without a Smile` and ably assisted by the quartet of Boylan Sisters played wonderfully by Andria Jones Bradley, Fiona Murphy, Rebecca Grey and Danielle Bradley.

Set design and lighting were in the very capable hands of society stalwart Mark Redmond. The set was simple, effective and had great detail in its finish. Lighting was most impressive. `NYC` was performed on a `black box` stage with no set whatsoever. However Mr Redmond`s brilliant use of skyscraper gobos, which filled the stage and cleverly faded in and out, was inspired.

Slick, well-choreographed scene changes were the order of the day from stage manager Greg O`Leary. This was a huge job given the size of the cast he had to contend with but everything ran very smoothly indeed.

There was great attention to detail in the wonderful array of costumes co-ordinated by Elaine Murphy. The down and outs of Hooverville were a dishevelled, motley crew and the maids and butlers were suitably crisp and uniform. I loved the transformation of the orphans at the end into their Christmas finery.

Sound was, bizarrely, a game of two halves. Act one was perfect and I kept noting what a wonderful job the designer/ operator was doing. However, from the cabinet scene onwards we had problems and there were issues with feedback which was distracting.

Hair and make-up were well looked after by Mary Stafford and Ellie Doyle and Annie`s obligatory red curls, although not her own, were deceptively natural looking. Like it or loathe it, at the core of `Annie` is a heart-warming, optimistic outlook on life which, God knows, we could all do with a bit more of in this current climate of. It was impossible to leave Oyster Lane`s wonderful production without a smile on your face or a spring in your step. It may have rained non-stop but I sang all the way home!

Meredith Willson`s The Music Man is, surprisingly, not as often performed as it might be. It is a show crammed full of catchy, but challenging, tunes, some great roles and plenty of ensemble involvement. Philippa Alford`s production for the Pioneer Musical and Dramatic Society was entertaining and heartfelt, playing to a most appreciative audience.

Ms Alford assembled a fine cast for this production. Her strength lay in the development of relationships and the wonderful chemistry between Marian and Harold was indicative of this.

In spite of some pacing issues on occasion, we had good delivery of dialogue, crisp and clear diction, and some excellent comic business. The ensemble was in need of more guidance when it came to furthering the dramatic action throughout the show. The final meeting scene needed much more to give the impression of an irate community which had been swindled out of its hard-earned cash.

There was excellent work from MD Yvonne McQuillan in a show which throws up many musical challenges including complex `patter` songs, counter tunes and, of course, the close vocal harmonies of the barbershop quartet. Rock Island, the acapella, syncopated, spoken opening which replicates the rhythms of a moving train, was excellently performed. Choral singing was of a very high standard. There was excellent diction and phrasing from the ladies in `Pick-a-Little` and the barbershop quartet had a lovely blend of voices.

The ensemble sang and danced with great enthusiasm and expression. They did need to be integrated into the dramatic action a little better however. The ridiculously catchy Shipoopi showed this ensemble at its very best as they bounced off the stage with sheer abandon.

The success of The Music Man is determined to a large extent by the actor playing the central character of the lovable scam artist Harold Hill. Seasoned performer Michael Evans brought a wealth of experience to the role. Movement and dance were exceptional and he sang with a rich baritone. Whilst there is no doubting that Mr Evans is an exceptional actor and performer, I did feel that pace needed attention at times. He was at his very best in his scenes with Marian where the chemistry between the two was excellent. Jean Sweeney as Marian Paroo gave a very fine portrayal of the suspicious librarian who is steadfastly aloof towards Harold and his advances. Her wonderful soprano was simply spellbinding at times and her considerable range was a joy to behold. `My White Knight` was a standout musical moment in the show. Ms Sweeney combined technique, purity of tone and exceptional vocal and emotional range to give us a most memorable rendition of one of Willson`s most heartfelt ballads.

Valerie Andrews gave a very funny characterisation of Marian and Winthrop`s strong-willed and excitable `Oirish` mother. Ms Andrews` comic timing was so sharp throughout and we were treated to some classic one-liners as she fought a losing battle to try to get Marian to at least look interested in Harold. I did feel that Ms Andrews was aged too much though. Her son, Winthrop, is only nine so there is no need to go too far with the aging process.

John Furlong was in top form as Shinn giving a very comical portrayal of the long- winded, blustering, River City mayor who wants to expose Hill for the conman that he is. Mr Furlong gave us an extremely well-studied character and his timing of the mayor`s many malapropisms was wonderful.

There was an absolutely delightful comedic performance from Siobhán O`Sullivan who played the mayor`s wife, Eulalie Shinn. Here was an actress with an innate understanding of comedy and timing. Delivery and diction were of the highest order and she really did inhabit the quirkiness of Eulalie in what was a wonderfully consistent portrayal throughout.

William Burke was impressive as Harold`s old confidante and right hand conman, Marcellus, who has gone straight and relocated to River City, Iowa. This was a lively, comical performance from Mr Burke. We got a real sense that, even though he had chosen to give up his shady ways, he was getting a real thrill out of being back in the game. His `Shipoopi` was a riot of fun and energy.

Brendan Keenan, Joe Murphy, Conor Cronin and Pat O`Keeffe were most impressive as the quartet thrown together quicker than an X Factor boyband.

Of course the analogy ends there as this unlikely barbershop could really sing and their voices blended perfectly. They had obviously worked extremely hard to master the complex vocal harmonies. Monica Griffin, Mary Keane, Tracy Armstrong and Paula Meehan as Alma Hix, Maud Dunlop, Ethel Toffelmier and Mrs Squires respectively, were an equally impressive quartet as the hilarious assortment of village gossips. These four ladies worked so well together and were perfectly cast. Their crisp, articulated diction in the Pick-a-Little number was simply superb.
