Jack Carolan`s performance as the town tearaway Tommy Djilas was most believable. It was a very intelligent interpretation and he displayed an excellent command of dialogue.

Lucy Murphy played a very pleasant Zaneeta Shinn and her chemistry with Mr Carolan was most natural. She sang very well in The Wells Fargo Wagon and had a strong stage presence.

John Cryan played the role of bitter anvil salesman Charlie Cowell with great energy and enthusiasm and elicited much humour from his scenes.

Lauren Murphy as Amaryllis, Adam Doherty as Winthrop and Alice Hunter as Gracie were three very talented children who will have gained a lot from this production and will no doubt have been inspired to go on to bigger and better things. Lauren and Adam sang beautifully and Alice`s dancing was a joy.

Leslie McShane was very impressive doubling up as the conductor and constable.

Choreography was in the very capable hands of Orla Savage and was fresh, well-executed and uplifting. The library number and `Pick-a-Little` were excellent in their precision and there was great energy and performance in `Trouble` and `76 Trombones`. There was an overriding sense of fun and enjoyment in the excellently performed `Shipoopi` and we also had a very elegant waltz number. Stage management by Richard Levins was, in the main, slick and well-choreographed. There was good movement of trucks to facilitate the interior and exterior of the Paroo house. However the premature arrival of some bookcases heralded a moment of some unfortunate confusion when we were meant to have a street scene. Good work apart from this mishap. There was excellent attention to detail from the ever-resourceful Maire Monaghan and her team on props and the superb array of costumes was in the expert hands of Trish Mooney who had the cast looking splendid from head to toe. Hair and make-up were looked after by Val Andrews (was she not busy enough?!) and Leona O`Neill and they did a fine job.

Pretty much a flawless night`s work from Vinny Osborne who did a splendid job on this show. Radio mics were expertly fitted by Mary Galligan.

An excellent stage/pit balance throughout. There was wonderful work in picking up the ensemble vocals over a band which had a considerable dynamic range.

Richard Levins designed a functional set which worked quite well but needed a lot more finish to live up to the high standards set elsewhere in this production.

Tony Martin and Denis Twomey did sterling work on lights, transforming the set and stage beyond recognition at times. There was a good choice of gels and excellent use of gobos and the cyc all through the show.

Nice use of the two moving heads which created some lovely specials, doing away with the need for a follow spot and some lovely cross lighting during the beautiful footbridge scene.

Overall this was an engaging production of a seldom performed show. Some fine comic playing, enthusiastic dancing and a superb barbershop quartet were the highlights of this entertaining show which still has legs after over fifty years.

There is an unquestionable feeling of driving 'down' to some place secluded and exclusive as you make your approach into Banbridge, an exquisite tranquil town in the County Down. The wide open main street with its large War Memorial statue has character and an authentic sense of historical context. It feels somewhat appropriate for a production of Fiddler on The Roof.

One can just imagine this main street crowded with market stalls and merchants selling their produce in the past. The accents abound with the hustle and bustle of activity but in a relaxed atmosphere. This is just what we got from Banbridge Musical Society as the lights dimmed and the curtain was raised in the Iveagh Movie Studios Complex for their annual production of 'Fiddler On the Roof'. The impressive projected village image faded as the ensemble was revealed behind a large gauze in the market square. They sang 'Anatevka' as they went about their business. The side stage portals revealed with large trees pruned in autumn colours complemented by an expansive stage backdrop of detailed autumn foliage with tall trees. The internal setting for this production with wooden fencing, solid moving trucks and rural accoutrements placed downstage was for the most part appropriate.

A young Fiddler was revealed upstage on a roof.  Tevye (Jim McGuigan) was joined on stage to the harmonious, well rehearsed, eager faced ensemble for the all anticipated rendition of 'Tradition'. We knew we were in for a treat!

Banbridge Musical Society assembled a large skilled cast displaying steadfastness and understanding of the nuances of war- torn Tsarist Russia of 1907. They were well clad in a wonderful multiplicity of colourful well thought-out earthy toned costumes; from head to toe. They sang with delight and character under the attentive eye of Musical Director (Colin Loughead). The Director (Leonard Anderson) gave us a bright assorted mix to the overall production with some very fastidious touches and particular awareness of character and accent. The colour may have lasted too long as the show should deteriorate into darker nuances getting colder as we head into winter and more distressing deeds.

Principal characters were suitably cast with secondary and cameo roles delivered with recognisable detail. A burly Tevye was esteemed and supported by a compassionate and maternal Golde (Rosemary Kelly) at all times, even if they did have to sit on the floor for 'Do You Love Me. Bench gone missing I presume?. Their daughters, (Lorainne Jackson Brown; Tzeital, Emma Woods; Hodel, Claire Costello; Chava), were zealous and suitably daughter-like. We would have liked a clear 'steps of stairs' look in casting here. The daughters should obviously get younger looking for Sprintze (Emma Kelly) and Bielke (Mallory Lutton). We weren't sure if we had twins or triplets, but this did not take from their warm performances. The speckled suitors (Anthony Fitzpatrick; Motel, Ryan McCart; Perchik, Lee Carins; Fyedka) engaged and entertained, albeit slightly underplayed while Yente (Linda McWilliams) showed spirit and passion as she tried to match up the somewhat clean-cut Lazar Wolf (Ian Davidson). The feeble Rabi (Eddie Orr) hiked up on a stool by his never to be missed Son (David McClelland), who must have been twelve foot tall, was great fun. They both delighted us with some great comedy, particularly during the wedding scene supported by the whole ensemble.

Getting the supporting roles right in Fiddler is an essential task and Banbridge got it right. Supporting roles were skilfully realised by Brian Doyle - Nachum, Paul Brown - Avram, Gerard Kerr - Mordcha, Kate Adams - Grandma Tzeitel, Nicola Johnston - Fruma-Sarah and John McCourt - The Constable.

Dance was well accomplished by the ensemble with spirit and precision. We would have liked to have seen more involvement of the chorus in 'The Dream'. More collective movement and less dependency on the small troupe of coupled dancers. The 'Bottle Dance' was precise and nerve racking, just as it should be.

We were impressed with the Set Design and Construction (Anthony Fairley and crew). It was well thought out, solid and integrated into the production with seamless accuracy and efficiency. We particularly enjoyed the wobbly bedroom furniture. The use of gauze panels in the side portals was inventive revealing the ensemble during 'Sabbath Prayer' and 'The Dream'.

Sound was at times overpowering, maybe because we were in a cinematic environment. Queuing however very well handled by Enda MacCusker. Lighting was modern in concept with appropriate geling and colour adding to the atmosphere and production values. We were distracted at times with the LED lighting as this type of device can become too obvious and does not have the dramatic impact of traditional theatre lighting. Rodney Ellis's design did support the bright colourful scenes and enhanced the more atmospheric tender moments. We did enjoy the snow effect during 'Far From the Home I Love', a lovely touch.

Hairdressing and makeup was well attended to. A little more distressing needed, particularly for the male chorus and Lazar Wolf. Yente, Gradma Zeitel and Fruma-Sarah showed great attention in costume, hair and makeup. Hairdressing for the female chorus was fitting.

Jennifer Orr made me very welcome for my first outing as AIMS adjudicator for this season. I very much enjoyed the experience and joined with the audience on the night in applauding the hard work of everyone involved. The 'Tradition' of musical theatre is alive and well in the capable hands of the talented members of Banbridge Musical Society. Thanks to Paul Brown for his help with accommodation. It was nice to chat with the cast and Leonard after the show. Well done everyone!

Footloose - The Musical is a very good choice of musical for a young company. Bosco Dram Group, Newry, based at the St. John Bosco Youth Centre was set up to develop the abundant energies and talents of the young people in this area. They captured just that with their recent production of the 1990's 'Footloose' based on the 1984 film of the same name. The difficulty with transferring a musical film to the stage applies again to this show; the challenge of making a film work for the stage needs ingenuity and creativity particularly for this rock combo style musical.

Bosco achieved this for the most part. We opened in a dance club in Chicago, met the main protagonist Ren, played by Killian Foy and moved after the opening theme song to the more subdued small time town of Bonmont. 'Were the hell is Bonmont? Here we meet the Reverend Shaw Moore 'On a Sunday'. He is a conservative and authoritative figure in this small sleepy town who lambastes the evils of "Rock and Roll' music which is banned. His daughter then proceeds to run off to meet her 'Trailer Trash' oversexed boyfriend as 'The Girl Gets Around'. This show is about the challenges facing middle class conservative America. Things don't change that much!

The production in the capable hands of Jim McGuigan and Corinna Cunnigham was exciting and fast paced. The stage pictures were good and the overall concept worked very well. We did need a little more attention in the dialogue scenes and needed to be careful of upstaging at times. Diction and accents needed more attention but characterisation was well defined. Niamh Morgan and Shane McKeever captured the 1990's feel to the dance routines. The line dancing was precise and well rehearsed. The dancing was well within the capabilities of the cast although we did need more rehearsal. The cast were strong in the title number 'Footloose' and 'Let's Make Believe We're In Love'. Musical Director Aislinn Mulholland Hughes was in good control of the orchestra and playing was solid under vocalists and chorus. Playing from the orchestra was controlled and the different styles well accomplished. We had some excellent playing from the lead guitarist, Kevin Canavan. There were some tempo problems and pitching issues at times, but overall a very fine performance from our musical director. This is a very exhaustive score and we needed to be more careful not to over sing, sometimes leading to excessive sharpness and loss of balance in harmonies. The harmonies from the chorus were well rehearsed and secure leading to a very appropriate gospel choir feel at times. Soloists were safe and secure.

Killian Foy was a very imposing 'Ren', delivering his singing and dialogue with confidence and charm. This is a very taxing role and Killian rose to the challenge. Killian caught the witty teenager attitude of the character and the journey from boyhood to manhood. He was a fine dancer too. Jane McAteer was a stealthy performer with fine singing and stage presence as Ariel. Jane understood the different worlds that this character inhabits; the buttoned-up and demure world of her father and the playful expressive thrill-seeking world of boyfriend Chuck and eventually Ren. Paddy Charlie Heaney gave a very committed performance as Chuck. Ronan Sharkey was perfectly cast as the innocent and giddy Willard Hewitt. Ronan was a tour de force in the role capturing the gentle soul with quick fists while Ruby Crowthers was a lovely sassy and self assured Rusty, Ariel's best friend. Martin Morgan brought a lot to the role of the Reverend Shaw, the minister of Bomont County. He was for the most part charismatic and believable. We were impressed with his demeanor and his eventual deterioration into frustration. Eithne Bell gave a solid performance and wonderful sing as the mother; Vi Moore. A wonderful heartfelt performance of 'Can't You Find it in Your Heart'. Eithne gave us a plucky performance, showing what life was like with Shaw before the tragic loss of their son. Neil Heaney was energised and playful as Lyle and Ciaran Henry was perfectly buddy-like as Travis. Seasoned actor Denis Walsh did very well as the gym teacher and Claire O'Neill was a suitable school principle. Ronan Lavery was a solid performer as Ren's friend Jetter and Maille Connolly was well cast as Ariel's friend Wendy Joe. Urleen: Chloe Copas; Betty Blast/Irene: Rita Copas and Coyboy Bob/Cop: James Maginn gave good performances in supporting roles. The boys and girls of the chorus did very well. Singing was strong and secure for the most part and the dancing was exciting and full of energy. The dancing needed some more rehearsal as some of the moves were a bit sloppy at times. This company of young people showed great promise and are to be commended for their hard work and commitment.

The overall set design was functional and worked well for this show. The use of steps leading to a central raised area worked very well for the train scene. The central opening area was fine and the double sided red lockers were inventive. The side portals needed more attention. Stage Manager, Anna Rose Heatley did a fine job on the backstage area with good set changing. Props were well attended to, particularity the motorbike. Sean Keenan and team did very well on sound. Cueing was good. The sound effect for the motor bike could have been more appropriate though. Sarah Smith and her team did very well on lighting. The gelling was colourful and the states suitably defined. Costumes, hair and makeup were all fine.

This company gave the capacity audience a wonderful night's entertainment. They were committed and full of energy. The talent was abundant and Newry can look forward to many more exciting shows from this young talent It was great to meet all the cast afterwards and thanks to Gerry Mulholland for the hospitality.

As I drove from Limerick City to Clane, Co Kildare on Halloween night to see Sweeney Todd, I was reminded of the night that was in it with the many bonfires along the route. As I arrived into the beautiful isolated village of Clane there were fireworks on display and the fog was slowly descending. I passed the neatly tucked old Abbey on my first pass through the village and then had to return through the village, park the car and walk in the chilled dark into the old Abbey grounds surrounded with headstones. I was greeted at the Abbey door, brought through the tiny foyer and escorted to my seat in a most charming atmosphere. Having settled myself and trying to look inconspicuous, I was then greeted with 'Hi Richie Ryan' from my left, Alice Hughes and Moira Nolan, AIMS veterans. No pressure!

Sweeney Todd is one of my all time favourite shows and I have seen it several times, but never so up close and personal. The Abbey in Clane is a small space with the stage set, high up, in front of you. No pit, few lights and even fewer entrances, perfect for a story set in 1846.

The set was very striking with the apartment set high up stage centre, steps leading to doors stage R and stage L, appropriately Londonised and Mrs Lovett's meat pie shop seen through a glass panelled door, underneath the soon to be barber shop. We are drawn into the story with a magnificent organ prelude, followed with the companies entrance for "The Ballad of Sweeney Todd" as Todd himself rises from the ashes DSC with accompanying smoke and floodlights. Prologue finished, let the tale begin!

Clane Musical Society was in full flight with a very strong ensemble, powerful singing and first class musical accompaniment. The company are required to appear throughout this show to comment on the action of the play through song. They achieved this!

Rory Dunne brought a quirky yet demonstrative interpretation to the very important and hugely significant role of Todd. I am not going to procrastinate around the character, suffice to say that this actor/singer was a motivating force in each and every scene. He delivered the role with intelligence, inspiration and a wonderful singing sensation.

Helena Reynolds Begley was a wonderful Mrs Lovett. Her facial interpretations were magnificent and her physical manifestation a joy. Helen is a seasoned actress and this was very perceptible from her finesse and impeccable comedy timing.

Paul Mescal Jnr was the perfect young sailor Anthony Hope. He brought sincerity and youthful naivety to the role. A fine singer and lovely actor!

Peter Manning captured the deterioration in the character of Tobias Ragg's mental state with astuteness and bravery. Peter's singing ability was highlighted in 'Not While I'm Around', beautifully delivered and perfectly measured.

Jessica Hackett was a beautiful Johanna. A true soprano with bird-like qualities! This underestimated role was captured with ease and gentle understanding.

Paul Mescal was a nasty, sleazy Judge and caught the essence of this character at every opportunity. Peter Fay was a strong Beadle, good accent and solid delivery while half mad Beggar Woman, Sharon Murphy, was a fine actress and we were riveted by her presence.

Chris Currid captured the caricature of his character, Adolfo Pirelli with pomp and ceremony.

A confident well rounded company who knew what they were doing and engaged in the overall story delivered with assurance and ease.

What little dancing there is in this show was well accomplished by the ensemble with spirit and precision under choreographer Deirdre Browne.

The overall set was functional, if not slightly unfinished in places. It was purposeful and simple. The use of the trap door for Todd's first entrance was masterful and Todd's chair impressive. We had a wonderful set piece for the oven, opening and revealing a fire with flames and smoke ensuing in the basement of Mrs Lovett's shop, another great touch. The high window at Johanna's house worked well. The interior scenes needed more definition as did Mrs Lovett's shop interior but overall the set was solid.

Sound was excellent under the stewardship of Vinnie Osborne. Cueing was tight. We could have used some additional mics on the chorus as harmonic balance was an issue. Brigid Loughlin did a great job on lighting with appropriate geling and colour adding to the atmosphere and production values. Cueing here too was excellent. Hairdressing and makeup was appropriate. The makeup and hair was great for 'City on Fire', backcombed and zombified. Costumes were a little disappointing. They seemed a bit hit and miss. I would have liked more creativity here with a defined colour pallet. Character costumes were appropriate and Pirelli's frumpy suit was a highlight.

One of the highlights in this production was the orchestra under Musical Director Dave McGauran. It was hidden behind the production with efficient high tech communication for cast and conductor. This is a huge musical challenge and it was remarkably achieved from the outset. The balance was excellent as was the cueing and management between pit and stage. Dave is to be commended! The orchestra was also first class!

This overall production was energised with some wonderful direction from Art McGauran; yes, brother of Dave. They make a fantastic team! The directorial touches were precise and perfectly timed. It is great to give quality actors the space to breathe and embellish. This director showed superior judgement throughout the production although we did need some more attention in the group scenes and with some secondary roles.

Thank you to Ann Keegan for her hospitality. I am looking forward to visiting Clane again soon!

The Sound of Music in Dundalk was a real treat for me! I have to admit to not having seen the show in over twenty years, much to my shame. My memory of the last time was a slow show with little to remember, but thankfully this time it was very different. Under the direction of Alan Kinsella, this production marched on. We opened with a magnificent psalm "Preludium" by the reverend nuns. Beautifully sung by the sisters behind glorious gauze: the lights revealed, the gauze rose into the flies and we were in mountainous heaven. The set design from Proscenium Set Hire was very impressive, revealing the Nuns abbey and later the large interior of Captain Von Trapp's house, adorned with large impressive columns. The stage crew, under stage manager Niall McCooey, were on the mark. Some of the stage furniture was not as impressive as the stage backdrops and this is always a challenge when complete sets are rented from scenic suppliers. It is important to match the stage furniture with the overall effect. The gates for the abbey garden were well realised!

Lighting was impressive under the watchful eye of Peter McDonnell. Good gelling and cueing all-round.

Musical Director; Mary McCague was very much in touch with her eleven piece orchestra. Some beautiful warm sounds from the Trombone and French Horn. Choral Mistress; Geraldine Casey had this choir of nuns singing beautifully, any Abbey congregation would be envious. Beautiful harmonies particularly for 'Preludium', 'Morning Hymn', 'Gaudeamus Domino' and  'Confitemini Domino'.

The Children were marvellous throughout the production. Perfectly cast and with all the fun and nuance expected from mischievous children. 'Do-re-Me'. 'Lonely Goatherd' and 'So Long, Farewell', were great. It is fantastic to see new and emerging talent.

The supporting roles were also well cast and the ensemble very supportive. There isn't a whole lot for chorus in this show, except for the Nun's, but what was required was executed very well.

Aisling McCormack was a beautiful Maria. Her singing was heartfelt and secure. Her rapport with the children was one of trust and mutual affinity as their relationship grew and blossomed through the show. Peter Lawless was a very imposing Captain. This role requires a stern head and a soft heart.

We had a lovely performance from Juliette Crosbie as Liesl. Confident and energised! 'Sixteen, Going on Seventeen' was a highlight.

Pauric McConville was great as the eldest son, Fredrick. He was always secure in the role, trying to be a man, but with a suitable adolescent insecurity. Ciara Quigley was a gorgeous Louisa and played with appropriate pomp and confidence. Padraic Craven was a very strong Kurt. This young actor was convincing and displayed a wonderful stage presence at all times! We had lovely performance from Niamh Baily as Brigita. Ellen McCourt gave a wholesome performance as Martha. Eabha Woods Enright was a delightful Gretl, full of fun and enchantment.

We had a standout performance from Lorraine Quigley as The Baroness. Lorraine understood the role and brought supremacy on to the stage at all times and at every entrance and exit. Tim Ahern brought experience and panache to this role. Tim was consistent and built up a lovely relationship with the children. Paudie Breen was a powerful performer. We enjoyed the potency of his acting and his dancing. Paudie showed his experience in this sometimes underestimated role. Orlaith Crosbie was a wonderful performer and powerful singer as Mother Abbess. Her rendition of 'Climb Ev'ry Mountain' was a highlight of the evening as "the hair stood on the back of our necks", while Sister Berthe; Una Cleary, Sister Margaretta; Bernie McMahon and Sister Sophia; Breda Kiernan were a great foil as the head sisters.

Dominic Keating was suitability butler- like while Phyllis Woods make a great housekeeper and proves that there is no such thing as a small part. Paul McGee was suitably cast as Herr Zeller.

Choreography by Robert Murphy needed more attention. There is very little movement in this show, and it is important to make an impression and to keep it; in its time.

Principle costumes were very good, under the watchful eye of Phyllis Woods. The Nuns were appropriate, but we needed Mother Abbess to be more distinguishable from the other nuns. Maybe a different over-piece?

The children's costumes were great and we loved the all-white uniform. Hairdressing and makeup was well attended to.

Thank you to all in Dundalk for reestablishing my faith in 'The Sound of Music'. It was a pleasure to see your show!

A large school hall was the venue for 'Flashdance' The Musical in Tuam, Co Galway. The cast from Marian Choral Society were proud to be presenting the Irish premiere of the 1983 adaptation of the musical film 'Flashdance'. The story revolves around 18 year old Alex, a welder by day and a 'flashdancer' by night and her dream of attending the prestigious Shipley Dance Academy. Set in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania this musical is a great show for a young cast. Most of the roles are for young people and it is full of great dance numbers and tells the story of holding on to your dreams against all the odds. The show includes hits "Maniac", "Manhunt", "Gloria" and the award-winning title track "Flashdance - What a Feeling".

This energetic cast certainly enjoyed their experience as the stage was full of liveliness and some great dancing and singing.

We had a very imposing backdrop for this production, a large set with a front stage expansion of over fifty feet. You could have been in the O2. The setting was very impressive with three large circular holes or loops set high up backstage and bedroom's stage right and stage left. We opened in the welding shop with the cast busy welding, flashing welding irons and smoke ensuing from all sides for 'Working Man's Orchestra'. A great opening for what was sure to be a great night.

Musical Director, Shane Farrell gave us a very imposing and forthright eleven piece orchestra. He was in control of the musicians at all times, even though they were spread out over a very wide expansive pit area. Shane was obviously very familiar with the music and guided the singers with precision and expertise. This was a fine production from Directors Enda Burke and Aoife McCafferty. It was inventive and full of energy. There were some issues around difficult staging options up on the two high risers, SR and SL, but overall the staging was confident and worked well. Entrances were well managed even with the confined backstage area and the dialogue and dancing was seamless. A great team effort!

Aoife McClaffery managed all the dance routines very well. The dances were well rehearsed and within the capabilities of the overall cast. This show gave us great options for inventive dance numbers and Aoife was well up for the challenge.

This was a very busy show, backstage wise.  It is always a challenge when we are confronted with any musical film adaptation for stage. Sean Callaghan managed the backstage quarter, with the help of his efficient crew, with effectiveness and determination. We did have some hurried set changes that needed more rehearsal and planning. Derval Sound had a difficult task throughout this production trying to get balance between the stage and pit. This was obvious and I am afraid we missed too much of the dialogue and the song lyrics for it to be satisfactory.

The set design added greatly to this production. The large circular units up stage centre were very imposing and gave great options for exciting lighting and pictures. The SR and SL raised areas ie: The Bedrooms, were also very striking. They might have been placed a little more downstage as we were very far from the action. The change into the laundry shop was very effective and inventive. The lap dancing club was well defined.

Gerry Traynor's lighting design enhanced the experience. He did an excellent job on the lighting design. There were many options and moving heads, all six of them, were well used. We did have an issue with a flickering LED light in one of the upstage circles which was a continuous distraction. Costume designer, Bronagh McLoughlin, caught the 1980's atmosphere with the individual array of costumes. They were well thought out and colourful. The boiler suits were effective and the character costumes well attended to.

Heather Doyle gave us a consistent performance in the lead role of Alex Owens. She had a very busy show with over ten musical numbers. We had a striking performance from this young performer. Her singing was impressive and her character very well defined and fantastic dancing particularly in 'What a Feeling'.

Shane Kelly was a very convincing Nick Hurley. A fine actor and singer! He portrayed the character with enthusiasm and spirit. Jennifer Duggan was a solid actress in the role of Hannagh Owens, mother of Alex. This actress did her best in what is a thankless role. Her singing in 'You're Not Done' was very impressive. It is always difficult within a youth production to cast adult roles. We sometimes need to cast age appropriate. Louis Brenan gave a fine performance as Jimmy Kaminsky, the drug addict and his performance of 'You Can't Keep Me Down' was a highlight. The three friends of Alex, Keisha; Amy Byrne, Jazmine; Aileen Newell and Gloria; Michelle Lawless were powerful singers, actors and dancers. They were excellent in every scene and delivered the comedy and pathos with conviction. A great job on 'Maniac'!

We had a great performance from Conor Hurst as Abe and seasoned actor John Mulrooney as Harry Green. Paul Kelly gave a very strong and dominating performance as the drug dealing, lap dancing club owner as did John Duggan as Joe. Suzanne Garvey-Brennan did an excellent job as the elusive Ms Wilde and Rory Kitt was a solid performer as C.C. La Drue. This company was full of confidence and energy during this very exciting production. They were determined and well rehearsed with strong singing and fantastic dancing. Well done everyone!

This is a great show for a youthful cast with great dance numbers and songs. Marian Choral Society rose to the challenge and obviously continues to encourage emerging talent. Through this ethos, they are sure to unearth new talent and secure the societies future. Well done everyone. It was lovely to chat with the cast and production team afterwards.

May thanks for solving my 'Car' issue! Sometimes when you arrive at an unknown location you are not familiar with the parking arrangements. In this case, as I went to park, the car park was full; I decided to drive around once more and in the dark ended up driving my car directly over five steps. Stuck at forty five degrees the car would not move forward or backwards. I decided to leave it as was and go to the show. After the show stage manager Sean Callaghan and about ten lads helped to get the car off the steps! The joys of Adjudicating!

The Solstice Arts Centre in Navan is a very imposing new build, with dynamic features wrapping the sloping theatre space and offering the fly tower integrated into the roof/courthouse level while actors' dressing rooms and scene dock are located at the lower ground floor level. This theatre would be the envy of many a musical society!

Meath Youth Musical Society is to be commended for facing the enormous challenge of staging a show like Les Miserables (SE). A large cast, large orchestra, large sets and a costume list of over one hundred costumes, might just put one off staging this show, but no so for Meath Youth, under the secure direction of Gareth Mahony. This group embraced the challenge with confidence and bravery. We opened with a black gauze backdrop for "Prologue" as the Chain Gang set the scene. Prisoner 24601, imprisoned for 19 years, revealed hard at work 'Work Song' under the watchful eye of the torturous guards as he is released "On Parole". Set in early 19th-century France Les Mis follows the stories of the escaped prisoner Jean Valjean through love, loot, redemption and revolution all in the milieu of 'What Have I Done' as he breaks parole. Montreuil-Sur-Mer, in northern France was depicted by two large imposing pillars with a huge gate set in the centre. Paris, 1832 was beautifully outlined with tall stone clad buildings, windows, steps and a suitable level upstage.

The impressive set designed by Sean Henderson was very striking, complemented by epic lighting from Darren Kelleher. The set and lighting design complementing each other.

The ensemble arrived on stage for "At the End of the Day" with confidence and determination. That was the tone for the evening; confidence, determination and bravery.

Tom Moran (Jean Valjean) was an imposing performer, capturing the determination with a dramatic performance and wonderful singing. A standout performance of "Bring Him Home"! Relentless 'Javert', played by Paul Mescal, was suitably dutiful to the law in "Stars". His performance was powerful as he captured the shame in "Soliloquy- Javert's Suicide". Brandon Walsh was a convincing and kindly bishop while Liam Egan was suitably credible as the demonstrative foreman Maria Branagan gave a magnificent performance as 'Fantine'. Convincing and heartfelt singing, as she reflected on her broken dreams and about her lover, "I Dreamed a Dream". Ellen Dennis was a beautiful 'Young Cosette' capturing her dreams of a better life in 'Castle on a Cloud" while Niamh Mahony was suitably pampered and unkind as 'Young Eponine' in her lovely red hat.

Madame Thenardier was in charge of that stage at all times. Aine Fox gave a duly large performance with great comic timing from this actress. Her reactions and interactions were hilarious! Mr Thenardier, Colin Flynn, showed perfect comic timing and captured the essence of the character both physically and vocally, particularly in "Master of the House". Great costumes for these two characters in the ballroom scene! We had a lovely performance from Daniel Kinnane as Gavroche. Perfectly timed dying scene and he enjoyed the mischief nature of this character in 'Little People", as did we!

Elisa Teyssier was a tour de force in this production. A fittingly ragged 'Eponine', measured and heartfelt! "On my Own" was effortless. The revolutionary 'Enjoiris" played by Sean Kenny captured the urgency and passion of this character. A very fine singer too, especially in "Dawn of Anguish"! Jamie Reynolds was a perfect 'Marius" and delivered with beautiful tone and pathos. "Empty Chairs at Empty Tables" was a highlight! Liam Egan gave us a solid performance as "Combferre', Dylan Ryan captured the youth and innocence of 'Courfeyrac', great performance from Gavin Ryan as 'Feuille", consistent drunk from Fionn Foley as "Grantaire" and a solid performance from Kevin Cleary as 'Joly'. Megan Walsh had a wonderful presence as 'Cosette". A beautiful rich soprano voice from this actress and we loved her "In My Life" and "Every Day", essentially loving.

Meath Youth Musical Society was well served by the talented ensemble. The company showed conviction and bravery right the way through this massive production. Excellent singing and commitment to their acting roles accomplished by what was for the most part a young cast.  Director Gareth Mahony gave us an excellent production with fine attention to detail and self-belief. Some scenes were set too far upstage, but overall a great achievement in staging. The moods were well achieved!

Musical Director, Olivia Torman, assisted by Helen McHugh, managed the eleven piece orchestra with control and trustworthiness.

Choreography was appropriate with lovely couples dancing in the ballroom and great ensemble fun in "Master of the House" under the watchful eye of Choreographer Erin Kenny.

The props under the stewardship of Marty O'Flaherty and Trish Durney were appropriate. A great number of rifles! Well done!

Hairdressing and makeup was well attended to by Ali Murphy, Claire Farrell and Bairbre Ni Bhraion. We had wide variation in wigs and hair dressing for men and women, a rare achievement. Alan White was in control of the sound at all times.

We had a magnificent array of costumes from costume mistress Debbie Walsh. We do need to be careful to fill the musical interludes and introduction music with action in this show, as it is continuous! There should be no standing idly on stage waiting for a song to start.

Congratulations to Meath Youth Musical Society for their bravery and commitment to this wonderful show.

Thank you to Angela Mitchel and the FOH team. It was also wonderful to meet all the young cast afterwards and to get a tour of the backstage from stage manager Collette Walsh. Thank you to Meath Youth Musical Society for their hospitality.

The CBS Secondary School is neatly tucked in Summerhill, Nenagh! This school type venue is your typical school hall with flat floor and raised stage area, fluorescent lighting and a common room type feel. Staging 'West Side Story' in this environment is no mean feat and requires ingenuity and much hard work, particularly if you have a large cast, crew and orchestra. It was jam packed on my visit and the atmosphere was palpable with excitement for this young local cast. Under the Musical Direction of Laura Kearney, 'West Side Story' opened with the solid Bernstein music engulfing the hall. The curtain opened to reveal the New York skyline slowly and atmospherically. The lighting made known, the smoke pouring and then the young cast entering the neighbourhood arena, Entrances and exits were somewhat restricted by the large set, as the Jets and Sharks struggled to control the neighbourhood with apposite taunts. Energy levels high as gang fighting ensued.

Doc's Drugstore was revealed downstage left as a panel was opened and Tony arrived on to his steps. Opening panels downstage right were also used for the Bridal Shop and these complete units were turned 360 degrees for the balcony scenes.

The set was cumbersome at times but overall served the show very well. Director Greg Browne is to be commended for bringing West Side Story to this young cast. The direction was well paced. We do need to be careful with some dialogue scenes, not over-stretching the actors and being secure that they are aware of their place in the production and the overall arc of the show. There is no such thing as a small part!

Set painting needed some attention. The overall backdrop was too one-dimensional and cartoon or child like. It needed more definition. The drug store, bridal shop and Maria's living room needed more distressing and appropriate detail. The lighting was hit-and-miss with some slow cueing. I am not a fan of moving heads being used as spot lights and distracting colour changers being used as the main lighting rig. When we are using moving heads or colour changers we need to make sure they are given sufficient down time so as not to be a distraction as they move through the colours and come up into the next cue. This technology needs to be precise and needs to be well rehearsed. Paul Browne gave a fine performance as Tony. He delivered his dialogue with pathos and sincerity. A fine young singer as we enjoyed "Something's Coming", "Maria" and "One Hand - One Heart". Roisin Heehan was a lovely Maria, another fine young actress and singer. Her top range was beautifully measured and she looked gorgeous. (It is interesting to note that in the whole show, Maria does not have any solo?) Mark Hynes was a good Riff, delivering the quick tempered character with energy and appropriate vigour. Dylan Rooney was a convincing Bernardo. Stephanie Browne was a powerful Anita. Her performance was consistent and natural. This character was well developed from "A Boy Like That" to "The Taunting" trauma. Stephanie brought maturity to the role. Andrew Whelan was a good action, keeping the pace energised. The Jets, Cathal Milner (Arab), Shane Slatter (Baby John), Brian Slatter (Diesel) and Eddie Darcy (Big Deal) were well cast and worked well together. Vivienne Mulcahy (Anybodys) was a great tagalong tomboy. Anthony White (Chino), Jodie McGee (Pepe) with John Harty and Jack Buckley were appropriately intense as The Sharks.

Aoibhinn Slattery (Margarita) gave a beautiful rendition of "Somewhere" during the ballet sequence. Megan Neiland (Rosalia) and Billie Kelly (Consuelo) and Aoibhlinn were very strong in "I feel Pretty" joined by the Shark girls.

Killian Fitzgerald was a very committed and strong 'Detective Shrank' and Michael Cormack was a very funny and fidgety 'Glad Hand'. Theatre stalwart Gerry Scanlon was a very fine and compassionate 'Doc' while Alan White was appropriate as 'Krupke'.

Nenagh Choral Society amassed a fine young cast for what was primarily their youth production. They were stretched and are to be congratulated for attempting this powerful show.

Musical Director, Laura Kearney, amassed a fine twelve piece orchestra with strings, trombone, reed, trumpet, bass and percussion.

These fine players came into their own for "Dance at the Gym", "The Rumble", "Scherzo" and 'the Taunting Scene" under Laura's watchful eye and ear. Generally the singers had been well prepared with some lovely singing. Harmonies were well rehearsed and apparent; particularly during "Tonight Quintet". Well done Laura! Stephanie Browne's choreography interpreted the music very well and was appropriate for the young cast. Stephanie is to be highly praised in constructing the moves within the capabilities of the cast. We enjoyed "America" and "Dance at the Gym" particularly.

Brendan Manning's backstage area was obviously well organised and things moved quite smoothly - I was impressed with the ingenuity and easy set up of the opening side panels. We might have used the cast a little more in some scenic set- ups.

Kathryn Condon with Laura McCarthy looked after props and did a good job. The shop mannequins were impressive and well tailored.

Hair and makeup was good and suitably of the times.

The ladies costumes looked well throughout and were appropriate. The men's costumers needed more attention. There were too many leather jackets and we needed some more attention to day and evening or night clothing. It is unlikely that Detective Shrank would visit Maria's house at evening time without an over jacket or Mac. Maria's costumes were beautiful, especially her white dress! We really enjoyed this production of 'West Side Story'.

Paul Shesgreen and all the team looked after me very well for my visit to Nenagh Choral Society. I was reminded that I played 'Tommy Albright' in their production of "Brigadoon' over seventeen years ago. Where did that time go? It was very special to be revisiting now as AIMS adjudicator.

Continued success to Nenagh Choral Society!

show_raw: Joseph And The Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat
review_text:
We are in a wonderful Great Hall in Downpatrick, Co Down. This old asylum building is very impressive from the front; large imposing redbrick build that has been renovated to pristine condition. The Great Hall, has a wonderful grand meeting hall ambience. A flat stalled area with a sloping type balcony area facing a large expansive proscenium arched stage with curtains. This youth production of 'Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat' is much anticipated by the excited audience.

This story is based on "the coat of many colours', the story of Joseph from the Bible's, book of Genesis. It is set in a frame of a narrator telling a story to a group of young children encouraging them to dream 'Amy Dream Will Do'. A story about a dreamer 'Joseph'! a great musical for a mixed youth group.

The curtain opened revealing what was a beautiful set. Very large steps leading to a high platform USC, back dropped with a gauzed entrance. The steps went right across the stage, taking up the complete area and the centre section was eventually moved to reveal a USC entrance. Very inventive!

The children's choir entered through the audience taking up their positions SR and SL on choir risers and joined in 'The Prologue'.

The children's choir are a very important element of this show. They need to be engaging and well disciplined as much of their singing is backing for soloists. This group of children, in Downpatrick, were well disciplined and very sweet indeed. Ages ranged from 6 to 10 years.

Director Garry Warnock did a fine job on the overall production. Staging was active and energised. The use of the stage was well attended too. Garry captured the 'magic' that is Joseph.

Niamh Conway did a great job on the choreography. Dancers were well positioned and well rehearsed.

Stage Management under the direction of Conor McCann was slick and efficient. Musical Director and chorus mistress Denise Kelly brought together a fine band for this production. It was a little light with just bass, drums, woodwind and piano but this did not distract from the fine playing. Denise was focused on the young cast at all times. Singing was very impressive from soloists and ensemble. The Children's chorus was well rehearsed. Denise captured the wide variety of musical styles that are apparent in this show and kept the pace going at all times.

Matthew Campbell was a fantastic Joseph. His singing was tuneful with rich baritone tones and excellent delivery from this young actor. Courtney Burns was a beautiful Narrator and a powerful storyteller. Courtney had confidence and precision throughout her singing and delivered meaning with every song. This actress also had a very strong relationship with the children.

Michael Sims was a great Jacob. This fine actor was sensitive and at the same time comical. Mark McMullan was great as Ruben with immense stage presence. Sarah McVeigh was strong as Zebulum, while Alice Magorrian was believable as Levi. Georgia Forde was a sturdy Dan and Kirsten Jennings was a first-rate Gad. Christopher Rice was very authentic as Simeon and Anna McMullan was admirable as Judah. Dylan Scullion was a lovely slight Benjamin and did very well as the youngest son.

Napthli: Louise Carney; Issachar: Una McErlean and Asher: Blaithaid Evans, were well cast and always engaging. The wives were very strong throughout the production with excellent singing and dancing. They also captured the fun! Mark McMullan was a fantastic performer. 'Elvis' supreme in the role of Pharoah while Michael Simms was an imposing Potifer. Laoise Carney was suitably scheming as Potifer's wife. Alice Magorrian  and Laura McCann were very funny as Butler and Baker respectively.

The sound levels were well balanced overall. We would have like more volume from the Children's choir. Lighting designer Danny Doherty gave us some lovely lighting options. We did have some issues with LED flickering upstage. The colours were well defined and the gauze upstage well lit. Using moving heads as spotlights can be distracting and inefficient at times. The costumes were colourful and exciting. We really enjoyed this show. It was sweet and engaging. Well done to everyone in Downpatrick!

Disastrously, Coolmine Musical Society, with two weeks to go, found itself with no leading man. Director, Colin Hughes, stepped into the breach and did a marvellous job playing the cockney costermonger who transcends the social divide to assume his position as Lord Hareford. It was an excellent production with underlying themes of class, fate and love underpinning some riotous comic antics.

Mr Hughes`s direction was of a very high standard. Pace was absolutely cracking and continuity was quite obviously an important concern. Comedy was brilliantly handled with a very definite vaudevillian feel to some wonderfully timed slapstick, pratfalls and double-takes which had the audience in hysterics. The heart at the centre of the show was given great attention also and we had some beautifully poignant moments.

I was very impressed with the ensemble in this production. There was a great mix of youth and maturity in the group and they showed great focus and purpose throughout. Singing was of a very high standard and diction was excellent. The kitchen scene was an example of ensemble acting at its very best with wonderful expression, diction and comic business from a uniformly committed group.

MD Caitríona Ní Threasaigh`s energetic and enthusiastic conducting was a production in itself as she got every last note and nuance out of cast and her exceptional orchestra. There was beautifully sympathetic piano at the top of `Once You Lose Your Heart` and the tutti of `The Lambeth Walk` was suitably big and brash. Principal singing was strong across the board. A temporary lyrical diversion during `Take It On The Chin` was cleverly steered back on course and was indicative of Ms Ní Threasaigh`s strong connection with her cast.

Brian Keogh`s choreography was sharp, well-rehearsed and, above all, fun! `The Family Solicitor` was a riotous romp which was hilariously performed and the wildly contagious `Lambeth Walk` was full of the necessary life, vigour and swagger from an excellent group of cockneys.

Mr Hughes`s sublime performance as the wisecracking, cockney barrow-boy was the glue that held this production together. His instinctive sense of comic timing was stamped all over the show and he displayed a physicality and athleticism which was quite exhilarating. He exuded a natural charm which captivated the audience from his very first appearance. His impressive vocal ability was evident throughout with `Leaning On A Lamppost` being a standout musical moment full of sincerity and heart.

The role of Sally is at the emotional centre of this charming show and Alison Dennan turned in a wonderfully layered performance of the cockney fish vendor who finds herself way out of her comfort zone at Hareford Hall. She exuded a warmth and dignity throughout which was most endearing. The chemistry with Mr Hughes was most credible and we had some beautiful moments with the two of them. Ms Dennan possesses a most captivating singing voice. `Once You Lose Your Heart` was a very touching and heartfelt rendition. `Take It On The Chin` went a little awry lyrically but the recovery was impressive and it didn`t take away from a superb overall performance.

Paula Fay played Maria, Duchess of Dene, with a most stuffy and autocratic air. She carried herself with the necessary haughtiness and really knew how to point an insult.  Her brilliantly delivered "Oh do be quiet you futile man!" cut poor Sir John to the quick whilst leaving the audience in stitches. `Song of Hareford` was a real musical gem and showed Ms Fay`s stunning soprano at it`s very best.

Paul Holloway is a fine actor and he performed the role of Sir John in a very thoughtful and intelligent manner. Comedy was very well handled and his drunk scene with Bill and Cedric was great fun. There was a nice chemistry between himself and Ms Fay and I really loved their `proposal` scene which had just the right mix of humour and sincerity. I did feel that more attention was needed to Mr Holloway`s overall appearance. His suits were too modern looking which was a pity. The addition of a moustache, or even a monocle, would have transformed him, giving him much more character.

Séamus Sullivan was in top form as a tewwibly, widiculous Gewald and he certainly got every last ounce of humour out of the wole...sorry, role! This was a superb comedic performance from Mr Sullivan who cast aside all notions of subtlety and treated us to some excellent physical comedy as he suffered for his art at the hands of Jacquie during `Thinking of No-One But Me`. His facial expressions as he repeatedly hit the deck were cartoon- like at times and perfectly in keeping with the style of the piece. `The Sun Has Got His Hat On` was a veritable campfest and Mr Sullivan appeared most comfortable with such proceedings!

Robyn Poole did well as the self-centred Jacquie whose heart is irresistibly drawn to Bill`s money. `Thinking of No-One But Me` was very well sung although timing of some of the gags needed some work. I loved her expression as Bill mistook her knee for the arm of the chaise. `You Would If You Could` was full of fun and energy and excellently sung. Focus during ensemble scenes was something which needed to be addressed at times. Her face `post-slap` was just hilarious.

What can I say about the role of Parchester played by seventeen-year-old Liam Egan? His performance during the preposterous `Family Solicitor` was akin to watching Mr Bean on acid! His facial expressions and swivel-jointed movements were hilarious. What a stunning vocal range and breath control he displayed to wonderful comic effect as well. Comedy gold!

David Kennedy was a wonderful, if unlikely looking, Charles who took his butler duties very seriously indeed if his fixed expression and monotone delivery were anything to go by. He was wonderfully consistent throughout and elicited much hilarity from his classic line in reply to whether or not he had ever been in love. "Oh no sir...I`m married" was delivered with brilliant dead-pan timing and brought the house down.

Lord and Lady Battersby were expertly played by two fine actors, James O`Higgins Norman and Dolores Hughes. They were an austere duo who complemented each other wonderfully, he with an inclination towards the bottle and she with an inclination to thwart him.

Eddie Burke looked every inch the part of the aging, hard of hearing eccentric. His monosyllabic utterances were delivered with gusto and he was a most generous observer of Sally`s `Take It On The Chin`. Michelle Tobin was an unapologetic busybody as the nosy Mrs Brown and she clearly enjoyed her scene.

A top-notch set from Proscenieum was brilliantly moved by Mo McMahon and her expert crew who combined wonderfully with cast to make transitions as slick as possible.

With the exception of Sir John`s suits, costumes from thatlooksgood were excellent. The ancestors were particularly impressive although one pair of luminous green tights did jar.

Props were of a very high standard generally. The vertically challenged suit of armour was hilarious. It was disappointing to see the same two chairs appearing in every scene though. Poor Jacquie was left to improvise without a croquet ball but managed admirably.

Sound designer Jody Trehy did a very good job generally. Stage/pit balance was excellent and there was superb work in featuring various instruments as required during instrumental sequences.

Lighting design by Denis Twomey was wonderful with excellent use of gobos and some lovely effects created. `Leaning On A Lamppost` was a particular highlight. I did question the decision to have the arrival of the ancestors in the library performed in full light. They are not `real`. They are a figment of Bill`s drunken imagination and the lighting should reflect this.

Linda Tristram oversaw hair and make-up. There was good attention to detail here for the most part although a hussy of a maid in the kitchen scene was obviously trying to catch Bill`s eye with her red lipstick! This was an excellent production of a highly entertaining, feel-good show. There was a real sense of a very tightly-knit group working very hard and having an "absolutely wonderful and marvellous and beautiful" time whilst doing so!

There have been many re-imaginings and re-hashings of Frank L. Baum`s book `The Wonderful Wizard of Oz` which was written over one hundred years ago. From the African American `The Wiz`, to the blockbusting `Wicked`, to its most recent incarnation `Tom and Jerry and the Wizard of Oz` (I kid you not!) it is a story which never grows old. But it is the 1939 MGM musical version which has fired the imagination for over seventy years now and its characters are the ones which are etched indelibly on our minds. It can be difficult to look beyond such iconic characterisations and therein lies one of the biggest problems for any director tackling the stage version. Does one try to replicate the MGM template or is it possible to approach things in a fresh and memorable way?

Director and society stalwart Diarmuid Vaughan went for a traditional telling of the classic tale. A man of many talents, he also designed, constructed and painted the set and is even credited as head of the make-up department! Mr Vaughan has a good visual eye and there were some fine comic moments. Characterisation and delivery of dialogue were in need of attention with some performers. I attended on the second night of the run and the cast wasn`t quite as on top of things as they might have been. Some performers appeared under-rehearsed and uncomfortable. I have no doubt that things tightened up during the run and I am only sorry that, due to a particularly busy week, I was unable to attend a later performance.

MD Danny Carroll conducted a scaled- down seven piece orchestra. There was some beautiful violin playing throughout. Keyboards filled in as many of the missing orchestrations as possible although some of the patches chosen were overly synthesised sounding at times. Underscoring needed to be pulled back on occasion especially during the `conferring` of diploma, heart and triple cross. Some musicians needed to be mindful of the fact that openly conversing during a show, even if a dog is going bananas on stage, is not acceptable. There was good choral work generally with the delightfully turned out little munchkins benefitting greatly from the inclusion of some adults in their numbers.

Gillian Hewitt-Fitzgerald and Majella Louise Fitzgerald devised some nice dance routines to suit their charges. These ranged from the simple but precise `Ding Dong The Witch Is Dead` to the brilliantly conceived and performed `Jitterbug` which was full of impressive cartwheels, athleticism and agility. The latter was a standout moment in the show.

As an ensemble this group sang very well. The inclusion of `Home is a Place in Your Heart` allowed them to showcase their choral skills. It was very static but their singing compensated for that admirably. The children worked hard and there were some fine performers in their midst. Some required more focus but will have learned greatly from being involved.

Fourteen-year-old Ciara Laste got the opportunity of a lifetime when she landed the role of Dorothy Gale. She will have gained so much from the experience. She was assured and sang well. Her `Over the Rainbow` reprise was beautifully heartfelt. I have to commend her maturity and level-headedness in her dealings with her canine accomplice who was less than co- operative.

George Barry played the dual roles of Professor Marvel and the Wizard. He certainly looked the parts and there was some nice comic playing throughout. His Marvel could have been a tad more knowing though as he convinced Dorothy to make her way home.

Noel Cairns was a very laid back Uncle Henry. Dialogue needed some work. His Emerald City Guard greeted Dorothy and her trio of friends with a hearty, Tipperary "How`re you now?" in what was a most bizarre moment. Mr Cairns has a fine voice but his `Merry Old Land of Oz` was ironic in that it couldn`t have been any less merry. The potential was there but Mr Cairns needed to relax and smile.

Grainne Vaughan was a most glamorous Aunt Em. Bright red lipstick, blusher and perfectly French manicured nails were totally at odds with what one might expect of a Kansas farmer`s wife in the early 1900s. Cueing at the top of the show was poor but improved as she settled.

Michelle Moloney played a rather serious Glinda with a nicely clipped accent. Again, she was a performer who needed to smile and enjoy the experience. Her `Home is a Place in Your Heart` was beautifully sung and showed what great potential she had. Michelle Smith was a fine Wicked Witch who revelled in playing such an evil role. She was full of energy and displayed a great twisted physicality which complemented her character so well. Her solo, (not listed in the programme), which I had never heard before, was well handled. Kevin Fahey was a superb scarecrow and really brought the show to another level every time he appeared on stage. He was always thinking and reacting and displayed great athleticism and agility as he threw himself around. His facial expressions were wonderful and he sang with great character.

David Hughes was less than assured as the Tin Woodsman on the night I attended. Lines were dropped and cueing was poor. He sang very well indeed and was clearly at his most comfortable when singing. Sheena Fennessy played the Lion with wonderful energy. She had a good comic flair and her singing was very strong indeed. However I do have to question the decision to cast a female, no matter how good, as the KING of the forest. It just didn`t fit no matter how hard I tried to be open to it.

Tootsie Vaughan was a most vocal Toto who seemed intent on overshadowing her co-stars at every turn. The cast coped admirably with her interjections especially Ms Laste who had the patience of Job. Stage managers Ruth Butler and Pat McGrath kept the show moving with efficient changes of a most effective set designed by the director. The gates of the Emerald City had a real "wow!" factor and the witch`s castle, using two very cleverly hinged pieces which opened out onto the stage, was excellently painted. The `Oz` head was the finest I have seen in all its rusty, metallic and hugely imposing glory. The props team did sterling work on this show with great attention to detail throughout. The Lion`s crown, fashioned from a flowerpot and the flower stem sceptre were wonderfully clever!

Dirk Beaumann`s lighting plot made great use of LEDs and there were some great effects achieved particularly during the twister. His sound design was equally impressive although I have to admit that the less than discreet headsets which made everyone look like they had a growth on their right ear were disappointing. There was great work from the make-up department on the munchkins, Witch, Lion, Tinman and Scarecrow.

Costumes, from a variety of sources, were generally well-chosen. Scarecrow, Lion and Tinman were excellently attired as were the munchkins in an eclectic, colourful array of quirky styles. The jitterbugs` costumes needed to be seen to be believed. They were brilliant creations bedecked with vibrantly coloured feathers and fur and the most wonderful headdresses of mohawk-like plumage. The witch, in her little black number was far too attractive looking to be such a nasty, evil lady.

Front of house were most hospitable and efficient. Particular thanks to James and Patsy for their warm welcome.

This was St Mary`s Choral Society`s 109th production. It was great to see so many young people from the local area involved as they will, no doubt, ensure that many more productions will grace the stage of the White Memorial Theatre for years to come.

Hope: Charity Valentine`s middle name. Hope: The feeling we were left with as the curtain closed on Philippa Alford`s production of `Sweet Charity` for HXT MS. Ms Alford dispensed with Neil Simon`s original, unexpected ending which finds our heroine submerged in water thanks to the neurotic Oscar. She opted instead to leave us with a Charity determined to overcome the slings and arrows which life had dealt her. Simon himself was never happy with the ending as written. Charity is an eternal optimist, albeit a terribly naive one, and Ms Alford`s alternative ending worked so well in creating a fittingly renewed sense of...well...hope.

This was a minimalist interpretation in a `black box` setting. It takes guts to stage any show in this way. A director must have a very clear vision, a very committed, talented cast and a top notch lighting designer. Thankfully, all of the above were in evidence. Ms Alford gave us a highly entertaining, high energy production with wonderful heart and some great comic moments. The stripped back approach allowed for great fluidity with minimal disruption to flow.

MD and chorus master Dermot O`Callaghan conducted a flawless orchestra which gave a top-notch performance of Cy Coleman`s classic score. Tempi were well chosen and there was an excellent stage/pit balance. There were some fine choral moments in the show with `The Rhythm of Life` being a real highlight. The arrangement, not one I`d heard before, showcased the group`s impressive vocal abilities. An excellent job all-round from Mr O`Callaghan.

Sonya Dunne`s choreography was so sharp and well-rehearsed. `Rich Man`s Frug` was a standout moment in the show with a wonderfully precise group recreating the iconic dance moves of the day. A spirited and excellently sung `Rhythm of Life` brought the house down and a red hot `Big Spender` heralded collar-loosening aplenty as the hostesses bumped and grinded their way through an excellent routine.

There was a most enthusiastic and focused ensemble at work in this show. From passersby, to worshippers, to hostesses, this was a very committed and well-rehearsed cast who knew exactly what was expected of them in their various guises. Diction was excellent, particularly in the very wordy `Rhythm of Life`. The hostesses were superb as each assumed their individual characterisations.

Likeability: Sharon Osborne`s middle name. Or at least it should be, given her idiosyncratic portrayal of Charity Hope Valentine...a woman "caught in the flypaper of life". There was a naivety and hopefulness to the role which drew the audience in from her very first scene. Humour was never forced but still the laughs came as Ms Osborne trusted the book and focused on eliciting compassion for her quirky, enthusiastic character. We felt her heartbreak too and there were some lovely poignant moments. She danced well and singing was strong and expressive. `Charity`s Soliloquy` was a particular highlight vocally.

It would be difficult to find a better Oscar Lindquist than Damien Hurley. This was a most truthful, unforced and real portrayal from a very skilled character actor living in the moment. He was deliciously self- deprecating and his neurotic behaviour gave rise to much hilarity. Mr Hurley was superb in the elevator scene and his chemistry with Ms Osborne was excellent. He had a lovely full tone to his voice which was shown off perfectly in `I`m the Bravest Individual` which he sang with most heartfelt expression.

Kelly Marie Davy and Julie Donnelly impressed as Charity`s hardnosed co- workers and confidantes Nickie and Helene. Strong acting from both helped to paint what a dismal, seedy, dead-end dump the Fan-Dango Ballroom really was. They were a perfect contrast to the dreamy Charity. Ms Davy sang so well in `Big Spender` and Ms Donnelly showed her dancing prowess in the same number. The two combined so well with Ms Osborne for `There`s Gotta Be Something Better Than This` and the chemistry between the three was very strong as they sang and danced up a storm.

Frank Beadle`s appropriately two- dimensional Vittorio was a fun characterisation. His scene with Charity in his boudoir had many fine comic moments and his `Too Many Tomorrows` took the roof off the theatre as Mr Beadle gave a masterclass in vocal performance, soaring to dizzying heights as the number reached its climax.

Sharon O`Callaghan clearly enjoyed herself as Vittorio`s love-interest Ursula. She was feisty and brash outside the Pompeii and, back at his apartment, her apology for accusing him of an indiscretion with Charity was so well-timed.

Chris Currid was a superb Daddy Brubeck, the leader of the Rhythm of Life Church. His `Rhythm of Life` was outstanding! Mr Currid has an incredibly powerful yet controlled voice with a most impressive upper register. His final note brought deserved rapturous applause for what was easily the standout ensemble number of the show.

I loved Andrew Docherty`s performance as dance-hall manager Herman. He was full of the necessary, bellowing bluster and he really drove home the reality of Charity`s seedy surroundings.

His `I Love to Cry at Weddings` was a great number and he was cleverly assisted by a hobo-like Chris Currid to great effect. All smaller roles were well played with particularly good work from Aoife Small as Rosie, Mark Keegan as love-rat Charlie and a deliciously funny cameo from Rosaleen Nolan as a harried receptionist. Even though this was a minimalist approach in terms of set, Marie Cusack and her crew were kept on their toes and carried out their duties with their typical efficiency, allowing for fluid transitions between scenes.

Andrew Reddy did excellent work on costumes with attention to detail in evidence throughout. The black and white theme in `Rich Man`s Frug` looked very well and there was wonderful colour in `The Rhythm of Life`.

A resourceful Karen Morrin was kept busy on props and there was nice dressing of the sparse set especially Vittorio`s apartment.

There was excellent sound from Vinny Osborne with typical attention to detail. `The Rhythm of Life` was a triumph.

With so much going on vocally and so many radio mics on stage Mr Osborne achieved a perfect balance in this difficult number between cast, orchestra and some very strong pit singers.

The single-most important technical element in a stripped back show like this can often be the lighting.

Without the considerable expertise of Richie O`Neill this could have been a very different show. A dropped cue right at the first scene change did not take away from what was an excellent plot throughout. There were subtle and not-so-subtle mood changes from scene to scene. `Rich Man`s Frug` included excellent use of movers evocative of 1960s psychedelia.

Make-up and hair were treated with the necessary attention to detail by Feebee Foran and front of house, complete with floral displays, was efficiently presided over by Philip Coventry and society members.

The minimalist approach chosen for this production was a brave one. It paid off though and HXT should be proud of

It poured rain as I drove to Portlaoise. It poured rain as I walked to the theatre. It poured rain IN the theatre and as I left the Dunamaise Arts Centre I was greeted with a further downpour. Walking the streets to return to my car I was sorely tempted to swing out of lampposts and splash my way through a myriad puddles such was the feeling of exhilaration after Portlaoise Musical Society`s feel-good production of the classic `Singin` In The Rain`. It was a charming show with some great characterisations, a stunning orchestra, marvellous silent movie sequences and the requisite amount of precipitation to put a broad smile on the faces of a most appreciative audience.

Direction was in the very experienced hands of Alan Kinsella. `Screen to stage` musicals can be notoriously difficult to stage. The all-important opening sequence of `Singin` in the Rain` is particularly tricky as there is no opening number to speak of and instead we are treated to a series of bitty episodes and a huge chunk of quick- fire exposition. Mr Kinsella handled this very well indeed, incorporating some well- timed freezes into the action which allowed us to focus on excellently enunciated reporting from Joan White playing intrepid Hollywood reporter, Dora Bailey.

Sarah Lynch Barrett lived up to her deserved reputation at the musical helm. She had assembled a top-notch orchestra which brought the iconic score to life. There was outstanding work from the brass in the incredibly challenging `Moses Supposes` and I am still laughing at the inspired, ad-libbed and perfectly timed piano accompaniment to the silent movie sequences. Choral singing was of a very high standard and the ensemble harmonies in the finale were just superb. Grace McGrath`s choreography was strong throughout. Performance levels were high and bigger numbers were full of energy. `Moses Supposes` was a triumph in its energy and execution and the titular number was splashingly good fun.

There was great enthusiasm and energy from the ensemble in this show. From the very disciplined freezes of their opening scene to the wonderful harmonies and performance of the finale we were left in no doubt that this was a most committed group which had been very well prepared. The crossovers during Don and Kathy`s `trolley bus` scene needed more consideration though. Whilst most were conscious of not stealing focus, there were some who were overly animated thus distracting from the intended point of focus.

As Kathy Seldon, Karen Hackett really set the performance bar for this production. A most clever actress, Ms Hackett exuded charm and likeability as the Hollywood ingénue. Her singing was simply exquisite and she connected beautifully with every song both lyrically and musically. `You Are My Lucky Star` was one of those `could have heard a pin drop` moments. Ms Hackett danced with such grace and poise and showed herself to be that rarest of performers "a triple threat".

Don Lockwood was played with warmth and confidence by Craig Regan. He was a fine actor with a natural presence and a most pleasing baritone voice. His chemistry with both Kathy and Cosmo was wonderful. Indeed, the connection between this trio of performers was a highlight of the show in itself. The signature number at the end of the first act was so much fun. Mr. Regan danced up a storm and was clearly having the time of his life! As the third piece of the jigsaw, Pat Cullen played Don`s hilarious sidekick, Cosmo Brown. With a range of rubberised facial expressions reminiscent of Stan Laurel, here was a comedian who appeared to have stepped right out of the silent movie era himself. Timing was impeccable and his `Make `Em Laugh` was simply exhausting to watch due to the energy and physical exertion involved. Accent was not always consistent but that was forgiven, such was the calibre of this performance. Sarah O`Sullivan was perfectly cast as the screechy-voiced diva, Lina Lamont, whose demise is heralded by the introduction of `talkies`. Ms O`Sullivan was careful not to fall into two common traps when playing this gem of a role. She did not sacrifice diction for the `squawk factor` nor did she start proceedings at a level so high that she had nowhere to go with it as her frustrations built over time. It was a very funny portrayal indeed and `What`s Wrong With Me?` was a real comic highlight. Studio boss R.F. Simpson was well played by John McEvoy. It was a good solid characterisation from Mr. McEvoy who was commanding and authoritative whilst at the same time handling humour well. His on-screen appearance at the Coconut Grove as he introduced the new technology of `talkies` was very funny. Damien Halpin, as movie director Roscoe Dexter, was a `colourful` and `flamboyant` character. Okay, he was as camp as Butlins but it really worked! His increasing frustration with Lina as she ruined scene after scene was perfectly pitched and paced.

Gillian Haslam as Miss Dinsmore/Vocal coach enunciated perfectly and her timing with Cosmo in particular was wonderfully precise. John Coss sang the very high `Beautiful Girl` well. He had a good strong presence and performed with confidence. Colm O`Toole was an `eleventh hour` stand-in as publicity guru Rod and did so well that, apart from a slight positioning issue in the final scene, I had no idea that he was a last second addition just before curtain on the night! Richard Finnegan was outstandingly hilarious as the villain in the silent movie sequence but he was not as strong as Sid Phillips. Dialogue needed attention, particularly in the scene where he attempts to convince Kathy to sing for Simpson. Paula Byrne`s Zelda Zanders was very well performed but I did feel that the decision to have her suffering from the same `vocal affliction` as Lina was ill- judged. It was amusing to begin with but the gag wore off very quickly.

The silent movie sequences, which are such a key element of this show, were brilliantly directed, performed, shot and edited. I have to applaud the huge amount of work which went into putting these together.

Bob O`Kelly`s stage management was, in the main, really slick and well thought out. The rain was a triumph of engineering and the logistics of preparing the stage for Act Two had been carefully thought through. Bringing in a black border to mask the mechanics of the sprinklers from the audience would have added to the `magic`. Seeing the source of the downpour took away from it slightly.

Set design was quite basic and in need of a lot more detail and finish. The Hollywood sign backdrop looked very well. The interior of Miss Dinsmore`s office was indicative of the lack of detail in general. Trying to fit five vowels onto four trucked pieces looked quite distracting visually as one pillar had to accommodate two. Annette McCaul`s props were generally of a high standard. However, the upholstery on Don`s couch needed to be of a uniform colour and Cosmo should really have had a watch in order to know that it was 1.30am.

Nick Anton`s lighting was basic but effective with well-timed cues throughout. There was good use of a glitter ball in `Beautiful Girl` and the various effects on the soundstage were well executed. More backlighting would have enhanced the title number greatly.

Vinny Osborne`s sound design and operation were first rate. All of the underscored dialogue of the opening sequence was perfectly set above the dynamic orchestra and the chorus level was excellent throughout. Nice work too in picking up tap dancing as required. Costumes were of a high standard with appropriate attention given to the period. The polka-dot dresses and flapper- style `Broadway Melody` costumes were suitably OTT and the arrival of everyone in raincoats for the finale was a great touch. This was a most entertaining production by Portlaoise Musical Society of a very ambitious and technical show. Blessed with some excellent principals, a fully-committed ensemble and a very experienced production team, this was a show in safe hands from the off which had everyone in high spirits from start to finish.

The basic premise of `The Producers`, that a theatre flop can be more lucrative than a hit, is one which would never wash with the musical society treasurers of this world who spend their lives frantically adding up bills, checking bookings and losing sleep. You`ve got to be pretty certain in these times of bums on seats. Taking on a show which gives a wide berth to political correctness and is as vulgar as it is manic, is a brave move. As I overheard a shell-shocked member of the clergy mutter that it wasn`t exactly his cup of tea, I couldn`t help but think that the absence of `Down With This Sort Of Thing` placards outside St. Joseph`s Hall in Boyle was an indication of how far we have come in this country that a show as close to the bone as this can be accepted for the irreverent, absurdist romp that it is and nothing more. Vivienne Caldbeck-Moran was the driving force behind this production in her capacity as director/choreographer. It was a solid piece of direction. Pace was fluid and staging was generally well- handled. There was great use made of a walkway surrounding the orchestra. Ms Caldbeck-Moran had a good comic eye and we were treated to some well-timed slapstick throughout. Some decisions left me puzzled though. Front of house personnel walked up the hall early in Act Two to strike two stools from the stage. It was an odd choice which I couldn`t see any reason for.
