Ms Caldbeck-Moran devised some really enjoyable routines which were perfectly suited to the dance abilities of the group. `I Wanna Be A Producer` was typically Broadway with broadly smiling showgirls strutting their stuff. Some of their `hat work` could have been a little sharper though. `Der Guten Tag Hop-Clop` was an absolute riot, brilliantly performed and the all-singing, all-dancing Nazifest, `Springtime for Hitler`, integrated some very precise choreography with excellent projections of marching stormtroopers and swastikas aplenty.

MD Anne Kielty conducted her eight fellow musicians from her piano and was well in control of the talented orchestra. She provided a great support for her cast who appeared extremely well-rehearsed and sounded excellent chorally. I have to admit to finding the band far too loud throughout the show. Some solo numbers suffered as a result and underscored dialogue was almost impossible to make out at times. Danny Doherty was a commanding presence as the larger-than-life, washed-up Broadway producer, Max Bialystock. It was a wonderfully physical performance which showcased Mr Doherty`s exceptional comic timing. He had a superb chemistry with Leo and his marvellously expressive face suited this kind of `no holds barred` physical comedy down to the ground. He had a fine singing voice and his `Betrayed` was a real tour de force from a most skilful performer.

Bialystock`s neurotic sidekick, Leo Bloom, was played by Jamie Dockery and boy did he have a ball playing this anxious, nebbish accountant. It was a really powerful physical characterisation which I can only describe as a touch of Robin Williams with a dash of George McFly! His chemistry with Mr Doherty was wonderful and their combined comedic talents created a typical old-time comic duo. What a singing voice he possessed too. It was powerful and expressive and almost seemed at odds with his mousey character. Mr Dockery did need to watch diction and projection at times as both occasionally got lost in his nervy characterisation.

Grainne Caldbeck played Scandinavian bombshell and token love/lust interest Ulla Inga Hanson Benson Yanson Tallen Hallen Svadon Swanson. She certainly had it...the talent...but I didn`t feel that she flaunted it as much as she might have to get the most from this outrageously oversexed ingénue. `When You`ve Got It, Flaunt It` was in need of an injection of sassiness and sultriness of movement to be in keeping with the OTT nature of the show. `That Face` was a beautiful duet with Leo and showed what a lovely voice Ms Caldbeck has.

Stephen Tighe`s cross-dressing director, Roger de Bris, was stereotypically outrageous and flamboyant. It was a very funny portrayal greatly enhanced by some of the stunningly vulgar `creations` which he wore.

Ronan Smith walked the walk and talked the talk as de Roger`s "common law assistant" Carmen Ghia. It was a hilarious performance full of flouncing, mincing and razor-sharp comic delivery. Mr Smith wore his leather trousers with style and was in his element as he threw himself into `Keep It Gay` with...well...gay abandon!

Ivan Moran provided one of the high points of the show as Franz, the demented Nazi playwright whose `Springtime For Hitler: A Gay Romp With Adolf and Eva at Berchtesgaden` is chosen by Bialystock and Bloom as their sure-fire flop. It was a superb comic turn full of energy and psychotic instability. His `Der Guten Tag Hop Clop` was a comic highlight of the show and I am still laughing at his rooftop pigeons cooing the German national anthem!

Eugene Beirne as Bialystock`s geriatric ladyfriend/investor did well and showed his comic abilities throughout. However, I really didn`t see the need for casting the role with a male performer. Yes, it got the laughs, but I would suggest that the laughs came for the wrong reason. Mr Beirne is obviously a strong performer and did what was required of him but I did feel that the very notion of an oversexed octogenarian woman is hilarious in itself without going to such lengths.

Stage manager Nigel Cleary kept things moving at a good pace and his crew was efficient and well-rehearsed.

Set design by Ms Caldbeck-Moran (is there anything she can`t do?!) was practical and allowed for good continuity and flow. I particularly liked the `Leo Bloom Presents` backdrop and Bialystock`s office was impressive if a little in need of more dressing. The glaring omission of the `s` on Max`s office door (MAX` OFFICE) was a mystery which bothered the hell out of a self-confessed `Spelling Nazi` like myself. I loved the Third Reich eagle which lit up on cue during `Springtime for Hitler`.

Props were generally well-chosen by Patricia Golden. It is important to remember though that if a prop is specifically referred to in the script then it must fit the description offered. The full title of Franz`s script was not on the front cover as per the dialogue. Franz`s pistol was quite clearly a toy gun complete with the red plastic tip on its barrel. This kind of detail is important.

Lighting was effective, if a little safe, throughout. Gels were well chosen and the LX on both the side flats and the Third Reich eagle were used to good effect. Cues needed to fade in and out over a couple of seconds rather than snapping on and off which was most unusual.

Sound was a mixed bag. Dialogue was clear and there were no missed cues. The band was overly amplified with the piano being too high in the mix in places. Stage/pit balance was poor during solos/ duets/trios but was better during choral numbers.

Doreen Caldbeck did a wonderful job with costumes. The girls looked great during `I Wanna Be A Producer` but Leo needed a top hat as per the lyrics. Roger`s entire wardrobe was suitably outrageous and the `Keep It Gay` number was appropriately costumed with every gay stereotype imaginable in attendance. The hilarious uniformity of the little old ladies was a visual treat.

Front of House personnel were super efficient, helpful and well-attired.

Boyle Musical Society made a brave decision in choosing `The Producers`. It is a monster of a show in every respect. In spite of a few technical shortcomings it was a hugely entertaining experience. To quote the show itself "It was crass and crude and I enjoyed every minute of it!"

I have countless fond memories of drama productions I was in whilst in college. Many were highly ambitious as we took on difficult works of Yeats, Pinter, Friel and Beckett. Looking back, we didn`t always get things right but the process of putting on such challenging pieces of theatre without a budget or a fear in the world was an incredible learning experience. I was brought back to those days as I watched UCD Musical Society`s production of `Sweeney Todd`. With the exception of a professional sound designer, every single person involved in this highly ambitious show was a current UCD student. All that said, there were some exceptional performances in this show that could have graced any stage in the country such was the calibre of some of the cast.

Director/choreographer Nicole Doyle had put her heart and soul into this show. The cast was disciplined and focused and she utilised an exceptionally simple set to good effect creating some strong images. Ms Doyle allowed her talented young cast to tell a complex story with a clarity of narrative which I have rarely seen in this show.

Colm Ferrari made his debut as MD and conductor of a nineteen-piece orchestra made up entirely of students. To be able to assemble an orchestra from the student body is most impressive. However, it was clear that not all players were able for the intricacies of Sondheim`s incredibly difficult score. It was a baptism of fire for Mr Ferrari and one I`m sure he will have gained invaluable experience from.

There was a most committed and focused ensemble at work here. Movement was strong and purposeful. I was so impressed with the maturity of the group and how at ease they were with the rhythmic complexities and challenging, multi-layered harmonies. They were an exceptional group chorally and full credit is due to vocal director Deirdre Hogan for eliciting such a wonderful sound from them. `The Ballad of Sweeney Todd` was powerful in its delivery and there was really good work from the quintet during `The Letter`.

Kevin Moran played the title role with intensity and detachment. He had a most pleasing baritone voice which, although lacking some bottom end, was both expressive and haunting. His youthful, clean-cut appearance needed to be addressed by the make-up department. It was a fine acting performance from Mr Moran, full of bloody vengeance but balanced with a sadness that elicited our sympathy throughout. A few more years of life experience will help Mr Moran explore the full gravitas of this deeply disturbed character in what I hope will be future incarnations of his demon barber.

Aisleen Murphy provided much-needed levity in this tale of rape, murder and cannibalism. She revelled in playing the role of the opportunistic pie-shop owner and displayed exceptional comic timing and a powerful singing voice in so doing. She was a marvellously intelligent actress as she balanced humour and deceit with ease in what was a deeply layered, nuanced performance. Her `A Little Priest` was a highlight vocally and dramatically. Shane McKenna as Anthony Hope possessed a most lyrical quality to his voice which soared into effortless falsetto in the beautiful `Johanna`.  Mr McKenna had a relaxed presence and was a capable actor. There was a sincerity to his performance which was most engaging. His `No Place Like London` introduced us to his fine vocal capabilities and `Kiss Me` with Johanna was beautifully sung.

Susannah Hughes-Jordan was most impressive as Johanna. She had the most hauntingly beautiful voice with a remarkable purity of tone and impeccable control. `Green Finch and Linnet Bird` was a real highlight as was her soaring, pitch- perfect soprano in `Kiss Me`. Her deeply disturbing asylum scene showed what a fine actress she was too.

Ciarán Murphy did well as Tobias Ragg. He has a fine singing voice and is full of energy however I did feel that he pushed things slightly at times and we lost the sincerity of the simple-minded, childlike character. His descent into madness was really well played but his hair was simply bizarre and was more reminiscent of recent Irish Eurovision entries than a nineteenth century street urchin.

Judge Turpin was played by Rory Crean with a most self-important air. Mr Crean`s diction was superb and he had a great resonance to his voice befitting of a man of such lofty legal standing. There were some issues with regard to timing and `Pretty Women` was taken at such a lick that Mr Ferrari and his orchestra struggled to keep up.

Shauna Carrick as the beggar woman needed to be careful not to lose words through over-characterisation. Diction was in need of attention at times as she became increasingly more frantic. She displayed a fine singing voice which was full of character and expression.

Diarmuid Sugrue was solid as the Beadle Bamford but needed to think about the more menacing edge of the character. His killing of the bird needed to be looked at with Ms Doyle. `Ladies in Their Sensitivities` was nicely sung with a fine rich tone to his voice.

Jonathan Dungan`s Pirelli was wildly comedic and boy did he have the voice to go with it! He had a wonderful upper register which appeared effortless as he strutted around the stage proclaiming his prowess as a barber. `The Contest` was perfectly sung and acted by Mr Dungan and the spontaneous applause upon his exit was well-deserved.

I have to admit that I struggled with the extremely stark set design to begin with. The series of raised platforms to suggest various locations was low-tech in the extreme. However, its simplicity grew on me and it worked in many ways even if it rarely evoked any real sense of nineteenth century London.

Lighting was simple but effective and brilliantly timed with the onstage action. There was a real sense of time having been spent working with the director and a lot of rehearsals having been sat at. I loved the effect of the red lighting underneath the platforms each time someone met a grisly end.

Sound design and operation were in the hands of Eoin O`Grady and he did an excellent job on this show. Some lovely unobtrusive sound effects were used and there was an exceptional balance in the choral pieces, particularly in `The Ballad of Sweeney Todd`.

Props were a mixed bag. Lovely authentic razors for Todd and Mrs Lovett`s implements looked the part. However, there were far more pies needed for `A Little Priest`. It was unfair to expect Ms Murphy to improvise with the paltry few she had. The pistol was not of the correct vintage.

Stage Manager Alex Owens kept things moving at a brisk pace and all was in order apart from a misplaced chaise which needed to be re-positioned just before `By The Sea`, thus causing a momentary delay.

Costumes were in need of more attention to detail. Footwear, in general, was too modern and white socks with black shoes were as much of a fashion faux pas for gentlemen in the 1800s as they are today! The short, white dress in the asylum scene jarred and Johanna`s final costume needed to be looked at so that Todd`s mistaken assumption that she was a man made sense.

Not every group can attempt to produce as ambitious a production as `Sweeney Todd`. It requires an exceptional cast and countless other resources in order to meet the demands of what is one of Sondheim`s most challenging shows. It wasn`t a production without its flaws but given the limited resources, the age profile and the relative inexperience of this group, the end product was far better than the sum of its parts. Musical It's beginning to look a lot like Christmas! It's my first visit to The Mill Theatre, Dundrum, South County Dublin. It opened in 2006 and is a wonderful new arts venue. The theatre is a beautiful 200 seated raked auditorium and is high spec with stage Unibars and fly tower facilities. There is also a studio space for showcase performances and a smaller space for rehearsals. The DLI (Drama League of Ireland) offices and library are also located in the building.

Could the department store Santa be the real thing? Kris Kringle takes on the cynics among us in this musical adaptation of the popular holiday favourite. A white-bearded gentleman claiming to be the real Santa Claus brings about a genuine miracle, spreading a wave of love throughout New York City, fostering camaraderie between Macy's and Gimbel's Department Stores and convincing a divorced, cynical single mother, her sombre daughter and the entire state of New York that Santa Claus is no myth. Filled with humour and spectacle, Miracle on 34th Street is a musical and joyful treat for families during the holiday season.

After the big brass band overture the curtain opened to reveal the West 70's in New York City, time present. We are in preparations for The Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade. 'Big Ca-lown Balloons' introducing us to the ensemble with energy and enthusiasm!

I am sure, if you have been following my reports, that I have an issue with Movies or Film being adapted as Stage Musicals. It causes major issues for cast, production teams and audiences. I believe that it is probably easier to convert Stage Musicals to Film, but hey, we will see when Les Miserables hits the big screen!

Glencullen Musical and Dramatic Society took 'Miracle on 34th Street' in their stride. They captured the magic that is Christmas and the audience had a wonderful family experience with this production.

Casting Liam Corrigan as Kris Kringle was a masterpiece. He was the perfect 'SANTA', kind, thoughtful and endearing! He looked every inch the part and had the audience captivated as the perfect kind hearted old man who believes he is Santa. This performer was inspiring and captured the iconic jolly and friendly characteristics of his character at all times. His singing was heartfelt and charming. He was perfectly believable! Leona McEvoy was a very imposing Doris Walker, Macy's Store event manager and mother of Susan. Leona gave us some wonderful tuneful, heartfelt singing. Her acting was confident and self assured. She captured the drive of this cynical and driven character. Shane Morgan gave us a wonderful assertive performance as Fred Gally, the smart, handsome, fun filled ex-military captain. We had some lovely warm singing and interpretation from this first rate performer. Rimear Nic Giolla Padraic gave a spirited performance with joyous singing and wonderful acting as the young Susan Walker. We had a compact performance from Christopher Bass. He was steadfast and imposing at all times as the aggressive and somewhat bungling junior executive Marvin Shellhammer. Eamon Murphy gave a solid and impressive performance as 'The Boss' Mr Macy, himself. George Ward was the perfect 'Judge'! He was hilarious with fantastic comic timing and delivery. This company had great fun in this festive production. They were suitable engaging and their singing was awe- inspiring. The delivered their varied roles with determination and we were engaged and entertained at all times. They captured the miracle!

We had a very fine production from Director Tom Ronayne. Ensemble work was good and characters were very well defined and confident. We needed to push the plot along with more pace and energy. There was a feeling that energy levels were below par as we travelled through the show. This show needs impact from the very start. Helen McCann gave us very suitable dance for the overall production. It was precise and well executed by the cast. Aoife Ryan did a great job with the set changes and stage management and props were appropriate. The Sound and Music Company did a first class job on sound. Well balanced with precise cueing and the set design was effective. Barry Donaldson did a good job on lighting design and Helen McCann did a great job on costumes.

Musical Director, Gerry Connolly, gave us a very confident full brass band musical experience from the wonderful orchestra. The score is very full and Gerry captured the iconic sounds needed for this type of show! The emphatic sounds achieved and the tender moments realised. The tempo's needed more energy, drive and delivery for some of the ensemble numbers. Pace was tentative at times and we needed to be more confident in our singing and delivery. This show needs heaps of energy and enthusiasm from the pit and the MD needs to drive the pace otherwise this show can come across as lackluster! I was delighted to visit this enthusiastic group and the night certainly put me in the Christmas spirit.

It is always a pleasure to visit Siama Tire,Tralee, a first class theatre, very well fitted-out with a magnificent expansive stage and wonderful fly towers! The facilities in this venue are fantastic and the Light Opera Society of Tralee (LOST) made every use of them. The stage area was framed with wonderful Victorian arched units and a wonderful cyc for this production of Jekyll and Hyde. The pre-set was a most atmospheric scene, bed set centre stage, with smoke seeping and a wonderful gas lamp, a vivid red cyc and we were drawn in! We knew we were in for a treat and we were not disappointed. This new society; under the aegis of the Kerry School of Music, are obviously very ambitious having presented 'The Mikado', 'West Side Story' and 'Footloose' in their very short two years existence.

This was a first class production with some beautiful picturesque staging from Director Aidan O'Carroll. The company worked very well and the principles were secure for the most part. At times it was like watching a work of art unfold. Visuals were superb! The set design for this production was excellent; Aidan O'Carroll, simple yet effective!  Each scene was well framed and the overall impact was full of imagination and creativity. Lighting was first class in design and execution by John Hurley.

Musical Director, Aidan O'Carroll captured the atmospheric nuances of this score at all times. He amassed a wonderful orchestra of fine musicians who engaged us with some superb playing. The Cellos and Violin playing was magnificent. We did feel that the orchestra was constrained at times with the slow tempos, but after a while this became a strong element to the overall experience as the score was given the opportunity to breath.

Garry Murphy was a very fine Henry Jekyll. His singing was excellent and he was a magnum opus in the demanding role. He captured our attention, particularly with magnificent performance in 'Lost in The Darkness', 'I Need to Know', 'This is The Moment' and a spellbinding 'Transformation'. Here, we had a most competent actor who was engaging and forceful. Aki O'Rourke did a good job as John Utterson. He was commanding and sincere. We would have liked a little more confidence from this young actor. Tim Landers was very solid in the mature role of Sr Carew. He was compelling and imposing at all times capturing the concerned father figure character.  James Brennan gave a steadfast performance as the secretary of the board, Simon Stride. We had a firm performance from Karen Soffe in this role of Lady Beaconsfield. Karen was a fine performer with appropriate enduring caricature, imposing and confident. Chris Armstrong gave a good performance as the Bishop of Beaconstoke. Danny Rigg was fine as Lord Savage. We had a solid performance from Shane Hannon as General Lord Gossop while Shane Curtin gave a good performance as Sr Archibald Poops. Aisling O'Carroll was a beautiful Emma Carew with a glorious soprano voice. Aisling was also a very fine actress and Jackie O'Mahoney captured all that is Lucy Harris. Magnificent singing from this most competent actress! 'No One knows Who I am', 'Sympathy, Tenderness' and 'Someone Like You' beautifully measured and delivered. Grainne O'Carroll was a very strong Nellie. Niall Fitzgerald was a much energized performer. He was focused and compelling at all times as Spider. Kerry Fleming was a good manservant, Poole while Tom Baily was believable as Bissett. This company worked hard to recreate the rich and poor of nineteenth century London. Their singing was very compelling as they were secure with harmonies. Jekyll and Hyde would not be considered a dance show, but Aisling O'Carroll and Tara Dore gave us some wonderful dance sequences, full of imagination and creativity. The dance sequence for 'I Feel You' was beautiful. Stage Management under the attentive and crafted watch of Des Hurley was very well executed. The trucks worked very well and the scene changes were seamless. Props were time appropriate. Shane Murphy did a very fine with sound balance and cueing. Ellen O'Carroll and Kay Fernane did a good job on costumes. They were appropriate for the time. We would have liked more coats and hats for exterior scenes. Miriam Owens did a fine job on hair and makeup. Thank you to Light Opera Society of Tralee for a wonderful experience. Continued success!

society_raw: North East Musical and Dramatic Society
review_text:
The end of World War II brought thousands of young servicemen back to America to pick up their lives and start new families in new homes with new jobs. With an energy never before experienced, American industry expanded to meet peacetime needs. Americans began buying goods not available during the war, which created corporate expansion and jobs. Growth everywhere. The baby boom was underway as was the introduction of a new type of music; 'Rock and Roll'. Developed from a blend of Southern blues and gospel music with an added strong back beat, this type of music was popular with teenagers who were trying to break out of the mainstream, conservative, American middle class mold As we enter the Temperance Hall in Loughrea, Co Galway we are brought right back to the mid 1950's. James Dean, Marlon Brando, Elvis Presley, Grace Kelly and Marilyn Monroe are brought to mind. This old hall has been transformed into a 1950's festival experience with posters, guitars and even 'bumpers' as we step in the front door. There is a fantastic sense of something about to happen, a great expectation!

"All Shook Up", is a new jukebox musical comedy written by Joe DiPietro that was inspired by and features the songs of Elvis Presley and loosely based on Shakespeare's comedy Twelfth Night. "All Shook Up" tells the romantic tale of how a young girl's dream comes true when a guitar-playin' roustabout rides into a square state in 1955 on his motorcycle and turns the town upside down with is hip-swivelin', lip-curlin' and sexy song singin'. The show features 24 Elvis classic hit songs including "Heartbreak Hotel", "Jailhouse Rock", "Blue Suede Shoes", "It's Now or Never" and "Don't Be Cruel". The mayor of the town, Matilda Hyde, has banned necking and having fun because it's a sin. When sexy Chad rides into town, he brings the town back to life. He pursues the town's sexpot, Miss Sandra who can't stand him while sweet grease monkey, Natalie pines for him. Nerdy Dennis is secretly in love with Natalie while her father lusts after Miss Sandra, Sylvia is secretly in love Natalie's father. Sylvia's daughter, Lorraine falls in love with the Mayor's son, Dean while the hen pecked sheriff, Earl is secretly in love with the Mayor. The songs of Elvis are woven into the story line about love finding rock and roll. It's a rollercoaster from start to finish! This is just what we got from St. Brendan's Choral and Dramatic Society, a fun filled, snappy, fabulous fifties experience. We had some wonderful direction from accomplished directors Brian and Sean Power. The scenes flowed with energy and pace as every comic moment was chased and realised. The stage pictures were superb and the cast were appropriately used at every opportunity. There was obviously some great work done with principles as they were all secure in their roles. Some of the dialogue was placed too far upstage and we did need to remind some principles to find their light at times but overall we had some lovely set pieces from Brian and Sean. There were many highlights in this production including 'Hound Dog/Teddy Bear', 'That's all Right', 'Blue Suede Shoes', Wise Men Say' and particularly 'Falling In Love'. Elaine and Ally O'Hanlon did a wonderful job on the choreography. It was cast and period appropriate, full of energy and excitement. It was very well rehearsed and precise. The cast enjoyed dancing to this fantastic music and the dancing was never too difficult or indulgent. It was what it was! Fun! Group pictures were gorgeous and variation within each dance routine was perfectly accomplished.

The orchestra under the expert guidance of Shane Farell gave us some supreme playing from the pit. Shane drove the 1950's music with passion and energy at all times. The twelve piece orchestra, with keyboards, reeds, trumpets, trombone, guitars, bass and drums were very much part of the overall experience. They supported the 'Rock and Roll' dynamic that enthused from the stage. Singing was secure and vibrant at all times from soloists and ensemble, engaging the audience for what was a wonderful juke- box musical pleasure. This show has over twenty five magnificent Elvis greats and we were captivated from the outset. This MD was in control at all times with precise entrances and crisp clean finishing beats. Guitar playing was magnificent at times and there was a wonderful connection with the ensemble and soloists. Harmonies were very secure. Tempos were excellent. Well done Shane!

Mickey Walsh was a fantastic dynamic and sexy Chad. He had all the attitude of James Dean, the hip swiveling moves of Elvis and the innate appeal of Marlon Brando. Mickey was a likeable rogue! His singing was a tour de force and his comedy timing and panache abounded from the stage at every opportunity from his 'Roustabout' to 'I Don't Want To'. Amy Byrne brought a sincere likeable appeal to the character of Natalie/Ed. Her dialogue was well paced and believable, as she dreamed of falling in love with that special guy. Amy's singing was nicely measured particularly in 'Love me Tender' and 'One Night With You', powerful yet musical. We really enjoyed her rendition of 'Fools Fall in Love'!  Congratulations to this young actress on a first class performance as she embraced the role, showing her versatility as she put on the pants as Ed.

Christopher McDonald was a hilarious Dennis. He was ridiculous yet sincere. He balanced the humor with the naivety of this character in a loveable way. Christopher was an accomplished comedian with wonderful comic timing, great physical expression, as we the audience felt sorry for him but at the same time laughed our heads off. His singing was great too particularly for 'It Hurts Me'! What a performer! What a fantastic performance from Louise Colohan as Miss Sandra, the beautiful curator of the town's museum. Her performance of 'Let Yourself Go' was magnificent. Louise was imposing, blatantly overt and delicious!

John Kelly brought a lot to the role of Jim, the recently widowed father of Natalie. He was compassionate and poignant. Madeleine Fleming was great as Honky- tonk bar owner Sylvia. Fine acting and a wonderful rendition of 'There's Always Me', sung with tenderness. A powerful performer! Conor Hanley performed the role of Dean Hyde admirably. As the young browbeaten son of Matilda, this role was delivered with a very sentimental and youthful suffering. Emer Dolan was very secure as Lorraine, Sylvia's daughter with great energy in 'That's all Right'.

We had a stand out performance from Joanne Kelly as the ever present Mayor of this small town. Joanne was expressive and commanding in the role with a wonderful performance of 'Devil in Disguise'. Michael Holohan was the perfect conservative Sheriff and a great foil for Matilda. Henrietta: Peggy Marmion, Bus Driver: Dannie Cunane, Prison Warden: Padraig Larkin and Jailhouse Rick: Johnathan Hopper were all very good in their supporting roles.

The ensemble chorus was to be celebrated in this production. They never faltered and were committed to each and every scene with wonderful singing and performance. We had a great mixed age profile and yet each and every member was focused and engaging. This ensemble certainly enjoyed their time on stage and we in the audience had a great evening's entertainment in their company. Well done everyone! Justin Lynch's; Stage Manager's, backstage crew and area was obviously well rehearsed and busy for this show. There were some lovely set pieces and set changes were for the most part efficient and seamless. We could probably have removed the motorbike a little earlier during the overture. Overall the stage management was very well accomplished and the set up for the bar scene was very impressive.  Props and larger set pieces were excellent with a fantastic Motorbike, Greyhound Bus and Petrol Pump. The sound management was first class from Derval Sound. Cueing was excellent and balance was very well accomplished. Sound effects were appropriate. The lighting was dynamic and full of colour. States were very well established and cues well executed by Pascal Gough assisted by Danny Cronin. We could have used a spotlight for Chad in 'Jailhouse Rock'. Some principles needed guidance to find their light for some musical numbers! Caroline Kelly did a first class job on costume. The array of costumes was excellent. The costumes for Miss Sandra were fantastic. Very clever moment revealing the shorter skirts and hair and makeup was period appropriate.

There was a fantastic overall aesthetic to the stage design for this production, with wonderful full use of the stage area. We loved the large guitars, the guitar frets and the moving trucks as they depicted rural America. This set design was imaginative and inventive, yet suitably appropriate for this fun show. Great adaptation for the fairground/rollercoaster scene into Act two. Great work, let's see more of this! I really enjoyed my visit to Loughrea. I was very well looked after by PRO, the charming Mark Burke. It was lovely to join the cast afterward for a quiet drink in the theatre bar. Thanks for the Sambos, much appreciated!

I headed to New Ross with excited anticipation for 'The Producers'. This has to be one of my most favorite comedy shows. My memory of seeing the Drury Lane production in London was a night of side splitting laughter. Therefore, I was very interested to see how St Michael's Musical Society would handle not just the unconcealed comedy but the very many scene changes and costume issues. The Producers also demands very strong casting with diverse caricature roles and demanding ensemble work. I am glad to report that I was not disappointed. St Michael's Theatre MS gave us a highly charged and hilarious nights entertainment.

This production, in the very capable hands of Director Kevin Kennedy and Assistant Director Lorainne Cooper, brought to life the spirit and humor of Mel Brooks musical at every opportunity. It was broad and overtly driven into the extreme ridiculousness of over emphasised caricature and show business in-jokes. Comedy timing from the cast was perfectly realised with some of the great moments captured and delivered with confidence. Something you don't always get in broad comedy. We were entertained, enthralled and shocked as the cast brought us into this ridiculous world of Max Bialystock. Choreographer Claire Buckey brought us brusque and precise dancing from the 'Opening Night' sequence with the Usherettes right through to the finale. It was steady, well executed and full of fun! Great tapping in 'I Wanta Be a Producer', precise and well rehearsed Zimmer framed 'Along Came Bialy' and gorgeous ladies in 'Springtime for Hitler'. All fantastic! Lizzy Heffernan did a first class job as Stage Manager. The stage crew worked hard on the seamless set changes for what is a very busy show, and this was achieved for the most part. We did have issues with the flying gauze on the night as the apparatus needed to be better timed. But, overall a great job! Set design by Terry Brennan was excellent. The scenic states were appropriate and fulfilling. The props for this production were well executed by Philip Erskine with fantastic accounting machines! Lighting under the attentive eye of Paul Malone was seamless. The geling was exciting and colorful. There were no issues with shadows and cueing was precise and integrated with the music. Getting lighting cues to the point of matching the musical beats within a show is a great achievement and Paul achieved this! Joe Murphy did a first class job on sound management. The balance was superb and the singing never missing a lyric. This was no mean feat considering the large and explosive nature of the orchestra. We heard every punch line in dialogue too!

Kevin Kennedy; Musical Director, is to be commended and highly praised for bringing together such a wonderful company orchestra. His attention to detail was evident with fantastic control of the eleven piece orchestra including Strings, Reed, Trumpet, Trombone, Synth keys, Bass, Percussion, and piano at all times. This orchestra was on the mark with spirited and manifest playing. The score of The Producers needs control yet a free spirit and this group of musicians was given the space to embellish but never taking from the overall collaborative experience. Tempe were precise and timbre full and rounded. The singing from the chorus was confident, well rehearsed and harmonies protected.

This company had all the essentials necessary to carry off this massive production with style and self-belief. Their singing was excellent with harmonies, diction and accents never faltering. They were secure and excelled in the many supporting and doubling roles. We were entertained and appreciative of their commitment to the comedy as they embraced the challenge. The dancing was first class and 'Opening Night' exciting, 'I Wanna Be a Producer' marvelous, Keep It Gay' excellent, 'Along Came Bialy' riveting and 'Springtime for Hitler' magnificent. Well done to all the little old ladies of New York too!

Paul Walsh was the ever present Max Bialystock with great fastidious character singing at every level from 'The King of Broadway' to 'Betrayed'. His comedy timing was superb and his interaction wholehearted throughout his performance. Dylan Walsh was the near perfect Leo Bloom. A wonderful performer with sensitivity and ruggedness when needed! His singing was magnificent capturing the innocent and the more romantic adventures with candor and aplomb. His comedy timing and attention to detail was a joy to watch. Lorraine Kennedy Cooper was a believable as Hold-Me-Touch-Me with some great comedy moments. Martin Conway was a very imposing Mr Marks, the arrogant boss. He was suitably demonstrative and overbearing. Keith Flanagan was the essence of comedy having us rolling in the isles' with his idiosyncratic style at every opportunity as the Ex-Nazi Franz Liebkind. He was masterful, hilarious and ever present, particularly during 'Der Guten Tag Hop-Clop'. James Dobbs was perfectly capricious and excellently gay in the role of common law assistant Carmen Ghia. What a wonderful unswerving performance from this comedy actor who never dropped the orb for one moment. A triumph! Kevin Reade gave an outstanding performance in the role of the flamboyant homosexual director Roger De Bris. His performance was measured and unfailing. This actor knows how to incarcerate the audience with first class comedy singing and excellent comedy timing. He was a tour-de-force! Bryan; Paddy Butler, Kevin; Rory Cooper, Scott; Sean O'Brien and Shirley; Jan Kennedy made for a wonderful variety of a production team. Their 'Keep it Gay' was a highlight. What a wonderful Ulla Inga Hansen Benson Yansen Tallen Hallen Svaden Swanson in Ashley Doran. She looked wonderful and her acting, singing and dancing was first rate. Ashley was sexy, funny and her delivery of 'When You've Got it Flaunt It' was magnificent, finishing with a fully extended splits!

Lick-Me-Bite-Me; Claire Buckley, Kiss- Me-Feel-Me; Jane Kent were suitably little old lady like. Hilarious! Jack; Paddy Butler, Donald; Philip Erskine and Jason; Rory Cooper were all fine cameo actors. Well done! Ticket Taker; Willie Walsh, Storm Trooper; Andrew Smith, Storm trooper Rolf; Paddy Butler, Storm Trooper Mel; Sean O'Brien. Stalin; Philip Erskine, and Churchil; Rory Cooper all did very well for their moment in the spotlight! Seargant O'Brien; Terry Brennan, Seargent O'Rourke; Philip Erskine and Seargent O'Reilly; Sean O'Brien were suitably Irish and Judge; John Dwyer was perfectly cast as the mature Judge while Forman/Prison Guard; Brian Geoghan was very imposing. The costume plot for this show was well delivered by Una Hayden and Jane Kent. The ensemble costumes were first class, particularly the Braviarian costumes and the elaborate head dressing for 'Springtime for Hitler'. The hair and makeup was well attended to by Treasa Dollard and Kitty Warren respectively. We had beautiful hair pieces, wigs for the usherettes and styles were time appropriate.

St Michael's Theatre Musical Society gave us a wonderful night's entertainment. We enjoyed every minute and of this slide splitting musical extravaganza!  Many thanks to Lizzy Heffernan for looking after me and it was lovely to meet everybody afterwards for a quite pint!

Framed against the sombre backdrop of the Spanish Inquisition, `Man of La Mancha` is not a show which is universally popular. Its lofty premise, complex `play within a play` structure and myriad layers challenge its audience on so many levels. Carnew Musical Society`s production, directed by Michael Dunbar, certainly challenged its audience. Mr Dunbar gave us a visually stunning show with some exceptional ensemble work and some beautifully realised pictures. Care did need to be taken at times not to assume that the audience was familiar with the premise. It is a very difficult narrative to negotiate and, as such, clarity is of utmost importance. An MD who builds sets and works on props too?! Lar Duffy is such a man. His ten piece orchestra hit us with a superb overture featuring some excellent playing on piccolo and trumpet and some wonderfully atmospheric timpani. However, the poorly amplified acoustic guitar cut through very harshly and I missed a more appropriate Spanish guitar sound which would have been much softer and warmer. Choral singing was very strong, especially the lovely, sweet harmonies of `Little Bird, Little Bird` and the finale of `The Impossible Dream`. Julie Kinsella handled the limited choreography very well with the Moorish dancers relishing their moment to shine in a routine which was appropriately energetic and precise.

There was excellent work from a fine ensemble which made the transition from observers to participants appear seamless as they moved fluidly from the `reality` of the dungeon to the imaginative world of Don Quixote`s tale. They did so well in the opening scene assuming roles of various unsavoury, predatory characters intent on relieving Cervantes of his belongings. The decision to allow the ensemble to `escape` the confines of their claustrophobic cell as they repeatedly left the stage for no apparent reason may well have been ill-judged. If the audience is to believe that the prisoners are incarcerated in this dungeon and that they are the observers of the tale played out by Cervantes, it is important to be consistent in this regard.

Brendan Fitzpatrick gave a strong portrayal as Cervantes/Don Quixote. He was smooth and assured as Cervantes and grandiose as the daft but noble Quixote. His senility was well-pitched and he was excellent in his deathbed scene which was so emotional. He displayed a nice baritone voice which was at its best in the show`s signature number `The Impossible Dream`.

Therese Canavan-Bolger played Aldonza with a fiery ferocity which was most engaging. "I`ll crush you like an egg!" she bellowed...and we believed her! It was a most compelling performance from Ms Canavan-Bolger who was coarse and raw but capable of tender moments when required. Her `Aldonza` was a definite highlight of the show. It was beautifully expressive and showcased her fine singing voice.

We had some welcome levity in the guise of the very talented Brian O`Gorman who played the endearing sidekick, Sancho Panza, with a comic flair. Crucially, given the style of the piece, Mr O`Gorman never pushed things too far. He had a great chemistry with Mr Fitzpatrick and sang superbly in `I Really Like Him`.

Jimmy Spellacy handled the dual role of Governor/Innkeeper very well. As the Governor he was a thoughtful actor with an authoritative air. His Innkeeper was a kind soul and he displayed some fine comic timing during `The Dubbing` of Quixote.

Catherine Stafford was an excellent member of the ensemble and a most generous performer. As Antonia, she sang well but needed to watch her timing in `I`m Only Thinking of Him`.

I was very impressed with John Young who played the Duke and Quixote`s nemesis, the pompous Dr. Carasco. Mr Young had a wonderfully resonant speaking voice and superb diction. He had a most commanding presence and gave a very well thought out portrayal. Joan Duignan`s beautiful soprano was a highlight in `I`m Only Thinking of Him`. She was well cast as the Housekeeper and added greatly to the ensemble. Mandie O`Keeffe was another thoughtful performer as Innkeeper`s Wife/Maria with great mannerisms and Paul Doran was a most imposing Captain of the Inquisition. John Duignan`s `Barber`s Song` was most impressive and he showed some good timing in his altercation with Quixote over the `Golden Helmet`. A very hirstute David Cox was a ruthless Pedro who was at his vicious best in his scenes with Aldonza and Seán Hallahan sang a wonderfully haunting `Psalm` as the show neared its conclusion.

Tony Barry designed a stunning dungeon set, complete with drawbridge, which had an incredible attention to detail. It was an amazingly realistic dark, communal cell. The perfect backdrop for Cervantes` tale. Stage manager Tommy Kavanagh had a relatively quiet time. The operation of the formidable `drawbridge` door was faultless. Cast were responsible for all changes on stage bar one where a crew member assisted in moving one piece. This seemed at odds with the rest of the show and the arrival of the black-clad individual on stage was rather incongruous when cast could feasibly have managed the change.

Society stalwart Kevin McEvoy was responsible for the top notch lighting design. Lighting is such a key element when trying to suggest the changes of location and mood which the `play within a play` format requires. There was excellent use of LEDs throughout, some fine gobos and, even though the strobe effect for the `Enchanter` was a little harsh, the overall lighting plot was simply superb.

Not for the first time on my travels, sound was a problem. The stage/pit balance was not always favourable and the guitar sound was obtrusive. Ironically, the onstage guitar at the top of the beautiful `Little Bird, Little Bird` did have a lovely warm sound. I found dialogue most difficult to hear at times and I was thankful that I was familiar with the script. Raymond Brennan, who worked independently of the sound designer, did an excellent job with his well-chosen sound effects.

Costumes from NoMac were suitably earthy for the prisoners and there was good attention to detail for the `play within a play`. Some of the sequined costumes for the Moorish dancers, although they looked very colourful, seemed a little too modern in appearance. A small point in what was an excellent costume plot. Hair and make-up were excellent and I particularly liked the authentic scars and occasional open wound sported by many of the cast. Props were of a very high standard. From Quixote`s lance to the chains and ropes which dressed the set, there was a lot of attention lavished on the finer details here.

There was a most efficient and friendly front of house team at work under the watchful eye of Debbie Furlong.

`Man of La Mancha` is a big ask of any society. There are so many vital elements which need to be right if the piece is to be accessible to those who are not familiar with its complexities. In spite of one or two shortcomings which affected the clarity of the narrative, many of those elements were in evidence and appreciated by Carnew Musical Society`s very enthusiastic audience.

It was a brave choice of show and one I`m sure all involved will remember for some time.

"Everyone of you hates everyone of us and we hate you right back." The stark, angry reality of the rivalries of West Side Story`s gang culture is nailed in one sentence by the Sharks` leader Bernardo. It is a timeless tale of racial tensions and violence juxtaposed with a forbidden, passionate and doomed romance which is as relevant today as when first conceived 37<2/

Director Des Henn gave us a stunningly vibrant and fast-moving production of this classic musical based on Shakespeare`s tale of star-crossed lovers. It was a triumph from start to finish, full of life and raw emotion. Mr Henn created some beautifully staged pictures and there was a great attention to detail in the narrative. He maintained a palpable tension throughout the show through attention to delivery of dialogue and a gritty realism. Anita`s `taunting` scene was a deeply disturbing moment which was typical of Mr Henn`s eye for visceral, dramatic tension.

Noel Lennon conducted a fine twelve- piece orchestra, most of whom did very well with Bernstein`s hugely challenging score. There was excellent work on percussion and exquisite violin playing throughout. Mr Lennon was a most skilled and enthusiastic conductor. From the syncopated rhythms of `Something`s Coming` to the polyphonic `Tonight Ensemble` he was very much in control of his charges. Ensemble singing was excellent throughout. There was a big issue with underscored dialogue which was very difficult to hear at times.

It is difficult to do justice to the standard of Barbara Meany`s choreography in this show. It was colourful, athletic and exhilarating with more than a nod to the iconic style of Jerome Robbins. To have assembled so many young men who could dance in such a graceful, yet masculine and vigorous manner was some feat. Each and every number was outstanding in its own way. From the hormonal abandon of the `Dance at the Gym`, to the slightly incongruous but beautifully balletic dream sequence, to the hilariously slapstick yet angst-ridden `Gee Officer Krupke` these were inspired and excellently performed routines. However, it was the superb precision and powerful intensity of `Cool` which stole the show for me. Simply wonderful.

West Side Story is very much an ensemble show and what an ensemble this was. Apart from the undoubted dancing abilities of the group there was a fantastic choral sound also. The `Tonight Ensemble` was stunning in this regard with the multi- layered melodies building to a wonderfully climactic finish. There was an incredible focus and energy from the ensemble with every individual totally committed to this production. The Jets and Sharks were most credible and cohesive units. Jared Nadin as Action was bursting with pent up anger in a very strong characterisation. Jamie Sheehan as Baby John and David Billy Tidswell as A-Rab also impressed as did the excellent Darren Nash as Diesel. The statuesque Pamela McGlynn looked every inch the gang leader`s girl and her dancing was a joy. Wannabe gang member Anybodys was played by Morna Canty and she was full of tomboyish bluster and bravado as she tried to impress the guys. Nigel Dugdale was very well cast as Tony who, unlike many who play this role, was a very credible former gang leader. He had a great presence and command of dialogue and he sang with a most lyrical tenor voice which shone in the testing `Something`s Coming` and in his stunning duets with Maria. He was a strong actor but I felt he needed to lose himself more in the emotion of the role at times. Having learned of Maria`s `death` from Doc I felt he needed to push the anguish more as his reaction was eclipsed somewhat by the gritty realism and emotion of Anita`s harrowing taunting scene just before. Jean Wallace was a wonderful Maria with one of the most magnificent soprano voices imaginable. It was so beautifully crystal-clear, full of expression with a superb tone. Ms Wallace`s range was simply stunning as she soared to the final top note of `Tonight`. She was a fine actress also, displaying vulnerability, innocence, defiance and anger as required.

Bernardo was played with a very strong presence by Derek McMahon. He was most believable as gang leader, and he was an excellent physical actor as he carried himself with authority and dignity throughout.

I felt, at times, that Orla Walsh`s Anita needed to own the stage a bit more in the early stages of the show. More pace, physicality and swagger would have turned a very good performance into a great performance. She was a strong singer, particularly in `A Boy Like That` which she sang with Ms Wallace. She really let go in the taunting scene and it was then that we saw the excellent potential she has as an actress. It was disturbing, gut-wrenching and heartbreaking.

What a Mercutio Michael O`Dwyer was. His Riff had excellent presence, great command of dialogue and a natural sense of pace. The audience was drawn to his every move and word and it was this magnetism which made him the perfect gang leader. `Cool` was out of the park in every respect and showed Mr O`Dwyer`s strong singing voice at its best.

Garry Murphy was well cast as Chino and was most impressive in telling Maria of Tony`s alleged demise.

The voice of reason was provided by Rob O`Leary`s Doc. He was very sympathetic and yet was convincing in his more emotional scenes also.

Brian Henry was a humorous Gladhand and Paul Donnellan impressed as Krupke. Glen Carr`s Shrank was more aggressive than authoritative. The ability was there but more light and shade was required. Des Henn`s impressively designed set was excellently managed by Ray Burke and his very efficient stage crew. Cast did need to be conscious of the cyclorama billowing as they ran behind though.

Olivia Parkinson and Carol Murphy were responsible for props and they did a fine job with nothing standing out as inappropriate in any way. The bridal-shop dummies were impressive, as were the authentic looking knives for the rumble. There was magnificent lighting from Mike Finneran and Ger O`Gorman with excellent use of gobos, moving lights and haze. Some superb pictures were created using specials and some very atmospheric cross-lighting. The soft focus follow spot was most effective during `Tonight`.

I had a major gripe with one aspect of the sound design. Whilst dialogue and singing were perfectly amplified for the most part, with no missed cues noted, underscored dialogue was often marred by an over amplification of the orchestra which was most obtrusive. Underscoring should complement and bring mood to dialogue. It should never compete with or overpower it.

Costumes, overseen by Jacinta Florish, were excellent. I loved the co-ordinated look of the Sharks at the dance in the gym and the entire ensemble in white for the dream sequence was stunning.

This was a triumph of a production for the Cecilian Musical Society. Yes, the sound issue was frustrating, but only because everything else was so incredibly good. It was a fittingly, fantastic start to what I hope will be a long and happy tenure at the magnificent new Lime Tree Theatre.

The ethos of the Sligo Fun Company over the past thirty years has been to allow young people from all backgrounds to experience the world of theatre with an emphasis on fun, personal development, self-esteem and mutual respect. And boy is it working! One couldn`t but be moved by the huge number of talented youngsters which took to the Hawk`s Well stage singing `Food Glorious Food` as if their very lives depended on it.

Mary McDonagh, assisted by Steffen Jorgensen, directed and choreographed this fast-paced show. She elicited some excellent performances from the children who were so well-drilled and assured. There was a nicely-struck balance between the dark and nasty elements of Dickens`s original story and the comical levity provided by some of the more colourful characters. Choreography was original, appropriate and well executed. `Consider Yourself` was a fine ensemble number with a wonderful group of featured dancers excelling as they came to the fore. All of the numbers in Fagin`s den were very well performed by the thirty boys who were clearly enjoying every minute.

MD Niamh Crowley conducted a scaled down five piece combo from her piano and, whilst I missed some of Lionel Bart`s rich orchestrations, this was a very tight and accomplished group of musicians. The three delicious violin cadenzas in `Reviewing the Situation` were expertly played and beautifully enhanced in turn by the sound engineer. Choral singing was of a high standard and a huge amount of work had obviously gone in to the children`s singing and diction.

The adult ensemble was very strong and focused. They sang well in `Consider Yourself`, although they could have done with more support from the sound department, and there was a palpable energy from behind the curtain as they geared up for a rousing rendition of `Oom- Pah-Pah` at the top of Act Two. Those who remained on stage for Bill`s `My Name` greatly enhanced the dramatic action. The tightly-drilled workhouse children excelled in `Food Glorious Food` with superb diction and a fine upper range. Fagin`s gang was equally impressive with great singing, movement and some superbly improvised background business which never pulled focus. Some needed to be careful though, as Fagin examined his treasures, not to forget that they were meant to be asleep and that any movement might distract the audience.

Mark Kilcawley gave a heart-warming performance in the title role. It was a portrayal full of wide-eyed wonder and optimism which Mark skilfully balanced with fear and despair. He had a most expressive face and his `Where is Love?` showcased his fine singing voice and the emotional depth to his playing.

Micheál Kearney was a Dodger with no rough edges and he was an excellent singer and dancer. `Consider Yourself` was so well sung and he had great fun with Nancy in `I`d Do Anything`. Both Micheál and Mark had a great onstage rapport which added so much to the show.

Mr Bumble was played with fine comic expression by Damien Brennan who, in spite of no attempt at an English accent, was consistent in his characterisation. `Boy For Sale` was very well sung, showing his impressive range and full tone. His sidekick, Widow Corney, was delightfully played by a deliciously funny Angela McGuire in what was one of the standout performances of the show. Ms McGuire`s comic timing was impeccable and she really knew how to deliver a song. `I Shall Scream` was hilarious as she hit her final shrill note whilst forcing Bumble to inspect her bosom area at close quarters.

Robert Fitzpatrick made the manipulative, criminal Fagin a most engaging and likeable individual whilst still maintaining the necessary dark edge which underpins this iconic character. He was a clever actor with superb comic timing and a `knowingness` which permeated his performance. `Reviewing the Situation` was very cleverly performed as he pondered the grim opportunities left open to him.

I was very impressed by the all-round strength of Maggie Villarini in the role of Nancy. It was a superb acting and singing performance with lots of layers, a rough edge and a considerable emotional range. `As Long As He Needs Me` was sung with a most melodic tone and a wonderful passion. Ms Villarini was a most generous performer on stage and was superb when it came to including and involving younger cast members. She also had a wonderful connection with her sidekick Bet, so pleasantly played by Amy Gilligan.

Gerry Ryan had a most menacing presence as Fagin`s murderous protégé Bill Sykes. His looming presence at the end of `Oom- Pah-Pah` set the tone for what was a particularly vicious portrayal. `My Name` was well delivered with a combination of intimidation and seething rage.

Franny Curley did well as the undertaker Mr Sowerberry, showing plenty of comic potential. His onstage partner- in-crime, Maureen Howley, turned in a top-notch performance as the cold and avaricious Mrs Sowerberry in what was a marvellously funny characterisation. Ms Howley was delightfully Dickensian in what is essentially a caricature role. Her mannerisms and consistency of physicality were indicative of a well-studied character. Killian Filan was an excellent Noah Claypole who combined very well with Evanne Kilgallon`s abrasive Charlotte. Cormac Gilligan was a strong presence as Charlie Bates and Siobhán Terry did very well as Old Sally in what can often be a throwaway role.

Michael Kilcoyne`s Mr Brownlow had a most pleasant and warm demeanour, however the absence of an English accent did detract somewhat from what was a solid performance otherwise.

Marcel Gordon favoured the comic elements of Dr Grimwig`s character and Orla McSharry performed well as the kind- hearted Mrs Bedwin although her `Where is Love?` was in need of some fine-tuning. John O`Donoghue`s impressive, multi-level set design, although not built specifically for the venue, worked well. I did feel though that a backdrop of some sort was required to give a more definite change for the London street scenes. Stage manager Frances Ryan ensured that a very well-drilled cast handled the difficult scene changes with utmost efficiency and precision.

Michele Feeney`s lighting design was in need of some tweaking but I have no doubt it tightened up as the week went on. Cues were tentative at times and things weren`t helped by the placing of some items of furniture slightly off their spots. Sound, by Vinnie Higgins, was generally very good, although cueing for the soloists (not credited in programme) in `Who Will Buy?` was not what it should have been. Ensemble vocals were not always picked up by the hanging mics and this was most noticeable during `Consider Yourself`. Wig designer Ali Murphy did sterling work, with Ms McGuire`s ringlets and Mr Fitzpatrick`s flowing locks being two particular highlights.

Ms McGuire is also credited with overseeing the wardrobe department. From the threadbare workhouse inmates to Nancy`s signature red dress, this was a fine costume plot. However, it needed to be kept in mind that men would always have worn hats outdoors. Overcoats were a notable absence from the final scene which takes place at night.

Props were well-chosen by Mary Phillips with some great attention to detail. The workhouse children were quite clearly being served fresh air though and Nancy poured more of the same at the top of `It`s a Fine Life`. Small details like this do stand out.

`Oliver!` is a most entertaining and, in spite of three people dying in the latter stages, uplifting show. The Sligo Fun Company pulled out all the stops in presenting a thoroughly enjoyable production which showcased some fine young talent and left its appreciative audience wanting even "More!".

The Claremorris Musical Society production of 'The Sound of Music' opened as the Nuns, holding candles, made their way through the audience in procession singing 'Alleluia'. They arrived on to the stage and took up their positions as the curtain open to reveal the Abbey. The Sound of Music is imbedded into our popular culture with many iconic moments and beautiful songs brought together in the award winning movie starring Julie Andrews and Christopher Plummer.  This society embraced the musical warmly and with enthusiasm.

Vivienne Lee gave us a very confident Maria capturing the feisty nature and the fun of the character throughout her demanding performance. Her singing was excellent and her acting was defined and engaging. Vivienne had a lovely natural bond with the children and built a very endearing relationship with Mother Abbess. Her interaction with Captain Von Trapp was contained and believable. Grainne Conroy was a near-perfect Mother Abbess. Her performance was heartfelt and sacred as she was soft-hearted and understanding of Maria's plight. Her singing of 'Climb Every Mountain' was a tour-de-force. Richie Heneghan was fine as Captain Von Trapp. This performer was solid. There were moments when he did appear a little taut and nervous, but overall a good performance from this actor. Sister Bertha; Angela Prenty, Sister Margaretta; Kate Hughes, Sister Sophia; Rachael Comer were all fine performers. They worked very well together and caught the supporting nuns' fun side at all times. Liam Newman was the perfect butler while Christina Jordan was hilarious as Frau Schmidt the busy housekeeper. Laura Beston was a lovely Liesel with wonderful singing and capturing the appropriate teenage innocence and Cathal Owens was a very fine Fredrich. Rachael Walsh was a delightful Louisa. Joe Kelly was a charming Kurt. Ava Fitzpatrick was a very appealing Brigitta. Susan Flynn was engaging as Martha and Beth Lloyd was a very sweet Gretl. All the children were delightful.

Kevin Murphy was a solid Rolf. Mary Dempsey gave a very compelling performance as Elsa Schraefer and Michael Goulding was a very energetic and an animated Max Detweiler. They worked very well together. Jarleth Owens was a solid Zeller. Ronan Egan was a sombre Von Schrieber.  The ensemble gave a very committed performance and their singing is to be commended.

This production, under the direction of Hazel McLynn was secure for the most part. This is always a difficult show with so many large set changes and Hazel gave us a solid and steadfast production.

Hazel McLynn, Director, was also in charge of choreography and did very well here too.

David Keane did a solid job backstage and his team was hardworking and efficient. I am afraid that set changes were too slow and needed more rehearsal and planning. Props were fine and sound under the stewardship of Alan Dunne was good. Peter McGallaig did a fine job on lighting design.

The costumes were a little hit and miss, I am afraid. They needed more attention and unfortunately shoes also needed more attention overall. Hair and makeup was fine.

Deirdre Lee, Musical Director and Choral Mistress, brought together a competent group of musicians who played with ease under her vigilant eye. Tempos were steady and we had some beautiful guitar playing from Tom Lyons. Singing was well rehearsed and confident while playing during set changes enduring. Harmonies were secure and solo singing was controlled and engaging. Diction was excellent particularly for the Latin text with rich, open and warm vowel sounds. Congratulations!

Tullamore, Co Offaly is a beautiful heritage town in the midlands. The main street is filled with a wonderful array of small shops, bars and restaurants. Tullamore Musical Society are based in the Tullamore Court Hotel, a magnificent modern hotel, just outside the town.

The Hotel facilities are put at their disposal and obviously the management embrace this group, apparent from the Pre Show Dinner Menu and the array of Cocktails all based around 'Annie Get Your Gun', this seasons offering from this historic society. There were bales of hay and cowboy accoutrements on display in the foyer and the front of house experience was full of fairground flair.

Annie Get Your Gun is a fictionalised portrayal of the life and love of sharpshooter Annie Oakley with music and lyrics by renowned songwriter Irving Berlin.

The story is quite simple in real terms, Annie meets Frank Butler, beats him in a sharpshooting contest at Buffalo Bill's Wild West Show, and they both have to compete between their competitive side and their new found love for each other. Tullamore Musical Society brought us a very colourful entertaining evening in Cincinnati, Ohio. It is well that Tullamore Musical Society could celebrate! The set was very impressive with stars and stripes abounding from pros arch to portals. John O'Donoghue did an excellent job on the set design for this production. The moving panels to the rear worked very well and gave us great variety for the many states. Lighting from Gerry Taylor was excellent. Cueing was good. The colours worked well. Pat McGann's costumes were very colourful and fitted the cast very well. The Indian costumes were excellent as were the Pitch dancer's ensemble. Principal costumes were first class. The costumes for Annie Oakley and Frank Butler were near perfect. Well done to whoever looked after shoes, perfect!  Makeup was good and hair suitably of the times under the supervision of Ultan Keena and Martina Byrne. Wayne Handy did a very good job as Stage Manager. His team was efficient and worked very well together. We were very impressed with the Motorbike and the Circle of Death scene. The large set pieces were all fine.

This production under the direction of Damien Douglas was solid. The overall story was well told and a team effort from the cast was apparent. Casting was appropriate and we had some fine performances. Staging was good and we had some good use of the stage and riser areas. Some entrances needed attention, particularly those from upstage centre. Ensemble work was good with some nice pictures. Some dialogue scenes needed more attention as we needed to embrace the comedy moments more. We had too many straight lines in dialogue at times and some moments needed more directorial attention. Laura Martin did a good job on Choreography. We had some good dancing, well placed and some nice final pictures. Some of the formations were very similar at times. The 'Tribal Dance' was a particular highlight!

We had a wonderful eight piece orchestra for this production under the attentive musical direction of Enda O'Connor. Solid wind playing; particularly the trumpet, excellent bass and exciting percussion! The strings were however slightly exposed at times. The MD kept the pace affecting as he focused on this very busy score with confidence and perception. Singing from the ensemble was self-assured and well rehearsed. The harmonies were secure and diction first class, particularly in 'There's No Business Like Show Business' and 'I've Got the Sun in the Morning'. Tempos could have been a little sharper and more energetic at times in order to drive the show along; this type of show needs to be animated. Principals were secure in their singing.

Amanda Cunningham was a powerful Annie Oakley. Her singing was strong, tuneful and sufficiently brash. This performer captured the wildness and equally the tenderness and insecurity of the character. Dialogue was strong and comedy lines were well delivered. We enjoyed her performance! Stephen Rabbette gave a nicely understated performance as Frank Butler with some lovely singing. This actor needed to embrace the showmanship of the role with more confidence! Natalee Kelly was very self assured as Dolly Tate, Frank's assistant. Natalee brought energy to every scene. Eoghan Fingleton was great as the manager of the Wild West Show; Charlie Davenport. He was a very strong actor and fine singer. Frank Nicholson was excellent as Buffalo Bill. He owned the stage at all times. Alan Conroy did very well as Pawnee Bill. Nigel Sammon was a great Chief Sitting Bull. Excellent comedy and a great voice and accent for this role! Roy Cunningham gave a very robust performance as Hotel owner Foster Wilson. John Coss was a very energetic Mac. Minnie; Ciara Coughlan, Jessie; Ciana Luskin, Nellie; Sophia Shiel and Little Jake; Kenny Heffernan were all great young performers as Annie's siblings. The ensemble were very focused and committed to their roles. Their singing was excellent and harmonies were secure. Well done everyone!

It was lovely to meet Nicola Heffernan, Aoife, Douglas, Laura and all the cast after the show. Many thanks to Karen Martin for the beautiful deserts,  the warm welcome +7.<2/,/+=<30=5130<80F	85./7)/+:; The Story of Tullamore Musical Society', a wonderful hard copy publication.

Continued success!

'Songs for a New World' is an abstract musical. It tells a collection of stories. It is not a book musical, as it has no over- arching plot and no consistent characters throughout the evening. Yet, there are consistent threads running through Jason Robert Brown's music; rhythmic, melodic and orchestration patterns, that link our experience. It is a collection of scene songs where each song in the show is essentially about the same thing; those moments in life when everything seems perfect and then disaster strikes.

There is no specific location other than the natural ambiguity of the human heart and mind. It is ultimately about survival. It is about the way we regroup and survive in a new set of circumstances - a new world. The world is constantly changing and this musical challenges our innate ability to change and survive.

The small ensemble, that is UCC Musical Society, rose to that challenge with youthful naivety and intelligence. The ensemble was committed to the project and gave brave performances in what is a demanding musical. They embraced the many challenges and delivered each song with determination and penetrating concentration. Is that enough for a musical production?

The opening number - 'The New World'- is in fact a prologue, a survey of all that is to come for the rest of the evening. "It's about one moment, when you are on the verge of success, the sky starts to change and the wind starts to blow".

The Orchestra or small band was placed upstage behind the action, Maybe a gauze in front of the band may have offered a less intrusive backdrop? That being said, Musical Director Lauren Ronan assembled a wonderful band of musicians on Piano, Bass and Percussion. Tempos were consistent and the many genres including gospel, jazz, pop and classical were very well released. The piano features extensively and Michael Young is to be congratulated for his fine playing. Lauren was precise and decisive on entrances and we had some excellent percussion playing from Eamon Cagney. The bass playing was also very supportive from the accomplished bass player, Deirdre Brett. This band was controlled and we had wonderful ensemble playing under the direction of a self-assured musical director. Singing was first class from soloists and ensemble with harmonies excellently defined and delivered with confidence. Balance was excellent.

Shona Lanigan was a beautifully rounded performer, focused and lyrical as woman one. Shona has a beautiful singing voice. Unfortunately her top range was a little stretched on the night I attended but this in no way took from her wonderful performance.

Vicky Sheridan was a tour-de-force as woman two. This actress gave a powerful performance and her singing was rounded, focused and very full bodied. Vicky also delivered the comedy moments with panache and great comic timing.

Mark O'Sullivan gave a sterling performance as Man one. His singing was excellent even though his vocal range was somewhat strained on the night. A tired voice, I presume? Volume was an issue at times but this did not take from his commitment to each and every song. David Lynch was a great robust performer with strong vocals and resolute delivery as man two. His characters were intense and smoothed and David was imposing at all times.

Aoife Bradley, Niamh Byrne, Ali Coady, Melissa Craig, Maeve Guilfoyle, Johanna Hartigan, Cassie McElligott, Clara O'Keeffe and Fiona O'Sullivan made up the excellent chorus. They were all focused and very well rehearsed. Their singing was excellent particularly for 'The World was Dancing' and 'Hear My Song' with secure harmonies.

Grace Voughan did a fine job on the overall direction. Moments were well released and each of the performers was focused and resourceful. This show offers the opportunity for some creative directorial touches but unfortunately this was not released for this production. The direction was overtly one-dimensional and safe. That is not to take from what was achieved, but with a small company it does offer opportunities for the director to 'think outside the box'. The lighting from Rob Moloney was adequate and cueing was sufficiently tight. The gobos were a nice touch. The costumes were adequate. This new society in UCC are to be congratulated on their inaugural production.

Johnny Depp and his cohorts have been responsible for a recent resurgence of coolness amongst those who sail the seven seas sporting eye-patches, prosthetic hooks and peg legs. Ballinasloe MS capitalised on such piratical popularity with its hilariously upbeat Pirates of Penzance (Australian Version).

Paul Norton`s outrageously funny version of the G&S classic culminated in a no holds barred Megamix finale which featured rollerbladers on stage, cast in the audience and Queen Victoria waving a large Jolly Roger a la `Les Mis`! Pace was relentless throughout and Mr Norton skilfully led his talented cast from comic highlight to comic highlight in a show which scarcely allowed us to breathe as the gags, old and new, kept on coming. MD Shane Farrell presided over a six piece combo, each of whom sported an obligatory bandana. As well as maintaining a tight rein on his charges, Mr Farrell proved himself to be quite the performer. His altercation with the Pirate King was very funny indeed. Principal singing was generally strong. Ensemble singing was strong when in unison but the alto line could have done with some additional support, particularly in `Climbing Over Rocky Mountain`.

Sarah Griffin`s choreography was well- rehearsed and appropriate, capturing the zany humour of the piece very well. `A Modern Major General` was a fun number with great precision adhered to by all and the multiple encores of the excellently performed `With Cat-like Tread` were rousingly riotous as the audience cheered for more and the clearly exhausted pirates dared not disappoint.

The gentlemen`s ensemble was excellent in this production as they treated us to many an "Argh!", a swash and a buckle. Mr Norton had clearly worked very hard with the pirates and policemen as their positioning, reactions and timing of comic business were impeccable. The ladies too did well. Their OTT infatuation with Frederic as they became his desperate `groupies` was hilarious. I loved their well-timed swoons as he gyrated his piratical pelvis. Patrick Byrne proved himself a very skilled actor and comedian as a flamboyant Pirate King. He was bodacious and dramatic, clearly in tune with the zaniness of the piece. His crotch-grabbing, moonwalking, celebratory "Who`s bad?!" was a comic highlight, as was his swinging over the heads of the audience as he narrowly avoided decapitating the MD. Mr Byrne had a fine singing voice particularly in `Oh, Better Far to Live and Die`.

Sixteen year old Ailbhe Lohan is a talented young lady who was supremely confident in the role of Mabel. She had a nice, pleasing soprano which belied her years. `Poor Wandering One` displayed her sweet voice at its best. If this is what Ms Lohan can sing like at sixteen then she will be a force to be reckoned as her voice matures and her upper register develops fully. Definitely a star of the future. There was no end of narcissistic posturing and posing from Paul Conroy as Frederic. Mr Conroy is a most clever performer with superb comic timing and expression. His tongue in cheek approach led to much hilarity as he lapped up the daughters` overly amorous attentions with barrel-chested delight. He also had a most wonderful tenor voice which was controlled and expressive. Louise Colohan was a brilliantly comical Ruth. Her efforts to convince Frederic that she is, in fact, aesthetically pleasing were very humorous and her confusion over the word "circumspect" as she focused on Frederic`s `nether regions` was side-splittingly funny. Ms Colohan was far from a one trick pony though and she had a powerful, expressive voice which was comfortable in both higher and lower registers.

Séamus Feerick stole the show as Major-General Stanley whose prolixity is rivalled only by his fertility, considering the number of daughters filling the stage. His inspired trapdoor entrance through a cleverly positioned treasure chest was brilliantly theatrical. Mr Feerick was so comically doddery as he treated us to sight gags, physical humour and impeccable timing aplenty. His signature tune `A Modern Major General`, with its tongue-twisting lyrics, may have suffered slightly from lapses in enunciation but all was forgiven, such was the calibre of Mr Feerick`s performance.

Eoin Croffy was a Monty Pythonesque Sergeant delivering a superbly consistent portrayal full of physical comedy which was only matched by his remarkable `comb-over`, in itself worthy of accolades. `When the Foeman Bares his Steel` was a triumph of comic business and movement and, under the exterior silliness, Mr Croffy indicated a fine sense of musicality.

Karl O`Doherty provided good support as Samuel and, although there were some tuning issues in `Pour, O Pour the Pirate Sherry` he compensated in no small way with his commitment and energy in the ensemble numbers.

Sarah Corcoran, Catherine Madden and Hannah McCreanor were a very funny trio as Edith, Isabel and Kate. Each had their own distinct and quirky character. Ms Corcoran, in particular, shone both vocally and comically.
