Seventeen year old Niall Callaghan was hilarious as a camp, kilt-wearing, blue and white faced Willie Wallace. Cue grave-turning aplenty from Gilbert and Sullivan! Mr Callaghan has a brilliant comic flair and his interjections added so much to the zaniness of the show.

Pat McGovern and his crew did well with plenty of trapdoor business to keep them busy throughout. The pre-set for Act Two made for an industrious interval although the backdrop did need to be pulled taut at the bottom.

Set design was most appropriate and excellently painted by scenic artist Grainne Moore. The seascape background for Act One was superbly detailed, as was the pirate ship which sailed on and off from stage left. The Act Two arches and gravestones transformed the stage, as did the well- painted backdrop.

Pascal Gough`s lighting was cleverly in tune with the show`s fusion of traditional and more modern elements. Colours were carefully selected and we had good use of follow-spot when appropriate. The strobe effect for the pirates` confrontation with the police worked well and the all out craziness of the Megamix was suitably enhanced in a frenzy of moving lights. Sound was in the very capable hands of Derek Recks who maintained a good stage/pit balance throughout. Some cleverly chosen sound effects added to the humour of the piece. The Major- General`s `Pinocchioesque` elongating nose was a particular favourite. Additional radio mics could have been spread amongst the altos in the interest of balance but this is a small point in what was a great job.

Eithne Blackwell headed up the wardrobe department and did a great job in co- ordinating the fusion of tradition G & S with the more contemporary elements of this version. Frederic`s yellow shirt and red trousers were suitably loud in keeping with his OTT characterisation and the Major-General`s plumage was a delight. There was great detail in the pirates` costumes yet all were uniquely individual. The funky, Converse footwear of the ladies combined brilliantly with the traditional costuming in what was a very quirky look.

Hair and make-up were well looked after from Ruth`s not-so-flattering wig to the `five o`clock shadow` of some younger policemen to Mr Croffy`s show-stealing comb-over.

Greg Blackwell`s props were well-chosen and appropriate with great attention to minute detail in evidence and the superb front of house display was most impressive with an abundance of pirate paraphernalia.

This was a most entertaining and clever presentation which breathed new life into the classic original. A very strong front line and a skilled director ensured that everyone was jolly (Even Roger!) as we left Ballinasloe`s Town Hall Theatre.

Legendary American director Hal Prince agreed to come on board for the original 1978 production of `Evita`, famously saying "Any opera that begins with a funeral can't be all bad." How right he was. The show has enjoyed massive worldwide popularity over the past thirty five years. Documenting the rise and fall of Maria Eva Duarte, it is a show which deals with complex political themes, corruption and a healthy dash of manipulation for good measure. Ballinrobe Musical Society managed to secure the much sought after performing rights and their production was a veritable triumph from beginning to end.

Director Liam Butler gave us a highly polished, visually dynamic and powerfully dramatic presentation. Attention to detail was in evidence throughout with so many clever touches in evidence. Mr. Butler moved things along at a frenetic pace, hardly allowing the audience time to breathe. Excellent work had been done with a very committed and disciplined ensemble and principal characterisation was exceptional. I did feel that the ending needed a little more clarity but that is a small point in what was an excellent job from Mr. Butler.

Finola Higgins-Cosgrove conducted a very tight nine-piece orchestra which handled the eclectic styles of Lloyd Webber`s score very well indeed. There was some stunning violin right through the show, particularly during `The Art of the Possible` and the beautifully warm tone of the Spanish guitar at the top of `Don`t Cry for Me Argentina` was a joy. Choral singing was excellent. The difficult `Requiem for Evita` with its dissonant harmonies was very secure and the six girls in `Oh What a Circus` displayed a beautiful blend of voices. One rogue male voice was less than accurate in `Rainbow High` but this was an exception to what was otherwise an excellent show chorally.

Choreographer Aoife McClafferty devised some well-rehearsed, energetic routines. `Buenos Aires` was a great routine but, whilst movement was very secure and well-drilled, more Latin swagger and abandon was required as performance levels and facial expressions from some cast members needed to reflect the dramatic Latin rhythms. `Peron`s Latest Flame` was a triumph. The strength, focus and military precision of the gentlemen were breathtaking in this number. Huge kudos to Ms. McClafferty for what must have been painstaking work in putting this routine together. The enormous ensemble was a central element to the huge success of this show. Each and every individual was in tune with Mr. Butler`s vision. From the heartfelt grief of Requiem to the precision of the military to the aloof expressions of the aristocracy there was careful attention given to ensemble characterisation which paid off hugely. Superbly disciplined freezes and difficult `slow motion` sequences were very well timed. The two nurses were incredibly focused as they slowly went about their business, adding so much to the heart-wrenching final moments of the titular character.

What a find Angela Curley-Staunton was for the society. She was perfectly cast in the title role, giving an outstanding performance which was fascinating in its depth and range. From the ambitious teenage Eva to the manipulative seductress to the conniving First Lady to the tragic, cancer-stricken figure, Ms Curley Staunton really did bring us on a cleverly thought out journey. Diction was exceptional, even in her weakened state. Eva Perón`s hand gestures and body language had been carefully studied. Excellent attention to detail. Singing was powerful and effortless. There were so many standout moments vocally. `Buenos Aires` was so strong and `Don`t Cry For Me Argentina` was captivatingly interpreted.

Dave Langan, as a charismatic `Everyman` Che, had a distinctive narrative style. He had an instant rapport with the audience and came across as comfortable and relaxed throughout. It was a very clever interpretation as we could see Mr. Langan thinking and reacting at every turn, never once losing focus. His increasing frustration and cynicism with Eva was so well judged. Vocally, Mr. Langan was very strong indeed. `High Flying Adored` sat on his fine, lyrical voice beautifully and I loved his `Goodnight and Thank You` which displayed his ability to infuse a song with subtle humour.

The multi-tasking Michael Coen gave a compelling portrayal of Argentine president Juan Perón. Mr. Coen had a very strong presence and his diction, timing and innate stagecraft shone through. There was a wonderful chemistry between himself and Ms Curley-Staunton from their initial meeting right through to her ultimate tragic demise. His rise through the ranks of the Argentine military was performed with excellent focus in `The Art of the Possible` and there was some lovely tenderness in `The Dice are Rolling`.

Niall Conway impressed with a suitably OTT performance of tango singer and heartthrob Magaldi. It was a really fun characterisation backed up by a quality tenor voice in `On This Night of a Thousand Stars`.

Sadbh Langan gave a memorable performance of Perón`s mistress. Her `Another Suitcase in Another Hall` was beautifully sung with a grace and fragility that was most engaging.

Michael Coen and his team designed a stunning set dominated by an imposing balcony and archways. In a coup of engineering and stage management the balcony came downstage for `Don`t Cry For Me Argentina` before returning to its original position.  Downstage left and right there were two raised revolves which allowed for some clever staging, particularly with ensemble groupings. Karen Forde`s scenic artistry was excellent with great attention to detail. Niall Heaney`s stage management was pretty much flawless. I did feel that, given the continuous nature of the show, costuming the crew would have added greatly to the seamlessness. That said, I couldn`t help but marvel at the efficiency and precision of the crew who, wearing in-ear monitors, were marshaled expertly by Mr. Heaney from the back of the hall. Derek Recks did a superb job on sound. Cueing was perfect all night. There was a lovely reverb on the ensemble for the haunting `Requiem` and individual instruments were featured in the mix as required. There were some nice, unobtrusive sound effects also, including fireworks at the top of Act Two.

Gerry Taylor`s lighting design was suitably epic. There were some excellent effects throughout including very clever use of five LEDs built into the floor for `The Art of the Possible` and some stunning, well-timed pictures created for the ensemble freezes. June Young of thatlooksgood, assisted by Finola and Edel O`Neill, provided a wonderful array of refreshingly authentic costumes with June`s usual attention to minute detail. Eva`s iconic white dress had the required `wow factor`. From the aristocrats` furs to the soldiers` white helmets it was clear that a lot of thought had gone into getting everything just right.

Hair and make-up were very well looked after by society members who had obviously done their homework on the ladies` hairstyles in particular.

Front of House, presided over by Seán Costello Snr, was buzzing before and after the show and all appeared efficient and under control.

For years I have been hearing of the exploits of Ballinrobe MS on the grapevine. My first trip to see one of their shows did not disappoint. I hope it`s not my last.

(SCHOOLS EDITION) It would appear that a freak of geography and genetics has somehow pre-determined that young people in the environs of Lisburn, Co Down are naturally gifted vocalists. Whatever else could explain the incredible talent in depth that Fusion Theatre had at its disposal for this wonderful production of Les Miserables (Schools Edition)? One by one, performer after performer, we were treated to exceptional vocals, stunning choral singing and startlingly layered and nuanced performances from this breathtakingly talented young cast, all of whom were aged nineteen or younger. It was a grim and gritty telling of Victor Hugo`s tale from director/MD Ian Milford who was deeply au fait with the show`s themes and dramatic possibilities. Mr Milford`s direction was most insightful and he got every last ounce out of his talented cast with a great attention to the narrative and some exceptionally staged sequences.Mr Milford led a wonderful fourteen piece orchestra which impressed right from the off with a stunning overture. `I Dreamed a Dream` was an outstanding combination of crystal clear vocals and beautifully sympathetic accompaniment, with superb playing from violins and guitar. Principal singing was outstanding throughout and the choral work was exceptional.

It`s no coincidence that some of the best sound engineers in the business are also accomplished musicians in their own right. Jody Trehy put his years of experience and excellent ear to great use by maintaining an incredibly balanced choral sound, a job which kept him on his toes given that there were over eighty singers on stage and over twenty radio mics in operation. An exceptional job! Choreographer Rebecca Leonard devised some well-rehearsed routines which were full of energy and spirit and in keeping with the style of the piece. `Lovely Ladies` was suitably bawdy and excellently performed and `One Day More` was a triumph of simple but precise movement from the entire cast in what was a standout moment in the show. `Javert`s Suicide` incorporated some excellent movement from a smaller ensemble group, dressed in black, appearing to represent the darkness and turmoil of Javert`s mind. It was a very clever concept, superbly performed but was let down slightly by the incongruity of some modern looking costumes. Boyd Rodgers was an excellent Jean Valjean with a wonderful vocal range. He was passionate, determined and desperate when necessary. Diction and phrasing was top drawer and there was a real emotional depth to his playing. `Bring Him Home` was a musical highlight of the show although he did need to be careful of pitching when moving from chest voice to falsetto at the end. A powerful performance from start to finish.

Valjean`s nemesis, Javert, was played by seventeen year old Rory McCollum who was playing his first principal role. I struggled to get my head around both his age and lack of experience as they were completely at odds with the maturity of his multi-layered performance and his vocal dexterity. It was a stunning debut by any standards. `Stars` was so beautifully sung and his suicide was a powerful dramatic moment.

Hannah Conlon gave a captivating performance as Fantine. This was a wonderful interpretation full of shame, determination and fear. `I Dreamed a Dream` was stunningly heartfelt and what a voice she had to go with it. A real "wow!" moment. There was excellent, heart-wrenching playing from her as she lay dying, imagining she could see Cosette in front of her.

Monsieur Thenardier could hardly have been cast any better than Conal Corr. He is a very talented comedian with impeccable timing and a remarkable physicality which allowed him to completely inhabit this role. He balanced his comedic prowess with a malevolent edge which made him deliciously obnoxious. He worked very well with Madame Thenardier, played with great energy and comic business by Jordin Mackin. She, too, was a riotous character with wonderful timing and a face full of comic expression. They made a delightfully funny duo.

Just when I thought that the well of talent had surely run dry, along comes Connor Carson as Marius! This was an acting and singing performance of the highest quality from a gifted performer with wonderful expression and a most effortless singing voice.  `Empty Chairs at Empty Tables` was one of many vocal highlights. It was note perfect and sung with an emotional range that was so genuine and honest. The chemistry between himself and Cosette was superb and their voices blended perfectly.

Perhaps the vocal performance of the night came from Jessica Webb as the ill-fated Eponine. She sang so well throughout but really blew us away with her rendition of `On My Own`. Her expression, tone, and control of a most beautifully lyrical voice combined to deliver what was yet another highlight of this wonderfully crafted show.

Eleven year old Gavin McNally, playing his first role, was simply outstanding as Gavroche. Take note of his name because this young man is going places! He had amazing presence for one so young and a huge voice into the bargain. I cannot imagine `Little People` being performed any better by anyone.

Aisling Quinn was an excellent Cosette who combined so well with Marius for some of the show`s most tender and memorable moments. There was an honesty and believability to her acting which was complemented by her beautifully expressive voice.

Matt Good was a very strong, revolutionary Enjolras. He had marvellous presence and sang so well in `Do You Hear The People Sing?` Aideen Nolan sang beautifully as Little Cosette and her `Castle on a Cloud` was poignant and sweet. David Bailie was an impressive Bishop of Digne and Emily McNally was a lovely Little Eponine. All cameo roles were to a very high standard.

The stunning set design, used in Waterford last season, was added to by society members to fit the huge stage of Lisburn`s Island Centre. The gates glided on magically as if by remote control and the imposing barricade was a sight to behold. Stage manager, Neil McGarry, utilised cast very well to ensure seamless transitions between scenes which added greatly to the continuity of the show. Costumes, overseen by Bernie Forde, were excellent for the most part, appropriate to the era and had great attention to detail. I loved the Thenardiers` wedding costumes which were suitably OTT and in extremely bad taste. The black costumes worn for Javert`s suicide were in need of attention though.

Props were in the capable hands of Anne McCleary and Neil McGarry and they did a fine job ensuring that everything was consistent with the timeframe and location.

Hair and make-up were well handled by Margaret Corbett and Denise Moran with particularly good work on the Thenardiers. Javert`s wig was superb. I did, however, feel that the passage of time needed to be reflected more in Valjean and Javert`s make-up as the show progressed.

Lighting could have been more consistent. If I`m honest this was the one area where things fell short of the incredibly high standards set in every other area of production. At times we had some stunning pictures with some lovely transitions. `I Dreamed a Dream` was a fine example of this. However, some cues were far too abrupt and moving lights were a little temperamental on occasion. Youth groups and adult groups are all treated equally in the present adjudication scheme. Some may think that unfair. However, anyone who has seen a Fusion show will join with me when I say that this group can more than hold its own and then some; such is the wealth of talent and energy within this remarkable group. Ian Milford and his team should be very proud.

Boy meets girl. Girl falls for boy disguised as older Hungarian guy. Older Hungarian guy arrives in town. Boy, disguised as older Hungarian guy, meets older Hungarian guy. Girl eventually falls for boy...no longer disguised as older Hungarian guy. Ya gotta love musical theatre really! Malahide Musical and Dramatic Society embraced the silliness of plot of `Crazy For You` with open arms and had an absolute ball doing so as they `yee-hawed` and tap danced their way through what is essentially a Gershwin `jukebox` musical with an hilariously corny script.

Lynda O`Neill`s direction was strong throughout. A corny book like this must be tackled head-on with no apologies and Ms O`Neill clearly understood this. There was plenty of well-timed slapstick and physical humour which culminated in a wonderful mirroring scene which was very precise, bringing the house down with every carefully co-ordinated move. Pace was cracking throughout and principal characterisation was uniformly strong.

Graham Walsh and his outstanding orchestra brought Gershwin`s marvellous score to life. Excellent playing from reeds and trumpet created a classic 1930s Broadway sound. The pit was suitably loud but never overwhelming with a great stage/pit balance noted throughout. Choral singing was strong particularly in the climactic `I Got Rhythm` at the end of the first act.

Sonya Dunne devised a lively set of routines which suited the wide range of abilities in the group. There was great energy and performance from the eight Follies who worked really well as a group. `I Got Rhythm` was a fantastic routine. Clever integration of various props made this the standout number of the show. The ensemble in this show was, generally, a strong, committed group. Some of the gentlemen needed to think more about their reaction to the arrival of the showgirls in Deadrock. However the gents redeemed themselves as they were brilliantly un-coordinated during Patsy`s attempt to put them through their dancing paces. The huge energy and life in all of the big production numbers was infectious.

Stephen Ryan had a baptism of fire playing his first lead role and what a great job he did too as Broadway wannabe Bobby Child. He had an engaging charm and a winning smile which had the audience on his side from the get go. Comedy was well-handled, from his impromptu audition for Zangler to his drunken pratfall in Act Two. He was strong vocally, whether singing the infectious "Slap that Bass" or the beautiful "They Can`t Take That Away From Me" which he delivered so well. Dancing was top notch, especially in numbers with Polly with whom he had a very strong onstage rapport.

Orla Jennings gets better and better every time I see her on stage. She was perfectly cast as Polly Baker, Deadrock`s lone woman. Ms Jennings was sassy and boisterous as required but displayed an emotional depth in the more tender moments which was very real. Her touching `But Not For Me` reprise led to many a sympathetic sniffle. `Someone to Watch Over Me` showed Ms Jennings` delightfully warm vocal, gorgeous expression and wonderful phrasing. The aforementioned older Hungarian guy was played in an appropriately OTT fashion by Bobby McWilliams. From his less-than-subtle eastern European accent to his larger than life gesticulations, this was a most humorous portrayal full of comic business and excellent timing. His mirroring scene with Bobby extracted every last ounce of humour from what was the comic highlight of the evening. The ever versatile Damien Hurley gave a near flawless performance as the gun totin`, hotel ownin` Lank Hawkins. Mr Hurley showed outstanding presence, focus and intelligence throughout. He was always thinking, always working hard, even when engaged in background business. Comic timing was exceptional, underlined by his delivery of some classic one-liners. Jennifer McGuire was a superbly caustic Irene Roth. This was a very funny characterisation with excellent comic timing and delivery. Her analogy of a besotted Bobby being akin to a "cow who needs milking!" was typical of such delivery. She vamped it up and owned the stage in the very well sung `Naughty Baby`, as the unfortunate Lank became the object of her amorous advances. Lottie, Bobby`s battle-axe of a matriarch, was expertly played by Mary Gamble who was domineering and materialistic in equal measure. She was a force to be reckoned with and was more than a match for Irene when the two went toe to toe. I loved her overly dramatic reaction to Bobby`s sacrilegious assertion that he actually didn`t care about money.

David Clarke did very well as Polly`s doting and somewhat doddery father Everett. He showed a lovely paternal warmth and I found his repeated referencing of Polly`s mother funny yet poignant.

Eugene and Patricia Fodor were a delightfully comic duo played by Robbie Keogh and Colette Moran. Mr Keogh had a wonderfully clipped accent, great comic timing and a range of facial expressions which helped him to inhabit this hilarious character. His sidekick, Ms Moran, gave a most likeable and quirky portrayal. She too had excellent timing and had great fun throughout.

As Tess, Kirstin Smith was a standout member of the Follies. She clearly understood the cheesiness required. She danced well and was always leading by example as she performed her socks off in every number.

Michelle O`Hara was an excellent Patsy with a natural comic flair which made this small role memorable for all the right reasons. Apart from being a strong comedienne she was another standout member of the Follies as she danced with great expression.

The cowboy trio were suitably hokum and sang well. They needed to be careful at times not to pull focus though with their background business.

A very basic but functional set was moved with good efficiency, for the most part, by Stuart Bourke and his young crew. It was great to see the stage managers of tomorrow getting a taste for things. The `Stage Door` caused a problem in Act Two but was eventually placed with some gentle persuasion.

Lighting was a real issue. Production numbers were marred by flashing lights on stage and distracting moving lights on the proscenium and in the audience. It was most inappropriate for this style of show, supposedly set in the 1930s. The sharp silhouettes of Zangler and the dancers behind the upstage gauze in the opening scene were very effectively created.

Jason Fallon`s sound design was superb. School halls can often present a difficult acoustic, but Mr Fallon maintained a great stage/pit balance with every word being heard even when the band was at full tilt. An excellent job.

Hair and make-up were given great attention to detail by Jane Lynch. The Follies looked the part. I particularly liked Ms Smith`s red wig. A great handlebar moustache for Mr Keogh and the wigs and moustaches for the `Zanglers` were well chosen.

Costumes by Monica Fitzsimons and Deirdre O`Brien were well-sourced and appropriate to the era. The showgirl costumes for `I Got Rhythm` were great and Lottie`s ensembles were appropriate to her status. The Fodor`s attire was great fun, particularly Eugene`s plus fours which were a delight.

I wasn`t sure at first about the cut out props including the double bass and vacuum cleaner. However, once I got used to them I actually bought into the idea and felt they worked quite well. All other props were well chosen.

`Crazy For You` is feelgood musical theatre at its best. Only those devoid of a pulse could have left Malahide`s production without a smile on their face and a spring in their step. Well done to all.

Ushered to our seats by some interesting characters yelling instructions in New York accents, it was clear that Galway University Musical Society was keen to set the tone before a note was played in anger. As I surveyed the auditorium and the stage area I caught sight of groups of cold, hungry, disenfranchised individuals huddled together, drinking and smoking as they tried to keep warm, belongings stashed in an old, battered supermarket trolley. It was a lovely touch from director Kate Costello who had assembled a wonderful cast for this gutsy presentation which she moved along with a frenetic pace and intensity, balancing sequences of explosive energy with moments of raw emotion in a superb production from start to finish.

Musical director, Megan Lohan, presided over a tight six-piece combo which brought John Larson`s eclectic score to life. Her conducting was most assured and we had some outstanding playing on acoustic guitar and piano in particular. Backing tracks used for `Today 4 You` and `Contact` were well produced and kept at suitable levels by the sound technician. Choral singing was stunning throughout with `Will I?` and `Seasons of Love` being two of many standout musical moments. The ensemble was incredibly strong in this production. Scanning the stage at any time it was clear that every individual was giving his or her all and was fully engaged with the narrative process. There was excellent work during the "Follow the Man" sequence as `addicts` filled the stage in what was a most skilful and controlled performance from all involved. Even when just standing and singing `Seasons of Love` every single person was performing and working hard.

Something which has impressed me so much on my travels has been the standard of choreography and dancing around the country. Both were outstanding in this show. Michael Flanagan had devised routines which were brilliantly original, clever, exciting and so brilliantly performed by a wonderfully strong group of dancers. The precision was breathtaking at times. From the explosive `Rent` to the clever theatricality of `Contact`, performance levels were through the roof. The two exotic dancers in `Out Tonight` moved very...um...`nicely` indeed!

Diarmuid Scahill gave a very honest and natural portrayal of Mark. He had a great narrative style, a good sense of comic timing and a super voice which was at its best in the title number and also in the stunning `La Vie Boheme`. Mr Scahill walked the line between being a detached observer and a central character very skilfully.

One of the performances of the night came from Deirdre Ní Chloscaí who ignited the stage as she brought the complex character of Mimi Marquez to life. This was an excellent characterisation with a most engaging emotional depth to her playing backed up by a powerful singing voice. `Out Tonight` released her inner `rock chick` as she let go with a drug-induced fervour and `I Should Tell You` was so poignantly and tenderly delivered. The chemistry between her and Roger was palpable as their relationship ultimately overcame their jealousy and fears.

Adam Keegan was an excellent Roger who was passionate, strong and dramatic throughout. He worked so well with Ms Ní Chloscaí. Their `I Should Tell You` was touching and he displayed marvellous range and control in `One Song Glory`. John Joyce was a strong Tom Collins. He had a very impressive, soulful and deeply resonant baritone which shone in the beautiful `I`ll Cover You`. There was a real sincerity to Mr Joyce`s performance. His pained expression as he carried Angel in his arms was heartbreaking. A lovely, honest performance.

Neil Delaney was perfectly cast as the cross-dressing musician, Angel. He never fell into the trap of resorting to caricature or playing for laughs. He created a real character which made his tragic demise all the more poignant. His `drum` solo in `Today 4 You` was great fun and his ability to maintain the consistency of his weakened state during the brilliant `Contact` was most impressive.

The role of bisexual performance artist, Maureen, was played by Julie Breen with wonderful energy and more than a hint of quirkiness. She performed the very difficult `Over the Moon` brilliantly, culminating in an invitation to a responsive audience to "Moo with me!" She handled the playful eroticism of `Take Me or Leave Me` very well in what was a great vocal performance.

Orna Ní Bhroin gave a powerful performance as Joanne, the no nonsense lawyer in a relationship with Mark`s ex Maureen. Her reactions to Maureen`s seduction techniques in `Take Me or Leave Me` were very funny and the timing between them was perfect. Ms Ní Bhroin quite clearly has a quality voice with a beautiful tone but I did feel that her voice appeared tired at times after what must have been an exhausting week.

Caoimhín O`Higgins was a wheeling dealing Benny. He had a strong presence and displayed a lovely vocal tone in `You`ll See`.

All cameo roles were very strong. I was particularly impressed with Brendan McGuinness`s fine singing voice in Seasons of Love and Jonathan Ryan was sleazy and ominous as The Man. Amy Jordan showed a fine flair for comedy as Alexi, as did Amy King as Mark`s mom. Sam Iredale was responsible for the fine split-level set which spanned the very wide stage of the Black Box Theatre. The various levels worked very well and there was a great attention to detail throughout the set, including the clever inclusion of the CBGB posters and the various graffiti offerings. Mr Iredale also headed up the stage crew and there was a great continuity to this production as the crew, dressed as various characters one would expect to see wandering the streets of New York, ensured slick changes in what was seamless stage management throughout.

Sound (not credited) was excellent throughout. From the traffic sound effects as we took our seats to the superbly balanced harmony lines, this was a great night`s work. Every single line spoken was heard clearly, ensuring all of the finer plot points were heard. Lighting (not credited) was atmospheric and some lovely effects were realised. I particularly liked `One Song Glory` in which Roger`s shadow was cast on the back wall. It was most effective.

Costumes were grungy, bohemian and funky all rolled into one. Thankfully, a close eye had been kept on the overall picture by Jessica Mullins and her team who had gone to great lengths to ensure a cohesive costume plot. Angel`s Santa garb was most entertaining. Great fun was also had with Angel`s make-up which was suitably OTT as was Mr Delaney`s black wig.

Galway University Musical Society (GUMS) has gone from strength to strength since its relatively recent formation in 2001. It was a pleasure to attend what was an exhilarating production from start to finish. The future is in very safe hands!

"When your heart is in the right place you don`t have to worry about being politically incorrect!" So says the undoubted `King of Political Incorrectness` and creator of `The Producers` Mel Brooks. Never one to sidestep taboo during his illustrious career, Brooks has infused some of the most sensitive subjects with his unique brand of humour. Racism, sexual orientation and religious persuasion have all been given the irreverent Brooks treatment over the years. `The Producers` pulls no punches either and Tipperary Musical Society embraced its irreverence giving us a highly entertaining, often side-splitting production.

Director David Hennessy was keenly aware of the potential pitfalls when producing this sort of `screen to stage` musical. Continuity is key and this was uppermost in Mr Hennessy`s mind as the show moved along with remarkable fluidity and pace. Downstage business, such as the overtly camp conga line, cleverly distracted from longer scene changes. There were comic highlights galore and a `no holds barred` approach to some outrageously absurd physical humour. The compromising position in which Roger and Carmen found Max and Leo, as well as Hold Me Touch Me`s `moment` with Max on the couch were moments which would have scandalised your maiden aunt!

Mr Hennessy`s choreography broadly suited the mixed abilities of the cast. There was great life in the `Fiddleresque` sequence of `The King of Broadway` and `Along Came Bialy` was a showstopper, well-rehearsed and great fun as the `little old ladies` shook their wrinkly booties (presumably?) with geriatric gusto. The accountants` routine was well conceived but lacked the precision of movement required from all. `Springtime for Hitler` was a riotous number with excellent ensemble movement and the six tapping ladies in particular did very well.

MD Danny Carroll did a wonderful job with his fine twelve piece orchestra which played with considerable flair. Three saxophones gave a big Broadway feel to a stunning overture and the excellent first violin provided lovely Jewish ethnicity to `The King of Broadway`. Singing was top notch from both ensemble and principals. A strong ensemble sang well throughout, particularly during `Springtime for Hitler` and there was great work from the showgirls during `I Wanna Be A Producer`. The gentlemen threw themselves into `Keep it Gay` with outrageously camp abandon, clearly enjoying their moment of flamboyance. Willie `Bun` Ryan, as washed-up Broadway producer Max Bialystock, had impeccable comic timing and was well able to deliver a one-liner. He had a wonderful singing voice which was at its very best in his marvellously performed `Betrayed`. Accent was not always secure with certain vowel sounds needing particular attention but his energy and comedic flair made up for this in what was a strong characterisation generally.

John Murray was a very impressive Leo Bloom with a disarming naivety that made his performance most engaging. He was a superb comic actor with a great physical awareness and timing. Stan Laurel would have been proud of Mr Murray`s wide range of comic facial expressions. His reactions to Ulla`s advances were just hilarious and his lead into the beautifully sung `Til Him` drew us all into Max and Leo`s `bromance` in a skilled yet amusing way.

A robust John Murphy delivered a spirited performance as the psychotic, neo-Nazi playwright Franz Liebkind. It was a very funny portrayal. His `Der Guten Tag Hop Clop` was an uproarious number with thigh slapping aplenty coupled with ridiculously silly movement and a remarkably full baritone.

Cathal O`Donoghue was a cross- dressing, heel-wearing delight as flamboyant theatre director Roger de Bris. This was a deliciously funny portrayal which never descended into overplaying, preferring to teeter on the precipice in a superbly pitched characterisation. Mr O`Donoghue`s timing and diction were exquisite as he inhabited the outrageousness of the role with an innate comic style. I am still laughing at the milking of his exit after `Springtime For Hitler` and his right hand momentarily delaying its moment in the follow spot! We all know someone who ticks that particular box!

Roger`s "common law assistant", Carmen Ghia, was energetically played by John Ryan and, whilst it wasn`t as outrageously camp as this role is often played, it was a solid performance nonetheless. I really enjoyed his `Julian Marsh` moment as he tried to convince Roger that he COULD play Hitler!

Lynda Breen brought a great vivacity to the role of the oversexed, Swedish bombshell Ulla. She really had fun with this gem of a role and cast inhibition to the wind as she set Max and Leo`s hearts (and other anatomical areas!) racing. Comic delivery was strong throughout and she really let go with the aptly titled `When You`ve Got it, Flaunt it`. Her Scandinavian accent was suitably OTT but she was always mindful of clarity of diction.

Deirdre Ryan was hilariously funny as Max`s randy octogenarian benefactor Hold Me, Touch Me. Her milkmaid routine had me in knots with her Penelope Pitstop-like "Hay-ulp! Hay-ulp!" and, given her age, her antics with Max on the couch would have shocked her chiropractor no end!

Dermot Quinn`s set design was the best I`ve seen for this show with a very clever, large revolve beginning as the theatre exterior and turning to reveal Max`s office. This revolve was a stroke of genius as it allowed stage manager Denis Wade and his crew to keep the show moving with great efficiency and the minimum of fuss. Props were generally well-chosen. There was good detail in the office with a goldfish bowl and wastepaper basket adding nicely to the reality. A banana and two apples became an outrageously phallic arrangement in Roger`s fruit bowl and both the decor and furniture in this scene flew the pink flag nicely. Ulla`s photograph should have been a  theatre headshot as opposed to a framed picture and it was a puzzling oversight to have her painting from a tin which clearly had a lid on it. The IBM logo on the reverse of one lady`s protest placard was unfortunate. I have seen a lot of shows costumed by Thatlooksgood this season and their typical attention to detail was in evidence right through this production. The showgirls were well turned out and Franz`s lederhosen and helmet were most humorous. Headdresses in `Springtime for Hitler` were fabulously ostentatious creations with a beerkeg, pretzel and even a sausage adorning the ladies` heads.

Gerry Taylor`s lighting design was up to his usual high standards with great use of colours and some very clever cues to complement the more dramatic and key comic moments. "Think of the TONY!!" was one of my favourites. There was nice use of follow-spot as required. Unfortunately the projection used during `Springtime for Hitler` was not fully visible as lights were focused on the screen. As the designer is not listed as operator, I`m guessing there was a missed cue.

Sound operation was not as slick as it should be considering it was so late in the run. A couple of late cues and a missed gunshot took away from the overall polish of the show. Stage/pit balance was excellent throughout though and underscored dialogue sat nicely above the orchestra at all times.

The large front of house team was super efficient and most courteous to all.

Last year Tipperary had huge success with its production of `Man of La Mancha`, a show which couldn`t be any further from `The Producers` on the musical theatre spectrum. This year`s offering showed David Hennessy`s undoubted versatility as a director and the group`s versatility as a whole. Thank you for a thoroughly entertaining evening.

In the unlikely event that you grew up under an uncultured rock, here are a few key details on 'OKLAHOMA!'. This was Rodgers and Hammerstein's first hit book musical, and it is now over 70 years old. It is set in pre-statehood Oklahoma Territory in 1906, and is an age-old love story of men fighting for the love of lovely young prairie gals, and conflict abounds. Besides the title track, there are quite a few great songs, including "Kansas City," "People Will Say We're in Love," and "I Cain't Say No." And there is also a Rodgers and Hammerstein dream ballet, which they revisited in subsequent shows, such as Carousel.

In addition to a slice of Americana, it is a story about love triangles in a small community, between the female protagonist Laurey, her would-be beau Curly, the hired hand, Jud Fry and also between silly Ado Annie, peddler-man Ali Hakim and cowboy extraordinaire Will Parker.

The Dean Crowe Theatre, probably better known as the home of the all-Ireland Drama festival finals, was the venue for Athlone Musical Societies annual production 'Oklahoma!'. The overall production was good with solid pace and energy. The chorus were well used and the principal roles were safe and secure. We had some lovely moments and the comedy was well constructed and realised by director; Mary McDonagh, assisted by Steffan Jorgensen. Some stage movement needed more attention as actors migrated to DSC just for the sake of being there. Some of the finer 'detail' needed more attention ie; Rabbits for Carnes, Better Shoes for Ali Hakim, Carpet Bag for Ali/Will, better food baskets etc. It was also very odd to find some dialogue moments placed sitting on the floor and the shirtless males in 'It's a Scandal' were off- putting and unnecessary. But, overall a very entertaining and highly charged production!

The dance for the production by Choreographer; Mary McDonagh, assisted by Steffan Jorgensen was very strong. We did find some of the routines slightly too modern and would have liked more 'Hip/belt or hat work from the guys and more use of the dresses from the ladies. The 'Ballet' dance was stunning with special guest artiste, Maggie Villarini. Formations were good, but some final pictures needed more definition and attention.

Enda O'Connor excelled in the demanding role of Musical Director. We had a great eight piece orchestra who captured the sounds, tempos and dynamics required for this full and demanding score. Entrances were tight, balance was measured and underscoring precise. Chorus Mistress; Heather Shine did an excellent job on choral singing with great harmonies and secure soloists. The 'Oklahoma' chorus was outstanding. This company embraced the energy that is needed for this show. The group scenes were full of energy and each and every member was focused and animated. Singing was excellent with great harmonies and commitment. Kenneth Kennedy was a very imposing and believable Curly. This fantastic actor and beautiful singer brought great energy and enthusiasm to this role. Mr Kennedy used every opportunity to work the stage with wonderful touches and intelligent interpretation. His vocal range was excellently measured with wonderful lower tones and a secure higher range. Audrey O'Meara was a beautiful Laurey with beautiful singing and a fantastic stage presence. This actress captured the feisty and emotionally engaging nature of this role with confidence and pragmatism.  Her scenes with Curly were playful and her scenes with Jud frightening. Excellent! Joan Larkin was a driving force as Aunt Eller keeping the pace and energy levels moving at all times. Ms Larkin was effusive and understood the demands of this role. She was pleasantly ever-present! Ultan Keena was a fine Will Parker. This young looking actor had a great smile augmented with a fantastic singing voice and great tap dancing ability. His dialogue was focused with great comedy timing. A tour-de-force! Hilary Orpen was the perfect Ado Annie with fantastic vocal agility, wonderful comic timing and great facial expressions. Ms Orpen needs to be mindful of keeping in character throughout the scenes as there were times when her character was dropped. Overall a fantastic performance. Fidalgo Romo, from Spain, was hilarious as Ali Hakim. His accent was fantastic and his comic timing excellent. He needed to work on delivery a little, but a great performance. Ollie Berry had a great presence as Jud Fry. He was compelling, strong and appropriately rugged and evil. Alffie Kilduff was fantastic as Andrew Carnes, father to ado Annie. He was hilarious and entertaining. Margaret Mulligan was a powerful Gertie with a great laugh. This actress needed reminding that it's ok to be funny!

The set design was fantastic for this production, by John O'Donoghue. The shapes and texture was very appropriate. The trucks were very inventive and imaginative and it moved with ease. Well done! The props, under the stewardship of Camilla Flanagan needed more attention. Some props were excellent; particularly the Rifle and Gun's, but we did need more attention to the smaller prop detail. It is unlikely that Aunt Eller would have a plastic jug!  Props need to be 'time and place appropriate'. Jonathan O'Brien did a very good job as Stage Manager and his team were efficient and smart. Some set changes were unnecessarily slow. We had a very good transformation into 'Jud's House'. The sound was well balanced with good cueing from Reck's audio, Clara. Pascal Gough did an excellent job on the lighting design and execution. We had some beautiful use of the cyc. The dialogue states were bright and the 'Ballet Sequence' was beautifully realised. Well done!

Hair and makeup needed more variation. We had an overemphasis on ringlets for the girls. Wardrobe mistresses; Kathleen Sweeney and Anne Kelly brought together a fantastic collage of costumes, supplied by Pat McGann. The ladies dresses were excellent. The male costumes needed more definition between Farmer and Cowboy. Some of the waistcoats were not appropriate. Principal costumes were excellent, particularly Laurey's.

It was lovely to meet Society Chairman, Paschal Gough and to chat over past Tops of the Town endeavours.

Well done Athlone Musical Society.

Coast. What is predominantly noticeable are the large and impressive rows of Victorian houses as you enter the town. The Riverside Theatre, built in 1976, is located in the campus of the University of Ulster just outside the town and offers a very comfortable audience experience and a wonderful wide and high expansive stage area. It boasts its flexible staging facilities. Ballywillan Drama Group is in existence since 1952 and provides a rich mix of productions in the area. Their choice this year was the Irish premier 'Whistle Down the Wind'.

The show, with music by Andrew Lloyd Webber and lyrics by Jim Steinman, has certainly a unique blend of two musical genres with some songs having the feel of Lloyd Webber's traditional Phantom/ Superstar creations, but many clearly having an influence from Jim Steinman's Meatloaf years. While the songs are not as widely known as some of Lloyd Webber's others, there are some really stirring melodies and powerful rock-style anthems in this show.

The storyline revolves around three children, whose mother has recently died. Swallow, the eldest, discovers a man hiding in the family barn. The first words he utters are "Jesus Christ," (the shock of being discovered, for he's actually an escaped convict) and Swallow takes it literally and believes the Son of God has returned and could well bring mum back from the dead. The core storyline follows Swallow's emotional involvement with the 'Man' and the way her innocent faith shapes both of them. Of course, while this is happening, the Sheriff and the townsfolk are all seeking a prisoner on the run and so the plot unfolds.

The title song 'Whistle Down The Wind' is probably the best know tune in the show, but it also depends heavily on 'No Matter What' popularised by Boyzone in 1998. The show itself has many dynamics to contend with - a big set, big orchestrations, some tough vocal parts, complex moods and therefore the need for strong actors playing the leads and a need for a quality children's chorus. This is just what was delivered by Ballywillan Drama Group.

The overall production was compelling under the instinctive drive and vision of Director Brian Logan. Each and every dramatic nuance was crafted with precision and effect. The visual impact was breathtaking at times as every scene was visibly picturesque. We did have some issues with some unnecessary movement through some numbers and some dialogue set too far upstage. The ensemble work was focused and well rehearsed. The production was excellently paced and scene changes well thought out. Sharon Logan brought great energy and some lovely moments to the musical staging and choreography. The ensemble was well placed and pictures nicely configured. We did feel that some ensemble patterns were repetitive at times, with too many static pictures. The dance and staging for the children's chorus was excellent. The children were magnificent in every vista, delivering their cameo dialogue with confidence and singing with focused determination and delight. All our wishes were granted for their primary number 'When Children Rule the World'. It was a highlight! This company had all the drive and enthusiasm needed for the townsfolk, mob and minor roles in this compelling musical. The ensemble set pieces were very strong with magnificent singing with each and every member focused and resolute. The choral singing was fantastic!  Musical Director Eric Boyd brought together a first class group of musicians for this very challenging score. Their playing was tremendous with wonderful strings, keyboard, cello, flute, saxophone, clarinet, lead guitar, bass and percussion. The orchestra captured the stirring melodies and the powerful rock style anthems with exactitude and symphonic approach. The Musical Director was engaged and a driving force at every opportunity. Sounds were expansive, filled and expressive throughout this production. Singing was wonderful from our ensemble. Harmonies were secure, diction precise and delivery confident. Fantastic work with the Children's chorus! Soloists were safe and supported at all times. This was a stunning success from a much affianced musical director.

Set Design by Director Brian Logan, was very impressive. The overall aesthetic was wonderful with breathtaking picturesque-like opportunities that were realised and added greatly to the overall production. The level (USL) Up Stage left, needed more attention. This roster unit seemed to 'stick out' and it might have been better to slope or rake this unit and use it as a walkway. Just an idea! But, overall a very exciting set. Lighting also under the attentive eye of Brain Logan was picture perfect. The gelling was stimulating and colourful. There was excellent use of colour changers, movers and gobo's while cueing was precise and enhanced the production. Follow spots in the hands of Joe McClelland and Brian Wilkinson also enhanced the production. There were some issues around actors face light far up stage left, on the riser particularly during the duet. I presume it was the intruding pros arch and the angle of the special or spotlight? The video projection for the fire scene was also very impressive!

The costumes, designed by Ewan Campbell, were well thought out and delivered. They were in keeping with the overall look of the production. It is great to get costumes that enhance the experience. The hair and makeup was well attended to by Sharon Logan. We had beautiful hair pieces and wigs. Stage management under the expert supervision of David Wray was smooth and decisive. The crew was efficient and the many scene changes were seamless. The setup of the barn was particularly inventive and this team is to be commended for some wonderful work backstage.  The props for this production were excellent under the direction of Karen Hunter. The props in the barn were very impressive. Darren McLoughlin did a first rate job on sound management with excellent balance and precise cueing for this ambitious production. Harmonies and dialogue never missed!

Ashling Reynolds held the stage at all times in the very demanding role of Swallow. This relatively young actress had a beautiful singing voice and was ever present and confident in each and every scene. Her southern accent was excellent and Ashling was delightful in the role capturing the innocence and naivety necessary for this demanding role. Alan McClarty gave a compelling performance as the fugitive; The Man. His performance was focused and never faltering for what is a very emotional challenge for any actor. His singing was equally connected with soaring arias, wonderful storytelling and compelling conflict all brought to life with manic insecurities. A credible tour- de-force! David Ferguson was suitably sombre as the recently widowed father dealing with a young family and an almost grown-up teenage daughter. David was believable and caught the struggles through his lovely singing moments. Colin McClarty had a fantastic rock voice for his role, the cocky Harley Davidson- riding 'James Dean' type character Amos. He was energized, rebellious and gave a robust solid performance.  Vicky Creelman was a very strong and powerful performer as Candy. This role is very demanding vocally and Vicky rose to the challenge. Annie Levy brought great attitude to young sister; Brat. She was gorgeous and her singing was confident and determined. Well done! Leon Woods was a fantastic Poor Baby. He was focused and enthusiastic. A great young performer! Adam Goudy managed the difficult role of Edward with confidence and pathos. A fine singing job on 'Cold'! Shay Reynolds was fine as the Sheriff while Ben Levy was good as Earl and Richard Campbell was a very imposing Preacher.

Thank you to Carlton for looking after me and continued success to Ballywillan Drama Group.

Me and My Girl is a simple little tale about a male equivalent of Pygmalion's Eliza Doolittle. London barrow boy Bill Snibson inherits a title "Earl of Hareford" and a fortune, but appears to be losing his Lambeth girl. Of course, he gets her back again, while charming his initially aghast new posh relatives, who eventually accept him as lord of the manor. Toffs abound in this show, surrounded by a clutch of caricatures including the formidable Duchess, the vampy 'Lady Jacqueline, the petulant 'Gerald', and Singing and Dancing ancestors. This show is a hoot! The play uses a classic '30s theme of class differences, along with the eternal theme of romance, both new and old.

Ennis Musical Society presented their annual production in the magnificent Glor Theatre in Ennis. We were entertained with heights of laughter and foot tapping dances. This company were full of the nonsense that is 'Me and My Girl'. They were excellent in the many roles, including guests, servants and cockneys. 'A Weekend in Hareford' was delightful, 'An English Gentleman', beautifully sung, 'The Lambeth Walk', full of energy, 'The Sun has Got His Hat On' perfectly silly, 'The Song of Hareford' majestic and 'The Finale' full of liveliness. Well done everyone!

The overall production was very well accomplished from Director Des Henn. It was funny, face paced and full of energy. There were some great comedy moments and the show entertained the capacity audience at every opportunity. This director brought to life what is a simple story with confidence and determination. The Choreography under the creative eye of Barbara Meany (Henn) was very well accomplished. Dancing was secure and within the capabilities of the cast. 'Lambeth Walk' was excellent with great spoon work. The orchestra under the Musical Direction of Shane Farrell was very secure for this obscure brassy score, full of colourful musical numbers, intermeshed with some beautiful endearing ballads. The nine piece orchestra was attentive to tempos and percussion brought many exciting sounds, just what is needed for this show! Brass sounds were explosive, sultry and underscoring was secure. Support for the tap dancing routines was expressive but never overbearing. Strings were however slightly underplayed at times. Chorus Mistress; Martha O'Toole brought the chorus through the singing with confidence as lyrics and musicality was ever present. Harmonies were secure and tuneful, dynamics delivered and timbre exciting. Soloists were secure. Brian Henry was ever presenting, cheerful and majestically entertaining as Bill Snipson. This fine actor was comically skilful and embraced this full-on role with energy and fantastical facial expression adding physical manifestation at every opportunity to this costermonger role. Mr. Henry was a fine singer with a beautiful measured rendition of 'Leaning on a Lamp'. His dancing was also excellently convincing, perpetuating the vaudeville tradition. Well done Brian! Lauren Dunne was a beautiful Sally Smith showing great potential. Ms. Dunne needed to engage physically and emotionally with the role as this is a 'wiry cockney', innocent and impressionable. This role needs to be dynamic and contrasting as her world is turned on its head. Ms. Dunne was a fine singer and a great dancer.

Kate Corrigan was strong and convincing as the Duchess while Neil Haran was a very fine actor and a great foil for the Duchess as Sir John.

Mary Healy was lithe and explosive as the hilarious Lady Jacqueline. The comedy moments were very well delivered and her 'You Would If You Could' was a highlight, sultry and manic! A joy!

Sarah Griffin showed her versatility as Lady Battersby and Mrs Brown (The Cockney Landlady) and Richard Donnellan was fine as Charles the Butler. Ger Daly did very well as the hard of hearing Sir Jasper. Good comedy timing! Joe Morgan was a solid Lord Battersby. Morgan Lahiffe was perpetually cheerful as the uncomplicated Gerald Bolingbroke. A romping performance from this fine comedy actor and Tony Murray, the all singing, all dancing all drinking and eating family Solicitor was hilarious.

Set Design by Brian Burke and Liam Hansbury was appropriate and worked well. Some of the trucks were probably too small for the stage width, but overall they worked well. The transformation into the house was great. Some of the chairs were set in very odd positions, particularly facing away from the table? Marina Mulqueen and Colette Browne did a very good job on Props. Lighting, not credited in the programme, was fine. Declan O'Sullivan (Jnr) from Star Sound Systems did an excellent job on sound design and execution with some great sound effects.

Costumes were well attended to my Jacinta Florish and her team. The chorus guests needed more attention; Lady Jacqueline was wearing too much red, clashing with Sally; the Cockney costumes were excellent as were the maid's costumes. I would have preferred a 'negligee' for Jackie for 'You Would If You Could'. We needed more bags and coats for exterior scenes and hats for 'The Sun Has Got His Hat On'. The ancestor's costumes also needed to be more historically appropriate.  Hair and makeup was fine.

Ennis Musical Society is to be congratulated on a great night's entertainment.

It's always a pleasure to visit Shannon for their annual production. I had the satisfaction of performing with and directing for this company in the past. I am at all times in awe of their community spirit and commitment to the task at hand. In fact, an aunt of mine, Kathleen Ryan (RIP) was the Mayor of Shannon three times! This fine group have produced some inspiring productions throughout its thirty five year history and always set the bar very high for themselves. This year was no exception as they took on the onerous task of bringing to life what is a Broadway extravaganza, The Producers by Mel Brooks and Thomas Meehan. Casting Aodan Fox in the role of Max Bialystock was a no- brainer, seeing as he fits into the many roles previously done by Nathan Lane. He is Shannon's Nathan Lane! Fox relished the role of Max Bialystock with his wonderful comedy timing, taking on the tongue and cheek pastiches with tremendous energy and commitment. His performance was a tour de force at every level coming into his own in "Betrayal," a dizzying one man musical re-enactment of everything in the show leading up to it. Mr. Fox, a commendable comedy actor, captured the fiery and erratic nature of this character with first class ultra-hilarious slapstick and sidesplitting facial expose and lecherous nature. Well done Aodan, always a pleasure! Chris Willetts embraced the mousey, nervous and fearful account Leo Bloom with faultless security. He was perfectly panic ridden, blanket hugging and love-struck. This actor embellished the role in his own unique style leaving the audience feeling sorry for him and eventually admiring his elevation to a life in 'Rio'. Mr. Willetts, a fine singer and equally fine dancer, gave a germane and manifest performance. Pamela McGlynn was the perfect Ulla Inga Hansen Benson Yansen Tallen Hallen Svaden Swanson! Miss McGlynn was voluptuous, leggy and the ultimate sex-pot.  She looked wonderful while her acting, singing and dancing was unsurpassed. 'When You've Got it Flaunt It' was a highlight! Eoin Sheedy was undeniable in the demanding role of Franz Liebkind, the narcissistic ex-Nazi. 'Der Guten Tag Hop-Clop' was a comic delight.

This production, in the very capable hands of Director Oliver Hurley was fast paced as it chased the colorful characters, the witty songs filled with sly cultural references, the mincing gays, sex-object women, greedy Jews, bubble- headed Swedes, oversexed old ladies, gruff Irish cops, and kick lines of singing Nazis masquerading as a comedy. Hurley achieved all this with a production that was hilarious at times and submissive at other moments. Overall the production was a rollercoaster with distinguishable highs and lows. We did feel that by the end of the show it had run out of steam. We had some stock comedy production touches that worked, but overall the production needed more precision, attention to detail and flamboyancy. The dancing was, for the most part, within the capabilities of the cast and appropriate, but overall it needed more rehearsal and an infusion of style from choreographer Oliver Hurley. 'Along Came Bialy' and 'Springtime for Hitler' were very impressive.

This company worked very hard to recreate the essence of this Broadway Musical extravaganza.  They were committed and determined to entertain and they certainly achieved that. We did feel that the 1950's Broadway style was at times absent and in need of more definition. It is important to walk, stand and move in a distinct lampoon caricature fashion, particularly for this unconcealed comedy.

But what of the rest of the cast?  Anna Maria Barrett (Fox) was the perfectly hearty Hold-Me-Touch-Me little old lady. This actress was zingy, zany and zappy at every opportunity and vociferously entertaining! Eoghan Rice was the ever present 'common-law assistant' to Roger De Bris, Carmen Ghia. This role requires an abundance of swinging hips and clenched buttocks, screaming gay pride with every subtle movement and uttered consonant. I am afraid Mr Rice needs to get out more, but nevertheless a very entertaining performance! Pat Hayes was the ultimate flamboyant, larger than life, butch Roger De Bris. He gave a fantastic performance from 'Keep it Gay' to 'Springtime for Hitler' with hilarious difficulty walking in high heeds to a truly gay 'Hitler' enraptured with public attention. Well done!

Bryan (Set Designer); Derek McMahon, Kevin (Costume Designer); Daniel Flanagan, Scott (Choreographer); Darren Nash and Shirley (Lighting Designer); Anna Maria Barrett made for a wonderful screaming production team. Their 'Keep it Gay' was action-packed. Lick- Me-Bite-Me; Rachel McIntyre, Kiss- Me-Feel-Me; Maria Kelly were suitably little old lady like. Hilarious! While, Noel McNamara was a very commanding Mr. Marks, the egotistical boss. He was suitably expressive and domineering at all times.

Carmel Griffin; Musical Director, brought together a wonderful ten piece orchestra for this expansive score with some wonderful playing from brass, saxophone and the 'Yiddish' sounding violins. This cartoon type musical genre tips its hat to the big jazzy MGM Musical style and this orchestra embraced those obvious rhythms as our Musical Director was in control at all times. The brash overture set the scene and playing throughout the evening was riotous when needed and classic Broadway. A musical victory! The singing from the ensemble and soloists was confident and pleasing. This well rehearsed group was secure and tuneful. Set design by Oliver Hurley was impressive and inventive. The moving and rotating side flats were an excellent idea and worked very well in this type of space. The inventive set made for interior and exterior states being nicely defined and accomplished with relative ease. The scenic states were appropriate but unfulfilled with scenic painting by Thomas O'Maoldomhnaigh, needing more attention to detail. Martin Gough and his team were in control backstage. Scene changes were smooth with very little delay. This is a very busy show, backstage wise, and the crew did their very best in what is a restricted space and a complicated and busy show. The props for this production needed much more attention. Max's office was excessively bare and we needed to infuse it with appropriate props and stage furniture depicting the chaos in his life.

Lighting under the dutiful eye of Michael Finneran was somewhat hit and miss at times. There were obvious dark spots along the front area and the mid to up- upstage area needed more attention. We also needed two spotlights as much of the action involves two actors. Colors were appropriate and dressing with moving gobos a nice touch. The video projection for the 'Shows' was too fast and hard to decipher. Cueing was good but we did have some distraction as additional lights were obviously added to the cue mid scene.

The costume plot for this show was well delivered by Karen Barrett and her team. The ensemble costumes were a bit hit and miss and needed to be more stylish and in keeping with the time and place. The Usherettes costumes were beautiful, with nice hats. The Bavarian costumes were excellent. The gold sequent costumes were impressive. The elaborate head dressing for 'Springtime for Hitler' were disappointing. Principal costumes were appropriate, although I did have an issue with Max's waistcoat as the color faded into his black cape. The Little Old ladies costumes were fantastic. The production team costumes needed to be much more flamboyant and inventive. Ulla's costumes were incredible. The hair and makeup was well attended to by Rachel McIntyre.

Liz O'Sullivan (Star Sound Systems) did an excellent job on sound balance and cueing.

As is traditional in Shannon, Front of House décor was a marvel, with a fantastic 'Broadway' experience from the marvelous props to the very well mannequined FOH staff! Many Thanks to Martin McNelis for meet and greet and to Tom Keane for looking after me.

West Side Story heralded a new beginning for the American musical when it premiered in 1957. It departed from the sweetness and light of conventional musical theatre and dared to explore the dark underbelly of society and its myriad problems. Themes such as racism, broken homes, interracial relationships and unrest caused by increasing levels of immigration were tackled head on in what is considered by many to be one of the most important theatrical works of the twentieth century. It was fitting that Carrick on Suir Musical Society would take on such a groundbreaking show to mark their 100th production.

Liam Butler gave us a production with exceptional pace and flow which was gritty, raw and full of attention to detail. There were some beautifully realised moments and a palpable tension which gripped us from the first notes of the Prologue to the show`s tragic conclusion. The final image of the show`s four adults left on stage contemplating the gravity of the tragic events was a deeply and despairingly symbolic moment typical of this thought-provoking production. Patricia Woods` choreography was well-rehearsed and complemented the narrative perfectly. It was strong and visceral in the `Prologue` and `Jet Song`, suitably flamboyant in `America` and full of energy and humour in the brilliantly performed `Gee, Officer Krupke`. The dream `ballet` sequence integrated some lovely dramatic symbolism with fine, appropriate movement and the angst- ridden `Cool` was a standout moment. MD Fergal Carroll`s eleven-piece orchestra hit us with an exhilarating `Prologue` which featured exceptional work from the very accomplished percussionist. Mr Carroll`s conducting of this difficult score was most assured. Underscored dialogue was beautifully accompanied and always audible. The `Tonight Quintet` was outstanding chorally and principal vocals were, generally, of a high standard. Mr Carroll deserves full credit for rescuing `Something`s Coming` when it went badly awry.

The ensemble worked really hard in this show. Dance routines were sharp and harmonies secure. Diction was excellent throughout and entrances/exits sharp and well-rehearsed.

Michael Raggett was a robust Tony who was an entirely credible former street hoodlum. He was a fine singer with a beautifully round tone to his most expressive voice. The tricky syncopation of `Something`s Coming` caused problems on the night I attended but I am sure things improved as the week went on. Mr Raggett`s characterisation was generally strong and he had some beautifully tender moments with Maria. Louise Mulcahy was a wonderfully engaging Maria. Not as wide-eyed and innocent as the role is often portrayed, this was a more mature, confident Maria but a superb performance nonetheless. There was a beautiful subtlety to Ms Mulcahy`s playing and she and Mr Raggett had some lovely moments. Her crystal-clear, sweet soprano was a joy. `A Boy Like That` was an emotionally- charged, dramatic highlight as she lived every single note and word.

Sandra Power`s Anita was strong and feisty with superb stage presence. Initially, I felt that her accent was being forced too much but I warmed to her compelling characterisation. `A Boy Like That` was outstandingly sung and full of the raw emotion required. The harrowing taunting scene showed Ms Power`s wonderful acting ability at its best. She was simply magnificent in this excellently directed, highly disturbing scene which culminated in her fateful lie setting a tragic chain of events in motion.

Russ Tamblyn, who played the impetuous Riff in the classic movie, was a trained gymnast and acrobat. Matthew Williams had clearly taken a leaf out of his predecessor`s book in a portrayal of the Jets` leader which was full of remarkable athleticism and agility. I had my heart in my mouth as I watched him swing upside down from bars, jump onto fences and turn cartwheels effortlessly! He was an excellent actor into the bargain with superb pace and understanding of dialogue. He never once dropped out of character, even during the physically demanding dance routines.

Dermot Keyes was a more mature Bernardo than we might be used to but this was soon forgotten such was the strength of his performance. Mr Keyes is a most clever performer. He displayed exceptional presence and focus throughout in an authoritative, physically intimidating portrayal. Excellent timing during the war council helped to create an excruciating tension and he was superb during the rumble as he pushed Tony over the edge.

I was very impressed with Ray Nolan in the role of Chino. His scene with Maria post rumble was gut-wrenching as he went from agonising despair to unbridled rage at the realisation of Maria and Tony`s relationship.

Bobby Landers was a very believable Action who was bursting with resentment and frustration and Amy Walsh had superb presence in a very physical performance of the tomboyish Anybody`s.

A gravelly-voiced Fergus Power was a credible Doc as he tried in vain to talk sense to the warring factions. I did feel though that his anger with Tony may have been overcooked a little in their final scene and that the poignancy might have been more pointed had his outburst been more measured.

Pádraig Sheehan was superb as the hard-nosed, racist Lieutenant Schrank. It was a very well-studied characterisation emphasising the less than appealing side of the local police force. His sidekick Officer Krupke was played with a nice comic touch by Declan Robinson and Séamus Power provided some excellent comic relief as he tried in vain to assimilate the Jets and Sharks at the dance.

Chris Hennessy designed an impressive set for this production, utilising the main stage area as well as two small extensions left and right. The downstage fencing, behind which the `Prologue` and `Rumble` played out, was most effective and a great feat of engineering as it rose up between scenes.

Stage management was generally slick from Michael O`Hara and his team. I did have a big issue though with the two crew members who repeatedly walked up the side of the theatre during scenes as they preparing to set and strike the bridal shop. Their arrival during the beautiful `One Hand, One Heart` was ill- judged and distracting.

I am fast becoming a fan of Gerry Taylor`s excellent lighting designs as I have seen a lot of his work this year. This show was no exception and there was evidence of close collaboration between Mr Taylor and Mr Butler as the design complemented the narrative perfectly. The dream scene was stunningly lit with great use of moving heads and haze and there were some beautiful transitions and atmospheric use of colour during `Somewhere`.

Sound by Star Systems was pretty flawless throughout. Excellent cueing and a really good balance between vocals and orchestra were noted. Underscored dialogue was perfectly audible and there was appropriate use of some well-chosen sound effects.

Breda Butler co-ordinated a fine costume plot with appropriate attention to detail. I particularly liked the Puerto Rican girls` dresses with colourful underskirts and the various floral prints for the American girls. An apron for Doc might have established his character more in his opening scene. Denise Hunt and her team did a good job on hair/make-up with appropriate hairstyles for the ladies and some authentic blood and bruising for the guys in Act Two.

Front of house was most welcoming and highly efficient.

One hundred productions is a milestone that Carrick on Suir Musical Society is justly proud of. Their 100th production was, in itself, worthy of great pride and speaking to Mr Butler it was clear how incredibly proud he was of his hard- working cast. His pride was justified. Congrats to all!

`Me and My Girl` has become a popular choice for societies since the rights have recently been re-released. With its wall-to-wall, feel-good numbers and its hilariously corny book, it is a guaranteed crowd-pleaser and the perfect antidote to all things gloomy. St Mary`s Musical Society, Navan had its audience in the palm of its hand with a very funny, lively production which put a smile on the face and a spring in the step of all.

Ray O`Hare`s direction was intelligent and controlled with lots of clever little touches throughout. There was a great attention to both the narrative detail and the myriad comic opportunities of this delightfully funny show. The very tricky `Fugue` utilised three upper- level windows to frame the principal characters in a cleverly realised scene. Staging was generally very strong apart from some missed opportunities to use the full depth and width of the stage but this is a minor quibble in what was a strong piece of direction generally.

MD Jacqui McGowan and her top-notch orchestra gave a rousing interpretation of Noel Gay`s infectious score. Ms McGowan`s lively, assured conducting got the most out of musicians and cast alike. We had some excellent muted trumpet in the superbly played overture and exquisite violin playing throughout. Choral singing was generally strong with the exception of the difficult `An English Gentleman` where one confident male voice was less than accurate in a capella sections.

Jane Wardick`s choreography captured the style and era of this show perfectly. It was very well-drilled and suited the abilities of the cast. `The Family Solicitor` was hilariously silly with principals entering into the spirit of things with joyous abandon. `The Lambeth Walk` was suitably lively with some great `spoon work` and the eight ladies tapping in `The Sun Has Got His Hat On` added so much to what was a wonderfully strong opening to Act Two.

The ensemble for this show was exceptionally well-prepared. Mr O`Hare clearly realises how invaluable a confident, purposeful ensemble is. From the marvellous poise and clipped diction of the aristocrats in the opening number to the appropriate business and sense of purpose of the Hareford staff, it was evident that every person on stage was a character and not just a `chorus` member. This doesn`t happen by accident. Great work from all.

The central character of the streetwise cockney Bill Snibson is the key to a successful `Me and My Girl`. Kevin Fagan was clearly a fine actor, singer and dancer. He was a less animated Bill than one might be used to and I felt that more drive was needed at times to tie in with the whirlwind of energy and comic business usually associated with the role. When he let go, Mr Fagan was full of exuberance and life and his scene with the Duchess as she attempted to turn him into a gentleman was comedy gold. He had a very impressive lyrical quality to his voice, with `Leaning on a Lamppost` being a standout musical moment.

Danielle Williamson was a really strong and feisty Sally Smith. She was suitably rough around the edges as the cockney fish vendor and showed her versatility in her virtually unrecognisable incarnation at the end of the show. There was a great chemistry with Bill particularly during the eponymous `Me and My Girl` where the two played off one another like a well- oiled machine. Sally is the heart of the show and Ms Williamson underlined this with a beautifully touching rendition of `Once You Lose Your Heart`.

Mairéad Murray was superbly condescending as the imperious Duchess of Dene. It was a commanding performance which balanced a no- nonsense, stern exterior with a genuine but guarded warmth for her costermonger nephew. Her encounter with the diminutive Lady Lind was side- splitting stuff indeed! Ms Murray sang well in `Song of Hareford` although she was stretched slightly in the upper register.

Bill Slattery was a very real and believable Sir John. It was a great performance from a fine comic actor who was capable of great subtlety and great silliness in equal measure. His scene with Sally in the "rub- a-dub-dub` was sympathetically played and there was great hilarity in his drunken shenanigans with Bill during Act Two. Colin Flynn, as Gerald Bolingbroke, gave an exceptional comic performance as the upper-class twit with an aversion to working for a living. It was a very well- studied characterisation with excellent diction and a remarkable physicality. He really did inhabit his role as the aristocratic nincompoop and his facial expressions and impeccable timing set him apart in what was a comic tour de force. `The Sun Has Got His Hat On` was superbly sung, underlining what a fine talent Mr Flynn is.

The conniving, materialistic Lady Jacqueline was played with great energy and comic flair by the talented Emma Stowe.
