She combined excellently with Mr Flynn for some of the show`s comic highlights, her `posterior slapping` being foremost amongst these! `You Would If You Could` was hilariously uninhibited as she used her womanly charms in an attempt to snare the newly found Lord Hareford.

Ian Rountree had a good command of dialogue as the `legal eagle` Parchester whose side-splitting, idiosyncratic performance during `The Family Solicitor` was exhilaratingly incongruous.

Ronan Walsh and Caitríona Mongey were perfectly matched as Lord and Lady Battersby in what were very convincing portrayals of a man with a fondness for a tipple and his overbearing other half. Great comic timing from both throughout. Seán Flanagan was an impressive Charles as he maintained a quiet background presence before unleashing some of the show`s best one-liners at the eleventh hour. Doug Hammond was a barking mad Sir Jasper and Michelle O`Connell was a fine Mrs Brown full of nosy intent.

Stage manager Mark Duffy presided over a wonderfully efficient crew which worked closely with cast to ensure excellent continuity throughout. They utilised all of the key elements of the exceptional set from Proscenium with the rose drawing room being particularly impressive. The interior of Hareford Hall did look terribly bare at times and was crying out for dressing. Appropriate curtains on the large windows would have added greatly to the required opulence.

Noel Ryan`s sound design was pretty much flawless throughout. No cues were missed and balance was superb, both vocally and instrumentally. Johnny McDonagh`s lighting was equally impressive with some lovely effects achieved especially during `Leaning on a Lamppost`. I did feel that there was a missed opportunity to close things in and create a more intimate atmosphere for `Once You Lose Your Heart` which was performed in full light.

Tom Walsh and Hugh Hennelly did a great job on props with well chosen furniture, floral centrepiece, tankards and tiger-skin rug standing out as being particularly authentic. A different desk and phone in the library to that in the the rose drawing room would have been preferred.

Costumes, co-ordinated by Rita Monaghan and Carmel Mongey were of a high standard generally. There was a nice distinction between the `upstairs` and `downstairs` staff at Hareford and the aristocrats were suitably attired in their formal wear. The ancestors looked very well. However, their costumes needed to replicate the gauzed `portraits` as closely as possible for their `coming to life` to make sense.

St Mary`s Musical Society has long had a reputation for staging top notch productions. This year was no different thanks to the talented cast and production team which was fully in tune with Ray O`Hare`s vision for what was a thoroughly enjoyable production.

So, `All Shook Up` is an Elvis Presley `jukebox musical` featuring unrequited love aplenty, misunderstandings galore, a dash of mistaken identity and a leading lady who, when masquerading as a guy, gets it on with the MALE object of female desire in a mundane, mid-western U.S. town circa 1955. William Shakespeare (yes, you heard me right!) has a lot to answer for, as it was his `Twelfth Night` which provided the basic plot for such cross-dressing shenanigans! New Ross Musical Society, skilfully guided by director Bill Stafford, accepted the script for the giant ball of camembert that it is, embracing its cheesiness to give us an often side-splittingly funny production. Mr Stafford used cleverly chosen projections to suggest a variety of locations, ensuring that continuity was never compromised. Pace was snappy, as it should be for such corny comedy, and the director balanced hilarity with some unlikely, but beautifully played, emotional moments.

Nick Cooney got a superb sound from his nine-piece band which churned out some very interesting arrangements of twenty- five Elvis tunes. Some wonderful guitar playing in `Roustabout` and saxophone in the heartfelt `There`s Always Me` underlined the quality of musicians in the pit. Mr Cooney was a skilled conductor who had the cast aware of his presence at all times.

Anne-Marie Stafford`s choreography was highly-charged and fun-filled. `Jailhouse Rock` grabbed our attention at the top of the show with its electric energy and the rather bizarre `Devil in Disguise` featuring angels and devils and a `battle of the guitarists` between the mayor and Chad was typical of the close work between choreographer and director as off-beat comedy combined with movement to hilarious effect.

The ensemble in any show is of key importance. Whilst this group was great chorally and showed good potential dramatically, performance and concentration levels were not always strong. A quick scan of the stage during both `If I Can Dream` and `Burning Love` confirmed my thoughts on this. Whilst there were some excellent performers, Graham Finnerty being chief amongst them, some were left wanting when it came to performance and expression. Sometimes all that was needed was a smile.

Alan Whelan was well cast as the hip- swivelling, lady-killing, transvestite- kissing Chad who rides into town to get his motorcycle serviced and brings the female population to its knees as they fall for his charms. Mr Whelan`s performance was perfectly tongue-in-cheek as he took narcissistic coolness to another level. He had a fine singing voice too, displaying a really strong upper register in `Hound Dog`. `I Don`t Want To` was beautifully sung and very cleverly performed as he realised that he loved `Ed`.

Claire Buckley was a charming, somewhat naive, type as the local grease-monkey and love-starved tomboy Natalie. As Natalie`s alter-ego `Ed` she was downright hilarious. It was a very strong comic turn from Ms Buckley who played the role with just the right amount of knowingness. There were so many comic highlights but my favourite had to be her (his!) attempts to resist the amorous advances of Miss Sandra. Comedy gold! She was well able to deliver a song, with `A Little Less Conversation` standing out in particular. Teresa Buckley, as bar proprietor Sylvia, provided the vocal performance of the night when singing `There`s Always Me`. It was a standout musical moment in which Ms Buckley skilfully combined beautiful expression, tone, control, phrasing and powerful emotional range. Ms Buckley was a clever comedienne into the bargain and could sure deliver a one-liner.

James Dobbs was a brilliantly nebbish, self-deprecating Dennis in a very funny portrayal of Chad`s unlucky in love sidekick. His nerdiness was pitched at just the right level as he vied for Natalie`s attention. Mr Dobbs was no `one trick pony` though, as he showed with his stunning rendition of `It Hurts Me` which was full of heartfelt expression and showed his powerful, soaring voice at its best.

Natalie`s father, Jim Haller, was played by Johnny Aylward. Although I had reservations to begin with due to inconsistencies in his accent, this was a performance which balanced comedy and heart very well indeed. His attempts to follow Chad`s lead in becoming more hip were most humorous. Mr Aylward sang very well, particularly in `The Power of My Love`, a duet with Chad which featured some excellent harmonies from both.

Philip Erskine sang excellently as Dean, with `It`s Now or Never` showing off his great range. Dialogue and characterisation needed a bit more guidance but that is something that will come with experience. His love interest, Lorraine, was nicely played by Melanie Cleary who shone as she taught Dean to dance. Ms Cleary had a most pleasant voice even if her harmony line in `If I Can Dream` was not as secure as it could be. Monica Pringle`s repressed Mayor Matilda Hyde was a deliciously funny portrayal. As the town`s moral guardian she denounced "public necking" (and Chad`s pelvis!) and her OTT movement in `Devil in Disguise` had me in stitches. Ms Pringle was flanked throughout by Seán O`Brien as Sheriff Earl. Not being allowed to get a word in edgeways for the duration of the show, his hilarious outburst at the eleventh hour brought the house down.

Caitríona Morrissey had a ball with the role of the prim and proper museum curator Miss Sandra who loses the run of herself and becomes a man-eating, predator. `Let Yourself Go` was brilliantly performed as inhibitions were thrown to the wind and she attempted to seduce `Ed`.

A minimalist set design by Mr Stafford and Tom Reddy worked very well combined with the projected images. A raised platform area, steps and even poles to slide down, provided scope for interesting staging ideas.

Stage Manager, Deborah O`Neill, had a relatively quiet night but performed all duties efficiently allowing for good continuity throughout.

Paul Malone and John Caulfield`s impressive lighting design added so much to the show. There were excellently timed cues for the `One Night With You` running gag and we had some nice, atmospheric mood lighting when required.

Apart from what appeared to be a loose lead issue during the opening number which caused quite a bit of interference, John Coffey`s sound design was solid. Cueing was good and there was a nice balance between the band and performers.

There was great attention to detail from Deborah O`Neill and Seán O`Brien who co-ordinated the impressive costume plot. The blue `suede` shoes for the entire ensemble looked very well. We had leather jackets, glitzy prisoner uniforms, angel/devil outfits and even `statues` which came to life.

Good work too from Peggy Hussey and Julie Rigley on props who ensured everything was appropriate. I particularly liked the mayor`s megaphone which was great fun.

Hair and make-up reflected the 1950s setting and Mr O`Brien`s moustache was a triumph in itself.

`All Shook Up` is becoming a firm favourite with societies at the moment and it`s not hard to see why. Above all else, it is a fun show. Fun to watch and fun to be in, I`m sure. New Ross Musical Society embraced this fun in spades in a most entertaining production.

A marvellous score, wonderfully strong yet humorous characters, heart- wrenching despair and the universal theme of tradition which is as pertinent today as it was in Russia a century ago, all combine to make `Fiddler on the Roof` the iconic musical which it is. Sligo Musical Society presented a very entertaining version of the much-loved classic which went down a storm in the fine Hawk`s Well Theatre.

Sarah Burns` direction was very solid, with some wonderfully imaginative touches. She utilised a very clever revolving set to great effect which allowed for good continuity. The role of the ensemble was clearly a priority for Ms Burns with assurance, confidence and purpose in evidence throughout. The use of the very loud snow machine which only gave partial coverage to one area of the stage did, I feel, take away from what would otherwise have been a touchingly sombre `Anatevka`.

There was a great sound from MD David McEvoy`s eight-piece orchestra. We had superb clarinet during the bottle dance and beautifully played flute in `Now I Have Everything`. A nicely chosen accordion patch on keyboards added much to the ethnic feel throughout. Choral singing was strong, with the men shining in particular during `Sabbath Prayer`. Principal singing was generally strong but Fruma Sarah`s song was taken at such a lick that it was most difficult to make out what was being sung.

Sarah Middleton devised some well- rehearsed routines, perfectly suited to the abilities of her cast. There was great strength and pride in `Tradition`. Superb movement from all during a most entertaining dream sequence culminated in the cast spinning the bed around and a very brave Fruma Sarah flying overhead! The bottle dancers looked suitably terrified and did so well not to `lose their bottle`.

There was a great sense of community from a very involved and dedicated ensemble. `Tradition` was powerful in sound and movement with a great sense of pride etched on the faces of this committed group. The gentlemen made a fine group of vodka-sodden drunkards in the inn scene and the dream was great fun as everyone entered into the `spirit` of things with great gusto. There were superb reactions and ad lobbing aplenty during the wedding scene but people did need to be mindful of the fact that scripted dialogue must be given priority. Paul Maitland looked every inch the perfect Tevye. He made an instant connection with the audience with his warm, honest delivery. We got the impression of a very loving father in what was a most likeable characterisation. Mr Maitland showed a beautifully rich baritone and a full, round tone during `If I Were a Rich Man`. I`m not altogether sure that Mr Maitland had his best night when I attended. We had some tentative moments, dropped cues and `Tevye`s Monologue` lost its way completely. It was a shaky start but he went on to show what a fine performer he is and had the audience eating out of his palm as things progressed.

Margaret Curley was a very strong Golde. Acting was thoughtful and clever and she nailed some comic gems with her acerbic delivery. Her emotional range was exceptional and she was outstanding as she told Tevye of Chava and Fyedka`s marriage. This was a most touching scene pitched at just the right level of emotional intensity. She had a nice quality to her voice in `Sabbath Prayer`. Emily Tansey impressed as Tzeitel, Tevye`s eldest daughter. There was a nice chemistry between herself and Motel and I loved her reactions during `Miracle of Miracles`. Her pleading with Tevye not to make her marry Lazar was nicely measured.

Motel the tailor was played by Eoin Ó Súilleabháin. It was a lovely portrayal which never fell into the trap of overplaying. He was a very real character. There was a great chemistry with Ms Tansey and his diction was excellent. I`m not altogether sure that the substitution of the `v` for `Vonder of Vonders` worked very well but Mr Ó Súilleabháin did sing very well indeed.

Sinéad Sexton sang beautifully as Hodel. Her `Far From the Home I Love` was the musical highlight of the show for me, such was the purity of tone, control and the effortless delivery. Dialogue needed more work though. The potential was there but more attention to subtext and not just the words on the page was required.

Kieran Cunnane made his stage debut as the revolutionary Perchik. He will have learned a lot from being involved. Hand gestures needed to be toned down and some dialogue was rushed but this is the sort of thing that comes with experience. The difficult `Now I Have Everything` was secure right up until the final note. Jennifer Healy, as Chava, gave the performance of the night. It was an excellent characterisation from a very clever actress. Ms Healy lived the character and was always in tune with what was going on around her. She had a wonderful rapport with Fyedka and her scene with Tevye as she pleaded with him to accept her marriage to Fyedka was heart-wrenchingly real.

Ms Healy was indeed fortunate to be playing opposite George Hynes as Fyedka. Mr Hynes was a perfectly credible character with a great natural command of dialogue.

Micki Murray was a larger-than-life Lazar Wolf. Mr Murray is clearly a good comic actor but at times he needed to tone things down so as not to become a complete caricature.

Denise Burns showed herself to be a fine character actress as Yente the matchmaker with a good understanding of pace and comic timing in her opening scene with Golde.

Ultan Burke was a humorous Rabbi and Mark Elliott, as his son Mendel, was quite aggressive at times in his first stage role. It can`t have been easy for Jean McConnell, who played Fruma Sarah, to sing her song as she dangled above the cast. She had a powerful belt voice and deserves accolades galore for bravery! Gia Kilia, from Georgia no less, had the most authentic Russian accent on stage! He had an imposing presence and worked well in his scenes with Mr Maitland. Tommie Bree was excellent as the innkeeper Mordcha.

Stage management was generally good and the main revolving piece facilitated quick transitions. We had a bit of a hiatus going into the inn scene. There was also a rather long delay as the train-station truck was set downstage of the curtain. Jean McConnell did a very good job on props with everything appearing appropriate to the context. The only exception was the very obvious doll which represented the baby.

Lighting was most effective from Frances McGowan. The cyc was used so well to complement the atmosphere. Excellent work in the dream scene and timing of cues during Tevye`s monologue and rebuttal were spot on.

Sound was impressive throughout with a good balance between stage and pit and sharp cueing. Sound effects were appropriate although the operator needed to be mindful of the fact that an abrupt cessation of howling wind just before a song is due to start will not work. Best to fade out slowly.

Wayne Handy built the magnificent set with guidance from the director. The revolve was an inspired idea and I loved the levels provided by the upstage steps. Costumes were a mixed bag. The gentlemen`s Ugg-style boots were not always appropriate. Some colours chosen for the ladies were too bright and some floral designs on the ladies` blouses and scarves too fussy. Perchik`s leather jacket and tan jeans needed serious attention. Gentlemen`s costumes were good generally, particularly the Russian soldiers.

This was a very entertaining, well- directed production from Sligo Musical Society with many dramatic and musical highlights. Thanks to all for a most enjoyable evening.

With The Sound of Music the epoch- making collaboration of Rodgers and Hammerstein came to an end: Oscar Hammerstein II died on August 23, 1960. Happily, this partnership, which changed the destiny of the American musical theatre, ended on a note of triumph. The Sound of Music continues to entertain audiences all over the globe with such favourites as ' I Have Confidence', 'Do- Re-Me', 'Sixteen Going On Seventeen', 'My Favourite Things', 'So Long, Farewell', 'Edelweiss' and many more. Enniscorthy Musical Society continued this tradition with a very entertaining production.

Lorna Mahon Wall was a salient, unbending, pleasant Maria with a beautiful secure singing range. Miss Wall gave a strong performance with gusto and determination in every scene. Anthony Jones gave a fine performance as Captain Von Trapp. He was unduly strict and serious. This experienced actor was secure and imposing. A solid performance! Caroline Daly Jones gave a striking performance as matronly Mother Abbess. This actress was truthful and uplifting. 'Climb every Mountain' was magnificently sung.  Danny Cooper was affable as the vigorous Max Detweiller. Theresa Buckley gave a full-bodied performance as the glamorous Baroness Schraeder.

Stephanie Kinsella was an impressive Liesel. This young actress was heart- warming with a beautiful singing voice. Niall Kavanagh gave a persistent performance as the adolescent Rolf. This young actor was particularly strong in the confrontational dialogue scenes.

Sister Bertha: Rebecca Murphy, Sister Margaretta: Jennifer Byrne, Sister Sophia: Ashley Doran, Sister Therese; Therese Canavan Bolger did very well in their character roles and were very entertaining. Dick Butler gave a spirited performance as Franz, the prescribed Butler and Jan Kennedy had a lovely charm as Frau Schmidt, the competent housekeeper.

Adam O'Leary was a fearless Fredrich. Leanne Cullen was a wonderful rebellious Louisa. Ronan Cloney was a lovely natural young actor and brought great likeability to Kurt. Alice Medcalf captured the bright and honest Brigitta. Eryn Buckley was a delightful and caring Martha and Ailbhe Murphy was a beautiful Gretl.

Musical Director; Kevin Kennedy brought great energy to the temperate score of Richard Rogers with excellent playing from the eight piece orchestra. We had some lovely trumpet playing from Thomas Kavanagh and splendid guitar playing from Rory Cooper. Mr Kennedy moved the show on with undulating pace that was in need of some reining back at times. 'Do-Re-Me' and 'So Long Farewell' were too fast and the Waltz tempo needed to be more measured. Vocal work was very resolute, particularly for 'Praeludium', 'Dixit Dominus' and 'Morning Hymn' with wonderful harmonies and diction. Principles were protected and we also had excellent singing from the children. The female chorus was superb with wonderful harmony singing and devout devotion. They were steady and secure. Director: Ray Quigley gave us a very entertaining production. The pace was maintained as we had some lovely moments. Some exits and entrances were in need of more attention and the lack of a second chair in Mother Abbess's office made for some awkward moments. This production was in need of more attention to detail, i.e. bedclothes, sofa, furniture, garden furniture, presents. Characters were well defined but we did have some very unnatural staging. Stage Manager; Jamie Murphy and his team did a superb job on set changes. Every scene change was resourceful and efficient. Pat Bolger did a good job with props. The set design by Mark Redmond worked very well for this production. We had a very good lighting design from Stage It. We did have some dark spots, particularly mid-stage. Global Sound Systems did a fine job on sound. We did have issues with balance at times and some of the sound effects needed better attention, particularly the storm sound effect.

Costumes from EMS Costume Design were excellent. The children's costumes were superb and the bridesmaids costumes beautiful.  Makeup was good and hair suitably attended too by Nicola Franklin.

Continued success to Enniscorthy Musical Society and thanks to Douglas for looking after me!

Fortwilliam Musical Society relished their time in getting away from it all at the magnificent Theatre at the Mill, Newtownabbey, County Down for their production of Me and My Girl. This show is the very essence of a bit of good old fashioned escapism, a show with a shallow plot, but full of slap-stick entertainment. The challenge with this show is to keep that narrow line between pantomime and comedy. It's a musical comedy, not a pantomime!

Siobhan Mullin; Director gave us a very entertaining and fast moving production. The comedy moments were realised for the most part. Chorus work needed more attention at times. We had some very nice pictures and staging. We did find the Ancestors moving during the Library scene a distraction, but overall a very enjoyable production.  The dancing was very good throughout the production by Choreographer Angela Harding. It was secure and well rehearsed.

The overall company did a sterling job in the many roles i.e. House Guests, Staff, Cockneys, and Townsfolk. Singing was secure for the most part and they were confident and entertaining. Dancing was very good. The Children's chorus was also a great addition!

Tony Young gave a powerful performance as Bill Snibson. This performer had the audience eating out of his hand with some great comic timing and confident delivery. Singing and dancing was first class.  There were times when it became slightly too pantomime, but overall a very enjoyable and entertaining performance. Angela Harding was a very confident Sally Smith. This fine actress and singer gave a secure performance and was also an excellent dancer. Ms Harding captured the tender moments and had all the swagger of a genuine cockney lass. Dawn Patton was a fantastic Lady Jacqueline, full or energy and self- assuredness. This actress was a joy to watch and delivered the comedy with exactitude. 'You Would if You Could' was a highlight, sassy, sexy and hilarious! Barry O'Kelly gave a full-on performance in the grandiloquent role of Gerald, the nincompoop. This actor delivered his dialogue with great energy. We had a fantastic performance from Siobhan Farrell as the imposing Maria; Duchess of Dene. We were reminded many times of that comic genius Hyacinth Bucket from 'Keeping up Appearances'.

Eamon Connolly did a fine job with the always picked-on, thankless role of Sr. John. The drunken scene was great!  Drew Reid was a very imposing Parchester. This utmost actor was ever present. We had an unyielding performance from Denis Cooke as Sir Jasper. Charles O'Kelly was fine as Charles. Maria Sweeney was good as Mrs Brown, with a good accent. Fergal McCarry did very well as Lord Battersby and Elizabeth McGeown was secure as Lady Battersby.

Musical Director, William Cairns, managed this group of musicians with determination and immense control at all times. We had some lovely playing from the strings particularly during 'Once you Lose Your Heart' and the piano accompaniment was also beautiful. Harmonies were secure for the most part from the chorus but they were not confident with words at all times. There were some issues with pit/stage balance. Male singing also needed more attention. We had some very nice work with the principles.

Costumes were a little hit and miss from Triple C's Costume Hire. We would have liked hats for 'The Sun has Got It's Hat On'. Sr. John needed an overcoat for the bar scene. We needed some Red Costumes for the Fox Hunt scene, there was too much black. Well done on shoes! Hair and Make-up was well attended to by Siobhan Morris and her team.

The set design by Siobhan Mullin and Liam Berry, was functional and worked very well. Stage Management was efficient under the stewardship of Gerard Kelly. Scene changes were efficient. It was probably not a good idea to use one of the cockney characters in costume to strike the bar scene? The props were well attended to by Eleanor O'Neill. They were appropriate for the most part. Parchester could have done with more 'papers'. The earpiece for Sr. Jasper was very imposing. The stage furniture was excellent. The suitcases needed to be larger!

David Walker looked after sound. The sound balance was not very consistent and we had some obvious feedback. Lighting was looked after by Siobhan Mullin and Kevin McReynolds. Lighting cues were excellent and we had some lovely pools or light. The spotlights were nicely defused.

Continued success and thank you to for a great night's entertainment!

Guys and Dolls is a musical that has it all: Larger-than-life characters who are at the same time wonderfully real, a score that is the very definition of musical comedy perfection, and a story that captures Manhattan at its vintage best (1950) - when there were newsstands lining the streets, cinched waist suits for women and Salvation Army missions competing for customers with such clubs as the "Hot Box," where sassy chorus girls took to the stage. And if you are in search of even more nostalgia, there is that island called Cuba, a wonderfully exotic playground ideal for an overnight romp fuelled by Bacardi. Add to that a battle of the sexes and you have a great show. Kilmacud Musical Society brought together a stellar cast for their recent production in The Mill Theatre, Dundrum. The overture opened well under Musical Director David 'Doc' O'Connor, with solid playing from an accomplished band of musicians. Trombone was slightly insecure at times. The balance was good. Choral singing was secure, but overall it required more accent and attack. The band needed to be slightly more playful at times with the various time signatures and needed to embrace the quirkiness of this score and the overriding style of the 1940's jazz and swing. We needed the bustle of city life in Runyonland with many contrasting threads to the beautifully crafted soaring melodies with wide leaps (sixths, sevenths and octaves) of 'I've Never Been in Love Before' to the syncopated 'Gamblers Ballet'.

Amy Byrne did very well as buttoned-up Sarah Brown, our innocent and conviction-driven sergeant of the mission 'Save a Soul'. Amy was strong vocally, although her upper range was stretched. Her acting was hit and miss at times where some reactions were over reached. This young actress needs to trust her instincts more and relax. Niall MacCarthy was a very imposing and commanding Sky Masterson. This singer had a beautiful tone to his voice and a very expressive vocal quality. Mr MacCarthy was vocally exposed on 'My Time of Day', but was consistent. Well done! Jennifer Fahy was perfectly cast as Miss Adelaide showing lots of potential. This actress needed to embrace this character with more physical energy and animation. Her comedy timing was excellent but not consistent. We needed Adelaide to stand out more, particularly for 'Bushel and a Peck'.  A very enjoyable performance! Making up our quartet was Alan Davoren, a very accomplished Nathan Detroit. This fine actor and singer was animated, energized and delivered each and every gag with confidence and excellent timing. He was a great master of comedy and had wonderful physical presence and piercing eyes. Excellent! Orbiting around this quartet was Paul Holloway as the skirt-chasing Benny. He was hilarious, confident and always in character. A fantastic rounded genial performance from Chris O'Connor as Nicely-Nicely. Fantastic comedy moments, animated and driven. Sit Down You're Rockin The Boat' was a highlight! A great performance from Carl Mageean as Harry the Horse and Pat O'Keeffe was magnificent as pistol packing Big Jule. He sustained the character and delivered each and every line with confidence and excellent timing. We had a fine performance from Pat Hennessy as Joey Biltmore with great comedy timing! Billy Andrews was fine as Rusty Charlie and Ian Tighe did fine as Lieutenant Brannigan, although accent was an issue at times. Marijka Walsh was a lovely compassionate Abigail. Kim Bolger gave a convincing portrayal of General Cartwright. The company worked very hard to recreate the fun that is 'Guys and Dolls'. They were secure but needed to be more confident. Singing was good. This production needed much more attention to detail under the stewardship of Director; Justin Parkes, with many obvious comedy opportunities missed and a certain lack of props. Staging was insecure with too many moments of upstaging and a mixed bag of stage direction. The stage pictures needed more definition and construction. We had some staging set too far upstage and behind desk and chairs. The dialogue was missing much of the tension required. Some stage entrances and exits also needed further attention as they were inconsistent. Dancing was a mixed bag under choreographer Nicola McDonald. The Crapshooters ballet was disappointing and needed more work. Stage management under the watchful eye of Gerry McCann was efficient. Props needed much more attention in the overall production. The Sound and Music Company did a good job on sound. The overall set design was functional and worked well for the show in this venue. It was in need of more definition; maybe some silver on the backdrop to pick out lights in buildings. It was a little flimsy but worked well. Gary O'Daly did a good job on lights. We would have liked more colour.

The costume team brought together a mixed bag of costumes. I had an issue with Sky's suit as it was in need of a pressing! Adelaide's costumes also needed attention as there was a distinct lack of style and an obvious lack of a bag or bags. We also had a fantastic mac coat on one chorus member that would have been better served on Lieutenant Brannigan.

Hair and makeup was well attended to by Portobello Institute, although Sarah had too much make-up applied.

Overall the production needed more attention to detail, but we had a good night in Dundrum.

What singles out The Wizard of Oz from our more conventional musicals is the fact that it is a fantasy musical. My understanding is that it was a response by MGM in 1939 to the production of the highly successful Disney film 'Snow White and The Seven Dwarfs' (1937). A fairy-book tail in a fairy-book style! In the broader sense we could categorise it as a good road movie similar to Priscilla - Queen of the Desert, but whatever it is, it is a good night's entertainment. That is just what we got in Naas from LARK, the musical society based in Kildare Town. The stage production was full of imagination, creativity, fantasy and magic and yet they brought some parts of the stage experience into the twenty first century with a backdrop of slides and film iconography. Did this work? I think… yes! This production was full of creativity and imagination under the excellent direction of Padraig J. Dunne. The story was clear and the ingenious collaboration with video introduction and interludes made for a very exciting presentation. The video projections were expertly produced and added greatly to our experience. The staging was inventive and original with some lovely stage pictures and states making for a wonderful magical journey. This director kept the pace brisk and moving.  The dance for the production by Choreographer; Deirdre Browne was within the capabilities of this mixed cast. It was original and resourceful and well executed by the cast. There were some lovely moments and the younger cast were integrated appropriately into the dance routines. We loved the Rabbits, The Munchkins, Lollipop Guild, the Ballerinas and The Merry Old Land of Oz. There was great energy in the dance for 'The Witch Is Dead'. Well done! The set design was excellent for this production. The walkway gave great heights and the centre stage area made for a good acting area. The upstage fence could probably have been removed as the show progressed. Noreen Quinlivan did a very good job as Stage Manager and her team were efficient. Set changes were slick and well managed. Well done on the mopping-up of the water!

The props were excellent also full of imagination, creativity and colour under the artistic eye of Noreen Quinlivan, Valerie Boyle and Jean Moroney. The props added greatly to the production values. The costumes were fantastic, under the creative touch of Brid O'Shea and Linda Heffernan. They were magical, colourful, inventive and most appropriate with the addition of excellent head gear adding to the overall experience. Well done! Hair and makeup was also inventive from Ashlea Cox and her team. Dawn Broughan was the perfect Dorothy. This beautiful singer and fine actress captured the essence of the character with appropriate naivety and youthfulness. 'Over The Rainbow' was a highlight. Miss Broughan brought energy to every dialogue scene and her southern accent was perfect. A joy! Ellen Heffernan was a fine actress in the role of Scarecrow. Her gender did not take from her performance as she represented the Midwestern farmers and the tension between knowledge and wisdom. This young actress was a physical joy to watch as she slid from scene to scene. 'If I Only Had a Brain' was well delivered. Kevin McCarthy was a stiffened and yet robust Tin Man. This fine actor delivered his character with determination as he represented the hardened Industrial worker. 'If I Only Had a Heart' was very well delivered. Director Padraig J Dunne was a wonderful cowardly Lion. This seasoned actor displayed excellent comedy timing and great vocal expression in every scene. He had a natural aplomb and connection with the audience. His delivery of 'If I Only Had the Nerve' was excellent. Trina Byrne was fine as aunt Em. This actress had good physical presence but needed to be more secure with her accent.  Paul Heffernan was secure as Uncle Henry. Evelyn Kelly was a powerful Miss Culch with a fiery and deliciously tyrannical accent. Grace Philips was secure as our good witch 'Glinda'. A lovely gently performance! Helena Duggan was a tour-de-force as The Wicked Witch of The West. This actress was full of energy and consumed the role with dynamism and vitality at all times. Ollie Byrne was very good as the Guard. Francis Gatley made a lovely Zeke. Laura Hannon was very good as Hickory. Carol O'Suillivan was great as Hunk. Michael Collins was a very gentle professor Marvel. Dave Wilson gave a very solid performance as the kind, ordinary man 'The Wizard'. Cormac Dredge was very good as The General and the young actor Tom Dunne, aged 9yrs was great as the Munchkin Mayor. This company were committed to the magic and mystery of this show. They showed their versatility and creativity throughout the production.

Musical Director; Lisa Nagle and her fine band captured the simplicity and lightness of this Harold Arlen score with some fine playing. Tempos were energetic and cueing was precise. Underscoring was full and broad when needed. Singing was secure from the mixed chorus with harmonies satisfactorily achieved. Soloists were protected and supported at all times.

Well done LARK!

Aidan Donoghue was a wonderful Bill Snibson. A fantastic singer and dancer, a perfect vaudeville performer with excellent comedy timing and delivery throughout the show. He embraced the challenging role with confidence and energy. 'Leaning on the Lampost' was a highlight. His Michael Crawford (Frank Spencer) moments were hilarious! His timing with the hat (gag) on the sofa was perfect! Carol Gleeson was a beautifully measured Sally. This supreme actress could sing and dance too, wonderful rapport with Bill and beautiful tender moments when needed. A stunning successful performance! Gearoid McGauran gave the full on, silly, perpetually cheerful interpretation of Gerald. He was hilarious! A great performance. Julie Donnelly was the perfect bombshell, scheming and calculating Jacquie, always dynamic and self-absorbed. Ms Donnelly entertained in every scene and her performance of 'You Would If You Could' was magnificent!  We had an imperial performance from Mona Conroy as the Duchess. This grand lady was impressive and we couldn't keep our eyes off of her! A real treat! William Lacy was a perfect Sir John, the kindly older gentleman, rather fond of the drink but sympatric to Bill and Sally. Peter Fay was imposing as Parchester the family solicitor. We had a solid performance from Val Brennan as Sir Jasper. Conor Byrne was fine as Charles and Eileen Flannery was very good as Mrs Brown with a great accent. Brian Kiernan did fine as Lord Battersby. Carmel Geissel was solid as Lady Battersby. Peter Nolan did very well as The Telegram Boy. A very special moment. Well done! This company were committed to the comedy moments and their singing was excellent particularly for 'An English Gentleman'. This was a very solid and secure production from Director Arthur McGauran with some striking staging and comedy direction. We had some lovely production touches and great attention to detail. The overall style of the show was well delivered and appreciated. This production had confidence and the pace moved very well from scene to scene. The choreography was outstanding for this production with magnificent tap dancing and group involvement by Deirdre Browne. We would have liked some movement for the finale reprise. The dream ballet was beautiful.

The set design for this production was excellent and effective by Bob O'Kelly and Arthur McGauran.  Scenes were very well defined. The library was very impressive as was the very inventive transformation into and out of the car. Stage Management under the attentive and crafted talent of Bob O'Kelly was efficient and very impressive. We were impressed with the scene change into and out off the street scene, a great transformation. We could have been a little more precise with the turning panels. Well done! Props for this production were excellent under the attentive eye of Ger Cullen and Deirdre Delahunty. A reminder to some cast to use props more appropriately e.g. Sally's case would probably have been slightly heavier! Some 'soap' on the trays may have sorted the reflection problem. We could have used ashtrays and more glasses in the bar and the letters would probably have been on a variety/different types of papers. The large book in the library was great!

Tom Kelly did a very good job on lighting design and execution. Excellent star cloth. Vinnie Osborne, The Sound and Music Company did well on sound. I did have an issue with balance at times. Costumes were first-rate under the stewardship of Trish Mooney full of colour and variety. We would have liked to have seen more hats, bags and coats. We had some excellent jewellery. Hair and Make-up was well attended to by Sinead Smullen and her team.

Congratulations to Naas Musical society on a most enjoyable show!

Nenagh Choral Society were delighted to be finally staging what is a universally dearly loved musical; The Sound Of Music.

Emily Sheary was a striking, strong- willed, temperate Maria with a beautiful secure singing range. Acting was slightly too flamboyant at times as we had too much 'familiarity' with the captain, but, overall we had a very strong performance from this actress for what is a very demanding iconic role. Paul Shesgreen gave a good performance as Captain Von Trapp. He was suitably austere and sober. The gentler and more emotional side of the character needed more work in order to bring this performance to life. Niamh Chadwick gave a beautiful performance as Mother Abbess. This actress was sincere and heart-warming with a beautiful rendition of 'Climb Every Mountain' while Patrick Rohan was amiable as the energetic Max Detweiller. Louise Cormack gave a robust performance as the glamorous Baroness Schraeder, ever present and demanding. Billie Kelly was a dazzling Liesel.

Paul Browne gave a steadfast performance as the young Rolf. This actor was particularly strong in the aggressive dialogue, showing his versatility. Sister Bertha: Caoimhe Geaney, Sister Margarettta: Zelda Dillon, Sister Sophia: Naomi Morrissey did very well in their character part roles and all were very well cast. Michael Cormack gave a feisty performance as Franz, the formal butler and Amy Ryan had a strong charisma as Frau Schmidt, the efficient housekeeper. The children in this production never faltered. They were a real treat! Shane Slattery was a brave Fredrich. Eva McKeogh was a great defiant Louisa. Manus Heehan was a lovely part-brave, part-kind Kurt. Caroline Browne captured the intelligent and truthful Brigitta. Grace Shesgreen was a cute and tender Martha while Alannah Slattery was a gorgeous sweet Gretl.

The Nuns chorus was superb with wonderful harmony singing of Godly devotion. They were constant and well rehearsed.

Director; Greg Browne gave us a production that moved along well with some fastidious touches. We had some lovely staged pictures, well devised scene changes but unfortunately some musical scenes were over directed and missing genuine motivation and soul. Entrances and exits needed to be thought out more and some wandering around the stage for dialogue scenes was noticeable. The production was nonetheless going in the right direction, but needed much more consistency and authority in direction. The inclusion of the real live dogs was a nice touch. Musical Director; Laura Kearney was in command of this solid orchestra at all times with secure direction and control. Playing was protected, cueing was tight and our musical director interpreted the score with a beautiful sense of appropriate musicality. Choral vocal work was very unyielding, particularly for 'Praeludium', 'Dixit Dominus' and 'Morning Hymn'. Principals were secure in their singing and we had excellent work with the children.

The set design by Greg Browne worked very well for this production. The design was inventive and added to the production values. The stain-glass windows were beautiful. The Austrian flag could have been better placed. Stage Manager; Brendan Manning and his team did an excellent job on scene changes. Every scene change was efficient and propitious. Catherine Condon and Rachel Browne did an excellent job on props. We would have liked a better whistle for Van Trapp. John Coffey did a fine job on sound. Cueing was excellent and balance secure.

Costumes from Pat McGann Productions were very suitable. Nun's habits, uniforms and the children's costumes were excellent. I was somewhat disappointed that the children's costumes did not match the bedroom curtains. Makeup was good and hair suitably attended to by Judith Hassett and her team. We did have too much eye makeup on Mother Abbess.

We had a very good lighting design from John Coffey. The cueing was efficient and the lighting complemented the set design. We did have some dark spots, particularly mid-up-stage. We also had lighting issues in the bedroom scene. Thank you Nenagh Coral Society for another warm welcome!

South Eastern Youth Theatre Group was founded in 2011 by Brian Collins and David Hennessy to give youths of Waterford and the South East area an opportunity to perform in quality musical productions and that is just what we got in the magnificent Theatre Royal, Waterford City.

The overall production was very well accomplished by director David Hennessy as this young cast were well rehearsed and committed to the task on hand. The pace was steady with good use of the acting space. Heights upstage could have been better used at times by overall the direction was tight and forceful as the complex story of love and tragedy was unearthed by this talented cast. The young actress, Holly Ryan, was magnificent in the emotionally challenging role of orphan Kim, capturing not only the mature themes, but bringing a maturity way beyond her years. Ms Ryan, a remarkable singer, left not a dry eye in the house. 'I'd Give My Life For You' was a highlight!

Paul Mescal gave a powerful performance as the conflicted and passionate American marine Chris. Singing was explosive and emotionally charged at all times from this imposing actor. 'Why God Why' was very impressive.  Adam Phelan was mightily charismatic as the sleazy pimp Engineer.

This performer was bigger than life and relished the role with pace and energy. 'If You Want to Die in Bed' and 'The American Dream' were captivating. Megan DeCourcey gave a standout performance as Ellen, Chris's wife. This actress brought style and presence to this role. Singing was secure and 'Now That I've Seen Her' was beautifully sung. Conor Clancy was a passionate and engaging John, best friend to Chris with fine vocals from this sensitive actor. Joshua Hurley gave a supreme performance in the demanding role of self-obsessed Thuy. Characterisation was very well defined and delivered with passion and asceticism. We had a preponderate performance from Julie Power as the sexy bar girl Gigi. Singing was dynamic, particularly for 'Movie In My Mind'. Thi-Yen Alward was a lovely Tam, son of Kim. This young company were fully engaged in this production. Bargirls were suitably brave, marines were energised and towns people/mob rightfully forceful. Choral singing was powerful and excellently delivered. It was a triumph!

The fine orchestra under the Musical Direction of Wayne Browne was very secure for this enormously complex score, full of dynamic musical numbers and some beautiful endearing ballads. The fourteen piece orchestra including Violins, Cello, Bass, Flute, Reeds, Trumpet, Trombone, Horn, Keyboards, and Percussion was conscientious of tempos. Flute was exposed at times. Underscoring was secure. Sounds were broad and engulfing. Singing from the female chorus was very strong, but the male chorus singing was not as secure, particularly with harmonies for 'Bui Doi'. Soloists were protected and supported by the musical director at all times. We did have some over-stretching vocally for some numbers, but overall a musical treat!

The choreography under the innovative eye of Michelle Condon was very well accomplished. Dancing was secure and within the capabilities of the cast. 'The Morning Of The Dragon' was a highlight! Stage management was excellently delivered by stage Manager Brian Collins and his crew. The set changes were smooth and slick. Mary Doherty and her team did an excellent job on prop procurement.

Set Design by Dermot Quin was inventive and made for very smooth transitions between the scenes. The overall aesthetic was beautiful. Fantastic helicopter moment. Well done! Paul Brown, lighting designer, brought some very nice dimensions to the overall lighting experience. There was a tendency to over-use the movers, but overall a well attended rig. Gelling was good.

Costumes were well attended to by Avril Musgrave and her team. We had great uniforms, street girls and mob costumes. Principal costumes were very well attended to. Congratulations! Ali Murphy and her team did an excellent job on hair and make-up. Wigs were excellent. Sound design by Jodie Trehy was excellent. Balance was an issue at times. Cueing was excellent.

Congratulations to all involved!

Co. Down embraced the challenge with enthusiasm and dedication. Musical Director Denise Kelly was in control of the small band at all times. Playing was secure, cueing was relatively tight and the band interpreted the score with passion. Vocal work was very solid, particularly for 'Praeludium', 'Dixit Dominus' and 'Morning Hymn'. Principals were secure in their singing and great work was achieved with the children. Director: Garry Warnock gave us a good overall experience. The production moved along well with some nice touches. There was more need for inventive direction. Some dialogue scenes needed a better natural staging structure and we had some over animation for songs. Pauline McCarthy did a good job with the dancing in the Ballroom scene. The set design by Francie Morgan worked very well for this production. Stage Management under the stewardship of Cathal McKervey was efficient and also worked very well. Scene changes were secure and well planned. Well done! Mathew Campbell and Mel Carney did a fine job on props. We had a very good lighting design from Danny Doherty. The cueing from Eoin Quail was efficient. The sound levels were a little hit and miss, unfortunately we had some intrusive feedback at times.

Costumes from Utopia and managed by Paul Kelly were a mixed bag. Nun's costumes, uniforms and the children's costumes were fine, but the chorus costumes needed more attention. Be mindful of black tights under ballroom dresses! Night attire for Maria needed more attention. The wedding gown was excellent, but we needed better bridesmaid's dresses for the children. We needed a hat and coat for Maria as she returns to the Abby. We had a beautiful red cape for Mother Abbess! Makeup was good and hair suitably attended too by Aine Barron.

Charlotte Burke was a beautiful free spirited, warm and kind Maria. Singing was secure. Acting needed to be more natural and this actress needs to trust her own intuition. The dialogue was somewhat forced at times leading to over animation. Brian McElroy gave a good performance as Captain Von Trapp. He was appropriately strict and military- like. This actor needed to embrace the warmth of the character and his journey from grief stricken widower to reigniting his passion for life through music and new found love. Audrey Neil captured the maternal nature of the Mother Abbess. 'Climb Every Mountain' was wonderful. Diarmuid Taggart was charming as the always plotting Max Detweiller. Kathryn-Anne Millar gave a very strong performance as the glamorous Baroness Schraeder. Courtney Burns was a gorgeous Liesel while Mathew Campbell gave an unyielding performance as the pleasant and young suitor Rolf.

Sister Bertha: Dolores Kearney, Sister Margaretta: Karen Laverty, Sister Sophia: Niamh Conway did very well in these cameo roles. Mel Carney gave a spirited performance as Franz, the formal butler. Lorna Maguire had a strong presence as Frau Schmidt, the efficient housekeeper. Maybe a tad too young for the role? Dermot Carney was a spirited Fredrich. Zoe Hanna was a great rebellious Louisa. Ciaran Rowan was a lovely part spirited, part gentle Kurt. Sara Kelly captured the smart and overly honest Brigitta. Maebh Barnes was a sweet and gentle Martha while Cliona Hanna as Gretl tugged the audience's heartstrings with her sore finger The Nuns chorus was excellent with wonderful singing. They were committed and well rehearsed.

Thank you Downpatrick for a great night's entertainment!

The Witches of Eastwick is a funny, sexy, not for children show, but that didn't deter Trim Musical Society as they took the risk!

Director Gareth Mahony pulled out all the stops for this production. The dialogue was very well pointed and the jokes were on the rampage and forthcoming. The staging was very satisfactory with internal states excellently defined with various appropriate furniture items. External states, including the tennis court, were also well defined. The 'Flying' of the three Witches was a marvel and worked extremely well. The turntable was also a delightful moment. This production was bursting with very well directed and worked out 'comedy moments'. This production soared along with energy and meticulousness. The dancing for this production complimented the overall arc of the show, from choreographer Julie Donnelly. The routines were congruent and within the capabilities of the cast. Final pictures were well delivered and precise. 'Dance With the Devil' was fun, hot and sexy! The overture opened with exuberantly brassy vaudevillian music played by skilled and multitalented musicians under Musical Director Graham Walsh. He was in calm measured control and the orchestra playing was solid under vocalists and chorus. The different styles, 1960's pop-rock and 1950's Las Vegas, were well accomplished. We had some excellent underscore playing from lead guitar and exciting playing from brass. The Cello playing for 'Waiting for the Music to Begin' was superb. The harmonies were well rehearsed with the chorus and secure, leading to a very appropriate choir feel at times. 'I Love a Little Town', 'Dirty Laundry' and 'The Glory of Me' were a highlight. Soloists were safe and secure at all times. It was a musical victory!

The overall set design was well-designed and worked well for this show. Frank Connolly and his team did a fine job in the backstage area with sublime set changes, exact and strict.  Props were very well attended to by Marty Flaherty and Susan Murphy. We loved the phones! The martini glasses were perfect. The sound was very well delivered by Alan White. Balance was excellent and cueing was always on-cue. Brendan Fox had some issues with lighting. We needed to have better face lighting covering U/S and Mid/Stage areas as we did have some dark areas. Some lighting cues were too slow and inconsistent. Lighting for the 'flying sequence' needed to be looked at as it was hard to see them. It is always a challenge to use moving heads as spotlights and they need to be well rehearsed and timed with the cast. Great moon Gobo!

Makeup and hair was well attended to by Claire Farrell, Gillian Kavanagh and Aisling Murphy. Wardrobe was looked after by Margaret Dunne and Debbie Walsh. The costumes were excellent with fantastic costumes for the principles, particularly Darryl. The red zoot-suit was fantastic. The three witches cream jackets were perfect, the black suit and red braces was excellent and the chorus costumes all worked.

Niall Dempsey was the consummate charismatic "Ladies Man" with a wildly wicked streak. This actor had excellent comedy timing, broad when required and subtle when needed. It was never a case of 'lampoon', it was always measured and at all times in character and plot driven, full of testosterone and tongue. He was crude and rude and it worked. Singing was stretched at times, but even so, an extravagance! Helen McHugh delivered Alexandra, the single parent, struggling sculptor character with delightful proficiency. Singing was potent, full-bodied and tuneful. A delight! Louise Cassidy was perfectly cast as Jane Smart, the music teacher, tense and cynical cellist. This actress was a wonderful comedy actor displaying immense vocal agility and physical expression through dialogue and song. A treat! Siobhan McAleese displayed preferential acting as the tongue-tied, insecure newspaper writer Sukie. Ms McAleese was also a wonderful singer, committed and focused giving a tour- de-force performance. A joy! The mean spirited Felicia, whose blue nose is out of joint because of the carnal cavorting was played by Gwen Bagnall, with facial expressions capable of stopping a battleship, singing and doing what should be impossible by simultaneously spitting up golf balls, spiders, cherry pits, an egg, and even a tennis ball was overwhelming. A spectacle!

Aidan Mitchell did very well as Clyde Gabriel. Funny and entertaining! What a fantastic rounded performance from Tom Moran as Michael, son of Alexandra. This young man can certainly act and sing. Jane Brogan was spirited and strong as Jennifer Gabriel. Megan Pottinger was compelling and mysterious as little Girl with excellent singing and stage presence.

The men and women of the chorus did very well. Singing was strong and secure and the dancing was exciting and full of energy. Each and every member was committed to the production.

I hope to see The Witches of Eastwick again in the future and thank you to Trim for my first experience of seeing this hilarious show on stage!

First published in the 1700s, `Beauty and the Beast is indeed the "tale as old as time" the song professes it to be. It`s hard to believe that the Disney treatment of this fairytale is over twenty years old. Avonmore Musical Society`s extremely entertaining production remained true to this animated classic and we were treated to a visual, comical and emotional feast which thrilled adults and children alike.

Bill Stafford brought his wealth of experience to bear on this huge show. There was comic business aplenty, great attention to the relationships at the emotional centre of the piece and superb work with a suitably `animated` ensemble. Staging was generally strong although there were issues with sightlines which needed attention at times.

Musical director Mairéad McKenna did a superb job on this show, bringing out the Disney magic at every turn. She presided over a wonderful orchestra, conducting with great control and sensitivity. From the beautifully sympathetic piano accompaniment at the start of `Home`, to the unrestrained fervour of `The Mob Song` this was an MD and orchestra at the top of their respective games. Principal singing was first rate and the ensemble sang well throughout.

Martina Lynch not only choreographed some impressive and hugely fun routines, she also found time to perform in them as a standout member of the ensemble. The tankard `chorus- line` in `Gaston` was superbly realised and the visual extravaganza that was `Be Our Guest` was suitably Busby Berkeley in its creation and execution in what was the showstopping number of this fine production.

There was great expression and life in this ensemble which played everything from villagers to kitchen utensils and clearly Mr Stafford had worked hard to get his charges in tune with the animated roots of this version of the timeless tale. Chorally the group was strong, especially in the wild abandon of `The Mob Song` which built to a marvellously threatening crescendo. Denise Brennan was most convincing as our book-loving heroine. She was tough and feisty when required but melted hearts in her more tender moments. Ms Brennan had a remarkable singing voice which had the most crystal clear tone. `Home` was beautifully sung in what appeared to be an effortless rendition which tugged at the heartstrings.

Chris Currid gave a stellar performance as a brooding but endearing Beast. There was a great physicality to this portrayal as Mr Currid balanced his vulnerable human side with his more hideous animal side. Mr Currid was wonderful vocally. His incredible interpretation of the sentimental `If I Can`t Love Her` was simply stunning as he combined power and exceptional control with heartfelt angst.

Gaston was played with muscle- flexing buffoonery by the towering Seán Hendley who was clearly having the time of his life with this gem of a role. Mr Hendley brought narcissism to a new level as he proclaimed himself to be the epitome of human perfection in the well performed `Gaston` which showcased his fine baritone voice. His hapless sidekick Le Fou was cartoonishly played by Tomás Byrne. Mr Byrne is a great physical comedian and filled the role of Gaston`s `whipping boy` admirably as he literally suffered for his art at Mr Hendley`s hands. Equipped with a fine store of cartoon-like, rubberised facial expressions, Mr Byrne got the most out of this very funny portrayal.

James Kearon was a gloriously dotty Maurice. There was a gorgeous connection with Ms Brennan in what was a very believable father/daughter relationship. Although his was an often humorous portrayal, we really felt for him as the show progressed. French candelabra and serial flirt Lumiére was played by Brendan Kenny. Whilst I thought that Mr Kenny did well in the role, I felt that better diction and a less speedy delivery would have helped him to fulfil his comic potential even further. His `Be Our Guest` was excellent vocally and performance wise, underlining what a talented performer Mr Kenny is.

The highly-strung Cogsworth was played with great comedic banter by Patrick Bracken. Mr Bracken was full of indignant stuffiness and had impeccable timing (of course!). He played well off Mr Kenny and was well able to deliver a one-liner. "If it`s not Baroque...don`t fix it!" was my personal favourite.

Naoimh Penston was a motherly Mrs Potts in a superb performance which had echoes of Angela Lansbury who voiced the role in the animated film. This was first rate acting and singing from Ms Penston whose beautifully controlled soprano brought the Disney magic to life in the title number. How Ms Penston negotiated the tight entrances and exits in her enormous teapot is just beyond me!

Elaine Sweeney was a marvellous Madame de la Grande Bouche. She played the enchanted wardrobe with a deft comic touch and proved no slacker in the vocal department either. Ciara Spellman got great fun out of her role of feather duster Babette in a flirtatiously humorous portrayal. Eleven year old Luke Heffernan was a most impressive Chip, proving that the society need not worry about the talent pool drying up anytime soon. Seanna Connolly, Tara Sterling Byrne and Fiona Byrne worked very well as a unit and were excellent as Gaston`s fawning `groupies` the Silly Girls. Rob Donnelly was a dead ringer for Danny de Vito in his penguin days as the malevolent Monsieur D`Arque. He had a scarily ominous presence in what was a very impressive performance.

Padraig Reid`s lighting design was strong throughout. Colours were well chosen and there was very good use of gobos. `The Mob Song` was particularly well lit.

The elaborate set, designed by Dermot Quinn, was a visual treat. From the imposing gates at the top of the show to the majestic castle interior, there was attention to detail everywhere. I did not feel, however, that it was a very crew friendly set as the flow of the show was often compromised by crew trying to negotiate the very large pieces. Crew, under Barry Ryan`s management, did well considering the tight space and the colossal set. However the decision to strike some items in full light was, I felt, ill-judged.

There were excellent props in evidence throughout. Maurice`s `invention` was most impressive and the various implements used by the mob were well chosen.

Hair and make-up were, as one would expect for this particular show, of a very high standard. The Beast was a wonderfully hideous creation and Mr Hendley`s hilarious wig nearly stole every scene it was in!

Costumes, hired from the UK touring company, were the icing on the cake in this visual spectacular.

The authenticity of the breathtaking costumes added so much and anchored the production firmly in its animated film roots.

Jason Fallon`s sound design was, as usual, of a very high standard with excellent cueing throughout and some superbly chosen sound effects integrated seamlessly into the action. Avonmore Musical Society proved that its reputation is well deserved with this thoroughly enchanting production of the much-loved Disney show. I very much look forward to their next production.

"If you open your mind, oh the thinks you will find, lining up to get loose!" So announces the mischievous Cat in the Hat during the opening number of `Seussical the Musical` as he invites us to suspend disbelief and enter the whimsical, Seussian world inspired by the tales of Theodore Geisel, written over fifty years ago. The success of `Seussical` depends largely on the willingness of its audience to buy into this fantasy as well as the ability of cast and production team to maintain a clarity of narrative throughout this challenging show.

Alan Recks`s production for Clara Musical Society was a visual treat full of colour and creativity from all involved. There were some excellent principal performances and some beautifully staged pictures, the most impressive being during the `Solla Sollew` number, gorgeously framed by twinkling stars behind an upstage gauze. Some choices affected the clarity of narrative significantly, however. Amongst these was the splitting of the Jojo role between two different children which was confusing and served no clear purpose. Mayzie`s egg should not have been seen until she got herself `in trouble` courtesy of the rogue Tweet McFirth and we could clearly see Horton`s clover in Gertrude`s hair before the big revelation at the end of `All for You` that she had found it. Such attention to detail is important if the tricky narrative is to be negotiated.

Directing  Seussical is a big job but to double up as MD is a mammoth task. "Anything`s possible" though and full credit to Mr Recks who guided his eight piece band from his keyboard through the eclectic musical styles ranging from powerful ballads to Latin rhythms. There was a great sound from the band generally but bass and drums needed to keep more of an eye on Mr Recks`s conducting at times and there were some less than accurate trombone playing throughout. Choral singing was very strong in `Solla Sollew` but `The Grinch Carved the Roast Beast` was in need of tidying up.

Sarah Griffin`s choreography was clever, clean and full of the great energy and life required for a fantastical show like this. There was excellent focus and precision from the talented children in `The Military` and `Havin` a Hunch` was a superbly clever number combining white gloves, UV lighting and exceptionally executed, sharp movement which was extremely effective.

There was a talented ensemble at work here which was at its best during the difficult courtroom scene requiring a lot of concentration and focus. The Whos evoked much pity for their plight as we willed the citizens of Nool to believe in their existence. There was a sense of everyone working hard on stage, however lyrics were not secure from everyone in the finale `Green Eggs and Ham` which was disappointing.

John Coss was a whirlwind of energy and agility as the madcap Cat in the Hat. He displayed great versatility assuming multiple manic roles from talk-show host to circus ringmaster to auctioneer with great comic flair. Mr Coss was an excellent mover and had a most pleasing vocal tone which was at its best in `Havin` a Hunch`.

Sinéad Handy combined exceptional physicality with more than a hint of quirkiness as she embraced the awkwardness of Gertrude, the bird who laments her lack of plumage. Comic delivery was wonderful in the hilarious but touching `All For You` and she sang so well in the despairing `Notice Me Horton`.

John Conroy was perfectly cast as the steadfastly loyal Horton whose acute sense of hearing discovers the microscopic citizens of Whoville. It was a top notch performance played with an honesty and depth which made this more than just a one dimensional cartoon character. His heartfelt delivery of `Alone in the Universe` with his superb, soaring vocal was a standout musical moment in the show. An excellent portrayal. Linda Murray was a glitzy, fun-loving and flamboyant Mayzie who thought nothing of leaving poor Horton holding the egg as she skipped town for some `r and r`. Ms Murray had a great comic touch and a powerful belt voice which featured superbly in her narcissistic `Amazing Mayzie`.

Although a little hesitant at times, James Paradise was a quirky, comical Mr Mayor with great facial expression. His `other half` was played with great comic flair and expression by Aoife Fitzsimons who was hilariously inebriated in the Christmas sequence. The splitting of the Jojo role was most confusing; however this did not take away from the performances of the very talented duo of Conor Dolan and Ciarán Ennis who were both equally comfortable on stage. Conor and Ciarán were very focused and sang well.

Natalee Kelly, Gráinne Kinsella and Jean Feery were a flamboyant threesome of Bird Girls who worked their collective plumage with considerable style. Harmonies were secure and they were at all times engaged with the action.

Stephen Rabbette, Wayne Handy and Nathan Meehan were an excellent trio as the Wickershams, the intimidating jungle bullies who taunt Horton for his `delusions`.

They brought a great agility to their roles and singing was strong in their signature `Monkey Around`.

Gráinne Donoghue was a sassy, bluesy Sour Kangaroo with a big voice and Derek Dalton gave a hilariously funny cameo as the psychotic military leader Schmitz. Michael Murray and Tommy Scanlon impressed as the Grinch and Yertle the Turtle respectively. The `Aw Factor` was provided by the lovely Ava O`Connor as Young Kangaroo and Dubhan Goulding as a very cute Elephant Bird.

Wayne Handy and his crew designed a brilliantly Seussian set which was so closely based on the iconic illustrations from Geisel`s books. It was such a visual spectacle, bringing the magical fantasy world to life before our eyes. The flowers which lit up on the proscenium were an inspired inclusion.

Lighting by Pascal Gough and Ronan Kenny was superbly creative and colourful. There was excellent use of moving heads, particularly in `Monkey Around` and an excellently lit reveal of the Whos behind the upstage gauze. There was great use of the starcloth during `Solla Sollew` but Horton was poorly lit from above for this number with the result that we couldn`t see his face clearly.

A pity, given his wonderful performance of the song. Using the soft focus follow spot here would have picked him out nicely.

This will not be a popular observation but the biggest issue with this show was the poor sound quality and operation. Performers were frequently drowned out by the band during musical numbers and underscoring. In a little known show, where the key plot points are contained in the songs it is imperative that your audience hears what is being sung. I know this show very well and I struggled to hear familiar lyrics right through the show. There was a wonderful array of colourful costumes coordinated by Liz Rickard and Mary Cornally. Creativity and attention to detail were in evidence throughout. I loved the oversized buttons on the Who costuming and Mayzie`s impressive plumage was great fun.

Edel Kennedy`s props were perfectly in keeping with the bizarre Seussian world, as were the fabulous make-up and hair design which captured the offbeat quirkiness superbly.

Seussical appeals most to those with imagination. Its celebration of diversity and its assertion that everyone can make a difference, no matter how insignificant they may feel equates to more than just a simple children`s story. Clara Musical Society`s production captured these universal themes admirably thanks to some superb performances and stunning visual elements. Striped hats off to all!

Hyde` is widely believed to have been written during a six-day cocaine binge in 1886. Such drug-induced creativity has given rise to countless literary and film spin-offs. It was only a matter of time before a musical version was conceived. Wildhorn and Briscusse`s fast-paced tale of inner conflict and good versus evil was the choice of Galway Musical Society this season. It was a powerful production, excellently cast and directed with some powerhouse performances from an exceptional front line and ensemble. Brian and Seán Power gave us a gripping interpretation. Attention to narrative detail was everywhere in this show. Dramatic tension was skilfully created throughout and technical aspects were seamlessly integrated to further continuity and the dramatic action of the piece. This production was all about the drama and the Power brothers got the very best from their wonderfully talented cast which was fully in tune with their vision for the show.

Shane Farrell musically directed and Paddy Daly took charge of the choral work. This was a first rate show musically. Mr Farrell`s eleven-piece orchestra was in fine form and, as always, he conducted with considerable flair and aplomb. Principal singing was top notch and the choral sound was exquisite at times. The quartet for `His Work and Nothing More` provided one of many musical highlights.

Mary McDonagh`s choreography was typically strong, precise and well- rehearsed. It was perfectly appropriate to the style of the piece. `Facade` was a standout number with its continuous fluidity of movement into very definite groupings. `Bring on the Men` was suitably raunchy from the Red Rat ladies and their chair routine was executed without a hint of inhibition. From the very first note of `Facade` we knew that this was an exceptional ensemble. Not only was their singing of a wonderfully high standard but performance levels were through the roof from every individual on stage. The production team had clearly instilled a wonderful sense of confidence in their charges which combined with hard work and talent to deliver some spine-tingling moments throughout.

Stephen Macken delivered a tour de force performance in the dual role of Jekyll/Hyde. Diction was exceptional from this fine actor, as was his ability to use pause for dramatic effect. He fully inhabited both characters in what was an incredibly physical and mentally exhausting portrayal. Mr Macken`s singing was simply stunning at times. `This is the Moment` was a virtuoso rendition infused with angst, power and feeling. The incredible dynamism of his voice was most impressive as Jekyll descended into the monstrosity that was Mr Hyde. `Lady of the night` Lucy Harris was brilliantly played by Louise Colohan. She struck just the right balance between her seductive side in the raunchy `Bring on the Men` and the vulnerability of the tender `Someone Like You`. Ms Colohan sang superbly , especially in the outstanding duet `In His Eyes`. Her quality as an actress was underlined in the steamy, animalistic `Dangerous Game`.

Megan Lohan was a most intelligent actress who fleshed out the role of Emma Carew, a part which can often suffer from a one dimensional portrayal. She sang exquisitely throughout, particularly in `Once Upon a Dream` where she carried herself with an elegance, beauty and poise which was in complete contrast to Hyde`s grotesque monstrosity.

Seán Hosty was Jekyll`s friend and lawyer John Utterson who was torn between his loyalty to the Dr. and his concern at the unfolding horrors. Mr Hosty was most empathetic in a portrayal which was underpinned by a quiet dignity. At times I felt that diction needed attention though and that a more `clipped` delivery was required. The patriarchal Sir Danvers Carew was played with a warmth towards Lucy which was most engaging. We were constantly aware of his wariness of Jekyll and his overriding concern for his daughter. Mr Feerick`s diction was excellent and he sang with a fine baritone which was at its best in the heartfelt duet `Letting Go`.

A strong actor, Jim Dillon did very well in the underwritten role of Simon Stride. His affections towards Emma were clear and his singing in `Emma`s Reasons` was impressive. The Board of Governors was excellent in their performance of `Jekyll`s Plea` with standout performances from Liam Brennan as the hypocritical Bishop of Basingstoke and Ailbhe Slevin as the obnoxiously imperious Lady Beaconsfield. Ms Slevin combined brilliantly with Jonathan Hopper as Lord Savage in the darkly funny `Bitch! Bitch! Bitch!` Kevin Griffin was an ominous presence as Lucy`s vicious pimp Spider and Katie Creaven turned in a stellar performance as the Red Rat manageress Nellie. Ms Creaven was a standout performer in the ensemble also, living every second on stage. The colossal, multi-level set designed by Sam Holmes was perfectly evocative of darkest, Victorian London. There was a superb finish and texture to this set and we could almost smell the dank streets such was the attention to minute detail. Stage manager Leonard Power kept this show moving at a cracking pace. Scene changes were slick and unfussy, particularly those which took place during musical numbers.

Paul Kelly`s lighting design was an absolute joy such were the stunningly atmospheric pictures created. Great effects were created using cross lighting, back lighting and strobe. Unfortunately, two key lighting moments were badly operated on the night I attended. During `Murder, Murder` two `dead` bodies were caught crawling back through the ensemble as the lights came up too soon. `Confrontation` was marred by poor operation. Timing is crucial here as Jekyll becomes Hyde and vice versa in the blink of an eye. This essential element was not good on the night I attended. I got the impression that the operator was following the script rather than the visual which would have been a better bet given the need for split second precision in this number.

Mike and Sally Dervan`s sound design was excellent with a marvellous balance achieved between a very dynamic pit and the cast. `Jekyll`s Plea` was outstanding from a sound point of view as every one of the Board of Governors was clearly heard delivering their protestations. Cueing was excellent throughout.

June Young is fast becoming the costume supplier of choice on the circuit and it is easy to see why. Attention to detail was the hallmark of this excellently costumed show. We had wonderful gowns and formal wear at the engagement party and the red and black motif worked well for the Red Rat ladies who were suitably attired for their chosen `profession`. Very authentic props were noted including Jekyll`s wonderful doctor`s bag, journal and a fine set of vessels and bottles for the laboratory scenes. I did feel that more drinks were needed for the engagement party. Sir Danvers was obviously feeling the pinch!

Hair and make-up were well thought out and authentic to the era. Ali Murphy`s wig plot added so much to the show`s visual appeal.

This was a wonderful production from a very skilled team. It may have taken six days on cocaine for the original story to be conceived but this was a production which left its audience with an exhilarating `high` of its own. Bravo to all!

Kilkenny Musical celebrated its 40th birthday with vibrant, fast-paced show billed as `A New Version of Gilbert and Sullivan`s The Pirates of Penzance`. There was an expectant atmosphere in the Watergate theatre as we awaited the MD`s cue to get proceedings underway and the very talented cast did not disappoint in the slightest. Directed and choreographed by David Heffernan, this excellently rehearsed and very funny show borrowed much from Simon Gallaher`s Essgee `Australian` version of the show. Much of Gallaher`s comic business and detail was replicated with great accuracy, giving us a rip- roaring, exhilarating show which had its audience rolling in the aisles from the off.
