Dance numbers were slick and sharp with excellent performance levels from an exceptionally talented ensemble. `Poor Wandering One` was typical of such slickness. Some of the movement bordered on the ridiculous but it was so well performed by all with tongue firmly in cheek that we couldn`t but buy into their collective silliness. `With Cat-Like Tread` was very strong from the gentlemen who had clearly been worked hard.

MD Kevin Kennedy did great work with this show. There was a superb sound from an excellent orchestra which more than did justice to Sullivan`s wonderful score. Choral singing was very strong throughout with the exception of `With Cat-Like Tread` where one lone voice belted out a line which was less than harmonious. Principal singing was generally good, particularly from the ladies.

This was one of the strongest ensembles I have seen this season from an acting point of view. Scanning the stage during bigger company scenes it was almost impossible to find any `passengers` as everyone was engaged and meaningfully so. Full credit to Mr Heffernan for eliciting such high performance levels. Singing too was of a high standard. The finales of both acts sounded superb chorally. Seán Gaffney was not your typical Pirate King. This gentleman looked about as pirate-like as Mother Teresa! It really worked though as Mr Gaffney was an excellent comedian with a zany physicality which lent itself perfectly to his madcap characterisation which was not unlike Simon Gallaher`s hilarious portrayal in the Aussie version. Mr Gaffney`s singing was adequate for the role although he did struggle in the upper register occasionally.

Kevin Reade was a fine Frederic. Diction was excellent from Mr Reade and he had a great natural understanding of pace and dialogue. Comedy was very well handled. His trying to cope with Ruth`s assertions regarding how she compared to other women was particularly funny. Mr Reade sang with a beautiful quality to his soaring tenor voice in `Oh False One, You Have Deceived Me` and `How Beautifully Blue the Sky`.

Mabel was played by the very talented Joanne McCabe who sang with exceptional technique and heart. Her crystal clear soprano was a joy with the vocal gymnastics of `Poor Wand`ring One` really stealing the show for me. `How Beautifully Blue the Sky` was a gorgeous duet with Mr Reade. Ms McCabe`s diction and presence were first rate throughout. Olivia Smith`s less than charming demeanour and exquisite comic timing combined to make her portrayal of Ruth the standout performance of the show for me. It was a marvellous characterisation from a most clever actress. Singing was top drawer also with `Oh! False One, You Have Deceived Me` showcasing her superb vocal talents. My only quibble was that the make-up department needed to look at making a fresh-faced Ms Smith look less `aesthetically pleasing` as is required for this character. A criticism BUT a compliment nonetheless! There was great comic business and quirkiness to Matthew Berry`s Major General Stanley. Mr Berry had exceptional diction in the very wordy patter of `I Am the Very Model of a Modern Major-General`. He was nicely paternal with Mabel and the vision of him with his teddy bear was heart-warming and hilarious in equal measure. Comic timing was superb and his `shuddering` had me in stitches.

Having played the Sergeant of Police with the society in 1986 and 1993, John Byrne reprised the role yet AGAIN! Any AIMS statisticians know if this is a record?! As one would expect from such a seasoned campaigner, Mr Byrne delivered a very funny performance which was full of comical expression and energy. `When the Foeman Bares His Steel` was wonderfully physical and was sung very well into the bargain.

Kevina Hayes, Nicola Brennan and Sarah Brennan were a delightful trio as Kate, Edith and Isobel. They combined very well musically and bounced off each other in their comic exchanges. Ms Hayes was an exceptionally clever actress throughout. She was always thinking, always engaged and was outstanding in ensemble numbers as she clearly lived every second on stage.

Fergal Millar was a really strong Samuel whose delivery and diction were most impressive.

In a gesture which epitomises the camaraderie of AIMS the Rathmines and Rathgar Musical Society donated a wonderful John O`Donoghue designed set to mark the occasion of their centenary. It helped create a very professional overall look to the show with its imposing statues of the Pirate King and Ruth and the gorgeous archways featured in Act Two. I did feel that the chrome hinges and handles on the doors were in need of attention as they were brand, sparkling new and I would hazard a guess that these weren`t part of the original set.

Gerry Taylor`s lighting was up to his usual high standards with some excellent effects created and some superbly timed cues adding to the dramatic effect. Break up gobos were well used and strobe during the ambush scene was most effective. Coffey`s of Templemore were responsible for a first rate sound design. There was an exceptional stage/pit balance and no cues were missed all night.

Bill and Rena Kennedy did sterling work on props. Swords, truncheons, and the very effective battery-operated candles were most impressive. The finale of Act One benefited greatly from the authentic Union Jack and Jolly Roger flags.

Costumes from Thatlooksgood were the icing on the cake for this superbly visual show. The motley crew of pirates was superbly dressed and the various dresses and bonnets for the ladies were delightfully Victorian. The arrival of the policemen was a real treat as their authentic uniforms and `bobby` hats added so much to the number.

Stage manager Séamus Reade had a relatively quiet night with most of the crew`s work being done at the interval as the set was changed. One small point would be to ensure that the haze machine only pumps haze during louder, more dynamic numbers to cover the sound. At one very quiet point we did get a blast of haze which distracted somewhat from proceedings.

Hair and make-up were well looked after with excellent wigs for some of the pirates and appropriate make-up for the ladies throughout.

Forty years is a wonderful milestone for any society. Kilkenny Musical Society has every reason to look forward to the future with great optimism and enthusiasm considering the great talent at their disposal. What are the bets on John Byrne playing Sergeant of Police again sometime over the next forty years?!

Seventy years on from its Broadway debut, `Oklahoma! ` is still a favourite amongst theatregoers everywhere. Whilst the score is universally acknowledged as a classic in the musical theatre canon it is often forgotten how wonderful the book is. Drama, romance and comic situations aplenty make it a script full of opportunity for performers and directors alike. Des Henn`s production for Limerick Musical Society explored many of these opportunities in what was a thoroughly entertaining presentation.

Mr Henn maintained a very snappy pace throughout this energetic and vibrant show. There were some excellently realised scenes with the smokehouse sequence standing out in particular as a superbly crafted and performed piece of theatre.

Máire Keary-Scanlon did a fine job as musical director and choral director. She conducted a really tight orchestra which brought the wonderful Rodgers score to life. The dream sequence was stunning musically with exquisite playing on violin and percussion in particular. Choral singing was generally good although the alto line in `Many a New Day` was in need of some additional support.

Niamh Twomey`s choreography was fresh, exciting and extremely sharp from a very well rehearsed ensemble. `Kansas City` was a brilliant routine, superbly performed with an energy which hit the appreciative audience right between the eyes. The dream ballet sequence was equally impressive and there was a marvellous sense of community and life in the excellent `Farmer and the Cowman`. The ensemble in this show was excellent at times, particularly in the bigger production numbers which they approached with considerable gusto. There were times though when they needed to engage more. The auction scene could have benefited from more involvement to enhance the tension and Jud`s gory demise could have provoked more of a response from the lady folk in particular as some seemed none too upset at the violent events. Michael O`Dwyer was a very smooth Curly with a most engaging presence and confidence. Likeability was the key here and Mr O`Dwyer had this in spades. He was a very clever actor and every word spoken had been thought about and was delivered in a most natural and believable manner. His preacher moment in `Pore Jud is Daid` was a real highlight, showing a real knowingness and intelligence as an actor. Singing was generally strong although I would suggest that Mr O`Dwyer is a more confident baritone than tenor as he occasionally lacked the control in his upper register.

Orla Walsh was one of the finest Laureys I have seen. I loved her very relaxed, natural delivery. Again, she was an intelligent actress who made the book come to life. There was a great strength and stubbornness to her portrayal which balanced nicely with a naivety which was most compelling. Singing was wonderful. Ms Walsh`s soprano was simply superb, soaring effortlessly in `Many a New Day` and `People Will Say We`re in Love`.

There was a great energy to Jamie Sheehan`s portrayal of Will Parker which was full of comic business and expression. Mr Sheehan was a most likeable, dim-witted type and he excelled vocally and choreographically in his big number `Kansas City`. Diction and projection did require attention at times as clarity was occasionally lost in his whirlwind of energy.

Kim Burke`s Ado Annie was a comic tour de force from start to finish. Her very natural comedic style was a joy. Timing was razor sharp and she never once pushed things too far as can often happen with this role. Ms Burke trusted the book, getting maximum impact from some very subtle delivery at times. Singing was impressive, from both a performance and musical point of view, with `Cain`t Say No` being a hugely entertaining rendition.

Martin McNelis gave a superb performance, reminiscent of the wonderful Shuler Hensley, in a carefully studied, sympathetic, yet menacing portrayal of Jud Fry. Mr McNelis was able to capture Jud`s threatening edge whilst maintaining a vulnerability and emotional depth not often seen in this role. `Lonely Room` was outstanding both vocally and dramatically as his tortured soul was laid bare.

Nigel Dugdale has huge potential as a comedian. All of the ingredients were there. Good physical capabilities, great energy, a myriad comic expressions and good timing were all in evidence in Mr Dugdale`s performance of travelling salesman Ali Hakim. However, from his first appearance he was so outrageously over the top that he allowed himself nowhere to go with the role. It was such a pity as the potential was enormous from this talented performer. Mr Henn must share part of the responsibility for this as he allowed Mr Dugdale to push things too far.

Aunt Eller refers to herself as an `ole woman` in the opening scene. It was difficult therefore to see beyond Laura Henebry`s youthful appearance and movement which seemed at odds with her character. This, of course, was not Ms Henebry`s fault and she worked very hard throughout, particularly during the difficult auction scene which she dominated and controlled very well.

There was good work too from Dermot Winston as Carnes whose comic flair and expression were impressive. He did, however, need to be careful not to play lines directly to the audience at times.

Elaine Rowlands` laugh was suitably grating as Gertie and Steven McCall and Patrick Woulfe did well as Cord Elam and Ike Skidmore respectively. Mr Henn`s set design suited the space well with a fine house for Eller and an impressive barn dominating the large stage. The absence of an apostrophe in `Skidmores` (sic) was unfortunate as was the unsightly ground row lighting which could so easily have been disguised. Stage manager Tom Enright ensured that slick transitions contributed to what was generally a very well paced show.

Props were well chosen for the most part with a well dressed smokehouse being particularly impressive. There was a distinct lack of holsters and guns for cowboys which was a pity and Jud`s $3.50 for Will comprised of notes only. Ali`s cart was superb and the full-sized surrey was the icing on the cake in the final scene.

Lighting from Paul Kelly was basic but functional throughout. I did feel that there were missed opportunities in the dream ballet which was crying out for more in the early stages.

Sound was impeccable right throughout the show from Star Systems. Cueing was sharp and there was an excellent balance between orchestra and cast. Perhaps a radio or two could have been spread amongst the alto line for `Many a New Day` but this is a small point in what was a most impressive job.

Costumes were a mixed bag. Great chaps for the gentlemen and some excellent attire for Ado and Will in particular. Hats needed a lot more attention as many were of poor quality and Carnes looked as though he had just walked in off the street. Curly and Laurey`s wedding clothes were excellent but Laurey`s dungarees were far too pristine and the `frayed` ends had clearly been distressed by a scissors.

Hair was appropriate to the era but make-up was in need of attention at times with two ladies in `Many a New Day` standing out for their inappropriately bright, red lipstick. The audience in Limerick`s University Concert Hall was enthralled by this production of the Rodgers and Hammerstein classic. The abundance of talent, infectious energy, exciting choreography and familiar tunes sent all away with a collective smile. Many thanks for what was a most entertaining evening.

The Venue, Ebrington is a temporary marquee erected in Londonderry for the duration of the City of Culture 2013 celebrations. Londonderry Musical Society was delighted when asked to perform their production of `Annie` in the prestigious venue with a seating capacity of 2,500. There was a fine wealth of talent on display in a show which was unfortunately marred by poor technical standards. My heart went out to a cast and crew which had worked so hard for months only to have their efforts compromised by shockingly poor sound operation. Director Deigh Reid had put his heart and soul into this production. There was exceptional work done with the very talented orphans and great attention to detail with ensemble business. Sightlines were sometimes an issue and more work needed to be done with crew to improve continuity and more seamless transitions which occasionally affected pace.

Jim Goodman did excellent work with a stunning nine piece orchestra. Trumpet and trombone were outstanding in the superb overture and there was gorgeous, sympathetic violin in `Maybe`. Underscoring was well handled and choral singing was impressive throughout.

I was very impressed with Venessa Chapman`s choreography. There was wonderful strength and focus from the orphans in the excellent `Hard Knock Life` which was performed with marvellous precision. A lovely tap sequence was inserted into `NYC` and `Easy Street` had a great element of raucous fun about it. `Never Fully Dressed` was outstanding from the exceptional group of orphans.

The adult ensemble worked really well as a unit, always acting and reacting appropriately. There was great business amongst the maids and staff at Warbucks` mansion and the down and outs of Hooverville were suitably haggard and decrepit.

Lauryn Mulholland was excellent in the title role. A clever actress, she had obviously worked hard with Mr Reid to explore her character and she brought so much sincerity and honesty to her portrayal. What a stunning voice she had too! `Maybe` was outstanding as she sang with such clarity of tone in what appeared to be an effortless style. A definite name for the future. Muire McCallion was a most intelligent actress as the perpetually inebriated Miss Hannigan. Comic timing was first rate and her `Little Girls` was a very humorous rendition. She threw herself into `Easy Street` with drunken abandon, never thrown by the fact that her microphone wasn`t working. Warbucks was played with great presence and bluster by Kris Doherty. After a hesitant start with poor cueing he settled into the role, giving a very sympathetic portrayal. He possessed a fine baritone voice with `Why Should I Change a Thing?` showing his vocal prowess. However, his constant pacing during this number did take away from it slightly.

Katie Patton as Grace needed more input from Mr Reid to make her performance more natural. Clearly a very talented lady, she had a most unnatural tendency to play almost every line to the audience rather than to the character with whom she was interacting. The potential was there but this style of performance was out of place in this show. Ms Patton had a beautifully clear singing voice which impressed throughout.

David Keown was a great physical comedian with superb expression and he played the role of Hannigan`s scoundrel brother, Rooster, with a great comic flair. Vocally, he wasn`t as secure as he might have been on the higher notes but his excellent performance compensated for such inaccuracies. His partner in crime and dumb blonde, Lily, was brilliantly played by a very funny Aoibheann Biddle. This was an exceptional performance from a very talented lady who had exquisite timing and superb diction. Both performers had a blast in the excellent `Easy Street`.

Take note of the name Kate McCafferty. This nine year old nearly stole the show as Molly. Acting, singing and dancing were outstanding from this young lady who is already a You Tube sensation for her Irish dancing prowess. This girl is going places!

David Thomas was a sympathetic President Roosevelt, Eaman Craig was full of life and character as radio presenter Bert Healy and Simon Quigg was a hilariously camp Drake with an excellent singing voice.

Caroline Gilliland had a baptism of fire with this huge show in her stage management debut. She will have learned a lot from the experience. It may have been an idea to use the maids and staff in character to assist with changes to and from Warbucks` mansion.

Sara Polley coordinated an excellent costume plot. Hooverville had a suitable mishmash of distressed attire and Warbucks` staff were pristine and crisp. I loved Rooster`s black and yellow pinstripe and the dresses for the orphans in the final scene were a lovely touch.

Jayne Black was at the helm in what was a huge props show. Everything was appropriate to the era from authentic shopping bags and hatboxes in `NYC` to Warbucks` beautifully ornate phone. Warbucks` mansion was screaming out for a suggestion of Christmas other than the solitary tree. The bare fireplace and staircase were in real need of dressing.

Albemarle Scenic Studios provided a most professional looking set. It was huge but needed to be to fill the enormous stage. The orphanage was most impressive and Warbucks` mansion was suitably lavish. With no flying facilities, the tracking of the NYC cloth worked very well.

Make-up design by Grace McAllister and Patricia O`Brien was well looked after with nothing inappropriate noted. Lighting was provided by Unit 7 Audio Visual. It was not appropriate for a theatrical production. There were so many missed opportunities to create mood and atmosphere and the flashing lights for `Easy Street` would have been more applicable to a concert setting.

Those who have been reading my reviews over the past year will know that the tone is always as positive as possible and that I always give credit where credit is due. However, on this occasion it is impossible to gloss over how bad the sound operation was for this show. I lost count of the missed cues and the number of times microphones were left on backstage as we heard full blown conversations from cast members. I accept that this can sometimes happen but this occurred all through the show and was incredibly frustrating. I do not accept that unfamiliar surroundings were to blame. This does not happen if the sound engineer has a clearly marked script and is familiar with the run of the show. It takes an awful lot for me to say this but I would not be accepting an invoice for that level of work if it was my society. I really felt for this talented group as I watched the show. They deserved better. Poor sound is possibly the one element of production which can do the most damage to a show. Costs should never be cut at the expense of professional sound design and operation.

Technical issues aside, Londonderry Musical Society gave their all to packed crowds at this unique venue. The talent within the group and production team was clear to see, particularly amongst the excellent orphans who stole the show with their energy and professionalism. I wish them the very best with their next venture.

The jukebox musical genre has been much maligned over the years and I have to admit to having been one of its greatest critics. A show tenuously constructed around the songs of a particular artist or era has never quite been my cup of tea. However, Newbridge Musical Society`s outstanding production of `All Shook Up`, a loose adaptation of Shakespeare`s `Twelfth Night`, taught me a valuable lesson. Yes, it`s silly and yes, it`s cheesy but in the right hands it has at its centre a real heart. This show was most definitely in the right hands and the heart of the show was so beautifully captured by director Sharon McNamara and her talented team. It was a celebration. A celebration of life and a celebration of music.

The old showbiz adage "Dying is easy. Comedy is hard" refers to how much more difficult it is for directors and performers who tackle comedy. Getting comedy right is not as easy as some would think but Ms McNamara made it look easy. Having assembled an excellent cast, she skilfully guided them through the corniest of books, making no apologies whatsoever and squeezing every last ounce of mirth from the script. Attention to detail was everywhere, especially in her exceptional work with a very committed ensemble.

MD Owen C. Lynch conducted his exceptional orchestra with considerable energy. Indeed, had he not been otherwise occupied he would have been a great addition to the dance troupe! The brass section was particularly impressive and there was a beautiful acoustic guitar intro to `I Can`t Help Falling in Love`. Choral singing was outstanding at times and principals sang so well throughout. Julianne McNamara devised some lively dance routines which had clearly been painstakingly rehearsed. Precision and performance levels were the order of the day as everyone on stage knew exactly what they were doing. The `Burning Love` routine was simply exhilarating, such was the energy and enthusiasm which bounded off the stage.

A very well-rehearsed ensemble added hugely to this joyous show. Choral singing, background business and disciplined freezes were all excellently handled and people danced with their faces as well as with their feet displaying pleasant and animated facial expressions.

Mark Trundle was superbly cast as the narcissistic, eyebrow-raising, hip-swivelling roustabout Chad. Mr Trundle played the role in a most knowing manner, clearly in tune with the corniness of his character. His recurring "I`ve been with a lot of women...a LOT of women!" was infused with such cheesy bravado that, at times, it brought the house down before he could even finish his line. What a voice Mr Trundle had too. `I Don`t Want To` was a vocal highlight of the show for me in what was an outstanding rendition.

Aideen Leacy was absolutely wonderful as local mechanic Natalie who transforms herself into `Ed` in order to get closer to Chad. When you know what`s coming in a comedy show it can often be difficult to appreciate its humour fully. In spite of knowing the show, I could not stop myself from laughing at Ms Leacy`s brilliant portrayal as she got herself tied up in a myriad knots as her male alter ego! Comic timing was excellent. Ms Leacy was also an accomplished singer with her considerable vocal talents shining in `A Little Less Conversation` in particular.

Phil Mac Sheóinín delivered a top drawer comic performance as Chad`s nerdy sidekick Dennis. Mr Mac Sheóinín is a superbly gifted comic actor whose entire being was immersed in the physicality of this role. His comic timing was exceptional and he never once lost his brilliantly consistent characterisation. His hangdog expression as he relinquished his sidekick tag to `Ed` had me in hysterics. Mr Mac Sheóinín sang `It Hurts Me` beautifully but still managed to lather it in as much camembert, edam and cheddar as possible for maximum comic effect. Helen Spring was an excellent Lorraine. A most clever actress, she had superb expression and presence and sang really well in `If I Can Dream`. Eoghan Fingleton played Ms Spring`s beau Dean. A strong performer, he needed to be conscious of not tuning out when the focus wasn`t directly on him. Mr Fingleton showed a wonderful upper register in `It`s Now or Never` which he sang superbly.

Yvonne Q. Cummins impressed greatly as the stuffy museum curator Miss Sandra. She was superb as she lost the run of herself and attempted to get her amorous claws into poor `Ed`. Ms Cummins had some of the very best lines in the show "Quote Shakespeare and peel me like a banana!" was hilariously delivered. She was excellent in her big number `Let Yourself Go` where she did just that!

Helena Begley was a very strong Sylvia. Her various sarcastic put downs were well delivered and her unlikely relationship with Jim was nicely played. `There`s Always Me` was gorgeously sung with exceptional control as it built to its climactic conclusion.

Conor Kilduff displayed a lovely paternal warmth as Natalie`s widowed father Jim. He balanced comedy with emotion very well and sang superbly throughout. `The Power of My Love` was really well sung by this very talented performer.

Cora Coffey Maher gave a very comic portrayal as the moral guardian of the townsfolk, Mayor Matilda Hyde. Ms Coffey Maher clearly enjoyed every minute on stage as she denounced Chad and his influences. Her `Devil in Disguise` number was hilarious.

Michael F. Malone was a mute Sheriff Earl right up until the eleventh hour when he unleashed his frustrations upon the unsuspecting mayor. It was a most humorous portrayal and Mr Malone ensured that, once he was allowed to speak, he was given full attention!

Andrew Reddy`s costume design was most impressive. From the ladies` jailhouse costumes to the transition from drab to colourful for the ensemble there was attention to detail everywhere. The `brides` at the end looked great but a suggestion for the `grooms` might have been a nice touch. A small point in an excellent plot.

The simple but clever set design which featured a huge upstage guitar which became a rollercoaster in Act Two was extremely effective. The gas station, complete with gas pump was excellent. Some unsightly blemishes on the back wall were unfortunate. Hanging a cyc might have been the best way to go. Tom Kavanagh and his crew ensured that everything moved exceptionally well in a show where continuity was key.

Liam Fitzgerald`s lighting made great use of moving heads and haze for some excellent effects. Soft focus follow spot was used in `There`s Always Me`. Timing of the recurring `One Night With You` gag was perfect every time.

Noel Ryan`s sound design and operation were excellent with no cues missed all night. There was an excellent balance between stage and pit and some clever use made of judiciously spread ensemble mics to embellish the marvellous choral numbers.

Hair and make-up were very much in keeping with the 1950s theme with some brilliantly authentic beehives hairstyles in evidence and Mr Trundle`s quiff being a feature in itself.

Props were all authentic to the era and appropriate. Sylvia`s bar was particularly well dressed.

This was a truly marvellous production by Newbridge Musical Society, fully deserving of the wildly enthusiastic reception which greeted it on the night I attended. Continued success to the group and thank you for a hugely entertaining production.

is often dismissed as a saccharine- sweet, superficial piece of musical theatre fluff, broken out by societies in need of a guaranteed audience and much needed funds. However, in the right hands it is a compelling piece and a story which runs much deeper than many give it credit for. St Agnes` Choral Society certainly had the right hands moulding their production. Director Tony Finnegan skilfully explored the more weighty, underlying universal issues such as freedom, political oppression and standing up for beliefs whilst maintaining a balance with an upbeat, cheery mood which underpins the real heart at the centre of this charming show.

Mr Finnegan created so many wonderful moments in this excellently- crafted production. Exceptional work with an extremely talented group of children was in evidence throughout. Pace was brisk and dialogue thoughtfully delivered. Attention to the detail of the book was always adhered to and so many clever and original touches were added. I smiled and shook my head in admiration as Maria placed her note on the teddy bear and the curtain fell on the first act. A beautiful moment. I can only describe the wedding scene as being akin to watching a scene from a movie. The scale, setting, staging, lighting, sound, costuming and attention to minute detail made this one of the standout theatrical moments of my travels. Wilson Shields elicited a wonderfully full sound from his orchestra which played exceptionally well. Two orchestra members appeared to consider themselves invisible to the audience when not playing and their antics from start to finish were a constant frustration. Choral singing was exquisite from the wonderful nuns` chorus and the children had been so well rehearsed.

It may not be a show which is renowned for its dance numbers but Rebecca Leonard`s choreography added so much to the professional feel of this show. In particular her work with the children was exceptionally sharp in `Do-Re-Me` and `So Long, Farewell`. `The Lonely Goatherd` was an outstanding number as the stage filled with brightly attired `puppets` who danced their hearts out and earned a sustained applause which was richly deserved.

The casting of Ceara Grehan as Maria, the unmanageable postulant turned governess, was a key element in the success of this production. She WAS Maria. Ms Grehan totally inhabited the role in a most endearing portrayal which had us from the very first note of the title number as she lay on her back in the Austrian hills. It was a superbly clever acting performance which was backed up by a most stunning soprano voice.

The role of Captain von Trapp is a difficult one to pitch. The talented Brian Trainor managed to skilfully balance an exterior, military gruffness with a softer, more paternal side. This is key to the development of the character and was so well achieved by Mr Trainor. Diction was excellent and he combined beautifully with Ms Grehan in `Something Good`, displaying a fine baritone with a lovely, full tone.

It is impossible to do justice to the performances of the seven children in this production. They were, without exception, stunning. Individually and collectively they sang, danced and acted with such maturity and professionalism. Alexandra Dick, Ben Redden, Sarah McFarlane, Owen McKavanagh, Olivia Rainey, Lára Mulgrew and Cara Magennis shone in their respective roles. It seemed beyond the bounds of credibility that this was only one of two equally excellent teams of youngsters playing these roles. My sources tell me that the Purple Team was just as brilliant. Marion Jordan was an excellent Mother Abbess. She was stern and authoritative yet warm when required. Her stunning soprano voice was a joy in the show-stopping `Climb Every Mountain`.

Emma Lundy was a rather more youthful Baroness than we might be used to and perhaps could have done with some aging from the hair and make-up department. Some nicely subtle yet pointed delivery left us in no doubt as to her intentions. She did need to watch her tendency to stand with her right foot out to the side in what was a rather unnatural stance. Mark McGuire provided comic relief as the wheeling, dealing Max who pandered to anyone he could gain from. An intelligent portrayal, Mr McGuire resisted the temptation to go too over the top for the cheap laughs. Ben McDaid did well as Rolf and his transformation from teenage suitor to hardened Nazi was well handled. All cameo roles were well performed, with Seán Allen as Herr Zeller delivering a standout, intimidating performance. Ditanya McKinty also impressed as Frau Schmidt.

The excellent set from Festival Productions was beautifully detailed and complemented perfectly by some very well chosen projections. It was moved with stunning efficiency by Clare Donnelly and her outstanding crew. Nothing was left to chance as every single detail of every single transition was carefully choreographed and rehearsed.

MK Audio was responsible for a flawless sound design and operation. Cueing was sharp and there was an excellent balance between stage and pit at all times.

Alastair Kerr`s lighting design was typically excellent. With a designer this good and a director who understands the myriad possibilities that clever lighting affords, this was always going to be a visually appealing show. Stunning pictures were created over and over again with clever use of backlighting, crosslighting and follow spot.

Triple C provided the very impressive costumes for this show. Attention to detail was in evidence throughout. The children`s `play clothes` were excellent, as was the formal attire for the various guests at von Trapp`s party. The wedding scene was outstanding from a costume point of view with Captain von Trapp`s uniform, Maria`s stunning dress and authentic attire for the multitude of altar boys, clergy and nuns adding greatly to the visual impact of this wonderful scene.

Maeve Gillen and her team provided a most authentic array of props. Again, there was great attention to detail here. Authentic thuribles and chalices were a visual treat and the descending sizes of the prize cups for the festival concert were a most humorous detail. St. Agnes` Choral Society was founded in 1957, two years before `The Sound of Music` first hit the Broadway stage. Half a century on, both are very much alive and together with a top notch production team and an excellent cast provided the ingredients for a truly memorable night at the theatre. Bravo to all!

A quarter of a century on from when they first staged Lionel Bart`s much- loved take on the Dickens classic tale, Tralee Musical Society took to the magnificent Siamsa Tíre stage with their production of `Oliver!` It was a well crafted production with some superb talent on display which was in the ever capable and experienced hands of Oliver Hurley.

Mr Hurley`s direction was slick and insightful, exploring the central, dark themes whilst ensuring that the book`s comic opportunities were also realised. As we observed the excellent focus of the children filing through the theatre during the opening vamp of `Food Glorious Food` we knew that this was going to be a secure production. Mr Hurley created some beautiful moments on stage which included a very long but disciplined freeze from the ensemble during `Who Will Buy?` Not content with just directing the show, Mr Hurley also choreographed a wonderful set of dance routines which were well rehearsed and performed with confidence. The children were particularly well drilled and performed with super precision and maturity. They really were so assured especially in the very sharp `Be Back Soon`. `Consider Yourself` and `Who Will Buy` allowed the adult ensemble to show their movement skills and both were full of life and high performance levels. Áine Murray did a fine job as musical director with her scaled-down six piece orchestra. Whilst I did miss some of the wonderful orchestrations it has to be said that this was a stunningly tight group of musicians with some exceptional playing in evidence. Lucy Tanner`s violin cadenzas in `Reviewing the Situation` were, in themselves, worth the trip from Dublin! Choral and principal singing were very strong although we did have a timing issue in `Be Back Soon` when Fagin`s gang raced ahead of poor Ms Murray in their enthusiasm.

Matthew Dineen was very well cast in the title role. He displayed the necessary vulnerability but balanced this very well with a feistiness and inner strength which shone through as he stood up to Noah, Bumble and even Sykes. Matthew had a lovely, expressive tone to his voice and his `Where is Love` was one of those `pin dropping` moments.

From his biog it would appear that Máirtín Ó Cathasaigh is a marvellously talented all-rounder who excels at just about everything he turns his hand to! This talent was evident in abundance as he assumed the role of likeable pickpocket, the Artful Dodger. It was a superb performance in every respect but Máirtín`s singing was something else. A bright future lies ahead. Watch this space!

I loved John Drummey`s performance as the wily Fagin. Twenty five years previously he had played Dodger with the society. Talk about coming full circle! Mr Drummey`s timing and physical awareness were exceptional. A very clever actor, his diction was exceptional as he totally inhabited the role. `Reviewing the Situation` was both humorous and contemplative in an excellent interpretation of the iconic song.

Jackie O`Mahony was a real `diamond in the rough` as the ill-fated Nancy. Ms O`Mahony had the most superb singing voice and exercised super control in the stunning `As Long As He Needs Me`. The reprise of this number was a standout musical and dramatic point in the show which built to a powerfully heartfelt crescendo as Ms O`Mahony struggled between her love for Bill and her concern for Oliver. Tim Landers had a chilling and intimidating presence as the villainous Bill Sykes. It was an excellent performance, very physical, with a cold, measured delivery which was most unnerving. `My Name` was suitably ominous and Mr Landers held nothing back as he terrorised the patrons of the `Three Cripples`.

Tim Moran and Clair McEvoy were a delightfully comic duo as Mr Bumble and Widow Corney. The shenanigans on the chaise between the two were hilarious as Ms McEvoy`s faux reluctance to succumb to Mr Moran`s amorous advances were short lived. Mr Moran sang well in `Boy For Sale` but Ms McEvoy`s voice did appeared a bit tired.

There was a real lack of pace and cueing between Mike Lynch and Karen Soffe as Mr and Mrs Sowerberry during the performance I attended. This was a pity as their characterisations were strong and both sang well in `That`s Your Funeral`. Edel Crowley had a gorgeous, natural presence and sang well as Bet, Nancy`s sidekick. Eve Dowling and Enda Sugrue impressed in their first roles with the society as Charlotte and Noah and both will have gained great experience.

John Fraher gave one of the performances of the show as a most kindly, compassionate Mr Brownlow and James Brennan was a very humorous Dr Grimwig. Mairéad Edmonds was a gorgeous Mrs Bedwin with a most reassuring presence. Her singing was beautiful as she gave great support to Oliver in `Who Will Buy?` The set, designed by the very busy Oliver Hurley, was more than adequate structurally. With its various levels and flying pieces there were great changes of location from scene to scene. There was a very cleverly concealed bedroom area on stage left which was revealed for the `Who Will Buy` sequence. Some set pieces were in need of attention though, particularly Sowerberry`s counter and the two doors during `Who Will Buy` which were poorly finished.

Ken Murphy and his crew were exceptionally well rehearsed and ensured superbly slick transitions between scenes. The timing of the change into Sowerberry`s was perfectly coordinated with Bumble and Oliver`s arrival on floor level.

Props were, for the most part, well chosen and appropriate. There was, however, a lack of attention to detail at times. Sowerberry`s coffin was far too modern and Nancy poured nothing from the ladle as she `filled` the boys` cups. Some upholstered bar stools in The Three Cripples were inappropriate. Wooden stools would have been more fitting.

Karen Soffe and her team did a truly wonderful and painstaking job in creating the vast number of costumes required for this large cast. Excellent attention to detail was in evidence with appropriate distressing of attire when appropriate and great care taken with the more upper class characters. Fagin`s coat was marvellous, as were the orphans in the opening number. Bravo to all involved!

Hair and make-up were generally well attended to. Excellent sideburns for Mr Bumble and wig for Fagin added greatly to their overall looks. Some black smudging on the orphans` faces were less than natural looking, I felt. John Hurley`s lighting design was a joy, creating exceptional mood and atmosphere throughout. There was superb use of follow spot, break up gobos and cross lighting to great effect. An excellent job!

Murt Whelan and Shane Murphy were responsible for what was a flawless sound design and operation. Exceptional cueing and a marvellous balance between stage and pit were noted right through the show.

There was a great atmosphere front of house with a lot of young people attending and a most efficient team at work ushering people to their seats. This was a really fine production from Oliver Hurley and his talented team. It was so heart warming to see such wonderful young talent and enthusiasm on the Siamsa Tíre stage. Well done to all!

Mack and Mabel is full of amusing vaudeville-style slapstick, pratfalls, chase scenes and hilarious pie-in-the- face routines all intertwined in a tragic love story.

This is just what we got from Kilcock Musical and Dramatic Society in St Joseph's Hall.

The overall production was nicely realised by Director Philippa Alford. The blocking was secure for the most part, albeit we did have some migrating to the front and some straight lines. Some frozen tableaus were beautifully constructed and added to the production. We did have some inconsistencies' with entrances and exits. The Keystone Cops were very funny. We did feel that the dialogue needed more connection to the musical journey in order to capture and unearth the real story of tragic love. Julie Donnelly; choreographer did a good job on the dance routines. We enjoyed the tap. Some formations were excellent and some were repetitive. We had too much of the same side stepping step in most routines. We would have liked more variation. Musical Director; Dave McGauran brought together a wonderful ten piece show band for this explosive score with strings, trumpets, trombone, clarinet, saxophone, flute, cello, bass, percussion and piano. We had wonderful playing from Mark Adams and Dave Collins on trumpets, Robert Geraghty on Clarinet and Carl Geraghty on Saxophone.

The band was playful, explosive at times, and equally melodic when required. Sometimes the brass was too big and needed reining in. Choral singing was secure and forthright. Principals were well supported. John Furlong gave us a very secure and effusive performance as the brooding Mack Sennett, the once successful silent film pioneer. This charismatic actor was committed to the role. He was engaging, truthful and believable. Mr Furlong sang with emotion and ardent pathos. 'I Won't Send Roses' was a highlight. We had a wonderful stand-out performance from Sharon Murphy as deli delivery girl turn star and lover, Mabel. This actress was successful and sincere in every scene. Ms Murphy was bright, bubbly and delivered her singing and dancing with energy and commitment. Sinead McLoughlin gave us a wonderful performance as tough talking Lottie.  'Big Time' and 'Tap Your Troubles Away' were delivered with personality and confidence. Peter Manning was very balanced and sincere as the tactful up and coming director Frank Wyman. Mr. Manning had a lovely genuine stage presence. William Lacey was strident and serious as W.D.Taylor, serious director and drug and alcohol user. We had a very secure performance from Eamon Nolan as Wally. Kenny Gribbin was fine as Harry. Linday Tapley was very solid as piano playing Ella. Andrew Docherty was suitable expressive as Mr. Kleiman. Peter Fay was good as Mr. Fox. Mick Amoruso was very nice as Eddie the Watchman, the Scottish accent worked. Gary O'Shaughnessy was very good as Andy and Lorainne Murphy did very well as Iris. The chorus was strong and imposing in every scene. This company were engaged and forthcoming in the many roles with typical vaudevillian style. Some chorus members needed to work on their words! The cast engaged us in amusing slapstick, pratfalls, chase scenes and hilarious pie-in-the-face routines.

Set design by Philippa Alford was fine. We would have liked more imagination in the overall design. The use of the USC cyc door was a lovely effect. Stage Manager; Dermot Anglin had a very competent team backstage. Scene changes were smooth and well rehearsed. The props were time and era appropriate. We would have liked larger suitcases. Lighting under the vigilant eye of Liam Fitzgerald was successful. We did have a little flickering as the LED's were lowered. The overall costume plot, supplied by Pat McGann was fine under the stewardship of Andrew Reddy. We would have liked alternate suit for Mack in Act 1 and an imposing overcoat. Hairdressing and Makeup was nicely attended to in this production by Maria Mallon and Ginny Breslin. The sound by Vinnie Osborne was well balanced and we had no issues with cueing, except for the start of the dialogue in Act 2.  Unfortunately we did have a faulty mic towards the end of the show, but Mr. Osborne managed to minimise the problem. Congratulations to everyone in Kilcock for a great upbeat show!

Portrush is a small seaside resort town in Co Antrim, Northern Ireland. It boasts a mile long peninsula with beautiful sea views. Well known for its sandy beaches it has a somewhat lazy feel, laid back and reserved. The last place you would expect to find retro sexy, sassy, Gangnam Style in abundance? But, that is just what we got for Portrush Music Society's recent production of the Hot Mikado. Hot Mikado is a jazz-swing 1940′s era adaptation of Gilbert and Sullivan's beloved 1885 operetta - The Mikado. David H. Bell, a theatre historian, knew of the "Swing Mikado" and a rival show "The Hot Mikado" staring Bojangles Robinson that opened across the street from one another in 1938 on Broadway. Bell decided to produce that version of "The Hot Mikado" at his Ford's Theatre in Washington D.C. for the 1986 season. Problem -practically no orchestrations or vocal arrangements existed from the 1938 show. So Bell and composer Rob Bowman scrambled to create a show. Bell wrote the book and new lyrics, Bowman created the orchestrations and arrangements. The result was their amazingly fun Hot Mikado!

The overall production in Portrush was sassy, sexy and very funny. Director Kerry Dunn is to be congratulated for being brave and forthright with her vision and certainly it worked. The overall production had a wonderful style that was colourful and broad, just what is needed for this show. It was visually explosive. Blocking was secure and the comedy was defined and delivered with confidence. The dance for the production by Choreographer; Ditanya McKinty, was also fun and expressive. The dance routines were well conceived and delivered. It had style and panache. Formations were interesting and diverse. The wardrobe team did an excellent job on costumes. They were creative and we loved the boots, stripy socks, men's jackets, hats and accessories. A Triumph! Hair and makeup was fantastic from Vikki Mitchell. The set design was fantastic for this production by Kerry Dunn. The overall aesthetic was beautiful and functional and Philip Bradshaw did an excellent job on the lighting design and execution. The backstage team under the stewardship of Sean Magee did very well with few changes. Props were creative. The sound was well balanced with good cueing from Chris Fulton, Ricky Ferguson, Stephen Henry and Sarah Quigley. The animation video production for Tit Willow was fantastic. This production was very creative.

This company embraced the vigour that is needed for 'Hot Mikado'. The group scenes were full of energy and each and every member was energised and animated. Overall a very strong and committed company. Harry Coates was every inch the Hot Mikado in this production. This fine actor, singer and sometimes dancer had all the moves and attitude and was hilarious in a carefree and relaxed fashion. Peter Olphert gave a great performance as Hanki Poo the disguised saxophonist and son of the Mikado. He captured the naive and hopelessly romantic nature of the character. Unfortunately, his singing was stretched in the upper range. Alan McClarty gave us a tour-de-force performance as Ko-Ko. This performer had excellent comedy timing, facial expressions and delivered each scene with energy and merriment. Singing was secure as the theatrical, clumsy and cowardly lord high executioner to be! Harry Stinson gave us a great performance as the pompous Pooh- Bah, the lord high everything. This actor hit all the marks in comedy and musical interpretation. Rory Sheehan gave a very entertaining performance as Pish-Tush. A cool performance. Louise McClarty was a beautiful sweet and bubbly Yum-Yum. Singing was beautifully measured. Laura Fisher was a formidable, sarcastic Pitti Sing with a fantastic belter voice. Amy Rankin gave a very good performance as sassy Peep-Bo. We had a fantastic performance from Helen Wilkinson as the fierce and fiery Katisha. This actress was superb in the role and her singing was a tour-de-force. Mary Byrne came to mind!

Richard Cambell brought together a fine seven piece band for this exhilarating big band score. We had some lovely brass playing from Derek McGillion and excellent flute playing from Suzanne Cameron. Mr Cambell gave us some great swing, jazz, blues, gospel, R & B, Be-Bop, rock and torch songs from the pit as it supported the overall production. The tempos needed some work and entrances and finishes were not as crisp as we would have liked. The singing from the chorus was strong but we did need more work on harmonies. Soloists had a tendency to check in with the MD.

Thank you to Portrush Music Society for a wonderfully entertaining evening.

Director/Choreographer Peter Kennedy brought out all the comedy in this fine production in Roscrea, with some lovely touches. Blocking was secure and fast paced. Staging was secure. Dancing was lively and colourful with some lovely formations and final pictures. The barn dance was great. The capturing of the girls was hilarious. We had some very secure Musical Direction from MD Mary Rose McNally (pictured). The nine piece orchestra was beautifully musical with some lovely string and effective flute playing. This skilfully played expansive and expressive score exposed a wonderful musical style and folky flavour from our versatile and competent players, just what is needed for this style of show. Singing was very secure from the chorus with lovely harmonies and timbre while our soloists were secure and supported. The piano was a little too dominant in the overture, but balance was forthcoming as the show progressed. 'Sobbing' Women was slightly exposed. The score is written purposefully to lend itself to lively dance and that is just what we got from Ms. McNally.

We had a very secure performance from Frank Jordan as bull-headed protagonist Adam Pontipee. The character of Adam is a stubborn male chauvinistic pig that eventually gets tamed by a woman. Mr. Jordan was impressive not just vocally but equally physically giving a very solid performance. Accent was an issue at moments, but overall we had a secure interpretation. Rachael McMahon gave a very spunky yet charming performance as Milly, our frontier woman. This actress captured the fiery and also the poignant nature of this character. Singing was beautifully measured and a highlight.

All the brothers were tremendous in their roles, Singing was good, and dialogue was packed with energy and fun. Paul Spenser gave a charming secure performance as Benjamin. Hilarious! Tadhg Maher gave a great energised performance as Caleb. Great! Eunan Carrol was great as cool and calm Daniel. Well done! Mark Delahunty was impressive as Ephraim. Focused! Colum Doyle gave a steady performance as Frank. Looked great! Fergal Flanagan was lovely as youngest brother Gideon. Excellent!

All the brides were fine singers and also caught the fun of the show. Laura Dolan was gorgeous as Ruth. Shanna Kenny was impressive as Liza. Caoimhe Kirby was hilarious as Martha. Roisin Heenan was focused as Sarah and Breffni Fitzpatrick was lovely as Alice.

The ensemble were very focused and committed to their many roles. Singing was excellent and the suitors did a great job! Paddy O'Dwyer was fine as Mr. Hoallum. Siobhan Bowe was very strong in the role of Mrs. Hoallum. A stand out performance with great physical and facial expression!

The overall set design worked very well in this confined space. Some of the centre stage panels were a little light and flimsy. The painted backdrops were excellent. Mark McLoughlin, Stage Manager, and his team did an excellent job backstage. Scene changes were slick and nicely planned. The props were appropriate and well throughout. Sound balance was an issue at times from John Coffey of Templemore. Cueing was good.

Pat McGann's costumes were suitable and fitted very well. The overcoats were excellent. We could have done with more hats for the men, particularly the Mayor. All black shoes would have been better. We could have done with a veil for the wedding. Underwear for the lads could have been more distressed. We needed to weight the costumes as the show headed into winter time. Makeup was good and hair suitably of the times. Lighting from Gerry Taylor was excellent. Cueing was good. The colours worked well for this type of show. We did have a slight issue with flickering LED's. Lovely lighting in the barn scene.

Thank you to everyone in Roscrea for a great night's entertainment!

I have to admit to having all sorts of negative pre-conceived notions when I heard that the venue for Banbridge Musical Society`s `Me and My Girl` was a cinema. Over the past year I have seen shows in theatres, sports halls, community centres and even lecture halls and it always amazes me how groups overcome venue limitations. But a cinema?? Not for the first time on my travels, I was proven wrong. A generously sized playing area which accommodated one of the finest sets I have seen for this show and, remarkably, flying facilities which most societies would kill for, made this a superb venue for what was a highly entertaining production.

Director/choreographer Leonard Anderson gave us a fast-paced and lively show from start to finish. There was a wealth of comic business throughout and Mr Anderson had worked hard with the ensemble who were busy and engaged as required. The difficult library scene was extremely well blocked and performed. I did, however, feel that the end of the show was thrown away somewhat which was a terrible pity. Choreography was generally well rehearsed and precise. `The Family Solicitor` was great fun and `An English Gentleman` was superbly effective as the ensemble nodded and shook heads with remarkable precision. We had a nice tap sequence from four maids in `The Sun Has Got Its Hat On`. `You Would if You Could` was excellently performed by Bill and Jacquie, however the ending was terribly weak with no `compromising position` for Gerald to be either "shocked" or "astonished" at.

MD Colin Loughead conducted very well in a very tight corner to the audience`s right. There was a good sound from the band generally although the decision to drop the violin did leave noticeable gaps, particularly at the top of Act Two. Perhaps dropping one of the trumpets would have been a better call. Choral singing was generally strong although there was a lack of balance in `An English Gentleman`. Incessant, animated conversation between the trombone player and clarinettist during Act Two was distracting and unprofessional. Anthony Fitzpatrick was as fine a Bill Snibson as I have seen. He was a whirlwind of comic energy as the cockney costermonger and hardly came up for breath from the second he appeared. There was more to him than comic business though. Mr Fitzpatrick was a very clever performer and there was a gorgeous chemistry with Sally which was so believable. Singing was very strong, particularly in the excellent `Leaning on a Lamppost` which was superbly performed.

Lorraine Jackson-Brown was an excellent Sally. Sally is the heart of the show and Ms Jackson Brown`s intelligent, sensitive approach ensured that we experienced great heart and warmth from her most engaging performance. Chemistry with Mr Fitzpatrick was superb. They really were a great pairing. What a magnificent voice she had too. `Once You Lose Your Heart` was very thoughtfully sung with gorgeous expression and phrasing.

The imperious Duchess of Dene was most impressively played by the very experienced Rosemary Kelly. Ms Kelly was an excellent actress and her comic timing was exquisite as she skilfully nailed each cutting remark. Her superb soprano voice was a joy in `Song of Hareford`.

Ian Davidson was more than a little flamboyant and over the top as Sir John Tremayne. This may have been a directorial decision. Whatever the thinking, it was an unfortunate choice which drew focus from other performers and should have been reeled in by Mr Anderson on the rehearsal room floor. Potential was undoubtedly there but Mr Davidson`s performance was in need of toning down.

Claire Costello was wonderful as the self-obsessed, materialistic man- eater Lady Jacqueline. It was a most humorous portrayal. Ms Costello`s powerful belt voice was excellent in the very funny `Thinking of No-One but Me`.

Ryan McCourt was impressive as Gerald Bolingbroke, playing well off Ms Costello. However, he too needed to pull things back from time to time. His pronunciation of "Jacquie" as "Jack-We" was quite odd. `The Sun Has Got His Hat On` was as camp as a row of tents but it worked. Mr McCourt had a fine tone to his voice with an impressive range.

It was a case of art imitating life as local solicitor Eddy Orr took on the role of Herbert Parchester, the family solicitor. Mr Orr was a fine performer with a most natural acting style. He enjoyed himself no end in the very funny `Family Solicitor` number. Paul Brown was an excellent Charles who went about his butler duties in a subtle, understated manner. The funniest line in the show "No sir, I`m married" was delivered with perfect dead pan timing. Chris Gorman enjoyed his cameo as Sir Jasper, throwing himself into the role with geriatric glee. Gerard Kerr and Kate Adams were a superb pairing as Lord and Lady Battersby. We really did feel for the poor Lord and understood perfectly why he sought solace in the bottle!

I loved Russell Caughey`s set which deviated from the standard design for the show. Utilising the huge width of the stage he gave us a most opulent Hareford Hall with lots of attention to the finer details. Scenic painting was excellent. The impressive garden backdrop in the second act looked very well.

Stage management was in the hands of Anthony Fairley and he ensured that pace was maintained through well rehearsed scene changes from his efficient crew. We did have a serious health and safety issue with a wheelchair which was not fit for use and an accident occurred on the night which should have been avoided. Thankfully, no major injury was caused but it could so easily have been more serious. The chair looked authentic to the era but safety must come first.

Rodney Ellis`s lighting design was simple but effective. There was good use of LED lighting throughout and some nicely chosen break up gobos on the floor for the garden scene were a welcome contrast. Unfortunately, the follow spot used in `Once You Lose Your Heart` was on a very sharp focus setting and required more subtlety.

Sound was generally well handled by Enda and Barry McCusker. There was a good balance between stage and pit and well chosen sound effects were most effective.

Dympna McConville did an excellent job on props. From the floral arrangements in Hareford Hall to the authentic, wooden tennis racquets, there was a lot of attention to detail in evidence. The difficult to source tiger- skin rug was a bit disappointing but that was a small thing in what was a very impressive props plot.

We had an excellent costume plot from Denise Bryson and Rosemary Kelly. Bill`s checked suit was perfect and the Pearlies were most impressive in their attire. One of the ancestors in the portraits is clearly referred to as a seafarer but was dressed as a clergyman. This was an unfortunate oversight.

Hair and make-up were generally well attended to. The Duchess sported a fine grey wig which added greatly to her aristocratic air. One jokeshop `bald wig` used in the kitchen scene was so out of place and distracting. This was a fine production from Banbridge Musical Society. Highlights included excellent work from Bill, Sally and the Duchess as well as a most impressive set. Thank you all for a most entertaining evening.

My second visit to the enchanting White Memorial Theatre this season, this time for St. Mary`s Choral Society Clonmel`s version of `Jekyll and Hyde` Wildhorn and Briscusse`s bloody tale of man`s inner struggle between good and evil. Even a catastrophic technical hitch, tinged with the bitterest of ironies could not take away from what was a quality production. Excellent direction, a superbly engaged ensemble and a towering central performance were central to the success of this wonderful show.

Michael O`Donoghue`s interpretation was a compelling one. Attention to minute detail was in evidence throughout as every dramatic possibility was explored.

Mr O`Donoghue created some exceptionally imaginative moments. The `prologue` of asylum inmates in various stages of agitation and distress was a disturbing enactment which set a suitably uneasy tone for what was to follow. Exceptionally clever utilisation and integration of the sinister character of Spider maintained an ominous thread throughout and was a standout feature of an intelligently crafted show.

Fergal Carroll`s musical direction and Mary Rose McNally`s choral work were magnificent with many musical highlights in evidence.  Excellent playing from a most accomplished nine-piece orchestra and some powerfully delivered ensemble vocals added so much to the overall professionalism. Mr Carroll`s conducting was most assured as he provided wonderful support to the large cast. The quartet `His Work and Nothing More` was a stunning rendition, brilliantly played and sung with exceptional diction and a beautiful blend of voices.

Mr O`Donoghue was responsible for much of the choreography which was strong, definite and assured. There was superbly controlled and fluid movement of groups during the powerful `Facade` and `Murder Murder` was exceptional in its realisation and execution. `Bring on the Men`, choreographed by Gillian Hewitt-Fitzgerald and Majella Louise Fitzgerald was excellent with Sheena Fennessy standing out for her impressive performance as a Red Rat Dancer.

The ensemble in this show was exceptionally well prepared and involved. Focus was wonderful and each and every person knew what was expected of them. Singing was of a very high standard and performance levels were most impressive. `Murder Murder` was brilliant musically and dramatically as the various scenes played out downstage of superbly disciplined ensemble freezes.

Diarmuid Vaughan`s portrayal of Jekyll/Hyde was stunning at times. His command of dialogue, pace and overall presence were indicative of this man`s exceptional talent. There was an incredible physicality to his first transformation as he threw himself about the stage. His ability to morph into the grotesque Hyde in the blink of an eye was unnerving as his entire face changed before us. A most skilful portrayal. The irony to which I alluded centred around the electrical fault which plunged the stage into darkness as Mr Vaughan sang the words "Lost in the darkness..." at the top of `The Confrontation`. It took quite some time for this glitch to be remedied but Mr Vaughan displayed incredible presence of mind to come downstage where he was lit by the spill from the orchestra lights. Brilliant! Singing was strong throughout with `This is the Moment` showing off Mr Vaughan`s vocal and emotional range very well.

Holly Jean Williamson was an impressive Lucy Harris who maintained a balance between the more sleazy elements of her character and a more vulnerable side which was laid bare in the excellent `Someone Like You`. Ms Williamson had a lovely tone to her voice which was at its best in the duet `In His Eyes`. Both herself and Mr Vaughan were excellent in the sensual but disturbing `Dangerous Game`.

Andrea Ruth Houlihan gave a really strong performance as Jekyll`s fiancée Emma Carew. It was a clever portrayal with some lovely moments. Singing was just wonderful from this very technically accomplished vocalist although, for me, there was a little bit too much vibrato at times, particularly in `Once Upon a Dream`. `In His Eyes` was superbly sung with Ms Williamson.

David Hughes played Jekyll`s confidante John Utterson who experienced his own internal struggle as he attempted to come to terms with the horrific events surrounding him. Mr Hughes sang well in the excellent `His Work and Nothing More`. It was a sincere portrayal but delivery of dialogue was not as strong as it could have been and I felt that Mr Hughes could have done with some more guidance in this regard.

Derek Ryan`s portrayal of Emma`s father, Sir Danvers Carew, was warm and engaging. His big, resonant voice and wonderful diction were a joy. Singing was first rate, his fine duet with Emma, `Letting Go` being a musical highlight.

The Board of Governors sang excellently in `Jekyll`s Plea`. George Barry was a wonderfully pompous Bishop of Basingstoke and Fiona Corcoran was a very OTT Lady Beaconsfield. Ms Corcoran could have held back slightly in her duet with the impressive Jack Hickey, `Bitch! Bitch! Bitch!` Her high pitched delivery and lack of subtlety got in the way of the dark humour of the piece. Cian Corcoran was simply outstanding as Lucy`s violent pimp Spider. His `Marilyn Mansonesque` appearance and incredibly ominous presence made for a most chilling portrayal. Kiya Donlan was strong as Red Rat manageress Nellie. She was also a key member of the Red Rat Dancers. It is sometimes hard to imagine how certain shows are going to fit into what may be perceived as restrictive venues. Imagination is often the only real obstacle and Diarmuid Vaughan`s very clever design was evidence of this. The use of scaffolding which came out over the pit was inspired and meant that those of us in the balcony were often eyeball to eyeball with cast as they screamed of murderous deeds and deception. The stunning, mirrored lab was a triumph, brilliantly dressed with exceptional attention to detail. Kay Sheehan`s stage management was extremely slick with great co- ordination and timing of opening and closing of the lab in particular.

Dirk Bauman`s lighting design was imaginative, clever and very well operated with split second timing for important cues. A pity that the most crucial lighting moment of the show `The Confrontation` was marred by a rogue fuse through no fault of the lighting department.

Sound design by Pat Marnane was excellent with a good balance maintained between a powerful pit and cast. There was great use of sound effects throughout including flies in the asylum, horses in the street scenes and atmospheric bubbling in the lab. Cueing was excellent throughout.

Wardrobe did an excellent job on this show with Nomac supplying costumes and Ollie Connellan and Anne O`Connor co-ordinating. There were fine gowns and formal wear at Danvers` party and the Red Rat ladies looked well in their red and black attire.

The props department outdid itself on this show. The lab was a veritable treasure trove of props with its bottles, vials, books and lamps... not to mention a most imposing and authentic looking syringe which made many an audience members` eyes water!

Hair and make-up were well looked after and authentic to the era. Ali Murphy provided excellent wigs which added so much to the overall look. Spider`s `anaemic` appearance was most disturbing.

The standard of shows I have witnessed this season has been incredibly high at the business end of proceedings. Yet, as I watched the opening minutes of Wexford Light Opera Society`s `The Witches of Eastwick` I knew that this was a show which was in a different league to much of what had gone before. It was a spectacular offering, with every aspect of its production reaching exceptionally high standards. For me, a new benchmark had been set. It really was that good.

John Donnelly`s production was exactly what one would expect of a director of his calibre. This was a mammoth show artistically, visually, logistically and technically. Mr Donnelly pulled out all the stops in what was a most professional interpretation full of pace and brilliantly clever comic scenarios. Casting was a key aspect in the success of this exceptional production and Mr Donnelly had built a stunning cast around what can only be described as a phenomenal trio of female protagonists. The breathtaking flying sequence and the incredibly professional and effective use of jaw- dropping projections underlined the brilliance of the production.

Fintan Cleary`s orchestra was a veritable `who`s who` of some of the finest musicians in the country and they certainly earned their keep as they brought Dana Rowe`s score to life. The woodwind section was kept on its toes with much doubling up and no less than eight instruments between two excellent players! From the brilliant overture we knew that this was going to be a musical treat and it did not disappoint. Vocally, this was a phenomenal show. Each of the three witches was stunning individually but it was when they came together that their real `magic` took hold. `I Wish I May` and `Make Him Mine` were outstanding as their three voices blended in numbers which would not have been out of place in any professional production. Sublime! Choral singing too was excellent with a really strong sound in the excellent `Dirty Laundry`.

I loved Nicole McDonald`s choreography. It was so in tune with the quirky, irreverent tone of the show and the exceptionally clever ideas were integrated seamlessly into the dramatic action. `Dirty Laundry` was a wonderful routine, so sharp and precise and `Dance With the Devil` was a brilliantly clever and superbly performed number during which the gentlemen evolved from dull, `ordinary Joes` to uninhibited sex gods!

Clever choreography and direction don`t always translate into a good show. You`ve got to have a cast which is in tune with the vision. The ensemble in this show were very much on the same page as their production team and entered into the show`s dark quirkiness with an incredible energy and relish. There was a sense of a great confidence in a special show and everyone working hard towards making it work.

George Lawlor was wonderful as the self-professed "horny little devil" Darryl Van Horne. He was both sinister and charming at the same time which is a difficult balance to create. Comic timing was excellent and this guy`s ability to deliver a one-liner was simply brilliant at times. Every glance, every raised eyebrow was timed to perfection in a brilliantly anarchic portrayal.

Mr Donnelly must have cried tears of joy when the three ladies playing the title roles walked in to audition. We often say that someone was "perfectly cast". That term was never truer than when used in reference to this unbelievable trio. The remarkable Siobhán Meyler Fawsitt was magnificent as the leader of the pack. She owned the stage. Her diction, timing and delivery of dialogue were so strong. She was outstanding vocally in the brilliant `Your Wildest Dreams` and exuded confidence and sensuality in `Another Night at Darryl`s`. Sharon Clancy`s performance of repressed spinster Jane Smart was the performance of the show for me. Her transformation into a sexually liberated vamp in `Waiting For the Music to Begin` was one of the funniest things I have seen on stage in years. Timing was exquisite from this very talented comedienne and she sang up a storm throughout. Naoimh Penston was a delightfully cookie Sukie Rougement, who longed to be more like the heroines of her vast collection of books. Full of words but unable to articulate, she was hilarious as she underwent her transformation in `Words, Words, Words`. Diction was incredible in this number. However, it was the often omitted `Loose Ends` which really blew us away. Beautifully emoted and technically perfect, it was yet another standout moment in a show with many, many such moments.

The excellence just kept on coming and Catherine Walsh as the officious battleaxe Felicia was testament to the talent in depth in this brilliant cast. She was both hilarious and despicable in equal measure and her final scene with her long-suffering, henpecked husband Clyde, played superbly by Pat Lawlor, was comedy gold.

James McDermott and Catriona Brady were a brilliantly comic couple as Michael and Jennifer. They were as cheesy as camembert in a very funny `Something`. Mr McDermott was exceptional in `Dance With the Devil` and Ms Brady`s transformation from `innocent girl next door` to `smouldering object of lust` was brilliantly portrayed.

Owen Brady was very funny as Darryl`s manservant Fidel and Maggs Jacob was wonderful as the slightly obnoxious but hilarious Little Girl. Ms Jacobs also understudied all three witches roles which is no mean feat! I loved the exquisite attention to detail of John O`Donoghue`s quirky set with its picket fence motif. Darryl`s gothic love nest was simply stunning and the collapsing church complete with pyrotechnics was a triumph. The set worked magnificently against the backdrop of the superb projections. Stage manager Colin Murphy ensured the scintillating pace of the show was maintained throughout with excellent work from a well-rehearsed crew. There was great authenticity in the wonderful array of props managed by Linda Hynes. Nothing was out of place and so much thought had gone in to the finer details.

It is difficult to do justice to the standard of Anne Recks` costuming in this show. Again, excellence and attention to detail shone through. The clever colour palette was carefully planned and reflected the overall quirky feel brilliantly.

The hair and make-up team did very well. Felicia`s hair provided a standout (or is it stand up?) moment!

To say that Gerry Taylor threw the kitchen sink at this show with his lighting design is an understatement. He threw that and every available piece of kitchen apparatus too! This was Mr Taylor at his very best and again I find myself running out of superlatives. So many brilliant effects and transitions, perfectly timed, complemented and enhanced the brilliantly high standards of production set elsewhere.

Sound from Jason Fallon was as flawless as I have come to expect of this designer. Superb stage/ pit balance and well chosen sound effects added greatly to the overall presentation.

I am rarely `blown away` by a production. I rarely consider a production to be `flawless`. This was one of those rare productions. It ticked every single box and then some. It was a triumph for John Donnelly and his team and a fitting tribute to the late Fr John O`Brien who (ironically, given the tone of this irreverent piece) must have been smiling down on his friends in Eastwick. Thank you all!

Decades on from watching Superstar for the first time, I've finally seen the light.

Despite the show's title, the role of Judas is at least central to this tale and, at last, I've come across someone who not only can sing the role but has the ability to enunciate his words.

Even recordings, at times, might as well just have been white noise but a big hallelujah then for teenager Tom Moran who finally made sense of the part with a commanding performance as the frightened and confused mortal doomed to go down in western history as synonymous with betrayal.

If his tearing pop tenor was good in Heaven on their Minds at the start of the night it had really warmed up by the time we got to Damned for all Time at the end of Act One and simply went into overdrive in Superstar at the end of the night. Mr Moran's general air of agitation as he senses the loss of control over their crusade was also correct for the role and proved a counterpoint to the passivity of Adam O'Brien's Jesus, an 18-year-old with another frighteningly good tenor voice complete with a sixth gear of an easy accessed falsetto. His version of Gethsemane was another highlight of the show.

In fact, Gareth Mahoney's well dressed, fast-paced production, played in front of Sean Henderson's solid Temple set, which dominated the Solstice Arts Centre's big stage, was littered with good voices. Graham Hutchinson has that rare instrument for a boy still at school - a potential bass-baritone voice, one that he made good use of as Caiaphas the high priest. Together with his excellent lieutenant, Liam Egan as the counter-tenor Annas, they captured the menace of men out to protect their own little empire in a country invaded by a foreign power.

Megan Walsh gave us a sweet- voiced Mary Magdelene, the prostitute who confesses she has fallen in love with the world-weary Christ as she attempts to calm him from the clamour which surrounds him, while Jamie Reynolds as Peter and Bob McQuaid as Simon proved they could handle meatier material in their short time in the spotlight. Sean Keany's cameo as Herod went down a storm with the audience while Shane Fox as Pilate portrayed the anguish of an outsider who didn't seek to be the arbiter of what he saw as a wholly Jewish dispute. The 40-strong chorus, predominantly female, was sensibly cut back at key times to allow for better balance while musical director Olivia Toman's nine-piece band, anchored by an excellent drummer and aided by Alan White and Darren Kelleher's fine sound plot, was supportive of the cast without threatening to overwhelm them.

That chorus, again blessed with decent diction, also got its chance to shine in concerted scenes such the beggars and cripples clamouring for Jesus to help them, neatly choreographed by Erin Kenny.

Mr Henderson's set, well lit by the aforementioned Messrs White and Kelleher, certainly helped the action whizz along as one scene flowed seamlessly into the next. Unfortunately, as all the action was played in front of the temple or its steps, it was a stretch then to imagine other iconic settings in the story such as the garden of Gethsemane or Herod's Galilean palace.
