Minor gripes perhaps on a night which was another good advert for the future of musical theatre here and a credit to a production team which gave up part of their summer to make it happen.

The year is 1959, a pivotal moment in American cultural history, when rock and roll was giving birth to the Sexual Revolution and everything in America culture was about to be turned upside down. Record companies were releasing more than a hundred singles every week and the country was about to explode. Grease, generally considered a trivial little musical about The Fabulous Fifties, is really the story of America's tumultuous crossing over from the 50s to the 60s, throwing over repression and tradition for freedom and adventure (and a generous helping of cultural chaos), a time when the styles and culture of the disengaged and disenfranchised became overpowering symbols of teenage power and autonomy. Originally a rowdy, dangerous, over-sexed, and insightful piece of alternative theatre, Grease was inspired by the rule-busting success of Hair and shows like it, rejecting the trappings of other Broadway musicals for a more authentic, more visceral, more radical theatre experience that revealed great cultural truths about America. In more recent productions Grease has had a tendency to create a succession of musical numbers rather than a strong sweep of narrative; anxieties and yearnings that are universal. This is a shame! That being said, it can also be seen as a teen-trivia musical, where broad strokes, big voices and flourishing high energy dances are the order of the day. This is what we got from Ulster Operatic Companies recent production in the Grand Opera House in Belfast. A broad comedy; high energy production full of colour!

The band was placed on a platform upstage centre in what seemed like a miniature radio backdrop. The side portals were decorated with large templates of Elvis and Marilyn Monroe and additional scene changes were flown in, trucked on or walked on by the stage crew. This production was entertaining and exuberant from Director/ Choreographer Peter Kennedy. High energy was forthcoming and the comedy moments were broad and crass. The overall production was well delivered by a solid and rehearsed cast. Scene changes could have been faster and tighter and it would have been nice if scene changes had been timed with the interlude and introduction music. We did have some empty gaps during scene changes. Some scenes could have been changed by the cast. Entrances and exits needed more direction; maybe dancing on and off would have helped the overall pace and continuity. The overall production, albeit entertaining, was in need of more nuances pertaining to the overall themes as "Grease" tackling social issues pertinent to 1950s teens and touching on matters of friendship, rebellion, acceptance, class conflict, dreams and love requited. It did lack the kind of magic that is needed between Sandy and Danny and the tension between Kenickie and Betty Rizzo in order to bring this musical to its full conclusion.

Musical Director Chris Tingley brought together a solid tight six piece band for this production. We had some lovely trumpet playing from Alisdair Wallace. We needed to restrain the saxophone and the guitar for some numbers; particularly the saxophone during 'There Are Worse Things I Could Do' and the guitar playing for 'Hopelessly Devoted To You' was too finger-picked and spiky. The band was suitably confident and musically explosive. Pit-Stage balance for this type of show is paramount to its success as the musical content is overtly large and broad. Getting appropriate balance when the band is placed upstage of the cast is even a greater challenge; we need the musical director to be very cognisant of pit-stage balance. There were times when the band came across too loud for some solo and chorus numbers; particularly obvious for 'Magic Changes' and 'Hopelessly Devoted To You'. Tempi were too fast for 'Look At Me, I'm Sandra Dee' and 'Sandy'. Singing from soloists was secure and well rehearsed. Harmonies were good for 'Freddie My Love' but needed more attention for the larger chorus numbers. Music was too loud over the dialogue during the start of Act 2. Overall, I would have to say that pit-stage balance and tempi was an issue for this production. This may have been in part due to the large auditorium, the band being placed upstage and behind the cast and the age profile of the cast.

Stage Management under the stewardship of Andrew McKnight was exact and skilful. Scene changes were efficient but could have done with more pace in order to support continuity. It is important to get scene changes tight, but at the same time be mindful of getting the job done quickly. Involving the cast in some setting and striking may have helped continuity, particularly the striking of the car. The set-up into the bedroom scene was particularly slow. The props for this production were basic. Be mindful to have props that are era and time appropriate; the car Cromer's looked too modern. Lighting design by Paul Hinchliffe was efficient and worked well. Spotlights were a little insecure at times. The sound balance needed more attention. There were times when dialogue and entrances were overpowered by the band. The soloist in Magic Changes could have been louder. The radio voice needed to sound more radio-like and some offstage dialogue was missed.

Costumes from Theatrical Costume Hire were excellent. Congratulations to Meike White in the wardrobe team for excellent shoes and attention to detail. Hair styles and wigs were appropriate from Bill Galloway and Kerry Orr. Make-up was excellent. Choreographer; Peter Kennedy assisted by Brook Aillen gave us great fast paced and interesting routines throughout the show. The dances were well devised with interesting formations and quirky moments i.e.; the male 'CRAB' walk! The cast worked hard to deliver the routines. Some cast members needed more rehearsal. The high kicking in the Rydell High routine was excellent. 'Born to Hand Jive' was a highlight and the final picture was excellent as was the final picture for 'You're The One That I Want'. Mathew Blaney was a very alluring Danny Zuko. Singing was secure and intuitively musical. This fine actor had great stage presence keeping his cool macho image in each and every scene. Mr. Blaney was imposing and determined in every scene and had lovely comedy nuances when required. This actor needed to embrace the T-Bird leadership role with a broader personality. This character needs to be the essence of the late 1950's and the sexual revolution that imploded on the one hand and the struggle of being cool and yet earning Sandy's affections on the other. We had a very sweet and compassionate performance from Claire Howell as Sandy Dumbrowski. Ms. Howell gave a very secure performance with some lovely singing. This actress was self-assured, calm and demure. The challenge for this character is to be naïve and innocent but at the same time to be 'interesting' to Danny. Aaron Butler gave a very energised and forthcoming portrayal of the tough and rude second in command Kenickie. This fine actor and singer was ever present and engaging in every scene. We had a very tough and steadfast performance from Annika Graham as Betty Rizzo. This actress has great potential. Singing was dynamic and hearty. Dialogue was too rushed and diction was an issue at time. This actress needed to slow down her dialogue and stand out more from the rest of the Pink Ladies, principally as the wild one! Ande Gray was solid in the role of gullible Doody. A fine singer and a very imposing actor. Rachael Stewart gave us a very likeable portrayal of Frenchy, the beauty school dropout. This actress captured the friendly and dreamy nature of the character. Singing was delightful. The school mooner 'Roger' was in the capable hands of actor Sean Larkin. Mr. Larkin was the perfect prankster. Hannah Dwyer gave us a very believable portrayal of Marty, the sailor love- struck pink lady. This actress captured the fun and the energy of this character in every scene. Marc Dallas gave us a very quirky, wise- guy performance as Sonny and Cherelle Hinds was ever present in the role of ever-eating Jan. Chris Pattison gave a great performance in the role of Eugene, the bullied nerd of Rydell. Mr. Pattison was hilarious and gave us a brave and steadfast comedy performance. This actor kept our interest and delivered every moment through to the last beat. We had a nicely measured performance from Joan Grenville as Miss Lynch, the English teacher while Shane McCaffrey was secure in the role of radio DJ and compare of the Prom, Vince Fontaine. We had a stand-out performance from Faith Stevenson as want-to-be pink Lady and cheerleader Patty Simcox. This actress was strong and engaging in every scene. David McCrossan was very imposing as rock star student Johnny Casino. Singing was secure and Ruth Reid had great stage presence as the girl from a different school, Cha Cha. A very confident performance! Mal Hanna was very secure as Teen Angel, our dreamed up guardian angel. Singing was excellent.

This company gave us a great night's entertainment. They were bold and broad in every scene and they were full of the style that is the 1950's rock and roll. Energy and commitment was apparent. Singing was secure and forthcoming. Dancing was a flourish of high energy and very well executed. Congratulations to everyone at Ulster Operatic Company.

Be mindful to seat the adjudicator in a position where he/she can see the whole stage. Unfortunately, this adjudicator was placed in a seat that made seeing stage right very difficult.

Midway through Act Two of Dundalk Musical Society's latest version of The King and I, the all-powerful but wily potentate slipped his arm around Anna Leonowens' waist as she sang "Shall We Dance" and they glided around the stage.

It was the first physical sign of the growing thaw in the relations between sparring combatants from clashing cultures, even a hint of the possibilities to come and it was clearly a moment the Sunday matinee audience at the border town's An Tain theatre had been waiting for, as they burst into spontaneous rhythmic applause in the best Viennese tradition accompanying musical director Mary McCague's tight 10-piece band.

In fact, it was so sudden and unexpected that it felt almost choreographed, something that had been rehearsed before I took my seat. Instead, I quickly realised it was merely a sign of how much the crowd were enjoying the performance and a measure of how the company is embedded in the community.

And there was much to enjoy in Donal Cantwell's production of the most romantic of Rodgers and Hammerstein's classics.

The show is a gift for a confident leading lady who is not frightened to command the stage, bossy yet endearing - cue Karyn McCooey with her effortless mezzo as Anna. She grabbed the role by the throat as soon as the boat from Singapore docked and refused to let it go for the rest of the performance.

Gerry O'Hara as the King of Siam, a more than capable actor on this performance, was an excellent foil for her. By turn imperious, autocratic, cunning, jealous and pragmatic, he was in his element stomping around his palace.

The Kings of Broadway may have been employed by ageing star, Gertrude Lawrence, to turn the story into a vehicle for her but they saved the best song of the piece for the leading supporting player and "Something Wonderful" got what it deserves from Orlaith Crosbie as a lovely toned Lady Thiang.

Aisling McCormick with her engaging soprano voice and Alan Doherty with his impressive tenor were well matched as the Burmese lovers Tuptim and Lun Tha.

Paul Kinahan brought his considerable stage experience to bear as an extremely natural Captain Orton, proving there is no such thing as a small part while Paul McGee was an ever-so-English Sir Edward Ramsey.

Youngsters Scott McHugh as an impressive looking Chulalongkorn and Pauric Craven as Louis have promise and will hopefully go on to enjoy many years on the stage. Mr Cantwell's well-paced production was also blessed with a troupe of well-drilled kids representing the scores of the King's children and enhanced by Roisin Walsh's unfussy choreography which culminated in an excellent version of the set- piece ballet, The Small House of Uncle Thomas, complete with a shimmering curtain sea and all-too- realistic wolf masks which would meet with the approval of Love/ Hate's Fran The show was also embellished with an impressive and highly functional set from Proscenium Set Hire, expertly managed by Niall McCooey and his 13-strong stage crew and well lit by Peter McDonnell.

To top it all off, an excellent set of colourful costumes proved a feast for the eyes. I would hate to see the final bill for those glad rags as I lost count of the number of changes for the King and, in particular, Anna. Splashing the cash however, meant the end result was great value for money at the box office for an appreciative audience that went home impressed. In common with them I thought it was a sunny antidote to the late October northern monsoons.

Deep into Act Two of Oyster Lane Theatre Group's version of Frank Baum's famous story, Dorothy instinctively reaches for a bucket in the pivotal scene of the show.

For the benefit of the few who have never travelled the Yellow Brick road, the Wicked Witch of the West is threatening Dot's mate, the Scarecrow, with fire. The innocent girl from Kansas intends to douse the flames with water but accidently soaks the Witch who melts before their eyes.

However, with a Sunday matinee full house of 600 looking on - many of them enraptured kids, some even in costume - no water hits the floor of the Dun Mhuire stage. Instead, in a moment of theatrical magic, coloured glitter is hurled from the pail, glinting in the light as it falls on the Witch's cloak and into the clouds of dry ice which rapidly envelopes her.

It was another little visual touch from debutant director Thomas O'Leary in a show littered with impressive technical trickery and tailored for the cinematic age.

It might have been Mr O'Leary's first time with his hands on the tiller of a musical but he is no stage novice. Indeed, he is a founder member of OLTG with a string of panto and drama credits to his name and all that experience was evident as he and set and lighting designer Mark Redmond put their creative heads together to come up with a platform that allowed this old tale to rattle along while creating a feast for the eye.

The production team - with choreographer Suzanne O'Leary creating some neat stage pictures with her dance routines and musical director and chorus master Patrick Clancy a relaxed but assured presence in front of his 12-piece band - then proceeded to cleverly mesh together the technical and the physical.

Making her principal debut by stepping out on that famous road was 16-year-old Megan Power who did enough in the role of Dorothy to suggest that she is another of those talented youngsters to keep an eye on in future.

Mr O'Leary's well-paced production was also blessed by a finely judged performance from Ruth Donegan who, I'll swear, delighted in the twin role of the uptight Miss Gultch and the loathsome Wicked Witch of the West.

It was also bolstered by well conceived turns by Mick Farrell, Stephen Byrne and Neal O'Leary as the Scarecrow, the Tin Man and the Cowardly Lion respectively.

Rosemary Furlong as a fabulous looking Glinda straight out of every little girl's Princess magazines and Robbie Duggan, all elbows and energy as that early bureaucrat, the Oz gatekeeper, also had their moments in the Oz sun.

Marian O'Leary was a well-pitched, homely Aunt Em playing against the authoritative Kevin McDermott as Uncle Henry while Lorcan Dunne with his rich speaking voice was believable as both the kindly Professor Marvel and the hectoring charlatan that is the Wizard of Oz. Oyster Lane's smallish adult chorus delivered exactly what was asked of them by the show's production team while a 30-strong children's chorus showed highly impressive commitment and concentration as Munchkins, monkeys and, at times, stagehands.

The overall look of the show was enhanced by a set of costumes supplied by the That Looks Good Company, who, happily, lived up to their name.

And the sound engineers from Star Systems worked their own little piece of magic, pitching levels correctly to keep the music and plot audible over the constant murmur of the little Munchkins sitting in the stalls.

A pity then that the cyclorama - such an important part of the production - kept rippling in Act Two as actors crossed the stage behind it too close and too fast.

Most major musicals bring their own set of challenges and dilemmas to an amateur adaptation, be it a requirement for expansive sets and staging, period or niche costume and production design or elaborate, demanding choreography, all of which often have to face the constraints and practicality of budget and available talent. Relatively speaking, RENT is a somewhat barer, rawer piece of musical theatre in those particular regards, and one whose expressionist, bohemian slant makes it a more flexible beast for the amateur treatment. However, therein lies the inherent challenge of tackling the show - there are no major set pieces or spectacle to hide behind, it is a story and production that is raw, pure, innately human and relatively uncompromising - and if the cast cannot rise to the occasion the show can be a floundering mess of youthful post-modernism and half-baked theatrical expressionism. It truly is a show that is only as good as those in whose hands it is placed. Based on Giacomo Puccini's opera, La boheme, RENT follows the lives of a group of struggling artists and musicians living in New York's Bohemian Alphabet City during the AIDS/HIV epidemic of the 90s. Its rock score highlights the anguish and tribulations these people endure over a year of their lives whilst examining contemporary and universal issues including sexuality, relationships, prejudice and addiction. This is just what we got from Portmarnock Musical Society, a raw interpretation of this groundbreaking Musical.

Donal Brennan was a tour-de-force in the demanding role of HIV-positive songwriter Roger. This actor was secure and forthcoming in every scene. Singing was excellent particularly for 'One Song Glory' and 'Your Eyes'. Sean McMahon gave us a solid and determined performance as Mark the young filmmaker. This actor was agile, appealing and very accomplished in the role. Singing was secure and nicely measured. Ciarán Mooney was very imposing as the gay philosopher and AIDS sufferer Tom Collins. This performer was brave and indomitable in this challenging role capturing the kind and playful nature of the character. Singing was determined and innately musical particularly for 'I'll Cover You'.  Neil Reid gave a solid performance as former roommate now turned entrepreneurial landlord Benjamin Coffin III. This actor was solid in every scene. We had a robust performance from Jennifer O'Donovan in the role of lawyer Joanne Jefferson. This formidable actress gave a standout performance in the role. Diction was an issue during 'We're Ok'. 'Take Me or Leave Me' was excellent. Sean Keany was the perfect Drag-Queen optimist Angel Schunard. This fine young actor gave a very compelling performance in the role and his singing was excellent.

The role of Mimi Marquez, the drug addict, HIV positive erotic dancer was perfectly captured by Orla Jennings.

This actress was confident and unwavering in every scene. Singing was superb. Highlights were ' Would You Light My Candle' and 'Out Tonight'. We had a standout performance from Roisin Walshe in the demanding role of now lesbian actress and protestor Maureen Johnson. 'Over The Moon' was very strong. 'Take Me or Leave Me' was excellent. Eva Kelly was very secure as Alex Darling. Joe Bulger was fine as Mr. Grey. Les Riley did well as the Pastor. The chorus of police officers', vendors, support group, homeless people, junkies and parents worked very hard to recreate and engage with us throughout the evening. Choral singing was exciting, poignant when required and diction was excellent. 'La Vie Boheme' was suitably brave, crass and rude. 'Seasons of Love' was a highlight. Well done!

Costumes were a diverse mix and match and suited the overall aesthetic. We would have liked some jewellery for the mother's. The overcoat and gloves for Benjamin Coffin II were very appropriate. The helmets on the police officers were peculiar. Makeup was well attended to by the wardrobe department. Makeup for the Mother did need to be older. Dean Kelly gave us some interesting lighting stages. We needed to be more careful with spotlights and face light was an issue at times. We also had some flickering from the LED's. We would have liked more Blue light for ' Would You Light My Candle' scene. Snapper DBO's needed at times, particularly at the end of 'We're Ok'. The set design was appropriate and worked very well in the constrained setting. The levels worked very well. The sound cueing and steadiness was admirable from Jody Trehy. Props were appropriate albeit the coal fire unit too new looking. Stage Management under the leadership of Mary Murphy was exact and proficient for a show that had very few set changes. Nikki Lynch did very well on the Choreography. We had some lovely 'Still's' from the cast. Tango Maureen needed more work.

Musical Director Marian Mullen amassed a fine rock band for this production. The musical content in Rent could be considered Rock- Opera, and this musical director was certainly up for the challenge. The musical content was raw and vibrant. Solo work was eagerly anticipated by Ms. Mullen at all times with support and solid entrances and finishes. Choral work was excellently rehearsed and delivered. Tempi were secure and confident throughout the evening. This musical contains over forty musical numbers of an eclectic and allegorical mix and this MD was always resolute and perceptible in her delivery. 'No Day But Today' needed reining-in. We had some lovely harmonies in 'Will I'. 'Seasons of Love' needed to build more. The overall production was accomplished and resolute from Director Chris Currid (pictured above). This director knew what he wanted, chassed the nuisances and let the issues or irony leap from the stage through the determination of each character. There was nothing forced during the production as each scene felt appropriately organic and self-determined. That being said, it is important to be mindful of meaningful entrances and exits and to be brave and resolute to stage 'important moments' throughout your production. This director gave us a very skilful production and is to be admired. We would have expected Roger to use the video camera more on him and his surrounds. The Homeless people needed to be more downtrodden. The set-up for the support group meeting was a little slow but overall a very accomplished production. Continued success to this young and upcoming director!

Many thanks for the hospitality.

A Society is always onto a winner when it gets a live audience on its side.

Never mind what the critics say, what adjudicators with lofty ideals write or those end of season awards. If you can please the paying public that's the biggest prize of all.

Such a moment arrived early during this fast-paced Peter Kennedy production at Galway's Town Hall Theatre when I was serenaded in quad by several budding Annies around me as Sarah McGuire launched into "Tomorrow".

Eleven-year-old Sarah may look young for her age but she turned in a mature performance as the Depression-age foundling who gets a happy ending that had the adults in the stalls captivated as well.

Mr Kennedy's production, played out in front of a set with backdrops and flats of almost photographic quality, was also blessed with a raft of other quality leading players who maintained plausible American accents all evening.

Amanda Stuart was excellent as Miss Hannigan, a clever measured portrait of the harridan in charge of a city orphanage, so weary of a world that has left her in charge of little girls that she seeks solace in the bottom of a bottle and barrelling around the stage on a pair of bow legs berating anyone foolish enough to listen.

Louis Brennan, in a convincing bald wig which completely changed his appearance, brought his lyrical voice and some sharp suits to the role of Oliver Warbucks, a man so powerful he can effect the removal of crime buster Elliot Ness from his pursuit of Al Capone to engage in the search for Annie's long-lost parents.

Roisin Egenton's commanding Grace Farrell was a fashion plate with a classy singing voice although her hairstyle was too modern.

Nicky Lawless was lively as Hannigan's brother, Rooster, a man in a suit so vivid it could have lit up the Christmas market in nearby Eyre Square while Tara Spelman as his broad, the splendidly named Lily St Regis, is an excellent dancer.

Debutant Donal Gill as Bert Healy looked as if he had been on stage all his life, Karl O'Doherty was a forceful President Roosevelt while Adrian Mooney was highly impressive as Drake the butler.

With Mr Kennedy's trademark choreography pushing the action on the very lively kids' chorus as the residents of the city orphanage and the adult ensemble had their work cut out for them.

Musical director Shane Farrell, who had clearly note-bashed the kids' chorus, also produced a good sound from the adult chorus despite the imbalance between the sexes. His small but punchy band also never threatened to overwhelm the singers thanks to the help of a first-rate sound plot from Fintan Higgins.

Annette and Feargal Cavanagh's costume plot didn't just concentrate on the principals but turned out an ensemble as a sharply dressed set of New Yorkers with the guys in double breasted suits and their women in coats with velvet facing cloche hats and then turned them into a smartly turned out set of servants at Warbucks' mansion.

However, the look of the down-at- heel residents of Hooverville was less uniform and, in some cases jarringly modern.

David Lane and Tara Killilea's treasure hunt for what seemed like a ton of props must have been started several months before the curtain went up yielding big ticket lots such as a laundry basket and a couple of real gems in an old valve radio and telephone.

Behind the scenes, stage manager Chontelle Kenny and her team ensured the action on stage zipped along all evening with scenes flowing into each other seamlessly.

show_raw: Joseph And The Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat
review_text:
One hour and fifty minutes into Joseph and the Amazing Dreamcoat and the sweat stains visible on the back of Paddy McGennity's shirt are all too noticeable as Bosco Drama Group swing into the Mega-mix ending for the last time in this run.

Mr McGennity - Naphtali in this version of Lloyd Webber and Rice's Biblical cracker - was starting to melt. A glance along the line and it was the same for Ronan Sharkey's Issachar, another who had lost another few pounds after an all-action night on Newry's Town Hall stage.

This was a big production from a big production team that consisted of not one but two directors, not one, not two but three choreographers but only one musical director. To me that configuration could be a recipe for disaster. We've all seen school shows where the three from the drama department are meant to mesh with the two from the music department and the guy from the science block but the result is staff warfare, pupils short-changed and a show that never realises its potential.

Instead Bosco's structure harnessed the teams considerable talent and turned it into the stage equivalent of one of those multi-valve engines that lurk under the bonnet of sleek, high- performance cars.

This super powered beast then created a fast paced Joseph that flowed brilliantly from start to finish and defied you to take your eye off it. Jim McGuigan learned his craft from the man who broke the mould of amateur musical theatre in Northern Ireland so it should not have been a surprise when he and co-director Corinna Cunningham framed a show that was big on detail and high on precision and played out on Anthony Fairley's clever set.

Ann Marie Morgan is northern musical theatre's most hidden dance gem. She has worked with the best in the past and frankly, should do so again given that together with daughter Niamh and assistant Donna Magee she fashioned imaginative and inventive routines that were then drilled remorselessly into that hard working ensemble and which contributed mightily to the overall flow of the show.

Musical director Aislinn Mulholland, the public face of the production team, put on a show all of her own. This bouncing ball of energy drove on her seven-piece band while giving the clearest of commands to her cast including a 35-strong junior chorus, seated on steps leading to the stage and who were a joy to watch all evening.

Killian Foy in the title role was a strong Joseph with a very lyrical voice while 15-year-old schoolgirl Emma Martin, all eyes and facial expressions and loose of limb was commanding as the Narrator.

They headed a cast list that included a Jacob of gravitas in Martin Morgan, a neatly camp Potiphar from John Heatley together with his lusty wife, Catherine McLoughlin and an eye- catching, hip-swinging Damien Lavery as the Pharaoh.

Messrs Sharkey and McGennity together with Michael White headed up a tuneful all-action band of brothers that worked at times in tandem with a girls' ensemble that boasted some excellent dancers. While the boys sweated, the girls merely glowed, of course.

Every part of an extensive, appropriate and highly colourful wardrobe was made by Christine Magee and Paula O'Hare including, of course, a multi- coloured coat that virtually filled the stage at the end of the show.

Panic Hire's good lighting plot added to the production but the company blotted their copybook a little with a sound plot that on a few occasion felt it was being fed through a filter.

This show is often dubbed the only Rodgers and Hammerstein show the Kings of old Broadway didn't write. Instead, they acted as producers and when Hammerstein's former collaborator, Jerome Kern, died before the project really got off the ground, the duo turned to Irving Berlin to write the score.

Ace innovator Hammerstein, a driver of the integration of the plot, score and movement in musical theatre, would have given a warm welcome to Carnew Musical Society's latest version of Annie Get Your Gun.

Michael Dunbar's clever production relied as much on Mark Flynn's choreography, Kevin McEvoy's lighting and projection plot and Raymond Brennan's sound effects as much as it did on the director's little touches.

It was played out on Tony Barry's economical but highly effective set and driven along by Lar Duffy's tight seven-piece band. A further example of that integration is the fact that Mr Duffy had a hand in constructing the set - a musical director who truly knew every inch of the St Brigid's Hall stage. The lights were no sooner down and Mr Duffy's band in full flight in the overture than they were lifted again as Cody's Wild West showgirls moved into the audience selling candy and balloons. A similar trick, involving costumed customers for Buffalo Bill's entertainment, was also built into the orchestra's scene setter.

They were the first in a host of visual and technical tricks which ensured the pace of the show never flagged and kept the audience fully engaged. Annie's entrance, shooting a decoration off Dolly Tate's hat, set the comedic tone for the evening with the rifle shot marking the first of a slew of perfectly timed sound effects from Mr Brennan.

The action flowed seamlessly from scene to scene with Tommy Kavanagh's efficient stage crew adapting the physical part of the set while the mood and often the location was denoted by Mr McEvoy's subtle lighting effects and his big screen images projected onto a solid white board at the back of the stage.

Mr Flynn, who joined the production team after rehearsals had begun, ensured his work always moved the action on and gave us some memorable routines and stage pictures, particularly in the opening number and in a beautifully costumed Indian dance.

Ellie Condren's excellent all-action Annie commanded the stage and evolved from a waif-like backwoods girl to a beautiful bride opposite Padraig d'Arcy's handsome smooth- voiced Frank Butler.

Catherine Stafford was an impressive put-upon Dolly who sportingly subjected herself to a tremendous visual trick on a spinning wheel.

Jimmy Spellacy's Cody embodied the sentiments of the show's most famous song, toiling on in spite of suffering from a chest infection while Gary Lombard was a commanding Chief Sitting Bull.

Sean Hallahan's Charlie Davenport was a typical showbiz hustler; John Duignan's Foster Wilson was a wily hotelier with an eye for the main chance while Paul Doran's Mac was easy around the stage, adding his pleasing voice to some good harmonies.

Seamus Burnell as Pawnee Bill was an effective showbiz foil to Cody with Joan Duignan a star-struck Sylvia Potter Porter.

Four budding actors, Anna Rose Hennessy, Cliona Byrne, Cora Tyrell and Simon Thibault completed Annie's suitably Hicksville family.

Teamwork was the order of the day vocally as well, with some of the male principals adding their services to the outnumbered men's chorus to create a decent sound in the big numbers. Realistic props including those all- important rifles were conjured up by Jane Kinsella and Cathy Tighe; a good sound plot from Coffey's Templemore Sound ensured the full house in the south Wicklow village heard every word while the company had clearly spent a few bob on dressing the show with some striking costumes from No Mac Productions.

ME AND MY GIRL Never mind the old adage behind every great man there is a great woman, behind every great country house is a great butler.

And I bet Glencullen Dundrum's debutant director, Helen McCann, is glad she cast the unflappable Brendan Phelan as Charles, the man who really knew how the ancient Hareford pile ticked in this Noel Gay comedy.

Midway through Act One as Lady Jacqueline lined up new Earl, Bill Snibson, for a spot of seduction on a fancy looking chaise longue, she made one move too many and the back leg of the furniture dropped off. Maybe the errant couch had taken enough of their shenanigans earlier in the run and decided to spoil their fun. Whatever the reason, a crucial piece of the set was down and Ms McCann's plans for the scene with it. With Ruth Fitzsimon's Jacqueline and Kevin Hynes' Bill improvising like mad without the use of their most crucial prop, out stepped Mr Phelan to sweep up.

As well as organising the staff and dispensing advice to some of the dimmer characters in his role in the show, he had been acting as chief stage hand, drawing and removing many of the back cloths used to depict locations on the Mill Theatre's small stage.

The audience were accustomed to seeing him by this stage and thought nothing of it when he walked on from the wings with two serving girls in tow and directed the removal of the offending chaise, bravely carrying off the leg while the girls shouldered the heavy lifting.

His unscheduled appearance was so perfectly timed it looked as if it was just another part of the action -even momentarily  throwing doubt into my mind - and what could have been a disaster was dealt with calmly and in character - a tremendous piece of work.

It was symptomatic of the stage experience this cast possessed. The front line actors possess a wealth of dramatic experience.

Mr Hynes was terrific as the East End boy who inherits a title and a fortune. He was by turn flash, brash and resigned and possesses a decent voice and twinkle toes. His eventual bride, Niamh Cartwright's Sally Smith, was another good hoofer; had a voice with a bit of a belt to it and a smile that lit up the room.

Dorothy Clements as Maria, Duchess of Dene, oozed stagecraft with her stature, great delivery and timing while Liam Corrigan, another fine actor, proved a good foil for her as the snobbish Sir John Treymayne.

Ms Fitzsimon's Jacqueline was comfortable around the stage and had a good voice while John Paul McGouran as Gerald invested the indolent fop with a speech impediment.

Eamonn Murray's lively Parchester was in good voice while Robert Coventry's chair-bound and deaf Sir Jasper Tring displayed a range of facial expressions as he battled to keep abreast of developments. Imelda Sullivan's slightly scary Lady Battersby looked to be losing her battle to rein in her husband, Frederick, portrayed by Tom Ronayne as a clubbable type, likely to accept a drink when offered. And Carmel Tubbert's Mrs Brown was a chirpy nosey parker who looked as if she was game for a double act with that other Mrs Brown from Dublin. Ms McCann's fast-paced production was driven along by Dave O'Connor's fine eight-piece band, enhanced by Nicole McDonald's choreography and played on a set devised by Messrs Ronayne and Corrigan with Colm Mac Ghiolla Padraig.

The biggest problem faced by this well dressed show was a lack of space. It was a full house the night I was there but when the whole company was on stage it was a similar story on the other side of the front curtains.

Like all good wedding venues it looked fabulous. White muslin draped the walls and disguised the ceiling as it hung in voluminous folds.

The band too, was excellent. Any bride and groom would have been proud to have had them entertain the guests on their big day.

Sadly, like some weddings we've all been to, there was also that nagging feeling that both parties at this bash were not entirely at ease with each other.

So it was with the Marian Choral Society's version of The Wedding Singer staged at Tuam's St Jarlath's College.

Given that this was a relatively small company, the work of the ensemble at times was less than precise.

An impressive opening by the group flattered to deceive as more work was clearly required in big numbers such as "Saturday Night in the City" and "Pop". And it's not that the chorus were incapable of delivering it, with their execution of choreographer Aoife McClafferty's routine for "Casualty of Love" much better.

Ms McClafferty, who doubled up as co-director with Enda Burke, procured a more rounded performance dramatically from the show's two main characters, Shane Kelly, as lovelorn band leader Robbie Hart and Emer Kelly as Julia, the unassuming waitress who forgoes an opportunity to experience a wealthy lifestyle with a Wall Street financier to become Robbie's eventual wife.

Both were convincing individually, believable as a growing partnership and blessed with high quality voices. Amy Byrne as Holly, Julia's cousin and best friend, produced an engaging performance, Jane McNamara as Rosie, Robbie's loose-lipped trendy grandmother, was animated and acerbic while Suzanne Garvey- Brennan, who maintained the best accent of the evening, was a convincing mum of a young woman. Stephen Cassidy as Robbie's best mate and fellow band member Sam tried his best with some less than sparkling material while Paul Singleton as George, the third member of New Jersey's premier wedding band and the comedian of the piece, was a little too over the top at times for me.

Louis Brennan as Glen was almost too nice to be a Wall Street shark while newcomer Ailish Flaherty as Robbie's initial love interest Linda, will have bigger, better crafted roles in which to make a real impact.

Shane Farrell's excellent eleven-piece band helped drive the action on, giving us some fine individual and collective playing along the way.

But the musical director, wearing his other hat as chorus master, had less success with the ensemble, which, at times, was less than certain of the score.

This trip into 80s nostalgia was bolstered by some excellent period props and had the benefit of  a good sound plot from Dervan Sound with the team ensuring a good balance between the band and stage all evening.

And while the costume plot - put together by Bronagh McLoughney and Joanie Rathbone with the help of the cast - was generally good, some small details needed attended to.

If proof were needed of the value of a society having a youth wing, this show confirmed it.

The majority of St Patrick's Choral Society's production team are graduates of the company's underage section.  A couple of the older hands in the principal line-up came out of the same stable while the current crop of kids threatens to beef up the talent in the adult company.

And those kids are now learning stagecraft while delivering shows with high production values to paying audiences.

Director Gary Warnock's well thought out version of this famous old tale had been in gestation since last June. That's when the company decided to design and build their own set for the show by way of a summer workshop. However, with comparative novices in the team that had agreed to carry out the task, including some of their young stars, they wisely turned for guidance to professional set designer, Francie Morgan, who, conveniently lives on the Society's doorstep.

The result was a clever, adaptable set which bore the hallmark of an old master whose work has graced many Belfast theatres in his time. Its clever revolves, reversible and fold-out flats, a cabin with a tilting front and a delightful Yellow Brick road which lit up, allowed this show to move at a fast pace.

It was pushed on by musical director Gareth McGreevy's nine-piece band which despite shedding strings for a synth still had plenty of poke in the right places and aided by Niamh Conway's choreography which was tailored for the young cast.

Sweet-voiced Katie Melua lookalike, Courtney Burns, looked and sounded the part as Dorothy, our heroine who meets some strange bedfellows on the charge to the Emerald City.

Her compatriots on the long march included Matthew Campbell's highly consistent loose-limbed Scarecrow, Catherine McGrath's high soprano take on the Tin Man and another female, Laoise Carney, as the Lion. It took both girls a little while to settle but Ms McGrath went on to maintain a manufactured stiltedness all evening while Ms Carney, another good voice, has the makings of a fine comedienne when she slows down the action. Standing in the way of their various ambitions was Catriona Smyth as a high-energy Wicked Witch of the West, green of face and black of heart whose demise, in folds of light and clouds of ice, was handled expertly. Brian McElroy was a kindly Professor Marvel who then flipped to the other side of his coin to reveal the booming voice and bombastic tendencies of the charlatan Wizard of Oz. Charlotte Burke's Glinda was a fairytale princess of a good witch while Mel Carney was a fussy gatekeeper.

And buckets of experience came in the shape of Audrey Neill and Diarmuid Taggart who were highly believable as Dorothy's kindly Aunt Em and Uncle Henry.

Ciara McElroy came up with a fine costume plot including effective outfits for the Scarecrow, Tin Man and the Lion and some excellent threads for the Munchkins.

A lighting team which included the aforementioned Ms McGrath - one of the many instances of cast members immersing themselves in the creative process - did a great job in building atmospheres while a very competent sound desk ensured the balance between Mr McGreevy's musicians and the performers was spot on during the evening.

The company's aim may be to generate fresh talent to perpetuate a 50-plus-year-old tradition but it would be a disservice to label this as simply a youth production.

Instead the Downpatrick audience got value for money from a show which graced the old-money magnificence of the re-furbished Downshire Great Hall with its beautiful high vaulted ceiling.

I hope some of the Dublin companies took the time to cast their eye over the talent pool that is the UCD Musical Society.

Champion jump jockey, Tony McCoy, would admire the students' collective ability to clear hurdles.

Not only are the players, by definition, young and the production team relative novices, they decided to tackle one of modern musical theatre's most difficult works in a venue that's not exactly theatre-friendly.

Belfield's Astra Hall has no natural stage and hence, no entrances/exits for the cast. They have to enter and leave the stage through the same walkways the audience uses to make its way to their seats.

Debutant director, Sarah Martin's achievement of pulling off a rarely performed work, given those kind of handicaps, is all the more credible. Together with assistant director and choreographer, Aly Coyne, musical director Sharon Ryan and vocal director, Grainne Larkin, Sarah fashioned a fast-paced version of Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine's clever and most accessible piece.

Like Ms Martin, Ms Ryan and Ms Larkin, fourth and second year medical students respectively, were tackling their jobs for the first time. Only Ms Coyne, a second year Law and Politics student, has been down this road before.

Together they created a version of the show woven around well known fairytales that was played at times with a very serious face, at others with a knowing glance to the audience and, on occasions, with tongue firmly in cheek, yet the comedy never veered into pantomime.

Essentially this story about human inter-dependence comes about with the introduction of a married couple seeking a child who then barge in and out of familiar childhood stories in search of their dream, messing up plotlines as they go.

Aided by the excellent all-rounders Daniel Rosenthal and Wallis Hamilton- Felton as those central characters, the Baker and his wife, a suave Narrator in Ryan Gillespie and the impressive Maurice Wright as the Mysterious Man, the production moved along at a lick.

Another pivotal character, Aisleen Murphy's witch, was a marvellous old crone who morphed into a cynical overbearing mother once a curse was lifted and her beauty restored while Cormac Todd was a wonderfully goofy Jack who ultimately brings tragedy to the village.

His mother, Gill Lambert, was an engaging actress with a lovely mezzo voice; Clodagh Lalor invested her Cinderella with a lovely soprano while Amy O'Brien's juvenile Little Red Riding Hood was all pigtails and stamping feet.

Jamie Whitehouse was eye-catching as a lascivious and carnivorous Wolf and comically carnal as a strong voiced Cinderella's Prince matched against another big vocalist in Aidan Byrne as Rapunzel's Prince.

Ciara Finnerty's Rapunzel had yards of golden hair and a silvery voice, Colin Doran's Steward was an uptight jobsworth while Laura Davenport as Red Riding Hood's bloodthirsty Granny possessed fine comic timing. Amy Behan as Cinderella's stepmother was wonderfully glam, Tiarna Devlin and Sarah Egan were a good double act as her shallow stepsisters and Joseph O'Sullivan was a vain, well- aged Cinder's dad while Shauna Carrick as Cinder's mother was another fine singer.

The rest of Ms Martin's 29-strong ensemble were as disciplined as the main players with everyone remaining firmly in character throughout the evening while Ms Coyne's choreography was suited to the cast and stage and integrated into the production.

Musically the show was what the doctors ordered with an excellent choral sound, some fine individual voices and some excellent orchestral players taking on a typically difficult Sondheim score under Ms Ryan's baton.

Christina Olwill and Jenny Keogh, the girls behind the costumes, make-up and props, gave the production an updated feel with more naturalistic outfits than are sometimes used for this show while some of the make-up was excellent.

Rebecca Watkin's lighting plot and first-rate sound were perfectly meshed into the action. Settings were the weak link of the night, largely because of the limitations of the venue.

If only I could have seen this production in a real theatre, then I really would have lived happily ever after.

As soon as we took to our seats in the Grand Opera House in Belfast we stepped back in time to the 19th Century with Belfast Operatic Society. The Overall production was classic in its concept, yet modern in visual design. The backdrops we faced were huge crystal clear projections depicting the various locations, interior and exterior. A Treat!

This production from Belfast Operatic Company, in the capable hands of Director; Wilife Pyper was compelling. The production moved with ease and the staging was vastly interesting and imaginative. This production was confident and the cast were excellently rehearsed. The overall production was exciting and gripping. The scene changes moved with assurance as each state was appealing and delightful. We had some excellent attention to accents. There were many highlights including the Funeral Procession, The Ghosts in 'Link by Link'. Headless man, the flying over the London City scape was fantastic, slow motion was impressive and many more. This was a very polished and intelligent production. A Triumph!  The dancing was very energetic and imaginative from Choreographer Michael Evans. The style of dance was in keeping with the overall vision and formations were interesting and exciting. We had some lovely frozen tableaus, fantastic Tap dancing and the Sailors dance was excellent. The costumes for this production were a highlight from Triple C and the costume team. The various costumes were time and era appropriate and layered with underskirts and headdresses, hats from the outset. Hats were an issue for some of the men; we could have done with a few more Top Hats. We would also have liked more gloves and scarves and overcoats. Principal costumes were also very well attended to.  Shoes were excellent. It would have been nice if the four men in the couples dance had the same black trousers and similar style of shoes for ladies would have been nice. We would have liked more cape style coats for the ladies in the exterior scenes. Congratulations. Hair styles and make-up was very well attended to by Shelly Blair and the team. Wigs were excellent from Dauphines of Bristol. Lighting design and operation Alastair Kerr - ACK Productions Ltd was excellent. Gelling was interesting and varied. States were colourful when needed and atmospheric when required. The lighting design added greatly to the overall production values. The overall set design worked very well for this production from Set Designers Wilfe Pyper and David Robinson with set building from Encore. We would have liked some heights as the flat stage became tiresome. The projections were excellent and added to the overall production values. The Grave Stone slide was epic! The Snow was fantastic. The sound balance and cueing was flawless from Tim Dougherty. Cueing and sound effects were excellent. Balance was perfect. The Props team gave us a very good mix of authentic props in the various scenes. Be mindful of sellotape on Parcels. We had great dinner table props. Stage Manager Claire Donnelly gave us a very measured and slick production back stage. Scene changes were efficient and well-rehearsed. Seamless was the order of the day! The flying was also a major success.

Colin Boyd was the perfect Scrooge. This fantastic actor/singer was intuitive, engaging and appealing.  Mr Boyd gave us a high energy and a gritty performance intermeshed with moments of tenderness and pathos. This actor had fantastic stage presence and was compelling to watch.  'Nothing to Do With Me' was measured and tight. 'Yesterday, Tomorrow and Today' was a highlight. Ian McMaster gave a lovely performance as Mr. Smythe as he pleaded for leniency with his debts. Mark Leeman had great stage presence as the hardworking clerk Bob Cratchit. 'You Mean More to Me' was beautifully sung and delivered. The hopeful and generous role of Mrs Cratchit was delightfully played by Sinead Coll. This actress had lovely stage presence and built a wonderful relationship with the children. Scrooge's nephew, Fred Anderson was very nicely portrayed by Keith Pyper. This actor was pleasant and very focused. Alice Johnston was excellent as The Ghost of Christmas Past. This fine singer had great sprightly stage presence and youthful energy. Heather McCloskey was excellent as the blind old hag. We had a very nice moment from Fiona Clarke as Mrs. Mops in 'Dancing on your Grave'. Samuel Moore was notable as returned ghost Jacob Marley. Gary Redpath was impressive as Scrooge's Dad. Shirley Adair gave a very lovely moment as Scrooge's Mother. Wilfe Pyper was hilarious as Mr. Fezziwig. Laura Kerr gave a standout performance as Mrs. Fezziwig. This actress had fantastic stage presence and comedy timing. We had a lovely good-hearted performance from Ellen Mawhinney as Emily. This young actress was delightful and had a lovely voice. 'A Place Called Home' was beautiful. David Hassard did very well as employee Mr. Beadle. Jill Morrow gave a wonderful moment as Ghost of Christmas Future. Brian Trainor was very impressive as The Ghost of Christmas Present. This seasoned actor held the stage and gave a very funny and entertaining performance. A tour-de-force! Anna Nelson was secure as Sally Anderson. Oliver Havin was very impressive as young Scrooge. A beautiful singer! Young Michael Nevin was wonderful as Tiny Tim. This young actor pulled our heart strings. This chorus made up of middle class ladies, tarts, bankers, businessmen, wealthy women, ladies and dancers were excellent in each and every scene. They were always committed and focused and delivered the various scenes with expression and confidence. Entrances and exits were particularly confident and we were impressed with the clarity and performance standard from this expansive chorus. Singing was superb with excellent diction and impact. Congratulations! The children added greatly to the overall experience. They were excellently focused.

Musical Director; Colin Scott gave us a powerful musical triumph at the helm of a magnificent twenty-five piece orchestra. The orchestra was supreme with magnificent playing from strings to wind and bass. This was a very expansive score with over seventeen soaring songs and was delivered with essence and precision from this astonishing musical director. Musical interlude music was also complete. The soloists were secure, supported and comfortable at all times. Ensemble work was exciting, well-paced and supreme. Harmonies were forthcoming and tempi measured and robust. Mr. Scott was on the mark at every moment, it was as though a soundtrack was being played, albeit we knew we were at a live performance. The overture set the momentum and this energy and competence was continuous throughout the evening. There were many highlights from the pit, suffice to say, we were very impressed. We had some very impressive Trumpet playing. Diction from the ensemble was crisp and accented.

Congratulations to everyone in Belfast Operatic Company and many thanks for the hospitality and the very warm welcome.

Anne Kielty was in control of the six piece band for this energetic score. We had some lovely guitar playing from Johnny McGlynn and explosive trumpet playing from Paul Kiernan. The score was nicely realised bringing to life the doo-wop and pop styles within the music with confidence. The fine vocal work with the Ronnie's was appreciated. Soloists were secure and ensemble work was measured and delivered with confidence. The starting Tempi for 'Feed Me' was a little shaky, but settled after a short time. Musical finishes from this MD were confident and crisp. The drums/percussion struggled with the entr'acte and took a little time to settle back in for Act 2. 'Suddenly Seymour' was a musical triumph. Harmonies were very well balanced and delivered from the ensemble.

The various costumes from the wardrobe team; Doreen Caldbeck and Joanne McPhearson were nicely procured and looked very well on the cast. The costumes for Audrey were excellent. Seymour's costumes were a little too classy. The black/purple sequined Ronnie's costumes were excellent with accompanying high heels.. The Dentist costume, with accompanying lights was fantastic.  Shoes were very good.

Tom Cleary did well on the lights. We did have some dark areas up mid-stage DSC and spotlights needed to be more secure and held steady. Some lighting changes were very sudden. I am not sure how many packs or channels were available, but some lighting changes were distracting at times. The thunder effect was excellent. The set design was very appropriate and worked very well in this constrained stage area. Damien Regan did an excellent job as Stage manager. The scene changes were seamless and very well rehearsed. Stage crew worked hard and continuity was maintained. The striking of the dentist scene needed more rehearsal. Sound under the supervision of Liam Feeney was secure. We would have liked a little more impact, volume in 'Downtown'. Sound echoes and effects were well delivered. Props were excellent and very appropriate from Patricia Golden and Sadhabh Duignan. The many props in the 'Flower Shop' were excellent.

The demanding role of Seymour Krelborn was played by Jamie Dockery with confidence. This fine comedy actor was physically exciting and chassed the comedy moments with energy and enthusiasm. The look was perfect and this fine actor had great stage presence. The comedy moments were well delivered and nicely timed. Singing was excellent from Mr. Dockery, but he did need to be more confident on falsetto.  This accomplished actor worked very well with Mr Mushnick and Audrey. The scenes with the plant were hilarious as was the 'Jacket' moment. Mr. Dockery came into his own as the show progressed. Elissa O'Dowd gave a standout performance as the 'Goldie Hawn' type interpretation of Audrey. This bright comedy actress was very impressive as she waddled and strutted on and off the stage with vigour and style. Ms. O'Dowd was a very fine comedy actress but what was most impressive was her gentle nature and demure manner. We were taken in by this young actress who was brave and had great stage presence. Dialogue was secure. Costumes were worn with confidence. Comedy moments, particularly her 'fainting moments' were hilarious. 'Somewhere That's Green' was outstanding! Brendan Reid was very impressive as Mr. Mushnik. This seasoned actor had great stage presence. Dialogue needed to be stronger and more confident. Energy and accent was an issue at times. The character of Mr. Mushnik needs to be domineering and dialogue needs to be clear and delivered with energy, driving the pace of each scene. This actor was more confident in his singing, where we saw Mr. Reid come into his own with a big Tevye moment in 'Mushnik and Son'.

CHIFFON / CRYSTAL / RONNETTE: Lizi Hannon, Ceara Conlon and Lynda Morgan, respectively, gave impressive performances as our backing Trio 'The Ronnettes'. These ladies had panache and excellent stage presence. They were full of self-belief, coolness and worked excellently together. Singing was secure with meticulous clear harmonies delivered with poise and clarity. Ms. Hannon, Ms. Conlon and Ms. Morgan were very clear of their function within this production; narration, commenting on the ensuing action. They also carried their various costumes with assurance and ease. We had a standout performance from Danny Doherty as our sadist dentist Orin Scrivello. Mr. Scrivello was clad in leather gear and made his big entrance through the audience on a large and impressive motorbike, surrounded by a bunch of bouncers. The performance was sharp, big and compelling. Hip movements were hilarious and Mr. Doherty was a very impressive singer. A Triumph!   The Voice: Matt Mannion and Robert Reid gave us a very imposing vocal performance as Audrey II our wise-cracking anthropomorphic cross between a Venus flytrap and an avocado with teeth. 'Suppertime' was excellent with clear diction and apt attitude. The Puppeteer. Shane McPhearson did very well as Audrey II, the puppeteer. Timing was good. Darragh Bernie gave a very fine performance as Mr. Bernstein, the big shot from NBC. Mr Bernie was a fine singer. Mardette Lynch proved that there is no such thing as a small part as she gave a wonderful cameo performance as Life Magazine supremo Mrs Luce. Costume jewellery and character costume was excellent. The ensemble for this production worked very well together. It was all about team work and the various characters from hobos to customers supported every scene. Singing was excellent and harmonies were secure. Director/Choreographer; Vivienne Moran gave us a well paced comedy production. The many comedy moments were very nicely realised and the overall production was confident and forthcoming. 'Little Shop of Horrors' requires tight and secure staging and this director gave us just that. The style of the production delivered the hilarious comedy and at the same time the more poignant moments were not forgotten or underestimated. Some exits and entrances needed more energy, particularly Mr. Mushnik. The telephone scene needed to be more precise, as on the night I attended the telephone lines got caught up. We did need more use of hand bags and overcoats, particularly for exits of Audrey and Mr. Mushnik. What was achieved in this tight space was a credit to this director. We really enjoyed the many varied pop-up locations and animation for the 'Ronnie's'. The 'Motorbike' coming through the audience was a marvellous moment. The dancing was well within the casts capabilities and delivered with confidence and energy from the whole cast. Formations were interesting and final pictures were very nicely shaped and executed. The final head drop moment in 'Downtown' was precise. The sways needed to be more together. Congratulations to everyone in Boyle for a fantastic evening!

Copacabana opens with a contemporary songwriter getting the idea for a song about a woman who gets a job as a showgirl at the Copacabana, and we see the story unfold as it unrolls in his mind. Director: Des Henn gave us a fast moving, animated, ostentatious production. The pace was determined and the production ambitious. Company numbers were well attended too. Some dialogue scenes needed more consideration and direction. Comedy moments were nicely chased and achieved. The stereotypical New York accents needed more attention from the cameo roles. Mr Henn gave us a very flamboyant Hollywood style to the overall production. Choreographer; Barbara Meany (Henn) complemented this style and gave us some very exciting and interesting dance routines. 'Copa Opening' had some interesting head work; 'Just Arrived' was nicely worked out; 'Dancing Fool' was appropriately reminiscent of a fitness endurance test; 'Night on The Town' looked fantastic with good work with the large New York City scapes; 'Sweet Heaven' looked great with good feather work and an excellent final picture. 'Ay Caramba' was exciting; 'Bolero de Amor' had some very good couples work; 'Welcome to Havana' was active; 'El Bravo' was energetic and exciting with some excellent formations and 'The Finale' was exciting. The dance routines had the appropriate style and imagination intermeshed with excellent formations and final pictures. Accomplished Musical Director; Shane Farrell, brought together a fantastic showy big-band sound for this solid production. Playing was secure from the ten piece orchestra with exacting rhythms, vivacious tempi and resonating with large broad Broadway show sounds. We had some wonderful large explosive brass, excellent work from the reed section and exciting percussion. This show requires big brash accompaniment from the pit and Mr. Farrell succeeded in achieving just this from the big-band workout 'Dancing Fool' to the bombastic 'Bolero de Amor'.  The clichéd 'Just Arrived' and the tepid ballad 'Who Needs to Dream' were equally acknowledged in this genre-shifting show by this musical director. Harmonies were secure from the well rehearsed and confident ensemble and soloists were nicely supported. Diction was excellent and the energy from the pit transcended onto the stage with some great musical moments including 'Ay Caramba'. Balance was an issue at times. The challenge with this explosive score is to achieve stage/pit balance and yet not pull back on the large broad verbose musical content. Stage Management under the stewardship of Tom Enright was efficient and well planned. Scene changes worked very well and the stage crew were well managed. We had appropriate props from the props team. The set design was functional from Des Henn while the lighting under the dutiful eye of Mike Finneran worked well. We had a wonderful array of flamboyant 1940's costumes from wardrobe mistress: Jacinta Florish. The attention to detail was apparent and shoes were well attended to.  Makeup and Wigs were very well attended to.

Mikey O'Gorman gave us a gentle and compassionate performance as Stephen/Tony. Mr. O'Gorman had a lovely stage presence and was physically relaxed and nonchalant as he embraced the title role. Singing was secure and tuneful for the most part. The character of Tony Forte is stereotypical of the movie musical era and this fine performer gave us just that. We would have like more colour within the performance as this character can slip into irrelevance as the show perpetuates the other more dramatic characters within the absurd plot. Sadhbh McCoy was a beautiful spoil for Tony in the demanding role of Lola La Mar. This role requires accomplished singing, dancing and acting. This fine young actress gave a very solid performance. We did feel that the comedy moments were her strong point and that Ms. McCoy needed to relax more on the stage. This actress was also very comfortable in the confrontational scenes. Singing was secure. Jessica Bray gave a knockout performance as the pert, sympathetic cigarette girl Gladys Murphy. The character was full of animation and style and Ms. Bray was at ease on the stage at all times. Entrances were decisive and dialogue was vibrant. A tour-de-force! We had a great crotchety and forceful performance from Brian Henry as Copacabana manager Sam Silver. Dialogue was by rights energetic and this actor had great comedy timing and delivery. This actor was a very solid physical comedian and he brought liveliness and determination to every scene. Des Henn gave a solid performance as Rico, the chic but precarious gangster who owns the Tropicana. Acting was secure and stylish, albeit slightly underplayed. Dialogue became incoherent at times as Mr. Henn tended to underplay the nasty and egotistical elements to this pompous stock character. Singing was exposed, particularly for "Bolero de Amor". Grainne Hartnett was superb in the role of Conchita. Ms. Hartnett gave a standout performance as she owned the stage and looked fantastic. A Triumph! This company captured the Show-Girls, the Show-Boys, Copa Girls and Boys, Tropicana Dancers, Pirates and Customers with energy and unmistakable self-belief. Singing was secure, harmonies well achieved and commitment forthcoming. This company was passionate and unyielding.

Thank you for a warm welcome and continued success to everyone in The Cecilian Musical Society.

Little Shop is a motown, doo-wop, musical comedy. The challenge with show is to achieve the broad comedy but at the same time give the musical diversity the space to breath and live. This is just what we got from Clane Musical Society.

Director; Arthur McGauran gave us a very exciting 'broad stroke' comedy style to this accomplished production. Moments were very well worked out and delivered with confidence. There were some fantastic slap-stick comedy moments throughout the evening. The overall production was secure, well- paced and very well staged on this somewhat confined stage area. The scenes moved with energy, blocking was nicely framed and delivered in every scene. This director gave us a confident comedy production, where Mr. McGauran chased the broad comedy moments and succeeded. This show should be funny, in your face, musically diverse and a galloping good nights entertainment. That is just what we got from this experienced director. We did have some repetition in staging positioning for Crystal, Chiffon and Ronnette and we could have probably have moved the counter for the Audrey II scene. The set changes were nicely timed and props were very thought out and appropriate. The timing of the smacks were excellently timed and delivered. The dancing was very appropriate for the production from choreographer Deirdre Browne. The styles were broad and very well delivered by a confident and enthusiastic cast. The formations and staging were cast and venue suitable. This cast were obviously well rehearsed and entertaining.

Peter Manning was the perfect Seymour Krelborn, the bumbling, lovesick, dreamer-with-no-talent character that comes into his own as the show gets more grotesque and unbelievably hilarious. This actor made his comedic impression from the start and continued to entertain with his acting prowess. The challenging role was embraced by Mr. Manning as he enveloped and peeled back the layers and deliver with self-belief. Singing was a highlight with great solo work and generous duets. This fine actor brought energy and enthusiasm to every scene, but never upstaging or pulling focus at any time. A very compelling and measured comedy performance! Helen Spring gave us a fantastical performance as the fragile Audrey - Seymour's paramour with a past. Teetering around with high heels and low self-esteem, Audrey is a character who could easily be portrayed as just a 'dumb broad'. In this production, though, Spring creates an Audrey who is subtle and street wise, even if she does have appalling taste in men. Her power ballads were delivered with much passion and power. Ms. Spring was cute and ditzy when needed and equally compassionate as this formidable comedy actress swished and swaggered all evening. 'Suddenly Seymour' was a highlight. A tour-de- force in comedy acting and singing! The grumpy shop owner Mr Mushnik, was played with confidence by Martin Fahy. This role is a pivotal role in any production of 'Little Shop', as he is required to be present and drive the pace, thanklessly, in so many scenes. We were very impressed with the Jewish, Walter Matthau style of Mr. Fahy's performance and interpretation. The dialogue was hilarious as Mr. Fahy engaged and entertained in every scene. Accent was perfection and this actor was always physically present. This actor has great eyes and excellent use of hand gestures. Congratulations! We were entertained and rolling in the aisles with the fantastic comedy moments from Séamus Sullivan as the obnoxious Orin who gets his kicks from nitrous oxide and misogyny. He's one of the all-time great musical villains without a single sympathetic quality.  His demise in this production was sinister and protracted. Big broad comedy was the order of the day and Mr. Sullivan delivered in buckets. Hilarious!

CRYSTAL/CHIFFON/RONNETTE (DYNAMIC TRIO): Lorraine Murphy, Louise Moore and Keelin Kilduff respectively, were the absolute highlights of this production in their 'Greek Chorus' capacity. These ladies brought the flair, the sass, and the fantastic vocals, required for this dynamo trio. And all while dancing in perfect synchronisation and looking very sexy. Whether they were doo- wopping in the background of someone else's song or crushing that high note, their energy levels and enthusiasm were way up there throughout the entire show. These ladies gave us that kick of adrenaline sorely needed in this show. These ladies had stage presence and worked extremely well together. Harmonies were also really tight.

Philip Emmett had the perfect Audrey II voice. This actor was vocally perfect and a resounding success. Timing and intonation was dynamic. We had a very secure and confident moment from Ciarán Lalor as Mr. Bernstein, the media hotshot. Dearbhail Downey proved there is no such thing as a small part as Mrs Luce, the business woman. Peter Fay did very well as Skip Snip, the talent agent.

The chorus for this show were very confident, well-rehearsed and enthusiastic in every scene. Singing was secure and harmonies were very well delivered and rehearsed. 'Downtown' was very impressive, vocally. The chorus captured the broad comedy style of this production, somewhat 'Sam Smith' style. Dancing was secure and stage business was well delivered as they were random bums on Skid Row, patients in the dentist office, indiscriminate business people in different songs that entice Seymour. Stage Management under the stewardship of Marie Cusack (Pro Staging) was secure. The set changes were efficient and very well worked- out. Scene changes were excellent, particularly the scene change into the Dentist scene. The stage crew worked extremely well. The props were excellent for this production under the fervent eye of Orla Reidy. Telephones, flowers, vases, gardening tools, roses etc. were all time and era-appropriate. Excellent gas-mask. Congratulations! The sound balance and cueing was protected from Vinnie Osborne (Sound & Music Company). We did have some throw from the chorus in 'Downtown'. Excellent sound effect in gasmask scene. The overall set design was excellent from Kilkenny Musical Society. The various plants were fantastic and the overall set design, moving panels, worked extremely well in this confined space.  We particularly liked the New York upstage pieces as they set the scene very well. Lighting design and operation from Colm Eaton, was hit and miss at times. Cueing was slow at times. The lighting changes were also intrusive. I am not sure what the capacity for lighting/packs/channels is in this venue, but unfortunately the LED's needed more work as the flickering was distractive. The mid-stage area had some black spots and the overall FOH wash needed better overall wash. Costumes were well looked after by Andrew Reddy and cast. The ensemble costumes were appropriate. Principle costumes were good. The highlight was the fantastic costumes for Crystal, Chiffon and Ronnette. The various sequin dresses were spectacular and fitted very well. Audrey's costumes were also excellent, particularly the leopard skin. Hair styles and make-up was very good from Fran Styles; no pun intended, and the team. Great attention to detail in hair design.

Musical Director; Dave McGauran brought together a fine solid explosive band for this production. The sounds from the pit; set behind the stage area, was ever present and focused throughout the evening, giving us a very classic Broadway sound infused with rock/pop energy. Playing from Trumpet/ Horn was particularly impressive and piano work was excellent. This MD knows how to control, drive pace and release tempi as the musical numbers were seamless for this production. The variation of motown and doo- wop genres within this pop/rock score were delivered with confidence as we were treated to great melodies, lots of tambourines and hand clapping, blaring horns, interplay between the lead singer's and his or her backup vocalists, driving bass lines and foot-slapping drum parts. The Entr'acte was excellent. Soloists were very well supported and harmonies were secure from the singing trio and the accomplished ensemble. A musical triumph!

Congratulations to everyone in Clane Musical Society for a galloping good time.

Robert Vickers was the supreme Jesus Christ. This dynamic singer and compelling actor was exciting to watch and alluring to listen too.  This musical is very challenging for any Jesus as it is exposed both musically and emotionally. The emotional journey is copper fastened with the desire to be dynamic and yet compassionate when required. This takes flexibility and understanding in all areas; singing and acting. This very fine performer was electrifying in each scene but tended to be trying too hard. The essence of any performance, especially a leading role, is to be believable. The actor must pace the journey and 'not peak too soon'. An example of this was in 'Gethsemane', where this actor needed to find the emotional journey. That is not to say that it was not a vocal triumph, but unfortunately it needed more attention to the emotional journey. 'Let it Breathe!' We were very impressed with the performance from Kevin Fagan as Judas. This excellent singer gave a very compelling vocal master class. The vocal range for Judas is breath-taking and Mr. Fagan rose to the challenge. This actor was brave and inspiring. 'Heaven On Their Minds' and 'Judas Death' were beautifully measured and convincing. 'Superstar' was a highlight. Bronwyn Andrews was a beautiful Mary Magdalene. This superb singer and actress gave a very heartfelt and idiosyncratic performance. This role is about emotional connection with JC and Ms. Andrews was convincing. Vocal range was secure and delightful. We would have like a more noticeable relationship between Mary and Peter. The chorus for this show were magnificent. Each and every member was committed to the production and energy was abundant. The singing was superb with secure harmonies and diction. The magnificent chorus added greatly to our enjoyment on the night. It was evident that they had worked hard and tirelessly to bring to the stage a wonderful spectacle.  Congratulations! Jim Walsh was excellent as the scorned and insecure Pontius Pilot. The role was made for him as he embraced the scenes with platitude and aplomb. Mr. Walsh was vocally agile and articulate and every scene was delivered with authority. 'Pilates dream' was beautifully measured as was 'Trial Before Pilate'. Congratulations! Justin Parkes gave us a nice decorous but yet egocentric King Herod. This fine actor and singer was spirited and entertaining. David Kennedy was solid and secure in the demanding role of Caiaphas, the high Priest. Mr. Kennedy embraced the octave leaps with confidence. His lower range was booming and his upper range edgy, just what is needed for this role. Diction was excellent. A success!  Liam Egan was the perfect Annas, sly and demure. This fine singer gave a seamless and protected performance.  Adam O'Brien was suitable as Peter, but needed to embrace the role more and stand out from the other apostles. This role can be underestimated and Mr. O'Brien needed to find his place in the pecking order. Singing was secure. The role of Simon Zealotes is to convince Jesus to stir hatred among the masses; John Conroy was fine as Simon, but needed to be more passionate and determined. The apostles were secure musically and gave a very cohesive performance. Director; Colin Hughes gave us a very appealing spectacle. The overall aesthetic was pleasant and sanitary. The staging was inventive and worked well giving beautiful pictures and was a pleasure to watch. Some pictures and entrances needed more acute definition, particularly 'JCS's first entrance. He was unduly masked. The overall production was somewhat sparse at times with very little use of Props or where they were used they were basic. We would have liked more use of props to enhance the overall aesthetic. There were times when lighting changes were unnecessary and over used. Be mindful to only change lighting states if you feel it adds to the tension or enhances the location or scene. Some of the emotional moments were missed in this production. Example; 'Everything's Alright', should be Mary Magdalene appeasing JC from his headache as the girls sooth the apostles….close your eyes!
