Overall we did feel that the director needed to chase and secure the emotional journey of this show. We had a very nice end to act 1. 'Hosanna' reprise needed to be more aggressive. Judas needed to make a very distinctive 'move or moment' for his final death. Pilot needed to be placed closer to JC to talk in his ear. The lashes needed more rehearsal as they were implausible. Taking JC off the cross needed to be more poignant and slower. The reincarnation didn't work for this adjudicator. Overall this production was too clinical and clean to capture my emotional connection and missed far too many possibilities and important moments. That being said, it was entertaining and we enjoyed it. We could see the amount of work put in by everyone involved and the audience had a great night's entertainment.

Orla Savage did an excellent job on the dancing for this production. Routines were well rehearsed and very appropriate for the varied cast profile. Formations were interesting and imaginative. Final pictures were secure apart from the end of 'The Overture' where it was slightly too D/S/L. Variation in style was apparent and is to be commended. Smiles from the dancing ladies were excellent. The Charleston routine was first class. Stage Management under the stewardship of Maureen McMahon was secure. We should have 'marked' the table for the last supper. The props were very sparse in this production. We would have liked more use of props to enhance the production. It is sometimes appropriate for the Props manager to suggest props, as the production is being set. The sound balance and cueing was secure from Jody Trehy. We did have a little feedback, but nothing major. Offstage singing was very well 'managed. Lighting design by Denis Twomey was a little hit and miss at times. We did need one or two spotlights. Gelling was fine, apart from the different gels on the specials. If you have a few specials on at the same time, it is very important to have them at the same level or with the same diffusion/ gel. We did feel at times that some lighting changes were unnecessary. We enjoyed the dramatic lighting at the start of the show. The overall set design was inventive and gave the director some fantastic options with heights, stairs and excellent entrances. Well done Colin Hughes and Wayne Handy (no pun intended) Costumes were well looked after by various suppliers and Gráinne Ui Chaomhánaigh, Geraldine Meade and Margaret Galvin. They were appropriate. We would have like more distressing as the show progressed and the Lepers needed to more attention. The Red costume for Judas and the Red Costume for Mary incongruous. Dancer's costumes were excellent. Head gear on the men would have been nice. The costumes were a little too clean for this adjudicator and needed more edge. Hair styles and make-up was very good from Valerie Andrews. The make-up on JC for the crucifixion was very believable. FOH was efficient and friendly.

Musical Director; Caitríona Ní Threasaigh gathered together a fantastic first rate rock band, not credited in the programme, for this mammoth musical score. We had wonderful Guitar, Brass, Flute and some big rock playing from the band. The musical content is the essence of this classic rock opera, challenging the soloists and the chorus with massive leaps and variations in rhythms, alongside ridged instrumentation and the ensemble creating the rock-pop feel. This cast and chorus achieved this in abundance and at every opportunity. Singing was supreme with perfect pitch, dynamic and energy as the telling of the Easter story with passion was malign and forthcoming. This Chorus were very well rehearsed vocally by Chorus Mistress; Elizabeth Kelly, with secure harmonies and confidence. Some variation in vocal roughness and severity was needed at times, as many of the numbers came over vocally too nice. This was particularly apparent for 'The Lepers'' and 'The Lashing' scenes where we would have liked more edge in vocal work. The vocal work needed more variation in timbre in order to emphasise the emotional journey of the mob! The soloists were excellently supported by the band at all times. Cueing was supreme from our M.D. and the music moved on with beguiling pace. Congratulations on a musical tour-de-force!

Grease may have been the word for my recent visit, but comedy was the order of the day. Accomplished Director Paul Norton gave us a bold, crass, in your face comedy production of Grease. The comedy moments were rude, hilarious and constantly forthcoming. This type of comedy takes confidence and it is obvious Mr. Norton instilled the 'trust me' approach with the entire cast. The comedy moments were everywhere from start to finish. We loved his brash set comedy moments; very well timed and delivered. The comedy included, arses, burping, flees in trousers, half- clad males, smelling Miss Lynch, finger moments and many, many more. This director gave us some very nice cover for some scene changes, particularly the scene change coming after the high school hop. The Beauty School dropout scene was very nicely set and staged. That being said, the dramatic scenes with Rizzo and Kenickie were nicely measured and staged. The overall production had confidence and this director knew what he was chasing. The movie scene was hilarious with excellent timing for the ring and the door moments. We loved the young girl on the roller skates! Some of the solo numbers needed more direction.

Dancing was very strong from choreographer Sarah Griffin. Formations were inventive and routines secure. The various dance routines were well rehearsed and the style was appropriate. Ms. Griffin gave us some lovely final pictures and exits and entrances were well thought out. The opening number built up very well as the cast joined. 'Summer Nights' was very strong. 'Those Magic Changes' was hilarious. 'Greased Lightening' was very energetic and had a very strong impact. 'Rydell High' was excellent. 'We Go Together' was a great end to Act 1 with a very nice final picture. 'Shakin at the High School Hop' was nicely varied and happy. The couples dancing were secure. 'Born To Hand Jive' was full of energy with another excellent final picture. 'Beauty School Dropout' was very nicely staged. The dance for 'We Go Together' needed more work. The 'Megamix' was very well delivered. Congratulations!

Seamus Carroll gave us the ultimate daffy, limber swaggering Danny Zucko in this production. This actor was bold, funny and showed his comedy timing superbly at every opportunity. There were many moments in the spotlight for this fine performer, as he indulged in the coolness that is Danny. Singing was excellent and not taken too seriously. This actor moved through the evening with comedic aptitude; the apple moment, and a broad sense of indulgence. This actor chased the comedy and succeeded. A tour-de- force! Grainne Donoghue gave us a very steady performance as Sandy Dumbrowsky, sexy but sweet. This actress was mindful of the challenges in going from a shy wallflower to leather clad babe and succeeded. Ms. Donoghue was nicely present and gave us some lovely moments of wide-eyed innocence, particularly during the drive-in movie scene. This actress was stretched vocally and accent wise, but managed to convey a sense of confidence and gave a heartfelt interpretation to her songs. Some scenes were static as this actress needed to relax a little more, the offstage puke moment needed to be bigger, but I am sure that will come with experience. 'Sandra Dee' reprise had some tuning issues. Suzanne Lillis gave a very compelling performance in the demanding role of Betty Rizzo. This up-front actress was candid and edgy in every scene as she stood out as the leader of the Pink ladies and a woman of the world. Ms. Lillis was strong in the dialogue scenes and gave a solid focused performance throughout the evening. We would have liked a braver interpretation of 'Look at me I'm Sandra Dee', but 'There are worse things I could do' was a very emotional experience. This actress did have an issue walking comfortably in very high heels, which made us uncomfortable at times. That being said it was a very accomplished performance from a very fine performer who was more at home in the aggressive scenes. This excellent comedian; Craig Regan, brought energy and comedy in abundance to the role of Kenickie, the hard talking T-Bird. We were impressed with this 'talking through the side of your mouth' characterisation as it gave us much laughter. Mr. Regan was bold and stubborn in a nice way. Singing was excellent and this actor added greatly to our enjoyment of the evening. Congratulations! Alex Cathcart was excellent as the foolish, gullible Doody. This actor was high maintenance in a good way as he ripped his way through the evening with high energy and bold, in your face fun. Mr. Cathcart delivered his comedy moments with a brave innocence that made for a most enjoyable performance. Fantastic! Rory Chadwick captured the wise-guy nature of Sonny in every scene. This actor was measured and never took the focus, but at the same time gave us a Sonny that mattered. We enjoyed his moments in the limelight! Eoghan Fingleton was excellent as Roger, the prankster. 'Mooning' was a highlight as was 'Rock and Roll Party Queen'. This fine comedy actor had immense energy and commitment to the role in every scene. Excellent!

Jane-Louise Kelly was hilarious as fun loving, light headed Frenchy. This comedy actress had us rolling in our seats as she delivered every comedy moment with enthusiasm and excellent comedic timing. Energy was the order of the day and Ms Kelly had that in abundance as she captured our sympathy in the nicest way. This actress was far-fetched and a delight to watch!   Sarah O'Sullivan gave an all-out perfect performance as the want to be, mature and sexy Pink Lady Marty. Ms. O'Sullivan was brave and full of fun in every scene. 'Freddie my Love' was a highlight. This fine comedy actress was secure as she tumbled through the show in a very positive way, always focused and mindful. Olive Maher gave a robust and 'Celery' eating interpretation of Marty. This actress gave a very strong and bold performance as she captured some excellent comedy moments. Her reactions in 'Mooning' were a delight. Ms. Maher made for great impact in every scene. Aoife Fingleton was very imposing, perky and energised in the role of Patty Simcox. She may be unpopular with the Pink Ladies, but this actress was very popular with the audience. Ms. Fingleton gave a very determined and spirited performance as she hit the stage running. A Delight! Joan White was a delight as the no nonsense English teacher, Miss Lynch. The part was made for this formidable actress. We laughed, cried and followed her antics at every moment. This actress showed her experience and fantastical comedy timing in every scene. We loved her moment singing in the Gym. This actress was full of performance. A Tour-de-Force! Pat Cullen gave a high energy, overtly manic portrayal of Eugene Florczyk, the Rydell nerd. Mr. Cullen displayed his experience in comedy roles as he brushed aside any self-consciousness and embraced the comedy with enthusiasm and panache. This actor was hilarious in every scene. Mr. Cullen was a comedic delight in the role. Richard Finnegan was the perfect, smoothie Vince Fontaine. This broad actor maybe small in stature but he proved to be extra-large in stage presence. The look was sleazy, the smile was compelling and the hips were moving, not to mention the hairy chest. Fantastic! John McEvoy gave a very nice performance as, lookalike Jon Kenny (The Unbelievables); Johnny Casino. Singing was secure. John Coss was perfectly camp, brave and out- there as Teen Angel. A very fine vocal performance. The fine actress; Marie Cashin, was sexy and stand-alone as Cha Cha, the outsider in Rydell. This beauty moved with grace and poise, just what was needed for this cameo role. Dialogue needed more impact but we did have a very exotic performance. The energy was apparent from this diverse chorus, who brought this production to life. Dancing was secure and singing was energised and exciting. The chorus worked the stage area very well and stage freezes were secure. 'Summer Nights' was a highlight. The chorus looked very confident and enjoyed every scene. Congratulations to the ladies who joined 'Grease Lightning', for their commitment to the male look. The male chorus was full of testosterone and were bold and crass, just what was needed. 'Those Magic Changes', in the showers, was hilarious. Rydell High pom-poms were excellent from the female chorus with precise synchronised timing and the singing was secure. 'We Go Together' was excellent with a very secure final picture. We had very nice couples dancing in 'High School Hop'. Hair styles and wigs were appropriate from John Coss. The costumes were excellent for this production; Olive Maher, Sharon Dunphy and Zeta O'Reilly. The character costumes were very good and the highlight was the 'Beauty School Dropout' with excellent silver sandals. Excellent shoes. Great yellow jacket on Doody! We had some lovely costumes for Sandy. Lighting design by Nick Antom was fitting. We did feel that the lighting rig could have had better gelling. We would have liked break-ups and green gelling for the park scene. Cueing was excellent. A spotlight on Vince Fontaine would have been appropriate as he gorged Frenchy. There were some problems with FOH face light. The overall set design; Paul Norton was inventive and served the production very well. Heights were well used. Some of the projections were too modern, particularly 'prom night'. The sound balance and cueing was excellent from Abe Scheele. Sound effects were appropriate and enhanced the production. We did have a little feedback/cracking at the outset of the show, but it steadied. There was some feedback from the wings at times. The radio jingle could have come in earlier for Vince Fontaine on a number of times. The car sound effect needed to be better. Excellent movie track. The props, under the dutiful eye of Annette McCaul and Eleanor Ryan, were appropriate and time appropriate. We would have liked more props in the bedroom scene. A different colour radio may have been better. Stage Management under the stewardship of Bob O'Kelly was efficient and skillful. The stage crew was well organised and resourceful. We had some seamless work here with some nice clean set changes. The entrance and the exit of the car was excellent and nicely timed with the MD.

Niall Mulpeter, Musical Director gave us the perfect rock and roll, jukebox high energy band type feel from some very accomplished and focused musicians in a very exposed environment. The sounds from the band, set on stage under a platform on right, were broad and inane and a musical triumph. Stage/ pit balance was excellent and we had some lovely playing from saxophone and guitar throughout the evening, never overpowering or intrusive. The general cast was confident with harmonies and tempi. They were well rehearsed and filled the stage and auditorium with energy under the capable baton of a very competent and forthright Mr. Mulpeter. Soloists were very nicely supported and the many atmospheres' created with co-operation and understanding from the M.D. We had some very fine scene change music and this MD was always in the controlling seat. Congratulations! Thank you to Annette McCaul for looking after me so well.

Little Women is a compelling opera. It follows the saga of the March sisters- Meg, Jo, Beth and Amy-as they grow up in Civil War America. With a book by Allan Knee, music by Jason Howland and lyrics by Mindi Dickstein this music is modern, yet not too difficult to take in. SONG in Dundalk gave us a compelling tale in the beautiful surrounds of An Táin Theatre. Sinead O'Callaghan gave us a powerful performance in the lead role of Josephine March (Joe), the tomboy like, brassy, bossy, demanding female writer. This character is the central character and the show tells her story and her journey. Ms. O'Callaghan gave us a magnificent vocal workshop with total control, interpretation and stage presence in each and every scene. This magnificent singer was outstanding and 'Astonishing' was just that! 'The Fire Within Me' and 'Sometimes When You Dream (Reprise) were excellent. The character needs to be rebellious, angry and outspoken yet needs to bring to life the human nature and passion of a loveable rebellious female. This actress gave us all this, as we followed her experience with interest. This show offers some wonderful songs for this role and Ms O'Callaghan gave us a magnificent rounded performance! The role of Meg March was played by Leanna Carragher. This actress captured the eldest and somewhat spoilt sister with determination and steadfastness. This character represents the convention and the good. This actress had great stage presence in every scene and delivered her dialogue with confidence. A fine singing performance with excellent high notes! Ciara Quigley gave a lovely, sweet performance as the somewhat shy and quiet younger sister Beth March. This young actress was full of energy and pathos, capturing the angelic and quite nature of the character. The youngest sister; Amy March, was played with confidence by Lisa Rose McMahon. This young actress gave a tour-de-force performance in the role. This character demands an obvious manipulative demeanor as she seeks popularity and seeks to achieve her goals. Ms. McMahon was ever present with fun, high energy and excellent diction. This actress also had great comedy timing. Jacqui Browne gave us a wonderful and heartfelt performance as the mother; Marmee March. This wonderful actress gave a very wholesome and touching performance. The tenderness and struggles were forthcoming in every scene. 'Days of Plenty' was a highlight! The overbearing great-aunt to the March sisters was played by Jane Stanley. Ms Stanley gave a very strong and formidable interpretation to the role. This role emphasises society wealth at this time (1869) and this seasoned actress gave a formidable and standout performance. Siobhan McNamara was excellent as the older Amy.  'The Most Amazing Thing' was very fiery.  Nik Parks gave a very fine performance in the role of boy next door Theodore Lawrence III. This fine handsome young actor had great stage presence and delivered his dialogue with confidence. This actor had a very secure accent. 'Take A Chance On Me' was excellent!   Jackie Winkless gave a good performance as Mr. Laurence, Laurie's grandfather. Mr. Winkless, a seasoned actor and singer was secure and gave a very fine performance. We would have liked a little more confidence on entrances from Mr. Winkless.  The role of Mr. John Brooke, Laurie's tutor, was nicely played by Andrew Browne. Brendan Cleary gave a very solid performance as the boarder in Mrs Kirks, Professor Bhaer. The role of Mrs Kirks was nicely played by Paula Murray. Rodrigo; the hero of the operatic tragedy, was nicely played by Cathal Grennan. The role of Sr. Baxton; the villain in the operatic tragedy was nicely measured by Darie Stanly. Roisin Roslyn was lovely as the heroine; The Fair Clarissa in the operatic tragedy.  HAG: Carol McCourt, TROLL: Irene Dunne and KNIGHT: Brendan Gormley did very well in their cameo roles. The chorus for this show captured the essential period and stature of the time. They gave us a very real sense of commitment and determination to recreate for us essence of the period. Singing was excellent in 'The weekly Volcano Press'.

Directors: Teresa Dunne and Rosemary Winkless gave us a very compelling and classical style production. Staging was secure and scene changes were full realised and integrated into the overall production adding to the production values. Some of the dialogue was set too far upstage and could have been placed more downstage. There were some lovely set pieces. Stage pictures were very nicely realised and work behind the gauze was secure. The dramatic tensions within the text needed more work. This opera is full of emotional energy and is highly physiological as it all about the demands of family, resistance to change, and the need to live a creative life. We would have liked a more highly charged operatic production. 'Here Alone' was set too far upstage at the start. The initial picture was very nice, but it needed to move downstage. The piano was intrusive at times. The characters were very nicely established by the director duo and the classic style was chassed and achieved. Dialogue was well paced for the most part. Some of the stage furniture was very dull, particularly the black Chaise Lounge. Set changes were nicely timed with lighting and music. 'My First Kiss' was a lovely moment. Overall this was a very exciting production. The dancing, staging was very appropriate for the production from choreographer Terrence Dunne. Stage Management was looked after by a very competent stage manager Ultan Hodgers and his excellent team. Scene changes were very nicely timed with the music and changes were clean and efficient. The dropping of the red drapes was very well timed to the music. I was not sure about the hats on the stage crew? The props were nicely brought together by the props team under the stewardship of Andrew Browne and Danny O'Shea. Remind cast to weight suitcases and to carry them as though they are heavy. An ink well was needed for the office scene. The wheel chair was excellent. Confetti would have been a nice touch. The sound balance and cueing was an issue in this production. We had many mics popping. It may have been technical issues on the night I attended, but it did take from the overall experience.  The overall set design was very nice from Bobby White - Scenemaker. Some scenes seemed far too dull and the pictures on set needed better painting. The attic scene needed better definition. Lighting design and operation from Darren Kelleher was effective and added to the overall production values. We did have lighting queue issues going ahead, particularly after the first scene and behind the gauze.  Costumes were a highlight for this production under Costume Mistress Bronwyn Walsh and her team. The period costumes were very appropriate and fitted very well. Some costume jewellery would have been appropriate for Aunt March. Be mindful to remind people not to sit on their coat tails. We would have liked an overcoat for Mr. Laurence. Hair styles and make-up were excellent from Paula Murray. FOH was efficient and friendly. Musical Director and Chorus Master; Patrick Dunne brought together a fantastic nine piece orchestra for this production. We had particular beautiful Viola playing from Jane Graham, for 'The Tragic Opera' moments. This orchestra under the dutiful baton of Mr. Dunne related the intelligence and emotional journey within the score at every musical opportunity and during the underscore music. Support for solos, duets, trios and the larger groups was forthcoming and very secure at all times for this very difficult and explosive score. Harmonies were secure, particularly for 'Five Forever'. This musical score is filled with soaring arias, duets and ensembles. This modern contemporary opera challenges the MD to embrace modernism and yet not lose sight of the classical operatic impact. Ethereal moments were realised and the gamut from open-throated Broadway song to serpentine twelve- tonish singing offstage, were all realised by this competent Musical Director. This elaborate opera score is built in rhymed couplets of seemingly effortless naturalness, something that can be difficult balance and achieve. This Musical Director accomplished all this. Congratulations!

It was a great pleasure to witness this Irish Premiere in Dundalk.

There was no second guessing for the recent production of Chess, by the enthusiastic group that is St. Michael's Theatre Musical Society in New Ross, Co Waterford. Director; Kevin Kennedy gave us a decisive and infused production of Chess. This director brought confidence and fortitude to the production as we are challenged for what is a confusing storyline and timeline. The overarching story and character tensions were nicely measured and pointed through dramatic impulses at every opportunity. This is a Rock-Opera and needs to be treated as such, full of Drama! What was achieved in this production was that the text was revealed and dramatised in abundance. We had some nice directorial touches particularly in principal work. The chorus staging was in need of more attention. We would have liked more energy and engagement for 'Merano' as this should depict a village carnival atmosphere as they welcome in traditional fashion the World Chess Championship games. 'The Soviet Machine' needed more direction in order to achieve the impending drunkenness inherent in this scene. The overall production also needed more attention to some finer detail; particularly we would have like suitcases and coats for the arrival of Svetlana at the airport and more American attire for Freddie. The projections on the cyc worked very well in establishing the various locations, interior and exterior but some props and costumes did not back this up. Claire Kickham (nee Buckley) gave us some lovely work on the dancing and formations for this production. The routines were exciting and dynamic. Pictures were interesting and added to the production values of this show.  The chess dance/movement was excellent. Well done! Dancing for 'One Night In Bangkok' needed more rehearsal. We had a compounding performance from Keith Flanagan in the demanding role of Anatoly Sergievesky, our determined and somewhat dull Russian chess champion. Mr. Flanagan gave us a very strict and appropriate interpretation. 'Anthem' was a highlight of the evening.

Kevin Reade gave us a smooth and competing performance as Fredrick (Freddie) Trumper, the American chess fanatic. This fine actor brought us through the struggles and strife's that follow celebrity with the new power of TV and Press and the emergence of the paparazzi. The dialogue and physical staging in the bedroom scene was very believable. 'Pity The Child' needed more emotional construal and the high notes were slightly exposed. Claire O'Connor was a wonderful Florence, the woman who betrays one love for another and spends the rest of her time wondering why. This actress was imposing and self-assured in every scene. Singing was forthright and compelling. 'Heaven Help My Heart' was a highlight. The strength of this character became apparent through the confrontational scenes with Molokov where we had some fine work. We were a bit stretched vocally in 'Mountain Duet'. The role of, the wronged wife, Svetlana was very poignantly played by Ashley Doran. This fine singer was believable and complimented the principal line-up. A smaller role, but this actress knew her position on the chess board!  'I know Him So Well' was excellent. Declan Taylor was very imposing in the role of Molokov, the Soviet manipulator. Mr. Taylor gave us a decisive and compelling performance showing imperial strength and stage presence in every scene. Singing was imperious and commanding. A tour-de-force vocally. The role of American media personality and secret CIA agent Walter DeCoursey was nicely measured in this production by actor James Dobbs. Mr. Dobbs was self-assured and engaging in the role and moved throughout the production with ease and clarity. Nigel O'Neill gave us a very compelling performance as The Arbiter, the no nonsense referee of the championship. We would have like a little more edge from the character. We were nicely entertained by David Burke as The Mayor of Merano.

Stage Management under the stewardship of Lizzy Heffernan was exact and well managed. Set changes i.e.; tables, chairs etc. were set efficiently and with confidence. The scene change into the bedroom was a little slow.  We had some issues setting up the interview scene. It needed to be better organised. Philip Erskine did a good job on Props. We would have liked some coats and bags at the Airport scene. Sound balance and cueing was exact and seamless from Joe Murphy. We did have a little 'feedback at times and we did hear some backstage chat. We had a very workable set design that enhanced the overall aesthetic from Terry Brennan. It was workable. The projections were excellent and appropriate. Congratulations! The Video projection of Svetlana was excellent. Lighting under the stewardship of Paul Malone was inventive with nice gelling and excellent cueing and delivery. Slides were excellent; the Studio Slide was particularly good. Spotlight work was good.  The costumes were excellent for the production by Costume Mistress; Marianne Furlong. We would have liked 'Fredrick Trumper' to have been dressed in more appropriate American clothes. We also needed more jackets, hats for the Russians and Americans. The Arbiter dancer's costumes were very good. Costumes for Florence were excellent. The yellow costumes at the start of Act 2 were also excellent. The hats were odd in the 'Russian Bedroom scene. Anatoly needed a tie for the TV interview scene. We lacked overcoats for the men, be mindful of the time of day. Hair styles and make-up was fine by Kitty Warren and her team. FOH was efficient and friendly. The Theatre was a little cold.

Musical Director Philip Kennedy brought together a fine blend of ten skilled musicians including Bass, Reed, Guitar, Trumpet, Trombone, Violin, Keys and Percussion for this exciting and enthusiastic rock-opera. The musical variety within this massive score was emphatically chased by this competent Musical Director who was in control and dedicated to the gargantuan job on hand. The band was not as full as we would have liked and there were times when it did seem slightly lighter than our musical ear required. This was particularly evident in at 'The Entr'acte' and 'One Night in Bangkok'. The keyboard string sounds needed better formulation and precision in order to bring the epic and soaring melodies to fruition, particularly for 'Chess' instrumental. Choral work was outstanding with unyielding harmonies and determination from all the cast. 'Anthem' was a highlight. 'The Story of Chess' was a musical and vocal triumph where the cast were prevailing and unassailable. Congratulations. The chorus for this production was assured and imminent in each and every scene. The choral work was excellent with secure harmonies and diction. This chorus came into their own for 'Endgame' where we had confidence and strength of character. It was a musical triumph and captured the dramatic exasperation in abundance. The chorus also fulfilled the various roles such as reporters, chess players, the people of Merano, Italy and Bangkok with determination and accomplishment. This chorus were suitably focused and committed.

Congratulations and continued success to St. Michael's Theatre Musical Society. Thank you for your hospitality!

The recent production of The Witches of Eastwick from Harold's Cross Tallaght Musical Society was full of dark nuances' and flying witchcraft abounding. The overall production was well paced and delivered with confidence from Director Philippa Alford. Scenes were well thought-out and stage action was detailed and dramatic. The work with the three witches was apparent and this director gave us a very exciting and intelligent production. Scene changes were secure and stage pictures interesting. We had some very nice use of the ensemble with some excellent production touches and suitable style for this type of show. Dialogue needed a little more pointing at times and the dramatic tensions needed to be more apparent in some scenes. Don't be afraid to hold the dramatic moments. The flying sequence was excellent. Congratulations!   We had some very nice dance sequences from choreographer Evelyn Donnelly. The routines were well planned and delivered with some creative groupings. Some of the formations became repetitive at times, particularly apparent during 'Dirty Laundry' and 'Dance with the Devil' and 'The Glory of Me'.  Stage management under the watchful eye of Marie Cusack was excellent. Scene changes were seamless and stage markings were exact and faultless. The timing of some scene changes needed some further thought. The striking of the Church scene could have been delayed a little. It is sometimes appropriate to strike or set scenes a little after the music or slightly into the next scene. The stage furniture was a little dull. The flying sequence was fantastic. The props, under the stewardship of Pauleen Boyle and Máirin Heffernan were suitable and appropriate. A few more umbrellas during the opening number would have been nice. Sound balance and sound effects by Vinnie Osborne were exact and precise. Some secondary roles were overpowered by the band at times, the sound operator should never fear articulating this to the MD, if needs be. The set design by Bobby White from Scenemaker added greatly to this production. The portals were appropriate and the central trucked units excellent.  Stage furniture did need better attention. The set design was effective and inventive.  Darren Kelliher did an excellent job on the lighting design for what is a very busy show lighting-wise. This lighting designer gave us some lovely lighting moments during the evening. Stage areas were well covered and states colourful and appropriate. The lighting was very nicely integrated with the excellent projections, by Sound and Music Co. Go-Bos were nicely used and cueing was confident and precise. We did have a late DBO at the end of scene seven and it would have been nice if we had a spotlight on Daryll during the flying sequence. The graveyard scene was beautifully lit. It would have been a nice touch if we had appropriate thunder lighting effect. The overall costumes were well attended to by the costume team; Martina Foreman, Joan Kelly, Rosaleen Coventry and Máirin Heffernan. There was an obvious lack of overcoats. The costume team need to be mindful of the time of day during the production and costume appropriately. Accessories were excellent with gloves, hair-bands and glasses. We did have a variation in shoes, some character shoes and some flats. The wedding dress was fantastic. Leona O'Neill did a good job on hair. House management was efficient and well turned out in their Dress Suits etc. Damien Hurley was everything we could expect from devilish Darryl Van Horne. This actor was a smooth operator. He was sly, mischievous and scandalously seductive. This actor was creepy and commanding. Mr. Hurley gave a formidable and likeable brash and crude performance. We did feel that this character needed more energy and physical presence as the show progressed. Overall a very enjoyable performance! Julie Donnelly gave a very commanding and forthright performance as Alexandra Spofford, the sculptor who creates small female statues in clay. This actress was steady and delightful in every scene. Ms. Donnelly came into her own in 'Your Wildest Dreams'. Singing was a tour-de-force. We really enjoyed Sharon Osborne in the role of Suki Rougemont, the ever stuck for words news reporter. Ms. Osborne gave a wonderful nerdy interpretation and was delightful in this demanding role. Dialogue was excellently delivered by this performer. Ms. Osborne needs to be mindful not to check in with the MD. Singing was a tour-de-force with secure harmonies.  Kelly-Marie Davy gave a standout performance as our not so successful Cello player, music teacher, Jane Smart. This actress was resolute and exhilarating with wonderful stage presence. Singing was terrific. The three witches deserve mention as a masterful trio. Singing was resolute and formidable with wonderful harmonies and attention to detail. They worked exceptionally well together and we really enjoyed their solidarity and legitimacy. 'Make Him Mine' was outstanding! We were treated to a hilarious and spunky performance from Catherine Lambe as Felicia Gabriel, the dominant matriarchal figure within the story. Ms. Lambe was confident and impressive in the role and moved through each scene with energy and insightfulness. A grandiose performance! Stephen Ryan gave a lovely measured performance as young teenager Michael Spofford. This fine actor also had a wonderful singing voice and lovely stage presence. 'Something' was a highlight. Aoife Small was gorgeous as Felicia's daughter Jennifer Gabriel. This actress and beautiful singer gave us a very believable performance coming into her own with 'I Wish I May - reprise'. Paul Laycock was secure and restrained as browbeaten husband Clyde Gabriel. Niamh Hanley was delightful as Little Girl.  Supporting roles were secure and well delivered. This company or Choir of Townspeople was full of confidence and vigour during this very exhilarating production. Company scenes were secure and choral singing was a highlight. This was a confident and disciplined company. Musical Director, Sarah Lynch gave us very strong and secure big sounds from the competent and exuberant band of musicians for this expansive score. Balance was an issue at times as the band outplayed the stage action and it was difficult to catch some of the lyrics and dialogue. The entr'acte was somewhat insecure and percussion was too strong at times. We were particularly impressed with the Cello and Trumpet playing. Soloists were well protected and supported. We did have some checking in with the MD from one or two principles. Choral singing was excellent from the entire chorus; they were confident and very well rehearsed. Tempi were secure and harmonies superb.

Thank you to everyone in Harold's Cross Tallaght Musical Society for making me so welcome.

In one of life's little ironies and with the country slowly sinking into the Atlantic, the troupers at Claremorris decided to stage Singin' in the Rain at the fag end of January.

The running joke on the opening night of a short run was that the show could have been staged outdoors in the town square Mediterranean-style (minus the sunshine and the heat, of course,) such was the volume of water - and snow - that was falling.

To do so however, would have deprived the big crowd in the Town Hall theatre from witnessing one of those acts of ingenuity that make watching live theatre such a joy.

As the title proclaims this show needs a believable indoors downpour to avoid breaching the Trades Description Act. How to achieve that in a west of Ireland venue not constructed for the staging of musical spectaculars and that has, frankly, seen better days, becomes the big question.

Step forward Michael Prenty, local FAS supervisor, and technical supremo who decided to turn the stage into a giant wet room at the critical turns in the storyline by overlaying it with ply board sheeting coated in roofing mastic, complete with its own drainage system. A tank beneath the stage connected to a pumping system then delivered the storm from an overhead rig through a giant showerhead with the in-built plug holes allowing the water to be continuously recycled.

The end result was a thorough soaking for David Gallagher's Don Lockwood and Liam Newman's policeman at the end of Act One as they re-created the iconic scene from the 1952 movie, a splashing colourful finale to the show with the cast in multi-hued Macs and much wonderment from an appreciative audience as to how it had all been achieved.

Mr Prenty's settings - handled expertly all evening by his aide de comte, David Keane and a five-man stage team - admirably created locations such as Grauman's Chinese Theatre, Monumental's studios and a movie executive's mansion complete with grand piano. He also fashioned highly portable pieces of kit including a screen that allowed the cast's excellent cinematic work with local firm, PhantoFilms, to be displayed at its best. It created an excellent platform for Hazel McLynn's well-paced, colourful, version of the movie classic driven along by her own choreography with a nod to assistant Orla McHugh and supported by musical director's Deidre Lee's five- piece band.

The men in this show may have been heavily outnumbered but they were uniformly strong. Mr Gallagher with his good singing voice and twinkle toes was a handsome, confident Lockwood, star of the silent era who morphed effortlessly into the talkies while another good dancer, Michael Goulding gave us a Cosmo Brown that was a bright, lively foil to his boyhood pal.

John Farragher looked the part as the increasingly exasperated film director Roscoe Dexter, Ronan Egan was a convincing studio boss, R F Simpson and Richie Heneghan - who doubled up on roles - was particularly good as the male voice coach to Lockwood.

Mary Dempsey was a sweet, lovely voiced Kathy Selden, Lockwood's love interest who becomes a star in her own right, Angela Prenty was a waspish Zelda Zanders, Karen Ronane gave us a couple of confident cameos as vocal coach Miss Dinsmore and actress Olga Mara while Kate Hughes was a convincing Hollywood reporter on the red carpet.

But the big star of the night was Vivienne Lee as Lina Lamont, the girl fated to be seen and not heard as the talkies usurp the silent era and all because she possesses a voice like the strimmers that mar sunny Sundays in suburbia. Miss Lee is an excellent actress and, as befits a movie star, looked a million dollars throughout.

In the never-ending quest for a box office draw, I can't envisage too many societies picking on Avenue Q.

For a start it is not suitable for children with its adult themes and liberal use of profanities. With its high dependency on puppetry, it also requires a huge suspension of disbelief. It would work best in bigger centres of population where there is a larger pool of prospective customers raised on its particularly American cartoon-style humour. As for the average Irish small town where even The Scarlet Pimpernel comes a distant second to a version of South Pacific, forget it.

It tells of the anxieties of young adults encountering the realities of the western world while searching for the meaning of their lives and touches on themes such as racism, homophobia and pornography.

Despite the health warning - it might not be a night for your Victorian maiden aunt, if such a creature still exists - the show is a great vehicle for a student company such as University College Cork Musical Society.

Director Grace Vaughan framed this production as theatre in the round, although one played out on a rectangle no bigger than the lounge of a millionaire's new-build. Danny Buckley's sturdy settings, depicting the homes on low-rent Avenue Q were positioned at either end of the Granary Theatre's space with the audience split into bleacher-style seats on the other two sides of the room, boxing in the playing area.

Thankfully Ms Vaughan had thought through the dangers with this type of staging and sensibly kept much of the solo or small ensemble work near the settings, allowing all of the audience's eyes to focus on the performers.

When the full company of 16 were onstage together she and choreographer Maeve Guilfoyle cleverly split the ensemble in two allowing each half of the company to address the side of the audience they faced, keeping them fully engaged. As a result the theatrical crime of looking at an actor's back was largely negated.

If Ms Vaughan's production was well conceived it was also well executed by the eleven principal players - eight of whom act as puppet masters - and the five chorus members.

Josh Spink and Cassandra McElligott who evoked sympathy for the central characters, Princeton, a recent English graduate fresh to the area, and Kate Monster, a teaching assistant, acted with their voices to the extent that the audiences' eyes became fixed on the puppet rather than the actor's face. Indeed, the trend of the puppet masters taking on the personas of their fluffy Sesame Street-style charges ran through the production. The cast also possessed good singing voices and when all 16 were together the tone and harmonies were of high quality.

Conor Prendiville became a funny Trekkie Monster; a malevolent Honey Monster with a certain take on the use of the internet, Emmet Crotty was a buttoned-up Rod, a closet gay, with the rangy Darren O'Dea as Nicky, his messy lodger.

Big-voiced Vicky Sheridan was sultry temptress, Lucy the Slut, while Aaron O'Sullivan and Melissa Craig were energised as the Bad Idea Bears, sprite- like characters with a taste for alcohol seeking to lead others astray.

The eternally busy Ali Coady took on the physical and vocal mannerisms of juvenile soap star, Gary Coleman; Fiona O'Sullivan was Christmas Eve, a scary Japanese therapist always one step away from erupting into fury, while the impressive Michael Phelan was her slacker boyfriend, Brian.

The production also benefited greatly from the work of musical director's Lauren Ronan's six-piece band which drove along the action while making light work of Jeff Marx and Robert Lopez's sometimes quirky score.

Under the directorial guidance of the innovative Brian Logan, who also doubled here as both lighting and set designer, this was a busy production with lots of stage activity from an extremely large ensemble, including some children, right from the off. Logan's biggest innovation was his departure from the norm by casting female performers in the established male roles of Caiaphas, Annas and the Priests.

I have never before come across a lady playing the part of the High Priest (or Priestess, in this case) and what a delightful job Maxine McAleenon made of it, maintaining a nice stage presence throughout and, along with her female sidekicks, quickly establishing her darker role and authority within the piece.

The Priestesses, played by Maelissa Cunning, Olive Hemphill and Megan McKenna, respectively, gelled well to produce a subtle, but no less intimidating, evil force, while producing much clearer vocal results than we normally get.

I felt this was a bold but clever move, especially for any company with that perennial problem … a shortage of men.

Apart from this, it was a fairly traditional staging of the biblical story with a modern edge and played out under Logan's commanding and majestic set, which, despite the stage-left band platform (due to no traditional pit space), remained visually pleasing and, for the most part, fully functional. This large multi-level single static set in the style of a Roman amphitheatre worked well with the venue's steeply racked semi-circular seating area and provided plenty of scope for interesting group positioning and clever lighting effects.

Due to the show's 'sung-through' format the hard-working musicians in Eric Boyd's confident and well- balanced 10-piece band were definitely the back-bone of this production, producing an impressively even music/vocal balance throughout, although there were small instances when, due to the large ensemble, the chorus was a little too loud for the soloists.

Generally, there were no problems with the music and indeed the high degree of musical suspense created by Boyd during Blood Money was a great example of how an MD can bring more to the table with a clear understanding of what is happening on stage.

The big colourful set piece, Jesus Christ Superstar, really stood out, not only because of its great integration of chorus, dancers, lighting and music with a top-notch performance by Judas, but also for coping so well with the additional technical demands of projecting live close-up video footage of the on-stage action onto two large screens.

The quality of choral singing remained uniformly good throughout, and, apart from some slow exits in an otherwise well-paced production, ensemble movement and positioning was good with some believable interaction to the words and actions of the principals. There was a vast range of mixed abilities on display in terms of movement and co-ordination and, Choreographer, Sharon Logan, did have her work cut out for her, yet movement and integration was generally well executed, but, with few obvious stand-out dancers, the routines, by necessity, proved to be adequate.

Richard Campbell's understated playing of the title role worked well and we warmed to his portrayal of the character with his expressive performance and vocal characterisation during Gethsemane, but his main strength as a performer was his vocals.

As this story is told through the eyes of Judas, young Adam Goudy was well-cast in this part. Unusual in this role, his vocals were amazingly clear throughout and combined with some great acting to provide a well- balanced portrayal of the deeply- troubled apostle and showed a great understanding of his character.

As Mary Magdalene, young Louise McClarty had a difficult and important role and I felt that, vocally, this performer was good, while, as Pontius Pilate, there was a solid and consistently good performance from David Ferguson, offering particularly clear diction and with a voice that was always fully controlled.

Although Darren Gardiner's overall sound mix appeared much more subdued than normal, I felt that it was a brave, if risky, decision and one that provided a double-edged sword in terms of creative success … working on some levels (excuse the pun) while not so well on others.

On the positive side, it helped us hear the lyrics more clearly without the soloists having to force their vocals, but the lack of volume sometimes diluted the 'rock' feel of the piece. With lots of evenly-washed mood lighting, some eye-catching atmospheric lighting and many dramatic moments, from the blinding entrance light for Jesus to the blood red backdrop lighting for Judas' hanging scene (adding a degree of eeriness to the shock value of the piece), Logan's lighting design was one of the most impressive elements of this production.

In dress, there was a wide variety of styles on show throughout, from the ragged shawls of the lepers to Herod's glitzy showbiz girls and the many white-winged Angels, Soul Girls and gospel choir members and Costume Designer, Ewan Campbell, and team were certainly kept on their toes.

Although the clichéd colour coding is probably no longer essential with such a universally-known piece, the costumes, generally, remained ambiguous enough as not to confirm either the time or geographical setting of this production.

One of the most interesting, and uniformly good, designs was dressing the female Priestesses in full length military-style overcoats, while Caiaphas looked a little more feminine with the sparkling accessories worthy of her station.

Generally, thanks to Chantelle O'Neill and her team, the hair and make-up were all well presented, while David Wray's stage management team had a lot to contend with coping with such a large ensemble, but this was generally well managed with a few exceptions.

Karen Hunter's many props (apart from the large Crucifixion cross, which was cleverly integrated within the set) were, for the most part, kept low key although I felt that the water bowl for Pilate was suitably large and exaggerated enough to help symbolise his total frustration when washing his hands of everything. Overall, there was great team work in evidence here with particularly successful input from music and lighting departments and from some soloists in this well-paced, well- directed, well-dressed and well-lit show.

Although the original show ends with no reference to the Resurrection, this was tastefully realised here when Jesus was escorted off stage by an angelic group of young children dressed in white … offering a touching and innovative message of hope.

There is something special about the local Musical Society's annual production in most rural towns throughout Ireland that causes a bit of a buzz in the town.

Castlerea is no exception, for when I arrived at the venue there was a great sense of expectation as the audience took its seats for this epic show about the birth of modern America … warts and all.

The foyer was filled with iconic imagery of America, including flags, bunting and even the image of the statue of liberty, and I also liked the fact that this company treasured its previous AIMS awards enough to publicly display them.

Directed by Peter Kennedy, who also doubled as Choreographer, this was not only a big show but also an equally epic production of it.

Lying somewhere between Fiddler On The Roof and Showboat in some respects, the gritty and disturbing subject matter was never going to be a 'barrel of laughs', but rather a theatrical reflection of the harsh realities of the time.

The staging of this show is a difficult enough challenge for any company, but to stage it from scratch in a sports hall of a multi-purpose community hub in an industrial estate with neither stage nor other theatrical facilities was nothing short of a monumental task. The set design team's work could only be realised after the building of a full, workable stage and lighting rig was in place. Comprising two large double-level set pieces at either side of the stage, this was an impressive design, which proved to be functional, symbolic and visually pleasing, with its black/white colour-coding capturing the racial significance within the story. The piece on stage left was a black open-framed staircase structure (where the Afro/Americans in the story would often be found), while the one on stage right was a white open- framed revolving house structure (the home of the wealthy white American family), but - due to height restrictions - the lower level of this one was merely symbolic.

The black structure also doubled as a ship and good use was made of two high mobile rostra, which, in keeping with other parts of set, were also open-framed structures.

The set also included full stage size projections onto the flat cyc screen above a stage-wide back platform, with continuous and relevant imagery to help tell the story or to set the scene. Thankfully, this was thoughtfully and very successfully used and - as the synopsis of the story is complicated for anyone new to the show - was a good tool for simplifying the story. Indeed, it is a credit to all involved here for bringing this story from page to stage so simply for its audience to understand.

All those playing members of the Afro/American community in this production wore black wigs and were 'blackened up' for the performance. While this is potentially controversial, the decision on whether or not to do this is totally at the discretion of the company and it must be noted that it does not affect the adjudication of the show.

There was good use of children throughout, and special mention must go to Cian Haynes as Little Boy and Nancy Henry as Little Girl for their important performances, while it was excellent to see a real Model T Ford car on stage, providing both great attention to detail and a high degree of authenticity.

Although not totally sung through, this show was 'as good as' for the busy 15-piece orchestra and their hard- working Musical Director, Chorus Master and Conductor, Shane Farrell, who, thankfully, chose only to conduct in order to give this busy choral show all the attention it deserved; a move that worked well as the choral diction was always close to perfect.

Following the Little Boy setting the scene with dialogue over the appropriately piano-based Overture, the rousing title song was accompanied by some busy stage activity with great use of space on all levels for groupings to provide a colourful opening with the amazing and unexpected arrival of Kevin Heaney's Harry Houdini from the back of the auditorium, suspended upside down from a high wire above the audience.

A lot of Kennedy's choreography was about groupings, positioning, movement and integration rather than conventional dance routines, and he certainly made use of all of the different height levels to maximise variation.

However, the dancers did get a chance to shine during the lively and colourful production piece, Crime Of The Century, and I particularly liked the ensemble dancing in Henry Ford with its use of hands to form the letter 'T', while the fast-paced playing by the orchestra combined with good ensemble movement to make The Gettin' Ready Rag a success.

Other musical highlights included: the harmonies during Journey On; the pounding musical suspense created as the car was being damaged; the amazingly effective off-stage choral work during both Justice and Epilogue; and the duet, Wheels Of A Dream, which really did cause the hairs on the back of my neck to rise. Generally, Liam Feeney's sound was good, but numerous late mic cues were annoying, as were a few late lighting cues. However, Kennedy and Feeney's warm lighting plot enhanced some great pictures in A Shtetl Iz Amereke, while the freeze moments and slow motion movement during The Night That Goldman Spoke was well-lit with impressive red lighting to express Tateh's rage.

While death scenes can sometimes be difficult to stage, Sarah's burial through the trap door in the Act 1 finale (Till We Reach That Day) was both effective and harrowing.

Boasting colourful and perfect period costumes, there was great attention to detail in dress, hair & make-up and props throughout, while the arrival of the Jewish community at Ellis Island provided very authentic costuming. There were no problems with entrances and exits and the hard- working ensemble/chorus gave great support to the generally well-cast Principals, although a few need to try to sustain their accents and diction, especially when expressing anger or arguing on stage.

With his soulful vocals and good acting, Shane Kelly gave a gentle and patient portrayal of the Afro/American immigrant and ragtime musician, Coalhouse Walker, who eventually seeks revenge and justice, against Julie Connolly's good performance as his girl, Sarah.

Displaying great stage presence, Jaqueline Kenny was outstanding with her gentle, warm and thoughtful performance of Mother, while her well controlled vocals in songs like Goodbye, My Love and the duet with Tateh, Nothing Like The City, easily made them highlights.

As the Eastern European immigrant and artist, Tateh, Niall Heaney proved to be a great actor with that rare ability to act through his expressive vocal skills; singing both gently (Our Children) and in anger (A Shtetl Iz Amereke and Success) yet retaining his clear vocals and perfect diction. Finally, Sarah's Friend was the voice of reason and hope here and her character was so well performed by Caroline Madigan that she proved that there is no such a thing as a small role.

(Youth Group Production) The staging of any musical theatre production is always a challenge for any company, but Sir Andrew Lloyd Webber and Charles Hart's record- breaking show, The Phantom Of The Opera, must raise the level of that challenge, both in staging and performance … especially for a youth group.

However, Fusion Theatre, who in the past have successfully tackled the likes of Les Miserable, Titanic, Chess, Evita and The Boys In The Picture, were certainly up for yet another challenge … and, being well passed 'the point of no return' on the night I attended, managed to pull it off, again. Set in front of the main tabs, the Prologue offered a busy opening auction scene, before Director and Musical Director, Ian Milford's 14- piece orchestra played that most stunning of Overtures to transport us back in time to a rehearsal at the Paris Opera House.

From such dramatic playing of this well-known piece, which simply demanded the audience's attention, to the lovely delicate picture achieved at the final scene with the gentleness of ballet dancer, Meg, holding the disappeared Phantom's mask, Milford easily set the scene, and the standards, for the rest of the evening. While the cloth backdrop for the Hannibal rehearsal scene may, on the surface, not have appeared overly sumptuous, full marks must go here for using these clothes and adding greatly to the authenticity of the scenes, while the accident with the cloths was nicely and simply staged to keep the production pace going. There was obviously a lot of work to ensure that this multi-purpose venue space reflected the feel of an old Opera House with the provision of theatre boxes at either side of the auditorium; essential both to the ambience of the room and to the staging of the story, while the Manager's office scene boasted a great central fireplace, assorted furnishings and black tabs all complemented by amazingly detailed props and great attention to detail with some very good sound effects throughout.

However, the wow factor was reserved for the underground setting into the Phantom's lair (which cleverly, and easily, doubled for the graveyard scene) with its sewage gate under a foot bridge with steep stone steps, motorised boat (complete with its own lit lantern at the front) and large candle holders.

Lit by cross-stage lighting, with effective use of smoke adding to the atmosphere, this was impressive. While the ever-present chandelier was never going to be as visually impressive as one would hope, the staging of its falling was well achieved, despite it dropping rather than swinging on to the stage.

Another well realised moment was the famous mirror scene (the Phantom's first appearance), while having Madame Giry lip-synch the Phantom's voice as she read his letters not only added eeriness to the moment, but also highlighted a certain relationship between the two.

There was a nice touch of natural integration displayed when the ballet was brought forward in the story and the pit musicians were, momentarily, involved in the action as they searched for their supposed place in their music scores.

Indeed, with its almost sung-through operatic style score, Musical Director, Ian Milford, and his hard-working musicians provided solid musical support for the young performers, providing such musical highlights as Think Of Me, The Phantom Of The Opera, The Music Of The Night and Wishing You Were Somehow Here Again, while the chorus really got to shine in Masquerade.

It must also be stated that, as part of the contractual agreement for this show, two tracks were provided by the Really Useful Group as a mandatory part of the band.

The main principals were well cast here with some outstanding young voices effortlessly coping with the show's demanding vocal challenges. With his commanding vocals and strong stage presence, David McCrossan excelled as the much misunderstood Phantom, while another great voice, Connor Carson, provided a Raoul with a believable romantic chemistry between himself and Bronagh Walsh's Christine.

As a delightfully innocent Christine, Walsh, whose songs were all close to perfection, was a most consistent performer, while Hannah Conlon's Carlotta really was that temperamental diva, complete with comical facial expressions and a confident voice. Jessica Teague turned in a great performance as the sinister choreographer, Madame Giry.

Due to the nature of this show, the costume, hair and make-up departments had a busy task trying to make so many young people look so out of age, with varying degrees of success. Apart from this, and some overcrowding at times with such a large ensemble, the main problems in this production were in the lighting and costume departments, with each requiring a little more attention to detail.

Overall, Rebecca Leonard's choreography and movement with such a large ensemble was an important element in this production's success.

After driving for five hours from Belfast to Galway through the lousiest of weather conditions (yes, it was that famous Wednesday in February!), I am glad to say that this Chaperone production turned out to be a lot more Drowsy than 'lousy'.

This laugh-a-minute 'show within a show' is a tongue-in-cheek satire of American musical comedy during the Jazz era.

Set around the frantic preparations for a wedding, this fun show was totally irreverent and hammed-up by director, Conor Kennedy-Burke, who - with a big student following for the company - always played to the gallery and never missed a trick when it came to comedy, innuendo or double entendre.

In keeping with the Jazz age setting of the show, some gentle jazz music was playing in the auditorium as the patrons were being shown to their seats to help set the mood and ambience for the piece.

With no front tabs, the single static stage set sprawled across one of the widest stages I have ever came across in any theatre.

Boasting wall lights, two side doors, two upstage entrances and a fridge that was also used for quick exits and entrances plus a large pull-out bed, this representation of the narrator's apartment was very functional and there were certainly no problems with entrances and exits.

However, Ronan Gallagher and Jack Scullion's set, an open-plan apartment with kitchen, living room and bedroom, was not visually attractive as, with so much empty space, it lacked character and, with little colour in design or from the lighting plot, it also lacked atmosphere.

The tone for the rest of the evening was firmly set when, in total darkness, the narrator's first words in his opening monologue were "I hate theatre". As he offered his opinions on musical theatre and relaxed in his chair beside his record player to enjoy listening to the soundtrack recording of his favourite musical comedy, The Drowsy Chaperone, the show magically came to life and was played out in a fantasy world in his lonely apartment.

Played straight through without an interval but with a hilarious sequence when the narrator changes the record to play Act II, this send-up loses touch with reality in more ways than one. The beginning of the Overture was pre-recorded, as per the script, to represent it being played on the record player in his reality world, before the live orchestra took over at the transition from the narrator's world to the fantasy of the show within a show.

Making his directorial debut here, Musical Director, Dean Reidy, was really getting into the spirit of the piece dressed in black tux and conducting with his back to stage (I can only presume that the principals and chorus could see him on a screen somewhere).

The score was generally bright and breezy jazz-inspired musical comedy fare and Reidy and his 12-piece orchestra, who (unlike their M.D.) were well hidden in a stage left pit, provided a nice light touch and some fast-paced playing.

The songs ranged from the lively cast introduction of Fancy Dress, to the song-and-dance number, Cold Feet, and from the anthem to alcoholism, Stumble Along, to the big production piece, Toledo Surprise.

However, it is a strange show in that it relies on duets and ensemble pieces and, sadly, no-one really gets a complete solo song.

Hannah O'Reilly and Charlotte Moore's choreography provided some lovely moments, like when the cast grouping symbolised the aeroplane at top of the show and when the diva appeared on the back of a human elephant, while all of the frozen cast moments, when the narrator paused the action to speak, were all well conceived and executed.

Although the use of old sea-shell footlights was a particularly nice visual touch, the lighting, with its abundance of bright wide washes and follow spots was not adventurous enough and lacked atmosphere.

Blathnaid McKevitt and Yvonne McHugh's costumes appropriately included many Charleston-style dresses for the ladies, with lots of fringes and head bands, and some typical maid costumes, while the gents sported a good mix of apt styles. Peppered with almost every stereotypical character that musical comedy has ever introduced, this satirical slant on 1920's melodrama boasted principals and a chorus with good voices, but with mixed acting and dancing abilities.

In his Man In Chair narrator role, Shane Egan possessed perfect timing throughout with his interjections and comic asides in a believable and relaxed performance, while, in the title role, Elizabeth Moon's upper class drunk provided great diction.

Grainne White really threw herself into the spirit of her role as the successful showgirl, Janet Van De Graff, while apart from his talent for blind-folded roller skating, Robert Browne's wealthy oil tycoon, Robert Martin, had the perfect vocal tone to play a singer from this period.

Keegan Charlier's wealthy Mrs Tottendale displayed nice teamwork with her butler, Underling, and some great comic timing, while Neil Delaney's outstanding portrayal of her unflappable upper class English butler stole the show with his comical awkwardness.

When everyone discovers that there is no Minister to conduct the wedding, everything slides into total chaos and the director, choreographer and cast deserve credit for how well this was conveyed in the piece and also for the enforced black-out scene when the lights fuse mid-song and the ensemble freeze until it is rectified, before continuing as if nothing had happened.

It is a great talent to be able to sing or act badly, but, in this piece, the performers get lots of opportunities to do just that.

The last time there was an apparition in the West of Ireland, the small village of Knock was firmly placed on the world map. So, when I witnessed what appeared to be a miracle happening in front of my eyes at the end of this performance, with Jesus clearly visible centre-stage on the Cross and the same Jesus (!) appearing stage right behind him to suggest the Resurrection, I thought I had been sent a spiritual sign to help me with my adjudication.

No such luck … but just how did the Sligo Fun Company achieve this unexpected and innovative twist in its production? … Smoke and mirrors? … No … but a simple case of 'double- casting' or casting double - identical twins!

Such dual casting of Anthony and Graham Kelly as Jesus (sharing the main role and the ghostly resurrected Jesus on alternate performances) was a great way to ensure an understudy for the title role.

There were many other small but significant moments in this production when director and choreographer, Mary MacDonagh, along with co- director and co-choreographer, Steffen Jorgensen, played to the strengths within this mostly youthful company.

These included the use of some risqué costumes that only a young cast could get away with wearing and some highly energetic dance routines and ensemble movement that the young performers all took in their stride. Right from the start, lying across the open stage as the audience entered, ensemble members displayed amazing discipline as they lay for what must have seemed like an eternity, before coming alive and bursting with energy in a busy and fast-paced routine during the Overture, which really set the scene for what was to follow in this bright and fast-paced production.

Like those on stage, an equally determined impact was being established in the pit under Niamh Crowley's unforced but precise musical direction, keeping her 17- piece orchestra in line with a measured pit/stage balance throughout.

A mix of seasoned musicians (some professional) and some very young players (Crowley's own music students) combined and worked hard to deal with the sung-through format of the show.

Although reverting back to the original use of an orchestra rather than the more recently accepted 'band' approach, what this production lost in 'rock' feel was well compensated for with lovely sweeping strings in the bigger musical numbers and good vocal clarity with no forced singing, as voices did not need to compete with overly loud music.

Played out on John O'Donoghue's functional, open and uncluttered single box-style set with a central rostrum, serviceable steps to a upstage platform with six large symbolic crosses embedded in the flats and equally symbolic extracts of biblical text, Frances Ryan's stage management was greatly assisted here and there were no problems with entrances and exits.

Although Nick McCall's lighting plot was never bad, I felt that, generally, there was perhaps too much reliance on bright full-stage washes and that being a little more adventurous may have created a few more atmospheric moments.

However, it was great to see footlights being used and the white lighting during Gethsemane (I Only Want To Say) was certainly effective.

Indeed, Gethsemane (I Only Want To Say) was a stand-out scene not only for its lighting, sound and musical input, but also because it represented the first time that Anthony Kelly managed to convey Jesus as a real vulnerable person in the show, with a most impressive vocal performance and characterisation of the part.

Although a more mature performer than his perceived peers in the show, Eoin O Suilleabhain's Judas offered a stand-out acting performance and a much softer vocal approach than expected, yet still with the ability to hit those high falsetto notes when required. He turned in an excellent performance during the lively and colourful title song to make it a true highlight.

Michele Feeney was a pale young performer with great facial expressions, body positioning and a clear understanding of her role as Mary. She was very gentle and caring with an almost motherly characterisation as she came to terms with her new role as someone who had finally found someone to care for. Feeney also provided beautiful vocals to Everything's Alright, I Don't Know How To Love Him and Could We Start Again Please? three musical highlights of this production.

Indeed, the harmonies during Could We Start Again Please? along with Luke Devaney's Peter - another young performer who carried his role well - were outstanding.

Dressed as a wealthy gentleman, Hugh O'Neill's suave-looking Pilate displayed great experience and we got a laid-back and gentle approach from this mature performer with clear vocals and perfect diction.

The enthusiastic ensemble were almost unique in that there was a high number of males involved and chorus work was uniformly good throughout, whilst movement, groupings and integration between those on stage all worked well.

As a youthful company with lots of energy, the performers had no problem coping with MacDonagh and Jorgensen's demanding choreography, which worked particularly well during the title number.

Let us hope that this aptly-named young company's enthusiasm, commitment and great sense of fun may continue for many years to come.

Imagine, for a moment, 30 One Direction fans milling around you night and day. Or, if you are from the older generation, 30 little horrors from the prep school version of St Trinian's. That was the reality of Andrea Doolan Browne's Aggie Hannigan as she carefully picked her way down the stairs to work each morning. It's no wonder she had a permanent headache.

Ennis Musical Society had so many girls interested in this show they fielded two teams of orphans on alternate nights with the six named girls and Annie bridging the groups. The kids were very well drilled by director and choreographer Sarah Griffin and by chorus mistress Fiona Walsh; were highly enthusiastic and possessed some good individual voices but when they screamed in unison or slammed down the buckets as they cleaned the orphanage floor in "Hard Knock Life", they made some racket.

Ms Griffin ensured her choreography - tailored for the company - added to the action and kept up the pace by bleeding one scene into another while the backstage crew changed the set in the background. It was highly effective and less distracting than it sounds with stage business always diverting the eye away from Maeve Fox's hardworking team as they went about their job.

The device also allowed Shane Farrell's excellent 10-piece band to let rip during the changes as opposed to supporting the performers at other times.

Ms Doolan Brown with her Broadway belt of a voice made a wonderfully tousled-hair Hannigan who was a more mean spirited matron than most, lifting Molly by the hair at one point, pinching Annie on the cheeks and then banishing her to a cupboard at another.

Aoibh O'Reilly whose Annie is probably the tallest I've come across, has a light voice which is worth developing and shows promise as an actress. Her rival in the cuteness stakes, Sandy an 18-month Bichon- cross called Freddie got on with her so well he even rolled over as Aoibh kneeled to sing "Tomorrow".

Annie's adoptive father, Oliver Warbucks, was played by Ken O'Shaughnessy as a man used to getting his own way while Edel Heaney's Grace Farrell was an efficient personal assistant with her eye clearly on the fashion magazines. The rangy Neil Haran invested Rooster with something of a strut as he strode around the Glor's big stage with Zoe Halpin's excellent Lily St Regis, with her great accent and diction, in tow. Ms Griffin was also blessed with good performers in the show's smaller roles exemplified by Paul Curley who took on the guises of Lt Ward, Bert Healy and a dottery Judge Brandeis and made them three credible and very different characters. I suspect audience members without a programme were not aware they played by the same man.

Richard Donnellan was a terrifically precise Drake, complete with an excellent received pronunciation English accent; Joe Moran played a sympathetic President Roosevelt, Fiona Coughlan, in her first role with the company, was a confident Star- To-Be while Kate Corrigan, Elaine Gavin and Shona Connellan looked and sounded great as the Boylan Sisters.

Ms Gavin also had a big hand in the overall looked of the show acting as the scenic artist on Brian Burke and Liam Hansbury's clever set and, with Teresa Larkin, coming up with a handsome costume plot for the production.

Star Systems sound plot ensured the audience heard every word, kept a good balance between the band and the performers and added to the atmosphere with some great sound effects.

However, Paul Kelly's lighting plot was a mixed bag with some great ideas well executed while at other times leaving players in semi-shade during routines.

There's a touch of the international brigade about the Light Opera Society of Tralee.

Scots, English and even Lithuanian accents mix with the Kerry and other Irish voices in this fledgling group but it was a local boy who showed his fellow cast members how to steal the show.

Tim Landers played the psychotic Nazi sympathiser, Franz Liebkind, with relish.  He grabbed the role of the pigeon-fancying playwright by the throat from the moment we first encountered him in his lederhosen and World War 2 helmet on the rooftop of his New York home.

He was a physical and comedic force very much at home on the wide open spaces of the fabulous Siamsa Tire stage, showing a level of attack that General Rommel would have been proud of.

James Finnegan as Max Bialystock is a good actor and certainly understood the role of the washed-up Broadway producer who hits on a crooked wheeze to make one big killing. He was physically perfect for the role and looked smart. He got the jokes, knew how to play them, had fabulous facial expressions but at times his gestures looked small in comparison to Mr Landers. With more of Mr Landers' pizazz this could have been an outstanding performance.

It was a similar story with Ciaran Higgins' Leopold Bloom, the accountant with all the courage of the Lion from the Wizard of Oz who gets his eyes opened by Max and his buttons undone by blonde bombshell Ulla. His studied nervousness was almost too timid.

Dovile Baltoniene, a blonde Lithuanian with Mermaid hair, was more outgoing and had fun in the role of Ulla, the Swede with a name almost as long as the bridge that connects Malmo and Copenhagen in Denmark. Naturally she looked the part.
