James Brennan played arty theatre director Roger de Bris with an understated campness, if I really can say that about a man in a green evening dress while Kerry Fleming as his assistant, Carmen, was highly consistent as a much more flamboyant gatekeeper to his boss.

Aki O'Rourke as Scott, another of Roger's boys, was a good mover good around the stage while Grainne O'Carroll took delight in the role of Hold Me, Touch Me, one of the sexed-up old biddies that Max taps for cash and Niall Fitzgerald was aggressive as accountancy boss Marks.

The driving force behind L.O.S.T., which is underpinned by the Kerry School of Music and performing arts, is Aidan O'Carroll, who not only directed the show and acted as musical director but came up with a well conceived set for the show.

His design and production were enhanced by Joseph Betts fine lighting plot but the loss on the night of some of the channels in Shane Murphy's sound plot left things underpowered for a time.

Mr O'Carroll is clearly steeped in musicianship and ensured his cast were well drilled vocally while keeping his band moving with a firm and steady beat.

Choreographer Tara Dore's clever routines were well executed by a small troupe of dancers. In fact, there were only a total 22 players on the Siamsa stage for this production, the majority of them gifted musically Mr O'Carroll describes L.O.S.T. as a boutique company. I longed for more bodies on a big stage that could easily accommodate an ensemble three times as big.

A lot of the fundamentals were in place for this production and, I suspect, for the group as a whole. Now I want to see things grow.

It was almost 11pm in tiny Clarinbridge outside Galway city and I'd just slipped on my coat to make the trek back to Belfast. I'd pick up my bag from where I'd left it when I was speaking to Maree Musical Society members after their show, grabbed a programme from where I had sat it but found that my notebook which was accompanying it had gone AWOL. My 16 pages of notes on the show (and those from Ennis Musical Society's "Annie" the previous evening) had vanished.

Before blind panic set in, Maree's chairman, Mike Kerrigan, nipped into the wings and returned with a selection of reporter's pads cleared from the set by a fastidious props team putting things to bed on the last night of the run. Thankfully, my notebook was on top of the pile and all, once more, was right with the world.

Looking back I shouldn't have been surprised at the final turn of events. It was just one more surprise on a night of surprises. For a start the company's shows take place in a surprisingly big complex buried in parkland a mile from the main Galway to Gort road which the group kits out from top to bottom, building a stage and importing tiered seating for a 600-strong audience. Five minutes into the show and John Wright's handsome looking set springs a major surprise - it sports not only an in-built video screen but a Les Miserables-style revolve - and then just when I'm coming to terms with this big crowd rocking along to Ashman and Menken's witty, tuneful show in what seems like the middle of nowhere, the plant opens its mouth. Audrey Two - voiced by a thousand burly men down the years speaks those immortal words "Feed me Seymour" - and it's a girl's voice I hear.

Later when Twoey appears during the curtain calls, it's the glamorous Antoinette Van Ravestijn, decked out in a flashy green evening dress slashed to the thigh who takes a bow. Puppeteer Rick Officer, the man who brought the plants to life and who literally sweated off pounds for the society, looked plain in comparison. As I discovered, producer, director and choreographer, Caroline Cawley, isn't frightened of challenging convention. The Ronettes, normally Ronette, Crystal and Chiffon - played in this case by teenage girls - were supplemented by Darlene and Patti and re-named the urchins while three Dream Girls (think any Motown girl trio) provided the vocal muscle.

Ms Cawley even had the temerity to omit Seymour's "Sudden Changes" and restore to the score, the beautiful - and highly effective - "The worse he treats me", a duet for Audrey and Seymour dropped by the writers before the show opened off-Broadway in 1982.

And she cast a couple of crackers in her lead roles. Yvonne Spelman was all we have come to expect  as Audrey, a breathy, clipped, high-pitched blue collar accent and movement hobbled by tight skirts and towering heels while Padraic McDonagh's was a terrific wimp, awkward, nervous and introverted. Both were on the ball vocally.

Paul O'Dowd, another good actor, made flower shop owner Mushnik a real Jewish poppa but needed to watch timing in his songs while Mike Kerrigan was a suitably over-the-top Orin Scrivello, the dangerous dentist. Those Dream Girls, Ciara McWilliams, Claire Gill and Ruth Randles not only looked well with their glam dresses and up-do hairstyles but sang well all evening. The Ronettes, Hannah Wright, Katie Gill, Katie McGrath, Naoise Costelloe and Aisling Officer added to the vocals and were great movers, often leading the 40-strong cast in Ms Cawley's 60s routines. And that chorus, with a healthy number of men, sounded well in the big numbers and boasted some high quality individuals. Dawn McGoldrick, who also doubled up as Ms Luce and a Skid Row momma, has a dynamite voice.

The action was played out on Mr Wright's cleverly conceived and well- built set and enhanced by a classy, period looking wardrobe and a good sound plot from Dervan Sound. The one disappointment of the evening was that Paul Kelly's ambitious lighting plot, which truly soared at times, also fell to the Earth with a bump at times.

With the running joke in AIMS of it being the year of Jesus Christ Superstar, it's time I made my way into the confessional (now that will amuse those who know me).

I'm not a big fan of women playing priests or apostles in Lloyd Webber and Rice's blockbuster,  finding myself cast as a liturgical traditionalist, (cue more laughter) preferring to see 12 men in those places around the table. With Shannon Musical Society short of the requisite number of younger men to fill all the roles in the show, they used five girls as apostles in the Last Supper scene that opens Act Two.

Earlier, director Sean Power had introduced Pamela McGlynn as Annas and used Edel Halliday with Derek McMahon to complete the priests' line-up.

To be fair to Ms McGlynn, she exuded a carefully controlled air of soprano- pitched menace all night, displaying a thinly veiled contempt for their prized informer Judas while acting as a counterpoint to Ger Treacy's basso profundo Caiaphas, a Judean empire builder not to be trifled with, and a man who could easily take his place as a lock in any rugby pack in the country.

I might not prefer it if societies go down that route but with so much else right about this show it seems churlish to find fault. Pragmatism won out over dogmatism and a first night full house at Shannon comprehensive school, sitting on specially imported raised tier seating, loved it.

In many ways it is easy to see why. This was a thoughtful production with the action invariably adding meaning to the words - something that doesn't always happen - with some sequences beautifully drawn and more realistic brutality than audiences often get to see in Superstar.

It was fast-paced, driven along by Carmel Griffin's synth-heavy band which sacrificed strings, woodwind and brass but gave us two formidable guitarists and an excellent drummer and the show looked well with an excellent earth-toned costume plot which neatly sat on a fence between the contemporary and ancient yet was adaptable enough to convey changes of atmosphere and mood.

Eoin Sheedy was a gentle Jesus - almost too gentle at times - with the necessary height in the voice while Jared Nadin, although small in stature, made a super Judas with his vaulting voice and great diction.

Lauren Dunne was a gorgeous Mary with a lovely voice; Ciaran Collins made a commanding Pilate, suitably anguished about condemning a man he could find no fault in while Eoghan Rice's Herod was stripped of the standard campness. Hallelujah!

James Kelly was a powerful Simon while Joe Bracken gave us a Peter who was physically frightened by what he had become caught up in. While Shannon's male line-up may have been lacking in quantity, it possesses real quality with some beautiful voices adding to a vibrant chorus that was vocally on the ball and possessed near faultless diction while choreographically working as one in effecting Sean Power's flowing moves.

The action was played out on Mr Power's own minimalist set comprising of those photographic quality flats that his home city of Galway seems to specialise in, some rostra, a white screen and curtains which were truly used theatrically.

The production was aided greatly by a first class sound plot from Star Systems of Thurles which included some excellent sound effects and by Mike Finneran's lighting with its great mix of colour and atmosphere.

It's thirty minutes to curtain up at Bray's Mermaid Arts Centre and I've just been given the potentially show- destroying news that Sheevawn Musical Society's Judas is down with laryngitis and, naturally, won't be singing in the performance.

I was still absorbing the shock when the solution to overcoming the problem was outlined to me even before I got around to asking the question: "What happens now?"

The afflicted Chris Currid would be appearing on stage despite his illness but his part would be sung and spoken by Conor Cronin, doubling up on his duties as Herod and delivering the words from downstage wing positions.

As it turned out Mr Currid had lost his voice earlier in the run and the new practice had been in place for a few nights.

The audience was made aware of the move just before the curtain went up but, like me, they quickly adjusted to the new regime.

Mr Currid proved a skilful mimer with an almost perfect lip-synchs technique and he must have some voice to have beaten the excellent Mr Cronin to the role in the first place.

Mind you, it wasn't the only thing the audience had to come to terms with. This was a Superstar removed from its traditional presentation. Gone was the ancient setting and costumes with the show being placed in what was effectively a black box framed by four metal columns and dominated by a large screen on the back wall with the players adorned in modern day clothes.

The Romans and Judean hierarchy appeared as the suited bureaucrats and bankers that Western society has come to despise while the Priests were not even afforded that title in the play, instead they were simply named as Caiaphas, Annas and Conspirators 1 and 2.

Christ's followers - in this case mainly the bright young things of tomorrow including a healthy number of teenage boys and young men - came along in their jeans, tee-shirts and trainers before morphing into the black-robed mob that calls for his death as the show comes to its climax.

Director Siobhan Gallagher's action was also accompanied by a running commentary of imagery on the screen, some of it immediately relevant to the story while others parts broke out into a social commentary on issues such as poverty, homelessness, drug abuse and animal cruelty.

She also had the best seat in the house to keep an eye on the action as she doubled up as conductor while musical director John Morris played keyboard in a small band whose arching guitar and driving drums helped push along the action.

Yvonne Prendergast's flowing choreography help maintain a fast pace while the production was also enhanced by Vinny Osborne's good sound plot and Darren Kelleher's fabulous lighting.

While the commendable ethos of this group is to develop young musical theatre talent, Ms Gallagher wisely sprinkled a few older hands in key positions.

Sean McMahon was excellent as Jesus; Ciaran Mooney's Pilate was eye-catchingly detailed and although I don't agree with placing a woman in the role of Annas, Joanna Logue is an actress with great stage poise with terrific arm movements and facial expressions.

Of the younger set, Roisin Walsh was a beautiful blonde warm-voiced Mary while Mr Cronin's turn as Herod became merely a neat cameo in relation to the work he shouldered the rest of the evening with Cormac Gleeson and Mark O'Looney giving us confident performances as Peter and Simon respectively.

Any company staging Annie needs three big planks upon which to build a platform for success.

Firstly they need a loud but vulnerable kid in the title role, secondly they need a cute dog to ladle on more of the Aah factor and finally, they need a gifted comedic actress to play Aggie Hannigan.

Director Paul Norton came up trumps on all three accounts by casting 13-year-old belter, Aoibhin Walsh, in the eponymous role, persuading husband and wife team Nigel and Niamh Sammon to let their Springer spaniel, Chester, roam the stage for the week and allowing Karen Martin to give the audience at the town's GAA Centre a studied lesson in drunkenness as the matron of the New York orphanage.

Miss Martin's performance went a great deal further than the mere comedic however, with a lot of subtle touches and facial reactions that invested her character with depth and never once veered into pantomime. Young Aoibhin is one to keep an eye on with a voice that's huge for one just entering her teens and an ability to react to her fellow orphans and adult principals alike. As for Chester, well you just can't beat a cute mutt to steal a scene simply by walking on stage. But there was more to this production by a tight group working in a constrained space and playing on a typically clever John O'Donoghue set complete with sliding panels on the main structure, built-in pull out columns and pieces on trucks.

Diarmuid Guinan, as befits a company director, gave business magnate Oliver Warbucks an initial hard edge to his character before succumbing to Annie's orphan charms while Marguerite McDonnell was an understated Grace Farrell with a good voice although she could have projected it a little more at the start. Shane Fox as a brash and cocky Rooster attacked the role, literally strutting around the stage. Blathnaid Fitzsimons as his girlfriend, Lily St Regis, arrived with a nasal accent so hooty I could barely make her out but was much better by the time she had morphed into Mrs Mudge in Act Two and reined in the accent.

Jim Smyth, a man who knows a bit about broadcasting, was a confident Bert Healy with a decent voice and an easy manner around the stage.

The aforementioned Nigel Sammon displayed a penchant for accents, taking the stage initially as New York cop, Lt Ward, before taking up residence at the Warbuck's mansion as Drake, a very plummy English butler.

Miss Hannigan's little charges were a 16-strong girls' ensemble that ranged considerably in age and height but were well drilled and worked as a unit in the big numbers and set pieces. They also displayed commendable diction.

Choreographers Ultan Keena, who doubled up as a bright Bundles, the laundry man, and Graham Finnerty helped the action flow and ensured that the adult chorus were precise in their movements all evening. A mark of their attention to detail was the synchronisation of head movements, not an easy task by any measure. Niall Mulpeter's seven-piece band brought some colour to the orchestration with some fine violin playing by Caroline Sutton and good toned reeds and brass. The band and players alike benefited from his clear direction and firm beat.

Over the years, I have seen in excess of 80 different productions (not performances) of this teenage musical romp by Jim Jacobs and Warren Casey … I stopped counting productions after 80!

With such a vast experience of past productions, I thought it would be impossible for me to find anything new about yet another production of the show, but - to my surprise and delight - this production by Athlone Musical Society was every bit as fresh and innovative as I could ever have imagined.

This colourful, vibrant and lively production really stood out with Music, Choreography, Direction, Lighting, Costumes and the amazingly enthusiastic performances from the young cast all combining as key elements in the success of this fast-paced and energetic show.

There was assured direction from director/choreographer, Mary MacDonagh, and her assistant director/choreographer, Steffen Jorgensen, who opted for a minimal approach in this well-cast production.

With virtually no formal settings, the design teams (lighting and sets) worked theatrical wonders with flats plus clever projections and amazing lighting effects and the show had terrific pace because of the lack of cumbersome set changes.

Jonathan O'Brien's minimal approach to sets included attractive coloured side flats with holes and concealed lighting, a back balcony platform, a giant jukebox and bleachers.

This production boasted great attention to detail in costumes, props and direction throughout with some nice touches, particularly comic touches, while the final megamix and fast-paced curtain call ensured that the audience left in a feel-good mood.

I thought it was unusual, but innovative, during It's Raining On Prom Night, when Jan was singing the song as if she was on the radio, while Sandy joined in, as if she was listening to Jan singing the song. I thought this brought some teenage realism to this scene.

Musically, Grease may be a rock'n'roll style musical, but the popular score is well balanced between loud up-tempo numbers and some softer and truly beautiful ballads.

Unusually, this production featured the song Sandy as part of an opening Prologue and also renamed the Scene 1 song, Summer Nights, to Summer Lovin'.

Musical Director, Enda O'Connor, had a firm hand on his musical T-Birds and Pink Ladies and he and his six-piece orchestra provided a suitably lively tempo when required and maintained good stage/pit balance throughout.

Chorus Mistress, Heather Shine, may have been playing keyboard in the pit, but her on-stage charges in the ensemble were doing her proud with particularly strong choral work during Summer Lovin' and during the up-tempo, Greased Lightnin'. The sterling work of choreographer, Mary MacDonagh, and her assistant, Steffen Jorgensen, played an important role in this youthful production, with the young cast members having both the talent and energy to bring the concepts of the routines to life.

Niamh O'Shea (Sandy) and Chris Corroon (Danny) had believable romantic chemistry right from the start, with O'Shea being well-cast as a very prim and proper Sandy with a suitable voice for the role, while Corroon really was Mr Cool with a romantic heart for Sandy. Linda Murray's Rizzo really stood out here, especially during her emotional rendition of There Are Worse Things I Could Do; probably the best performance of this show. Sinead Handy may not have looked large enough to be compulsive eater, Jan, but she was good acting the part and certainly had an appetite for delivering strong vocals in all of her songs, Lisa Ann Roche brought a lot to her smaller role as the annoying, Patty Simcox. Apart from her real baton twirling, this performer had good acting abilities and particularly good facial expressions, while Paul McCarrick's 'over-the-top' timid geek, Eugene, was well realised and Joe McCaul's food-loving Roger had a great voice and supplied strong vocals.

Maggie Villarini's Cha Cha was a truly great dancer and deservedly brought the house down with her sexy show-stopping routine in Born To Hand Jive, while Darren O'Hara's Teen Angel may have been self- important and camp and played for laughs, but, beneath the hilarity, his was a great voice.

There was strong support off-stage too from Stage Manager, Jonathan O'Brien, and his team, while Property Manager, Camilla Flanagan's props were always authentic.

Derek Recks and Emer Kenny's overall sound mix was consistently good, and all sound effects worked well, while Paschal Gough's Lighting Design, was both clever and attractive and made everything look so good.

Wardrobe Mistresses, Kathleen Sweeney and Anne Kelly's many costumes included a wide variety of appropriate styles and there was great attention to detail here, particularly with footwear, while the Hair & Make-up team made sure that all were well presented In many ways, the sentiments of We Go Together sum up the qualities of the perfect ensemble and the young players in this production certainly went well together, with a great unity of purpose to everything they did on stage, from the well-drilled choral work to the most energetic dance routines and to the full integration with one another throughout the performance.

Ballinrobe Musical Society wanted to stage something special and something big for its 40th Anniversary show and it really pushed the boat out with this epic production of Jill Santoriello's A Tale Of Two Cities.

With show banners across the town's main street and a big front of house display of past productions and successes, the company was certainly in celebratory mood to mark its 'best of times', yet this dark show was anything but party material.

The cream on top of this musical birthday cake for the company on the night I attended was the presence of the American author, composer and lyricist of this Broadway musical, Jill Santoriello, and it was a great privilege for me to spend time with her and to get a deeper understanding of the piece. Whilst there will be obvious comparisons to Les Miserables (with its French setting, large ensemble and the many and varied characters to be found within), this show had drama, song, music, choral work, movement, romance and violence, but virtually no humour to give it light and shade.

As if the staging of such a big show was not challenging enough, full credit must go to all involved here for dealing with the additional task of converting a school sport's hall - with no theatrical facilities - into an impressively workable theatre.

Under Liam Butler's direction, there were lots of small, but effective, touches here, including: the atmospheric Christmas snowfall before I Can't Recall; the transition of focus from the child's bedroom to the funeral of Gabelle's son during Little One; the use of echo at times for dramatic effect on microphones; clear diction and vocals throughout; the Marquis singing the words of the letter as Darnay read it in Letter From Uncle; the great dramatic build up with blood-red lighting, silhouettes and slow motion action during the execution scene and the heavy thud of the blood-stained guillotine (helped by the snare drum) which was as important here as the final closing of the door in Ibsen's play, A Doll's House; and the individual groupings in the curtain call provided very effective pictures. There was particularly beautiful staging during If Dreams Came True, with Carton singing downstage as Darnay and Lucie's married life was depicted behind him, including their daughter growing up.

Played out on Butler and the design team's exceptionally wide double- level set on a deep stage to give plenty of central performance space for most of the ensemble action and, with good opportunities for variation within groupings and movement, it proved functional with upstage exits and entrances on both levels.

The show opened with the Bastille in Paris centre stage and, stage right, the inside of the house, complete with a staircase, a landing with a wall portrait and wall candles, a table and chairs with a heavy tablecloth, while upstairs had a wall portrait, a chair and a table-light for the Marquis. Stage right also doubled as Carton's office and the upstairs became the child's bedroom, while, stage left, the external frontage of the Defarge Tavern was represented together with narrow steps leading to the upstairs back-room.

Although predominantly concerned with the movement and grouping of such a large ensemble, there were some interesting dance routines from choreographer, Aoife McClafferty, during songs like No Honest Way (which also highlighted the mixed abilities within the ensemble) and Everything Stays The Same (with the symbolic beheading at the end of the scene). There were also some impressive groupings utilising every bit of the set in The Trial.

The decision by Musical Director, Finola Higgins Cosgrove, to only conduct her 13-piece orchestra and her other musical charges on-stage paid off with particularly good choral results in such numbers as The Trial and the Finale, I Can't Recall, while the rousing ensemble piece, The Way It Ought To Be, really stood out and the equally rousing Act 1 finale, Until Tomorrow, was delivered with great passion from both singers and players.

A high degree of suspense was well achieved with the foreboding music in Out Of Sight, Out Of Mind, while other musical highlights included: the almost operatic style father/ daughter duet, You'll Never Be Alone; the lovely gentle and moving piece, Little One; Without A Word, with its great ending and perfectly held note; the busy percussion during The Bluff; and the gentle duet, Let Her Be A Child. The ensemble integrated well here and provided some great choral work, while the principals managed to maintain clear diction and accents throughout.

For me, the most consistently good performances came from David Langan as the self depreciating British legal person, Sydney Carton, who - bringing the story to life in song and action - was the ultimate hero of the piece and, in performance, the ultimate hero of this production, while Angela Curley-Staunton, as the ever plotting and scheming Madame Defarge, provided beautiful vocals and had a great stage presence.

Although there were no problems with Niall Heaney's stage management, Liam Feeney's sound, the props department, Edel O'Neill's wardrobe department or the hair and make-up department, the lighting was the main weakness of this production.

Right from the opening of the show when the light was not on the opening performer, there were numerous and similar lighting problems throughout the night, including no follow spots on singers when they were moving in darkness and late lighting cues.

However, all was not lost because the final black out cue was crucial to this production and it worked perfectly, while other successful lighting moments included the good use of footlights for the murder of the Marquis, the mood inspiring purple backlight for the proposal and the blood-red lighting for the execution scene.

While some young performers can feel intimidated because an adjudicator is in the house, you can guess how I felt with the writer of the show standing beside me during my after show chat with company.

Jill Santoriello was more than happy with this production of her show and, surely, that must be an award in itself for the hard working members of Ballinrobe Musical Society - Congratulations on your 40th Anniversary!

As a Director, Peter Kennedy has a reputation of being someone who never misses an opportunity to 'ham' things up or to milk the comedy (and any double entendre) out of a show. So, when the show in question is the already 'over the top' Mel Brooks and Thomas Meehan comedy, The Producers, then you know you are in for a night at the theatre like no other.

It was no surprise therefore that, under the control of the Irish master of fun and irreverence (Kennedy), this was a relentlessly funny production from start to side-splitting finish with, probably, a more comic interpretation than usual.

By necessity, Peter Kennedy's set design had to be a mixed bag to cope with the many and varied scene changes; some were 'cheap and cheerful' while others proved more lavish. However, in order to maintain pace and functionality, there was a big reliance on cloths. Despite the many changes, this production was directed and staged with relatively good pace, and offered a great night's entertainment to its audience and I particularly liked the comic send-up of stage show titles as a backdrop to the end of the show.

Although a lot smaller than the number of musicians for the original productions of this show, the 12- piece orchestra, under the firm baton of Musical Director, John Roe, provided a lively tempo and good pit balance throughout.

Opening Night displayed promising choral work from the off, thanks to the sterling work of Chorus Mistress, Martha O'Toole, while the Act 1 Finale was also a highlight on the choral front.

Totally in keeping with this fun show, Peter Kennedy's choreography was, generally, very lively and energetic throughout, with a lot of visual choreographed comedy in hilarious numbers like Der Guten Tag Hop- Clop and the Act 1 Finale, with its amazingly funny routine from the old ladies, complete with walking frames.

Keep It Gay was also a very busy number on stage and full of comic moments in terms of movement (some a lot less subtle than others!), with a great conga line through the auditorium at the end (also acting as a great distraction for a scene change).

When it came to big production numbers, they didn't come much busier than Springtime For Hitler with its mass groupings, show girls and Kennedy's famous human carousel choreography.

I Wanna Be A Producer was a well achieved production number, with Leo's voice full of hope at the start and gradually gaining confidence as the song - and his belief in the idea of being a Producer - progressed, while, in contrast, Leo's beautiful duet with Ulla, That Face, stood out for its gentleness and When You've Got It, Flaunt It really captured Ulla's character with a very sexy routine. One of Peter Kennedy's many talents is that he is a naturally great comedy performer and comic actor, especially in the Groucho Marx style of one-liner delivery.

So, the part of the washed-up Broadway producer, Max, could have been written for him Nicky Lawless was suitably timid, nervous and indecisive in the role of Leo Bloom; the boring accountant with an escapist ambition of being a producer, while his softer vocals were suited to the more romantic songs.

Roisin Egenton's well sustained broken English accent, attractive looks and sexy posturing, dancing and vocals made her perfect in the role of the blonde Swedish bimbo, Ulla.

Declan Kelly turned in a show- stopping comic performance as the Nazi sympathiser, Franz Liebkind, particularly during the hilarious Der Guten Tag Hop-Clop.

As mature homosexual director, Roger DeBris, Tim Landers was, thankfully, a bit more butch than most of the others in his entourage, but still managed an 'over-the-top' comedy performance With his believable camp manner, Declan Gardiner did well as DeBris' ever dancing and ever twirling assistant, Carmen Ghia, The Properties Team - Marion Heery, Christine Bourke-Clancy, Niall Clancy and Helen Cooke - came up with the goods when necessary and, with so many scene changes, Stage Manager, Chontelle Kenny, and her team had a lot to contend with but there were no major problems.

Although rarely atmospheric, Emma O'Grady's lighting design reflected the brightness of the piece, while Mike Dervan's sound mix was consistently good and the sound effects all worked well Christine Bourke-Clancy, Helene Boyce and Martin Feeney ensured that all looked well in the wardrobe department with a wide variety of appropriate styles for old ladies, German soldiers, chorus girls, accountants and prisoners.

With comedy to the fore, Franz was dressed in a German helmet, lederhosen and big boots, while Roger's choice was a 'Chrysler building' glittering dress and jewelled accessories with white arm-gloves; both visually comical to add to the hilarity of the piece.

Considering the large number of old ladies playing 'out of age' and the number of performers playing homosexual men (who all needed serviced with hair and make-up), David Browne and Valerie Egan had a busy time, but - like everything about this production - all was achieved with more than an eye to comedy.

Some shows are dark and dramatic by nature, while others, less serious, rely on being just good fun for all involved and Paul Francis Webster and Sammy Fain's Calamity Jane certainly fits into this latter category. With an energetic cast of mostly young players, this was a good show choice for the Sligo Musical Society's annual production.

Directed by Aine Gilmore, this take on the old 'evergreen' western musical comedy rattled along at a pace that would have put the Deadwood stage itself to shame. Right from the suitably bright and breezy Overture, played with gusto by, Musical Director, David McEvoy's eight-piece orchestra of professional players, the mood was set for a fun family show.

This atmosphere continued with the lively, well sung opening, The Deadwood Stage, which - despite the busy stage activity - produced some early and impressive choral work, with good tempo and pace from the musicians.

Although there was no programme credit for set design, the 'room- style' set was well made by local company, WD Construction, and consisted of a typical saloon bar- room with a brightly lit back cyc, moveable flats and two staircases at either side of the cabaret stage within a stage, which - with attention to detail - was well decorated with flowers and drapes.

Although not generally inspiring, visually, the set was functional with openings on either side and on both levels for entrances and exits plus another through the saloon's cabaret stage.

However, the actual bar, stage right and at right angles to the audience caused obvious sight-line problems when performers masked one another as they crowded around it. Later scenes such as the Chicago dressing room, using simple props like changing screen etc, and Calamity's cabin, using a painted log cabin wall with white cloths, greatly quickened scene changes.

Gilmore's direction produced some nice touches, including the way Calamity was joined during Men by the other girls as the song progressed, audibly increasing the ladies' frustrations of the gender and the stage activity, at times, of the saloon cleaners dusting on the staircase was good.

Their high standard chorus moments made Adelaide and The Black Hills Of Dakota musical highlights, while Men was, appropriately, sung with conviction and the gentle violin and piano accompaniment at the start of Secret Love worked well.

Full marks must go to Alan McEvoy on percussion for his quick thinking in making the gun noise when Calamity's gun jammed and also for his nice Native American style rhythms during Windy City.

Choreographer, Sarah Middleton's use of five main dancers as the attractive group of showgirls was good at focusing dance routines on those who could really dance and some of her other ideas also worked well, including: the send-up comedy with the male ensemble during Adelaide, with the men pretending to be her dancing girls; the great song-and-dance routine in Ev'ryone Complains About The Weather; the different level groupings during Men and the realistic conversational groupings of The Black Hills Of Dakota.

Karen Gordon was good in the title role, with confident vocal support from Paul Maitland's Wild Bill Hickock and Olivia O'Hanlon's Katie Brown, while George Hynes proved to be a real song-and-dance performer as Francis Fryer.

However, it was Jennifer Healy's gentle performance as Susan Miller with great vocals, nice stage presence and good footwork that impressed here to show that she is a lot more talented than this role allows for.

All other departments of this production (Sarah Burns' stage management, Vinney Osborne and Eoin O'Grady's sound and Karen Fox and Pam Lindey's props) were, generally, good with no major problems arising.

Although mostly rented or brought in, the wardrobe team ensured that costumes and accessories looked well (only perhaps too clean at times for rough cowboys) and it was a nice touch for Props Manager, Anne McElhone, to provide gingham seat covers and tablecloth for Calamity's cabin transformation along with her other authentic props.

My main problem with this production was in Nick McCall's lighting design, which - although suitably bright for this fun show - lacked atmosphere.

This was particularly noticeable during The Black Hills Of Dakota, when an atmospheric lighting opportunity was missed and the bright lighting on the back cyc was neither off nor dimmed sufficiently to suggest it was night time.

While I love the use of footlights, it is important to watch their overuse (sadly, not the case here) as this dilutes both their effectiveness and impact.

Apart from that, this was a well- paced lively show for the whole family to enjoy.

The staging of such a complex and complicated show as Ragtime is a massive challenge for any company, for, with its depiction of three totally separate communities and cultures - the wealthy white Americans, the Eastern Europeans and the Afro- Americans - this show has few light moments to offer any respite from its strong and dramatic storyline, which reflects the harsh realities of the time as the birth of modern America gets underway.

Director and Set Designer, Eoin Cannon, certainly appeared to have a good understanding of all three communities and cultures within the piece and managed to reflect clear distinctions and frictions between them with good interpretation and pace here with Music, Lighting, Sound and Costumes all playing particularly key roles in its success. With a simple minimal approach, Cannon's open set had up-stage moveable steps to an upper level, which continued round onto two long balconies, and it really looked both functional and visually pleasing. The deep stage, or performing space as this was staged on flat ground level with no raised platform, allowed for lots of exits and entrances both up-stage and on either side on both levels, which greatly aided the pace of the production..

While the clear distinction between the three communities utilising clever costuming to identify each grouping was successful here, there were other nice touches, including great use of children in the production; the appropriate bunting on the stairs of the theatre and the Ragtime-style walk in music; the innovative use of the set's mobile steps to help create the lovely end picture with the symbolic birth of a new family; good romantic chemistry between Sarah and Coalhouse; and the realistic staging of The Trashing Of The Car. As Musical Director, Conductor and Chorus Master for such a long and almost sung-through piece, Dermot O'Callaghan really did have a lot on his plate. However, not nearly enough it would appear, for he also decided to play keyboards as part of his eleven-piece orchestra, which maintained good stage/pit balance and pace throughout.

In terms of ensemble movement, groupings, positioning and integration within the production, Orla Savage's choreographic concepts appeared to be extremely well realised and effective here. The strong opening, Prologue: Ragtime, with its gentle promenade style choreography and groupings combined with impressive lighting to create pictures that reflected the confrontation between, and the identity of, the three communities in the piece.

Choral work was always to the fore here, especially during Henry Ford, Atlantic City, The Night That Goldman Spoke At Union Square, New Music and in the Act 1 finale, Till We Reach That Day.

Shay Griffen offered a good portrayal of the Afro/American immigrant and ragtime musician, Coalhouse Walker, with a great romantic chemistry between Sarah and himself, while, as Harlem native, Sarah, Fiona McManus provided great diction and strong vocals. Marie Therese Purcell also displayed impressive vocals and diction in the role of Mother, while Jim Walsh, as the Eastern European immigrant and artist, Tateh, provided some lovely vocal moments, and Kris Kendellen, as head of the upper-class, rich white Protestant family, Father, was as pompous and upper class as one would expect with a brilliant voice. Special mention and credit must also go to young child performers, Luke Cummins and Ella Coughlan, who did such a good job playing the Little Boy and Little Girl, respectively. Also playing important roles in the success of this production were Stage Manager, Gerry McCann, and his team; Property Mistress, Maire Monaghan; Ali Murphy's Hair & Make-up design; and Costume Designer, Andrew Reddy, whose many outfits all looked beautiful, especially those for the American community, which also made good use of hats and bonnets.

Vinney Osbourne's sound mix was consistently good, while Denis Twomey's Lighting Design, was clever, attractive and atmospheric. Having offered such a positive production, I felt it was such a pity that this company did not take more drastic steps to remedy the major sight-line problem that is caused when a production, like this one, is not performed on a raised stage.

Tipperary Musical Society really 'pushed the boat out' (if you will pardon the pun) and went to a lot of trouble, especially in the Front of House area, to make sure that all was ship-shape for this production of H.M.S. Pinafore.

The foyer was decorated with maritime-style bunting, life belts were strategically placed in case the weather would get worse and costumed crew members were to be seen, while the intermittent sound of seagulls above my head was so realistic that I found myself looking up for reassurance from time to time (…just in case they might be getting a little nervous as show time approached!).

Indeed, Pat Marnane's sound effects also continued inside the auditorium as the audience was taking its seats, which really helped to set the mood. As the only Gilbert & Sullivan show that I have came across in this year's adjudication, it was nice to hear some truly traditional-style G&S choral work and singing, delivered by a company with such an obvious passion for the genre in this production, which was directed and choreographed by G&S buff, Leonard Anderson.

Anderson's set design (along with Derek and Kenny Ryan) was a functional single static set for the whole show; a ship deck with steps on either side to an upper deck and side flats with painted lifeboats plus nice red concealed lighting through portholes in the downstairs door. The upper deck boasted painted portholes, various lifebelts, rope rigging, bunting and a mast pole with the ship's wheel centrepiece. The 15-piece orchestra and performers on stage soon realised that even Captain Corcoran had strong competition here from the real musical boss on this ship as Musical Director, Danny Carroll, effortlessly steered his crew through the score.

As one of the old school musical directors, Carroll, who was well used to the musical nuances of G&S, chose to conduct only and maintained great balance and control at all times to offer an evenly paced and good interpretation here, while Chorus Mistress, Helen Colbert, ensured a high standard of choral singing from all.

It was nice to see the Conductor lit-up by a spotlight during the Overture, as this helps the audience to focus on the music (the MD and orchestra are, sadly, often forgotten about once most shows actually begin).

This was one of many nice touches in this production while other notable aspects included: the realistic stage activity; good use of space for groupings; costumed crew or performers being used to move props; good accents; and some performers remaining in character during the curtain call.

The comic moments included: Buttercup's unexpected arrival in a rowing a boat; Sir Joseph's female entourage arriving out of large sea packing case; and the blast of the Titanic film theme from the ensemble, complete with the iconic open arms visual.

As a company who appear to be stronger at singing than dancing, Anderson's choreography was, rightly, more about groupings and positioning with routines being kept simple and to a minimum.

There was some good casting with John Murphy's Ralph Rackstraw particularly suited to the more melodic songs, while Maria McGrath's Josephine offered the perfect voice for Gilbert & Sullivan and Aidan O'Connell's Sir Joseph Porter provided some nice comical touches.

Lena Hally gave a strong performance as Buttercup, but Derek Ryan was the star of this show as Captain Corcoran. Boasting a great stage presence, he proved to be a G&S natural with a very confident performance and great vocal control.

Although there were no major problems with the work of Stage Manager, Kieran Hickey and his team; Eileen O'Connor's props; Pat Marnane's sound mix; Leonard Anderson, Phyllis Hickey, Antoinette Kelly, Jane Green, Maureen Wade and Laura Hadnett's costumes; Evelyn O'Meara, Leah O'Neill and Aoife O'Meara's hair and make-up team or Orla Kavanagh's Lighting Design, I felt that the lighting could have been, perhaps, a little more adventurous.

One thing all companies need to watch is the staging of a curtain call with singing, as this can be a bit messy sometimes because the audience is never sure when to applaud.

After the long drive from Belfast to Tipperary for this show, it was nice to return to Belfast directly after the performance with the sound of Tipperary Musical Society ringing in my ears following an impromptu rendition of It's A Long Way To Tipperary by the members of the company as I was leaving - a delightful and nice touch. Thank you.

It is often said that one should never judge a book by its cover and this also holds true for musical theatre productions as I travel around the country to a wide variety of venues to see the many shows on offer within this year's Adjudication scheme. When I visit a professional theatre venue, it is, perhaps, only natural that I am expecting a higher standard of production than I would find in, say … a school hall … but, how wrong I would be if I believed this!

For, despite being staged in the local school hall, Trim Musical Society's impressive production of Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice's Evita proved that this is not always the case.

As I waited for the show to begin, I looked at the small 'hole in the wall' sized stage with house tabs and small extended aprons on either side of the stage and wondered how this massive story about the rise and fall of Eva Peron was going to be staged.

The answer was with some assured direction from Justin Parkes, who made two vital decisions to ensure the success of this production; he opted for a most minimal approach and, without exception, his Principal line-up was perfectly cast.

This minimal style may have been taken almost to extreme here with virtually no formal settings, but the design teams (lighting and sets) worked theatrical wonders with plain blue and white (Argentinian colours) flats plus clever projections and amazing lighting effects.

This show cracked on at a terrific pace, not only because of the lack of cumbersome set changes, but because the director produced plenty of downstage action as a distraction during scene changes to make the production flow seamlessly.

Dressed on either side by the Argentinian flag above the side aprons, the show began with an on- stage public announcement of Eva's death during the opening musical passage, which was played by a 12-piece orchestra of professional players.

The contemporary sounding score, which offered a high degree of musical input made life busy for the hard-working Musical Director, Chorus Mistress and Conductor, Olivia Toman, who, thankfully, chose only to conduct, and there were many exceptionally good highlights under her musical direction.

These included: the choral work in both Requiem For Evita and The Actress Hasn't Learned The Lines (You'd Like To Hear); the lovely slow piece in the arrangement with romantic strings during I'd Be Surprisingly Good For You; the nice work from string and wind sections of the orchestra in Don't Cry For Me Argentina; the most sympathetic playing during Eva's death scene and the amazing arrangement of Don't Cry For Me Argentina for the finale.

Officially, there may only be a few production numbers in this show to highlight the dancers, but choreographer, Aisling Toher, had other ideas … lots of them … and never missed a trick when it came to developing a routine.

While the two big production numbers, And The Money Kept Rolling In (And Out) and Buenos Aires, provided lots of brilliantly staged movement and lively choreography, there was also confident footwork in A Waltz For Eva And Che and in the black/white themed, Rainbow High.

There was a nice little bit of humour between the dancers and the singer (On This Night Of A Thousand Stars), and some impressive tango moves with chairs (I'd Be Surprisingly Good For You) while the top of the show had a gentle ballet from four female singer/dancers, as Eva's coffin was respectfully carried off stage.

However, the military precision marching movement (Peron's Latest Flame) summed up the high standard of choreography here with all groupings, ensemble movements and integration being visually pleasing and carried out with almost military precision, while good use was made of the well-lit aprons on either side of stage for the larger ensemble moments.

Indeed, not only was the ensemble and chorus a great strength of this production, but the Principals all had that winning combination; great stage presence and diction with good individual voices.

All impressed and it is unfair to single some out for special praise, but Helen McHugh and Kevin Fagin really stood out as Eva Peron and the ever-present narrator, Che, respectively, with each making their role totally believable, while young Grace Collender provided the purest of vocals as the Santa Evita soloist. All other departments, including Stage Management (Frank Connolly), Props (Marty Flaherty and Susan Gantley Murphy), Sound (Alan White), Wardrobe (Debby Walsh) and Hair & Make-up (Gail Clarke, Graham Dunne and Susan Gantley Murphy) pulled their weight here in a great team effort with Darren Kelleher's attractive Lighting Design making everything look so good. Kept simple but extremely effective at all times, his plot provided atmospheric blue hue with smoke (Requiem For Evita), flashing overhead spots (The Art Of Possible), great off-stage lighting for the show within a show (Charity Concert) and great backlighting (Another Suitcase In Another Hall).

A nice quick curtain call brought an end to this slick show in which Che has the line: "One has to admire the stage management" … It appears to me that there was a lot more than Stage Management to be admired in this production.

There's a posse of directors around at the moment who, while not exactly ripping up the rule book on productions, are re-writing or bending the rules. This re-shaping of shows is evidence of a thought process that is re-defining amateur musical theatre here.

As a result on a Saturday night in Ballinasloe, Cedric Parchester, family solicitor to the haughty Harefords and a man normally played with a cut glass English accent and dressed in an upper middle class morning suit, becomes a kilted canny Scotsman.

And Cockney landlady Mrs Brown, known best for her jellied eel's vowels and her nosey attitude, becomes Corkonian Bridie Brennan. However, the man at the helm in this case, Paul Norton, had to alter his own plans just before going into rehearsals when he had to introduce two new cast members. His changes saw him bringing in actors at differing ends of the experience scale.

Bernie Dudgeon, who filled in as Lady Clara has been there and got the Tee shirt. By contrast, teenager Eoin Costello, who stepped in as Bill Snibson, is only starting out on what could be a promising stage career. He's not the finished article by any means but there's a lot going for him, not least the guts he showed in agreeing to take on the role in the first place.

It says a lot for Mr Costello that he was able to play up to Sarah Corcoran, who as Sally Smith was not just terrific looking but displayed great control of her singing voice and acted and danced well.

He was not overawed either in the presence of another feisty female, the Lady Jacqueline of Joanne Kelly, who was not just bubbly on and off stage but got physical with the new Lord Hareford.

Seamus Feerick's excellent Parchester - he even sung in a Scots accent - and Catherine Madden's neatly judged Cork fishwife were not the only quirks in this Midlands line-up.

Patrick Byrne catapulted the Hon. Gerald Bolingbroke, so often a peripheral figure of fun into a real character. Here was an actor who had studied the role to see what he could bring to it and invested the upper class toff with a terrific foppish look and great mannerisms. Majella Flanagan was a full-voiced Duchess of Dene who gave "Men of Hareford" the kind of poke it needs while Mike O'Reilly as Sir John Treymayne neatly graduated from a terrible snob to a likeable guy with a big heart.

Brian Derrane, fetching in a flash blazer, was a typical put-upon Lord Battersby; Dave Hardiman gave us a staid butler while Micheal Breathnach's Sir Jasper Tring had the longest hair seen on stage since Dave Crosbie retired from rock in a fog of alcohol and drugs. Think early Billy Connollly.

This well-paced production was handsomely dressed by Eithne Blackwell and played on Dave Hardiman's colourful settings which gave a big-sounding chorus plenty of room to execute Sarah Griffin's routines.

The ensemble however, could have done with throwing off the shackles a bit more and could have taken after Pearly King Aidan Flanagan who made a big impression as East End nobility and in another small role, the educated French speaking London Bobbie.

If ever a show was a metaphor for a Society's current standing, then this was it.

Back in the last Millennium when I reviewed the group's productions regularly, Fortwilliam were a bunch who would tackle operetta with elan. The voice was the thing you see, the formation of the company was presaged by a love of singing and a show featuring hoofers wouldn't have been high on the list of choices. These days while the north Belfast company haven't exactly banished light opera from the repertoire, well, they're modern just like Millie, and moving with the times.

The company now stage its shows outside of Belfast's centre where they had been resident for quite a while after moving from their home turf in the north of the city and play at Newtownabbey's shiny new Mill Theatre, not far from where the group was formed. It's a move that is as far-sighted as their establishment of a youth wing two decades ago. Graduates from that junior section now guide the main group and a healthy percentage of those on stage in Simon Pyper's energetic and colourful production have travelled the same road.

Mr Pyper and choreographer Angela Harding cleverly disguised the split in the company's talents in the show's set-piece numbers with the dancers working up a sweat and taking the eye in prime spots on the Mill's big stage while the singers, given less onerous moves to concentrate on, added vocal weight from behind. Some performers, of course, can do it all, like Dawn Patton as Millie Dillmount and Brian Trainor as Trevor Graydon the Third.

Ms Patton is a good actress and dancer with a big voice and she imposed herself on the title role in this show, as the small town girl up in the big city to earn her fortune and bag a husband in the process. She also looked for all the world like Aussie television detective Frynnie Fisher in her short black bob hairstyle.

Mr Trainor, a man with theatrical X factor who can turn his hand to a thousand different stage tasks, is an actor and singer with fine comedic timing and an excellent mover, and brought all of that significant ammunition to his portrayal of insurance boss Graydon.

To dismiss this as a two-man show however, would be far from the truth. Tony Young, another guy with a good voice gave a lovely, gentle performance as Jimmy Smith, the man who ultimately woos Millie, Sara Donnelly's Dorothy Brown was all wide eyes, tumbling tresses and trembling legs while Maria Sweeney as failed actress and white slaver, Mrs Meers, was impressive.

The aforementioned Miss Harding doubled up on stage as Graydon's gatekeeper, Peg Flannery, in this case a mad-haired, tap dancing loon with a huge bum, Siobhan Farrell's Muzzie had a good voice and stage presence while Vijay Sharma and Charles O'Kelly, the put-upon Chinese laundry workers Ching Ho and Bun Foo respectively, turned in their own solid shifts.Miss Harding's lively routines, in keeping with the era and with a huge nod to the Flapper times, added much to the show while not getting in the way of the narrative and her dance ensemble was thoroughly drilled. Highly experienced musical director Billy Cairns' excellent band, featuring some top class individual players, drove the action on relentlessly. Fabulous authentic and highly colourful costumes, a beautiful set, all angled geometric flats and Art Deco drops and some terrific atmospheric lighting from Alastair Kerr added to the spectacle.

However, a couple of uncharacteristic glitches at Geoff Clarke's sound desk marred the technical side of the evening.

Mad March brought that rarest of opportunities - a chance to see Show Boat, one of the seminal staging posts along the musical theatre road.

A young Oscar Hammerstein the second broke the mould in his book for the show by tackling the subject of racism and specifically miscegenation.

These days, however, licence requirements stipulate what you can and can't do if you don't have a mixed race cast. It means that in a digital age, leaving aside arguments on race and political correctness, Show Boat is stuck in the analogue era.

It forces the hand of directors like Arthur McGauran who opted to denote his cast through clothing. In this case coloured females wore headscarves, their men folk tattered boaters and overalls.

Mr McGauran sported one of those boaters as a rich bass-voiced Joe and delivered a finely gauged version of Hammerstein and Kern's classic "Ol' Man River". Wearing his other hat as director he guided his charges around Dundrum's Mill theatre's small stage.

Another man who did justice to the terrific score was Niall MacCarthy with a high baritone voice that's perfect for operetta and the looks and physique to carry off the role of Gaylord Ravenal, gentleman killer and king of the riverboat gamblers. He wins and breaks the heart of Noirin Sheridan's high soprano Magnolia - particularly powerful in "After the ball" - before re-uniting with her and their daughter in middle aged.

The experienced Eamonn Murphy held the ring brilliantly as the central character of Captain Andy Hawks, show boat hustler, producer and director and bon viveur while battling with and against his stage wife, Marion Holohan's strong willed Parthy.

Amy Byrne as Julie La Verne, the riverboat entertainer on whose background this tale turns, showed a decent soprano voice, particularly in "Bill" while stage husband Chris O'Connor as Steve Baker has a big voice with good tone that would be suited to bigger roles than this.

Song and dance couple Frank and Ellie May Schultz - Carl Mageean and Jennifer Fahy - did exactly what it says on the tin and showed neat comic timing with some great facial reactions.

It was a brave move to mount such a rarely tackled show on such a small playing area.

The physical structure for the production was an adaptable set by SceneMaker with a central truck with the exterior of boat on one side and the boats interior and the Trocadero theatre on the other with wing flats on castors and portable pieces and props. Much of the scene changing was carried by the male cast, helping the action to flow along like the Mississippi itself.

Much of Louise Dodrill's choreography rested with a small troupe of younger girls who covered a range of styles as big as the show's time span, a sensible move here as big production numbers on a playing area this size are not really possible.

It also meant that while most of the interplay between principals and smaller groups was good, some of the bigger chorus scenes were a little static.

Dave O'Connor's eight piece band made a big sound with some fine individual players showing what they could do from time to time and I have to admire their discipline, perched as they were up against the theatre wall and encroaching into the auditorium surrounded by paying customers members on two other sides and the performers on a forth.

Barry Donaldson, a man who knows this theatre well, delivered a simple but effective lighting plot while the sound from SoundLease Ltd warmed up after a slow start.

Two thirds of the way into the first act at Limerick's plush University Concert Hall, newly established radio actress Eva Duarte cosies up to Army colonel Juan Peron in a red evening dress that's split to the thigh.

An alliance is constructed, an affair is in the air and a white suspender button is on show. It's just part of the detail the Limerick costume team went to make this Evita as authentic as possible.

Gemma Galvin as Eva Duarte had been persuaded by wardrobe mistress Jacinta Florish to don a corselet and stockings all in the name of her art, of course but no doubt appreciated by the men in the audience during the scene when her maids strip her off before dressing her again and packing her off on the Rainbow tour.

It was evidence of the concerted planning and thought that went into making Des Henn's fast paced production a fitting pillar of the city's year of culture celebrations.

The set, in which Mr Henn had a hand, was practical, sturdy and handsome and boasted not just one but two screens to show imagery of Argentine's most famous couple of the 20th Century, the sound from Star Systems was well balanced and Marie Keary-Scanlon's 12-piece band, featuring an excellent guitarist and drummer, drove the action on relentlessly.

In similar fashion Niamh Twomey's cleverly conceived and fluent choreography added enormously to the overall flow of the piece.

And then, of course, was the human face of the show. Ms Galvin was a lot more than a simple leg-flasher giving a high-energy performance in one of modern musical theatre's most demanding female roles. She firmly put her stamp on a part that travels 20 years in under two hours and gave us a portrayal of a hard- nosed poor girl who elbowed her way to the top casting aside the sneers and stuffing derision down the throats of her detractors before realising how fragile and short life can be.

Martin McNeilis, as the man who gave Eva her passport to riches and fame, was an excellent Peron. Not alone does he have a baritone voice with a beautiful tone but he is an actor who uses his body as well as his voice to convey emotions. The University Concert Hall is a big stage to fill and he commanded it. Michael O'Gorman as Che was also blessed with a good voice and had that ability needed to act as the narrator of the piece one minute, its conscience the next and then in another bound to immerse himself in the action.

Amy McKenna was a sweet-voiced Mistress while Ciaran Collins has the voice that can bring the necessary vocal pyrotechnics to the role of Magaldi.

Mr Henn brought a lovely touch to Ms McKenna's role, re-introducing her as Peron's mistress on a couple of occasions, firstly when Eva is on her European tour and later when Evita is on her death bed and extending the character a little while implying unfaithfulness on the part of the Argentinean president.

However, Mr Henn got it wrong when on that Rainbow tour Evita runs her hand up those nyloned legs to get a reaction from the Pope and his entourage. Even if she had behaved that way, I can't imagine the Papal party would have reacted in the manner they did.

Paul Kelly's lighting was also problematic.

The design incorporated some good ideas but too often cues were late with characters left in darkness.

Director Wilfie Pyper years of experience led him to make two small but highly significant decisions in this warm hearted show.

Firstly he allowed Colin Boyd as Sir John Treymayne to linger in the Hareford Arms while Sally Smith pours out her heart. Often in productions of the show Sir John does a bunk almost as soon as the poor girl starts singing which never made sense to me.

In this case the talented Mr Boyd as a suitably posh upper crust gent - he pronounced house as "hice" - stayed for almost her entire song before slipping out to get ready for the ensuing ball scene.

And he had a more complicated costume change to attend to than is often the case for his character so it can be done.

Later Mr Pyper kept the show's educated policeman, in this case Andy McKnight, another seasoned performer, on the stage while Andy Scott as Bill Snibson sings "Leaning on a lamp".

I've always believed that moment should be something of a conversation between Snibson and the law and clearly Mr Pyper does too.

Here I have to put on record that Mr Pyper is a director I have worked with closely on projects down the years and we come from the same school in musical theatre terms as well as in an educational sense. His production at Lisburn's Island Hall was aided by Angela Harding's choreography which maintained the flow of the show while musical director Ian Milford's eleven-piece band pushed the pace along.

The aforementioned Mr Scott was a rangy Snibson with a big voice not frightened of taking on his newly discovered relatives or the width that the Island Hall's stage provides. His Sally was Gillian McQuade, a fine actress who conveyed the sweeping emotions the East End fishmonger goes through fearing for her relationship with her newly ennobled boyfriend.

Vivian Shepherd was a confident Maria Duchess of Dene with a posh accent and precise diction who finally gave in to Mr Boyd's transformed Sir John.

Mark Maguire with his ringing tenor voice as Gerald was one half of the third couple that dominates this show opposite Claire Cranston's Lady Jacqueline, a woman not frightened of putting herself about as evidenced by a seduction scene which was more of an attack on Bill. Mr Pyper's thought process also extended to a quirky take on Parchester, the Hareford's family solicitor. Actor Tim Pentland, a tall man who is very light on his feet, played him as a goofy creation, almost detached from this world and complete with an excellent awful comb over hairstyle.

The highly experienced Liz Pentland made light work of East End landlady Mrs Brown but I felt that Desi Martin's Charles did not impose himself enough as the butler despite an officious start to his evening.

If anything the Island Hall is too wide and not deep enough, a problem set designer Alan Marshall overcame with a mixture of set pieces, flats and trucks.

His creation was well lit by Alastair Kerr while Damian Hughes' sound plot was first class.

We are coming to the conclusion of South Pacific and the nurses, marines and See Bees are gearing up to leave their island base to advance against the Japanese. It's a scene that calls for a huge cast to support the action of a mass decampment of American forces. So what does director Damien Douglas do on the Solstice Arts Centre's big stage in Navan with a company that numbers no more than 40?

He gets his ensemble to filter across the stage from the wings stage right, march up the rostra at the back of the set which is serving as a landing jetty at this time and gets them to walk around the back of the set out of sight of the audience and then repeat the exercise.

I don't know how many passes they made during the scene but it made it look as if the show had a cast of thousands. It was a simple but highly effective trick which kept up the pace of a show that can be often flag in the second half.

It was just one of several clever and often subtle ideas he employed that added to the look and the atmosphere of this show and which kept the action flowing.

Mr Douglas was also clearly as keen as possible to cast this show as close to the character's age on the page.

That brought a youthful Danielle Williamson to the part of Nellie Forbush, the girl a long way from her Little Rock home but who had brought her partially closed mind thousands of miles across the ocean with her. It's a big role but the beautiful Ms Williamson, a good actress with a good voice was impressive all evening in a very confident performance.

Similarly, Ronan Walsh, big of stature, a decent actor and with a big baritone voice was also a younger Emile de Becque than we often see while 22-year-old Kevin Fagan, a young man with a fabulous tenor voice, was an engaging Joe Cable, the epitome of impatient young men who lived life in a hurry in the middle of conflict, determined to make as much of every moment they had.

Craig Regan's slightly undercooked Luther Billis and Megan Monerawela's lithe Liat continued the youthful theme while Mairead Murray as a typically abrasive Bloody Mary and the excellent Des Lynch as a Captain Brackett with plenty of fire in his belly flew the flag for the more mature element of the cast. Only Enda Gill's blustering Harbison bucked the age trend in the show's front line.

The players were given good support all evening from Jacqui McGowan's rich sounding and sharply dressed nine-piece band.

And the actors had plenty of room to roam around the Solstice's wide open spaces thanks to a minimalist, multi-purpose but highly functional set from Mr Douglas and Enda Nugent.

It allowed choreographer Jane Wardick to give a little air to her routines, best in "There is nothing like a dame" and a towel themed dance in "I'm gonna wash that man right outta my hair".

The technical teams were also on the ball with those settings beautifully lit throughout the evening by Johnny McDonagh while Noel Ryan's sound desk ensured correct levels and produced some terrific effects during the show.

I have to admit I broke into a fit of laughter as I rolled up to Longford's Backstage Theatre, a little gem on the outskirts of the small Midlands town.

Even before I'd made it to nearby Edgeworthstown on my way there I knew I would probably tell the kids in the show about my views on a stage show being like a team sport with everyone playing their part. Little did I know that the Backstage was effectively part of the local GAA set-up, operating on the same site as the brilliantly named Longford Slashers. Somehow, it couldn't be more appropriate.

And those Longford youngsters have taken to our particular team sport like ducks to water. St Mel's chairwoman, June Belton, had been hoping to put 12 children on stage for the show. The response the group received was so great they fielded 24 kids including Oliver and the Dodger - 18 of them boys.

The end result was as impressive as the figures, with the kids musically, dramatically and choreographically secure throughout Paul Norton's slick production which was in the middle of a sell out run.

This was a typically tidy show from Mr Norton with attention paid to detail and a few scenes played in a way audiences are not always accustomed to.

For instance Dermot Deely's rotund, rich-voiced Bumble and Christine O'Brien's Widow Corney, who had a scream like a siren, took their courtship and later their marriage to places not often seen in what is a kids' favourite.

Benny O'Brien was a more conventional Fagin.

This experienced actor was a scheming, streetwise but kindly gang master, fleet of foot but stooped in stature. By contrast Tony Wadd's Bill Sykes was an upright, aggressive and very threatening man mountain stomping around on Eddie Kiernan and Robert Belton's clever set with sets of steps leading to a fixed gangway that doubled as London bridge and the Brownlow residence on high and Fagin's lair and the Three Cripples pub at stage level with other locations in the storyline trucked in.

Mr Wadd may have dwarfed Lyndsay Clyne's Nancy physically but not vocally. Ms Clyne brought some anguished raw emotion to the role through her Broadway belt voice.

A pair of good actors, Kevin Leavy and Liz Leavy made a ghostly couple of the Sowerberrys while another experienced hand, John Kelly, played a Patrician Mr Brownlow. Oliver was a confident Jack Oates while another gifted little actor, Dylan Murray as the Dodger is clearly going through that awkward time for boys as their adult voice starts to settle. The big cast was completed with Grainne Fox, Anthony Heavey, Michelle Kelly Conlon, Damien Bennett and Lorraine Faye touching in the roles of Bet, Claypole, Charlotte, Dr Grimwig and Mrs Bedwin respectively.

Emer O'Brien's choreography - executed well by both the children and adult ensembles - showed what is possible in a confined space with military precision moves mixed with milling crowd scenes. Incidentally, some of the individual voices within that adult chorus are very good. The players were well supported by musical director Fintan Farrelly and a group of musicians who revel in the title the Urban Day Spa orchestra while Rodney Ellis' first class lighting plot captured the gloom of London at the time, creating atmosphere and throwing up a few surprises along the way.

Amid all of the darker and newer shows on the amateur circuit this year, it was refreshing to see a staging of one of Rodgers & Hammerstein's 'big five' shows.

Although as controversial and ground-breaking in the world of musical theatre in its day as, say, the work of Andrew Lloyd Webber has been in more recent decades, this classic can still hold its own as it is hard to beat Rodgers & Hammerstein for pure melody.

Directed by Colin Hughes, this was a bright, safe and fairly traditional staging of the popular western musical comedy, with a few nice touches.

There was a lot of extra effort put in place here with the company's front of house team all dressed as cowboys and cowgirls to greet the audience in the foyer.

The set design by All Set Scenery was mainly based around Aunt Eller's house (stage left) complete with its porch, door and windows, with a wooden fence, arched gateway and bench (stage right).

Eller's house (moved to stage right) also doubled as Jud's smoke-house, while an open stage was used for the more crowded scene (The Farmer And The Cowboy) with four symbolic house-frame pillars, which also joined together to form an arch (All Or Nothing).

Sadly, the restricted entrance to, and exit from, Aunt Eller's house on stage-right through the narrow arched gateway caused a bottle- neck effect at times.

However, this production had much to enjoy and I thought Colin Hughes and the production team did well. It was good, for a change, to see that Ali Hakim was not directed as a total clown.

The beautiful love duet, People Will Say We're In Love, worked really well here because it was truly believable with the great romantic chemistry that existed between Curley and Laurey and the appropriately sympathetic playing from the orchestra also ensured the right mood for the success of this number.

The reprise of the song was even more in context following the on- stage proposal scene.

The cat-fight between Ado and Gertie was particularly realistic, while the fight between Jud and Curley - although well-choreographed - was, perhaps, too short.

The use of a real surrey with a fringe on the top was a nice touch, while the quick, clean curtain call and finale chorus were both impressive. It was so nice to hear Musical Director, Conductor and Chorus Master, Aidan Faughey, and his 8-piece orchestra playing the Overture in its entirety to get us in the mood for this melodic classic. With a traditional musical interpretation of the score, Oh What A Beautiful Mornin' proved to be a nice bright and optimistic opening with Curley beginning to sing after coming on stage and not having to go through the more difficult task of having to sing off-stage before appearing, which has long been the norm with this show.

The Surrey With The Fringe On Top coaxed a great vocal performance from Curley and good musical variation in both pace and softness from the musicians, with some great underscoring under the dialogue, while a good male chorus with a well executed musical build up was achieved during It's A Scandal! It's An Outrage!

Choreographer, Sonya Dunne, had some nice ideas for routines here and her concepts were always appropriate and, generally, well- executed.

There was good grouping, movement and positioning of the ensemble and the main dance routine in Kansas City was well delivered with some 'line dancing' moves helping to produce a nice innocent country feel to the evening.

As the set did not offer any real height variations, it was important and apt that Dunne created different level positioning at times e.g. during Many A New Day, the girls were standing, sitting or kneeling.

The female chorus was nicely positioned stage left for the gentle ballet sequence in Out Of My Dreams/ Dream Ballet, with movement in the routine ranging from graceful and romantic to saucy, with four Can-Can dancers and chairs, and threatening with Jud's appearance.

Ensemble movement, groupings and integration with one another and with the Principals was, generally, good. Alec Ward turned in a good performance as Curley with particularly expressive vocals during The Surrey With The Fringe On Top, while his believable romantic chemistry with Laurey - especially with that kiss in the second half before the proposal - made the beautiful love duet, People Will Say We're In Love, most enjoyable and realistic.

Shona Henneberry displayed a beautiful vocal as Laurey, particularly in Many A New Day, and some good acting skills, especially with her early reluctance to get involved with Curley.

Brian Phillips had a very pleasant singing voice as Will; a kind of male equivalent of Kate McKeown's innocent bimbo, Ado Annie, and McKeown certainly delivered comedy in this role, while Eoin Salley's Jud had a good singing voice and he gave a powerful vocal performance of a difficult song in Lonely Room. Michael Keegan's mature peddler, Ali Hakim, really was a man of the world and, with his great comic timing, this experienced performer was totally suited to this role.

As Aunt Eller, Nicola Graham was another performer with great comic timing and she also had the rare ability to capture the impish humour of her character with some great facial expressions.

Thanks to all other departments - Stage Manager, Ger Keeling; Props Co-ordinator, Sally Crawford; Vinny Osborne's sound mix; Lighting Director, Gary O'Daly; and Ann Hennigan's costume team - we enjoyed this evergreen classic … Oh, What A Beautiful Evenin' indeed.

The staging of Galway Musical Society's production of Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice's Evita was both a happy and sad occasion for the company.

As the company's 30th production, it was dedicated to the memory of the late Len Wright, who died last October, and, so, was as much a celebration of Len's many years with the company as it was a celebration of 30 years of GMS.

A much respected member of the society since its inception, Len would have been proud of this production and, coming from the sets and props department, would have been particularly proud of its show- stealing set … a symbolic mansion in the spirit of  La Casa Rosada.

Directed by Brian Power and Assistant Director, Sean Power, this visually-pleasing production boasted a strong cast; all with very good diction and good voices.

Apart from solid performances from a good line-up of Principals and supporting cast, the technical side of things was impressive too in this well-paced and traditional staging of this show.
