Con O Ceallaigh's majestic set was impressive in visual appearance, detail and functionality and it dominated the stage throughout, with the action all played out on an open stage in front of the palace. It was a very stately looking palace with a stage-wide balcony and smaller ones running on either side with some open panels and backlighting through the windows and lanterns on the walls.

I especially liked the balcony revolve that allowed us to briefly contrast the public and private side of the President and First Lady.

As director and assistant director, Brian and Sean Power, respectively, brought some nice moments and touches to this production, including: the opening Requiem For Evita, which provided impact due to atmospheric lighting and lovely groupings; the clear diction in Good Night And Thank You captured the humour of the piece and the fact that Eva was on a higher level than all of the men, symbolically highlighting who was in control; the great stage discipline during Don't Cry For Me Argentina when the ensemble was frozen for such a long time; the beautiful children's choir in Santa Evita; the good transition to the next song with Eva collapsing at end of A Waltz For Eva And Che; the retrospective Montage segment with its well- drilled and building chorus; and the most beautiful ending with the bell tolling as Eva's ghost watches over her funeral from the balcony with an effectively slow curtain.

The contemporary sounding score offered a high degree of musical input and made life busy for the hard-working Musical Director and Conductor, Shane Farrell, and Chorus Master, Paddy Daly.

Together with his relatively modest 13-piece orchestra of professional players and Daly's well-drilled chorus, there was a lovely pit/ stage balance and there were many highlights under Farrell's musical direction.

These included: the good tight rock-style moments during Oh What A Circus with the eerie and atmospheric pounding of the drum as the mourners left the stage; the music was played with great gusto during a lively Buenos Aires and with a suitably moderate pace in both Good Night And Thank You and the waltz-time duel, A Waltz For Eva And Che; while the effective crashing percussion as Eva's fate looked certain really integrated well in a very emotional performance of Dice Are Rolling In/Eva's Sonnet.

Daly's chorus was strong throughout this performance, ranging from being suitably rousing in A New Argentina (to emphasis the rise of Eva) to being both delicate and beautiful when the children's choir provided a major highlight with Santa Evita.

While choreographer, Declan J Gardiner, was in charge of routines, groupings and movement, one of the best moves he made was to go for the option of fielding a group of core dancers for some of the routines as - all too often in shows - many companies are prepared to let the entire ensemble believe that they can dance.

This move ensured that his good concepts were well-executed and realised and, generally, his groupings, positioning, movement and integration were all good.

Ailbhe Hession, generally, made the role of Eva Peron believable and I really warmed to her changing characterisation as the show progressed.

Her show-stopping, You Must Love Me, with a most moving performance in which she lived the lyrics as the sick Eva highlighted her good acting skills, which were matched by her beautiful vocals and, in Don't Cry For Me Argentina, she did her big song justice.

Shane Kelly succeeded in making his role as the ever-present narrator and radical, Che, totally believable in terms of acting, while, musically, he displayed a wide vocal range and Padraic McDonagh was good as Eva's fat-cat and opportunistic husband, Juan Peron.

Nicky Lawless certainly captured the smarmy characterisation of the nightclub singer, Augustin Magaldi, and was good acting someone who had been used by Eva, while Heather Doyle, as Peron's Mistress, was a beautiful young performer with a gentle and innocent voice and very clear vocals, which she used to maximise her impact during her short moment on stage during Another Suitcase In Another Hall.

There was also strong support off- stage from Leonard Power (Stage Manager), Chontelle Kenny (Property Mistress), Mike and Sally Dervan (Sound), Paul Kelly (Lighting), Terri Dooley, Karen Soffe and Clodagh Farrell (Costumes) and Fiona Lawless, Ali Murphy and Deirdre McDermott (Hair & Make-up).

Congratulations on such a good show for your 30th production!

With so many shows to see in such quick succession on the adjudication circuit, it is perhaps surprising that I would have been remotely interested in seeing any particular production(s) again for my own enjoyment.

However, the standards were so high in this year's scheme that there were a few … and this was one of them. What makes it even more surprising is that there were so many other productions of Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice's rock musical, Jesus Christ Superstar, on the circuit that I really should have wanted to avoid this show for a while.

However, under Oliver Hurley's impressive direction (and choreographic control), this production was so stunning, particularly in direction, music, choreography, stage management, sets, sound and lighting, that - like every other show - I missed things due to my all-important note-taking. What made this production so attractive was the combination of its traditional interpretation, its modern hi-tech and multi-level staging and its high production values.

With a minimal approach to sets, this slick and seamless show was directed with purpose and pace, and boasted brilliant lighting, great sound balance and totally relentless movement throughout plus the fact that the music, choral work and performances were also top-notch. Sadly, and surprisingly, no individual or group was credited in the programme for the Set Design of this production, which is such a pity as it played such a basic, yet vital, role in the show's overall success.

So, I can only assume that it was a team effort and decision to adopt a minimal approach with a wide open staging, consisting of long ramps from either side onto the stage and also on stage, central white steps and white platform on wheels all towered over by a suspended bridge. Fully functional in every way and to facilitate the amazingly atmospheric lighting and many clever projections, the entire set and drapes were all white; providing a clean, clear and uncomplicated setting for the story with lots of performance levels for good groupings, movement and integration.

Director, Oliver Hurley, brought some clever touches to this fast-paced production and there was little not to like.

A strong impact was made from the first note of the Overture and the amazing lighting which highlighted the individual characters made it a most atmospheric and exciting opening sequence.

Everything's Alright highlighted good interaction between all three leads, with a nice fade away vocal as the ensemble slowly moved off into the auditorium, while the four white drapes dropped centre stage for Pilate's Dream provided a visually calming atmosphere for his clear and concise vocals with acoustic guitars accompaniment.

I loved the refrain of 'Poor Poor Judas' at the start of Act 2 with Judas and Jesus facing one another before the start of The Last Supper and the great gritty friction between the two during this piece, while Gethsemane was a highlight with its central white down-light perfectly focusing this important song and the amazingly good vocal performance from Jesus reaching its most climatic moment after the falsetto when Jesus fell and the music sounded cleverly and appropriately out of control.

The four solo women singing at Jesus as he was led away in The Arrest was most effective as was the suitably loud lashes with blood splats projected across the stage and cast in Trial Before Pilate.

Superstar was very tastefully staged, with soldiers leading Jesus and his cross off-stage at the start and this up-tempo send-up juxtaposed with the sad and pathetic return of Jesus and his cross.

Right from the opening electric guitar solo of the Overture, Conductor and Musical Director, Noel Lennon, and his orchestra left us in no doubt that this was a rock opera with a strong interpretation of the 11-piece orchestration as directed by the Really Useful Company.

Considering the rock-feel of this sung-through piece, there was a lovely pit/stage balance throughout and there were many highlights under Lennon's musical direction, including: the really solid rhythm section (Heaven On Their Minds); the acoustic guitar accompaniment (Pilate's Dream); the sympathetic flute playing at end of I Don't Know How To Love Him, which ran seamlessly into the next song; the great horn solos (Damned For All Time / Blood Money and The Last Supper); the piano/flute accompaniment and gentle vocals (Could We Start Again Please) and the important and poignant pause after the Crucifixion before playing John Nineteen; Forty-One.

Chorus Mistress, Anita Lakner, is also to be commended for the strong choral work both on-stage (What's The Buzz / Strange Thing Mystifying) and off-stage (This Jesus Must Die). All voices in the latter managed to be very threatening and, in total contrast there was the most joyous choral singing in Hosanna, while Everything's Alright provided nice fade-away vocals as the ensemble slowly walked off through the auditorium.

Boasting totally relentless movement throughout, there was no let up in movement and groupings and, choreographer, Oliver Hurley, ensured - or demanded - that his great concepts were well-executed and that all groupings, positioning, movement and integration was excellent at all times.

Although the Principal line-up was well-cast here, the keyword in the success of this production was the teamwork of all departments and, so, the ensemble played a major role in this show.

Gary Murphy turned in a good Jesus characterisation right from the start, which is unusual as most people in this role don't really connect with the audience until the song, Gethsemane.

Perfectly capturing Judas' frustration from the opening, Rory Ward was impressive in the role of the man who betrayed Jesus. This performer was always observing and had great vocals and stage presence.

Always reassuring, Michelle O'Callaghan, was a gentle yet strong Mary Magdalene with a beautifully clear vocals and good acting abilities, while Tim Landers also proved to be a strong actor with a good singing voice in the role of Pontius Pilate and Fergal Cleary's confident vocals and good comic timing as King Herod ensured that his mocking fun number was well executed.

John Hurley's Lighting & Projection Design was almost concert-like with its gig rig ensuring that the atmospheric lighting was never less than brilliant.There was perfect plotting and all performers were always in their correct position for specific lighting moments.

Costume Mistresses, Ann O'Shea and Sandra Waller, made sure that the costumes in this production all looked well and their attention to detail made the uniforms of the soldiers particularly realistic, complete with feathered helmets and sandals.

Other solid off-stage support came from Stage Manager, Pam Brosnan, and team; Property Team, Marie Moloney and Peter Cook, Sound from Star Systems; and everybody was well presented in terms of hair and make-up.

I truthfully could not suggest anything to improve on this production … apart from suggesting that it be re- staged sometime - so as I can see it again!

Although the venue for this production is a fully functional theatre, it is a studio-style performance space with tiered seating overlooking a ground- level flat performance space.

This is great for dance, drama etc. but - as there is nowhere to position an orchestra without obstructing sight-lines - it is unsuitable for a musical theatre production.

Therefore, full credit must go to the company who - before performing the run of their show - had to, first, build a complete stage from scratch on which to perform.

Directed by Colin Hughes, who was making his directorial debut here, this was a fun, bright, well-paced and well-dressed traditional take on the western musical classic, with a few nice innovations.

In keeping with the traditional approach of this production, Set Designer, Bob O'Kelly's concepts were authentic and functional with a realistic looking saloon as the main piece, complete with an internal balcony above the swinging entrance doors.

The saloon's small bar was centre stage, with a small raised cabaret stage on stage left and flats on either side.

There were entrances and exits on balcony level and at either side on the lower level in addition to through the cabaret stage and the saloon's central upstage doors.

Hughes' successful innovations and directorial ideas included: Calamity shooting the hat off Rattlesnake's head to provide a nice comic touch; the laboured ensemble freeze when Calamity admitted that Katie was not Adelaide was a good moment of theatrical suspense; the busy stage activity during A Woman's Touch was both well choreographed and realistic; Calamity really did get well messed up after falling into the stream; and the good use of levels and separation from the other performers with the nice closing picture of Calamity in her wedding dress on the balcony with Bill.

As Musical Director, Conductor and Chorus Master, Michael Fay, was busy and it was nice to hear his musicians play a full Overture with no stage action to distract, as the orchestra is too often forgotten once the first scene in a musical begins. During the Overture and the remainder of the show, which boasted a traditional musical interpretation of the score, Fay managed to coax a surprisingly big sound out of his small eight-piece band, which maintained good stage/ pit balance throughout.

With its lively accompaniment and rousing finish, Windy City was a musical highlight, as was The Black Hills Of Dakota, which produced great choral work, while the male chorus really stood out in Adelaide. Choreographer, Deirdre Browne's use of main dancers as the group of showgirls was good at focusing dance routines on those who could really dance, while her concepts were kept relatively simple and within the company's abilities.

With a voice that was best suited to the slower numbers, Dearbhail Downey was good in the title role with a confident performance, while Peter Manning offered lovely, gentle and relaxed vocals in the role of Wild Bill Hickock with a consistent and natural performance and Shane Byrne made the most of being Lt. Danny Gilmartin.

Generally, Helen Spring's Katie Brown provided a lot of beautiful vocals, while Peter Fay provided an understated performance as song- and-dance performer, Francis Fryer, and Julie Donnelly, as Adelaide Adams, displayed such beautiful and confident vocals in It's Harry I'm Planning To Marry that I would have loved to have heard more of her singing.

While there was no major problems with all other departments, including Bob O'Kelly's stage management; Jack Conroy's props; Vinny Osborne's sound mix; the wardrobe team (Mona Conroy, Mary Smyth, Mairin Dowling, Joy Donohoe and June Young); and the Hair & Make-up team (Mary O'Reilly, Aoife Talbot and Karen Kavanagh), I did feel that Tom Kennedy's lighting plot could have been a little more adventurous … but, keep it under your hat!

There is probably no more appropriate venue to stage any show premiere than the aptly-named Premier Hall in Thurles.

And so, it was here that Alan Menken and Glen Slater's musical comedy, Sister Act, received its local 'baptism' with the Irish premiere of the show. Directed by Tony Finnegan, and Assistant Director, Mary Butler, this was a very funny interpretation of a funny show and all the humour was well delivered with some great visual comedy thrown in for good measure. In keeping with Finnegan's trademark 'attention to detail' approach, the company certainly went that extra mile to ensure authenticity in this production.

The whole venue was touched by divine intervention - or at least Finnegan intervention - as it became a 'church' for the performance, with the windows in the foyer coloured like stained glass windows and 'parish notices' on the entrance notice- board, including, appropriately, news of the annual 'pilgrimage' to Killarney in mid-June.

At the back of the auditorium, a cut- out 'nun' board was available for personal photographs and, as the audience - sorry, the congregation - made its way to its seats, the pre- service announcements alerted the faithful patrons to the fact that "Our service will begin in three minutes." When the 'priest' came on stage just before the show with pre-show safety announcements, I was totally fooled and, for a while, thought it was a real priest (albeit one with a great sense of humour!); so good was Cathal O'Donoghue's performance as the show's Monsignor O'Hara. Beginning with "Good evening parishioners" as in a church with all manner of religious references, his delivery of the introduction to the evening was hilarious and perfectly set the mood for what was to follow. Finnegan and Tommy Sweeney's impressive set design, with its amazing stage-revolve, was both functional and realistic, with a central large cross above the stage, raised aprons/platforms on either side of the stage (over the fire escapes), a catwalk around the orchestra pit and back-lit church windows.

The side aprons/platforms became a police station, an office, a bedroom and a viewing gallery for the visiting Pope in turn, while large sliding gates added to the authenticity of the solid outside of a church piece with two large wooden arched doors.

The disco bar, filled with real bottles, was on a truck, while a large mirror ball helped to create the right ambience for that scene.

The revolving stage was well used to assist the overall pace of the show and for ensemble movement in some scenes.

It also provided comedy impact during the final chase with some inventive use to put a nun into the arms of the gangsters.

The Act 1 finale, Take Me To Heaven (Reprise) ensured that the soulful sisters in dark glasses provided a rousing finale with great use of levels on the various aprons and good use of altar boys to lift the collection. However, as his visit was such a big event within the show, I felt more could have been made of the Pope's appearance.

While she may not have been wearing her best 70s disco gear, Musical Director, Conductor and Chorus Mistress, Mary Rose McNally, and her 10-piece orchestra were certainly in-tune with the era when playing the mainly disco-based score in this fun- filled take on the genre.

Boasting lots of lively up-tempo numbers, Alan Menken and Glen Slater's score led McNally (herself on piano) to correctly forgo strings in favour of a great brass input for that fuller sound.

Yet, despite the sheer volume of a brass section, a good stage/pit balance was maintained throughout. When legs and feet are mainly covered by long nun habits, as in this show, choreography doesn't need a lot of fancy footwork but relies more on the movement of arms and bodies and in overall ensemble movement and positioning.

Yet, Chorographer, Debbie Kiernan, still insisted on plenty of movement and dance steps for the cast in this production.

Linda Ryan's performance as the wannabe diva, Deloris van Cartier, was that of a great worldly woman, who even smoked in the confessional box.

She also had a great gutsy soulful voice and her vocals really shone in the big production numbers, while Maria McElgunn had a truly gifted voice and was a wonderful Mother Superior with old-style traditional values.

As the shy and meek young novice, Sister Mary Robert, Cathy Keane is one of those performers with a natural stage presence that draws one's attention to her … and boasted an equally attractive voice to match. However, this postulant was no novice when it came to being on stage and she knew how to use her beautiful smile and expressive eyes to act well.

In addition to really living her song, The Life I Never Had, she also proved to be an energetic mover in the dance routines.

As Sister Mary Patrick, Olwyn Grogan had a good sense of comic timing and proved to be a lot of fun, while Nina Scott's Sister Mary Lazarus was loud with a dry, quirky sense of humour and good comic timing. Jonathan Gleeson gave a good performance as head conman and club-owning playboy, Curtis, with a nice balance of both the character's humorous and violent sides, while Barry Derby's portrayal of (Sweaty) Eddie, the shy cop with dreams of impressing Deloris, deservedly earned the sympathy of the audience.

These performers had great off- stage support throughout from Stage Manager, Tommy Sweeney, and his team; The Props Team - Rita Loughnane, Trisha Kirby, Noelle Butler and Anne Marie O'Brien; Star Systems' sound mix; Ger Egan and Collette Sweeney's Hair & Make-up; and Wardrobe Mistresses, Eidin Sweeney and Breda Sammon.

Gerry Taylor and Gary Dempsey's lighting was very good all round and varied from bright stage moments to atmospheric moments when appropriate.

Directed and choreographed by Oliver Hurley, this was a visually- stunning, beautifully-lit, well-cast and well-paced staging of the Andrew Lloyd Webber/Jim Steinman musical and all departments involved deserve the highest credit as, without exception, all were central to the overall success of this production. Oliver Hurley's minimal approach to settings was a key element to the success of this production, providing not only an appropriately wide scene space for the story, but also lots of room for big ensemble pieces with no cumbersome sets to hinder exits and entrances or the pace of the production.

This open staging consisted of a back stage-wide projection cyc (most effective in the portrayal of fields and space), with a series of moveable wooded gable framework structures to represent various buildings - some symbolic and some solid structures. The scenes included: a church, open fields, a trailer, the town, a bar, a tent, a realistic street scene (complete with a motorbike), a footbridge over the railway lines and an amazingly realistic barn.

The wooden plank-backed aprons (reflecting the 'wooden plank' theme of the flats and other set pieces) boasted fixed and authentic rural items like milk cans, a wagon wheel, bales of hay, lanterns and tools, while the authenticity even stretched to a wooden stile into a field.

At the start of each Act, a wooden box-panel was flown into centre stage with the name and logo of the show projected onto it.

Despite the contrasting anger of the adult townsfolk to the gentle innocence of the children in the piece, Hurley managed to instil a laid-back rural American feel in his interpretation of the show.

One of the great drawbacks of this show is that, if you don't have a children's chorus/ensemble of a certain standard then it can seriously infringe upon the overall success of the production as the role of the children - their voice, their innocence - is key to the story.

Thankfully, the children involved in this production were amongst the most disciplined and well-directed that I have ever come across and I constantly found it difficult to believe that this was not a professional production.

The integration of all departments and the attention to detail was excellent throughout, while the minimal approach and lack of cumbersome sets ensured the pace and seamlessness of the piece.

The burning of the barn was amazingly well achieved and very realistic, with straw on fire, lots of smoke, screaming children running onto the side aprons, the screen of projected flames and, generally, shadowy lighting.

While Musical Director, Aine Murray, led her ten-piece orchestra on piano to achieve some sympathetic and atmospheric musical accompaniment with the varied score of rock, pop and gospel, Chorus Mistress, Geraldine Heaslip had her singing ensemble already well-drilled to provide impressive choral work. The astonishingly successful Act 1 finale, No Matter What, produced a most moving and innocent moment of theatre with perfect integration of all departments and sterling work from the MD as it captured the theme of the show - innocence and anger. As this was a large cast of mixed age groups and dancing abilities, the key to the success of Oliver Hurley's choreography was in keeping the routines relatively simple and certainly within the capabilities of the performers.

Away from specific routines, the overall movement, positioning and groupings were always impressive and - despite the lack of height variations within the set - all areas were utilised, including the large side aprons and exits into the auditorium to provide great integration at all times.

Alan Teahan was excellent in the role of The Man with a great performance that was always controlled both in terms of acting and singing. He has a rare ability in that his very expressive vocals enable him to act with his voice while singing.

Janna Foley also turned in an excellent performance as the ever- believing Swallow, which was both gentle and innocent, while Mike Lynch's portrayal of Boone was that of a very caring father and worried widower doing his best for his family. Making her principal debut as Brat, Sarah Cleary's great accent and sense of innocence provided appropriately innocent vocals and characterisation, while Emma O'Shea provided good vocals and diction to her suitably angry and assured performance of girlfriend, Candy. As all departments really worked together here as a team, credit must go to Stage Manager, Des Hurley; Props Mistress, Gemma Hurley; Sound men, Murt Whelan and Shane Murphy; Costume Mistresses, Karen Soffe and Lena Lynch; and Noranne Gleeson's Hair & Make-up department.

Finally, John Hurley's warm, rich and atmospheric lighting plot was another strong element in this production's success.

Exceptionally good at all times, this most visually-pleasing plot was clever in creating mood and shadows and compensating for the lack of full sets, with good and effective use of many styles of lighting.

In keeping for a Society whose base is only a few hundred metres from a beautiful bay coastline, the cast of this show had already got their sea legs by the time I caught up with it. Richie Smith's version of the Cole Porter classic sailed along smoothly with some old hands with a few crossings between them among the somewhat disparate passenger list of the transAtlantic liner setting. And like the ship's funnel that spewed out smoke from the dry ice machine long before the orchestra struck up, this show fairly steamed along.

That pace owed much to James O'Keefe's clever composite set which kept scenery changes to a minimum, allowing the action to flow on the tight stage of St Mary's Girls School, a mere sea breeze away from Baldoyle's centre.

It was also bolstered by Trish McDermott's lively dance routines which pushed the narrative on rather than get in the way of it while Sarah Lynch Barrett's eight-piece band drove things along at a lick.

As in every sea journey space is at a premium so Mr Smith in a neat and very practical touch made great use of the auditorium's aisle to board his passengers.

Chief among them was Kathryn Gibbons who had her own take on Reno Sweeney, the evangelist turned nightclub singer (I always thought things were meant to be the other way round) who on this journey was more sophisticated and less brassy than usual.

The initial object of her romantic attentions, Damien Hurley's lovelorn Billy Crocker, was relaxed, witty and imbued with easy grace.

The show's Hope Harcourt was the sweet-voiced Ceri McEvoy who abandoned her fiance, Sir Evelyn Oakleigh, Karl Hoffman with a spiffing upper crust English accent and a flare for comedy, for the charms of Mr Hurley's Crocker.

Years of stage experience showed in Rory Robinson's portrayal of the somewhat less than criminal mastermind, Moonface Martin, with his comic timing finely judged.

Another seasoned performer, Lesley Byrne, turned in a lovely understated version of Evangeline Harcourt, a clucking mother of the bride-to-be while Nicola Pollard was a suitably nasally Erma, Moonie's sidekick, if not the real brains of the operation. Anthony Ennis took on the looks and mannerisms of a much older man to make a convincing Elisha Whitney, Paul Fay was an imposing and comic Captain, Mark Smith was an energetic ship's Purser while Thomas Dempsey was a highly realistic vicar. Add in a hard working chorus and it made for a good night's entertainment for the crowd that shoehorned themselves into the small hall.

This show, so representative of the wit and elegance of Cole Porter, needs good costumes and I have to say that the Society did not scrimp on the budget in spite of the limited income that a hall this size can generate.

My one real concern during the evening was the over-elaboration of Cathal Donohoe's lighting desk. At times I found the constant changes during songs almost distracting.

show_raw: How To Succeed In Business Without Really Trying
review_text:
J Pierpont Finch - king of musical theatre's chancers - would have been appalled.

In the run up to his dismissal as Manchester United boss, David Moye's choice of reading material on a flight back from a Champion's league game in Greece was openly mocked by his underperforming and increasingly hostile players.

The tome in question was a self help manual, exactly the kind that Brian Raftery in his guise as Finch in Cork Institute of Technology Musical Society's version of How to Succeed used to bluff his way to the top of the World Wide Wicket company.

Finch, in the Loesser and Burrows 1950s lampooning of American big business, understood that knowledge is power and uses facts like a stiletto knife to rid himself of whoever stands in his way.

It's a huge role, more so for an inexperienced player and while Mr Raftery shows a lot of promise as an actor, his character was too beguiling and not ruthless enough for me. An in-built problem for director Johnathon Tweedie was the role of JB Biggley, boss of the World Wide Wicket company and usually played by a man in his 50s or older. With an all student cast the part fell to Aaron Barriscale, another good actor who mimicked the tone and moves of a man much older than himself but whom, essentially, is too fresh faced. It's the same problems youth groups face when casting Valjean and Javert in the schools' version of Les Miserables.

Mr Tweedie's production which was otherwise well conceived, did however, boast the sweet soprano voice of Muirgen O'Mahony as Rosemary, the secretary who falls for and eventually marries Finch.

Declan Leonard proved his versatility by playing meek time-serving company man Arthur Twimble in Act One and then returning as WWW president Wally Womper, a character who could not have been more different.

Liam Cuthbert's Bert Bratt, a man with a big smile and a big voice, was also impressive while Emily Hutt made a good buttoned-up Josephine Jones, secretary to the big boss and Maria Branagan as Hedy, an office girl with a typing speed of 12 words a minute but whose business attributes lay in other places, was a nasally voiced New Yorker on the make.

Mr Tweedie's dance routines were varied, appropriate and well executed on the wide stage of the Curtis Auditorium at Cork's School of Music by an ensemble that was fully engaged in the action from the moment the curtain went up.

A clever composite set and judicious use of some floor space for a few of the scenes allowed the show to flow at pace while Deirdre Long's ten musicians - nearly all of them students - provided the big band sound that is needed for this show. This is a group that is only in its fourth year and which has grown out of all recognition in that time. While it is the first time they have entered the AIMS awards they have followed the classic college society route of staging shows that are a little out of the ordinary.

There is huge potential here both on and off stage. The society pulled in a full house the night I was there and could easily fit more into the Curtis Auditorium with different staging and seating configurations.

With the School of Music's central location by the river in Cork city they have great scope to develop an audience off campus should they decide to go down that route.

musical about boastful but socially crippled teenagers, this show was held in a school sports hall.

It might have been anathema to the cigarette smoking pupils of Rydell High but the basketball hoops were among the most prominent features of the Colaiste Bride hall.

At least two of the youthful cast - pupils of the Enniscorthy school - were at home here on the hall's wide stage while others in the cast are still at school elsewhere. Ironically some of the experience in the cast was provided by teachers.

Director Clodagh Cecil's version of the original teen musical was not as racy as some although quite a few of the Rydell High rebels sported those cigarettes throughout the performance while the Pink Ladies also dabbled with alcohol.

It was well staged thanks partly to Mark Redmond's subtle lighting and inventive settings which included wing adjuncts and a catwalk which corralled Kevin Kennedy's eight- piece band.

Those settings enabled Ms Cecil to mount shot through scenes with the action taking place consecutively on different parts of the stage allowing the show to flow at pace and left plenty of room for Anne-Marie Stafford's lively dance routines.

That youthful cast included couple of promising and energetic novices in the lead male roles. John Murphy as Danny Zuko and Naoise Dunbar as Kenickie were making their musical theatre debuts.

Schoolgirl Megan Power as Sandy - a teenager with a lot of potential - by way of contrast was appearing in her second leading role in the south east this season.

Yvette Walsh, one of the more experienced hands in the group, was a hard-nosed, combative Betty Rizzo. In contrast, Niamh Bolger brought out Frenchy's soft centre and gentle side.

Joanne McCabe, a girl with a big voice, a big smile, great facial reactions and a big appetite ensured Jan was eye catching while Megan Ryan got to show off a lovely voice as Marty, the fourth member of the Pink Ladies who somewhat reluctantly allow the new girl in town into their circle.

Darragh Kinsella was a goofy Doody with James Dobbs a convincing nerd as Eugene. Gearoid McCauley as Sonny and Sean O'Brien as Roger added experience to the male ranks. Michaela White was an enthusiastic Patty Simcox while her fellow Colaiste Bride student, Charlotte Morrissey, was a lithe Cha Cha DiGregorio.

Another couple of older hands brought some lovely characterisation to adult roles in the show. Pat Bolger was a slippery Vince Fontaine all honeyed words, wandering hands and a spectacularly awful wig.

And Ronan P Byrne showed tremendous flexibility by portraying singer Johnny Casino and the Teen Angel in scenes only minutes apart yet making the characters completely different. His conversational style of delivery as the Angel, complete with his backing vocals troupe, was excellent.

Society Chairwoman Jennifer Byrne was typecast here as school Principal Miss Lynch, keeping an anxious eye on her errant charges.

If Mr Redmond's lighting desk was subtle in its approach to the show the same can't be said of Global Sound Systems sound plot.

Too often band levels in particular were at the top end of the spectrum

As someone old enough to have heard of the horrors of World War One at first hand, I often think the house lights should be kept dimmed a little longer than usual at the end of this show and that Kleenex would be an ideal sponsor.

I vividly remember as an inquisitive child being quietly sat down when I was deemed old enough to understand and being told of the shock and devastation of seeing young men fall beside you, the noise of the German snipers' rifles, the deafening blasts of early 20th Century munitions, the Mustard gas that blinded temporarily and the cases of foot rot suffered by troops positioned in cold wet mud in foreign fields, often in poor equipment.

The narrator was a wise old cove, a great uncle who survived the conflict and taught me much in the time that I knew him. Mercifully he and two of his brothers came home to Belfast. All three were in one piece physically although variously they had been blinded for short periods and suffered what we now call shell shock and post traumatic stress disorder.

Their story to a degree mirrors the hard life of the working class Tallentire brothers of Howard Goodall and Melvyn Bragg's desperately sad musical. For the pre-war graft of the Cumbrian farms, the danger in the Whitehaven coal mines and fell hunting swap Belfast bar work, the city's famous shipyards and coastal fishing.

The awful tragedy and waste of war is encapsulated in the fate of Harry, John Tallentire and his wife Emily's teenage son. From the time we first meet him running freely across the fells at the start of Act Two as an innocent wide eyed boy, his character is drawn in two short scenes in the family kitchen when he announces he is going down the mines against his parents' wishes and then when he tells his mother he has joined the army, leaving her at home with his sister while his father is already in the trenches.

His demise after going over the top to try and take out a German sniper's position and his courage in so doing is recorded in a brief scene by way of a letter from his father to his mother as John prepares to come home after the fighting has ceased.

Trying to convey all that in the confined and under-equipped space of St Joseph's Hall in Kilcock was director Philippa Alford whose fast paced production benefited from the inclusion of the excellent voice of Peter Manning and the acting ability of Sharon Murphy as John and Emily Tallentire, the couple who move to the village of Crossbridge after marriage, then onto Whitehaven in pursuit of work and whose lives are changed irrevocably by the First World War.

Her guilt at an extra marital affair with the wealthier Jackson Pennington - an imposing Eddie Brady - was palpable while Beth Duberry was their wilful daughter May and Connor Griffin as Harry was a portrayal of earnest innocence.

James Paradise played the fun loving Isaac Tallentire with a big smile even through the trauma of losing a leg on the battlefield while John's other brother, Seth, was correctly portrayed as altogether more earnest by Eamonn Nolan.

Paul Byrne brought a hard edge to landowner Pennington, Jackson's father, Bert Carruthers was a combative Blacklock and Lorraine Murphy was a bright Sally.

Musical director Michael Fay took Goodall's score at a lick while choreographer Julie Donnelly sensibly kept routines simple in such a tight space.

Unsung heroine of the night was stage manager Sinead McLoughlin who with her five man team ensured the cast were on cue all the time and settings were changed with the minimum of fuss while working in their version of stage Hell.

A GAA club in Kildare isn't exactly London's West End but the man behind the lighting of this show wouldn't be out of place there.

Darren Kelleher's plot for Claire Tighe's version of the Lloyd Webber and Rice rock musical at Leixlip's Green Lane hall was ambitious in its scope and classy in its execution with warm colours, stark blues, atmospheric washes and striking effects.

Ms Tighe is a young director from the company who clearly knows what she is seeking to achieve and she pushed this production along at a lick aided by her own dance routines which moved the narrative on rather than getting in the way of it.

However, with the audience seated on the flat a couple of crucial scenes were set in an area of the stage partially blocked by musical director Caitriona Ni Threasaigh.

For the uninitiated (with the season we have just had, can there be such a creature left?) Superstar is more about Judas and Ms Tighe and her production team cast a smasher in Chris Currid, a young man with a big voice, outstanding diction and a good actor.

Brian Tighe, a big man with plenty of height in his voice was a gentle Jesus with Jenny McCabe lending more of a Broadway tone to Mary Magdalene than is sometimes the case.

Schoolboy Eoghain Kiernan as Caiaphas was truly a giant among men. The role of the High Priest requires a bass voice and while there is a bit of depth to his instrument I suspect it is still settling down due to his age. However, standing at around six ft six inches, he cast an imposing shadow on the proceedings.

In this version of the show he had only two henchmen instead of the normal three with John Dennehy bringing a powerful, lyrical hint of evil to Annas and Kevin Hynes adopting a controlled air of menace as the unnamed priest who watched everything through hawk-like eyes and expressed his thoughts through a series of hand movements.

Ross Murray portrayed Pilate as an angrier Roman Governor than is often the case while Daniel Frawley gave us a camp King Herod in a performance that was full of attack. Ian Tighe was untroubled by the vocal and dramatic d e m a n d s o f Simon while Dara MacGabhann as a frightened Peter revealed a very good baritone voice with a lovely tone.

A largely youthful ensemble including quite a number of young men brought great energy to Ms Tighe's dance routines in a performance that was never less than fully committed from the moment they set foot on the stage.

Musical director, Ms Ni Threasaigh's highly experienced nine-piece band gelled well as a unit, adding to the atmosphere of the show and driving the action along at a lick.

Elaine MacCauley is a striking beautiful blonde as those on the Northern circuit who know her will attest.

Her transformation therefore into the jive talking Deloris de Cartier, heroine of this piece, was all the more remarkable.

Aided by a Diana Ross-style Afro wig and a subtle make-up job, she tackled the role of sinner turned saint head on in the Northern Ireland premiere of Alan Menken and Glenn Slater's stage adaptation of the movie.

Mrs MacCauley is one of life's stage naturals. After a few years off the boards she was back commanding Coleraine's Riverside Theatre's deep space.

However, the score from Alan Menken, Disney darling and one of the busiest men on Broadway and Hollywood, does not always lie in the best part of her voice.

She may have been the figurehead of the ambitious north coast outfit in this feel good tale that does, however, open with a shocking murder but director Kerry Dunn also fashioned a host of other fine performances from her cast.

Una Culkin was a terribly posh Mother Superior with her nose so far in the air that I'm surprised she could breathe never mind pray. Rosemary O'Connor was funny as Sr Mary Patrick, Helen Wilkinson was eye catching as a growling Sr Mary Lazarus and Amy Rankin was a sweet voice postulant, Sr Mary Robert, who finally found her nerve after hanging out with bad girl Deloris.

Harry Coates looked and sounded right as nightclub owner and all- round bad guy Curtis Jackson who surrounded himself with four minders and messengers.

TJ, his nephew, was played by the promising Adam Goudy while the colourful Peter Olphert and Andy Shaw provided the muscle.

Only in the Northern Ireland premiere of a show based in a convent could the murder victim, the fourth member of Jackson's gang, be a real life priest, local PP, Rory Sheehan, who had to dash off between the Saturday matinee and evening performances to conduct Mass.

David McDowell was the timid cop who finally lost his inhibitions to save and then win Deloris in a well handled final scene, Harry Stinson found his new calling as Monsignor O'Hara, the man in charge of the rundown Queen of Angels parish while Society president, John McDowell, was promoted to an even higher office, making a brief appearance as the Pope as the show drew to a close. Ms Dunn, who trained as a set designer, opted to use projections as the basis of her production at the beautifully sited Riverside, surrounded on several sides by green fields on the University of Ulster's north east campus and close to the Society's home base of Portrush. It allowed the show to flow quickly from scene to scene while giving the company - particularly those bopping nuns - room to execute Ditanya McKinty's lively choreography.

Terry Cloughley's good ten-piece band drove the action on while experiencing for the first time another excellent Menken score that includes a couple of lovely songs in "The life I never led" and "I haven't got a prayer", the lively finale "Spread the love around" and the brilliantly titled Latin chant "Benedicta-ta for now".

They're a noisy lot in Ratoath - and that's only the audience.

A near full house at the intimate Venue Theatre started clapping in time during the overture from Olivia Toman's fine band and never really stopped.

The hollering of course, wasn't confined to the neatly raked seats with the well drilled cast clearly enjoying themselves in the big numbers with a couple of choreographer Aisling Toher's routines turning into real hooleys.

It was all a lot different from talking to Ratoath officials before the show. The signs were not good when they started getting their apologies in early.

They were only a small company, they told me, the stage at The Venue only has one wing entrance (yes honestly) and they weren't expecting a big crowd as it was the night before children went back to school after the Easter holidays.

But 15 minutes into Garry Moutaine's version of this Rodgers and Hammerstein classic I came to the conclusion this was a Society selling itself short.

Yes, there might only have been 33 adults on stage (backed up by eight children and a couple of pit singers) and some of the leads were lacking in experience but this was a good show by anyone's standards.

The old Kings of Broadway made Aunt Eller this show's leader on stage and the eye catching Clare Green more than filled that role for Mr Mountaine She was a great foil for Orla Mulreid's Laurey, a girl who can sing, dance and act.

Sean Keany as Curly was even younger than his eventual stage wife. In fact, he one of those teenagers I've found up and down the island with lots of promise. However, the night of my visit his voice was tired, a casualty of an earlier illness.

Another youthful player, Aisling Reid, a girl with great facial expressions and wonderful timing acted her bonnet off as a busy and very funny Ado Annie while yet another teenager, Liam Egan, another very good singer and actor came up with a scary portrayal of Jud Fry.

Ian Rountree, new to the Society, weighed in with a vivacious and highly committed performance as the dopey Will Parker while Niall Dempsey brought years of experience to bear in a fine comic perfomance as Ali Hakim the persian peddlar.

Emma Dalton was the giggly Gertie Cummings who eventually marries the door-to-door salesman; Joe Murphy was a suitably upright Andrew Carnes, out to uphold the law and his daughter's virtue, and Peter Finnegan as Ike Skidmore interacted well with the other principals.

Stage manager Bobby White and his team expertly handled the hired-in John O'Donoghue truck-based set - it had been used on a small stage before - while Nigel Lombard's first rate lighting plot added much to the atmosphere.

The production looked well with some great costumes, good hairstyles and a very good dream ballet conceived by Ms Toher and well executed by the cast members.

I saw the show on a Sunday night at the end of their first short run ahead of a few days off and before repeating the exercise all over again. With a big number of walk-ups on the night and word of mouth I'm sure they were turning people away in the second part of the run.

The audience was settling into the fifth scene of Paul Norton's typically fast-moving Annie at Roscrea's Abbey Hall when one of those little lights went off in my head.

Paul Donegan's Oliver Warbucks had just strode into his New York mansion back from a tour of his Depression- hit factories and something was definitely different.

Warbucks is usually played with a generic American middle class accent but here was an actor stepping outside that mould.

Instead, Mr Donegan invested his billionaire with a blue collar accent that Bruce Springsteen and Jon Bon Jovi would have been proud of. The rationale, of course, is that W a r b u c k s - as he tells orphan Annie when he seeks to adopt her - is from New York's famous Hell's Kitchen and there was nowhere more working class in the city at the time.

So, at last, we were treated to a character that we could believe came from virtually nothing in an eye catching performance from an actor who whispered conspiratorially at times, hollered loudly at others and probed other dynamics in between. It was just one of the devices that Mr Norton (above) used in the Abbey's confined space to bring alive the story of the orphan girl who strikes it lucky.

When things were going the couple's way and it looked as if he would get the green light to adopt her, Warbucks, by way of celebration broke into a waltz with his prospective ward with Annie's feet  perched on each of his highly polished shoes as he carried her around the stage. Hannigan's "Little Girls" rant came with the children in a freeze as the orphanage matron mentally struck them out of her mind while the ventriloquist's dummy in the radio studio scene was a child (Claudia Gleeson) given a brilliant make-up job.

Kate Williams, a girl with both a serious face and a luminous smile Competition was a confident Annie who worked well with her fellow inmates at the orphanage, Miss Hannigan, Miss Farrell and Mr Warbucks.

The highly experienced Siobhan Bowe delivered a lovely turn as Miss Hannigan and used a Broadway belt voice to good effect in her big moments while Rachael McMahon with her lovely soprano voice was a businesslike Grace Farrell.

Another experienced actor, Paul Spencer, was able to show his ability to play different styles of characters in Rooster and his alter ego, Ralph Mudge. His moll, Sarah Gene Loughnane as Lily St Regis fell into the trap of being too nasally as the Broadway broad but was much more distinct in the persona of Shirley Mudge. Colin Williams was a bright and efficient Drake, Seamus Mullaney, a statesmanlike President Roosevelt while John Lynch, who played a trio of characters during the evening, made beat cop, Lt Ward, much more of a hard-nosed policeman than is often the case.

Platinum blondes the Boylan Sisters, played here by Niamh O'Donnell Margaret Stanley and Maebh Campion, played up the boredom of their radio studio bit part, Paul Tobin O'Brien was a cheery Bundles as well as serving as a Roosevelt adviser and a dusty old Judge while Gillian Wallace swapped the glamour of a wide eyed would-be Broadway starlet for a later role as the fourth member of the President's kitchen cabinet.

Finger clicking good!! - That is how I would best describe this Irish premiere production of the musical comedy, The Addams Family … or, at least, its finger-clicking opening number, When You're An Addams. Under the directorial hand of Bill Stafford, this was an entertaining and fast-paced production of Andrew Lippa's funny musical about a less than conventional family and its fully-active ancestors.

Right from the off, it was obvious that this was not going to be 'One Normal Night', as the patrons were greeted by an array of weird and ghoulish characters outside of the venue before entering a foyer decorated with a star curtain and coffin lids.

However, the smartly-dressed and efficient Front of House Team brought a sense of normality to things and a sense of uniformity as all wore flowers in their lapel.

Mick Russell and Tomas Byrne's Set Design was not only visually perfect but also extremely functional.

Ranging from star curtains to a moonlit graveyard and from an open stage with black curtains with the effective use of split house tabs for different scenes to the Addams family's eerie mansion, the designs were varied, but - being generally minimal in approach - all helped with the good pace of this production. The main set piece, the inside of the mansion, had two sets of stairs to the balcony, dark-coloured side flats, while - although they could have been used more - side aprons were also used at times, especially at the end.

The costumes and the make-up for the Ancestors were to die for (… and they obviously did!!), while the Act 1 finale, Full Disclosure (Part 2) was a great production number and an amazing ensemble piece with good integration and choreography on all levels and atmospheric purple/blue lighting.

Musical Director, Conductor and Chorus Mistress, Mairead McKenna, and her 7-piece orchestra really rose to the challenge here with this varied and difficult score and managed to maintain a good stage/pit balance throughout.

Apart from the variety of tempo changes from one song to the next, a lot of the music was fragmented with lots of start/stops throughout many songs.

This did not make a musical director's job easy and there were also lots of tempo changes to be found within songs e.g. the big production number, Full Disclosure, like many others, also had dialogue to be played under.

While the great musicality of the tango rhythms made numbers like Trapped, Secrets and Not Today stand out here, it was the orchestra's sheer accuracy of performance and the visual impact of the dancers in the production number, Tango De Amour, that combined to make this an irresistible musical highlight. Choreography was a strong element in this production and Choreographer, Martina Lynch, knew exactly what she wanted and how to get it from her young charges.

Her concepts were well-executed and all groupings, positioning, movement and integration were great and there was good use of all levels for groups.

The big opening production number, When You're An Addams, was well- executed and, from the word go, one knew that there was going to be no problems with dance or movement for this song's varied choreography included lots of arm movements and samples of line dancing, the bunny hop and the twist.

Brian O'Gorman gave a good performance as the head of the family, Gomez, and supplied some touching moments in the song, Happy / Sad, yet also managed to deliver the song's humorous lines on cue.

As the tall, elegant mother, Morticia, Leah Penston looked the part in her long black ankle-length dress and long black hair like Crystal Gale. This was a very confident performance from a total all-rounder with a great voice and good stage presence who perfectly captured her character's dry wit.

She also proved to be a most impressive and energetic dancer, especially in the song and dance number, Just Around The Corner, and even managed the splits during Tango De Amour. This performer is an amazing talent.

Amy Penston, who played family daughter, Wednesday, is another amazing talent. She is a strong performer with a great voice and a good stage presence and this was highlighted in her performance throughout, but especially during Pulled.

Despite playing the weird uncle, Fester, Brendan Kenny provided lovely vocals during his gentle ballad, The Moon And Me and proved himself more than capable as the show's narrator.

Boasting what was probably the best make-up in Ireland this year, Sinead Rees, as Grandma, may have looked like Alice Cooper in drag, but - perfectly capturing her character's outspoken and irreverent attitude - she provided faultless comic delivery, timing and accent throughout.

Naoimh Penston is another amazingly talented performer and, in playing Alice, turned in a great performance, In addition to the talented cast, another star of this production was the range of costumes, particularly the amazingly detailed and atmospheric outfits worn by the Ancestors. Wardrobe Mistress, Els Penston and Elaine Sweeney, are to be highly praised for the visual effect of these outfits (combined with the work of Nationwide Respray Specialists, Sharon Kavanagh's Hair and Make-up Team and Padraig Reid's Lighting) and how important they were to the overall success of this production. Suffice to say that the costumes were amazing!

Likewise, Sharon Kavanagh and her Hair and Make-up Team - Nicol Hempenstall and Sharon Kenny - are also to be highly praised for their vitally important work in this production. For not only were they responsible for the impressive look of the Ancestors, but also for the hair, eyes and scary skin tones of all of the performers, especially the Principal line-up, who were all amazing. This was a truly great job by all.

There was also solid off-stage support from Stage Manager, Barry Ryan, and his team; Props Mistresses, Karen Kavanagh and Stacey Myler; sound mix by All Around Sound; and Padraig Reid's Lighting.

Finally, this show could well have been renamed, The Penston Family, for this production; so strong and important was the input from members of this family.

They say that variety is the spice of life. So, whilst touring around the country to see the various shows on the adjudication circuit, my life was certainly spiced-up with the wide variety of shows, performances and voices on offer.

However, another variant was the style and size of venue for the shows and this one must surely have been one of the smallest of all.

Seating around 200 people, it was very deceiving from the outside but extremely well-designed with tiered seating and no space going to waste.

While it was intimate and cosy, the down-side was that the stage had no wing space at all and I sympathise with, and salute, the company, the director, the choreographer and the stage manager in achieving the almost impossible by staging musicals in such a restricted space. One nice touch here was the fact that everyone in the very efficient and smartly dressed Front of House team wore a brightly coloured flower in either their lapel or hair, which tied in well with the exotic setting of Rodgers & Hammerstein's South Pacific.

Despite the obvious restrictions which badly affected the pace of the piece, Director, Sharon McNamara's intimate production boasted a traditional interpretation, some nice comic moments, good discipline, pleasant vocals and some great choral work.

Olan Wrynn's set consisted of traditional theatrical flats with painted views of the islands plus trees, bushes and painted windows. These hinged flats opened out for the painted beach scenes, complete with a shower unit, while heavy army rope, office furniture and small platform risers were also utilised for other scenes.

While this design worked to an extent, scene/set changes were still very long - mainly due to the lack of space - and I would suggest that in venues such as this, the minimal approach to set design is the only way to go to give the production pace and to do away with cumbersome set/scene changes Musical Director, Conductor and Chorus Master, Enda O'Connor, and his 7-piece orchestra were kept busy here not just with the score but also playing during some long scene changes.

Positioned out of sight at the front of the tiered seating block, there was a lovely pit/stage balance, especially during Some Enchanted Evening, and right from the beautifully paced and gentle Overture, there were many highlights under O'Connor's musical direction.

However, the musical highlight must have been the surprising reprise of the comic number, Honey Bun, which was played in slow time with the company doing marching steps in respect for the death of Cable. Although good, sadly, Choreographer, Julianne McNamara's concepts and ideas during dance routines were seldom realised here as, all too often, they fell victim of the space restrictions offered by this venue.

There were exceptions, of course, and despite the space restrictions, McNamara worked wonders with groupings, positioning and integration - an amazing feat in itself - but, movement and routines were problematic at times.

Faced with these restrictions on stage and in the wings, the ensemble did well, especially in terms of exits and entrances and the good discipline displayed by all of the sailors who were 'frozen' during Bali Ha'i was impressive.

Playing out-of-age, Shane Broderick displayed good control and confident vocals as the mature, suave and wealthy planter, Emile de Becque. As the confused young girl in love with an older man, Audrey O'Meara was both upbeat and unsure in turns. She gave a good vocal performance of I'm Gonna Wash That Main Right Outa My Hair and a joyous rendition of I'm In Love With A Wonderful Guy. Adrian Sheils supplied some nice comic moments in the comedy role of Luther Billis. These were well- played, especially during Honey Bun and Bali Ha'i.

Heather Colohan's great singing voice was really suited to the role of the native lady, Bloody Mary, especially in her atmospheric rendition of Bali Ha'i With his nice vocal performance in Younger Than Springtime, Daniel Ryan coped well in the role of the heroic Lt. Joe Cable, but looked way too young to be the strong heroic type The children, Sarah O'Rourke as Ngana and Patrick Bergin as Jerome, did a splendid job, especially as they had the difficult job of being the first on stage to open the production. Like the Director and the Choreographer, Stage Manager, Liz Kennedy is another person who needs to be singled out for praise here as, with no wing space, she also achieved the impossible and did a great job with the movement of sets, props and people during all exits and entrances.

There was solid support off-stage from the Props Team, Roisin Gilmore and Alma Naughton, and from Recks Audio's overall sound mix.

Paschal Gough's lighting was fairly basic with few atmospheric moments and, overall, I felt that the lighting could have been a bit more adventurous.

Although the costumes were supplied from a number of different sources, Wardrobe Mistresses, Maureen de Forge, Gerri Hynes and Marguerite McDonnell, made sure all looked well, but the styles of jeans on the sailors were a bit too varied and as the programme did not credit anyone for hair and make-up, I can only presume that everyone looked after their own. Well done therefore to all the ladies for their hair styles and to Billis for his make-up in Honey Bun.

Falling so close before Easter, this was a most timely staging of this musical from the energetic and enthusiastic members of Clara Musical Society, especially as I had attended a Palm Sunday service immediately before the performance (Hosanna never seemed so real before in my mind's eye!).

Credit must go to the company for its great modern-looking set and lighting here, which was no mean feat when one considers the additional work involved in turning this non-theatrical sports/community hall into a theatre for this production. Under the direction of Alan Recks, who opted for a minimal approach with sets stripped back to concentrate on the music of the piece, the sets, lighting, choreography and music were all particularly strong elements in this more modern interpretation of Sir Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice's early rock opera.

While the music was loud and suitably aggressive in places and there was great integration and use of all levels by the very young company, there was an unusual camp feel about this colourful and fast-paced production, which added little to it apart from some novelty value.

The Set Design by Stephen Rabbette, Wayne Handy, Alan Recks, Ronan Kenny and Derek Recks was very modern, clinical and, most importantly, functional. With a minimal approach, the open- set offered a deep and narrow rectangular performance space on ground level in front of a tiered seating auditorium.

Its split level accommodated the orchestra underneath the back balcony platform with steep steps at the sides up to the balcony and one wider set of central upstage steps, while some of the lighting rig was integrated into the set design with warmly lit scaffolding structures at either side.

Due to the fact that there is tiered seating here and that the performance space is at floor level and not raised, the company needs to be aware of potential sight- line problems and ensure that any action on the performance space is always within sight of everyone in the audience.

With such a deep performance space this was, generally, not a problem, but during Heaven On Their Minds, the action on the floor was just about within sight-line, while Jesus on the floor at the end of Trial By Pilate did cause a sight-line problem and really needed to be staged more upstage. The show's original and iconic 'two angels' image was projected, as was some gospel text, on to the stage during the Overture, while the projection of images of war and death were effective during Gethsemane and the use of the cast to carry on the scene's bench-like tables for The Last Supper worked well to help pace.

Integration was a big part of this production and even in the early Everything's Alright scene, the ensemble were integrated into the action, while, at the end of this scene, the ensemble crowded around the front of the stage hiding the scene change - this again integrated the ensemble, while adding to the fast pace of the production.

Judas' Death was staged almost in silhouette against red lighting and I liked the echo on the last notes of the music at the point of the hanging before the effective silence.

The Crucifixion was a major highlight in this production with its very eerie and foreboding music, red lighting on the steps with every hammer blow and disturbing mocking sounds as the cross was positioned close to the audience.

The death scene itself was amazingly realistic, harrowing and moving and will live in the memory for a long time.

Due to the open design of the sets in this production, there was no 'pit' for the 8-piece orchestra and, along with Musical Director, Conductor and Chorus Master, Alan Recks, they, therefore, found themselves hidden below the balcony at the back of the performing space.

Under such circumstances, they did very well not only in coping with the show's busy sung-through format but also maintaining a good stage/ orchestra balance, particularly with such a rock-inspired score.

Judging by her impressive work on this production, Choreographer, Lea Carroll is obviously a lady with lots of potential, who - being young herself - managed to get the best from her energetic and youthful peers.

Her concepts were well-executed and all groupings, positioning, movement and integration were great and there was good use of all levels for groups.

Carroll came up with some nice touches, particularly with the angels dancing in a 'cross' formation during Superstar, Although his vocals were sounding a little tired on the last night of run in this vocally demanding role, Stephen Rabbette's Jesus captured the friction between Judas and himself from early in the show and he still managed an impressive interpretation of Gethsemane. However, he should be justly proud of his most realistic and memorable death scene.

When Jesus met up with the apostles at the start, John Conroy's Judas watched from a distance; immediately establishing the friction that was building between Jesus and himself. This performer had great diction and very strong and loud vocals, throughout, and delivered what can best be described as powerhouse vocals in the big production number, Jesus Christ Superstar.

Sinead Farrell, who played Mary Magdalene, is undoubtedly an amazingly good singer, while Damien Keating's Pontius Pilate provided a clear and determined vocal interpretation of Pilate's Dream. Darren O'Hara was a particularly strong vocalist and displayed amazingly good clarity and diction in his performance as Peter. A great actor and singer, he portrayed a determined denial with fear during Peter's Denial.

There was solid off-stage support from Stage Manager, Wayne Handy, and his team; Props Mistress, Edel Kennedy; sound mix by Recks Audio; Wardrobe Mistresses, Liz Rickard and Mary Cornally; and Hair & Make-Up team - John Coss, Bankz Hair Salon, Liz Rickard, Mary Cornally and Kellie Cornally.

The Lighting Design, again by Stephen Rabbette, Wayne Handy, Alan Recks, Ronan Kenny and Derek Recks, was bright and colourful with atmospheric effects when necessary.

Gorey Musical Society celebrated its 50th anniversary with the staging of Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice's Evita and fittingly remembered one of its founding members, the late Oona O'Carroll, in its show programme.

A founding member of the original Gorey Operatic Society, she remained a stalwart of the evolving musical society until her death last Christmas, aged 92.

Although a fairly traditional staging of the popular show, this production was extremely well-directed by Imelda McDonagh with fast pace and particularly good sets, choreography, chorus, costumes and individual voices and performances.

As a symbolic mansion in the spirit of La Casa Rosada, Imelda McDonagh's majestic set was impressive in visual appearance, detail and functionality.

I particularly liked the great use of the two sets of mobile steps in varying positions in different scenes and the many entrances and exits to assist the pace of the show.

Having the balcony move forward to bring the audience into the piece during Don't Cry For Me Argentina made the song more intimate and was an effective touch.

While McDonagh's well-thought direction and a functional set greatly aided the fast pace of this production, other important factors came into play, including splitting the ensemble for various scenes, using cast members to move sets and props, and the inventive use of the set's two mobile steps.

All too often, acting becomes secondary to singing in most musical theatre productions, and it was an advantage to have a director from a drama background who ensured that the drama in the piece was not forgotten.

The tasteful opening with the military and the music full of pomp and ceremony during Requiem For Evita really set the scene in this production, complete with a body in the coffin lying in state and a mournful chorus.

Although I felt her accent was getting in the way of her diction at the start, I liked the way Eva's character transformed and evolved throughout this production and this was first realised during the Charity Concert when there was a visual transformation in her dress style before her new found vocal clarity and elegance was highlighted in I'd Be Surprisingly Good For You with its elegant dancing from Peron, Eva and the dancers.

There were lovely groupings throughout and during Don't Cry For Me Argentina with the inclusion of children and the little boy on his father's shoulders giving Eva flowers during the song was a particularly nice touch.

Clever localised lighting helped the great moments of contrast between the death bed and past realities during Montage to make it a highlight, while Lament provided a well-realised death scene, complete with the ever-present portrait of Eva in La Casa Rosada.

While costumes had good attention to detail, Eva's costumes were extremely impressive for authenticity, variety and the sheer number of changes, while the female hairstyles were particularly good.

Musical Director, Conductor and Chorus Master, Lar Duffy, and his 9-piece orchestra were busy as the contemporary sounding score offered a high degree of musical input and they managed to maintain a lovely pit/stage balance throughout.

Chorus standards were high throughout this show and there was a particularly strong chorus during Rainbow Tour, while the children's vocals, with sympathetic accompaniment, which built up to a full adult chorus in Santa Evita were truly amazing.

Choreographer, Frances Ryan, did a fantastic job here as all of her work was visually-pleasing. This was in no small way because the decision was taken to split the ensemble for various scenes, which guaranteed not only no over-crowding on stage, but also ample room for the good work put into routines to be realised. Another major factor in the success of the choreography was the use of dedicated dancers (as opposed to everyone in the ensemble) for main routines, which ensured the successful execution of the choreographer's concepts e.g. as in the lively Buenos Aires, when the formation-style choreography also boasted good ensemble groupings, positioning and integration.

The styles were varied throughout with I'd Be Surprisingly Good For You providing elegant dancing while And The Money Kept Rolling In (And Out) was an opportunity for the good dancers to be really energetic, with a great final picture of Eva held aloft. Showing ambition from the early scenes, Ciara Herron really captured the character of her role as Eva Peron and developed the part as the piece evolved with great vocals and acting skills.

This particularly stood out with her strong interpretation of Don't Cry For Me Argentina, her emotional performance of You Must Love Me and in her most impressive performance during Eva's Final Broadcast when she became believably weaker with each broken breath. As the ever present narrator, Che, Gary Stephens offered well- controlled vocals throughout and, although he was quite laid-back in style, held the story together well. He turned in a strong performance during Oh What A Circus and, thanks to good diction and a good performance, helped to capture the only humour in the show during Good Night And Thank You.

Malcolm Byrne's towering physical frame really suited him to the role of Juan Peron and he certainly captured the character's ambitious nature, while showing his gentler side in She Is A Diamond; the first time Peron displayed any sentimentality.

As the tango singer and woman's man, Magaldi, Dermot Wildes turned in a confident performance with controlled vocals (especially in Eva Beware Of The City) and good diction. He really sounded like an authentic tango singer in On This Night Of A Thousand Stars and in the Charity Concert showed that he had moved on from his time in nightclubs.

Clodagh Leacy offered the most beautiful vocals as the Mistress during Another Suitcase In Another Hall, while young Grace and Niall Kehoe provided perfect angelic voices to this production as the Santa Evita children and produced one of the most poignant moments in the show.

Considering that, on the night of my visit, the lighting control board had broken and the lights had to be controlled using a keyboard, I thought Mark Redmond's lighting was, generally, good.

Although the costumes were supplied by Utopia, the Wardrobe Mistresses, Mary Spellman, Theresa Donegan and Betty Kelly, made sure that all looked well and there was other solid off-stage support from Stage Manager, Paul Doran, and his team; The Props Team did well; the sound mix by I-Tech Productions; and Linda Collier's Hair & Make-up team.

Congratulations to all involved on such a good show for your 50th Anniversary production.

- A MUSICAL DRAMA Well ahead of its opening, the posters for this show said it all by publicly and proudly stating: 'Michael Collins - Sold Out'.

While that quotation may, perhaps, be a political statement for some, in this case, it was a definite confirmation of commercial success … and if ever a production deserved such support, it was this one.

This musical slice of Irish history by the late Bryan Flynn, with its almost sung-through format, was epic in both content and staging and everyone involved here deserves the highest praise for producing one of the most riveting nights of theatre that I have witnessed in a long time. Billed as a 'musical drama', this production, directed so superbly and meticulously by Christine Scarry, was an even mix of both music and drama in equal turns.

Indeed, when Bryan Flynn watched this production only weeks before his most untimely death, he must have been a very proud man because it is obvious that not only is this a home-grown masterpiece of musical theatre, but also because his peers in a company so close to his native home were able to bring his work so vividly to life.

I cannot praise this well-paced, slick and seamless production enough as there was not a weak link in it.

The key to its success was the amazing team work and high degree of integration, even down to a style of integration within the set (i.e. the hidden smoke machines, the ship's gangway being concealed within the walls and the car seat that metamorphosed into a coffin for Collins).

The fact that this was an amazing period piece of Irish history … and there was not a single Dublin tenement house in sight sums up the inventiveness and originality of John O'Donoghue's Set Design.

The dark brick-work set wrapped around the walls of the proscenium arch with iconic imagery of the period, including photographs, an Abbey Theatre bill poster and a representation of the Proclamation. With entrances and stone upstage steps at the sides and a central upstage door, this was a totally functional open box-set.

It also boasted an inventive second centrally-positioned stage platform (for the play within a play) with sliding doors, which were used for projections, usually newspaper headlines.

Combining with the lighting and smoke, this was a visually atmospheric design, which greatly added to the success and to the pace of the production.

Although there was lots of fragmentation within the gritty story and amongst the characters, the full integration of all parts of this production offered its audience a single experience that was total theatre at its best.

Director, Christine Scarry, her team and the entire company brought so many highlights to this production, including the atmospheric opening with its busy stage activity during the Prologue with smoke and three dancers who were joined by the ensemble, while the mystical figure, Mother Ireland, appeared centre stage above.

The Celtic music for the Act 1 finale, Every Heart Awaken, was real stirring stuff, while the short cameo by Se Nicholson, as the Volunteer, was simply stunning here and the slow motion ambush scene in Revolution was well-achieved.

In the show programme, Musical Director, Conductor and Chorus Master, Patrick Clancy's six musicians are referred to as a Band and between them they overcame the vast challenge that was supplying the varied music for this busy, almost sung-through score. There were many highlights under Clancy's direction, including the atmospheric pipe opening of the lament in the Prologue; the robust playing of the full Irish flavoured music in the rousing number, Price To Be Paid; and the stirring interpretation of the Celtic music for the Act 1 finale, Every Heart Awaken. Choral work was to the fore also with the strong manly vocals in Prison Song and the great male chorus of the call to arms, Fly The Flag Of Freedom, which began with piano accompaniment before building up musically and vocally to a stirring anthem, sung with anger, conviction and commitment.

Choreographer, Gemma Grant ensured a high standard of choreography throughout and, although it was more about movement and positioning than big production routines, her concepts were well-executed and all groupings, positioning, movement and integration was excellent at all times.

While there were many choreographic highlights, a key feature was the vast array of lovely groupings, particularly the nice picture endings in most musical numbers.
