Michael Hayes portrayed Michael Collins as a strong man who was a public speaker and a fighter out of pure conviction. Although he was cocky and joked at times, he insisted that he was a soldier and not a negotiator and, frustrated at what he had to do, was a most reluctant negotiator.

Hayes really captured all of these character traits in a great performance, which also displayed Collins' softer, gentler and romantic side during the big romantic duet, Our Love Will Never End, and with his genteel dancing during Collins in London. This was a very strong performer and singer.

Tall and thin in stature, Ciaran Dunphy was a very realistic looking Eamon De Valera and perfectly captured his character's growing confrontation with Collins.

While his first appearance showed the human side of his character, Dunphy's clear and precise performance throughout soon highlighted the controlling aspects of his character's nature. Indeed, this was a most controlled and convincing piece of acting, while his patter-style vocal was exactly what one would imagine this character to sound like in song.

As Collins' friend and his rival for Kitty, Eoghan Fingleton's interpretation of Harry Boland was that of a stubborn man who would not entertain any reconciliation with Collins. This performer made a great job of this.

As Collins' girl, Kitty Kiernan, Kevina Hayes delivered some beautiful soft vocals and her romantic relationship with Collins was very believable. As the mythical Mother Ireland ('Kathleen Ni Houlihan'), Delia Larkin was the almost ever-present figure who watches over her country and guides her sons to do what is right for her and, overlooking the action in both the Collins story and the parallel staging of the play within a play, she was a vital link between the two. This performer and her physical appearance successfully achieved this.

In addition to their respective roles in the parallel staging of the play within a play by the Abbey Players, the four Players - Declan Taylor, Kevin Reade, Nicola Brennan and Sarah Brennan - also acted as a chorus of narrators in the Collins story. Performing in total unison at times, they were a strong grouping and brought a lot to this production with excellent diction and amazingly good vocals.

Gerry Taylor's Lighting Design ensured that the atmospheric lighting was never less than brilliant. There was perfect plotting and all performers were always in their correct position for specific lighting moments.

Other solid off-stage support came from: Stage Manager, Seamus Reade, and team; Properties Master, Bill Kennedy; Star Systems' sound mix; Costume Co-ordinators, Claire Gibbs and Sarah Brennan; and Val Sherlock, Catriona Barrett and Emma McGuinness' hair and make-up.

I truthfully could not suggest anything to improve on this production as there wasn't anything that I did not like.

As the most staged show of the season, there have been many innovations to, and variations of, Sir Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice's early rock opera, Jesus Christ Superstar.

Boasting an energetic young company and large ensemble, this production by Loughrea Musical Society was by far the darkest and grittiest interpretation of all.

Director and choreographer, Peter Kennedy - who also turned in a powerful performance as Pontius Pilate - installed an almost frantic pace to this brutally realistic and hard-hitting production.

It was a very edgy, contemporary, urban, violent, disturbing and threatening piece of theatre and, more than anything … it rocked! Surprisingly, this was the first time that Kennedy had ever tackled this popular title and it showed a whole new side of the man; both as a director and as a performer.

For here, there was little to laugh about as Kennedy's trademark double entendres and comical send- ups were replaced by a much more mature approach which got to the heart of the piece to reveal the harsh reality of it all.

(Perhaps, this modern take on this one-time controversial show could see the arrival of a new, more serious Kennedy? - I doubt it, as even the namesake of this show would probably need to call for divine intervention to achieve that miracle!) With its use of metal fencing, graffiti on walls and a cityscape backdrop, Peter Kennedy's dark Set Design was very urban with a rough edge and could easily have come straight from a production of West Side Story or Grease.

There were side aprons and steps up either side to an up-stage balcony platform with black side flats and a large ramp running down into the middle aisle of the auditorium.

With a blinding cross of lights, the Overture boasted an on-stage guitarist to reinforce the fact that this was a rock opera, while the character introductions took place under fixed spots as busy stage activity, including violence and graffiti spray painting, unfolded to set the mood of this interpretation.

The large cross was carried through the audience along the brightly lit middle aisle during Heaven On Their Minds, while, at the end of two of her songs, Everything's Alright and I Don't Know How To Love Him, Mary left the stage with Jesus, which reinforced the strength of their relationship more than normal.

The ensemble entrance through the audience at the start of Hosanna was joyous and infectious and helped to bring the audience closer into the show, while the backlighting at the end of this song was suitably threatening for the violent dispersal. Judas joining in with Could We Start Again Please was unusual as he normally would not have a prominent role in this song, yet - leading up to his death - it was most appropriate that he was involved with the sentiments of this song. This was a nice innovation.

The realistic cries with each hammer blow during the Crucifixion was harrowing to listen to and having the ensemble echoing Jesus' tortuous breathing pattern as he was dying was a great way of highlighting his pain and what he went through for us.

Everything about this production had a hard edge to it, and - in keeping with this approach - Musical Director and Conductor, Shane Farrell, and his ten-piece orchestra, ensured that the rock-inspired score of this rock opera was loud, in your face and always rocking.

Indeed, special mention must go to the very enthusiastic percussionist, Terry Cooke and drummer, Pat Corless for their outstanding work, particularly during the Overture and in the gritty version of Gethsemane, and - despite the success of the work of these musicians - also to Shane Farrell for managing to sustain a good stage/pit balance throughout.

Chorus Mistress, Martha O'Toole, was taking no chances with her choral work being overshadowed by the loud score and opted for an additional seven-piece pit choir to assist those on stage.

Choreographer, Peter Kennedy, supplied many varied routines here and this young company had no problems in executing his energetic dance moves, which - combined with some great movement, groupings, positioning and integration - ensured the realisation of his, sometimes, rough-edged concepts.

Although he had clear conversational vocals from the start as Jesus, Alan Greaney proved that he could also express both confusion and anger and his gritty interpretation of Gethsemane took him through many emotions in song.

With good acting skills and powerful and wide-ranging vocals, Shane Kelly was a great Judas who captured his character's confusion and anger.

We could see his initial troubled annoyance become frustration before turning to anger and despair. Vocally, he provided many highlights and it was nice to hear him joining in with Could We Start Again Please as, so close to his own suicide, the sentiments of the song were relevant.

As Mary Magdalene, Althea Kerr's pop-inspired vocals worked here because of the show's interpretation being so modern.

Amazingly, this was this performer's first show and her great vocals ensured that she made an impressive debut.

Peter Kennedy's interpretation of Pilate was a revelation. It offered a surprisingly strong and believable performance and some amazing vocals from a performer who is rarely associated with serious roles.

In Pilate's Dream, he provided good clear vocals before becoming serious and commanding in Pilate And Christ and, finally, turned in a powerful performance during Trial By Pilate.

The role of King Herod is a difficult one to sell in a few minutes, but Declan J Gardiner did well her with good vocals as the flamboyant mocker.

Fr. Mike Byrnes gave an impressive performance as Peter with a very strong denial scene showing both fear and regret.

His duet with Mary, Could We Start Again Please, was a highlight because of the strong vocals and excellent harmonies.

Off-stage support from Stage Manager, Justin Lynch and team; Props Mistress, Catherine Hynes; Recks Audio's sound mix; the company for the costumes; and the Hair & Make-Up team - Joanne Kelly/Waves Hair Salon plus Maude Mahony, Ethna Mahoney, Connie Bolton, Maureen Conway and Madeline Fleming - was all impressive.

Paul Kelly's Lighting was, generally very good, but - with an appropriate dark edge (using a lot of back-lighting to create a threatening atmosphere, at times) - it was, rightly, more about bringing the director's interpretation to life than being attractive.

The venue for this production, Newcastle's Annesley Hall, was undoubtedly the smallest on this year's adjudication circuit and this company, which is lucky enough to own the venue, is one of the scheme's smallest companies.

However, proving that 'big' isn't always best, this very funny show by Richard Morris, Dick Scanlan and Jeanine Tesori was given impressive direction by Gary Warnock here and succeeded on a lot of levels, particularly music, choreography, characterisation, comedy and set- design.

Carol-Anne McKay's set design was both clever and functional with central double doors and brick wall flats around the stage and side exits for the opening street scene.

The set opened to reveal a minimal setting for various scenes - all well- dressed with flats and props - and was easily and quickly changed to the lobby of the hotel, a laundry room, an insurance office, a penthouse and a speakeasy, when required.

Projections were used for scene descriptions and translations, while - to aid pace - a black gauze was used for downstage action while the next scene was set.

There was a New York skyline from the windows in the penthouse and the hotel lift looked authentic with its small inside lighting and the window ledge scene was positioned downstage, stage right.

This was a well-cast, well-paced and well-directed production with a great cast of Principals; all with particularly good diction.

Projected imagery of the period helped to set the mood during the Overture, while the stage activity was a visual introduction to the characters.

There was great choreography during The Speed Test using the speed of the tap shoes to reflect the speed of the typing in this good ensemble piece, while the dance on the window ledge during I Turned The Corner / Falling In Love With Someone Reprise was a great concept and was well executed. Musical Director and Conductor, Gareth McGreevy, and his 11-piece orchestra were positioned above the set and, with mainly jazz-orientated instrumentation, made a great job of the varied score and managed to maintain a good performer/orchestra balance throughout.

Despite this venue's general space restrictions and height limits that prevented there being a variation of performance levels, Choreographer, Timmy Bell, came up with well- realised concepts for routines in this production and his work on integration, movement, positioning and groupings were all good.

This young choreographer showed a lot of promise here and his hard- work threw up a lot of memorable moments and there was a high degree of teamwork on display throughout this production from an enthusiastic ensemble.

Emma Nugent was a funny and energetic Millie Dillmount with a sense of humour and lots of charisma.

She displayed good acting skills, great facial expressions and impressive comic timing, especially with her comical body movements, and all combined to make her a noteworthy comedienne.

In addition, she was a good dancer, especially in her comic routines and offered strong, controlled and expressive vocals during both Jimmy and Gimme Gimme.

Allen Gordon was a carefree and self-assured Jimmy Smith with a good voice and displayed his vocal talents well in What Do I Need With Love?, while Emma-Jane McKnight was a suitably posh and refined Dorothy Brown with a lovely voice and clear diction, both while singing and speaking.

Seamus Rooney was a pompous and suave-looking boss as Trevor Graydon.

Nicely dressed, with red braces and spats, he delivered a great patter- style vocal in The Speed Test.

With heavy make-up and a good, if stereotypical, accent, Careen Starkey was an appropriately villainous Mrs Meers and provided confident vocals during They Don't Know plus good comic timing throughout.

With appropriately glittery accessories, Bronagh Killough's Muzzy Van Hossmere looked the part and offered some powerful vocals on the big old-style ballad, Only In New York, while Aedin Hoey gave a great comic performance as the stern office manager, Miss Flannery, and was suitably bossy, outspoken and loud.

Meanwhile, there was thoroughly good off-stage support from Stage Manager, Suzanne Smyth, and her team; Properties Team - Lesley Craig, Emma-Jane McKnight and Suzanne Smyth; Geoff Clarke and Dean Hamilton's sound; Sean Keenan and Pat Brady's lighting; Wardrobe Mistress, Attracta Campbell; Lesley Craig's make-up; and Gordon Donaldson's hair care.

Many years ago, I spent a week of my annual holiday in Portmarnock … so, although this was my first time catching this particular show, it was my second 'Summer Holiday' in the North Dublin resort.

For me, it was a night of nostalgia from the start, but, if the smiling faces in the audience were anything to go by, then once the hit-filled Overture started, this was also a nostalgic night for many others too. Based on the original 1963 film with stage adaptation by Michael Gyngell and Mark Haddigan and orchestrations by Keith Strachan, this 'catalogue' show full of many hits by Cliff Richard (about a trans- European trip on a London bus) was positively bursting with musical memories for those of a certain age (yes, there are a few of us still around!).

Directed by Declan Keane and Co- Director, Breid Morris, this was a well-paced version of this light- hearted slice of musical fun, which remains every bit as corny as the original film.

Staged in a function lounge of a local sports club with its many restrictions on space and its total lack of theatrical facilities, the chances of this production being a serious contender in this year's adjudication scheme seemed as remote as the story's group of young bus mechanics actually driving a London bus to Athens.

Yet, like the successful, if eventful, trip in the piece, this young company of performers and all involved with this production also made it a success.

Indeed, this performance was also eventful, for, not long after the show had started, a fire alarm went off and I must admit to having been a bit concerned in terms of health & safety that, instead of being evacuated, the old adage 'the show must go on' came into play, as everyone on stage continued with the performance. We were later relieved to find out that it had all been a false alarm and, in hindsight, I must congratulate the company for its professionalism in not being 'put off' by the incident. Due to the enforced restrictions of the venue, Sinead McDonald's Set Design took the minimal approach almost to the extreme.

As a sports hall function room, the venue was totally lacking in any theatrical facilities and, by necessity, the setting was on a wide and open, low-platform style stage. It had little depth and just plain flat walls with a few tables and chairs stage-right to represent a café area with central doors, which would reveal the centre piece, the London bus.

What looked like a painting of a double-decker bus on a piece of scenery was both clever and good. The flat panels of the bus came off to leave a symbolic theatrical performance space inside the vehicle, complete with seats, table, stairs to the imaginary upper-level and even a shower.

Like the set design, Darren Kelleher's lighting options were greatly restricted by the venue's lack of space and low ceiling levels.

So, a minimal approach was adopted again here with mostly fairly basic bright lighting, good use of spots, some gobos (clouds, church window etc) and a mirror ball, while The Young Ones had nice atmospheric lighting with smoke.

In Summer Holiday, the representation of the movement of the bus was achieved by moving the various passers-by … and not the motionless bus.

It was also clever to have the broken down car made up of individual block shapes, which quickly became the girls' luggage when they opted to travel by bus.

We Say Yeah! provided a fun Act 1 finale and it was nice and natural to see a few of the more mature members of the ensemble reliving their youth and dancing along to the music, which also helped self- conscious members of the audience to relax and enjoy the music.

Representing the various countries on the journey by cast members waving the respective hand flags (France, Switzerland, Italy and Greece) was a simple but effective idea.

Do You Wanna Dance? was an undoubted highlight. As a fun celebratory wedding reception dance, this scene was lively and energetic and included the full ensemble and I particularly liked the end freeze-frame grouping like the guests in a wedding group picture. The all-white curtain call for On The Beach was suitably summer- like, while the all-singing and all- dancing Medley Finale was one big, bright sing-a-long with full cast and audience members all joining in - a great impact to send all home happy! With no space for a normal pit in front of the stage, Musical Director, Conductor and Chorus Mistress, Marian Mullen, and her band were positioned stage-right beside the audience.

With over 30 hits in the mostly up- tempo score, they were kept busy not only playing the authentic pop- based music (although there were some jazz and country influences too) but also supplying the many instrumentals played either between scenes or as underscoring for dialogue (e.g. the guitar-based instrumental, Foot Tapper), while managing to sustain a good stage/ pit balance throughout.

Although not a great show for highlighting good choral work, musical highlights included the soft and gentle Doo-Wop version of Living Doll and the gentle ballad, The Next Time, complete with underscoring for the proposal.

Despite the venue's very low ceiling, Choreographer, Roisin Walsh didn't allow it to totally restrict high jumps and lifts when they were needed, but, with no level variations available, her groupings and positioning of the ensemble was limited and, by necessity, was unavoidably linear in approach.

Although good, sadly, Walsh's concepts and ideas during dance routines were kept reasonably simple due to the space restrictions offered by this venue and the performers had no problem in achieving them. Being a catalogue show, this musical was a simple bit of fun and entertainment with no depth to either the story or to the characters and, as such, there was no great demand on the cast (apart from energetic dancing). Suffice to say that all did well in their respective roles.

While Props and Costumes were supplied by members of the company, Stage Manager, Mary Murphy, Sound engineer, Jodi Trehy's and Beth Kelly and stylists from Peter Mark's hair and make-up all deserve a mention for their solid off-stage support.

Finally, I felt it was most appropriate that the fire-alarm incident at the start of this show was caused by a barbecue in the building … well; you do expect the odd barbecue during a Summer Holiday!

Hidden away in a small side street in Clonmel, the small and intimate White Memorial Theatre is proudly owned by the society itself and boasts good, if restricted, facilities and a permanent display of past productions and of the company's great history.

While the overall size of the performing space was relatively small and caused a few problems with entrances and exits - especially for such a large ensemble piece as Jerry Bock and Sheldon Harnick's popular musical, Fiddler On The Roof - Michael O'Donoghue's production was given some nice touches to ensure a reasonably good pace. Directed by O'Donoghue (who was also responsible for the choreography and lighting design), this production, which was as traditional as its central character's religious beliefs, offered particularly strong performances from its orchestra, chorus and leading man. Apart from two extended aprons over the orchestra (both narrow but running deep into the auditorium), height restrictions prevented any variation of levels for groupings or positioning in Diarmuid Vaughan's wood-based set.

Complete with a window (with concealed lighting) for the Fiddler, a Star Of David on the floor and on the door of the house against a painted rural village scene backdrop, there was great detail in this set with slates on the roof of the buildings, trees and lots of small effective props. The house fronts were cleverly hinged to reveal internal house scenes, while the bed was integrated into the set.

The scene was well set before the start with various performers gradually coming on, one by one, and engaging in normal village activities, complete with the sound effect of chickens, while it was a nice touch having performers pretending to be musicians at the wedding. It is always a realistic touch to include children in a show like this, but having one eating an apple was just so natural and there was some great attention to detail in costumes and props and I liked the fact that Golde had flour on the table when she was baking and that she was also throwing authentic-looking 'chicken feed' on the ground when feeding them.

The building of suspense as a new arrival is rumoured at Motel's house was well-achieved, while Sabbath Prayer was well staged with an authentic looking ensemble and great choral work.

Tevye and the Fiddler doing a short routine during Tevye's Monologue worked well and I liked how Motel gained sudden confidence in song during Miracle Of Miracles.

The Dream was well-staged with nice ghostly images and lots of white costumes and blue light, followed by great colour-changing lighting, and while Far From The Home I Love is always a highlight in this show, here a simple touch like the sound of the train provided added poignancy to the song at the end.

Do You Love Me? was another highlight here and I liked the fading light at the end of the song with a simple spot as both Tevye and Golde realised that they did love one another, while the plodding musical beat depicting 'going nowhere fast' was very good in the final scene and the sound effect of the wind helped to convey the hopelessness of the situation.

The music and choral work spearheaded by Musical Director, Conductor and Chorus Mistress, Laura Cotter, and her 10-piece orchestra was the backbone of this production.

Together, they provided not only lots of underscoring during dialogue and scene changes, but also a fairly traditional interpretation of the score, a good stage/pit balance throughout and some lovely musical moments. Anatevka was an undoubted musical highlight as it was sung with both affection and anger and was accompanied by good choral work. Indeed, the standard of choral work was high throughout, particularly during Prologue/Tradition, Sabbath Prayer, Sunrise Sunset, while the male chorus ensured a rousing finish to the up-tempo and joyful, To Life. Although I would have liked to have seen a little more height variation in terms of groupings and positioning on the main stage, there was certainly good use of the high side aprons when possible and integration was good throughout.

However, movement was, generally, restricted due to a small performance space and a very large ensemble. Despite this, Choreographer, Michael O'Donoghue did coax some memorable routines, including: the choreography in To Life reflecting the rivalry between the soldiers and the locals.

Diarmuid Bolger was a really good Tevye. He was laid back and easy going and gave a very natural performance with great diction and a great accent.

He came across as very convincing and devout during Sabbath Prayer, while offering confident vocals throughout, especially in If I Were A Rich Man, while Elaine Bowe was suitably bossy and impatient as Golde.

Meanwhile, off-stage support came from Stage Manager, Diarmuid Vaughan; Properties Manager, Robert Donlan; Pat Marnane's overall sound mix; Michael O'Donoghue's lighting design; Nomac's costuming and Wardrobe-Co-ordinator, Anne O'Connor; and the Hair & Make-up Team - Ruth Butler, Marie Crowe, Grainne Boyle-Ryan, Fiona Murphy and Alison McNamara.

Having sold out long before opening night, tickets for this show were in high demand. No doubt, this was partly due to the company's reputation for quality following its success in winning the 'Best Overall Show' award with its previous outing.

No pressure at all for this talented group though, for, again, it easily lived up to all expectations with this production and sent everyone home singing its praises (or praising its singing!).

And deservedly so, for this was a fine example of total team work in action with John Donnelly's strong direction making sure that everyone (and not just the nuns) was 'singing from the same hymn sheet'.

Alan Menken and Glen Slater's musical comedy, Sister Act, is a very funny show and the comedy was delivered with good timing throughout which, no doubt, added to its success, as did the choreography and choral work.

After the show, I overheard one lady say that it was 'like a West-End show', and she was right - for this production (and a few others on this year's adjudication circuit) boasted high production values and had a high degree of visual impact.

By necessity, this show requires a large ensemble and, despite this, Donnelly - with more than a little help from good stage management - was able to maintain a fast pace in this production.

Although the set had the luxury of having fly facilities, Scenic Projects' set design did not overuse this facility and came up with numerous set pieces for various scenes that were all functional enough to help with the fast-pace of this production. These varied from the lit-up club sign to the police station with its big desk to the 'church window' flats in the down-stage performance space with an opening centre revealing a gate, a bronze cross and a deeper stage.

The massive hanging backdrop of the Last Supper, appropriately in the nun's dining room, was authentic, as was the many formations of well-lit stained-glass windows and the giant statue of Our Lord.

Authenticity was also a key element of the Bar scene, with its Christmas decorations, bottles and real jukebox. There was good use of flats for changing position in down- stage scenes, which was good as the one weakness of the set design was that there was no variation of performance levels.

With its 70s male vocal band routines, When I Find My Baby was a highlight and was used well as a distraction for a scene change, while the scene change at the end with bar patrons bringing on the bar as they danced to the previous song worked really well and added to the pace of the show.

Another highlight was the soulful fantasy ballad, I Could Be That Guy, when timid Eddie became a white- suited soul star (complete with deep soulful vocals replacing his high- pitched vocals) and delivered a good disco routine with the homeless street people. This was an excellent transformation scene.

The Act 1 finale, Take Me To Heaven (Reprise) had well-lit stained glass windows and a massive statue of Our Lord, which, along with the altar boys with real candles and the smell of real incense, added great authenticity to the piece.

This rousing all-singing all-dancing finale also boasted great integration and varied choreography and I particularly loved the 'Sign Of The Cross' movement to the beat.

The big Studio 54 production number, Fabulous Baby (Reprise) was a great ensemble piece and was well balanced between the celestial singing of the nuns on either side and energetic activities of the disco boys and girls.

The bright and colourful costumes and lights and energetic dancing all added to the atmosphere.

The relatively modern and soul- filled score offered lots of musical input and made life busy for the hard-working Musical Director and Conductor, Fintan Cleary, and Chorus Mistress, Eithne Corrigan. Together with his 14-piece orchestra and Corrigan's well-drilled chorus, there was a lovely pit/stage balance (after initial sound problems) and there were many highlights under Cleary's musical direction.

Corrigan ensured that choral work here was always strong, particularly during the ballad, I Could Be That Guy, while the chorus had a difficult job going from having to sing badly to singing with confidence in Raise Your Voice and the increased choral conviction in Sunday Morning Fever when they hear that they are going to sing for the Pope was well realised. Choreographer, Nicole McDonald had her work cut out for her having to deal with such a large ensemble and in the absence of any height variations within the set design for groupings. However, she did a great job and, despite the disco-orientated nature of the music, managed to vary her energetic routines with lots of gospel choir-styled arm movements. To this end, her concepts were well realised by the enthusiastic ensemble and, although linear by necessity, her groupings, positioning and general movement went a long way in ensuring some great integration at times.

Claudia Kariuki came across as the real deal in the role of wannabe diva, Deloris Van Cartier, as she was loud with a lot of street cred and had good comic timing.

Her soulful vocals ensured that she could not only belt out the big production numbers but was also capable of doing justice to slow ballads like the title song.

With old-style traditional values, Siobhan Meyler Fawsitt captured the character of Mother Superior, who tries to be firm and patient but is being pushed to the limit so much that she begins to doubt her faith. She was a good singer and delivered nicely controlled vocals in Here Within These Walls.

Maggs Jacob had no problems in the role of the shy and meek young postulant, Sister Mary Robert, and proved that there was nothing shy about her vocal range when she came out of her shell with a beautiful voice in her song of regret, The Life I Never Had.

With her good comic timing, Catherine Walsh was a lot of fun as the loud and witty Sister Mary Patrick, while Marian O'Leary was suitably loud with a great New York accent in the role of Sister Mary Lazarus. With a dry, quirky sense of humour and good comic timing, she may have fancied herself as a musical director but was more of a hip hop rapper.

Des Whelen's Monsignor O'Hara really was a stereotypical Irish priest. He was laid-back, gentle and unruffled at all times and, although softly spoken, delivered good diction and good comic timing throughout, while George Lawlor was a good singer and performed well as the sleazy club-owning head con-man, Curtis, with a funny and violent personality.

Tony Carty was really good and suitably awkward as Eddie, the hapless, nervous cop who lacks confidence. However, when his high- pitched voice was replaced by deep soulful vocals in the fantasy ballad, I Could Be That Guy, he became that soul star.

The soulful sisters in this divine musical were also well-supported by a lot of other talented angels in the heavenly back-up crew, including Stage Manager, Colin Murphy; Props Mistress, Emma Kehoe; Sound man, Jason Fallon's; Aidan McGrath's lighting; Wardrobe Mistress, Anne Reck and her team - Marie Brady, Maria Ruthledge, Jacinta Roche, Elaine Murphy, Dolores Kavanagh and Yvonne McGuire; and Pauline Roche's Hair & Make-up department.

To say that Newbridge Musical Society's production of Lionel Bart's Oliver! was busy would be an understatement, as this production boasted what was easily the largest cast of any show in this year's adjudication scheme.

Fielding such a large and wide- ranging ensemble (literally, aged from 8 years old to 80 years old), Director, Sharon McNamara, made full use of every inch of space on the multi-level set and vastly extended stage in this college hall and her firm direction - combined with sterling work in choreography and stage management - ensured that, against the odds, this remained a well-paced and traditional version of the popular show.

Tom Kavanagh, John O'Brien and Phil MacSheoinin's visually-pleasing multi-level set was deceiving in that it looked more complex than it actually was and, in fact, was a lot more functional than it first appeared. Vastly extended to cope with the extra large ensemble, it consisted of aprons on either side, with wide steps stage-right into the auditorium and a symbolic fly-bridge across the front of the stage at the start.

Very Dickensian in look, it had lots of brickwork on the main set with small level platforms mid stage and a wooden step structure with a crossover bridge at the higher level, while a smoking chimney pot was a nice touch to represent foggy London.

Food, Glorious Food was one of many examples of when the production team achieved the almost impossible by having a very disciplined ensemble positioned at all levels and filling all spaces with particularly good use of the front stage steps for both positioning and for mass exits and entrances through the auditorium.

The young choral work here was impressive not only because of the age of the children but also because they had to deal with some intense movement while singing.

Played for laughs, I Shall Scream, was successful not only due to the clear diction and good voices of the performers, but because it was risqué and saucy for the adults on one level and just funny in a silly way for the more innocent viewer - very well achieved.

I liked the use of projection in numbers like Boy For Sale and, particularly, the way that Bumble and Oliver's walk to the upper level and back again was used as a distraction for a scene change.

The nice yellow down-lighting when Fagin got his treasures as the urchins were asleep was effective and atmospheric.

Who Will Buy? was very well staged using five solo singers positioned on differing levels with Oliver and Mrs Bedwin watching them from the window.

Having these singers being individually lit was also very effective and combined well with the most amazing vocals to make this a truly visual and musical highlight.

The reprise of Reviewing The Situation provided a great ending with London projected and both Fagin and Dodger silhouetted against the lit skyline was such a nice touch.

Musical Director, Conductor and Chorus Mistress, Margaret Hayes-Mahon, and her 10-piece orchestra provided not only lots of underscoring during dialogue and scene changes, but also a fairly traditional interpretation of the score, a good stage/pit balance throughout and some lovely musical moments. Following a short Overture, there was good choral work from the young ensemble while That's Your Funeral was played at a slower tempo than normal and there was a nice change in the arrangement of Consider Yourself to suit the bigger ensemble.

Choreographer, Julianne McNamara's concepts were good and well-executed and the groupings, positioning, movement and integration were all well-handled with particularly good use of space and all levels.

This was even more successful when one considers the extra challenge here of having such a vast number of people fielded in the ensemble and the very young age of some of the cast.

The key to McNamara's success is that she knows how important it is to have, visually, nice groupings and her 'picture' groupings at the end of most songs were always very effective.

In the title role, young Kyle Dunne was suitably pale and timid, while showing a lot of promise, especially with his vocals, while Graham Butler Breen, who shared the part of Dodger with Elliot Nolan, made a good job of the role.

With his long red coat, Conor Kilduff really was a good Fagin, and while his character may have been leading his young charges astray in the piece, this experienced performer had a lovely way with him.

He not only kept a fatherly eye on the younger cast members but also brought the audience into things by asking boys and girls in the audience questions on occasions. His vocal interpretation of Reviewing The Situation made it a highlight.

With her amazingly expressive vocals, Deirdre Moloney's gin- drinking, loud voiced cockney, Nancy, could have been straight out of Eastenders.

She provided a great vocal build-up in her heartfelt version of As Long As He Needs Me, when she also proved that she has the rare ability to sing in character, while her powerhouse vocal work in songs like It's A Fine Life and Oom-Pah-Pah ensured that they too were also highlights. Overall, this was an outstanding performance.

Padraigh Munnelly was suitably well-dressed, authoritative, large and loud as Mr. Bumble, while Gill O'Brien was a large, voluptuous Widow Corney with a great laugh and a great voice.

With his pale makeup, limp, top hat with black ribbons and tails and tape measure around his neck, Keith Domican looked every inch the opportunistic, but hen-pecked undertaker, Mr. Sowerberry, while Louise Moore - who also doubled as a singing vendor - was suitably bossy as Mrs. Sowerberry.

With great expressive vocals and controlled singing, Martin Hennessy's Bill Sykes was suitably threatening, while her gentle vocals in the reprise of Where Is Love ensured that Cora Coffey made a good impact in the smaller role as Mrs. Bedwin.

Off-stage support from Stage Manager, Tom Kavanagh; Props Master, Tony Bird; Noel Ryan's sound mix; Liam Fitzgerald's lighting; Andrew Reddy and Utopia's costumes; Margaret O'Connor's hair design and the make-up team, Kirstie Duggan, Robyn Campbell, Aideen Stanley, Niamh O'Sullivan, Laura Duffy and Rachel Duffy, was all impressive.

Finally, with so many young performers displaying such a high standard of enthusiasm, commitment and talent, I feel that this company has a bright future for many years to come.

Some Irish societies stage their productions in old cinemas. Banbridge Musical Society takes things a step further and stages theirs in a working picture house. Some societies up and down the island stage premieres each season. Banbridge create and develop theirs. And so, the Northern Ireland, the Irish and indeed, the world premiere of Titanic Serenade came to pass at the Iveagh Movie Studios in the Co Down town in the middle of May. The group backed director Leonard Anderson and musical director Colin Loughead in turning Belfast playwright Stewart Love's 30-year- old work "Titanic" into a musical. Messrs Anderson and Loughead penned a couple of original numbers for the show and then completed the score by fusing old Belfast street songs, hymns and popular pieces of the time with the book.

In footballing parlance Titanic Serenade is a game of two halves with Act One depicting the often hard lives of the Belfast workers who built the ship while the second act tells of the liner's only voyage and its sinking through the eyes of the crew and passengers in a show that has 34 featured parts.

While some characters are common to both parts of the tale - Edward Orr's visionary but cowardly Bruce Ismay, Ian Davidson's solemn Thomas Andrews, the man credited with completing the plans for the doomed ship and the boyish Joe of Adam Maginnis, a shipyard apprentice and part of the Harland and Wolff Guarantee crew who sailed and perished with Titanic - Mr Anderson used a linking device in the shape of  the excellent Anthony Fitzpatrick as the narrator Harry, popping up around east Belfast at first before becoming a waiter on the ship.

Appropriately for a show staged in a cinema Mr Anderson and Russell Caughey's set design made great use of projections with some famous stills of Titanic and the Harland's shipyard of the time and some terrific movie footage of early 20th Century Belfast including once sequence shot from the front of the top deck of a tram.

The other main plank in the settings platform was a metal gantry accessed by steps either side of the stage which added height to the scenes, particularly in the second half, and which allowed acres of room for Mr Anderson's flowing routines in a show that was stylishly staged and handsomely costumed. Rosemary Kelly, Orla Reynolds and Lorraine Jackson-Brown as Belfast housewives Cissie, Bella and Georgina, all headscarves and pinnies, caught the pathos and the often black humour of the city, Ms Kelly in the recurring dream of losing her son Joe to the sea and Ms Brown in a busy performance that culminated in a raucous scene Granny wouldn't approve of.

Stage veterans Ken Hamilton and Brendan Magee were impish as Belfast men Willie and Rabbie; Gerard Kerr will always have an opening as an evangelical preacher after his splendid turn as a street corner pastor while Chris Gorman touched in Lord Pirrie, head of Harland and Wolff, in an Act One cameo before having a ball as brash American Hiram on board Titanic. Dennis McKeever was a rich voiced Captain Smith; Scott Skelton was a suitably Scottish Murdoch while Aaron Frazer made an impressive debut as radio operator Phillips. Together with the experienced trio of Jacqueline Mathews, Pamela McCullough and Nicola Johnston they were the pivotal figures of Act Two.

The production featured 22 men, the biggest number the company has put on stage for many years as well as 20 women and six children.

Stewart Love, who was also watching on makes no claim to historical accuracy. Instead he says his tale "is an imaginative account of the conception, construction and loss of the greatest ship of its time". His original play was written at a time before the wreckage of the mighty ship was discovered and before Belfast embraced the legend of the liner as part of its booming tourist drive. While the show will resonate with Northern Ireland audiences with its heavy references to a Belfast of a bygone age, complete with its humour and songs, I'm unsure of how it will travel.

Five-year-old Olivia Pyper epitomised the cast of this Boublil and Schonberg blockbuster with a sure-footed portrayal of Tam, the son borne by Vietnamese orphan Kim to her American Marine lover, Chris Scott, after the fall of Saigon to the Viet Cong forces.

The child from a theatrical family mirrored the confident performances of a rapidly maturing teenage front line and with her pudding-bowl wig, cute costumes and mini Teddy Bear threatened to steal scenes from the excellent Kim of Ellen Whitehead. Miss Whitehead, only eleven years older than Olivia, had the looks, the voice and the acting ability to portray the young South Eastern Asian mother driven to suicide after realising she has lost the love of her life.

Connor Carson as Chris showed the full house at Belfast's MAC theatre why he has just taken up a place at hoping to pursue acting as a career, brought an air of menace and some fine timing to the role of the Engineer. Ellen Mawhinney, who has just gone to the Royal Conservatoire of Scotland to further her music studies, brought a big voice and a big performance to the part of Ellen, Matthew McConnell, a Birmingham- based drama student brought emotion and aggression in equal measure to the role of Thuy while the youngest principal, Newry-based Emma Martin as Gigi, got to show a Belfast audience her promise.

Dubliner Sean Hanratty, making his second successive appearance with the company, was a highly confident John. He was joined on his cross border excursion by Waterford's Holly Ryan who shared the role of Ellen with Miss Whitehead as well as the important backstage task of keeping Miss Pyper amused between scenes over the six performance run. Director James Huish turned the show's famous helicopter scene into a sensory experience with a wig rustling rush of wind in the auditorium following on closely from the first thump of the aircraft's heavy rotors as it came into land at Saigon's US Embassy compound.

The collaboration on the episode between Alastair Kerr's lighting desk, Jody Trehy's sound team and Claire Donnelly's stage crew was the highlight of a good night's work from the backroom boys.

Also behind the scenes on the night was Wilson Shields' 17-piece band, housed behind the stage because of the lack of an orchestra pit at the city's newest space. Underpinned by some of Belfast's finest musicians but including a sprinkling of young talent, they produced a big, rich sound with some excellent percussion and fine brass work. Tidy choreography from Kirsten Magee was also the order of the day in a show that was rapidly put together by way of a fortnight-long summer project with the cast of 62 selected from 320 auditionees.

However, in a production that even went to the trouble of importing licenced authentic deactivated period weapons for its rival combatants, it's a pity that the same attention to detail wasn't paid to some other areas.

Fusion Theatre Company presented their version of Miss Saigon to a packed auditorium, with a host of young people, drilled and musically trained to effect those dark days of Saigon falling.

An impressive group of young principals supported by a well-drilled chorus were, I'm afraid, not always supported by the technical team of "adults ".

The technical difficulties were in part over-come by this talented bunch of principals. Jessica Webb as Kim showed a vocal resilience with a lovely quality voice. She was well matched vocally by Adam Williamson - as Chris but mind the words, Jessica, and know what you are singing about. Matthew Quinn as John has strength and presence with another fine voice. He shapes the words beautifully as does Conor Taggart as Thuy - who really bowled me over. A fine tenor voice which can only get better in time. A rich mezzo is hard to come by today, but Megan McGarry as Ellen has it. With a little more training she should sort out the top of the voice; so she can slip through the passagio more easily.

Orchestrally we had, by today's standards, a large band of fourteen players covering all the colours you'd expect from this Schönberg score. Beautiful Sax playing from Davy Mayes with haunting oboe playing from Paul McCrisken added to the sound of this excellent orchestra. Bravo!

The main set had some nice detail with rattan reeds on the risers of the steps, the moving mechanical trucks were a nice touch for quick scene changes, but what goes on these rostra must be specific and detailed. A curtain with hooks on one end is not good enough as a part bedspread. Some tight entrances due to stage left and right being curtained to allow changes of the mechanical pieces which hampered, to some entrances and exits for the cast.

Production and conducting were in the hands of Ian Milford. The show moved very well from scene to scene allowing good pace and clarity. Musically, I felt we needed more gear changes of tempi to heighten and convey emotionally what these young actors were trying to tell us. I did miss some of the oriental gongs etc. like the tams in the opening needed to be more pronounced. Some very good work from this young chorus with individual lines clearly making a cohesive sound. It was strong with excellent diction. The company executed some lovely work choreographically from Rebecca Leonard, especially the blockbuster numbers of American Dream, Dju vui vai and The Morning of the Dragon. Well drilled with some nice inventive chorus movement throughout.

Lighting was a bit rocky throughout. Over lit scenes taking impact away from many sensitive moments, and poor key light missing in others. Great projection work with very apt images especially the Vietnamese children for Bui Doi.

Costumes had an array of sleazy girls to well dressed GI's - mind those boots and accessories - they are important. Kimonos are Japanese and should not have appeared in the wedding scene. Principals were generally well attended to but a greater eye on distinction between the two armies.

Certainly, there was a great night had by the audience in the auditorium with a standing ovation for these talented young performers.

It is always a pleasure to sit in the Grand Opera House, one of the best appointed and beautiful opera houses in Ireland. Ulster Operatic Company presented Oliver! to a packed and very enthusiastic audience. It is always encouraging to see so many young people in the audience to encounter this well-known Dickensian tale. Although a dark work, Lionel Bart certainly brings much needed relief through his music to lighten moments throughout a very difficult story of child slavery and Victorian views on society.

The curtain rose on the first few bars of music to reveal a set by Festival Productions which sat comfortably on the Opera House Stage. With the walls and different levels within the one structure, it wrapped around the stage giving plenty of nooks and crannies for the adventure to unfold. I found that the production team could have used this structure more, especially in the larger chorus scenes and also for the Fagin's den scenes with the children.

Chris Tingley brought some great playing from the orchestra with many colours being brought to the fore, Bumbles bassoon, the glock giving such momentum to the gruel scene, the beautiful solo violin playing in Reviewing the Situation. Tempi and pace moved each scene along briskly but never intruded. Well-judged throughout.

Costumes generally needed more detail as there were many different era's represented on stage. The gents faired worst with no breeches and tights (especially for Mr. Bumble) and modern day morning suits for Mr. Sowerberry and for Mr. Brownlow. Shoes / boots were also a mix and match affair and needed more attention, especially the boots worn by Nancy. She really should have had heels and not flats.

Prop dressing in this production overall could have been better, leaving some scenes very sparse. However, some excellent individual props peppered this production like the sellers, especially the Long Sheet Seller - he should hold this higher- show off great props like this and the Yoke with the two pails. Nice work here. Mind the silverware - the sheen from stainless steel really jarred with this period. The two beautiful chairs in Mr. Brownlow's showed off his position in society.

Some lovely effects were created with the lighting especially the night scenes and the use of the star cloth created much depth to the stage. There were scenes, however, over lit and I felt didn't match the mood of the storyline, like Nancy's death scene where the stage became bright, flat and one dimensional. Not enough key light in the return to Fagin's scene in Act 2 when Oliver is hauled back by Sykes.

Principals could all have had more help in creating their characters both physically and through the spoken word. Luc Burns playing the leading role sang beautifully in tune with clear diction at all times but was left standing statically for most of the night. Conall McKenna as Dodger burst onto the scene with great animation and voice projection, but that dreaded thing happened with his voice breaking, rendering him in no man's land vocally. A great little actor who gave his all. Nancy was played with strength throughout and didn't disappoint in her "As long as he needs me". A weak position for Bill Sykes entrance didn't give this actor the punch he required to establish himself within this production. Shane McCaffrey never really scared, as the character remained on one level throughout with little subtlety.

With a beautiful speaking voice, Kevin McReynolds suffered the same fate where the character didn't journey. Gerry McBrien as Bumble and Pamela Todd as the Widow Corney worked well together creating some welcome comic relief, while family life in the funeral parlor never quite got that uncomfortable feeling that Oliver had jumped from the frying pan into the fire. Theo McGeough as Noah looked well with good projection and accent though, I am not sure he would eat with a knife and fork!!!

Brian Trainor is such an intelligent actor. An excellent wig added greatly to his portrayal of Fagin. Accent was generally good but it dropped here and there. Energetic body language enabled him to move nimbly around the stage.  However, more could have been created for this character. He is so wily and mischievous, lovable yet dangerous. You were capable of so much more.

In depth characterization and animation was the key feature missing in almost all characters this evening. They never became flesh and blood. A young and fresh faced adult chorus sang lustily throughout. They projected well and diction, in general, was of a high standard. Some great work here by the Chorus Master. The Children's chorus was precise - just a little falling away from the beat in their opening number, nerves may have got to them as this was their first performance. I missed the hustle and bustle of London life, the busyness of "Fagin's Gang" never materialized resulting in static positions and little integration in their various scenes. Choreography by Brooke Allen created safe moves for the young company at her disposal, focusing on tried and tested dance routines that didn't challenge. This was such a missed opportunity. Many scenes were left "unmoved" forming semi- circles which did not enhance visually or integrate chorus's with-in scenes. The children were left un-aided in most of their scenes and left standing about.

Production by Syd Ralph missed many opportunities in character development that left her cast fairly one dimensional. The show flowed well from scene to scene but generally lacked punch and energy. The themes of this gem of a show were not explored at all. More detail was required in the various departments - costumes, props etc. - which can only come from and insisted upon by a director.

society_raw: David Hennessy Musical and, Dramatic Society
review_text:
Once upon a time the mere suggestion of murder in a Broadway show such as the seminal Show Boat was enough to cause controversy. Almost 20 years later Oscar Hammerstein the second was at it again provoking an outcry over a stage killing in Carousel.

More than 40 more years down the line and the body count in Stephen Sondheim's eerily dark Into The Woods reached Midsomer Murders proportions.

Hammerstein acolyte Sondheim's story of fused fairy tales could not be accused of leading with the heart. It is definitely a show for the head and at the very least it is thought provoking, if not disturbing.

It was a big change for many of the audience at Waterford's smart Garter Lane Arts Centre who didn't realise the psychological thrills and spills they were in for.

Some confessed they were more used to seeing David Hennessy's young but surprisingly mature cast in productions that come with a much larger dollop of sugar.

Not that that mattered much to Mr Hennessy as the director ensured that a couple of the killings were carried out in an almost brutal fashion on Dermot Quinn's highly functional three level set that boasted more timber than the average small forest.

The show, which was dedicated to Waterford's Brian Flynn, also looked well with older characters aged properly while others had their look adjusted as we went through the tale. Adam Phelan, a fine actor, played the lynchpin role of the Baker while the impressive Megan DeCourcey as his wife more than matched him in a performance that grew in stature as the evening went on.

Jessica Hackett was a beautiful Cinderella with an excellent voice while there were big vocal performances from Sinead O'Donovan as the Witch and Chloe McGrath as Rapunzel. Pocket dynamo Holly Ryan turned Little Red Riding Hood from a bouncing, wide eyed child into a knife wielding psycho after she and Ciara Giles' bloodthirsty Granny were rescued from the clutches of Evan Croke's Wolf.

Mr Croke brought different characteristics to the role of the animal and that of Cinderella's philandering Prince while Conor Clancy lent a mature voice to Rapunzel's Prince. Kerill Kelly had that necessary naivety that is required of Jack while Kayleigh Quinlan was suitably busy as the boy's worried mother.

Nathan Carey, the youngest in the cast, showed promise as the Narrator; David Power brought a sarcastic edge to the Mysterious Man and Jack Casey played the camp bureaucratic Steward who mopped his boss's brow too feverishly.

Katie King had excellent diction as both a stylish Stepmother and the voice of the giant and worked well with her daughters, Hayley O'Brien and Eilish McLaughlin, who had their double act off pat.

Carrie Mullane split her evening between playing Cinderella's demure mother and the leggy temptress Jack brings down from the skies while Aaron Mooney brought Milky White, the cow, to life.

At a time when some groups lavish vast sums on an orchestra, the highly experienced David Hayes and his assistant, Shane French, brought Sondheim's rich score to life using only two keyboards and a little light percussion in the intimate venue tucked away behind the city's quayside.

Two thirds of the way through this tale of fiery passions, fabulous costumes and false identification set against a showbiz background, Rory Robinson, one of the two gangsters of the parish, makes a 'phone call to his boss.

In the ensuing conversation he discovers that his chief has been disposed of; that he and fellow hood Paul Laycock have a new head honcho to answer to and realises that their mission to recover a debt has died with the late Don thus unveiling one of the big turning points of this Porter and Spewack show.

Before the audience at Blanchardstown's Draoicht Theatre got their head around all that, the experienced Mr Robinson made a small move that crystallised the attention to detail in Pat McElwain's production - he made as if to put money into the excellent wall mounted old-style payphone at the Baltimore theatre's stage door before dialling the number he was trying to reach. It might only be a small point but a highly realistic one nonetheless even if the mobile' phone generation wondered what he was up to.

Messrs Robinson and Laycock unquestionably made a great team, two sides of the one coin if you like, each with different characteristics well drawn by the two actors but unlike many of their predecessors in the roles they didn't steal the show.

That particular round of applause in this show about a show went to Jennifer McGann who gave us both a sweet-voiced Lilli and a volcanic Kate constantly on the edge of erupting who, of course, ends up with a sore backside for her trouble when her husband retaliates after being bit, punched and kicked.

Bronwyn Andrews was a bubbly Lois, a small package of vocal tricks and suggestion, as the Broadway hoofer given her big stage break as Bianca, Kate's second class sister.

Damien Hurley was very much in charge of the stage in both his guises as producer Fred Graham, the head of the touring theatre company and in his stage role as Petruchio while Stephan Ryan was an easy moving Bill/Lucentio.

Gavin Quigley was a loose limbed Paul opposite Orla Walsh's confident Hattie while Justin Parkes served up a world-weary Harry and a Baptista in constant bemusement and John Furlong, somewhat appropriately for an army general, gave us a commanding Harrison Howell.

John Cryan had great timing in the small but important part of Ralph while Jack Carolan and David Darmody touched in the roles of Hortensio and Gremio respectively.

They were backed by a hard working female dominated ensemble that worked up a sweat in numbers such as "Too Darn Hot", bringing choreographer Orla Savage's routines to life. The male chorus, though smaller in number, was powerful vocally and had its fair share of movers.

This handsomely dressed production of a show that is often sadly overlooked by professionals and amateurs alike, was played out on Scenic Projects well-crafted and highly functional set and driven along by musical director Yvonne McQuillan's excellent ten- piece band.

show_raw: Whisper it quietly but this is one
review_text:
of those Marmite shows that looks destined to become a cult classic. Avenue Q is not to everyone's taste, especially if you are over the age of 30 or if you weren't raised on American television programmes such as Sesame Street or South Park, aimed at adolescents who wear baseball caps back to front.

It's been on or off Broadway almost continuously now for more than 11 years and even with its uncompromising North American references has gained an increasing foothold on this side of the Atlantic. Because of the influence of America on western culture, it resonates with a young audience and one of the men behind it, Robert Lopez has made it big, teaming up with the creators of the aforementioned South Park to create Broadway and London's current smash, The Book of Mormon, and with his wife, penned the songs for the Disney behemoth Frozen, including the omnipresent anthem of the last 12 months, "Let it go".

Avenue Q's latest incarnation on these shores was at Navan's Solstice Arts Centre where it looked like the younger element of St Mary's Musical Society had staged a coup d'etat and was having a ball on stage.

With its heavy reliance on puppetry, it was a giant sideways leap for many of the cast from the last time I saw them in Rodgers and Hammerstein's South Pacific.

Kevin Fagan, a fine lyrical Joe Cable in that production, had much more scope here to display his acting ability portraying recent university graduate Princeton, who in quick succession has to come to terms with low-rent accommodation away from home, unemployment, relationships and that nagging imponderable, what are we all here for?

Danielle Williamson, a lovely Nellie Forbush in South Pacific, lent her excellent soprano voice to a wistful Kate Monster while Ronan Walsh, a cultured Emile de Becque, used his rich baritone to articulate the deep- voiced, immensely rich and sex- obsessed Trekkie Monster, a kind of twisted relation of the Honey Monster. Colin Flynn gave us an energetic version of the buttoned up Rod, the repressed gay of the street while Craig Regan was a likeable, messy Nicky who provided some of the vocal highlights in league with Mr Fagan and Miss Williamson Louise Cassidy let rip with a big seductive voice as the predatory nightclub singer Lucy the slut and Sean Flanagan adopted the strolling mannerisms and quirky speech patterns of former juvenile television star, Gary Coleman.

Emma Stowe was a bossy Christmas Eve badgering and bullying her slacker partner Brian, a confident Matt McGuirk.

Fiona Keenan and Eoin Kenny became a theatrical double act joined at the hip as those malevolent sprites, the Bad Idea bears, always encouraging the rest of the cast to misbehave and Siobhain Sanders O'Brien gave a lesson on how to make the most of a small part as a haughty Mrs Thistletwat.

Director Richie Hayes' production, with its highly colourful puppets, was staged on his brother John's set, extended to meet the wide space that is the Solstice and played to backing tracks.

By slipping in an autumn show staffed by its younger element, St Mary's must be in the running for the title of the busiest society in the country. They staged South Pacific last March, mounted a late summer cabaret run, launched into Avenue Q and have a pantomime and a spring show in the offing.

The power stage performers hold over audiences was brought home to me as I walked down the stairs of Dundalk's An Tain theatre at the end of this Colin Hughes' production.

A lady who had been sitting beside me had a smile on her face but tears in her eyes as she made her way into the foyer. While the show had moved her, she told me her father had played the role of Tevye with the Louth group many years ago and confessed she had been in two minds before the curtain rose about whether or not to come to the production because of the memories it would stir. However, in company with a near full house that turned up in near monsoon conditions - very wet but exceedingly warm for October - she left the theatre glad she came.

Walking in Tevye's shoes in the 2014 version of this Broadway classic was Jim McGuigan who not only lent his rich baritone voice and magnificent beard to the part of the village milkman but also displayed a feel for the comedy of the role.

He was teamed with the Golde of AIMS award-winning singer Karyn McCooey, who once again proved that she can also act with the best of them.

Their five stage daughters looked the part with Fiona Mullen's Tzeitel the most impressive actress; Aisling McCormick's Hodel possessing the best voice while schoolgirl Niamh Craven as Chava was not overawed despite making her debut on the adult stage. Budding actresses Niamh McDonnell and Katie Doheny touched in the roles of Sprintze and Bielke respectively.

In a show with 20 named roles, Maeve Montgomery's busybody Yente was eye- catching while Gerry O'Hara brought his experience to Lazar Wolf and Paudie Breen's Motel was as strong as his character was weak.

Alan Doherty, with his big voice, brought some fire to the revolutionary Perchik while Patrick Brown was a very civil Fyedka.

Tim Ahern's excellent speaking voice belied the Rabbi's aged stooped frame and flowing white beard as he was shepherded around the stage by Sean Og Cairns' feisty Mendel; Jack Montgomery was well cast as innkeeper Mordcha while Brian Halpin and Colm Lally touched in the small roles of bookseller Avram and the Fiddler respectively. Excellent make-up and costumes transformed Phyllis Woods in Grandma Tzeitel and chorus mistress Geraldine Casey into Fruma Sarah for one of the show's pivotal scenes.

For a show that is about changing times, Mr Hughes opted for an unconventional ending with the remnants of Tevye's family joined by the Fiddler as they leave for America. The usual procession from the village that often serves as a final play-out had deviated from its traditional route and time, passing the back of Tevye's house before the milkman picked up the handles of his cart to start out on his trans-Atlantic journey.

The cast however, were allowed one more moment in the spotlight with a graduated curtain call introducing not just the principals but the various family units.

It was also great to see so many young people taking part. Like the villagers of Anatevka setting out on a new chapter in their lives, Dundalk MS with a lengthy, proud tradition of its own, has reason to be optimistic about the future.

The first time I came across this show in the early 1990s I naively thought a musical by the Heather Brothers might just be a fluffy bit of Scottish whimsy, the sort of thing the late Andy Stewart would sing from at Hogmanay.

Anyone who knows the piece will readily understand just how wrong I was. As advertising slogans go, this is a show which just about does what it says on the tin.

It's as true a representation as you will find on the stage of the nightmare that flashes in front of the eyes of every parent of a teenager as they wave them goodbye out of the door on a Friday or Saturday night.

This pastiche of the 1960s is also a fairly accurate mirror of teenage dramas, insecurity and awkwardness as they embark upon the road of breaking away from parental bonds - a kind of English answer to Grease, except it's much more irreverent.

Cue ballroom romances, dance-floor rejections, sexual anxieties, casual confessions, macho bravado, feminine protectionism, pill-popping and enough alcohol sunk at the fictional Club A-Go-Go to float a small ocean-going liner.

The man with his hands on the rudder that guides us through the flotsam and jetsam of this underage jamboree, club owner Eric "Rubberlegs" De Vere, part narrator, part confessor and part relationship guru, was played with gusto in this Gareth Mahony production by the experienced Sean Fox.

Heading up the male tribe in this piece about the rites of initiation was pouting peacock Gary, Sean Keany with a great voice, great accent and hands never far away from smoothing down his hair or fixing his skinny tie, teen inadequate Rick, a study in awkwardness from Kevin Cleary and social hand grenade Eddie, a terrific performance from Gavin Ryan as the gormless prat you wouldn't want living next door.

The female side of this meat market was led by the excellent Ainé Fox who lent her fabulous voice to the role of Sue, a girl who only wants to be as skinny as Twiggy, Grace Collender as the big- haired busybody Penny, Lisa Murray as Sharon, all folded arms and tilted head waiting for Rick to make a move and the Bridget of Keila Whelan, another good actress, whose realises during one of her big moments that her vision of the perfect man is her Dad.

It was all played out on Sean Henderson's open set at the Venue in Ratoath with its wing rostra which allowed the separated brethren of the big ensemble to act as a Greek chorus as required or to act as a visual backdrop to the action centre stage whenever the little wallflowers were not called into action to execute Erin Kenny's vigorous routines.

Her dance moves, like the score, mirrored the 1960s to a large extent. Indeed, many of the tunes, or more accurately, little riffs from them, are reminiscent of hit numbers of the era.

Those Heather Brothers songs were given full vent by a terrific five- piece onstage band anchored by the keyboards of joint musical directors, Pat Morris and Paul Strachan.

There was a bit of a buzz about Wexford during the opera festival in the middle of October.

And part of that buzz was centred on Paul Walsh's production of the Lloyd Webber and Rice blockbuster as Oyster Lane Theatre Group celebrated its 20th anniversary.

The audience comes from far and wide for the society's annual production - the woman beside me was from Dublin, a fan of the amateur musical movement, and has been a regular at the south eastern town's Dun Mhuire theatre during the group's October run for years.

Like others in a full house of around 600 she quickly learned that this version of the most famous tale in Western history is as much about Judas as it is about Jesus.

It is a view that seemed to be accepted by Mr Walsh and his colleagues in the production team who made a significant statement of intent in casting vocal powerhouse Chris Currid, a young man with strong links to the society, as the perceptive but increasingly disillusioned and hostile apostle who sees the crusade centred around Christ falling down around them.

Standing toe to toe with Mr Currid in the show's vocal scraps was James McDermott, a charismatic Jesus who put his own mark on the show's big number with a dramatic version of "Gethsemane". Yvette Walsh as a sweet-voiced Mary Magdalene was the source of a minor rift between the two men as the story edged towards its fatal conclusion while Mark Mahoney was a deep-voiced Caiaphas, the politician priest out to save his very own empire and the man who repeatedly pressed the civil authorities to put an end to the life of Jesus.

John Crosbie was a physically commanding Pilate who agonised over being backed into a corner over Christ's death while Lee Hynes, in his first major role with Oyster Lane, played that other authority figure, Herod, as dismissive of Jesus in a strong performance devoid of campness.

Mick Farrell made a real zealot out of Simon, portraying him as a revolutionary hard man and a street fighter whipping up the mob against the Roman conquerors at every opportunity while Neal O'Leary played Peter as a man frightened of the consequences of being associated with Christ after his arrest and Robert Duggan White as Annas was a creepy right hand man to the high priest.

While Mr Walsh's version of the show was not as graphic as some, he coaxed several big performances from his players while choreographer Suzanne O'Leary's flowing dance routines kept a big ensemble busy in this fast-paced production.

It was also evident that musical director Patrick Clancy - here in charge of a very good eleven-piece band - had real feeling for the show.

It was played out on Mark Redmond's curved stone-faced set which boasted wing adjuncts which housed video screens as well as catering for Pilate's palace and the garden of Gethsemane, all well lit by the man himself wearing another of his technical hats.

A fun night with some real issues central to the entire show. Bosco drama Group tackled this show full on with great energy and enthusiasm. Some delicate issues which focused in on segregation in the 1960's in Baltimore were the kernel of this show.

The eight piece orchestra played and blended to give that "Bid Band" sound we need from the major numbers in the show. Great Sax playing from Stephen Dolan with great control from the brass section all night. Very energetic and responsive conductor from Aislinn Mulholland. I think you were jumping off the floor at one point The production flowed from scene to scene with a good design that suited the Town Hall in Newry and also the production. The use of trucks helped scene changes enormously which were slick and efficiently done. Mind that the stage management are not too eager to change. Their speed is really off putting as it looks as if they are in a panic. A fine and capable young cast (in the younger parts) were very well cast. The evanescent Sarah Toner as Tracey Turnblad with endless energy and quick wit, good facials and a very fine singing voice. She is sensitive and heartfelt and always secure vocally. Her sidekick and friend, Emma Martin as Penny Pimgleton was just adorable. Accomplished actress and singer and relished every word. A great little performer and a star of the future.

Edna Turnblad was performed by James McGinn who turned out a fine performance. She looked great but needed a little more projection on lines. As large as life, this, overall, was a fine performance with a great duet with Martin Morgam as Wilbur her husband "Your Timeless to me". Annette Ward played Velma who was the acid tongued racist played to perfection ….which is a little worrying! And her daughter, with the silver spoon stuck firmly in her mouth, gave a rounded vivacious performance - a chip of the old block.

Ciaran McCormack played Link, a strong performance with a great voice, agile and performed with ease throughout. Thuli Ngebeni as Motormouth Maybelle was vocally very strong with great range. Her rendering of "I know where I've Been" was vocally one of the highlights of the show. Clarity of diction needed a little attention as did her son, Clinton Ngebeni playing the role of Seaweed. A little introverted but did well as his first ever performance on stage.

The good singing young chorus with a lot of energy worked hard all night with some creative and inventive routines by Anne Marie Morgan. A couple of scenes needed attention in the production to vary the position of chorus, but overall there was a good response in the choreography from the music itself. Good singing and attention to diction paid off well.

This production of Hairspray ran smoothly with solid back up from Stage Management. Costumes were well attended to especially the beautiful 1960's ladies dresses which looked as if they were individually hand made. Beautiful fabrics and colours, all with proper underskirts. Great work here. Men fared less well in general with some attention to be made with modern looking suits and trousers and ties. Lighting was hit and miss with a badly lit cyc all evening. It was the area that needed more attention in this production. Over lit scenes a problem and curing erratic. Hair and Make-up excellent with great "hair doos" for the ladies and wonderful wigs for the Dynamites. Again, men fared the worst here with little change from when they walked into the theatre. Greased back in this area would have helped.

Overall a very enjoyable and welcoming night in the Town Hall in Newry. It was lovely to see some old friends once again and to see the great work in nurturing young people to have a live of the stage.

The small but perfectly formed "Abbey Theatre" in Clane was the venue for Godspell. Stripped away to the bare walls leaving maximum space for this show to unfold was a brave decision by the production team. Even the orchestra was removed to the back of the stage with the cast using FOH monitors for conductor contact. This arrangement was seamless throughout.

The show started with the Philosophers in modern day costume with strong contributions from everyone. Clear and atmospheric lighting with costumes in black / grey, it was a fitting prelude to the wonderland of colour that was to ensue. Conductor Michael Fay led his troupe unobtrusively which created a seamless dynamic between stage and "backroom". The various colours of the score were brought out sensitively never drowning the singers on stage with some very fine guitar and kit playing, especially in "Oh! God, I'm dying".

Chorus Master, also Michael Fay was strong where diction was clean and you heard every word especially in "Babylon" which can get cacophonous when it builds to an ensemble piece. Harmonies were well exploited and strong especially in "Prepare ye the way of the Lord", beautiful balance in "Day by Day". Good job.

The cast, or should I say the entire company, worked their socks off ALL evening. The chorus participated so much that I would consider them a principal part all of their own. Each person in the chorus was their own character who really immersed themselves into the entire production assuming multi roles which combined, to give an exciting performance of this crazy show.

Séan McMahon was the corner-stone of this production. With plenty of charisma and energy he gave a fluid performance with many nuances throughout. A light high baritone voice he and cleanly especially "Beautiful City".  Dominic Read played John the Baptist with strong voice with a lovely a capella start to "Prepare Ye" from the back of the theatre. Again, an agile performer relishing all the multi role playing. Philip Emmett as Judas looked great - I'm a great supporter of the follicly challenged! Again, clear diction in a lovely duet with Jesus " All for the Best". A brooding dark performance. Peter Fay as Lamar worked hard throughout with a lovely tenor voice well suited in timbre for this type of show. "All good gifts" was well delivered and I loved the simple transformation with the mop head for Noah's beard.

Helen Moran as Joanne played many roles with relish and confidence. There is quite a comic streak with this performer with ability to producing good accents. Elaine Moore O'Donohoe as Peggy displayed a lovely voice in "By my Side" - she was a dedicated and a major player in this tight ensemble.

Fiona White as Sonia has a steady and rich voice and even throughout the range. "Turn back old Man" is her big number, sung with Aztec headdress and feather boa with an alarming glint in her eye.

Dearbhail Downey as Gilmer was a breath of fresh air.  She is a vivacious actress with a clean soprano voice and great understanding of text and musical nuances.
