Well suited to each of the characters she was playing, a real tour de force in this production. Well done. The last principal - The Chorus. They worked tirelessly during the whole production and were integrated throughout giving great support to the principals and their colleagues alike. Vocally a strong chorus with a good range, always in tune and some nice harmonies. An organic group of individuals that gave of themselves all evening.

Arthur McGauran directed this piece and allowed the show to flow smoothly getting great role play performances from his entire cast. It was slick thanks to the space he had created and telling us the story in many inventive ways. He allowed the telling of the parables to build and create a community incorporating the audience at every turn. The success of this production was its simplicity with minimal props and utilizing almost everything on stage. Choreography by Deirdre Browne kept things simple and always complimented the director's style. Bringing "Day by Day" into the audience was inclusive, the line dancing fun but just mind the synchronised Fosse scene. Precision is key to its success. This was a little out of sync at the beginning. Stage management was unobtrusive as most of this happened off stage.

All the props used on stage were virtually found within the set. However, I thought the 2 sets of steps were ugly and jarred with the rest of the set. A small quibble. The sound design by Vinnie Osborne was very successful with good balance from "Back Room to Stage". The tone was well judged and no lapses of mics not being turned on for first lines. Hurrah! I did feel, however, that the guitars did penetrate too much here and there but I guess this was the nature of those numbers.

With height and stage size issues, Colm Eaton delivered a good plot, key areas well lit, with seamless continuity right into the audience. The change of LX colour when Judas spoke worked very well. A nice detail. Not sure if we needed the projection of the cross at the end??? I think this should be left to the people's imaginations.

Costumes by Andrew Reddy went for a kaleidoscope of colour, all different - reflecting their characters. Bright vivid colours with everyone on stage having their own personal stamp on his costume. Nice touches with the colored Fossé hats and the sneak pinch from other eras, as in John the Baptist's gold jacket really worked well. Hair and make-up were of today and suited this style of production. If ever you wanted a bit of religion, this is how I would like it served up to me. Well done and thank you.

Andersson, Ulvaeus and Rice created this piece, they made sure the music lived on. Presented by Coolmine Musical Society at the Draíocht Theatre, no expense was spared on the visuals - an excellent set with large screen and many beautiful images projected onto it.

Musical Director, Caitríona Ní Threasaigh created a delicate opening with clean staccato which created a delicate atmosphere which was a precursor of the tension and gradual build to chaos in the unfolding story. The interpretation of the score did not ride the sweeps as it should, I missed the big crescendos and felt some numbers like "Pity the Child" could have moved on.

Mandy Geary took charge as chorus mistress. The ladies numbered more than the men so there was quite an imbalance in the desired choral effect. Some voices came across as loud and a little raucous which somewhat marred the overall sound. The piano sections were most successful as in the "Hymn to Chess" but there was a little bit of strain in "Endgame" and "The Arbiter". A well balanced orchestra of twelve with a heavy brass section that didn't overpower. Some beautiful flute playing in various sections shone through, but I never felt the full power of this group of musicians till the very end.

Karl Sheridan has a fine look for the Arbiter, but was hampered with little variation in his movement and position on stage which was played DSC most of the time. A fine voice but didn't command the stage as he should. Liam Egan played Freddie Trumper, the cool American, with a flexible and agile voice, well within his range with an easy facility for the stratosphere he has to sing in. He, however, had a tendency to stab at top notes which at times, became a little harsh.

Nicole Lamb, always the business women performed very well with great diction all night and a well-schooled voice.  A slight vibrato crept into "The Mountain Inn" scene but other than that, gave a personal and dramatic performance. Frank Beadle presented a thoughtful presence in his opening scene as Anatoly. A fine tenor voice; I have no doubt that you can sing this role. However, hardly a trace of an accent and a lack of using the text left this character hollow. This was a vocal performance with much of the character left by the wayside.

Bronwyn Andrews enters in Act two as Svetlana with an elegant presence and performance that stood out. She knows how to delve into text and present fully, a three dimensional character. A great voice with a delicious low register. Alexander Molokov . performed by Kris Kendellen rose to the occasion. Every inch a KGB spy, a fine (bass) baritone voice. Once again, text issues in interpretation prevented Kris from really bringing this manipulative role to full impact.  Robbie Kennedy as Walter de Courcy delivered the goods in this production, present and always authoritative in the scenes that he played.

A large chorus which demanded them to play many "roles" within the score of Chess. Musically varied throughout with good sense of fun in the "performing monkey's routine" to the tourists in the Merano scene but came into difficulties in the big ensemble scene at the end with "Endgame". A number of tuning problems peppered throughout the evening, with the English Embassy scene faring the worst. This scene sounded brittle culminating with problems in vocal balance.

This show is an old chestnut for this director John Donnelly.

The visual side with set and costumes were well looked after with beautiful chess pieces in three games and also the Merano costumes at the opening. The set allowed for plenty of space for the big ensemble numbers, but I felt the more intimate scenes needed the lighting to be more contained. There needed to be much more attention to props throughout this production.  Some were raggy and in poor taste for their specific location - as in the furniture in the Aurora Hotel. The same table appeared right across the globe in Italy, Bangkok and then in a TV studio? The show moved well from scene to scene ably stage managed by Maureen McMahon and her crew.

The director showed poor judgement in allowing some intrusive choreography into intimate scenes. He should also have encouraged his actors to lavish more attention on the text. Without text we have little drama or communication. It was such a shame as the cast were better than this.

A large chorus to move - but isn't that the joy of working with so many people. Choreography by Louise Dodrill certainly integrated the chorus well into the show but was somewhat a challenge for the majority of the company. There was a lack of precision which did not make the pictures effective. Dancers intruding into solo scenes detracting emotionally and dramatically.

Lighting by Denis Twomey created a fine lighting palette that was evocative and exotic. The main set lit beautifully allowing for the projections to be clearly seen all the time. Be careful with blackouts, as there were some delays at the end of scenes. The various hair designs were well attended to here with nice changes from Merano to the modern world. Good details in the traditional styles and accessories.

I received a lovely warm reception when I arrived at the theatre.  It brought back such great memories having worked with this company on several occasions. Courteous and pleasant, the house management even allowed me to change my seat. Loved the hats with chess pieces on top of them. Very inventive and

Fusion Theatre Company presented their version of Miss Saigon to a packed auditorium, with a host of young people, drilled and musically trained to effect those dark days of Saigon falling.

An impressive group of young principals supported by a well-drilled chorus were, I'm afraid, not always supported by the technical team of "adults ".

The technical difficulties were in part overcome by this talented bunch of principals. Jessica Webb as Kim showed a vocal resilience with a lovely quality voice. She was well matched vocally by Adam Williamson - as Chris but mind the words, Jessica, and know what you are singing about. Matthew Quinn as John has strength and presence with another fine voice. He shapes the words beautifully as does Conor Taggart as Thuy - who really bowled me over. A fine tenor voice which can only get better in time. A rich mezzo is hard to come by today, but Megan McGarry as Ellen has it. With a little more training she should sort out the top of the voice; so she can slip through the passagio more easily. Orchestrally we had, by today's standards, a large band of fourteen players covering all the colours you'd expect from this Schönberg score. Beautiful Sax playing from Davy Mayes with haunting oboe playing from Paul McCrisken added to the sound of this excellent orchestra. Bravo!

The main set had some nice detail with rattan reeds on the risers of the steps, the moving mechanical trucks were a nice touch for quick scene changes, but what goes on these rostra must be specific and detailed. A curtain with hooks on one end is not good enough as a part bedspread. Some tight entrances due to stage left and right being curtained to allow changes of the mechanical pieces which hampered, to some entrances and exits for the cast.

Production and conducting were in the hands of Ian Milford. The show moved very well from scene to scene allowing good pace and clarity. Musically, I felt we needed more gear changes of tempi to heighten and convey emotionally what these young actors were trying to tell us. I did miss some of the oriental gongs etc. like the tams in the opening needed to be more pronounced. Some very good work from this young chorus with individual lines clearly making a cohesive sound. It was strong with excellent diction.

The company executed some lovely work choreographically from Rebecca Leonard, especially the blockbuster numbers of American Dream, Dju vui vai and The Morning of the Dragon. Well drilled with some nice inventive chorus movement throughout.

Lighting was a bit rocky throughout. Over lit scenes taking impact away from many sensitive moments, and poor key light missing in others. Great projection work with very apt images especially the Vietnamese children for Bui Doi.

Costumes had an array of sleazy girls to well-dressed GI's - mind those boots and accessories - they are important. Kimonos are Japanese and should not have appeared in the wedding scene. Principals were generally well attended to but a greater eye on distinction between the two armies.

Certainly, there was a great night had by the audience in the auditorium with a standing ovation for these talented young performers.

A fond return to the Dunamaise Arts Centre to see a full house, meeting some old friends and a great buzz about the theatre. Another production with an invisible orchestra, conducted by Niall Mulpeter keeping everything together but lacking a little attack and bloom in the big forte sections of the score. Very clean segues throughout this show which helped drive it forward. More energy was required for "listen to that Howling Mob" and a little slower at the beginning of the "leper Scene" would have helped the transition and build up to this effecting number.

Paul Norton directed a traditional JCS with some subtle twists which shed some new light onto this show. . Jesus kissing Judas after "I don't know how to love him", it was calm and knowing - allowing Judas to carry out what he must do. Final images like Mary lying beside Jesus were very strong and different. The show had momentum and flowed freely bringing its audience through the last days of the greatest story ever told. The working of the upper level of the set could have been better utilised - it is precious space. However, these levels were well used in the Trial Scene. The working of the chorus in certain scenes needed more craft and focus - the temple scene needed more hustle and bustle with more sellers and buyers and more noise. Maybe overlay a sound effect on top of the natural babble - with animal noises etc. The bringing on of the lepers was premature which resulted in the chorus getting to their final positions too soon. Investment in the text should have been given more prominence as there is no dialogue in this work.

Choreography by Lea Carroll worked the company well and all within the capabilities of the cast. Much energy infused into "Christ you know I love you". A beautiful delicacy in "Everything's alright" - gentle and very caring. Be careful not to isolate Judas in the "Superstar" number as I felt he was left to his own devices throughout the song with little relation to the main number. Herod's "Jesus, I am overjoyed" lacked "an idea" which didn't punctuate this number, although the audience enjoyed the antics on stage………… it was a puzzlement.

This rock opera is not only about Jesus but also about Judas which you don't really see in some productions. Both actors worked well together, feeding off each other in their big moment. Two very fine performances in different ways. Alex Cathcart, traditional in look, gave us a calm and often a charismatic performance, with a heady rock tenor voice that was clear, vibrant but had a small tendancy to tighten a little on top. Some beautiful pianissimo singing - "Neither you, nor the fifty thousand". Gethsemane needed much more variation with the text and more time was required with the last words on the cross. But an excellent performance. Thank you.

Eoghan Fingleton as Judas, gave us a brooding, troubled portrayal, convincing in every way. He had a depth of truth in his character with clear text and emotions that was a welcome and effecting performance. An excellent rock tenor voice with extraordinary sustained top notes, allowed him to interpret this difficult score and its high tessitura with ease and, dare I say it, with some grace.  A pity he wasn't well integrated into his big number "Superstar". Another excellent performance. Thank you. Aisling Rohan as Mary Magdalene also interprets music clearly with a focus on text. Never forced, all within her range. A slight vibrato crept in at the beginning of "I don't know how to love him" but she was left a bit stranded with no focus on the direction in this number. Seamus Carroll as Pontius Pilate needed a bit more variation in tone for "The Dream" - it was a little monotone with only one dynamic and thought structure. The voice seemed a little rough at times but was well capable in the Trial scene.  More attention to his costume would have helped give him a stronger presence. Richard Finnegan certainly did what he was asked to do. A scene which lacked focus and direction. Direction here did not create a sufficient idea/theme for this scene. The actor struggled to find the tune throughout the number which also didn't help. John Coss as Simon is a very nimble performer with a strong high baritone voice. Again, he should have been highlighted more in his number and not merged with the chorus.

Nick Anton as Caiaphas gave us a deep resonant bass voice which carried well with clear diction. More investment into the text would have put the cherry on the cake for this actor, whilst, Jay Ritchie as Annas could have invested more slime and venom into his character. Vocally, the falsetto was greatly missed as it set the balance askew with this self- contained unit. A static quartet, their real presence was quiet underwhelming in the scheme of things. Jacko Maher was very plaintive in "Could we start again please" with a fine strong baritone. A distraught reaction to his accusation of knowing Jesus.

With a well-designed, single unit set, Bob O'Kelly and his crew worked the scenery well with slick cueing. Not much changed with the set which was a pity. It required a detailed lighting plot which I am afraid was a bit patchy and variable. The main issue here were focus of lamps and cueing. The walkway around the upper level was patchy and uneven with untidy cue times in the Opening of Act 2, - The Last Supper and a delay in the up cue for The Temple scene.

Costumes showed imagination and you felt you were in the Middle East. Good choice of fabrics and palette of colours helped the whole look of this production. Jesus' white robe needed to be lined as it was see-through. Pilate's costume needed more work done to it. A cloak would have helped, plus his gold laurel crown would have separated him from the crowd. His sandals were amazing. Guards also needed help with armlets and they needed better sandals. Overall though, a fine collection which enhanced the show.

Make-up and hair was all in order except for the blood for Christ's lashing. There should have been much more of it on his back.

A lovely welcome by David Delaney was appreciated on another freezing night. It's funny how you get a warm glow from a show such as this.

Evita, another of my favourite scores, was being performed by St. Michael's Theatre Musical Society in St Michael's Theatre, New Ross. With a composite set, well-built and painted, detailing the decaying nature of Buenos Aires of the 1930's, we were plunged right into the political upheaval  that surrounded the rise of one, Eva Duarte - better known as Eva Perón.

Great scope with the set that was not fully utilized, especially the upper side levels. In the famous number from the show, the central structure trucked DS with Evita on it. This was an impressive moment.

The nine piece orchestra played this difficult score very well with nice percussion instruments, the conga drums, adding flavour and location to the production. Relying on electronic instruments, I felt the sound seemed to be muted and the various builds in the orchestra never became powerful enough. There was, however, generally a good balance between stage and pit. Conductor Philip Kennedy had a firm grip on this piece and allowed the show to segue from scene to scene cleanly. A little more contact on stage would give more security to the performers.

The chorus was very even in the SATB sections with a greater number of ladies than men. This caused for an imbalance from the choral sound. There was a general tendency to push but some really fine piano singing from the ladies in "Requiem reprise" paid off. The men's chorus was challenged with all they had to do, especially in a score of this size. The sound was a tad raw at times and exposed with little connection with the text.  The chorus was well integrated into the overall production but needed help in expressing what to do.

Principals were, on the whole very good. Joanne McCabe performing the title role had all the vocal and colour requirements for this role. More attention to the text is vital to communicate to the audience. This was also the issue with Keith Flanagan performing Ché. A fine voice with no problems in range, but again, I would like to have had many more nuances throughout the text. Keith is easy and flexible on stage but I also felt, paced around too much with little focus. Kevin Reade as Juan Perón gave a very fine performance with great stage presence, a fine voice skillfully used. We believed in everything he sang as he gave weight to the text and music. Excellent diction and invested emotionally throughout.

Kevin Kennedy (who directed as well) played Augustin Magaldi looked perfect as the 1930's Latin tango / cabaret singer. Again, singing voice with the right colour for this character was not a problem, but was rather awkward and solid on crossing down stage centre. He needed much more fluid movement - especially to attract the eye of Eva,  Ashley Doran as Perón's Mistress was a joy with a beautiful mezzo voice. Performed simply, she vanished as quickly as she appeared. A very promising young lady.

Two beautiful child singers - Tomás Mulally and Niamh Lynge were exceptional in their tuning and singing for their age.

The production moved well throughout being driven by the music. More attention on props was needed. A pity about the plastic chairs amongst the beautiful wooden carved ones and the modern table and ballot box for the voting scene. Suitcases and newspapers very in period, but again the dressings on the coffin in the opening scene needed much attention. It was all so modern I thought there was someone actually in the coffin. Choreography by Claire Kickham used her skills to manage the company in the various dance forms throughout the score. The Chorus were challenged, which is good, but there has to be a point where style and capabilities are not compromised.  Men were a little tentative in their military formation but the ladies were most successful in Buenos Aires. Sound design was clear and generally balanced well with the orchestra. Just really missed the big crescendos through the score. No missed cues which was a joy and nice effects like the film in the cinema. Stage Management did their job efficiently and cleanly with no upsets. All props placed on stage in time.

The lighting was disappointing in many scenes with not enough focus on important moments. Areas not lit - the balcony scenes on several occasions, the lack of punctuation DSR with Eva and Magaldi in the restaurant. The colour palette was not evocative of the exotic location with missed opportunities. Good back light for the crowd scenes and also for the ladies chorus along the front towards the end.

A great ladies costume plot with attention to shoes but the principals did not fare well. Eva was just not lavish enough and not enough changes especially  "on her tour". I felt it was not  "Christian Dior Me" but " Penneys Dior Me". Unpolished shoes are not a replacement for military boots. Magaldi's suit was a modern dress suit which should have been period , 1930's double breasted.  Good attention to hair throughout with a great slick look for Migaldi. Men needed a little more attention as they needed short back and sides and a slick look also.

With so many areas having many positive things, it is always the little things that catch us out.

Best Little Whorehouse In Texas is one of those fun shows that belies its title. Great fun to be in and can be hilarious for an audience. The full house at the Civic theatre lapped it up and wanted more. With Sarah Lynch Barrett at the helm of the orchestra, the show moved along with a number of fine musicians in the pit. We even had Alan Smale, ex leader of the RTÉ Symphony orchestra as violinist for this performance. Nice work here for "Girl, You're a Women" and also in "Doatsy Mae". Some numbers were too fast which did not allow cast to "breath" within the music and allow the emotions to be conveyed. A fine country and western style with Hawaiian guitars and the honky-tonk piano evoking the southern feel for this score. Nice touch with the Wurlitzer organ in "The Side Step".

Chorus had a very fine sound with some good detailed harmonies. Nice tone throughout from the entire ensemble especially the ladies in "Hard Candy Christmas" with a strong, rich mezzo line which came through. The men's chorus shone in their "Aggies" number - not the usual shape for footballers but the audience loved their antics. Good control from the men backing "Good Ole' Girl". One niggle - I'd like to have had more text coming through the numbers.

Julie Donnelly played Miss Mona - not an easy role to play. Her voice is easy, in tune and well within the range of the score. I missed the country feel for a lot of her numbers, which should have been brought out by the MD and Director. The colour of the voice was right and could easily have achieved this. Investment in the text was a problem as I, at times, did not get involved emotionally - "No Lies" and "Bus to Amarillo" were examples. Just be careful that the dialogue does not run away with you.  Ed Earl Dodd, performed by Eoin Salley just wants an easy life. Good demeanor on stage with many rough edges which is his endearing quality. Text was driven too much, never quite finding the rhythm and flow of the lines resulting in problems with diction. A strong baritone voice but too projected for his number "Good Ole' Girl".  It needed to be more internalised. Good accent throughout. Mark Keegan as Melvin P. Thorpe was a bundle of energy all night with his sycophantic take on this TV Reporter. Opportunities with more comic turns for this character were missed. A fine voice used to its max in "Texas, has a Whorehouse in it".

Serena Salmon as Angel knows her way about town. A confident performer with great body language and vocally very strong with a bright forward sound. Loved her reactions to Miss Mona's rules. Lovely telephone scene with her Mama and son.

Beth DuBerry as Shy was a lovely take on this Hicksville kid with nowhere to go. It was a great journey for this character from gawky and naïve to a confident and able young women. Be careful you don't keep your head bowed too low. Her simple delivery of the lines was well judged and nicely paced. Celine Potter as Jewel gave us a singing performance. A vibrant and well placed voice with a huge belt. Good rendition of "Twenty four hours of Lovin'" but again, I did not feel anything for the text. The character was not integrated into the piece which kept her to the side lines a bit. A clear brassy delivery with good diction from Kelly- Marie Davy as Linda-Lou. Very much her own woman, with attitude. Ginger played by Sharon Osborne was a gem played with confidence and sweet nature. Hair style appropriate and well costumed. Mind some of the 't's in your words with this accent like "Late" and "Weight" in "Hard Candy Christmas". We shouldn't hear them. A lovely voice, always in tune. As the Bandleader and Rufus Poindexter, Damian Hurley gave us two characters poles apart. An easy delivery from the bandleader but would have liked him to have meandered around the stage and the groups more. He seemed a little stuck DSR and the DSR. Great Southern accent sustained throughout "20 Fans". As Rufus, a bored, drole and probably on the spectrum interpretation which worked very well for this character. Although a different interpretation, his lines always were clear and had truth in them. Well done, a fine study.

Paul Laycock played the Governor with agility but vocally chased his number "The Sidestep" all night. Pitched too high, he lost the tune and turned the vocal line into parlando. Kirstin Smith as Doatsey Mae exuded a tough life. A lovely voice with the right tone for her number but was let down with the direction of the song. Would have liked the narrative to come through more here also. Full of self-importance, Eddie Brady as Senator Wingwoah, got some fun out of this role. Costume department let him down with his modern style suit.

The set allowed for easy flow of this production though greater detail was needed in a number of areas. A basic unit set that did not give any idea of why this Chicken Ranch would be popular with the men-folk of the town. Poor judgment in the placing the Doatsey Mae's café DSR corner which hampered entrances and the following dialogue. Just having benches is not enough to say that we are in a locker room for the Aggies scene. Lack of dressing for most scenes especially in Ed Earl's office with hardly anything on his desk, the café and Miss Mona's suffered the same fate.

Permeating throughout this production, opportunities were missed to augment the fun and risqué business already written in the script. Director, Philippa Alford did not highlight these and missed the nuances in the dialogue and lyrics that would have integrated the characters more. Scenes were a little static and principals needed more help with extending their characters - through the text and lyrics. Choreography by Orla Savage kept things moving and in keeping with the style of the show. Nice traditional flair with lots of energy in The Aggies. I liked the double chorus idea in "Texas, has a Whorehouse in it", but it failed to inject the fun element; apart from Melvin. Precision was lacking in several numbers which made them uneven except the "Angelette March", which had great attention to detail. The props department was successful in some areas. Great work with carpet bag, the wheelchair and the various pieces of luggage but was let down with things like set dressing, the modern chairs and table in Doatsey Mae's and the choice of furniture in Miss Mona's would not have been seen…even in a whorehouse. Sound by Vinny Osborne was evenly balanced and had a lovely tone which added to the show. Just a tad heavy from the band in several areas but didn't offend in any way. Well timed effects especially the dialing of the phone. Lighting by Darren Kelleher was a mixed bag with a lack of subtlety and clarity.  The set did not inspire but I would suggest closing down more for the intimate scenes, focusing in more on the drama. Several cues timed incorrectly with a lack of key light on several principals. I feel more time was required to settle these areas. Costumes helped bring the 70's era to life with good attention to detail regarding shoes and socks/tights. Some nice detail with the principals' attire especially for Miss Mona. The girls looked great for daywear but be careful with the eveningwear - all the girls seemed to look similar and not honing in on their personalities. The Aggies needed more work with a very limited amount of football attire. The Governor looked terrific in all white including Stetson but Melvin P. Thorpe needed more fun in his costumes. It wasn't nearly over the top enough. Make-up and hairstyles all seemed to be order here with a difference between the girls. I felt Miss Mona's hair style was a bit too severe and not suitable for her face structure. It needed to be a lot softer.

It is a pleasure always to visit the Chicken Ranch and this version left the audience howling for more. Isn't that what it's all about?

The Wicklow village of Carnew with a population of barely more than 1,000 souls is one of, if not the smallest, stops on the AIMS circuit. The ambition, however, is on a different scale altogether.

Not content with being heavily involved in the impressive refurbishment of their St Brigid's Hall home, the group has now added staging a European premiere to its list of achievements.

This version of Dickens most famous tale by the American duo of composer Bruce Greer and writer Keith Ferguson, points up slightly different aspects of the story to Alan Menken's better known musicalisation while a liberal inclusion of Christmas carols betrays the roots of the collaborators in American Christian theatre.

Those carols combined with about a dozen original pieces told the story in eight different scenes played out on Tony Barry's clever composite set of early Victorian London which still allowed room for Mark Flynn's choreography. It still meant that the central character of Ebenezer Scrooge - played here by a terrific all-rounder in John Young, stooped of gait and big of voice - was on stage for most of the performance.

His Damascene conversion from miser to philanthropist came in the form of a nightmare kicked off by Peter Lewis who lent his excellent baritone voice to Scrooge's deceased partner Jacob Marley.

In an adaptation that is almost a literal re-telling of the story, Scrooge is then visited by the spritely Carol Byrne as the Ghost of Christmas Past, the towering David Cox as the Ghost of Christmas Present and Denis Fox as the menacing Christmas Future.

Director Michael Dunbar had cast another good actor/singer in John Egan as Bob Cratchit, who while timorous around Scrooge rejoiced in the company of his family headed by Amanda O'Keefe, another good all-rounder as his wife, and which included Niall Kehoe, a Tiny Tim to give this production the Aah factor. Gary Stephens was an optimistic Fred with a big hi-baritone voice while parts of the story were linked by narrators Joe Sinnot and Mairead Connaughton who doubled up as a sweet-voiced Belle, whom the young Scrooge loved and lost. Mr Dunbar's handsomely dressed detailed production was driven along by Lar Duffy's rich sounding pit band and aided by the work of both the sound and lighting desks with the latter making use of the improved facilities at the south Wicklow venue.

Both the front of house and stage crews were decked out in period gear, the former  to welcome a full house to the new facilities while the latter not only efficiently manoeuvred Mr Barry's cleverly engineered settings, aiding the flow of the show, they also kept a big ensemble in line.

In a day of firsts, it was not just the first time this version of the story had been staged in Europe, it was also the group's first show in the much-improved St Brigid's Hall and the first time the society has staged a matinee performance.

Castlebar might be the newest addition to the AIMS family but its members used their collective head in approaching this show.

With two musical theatre novices in a three-strong production team, the society's committee persuaded Michael Brett, the man behind the last three adult musicals to be staged in the western town, to come on board as producer to pass on a few tips.

And the woman at the helm of the project, director Alanna Ni Mhiochain, in conjunction with her colleagues, blended a hefty helping of experience into a cast that staged the first show in the town for 16 years.

Leading lady Vivienne Lee is an AIMS nominee and she was joined here by a few familiar faces from the long established Claremorris Musical Society just down the N60.

Ms Lee brought a combination of feistiness and vulnerability to the role of Laurey Williams as well as lending a pleasing soprano voice to the part.

She played coy around Paul O'Brien's Curly - a fine debut from the Westport man - before the increasing menace of Richie Heneghan's big-voiced Jud drove her into his arms.

Donna Ruane, a fine actress, was a classy Aunt Eller and, as befitting the stateswoman of this show, had helped develop some of the other talent around her on stage.

A case in point is student teacher Emma Daly who, as Ado Annie, matched up with David Gallagher's lithe but dim Will Parker.

Matthew Largent, making his Irish debut in the role of Ali Hakim displayed the timing and a feel for comedy of someone who is no stranger to the stage while newcomer Tracy Hanley was a fine giggling Gertie Cummins.

Another woman who had helped nurture some of the younger faces on show was musical director, Deidre Lee, who with a host of musicals behind her was the only member of the production team immersed in our form of show business. Ms Lee's colleagues, choreographer Collette McGinty and Ms Ni Mhiochain - the driving force behind the formation of the society and the choice of show - were making their musical theatre bows. Together they fashioned a fast-paced show and drew some fine performances from a cast that was almost 60-strong. However, even with so many people on stage, the company had plenty of room to roam around the wide open spaces of the town's TF Royal Theatre which mirrored the vast plains of the north American territory that was to become known as Oklahoma.

The production made a big impact on the audiences who attended the society's debut in early December with the crowds at the fabulously appointed venue bigger than the group had dared hope for. The latest venue on the AIMS circuit leaves most of the others in the shade. The 2,200 seater Royal Theatre, with its West End spec stage, even eclipses modern hi-tech houses such as Derry's Millennium Forum, Limerick's Concert Hall and Belfast's Grand Opera House, all of which hold around 1,000.

Kill made too big an impression on their return to action after nine years on the side lines.

Emer Hartnett's small but excellent band was allowed to dominate the first half of this show to the detriment of some of the lighter voiced singers. Fine players that they were - they even gave us an excellent play-out in this updated take on a 19th Century classic - the volume should have been lowered much earlier than it was.

While some of the cast could successfully hold their own in the musical battle with the band, others unfortunately were virtually swamped on occasions.

In these times when even a version of the Gilbert and Sullivan flagship show is amplified, it's not altogether the fault of the musicians.  Kiernan Sound Services must shoulder some of the blame for not adjusting the balance at the first opportunity.

Thankfully matters were put to rights for the second half of this bright and breezy Liam Butler production where the action takes place in a 1940s America populated by men in gaudy Zoot suits and ladies in tea dresses and French roll hairdos. It was almost as if the timing was decreed by The Mikado himself. After all he doesn't get involved until the final third of the show but Burl Ives lookalike Padraig Munnelly who played the big boss man as a Deep South gentleman made the most of his time on stage with a neatly crafted comic performance and an excellent accent.

His fearsome female accomplice, Jennifer Noirant's Katisha, was a force ten gale of a nightmare dressed as a daydream who, of course, had to settle for second best in marriage to Tom McCarthy's classic Gilbertian funny man Ko-Ko.

That's because the man of her dreams, Conor Cronin's Nanki-Poo, the son of The Mikado but here disguised as the terribly civil second trumpet in the Titipu Big Band in an attempt to hide from his would-be suitor, had gone and married Helen Spring's sweet-voiced Yum-Yum. Brian McCabe's Pooh Bah, the holder of too many offices to mention here, displayed a decent baritone voice across those swing and jazz rhythms while young baritone Rory Dignam touched in the role of Pish-Tush.

Ms Spring's cheeky schoolgirl friends Pitti-Sing and Peep-Bo were played by sisters Alison and Caroline Behan respectively.

The small ensemble was virtually doubled by pit singers while, with an eye on the future of the society, a juvenile chorus was used to introduce kids to the stage. With only 23 adults involved on stage the full company had plenty of room to execute Ciaran Keating and Julie Reilly's energetic 1940-style dance routines on the handsome set from All Set Scenery although, a little confusingly, this was a Japanese setting even though the action in this version is moved to New York. If the sound desk had room for improvement the same could not be said for Nigel Lombard's lighting plot which was sharp and atmospheric.

UCD's Musical Society is lauded on campus as being one of the busiest groups in the university. Their ambition not only runs to at least two shows a year plus concerts but they are about to inaugurate a competition for other third level musical societies around the island. Now the bright young things of Belfield have beaten every other Irish group to the rights to this Frank Wildhorn, Don Black and Ivan Menchell musical which had its world premiere five years ago and a brief run on Broadway in 2011.

For fans of Wildhorn who view him as an American Lloyd Webber, this show is a sharp turn away from the big overblown Broadway scores of Jekyll and Hyde and The Scarlet Pimpernel with the music often leaning on America's folk and bluegrass traditions.

It does contain a couple of Gospel-type belters in "Made in America" and "God's Arms Are Always Open" while Clyde's declamatory "This World Will Remember Me" is wonderfully apt. However, this score is at its best when the composer reduces the decibels as in the tender female duet "You Love Who You Love" and Bonnie's bizarrely beautiful solo "Dyin' Ain't So Bad".

Menchell's often witty book neatly condenses the back story of the States' most famous criminal duo of the 1930s to characterise Clyde Barrow as a financial victim of the great recession of the time and Bonnie Parker a star-crossed small town girl who falls for a charming rogue. It also cleverly pares back their criminal exploits to concentrate more on their relationship and of that of Clyde's brother Buck and his wife Blanche. Despite its short-lived Broadway tenure, there's a lot going for this show although there is not a lot for a big chorus to get its teeth into. It is however, suited to the smaller spaces many Irish societies work in. UCD have already proved that point, staging the show in the confines of the university's Astra Building, a space without a proper stage and hence no backstage facilities.

Cast entrances, exits and set changes are made through the same doors the audience use to get to their seats.

This battle against the theatrical odds was alleviated somewhat by Joe Murphy's composite and adaptable pallet-based set which afforded the cast levels on which to work and which employed the use of projections.

It also allowed Shauna Carrick's thoughtful and lively production - it contained more gunshots than a 1970s Belfast gun battle - to run at a lick with the aid of some diligent scurrying from stage manager Katie Lyons and her big team.

While I might have had reservations about the hair colourings of leading ladies Clodagh Lalor and Aly Coyne as Bonnie Parker and Blanche Barrow respectively, I had no quibbles about their performances. Both are fine actresses with terrific voices.

Ms Lalor's stage partner and fellow second year medic, James Bergin, lent a powerful high baritone and easy manner to Clyde Barrow and, importantly, possessed the kind of winning smile that so disarmed Bonnie while Ause Braike was believable as his admiring and easily-led brother Buck. Aidan Byrne was a forceful, big-voiced Preacher; Oisin Nolan was a buttoned-up local cop Ted Hinton while American student Simone Lieban Levine aged herself to play Bonnie's widowed mother in a quietly effective performance.

Natasha King and Aoife O'Donnell had plenty of vocal poke as the young Bonnie and Clyde while Joseph Lawlor was a tough-talking sheriff on the trail of the Barrow boys.

It was a good night too for musical director Simon Shaw and his tight nine-piece band anchored by drummer Abdulaziz Siddiqui.

Arriving to a full house at the Hawkes Well Theatre boded well for The Little Shop of Horrors performed by the Sligo Fun Company. Directors and Choreographers, Mary MacDonagh and Steffen Jorgensen worked as a team in both disciplines and moulded their cast into delivering a fine performance of this early 1980's mad cap story of the man eating plant - Audrey II.

Although the Hawkes Well has a dry acoustic, Musical Director Niamh Crowley provided a tight well balanced band of seven, with excellent cueing, yielded a firm hand to tempi which added greatly to the performance. Good dynamic work on stage and a nice collection of sounds coming from the kit and keyboards augmented to the show, with the band really listening to each other. Chorus work is not too plentiful in this show but the sound was always pleasing with a good blend of voices with clear harmonies being heard in "Skid Row" and in "The Meek shall Inherit". They were well integrated into their scene with good detail on building characters.

Arron McDonagh as Seymour is a fine young actor who achieved a good rhythm with his dialogue and possesses a strong baritone voice. I would have liked a bit more awkwardness and shyness with a few nervous ticks thrown in. He has a flare for dance, moving easily in all his numbers especially in "Mushnik and Son". Be careful not to drop projection with dialogue in numbers such as "Now".

Michele Feeney as Audrey was consistent but I felt her character wasn't helped by her walk - I feel her shoes may have been too big for her as it was quite distracting - it wasn't believable. Dialogue was well projected but wait a little after your laugh line - "There's something wrong here".  She has a nice voice but be careful with the ends of the duets as there was a tendency to go off the note. Gerry Ryan as Mr. Mushnik revealed the exploitive nature of this flower shop keeper but missed the Yiddish aspect of the character. Uncertain tuning at the start of 'Ya Never Know" I fear the moves in "Mushnik and Son" overtook his concentration quite a bit.

Luke Devaney as Orin Scrivello was a bundle of energy as he psychopathically gave us his mad dentist. A well projected voice which also carried into his singing, he moved with ease especially with the Nitro - gas contraption on his back. He was quite fearless and captured the duality - even trialty of this role well.

The three girls; Crystal - Angela McGuire, Ronette - Kelesa Mulcahy and Chiffon - Evanne Kilgallon all worked tirelessly throughout the show. Each well-defined through costume and hairstyle, providing a narrative that was clear and harmonically secure. A great blend of voices throughout with very well timed moves. A good team.

Audrey II was played by Graham Kelly giving a fun performance. I personally would have liked more variation from his dialogue. I feel he could have used the text more, giving it more energy and, dare I say it, some sexual nuances. "Little Lady, Hello".

Wisely split into three characters, Donal Ryan as Bernstein was energetic with a good presence and clear vocals, Rebecca Friel as Mrs Luce gave a well projected confident performance and looked terrific in her Jackie Kennedy peach outfit, and finally Skip-Snip played by Conor Bastible grabbed your attention. A fine voice but a tad nasal at times. Mary MacDonagh and Steffen Jorgensen working jointly as directors and choreographers moved their cast and chorus well with some lovely ideas and using the upstairs windows to great advantage. Some nice character building amongst the chorus and a production that had an easy natural flow.   Some good work with the principals although I think more depth could have been drawn from them. More ditzy from Audrey and Orin could have gone even further with his madness and his sadism. Great work with the "3 girls" with lovely movement throughout capturing the 80's perfectly.

The chorus number "The Meek Shall Inherit" was well conceived and well executed as "budding" Audrey II's. Stage Manager was also Stefen Jorgensen who ran a well-oiled ship with scene changes generally smooth, clean and efficient. Set Design by John O'Donoghue provided an all in one set which worked extremely well. With sliding panels and extra truck wall it could transform into various locations. Well painted giving us a run down Mushnik's Flower Shop. Costumes created by the company themselves were in period and evocative of the era. In particular, I loved the dyed body stockings for the "Meek Shall Inherit". They looked wonderful ….except for the extra boy who didn't complete this look all complemented nicely with some great work from the Hair and Make-up team.

Some excellent props provided by Mary Philips and Angela McGuire augmented to the set brilliantly. Too numerous to name, but especially the dentist's chair, the radio, camera and the bicycle and of course, the Audrey II. Great work here. Lighting by Derek O'Neill was creative with a great use of gel colours. The choice of dense colours - deep reds with vivid burnt ambers - worked well which made a great impact on the set and the various scenes. Cast didn't always work to the specials but, it was a first night.

Overall, a fun night with The Fun Company and a very enthusiastic youthful audience put a smile on my face as I left the Hawkes Well Theatre.

A more accurate name for this Cy Coleman classic - Broadway's first big hit of 1966 - would be Bittersweet Charity.

The sting in the tail, when the neurotic Oscar Lindquist dumps his prospective bride Charity Valentine at the eleventh hour, brought an audible gasp from some audience members unaware of the story. It was particularly evident from females who thought the couple were coasting to a happy ending. It was a tribute to director Hazel McLynn and to the show's two leads, recent AIMS nominee Vivienne Lee and Richie Heneghan that the big crowd were sucked into the story of the club hostess who is eternally unlucky in love.

Ms Lee is an excellent actress with a good voice and the role of Charity lies slap bang in the middle of her vocal range. The result was a performance that not only entertained the final night crowd but evoked their sympathy.

Mr Heneghan, another fine actor/ singer, was a convincing Oscar, conveying his buttoned-up character's initial nervousness then his blossoming confidence before reverting back to neurosis.

The show, the idea of the Society's triple driving forces of Ms McLynn, musical director, Deirdre Lee and producer, June Allison-Keane, was staged in the western town's refurbished Town Hall with its newly installed tiered seating offering the greater part of the audience significantly higher levels of comfort and a much better view.

This version was stripped of one of Charity's two pond dunkings and a few of the original songs although it still left a score rich in high quality tunes with theatregoers later confessing they were surprised how many of the songs they knew.

Ms McLynn's well-paced show was aided by her choreography which ranged from the bump and grind of "Big Spender" to the frivolity of "I love to cry at weddings" while musical director Deirdre Lee extracted a big but well-rounded sound from her small pit band.

Karen Ronane was a strong Nickie, combining particularly well with Mary Dempsey, another of Charity's hostess friends, in "Baby, dream your dream".

The big voices of Kate Hughes as Carmen and Angela Prenty as Betsy completed the cynical line-up at New York's Fandango Ballroom while Liam Newman was a gentler Herman than is sometimes the case. Sharlene Ruane was the naïve Rosie, the new girl the old hands recognised as themselves a million dances ago. Michael Goulding, as befitting someone in the rag trade, looked suave as film star Vittorio Vidal, while Simone Dooley was his eye- catching on-off love, Ursula March. Paul O'Brien, a relative newcomer to the stage, is a natural performer who took the role of the hippie Daddy Brubeck in his stride.

The show consolidated the Society's place as an increasing force in the west. The group's growing reputation and the increased comfort of the Town Hall space leaves the door ajar for the company to kick on to another level.

GREASE The more I see of this Downpatrick- based outfit the more I am convinced they are re-generating from within. Teenagers have bolstered the adult company in recent seasons and increasingly the creative teams behind the group's shows have all come through the ranks.

For this version of the American high school coming of age musical, the four-strong production team was not just home grown but the youngest I have encountered. Debutant musical director Matthew Campbell is only a tender 18 and the combined age of the team doesn't reach three figures. The society re-visited Grease - the first show the youth wing tackled - to celebrate the tenth anniversary of the underage group.

Director Gary Warnock, a comparative veteran in this company, and his assistant Catherine McGrath fashioned a fast flowing version of the Jacobs and Casey show using the burgeoning young talent attracted to the society.

Further evidence of the group's expansion was that the two leads, Sandy and Danny, Naomi Smyth and Brendan Mageean, were new to the Society.

Ms Smyth, tall, rangy and with a good voice and a flowing mane of blonde hair played the 1950s good girl to a T before emerging as a firecracker after her finale transformation. Mr Mageean, in his final year at school, had the necessary height in his voice for the role, a body for skinny, skinny jeans and mannerisms which saw his hands never far away from his greased back hair.

Regulars Courtney Burns and Charlotte Burke gave us a confident Rizzo and comedic Frenchie respectively with strong performances from Claire Keenan as Marty and Katie Quinn as Jan.

Alice Magorrian brought a tougher edge to Patty Simcox than is sometimes the case while Karen Mullan was a lithe and sultry Cha Cha DiGregoria.

University fresher Mark McMullan not only weighed in with a big-voiced Kenickie but designed the set for the production while Chris Noade lent a very good voice to Doody.

Tiarnán Donaghy as Roger and Donal Carney as Sonny are decent actors with good voices while Patrick Rowan, who has specialised in comedy roles since joining the group, gave us a gawky Eugene. Experience came in the form of Karen Laverty as schoolteacher Miss Lynch, reprising her day job on stage and Brian McElroy who slipped easily into the dual roles of Vince Fontaine and the Teen Angel.

Despite the creative team's relative inexperience they brought some innovation to the production but resisted the temptation to opt for the outrageous.

Choreographer Kathryn-Ann Simpson, another debutant at this level, injected her varied routines with energy.

The aforementioned Mr Campbell had ensured his principal line-up and ensemble knew exactly what they were doing musically, a necessity with his nine-piece band perched high on top of Mr McMullan's set and out of the performers' sightline.

Not only did the youthful musical director keep a tight grip on the eight musicians he was working with, he also found time to play Johnny Casino from his position on the bandstand with his big voice ringing around the vaulted heights of the beautiful Downshire Great Hall.

society_raw: North East Musical and Dramatic Society
review_text:
It's not often one comes across a show that generated more electricity on stage than it expended in the lighting rig. Then again it's rare that this Sondheim and Weidman tale about murderers, wannabe killers and misfits gets an outing.

Colm Eaton's lighting plot at Dublin's Helix Theatre was atmospherically stark and spare with occasional and highly dramatic shafts piercing the gloom at key moments while onstage the ESB company bubbled away from start to finish.

At times Electric Ireland could have tapped into the performances of some of the principals to supplement the national grid such was the frissons of excitement and fear. This is not one of Sondheim's readily accessible shows but it does give musical theatre performers a chance to display their acting skills.

It was an opportunity grasped willingly by many of the cast including the John Wilkes Booth of David Latham, the Southern gentleman actor who killed Abraham Lincoln and - in the context of this show, the catalyst of this musical fantasy. After his death at the hands of Union army soldiers, a large dose of suspension of disbelief is called for as Booth returns to the action, interacting with and, on occasions, inciting some of the other Presidential killers and plotters in a story that spans almost 120 years. In a show that most definitely leads with the head and not the heart we encountered the deluded but dapper Charles Guiteau of Brian O'Gorman, a man with dangerously mad eyes, glorious twinkle toes and a ringing tenor voice.

Chris Currid as Guiseppe Zangara found himself in the rare position where his acting eclipsed his singing, Nick Sheridan lent his rich bass-baritone to a disturbed Leon Czolgosz, Kathy Kelly was a bungling Sara Jane Moore while Ranae Von Meding was convincing as the dropout Lynette Fromme. Christine Scarry's detailed production also boasted Pat McElwain's powerful and manic Sam Byck with Maurice Treacy a melodic John Hinckley, Ian Tighe a sceptical but malleable Lee Harvey Oswald and Adam O'Brien a bright Balladeer. A cast with loads of stage presence also included Justin Parkes, Sean Keany, Seamus Sullivan and Claire O'Neill as well as boasting an ensemble, a feature missing in the original version of the show but used to good effect here.

Musical director David Wray ensured the cast were secure in the sometimes spiky score which has part of its roots in American folk and bluegrass music while his biggish band with its prominent brass and reed sections helped drive on the action.

And Terry Heron's expertly timed sound effects added a lot to a show that was played out on John O'Donoghue's highly functional but lean setting dominated by representations of the Stars and Stripes flag.

Meehan show big out in Tuam.

Kevin Griffin was bulked up with padding to take on the now traditional cross-dressing role of Edna, Roisin Egenton as Motormouth Maybelle had her body shape altered to give her more of a J-Lo bum and Jennifer Reilly's Tracy was given the big hair the storyline calls for.

Musical director Shane Farrell had assembled an eleven-piece pit band which delivered plenty of oomph and co-director and choreographer, Aoife McClafferty, didn't stint with her energetic and varied routines. But with the composers' ban on all-white groups blacking up, Ms McClafferty and Enda Burke's production lost an edge, in spite of some fine performances from a big cast on the stage at St Jarlath's College.

Debutant Jennifer Reilly with her big eyes, big smile and big hair was so at ease as the schoolgirl heroine Tracy Turnblad, it was hard to believe this was her first show.

The aforementioned Mr Griffin was a soft-centred growler of an Edna who not only pointed up some feminine movements but struck up a good relationship with his stage husband, Nicky Lawless' goofy giggler of a joke shop proprietor, Wilbur.

Ms Egenton's voice was as different as her look, resulting in a terrific take on the big gospel number, "I know where I've been" while Declan Gardiner, a brilliant mover, gave us a lithe Seaweed Stubbs.

Katie St John's Penny Pingleton with her stooped gait, pig tails and glasses was a picture of daft innocence; Louis Brennan as Corny Collins gave us a slick all-American television host, while Stuart Barrows, complete with kiss curl, was a confident Link Larkin.

Suzanne Brennan's Velma, the villain of the piece, was a Cruella de Ville of the television studio eating presenters and performers alike while Emer Kelly caught the essence of her spoilt daughter, Amber.

Jennifer Duggan as Prudy Pingleton was a dragon of a mother whose fire was put out by prospective son-in- in-law Seaweed while Mervyn Fahy made Harriman Spritzer a spluttering business entrepreneur.

Jane McNamara gave us a scary prison matron, Martina O'Brien was a martinet Patterson High principal and another debutant, Chloe Donnellan as Inez, displayed a big voice in a small role.

Kevin O'Dwyer was a suitably over the top Mr Pinky while Mike Flaherty touched in the roles of the gym teacher and prison guard.

The show, which was teased up and given a lacquered finish in just eight weeks, was played out on Eugene Finnegan and Paidraig Neenan's set which was given a gloss of its own by excellent scenic artist, Mairead Brennan.

Mark Shaiman's show is gloriously over the top -unsurprising for a man who works with Bette Midler. It proved a hit with the public out in the west with big crowds all week and a full house on the night of my visit that really enjoyed themselves.

No one can have failed to notice the way standing ovations have become the norm at the end of shows these days. It's a development that snowballed in my years away from theatre and, ever the detached contrarian; it's a display that rarely moves me.

The ovation at the end of this production though was a different kind of animal, an outpouring of affection not solely based on the production by a young cast that had just ended its short run. That's not to say that some of the torrent of applause wasn't designed to show approval for the efforts of the next generation of mid-western talent. However, the overwhelming sense I got was that the crowd, who were on their feet from the moment Billie Kelly's Meg Giry removed the black cloth covering the seat Paul Brown's Phantom used to effect his escape from the mob, until the end of the curtain calls almost five minutes later,  were celebrating something greater again.

This was, after all, the first production staged in the newly refurbished Scouts Hall in the Tipperary town for 14 years and the locals were queueing up to welcome back Nenagh Choral Society to its spiritual base.

After four years of graft, the group only got the keys to the hall nine days before Phantom's opening night, barely enough time to prepare to stage one of modern musical theatre's blockbusters. At the moment it is a building - albeit a highly comfortable one - but by the time of its official opening at the start of 2015 and with further improvements scheduled as well as the important return of the Society's memorabilia, it will become a real home to the group.

The near 500-strong crowd at the Sunday finale were virtually shoehorned into the hall with others disappointed through not booking on time. Together with an interval that had to be extended such was the demand for the fundraising raffle as well as that prolonged ovation, it rammed home to me just how enmeshed many of AIMS member societies are in their local communities.

To earn their support and trust of audiences down the years those groups have had to constantly entertain their peers while pushing their own boundaries and it's safe to say Phantom followed a well- trodden path.

A little like those standing ovations, I've become a bit blasé about the burgeoning base of young talent stepping onto stages all over Ireland at the moment.

It no longer surprises me that 18-year-old university fresher Paul Browne carried off the title role with ease or that final year schoolgirls Roisin Heenan and Breffni Fitzpatrick can effortlessly deliver the difficult vocal roles of Christine and Carlotta respectively.

Dylan Rooney (17) and still at school was an impressive Raoul while the diminutive 18-year-old Niamh McDermott  was well cast as Madame Giry and the aforementioned Billie Kelly was a strong Meg.

Trinity student Johnny Burke was a high tenor Piangi while the father of the company, 21-year-old Killian Fitzgerald and 19-year-old Anthony White were cast as theatre owners Andre and Firmin respectively.

Gary Clarke was a believable Maestro Reyer while Timmy Cullinan touched in both the roles of theatre owner Lefevre and the police chief and Jordan Noon was a confident Auctioneer.

They were guided by a clever director in Greg Browne and backed by Laura Kearney's big sounding orchestra which also included Academy musical director William Cullagh, who had worked with the group from August.

Conductor Finola Higgins-Cosgrove gave us a very involved and accurate reading of this Oremus and Eriksmoen score. Many of the iconic Elvis numbers flooding back into the memory bank. Nice, tidy transitions into scene changes and a good control of this eleven piece orchestra. A clear beat all evening and unobtrusive contact with the stage at all times. Finola also acted as Chorus Mistress putting shape onto this large company. An imbalance with the chorus sound due to a larger number of women, yet some harmonies were still audible. The Chorus generally projected well with clean diction but there were numbers like 'It hurts Me' where the sound was muted. This could be a sound issue.

Louis Brennan as Chad is a good looking lad who had the right attitude from the moment he came on stage. He has a certain swagger and charm but his performance lacked energy. Vocally no problems, well within his range. I believe he could have given more. At times he got a little lost in the crowd due to lack of character projection. This could have been a directorial issue. Overall, a likable, easy sounding, lovable Chad that needed to be pushed a little more. Emer Kelly played Natalie who displayed a great voice with a very good grip and understanding of the lyrics. An easy way on stage, she is always involved and committed to her fellow actors. As Ed, the accent did drop on several occasions. Good body language and aware of new things happening to her - like wearing a dress and proper shoes. Alison Madden as Lorraine is a flighty and energetic young performer with lots of teenage attitude….especially to her mother. A lovely lemon A-line dress suited her very well. She displayed a bright even voice with a great handle on text delivered with a real natural flow. Jamie Dockery as Denis was another diverse and energetic character who gave much to the role and to his colleagues. A lovely comedian surfaced without pushing for laughs, with a well- focused, strongly projected voice. Good accent and a thorough knowledge of the text. His 'It Hurts Me' was a highlight for me.

The Blonde bombshell - Miss Sandra was played by Liz Parsons showing plenty of sass to all around her. A fine voice with a great rock belt, and had the right vocal feel - 'Let Yourself Go' also in - 'The Power of Love'.

Laura Rochford played Sylvia, the bored owner of the Honky Tonk bar. A very convincing performance giving us an easy delivery of text. A lovely mezzo, Sylvia sometimes just glided over the lyrics which lost the true value.

Niall Conway as Jim Haller was in a slightly similar situation trying to bring up his daughter single handedly. He was fully involved in his character and you could sense his frustration in trying to get noticed by Miss Sandra. Nothing like a good midlife crisis!! Siobhán Campbell as Mayor Matilda was suitably unctuous and bossy with well projected dialogue, agility on stage and displaying a fine singing voice which was always in tune. Sheriff Earl was performed by the well- seasoned Pat McGovern who waited till the end to take control of the Mayor. You could sense his frustration with her throughout. A nice rendition of 'Wise Men Say'.

A large chorus in Ballinrobe populated the stage to capacity at times. Thankfully it is a large stage. An energetic and willing group of people who worked hard together, but who were not always together in the choreography. They were let down by the production team in certain scenes were the chorus was not integrated well enough with the principals. The freeze could have been a little more animated. The six girls who joined for 'That's alright, Mama' looked terrific in their A-lines skirts.

Brian and Sean Power provided a fine look to this show with and a fine set that changed and adapted to suit the show's needs. The Rollercoaster effect was well achieved but I felt it was underused especially with the placement of chorus. Chorus needed more attention all evening. Principals will always look after themselves if they have to. I also felt that there was much more in the musical numbers - many were left under- directed with little response to the lyrics. Characters were well crafted and moved well.

Choreographically, Aoife McClafferty, I felt, the routines were a little too much on the aerobics plateau. Too many people at times didn't help the overall pictures. Stage Management, led by John O'Shea, was quick and efficient with some nice work from props. Lovely jukebox and a fantastic bike for Chad. The well thought out set fitted well on the stage. The multi-functional pieces worked well throughout. Karen Forde designed and painted the terrific western landscape to great effect.

Sound by Derek Recks brought a bright tone to the band making the instruments alive and very of its time. Good balance between stage and pit except for some of the chorus scenes. Some mic mishaps with mics not on at the start of lines was a little off-putting. Lighting by Pat Gallagher had a mixed evening. Some issues with accuracy of cues, with over lit intimate scenes. Key light was needed in several scenes especially DSL in the Pub. A little less spread on Denis in 'It Hurts Me' would have worked better. Andrew Reddy and Edel O'Neill presided over a great looking set of costumes. Great colours with attention to underskirts for the A-line dresses and skirts. There were, in my opinion too many black dresses and cardigans in Act 1. It looked a bit too dark. White gloves for Dean were needed and not mustard coloured socks. I felt the angels needed white gloves and the Devils, red ones. Makeup and hair were well attended to with some very fine styles which certainly whisks you back to a long forgotten era.

Snowy blizzards accompanied me on my way to The Riverside Theatre in Coleraine for Ballywillan Drama Group's production of Hairspray. A non-proscenium stage with the orchestra situated up stage on ground level, leaving the large central area and two raised areas stage left and right for the performance. A clever and colourful set designed by Brian Logan allowed the action to flow with facades of houses and shops opening to reveal interiors with the addition of trucks being brought into the central area from time to time.

A neat nine-piece band was put together by Eric Boyd, which produced an even sound with a nod to the 50's. Good brass playing, which didn't intrude and overpower the rest of the instruments. I felt, however, that the overall sound was a little muted - in many of the big numbers, the big forte sections never made impact. With the conductor, Eric Boyd, behind the cast all night, he coped remarkably well - most of the time. A couple of mishaps; like the entrance to "Mama. I'm a Big Girl Now" and some solo lines in "The Big Doll House" needed security from the conductor. The score zipped along with clear tempi and a great sense of style.

Chorus Master, again Eric Boyd, produced - from this large, young company - a vibrant sound but I would like to have heard more harmonies throughout the work. The sound design was an issue here with an uneven balance between band and performers. The energy from the cast seemed "zapped" and un-energised. I also would have liked to have more engagement with the words.

Megan Cunning as Tracy Turnblad looked the part and gave an energised and involved performance. Megan had a good forward singing voice with great diction but some tuning problems plagued her performance throughout the evening. Please keep an eye on your posture as it sometimes looks a little contrived. Alan McClarty created a very successful interpretation of Edna Turnblad, which was unforced and very believable. A truthful and sincere performance with clear diction that was rounded off with a great duet in "Timeless to Me". Helen Wilkinson as Motormouth Maybell gave a confident performance with a mighty, big and flexible voice. Costumed and wigged well, her "I know where I've Been" was the deserved musical hit of the evening. A very classy act.

Louise McClarty was a bundle of energy as Penny Pingleton who worked well with her colleagues all night. Great projection of dialogue in this difficult acoustic. Laura Fisher as Amber Von Tussle needed to be bigger in character, making the put downs and spiteful remarks even more bitchy. Laura has a great singing voice, all within range. Link Larkin, performed by David Mullan was very comfortable on stage and used his previous stage experience with well-projected lines and a fine singing voice with very good interpretive skills. Clumsy staging for "Without Love" left him singing up stage for most of the number. I felt he needed to be more passionate about the cause. A flexible and agile Seaweed, with a terrific rock tenor voice swaggered through the show with great confidence. Adam Goudy who played this role took advantage of all his skills, displaying a big flexible voice, with good well- projected dialogue.

Maxine McAleenon as Velma Von Tussle didn't quite get the subtle nuances of this ghastly character. It was treated more with a cleaver than with a razor sharp scalpel. Vocally a little stretched at the top of her range and I felt she should have let go more in "Miss Baltimore Crabs". Richard Mairs as Wilbur was the devoted father and doting husband. A little too much on the "off the line" moments but a very solid performer with a hilarious " Timeless to me".

We needed a much bigger personality from Warren McCook as Corny Collins. We missed the showman and pizzazz associated with this type of character. More energy in his personality would have helped to drive the dialogue more forward. And also a different, brighter costume would have helped rather than the dark funereal one he wore.

Maelisa Cunning as Prudy Pingleton lacked some character as she blended in with the rest of the cast. Prudy is an odd ball, austere with different ideas and thoughts about life and youth. Dressed beautifully she became one of the "ordinary folk" and I felt she needed to be more self-absorbed in her oddness. Tying your daughter up is a little odd. A lovely presence on stage and vocally steady, Jasmine Gardiner was a ray of sunshine and a bundle of energy as Little Inez. Great projection of lines with a strong singing voice. She moved easily on stage but I felt she was cast a little too old for this role.

Ken Bolton played the flash in the pan part of Mr Pinky, but he nailed every second on stage with a well-observed and disciplined performance. Bravo. A large chorus, even with the juniors, worked hard all night. They sang well, but I missed quite a lot of the harmonies in the score. Balance also was an issue due to the young age profile and the percentage SA to TB in the chorus. I felt Sharon Logan and Victoria Lagan (choreographers) probably needed more rehearsal time as the cast needed further precision drilling. A stronger hand needed to be taken here. Some great work in "Timeless to me" and the Act 2 Finale brought the house down.

Jeni Campbell looked after the wardrobe department. Costumes were beautifully presented in general, with great detail given to the 50's period and accessories. Gorgeous A line skirts with great underskirts, beautiful day suits for Prudy and Velma all created the correct look for this show and period. Karen Hunter (Props Designer) did a fine job with suitable microphones and props positioned behind the set facades. The TV was not of the correct period. ….even though we only saw the back end of it. Stage management under David Wray marshaled his team with precision and efficiency all night. Wigs were a great success also which added greatly to the period. All age appropriate - quite amazing and then we had the "fantasy" 50's wigs at the end…great thinking here. Director Brian Logan used the space of the Riverside theatre cleverly and with some imagination. The show moved very well with no hitches, cast making clear entrances and exits. Principals were well directed but I would have liked a little more from some characters.

Sound by Darren Gardiner was a major issue in this production, which varied throughout the entire evening. Too many microphones not on for the start of dialogue with much fluffing and hissing throughout. The overall sound needed to be brighter in order to give clarity - especially for the chorus.

Racism and segregation are the two strategic elements, which are central to this musical. The kernel of the show lies in the fact that this overweight white girl, against adversity, fulfills her dream of making it on to the popular TV programme, The Corney Collins Show, only to give everything up for a minority group - the black kids. The ugliness of white supremacy in the 1950's is strong subject matter. Without black actors in this show, for me, it is bubble gum without the flavour. If you don't have men in your company, you don't produce Guys and Dolls………if you are doing Hairspray, you need the correct ethnicity for the storyline to hit the audience hard…. where it hurts…their hearts. Without a put upon minority, this show is hollow. The three principal characters, which should have been black, were very talented but their performances were diminished because of their ethnicity. It's a problem that has no answer other than…if you don't have the cast, then don't do the show.

A special thank you to Carlton Molyneaux at front of house who treated me and my guest with great attention. One of life's gentlemen. Thank you once again for your generous hospitality.

An interesting and quite a large perfuming space at The Black Box in Galway City. The open stage showed a great parquet floor with some raised levels up stage centre with the large orchestra to stage right.

Fionnula Hannigan-Dunkley was the conductor for this and had quite a large orchestra of fifteen to control in this Kander and Ebb blockbuster. The trumpet and the trombone marred much of the orchestral playing, I feel through lack of experience. Lovely string playing - with delicate pizzicato work, - kit and woodwind playing also good.

Not a huge amount of work for the chorus in this show, with the choral sound unbalanced due to so many ladies versus the men and the tessitura also being too high. The chorus had problems with precision, raggy cut-offs and late entries.

Peter Kenny as Cliff showed good presence and looked well as the American. A stronger American accent was needed but vocally had an easy tone suitable for this role. Be careful with the tuning.

Róisín Egan as Sally Bowles gave a stilted performance - more of primness rather than a lost English girl trying to deal with her demons in the tacky quarter of 1933, Berlin. Her first entrance was not strong enough. The character lacked fun and excitement. Vocally fine, but with a slight strain on the voice in 'Mein Herr'. Care must always be taken with text and lyrics. This was the problem with the title song.

Martin Kenny as the Emcee had 'moments' in this role, but again, attention to detail with accent, lyrics and text let him down. A character with multiple personalities… did not come through. Vocally variable with tone and at times flat. Lack of understanding of text of was a constant shadow in this performance and, unfortunately, hovered over this character all evening.

Julie Breen as Fraulein Schneider showed a great concern for her home. She worked hard all evening giving to her fellow cast members. Text was well understood which was clear. A lovely mezzo voice, her number 'What Would You Do' was beautifully and sincerely delivered.

I am afraid that Jack Fitzgerald was cast beyond his capabilities. Although he gave us a certain agitation in the role, he was far too young for the part and just had a bad evening. A strong energetic performance from Chris Moran as Ernst Ludwig with fine projection of text throughout. Fraulein Kost entertained 'her cousins' all night. More of an accent was needed and also a freer Bohemian look would have worked better.

The hard working chorus was dealt a bad hand from the production team and I felt this show was under rehearsed. There was a lack of real involvement in the dialogue scenes and vocally ill prepared in others. Too many on stage, at times, prevented clarity of moves.

Kori Kilduff was the director for this production. It was a presentation that did not probe any of the issues inherent in this dramatic Kander and Ebb show. More attention was needed with accents, energy in characterisation, delivery of text and having your finger on the pulse regarding the technical. Choreography was simple in nature and lacked real understanding of the piece. Nice doll like movements and freezes in 'Money' and some good chair work in 'Mein Herr'. Not a great night for the Stage Management who took an age to change sets - mind you, they weren't helped by music running out and not having ANY light. Ray Hehir designed the set which generally worked well for this space. An erratic evening with the sound design gave us inaccurate cues and a lack of balance with everything.
