Costumes over all had a taste of Berlin 1930's but didn't make you uneasy at any time. Some lovely costumes like Frau Schneilders' black with beige trim looked wonderful as did Frau Kost in the red shoes. Men's shoes needed more attention and I felt the Emcee needed more changes. Some work and research had been done by the wigs and make-up department which showed. We missed Sally's iconic black bob hair style. Men's styles needed looking at.

Opportunities were missed with this show. Being a university, I expected this production to have energy and a greater degree of risqué business that some other companies may not have tackled. This, I am afraid did not happen.

This is a show I know very well and the trick with producing it is to try and provide a Dickensian feel to its dark and unpleasant story lines. If you capture this, then you have an essence which will help with the rest of the storytelling. I am sorry to say that we did not receive this this evening. A fine orchestra was present with conductor Elizabeth Kelly giving quite varied tempi throughout. A slow start to 'Consider Yourself' did not help Dodger and then quickening it up for the dance section didn't really help the dancers. Great sound coming from the band with some good sliding work from the trombone, and some lovely violin obligato work from the violinist in 'Reviewing the Situation'. I feel the score needed more momentum in general. The children's' chorus sang lustily, in tune and with good diction. Movement was mainly marching. Some nice harmonies but were let down by the production team in the Den scenes where they were left standing about and uninvolved. Tom Bennett as Oliver Twist has good rhythms and a lovely voice which he uses well. He tends to drop out and does only what he has been requested to do. Ciarán Mooney as Fagin gave a very one dimensional portrayal of this iconic role. A performance that didn't burrow into the skin of this immensely rich and varied character. There was very little trace of an accent which was not placed anywhere in particular and the tasting of the words was lacking. Tuning was a problem here and there throughout the evening.

Orla Walsh performed a truthful and well voiced Nancy, really working hard and taking care with the text. Clear diction and a lovely voice that was well able to deliver 'As long As He Needs Me' soaring to a belt at the end.

Unwashed and looking every bit a Bill Sykes was Paul Laycock who provided menace except for the murder scene at the end which made the character look weak. Be careful with the accent which dropped a number of times. Cian O'Sullivan as the Artful Dodger was too refined and not a kid of the streets. A few tuning problems and lack of direction and movement left this Dodger a bit under nourished.

Well projected dialogue and an understanding of the text was well put across by Jean Bennett as Widow Corney. Robbie Kennedy was a little shaky at the beginning but rallied as Mr Bumble. Again, a lack of things to do from the production team rendered this character a shell of what he should be. Wigs were essential for the Sowerberry's. Modern haircuts don't work in this period piece, Vincent Oliver needed to develop more of a Dickensian character while Ciara Hanratty needed to be more animated and fluid in her lines. The 'Nancy in training' role of Bet has a bright forward personae in her lines and a well projected voice. She complemented Nancy very well.

Marissa Magner as Mrs Bedwin was cast far too young as we should have some indication that she is interested in Mr. Brownlow, played by Paul McGuire. A fine speaking voice resonated with clarity and projection. His tone was that of a 'Mr Meldrew'.

The adult chorus, despite being given uninteresting choreography to execute - needed more rehearsal time - worked hard all evening given the various jobs they had to do. Choreography by Sonya Dunne Johnson was not well thought through with semi circles for dialogue with hardly any integration amongst the principals, created a dip in the dramatic intention of several scenes.

Many opportunities were missed in this production where the story oozes great characters, atmosphere and changes of moods. Director, Lynda O'Neill did not draw the necessary qualities from the cast to create such characters. Attention to the text was very lacking with also a lack of persistence on accent work. Uneven choreography created peaks and troughs in this Oliver! Why was so much music cut from the end to render the entire Sykes death to an almost nonevent.

Some more attention needed to be lavished on the props like better tea service for Widow Corney, Sykes' Jemmy, and Fagin's jewellery box. The set designed by Lynda O'Neill was sparse and not informative of period or location, as a result it left very little for Stewart Bourke, Stage Manager to do. Projections were ill chosen - Why was there a projection of Calvary in the Sowerberry's scene? Jean Bennett and team sorted costumes with a lot of dying for the kid's orphanage scene. Be careful using modern trousers for chorus men; also be careful with footwear - that's if you want to go the extra mile. Some good looks for Nancy, Sykes and Fagin with all his layers. Make up and Wigs is another area that needed more attention in this production. The character names that Dickens gives his dramatis personae indicate what we must do to bring these personalities to life. We must listen to the master.

Happiness and excitement certainly does generate a mood before you go into a production and this was easily palpable before Sister Act began. There was a joy coming from the stage which carried the audience through this up lifting score to the very end.

Carmel Griffin led her ten piece, well balanced orchestra with good control and discipline, bringing certain instruments like sax, double flutes and clarinets to the fore. A sense of freedom in the conducting helped the flow of the music with good judgment on tempi and balance. There was just an issue with some of the scoring under dialogue which was a bit loud. Her work was evident in the chorus preparation with projected delivery and clean diction in the most part. A good number of 'solo' singers in the chorus helped to raise the standard of this almost all female chorus. High standards with tuning and rhythms bringing energy to this music.

The leading lady, Deloris Von Cartier, was played by Jessica Bray. A confident and well-presented artist, projecting this sassy Philadelphian with lots of attitude. Very flexible and easy on stage. Vocally a clear voice with a strong belt captured many of the numbers. Be careful with dialogue speed - you tended to deliver too fast at times, and we didn't catch everything. Edel McFadden as Mother Superior gave a variable performance. I felt there was a character imposed onto this role which restricted the artist quite a bit. Didn't understand why she should have an English accent - it's not indicated in the script! Some nicely timed parlando in the opening of 'Here, within these walls' with good understanding of text.

Ciaran Collins as Eddie sometimes dipped in volume with some dialogue but he performed with a good accent and with an easy baritone voice. Good progression in the number 'I could be that guy' but more attention to lyrics would have helped in this piece. More sweat stains on his costumes would also have aided his portrayal.

Derek Barrett gave us his suavely measured thug like performance, immaculately groomed in a blue / grey suit. More energy in the script would have helped his character - this was due to the 'cool' nature he created for Curtis sacrificing the dangerous side.

Hazel Park was a loud and vivacious Mary Roberts who 'bubbled' her way through the show with a tendency to run away with her lines. Be careful as every word matters. Anna Maria Barrett as Sister Lazarus was tough as old boots who created this façade with a hard voice and forthright manner. She had great body language, good pace with dialogue and true understanding and timing of lines. Sister Mary Patrick played by Grace O'Connor had a big sunny disposition, loud and vivacious but was a little fast on the delivery of lines. Great voice with body language to match. An infectious performance.

An old ham who spoke with clarity and projected a typical 'Fr Ted' version of his role, Aodan Fox was consistent in every way with excellent diction and delivery of lines and reactions. James Kelly as Joey, Eoghan Rice as Pablo and Joe Bracken as TJ all worked well together giving diverse characters in this group of thugs. All well capable singing in 'Long Black Dress' - Difficult falsetto line for Pablo. Some fine choral work which developed from the four backing singer's right through to the full nun's chorus. Good rhythms and an eagerness to create their own characters. The chorus was well integrated into their scenes with good reactions to the various situations. A well paced production by Jean McGlynn with a well drilled cast and quick scene changes allowed the production to flow. Just one scene change delayed - the first office scene. Good use of the space with some clever touches like the LX behind the stained glass window, the smiling altar boys. Numbers were well developed with some nice creative touches. Choreography devised by Pamela McGlynn was energetic with plenty of movement and ideas permeating through the production. It was the less upbeat numbers that slid down the scale a bit. Standards were high in the execution of moves and created the '70's feel very well.

Stage management headed by Francis Maloney took charge of the slick scene changes, executed with efficiency - apart from the one mentioned above.

Some great looking props were gathered by Mary Forde. The only thing that jarred for me was the style of bed in the nun's quarters. Needed a little bit more dressing in the office scene. Good work though.

Great multiplicity of uses for tables as walls, confessional boxes and long refectory tables. Good use of materials which saved so much space. Great stained glass window, lit in different colours, was a fine central piece in the convent scenes. Lighting was a challenge for the designer with low ceilings in this space. Michael Farrell used a really good selection of gels and produced some lovely effects with back lighting on the stained glass window. There were a few focus issues of lamps and some cuing moments that were a little off.

Costume management by Rosie Byrne, brought some lovely attention to detail and ideas for the costumes in this show. Good choice for some costumes which brought us instantly to the correct period. Eddie is a detective not rank and file policeman, I loved Mary Robert's sandals - indeed, good footwear throughout including Deloris's FM Boots! Makeup by Rachel McIntyre and team was all suitable with nothing jarring. Great wig for Monsignor O'Hara. House Management was busy with a full house to settle which they did unobtrusively. Escorts included Sister Susan, and Fathers Tom and Martin who looked after me extremely well - nothing was too much trouble.

An Táin, with its steep auditorium giving great sightlines to the stage was the venue for this 'Sweeney Todd'. Conducting this complex score was Patrick Dunne who maneuvered his nine piece orchestra through all the pit falls and where all the colours from this extraordinary score could be heard. A little loud under dialogue, it was generally sensitive to the singers. All moved along nicely without any obvious delays. The score never seemed rushed and singers and chorus alike were well prepared. A strong opening section vocally for the chorus with some excellent solo lines. Men lost it slightly coming into the tutti section of 'The Ballad of Sweeny Todd'. Good harmonies coming through but needed a little more bite with the words in areas like 'His hands were quick'. Good work though.

Brendan Cleary as Sweeney Todd gave a brooding psychopathically troubled man bent on revenge. He needed more energy from his character which, unfortunately, remained on a plateau of emotion. Irene Dunne as Mrs. Lovett did a fine job with this difficult role. She generally needed more business and needed to be more flippant in character. Relish and point the text more and be careful to sustain the breath more in singing. There was a tendency to go off the note when put under pressure.

The insipid role of Johanna was nicely performed by Leanna Carragher. With a bright and clear voice she was ideal in this role. Be careful also not to put pressure on the top of the voice, it became tight and pinched. Nimble on stage but a little static in the first balcony scene.

A confident and compelling performance from Gavin Quigley as Anthony. A healthy tenor voice but also was stretched at the top of the range becoming a little raspy. Lyrics and text were sincerely performed and his emotions were always believable. With a focused and well-rounded voice, the Beggar Women - Lynsey O'Neill was a treat all evening. Nice playful scenes with Anthony, she ran away with her riddles a bit. Sincerely delivered and nicely paced performance. The journey for Cormac Todd's character as Tobias was not long enough and lacked a certain knowledge of life. The simpleton side of the character was not adequately drawn; hence the end of the show was not as shocking as it should have been. Vocally the timbre was right for this part, but unsure in several areas musically with tuning and stamina problems.

Beadle Bamford should be more of a bully. Andrew Browne is a gentle giant really and this different approach somewhat worked against this crooked rogue. A beautiful tenor voice, he was vocally strong with a clear upper register and diction. Kevin Stanley as Judge Turpin gave a strong and confident performance with a great understanding of the dialogue. A rich Bass Baritone voice gave real justice to the opening recit 'You see, Sir, A Man Infatuated with Love' which displayed a very even range and well projected voice. A weak entrance for Pirelli, performed by Tom Maher, also revealed an actor that was over stretched in this role. Vocally too high and out of his natural range. He lacked a certain ego and larger than life acting which is the hallmark of this role. One of the best singers on the stage came to us from Mr. Fogg played by Tom Doonan. An excellent baritone evenly produced and well projected. He has a bright future ahead of him.

A very reactive group of people who were drilled well musically. Good blend of voices with diction well handled. More bite required from the men's chorus with words in 'The Ballad' reprise. Great chorus integration in 'By the Sea'.

A creative approach to this production from Rob Vickers, who used his cast well with a unified harmony that worked well within this space. Some lapses in giving his principals things to do, Mrs Lovett and Sweeney Todd fell victim to this a few times. A brooding approach with Todd's character sucked all the energy from this role. Not using blood in a production such as this really baffles me especially if no alternative device is sought. Choral movement in Mrs Lovett's was very much muted at the beginning of Act 2. This needed to be more vibrant and chaotic. Great entrances and exits for the mini-ensembles were efficient and direct.

Scene changes by Lisa Dunbar and her team were effective with the flying cues timed very well. Some projection images were ill timed. A fine collection of props by Nessa Toale with lovely attention to the bird cages and the bottle of elixir for Toby. Be careful with bulbs in lanterns - it looked too modern.

A multi layered set with all its rough edges gave us the playing field for this penny dreadful piece. It looked sturdy but I thought Mrs. Lovett's basement/bake house was not well thought through. It didn't capture the horror of the place. The mangle and the oven door worked very well. Size really does count. Sound by Vinnie Osborne was evenly mixed throughout the evening. A few fluffs with mics not being on for first words. Lovely reverb on 'City on Fire'.

The lighting board seemingly crashed in the morning of the first performance and so we had a skeletal design. It really would not be fair for me to comment on this unfortunate incident. But well- handled on the night.

Costumes gave a good impression of Victorian London in all its colour and grotesqueness. Good mix of fabrics and colours in all the costumes. Things did jar like Todd's coat being too short and the Masquerade look was not correct with costumes of a later period. It wasn't 'grand' enough. Footwear was also a mixed affair. Research and details with a period show is a must. Overall, a very good look for the entire show. Complementing the costumes was the Make up and Hair team led by Paula Murray. All looked in order except the BEARD!!!! And I would have insisted on the use of blood. A great evening with the audience at the edge of their seats.

Danny Carroll is a master at guiding and bringing together both cast and orchestra with great control. With an orchestra of 10 players, he drew some lovely playing from this brass and woodwind dominated band to great effect. The show flowed well integrating both score and dialogue neatly. Balance for such a wind and brass dominated orchestra worked very well and never overshadowed the singers and chorus on stage.

Helen Colbert, as chorus Mistress, did great work in spite of a gender imbalance within the company. The sound impaired the vocal reproduction coming from the stage which was a pity.

A good looking Liam Quigley as Chad gave a rounded performance with a pleasant singing voice. Be careful of your tuning you went flat a number of times. A little more projection of dialogue would help and invest more into the text and lyrics. Lena Hally looked great as the mechanic - Natalie. A natural performer with a good singing voice and clear diction, just right for this '50's score. Again, analyse the text more.

Derek Ryan as Jim gave an earnest performance and a great commitment to the character. Clear projected dialogue with no problems vocally with this score ……neither would he have with Wagners Ring Cycle! He made a good fist of the dancing which worked out well for him. Tracey Walsh as Sylvia is an attractive performer on stage, a little stilted due to lack of business to do on stage. Her casual way of standing back and assessing the situation was lovely to see…..the way Jim behaves, she can see right through it. Orla Purcell is a bundle of energy as Lorraine. Ever romantic, she tended to drop dialogue in more intimate scenes with Dean. More focus required here. Vocally, a little stretched.

Gary Sheppard is a constant worker on stage in the role of Denis. A lovely comedic actor exuding all the nerdyness of this character. Vocally reliable and a lovely rendition of 'It hurts Me'. Anthony Flynn as Sheriff Earl reminded me of Boss Hog from The Dukes of Hazards. A distortion with the dialogue due to the thick American accent and some difficulty in pitching notes for his number. Fiona O'Connor as Miss Sandra is an attractive actress stepping into her first stage role. An easy manner, she vamped her way through with some confidence as belies her experience. A little more sexuality in the garden scene would have nailed this perfectly. Vocally a few tuning issues, down to nerves I am sure, and watch out for lighting specials.

The juvenile lead, John Ryan as Dean, has much to contend with. Dodging his bossy mother in the first blushes of love doesn't prevent a good bond to develop between him and Lorraine. His text was true and believable and a pleasant singing voice. However, lyrics needed more emotional content.

The chorus worked very hard all evening but felt the production team should have integrated them more into the show. More energy was required for entrances and exits.

Des Henn was director of this production and he needed to give more time to the chorus and in the production of some of the numbers. Technical areas of the production needed more time. I loved the idea of Lorraine chasing after the bus. Nice touch. Production flowed well with small delays only in some scene changes. Motor bike access was one of the main problems.

The choreography of Barbara Meany in this production did not trail blaze and infuse that 1950's frenzy and energy that you associate with this most dynamic of decades in America. Too many frantic arm movements on the spot did not make up the '50's feel that is required for this show. Numbers lacked precision with faces lacking energised attitude. Nice touches with the angels and devils but I feel this should have gone further. Stage crew guided by Francis Hickey worked hard all evening given the tight space they were working in. Small things like stretching the cyc would help visually. A speedier response to changing scenes would also assist show pace.

Good array of props with leather suitcases and mechanical paraphernalia was collected Derek Ryan and team. More props were needed in the Honky Tonk.

Set design by Dermott Quinn and built by An Tus, was clever in its design, slotting any piece together to form a new space or scene. More detailed painting was required as some of it was a little approximate. Sound by Pat Murnane did not achieve a suitable audio balance for this auditorium. The sound quality lacked warmth and sounded too brittle and bright. Some dialogue became distorted with some cues missed on cast entrances. Lighting by Seamus Recks was a travesty from the start. Cue times ill judged, focus of lamps not suitable for the production and an over reliance on three sets of baton stripes along the front of the stage. It was not a good night in this department. The colourful costumes were looked after by Phyllis Hickey and team. Good attention to detail with the appropriate footwear and underskirts. Be careful with trouser lengths - Denis's trousers needed taking up approx 6". Chad needed brightening up - a white T shirt would have looked much better than the black - as with Denis and Jim. Great hair styles for the chorus in this production thanks to Bridget Hadnett and her team. A great job done.

A lovely welcome from the FOH at the Excel. Announcements were made from the sound desk which lacked energy and were not terribly loud. The interval snack was very welcome. Many thanks.

Scoil Mhuire in Trim was the ghostly location for this well put together production of the rarely performed The Addams Family. With various sounds coming from the keyboards, the twelve piece orchestra gave some lush sounds and an even balance throughout the evening. Conducted by Olivia Toman. Physically, her beat was clear at all times but quite metronomic and a little four square. The job of Chorus Mistress was entrusted to the same lady, brought a vibrant sound from this well worked and tutored chorus. They were always involved dramatically with some good SATB harmonies with clear diction coming through despite the differences in numbers between men and women. The fulcrum of the show, Colin Flynn as Gomez was well focused and prepared in this role. Great body language with well projected text and vocally very clear. His sexual innuendos needed to be greater and needed to be nearer the surface especially with Morticia. Danilelle Williamson as Morticia captured the iconic look with the long straight hair. Sleek and rigid, she had many of the stoic attributes for this character. A tease with her husband, but I wanted more to make this character truly work. 'Secrets' showed a lovely mezzo voice with a fine shape on the dialogue. Keila Whelan as Wednesday had an excellent attitude with a serious expression most of the night. Clear diction, punctuating her text with clarity showed a great understanding of the script and lyrics. Vocally very secure with a full even range. She has an innate sense of the stage.

Shane Fox as Uncle Fester was a tour de force all evening despite his youthful age. He threw himself into this role, cultivating a character with mannerisms and body language which was sustained throughout the evening. A very well defined accent with fine make-up helped him find this zany character. His 'Moon and Me' was one of the highlights of the evening.

Lurch came in the form of Niall Dempsey in this production. A fine and even study with only movement to communicate. A fine strong baritone voice revealed at the end. A measured and well controlled performance. Granny, played by Gwen Bagnall looked great in her layered costume. She brought plenty of character to this part, good facial reactions and lots of madness. Dialogue had lots of character with the lovely line 'I just peed.' Brian Higgins as Pugsley was visually correct for this role who interacted with this mad family on every level. Great reactions in the shock treatment scene. Although having some very clear diction, it did lapse in the bedroom scene. A nice voice but he had some problems with tuning.

Lucas, the romantic lead was played by Craig Regan who gave us an energised and youthful performance. He looked great and had a very tangible relationship with Wednesday. A good understanding with the text which was well articulated. He need to project more when there was underscoring. Emma Stowe gave us a very well-studied, terrified mother with plenty of subtle acting. A lovely change of character in 'Full Disclosure', showing us a real outpouring of truth with a fine voice that belted her frustrations out along the table. A really well judged performance. With excellent makeup and wig, Sean Flanagan was transformed into Alice's urban and conservative husband, Mal. A strong performer with good delivery of text and he performed well with his fellow cast members.

The only thing I can say about Eoin Kenny as Thing was that he needed make up on his hand to give it more definition Great attention to detail in this production by Pat McElwain with his eye on every ball. Very good attention to the visuals - set, lighting and costumes. The production was generally slick except for one scene change. Good use of space and well-drawn characters made for an entertaining show. Certain things which did not come across - the bewitching effect Morticia has on Gomez…..I felt Gomez needed more energy and freedom and to get much more fun out of it all. On the whole, very well done.

Choreographer Aisling Toher devised and executed some animated routines which were in keeping with the feel of the entire production. She had an awareness of space and the moves were well generally well drilled. There was good precision in the arm movements and clicks. The ancestors moved well within the piece. Apart from the long bedroom scene change, Frank Connolly and his team were well prepared with clean and efficient changes, Props were well in order especially Granny's 'Private stash" cart and Gomez's torture chair.

The set looked great with some nice details on it. Not a big stage but it fitted well into the space. I think a missed opportunity for some more magic tricks and more of the gothic in the interiors would have created more atmosphere. The moon and her glitter lips……did the moon stray into Ali Murphy's make-up room?

Sound was variable between pit and stage. The pit seemed to dominate over the stage especially in the numbers - 'Not today' and 'Crazier than you'. Well cued sound effects with good clarity from the actors on stage.

Lighting by Darren Kelleher was very atmospheric and created some beautiful states throughout the evening. A lovely pink state complementing the star cloth with Morticia in 'Just around the corner', the blue state with the special on the moon to highlight the glitter lips worked well.

Costumes were by Debby White and her team. She did an excellent job both on the Iconic TV reproduction of the principals and the varied all-white costumes for the ancestors. Some feat working through all the eras. The only issue here was that some of the footwear was not in period. Some issues with long trousers - Gomez's needed taken up 4/5 inches and Fester's flying hat need trimming. Small quibbles to an overall, great job.

Hair and make-up created another dimension to this show with excellent attention to detail for all characters. Great depth was achieved with shading on the white faces. Hardly any colour make-up was used. Great wigs finished off each look with style.

With plenty of children in the audience, this show went down a bomb with great entertainment values. It just hit the spot.

One of the great joys of this job is seeing how different societies cope in adverse circumstances.

Castlerea, in the west of Roscommon and closer to the borders of Galway and Mayo than the county town, is one such musical society.

With the small town stripped of both the old cinema and the night club that previously hosted the group's shows, the company take over a sports hall in an unprepossessing industrial estate on the eastern edge of the town a week before opening night and turn it into a mini-theatre.

Like some of their western counterparts they have to build a stage and import essentials such as lighting trusses.

The end result in this particular case was a decent playing space in a comfortable auditorium named The Hub which pulled in full houses for Colin Hughes' upbeat version of this feel-good tale of rags to riches set against the background of a gangland murder.

This was a production that benefited greatly from the excellent support of Shane Farrell's eight-piece pit band which backed the actors perfectly without drawing unnecessary attention to themselves.

Choreographer Patricia McDermott had drilled the chorus in her 70s-inspired routines while chorus mistress Heather Shine had also put in a considerable amount of graft with the ensemble. The work of both ladies ensured that the nuns were sure of foot and note and as a result, thoroughly enjoyed themselves onstage.

The heroine of the piece, Linda Murray, was an all-action big-voiced Deloris Van Cartier who morphs from a gangster's girlfriend to the saviour of the run-down Philadelphia parish of Mary, Queen of the Angels, inveigling her new found sisters into Sunday Morning Fever along the way with her showbiz wiles.

Majella Flanagan was a haughty Mother Superior who took an instant dislike to the interloper in her ranks while Ivan Moran's Monsignor O'Hara was by turns dejected and enthusiastic as the cards were stacked firstly against and then dramatically for him and Niall Heaney a soft-hearted Eddie Souther.

Daniel Doherty gave gang boss Curtis a believable edge while David Cooke was his comically dim lieutenant TJ, part of a rat pack that included Aidan Flanagan as the mumbling Latino Pablo and Stephen Fagan as ladies' man Joey.

Julie Connolly as Sister Mary Robert blossomed from the shy postulant to a more worldly wise adult who would defy her Superior while Caroline Madigan invested Sister Mary Patrick with giddy humour and a mellow mezzo voice and Francis Cooke was a gravelly voiced Sister Mary Lazarus, an old groaner who discovered the joys of rap music

If Jesus Christ Superstar is as much about Judas as Christ, this show is as much about Sue Snell as Carrie White. As Stephen King's tale about a repressed teenager with telekinetic powers unfolded I also couldn't help thinking of Elphaba's powerful song from Steven Schwartz's Wicked, "No good deed goes unpunished".

For it is Sue's insistence on making it up to the class loner Carrie after a public belittling that unleashes the chain of events that leads to the deaths of so many in small town America. She inveigles her boyfriend Tommy Ross to take Carrie to the high school Prom as a way of assuaging her guilt.

However, unknown to Sue, the frat brats, headed by the aggrieved Chris Hargensen and her boorish boyfriend Billy Nolan; plot to humiliate Carrie all over again at the dance.

A running joke about the spilling of blood, re-enacted here from the top of one of two towers in Nisei Kobayashi's minimalistic set, means that all Hell breaks loose as the child on the outside of the group takes her revenge in the most savage of fashion.

In this Irish premiere of the work, CIT's first AIMS nominee, Muirgen O'Mahoney, was excellent as Sue in a commanding performance as the sole survivor of a horrific night in Chamberlain, Maine. Madeleine White, a first year student in the title role, is a promising actress with a good soprano voice and a neat line in murderous magic.

The adult partly to blame for laying the groundwork for her daughter's unhinged actions, Carrie's mum, the evangelically religious Margaret White, was played by post-graduate student Jean Elliot- Murphy, another expressive soprano, who captured the emotion of a tortured, possessive zealot who had persuaded herself that she was trying to protect her only child.

Maria Branagan had an edge to her character as the self-centred Chris while Society chairman Aaron Barriscale as Nolan came across as a timewasting prat.

Cathal Broderick's Tommy Ross showed the makings of a good tenor voice as the boy caught in the middle of the maelstrom by honouring his girlfriend's wishes; Aisling McCarthy - another fine female voice - was the tough but well- meaning PE teacher Miss Gardner while Joy Mulcahy made a stern class teacher as Mrs Stephens.

Director Joseph Walsh and his assistant Katrina Foley were proven correct in their decision to stage this piece as theatre in the round, drawing in the audience in the Curtis Auditorium at Cork's School of Music, a venue that can seem cavernous. Musical director Michael Young fronted a fine band and together with musical supervisor Deirdre Long prepared not just soloists but moulded the 20-strong cast into a terrific ensemble.

The student Society are not frightened to tackle shows that are not in the mainstream - most of their work to date has been on that track - and, encouragingly, they were rewarded with full houses including a large part of the audience from off-campus.

While the original production of this show is known as Broadway's biggest flop of the modern era, I suspect this revised version by Michael Gore and Dean Pitchford, the team behind Fame and Lawrence D Cohen, the screenwriter of the film, will have a longer life.

Pity the adults of Ennis Musical Society good people. Never work with kids or animals was the advice drummed into them in days gone by - advice they casually ignored in this Sarah Griffin production.

Not content with taking their chances of being outshone by the armies of children in this show, they had to contend with the devastating charm of a little Pomeranian called Charley, a real little diva in the role of Toto.

And any last residue of empathy from the full houses at the spacious Glor theatre in the Clare town was mopped up by 16-year-old Sinead Coughlan in a mature and neatly crafted portrayal of Dorothy as she made her way along the Yellow Brick road in this Frank Baum classic. It meant a fine musical theatre debut by Rachael Culligan in the twin roles of Almira Gulch and the Wicked Witch was slightly overlooked by the big crowd. Miss Culligan, no stranger to the drama circuit, brought her experience to bear here.

Joe Varden - here cast in the roles of Professor Marvel and The Wizard - was another whose drama background shone through with his clear speaking voice and excellent diction.

Mr Varden joined a cast that included Ennis regular Neil Honan as a very credible Scarecrow who grew into this production although he was a little less rubber-legged than some of the straw men I've encountered in this role.

Declan Honan, one of the men the Society has added to its ranks in the last couple of seasons, was a humorous Lion with a good speaking and singing voice while recent university graduate, Adam Bluett, lent a light baritone voice to the role of the Tin Man.

Society chairwoman, Kate Corrigan, as Glinda, was a Disney-like princess while Laurence O'Brien, back on the stage after a long break, brought a manic touch to the Emerald City gatekeeper.

Joe Moran was a gruff Uncle Henry, played here with a limp while Gillian Dunphy was a very sympathetic Aunt Em although I thought she looked a little young looking for the role.

Ms Griffin also threw a highly mobile set of crows and a glamorous trio of trees into the mix in a production that handled all the pivotal moments cleverly, presenting a bit of magic before the cluster of young eyes dotted around the audience.

Ms Griffin's choreography was tailored to an ensemble, which as well as an adult chorus, included so many kids that they had to be split into sections and used on alternate nights.

The production, driven along by musical director Shane Farrell's fine ten-piece band, also delivered the unexpected pleasure of a surprise ending.

A clever set by a design team headed by Elaine Gavin, which allowed changes to be carried out swiftly and smoothly, also aided the flow of the show on what is a big performing space.

Elvis will never really leave the building when there are shows like this.

Joe DiPietro's book is constructed around 25 songs associated with the King of rock and roll.

Mr DiPietro's work may be one of the better storylines of the rash of jukebox musicals that have appeared over the last couple of decades.

And while it is claimed that the story is loosely based on Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, one thing it is certainly not is a biography and with its unlikely fantasy, has the potential to verge into pantomime.

Director Paul Norton avoided that pitfall by aiming for the vibrancy and colour of a stage cartoon with characters that are drawn with big brush strokes rather than fine detail and where the audience suspends disbelief for the sake of a good night out.

Leading man Chris Corroon as Chad certainly understood the brief. With a tongue firmly in his cheek, his long legs in tight trousers and a seriously expressive face this was a man who elevated two highly defined eyebrows to weapons of mass seduction raising alternate sniggers and guffaws from middle-aged women who should know better. He can also deliver a song.

As the run headed towards its conclusion, Sinead Handy as Natalie/Ed suffered for her art with armfuls of bruises thanks to the stage action. Thankfully her vocal chords were in better nick with a strong pop soprano voice as Natalie the motor mechanic which descended surprisingly easily into a much lower register as Ed, her alter ego.

Hardworking Tom Maher as Jim had also taken serious direction to effect a stammer as his tongue tied character vainly pursued the statuesque Sandra of Aoife Fitzsimons, the sultry sex bomb of this piece.

Jim Smyth's Earl was another of small town America's citizens who had trouble with words - he doesn't say anything until the last ten minutes - leaving the ShowTimes Reviews/Feature actor to win over the audience with a series of shrugs, glances and stares. He eventually pipes up to silence the somewhat louder Matilda, the bossy handbag toting Fiona Goulding, a one-woman McCarthyite campaign determined to crack down on loose morals and indecency.

Roddy Shaw was a quirky Denis, complete with Buddy Holly glasses, Chad's not-so-little helper at well over six feet tall, while Grainne Donoghue as Lorraine had an edge to her voice as another of the pop princesses in this cast. Her stage mother, Amanda Cunningham From: Lucy O'Byrne By the time this goes to print my fate may already have been decided, but for now, I write this on my day off from rehearsals for the live shows of series four of The Voice UK. How I ended up on Team Will.i.am, as the first ever classically trained singer to make it to the live rounds of The Voice, is a very long and convoluted story. However, I can assure you it started in a community hall in Baldoyle, Co. Dublin.

My parents, Jimmy and Carol have worked, for longer than I can remember, both as a team and individually, as directors, choreographer, musical director, and even actors and singers all over the country. There are probably many of you reading this now who have worked with them in some capacity as part of AIMS over the years. As well as both being former AIMS Nominees they have worked professionally in the Business for most of their lives... What I'm saying really is - it's their fault! They instilled in myself and my sister Rachel at a young age a love of performing that has only strengthened and grown with their encouragement and support (... And their driving us halfway around the country to rehearsals when it was our turn to try our luck on the AIMS circuit!)

Mam and Dad founded Song and Dance Stage School and Youth Theatre for us and our friends. I sang my first solo (On My Own from Les Miserables - a role for which I later earned my own AIMS Best as bar owner Sylvia, also invested her character with a big pop voice while John Conroy as Dean has a cracker of a tenor voice that would be suited to much more classical work than this fun night. John Roe's fine band got into the swing of things pushing along Graham Finnerty's flowing dance routines, a big feature of this show.

A colourful costume plot added to the visual aspect of the production at the Midland town's GAA Centre, played out on a fabulously economical set by the innovative John O'Donoghue.

A snowy countryside as I drove to the matinée performance of this production of Hairspray by Athlone Musical Society.  A full house with a very enthusiastic audience awaited. Ger Madden, hidden behind the set, conducted the seven piece band providing a great sound and colour for this fast moving score. Good judgement of tempi with a good sixties feel showed good leadership - it was a pity we couldn't see him. Chorus Mistress Heather Shine drilled the chorus to a very high standard of singing - a little muted in 'Good Morning, Baltimore' the lyrics needed a little more bite for them to really live. 'Big Dolls House' with the Wurlitzwer and restrained trumpet, was vibrant with attractive vocal harmonies happening throughout. Generally, a fine set of principals was assembled. Size and segregation are the two main issues in this show and we got one of them - segregation - in this evening's performance. Jennifer Clogher as Tracy should have been bigger than she was with the iconic hairstyle - which should have been a little higher in the front. Dialogue was always well projected but could have a little more variation of tone and pitch.  Vocally a fine voice with a touch of vibrato and be careful with pitching some notes - 'Oh! Oh!, Oh!' was slightly out of tune.  Mind you don't punctuate each line with a pose - which got a little tedious after a while.

Charlie Doherty as Corney Collins is a very accomplished performer with an excellent manner on stage, great voice for TV and also a great look. Vocally on top of his game, full sounding and always in tune.

Caoimhe Crowe O'Connor as Penny is a lively performer but needs to calm things down and not try so hard. Tends to drop the level of dialogue leaving us straining to hear text. Vocally fine but needed to punch through more in 'Without love'. Paul Holloway as Edna Turnblad gave us many qualities but I think he needs to toughen it up a bit. It needs to have more energy to it. A level was reached and it cut off. The personae needed to be much bigger - all the time. I also feel that you needed to be padded up.

Mary Helen Hensley as Prudy needed to show us a bit more of the religious fanatical side to her character. Loved the look and she needed just a bit more projection of text. I feel she needed a second costume! Amy Kelly as Amber Von Tussle brought the spoilt and preening characteristics out in this role. Needs more vocal projection especially in 'Big Dolls House'.

Wigged disastrously, Joan Larkin as Velma understood this character well and got some fun from her even if she is ghastly. Vocally all fine except you need a stronger technique for the final few bars of 'Baltimore Crabs'. Bernard Coyle as Wilbur has a huge fun personality with dialogue full of energy. A very easy voice with a lovely duet with Edna.

Shoro Omotosho as Little Inez was cast a little too old for this role. Be careful to slow down the dialogue as it was rattled off too quickly. Sammy Rosney as Seaweed did a marvellous job as this was his first role ever. He looked at ease but needs to slow down in the dialogue and really listen to the text. Vocally no problems with only a small hic-cup when coming in during 'Without you'.

Lucia Evans was a dynamic presence with the right amount of attitude. A natural well projected voice both in dialogue and vocally. Costumed in trousers was not correct for the period. A big, clear bluesy voice well capable for this score, making it do anything you wanted. 'I know where I've been' was focused and truthful and a joy.

A large well focused and energised chorus with some very good dance skills. Synchronisation wasn't always together, strong musically with good detail in the dynamics and harmonies. 'You Can't Stop the music' raised the roof. Alfie Kilduff created a well-paced and punchy production while Nicole McDonald kept the show moving in the right groove all evening presenting some nice variations to the routines. Stage Management (& Set Design) led by Jonathan O'Brien was alert and efficient. Be careful of stray hands being seen in turning the Toblerones. Camilla Flannigan brought some lovely props together - mind the acanthus leaf chair which was too modern.  A well-designed set flowed nicely and was well painted, capturing the feel of the '50's. Prison bars worked very well at the beginning of Act 2.

Sound by Derek Recks was well balanced and integrated well to the acoustics of this theatre. Some mic issues of cuing and mics just going off and on was a slight problem. Lighting by Paschal Gough created many moods for this show with follow spotting a little erratic. Kathleen Sweeney and her team styled the costumes very well including proper underskirts and great coloured jackets for the men. Motormouth's costumes needed some looking at but overall, a good combination of colours and period pieces which looked attractive on stage. No issues with Make-up and the hairstyles were very well put together, some great looks which were individual. Overall a really entertaining afternoon in the Deane Crowe Theatre where much happiness poured forth.

that brought some beautiful playing from the thirteen musicians he assembled. There was much clarity in the interpretation of the score and allowed for the music to flow throughout the evening. Percussion was missing from the orchestral mix which created a major gap in the orchestral landscape. Overture had some lovely brass falling away and some really well executed pizzicato. Good balance between stage and pit all evening.

Chorus Mistress Marta O'Toole needed more time in bringing the chorus to the level they should have been. Entries were raggy with not enough detail on harmonies. Precision on text was also wanting. The best singing of the night was the atmospheric and beautiful 'There's a Place for Us'.

Alan Greaney as Tony gave a well projected performance but needed to embrace some improvisation more. A very well controlled voice which he can sing some fine ppp notes. I am afraid there was little connection emotionally with Maria, Advertisement it just didn't happen the evening I attended. Iona le Gros performed Maria. More care was required with the accent and she tended to run away with dialogue. Stronger accent in 'To-night' and a very awkward scene with Tony on the balcony. It remained static and un- directed. Katie Creaven as Anita needed longer vowel sounds and rolling 'r's 'to correct the accent deficiencies. I felt her character needed to be more fiery and explosive. Vocally a nice mezzo, not dark but more in a soprano range but needed more weight in 'America' and 'A Boy Like That'. A beautiful demeanour, great poise and very stylish. Johnny Garvey as Riff was agile on stage and needed to give much more in the text and lyrics which were undernourished. Declan Gardiner as Bernardo also moved well with very good poise. Some very good dance solos but dramatically needed to be much stronger. Stuart Barrows as Action played him manic and slightly crazy. I know he is like a coiled up spring, but I found him to be quite psychologically removed and aggressive most of the time. Richard Brown as Chino was earnest in his characterisation with a good accent and well projected dialogue. Peter Kennedy as Doc provided a social barometer whose weariness was tangible and whose council rarely taken on board and Paul Hughes as Shrank projecting well but with a ponderous way with his dialogue. Kevin Flannery as Gladhand was quite disgraceful, ill prepared, forgetting lines and then laughing about it on stage. It was quite unforgivable. Niamh O'Brien as Anybody's was nicely energetic but for my taste, a little too tall for this role. Could not understand why she appeared at the dance. Maeve Browne as Rosalia is a confident performer but needs to throw out words more in 'America' and 'I feel Pretty'.

The chorus worked very hard all evening, especially in a show like this, but, there was a distinct lack of rehearsals which did not show off this group of players to their best. Generally the dances lacked energy, precision and style which is demanded from such a score. Big moments like the Finalé Act 1 just about came off with good powerful singing from the whole ensemble. Men appeared a little awkward with issues in rhythm and styles. This should have been spotted by the director Peter Kennedy. Cast, almost age appropriate, he should have had a stronger influence on visual and emotional content of the production. The show did move well except for a crazy bedroom scene change which went off and then came back in again.

Choreographer Declan Gardiner did not gauge properly the capabilities of the cast. Although they worked hard the required style was not drilled into them. This is our job as directors and choreographers - it's to make the cast look well. The cast on this occasion lacked precision and did not know their steps. Stage Management by Marion Heery worked well in general apart from two, quite slow, scene changes - the bedroom scene and also into the Drug Store in Act 2.

The set designed by Peter Kennedy was functional - like an enclosed courtyard effect - creating a sense of NY city streets. Some areas looked untidy with badly creased fabric in some windows and also LX cabling hanging down. The bedroom scene needed more space for the players and certain scenes like the Drug Store needed to have more dressings.

The sound by Fintan Higgins was variable. Balance from the pit needed altering due to some of the instrumental gaps in the band make-up. The orchestra just never seemed to bloom. Some missed cues for characters first lines was recurring. Maria, I felt, sounded a little thin at the top of her voice. It must be a nightmare of a show for sound with all the movement etc. Lighting Designer - Emma O'Grady created a simple palette of colours . Quickness and timing of cues were a slight problem all evening and mood creation also needed to be looked at. Costumes for this sixties classic show are actually about today on the main streets. Some lovely attention to detail like Anita's house coat and Maria's simple white dress. Anita's beautiful black outfit for Act 2. Tony did not look his best at the gym - in fact he looked like an accountant. Be careful with underskirts and freshness of tulle and also the length of the underskirts. Policeman needed some major work - He needed a belt and also the trousers needed turning up.

Make-up and Hair by David Browne and team worked well here but we needed some differentiation between day and evening wear. The Shark boys looked slick but the girls needed wigs/hairpieces.

Some announcements were made in Irish which was lovely to hear. Good order out Front of House where I was well looked after.

A fabulous score and Michael Fay and his nine piece band gave a fine rendition to this great Ludwig and Gershwin musical. A great feel and sense of the old MGM 1930's musicals swept over us all evening. Good contact was made with the cast on stage and in general, the various numbers in this score were judged correctly and flowed well. Chorus was well taught but there were issues with audibility all evening. The sound from the chorus was much muted and I think this was due to some imbalance with sound. It was very apparent in numbers like 'Tonight's the Night' and 'I've Got Rhythm'. Be careful with diction throughout especially in 'Stiff Upper Lip'. This did not help with balance between pit and stage. Good use of the muted trumpets and trombone added some nice colour to the textures in several numbers and some lovely brush work on 'Someone To Watch Over Me'. Accuracy came into question with some unsteadiness in the 'New York Interlude', in fact, the orchestra nearly fell apart in the opening section.

Colin Hughes playing Bobby Child, (and also directed) for me, always seemed to be a step behind the true potential of where this character should have been. The playing was a little over exaggerated. Dialogue was clean and projected with good comic elements and a great mirror scene with Zangler. You need to be aware of costume presentation for the entire performance and what were on your feet?

Dearbhail Downey as Polly brought some feistiness to the role together with great vocals where the lyrics were always given their true value. Dialogue was slow to begin with but got into a natural groove thereafter. I felt she was poorly served by the production team for blocking of her numbers. She was given little or nothing to do. Dominic Reid (pictured above) as Bella Zangler was full of energy and played the drunk extremely well. Well projected dialogue which flowed naturally and a nice baritone voice. A very committed actor.

Trish McMahon as Irene Roth takes no prisoners. Fine accent throughout with a good understanding of text. 'Naughty Baby' was a little disjointed but she sang it very well, no problems with range. A confident performer. Daniel Nolan as Lank Hawkins knows how to dish out an insult. Good strong personality on stage with a natural flare for 'black' comedy. Good work between himself and Irene. Their clashes worked very well. Siobhán Clifford playing the role of Tess was vivacious and bubbly. No problem with dialogue and a lovely mover as was Mona Conroy (in a different way) as Mother. Once in the gal, always in the gal. This was a fine performance in style and timing. Well-groomed all evening - the bag not correct in the first scene. Good understanding and delivery of dialogue.

Val Brennan as Everett Baker needed more clarity with lines but maintained a good accent. Vocally a little shady' in pitching notes. The 'Fodors' worked well as a team but Gary Lanigan as Eugene, whose accent was well created, needed to be much bigger with more fluid and connected moves. Carmel Geissel as Patricia needed more eccentricity and affectation. Just so much more over the top playing was required. Good choral work throughout with good tap numbers from the ladies who were well drilled. The men's chorus on my first seeing them looked suitably bone idle in this God forsaken town. Needed more work with choral reactions to the various situations. They needed to be integrated more.

Director Colin Hughes had a few issues during this production. Being a classy 1930's MGM Musical, it lacked style and sophistication. This was prevalent in most departments, I am afraid. Directional issues with musical numbers were left alone with some principals needing help. This was also the same for accents, Things just needed to go further. An eye to the technicals was also required. Pace was broken and slow at times.

Stage Manager, Bob O'Kelly, had some problems with flying cloths which jammed or got stuck throughout the night. Placement of furniture also caused some delays. The stage piano should have been turned more US. Synchronicity of truck movement would have been great and a bonus but I fear the scene changes needed more work. Some lovely moves from Deirdre Browne who conscientiously and faithfully gave us moves reminiscent of the 1930s with good movement and formations in the most part. Style is vital for a show like this and she achieved this, to a certain degree, a flavour of this elegant era. Good clean tap in 'I Got Rhythm', the pick axe movement needed to be cleaner. All in all a good job.

Props by James O'Connor needed to be careful with the ageing of props like the envelope given to Polly which was too modern. The luggage needed breaking down. The Hoover was incorrect for period (more 1970's style) not 1930's.

Set Design by Bob O'Kelly and Colin Hughes was functional but appeared really not to fit and do what this show wanted it to do. Health and safety was an issue with stairs not braked and a hand held from behind to hold it in place. Masking issues all evening USR and SL.

Sound by Vinnie Osborne had a few problems during the evening with cue failures dotted throughout the evening. The balance between stage and pit favored the latter with choral singing suffering. Principals were well judged with no problems except for cue problems.

Tom Kennedy as Lighting designer also had some issues. The main problem was too much light on stage in areas not being used. The mixture of colours did not always succeed and did not create depth in some scenes. I think a follow spot would have helped this show. Also had issues with the timing of cues. Costumes got the right feel for this show with lots of nice period touches. Good attention to shoes for the ladies but too many slip on shoes for the men. No, No, No! Bobby looked great in scene one but there after he needed someone with him all the time to keep him "costume tidy'. The walk down at the end looked great with the feathered showgirl costumes.

Mary O'Reilly and Clare McMullen looked after the makeup and hair. Whilst there were some lovely blonde and dark brown wigs on the dancers, there were several ladies in the chorus who remained with their modern hairstyles all evening. The foam cut out of a goatie for Bobby as Zangler was NOT good.

Rosemarie O'Dowd looked after me royally for the evening and was just lovely. Great to catch up with so many people and friends.

Virtually a full house for Teachers Musical Society started this company off in good stead for their weeks run. Energy permeated through the score which was well handled by Dermot O'Callaghan. A very fine band was brought together but I had real difficulty trying to assess the conducting skills of the conductor due to the fact that he was hidden most of the night behind the set. Lovely segues working seamlessly in the overture and overall pace was well judged depending on the style of the music. Some numbers did move a little too fast like the 'Jailhouse Rock' and the 'Burning love' number was pushed a little bit too much. A very well-schooled chorus was well trained by Dermot O'Callaghan who prepared them with fine details in both music and lyrics. A very rounded sound coming from the rather large chorus with plenty of harmonies coming through the big numbers. One exception was the 'Fools Fall in Love' where diction was a problem. Some great individual playing from the band members but there was a tendency for them to overpower the balance of some numbers.

Looking every inch the part, Ian Tighe as Chad, strutted his stuff around the whole stage with confidence and charm. Vocally he was well equipped for the many different numbers in the score. Perhaps a little nasal at the top of his voice, he, however, sang with understanding and well-crafted text. Be careful with the accent, it was uneven throughout the night. Alison Dennan as Natalie was ideally cast giving a vivacious and natural performance. With a clear and well- focused voice, text was always clear with no problems in the vocal range at all.

Jim played by Eddie Brady has lost his way a little in life. He shaped his dialogue nicely with lovely reactions to Sandra - especially his stuttering. Good belt for the forte section of 'Don't be Cruel'. Good comedy also with 'The Power of my Love'. Jenny Noirant as Sylvia is a natural actress with plenty of stage experience. Probably too well groomed for the earlier scenes, she has a natural and firm understanding of the text conveying a truthfulness which was refreshing. Her scene with Jim in act 2 was heartfelt and sincere. Lorraine - the juvenile lead was well played by Sarah O'Driscoll who has a flare for stage, reacting well to people around her. Great projection with text and lyrics. She connected well with Dean.

Sean McMahon played a spirited and well-rounded character in the guise of Denis. A natural comic flare ran through this performance, not only in personality but also in costume and antics. Excellent body language and awareness of everyone else around him. Nice reaction to Chad's gyrations. 'It Hurts Me' revealed a fine voice, clear and well projected with a sincere shape to the lyrics which were heartfelt, all accompanied to well sculpted body language.

Some nicely timed moves for Denise King as Miss Sandra with an excellent singing voice moving easily into belt. Loved the line "Throw me to the ground and start me like a Chevy. Slightly restricted with her pencil skirt, it remained a sophisticated performance. Joanne Logue as the Mayor was suitable bossy in every way and giving a dog's life to both her son, Mark O'Looney as Dean trying to find his adult feet. His 'It's now or never' displayed a young tenor voice with good diction. Kevin Heaney also got the brunt of the Mayor's wrath. With a Jeff style delivery from 'Rules of Engagement', he showed clear and cool delivery of lines with a nice voice with a slight vibrato which was very endearing.

The chorus delivered a well sung and committed performance from beginning to end. Well drilled in imaginative choreography by Mary McDonagh, they displayed great energy and precision in most of their numbers. Moves were slick with good head and arm movements. Some fine harmonies emerged especially in 'It Hurts Me' off stage. Reactions just needed to be worked on, for example: the dialogue before 'Burning Love' needed to be more varied and reactions just a little bit more intentional.

The director, Eoin Cannon, above, controlled things very well and had his finger on the pulse all evening. It was a well finished production with lots of 60's details. Good integration of cast and chorus and a natural rapport with the principals. The reveal of the bike was a little too contrived but I loved the 3D bus scene which was well structured and put together. The show flowed well with good segues from dialogue into vocal numbers. Be careful with a deficiency in chorus participation towards the end of the show. They too, with their reactions, contribute to the outcome of the show. Stage Manager Gerry McCann kept a clean slate with efficient and brisk scene changes. Props by Marie Monaghan and team succeeded on many levels with well-dressed scenes both for the set and also personal items. Set Design by Eoin Cannon brought a sense of period to the stage with two giant guitars dominating. Well- made but I felt the small trucks for the garage etc. were too small and d i d n o t make a huge impression.

The second act did not tell us we were at the fairground.

T h e additions to the set just didn't give that impression.

Sound by Derek Williams created a slightly mixed bag all evening. The most alarming issue was sheer decibels. The sound levels all evening were painful. Orchestra and vocals battled all evening which was a shame. It was also very bright and forward. Less treble might have made it less uncomfortable. Some very nice lighting from Denis Twomey complemented the set and costumes well with some very good cuing. He used a very nice palette of colours which worked well. Night time needed to be a little bit darker for my taste - a small quibble.

Costume team, headed by Andrew Reddy created a very fine array of period costumes - probably a bit too much black with the ladies cardigans. A lot of the costumes looked bright and summary and worked well with this production. Good attention to detail with hair and makeup especially with the ladies. Alison Murphy, assisted by Sinead Judd gave us the 50's flare in a natural way. Ed's beard was really something to look at.

Thank you to Leo Kilroy who looked after me and my guest extremely well. Wishing you and the company much success in the future.

It was appropriate that a group which has grown out of a school of music should field the largest string section that I've come across on my travels in the Sullivan section in the last two seasons.

With economics increasingly dictating the demise of strings in pit bands all over the island, it was a treat to listen to the rich tones of the violins and cellos in an orchestra that also included a bassoon, give real depth to musical director Aidan O'Carroll's reading of this Sondheim score.

Mr O'Carroll's cast - he also doubled up as director - also boasted some excellent singers and actors as they set about work on the wide open spaces of Tralee's beautiful Siamsa Tire theatre on a clever and atmospheric set which made good use of Alan Johnston's projections. Shane Murphy's sound desk added some fine effects culminating in the footsteps of the giant that built into a crescendo that made seats bounce and chest cavities rattle.

This was a show where Mairtin O'Cathasaigh's simpleton Jack and his mother - the eternally worried Mary Barry - profited materially from his raids on the kingdom of the Giants with significant upgrades in both clothes and furnishings as Act Two got underway.

James Brennan carried the central figure of the Baker well, helping to weave together the various fairy tales this show is based upon; Grainne O'Carroll as his wife is a very good actress with a terrific singing voice while Aisling O'Carroll's Cinderella had a beautiful voice with a lovely tone.

Pearl Kennedy, another good actress with a more than useful singing voice, was a stooped, snarling Witch who morphed into a classy looking middle-class mother.

The impressive Alan McLoughlin, who had a good feel for the comedy of Rapunzel's Prince also showed off a good singing voice as an excellent foil for Proinnsias O'Cathasaigh's more serious Cinderella's Prince. Noel King in the dual roles of the Narrator and the Mysterious Man had a terrific speaking voice and was nimble around a stage while Karen Soffe, another fine actress, made the most of the small role of Cinderella's haughty Stepmother as she flitted in and out of the action.

Kerry Fleming invested the Wolf with a terrific look and a great howl while Katrina Galvin's Red Riding Hood soldiered on bravely through her big first half number after a major problem with the lighting desk and grew into the role after being rescued from the Wolf's belly.

For those of you who didn't catch it, this was a production that literally brought the house down.

Director Paul Norton and fellow mischief-maker, stage manager and technical boffin Pat McGovern, pulled off an early trick.

When the relatively normal Beineke family shipped up to the Addams' Central Park mansion for the first time and ring the bell, they were left standing in the doorway of the house as the façade of the building falls forward to the floor.

Musical director Shane Farrell threw up a sheaf of sheet music timed to catch the downdraught of the fall, the front row ducked instinctively and the rest of the audience sucked in a deep breath before exploding into riotous applause when they realised it was part of the action. The bemused Beinekes - Patrick Byrne's uptight Mal, Joanne Kelly's Alice and Bryan Mulry's Lucas- were then faced with Paul Drysdale's gurgling Lurch - he spoke in a low register language decipherable only to watching spooks and passing alien spaceships - as the giant South African actor opened the door to them.

Ballinasloe's demolition men's stunt may have been the icing on the cake but they invested this production with a couple of other explosive tricks as well as several eye-catching effects.

The aforementioned Mr Farrell took control of a tight pit band while choreographer Sarah Griffin had drilled a ghoulish ensemble in her cleverly conceived routines.

Seamus Feerick loaned Gomez a Mediterranean accent, painted-on hair, subtle comedy, great mannerisms and a big baritone voice while Bernie Dudgeon's statuesque Morticia had a smoky voice.

Sarah Corcoran as Wednesday stormed through her big numbers in a Broadway belt in a terrific performance while David Kennedy as her younger brother, Pugsley, is a sub-teen with a crystal clear cathedral chorister voice and the makings of fine actor.

Patrick Byrne as Mal Beineke gave a neat interpretation of the buttoned up former rocker while Joanne Kelly as his wife Alice slipped through the acting gears to move from a prim and proper New York social climber to wanton sexpot in the time it took her to complete her big number. Bryan Mulry as Lucas, another member of the cast still at school, was unfazed in a fine principal debut; Amanda Stuart was a stooped sour faced old hag of a Grandma while Brian Derrane was a fun-filled Fester whose lightness of feet belied his bulk.

While this show was derided by the critics when it made its debut on Broadway in 2010 it was loved by the audiences. I suspect Irish audiences will also take it to their collective heart.

Some societies with greater stage facilities than Kilmacud would baulk at tackling this show full point. Others would long and hard consider the technical difficulties in mounting it before deciding to take the plunge. The south Dublin group stage their shows in the confined space of the Mill Theatre situated at the back of Dundrum's sprawling town centre development and just down the road from their spiritual home.

Given the size of the stage, it was a triumph for director Siobhan Gallagher and her technical crew that the magic of the three witches rising into the air at the end of Act One, a pivotal moment in this show, took place.

Flight rig technician Johann Hattingh ensured Jillian Fagan's Alex, Amy Louise Byrne's Jane and Jennifer Fahy's Sukie rose elegantly - and safely - as Alan Davoren's Darryl Van Horne worked his biggest piece of magic on them.

Ms Gallagher's direction was similarly nimble and sure in a tackling a storyline that could frighten the horses. She walked a line that kept the more overtly sexual scenes suggestive rather than explicit.

Her pacey production was also well cast with a sonorous and well- blended trio of female leads in Ms Fagan, Ms Byrne and Ms Fahy set against a devilish looking Alan Davoren and had an eye for detail. Marion Holohan was impressive as the buttoned up self-appointed town busybody Felicia Gabriel who harboured her own secrets behind closed doors with husband Clyde, a man with a roving eye and sour tongue, captured well here by Aidan Ffrench.

Steven Halion and Jacqueline Drew touched in the roles of the young lovers from different sides of the tracks in the small town where everyone knows each other's business while Alison Cuffe had the thankless task of portraying the little girl who sees everything but rarely gets a chance to speak - a kind of silent narrator almost.

In a show where John Dempsey and Dana Rowe's re-telling of John Updike's novel re-inforces the line that women often prefer bad boys, nine other actors in the Society's terrific ensemble brought less prominent characters in the story to life.

This was a chorus that produced a lovely sound when together and delivered choreographer Rachel Sheahan's varied dance routines without losing vocal power.

The show, driven on by Geoff Woods big-sounding pit band, here shoehorned into a corner of the theatre between the stage and the front rows of the auditorium, was played out on Scenemaker's clever set which allowed the performers as much room as possible in a tight space.

Good technical back-up from the lighting and sound desks throughout the night added atmosphere to a production that was great value for money for the Mill Theatre full house.

Without a doubt Bill Stafford was the real governor in this show, tackling not just one but a variety of roles. New Ross Musical Society's vice chairman was multi-tasking here as director, set designer, lighting designer and actor in his version of Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice's rock opera at the town's St Michael's Theatre.

Mr Stafford made sure his rehearsal schedule allowed him to undertake the role of Pontius Pilate with his wife and choreographer Anne-Marie Cooney taking over the reins in parts of the final run up to opening night. And happily Mr Stafford seemed to take matters in his stride producing a commanding performance in the role of the Roman governor in his take on the 70s classic.

This fast-paced glimpse of the story of the last seven days of Christ's life on Earth gave us one of the most prolonged crucifixion scenes I have witnessed in productions of the show down the years but conversely I would have liked to see some other elements pointed up more brutally. The framework for the aggravated action was already in place with Mr Stafford's fine staging of the Trial and the subsequent 39 lashes a highlight of the show.

However, I felt the Jewish revolutionaries let their Roman oppressors off the hook too lightly in the street scene when we first encounter the conquerors and later, when they come to arrest Jesus. Christ's subsequent treatment at the hands of the Romans could have been more graphic. Indeed, this was the only time the action slowed down a production that raced along without ever feeling rushed.

Padraig D'Arcy in the title role had great control of his voice and gave us a Jesus that was less compliant than some I've seen down the years. He was matched for power by the energetic Judas of Keith Flanagan while Claire O'Connor lent her pop soprano to Mary Magdalene.

The physically imposing Martyn Gladney was a commanding Caiaphas while James Dobbs, with long black talons for fingernails, fashioned an Annas dripping in vitriol.

Trevor Kent as Simon and Nigel O'Neill as Peter have voices which deserve to be heard in bigger parts while Joe Malone and Thomas Byrne touched in the roles of the other priests.

The gloss was taken off Derek Shannon's turn as a camp Herod due to a dead microphone while a big ensemble had no difficulties with either the score or Ms Cooney's flowing dance routines.

Philip Kennedy's eight-piece band, with keyboards replacing the string section, helped drive along a production that was played on a composite set that allowed the action to flow seamlessly from one scene to the next.

I learned a long time ago that a musical can be created out of almost anything.

Sondheim has proved it consistently over his career, sometimes fashioning tales out of the unlikeliest material.

This season, long before I pitched up at Cork's Firkin Crane - an old butter market on the city's north bank now re-fashioned into a three theatre space and used a lot by modern dance companies - I'd already witnessed a rare Irish performance of his Assassins.

The Sullivan trail has also led me to performances of Titanic Serenade, Bonnie and Clyde and barely a week earlier and across the river in Cork I had caught the Irish premiere of Carrie, The Musical, Stephen King's horror story, none of which at first glance seem instant candidates for the musical stage.

However, even they seem almost normal when set beside Seussical by Lynn Ahrens and Stephen Flaherty. The writers - best known for the epic Ragtime and the charming Once On This Island, a kind of Caribbean-style Little Mermaid - pulled together a complex tale based mainly on three of Theodor Seuss Geisel's children's books but drawing on strands from another 16 or so.

Despite its huge success - it is one of the most performed works in current musical theatre - it is one of the strangest animals in the Broadway canon.

Fittingly perhaps, one of the stand- out performances here was from 12-year-old Cork schoolgirl Abigail Murphy as Jo-Jo the child who eventually saves the citizens of Whoville from destruction.

The company had brought in Ciaran Bermingham, active on Cork's professional scene, to direct and he fashioned a fast-paced version of the show drawing out some fine performances from his young cast. Alison Coady as the Cat in the Hat pulled the strings as both narrator and performer while Thomas Grogan in the other central role lent a strong baritone voice and easy stage presence to Horton the Elephant. Fiona O'Sullivan evoked sympathy as the often overlooked Gertrude, a bird with only one tail feather who wished she was more like the flighty Amazing Mayzie, played here by a confident Jane O'Regan.

Clodagh O'Callaghan was a big- voiced Sour Kangaroo while Ryan Grace and Alex Bermingham were convincing as the first citizens of Whoville who enjoyed the good life. Aisling Crotty was a believable General Schmitz while Faith Jacobson lent Yurtle the Turtle a big Gospel voice.

Aidan Fitzgerald, Vicky Sheridan and Meghan Papp were a lively unit as the mischief-making Wickersham Brothers while the talented trio of Aine Gallagher, Laura Butler Synott and Aoife Bradley as the Birds sacrificed their individuality to forge a solid unit which moved and sang as one while acting as a fabulous backing group to the selfish Mayzie. The lively ensemble, while not carrying out other roles in the show, watched the action from seats at the edge of the stage in full view of the audience.

They had been coached musically by Louise Luddy who had clearly put in the necessary hours in the rehearsal room and had mastered the flowing routines of choreographer Maura Lyons and her assistant Roza Karim. Another striking element of the production was a 17-piece orchestra directed by past AIMS nominee Lauren Ronan and which included Michael Young, the man behind CIT Musical Society's Irish premiere of Carrie the Musical.

Arriving to a full house at the Hawkes My role with AIMS is to analyse and dissect and deliberate but there are nights when the occasion should take precedence over the deliberations.

The mid-point in Banagher Musical Society's inaugural production was one such occasion.

To bring live entertainment on the scale of our often expensive hobby to a small midlands town that has been buffeted by the prevailing economic winds all its life is a huge achievement in its own right.

As is often the case in circumstances such as this, it's one person or a small group who provided the spark or the drive to create a new company.

Here it was Jared Madden, a speech and drama teacher from the area who convinced members of the local drama group and friends to back him in his quest.

If this sounds like the occasion overshadowed the production then that's wrong. In spite of an inexperienced cast - only four had been in a musical before - this was a well put together show Mr Madden and his committee had the sense to bring in an experienced director in Athlone's Alfie Kilduff and musical director Alan Recks fresh from a run with Clara Musical Society.

The show itself was also a great strategic choice for the group's first venture into musical theatre, it's light, lively, great fun and packed with familiar tunes that appeal to both children and their grandparents. The company were rewarded by near full houses each of its three nights in the converted gym of the very modern Banagher College, pulling in around 1,000 customers, a little more than half of the town's population - that's market reach on a huge scale.
