Mr Madden, apart from driving the whole idea, also played the lead role of Chad, the roustabout who gets drags a small American town out of the dark ages and gets it moving - literally. He has a good voice, was lithe on stage but could have eased up on the facial expressions a little. His leading lady, Aoife Horan in the twin roles of Natalie and Ed, made an impression on her stage debut while Patrick Kelly lent his experience to Dennis as well as a stratospheric voice to the role.

Gemma Flynn was confident, bringing a powerful voice to the part of Lorraine while David Broderick, a late replacement in the role of Dean Hyde, grew into the role.

Ann Marie McLoughlin was a sassy Sandra; Brendan Dolan as Jim Hiller showed his background as a singer and Caroline Clancy was a domineering Matilda, the town busybody.

Marita Fogarty was a kindly Sylvia; John Kennedy was Earl, the town sheriff who thinks he is playing in a silent movie while Sonya Cuddy provided an explosive opening to "Heartbreak Hotel".

The show was played out on a handsome looking set that was bought in and while its provenance was unknown bore all the hallmarks of a John O'Donoghue work. It allowed the cast plenty of room to execute Niamh Donahoe's energetic dance routines.

title for this trip to the Kingdom. Another first was attending a show at the INEC which is quite an auditorium for any production. It's big, and any company wanting to produce anything here needs to also think big.

A great rock sound for this score was achieved by musical director Noël Lennon and his nine piece band. With good balance, the score took to life with energy and atmosphere. Well in control of this piece you could hear many layered sounds emanating from the pit. A fine awareness with underscoring and always sympathetic to the singers. A good orchestral balance was achieved from its modern sounding overture to the complex rhythm section in the Subway Ghost scene to the sensitive playing through 'Without You' and Three Little Words'. Choral work brought a large company together with a large sound. A natural imbalance due to the vast number of women compared to the number of men in this chorus caused some problems with the SATB arrangements. Some untidy cut offs with 'Hallelujah' in 'Talkin' Bout a Miracle'.

Gary Murphy as Sam Wheat created a personal interpretation which was free and natural which also reflected in his dialogue and lyrics. Good pace generally with the dialogue but he has a tendency to speed up. Would have liked more playfulness in 'Unchained Melody' and general animation with numbers to reveal more of the emotional content. Roza Karim played Molly and she was well capable for this difficult modern score. Great range vocally and another natural performance well used to being on stage. Be careful with the accent which needed to be stronger and also be careful with the colour of your voice on sustained notes - the colour loses its bloom and a certain quality. The inextricable bond that has to exist between these two people just didn't work its magic for me unfortunately. Confident and easy on stage was Jack Healy as Carl Bruner. He needed more drive and energy in his performance. Relaxed also needs to have energy on stage. Pitching the voice so low caused issues in variation of delivery. A clear ringing top vocally was used to great effect in 'I Had A Life' - it did need more text however.

Oda-Mae Brow was played by Hazel Devane and I found that this actress fought all evening to find her niche in this production. The problem was that the role was not cast black which should be a pre-requisite as with other shows in the repertoire. The language for this role is written for an ethnic / black person. The accent slipped in and out all evening giving a very varied performance. More attention needed to be given to when she is talking to the invisible Sam than to humans in the real world. Much comedy was lost here. A fine range vocally which she uses fearlessly and is well able for what the score demands.

Des Furlong was perfect for the role of Willie Lopez - cultivating and sustaining a Latino accent all evening. Great text and body language but could be a little more dangerous.  The Subway Ghost, performed by Ronan O'Shea showed much anger and hostility. Well performed with much intensity through his lines, they did not always come across too clearly. Be careful that you don't let the emotional side of the role take you over completely. Louise and Clara played by Brid Mills and Michelle O'Callaghan supported Ode-Mae in her sham dealings as a clairvoyant. Both had well projected dialogue and strong vocals in 'Are you a Believer'; Mike Moloney as the detective spoke clearly in a good accent as did Fergal Cleary as the bank manager with some good expressions for Oda-Mae's asides with Sam.

The large Chorus filled the INEC with efficient entrances which were focused and well executed. Much of the movement was stylised and not exactly dance - some of it walks with specific journeys. The 'Rain' number needed more precision with the umbrellas. Movement, by Oliver Hurley, on the whole was on the lines of the Broadway production which created their own language for this production.

Oliver Hurley as Director lavished a high tech look to this premiere, marshalling his cast around the large stage confidently. Good casting in general except, in my opinion, the role of Oda-Mae. - for the reasons above. Be careful with some of the dialogue and the accents.  - flow and continuity need to be maintained. Stage Manager Frank Ashe executed clear and efficient scene changes. Crew were well drilled and are to be congratulated on a job well done. Props by Marie Moloney were well chosen from the multi coloured Chaise Lounge to the chairs and tables for the restaurant. Everything can be seen….. even the badly covered flight case with the coffin on it.

The set and lighting all became one in an amazing technical achievement that was brilliant from it conception to its execution. John Hurley is quite a man and created and designed his own stunning projections. NY Skyscrapers, the subway, even to the flat lining images were well devised and executed.  You should have them copyrighted. There were, however, some masking issues with the set. The lighting worked in tandem with the projections. A good colour palette was used which didn't bleed out the projections. Loved the use of the Congo Blue. Nice rich ambers in the apartment.

A fine job done by Star Systems who conceived a well-balanced sound design, never noisy and the pit complementing the stage. Good sound effects which were well judged. Costumes by Siobháin Bustin brought together a feel for the eighties, and while not flattering, gave us an era to work from. Sam for my taste did not look relaxed. His trousers needed taking up 6 inches. He looked a little unkempt most of the time. The cut of the suits for Carl looked a tad too modern and did not reflect his position in the organisation.  Oda-Mae's entire wardrobe needed a rethink as they weren't funky enough. The Chorus generally wore black which worked well.

Hair and make-up was done by the cast and while this was fine, the subtleties and details were lacking to give an overall impression of the '80's.  All in all, things were fine but Oda-Mae should have had her hair up with hat going to the bank manager.

I was very warmly received by Donnacha Galvin and Nanette O'Leary who stayed with me all evening and entertained me with laughs and stories over the years. An enthusiastic audience showed their appreciation with a standing ovation.

A beautiful spring evening traveling through the countryside to the seaside town of Newcastle. The last time I was there was with an AIMS Seminar, many years ago.

A fine ornamental building at the far end of the prom, beautifully renovated is the home for this company. A very good ten piece band that produced some great colours and textures for this show was well judged by Musical Director Gareth McGreevy. The band started very well with a good balance maintained but gradually became a problem as it over powered the artists on stage. Tempi all evening were well judged with everything moving on.

Chorus was well prepared and sang with clarity and with tight, meticulous harmonies. Good tone with some very good singers was evidenced even when whittled down to five or six singers. Sound was also an issue here where volume was too much and over amplification just not needed.

Niall McLean as Gomez created a good father figure and Lothario for this dysfunctional family. Work was needed with his accent but he projected his dialogue well. Passion is important for Gomez and we had moments of this throughout with Morticia. Be careful not to push the laugh line. Trust the dialogue. Carol-Anne McKay performed the role of Morticia creating her own interpretation which worked very well. But I still would like to see a more stoic and deadpan delivery, oozing with sexuality. The black wig was too short and costume needed to be a bit longer. Be careful not to run on with dialogue as we lost many of the innuendos.

Sarah King in the role of Wednesday is a talented young lady with an excellent voice, always in tune and has the full range for this role. A large sound with a great belt. Too quick in the dialogue all evening but just slow down and give each word its due value.

A good preppy look for Chris Poland as Lucas (pity about the slip-on shoes). Cast a little bit too young, he had a great relationship with Wednesday. Good team work here. Too explosive with his text marred his dialogue.  Pugsley, played by Eoin McGuinness needed to be larger. Great scene for him in the torture chamber and with Granny and the trolley. Good singing voice, in tune and handled the syncopation moments in 'Secrets' very well. Paula Kearney performed Granny in a quirky and funky way. Good with dialogue and getting most fun from the text. A very agile tongue!! I'll not say any more!  Fester was played by a female actress - Careen Starkey. Odd, but I waited to see. The role was played with conviction and with relish. She was reason in this presentation with a caring side. The Bald cap did her no favours as it was dreadfully put on. 'The Moon and Me' was beautifully paced and delivered.

Well focused and stiffly delivered, Lurch was played by Andy McKnight. Pitch for the gurgling should have been much lower. In itself, creates a great laugh. Loved the lifts in his shoes. Emma-Jane McKnight as Alice was a giddy, selfless actress all evening who spoke her lines with crystal clarity and whose giddiness was infectious. Great off the line reactions. Good voice with well projected lyrics. A tiny tuning problem at the beginning of 'Secrets' but was quickly sorted. Another fine character, Dean Richman as Mal, is an accomplished actor with natural flare for the stage. A light tenor voice but needs to be careful with the tuning...understanding the lyrics made up for it.  A lovely transformation into the 'Rocker' was well achieved at the end.

A well moved and vocally drilled chorus worked hard throughout this production. Great set of white costumes, all different and fine attention to detail for each one. I loved 'Death' with the scythe - very acrobatic and a great mover. They did all they were asked with relish and with clean, fluid movements. Neil Keery as director drew some lovely performances from a cast that knew what was required of them. Be careful that cast doesn't shout their lines. This was a common feature with some of the cast. A brave decision to cast Fester female which paid off. Well done. A good tight rein on scene changes which helped the pace of the show. More development of interpreting the musical side of things would be helpful to actor and audience. He has a good eye for the visuals also.

Timmy Bell as choreographer approached the score creatively with some interesting numbers devised. Full Disclosure was complex and tricky with several things going on at once. A very good response to the score which contributed a lot to the production.

Martin Bradley was on top form as stage manager and controlled a tight ship. Props were of a very high standard in this production thanks to Bronagh Killough and her team. Four great umbrellas for 'The Moon and Me' which lit up - for example. Set Design by Carol-Anne McKay brought together an open stage with the main interior house structure behind a moonscape backcloth. The animated feel to the painting helped and worked well for this production. Sound by Geoff Clarke was very mixed all evening with different instruments sharing the lime-light. The mix between pit and stage was not well balanced losing any natural bloom from the musical instruments. Good timing for sound effects but I feel the explosion needed to rock the building - it was too soft. Lighting by Sean Keenan was well managed despite lack of room in this particular venue. Lighting the backdrop was very successful - be a little more sensitive with some cues, they need to be felt well. Costumes were well thought through except for glaring errors like Gomez' striped jacket and evening dress trousers!!! Morticia's black dresses needed to be longer. Some great work achieved by Attracta Campbell especially with the chorus in all white and from different periods.

Great that Thing had make up on his hand - Fester needed makeup on his hands. Great detail with the chorus and I felt that the principals needed to be paler. Good 'tache for Gomez and his hair slicked back and Morticia needed a much longer wig. More attention to festers bald cap was required. It really takes two to put on a bald cap. I missed Cousin 'It'. Now there's a challenge!

Some of the people I've had most time for in this business have been connected with Fortwilliam Musical Society.

Back in the day as a young (ish) reporter I covered the North Belfast society's foundation and its initial productions, Gilbert and Sullivan naturally, as was the custom then. Many of those I referred to in the intro to this piece are sadly no longer with us and the society, regenerated by a productive youth group, is a different animal these days.

Their growing confidence has reached the point where they tackled Stephen Sondheim's most famous work at Newtownabbey's spacious Theatre at the Mill, a fine space set into a wonderful piece of industrial architecture in greater Belfast's northern outskirts.

It was a case of bringing gristle to the Mill as director Simon Pyper put together a strong cast for the Northern Ireland amateur premiere of the show.

At its heart of this tale of dark comedy and murderous revenge was the brooding presence of Fortwilliam newcomer Karl McGuckin in the title role of the wronged London barber. Mr McGuckin here was a man armed with the twin weapons of menacing eyes that chilled the soul and a thunderous bass-baritone voice dipped in chocolate and allied to excellent diction.

He may not possess the natural stagecraft of Angela Harding who portrayed Mrs Lovett as cuddly but conniving and sharp at the same time in her best cor blimey, luvaduck East End accent, but he had an aura nonetheless.

The couple cooked their pies and their plans under the atmospherically dim lighting plot of Alastair Kerr on a composite set from English professionals, Scenic Projects Ltd which filled the Mill's wide stage but left Mr Pyper plenty of room to drive on his action while creating pictures. Drama student, Sean Harkin, another making his debut with the company, showed off a lovely tenor voice as Anthony, the sailor back from Australia with Todd who then falls in love with the barber's daughter. His real-life partner, Orla McCormack, a fine-voiced soprano was his stage love, Johanna, separated from the barber by the corrupt Judge Turpin, here played by Eamonn Connolly as sour-faced and self-serving.

The well-rounded Drew Reid gave one of his most impressive performances for years as Beadle Bamford, a man with too much respect for authority eager to suppress disquiet about the actions of society's ruling class. And Mr Reid showed that he still has a fine singing voice.

Kerry Rooney, a man with a flair for accents and a fine tenor voice, was Adolfo Pirelli, the charlatan who is too clever for his own good and who ignites the smouldering fuse of destruction within Todd while Maria Sweeney was an agitated Beggar Woman, the barber's last victim as he reaches his Damascene moment. Vijay Sharma was a suitably nervous but clear-voiced Tobias Ragg while Tony Young was an oily Jonas Fogg, director of the Bedlam asylum.

An ensemble that included a number of stratospheric sopranos played a full role under Mr Pyper and musical director Wilson Shields who had pulled together some of Belfast's finest instrumentalists in a terrific sounding ten-piece pit band sunk low below the Mill's stage.

ANYTHING GOES By necessity this south Dublin group have become experts in staging big shows in small spaces.

Once again they showed it is not what you do it is how you do it as they tackled Cole Porter's witty classic on the cramped confines of the Mill Theatre, tucked away at the back of the huge Dundrum Shopping Centre.

Director Helen McCann called on the experienced Tom Ronayne to help her design a composite set to depict an ocean-going liner and to lay the foundation for a successful production.

The pair worked along the lines of garden and theatre designers alike - if you can't build out, build up.

They came up with a structure which not only suggested the façade of the SS American but incorporated interior cabins with pull-out beds and added a working bridge on top to give the performers the maximum amount of room in which to move. As a result the hard-working ensemble had enough floor space to do justice to choreographer Nicole McDonald's energetic dance routines while creating stage pictures.

Ms McCann and Mr Ronanyne also removed Dave O'Connor's big- sounding small band from its usual position wedged right up against the front rows of the audience - and sometimes almost as part of it - and placed the musicians on a eyrie above and behind the ship's bridge with the performers relying on a monitor in the auditorium to keep an eye on the musical director.

Ruth Fitzsimon as showgirl turned evangelist Reno Sweeney, employed a rapier in this role rather than the bludgeon we often see.

Kevin Hynes as Billy Cocker had twinkle toes, a flashing smile, a good top to his tenor voice and worked well with not only Ms Fitzsimon but Kate McKeown's demure Hope Harcourt, who at times throughout the night produced a big Broadway belt of a voice.

Kevin Macken's Moonface Martin had an old comedy head on young shoulders allied to a melodic high baritone singing voice while the aforementioned Tom Ronanye grabbed the role of Elisha Whitney by the scruff of the neck and never let go in a forceful portrayal of the millionaire.

Emma Mae West's Erma was a sassy Broadway broad with a knowing smile while Dorothy Clement and John Paul McGouran as Evangeline Harcourt and Lord Evelyn Oakleigh respectively showed the depth of dramatic talent the Society possesses.

Liam Corrigan made a wry and very English captain of the vessel, Chris Bass was a high camp purser and another experienced actor, Robert Coventry lent his skills to the small role of Henry T Dobson, the vicar who is mistaken by the cops for Moonface and hauled off to custody just before the boat sails.

A rather mature theatre critic of my acquaintance these days quails at the very mention of Grease.

At the last count he had seen over 100 versions of the show both professional and amateur from schools halls to Carnegie Hall and he maintains there's nothing anyone can do with it that he hasn't seen. I would like to have had him sitting alongside me to see Claire's Tighe's take on Jacobs and Casey's 70s blockbuster.

This was a different Grease with an invention and an edge rather than the standard version so often served up to audiences. And it all started with a very different opening.

Catriona Ni Threasaigh's band had played only a few chords of the show's rousing opening number before Vince Fontaine came to life on the big screen long before he set foot on stage, courtesy of a very old television model built into the stage left wing adjunct.

And in Act Two the radio host wasn't accompanied by band leader Johnny Casino, a character dropped from Ms Tighe's version, with Fontaine not just introducing the high school hop but also singing the Hand Jive. Roger and Sonny, played here with relish by Ross Murray and Dylan McQuaid respectively, so often mere incidentals in this story, were elevated from bit parts to the point where they almost eclipsed Doody, the recognised third male lead in this show while Sandy and Patty showed a strength of character that is often absent.

Ms Tighe's hand was all over this production - directing, choreographing and designing the set.

Orla Jennings was the new girl in town who finally succumbed to peer pressure; Brian Tighe was a strutting Danny, Avril Doyle was a bossy Rizzo and Ian Tighe made for an aggressive Kenickie.

Jamie Hennessy's well played Doody gained new status as a pop star in this version while Aoife Cartwright was a minx of a Marty and Aoife Masterson breathed new life into would-be beautician Frenchy.

Lynn Brennan's lively Jan was another variation from the norm while Jordan Donnelly's Eugene was much more integrated into the gang than usual.

Brian Phillips' coped manfully with his increased workload as super smooth Vince Fontaine while Jennifer Dawson made Cha Cha di Gregorio more of the fiery Latin man-eater she is meant to be.

Ms Tighe's choreography built throughout the evening to the point where we had an electric hand jive delivered with a high degree of precision.

This was a show that was dressed well with some fabulous wigs on show; had fine technical support and was played out on an interesting composite set in front of an appreciative and somewhat noisy audience.

John Dempsey and Dana Rowe's musicalisation of this show is one of modern musical theatre's most underrated works.

It has a lot to offer amateur societies and Limerick Musical Society gave it a lot in return.

Director Des Henn put together a strong cast for this raunchy night on the wide open spaces of the city's University Concert Hall.

Dave Griffin was a dashing devil of a Darryl Van Horne, a terrific actor and a man who has a much better baritone singing voice than he allowed himself to show.

There were no such inhibitions from the powerful trio of Mr Griffin's pupils - or were they his victims? - Laura Henebry's Alex Spofford, Sinead O'Sullivan's Jane Smart and Rebecca Ballinger's  Sukie Rougemont.

All three sounded well on their own and combined beautifully on big numbers like "Make Him Mine" and "I Wish I May".

Judy O'Connor's Felicia Gabriel was an all-action, fleet-footed and sour faced town busybody with Adrian Egan her brooding and disenchanted husband who eventually kills her. The couple's stage daughter Jennifer was played by good young soprano Zara Walsh who linked well with Jamie Sheehan's lively Michael Spofford, a young man who can dance as well as he can sing.

A terrific ensemble who did both musical director Maire Keary- Scanlon and choreographer Niamh Twomey proud, had loads of space in which to work on Tom Lynch's storybook set which also incorporated a catwalk which corralled Ms Keary-Scanlon's big- sounding orchestra in a pit.

Mr Henn's production also had great technical support from the Star Systems boys on the sound desk and Joe Betts' lighting plot. Both disciplines played an integral part in the show while another huge effort saw Jacinta Florish and Barbara Meany make the wardrobe for a company that was almost 60-strong. The one off-key moment in a strong production in a lovely venue was the manner of the way the three ladies were rigged for their flight at the end of the Act One. It took a little bit of the magic away from the moment.

A little like the Phantom in his last production, the shadow of Greg Browne was all over this show.

Not only did he direct the piece, he choreographed it and went on to design the set and the lighting.

With such control it's not surprising that this was a tight production staged in the much renovated Scout's Hall which takes on a glossier look on each successive visit.

Mr Browne does the simple things well. He pulled together a strong principal line and then extracted good performances from them as well as devising high energy routines for a big ensemble.

Indeed, this show was often at its best during sequences such as the Indian Ceremonial Dance, although a clever routine at the end of "I'm A Bad, Bad Man" involving only hands, heels and toes and with the ensemble seated on wooden benches rivalled it closely.

Zelda Dillon in the title role captured the essence of a bemused backwoods girl catapulted to stardom but really only seeking domestic harmony with Frank Butler. The famous sharpshooter was played by the big-voiced Kevin Prout who is very easy around a stage while Shane Connolly was a forceful Buffalo Bill Cody.

Patrick Rohan as amiable hustler, Charlie Davenport, was a schemer with a fat cigar and a chuckle never far from his lips while Anthony White was a very distinctive Pawnee Bill and Niamh Chadwick a busy Dolly Tate.

Gerry Scanlon, a man with great mannerisms and excellent diction, was a calm but commanding Chief Sitting Bull.

Mr Browne's settings, which included a toy train racing along the back of the set as a precursor to the rail journey the travelling show takes, allowed the maximum amount of room for the big company to move around in while creating locations such as a fabulous red and white striped marquee.

The director also created some excellent stage pictures throughout the evening and gave us a fabulous expertly choreographed slow motion sequence under strobe lighting in the initial shooting match between Annie and Frank.

A handsome costume plot and some fine props, including a few from the Society's 1982 production of the show at the venue, added to the eye appeal.

A healthy box office with the house full signs up for several of the performances was also further proof that the north Tipperary group correct in making the move to acquire and renovate their spiritual home.

Unsurprisingly, UCD MS have just picked up an award. Not from me I hasten to add, but a few days after the curtain came down on this Broadway blockbuster the group were named UCD's Society of the year.

It comes in a season when they have staged the Irish premiere of Bonnie and Clyde, organised an inter-varsity competition, tackled A Chorus Line and then announced they have secured the rights to Legally Blonde for next spring.

This well organised, thriving group has made a point of mixing the new and the neglected with the popular in its short life, as evidenced by next year's plans which still holds out a 50/50 prospect of a run of a rarely performed modern work in the autumn.

The Society's biggest problem is that they usually work in the far from ideal Astra Hall on the university's campus, a space without a proper stage, wing space and where the performers enter through the same doors as the audience.

On this occasion musical director Conal Duffy's rich-toned 15-piece orchestra were placed to the right of the stage area, not ideal for the performers, who without the aid of monitors, had to be extremely well drilled in their knowledge of the score.

Cormac Gleeson, a second year actuarial student making his directorial debut, was the man at the helm of this rarely performed Pulitzer Prize winning show which explores the private lives and thoughts of chorus line dancers on New York's theatre scene.

It was derived from a string of interviews conducted by director and choreographer, Michael Bennett, himself a former hoofer, with 24 Broadway-based dancers on topics ranging from their private lives to their theatre careers.

While the tension between Maurice Wright's Zach and Jessica Concannon's Cassie over a failed relationship wasn't as good as it could have been many of the other characters were well drawn.

Amy Gilligan's giddy Kristine and Naoise Dunbar's protective Al made a convincing couple; Lorraine Stack was a strong, feisty and confident Sheila while Conor O'Rourke was a dry, witty, middle-class Bobby.

Niamh Casey could have been a little sourer as Diana Morales, the girl who still viewed herself as an outsider while Grainne Larkin's Maggie and Aisling Gilligan's Bebe brought vocal power to the table.

Katie Stevens was an assured Val while Oisin Nolan's confessional monologue as Paul was powerful. Lorna Bailey, Kevin Bates, James Bergin, Daragh Cushen, James Glynn, David Kennedy, Kevin Moran, Sophie O'Sullivan and a 13-strong ensemble also played their part in a production that moved at great pace, engaging the audience, some of whom came from off campus. A typically spare set from Scenemaker, this time turning the back of the theatre into a mirrored rehearsal room by the reversal of flats on trucks,  allowed the cast plenty of room to execute choreographer Aly Coyne's well-conceived dance routines.

Joining Thurles Musical Society for their first performance of Curtains brought back a little nostalgia. A work I had only seen once before. A 'Who done it' style musical - so different from many of the musicals on the scene today. I really was not prepared for what received me in the auditorium when I entered. With a complete gold pros arch and opera boxes - you could have entered the Theater an der Wien in Vienna - plus the orchestra was encased in an elaborate enclosure of gold pillars and red fabric. It was truly extraordinary. This complex show moved swiftly from scene to scene, each scene carefully gauged with a strong momentum from Mary Rose McNally's ten piece orchestra creating a fifties feel to this lush score. A large brass section including sax, trombones, horns and trumpets brought some beautiful sounds reminiscent of the MGM Movies. A clear beat, stage and pit was always balanced except for some underscoring which was a little too loud at the beginning. Muted trumpets in 'Show People' was nicely judged and some lovely clarinet playing in the 'Coffee Shop Nights'. Good attention to the dynamics throughout the score with some nice accelerando in 'What Kind of Man'. With tight control of accents, Tony Finnegan was in his element executing the Bostonian tongue. Interpretation of the text was natural and flowed well with characters well drawn. The chorus was well integrated throughout the show with all technicals of a high standard. He brought his considerable skills to the fore in tackling this war horse of a show. Choreography by Debbie Kiernan showed imagination in the interpretation of this show, incorporating many of the company members in a considerable amount of musical numbers. Moves were varied and different like the Wide Open Spaces with a circle of piggybacks, and the four boys in 'Thataway' using the chairs. It was very creative and clever. The Fred and Ginger number was quite magical with all the ingredients of a MGM musical fantasy. A mammoth job for Stage Manager Tommy Sweeney and team who were in control all evening with this large and varied set. Using some cast for scene changes allowed sets to be changed at great speed helping the flow of the production. Great attention to props by Rita Loughnane who brought a nice 1950's authenticity to many props in this show. Set designed by Tony Finnegan was impressive and well executed by Tommy Sweeney and crew. The set was a feat of engineering that was imposing by its size and lavish in its finish. Even the pros curtains were sumptuous with tails and swags. The fantasy scene was pure MGM Hollywood with its double width white staircase - even to the pink trim on the lavish white drapes. Excellent detail. Star Systems kept an even balance with the sound most of the evening. I felt the chorus were a little muted in the beginning but this was quickly remedied. The tone Advertisement was mellow and worked well in this auditorium. Lighting by Ali Kerr created a varied pallet which complemented the set. Some lovely closing down of scenes especially Aaron on the piano in 'I miss the Music'. Cueing was of a high standard which, again, helped with the flow of the production. Costumes were well looked after by Eidin Sweeney. The '50's period was well observed with some lovely touches that gave an authentic feel like the fur wraps and jackets which added a sophistication to the look. Belling looked a treat all evening and there was a beautiful set of white costumes, á la 'Fred & Ginger', plus showgirls for the fantasy scene. Footwear was well observed - but please remember, nude shoes do not work for black dresses. Also, be mindful of trouser lengths for the gentlemen. Make-up and hair was very well attended to by Ger Egan and her team with styles well suited for many of the characters. The titanic role of Cioffi was played by Aodán Fox. This was a tour de Force of a performance which never stopped from the moment he entered the "on stage' theatre. Good control of script with an innate understanding of the text which kept the dialogue interesting and well observed. Vocally the score was well within his range with clean lyrics. I loved the way he looks after Belling when he exits. This was a very accomplished performance. Maria McElgunn consistently engaged as Carmen with a droll, dry delivery. Dialogue needed to be projected more and I thought she needed to turn up the 'bitch' button more ….just to round her off nicely. The explosive moments needed just a little more heat. Cathal O'Donoghue as Belling, the camp director, was a treat all evening - never overplaying - this was his secret weapon. A natural performer with clear diction and well projected lines manipulated and delivered dialogue with flair. Georgia, with a beautiful wig, was played by Fiona Delaney who needed to be bigger in character to match the other performers on stage. This, too, carried into the singing. 'Thinking of Him' displayed a lovely mezzo. John Hayes as Aaron projected text clearly with a well sustained accent all evening. Vocally, for me, he has the hit of the show with 'I Miss the Music' which has a haunting melody and some sentimental lyrics. A little high for him - it non-the-less never marred the integrity of his performance. A nicely drawn 'blonde' performance from Danielle Martin as Niki playing the innocent to a tee. Dixie Byrne played Oscar who took a while to establish himself in the production. Some lapses of accent with some difficulty working off the line. Loved him finding the take away in Cioffi's briefcase. Frank Touhy as Bobby gave an energetic performance with clarity and focus of character. A natural performer with some very good dancing skills - performed a lovely pas de deux with Bambi, played by Mairead Hackett. Bambi was a vivacious and attractive performance well able to handle the go getting ingénue. Great working off the line with a natural flare for the stage. Pat Hayes as Sidney made a grand entrance through the auditorium. He was suitably gruff with a fine Brooklyn accent. Peter Donnelly as Randy has oodles of talent with a bright personality and a fine singing voice. He projected clearly all evening and is a great asset to the company. Nina Scott as Jessica was, Oh! All too brief. With her 'no musical talent', she revealed good comedic timing. God bless Gary Dempsey as Johnny - who would want to be stage manager for this Bernstein and Shapiro Company. Attentive in all his duties he displayed good understanding of text and kept things moving along nicely. John Butler as Daryl gave a reliable performance with a good grasp and a well maintained Boston accent. Clear projection but a little too much resistance with O'Farrell the detective! A great show for the chorus as they have several great numbers from 'Wide Open Spaces' to 'Show People', 'Thataway' and ' He Did It'. Well-balanced choral work with attention to some complex harmonies, which rang into the auditorium. The tricky soprano leaps in 'The Women's Dead' were well handled with the split chord at the end of this number well sustained and with rich tone. A slight imbalance in 'A Tough Act to Follow' and a rather sluggish and tentative entry at the end of Wide Open Spaces reprise. A fine representation of this new(ish) show. Thank you once again for inviting me, to Mary Butler for her hospitality and even to Anne Heffernan doing an act of mercy at the interval. As discussed with AIMS at the beginning of the 2014/15 season, Tony Finnegan wishes to state that he does not want to be considered for any nominations in relation to any production with which he was involved this year. Thus, as Director for Thurles Musical Society's Curtains, his wishes will be respected.

A lovely 1930's feel to this production as if the sound was coming from a record player. Evocative of the period, the band was perched on the poop deck enclosed by a canvas wall. The conductor, Shane Farrell, brought the band together with a clear beat - gleaned only when the canvas wall rose. Clean playing from all sections of the band - individual sections of the overture segued nicely into each other with smooth changes of tempi and some lovely colours coming from the sometimes muted brass section and the saxophones. Great tone from band with this Cole Porter score littered with different tempi - some slow and smoochy with others full of energy and pizzazz. Piano came several times too much to the fore as in 'Easy to Love' but lovely playing especially from the flute and violin in 'It's de lovely'. Paddy Daly brought some nice coaching and effects from the choral singing as Chorus Master. Bon Voyage was left a little too static which does not help the momentum of the number - the pizzicato section could have been cleaner and some tuning problems in the final chord. The quintet showed a good blend of voices but a couple were rather exposed in solo lines. Style, posture and deportment was lacking in bringing us back to the 1930's. Some good work from the men in 'Anything Goes' and some well executed and precise tapping from the ladies which showed them off to good effect. 'Blow Gabriel Blow' didn't leap off the stage but loved the idea of the boxes for Reno USC. Michael Evans as Billy Crocker gave a relaxed performance with clear diction and a well - sustained American accent. He could have had more fun with playing around more with the various accents. The score was not an easy fit for this performer as anything over a G or an A, the actor slipped into falsetto. A confident performer with an easy flow to his movement. Dancing is second nature to this actor with a lovely style and he could have benefited from more challenging choreography. Roisin Egenton as Reno Sweeney gave an attractive performance with a good grip and understanding of text. Full of fun, she could have gone further with her performance, making the character much bigger and more theatrical. More could have been made with the lyrics but this actress has a fine voice well able for the wonderful Cole Porter score. Sean Hosty as Lord Evelyn Oakleigh brought great fun and over the top accuracy to this fop of a character. An excellent accent, with a fine resonant voice was well sustained throughout the evening and displayed an innate understanding of the text. More attention to vocal pitch would help this character - and be careful you don't 'drop out' of character during scenes. An engaging performance from Megan Lohan as Hope Harcourt with a character that isn't too developed in this book. Some very good dialogue and always involved in her scenes. She was always in character and I loved her 'seeing' all the pictures painted by Billy in 'Easy to Love'. Good vocal range in this well produced voice but needed to colour your solo with a bit more sentimentality. The nude colour evening gown looked beautiful. Nicky Lawless as Moonface Martin was too laid back for my taste. Hardly any attempt at an accent and not different enough from the other characters which was a shame as this actor could have given more. Dialogue lacked colour and energy where text was thrown away. Being laid back does not create a cool character and I felt that this performer was playing to a gallery of 'mates' attending that evening and feeding from their reaction. Edel Garvey as Erma gave a variable performance with an unevenness in her accent. The character was not established due to that fact that I did not believe the relationship she had with Moonface. 'Just practicing' was nicely delivered and showed much potential which was not developed. Her maiden voyage in musical theatre, I feel that this sophisticated character role might have been a step too far. Vocally a fine voice with a great range. Ailbhe Slevin as Evageline Harcourt was suitably motherly and gave a myriad of reactions throughout her performance. She was always attentive and presented well in every scene. Patrick Byrne as Eli Whitley is a creative actor who draws your eye whenever on stage. He knows his craft with a nicely judged drunk that never lapsed into farce. Unforced comedy was always a delight and loved the small touches of him shaving his chest and posturing in the chair before Reno was to arrive. Eoin Grealis was always on the ball as The Captain with attention paid to the delivery of text. Obviously very reliable as he was placed in many scenes….. possibly some that he should not have been in. Karl O'Doherty as The Purser had great energy with a clear well projected voice. Well integrated within the production but a tendency to go off the note in his singing which is a shame. This could be easily remedied with some technical vocal exercises. An unusual interpretation for Rev. Henry T. Dobson. Kevin Griffin brought a character full of affectation and loaded with campery which was not required for this character. Directors Brian and Sean Power used the space well on stage except for the cabin scenes which seemed cramped and too small. Energy was lacking in some scenes as dialogue needed to be quickened in several places. Some opportunities were missed in vocal numbers such as 'Be like a Bluebird' and 'Bon Voyage'. A keener eye to costumes and shoes was also required and stronger accents to be insisted upon especially with Moonface and Erma. Claire Rigney as choreographer gave a varied collection of routines which needed more precision and style to evoke the era. Good response and inventiveness to numbers such as 'Easy to Love' and 'You're the Tops'. Good tap work in Anything Goes' with the men doing extremely well in this number. Scenes changes were carried out smartly and efficiently by Leonard Power and team. Some masking issues US centre in the first scene behind the bar was a distraction. Props needed some attention and needed more care in locating items of the period. A lot of the dressings were not up to the standard. Some looked great like the leather chair, but why cover it up and pretend it's another chair in a cabin???? The black tablecloths did not fit in with the rest of décor. The tea trolley looked like an industrial case. Plenty of space given with a clean a spacious set design by Scenemaker. The finish was far from complete with handles for doors needing looked at. Stage breaks were required for the trucks and more slash curtain was also required to create a better finish. Sound by Fintan Higgins and Marion Heery was a bit hit and miss throughout the evening. Cuing variable with many missed entry lines. Sometimes mics not even on. Lighting by Paul Kelly had some success with a nice palette of colour used. Nice variance with LX for the 1st and 3rd class cabins. Some problems also with cuing but some good use of gobos throughout. Costumes were a bit of a mixed bag. Need to be careful with fabrics and prints that they are of the right period. The cat-suits were not appropriate and the choice of fabrics was more suitable to Sweet Charity than Anything Goes. Trousers in general need to be looked at - length and fit. Erma needed to wear tights. The sailor's uniforms were mostly ill fitting. Aine and Fiona Lawless looked after make-up which was fine but wigs needed to be employed to get the full '30's effect for this iconic show. Hope needed some major work done on her hairstyle. Good attempt with some of the chorus ladies with their hair but there were others who just didn't bother. House management was courteous and it was lovely to hear announcements made in the national tongue.

stage.  A good orchestra was put together but off stage behind the stage with conductor Fintan Farrelly also playing. Variances of sound levels plagued this performance and I was wondering if there was a proper sound check done during the technical rehearsal. More breadth was required in shaping the score to give the cast a chance. 'To Life' was taken too fast and the orchestra lost its way towards the end creating confusion on stage. Sabbath Prayer needed a little more time and freedom of expression especially with Tevye's musical 'turn' at the end. He didn't have enough time. Due to the sound design, a more ensemble sound from the instruments was required with a number of instruments, at times, over-loud and confusing.

A nice sounding chorus with some very good harmonies coming through, especially in the 'Sabbath Prayer' and 'Sunrise, Sunset'. Men were somewhat untidy in the 'To life' number. More dynamics would have been the cherry on the cake.

Benny O'Brien as Tevye relied on a softer approach in general to his interpretation. We didn't get the twists and turmoils which plague his mind. He needed to be freer flowing in his thinking and body movements. A tendency to drop lines and he needs to use the words of the text more. 'Rich man' was too busy and should grow from your daily work. Relationship with Golde worked very well with the duet really working.

Christine O'Brien as Golde won our hearts with a lovely thought through performance, with a natural flare for working with children and trying to co- exist with that man of yours. Vocally, more than fine for this role giving extra to the lyrics making sure they were communicated.

Liz Leavy as Tzeitel was cast older than the other sisters - which didn't really match up. Nicely drawn performance with well projected dialogue and was close to her other sisters. Good animated scene in 'Matchmaker' with an easy way on stage. Eimear Reynolds as Hodel showed lots of personality with a certain amount of cheek. Uses her light mezzo voice very well culminating in a lovely 'Far From the Home'. Be careful of diction in this number and the amount of vibrato you put into the voice.

Natasha Fitzpatrick playing Chava is the more reserved of the three sisters. A lovely voice with clear diction in 'Matchmaker' - I loved her asking 'Please, take your time'. Lovely flare with dialogue and reaction to text. Remember to stay in character till you have fully exited. Both Sprintze and Bielke, Derfhinn Bushell and Aoife Wadd created a great bond with their elder sisters and added greatly to the scenes that they were in. Both seemed to be having great fun which spilled over into the audience.  The nervous and slightly eccentric Motel was played by David Flaherty who needed greater volume in his dialogue. Some of the comedy did not come naturally to him and seemed imposed on him. Could really draw and use the lines more in the 'perfect fit', 'fits like a glove' scene with Tevye. Same with the lyrics of 'Miracle of Miracles' but vocally well within his range. Blocking in this number did not mean a lot. The perfect looking Lazar Wolf played by Michael O'Driscoll seemed a shy man but never got lost in the crowd. Again, more projection with the voice as we lost a lot of lines. This was more like TV acting but for stage it needs to be much bigger. A nice baritone voice, always in tune. Sean Rooney as Perchik has a nice presence on stage but needs to believe more and become more passionate with what he believes in. Needed to be more persuasive with Hodel.  Liam Brady as Fyedka developed his character well throughout the night. Volume of dialogue was an issue - and he needed to be a little freer with his approach to the character. Phrasing of text was well marked.

Maureen Dunne playing Yente was full of business and on a mission. At times, text was too fast and we missed quite a bit. The natural gear changes in the text were not evident and the scene with Golde needed to be more conversational. A lovely actor in the role of the Rabbi. This was Gus Hanley who looked the part and delivered his lines cleanly. Not sure about the wedding shawl - this one looked odd. Micelle Kelly Conlon has a good strong voice with a good understanding of the text - a little bit like Miranda Richardson in 'Black Adder'. An apparition from the bed clothes revealed Sarah Duke as Fruma Sarah - great start with her number but was inaudible by the time we got to the curse. This could have been a sound issue. Well made up - she looked a fright!

The chorus was well drilled in most of the routines except for the 'To Life' scene which needed more rehearsal time. Lovely groupings and always well disciplined. They need a little more work in reacting with each other. More musical dynamics could have been displayed as they were capable of it.

Director Liam Butler marshalled his forces well with this large company and drew some nice playing from a lot of the cast but I felt they could have opened up more within their characters - like Perchik and his revolutionary ideas. The community disliking the Russians needed to be stronger - nobody reacted to them in the pub for instance. More careful observance with footwear and to sound.

Choreographer Emer O'Brien created well devised routines which responded well to the score. Traditional in style, most of the company were well capable of executing her ideas. The spinning bed in the dream sequence was very novel and added a different dimension to the number. Well done. Stage Manager Eddie Kiernan devised the scene changes very efficiently and were cleanly executed. Smooth transitions helped the run of the production. Well-crafted farm tools and a great attention to period props by Maureen Flaherty gave authenticity to this show. Set design by Robert Belton, Eddie Kiernan and Liam Butler devised a simple all-encompassing set which was effective and evocative and more than etched out an idea of where this show was set. The four wooden 'islands' were a puzzle to me all evening as they were not hugely used throughout the night!

Sound by Jody Trehy was not the best I have heard from this normally meticulous designer. It was a litany of cues missed, major woofing and fizzing, and general inability to hear artists on stage with very little balance between stage and pit.

Lighting design by Rodney Ellis created some very evocative and sensitive moods for this show which worked 'hand in glove' with a lot of the scenes. Some cueing needed to be looked at with ends of numbers needed to be punctuated more. Costumes from Pat McGann were a breath of fresh air. An excellent selection of fabrics and colours which bring a sort of Technicolor to the production. Fiddler does not have to be dull and earthy. More coats were needed for the exodus at the end - I don't think many would have survived their journey. Make-Up and Hair was kept very simple except where all the drama occurs in the Dream Scene which was well designed and executed by Teresa Morgan, Fiona Fenelon and team. Hodel needed some work done to her hair - it just looked unkempt all evening.

I was met by Padraig O'Brien and was extremely well looked after. Lovely to meet with some people I recognised from over the years on this busy first night.

As I rolled up to the Abbey Hall in the north Tipperary town a little over a week before the end of the Sullivan season I wondered just what I would be in line for.

It was about 13 months since I had seen a version of the Noel Gay show directed by Paul Norton closer to the centre of the Midlands patch he serves.

Would it simply be a re-hash of that production, would it a development on that show or would it be something entirely different?

The answer, of course, was probably irrelevant, given that one of Mr Norton's principal tenets is to entertain his audience, a job he invariably succeeds in.

For the record the production was probably closest to answer number two but sufficiently different so as not to be a carbon copy of last year's model.

Like all good directors Mr Norton doesn't stand still, adding to the characters and shaping the show using the abilities of the personnel he is working with.

While his decision to make the family solicitor Parchester a Scot was no longer a surprise to me, John Lynch's version was not the dour Calvinist notary I remember. Somewhat surprisingly this Parchester was a sly drinker, reaching for the hip flask in his briefcase at every available opportunity.

Mr Norton's London landlady was once again, a nosy Irishwoman, far removed from the typically East End harridan we normally see but Margaret Stanley's take on the role was, once again a development of the character. Tadgh Maher's Gerald was much more of the conventional fop while Siobhan Bowe as the Duchess of Dene was given a more imperious tone in this version and Gary Clarke lent a deep voice and deadpan humour to a very different take on the Hareford's butler Charles.

The director also produced big performances from his central characters, the all-action and acrobatic Pat Cullen as Bill and Aisling Rohan who was easy on the eye and ear as Sally.

Brid Delaney's Lady Jacqueline was still a self-serving man-eater while Paul Spencer repeatedly threatened to hog the limelight as Sir John Tremayne. Tim Keane, Andrew Walsh and Niamh O'Donnell touched in the roles of Sir Jasper Tring and Lord and Lady Battersby respectively while Ronan Foyle was a cheery policeman.

Choreographer Sarah Griffin came up with routines for the full company and principals alike that were integrated into a production which was played on a set designed by Mr Norton and stage manager Ian Hanrahan that was tailored to the confines of the Abbey Hall.

Nestled in North County Dublin in the seaside resort of Rush lies the small auditorium of the Millbank Theatre which allows Rush Musical Society to perform over ten days thus giving more opportunity to audiences to see the work this company does. A full house for the opening performance brought a great atmosphere to this 'Best little Whorehouse in Texas'. In full flight was Sarah Lynch Barrett who controlled a fine group of musicians - from behind the stage - to great effect. She brought a great country feel to the sound of this musical with pace and tempi well judged. Also acting as Chorus Mistress, some good work was evident with good articulation generally with text and harmonies coming through easily. There were some tuning problems with the Dogettes in 'Watchdog' interlude and The Aggies number was overly raucous. The men redeemed themselves in 'Good Ole Girl' which was sensitively sung and very well balanced vocally. The girls were generally in better shape with clear voices and tone ably making 'Hard Candy Christmas' one of the highlights of the show. More bite to text was needed throughout. A very glamorous Miss Mona, performed by Niamh Carroll, gave us a well thought through character with a rich smoky mezzo, well-pitched voice. The voice fully in range of her given musical numbers; she invested a lot in the text and gave a very fine sensitive and rounded performance. 'Bus to Amarillo' needed to be simpler from the start and then moving in gears to the climax. Seamus Griffin as Ed Earl provided a sure confident and well- paced performance and was every bit a match for his Miss Mona. For once, we really did believe that these two had a past …….and a present. Good Southern accent with attention to text and rhythm of lines created a natural, warm portrayal. Vocally, a well felt 'Good ole Girl' in an easy baritone - never pushed but always in range. Gary Finegan as Melvin P. Thorpe was, I feel slightly stifled and the real comedian never quite emerged. With the ghastly blond wig - was Ali Murphy punishing him for something? A great accent with detail to phrasing, there were some problems with diction as words were not projected as well as they could have been. Michelle Harris Farrell as Angel was the street wise, lippy arrival who delivered lines well - a little rushed at times - but always with clear diction. Loved the chewing gum and an endearing scene on the telephone. Good forward tone to the voice, lyrics were well projected and sincerely delivered. Shy was ably portrayed by Niamh Kavanagh in her pig-tails, dungarees and I loved her walk in the high heels. She should watch the posture as it was too refined and also she had a tad too much make-up on. She's a country hick. Less is much better here than more. Celine Potter as Jewel gave her powerhouse performance of 'Twenty Four Hours of lovin' to a thrilled audience. Her dialogue was dark and 'black' but she was not hugely integrated into the show. The dillusional and "happy with her lot in life" character of Doatsey Mae was well-judged by Noreen Fynes. Real understanding of dialogue brought her life into focus. A perceptive comedienne it was delicately performed with the range to tackle another song highlight 'Doatsey Mae'. Barry Kavanagh as the Governor was nimble with some fancy footwork in dodging the awkward questions. Text and lyrics always clear and projected. But he required stronger make up. Peter O'Brien as Senator Wingwood was dressed immaculately and was suitably raucous and falsely loud with the Aggies team rousing them for their nights stand at the Chicken Ranch. Stephen Ryan confidently delivered 'The Prologue' with a good accent but not always in his vocal range - the lower sections were at times a little weak. A fine, energetic mover, he was the fulcrum later on in many of the dance sections. A strong chorus with good attention to harmonies was the hallmark of this group of singers. There were times when pitch was a problem for the men as in the 'Aggies Dance' but this didn't apply to 'Good ole Girl' which was sensitively sung. The ladies shone through in several numbers especially in 'Hard Candy Christmas.' More investment in the text would make many of the numbers come alive more. Director Pat McElwain directed a slick and well thought through production. Good attention to dialogue with a keen eye to costumes and set which firmly set this show in period and location. Good accents throughout but some words needed to be more exaggerated to put the Southern stamp on the dialect. Choreography by Denise Donohue brought the Southern style to many of the routines. Numbers like 'Texas, has a Whorehouse in it' was well devised but needed to be more together. Chorus was well integrated into the production with some good pom-pom work and some great poses with the girls. Damian Hurley was more than capable as stage manager in executing clean and slick scene changes all evening. Props by Connie Murray were well detailed and in period especially the wooden wheelchair for Miss Wulla Jean, carpet bag for Shy and the various paraphernalia in the café and office scenes. Set design by John O'Donoghue was inventive, creative and extremely clever in utilising the small space that is the Millbank Theatre. Sandy in colour with ox-blood highlights, it created clean lines and everything for the various scenes were built into the structure. It left the maximum space for the show to unfold. Lighting by Alastair Kerr expertly chose a great palette of colours enhancing the set and costumes to great effect. Cueing was not always spot on but the effects were quite beautiful. Nice effect of closing down the stage to the scene being performed brought more focus to the action. Jody Trehy brought a fine balance to the whole evening with sound - considering the orchestra were in a different part of the building. A keen ear, everything was in order. Gunshot sound effects needed to be looked at as they were not realistic. A fine set of period costumes for the '70's were selected by Lisa Collins and Noreen Fynes with particular mention to Miss Mona's wardrobe which was just beautiful. Be careful with trouser lengths as Ed Earls needed attention. Hair and make-up was very much in order with great detail - as you would expect from Ali Murphy. Styles were tasteful and also suited the characters; especially the ladies. House management was extremely attentive and we were looked after royally by Helen Kavanagh all evening. I have to say, I did 'a little side kick 'on crossing to my car.

My first time in the beautiful town of Birr and their wonderful Theatre & Arts Centre. Due to unforeseen circumstances, Vincent Lynch stepped into the breach at the last minute to act as MD. He did a fine job throughout with just a few things that needed a little attention. There was a raggy ending to 'Rich Man' and tempi was a little fast for the 'To Life' number. More control was needed for the big Fruma Sarah ensemble section - it need to be more together. Good balance from the band, which allowed certain instruments to come to the fore when required. A lovely rustic feel with the inclusion of the accordion. Violinist worked great as 'The Fiddler' in the show also. Nicely segued into the various scenes from her position in the band. Lovely clarinet playing in the 'Bottle Dance'. Very good balance and accuracy maintained.

The ladies were more secure in their singing than the men, but the large ensemble numbers had great quality of tone with carefully rehearsed harmonies and clean diction. 'Sabbath Prayer' was very successful but the men needed to take more care in 'To Life' which sounded a little discordant. More dynamics would have helped throughout to give the music more dimensions. Great opening number (Tradition) introducing the entire village to us. Great movement with lots of energy in the Dream Scene. Good work in reacting to the confusion in the Wedding Scene.

Michael Donegan as Tevye looked great in this role - the central figure to the family and to the show. Too declaimed at first, he levelled it off to a normal level but I felt there was a lot of humour missing in this performance. Vocally, too much movement in 'Rich Man' over exerted the actor, which put a strain on this number. More care needs to be taken with rhythms and also be mindful of pitch. Barbara Hanamy as Golde gave a lovely, all- encompassing performance. A caring performance rather than the tough ole' boot character you normally get. A lovely Yiddish prayer before the 'Sabbath Prayer' was well judged with a steady mezzo voice. The 'Do You Love Me' was a little over-sung and needed more variation of emotions. Darren Madden performed the role of Motel. A meek interpretation is fine towards Tevye, so long as you are strong in 'Even a poor tailor deserves some happiness'. This is the turning point for Motel becoming a man. Some of the personal moments with Tzeitel were too low and inaudible. Be careful of vocal pitch for 'Miracle of Miracles'. A good journey with this role though. Marguerite McDonnell as Tzeitel has a playful and natural demeanour on stage. Good understanding of the text with clear projection. Her happiness being with Motel was very real; she sings well and in tune.

Darragh Molloy as Perchik looked well as the wandering 'student' with great ideas, which I felt you could have defended more strongly. It lacked a certain passion. The only problem with this performance was lack of projection in dialogue in certain scenes. Nice nifty moves with Hodel in the dances and a very pleasant baritone, which was well schooled. Hodel, played by Yvonne O'Toole, had lots of spark and a vivacious personality. Dialogue lovely and clear with a forward momentum to this character. Vocally, 'Far from the Home' was one of the highlights of the show. It was sensitively sung with good weight to the lyrics.

Alex Kearns as Fyedka needed more weight in his dialogue. It was a caring performance and worked well with Claire Connors as Chava - the "dreamer" of the sisters. Claire must be careful with the text in 'Matchmaker'. Lovely dramatic scene with Papa when he disowns her. Just a little more thought into various moments within the role - more impatience while waiting for Tevye, and a stronger persona while waiting for the celebrations to begin at the wedding. Every inch the Matchmaker, Heather Colohan as Yente left her mark on every arrangement….almost. This performance suffered due to non- projection of dialogue, which occurred throughout the night. Be careful not to lose text due to speed.

SarahJane Cleary as Fruma-Sarah was suitably strong but vocally unsteady with some tuning problems in her wailing at Tevye and Golde. Well costumed, the constable - played by John Lynch - needed to invest in more understanding of the text. Tommy Lyndon as the Rabbi extracted some humour from this character. He looked great but I would have liked a little more detailed work done with accent. Director Paul Norton created good pace in this production. Some more detailed work on accents and characterisation was required. More projection was need by most of the cast. The destruction scene needed more build up and momentum and was not dramatic enough. Good eye on set and costumes. Some varied and interesting work from Choreographer Grace McGrath who guided the cast through many great numbers in this score. 'To Life' needed more rehearsals; as I felt the men were not ready for this number. Be careful not to impose moves on numbers. Keep them simple - like 'Miracle of Miracles'. Scene changes were mostly done by cast but well led by Liz Kennedy. Props were well executed and beautifully chosen by Roisin Gilmore and team. Set design by George Dempsey Flanagan & Michelle Makim created a most beautiful set which was almost in miniature. Accurate and evocatively painted. Loved the LX in the back wall coming on for 'Sabbath Prayer'. Sound by Recks Studio, although a nice balance was achieved between pit and stage, there were issues with dialogue all evening. Pascal Gough designed lighting which created its own difficulty with a white box set. Closing down scenes was the main problem here with many scenes over lit. A vibrant set of costumes was well chosen bringing colour into Anatevka's dark and dull lives. Good natural style to the makeup - with fine character make-up for Fruma Sarah. Maybe a suggestion….I would have painted the masks up for added effect - they were a bit sterile. House management was great and no matter how busy, took plenty of time to make me welcome. Thank you for the Neurofen for my guest.

An early visual snapshot at Bray's Mermaid Arts Centre summed up the enduring appeal of this infectious Joe DiPietro show based on the music of Elvis Presley.

The audience's ages ranged from pensioners down to a five-year-old a few seats away from me who was clearly engrossed in the action.

Onstage, the majority of the performers were born a long time after the death of Elvis, but were obviously enjoying themselves while entertaining the Sunday afternoon matinee full house. The group had all the appearance of a society building from the bottom up. The few old hands in the company were vastly outnumbered by the fresh faces around them. A few of the principals were even making their stage debut. Wisely the group had turned to experienced director Siobhan Gallagher to guide them through a show that could all too easily veer into the realms of pantomime in the wrong hands.

Ms Gallagher gauged it correctly, was not frightened of making cuts and delivered a fast-paced, lively and highly entertaining production.

Ross Loughran, although new to the society, was one of the few leads with any real stage experience. He played the youthful rebel Chad with his jeans turned up at the bottom, a twinkle in his eye and his tongue firmly placed in his cheek.

Ms Gallagher also produced fine performances from the rest of her frontline players with Fiona Hickey taking the dual role of Natalie/Ed in her stride and Shauna Temple giving us a dismissive Sandra, the sex-bomb stranded in a small town.

Caitriona Woodcock, making her stage debut as bar owner Sylvia, is a real find while Karl O'Leary, a decent baritone in the role of garage owner Jim Halley, was another making his first stage appearance.

Jonathan Buckley as Dennis has the makings of very good musical theatre comedian while teenagers Sean Luby as Dean and Isabella Vance who played Lorraine are young people the Society will hope to build around in future years.

Jackie Fisher as the meddling Matilda, the villain of this piece, brought very good timing to the role while Nick Russell was a stoic Earl, the only figure who could put her in her place.

This energetic affair, where every other principal gets to wear blue suede shoes, was aided by Ciara Heaslip's lively choreography and driven along by a fine band under the direction of Elizabeth Gregan.

It was played out on a clever John O'Donoghue set with terrific technical backing from Cathal O'Donaghue's lighting desk and Vinny Osborne on sound.

One of my favourite shows, I entered Clara on a beautiful evening to attend Evita. Front of house was very busy which was wonderful to see with a lot of young faces in the audience.

No sign of an orchestra as they were hidden behind the set. This caused a few problems with synchronicity during the evening. I am not sure the company had visual monitors to see the conductor - Alan Recks - as I could not see any from where I was sitting. A good sound from the orchestra from this complex score except for the synthesised sound of keyboards for the string section which sound tinny and hollow. Good rhythms permeated the playing with good attention segues and tempi. What can I say about the conductor as I never saw him all evening? He did keep things moving and the score appeared to be played accurately.

More precision in duet work was needed from the conductor 'Good Night and Thank You' and the chorus needed tightening up as they were out of sync with the orchestra on several occasions. The SATB divisions were weak due to a large number of ladies, with the men needing to be more secure working within the ensembles. Lyrics could have been projected more throughout as they needed more bite. The chorus, nevertheless made a strong sound when singing tutti. Principals generally made a strong impression with some strong interpretations. Georgina Ireland Cathcart in the title role gave an emotional rollercoaster with expressive singing especially in her lower register. Visually excellent in the 'Balcony Scene' with great use of text. This was a very touching performance. Stephen Rabbette as Ché brought a free and fine tenor voice to this role but needs to relax much more to get the freedom that this role requires. It is a strong, flexible voice all well within his range. I felt that he needed to be really integrated more within the triangle more.

Juan Perón was sensitively and naturally performed by Chris Carroon. A joy to listen to he has a lovely baritone voice which he uses expertly and to great effect. A strong commitment to the lyrics was in evidence. The seduction scene was quite lame butthis problem may lie on the director's doorstep. Much was heartfelt and worked on the emotions. He gave much to his fellow actors who in turn fed from it.

Quite the opposite, Darren O'Hara fielded a very strong tenor voice for Magaldi but this actor must simply understand the importance of text. If there isn't investment in lyrics then singing becomes vocal exercises. Arm movements spinning out vocal line should be kept to the rehearsal room. Every word has a meaning and that is what is to be communicated by the actor.

A lovely cameo role for Joanne MacDonagh as the mistress with a lovely rich modern mezzo. Great colour to the voice and expressively sung. Ava O'Connor as the Child Soloist did a splendid job and is going to be a little star in years to come with that voice on her. This was a large voice and was well able for the 'Santa Evita'. In singing to Evita, why then was she turned out to the audience??? It made no sense.

The Chorus has a big job to do in this show and much to contribute. They were well drilled and had flare - the ladies relishing the challenge more, I think, than the men.  At times the chorus was tentative with their entries musically but worked hard at the dance routines which confidently evoked the exotic rhythms of South America. Some lovely ideas by Choreographer Lea Carroll who gave us the exotic and heat filled flavours of Latin American dance through her routines. There were some good details and creativity put into the routines some of which were a step too far for a number of the men. The slide movement in 'Perón's Latest Flame' looked a little bit too camp for the men's chorus. Excellent use of the chairs in 'The Art of the Possible. Director Alan Recks spread himself a little thin on this production trying to maintain several large positions in the production. This had, I feel, an effect on the production and musical side of this show. More care was needed with lyrics as certain scenes were not directed and so created a gap in the production -  like the seduction scene ' I'll be Surprisingly Good For You',  and a weak tableau for 'A New Argentina'. The slow motion needed to be sculpted better and slower to get the desired effect.

Scene changes supervised by Wayne Handy and his team happened quickly and smoothly using at times the cast to create a seamless transition from scene to scene. Some lovely props brought into the production by Edel Kennedy and Alex Cornally. Everything generally in order here. You should have lit the Thurible and also the red tablecloth should have been ironed ……big time.

The set was well designed by Stephen Rabbette, the director and Wayne Handy. A dusty and grime covered (with age) of a once elegant house. It allowed for it to be changed swiftly. Sound suffered badly in this production due to the sound levels which were too high, resulting in distortion of text and music - especially in the higher ranges. The GAA hall in Clara has a strange acoustic. It is bright and forward sounding and nothing to absorb the sound in the auditorium. A fine collection of costumes with special attention to the ladies daywear and their jewel coloured evening gowns. All looked great with marvellous accessories ….  sadly, not the shoes. Principals were well catered for especially Eva and Perón. Suitable sashes were worn by the presidential party. A beautiful soft pink/nude evening gown for Eva really stood out. Be careful with trouser lengths - each man should really have braces.  Make-up and Hair was very well devised with special mention to the several styles within the show. This was ably looked after by Liz Rickard and team.

Thank you to the FOH team who organised efficiently and without fuss. Thank you for the interval drinks. Regarding suggestions, I would suggest that the director/conductor/ designer and keyboard player relinquish something to give more time to the cast.

There are not many suggestions as the company generally are in a great position. Continue and keep doing what you are doing. With every best wish for the future.

Tucked away in a small side-street in Clonmel is the bijou White Memorial Theatre. A small, perfectly formed building where Man of La Mancha was being presented.

A great score with some wonderful numbers, it is one of those shows that we don't see too much of and it's a great pity. Laura Cotter held everything together very well, working the twists and turns from ballads to much underscoring. A little overpowering at times, she brought out the myriad of rhythms and colours from this kaleidoscopic score. The fight music should have been reduced as it is monotonous and un-focused. The make-up of the band was nicely put together with the inclusion of the Euphonium/Baritone. A rich tone with good tempi throughout kept the show flowing. Good ensemble playing with lovely contributions from the flute and piccolo adding some nice colour to numbers.

The choral singing, tutored by Laura Cotter, was well balanced with good divisions between SATB. The singing, at times, needed more elegance and care in its production, there were times the singing became raucous. There needed to be more dynamics and more effective divisions in the music. The choral pick up in 'Dulcinea' was raggy and late. I was puzzled as to why the chorus was off so much of the time - this is a trial they are holding and would be privy to all of the 'evidence'. Choral acting needed more freedom for the individuals to create and immerse themselves in their characters. There was quite a bit of participation that didn't ring true. The opening sequence needed more animation and stories better told.

The pivotal role of Cervantes was taken by the experienced Diarmuid Vaughan bringing a well-developed character which nicely progressed all evening to a very sincere and well imagined death scene. Fine projection of lines with great investment into the spoken word, relishing every vowel and nuance. The transformation was well executed on stage with a suitable baritone voice singing 'Dulcinea' and 'The Golden Helmet of Mambrino' with feeling. A slight lack of diction with the lyrics was a small problem with vocals form this actor.

James O'Donovan worked hand in glove with his Cervantes. His accent was more Mexican and became a little annoying after a while due mostly to the fact that I could not understand that he was saying. He has a strong voice but with a tendency to lose tuning - especially in the opening numbers. Believing in the lyrics is also important which I felt this actor did not do. The lack of words in 'A little gossip' - not strong enough.

Holly Jean Williamson as Aldonza suffered in this role as she was cast far too young. This 'alley-cat' personality needs to have years of experience - of life - to work this role. There were problems also with the vocal line as you could hear several gear changes in the voice. 'It's all the same' was too high. Issues also with the accent - it was not Spanish and it became confusing to the audience. Be careful that you invest much more into your text. It is so important.

One of the few who get to wear a period costume is the Governor played by George Barr. A fine presence on stage who had difficulty in picking up lines; upsetting the natural flow of the scene. A nice baritone voice well capable of 'Knight of the woeful countenance'. David Hughes as The Duke/Carasco/Knight needed to be more involved in some scenes. Fine speaking voice - Why was Carasco so English? This actor could have worked more off the line to involve him more in his scenes. Vocally in tune with a nice baritone voice.

Siobhan Dempsey as Antonia has a clear voice with good attention to text. Vocally, careful of the vocal line of the phrase as you go off the note at times. It just needs more technique. More business on stage would help flesh out the character. Liam Hunter a Padre Perez revealed a high baritone voice - there were some tuning problems here in 'I'm only thinking of him' with a little more work on the accent needed. More text required in 'To each his Dulcinea'. Needed to put the monk's hood up of the costume as you didn't have a skull cap or a tonsure wig.
