A nice performance from Tracey Walsh as The Housekeeper but she could have exploited the comedy more. The hysterics at times were a little untrue. Emmet Donlan as The Barber has a strong singing voice and was well- integrated into the scene. Nice fluid performance - including excellent on- stage trumpet playing! Ricky Dunne as Pedro was suitably rough but the nuance and projection in the dialogue were not always pronounced enough. Being more physical with Aldonza would have made the scene more real. Sheena Fennessy as the Moorish girl needed to have a dark wig and had too many repetitions of the same dance moves.

Director Michael O'Donoghue made a lot with so little as the stage is not very big. Some scenes were over simplified but had a strong leading role in the character of Cervantes. Attention to accents and dialogue and intonation patterns needed more attention. Some scenes were a little over simplified and the more dramatic moments needed to go further like the rape scene - possibly the reason being that the Aldonza was so young.

I missed the chorus being present on stage and although there was some good work with Rocinante and Dapple, I think the comic value could have been exploited more. Lovely work with the use of tables and I loved the creation of the stable. A good pace with this production which generally brought a natural rhythm to each scene.

What scene changes there were, were created through the use of props and by means of the cast.

Excellent attention to detail with props by Grainne Vaughan and team. Beautifully made and well researched. Set designed by Diarmuid Vaughan was beautifully crafted and fitted like a glove in this theatre. Detailed painting capturing centuries of grime and torture stains within these walls.

Authentic looking candelabras and torches, even to their scorch stains on the walls, the chains were evident. A fine creation.

Pat Marnane on sound worked his magic with a tight balance all round. Sound effects were well handled with good use of reverb for the Green Knight. Lighting by Michael O'Donoghue was atmospheric using a good palette of colours. Top of Act 2 with the straw colour focused on Cervantes USC and with the steely blues later in 'To each his Dulcinea worked its own magic. Lx cues for the end of the rape scene did not punctuate the scene as they were in the wrong place.

Ruth Butler and team worked hard to create a look for this production, which on the whole, more than succeeded. Fabric choices for the rags for the chorus were a bit on the light weight side but the period costumes looked well with appropriate accessories. Good attention here with Make-up and hair. A few dodgy wigs in the chorus that made no sense. Good transition scene for Cervantes into Don Quixote. Needed to look at the shape of his sideburns. Good transformations on stage from the other characters.

I arrived at the White Memorial Theatre to a very warm reception. It as Mary Cummins R.I.P who directed me in my very first show with Bray Musical Society….many moons ago. Thank you indeed for your kindness and hospitality.

It was my first time in the Siamsa Tíre in Tralee and was looking forward to seeing Sister Act there. Aine Murray took the baton for this evening's performance and controlled things to a very high order with flare, style and with a sympathetic ear to the cast on stage. She is a natural metronome as she was always keeping beat with body - I think she might have been enjoying herself. Generally she had a good control of the orchestra but here and there it did overpower in 'I haven't got a Prayer'. Tempi were mostly all well-judged and a good adherence to the score brought lots of colour and shape to the musical preparation. Incisive control from the conductor maintained balance between pit and stage.

Jackie O'Mahoney as Deloris gave a very complete interpretation, a fluid performance with a great accent, punching out the comedy like a machine gun. An excellent singer with lots of tone and easy ride into the belt voice, I did think however, that this might have been a little bit of a stretch for her. A real tour de force.

Maura Jones as Mother Superior was nicely conceived and I felt for her building frustration. More projection Calendar ShowTimes of the dialogue in general especially asides to the audience would help. Vocally there is a little vibrato in the voice with some lapses of tuning in 'Here within these walls'. Costume was a little bit too short for the Mother Superior. Lauralee Curtin as Mary Roberts looked great with her fringe and white socks but needed better footwear - possibly some sandals. She grew in character being nicely timid in the 'Gloria in excelsis Deo'. Good progression for this character with a sincere understanding of text in The life I never lead' which came across very well.

Claire McEvoy playing Mary Lazarus caught this character very well. Tough, rough and forthright with good projection of lines. Vocally well in tune in 'It's good to be a nun' and blended well with the other principals and chorus. Great pick up tempo and much energy in the number which was hilarious. Loved the yellow cap and sun glasses in 'Sunday Morning Fever'. Mike Lynch as Eddie Souther is a police officer - I don't think he is that accident prone and with so much shyness. This was I feel too much for this character. Good rhythm and feel for the dialogue and he projected his only number very well 'I could be that guy' even if it was a bit too low for him. Tim Moran as Curtis offered us his smooth and suave character who ruled the roost. Vocally fine in his number with good projection but not a great mover. It rendered the number weak. Jonathon Lynch as TJ is a natural comedian with a good strong tenor voice. Well able to go into falsetto. Loved his over the top antics DSL at the wall for 'Lady in the long black dress.' Shoes were an issue and needed to be addressed. Aaron McLarnon as Joey gave a solid interpretation. Tight-knit with the other two, there was some great ensemble playing here. Vocally well able to tackle any challenge given Competition ShowTimes to him with a slick slip into falsetto which was well placed.

Gary Murphy as Pablo worked well as the third member of the team with a very good Spanish accent in his dialogue. Good comedic skills also with clearly projected dialogue. Tim Landers as Monsignor O'Hara played the role fluidly but needed more genuine comedy to set this role apart from the ordinary. He didn't push the dialogue - comedy is not inserting an 'h' into words like 'musht' for must. The transition from bored priest to elated priest with the new music was evident but it appeared he was at the local disco.

Andrea Brosnan and Suzan O'Gara both supported Deloris with style and with great voices as backing singers in the first scene. Both are confident and have great flare, projecting words and lyrics clearly throughout.

This show was filled with so much energy it ripped through the audience who responded in a suitable fashion. It was really contagious and the production team ignited a bomb of sorts that lasted over two hours. Well drilled in their routines, with great singing ensembles and tight harmonies brought the house down by the end of the evening.

Director and Choreographer Oliver Hurley showed a great understanding of this show. It was tight, with lots of flare and energy which heightened the experience of this 'Devine Comedy'. High level of work with most principals with very good integration of the chorus throughout. Routines were well devised and drilled for smooth execution. Good routine for the 3 boys in their 'Lady in the long black dress' but they could have pushed this further. A lovely ensemble number in 'Bless our show' which highlighted the individuality of the nuns.

Certain other areas needed looking at like hair styles and some footwear and some issues with sound. An excellent use of stage space and creative ideas that worked extremely well as in the arm for Deloris in' Fabulous Baby Reprise'.

Des Hurley stage managed a very tight ship with precision in flying cues and also in the scene changes. All ran like clockwork. Props were all well catered for with excellent choices for the convent and various other locations. Some very good detail here.

A clever design that allowed for the use of levels, all painted a biscuit colour to allow for the projections which really was the set. They were stunning and well-conceived - the images well chosen. Confessional boxes further down at the sides of the audience worked well and revolved around at certain times. Sound by Brian Irwin was very mixed with a considerable number of missed cues, mics going down and on one occasion mics left on when cast off stage. Good balance and tone, however, between stage and pit, which is not easy to get in this type of show, was well achieved.

John Hurley masterminded the whole look for this show. He created some beautiful lighting states. So easily these could have been bled out by the projections or the states bled out by the projections, happily, he was the creator for both, so both worked hand in hand. Moments of sheer beauty were realised between the two.

A Trojan task was undertaken by Karen Soffe and her team and created the whole wardrobe from in-house. An achievement well worth the trouble. Nuns had a myriad of changes from plain black right through to white sequenced habits. All the females were well catered for but tailoring for the men is a huge skill with many of the items bought in. These costumes needed better fitting and most trousers needed taking up considerably.

The ecclesiastical costume looked great even to the white and red altar boys. On the whole, a terrific job done. More detail in hairstyles was required for those not in a habit. Attention to period for both men and women was required. Make-up was well in order and very natural. No problem there. On the whole, a great show full of energy - it was like getting Mass on a Saturday evening.

Kathy Kelly's first act showstopper is almost a metaphor for this Society. She sang I'm Still Here, glass in hand, eyeing up an audience she had in the palm of her hand.

Her character, Carlotta Campion, of course, has been away from the stage but the song serves to remind her fans that she has still got it.

This was O'Connell's first show in four years and what a way to make an entrance with a super cast, clever set and a fabulous overall look.

Follies is the Sondheim show that explodes the myth that the man never wrote a tune. The storyline of fractured marriages, missed opportunities and wrong turns forced into the light at a showbiz reunion requires a number of old hands reprising their former glories.

Maria Kavanagh took the suggestion literally in the role of Hattie Walker. Her rendition of Broadway Baby practically stopped the show. I wonder has the 85-year-old Sondheim ever considered extracting it from the montage it is part of?

Delores Hughes as Heidi Schiller rolled back the years while Eileen Gill was a lovely Solange Lafitte complete with French accent and Liza Minnelli hairdo. This was a show that saw Jean Sweeney as Sally, one of the four central roles here, in fine voice with beautiful renditions of In Buddy's Eyes and the haunting Losing My Mind. Jennifer McGann as Phyllis gave the audience another glimpse of the firebrand she can bring to the stage in a performance that was laced with good comic timing and some excellent movement.

The An Clasac audience also saw a weighty performance from Michael Evans as Ben Stone while Conor Kilduff, who only took the last of the four leading parts at short notice, was terrific as Bobby.

Stylish choreography from Denise O'Donoghue matched the tone of Eoin Cannon's production while fabulous hairstyles and some stunning costumes gave this show a look that was fabulous.

The cast of Dublin heavyweights also included Barry Kavanagh as the theatre proprietor who brings together his old friend for the reunion that fanned the flames of the central characters' disillusionment over their marriages. My one real concern during the evening was that Gay Kirwan's band were often too loud.

While they were undoubtedly excellent musicians I could have done with hearing a little less of them, particularly the brass section.

If this theatre, which looks as if it was designed by committee, is to be the Society's new home, the siting of the band needs to be addressed.

This was a production tailored to the tight confines of Ratoath's Venue, a centre with a small playing space, one entrance to the stage and little by way of wing space.

Director Richie Hayes took full control here shaping not just the physical action but also designing a clever set in which truck-based exteriors opened to create interiors such as Tevye's home and Motel's shop.

He supplemented the physical pieces with projections that helped set locations such as the exterior of Tevye's home, the streets of Anatevka and the village's railway halt.

The device though was at its best when it became an integral part of the scene where Tevye persuades his wife to let him break the agreement he made allowing Lazar Wolf to marry his eldest daughter.

As he invoked the ghost of Lazar's first wife, Fruma-Sarah, in his bid to frighten Golde into agreement, the character played by Aisling Campbell, appeared in all her ghoulish glory on the big screen before popping up on cue on the floor behind the headboard of Tevye and Golde's bed.

Mr Hayes also created some good pictures on the stage using the Ratoath cast. Big numbers such as the Sabbath Prayer and Sunrise, Sunset, were well grouped giving the audience a strong image and allowing the cast to display its vocal power.

The show was also packed with small, everyday details which were not only believable but helped round out the production.

Fiddler's big cast was headed up by Niall Dempsey's Tevye, a tall, lean and commanding figure with a rich speaking voice and a pleasing baritone.

Clare Green, who knows how to use a stage, was a good match for Mr Dempsey as his long-suffering Golde. Niamh Parkes, a good soprano, played the couple's eldest daughter, Tzeitel who breaks the accepted mould of relationships when refusing to enter an arranged marriage; Keila Whelan, a girl I suspect we will hear more of, was Hodel, who falls for the radical Perchik and Aisling Reid, a fine young actress, made an excellent feisty Chava, the girl who turns Tevye's world upside down. Their three suitors were played by young men rich in dramatic and musical talent. Colin Flynn was a suitably timid Motel, the tailor in love with Tzeitel; Sean Keany with his fine voice was the Kiev student Perchik while Gavin Ryan was a courteous Fyedka, the Russian who steals Chava's heart with his love of literature.

Monica Hannigan created a self- obsessed Yente, the village matchmaker; Justin Parkes weighed in with a Constable with a bit of an edge while Gerry Hannigan caught the eye in the small role of Mordcha the innkeeper.

The older hands added experience to an ensemble that contained a high proportion of young adults. If they stick together it will be interesting to see just what they can achieve.

This young group is clearly not lacking in ambition. Apart from being one of the newest members of AIMS, the Society is reviving a tradition in the south east's most famous seaside town.

The company was formed in late 2012 and has a couple of Christmas pantomimes under its belt, staged in a school hall in Tramore.

However, for its first venture into musical theatre the group decided to de-camp and move into the Garter Lane arts centre, close to the river front in nearby Waterford.

They also chose the daunting task of staging the rock opera Rent, the late Jonathan Larson's best known work. At the moment the group is almost self-contained. Musical director Izzy Carr and Co-directors John Power and Stephen Carr were not just on stage but also played key roles in the show. Izzy and Stephen also took on board the task of choreographing the show. Therein lies part of the problem. It's hard enough for a principal to worry about his or her role without taking on the task of worrying about what everyone else in the cast is doing. While the group has some talent it would be better if the production team or part of it removed itself from the stage to concentrate on bringing out the best in the others.

Mr Power, who played videographer Mark Cohen here, is a capable actor and had a good baritone voice, Stephen Carr, anarchist technology boffin Tom Collins in this production, had probably the best voice on display while Izzy Carr, cast here as junkie club dancer Mimi Marquez, can sing, act and dance.

Dominic Kenneally as Roger has the makings of a rock voice; Chloe Quilty was a fine Angel Schunard, although it's the first time I've seen a girl in the role, Ross Kavanagh as millionaire property developer Benny Coffin was confident around the stage while Lydia McGovern in her principal debut did well with the tricky role of Joanne Jefferson.

Some of the more experienced members of the small ensemble touched in the roles of the parents and television agent Alexi Darling.

However, none of the performances had the intensity or the power of Christine Poole's Maureen Johnston, the self-obsessed bi-sexual actress. Ms Poole made an entrance with Over the Moon as the first half neared its end and continued to operate at high octane until the final bows.

And while the chorus sounded well when all together as in Seasons of Love, led by Jenny Hogan, probably the most experienced musical theatre hand on stage, at other times the action was a little uneven.

Kevin Kennedy's small band, housed under a balcony of Scenemaker's space-saving set, helped power along the action.

If, like me, you are of a certain age, the words Waterford and musical naturally go together.

For anyone over the age of 50 the southern city was often regarded as the Mecca of musical theatre on the island.

It was largely due to the much missed Waterford International Festival of Light Opera but the city also had thriving musical societies in their own right.

You won't be surprised then that one of the many joys of the 2014/15 Sullivan season was my opportunity to welcome the newly-formed Waterford Musical Society to the AIMS fold. Naturally, for a place with musical theatre coursing through its veins, the new company was not only welcomed by the locals but backed to the hilt. A Theatre Royal packed to the rafters laughed along, swayed along and sang along as the new society with members aged from five-years-old up to one 80-year-old, delivered a classy version of Rodgers and Hammerstein's Carousel from director David Hennessy.

While a working fairground carousel constructed from folding metal bars provided the full house with an early quirky moment the old Festival audience loved to applaud, this show settled into a rhythm that promises much for the future of musical theatre in the city.

Solid performances from Derek McGrath, a man who hadn't been on stage for 20 years, as Billy Bigelow, and bright-voiced soprano Joanne McCabe as Julie Jordan set the tone for the show.

Olga Greene and Bill Stafford as Mrs Mullin and Jigger Craigin respectively left their individual marks on two less than empathetic characters while Lupita DeBhail Sheehan revelled in the big songs given to Nettie Fowler.

The new company made a real find in the Carrie Pipperidge of Avril Hartrey while her stage husband Ray Collins was terrific as the moralistic and social climbing Enoch Snow.

Old hand, Des Manahan, gave the audience a glimpse of what they had been missing with a beautifully gauged turn in the dual role of the Starkeeper and Dr Seldon, a little masterclass in unhurried characterisation.

It is fitting that 80-year-old Mr Manahan with his long association with Waterford, has agreed to become the patron of the south eastern city's new Society.

At the other end of the age spectrum teenagers Phoebe Dipple and Nathan Carey as Louise Bigelow and Enoch Snow Junior turned in confident performances while Dee Lanigan was a clear-voiced factory owner David Bascombe.

Above all though, it was the delivery of the music of this old standard that lifted the heart at the end of a long season. Musical director Wayne Brown did a sterling job in guiding singers old and new and then backing their work with a rich sounding orchestra in the fabulous surrounds of the Theatre Royal.

Director Kerry Kane's big innovation here resolved one problem but may have inadvertently caused another. Ms Kane split the role of Evita between two actresses with the young Eva taking to the stage at the start and not relinquishing the part until her thirst for fame and fortune had seen her acquire a reputation - and several lovers - in Buenos Aires, halfway through Act One.

Donelle Reynolds, a girl who can sing, act and move well, played the younger Evita on the night of my visit to Coleraine's Riverside Theatre on the town's university campus.

It meant that the make-up team didn't have to worry about ageing the lead character at a crucial tie in the show or changing another wig.

However, with Fiona Flynn, who played the role for the rest of the night never becoming the force of nature this character should quickly become, it may have upset the natural rhythm of the show with Evita not getting the lead in time she needs.

I felt that the other big figure in this show, Adam Goudy as Che, didn't impose himself on the show enough either. While Mr Goudy has the vocal equipment for the role, he didn't really pull off the difficult of act of being both narrator and player.

It all meant that while the production had pace and flow aplenty - it was only 135 minutes from the moment the band struck up its first note to the end of the night, including the interval - the show stayed pretty much on one level throughout the night.

Harry Coates was contemplative as Peron rather than scheming, lacking the aura of menace that should surround this huge figure of Argentinian political life.

Anna Warke, as Peron's mistress, displayed a lovely voice and an ability to convey the dashed hopes of a young girl who realises her ambitions have been thwarted by an older, more ruthless rival.

Like Ms Reynolds she is capable of taking on bigger roles with the society in the future.

Andy Shaw was a confident Magaldi, taking control of the scenes he was involved in.

And another young performer, Rachel Wilkinson, still at primary school, showed of a lovely voice as she embodied the children of Argentina in Act Two.

Anthony Ennis - a man who played two men and a woman in this production if you follow me - is the kind of guy W S Gilbert would have loved.

Mr Ennis is one of those baritone showmen who would make a fine Major General in the Pirates of Penzance or Sir Joseph Porter in HMS Pinafore. He has the bearing, stage authority and I suspect the patter to pull it off.

He was one half of a comic double act here in the rarely performed Jule Styne, Peter Stone and Bob Merrill re- working of Billy Wilder's famous film. His partner in crime, Karl Hoffman, a fine actor and singer with a lovely baritone voice, can always fall back on a career as a drag artist should he have too. I hope he forgives me when I say that, as a woman, he is almost attractive.

The two romped their way through this tale of luckless musicians who witness a Chicago gangland hit and spend the rest of the time evading the gangsters by hiding out in an-all female band making their way to a residency in far- off Miami.

Director Paul Fay brought a lovely light touch to proceedings with choreographer Catherine McCourt delivering some inventive routines, including one excellent prolonged tap sequence.

Nicola Pollard, in the title role complete with a dazzling blonde bombshell wig, provided the real glamour here as the Broadway babe with a drink problem. Kathryn Gibbons was the hard-nosed band leader heading up the girls' ensemble, the inappropriately named Sweet Sue. Like Ms Pollard she displayed a fine soprano singing voice. The bulk of the band-leader's anger was directed at the put upon Bienstock, a neat interpretation by Mark Smith of the cowed administrative assistant. James O'Keefe, when his overcoat wasn't draped over his shoulders, was so light on his feet he gave the impression of running everywhere as Chicago hard man Spats Palazzo. And the Sir Oscar Fielding of Pat Forde brought us a tenor voice that was evocative of another, earlier era in musical theatre.

Musical director Dave McGauran's fine band drove the action on relentlessly, although a little too loud in places for my liking.

The well-dressed action on the St Mary's school stage took place on a clever set designed by the aforementioned Mr O'Keefe.

A fun show for Avonmore M.S. to present this year which was a great hit with the audience. It has much for principals and chorus alike and they appeared to revel in its madness and crazy plot. Great sound from the orchestra which gave us a sophisticated tone to this nightmare in Eastwick. Tempi could have been picked up in certain numbers which did slow things. The conductor, Mairead McKenna I felt needed to support the cast on stage more in numbers such as 'Waiting for the Music' and 'Words, Words, Words'. 'Dirty Laundry' needed to be more tidy especially the ending. Nicely drawn out instruments like the harpsichord in 'Waiting for the Music' but the cello sound was no substitute by the keyboards. A complex piece, there was a good accurate collective reading of this score with a good balance had between pit and stage. The chorus was tutored by Mairead McKenna also; where there was a little uncertainty in the odd number. The SATB arrangement was not balanced with more ladies to men and so the vocal equilibrium was not great. More control with legato singing in the opening number would have been nice. More variations with positioning on stage would have helped the chorus a lot, especially in the opening number to introduce the community. Good reactions for Darryl's entrance and also good big reactions in the church scene. They all moved well but the boys' routine was calmed down in 'Dance with the Devil. 'Paul Laycock as Darryl Van Horne looked great as the devil with a certain confidence. He needed to free himself more and really go into the role for the character to really come alive. Much was measured which killed the spontaneity and cheekiness of this role. Much more twinkle in the eye was needed to hook these women into his lair. Always remember, you control what happens on stage in this production. Jennifer Lee as Alexandra Spofford has a lovely rich, mezzo timbre to the voice which was always well projected, but there were gear changes to it and not always progressed easily up the through the voice. Great understanding to text and worked very well with the other two witches. Naoimh Penston as Jane Smart was the driving force of the three. Total understanding of her character with excellent diction, there were moments when dialogue was too fast. Needed to give us a slightly more peeved and fed up rendition to the beginning of her number 'Waiting for the Music'. Denise Brennan playing Sukie Rougemount completed this ensemble playing trio with another different character to the other two. Shyer at first, this soon changed. Starting off 'Word Words, Words' needed to be more demure and then building up to the confident Sukie. The allegro section was a bit too fast which jeopardised the text. Elaine Sweeney soft interpretation needed more ferocity as Felicia Gabriel and needed to be a force to be reckoned with. It is a big character which needed broad strokes. Michael Pluck as Michael Spofford required more freedom and sense of being in love with Jennifer. It came over as rather solid and restrictive. Jennifer Gabriel played by Alison Coyne was also capable of more. It seemed that you were stifled, inhibiting your natural flair for comedy. Dialogue was well projected and believable. Tuning problems with this Little Girl played by Fiona Walker. She was by no means a little girl and this baffled me. Rob Donnelly as Clyde brought out the downtrodden husband with clarity -projecting lines well. Not a huge deal was made with this character and I would have liked to have seen him grow more in this production. The difficult aspect of this show is whether or not the characters live and are they animated enough? This is where this production could have gone further. They need also to be given a certain freedom for them to risk things and also to improve the flow of the production. Dialogue needed to be pushed more with more emphasis on projection and keep an eye to actual formations on stage that they are interesting. Martina Lynch as Choreographer developed some good routines throughout this show involving the whole company. There was a good response to the music and also gave a flavour of the period as well. 'Dance with the Devil' worked well for the girls but was tamed down for the boys. A composite set with a large projection screen USC worked a treat for this venue. Barry Ryan worked his magic as stage manager to create efficient and effective scene changes which ultimately helped with the run of the production. Props were looked after correctly by Karen Kavanagh and team. A pity about the large green sofa which was too modern for Alex's house. Loved the cello playing on its own and the 'Booby Dolls' were well made and plenty of them. Projections were well chosen but I did miss the 'Stepford' feel to the housing developments. They were fairly modern and shoe-horned us into a modern interpretation of 1950's. The fire and windows all looked great. Sound by Jody Trehy created a clean balance between stage and pit but there were some needless cue errors which should not have happened. The sound was forward and clear with a natural tone to the show. Lighting by Padraig Reid created some lovely atmospheres by using a good palette of colour which complemented the set and costumes very well. Small details like a faster black out was required at the end on 'I am Eastwick' which would have punctuated the end of the scene nicely. Good attention not to drain the projections most of the time from colour. Little more separation of split stage would have helped; for instance in the last scene. It looked as if the three witches were actually in the church. Costumes were well brought together by Els Penston who has a great eye for detail and period. The 'A' line skirts needed underskirts to give the kick and principals in general were well catered for. Darryl, however, needed a red cravat towards the end of Act one (I think the one he wore was burgundy) and his shorts for the tennis scene needed also to be - perhaps red and not blue. Keep an eye on the nude shoes. They are not suitable for just every costume. Hair and Make-up by Sharon Kavanagh did a great job in trying to keep everyone within the period with many styles of the era in evidence. Men too were looked after with side partings. All in order. Thank you for your kindness and your hospitality during my stay with you and as I always say, the devil is in the detail. With every best wish,

A pleasant drive cross country to Gorey brought me to the Little Theatre with still a stretch in the evening. This would be my first Gilbert and Sullivan in 44 shows and I was really looking forward to it. The nicely appointed Little Theatre filled to about half full and at eight bells we were off. Lar Duffy struck up the familiar opening chords. With his nine piece orchestra there was a nice balanced sound. He showed care for the singers in general but there were some late pick up of cues - as in for Ruth's 'When Frederic was a little Lad'. 'Now, for the Pirates lair' where more attack could have been given to the double chords at the end of each phrase.

More style and attention to musical accuracy vocally was needed. Trumpets a little wayward in 'O men of dark and dismal fate' with no observance to many dynamics in 'Hail Poetry'. Lar Duffy has a contained style of conducting but everyone knows what he wants.

Trained by the same person, the chorus was very unbalanced with gaps in the SATB divisions. The overall sound was weak and never bloomed in the big ensembles with more attention and attack to the lyrics required. As a unit, it lacked vocal heft and thus the loss of some thrilling moments in this well know operetta.

David Cox as The Pirate King had all the alertness and swagger for this great show-off role; projecting well his dialogue and lyrics. His sidekick Samuel, played by Danny Cooper needed to focus in on the conductor more. An approximate performance with unsteady musical cues and a slight memory lapse for 'Here's your crowbar' section.

Gary Stephens as Frederic was sincere and also played up the role. Why did Frederic have a Northern Ireland accent? He was agile on stage and worked well with his Mabel. Bridin Higgins O'Keefe as Ruth needed much more energy and truthfulness in her delivery of dialogue. A nice Mezzo voice, it was unsteady at the start of the three verses in her Act one number. Little was done with any conviction and I am afraid you looked bored which translated across the forth wall. Mabel - A different interpretation that lost the winsome and Victorian bloom of the English rose. More leader of the pack sort of portrayal, knowing what she wanted and got. Yvette Walsh had all the notes but with a heavier timbre than the usual coloratura. Needs more investment in the lyrics - this would help enormously. 'Sorry her lot' was most convincing with thoughtful lyrics portrayed. All three girls, Clodagh Leacy, Karen Dunbar and Fauve Byrne as Edith, Kate and Isabel showed off their personalities and charms. They needed a stronger hand with direction and their characters needed further delineation. Kate's vocal line was transposed due to the vocal height of the role with alternative endings to some sections.

The Major General played by Malcolm Byrne has a lovely baritone voice but again was under directed in this peach of a role. No attempt was made to age him and he should have had a wig. Good precise dialogue which was clear and well focused. Playing off the line would also have helped the continuity of the character more. Sean Hallahan as Sergeant of the Police was not a Bass - which is required for this role. Once again, this was learnt 'approximately' with little flexibility in the performance. Lines lapsed on several occasions.

Chorus was under directed all evening with more interaction necessary to make scenes come alive. Girls slow entrance for 'Climbing over rocky mountains' did not match the energy of the music. Throughout, more time was required for drilling.

Director Imelda McDonagh went outside the box with a new idea for this production, and whilst there was a germ of an idea, I felt it needed a longer gestation time for it to mature. We lost the essence of this thrilling score with more investment into the dialogue and lyric required. Characters needed to be broadened out all round and blocking made more interesting. More energy needed to be instilled into most areas of the production. Choreographer, Frances Ryan tipped at the iceberg with many missed opportunities. Routines were kept simple and did not challenge with little response to the music.

Paul Doran as Stage Manager managed a clean slate for this production with efficient cueing of cast. Liz Bush paid much attention to swords and pistols. Again all in order here. Set Design by Imelda McDonagh worked a treat and gave important levels for the company to play. Good elevation of the company and easily configured into the Act 2 ruined churchyard. Great detail in the painting of the set which was able to take light easily. Sound by I-Tech Productions provided a good tone for voices to naturally come through. A good balance was maintained between stage and pit all evening. Mark Redmond provided some lovely lighting states with good use of gobos. Some lovely broken beams coming from USL in Act 2 created a lovely atmosphere but it wasn't dark enough for Act 2.

This was not your traditional set of costumes. Looked after by Mary Spellman and team, it was audacious and nearly took off but for the choice of colours and the very mixed accessories added to create this look. It was Moulin Rough meets The Land of the Vampire. Attention to detail was missed in several areas which included footwear, men's socks, and the governesses which looked out of place in this scenario. Mabel should have stood out more from the others and her boots needed a major rethink. Some nice ideas permeated this costume plot; was rather less than the sum of its parts.

Make-Up - Good work here with a good differentiation between day and going into the evening/night scene. Linda Collier and her team were busy as there was some detailed work with the hairstyles. The Major General needed a wig and the men's modern styles needed taming down Gorey certainly put the NEW in this Pirates of Penzance. I just wish it had gone further.

One of my favourite theatres in both Ireland and England, it is like going home. The expectations were palpable with this production of Sister Act; sold out for over ten weeks before it opened at the Grand Opera House.

A terrific sound was established in the pit from the first note of the overture. A big sound with sixteen in the pit drove the music forward filling the auditorium with energy and pace. Conductor Colin Scott certainly knows how to put an orchestra together, but, as I have said before, this is no ordinary set of orchestrations - it is a beast. The sheer volume was huge and created a blanket of sound over the audience despite having a cover over the pit itself. The playing from the orchestra was top notch all evening with a terrific ensemble sound achieved. Fine brass playing dominated with some funky sounds added into the beginning of Act 2 to give a nod to the period of the '80's.

Chorus master Colin Scott had the chorus well drilled musically for this high octane show with a good balance achieved among the voices. Not a great show for the men's chorus. The ladies sang and moved to great effect throughout the evening.

Most of the roles well cast with a strong and able Mother Superior from Laura Kerr tirelessly working off the line with facial and well thought through, pensive replies. The pensive replies did however at times become a little too ponderous and could have moved scenes along. However, a great investment in words and lyrics with a beautiful take on 'Haven't got a prayer' which was like a nun's Gethsemane, well-paced with great feeling.

Nuala Mannion as Mary Roberts vocally had the range with great care to punctuations and clarity in dialogue and lyrics. Suitably shy, her journey was easy to follow as she spread her wings and gave us an excellent 'The Life I never Led' - with an excellent sustained last note showing good technique and beauty of tone. Mary Patrick performed by Shirley Adair, the happy nun, was certainly happy but her performance needed to be bigger in this company of girls. Needed to relish the words more and let go even further in the up tempi moments. Heather McCloskey as Mary Martin gave us a lovely secondary role clear dialogue and settled in amongst her 'community' very well.

Colin Boyd as the Monsignor needed to inject more humour and energy into the character. Dialogue was a little stilted in Act 1 but came alive in Act 2 when the 'beat' got to him. Great ad libs to the balconies were very appropriate. Accent drifted from scene to scene!

Curtis performed by Joff Manning processed a good accent but too much anger dominated this character which didn't reveal the other threatening aspects to this role. Needs to be aware of pitch and tuning in 'When I find my baby'. Also, the music was a little too approximate. Samuel Moore as Eddie has a natural delivery with an easy way on stage. A lovely mover with a very suitable voice, well within his range for his solo. A pity he didn't have any sweat on his costumes.

Vijay Sharma was called at a late stage to perform T.J. He fitted into the production like a glove shaping up as good as the rest. A lovely mover with a clear and direct voice, he projected dialogue and lyrics cleanly. Slipping into the falsetto was no problem for him.

Martin Bannon as Joey and Mark Leeman as Pablo both worked well and looked great in their 'zoot 'suits. Both well styled and both vocally well able for the 'Lady in the long black dress'. The latter had a good Spanish accent which he threw away with aplomb. The chorus worked tirelessly all evening - most especially the ladies. The energy levels were ignited from the overture and continued right through to the end of the show. They were always well drilled in creative and fresh routines.

I have left Deloris till last, played by Jean Michelo. It was great to see a black actress take on this role but I think the production team didn't do themselves nor Miss Michelo any favours as this actress was very much out of her depth in this role. There were tuning and rhythmical problems dotted throughout the performance, with considerable problems to the vocal range. A dangerous game to play with someone's vocal instrument. Dialogue seemed imposed with strange inflections and intonation patterns that did not seem natural. Lateness into several scenes was an issue also. You can forgive once; but this happened several times with cast trying to ad lib through the non-appearance.

Director, Wilfie Pyper presented a slick show which looked well on the Opera House stage. Good energy came across for the most part but some scenes with the Mother Superior and Monsignor could have been moved on. Characters were well drawn, apart from Eddie falling off a few tables which, for me, didn't work. Lovely work with the nun's bedroom scene and also the bar scene. More attention to the sound issues and the issue regarding the leading lady should have been tackled. Timmy Bell as choreographer devised a myriad of fresh routines and did as much as he could do, given ladies wearing habits. He created movement with energy and with some lovely formations about the stage which the company responded to easily. More creativity was required for 'Lady in the long black dress' - a lot of this number I had seen before!

Stage Manager Patrick Freeman marshalled his crew well with efficient scene changes and some nice cuing of flies. Getting into Eddie's office was a little slow in establishing itself. Good masking all around and each scene looked clean and well placed.

Valerie Greenlee looked after props meticulously. Everything here was well in order. A great set from UK Productions dressed this beautiful stage and sat well within the pros arch. Vaulted and filled with stain glass windows with piped organ peeking down from the borders, it looked handsome.

Sound designed by Jody Trehy and Jason Fallon needed more balance between the pit and stage with a re-balance of the orchestra as the decibels were pretty mighty. There was no problem with the actual quality of the sound as tone was nicely judged and cuing was also of a high order. Lighting by Alastair Kerr was professional and with a great eye to the colour palette for this set and costumes. Some beautiful states were achieved especially the use of the congo blues, red and greens for 'Here within these walls'.

Costumes were looked after by Margaret Mehaffey and her team. Men looked great in the 70's styled 'zoot suits' and the nuns constantly changing - to their white and silver habits at the end. Good nightwear for the nuns - mostly all individual, but be careful; the Pope would not wear a mitre at the end - it would be a white skull cap.

Hair and makeup was well attended to with good attention to the men with styles and colouring. Great front of house which attended to my guest and me in a courteous and welcoming manner. Thank you Anne.

With the weather on the alleged spring night I caught this show rapidly swelling the nearby Royal Canal, the SS American could easily have floated down School Street and sailed off to Dublin port.

As I raced into St Joseph's Hall to escape the pre-show downpour, the fabric of the building was being tested to the limit with buckets strategically placed around to catch the drips coming through the roof.

On top of that, the technicians on duty had both lost considerable amounts of equipment in the fire that had swept through the Dublin warehouse they shared a few days earlier.

Thankfully Philippa Alford's treatment of Cole Porter's frothy comedy was the perfect antidote to all the doom and gloom. Ms Alford with the aid of a good cast brought a bit of sunshine back into people's lives for a few hours. Louise Cassidy as the nightclub singer turned evangelist Reno Sweeney was a powerhouse. She loaned her character a big voice and a big presence in a performance that generated enough wattage to power an ocean going liner. Stephen Ryan's Billy Crocker was an American smoothie, gliding his way through the various obstacles and barriers placed in his way of the pursuit of socialite Hope Harcourt, displaying a voice that was easy on the ear and moves that were easy on the eye. The object of his affection was played by Naomi Cleary, a big voiced soprano with more than a hint of a Broadway belt at times.

Andrew Docherty as the blustering gangster Moonface Martin attacked the role from the moment he walked onto the stage until the curtain finally came down.

Broadway broad Erma, his partner in crime, was given pretty much the same treatment by Lorraine Murphy who sang, danced and pouted her way through the evening.

With Bert Carruthers as Crocker's short-sighted boss also chasing Aine Grace's Evangeline Harcourt on the high seas, this production moved along at a rate of knots any liner captain would be proud of.

Wearing a different hat Ms Alford had designed the set, wisely deciding to build upwards rather than outwards, thus freeing up space for the company to execute Deirdre Brown's energetic dance routines while simultaneously creating two new playing areas with a balcony and the access steps to it. The technical teams also provided terrific support for the production in spite of the turmoil they were going through

This is one of the most difficult jobs I have faced in my time in the Sullivan hot seat because of the personnel involved.

I don't have a direct connection with Lisnagarvey Operatic although I know many of the figures who have guided it down the years.

However, I have to declare an interest when it comes to the show's production team. The director, Wilfie Pyper, is an old friend and we have worked with and for each other in the past; musical director Ian Milford and I have been known to share a stage and choreographer Claire Donnelly is not exactly a stranger either.

This was a modern Superstar for a modern audience. The old line about Israel in 4BC having no mass communication was rendered irrelevant in Mr Pyper's production with many of the characters on stage having an email address courtesy of Gary Redpath's projections which were often used as a narrative device to push on the story.

"Just saw Jesus losing it at the Temple" was one of the messages flashed up to the big house at Lisburn's Island Hall as Adam Williamson's Christ lost his temper with the Jerusalem traders. This was a powerful performance from Mr Williamson straddling the line between man and God, summed up in a beautifully gauged "Gethsemane" and later delivering the very real agonies of someone being put to death.

Sean Harkin was a big-voiced troubled Judas, Jamie Ewing was a classy Pilate, calculating but almost sympathetic while Simon Pyper as Herod was highly energetic but strong and dominant and not remotely camp. Orla McCormack lent Mary Magdalene a lovely soprano, Colin Gregg's Caiaphas was an Empire builder while Andy Scott's Annas was suitably repellent.

Mr Scott, like Noel Marsden as Simon and the aforementioned Mr Redpath as Peter all displayed fine singing voices. Unsurprisingly as a result the men's chorus was the best 'Garvey have fielded in a couple of decades. The pace here was turbo-powered with both acts coming in at 50 minutes and yet the production did not feel rushed. It was played out on a minimalist setting with towers constructed from scaffolding and accessed by steps from the stage floor. Platforms at the top of the towers stage left and right reached into the centre stage area but did not meet allowing Mr Redpath's projections to suggest the locations in the story.

While Jesus was dressed in his traditional white tabard and trousers and the ensemble in outfits that could be construed as either modern or traditional, much of the rest of the plot was decidedly modern.

Pilate was in a lounge suit and a dress suit, both with open neck shirts, Herod was in a Sci-Fi black leather number and the Roman guards were incredibly well equipped to deal with street disturbances involving the Jewish mob, being kitted out from head to toe in authentic RUC riot squad gear in flame-proof Kevlar.

show_raw: The Best Little Whorehouse In Texas
review_text: A wet blizzardy night escorted me to the Millennium Form in Londonderry to attend a performance of 'Best Little Whorehouse in Texas'. A large comfortable 'A' house with a large stage and auditorium. Peter Doherty conducted this fun score with the right feel and nuances. He drew a nice balance from the musicians giving us a lovely flavour of Southern sound with good attention to dynamics. More care should have been taken with choral contribution with some trimming done to 'The Sidestep' which unusually went on at great length. Chorus, also tutored by Peter Doherty needed more time in the rehearsal room as certain numbers were weak and not musically strong. An imbalance with the SATB didn't help as we rarely got a balanced ensemble due to more ladies than men. Men had tuning problems with cut offs a little raggy and not together. This was evident in 'Good old Girl'. A great sound from the orchestra including the Hawaiian guitar added colour and livened up the texture of the sound palette. Solo instruments coming nicely through like the violin in 'Texas, has a Whorehouse in it'. The overall sound, however, was a little over blown due to the insensitivity of the audio system. Too many decibels which competed with the cast on stage. Kris Doherty performed the Bandleader in a confident and easy manner. He really loves the stage and sported a really 'fine' Southern accent. Muire McCallion as Miss Mona gave a more grounded performance - gritty and matter-a-fact.  Accent wasn't quite located properly with well projected dialogue with a well-focused, forward sound. Lyrics could have been a little clearer at times and she tended to go off the note in 'Girl, You're a Woman'. A little let down by the production team, you were left to walk a little bit aimlessly throughout.  Rory Mullan as Sheriff Ed Earl tended to shout all evening which became quite unrelenting. There is not a problem with his projection of dialogue. This actor should also keep his head up as he has a tendency to look at the floor. A lovely baritone voice with which he shaped 'Good Old Girl' very well. I didn't feel the embers of the relationship with Miss Mona between these two actors which is an intrinsic part of this show. Simon Quigg as Melvin P. Thorpe created an effeminate interpretation of this lovely comedic role. The director is partially responsible for allowing him to go so far. There were slow pick-up of lines from Ed Earl and much was played to the audience. Enough said. Rebecca Morgan as Angel developed a confident and well-articulated character with a fine accent. She understands dialogue very well and vocally has a fine vibrant voice which came through in 'Hard Candy Christmas'.  Johanna Johnston as Shy could have been more styled as a Hickesville gal. The white boots didn't work as we have to travel a great journey with this character through the show. Good comedic skills with a natural way in using dialogue. A little too pretty and made-up for the first scene. Penny McGonagle looked great as Jewel with a clear voice that rocked 'Twenty Four Hours of Lovin'. She was a little isolated and not integrated very well into the number. Katie Patton as Doatsey Mae, I felt, took the wrong end of this character. Instead of being a bit tired of life and is thinking "is that all it's got to offer", this actress was quite bright and bubbly. It's another interpretation which she played well but it doesn't really give her emotional response for when she sings her number. No problems with her vocal delivery, fully in range and perhaps, a little over sung. Lack of energy dogged Greg Doherty performing Senator Wingwood most of the evening; which was emphasised in the pre Aggies number. Dialogue was underpowered and not projected. Gerald McQuilken looked suitably dull as Rufus Poindexter with his wide trousers and his great looking glasses. He had a good hold of his lines but at times the Café scene was a bit slow. Kieran Conor created a lovely cameo role as C.J.  Scruggs with attention to accent and well projected lines. Maybe your lines should have been directed more to Ed Earl as you were having a conversation with him. Chorus worked hard all evening and certainly got into the 'rhythm' of things in the opening scene. Perhaps a bit risqué - I'll let the audience decide. Vocally, the chorus needed a firmer hand to get more dynamics and vocal discipline. Girls nudged well in front for in-tune singing but the men had some difficulties with tuning. The SATB was not even - in favour of the ladies so the balance was not there. Movement on stage was very erratic where more drilling was needed to clean up routines. However, there was good precision with the Angelettes but I missed the pom-poms. Deigh Reid directed and the production moved along at a good pace. Good delineation of characters but more attention to accent work and creativity in some numbers needed tending to. Dialogue had good pace and some flare with different things tried - some worked, some didn't. A closer eye to Wardrobe was also required and to the lighting - to try and create more closed down lighting states to focus more on the drama of the piece. Venessa Chapman was choreographer who worked the company hard. Some numbers did lack a certain creativity - Aggies Number for example. Overall, it should have allowed the company to shine but the routines needed more rehearsal. Precision of moves must be insisted upon especially when performing in such a venue. It is the least we can expect. Moves in 'The Sidestep' were a bit repetitive. Stage Management, in the hands of Christine Deane, made sure that most scene changes were done as efficiently as possible. There was just one delay - striking the table and flying out the wall from Act 2 - Ed Earls Office. All in all, very much in order. Props were disappointing in this show with a miss match of furniture everywhere, not suitable for Miss Mona's. Loved the leather office chair for Ed Earl. Set design by Deigh Reid was a composite structure that worked well for the ranch. The upper section was a little underused but it was quite impressive. Unfortunately, the set didn't "do anything" and became limiting for the other scenes. Sound - by 'No Name' was pretty disgraceful all evening with bad cuing and fluffing intermittent all evening. The sound levels were at times very uncomfortable with no sense of balance on or off stage. Mics were also left on back stage and voices became distorted owing to the high levels of the sound. Lighting by Martin McDonald had some nice creative touches with the spinning gobos acting as fans. Be careful that there is enough key light especially on upper levels. Costumes by Elayne McNicholl brought together some very appropriate attire. Some great individual looks with Angel at the beginning, Jewel, the Governor. A better wardrobe was needed for Miss Mona all evening as it wasn't elegant enough. On the whole, a good job done. No credit in the programme for Make-up and hair which seemed well in order. Work had been done to get the 1970's feel to this show through hair styles. A lovely welcome to this theatre was afforded me by a number of the committee members who looked after me royally. It was wonderful to catch up with so many old friends. Thank you for your lovely hospitality. Wishing you every best with you future productions.

A lively and energetic production for my last review for AIMS as the Gilbert Adjudicator. A very fine response to this score by Wilson Shields who assembled a big band sound. Great tempi taken for each number with the brass section relishing the 'big blow' required for this score to come alive. Sometimes a little loud for the underscoring but in general lyrics were allowed to come through.

No name given for chorus master but this was a well-trained chorus with attention to tone and expression of lyrics. A very strong SATB balance was delivered with some ballsy articulation and forward projection. Great harmonies were learnt and came across very well despite the decibel level of the sound. The addition of the Belfast Community Gospel Choir was an excellent idea which powered up the 'I know where I've been' number to a stirring level. A great level of commitment was given all evening with vibrant and well drilled dance routines which were at times complex in their design. They showed precision and flair throughout.

Principals were well cast throughout - an energetic and articulate performance of the lead role, Tracy. A bright and infectious performance ran through this interpretation with clear dialogue and vocals generally well within her range. Slightly weak in the lower register it really didn't hamper the vocals.

Glen Branney as Corney Collins gave us an all American, cool cut TV presenter. Dressed immaculately with two tone shoes he really looked the business. Velma Van Tussle performed by Fiona Keegan brought experience and depth to this role emphasising the racist element to this production. She is forthright and full of attitude and takes no prisoners. Diction always clear with more than a hint of Dixieland coming through in the accent. Dialogue was animated and I loved the line 'Miss. Tracey Tugboat'. Vocally, well capable of singing this role with a 'broad' sound to the voice, investing with all lyrics in 'Baltimore Crabs'.

Corrie Earley as Amber Von Tussle was a chip off the old block in terms of morals and imperfections. A fine personality who projected her dialogue clearly with accent. The sound design added problems which over distorted the voice making it shrill and very uncomfortable. She was vocally well able for this role.

Penny Pingleton, performed by Jenney Coates gave us a vivacious and energised performance that was always charming and hot on the heels of Tracey. Excellent in 'Mama, I'm a big girl now'. She constantly works off the line and never slipped out of character. Her wigs were a disaster all evening but her dowdy costume represented well her mother's ideals on life. Tony Young as Edna was a fine transformation always working on stage with great diction and tongue in cheek delivery, yet sympathetic and meaningful. Great body language and fine attention to dialogue and lyrics made this character all the more believable. He was well able to move with a lovely duet with Wilbur 'Timeless to Me'. A really fine performance. Michael McDowell as Edna's husband Wilbur brought his own energy and pizazz to his performance. There is a dangerous twinkle in his eye which, if I was Edna, I'd give a wide berth to. Fine dialogue, well projected with a tendency to sing, at times, under the note. Good comedic skills at play here also.

Andrew Keeney as Seaweed had a great funky and cool look with his braces and red socks. Another agile and flexible performer, great ease on stage with a natural delivery of dialogue. Some projection problems here and there which also occurred with the lyrics. The vocals all within range with some pitch problems which were evident in 'Without Love'. The matinee idol, Link, being groomed for stardom looked great in his costume, slick hair-do and very cool attitude. Great posture for the rock star - a very good voice which projected easily. Good bite to the lyrics and nice agility in his performance Motormouth played by Marlene Hill was a tour de force. Great big performance with a great stage presence. Natural flare for this score with great rhythm and style. A clear, clean sound with great attention to the lyrics. An even voice the whole way through her range. Little Inez was played by Ellie Reynolds - quite an amazing performance for such a young age - I think maybe eight years old! With natural flair for the stage, she never faltered in dialogue or singing giving an extraordinary performance many adults would be proud of. This is really a child star. The production was in the hands of Kieran Griffiths who presented a well finished production which ran smoothly with some clever ideas thrown in for great effect. The use of the two camera's on stage and projecting them onto a central screen worked terrifically well in the TV studios. Good attention to character work and accents. He got the differences between the blacks and whites which was also reflected into the choreography.

Rebecca Leonard created the choreography. She has an innate ability to get to the music and feel of a score. It was fast moving, creative and used her cast to the maximum. Everyone was well integrated into the production especially the big ensembles which took the roof off the house. Scene changes were well looked after by Clare Donnelly. Cueing was very efficient and well timed. Changes were mostly done by cast members who forgot to bring a TV on DSL at one point. Props by Maeve Gillen were generally well chosen. Pity the audience had to see the smashed up front of the TV set coming in from DSR.

Scenic Projects, UK provided the set and although it generally looked well it appeared as if it was scaled up for this stage. The two flats US were ill fitting and too short for the height of this stage.

Sound was an issue all evening mainly trying to get a balance with this large sounding orchestra and the cast. The vocal sound was so high at times that the voices became distorted and shrill. Cuing problems persisted also with a number of mics not on for lines.

Alastair Kerr brought some more atmosphere and mood to this show again with a varied palette of colours. Well timed cues worked well. A few key light issues but nothing major. Some of the cues were striking in their simplicity like Tracy in the prison cell on her own.

A beautiful set of costumes was assembled for this production by Maeve McLoughlin. Care was taken with the 60's look and the age profile of the character wearing the costumes. Boys looking smart and dapper with great hair-cuts and the ladies always fresh with good attention to footwear all evening. All in good order here. Make-up and hair by Dawn Sutton achieved the right look for this show except for the wigs for Penny and the striped disaster that just sat on Tracy's head. The last principal wigs did not really work either. Make-up was all in order.

A lovely welcome Greg Flood who then left us in the more than capable hands of Emma Lundy who looked after me and my guest extremely well before the show and during the interval. Thank you for your kindness.

begins we welcome two new adjudicators, Peter Kennedy and Greg Currid and wish them well in their travels. In keeping with the rules of the adjucication scheme they will not be going backstage to meet the cast but may wish to see particular technical aspects of the stage facilities.

By way of introduction here are some biographical details.

A Friday evening visit to the Helix Theatre to The Phantom of the Opera. Another youth company taking advantage of performing rights to put on Andrew Lloyd Webbers masterpiece. The orchestra produced a most wonderful musical sound throughout the whole performance. Only on the odd occasion did the 6 brass instruments stray from the conductors control to let loose. I must also compliment the percussionist who from my vantage point in the balcony gave a virtuoso performance worth watching in itself. She was superb. The conductor Killian Grumley Trainor was in complete control throughout and gave a most perfect downbeat. He brought musicians in with both his left hand or the occasional nod of his head and gave the players on stage every possible aid to assist them in their performance. The chorus' rendition of "Masquerade" was brilliant, in fact, that whole musical number with the flowing dancing movement of the whole ensemble was visually super. The choreographer (Caoimhe Dalton) had the chorus numbers all exactly to a tee and then when she had the specific "ballet dancers" on stage, they all danced with preciseness, grace and a smile on their faces which was wonderful to watch. Josh Hurley (Phantom) had the onerous task of filling the leading title role. Josh has a booming, but well controlled, rounded baritone voice with very good diction and carried the songs perfectly. What really impressed me was his characterisation. He acted throughout with anger to the crowd but with tenderness to Jessica Hackett (Christine) and in the final scene where he let her go you could feel the emotion within him. In the same way when he was kissed he gave the impression of never having been kissed before and you could feel the pleasure that he derived from it. Opposite him Jessica was the perfect foil. She sang the duets with Josh so well and their voices blended so sweetly together. In her own singing she has the most fantastic quality to her voice and when she sang "The Phantom of the Opera" she hit every note right in the middle. Marvellous. Jessica's acting was excellent throughout and she gave every attention to Cian Judd (Raoul). Cian was not intimidated and performed to the same high standard, he must be careful, though not to upstage. Anna Bergin (Carlotta) looked resplendent in her flowing ball gowns and was suitably bossy to all, just be careful of the accent as some words were lost. Stephen Perry (Piangi) also had the problem of concentrating too much on the accent which led to words not being clear but he does possess a wonderful tenor voice. Rachel Galvin (Madame Giry) played the archetypal Dance Teacher, with straight back and cane, and commanded every scene she was in. Rachel also possesses a wonderful singing voice, but be careful not to be too quiet on the dialogue. A super cameo performance by Aly Coyne (Meg) who not only spoke and sang with perfect clarity, but was also forefront in a number of the dance scenes which she led wonderfully. Which leads me to Kerrill Kelly (Firmin) and Callum Martin (Andre). They were brilliant. Great timing. Good expressions. Quick sharp dialogue with neither trying to better the other but more to give support to the other. No finer double act will you see. The props in this show were numerous but I must mention a few. The working Pianola, the chandelier which fell on cue spectacularly were excellent but the highlight was the boat. It glided across the stage on a cloud of dry ice and with a backdrop behind of rippling water and candles...marvellous. The attention to detail in this production was second to none and Sean Gilligan (Director) is to be congratulated for the way, not only did he give personal attention to detail with the actors but also his attention to detail with the technical side of the show. Sound and lighting cues were all spot on. His use of technology with picture backdrops worked magnificently and gave such depth in scenes. Perhaps his greatest accomplishment in this show was to dress over 100 cast members in costumes that were absolutely exquisite. Each member had at least three changes and each costume could not be faulted, including an extraordinary selection of perfect white wigs which the dancers wore.

It was a marvellous night's entertainment.

My first visit to the lovely An Tain Theatre in Dundalk for the musical comedy that is Sister Act. When your director, Colin Hughes, is a panto legend, you can be sure that he will milk the script for every laugh going and have his players primed for every conceivable comedy moment. I wasn't disappointed. His comedic "chase" scene was absolutely brilliantly conceived and executed. Away from the comedy his direction of the quieter dialogue, particularly the two and three handed scenes, was excellent. This show has big musical chorus numbers and the chorus were drilled in both diction and singing by chorus mistress Geraldine Casey, a wonderful all round performance by the chorus. Allied to that the Nuns chorus were also foot and hand perfect in the big dance numbers choreographed by Gilda Turner, unfortunately some of the characters were not up to the task in the smaller dance routines. When you have a nine piece orchestra, of which three instruments are brass, it is the responsibility of the musical director, Ronan Dennedy, to ensure that the orchestra accompanies the singers on stage. On too many occasions it felt like the players on stage were competing with the orchestra.

I must compliment all the players who had cameo roles in this production, all knew their roles with uniform accents and the pace of the dialogue was kept at a premium. TJ, Pablo and Joey (Sean Og Cairns, James Brennan and Brian Halpin) played the comedy up, but dance steps in the routines were lacking in timing. Curtis (Gerry O'Hara) had a good New York accent throughout and I loved his performance in his main song "When I Find my Baby". These four characters were pursued by Lt Eddie (Paudie Breen). Paudie gave a most sublime rendition of "I Could Be That Guy". He sang passionately throughout and performed with good diction and comedic timing. Sr Mary Robert (Niamh Craven) sang with a small timid voice perfectly, and I was awaiting a big booming voice at the end of the show when she got her mojo back but, sadly, it never arrived. The other supporting Nuns all acted suitably demonstrative throughout especially Sr Mary Patrick (Karyn McCooey) who played the character on the verge of hysteria. Karyn also possesses a wonderful singing voice and led throughout in all of the Nuns pieces. The lone man amongst the Nuns was Mgr O'Hara (Tim Ahern) who gave us another wonderful comedy performance. A leading lady needs to be front and centre and never fearful of what she is required or expected to do. Deloris Van Cartier (Carol McCourt) played the part wonderfully and commanded every scene that she was in. Her singing was bold and brash, with great intonation, she could dance and her interpretation of the part was excellent particularly in the two and three handed dialogue scenes. Her scenes with Mother Superior (Oirlaith Crosbie) were excellent. Oirlaith has a most wonderful singing voice and sang with beautiful vowel sounds and perfect phrasing. Her dialogue was smooth and precise and her comedy, especially when she spoke to God, was brilliant. Costumes were typical 70's style and it was great to see bell bottomed trousers again. The sets had some very good backdrops highlighted by the stained glass windows and the cross. There were, however, a number of issues with sound and sound effects which shouldn't happen on a Saturday night performance. The audience gave the company a standing ovation and an extra matinee was put on for the Sunday afternoon, a good result all round for the Dundalk Musical Society.

They say that "The Best Things Happen While You're Dancing", and for Coolmine Musical Director, Caitriona Ni Threasaigh, this was undoubtedly the truth, for while she literally danced in front of the orchestra, they treated the audience in the Draíocht to a musical feast. Rarely have I witnessed such an animated performance from a conductor, her style of movement changing with the changing tempo of the music. It was a pleasure to watch someone lost in their music, and enjoying every note, and I'm delighted to report that it was only the prelude to a night that scored highly on musicality. Whether it was Mandy Geary's well drilled choral pieces, or the individual voices of a highly impressive front line of principals, "White Christmas" was a show beautifully sung... even the audience impressed when they sang along.

When a single split note from the trumpet player is the only thing I can pinpoint to criticise, it says a lot for the people in control of the music. The orchestra were always balanced and always under control. The harmonies from the Quintet were spot on, and the chorus had both control and energy. Indeed, the chorus were notably well rehearsed and precise in all their business. There was always a reason for them being onstage and they never looked like they were loitering purely in anticipation of a song or dance. Good attention was given to creating cameo characters.

Principal voices were melodic and confident, and the harmonies in the duets and trios were polished. Musically, the show was obviously very well rehearsed. Another success was the principal pairing in the show. Séamus Sullivan and Mary Beth Jennings as Bob and Betty, were a comfortable couple, both playing the awkwardness of their initial meeting with a good sense of comedy, and they were equally at ease as they gradually realised their love for one another. Vocally, they blended beautifully, and individually their voices were melodic and strong. I particularly enjoyed Mary- Beth's rendition of "Love, you didn't do right by me."

As Phil and Judy, Damien Douglas and Alison Dennan sparked off one another with strong comic ability. Both made the most of their dialogue and their dance numbers were delightful. Damien oozed confidence and was suitably roguish as the play-boy of the piece, while Alison had warmth of personality that made her instantly likeable. Again, they both had easy-listening voices and performed their songs with polish. Indeed, these four performers worked very well together as a team, always at ease and comfortable to watch.

Equally in tune with each other were Rory Robinson's General Waverly and Kathryn Gibbons in the role of Martha. Rory had more of a hint of James Cagney about him, both in deportment and in tone of voice. His stubborn and headstrong personality was nicely contrasted by the comedic busy-body antics of Kathryn, and as the show progressed, their affection for one another was well portrayed. Rory was at his best wringing every ounce of value out of the self-indulgent, overtly sentimental and unapologetically patriotic speech of the finale, while Kathryn soared to great heights with her rendition of "Let me sing and I'm happy". Her trio with Mary-Beth and Alison, "Falling Out of Love", was a musical high point of the show.

Andrew Gallagher contributed well to the show with a secure, confident and likeable Ralph Sheldrake.

Niamh Kiernan is a young lady with a lot of promise and with plenty of talent on display in her role as Susan Waverly. If anything, she may have been a tad too mature to capture the cute innocence of the granddaughter, but nevertheless, she's a performer to watch for in the future.

Amie Preston and Amy Ward as Rita and Rhoda were delightfully over the top in creating their ditzy characters, and Seán Fay was consistently funny as Mike. Crystal Murphy, Kate Furlong, Susie Murray, Wendy Storey and Yvonne Kennedy were delightful and pitch perfect as the quintet, and from a long list of supporting roles, all of whom were very capable, James O'Higgins Norman as Ezekiel and Colm McGrattan as Jimmy, created very comical caricatures, and Maria Kavanagh displayed a fine voice and character with the little opportunity she was given.

Louise Dodrill gave us plenty of variety in her choreography, from the light- hearted routines with Bob and Phil and the Fred and Ginger style of the duets to the well polished show stoppers of the dance ensemble. Never over complicated, the routines were precise and well rehearsed, with "Blue Skies" and "I Love a Piano" making the biggest impact. Make-up was consistently good, and great work was done with creating the hairstyles of the era. Costumes were always appropriate, and the principals looked comfortable wearing them. There was plenty of glitz for the big chorus numbers, and the traditional Christmas outfits for the finale were beautiful.

The set for the show was well constructed, with the train carriages and the television screen being particularly impressive. Stage management was an efficient, no-fuss affair, with smooth and well paced transitions. Good props apparent throughout, but I would have liked a bigger Christmas tree, and might have set it as a centre-piece, rather than almost losing it in the SR wings. Lighting was well designed with great attempts made to capture the atmosphere of each scene, and the greatest praise I can give to the sound engineer is that I didn't even have to think about the quality of sound. It was spot on.

Director John Furlong presented us with a straightforward, no nonsense, well rehearsed, by the book production. Stage pictures were tidy, and the chorus were well integrated into the action. Entrances and exits were well structured, giving the action a very natural flow, and the pace was generally very good. The train scene was particularly well worked to give the impression of over-crowding and discomfort. I also liked that attention was given to establishing the identity of the many cameo characters. There was a tendency for principals to play very face-front to the audience, and indeed it's a style that some directors seem to favour. I do feel that it looks somewhat un-natural at times, and weakens the connection between characters. We communicate so much through eye contact, and I feel it adds intimacy to relationships to play more to each other. On a more minor point, Susan entered the bedroom through an invisible wall to give her message to Martha after the "Falling Out of Love" trio.

Regrettably, I have to say that the main neutral set, visible throughout the show, was an unpleasant distraction. I'm all for innovation, and often a 'concept' set can have a clever significance to the production, but on this occasion, I completely failed to understand what the concept was! In a production that was 'traditional' in every other respect, the neutral and rather dull permanent pieces seemed completely out of place. I wouldn't labour the point except that, unfortunately, it impacted on so many other aspects of the production. Lighting could have been even more dynamic had it been focused on a more attractive canvas, and even the glitziest costumes couldn't give a real feeling of the razzle- dazzle of show-business, when set against a drab background. During the otherwise beautiful finale, the addition of twinkling stars merely transformed the main set from dull, to dull with fairy lights.

The other disappointment was that after all the effort that went into organising the 'big surprise' for General Waverly, having just four members of his division on stage at the end was a bit of an anti-climax. While assuming that the audience were his regiment in the opening scene worked well, it failed to have much impact at the end. It might have been worth dressing the entire chorus in uniform to let the audience actually see the love and respect that was felt for the General.
