To return, however to a positive note, despite the above mentioned distraction, every performing member of this talented cast gave a very good account of themselves, and the direction was clean and concise. It is certainly fair to say that my most positive memories of my visit to Coolmine will be of a night of beautiful music, beautifully performed. Thank you so much to all concerned and to Santa Claus and his front of house team for the warm welcome and hospitality.

Not for the faint hearted is the racy, raunchy and often ridiculous musical version of The Addams Family, with Music and Lyrics by Andrew Lippa, and a book by Marshall Brickman and Rick Elice. But if you like a bit of spice and a bit of Hammer horror humour, then this show is just the ticket. The seemingly disembodied hand clicking and conducting the overture through the curtains was an early indication that this was going to be something different. And different it certainly was.

Musical Director, Niall Mulpeter had a fine orchestra around him, and their energy and volume during the overture had me initially worried that they would be over-powering during the performance, but my worries were unfounded. The balance between stage and pit was consistently good throughout the show, and when the opportunity arose, during dance numbers, the musicians let rip with energy and precision. As no-one else is credited, I'll assume that Niall was also the chorus master, and in this respect, he did a good job in teaching some very intricate and often discordant harmonies. There was a tendency for individuals in the chorus to over-sing the final note, and they perhaps needed a more definite cut-off. This isn't an easy show, musically, and Niall was required to sing along on a couple of occasions to keep principals in tempo, which quickly resolved any problems.

The principal line-up included many fine voices, and the chorus scored well on harmony, with some very difficult music. The chorus generally contributed to the action with good focus and good expression.

But comedy was the backbone of this show, with all the central characters requiring good timing and delivery of a very racy script.

Paul Spencer as Gomez gave an entertaining performance, at his best when trying to seduce his own wife, and at his most sincere when showing fatherly affection to his daughter. He is a fine comedian, but I felt that much of the dialogue between himself and Morticia in the earlier scenes lacked a bit of pace. Musically, he got off to a dodgy start, but thankfully he quickly recovered and handled his songs with gusto. Joan White looked fabulous as Morticia, and after a subdued opening scene, she grew in stature as the show progressed. Her delivery of "Death is just around the corner" was spot on, displaying a good voice and a good sense of comedy. Aishling Rohan, as Wednesday, impressed from the outset, full of confidence and a strong melodic voice. "Pulled" was an excellent solo, where she really made the most of the comical lyrics. She worked well with Gary Sheppard, as Lucas, to establish their weird relationship. Gary started rather timidly, but again, he blossomed as he got further into the story. Uncle Fester, delightfully played by Paul Kenna, who played very well to the audience and almost stole the show with his terribly silly rendition of "The Moon and Me". Good work!

And talking of show stealers, the youngest member of the cast, Richard Mansworth in the role of Pugsley, displayed a remarkably wide range of performance ability for his tender years. I have to say that his comic timing and delivery was possibly the best in the show, and despite being the obnoxious little brother from hell, I, and the whole audience, loved him. Physically, JJ Tynan in the role of Lurch was a sight to behold, towering above the rest of the cast, and not once did he wobble on his stilts. He wasn't very articulate.... (that's a joke, by the way!) but his grunting was most effective, and at the finale, he showed that he had a fine speaking and singing voice. It was a masterful touch when he lifted Morticia high into the air to give her a goodbye kiss.

If I live to one hundred and two, I hope I will still be as sexually vibrant as Grandma, ever so naughtily portrayed by Dawn Kavanagh. She was very funny, and her scene with Pugsley was a highlight of the show. Pat Cullen was a convincing stuffed-shirt in the role of Mal Beineke, and a good contrast to the insanity around him, and his wife Alice, a role very obviously enjoyed by Sarah O'Sullivan, was pleasingly comical as the frustrated housewife, and positively animal-like when she let rip with an outrageously sexual rendition of "Waiting"! Very nicely done.

Lea Carroll's choreography was inclusive, tidy and performed with great enthusiasm, but a little 'safe' for this production. A bit less 'Cabaret' and a bit more 'Freak Show' might have had a stronger impact, Given the outrageous nature of this show, and the scope for creativity, I think she missed opportunities to inject comedy into her routines.

Paul Norton demanded a lot from his cast, in terms of physical comedy. He employed every gag and gimmick he could to make the most of the comedic potential of the piece, and his bawdy sense of humour was always appropriate and well placed. There were pace issues with the opening scenes that got the show off to a sluggish start, but it did gather momentum as the night progressed. Good comedy is a serious art form, and while I could see his intentions, they were not always executed to perfection. A lot of effort went into the preparation of some excellent props, especially the 'rack' for stretching Pugsley, and that extremely dangerous chair that made my eyes water at the very thought of it. Nice attention to detail.

I'm well aware of the technical limitations of the Dunamaise Arts Centre, but it would have been nice to see a bit more scenic variety within the Addams home. Good effort was made with the graveyard and the gates to the crypt, and I loved the trees in the park, but I would like to have seen the 'rack' in a dungeon setting, and maybe a spooky bedroom setting for Pugsley or the guests. The stage crew did an efficient job of moving furniture on and off the stage with minimum fuss. I loved the moon, (and especially the baby-moon in the pram.) and the projection of Fester on the star cloth was well achieved. The star cloth was a nice feature of a lighting plot that did well to create appropriate atmospheres. Sound, with the exception of one grumbling mic in an early scene, was of a good standard, with good balance and some very good sound effects.

Generally, the wardrobe was good and appropriate, except for that awful yellow dress on Wednesday, which clashed horrendously with the much nicer yellow dress worn by Alice. Wigs were very good, and congratulations to the make-up team for what must have been an arduous task.

The Addams Family is an outrageous show, and the director took the right approach to it, taking liberties and playing it over the top. I had a sense that in other departments, the tendency was to be more cautious and traditional. My only real suggestion would be to assess the mood and nature of the show, and allow that to determine your approach to it. Wallow in the freedom of creativity, and don't be afraid to take risks. This is a very competent company, and, as your show selection suggests, a company that enjoys a challenge. Thank you sincerely for a very entertaining evening, for your hospitality, and most importantly, for sending your audience home with smiles on their faces.

TThe Wexford Opera Festival is preceded by Oyster Lane Theatre Group's annual production by one day. So it was not to the National Opera House but to the Dun Mhuire Theatre I visited to see their 21st birthday presentation of "Hairspray". This show absolutely bounced off the stage from the first moment to the last with a young vibrant chorus all word and note perfect under the baton of Patrick Clancy; however the orchestra were a little loud in places particularly during under scoring. There was also a major issue with sound cues some of which were late or, on occasions, missing completely. Good set, with a super replica TV Camera, and a well thought out lighting plot was provided by Mark Redmond. Greg O'Leary ran a tight stage crew where set changes were swift and unobtrusive. Wonderful bright costumes for the entire chorus and the wigs for the leading players were perfect. "Hairspray" is a show with a large number of cameo roles which allows new members of societies to gain experience. All of Oyster Lane's cast performed the cameo roles splendidly. Despite the success of the movie version of this show the pivotal part revolves around Tracey Turnblad (Yvette Walsh). Yvette was a tour de force playing this role, her singing and dancing were absolutely spot on and in the scene where she met Link Larkin (Stephen Byrne) she was apoplectic with excitement. A truly marvellous performance. Stephen played the relationship with Tracey in a tender compassionate way, his singing was excellent with very good intonation and he glided around the stage in his dance numbers. Neal O'Leary put the corn into (Corny Collins) with a suave performance of a TV host. He played the part with good diction for his dialogue and a smooth singing voice. Gearoid McCauley (Edna Turnblad) played with good accent at a pitch which didn't drop or falter at all and then sang with a lovely controlled baritone voice. He was ably assisted by Seamus Murphy (Wilbur Turnblad) who milked each comedy line for what it was worth and gave a most sincere performance. Majella Londra (Prudy Pingleton) played the stereotypical mother who constantly chased and chastised her much maligned daughter Emily Brazzil (Penny Pingleton). Emily has a most powerful voice with excellent diction and she played the dizzy, mad, over exuberant part to a tee. The audience were asked to "suspend belief" as Sadbhb Roche (Little Inez), Michael Farrell (Seaweed J Stubbs) and Ann Marie Walsh (Motormouth Maybelle) all performed extremely well the onerous task that befell them, particularly Ms Walsh who gave us a most marvellous rendition of "I Know Where I've Been". Aishling Jones (Amber Von Tussle) strode around the stage like a mirror image of her stage mother (Velma). Wearing super costumes Aishling stood tall and straight and has a wonderful stage presence. She delivered her dialogue crisply with a perfect hint of sarcasm that belittled all around her. Nicola Roche's (Velma Von Tussle) rendition of "Velma's Revenge" was marvellous. She has superb voice control, sang with a passion and perfect intonation. Her dialogue was spot on and she commanded every scene she was in. She directed the proceedings in the studio with a regimental attitude and woe betide anyone who got in her way. It was a most wonderful performance. For this show to work properly it is absolutely imperative that the dancing is flawless. Suzanne O'Leary (Choreographer) not only knew the capabilities of her cast and chorus but she knew exactly how far to push them. The opening number "Good Morning, Baltimore" gave us a cast and chorus bursting onto the stage, the girls in their bobby socks all immaculately turned out and absolutely foot perfect. Then in the smaller duets and ensemble numbers each character was choreographed within their capabilities which made every dance look like a master class. Then the final number possessed so much energy that it brought the show to a wonderful climactic finish. It was a wonderful evening's entertainment and I thank Paula and Jamie who chaperoned me and my guest on the evening.

As a Daddy myself, I'm a great believer in family values, and the importance of a strong father figure, always putting the needs and concerns of his family before himself. And of course, if the father also happens to be clever and crafty, he can manoeuvre any situation to ensure that he also has a lot of fun. And when the family in question is The Addams Family, you're guaranteed there's going to be a lot of fun on the menu. The St. Michael's Theatre Musical Society benefitted from having a remarkably fine father figure, steering the show to a highly successful conclusion, but more of that later.

It took Musical Director Philip Kennedy a couple of songs to rein in a strong and accurate orchestra, to a volume level that was appropriate to allow the performers on stage to be properly heard. From the outset, they were somewhat overpowering, but once the balance was achieved, it was consistent for the rest of the show. When there were opportunities to let loose in the dance numbers, the brass and woodwind players seemed to really enjoy the varied rhythms of the score. The tricky vocal score was well mastered by chorus and principals alike, with harmonies well defined. The principals were supported by a company of dead ancestors who contributed significantly to the chaos of the piece. Their singing was always secure, and they were animated in gesture and expression. Choreographer, Claire Kickham, (also Morticia) led from the front with a well drilled chorus of dancers, full of energy and expression, and a great sense of fun in all their routines. They got the show off to a good start with "When you're an Addams", and were a slick Greek chorus behind "Full Disclosure". But the Tango was the terpsichorean highlight of the show. My only crib was that, on occasions, the stage looked a little over crowded. Keith Flanagan was a confident, charming and extremely witty Gomez, with a crafted accent that was rich and always articulate. His tone and clarity in song allowed the clever lyrics to be clearly understood, adding nuance and emphasis to enhance his comedy. There was also great tenderness in his rendition of "Happy/sad". This was a really fine characterisation, which also brought out the best in his seductively, sultry side- kick, Morticia, delightfully captured by Claire Kickham. Her performance was most impressive and peaked with the superbly executed "Tango de Amor". Wednesday has become my favourite day of the week, thanks to the somewhat psycho, yet sensitive treatment she was given by Roisin Barry. I wasn't mad about her eye make-up, which looked a bit smudged, but it didn't take away from her secure stage presence and her commanding voice. Her love interest, Lucas, was well portrayed by a very confident Tom Joyce.

Fester is another character whose make-up needed a bit more care to make the bald cap a little less obvious, but Andrew Smith gave a rib-tickling performance, playing beautifully to the audience, and stealing the show with an hilarious "The Moon and Me", for which puppeteer Ray Shannon deserves lot of credit. Excellent comedy.

Edward O'Dowd came across as a street-wise brat, cheeky yet charming as the disturbed, juvenile masochist, Pugsley. He can sing a bit too!

Ciarán Power gave a secure comedic treatment to Lurch, and what a fine voice he revealed at the end of the show. Margaret Dunne's crazy Grandma peed herself superbly, with great timing and suitably contorted expression. Another slick performance.

Seán O'Brien and Joanne McCabe as Mal and Alice Beineke, played their roles with secure comfort, but given the outrageous nature of the show, both could probably have gone crazier when their subdued inner selves were exposed.

Well done to stage manager Lizzy Heffernan for keeping on top of the technical requirements of the show, and her stage crew were invisible. The main set, with its balustrades and double staircase, was a well constructed piece, and well used throughout the show. I loved the dungeon trucks, complete with skeletons and cobwebs. You could almost taste the mustiness of the setting. I did think that the white gauze behind the rather sparse grave yard made the scene a little too bright. Furniture and props were of good quality and well employed.

Lighting for the show was decent and adequate. I do feel that some scenes were over-lit, where more atmosphere could have been created with specials or better colour use. It was difficult to create atmosphere in the scenes that included the white gauze. But everyone could be seen, which is of primary importance. It's the first show I've seen in a long time where follow spots were effectively used. Nice effects with the lightning, and superb UV scene. Apart from the requirement to boost mics at the start of the show to get over the over-zealous orchestra, the quality and balance of sound was generally very good.

Well done to the hard working make-up and hair teams. Generally, very good work, although a few of the principals needed a bit more definition in their make-up. Costumes, too, were appropriate and varied, with good definition of characters within the chorus. When Gomez slashed at the curtain with his sword, and a curtain tassel suddenly fell to the floor and took on a life of its own, I knew I was watching a production where director Kevin Kennedy had put a great deal of thought into every detail of his show. His use of this kind of puppetry was such a clever and creative touch, which reached its pinnacle when Gomez suddenly began dancing above the heads of the chorus. Excellent use of black light.

I was initially concerned when I thought that the black curtain had jammed, then realised that it was being used as an effect, a process that became a feature of the show. I'm not a fan of scenes being played in front of black tabs, but this was quite clever, with one half of the curtain being raised like a drape to reveal one location, then switching to the other side to give a different location. Had this been a device to mask an inadequate set, I would have been much more critical, but in truth, the rest of the set was most effective. So, while I didn't love the black drapes, I acknowledge that they were cleverly employed.

This was, indeed, a production peppered with innovation and attention to detail. (Gomez side-stepping a lightning flash, Fester illuminating light bulbs in his mouth, the 'slow-motion' of the arrow hitting the apple, and what could only be described as an animated mop-head chasing after that elusive curtain tassel at the start of act two, are just a few examples.) Kevin Kennedy's approach to his task was entirely appropriate and true to the mood and tone of the material. A most enjoyable and well presented show by all concerned, and I am grateful to have been in the audience

Technicolor Dreamcoat It was a nostalgic visit to Nenagh this evening, and a shock to the system to see how the Choral Society have transformed what used to be a draughty, rather weather-beaten Scout Hall into a splendid, bright and well equipped Regional Round-Up theatrical venue. Congratulations to the company and their committee on such a wonderful achievement. And how lovely it was to meet old acquaintances from by-gone days, like Dick Gough, Una Collins, Gerry Scanlon, Paddy Rohan and of course, the director/choreographer of tonight's show, Greg Browne.

As the house lights dimmed, attention swiftly moved from the past to the future, as a new generation of musical thespians stepped into the limelight, full of raw energy and heart-warming enthusiasm. "Joseph" is a very good vehicle for a youth company, and Greg Browne made a good decision to have a group of narrators, rather than the normal solo performance, thus giving more young performers the opportunity to play principal roles. With seven narrators, 12 brothers, half a dozen other named principals, and an ensemble of more than 20, this was very much a team effort, and in many respects, a highly successful one.

Company Chairperson, Ger McCathy, hit the nail on the head after the performance when he told the young cast "You won over the audience and sent people home with smiles on their faces", and as a member of that audience, I entirely concur with his sentiments. A Youth Academy is a place of learning, and it takes time and experience to become perfectionists, but each and every one of you have already learned that musical theatre is all about entertaining an audience, and you most certainly managed to achieve that.

There was a touch of "Lawrence of Arabia" about the attire of the orchestra, a very nice touch, and I'm delighted to say that they sounded as good as they looked. I found the drum rhythms a bit pedantic at times, and some of the transitions from one number to another were a little uncertain, but by and large, there was a pleasant sound from the pit, and it's nice to hear the brass and woodwind sections showing consideration for the performers on stage. The balance was good, and they never overpowered. Similarly, the chorus and various groups of performers were well drilled in their harmonies and in their diction. Musical Director, William Cullagh, led efficiently from the piano, but on one or two occasions, the young performers would have benefitted from a conductor, or a larger gesture, to bring them off their final notes more cleanly. Calvin O'Rourke as Joseph is a young man with a heap of potential, particularly as an actor. He created a cocky but likeable character, and worked hard to inject his role with comedy. He's a fine figure of a lad, and obviously enjoyed confidently strutting 'topless' on the stage. Vocally, he needs to 'listen' more to his accompaniment to rid himself of a tendency to pitch slightly below the note. Timmy Cullinan enjoyed the role of Pharaoh, and persuaded us to enjoy him too. The inclusion of an "Elvis" sing-a- long medley was a clever gimmick, and he had a good comedic rapport with the audience. Nicely done. I liked that the chorus were even included in the comedy business, providing good vocal harmonies for the medley of Elvis songs. Anthony White and Alannah Shesgreen as Mr and Mrs Potiphar were a pleasant couple. Neither part is vocally demanding, but they were confidently played, and Mrs Potiphar made a good effort at being as provocative as a youth production would allow. Anthony also gave a secure performance as Jacob, shining particularly in his comedy Tango with the gymnastic dancers.

As a group, the Narrators charmingly told the tale of Joseph. They looked well in their purple outfits, and vocally, they were more than delightful. I have to give special mention to Caroline Browne, Megan Maher and Grace Shesgreen, whose smiles and facial expressions lit up the stage. The less experienced chorus members could learn a lot from them.

Joseph's brothers had a lot of fun with their roles, and were at their best with their comic antics during "One More Angel in Heaven". The solo voice in "Those Canaan Days" was notably good. Both musically, and in their execution of dance routines, the company were extremely well drilled, realising good harmonies throughout, and a vibrant and disciplined energy in their dances. I was impressed not only with the simple and effective choreography throughout the show, but also by the standards achieved by the young performers. Pharaohs Song, One More Angel and Oh No, Not He were notably slick and energetic, but the show-stopper was the comedy Tango performed by Jacob and his dancers. It was a beautiful comedic touch to see Jacob revert to the stature of a feeble old man as the dance concluded.

There was a great sense fun and inclusivity about Greg's direction of the show. Opportunities to shine were given to as many individuals as possible. I was delighted to see in the programme that there was a lot of family involvement in the production, giving it a real sense of community theatre.

There were times when the stage seemed a bit over-crowded, most notably during the "One More Angel in Heaven" hoe- down dance, which although well performed, would have benefitted from being a bit less cluttered. I also felt that the interpretation of dreams was a bit lost amid the activity around the central character.

The show was peppered with nice comedic touches, like Jacob presenting his favourite son with a Tipperary jersey before giving him the coat of many colours. The Pharaoh scene was particularly creative.

Hand movements throughout the show were a bit of a distraction. I've always felt that you can judge the confident of a performer by how they use their hands, and perhaps a workshop in the future on natural hand movement might be a worthwhile venture.

The set for the show was bright and functional, with particularly good use of props. The camel was a gem, as was Joseph's chariot arriving through the audience for the finale. This was a multi-level set, and the levels were well utilised. Scenic art was at its best for the opening scene.

Sound, throughout the show, was well balanced and cueing was excellent. Lighting, however, was much more sporadic. There was a considerable lighting rig, and many lovely effects, such as a virtual rainbow of backlight when Joseph received his amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat. But the first rule of lighting, even during atmospheric scenes, is that the performers must be clearly seen. I think perhaps it was a lack of communication between lighting operator and director that led to many scenes where principals were in shadow or inadequately highlighted. I appreciate that with an inexperienced cast there's more chance that principals will miss their 'spot', but in such circumstances, a more sympathetic general wash might help to eliminate the dark shadows. A beautiful lighting effect was created during "Close Every Door To Me" with haunting backlight and an overhead spot on Joseph, but its impact was lost because Joseph sang most of the song with his head down.

Visually, there was an explosion of colour from the costumes of Pat McGann, well accessorised by your wardrobe department, with a wide selection of hats, scarves, waist-coats and head- pieces, all blending nicely together to create the varied atmospheres of the musical numbers. There was good work done by the make-up team, including a profusion of wigs and beards.

As mentioned above, the venue was beautiful and well presented, and the front of house staff, led by Una Collins and company chairperson, Ger McCarthy, were polite and welcoming. I very much appreciated the coffee (I'm an addict), cake and biscuits at the interval and the guided tour of the venue after the show.

I would advise Greg, William and the committee to keep going at full stream with what is obviously a very enthusiastic and energetic youth policy. It was an absolute pleasure to see so many young performances having the courage and confidence to take to the stage, and their sense of enjoyment was infectious. Their efforts were fully appreciated by the entire audience, and with the degree of talent on display, the future of this group seems to be in a very healthy condition. Thank you all sincerely for a most enjoyable experience.

For anyone who doesn't know the show, "Urinetown" is about a future world where people have to pay to pee because of an eternal drought, and below the surface, it's a clever commentary on corporate greed and abuse of power, and on an even deeper level, it questions the whole futility of life. Heavy or what? Well no. Not at all, in fact, for the story is hilariously told in an almost pantomime style that pokes fun at the feel-good frivolity of musical theatre, and turns the notion of life's happy ending on its head. "Urinetown" may be easy on an audience, but it is demanding on its cast, filled with a plethora of principal roles, intricate choral harmonies and opportunities for dance. In the right hands, it's a jewel of opportunity to be creative and outrageous, and it was certainly in safe hands with Director Eoin Cannon, Musical Director Dermot O'Callaghan and Choreographer Michael Evans.

Throw in a cast who wallowed in the craziness of the whole experience, a technical team who enjoyed the licence to be experimental, and a well tuned orchestra, and the result was a production that certainly packed a punch.

A tight orchestra (sadly not named in the show programme) were well positioned beneath the upper level of the stage set, and despite being on-stage, never overwhelmed the singers. Tempi throughout were secure and under- scoring was just that, an accompaniment that allowed script to be clearly delivered. Dramatic moments on stage were well punctuated by the musicians. Good direction and coordination from Dermot O'Callaghan, who, I assume, was also responsible for the quality of the choral singing. On this front, a masterful job was done on "Run, Freedom, Run", which deserved an ovation from the audience, and throughout the show, harmony and dynamics were always apparent and precise.

Eoin Cannon embraced the nature of this craziest of musicals, and approached it in precisely the correct manner, taking every opportunity to punctuate that craziness. It's one thing to walk a cast through a very funny  script, (and in fairness, it would take a director with no sense of humour to fail with this script) but it's an art form to enhance what is on the page with gestures and nuances, glances and gimmicks that raise it above the ordinary. Such was the attention to detail in this production. Even the chorus members performed as individuals, not merely as an ensemble. The show was beautifully designed and presented, with obvious good communication between director and technicians, to achieve the many desired effects. The various levels on stage were well used, and chorus entrances, exits and groupings were always in keeping with the action.

This is not a particularly difficult show to stage, but Eoin Cannon's clever set design was well realised by Stage Manager and Set Construction supervisor, Marie Cusack. Good use was made of the available space, including the functional upper levels. The dreary, darkness of the main set was appropriate and a nice contrast to the cleaner pieces for the Urine Good Company setting. Set changes from the public amenity to the UGC offices were not speedy, but very tidy, and other changes were very smooth. Props and furniture, courtesy of Pauline Boyle and Evelyn Donnelly, were always appropriate, and appeared with minimum fuss and often 'driven' on by cast members. Good organisation. The circular silhouette screen USC was superbly used, hilariously during the Cop Song, and with stunning effect for Bobby's death. These were just two of an array of first class effects in Darren Kelleher's lighting plot, which was a show in itself. There were occasional moments of patchiness, when dark spots were apparent, but principals, or the operator, always quickly rectified the problem, and the overall impact of the lighting was a feast of dramatic and colourful delight. Two late cues were the only blemishes on an otherwise well balanced and perfectly pitched sound plot from Vinny Osborne. An effective wig on Penelope Pennywise, and an hilarious one on Caldwell, were noted. There were no problems with make-up, and costumes were suitably unglamorous (when required) and well coordinated.

As mentioned above, the chorus were presented as a troupe of individual characterisations, each player maintaining their own distinct personality throughout, which added great strength of their performance. They were never lacking in energy and enthusiasm, and they nailed some excellent choral pieces. "Run, Freedom, Run" was awesome. Kevin Fagan as Bobby Strong was heroic in a James Dean kind of way. Cool, yet gullible, street wise but also innocent... a rebel without a cause that he understood! In a well balanced performance, which highlighted his acting and comedic talents, it was his voice that impressed most. Smooth, melodic and in "Run Freedom Run", powerful and commanding.

It would have been impossible not to love Aoife Small as Hope Cladwell, so dumb, fragile and vulnerable was her character. Her duet with Bobby, "Follow your Heart" was romantic and beautiful in the silliest possible way. What a lovely performance.

Damien Hurley was born to play Officer Lockstock. This was such a complete comedy performance, with every word, every movement and every gesture contributing to his character. His timing was extraordinary, and the "Cop Song" had me, and the entire audience, in hysterics. Superb work from Damien. Alongside him for much of his narration was an endearing performance from Vourneen MacElwain as Little Sally, the waif with advanced intellect. She captured the innocence and unintentional intelligence of the character beautifully. (Her teddy bear also gave a memorable performance!) Kelly Marie Davy was a convincing Penelope Pennywise, who opened the show strongly with "It's a Privilege to Pee" and grew in stature at the revelation of her being the mother of Hope.

John Sweeney brought a wealth of experience and an hilarious wig to the role of Caldwell. His greed and devious arrogance wouldn't seem out of place in the Ireland of the past decade. Suitably smarmy, and strong in delivery of his musical numbers.  As his side kicks, Gary Finnegan and Mark Keegan created much hilarity with their interpretations of Senator Fipp and Mr McQueen, respectively. Gary convinced as the lecherous money-grubber, and Mark revelled in the 'campness' both of his character and of his bunny rabbit impersonation. Eoin Salley was a comically menacing Office Barrel, who bounced well of his partner.

Paul Laycock was a credible Old Man Strong, making the most of a relatively minor role, and as Josephine Strong, Rosaleen Nolan contributed a delightfully emotional and sincere performance. Catherine Griffin (Soupey Sue), James Place (Tiny Tom), Mary Galligan (Mrs Millenium, and Kirstin Smith (Rhonda the Stockfish) all made the most of their opportunities to shine in Act Two, and while Dylan Kelly, as Hot Blades Harry, was never lacking in energy or ability, he needs to mind his diction when using such an exaggerated accent. Of the supporting roles, Sharon Osborne as Little Becky Two Shoes was on fire, full of craziness, energy and confidence in delivery.

"Urinetown" is an excellent piece of writing, and it will hopefully become a popular addition to the amateur musical theatre repertoire. In presenting the Irish amateur premiere, Harold's Cross pulled out all the stops to show it off to its best advantage. I'm sure the writers, had they seen it, would be proud of their creation, and immensely grateful to HXT for their exceptional production. A truly memorable night of musical magic. Thank you for the experience.evening,

On The day I attended Sister Act in Letterkenny Hurricane Desmond was firmly assaulting all parts of the country particularly Donegal. But have no fear the wonderful An Grianan Theatre was built to withstand much more than a hurricane. It was also built to house Sister Act. This fast, slick show was directed by Pluincerd O'Fearraigh and he had the cast and crew suitably prepared for the task in hand. His direction had the cast on their marks and ready for every cue, no slacking in the pace of the dialogue which was crisp and precise. In the pit md and chorus master, Pat Campbell had the orchestra rattling along at a super speed, but never too quick to upset the players, and he had a wonderful control of the chorus who never faulted on their job, especially the larger chorus numbers which were sung with passion and intensity. Similarly the big chorus numbers were choreographed superbly by Phil Dalton. The cast were led by Maire Kelly (Deloris) who sang with plenty of passion and gave a marvellous rendition of "Raise your voice" all ably assisted by a chorus of 23 nuns. Jean Curran (Mother Superior) managed to get every bit out the comedy and she spoke with a most wonderful controlled accent especially when talking to "God". Kieran Kelly (Curtis) led the bad guys in this musical, whilst his dialogue was smooth and with a good nasally New York accent he could have been more intimidating.

Supporting roles included Geraldine Galligan (Sr M Lazarus) who gave us a most wonderful display of enthusiasm with the most marvellous facial expressions from pathos to joy and Karen McNulty (Sr M Robert) whose dialogue in the end scene where she protected Deloris was a most touching piece of theatre. The society managed to get every last bit of comedy out of this show led by Diarmuid O'Gallchoir (Monsignor O'Hara), he gave a most superb display of comedy with all the nuances and subtleties at his disposal. Sets were suitably designed and constructed, although set changes could have been quicker and quieter. Lighting cues were, on occasion, a little late and, on occasion, too early. Sound cues were not as correct as might have been expected. All in all a most wonderful afternoon's entertainment and the society took their curtain calls to a standing ovation.

My journey took me to the foot of the Wicklow mountains to St Brigid's Hall for the classic musical "Me and My Girl". Carnew MS was presenting its 49th show and has the wonderful local talent of Michael Dunbar to direct and Lar Duffy to musically direct their productions. Mr Dunbar directed the show and managed to get every laugh possible out of every scene which enthralled the packed Saturday night audience. Lar Duffy had wonderful control over his orchestra and they played with the most melodic harmony all night, never too loud and always accompanying the singers, a super job. Mr Duffy also doubled as the chorus master, thus ensuring that the high quality in the pit was surpassed by the beautiful harmonic voices of his chorus, they sang with wonderful phrasing and diction. The show revolves around a cockney boy who found himself heir to a rather large fortune. The leading man Bill Snibson (Bill Stafford) was the all singing, tap dancing comedian who performed with lightning feet and a ready wit. His performance was outstanding. His love interest Sally Smith (Eliie Willoughby) was equal to him in every department and they were a wonderful duo. Her rendition of "Once You Lose Your Heart" was a showstopper. A most beautiful clear soprano voice with perfect diction she got every bit of pathos out of the song and out of her performance. Whilst the comedy ran through the show Gerald (Gary Stephens) played the haughty, "hoorah henry" part to a tee. Wonderfully over the top expressions with an exuberance that was nearly demonic. His love interest was Lady Jacqui (Catherine Stafford) who played the femme fatale brilliantly. Her scene where she attempted to seduce Bill, to no avail, was marvellously played. There were numerous cameo roles who all ably assisted the front line, but I must mention Herbert Parchester (Rob Donnelly), there was such great energy in his portrayal of this typical, although slightly eccentric, English solicitor. Costumes were wonderful throughout climaxing in a selection of Pearly King and Queen outfits for the finale of "Lambeth Walk". Technically the sets and scene changes were all in the safe hands of stage manager Tommy Kavanagh and the lighting plot was expertly executed. A few late sound cues didn't spoil the evening's entertainment of what was a super production.

The TF Theatre Royal in Castlebar is one of the most modern theatres in the country. The facilities are second to none with one of the largest stages to be found anywhere in the country. A large stage was required as the cast numbered over 70. It is always pleasurable to see a new society with the passion and excitement of starting out on a new venture. Ronan Egan (Tevye) was in full control of his performance throughout the evening, with good clean diction a good accent and a nice melodious voice. He was assisted by Donna Ruane (Golde) who played the dutiful wife intent on marrying off her daughters as quickly as possible. Her performance was precise but perhaps she could have harassed Tevye a little bit more. Her dialogue scenes with Vivienne Lee (Yente) were nice and crisp but both characters failed to wait for the laughter to subside so further dialogue was lost. The three daughters Niamh Gavin (Tzeitel), Sandra Gibbons (Hodel) and Stephanie Cassol (Chava) gave a beautiful singing performance of "Matchmaker" but I would have liked the piece to have been choreographed. Sandra sang with wonderful melancholy "Far from the home I love", perfect diction and intonation. James Garvey (Motel) was suitably busy with a good accent and wonderful facial expressions, Ollie Kennedy (Perchik) has great stage presence and performed his role with a perfect accent and super diction, whilst Tommy Morahan (Fyedka) performed well with a slightly different Russian accent. In the dream scene Mairead McDonnell (Fruma Sarah) gave us a most marvellous performance as Lazar Wolfe's dead wife, with marvellous costume, hair and make-up she shrieked and cackled throughout her performance but never losing the words or the notes. The stage was so large that a minimalist set was used to great efficiency although scene changes could have been a little tighter. There were a number of sound issues with late cues and the lighting plot needed to be fine tuned a little better. Director (Alana ni Mhiochain) kept the pace of the show nice and tight although in places dialogue was a little laboured. Similarly the orchestra were a little too far apart which led to a number of intonation problems for the singers on the stage. Musical Director Deirdre Lee chose to play the keyboard, this meant that some of the more difficult chorus pieces which needed a conductors direction, i.e. the dream scene and the rumour, were not performed as correctly as would have been hoped. I enjoyed my visit to Castlebar and I thank Sarah Ronayne for her kind hospitality.

The magic of Cole Porter is the backbone of "Anything Goes", with a string of his most memorable hits, threaded together in a paper-thin storyline that relies heavily on farce and slapstick comedy. "I Get A Kick Out of You", "It's De-lovely", "Easy To Love" and of course the title song, are thrown in regardless of whether or not they perfectly fit the story-line. But it's a show that throws up plenty of opportunities for character comedy, and a sense of the ridiculous. Only in such bizarre musicals can people meet, fall in love and get married all in one day, and if one accepts that premise, and plays it for laughs, well.... that's entertainment! Musical Director, Deirdre Lee, led a band of eight well tuned musicians from the keyboard, and did so with comfort and balance. Some of the cuts, to reduce dance routines, seemed a little awkward, but the overall performance of the musicians was very pleasing. A good job had been done also on preparing the vocal chorus, with well realised harmonies throughout the show. The gentlemen were particularly delightful in "There'll Always be a Lady Fair" and supporting Erma in "Buddy Beware". Visually, the chorus did all that was asked of them with ease and a natural flow. It would have been nice to see chorus members mingling in the 'on- deck' scenes, as you would expect on a passenger liner, rather than appearing only when they had a few lines to say, and the Evangelist meeting, in particular, needed more involvement from the crowd. This was a production light on choreography, but when the opportunity arose, the chorus were tidy and well coordinated.

Vivienne Lee made an impact from the moment she stepped on to the stage as Reno Sweeney. She had a relaxed, easy manner, and was confident and convincing as the night club evangelist. Added to that, was a good sense of comedy and a very "easy listening" voice that lent itself beautifully to the style of the Porter melodies.  Equally relaxed and confident was David Gallagher's Billy Crocker, with a most pleasant tenor voice and comedic talent that was highlighted in his very funny falsetto at the start of "It's De-lovely". His relationships with both Reno and Hope were believable and comfortable Mary Dempsey was delightfully likeable in the somewhat under-written role of Hope Harcourt. Here was another lovely voice, best exhibited in "Goodbye Little Dream", and she was as suitably awkward with Lord Evelyn as she was comfortable with Billy Crocker. Séamas Cafferky as Lord Evelyn Oakleigh provided the comedic highlight of the show with his "The Gypsy in Me" which rounded off a performance that consistently tickled the funny-bone of the audience. Both in accent and delivery, this was a confident and very capable performance. Richie Heneghan was a secure and articulate Moonface Martin, though perhaps not fully realising the ridiculousness of a character whose only ambition was to be higher up the ladder as a Public Enemy. He did display a good voice and comic ability, but his character needed to be further developed.

Sharlene Ruane was a feisty Erma, enjoying the silliness of her role. Her Brooklyn accent (which made one or two excursions into Cockney English) needed to be slightly more articulate, but her enthusiasm was infectious and very enjoyable. Ciaran Kiely and Carmel Glynn as Elisha Whitney and Evangeline Harcourt respectively, added mature experience and a great sense of fun to their characters. Ronan Egan as the Captain, Damien Conway as the Purser and Michael Goulding as Henry T. Dobson all made worthy contributions to the continuity of the show, while John Farragher and Cathal Owens got good comedy from their cameo roles as Luke and John. Reno's "Fallen Angels", played by Angela Prenty, Mairead Mullaney, Imelda Reilly and Jane Kelleher, provided an eye-catching back-up to Reno, despite their limited involvement. The main setting for the show was practical and well constructed, with sections opening to reveal the cabins, although these in-sets could have been dressed with a few more props. There was a secure upper deck which was effectively used. I was concerned that the opening scene, including the beautiful rendition of "I Get A Kick" was a bit too long to be played in front of house curtains, and might have benefitted from being played on a centre-stage in-set, framed by the curtain. This would also have lessened the delay while the bar and stools and dressing were being cleared during the scene change. It had the effect of getting the show off to a rather sluggish start. Stage Manager, David Keane, ensured that scene changes were generally tidy and fuss-free, but they did seem to take longer than necessary. Similarly, the lights down/lights up between scenes tended to happen at a leisurely pace. Alan Dunne's lighting plot came up with some effective moods, although I would question some of the colour washes. One of the duets, "Easy To Love" was played against a green background, which was anything but romantic. He did, however, ensure that no one was playing in darkness, with very secure key lighting. Sound was extremely reliable, with good balance and cueing.

There was good attention to detail in the costuming of the show, with beautiful gowns in abundance, complimented by appropriate hairstyles and well applied make-up. Reno and her Angels always looked stunning, while Hope (despite one dodgy ball gown) and Mrs Harcourt were the epitome of elegance. Male costumes were tidy and appropriate, and overall, the production was visually splendid.

What was apparent throughout this production, was a sense of community spirit and involvement, and a company who were enjoying being on the stage, and that comes from good leadership and efficient preparation. Director/ choreographer Hazel McLynn should be justly proud of her cast for establishing competent, confident characterisations, and for putting their best foot forward, in a show that had all the signs of being meticulously rehearsed, which is the very reason that I felt a sense of frustration that, for me, it just didn't ignite the stage as it should have done. This style of zany comedy, with a ludicrous story- line, requires exaggeration to bring the characters fully to life. Moonface and Erma, and even Billy, are almost cartoon-like on the page, and that sense of the ridiculous needs to be articulated to translate to the stage. More than anything, though, farce/slapstick relies heavily on pace, and often I had the feeling of sitting in a sleek and polished Ferrari that was being driven by a very nervous chauffeur. Blow Gabriel Blow and the title song should explode from the stage, and while they were undoubtedly tidy routines, they needed more punch, and probably more choreography, to raise them above the ordinary. There's no doubt at all, however, that this was a smooth, if leisurely, sailing on the SS American, and a very enjoyable evening of entertainment. It was a pleasure for me to meet and enjoy so many talented people. Thank you to June Allison-Keane and her Front of House team, for their warm welcome and their hospitality,

It was a very nice touch to be able to shake hands with "The Hand" in the foyer of the Black Box Theatre, Galway, prior to the start of "The Addams Family". It set the tone nicely for an evening of fun and hilarity, in the company of an energetic and enthusiastic cast of Galway University students.

"The Addams Family" is a romp in the realms of the ridiculous, and Director Julie Breen approached it with just the right amount of silliness, displaying a good understanding of comedy throughout this production. She developed strong c h a r a c t e r s and gave them enough free rein to indulge in their antics.

The show was generally very well cast, and much effort went into visual appearance.

One or two of the scene changes were on the slow side, but a cracking pace was maintained from start to finish. There were also some very well defined cameo roles, such as the Forlorn Bride (Aisling Bonner) and the Cavewoman (Sive Neary), which showed innovation and attention to detail.

Dean Reidy is a young Musical Director who will grow in stature when he learns to relax more into his music. A tendency to be somewhat pedantic with his rhythms, and possibly intimidated by the demands of the score, led to a production that was musically subdued. More confidence would have allowed the well tuned orchestra to make a greater impact throughout the show. The chorus showed great promise in a rousing and well presented opening number, with good energy and clear harmonies, but they did tend to lack the same vocal confidence as the show progressed. Despite this, there were many splendid vocal contributions to the show, and from a visual point of view, the chorus never lacked enthusiasm nor conviction. They also made the most of the choreography of Rory McNamara and Lorna O'Connor, which was generally inventive and appropriate to the style of the production. Some of their routines would have benefitted considerably from a little more "Oomph" from the orchestra. The great strength of this production was a well selected and confident principal line. Paddy Quinn gave a highly entertaining performance as Gomez, with good comic timing, a well maintained accent and an abundance of stage presence. He 'lusted' beautifully after his wife, and was suitably sentimental towards his daughter. Despite rhythm issues in some of his musical numbers, he also displayed a fine vocal ability. Gráinne White was a remarkably good Morticia, well able to put her songs across with gusto. She had a fluent stage presence, was visually perfect for the role, and above all, she played her comedy with style and hilarity. Her facial expressions were wonderful and her affected laugh was top notch. Excellent work.

Kevin Murphy's strength as a performer, in his portrayal of Fester, was his physicality on stage. He used his voice, his hands, his face and his body shapes to become absorbed in his character, making the most of every move and gesture. A prime example was "The Moon and Me" which, truthfully, was not inspirational in design, but was saved by his determination to extract as much comedy as possible from the number. I would have liked him to exaggerate his insanity with wide eyes and more of a demented smile on occasions, but this was a thoroughly entertaining performance.

Niamh Roche was a formidable Wednesday, quirky and feisty in equal measure. She was believably in love with Lucas, and endearingly comical in her relationship with her parents. Apart from a hint of insecurity between her pure voice and her 'belter' voice, she had a strong and pleasant vocal quality.

Understandably, GUMS didn't have the luxury of going 'outside' to import a Pugsley of the right age, but while David Nagle was obviously too old for the role, he injected it with a good dose of 'childlike' energy and tantrum. Good comedic ability and a fascinating falsetto!

Niamh Ni Fhlatharta defied her youthfulness to present a very credible and hilarious Grandma! Good work on her hair/make-up, but particularly on her characterisation. Most enjoyable.

Eoghan Walls-Tuite was most impressive as Lurch. Again, he was well made up, and kept in character throughout the show, with some beautifully timed reactions.

Lucas Beineke is a role that can be rather understated, but in his portrayal of the character, Cathal Ryan indicated his intentions of being a confident leading man of the future. Good comedy, sensitive acting and a fine and confident singing voice. His scenes with Wednesday were delightfully cute and cheesy, as they should be! Very well done.

Claire O'Brien's Alice and Alex Murphy's Mal were wonderfully acted roles. There was a genuine feel to their wayward relationship, highlighted by his 'squareness' and by her frustration. When they were called upon to reveal their inner souls, they both achieved this with great comedic effect. Alex was some way short of being pitch perfect, but he totally nailed his acting. Claire, on the other hand, displayed a fine vocal range, particularly powerful in her lower register.

The show was also a visual delight, with great attention to the costuming and make-up, not just for the principals, but for every individual chorus member. This was very good work. The set, also, was well presented, if somewhat minimal, which was more a reflection of the limitations of the theatre than any lack of design by the stage team. Some of the scene changes were a bit laboured, and this was amplified by the use of the repetitive "Addams Family" number, which was over-used to cover scene changes. Lighting was generally good, with effective use of colours to create atmosphere, and follow spots which only faltered on blackouts. The sound engineers provided good balance and good cueing throughout.

If this production was being assessed as part the students' University course work, they would all be passing with flying colours; such was the enthusiasm that was on display throughout the production. There were moments of excellence, as well as a few problems, but the overall package was a night of great fun and entertainment. The ability is there, in abundance, and in some instances, just needs to be nurtured and developed. Thank you all, sincerely, for a most enjoyable night.

O'Reilly Hall in UCD is used for numerous events and this week's turn was the Musical Society's production of Legally Blonde. A man made stage gave the players plenty of room to manoeuvre the intricate dance routines courtesy of Conor Nolan. Each routine was perfectly choreographed and executed and the young vibrant chorus took on the challenge and never missed a beat. In a similar fashion the directorial skills of Amy Gilligan had the chorus and front line co-ordinated perfectly. Ms Gilligan ensured the pace of the show rattled along with never a fault in dialogue nor a delay in scene changes. The set, designed by Miriam King, was intricately designed with plenty of height at the start and a most ingenious transformation in the courtroom. Technically there were a number of issues, particularly with late sound cueing which is extremely frustrating for both players and audience. The orchestra, under the baton of Simon Sharpe, played together as a very tight unit however, they just needed to be a little quieter especially during underscoring. Sharp suits for the men and marvellous dresses for the leading lady, gave us a sense of opulence in the college and courtroom scenes but the cheerleader's costumes stole the show. This show cannot work unless you have a chorus who not only must have the technical ability to sing and dance but also have the nous to act in quiet moments, where they can be seen but not heard, this chorus were magnificent in achieving this result. The three "BFF's" of Elle, played by Niamh Casey, Katie Stevens and Niamh McGowan, were tremendous in their singing and dancing and supported wonderfully. Gill Lambert (Paulette) gave a most beautiful rendition of "Ireland", with wonderful phrasing and perfect pitch. Sarah Gordon (Brooke) gave us a workout dance routine and, to her credit, never missed a note. To sing and dance is an art in itself, to sing and work out is a very special talent. As for the male leads Conor O'Rourke (Callaghan) sang in a most wonderful baritone voice and spoke with gravitas, Daragh McArdle (Warner) was suitably haughty and delivered his comedy superbly. Her singing has a most marvellous quality to it with beautiful vowel sounds and the audience heard every word. Her timing was absolutely spot on in all her comedy, never over the top and her accent was consistent throughout the whole performance never dropping for an instant. All in all, my guest and I had a most marvellous evening's entertainment and I thank Miriam for her kind hospitality.

In so many respects, Ballinrobe Musical Society realised the full potential of The Addams Family, and pulled out all the stops to make it a truly memorable production. From an amazing set, through to a dazzling front line, audiences were treated to a night of magical madness and mayhem.

Musical Director, Finola Higgins had assembled a very talented band of musicians who were robust in their playing, while never over-powering the on stage action. Percussionist Terry Cooke was as entertaining to watch as he was to listen to, as he added great variety to the sounds emanating from 'the pit'. Pace and tempi were strong and precise throughout the show, as indeed were the vocal harmonies from a well drilled chorus. As a package, the show was extremely musically sound.

As co-directors, Liam Butler and Aoife McClafferty were obviously very much in tune, and focusing on making the show as diverse as possible. There was a very effective use of the chorus virtually as part of the scenery, as they spent a couple of scenes plastered to the walls like a living tapestry. It really was most creative. In other scenes they intertwined and became living (or maybe dead) trees. The pace throughout the show was excellent, benefitting considerably from a slick and clever set, and what a set! With the exception of the forestry side flats, which were not superbly painted, the rest of the set was simply stunning, and managed with precision. When it was fully displayed, the interior of the home was full of style, detail and character. Wall panels opened to reveal detailed bedrooms, with coffins. Another panel hid the rack that gave so much please to Pugsley, and another revealed the torture chamber with Gomez's 'persuasion' chair. A panel in the floor was opened by Lurch to allow Gomez and Mal to go to the basement. Needless to say, a vast array of perfect props had also been assembled for the purpose of dressing such a vast stage. But behind the physical appearance of the set, a stage crew, led by John O'Shea, worked miracles, making sure that everything functioned and flowed with a minimum of fuss. This included the device that allowed Fester to fly above the heads of the chorus in pursuit of his beloved moon. Extraordinary team work. Very well done to all concerned.

The directors were blessed in having had several amazingly talented players in their principal line, but if I had to be picky, the great strength of some highlighted a little insecurity in others. While Wednesday, Lucas and Mal all performed with energy and enthusiasm, they could maybe have had their characters a little more developed and defined.

Michael Coen in the role of Gomez had everything that the character required. Stature, charisma, perfect comedy timing, sincerity, vocal quality, abundant energy, and he used them all to the max in his performance. From the get go to the final curtain, he commanded the stage and delighted the audience. His stepping in and out of a 'private thoughts' spotlight was a clever touch. Hot on his heels was Niall Conway as a flamboyant, crazy, deliciously likeable Fester. He was like a prankster, always trying to put one over on his family, on the Beineckes and even on the audience. This was a powerful physical performance, as well as being vocally delightful, and a beautifully crafted characterisation.

James Conway's Lurch gave a master class in the art of mime, making the absolute most of every grunt and gesture, and realising the comedy of his character. Then, just when you thought the show was over... Wow! A booming baritone voice revealed itself, and added a final layer of class to a top notch performance.

Despite his tender age, James Murphy had no intentions of being over- shadowed by the adults around him. His Pugsley was delightfully secure in acting and singing, and he showed a remarkably good sense of comedy for one so young.

Suzanne Garvey-Brennan brought a fine voice and a strong character to the role of Morticia, always looking comfortable on the stage, and playing particularly well when in the company of her mischievous husband.

As Wednesday, Heather Doyle displayed a powerful and melodious voice. "Pulled in a new direction" was a tour de force, and "Crazier than you" showed off her potential to be feisty. While she managed to very effectively put across her sinister streak, the story revolves around the fact that she is changing, and has fallen in love, and her performance would have benefitted from a bit more expression of the 'new' Wednesday. The script even states that love has her "smiling". Even in her scenes with Lucas, we didn't see that smile often enough.

Donna Ruane was a fun-filled and hilariously inappropriate (in behaviour) Grandma. Her aged posture was beautifully accentuated, her diction was excellent, and her comedy timing was extremely good.

Ciarán Hennelly was a credible and enthusiastic Lucas, believably afraid of his potential in-laws, but equally determined to prove himself to Wednesday. As a couple, they performed "Crazier Than You" extremely well.

John Byrne as Mal Beinecke, was at his best when he relaxed and released his inner self. His playing of the grumpier stuffed shirt in the opening scenes seemed a little forced, but was still commendable.

Siobhán Campbell was a convincing subservient housewife as Alice, and revelled in the craziness of letting her hair down and recognising her wild and vivacious inner being. "Waiting" gave her the perfect opportunity to let her skills as a comedienne shine.

The chorus did all that was asked of them with conviction. They were musically secure and made the most of limited opportunities to get involved in the action.

Aoife McClafferty's choreography got the show off to a cracking start with a high energy "Addams Family" routine, but the highlight of the show was a combination of choral movement and choreographed scenery, during "One Normal Night", when everything was perfectly synchronised, and the final picture was the stunning interior of the Addams family home. This was very well done. The "weather" provided by the chorus in "Full Disclosure" was most effective too, but with other routines, there was a minor problem with over- crowding. Choreography was generally very well rehearsed, but with some of the more 'hip-hop' movements looking a little awkward for some of the older dancers. I did feel that the "Tango de Amor" needed to be either highly seductively stylised, or played for comedy, and it kind of fell between two stools. While it was danced with conviction, particularly by Gomez and Morticia, it did disappoint a little. However, Aoife deserves full credit for a company who were well polished, and clearly enjoying their dancing.

Lighting was generally acceptable, and on occasions, very accurate and precise. The close-to-the-stage follow spots were well used, most of the time, and allowed for some very atmospheric states. There were areas, however, further up-stage and in corners, which the follow spots couldn't access, and unfortunately these areas were frequently used for action. For example, poor Wednesday was mostly in shadow on the swing, as Gomez drifted in and out of well lit areas for "Happy/Sad". But in general, good colours were used, good mood were created, and cueing was spot on. The beast below the bed was excellent. Sound quality was very good throughout the show, with good balance and excellent cueing, even of the one-liners. Principal costumes were good and appropriate, and the chorus had plenty of character and variety, although they were a bit stark white, and possibly something off-white or green/grey might have been more ghostly and atmospheric. Good attention had been given to making sure that everyone was kitted out with wigs and appropriate hairstyles. . Make up, universally, was excellent, with good contouring and definition. Fester looked brilliant, and Grandma was a wonderful caricature.

Ballinrobe is community theatre of the most impressive kind, with so many giving so much dedication in every aspect of the production. Long may you continue to flourish and thank you most sincerely for your hospitality and for a superb night of entertainment.

My first visit to The Mill Theatre in Dundrum, in anticipation of the all singing and dancing "Singing in the Rain", Kilmacud's production for this season. In a very small corner of the auditorium I found the orchestra. It is very intimidating even for the most accomplished of players to have the audience that close to you especially if you are a brass player. It must have been also very disconcerting for Musical Director Geoff Woods to have to stand amongst the audience in order to conduct. It certainly stopped Mr Woods from showing his conducting skills as he gave a very regimented performance. The show is written from the film. This means that if you are going to copy dance numbers then you must copy them precisely because the audience will remember the originals. Unfortunately a lot of the dance numbers were copied only in part, this meant that the highlights of the dance numbers for example Cosmo's "Make Em Laugh", which had a big finish did not happen, this was a shame. It is also very important that all the cast are exactly precise on the dance steps otherwise it can look ragged and disjointed. Director Paul Fay kept the show running at a good speed throughout although there were some delays on scene changes. He had accents all correct and there was some nice pathos when required. The show is a movie within a show and I must congratulate the director on an absolutely marvellous video of their own "silent movie." This was delivered perfectly on screen with wonderful cue cards to give us the storyline, congratulations. Another marvellous effect was the "rain". It worked absolutely perfectly with a steady stream of water which allowed the theme song of the show to be delivered correctly.  Lighting was good and unobtrusive although we did have a wobbly moon in the first act, but the travelling spot work was excellent. Sound technicians invariably have problems and this one had "feedback issues", this shouldn't happen especially in a professional theatre. The ensemble and supporting characters gave 100% commitment to delivery and all sang and danced with smiles on their faces there were some nice cameo performances particularly by Dave Supple (Roscoe Tanner) and Marion Holohan (Dora Bailey). The show, however, revolves around four main characters. Carl MaGeean (Cosmo Brown) threw himself into the part and got all of the comedy and slapstick correct. His dancing was not as precise as it should have been and he had a few issues with his timing on his piano playing, whilst his dialogue was delivered wonderfully he did have a few intonation problems when singing. Anthony Ennis (Don Lockwood) had the unenviable task of portraying this character. Mr Ennis certainly put his own mark on the part with wonderful dialogue and acting but his singing and dancing needed to be more exact. Aisling Cuffe (Lina Lamont) performed with the most perfect squeaky New York accent, she kept the accent up throughout and even when she sang her big number she still sang with the same nasally accent, a most marvellous performance.  Sarah Lawlor (Kathy Selden) acted her role with a wonderful accented dialogue, superb diction and when she smiled she lit up the whole auditorium. She then sang with so much controlled passion, beautiful phrasing and she was absolutely note perfect, to complete her performance her tap dancing was spot on.  My guest and I were looked after by James the FOH manager and I thank him and his team.

From the moment Musical Director Sarah Lynch Barrett gave the downbeat for the start of the overture, it was apparent that this was going to be a sizzling "Hot Mikado". Her seven piece band, (sadly, un-credited in the programme) was one of the highlights of a production that was vibrant, racy, comical, colourful and highly musical.  She set a cracking pace from the outset, and maintained it throughout the performance. Her musicians were note perfect, and performed with zeal, obviously enjoying every moment of the racy score. The balance between stage and pit was excellent, and the chorus were generally secure in their entrances and their cut-offs at the end of musical numbers. Choral harmonies were well achieved, and principals seemed confident and musically well rehearsed. Excellent Musical Direction.

Director Barry Kavanagh presented a clean and tidy production that played successfully to the limitations of the venue, and to the abilities of his performers. Koko's entrance through the audience was well conceived, and indeed the chorus exit through the audience at the end of Act One doubtless eased what would have been a very congested exit on stage. When the chorus weren't moving, they were well arranged into pleasant pictures, and there was a good awareness of space, preventing the stage from ever looking over-crowded. Chorus entrances seemed a little contrived, on occasions, suddenly appearing to perform a song and dance, rather than gradually blending into the scene, but they were well directed in their involvement and reactions, always looking like participants rather than spectators of the action. Principal characters were well developed, and allowed to play to their strengths. The strength of the direction of this show was undoubtedly the pace at which it was played. There was never a dull moment, nor a lull in activity, with ever changing pictures, and enough action and variety to keep the audience thoroughly engaged.

Choreographer Jean Gill showed great wisdom in keeping her choreography at a level that was manageable for her dancers.  The male chorus made a good solid effort with the opening chorus, if slightly hampered by the canes they carried, which were a little untidily used in the routine. Having said that, Jean bravely introduced a lot of business with hats during the "Mikado" number, and it worked remarkably well. Nice creativity. There was a very good flow to the choreography throughout the show, and while the execution wasn't always precise and completely together, her dancers did themselves proud in enthusiastically putting their best foot forward. The Act One finale sequence was vibrant and full of energy, and the tap routine was appropriate and appreciated.

Koko is one of those roles that requires physical comedy, facial expression, a good vocal quality, and above all, strong comedy timing, and I'm delighted to say that James McDermott had it all, by the bucketful. This was a performer who knew how to use the stage, and how to play to the audience, which he did perfectly, without ever going over the top. I'm not quite sure why he, rather than Pish-Tush, sang "Braid the Raven Hair", but it did give him an additional opportunity to display the quality of his voice. Excellent work.

Vocally, Maggs Jacob stole the show with her "Alone and Yet Alive", and she seemed to thoroughly enjoy the role of Katisha. She was strong and domineering throughout.

Kirstin Smith was a fun and feisty Yum- Yum, who extracted as much comedy as was possible from the role. She sang her songs with comfort, and filled them with expression, and her switch from doting wife to one who was hell-bent on self- preservation, was delightfully achieved. Eoghan Fingleton, gave a strong and versatile vocal performance and displayed good stage presence, but he did need to relax into the silliness of the story and smile more often. He was at his best during "This is What I'll Never Do" and a well-devised "Here's A Howdy-Do".

Vincent Oliver was a robust being, in his portrayal of Pooh-Bah, who could have gone even further with his comedic superiority. Most impressive was his rich, resonant baritone voice, and his perfect diction. Along with Koko and Pish- Tush, his "I Am So Proud" was superbly performed. Similarly, Colm Lombard, as Pish-Tush, made the most of his vocal opportunities, and always looked comfortable and confident in his role. Pauline Maguire had the perfect range and tone to carry off the vocal demands of Pitti-Sing, holding her ground against Katisha with an assured nonchalance. Along with a vibrant performance as Peep-Bo from Celine Byrne, these two provided secure support for Yum-Yum in "Three Little Maids", capturing the style and close-harmonies of the piece most effectively.

Arriving into the action half way through Act Two requires an immediate impact, to quickly establish a character, and both in appearance and delivery, Paraic Kelly, as The Mikado, was up to the task. His Mikado song oozed confidence, comedy and choreography.

The simplicity of the set must have been welcomed by the stage crew, under Denise Flood, who when called upon to move a screen or a bench, did so with no fuss whatsoever. This is a show short on demand for props, and those that were required were always appropriate. The raised platform centre stage was well utilised and helped to create interesting stage pictures. The opaque screens stage right and left required, and indeed received, good lighting, but with the simplicity of the set, the large fan up centre could have been a little more elaborate in design.  Good use was also made of back lights. General lighting at the front of the stage wasn't as sharp as the beautiful moods created on the raised platform. There was a tendency for principals to pass through shadowy areas when moving from one hot spot to another. The idea of a shadow show through the centre stage screens was a very creative concept that didn't quite reach its potential in practise. Overall though, a bright and colourful plot that added much to the tone of the show. Thank God the sound quality and balance was absolutely spot on, for it allowed the band to play their music as it should be played, without ever drowning out the singers. Very good quality!

Costumes for this production were well presented and well worn, bright and colourful, and with good attention to detail. Hats and shoes were appropriate, and I particularly loved the "spats" in the Mikado routine. There was good attention to hair-styles, and a natural feel to the make-up, although I would have been inclined to make Katisha a bit more severe/grotesque.

Overall, this was a lively and well presented production, with a high entertainment value. Thank you for a lot of laughs, and an abundance of beautiful music.

St Michael's Theatre in New Ross has, over the years, seen a whole range of plays and musicals performed on its stage. However I doubt if it has seen such a passionate and vibrant production as Sister Act. It absolutely bounced off the stage led by their leading lady Yvette Walsh. Ms Walsh's portrayal of Deloris van Cartier was delivered with style, panache, precision and she also gave us a most powerful singing performance. Ably assisted by Teresa Buckley (Mother Superior) who rose to the task and gave the audience every comedy moment, she also sang with a beautiful mezzo voice and her rendition of "Haven't Got A Prayer" was perfect. These two characters were ably supported by a chorus of nuns who all performed together and sang with wonderful harmony and phrasing, credit to Chorus Mistress Maeve Wilson for this, although some of the dancing could have been a bit more precise. The transformation by Niamh Bolger (Sr Mary Robert) from shy, timid nun to defender of Deloris was spectacular. Her song "The Life I never Led" was sung with gusto and passion and her final note seemed to go on forever. The "baddie" of the show Gearoid McCauley (Curtis) could have been a bit more sinister and he played the character more as a panto villain! His three henchmen James Dobbs (PJ), Trevor Kent (Joey) and Tom Joyce (Pablo) all played their manic characters to a tee with good and varied styles however the dance numbers were not as precise as they might have been. The job of trying to capture Curtis and his gang fell to Keith Flanagan (Eddie) who performed with good diction and a nice steady accent, his singing in the quiet moments might have been more controlled but his forte singing was excellent. He also gave us this goofy characters persona and exuded happiness when he kissed Deloris. Ken Moroney (Monsignor O'Hara) was always on his cue and his mark although he had a tendency to be a little too loud in his dialogue. The whole production under Director Derek Shannon moved along at a very good pace with nice crisp diction and consistent accents from all of the principals, he also assisted in designing the set. The fixed backdrop and rotating flats were very good and set the scene in the convent although I didn't think that the "last supper" backdrop was required. Half stage lighting was very good but the spot was a little too large. Sound technician did a good job only dropping the baton a couple of times. The costumes were marvellous, all correct from the 70's winged collars and bell bottomed trousers through to the transformation of the nun's habits. A lot of 70's hairstyles were in evidence for the men but I must say that Deloris' "afro" hair was brilliant. The big chorus numbers were choreographed exceptionally well by Anne Marie Cooney but the smaller dance numbers, both the opening and the "baddies" could have been more precise. Philip Kennedy's conducting skills were in evidence with a nicely controlled sound from the orchestra, although they could have been a little quieter when under scoring and perhaps a bit more precise when finishing chorus numbers. He also played a good cameo role when doubling as the Pope. I and my guest were looked after by Dorrie Godkin and her team and I thank her for her kind hospitality. The show was sold out prior to the run even starting and the people of New Ross were not disappointed.

I learnt that the Annesley Hall in Newcastle where I attended 9 to 5 was gifted to the society and what a wonderful facility it is. 9 to 5 is based on the Dolly Parton film and is an absolute rip roaring roller coaster of comedy. The lead male character played by Jay Walsh (Franklin Hart Jnr) climbs the ladder of success by either deceit or bullying. He was obnoxious and smarmy in his portrayal with perfect accent and diction, a super performance. The three main female parts were played by Orla McCrickard (Doralee), Emma-Jane McKnight (Judy) and Emma Nugent (Violet).
