Ms McCrickard doubled and played the Dolly Parton movie role, and she looked the image of her, sang like her and spoke with a believable nasally Texas accent. Ms McKnight started off as a shy and nervous character but transformed in to a well adjusted forceful woman and her rendition of "Get Out and Stay Out" was fantastic. But the show is held together by Ms Nugent's character Violet. Superb delivery of dialogue, wonderful comedy, super singing and her effortless dancing gave us a most complete performance. The society has a number of highly talented players who performed secondary roles and contributed to the overall performance but I must single out Sheila Paolinelli (Margaret). Margaret is the office lush and Ms Paolinelli's delivery of performance was mastered expertly. Never did she stumble too much to lose control, never was she late for any cue and every time she had a line it was delivered audibly, never too slurred not to be understandable. I laughed out loud at her theatrics. Choreography by Timmy Bell was simple and precise and he is obviously aware of the abilities of his cast as they were all able for the task. Director Neil Keery, had all the players with correct and steady accents throughout, a good pace and because of the foresight to use the cast to change the very cleverly designed set there was not delay to the proceedings whatsoever. Gareth McGreevy's musical direction and control of his orchestra was always in time but as the orchestra were in another part of the building the sound relayed in was somewhat loud in places. It was a most marvellous evening's entertainment and I thank Aline for her kind hospitality.

A great new generation of enthusiastic performers provided a night of energy, colour, and laughter, with a production that was a real winner for entertainment value. It ticked so many boxes and sent the audience home laughing and singing, and that's what it's all about.

The pace of the show, from the outset, was excellent, and was helped considerably by a clean and tidy, if over-simplistic, set design. Characters were clearly established, and the chorus were integrated very well into the action. Some of the principals were set very down stage, and continually upstaged themselves, and in the courtroom, the judge and witness were too far upstage, forcing others to face the back wall when delivering lines to them. Having said that, the staging of "Gay or European" was excellent.

But Director, Jessica Bray's crowning glory in this production was her excellent use of the Delta Nu girls for setting up Paulette's salon. It was a clever and classy gimmick that helped the flow of the scene changes, enhanced the girls contribution to the show, and turned a technical necessity into an entertainment.

This was inventive and very well executed by the girls. I would also suggest that the Director needed to spend a bit more time plotting the show with the Lighting Designer.

There was a lot of excellent comedy throughout the show, and despite the criticisms above, Jessica should be very proud of achieving such a fluent and entertaining production.

There was very good work from choreographer, Pamela McGlynn, especially with the Delta Nu girls. Everything about them was vibrant and energetic, and I particularly liked that they were individually choreographed, rather than performing patterned routines. "What You Want" was a well worked routine, with good fluency through the various settings. Likewise, "Chip on my Shoulder" and "So Much Better" were well designed and executed. There was wisdom in not including too many dancers in a tidy skipping routine for "Whipped into Shape". Indeed, I liked that Pamela didn't feel the necessity to over-crowd the stage, allowing smaller groups of dancers to shine. "Bend and Snap" and "Gay or European" were well staged, and the Remix was full of energy. Routines throughout were well rehearsed and polished.

As Elle Woods, Kim Burke's singing was wonderful, and she displayed a sense of comedy that was as fluent as her natural dance rhythm. She did have insecurity, which was a tendency to underplay her facial reactions in some moments of drama. That said, there is no question that this was a powerful enough performance to indicate that audiences will be seeing a lot more from Kim in the future.

Anna Maria Barrett took to the role of Paulette as a duck takes to orange sauce.... a perfect pairing, deliciously tasty, and a feast for the audience. There was a raw warmth and sincerity about her interpretation of the role, awesome in its comedic impact, and robust in its vocal delivery.

Grace Collins was a right nasty piece of work in the role of Vivienne, with a perfect amount of smug superiority, and when she eventually redeemed herself; her delivery of the Remix was a powerful vocal contribution to the show. She was ably supported throughout by Georgia Henley in the role of Whitney.

Hilary Orpen gave an energetic portrayal of Brooke Wyndham, skipping and singing perfectly through "Whipped into Shape". This was another good comedic performance.

Hilary Parkinson presented us with the feisty but well controlled tomboy/ feminist/lesbian, Enid. She had a good voice and made the most of some lovely moments of comedy.

While Hilary Burke, Hazel Park, Kate Barrett, Sarah Allen, Laura Gough and Sinéad Liddy all gave strong individual performances as Delta Nu girls Serena, Margot, Pilar, Kate, Gabby and Cece, it was as a team that they made a superb contribution to the show. I suspect they had been fitted with Duracell batteries; such was the level of their boundless energy. This new generation of Shannon are a force to be reckoned with, each girl displaying acting, singing and dancing abilities in abundance. Great work. Outstanding amid the myriad of supporting female roles was a delightfully ditzy Chutney, hilariously played by Rachel McIntyre, but great support was also offered by Clare McNellis as the Judge, Ruth Byrne as the DA, Debbie Reddan as Elle's Mom, Alison Waldron Cusack as the Reporter, Maria Kelly as the stenographer and Karen Barrett as the Hairdresser.

Mikey O'Gorman gave an assured and likeable performance as Emmet, musically very capable, and sincere in his dealings with Elle. He could have looked a little more dishevelled in the early scenes, which would have added an extra "Wow" factor to his transformation, but his acting compensated for that. Richie Hayes impressed as Warner, having the look, the mannerisms and the arrogance to be totally in love with himself. I loved that when things weren't going his way, he became a bit of a cry-baby! His "Serious" was very well delivered.

Martin McNellis was secure, relaxed and confident in the role of Callahan. "Blood in the Water" was perfectly delivered with a strong and resonant baritone voice, and his performance displayed the maturity of one who is completely at ease on the stage. Very good work. Stephen Byrne as Aaron Schultz, and Brian Roche as Padamadan gave confident support in the Harvard scenes, with well defined characters and good vocals, while Gary Loughnane, Derek Barrett and Daniel Flannagan as Winthrop, Pforzheimer and Lowell gave mature back-up, and were delightfully funny trying to copy the dance styles of the young chorus.

Joe Bracken as Nikos and Chris Willets played their roles with so much conviction that one might have questioned if they were real life partners! Very good comedy from both.

More comedy could have been drawn out of Stephen Ryan in the role of Kyle, but his natural stature served him well, and his "Oirish" dancing was only hilarious. Glen Carr was a suitable 'slob' as Dewey, and in the cameo role of Elle's Dad, Aidan Fox proved two things. There's no such thing as a small part, and he knows absolutely nothing about playing golf. Great visual comedy, timing and twerking!

Ronan Mitchell was an interesting and very amusing Kiki, and Jamie Hickey and Tom Barrett (the Chads) would both give Eminem a run for his money. Good rap! Bruiser and Rufus were superbly played by Mini and Buddy. Did they go to acting school?

Stage Manager Francis Maloney had done a good job on both his stage crew, and ensuring that the members of cast who moved much of the set, were extremely well rehearsed. The set design was a good concept, and while it was clean, tidy and well constructed, it was perhaps a little too simplified, leaving the stage looking a little empty on occasions. What there was, however, was very skilfully manoeuvred around the stage, with a minimum of fuss. The Props team did an excellent job on the bedroom and the salon, with an array of appropriate props. A good job all round.

There's really no need to mention the sound when the balance and cueing are so clean that you aren't even aware of it, so.....

The simplicity of the set required an extensive lighting plot to add atmosphere to the visual impact of the show, and while Michael Finneran's design wasn't lacking in colour, and did present some effective pictures, his washes were all rather general, with not enough attention to specific area lighting. When attempts were made to create pools of light for the more intimate romantic scenes, the back light was often too intense, and it made faces difficult to see. A very 70's style disco effect was over-used in many of the big musical numbers.

A very beautiful set of costumes were created for this show. My only quibble, as mentioned above, was that Emmet could have been a bit dowdier early on to give greater emphasis to his transformation. Elle was always the epitome of glamour, even in her pink sweats, and the Delta Nu girls looked funky and appropriate. A brilliant touch was that when they appeared as the Greek Chorus, they were wearing replicas of their opening costumes, but in white. Attention to wig and hairstyles was noted, and very consistent. Make-up looked natural and nicely over-the-top for the glam girls. Outside the venue doors, there was an enormous pink handbag, and an enormous pink high-heeled shoe. Inside the doors was a treasure trove of memorabilia, photographs and information, and three live mannequins, who were under orders not to flinch. Not contented with that, the entire front-of house staff was adorned with pink ribbon sashes, including the ice-cream sellers. There was such wonderful attention to detail, and all under the supervision of Kathleen Browne.

This was a show that heralded the arrival of the new generation of Shannon, bolstered, of course, by many older and more experienced members. Well I'm delighted to report that, based on their production of "Legally Blonde"; their future is in very safe hands. Thank you for a fun-filled adventure, and an array of wonderful talent.

"42nd Street" is theatrical escapism of the exaggerated variety, full of colour, and life and fun, and theatrical stereotypes. The hard-nosed, successful but down on his luck Director, the chorus girl with the talent to take on the world, the swaggering, self-obsessed tenor, and the ageing-and-conscious-of-it Prima Donna, and so forth. With so many caricatures under one roof, the show is heavy on schmaltz and delightfully pastiche of a certain era.

For pastiche to work, the performers need to play their roles as if they really believe in them. To send up a send-up is to resort to pantomime, and one of the great strengths of this production was the Director's ability, generally, to prevent that from happening.

Director Pat McElwain knew the right approach to his material, and delivered a show that was strong on character, alive with comedy, and brimming with energy. My only concern from a character point of view was the pairing of Dorothy and Abner, whose interpretation of their roles seemed somewhat out of keeping with the rest of the cast, but I'll elaborate on that below.

What was extremely successful, however, was a cracking pace that was sustained throughout the show. The chorus were extremely well integrated into the action, and quite separate from their dancing, they were perfectly choreographed in their reactions. Whatever other issues I may raise with other aspects of the show, the Director had instilled in his performers a level of energy, commitment and self belief that extended beyond the footlights and infected the audience with an appreciation of their talents.

With the exception of a moment of insecurity during the Shadow Waltz, this show was a secure, robust and precise musical delight. The orchestra seemed to really enjoy their music, and thanks to a good sound system, they never sounded restrained nor inhibited. The "42nd Street" Ballet was superbly played. Musical Director, Dermot O'Callaghan, maintained a good balance and control between stage and pit, and as Chorus Master, extracted some excellent vocal harmonies from a well drilled chorus. "Lullaby of Broadway" and "Sunny Side to Every Situation" were particularly impressive; the latter also highlighting many fine solo voices.

At a guess, and by no means as a criticism, I'd say that a large number of the 'hoofers' in this show were not experienced tap dancers, which is a massive compliment in itself to the talent of choreographer Orla Savage, for the opening rehearsal sequence exploded off the stage with excitement, energy and accuracy. Indeed, the tap numbers throughout the show were highlights of the choreography. They had flow, rhythm and plenty of variety, but most important of all, they were performed with total conviction and radiant smiling faces. "Getting Out Of Town" and "Lullaby of Broadway" were well moved, but I'm not sure that the middle section of the "Dames" number reflected the quirkiness of the musical accompaniment. There was a good attempt at story-telling in the 42nd Street Ballet, the atmosphere of which wasn't helped at all by the scenery, which in turn made the costumes look a little drab, but it was very well performed, and built to a good climax. I'm sure Orla was well pleased to have Bronwyn Andrews, Stuart Pollock and Stephen Ryan as her main dancing principals, all of whom performed with panache. Very good work.

Conor Kilduff, as Julian Marsh, established his character from the moment he stepped on to the stage. He was confident and convincing, striking a nice balance between the bravado of the successful Broadway director, and the insecurity of the guy who desperately needs to re-establish his career. I particularly liked his playing of the final scenes with Peggy, with a touching sincerity in his recognition that she was but a young girl, beguiled, perhaps, by his charisma. His final solo was delightful and strong.

Bronwyn Andrews had the acting, the singing and the dancing skills required to make the most of the demanding role of Peggy Sawyer. She displayed beautiful comedy timing throughout, but also a warm sincerity in her scenes with Julian. I totally believed that she was overwhelmed at being that "speck of dust". Beautiful work.

Kathy Kelly as Maggie was a well defined and extremely funny character. She had the perfect diction that is needed to accompany an exaggerated accent, and when required, she could certainly belt out a song! Good comedy acting and a fine voice. A very 'natural' performance. As a young director, I once suggested to a performer that he needed to focus more on his acting, to which he unashamedly replied, "I'm not an actor, dear. I'm a tenor!" Times, thankfully, have changed, and in re-creating that old school attitude, tenor Stuart Pollock, ironically acted, sang and even danced his pants off with a beautifully crafted performance.

Brian O'Gorman gave a warm and very likeable quality to Bert Barry, noticeably respectful of Marsh, intimidated by Dorothy, dominated by his writing partner, and comfortable in the silliness of "Shuffle off to Buffalo".

There was no question mark regarding Joanne Logue's talent and ability, performing Dorothy Brock, as she did, with comedy and confidence, but I think her credibility as a caustic Diva was weakened by her 'clowning' of the early scenes. The Shadow Waltz should have been funny at her expense, rather than by her antics. She did end Act One most dramatically, and thankfully, upon her return in Act Two, she shone in her acceptance of her circumstances, and there was great sincerity in her speech to Peggy, and her delivery of "About A Quarter To Nine".

In appearance, I'm not convinced that Kris Kendellen, as Abner Dillon, would have appealed to Dorothy, even if he had been twice as rich. He did look more of a backwoodsman than a business tycoon, and while the outfit and facial hair were obviously for comedic effect, I think he proved, through his competent acting of the role, that he could achieve the goofiness of the character without the somewhat out of place trimmings.

Stage presence and top notch terpsichorean talent, made Stephen Ryan the perfect choice as choreographer Andy Lee. He led the opening number with authority, and sustained his strong character throughout the show. Delightful.

Ciarán Lenehen had a good 'washed up' look about himself as Pat Denning. It's a fairly thankless role, but he played it with sincerity and always looked at ease on the stage.

Aisling O'Callaghan was pretty and perky, but could perhaps have been a tad more provocative as Anytime Annie. She performed well with Bert in "Shuffle off to Buffalo". Teresa Gallagher had a few 'foot loose' moments as Lorraine, but alongside Sarah O'Driscoll's accomplished Phyllis, they provided good back-up to Annie and Maggie. James MacEoin as Mac gave good support.

Scenic Projects supplied a set that was sufficient to create the drab 'empty stage', back stage, and rehearsal sections of the show. Its raised level and stairways worked well for the train station and the split level party/Dorothy's room sequence, and the truck piece with the Dressing room mirrors on one side and the train sleeping carriages on the reverse was a very sturdy and well designed piece. There was also a good "dressing room" truck that had an authentic cluttered feel to it. But "42nd Street" is probably the ultimate "showbiz" show, depending, particularly for the show within the show, on glitz and glamour, and I'm sorry to say that, on this score, they missed the mark by a long shot. For "Pretty Lady" to be "the best show that Broadway has seen in 20 years", it really did require spectacular pieces for "Dames", "We're in the Money" and particularly the "42nd Street Ballet". The whole mood of this piece is dark and jazzy, with a tragic love story being swallowed up by the ever moving, ever pretentious glitz of that "glittering gulch". But the centre piece was psychedelic, loud and distracting. Despite the best efforts of the lighting designer, it was almost impossible to create atmosphere with something close to a 'day-glow' background. Lighting Designer, Denis Twomey, did however make the most of his opportunities to display his capabilities, with excellent lighting through the gauze, tight and precise cues for the 'dressing room' lights, and good cueing generally. The rope lights, etc, on the set were well used, and not over-used. There were well defined playing areas, with everyone clearly lit, and again, good cueing between upper and lower levels in the party scene.

Stage Manager Gerry McCann and his team did their utmost to compensate, by providing a smooth running show with tidy and efficient scene changes, and there were plenty of appropriate props and furniture to help create the atmosphere of the piece. There were no problems with the sound system.

With the exception of the somewhat outrageous styling of Abner Dillon, very good work was done on the hairstyles, wigs and make-up, although I did think that Peggy's finale wig, or maybe just the style of it, was a bit severe.

Day costumes were very good and well worn, and the red set of dance costumes for "Dames" were a nice design, but might have been better displayed had the girls entered in fashion show style, down the centre stairway, instead of streaming in from right and left, obscured by the men. To follow that routine with more red (and gold) in the "We're in the Money" routine, was just too much red! The frenzy of fluorescent colour on the back piece for the ballet tended to make the costumes look dull in comparison. (Not the fault of the costumes.)

Despite the criticisms, it is a credit to director, choreographer, musicians and performers alike that this show still bounced off the stage with enthusiasm, life and energy. I thoroughly enjoyed the performances of a very dedicated and talented company, and am thankful to all concerned for a most enjoyable evening. Thanks also to Leo Kilroy who met Donna and myself in the foyer and looked after us very well before, during and after the show.

I hate that feeling when you're watching a good movie and something happens to prevent you from seeing the end of it... oh God, it's so frustrating. Mind you, when the interruption is the breaking news that Eva Peron has died... well, you quickly forget all about the movie, and realise that you are caught up in a moment of history. Such was the case in the Simon Ryan Theatre, Tipperary when the curtain rose on what was to prove a visually delightful, musically powerful and dramatically absorbing production of Evita.

A twelve piece orchestra, under the baton of Musical Director Danny Carroll, sounded balanced and secure in their playing. I would have to single out that the most sublime and beautiful solos from guitarist, Dave Keary, were such a pleasure to listen to. Tempos were good, balance between players was good, and while I initially worried that the orchestra were a tad loud for the singers on stage, within a scene, the balance had been achieved. Chorus and principals alike were very secure in their music. And what a chorus. Helen Colbert, as chorus mistress, extracted wonderful harmony and expression from her singers. "Peron's Latest Flame" and "A New Argentina" brought a powerful and impressive end to the first act, and in Act Two, even the children in "Santa Evita" were well disciplined. Very good work.

Director, Des Henn took a good no-frills approach to this production. Without feeling the need to swamp the show with gimmicks, it was generally clean, precise and visually perfect, allowing the performers and the music to be the true stars of the piece. The set was quite simple, but beautifully constructed, and stunning in its simplicity. It was extremely well used to give the feeling of space and a variety of locations, and many beautiful pictures were painted on the stage with good use of the performers. The projection screens were well used, but not over-used, and the images were always relevant to the stage action. I was initially concerned that the show was going to drag, for the opening scenes, from the cinema up to the introduction of Migaldi, albeit beautifully presented, did seem to happen rather slowly, but I'm happy to report that from then on, the pace was excellent, and the action totally engaging.

I would have liked Eva to have shown a little more rawness in the early scenes, and perhaps that might have been created by spicing up the "Good Night and Thank You" routine, indicating that her ability to seduce a nation, stemmed from the practice that she put in along the way. By the time she cast off Peron's in-house mistress, however, she began to illuminate the stage.

"The Art of the Possible" was sinister, and very well executed (excuse the pun)! The final scenes of the show were extremely emotional.

One minor quibble and I know that as a show, Evita lacks comedy, but I'm not convinced that the dancing Pope and Bishops were in keeping with all that went before and after.

Barbara Meany presented very clean and uncomplicated choreography. Much of the show requires 'movement' as opposed to dance, and it was a credit to Barbara that patterns and pictures were always tidy, interesting and well executed. Of the opportunities for dance, "Buenos Aires" was lively and effective, and while the second act waltz was nicely performed, it's almost a taunting scene, and perhaps could have been a little more provocative. All in all, the tidy precision of all the movement contributed significantly to the tone of this production, and as such, was extremely good work.

Deirdre Ryan's development in performance paralleled Eva Peron's growth as a personality through the show. I was unsure of her at the beginning, wishing she was more flirtatious, more of a seductress, unsophisticated and a little more brash and obvious. But within a few scenes, she gradually became her character, acquiring a calculated charm, an unflinching resolve and a controlling, manipulative force. By the end of Act One, she truly was Eva, and in Act Two she was sublime. Her singing, from the outset, was quite excellent.

The power of the voice of Derek Ryan was the strength of his characterisation of Peron. He had a commanding presence on the stage, and yet, was sensitive enough to appear mesmerised by Eva, and vulnerable enough to be overwhelmed by her. A very balanced and emotional performance, and sung to perfection.

Ray Nolan was a relaxed and assured Ché, vocally secure and confident in his narration of the story. He was well integrated into the action of the scenes, and the only place I would have liked to see him exhibit a bit more fire was in his taunting of Eva during the "Waltz" scene. He handled this demanding role comfortably, and connected well with the audience. Very nicely done.

Jack Sharpe displayed a very melodic tenor voice as Magaldi, and from his demeanour, there was little question that he would be duped and abandoned by Eva. This was a good steady performer. Fiona O'Connor, as the mistress, acted and reacted very well to being summarily dismissed by Eva, and her rendition of "Another Suitcase" was beautiful and expressive. I loved that she cheekily reappeared beside Peron while Eva was off on her Rainbow Tour.

The set for this production was simply beautiful, with a stone appearance of crafted arches on the high level, with good functional balconies right and left, the centre balcony and staircases leading down to the main stage, with its enclosed courtyard feeling. Stage Manager, Brian English, was probably delighted that the set had no moving parts, and it gave him and his crew plenty of time to move the props that were effectively utilised to suggest the changes of location. The props were well selected, and plentiful, and much work went into the array of flags, bunting, placards, etc, that graced the Act One finale.

In all likelihood, the single set may have become tiresome had it not been for an absolutely excellent lighting plot, which saw the structure of the castle take on an entirely new life and atmosphere with a simple colour change. A lavender- washed love chalet became a green and shadowy dungeon, or the peaches and cream courtyard of the aristocracy. Colour selections were perfect and out of the ordinary, and a multitude of well positioned specials ensured that the focus of attention was always illuminated without losing the atmosphere. There was nothing pretentious or flashy about the plot... it's was quite simply comparable to looking at a series of perfectly painted landscapes. Congratulations to the artist, lighting designer, Joe Betts. As mentioned above, the projections contributed beautifully to the show, courtesy of Star Systems, who also provided a sound system which, in keeping with the other technical aspects of the show, was precise and perfectly in balance. Costumes for the show were excellent. Military uniforms were appropriate, the common people looked plain without looking shabby, and the aristocratic costumes were radiant. More importantly, the cast wore the costumes with good attention to presentation. Hairstyles/wigs were always in keeping, and make-up was natural, with Eva losing colour effectively as her sickness developed.

I left Tipperary town with a glow of appreciation for a very beautiful, highly emotional and thoroughly entertaining night of quality musical theatre. Thank you so much for the enjoyment.

Director, Tony Finnegan, deserves top marks for the inspirational concept of transporting The Pirates of Penzance from the Cornish Coast to the bedroom of a little boy, and presenting the entire show as dream sequence, in the young fellow's imagination. Not only was it a charming twist on the original, but it had good practical implications. Beds that became a boat, and then became crypts, made life easier for the stage crew, and the "child's dream" scenario allowed for an interesting and creative opening sequence.

The chorus had been thoroughly directed to be constantly animated, which was always the case. The men were the roughest of rough pirates, and the females were deliciously ditzy. There was also a lot of individuality within the chorus.

It was, perhaps, because the first act of the show was so powerfully delivered, that it seemed to lose a bit of momentum in act two. Having marvelled at "Hail Poetry", I expected "When The Foeman Bares His Steel" to bring the house down, which sadly wasn't the case. There was a tendency with the policemen to sacrifice accuracy for the sake of outrageous comedy, and perhaps a better balance could have been achieved. I was surprised that, in the wake of so much innovation and creativity, the finale of the show was a little ordinary. However, the final picture, of all the crazy characters surrounding the sleeping child in his bed as the dream draws to a close, will stay with. A little moment of pure magic. Aisling Toher did a very good job of echoing the director's vision of a racy and energy-packed production. It's a show with limited opportunities for indulgent choreography, but when they arose, Aisling impressed not only with steps and patterns, but also with a fine sense of comedy in her routines. My only concern was that the polish of routines involving the policemen suffered a little from over-exaggerated silliness.

Kevin Fagan, as Frederic, was excellent in every respect. As singer, actor, comedian or dancer, this is a performer who works incredibly hard at every aspect of his performance, without ever looking as if it requires any effort, so natural and assured is his stage presence.

Trim must have been delighted to welcome Jessica Hackett into their ranks, to undertake the role of Mabel, with the most beautiful soprano voice. She displayed great control, and good comic ability in her delivery of her 'trills' during "Poor Wand'ring One", and her duet with Frederic, "Ah, leave me not to pine alone", was a musical highlight of the show. Her ability to act as well as she sings made her the perfect Mabel.

As her sisters, Edith, Kate and Isabel, there were strong performances from Siobhan McAleese, Emma Stowe and Megan Pottinger, respectively. Siobhan had a strong mezzo range and good comical indignation. Emma was hilariously feisty and provocative, and Megan was playful, serene and delightful.

The female cast was completed by a stalwart and robust performance from Siobhan Fawsitt as Ruth, exhibiting excellent comedy timing, and the perfect vocal requirement for the role.

As the Pirate King, Craig Regan was somewhere between Johnny Depp's Jack Sparrow and Kevin Kline's Pirate King, playing the role with a kind of quirky, confused arrogance. He had good confidence and a fine baritone voice.

As his side-kick, Samuel, Ian Rountree made the most of his opportunities to shine, showing a good sense of character comedy.

Colin Flynn's Major General was articulate and precise, clearly putting across the patter of his song. He had lovely inter-play with the children, and his comedic ability was well accentuated in his "Orphan boy" sequence.

Sean Fox was a visually effective Sergeant of Police, but as with the policemen's chorus, diction tended to suffer amid the extremes of comedy business. When it was articulate, he displayed a secure bass/baritone voice. Young Daniel Barniville as Bart, and Jim Harrigan as his playmate, did a splendid job of realising the Director's inventive approach to the telling of the story. As already mentioned, the Director's vision of a show set entirely within the confines of a child's bedroom, allowed Stage Manager, Frank Connolly, to have very much a supervisory role. Most of the movement of props and furniture on stage was carried out, in a disciplined manner, by members of the cast. A vast array of appropriate props had been gathered and were well utilised during the performance. The lanterns were Programme Adjudicator Seeks Email Addresses Programme Adjudicator, Noel Dundon, has requested that each group includes an e-mail address when submitting programmes for adjudication. The completed adjudication will then be e-mailed back thereby ensuring that it is returned much more efficiently. Simply include an email address for the intended recipient or officers of the group along with the programme and this will suffice.

particularly delightful and well used to create atmosphere. The set itself was solid and well painted, giving the enclosed sense of the bedroom, but also the strong hint of the more traditional seaside location.

The lighting plot was generally very acceptable, with good atmospheric blends of colour. Principals were occasionally in shadow, particularly on the periphery of the set. I appreciate that the designer didn't want to throw over-powering pools of light and distracting shadows on the walls, but when principals were elevated up-stage or standing on the bed stage right, this resulted in them being a little under-lit. The star cloth above and behind the bedroom was well utilised.

Sound quality throughout the show was most satisfactory, with the exception of a late cue on Frederic at one stage. A good balance was struck between the orchestra and the on-stage performers. The visual impact of this show was one of its great strengths. Costumes were appropriate and well worn, with much attention to the detail of gloves, shoes, etc. The children were charmingly attired throughout. An abundance of wigs and facial hair added tremendously to the authentic look of the pirates, and female styles were well achieved. Make-up looked natural, including successful ageing of the Major General, and the requisite paling of the policemen.

With an excellent company spirit, and the employment of extremely competent professional services, Trim seem to be getting the recipe perfectly right and it was such a pleasure to be carried along on the crest of a wave with the famous Pirates of Penzance. Sincere thanks.

Director Paul Norton tried to put himself inside the mind of Mel Brookes when putting together this raunchy, rambunctious production of The Producers. He wasn't afraid to go for the jugular in his efforts to entertain in the bawdiest of manners. From maximising the comedy potential of a person of short stature, to accentuating the frolics of sexually gymnastic Grannies, glamorising Adolph Hitler was probably the least politically insensitive aspect of the show.

The combination of irreverent humour and excellent comedic performers resulted in a highly entertaining romp of the risqué variety! It was most certainly a crowd pleaser....assuming the crowd didn't include any aged, vertically challenged, gay, Jewish, politically correct, feminist puritans. There were moments when the humour walked the very thin line between good and bad taste.

The pace of the show was very good, and efforts were made to cover difficult scene changes, either with dialogue or comedy business. I did find some of the duets and principals numbers a bit static when balanced against the very animated direction of the script.

Technically, the show is very demanding, with so many scene changes, and by and large, the concept of the set was good, but it did lack 'show-biz' glamour, and with Paul also performing in the show, he possibly needed a second pair of eyes to draw his attention to visual problems, such as poor lighting during his otherwise brilliantly performed "Betrayed" number. There was good integration of the chorus into the action, all of whom were well focused and highly spirited.

Musical Director Shane Farrell led a strong orchestra with confidence and control, keeping a good pace to the music and a tight rein on the volume. The balance between stage and pit was spot on, and Shane even took part in the action, when he was taunted from the stage. Good work had been done on vocal harmonies, which were evident throughout the show, and all of his principals were vocally secure.

Choreographer, Aoife McClafferty, made a good impact with the opening numbers, setting the scene nicely with "Opening Night", and having a well drilled and energetic chorus in "The King of Broadway". "I Want to be a Producer" was tidy and well presented, but with an over-use of very modern 'hip-hop' movements. "Along Came Bialy" was a very strong routine, making excellent use of the demented grannies and their Zimmer frames. "Springtime for Hitler" was simple but effective, and Aoife should feel justly proud of her chorus and dancers for always looking enthusiastic and comfortable in their routines.

In the role of Max Bialystock, Paul Norton led from the front, with a rock solid performance, filled with great comical delivery of his lines and intuitive stage awareness. It was notable that he was also generous with the lime-light, never appearing to upstage his fellow performers. He established his character right from the outset, and impressed with his vocal ability throughout. A strong and balanced performance.

Patrick Byrne was comically and delightfully fragile as Leo Bloom. His physical comedy was excellent, and beside Paul, there was a touch of Laurel and Hardy about their antics. Patrick nailed his songs with confidence, but was at his best with blue-blankey in hand, and trying to cope with the affections of Ulla. Such an enjoyable performance. Sarah Corcoran was a sassy Ulla, with a strong voice and a good sense of comedy. Good diction accompanied a good accent, and she used her natural assets comfortably to seduce Leo and to tease Max. I think more could have been made of her dance during "When You've Got it", but that aside, she was vivacious and entertaining throughout.

Excellent facial expressions were a great strength of Brian Derrane's performance as Roger De Bris. He kept it gay from start to finish, obviously enjoying the diversity of his character. He was very musically secure in all his numbers, and performed "Heil Myself" with aplomb. As Roger's partner, Carmen Ghia, Nicky Lawless had more mince than a Christmas hamper, he was skippier than a bush kangaroo, and camper than a boys scout jamboree! This was a deliciously silly caricature, played for every ounce of fun. I loved the signature 'flick' of the heel.

Séamus Feerick added a wealth of experience to his performance as Franz Liebkind, with secure timing and delivery. There was plenty of silliness in his "Der Guten Tag Hop-Clop", and was particularly funny brandishing his gun and limping around the stage in a cast. Bernie Dudgeon turned a cameo role into a Tour de Force, as Hold Me, Touch Me, not a bit afraid to fill her granny character with the most outlandish sexuality. Extremely funny and surprisingly agile, for her age!

Mike O'Reilly competently played a string of cameo roles, each with a distinct individuality, and of the plethora of supporting roles, Kevin Griffin wallowed in being outrageously attired. His dancing Hitler was hilarious, and he sang and moved well as the Storm Trooper.

Mark Mulligan, un-credited for any specific role in the show programme, gave a performance of monumental stature every time he appeared on the stage. His mischief was a comedy highlight of the production.

The chorus, in their various guises, performed with energy and a great sense of fun, with the Grannies being particularly funny and outrageous. Stage Manager, Pat McGovern, and a well organised crew, worked a difficult set with a minimum of fuss. Early changes were on the slow side, but by no means untidy. A very good job was done by the props team in assembling a vast array of appropriate props. The pigeons were excellent.

While the set was functional and adequate enough to suggest the various locations, the painting of much of it was flat and two-dimensional. Theatre signs looked roughly hand painted and had little impact, and when doors are only painted as doors on one side, it would be better to have them open out, so the door reverse remains unseen. The office interior was full of good detail, the safe, the cabinet with photos, etc.

Paul Kelly's lighting design was generally good and well balanced, with good use of colours and nicely highlighted areas, but the cueing did tend to be a little lethargic, with background lighting in place for a few seconds before face light arrived. The Max in Jail scene was frustrating. I appreciate the effect that was being attempted (shafts of light through the bars), but in a number that requires so much facial expression, the actor was extremely difficult to see clearly.

Sound, throughout, was of a good quality, with the performers always audible, and there were very good sound effects. I particularly loved the sound of traffic and the street below when Max opened the window in his office.

Principal costumes throughout the show were very good and appropriate. Chorus day costumes were more than adequate, and the 'show' costumes were beautiful, and in keeping with the glitzy 'show-biz' style of the show.

There were good wigs and hair styles in abundance, even if Roger's 'Hitler' wig was a tad 'bouffant', and make-up was always appropriate. Very good work on the grannies, and delicious blue eye- shadow for the...erm... effeminate men! Sincere thanks to everyone involved in this crazy, fun-filled production. I laughed the whole way home.

I thought I had mistakenly walked into a church when I entered the auditorium of the Strand Theatre in Carrick-on- Suir, so stunning and realistic were the projections that were being used as a pre-set for the show. This was just a teaser for a brilliantly presented projection show that became the backdrop for the action throughout the performance. It was a courageous piece of innovation on the part of director Liam Butler, to put so much faith in technology, but then again... isn't this a show all about faith?

This was unquestionably the best attempt at projecting the scenery onto the stage that I have witnessed in an amateur show. Not only were the projections well selected, but they had strength of tone, good definition and a very 3D effect. And the feast continued with offices, brick-lined streets, pubs and nightclubs, all appropriate and to scale for the stage. The sharpness of the projections was largely due to the surfaces not being flooded with light, wherein, sadly, a dilemma arose.

Lighting Designers John Hurley and Liam Butler put so much effort into trying to light the stage effectively without washing out the projections, but unfortunately this led to dark patches here and there, and quite a lot of principal work played in shadow and half-shadow, a problem that was consistent throughout the show. Excellent use was made of back light and side light to create acting pools, and when these worked, the effect was powerful and atmospheric, and I'm convinced that with more experimentation, your design team are only steps away from refining this style of presentation. Perhaps a combination of all that you got right, and the use of 'moving heads' to follow principals might be part of the solution?

Just when I was thinking "This is awesome", the bar was raised even higher with the introduction of 'moving' projections, creating a spectacular techno-show behind some of the musical numbers. What a visual delight.

The set, consisting of a number of white moving screens, was beautifully used to create smaller spaces, and particularly effective was the "Fabulous Baby" Reprise, when the screens opened and closed, revealing the nuns in Deloris's mind. The confessional booth was a wonderful piece of furniture. Stage Manager, Michael O'Hara, and his team, ensured that everything was in its proper place with a minimum of fuss.

The stage space was generally very well used, with chorus entrances and exits being smooth and natural.

Perhaps Monsignor O'Hara and the Mother Superior could have been boosted slightly in the Act One finale to make their solo lines more audible above a powerful chorus.

And what a chorus! Whether on or off stage, choruses were strong and accurate, with well realised harmonies, "Raise Your Voice" and "Take Me To Heaven" at the end of Act One being particularly up-lifting. Principals were well rehearsed and extremely musically secure. I really liked that the 'bad' singing by the nuns was delightfully controlled and off-key, rather than pantomimed shrieks. Apart from abruptly interrupting the 'house' announcements, by starting the overture prematurely, Fergal Carroll led an excellent orchestra with authority and control. The sound that emanated from the pit was consistently of the highest calibre. Pace was perfect, with the nun's numbers being punctuated with a great 'gospel' feel.

I'm sure choreographer Patricia Woods was very proud of the commitment, energy and discipline of her chorus and dancers. She used every opportunity to display her choreographic range, from the funky pop styles of the Fantasy Dancers, to the polished gospel routines of the nun's chorus. With so many show- stopper numbers, it's easy to become repetitive, but she varied her steps and used ever-changing patterns to keep the show constantly fresh and alive.

What a complete performance from Irene Malone as Deloris Van Cartier. I laughed at her comedy, delighted in her vocals, and melted in her moments of sincerity. Her timing was immaculate, her body language inspired, her accent superb, and when she let rip in the big vocal numbers, she was a power house of confidence and excellence. Truly inspiring.

Pat Quinn-Bolger was a sober and spiritually salubrious Mother Superior, maintaining a dignified deportment amid the surrounding mayhem. Her delivery of "I Haven't Got a Prayer" was excellent, and she underwent a very believable conversion when she accepted Deloris as a Godsend. A very nicely balanced performance.

Louise Mulcahy was a delight in the role of Sr Mary Robert, putting across the youthful insecurities of a spiritually confused postulant, and then the strident confidence of self-discovery. "The Life I Never Led" was beautifully and emotionally delivered.

Sandra Power was a vivacious Sr Mary Patrick, buzzing with energy and enthusiasm... the kind of person who would wreck your head if you had a hang-over! A highly amusing portrayal and a strong and confident vocal performance.

I thought I would burst a blood vessel laughing at Marie Kelly as Sr Mary Lazarus. She was visually excellent, her 'rapping' was even better than her singing, and when she started break dancing, I could hardly catch a breath. A hilarious performance from start to finish. Fergus Power really looked the part, and extracted good comedy from the role of Monsignor O'Hara. He provided strong and confident support to the sisters, and played well to the 'congregation' i n t h e auditorium.

Ray Nolan created a very likeable Eddie Souther, with a secure singing voice, and good stage presence.

His quick change routine for "I Could Be That Guy" was very well done, and he handled the awkwardness of the would-be lover very effectively.

Seamus Power (above) was a convincing and amusingly goofy Curtis Jackson. His stature gave him the look of a natural leader, and it was a close call, but I think he was just ever so slightly more intelligent than his gang members TJ, Joey and Pablo, played with good effect by Bobby Landers, Jimsy Dowley and Caolán Deehy-Power respectively. I did find that the pace of dialogue slowed a little too much during their scenes, but they provided good back up to a nice performance of "When I Find My Baby" from Seamus, and their own "Lady in the Long Black Dress" was highly comical. A host of well realised cameo roles were strongly led by Jenny Hogan as Sr Mary Martin of Tours and Helen Hahessy as Sr Mary Theresa. Indeed, most of the nuns chorus displayed good individuality, as well as functioning as part of a slick chorus group.

How many variations of a nun's costume is it possible to create in one production? Well, I think I counted 4 or 5 at least, with a bit more glitz and glamour being added to the plain habits as the nuns grew in confidence. Very nice work. Deloris looked fabulous; wig included, and was particularly striking in the finale. The Fantasy dancers were appropriately attired and very colourful. "Street" characters had good personality in costume and wigs/hair-styles, as did the gangsters. A very well presented visual treat. Sister Mary Lazarus's make-up was excellent.

I greatly admire the courage and creativity of the company for the direction in which they took this adventurous production, and I hope they continue to be adventurous in the future. Thank you for a wonderful night of entertainment, where technical innovation provided a delightful enhancement to a musical treasure chest and some stunning theatrical performances.

The magnificent "Glor" theatre is situated in the heart of Ennis and what a most wonderful venue it is. I met with the Chairperson Anne Marie Hassett who extolled on me how lucky they were to be able to avail of such a wonderful venue for performances. "Footloose" is not a musical that is performed very often but after seeing this production I wonder why? It has numerous parts for all ages both male and female and has the most wonderful rip-roaring score full of songs that brought me back to my youth. The show revolves around Ren McCormack (Jamie Sheahan) who along with his mother move to a small town in middle USA called Bomont. The town is run by the Reverend and his committee and dancing is banned!  Jamie Sheahan led from the front in both singing and dancing and his accent and dialogue were excellent. His opposite number Siofra Ni Eili Duggan (Ariel) gave us an acting performance of warmth, passion and forgiveness and was also very feisty when needed to be, and her singing was perfectly in tune. She was ably assisted by her three "bff's" Shona Connellan (Urleen) and Ciara Lynch (Wendy Jo) who sang beautiful harmonies in the Burger Blast scene, and Sinead Coughlan (Rusty). Ms Coughlan also performed most wonderfully and she had some marvellous acting moments with Declan Honan (Willett). Mr Honan was the comedy foil for most of the show and he carried off this role superbly. There are a number of adult parts for older players in "Footloose" but I must single out two. Andie Doolan played Ren's mother, and she opened the show with a wonderful musical rendition full of controlled power and superb diction and then later she sang most beautifully in the trio. Neil Haran (Rev Moore) was excellent in his portrayal of the dominant member of the council, his anger and rage bubbled throughout his performance and then at the end when he recognised the error of his ways he acted with suitable melancholy and grace. The set gave us suitable height for the chapel and railway scenes, the lighting was varied and concise and the sound was correct throughout. A lot of work went into the costumes particularly the "BHS" school shirts and the cowboy line dancers. Sarah Griffin took on the dual role of Director and Choreographer which was admirable, perhaps more time could have been spent on the dancing, particularly the male chorus. Shane Farrell was musical director and his control of the chorus, principals and orchestra was superb when he conducted. Overall a most wonderful afternoon's entertainment and I look forward to visiting this wonderful theatre again in the future.

Enniscorthy Musical Society's production of this musical, of some of the writings of Dr Seuss, was a most vibrant spectacle of colour and imagination. The set was perfectly situated with a towering tree, the centrepiece in which Paul Walsh (Horton) perched in as he looked after his egg! The egg was owned by Therese Bolger (Mayzie) who gave us a most wonderful singing performance throughout the show culminating in a perfectly powerful rendition of Mayzie in Palm Beach. Emily Brazzill (Gertrude) was Horton's love interest and she sang with wonderful diction and voice control and eased herself around the stage not letting her over long tail distract her. Marian O'Leary (Sour Kangaroo) delivered her dialogue crisply and sang with power and punch and then at the end she capitulated so gracefully. Dylan Walsh (The Cat in the hat) played the role with a suitably manic characterisation and he bounded around the stage with endless energy. The performance of the evening belonged to Eryn Buckley (Jojo). This young girl sang with a voice that belied her tender age, perfectly in tune and superb diction, a marvellous performance. The technical side of the show required a little bit more care and attention as the lighting and sound cues were not as tight as they might have been. Anne Marie Cooney's choreography of the large chorus numbers used fluent and controlled movements but the smaller cameo dancers needed a bit more precision. Musical director Kevin Kennedy allowed the volume of the orchestra to impede some of the singers and he just needed to keep a firmer grip on the musicians. This show requires vibrant colours top bring Dr Seuss' characters to life and the costume department absolutely achieved this perfectly, throw in a most wonderful all round presentation of hair and make-up the ladies in these three departments all worked perfectly together to give a marvellous visual display. The audience of adults and children had a marvellous night's entertainment as did I.

show_raw: The 25Th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee
review_text: My second visit to the small and compact Belvoir Players Studio in Belfast. This show is not performed very often and yet with only a cast of 15 players required it would be perfect for a youth society in which to improve and hone their stagecraft. A fixed set consisting of two tables and some steps allows for set spots to be in situ with only small adjustments required in the lighting department. A particularly good sound technician is required as the audience have to hear the spelling of words as this is paramount to the performance. The characters include three adults, two of which are schoolteachers and the other adult in attendance is on "community service", these players keep the momentum of the show going. They also have to integrate the "four guinea pigs" that are chosen from the audience and who are entered into the actual spelling bee competition. This is a fundamental part of the show and provides great fun and merriment particularly from those in the audience related to the guinea pigs. Director Jordan Walsh kept the show moving along rapidly and ensured that each characterisation was defined, the choreography by Alex McFarlane was sharp and precise and full of energy. Musical director Drew Vincent kept reasonable control over his 5 piece band which had good balance and tone but on occasion was a bit loud for the players. The story revolves around the six main spellers ably supported by the "adults" and the "ensemble". The leading lady was played by Jenny Coates (Olive Ostrovsky), who possesses so much energy in her portrayal that she bounces around the stage fully in control of her accent and her singing which was delivered perfectly in tune. Ethan Haddock (William Barfee) played the geeky scientist to a tee, and along with a mad hairstyle performed his part by delivering dialogue so crisply assisted by his "magic foot"! Johnathan Brown played (Leaf Coneybear), his character was introverted and very babyish but he still managed to give us perfect diction in his dialogue. Amy Cahoon (Marcy) played the straight laced lady with perfect hair and costumes, wonderful stage presence and she danced most sublimely. Josh Trainor (Chip Tolentino) was a boy scout and was the spitting image of Russell in "Up". He gave us a good characterisation and he has a wonderful comedic number at the start of Act 2 which leads to his demise. Finally we get to Holly McConville, (Logainne Schwartzandgrubenniere), she has two dads who dote upon her but also put enormous pressure on her to succeed which she handles quite wonderfully. Unfortunately two dads results in her very long surname which is an amalgamation of her two dads! This show can be played as a one Act but on this occasion two short 45 minute acts, meant that the audience were treated to a marvellous night's entertainment.

"Whistle Down The Wind" is a challenging show, but the cast of Fusion Theatre Group took to the stage with confidence and an abundance of talent. There were some outstanding voices, many accomplished actors and a whole company of good movers and shakers. Technically and visually, the show was very tidy, and all in all, it was easy for the audience to become completely absorbed by this production.

Musical Director, Ian Milford, led a very neat orchestra who comfortably met the demands of the music for this show. They were always sympathetic to the on stage performers and pace and rhythm was consistent throughout. As Chorus Master, he presented a well-rehearsed group who were true to their harmonies, and full of expression. The Vaults of Heaven and Wrestle With the Devil were particularly good numbers. Principals, likewise, seemed very secure and well- rehearsed.

The opening number, "The Vaults of Heaven" can often be a dreary, rather Presbyterian affair, but Ian Milford (who also directed) went for instant impact by presenting it as a joyous Gospel style hymn, with a congregation who were rocking in the aisles. Throughout the show, the chorus were generally well used and involved in the action, with entrances and exits forming part of the natural flow of the scenes.

I had issues with Amos being allowed to over-sexualise his scenes with Candy and particularly with Swallow. A bit more subtlety was required.

The real snakes were a nice touch, and indeed the Wrestle With the Devil scene was excellent. It had the creepily authentic feel of a revivalist meeting, with Swallow very well integrated into the action.

There was a good level of confidence among the main principals, but I do feel that some of the more minor principal roles could have done with a little more assistance with their character development. But it has to be said that, by and large, this was a very competently directed show.

Jillian Liggett did a really good job of injecting life into the chorus, from the lively and animated gospel movements of the opening number, to a well presented dance sequence in the "Cold" number. Good pairs dance. The children's chorus have only a few opportunities to dance, but when they did, their movement was appropriate and well-rehearsed.

Sean Harkin, as The Man, made his mark on this role with a passionate and spirited vocal performance. He had a fine tenor voice, with a most effective falsetto, and he used it well to give emotion to his character. He worked his socks off to make him believable, but he does need to focus on his hands and arms, which moved awkwardly and were a bit of a distraction. The suddenness of some of his gestures (especially his passionate 'attack' of Swallow in the penultimate scene), was bordering on melodramatic. Lucy Donnelly, as Swallow, was a delight to watch, and had an absolutely beautiful young voice. There was a vulnerability about her, and yet a great inner strength, and for one so young, she realised all the subtleties of expressing those qualities. A really heart-warming performance. She was also very well supported by Aimme McVeigh as Brat and Patrick Glover as Poor Baby, the former being a vibrant bundle of energy, and the latter full of mischief and charm. They were also two great little singers.

Cameron Mack gave a very tender and emotional portrayal to Boone, a father struggling with the loss of his wife and trying to raise his children alone. This was a totally believable performance, not only very well acted, but sung with a perfectly melodic voice, and a great depth of emotion.

James Marsden had a good voice for the role of Amos, and while he was certainly animated, he did need to be reined in regarding the intensity of his attentions towards Swallow. (His physicality with her was a little uncomfortable, I detected, for the audience.)

Beth McNally was a very sassy Candy, and any awkwardness at trying to appear 'sexy', was forgotten in her fiery display of anger at being stood up by Amos. Good emotions and good singing of her musical numbers.

Rory Jeffries made a very decent effort at the role of Edward, and "Cold" was a very well put over number. Elsewhere, he was a good friend to Boone, and a good voice of reason for Candy.

Ian Simpson seemed to enjoy the role of the Sheriff, complete with cool-dude sunglasses, and he was consistent throughout the show.

Connor Richardson as the Snake Preacher, and Tiarnan Daykin as Earl, were very credible, if a little melo- dramatic, and Connor did very well with the very difficult "Wrestle with the Devil" number.

Samuel Milford as the Deputy, and Andrew Johnston as the Church Singer, led a host of other cameo roles in providing good back up. Andrew sang "The Vaults of Heaven" well, but could have done with being amplified a bit more when the chorus joined in.

As mentioned above, the chorus contributed very well to every aspect throughout.

The set was well designed and painted, and while the larger barn piece took time to set on a few occasions, the crew, under Stage Manager Peter Kay, did an excellent job of keeping the show moving smoothly. The house stage left and the railway cutting on stage right was ample enough to suggest the settings. Props throughout were very good, and the motorbike was excellent. The 'gimmick' at the end with the charred cross was well done, although personally I found it a bit cheesy.

The general lighting was good, with everyone visible when they should have been, and some lovely atmospheric pictures were achieved. The 'moving' highway was a nice effect for "Tyre Tracks" and en route to the railway tracks. The psychedelic effects for the revival tent were also effective, but I'm not sure that they were in keeping with the rest of the plot. Sound, throughout, was balanced and secure, with some very good sound effects.

In the area of costuming, more distinction could have been made between the black and white characters, or, as suggested, between folks from different sides of the tracks. Other than that, costumes were appropriate and good effort was made with the gospel robes, policemen uniforms, etc. There were no noticeably out of place hair-styles, and make-up seemed natural, even the bruising of Amos's eye.

I noted that as far back as 2005, at the Waterford Festival, Fusion won an award for "Youthful vitality and promise for the future". Well, more than 10 years down the road, and you have certainly fulfilled that promise, and more significantly, you successfully continue to ooze with youthful vitality. My only suggestion is that you continue to aim high, and to uphold the well-deserved reputation of this excellent youth company. Thank you so much for another wonderful evening of heart-warming entertainment.

Sweeney Todd is basically a macabre horror story, injected with twists of sinister comedy in the shape of clever lyrics and exaggerated characters. As a package, it needs pace and creative staging to bring it to life. Perhaps it was an opening night nervousness that caused Aidan O'Carroll's direction of this production to seem somewhat flat and one dimensional. It did start very encouragingly with the demented girls entering through the audience, and creating an atmosphere of insanity, and the raising of the dead from behind the graveyard headstones was innovative and most effective, but the use of the chorus thereafter seemed minimal, and on occasions, musically insecure.

Physically, the set was better in design than in presentation. The main truck piece needed more detail to give it life, and the upper level was awkwardly high to be lit effectively. Mrs Lovett's shop needed more detail and more props to give it a really dirty and pest ridden feel. The barred asylum on the reverse was very good, as was the down stage left living room. The oven was a decent practical piece. The slide from barber's shop to the kitchen worked well, but I suspect that the new barber's chair was a little modern. The use of blood capsules only worked on one occasion, and when it did, it was most effective. Pirelli's caravan was a good set piece, and as mentioned, the use of projections to suggest location was quite effective. Eileen O'Connell's stage crew were generally efficient, if a little laid back, with the scene changes, and due to insecure lighting cues, were caught on stage on a few occasions.

The production did seem a little static, with principals often rooted to the spot. Anthony, for example, spent a lot of time with his lamp down stage right, seemingly searching for Johanna, but doing nothing in particular, while poor Johanna seemed to spend an eternity kneeling upstage with nothing to do but look demented. The 'crazy' girls from the opening might have been effectively used in this scene to emphasis Johanna's ordeal. The principals were well directed in the final scenes as the show reached its climax. The sound system throughout the show was consistent and balanced.

Musical Director Anna Connolly was fortunate to have both a good orchestra and good principal singers at her disposal. The orchestra, conducted by Aidan O'Carroll, made most pleasing sounds throughout the show, with good balance and consideration for the singers, and most of the principals seemed secure with their solos. The chorus were at their best at the opening, with a strong presentation of "The Ballad of Sweeney Todd", while on other occasions they were a little insecure with entrances and harmonies, which I'm quite prepared to put down to first night nerves. When they did get it right, they produced a fine sound.

There are limited opportunities for a choreographer to shine in Sweeney Todd, but Grainne O'Carroll did good work on the masquerade dance, and presented a nice ballet to accompany "By The Sea". Her use of the demented girls at the start of the show and in the asylum scene was very effective.

There was a solemn timbre to the voice of Alan McLoughlin that made him a natural choice for the role of Sweeney Todd. He captured the darkness of the character in all his vocals, and for one so young, there was a good intensity to his acting.

Grainne O'Carroll gave a well constructed performance as Mrs Lovett, with a strong and secure voice, making easy work of a very difficult musical score. She displayed excellent ability as a character comedienne.

Cormac Sertutxa seemed a little insecure musically, and uncertain in his timing, but he had a pleasant voice that grew in confidence as the show progressed, and he played his role with a pleasing naive sincerity.

There was a genuine vulnerability about Tracy O'Keefe as Johanna, and her singing of "Green Finch and Linnet Bird" was delightful.

Ian Dillane gave great credibility to the role of Tobias Ragg, particularly through his acting. He wasn't always pitch perfect vocally, but he performed his numbers with great character, growing in stature as the show reached its climax.

Tim Landers was a formidable Judge Turpin, towering over most of his fellow performers, not just in stature, but in strength of character. First night nerves may have caused him to be a little tentative, but unnecessarily, as he was vocally secure and well cast in his role. Kim Harris was visually excellent as the Beggar Woman, although her diction in the early scenes needed more attention. It did improve as the night progressed and her singing by the end was strong and true.

Noel King was a grouchy Beadle, as he should be, and Sean Lyons was a credible Fogg, and while Catriona Fitzmaurice displayed a very fine and secure singing voice and good acting ability, having a girl playing Pirelli didn't really work for me.

A good job was done on costumes, with outfits being appropriate and tidy, and hair similarly was always appropriate to the era and the character. The masks for the Masquerade were very good. There was excellent make-up for Sweeney, Mrs Lovett, the Beggar Woman and Tobias and indeed for the poor demented chorus girls.

It's the very complexity of Sondheim pieces, both musically and lyrically, that almost suggests that production values should be as creative and interesting as the material. Sweeney Todd, maybe more than most, is open to imaginative interpretation of the most macabre and sinister nature. It is also a comedy at heart, and perhaps needed the dark comedy of the story to be emphasised more. I think perhaps this production was just a little safe. That's not to say that it wasn't a good effort at a very difficult piece. Good performances and the quality of the musicians suggest that it was likely to grow and blossom over the week. It was still very worth seeing, and I thank you all sincerely for a most enjoyable evening.

Projection is becoming a feature of many productions this year, with varying levels of success. For Derry's production of "Sister Act", Director Deigh Reid took the wise precaution of backing up the projections with good physical set pieces. The combination worked very well. Lee Thomas led a competent stage crew who managed the scene changes with a minimum of fuss. The changes involving the placing of many benches tended to be a tad slow, but they were not untidy. The show benefitted from the ability to smoothly fly in set pieces, all of which were nicely painted and appropriate to the settings. It frustrated me somewhat that the black curtain was used quite a bit, considering the option of playing in front of another projection. The weakest feature of the set was the white material side flats, in so far as they were frequently not smooth, and the light hitting them emphasised their creases and folds. The concept was good, but they needed to be taut and still. Ultimately, though, the staging of the show was pleasing to the eye and appropriate to the stage space. Props were more than adequate throughout, with a good confessional booth and decent furniture. Otherwise, this was a safe production, with well realised characters, an enthusiastic chorus and well used stage space. Most of the errors on the night were what might be expected on an opening night.... chorus false starting on a dance routine, an occasional body in the wrong place and hesitant lighting and microphone cues. I did have a problem, in one or two scenes, locating Deloris amid the crowd of nuns, and perhaps some slight difference in her costume, or a follow spot to highlight her, might have been appropriate. The gang of gangsters performed their comedy number very well indeed, but I felt that their dialogue needed more work to capitalise on its comedic potential. I also felt that the relationship between Deloris and Eddie could have been better developed before they eventually kissed. It kind of happened rather suddenly. Having the television interview happening stage right while the gangsters watched it on TV stage left was a nice touch. Overall, a very nice and tidy production.

Musical Director, Peter Doherty had good control of a proficient orchestra who attacked their music with energy, as comfortable with the pop/rock rhythms as with the gospel feel. They made a strong contribution to the quality of the production, and Peter kept the balance right to allow his singers to be heard. Chorally, the performance ranged from slightly insecure and hesitant to confident and competent, although there was a tendency for volume, and occasionally harmony, to slip when the singing was accompanied by a lot of movement. The balance of sound took a little while to settle, and a few cues were late, especially during the "Raise Your Voice" number, where several nuns had solo verses.

Choreographer, Vanessa Chapman, produced some excellent work, with changing patterns and a good variety of steps in the nuns' gospel numbers, and some exciting funky routines from the fantasy dancers. For a first night performance, she should be very pleased that, by and large, her dancers were well synchronised.

A good stage presence, a fine sense of comedy, and strong vocal ability were the hallmarks of Emer McCaffrey's performance of Deloris Van Cartier. She performed with confidence and authority, and contrasted well with the more refined personalities of the Sisterhood. There was a good sense of the 'street' about her demeanour.

Judith O'Hare brought refinement and severity to the role of the Mother Superior, growing nicely in frustration as the story progresses. She handled her songs well, and I enjoyed her chatty relationship with God.

At only 18, Enya Loughlin is a star in the making, giving an excellent voice and very capable acting ability to the role of Sr Mary Robert. She was quite delightful, and "The Life I Never Led" was a highlight of her performance, and of the show. Muire McCallion was a bubbly and charismatic Sr Mary Patrick, with a strong and secure voice and an infectious joie de vivre. She played her role with a great sense of fun. Joanne Palmer got plenty of laughs for her portrayal of Sr Mary Lazarus, with good comedic ability and a fine voice.

Geoff Coke was a subdued Monsignor O'Hara at the outset who grew in stature as the night progressed, to the point of becoming a virtual rock star by the end. A good performance.

Vincent Lynch was suitably menacing as Curtis, more comfortable with his acting than his singing, but he performed "When I Find My Baby" with good expression. Joey, Pablo and TJ, played competently by Rory Mullan, Michael Poole and James Nangle, were at their best in "Lady in the Long Black Dress".

Kate Porter and Christine Deane impressed as sisters Mary Theresa and Mary-of-Tours, respectively, and Amy Smith and Hannah Deane gave good support as Deloris's side-kicks, Michelle and Tina.

David Keown gave a mellow and engaging performance as the love-shy cop, Eddie Souther, with nice delivery of "I Could Be That Guy".

There were fine cameo performances from various members of the chorus, with company President Donald Hill making a brief but welcomed appearance as the Pope.

The Chorus were generally well animated, and vocal quality was good if a little insecure on occasions, but it was opening night, and I don't doubt that they sharpened up as the run progressed. I enjoyed watching the gradual jazzing up of the nuns habits, building up to a stunning set for the finale. And I loved that the Monsignor was included in the progression. Great costumes throughout, and great wigs where appropriate. Good ageing make up for some of the nuns. There were no problems really in these departments.

With a long and successful history of presenting a high standard of musical theatre, I suggest that you continue to aim high, and enjoy your shows with the same energy that flowed from the stage during "Sister Act". Thank you for a very entertaining night.

When you approach St Finian's College and dusk is falling, all that was required was a clap of thunder and a bolt of lightning to firmly establish the fact that you were attending The Addams Family. Mullingar Charity Variety Group had not put on a full scale musical since 2011 and to re-open with this very technical show was a mighty challenge. Paul Curley took the mantle of Director and guided this very capable team of players through this marvellous comedic romp. A superbly designed "book" set opened up intimately into each scene with excellent props and super dressing of the stage. The lighting might have been more precise on the cues but the overall effect worked splendidly. Musical Director Petrina Mills had the difficult task of keeping everything together as the orchestra had a tendency to get a bit carried away in the louder pieces which hampered the audibility of the singers on stage for the audience. Costumes were excellent, particularly the ghostly ancestors although the make-up could have been a bit more on the pale side, especially Morticia who should have been transparent. The male principals all performed in character led by Alan Conroy (Gomez). His accent was very good but when singing with an accent you must emphasise the words a little more. Richie Geoghegan (Fester) perfected the waddling walk and his song to the moon was delivered expertly. The youngest male principal was Finn Sheahan (Pugsley) who sang with a big booming voice and delivered his lines perfectly. The female principals were led by Elaine Purdue (Morticia) who has the most wonderful stage presence. She glided around the stage and her long black hair was spectacular, she sang beautifully and her dialogue was crisp and precise. Joanne MacDonagh (Wednesday) took on the role of being half Addams and half normal and was completely in control throughout all of her performance. The comedy performance of the evening was delivered by Eleanor MacDonagh (Alice) who threw herself into her characterisation and gave us a most wonderful performance of comedy acting and when she crawled across the table the audience's laughter rocked the auditorium. There were some good dance routines particularly by the principals but the Choreographer Joanne Daly excelled herself in the opening number "When You're an Addams".  A most enjoyable evening's entertainment and I thank Joanne and her front of house team for their hospitality.

Good management of the chorus was one of the strengths of Philippa Alford's direction of Naas Musical Society's Wedding Singer. With a plethora of weddings and bar mitzvahs, there are many scenes where the chorus are required to be present and constantly acting and reacting to the action. These were very well handled and always interesting. There was also good character development, with most of the principals being very assured in their roles. Comedy was well realised, and the pace of the show was well balanced. While I fully appreciated the intentions and innovation of using projections as a background to the scenes, it wasn't, sadly, altogether successful. Without a much tighter and more specific lighting plot, the tendency was for the backgrounds to virtually disappear, leaving the stage looking rather empty. To work effectively, projection needs to be on more surfaces than just the back wall, and images need to be very sharp and well defined. Stage Manager, Bob O'Kelly, and his team did an efficient job of placing props and furniture, all of which were appropriate to the show, but as mentioned, with no solid set around them, they did tend to seem very isolated. I'm loathe to be over-critical, because I applaud your bravery, and this seems to be the direction in which set presentation is headed, but it will probably take much trial and error to get it just right. I was aware, however, of the efforts made by the lighting designer to create atmosphere with good use of colour and effects.

Thankfully, the strength of principal direction did compensate largely for the problems, and to remain positive, the overwhelming emotion that emanated from the stage was a sense of enjoyment and involvement from the entire cast.
