Michael Fay did an excellent job of preparing his chorus and principals for the stage. Vocal harmonies were well established, and principals were very musically secure. The orchestra were extremely talented, but also extremely loud on occasions, and did need to be reined in. Having said that, their tempos and rhythms were spot on throughout the show, and during the dance sequences, they added great energy to the routines. And speaking of routines, Choreographer Deirdre Browne did a fabulous job of creating dances that were entirely appropriate to the era of the show. The opening number set the scene brilliantly, and there was good variety from one routine to the next. "All About the Green" had very good business and changing patterns that made it interesting. "Casualty of Love" was fun and energetic, and "Saturday Night in the City" was vibrant and explosive. Deirdre also made the most of the obviously considerable dance abilities of both Holly and Linda. Very good work.

Seán McMahon gave a strong and sensitive performance as Robbie Hart, expressing his hurt at being jilted with venom, but then so tender in losing his heart to Julia. He has a wonderful voice, which was at its best during the romantic songs. Dearbhail Downey was a perfect Julia, sweet, sensitive, vulnerable and beautiful. She achieved the quirkiness required for "Someday", the comic timing for "Come Out of the Dumpster", and her delivery of "If I Told You" was exquisite. As a couple, Seán and Dearbhail seemed perfectly suited, and together they made the story completely believable.

James Place had the arrogance and attitude appropriate to the character of Sammy, combined with the necessary cheekiness to make him believably appealing to Holly. His vocal ability was very secure. Serena Salmon, as Holly, dazzled when she danced, and had the vocal punch to put across her numbers with energy and vitality. She led "Saturday Night in the City" with confidence, and excelled in "Right in Front of Your Eyes".

Dominic Reid could have been more flamboyant as George, but he did give a likeable, gentleness to his role, backed up with good vocal quality. He was delightfully funny during "Single".

Mona Conroy clearly enjoyed the silliness of Rosie, and she delivered her 'rap' like she'd been doing it all her life. Her "Note from Grandma" was very funny, and her unapologetic Irish-ness added to the comedy.

Joe Egan gave an assured performance as Glen, in his first musical theatre role, impressively selling the "All About the Green" number. Had he relaxed a little more, he could probably have found more comedy in exaggerating the arrogance of his character.

Julie Donnelly was a feisty, fiery Linda, not at all afraid to use her natural assets to accentuate her character. Good delivery of her musical numbers.

Joy Donohoe comically achieved the superficiality of a mother who wanted the best (financially) for her daughter, whether or not it included happiness. Nicely sung and performed.

Aisling Conway, Tina O'Kelly and Stephen Fagan made the most of their look-alike characters, albeit in a scene that should be radically re-written. From within the chorus, there were plenty of other well played and credible cameo roles, most notably the Bum, who added much humour to the "Single" scene. Very good work was done on creating an authentic look of the era, through costumes and hair-styles. I remember very well looking as horrendous in the 80's as some of the visions on stage. Principals were well presented, especially Holly, who was always appropriately sassy. The same attention was given to wigs/hairstyles... even for the boys, and there were lashings of over-the-top glam make-up. A very good job all round in visual presentation.

The use of projections in amateur theatre is really in its infancy, and while I obviously can't ignore the problems that it presents, I am full of admiration for companies who are prepared to be leaders in exploring the possibilities in this area. I applaud your courage and hope you will continue to be experimental. I'm also happy to acknowledge that, despite the problems, Naas presented a standard of show that sent their audience home filled with laughter and fun. Thank you for a very enjoyable experience.

The Witches of Eastwick is a very technical show, not just because the three ladies have to fly but scene changes and lighting plots have to be executed perfectly to allow the flow of the show to be consistent. Baldoyle Musical Society managed to do this with consummate ease. The stage manager James O'Keeffe had his crew all prepared and they delivered on cue each time. Director Clive Jackson probably had a hand in these proceedings and I found his direction to be precise and concise. The direction for Felicia's demise was a wonderful piece of theatre which required both, actors, lighting and orchestra to be perfectly in sync with each other. Rory Robinson (Darryl) gave us a most assured acting performance, with wonderful diction and superb facial expressions which enhanced his ability to deliver the sexual nuances of his character. Kathryn McGibbon (Alex) sang marvellously throughout her performance with good tonal quality and wonderful diction and she delivered her dialogue in a most relaxed, laid back manner. Kate Headon (Jane) sang throughout her performance with good crisp delivery of all of her lyrics and wonderfully in tune. Ms Headon appeared completely at ease throughout her performance and her dialogue was full of inflection and she always kept the pace of each scene moving swiftly. Karen McCourt's (Suki) voice is simply fantastic. She has a wonderful lilting melodic tone with a marvellous control of her crescendo and super diction. Her acting was more flirtatious and she gave us superb facial expressions. Collectively the three ladies sang together most harmoniously. Colete O'Beirne (Felicia) sang with perfect diction and gave us a terrific performance of her solo number "Evil", her dialogue was crisp and her stage presence excellent, she acted most superbly in the scene when she was "bewitched" by the three ladies. Her husband Karl Hoffman (Clyde) gave a most assured display of a drunk with a wonderful stagger but it never impeded his delivery of dialogue. His acting in Felicia's demise was excellent. Ciara Roche (Jennifer) committed to every scene and gave us every emotion from joy when she finally got her boyfriend to commit to despair and resignation when her parents had died. Mark Smith (Michael) was a little hesitant in his delivery and he just needed to commit to Jennifer a little more. Their duets were beautifully sung with wonderful harmonies. Caoimhe Doody (Little Girl) was never late for a cue, always on her mark and sang perfectly in tune. The orchestra under Dave McGauran were in balance with themselves but on occasion were a little too loud for the soloists which was a shame, choreography by Catherine McCourt was imaginative and the chorus danced all of the routines perfectly together. It was a marvellous production and a great night's entertainment.

It is a very long time since I first saw Cats on the London stage, and fell instantly in love with the whole concept of the show. That there was no story-line worth talking about didn't matter at all, for in transforming people into felines with human characteristics and back-stories, Lloyd Weber turned T.S. Eliot's poetry into a feast for all the senses.

The amazing thing is that for Ballywillan Youth, even with an entire cast of young teenagers, without the years of training that the West End cast had been through, the concept still functioned quite brilliantly. Routines were devised to suit the capabilities of the young performers, and the costumes, wigs and make-up were as close to the professional show as made little difference. From the very youngest (probably about 6 or 7) to the older teenagers, the energy and determination of these amazing children was quite awesome.

Director Brian Logan, Choreographers Sharon Logan and Victoria Lagan, Musical Director Eric Boyd, and their many assistants, have created something magical, inclusive, vibrant and spectacular, where all their students, regardless of ability levels, were given their moment to shine and to impress, in a most creative endeavour. In years to come, very many of these children will have an abundant appreciation of musical theatre and arts in general, because at an early age, they were given the kind of encouragement and opportunities that this production team have afforded them. From a production point of view, it was notable how every performer stayed in their feline character at all times. There were kittens who crawled and scratched, and washed their whiskers with their paws, and snuggled up to the older cats when stories were being told. Body language was so detailed and constant, suggesting great attention to detail at rehearsals. Entrances and exits were tidy on the well laid out stage, and the choruses focused and responded well to the main action. But maybe most impressive of all was the varied and non-stop choreography, giving opportunities for gymnasts and acrobats to have their moments, and ballerinas to impress with their grace and elegance. The ever changing pictures on stage were delightful and intelligent.

A six piece band, under Musical Director, Eric Boyd, included two keyboard players, who successfully managed to create a fairly full orchestral sound. The accompaniment was always sympathetic to the singers, and tempi throughout the show were spot on. All the performers on stage appeared to be well rehearsed, and the vocal quality of the choruses was generally very good.

Shea Eastwood as Munkustrap got the show off to a fine start as the main narrator of the piece, with a clear and tuneful voice, and a confident manner. There were very fine performances from Niamh Cunning and Hannah Baxter as Mungojerrie and Rumpleteazer, and a well realised characterisation from Chloe Barclay as Jennyanydots, sleepy and lazy during the day, and alive and animated at night. Leon Woods was most impressive as the strutting, self confident Rum-tum- tugger, and had a fine and confident voice. Abby Robinson was a blustering, bumbling Bustopher Jones, and Annie Levy was an animated Skimbleshanks, the railway cat. Joel Murphy added a nice bit of maturity to the role of Old Deuteronomy, always authoritative and with a good commanding voice. Likewise, Ross McAllister gave a warm performance and a very pleasing voice to the role of Gus the Theatre cat. The introduction to his song was beautifully performed by Hannah McAleenon as Jellyorum.

Erin White impressed as Jemima, and Mollie Cochrane was an imposing and scary Macavity, and when Old Deuteronomy was kidnapped, a very capable Zahra Carmichael as Mr Mistoffelees was quick to rescue him. There were many other fine performers in a host of cameo roles, but quite outstanding was Olivia Baker, as Victoria, whose ballet had me completely entranced.

Central to the show, of course, is the fortune of Grizabella, which gave Lucy McDowell the opportunity to display her fine acting ability and to lend her lovely voice to the shows most popular song, "Memory".

I make no apologies for saving the best for last, for while every member of the cast was notable for their energy and enthusiasm, it was the exceptional performance of "Macavity" by Jasmine Gardiner as Demeter and Ellen Duguid as Bombalurina that completely stole the show. Excellent characterisation, and excellent delivery from these two very talented girls.

The Kitten Chorus were simply charming, and totally engrossed in their task, and the Dance and Chorus Cats gave a remarkable display, with some very outstanding dancing.

The staging of the show was simple and effective, with a rubbish dump featuring over-sized empty tins and cereal boxes, etc. Lighting, throughout, was colourful, effective and atmospheric, with principal performers well highlighted, and a very hard working team came up with a vast array of appropriate props for the show. With so many individuals to mic, there were one or two minor problems with cueing of the sound, but generally there was a good sound balanced and any slight cueing delays were quickly remedied. The visual department of the show was remarkably good, with costumes being colourful, eye-catching and totally in keeping with character requirements. The long list of make-up assistants is evidence of the great work that was put in to making every person look feline and individual. Likewise, the detail in wigs, and ears, and many of the performers even had microphone packs embedded in their wigs, because of their dancing and rolling on the floor. Really excellent work all round.

If you could find a way to bottle the energy and dedication that the young people of Ballywillan Youth put into their performance, you could make a fortune selling it! This was such a wonderful night of captivating and mesmerising atmosphere and entertainment. Long may you continue to flourish, and thank you for an unforgettable experience.

The Addams Family is full of macabre fun and mischief that Banbridge Musical Society delivered to their audience in style. Under the baton of Colin Loughead the well-known theme tune from the 60's was played with wonderful timing and had the audience clapping along in time with it. Mr Loughead had super control of his orchestra and he gave good visual direction to his players on stage. Leonard Anderson took control of the direction and choreography. The larger chorus scenes were expertly delivered and his ghoulish ancestors were all suitably prepared for their interaction with the principals. The opening number was performed expertly by all concerned. There were also a few innovations in his direction and I must mention the "motorised electric hand" which wandered around the stage seemingly with a mind of its own. The costumes, make-up and hair department worked their socks off to give us ghoulish ancestors from the grave and they all looked superb. As for the players Paddy McGennitty (Gomez) delivered with a wonderful accent throughout, even when he sang he kept the inflection perfect and his dialogue and diction were excellent. Opposite him was Emma Kelly (Morticia), this young lady glided around the stage as if on wheels. Her costumes and make-up were perfect and she sang, spoke and danced sublimely. Jim McGuigan (Fester) with his shiny bald pate fell in love with the moon and his scene with the moon and stars was visually and theatrically excellent. Anna-Maria Boyle (Wednesday) has a most clear and powerful voice which she used to wonderful effect in "Pulled". Nicola Brenchley (Grandma) adopted a stooped walk for her character and got every bit of comedy out of her part and James Woods (Pugsley) played the suitably horrid little brother intent on evil throughout. The minor characters all have roles to play in the storyline even David McClelland (Lurch), who stood very straight and tall and had a booming Bass voice which he delivered long and loud at the end. The Beinke's Ian Davidson (Mal), Rosemary Kelly (Alice) and Scott Skelton (Lucas) all assisted in making this production one of fun and laughter, albeit with a little macabre humour thrown in. A super evening's entertainment sent the audience home with smiles on their faces and wonderful memories..

On the day I attended Clara Musical Societies production of 9 To 5 one of their most famous inhabitants, Golfer Shane Lowry, was tying the knot in New York. Alan Recks took on the task of director and musical director which automatically doubled his workload. However his cast never let him down and they delivered by acting out this extremely funny musical expertly. His direction ticked all the boxes in tempo and the accents of all of his principals were perfect. His stage manager Wayne Handy took on the task of ensuring that every scene delivered and gave us expertly swift scene changes. Where there were problems was musically. In so far as having the band backstage means that the musical director is only visible on a video screen and this didn't work, as a lot of the finishes of musical numbers were ragged. Amanda Cunningham (Violet) gave us a wonderful singing performance and her acting, especially in the "doobie" scene was hilarious. She was ably assisted firstly by Natalee Kelly (Doralee) who looked like, sounded like and sang like the protagonist of the show Dolly Parton, and secondly by Karen Monaghan (Judy) who started off as a hesitant lady in her first job and then as the show progressed transformed into this passionate, confident woman. Her big number "Get out and Stay Out" brought the house down. The show is about these three leading ladies and how their boss (Franklyn Hart) treats them so appallingly, Hart was played by John Conroy. Mr Conroy got all the acting and innuendo perfect and took his comeuppance on the chin at the end, he just needed to be more positive in his vocals. There are numerous cameo roles in this show however Chris Corroon (Joe) pursued Violet throughout, with super diction and dialogue delivered perfectly he then sang most wonderfully to her in "Let Love Grow". Choreography was by Lea Carroll and she had the chorus dancing in perfect rhythm together and it was wonderful to see them all dancing with happy smiling faces. In fact the chorus performed with energy and enthusiasm throughout all of the show which was terrific to see. It was a most wonderful nights entertainment and the sell out audience went home humming all of the well known tunes..

The great strength and beauty of West Side Story comes from its source, William Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet. This classic love story has been told in so many varied ways, but none more effectively than through the medium of musical theatre, and the combined genius of Leonard Bernstein, Stephen Sondheim and Arthur Laurents. They chose, obviously, to soften the ending to a message of hope, by allowing Maria (Juliet) the honour of living to love another day, which undoubtedly made it more palatable to a light entertainment audience. It was the right choice. What they created was, in its day, a modern masterpiece, with one of the most entrancing musical scores ever written... and so it remains, ever popular, and ever relevant.

Michael O'Donoghoe's production had plenty of novel twists that gave the show a fresh treatment. The introduction of a Denizens chorus, particularly at the start of the show, gave an insight into how the gang war between the Jets and the Sharks, might have affected other street people. They were re-introduced very effectively in the Dream sequence, showing how their lives could be different in the Utopian world of Tony's imagination. This was both creative and beautiful. Diarmuid Vaughan's set was well painted, and clean and efficient in design, if slightly less effective for interior scenes than exterior.

Stage Managers, Ruth Butler and Kay Sheehan, controlled the placing and removal of a wide range of very good props, with efficiency, hence preventing scene changes from disrupting the pace of the show. Good choice of colours helped the lighting design to enhance the set, and generally, lighting added to the tone and atmosphere of the production. There were very few problems with sound quality or balance, with the exception of a microphone cutting out on one of the girls in the bedroom scene.

Michael's choreography, with more than a little input, I imagine, from Gillian Hewitt- Fitzgerald and Majella Louise Fitzgerald, was always interesting, often dynamic, and occasionally very precise. The girls tended to be more together than the boys, but what the boys lacked in finesse, they made up for in energy and determination. The dance at the gym had moments of magic, particularly when Riff and Velma took the floor, and there was some nice acrobatic work. At the start of the Dream sequence, I was wondering "Where is this going?", as it seemed a little vague in concept, but when the intention became apparent, it revealed itself to be a very clever and creative piece of choreography. America was a good showcase for the girls, and Officer Krupke was great fun for the lads, brilliantly led by Action.

Laura Cotter, I'm sure, would have liked a few more musicians for the complexity of West Side Story, but the musicians she had made a good job of filling out the score. The ever changing rhythms and time signatures were well realised, although I did feel that a few numbers needed a little more pace to capture the frenetic energy and urgency of the action. There were also a few split notes from an otherwise impressive brass section. The "Tonight Ensemble" is one of the few opportunities for good choral work, and along with "Somewhere", highlighted some very fine vocals. The Jets were also extremely impressive during the Jet song. Most of the principals were musically secure, but I would like to have seen more attention given to acting during songs. In this department, Diarmuid Vaughan led by example.

Emmet Donlan, as Tony, displayed a very fine, if on occasions, too forceful, tenor voice, well able to hit the high notes. He needed to let the emotion of the lyrics show more on his face. I found the chemistry between himself and Maria a little forced, and upon hearing the news of Maria being shot, I would like to have seen him crumble at least a little. He was much more successful with Riff and the boys, where he convincingly showed signs of once having been a leader.

Eva McNally grew in every department as the show progressed. At the outset, she was somewhat tentative and insecure, but her confidence grew when she sang "Tonight", and by the time she sang "I Feel Pretty" she had settled into character. I didn't truly believe the love between herself and Tony until he was dead, at which point, she gave a very moving final speech. Vocally, Eva has a voice that has yet to reach full maturity, but it is certainly headed in a very positive direction.

Keith Greene exuded confidence as Riff, and was largely responsible for getting the show off to a cracking start. He was extremely enthusiastic in his dancing, so much so that I choose to believe that he performed every step perfectly! He had confidence in his acting too, although a little rushed on occasions. He was vocally sound in delivery of his songs.

Ian Purcell gave a quiet confidence to the role of Bernardo, and was a plausible leader of his gang. Unfortunately he also gave a very quiet delivery of his lines in the opening scenes, and it wasn't until the Doc's store scene that I really got a sense of how strong his character really was. He did have very good stage presence, and danced well at the gym.

Michelle Smith was a very convincing Anita, with a perfect look, a good sense of comedy, and a salty attitude. Her taunting scene with the Jets was well acted, and suitably uncomfortable to watch. I believed her hurt. Vocally, she was at her best during "America", and while she did put passionate emotion into "A Boy Like That", she did seem a little insecure. Hers was a very enjoyable performance, nonetheless.

Diarmuid Vaughan, as Action, gave the most confident performance of the night, involving himself constantly and believably in the action, even when not the focus of attention. His fiery attitude was always apparent, and it built to a perfectly presented rendition of "Officer Krupke". Likewise, Rosie Mai Fitzgerald, as Anybodys, maintained her character strongly throughout the show, enjoying the tough Tom-boy attitude, and enhancing her performance with a good accent and excellent dancing. This was very nice work.

Sheena Fennessy as Velma, and Clare Murray as Graziella made their presence felt in the few opportunities they had, with Sheena being particularly noteworthy in the dance numbers.

Likewise, Lisa O'Brien as Consuela and Rebecca Laste as Rosalia made a good impact with their dialogue and vocally in America and I Feel Pretty, where they were ably supported by Nicole Butler as Francisca.

Cian Corcoran (A-rab), Ruairi Doyle (Snowboy), Joe Shehan (Big Deal), Darragh Johnston (Diesel) and Daniel Traas as Baby John, gave great support as the Jets, and their dancing, though not always perfectly co-ordinated, was buzzing with raw energy and effort.

Jason Ryan, as Chino, made a good job of reporting the "Rumble" to Maria, and he played the shooting scene very well. He had good back-up from Alan McCormack as Pepe and Jack Houze as Indio.

Denis O'Sullivan was a quaint, put-upon store owner as Doc, and his delicate scene with Tony was nicely handled. Similarly, an eccentric and quirky performance was given by Kevin Fahey as Glad Hand. David Hogan had a good stage presence as Lt. Schrank, but could have been a tad more aggressive in his confrontation scene with the Jets, while Ricky Dunne's Officer Krupke was suitably angry and abrupt.

Sadhbh Treacy had a pleasant, but gentle and slightly nervous voice as the "Somewhere" soloist, but will no doubt be a young performer to keep an eye on in the future.

The chorus for this production, from the "oldies" of the Denizens, to the youngest dancers, gave one hundred per cent commitment to maintaining a high energy performance, with great physical presence and enthusiastic vocals.

The wardrobe plot for the show was very appropriate and tidy. There was good attention to torn t-shirts after the fight and good injury make-up. Girls, both in costume and hair-styles looked perfectly turned out, although Maria's dresses could have fitted a little better.

I had the sense of a new generation working its way into the ranks of St. Mary's Choral Society, full of enthusiasm and adventure, which is a great sign for the future of the company. There is also a wealth of experience in the company to give them good guidance, and based on this production of West Side Story, the young ones are already stepping well up to the mark. Thank you for a thoughtful and varied production of one of my favourite shows. It was a lovely night of entertainment.

It is a shame that when designers build brand new theatres that they only think of plays rather than all types of theatrical productions. The Mill Theatre is a super venue but does not have a facility for an orchestra. This means that the musicians have to contend with sitting in the front row of the auditorium which is not pleasant for them or the audience. In saying this I was most impressed with the control that Musical Director, Graham Walsh, had over his orchestra. He has a most wonderful conducting technique and controls the volume of his orchestra as if he had them on a dial. The beautiful playing gave wonderful support to a large cast in this well known and some might say iconic musical, which is Calamity Jane. Our heroine, Calamity was played by Ema-Mae West. In her performance she gave us wonderful stage presence, a super accent, which was consistent throughout, she was feisty with Bill and the boys and her singing was passionate and precise. Her dialogue just needed to be slowed down a little as it was sometimes a little rushed. Her relationship with Andrew Torsney (Bill Hickock) developed perfectly from anger and cajoling to eventually a commitment of love. Their duets together were sung perfectly in tune and the dialogue was clean and precise. Amy Louise Byrne (Katie Brown) sang with complete ease with wonderful clarity in her voice and she never missed a beat and in her acting she was marvellous in her commitment to Aaron Tierney (Danny Gilmartin). Aaron needed to be a bit more soldierly and stand straighter but his accent was good and he was always on his mark. The third duo in the show consisted of Kevin Macken (Francis Fryer) and Niamh Thornton (Susan). Kevin gave us a wonderful stage dance in his opening scene and then he gave us a superb cameo as female impersonator. He was suitably embarrassed throughout and he portrayed this excellently. The part of Susan is often overlooked but it is an important cameo role for the plot of the show and Ms Thornton, with good timing and cueing played the role perfectly. I would have liked more harmonies from the chorus as some of the numbers were sung in unison. As the stage is very small and the chorus large it was a wonderful achievement to get everybody on and off and in position properly, Director Helen McCann is to be credited for this. Nicole McDonald choreographed and is to be complemented for a wonderful array of 12 can can dancers who worked perfectly together. The small venue did not help the stage crew and they struggled with set changes. The society sold out before the show started which is testament to the support that this society has in south county Dublin, long may it continue..

An excellent orchestra, good singing, vivid characterisations and very competent choreography were the positive aspects of Kilcock's production of "42nd Street" in the uncompromising, cramped conditions of St. Joseph's Hall.

If lack of facilities had a negative impact on the technical aspects of the show, it certainly didn't stand in the way of a troupe of performers who gave their all to entertain their audience.

Siobhán Clifford was an engaging Peggy Sawyer, nervous and vulnerable at the outset, growing in stature and confidence as the story progressed. As required in this demanding role, her acting was as accomplished as her singing and dancing, as she put in a powerhouse performance. She is blessed with a delightfully expressive face which always conveyed the correct emotions. Very good work indeed.

Lorraine Murphy was a caustic Prima Donna in the role of Dorothy Brock, well able to command the stage and to turn her nose up at her supporting cast. Her vocals were strong, and when she softened in Act Two, her sincerity was gentle and believable. She got good comedy from her relationship with Abner Dillon.

Louise Moore was a delightfully bubbly and vivacious Maggie Jones, making the most of her vocal opportunities, and delivering her comedy with confidence. Sharon Murphy was a feisty Anytime Annie, and along with very capable performances from Maeve Cunningham as Phyllis, and Charlene Masterson as Lorraine, she fronted much of the dancing with great energy and ability.

Colin Stephens as Julian Marsh, was at his best in his encounters with Peggy, but I did feel that he could have been more animated in some of his other scenes. He was vocally impressive, especially in his delivery of his final solo.

It was a huge benefit to the show to have a dancer of Stephen Ryan's ability in the role of Billy Lawlor. His foot work was always secure and reliable, and he was well able for the vocal demands of the role. I would have liked him to be a bit more cocky in his dialogue, but he was still a strong and very credible character. James Place looked and acted the role of Andy, the choreographer, with good authority, and was relaxed and very much at home on the stage. Nicely played. Similarly, there was an air of confidence about Liam Brennan as Bert Barry, who played well against Maggie, and was pitch perfect and secure in all his music. He and Annie made a very good job of "Shuffle off to Buffalo."

Bert Carruthers, in the role of Abner Dillon, was almost laconic in his interest in show- business, and fawning in his love for Dorothy. His laid back style was unusual for this character, but it worked extremely well.

Ronan McCabe was an effective Pat Denning, both humble and likeable as the down on his luck performer. Good support was given by Sinéad McLoughlin as Diane, Maria Fowler as Gladys, Grace Cosgrave as Ethel, Olwyn Boyle as Olive, Matt Sands as a Thug, and Michéal Hogan as a Young Man, while Stephen Fagan gave a consistent and noteworthy performance as Mac.

The chorus were energised and focused on the action of the story, responding appropriately at all time, and both in vocal quality and dance ability, their contribution to the overall show was more than satisfactory.

A wonderful musical score is the backbone of "42nd Street", the melodies, the rhythms and excellent arrangements all come together to create a musical feast that is guaranteed to set feet tapping and hearts racing. Well, in the right hands, and with the right musicians, that is the case, and under the secure baton of Sarah Lynch Barrett, this orchestra gave a sparkling and triumphant display of musicianship. Brass and woodwind were particularly outstanding in the dance numbers, reaching a peak with the jazzy, rhythmic strains of the 42nd Street Ballet. Sarah was also responsible for ensuring that the chorus delivered their harmonies effectively, which they certainly did, particularly the females in "Shadow Waltz", "Sunny Side" and "Shuffle of to Buffalo". Principal music was strong and secure. An excellent job all round.

Variety was the spice of Choreographer Deirdre Browne's work on this production. There was a good solid tap opening, very well led by Stephen Ryan, and indeed the tap throughout the show was consistently impressive. The Shadow Waltz, though technically awkward, was well danced with nice comedy touches. The inexperience of Peggy Sawyer was well comically highlighted in "Getting to Be a Habit", and "Getting Out of Town" had great movement. Similarly, "Lullaby of Broadway built beautifully to a strong finish, and there was good creativity in the 42nd Street Ballet. There was plenty of bluffing going on in the tap routines, which is not unusual, but the trick is to bluff with confidence, and this was certainly the case, for the dancers looked confident at all times. All in all, a very well choreographed show.

The difficulty with presenting a glamorous "Show-biz" show is that the script almost dictates the material needs of the production. 42nd Street is littered with references like "The greatest show Broadway has seen in 20 years", "that glittering gulch" and "the tinsel and glitter of musical comedy", and while Director Philippa Alford got great work and energy from her cast, the show was technically lacking in variety and glamour. There was little visual indication throughout the show of location, except for the opening, which had the look of an undressed empty stage. The drop in lights for the dressing rooms were a good effort, and the curtains for "Shuffle of to Buffalo" brought a welcomed change of appearance, but costumes alone didn't give a glamorous enough feel to numbers like "Dames", "We're in the Money" and The 42nd Street Ballet. The venue also made scenes like "The Shadow Waltz", and the front of curtain/ back of curtain scenes very difficult to realise.

Thankfully, as mentioned, the direction of principals and chorus was a very different ball game. Good emphasis was given to characterisation, positioning and pictures on stage were well established, and attention to the comedy of the script was very evident.

The "Pretty Lady" costumes were generally very effective, with good ball gowns for "Dames", great dance costumes for "We're in the Money" and the Ballet, and a colourful array of night gowns for "Shuffle off to Buffalo". Principals were smartly dressed in their day outfits, although I'm pretty sure Julian Marsh would have been wearing White Tie and Tails on the opening night of "Pretty Lady". Wigs and hairstyles were very good, and of the era, and make-up was well exaggerated without going over-the-top.

I'm delighted to be able to say that, despite technical issues, this was a wonderfully well presented and performed night of fun and entertainment, that ticked all the boxes for character, comedy, vocal quality and great musicianship. Thank you to one and all for your dedication, and for a most enjoyable experience.

There are a host of Juke-box, compilation musicals that are poor in quality and instantly forgettable, but that certainly isn't the case with Rock of Ages, for, like it or loathe it, it has the potential to explode off the stage with vibrant, pounding music, a racy and very comical script, an excuse to dress crazy, and a score so familiar that you can hardly resist the temptation to sing along. (Well, for my generation, it has that effect!)

Spit and polish had been applied to every element of Director/Choreographer Claire Tighe's production, from a detailed and practical set, to colourful/sexy/outrageous costumes, from dynamic dance routines to sparkling comedy, and from carefully crafted characters to technical excellence. This was a slick technical show, with a well devised set, beautifully dressed with a vast array of memorabilia. The insets stage right worked well, as did the steps in the front right corner, and the upper window of the strip club, stage left, was excellent. Stage Manager, Mary Purcell, and her team kept the action flowing with slick, effortless scene changes. Lighting was excellent, capturing the essence of a Rock concert for the up tempo numbers, and dropping to well focused mood lighting for the more mellow numbers. Special areas were well achieved, which again helped to keep the flow of action unbroken. The lighting and smoke for Dennis' exit to immortality, was superb! The pace of the show was electrifying, with never a dull moment, and yet the sentimental and romantic encounters were sensitively handled, allowing the principal characters to display the full range of their emotions. Some of the brilliant touches that really stood out were Drew's very un-cool moped, the pole dancers in the upstairs window, and the "walk into the light" exit of Dennis when he was told he was dead. Hilarious! But it was the choreography that really drove the show forward, with every possible opportunity taken to dazzle the audience with fancy footwork, gyrating hips, thrusting groins and even jazz hands. It was virtually non- stop throughout the show, filled with variety, vivacity and captivating creativity. The lap dancing during "I Hate Myself" was superb, and "Here I Go Again" brought the house down. The dancers were exceptionally fit, and there was no awkwardness to their raunchiness. Principals were equally energetic, with great routines, particularly for "I Wanna Know What Love Is" and the hilarious "Hit Me With Your Best Shot".

It was the ability to switch from outrageous rock to easy, laid back sensitivity that demonstrated how much Musical Director, David Hayes, was in touch with this show. A superb band raised the roof with the rock anthems, safe in the knowledge that the singers were well amplified to carry above them. The sound balance throughout the show was absolutely perfect, with accurate cueing and good reverb effects when required. But it was the mellow accompaniment to "More Than Words", "Waiting For A Girl Like You" and "Every Rose" that showed the quality of the musicianship on display. Choral harmonies were always evident, and always sung with energy, and the principal line were musically excellent. In many ways, this was a rock concert, interrupted by a very amusing script. Very impressive.

As with the band, it was the effortlessly switch from sensitive and emotional ballads to a powerful rock tenor, that showed the musicianship and versatility of Kevin Fagan in the role of Drew. Similarly, we felt his insecurities and his hurt as his relationship with Sherrie kept going amiss, thanks to sincere, emotional and totally believable acting. This was a superb performance.

Sincerity was also the key to the brilliant performance of Orla Jennings in the role of Sherrie. Loveable from the outset, her optimism was palpable, and we consequently felt deeply for her in her disappointments. Contrasting that vulnerability was a fiery, feisty ability to strut and seduce, combined with excellent dance ability. And did I mention how well she can sing? Excellent.

Ian Tighe really enjoyed the license to thrill offered by the role of Lonnie. As the narrator of the piece, his rapport with the audience was excellent, his comedic timing perfect, and he was well able for the vocal demands of the role. His antics with the haze machine were excellent. Ciarán Tighe, as Dennis, was a convincing club owner, and had the air of someone who had missed the era from being on a constant "trip". Nice characterisation, and believably passionate about his club. His affection for  Lonnie was very funny, and his exit was superb.

Rob Vickers nailed the vocals of ageing rock star, Stacee Jaxx, and was hilariously morose in his "Wham-bam-thank-you- ma'am" attitude to women. He revelled in his semi-naked cavorting, and "I Wanna Know What Love Is" was a comedic highlight.

Serena Salmon was a delightfully loveable and quirky Regina, was quirky, comical and passionate in her rebellious defence of the culture to which she ascribed, and cookie and convincing in her admiration for Franz. She was a naturally good dancer, and very secure vocally.

Seán McMahon attacked the funny bones of his audience with his hilariously funny interpretation of Franz. His body language, his accent and his delivery were perfect, and he was vocally strong. This was a most entertaining performance.

Kevin Hynes as Hertz, gave a good comical and authoritative performance as the heartless, aggressive German, at his funniest when he realises his affection for his son.

Avril Doyle was impressively imposing and yet sweetly sympathetic as Justice, with the highlight of her performance being her commanding and melodic vocals.

Sean Duffy was a funny and convincing Mayor, reminiscent of many of our local politicians, and good support was given by Ciarán Austin as Father, and Ailish Byrne as Mother.

Aoife Masterson was delightful as Waitress #1, and considerably more appealing than Dylan McQuaid as Candi.... but I guess that's just my personal preference! (Dylan was extremely funny!)

Also worthy of mention were very competent performances from Jamie Hennessy as Joey Primo, Francesca White as Constance, Damien Scanlan as a Sleazy Producer and John Dennehy as Ja'Keith Gill.

The chorus and dancers throughout the show were committed, energetic and precise in all their action and music. This is a real fun show, when it comes to costumes and wigs, and Leixlip went all out to make it flamboyant and outrageous. Wigs were excellent, particularly for the boys. I loved the matching outfits of the nightclub dancers, which were slick and sexy without being too tacky. The mock choir robes also worked very well. Make-up was universally good.

This company has talent in abundance, and a production team who have served them extremely well. With this production, they have hit the nail firmly on the head. Thank you sincerely for a very polished, precise and enjoyable night of craziness!

This is a 1960's musical full of hope and expectation incorporating a little bit of that 60's swing to it. Lisnagarvey Operatic Society took on this challenge in the magnificent auditorium that is the Island Hall Theatre in Lisburn. As would suggest in the show's title everything revolves around our main character Charity. This task was bestowed upon Lauren Molloy who took on the challenge, held on to it and produced a passionate display of singing, dancing and pathos throughout. Her comedy timing was wonderful and her relationship with Rea Campbell (Oscar) was marvellous. Rea used all of his comedy genius to get every laugh out of the script and his scene in the lift had the audience in hysterics. Whilst the show revolves around Charity there are numerous characters who interface with her throughout. Claire Cranston (Helene) and Ashleigh Gault (Nickie) worked with her as "dance hall hostesses", their characters were there "temporary" but that was only a ruse. They were there for the long haul and both Claire and Ashleigh played this out in their performances. Claire's dialogue was crisp and precise against Ashleigh's singing which was perfect in both diction and intonation which allowed them to be most supportive in their roles. Such is this show that every role is trying its best to get a laugh, this was evident in the cameo role of Sean Harkin (Vittorio), who played the suave Italian film star to a tee with perfect accent throughout and an over the top delivery of dialogue. These performances were all down to Director Wilfie Pyper, who allowed the show to run at an even pace, allowing all the comedy to be the highlight of the production as the actual story is one of pathos and ends in rejection. Clare Donnelly's choreography of the big chorus numbers was marvellous especially "I'm a Brass Band" which was excellent although the show stopper "Big Spender" just needed a little bit more sexy pizzazz. The orchestra were kept in check by Musical Director Ian Milford which allowed all the singers to be heard and his brass section supported the singers wonderfully. There were a number of issues with late sound cues and I would have liked the lighting to have been a little brighter throughout if only to showcase the most marvellous array of costumes that were on display. From the "I'm A Brass Band" costumes which were pristine and perfect through to the 60's hippie costumes for the "Rhythm of Life" scene which were all fantastic. I was treated to a most wonderful evening of nostalgia and entertainment.

The New Lyric production of High Society was high on design quality and on performance ability. From a beautiful set to luxurious costumes, from fine singing to robust acting, creative choreography and direction, there was much to be admired. I think there was an element of telling the story from the viewpoint of the domestic staff in Director Kieran Griffiths' production, using the chorus as he did almost as narrators and commentators of the action. It was a novel approach, which worked well on occasions, but was possibly over-used, as the chorus did become a bit of a distraction from the focal point of the action.

Technical and visual aspects of this show were very well achieved, and I liked the use of the picture frames, which were a lovely piece of innovation. I did feel that the pacing of dialogue was a bit of an issue throughout the show. Everything seemed very rushed, and on several occasions, the audience didn't have time to appreciate the humour before the dialogue had resumed and raced away from them. This was particularly the case in encounters between Tracy and Dexter. Having said that, there was a very good realisation of individual characters, and a strong sense of security in the delivery of lines.

Musical Director Wilson Shields had very fine musicians in the pit and very secure singers on stage. The orchestra were well controlled in tempo, pace and volume, and there was great security in harmonies from the chorus. Principals were all more than satisfactory in their vocal ability. A very good show, musically.

Apart from some routines and business that seemed a bit superfluous to the story, Wendy Mairs' choreography of the show was slick and varied, with a real feeling of enjoyment emanating from the dancers. There was a very inventive picture frame routine which working extremely well, literally creating a beautiful collection of pictures on the stage.

Caitlin McClurg was most impressive in the role of Tracy Lord. To begin with, she looked radiant, and her costumes were simply stunning. Add to that the fact that her acting was very good, her singing was very secure and her comedy was on the ball, and you have a beautiful all round performance.

Ciara Mackey's beautiful voice was best displayed in a touching rendition of "He's The Right Guy", which was the highlight of her performance as Liz. Aside from that, she had wonderful stage presence and was most expressive in her delivery of comedy and sentiment.

Alison McAllister gave a well balanced performance as the Lord matriarch, Margaret, the very forgiving wife of a cheating husband. She embodied the out of date notion of "Well he's a louse, but what can I do, I love him", and did so very convincingly. She also had a commanding vocal quality that enhanced her performance.

Bonnie Lennox gave an enchanting performance as Dinah, full of mischief and gossip, and abundant in her love for Dexter. A very nice performance indeed. John Lindop was relaxed and confident in the role of Dexter Haven, seemingly unruffled by the chaos around him, and well in control of manipulating his reunion with Tracy. He also had a most pleasing lyrical baritone voice, well suited to his songs. There was a warmth and believability about his relationship with young Dinah, like two rogues with a common purpose.

Jamie Johnston was excellent as the somewhat confused writer/journalist, Mike Connor. He had great facial and vocal expression, and made the most of his comedic opportunities, being particularly impressive in his scenes with Tracy. His timing throughout was very good, and he also had a very fine voice.

Colin Boyd was the perfect Uncle Willie, giving great authenticity to a character full of alcohol and impropriety. Delightfully comical and very articulate, even when in an alcoholic haze.

Gary McAlorum was suitably priggish in the role of George Kitteridge. Knowing Gary to be a person with a great sense of fun and humour, he showed very good discipline in maintaining the dull sobriety of his role. Very nicely played.

Chris Curry was a very credible repentant husband, and charming enough to win back his forsaken wife.

The chorus did all that was asked of them with a great sense of fun, and with a high level of commitment. Their singing was worthy of note and their dancing was precise and well rehearsed.

This was a slickly presented technical show. The excellent set didn't change too often, but when it did, it was done with efficiency by Stage Manager Andrew McKnight and his team. Props were suitably grand and appropriate and again, well handled. The main set was of beautiful design and construction, and the drapes were top quality. I loved the impression of a swimming pool in the garden. The only set piece that disappointed was the kitchen cloth, which was dull in comparison to the rest of the set.

Lighting was very impressive throughout the show, always helping to create atmosphere, and brilliant in its use of colour. Great design and execution.

Similarly, there were no problems apparent with the sound, and the balance with the orchestra pit was spot on.

The costumes for this production were stunning, and in particular, the gowns worn by Tracy, but generally, the standard was absolutely out of the top drawer. Added to that, there was great attention to the detail of wigs, hairstyles and make-up, beautifully crafted to capture the era of the show. The overall effect was a sumptuous feast of visual excellence, which was the crowning glory of a night of wonderful entertainment from a dedicated company. Thank you all for a most enjoyable evening.

There was a strong sense, from the outset of this production of 9 To 5, that Newbridge Musical Society were thoroughly enjoying their material, and their enthusiasm certainly infected the audience. In what is a fairly un-glamorous show, it is the colour and diversity of the characters that carry the show, and the audience were treated to a night of much laughter, and many outstanding performances.

The strength of Director Sharon McNamara was evident in her direction of her central female characters, for while she presented them with a great grasp of comedy and sensitivity, she quite rightly didn't hold back on the power of the feminist speeches towards the shows conclusion. For a show that is frivolous on many levels, it does make a poignant commentary on the role of women in the workplace, and this was well highlighted. From a staging point of view, a good effort was made with projections which only occasionally became a little washed out by lights. When neutral side flats are being used, it's best to leave them a more neutral colour and let the lighting differentiate the various scenes, but the blocks of strong red and blue were hard to disguise and were consequently over- prominent throughout the show.

It's as well that Stage Manager Phil MacSheoinin had a good stage crew, for they had a lot of furniture to shift around the stage, and they did so with no real sense of panic or disorganisation. Tidy work. Props, however cumbersome, were always appropriate and authentic. Projections were suitable, if somewhat unspectacular for the various office scenes, and on occasions light-spill weakened the images, but the moving images behind the "Potion Notion" dream sequence, were excellent. Lighting of the dance routines was colourful and creative, and the general lighting was more than adequate to ensure that the action was clearly seen. Sound quality, balance and cueing were very good throughout.

Costumes were well selected to suit the characters who were wearing them, and the children's costumes for "Potion Notion" were delightful. Being set mostly in an office, there aren't many opportunities for glitz and glamour, and while the outfits were very nice for the dream sequence, I felt you could have been even more flamboyant. Good work was done on hairstyles and make-up. Musical Director, Dave McGauran, led a very efficient orchestra who seemed to enjoy the genre of music of this show. Volume was well controlled, and there was good balance between the musicians. Likewise, the chorus were well rehearsed and very accomplished vocally. Whether on stage or singing from the wings, harmonies were clear and well realised. Principally, the show was vocally strong and precise.

Choreographer, Julianne McNamara, took every opportunity to inject the show with energetic routines, and she was fortunate enough to have a great team of funky, youthful dancers. There was good variety in the three dream sequences, and her dancers were very disciplined. The full chorus numbers were always vibrant and interesting. It's not a major criticism, but I would like to have seen the "One For The Boys" routine performed by Violet and boys, rather than the girls.

Helena Begley gave a powerful all round performance as the formidable Violet, strong on personality, vocally secure, and particularly excellent in her delivery of comedy. This is a role that requires a combination of vulnerability, insecurity and ultimately, supreme confidence, and in all areas, Helena was most appealing. Aideen Leacy was a delightfully likeable Doralee, capturing the essence of the cowgirl/country style Queen, and injecting it with a brassiness that would make any man feel ill at ease. Great delivery of her musical numbers.

Keelin Kilduff played Judy with hilarious simplicity and naivety, making the most of her beautiful comedic situations, and being totally believable and sympathetic as the heart-broken, jilted wife. A lovely performance.

Gill O'Brien could not have extracted much more comedy from the role of Roz. Her delivery of "Heart to Hart" was a highlight of the show, and her look and attitude when she became 'French-ised' was impressive!

Paul Laycock convincingly played the misogynist, Franklin Hart Jnr, as a complete weasel, with no redeeming features. A stronger dose of smarmy charm may have added a further dimension to his character, but he was, nevertheless, strong on brash and brutish comedy. "Here For You" was a tad unnecessarily vulgar, but his delivery of the number was particularly crass and enjoyable.

Margaret, the lush, was played to perfection by Ann Ryan. Her comic delivery was excellent.

I was sorry that Rory Dignam, in the role of Joe, didn't have more singing, so pleasant was his vocal quality in "Let Love Grow". He also very believably created his character, and played well beside Violet. Conor Kilduff brought a wealth of experience to the supporting role of Mr Tinsworthy, as well as adding gravitas to the male chorus.

Claire McMullan gave secure support in the role of Missy, while Daniel Ryan, Keith Domican and Cian Dowling made the most of their opportunities as Dwayne, Dick and Josh respectively. Emma Kilduff (Maria), Clodagh Donnelly (Kathy), Hannah Ryan (Candy Stripper) and Jen Martin (Doctor) competently completed the principal line-up.

This was a thoroughly entertaining production by an extremely competent cast and production team, and I thank you all sincerely for a very enjoyable visit to Newbridge.

It says something for a musical society when they can proudly proclaim that they are doing their 76th annual show in the same venue.

Well that proud statistic belongs to Roscrea Musical Society. A society founded on the traditions of musicals throughout the 20th century and now performing more modern musicals in the 21st century. The Addams Family is becoming one of the more regularly done shows as it has everything in it. A macabre chorus of ancestors, a number of well known songs, the chance for innovative choreography and good witty dialogue that allows comedy to be at the forefront of the production.

Our leading man Paul Spencer (Gomez) sang and danced so sublimely and delivered his dialogue with perfect comic timing in his desire to ensure that Rhea Smith (Morticia) his stage wife would not leave him  for keeping a secret. Ms Smith delivered her dialogue using wonderful inflection in her voice, seizing every moment to upset her husband and her daughter. Aishling Rohan (Wednesday) in return used all her acting skills to marvellous effect to harangue her mother, cajole her father and tease her boyfriend Mark Delahunty (Lucas). Throw in Andrew Walsh (Fester) whose manic characterisation was always in evidence, Siobhan Bowe (Grandma) who adopted a high pitched voice with perfect enunciation and Liam Murphy (Pugsley) who revelled in being put through the torture wheel it is a strange household. Another strange character in the Addams household was Ronan Foyle (Lurch) who not only mumbled in such a way that you thought you knew what he was saying, but he also mastered the stilts so he stood head and shoulders above the rest. When the Beinke's came to visit and rang the bell the set fell down, the Orchestra threw music in the air and the audience gasped thinking that disaster had befallen the show. It hadn't. It was director Paul Norton's magnificent curveball which was a wonderful theatrical moment. Another theatrical moment was made of Fester singing to the moon with a marvellous lighting plot which gave the impression that he had actually reached the moon, with a sleight of hand we then had the pleasure of a Fester Puppet who played gleefully with the moon, just superb. The choreography by Julieanne McNamara was precise and the chorus all performed it perfectly in time. Also perfectly in time were the orchestra under the baton of Mary Rose McNally. The Orchestra were beautifully balanced and played some most wonderful accompaniment and the chorus were correct on every entrance and ending of each phrase, beautifully in tune and with superb diction. With productions like this one that Roscrea's community were treated to the society will have no problem performing for the next 76 years.

My second visit of the season to the An Tain Theatre in Dundalk this time to see Stage One New Musical Group's production of Oliver!. A small band requires every musician to be precise and we were treated to this by a five piece orchestra with most wonderful clarity in their playing. Each instrument was played with consummate ease by the musicians and under the baton of Patrick Dunne they gave support throughout the performance to each and every member of the cast. Oliver! is a show with rip-roaring musical numbers, pathos, comedy and eventually a happy ending. Dual directors Terese Dunne (who also doubled up as the choreographer) and Rosemary Winkless ensured that each principal was always on their mark which enabled the players to produce good quality diction and a perfect selection of cockney accents. Barry Murphy was our waif-like Oliver, he has a most beautiful boy soprano voice and his rendition of "Where is Love" was lovely. He sang each of his numbers perfectly in tune and his diction was excellent. Aaron Duffy (Dodger) was extremely relaxed on stage as he paraded around the town doffing his cap and teaching young Oliver the tricks of the trade. He also sang perfectly in tune and enunciated so well. The children's chorus gave us a most marvellous opening number full of passionate singing but it sort of tapered off throughout the show as their energy levels dropped. Similarly the adult chorus, although small in number, gave us some excellent singing but needed to be more precise in their steps in the large dance numbers. Leading lady Lynsey O'Neill's (Nancy) acting with the children's chorus was super, she took them under her wing and guided them through the musical numbers in the den, although I would have liked her big solo "As long as he needs me" to have been sung with more pathos and a bit more reflectively. Tom Doonan (Fagin) was susceptible to singing a little too quickly and needed to enunciate more clearly but his acting was absolutely first class. With a perfect accent, wonderful stage presence and mannerisms he gave us a wonderful portrayal of his character. Andrew Browne (Bill Sykes) allowed his stature to command attention from the audience and the cast, and his singing was perfectly gruff and aggressive. These main characters were all suitably supported by the smaller roles but I must compliment Siobhan Jordan (Charlotte). Whilst only a small part she commanded her scenes with a wonderful accent and diction, playfully enticing Paraic McGeough (Noah) to do his worst and then she was simply horrid to poor Oliver. The sets gave us the dark foreboding London which is synonymous with the show and the costumes were bright and garish and were shown off fully by the superb lighting plot of Darren Kelleher. The sold out audience went home humming all the well known songs and had smiles on their faces which is what musical theatre is all about.

Tattersalls Ireland is where, back in the day, they use to sell horses. Now the venue is not being used for that anymore so they are upgrading it which meant that the local Ratoath Musical Society, could take on the venture of producing their show Legally Blonde there. The venue is a magnificent amphitheatre of over 600 seats, all with a perfect view of the circular stage. This calls for an enormous amount of pre-production as the design of the set and the actual technical manoeuvring of the set has to be planned precisely. Director Richie Hayes obviously put a lot of thought into this as every set was built to the correct dimensions, the stage crew, under stage manager Elaine McLoughlin, were superb in changing and re-arranging and never stopped the flow of the show one iota. Legally Blonde is a powerhouse of a show that hits the ground running and doesn't stop. The choreography by Erica Delaney Hayes was precise, full of energy and, more importantly, every member of the cast was up to the task especially the ladies of the Delta Nu sorority. These nine ladies never stopped for a minute. Their singing and dancing was absolutely wonderful, which they performed throughout all of the show and they supported their leading lady superbly. That leading lady was Danielle Williamson (Elle) whose singing was absolutely superb, she has wonderful diction and marvellous control of her powerful crescendos all delivered perfectly in pitch. Opposite Danielle was Kevin Hartnett (Emmet) who has the most wonderful stage presence and he carried off his role perfectly. Gavin Ryan (Warner) sang his opening number with wonderful comedic timing. Keila Whelan (Vivienne) played the dominating, aloof stereotypical law graduate with good clear diction and wonderful dialogue and at the end she sang so passionately. Gerry Hannigan (Callaghan) played the elder statesman at the university and delivered with superb enunciation and was in complete control of every scene, he also has a very commanding stage presence which he used to great effect in the court room scene. This show is full of wonderful comedy both in dialogue and visually, no more so than when the UPS man shows up and he transforms Louise Cassidy's (Paulette) life. Ms Cassidy delivered terrific dialogue and sang her song "Ireland" with a beautiful lilting voice. The costumes for the lawyers all oozed quality and the Delta Nu's costumes were all pristine and uniform throughout. With it being an open stage the technical side of the show needed to be specific and correct and Colm Eaton managed the lighting perfectly, although the sound needed some enhancement. Perhaps the sound also adjusted the volume of the orchestra as they were a little loud in places especially in underscoring but they sorted out the errors in the second act. Overall it was a wonderful evening's entertainment and a standing ovation was duly afforded..

The Solstice Theatre in Navan is built like an amphitheatre in Roman times of old. Some Like It Hot is a show that is not put on very regularly and yet it ticks all the boxes. Well known music, plenty of dancing and some super comedy run through the show with an abundance of parts for all ages. Richie Hayes, assisted by Liam Butler, oversaw this performance and gave us a most wonderful production. Super scenes that ran effortlessly into one another with marvellous accents and enunciation from all the cast meant that the audience were treated to a visual delight. Visually the costumes were magnificent, but singularly the costumes were made and fitted so precisely. Special word to the costume department who managed to dress our leading men in the most perfectly fitted and glamorous dresses. Ciara O'Donoghue (Sugar) played the "Marilyn Monroe" part to a tee. Her style and elegance along with her perfectly pitched accent and blonde wig enabled her to perform marvellously. Her dancing and singing was precise and the delivery of her dialogue was exact. There are a number of cameo roles in this show and all performed in tandem to assist the main players.

The stage management of Elaine McLoughlin was excellent, she and her crew made the scene changes swiftly and never delayed the show one bit. Aisling Toher's choreography was precise and inventive and the female chorus all performed together superbly, especially in the larger chorus numbers, with wonderful smiles on their faces which was lovely to see.

Our orchestra played most beautifully in the quieter moments with a lovely quality, however as they were at the back of the stage our musical director had to rely on a video screen to show his conducting skills, this is never a good idea as the communication is not instant and led to a few problems at the end of phrases. The main protagonists in this show were played by Ultan O'Cinneide (Joe/ Josephine) and Ronan Walsh (Jerry/ Daphne). Mr O'Cinneide's character is often thought of as the straight man but in fact his comedy is mostly spoken, not with Jerry but with Sugar. His scenes in the second half of the show when he transforms from Joe to Josephine to Junior, were played with comedy and poignancy as he struggled with himself about telling Sugar of his love for her. The final scene when he "owns up" was played superbly with wonderful pathos. Mr Walsh (Jerry/Daphne) delivered his comedy superbly and precisely, he got every laugh and his timing was impeccable. His delight when he announced his "engagement" had the audience in hysterics. The three leading players led from the front and assisted by the rest of the company gave their audience a most wonderful evening's entertainment.

Director Tim Landers presented us with a show in which the basic ingredients were securely in place, and then put much thought and effort into injecting it with creative touches and innovative ideas. The "Thing" (the hand) beautifully conducted the orchestra during the overture, his gestures indicating that he had a thorough knowledge of the music. He also impressively showed up unexpectedly during the action of the show, which worked nicely. (Having him conduct the Enteract was possibly stretching the joke a bit too far.) The Graveyard Gatekeeper, a kind of Frankenstein's "Igor", was another nice touch, hovering as a spooky presence in the background, and even assisting with scene changes. The addition of the character "Cousin It", however, despite looking very funny, served no real purpose and contributed little to the content of the show. I liked the use of statues, gargoyles, etc, to enhance the set, and I was delighted to see such detail stretching as far as the foyer, getting the audience into the flavour of the show even before they were seated.

The opening of the show suffered because of too much smoke, through which the lights had little effect. Consequently, the first seven or eight lines of script, including some very funny visual gags, were lost completely.

Positionings on stage were good, and much work was done on realising the comedy of the show, but I think one or two of the principals needed a little more guidance on delivery of punch lines, and the pace of some of the extra business was a tad slow. (The comedy of Lurch "rushing" to open the door was weakened by the business with the breath freshener, which seemed to take an age.) The chorus provided good back-up throughout the show, but one of two younger members were guilty of coming out of character before they left the stage.

All in all, however, this was a well directed and smooth running production.

Musical Director, Fintan Farrelly, had good control of a very competent orchestra, who were energetic, yet sympathetic to the on-stage performers. Balance was always well maintained. There was great pace to all the musical pieces, and good dynamics in the interpretation of the score. This was complemented by an enthusiastic performance from the chorus, with harmonies generally secure and confident. Principals also appeared to be very well musically rehearsed.

Choreographer, Emer O'Brien, had her chorus and dancers displaying high energy and heaps of ability right from the get go, with a lively and engaging "When You're An Addams". From there on, they were well involved in "Full Disclosure", showed their best during "Just Around The Corner" and worked hard in "Tango De Amor". There was good variety in the choreography, and it took into account the level of ability of the dancers, which allowed the routines to be well polished. The dancers' involvement in "The Moon and Me" was fine, but the number suffered from a need for more creativity. Arm movements, generally, weren't always precisely together, but that's a minor flaw in what was a very good display of dance throughout the show.

In the role of Gomez, Tony Wadd performed confidently and sang with an assured vocal. While he deservedly earned plenty of laughs from the audience, I did feel that he worked too hard at trying to be funny, rather than allowing the script to do the work for him. He played the role as a comedian, rather than a comedy actor, and perhaps being more suave and sophisticated would have added comedy and awkwardness to his "stuck-in-the- middle" dilemma.

Janice Gibney had the perfect look and ambiance for the role of Morticia, strutting beautifully, and clearly having the upper hand with her husband. Her delivery of "Death is Just Around the Corner" was very good, and she pointed the "cor-o- ner" joke very well. Her false laugh could have been funnier, had it been more dead- pan, but this was a fine performance. Liam Brady played well to the audience as Fester and Narrator. There was a pleasant gentleness combined with a wide-eyed insanity about his interpretation, which worked well. "The Moon and Me" was sung very nicely, but I do feel that more could have been done with the routine. Lindsay Clyne impressed as Wednesday, largely because we were allowed to see the lighter side of her personality when she was with Lucas. "Pulled" was particularly well performed, and she and Lucas had good chemistry in "Crazier Than You". Iarlaith O'Rourke was a Pugsley with attitude, who enjoyed the cheekiness of his character, and was full of mischief. He did struggle a little with his music, I suspect because his voice is at that awkward breaking stage, but he did, nevertheless give a very likeable and credible performance.

Michelle Kelly Conlon was a well aged, feisty and mischievous Grandma Addams, who handled her character and her comedy very comfortably.

Conor Lynn-McLoughlin had a good look and stature for the role of Lurch, and delivered his grunts with aplomb, but the real comedy of the character comes from being completely deadpan, and a tendency to smile weakened his impact. Some of his extra business also seemed a bit laboured.

Sean Rooney was a very credible Lucas, strong in delivery of his lines and confident in his music. In a nicely established relationship with Wednesday, "Crazier Then You" was very well performed number.

Michael O'Driscoll and Valerie Nolan as Mal and Alice Beineke were a very plausible couple, and displayed very humorous discomfort in their stagnant relationship in the early scenes. Valerie showed great vocal ability during "Waiting", although I do think she could have been even more extreme in unleashing her inner self. But both performed with conviction, and they played off each other well as they reignited their flames of passion.

The chorus made a worthy contribution to the action of the show, whether singing and dancing with confidence, or providing a "Greek Chorus" of reaction in the background.

With the exception of the portable trees, which were a tad untidy, I really liked the set for this show. There was great attention to detail with many interesting and unusual statues and carved heads, etc, all of which looked very spooky and effective. The rack and the chair were decent props, and there was always plenty to look at. The tree for the shooting of the apple was good, with some kind of freak hidden inside it, which I couldn't clearly define. Several house interior projections were used, and while they tended to be a little bit pale to make a more powerful impact, they did look very good and appropriate.

Stage Manager, Eddie Kiernan and his crew weren't in a hurry with their scene changes, but they did do an efficient job. Lighting was competent as opposed to spectacular, with good colour and atmosphere creation, and it was certainly good enough to ensure that all the action was clearly seen. I did like the "weather" effects during "Full Disclosure Part 2" and a good effort was made to keep the general washes from spilling too much onto the projected backgrounds. Sound quality was fine throughout, with good balance and cueing.

Much time and effort was obviously spent on presenting a weird and wonderful chorus of dead ancestors, from good individual costumes to outrageous hair and make-up. Very effective work was done here by all concerned. Principals were equally well attired.

How delightful to see the effort that went into giving the audience a taste of what was to come, the moment they arrived at the venue, with cobwebs, ghouls and all manner of spooky items dressing the entrance to the auditorium.

A spirit of adventure was reflected in the fun, energy and sense of community that was evident throughout this show, from all who participated. Thanks to all concerned for a bright, entertaining and feel-good production. It was a most enjoyable night.

It was with great anticipation that I made my first trip to the National Opera House in Wexford, having heard so many wonderful reports about the venue, and I wasn't to be disappointed. The place is superbly designed, materially beautiful, technically excellent and acoustically perfect. But its greatest charm is that, at heart, it has been created in the style of a wonderfully traditional proscenium theatre.

I don't like to be repetitive, so it's sufficient to say that the above description can be equally applied to Wexford Light Opera Society's production of Evita. Director, John Donnelly, offered his audience a superbly slick and lavish, traditional telling of the story of Eva Duarte. Principals and chorus were sure-footed, from entrances and exits to polished routines and beautiful pictures. The technical preparation for the show was evident in an excellent blend of physical staging and projected images, appropriate and beautiful costumes, an almost perfect lighting design and close to flawless sound quality. In just about every way, this show was a shining example of the golden rule, get the basics right, and the rest will follow.

"The Art of the Possible" followed a well tried and tested pattern, but the perfect timing of Peron 'stealing' the final chair in the game of musical chairs, was a touch of class. Similarly, what seemed like a common-place "Rainbow Tour" was transformed into something special by Che's quite excellent jumping into the accent and character of the various countries being visited. The simple magnificence of the Act One finale needed no tricks or gimmicks. It was simply as brilliant visually as it was musically.

The 16-piece orchestra, under Musical Director Fintan Cleary, was truly sublime, whether it was the varied effects from keyboards and percussion, the vibrant tones of the brass and woodwind, or the stirring swell from the strings, their accompaniment of the on-stage action was top class. Equally accomplished was the vocal contribution of a well drilled chorus, under Chorus Mistress, Eithne Corrigan. Whether on stage or off, harmonies, lyrics and dynamics were crisp, clear and precise. From full choruses to smaller groups, and including the children's chorus, the music of the show was truly excellent.

Choreographer, Nicole McDonald made the most of her opportunities to show the chorus in the best possible light, with routines that were very well devised. No- one looked uncomfortable in their dancing, which suggested thorough rehearsal and attention to detail. "Buenos Aires" was lively and varied, and performed with zeal by the chorus. "Peron's Latest Flame" was suitably refined for the aristocrats and the soldiers performed with military precision.

There was excellent dancing from the Tango couple on the balcony, for "I'd Be Surprisingly Good For You", but truthfully, I did find it a bit of a distraction… "The Money Kept Rolling In" was very well staged, and the "Waltz for Eva and Che" was nicely choreographed. Overall, the choreography made a significant and enchanting contribution to the success of the show.

Aileen Donohoe was an engaging Eva, fresh and flirtatious from the outset, and growing in confidence and stature as the story progressed. Her acting was always secure, and particularly impressive in her illness at the shows climax, but it was the quality of her vocals that made the biggest impact, from a rich, rounded earthiness in her lower register, to a controlled melodic soprano. A very nicely balanced performance.

Tony Carty sang Peron with ease, and excellent expression. He was a very believable General and leader at the outset, and there was very good chemistry between himself and Eva. Like her, his prowess as an actor grew brilliantly during Act Two, and his handling of Eva's deterioration and eventual demise, was remarkably emotional.

James McDermott was an outstanding Che, strong in his vocal delivery and thoroughly comfortable in the role of narrator. He gave much variety to the character, slipping from his regular voice to a Spanish, then an Italian and a French accent with ease during a brilliantly performed "Rainbow Tour". With an excellent stage presence, his running commentary on Eva's life was acted and sung with great energy and emotion. Eric Hayes, both in appearance and in performance, was a delightfully cheesy Magaldi, capturing the essence of a character whose ambitions were far beyond his capabilities.
