The magnificent setting of the Grand Opera House in Belfast was this year's venue for BSPA's production, Les Miserables. My guest and I attended on the second Friday and witnessed a committed performance by a talented cast of teenagers. Leading the way was Valjean played by Matthew Quinn. He led from the front with a passionate performance, his acting matched his singing and we were left in no doubt as to who or what the show was about. He was pursued throughout by Tom O'Kelly as Javert. Tom has excellent stage presence although a bit more menace to his character would have been an advantage. Naomi Smyth gave us every emotion in her portrayal of Fantine, she sang most perfectly and died most graciously. Holly Ryan as Eponine was pivotal in every scene. Her rendition of "On My Own" brought the house down and at her demise she conveyed the most poignant emotion. Alexandra Dick played the adult Cosette and sang with a wonderful soprano voice and her relationship with Marius was acted most precisely. Ciaran McCormack led the students with passion and precision as Enjolras. He has a very good singing voice and he was most commanding in all of the scenes at the barricade. The comedy was delivered by the two Thenardiers, Malachy Conlon and Maebh Quinn. The emphasis was on the comedy, too much sometimes, leaving the words and notes not supported as well as they might have been. The highlight of the evening was Robert Kelly's portrayal of Marius. Every word, every note, every movement were all perfect. Not a foot wrong, not a word delivered incorrectly, not an emotion misplaced. When he climbed into Cosette's garden and met her for the first time, the awkward embarrassment was delivered superbly. Similarly when he realised that Eponine loved him but only at her death it was heartbreaking. It was a wonderful all round performance.

As for the technical side of this production, led by Director James Huish, it was not as slick as it could have been. Scene changes were laboured. Lighting was very good but every scene was too dark, daylight never appeared at all. Sound cues were very poor, a pity. The orchestra under Wilson Shields started at a most frantic pace and then got quicker! There also needed to be a little quieting of the brass section who overpowered all comers in the first act. The set design was very disappointing. A pre-requisite of a barricade is that it is taller than the members of the cast, this was not so. Players could clearly be seen behind the barricade awaiting their entrance. With the most marvellous facilities of a professional theatre a bit more thought in the technical side of this production would have assisted enormously. The chorus were note and word perfect and they sang with gusto and commitment. The opening convict's number was superb as was the female chorus in the factory. Well done to all concerned. Costumes were wonderful and correct to the time especially the prostitutes who were dressed most colourfully. The audience afforded the cast a standing ovation, well deserved for all their labours.

The town hall theatre in Claremorris, I am reliably advised, will soon be an 800 seat venue. The well-known professional musicians who are booked to perform there will have the pleasure of performing in a wonderfully appointed venue right in the heart of the town. Claremorris Musical Society performed their 11th production, Me and My Girl, to a packed theatre and how well they entertained their patrons. This show is a rarity in that the leading man is also the comedy lead. John Byrne (Bill) took on the challenge and played it quite superbly. His accent, dialogue and singing were marvellous but his forte was his dancing. He excelled in all his musical dance numbers and his tap was terrific. He was ably assisted by his leading lady Mary Dempsey (Sally). She took on his challenge and together they danced most sublimely. Her dialogue was enunciated perfectly and her singing of "Once you lose your heart" was beautifully melodic. Director and Choreographer Hazel McLynn kept the show moving at a wonderful pace, with the dialogue cues precise and she ensured that every last bit of comedy was garnered from the script to its fullest. Not only were the front two precise in their dance steps but Ms McLynn also had eight dancers who danced superbly in every number. Michael Goulding (Gerald) played the typical toffee nosed gent with a perfect high pitched accent and an air of despair each time his "true love" Lady Jacqueline rejected him. Vivienne Lee (Lady Jacqueline) played the femme fatale brilliantly, her scene on the couch with Bill left little to the imagination as she teased and tempted him. Her acting was marvellous and her singing was wonderful. Ciaran Kiely (Parchester) played the straight laced family solicitor, his dialogue was excellently delivered but we also saw him perform the comedy side of his character perfectly. The manor was ruled by Rosemary Noone (Duchess of Dene) who gave a most commanding performance. Her intonation was marvellous and she was in full control of her performance. Ms Noone gave us a typical, stereotype of an English Lady. Most formidable in her actions and her deportment, her dialogue was pronounced correctly and precisely. Seamus Cafferkey (Sir John) played extremely well in Act 1 as the Lord of the Manor although in the shadow of his wife the Duchess. His dialogue was precise as was his accent. He excelled in Act 2 and his duet with Bill took us back to the music hall where their rendition of "love makes the world go round" was a singing, dancing and comedy gem. The technical side of the show gave us perfect cueing from the sound technician and the lighting plot worked very well although a travel spot for some dances would have added to the visual. The set was well designed with the main three piece set swivelling for particular scenes and the interior scenes were very well dressed. The costumes were terrific, all fitting perfectly and very correct to the era. The orchestra led by Deirdre Lee accompanied with wonderful control and the tempi were perfect not only for the dance numbers but also for the quieter, melancholy number.

I am told that there is nothing unusual about a rainy Friday night in May in Galway. However the rain didn't stop me and a host of patrons and sponsors attending Corofin Musical Society's second musical offering. Hot Mikado is based on the Gilbert & Sullivan operetta with only a few modern adaptations to the music. It still requires a talented singing chorus and a raft of musical principals. Founder of the society Joey Power made his debut in directing and what a wonderful job of it he did too. He got the most out of his cast with special emphasis on the comedy, and his players all took up the challenge and never faltered.  Our wandering minstrel, Robert Reed (Nanki Poo) delivered his dialogue in a most crisp manner and never tired. He was a bly assisted by Alana Power (Yum Yum) whose dialogue was enunciated wonderfully. Their duet was sung most musically and the timing of the lyrics interspersed with the kisses was timed perfectly. The main comedy role fell to Stuart Barrows (Ko Ko), who gave us a wonderful character accent which he kept up throughout, his singing was delivered perfectly in tune and his comedy timing was exemplary. The arrival of Olibhia Donnelly (Katisha) was a show stopper in itself as she strode around the stage with a stare of displeasure... and then she sang. Her phrasing was sublime, her diction was perfect and she not only sang every note right in the middle but sang each note for its full value. Allied to her singing Ms Donnelly also gave us wonderful comedy with Ko Ko particularly in "tit willow". It is a very small stage in Corofin but the Power sisters, choreographers, managed to get the cast to move and dance and tap without any fear of mishap and they also got the chorus to get every bow and scrape timed perfectly when the Mikado spoke. Eoin Fahy (Mikado) made a grand entrance from the auditorium and spoke slowly and precisely asserting his authority throughout. The main principals were ably assisted by Elaine Hynes (Pitti Sing) and Roisin Broderick (Peep Bo) who along with Yum Yum gave us a wonderful musical trio and cameo of the Andrews Sisters, the harmonies were perfectly sung and perfectly balanced. It would be remiss of me not to mention Kevin Murphy (Pooh Bah) whose facial expressions were excellent, this assisted him in his many characters all of which he played with different accents and mannerisms, a most accomplished feat in itself. The set was simple and perfectly functional with a marvellous "fan" design at the back. The lighting complemented the set and in the opening of Act 2 gave us a most visual silhouette of the bride to be, Yum Yum. The sound technician knew his cues and his directions as he performed perfectly. The small orchestra under John Flatley's direction gave wonderful support to the performers, and Mr Flatley's accompaniment on the keyboards was terrific. The chorus mistress Martha O'Toole managed to get a wonderful sound from the chorus and they all sang with passion and gusto throughout. It was a wonderful night's entertainment to start the new season.

This show requires the chorus to hit the stage running and never stop, which is exactly what Fermoy Musical Society gave us. The male chorus was limited in numbers but they were positive in all their actions. The female chorus was marvellous. The energy that each gave was super. The choreographer Stephen Cullinane O'Regan had the chorus dancing and tapping their way through the show and the female chorus led by six dancers were terrific. The music from this show is based on the G & S "Mikado" but is adapted to give us a more, bluesy/jazzy accompaniment. Musical Director Deirdre Long led a very tight band of musicians. Three gentlemen who immersed themselves into the production also and their playing of trumpet, trombone and clarinet/saxophone was fantastic, and they even joined in on the ad libs where required. A small gripe was that the "electric" instruments were a little overpowering and the balance was a tad off. The sound technician had all his cues correct, the costumes were an abundance of colours, particularly the leading ladies whose dresses were fantastic. The six dancers in particular had wonderful matching outfits. The lighting plot had too similar back lighting which meant facial features in some scenes were not visually clear. Sarah Berry (Yum Yum) sang very positively, with good diction and good intonation. Her dialogue was precise and her commitment to Cian Daly (Nanki Pooh) was excellent. She just needed a little more precision in the dances. Aine Carroll (Pitti Sing) sang with a control and passion above her 17 years. Her phrasing and breath control were marvellous. Her dialogue was secure and she was very light on her feet. Gillian Fenton (Peep Bo) sang perfectly in the trio's with Yum Yum and Pitti Sing and held her line wonderfully, her dialogue was super and her acting whilst miming was hilarious. Colette Daly (Katisha) entered with a powerful voice which she controlled perfectly. Superb diction and intonation, she phrased all of her songs superbly. She performed the comedy scenes with Ko Ko in a relaxed manner. Cian Daly (Nanki Pooh) started off a little hesitantly but grew into both his singing and acting roles. Paul Finn (Pooh Bah) delivered his dialogue quite precisely with clean crisp enunciation. He has a most luxurious baritone voice with superb resonance and his lower register was velvety. Rory Ward (Pish Tush) has a superb upper register and carried the notes perfectly, just needs to enunciate a little better. His acting was always on cue and his attention to his fellow performers was excellent. Declan Woulfe (Koko) played the comedy role. The character requires boundless energy and Mr Woulfe gave us this. His characterisation appeared to be based on The Mask with his stance and facial expressions, and then his accent was mostly German, which sometimes interfered with the delivery of his dialogue. His singing was perfectly in pitch and his comedy dancing was good. Director Killian Collins kept the pace of the show nice and tight, his set was designed like an old time speak-easy with orchestra at the back and a flowing staircase u/s/r to allow prominent entrances of the principals. In 2024 the society will be 100 years old, and with a full house on a Tuesday night you can see that musical theatre is alive and well in Fermoy.

Guys & Dolls is one of those shows that require a mixture of performers. From the more established players who give us the back bone of the chorus through to the young female Hot Box dancers and a male chorus who need to be able to move rather than dance. The chorus, ably taught by Dave O'Connor, gave us good clean diction and the harmonies were precise when required. This show has some big dance numbers. For the men the movement in "lady luck" was a little too regimented, but the females, firstly the Hot Box singers danced and can- canned most precisely in "take back your mink" and then gave us wonderful slow suggestive dance moves in the Havana scene. The costumes for the ladies were beautiful in style and colour particularly the Havana scene with wonderful red, blue and gold dresses. Joanne Logue (Sarah Brown) has the most wonderful soprano voice, beautiful tone and vowel sounds and she sang in complete control of her voice. Her acting went from being strict and standoffish to being in Love with Sky and her committment to him was played perfectly. Kevin Hartnett (Sky Masterson) has the most wonderful stage presence. He strolled around each scene, delivering dialogue perfectly with a marvellous specific American accent. His singing has wonderful intonation and clean precise diction. The relationship between Sarah and Sky was played perfectly and their commitment to each other was terrific. Their voices blended marvellously in their duets with each giving marvellous support to the other. Terry Martin (Nathan Detroit) was the busiest man on stage, quick movements, super facial expressions relaying complete panic to the audience as everything he tried to achieve went pear shaped. His accent was precise, his dialogue was delivered quickly and his enunciation was excellent. Katy Nicholas' (Miss Adelaide) portrayal was spot on. Her nasally accent and shrill delivery of her dialogue, when talking to Nathan, was perfect. Her dancing was full of energy, her comedy timing was marvellous, and when she sang she had a most powerful voice perfectly in pitch and always well supported. All of the main players were well assisted by the supporting players. The opening musical trio sung by Chris O'Connor (Nicely Nicely), Kevin Macken (Benny) and Sean Button (Rusty) was wonderfully performed and they got all the rhythms spot on. There was also an excellent cameo performance by Aaron Tierney who played Harry the Horse. Helen McCann (director) managed to get the players dialogue delivered at a nice brisk pace, the sets were constructed and painted very well, the sound technician got all his cues correct, but the lighting plot was a little too repetitive. David (doc) O'Connor was the musical director and he gave a very good conducting beat to the orchestra and both hand and visual direction to the players on stage.

Chess is a musical that requires a large stage area to ensure that full respect is given to the wonderful chorus arrangements in this show. The Mercy School in Tuam has that space. The large open stage stretched across the entire width of the auditorium, wonderful painted chess pieces either side, the American and Russian offices down stage left and right, a marvellously lit chess board front and centre and to finish it off superb video screen shots that ran through the whole production. The musical director John Roe had a very tight and precise orchestra who, with the odd exception, played and accompanied wonderfully. Choreographer Ciara Kavanagh had some intricate dance steps which some of the chorus struggled with, but the corps de ballet who were used in the Chess games, were wonderful. The wardrobe department worked overtime to produce the most marvellous array of colourful costumes which enhanced the production. Sound cues and effects were good and the lighting plot was excellent. The show revolves around three main characters and supported by four others. James Conway (Arbiter) stood very straight and oversaw the games, good crisp dialogue and wonderful diction in his opening singing piece. Steffen Knauer (Molotov) spoke with a most pronounced Russian accent, which occasionally was too strong and it impeded his dialogue and singing. Damien Conway (Walter) had a good stage American accent and his portrayal was excellent particularly towards the end when we saw his true colours. Karen Ronane (Svetlana) sang most beautifully, with super breath control and wonderful diction and intonation. The duet with Florence was sung quite perfectly. Niall Conway's (Trumper) acting and dialogue was brash and brusque at the start and then his attempt to try and woo Florence back was played marvellously. His singing required more support as his diction was laboured, and he had problems with his intonation. Emily Lohan (Florence) sang with wonderful poise and control, her breath control enabled her voice to carry the lyrics and harmonies beautifully. She gave us anger and despair at Trumper and then gave us the most wonderful commitment to Anatoly. Shane Kelly (Anatoly) sang magnificently. Every note, every word was delivered perfectly, his acting was very relaxed and his commitment to Florence was wonderful. He led from the front and gave us a superb performance. Peter Kennedy directed and gave us as a show that had slick dialogue, smooth scene changes, pathos and humour. On their 40th anniversary a wonderful evening out at Marian Choral Society.

This show is not done very often, probably because it would not suit a vast number of societies due to the relatively small number required in the cast. So it was with eager anticipation that I travelled to Shannon to see Muse Productions' presentation. The show is set in a communal prison cell which means that all the players are on stage for the whole performance, they wait their turn and observe and interact in all aspects of the show, a difficult task in itself. Director Martin McNelis designed a most marvellous set full of niches, cubby holes, dungeons and a most magnificent trap door that opened from the roof down. He then used two tables and four forms throughout the show to make objects allied to the story, a castle, two horses and a windmill. Add to that a box of props which held more than seemed possible and we were all set for the performance. The play revolves around our leading man Chris Willetts (Cervantes). It is a mammoth part, not only singing and speaking but his characterisation requires him to lose his faculties whilst slowly going mad. He affected a pause in his dialogue which looked and sounded as if he was searching for lines, but it was all part of his character. His dialogue was excellent and his singing was strong and secure, fantastic. He was supported by his assistant Brian Roche (Sancho). Mr Roche had boundless energy as he threw himself into his character and supported throughout, super dialogue and a most marvellous tenor singing voice. Our heroine in the piece Jessica Bray (Aldonza) sang with a guttural rasp in her melodic voice. She used her accent to accentuate the vowels and her diction was excellent. Her acting was broad and brash and she commanded the stage. In Act 2 after she was attacked, she returned from the dungeon and her acting was quite superb, she was composed and timid and fearful, marvellous.

What was terrific about this group of assembled players, and what was required for this show, was that they were singers who could act. The singing in this show is difficult and challenging and every member of the cast took up that responsibility. Noel Murphy (Innkeeper) sang tongue in cheek with "woeful countenance". Lauren Dunne (Antonia), Mikey O'Gorman (Padre) and Clare McNelis (Housekeeper) sang as a trio most marvellously in "only thinking of him", and the padre's comedy timing in that number was hilarious.

Choreography was by Gary Loughnane, and whilst there were various movements throughout the only choreographed piece was danced by Ciaran Collins (The Moor) and Tara Monaghan (The Gypsy). This was a most wonderful sensuous dance, where they both committed to a routine of tantric temptation.

Costumes were suitably ragged and dirty for the prisoners although style of footwear could have been looked at a little closer. Sound technician was very good and the lighting plot was terrific. The chorus work which was excellent was overseen by musical director Shane Farrell.

Due to space the orchestra were positioned in another room and a live feed was visible to players. There were a few delays in the feed, but nothing to hamper nor upset what was a most entertaining and enjoyable performance.

In Castlemahon there is a newly built community centre where the Newcastle West Musical Society has taken up residence and to where I travelled for their production of The Wizard of Oz. An absolute guaranteed crowd puller so much so that they put the show on over two weekends instead of a whole week. A very large cast of children and adults all portrayed their respective characters wonderfully be they townsfolk, munchkins or winkies. Dorothy Gale, on the night I attended, was played by Cori Greaney. Dressed perfectly and with little Toto by her side, she took on this role with the confidence that belied her 16 years. Superb accent with wonderful crisp dialogue, marvellous dancing and then to cap it off a truly perfect rendition of her signature song "Over the Rainbow". Nick Cotter (Scarecrow) could have had more stuffing in the costume department and his singing needed a little more care. Liam Cronin (Tinman) had a tendency to over sing which caused a few intonation problems and Paul Keyes (Lion) needed to slow down his dialogue especially when delivering the punch lines. Olivia Lynch (Ms Gulch/Wicked Witch) unfortunately didn't convey to us the fear from the Wicked Witch of the West which was expected, perhaps more emphasis on the cackling and shrieking voice, there was also a distinct lack of a broomstick!

Direction was a joint effort by Tom Madigan and Susan Browne who also choreographed. Dialogue was kept at a good pace, but there was not enough concentration to make the accents uniform.

Having a very large children's chorus did not help the choreographer's task as they were prone to drift away from their allotted positions. Musical Director Michael Young played the keyboards and had three musicians to accompany; they had a lovely balance and good support for all the pieces. Perhaps he should have been centre in front of the stage to allow better eye contact for entrances and endings. Sound was good throughout, the lighting plot could have been more precise and the scene changes were not as quick as would have been expected considering that the show was running three performances. I was afforded lovely hospitality and the audience all left singing and humming the well-known tunes, well done to all concerned.

When a show is performed so rarely it is always wonderful to re-visit. Hello Dolly! is one of the most classic musicals of all time, full of song and dance, and one of the few roles for a leading lady to headline. This production had Dawn Kavanagh playing Dolly Levi, costumes maketh the lady all of which were marvellous. Her dialogue was wonderfully precise and she kept a certain metre to her delivery. She sang with controlled power and her signature song was sung as a standout crowd pleaser. Yvonne Murphy (Mrs Molloy) was the proprietor of a most wonderful hat shop. The set was superb and the array of hats was terrific. Ms Murphy spoke with a most precise accent and her intonation and diction were excellent. Jayne Louise Kelly (Minnie Fay) gave us the most marvellous facial expressions of awe and wonderment. Her dialogue was superb and her comedy was terrific. Rory Chadwick (Horace) needed to get more anger into his personality; he berated his staff until his capitulation at the end. Good speaking voice with a clear accent, the diction of his lyrics needed a little more attention. Paul Kenna (Barnaby) played the down at heel, embarrassed fool quite perfectly. His facial expressions were very good particularly with Minnie. Pat Cullen (Cornelius) had the comedy part of his character perfect, good timing and his dialogue was excellent. When singing he just needed to hold the notes through to the end and support the voice a little better. Musically the orchestra gave wonderful accompaniment and was never too loud. I would question some of the tempi which Mary Rose McNally used. Some pieces were slow instead of quick and vice versa. The costume department worked overtime, the female chorus dresses were spectacular, with all shades of pastel colours, and the uniforms for the parade were super. The main backdrop was a wonderfully painted street scene, and the addition of the shop in the opening with steps and a basement door entrance worked splendidly. The Hat shop was wonderfully conceived and dressed. The restaurant was most plush in Act 2 although the tread of the stairs was a little too big which caused some problems. The big chorus numbers were well designed by Choreographer Grace McGrath. The movement in "Sunday clothes" was excellent. Simple steps all on the beat and with plenty of happy smiling faces. The "parade" was superb. Not only did the costumes help but the marching of the chorus was quite intricate and looked visually spectacular. No errors from the sound department who gave us a lovely reverb when Dolly talked to her dead husband Ephraim but the lighting plot needed a little more work.

The beautiful Theatre Royal in Waterford is an old fashioned theatre in which I attended this relatively modern musical Starlight Express. The story of a child who, in her dreams, has her trains come alive and race against each other. A cast of 25, all with specific costumes relative to their character, took to the stage and roller skated their way through the performance. Roller Skating was something all the kids did in the 80's, so it was a great to see the cast skating, singing and dancing. David Hennessy directed this show and he had the cast performing in a most fluid manner. No member of the company struggled with the skates, they were never out of position and including the wings for the race scenes gave us a sense of a racetrack. The choreography by Michelle Condon gave us movement of locomotive trains and using wonderful arm movements and gestures meant that visually it was very precise. The individual costumes were fantastic, each specific to the character and were enhanced by wonderful lighting. The lighting plot was sure and precise. They used the metallic stanchion of the set to bounce the lights around the stage and the travel spots were perfect. This production used backing tracks throughout the entire show which I do not like. I still believe that when a song is sung in a musical it should be a joint collaboration between singer, musicians and conductor. Using backing tracks should have made it easier to ensure that the sound balance was correct but there were still some performers who were not audible over the volume of the backing tracks! Danny Brockie (Rusty) sang with super diction and wonderful phrasing. His duet at the end with Phoebe Dipple (Pearl) was marvellous with beautiful harmony blending the two voices together. Phoebe gave a wonderful performance with superb enunciation of her dialogue. Padraig Di Fusco (Greaseball) had a most wonderful wig, like an old time rocker, he danced sublimely on his roller skates and sang with anger and contempt. Sinead O'Donovan (Dinah) gave us a terrific performance throughout. Her country and western style song UNCOUPLED was delivered with wonderful humour and her comic timing throughout the show was super. These leading characters were ably supported by this small but very talented cast. The show finished with a full cast rendition of "Light at the end of the tunnel" which they sang and danced with carefree abandon and rocked the auditorium to its close. A truly rousing climax to what was a most wonderful production.

A brand new society joining the ranks of AIMS and a first for Cavan. Calamity Jane is a perfect show for a new society to showcase its talents as it has a bit of everything. Lots of character parts with an opportunity for specific dancing and choral singing. As the show progressed Andrea Fitzpatrick (Calamity) shrugged off her initial nervousness and fully committed to her role. Her dialogue was positive, her comedy was delivered with good timing, her relationship with Bill was feisty at the start and then slowly she fell for him. Chris Corroon (Bill) gave a most assured performance. Wonderful stage presence, a good American drawl on his dialogue and his Baritone voice had wonderful resonance. Enda Shalvey's (Danny) dialogue was crisp and precise and he sang well within himself. His duet with Katie Brown was perfectly melodic. Shannon O'Flynn's (Katie Brown) first scene with Calamity was very good. She got the pace of the dialogue correct and her accent and diction were super. John Grogan (Francis Fryer) performed a good precise dance routine and his intonation was good. His dialogue and enunciation, particularly in Act 2 in the scene with Miller, was excellent. Seamus Smith (Miller) was obviously a well known local man as every entrance was greeted with anticipation by the audience, his performance was terrific. He got all the nuances correct of his character, his delivery of dialogue was always on cue, his timing and pauses were correct. There were a number of cameo roles all played correctly in character, however I must single out Conor Martin (Joe the Barman), he played the part with his dialogue always on cue and his singing was assured in the reprise of "Adelaide". Due to the small back stage space he was also Joe the stage hand. His work was very good throughout and his efforts were of great advantage to the production. Costumes were all period correct and ball dresses were super. Choreographer Roisin Currid also played Adelaide Adams. Her singing was very secure and her dialogue was suitably dismissive of her suitors. In her choreography she produced simple but precise dances steps for the big chorus numbers whilst her routine for the 4 can-can dancers was excellent. Director Chris Currid used the small stage area to the full with the saloon being the main set. Clever dressing of the stage allowed for the other scenes to be played within this set. He also made good use of the auditorium with entrances of the chorus from the hall for "Black Hills of Dakota" and the scene leading up to Calamity and Bill's rendition of "Secret Love". The orchestra were a little loud and had a reliance on a synthesiser for strings which didn't help the balance. Musical Director Vincent Tully gave most of his direction to the orchestra which meant that chorus work was affected. There was one notable exception being "Black Hills of Dakota", which was sung a Capella with wonderful precise harmonies. A first production for this new society and with plans in place for next year, community theatre is alive and well in a small corner of Co Cavan.

Director Brian Logan set the scene and the tone of the show very well from the outset with a vibrant and unusual opening chorus sequence. I liked that he and Choreographer Sharon Logan were courageous enough to veer away from the norm, even if it presented a show of contradictions. The presence of Roosevelt and his New Deal firmly establishes a specific era, which immediately knocked Annie's frizzy hairstyle and the hip-hop elements of the choreography at odds with the period. But with the current success of "Hamilton" and other modernisations of dated stories, I suppose this is a trend that must be accepted as a new norm. While it didn't always sit comfortably with me, that in no way detracted from very well-rehearsed and performed dance routines, and an abundance of energy from both principals and chorus. The set was consistent with the modernisation, a collage of "Annie" posters and images, which were well selected and attractive, although it resulted in a less defined contrast between the squalor of Annie's orphan life and the grandeur of life with Warbucks. The composite set made life a little easier than usual for Stage Manager David Wray, but there was still plenty to do with moving flats, doors and furniture pieces. This was efficiently handled. Props were appropriate and everything was nicely painted.

Both as MD and Chorus Master, Eric Boyd did a fine job of adapting to this modernised version of the show. The accompaniment was fresh and exciting, and some intricate harmonies and tempos were nicely realised. I'm not sure that all the modernisations necessarily enhanced the original, some numbers being somewhat heavy on beat and rhythm, at the expense of melody. Singers were well prepared and uniformly capable and competent in their delivery. Dancing throughout the show was of a good standard with some excellent work particularly from "Cecille", "Annette" and several other maids. Orphans were well disciplined, and the named orphans all gave very good account of themselves. "Molly" was simply delightful!

Abigail Mairs gave a strikingly good performance in the title role, full of feisty energy and likeability. She was an accomplished dancer and captured her character with great confidence. She has the makings of a very good voice also, although there were a few pitch issues, on this occasion, on some of her top notes, but overall, she was delightful to watch and to listen to.

Abigail's real-life Daddy was also her Daddy Warbucks, and from Richard Mairs came a decisive and assertive performance, capturing the initial coolness of the business tycoon, and then melting beautifully at the antics and warmth of Annie. Good vocal quality here also.

Niaomh Rodgers was a delightfully sincere Grace Farrell, as comfortable being a nanny to Annie as she was being a business secretary to Warbucks. Again, strong vocal quality enhanced her performance.

Maxine McAleenon as Miss Hannigan, obviously relishing the opportunity to torment her poor orphan charges. One could almost smell the gin, as she staggered the stage. Her scenes with Rooster and Lily were her strongest, and she gave character and commitment to her music.

Alan McClarty sleazed his way around the stage as the comical con-man, Rooster Hannigan, and he displayed the range of his character acting with a hilarious performance as the raspy Ralph Mudge. A thoroughly entertaining performance, with strong, confident vocals.

Kellyann McKillen was a competent Lily St Regis but maybe a bit too gentle in the role. With few opportunities to shine, a more exaggerated characterisation might have made a bigger impact and enhanced her change to Shirley Mudge, which was very nicely played.

Leon Woods was an enthusiastic Bert Healy with a clear, articulate voice. Shea Eastwood gave an amusing quality to Drake, the young butler, and Jim Everett was a convincing and sincere Roosevelt. There was good support from Vicky Hogg as Mrs Pugh, Audrey Hull as Mrs Greer, and Tom Waddell as Officer Ward. Lucy McDowell, Jasmine Gardiner and Chloe Barclay made the most of their silliness as The Boylan Sisters, and Sandy the Dog, played by Mylo, was outstanding! Individual members of the chorus made good impact as Hooverville residents and Presidents men.

Lighting was a mixed bag of nice atmospheric tones and occasional missed spotlights, but it did contribute significantly to the overall effect of the set and the action. Sound was secure and nicely balanced throughout. Costumes were well selected and appropriate, and with the exception of Annie's red duffle- coat, seemed to follow the traditional era of the show. Grace, Miss Hannigan and Lily were very nicely attired. Wigs and hair-pieces were good and well-worn. Make-up was very satisfactory.

This was Annie with a difference, borrowing, as it did, from the original and the new modern movie of the show, and with the exception of the replacement of the original showcase of "Little Girls" with an altered and altogether less appealing version of the same song, it was a successful experiment, and quite refreshing to see "Annie" with a twist. I'm grateful for having had the opportunity to enjoy the fine work of Ballywillan and their production team once again. Sincere thanks.

The Wedding Singer is a show that is becoming a staple on many a societies list for "to do" shows. It has an array of roles to suit all ages and genders and the music is an amalgamation of modern 80's songs. John Larkin (Robbie Hart) was our wedding singer and he carried off the role with style and panache, a good musical voice and superb diction allowed him to deliver all the well-known tunes. He played opposite Farrah Bogle (Julia) who matched Robbie for his singing with wonderful phrasing of lyrics and a powerful punch in her voice. Their dialogue was smooth and quirky and they gave each other tremendous support. Julia's supposed boyfriend was played by Frankie O'Donnell (Glen). He eased his way around the stage, full of self-belief and confidence, man about town with the lads and mocking at poor Julia's attempt to get them married. His dialogue was precise and delivered with a perfect accent. Ronan Drummond (Sammy) interacted perfectly with Andrea Keeney (Holly) who gave a most wonderful performance full of vivaciousness. Audrey Davitt (Grandma Rosie) ensured that none of the comedy would go astray as she mastered a jittery walk. When she sang the rap song it was full of energy and with perfect rhythm. Director Moya Ferguson ensured that all the dialogue was promptly cued and never a player missed a mark. Musical Director Niamh Currid, played keyboards quite masterfully throughout the show, but this led to some errors in balance between stage and pit. Choreographer Karla Gallagher never really got the full use of the chorus as some of her moves were a little too intricate for the cast. The lighting plot was a little tentative in delivery and the sound technician had a number of issues with late cues and feedback. The scene changes were cumbersome and slow, perhaps they needed extra hands at crucial times. The audience afforded the cast a standing ovation and community theatre is alive and well in Co Donegal. This society is celebrating 65 years in existence and playing in the pit was Tom Gallagher who has been involved in every production. He was duly afforded a standing ovation in recognition of his service to the society, congratulations to him on an amazing achievement.

show_raw: Joseph And The Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat
review_text:
It's hardly surprising that a show with a biblical theme is male-dominated, so Joseph is definitely one to avoid unless you have a good line-up of men. Thankfully, Birr were not found wanting, and indeed, it was the powerful vocal performance of Jacob's sons that absolutely stole the show. As Director, Tommy Lyndon presented a show that was tidy and thoroughly entertaining, even if it seemed, on occasions, a little disjointed, rather like a series of sketches as opposed to a free flowing piece, and might have benefitted from keeping the company on stage more often. However, there's no questioning the strength of the performances, with well-directed action, a decent focus on comedy, and very nice staging of the musical numbers.

Musical Director Enda O'Connor led a small but secure orchestra from the keyboard. From within their ranks, Bertrand Huvé gave a virtuoso performance, tripling on sax, clarinet and flute, producing beautiful and precise sounds from each instrument. Rhythms and tempi throughout the show were very good, and there was a fine balance between pit and stage. As Chorus Master, Enda did sterling work, with clear well-rehearsed harmonies in abundance, sung with feeling and energy. His work with the male chorus, in particular, was superb, and raised the overall level of the production.

Ciaran Cooney was a confident Joseph, looking at ease on the stage, and singing with a melodic and well-controlled pop tenor range which suited his character perfectly. The only thing that detracted from his performance was his apparel, which, on occasions, looked like he was casually dressed for rehearsals.

Claire Connors and Marguerite McDonnell were the delightful narrators of the story. Both were extremely capable both as actresses and singers, Claire in particular having a beautifully rounded vocal tone, while Marguerite was the more natural story-teller, with captivating facial expression and body language. They combined very well together as the engine that drives the show forward.

Adrian Sheils was the most traditional "Biblical" character in appearance, sporting a very good costume and a superb abundance of facial hair. His emotions throughout were appropriate and well balanced.

Dickie Donnelly clearly enjoyed every moment of his Elvis-style performance as Pharoah, as did the audience. His vocal performance was strong and reliable, and he had the confidence and humour to make the most of that wonderful costume! Adrian Shine and Mary Lyndon, as Potiphar and his promiscuous wife, really made the most of their limited opportunities to add a touch of comedy to the story. Nicely played.

While the solo performances of Barry Kennedy (Reuben), Darren Madden (Simeon) and Gerry Clarke (Judah) richly enhanced their respective Musical numbers with good vocals and clear lyrics, it was the vocal contribution of the entire family of brothers that absolutely stole the show. Number after number, there was an assurance about every note they sang, with harmonies ringing out clear and loud. They were hardly a Corps de Ballet when it came to movement, but they were abundant in energy, and enjoyed the silliness of their scenes. Bravo gentlemen. Excellent work.

There were interesting, and extrovert, caricatures from Kevin Murphy and Damien Dillon, as the Butler and the Baker respectively, and the children's choir were well disciplined and made a splendid vocal contribution to many of the big musical numbers.

The female chorus and wives were well integrated into the show and performed with great enthusiasm and very secure vocals.

Stage Manager, Keith Wolfe, was lucky to have a tidy set with few moving parts, and as the show was quite shy of sizeable props, I'd say the stage crew were never over-exerted. However, the movement of stairs, platforms, etc., was all handled with minimal fuss, and never interfered with the smooth running of the show. As mentioned, the set was very nicely painted, and a good lighting plot allowed for plenty of visual variety. Sound throughout was set at a good level, and cueing was accurate. With the exception of Joseph's over-casual look on occasions, the costumes were generally good, with Jacob looking particularly effective. The narrators were very nicely attired, and Pharaoh was visually most amusing. The various hats to relate to the style of music of each number was appropriate, and could even have been taken further, but all in all, combined with good wigs, beards, etc. and tidy make-up, the visual impact of the show was impressive.

This was a most enjoyable show, performed by an enthusiastic company who should be proud of bringing exciting musical theatre to their very appreciative audiences. Thank you so much for a wonderfully entertaining night in Birr.

The Waterfront Hall is a colossus of a building in which numerous function rooms and auditoriums are available for hire. It is a shame that the planners never thought to consult people who actually perform in musicals as there is no space for an orchestra nor space in the wings for sets! The orchestra, led by Wilson Shields, performed in a small cramped space quite marvellously. They were compact and precise and using two keyboards allowed Mr Shields to direct chorus and principal entrances and endings quite perfectly. Footloose is a helter-skelter ride of emotions with a "no dancing" theme. However, when the young cast were given the chance to perform the enthusiasm that they gave in their performance was terrific. Choreographer Alex McFarlane's dance routines were sleek and precise and the players performed exactly and precisely. Ciaran McCormack (Ren) sang with passion and purpose, his quiet duet singing was controlled and a wonderful contrast to when he sang in the big chorus numbers and his dancing was superb. Jenny Johnston (Ariel) has the wonderful ability to glide across the stage and her dancing was perfect. The dialogue scenes with Ren where she was quiet and unassuming were in complete contrast to the feisty scenes with her father. Her father Tony Young (Rev. Shaw) ran us through the whole gamut of emotions. His practical philosophy as a preacher at the start, his stubbornness with his wife and daughter, and then his capitulation at the end. All were played quite perfectly with all the emotions of each situation displayed. This show has plenty of comedy throughout and was given to us by a wonderful duo. Sarah McFarlane (Rusty) gave us a slightly weird insecure characterisation. Superb dialogue and accent, good specific dancing and then when she performed "Let's hear it for the boy" her powerful voice was superbly controlled. Curtis Patrick (Willard) never let up for an instant. His characterisation was over the top and in your face. His dialogue was delivered quickly, with a super American accent, and his enunciation was perfectly precise. His singing was broad and raucous and then when he had his solo dance he brought the house down with an over the top display of raw emotion. The chorus worked their socks off and the choral singing was precise and correct throughout and the dancing was performed with an abundance of energy and precision. Sets were suitable although quite large and, due to the lack of wing space, there were a few delays. Director Jordan Walsh kept a very good pace to the show, with particular reference to the two handers, whereby dialogue was precise and sharp and always on cue. He ensured accents were correct and similar and garnered great pathos from his principals at critical points. It was also his 21st birthday the night that I attended. Even at a young age his musical nous was evident for all to see.

The music of Dolly Parton, along with a tale of sexual transgressions of a leading man and the desire of three ladies to do away with him is the basic premise of this musical. Banagher Musical Society Chairman took the male lead and what a super job he did with it. Jared Madden got all the sexual innuendo correct as he used his chauvinistic tendencies to rule roughshod over all. A good southern accent, along with an extremely slimy disposition, made the life of his three leading ladies, hell! So they took matters into their own hands led by Alanna Kenny (Violet). Ms Kenny gave a wonderful performance of singing, dancing and very determined acting with a most passionate speech delivered forthrightly at the end. Ann Marie McLoughlin (Doralee) looked and sounded exactly like Ms Parton, with a walk and a wiggle and a precise nasally accent, which never impeded her dialogue or her lyrics. Sharon Donohoe (Judy) started off as a quiet, shy, timid girl but gradually transformed into a brave and bold woman. Her rendition of "Get out and stay out" was sung superbly finishing with an amazing crescendo. Hart did have one admirer and that was played by Kate Flynn (Roz). She was not one for tittle tattle and ruled the roost in the office, she sang most powerfully and her phrasing was excellent as she used the lyrics to their fullest but her actions were somewhat toned down which inhibited the style of her performance. Alfie Kilduff directed the show and whilst his production was delivered at a crisp precise pace his overview of the show was a little awry. Musical Director Alan Recks played wonderfully in the pit but the balance within his orchestra needed tweaking. Choreography was by Lea Carroll and whilst some of her routines were excellent, sometimes they need to be made a little simpler to facilitate the abilities of the dancing chorus. The chorus singing was very good although endings were a little ragged. Stage Manager Michael Flannery worked his stage crew very hard and it paid off as the set changes for each scene were precise and exact. Sound technician got all his cues correct although the balance between pit and stage was under his remit and some adjustment was required. Lighting was nice and bright but when a player misses their mark an adjustment must be made so that we can see them. The costumes department worked very hard and produced a wonderful array of pastel colours for the office workers but maybe needed a few more animal costumes for Violets doobie dream.

On a beautifully designed set, Director Niall Heaney presented a well selected cast, in a clean and tidy production that showed a good understanding of the material and the era in which it was set. Costumes, props, etc. were all visually pleasing and appropriate, and the cast, small by Castlerea standards, were never lacking in enthusiasm. And yet, while there were few performance flaws, the pace of comedy delivery seemed a little off the boil, and it's a show that requires good pace to achieve maximum impact. There was little about this production that could not have been mended with a bit more attention to the technical needs of the show. Particularly with unknown or lesser known material, it is so important that everything can be heard and seen for the piece to be fully appreciated. On this score, there was a major issue with the balance of principal microphones, with underscored dialogue and solos against choral singing, on occasions, being almost inaudible. Lighting was a bit of a mixed bag, ranging from some absolutely beautiful atmospheres created on the cyc, to poorly lit playing areas and missed spots, which were a bit of a distraction. Particularly where there are scripted "effects", the timing of cues needs to be more accurate. Stage Manager, Noel Kelly, had his crew efficient and well-organised to cope with the numerous changes of location. With a static main set, most of the movement was of props and insets, all of which were seamlessly handled. The design and painting of the set were both excellent, and the myriad of props were authentic and appropriate to the era. I'd be reluctant to lay any blame for the imbalance of sound at the feet of the musicians, or the musical director, Shane Farrell, given that the sounds emanating from the pit were disciplined, accurate and by no means overwhelming. Indeed, the quality of the music throughout the show was very good. Chorus were disciplined, harmonious and well-rehearsed.

Deirdre Browne's Choreography was varied and appropriate to the music, and more significantly, appropriate to the capabilities of her chorus and dancers, who generally looked at ease while performing.

A mellow voiced David Cooke, with a well sustained English accent, gave a lot of energy to the role of Lawrence Jameson. While the timing of some of his comedic reactions could have been sharper, the self-belief and superiority of the character were nicely captured, and his vocals (except those that were lost to poor sound) were delightful.

Kieran Croghan needed more charm to make the character of Freddie Benson a bit more believable. He was extremely funny as Ruprecht, and indeed in his antics in and out of the wheelchair, but it would have been nice to see him more roguishly charming in his dealings with Christine.

Julie Heaney gave an excellent acting performance as Christine, delightfully flaky and gullible to the point that audience members unfamiliar with the story were audibly surprised to discover that she was the scheming villainess of the piece. At the shows end, her Nu Yoik accent was equally convincing. The music didn't really highlight her vocal range.

It took a while for Thomas Mearon to relax into the role of Andre Thibault, which was exacerbated by poor microphone balance in his "Chimp in a Suit" number, but as his relationship with Muriel Eubanks developed, so did the confidence of his performance, resulting in some fine comedy episodes in Act Two.

Jaqueline Kenny, as Muriel, hit the mark from the get-go, with a quality performance of the philanthropist on the look-out for a worthy cause and a taste of romance. Vocally very secure, and with great comic timing, Jaqueline was believable and beautifully cast in her role. Julie Mannion gave a whole heap of down-home, country-cousin, caricature to her portrayal of Jolene Oakes, making the most of her comedic opportunities, and selling her "Oklahoma" number with energy and enthusiasm. A very nice performance.

The chorus, few in number, made a valiant effort to make the crowd scenes look busy and energetic. Routines were tidy and well sung, and everyone seemed to know their place. It's not a show that relies heavily on the chorus, but when they were present, they made a good contribution to the overall production.

This was also a very nicely costumed show, with outfits always appropriate to character and era. The gentlemen looked dapper, and the ladies elegant, when required. Good variety of costumes too for Freddy, with a notable change in elegance when Lawrence takes him in hand. Ladies, both in hairstyles and make-up, looked perfectly in place.

The foyer of the Hub had been given a French Riviera make-over, and was very well dressed to greet the audience. Front of house staff were welcoming and friendly. Castlerea have, as always, presented a high standard of musical theatre performance, which was greatly appreciated by their audience. Long may your success continue, and thank you sincerely for a most enjoyable evening.

Having the orchestra hidden in some back room, behind the stage, didn't prevent Musical Director, Dave McGauran, and his orchestra from being the driving force behind a musically excellent production of The Wedding singer, delivered by a talented and enthusiastic group of chorus and principals. The eponymous leading man got proceedings off to a fine start by acting as MC, and doing the safety announcement, in character, before launching into the opening number. This was a delightful opening, enhanced by the fact that Choreographer, Jean Gill, nicely captured the mood of this and other wedding scenes by having a kind of organised chaos to the dancing, with lots of individual moves, rather than big synchronised routines. This gave a very natural feel to the weddings. There were also big exciting routines, filled with energy and invention, such as "Saturday Night in the City", "Casualty of Love", "All About the Green" and a delightfully light hearted "Single". If I had one choreographic quibble, it would be that a few of the dancers needed to use their smiles as ably as their feet.

Director, Lynda O'Neill, seemed to have focused on character and comedy, in this well-paced and delightfully funny production. Front line and cameo roles alike were well defined, and comic delivery was of an excellent standard. Lighting throughout the production added significantly to the atmosphere, but sadly, the set was rather disappointing. If you take the decision to have a neutral set, then it needs to be artistic and creative enough to visually stimulate for virtually the whole show. In this case, it was somewhat drab and unfinished looking. A centre revolve was an effective way of facilitating the arrival of various props, and indeed, the Stage Management of Therese Farrell and her team kept everything running smoothly, but there again, that revolve just needed to be more visually appealing. Happily, just about everything that happened in front of the set drew attention away from it, with a show that was very well cast.

Chris Currid, as Robbie Hart, was charming and charismatic from the start, with a strong and appealing tenor voice. Coupled with his charm was a great sense of comedy, and his heart-ache was very believable. A very well portrayed character.

Orla Connelly was sweet and sensitive in the role of Julia, and also well able to carry off the drunk and the heart-broken scenes. She had a mellow tone that was very easy on the ears, and was very believable as Robbie's love interest.

Michael McCormack had a confident air and a good sense of swagger in the role of Sammy, again, making the most of his comedy opportunities. His relationship with Holly was well developed, and he performed as a believable band member. Jenny McGrath was a cookie, crazy, life of the party type in the role of Holly, always animated and full of energy, and boy could she let rip vocally. This was a very well judged all round performance from a very talented lady.

Equally energetic, in a geriatric kind of way, was Mary Gamble as Rosie, the type of Grandmother we'd all love to have. She wasn't at all backward about sexuality, and played her role for all the comedy it was worth. And what a rapper!

A tastefully and never over-the-top camp performance made Stephen Rixon's George loveable and believable. His dancing was hilarious, and his singing was… well, it was certainly different, and perfect for the role.

Ben Lawless gave a good conceited performance as Glen Guglia, and performed "All About The Green" very well. I did feel he could have been even more repugnant by upping the level of his arrogance.

Kate Headon didn't hold back her bawdiness in the role of Linda, quite happy to lose herself in gyrating hips and abdominal thrusts. She performed both of her songs with an energetic confidence, and a great sense of fun.

Therese Farrell was very believable as Julia's pushy mother, Angie, making the most of an under-written role, and well able to deliver her comedy.

There were several chorus/cameo roles that were all very capably performed, and as stated above, the chorus contribution was extremely good and energetic.

Lighting throughout the show was consistently good, with nice use of colours to help create different atmospheres, and key lighting was mostly on target. Sound quality was also extremely pleasing and, given the concealed orchestra, a good balance was always maintained. Cueing was excellent.

Julia's Wedding Dress provided the aesthetic highlight of the costume plot, which was generally very acceptable. It was nice to see different sets of bridesmaids at the different weddings. George's wig was as delightful as his performance, and was the show-case of the hair and make-up department, who got everything just about right.

Apart from the issue of the neutral set needing more detail and attention, Malahide presented a wonderful show, and long may they continue to achieve such a good standard. Thank you so much for a night of feel-good entertainment.

Director, Jessica Bray, peppered this production with many clever and appealing gimmicks. The movement of props and furniture by cast members followed on beautifully from the success of that device in last year's show, and indeed was maybe even cleverer, as the changes seemed to be echoed by various lines in the script. (The tables are turning…. Etc.) Stage Manager, Francis Moloney, obviously had everyone very well drilled. There was also the clever and comical use of Joe, mimicking the actions of the girls, which was a nice touch. The use of the chorus, front of stage, miming a ride on the subway was most effective.

There was an abundance of very good and appropriate props which were essential to create the various office and bedroom settings, particularly since the set itself did little to create any atmosphere. Technically, the show suffered from a set that was not neutral enough to allow the suggestion of various settings, painted in a manner that didn't allow the lighting to achieve significant differences. While I could detect what you were trying to achieve with the projections, sadly, they lacked definition and on occasions were more of a distraction. There were occasions when principals were performing in semi- darkness.

Choreographer, Karen Barrett, given the restrictions of space, due to the number of props on stage, made a very good job of keeping routines varied and inventive. She was ably assisted by a chorus who were always well drilled and capable of meeting the demands of the choreography. Routines such as the Dance of Death, the Cowgirl's Revenge and One of the Boys would have been enhanced by a more interesting background, but they were very good routines nonetheless.

A strong and positive feature of the show was a well-tuned, well-balanced and sympathetic orchestra, under the leadership of Musical Director, Carmel Griffin. Choral vocals were thin, on occasions, due to small numbers, but they were never lacking in clarity or harmony, including some strong and melodic off- stage singing. There was consistently a good balance between pit and stage. Clare McNelis struck a beautiful balance between downtrodden female employee and ambitious business woman in her role as Violet Newstead. She didn't allow her early tolerance of Hart to disguise the frustration and volatility that were brewing below the surface, and when it was finally unleashed, she championed the feminist cause with a robust but palpable sincerity. Her vocal quality seemed to strengthen as the performance progressed, culminating in a beautifully sensitive duet between herself and Joe.

Hilary Orpen Ryan did well not to topple into the orchestra, given the breast enhancements that were a feature of her character as Doralee. This was a confident and raunchy performance that still allowed her to be sweet and vulnerable. She delivered her comedy lines with bravado, and when she let rip, she was a vocal powerhouse.

The beautifully measured naivety of Lauren Dunne's Judy was the backbone of a very loveable and believable characterisation. As she attempted to grow in confidence, her comedy was delightfully quirky, and her vocal delivery throughout was of an excellent standard. A very nicely controlled performance.

Debbie Reddan gave a capable and competent performance in the role of Roz, which could perhaps have been stronger on comedy, had she been a tad less glamorous. Dull colours and a colourless personality would have made her raunchy comedy number even funnier than it was. Similarly, Maria Kelly as Margaret could have been a tad more extreme as the lush of the early scenes, which would have pointed her triumphant return from rehab more comically. Nevertheless, this was a good performance.

Good support was given by Alice Barnes as Kathy, Hazel Park as Maria, Lauren- Kate Browne as Candy Stripper and particularly by Rachel McIntyre as the gormless wife, Missy Hart.

The high point of Martin McNelis's performance as Hart was a joyously delivered solo, "Here For You", as he lusted after the buxom Doralee, and throughout the show, Martin kept his loathsome character strong and obnoxious. I just wish he had been given leave to caricature the role more, replacing anger with sleaziness, and his scowl with a sickly smile. (I can't help thinking "Trump"!!)

Brian Roche played Mr Nice Guy, Joe, with a touching empathy, and warm sincerity. This was a beautiful performance, which also displayed a smooth, melodic voice, his duet with Violet being the musical highlight of the show. His mimicking of the girls moving the props displayed a good understanding of comedy too.

Stephen Byrne could have been a bit more of a sleaze-ball as Dick, but still delivered his lines with confidence, and Eoghan Rice was sincere enough to be likeable in the thankless role of Dwayne. Derek Barrett made his presence felt in the latter stages of the story, as Tinsworthy, the honourable boss, and good support was given by Shane Logan as Josh and Stephen Ryan as the detective.

The children who played the animals during Potion Notion displayed good discipline, and certainly seemed to enjoy their moment in the limelight.

The chorus did everything that was asked of them, be it harmonising, dancing or background acting, with good energy and precision, and they deserve so much credit, as on-stage stage crew, for the smooth transitions from scene to scene. In what is a functional, as opposed to glamorous, costume show, costumes were always appropriate and well selected. On those few opportunities when licence could be taken, the dancers were nicely attired, their number with Roz being particularly effectively dressed. In a fairly modern setting, the variety of wigs/hairstyles was acceptable and appropriate, and make-up was all proper and correct.

The large ticking clock outside the main entrance of the hall was a very nice welcome for the audience, as was the kind of nostalgic display that Shannon has become so accomplished at providing. The live mannequins, frozen in working poses, were extremely well disciplined. Shannon Musical Society never fails to impress, with an abundance of new and older talent, performing to the highest standards and providing their audiences with wonderful entertainment.

Thank you all for a most enjoyable night of musical theatre.

There are not many musical societies who would have at their disposal a cast young enough to attempt this show. Not only does it require specific particular singing it relies heavily on a company who can dance modern day hip-hop through the duration of the show. It really is full on for the whole show and UCD's chorus were fit and able and were as energetic at the end as at the start. The choreography in this show was conceived by Katie Duffy. It was simply breath taking. Passionate and powerful she had the chorus dancing in perfect synchronisation from the turn of their heads to the balls of their feet. Cathal Grennan (Usnavi) opened the show in a narrative style introducing the main players whilst rapping at 100 miles an hour, his diction was superb. He later gave us wonderful pathos when Anna Bergin (Abuela) died. Ms Bergin played the grandmother role splendidly, good steady dialogue, never rushed or hurried, and a wonderful singing voice that resonated around the auditorium. Lauren McMahon (Vanessa) led from the front with a wonderful display of acting and singing and her relationship with Usnavi was tender and affectionate. Colin Gilligan (Kevin) and Hazel Madden (Camila) were the hard working parents to their daughter, the first one to ever go to college. Mr Gilligan has wonderful stage presence and the timbre in his voice when delivering his dialogue is marvellous. Ms Madden started out in Kevin's shadow but came into her own and sang with passion and conviction in her number "enough" and this transformed her character completely. Caoilfhionn Ni Dhulaing (Nina) played the daughter back from college. Her acting was terrific but was surpassed by her singing. She sang with a beautiful melodic voice and her phrasing was perfect. Comedy was at the forefront of this musical and whilst Jack Carolan (Piragua Guy) was continually playing, and getting, the laughs, the duo of Eimear Finnegan (Daniela) and Amy Gilligan (Carla) stole the show. Ms Gilligan's ability to arrive on her mark and deliver a one- liner was simply brilliant. Coupled with their duet singing, which Ms Finnegan led quite superbly, they were a wonderful double team. A cleverly designed fixed set enabled specific scenes to be played within its confines, lighting cues were very good but some sound cues needed to be a little tighter. A big band, under the direction of Barry Power supported the solos and duets marvellously, but in the big chorus numbers they did get a little raucous in their playing and brass and percussion got a little carried away. The show was directed by Kevin Bates and not only did he instil good comedy timing, he got all the pathos correct at the most crucial times. He allowed the actors freedom to explore and develop their roles and his overall direction of the big chorus scenes was excellent.

Making his directorial debut with Tipperary Musical Society, John Murray was handed a show that can be a technical nightmare, and to give him credit, the concept of his set was extremely good, if not always practical. What he achieved very well indeed was to inspire his cast to give a performance that was energetic, spirited and thoroughly entertaining. From the get-go, there was a bit of over-acting from much of the front line, but as the pace settled and the story developed, the quality of the individual performers began to surface.

Caroline Brahan gave bucket loads of energy to her portrayal of Violet Newstead, even if she had a tendency, early on, to be over-animated. Perhaps a more tired and put-upon countenance at the start of the show would have better emphasised her transformation into the stronger, more confident Violet of Act Two. She played her 'murderess' scene in the hospital very well, and she was on fire performing her "One of the Boys" number.

Siobhán Dempsey had a perfect look for the role of Doralee, and delivered her script throughout very effectively, once she toned down her Southern drawl which was uncomfortably high pitched at the start of the show. She had a pleasant and secure singing voice and she performed with sincerity and believability.

Deirdre Ryan gave the performance of the night, as the fragile, but eager to embrace a new life, Judy Bernly. Her comic delivery was always perfectly timed, and her vocal quality was most delightful, with "Get Out and Stay Out" being a musical highlight of the show. This was a very strong performer. After an opening scene where he delivered most of his lines to the audience, much in the style of a pantomime villain, Willie Ryan mellowed, and turned in a very good comedic performance as the male chauvinistic pig of a boss, Franklin Hart Jnr. "Here for You" was very nicely performed.

Tracey Walsh had very good presence and a fine sense of comedy in the role of Roz Keith, but a few of her lines were lost through being spoken too softly. "Heart to Hart" was a memorable number.

Conor Ryan was a convincing and sympathetic Joe, who delivered his lines and his duet with Violet with good confidence.

Much of the early comedy of Aoife O'Meara's Margaret was lost because it was not apparent enough that she was the office lush. Once her hip flask got some attention, that situation improved, and she grew into the role.

Seán Ó Maoilriain was a good Dwayne, and Jason Ryan gave a nice quirky arrogance to the role of Dick. Richie Crowe was a convincing Josh, and Joe Franklin proved that a small cameo role can make a big impact with a very funny Bob Enwright. Fine support came from Claire O'Dwyer as Kathy, Denis Fitzgerald as Tinsworthy, Alma Quinn as Maria and several other chorus parts. Mairéad Breen looked good as Missy, but again, the high pitch of her accent detracted from her delivery.

The chorus made a lively and energetic contribution to the show, with good clear vocals and plenty of ability in their movements.

Helen Colbert made a very good impact as Chorus Mistress, punctuated by some well-rehearsed and strongly presented vocal harmonies, with the Finale of Act One being particularly impressive. While the fine assembly of musicians in the pit played the score with confidence, there were occasions when rhythms became a little pedantic, and perhaps Helen needed to tighten her coordination between the pit and the stage. One or two song endings were loose or untidy, and scene change music (of which there was a lot!) often ended too abruptly rather than fading out. Generally, Miriam Ball's choreography had a good shape and was danced with great enthusiasm by a competent cast, although I feel she could have asked more of them in the Dream sequences. The outstanding number of the show was "One of the Boys" which fairly bounced of the stage, with great energy from Violet and the dancers. The choreography did contribute significantly to the overall impact of the show.

An uneven pace to the show was largely down to technical issues. The almost psychedelic artwork of the set had a very good visual impact as the audience entered the theatre, accompanied by images on screen and music of the era. In practice, however, the set proved to be over-complicated, which caused Stage Managers, Brian English and Aidan O'Connell, and their team, some very laboured and long scene changes. The on screen images also became a bit random and chaotic, distracting, rather than contributing to the performance. The props team had done a mountain of work presenting a plethora of good and appropriate props, and the quality of sound throughout the show was very good indeed. The lighting, as with the projections, seemed rather random, with lots of special effects and flashing lights, but perhaps not enough attention to the key lighting, which, on occasions, was out of kilter with the action on stage. The beautiful, romantic duet "Let Love Grow" was lit almost entirely in a ghastly shade of yellow, which had also been used as front light a few scenes earlier. The result was that the principals in those scenes had a sickly pallor.

In what, by its nature, is a rather unglamorous show, the very nice costumes for the Joy to the Girls ending of "Potion Notion" were a highlight of a generally good costume plot, with everything in its place and appropriate, and occasionally (as in "One of The Boys") a bit of glam was a welcomed surprise. Wigs and hairstyles were neatly presented, and everything looked natural and pleasing on the make-up front.

Criticisms aside, Tipperary have continued to impress with a standard of performance that they should feel rightly proud of. Their new production team gave the show a great sense of fun and energy, and the sense of community spirit surrounding the whole show was always in evidence. Thank you so much for a most enjoyable evening.

The classic West Side Story is that famous tale of Romeo and Juliet set in inner city New York. Newry Musical Society took up the challenge and under the baton of Danny O'Neill gave us an orchestra perfectly in tune with the subtle nuances of Leonard Bernstein's score. Act 1 was played at a wonderful tempo with superb accompaniment throughout allowing the talented cast of singers to perform to the fullest. Whilst there was the occasional wobble and misplaced note in Act 2 nothing to the detriment of the production. Fiona Flynn (Maria) sang with a most melodious voice, superb phrasing and diction and her dialogue was delivered perfectly with strong Latino accent. Ronan Sharkey (Tony) was perfect from the outset. His first number was delivered with anticipation and expectation, beautifully in tune and a super ability to tell the story. Their work together was excellent and they gave us every emotion from laughter through to pathos. Paddy Heaney (Bernardo) was suitably suave and his accent was precise and clean. He ruled the roost giving orders to the Sharks, advice to his sister Maria but he never really was in control of his girlfriend Anita. Maille Connolly's (Anita) singing was feisty and spirited, good accent and a fiery delivery when scolding Maria. Her dialogue was precise and in Doc's store she played it quite superbly, where she spat out her anger, rage and disgust with the Jets. Conor Mathers (Riff) opened the show by leading the Jets in their opening number and then in "Cool" he got all the rhythms correct and his diction was terrific. The chorus all worked extremely hard especially in the dance at the gym which was danced sublimely and was a visual delight with the wonderful costumes prepared by Nadine O'Hare. This show revolves around the ability of the cast to dance. The emphasis on the choreography is paramount and it was provided to us by Ann Marie Morgan. The dance at the gym was quick and slick with wonderful choreography giving us both American and Latino dance moves contrasting both gangs. The ballet sequence was absolutely perfect in both its design and execution. Director David Cunningham had the show running at a wonderful pace with dialogue cues precise and accents consistent throughout. There was a problem with other technical issues though. The lighting plot was not as precise as was required and the sound technician needed to be more aware particularly in "Gee! Officer Krupke". This performance was in the magnificent Newry Town Hall which is full of history and nostalgia, a most fitting venue for a wonderful production.

Much as Man of La Mancha sees Cervantes tell his dramatic story within the confines, and performed by the occupants of his prison cell, so Paul Norton's production sees poor Tobias Ragg relating the story of Sweeney Todd within the confines, and performed by the occupants of the Fogg Asylum. The concept has superb effect, played on a brilliantly designed and painted set, with the company of 'disturbed' inmates roaming the stage and the auditorium as the audience enter the venue. It was impossible to not feel a part of the action and the atmosphere.

Decide on a concept and see it through, may have been Paul Norton's maxim as he approached Sweeney Todd, and indeed, he did see it through to a most successful conclusion, with an artistically brilliant production. The set, designed by John O'Donoghue and built by Stage Manager Wayne Handy and his team, was superbly detailed and dramatic, and dark and dreary. Stage Management consisted of organising the cast to move and remove the various props that became the centre pieces within the asylum. This was always carried out in character and with precision. A good and varied lighting plot contributed to the action, and only on one or two occasions some principals could have done with a tad more highlighting. There was great use of colours in creating appropriate atmospheres. Sound quality, including audio effects, was excellent throughout.

Wigs, hairstyles and make-up were a wonderful feature of this production, and would have been fun for the cast as well as those responsible for creating the looks. There was a hungry, death-mask look to the whole assembly that was powerful and quite chilling. Costumes were stark, simple and superbly effective, with just enough frills and add-ons to distinguish the main characters from the rest of the asylum inmates.

Much of the show requires musical staging, as opposed to routine choreography, and every scene was convincing, detailed and often surreal. When there was an opportunity to inject dance steps, it was done very much in keeping with the demented style of the production. The rape ballet was artistically superb. Enjoyable and inventive work from Choreographer Graham Finnerty.

The immensely intricate musical score was given first class treatment by a most accomplished 16 piece orchestra, under the baton of Shane Farrell, whose control and sensitivity were top notch. The strings, in particular were sublime during the more melodic sections of the score. The balance from the pit was perfect, ranging from robust pronounced moments of drama and tension to an affecting mellow tone when required. Added to all the above, Shane led the chorus with care and precision, a chorus who were very precise and nailed the intricate harmonies almost all the time. The Epilogue was a tour de force. Excellent work from all concerned.
