There was a sinister countenance about Stephen Rabbette's Sweeney, a kind of humourless hue that he maintained even when being comically taunted by Mrs Lovett, and while it gave great strength to the depth of his resolve to have his revenge, it might have been nice to see another, lighter, dimension to his character. He had a strong and menacing voice, but with an occasional tendency to slide onto notes, which, given Sondheim's intricate harmonies, came close to sounding off-key before resolving. This was, nevertheless, a strong performance. Jay Origan, as Mrs Lovett, was superb, not just with an amazing vocal clarity and a masterful control of the complicated lyrics and rhythms, but her facial expressions were an extraordinarily powerful extension of her mood and tone. Her playfulness was infectious, her vulgarity was palpable, and when confronted by danger, you could see terror in her eyes. A remarkably fine performance.

There was a spidery quality about the appearance of Chris Corroon as Judge Turpin that added a creepy and sinister intensity to the personality traits that make the judge the most repugnant character on stage. His singing was strong and intense, and his self-flagellation scene was excellently played. I could feel the pain! Alex Cathcart gave a fine tenor quality to his portrayal of Anthony Hope, and his naïve simplicity was a nice contrast to the intensity of Sweeney. I would perhaps have liked to see a little more despair and desperation in his demeanour as he searched to find his captive Johanna, but he maintained likeability throughout the madness of the action.

Yvonne O'Toole as Johanna graced the stage with a beautiful soprano quality, best displayed during "Green Finch and Linnet Bird". She very convincingly expressed her revulsion at the thought of being wed to the Judge, and after a spell in the asylum, there was a good demented quality to her acceptance of her circumstances. Very nicely acted.

Amanda Cunningham impressed greatly as the Beggar Woman, not least because even with a demented persona and a thick haggard voice, she remained beautifully articulate throughout. Delightful in her vulgarity, and sincere in her yearning for her daughter and husband, this was a very well balanced and studied portrayal of an often under-developed character.

Tomás Glynn gave a spirited sense of the ridiculous to the character of Pirelli, with almost a cartoon quality to his vocals. His well sustained Italian accent gave way to an equally comical Irish brogue, and while not every note he sang was pitch perfect, it was always entertaining.

Eoghan Fingelton as Tobias Ragg provided the breathtakingly, poignant and emotional high points of this production. From his calipered leg to the top of his wigged head, he was superbly absorbed in his character, and his devotion to Mrs Lovett tugged at the heart-strings. "Not While I'm Around" was theatrical gold. A surprising falsetto tenor voice was a notable feature of Tommy Maher's interpretation of the Beadle. Clear and precise in his diction, appropriately sycophantic towards the Judge and menacing in his attitude to his underlings, this was a very good stalwart performance. Rory Chadwick gave a good cameo account of himself as a hard-nosed and un-sympathetic Jonas Fogg. No-one was sorry to see him die!

The contribution of the chorus to the intensity of the production was excellent. Their vocal quality was top drawer, with the Ballad at the start and the Epilogue at the end being particularly powerful, but it was their constant presence and reactions to the action that helped in no small measure to keep the eerie atmosphere consistent throughout the show. Their presence as the audience entered the auditorium was extremely disciplined and disturbing. Sweeney Todd is one of those shows that can show up the strengths or weaknesses of a musical society, such are the heavy dramatic and musical demands of the piece. On this occasion, it has highlighted the strengths, talents, ambitions and dedication of an exciting and vibrant company and production team. Thank you so much for a wonderful experience.

Alfie Kilduff captured the tone and atmosphere of this extremely funny and energetic show right from the outset, with good pace, an attractive opening set piece, and well established characters. While his set for the show was not artistically awesome, it was practical and functional, and well manoeuvred by Stage Manager, Jonathan O'Brien and his team, and combined with a good lighting plot, it served its purpose of suggesting the various locations and of creating atmosphere. Only rarely could the comedy have been more exaggerated, but this was an efficient, tidy, no-nonsense production that never allowed its audience to lose interest. While virtually all of the players were well directed, the brilliant antics of the three Delta Nu leaders were hilariously presented and delivered.

Equally proficient at presenting the show to its best advantage, Musical Director, Ger Madden, kept good control of his orchestra, with strong rhythms and well- balanced tones throughout. The whole package was vocally impressive, with secure harmonies and good clear diction from an obviously well-rehearsed chorus. Nicole McDonald's choreography, made the most of an energetic chorus of very able dancers. Her work with the Delta Nu was funky and impressive, with "Omigod You Guys" getting the show off to a great start, and "What You Want" being particularly well designed. "Bend and Snap" was great fun, and the "Legally Blonde Remix", featuring a highly comedic Irish dance, was an audience favourite. There was a youthful energy and charm about Cherise O'Moore in the role of Elle Woods that fitted the character perfectly. Her vocals were beautifully lyrical, and she displayed a very good sense of comedy. When required, she was also very adept in the dancing department. She does need to occasionally check the speed of her line delivery, but over-all, this was such an enjoyable performance.

Chris Currid had a relaxed confidence in the role of Emmett which gave him an instant charm. He beautifully managed to be a friend to Elle without ever imposing himself on her, but when his feelings for her grew, there was great sincerity in his affection. His strong and secure tenor voice was well displayed by the requirements of the vocal score.

Equally assured in his fine vocal quality was Chris Coroon as Warner, who also ably captured the shallowness and vanity of the role. His transition from arrogant Frat boy to sulky loser was very well achieved, with both personas being strongly realised.

Linda Murray was a confident Paulette, secure and energetic in her physical comedy, articulate and pitch perfect in her vocals. I did feel that she could have played the role with more caricature, but she did nothing out of place in a well- balanced performance.

Joe Steiner was impressive as Callahan, strutting with superiority in his early scenes, and suitably smarmy as he made his advance on Elle. "Blood in the Water" and "Gay or European" were nicely performed.

Róisín Currid made a strong visual impact as fitness guru, Brooke Wyndham. Her energy allowed her to put over "Whipped into Shape" with ease, despite the accompanying physical workout. She had a strong character, and yet was well-able to become the giggly sorority sister in the presence of Elle.

There was a hint of dominatrix about the appearance of Róisín Jackman, with the severe black wig and the dark suit, which seemed perfectly appropriate to her portrayal of Vivienne. She was almost like an evil force, dragging Warner away from Elle, but she redeemed herself with sincerity when she sided with Elle, and punctuated the "Legally Blonde Remix" with fine vocal quality.

Show stealers, Niamh O'Shea, Amy Kelly and Jennifer Clogher, performed out of their skins in the roles of Serena, Margot and Pilar, respectively. They were the energy that drove the show forward, dynamic in their routines, crystal clear in their vocals and outrageously funny in their comedic antics. They were such a pleasure to watch and enjoy.

Alanna Kenny made a strong and engaging Enid Hoops, butch but not unfeminine, angry but not aggressive, comedic but not outrageous. This was a well-judged interpretation of the character.

Good support was given by Paul Fogarty as Aaron, Barry Coughlan as Sundeep, Paul Donnelly as Lowell, John McGlynn as Winthrop, Tony Dalton as Pforzheimer, Anna Boles as Whitney, Blanaid Casserly as the DA, Mary-Helen Hensley as the Judge, Grainne Keane as Kate and Ruth Foy made a strong cameo role out of Chutney. Colin Kelly and Joan Larkin were convincing as Elle's Dad and Mom, and Paul Donnelly got good laughter as the slob, Dewey.

Jonathan Kilduff as Nikos and Darren O'Hara as Carlos, played their parts with high-camp and deserved their excellent response from the audience, while Tomás Glynn had a touch of Schwarzenegger swagger as he strutted the stage as Kyle. Nice comedy Irish dancing from him and Paulette as well.

A host of cameo roles were played efficiently by members of the chorus, while Enoki and Kodi made the desired impact as Bruiser and Rufus.

The wardrobe department did a good job of making costumes suit the characters wearing them, like a severe appearance to Vivienne, the initial dishevelled look of Emmett, and a very funky Paulette. Elle's Bunny costume was particularly delightful, but I would have liked her majorette costume for "What You Want" to be somewhat glitzier. Hair and make-up were universally good. There were no problems with the sound.

From front of house to backstage crew, there was a wonderful sense of being part of a team, and it displayed itself energetically in the performance by a wonderful cast. My sincere thanks go to all in Athlone for a thoroughly entertaining production of Legally Blonde.

This musical is a horror, rock musical based on a plant named by the leading man as Audrey II. It has small beginnings but grows quickly as it becomes blood thirsty. The actual puppetry of Audrey II was brilliantly worked. It was controlled by one man and voiced by a woman, Cleo Meaney. She sang the role most beautifully for a plant that was not nice at all. Eoghan Rice (Seymour) played the hapless love struck flower shop assistant who only loved one girl and spent his whole life trying to impress her. His accent and dialogue was clear and precise, his facial features were marvellous and his attention and concentration to Audrey was excellent, although his singing needed a little more support. Sarah Corcoran (Audrey) gave us a range of emotions, initially shy and timid from the abuse from her dentist boyfriend but then she slowly developed an understanding with Seymour. Her accent and dialogue was marvellous, the pair worked really well together and her singing was super. The owner of the flower shop was Gary Loughnane (Mr Mushnik), he played the role with a very heavy foreign accent which required better delivery to enable the audience to hear every word. Patrick Woulfe (Orin the Dentist) is a role played like a mad-cap scientist prevalent in the old 60's movies. He started off as the big bully boyfriend and then changed to a sadistic, vicious dentist whose aim was to create pain to all who attended him. He acted this role quite superbly, his dialogue was clean and precise and his facial expressions were terrific. Sarah Griffin directed and choreographed. A very big task to combine the two but to her credit she achieved both remarkably well. Her direction of the dialogue scenes was precise and clean, she had all the principals perfectly on cue and on their marks, and then her dancing routines were simple but very well executed. Shane Farrell had wonderful control over the orchestra, the balance between the pit and the stage was super. The chorus sang all their numbers perfectly and he gave the principals super direction. A special word of mention to Elaine Gavin (Crystal), Kate Corrigan (Ronette) and Carol Hackett (Chiffon). These three ladies played the backing singers roles quite splendidly. Their singing was perfectly precise and their harmonies most melodic. They then danced in a wonderful relaxed attitude giving super support to all the main principals. The evening finished with two presentations to long serving members of the society, Barry O'Loughlin and Sharon Cullinan, a fitting tribute to a wonderful evening's entertainment.

One of the pleasures of being adjudicator is that you get to see a lot of Premieres, and Clara Musical Society did just that with CATS. Now there are numerous musical numbers in this show that have been recorded by various artists but it is only when you see the show in its proper context that you realise how wonderful the score is. Alan Recks took on the role of director and musical director. Probably a good idea to have a musical director so involved as the show is non- stop music. Firstly he had a wonderfully balanced orchestra who covered all the orchestrations marvellously and, probably in conjunction with the sound technician, was never overbearing or too loud. The orchestra were excellent and accompanied superbly throughout. CATS is a selection of poems set in separate scenes that all blend together. His direction of the cast was excellent and the wonderful visual that they all displayed was the constant animated gestures that Cats make. The cleaning and stretching, the rubbing against each other and the sleeping. It was such cleverly devised direction. There is a substantial amount of chorus singing in this show, with plenty of harmonies, and the entire cast sang splendidly, without any breath control issues, which was very impressive considering the energetic dance numbers. Lea Carroll was choreographer and she is to be complimented for her imagination. To be able to conceive so many individual routines, to teach them, to insist on perfection, and then to acknowledge that they have been correctly performed was marvellous. The set was fixed and had all the wonderful nooks and cubby holes that a cat would find to sleep in. It also had a wonderful walkway at the back of the stage which was used to its fullest in Ms Carroll's choreography. Sound and lighting was perfectly correct and even in the darkness of certain scenes the pin point spots were perfectly positioned. John Coss (Rum Tum Tugger) showed super stage presence and gave a wonderful display as he set the scene, swiftly followed Stephen Rabbette (Munkustrap) who sang superbly with wonderful diction and intonation. The Georgina Ireland Cathcart (Grizabella) gave a most pronounced slow walk as she traversed the stage looking for comfort, her interpretation of "Memory" was hauntingly beautiful. There was wonderful support singing of close harmonies by Janet Murphy (Jellyorum), Joanne McDonagh (Demeter), Ruth Maher (Jellyanddots) and Grainne Donoghue (Bombalurina). This production's dancing was superb throughout but I must pick out a couple of things. The dance of Chris Corroon (Mungojerrie) and Niamh Moore (Rumpleteazer) was absolutely astonishing. Their movements together were entwined as one, the control and the physical support they gave to each other was fantastic and their concentration upon each other was beautiful. Then we had Skimbleshanks: The Railway Cat. This scene from start to finish absolutely blew me away. The design of the dance, the singing of both the soloist and the chorus, then the building of the Railway Train…astonishing in its complexity and its execution. It would be remiss of me not to mention Liz Rackard and Mary Cornally who took on the role of making the costumes for the entire cast. Not only was it an incredible undertaking but the end result was magnificent. It was a most wonderful production, full of everything that is good about amateur theatre in Ireland….. Just a little bit better.

It is the responsibility of the Director to ensure that when leaving an auditorium you have a memory that will linger in your mind. Ian Milford gave the audience of Banbridge Musical Societies "Little Shop of Horrors" just that in his curtain calls. By simply trailing the roots of Audrey II from the balcony over the audience and then having Audrey II move whilst the puppeteers were taking their bows was a visual delight and had the audience in stitches. Not only did he plan the ending well but his cleverly designed set delivered for every scene, the dialogue came with sharp cues and wonderful accents, and his cast all combined to provide a super production. Niall O'Flaherty, positioned front and centre, gave wonderful direction to his orchestra and his visual rapport with the cast was first class. Lynn Gourley oversaw the choreography and her simple but precise routines were delivered quite perfectly by the chorus and principals alike. James M a r s d e n ( S e y m o u r ) g a v e a w o n d e r f u l display from start to finish, initially a bit awkward he changed his characterisation to finally loathe Audrey II. He gave good attention to leading lady Lorraine Jackson-Brown (Audrey) .above). She gave a most consummate display of singing and her movement around the stage was mastered quite superbly with a manufactured walk on her high heels. Eddie Orr (Mushnik) gave a super singing display and his dance was a comedy masterpiece, he just needed to watch his accent in his dialogue and enunciate clearer. Ruairi McAlinden (Orin) played his comedy in a manic manner, dialogue soared from loud down to a whisper in less than a heartbeat and his facial expressions added to his demeanour. Emma Kelly (Crystal), Claire Costello (Chiffon) and Lauren Hill (Ronnette) were absolutely superb as the three backing singers. They sang in wonderful harmony, with wonderful accents and super phrasing. Their dialogue was nice and tight and their dancing was marvellous. Technically there were no issues, sound was correct, the lighting plot was excellent and the costumes were super. Audrey II was worked with wonderful puppetry although her voice needed to be a little cleaner and her words a little crisper. It was a most wonderful evening's entertainment enjoyed by the entire audience and the cast were afforded a suitable ovation.

As much as I love the frivolity of "Me and My Girl", the song and dance of "42nd Street", the outrageous comedy of "The Producers", et al, there's nothing quite like being mentally and emotionally challenged by a heart-wrenching, and heart-warming dramatic musical. Such, was the offering from Kilkenny Musical Society's passionate and superbly produced "Parade".

You can always tell when a Director has a passion for a show. It's evident in the attention to detail, the commitment, the energy that pervades every scene, and the emotion that they wrench from their performers. All of that was the case with this enthralling production from Christine Scarry. She managed to tell this disturbing story of racial and religious prejudice without allowing it to become maudlin. This was achieved by recognising and highlighting the lighter moments and the comedy of the piece, of which there is plenty. As with Tevye in Fiddler on the Roof, Leo Frank had that very Jewish, self-effacing sense of ironic comedy about his circumstances. These were beautifully played out in this production.

Christine's other great achievements were ensuring that all the technical aspects of the show enhanced and realised her own vision of how it should be presented. There were no weaknesses, no-one not pulling their weight.

From the keyboard, David Hayes led an orchestra which played with precision and sensitivity, giving energy to the more robust musical pieces, and sublime accompaniment to the highly emotionally charged moments. With any such lesser known piece of work, clarity is of the essence to make sure the story is understood, and the chorus were as precise in their diction as they were in their harmonies, suggesting very thorough rehearsal. From start to finish, the show was musically delightful.

The choreography throughout was a perfect extension of the director's style and gave a sense of seamless continuity. Nicole McDonald used a beautiful fusion of stylised dance of the era and wonderfully effective, almost aggressive movement that added power and punch to the likes of "Hammer of Justice" and "Where Will You Stand". The ironically joyful dance as Leo is found guilty of murder was as sinister as it was brilliantly executed. A beautifully simple and effective set did all that was required of it to create atmosphere and location, with good use of the various levels. With few moving pieces, Stage Manager, Aidan Dohney and his efficient crew were free to assure the smooth movement of the appropriate assembly of props and furniture. Lighting throughout the show was subtle and discreet, highlighting the action, and almost unobtrusively creating beautiful background atmosphere. I wasn't aware of the sound, which is a compliment. Balance and cueing was always perfect. Michael Hayes' performance in the role of Leo Frank was sublime. He captured every nuance of a character who was as uncomfortable with romance as he was with living in alien surroundings, unable to properly connect with anyone. He managed to be stubborn without losing our sympathy, and his sense of the injustice surrounding him was palpable. His relationship with his wife was as sad as it was beautiful. He also enacted his "evil self" most effectively during "Come Up To My Office". The quality of his vocal performance was superb, from a gentle mellow tone to passionate heights of anger and indignation, he never lost control nor clarity.

Sarah Brennan was gave an emotional performance as Lucille Frank, dedicated to her husband, and almost more at odds with his personality than she was with her unfortunate circumstances. She combined humility with a powerful resolve and the deepest sincerity, in a performance that touched my heart. The final picnic and its accompanying duet were quite simply heart-wrenching. She was also vocally beautiful.

Kevin Reade (above), should consider a career in politics, so convincingly sly and underhand was his performance as Hugh Dorsey, with an outward show of buttery pleasantry disguising the deeper ruthlessness of a self-serving, manipulative gangster. This was a well measured performance, with strong vocals and attitude.

C a o i m h e Kelly perfectly c a p t u r e d the playful innocence of Mary Phagan, bright and secure in her duet with Frankie, and when she reappeared during the court case, blissfully unaware of the cruel nature of her demise, which only heightened our sympathy for her character.

David Doyle successfully made the transition from jocular Jack-the-lad to bitter and resentful bereavement. He was extremely likeable as the playful young rogue, and frightening in his anger. He got the balance just right, and was vocally very secure.

If Kevin Reade was the respectable face of bigotry, then Eoghan Fingleton was the darker and more sinister force at work in the background. His portrayal of Tom Watson was cold, calculated and ruthless, inciting hatred and perverting justice. With a wonderful vocal delivery, there was an icy resolve in his delivery which was far more effective than bullish aggression. Eoin Gleeson gave energy and a level of sleaziness to wannabe top journalist, Britt Craig, adding fuel to the already volatile situation. "Real Big News" was a well performed number.

Tervine Wallace captured the essence of the dodgy character of Jim Conley with confidence and excellent physical presence. His diction wasn't always the clearest, but the message of "That's What He Said" got through loud and clear. Paul Spencer gave a stalwart and convincing performance as Governor Slaton, the man trapped between his political career and his sense of fair play. A wonderfully believable cameo of confusion was given by John Rice as the befuddled Newt Lee. Lolley Sinyan gave vulnerability and self-preservation in equal measure to a very able performance as Minola McKnight.

Other memorable and delightfully articulate performances came from Tony Murray as an excellent Judge and as the bitter old soldier; Brendan Corcoran as an ineffectual lawyer Luther Rosser; Rebecca Murphy as the grieving mother Mrs Phagan; Ciara Laste, Rachel Madden and Kate Brosnan as Mary's easily corrupted school friends Iola, Essie and Monteen, and Kevina Hayes as the loyal Governor's wife, Sally Slaton.

Good solid support also came from James Brennan as Det. Starnes, Jerry Gardner as the Guard, Ciarán Dunphy as Mr Peavy and David Brydone as Officer Ivey.

The same attention to detail that went into every other aspect of the show went into assuring that the costumes were well presented and appropriate to the era, with good delineation of race and social standing. Likewise, hair and make-up blended into a perfectly presented visual delight. Thank you sincerely to Kilkenny Musical Society for introducing me to this wonderful show, and for doing so with a brilliantly emotional and precise production.

A very attractive set, combined with a beautiful lighting plot, were the outstanding visual features of this production of the Rodgers and Hammerstein classic, "The King and I". It's a show not so frequently performed these days, but the richness of the musical score remains as powerful today as it was when it premiered on Broadway in 1951. Director, Michael Dunbar, presented his audience with a very fine traditional production, relying on the performers and the music to shine. The pace was generally good and there was plenty of attention given to chorus involvement. Visually, the show was delightful, and while there was nothing at all wrong with the direction of the principals, it was rather "old school" in style, with a lot of playing out to the audience, especially during musical numbers. I loved the set for the show. It was creative, artistic, and above all, extremely practical, not to mention that it was excellently manipulated by a very efficient stage crew, under the management of Paul Doran and Frank Byrne. The lighting was a visual treat, with most effective use of colours, and the effects on the back pieces were truly beautiful. Principals were always well lit, and every scene was filled with atmosphere. The sound engineer also did a splendid job with cueing and balance, making the overall technical presentation of the show quite excellent.

The orchestra, under the mindful direction of Conor McCarthy and Kelli Ann Masterson, played with precision and sensitivity, especially during the more gentle and rhapsodic passages of the score. They were also respectful to the on-stage performers, maintaining a good balance throughout the show. There aren't many opportunities for the chorus to shine vocally in this show, but what they had to do, they did well. Only during the "Small House of Uncle Thomas" sequence did there seem to be a little vocal insecurity. The show was, overall, musically beautiful. From a dance point of view, that "Small House of Uncle Thomas" was the highlight of the show, and performed with confidence, especially by the lead dancers. There were few other opportunities for Choreographer Frances Ryan, to display her talents, but the march of the children was impressive, and "Getting to Know You" was tidy.

Kevin Bolger gave an excellent performance in the role of The King, combining authority with a fine sense of mischief. Most of the comedy stems from his treatment of Anna, and these scenes were particularly well played, but he had the gravity, too, to give vent to his anger and frustration at being unable to adapt to a modern world. His demise was poignant. This was a very thorough performance, and he was the most relaxed person on the stage. Musically, he talked/sang his numbers very capably in character.

There was an old school charm about Avril O'Toole's Anna. Her accent was delightfully English, her manner delicate and very proper. Her songs tended to be akin to concert performances, played more out front than to the characters on stage, but this was indicative of the era of the musical. Her voice was most pleasant to listen too, and there was good sincerity in her overall performance.

Bridin O'Keefe captured the obedient yet authoritative rank of First Wife very convincingly, and her rendition of the melodically beautiful "Something Wonderful", was a musical highlight of the show.

Cara O'Connor was a charming Tuptim, the very essence of the frightened servant, and heart-broken lover. Her narration of the Uncle Thomas number could have been a little more animated, but it improved significantly as her anger grew towards the King. Her singing was very good, although I would have liked both herself and Lun Tha to be a bit more passionate in their moments alone. "We Kiss in a Shadow" was a tad formulaic in style, rather than free flowing.

Callan McCarthy Coughlan had a good presence as Lun Tha, but as stated above, he could have displayed a more unleashed passion in his stolen moments with Tuptim. His vocal quality was very good, but he tended to be over-operatic, when a more relaxed and lyrical tone might have displayed more emotion.

David Cox looked good as the Kralahome, and when he ultimately expressed his devotion to King and country, he was passionate and authoritative, but I do think he was a tad too informal in some of his earlier scenes.

Jirat O'Neill was very impressive indeed as Prince Chulalongkorn, naturally inquisitive as a young boy should be, but with the confidence to assume authority as his father falls ill. Very well played.

Likewise, there was a great confidence in the performance of Niall Kehoe as Louis, whose diction was perfect, and his singing was really delightful. Here was a young star in the making.

George Percival displayed a kind of stiff- upper-lip English awkwardness in his portrayal of Sir Edward Ramsey, and good confident support was given by Paul Doran as Captain Orton, and Eamonn O'Connor as the Interpreter.

The King and I doesn't really demand a lot of its chorus, but the many wives of the King were suitably confused and uncomfortable by the intrusion of a westerner, and most amusing in wearing ball gowns and high heels. In their few opportunities to sing, the chorus produced a pleasant sound.

The chorus of children were absolutely lovely, and played their moments of comedy extremely well.

While all of the Eastern costumes were delightful, especially those for the Ballet and by the many children, the western style ball gowns for the ladies were a bit tawdry, and should really have been in the style of the wide-hooped outfits worn by Anna. The ladies chorus wigs were satisfactory and well worn, and make-up was of a good standard.

It is always a pleasure and delight to visit Gorey, and to applaud their efforts. Thank you for a thoroughly entertaining revival of a great 'older' musical.

Des Henn's production OF Chess opened in Budapest, with a young Florence being told the Story of Chess by her father, just before he is arrested by Communist soldiers. It was a beautiful cameo that made sense of the references to Budapest later in the show, thus making Florence more identifiably relevant to the action, and I came to the opinion that if you accept the musical is really the story of Florence, it all seems to make much more sense. The whole production was inventive, alternative and extremely well performed. The music of the show is dynamic and often stunningly beautiful, and from her perch somewhere above and behind the set, Musical Director, Maire Keary-Scanlon, was in good control of her orchestra. I found the opening of the show a tad slow, and the crescendo in the middle of the Chess Game, which signals the dramatic start of the dance, didn't quite hit the mark, but those small issues aside, this was a well-paced and well played musical treat. Maire had also done excellent work on the chorus, who delivered a fine vocal display with clear harmonies and good diction throughout. Des Henn set his production in a stunning, Colosseum-style amphitheatre, a clever setting for a gladiatorial meeting of two Chess giants. Other locations were suggested throughout the show by simple images on three projection screens within the back arches. The show was littered with excellent touches, like the opening with young Florence and her father, or like the superbly staged "Pity the Child" as Freddie looked back over his upbringing. There was a strong focus on characterisation, with well- defined personas, and the chorus were neatly weaved into the action. The whole production had the clinical discipline of a game of chess, with neat pristine costumes, efficient changes of location, well-rehearsed moves, and precise routines.

I wasn't prepared for a dance spectacle when visiting Limerick, but that is what the audience were treated to, with Barbara Meany going to town on the Chess Game ballet. Even more appealing was a superb routine akin to a military tattoo for the Diplomats' Number, followed up by a most remarkable and artistic production number for "The Arbiter Song". It was very well sung, but it was the dancing that took the plaudits, being slick, precise and energetic. "One Night in Bangkok" could have been a tad sleazier, but it was still a very well presented number. The Embassy Civil Servants performed a very comical routine. All in all, this was a wonderfully choreographed show.

As mentioned, the show was played against a stunningly beautiful, excellently constructed and very well painted, amphitheatre set, with screen filled arches, upon which appropriate and effective projections helped to add to the atmosphere of the various scenes. It was a credit to Stage Manager, Glen Carr, and his team, that I was hardly aware of the moving of props and furniture around the stage. Their business never interfered with the flow of the action.

The lighting of the set was most effective and atmospheric, and some of the effects were beautiful, although the moving heads didn't always highlight the people they were following and were perhaps slightly over-used. Lighting of the upper areas and the front ramp was very good. Sound was consistently good, allowing every word to be heard cleanly and efficiently.

Niall O'Halloran in the role of Anatoly gave a remarkably convincing performance as the cold natured Russian, who eventually falls for Florence. His vocal quality was of the highest order, with a superb "Anthem" and beautiful duets with Florence.

As Florence, Claire Heffernan perfectly captured the balance of juggling her professional role with matters of the heart. Her acting was delightful and her voice was melodic and easy on the ear, even if she didn't dominate the action as much as she could have.

James Malone gave a secure, cocky attitude to Freddie, but managed to display his vulnerability during a beautifully staged "Pity the Child". Vocally, this role is a real challenge, and one to which he rose with a fine tenor quality and a pleasing falsetto. Molokov is a nasty piece of work. Strong, manipulative and unforgiving, and Aidan O'Connell successfully captured all those qualities to give a performance of immense stature. He also had a strong, resonant vocal quality.

Ciarán Collins was a relaxed and secure Arbiter, personable, yet commanding. Rigid in his authority, he was fluid and flexible in his movement, as he fronted the amazing "Arbiter Song". This was a very nice performance, with good vocal quality. Jason Ronan was a convincing Walter, brash and all-American on the one hand, and snide and underhand in his bargaining with Molokov. He sang with an assured confidence.

Laura Henebry made the most of the under-written role of Svetlana, with strong delivery of "Someone Else's Story", and melodic quality in the "I Know Him So Well" duet. She also nicely transmitted the wrath of a woman scorned as she chastised Anatoly in the Endgame.

The Chorus throughout the night performed with great precision and enthusiasm, both vocally and physically. The combined effect of the wonderful set, very effective lighting, beautiful and appropriate costumes, well sourced props and well-presented hair and make-up made this show an outstanding visual treat to savour and enjoy. Limerick Musical Society achieved a wonderful standard with this thoroughly enjoyable, accomplished and memorable performance. Thank you for a great night, with some very pleasant surprises.

The Mill Theatre in Dundrum was not designed to stage musicals as there is no pit for an orchestra. This meant that the orchestra were positioned on the stage under part of the set. A video link to a screen out front enabled the cast to observe Geoff Woods', the musical director, downbeat and instructions. Whilst his direction to the players was good, unfortunately his control of the volume of the orchestra was not, and the principals and chorus struggled to compete. Director Paul Fay ensured standard uniform accents from the cast, dialogue was kept at a premium and interaction between the chorus and principals was excellent. Where he needed to be more precise was in his direction at scene changes which were slow and cumbersome. Rachel Sheahan (choreographer) obviously knew the limitations of the chorus as the routines were designed and executed in a very precise manner by all of the cast. Technically the sound was very good and the lighting plot worked expertly particularly on the set spots for each rendition of "One night with you". Ross Loughran (Chad) needed to pay more attention to his leading lady as a lot of dialogue was delivered to the audience rather than directly to her and his intonation needed to be more precise on his forte's. Emma Coast (Natalie/Ed), whilst speaking as Ed her lower register never impeded her upper register singing voice which was excellent. She was always on her mark and her cueing was excellent. Niall Gallagher (Dennis) dragged every laugh out of this comedy role. His facial expressions were excellent and he still managed to muster support from the audience when rejected. Laura Murphy (Miss Sandra) played the stoic museum curator perfectly and then unleashed a wonderful femme fatale persona. The supporting principals all played their roles correctly but I must mention Noirin Sheridan (Sylvia) who performed her role as the despairing widow quite perfectly and then sang most beautifully. The audience gave the cast a tumultuous reception and all went away singing the wonderful music of Elvis Presley.

The Pirates of Penzance is one of Gilbert & Sullivan's most famous operettas and is so rarely done nowadays, mainly because of the large double chorus of men required as Pirates and Policemen. There were not a huge number of men in the Little Sea's chorus and they were spread liberally, but with the addition of some quite comically funny Lady Police it bolstered the numbers considerably. Unfortunately not having enough men meant that the chorus work, particularly the four part harmony, suffered as a result. Conductor Robert Mahon, along with his wife Angela, took control of the orchestra all of whom were members of the Kiltra School of Music. Whilst they are a fine body of young string musicians they did require some brass and percussion to assist them in the accompaniment. The community hall in Bannow does not possess a very large stage and this impeded any large dance numbers. The smaller ones were designed by Diana Martinez Sanchez and "With cat like thread" being the highlight. Teresa Buckley Directed and kept a very good pace in the dialogue with the front line delivering excellent cueing. The supporting leads, however, needed to up their game to compete. More emphasis should have been placed on the accents of the cast which were not as expected. Mairead McGuire (Mabel) sang splendidly, although she did struggle with some of the slow tempi from the pit. Her accent was excellent but perhaps she could have been a little more committed to her leading man Michael McKenny (Frederic). He also did not commit as passionately as might have been expected, his dialogue and accent were excellent, but his singing was a little wayward. The Pirate King was played by Michael Curtis. He gave us a very robust singing performance but his dialogue could have been more precise. Paddy Hannon (Major General) and Derek O'Reilly (Sergeant) both suffered from hesitancy in delivery of dialogue and lyrics, and needed to be more precise on dance steps. Mandy O'Leary Murphy (Ruth) was making her debut in a musical and what a superb performance she gave. A super Cornwall accent, her dialogue was delivered perfectly whilst her singing was precise and perfectly in pitch. A wonderful all round performance. The costumes gave us wonderful bright dresses for the female chorus all suitably decked out with an array of bonnets. The Pirates needed a little additional accoutrements to their costumes but the Policemen's costumes were period correct. The local audience were all suitably impressed at the first ever production of their new musical society and I am sure they will return again in the future.

While there were aspects of this production that disappointed, the choreography elevated the overall production of Londonderry's "7 Brides for 7 Brothers" to a highly enjoyable experience. Choreographer, Venessa Chapman must have been delighted to have such a talented team of dancers at her disposal, enabling her to choreograph vibrant and adventurous routines. The challenge dance was the highlight of the show, full of energy and style, ballet, gymnastics and great patterns. The spring dance was another beautifully designed number, with very tidy lifts, and beautiful shapes from the girls. There was also good comedy in the "Goin' Courtin'" routine. Indeed, comedy was probably the strongest element of Deigh Reid's direction of this show, making the most of the antics of the brothers, when they met Millie, having their breakfast, learning to court a lady, and of course learning to dance. These scenes were all very funny. My main concern about the show was a lack of pace. This was contributed to by very slow scene changes, and slow lighting cues, even when a scene was set. This aspect of the show needed a lot of tightening up. Indeed, the effect of the avalanche, which was well designed, was virtually lost through late cueing. The set was both visually pleasing and very practical, but the stage crew, under Lee Thomas, seemed rather leisurely about getting things into place. Lighting very generally very effective, with some beautiful atmospheres created, but cueing was an issue, and at most scene changes, there seemed to be a long pause before lights up, even after everything was in place. This did significantly hinder the pace and fluency of the action.

Peter Doherty had a very capable orchestra to control, who played the score with precision, but there were several tempos that seemed to drag the show to a very slow pace. "Bless Your Beautiful Hide" needed to bounce along with much more vibrancy to get the show off to a lively start. The slow numbers were a bit laboured and, on occasions, almost funereal. The repeated scene change music to cover slow scene changes became irritating, but I accept, of course, that the MD had little option but to keep playing. On a more positive note, the musicians were excellent, and a good balance was struck between stage and pit. There was also very good vocal work from both chorus and principals.

David Keown did enough in the role of Adam Pontipee to leave no doubt in my mind that he is a very capable actor, but if I'm honest, a tendency to play for laughs weakened his role as the surrogate father of his brothers, I'd have liked to see him more authoritative, and maybe less "one of the boys". His relationship with Millie consequently came across as cold and thoughtless, rather than a man struggling to adapt to new circumstances. He was by no means unlikeable, and it was evident that he has a fine sense of comedy.

Emer McCaffrey was comfortable in the role of Millie, light hearted when required, but she also had the maturity to look after the well-being of the other girls. This was a nicely balanced performance, and was very vocally secure.

Rory Mullin had a calm, maturity as Benjamin, the second oldest brother, which befitted his character.

Robert Kelly was the perfect hormonal teenager in the role of Gideon, and if I'd been Alice, I'd have been petrified by his passion! He did, however, express his more sensitive and responsible side in his dealings with Adam. Very nicely played, and equally nicely sung.

Áine O'Riordan was a delightfully giddy and adorable Alice, playing her scenes with Gideon most believably… and what a lovely dancer.

Collectively, Simon Quigg as Caleb, Eoin Callaghan as Daniel, Gregg Parkhill as Ephraim and Thorin Coffey as Frank, worked brilliantly together as a team, but all displayed good individuality, especially the angst from Frank.

Similarly, Amy Kilgore as Dorcas, Amy Smith as Ruth, Hannah Deane as Lisa, Zoe Kyte as Martha and Niamh Long as Sarah, came across as best buddies, and still managed to have their own personalities. Their dancing was superb!

Together, the Brides and Brothers worked so well at their comedy, their dancing and their singing. Marvellous work.

Good support was given by the 'oldies', Judith O'Hare and Greg Doherty as Mrs and Mr Hoallum, Brendan Brady and Joanne Palmer as Mr and Mrs Sander, and Tom Stockman as the preacher.

The Suitors, Corey O'Connor as Jeb, Oisin McCool as Nathan, Ethan McKeegan as Luke, Conor Polley as Matt, Stephen Carlin as Joel and Ross Wilders as Zeke, need to be as convincing as the Brothers for the show to work, and this group of boys were very strong, particularly as dancers, with Ethan McKeegan beautifully demonstrating what a bit of ballet training can do.

The chorus, who have few opportunities to shine in this show, acquitted themselves most satisfactorily, both vocally and as movers and shakers.

Costumes were very good, and well worn, and hair and make-up were consistently good. Adam's beard at the opening was a tad sparse. There was a good wide range of props which were all authentic and appropriate, and sound was good throughout, with the exception of the odd bit of feedback.

Despite the issue of pace, this was still a highly enjoyable experience, performed by a talented and very enthusiastic company. Thank you for a super show and for a terpsichorean treat.

Under the Direction of Paul Norton, "All Shook Up" proved to be the perfect vehicle for a young, energetic company, who performed with an abundant sense of fun. This was a production filled with fun and energy, with a lively and comedic cast of principals and a colourful and practical set. Nice silhouetted fairground pieces in act two, and effective town pieces in Act One were sufficient to create the necessary atmosphere. The practical Tunnel of Love with the fairground car was a lovely piece, and the bus, made up of suitcases worked very well. The stage crew, under Eddie Kiernan, did a good job, and changes weren't overly long. The lighting was colourful and effective, and apart from when they ventured too far on the periphery of the stage, principal action was well highlighted. Comedy throughout the show was well pointed, and I particularly liked how Chad was directed. Positioning on stage was good, with nice use of practical props, although there was a tendency to bring everyone on stage for virtually every number, when perhaps a scattering of chorus in the café scenes might have been more effective and less crowded.

Emer O'Brien kept her choreography funky and fresh throughout the show, and was fortunate to have a fit young company to carry off the routines with energy and precision. Again, there were occasions when she probably didn't need to have so many people on stage, but numbers were well fronted by principals who all had very good dance ability. "Devil in Disguise" could possibly have been a tad more imaginative, but that aside, this was good, tidy work.

Fintan Farrelly led an enthusiastic orchestra from the keyboards, and kept the show moving at a cracking pace, with lively, vibrant tempos, and a nice mellow feel to the more romantic numbers. The Chorus had been well-prepared in their harmonies, but perhaps just a touch more work was needed on dynamics, particularly in "Can't Help Falling in Love" and "Fools Fall in Love", which both had excellent harmony, but tended to be all at the one level.

Natasha Fitzpatrick-Brady proved to be a feisty and formidable Natalie, and a very comedic Ed. She had a fine vocal quality, well able to punch out the belter notes, and still gentle enough for the sentimental numbers. This was a very nicely portrayed character.

Sean Rooney, in the role of Chad, reminded me a lot of Fonzie from "Happy Days", playing the role with a quirkier comedic feel than I've become used to. Normally, it's very much about testosterone and posing, but this guy had a bit more personality, which was very agreeable. He was also very good at putting across the Elvis numbers.

Tony Wadd is clearly a fine comedic actor, and indeed he managed to elicit much laughter from the audience as Jim Haller, but it was, I feel, slightly at the expense of the more sentimental aspect of his character, the grieving widower, who finds new love. He still gave a very credible performance, displaying a good vocal quality.

Valerie Nolan captured the hard edge of the single mom of a feisty teenager, and blended it perfectly with the soft-centre of a woman re-discovering love, in her portrayal of Sylvia. A beautiful rendition of "There's Always Me" was the highlight of her excellent performance.

Eimear Reynolds gave superiority and then sass to the role of Miss Sandra, using her sultry tones in her attempts to seduce Ed. She could have been a tad more animalistic in her advances, but she was, nevertheless, a convincing seductress. Sinead Mullally was perfectly cast as young Lorraine, full of feisty teenage mischief, and her voice and manner were both appropriate to the role. Very nicely played.

Conor Lynn-McLoughlin's stature gave an excellent sense of an over-pampered child to his role as Dean, and he played the awkwardness of the Mommy's boy very well. He was equally convincing when he unleashed his inner passion and fell for Lorraine. Good singing of "It's Now or Never".

Aaron Nelson had great youthful exuberance as the wannabe hero, Dennis. We wanted him to be successful with Natalie because he was so cute. He played the part with energy, focus, and wonderful expression, combined with a very good vocal quality.

Joanne Sexton was a powerhouse in the role of grumpy killjoy, Mayor Matilda. She gave a great performance of "Devil in Disguise", and was equally convincing when she melted under the sudden manliness of Earl. This was good comedy. John Kelly got Earl just right. He impressed as the silent subservient slave to his domineering Mayor, using great facial expression to highlight both his frustration and his acceptance of his lot. He then made great fun of turning the tables on her.

The chorus made a very good vocal and physical contribution to the show, although there were times when they were just brought on stage to stand and sing, rather than be integral to creating an atmosphere. Very good work, nevertheless.

Costumes were as one would expect for the era of the show, and nothing stood out as being inappropriate. Hair and Make-up presented no problems, although I'd have made Ed's stubble a bit more obvious. From where I was sitting, it wasn't that noticeable. Props were very good throughout. Sound was consistent with good cueing and a secure balance between pit and stage.

There was a wonderful youthful feel about this production, as a new generation takes centre stage, and this is so essential for the future of any company. Thank you for a most pleasant and entertaining visit to Longford.

Arguably the best comedy movie of the 20th Century, "Some Like it Hot" first appeared in 1959, and wasn't made into a stage musical until 1972. Retitled "Sugar", the show sticks closely to the script and settings of the original movie, keeping alive the wonderful comedy, but also presenting technicians with a tough challenge. Stage Manager, Bob O'Kelly, and his team did a fine job of rearranging the various, and numerous, pieces of the set. The neutral white boxes, despite being very practical, were a bit stark, but were used to their best advantage as the train carriages. On other occasions they didn't really give a strong sense of location, due to artwork that was a tad bland. The props team had done a mountain of good work in obtaining all that was necessary for the production, the lighting design, throughout, made a very good effort to create atmosphere, and sound quality was consistently good. Philippa Alford got plenty of style and atmosphere into this production of an old classic. There was a good sense of the era and some very good characterisation, but it might have been nice to see Joe and Jerry actually playing their instruments at some stage, being as how their careers are pretty central to the plot. While the pace of the show was generally good, some of the comedy sequences, and particularly between Daphne and Osgood, were a little laboured. The yacht scene, with Junior and Sugar, in contrast, was very nicely played. Some of the principal musical numbers were a bit static, and particularly for "It's Always Love", a bit more drama or movement would have distracted from what was a challenging sing for the actor. Michael Fay's orchestra were positioned high above the action, where they played a well-tuned and lively rendition of the musical score, and given their location, Michael did a very good job of keeping everyone together. Tempi were precise, and there was no over-powering of the singers on stage. The chorus vocals were ever-present and correct, even when sung from off-stage, and harmonies were strong.

Deirdre Browne's choreography was very much of the era, with a great "Maple Leaf Rag" Charleston to get things going, followed up by a well-executed tap routine for the gangsters. There was a touch of the Busby Berkeley's about her "Shell Oil" routine, and "When You Meet a Man in Chicago" was the dance highlight of Act Two. Overall, the show was very nicely moved.

Stephen Fagan gave a positive performance as Joe/Josephine/Junior, with good distinctive accents and personas for his three roles. The vocal demands of his character tested him quite a lot, and had his solo's been physically staged with more business, they might have made a greater impact, but his acting didn't fail to impress, even as a woman! The dead-pan delivery of Martin Fahy in the twin roles of Jerry/Daphne was more in keeping with Walter Matthau than Jack Lemmon, and it suited the character beautifully. There was a rich "innocent abroad" quality to the situations in which he found himself, and excellent facial expressions often spoke louder than his actual words. "Magic Nights" was expertly delivered.

Siobhan Clifford is a performer of immense stature and ability, both vocally and as an actress, but in mimicking Marilyn Munroe in the role of Sugar, I thought her focus was more on the physical impression than on the script. Her delivery was exceptionally good, and I believe she can be even better. She was very well cast in this role.

Claire O'Reilly was a confident and very capable Sweet Sue, fronting her band with authority and keeping Beinstock and the girls in line. She had a very good voice and made the most of her comedic opportunities.

Brian Patrick Gallagher maintained a cartoon-esque quality throughout his performance as Bienstock, with a nervous high pitched voice and a 'put upon' nature. He was believably afraid of Sweet Sue, and made the most of the comedy of his situation.

Shane Byrne, with his fancy footwork, led the group of gangsters very convincingly in the role of Spats Palazzo.

Rory Robinson added more than a touch of old-school charm to the role of Sir Osgood Fielding. He knows how to play to an audience and to make the most of a well written character. He was vocally secure, with perfect diction, although I did feel that some of the comedy between himself and Daphne was a little slow- paced.

There was good support from Paul Dicker as Knuckles and from several other cameo performers. The chorus contributed in a very positive manner to the atmosphere in several scenes, dancing with energy and singing very well.

The show was very nicely costumed, with Daphne's outfits being particularly fetching. Sugar always looked stunning, and the dancers were always appropriately and beautifully attired. Wigs/hairpieces/ hairstyles were true to the era and well worn, and make-up did a fine job of everything… even if they fell short of making Josephine and Daphne beautiful… but given the surfaces they had to work on, that was maybe too much to expect! What made this a successful show was the sense of community spirit that pervaded the production. You all looked as if you were thoroughly enjoying what you were doing. Thank you sincerely for a most enjoyable night of entertainment.

This musical is based on the film and includes all the memorable well known tunes especially the title song, which requires a continuous cascade of water enabling our leading man to dance and tap his way home. The special effects used for this production were superb. Not only did the rain cover all of the stage area it was also used at the end of the show where the whole cast donned yellow rain coats and tapped their way into a magnificent finale. The special effects didn't stop there either. The video projections of the silent films were displayed and produced splendidly. The vision of these special effects came from Director Derek Shannon, who gave us a very slick production and oversaw a cast, all of whom were aware of their characterisations. James McDermott (Don) led from the front, his singing was precise and the lyrics delivered perfectly. His dialogue was tight and sharp and his dancing was effortless. Yvette Walsh (Kathy) sang beautifully with wonderful phrasing and a lilting soprano voice. Her dancing was relaxed and precise and she gave us poignant pathos at the end when discovered to be Lena's voice. James Dobbs (Cosmo) performed as a wonderful madcap entertainer. His dialogue was crisp and his gags were delivered with perfect timing. His forte was his dancing which was marvellous. With wonderful rhythm and tapping his "make 'em laugh!" song was a showstopper. Caroline O'Connell played Lena Lamont. With a perfect high pitched nasally American accent and a selection of fitted wigs, Ms O'Connell paraded around the stage with an air of a diva so perfect for her character. Her dialogue was delivered perfectly on cue, her over the top exaggerated hand movements, especially her goodbyes with Zelda, and finally her singing all encapsulated a quite magnificent performance. Musical director Philip Kennedy gave good support and strict tempo to all the numbers but allowed the Brass section to be a little lax in delivery of some notes. Choreographer Anne Marie Cooney designed routines for the chorus which were precise and sharp and all within their compass. The solo dances and routines allowed the three main leads to shine, particularly their routine in "Good Morning" which finished on a wonderful toppling of the couch, a most difficult thing to perform but visually terrific. The costumes were period correct with an array of wonderful dresses for the ladies, especially the tiller girls costumes at the birthday party. The stage crew worked extremely hard, as this show has numerous scene changes, and kept the flow of the show correct. The sound had a stuttering start but balanced out quickly and the lighting plot was delivered on cue. It was a wonderful production and a marvellous evening's entertainment.

With an eye for perfection, Director, Eoin Cannon, gave attention to every aspect of this production, from establishing characters to ensuring that not a line was lost, and wrapping the whole story in a very tidy technical package. It was a production with minimal choreography, but all of the choral movement had purpose and direction and added significantly to the overall package. A dynamic set was brilliantly manipulated around the stage by a very efficient crew, and this contributed greatly to pace of the production. Beautiful lighting made this show visually delightful, with great creation of atmosphere. I particularly liked that the lighting wasn't over-elaborate. Moods were created with subtlety, rather than through exhibitionism. Stage Manager, Gerry McCann, and his team, worked efficiently and with silent stealth to have everything in the right place at the right time. Props were well- sourced and appropriate to the era of the show. Sound was clean and balanced. Hair and wigs were top class and very natural in appearance, and considering the abuse many of the wig-wearers had to endure, they were also very securely fitted. Similarly, there was lovely attention to detail in the make-up department, with some of the performers hardly recognisable. Costumes were excellent throughout, clearly defining the wealthy from the impoverished.

With the exception of a few hints of vocal tiredness in Sweeney himself from the demands of his role, there is little I could criticise in what was a magnificent musical display from musicians, chorus and principals. The orchestra captured the tone and mood of every musical number, while on stage, the clarity and diction of the vocals was quite brilliant. Altogether, Musical Director, Dermot O'Callaghan made this highly intricate musical score seem like a piece of pie. This was excellent work.

Ciarán Mooney gave presence and authority to the role of Sweeney Todd, dominating the stage and filled with an intense sense of wrongful persecution and an obsession with vengeance, as you might expect, but what stood out even more was his superb comedic ability. His timing and facial expressions, when a customer arrived for a shave accompanied by his wife and child, were priceless. The mirth that he shared with Mrs Lovett gave so much additional dimension to his character. While his singing voice sounded a little tired, he still managed to reach great heights of passion, in an overall performance that was awesome. It was that same balance between sinister acting and brilliant comedy that made Bronwyn Andrews outstanding as Mrs Lovett, not to mention that her singing was delivered with immaculate diction and expression. This was the performance of the show for me, using every device in her repertoire to create a perfect characterisation. "A Little Priest" and "By The Sea" were simply stunning.

Pat McElwain's Judge Turpin was as cold as ice and clinically menacing, from his tone of voice, to his leering expression and his impassioned self-flagellation. With vocal authority, he presented himself as a most dislikable character. I'm glad to know that he is recovering nicely from the nasty accident that befell him during performance.

There was a wealth of innocence and sincerity in Peter Manning's portrayal of Anthony, combined with a smooth, lyrical tenor quality. His love for Johanna was completely believable.

Fiona Hiney gave vocal security and an intense vulnerability to the character of Johanna, in an emotionally charged performance. ""Green Finch and Linnet Bird" highlighted her vocal quality, and her duets with Anthony were beautifully rendered.

Sean McMahon was a credible Tobias, and delivered his vocals with conviction. He was perhaps a tad too street-wise at the start to establish the simplicity that engulfs his character in later scenes, but this was, none-the-less, a well-acted performance. "Not While I'm Around" was beautifully delivered.

I would have liked a few rougher edges on Jim Walsh's interpretation of the Beadle, for while he established a smug superiority over most characters, his tone and demeanour didn't capture the grovelling, sycophantic nature of his relationship with the Judge. After all, he knowingly sheltered the Judge's immoral behaviour. His vocal delivery, never-the- less, was excellent, and he maintained his superiority throughout.

Louise Cassidy managed to be very convincing and manic as the Beggar Woman without losing any clarity in her delivery of lines. Her vulgarity was counter- balanced by her sympathetic love for her daughter and her estranged partner. Very nicely done.

Pirelli sang with the prowess of an Italian opera singer, and Frank Beadle seemed to enjoy the mischief of his character. He was delightfully slimy as he appeared to the assembled crowd, and devilishly devious when he revealed his Irish roots and his evil intent to Sweeney.

Eoin Kenny made the most of his opportunities to present himself as the loathsome Jonas Fogg.

The chorus were very well integrated into the action, and made a brilliant contribution, both vocally and visually, to the proceedings.

This was a beautiful production of what has rapidly become one of my favourite shows. Thank you for such a thoughtful, excellent and entertaining standard of performance.

Aidan Fox showed that there's more to his talent than just as a performer, by making a very favourable impact on Thurles as their director, in a well-balanced and thoroughly enjoyable show. I wasn't sure about the set when I entered the Premier Hall, with those seemingly over-elaborate structures on the stage extensions, which in act one, gave a very enclosed feeling to the town, albeit very well constructed and painted. It was only when it suddenly transformed into a colourful and eye- catching fair-ground in act two that one could appreciate the thought and effort that went into it. The manipulation of such an intricate set presented no problems to an expertly efficient stage team, under the management of Tommy Sweeney, and props throughout were of a very good standard. Good attention had been given to characterisation, and to playing for a strong comedic impact. The one area that perhaps needed a tighter rein was the lighting plot, which had some very good creation of atmosphere, with good colour use and well defined acting areas, but there was also an over-use of flashing disco effects. While they were perfect for the Juke Box coming to life in "C'mon Everybody", they became a bit repetitive and predictable. Occasionally, some of the principal action also needed a tad more key light. There were no problems with sound quality.

A tight ten piece orchestra was sufficient to the requirements of a racy score, under the direction of Mary Rose McNally. A vocally capable front-line of principals were very well supported by an excellent vocal chorus, who epitomised the strength of good harmony and diction, "Can't Help Falling in Love" being their most obvious show-case. "Heartbreak Hotel" was also powerful in performance. It's always nice to hear a male ensemble holding their own against a much larger female chorus. Excellent vocal work.

Debbie Kiernan played to the ability of her dancers and chorus in a very tidy and fun filled display of choreography. Much of it was straight-line, but it was always effective and well-rehearsed. The movers and shakers displayed good energy and precision.

Frank Tuohy gave a convincing performance in the central role of Chad. He had plenty of swagger and confidence, and a decent vocal quality, but I'd have liked to see him be more comically self- obsessed in the hip-swivel department. Shelley Martin was a delightful Natalie, petite and perky as a young lady, and well able to deliver her comedy as Ed. Her singing was very pleasant, and my only suggestion would be that she needed to be slightly more exaggerated for her expressions to reach the back of the auditorium.

Peter Donnelly was extremely well cast in the role of Dennis, and used his stature, his voice and great facial expression to portray the loveable nerd of the show. He was also very competent as a vocalist. Mairéad Hackett was a show-stopper in the role of Miss Sandra. She looked a million dollars, but it was her comedy and her delivery that was most eye-catching. She moved with feline sensuality, and sang with expression and energy, resulting in an immensely enjoyable performance. Barry Derby sang Jim Haller with sincerity, and created a nice sympathetic character, although I'd have liked to see him a tad more fatherly towards Natalie, with maybe a warm hug or kiss as she launched into her "Fools Fall in Love".

Linda Ryan was a most beautiful and sympathetic Sylvia, yet well able to be the scolding mother of her angst-ridden teenage daughter. Her care and concern for Jim were palpable, and there was great sensitivity in her rendition of "There's Always Me".

Damien Sweeney really looked the part of the young military academic type, in the role of Dean, very proper and correct, until something stirs within him on meeting Lorraine. The transition to rebel was well achieved, and he gave a very strong rendition of "Now or Never".

Equally capable and convincing was Aoife Ryan, who contributed great energy and feistiness to the role of Lorraine. She competently led Dean astray with playful glee, and made the most of her vocal opportunities.

Nina Scott gave a Trojan performance, using experience and comedic talent to make the most of a delightfully silly role. "Devil in Disguise" was a good vehicle to display her vocal confidence and quality. Finbarr Shelley as Earl, delightfully relied on good facial expression to portray his emotions in Act One, and contributed most successfully to the comedy when he became vocal in Act Two. He also sang his few solo lines most pleasantly.

The chorus made their strongest contribution to the show through their music, which was of an excellent standard, but they also acted and reacted well, and did all that was asked of them in their routines.

Costumes were effective and eye- catching, with good attention to detail. That stunning red dress on Miss Sandra instantly set her apart from the rest of the small town yokels, and immediately established her character. Dean was effective attired for his military school, and the choir robes were a nice touch for the chorus backing up the later emotional numbers. Hair and make-up were all well taken care of, even if I did find Chad's hairstyle a tad bouffant.

There is a wonderful sense of togetherness about the generations of this Musical Society sharing their stage experiences, and as always, the fun and energy of musical theatre was well-realised in this most enjoyable production.

Ian Charleston as Sky, Julie Covington as Sarah, Bob Hoskins as Nathan and the supremely talented Julia McKenzie as Adelaide was one of the finest principal line-ups I've ever had the pleasure of watching on-stage, (National Theatre, London, 1982) and they are largely responsible for my love of "Guys and Dolls". With its timeless comedy, and superb score, it remains a popular favourite, 67 years after its Broadway premiere.

Pat McElwain's production for Trim Musical Society had a cast that, although they haven't yet reached the dizzy heights of that London cast, brought the book to life with energy, confidence and an abundance of talent.

It was the cracking pace of this production that really made a great impression in what can be a lengthy show. Attention to characterisation was also of the essence, with a few quirky variations on what one has become used to with this tried and tested piece. Nicely and Benny were cartoon-esque, Nathan more up-beat than usual, Harry the Horse was… well, different! With an old chestnut, it takes courage and imagination to go off the beaten track, and it certainly paid off. The design of the set was abstract and efficient, with just enough variations to establish the different settings, and good painting allowed the permanent pieces to change in appearance with the use of good lighting. Stage Manager, Frank Connolly, and his team ran a very smooth and efficient show, with few pauses in the action.

Judicious pruning by Musical Director, Dermot O'Callaghan, reduced the overly long prologue, the Havana dance and the Crapshooters Ballet to more acceptable lengths, which I'm sure, was appreciated by the choreographer and the dancers. The cuts were seamless. Under his direction, the orchestra gave a great performance of this popular score, with strong and constant rhythms and good balance. As Chorus Master, Dermot presented a well drilled chorus with good strength and perfect harmonies.

Choreographer, Aisling Rountree, played beautifully to the strengths of her performers, with her most inventive and exciting routines being energetically presented by the fabulous Hot Box Girls. I loved the sense of these being dancers in a seedy night-club, and the routines were appropriately teasing and provocative. The male chorus were full of energy and enthusiasm, if not quite the same finesse, in their routines, which were suitably, and wisely, less demanding. Overall, the choreography was in keeping with the flavour and the tone of the whole production. "Sit Down You're Rockin' The Boat" was abstract and great fun!

Jessica Hackett, in the role of Sarah Brown, sang with rich soprano tones, and displayed a great sense of comedy and straight acting, switching effortlessly from the staid and refined Mission girl of the early scenes to the intoxicated flirt of Havana. This was a beautifully balanced performance.

Kevin Hartnett played the role of Sky Masterson with a cocky charm in the early scenes, but when he suddenly became loved up towards Sarah, I felt he became a bit boyishly love-stuck, when you might have expected this revelation to bring him to a new maturity. Nevertheless, he displayed fine confidence and ability in his performance.

Damien Hurley was the most jovial Nathan Detroit I've ever watched, with hardly a hint of the world-weary pessimist who's scared of marriage and bankruptcy, and yet it worked deliciously because of superb comic delivery, hilarious facial reactions, and a remarkably reassuring ease and presence on stage. Top notch! Emma Stowe had a perfect combination of feisty and fragile, venomous and vulnerable and sexy and sensitive in a delightful portrayal as Adelaide. Her singing was also perfect for the role. Ian Rountree and Colin Kelly worked very well together as Benny Southstreet and Nicely Nicely Johnston, both characters receiving a quick-witted and quirky treatment. I did feel that more comedy could have been squeezed out of their "Guys and Dolls" duet, but that didn't detract from two very fine, cartoon-like, performances. Nicely gave great energy to "Sit Down You're Rockin' The Boat". Shane Fox was hilarious as the nervy, techy, aggressive thug, Harry the Horse. That's how to play a minor role!

Eoin Kenny made the point that good things can come in small packages with a very amusing portrayal of Big Jule.

Cormac O'Reilly was a convincing and sympathetic Arvide Abernathy, and Sean Fox was a suitably buffoonish Lieutenant Brannigan, full of bluster and ineffectual authority. Gwen Bagnall made the most of her few opportunities to impress as General Cartwright, and Sean Flanagan's Rusty Charlie provided a good third voice to the Fugue for Tinhorns, and maintained a good accent as Joey Biltmore.

In a show that doesn't provide many opportunities, the chorus were vocally secure and always full of energy. The Hot Box Girls were excellent both visually and vocally, and really seemed to enjoy their routines. The male chorus gave strong vocal power to "Oldest Established" and "Luck be a Lady Tonight" and performed all their dances with enthusiasm. "Sit Down You're Rockin' The Boat" was a great fun number.

Key lighting was generally good, with most of the action clearly visible, but there were occasions when the combination of haze and back-lighting overpowered the key lights. There were a few too many colour changes during some of the scenes, and in particular in the sewers, which looked initially excellent in atmospheric greens and blues, but included romantic pinks and reds during "Luck be a Lady", which seemed somehow out of place. "Guys and Dolls" can be a prop heavy show, and on this occasion they were well selected, appropriate and efficiently handled. Sound quality throughout the show was very good, with perfect cueing and a nice balance between stage and pit.

Excellent work with wigs and make-up on both men and women, and particularly the Hot Box girls, who were splendidly turned out all night. Costumes were generally very good, from the traditional Mission uniforms to the colourful Havana outfits, and the gentlemen wore their suits with panache.

All in all, there was a level of production of this classic musical that will make thespians who saw it, want to do it, thus keeping "Guys and Dolls" alive and well for another generation. Thank you for a wonderfully entertaining night.

Another new musical society, this time formed in Trinity College, who strolled up O'Connell Street to perform in the O'Reilly Theatre. West Side Story is the epic tale of love across boundaries set in New York. There were four named choreographers who all had an input and each achieved the requisite accomplished performance. From the comical "Gee, Officer Krupke!" through to the wonderfully staged taunting scene in Doc's store. The performers carried out the choreographers directions quite superbly. Director Seimi Campbell had a simply designed set with scaffolds with three tiers to them as the centre piece, which he used well in various scenes throughout the show. His players all had specific American accents and were always on cue and on their mark. A very large orchestra, comprising all players from the college, were under the baton of Cian Flynn. Mr Flynn worked extremely hard all evening managing to keep tempi strict and allowing the singers plenty of support. Costumes were excellent and I liked the nice touch of denims for the Jets and shiny suits for the Sharks. Sound technician had a trying evening and the lighting plot needed to be more specific. Lainey O'Sullivan (Maria) sang most beautifully with wonderful phrasing, superb pitch and her diction was marvellous. Josh Hurley (Tony) gave her every support and confidence and their acting together was marvellous. He sang with great energy but had a slight tendency to get ahead of the music. His demise was performed poignantly and the passionate outpouring of grief by Maria was heartfelt. Berus Komarschela (Bernardo) has a wonderful stage presence and he managed to give us three different personalities in his relationship with Maria, the Sharks and Anita, all of which were excellently played. Katie Clarke (Anita) gave us a super singing performance, firstly comically in "America", where she delivered the nuances of the lyrics perfectly and then she sang so passionately to Maria in "A boy like that". The chorus all worked extremely hard, they were all on cue and their dance steps were precise. Then they all sang "Tonight" with raucous passion. The secondary leads all assisted with particular note to Alex Gogarty (Schrank), who appeared in each scene as if from nowhere, delivering his lines in a laid back style. His accent was terrific and he used his jacket and cigarettes as personal props assisting him in his characterisation. All in all it was a wonderful opening debut from this new society and I have no doubt they will go on to produce and perform many successful shows in the future.
