Director, Stephen Acton removed the need for an abundance of set pieces and weighty furniture by playing the show on a very effective neutral and somewhat abstract set. There was a sense, throughout the show, that he was aiming at realism, including flaws and all, in the presentation of his characters. There was a bawdiness about the working classes, with a distinct lack of propriety, and a world of difference between their manners and those of the upper class. There was a strong suggestion of the lowly accepting their lot in life, most beautifully emphasised at the end of "As Long as He Needs Me", as Nancy rushed straight back into the arms of her abuser.

Using a revised script, this production of Oliver! threw up some highly entertaining extra pieces that made it stand out from the norm. A wonderful monologue for Fagin in Act One and the inclusion of Widow Corney on Bumble's visit to Mr Brownlow were notable comedic gems. There was a strong, but not an offensive, emphasis on the bawdy in this production, seeing much physicality between Bumble and Corney, hints of it between Noah and Charlotte, and a fair amount of slap and tickle in the pub scene. While there was a nice reality to nearly all the characters, Bill Sykes stood out as being out of keeping with the Director's vision, in so far as he came across almost as an exaggerated pantomime villain. The prelude to this production, depicting Oliver's pregnant mother seeking refuge at the orphanage, was very effectively achieved.

There was an obvious flaw at the close of Act One, when we clearly did see Oliver pocket-picking, rather than Dodger committing the crime and passing the buck to Oliver, while in Act Two Mr Brownlow claims that it was all a mistake. The final scene of the show with the shooting of Sykes is always a tricky one, and on this occasion, I just felt it was a tad rushed or abrupt, but the final image of Fagin and Dodger was nicely effective. All in all, this was a well presented show, with good pace and good comedy.

With this version of the show featuring some arrangements I hadn't heard before, and with some effectively added ambient vocals at the opening of the show, Naoimh Penston did a very good job of guiding both orchestra and vocalists through the musical score. There was a slight problem at the start of the show with off-stage singers falling slightly behind the musicians, but it was, happily, quickly resolved, and a strong line-up of principals, backed by an efficient chorus, made the most of their opportunities to display their well-rehearsed harmonies. There was a good balance between pit and stage.

Choreographer, Martina Lynch, did very good work with the chorus of children, and there were effective routines for "Consider Yourself" and "Who Will Buy". Particularly among her Fagin's gang, there was energy and precision combined in the colourful routines. "I'd Do Anything" was nicely devised. Martina did great work with a show that really doesn't offer too many opportunities for choreography to shine. Brian O'Gorman proved to be the perfect actor to make the most of the additional dialogue that this version of the show offers. Apart from delivering his songs with panache, his monologue in the middle of the Fagin's Den scene was a masterful piece of vocal and visual comedy. He related well to the children around him and was at ease with the other principals, in a wonderfully strong yet delightfully understated characterisation.

It was the vocal quality of Joanne Logue that made her portrayal of Nancy particularly appealing, but there was passion behind the voice that made "As Long As He Needs Me" a showcase piece for her. She played her character with a good sense of fun in Act One, and a nice dimension of tragedy in Act Two.

Sean Hendley, as Bill Sykes, dominated the stage with menace and aggression, and despite the above mentioned reservation about the style of his characterisation, this was a strong and worthy performance. His "My Name" was chilling.

Seán Fox was a bumbling Mr Bumble, comically austere with the children, and somewhat depraved as a companion to Widow Corney. The role was played for laughs with a strong element of relatively innocent bawdiness, and Seán made the most of it. I laughed most when he was being joyously hen-pecked by his partner. And speaking of his partner, Widow Corney was given a fiery interpretation by Siobhán Fawsitt, hilariously funny in the "wants to be seduced but playing hard to get" Scream duet, and even funnier as the eventual battle-axe of a wife. Timing and delivery were superb throughout.

Brendan Kenny and Elaine Sweeney were a formidable, creepy pair as the undertakers, Mr and Mrs Sowerberry, with a gothic appearance and demeanour. Their "That's Your Funeral" number was performed with a nice flavour of cynicism. Jayson Murray was a spirited and cocky Noah Claypole, who flirted nicely with Charlotte, teased Oliver mercilessly and eventually revealed himself as a whimpering coward. Nicely played. Lisa Hamilton made the most of the few opportunities presented to the character of Charlotte.

Anna Kenny was a sympathetic Bet, sincere in her concern for Nancy, and very competent with her vocals in "It's A Fine Life".

Niall Hunter as Mr Brownlow and Rob Donnelly gave strong support in their roles, the former being a perfect gentleman, and the latter, suitably befuddled.

While proving that there's no such thing as a small role, Aisling Green Madden made a welcomed return to the stage, with a sympathetic and sincere Mrs Bedwin. Two young gentlemen to watch out for in the future are Conor Christian, who was a beautifully believable, well-sung and disciplined Oliver, and Luke Andrew Feeney, who gave spice, character and comedy to the challenging role of the Artful Dodger. These boys illuminated the stage with their charm and presence. There were nice cameo performances from Kerry Reid as Old Sally, young Jake Molloy as Charley Bates and Fiona Walker as the pregnant mother of Oliver in the opening sequence.

The chorus made wonderful vocal contributions to the show, and while the show isn't exactly a choreographers dream, the movement and dances throughout were executed with energy and precision, particularly by the orphans and Fagin's gang, who performed their socks off.

The neutral set featured random windows, entrances, sets of steps, etc, which were all well integrated into the action, with the raised areas providing plenty of placement variety, and thanks to an efficient stage crew, under Barry Ryan, furniture and props were quickly put in place. The lighting was generally very good, with the action well highlighted, and the creation of some good atmosphere. Sound levels were well controlled, and the balance was just about perfect. Costumes throughout were of a very good standard, while hair and wigs were appropriate and nicely attended to, and with excellent make-up, Fagin and Bill Sykes in particular were outstandingly transformed performers. Selecting the revised version of the show was an excellent move, as it offered a few nice touches of variety from the norm, but at the end of the day, this was a disciplined and enthusiastic presentation of a highly popular show. Thank you for yet another wonderful night of entertainment.

From the very outset Director Bill Stafford established the grim reality of life in prison. The set was visibly superb. Dark corners to hide in, subdued lighting giving us the impression of dirtiness and grime, flickering candle lights, men roaming in gangs and girls hiding fearful in the shadows. The sound effects were excellent throughout the show, particularly the opening of the roof to allow new prisoners or guards in. It was perfect on the ear and gave us an absolute feeling of containment. His lighting plot was still bright enough to ensure all characters facial features were visible and to show off the marvellous make-up artistry. Costumes were suitably dirty and grimy except when the stories were being told and then they changed into costumes of the tale and these, especially the ladies dresses, were beautiful in colour and design. Keith Flanagan (Cervantes/ Don Quixote) was required to hold the show together with his story telling at the centre of everything. His dialogue was precise and correct and his singing was passionate. He worked very well with his servant Tobie Hickey (Sancho). Mr Hickey got every last ounce of comedy from the role, with wonderful double takes and dead pan delivery of gags. Jennifer White (Aldonza/Dulcinea) sang wonderfully in her lower register with good control and she sang through her lyrics. Her upper register needed, on the top notes, to be more precise. Her acting was positive and forthright until she was attacked. She then returned quiet and subdued which she portrayed poignantly. The supporting cast are many in this show. Each is able to perform in the limelight as their story is told. The comedy throughout this show both in dialogue and musically was at the forefront throughout which lightened the production. Never more so than in the confessional scene. Avril Hartrey (Antonia), Trish Orpen (Housekeeper) and Dermot Keyes (Padre) all sang beautifully. Their diction was marvellous and they got all the inflection in their delivery to allow the very clever comedy lyrics to come through. Choreography is not a major part of this show but what was performed was perfectly adapted to the tale it was part of. The female moors dancers put on a marvellous show, the male chorus sang very passionately and gave enormous energy to their stage movements. The chorus all worked extremely hard as they were on set for long periods. They interacted whenever required, they listened to the stories and gave good quiet supporting acting in the background. The score in this show is full of beautiful tunes and off beat rhythms which musical director Wayne Brown had complete control of. His direction to the cast was quite perfect both visually and with good hand directions. His control over the orchestra was terrific and he never allowed them to overpower the singers in any number. Technically the sound cues were all correct, the lighting plot was very specific and used wonderful set spots for emphasis and the scene changes, mostly done by the cast, were all carried out quickly and smoothly. It was a wonderful evening's theatre and the audience gave the assembled cast an appropriate ovation.

Very rarely is it possible for a show to be performed without a musical director out front giving direction. It is not usually possible for an entire cast to be correct on all of their entrances and exits without a focal point giving specific direction. However this production was the rare one. The singing was perfectly on cue, not only the soloists but the chorus also. The energy and passion that the chorus put into their dancing was terrific. They sang out loud, they were always on the beat. The amount of work that went in to ensure this level of precision must have been enormous. So congratulations to all involved, it was superb. Director Liam Butler, had the show rattle along at a super pace, the scene changes were very quick, and the dialogue was on cue, but never rushed. Kevin Hartnett (Chad) was the roustabout who came to woo the women and change the emotions within the town. His stage presence was excellent, with guitar on shoulder he rode into town on his broken motorbike and looked the epitome of a young Elvis. His singing was excellent, he got all the rock and roll correct and his diction was marvellous on every lyric. Facial expressions were used to full effect and the scene where he was kissed by Ed/ Natalie, brought the house down. Eimear Donnelly (Natalie/Ed) sang with wonderful phrasing and always in tune. Her acting as Natalie was very secure but when playing Ed she needed to lower the tone in her voice a little. Ultan O'Cinneide (Dennis) gave us a most wonderful comedy performance. He was full of nervous energy and his facial expressions, played straight to the audience, were brilliant. Ciara O'Donoghue (Miss Sandra) gave us a prim and proper museum curator at the start then turned into a wonderful femme fatale as she danced, particularly in the scene with the statues which was wonderfully suggestive with all the right sexual nuances. Sean Flanagan (Jim) and Caithriona Mongey (Sylvia) played a marvellous double act together with super dialogue scenes as they gradually fell for each other and their singing was terrific. Mary Murphy (Mayor Matilda) gave everybody the run around especially poor old Barry Murphy (Earl) with her general bossiness she ruled the roost. However Barry got his own back as he delivered his speech at the end to the audiences delight. Technically the sound was correct, the stage crew all worked extremely hard to give us very swift changes and the lighting plot was marvellous, especially in the running gag of "one night with you". It was a wonderful production and a marvellous night's theatre.

American Idiot is not a show for the faint-hearted, nor for your children, nor your grand-parents, probably not for people who like to keep their ear-drums intact, nor for those who are purist about the excessive use of bad language. Aficionados of light opera, traditional musicals or anything that falls into the wide scope of "easy listening", might want to think twice about connecting with this show, but if you're the kind of person who really enjoys listening to the self-indulgent ramblings of foul-mouthed, angsty, obnoxious kids who think no generation has ever had it as bad as theirs…… or if you're a Green Day fan… you'll most likely think it's the greatest piece of contemporary theatre ever penned, with a deep meaningful message that captures the essence of a generation of disillusioned youth. Needless-to-say, it wasn't exactly my cup of tea, but on a more positive note, and fortunately for Loughrea Musical Society, it's my job to critique the production, not the show itself, and as far as the production goes, well… they kind of nailed it! The fact that I found it oppressive, negative and frankly quite disturbing, has a significant bearing on the comments that follow, in so far as the more I believed in these characters, the more I hated them, and ironically, the more I admired the performers for their credibility.

Director/Choreographer, Sarah Griffin, who is obviously much younger than myself and more in tune with this kind of outrageous art, did an excellent job of making this an "in-your-face" production, which, let's be honest, was exactly what punk was all about. The show opened long before it opened, with members of the cast on stage watching television, seemingly suggesting how a generation is brain-washed by mind-numbing banality. It was an effective gimmick, although I'm not sure how it related to what came after. On a very simple set, comprised a few levels of scaffolding, a very well used projection screen, a living room area and a… well, a romping room, with a duvet, there was a great sense of space, and free flowing movement throughout the show. Sarah's choreography was suitably reminiscent of the style I witnessed when (for my sins) I attended gigs by The Stranglers and The Boom Town Rats, and the dancers performed each number with a frenzied energy. As one might expect of a virtual rock concert, the lighting was anything but standard, with constant mind-numbing flashing and moving lights, frequently challenging the audience to watch the antics without being blinded or having a seizure. That was entirely appropriate, I think, but it didn't mask the fact that several dramatic (I can't believe I'm using that word) scenes were badly under-lit. The upper left raised level was perhaps just a bit too high to light effectively, as heads tended to be cut out of the lights. The down left living room seemed, on several occasions, to have been completely overlooked. Props, I assume, (what would I know about rubber tubing and needles?) were well sourced, especially the hospital beds and fittings, and Tunney's prosthetic leg. Heather's baby was a tad artificial looking when it was visible.

St Jimmy's entrance to the show was spectacular, exploding… almost literally, from a box in the middle of the auditorium. At least I'm now reassured that I have a strong heart! Costuming was varied and very acceptable. Where Sarah really scored was in making her cast believe in what they were performing, as the level of commitment was extremely high.

Green Day themselves would have been proud of the musicianship of the band assembled for this production. They were awesome, and their sound was raw and authentic. Shane Farrell kept them together from the keyboard, and also gave plenty of direction to the demented souls on stage, ensuring that their timing and their harmonies were all neatly in place. Chorus Mistress, Louise Moran, will be delighted to know that Chorus vocals were strong, and most of the principals had tuneful and appropriate voices for the style of the music. One or two of the supporting roles could have done with a bit more attention to their pitching, but overall, this was like a punk rock concert, loud, committed, brilliantly played and very well sung.

Joseph Ryan did an excellent job of becoming Johnny, the self-obsessed jerk who doesn't care how his actions affect others. Basically, he narrates his own journey through dropping out of society, into and out of drug addiction, before "finding" himself…… whatever THAT means. This was very well acted, and beautifully sung. He was even almost likeable when he reflected on how he had lost what's Her Name.

By contrast, St Jimmy was completely dislikeable. In fact, I really wanted to get up on the stage and hit him. Fergal D'Arcy exploded onto the stage and gave the performance of his life as a character representative of drug-addiction. His aggression was awesome and totally obnoxious. He was vicious, unrelenting and uncaring. Fergal's body language and his tone were perfect, and his suicide (representing Johnny's victory over addiction) was dramatic, and quite frankly, a great relief. Watching him actually gave me a headache! Brilliant performance though.

Louis Brennan turned the clock back and pretended he was a young man with no hopes, plans or ambitions, in the role of Tunny, who might have escaped from "Born on the 4th of July". Like Tom Cruise, Louis had to act out going to Vietnam and becoming a crippled hero of sorts, which left him short of a leg, and any hopes of future happiness…… oh, except for that nurse, about whom he had strange trippy dreams. Louis was vocally perfect for the role, and his acting was very convincing. His stump also gave a wonderful performance!

At only 13 years old, Gearóid Treacy played Will, the irresponsible kid who gets his girlfriend pregnant, then isn't man enough to stand by her. This was a selfish, sulky character who Gearóid acted confidently and convincingly. At 13, however, he didn't quite have the vocal maturity to do justice to the demanding vocals, but he will doubtless mature into a very fine performer.

It's indicative of the mentality of this show that the "All American Hero" type character of Joshua is portrayed as a soldier and a babe-magnet. How Donald Trump-ish is that? Eoin Mullins, however, played it with fervour, and wrapped it all up with a smooth, velvety young voice. Sarah Corcoran played… what's her name? No, I haven't forgotten… that was her name. What's Her Name! She's the love interest for Johnny, whom he loves so sincerely that he never remembers her name, and persuades her to "shoot up" on drugs. (Nice guy!) Sarah gave an excellent performance, filled with feisty energy and understandable anger as the story progresses. Her voice was strong and appropriate without ever losing its musicality.

The only truly likeable character in the show was Heather, Will's girlfriend, who was literally left holding the baby. She's the only sincere "victim" of the piece, and it was played with great sincerity and a beautiful young and powerful voice, by Laura Charleton.

Another beautiful voice and well-played character was Extraordinary Girl, the nurse about whom Tunney has those strange dreams. It's not a meaty role, but a very talented Andrea Treacy played it sympathetically and with great assurance. Ciara Lynch, as Heather's friend Alysha, got caught a couple of times between her head voice and her chest voice, but she gave good support to her friend. Fine support also came from Roisin Finn as Libby and Ellie Worcester as Leslie. The small chorus really did perform with zeal and conviction throughout the show, putting energy into their vocals and their movement.

The costumes for the show were very good and always appropriate, defining individual characters and adding a touch of glitz and glamour when required. Make-up was, likewise, perfectly suitable to the production. St Jimmy's hair and make-up were outstandingly frightening. Oh, how I hated him!

Sound, for a show of this nature, needs to be extremely on-point, to allow the band to realise the rock score, and still ensure that lyrics are heard. Happily, this was the case, and while I might have found much of what I heard highly obnoxious… at least I heard it all.

While "American Idiot", as a show, doesn't really rock my boat, I'm full of admiration for the way in which it was presented. Loughrea took the bull by the horns and went for the jugular, with that inane sense of anarchy and nihilism that epitomised punk rock, (well, that's my opinion anyway), and in so doing, they brought out some extremely fine performances and theatrical ideas. I greatly admire such commitment and spirit of adventure. Well, what is there left to say? I'm off to take some headache tablets!

Director, Wilfie Pyper, gave us an opening set of ten beds in the orphanage, with a twist and a twirl of the freestanding set he then gave us Hooverville, cleverly designed and very effective. His setting for Warbucks' house was very plush and with a very good bright lighting plot and specific dressing using flowers it was visually marvellous. He had the dialogue delivered crisply and cleanly with a good variation of New York accents. Musical Director, Wilson Shields, had marvellous control of his orchestra and they played wonderfully throughout. Never too loud for the singers, they accompanied perfectly. Choreographer, Oprah Devitt, gave us a rumbustious opening with "It's a Hard Knock Life". The orphans gave 100% commitment and attitude and sang very forcefully. The highlight though was the "NYC" number. This had a myriad of both individual and sets of dancers who all intermingled splendidly. It made the stage appear like a busy New York street. Technically there were issues with the travel spot which was not accurate, the stage crew needed extra hands as scene changes were terribly slow, and the sound technician needed to be on his toes a little more with his cueing. The show revolves around Charlotte Houston (Annie) and she was just tremendous. She sang correctly and loudly throughout the entire performance, her accent was steady and precise and her dialogue was delivered in a manner well above her tender years. She even managed to sing "Tomorrow" whilst Sandy the dog climbed all over looking for his next treat! The orphans were superb in their assistance to Annie, they were all on their toes, their cueing and actions were excellent and they all looked very happy to be performing. Billy Rea (Warbucks) was stern and dictatorial at the outset but soon lost his gruffness as his acting and support of Annie was super. His dialogue was very secure, his singing correct and his diction very good, just needed to dance a little more precisely. Claire Cranston (Grace) sang with a wonderful melodic voice, super pitch and the control of her upper register allowed her to phrase perfectly. Her dialogue was clean and crisp and she wore her heart on her sleeve. Gillian McQuade (Miss Hannigan) gave us a tremendous walk as she tottered around the stage in various states of inebriation. Her slurred dialogue never impeded her enunciation which was excellent. Her singing was secure although there appeared to be some cuts made to the score! Ashleigh Gault (Lily) gave us a squeaky New York accent, a wonderful laugh, a blonde wig and a wiggle as she paraded around the stage. Sean Harkin (Rooster) needed to be more vociferous in his dialogue, a little bit more over the top in this role. The dance steps in the trio "Easy Street" needed to be a little more precise. Of the other small supporting roles Andrew Scott Snr (Roosevelt) gave a powerful display as President with strong tuneful singing and a super accent. He also gave Annie particular attention and assisted her in her performance, excellent acting all round. This show is wonderful to introduce young people to the theatre. The families around me were enthralled by the entire production and gave a most deserved extended round of applause at the finale.

St Joseph's Hall in Kilcock is under some renovations at the moment. It is a wonderful building steeped in history of a bygone era and it is also where Kilcock M & DS performed Hot Mikado. The stage area is not huge and the back stage area is even less so putting on a show with one main set is the ideal way to utilise the facilities. The show opened with a wonderful overture performed by a small orchestra led by musical director Sarah Lynch Barrett. As with small venues it is very difficult to ensure that balance is correct between pit and stage and at times the orchestra overpowered the singers a little too much. However Ms Barrett gave good direction to all involved. Director Philippa Alford had the cast extremely well prepared with cueing and diction of the dialogue excellently delivered. This show has numerous opportunities for the audience to laugh heartily and the players just needed to be more aware of this and should allow laughter to die down before the next line. Deirdre Browne devised the routines with the stage size in mind and the chorus worked superbly to ensure that the steps and moves were executed correctly. Chorus singing was very good in volume but phrasing needed to be finished cleaner. Sound cues were excellent and sound effects, particularly the bird song in "Tit Willow" added to the piece. Lighting plot was excellently devised and delivered, enhancing the colourful varied costumes prepared by Andrew Reddy. Leading lady Naomi Cleary (Yum Yum) gave a lovely display as bride to be, with super dialogue, wonderful comedy and she sang the quick songs superbly with good intonation and diction. Adam McGealy (Nanki Pooh) has a wonderful range to his voice and he sang most superbly, just needs to be more specific with diction. His acting was delivered in a very straight manner and his concentration upon Yum Yum was terrific. Dominic Reid's (Pish Tush) singing was first class and his diction exact. Paul Laycock (Pooh Bah) played this role in a very stern manner, but changed his persona with the wonderful speech of all his individual characters. His accent changed for each one and they were all exact and precise. Charlene Masterson (Pitti Sing) and Sharon Murphy (Peep Bo) worked together marvellously and gave great support throughout. They both sang quite perfectly in the trio "Three little maids" and their diction and dialogue was excellent. Pat Cullen (Ko Ko) was the main comedy role in this show and he worked extremely hard in delivering this. He got every laugh possible from the script and the audience went along with all his gags especially when he directed questions to the front row. His patter songs were in tune, but he needed to be more precise with his lyrics. Maria Mallon McGarry (Katisha) strode around the stage like a typical femme fatale, she got her hooks into Ko Ko and then she gave us the most wonderful comedy from facial expressions towards Ko Ko to marvellous dead pan expressions to the audience. She was the perfect foil to Ko Ko's comedy.

Beautifully directed by the multi- talented Sean Gilligan, who was also required to become an excellent last minute replacement in the role of Daddy Warbucks, this was a vibrant, energetic and fun filled production of "Annie", raced along with nary a dull moment. On a vast stage that was mostly dressed with excellent projections and drapes, we were treated to an opening Street montage that introduced the various characters of the show, and gave us an insight into their personality types, all accompanied by projected newspaper articles of the era. From then on, the show moved swiftly from scene to scene, with most of the changes covered by added business or cross-overs which ensured the stage was never inactive. There was strong attention to character, even among the orphans, and especially in the principal line-up. Comedy was well highlighted throughout, but not at the expense of the more touching moments of the story, which were always well realised.

The technical balance of the show was a combination of the very effective projections and good lighting which rarely missed the mark. Perhaps the scarcity of furniture and props diminished the look of several scenes. The drapes and stairs of the mansion were very effective, but the scene cried out for a big sumptuous chaise longue or a carved office desk and chair to create that mansion effect. Given his wealth, and his desire to make Annie's first Christmas in his home an unforgettable experience, I'm sure Warbucks would have demanded a less dowdy and under-dressed Christmas tree. Similarly, the orphanage could have done with a lot more clutter and jumble to make it inhospitable and oppressive. On two occasions, Miss Hannigan's office had a wall and a door, but these were left out in the final orphanage scene. Given that the show is set during the winter, it might have been appropriate to have top- sheets at least on the children's beds. There were times when the cueing of the projections got a bit out of kilter, but they were all well-chosen and created good atmosphere. Congratulations to the lighting team for ensuring that they were never washed out. Lighting generally was very good and precise, and atmospheric without over-doing the special effects. The sound engineer missed a few cues, and poor old Roosevelt seemed to be rather muted during the Cabinet scene. There were one or two occasions when single voices were too strongly amplified against the chorus, giving a sense of imbalance. The stage crew, under Stage Manager, Sarah Hall, did an efficient job of keeping the show smooth-running.

Laura Bella Griffin's choreography was generally very impressive, but her work with the orphan's chorus was exceptional. Her beautifully disciplined charges filled the stage with raw energy and dynamism. "It's a Hard Knock Life" set the standard with a vibrant and exhausting treatment, which continued with a well-constructed "Never Fully Dressed". These children loved what they were asked to do, and did it with panache. The servant's chorus were equally enthusiastic, performing excellent steps and patterns in all their pieces, and "NYC" was a show-stopper of ever- changing activity and boundless energy. Beautiful work throughout the show. Killian Grumley Traynor led a precise and vibrant orchestra with great diligence, maintaining great pace and tempo from overture to finale. While few in number, the second keyboard helped significantly to fill out the score and produce a full sound. The show was vocally strong, both from principals and the various choruses, although the wannabe star during "NYC" was a tad flat in places, and Miss Hannigan's slurring came dangerously close to sounding off-key on one or two notes. The overall vocal effect, however, was of an extremely good standard. In the title role of Annie, Hana Kelly showed her strength as a performer during the more emotional moments of the show. This wasn't just a cute kid who could sing and smile, but a young actress who believably wept when she heard of her parents' death, and showed genuine affection for Warbucks. This was an endearing performance, from her protective care of Molly, to her sense of mischief with Miss Hannigan, and the sincerity of her love for her adoptive Daddy.

Sean Gilligan stepped in at very short notice as a replacement Pat in the role of Daddy Warbucks, and gloriously led by example, turning in a very fine portrayal of the business-like Multi-millionaire. There was great warmth in his rendition of "Something Was Missing", and a nice development of his relationships with both Annie and Grace Farrell.

Amy Fidgeon, as Grace, had good presence and likeability, combined with a very secure vocal quality. She played particularly well with Annie, with an almost motherly affection, but she did tend to over-react to the attention that she received in the later scenes from Warbucks. I know this was for comedic effect, but it seemed a tad out of keeping with her demeanour.

In contrast, the blatantly abundant over- reactions of Emma Barry, in the role of Miss Hannigan, were the backbone of a hilarious portrayal of the character. Her performance was filled with brash, vocal and physical comedy, expertly delivered by a very good comedienne. Vocally, she had a delightful drunken slur, but it did, on occasions, sound a little pitchy, but she performed with gusto.

James Deegan turned in a solid and comical performance as Rooster, with good movement and strong vocal delivery of "Easy Street". There was a nice contrast between his Rooster and his Ralph Mudge. Jenny McGrath was a very good combination of dumb, ditzy and deliciously devious, in the role of Lily St Regis. Strong on comedy, she even managed to get laughs when she accidentally lost, and then reclaimed her hat. She certainly made the most of an under-written role. Of the supporting roles, very good work came from Callum Martin as a cheesy Bert Healey and Eoin Harrington as the loyal butler, Drake.

Worthy of special mention were the excellent named orphans, Niamh O'Reilly as July, Caitriona O'Connor as a very amusing Tessie, Andrea Hickey as Pepper, Caireann Teggart as Duffy, Sarah Kate Bradley as Kate, and especially a delightful performance from Brianne Byrne as the loveable Molly.

The various choruses performed with unbounded energy, adding so much to the production, visually and vocally, but special mention must be given to the superbly animated and enthusiastic chorus of orphans, who really deserved the excellent response they elicited from a most appreciative audience.

Juno, as Sandy, was wonderful.

Costumes were very good, and I particularly liked the outfits sported by Miss Hannigan, Grace and Lily. Warbucks was very dapper, and it was nice to see a young chorus of servants in costumes that actually fitted them. Great work was done on the wigs/hairstyles of the ladies, and make-up was always appropriate. Miss Hannigan, in particular, had a weathered and weary aspect. Thank you to all concerned for a most enjoyable performance of "Annie", where the younger element were the real stars of a delightful show.

A simply designed set allowed the chorus full movement around the stage in this comic sci-fi tale. Choreographer, Anne Marie Cooney, had the small, but very energetic chorus, step perfect in their routines in which each member of the chorus performed admirably. Their singing was very powerful, but at the same time very controlled, and intonation along with diction was excellent. Sound cues were good, although sound effects were a little too loud, whilst the lighting plot was conceived and executed very well. Musical Director, Kevin Kennedy, gave a steady controlled beat to his orchestra with good visual direction to the players on stage, perhaps he needed to control the volume of the orchestra who at times were on the loud side. James Dobbs (Seymour), started out as a mild mannered, simple kind of guy in love with Audrey. Good hesitant dialogue allied to super stage presence, in which he got all the slap stick comedy perfect. His accent was excellent and his singing was perfect. He wore his love on his sleeve for his leading lady and his rapport with her was superb. Niamh Bolger (Audrey) adopted a wonderful walk, her nervous disposition was excellent around Orin, her accent was correct and constant, and her facial expressions were super. Her singing was precise and clear and her intonation and diction was excellent. Lorcan Dunne (Mushniq) had a tendency to rush his dialogue which meant that words were not as clear as required and his accent needed to be more precise. Neal O'Leary (Orin) got all the subtle nuances of the psychopathic Dentist. He used an affected voice to make him sound odd and his actions in controlling Audrey were frightening. He then gave a wonderful over acting display in the dentists, scaring his patients, along with some of the audience. His struggle to save himself at the end was played superbly. He was a little unsure as to whether he should save himself or enjoy the nitrous oxide a little more. The puppetry of Audrey II was very good and precise and perfectly on cue. The voice needed to be extra careful as whilst volume is important when Audrey II is shouting, enunciation is just as important. Throughout this show there are three backing singers who play cameo roles continuously, Therese Canavan Bolger (Chiffon), Ashley Doran (Ronnette) and Michaela White (Crystal) gave wonderful support to the main characters. Their dialogue was clearly spoken, their singing had wonderful harmonies and was always in pitch, they gave plenty of energy to each situation and then, they sat on the stoop and acted silently in the quiet moments. They were a wonderful addition to the production. Director Paul Walsh used these three girls to super effect throughout the show. He had the front line dialogue nice and crisp, and yet also directed the players to wait for the laughs, which is so important. Clever stage design allowed the movement from each scene to be very precise and delays were rare. The stage manager kept the crew on their toes as scene changes were very swift and unobtrusive.

Colin Hughes was the Director of Dunboyne's production and he had his finger perfectly on the pulse of the nuances and intricacies of the characters in Rent. He allowed each player to establish and then develop each role which gave the audience a wonderful array of performances. Kevin Fagan (Roger) was moody and self-indulgent, his dialogue was crisp and clean and his song to Mimi at the end was delivered with wonderful pathos. Danielle Williamson (Mimi) got the balance between hard-up junkie looking for a fix to happy-go-lucky girl after her fix absolutely perfect. She sang passionately and used her voice to its fullest, her dialogue was delivered crisply and she never missed a mark. Sean Keany (Angel) was marvellous. Perfect hair and make-up allied to wonderful costumes allowed the actor to perform the role precisely. His balance on his platform shoes was terrific and he adapted a wonderful walk. His acting was forceful when required but also played with great tenderness particularly with Liam Egan (Collins). They worked superbly together and when Angel died, it was a wonderful moment of theatre. Mr Egan's ability to commit to a scene was very evident and his stage craft was fantastic. Oisin Nolan (Mark) played the narrator and film director and kept the pace of the show flowing very smoothly. He was always upbeat and his dialogue was excellent. Ciara O'Leary (Joanne) gave a wonderful cameo singing performance in "Seasons of Love" and performed (with Mark) "Tango Maureen" brilliantly. The acting performance of the evening went to Nicole Lamb (Maureen). Not only was her character perfectly portrayed with excellent dialogue, a super accent and wonderful commitment to Joanne, but her solo scene "Over the Moon" was absolutely marvellous and her energy and commitment was superb. Technically the lighting plot was very well executed, there were numerous screen projections used throughout the production all of which were specific and enhanced the production wonderfully. The set was very cleverly designed and the stage crew all worked very hard to ensure there were no delays. Musical Director Paul Strachan, kept a good beat going within the orchestra but occasionally was guilty of not controlling the volume particularly of the bass guitar. This production had a very strong cast who could all sing, but at times, struggled to be heard.

There was a no-nonsense approach to the direction of this show from Jim McGuigan and Corinna Cunningham. It was traditional and very well disciplined, with good attention given to presenting the younger performers at their absolute best. Combined with the tidy and effective choreography of Donna King, the team managed to show off the great talents of the children of the orphanage and of Fagin's gang. The choreography of "Consider Yourself" was lively and varied, "Who Will Buy" was delightful, and "Oom- pah-pah" had energy and a great sense of fun. While direction was precise and very clean and tidy, possibly opportunities for a more comedic effect were missed to exaggerate the beautifully drawn Dickensian characters.

A very effective and practical set was nicely used, with enough suggestion of the various locations to keep the show visually interesting, and the very good pace of the show was assisted by Stage Manager Ryan Walsh in guiding his stage crew through a tidy presentation that made good use of the space available. There was a wide array of good and effective props apparent throughout. Lighting, in keeping with the production trend, was tidy and un-fussy, with action well-highlighted and good atmospheres created by a sensible choice of colours. The dramatically "darker" scenes of the show were nicely plotted. Sound, throughout was even and on cue.

Costuming "Oliver!" isn't the most glamorous job in the show catalogue, but there was nothing eye-catchingly out of place, and one could easily distinguish the wealthy from the poor. The children's chorus were very nicely and appropriately dressed, and the principals all looked comfortable and correct in their outfits. Good work was done on wigs and hairstyles and those that required character make-up we're not let down by the make-up team. Overall, the Visual Presentation was very satisfactory.

Ronan Caldwell had a delightful innocence in the role of Oliver, not at all lacking in confidence or vocal ability. Well played young man.

Finnén McCann created a very credible Artful Dodger, with a good accent and plenty of personality. He put his vocal pieces across well, and is a promising young performer for the future.

Lowry Hodgett was a gentle Fagin, taking the role in his stride and always looking relaxed in his business. His work with the boys was very good, but it might have been nice to see an edgier, sinister side to him as well. "Reviewing the situation" was nicely performed.

Ciara McPartland was a feisty Nancy in Act One, full of spirit and at ease with Fagin's gang. In Act Two, she sang a passionate rendition of "As Long as He Needs Me", and put up a credible fight to save the life of Oliver, in a well-balanced performance. I loved Cathal Markey's interpretation of Bill Sykes. Not being burly in stature, he chose to be like a vicious pitbull-terrier, poised and ready to attack. There was something thug-like about his laugh, and seeming cordiality at moments when he was about to unleash his bile. "My Name" was a tad too gentle for my liking, but in every other respect, he was scarily credible.

Eithne Bell gave strong characterisation to Widow Corney, focusing more on her angry, discontented persona than on the comedic possibilities of the role, which was probably more Dickensian that Lionel Bart, but that is by no means a criticism. This was a solid believable performance. Likewise, Jim McGuigan was a robust and formidable Mr Bumble, without the more blustering, buffoon-ish treatment that he often receives. His stage presence was excellent, and his vocals clear and secure. Donal O'Hanlon and Anne Marie Campbell were well-paired as Mr and Mrs Sowerberry, he being pendulous and hen-pecked and she the blustering bossy wife. These were nicely played characters who delivered "That's Your Funeral" very effectively.

Another confident pairing was Neil Heaney as Noah Claypole and Emma Slater as Charlotte. With limited opportunities, they established a teasing relationship, and Neil was a perfect bully who got his comeuppance at the hands of young Oliver.

Niamh Walsh made the most of her few opportunities to impress as Bet, with a pleasant voice and good presence.

Mark Hughes was a credible and sympathetic Mr Brownlow, and Dennis Walsh a suitably befuddled Dr Grimwig. Good support and a clear and tuneful voice was offered by Helena Hughes as Mrs Bedwin, while Conor Downey as young Charley Bates, Claire O'Neill as Old Sally and Annette Ward as the old Lady all gave what was required to their roles. Good individual voices from the chorus were apparent during "Who Will Buy", and the chorus generally performed with good energy and focus.

Discipline, combined with a great sense of fun and energy, is always apparent in Bosco productions, and I hope they continue to provide such wonderful opportunities and experience to their enthusiastic membership. Thank you for a tidy and precise production of "Oliver!" and yet another great night of entertainment, where the young talent of the future was so impressively on display.

This show is a collection of characters from stories by Dr Seuss. It is required to be a light hearted romp through a child's eyes with lots of overacting by the cast and to be spectacular, visually. Director Damien Hurley gave us exactly that. The set was on two levels with a wonderful walkway from stage left across the back which allowed individual characters and scenes to be played with all the players visible throughout. The costumes were superb in colour and, it should be noted, were all made by the costume department. The show revolves around "Horton" played by Karl Hoffman. He is a very lonely elephant who finds a village of small creatures, "The Who's", who he is determined to protect. His dialogue and diction were very good but had a few problems with singing in some of the high pitched numbers. These villagers are led by Fergal Sweeney (Mayor) and Colette O'Beirne (Mayoress). Fergal was very eloquent in his dialogue and Colette spoke with wonderful precision and sang superbly. The narrator was played by Kathryn Gibbons (The Cat in the Hat). A wonderful costume, and a very large hat, allowed Kathryn to dance, sing and act in a wonderful relaxed manner. She kept the flow of the show going wonderfully and her timing with all her stage props was excellent. She befriended Amy Molloy (Jo Jo). This young lady was full of energy and excitement, her dialogue was very precise and her singing and dancing were wonderful. There are a number of other characters who all interjected throughout the production, Keeva Kavanagh (Sour Kangaroo), had a super belting voice with marvellous control, Anthony Ennis (Schmitz), gave a performance of military precision, and a super pencil moustache to boot. Karen McCourt (Gertrude McFuzz) was wonderful in her portrayal of this lonely little bird with a small tail. Her dialogue was perfect and her singing marvellous. The three ladies Ciara Roche, Helen Cahill and Sinead McCrohan (The Three Bird Girls) were superb in their singing and dancing. They were a very focal part of the production and all had super stage presence and were always on their mark. The choreography was delivered by Patricia McDermott and she ensured that the dance routines were cleverly designed and their execution was marvellous. Scene changes were executed in a swift precise manner with exemplary delivery of props. Make up was superb, and once under the very precise lighting plot added to the overall visual nature of the show. Sound cues, including sound effects, were timed perfectly and all the cast were heard clearly. The orchestra, under the baton of Antonio Cafolla were a little loud in Act 1 but this balanced itself out in Act 2 and their accompaniment became very good all round. Baldoyle Musical Society has a strict policy of using members only, which is a return to the 80's when "all amateur shows" were the norm. It was a wonderful production and the audience afforded the society an appropriate ovation at the end.

n the design of this show, from stage to costumes to character realisation, Director Eoin Cannon, captured the mood of this piece perfectly, and had great fun with the frivolity of the story. From a comedic point of view, I might have been inclined to rein Freddy in a little and to exaggerate Jolene a little more, but this was a well- paced and extremely tidy production that was delightfully appealing to the audience. The set design for this production was bulky but beautiful, with revolving staircases and balconies, a very nice backdrop and pleasing neutral side-flats. The different locations were well enough established by the changes and by good lighting. The stage was nicely utilised, from scenes on the balcony to insets for the train scene and the bedroom. In fairness to Stage Manager, Maureen McMahon, and her team, they managed those sizeable trucked pieces efficiently, given the lack of space, and without too much delay. The wide range of props was well sourced and appropriate to the era and location of the show. The lighting, thankfully (as it is referenced in the script) was very good throughout the show, particularly when picking up the principals in "specials". There was also good use of colour for atmosphere.

The sound, with the exception of one momentary blip, was close to perfectly balanced and cued.

David Wray had a fine orchestra at his disposal, which would have been totally at home on the moon-lit veranda of a Riviera hotel, capturing the lazy-hazy, intoxicating flavour of the music. Their sound, with the exception of an occasionally heavy drum beat, was the perfect accompaniment to the goings-on on stage. Albeit played on a keyboard, the mood was deliciously heightened by several atmospheric accordion solos.

The art of good choreography is to make the dancers and chorus look comfortable in the execution of their routines, and Denise Donohoe hit the nail on the head in creating beautiful routines that were inventive yet manageable enough to be cleanly and precisely performed. Her routines were also delightfully appropriate to the era and mood of the show.

From the moment he appeared on the stage, Michael Evans oozed charm, smarm and complete confidence in the role of Lawrence Jameson. In a musical that frequently crosses the footlights to involve the audience, he had just the right amount of pantomime to make the most of his comedy, and he flipped easily from posh English gentleman to sadistic German Therapist, to sleazy Latin American for the final scene. Added to strong acting and excellent comic delivery, was a smooth voice and a dynamic sense of rhythm. Stuart Pollock was an immensely funny Freddy Benson, with a propensity for fidgeting with his groin. His best scene in the show was his reaction to being whipped while confined to a wheelchair, which was hilarious. I did feel that on occasions he needed a softer edge, as much of his comedy was very "slap in the face", but with strong vocal quality and fine mobility, this was a highly entertaining performance.

An excellent voice and a good sense of comedy made Katy Nicholas a great choice for the role of Christine Colgate. There was much sincerity in her little- girl-lost humility as she conned the boys, and a delightful enjoyment in her victory over them. This is a performer I will look forward to seeing in meatier roles in the future.

Philip Emmet was a strong and efficient Andre Thibault, always clear in his diction, despite his thick French accent. His singing was very good and he had a delightful comedy rapport with Muriel. Emma Jane Reilly enjoyed the silliness of her role as Muriel Eubanks, delivering much of her comedy straight out front to the audience, with wonderful timing and very funny facial expression. The timing of the scene on the balcony, where she and Andre discuss their night of passion in relaxed conversational tones, was perfect, and the lady can sing with conviction. Sophia Daly could have been a tad more exaggerated as the Oklahoma heiress, both in her accent and in her persuasive aggression, to make the most of a character that disappears all too swiftly, but she nevertheless impressed with a confident presence and a fine voice. Several fine voices from within the chorus made a strong impact as soloists, and there was a plethora of cameo roles which were all convincingly portrayed. The chorus of this show is generally superfluous to the action and frequently used to cover changes of scene or for time lapse, but within those parameters, this chorus gave all that was asked of them, both physically and vocally.

There was good attention to detail in costuming, hairstyles and make-up, all of which beautifully captured the feel of the French Riviera. This was a well presented production where nothing awkward stood out or captured the wrong kind of attention.

This was a truly delightful production of a light and fluffy musical comedy, with a musical score that I find highly forgettable, but also strangely intoxicating and appropriate to the mood and tone of the setting. It was, however, performed beautifully by an extremely talented cast and orchestra, and the production was full of commitment and energy.

Underneath a fluffy pink cover, Legally Blonde is a story that, at its heart, tackles gender equality, misogyny and bullying. It condemns stereotyping, targets pretentiousness, and kicks the ass of vanity, and it does all of this through cleverly devised wit and wisdom, wrapped up in an extremely challenging musical score, a physicality that requires a clever and creative technical team, and throws up a formidable list of Dramatis personae, including one of the most demanding roles in contemporary musical theatre. That is a hell of a lot to get right… but Leixlip succeeded on every level.

The pace was awesome, with crescendos of comedy and choreography. Under the direction and choreography of Claire Tighe, characterisations throughout the cast were spot on, and not an opportunity was missed to make the most of the comedy of the script. There was also physical comedy that was inspirational in design. The sudden formation of the heart of pink pom-poms surrounding Elle during "What You Want", was a masterpiece, and when the heart began pulsating, it became a moment of pure gold.

Attention to the technical aspects of the show was part and parcel of the smooth- running of the production, and in keeping the stage vividly painted with atmosphere. There was grandeur in Harvard and the Courtroom, and spacious elegance about the department store. The clutter of Elle's room was just as it should have been. Dewey's trailer looked like the real McCoy. Other cameo scenes were well-realised through the use of effective lighting which, throughout the show, was atmospheric without being over-stated. Follow spots were used discreetly and effectively. Stage Manager, Mary Purcell and her team were hardly evident at all, so tidy were the changes of scene. The props team had done an excellent job of accumulating a wide range of appropriate props and furniture. Sound quality was excellent.

But it was superb choreography that raised this show to incredible heights. There was a fusion of dance, drama and comedy in almost every routine. There was invention, energy and superb execution by chorus and principals alike.

With the need to excel in the four disciplines of acting, singing, dancing and comedy, Elle Woods has become the present day Dolly, or Charity, and an opportunity to show off an awesome individual female. In casting Jacqueline Brunton in the role, Leixlip hit the bullseye. Here is a lady who gave the role more comedy than I've hitherto seen, a powerhouse vocal performance, stylish and often comical dance ability, and a sincerity in her acting that was heart-melting. She was quite simply dynamic in every respect.

Ross Murray was such a likeable and sincere Emmett that the whole audience were rooting for him. He had a very fine vocal quality, but it was his charm and affability that made the greatest impact in a well-realised characterisation.

Ian Tighe nailed the arrogance and conceit of Warner, and along the way displayed a very strong sense of comedy. His singing was perfect for the role, and his interpretation never faltered. A very well played role.

Jenny McCabe stepped up to the wonderfully comical role of Paulette with ease and confidence, making the most of the excellent dialogue and selling her "Ireland" number with aplomb.

Ciarán Mooney was as sleazy as he was authoritative in the highly dis-likeable character of misogynist boss, Professor Callahan. He also played the comedic elements of the role with a relaxed assurance.

There was a delightfully bitchy edge to Kirstin Smith in the role of Vivienne, successfully making her the character the audience love to hate, but there was an equally charming sincerity in her admission of misjudging Elle in the later scenes of the show, where she also let vent to a strong and capable vocal display.

Breathtakingly brilliant was the energy displayed by Orla Jennings as she took to the stage as Brooke Wyndham with a superbly executed skipping routine, all the time bellowing the musical number with a powerful and tuneful vocal. If that wasn't enough, she also demonstrated a great sense of comedy and timing in her delivery of lines.

Watching Serena, Margot, Pilar and Kate left me absolutely exhausted, such was their energy level. Orla Maher, Avril Doyle, Aoife Masterson and Aoife Cartwright established great individual characters and worked brilliantly together as a team. Their energy was as high vocally as it was physically, resulting in powerful and exhilarating performances.

Colina McGarry gave a tough, tomboy personality to her Enid Hoops, playing strongly to the comedic elements of her character. This was a very good balanced performance, without going too over the top.

Ciarán Tighe looked confident and relaxed as Kyle, enjoying his strut, and boasting about his package. With a good sense of comedy, this was a well-delivered role, excuse the pun.

Strong support was offered by Jamie Hennessy as a delightfully funny Carlos, and doubling as Aaron Schultz, and from Conor Browne as the ridiculous Nikos. Other characters of note were Jordan Donnelly as the rapping Grandmaster Chad, Elaine Brunton as the caustic Chutney Wyndham, Fionn O'Dwyer as Sandeep Padamadan and Kevin Sherwin in a variety of cameo roles. Perrie was a cute Bruiser, and Lily was a beautiful and well-behaved Rufus.

David Hayes led a superb orchestra who captured every nuance of this excellent musical score, including a refreshing and impressive Moog synthesizer solo. Tempi and rhythms were strong throughout, and yet there was a delicate touch to those moments of emotion that required a gentler feel. Balance within the orchestra was just perfect, and the balance with the singers on-stage ensured that the lyrics and harmonies were always heard loud and clear. As well as a musically strong principal line-up, the chorus were top drawer in their vocal presentation.

I loved that the Delta Nus were all individually attired appropriate to their characteristics. Elle looked consistently radiant, and the dull characters were suitably more conservative in appearance. There was very good attention to detail in costuming, hairstyles and make-up, with no inappropriate distractions. All in all, there was excellent work on visual presentation.

Thank you to everyone for a superbly entertaining night of comedy, choreography and classy performances.

The gruesome story of the Demon Barber of Fleet Street in Clonmel, proved to be very dark indeed, enhanced by wonderful and well-presented music, highly dramatic acting and a vast array of technical and visual treats. I doubt if the audience will easily forget their encounter with Sweeney Todd.

Director Michael O'Donoghue went over to the dark side with this production, highlighting the sinister aspects of the show with great intensity. There was limited relief from the feeling of drudgery and begrudgery, on a set that was brilliant in its dismal aspect. With excellent design by Dairmuid Vaughan, the small stage of the White Memorial Theatre was transformed into a dour and dismal multi-level composite set that served its purpose brilliantly. To compliment the surroundings, very effective lighting created the perfect atmosphere for every scene, and the range of absolutely excellent props was quite outstanding. Todd's Chair was superb. The mincer was amazing. The shrouded cadavers hanging on meat hooks, awaiting mincing, were creepy and spine-chilling. The Stage Management of Kay Sheehan and Sean Deegan was efficient and fluent. Sound quality was very good throughout the show, with well-timed effects. Given the restrictions of the venue, this really was a wonderful use of space, with precise attention to detail. with props that were gruesome even to look at, and with characterisations that focused on the darkest side of human nature.

It really did feel like sitting through a horror story. The glory of Sondheim's writing, however, is that at its heart, Sweeney Todd is still regarded as a dark comedy, and I did feel that a few opportunities were missed to offer the audience some relief from the oppressive misery of this superb story. Perhaps a touch more charm about the character of Todd, a more exaggerated sense of the ridiculous about Pirelli, and more attention to the double standards of the Beadle. With the exception of a brilliantly devised "By The Sea", and some well pointed lines during "A Little Priest", the production seemed to stay very much on one level, albeit a very high level.

The pace at the start of the show was a little pedestrian, but it soon picked up and was well balanced for the rest of the performance.

This is not a show that requires much choreography, but the chorus were very well used, given the limitations of the stage, and movement was generally well designed and executed with good timing and delivery.

Dairmuid Vaughan was a very sinister Sweeney, rarely allowing a hint of a smile to cross his face, even during his comedic duet "A Little Priest". I laughed out loud when Mrs. Lovett dressed him up during "By The Sea", but bar that moment, this character was played with a sombre darkness. Diarmuid's accent sounded like an interesting blend of Australian and Cockney, which was clever and appropriate. There was no doubting the quality of his drama, nor his vocal ability, but I did feel that an additional element of charm, to attract the flow of unfortunate customers to his parlour, would have given another dimension to an extremely impressive performance.

Olwyn Grogan grew into the role of Mrs Lovett as the show progressed. A little timid at the outset, she was enjoying herself by the time she beautifully delivered "A Little Priest". "By The Sea" was a tour de force, and her panic when Tobias twigged that the pies might not be all they seemed, was palpable. Very nicely acted and securely sung throughout. Emmet Donlan had a most pleasing tenor voice and gave good character to the role of Anthony. He was always believably sincere, and his scenes with Johanna were emotionally strong.

There was a beautiful quality to the voice of Sinead O'Donovan in the role of Johanna, combined with a convincing vulnerability to her character. Her disdain for the Judge was well established through tone and body language, and she was at ease in her work with Anthony.

John Sharpe, as Tobias, played his later scenes with simplicity and great credibility, but I'd have liked to see him more vulnerable and put-upon from the outset. He initially came across as strong and able, which made him a tad less sympathetic at the story's conclusion. His singing was very good and secure.

David Hughes had a great voice, and the stature and severity for Judge Turpin, but being the real villain of the piece, I did feel that the loathsome nature of his character needed a more exaggerated and visible realisation.

James Sweeney was a very credible Beadle Bamford, but I think there's scope for more comedy if this character is appallingly sycophant towards the Judge, and smugly superior to everyone else. It was, nevertheless, well played and nicely sung, including a decent falsetto.

A wonderful performance was given by Michelle Smith in the demented role of the Beggar Woman, earning the laughs, but more significantly, the sympathy of the audience during the denouement. Her singing was perfect for the role.

James O'Donovan gave a strong performance, but could have had more fun with the role of Pirelli, especially in the almost "musical hall" style of the street scene. His Irish thug, when he visits Sweeney with his extortion plan, was excellent. The contest was well sung. Ricky Dunne was suitably nasty as Asylum owner, Jonas Fogg, and David Hogan gave good support as the Bird Seller. There was very good vocal work from the chorus throughout the show, and given the restrictions of a small stage, they managed all their movement most effectively.

Very good work was done on costuming the show to reflect the sinister tone and the settings of the piece, from the garb of the demented asylum residents to the dapper wear of the Judge and other gentry. The same level of attention was given to wigs and hairstyles, particularly for Mrs Lovett, and the delightfully dishevelled look of the Beggar Woman. Make-up, similarly, was detailed and extremely impressive. I'm not sure I would have trusted a barber with a wonky eye to hold a razor to my throat, but the effect was very good.

This was a great lesson in how to present a massive production on a tiny stage, with the use of good planning and invention. While I did feel that a tad more attention to comedy would have given it another dimension, the overall standard was, nevertheless, of a very high order. Thank you sincerely for a very enjoyable night.

To his credit, Paul Norton is a director who likes to push the boundaries in his interpretation of musicals, but his most outstanding achievement in this production of "Rock of Ages" was his ability to restrain his principals, allowing them to exaggerate their characters, but keeping a tight enough rein to prevent them from over-doing the caricatures. Hence, from a principal point of view, this was a well-paced, well-balanced and disciplined production which allowed the very funny script to take centre stage. It's all too easy for a show of this nature to turn into a pantomime, which was, thankfully, avoided. Chorus-wise, there were a few occasions where the ensemble seemingly appeared just to perform a dance, rather than slotting seamlessly into the action, but in most other respects, this was a very well-directed piece of work.

Alan Greaney took on the central comedy/ narrator role of Lonny, and did so with a very good degree of success. His singing was strong and inspiring, and the ease with which he played the comedy of the role was most impressive. The opening scene needed a little more pace to start the show more explosively, but from then on, he was relaxed, confident and very funny, with some good ad-libbing.

Eoghan Fingleton, as Drew, displayed a strong rock tenor range, putting over the tender romantic moments as effectively as the hard-rock belters. His character was very well established, and his scenes with Sherrie were sympathetic and believable. Hannah Wright was a radiant Sherrie, convincingly shy and determined at the outset, foolishly impetuous with Stacee Jaxx, vulnerable on the rebound from the hurt, and delightfully sincere in realising her love for Drew. She achieved all of this with supreme stage presence and a powerful vocal performance.

Kevin Griffin sustained a wonderfully comedic presence, attitude and accent in the role of Dennis, showing signs of having been an avid "Wayne's World" fan. This was an excellent performance, helped considerably by a strong vocal delivery. Patrick Byrne needed more amplification in the role of Stacee Jaxx, as a combination of a very husky voice and a kind of mesmerized character led to an issue with clarity. He truly looked and acted the part very convincingly and was extremely funny in his "I Want to Know What Love Is" duet with Sherrie.

Eoin Ryan was brilliantly cast as the highly amusing Franz, giving equal measures of character, comedy and "camp" to the role. He acted and sang with great confidence, and was perfectly matched with Kori Kilduff, who played a quaint and quirky Regina with character, energy and an impressive vocal ability. This was an excellent pairing, developing a very credible and comical romance as the show progressed.

David Alexander sustained a good accent and a stubborn character in the role of German property developer, Hertz. He was also delightfully funny as he eventually melted and became the loving, caring father of Franz.

Sarah Corcoran was relaxed and assured in the role of Strip-joint owner, Justice, displaying nice sentiment and a strong vocal quality, particularly impressive in "Every Rose Has It's Thorns".

Heather Doyle made the most of limited opportunities to impress with her vocal power in the role of Waitress #1. Caroline Greaney, likewise, made a good impact as Sherrie's Mother, and Claudia O'Sullivan was a believable, easily stimulated Constance Sack.

Michael Cooney was a suitable money- grubber as the Mayor, and appropriately sleazy and inappropriate as the lecherous Producer, and Richard Brown was a capable and confident Ja'Keith Gills. Jay Molyneux stood out, in more ways than one, with an excellent performance as transgender Candi. This role was beautifully danced, and comically alert, not to mention perfectly attired. He just needed to be aware of not upstaging the focal point, as happened when he did his extremely impressive splits.

The chorus and dancers, throughout the show, showed no embarrassment or discomfort, in appearing in frequently flimsy attire.

Declan Gardiner's choreography was at its best when there was a reduced number of dancers on the stage, particularly for "Heat of the Moment" which was delightfully sensual/ sexual, and danced with great conviction. On the bigger choral numbers, there were just too many bodies on the stage for the routines to be precise, despite there being many outstanding dancers and some challenging choreography. To cater for mixed abilities, these routines should perhaps have been simplified a little, with less repetitive arm movements, which notoriously highlight when dancers are out of sync. Nevertheless, it has to be said that no-one on the stage was lacking in energy or enthusiasm.

Shane Farrell, almost unrecognisable in his wig, got the show off to a fine start, taking centre stage with a keytar, before moving back to lead an excellent band, who played the classic rock score with precision and conviction.

Rhythms throughout were perfect, and the orchestration featured some fine solo work. Choral work was equally impressive, with abundant, well-sung harmonies, and plenty of strength, even when performing energetic dance moves.

The very good technical presentation of the show was marred only by an element of inconsistency in the lighting, which perhaps needed a tad more attention. The golden rule should be to prioritise that the focal point of the action is effectively lit, and then attend to the atmospheres and effects. There was some excellent use of moving lights and atmospheric colours in this production, but there were also many instances where groups or individuals were singing or speaking in half light or, once or twice, in no light. The imbalance causes an un-necessary distraction, and is easily remedied by plotting the key lighting first.

Sound was generally very good, and given that the band was prominently placed on-stage, a good balance was achieved. Just once or twice, principals could have benefitted from a tad more amplification to raise them above the chorus.

The several expletives uttered by the MD are, of course, part of the script, but I feel they'd have been more effective and funnier had they been background throw- aways, rather than so obviously amplified. The set for the show was beautifully designed, excellently dressed, and operated with efficiency. Stage Manager, Chontelle Kenny, albeit assisted throughout by an energetic "Lonny" on stage, kept the show running smoothly with effective movement of set pieces and furniture, all of which was appropriate to the show and the setting. The insets that folded out from the stage right flat were particularly impressive and sturdy. The various levels were well used.

The wardrobe department did an excellent job of blending the characters into the beautifully appropriate set. The rockers looked authentic, and the strippers were delightfully under-dressed, without being offensive. I loved the attention to detail with the clever use of logo-t-shirts on Lonny, the lederhosen on Franz and the cheesy boyband jacket for Drew. Principals were nicely individualised. Wigs and hairstyles varied from insane to outrageous, but all were highly appropriate and well-worn. Make-up was equally effective. All in all, this was a very well presented visual package.

For pure entertainment value, Galway hit the target and provided their audience with a very funny and memorable production. Thank you to all concerned.

To direct your first musical ever on possibly the smallest stage in Ireland is some achievement, and Sadie O'Reilly should feel well proud that she did a tidy job of it. Given the lack of space, she managed to get people, furniture and props on and off the stage without too many delays. While some scenes, on this occasion, took a while to set up, and some were a tad bland in dressing, Stage Manager Sarah Flynn did all in her power to keep things moving at a decent pace. There was great attention to detail in the props, the Carousel being a very clever device, and the wharf having enough pieces to strongly suggest the setting. Lighting was very good, and even on the limited stage, focal points were well highlighted and good atmospheres were created. Sound was sound, throughout the show.

Characters were nicely realised throughout, and the mood and pace of the show were impressive. There were times when more could have been made of the comedy. With the central story being dark and somewhat depressing, any opportunities for levity should be grasped. However, the story was well told, and both Billy and Julie worked hard to keep the whole tale credible. The opening scene is difficult, particularly on such a limiting stage, but good effort was put into presenting different characters, and giving a fairground feel to the setting.

Musical Director, Michael Fay, and his orchestra were tucked neatly away behind the set, but that didn't prevent good leadership and a fine balance between stage and musicians. From the flowing strains of the Carousel Waltz to the delightful "Never Walk Alone" finale, the tuning of both orchestra and chorus was pitch perfect. While one or two of the principals were vocally stretched, the show was strong on musicality and very pleasurable listening.

On a stage that is a choreographer's nightmare, Gráinne Jones managed to present some very fine work, sensibly using small numbers in the big dance section of "June" and creating some beautiful and effective ballet sequences with Louise and the Carnival dancers. The Pas de Deux, with Louise and Cian McKeon, was excellent. On other occasions, nice pictures, with minimal movement, were the sensible route to take, and the only scene that looked over-crowded and less effective was the opening, largely because of the action and props that had to accompany the movement.

There's virtually nothing likeable about Billy Bigelow, but Séamus Sullivan gave a wonderful acting performance, strong, thoughtless and bullying in the early scenes, and I even felt a bit sorry for him at the denouement. He was almost likeable as he flirted with Julie, and well oppressed by the weight of his association with Jigger. Apart from a couple of top notes that stretched his range, his vocal performance was also most pleasant. Michelle Bradley's Julie Jordan was vulnerable and nervous, but courageous enough to take a chance on Billy. She portrayed all of these emotions most effectively. Her acceptance of being beaten by her husband was hard to swallow, but she was very believable in her miserable devotion to him, and my heart went out to her. Musically, she performed with a pleasant, lyrical voice that was full of emotion.

Peter Fay gave a solid rendition of squeaky-clean Enoch Snow, playing the comedy of the character very confidently. Again, there were occasional top note issues, but it didn't detract from a very nicely judged acting performance. There was a nice smug-superiority about his fatherly scenes in Act Two.

Calina Cunningham, I feel, started off rather timidly in the role of Carrie Pipperidge and glossed over several opportunities to enhance the comedy of the character, but she did, without question, relax into it, and provided many more laughs as the story progressed. Her "When I Marry Mister Snow" was very sound, and "When The Children Are Asleep" was a delightfully performed duet.

Edel Marron O'Flaherty was a most animated and impressive Nettie Fowler, enjoying the lightness of "June is Bustin' Out All Over", the relaxed breeziness of "Clambake" and culminating in a beautiful and emotional "You'll Never Walk Alone". Very nicely played.

Equally secure was the performance of Elaine Moore O'Donohoe as Mrs Mullins, establishing her possessiveness of Billy, and her hostility towards anyone who got close to him. She nicely portrayed her love for him at the moment of his death.

Ronán MacCabe played a cold, calculating Jigger Craigin with great confidence, handling his limited opportunities for comedy with aplomb. "Blow High, Blow Low" and "Stonecutter" also revealed a confident vocal quality.

Arthur McGauran gave a solid performance as Mr Bascombe, and still managed to relate to Julie's plight with a sensitive nature. A very nicely portrayed character. I don't know how the religious elite would feel about a woman holding such a prominent office in Heaven, but I thought Áine Grace was a lovely Starkeeper, and put her character over with dignity and sympathy. Likewise, she was perfectly delightful as Doctor Seldon.

Andy Kelly was a very acceptable Heavenly Friend, with Sarah O'Flaherty as his able assistant.

Sinéad Byrne was a beautifully graceful Louise Bigelow, excellent in her ballet, and confident in her delivery of lines. Cillian Byrne was a casual and snobby Enoch Snow Jnr.

Cian McKeon proved the perfect dance partner for Sinéad, as the Carnival Boy. He had poise, balance and good strength for the lifts. Very well done.

Good support was given by a good clear voiced Arminy (Louise Tierney), Evan McGarr and Tommie Nolan as the Policemen, Robert Gallagher as the Captain and Brid Murphy as the Principal. The Snow Children, led by a very capable Kealy MacCabe, did all that was asked of them with charm and good discipline.
