The chorus throughout the show, involved themselves in the action with a good awareness of the point of focus and with fine reactions. Their singing was disciplined and very pleasant on the ear, with good harmonies and diction. Movement on such a small stage was limited, and occasionally looked over- crowded, but they all performed with spirit. The show was nicely costumed with no- one ever looking out of place or era. There was nice variety in the carnival costumes and for the ballet, and principals always seemed appropriately attired. There was good attention to detail in wigs and hairstyles, and make-up was generally acceptable, although perhaps Jigger could have had a more sinister aspect. This was a most enjoyable show, and for me, a nostalgic trip down memory lane. Thank you for a very entertaining night, and wishing you much success in your future productions.

The appeal of Oliver! is that it offers a great opportunity to introduce young performers to the joys of musical theatre, and there's certainly plenty of young talent in Roscrea, judging from the finished product. This was a well-directed, well-performed piece of traditional musical theatre with a few pinches of spice thrown in for good measure.

There were a few Paul Norton signature features to this production, particularly reflecting his bawdier-than-most approach to comedy, but it was all done tastefully, and presented with great energy and enthusiasm from a talented cast. The staging was very good. The set for the show was most effective, with fold- open units left and right, a bridge centre stage that kept changing in detail for the different scenes, and some beautifully painted backdrops that gave great depth to the stage. In a hall that has virtually no wing-space, stage manager, Ian Hanrahan and his team, did a splendid job of scene changes, and of getting furniture and props on and off the stage. Lighting throughout the show was tidy and effective, and sound quality was very good indeed, apart from a couple of slightly late cues.

Comedy, throughout the show, was well-accentuated, even by the smaller supporting roles.

Julianne McNamara presented clean, well-rehearsed choreography, with great energy from the younger choruses, and very good staging of the adult numbers. "Consider Yourself" was nicely varied and flowed smoothly from one group to the next. This isn't a great dance show, but the company did all that was required of them with precision and enthusiasm. With a confident, competent orchestra before her, Mary Rose McNally guided musicians and performers alike through a smooth and successful musical journey. I greatly admired how she pulled the orchestra along with her on the one occasion when the younger vocalists on stage got slightly ahead in their music. Harmonies were well realised and vocal quality was very good from the choruses. All in all, this was a very secure musical production.

The show is Oliver! by name, and the show-stealer was Oliver himself, after a wonderful performance from the 8 year old star of the future, Calum Mitchell. While he would certainly have won the audience over just because of his cuteness, he actually did it by being a dynamic little performer, full of good musical quality, a good sense of how to act and dance, and even a handling of comedy. Well done, young sir, on a really fabulous performance.

I'd normally be of the opinion that the Artful Dodger should be played by a confident kid of 12 or 13, but given that Oliver was only 8, I think that Fergal Flanagan was probably a great choice for the role. I'm certain that his experience was a great help to young Calum, as the two seemed to connect very well during the show. This was a nicely judged performance.

It was evident from his performance that Colin Williams relished the role of Fagin. He realised the comedy of his lyrics and delivered his songs with great conviction. His stature worked well beside the large and brooding figure of Bill Sykes, and he used this to give himself a weasel-like style of movement, always frantic and animated.

Brid Delaney immersed herself in the role of Nancy, and while her delivery of "As Long As He Needs Me" was emotional and beautifully performed, it was the vibrancy of her joyous, energy-filled first act performance that really illuminated her personality.

Prionnsias Loughnane was a menacing Sykes, prowling the stage like an angry bear, delivering "My Name" with almost casual insolence. Some of his body language during conversation was a tad weaker than his character demanded, but overall, he was a convincing menace. Andrew Walsh, despite an accent that wavered from London to Tipp and back a few times, gave great comedy to the role of Mr Bumble, and especially during his attempted seduction of Widow Corney during the "Scream" duet. He maintained his character well throughout the show, becoming a suitable wimp once he took the plunge to get married.

As Widow Corney, Siobhan Bowe initially fought valiantly to preserve her dignity, and progressed to becoming a hard- nosed, domineering wretch of a wife to Mr Bumble, but it was all achieved with a delightfully measured spirit of comedy, and a naturally relaxed stage presence. John Lynch had a good look and assumed stature for the role of Mr Sowerberry, and played the part with conviction, while Niamh O'Donnell seemed a little vocally subdued in the role of his busy-body wife, Mrs Sowerberry, especially during their duet. Their daughter Charlotte was effectively played with a hint of mischief by Charlene Duff, and Mark Delahunty gave a roguish element to the role of the bully, Noah Claypole.

Rory Chadwick was a convincing and gentlemanly Mr Brownlow, dignified yet severe when dealing with Bumble, and genuinely sympathetic to Oliver.

I'm not sure if it was a befuddled Tim Keane playing Dr Grimwig, or Tim Keane playing a befuddled Dr Grimwig, but either way, the tripping over the script didn't detract at all from the character, and earned him good laughter.

Maeve Conlon was a sympathetic Mrs Bedwin, and a crazy old crone as Old Sally.

The chorus made a more than worthy contribution to the production with good singing and plenty of enthusiasm in their routines. Some lovely solo voices were evident during "Who Will Buy". The children's choruses were lively, animated and well sung throughout. Nice work. Costuming was appropriate and effective. I loved the look of Fagin, and Sykes was appropriately slovenly and unwashed looking. These characters were also well made-up, and make-up generally was very good.

Overall, this was a tight and tidy production that highlighted the dedication and ability of a company who thrive on community spirit. Thank you so much for a great night in Roscrea.

Reading a beautiful tribute to the late John Donnelly in the show programme was an emotional, but also a lovely way to begin a night of great entertainment in Wexford, his spiritual home.

A million miles from the style and nature of last year's Evita was this year's production of the feminist struggle that is at the heart of "9 to 5". And yet, when it comes to production standards and dedication, the difference was minimal. Attention to detail would be a characteristic of a Vivian Coates production, and this offering of "9 to 5" was no exception. In what was a by-the-book approach, enhanced by a well-chosen set, a careful and considerate lighting plot, precision in the selection of costumes and well- realised characterisations, he presented a thoroughly balanced and precise show. If the show didn't exactly take my breath away, it's more down to a lack of depth in the material, rather than the performances, which were universally top-notch.

A very good set offered plenty of variety for the various office locations, and was very well furnished throughout. An efficient stage crew, led by Colin Murphy, ensured that the transitions from scene to scene were pretty much seamless. There was very good use of the harness to suspend Hart high above the ladies in the bedroom scene. The projections and dialogue of Dolly Parton were well timed with the music. Lighting was efficient, with a good emphasis on the key lights being sharp and focused so that no business was ever lost. There was good creation of atmosphere through good use of colours, with the dream sequences being particularly effective. Sound was constant and well balanced, with nice effects. As with other aspects of the show, there was nice attention to detail in the costuming, with good individuality in the leads. Opportunities to add a bit of glamour were well taken in the dream sequences and in the "One of the Boys" number. Colour coordination was good, with no costumes stealing the focus. Roz Keith was nicely severe in comparison to her co-workers. Hairstyles/wigs were well-worn and appropriate, as was make-up. This was a visually beautifully presented show.

Following the trend of the direction, Nicole McDonald's choreography was extremely tidy and well-rehearsed. With the benefit of a wonderfully spacious stage, there was room to manoeuvre around the office furniture without any traffic jams, resulting in good fluent movement. Numbers like the dream sequences and "One of The Boys" were inventive and slick, and there was good comedy attached to "Heart to Hart". It always pays dividends when a choreographer plays to the ability of their dancers, and in this production, Nicole did a perfectly measured job.

In the demanding role of Violet, Aileen Donohoe gave a wonderful all-round performance, capturing the frustration of the character in her acting, confident and competent with her comedy, and strong and assured in all her vocals. Her feminist speech at the denouement was delivered with passion and credibility.

Sharon Clancy got under the skin of Doralee, enjoying the style of the music and milking the comedy for all it was worth. She established a loving believable relationship with Dwayne, and having won them over, her friendship with the other girls was warm and delightfully comical. This was a beautifully balanced performance.

Maggs Jacob's rendition of "Get Out and Stay Out" highlighted her beautiful acting ability, and a note-worthy voice, in the role of Judy. This was a well thought out performance, moving from the fumbling, insecurity of a rejected wife to the wonderful comedy of an independent woman re-born.

George Lawlor struck the balance between misogynist and comedic arch-villain at just the right level, being nasty enough to despise, but silly enough to be laughed at, as Franklin Hart. It's a difficult enough role in which to earn any sympathy, but George handled it confidently and deserved both the boos and the cheers from the audience. His ""Here For You" was expertly delivered.

Elizabeth Rose-Browne had no shame whatsoever in the roll of Roz, lying spread eagle on a desk, flashing her knickers to the world. Up to that point, she had been the epitome of stern, humourless sobriety, with just a pinch of lust directed at her employer. This role was played with a great sense of fun, and beautifully performed.

Eric Hayes was a genuine and sincere Joe, combining wonderfully with Violet for the "Let Love Grow" duet. He was very believable as the wannabe toy-boy lover, and equally determined to achieve his objective, which he did with charm.

Dwayne is not a prominent role, but I very much admired that Stephen Byrne used his few opportunities to establish a sincere loving and supportive relationship with Doralee.

Similarly, Stephen Schokman, as Dick, only had a few opportunities to make himself a believable smug and conceited ex-husband, which he did very effectively. Marian O'Leary gave a staggering performance as office-lush, Margaret. It's a fine art to play a drunk without going over the top, and she really did keep it under control with a very good sense of comedy.

Jane Kent could maybe have played Missy with a slightly more vacant quality, as her gullibility seemed to disappear with the aggression of her final few lines, but I was still delighted to see her triumphant return to find true love with Roz.

Very good support came from Cillian Tobin as a credible teenage son, Josh, Sarah O'Leary as Maria, Antonia Close as Kathy and Pat Lawlor as Bob, while Fintan O'Leary made a strong impact as Company boss, Mr Tinsworthy.

There was very good vocal strength from the chorus, and precision to their movement throughout the show, whether dancing or going about their business in the offices.

This is a dedicated company who are consistent in presenting a wonderful standard of production and performance. Thank you sincerely for a most enjoyable 9 to 5.

Tralee Musical Society presented Jesus Christ Spectacular Superstar, with a technical and visual display that was nothing short of awesome. Director/ Choreographer, Oliver Hurley's focus was definitely on getting the look and atmosphere of this piece as close to perfection as possible. Technically, it was simply stunning, and one could feel the audience gasp at some of the serenely beautiful effects that were created by that perfect blend of projections and lighting. Every available piece of scenery had depth and dimension, moving from detailed stone-work to garden shrubbery, to thunder filled skies, to burning flames of passion. It was delightful to the senses, and the perfectly selected images intensified the atmosphere of every scene. Follow spots were very well used to make sure that soloists were properly illuminated, which left the lighting designer free to really go to town on mood creation. The various levels of the stage were also very well used to create attractive pictures, with placings and entrances and exits always beautifully structured and manoeuvred. Stage Manager, Des Hurley, kept everything moving smoothly, as pieces of the physical set came and went almost un-noticed. A couple of late sound cues, early on, were quickly forgotten, thanks to a very well-balanced system that allowed orchestra and vocalists to co-exist harmoniously. There were also extremely good sound effects throughout. Choreography was always precise and engaging, although there were occasions when I did feel that less might have been more, when stillness might have better reflected the mood of some scenes. Characterisation was strong throughout the show, even if, on occasions, there was a question mark over the vocal ranges of the actors in their given roles.

Musical Director, Áine Murray did a very good job of controlling both the volume and the quality of a fine orchestra, and of keeping the stage and the pit together. I was a tad surprised to hear some of the guitar solos played on keyboards with two fine guitarists in the pit, but the balance was always good, and the brass and woodwind made beautiful sounds, and there was a nice contribution made by the percussionist.

Vocally, Elaine Canning had done a great job in teaching harmonies and dynamics to her chorus, with the only frustration being that, on several occasions, the female voices tended to dominate.

There was a reassuring tone and texture to Jerry Lynch's voice in his comfort zone, but a tendency for his falsetto to sound rather more operatic than rock, but this was a strong performance of Jesus, with good emotion. The crucifixion scene was beautifully played.

Sean McElligott played Judas with great strength of character, nicely portraying the confused dilemma of loving Jesus and betraying him. For most of the performance, his vocals were strong and secure, but I suspect the strain of the week was telling on a few top notes that he cracked or fell away from.

The vocal performance of the night came from the velvety tones of Sharon Walsh in a warm and sincere interpretation of Mary Magdalene, believably adoring and respectful towards her inspiration. Very nicely played.

Mike Lynch had good poise and stature in the role of Pontius Pilate. His talk/ sing style suited the role, yet he had a good vocal ferocity when he belted out his eventual condemnation. He nicely portrayed Pilate's reluctance to persecute Jesus, which gives the character a level of humanity.

Tim Landers relished the opportunity to bring the only character of levity in the story to life, with a highly amusing rendition of Herod. I didn't much like his wig, but he wore a fetching little number that blended beautifully with his chorus dancers. A nicely played role and the songs were put-over effectively.

Tim Moran acted well, and despite looking physically imposing, and maintaining a good countenance, didn't quite have the sonorous bass tones to vocally capture the gravitas of Caiaphas.

Annas is normally sung with a high falsetto, but it worked well, coming down the octave to allow James Finnegan to give a strong vocal quality and confidence to the role.

Jonathan Lynch and Gary Murphy, as Peter and Simon, respectively, were strong and secure, both in their acting and their singing, giving good definition to their characters. Jonathan, along with Sharon, sang "Could We Start Again Please" with great emotion.

There was very good support from the other, uncredited, high priests, and the apostles worked well together.

Choral work was very good throughout the show, even if it often sounded very female dominated. The chorus added so much to the atmosphere of the show in their reactions and their movement. They were always graceful and precise.

The costumes for this production were beautifully produced and worn with style and panache. Colours were subtle, adding a hint of glamour to the outfits, and the costumes for "Herod's Song" were delightfully camp and perfectly suited to the routine. It was clever that Herod was able to peel off his traditional outer garment to blend in with the chorus. The High Priests Costumes were excellent. There was superb attention to detail in veils, head-dresses and hair-styles, especially the wigs, which looked very real. There were no issues with make-up. This really was a delightfully picturesque visual production.

Thank you to Tralee Musical Society for a thoroughly engaging production of Jesus Christ Superstar. It was a night to savour, and the display of technological genius will stay long in my memory.

Me and My Girl is a wonderful vehicle for a large scale musical society, offering excellent leading roles, an abundance of supporting roles, lots of choral work and plenty of fun for a dance troupe. The humour of the show works as well today as it did back in the day, and the musical score is a classic. Little wonder then that St Agnes' Choral Society found it the appropriate choice for the celebration of their 60th Anniversary production.

Laura Kerr took on the Director's mantle at short notice, and it's an immense achievement that she and the cast and production team managed to achieve such a wonderful standard of presentation. The many strands that weave together to produce the final product were fortunate to have someone so capable to draw them all together in time for opening night. Comedy was the order of the day, and it was served up in copious amounts, with the script being well delivered, and plenty of additional visual comedy, much of it harping back to a bygone era of traditional music hall sketches. These were beautifully presented.

Good work was done on establishing character among the principal roles, each defined by their own idiosyncrasies, although I did have reservations about Maria, the Duchess of Deane. Powerful performer though she was, I felt that she needed to be more demure and dignified to capitalise on the comedy that flows from the juxtaposition between herself and Bill. That aside, this was generally a very balanced and accomplished production. While the well-tuned, well-balanced orchestra were very good, under the baton of Wilson Shields, it was the chorus who musically stole the show, with abundant harmonies, strength of delivery and excellent diction. With the help of a fine line-up of pit singers, the mostly unison delivery of "Lambert Walk" was infused with fun and energy, but it was the opening of the show, and "An English Gentleman", "Men of Hareford" and "The Sun Has Got His Hat On" where the vocals were most delightful. This was excellent choral work, at the heart of a wonderfully musically secure presentation.

The contribution of the super talented choreographer, Ann Marie Morgan, was top notch. From the simple yet stunning effect of the step-ladder pyramid in "Men of Hareford", through the high-energy, ever-changing patterns of "The Sun Has Got His Hat On" to the sublime "Leaning on a Lamppost" ballet, the show was a choreographic treat, and performed beautifully throughout by a very talented dance ensemble. Principal dance numbers were treated with the same respect, playing to the abilities of the dancers, and always creative and fun.

There was very good attention to the technical demands of the show, with the set having a beautiful revolving centre piece for the interior and exterior of Hareford Hall. The insets for the pub, the kitchen and Sally's residence in London were less dramatic, but still well painted and appropriate. Stage Manager, Andy McKnight, and his team had no problems getting everything in place quickly and quietly, including a significant number of very good furniture props. The lighting plot for the show was top quality, full of atmosphere and well defined acting areas. The lighting of the Library scene was quite excellent. Sound was equally impressive with good balance and some lovely effects.

Everything was in order in the costume department, with elegance reigning at Hareford Hall, and a kind of tidy scruffiness to the Cockney characters. The Pearly King, Queen and Chorus looked excellent, and the staff of servants were always appropriately attired. There was good variety in the Ancestors and an excellent dancing suit of armour. Wigs and hairstyles were generally very good, and my only quibble with make-up was that Lady Battersby looked very young.

Bill Snibson is one of those roles that requires charm, romance, excellent physical comedy and an all-round ability to dominate proceeds from curtain up to curtain down, and in Kerry Rooney, St. Agnes found the perfect performer. His likeability was of the highest order, his timing was impeccable and as a song and dance man, he was tender of tone and fleet of foot. An excellent performance. If this was Aideen Fox's first principal role, I can't wait to see her in future productions, for as a novice, her Sally Smith was confidently portrayed and very nicely sung. She had a good awareness of comedy timing, and a natural stage presence. She could have been a little softer of tone during some of her more emotional scenes, but this is certainly a performer who has much more in store. Fiona Keegan had great stage presence as the Duchess of Deane, albeit steered in the wrong direction. Her stature as an actress and comedienne was ever apparent, and the pinnacle of her performance was a powerhouse vocal presentation of "Men of Hareford". There were nice moments of tenderness, too, in her relationship with Sir John.

There was a twinkle in the eye of Michael McDowell as he effortlessly portrayed the roguish old gentleman of Sir John. His pomposity was nicely tempered with a playful eye for the waiting staff, an appreciation of Bill's free spirit and a highly believable sympathetic nature towards Sally. His scenes with the Duchess were very nicely played.

Apart from the ease of costuming him throughout in a formal kilt, I'm not sure if there was much benefit in playing Parchester as a Scotsman, but Peter Burke sustained his accent very well, and performed "The Family Solicitor" with a great sense of the ridiculous. A wealth of experience was evident in his relaxed and easy manner.

Lorraine Jackson-Brown slithered around the stage as the provocative, money- hungry Lady Jacqueline. This was a strongly sensual and charmingly comical interpretation of the role, and her "Thinking of No-one But Me" was deliciously self- indulgent. Her vocals were always strong, and she proved a natural leader in many of the dances.

Gareth McGreevy started timidly, but grew in confidence to become a wonderfully cheesy upper-class twit in the comical role of Gerald. He led "The Sun Has Got His Hat On" with zeal, and used good visual comedy to portray his wimpish character. A remarkably fine cameo performance was given by Ditanya McKinty in the role of Mrs Brown, demonstrating excellent character and comedic ability.

Gerry McBrien made the most of his opportunities to earn audience laughter and approval in the supporting role of Sir Jasper Tring, and was in the good company of Jim McGuigan's convincingly hen-pecked Lord Battersby, and a delightfully bossy Lady Battersby, in which a fresh faced Michelle Harkin could have done with a tad more aging.

Kevin McReynolds as Charles, the butler, was like a cross between Jeeves and Lurch, delightfully sombre and sober, yet comical when required.

The minor roles in this show were abundant, and all played with good credibility, particularly Matthew Dempsey as Bob Barking, Mary Hughes as Mrs Worthington-Worthington and Jim McBride as a very amusing Constable. The contribution of the chorus to the show was excellent, particularly in the vocal department. Physically, they were consistently animated, and dance routines were delightful and precisely delivered. Might I also say how wonderful it was to see David Smyth making such a worthy contribution as a member of the Chorus. St Agnes' celebrated in style with this production. Sincere thanks to all for making my final show of the season such a wonderfully enjoyable one.

Celebrating their 10th anniversary SONG's 2016 production is that classic of Musicals Evita. Not only for famously putting Elaine Paige on the map but also for the movie version where Madonna and Banderas strutted their stuff in the classic tale of corruption, greed and death. The title role was played by Sinead O'Callaghan. A passionate display of suggestive carefree dance, and sung with wonderful tone and technique. Her signature solo "Don't Cry for me Argentina" was delivered most perfectly. Opposite Evita was Brendan Cleary (Peron). His singing was very good, he has good support of his voice and he sang with good phrasing. He got all the pathos at her death. Nik Parks (Che) sang with excellent diction and enunciated every word and syllable. Perhaps a specific accent should have been considered for the whole performance as his altered from Spanish and English continuously. Tom Maher (Magaldi) needed to be more positive in his singing, he was a famous singer but he never performed in that manner. Lisa Rose McMahon (Mistress) was suitably affronted when put out by Evita and then she sang with a wonderful melodic voice her only song "Another suitcase in another hall". Her tone was wonderful, her diction excellent and she performed the piece most splendidly. Musical Director Patrick Dunne used only a keyboard, percussion and guitar as live instruments. He chose to use backing tracks for the rest of the show and this simply did not work. The music is written for a live performance. At a live performance the music is played at a slightly different tempo to allow for the mood of the performance, or the audience or simply just the right atmosphere. It does not work when soloists have to sing so regimented to a backing track. Unfortunately also the backing tracks did not give the same volume or crescendos as an orchestra would have. The chorus were very well prepared and sang in a most committed style. The opening scene was superb and the children's chorus sang most poignantly. Choreography in the show was by a triumvirate of Teresa Dunne, Aoife Feeney and Tara Gill and what a marvellous set of dance numbers they prepared. Good rhythms with Spanish flair throughout. Direction by Rosemary Winkless and Theresa Dunne allowed chorus interaction with principals to be at a premium. There was a large cast who were all aware of their positions, particularly in the opening and closing scenes, which allowed smooth transition throughout. Set design had a raised balcony which was well used throughout by all the cast, and then a simple balcony design for the Mistress' eviction. Costumes for the females were most colourful and the men's army uniforms were neat and precise. The sound was a little hampered as the backing tracks were a little loud and occasionally the singer's initial entrances were lost. Lighting was very good in the indoor scenes, but I would have liked daytime to have been brighter.

Wilfie Pyper was in tip-top form when he put this production of Jekyll and Hyde together, selecting an excellent cast, presenting a beautifully visual show, filled with the menace and atmosphere required for telling this shocking tale. While there was so much to admire, I make no apologies for stating that the outstanding star of the show was the lighting. It was quite simply stunning, and did so much to enhance and invigorate the overall production.

The stage space and levels were nicely used, and the chorus were always directed to be an integral part of the story, both in their movements and their reactions. While the opening of the show was engaging enough, there was perhaps an opportunity missed to show the horrors of mental derangement by surrounding Jekyll's father with other tortured souls, but that's a minor point.

The murders of Hyde's victims were very well devised and presented, indeed, in Lucy's case, it was positively disturbing. There's no easy way to present the Confrontation where Jekyll and Hyde sings a duet, and while the switching from up-light to down-light was acceptable, this was possibly a scene where some special effects might have enhanced the number. However, these are minor issues, and didn't really diminish the excellent standard of the production. What did diminish it, more than it should have, was poor sound quality which, sadly, resulted in the orchestra almost overpowering some of the best songs in the show. It was such a pity because there was an excellent orchestra, under the very capable direction of Colin Scott. In "This is the Moment", Jekyll's crescendo was all but lost behind the accompaniment. I noted that the orchestra were mic'ed, so I can't attribute all the blame to the musicians, but it's so important that the MD and sound engineer work together to strike a balance. That said, when the singers were clearly audible, the vocal quality of the show was astoundingly good, which suggested meticulous rehearsal.

Timmy Bell did a very tidy job of manoeuvring a large chorus around the stage, creating good pictures and capturing the atmosphere of the various scenes. The "Bring on the Men" number could perhaps have been more adventurous, but in fairness, it has a lousy tempo, and is probably the most un- musical number in an otherwise wonderful score. The chorus/dancers seemed very well-prepared and performed their moment with a great sense of drama. Despite the problem with sound, Karl McGuckin did enough hard work throughout the show to demonstrate that he had the vocal power, range and quality to do justice to the extremely demanding role of Jekyll/Hyde. His rich baritone was as effective in his gentler moments as when he raged as Hyde. There were moments, particularly in the earlier scenes, when his acting seemed a bit stilted, but he did grow in stature as the story progressed.

Acting honours for the night went to Emma Martin as Lucy. As well as having a strong and beautiful voice, her demeanour and her body-language were always powerful and completely indicative of her circumstances. She can also move extremely well, making her a bit of a wonderful all-rounder.

Delightful, too, was a highly convincing Emma Carew, played by Alice Johnston. She was a believably devoted lover to Jekyll, yet feisty when required to put the snobs in their places, and her singing was absolutely beautiful. This was a well-balanced and most enjoyable performance.

Joff Manning, as well as possessing a quality vocal ability, had great presence and sincerity in the role of John Utterson, secure and confident in everything he did. Iain Mercer convincingly portrayed the frustration of being supportive of Jekyll, but frightened for his daughter's future, in the well-acted and securely sung role of Sir Danvers.

Darryl Bowden was suitably obnoxious as Simon Stride, Debbie West was a staid and delightfully sneering Lady Beaconsfield, Keith Pyper gave a real sense of hypocrisy to his Bishop of Basingstoke, and Hall Graham, Ian McMaster and David Magowan confidently completed the pompous and patronising Board of Governors, as Sir Archibald, Lord Savage and General Glossop.

Martin Bannon was believably concerned for the welfare of Jekyll, and equally humble as his man-servant, Poole.

Mark Leeman was just about as creepy as a Spider should be, and perhaps could have been more prominent in the Red Rat scene.

Good support came from Sinead Coll, as a confident Nellie, Ken Hamilton as a Red Rat customer and, I believe, as Jekyll's disturbed father, David Mehaffey as a rather believable Vicar, and Ciaran Conlon as the reluctant Apothecary.

The chorus acting and reacting was of a very high standard, not to mention their well-polished movement and their strong vocal contribution to the overall show. As stated already, the lighting for this production was nothing short of superb, and precise enough to pick out each member of the Board of Governors individually as they were introduced. Colours, tones, atmospheres and timing were all top notch. The set was excellent, with its staircases and upper levels, the insets that appeared almost invisibly through the archways, and the abstract neutral flats which were perfect for creating wonderful lighting atmospheres. Furniture and props were excellent, with the Bunsen burner effects making a great impact, and everything moved in and out of place like well-oiled pieces of machinery, thanks to Stage Manager, Marie Cusack, and a disciplined team. Apart from afore- mentioned problematic issue of balance, there were several occasions when mic volume on some of the principals faded up and down, causing a distraction. I'm hopeful that this will have been remedied quickly for the greater enjoyment of the audiences, and perhaps it was just a case of first night teething problems.

The show was very nicely costumed throughout, with the exception of a far too risqué first outfit on Lucy. Her fellow brothel sisters were perfectly dressed. All other principal costumes quickly established their characters. Wigs were excellent throughout, and the make-up team did a very good job.

Thank you to Wilfie, Colin, Timothy and an excellent cast for such an enjoyable and memorable night of drama and music in the beautiful Opera House.

Legally Blonde as a perfect vehicle for a company like Carrick-on-Suir who have great strength in depth, offering, as it does an extensive list of character roles, plenty of work for the chorus and technical requires that can challenge and inspire a good technical team. Unlike some modern musicals, it is also testing to musicians and singers alike, filled with good and varied harmonies. On that score, (pardon the pun), this production was in the very safe hands of Musical Director, Fergal Carroll, who kept a tight rein on an excellent orchestra, always conscious of keeping a good balance between the pit and the stage. Tempi were perfect, with good attack of the upbeat numbers and equally good dynamics in the more melodious sections of the music. The equally proficient Chorus Master, Eamon O'Malley, had his singers were well-drilled and they sang with great harmony and confidence. Endings were precise, and diction was perfect.

Director, Liam Butler, offered us a well- directed piece, with great attention given to characterization, and maintaining a good pace throughout the show. The concept of the set was excellent, combining projections with sliding panels, even if the execution raised several problems, as outlined below, but transitions from one scene to another were smooth and effective. Chorus were well worked into the production, and played 'characters' rather than just appearing as a back-up mob.

Patricia Woods injected so much energy into her routines, and plenty of variety, and she was fortunate to have a team of dancers who could execute her moves with good precision. I've become used to seeing this show choreographed in hip-hop style, but the more tradition show-dance style employed by Patricia was classy and very entertaining, and a special mention has to go to a superbly effective "What You Want", which was a show-stopper. The skipping routine for "Whipped into Shape" was very good, even allowing for a couple of tangled ropes.

In the extremely demanding role of Elle Woods, Louise Mulcahy displayed abundant energy, excellent comedy and strong vocal delivery. There was great sincerity in her scenes with Emmet, and a convincing bond of friendship developed with Paulette.

Ray Nolan was a very believable and sincere Mr Nice-guy in the role of Emmet Forest, and it seemed perfectly feasible that Elle should fall for his warmth of personality, but he also put over the angst of his "Chip on my Should" with great conviction.

Keith Greene's physical presence aided considerably in giving strength and superiority to his portrayal of Callahan. He was a convincing boss, and equally believable as a predator. "Blood in the Water" was confidently performed.

Emmet Donlan nailed the smug, frat boy narcissism of Warner, full of smarm/charm in his opening scene, and then sinking to an amazing depth of shallowness. He handled his comedic lines, of which there are many, with a confident ease, and his vocal quality was evident in "Time To Get Serious".

The standard of delivery, the confidence, the stage presence, the vocal expertise and the outstanding comedy of Irene Malone, made her performance as Paulette quite simply stunning!

Marie Kelly skipped and bounced and gyrated with skill and energy, even while she sang the role of fitness guru, Brooke Wyndham, although it was hard to believe that she had attended Delta Nu some time before Elle, such was her youthful appearance. Regardless of that, she was feisty and secure in her portrayal.

Sandra Power was delightfully condescending as Vivienne Kensington in her early scenes, positively bitchy on occasions, and then completely convincing in transformation to the sincere and supportive friend of the final scenes. Vocally, she got the Legally Blonde Remix off to a great start.

Siobhan McCarthy made the most of her opportunities to impress as Enid Hoops, sensibly not going over the top with a stereotypical 'butch' lesbian portrayal. Her moments of comedy were well pointed, and her vocals were always secure.

Ashley Cooke as Serena, Siobhán Grace- Regan as Margot and Tarryn Attlee as Pilar performed very well as a team, but also managed to have good individuality. All three had impressive voices and a great ability to move with grace and energy. Bobby Landers loved himself in the role of Kyle, strutting his stuff in his shorts and charming the ladies, which is just as it should have been. This was very nicely played comedy.

Caolán Deehy-Power made an impression as Aaron Schultz, but was in danger of stealing the show as the ludicrous Carlos. Extremely funny.

Chris Hanlon might have offended the PC brigade by 'darkening' up to play turban- clad Sundeep Padamadan, but I enjoyed it, as much as I enjoyed his rapping Grandmaster Chad. Good work.

Kane Molloy was successful in leaving a question mark over his sexuality in the role of Nikos, a role that is often over-played, but he came convincingly out of the closet at the end of the courtroom scene.

Sadly, Penny had lost her voice in the role of Bruiser, but still managed to make herself understood when relating the whereabouts of Elle. That's professionalism!

Chuck, as Rufus, played to the audience a lot in a deliberate attempt to steal the show. He succeeded. What a star!

Padraig Sheehan, Fergus Power and Seamus Power had their moments in the limelight, which they enjoyed with comfort and reliability. Good support came from Jennifer Williams as Kate, Siobhan Whelan as Whitney, and a plethora of smaller cameo/chorus roles. Jenny Hogan doubled nicely as Winthrop and the Judge, and Fiona Hennessy fitted well into her various roles. Deckie Smith-Robinson didn't mind making himself look decidedly undesirable for the role of Dewey, and Sheridan Brady was a convincing Chutney.

The chorus, throughout the show, were precise and energetic both vocally and in their routines.

While much of the show was visually dynamic, there were too numerous occasions when principals were not clearly lit, or drifted from one hot-spot to another through patches of darkness. Many of the projections were vivid and super-effective, until they became bathed in general lighting, causing them to fade, almost to invisibility on occasions. Side lighting, when it was on-point, created some beautifully atmospheric effects, but frequently it was insufficient to highlight all of the action. The projections themselves were well selected and appropriate to each scene. Harvard looked austere, the department store had an authentic feel, and the gardens of Harvard were beautiful. The rising podium centre stage was a great mechanical piece, and very well used. The transitions from one projection to another were also very effective, as was the list of interns pinned to the wall and then enlarged. Full credit goes to stage manager, Michael O'Hara, for the smooth movement of sliding screens and the management of the large number of well- sourced props, which was all done very efficiently. There were no problems with sound quality or execution throughout the show.

Costumes were of a very good standard, uniformly appropriate to the action, and allowing for individuality of the various characters. Elle's early quick change was the fastest I've ever seen it performed, and she always looked perfect. A step above the average was the visual impact of the "What You Want" routine, which was a show-stopper. Wigs and hairstyles were very good and make-up very natural. It was a pleasant experience to see the Strand Theatre foyer beautifully dressed, and an even more pleasant experience to witness such an invigorating production of Legally Blonde. Thank you kindly for another wonderful night.

It takes a Director with an enlarged funny- bone, and a great deal of outrageous imagination to fully do justice to the high- spirited nonsense that is "The Addams Family", and on this occasion, the Director, Wilfie Pyper, approached this show with just the right attitude, playing it for maximum comedic impact that was evident in every aspect of the production. Even the scenery had a quirky cartoon quality to it. Costumes were well selected, and the chorus were directed to never look normal. Everything was exaggerated and larger than life…death… whatever! The levels of the stage were well used, and there was no fussiness about scene changes. Good lighting allowed cameo scenes to require only a tight pool of light and a suitable prop. The pace of the show was perfect, quick fire comedy, but with a principal line up who were well instructed in pausing for comedic effect and for audience reaction. Not a line was lost. An important detail of this show is that the players really looked like they were loving every moment of the madness. With the exception of a few moments of lighting issues right at the start of the show, the piece was also technically delicious. From star clothes to seemingly floating lanterns, to a stairway lined with candelabra, from tight pools of light creating well defined performance areas within the main set, to excellent pitch darkness for the "flying" of Fester, this was a very well plotted show. Doubtless, stage manager, Patrick Freeman, appreciated a well designed set that required minimum fuss, but the few moving pieces that were evident, were quietly and efficiently rolled into place. Props, throughout, were very well sourced. Sound quality was good enough for me to be able to say that I never had to think about it. Balance was perfect, cueing accurate, and effects well placed and achieved.

Musical Director, Colin Scott, had the benefit of a highly proficient 13 piece orchestra at his fingertips, including an excellent percussionist, and together they were responsible for the top quality sounds that emanated from the orchestra pit. They were accurate and balanced, and never overpowered the on-stage performers. A very tuneful and disciplined chorus enhanced every scene in which they appeared, hitting the high notes even when engaged in much exaggerated physical movement. And with an extremely strong cast of vocally capable principals, the entire musical performance was a delight to the ears.

Timmy Bell gave great variety to his choreography, and obviously a good amount of disciplined rehearsal time. He captured the craziness of the zombie chorus, with "Thriller-esque" eeriness, without ever stealing directly from the source. General movement was as well prepared as the bigger dances, and comical and exciting pictures were achieved. A very good piece of work all round.

Brian Trainor, in the role of Gomez, looked completely relaxed and in control of the Opera House stage, with a display of superb comedic timing. He also managed to melt the hearts of the audience with a sincere and emotional rendition of "Happy Sad", which served to highlight the breadth of his talents.

Kerry Cooper had the perfect look, demeanour and abilities to make the most of the role of Morticia. Her performance peaked with a delightfully sultry and sinister rendition of "Death is Just Around The Corner".

Eric Millar, as Uncle Fester, really enjoyed "playing" to, and with, the audience, making the most of his script, and the various topical ad libs, all of which he delivered with panache. He even proved to be able to "fly" with remarkable ability. Emma Martin was as sweet as she was scary in the role of Wednesday. Her strong sadistic streak gave way to mellow moments of cuteness as she discovered love, but it was as the angst-ridden teenager that she made the strongest impact. And what a great "pop" voice she displayed. Perfect for the role.

Ben McCambley, as Pugsley, proved himself to be a star of the future, having already grasped the rudiments of comedy timing and mimicry. He is also blessed with a very capable voice. This was a very nicely played role.

Shirley Adair may have been on leave from an asylum to play the role of Grandma, such was the authenticity of this crazy character. She was visually perfect, and made the most of her opportunities to be outrageous.

Keith Pyper was a convincing Lurch, articulate in his grunting, and fleet-of- foot in his movement. While his finale solo revealed a fine quality tenor, I think a resonant bass voice might have suited the character better, but that is not to diminish an otherwise very good performance. When you combine perfect line delivery, superb body language, hilarious facial expression and a willingness to sacrifice one's dignity to truly capture the ridiculousness of a character, you get Laura Kerr, playing the role of Alice Beineke. Enough said.

Samuel Moore proved as capable of recreating the craziness of his youthful past as he was of playing the stuffed- shirt, middle-life crisis spoilsport of Mal Beineke. A thoroughly good performer with a fine voice.

Josh Kelso was very believable in making Lucas Beineke as much in love with Wednesday as he was scared of her. He also made the most of his vocal opportunities, with "Crazier Than You" being a highlight.

Within the Chorus were many fine individual performers and voices, but as a unit, they functioned superbly. The "Addams Family" chorus contribution is largely as a visual support to the Halloween-esque nature of the show, but in this production, their vocal quality was quite exceptional, not to forget that they moved and danced with energy and precision. Very good work.

Costumes, provided by Utopia, Scotland, were good quality and there was great variety in the chorus outfits. They were also very well worn, which is not always the case. No-one looked ill-fitted or uncomfortable. There was superb attention to detail in wigs and make-up, ranging from the natural to the surreal. Every aspect of this production implied that in each department, the membership strove to achieve as professional a standard as possible, and on this occasion, the effort paid off. Thank you kindly for the silliest, spookiest entertainment I could have wished for so close to Halloween.

As Donegal is one of the most beautiful places on Earth, I was delighted to hear that I would be travelling northwest for Donegal Youth Musical Theatre's first production: The Phantom of the Opera. And what an amazing start for this very exciting group it was. Making sure we had enough time to pop around Glenveagh National Park and take a spin out to Mount Errigal, it was time to go to An Grianán Theatre in Letterkenny - a place that feels large and open, yet intimate at the same time. We were greeted in the theatre with the same warm welcome that we received in every establishment in Letterkenny. The people are unbelievably friendly there. Classical music filled the auditorium, setting the tone nicely. We were fooled into thinking that back-lit gauze was the front curtain, making the auction scene appear instantly before our eyes. Crimson lighting behind this gauze made the auction scene look very old-school, allowing for the stage to burst into colour and life as the chandelier rose.

The duo of André and Firmin, re-imagined as a married couple, was played very well by Colm McGroarty and Aoife Breslin. Madame Firmin hen-pecked, badgered or seduced her husband when necessary and, with great chemistry from these two, the whole thing worked very well. It was also nice to hear their numbers sung as male/female.

Siobhán McParland and Conor McAllister played the opera stars Carlotta and Piangi respectively. They swept in and out with the appropriate amount of diva behaviour and managed their vocals well. Carlotta's frog-like singing and Piangi's delivery of the line 'amateurs!' were both very funny. Anna Gallagher was excellent as Madame Giry. With stiff body language and stern facial expressions, she captured her role as disciplinarian and bidder to the Phantom with aplomb. Her singing was great and it was no surprise that she was understudy to Christine. I look forward to seeing more from this performer.

Madame Giry's daughter, Meg, was played by Rachel Reid and boy was I shocked to learn that this performer was only twelve years old. She captured her friendship with Christine very well, sang beautifully and had an intense presence in the final moment of the show that I would normally associate with a more mature actor. Well done.

Aodhán Gavigan was very sweet as Christine's old friend turned lover. He was the perfect foil to the complexity and darkness of the character of the Phantom. He sang 'All I Ask of You' very well and he played the final scenes of the show with great passion.

And now, we come to Niamh Long as Christine. She was stunning. The whole emotional journey Christine must go through, from nervous ingénue to captive to lover to fighter to forgiver was perfectly measured throughout. Her vocals, in parts, were as good as any Christine you would find in the West End, yet she never forgot to act through the songs.

Equally as stunning was Robert Kelly as the Phantom. His booming voice filled the auditorium, before we even saw him, and it was clear that we were in competent hands from the get-go. His bass-notes were particularly gorgeous. His 'Music of the Night' was brilliant, both vocally and dramatically. His anger and despair as Christine removed his mask was spot-on. He shook with rage and grief in the final moments of Act One as he declared 'I gave you my music…". He was the perfect baddie in 'Why So Silent' and the graveyard scene and his whole spectrum of emotions portrayed by him in the final sequence of the show brought wide- spread sniffling from the audience. I can't wait to see what he does next.

Set and costume design were both by Sinéad O'Donnell Carey, and this meant that the visual aspect of almost all of the scenes was pulled together very well. Props, hair and make-up were all to a high standard throughout also. For the most part, the show was visually stunning. Lighting design by Paul Kelly punctuated the more famous moments, such as the change from 'Masquerade' into 'Why So Silent'. Sound design by Vinny Osborne was excellent overall. The balance between the band and performers was perfect and the band swelled perfectly during those famous instrumental moments, such as the beginning of 'The Phantom of the Opera' number. Clever surround sound effects made it sound as though voices were coming from different parts of the auditorium.

There were, unfortunately, a couple of shaky scene changes but once the scenes started, we were back on track with a great show. It is no easy feat to change these set pieces while the performers are still singing and travelling. Unfortunately, a lot of tech rehearsal is required for such a big job. Those changes that could happen behind the scenes involved large set pieces and were more successful.

Choreography, by Amy Jordan, was very suited to the group. The ballet sequences were great and executed competently by the dancers. The Masquerade Ball had lots of different sequences happening around the stage at the same time, making it a feast for the eyes.

Musical Direction was provided by Herta Kelly. It was a tough job to get the balance right in the choral pieces when the females so heavily outweighed the males. The leads were very well prepared, however. The front-line numbers such as 'Prima Donna' (which is a nightmare to learn) and 'Masquerade' were excellent and it was clear a lot of work and rehearsal went into these. Conductor on the night, Daniel Dunne, kept everything steady in the pit. A helpful hand was provided by the piano if a performer got a little lost and the scene changes were handled as well as they could have been.

This was all possible thanks to one- man; Séimí Campbell. He assembled an excellent cast and a super line-up of behind-the-scenes professionals and managed to stage one of the most famous musicals in the world with style (and in three weeks!). The emotional journeys of the characters in the show were spot on. Props, costumes and set pieces were mostly fabulous and no doubt Séimí contributed to all these successful elements of this show. From performances to design, he should be very proud of himself for making the whole thing happen. This man is very talented and one to watch. It is also very exciting to think what the newly-founded Donegal Youth Musical Theatre might do next.

A very useful marque had been attached to the side of the Dr Duggan Hall, Corofin, to accommodate audience on arrival and for refreshments during the interval of their production of Guys and Dolls. This was a lovely idea, and indicative of the community spirit that was evident throughout the evening. Front of house staff were friendly and most welcoming. Director, Ronan Lardner, a very capable and much recognised performer, especially of comedy, presented a show that moved from start to finish with an acceptable pace, plenty of high points and a great sense of fun and enjoyment. When the Director is also performing in their show, it's always a good idea to appoint an assistant director, to keep an eye on those scenes in which the director is involved. On this occasion, it was often the scenes involving Sky where the pace was a little rushed. There were also one or two supporting characters who needed to do a little more script revision before taking to the stage. However, a front line that was good on vocal quality and extremely capable of playing comedy was the backbone of this Corofin production. Sonja Stevens, as Sarah Brown, captured the nervous man-wary character of the Mission doll, and played her role with great conviction. With more experience under her belt, the acting ability and vocal quality which are already apparent, will develop and become fine assets to her performances.

Ronan Lardner played Sky Masterson with confidence and a fine vocal delivery, especially in "Luck Be A Lady". His dialogue seemed a bit rushed, particularly in the romantic scenes, which made him appear a little abrupt in his efforts to charm and seduce Sarah.

Emily Lohan, in the role of Miss Adelaide, oozed personality, both verbally and in her wonderful facial expressions. Her comedy delivery was excellent and her vocal quality was quite exceptional. While I felt she could have been stretched more in her musical numbers, this in no way detracted from a top notch performance.

There was a hint of a nervous Yogi Bear about Niall Heaney's interpretation of Nathan Detroit, which suited the part very nicely. His comedy was consistently well- pointed and his singing was relaxed and effective. "Sue Me" was a great number, with very good rapport between himself and Adelaide.

David Alexander brought a strong vocal quality to the role of Nicely-Nicely Johnson, which was best demonstrated in an impressive "Sit Down, You're Rockin' The Boat". He maintained a secure character throughout the show.

Michael Cooney was competent and confident in the role of Benny Southstreet, but needs to be careful not to drop his voice at the end of sentences. His singing was good, and his partnership with Nicely- Nicely worked well.

Unaided by an awful costume, Gerry Curley gave a colloquial warmth to the role of Arvide Abernathy, gentle in his dealings with Sarah, and sincere in his performance of "More I Cannot Wish You".

There was an air of confidence and very good stage presence about Olibhia Donnelly in the role of General Cartwright. With limited opportunities, she established her character and her comedic ability. Michael Hurley displayed a wealth of experience as an effective, frustrated Lt Brannigan, with a work-weary and ready for retirement attitude.

Feargal MacMeanmain was insecure with his lines, which diluted the potential that he occasionally displayed in his interpretation of Harry the Horse.

Nathan Mannion had the stature and the dead-pan expression for the role of Big Jule, but possibly more could have been made of his delivery of some very funny lines.

Good support came from Cian Forde as a very secure Rusty Charlie, Thomas Hynes as Angie the Ox, Karina Harte as Agatha, and Jade Costello as Hot-Box dancer, Mimi.

The Hot-Box dancers were at their best during "Take Back Your Mink", but also sang "Bushel and a Peck" convincingly. The members of the Mission Band did all that was asked of them, and the chorus, though thin in number, gave spirited support to the line-up.

Jay Molyneux's strongest contributions came through the choreography "Luck Be A Lady", which made good use of a very small male chorus, and "Take Back Your Mink" with its fun and raunchy style. While the opening of the show rarely stopped moving, the movement didn't really seem to relate to the changes of rhythm and tempo in the music. Similarly, the Havana scene started well, and then seemed to become rather random in design. With limited numbers, it was probably a good idea to cut the Crapshooters ballet. The black-light, white-tights idea for "Bushel and a Peck" was novel, but would have been stronger with a more energetic supporting routine.

Musical Director, Shane Farrell, led a tidy band from the keyboards, and kept a good eye on the on-stage performers, bringing them in and cutting them off with efficiency. Given the very small chorus, he also managed to create some good harmony work, most evident in "Sit Down, You're Rockin' The Boat". He was also blessed with a vocally secure principal line-up. I very much appreciated that Shane "followed" his principals beautifully, particularly in their comedy numbers, allowing dramatic and comedic pauses and crescendos. Nice work.

I know that this company, like many others, work on a shoestring budget, but in opting for a neutral set, there did need to be a bit more attention to detail and visual impact. Reversible or revolving flats are always a good and accessible option, and perhaps more attention to the artwork would have made a significant difference to atmosphere of the various scenes. The projections on the back wall were a nice idea, but the images used weren't very strong. The lighting designer made a good effort to keep the light off the projected images, but on such a small stage, it was not always possible, and with only black curtains to light, creating atmospheres wasn't easy, but at least everyone and everything could be clearly seen. After a couple of hiccups in scene one, the sound quality was good, with a level balance and efficient cueing. The stage crew, under Padraig Neenan and Keith Fleming, were efficient with the movement of props and set pieces, if a tad leisurely.

While most of the costumes in the production were acceptable, there were a few chorus outfits that were too modern, and a few principal costumes that just didn't look right, particularly Arvide's Mission uniform, and Sky's finale costume. Corofin is an exciting new company, full of energy and good intentions, and the show, as presented, was a fun experience, and as mentioned above, provided a good standard of entertainment to an enthusiastic audience. I have no doubt that the company will continue to grow and prosper. Thank you for a most pleasant and enjoyable evening.

Here's my irritation about Hot Mikado. It's billed as a musical by David H. Bell and Rob Bowman, based on Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado. Well that simply isn't true. It's a musical by Gilbert and Sullivan, and played around with by Bell and Bowman, and when they couldn't think of anything to do to modify a section, they basically left it as it was, including virtually the entire script, which is what makes it so delightfully funny. Hot Mikado, which is a brilliant modification of The Mikado, makes the show slightly more relevant to a new generation, but perhaps it's the writer in me that insists that Gilbert and Sullivan deserve top credits! Rant over.

Director, Barry Kavanagh, took a no nonsense approach to this production, and rather than robbing it of originality, he enhanced the show by keeping it clean, tidy and traditional. There is a tendency to over-play pastiche, and by avoiding that temptation, the show is allowed to grow and blossom naturally. Strength and security came from a strong line up of principals who clearly enjoyed their roles, and from tidy and consistent chorus work. The set, making life easy for Stage Manager Petrona Devine and her team, consisted of plain Japanese screens, some of which opened or moved aside to allow entrances. It was simplicity itself, enhanced by an extremely effective lighting plot which changed the appearance of the screens with varied colours and tones, allowing for good changes of atmosphere.  Using the centre aisle for entrances also worked effectively.  Costumes were well selected, and contributed strongly to the look of the show. Hairstyles/wigs and make-up were all appropriate and in keeping with the clean and precise production values. A few moments of Musical Director Sarah Lynch Barrett on screen, confirmed that, even when out of sight of the audience, she effervesces in front of her orchestra, inspiring them to give their all to their performance. On this occasion, despite a few split notes in the brass section, they took her lead and played with strong tempi and spirit. As Chorus Mistress, she had put a lot of work into the vocals, with the women displaying good harmonies and diction, while the men suffering somewhat from lack of numbers. There were a few insecurities at the start of "Gentlemen of Japan" which were quickly resolved, and a couple of nervous moments during the Madrigal. Overall, however, the chorus performed with vocal confidence and great energy.

Choreographer, Sinead Lightley, created fine routines that were clean and precise without being beyond the capabilities of her chorus and dancers. There was plenty of variety and good stage pictures, and when the opportunity arose, the more adventurous hoofers were given their moment to shine, most notably during the Mikado song, which was a very nifty tap routine. The result was a relaxed and confident display from the chorus throughout.

The strength of Adam McGealy's performance in the role of Nanki Poo lay in a rich and melodic tenor voice, with a quality falsetto. His solos were beautifully sung and his kissing duet with Yum Yum was delightful. He did, however have a tendency to rush his dialogue and his reactions, which resulted in many of his lines being difficult to understand.

Niamh Kavanagh gave an articulate, charming and witty performance as Yum Yum, with a crystal clear vocal quality, which peaked during "The Sun And I". Here is an actress who uses her face as precisely as her voice to put across her emotions with wonderful effect.

Gary Finegan lit up the stage in an extremely funny portrayal of Koko, combining great physical comedy and perfect execution of his script. He has that natural ability to play an audience and to make every line and gesture count. Niamh Carroll dominated the stage in the role of Katisha. Perfectly costumed, and with severe make-up, she commanded attention, delivering her lines with comedic venom, and delivering her songs with a powerful tone and texture. "Alone and Yet Alive" was excellent.

Ciaran Canavan, physically towering above everyone on stage, was brilliantly cast as Pooh Bah. His different voices for his "Lord High" character list were hilarious, and he used his stature perfectly to his advantage throughout the show. Tracy Leonard played Pitti Sing with great caricature and mischief, always alive and animated on the stage. She led the "Going to Marry Yum Yum" number with vocal strength and authority. She has a very expressive face and a great sense of comic timing.

Paraic Kelly bounced into Act Two with confidence and charm, looking rather dapper as the Mikado. He tapped a little, sang a little and kept delightfully cheery as he sentenced Koko and his accomplices to death. A lovely performance from a talented all-rounder.

Jennifer Browne, as Peep Bo, had a radiant smile and bundles of energy, as she completed the three little maids line-up. Apart from a few tentative bars of music, she made a good job of providing the alto line, and stayed in character very well throughout the show.

There was a confidence about the acting of Brian Magennis, in the role of Pish Tush, that seemed to drain from him when he was singing. He was not lacking in musicality, only in confidence, which I'm quite sure can be developed.

Several members of the chorus had lines of dialogue, all of which were delivered with clarity and a sense of fun. The choral singing was impressive throughout, if a little unbalanced due to the small number of men. Physically, the chorus always looked enthusiastic and engaged in their performance.

This beautifully relaxed and enjoyable production put me in mind of sitting in your most comfortable chair, wearing your cosy slippers and pyjamas, sipping hot chocolate from your favourite mug, and listening to your favourite music. It was a "comfort" production, and my thanks go to the cast and production team for such a warm and relaxing night of musical theatre.

society_raw: North East Musical and Dramatic Society
review_text:
Rock of Ages is a riot of a show. While it is a juke box musical, the writers were not tied to any particular artist, meaning that there was a super selection of songs to choose from. It feels like an original score, yet has such familiarity that the audience cannot help but want to sing along. This show is for adults only, and that premise was worked to the extreme by director Jordan Walsh, making this production not for the faint-hearted. It was clear from the get-go that the audience, some of whom were in fancy dress, were here to enjoy themselves. As the evening went on, the crowd grew more and more ecstatic by they saw on stage until they were leaping out of their seats for the final number. Screams of laughter filled the theatre over the evening until tears of pride flowed from those behind the scenes. Here is why… Jordan Walsh is the head of Belfast Music and Drama Society. There is no doubt that the overall success of this production is thanks (or partly thanks) to him. He teased the comedy out this piece by peppering lots of filth throughout the show, ably provided by narrator/ringmaster Lonny, played with great energy by Matthew Campbell. A stand-out piece of direction was when Drew ran for the midnight train and various chorus couples formed a path of his memories with Sherrie.

The stage was mostly made up of an open stand-alone set, not too different to any other Rock of Ages set I have seen. There was a very good truck that pulled out from the set-wall to create a bathroom and this was magically transformed in Justice's office later in the show. A staircase led up to an upstairs office and wrapped around to make a balcony. All this space was well used to block the show. Costumes, hair and make-up were mostly likely a team effort and looked suitably 80s.

The positioning of the band, deep inside the set, meant that the connection between MD Wilson Shields and the cast was challenging. There were times when the actors were waiting on the music to continue with their performance, suggesting that the timing of underscored dialogue etc. was not as tight as we would have liked. The cast, however, appeared to be very comfortable with their singing so good preparation was evident there. When choreography, by Alex McFarlane, captured the essence of a number and/ or was framed by a sense of story-telling, it was very good. All dancers seemed well rehearsed and execution of the choreography was on point.

Lighting by Sandy McAllister highlighted the action well. There were some impressive floodlights used during some of the more rockin' moments, but caution is advised in how often they are used, as they can become a little uncomfortable. There were some issues with balance with sound by Jamie McAllister, something that was most likely rectified as the run continued.

In the part of Sherrie, we had a wonderful leading lady by the name of Karen Hawthorne. She is a skilled actress who cleverly structured her characterisation so that she presented in the beginning to be too big for a small-town life. She was ultimately humbled and grounded by her professional unhappiness and her love for Drew. Karen has a whopper of a voice and coupled it with such emotion that her songs sounded as though they were part of an original musical score. She was awesome.

Her leading man was played by Harry Lambert. He captured the essence of the wannabe singer/songwriter Drew who sometimes lacks confidence, sometimes like to goof around and has so much music inside of him that it has to burst out of him. He knew exactly when to play for laughs, exactly when to milk the audience's hysteria and exactly when to bring some honesty and pathos to his scenes. Well done.

Master of ceremonies Lonny was played with great showmanship by Matthew Campbell. He knew how the work the audience and there were no risqué lengths to which he would not go to elicit shrieks of laughter from the crowd. He gave enormous energy and commitment to this part and delivered it with the exact competence and confidence needed for this role.

Niall McClean was perfect as the clapped- out aging rock 'n' roller Dennis. He speaking voice, physicality and singing were perfectly in character. Along with Matthew Campbell, the brought the house down with 'Can't Fight This Feeling.

Seán Harkin as Stacee Jaxx was brilliant. He has the most amazing look for this character and is on par with Tom Cruise from the awful movie version. He has the perfect singing voice for this role. His characterisation was never predictable as he presented all sorts of sides to this character. At times, he was supercool and amorous, yet he was clever enough to show a few camped-up scaredy-cat moments also. Seán gave a scene-stealing rounded performance in a role that could have been dismissed as one-dimensional. Hertz, the German father of Franz, was played very well by Simon Pyper. He had a very good accent. He captured the soul- destroying dominance over his son in the initial scenes, yet showed great range by changing to a softer and more vulnerable man in the later scenes.

Ruairí McAlinden had the audience in complete hysterics as Hertz's son Franz. He showed a good sense of physical comedy in how he hopped/walked/ran/ minced about the stage. For me, the character choices were too over-the- top and I was not convinced that the vulnerability of Franz in the earlier scenes was captured. It is difficult to feel for Franz if he appears too comfortable in his own fabulous skin from the get go. Ruairí's Franz was a wonderfully happy character, so his rise to self-empowerment was not as noticeable. Somebody somewhere is probably saying that I need to lighten up and learn to have a laugh. Still, this moody so 'n' so thinks that there is a journey that Franz can take that should not be missed. No doubt the audience who whooped and hollered for Ruairí McAlinden disagree with me. He gave them such a brilliant night's entertainment and I cannot fault this man's ability to get a laugh.

Sarah MacFarlane was suitably uptight as Regina. She knocked her musical moments out of the park. She showed good acting range by bringing one or two serious moments to the overall madness of her part. I loved her scene when she gave it to Hertz over his lack of acceptance of his son. It was believable and moving, which is not what you might expect from a slightly bonkers character in a musical comedy.

Oprah Devitt understands something about acting: that a character's job is to change the minds of others. She showed such authority and persuasiveness as she lured the down-on-her-luck Sherrie into a strip club job. She captured the idea that Justice has been around the block, seen it all and doesn't allow herself to be taken for a fool.

Tony Owens was the perfect sleazy opportunistic manager Ja Keith. Waitress 1, a role split between two actresses it appears, showed off a belter of a voice. Jordan Humphries, who played Constance, has very good presence. I was sorry her part was not bigger. Wendy Pyper doubled up as Sherrie's Mum and the Mayor and did a great job. Both she and Stephen McQuillan sang well as Sherrie's parents.

So it is no surprise that the audience was leaping out of their seats to sing, dance and holler at the end of this show. This brilliantly fun score was delivered by a cast of superb performers, competently enabled to sock it to the crowd by their talented production team trio. What a blast.

Determined to be as objective as I could possibly be, I arrived to Lisburn's rather impressive Island Hall with a certain degree of private scepticism. Starlight Express is not the best show ever written. Still, I thought to myself, won't the kids enjoy being part of it? How naïve I was to be so dismissive. Fusion Theatre improved upon any online versions I had watched as I researched this show. I found myself engrossed in the characters, entertained by the action and ultimately far clearer on what was actually happening on stage. So how did this company manage to draw me in and prove me wrong?

Ian Milford's direction seemed determined to provide some much-needed clarity to the story-telling of this show. Traditionally, a child called Control narrates the story and is represented by a pre-recorded voice-over. The likely reason for this is because the child should be gigantic in comparison to the rest of the cast, made up of his toy trains. Perhaps ditching the kid is also very helpful for touring companies etc. Ian made the clever choice to bring all of Control's action onto the stage, ultimately clarifying what was going on, whilst heightening the tension between the boy and his trains. Control, played by a very well-rehearsed Tiernan Ryan, cleverly matched the movements of his model train-set (a replica of the main stage) with the blocking on stage. At one point, he roared at the trains for misbehaving in a race and this was very powerful to see in the flesh. His raised bedroom went some way to take care of the fact that he wasn't bigger than the trains. A prominently placed Barbie Doll in the boy's bedroom worked well as a symbol against gender stereotyping in children and served as a pre-cursor to the emphasis placed on diversity and inclusion throughout the rest of the show. The lights made rainbow patterns on the floor, further symbolising diversity, and the bullying scenes of underdog Rusty the Steam Train were saddening.

The large chorus of fifty wheeled performers were used to mark out the race-tracks, something that clearly isolated these sequences from the other skating in the show. Images were projected onto the upper part of the back wall adding extra clarity, excitement and humour to proceedings. Previously prepared 'photo-finish' shots appeared at the end of races and the when trains collided they were accompanied by those famous comic-book Batman images, with words such as 'Bish-Bosh', indicating the force of the fight.

It would have been far too simple to direct a cast of fifty performers on wheels, so Ian Milford also provided musical direction for this show. The employment of eight musicians is to be commended when the show's rights package comes with a set of tracks and pre-recorded material. If some numbers required a dance-track style accompaniment, some pre-recorded music was used. The rights dictate this. Nonetheless, there was a great balance between live music and the pre-recorded necessities. Ian gave great support to the band and the cast. Soloists and chorus alike sang excellently well and appeared confident in what they had to do. The brass section was too loud at times, but this was fleeting.

Jillian Liggett took on a challenge, far greater than many choreographers must, in getting a cast of over fifty people to perform on wheels. She made this look very easy indeed. Every number was exciting, varied and involved as many performers as possible. There were different sequences going on in various parts of the stage. The moves were competently executed by everyone the cast and timing was perfect. Choreography was simplistic and effective when it needed to be and was challenging and impressive at the right times also. For a steam-train, Ethan Haddock as the anti-hero Rusty appeared to have electricity pumping through him. His voice has the tone and resonance of someone with a lot of training. He captured the various sides of his character - goofy, vulnerable, awestruck and strong - with great taste. His reactions when not speaking were also great. He had a fantastic way of shoe-horning a plethora of emotions into a song, such as the title track 'Starlight Express', keeping his delivery engrossing at all times. A very clever performer.

Abbie Watson was adorable as Pearl. She has a mature alto sound to her singing voice that reminded me of Adele. She was very good at putting across the dilemma her character felt as she betrayed Rusty to race with a more impressive train. She worked brilliantly with the other female leads also.
