There was even a wonderful snow-machine effect to highlight the misery of their conditions. Choreography, by Erica Delaney Hayes, was simple with some synchronised tool movements in 'Worksong'. The highlight was the folk dancing which was inclusive of all ages and ability levels. This bounced off the stage, making sure we were as happy as could be before the sad bits, maximising their impact.

Kevin Fagan played our Everyman hero John. This somewhat timid character has to deal with learning of his wife's dalliance with another man and with a son who insists on going to war, only to meet disaster. It was a beautifully measured performance. While he was often understated, he never dismissed a moment as unimportant, always doing just enough to react to what was going on. He internalised his feelings rather than gesticulated every obvious emotion, making it all the more powerful when his feelings overflowed in private moments. The emotions seemed to surge from within, manifesting themselves into his voice and eyes in a way that was utterly convincing, truthful and honest. To top it off, his singing was professional, powerful and moving.

Like John, Emily is a massive part, with a huge amount to learn, and the role was in the competent hands of Kelly-Marie Davy. She was nice and affable and we were always on her side, which is important considering her betrayal of the faithful John. The scene in which Jackson wins her over was very well crafted; he would not take no for an answer and her lust for him dominated over her fear of sinning, leading to an inevitable and passionate kiss. Her reaction after the kiss was layered and fascinating: She trembled with lust, regret, fear and possibility. Seeing the complexity of the moment, we can stay on her side for the rest of the show. Her voice suited the lower part of the score best, but she emoted beautifully through song nonetheless. Her death was very touching, all the more because she had done enough things right to deserve the heartache of her loyal husband.

Damien Hurley's performance of Jackson made me wish that Jackson had a musical of his own, such was the subtle complexity of his interpretation. Does his darkness come from his overly-critical father or is his father right to be so harsh? Why does he want a married woman? How does he manage to win her over when she appears otherwise to be completely devoted to her lovely husband? (Getting the passionate nicey-nice treatment from a bad boy has won a few hearts in the past). How is he 15 years later? Slower, tamer, sadder but more settled. The war would have taken its toll, of course. All of this was measured very nicely by Damien, with just the right amount of ingredients, prompting more questions than answers, which is far more interesting.

Matthew Carpenter brought much-needed humour and energy in a characterful, persuasive and convincing performance of Isaac. His job was to bring vim, humour and strength to the very tame Tallentire household and he did this well. Such was his bravado that it was all the more painful when he broke down in tears, recalling the conditions of war that cost him dearly. It was completely convincing and avoided self-indulgence, which was great.

More drama was provided by Stephen Fagan as Seth. He had a more serious head on his shoulders than Isaac, bringing balance to their scenes. He was effective in the Miners' meeting. [Spoiler Alert] He added to the panic of Harry's youthful and misguided heroic attempt to flee the trenches to attack the other side and his embrace of the dead body was tense and moving. Charlene Masterson, as Sally, had great rapport with Emily and as such we saw more reason to like Emily throughout the show. Her discomfort at Jackson's arrival to Emily's house was cleverly acted and her singing of 'Who Will You Marry Then?' was very good.

Aoife Small, as May, had all the sass and confidence that her parents lacked, injecting energy and into the Tallentire household. She combined nice vocals with good story-telling ability in 'You Never See the Sun'. She was the perfect foil for her anxious brother. She took nonsense from nobody and, as such, was all the more effective when she became saddened in the later scenes.

In contrast, Jordan Bass as her brother Harry had all the nervous energy of an adolescent young man coming of age, looking for excitement and heroics. He was steadfast and persuasive as he told his mother that he lied about his age to join up, and his re-appearance at the end of the show was touching.

Eddie Brady showed his range as an actor by appearing as the criticising Pennington in the First Act, and the dithering and humorous clergyman later in the show. Paul Laycock was a pensive and committed Chairman of the Miners' meeting and added considerably wherever else he appeared. Julie Donnelly had great presence as the Landlady and established herself as the matriarchal boss of the proceedings in the pub.

Kevin Shirran was able to be funny or deadly serious depending on his function within a scene as Tom. Garrett Rogers, James Place and Robbie Keogh brought their experience to their roles of Bob, Joe Sharp and Ted Blacklock, ensuring that standards did not slip across the line of named parts.

Costumer, Andrew Reddy, has a great supply of costumes that are indicative of this time. Everyone was as cute as a button. I would argue that costumes could have been messier; with tears in the clothing, patches and grime that would make more of a suggestion towards the poverty and terrible working conditions of the mining families. The soldiers' uniforms looked great and those ladies of a higher caste stood out from the poorer women, such were their high-power rigouts. The use of modern-day spotlessly-clean overalls were neither suitable for the time period nor indicative of the awful working conditions of the men.

Couple this with a few too many Disney- like moments, where cast members pointed and gazed into the distance, all doe-eyed and dream-like, and I am not so sure that we got enough of the 'rugged' quality that Time Out magazine had once admired about The Hired Man.

Lighting was by Tomás Fitzgerald/Stage Lighting Centre who splayed some nice colours across the rocky wall of the set, giving atmosphere to various moments. The lighting of the mining scene where the men get trapped was too bright. This did not support the sense of position- cheating in the blocking or the sense of claustrophobia that was acted very well by those involved. There were some nice specials, such as when John had to deliver bad news to Emily from the Front. More specials might have clarified who was speaking in the opening sequence. They say that you have succeeded if you manage to split the audience and create debate in the aftermath of the show. Director Art McGauran managed this through his intelligent nurturing of scenes to explore the complexity of relationships. The audience may well have differed with each other about what actually happened, most notably with the kiss between Jackson and Emily. The final verdict of HXT's production of the Hired Man? Fantastic individual performances, overall, and superb choral singing, texturised with glorious dynamics. Scene changes were clever when stylised. But the chorus stood in too many straight lines. When I go to the theatre, I want to be moved to feel something; humour or sorrow or awe or elation. There were many tissues employed amongst the audience to wipe away a tear. This, in my book, means that the show induced such a catharsis and, as such, worked very well indeed.

I am reliably told that the Dun Mhuire Theatre in Wexford Town was once the third biggest theatre in Ireland. I would well believe it by the scope of this space that stretches far back to accommodate over 600 people. The large crowds this show pulled, despite the amount of other attractions in the town - such as the Opera Festival and the Spiegel Tent - was very impressive. Audience members were received with a relaxed, friendly yet effective manner by Box Office and Front of House personnel.

The official Footloose The Musical website describes the show as an "explosive rock 'n' roll musical sensation". I was expecting some fun, but I was not expecting so much substance in terms of drama. Little did I realise that this show is just as much about control and grief and eventual healing as it is about busting some moves. Dancing was banned in the town of Bomont after a group of young people died on their way home from a dance. Newcomer, Ren, whose job it was to help the townsfolk emerge from their grief, by re-establishing their love of dance, was undertaken by a very good actor and singer - Nathan Fitzpatrick. His abilities were equally matched by Niamh Bolger who played Ren's new-found love interest Ariel - a girl rebelling against her parents' grief. Niamh has great vocal range and sang brilliantly with sass or with softness as required. Ariel's father, the Reverend Moore (the man who banned dancing after his own son was killed), was played excellently by Greg Currid. He has a velvety yet booming voice that captured the authority and intention of the preacher-man. He could equally portray the vulnerability of a grieving father and he acted brilliantly through song. He and his wife Vi, played very well by Majella Londra, engaged in private arguments about how to heal from their past traumas and move forward for the sake of the youth in the town. These dramatic scenes, whether between husband and wife, father and tear-way daughter, or Reverend and advocate-of-dance Ren, were all excellently directed by Imelda McDonagh and had brilliantly varying emotional levels throughout. Additional tension to the piece was provided by Ren's struggling mother, Ethel, played with competence by a very good actor and singer, Caroline O'Connell. Poor Ethel is forced to take her son to live with his Uncle Wes (played by Andy Fanning with both comedy and crankiness) and his Aunt Lulu (played by Paula Malone Carty) who created the perfect foil for her uptight husband.

While these scenes brought more drama than I was expecting, there were still plenty of laughs too. James Dobbs played the slightly dim but very lovable protégé to Ren and provided some fantastic comedic moments in his portrayal as Willard, the honest hillbilly. More comedy was provided with a fine cameo from Marian O'Leary as Betty Blast, the owner of the local Burger Joint. This elder of the community took no nonsense as she sped dangerously around the diner with roller skates and Zimmer frame. Another competent cameo was provided by Neal O'Leary as Cowboy Bob who opened Act Two with a Country and Western number that inspired confidence. More colour was provided by town hunk Chuck Cranston who was played with all the bravado, cool and un-likeability necessary by Gary Stephens (who sang brilliantly with some nice falsetto moments). Such a baddie requires side-kicks of a lower status and these were provided with appropriate foolishness by the very good Luke Spellacy and Murt Murphy, who played the brain-dead Lyle and Travis respectively. More unlikeable characters emerged, making us fall in love more with our leads and their plights: The stricter- than-strict Principal Clark was played with great authority and presence by Donna Spellacy O'Leary and Dylan Walsh fulfilled the role of the revolting Coach Roger Dunbar with the right amount of pompous aggression. Ariel also needed some girly mates and received super support from Elaine Murphy as Rusty (who luckily enough finds love in the most unlikely places). Elaine joined Catherine Devereux as Urleen and Ceris Brown as Wendy Jo to form a competent trio of good singers with great accents.

These fine performances all took place on some very clever staging. Each set piece glided on and off with amazing ease and speed, thanks to stage manager Greg O'Leary and his team. The set pieces themselves, designed by Mark Redmond, were mainly presented as a series of trucks or stand-alone furniture that immediately and effectively defined the space and enhanced the narrative. Mark also provided lighting on the evening and he, with a clever cyc matching the colours present in the set pieces, created a synergy within the aesthetic.

While there was plenty of laughs and drama on stage, it is the case that the dancing in this show is a very important feature. With such belters as 'Holding out for a Hero' and 'Let's Hear it for the Boy', one expects this show, with its core message about the love of dance, to sock- it-to-'em in the dance numbers. This task, for the most part, was well realised by choreographer Suzanne O'Leary and her dance troupe. There were some central formations and V-shapes that seemed to work really well in a few of the numbers. Not all of the routines were as slick as one would have liked, such as the finale of Act One, but the finale of Act Two bounced off the stage and reminded everyone why dance can bring so much joy.

Singing throughout the show, by soloists in particular, was excellent and all the principal cast seemed to be very well prepared by Musical Director Patrick Clancy, who provided great support from the pit. Less successful was some of the group/choral work, particularly at the beginning of the show, which seemed to suffer from some gaffs from the sound desk. By the finale, however, the chorus belted out the famous 'Footloose' number and harmonies between the guys and girls were balanced here.

Director Imelda McDonagh has a talent for creating pictures; with each scene being so distinct from the previous one, while using a minimalistic and effective approach to staging. The clever structuring of the dramatic scenes, the individual performances, the solos, duets and small group numbers were, for me, the strength of the show. That said, it was also very uplifting when the entire company took to the stage for a final dance, leaving us with a feeling of healing and hope. Art imitated life and the more experienced 'cut loose' with the optimistic youth to celebrate the happiness music and dance can bring.

I'm indebted to Glencullen Dundrum MDS for the thought and effort they put into the re-telling of this very beautiful and emotional piece of theatre.

The Hired Man is really a play with music, and for a society with a background as much in drama as in music, it was a perfect choice to amalgamate the two disciplines. There was a simplicity to the direction of Tom Ronayne that allowed the script to tell the story without distraction. The neutral set functioned effectively and was nicely painted and constructed. There were sufficient appropriate props to add authenticity to the scenes, and lighting was effective if unadventurous. The flaming cyclorama for the war scene was a tad overpowering and might have been more effective with just occasional flashes of explosions or gunfire.

While there was some tidy choreography on occasions, this was more a production of attractive pictures and nice positioning of chorus for their musical numbers. The opening sequence, with the hirers on the back platform, and those up for hire on the forward stage, caused much of the opening dialogue to be directed away from the audience. There may also have been more potential for dramatic conflict if some of the revellers had left the pub and followed John home for his finale of act one encounter with Emily and Jackson. Amy MacCarthy gave a warm and sensitive portrayal of Emily Tallentire, a woman caught between love and duty. There was a believable resistance to Jackson, and a most convincing regret for her betrayal of John. She aged well, and played out her inner turmoil with a most affecting sincerity. She also sang with good tone and excellent emotion.

John Conroy excelled in the role of John Tallentire, with a smooth and passionate voice that thoroughly complemented his most tangible acting performance. His emotions were always apt and consistently credible.

And an equally endearing performance was given by Niall MacCarthy in the role of Jackson, with the one proviso being that on occasions, he seemed a little unsure of what to do with his hands. His vocal quality was appropriate to the demands of the role.

It was a touch of genius casting a Labour Councillor as a Union man, and Peter O'Brien, as Seth, preached with a natural ease at the meeting of the Miners. This was a well-acted and comfortably sung role.

Providing the all too rare moments of levity in the show, was James Paradise as Issac. This was a nicely exaggerated role, making the most of his opportunities to lighten the atmosphere, and again, the vocal requirements were well realised. Jack Farrell showed his potential as an actor in the role of young Harry Tallentire, earning the approval and the sympathies of the audience as he followed his father off to war.

Aisling McDonnell used a shrill voice to relate the youthfulness of May Tallentire, and managed to give a secure and light- hearted performance. She was also most convincing in her reactions to the death of her mother.

Emma O'Brien was a spirited Sally Edmonson, was a jovial aspect and some very good comedic timing in her early scenes. She could perhaps have been aged a little more convincingly by the time we reached the post-war era.

There was secure support from Liam Corrigan as Pennington, and several of the cameo roles who stepped out of the chorus to deliver their lines with conviction. The chorus acted and reacted well to what was happening around them, and were comfortable in their movement. Vocally, there were secure and tuneful harmonies throughout the performance.

The costumes for the show were generally very eye-catching and appropriate, although there's more poignancy to the Farewell scene when the men are all dressed in uniform. I saw nothing inappropriate or out of place in either hairstyles or make-up.

The small band of musicians made a worthy contribution to the show. The trumpets echoed refrain was always good in tone and tempo. The pace and volume of the music was generally good. I had a sense that the pianist was not entirely at home with sections of the score, but Musical Director, Róisin Ryan, kept a good control between the pit and the singers, and the choral numbers were very nicely performed throughout the show. Principals seemed well-rehearsed vocally, and the trio at the end of Act One was beautiful. This is a show that deserves to be performed more often, such is the quality of both script and music, and I'm delighted that Glencullen chose to present it, and to show it off with a very good standard of production and performance. Sincere thanks to all involved for a night of emotional entertainment.

show_raw: The 25Th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee
review_text:
The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee isn't at all about the glitz and glamour of show-business. It's all about the business of Spelling, and is appropriately set on a drab school stage, with a microphone, the contestants on school benches, and the panel of organisers seated at a school desk.

There's also no chorus, no need for fancy costume changes, and indeed, a very limited story line… all of which might make it sound rather uninteresting, but the very opposite is true.

The first thing that Director, Cian O'Dowd, got right was his selection of a cast of such highly talented individuals, for had that been wrong, the show may have faltered. Relying entirely on the strength of the nine principal characters (and a few members of the audience, I'll get to that later), this is a wonderfully clever and classy piece of comedy drama with musical interludes. The cast of ODD Theatre Company, I'm delighted to report, proved equal to the task, with every individual given a top- notch performance.

This is a show that has a strong element of improvisation, including involving a few members of the audience to become participants in the Spelling Bee. These scenes were brilliantly orchestrated, and added immensely to the enjoyment of the show. Fair play to the stooges who volunteered to appear on the stage with only a moment's notice.

In dress, idiosyncrasies, tone of voice, and emotional state of mind, each principal on the stage was very securely prepared and presented. The pace of the show was never allowed to drop, and comedy was brilliantly realised throughout. The good preparation of the vocals, and the musical accompaniment to the show, was secure enough to allow Musical Director, Keelin Kilduff, to also play a performance role, while leaving the conducting of the very capable 4 piece band in the safe hands of Grace Bergin. There were very good group harmony sections to the score, and again, the singers were very well able to produce a secure and tuneful sound. While some of the songs are hilariously funny, and many of the tunes and rhythms are tricky enough to present, the music is generally quite forgettable, but none-the-less, highly enjoyable in the moment.

For such a small show, there were plenty of opportunities to involve the whole cast in the cleverly devised, and often very funny, dance routines. Choreographer, Aine Foley, did a creative and well- rehearsed job on her charges, and the fun of their routines was evident in their performances.

I will preface the comments on the principals with the observation that, with the exception of three performers, the cast were all portraying 11-12 year olds, and did so with complete believability.

William Barfee, the Spelling Bee winner, was self-obsessed, OCD and extremely high maintenance, and in every respect, Daniel Ryan portrayed him with the most convincing reality. His frustration at having his name consistently mispronounced was hilarious, as was his "special" method of using his magic foot to spell out his words on the floor. His "Magic Foot" number was quirky, comical and very well performed, and his sentiment in "Second" was sincere and endearing.

2nd Place went to Olive Ostrovsky, beautifully and sensitively portrayed by Keelin Kilduff. This was the singular child, with only her dictionary as a friend. We get an affecting glimpse at her home life and her relationship with her parents, and finally we see a most engaging and sentimental bond between herself and William in the "Second" duet. Acting and singing were equally appealing.

Chip Tolentino, past winner of the Bee, is tormented by hormones, and when a sudden erection over a good looker in the audience breaks his concentration, he crashes out of the Bee. While every aspect of Fionán O'Carroll's performance was strong, it was his delivery of the "Lament" (the erection song) that best demonstrated his very fine sense of comedy.

The lisping and socially aware Logainne Schwartzandgrubenniere was given a delightful treatment by Emma Kilduff, as she came to terms with being the daughter of two gay daddies, and a birth mother who lives in a trailer park. Emma's facial reactions, her tuneful and emotional vocals and her consistent lisp, highlighted her beautiful and often hilarious performance. Clodagh Donnelly gave a spoilt brat, conceited, athletic and colourful portrait of Marcy Park, the child who's good at absolutely everything, and desperately just wants to be more ordinary. "I Speak Six Languages" was superbly performed, as she demonstrated every aspect of her Miss Perfect persona. Her exit from the Bee was a moment of personal triumph, both for Marcy and for Clodagh.

The final contestant in the Bee was lost, confused, gullible, childlike, and adorably Not-smart, Leaf Coneybear, played to absolute perfection by Eoin Gleeson, with what, for me, was the performance of the show. His facial reactions, body-language, tone of voice, comedy timing, ability to melt the audience, were all remarkably well handled. "I'm Not That Smart" was just fabulous.

Lynn Carter played the role of Grief Counsellor, Mitch Mahoney, the on- parole, attitude problem person with the task of consoling the contestants when they exit the Bee, which of course she did with little solace or empathy. Lynn gave a feisty and believable performance, with very good comedy and a strong voice. Winner of the first ever Putnam Spelling Bee, Rona Lisa Perretti, was the host of the 25th, full of the vanity and conceit of past glories. Fiona Hiney gave a valiant interpretation, epitomising the shallowness of the competition, and embracing her role with a great sense of fun. Her much repeated "My Favourite Moment", was musically delightful.

Last, but certainly not least, was Conor Kilduff in the role of Vice-Principal Douglas Panch. This was a wonderful character, at the heart of most of the improvised business with the "volunteer" audience members, and also the questionmaster of the Bee. In his delivery, Conor was crystal clear, constantly animated and ridiculously cheesy, reaching a high point when he had a minor breakdown over being Vice-Principal and not Principal. His empathy with second place Olive, presenting her with a runners-up prize from his own pocket, was as hilarious as it was sentimental.

There were several other roles, played by the same cast, all of which were very believable, including a very amusing and "not-my-concern" type Jesus, by Lynn Carter.

Now, I have to admit that I might have been inclined to do a little more with the dressing of the stage, for although the black drapes and minimal furniture were adequate, there would be potential to make the set more visually appealing, with perhaps a glitter cloth or even a nicely dressed doorway at the back for the entrance of the contestants, and if finances allowed, neon signs, or even painted signs, to give the feel of a studio or a well-dressed concert stage.

Lighting was basic, but important business was always well highlighted, and an occasional splash of colour added atmosphere to some of the musical numbers. The "freezes" were accentuated by good special area lighting. Sound, throughout, was very good.

I am indebted to all in the ODD Theatre Company for introducing me to, and hilariously entertaining me with, this wonderful little show. Sincere thanks.

A very obvious love of comedy came across loud and clear in Killian Collins' direction of this show. Characters were strongly painted, and there was plenty of good corn and slapstick to augment an already hilarious script. Indeed, when it comes to feel-good musicals of the modern era, "Sister Act" must surely rank highly for its level of unleashed frivolity and its happy-clappy musical score. It's also one of those musicals that offer so much more than usual for female performers, which is why it was such an excellent choice for Fermoy Musical Society, for here was an exhibition of strength in depth, from the leading lady to the cameo roles within the nuns chorus.

Christina McGrath was the epitome of "Glam" in the role of Deloris Van Cartier. She strutted on to the stage with supreme confidence, then withered delightfully when put in her place by Curtis. This was a strong acting performance, a vocal power- house and extremely funny in the comedy department. Overall, it was a performance of great stature.

Valerie O'Leary, as the Mother Superior, delivered her lines with authority, frustration, and excellent comedic timing. This was a highly competent and confident actress, with a voice that stood out for its strength and clarity.

Colette Daly was a hilariously silly Sr Mary Lazarus, reminding me a lot of a nun I once knew in Thurles, except that the Thurles nun didn't have the "Rap"- ability of Colette. A beautifully portrayed character and a definite favourite with the audience.

Aoife Collins got as much fun as possible from the character of Sr Mary Patrick, high on energy and silliness. Her voice was strong for the delivery of those high notes, and her over-enthusiasm for everything was addictive.

Maeve O'Callaghan was a sweet and loveable Sr Mary Robert, fragile and innocent at the outset, but displaying a growing feistiness as the show progressed. Her "The Life I Never Led" was very nicely performed. This was a young actress with great potential to be a star of the future. Mary O'Neill gave a noteworthy cameo performance as the anything-but-fragile "older" nun, Sr Mary Theresa. She was more than able to strut her stuff amid the younger sisters.

Áine Maye as Sr Mary Martin of Tours and Marie Kelleher as Sr Mary Margaret led a highly talented group of nuns who gave 100% to their characters and to their singing and dancing. Having spent many a summer in a convent in Thurles, I can honestly say that I've never seen a younger or more glamorous and athletic bunch of holy sisters in my life!

Lisa Feerick as Tina and Amy Clarke as Michelle, got the show off to a good start, giving good vocal backing and dancing to Deloris.

It would be remiss of me not to mention that the men in the show also made a significant contribution to the success of the production.

Rory Ward had the insecure, awkwardness of Sweaty Eddie down to a fine art, without ever losing the authority of a police officer. His delivery of "I Could Be That Guy" was delightful and funny, and also displayed a strong and capable voice. He became the romantic hero with grace and great comedy.

Paul Finn was a funny yet threatening Curtis, vocally secure and with a good stage presence. He had the gravitas and the leadership qualities for the role, and the comical tolerance to cope with his ineffectual thugs.

Michael Murphy as TJ, Hugh Mulqueen as Pablo and Brendan Daly as Joey, almost stole the show together in performing "Lady in the Long Black Dress", with an abundance of groin thrusting and gyrating, and indeed, throughout the show, they provided great comedy and characterisation.

Bill Cahill was a suitable Ernie, and also featured well as Mr Lardner and as a member of the "homeless" chorus.

Mikie Dunne was a highly amusing Monsignor O'Hara. I forgot to ascertain if his Northern accent was his own or put on for the character, but either way, it worked well in the role. He was delightfully "hip" when required.

A host of very good cameo appearances by members of the chorus, as hookers, homeless people, bar staff, dancers, taxi- driver, and of course The Pope, all added to the atmosphere throughout the show. The set was clever and effective, and usually well-manoeuvred about the stage. One or two of the changes could have been a tad speedier, but the Stage Manager (uncredited in the programme) and his/her crew worked hard to keep things running smoothly. There was an abundance of good and appropriate props used throughout the show. and while the lighting became a tad disco-esque for my liking, there were still some amazing effects and atmospheres. The front walk way around the orchestra was a great idea and very well used. Entrances and exits were clean and the stage never looked overcrowded.

Given that several of the big musical numbers have a similar rock-gospel feel, Choreographer, Stephen Cullinane- O'Regan, managed to keep his routines varied and non-repetitive. They were full of joy and energy, and were always well executed by his hyperactive nuns. There were also extremely funny routines for the gangsters, particularly "Lady in the Long Black Dress", which was deliciously non-PC.

There was an intelligent and thoughtful use of the chorus, as homeless people, meandering about the stage and assisting with the clearance of props.

Lighting was good, with some beautiful use of split beams, and moving heads, to create an ethereal effect. Back light was very well used to mask the entrance of chorus or principals in the background, and most of the action was well highlighted, but the Fund-raising thermometer was almost lost due to the smoke, which, frankly, there was a bit too much of throughout the show.

A very talented orchestra played the lively musical score with precision, energy, and on occasions, just a bit too much exuberance. An excellent brass section had a tendency in act one to overwhelm some of the solos, but they did pull back a little in act two. The leadership from Musical Director Deirdre Long was secure and animated, and the wonderful work she had done on preparing her vocal choruses was always evident. There was excellent contrast between the serenely beautiful start of Take Me to Heaven, and the powerfully uplifting gospel rock of the rest of the number. Sunday Morning Fever, from start to finish, was superb.

A very good job was done on costuming the show, with good nun costumes, which transformed throughout the show, culminating in a dazzling display for the finale. There was beautiful attention to detail in creating a down and out homeless chorus; there was great era-authenticity to the gangsters. All in all, a very good visual display. Make-up, or the limited use of it, was just right.

Thank you sincerely for a tremendously uplifting night of community spirit, abundant joy and high quality entertainment.

It hadn't been billed as the Sing-a- long version of "All Shook Up", but the audience in An Draíocht had other ideas. Elvis may not be alive and well, but he's apparently as popular as ever in Coolmine, whose audience members took it upon themselves to boost the on-stage singing for almost every musical number. Not that they needed too, mind you, for the choral singing was one of the outstanding features of this wonderful rendition of the show.

Pat McElwain presented an electrifying production of this brilliantly scripted Juke- box musical, with an emphasis on pace and comedy. Characters were strongly represented by an extremely well-cast line of principals. There was attention to the technical quality of the show, with good sound balance and a very nicely devised lighting plot. The set was simple but beautifully presented, with nice set pieces and a good industrial frame work. It was well-painted and the moving pieces were manoeuvred with ease by an efficient stage crew under Stage Manager, Mo M c M a h o n .

C o s t u m i n g t h r o u g h o u t w a s a p p ro p r i a t e and delightful, with principal outfits always in keeping with their character. Chorus outfits had plenty of colour and variety, with a particularly nice set for "Devil in Disguise". The brides in the finale looked superb. Wigs and hairstyles were very in keeping with the era, and there were no obvious problems with make-up.

Where direction scores highly, is where all these elements are brought seamlessly together to present a clean and precise overall production, as was the case with this performance.

The quality of both the orchestra and the on-stage chorus were so good that I would find it hard to select the musical number that had the strongest impact on me. The harmonies of "Can't Help Falling in Love" were perfection, but the combination of harmony and power-singing exhibited in "All Shook Up", quite possibly made it the number of the show. The point is, Musical Director, Dave McGauran, got just about everything right in this production.

Contributing so strongly to the quality of the production was the inventive and high-energy choreography of Nicole McDonald. She has that great knack of making her choruses look comfortable in their movements, by creating routines that perfectly suit the ability of those performing them. She was also blessed with a principal line-up who were as capable of the dance moves as her choruses, and what a principal line!

In the role of Chad, Kevin Hartnett has found himself the perfect character to best display his combined talents of comedy, energy and vocal quality. This was a beautifully crafted performance, making the most of an excellent script, an abundance of non-verbal communication, and an ability to put over those wonderful Elvis songs.

A feisty, feminine, yet exquisitely tom- boyish performance came from Keila-Ana Whelan in the role of Natalie/Ed. With a beautiful, modern vocal quality, she made the most of her ballads, and had plenty of energy in the rock and roll numbers, but it was her comfortable and competent acting that held the role together so successfully.

Liam Egan was an exceptionally funny Dennis, capturing the nerdy, self- deprecating humour to a T, and adding to it a strong and expressive vocal quality. His facial reactions were excellent, and his timing absolutely perfect.

In the role of Miss Sandra, Serena Salmon commanded the stage, with voluptuous charm, singing and dancing like a Broadway showgirl, and oozing sex- appeal and comedic delivery. This was a stunning performance.

Gerry Hannigan' shy and mild mannered Jim Haller gave way to a very funny wannabe rocker in his efforts to woo Miss Sandra. This was a very nicely gauged performance, strong on comedy, and believable in the realisation that Sylvia was his real saviour.

Niamh Carroll was a feisty Sylvia, stern in her concern for her daughter, and sincere in her feelings for Jim. Her "There's Always Me" was delivered with warmth, passion and a strong and tender voice.

In making the most of the role of Lorraine, Louise Hudson also showed that she would have been capable of playing Natalie or Miss Sandra; such was her abundant talent as an actress, singer and comedienne. She was effervescent on the stage.

Ben Hannigan had the perfect look for the role of Dean, and transformed very effectively from the timid mummy's boy into the rebellious teenager, encouraged by his love for Lorraine. A very well played role, displaying a fine tenor in "It's Now or Never".

Kathryn Gibbons gave a stalwart performance as the domineering Mayor Matilda, full of comical self-sanctimonious morality, and latterly, like a school girl on a first date with Earl. Very nicely played, with a fine rendition of "Devil in Disguise". Sheriff Earl relies heavily on facial and body language for most of the show, and Justin Parkes displayed excellent powers of mime in making him funny and believable. When he eventually got to speak, he did so with authority, and a resonant vocal in the "Can't Help Falling in Love" reprise. Seeking Adjudicator for 2018/'19 Season (Season begins June/July 2018) The AIMS adjudicator is required to visit productions by AIMS member societies throughout Ireland, to prepare a detailed report for the society on the show in a specified format, to write a review for publication in the Association's journal Show Times, to make nominations for the AIMS Awards at the end of the season and to select the Award Winners. A thorough knowledge of musicals and of amateur theatre in Ireland is essential. Membership of a recognised body will be a distinct advantage. A modest package covering fees/expenses will be offered to the person appointed.

Frank Foley, National Secretary AIMS 25 Harcourt Lodge, Inchicore, Dublin 8.

No later than Friday 12th January 2018. Shortlisting might apply.

There was a plethora of cameo roles, all of which were performed with conviction, especially the vocal contribution of Sinead Peris as Henrietta.

The chorus and dancers made a strong and precise contribution to the show physically, but vocally, they were superb. Scenically, perhaps there could have been a touch more variety in the fairground scenes, but what was there was very effective. There was a fine array of props throughout the show, even if the "alcohol enthusiasts" in the opening diner scene hadn't a drink between them.

Lighting was very good, with beautiful use of colour to create the right atmospheres. None of the key action was missed. Sound quality and cueing was very good throughout, with a fine balance between This was a top rate night of entertainment, enjoyed thoroughly by an audience highly enthused by the standard of performances on the stage. Thank you sincerely for an amazing night of fun and entertainment.

Within the confines of a fairly tight space, Director, Philippa Alford, managed to keep the stage from ever looking over-crowded, which was an achievement, given the size of the chorus and the numbers of children performing in this Kill M&DS production of "Oliver!". The set for the show was compact and appropriate, making the most practical use of the facilities available, with the front left apron proving useful for Mr Brownlow's House, and everything else played on the main set, with an effective bridge and well-utilised banners, depicting the various locations. It was also a very wise idea not to overflow the stage with furniture. The movement of furniture props and set pieces was done with quiet efficiency, under the guidance of Stage Manager, Tom Sheehy. Props were generally good. The lighting was tidy and effective, with a decent selection of colours to provide atmosphere. Cueing was good. There were no problems with the sound system.

While this was a tidy and entertaining production, I felt that there needed to be a stronger emphasis on the comedy of the piece with perhaps more slapstick between Bumble and Widow Corney, more comedic business at the undertakers, and a lighter side to the character of Fagin. As with most 'dark' stories, it is the moments of light-heartedness that add to the poignancy of the more sinister or depressing moments of reality. The show was well-paced and delivered by a cast who seemed relaxed in their stage- presence and secure in their vocal quality. While the children perhaps needed more business to perform, they were bright and delightful in everything they did.

Charlie Reid was a confident young man in the role of Oliver, with a lovely tuneful voice and nice facial expressions. He showed good fear in the presence of Bill Sykes, and a lovely cheerfulness when performing "Consider Yourself" with Dodger. A young star in the making.

Julie Finan gave her younger pal good guidance and leadership in the role of The Artful Dodger, with plenty of energy and character. She sang and danced well, and her acting was very capable.

Dominic Reid had a great look as Fagin, and indeed, captured the sinister nature of his character extremely well. As mentioned above, I'd have liked to see a more playful side to his nature when performing with the children, and there was scope for more comedy to be wrung from his fear of Sykes. He did show his comedic potential in "Reviewing the Situation", which was well-delivered.

Rossagh Cusack made a believable and sympathetic Nancy, with well-directed reaction to her every circumstance. "As Long As He Needs Me" was beautifully interpreted, and she gave a feisty rendition of "Oom-Pah-Pah!"

Beside Nancy, Alison Behan showed sensitivity while making the most of her cameo role of Bet. I really liked her little hug with Oliver after the demise of Nancy and Bill.

Ciaran O'Shea's gave an angry and aggressive interpretation to Bill Sykes, which worked in portraying him as a bully, but perhaps a more quiet, disturbing aspect would have made him even more sinister.

Tom McCarthy was a very good Mr Bumble, pompous at the outset, and rather blustery and bumbling as the story progressed. His vocal contribution to the show was also very appealing.

Mags O'Driscoll perhaps needed a little push to give her character more feistiness, but she looked well and made a very decent job of "I Shall Scream".

Damien Donegan as Sowerberry and Denise Donegan as Mrs Sowerberry worked well together, and were very believable as the grim undertakers. I just felt that there scenes needed a touch more physical comedy, but "That's Your Funeral" was nicely played.

Antoinette Agnew's Mrs Bedwin was warm and sympathetic, and she served her master well. Brian McCabe was a commendable Mr Brownlow, suitably aristocratic and ultimately kind-hearted. Brian Cummins and Sinead O'Brien put in a couple of highly credible performances as the smug bully, Noah Claypole and the full of attitude Charlotte.

There were several very capable performances in cameo roles, including a convincing Laura Sheehan as Old Sally, Karen Fogarty as the Matron and a blustery Tony Victory as Dr Grimwig. Lack of space dictated that the choreography of Julianne McNamara probably had to be reined in a little, but she did manage to keep patterns interesting, and those in her charge managed to despatch their routines with a good sense of security. The children were full of energy, and while I would have liked to see "Pick a Pocket or Two" with more comedic business relating to the lyrics, they performed with confidence throughout. "Consider Yourself", "Oom- pah-pah" and "Who Will Buy" were all apt to the atmosphere of their scenes.

Emer Hartnett gave secure leadership in front of a well-tuned and nicely balanced orchestra.

The string section was particularly appealing, including the fine solo work that accompanied "Reviewing the Situation". As Chorus Mistress, Emer's work was apparent in well delivered harmonies from the adults, and good diction and energy from the children's choruses. Pace and tempi were excellent throughout, with the possible exception of the "Fine Life" Reprise, which was a tad rushed.

From the drab uniforms of the orphanage to the colourful outfits of Fagin's gang, and from the lowly chorus to the higher stations of society, the costumes for this production were appropriate and very presentable, and good attention was given to hairstyles and make-up.

Cast, crew and the production team should all be commended for a thoroughly entertaining show, with good vocal and acting talent on display and complementary technical back-up. Thank you so much for a highly enjoyable night.

show_raw: Joseph And His Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat
review_text:
Of all the venues I have been to this year, The Limetree Theatre has so far been the most striking. The entrance is made up of an enormous hall of steps, that reminds one of the amphitheatre from the Ancient Greek tradition. And that's just the foyer! This venue has been the recent home of the Cecilian Musical Society. The theatre's vastness and modern décor contrasts beautifully with the extraordinary sense of tradition and community spirit evident within the society.

The box-office contained a lovely colouring competition that had been organised in aid of the local hospice. Photographs of recently deceased members where hung in the box office and tributes to them were put into the programme. Those young members who are following in the tradition of the families and continuing the participation in the society were also celebrated, proving that the future is just as exciting as the past.

Joseph and his Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat, like so many Andrew Lloyd Webber shows, barely comes with a script. There is a list of lyrics, from which a director has to make some sense of it all. There are those who see this as challenging because the production is starting from scratch each time. Others see this as a fantastic opportunity to start with a blank canvas and structure the show however the imagination allows them to. Every version of the show is unique. Every CD is different. Every time the score is heard, someone has done something new to it. When setting out to produce it, it can be a show that makes the head spin. On the other hand, if you're up for the challenge, it is a show that can provide endless fun opportunities for inventiveness, comedy and playful scoring. Even if one wanted to steal their every idea from YouTube, there are so many choices that it would be a job in itself to sift through them all and make a decision. So the Cecilian Musical Society had the challenge of making sense of this slightly bonkers show and uncovering all this inventiveness in terms of dance, comedy and music. How did they do? They completely and utterly smashed it. Dermot Quinn designed the set and he and Andrew Cusack built it. A huge projection welcomed the audience with its Elvis silhouette, large Sphinx cats and hind of Egyptian monuments and the welcoming words "The Cecilian Musical Society presents Joseph and his Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat". There were four columns, complete with impressively carved Pharaohs, and nicely finished off with two sets of symmetrical steps on either side that were used to house the young performers. Another curtain would eventually open to reveal some stunning set-pieces behind. The village-scene with canopy, with a well to dunk Joseph, was a real treat. The bed in Potiphar's home looked super. They used stand-alone black poles for Joseph's prison cell, which were surrealist but effective. The Pharaoh's set with its blue and gold head and lovely steps was complemented by the same colour scheme in the costumes to complete a super aesthetic. Projections were by Jason Ronan and contained movement to show Joseph's journey and add to the narrative. There was, for the most part, good continuity in terms of theme and tone.

From an audience point of view, it was impossible to tell where the direction or musical direction started and the choreography ended in this show. I imagine this is the case with many versions of Joseph and His Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat. Sufficed to say, this production seemed to marry all three elements of production seamlessly, hinting to a dynamic creative relationship between all three members of the production team, intertwining all three disciplines brilliantly. A poor production of Joseph and his Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat can leave an audience scratching their heads as to what on Earth is going on. Thankfully, the story-telling here, by director Des Henn was crystal-clear. He has a talent for comedy. He treated every moment with equal importance meaning that there was never a lull or a dull moment once those lights came on. It was the show that just kept on giving. Images and animations were projected onto the screen to show Joseph's journey to Egypt. At one point, the Brothers did an extremely impressive Diversity dance sequence that combined music, comedy, lighting and performance to create a very special moment. This is one example of how each moment was crafted, enhanced or expanded to tease out the comedy and provide a super night's entertainment.

Musically, this is the type of show that can be fairly straight-forward on paper but also allows for so much creativity in terms of music. I am delighted to report that this inventiveness was found throughout the musical aspects of this production by Musical Director Shane Farrell. The band were behind the set, and while we missed the aesthetic they add to the musical experience, the sound was so balanced as a result, making this a very good idea. There were two screens on either side of the back of the auditorium to support the cast onstage. There was a rich sound from the chorus. 'Benjamin Calypso' began in a fantastic slowed-down version and 'Those Canann Days' had some phrases that were held forever with powerful delivery of harmonies.

It was clear that an extraordinary amount of hard graft and inventiveness went into the choreography by Barbara Meany. I like to take a lot of notes and I can usually jot down comments about the essence of the choreography. There was so much to see that I gave up trying to write about it. Plus, I did not want to take my eyes off the stage such was the entertainment value of the dancing. Every genre of dance was explored, often intertwined with Ancient Egyptian movement which married the thematic with the contemporary. Each moment was original and special, maximising the talents of the group to make the show bounce off the stage. The man with the title role, Brian Finn, gave a solid performance. He had good rapport with the children at the get-go as he high-fived them or held their hands. I loved how, with the odd glance towards each other, he and the Narrator seemed to be complicit in the story-telling. His image was super for this part, considering it appeared as though he had single- handily built every pyramid and temple in the Middle East, such was his heroic physique. It could be argued that he is more of an actor than a singer in the strictest sense but when he sung in his baritone range it was very nice indeed. The Narrator, played very nicely by Hilary Phayer, had lovely charisma and carried the show with grace and competence. She too appeared to show great warmth towards the children. She told the story with lovely conviction and her singing was perfect. She looked like she was having a lot of fun in her story-telling and, with a slight glint in her eye, we too had lots of fun hearing it. She cleverly skipped off with feeling when it was time to leave the stage and she never broke character, even when observing from the background. Joseph's eleven brothers were absolutely awesome. There wasn't a weak-link amongst them and they presented as a troop of very good singers, dancers and actors who had clearly been well-prepared to give a competent, confident and highly entertaining performance. Their dancing, positioning, movement, harmonies and their comedy were all fabulous. I would encourage any lover of performance to play a Brother in this show, such was the extent of fantastic opportunities they were given to shine in this production.

Joseph's father Jacob was played by Paul Cable, who impressively doubled as Potiphar. He was good and caught the old-man characterisation very well. His contribution to the 'Any Dream Will Do' reprise was bizarrely quite moving for a show that one doesn't normally take too seriously. He sang with vulnerability as he tenderly carried Joseph's cloak.

The Pharoah was played by Barry Danaher who is a very good singer and excelled even more as his song came to a crescendo and he belted out the high notes. The Butler (Stephen Byrne) and the Baker (Jason Ronan) both had good characterisations. The Butler had a great PR accent and the Baker had a great Northern English accent. Mrs Potiphar was played by Edel Shinners who caught all the diva nature and mischievous seduction of the role with good comic effect.

The chorus, overall, was simply brilliant. Often considered to be too much of a 'male show', the contribution of the ladies to this production was fantastic. The wives' first entrance was very comical and hooked us into the fun to be had once the white curtain revealed the town set behind. The addition of their voices to the choral numbers was fabulous and they were highly entertaining in everything they did.

The children who stayed on for the entire show were very well behaved throughout. Their backing singing in 'Any Dream Will Do' was very good and they added their voices well to other choral parts. I think more could have been done to maximise their intentions and reactions to the story, but they did what they were told to do well. Costumes were mainly provided by Pat McGann Productions Ltd., Clarina Co. Limerick and the society themselves. They were absolutely stunning. They married the ancient with the modern and contained so much detail. You could have watched this show with the sound off such was the feast for the eyes in terms of costumes. Each scene was thematic, complementing the set and pulling the aesthetic together wonderfully. There was not a stitch on stage that was below par. No amount of effort was spared. It was as though the costumes were a character in themselves as I could not wait to see what happened next with them.

Sound was by Star Systems, Thurles. Cueing was good throughout and the balance between the band and the stage was excellent, all the more easily controlled with the band behind the stage. Unfortunately, there were some significant moments of feedback. The microphones on the males were too dominant over the female vocals in the finale of Act One, meaning the sound was not balanced enough here.

Lighting, by Joe Betts, had some lovely moments, punctuating the high-energy moments and giving atmosphere to those slower bits. Use of gobos to create stone- effects on the floor were very good. The lighting might have changed colour with every new musical motif introduced in the overture, just to give a little more energy to the stage. The blackouts needed to be reconsidered. They were not very dark and created lulls. Stage Management, by Ray Burke and a committed team, was very good overall but created some further lulls here and there. But once the lights were up and the scenes began, it was sock-it- to-'em magic. Some societies dismiss the idea of doing Joseph for many reasons. It is argued that it is a kids' show. Yet I found this version highly entertaining. It is argued that the show is male-dominated. I guess that is true, but this society worked their ladies in in so many ways, that their contribution could not be underestimated. So I recommend more societies consider this show. And you could do a lot worse than link in with the Cecilian Musical Society to get their advice on set and costumes. They were absolutely fabulous in what was a super production overall. Go go go Joe!

The perfect show for early December, to put one in the mood for Christmas, and in the hands of Castlebar Musical and Dramatic Society, it was given a warm and festive treatment, in the beautiful St Mary's Hall, GMIT. The principal line up was strong, the dancers were energetic, the chorus were harmonious, and even the audience got to sing-a-long to the beautiful title song.

The only draw-back about the performance venue was the surrounding white walls and ceiling, which tended to bounce the lighting all over the place, and made it difficult to isolate the stage as the centre of attention. Perhaps a black curtain above the cyc might have given the stage a more enclosed appearance. It also tended to slightly overpower the well-selected screen projections that were a feature of the set. The set was simplicity itself, a good idea, given the numerous scene changes, and set pieces and drops did enough to suggest the various locations. With not too much to trouble them, the crew under Stage Manager, Declan Gibbons, did an efficient job of keeping running smoothly. I was aware of the efforts being made by the lighting designer, in difficult conditions, and the stunning effects of the evening were the falling snow and the superbly atmospheric moving projection of the snowy landscape when the barn doors were opened in the finale. It was like a winter wonderland. Director, Donna Ruane focused on her performers and delightfully managed to capture the essence of the seasonal story. She was blessed with a very capable cast who realised the nature of their characters with great success. The relationship between Bob Wallace and Betty Haynes was particularly well- crafted, with their initial awkwardness beautifully portrayed by the performers, and their development to a loving couple by show's end was natural and totally believable. There was a suggestion of a "Greek Chorus" with singers brought on stage in picture formation to bolster some of the musical numbers, and while it's not a strategy I particularly like, I appreciate that it echoed the great sense of community and involvement that was a backbone of this society. Comedy, throughout the show, was well-pointed and equally well-delivered. There were a few occasions when dancers were on stage as background dressing when they could perhaps have been a tad more animated, but it's a minor point.

Choreographers, Hazel McLynn and Aoife Durcan, keep their routines nicely within the capabilities of their dance ensemble. "The Best Things" and "I Love A Piano" were the best worked routines. The little ballerinas in the finale were only delightful. That beautifully sculptured relationship between Bob and Betty lay at the heart of this show, and Ronan Egan as Bob Wallace, and Vivienne Lee as Betty Haynes, were equal to the task of making it work so effectively, with two crafted and highly accomplished performances. Their timing in that awkward first encounter was close to perfection, and their ever- strengthening bond was totally believable. It helped considerably that both were also blessed with delightful vocal ability. Ronan was also the perfect straight man to John Byrne's comedic antics in the role of Phil Davis, who was always comfortable and at ease on the stage. His musicality and sense of rhythm aided him strongly in being the song and dance man, and again, he was delightfully paired with the talents of Stephanie Cassol in the role of Judy Haynes. Here was a smile that beguiled, a fine sense of comedy, and as much energy as a Duracell Bunny. She was also a very pleasant chanteuse and dancer. Michael Goulding cut a fine figure in the role of General Waverly, with a fine sense of authority coupled with a kind heart. His relationship with Martha was well-realised, and vocally, he aged well between the opening scenes and his days of retirement. As mentioned above, I would just have liked him to look physically older as the show progressed, with perhaps a more exaggerated limp from the damned shrapnel. None-the-less, this was another fine performance.

Carrie Doran was the highlight of the show for me. When she first appeared as Martha Watson, I immediately thought "Too young!", but with excellent vocal technique and well-devised physical characteristics, she proved my first impression to be completely wrong. She was a comedy delight, who never missed an opportunity to make the most of her lines and her slap-stick comedy.

Brendan Mullins was a likeable and effective Ralph Sheldrake, a good pal to the central characters, and credible and cunning as the "arranger" of their little surprise.

Emma Daly and Sandra Gibbons had a lot of fun with their ditzy roles of Rita and Rhoda, with good comedy delivery and a fine sense of the ridiculousness of their characters.

Andy Hannon gave a camp-as-a-boy's- scout-jamboree performance as the hyper-thyroid stage manager, Mike, his English accent being a nice contrast to those around him. His physical gesticulations were very good.

Jim Finan was a suitably docile and befuddled Ezekiel, and showed a good sense of delivery when his character came to life in the latter stages of the show. Young Leah Rochford was well able for the role of work-shy, wannabe performer, Susan Waverly.

She had a lovely relationship with her grandfather, a fun relationship with Martha and a palpable, annoying persistence in her desire to impress Bob and Phil. Nicely played and well-sung, young lady.

The chorus and dancers made a very good vocal contribution to the show, and physically, doing all that was required of them with energy and enthusiasm.

With a vocally strong principal line, and equally accomplished musicians in the pit, it must have been a pleasure for Musical Director, Deirdre Lee, to be at the helm of this strong musical presentation. The balance throughout was spot-on, and there were consistently good harmonies from the choruses.

The strong final scene was also enhanced by the nicest costumes of the evening, particularly those worn by the main principals. Elsewhere, the girls wore some beautiful and authentic gowns, and the men looked appropriately dapper, but there were some of the chorus costumes that looked a bit modern, albeit, Christmassy. There was some good work done on hairstyles and make-up was generally very effective, including good ageing of the General.

I haven't stopped singing "White Christmas" since I left the venue, except to sing my children to sleep with "Counting My Blessings". Thank you sincerely for getting my Christmas spirit truly invigorated by this most entertaining production.

Boyle Musical Society JOSEPH AND HIS AMAZING TECHNICOLOR DREAMCOAT I arrived in Boyle in the middle of a snow storm, and chilly though it was, the warm reception I received at the beautiful, circular St Joseph's Church made me quickly forget about the weather. How appropriate to be performing "Joseph" in St Joseph's Church! And what a delightful production it turned out to be. Given that much of the movement of the show involved negotiating the steps of the church altar, Director/Choreographer, Vivienne Moran did a remarkably fine job of keeping everything running smoothly and at a good pace. The levels were well used for creating pictures and the chorus and dancers were up and down the steps like yo-yos, in some well-drilled routines. A simple and effective set was created on the altar, and what scenery there was had been beautifully painted and constructed, and very efficiently moved by stage manager, Enda Commons and his team. There were sufficient and appropriate props. The lighting of the show was very tidy, and while more variety could have enhanced the back wall on occasions, there were many moments of sublime beauty. The star cloth worked very well, and the lighting of the finale was breath- taking, with the entire roof of the church lighting up as a rainbow. It was quite simply stunning. Characters situated UC stage tended to be weakly lit until they moved forward, but overall, the lighting was most impressive. Sound quality was consistently good, and adapted nicely for the church setting.

Anne Kielty led an effective 7 piece band, seated at the keyboard, and managed to keep good control of them and the on-stage singers. Despite a venue that isn't ideally suited to stage productions, there was a good balance of sound, and generally the delightful harmonies of the various choruses came across very nicely. Principals seemed to be thoroughly rehearsed in their music. All in all, the musical offering was of a most pleasing standard.

Karen Gordon was a homely, confident Narrator, with a very pleasant vocal quality, and great energy to also be involved in so much of the movement. She told the story well, and engaged well with the children's chorus and with the audience.

The was a likeable nature to Jamie Dockery's Joseph, even during his bragging younger days, and he had extremely good facial reactions to what was going on around him. His singing was strong and consistently good.

Damien Wallace was a relaxed Jacob, and had no problems expressing the emotions of the proud or grieving father figure. Marc Egan made the most of milking his Elvis styled Pharaoh, with a fine physical and vocal performance, meriting the encore of his number.

Tomás Smyth looked excellent as Potiphar, and reacted beautifully to the mischievous antics of his very alluring wife, Daniela Beadnall as Mrs Potiphar.

Seán McInerney as Judah, Diarmuid Beirne as Simeon and Darragh Beirne as Reuben, each gave a strong individuality and presence to their characters, and all gave a fine vocal performance. Indeed, the group of brothers were collectively strong and assured in both voice and movement, with "Those Canaan Days" being their vocal highlight.

There was a lovely solo child's voice at the start of act two, and the children's chorus throughout the show were disciplined and most delightful.

The female chorus throughout sang beautifully and were enthusiastic in all their acting and reacting. This was a very strong team effort.

A special mention, too, for the female tango dancer whose movement was fluent and effortless.

With the exception of the wive's costumes, which were suitable in style and design, but a tad lacking in colour, the costume plot for the show was beautiful, particularly in the Egyptian scenes. Styles were mostly traditional, with a few modern touches, such as Potiphar and his wife, who both looked amazing. A very good job was done on make-up too. Hair, wigs, beards, etc were all very nicely presented. But the visual masterpiece of the show was Joseph's Technicolor Dreamcoat, which opened out during the final, to about a 30ft diameter of multi-coloured fabric, loving sewed together by wardrobe mistress, Mandy Toolan. It truly was AMAZING!

The zeal and enthusiasm of the cast and crew of Boyle Musical Society made this a wonderfully entertaining night of warmth and happiness, even amid the Christmas card weather! Thank you sincerely to one and all.

St Brigid's Hall, with its lovely patron saint's cross over a fantastic poster for the production, was a great setting for Carnew Musical Society's Sister Act. The venue used to be a cinema and the old- style red seats were very atmospheric for this show - a production that seemed firmly set in the seventies, such was the disco-era decorations around the walls. Stalwarts of the society, some gentlemen even in tuxes, expertly chaperoned the audience to their seats and there was a lovely welcome given to all by MC Eamon Doran.

Four closed trucks, (each one with set-pieces hidden inside) and a cyc covering the back wall were on display for the audience as we entered. Perhaps something more might have been done here with lighting or projections to make the stage feel more special and atmospheric. Thankfully, this somewhat dull set-up would turn into something far more exciting once this show, solidly directed by Michael Dunbar, began. The moving trucks reminded me of that game where a magician hides a marble under three cups and moves them around to see if you can remember under which cup the marble lies. There was always a surprise to be found when a truck was opened, and they were moved well. I could never remember which truck was which, as surprises continued to be revealed from inside each one. I imagine a lot of organisation and planning was necessary by Stage Manager Tommy Kavanagh. Scene changes were at their best when worked into the action - the most successful being when the nuns carried on the benches and plates etc. for a meal scene, which is what they might do in a convent anyway. Cleverly, the crew wore altar-server costumes, as though they were "serving" the show.

The journey Doloris goes on, from outwardly confident, but ultimately lost gangster-broad wannabe-singer, to a person of better self-awareness was well realised. The gangsters were all styled differently to tease out the individuality of their characterisations. The nuns arrived on stage, half-dead and out of tune which was comical, establishing the convent environment well, enabling them to go on the broadest journey possible. There was a well-thought-out chase scene with various groups of nuns protecting the convent, each with their own assigned prop (mops, brushes, kitchen utensils). Choreography was by Graham Finnerty and was suitable for the group. Armography was not always in sync but I guess it could be argued that this was suitable for the characterisations of the nuns. Positioning and picture-making in 'Raise Your Voice' was good in a very exciting version of this number. 'Take me to Heaven' hopped off the stage at the end of Act 1. The nuns' movements in 'Sunday Morning Fever' were great fun, as the lines moved forward one by one. 'Spread the Love Around' finished off the show with super energy, spreading delight amongst the audience as the show came to an end. Naoimh Penston is a machine. First of all, she was Musical Director for the show. Principal singing throughout was competent and well-rehearsed. Harmonies (when we could hear them) were secure. Not only did she do a great job as MD, and maintain her duties right up until the band call (until Philip Kennedy took over as conductor) but she managed to take on the lead role as well. She performed the role of Deloris Van Cartier with style. She had attack, energy and never wasted a moment she was given. She burst onto the stage with sass, and showed a more vulnerable side in later scenes. For all her sass, Delores really finds herself in this journey and over the show, Naoimh stripped away the mask of sass and messy loudness to uncover someone more centred and brave in a different way. Her fish-out-of-water persona, when she arrived at the convent, was funny and well- observed. Her witnessing of the murder, and her hilarious attempt to retreat from the scene, were very funny. The sequence where she awkwardly blesses herself and paraphrases the 'Our Father' and the 'Pledge of Allegiance' was really good. Her singing was excellent throughout; my goodness, what a belt this woman has! She owned the stage in 'Raise Your Voice' as she bounced around like an Energizer bunny inspiring the nuns to sing.

What a treat it was to hear to Naoimh sing with such another amazing vocalist in Jennifer Byrne. Her vocal performance of Mother Superior was phenomenal. She has the ability to belt with power or deliver beautifully in classical soprano, all the better when she would mix the two in one number. In terms of characterisation, I found her a little jolly in her first introduction and I am not sure if that is the impression we were looking for. Her arguments with Doloris in the later scenes better embodied a woman who was trying to keep the rest of the nuns safe from the dangers of the world. Her face when the nuns first started singing in the church was brilliant. The scene in which she performs 'I Haven't Got a Prayer' was excellent, as she took out the bottle of booze and treated us to a musical performance that grew more brilliantly frantic at the end. She deserved the huge cheer she received from the audience after this moment. Therese Canavan Bolger had a very well developed characterisation for Sister Mary Lazarus, with a low voice and dry way of speaking. She had great line-delivery and very good comic-timing. She got some extra duties with the rapping pieces and she delivered both these moments brilliantly.

Brian O'Gorman played the part of Sweaty Eddie. He has a beautiful voice with very good resonance and super power when required. The crowd really appreciated his double striptease scene. The awkwardness between himself and Deloris in the scene in which they reminisced on their school musical was adorable and showed lovely chemistry.

Erin Hogan, as Sister Mary Robert, had some lovely acting as the young novice questioning her future. She acted her newfound confidence well, without changing the central self of her character too much. She showed off some good vocals in 'Sunday Morning Fever'.

Marie Dunne was adorable as the friendly Sister Mary Patrick. It was a nice touch to keep her Irish brogue and she was suitably jolly and warm-hearted throughout.

Monsignor O' Hara was played by John Young who did well at portraying the reserve and grace of the priest who supports the Sisters' new style of singing. Bill Stafford, as Curtis, was masculine, authoritative and imposing with a great accent. He had great presence and influence and was utterly convincing as the mob-boss. He vocalised very well also. TJ (Jimmy Spellacy), Joey (David Cox) and Pablo (Pádraig D'Arcy) were all a scream as Curtis' idiot henchmen. TJ sent up his Irish brogue, Pablo had a great Spanish accent and brilliant falsetto, and Joey… those hips… I didn't know where to look during their 'Lady in the Long Black Dress'. Very well done to all the mob for giving the audience a belly full of laughs. Ellen Kinsella and Helena O' Flynn Roche, as the skanks in the police station, helped to establish the atmosphere of the place and they sold their laughing at Sweaty Eddie with good effect. Rob Donnelly, as the tortured cab driver, did very well as he cried and shook with fear convincingly. His "You just described everywoman in Philadelphia" line was very well delivered. Costumes for this production were by NoMac. The costumes on Monsignor O' Hara and Mother Superior looked particularly rich and convincing. All of the nuns looked spectacular, with their crosses hanging from their black and white habits. The addition of their gold bling with red hearts (with just a clever half-measure for Mary Robert) looked great. Different groups of nuns, in different colours looked fantastic in 'Sunday Morning Fever'. The final bling for 'Fabulous' coupled with Deloris' white sequins and white fur looked super.

I've seen this show where all the gangsters were dressed thematically, so it was nice to see the individuality of the characters expressed in their differing costumes. Deloris looked suitably uncouth in her Act One costume. I was not sure when she had time to pack her change of clothes for leaving the convent. Perhaps, as she was planning to leave Curtis, she might have organised it. Still, the silver trousers and brown leather jacket with fur cuffs and bling top blended nicely with an upcoming number so I guess we can write that off as a suspension of disbelief. The magic involved in Sweaty Eddie's striptease was pulled off with aplomb.

Sound was by iTech productions/Joe Murphy and was hit-and-miss throughout the evening. Those nuns who had solo lines in 'It's Good to be a Nun' were required to start singing so the desk could turn up their mic (and in the final show). There was a rogue mic left on taking away from a lovely silent moment. The body of sound coming from the large nuns' chorus in Act One really didn't hit the audience the way it could have, and when it did it was tardy. The body of singing was better here in the opening of Act Two. Balance was good between the band and the performers, with the band never appearing to drown out what was happening on stage, from my seat in the balcony anyway. The gun sound-effect was very good. The echo/ reverb, to create a sense of acoustics in the convent, was great.

Lighting was designed and operated by Kevin McEvoy. More might have been done to add texture to the sleeping set as the audience filed in. The spotlight on the MC was good. The cyc was well-lighted throughout, adding atmosphere to the stage. There was a good lighting change to punctuate 'It's Good to be a Nun'. The bar was suitably dim, to evoke the dingy atmosphere. There was disco-ball effect and rainbow of lights at the end which really added to the excitement of what was happening on stage in the finale. Congratulations to Carnew Musical Society for reaching their 50th year. So much hard work is required from volunteers to keep the show on the road for that length of time so they should be very proud of themselves. All those who took part in the show, whether it was a main role, a secondary role or as a member of the ensemble did so with great commitment and enthusiasm and I congratulate all on stage for a great night's entertainment. Here's to the next 50!.

The impressive town hall in Newry is 130 years old but was recently refurbished, with additional stage lighting. The building is a character in itself and made for such a sense of occasion for the staging of this show. The stage has a beautiful arch shape with a lovely red curtain. Annie is the perfect show to stage at this festive time of year. This production brought together experienced performers with an amazing troupe of young people. I saw one of the two casts of children (over 50 in each group). The casts are not streamed, and the group is very inclusive to all applicants. The evening would be full of fine principal performances from the adult cast, that brought laughs-a- plenty. The children had super energy and commitment in moments that bounced off the stage. Then, ladies and gentlemen, there was Aoife Hughes as Annie.

Her singing voice was as professional as you are going to get for a twelve-year- old, with a lovely vibrato that is rare for someone so young. She made space in her mouth and dropped her jaw, rather than tightening to reach the high notes, showing a well-developed sense of technique. She had a super accent and very believable line-delivery. She showed a great mix of likeability and toughness. Her ability to listen and react to Warbuck's was very impressive, as was her emotional speech about wanting to find her parents. This was such a mature performance. She was exceptionally good.

Corinna McGaughey co-directed with Jim McGuigan. I was so happy to see that that hideous red curly wig wasn't used for Annie. Her hair was beautiful in Act Two, showing her journey from rags to riches. Blocking was meaningful and the relationships between the characters were well teased-out.
