There were some beautiful aesthetics throughout the evening. The orphanage in the opening scene looked particularly brilliant. There were misshapen bunk beds, painted in fluorescent green and blues. They looked fabulous as they were bathed in an atmospheric blue light, that evoked night time without losing visibility. Torn wallpaper looked really well, revealing super brickwork behind. The backdrop of the Hooverville scene was great. There were magnificent lopsided filing cabinets in Hannigan's office. They were stuffed with confiscated teddy bears, furthering the theme of the dysfunctional orphanage and enhancing the story-telling, setting and characterisations within the piece. There was a glorious aesthetic created for Warbuck's mansion. The staircase with its red carpet, and marble effect on the walls looked super. A gold and black phone and the beautiful real leather furniture looked so expensive. The plush desk was cleverly set on a bed of red carpet that hid the wheels. The gorgeous garlands on the staircase and the enormous Christmas tree were divine.

Money doesn't grow on trees however and there were some dips in the aesthetic. The dog-catcher scene was in a black box, which felt like a real dip after the super orphanage setting. It was a shame that this backdrop could not have been used in this sequence, as a black box setting was a little underwhelming after such a fabulous orphanage aesthetic. The 'NYC' scene didn't really evoke the visual wonder of New York City either. The cinema moment, with its filmic flickering light on the cast, was one of the few scenes that got away with a black box setting. The Oval Office desk was nicely positioned at an angle (and the security guard blended in comically into the black curtain). The Seal of the President of the United States looked amazing and was finished off nicely with the two American flags.

What was particularly impressive was that this set was designed by Anne Marie Campbell who only went on to play Mrs. Hannigan. She constructed the set with Dennis Walsh so she must be one busy lady. There was much to admire about her performance as the tyrannical manager of the orphanage. She was scary, pathetic, sadistic and false all in one. "You will pay for it, I promise" was delivered to Annie in such a lovely natural and understated way, which in this instance was far more effective as a result. 'Little Girls' was performed with the appropriate amount of anguish. This despair and nervousness increased again during the reprise of this number. Her final scene, as she entered Warbuck's mansion, bowing comically while holding the edges of her coat and disingenuously conducting the choir of orphans was a scream.

James McGinn, as Daddy Warbucks, was cool-headed and authoritative in his own home. His characterisation was suitably confident and competent. He has a gorgeous, low, rich speaking voice that I could listen to all night. I wondered did he present as enough of a workaholic in his first scene? For me, a little more distracted franticness might have been considered. He had some tuning issues, such as on the letter "C" in 'NYC'. He chose to speak some of his lyrics, which I think was a nice choice. His relationship with Annie was adorable and we were really rooting for him at the end. He handled the later emotional moments with very good ability. The dynamic duo of Damien Lavery as Rooster and Annette Ward as Lily were highly entertaining. Damien immediately personified the bad guy boyo with a great New York accent. He showed some great vocalising also. His partner in crime, Lily St Regis, had a fantastically high-pitched speaking voice, her ditzy posing was a hoot and her facial expressions were excellent. The trios dance moves, kick lines and hip wiggling in this number was very good, as they transferred their weight with competence. 'Easy Street' was a quality moment full of great variety in acting. Physical comedy from this pair of baddies was very good in Warbucks' mansion. Their southern accents were excellent as they pretended to be Annie's long-lost parents, Mr. and Mrs Mudge. Roisin Fearon, as Grace, immediately established herself as a ray of light in her gorgeous baby blue three-piece outfit and hat. Her hair was also beautiful. She has a gorgeous singing voice and played her role with the appropriate amount of warmth, patience and loving care.

Paddy Heaney was very nice as Drake. Miceal White as Bert Healy was characterful and committed. He vocalised in a suitable old-school style in 'Never Fully Dressed Without a Smile'. Helena Hughes, Coleen Andrews and Aoife Cranny played Bonnie, Connie and Ronnie Boylan respectively. These three singing sisters had great character and their smiling and shimmying were comical. Their harmonies were not tight but they sold the heck out of their singing, bringing a smile to everyone's face. Richard Powell was very good as the radio announcer. Conor Cinnamond as Mr Bundles had a fantastically breaking nasal voice, with funny characterisation and great line delivery. Fred McCracken as Lt Ward had a great accent and a good sense of authority. Nicole Reynolds as the Rising Star was committed to her role. Dennis Walsh is no stranger to the stage and did very well as President Roosevelt. The cabinet of men in the Presidential scene were all very well cast and played their roles in a suitably stuffy manner. This scene was well-crafted, moving and funny. There was a fabulous a capella moment of which MD Aislinn Mullholland should be very proud.

Indeed, there were plenty of lovely moments of musical direction throughout. The volume of the underscoring under the dialogue in the first scene was lovely. The children's singing was very clear in 'Hard- Knock Life'. Harmonies at the end of the Hooverville sequence were excellent. The female harmony lines were particularly well sung in the finale of Act One. There was a super sound from the large number of orphans in 'You're Never Fully Dressed Without a Smile'. The ending of the choral singing of 'I Don't Need Anything but you' was great. The final 'Tomorrow' reprise stirred all the feelings and there was an awesome harmony on "day a waaaaay". Choreography was by Ann-Marie Morgan, who was assisted by Donna King. The talents of the company were well-utilised. 'Hard Knock Life' was completely slick with excellent moves that bounced off the stage. The scrubbing was blocked to the beat and there was super energy here. Slick head movements in 'Hooverville' (messy in the right way to evoke a sense of individualism in the crowd) were very good. There was super intention from the chorus here, in terms of the acting of their dire situation. 'I think I'm Gonna Like it Here' reminded me of 'Be Our Guest' from Beauty and the Beast, such was the warmth, energy and inventiveness in this number. The 'Easy Street' routine, with all its kicking and hip-wiggling was very well executed by our trio of baddies. The orphans did an excellent tap routine, with a great sense of spacing. There was a good sense of movement from Warbucks and Annie as four couples joined them in a ballroom number. There was a fabulous moment in the mansion when the President's wheelchair and the rest of the cast were used to make a human sleigh. Each moment the chorus appeared, it was a treat for the eyes.

Stage Management was by Aimee Yates. I know about the limitations of the stage, but the scene changes were a little slow. They appeared well-planned but extremely cautious. It was very helpful when performers in a particular scene were used to bring furniture on and off. Sound was by McKusker Audio Services and Sean Keenan. There were some good sound effects, such as whistling and a chiming clock. It appeared some people with stand-alone lines were expected to deliver without a mic, which is a thing of the past, in my opinion. The body of sound from the chorus was not present in their first singing moment of 'I Think You're Gonna Like It Here'. I am not sure if this was because of sound issues, forgetfulness from the performers or miscommunication from the pit. It was not clear what went wrong but it took a while to get going. Someone got their act together, however, as the choral ending to this song was good.

Lighting design was by Rodney Ellis. There was a series of nice gobos shone on the floor to enhance the atmosphere of different scenes. The flickering light in the cinema was very clever. A lighting moment, to show the inner torment of Hannigan's mind, worked really well. There was a great lighting change on the final beat of the 'You're Never Fully Dressed Without a Smile' reprise. There was a magical change in lighting as the song grew in the Presidential scene. Warbucks' Christmas tree and the rest of the stage was stunning in dimmed lights, as Annie sat on the stairs with her suitcase, ready to leave the mansion. A spotlight moved over the band for the bows which was a nice touch.

Wardrobe personnel were made up of Paula O'Hare, Deborah Gorman, Ciara Jennings and Kathleen McAteer. The orphans all looked super in their mismatch of old-style fabrics. The sailors, well-to- do ladies and the ushers looked really well in 'NYC'. Annie wore a red and white sailor costume to show her elevation from the orphanage, and this theme was nicely repeated later on in blue. She had a lovely tartan dress also. Warbucks looked very dashing in his grey power suit. Hannigan had a flowery dress, brown shoes, red tights and a cardigan that had a complementary (but not too obvious) triangular motif. The Boylan Sisters had dark grey glittery dresses, pearls and lovely headpieces. The grey suits on the cabinet members evoked their stuffiness. The female household staff wore rich wine and white uniforms and the males wore gorgeous gold/black waistcoats, white shirts, ties and black trousers. The Cook wore blue gingham to blend with Grace's beautiful blue costume, complementing the overall colour scheme. This large chorus of well-dress household staff really added to the aesthetic when they were all on.

So I left Newry Town Hall feeling full of festive optimism. With around about 150 performers taking to the stage during that week, the future looks bright for this group, as they work towards their 20th anniversary. This was my final show to adjudicate in 2017 and it was a lovely one with which to finish.

Life appeared to be imitating art, as national news declared that many counties, including Sligo had received a weather warning that they were to get the worst of the brunt of Storm Eleanor. Then word started to filter through that a good chunk of Sligo Fun Company's cast of The Wizard of Oz had been struck down with flu. Not something to laugh about with so many cases of Aussie flu around the country. So far, not so Fun Company. As fate would have it, I was travelling to Sligo from Cavan for this post New Year's excursion - such an incredible drive through the North and Leitrim, where the sweeping valleys, mountains and green fields were gorgeous. We passed the junction of Yellow Road and I thought "now, there is a good omen". Then suddenly, as we drove through the expanse of these sweeping valleys, two rainbows burst over our heads and, again, my optimism grew. One rainbow stayed with us for an hour and a half and still sat there proudly outside the Johnston Court Shopping Centre, as we went on the obligatory toothbrush hunt. These were good signs. "Come on Sligo Fun Company", I thought, "you can get over the rainbow and be the pot of gold at the end, despite all the drama off-stage". It was announced that Kerry Golding would replace Emily Tracey as Aunty Em/Glinda, with only a couple of hours' notice, and that this would require the use of a script in parts. Kerry was lovely in these roles, showing all the grace that Aunty Em would have, as well as the regal stature of Glinda. It is so commendable that she learnt as many lines as she did in such a short space of time and she even sang her piece, showing a lovely voice also.

Steffen Jorgensen is a very busy man: He directed and stage-managed the show, as well as providing primary choreography! The characters were well-drawn and blocking was very good for the most part. The tornado was inventive - with a wind machine that blew the leaves and hay around the place, with an appropriate lightning effect. The very young Munchkins were appropriately choreographed, in the context of their overall performance experience. The Crows and Trees were choreographed by our hero stand-in Kerry Golding. The Crows, played competently by Nessa Filan, Nicole Filan and Anna Ryan, were full of effective physical comedy. It was great when they were doing different dance steps to the principals, as this added variety to the scene, but it also worked really well when they all suddenly burst into the same moves. The Jitterbug dance was choreographed by Artistic Director, Mary MacDonagh, and was the best number in the show. It had endless formations, jumping, legwork, exciting armography, energy, intention and a fantastic final picture which delighted the audience. The number also utilised individual talents within the company with two super dancing monkeys.

Musical direction was provided by Niamh Crowley. She lost two musicians to flu but she was left with eight, which ain't so bad. It is unusual to see an MD play piano so intensively with ten other musicians and, with so many younger performers, I would have thought that the MD would want to conduct only. Still, there was very little wrong with entrances etc. suggesting that a lot of preparation was done to enable the MD to double-job. The band were at a lovely level, never overpowering the performers on stage. Principal singing was competent throughout. The choral singing was difficult to measure, as there were six people missing, but the final company version of 'Somewhere Over the Rainbow' was very nice indeed.

Dorothy was played by Zoe Gordon on the night that I saw the show. She had an enormous amount of dialogue to learn and it is clear that she worked very hard on this role. She was on the ball every step of the way. She even cued one of the adults at one point. She showed a lovely singing voice and was clever enough to check in with the MD whenever she needed to confirm that she was correct, which she inevitably was.

The Scarecrow/Hunk was played by Michael Donaghy. Michael had excellent physical comedy, giving an impressive, limber physicality to the Scarecrow. He performed 'If I Only Had a Brain' very well. He is a very good mover (such as in the Jitterbug sequence) and gave us an impressive one-handed hand-stand! He was nicely charismatic with a lovely soft and suitable speaking voice. He appears to be the man to trust with the harmony lines also, showing that he is an accomplished all-round performer.

The Tinman/Hickory was played by Trevor Gorman. He was suitably hysterical in his opening scenes and was fantastically emotional for a man with "no heart". 'If I Only Had a Heart' was very enjoyable. It is no easy feat to perform in that silver make-up and the silver suit, so well done on a very committed performance.

Kieran Cunnane nailed the roles of Zeke/ The Lion. He showed competent vocalising in 'King of the Forest' and 'If I Only Had the Nerve'. He was scared or adorable when needed and had great presence in the Lion's more competent moments. Angela McGuire was very good as Miss Gultch/The Wicked Witch of the West. She had the right amount of unlikeability as Miss Gultch and she nailed the speaking voice of the Wicked Witch. She was the perfect baddie overall.

The Professor/The Wizard of Oz was played with good presence by Darren Kerr. He had a very good accent and speaking voice and delivered his material with competence.

Uncle Henry/Guard was played by Franny Curley. As the Guard, he was characterful, and his comedic turn in the opening of Act Two was appreciated very much by the audience.

Trevor Horan, Sadhbh Hanley and Joseph Harrison as the Mayor, the Coroner and Barrister respectively all had great facial expressions and delivered their lines with very clear speaking voices. The rest of the Munchkins were adorable and reacted very well when Glinda suggested going to the Wizard. The trees, played by Alannah Donoghue, Saoirse O'Donovan and Annie Buick, were full of the appropriate amount of attitude and they sang well. There was huge energy and commitment by the chorus in the Emerald City and they deserved their huge cheer from the audience. The menacing movements by the Monkeys in the scene in which Dorothy is held captive were excellent and added energy to this moment.

Costumes were sourced and managed by Therese Lee, Martina Higgins and Angela McGuire and Make-Up was by Cillian Oates. Dorothy wore the infamous blue gingham dress, white socks and black shoes. Her red ribbons were the only hint of colour in the opening Kansas sequence.  The Professor wore a nice black suit with pinstriped waistcoat and a white shirt with black neck-ribbon. This suit was re-used when he appeared as the Wizard. I am sure this was symbolic of the ordinary man behind the façade of Oz, but all the other characters changed so it was still a little jarring that he did not. To go to Oz is to be transported over the rainbow and I think colour is important here. Otherwise, wouldn't Dorothy have just recognised him as the man she met in Kansas? Glinda's lovely pink dress, gorgeous head-piece and beautiful staff complimented her lovely blonde hair. The Wicked Witch of the West's black dress and bling belt looked very well, and her charcoal grey hat was fabulous.

The Scarecrow costume might have had more detail; such as patches in contrasting colours etc., as his clothing looked a little human, albeit well-stuffed with straw. His yellow face and wide mouth looked well. The Tin Man's silver face looked great in the beginning. His pores seemed to absorb the silver as the show went on, the poor man, and I would suggest a touch-up was needed. His costume looked great on the outset but his Velcro came apart and revealed red lining within. The Lion's costume and face-paint was perfect. There might not have been enough time for this trio to rehearse their quick change, but I assume this took place side-stage with as many people helping as possible? It was unusual that the Guard was not dressed in shades of Green, but rather a red tunic with a gold shield of arms. He wore a Lion symbol on his chest and I wondered was that on purpose. The Jitterbugs looked fantastic all dressed in black with their brilliant antennae on their heads. While I was surprised to see less green in the Emerald City than I might have expected, the polka dot embellished multicoloured costumes were very pretty. The boys wore tartan pyjama bottoms with white T-shirts, that prominently displayed the word 'Oz'. One man had a really cool green beard in the Emerald City. Nico, the main flying monkey, was wearing those tartan PJs worn by some of the Citizens of Oz. Was this a throwback to the idea that he used to be a person? Interesting.

Francis Heraghty and Rory Kelly constructed the set. Two ladders either side of the closed curtain framed the stage symmetrically which gave good opportunity for the Wicked Witch of the West to gain height on the rest of the characters. The curtain opened to reveal an impressive screen at the back that would feature a series of images over the course of the narrative. I think this show lends itself really well to the use of projections as the images required are to such an enormous scale. For the most part, the images chosen were successful. I think it was a shame to not grey-scale the Kansas images to give more impact to the eventual colour of Oz. Sometimes, the characters changed location but the slide didn't change. Slides were tardy at times. I suggest the following sequence: black- out, new slide (to establish the upcoming scene in lovely darkness and to give the audience something to take in while the rest of the staging is changed) and then lights up.

Lighting was designed by Maurice Power and operated by Gary Maguire. Oz had a burst of warm yellow light when Dorothy first arrived, which juxtaposed nicely with the dullness of Kansas, and this theme was repeated each time 'We're off the see the Wizard' kicked in. The blue and green light in the spooky forest really added to silhouettes of scary trees. A lighting change to isolate the snow might have been nice, particularly as this very good effect was still somewhat narrow. The Emerald City was texturised with green, blue and yellow lighting which was nice. I suggest that a blackout was necessary to allow the Wicked Witch of the West to leave after her melting scene. A special on Dorothy, as she chanted "There's no place like home", was very effective.

Sound was provided by Vinnie Higgins. Balance was good between the band and the performers, with the band never over-powering the performers on stage. The Munchkins' singing was hard to hear, but perhaps confidence was lowered by the loss of some cast members. An oil can sound effect in the Tin Man's first scene was good as was the echo when the Scarecrow banged on his new metallic friend's chest. The off-stage backing vocals for "You're Out of the Woods" were difficult to hear. The Wizard's voice had a nice gravelly sound effect.

Props were by the extremely busy Wicked Witch of the West/Costumer Angela McGuire. The Professor's black bag and "authentic crystal" looked well. The flowers in the hands of the Lullaby League and the lollipops for the Lollipop Guild looked great. The Wicked Witch of the West's broom was super. The apples thrown by the trees looked well. A large silver blinged scissors, used to pretty-up our heroes when they arrived in Oz, was fun. The hourglass used to time Dorothy's demise looked fantastic.

There is an old adage in theatre: If an animal appears on stage, everyone just stares at the animal. Why? Because the animal is simply 'being' and this is bizarrely mesmerising. It is told as advice to actors who should endeavour to be more like this, and 'be' the character rather than simply pull faces etc.  Toto had FAR too much free reign. Hardly anyone was listening to the well-learnt dialogue when he was running around the stage. If the audience weren't panicked about him falling off the stage, they were in hysterics when he was licking the ear of the trumpet player. I would suggest that this is unfair to the rest of the actors and disrespectful to the story-telling. An actor might have tripped over him either, which is a health and safety issue. When one actor fell to the floor screaming, the dog became startled. When the company bow was happening, and hands were raised, this choked the dog. I suggest a massive re-consideration of how animals are used in productions from now on. He should have been held more and disposed of whenever possible. Thankfully, with such a dramatic week off-stage for the entire company, the adorable Toto was the only 'disaster' I can report. Artistic Director Mary MacDonagh outlined a very lovely vision for the group in her programme address, firmly placing the focus on affording "young people an education in the world of theatre with an emphasis on fun, personal development, self-esteem and a mutual respect for all". The community pulled together to support each other that week, in a situation that might develop those skills more than any other theatrical experience. Society stalwart Fintan Whelan wisely stated that "the show must go on". And it did. And all was well that ended well in Hawk's Well Theatre.

I am not aware of another society associated with AIMS who does as long a run as Ballywillan Drama Group undertook with their 'loverly' production of My Fair Lady. Nor am I aware of a lengthier show. Sometimes the company performed this mammoth piece twice a day, which is an outstanding achievement. There was not a spare seat in the house in the University of Ulster's Riverside Theatre in Coleraine, as the mostly stand-alone set greeted the audience as they arrived. From the moment the ensemble first appeared, it was clear we were in good hands, as they burst onto the stage with character, energy and intention. There was no sign of fatigue here. Then we were introduced to the fantastic front line, and I knew, this is going to be good… Director Brian Logan, with Assistant Director Alan McClarty, did a fantastic job in a challenging space. While it is a pleasure to watch a show in this space, from an audience point of view, it is difficult to stage a musical in a theatre that appears to have little room backstage and barely any wings. This required Brian to design a stand-alone set for a narrative that very clearly changes from one famous place to another. This was, for the most part, cleverly actualised. There was a painted pink and light orange circular floor-design which added warmth and energy to the centre point of the stage. It was abstract enough to work as tiling in the street scenes or a plush carpet in the interior settings. It was a good idea to make the floor so striking in a theatre of this nature, with its amphitheatre of stadium seating, as the audience had a very definite view of the floor.

The rest of the set changed in subtle ways only. The opening street scene had a smoking fire-feature and crates shaped a nice space for the ensemble to naturally inhabit the street. The smoking fire itself was very atmospheric, cleverly off-centre, giving a focal point to some of the ensemble, while leaving centre stage free for the main action. This scene changed effortlessly to the interior scene (with its famous upper mezzanine level), simply by changing a fanned backdrop and removing a street lamp etc, opening up a hidden bookshelf and adding a desk (filled with props), a blue chair and the red chaise longue.

The Ascot scene was created by adding the looped curtain over an entrance and a silhouette of a horse and jockey in the upper background. A pair of Transylvanian flags were all that was needed for the Embassy Ball. An S-shaped garden furniture and background tree was just enough to establish Mrs Higgins' house. If I were to be picky about one aspect of set design, it was how Higgins' front door did not open in the street scene in which Freddy was waiting. The cast had to swoop in and out behind it. Of course, I know that it would have been the desired effect for the door to open and close, and no doubt the space challenges prevented this, but I still cannot say that this piece of scenery worked as cleverly as the rest. I was also unconvinced that the mezzanine level should have been used for this street scene either. With only a door to establish the sense of space, it was a little jarring that the chorus also walked on the level over the door. To me, they either looked like they were in the house or walking on top of the house. I suggest we have to be very clever, when designing sets in the abstract, that we use the blocking just as much as furniture to establish a sense of space. Elsewhere, the blocking was meaningful, and actors moved, sat, stood or lunged at one another with purpose. The choice to use furniture, primarily, to establish a sense of space would not have been so successful, if it were not for a committed large group of stage personnel who managed to change the scenery in a prompt but controlled fashion. While the skeleton of the set did not move, the design was clever and new places were established by changing small details in the aesthetic. Nonetheless, there were lots of small fiddly bits and this could have been a drawn out cumbersome exercise. Thankfully, the large committed stage crew seemed well prepared by Stage Manager David Wray; competent in their duties, carrying out their tasks in a speedy yet unpanicked fashion. No doubt this team were well organised and clear on their responsibilities. The ensemble was kept on for as long as possible, dancing and hollering to keep the energy and atmosphere up, meaning that each scene flowed into the other and the scene changes rarely felt like a lull.

Musical Direction was by Eric Boyd, who was assisted by Andrew Robinson. The musicians were nicely tucked in at the side, without much choice I would imagine. Still, the band felt part of the overall show nonetheless. Eric has that effortless ability to set tempo by playing the keyboard, rather than using hand signals. He had the aid of a page turner and the eight musicians played very well. Obvious engagement by the MD with the performers did not seem necessary either. This suggests to me that principals and ensemble were very well prepared for their roles. The front-line were so competent in what they had to do, and chorus sang with confidence throughout.

Choreography and Musical Staging was by Sharon Logan, who was assisted by Laura Fisher. Each time the chorus appeared they were fully in character while bringing a fun element to all they did. Talents were utilised throughout the company, as those who had a particular skill-set for dance were allowed to shine. There were different things happening around the stage during ensemble numbers, adding detail and variety, making everything feel very natural and holistic. Moves were indicative of the time, suitably simple in places, well- rehearsed and always delivered with energy, commitment and enthusiasm. The 'Ascot Gavotte' was filled with dynamic head, fan and umbrella movements. The final pictures were always lovely throughout. The ensemble appeared to be having fun and thus we had fun with them. The bows were danced; which kept up the energy right to the end, something that was necessary in such a long show. The role of Eliza Doolittle was played with competence by Katie Patton. She is an excellent singer who looks and sounds like she has had lots of training, a very good sense of technique and can mix her voice perfectly. She inspired confidence each time she sang. She captured the sense of the rough-around-the-edges earlier Eliza, she explored her transition with convincing and comic style and she emerged from her chrysalis as an elegant and mature product of Higgins' teaching, and her own hard work. She mapped Eliza's development very well from frantic flower girl to composed and confident ingénue. This was a super performance, overall.

Professor Henry Higgins was played by Assistant Director Alan McClarty. Higgins is so over-the-top misogynistic that it is comical and, rightly or wrongly, we enjoy the ridiculousness of his behaviour. He caught the ill-tempted dismissive ignorant way that he treats Eliza in the earlier scenes very well. The arc of Higgins' semi-transformation to a slightly softer, slightly more self-aware, slightly more humble man was well constructed, particularly evident in the change of tone at the end of 'I've Grown Accustomed to Her Face'. There were shades of Alan Rickman in places. His action and diction were very good, and his vocalising of these very wordy, high energy numbers was excellent. Like Katie, he had an extraordinary amount of material to learn and both inspired confidence with their masterful delivery of the work.

Richard Mairs was equally marvellous as the horrible yet highly entertaining Alfred P. Dolittle. His drunken acting, Del-Boy style attitude, his comic yet naturalistic line delivery, and his physical comedy were all excellent. There was a darkness to his character that I have not seen before. He was less ridiculous and more baddie than I am used to seeing. He was utterly convincing in his speech and movements and we got just enough of fun to enjoy his entertaining numbers, without losing that interesting darkness to his personality. Paul Sleet as Colonel Pickering was the perfect foil to Higgins. He was more balanced, fairer, more decent than the Professor. He is the type of actor that must be very good in plays, such was the naturalism to his acting. He played it straight, and less ridiculous-toff as I have seen in the past, yet like his fellow cast mates, delivered the comedy in a convincing way when necessary, such as the telephone call to the Home Office and some bullfighter dance moves in 'The Rain in Spain'. His reactions and listening skills were excellent.

This high standard of acting, that combined naturalism and convinceability with just the right amount of humour, was once again found in Olive Hemphill's performance as Mrs Higgins.

Olive appeared in this company's first ever musical twenty-three years ago and her experience has stood to her. She showed a suitable amount of shock at Ascot, without becoming a hysterical caricature. She was well able to handle her son and his antics and she was convincingly warm to Eliza when she took refuge at her home. She is another performer who knows how to listen and react very well and give us a giggle when required.

Another actress who managed to manoeuvre her way from stern to warm was Laura Fisher as Mrs Pearce. She showed all the suitable panic a housekeeper in such a home would when a common flower girl turns up at the house. She was perfectly insistent that Higgins establish the terms in which Eliza would stay and she gradually warmed to the young girl as the play moved on. Whether she was harsh or soft, she was always in the role of protector and measured her reactions very well indeed.

Peter Easton, as Freddy Eynsford-Hill, had all the wide-eyed love-sick youthful optimism required to play another form of foil to Higgins. He was the perfect goody for Eliza, who otherwise has to contend with various forms of abuse from the Professor and her father. He played the Ascot moments, in which he found Eliza charming and funny, very well. He had all the warmth necessary and his singing was very nice. He held the final note of 'On the Street Where You Live' beautifully.

Jim Everett showed a good range as an actor by playing George the Bartender and Professor Zoltan Karpathy. His accent was very good as George, suitably frustrated by Doolittle's earlier antics and suitably pandering towards him when Doolittle hits the big time. He made an appropriate nuisance of himself as Karpathy and he added a sense of comedy and tension to this part of the show.

Patrick O' Connor and Matt Suddaby were full of character as Doolittle's partners in crime, Jamie and Harry. They had great accents and all the energy and commitment needed to sell the fun of these sequences.

Tom Waddell played the Butler and Lord Boxington. His is upper-lip was suitably stiff throughout his performances and he managed his material well.

The relationships between the characters were well explored with convincing naturalism. There was plenty of dynamic drama sparking off Higgins and Eliza. Characters charted their way nicely through their own journeys: Higgins moved from stoic misogynist to self-doubting semi-romantic. Eliza moved from messy street urchin to an empowered woman of grace. Pickering moved from bystander to active defendant of Eliza. Mrs Pearce's harsh-exterior melted away as the entire household began to root for Eliza. Doolittle went from tortured bankrupt to tortured bank-roller and Mrs Higgins went from shocked snob to supportive champion of her son's student.

I might argue that Eliza delivered too much to the audience at times. This needed to be cheated more, so that the audience can see her face without it feeling like she is breaking the fourth wall and delivering so much directly to the audience, as though it were a concert. I might argue that Zoltan Karpathy's accent was a little thick. I acknowledge that he is Hungarian but if Higgins was able to transform Eliza's accent, so deeply embedded in her way of speaking, and Karpathy was his greatest student, who speaks 32 languages and claims to be able to cite Eliza's origins, I imagine that Higgins would have helped him establish more of an RP accent, like he did with Eliza.

The costumes, provided by Utopia Costumes and co-ordinated by Lisa Mairs, Sharon Logan and Ann McCubbin, were sublime throughout. The ensemble in the street scenes were cute as a button with their hats, caps, suits and petticoats, and when ladies and gentlemen of a higher caste appeared in the street, it was very obvious by their fine attire. The clothing worn by the principals was suitable throughout and completely convincing. Higgins and Pickering always looked as though their suits and smoking jackets were expensive, as was Doolittle's rig-out when he had made it good and was about to get married. The maids' black and white dresses and aprons looked fantastic. Mrs Pearce looked super in her smart, modest and sensible brown uniform dress. The chrome motif in the Ascot scene was stunning and everyone looked marvellous at the Embassy Ball. Eliza's first costume was lovely, and she looked gorgeous in her later, more upper-class, outfits. Some of the hats throughout caused sight-line issues. While they were fabulous, the performers needed to cheat their heads more, so their faces could always be seen. Hair and Wig design was by the very busy Sharon Logan. There was a long list of people to help with this backstage and make-up was supervised by Chloe Freedman. Katie Patton's real-life natural curls were gorgeous and the use of the hair-piece for the ball was clever. Mrs Pearce's wig gave her the perfect hair style. Zoltan's messy black-wig and long scraggly beard might have been a little over-the-top considering the naturalism of the rest of the show and the high quality of wigs and make-up elsewhere, but I understand the comedy that was intended. Those in the street-scenes were always suitably dirtied up.

The use of a follow-spot on principals was excellent and gave clear focus to those who were singing, particularly when they are surrounded by many other performers. The end part of 'I Could Have Danced All Night' used a nice spot-light effect. There was a super rain-effect that made it look as though it was lashing rain onto the whole stage A gobo before 'I'm Getting Married in the Morning' gave a lovely sense of twilight to the early morning session and the wash of warm yellow light gave great energy to the dawn.

Sound design was by Darren Gardiner and was excellent throughout. Balance between the band and the performers was very good and every word could be heard perfectly. Those who had solo lines within choral moments were always heard clearly. There was a good horse-racing effect used in the Ascot Race. The crackling behind the pre-recorded gramophone pieces was good. Mrs Higgins' microphone could have matched her own skin tone more closely, to enhance subtlety.

Properties designed by Karen Hunter were of a high quality. Higgins' desk was well-dressed. The gramophones looked excellent. The bird cage, the broadsheet newspapers, the pipes, the baskets with flowers, the goblets, the tea-cups were all high quality and excellently sourced. The ending chosen was more sentimental than I have previously seen, with Higgins walking towards Eliza on his final "slippers" line. It was the ending we all wanted, but perhaps should not have gotten. It suggested a very transformed Higgins, which is more optimistic than usually imagined for a man whose most romantic moment culminates in the line 'I've grown accustomed to her face'. Still, this was a tiny few seconds in what was, overall, a very well-produced and performed show. Each and every person who appeared as part of the ensemble was full of character and brought their acting skills to create engaging crowd scenes. The transition from street-workers to aristocratic society people to subordinate household staff was very well achieved. Each time the chorus appeared, it was a joy. The energy, commitment and pace of the front-line never lulled, as they dynamically drove the narrative forward with competence and skill, culminating in a great night's entertainment.

I believe that Sister Act: The Musical owes its success to those fantastic numbers performed by the nuns' chorus. Firstly, there ain't nothing funnier than a dancing nun. Secondly, these songs are absolute showstoppers and can even manage to fill this miserable old adjudicator with glee. But they have to be performed well, otherwise they never really live up to the expectations created by the studio versions. In this capacity, however, Trim Musical Society surpassed all expectations and gave versions of these choral bangers that I will not forget for a long time. Nothing less than perfect will do for Musical Director Dermot O'Callaghan and this was evident by the rich choral singing, texturised with varied and easy to hear lines of harmony. The intricacy of the harmonies in 'Sunday Morning Fever' was very impressive and the descant added another rich layer. 'Raise Your Voice' raised the roof, such was the power, accuracy and intention of the singing. My reaction was visceral. I was covered in goose-bumps from head to toe. I am not sure what was happening to me, but it was full-body. Someone needs to video Dermot conducting the 'Life I Never Led'. Dermot's signalling to the musicians was very clear and it was evident that he wanted certain dynamics from the players. He did not just keep time. He conducted in a committed and meaningful way.  The way he felt every moment of the score, it was as though he was caressing the music. It was like he was hypnotised by the orchestra, and this ensured rich and varied playing from the musicians.

At times we were teetering towards the edge of the band being too loud and overpowering the vocals slightly. This is the curse of these smaller venues with no pit or way of re-locating the band. And how can the MD know if this is happening halfway down the hall? How can the sound person control how loudly the band are playing? How can the musicians know? It is a shame when this happens, particularly when a cast would be rehearsed to the high standards enabled by this MD. Thankfully, it never got too bad and every moment was still very enjoyable. Director Peter Kennedy enabled fantastic acting performances from all on stage. The characters were well-drawn from the sassy but sincere Deloris to the stoic Mother Superior, the cruel Curtis and his henchmen of stooges, the troupe of nuns (who were all so individualised and absolutely hilarious), the highly entertaining Monsignor O'Hara and the nerdy but lovable Eddie. Peter's direction teased-out a lot of comedy with some slapstick moments that induced rolls of laughter in the audience.

Added lines, such as "This is the only time the Catholic Church allows protection", as Monsignor O'Hara places cotton wool in his ears, shocked the audience into laughter. Deloris' luggage contained a vibrating something or other, which was a good gag. There was plenty of slapstick in Curtis' song 'When I Find my Baby' as he was supported by his henchmen of clowns. Three nuns were added to 'Lady in the Long Black Dress', giving something original to this song, and I always congratulate innovation such as this. The function of the song, comically, is not worlds apart from the first gangster number, so it was nice to see something fresh. It was funny to see the Altar boys falling asleep in mass. The riot scene involved pulling Deloris into the washing basket, which was fun and functional. Pablo falling into the basket was a good stunt also. Deloris' brought back her original was a good stunt also. Deloris' brought back her original backing singers for the end, showing that she did right by these girls and never lost touch with her roots. Eddie appeared in his fantasy costume for the curtain call, proving that everyone's dreams had come true.

While comedy was to the fore in this version, I loved how the ever-hilarious Monsignor O'Hara played the news of the church/convent closing with honesty and how sincere the Mother Superior's response was. I would have liked a little more sprinkling of such sincerity throughout the rest of the narrative. With Deloris' court date being pushed out for a year, for example, I was not convinced that there was much really wrong with this news, as it was all sort of played for laughs. Mother Superior was a little baddie-ish when she got that call that Deloris would be transferred. I think this is more of a complicated moment than that. I think it is important that the characters carry themselves within what Stanislavski would call the given circumstances. It was, of course, funny when the nuns squared up the Mother Superior after she dismissed Deloris, but a part of me cannot help but think that this would never happen in such a scenario.

The nuns have taken an oath of obedience, and if they were to break it, it should be in a nun-like way. If you look at the movie versions of this tale, you will never see any of the characters step out of their station, despite being very funny.

I've seen the moment when Deloris has to say goodbye to the nuns played in a truly heart-breaking way, and I found that more impactful than playing it for laughs. It appeared, at time, that it was a case of 'anything for a laugh'. And laugh they did, so maybe I need to get in the party- mood and not take it all so seriously. The moment Deloris stepped in front of her sisters to protect them against Curtis was touching, however.

Choreography by Aisling Rountree was excellent. She left no stone unturned in devising her routines. It is unusual to see the opening number danced by the chorus. I understand why the production team would want to give more opportunity to the girls to perform and if you have a talented troupe of girls, you might as well use them. That said, the excitement of the number did not evoke the misery of Deloris' showbiz career to date and was in danger of taking away from some of her later date and was in danger of taking away from some of her later success. Perhaps more might have been done to illustrate that Deloris did not actually have twenty backing dancers in her rather tragic audition for Curtis. I am not sure that someone, who did not know the show in advance, would realise that the dancers were only in Deloris' head. Or were they? The slapstick choreography in 'When I Find my Baby' elicited great laughs from the audience, as the lads were massively committed to this number, selling every move. All of the elements combined for 'Raise Your Voice': great performances, amazing choral work and super spacing and movement to become an unforgettable showstopper. Seven nuns appeared elsewhere with lighted lettering spelling out D.E.L.O.R.I.S. which was inspired. Deloris Van Cartier is a mammoth role and Louise Cassidy performed it with confidence and competence. With those vocals, we always knew we were in good hands. She socked 'Fabulous, Baby!' to the audience, moving on every bit. Her intention in the 'Sister Act' number was really lovely, and we could really "recognise" the star she wanted to be. She carried the show superbly and, overall, she was fabulous, baby!

Siobhán Fawsett as Mother Superior had a commanding speaking voice, rolling her r's as she established herself with great presence. She has a very rich singing voice, with a lovely way of sustaining her vowel sounds. Her stoic face contrasted brilliantly with the glee of Monsignor O'Hara when Deloris pulled them into a routine.

Megan Pottinger was adorable as Sister Mary Robert and utterly convincing as this shy, meek little thing, desperately trying to unearth some self-confidence. Her tight arms and clenched fists never relaxed, more impressively when she stood up to Mother Superior, ensuring that she did not abandon the true quiet nature of her part, even if she was acting out-of- character. She knocked 'The Life I Never Led' out of the park, evident by the insane reaction she received from the audience. She varied the dynamics of her vocal from soft and vulnerable to eruptive belt. She re-started the song in a small and subtle way, so it had somewhere to grow and her final note was awesome. I believe she is 19, and heretofore, played child roles in the society. Well, ladies and gentlemen, a star is born.

Emma Stowe created excellent facial expressions, vocal quality and physicality as the foul-tempered Sister Mary Lazarus. Her waving of the baton and her lame laugh after "You made a joke" was hilarious. A super job. She was matched by Áine Fox as Sister Mary Martin-of-Tours who was equally hilarious in her forgetfulness and senility.

Jenny Seery as Sister Mary Patrick was wonderfully jolly throughout, evoking the fun that this character brings to proceedings. Her facial expressions were always entertaining. Her sultry delivery of "I don't know how…" was a hoot.

It was incredulous how old Gwen Bagnall looked as Sister Mary Teresa. She created a physical performance that added significantly to this characterisation and she added a lovely dimension to the scenes she was in.

Seán Fox as Monsignor O'Hara managed to combine sincerity over the future of the church/convent with hilarity with his reactions to the new-found success of the choir and the resources it was creating to save the day. His obligatory ramped- up Irish accent was fun, as was his faux American accent when the performer in his character burst out.

Ronan Walsh had a characterful speaking voice as Sweaty Eddie. He explored some physical comedy while banging his hand off the table or missing his seat. His change from nerdy to Mr Cool in 'I Could be That Guy' was comic and we got hints of this strong voice and great control here, particularly with the high note.

Ian Rountree as Curtis had a cool speaking voice. He performed 'I'm Gonna Find That Girl' well, as he growled and roared his vocals with character. Seán Flanagan as Joey led the posse of stooges well and was particularly funny in 'Lady in the Long Black Dress'. John Higgins played TJ very well as a goof-ball village idiot. Kevin Hartnett was very good as Pablo. He got a great reaction on his falsetto moment in 'Lady in the Long Black Dress'.

Laura Cahill as Tina and Helen McHugh as Michelle had good accents and gave good support to Deloris in her opening good accents and gave good support to Deloris in her opening scenes/numbers. Vincent Russell played his part as Ernie well and gave us a great laugh in his cameo as the Cross Dresser.

These aforementioned nuns and their unnamed counterparts were responsible for blowing the roof off the building with their amazing choral work. Each nun was perfectly individualised and every time they appeared, they had fantastic facial expressions and reactions and were a joy to behold.

Stage Management was by Frank Connolly. Scene changes were well- rehearsed and swift and utilised the cast where appropriate. It was a shame that some small vamp could not have been explored as the very swift scene changes seemed longer because of the silence. Andrew Reddy was in charge of wardrobe and ensured that everyone was very well turned-out on the evening. The black- sequined dresses with coloured belts (some matching with the wigs) on the dancers in the opening number looked well.

There were very genuine looking individual costumes on the gangsters. Deloris wore an animal-print dress with knee-high F.M. (Father Mulcahy) boots. Tina and Michelle wore pink and silver sequins with green jackets and silver belts. Curtis was dressed in menacing colours in his black suit/waistcoat, red shirt and white tie. Less 70s looking were the skanks in the cop station who wore long black boots red/black dresses and gorgeous contemporary curly blow- dries. The gold panels with red hearts looked great in the finale of Act One. The multi-coloured habits for the opening of the second act looked super also. The black-sequined above-the-knee dresses in the reprise of 'Fabulous, Baby!' were cool. The sunglasses on Monsignor O'Hara were a scream, as was the baseball cap on Mary Lazarus.

The pyjamas on the nuns in the night-time scene were wrong. My own mam, now in her sixties, did not start wearing PJs until the early 90s. Having given up all worldly possessions, as the script suggests, the nuns would most likely have had more feminine, yet gawdy, night dresses, possible standard issue and would not have looked like they just popped to Pennys, hun. Those who wore night dresses were much closer to the mark. Hair and Make-Up was by Ali Murphy, Jacquie Walsh and Sandra Byrne. Deloris' hair was an advanced hairspray-powered Ginger/Scary Spice hybrid, finished with a bucket full of glitter, giving her the physical presence of a star. The multi- coloured bobs on the dancers in the opening looked cool. The blonde Farrah Fawcett wigs on Tina and Michelle looked great and evoked the 70s nature of the scene. The Gangster's wigs/moustaches/ sideburns transformed the actors entirely and gave them a very definite 70s look. It was extraordinary how successful the aging make-up was on Gwen Bagnell. I was agog. The short wigs on the nuns, when in their nightdresses, was special, enhancing their characterisation and showing lovely attention to detail. The Elvis wig on Monsignor O'Hara was gas. The pink wigs on the Chorus in the reprise of 'Fabulous, Baby!' were groovy.

Set Design was by Wayne Handy. Set Construction by Enda Nugent and Frank Connolly used the space well to actualise the narrative. While the curtains were closed before the show, the confessional boxes were stored on stage right, the stained glass windows on stage left, and the two tables (with two and three chairs) sat in front of the curtain - using the space efficiently, giving us just enough to get us in the mood before the show started, without giving the whole set away in advance.

The intricate stained-glass windows looked great from the audience. The fuller set had lovely columns and brick work, with a piece that opened at the back, sporting various backdrops to change up the locations. It was very cool how the nuns entered from this location in the reprise of 'Fabulous, Baby!' An extra wing popped out to help make an extra sense of space, such as in the cop station, with its very nice police emblem. This space was quickly transformed into the Mother Superior's room by changing the detail on this extra flat and covering the desk with a tablecloth. The large statues of Jesus and Mary looked great. The giant TV was awesome and the best I've seen so far in terms of re-creating this slightly cumbersome moment.

Lighting was by Darren Kelleher and used specials to punctuate solos, celestial beams of back-lighting and some disco fun when the up-tempo numbers kicked in. The coloured movers and the disco ball added retro excitement to the opening and the movers kicked in again on 'Fabulous, Baby!'. Lights shone into the audience on the final 'Amen' of 'It's Good to be a Nun'. Purple seems to be Deloris' signature colour and there was nice use of purple light, combined with a nice white special on the leading lady, in the sequences in Eddie's house. The obligatory disco lights in the finale added to the energy of the party.

Sound was by Alan White and, for the most part, was successful at ensuring balance between the band and the performers. There were times when nothing could be done about the volume of the band. The counterpoint between Eddie and Mother Superior was hard to hear as it was all getting a bit deafening. Reverb, as Deloris shouted the word "Stop!", worked well as this was all happening in her head.

Peter Kennedy directed a solid show that treated every moment as important and aimed to create as much laughter as possible from the audience. The chorus were impressively prepared by Dermot and Aisling to blow the audience away with these choral numbers. I have to congratulate Dermot on getting into the spirit of things and transforming into the Pope for the final moment. His reveal was slick and gave everyone a great laugh. 'Spread the Love Around' was reprised after the bows to give the crowd one last moment of elation. And they had a ball, so this aim was well and truly achieved. My goodness me, do Trim Musical Society know how to throw a theatrical party. Such fun!

There were signs everywhere for My Fair Lady as I drove into Ballinrobe, including a lovely banner strewn across the main street. "You must be going to the musical", asked Bean an Tí Bríd knowingly as I checked into the B&B. I was not the only guest who had travelled to see the show and she couldn't wait to see it on Friday. In the local restaurant, before the show, as I was grabbing a lonely Valentine's bite to eat, I could hear a man asking the chef "Did the musical end like that when you did it?" "That's right" says she, "with just himself and herself left on the stage". Perhaps she had been involved in the society's 1993 production. The society was founded in the 1940s and was resurrected in the 1970s. The throngs of people attending Ballinrobe Musical Society's show were a final testament to the incredible community spirit and excitement that was evident during my trip there. "I've Grown Accustomed to her Face" was as romantic as this Valentine's Day was going to get. Thankfully the production was excellent, with direction that concerned itself very much with the pace of the beast, and fine principal performances that makes this classic show such an enthralling study of human relationships.

The inventive set, which took the breath away as we entered, was designed by David Nevin and John O' Shea (with scenic artistry by Michelle Conway). Its clever design meant it would be expertly manoeuvred by Stage Manager John O'Shea and his crew. Higgins' House, which had a lovely three-dimensional outer façade, was easily opened out to reveal an interior that exuded opulence and attention to detail. It was very well dressed, with numerous ornaments and props, by John Hyland, Gwen Costello and Anita Heneghan. There were excellent posters/diagrams exploring the elements of speech, which really evoked Higgins' profession. The staircase was very nicely placed on stage right, giving us just the right amount of upper-level. The pub had fantastic lettering - 'The Quiet Woman' - and looked quaint from the outside. A fence, white chairs, table and white double doors with plant pots and foliage were used to create Mrs Higgins' house. This looked minimalistic but very effective as Mrs Higgins' house and was a lovely surprise. It was the set that just kept on giving.

If I am to be picky, I was not convinced that the use of a dreamy star-cloth evoked the London skyline. For me, a star-cloth works much better in a highly romanticised show, such as Beauty and the Beast. If time and money grew on trees, I would have loved to have seen a London City backdrop.

But what about what the stuff that took place on this fabulous set? Peter Kennedy thankfully understood the onus on a director of My Fair Lady to problem solve the fact that the show is two and a half days long. This was significantly well- realised in the beginning of Act Two, which cleverly saw an amalgamation of the Embassy Ball scene and the Higgins' debrief afterwards. This felt filmic or cinematographic. As Higgins told the story of the ball, it happened before our eyes. If he quoted his old Hungarian student Zoltan Karpathy, for example, Karpathy spoke this line instead, really bringing the scene to life. It can be hard in any musical for an audience to pick up on every lyric and this a wordy show full of endless (but brilliant) monologues. To break the whole scene down into more accessible and comprehensible moments like this was inspired.

Elsewhere, pace and rhythm were well teased-out. Higgins' meandering up the stairs on the slow bit of 'I'm an Ordinary Man' and coming down on the fast bit made perfect sense in the context of the tempo of the music.

There were some lovely moments of inventiveness, such as a portrait of the King, which came to life at one point, with a live actor actually speaking the lines. This was another example of how a monologue could be broken-up so it continues to be engaging and clear to an audience. Similarly, placing Higgins behind the curtain, and including three soldiers to execute him, in 'Just You Wait' brought variety and clarity of story-telling to Eliza's rant. Higgins simply lowering his head when shot was nicely measured, avoiding any sense of a ridiculous death- scene.

Emotional levels were well-explored with Higgins going from angry tyrant to encouraging teacher. He warmly said to Eliza: "Conquer it you will". This change from stern to encouraging was more empowering, giving her the confidence to make her break-through. Was this an example of some genuine warmth from him or a more cynical change of tack to get what he wanted from her? We cannot be sure, and it doesn't matter. However, it made their dynamic more interesting and avoided that trip actors can fall into, where once they find the character/voice they deliver every moment the same way. Eliza's placed a flower into her father's lapel as he prepared to marry her "step- mother", symbolically offering him her best, suitably unsentimentalised, considering the toxicity of their relationship.

And while these moments provided nice amounts of pathos, this was the first time I have seen this show when it felt like a comedy. Wildean in nature almost. Mrs Higgins' put-downs of her son in the scene in her house, and the shade Eliza threw at Higgins in the same scene elicited great laughter and reaction from the audience. At one point, Higgins' hilariously sculpted Pickering's body when brainstorming a new gown for Eliza.

The ending was very impactful. Higgins' sat still, after a mesmerising 'I've Grown Accustomed to her Face', head in hands, clearly devastated in his stiff upper-lip way. Eliza's entered in a low-key, domesticated way. Yet, she strongly whipped out the slippers. Here she was not a victim, a lost woman who simply cannot leave, but Higgins' equal, making the bold choice to stay.

I would argue that that positioning of the mammoth chorus and their sense of function and intention needed more attention. At times, it seemed as though one clump of people were aimlessly standing around, pretending to talk. The scene might have benefitted from a couple of boxes for people to sit on, which could have created more levels, sub- groups, more identifiable business, and more people might have been seen. Also, I think the bows are more special and meaningful when everyone can be seen. It might have been an idea to spread out the bows more, using every inch of space so we could see more of the cast.

Another person responsible for ensuring that this show motored along was Musical Director Finola Higgins, who ensured all numbers moved along at a good speed. Her thirteen musicians made a rich and varied sound. She had a very clear conducting style which could be easily followed by the musicians and she provided excellent support to the performers on stage. The up-tempo section of 'I'm an Ordinary Man' was super and juxtaposed brilliantly with the slower verses. The slowing of the tempo temporarily, after Eliza was left alone in 'I Could Have Danced All Night', was a lovely touch, before cranking it up again. The inclusion of male voices in "Poor Professor Higgins" was new to me and gave an opportunity to the males, and I am a fan of such inventiveness. The alto mics might have been slightly dominant here, however.

I found the lack of female vocals in 'Wouldn't it be Loverly' sort of unusual, and if I'm honest I wanted the women to join in, rather than remaining mutely on the stage. Elsewhere, the maids and footmen did not all come off the note at the same time, which is a consequence of walking off with your back to the MD. Still, such moments require extra drilling as a result. Choreography was by Aoife McClafferty. The three consecutive lifts in 'Wouldn't it be Loverly' were great and very well executed. There were good twirling movements in 'With a Little Bit of Luck' reprise and the ensemble's exit was worked into the last moments of the routine, making it very slick. The drunken dance moves of 'I'm Getting Married in the Morning' were suitably messy and great fun. That's a party I'd like to go to. With its endless inventive sequences, this was the number that just kept on giving and was, by far, the dance number of the show.

I would have liked the moves to be less performative and more naturalistic, ad- hoc, and playful in 'The Rain in Spain'. The most enjoyable moment of this was the bullfight, which did not rely on formal choreography.

While I understand the comedic minimalism of the Ascot Gavotte, I feel this number was a little undercooked. I think more moves were required. I think that the uptight stoicism of the crowd is achievable without so much stillness or uprightness. For example, bending the body into various poses might have added to the comedy. The crowd seemed to be in a bit of a clump, meaning we really only saw the first row. This is a shame, considering the fabulous costumes. The brilliance of this scene is in the array of facial expressions, so I wished the crowd had been spread out more in front of the red door and the white furniture in order to make this number less squashed. The instrumental was given over to a few nods and a few exits and I think that the opportunity was lost for some ensemble dancing here, even by a few more-able dancers.

I think far more choreography was possible for 'With A Little Bit of Luck'. This song has a great hook and I think it could have hopped off the stage more. The ensemble "could have danced all night", but they didn't, unfortunately.

Michael Coen as Professor Henry Higgins is a wonderfully naturalistic, competent actor, and had an excellent speaking voice. He had lovely varied rhythms and excellent line delivery when talking. He was suitably hateful in his first scenes but grew softer as he moved through his own journey. This performance begged the question: Who is the Pygmalion in this play? He found lovely levels when fighting with Eliza after the Embassy Ball. His numbers, that can be almost completely spoken if the actor wishes, were tuneful and melodic to just the right degree. It is extraordinarily difficult to sell a song without any movement, yet 'I've Grown Accustomed to Her Face' was bizarrely captivating in its subtlety. There were some lovely moments of stillness here, coupled with a rush to the door and a sudden stop, that made this potentially boring song into a really impactful moment. "Marry Freddy!", he'd roar before being paralysed with grief. This was a fascinating portrayal. Ailbhe Doherty as Eliza was a very strong vocalist. She presented as though she has good training and understanding of technique, such was the production of her vowel sounds and diction, her change from chest to head voice and how she mixed these at times. Her voice seemed to sit best in her alto/belt range. She had wonderful projection when she sung. She got some great laughs when talking about her aunt in the Ascot scene. Her transformation could be clearly seen by the time she returned from the Embassy Ball. She had transformed her speaking voice and found poise, no longer needing to lurch her body at Higgins to make an angry point. Overall, this was a very good performance.

Niall Conway as Alfred P. Doolittle had an excellent accent and was nicely ridiculous. Like Michael, he had a fantastic way of mixing up the rhythms of how he spoke so that one never knew how the next line was going to come out. He found a lovely balance between convincing naturalism and heightened characterisation. His despair when singing the reprise of 'I'm Getting Married in The Morning' was hilarious and his vocalising throughout was great.

Richard Crumlish was very good as Eliza's true role model, Colonel Pickering, always pulling Higgins up on his lack of decorum with the girl. He too managed to marry naturalism with comedy, meaning we got the laughs when required without the need to resort to an over-the-top toff-like characterisation.

Siobhán Campbell was lovely as Mrs Pearce. It was nice to hear the Scottish accent as I have not seen it done this way before. Very Mrs Hughes from Downton Abbey. Her reaction when the cheeky Doolittle exited the house got a great reaction from the crowd. Her filthy looks for Eliza at the beginning of the play, changed to filthy looks for Higgins by the time he had come home from the Embassy Ball, such was her increasing fondness for Eliza and her understanding of how unjust all of the congratulations were.

John Byrne as Freddy got a few laughs at the beginning of 'On the Street Where You Live', which is rare, but impressive as he really sold the story of the song. He had a lovely singing voice and seemed to be able to put across this song with ease. I bet he can sing traditional Irish ballads very well too. He might have been a little cheesy in the 'Show Me' moment with Eliza and he might have explored a more genuine way to play this scene. Otherwise, he was an excellent foil for Higgins and was cast very well as Eliza's suitor.

Ronan Egan as Jamie and Michael Sweeney as Harry harmonised very well with Doolittle. It was lovely to see men of two different ages playing these roles, as this gave variety to the dynamic of their scenes and to the timbre of the vocals. Their few moves were very nicely done, as they evoked the men of the time having a bit of fun after a few pints.

Donna Ruane had very good presence as the formidable Mrs Higgins. She got a great reaction from the crowd when she turned her son's own words on him and wickedly told him to keep his conversation to his health and the weather.

Des Treacy as Lord Boxington and Aileen Feely as Lady Boxington added very nicely to the comedy of the hilarious Ascot scene in which Eliza talks about her aunt and those who had "done her in". Gerry Hughes, as Barman George, was suitably cross with Doolittle when the drunkard couldn't pay his bill, and suitably the opposite to that when Doolittle had come into his fortune. Collette Conway as Mrs Hopkins and Kenneth McCarthy as the Policeman both did very well in the street scenes. Zoltan Karpathy's lines (both spoken and sung) were borrowed from Higgins and the gentleman who performed them did very well.

There must be a huge local interest in taking part in this show, such was the enormity of the chorus. The more mature gentlemen in the opening scenes added lovely character, which is rarely seen throughout the country. Indeed, it is rare to see such a fine amount of men, of all vintages, grace the stage. It looked, at times, like they outweighed the females which is almost unheard of. The chorus were very committed to their performances and played their material given to them very well. 'I'm Getting Married in the Morning' was a great achievement, with its endless formations and sequences. It bounced off the stage, filling the audience with delight.

Costumes were in the capable hands of Niamh Lally who employed Utopia Costumes in parts to an amazing job at turning out the cast in such finery. There were some stunning pieces, such as the Ascot scene with its gorgeous purple, grey and white motif. The black, red and tartan costumes on the three male and three female dancers in the opening sequence looked special. The aristocrats in the opening street scene were instantly recognisable. Doolittle's brown leather waistcoat and matching hat made him look extra oily and he stood out from the crowd, making him also instantly recognisable. All of Pickering's and Higgins' costumes looked really well fitted and high quality. The maids and footmen really looked the part. Mrs Pearce was suitably practical-on-the-verge-of-dowdy. Her blue nightgown, over her white nightdress, looked well and distinguished her from the maids who wore the same thing but in green. Eliza was cute as a button in her earlier scenes and stunningly dressed in her later scenes. She was breath-taking when she came out for the Embassy Ball.

Eliza needed an extra pair of eyes to tell her that we could not see her face when she first arrived at Ascot. Freddy was more casual than I am used to seeing him in his final street scene and his sporty jacket looked at little more 1950s and a little less aristocratic.

Hair and Make-up had a huge team of fourteen volunteers that ensured that hair and make-up were kept naturalistic and believable. The faces of the working-class people, including Eliza, were suitably dirtied and the distinction between the different classes was very clear.

Sound was by Derek Recks. The balance was superb between the thirteen musicians and the performances on stage. The band never over-powered the actors and every word was crystal clear. The squealing noises from the gramophones were suitably horrific. There was too much male harmony in 'I'm Getting Married in The Morning', meaning the melody line was barely audible, creating a jarring lack of balance. It is next to impossible for the MD to hear this, as she is right up close to the cast and surrounded by 13 musicians. But, unfortunately, the work put in at rehearsals was not presented properly once the microphones came into the frame in this number.

Lighting was provided by Dirk Bauman/ DLB Lighting, which employed the use of specials and spotlights to enhance solos. Lighting changes punctuated some of the numbers. Higgins glowed white during 'I've Grown Accustomed to Her Face'. A spotlight on him, as he stopped dead in his tracks at the door, clearly struggling with his feelings towards Eliza, enhanced the drama of this moment.

These are small negative points in what was, otherwise, a very well-directed production that cleverly dealt with the length and pace of the show and explored the relationships between the characters in a fascinating, yet often comic way. The aesthetic is to be highly commended also, with a brilliant home-grown set.

Jesus Christ Superstar is a show I have always loved, and to see it performed to such a high standard is always a great pleasure. The relatively young Bardic Theatre company made the show relevant to a younger audience, without ever betraying the Lloyd Webber classic, or the ancient tome from which the story is lifted. Performance levels were high, production standards were ambitious but extremely well achieved, and the audience were totally absorbed by the whole presentation.

I must praise Director Stephanie Faloon for having the creativity and artistry to make the most of a show that is so open to individuality and interpretation. The neutral set with its multi-levelled steps, provided a great structure for inventive direction and choreography, which was well-achieved throughout. There was an awesome visual display that provided a background, through cleverly selected projected images, that captured the essence of the storyline precisely and tuned in perfectly to the modern re-telling of the Biblical tale. The amount of thought and precision (if not always entirely original) that went into the organisation of these images, was breath-taking in its completeness.

The decision to play every aspect of the show in modern dress was equally impressive and very well achieved. The t-shirted chorus donned hoodies to become a thug-like assembly. The soldiers wore S.W.A.T team flak-jackets. The priests had a suited "mob" appearance, and Pilate went from jogging gear to judge's robes. Even the Guantanamo Bay style orange prison garb on Jesus fitted in perfectly. Something as simple as the rucksack carried by Judas gave a sense of the impetuous student, always on the go, undecided whether to go or stay within the fold. The message here is, if you're going to go modern, do it with conviction, and Stephanie Faloon certainly did.

I did feel that the lighting of the show could have gone farther in adding to the atmosphere of a few scenes, particularly the crucifixion, although the lighting was generally very good. It might also have added solemnity to the occasion to see Mary and Disciples weeping at the foot of the cross. If I was to nit-pick, I'd suggest that Jesus' arrival in Jerusalem was a bit understated, and perhaps the debauchery of the market scene could have been more exaggerated. Sound quality throughout was very well balanced and well cued. I can only imagine that after the technical rehearsal, Stage Manager, Malachy McCullagh, and his team, appreciated having plenty of free time to sit back and enjoy the run of the show.

In the role of Jesus, Damien Kivlehan displayed a powerful vocal range that was at its best in the rock falsetto sections of the score. While there was no doubting his ability, I did feel that he had a tendency to over-sing some of the more tender moments. Gethsemane needed some quieter moments to give it more light and shade. He acted well throughout the show, with real human emotion about his fate and expectations, but I would have been inclined to pull back on the crying in his final moments, when the struggle becomes not about the physical pain, but about his soul and his purpose. Nevertheless, this was a performance of considerable stature.

The most profound moment of theatre came when Judas wept and clung to Jesus after he had betrayed him. This was the culmination of a performance, from Conor Begley, that was a fusion of impetuous youth and confused moralist. We witnessed a Judas whose love for Jesus was never in question, and who clearly but reluctantly realised his own tragic but essential involvement in advancing the cause of Christianity. I have not seen this role performed better. It was superbly sung and superbly acted.

Director Stephanie Faloon played the role of Mary Magdalene with dignity and emotion, and a relaxed and confident stage presence. "I Don't Know How To Love Him" was beautifully sung, though I would respectfully suggest that perhaps it may have been even more poignant had she been singing beside, or watching over, a sleeping Jesus. Her reactions, when she wasn't the focal point of the action, also strongly enhanced an excellent performance.

The menacing High Priests were superbly led by a growling Caiaphas (Mark Casey) and a high pitched and patronising Annas (Brian Mills). While both gentlemen gave excellent performances, the powerful vocals of the latter gave him a particularly chilling persona. Very good support was given by Stuart Richardson and Shane Coleman as the other High Priests/ S.W.A.T Soldiers.

The director's interpretation of Pontius Pilate allowed Declan McGrath plenty of scope to give character and personality to the role, which he obviously relished. This was another delightful portrayal, exhibiting very good vocal quality and an understanding of Pilate's reluctance to be labelled for the persecution of Christ. With the smarm, charm and charisma of a television reality show host, Finton Daly made the most of the one-song role of King Herod, with excellent delivery of his vocals and his "phone-in" cheesiness. While taking liberties with the patriarchal nature of the Bible, and transforming Simon to Simone, Lauren McCrory never-the-less presented the role with confidence and very good delivery, and I, for one, would concede that the original text could do with a few strong female characters.

A youthful Eoin Tennyson displayed a fine voice and good emotion in the role of Peter.

The young and energetic chorus did all that was asked of them in adding atmosphere, vocal ability and impressive movement to the overall production.

Choreographing a high-energy production, and maintaining the Director's vision and concept is a big enough challenge, but when you add in the fact that the entire stage was a series of steps, from about 6 feet at the back down to floor level, required even greater imagination and skill, and Choreographer, Jamie-Lee Meneely was not found wanting.
