The audience were treated to a consistent visual display of energy and enthusiasm from a very capable dance ensemble. Routines were well-devised and executed to perfection. The main dancers brought a touch of class to Herod's Song and to the title song. This was very good work. MD, Damien Cullen, had a fine group of musicians well under control, and gave a strong interpretation of the score, with the keyboards adding significantly to the breadth of the overall sound. There were good guitar solos and a consistent, but never over-powering, beat from the percussionist. While the standard of singing throughout was extremely high, my one criticism would be that some of the solo work needed more restraint to highlight the more tender moments in an otherwise racy rock score.

All in all, it's fair to say that this was an accomplished and stylish piece of musical theatre, with the strength of the company evident in every department. Thank you sincerely to Bardic for a most enjoyable night of great entertainment.

Just like a Max Bialystock production, Birr Stage Guild's production of The Producers opened and closed in the same night. But not because it was a flop. On the contrary; the society had such a successful run that they brought the show back for one night only - to a packed venue - and thankfully this gave me the opportunity to adjudicate it. With fine leading performances and a committed chorus, the audience were screeching with glee at the comedic delights provided by this brilliantly written farce. This was a production I was very glad not to have missed.

Director Paul Norton couldn't direct traffic. This is what criminal producer Bialystock has to say about him as he rants about all the wrongs done to him when locked up in prison. I, however, am of a different opinion. Paul Norton knows this show well and was able to tease out the comedy so that the audience was squealing with laughter. He also managed a challenging space very well. The Hold Me/Touch Me sequence was an absolute riot: as this Granny held the stick over her shoulders, pretending to be a milk-maid in some sex- fantasy, running and firing herself on top of Max, showing us her granny knickers in the process, leaving the audience screaming in glee. Elsewhere, the Granny swinging from the wings was brilliant! At one point, a puppet pigeon hilariously waved a Nazi flag. Carmen gave Roger the finger, which was hilarious, but this comes with a word of caution not to over-use this motif. Comedy comes from surprising the audience, so less is more. We don't want the audience to become immune to this. I fully support the fact that those presidential pieces in 'Heil Myself' were taken out. I am of the opinion that they wreck the momentum of the number. Having Franz in a wheelchair, playing the accordion, in prison was a great touch. Max and Leo wore Indian head dresses in the office after returning from their meeting with Roger which nicely linked the narrative between the two scenes. It is important in a scene to hint to where a character has just come from. This was nicely repeated with the lay around Leo's neck in the courtroom scene after returning from Rio.

Leo's positioning on the floor, reading the scripts, could be reconsidered considering the positioning of the MD. Floor work of any description should be done with caution on this very low stage. I think numbers such as 'Where did we go right?' might have benefitted from a little more structure with the blocking. The actors sort of just stood there.

Musical direction heretofore was provided by Enda O'Connor. Enda could not make this reprise of the show however, and his side-kick Shane Farrell stepped in as conductor for the evening. It may seem like a small thing, but I want to thank Shane for using two stacked up chairs on which to conduct. I understand that MDs are more visible to the musicians when they stand, but I have been to so many shows placed on low stages, where the MD has blocked half the action. The compromise to sit tall in this venue was the perfect choice. Shane conducted the musicians in a relaxed and easy manner and he did not present as someone who was deputising.

Principal singing was very secure throughout, indicating that the show was well-rehearsed. The chorus made a great sound, as their numbers bounced off the stage. Insuring that the Grannies sang their harmonies accurately, while maintaining their cackle in their voices, showed a good job at dynamics here. The band got a little loud at the end of 'I Want to be a Producer' and the girls were a little hard to hear. This is small fry in such a venue, where the danger is that the band can be too loud for the whole evening. Thankfully, this rarely happened, enabling us to hear everything clearly. The choreography, by Deirdre Browne was very good. It was not an easy job to fit everyone on this small stage, and the danger was there that it began to look a little crowded, particularly in the opening and during the Zimmer frame dance. In 'Springtime for Hitler' the perfect swastika was made, but I am not convinced everyone would have noticed. In a theatre with raised seating, this would have been more impactful. I would love to see this same choreography on a bigger stage. That said, there were plenty of successes. The Russian dancing to match the music in 'King of Broadway' looked great. The six showgirls did well with the tap. The big finish of 'I Want to be a Producer' was a lovely surprise, with the male office workers even joining in to give it as much welly as possible. 'Der Guten Tag Hop Clop' was suitably ridiculous. A great party erupted in Roger's house and the conga line down the aisle was great craic. The use of the walking sticks, before the introduction of the classic Zimmer frames, worked really well to give this number a little extra something. The Bavarian dancers executed their first series of moves very well. The tap from the Nazi girls was very nice. The curtain call contained some nice moves, and everyone seemed on top of it, showcasing that this was well-rehearsed. I think more might have been done with Ulla on those drums solos in 'If You've Got it, Flaunt it'.

Dickie Donnelly as Max Bialystock was a complete natural and had an imposing voice.  He had such a natural accent (and the moment he did the Yiddish accent was great). His jump from his hunkers to his feet was impressive. If I had one suggestion to make for an otherwise excellent job: Endeavour to be less performative in 'Betrayed'. He could see it and feel it unravel before his eyes rather than so much telling of the story to the audience. I know, I am an awful spoil-sport, considering the learning of the number in itself is a mammoth and impressive task. Elsewhere, however, he just 'lived' the part and we could not 'see' the acting. He was the perfect Max and I hope I get to see him play another role in the future.

Patrick Byrne was just as good as Leo Bloom. His commitment to his role was apparent from his first appearance - he managed to turn his face so red with anxiety that it looked like he could explode on the line "You're making me extremely nervous". He had a great speaking voice, whimpy and nasally, and a lovely singing voice. A super half of a super double act. Shanna Kenny had the perfect image for Ulla and did vell vit her Sveedish accent. She and Patrick had lovely chemistry together, evident in their moment at the beginning of Act Two. She captured all the warmth and adorability of this character. Michael Donegan as the bonkers Germanic Nazi-loving Franz Liebkind had great facial expressions and a good sense of physical comedy. He gave the role socks. It is important to really watch the diction when speaking in such a thick accent. Nonetheless, he gave us plenty of laughs in the knee-slapping in 'Der Guten Tag Hop Clop' and knee-bending in 'Haben Sie Gehört das Deutche Band?' His "fat legs" gag was a hoot.

Darragh Molloy was a committed Roger de Bris who looked as though he was having as much fun in the role as we had watching him play it. While I loathe stereotyping, if I am honest, I can imagine this guy playing a game of rugby and then meeting the lads down the pub for a few pints. Roger should be more… more… more… what's the word…? Also, watch that voice. It's the screaming that will do the damage so be very careful not to force the voice in the dialogue moments. His 'Heil Myself' brought the house down and he gave the audience a great night's entertainment.

Aidan Kelly was simply superb as Carmen. If this guy is not similar to his character in real-life I will collapse in shock, such was his ability to inhabit his character's body language and exist convincingly within the role. Either way, he was fabulous. His timing and his comic ability was excellent, and he had a look for this character of which the Broadway production would be jealous. Superb.

Kevin Murphy as Leo's boss Mr. Marks was suitably authoritative and mean. The solo guy in the office scene - the script calls him 'Black Man Accountant' - did very well at selling his material and showing his despair. Darren Madden as Jason Greene was great in the audition scene. Paddy Ryan as Donald Dinsmore had some lovely physical comedy, with his bent-over physique and robot arms. David Sheils sang very well as the Stormtrooper. Roger de Bris' production team elicited screams of laughter from the audience, such was the comedy created by each of them as they were introduced.

There was a great sound from this committed chorus, who had a dynamic sense of attack every time they appeared. Harmony was good from the eight guys in Whitehall and Marks. The showgirls in 'I Want to be a Producer' socked great energy to the audience. Those Village People who ruffled my rather tragic hair are in trouble. The three principal Grannies in 'Along Came Bialy' did very well. The Grannies over-all were super and their knicker-showing antics induced huge reactions from the audience. Everyone sang their brains out at the finale of Act One - the sound made here was awesome. Some people needed to remember to hold the pose at the very end of Act One as the curtain closed though. Perhaps a little more intention was needed in the faces from the Nazis in 'Springtime for Hitler'. The Grannies' reactions in the courtroom scene were hilarious. The gentleman who read the note in the prison was a very clear speaker. Overall, the chorus were great. Seven people worked on this set that used the available space well. The series of dotted lights for show titles e.g. 'Funny Boy', 'Bloom' and 'Springtime for Hitler' and the posters with the funny twists on classic show titles added brilliantly to the show. The vintage leather couch looked really rich. The office set was a smoke- stained yellow with two brown doors and a hat stand in the foreground. The rest of the office set suggested Max did not have a penny to his name, such was the simplicity of his surroundings. The funny posters idea was continued here, which I was glad to see as it takes a while to absorb these jokes when there is so much else happening on stage. The pigeons looked brilliant in their six cages covered in hay. Their movements were comical. They were placed on a red-bricked roof- top façade which did well at creating this sense of space.

Roger de Bris' house was suitably fabulous, all in pink with purple leafing, looped curtains and a pop of green from the two plants. The stage was completely transformed into a red set for 'Springtime for Hitler'. With its series of swastikas, it looked really well and was so different from what had come before. The way the Nazi symbols lit up was awesome. The bars in the prison scene, against the black and blue curtains, were minimalistic but effective.

The signs for 'Whitehall and Marks' might have been easily enough popped into picture frames to give them a little extra quality. I think a chair was required for Max in the courtroom scene. It was not very realistic that he would lean against a wall for this trial.

Lighting was by Pascal Gough. The lights looked great on the pigeon coops. The way the wings flipped so quickly to show the lights of Broadway during 'I Want to be a Producer' was really effective. The use of the spotlight, as director Roger de Bris came through the aisle at the audition scene, was a good idea and added clarity. The spotlight on Max as he began 'Betrayed' helped frame the space and the number. The final spot on Leo and Max as they embraced and looked over their shoulders at the audience was lovely. Stage Management was by Keith Wolfe. There were a few inventive ideas to 'cover' the scene changes. A blind fiddler from a street scene stayed on under special lighting to keep us entertained. After the conga line, the crew danced as they changed the scene, keeping the fun going. Similarly, Carmen was immediately in character during the scene change into Roger's house, making it as though he was creating the interior decorating of the home. The audition scene also began in earnest asap during the blackout giving us something to look at. The final scene change was managed exceptionally well, considering it happened in the middle of a scene.

I understand that this one-off show lost six members of the crew from its original crew and that it was like opening night all over again. There were so many bits and pieces to bring on and off that there is no doubt that the crew worked really hard on the evening to pull off this one-night- only performance. That said, the truck with the main entrance to the office was very wobbly, particularly for the second act, and was a little jarring when it shook as actors came on and off. It could have been held by a few people off-stage as the actors used it. There was one particularly hairy moment when the 'Bloom' sign and the lockers got stuck in the flat and the congestion here caused some delays. Costumes were by one of the Andrew Reddies. There appears to be a number of him around the country at the moment. The usherettes looked well in their burgundy jackets and skirts, complete with white frill. The aristocratic theatre attendees looked great in their tuxes and dresses and fur stoles. They were joined a by a fun group of people in nuns and sailor costumes etc. The blind fiddler wore sunglasses, a scarf and white rope belt around his trench coat. One man even wore tassels on his nipples, showing off the diverse nature of the New York streets. The production party that erupted in Roger's House was the scene that just kept on giving in terms of costumes: The leather, the pink, that crotch, the checked shirt/jeans/toolbelt, the village people and that oiled up Aladdin-esque manservant all looked fabulous. The sequined showgirl costumes looked swell. The matching blue outfits on the Grannies were well-sourced and looked professional. Ulla looked cute as a button in her blue top, skirt and beret. Some people in the audition scene, such as the blonde female Hitler looked a little modern perhaps. The silver head pieces on the chorus girls in 'Springtime for Hitler' looked fabulous and it was a clever idea to put Ulla in a black one to make her stand out. Her silver post-show gown was gorgeous. The striped mini- dress and green jackets on the 'Prisoners of Love' girls were great. The black sequined jackets and silver trousers on Roger looked perfect for the ending. The Stormtrooper's grey costume was great and the Nazi chorus girls in their shorts, shirts and hats looked fantastic.

I found the use of black shirts on some of the men a little jarring, particularly Leo. His black shirt with green and yellow accessories was quite masculine and dangerous looking, a kind of palette that might suit a mob boss, rather than a dweeb afraid of his own shadow. Patrick is a statuesque man and this palette coupled with the grey suit seemed a little high- powered to me. This motif was continued in the accounting firm scene, and I felt that the lads looked washed out against the black/blue background. The green eyeshades looked well though. Leo's white shirt and blue tie for the second act was far more suitable for this character, in my opinion. Was there enough support given to Max backstage for his quick changes? He appeared once with his bow tie around the skin of his neck and he appeared in prison with his tuxedo trousers on.

Hair and Make-Up was by Heather Colohan, Lindsay Murphy, Elaine Houlihan and Johanne Doorley. Leo's curly hair was nicely shaped into a parting that swopped up in curls on both sides. This gave him an almost mad scientist vibe and provided a nice opportunity to slick it down when he was playing producer later on. The white curly wigs on the six showgirls in 'I Want to be a Producer' looked well. I think more could have been done with make-up to add to Roger's fancy dress fitting; false eyelashes etc. Ulla's hair looked quite wig-like. The Grannies' wigs looked very well, but there was less need for realism here.

Sound was by Recks Audio, Clara. The crash and cat screaming sound effect as the Granny swung back into the wings was great, as was the motorbike effect when Franz arrived for opening night and his gun sound later on. The mics on the Grannies were not up on time at one point. Otherwise, cueing was good.

Props were by Róisín Gilmore and Alma Naughton. The adding machines, rolls of paper and pencils in Whitehall and Marks looked good. The pizza boxes were just written on with marker. Printed stickers might have looked better here. The walking sticks and the Zimmer frames, in particular, were excellently sourced. The truncheons in 'Prisoners of Love' were great.

I wonder would the society consider investing in some materials to build out the sides of the stage or to build a ramp around the orchestra that could be used year after year? Moments such as the conga line or the time when Leo tries to escape during 'We can do it' might have room to breathe if this were the case. Money doesn't grow on trees, I know, and a ramp might lose a line or two of chairs, but there is such talent on and off the stage in this group, that they need… nay deserve… to have their work showcased in the best space possible. Perhaps The Producers is just one of those scripts that demands so much from the space that it showed up the limitations. Another show might fit perfectly fine here.

If anyone had been walking by during Birr Stage Guild's performance of The Producers, they would have heard constant shrieks of laugher from the hall. This was thanks to a great production team trio, quality leads and a committed chorus. The audience left having had a ball which is exactly what this show aims to do. So it was job well done. town

society_raw: North East Musical and Dramatic Society
review_text:
"You make the world lousy", exclaims a broken Doc, summing up the contribution the feuding gangs in this story make to society. Thankfully, West Side Story makes a far greater contribution to musical theatre, and Belfast Music and Drama Society gave us an excellent version of this show. The Grand Opera House, with all its intricate red and gold designs contrasted brilliantly with the effective minimalism of the staging. The curtain opened to reveal a set provided by Prosceneium Ltd; two tall New York tenement buildings with balconies and windows that glowed amber light, brought together by fencing that would eventually fly in and out of the space. The rest of the places, such as Doc's Drug Store, the wedding shop or Maria's bedroom would be made by modest trucks and furniture that would be swiftly moved on and off by Stage Manager Andy McKnight and his crew. This was minimalistic, but symbolic and highly effective. Lighting by Declan Anthony brought great clarity to proceedings and the use of a cyc at the back that glowed blue for the Jets' scenes and red for the Sharks', or a continuum of the two when they were together created a lovely sense of symbolism and space. In this playing area, a group of talented performers, whose appearance suggested a modern take on a classic look (complete with red or blue wrist scarves depending on the gang they were in), would showcase a mixture of amazing vocals, tense performances and committed dancing to bring to life a tragic tale of love, loss, hatred and revenge.

Maria, played by Amber Dixon, sang like a nightingale. Her voice blended beautifully with Tony's. She was able to act excellently in 'A Boy Like That/I Have a Love', allowing vulnerability to be part of her vocal, without sacrificing its beauty or accuracy with the harmony lines - something which is very difficult to do. This girl was sixteen years old and she was absolutely brilliant.

Boyd Rogers as Tony had a superb singing voice. He had excellent diction with beautifully sustained notes and the most tasteful hint of vibrato at the end of a phrase. He had all the presence of a leading man. I would suggest trying to layer the singing with a little more expression in the face, to show what is happening behind the eyes. As beautiful as the singing was, he might endeavour to continue to find meaning in the lyrics. That said, the crowd went wild after his 'Tonight', so what do I know? He and Amber were simply gorgeous together and when they sung it was stunning.

Naomi Smith was very good as Anita. The complexity of her show-down with Maria was fascinating, such was the conflict she felt. For such a feisty character, her playing of the lower status, as she entered Doc's, was nerve-wracking as she was so vulnerable at the beginning of the scene. She portrayed the horror of being raped with aplomb and we could absolutely see why she would lie about Maria's "suicide" after this.

Seán O'Neill as Riff, the leader of the Jets, was the perfect foil to Tony. He was more impulsive and highly strung than his friend who was looking to give up all this rumbling with the Sharks. He had a great singing voice and carried his numbers with competence.

Vijay Sharma played Barnardo with all the menace, darkness, anger and bravado required for the role. He has a striking presence on stage and established a real sense of danger when he appeared, such was the intensity of his portrayal.

Colin Boyd, as a very convincing Detective Shrank, had an authoritative presence and brought great tension to the scenes in which he appeared. At the same time, we could sense how burnt-out the character was and sick to his back teeth of the juvenile antics of the Jets and Sharks. Paddy McGenity played Doc with a heaviness of a man with the weight of the world on his shoulders. Frustrated by worrying about these younger fellas, he clearly cared about them, even if sometimes presenting as a man of few words. He had great reactions when Shrank was trying to get information from the Jets about the location of the rumble, adding very nicely and convincingly to the tension of the moment.

Conor Johnston as A-Rab has a talent for physicalising his character in interesting ways and his commitment to this role cannot be questioned, such was his ability to stay in character in every moment. He was hilarious talking to Officer Krupke. I recommend, in this scene with Krupke, to double-check that the lines are delivered as though they have never been said before. It is important not to sound too articulate or well-rehearsed and that these ideas are coming to the character for the first time.

Jordan Walker as Baby-John captured all the innocence of this part, which cleverly brings balance to the piece by showing a more vulnerable side within the Jets. His so-called 'friends' forced him to perform the rape on Anita, which added to the horror of the situation and his distress after this moment was very upsetting. Conor Headley as Action performed his material well as one of the most quick- tempered Jets, and just like the rest of the whole cast, was hugely committed to his role. Ellie McKay as Anybodies was very good as the female-in-a-male-world and played her material, and the challenges she faced in fitting in with the boys, very well indeed. Shane Johnston as Officer Krupke had a humorous presence and gave us a laugh or two just in the right moments. Lauren McCann showed a beautiful singing voice as the Dream Sequence Soloist. Andrew Devonshire as Glad Hand, the over-the-top teacher in the gym scene, was humorous and added some light relief to a show that can be quiet dark. His function as one of the adults in the show, who are desperately trying to show the younger generation that their hatred and violence towards each other was unnecessary, was well realised. James McLoughlin, as Chino, made the hair stand on the back of my neck as he roared that Maria's lover had killed her brother.

The commitment of the entire ensemble to make this show as good as possible, and the amount of hard work that must have gone into getting this production to this standard could not be disputed. These performances were enabled by a production team trio that did a fabulous job at putting this show on the stage and adding interesting layers, whether such layers were musical, danced or acted. An hour into the show, I couldn't help but notice the woman sitting two seats to my right who was leaning forward, gripping to the balcony's edge in distress, as Bernardo and Riff were killed, clearly very moved by what was happening. This was a testament to the tension created by Director Jordan Walsh. My body turned cold when Chino shouted to Maria "He killed your brother". Shivers ran down my spine as Maria rightfully screamed "We all killed him" -  summing up the tragedy of these senseless deaths. It was clear, by the end, that I could become invested in these characters and the complexity of their tragedy.

From the get-go, it was evident that this production would aim to bring the audience hovering close to the edge of their comfort zone. The cutting of the ear was quite violent. The rape scene was very upsetting. If we weren't horrified enough for Anita, the decision to have the Jets force Baby John to perform the act, and his crying afterwards, created even another victim in an already unbearable situation.

Elsewhere, the odd, barely audible, ad- lib was very effective. Understated or ambiguous enough to sound natural, without taking away from the main material, but effective enough to pop an extra layer of tension in there, such as a random utterance of the word "Spik". There was a female dressed in a masculine suit, a girl swinging round the waist of another girl and females dancing together. A-Rab and Baby John briefly held hands on the line "Let's run away". These were interesting nods to some of the arguments about the multidimensionality of the writing, without reducing anything to the lowest common denominator. The beauty of this writing is how it works on different levels and so I think the balance was nicely found between exploring layers of meaning, while still allowing the audience to think for themselves.

The blocking for 'Something's Coming' appeared to lack intention and direction in how Tony moved around the space. I suggest that this could have been more structured, mixing moments of absolute stillness with moments of purposeful movement that enhanced the story-telling and gave additional meaning to the lyrics and emotions. I think that there could have been a little more tension during Tony and Maria's meeting on the fire-escape, with her looking over her shoulder once or twice more. He might have whispered the odd line of dialogue to illustrate the idea that what they were doing was dangerous and that there could be consequences if they were discovered. That way, the passion for each other might have felt even more intense, as it was more against-the-odds. Things were fantastically complicated between Maria and Anita in 'A Boy Like That'. There was more than one emotion or tone at play here, which was far more interesting. The creative characterisation and physicalising of A-Rab added a fascinating extra layer to some scenes, but this should come with a word of caution that these reactions do not steal focus from the primary action.

Musical Director Wilson Shields controlled the orchestra with the upmost expertise. He had an impressive ability to encourage the band to swell in instrumental moments and pull them right back when underscoring dialogue etc., meaning that we heard every word. This allowed the orchestra to be impactful at just the right moments, such as the pounding in the fight sequences, and gentle in the more tender moments. There was an impressive orchestra of 15 musicians, the biggest I have seen this season, providing such a wonderful variety of sounds, which was particularly enjoyable in the Entr'acte. There was a lovely sense of dynamics when the Jets started singing quietly for 'When You're a Jet' and they dramatically rose from the ground up, effectively amalgamating dynamics and choreography into one moment. At one point, the word 'Maria' echoed after Tony sung it. I am not sure how this was done. It was either an echo effect on the mic, a pre-recording of Tony's own voice or supplied live by off-stage males. Either way, it was very indicative of how the name was swirling around his head.

Choreographer Alex McFarlane did an excellent job with this production. The opening was suitably stylised. One could not tell where the dancing ended and the acting started. The choreography was used to establish tension, character and plot i.e. how Barnardo appeared to be controlling the others on his side. The shoulder action, clicks, high kicks etc. were all what we would come to expect from West Side Story, but it was masterfully pieced together nonetheless. The mixture of free-styling and official choreography in the gym scene was great, cleverly mixing naturalism with structure. A moment of folk dancing juxtaposed brilliantly against the raunchier moves in the rest of the gym sequence. We never knew what was going to happen in the encaptivating and emotive dream sequence and the three different lifts were very inventive. The 'Gee, Officer Krupke' sequence was very inventive and brilliantly executed.

The beginning of the 'Jet Song' felt as though the scene leading into the number had been blocked one way and the beginning of the song a different way, resulting in the guys artificially getting into their starting positions. I recommend blurring such a transition more. That said, there is no questioning the Trojan work this choreographer did in providing excellent choreography for this show and how utterly committed the ensemble was in making sure the routines bounced off the stage.

Stylised bows summed up the narrative, with the various groups posing into their signature moves and with the adults on the balconies. This was in good taste, considering the body count, but a respectful full-company bow might have been considered once the curtain had lowered and risen again. I always argue that the bows are taken by the actors, and not the characters themselves, and should not be in character (except for a laugh in very light comedies and children's shows). This amount of stoicism is possibly not necessary. If the crowd are roaring in appreciation, it would not be the end of the world to show more warmth for the final bow in acknowledgment of the audience response. Otherwise, it can feel a little jarring for the crowd to whoop and holler in appreciation, only to have glum faces staring back.

Numerous snot-rags were employed throughout the audience, in the final scene, as Maria clutched to her dead lover's body. I, too, was on the edge of my seat, despite knowing what was going to happen, and I was fully convinced that this production had succeeded in doing its job; to portray a tense and tragic tale, through the medium of evocative dance, wrapped up in a beautifully sung score. The set looked great, the scene changes were swift, the use of the space was clever, the relationships were excellently explored, the pace was speedy when necessary, yet the tension was palatable, and the horror of the tragedy was very well actualised. This was a superb production that was excellently directed, musically directed, choreographed and performed. A great achievement, overall..

The Front of House personnel were all dressed as prison officers, guardians of the theatre, letting people in and out as we arrived at the Cork School of Music for CIT's production of Bad Girls - a musical version of the original ITV prison drama. The announcements before the show stated that "lock-down would happen in 5 minutes", enhancing the whole theatrical experience. The introductory announcement contained violent threats and bad language which set the tone for everyone, allowing us to understand what we were about to see. Act One would culminate in a riot scene in the prison and the announcer would tell the audience to "Please take fifteen minutes while we get these women under control". This was functional yet added to the narrative and brought us out of the gloomy violence of the riot.

Bad Girls the musical has some problems with the writing. It is a show that does not really know what it wants to be. It aims to be gritty and show the horrors of prison- life but reverts too often to comedy and spectacle in its journey. There are too many protagonists and there are only rare glimpses of a plot-line worth following. The traditional well-made play tends to follow one or two protagonists and we invest ourselves in their attempts to achieve a particular goal. The TV show had been able to meander through all these characters' stories. The interwoven sub- plots in the musical, however, are never given any time to breathe with credibility. Ultimately it is difficult to care about these two-dimensional characters or the tension in their lives, particularly when a firework display suggests a sort of apologetic happy ending. But I believe that my job is not to adjudicate AIMS societies on the material they perform, but how they perform it. Thankfully, CIT Musical Society presented this show with aplomb and they deserve congratulations on doing an excellent good job with a flawed piece. I am not surprised to see that Director Eamonn B. Shanahan has an MA in Creative Producing and Theatre Studies, such was the calibre of his vision for the aesthetic of the piece. The minimalism of the set was perfect, utilising sterile white against harsh steel to create a gripping performance space. New parts within the prison were created effectively but symbolically, using a minimal amount of staging, but ensured that the aesthetic did not reduce itself to an amateurish use of a "few bits and pieces" to cheaply create a sense of space. At one point a body is found in a cell and, in this vein of minimalism, it was a very good idea not to show the dead body at all. Such moments are always cumbersome to stage and will invariably take the audience out of the story, for one reason or another.

The very good set used harsh angular lines, and metal, black and white colour scheme to create a minimalist, but highly structured and effective playing space, that was very atmospheric. It struck the perfect balance between the abstract and the concrete. The bed of white sheets and the stand-alone toilet with a back- drop of bars was all that was needed to create the idea of a cell. The large white rectangular partitions were used well as the staff-room, the urinal, the phone and piece which showed the silhouettes of Dockley's and Fenner's escapades. The massive screen at the back was used just the right amount, with its expanse of grey clouds. The falling golden embers, the fire during the riot and the fireworks for the bizarre happily ever after moment were good. The dowdy red and pink stripy chair in the staffroom contrasted excellently with the harsh sterile steel of the rest of the set. I would not have changed a thing. Lighting Design was by Declan Leonard. The lighting used harsh white specials very well indeed to create a sense of tenebrism that brought great focus to the leads during solos. The fluorescent lights were torture on the eyes, but I can see how that was the desired effect; to show the harshness of being locked indoors in such a place under artificial light.  The use of only one fluorescent light for Helen's office was clever. The strobe lighting, against the purple. was very effective in the slow-motion part of the riot. It is to be commended on how well the use of strobe lighting was advertised. The sudden blackout at the end of the riot was dramatic. The cold light of the prison bed contrasted brilliantly with the warmer light of Helen's sitting room.

The blocking of new inmate Rachel's admittance to the prison, opening her towel to the prison warden, set the right miserable tone, without being too in-your- face. A tap number very nicely utilised the talents of the group and added variety to proceedings. Three very contrasting characters performed this which I thought was also interesting. Various routines used truncheons, mops or chairs - all really inventive, using the banality of the prison to evoke the fabulousness of showbiz. At one point, the ensemble, clad in rubber gloves, were passing buckets to one another, turning the banal chores of the prison into a bit of a showstopper. There was one moment when a character was sent to solitary confinement and this was staged in the middle of the centre aisle. While I acknowledge this confinement was very separate from the rest of the playing space, I think this idea back-fired slightly: Most of the audience between the performer and the stage did not turn around. Perhaps they did not know where to look. I think it was a shame that only half the audience saw this moment. Had the chairs been in more of a V-shape, this might have been more impactful. Could pre-recorded images been used on the screen, for example, to show the separateness of the character to the main area? The using of the aisles in a riot scene was more effective, however, as we were drawn into the sense of chaos. Musical Direction was by Michael Young. He conducted six musicians with a competent and relaxed manner and he also assisted with keyboards. The cast appeared to be very well-prepared for their musical numbers as they performed with confidence, competence and ease. The vocals delivered throughout the evening were all top notch. The band was kept to a good level throughout, never over-powering the performers on stage. Harmonies were secure in the choral pieces.

Stage Management was by Michael Greene. The girls carried out tables in a stylised fashion and slammed the chairs with the music, turning what could have been a boring scene-change into an engaging moment. Elsewhere, while the scene changes were very well-rehearsed, they were dead-silent and created lulls in the narrative. Perhaps prison sirens going off each time a scene was changed would have added atmosphere, like the way that sharp whistle is often used in Sweeney Todd.

The performers in this show were all top- notch. The vocals, in particular, were excellent throughout. Each performer managed to evoke the function of the characters they were playing i.e. whether your job was to provide comedy, aggression, despair or corruption or to move from one of these to another. Each performer was 100% committed to their role. Harmonies were great throughout. The riot scene showed how hugely committed the cast were to show the aggression of the moment.

Seán McGearáilt was very good as the sleazebag Principal Officer Jim Fenner. He had just the right amount of sleaze to avoid becoming a caricature or a panto villain, while still churning our stomachs by his antics. If he had been over-the-top, he never would have won Rachel's naïve trust. He played it all very cool, which is just how a psycho might. With her mini- stature, Sarah O'Regan as the bitch-faced Senior Officer Sylvia Hollamby, achieved nice comic moments as she stood up to her two tall male colleagues beside her, or played up a fake bad back. She was suitably horrible to the inmates, bringing with her the appropriate wave of misery every time she appeared. Dillon Harris as Number One, the Governing Governor was suitably slimy and corrupt, and evoked the maturity necessary to play a role of more advanced years.

Lorraine Crowley played the part of Governor Helen Stewart well. Her Scottish accent, based on the TV actress, was absolutely flawless. If it weren't for the TV show, I would be inclined to think it was her own accent, as it was so convincing. Her character possibly showed up the flaws in the writing as I would argue she was a little too Ms Perfect. Brendan Morris, as the prison warden (who wanted not to be crooked and to do the best job he could), was played very well by Justin Mattisson. He provided some well-needed light in a dark world. It was adorable the way in which he fancied the Governor. Alison McCormack, as top-dog Shell Dockley, had a superb accent and was brilliantly aggressive as she chewed the rest of the characters up like a Rottweiler. Dannielle Hoban Maguire as Shell's sidekick Denny Blood was suitably less of a bulldog than Shell herself. She was the perfect side-kick - empowered to be intimidating by those with whom she hangs around, but would probably not have the same impact on the other inmates if she were left to handle them by herself. Ciara McCarthy as Nikki Wade, love interest of the Block Governor, gave us a character worth caring about with lovely acting through song and a great voice. Christine Caldbeck, as Crystal Gordon, had a brilliant Jamaican accent. She provided us with the variety of a lovely contrasting character to the rest of the rough cockney women. Her prayer-like ballad at the beginning of Act Two was touching and sung very well.

Sinéad Donnelly as Yvonne Atkins, exuded glamour and toughness as the wife of the mob boss. She took no prisoners (pardon the pun) when she arrived on the block, convincingly putting the intimidating Shell in her place and quickly establishing herself as the new top dog. Ciara O'Neill as Julie Saunders and Kayme O'Callaghan as Julie Johnston (two prostitutes who have styled themselves alike and taken the same name) brought plenty of character to proceedings and acted as the comic relief for the show. That said, the darker issue of losing their visiting rights was played with sincerity. Nuala Maunder as Rachel Hicks, the new terrified inmate, who eventually takes her own life, captured all the vulnerability of this character. Maggie Keating as the ancient Noreen Biggs, added some humour, especially when some drugs were found. There was not a weak-link on stage and Millie Ahern as Kat Clarke, Rebecca McCarthy as Shanel 'Spike' Dyson and Saoirse Murphy as Natalie Scott added to the high standards across the board.

Costumes were designed by Meghan Bartual-Smyth. Most likely, there was little need to rent any costumes, such was the day-to-day nature of the piece. That said, all costumes suitably enhanced the sense of characterisation of those wearing them. Dockley's grey tracksuit bottoms and loopy earrings, the gaudy style of the Julies, the fabulousness of Atkins, the brown pants and flowy purple top on Crystal are all examples of the subtlety in which the characters were effectively costumed. A pair of skinny trousers on Number One were too modern and youthful, however.

Sound Design was by Declan O'Sullivan, Star Systems. Cueing throughout was very good. Every word was crystal clear, and the band never over-powered the performers on stage. The sound of breaking bottles and a siren added to the drama of the riot scene. The tap dripping in the bathroom scene enhanced this sense of space. In the same vein, a sound effect when closing the cell door might have been considered. Such a sound effect might have been repeated during the scene changes to give them atmosphere. The bows were somewhat 'ranked', with a letch of a prison guard taking the final bow. I do not believe such an ensemble piece required this. You will notice in theatres like the Abbey that people rarely get their own bow. Indeed, no one ever gets their own dressing room because casts are always considered to be a company of equals. This show begged for such a company bow. It could be argued until kingdom come who were the leads in this show, but in a show full of girl-power, I would not have chosen to give the last bow to the male baddie who had been caught interfering with the female inmates. But one has little to be giving out about, if one is giving out about the bows, and the success of this production far outweighed the negatives.

This is a relatively unknown show, and most people I know haven't heard of it. Should more societies do it? Well, it most certainly lends itself to groups whose membership is primarily female. There are great moments to show off vocal prowess, and in the hands of a director who can do as much as possible to make a coherent story-line, then it should just work. Thankfully, CIT Musical Society, which is evidently dripping in talent, did a very good job indeed.

This society is known for taking on slightly unknown, often rarely performed pieces, and college is the perfect place to experience them. Whatever they decide to do next, whether it be obscure or well- known, I hope I get an opportunity to come see another CIT production in the future. Plus, I very much look forward to seeing what Eamonn B. Shanahan does next. Congratulations to Producers Lorraine Crowley and Maggie Keating, their committee, the production team and the cast for showcasing their talents in an interesting and inventive performance space. It was great to experience something rare from such talented performers..

When it comes to feel-good musicals, "Sister Act" is one of those shows that keep your toes tapping and a smile on your face from beginning to end, and it was a great choice for Malahide M&DS, giving so many opportunities to let their individual and collective talents shine. Lynda O'Neill presented a very clean and tidy show, with well-defined characters and good use of the space available. She drew out a wonderful performance from her leading lady, and while all the characters were strong and credible, there were opportunities to accentuate the comedy even more on occasions. Stage manager Therese Farrell and her team had no problems with getting things in place quickly and quietly. The black box set with a wonderful LED screen was most effective, if perhaps a little sparse, and I did feel that a more dominating pulpit, a more detailed Confessional and maybe more substantial furniture for the office scenes would have taken away from the occasional emptiness of the stage. But that is not to take away from an excellent use of that screen, and perfectly selected images. All in all, this was a great show to look at, and entertainment value was extremely high.

In the safe hands of Dave McGauran, the orchestra played with good balance and good rhythm throughout the show, and despite being well away from the stage, the coordination between stage and pit was perfect. Vocal preparation was evident, with the nuns choruses being particularly high on energy, with well- drilled harmony and good clear diction. The gangsters gave very good accounts of themselves in both their vocal numbers, and all of the principals performed their music with confidence.

This is a show with a vast amount of choreography, and Jean Gill made every effort to make each routine fresh and unique. The gospel numbers were filled with energy and invention, with hand movements just occasionally out of sync, but her chorus served her well in giving great life and enthusiasm to every number. I did feel that the gangster's routines could have done with a tad more comedy, despite being very capably performed. The levels of the stage were well used in many routines.

In the demanding role of Deloris Van Cartier, Emma Jane Reilly was at her best in her comedic delivery of her lines, displaying excellent timing and superb facial reactions. I think she took occasional optional low notes, but it didn't detract too much from a rounded and very polished vocal performance. She was always in control of the stage and oozed charm and charisma.

Jen McGuire Noriant was a sincere and gentle Mother Superior, precise in her vocals and well able to display her frustration and displeasure, when required, at the antics of Deloris. Her "I Haven't Got A Prayer" was most delightful.

Rebecca Gamble combined feistiness and insecurity in equal measure to give a most convincing character to Sister Mary Robert. "The Life I Never Led" was delivered with passion.

Pauline Maguire was a delightfully giddy and convincing Sister Mary Patrick, with great facial expression and a most pleasing voice. She was a good contrast to the angrier and bossier Sister Mary Lazarus of Eileen Gill. Her initial severity added greatly to the comedy of the "rap" sections of her vocal numbers. These two "sisters" worked very well together.

Orla Connolly and Kirstin Smith, as Michelle and Tina, gave good feisty and comedic support to Deloris, and hit the mark with their music and dancing.

There were note-worthy performances also from Jean Bennett as Sister Mary Martin-of-Tours, Fiona Dowling as Sister Mary Theresa and Caitriona Connolly as the female Cop.

Heading up the male cast of this predominantly female showcase, was the ever engaging Damien Hurley as "sweaty" Eddie. While he could have pushed the boundaries a tad to make himself even more sympathetic, this was a confident and controlled piece of acting with good vocal quality.

Ed Brady played the villain Curtis was a good thuggish attitude. "When I Find My Baby" was delivered with grit and an assured vocal quality, and he was a natural leader of his gang of incompetent sidekicks.

There was more than a touch of the homely Irish Parish Priest about Paul McGuire's portrayal of Monsignor O'Hara, business- like in his early scenes, and comical in his sudden passion for rock-gospel.

As a team, Jonathan McKenna as Joey, Stephen Rixon as Pablo and Mikey McCormack as TJ worked well together, doing all that was asked of them, and infusing each character with their own individuality. TJ in particular played the dumb-ass very effectively. Their routines were nicely performed but perhaps could have contained more comedy.

Sean Markey was a credible Ernie and Lorcan White an effective Taxi Driver, and the members of the ensemble who doubled in cameo roles all made a significant contribution to the overall enjoyment of the show. As a unit, the chorus sang exceptionally well, delivered their routines with great energy and were mostly tidy in the presentation of their dance steps. While generally facial reactions were good, one or two faces occasionally showed the concentration of trying to coordinate steps with words. The lighting for the show was very good, with nice use of colours and of special areas, and thanks to that great screen, there was never a problem of images being washed out. Sound quality was very good throughout. Costumes were very good and appropriate, with the nuns growing in colour and glitz as the show progressed. Bedroom attire was very effective, and the gangsters looked good, but I would have liked to see their hairstyles complimenting their outfits and the era with a bit more exaggeration. Dance costumes in the non- nun scenes were bright, colourful and era- appropriate. There were no problems with make-up.

It's easy to understand why this show is so popular at the moment, and from the spirit and energy of the Malahide cast, they were clearly enjoying every moment of the performance as much as I was. Thank you all for a thoroughly uplifting musical and religious experience.

Director, Claudia Glavey, presented a show that was vibrant and engaging, and despite some aspects that were a bit problematic, one always had the sense that the cast not only enjoyed, but totally believed in what they were doing. This sense of camaraderie always infects the audience and results in them showing supportive warmth towards the efforts being made.

The sheer expanse of the Black Box stage caused a few problems, with long walks to the coat-hooks, or to answer the door, slowing down a lot of the action, particularly in the opening scenes, where pace is crucial. The set was by no means unattractive, with a nicely painted background, and decent functional truck pieces, but it might have been better employed by creating smaller playing areas for scenes that only involved a couple of principals. The Props team had accumulated a good variety of pieces, but more thought could have gone into the dressing of Debris' "gay" apartment, which was rather sparse. The stage team, under the supervision of Stage Manager, Cadhla Boyle, worked hard to keep things moving, but many of the scene changes were unnecessarily lengthy. The lighting for the show was more functional than spectacular, but at least everything was well-illuminated and the focal point was always established. Sound quality throughout was very commendable. The director did a fine job in realising the various and varied characters of the show, and in presenting them with well- rehearsed confidence. "Keep it Gay" and "You Never Say Good Luck" were nicely plotted and performed.

Co-choreographers, Jess Harkin and Cian Elwood, piled plenty of energy and physicality into their routines, and were rewarded by a chorus who looked as well-drilled as they looked happy to be dancing. There was plenty of variety in the movement, from the silliness of "Keep it Gay" to the more disciplined "Springtime" routine. There was nice work in "I Want to be a Producer" and bundles of fun in the Granny number.

A very commendable orchestra handled what can be a tricky score with good rhythm and musicality, and under the direction of Eoin Corcoran, provided a secure accompaniment to the on-stage singers. I might suggest that when scene changes are lengthy, (which they were on several occasions) it's better to repeat a long phrase of music than just a few bars, which becomes very repetitive and only serves to emphasise the length of the scene change. Together with Oisin Feely, Eoin drew forth a good vocal performance from the chorus, and by and large, principals also seemed to be vocally well- rehearsed.

Costumes were generally acceptable and appropriate, although more attention to style and era would have enhanced Ulla, and I wasn't sure about Roger De Bris' costume at the end of Act One. The make-up team were on the ball, with very good work done on Hold Me Touch Me and the other old ladies. Roger should have had a wig of better quality to go with his Chrysler Building dress.

Congratulations, first and foremost, to Shane McCormack in the role of Max, for vocal dexterity, in handling so well the marathon solo that is "Betrayed". It was perfectly delivered. Shane gave a credible performance throughout the show, displaying a good sense of comedy, and breathing life into his musical numbers. Alongside him, in the role of Leo Bloom, John Rice showed a fine ability to present the appropriate characteristics of a highly nervous soul. His sensitivity was, on a few occasions, a little drawn out, causing a slackening of the pace of comic delivery. Although not pitch perfect on all occasions, he delivered his songs with charisma.

Una Valaine was a sassy and provocative Ulla, with a well-sustained accent and a good sense of comic timing. Musically, she performed with confidence and clarity. Kevin Murphy brought a wealth of experience to the role of Roger De Bris, enjoying the high camp of his character. His physical comedy was strong, and his diction excellent. He made a very good job of both the "Keep It Gay" song and "Springtime for Hitler".

Conor Duggan was also convincingly camp in the role of Carmen Ghia, although he did, once or twice, become a bit high pitched and shrill to be clearly audible. Physically, he captured his character very effectively.

Amie Donnellan, for one so young, achieved a very believable little old lady in the role of Hold Me Touch Me, delightful in her comedy and decidedly "naughty" in her lustful nature.

David McGowan gave a distinctly confident and rounded performance in creating the character of Franz Liebken. This fine young actor was as competent in song as he was in delivery of his very funny script.

Jess Harkin and Anna Campbell got the show off to a secure start as the Usherettes, while Patrick Conneely, as the Stormtrooper, gave an authoritative rendition of "Springtime for Hitler".

There were a plethora of well-defined cameo roles, most notably Niamh Bain as Mrs Marks.

The chorus did all that was required of them with energy, and a great sense of enjoyment (especially the camp male chorus), and made a more than adequate vocal contribution to the overall entertainment value of the show.

Criticisms aside, I reiterate that the palpable team spirit that glued this production together caused myself and the whole audience to be carried along on the crest of a wave of fun and frivolity. This was a thoroughly entertaining show, and I enjoyed it immensely. Thank you to all concerned.

At only 22 years of age, Séimí Campbell is a ridiculously talented young Director, who put his stamp on this Trinity production of Evita, right from the get-go. From the stylised movement of the funeral to the decision to split the narration between three performers instead of the normal one Che, one was immediately aware of a well- thought out plan of action. Stylish, rustic, original and vibrant, this version of the classic story of Eva Duarte was told with attitude, confidence and a cracking pace. At just over two hours, it was certainly the raciest production I have ever watched, but I'd be quick to acknowledge that the speed in no way detracted from the moments of beautiful emotion that were also achieved. The show also featured some of the most original and beautiful choreography I've seen in a long time. From that stylised opening scene, to the beautifully performed ballet leading into the finale, this whole show was a crafted and confidently presented terpsichorean treat. Choreographers, Cisca Devereux and Katie Mirocha, gave passion and variety to their routines, even turning something as simple as running into a visual delight, but it was a duet between Peron and Eva that really established their skills, and the aforementioned contemporary ballet that lifted this display to exceptional heights. Musical Director, Naoise Whearity, kept tight control of her orchestra throughout the show, and given the pace at which the show was delivered, that was no mean feat. There was always good balance between the musicians, and more impressive, given the orchestra size, they managed to never drown out the on-stage vocals. Those vocals were extremely well prepared, with vibrant harmonies and clear diction, and an impressive difference in tone and quality between the aristocracy and the common throng. Principals were all very secure in their music.

The show was very nicely costumed, with a good distinction between the common throng and the aristocracy. The exceptions were the military uniforms, which in a country with a strong military regime, needed to be more uniform. A variety of cap colours and shapes, and accessories (and one or two wayward hairstyles) gave the military a slight scruffiness, despite the superb discipline of their performances. Principals were perfectly costumed, with Eva Peron always looking radiant. Wigs, hairstyles (with those one or two exceptions) were generally very good, and make-up was very acceptable.

"The Art of the Possible" was one of the scenes that was abstract and confusing to me. There was a bit too much going on to clearly put across the meaning of the song. I also felt that "A New Argentina" would have benefitted from flags, banners, placards, props, the usual symbols of a revolutionary mob. They do help to intensify the atmosphere and to add colour to scenes that can appear dark and dreary. Also, bunting or national flags would have given a clearer sense of the various locations being visited during the Rainbow Tour. Despite both of these scenes being strongly performed, visually, they could have been enhanced.

The set was a clever combination of a suggestion of the Casa Rosada, mingled with a more rustic representation of the less glamorous architecture of an impoverished Argentina, and with its balcony, windows and elevated doorways, it was well utilised. Stage Manager, Cian Mulhall, and his team must have been delighted to have minimal physical work to do during the performance, as the only major moving parts, the staircases, were generally, and efficiently, moved by cast members. These functioned very well, even though I felt they were occasionally un-necessarily employed. Very nice use of the full length mirrors.

The ambient lighting of the set was most effective, creating tone and atmosphere, but there were several occasions when solo spotlights were either late or not quite focused on the intended target. Then again, there were the beautiful effects of the back lighting on the balcony, and the light emanating from the coffin. Sound quality was spot on throughout, with good quality in the "film" opening and a perfect balance between orchestra and stage. How fortunate Trinity were to have the talent of Lainey O'Sullivan available to them for the central and demanding role of Eva Duarte, giving one of the best performances of this role that I have had the pleasure to enjoy. Her singing was passionate and assured and her dancing was remarkable, but it was her acting and her attitude that impressed the most, capturing the capriciousness of the young Eva, the determination of the social climber and the confidence to stand tall even amongst those who consistently frowned upon her. Her desperation upon realising that she could not achieve her ultimate goals was palpable. A truly captivating performance.

Dave Quane overcame a somewhat youthful appearance to establish a mature and extremely capable performance as Juan Peron. He had gravitas when it was required, a believable cautiousness in the face of Eva's overpowering ambition, and a great sensitivity in coping with her demise. He was also vocally very competent. Apart from not always being illuminated when they started to sing, Cian Judd, Josh Hurley and Berus Komarschela gave energy, vitality and very fine vocal quality to the role of the narrator, including some very effective added harmonies. As the voices of Eva's conscience, they functioned almost as the devil on her shoulder, constantly reminding her of her beginnings and challenging her motives. This notion was fortified by having three voices rather than the usual one, and worked delightfully. Individually, they all exhibited a confident stage presence and a thorough understanding of their function. If Eoin Hand looked a tad young and innocent to be the experienced crooner and Casanova, Magaldi, he made up for it with a confident and very accomplished performance, well able for the vocal challenge of "On This Night of a Thousand Stars." This was a fine sense of him being trapped by Eva, and he displayed ample frustration at being subsequently discarded.

Rua Barron put good emotion into her delivery of "Another Suitcase", which really is as much as one can do with the role of the Mistress. She had an expressive face and strong vocal quality.

Lea Herron sang the role of the Little Girl with a crystal clear voice and an assured presence. Very nicely delivered.

The chorus and dancers were excellent throughout the show, giving power and emotion to their vocals, class and style to their movement, and constantly focused and reacting appropriately to the focal point.

Trinity Musical Theatre Society are a young and vibrant group, and judging from the thought and passion that went into this production of Evita, they will be a great addition to the AIMS family. My sincere thanks to cast, crew and committee for a truly inspirational night of musical theatre.

The theatrical experience that was Shannon Musical Society's production of The Wiz began long before the overture kicked in. Anne Barnes was in charge of House Management and created a pathway towards the auditorium that would have to be seen to be believed. It began with three road signs pointing to various locations in the script, which also included information about the society e.g. "SMS40 Northbound Emerald City", pointing to the fact that this was the society's 40th anniversary show. Poppies were everywhere. A house stood in the corridor, with real-life legs of a flattened witch wriggling underneath. A mannequin and a real person dressed as poppies (with the real person surprising the crowds by moving) was the right side of spooky. An ominous flame billowed up towards a troupe of flying monkeys, a gorgeous life- sized lion snoozed (with a real-life Dorothy asleep on him) and a bubble hung from the ceiling as an ode to the original Glinda. There were beautiful photos of the cast and crew (high definition with a lovely uniform white background) and all the 39 perfectly preserved programmes from the society's previous productions were presented. Some of the AIMS trophies awarded to the society were on display, which is a lovely way to celebrate the community's past successes. An army of ushers in white tops and black bottoms were lined up in single file on the steps of the auditorium, directed by Richard (in a lovely tux), showing excellent planning and organisation.

I must admit that there are better scripts out there than The Wiz. While there is more scope for comedy and invention in this version of The Wizard of Oz, and extra fun and energy to be had in the songs and dances, the narrative is hacked by a silver-sequined axe to its lowest common denominator. Dorothy's life in Kansas, with her very loving Aunt Em, is perfectly fine, and this version makes little effort at establishing any frustration in Dorothy's home life. The Wiz's Dorothy is immediately accepting of the Land of Oz, with no sense that she is overwhelmed by her arrival there. At the end of Act One, she and her companions are off to kill the Witch. At the beginning of Act Two, she is working for the Witch without any explanation. It's all a bit panto. When she finally clicks her heels together, the show ends, not even bothering to show her return to Kansas. Who cares anyway? We are not rooting for her to achieve her goal, because she never really misses home in the first instance. So as I arrived to Shannon Musical Society, I had already written off The Wiz as a show that serves the needs of the society, more than it serves the audience. But my Front of House experience was so special, that I sat looking at the blue wash on the closed curtains, with the band nicely placed behind an adorable picket fence, and I thought to myself that I might have been very wrong to feel apprehensive about watching this show. This society does not do things by halves. And it turns out I was right… about me being wrong. The show was such a treat.

Director Jessica Bray left no stone unturned and ensured a quirky and fantastical trip to Oz. The production, presented within an aesthetic that just kept on giving, whipped along at great pace, introducing one well-drawn and enjoyable character after another. A very well behaved Mini as Toto was held for the most part or kept on leash. S/he did not overly distract from the scene and was managed with care. Winged creatures dressed in black came on during the storm and moved Dorothy's small house around in a clever dance sequence, giving clarity to what was happening with the use of these personified storm-creatures. As Dorothy moved through her adventure in Oz, meeting these quirky versions of the classic characters, we had many laughs from larger than life performances in production that showed excellent attention to detail. Each scene change, for example, was a moment in itself, ensuring that lulls were kept to an absolute minimum.

Musical Direction was by Carmel Griffin. She gave clear conduction to her eight musicians and good support to the performers on stage. Everyone appeared to be well-rehearsed and comfortable with what they were doing. The vocal performances of all members of the front- line were to a very high standard across the board.

Choreography was by Pamela McGlynn. The production team utilised the talents in the group by having various dance troupes. The storm-creatures' moves were dramatic and well-rehearsed. A Munchkin kick-line, delivered in a slick yet tongue- in-cheek way, was fun. The Yellow Bricks' routine was brilliantly stylised, clever and inventive. The spinning of the bricks on their vertex on the floor looked really cool. The brick people moved the bricks from one side of the stage to the other, as the Scarecrow and Dorothy travelled, which was a cool idea. It is commendable that the same choreography was not repeated each time the 'Ease on Down the Road' motif came in, meaning these moments continued to be fresh and exciting. The routine for 'Everybody Rejoice' was slick, well-rehearsed and performed with competence, reminding me of some choreography one might see in Fame. The Crows very effectively flapped their arms and bobbed their heads, marrying their aviary nature with dancing. The energy in the reprise of 'Everybody Rejoice' bounced off the stage, leaving us on a high.

Hazel Park as Dorothy was such a strong leading lady with engaging facial expressions. She has a fantastic voice and sold all of her numbers with confidence and style. She was full of girl-power. What a star!

Hilary Phayer as Aunt Em had a good southern accent and had a soulful voice. Her character's love for Dorothy was very convincing. She embodied goodness and grace as Glinda and her poise created a nice foil for her slightly bonkers sister. Her final song was also super.

Grace Collins as Addaperle was suitably bonkers and entertaining. Her one eye closed, as she tried to cast a spell with her wand pointed firmly towards the sky was a hoot. She had a great voice and very good stage presence.

Brian Roche as the Scarecrow had fantastic characterisation and a super voice. It was great when he joined in with some of the dance moves in his first number. The production team utilised his skills, and he had a few nice acrobatic moments. He showed very good ability for physical comedy.

Ronan Mitchell played the Tin Man. He had a really cool speaking voice, some hilarious one-liners and his solo ballad was touching. A great all-round performance. Jason Ronan made a brief cameo as Uncle Henry and, most substantially played the Lion. He was completely 'fierce' as the Lion, full of sass and showmanship as he socked his first song to the audience. He had great timing and line-delivery.

Pa Woulfe was commanding in the title role of the Wiz. He had a super singing voice which soared throughout the auditorium. He played the contrast between the two sides of his character/accents very well, so much so I double checked that it was the same actor playing the psychotic and menacing Wiz and the wimpy guy who was tip-toeing away in his onesie and school bag. He told the story of his arrival in Oz with excellent clarity.

Hilary Orpen Ryan was fierce as Evillene. She had an excellently evil speaking voice and her riffing at the end of her number was awesome. She chewed up the stage in all her scenes.

Dara O'Callaghan as the Gatekeeper played his role with confidence, competence and humour. He managed the set pieces in his charge very well. Lord High Underling was played by Stephen Byrne and helped establish the Nazi-like regime created by the nasty Evillene. The Messenger was played very nicely by Alice Barnes. Mini as Toto behaved very well and did not become overwhelmed by this moment in the spotlight.

The chorus in this production were excellent, with grouping that utilised the talents of each person. The Storm- Creatures danced very well. The group of female Munchkins had fantastic characterful facial expressions. They looked like they were having fun, so we had fun with them, as they socked their high energy performance and great vocals to the audience. The People of the Corn's backing vocals and finger-clicking was cool and the Crows had great bird-like dance moves. The bricks did a wonderful job at manoeuvring the yellow-brick road, each time the number kicked in. The Ozians had superb presence and captured the quirkiness of the characters well. Each time the chorus appeared, it was a treat; in terms of aesthetic, characterisation and vocals. There was so much to do and there was no apparent weak-link amongst them.

Set Design was by Jessica Bray, Pamela McGlynn, Francis Maloney and Ultan McAvinue (who was also responsible for the exciting and quirky set artistry). Stage Management was by Francis Maloney, assisted by Martin Gough, and ensured that the pace never let up in this exciting show. When performers were utilised to move set pieces, they did so in character (or through dance) and was perfectly in time with the music.

The yellow and red swirl on the floor looked great and it was wise to do something with the floor, considering the seating in the auditorium was raised. The side panels had diagonal jagged lines, breaking the pieces into black and white with circular embellishments, which looked almost like futuristic poppies. A cloudy grey sky, on a vast expanse of land, on a large upstage screen looked suitably bleak for Oz. The transition into Oz gave us a burst of colour. The wings were graffitied to add excitement to the colourful aesthetic and furthered the narrative by adding slogans such as "There's no place like home" or "Oz is Evil". The covering of the picket fence when Dorothy arrived in Oz showed great attention to detail. The quirky trees in the Tin Man scene enhanced the magic of Oz. The corn pieces on the Scarecrow's pole matched brilliantly with the costumes in this scene. A flower-like person sitting on the flower-covered set piece was quirky. The entrance to Oz was like the front of an exclusive club, which was a nice metaphor. The Wiz's lair was awesome with the large head with lighted eyes. Evillene had a set of machine cogs which looked great.

While a large permanent back-drop of human silhouettes, looking as though they were enjoying a concert, was cool, I am not sure how well this worked overall. Its significance was not clear, other than to show people dancing and having fun. It felt as though it had been re-cycled from a variety concert. It made me wish that the screen had been used more. Perhaps the screen was not used because the images were bleached-out by too much upstage light. It is a compromise that has to be made so often: more light means less image. That said, I think that the changing areas in Oz might have been further enhanced by the use of projections, considering such an impressive screen was available. But I am being very picky here in a show that provided a wonderful aesthetic.

A fantastic job was done on costumes by Karen Barrett, Vie Leahy, Pamela McGlynn. Dorothy was in contemporary dress; with a cool blue leather jacket, a clever rainbow T-shirt as an ode to the famous song, and a funky gingham skirt as a nod to the original costuming in The Wizard of Oz. Aunt Em had a modern and practical top and jeans, making them both very normal against all of the wonderful and whacky characters we would meet along the way. Addaperle looked suitably bonkers in her strange hat, wine tights and multi-coloured dress with blue underskirt. The Munchkins added to the other-worldly-ness with their hot pink, blue and purple outfits with a variety of coloured underskirts, multi- coloured tights and shoes and ribbons. The fantastical black wings billowing out from the wings gave us our first clue that we were in for something special with the storm-creatures. The black flowy skirts on the girls, and the wide trousers on the guys, added to their wind-like movements. The People of the Corn looked brilliant in their yellow t-shirts, corn-head pieces and green overalls. The Crows were all in black with fabulous feathered mohawks. The Scarecrow had a pin-striped suit and black waistcoat. His straw wig matched the rest of the straw jutting out of the other parts of his clothing. Tin Man wore some very cool embellished jacket and trousers and his sparkling axe looked great. The Lion was a cool cat in a coat that nicely personified him while still looking animalistic. The Kalidahs wore a fantastical spin on a contemporary street-wise look with their long-hooded tops and masks. The variety of green costumes in the Oz scene was so exciting, nicely pulled together by the uniformity of green circular glasses. The Wiz looked like a high-fashionista in a fabulous coat. Evillene's head-piece was indicative of Maleficent. She wore an amazing dress of layered material with a dramatic skirt section. The eye masks with brown tunics over black costumes and the wheelies worn by the ensemble were so cool and evoked the Nazi-esque tone of the scene. The Poppies, with their head dresses and skin tight catsuits were sensual without being too risqué. The colourful skirts, cuffs and shoulders in 'Everybody Rejoice' were lovely. Glinda was fabulous in her pink Big Fat Ozian Wedding gown. She looked a little like a pageant girl.

Make-up was by Rachel McIntyre and Hair was by Ronan Mitchell and Pam McGlynn. The hair on the female storm creatures looked fantastic. If I were to be picky, I would say it was a shame that more was not done with the male heads, even a head scarf, just to de-personify them more and bring them in line with other-worldly-ness of their female counter-parts. Addaperle's glittery make-up added to her bonkers characterisation. The Scarecrow's straw wig and traditional face-paint, finished off his costumes marvellously. The Tin Man had embellishments on his face that complemented the detail in his jacket. His hair was also sprayed silver. The Lion, with his fantastic face-paint, had a cool head of dreadlocks. All genders in Oz wore green lipstick. The Wiz wore a white scraped- back wig, with green strip, which was menacing and highly effective at changing his look when he took it on or off.

Props were by Mary Forde. The yellow bricks had silvery-bling lines of cement, which showed fantastic attention to detail. Evillene's slaves carried buckets labelled H2No, which were a lovely touch.

Lighting, by Indigo, was meaningful and complemented the narrative. For example, as the Lion grew in confidence during his song, the light grew warmer around him. Lighting changed during different movements within the overture, something that is often ignored. Pink light on Addaperle's song, suited this number and specials were used throughout to isolate solos. There was a very cool growing gobo that brought us into the Spooky Forest. The red and green lighting made the poppies…well… pop. The green lighting complemented the variety of green costumes in Oz. The eyes and mouth of a gigantic head in the Wiz's layer lit up and was lovely against the white light on the Tin Man during his solo near the end of Act One.

Sound by Star Systems, Thurles, added some really cool sound effects. There was the tiniest bit of reverb on the Wiz's speaking voice - effective while remaining at a subliminal level. Baddies in Evillene's layer had an almost robotic sound to their voice and when the evil Witch melted, her voice was altered to an awesome drone.
