So while the script of The Wiz is not the best I have come across, Shannon Musical Society, with their exciting aesthetic, fine principal performances, talented chorus, inventive choreography and direction that showed great attention to detail, managed to turn a sow's ear into a silk purse. It was a feast for the eyes and a thoroughly enjoyable evening.

Sometimes when I watch Sister Act, I notice that the opportunity for comedic moments is lost. Other times, the cast work so hard to get laughs, that any sense of truth is lost. Tullamore Musical Society gave us a very funny version of this popular show, that brilliantly teased out comedy without turning the show into a pantomime. With the laughs, came a nice amount of sincerity, and I think this balance is what is required with this show. For example, I think Mother Superior and Monsignor O'Hara should be foils to one another. If one is the straight-laced one, it makes the other funnier. With this production, we got a Mother Superior who played her role, as protector of the nuns in her care, with great sincerity and conviction. She empathised with the struggles of her own character and was, therefore, accidentally funny, rather than obviously looking for laughs. This is how the evening progressed. Deloris' street wise-attitude contrasted nicely with Sweaty Eddie's goofiness. Mother Superior and Deloris met as equals in the end, both realising that they have something to teach each other. The troupe of nuns were fantastically individualistic, hilarious in the characterisation and physical comedy, yet were truly heart-broken by Deloris' sudden departure, resulting in a moving moment in an otherwise hilarious production. These examples are indicative of the balance struck by director Paul Norton and the cast of Tullamore Musical Society's production of this show.

Karen Martin was strong as our leading lady, Deloris Van Cartier. She showed an impressive set of pipes, really coming into her stride in her second song, showing how fierce she really was. She was able to be funny or emotional in equal measure. She sold her gags well, but could be emotional and introspective, such as at the end of the 'Sister Act' number. This is a mammoth role and one that suited this talented lady very much.

Some goofy comedy was teased out by Chris Corroon as Eddie, such as banging his hand off a table or missing a chair and falling to the ground. He was the perfect anti-hero. His vocals really came into their own when in his higher belt- register. He and Deloris had some nice chemistry together and it was lovely to see a different side to both these characters as they reminisced about the old days. Joan White as Mother Superior was stony- faced and stoic and suitably shocked by her first encounter with Deloris. This made her fleeting moments of warmth near the end quite impactful. Her singing was adorable. She grew brilliantly frantic in 'I Haven't Got a Prayer'. What I loved about this number is that she played it completely straight, which was what was very funny about it. An actor must have empathy for their character's cause, no matter how an audience might not agree with what the character believes. Joan did this so genuinely which was, for me, far better than trying to push the comedy towards the ridiculous.

Tomás Glynn had a deep bass-like voice as the nasty Curtis. He showed good vocalising in that 'When I Find My Baby'. His sweet singing juxtaposed dangerously with the menace of his intention in the reprise of this number, giving us some genuine baddie moments that did not only rely on comedy.

Aoife Fitzsimons as Sister Mary Lazarus created a memorable character with her glasses, aging physical frame and croaking voice. She has a talent for physical comedy. She really spelled out the words of 'How I got the Calling' with such clarity in her vocalising and physical gestures. Her 'You got the Boogie' rap was priceless. Linda Murray as Sister Mary Patrick was suitably jolly and bubbly in all her dealings.

Gráinne Donoghue as Sister Mary Robert was very nice indeed. She acted through song very well, showing us her despair in 'The Life I Never Led'. There was a nice moment when she stood up to the Mother Superior, showing the growth in her character.

The pre-show announcements informed us that Monsignor O'Hara would be played by Colin Hughes. Colin was adorable, warm and excitable as Monsignor O'Hara, everything the Mother Superior was not. With the mandatory send-up of the Irish accent, he had brilliant line-delivery. Wishing Jim Smyth a speedy recovery and I hope he got on stage at some point that week.

TJ was played by Rian Condron. He put on a funny voice that was indicative of his nerdy persona, such was its mid- pubescent quality. His higher register in 'Lady in the Long Black Dress' was great. In one raunchy number, he started thrusting towards the floor. My goodness. What can I say about Tom Maher as the brilliantly-wigged Joey and a particular hand placement in the same smooth number? Those hips. I didn't know where to look. Very funny indeed. Barry Dunne was great as Pablo. I have to give it to him - he certainly had the edge when it came to busting those dance moves to the audience. His falsetto in 'Lady in the Long Black Dress' took it to another level. Amanda Cunningham as Michelle and Marguerite McDonnell as Tina acted well in their opening scene with Deloris. The singing in this moment is very challenging but they managed with aplomb.

The chorus, which is arguably made up entirely of nuns, was super. It was clear how much work had gone into the scenes and songs performed by this troupe of committed ladies. Each time the nuns appeared, they were fully individualistic and in character and had fantastic reactions. They acted every moment, with great examples of physical comedy, socking the vocals and high-energy movement sequences. They looked like they were having fun, so we had fun, and their efforts were hugely appreciated. All of this fun was enabled by choreographer Graham Finnerty, who gave us some fantastic sequences of moves that one comes to expect from this show. That said, these were very well-rehearsed and slick, with some complicated sequences executed with style. There was one moment when the nuns finished a number by piecing together nine pages that made up the image of the Pope, which was surprising, inventive and married choreography with comedy.

All these well staged numbers were accompanied by quality singing, enabled by Musical Director Shane Farrell and Chorus Master Enda O'Connor. Vocal performances were lovely throughout and the nuns chorus knocked it out of the park. The band were at a good level and never over-powered the performances on stage. This would have been due to a combination of good musical direction and the excellent Jody Trehy on sound. Another star of the show, not mentioned yet was the set. The design and set-artistry were provided by All Set Scenery, Stephen Rabbette and Patrick Rabbette. A cross arch displayed the words "Benedictus qui est nomine domini. Hosanna in excelsis" and the lettering was really good here. The background contained a very nice, layered, texturised set with three dimensional arches, beautiful plaster- work, marble-façade and pillars. An arch shaped crucifix which turned to reveal red-brick on the other side, for the police station, club, Eddie's home and other non-convent places was clever. There were a series of faux stained-glass which were lovely. There were small white stone carvings with the gold detail on each side of the most downstage wings. Brick-work panels on the sides effectively covered/ created the wings. Purple and silver material looped around the room and foyer, adding a nice sense of atmosphere to the room and linked in brilliantly with the staging. Purple seemed to be Deloris' signature colour, linking back to her F.M. boots (Father Mulcahy apparently).

While the stand-alone structure of the set was excellent, I would argue that rest of the furniture used to create offices etc. was a little anaemic in places. If trucks could have been utilised to bring on certain secondary sets, there could have been the inclusion of some plant pots, or shelves or dustbins or something to frame the areas more and enhance the sense of space. I know money and wing-space does not grow on trees, but for me it was a set of two halves: a quality framework that could be found in a professional touring production of the show, with a few bits put out here and there that did not continue the professional tone created by the primary set. That said, there is no denying the opulence of the background scenery, which was very impressive.

The costumes, co-ordinated by Bláthnaid Fitzsimons and Graham Finnerty (with Costume Mistress Vlada Boravska), were just as opulent. Deloris wore an animal print dress with purple belt, purple boots and large purple bag, she looked over- the-top enough and put-together enough, which is indicative of her character. Her blue fur coat suitably clashed with the rest of her outfit. Her backing singers, Tina and Michelle, were dressed in spray-on colourful/shiny costumes, green stoles with pink scarves running down the middle, cinched in by a belt. Eddie's cop uniform was complete with sweat patches. The individual jeans/trousers/ wide collar shirts/leather jackets etc. on the mafia guys all evoked their individuality and were very much responsible for establishing the 70s theme. In a world full of glitzy showbiz costumes, cop uniforms and habits, these were the characters who could really establish a sense of time, and this was done very well. The skanks in the cop station, who turned up again in the bar scene, were suitably skanky in their leather caps and thigh-high boots. A group of fantasy dancers appeared in a dream- sequence during Deloris' 'Fabulous, Baby!' reprise and they were dressed in very groovy rainbow flapper dresses. Each time the Monsignor O'Hara appeared, his costumes were more outrageous, such was his enthusiasm for the choir's success and the money they were generating for the saving of the church.

The nuns were grouped into various colours in 'Sunday Morning Fever', which must have required a lot of co-ordination with the choreographer. Hard work like that often goes unnoticed. Youthful postulant versions of the costumes were provided for Sister Mary Robert, which was a clever touch. The nuns wore well-sourced dowdy white nightdresses and head-covers in a night-time scene. It could have been easy to scrimp here, citing the nightdresses as unimportant, but instead attention to detail and character was excellent. The silver- sequined costumes of the finale, with some of the more principal nuns in black, looked fabulous. The altar men looked great in white and red sequins. Deloris looked like a star in a white gown and fur. She was finally fabulous, even if it was a little Jessica Rabbit for the Pope!

Make-Up and Hair/Wigs were by the very busy Bláthnaid Fitzsimons and the very busy Ultan Keena-Robinson respectively. Sweaty Eddie had a moustache, evoking the 70s and his boy-trying-to-be-a-man sentimentality. Deloris had a lovely head of brown and blonde curls. The mafia guys, bar the youngest, all wore funny wigs, enhancing their comedic impact and evoking the 70s theme. The fantasy dancers wore some very cool black afro curls.

Highlights with the lighting by Ronan Kenny of Roken Lighting involved a series of warm-spotlights on the actors in their more intimate moments. Movers were shone out into the audience to evoke a chase scene and the excitement of the finale. Panels of purple/silver with golden strips opened out and lit up in various colours striping across. This was a lovely surprise and added excitement. There was a thermometer on a central crucifix, showing the rising funds for the church generated by the nuns' success. It was crude but brilliant. That said, the spotlight motif was the go-to decision in almost every special moment and I would suggest that more inventiveness was possible throughout. The bar scene, although employing the use of a mirror-ball, was not atmospheric enough. Perhaps more could have been done with lighting to isolate sets-within-the-set, so they looked less undercooked also.

However, it is a privilege to be so picky with a show that, overall, was extremely successful. There was a lovely balance struck between comedy and pathos, slap-stick and danger, and heightened characterisation with convincing honesty. The nuns' numbers, led by a talented leading lady, were slick and bounced off the stage. The stand-alone set was stunning. The costumes were gorgeous. What more could you want, I hear you ask? The Pope travelling up the aisle in a proper Pope-Mobile, guided by two priests and a candle-bearing nun? Well, we got that too. Fabulous, baby! to .

Athlone Musical Society were one of many societies effected by the freak Spring snow storms. Happily, they had a great house the night I was there. Roisin Carlin was central to the impressive Front of House design. The bar area was transformed with a rich red material across the walls and ceiling. Clay statues and wreaths were created by hand to evoke the Ancient Roman aspects of this story, that contrasted nicely with the treatment on stage. An extraordinary amount of work went into creating a fantastic atmosphere in this area. Massive congratulations must go to Roisin and her colleagues for the hard work and inventiveness in the transformation of this space.

I have been to musicals in the Dean Crowe Theatre before, but I've never seen this stage appear so spacious. The set was made up of three simple levels, which created an amazing sense of depth and perspective. A screen at the back displayed the Jesus Christ Superstar logo. Wooden structures at the sides of the stage (covered in graffiti statements such as "Love", "Hope", "Saviour", "#JC", "What's the buzz?" and "The Twelve" etc.) housed the band on top of them. The red and blue washes on the steps of the rested stage, as the audience filed in, looked very professional and the whole thing made for a very exciting set-up.

In a recent interview with the Independent, renowned Irish playwright Marina Carr said "Only a 19-year-old would talk about originality. A big thing [for writers] is escaping influence. It's impossible, and I'm convinced at this stage that anyone who says they have is lying. We get our ideas from other artists." One of her plays, By the Bog of Cats, is based on the ancient Greek work Medea. That said, she did not throw Medea on the photocopier and call it her own play.

I thought that the 2012 stadium-tour version of this show was highly effective at creating an interesting contemporary setting and exploring the idea of cult- life and celebrity in the modern context. I also think the mix of genders, in the Last Supper for example, works well dramatically and serves the needs of a society. Much of Athlone Musical Society's production was lifted from this version. Of course, there are certain shows that are difficult to mess with. Take The Producers, for example. The visuals are so heavily dictated by the script. Ulla paints the entire office white, so a white set is required. Jesus Christ Superstar is a rock- album, however, and the script is nothing more than a list of lyrics. There is so much scope for a director to come at this two- thousand-year-old story from their own angle. We may all pinch the odd idea, but I would avoid copying to this extent. Mary Magdalene's costume and hair were very like Melanie C's, for example, something I think was easily avoidable. Had I not seen this other production, I may well be gushing far more about the direction of this show.

That said, I believe that direction is about 10% inspiration and 90% perspiration and it no easy feat to get any show to a good standard without an extraordinary amount of hard work. Direction by Alfie Kilduff succeeded in getting this show on the stage to a very high level and there were lots of interesting moments. A masked ghost-like electric guitar player, which I interpreted as a rock-version of the Grim Reaper, was an impactful motif than appeared in just the right places to evoke sinister curiosity - such as Judas' suicide. Elsewhere, the rehearsed laughter by the crowd around Jesus in 'Heaven on their Minds' gave structure to the rhubarbing and was nicely timed. The chorus' exit after 'Heaven on their Minds' was nice and gradual with an effective spotlight on Jesus and Mary Magdalene holding hands, subtlety suggesting an intimate relationship between them. Later on, however, Jesus exited holding the hands of two girls, which made for a very interesting moment.

The contemporary use of mobile phones and selfie-sticks combined with the more traditional uses of placards to evoke the protests. The idea of the Temple as an exclusive nightclub, with bouncers (in their black sunglasses and clothing) and a velvet rope, was a good metaphor. A bunny-eared hen party with the blow- up doll, a mini girl group singing, a drag queen and a nudey man all added to the debauchery and was a nice contrast from the hippy vibe heretofore.

One particular moment of surprise was when a Donald Trump lookalike appeared as Herod. I cannot think of a more suitable modern reference for this bonkers king. His appearance alone brought the house down. Malcolm Whelan gave us a show- stealing Trump-like Herod. His singing, dancing and showmanship were very good. He sold the song very well and created a super modern reference for the bonkers Herod. The routine was very well put together and performed by the cast with gusto with a super tap number that included the man himself. He even said "You're fired" to Jesus at the end. These moments of, dare I say it - "originality", were a treat.

The flogging of Jesus was extremely violent, with the whips very effectively covering Jesus in 'blood'. There was the odd cackle here and the crucifixion was nuanced with some laughter, which was suitably unnerving. But the laughing was noticeably gone as the lights cut on Jesus' death and the metallic cross was lowered to the ground, with Jesus being carried off. The hanging scene was harrowing and pulled off with aplomb. It appeared as though Judas actually hung himself with his own scarf in front of a red backdrop. Choreography was by Lea Carroll. The energy in 'Hosanna' was amazing. The V-formation in 'Simon Zealotes' was awesome. Simon was played by Joe Steiner. He had a very good voice, particularly impressive in his higher belt. The person playing this role is responsible for really selling the 'Simon Zealotes' number, and he did very well in this regard. Simon and his fellow male dancers also busted some brilliant moves. The leper scene built and built with more and more people coming on. The white and black angels in 'Superstar' made for an excellent routine.

Musical Direction was by Ger Madden, whose work was well showcased by Recks Audio Clara. Sound from the stage was powerful but perfectly balanced, helped in some small part by the positioning of the band on top of the wooden structures. Every word was crystal clear. The "Hosanna Superstar" singing from the crowd during the Priests' scene really sounded like it was coming from the street.

The "aaahs" (as Jesus first appeared, bathed in white, but still one of the crowd) sounded great. They came in and out nicely, showing very good attention to dynamics. There were exciting choices made about when to bring in songs. 'What's the Buzz' came in immediately over the applause which created a great sense of pace. Mary Magdalene started singing a capella after the leper sequence, which contrasted brilliantly with all that mayhem. Harmonies in the first "Well done, Judas" sequence were very good, with lovely high and low lines giving great texture. The soprano line on "Take him to Pilate" was particularly impressive.

It was a treat to have the female voices in the Last Supper. That said, it was nice to have the recognisable male harmony- line maintained. I was baffled as to how the cast could see the MD, suggesting that preparation was very good here. That said, there is the odd moment when a visible conductor can be very helpful, such as bringing all of the chorus off on the "s" in "tribulations" at the same time, to keep it nice and clean.

Judas went off the melody a teeny bit too much for me in the reprise of 'I Don't Know How to Love Him'. I think it should echo what Mary sang more to illustrate the intertextuality here. The "awwwws" as the angels came on for 'Superstar' were awesome. There was good energy in the dance numbers. The very well-executed riot scenes sounded very well and the choral singing was excellent overall.

They say in theatre that one "cannot play the king". By this, it is meant that an actor can only be king-like if those around him act as though he is the king. This show does not work if the chorus are not good, as much of the narrative is to be found by their reactions to Jesus or with their protestations to the authorities. Thankfully, reactions from the crowd were excellent (such as when Mary Magdalene was wiping Jesus' brow) and it appeared as though the company had a very good understanding of their purpose and intention in each moment of the story. The solo lepers sang very clearly while showing their suffering.

Casting in this show was excellent throughout. It was great to see the high- powered characters be of a certain age, which felt very realistic in comparison to the youthfulness of Jesus and his followers. Shane Kelly (pictured above) gave us a charismatic Jesus in his earlier scenes, giving strong leadership, and it was clear why the crowds were obsessed with him. What a powerful voice. He had some incredible falsetto moments, particularly in 'Gethsemane'. His crying towards the ground during the first pause in this number was impactful and the audience reaction after this number was huge.

As a foil to Jesus, Seán Rooney gave us a lonely Judas, always on the outskirts.

There was so much clarity with this performance and for the first time, I really understood what the angry Judas' problem was. "People are hungry, people are starving". It was so clear what the issue was. His "whyyyyyy" was powerful yet guttural and rolling. 'Superstar' was sung with attack and gusto and the note on his final word - "are" - was awesome. Judas scrambling for the cigarette, enabled by Annas, was a good way to illustrate the stress he was under and how the Priests were manipulating him. I loved how Judas began his betrayal of Jesus to the Priests with his back to the audience. The torches on the hooded people for the first "Well done, Judas" was suitably sinister and dramatic. Their exit used the space very well as they travelled along the steps. Mary Magdalene was played by Caoimhe Croasdell (above). She sang so sweetly, with a voice as clear as a bell, like a cherub angel. This contrasted beautifully with her harsh styling. Her acting was understated but beautiful and she brought a softness to this character that I had not seen before.

Pilate was played by Kieran Kilduff. He had a lovely voice. I am glad he did not bawl his way through 'Pilates Dream' like so many do, instead giving us a professional man who has to deal with a lot of difficult situations on a daily basis. Strangely, the instrumental in 'Trial by Pilate' was not used for Pilate to realise Jesus was the man from his dream. I thought that was the purpose of that section. Pilate went from lambasting Jesus to defending him with no apparent reason.

Peter was played by Samuel Tuohy. He had a little vocal fatigue on the night I was in, something I'm all too familiar with myself as a performer. Hopefully, he got back to his full potential as the run went on. He acted the remorse of his betrayal with impactful passion, however.

Caiaphas and Annas were played by Tony Dalton and John McGee respectively. They carried themselves with imposing authority and their vocals, either bass-like or falsetto-fuelled, were very good.

The men and women of the well were dressed as down and outs, huddled around a fire. Their scene was very good, with Mary stopping Peter from attacking them with the bat, as he eventually handed it to her. Those involved in this scene did well and the male had a noticeably strong voice.

The performance space had that arena-like rock-concert openness, uncomplicated by too much unnecessary scenery. The sleeping stage, bathed in blue, showed a high definition Jesus Christ Superstar logo on a screen. A cyc covered the entire back wall, enabling some dramatic lighting choices. I was not sure how successful the images on the screen were: a dove, or the odd word such as "Believe" or "Heaven". The various moon images, in their varying monthly state were, I guess, successful at showing a passing of time. I think more bold, interesting choices were possible, however. The Priests' logo was Hunger Games-esque and evoked their high- powered positions. Pilate, as a Judge, got the traditional symbol of justice with the weighing scales.

A steel bin with fuel and flickering lights looked great, evoking the tent-city vibe. In contrast, the high-powered office scenes looked really well with a simple blacked out desk with laptop and expensive looking office chairs. This minimalism and colouring blended with the set, making it look stylised and professional. This enabled minimum fuss for scene changes also.

The steps enabled exciting lighting choices and all members of the ensemble could be clearly seen; which is a rare treat. From my seat, I could not always read what was on the screen during crowd scenes. Perhaps some of this writing could have been brought to the top of the screen, rather than in the centre, once this was noticed in the tech rehearsal.

In parts there was a real sense of musicality to the lighting, with the set-up changing in time with the score. Disco lights in 'Simon Zealotes' changed effectively to two spots on Jesus for "Neither you Simon or the fifty thousand" to punctuate this change in tone (and were adjusted nicely as Jesus stood up). A green wash to introduce the leper scene was suitably eerie. Two impactful beams of light shone on Judas as he betrayed Jesus. The black-out at the end of Act One took a few seconds before the house lights came in, allowing us to drink in the drama of the moment. The white flood lights on the 'Jesus Christ Superstar' melody, after Pilate places the thorns on Jesus' head, were dramatic. The rainbow of lights at the back for the 'Superstar' curtain call added to the excitement.

Costumes were by Anne Kelly and Michaela Barrington. There was a hippie cult-esque vibe about the crowd scenes that worked very well in the context of this tent-city treatment. The police riot-gear was very well sourced. Beads around Jesus' neck suggested a hippie vibe. Herod's Trump-like suit looked well and the change to the red sequined jacket was fabulous. Those men in authority and the Pilate as the judge all looked the part in their power-suit finery. Orange is the new shroud as Jesus appeared in a prisoner uniform after his arrest. Judas had the same silver star on his chest, linking him to the rest of the angels, but contrasted nicely with his leather jacket.

Production values on and off the stage of Athlone Musical Society's production of Jesus Christ Superstar were excellent overall. It is also commendable how this group seem to change it up each year and are not afraid to do comedies and tragedies. Their list of shows is highly eclectic, and they have a great reputation. Whatever they pick next, no doubt it will be fresh, and it will be great. What a joy it must be to be a member of this group.

Staging 'Into the Woods' is a rare brave choice for any musical society. There is little or no chorus in the show, making it difficult to produce, as a smaller cast can make it exceptionally problematic to finance and/or result in some members not taking part. Also, the timing of the score is massively challenging, in a way only Sondheim seems to manage, thus requiring painstaking work from the small cast. But it is a wonderful show, that combines the traditional narratives of a series of classic fairy tales. The bits we already know inform the first act, for the most part. The second act expands these fantastical narratives through a lens of domesticity; marriage, loss, temptation, betrayal, break-ups, cruelty, disappointment, love and how humans treat each other in a crisis. An extraordinary amount of hard graft and talent is required, on and off the stage, for this slightly left-of-centre show to work. Did Carrick-on-Suir Musical Society's production manage to pull off this massive challenge? Absolutely yes. They had all the necessary elements, the hard work and talent, in abundance. Their version was sublime.

Director Liam Butler staged this show in an enchanting aesthetic and ensured very clear story-telling with this difficult piece. It was a long show that whizzed along at great pace. Character, comedy and pathos were all teased-out in a balanced way, ensuring a magical evening, while exploring the ordinary just as effectively. We got some great giggles, from the Princes for example, yet the core characters' journeys were honest; entertaining in the first half, as they evoked the stories we know and love, and intriguing in the tensions of Act Two. Together with set-designer John O'Donoghue, a performance space was created that accommodated the various aspects of the narrative without ever feeling fussy or overly economical. The space was used very well; an almost stand-alone woods space that was moved about by a chorus of wood nymphs in a mystical way, as though we were forever finding ourselves in different locations. Both sides of the stage were built out to make Cinderella's house and the Baker's house. The main space was fully free for the adventure into the woods. Lighting was also a key feature to this enchanting aesthetic, which was cleverer than I have seen. With John O'Donoghue's beautiful paint work, enhanced by gorgeous lighting, the set looked incredible.

The lighting was gorgeous, atmospheric, and functional in framing each moment of the show. It was clear that light was a feature in the original design, as there were panels in the floor etc. that enabled the lighting to work wonders and bring this aesthetic to glorious life. The lighting sequences were endless. Each solo, duet, scene change and change in tone were bathed in lovely combinations of light that this show begs for, considering the mysteriousness of the piece. Certain nooks or crannies of the stage would remain lighted during transitions into new scenes, meaning we were never really taken out of the narrative. The lights in the most downstage section of the ramp were also an excellent idea, further enabling the beautiful set-work to glow with life and atmosphere. Truly magnificent.

This show is a mammoth undertaking musically.

The counterpoint and syncopation are so difficult, such is the way many Sondheim shows are written. When it is correct, however, there is nothing like it. Thankfully, it appeared to me that the cast nailed the timing of this challenging score, giving us a musical treat. This was enabled by Chorus Master Eamon O'Malley and Musical Director Fergal Carroll. The band were down in a pit, which is a blessing at any show. So low, in fact, one could barely see them. Signalling was clear from Fergal, however. The band were kept at an excellent level throughout, something that is more achievable when a theatre has a pit. The principal performances were exceptional, culminating in an evening which was a musical treat.

Sound was perfectly balanced throughout the evening. Thankfully, the pit ensured that the band never over-powered the singers, something that could easily happen when nearly a dozen named parts are singing against one another. Balance in these group numbers was also excellent. Cueing must be massively challenging in this show, and as far as I could see, it was spot-on. The pre-show announcements were provided by a first-class voice-over artist. The pre-recorded Giantess dialogue was spot-on (and very well performed by Peg Power). The baby crying sounded as though it was actually coming from the baby and sound effects, such as the squashing sound were excellent.

Interestingly, the costumes were not from long, long ago but the principal cast were quite modernised, marrying the contemporary with the fairy tale. The wood nymphs were more timeless, in their caps and waistcoats, contrasting with the modern stylings of the named parts. Rapunzel appeared in traditional Fairy Tale Princess garb, cleverly highlighting her captivity. The Prince's costumes, however, were highly stylised, with feathered shoulder pads that added to their pomp.

In parts, Hair and Make-up were kept simple, such was the modern-day realism of some of the characters. Elsewhere, the Witch's face looked well, albeit clearly a mask. Her striking wig, after her transformation to her former beauty looked great. Cinderella's Mother had some leaf detailing on her face and neck and foliage in her hair to blend her with the tree in which her spirit resides. The two step-sisters had large heads of curls and their mother had a fairy tale purple rinse. The Wolf's hair was turned up into two rolls on either side, blending bad- boy Elvis-style hair with the animalistic. The Prince's looked suitably suave with a quality wig provided for Keith Greene Dwyer. A superb balance between the theatrical and the day-to-day throughout the whole show was nicely struck.

The simple but highly effective puppet-like structure used for the cow Milky White was operated by Ellie O'Dwyer, Liadhain O'Shea and Henry Power with precision, resulting in the audience suspending disbelief and buying into the idea that this cow was really on stage. Those who appeared operating the goose that laid the golden eggs did very well also. The chorus of wood nymphs added considerably to the mysteriousness of the setting. Stage Manager Michael O'Hara gave very good training to his magical nymphs, who expertly moved the trees around to create different shapes in the woods. Other pieces were brought on, such as the quilt for Grandmamma's bed, and Rapunzel's tower would turn to appear as needed. Each moment was perfectly timed, free of fuss or obvious stage crew and enabled the show to flow beautifully.

An actor's job is to serve the writing and the story being told. This show is exceptionally well-written, and if performers are talented enough, the production becomes a captivating tale. Each actor is given an abundance of quality material on which to base their characterisations. In a long show that twists and turns towards the comic and the tragic with well-rounded characters, it almost seems reductive to pull apart each person's performance. This is because everyone was so good at playing such good roles. Acting and singing were of the highest quality throughout the production and each actor excellently actualised what Sondheim's material asked of them. The narrator of the piece was a young boy who had run away from home, experiencing this story unfold before him in the woods. He was played by Cristian Nolan. This young man had clearly put in a considerable amount of work in learning all of his material. He never broke character, even though at times he had to stay on stage watching the action for a considerable time. Very well done indeed on an excellent performance.

Ray Nolan was very good as the anti- hero Baker, certainly in love with his wife, longing for a child. It was a joy to watch him undertake the tasks that he was by no means prepared to do, in an effort to make a happy life for himself and his wife. He was perfectly cast, such was the likeability of his portrayal. This made his wife's brief indiscretion more impactful and [spoiler alert] his success in reuniting with his son at the end so touching. A lovely performance.

Sandra Power was equally impressive and likeable as The Baker's Wife, meaning that we sided with her even when she betrayed her husband. Her partnership with her sometimes-hopeless husband was very interesting, as she denied his pleas for her to stay in the kitchen and was quite successful in solving the challenges before them. She sang very well indeed. This was a gorgeous performance that was utterly captivating during her solo moments in Act Two.

David O'Donovan gave us a slightly vulnerable, slightly stupid, Jack. His efforts to improve life for himself and his mother result in some foolhardy decisions that have dire consequences. He evoked the young man very well indeed with this engaging performance.

Pat Quinn Bolger played Jack's poor struggling down-trodden mother, suffering her idiot-son and his inability to help her make a better life for them. Her costume in Act Two, when they have hit the big time, showed that style cannot be bought. While she despairs of Jack in the first act, she gives us a moving portrayal of a grief- stricken mother in the second act. Very well done.

Little Red Riding Hood was played brilliantly by Marie Kelly with all of the slightly annoying, yet highly comic, character traits required for this role. It is a great part; her voice and body language indicate that she is a young girl, yet there is a darker side hidden beneath (like when she adds her predatory wolf's fur to her red coat). All played quite innocently, yet there is always something more sociopathic or perhaps psychotic going on behind it all. Great job.

The Witch was played superbly by Irene Malone (above right). This is another character that is so well written. She is harsh yet shows vulnerability as mother/ kidnapper of Rapunzel. She is, at times, comic yet can be highly dramatic and emotional. She would betray any of them yet can be a rock of sense in a crisis. All of this was wonderfully evoked by Irene Malone in her star-turn as the Witch. We got plenty of laughs by Keith Greene- Dwyer as Cinderella's Prince and Dermot Keyes as Rapunzel's Prince. Both evoked the ridiculousness of their characters; which is to show all of the bravado of the fairy tale prince, yet do so in such a comic and over-the-top way that means there is little substance behind all of their pomp and posturing. Two great performances. Cinderella was played beautifully by Louise Mulcahy. In a world of very flawed characters, she appears to be the purest of them all. The abuse she suffers is the flaw in her story, as well as the presence of her dead mother. She is a dreamer, wishing for a better life. Yet, she is the one who breaks up with Prince Charming, showing us some more female empowerment, in this twist on happily ever after.

Rapunzel was played by Ashley Cooke. She has the voice of an angel. Unlike the rest of the cast, her costume belonged to a traditional fairy tale setting, evoking the idea that her kidnapper mother wanted to preserve her in the tower forever. She is clearly damaged by all that has happened to her, again showing that 'Happily Ever After' are just stories that have not ended yet. Her years of isolation and subsequent tragedies takes its toll and her all-too-brief demise is disturbingly fleeting and tragic. Cinderella's Stepmother was played by Helen Hahessy with all of the unapologetic abusiveness towards her step-daughter needed to tell this story. There is a lot of dark comedy (or comic darkness) provided by her as she chops off part of her other daughters' feet to force the slipper onto them. It is horrific, yet we find ourselves nervously laughing, which creates a fascinating dynamic.

These daughters, Lucinda and Florinda, were played by Tarryn Attlee and Sheridan Brady respectively. They were both very good. Sondheim's writing always gives us a side to a character that we are not expecting. These daughters are certainly nasty to Cinderella, learnt behaviour from their mother no doubt. But when parts of their feet get cut off and they are blinded by birds, one cannot help but see the flippant tragedy in their tales. We wash over their demise in a comic way, finding ourselves laughing at their suffering. Why? Because they are vein and demanding? Very interesting indeed.

The Wolf was played by Chris Hanlon with all of the predatory sleaze required for this role. It is one of the smallest roles in the show but was nonetheless impactful when he appeared. The Mysterious Man was played by Tobie Hickey with a realism fitting for this somewhat inexplicable presence, that drove the narrative or served as a mirror for the other characters. It is as though he is a spirit, yet in this Fairy Tale Land, he was paradoxically the most real. Michelle O'Sullivan gave us a nice cameo appearance as Little Red Riding Hood's Granny and Jennifer Williams was lovely as the spirit of Cinderella's Mother, who resides in a tree. The Steward was played by Caolán Deehy Power who is responsible for the death of Jack's mother. He kills her because he thinks she should die for the greater good but is far less enthused about giving his own life for the same purpose. Katie O'Shea sang beautifully as the Harp. These cameo performances ensured that the high standards set by the central characters never wavered.

This version featured the narrator as a child who had run away from home. In a beautifully emotive twist to the end; the Baker appears in search of this boy, his son from the primary narrative. This inventiveness by Director Liam Butler was a lovely surprise and caused quite a lot of sniffling throughout the audience. Each principal actor gave a wonderful performance; comedic and emotive, while nailing the difficult score. All of this took place on a set that had to be seen to be believed. Everything was so well presented, performed and executed. It was simply wonderful.

In presenting a no-nonsense production of the show, Director, Colin Hughes allowed the fine musical score and libretto to take centre stage, which is a very acceptable formula with a piece as popular and well-tested as Oliver!. The story was well-delivered by a very capable cast, who could possibly have been pushed further into developing the comedy of the piece. That, in itself, would probably have overcome the tendency for the action to appear a little too laid back. Technically and visually, the show worked well. The set design was very good, given the limitations of the venue, with the bridge at the rear of the stage being well used throughout, and the insets being appropriate and sufficient enough to suggest the various locations. There was a wide range of appropriate props, and the stage crew, under Stage Manager Aoife O'Connor, generally moved furniture and set pieces into place with a minimum of fuss. Lighting was atmospheric, with good selection of colours, and apart from revealing stage crew at the end of a couple of the scene changes, the timing of cues was good.

I think there needed to be a little more action and reaction around the arrest of Oliver at the close of Act One, and around the death of Sykes in Act Two, which happened very abruptly and without much tension. That said, it was a production free of any major flaws, and the entire cast gave good account of themselves. The youngest cast members were delightful and always committed to their scenes, and the mature chorus did all that was required of them with a fine energy and stage awareness.

The voice of young James Fennell was more than enough to merit him the central role of Oliver Twist, but added to that was a self-confidence, a good sense of the situation, and a bundle of cuteness that made him an absolute winner with the audience.

Then there was the cocky cockney lad, The Artful Dodger, played with character and comedy by Matthew Burke. He was a great partner for young Oliver and the two worked very well together. This is a lad with a vocal quality and an all-round ability that could take him much farther, if that is the direction he chooses.

Denis Sherlock had a good fussiness about his portrayal of Fagin, always agitated and on his toes. I did feel that his accent meandered a little, but it didn't detract from a very capable performance, and he worked extremely well with his young gang members. "Pick a Pocket or Two" and "Reviewing the Situation" were delivered with good diction and strong character.

Lauren McMahon was a lovely Nancy, happy-go-lucky in her early scenes and very believably tortured in her scenes with Bill. She gave a fine and passionate rendition of "As Long as He Needs Me" and worked well with the kids in "I'd Do Anything". She had good support from Holly Byrne in the role of Bet.

Paul Laycock had the appearance and demeanour to create a sinister Bill Sykes, and delivered his lines with ferocity. Vocally, he went astray at the end of "My Name" and again at the end of "Fine Life- Reprise" which detracted somewhat from an otherwise strong characterisation. Eamonn Murphy and Nell Rochford worked well together as Mr Bumble and Widow Corney, creating believable Dickensian caricatures, although I did feel that the comedy of their scenes could have been exaggerated a tad more. "I Shall Scream" was clearly delivered and "Boy For Sale" showed the quality of Eamonn's vocal ability.

Tom Delahunty was a credible Mr Sowerberry, accompanied by Janet McKennedy, who could perhaps have been a bit more austere as his domineering wife. "That's your Funeral" was articulate and tuneful, but again, could have been played to stronger comedic effect.

This scene was enhanced by a good performance from Luka Flanagan as a cheeky, thuggish Noah Claypole, and Katy Hanrahan gave good attitude to the role of Charlotte.

There was a nice sincerity to John Freeman's Mr Brownlow, and an equally delightful Mrs Bedwin, in the hands of Marian Holden. Derek Scott was a believably befuddled Doctor Grimwig. There were very good vocals from the chorus and particularly the solo voices in "Who Will Buy".

From a production point of view, Oliver! is one of those shows with many smaller/ cameo roles, and given how little time many of those roles have to make an impact, I did feel that perhaps they needed to be more exaggerated to make a more lasting impact. This would undoubtedly have given a more undulated feel to the pace of the show, in the same way that driving through rolling hills and valleys tends to be more exhilarating than driving a long, straight motorway.

The most striking feature of this production was an excellent orchestra, under Musical Director, Michael Fay, playing a revised studio version of the Oliver! score, which was quite exquisite, and allowed for the musicians to give virtuoso performances, which they did with panache. One or two of the tempos were a tad laid back for my liking, but they were, nevertheless, played with aplomb. The show has limited choral work, but what there was, was delivered confidently, with particularly well-executed harmonies in "Who Will Buy". While most of the principal singing was secure, more attention needed to be given to the "It's a Fine Life - Reprise", which lost its way a little towards the end.

With the exception of Old Sally possibly needing to look a little closer to death, the make-up for the show was nicely attended to, and wigs and hairstyles were always appropriate. Fagin and Bill Sykes were given good definition and character. The costumes for chorus and principals were well-selected, and with the exception of one or two of Fagin's gang wearing a few pieces that looked a tad modern, the general costuming was very pleasing. Sound quality throughout was of a very high standard, with the exception of "Food, Glorious Food", where some of the solo children's lines were virtually lost, which is a common problem when a lot of individual voices are used.

Dún Laoghaire put their best feet forward and delivered a show that displayed a wealth of talent, a tidy presentation, and a standard of entertainment that sent their audience home with contented smiles and their ears filled with popular and well- delivered music. Thank you very much for a very enjoyable night.

It's not often you get offered holy communion on the way into the theatre, but I was instantly set upon by a priest bearing bread and wine/Ribena, although being of a different religious persuasion, I respectfully declined. It was a nice touch from a front of house team who were polite and very hospitable.

The currently highly popular "Sister Act" proved to be the perfect vehicle for Ennis Musical Society to unleash a female tour de force. The standard of production and performance here was as good as and better than I have seen from Ennis throughout an association with them that goes back more than two decades. Much of the thanks for that lies in the hands of Director Jessica Bray who has surpassed herself with this production. She showed attention to detail in establishing very individual personalities within her chorus of nuns. The show was fresh and abundant with good comedy, and it was as visually pleasing as it was technically efficient. A well designed and equally well painted set provided a strong background to the action, and with the guidance of stage manager Roisín Dempsey, a combination of the stage crew and the nuns managed to keep the show moving at a very good pace. The set pieces were nicely constructed, and there were appropriate and well-sourced props. Equally appropriate was the well- selected wardrobe for the show, with the Sisters progressing from black and white to an eventual glitzy and glamorous outfit. A few nuns did need to be more careful in attaching their wimples. There were nice era-appropriate dance costumes used by Deloris's girls and in the dream scenes. Men were well attired, but it might have been nice to see the gangsters with varied wigs of the era, alongside Curtis, whose wig was very good.

A good balance between pit and stage was apparent in Shane Farrell's control of the orchestra, never allowing the musicians to overwhelm the singers. Pace and tempi were just about perfect and the show bounced along from start to finish, interrupted only by a more sympathetic accompaniment to the gentle ballads of Mary Robert and Deloris. How nice to see that among his other achievements, Shane appears to have been ordained as a Bishop, taking charge of a somewhat ecclesiastic band of players.

Eilís O'Neill took on the choral quality of the show, and did so with aplomb. Harmony and Diction was, indeed, the key to success. This was very good work on her first outing as a chorus mistress. Sarah Corcoran could have been a tad feistier in the central role of Deloris Van Cartier, but that does not diminish the strong impact she made, especially with her powerful and expressive vocal quality. She was the right choice to carry this demanding role with confidence and a relaxed stage presence.

Cleo Meaney had just the right amount of comedy intermingled with her severity and reverence in the role of the Mother Superior. Suffering from a dodgy throat on the night, she still managed to put across her musical numbers tunefully and with strong expression.

Sarah Kenny made a wonderful impact as the happiest of happy nuns, Sister Mary Patrick, with excellent comedic timing, an assured voice, and astounding physical capabilities.

There was a lovely vulnerability about Fiona Coughlan's Sister Mary Robert, always gentle and sincere, yet well able to stand up for herself when required. Her rendition of The Life I Never Led was very emotionally charged.

Rachael Culligan gave a stern but delightfully funny edge to Sister Mary Lazarus, with good diction even during her rap sections.

Patrick Woulfe looked a little young in the role of Sweaty Eddie, but that didn't stop him from making a good impression as the eventually heroic police officer. His songs were well delivered, and he showed good comic ability. The romantic nature of the relationship between himself and Deloris needed more emphasis.

Derek Barrett used a wealth of experience to give a sleazy character to the role of gangster Curtis. His "That Girl" solo was well performed, and he was a relaxed and natural leader of the pack.

Martin McNamara as Pablo, Nathan Bluett as TJ and Brian Roche as Joey worked effectively together as a team, with Brian standing out for his comic timing and excellent physical awareness, but each character had his own good individuality and earned laughter from the audience. Tony Murray was an effective Monsignor Ryan, believable in his religiosity, and enjoying the silliness of becoming the oldest swinger in town.

There was strong support offered from Emer O'Flaherty and Geraldine Cahir, as Sister Mary Martin-of-Tours and Sister Mary Teresa respectively, and in the opening scene, Deloris had good company on-stage from Claudia Ryan as Michelle, Elaine Gavin as Crystal, Kate Corrigan as Tina and Shauna Murphy as Diane.

The chorus did all that was asked of them with energy and abundant enthusiasm and also a high level of precision. Choreographer, Pamela McGlynn, took full advantage of that energy to provide the female chorus with a variety of high- octane routines, featuring choreography that was complex enough to be ever- interesting and yet simple enough to be performed with energy and accuracy. This is the hallmark of good choreography. There was a nice ad-lib quality to the Bless Our Show routine and good comedy in the Chase scene.

Both vocally and physically, the chorus contribution to the show was excellent. Lighting was varied and atmospheric and generally added to the visual impact of the action. Sound, throughout, was well- balanced and cueing was spot on. This was a highly competent and confident production, which enabled me to just sit back, relax and enjoy the fun. Thank you to all concerned for a most enjoyable night of religious fervour.

For those reading this who have not been to the INEC in Killarney, then quite frankly, you haven't lived. It was strange to be in this venue when not attending the annual AIMS Awards Ceremony held there each June. This time, however, the auditorium was transformed, with long rows of stadium seating facing the wide stage. The event was free-seating, but it would have been impossible to get a bad seat. Songs from the musicals, similar to the styling of the show itself, played as the audience took their seats, nicely setting the right tone. The two famous screens on either side of the stage beamed advertisements from the sponsors. The venue must seat about a thousand audience members. It was here that Killarney Musical Society staged a riveting version of Sweet Charity, with a superb front line of excellent performances in a unique aesthetic. What else do you want? About twenty musicians all brilliantly spaced on scaffolded levels, like a full-blown orchestra behind the performers? Well we got that too.

Director Killian Collins enabled fantastic performances from the principals and the ensemble alike, all set in a quirky and inventive space, that was abstract, yet highly effective at framing the narrative. Two large screens on either side of the stage (you know them if you have been to the awards) added nice clarity to the story, particularly useful with this minimalistic but professional-looking set. The slides, designed by Kieran Somers, contained some phrases which described Charity herself, "Who Wanted To Be… Loved". As this story of whether or not she would achieve this goal unfolded, more slides supported the narrative, such as "A Stroke of Luck", "The Heavyweight", "The Big Finish", "A Big Decision", "To Be Continued", "Back in the Elevator", "The Proposal", "At Last" and "Plans" etc. These were often written on a silhouette of Charity's body, which linked nicely with the theme of the poster and programme for the event. Elsewhere, at the Rhythm of Life Church, there were colourful images to evoke the flower-power era.

Principal performances were always highly engaging and clever. How the girls laughed at the end of 'Baby, Dream Your Dream' for example, played nicely against the drama before quickly changing to a moment of genuine sadness. Scenes which featured the entire ensemble where always well-directed. The crowd reactions in the park were excellent, with a very good mix of ad-libbing, while official dialogue continued, giving the park scene a highly authentic feel. There were also plenty of little touches, such as the roller- skater. Holding Charity upside down was very well executed. I loved how the "inner" monologue kept going as the customer kissed her neck. The Pompeii Club customers clapped along and enjoyed the band, as though the musicians were part of the narrative. The leader of the hippies, sitting on the red bin with his legs crossed, looked fantastic. The group formation in 'I Love to Cry at Weddings' was great, and the scene finished with a lovely picture. The use of the scaffolded structure was superb, for example when Charity was hiding in the closet or when she and Oscar where up high in the fairground. Other quirky moments, such as how the cast used their bodies to evoke the sense of being on the subway, were simple but highly effective.

Musical Direction was provided by John O'Brien, who ensured a musical feast with this enormous orchestra. When the brass section pounded those famous opening bars of 'Big Spender', I felt goose-bumps galore. When conducting, John was a little removed from the orchestra, who were positioned behind the performers. He stood on a podium, far more downstage, meaning the performers could see him also. Perhaps some might have found this distracting. Not me. The evening had the feel of one of those very well staged concerts (ref: Emma Thompson's Sweeney Todd) and the MD's positioning, with his lovely way of conducting that appeared to involve the musicality of his whole body, added to the evening for me. Principal singing was excellent throughout. There was a lovely sense of dynamics in 'Big Spender', such as that nice low "hey". The different "me", "good times" and "fun" coming in one after the other was great. The counter-point in 'The Rhythm of Life' was excellent in this show- stopping number. The reprise of 'See Me Now' made for a lovely finish to the show. A superb job was done with the choreography by Daniel "Cheech" Maguire.

There was beautiful interpretative movement in 'You Should See Yourself'. 'Big Spender' was a visual treat, as Daniel ensured that these ladies performed endlessly inventive moves. Also, the dance/movement during the inner monologue, as Charity danced with the customer, was awesome. The routine in the Pompeii Club was so cool, with the stoic yet sultry black-bobbed female dancers slickly performing this atmospheric number. The crossing here was so effective. A huge amount of work went into 'The Rhythm of Life'. It was so good I wanted to shout "again" and re- live the whole thing. The three groups that moved into two groups, then running to the side, and the hippie-esque circling all worked brilliantly.

The set was made by Made for Stage Ltd., Limerick. The scaffolding brought across the stage, to create the dance space for the stripper girls, was a very good idea - even if it looked like a bit of a job to get it there. It was very effective once placed. The make-up tables and mirrors worked really well for the backstage of the club. If I were to be very picky, I might say that it was a small shame that the bulbs did not light up. The velvet rope on the fancy apartment building, along with the uniform of the door man, was all that was needed to transform the central entrance in to a brand-new space. The four tables with the white tablecloths evoked the Pompeii Club nicely, and the silent movie style slide with "The Aloof" written on it, matched the green plants in this scene.

The side areas of scaffolding would move more central stage to create new areas - highly effective for the wardrobe scene, for example, or as the elevator where Charity meets Oscar and he has his panic attack. Vittorio's apartment looked wonderful, with its soft grey armchair, gorgeous bed with iron frame. All these set pieces were nicely decorated or enhanced by props. The use of two tyres and the red steel trash can, for example, created a super space for the Rhythm of Life Church. The candy-floss and balloons at Coney Island looked great. Charity's apartment set, which she shares with her two friends, was special, with its little sofa and footstools. The director might have gotten away with setting this back in the club, but this was a lovely new addition to the narrative. Its simplicity contrasted nicely with the lushness of Vittorio's' home. The three benches and two street lights were nicely re-used in different moments, effectively recycling some set-pieces.

Stage Management, by Pam Brosnan, ensured great flow to proceedings, bringing the clever vision of the set to fruition.

Costumes were by Pat McGann, Tralee Musical Society and Killarney Musical Society. The two cop uniforms looked great. There was a sense of uniformity in the 'Big Spender' scene, with the ladies all dressed in various combinations of red or black satin, or a mix of both. The doorman's uniform of the fancy apartment building looked super. The gowns, stoles and tuxes in the Pompeii Club looked gorgeous. Vittorio's red smoking jacket was very suave. The silver sequined mini-dresses, black shoes and black to-the-elbow gloves looked fabulous on the dancers in the Pompeii Club. The costumes for 'The Rhythm of Life' were so good; the wigs, afros, headbands, colourful flares and beads were all awesome. So much effort went into this stand-alone sequence. Seeing the stripper girls in their normal clothing in their apartment showed another interesting side to these characters. Not to be clichéd, but Charity's pink dress really evoked the idea of love. Her red dress linked in perfectly with the colouring of the lovely red and white costumes worn by the majorettes.

Hair and Make-up, by Ann Rohan, was mostly of the time. There was one young man in the chorus with a very contemporary up-to-the-minute hairstyle which could have been covered up. The girls' images worked best when wigged also. Charity's pixie hairstyle suited her so well. The black bobs on the dancers in the Pompeii club gave a fantastic sense of uniformity, giving the whole vibe a very Austin Powers style baddie look.

Lighting was by Kieran Somers. 'Big Spender', with the band in a red wash, and the blue and red on the girls, was very atmospheric. The yellow lighting on Vittorio's bed, at the end of 'If They Could See Me Now' is a good example of how songs were nicely punctuated. The light spilled all the way onto the side walls of the vast auditorium, bringing them closer to us and developing a sense of intimacy in this huge space. The disco-ball effect on the reprise in the strip club is an example of how newer technology can be used so well. The psychedelic lighting of yellow and purple on the floor (with the orchestra in a green wash) for 'Rhythm of Life' was cool and the red and blue lighting of the cops' siren worked well here. The lighting that followed this scene was lovely and simple, creating a nice contrast to that madness that had come before. The purple and greeny-yellow lighting for 'I'm a Brass Band' was somewhat sinister, nicely playing against the drama of this song where Charity celebrates that somebody loves her.

Lighting was perhaps a little abstract in the odd moment, such as when going into the Coney Island sequence. This is an example of how with great power, comes great responsibility. I have seen some examples of this around the country since the advent of LED lighting. Just because something weird and wacky can be done, does not mean it always should be done. There was also one blinding moment from the lights on the rig on the stage-right side of the audience, as they moved and came on at the same time.

Sound, by Star Systems Thurles, was very good throughout. Only in a space this big, would a society be able to have so many musicians, particularly on brass. Thankfully, the balance was spot-on for the most part. It was a joy to listen to the big band without panicking that all the vocals were going to be lost, as is too often the case. The seaside sound effects for Coney Island worked very well. There might have been the potential for a little more vocal in the showband scene. It was a little hard to hear them with the band at full gusto. The splash sound effect, as Charity fell into the water was great, as was the ping and hum of the elevator. There was not a weak-link between the principal characters and the chorus. The cops in the park were suitably full of bravado and attitude. Each of the female dancers in the club were excellent, both in their dancing, singing and during the separate dialogue scenes. Their entrance ensured that the setting-up of the scaffolding was not boring. Every hippie was very much in character. All those who provided solos and harmonies in 'I Love to Cry at Weddings' did a fantastic job. Pádraig Creedon had a lovely presence and a great accent as Daddy Brubeck, the hippie leader of the Rhythm of Life Church. Džana Bukvić was beautiful as the sultry Ursula March, acting a great foil to Charity's less than demure characterisation. Her exotic accent was wonderful also.

Gerry Adams, as Herman, had a great accent and characterisation in his no- nonsense approach to managing the working ladies in the club. He showed a lovely voice, putting across 'I Love to Cry at Weddings' very well indeed.

Derek O'Leary was very suave as the Italian stallion, Vittorio Vidal. He had a great accent, lovely rhythms when he spoke and a beautiful classically trained voice that resonated with professionalism around the room.

He simply and effortlessly made room for the high notes, rather than reaching up to push for them, such was the quality way in which he could support his voice.

With her great voice and sense of musicality, Siobhán Bustin as Helene ensured that the girls harmonies were awesome in 'Baby, Dream Your Dream'. She was perfectly matched with Amanda and completed the line-up of principal ladies perfectly.

Amanda Miura, who played Nickie, is a dancer with a capital D, such was the quality of her shaping when she moved. She was so convincing as the straight- talking tough-broad friend/colleague. I can see her being an amazing Anita in West Side Story also. A quality performance. Supporting our leading lady was a superb actor by the name of Rory Ward who played Oscar. His panic attack in the lift was absolutely awesome. He has a lovely voice and played the part with just the right amount of vulnerability. [SPOILER ALERT] We really wanted it to work between himself and Charity and it was heart-breaking to see that he could not commit.

Finally. Lily McMonagle. What a star! She had an excellent accent, a super singing voice, fabulous facial expressions and a great sense of nymph-like physicality in this top-class portrayal of Charity Hope Valentine. Her every reaction was so well thought-out. She never wasted a line or dismissed a moment as unimportant. She constantly changed it up, meaning we never quite knew what was coming next, and she ensured there was never a dull moment in her performance. She could go from excitable to defeated, comic to tragic, on the turn of a dime. "Did you ever have one of those days?", she'd asked and we'd all laugh, yet she'd immediately burst into tears and it was instantly harrowing. She was utterly captivating and deserved the immediate standing ovation on her bow.

Would I make it? Would I not? These were the words floating around my head all week, as us Dublin folk braced ourselves before Storm Emma. I was so pleased to make Fortwilliam Musical Society's production of Sister Act, thanks in no small part to the society themselves for supporting me on my journey. There was a lovely buzz in the theatre on the evening, aided partially by the food on sale and the bar licence. The venue enabled a complete night out. The theatre, with its lovely red seats and red curtain is an excellent resource. Almost all shows in the North start at 7.30pm. Almost all shows in the South start at 8pm. 7.45pm was a nice middle-ground between the two, giving the audience time to get there, without making the finishing time too late.

This was my second bout of the nuns that day and I wondered if Fortwilliam could hold my attention, considering how often this show has been staged. It is incredulous to me how each time I see this show, it feels fresh and new - a testament to the creativity abundant in this country. This Sister Act was treated like a drama, albeit with laughter song and dance. There was a realism and sincerity in which the whole show was based, treating it like a story about real people, not as a farce. This must have been in no small part thanks to Director Simon Pyper, who endeavoured to tell an honest story. Some treatments of this show will aim to do anything for a laugh but, for me, this can lack integrity. I am happy to report that this was not the case with Fortwilliam's version. Rather, we got a Deloris who has had it tough; who meets her match with a Mother Superior that was unrelenting in her mission to protect those in charge, while she falls in love with an Eddie who was neither farcical nor boring. Mother Superior was suitably straight-laced, cautious and stand-offish when Deloris arrived. Her induction to the convent re-located various locations, showing a passing of time that suggested we were getting snippets of this conversation, rather than the whole thing. This made the idea of Deloris pretending to be a nun more realistic, as normally I think that she buys into this idea too quickly.

Everything in this version made sense. As Deloris fled the bar, she made sure she had the food she had ordered in her mouth. This is an example of teasing out comedy, while remaining truthful. Of course she would grab the cheese steak, she was starving after a fast. This was the first time I saw a reason why Mother Superior addressed Sister Mary Clarence as "Deloris" in front of the nuns: she was rushing because of the squad cars lining the streets. It was also truly heart-breaking when Deloris left, having transformed these nuns' lives. Mother Superior getting rid of the Sisters while the kiss was happening was more realistic than staying in situ and reacting to it. This way there was a reason for the exit.

Mary Robert standing up to the Mother Superior was really given time to breathe and the moment when the gun was pointed at Deloris, the stage all in red, was genuinely tense. The final conversation between the Mother Superior and Deloris was a meeting of equals with a well- measured stress on the word "we".

The very professional and clever set was provided by Newbridge Musical Society. The surprise stained glass windows, that came through the gauze on the side panels, were very inventive. The revolver at the back worked so well at immediately establishing different locations, such as the cop station. (I also loved how it was used for Deloris' bow!). The stained- glass globe was gorgeous. The desk, two chairs, files, phone and Eddie's jacket on the chair created a busy work-space in the cop station. The steps were utilised well to create a bar and the two tables with two chairs at each shaped the space well. The confessional boxes needed two chairs on the side sections to allow the actors to sit. Their standing on either side did not quite make sense.

The clever design of this set, with its changeable stained-glass windows and very cool revolving wall at the back, meant that Stage Management by Andy McKnight could be pacey and efficient. The timing of the nuns carrying on the benches was excellent, coinciding with their backing-vocals for 'Here Within These Walls'. This made them and their lives part of this number. This included them more in the number, making it less weird that these vocals were happening, and avoided any sense of lull in the scene change.

The lighting in this show was a character in itself. It was provided by A Show in a Box who utilised excellent resources to make an impressive display. The mirror- ball in the centre of the theatre, created a fantastic effect, but comes with a word of warning not to over-do it. Keep it rare and special. There were some lovely specials used throughout, such as the celestial light shining on Deloris and Mother Superior during their counter-point moment. There were four white specials (with smoke cutting through them) beaming onto a red- wash floor, which was suitably menacing for 'When I Find My Baby'. That said, it was slightly lost on me why they were there if the lads did not dance in them: The three stooges were out of the light and in shadow for most of it. The various spotlights throughout 'Raise Your Voice' clearly established the idea that time was passing and that different rehearsals were taking place. The changing colours of the stained-glass window throughout was brilliant. The final blackout of Act One, with just the stained-glass windows left on, was very effective. The Pope looked so holy up there on the balcony, such was the power of the white light on him.

If I were to play devil's advocate, I did stop to ponder whether or not this impressive lighting display was a little far-out, particularly in the earlier nun numbers. At times, it was indicative of a Diversity concert. While this is an impressive achievement, I wondered whether this was indicative of the 70s and a simple choir of nuns in a church. But the advantages far outweighed any niggles here. The highly professional lighting framed every moment, added clarity, energy and movement to each number. There is no doubt about it: A lot of work went into the plotting of these lights to ensure a highly entertaining evening.

All of this lighting would have meant very little if the singing and dancing in the show were not to a good standard. Musical Director Niall O'Flaherty enabled excellent principal vocals and choral numbers that lifted the roof. The band were hidden backstage which was the right thing to do, ensuring that the band did not block the action. Normally this lends itself to ensuring that the band does not overpower the performers also. Alas, through no fault of anyone in the pit, the balance was not there in the first quarter of the show, with the volume of the music making us strain to hear to the vocals. Thankfully this settled as the evening went on. All of the principal vocals were impressive and competent, indicating that they were well-prepared. The nuns' numbers, which require an extraordinary amount of work, bounced off the stage and their harmonies were secure throughout.

Choreographer Alex McFarlane's routines bounced of the stage and gave space for the comedy also. They were well- rehearsed, simple, effective and slick. The show-choir nature of this piece requires those lined formations, and much in the way of armography. This was given to us in spades. It is difficult to be inventive when many of the numbers require the same treatment, but thankfully Alex was able to continue to devise exciting movement for the show. The reprise of 'Raise Your Voice' seriously got the crowd going and formations and spacing the finale were excellent.

None of this spectacle would have been enough without solid performances from the actors themselves. Deloris Van Cartier was played by the fierce Kelly Brown. She played a tough cookie who has been around the block and perhaps has been hardened by her experiences. She has a powerful voice, a true alto, who gave us vocals that Adele might give us if she were to play the role. She was funny when she needed to be, yet vulnerable or tough when required.

Her impassioned rendition of 'Fabulous Baby' (reprise)/ 'Sister Act' combined power and introspection.

By the end, she resembled a heroine from an action movie, who appeared as though she had really been through the mill. Other actresses can go right back to normal after nearly dying, but this was better thought-out than that. Mother Superior was played by Wendy Pyper. I have seen this role played for laughs, which for me is not the best way to approach this part. Personally, I am a champion of Wendy's treatment of the role: a head of a convent whose experience has taught her that "outside, life is grim" and she is unshakably committed to the protection of the nuns in her care. She is clearly disturbed by the threat Deloris poses to the convent. Of course, this makes for many occasions when moments are accidentally funny. It is because of her stoicism, that scenarios can be hilarious. This is more honest than mugging each moment in the hope of a laugh. I congratulate Wendy on creating a believable and honest character, which brought tension or comedy in just the right amounts.

Vijay Sharma played Eddie. He uncovered a speaking voice that evoked the sweaty police officer's nerdier side, while still remaining enough within the realms of realism that we could imagine him and Deloris together. This was a lovely balance. He has an impressive voice which is used to good effect to belt out some of his solo number - while showing off nice falsetto and lovely low notes. His obvious transition into his dream-like suave persona during 'I Could be that Guy' was great.

Curtis was played by the imposing Eamonn Connolly (above) who had all the tough-guy presence to evoke an intimidating mob-boss. Again, he was not a caricature but rather a believable presence that brought danger and tension to our leading lady's story. His accent was perfect, and he unnervingly relished in the menace of 'When I Find My Baby' reprise. Emma Dallas was suitably meek as postulant Sister Mary Robert and showed a good journey in her character. Her slight stutter made it more impressive when she found her voice. And what a voice. She knocked 'The Life I Never Led' out of the park, evident from the massive response she got from the audience. The woman in front of me muttered "unbelievable" after this.

Stephen McQuillan played Monsignor O'Hara with the obligatory southern Irish accent. He has a very clear speaking voice and managed all of his material in a competent straight-forward fashion. He did very well at getting the audience going and became hysterical at the mention of the pope.

Megan McGarry played Sister Mary Patrick with all the jolliness and positivity needed for this character. Her repetition of Pablo's Spanish phrases was hilarious. As the perfect foil to Megan's characterisation, Ditanya McKinty was a tough-cookie as Sister Mary Lazarus, with all the hilarious cynicism of this aging and sarcastic nun. She seized the opportunity to bring the house down with her various raps. Ella Taylor Campbell as Sister Mary Martin- of-Tours and Jaquie Hanley as Sister Mary Theresa brought extra comedy to the scenes they were in with their senile behaviour.

John Kelly as Joey was very good at being Mr Cool in 'Lady in the Long Black Dress' and would have a very smooth voice for radio. Jordan Walsh showed very good vocals, with good falsetto, as TJ. Daniel May played Pablo. His flamenco-style finger-clicking linked in perfectly with his characterisation and his chest-baring antics were a scream. The way these gangsters crawled towards the women in the audience during 'Lady in the Long Black Dress' had the place ecstatic with laughter. The woman beside me was genuinely fanning herself afterwards. These guys should start doing hen parties. Lucy and Annie McIllwaine played Tina and Michelle respectively.
