John Dooley had an imposing presence as the tough-guy producer Sidney Bernstein. He owned the stage whenever he appeared and was so suitably unlikeable that we were inevitably on Carmen's side when he was killed.

Jessica Cranshaw was played by Áine Coe. She was brilliant at being crap. Another performer who served the narrative by embracing the comic unlikability of her character. Another death that didn't bother us in the slightest. Stephen Fagan had specific responsibilities as highly featured member of the ensemble Randy Dexter and performed his material with competence and confidence.

There have been many compliments listed above about the Direction and  Choreography. None of those compliments would be possible without the talent and hard work of this chorus. Harmonies were well-learned and sung with power. The routines bounced off the stage and the reactions in the crowd scenes were excellent throughout.

June Young from That Looks Good and Claire O'Reilly were in charge of costumes. The country and western dresses and the male cowboy costumes in Robin Hood looked very well. Aaron's open bow tie, in comparison to how smartly dressed the other producers were, gave him a look, that evoked the emotional state of his character. Georgia's floral dressing gown was lovely. Darryl needed a coat, to illustrate that he had come from the outside. Carmen's mourning dress was suitably sexy and accessorised with a purple flower, showing that she wasn't that aggrieved (or going to sacrifice her sense of style) for a dead husband whom she could not stand. Pyjamas throughout were classic and evoked the old-style effectively (This is an area that can easily go wrong, and societies sometimes scrimp here, so well done). The Kansas dresses were gorgeous. The tanned Native American female costumes with brown frill and the yellow feather in the head-pieces (but red for Bambi) looked nice and theatrical.

Make-up was by Catherine Coventry and Hair was by Leona O'Neill. Wigs were excellent throughout, transforming some of these ladies' natural looks, and ensuring that the leads looked very much part of the period in question. Darryl's hair was somewhat modern in style and might have benefited by a little more slicking- down.

Lighting, designed and supplied by Stagelights.ie., was used well to punctuate the beginnings and the endings of songs and to add to the energy during the numbers. The eerie green lighting in 'The Woman's Dead' worked very well. The spotlight on the piano for 'I Miss the Music' was very nice for this sincerely performed ballad. The red wash to punctuate Aaron's "thinking of you" was very effective.

The play-within-the play calls for "Light Cue 5" to be shone on Georgia as she reluctantly performs one of her own songs. I think she needed her own spotlight to phase out a little of the business around her, rather than simply shining pink on the backdrop. I found some of the well- intentioned reactions from the crowd a little distracting after a while. I think she needed to be framed in her own intimate space for this, so that the chorus reactions were more subliminal.

Sound was by Vinny Osborne of The Sound and Music Company. There were numerous solos in 'The Woman's Dead' and each one was perfectly cued. There was a little bit of feedback caused by the chair dance, which I am sure was sorted as the week went on. Everywhere else, the balance between the band and the performers was excellent, thanks in part to the positioning of the band behind the performers and thanks to the sound desk, of course.

Philippa Alford directed a show that gave us sincere performances and believable relationships, presented in a very good aesthetic. The principals and chorus alike gave us impressive vocal performances. Trisha McDermott devised inventive numbers that bounced off the stage. This was all possible thanks to a talented cast and a committed chorus. Thankfully the impact of Storm Emma did not mean it was curtains for Curtains. "The show must go on" is a lyric repeated in this score. And the show did go on. And it was very good indeed.

Rush Musical Society stage their show each year in their local Millbank Theatre, a gorgeous intimate venue. With tiered seating, there is not a bad view in the house. They do a nine-night run, which deserves a round of applause in itself - no small ask for the leads of Jesus Christ Superstar. This show is never done the same way twice, something I enjoy about it. That said, sometimes versions can be a little overcooked, cramming as much in as possible, losing the run of itself in the process. This version was lovely and simple, easy to follow and clear in its interpretation, visual representation and style. There was many a red eye when the house lights came up, showing that it was an emotive night for some.

Director Barry Kavanagh chose to set the show in biblical times, unmuddled by too much referencing to modern day motifs. With no script and only a list of lyrics to go by, there is no end to the directions this show can take. However, with no boundaries, productions of this show can aim to do too much and as a result achieve too little. I appreciated the straight-forward simplicity of this version. We got biblical versions of the characters exploring the phenomenon on celebrity, leadership, politics and religion in the context of 2,000 years ago. Like all versions, the rule book is thrown out for the final 'Superstar' number, which reverted to modern showbiz pizazz, drawing parallels with modern superstardom.

The set was comprised of a triad of two- tiered playing areas of wooden scaffolding, that were connected when necessary. The middle area could move up and down stage and turn to become something else, and this was slickly executed by Stage Manager John Foley and his team. The crucifix would be attached to this section also. The low table for the Last Supper was about a foot off the ground, meaning that the Apostles could sit on the ground and the action never felt blocked. In the context of the traditional setting, the wood worked beautifully, and the various levels provided so many mini-performance spaces onto which moments could be staged and pictures created. Light could fall in these areas effectively also.

Lighting, by Colm Eaton, effectively created atmosphere and framed the narrative throughout. There was a dim red light on the top of the central steps and subtle gobos on the floor to bathe the sleeping stage as we filed in. The yellow light for the lepers was suitably eerie. Reds and purples evoked the menace of Pilate's layer. The crowd in green and the soldiers in red during 'Trial by Pilate' enhanced the danger of the moment. Jesus being backlit for the lashes was very effective. The celestial light on Jesus as he was on the cross was lovely.

Slow-motion montages during the 'Heaven on Their Minds' opening, walked us through a series of recognisable bible stories, summarising Jesus' ministry, thus bringing us up to the point that the narrative begins in earnest. The High Priests created an omnipresence within the show, forever observing from a height with defensive folded arms, not just appearing for their solo moments. These heights were also used effectively to allow Jesus to preach. There were some nice moments of sinful behaviour in the Temple, such as a Belly Dancer who was walked around on a lead. There was an interesting dynamic in 'I Don't Know How to Love Him', as the sleeping Jesus clung to Mary and she fobbed him off in her confusion. It can often be portrayed with her being all over him, so this role reversal was enjoyable and interesting.

Including the women as servers gave an extra dimension to the Last Supper and Jesus washing the feet of the Apostles was a nice touch also. Thankfully the Apostles did not fall asleep in one quick movement as though gassed. The crowd taking over from Pilate in the counting of the lashes was a clever way to signify how he had lost control of the situation. The slow-motion crowd movements during his "Where are you from, Jesus…" created an effective change in tone. Direction ensured that from the crucifixion straight through to the end was particularly successful and well-structured. Placing Jesus on the white sheet after the crucifixion was lovely.

In terms of the performers' image, the Biblical setting of this show was nicely actualised throughout the evening.

The coverings on the female heads were particularly important, I thought. Noticeably, Mary did not wear a head scarf, which set her apart and suggested a certain defiance or rejection of modesty in the context of the setting. Judas wore a red shirt with black waistcoat, two dangerous colours that pointed to the darkness of his character. The Priests were nicely uniform in their gold and black tunics. I might argue that some of the chainmail/ armour was a little unconvincing. Perhaps there was a tone of theatricality that was slightly lost on me. Either way, this contrasted with the realism of the rest of the costumes. That said, Herod's version of this was convincing, complimented by his purple cloak and broach. Pilate's gold chainmail over his wine costume established his authority, complete with a crown of golden leaves.

Hair and make-up designed by Ali Murphy was kept suitably simple throughout. Jesus' real-life image was dramatically transformed to create the iconic look we have come to associate with this man. The High Priests wore stylised eye make- up with thematic black strips in their white beards (the opposite with Caiaphas' beard). Herod's make-up enhanced his bonkers persona.

Musical direction was provided by Dave (Doc) O'Connor. In the context of this small theatre, it was not surprising that the band was in another room behind the stage. There were two small monitors on either side of downstage for the actors to see the MD. They were quite subtle, and I almost did not spot them.

Those infamous opening "aaawwwws" at the top of the show were performed onstage by the ensemble, which was really nice. The sopranos were particularly impressive in the "Superstaaaaaaaar" finish of 'Hosanna'. The bass-voice drone on the "well done, Judas" at the end of Act One was impactful. It was cool the way the ladies gave the "pool of wine" response during the Last Supper as they served the men. The harmony by the Apostles, after Jesus and Judas left this scene was lovely. "I wonder how he knew" was beautifully harmonised by Peter and Mary and I have not heard it done like that before. Their harmonies in 'Could We Start Again, Please?' were lovely also.

Unfortunately, the show was a bit loud. The band were behind the stage, which usually solves the problem of the music being over-powering. This was not to be the case, however. To counteract this volume, the mics appeared to be up sky-high, meaning that the top of the show was a tad deafening. The groups singing the "Tell me Christ…" bits after Gethsemane were hit and miss, with some groups containing people with mics and others who did not. It appeared to me that all mics were up here and it was pot-luck whether a group were heard or not.

There were a number of times when entrances were not secure e.g. Mary's initial entrance before the 'I Don't Know How to Love Him Scene' (I didn't get the impression it was her fault), the start of 'Hosanna' was a beat off and the entrance into the Temple singing was tentative and took a while to establish itself securely. It took a handful of confident people to get a verse going before everyone else knew they were to come in. Perhaps this was because the band were in another room and everyone was relying on technology to sync what was happening on stage with the band.

Choreographer Sinéad Lightley ensured that her cast were well-prepared in plenty of high energy entertaining dance routines. The opening number was very interesting. There was something hypnotic about it. It appeared to mix what looked like sign language with slow, quirky folk dancing that seemed unique and unlike much of what I have seen before. The crowd surfing in 'Hosanna' was awesome, really capturing the meaning of the number. The six dancers in 'Herod's Song' were great and their reaction to his entrance, as though irritated by him, was funny. It was clear that a lot of work went into the rest of the numbers. The cast had clearly been well-rehearsed by Sinéad and they executed the routines with energy and commitment, ensuring some highly entertaining up-tempo numbers.

Adam McGealy as Jesus had a cool, almost hippie vibe, as he moved hypnotically in some of the slow-motion scenes. He had all the warmth and likeability required for the role. It is often the case that Jesus is very angry and argumentative, and while some of the score and lyrics asks for this, I think that Jesus should have a calming, ultimately forgiving nature that contrasts with Judas' anger. I don't see how Jesus can spread the message of love and be constantly at war. Even in the betrayal and the passion, there is an apparent inevitability to it all. The death needs to happen, and perhaps Judas is being asked to play his part in it. Happily, Adam's interpretation found a lovely balance between a man who is made of flesh and bone, who has relationships, who is afraid, with a man who wants to inspire those around him. He has a lovely voice, with a bit of a rocker growl to it. That said, I am not convinced the right choices were always made in rehearsals. By far, my favourite rendition of 'Gethsemane' is by Michael Crawford, who steers clear of all of those hyper- falsetto moments. While Adam nailed some of them, such as his "Why should I die", others were not as natural to him such as the "get out" in the Last Supper. I think the natural voice of the actor should be the starting point when devising the vocals for this show. Do it simple and well, rather than reaching for an ideal that is not within the natural timbre of the voice. But hey. What do I know? The audience went wild after 'Gethsemane', indicating that there was much to be admired here (in particular how he sustained the word "mind" at the end).

In contrast to Jesus' balance, Jim Walsh as Judas gave us a man on the edge, both physically and emotionally. So much on the outskirts of the Jesus phenomenon, he could not reconcile with much of the hype surrounding his leader. Seeing things differently to everyone else, he sung "Everything's alright" with far less optimism than everyone else, like a mantra to calm himself down. There was always something interesting going on behind those eyes. He was clearly uncomfortable with some of the choices Jesus was making, between the superstardom and his relationship with Mary Magdalene. These tensions eventually drove him to shop Jesus to the High Priests, a decision he later came to hugely regret. He dove deep and unearthed some high-octane emotion in the moments that led him to suicide. He writhed on the ground in emotional pain and sobbed about his role in the demise of his lord. He showed off some serious power with his singing also. No need for a mic here. He absolutely belted it out, ensuring an excellent all- round performance.

With all of this agro, it was very nice to have a Mary Magdalene that brought balance, calm and gentleness to proceedings. Jennifer Browne has a lovely singing voice and she acted well through song in 'I Don't Know How to Love Him' (which got a great reaction from the crowd). She did very well in the reprise of 'Could We Start Again, Please?' at the end, which appeared to be highly emotive for the audience around me. This part is too small, in my opinion, so it was lovely to have more from Mary in the aftermath of Jesus' death.

Mary had a particularly close friendship with Peter, who was played nicely by Daire Kelly. Their singing/ harmonising of 'Could We Start Again, Please' was lovely. Daire did very well with his scenes that were concerned with his denial of Jesus. He joined Mary in this final reprise and matched her in emotion.

Colm Heaney played Pilate. There is something special about the timbre of his speaking voice. His 'Pilate's Dream' was very nice indeed. It was a simple interpretation of the song and I am glad to see he didn't wail his way through it. He moved well between the effortless arrogance, the aggressively intimidating and despairing loss of control, in this role that requires the actor to do so much in so little time.

Gary Finegan had superb showmanship as King Herod. His vocalising of his big number was highly entertaining as he socked it to the audience in a charismatic way.

Nathan Durkin as Simon gave us some lovely vocals, particularly in the lower sections of Simon Zealotes. His falsetto bit at the end was also cool. Another good showman who was able to give his number plenty of welly.

Brian Dennison as Caiaphas and Peter O'Brien as Annas (joined by an equally good third priest played by Paul Johnston) did very well as the High Priests. Their defensive body language and stoic omni- present leering towards Jesus worked very well. They were the perfect baddies, ladling the pressure on Judas to betray Jesus.

Kate Motherway as Maid by the Fire and Bob Crowther as Man by the Fire did well in their scene, placing pressure on Peter and causing him to deny Jesus.

This show contained a highly committed chorus. Dance routines were well-learnt and well-executed. Everyone appeared to be very clear on their intentions in each moment, whether they were supporting Jesus, reacting to the agro, putting pressure on Pilate or heartbroken after the crucifixion.

The ending, a choral reprise of "Could We Start Again, Please?" was a nice surprise. The lyrics were borrowed from various professional source-materials. The cast placed candles on the ground, forming the shape of a cross, which would remain after a final blackout. This was a lovely idea. I might argue that the performances were a little too overwrought with emotion for me. Sometimes it is more powerful to see someone trying not to cry than to seeing someone bawling. There was plenty of sniffling in the audience and many swollen red eyes when the house lights came up, suggesting that this production had been emotionally impactful on the audience. The instant standing ovation also suggests that the audience hugely appreciated the show.

Newbridge Musical Society is an inclusive organisation, and the community spirit alive within the group is evident when one moves around the hallowed halls of Newbridge College. They are a society that are not afraid to mix things up, with this show following last year's dark production of Sweeney Todd. Based on the 1998 movie, The Wedding Singer is a fun musical send-up of 80s culture, with a good dollop of romance. The characters are well-drawn and highly entertaining and if done right, the show can give the audience a great night out. This Wedding Singer was a blast. There was a lovely chemistry between all the leads and it appeared as though the entire cast were having as much fun as the audience were. The opening and closing numbers bounced off the stage and there was so much fun sandwiched in between.

The pre-show announcements began at 20:00 exactly, showing good organisational skills. This announcement was done with an accent in the style of the show, giving the information as though part of a wedding speech, which was a lovely touch. Director Sharon McNamara created a clever performance space and presented the narrative well. The comedy was nicely teased out throughout; subtle at times with Robbie's awkwardness, outrageous like as when Linda did her unforgettable seduction routine on Robbie, and thrilling like when Rosie had the audience in hysterics by her atypical Grandma characterisation. The rest of the show unfolded with hilarity, yet culminated in a touching finish, as we found ourselves really caring for the characters and hoping that they all find the love that they deserve. Musical Direction was provided by Dave McGauran. While it can be a shame for the audience not to see the band as part of the overall musical experience of an evening, I think placing them elsewhere is always the best compromise when staging full- blown musicals in smaller venues. From the ceiling, there was a screen facing the cast that would provide signalling for the performers. Another screen was flown in allowing Dave to wave at the audience through a camera, all dickied up in a wig and golden jacket, giving us a taster of the fun backstage happening in the live band. Principal singing was very good throughout and it appeared as though all were very well prepared for their performances. The ensemble singing was also great. There was a noticeably cool techno-vibe during the scene change after 'A Letter from Grandma'. Sound was by Jody Trehy and it was cool the way different instruments were fed into different speakers, giving a nice surround- sound feel to proceedings.

Choreographer Julianne McNamara utilised the talents of the group very well. She had some stunning dancers at her disposal and she gave them challenging moves that allowed their talents to shine forth. Elsewhere, she grouped the dancers appropriately and pitched the choreography to suit each group and to add variety to the numbers.

The movement in the opening number involved a series of punchy poses on the beat of the music. The fun moves set the tone brilliantly for the night, and we knew we were in for a good time. There was a nice mixture of individual and uniform movements in this number that was socked to the audience by the ensemble. There were lots of suitable eighties moves incorporated, such as those infamous high kicks.

'Saturday Night in the City' had so many surprises. The otherworldliness of the dancers in 'All About the Green' was atmospheric with cool inventive and highly effective moves that were excellently executed by the girls. A flown-in bar gave a new flavour, with the men all dancing behind it, giving us only their top halves and their lower legs. I love the use of props in choreography to enhance the narrative and the pink/ purple folders worked very well here. The final song - wow, what a number! It bounced off the stage, sending us off having had one hell of a party. If I were to be picky, I would point out that the odd moment of dialogue was upstaged by other action/ dance e.g. the famous water-pouring scene was slightly blocked by some dancing, and I think it was a shame not to let the audience see this more clearly. These few moments were fleeting and thankfully the vast majority of the show was very well staged, with a good aesthetic, clear and well-developed characterisations, quality laughs-a-plenty and some heart-warming romance.

The set was provided by Scenic Projects Ltd. It consisted of metallic-styled wings with lovely structural detail, working right over the top arch of the stage. Within this fairground style set, there resided a million coloured bulbs that would, in just the right moments, burst into life, adding plenty of visual excitement to some special moments in the show. Each wedding had its own colour scheme from the costumes to the props. The series of wedding cakes were incredible, each more impressive than the last. The three-layered ones all linked with the colour scheme of the wedding. The Bar Mitzvah Cake had lovely detail, with the piece on top and the words "Mazel Tov" on the bottom layer. The five layered one in the store begged a belief. One side of the cross-arch contained a blue dumpster, which looked perfectly of-the-time and had very good detailing to show dirt etc. There was a well-placed phone here also and the dumpster was surrounded by old bottles to add extra detail. The other side looked cool; with the stylised circular trees, beautiful flowers and a garden bench. Other pieces were brought on stage to suggest various other locations, such as a queen-sized bed for Robbie's room (complete with sound system shelves, alarm clock and lamp). There were steps in front of the stage that would be used very effectively throughout the evening. All of this was pulled together nicely by a backdrop which looked like a blend of watercolours, that would work very well with the lights to make the space pop with 80s colour. Finally, the use of the screen to show Glen calling on his cellular car phone was inspired, giving that much- needed something extra to this scene. A stained-glass window was flown in also and, when coupled with the two white chairs and pulpit, made for a convincing chapel space. A velvet rope and the "Disco" stand worked well at establishing the club scene. A gold fringe curtain for the Bar Mitzvah mixed things up again. Lighting was by Tomás Fitzgerald of Stage Lighting Centre. There was a musicality to the lighting, as the set ups changed to match the beat of the music. A dangerous red sky on the cyc and the smoke evoked the comic torment suffered by Robbie, as he lay in bed after being jilted at the altar. A blue mover enhanced the moments when he began to scream and the white special on his Grandma was lovely. Tacky fluorescent light in the club brought us back. Green lighting for 'All About the Green' was, of course, perfect. A rainbow of 80s colour moved over the backdrop at the end, enhancing the excitement in the final moments.

Stage Manager Tom Kavanagh ensured swift and speedy scene changes, with a focused crew that transformed the stage as quickly as possible. The first wedding scene, after the opening number was set up in the blink of an eye. From here we knew that the crew would be on the ball for the evening. The use of a silk black curtain in the dumpster scene not only created a new sense of space, but enabled the scene changes to happen on the sly behind it. The silk nature of the curtain, however, did mean that we saw the stage crew's torches working away unfortunately. It was a slight shame also that some pieces were crooked when first flown in, such as the stained-glass window, but no doubt something about the theatre caused this. Flying in the gaudy wedding dress made for a really cool moment, however.

Costumes were by Andrew Reddy. In an effort to make each wedding feel different, a specific colour scheme was assigned. The men's shirts were matching yet had individualised detailing on them (stripes etc.) that pulled the scene together nicely. It was a left-of-centre choice and I admire any production within AIMS that attempts to do something new and quirky. The principal characters did not follow these themes, meaning they were always easily identifiable in such crowd scenes.

There were some excellent nods to the 80s, such as Robbie's Grandmother's hilarious purple shell-suit tracksuit (with yellow Walkman) and Sammy's oversized blue jacket.

George was suitably outrageous in his sparkly trousers, yellow jacket and blue head band (both colours repeated in his wrist scarves). I am not sure the 80s motif was pushed to its potential, however. Glen and Robbie, for example, wore dashing office suits, but they could have worn them to work or to a wedding in this very year. Louder coloured suit-jackets, with shoulder pads and rolled up sleeves, for example, were missed in my opinion. This might have furthered the visual comedy of the piece.

Linda looked super in all her outfits. She looked like a Madonna-reject in her solo number on the steps. Her spray-on black leather shorts and Van Halen t-shirt evoked a real bad-girl image. This look contrasted nicely with Julia's safe floral- print dress. The long white shirts with detailed trim at the ends looked well in the Bar Mitzvah scene. The female office dancers' black pencil skirts and white shirts really captured their no-nonsense intentions. Julia's garish wedding dress resulted in her looking kinda pretty/ kinda comic, which is the perfect balance for this show.

George's messy hair, filled with dreadlocks and embellishments looked perfect. The gaudy fluorescent finger nails on some of the ladies were just the ticket. While the female hair-styles were from the 80s, I might argue that some people looked somewhat safe or subtle, like a kindergarten teacher. I think the opportunity was missed to really have fun with the hair. Wouldn't it have been good craic to back-comb the life out of the girls' hair, to really push the envelope of the 80s theme? More blue eye shadow, that's what I say! It might have been an idea to have more of the men sport those awful handle-bar moustaches also. Linda's orange crimped hair was amazing by the way. A group of poor unfortunates at Wedding Table 9 all looked hilarious; the woman with the sideburns, the man with the awful hair-cut, the man with the plaster holding his glasses together and the girl with chocolate cake smeared on her face. The costumes and wigs for a group of celebrity impersonators created their likenesses perfectly.

Fionán O'Carroll was excellent as Robbie Hart. His characterisation was more heightened than I have seen before, giving us splashes of Jim Carrey and/or Chandler Bing. This meant that we never got bored of this part, a role that otherwise could be played quite plainly. He constantly changed up how he delivered his lines, giving us an engaging and often comic performance. That said, he toned it down considerably as the show went on and as his heart began to break, which was lovely to see. And what a voice! It is so well placed that it resonated so clearly around the hall. I would doubt he was in much danger of losing his voice, such was the surety with which he sang. He has some belt. This young guy is one to watch. Keelin Kilduff as Julia has a beautiful voice, with lovely vibrato in her expertly sustained notes. Her final "will you sing at my wedding" was gorgeous. She had a simplicity and a softness to her balanced character that contrasted nicely with Robbie's edginess. She was adorable when enticing him out of the dumpster. We were rooting for this character every step of the way and we were very pleased when she got a partner that really appreciated and deserved her. Simply lovely.

Again, there was a lovely sense of contrast in the characterisation of Holly by Clodagh Donnelly. She had more sass and naughtiness to her than Julia, giving us plenty of laughs with that rough New York delivery. She was a hoot in the scene where Robbie and Julia rehearsed the kissing. She danced and sang brilliantly, socking it to us in 'Saturday Night in the City', as the water poured down on her in the final moments of Act One. Super job. Daniel Ryan also had a talent for mixing up his line delivery, finding constant new directions to take his dialogue as Sammy. He never wasted a line and spoke so clearly. If I were to have one piece of advice for this very good actor, it would be to marry each line without the need for a pause. I do not mean to speed up the words, I mean shave down the pauses in between sentences so one flows more into the next. Otherwise, another very likeable character was created here, and we also rejoiced in the partnering of himself and Holly (he was a hoot when he first tried to hit on her). He really got to show off his voice in 'Single'. Very well done.

All the bravado of Sammy was nicely contrasted against a very good performance by Rory Dignam as George. His camp nature was excellently observed, giving us many a giggle with his one liners or his physical comedy/ dance. He did a great job and showed off a good vocal range during his hilarious Jewish singing. Together with Daniel, they formed a highly entertaining comic duo, with Rory's hysteria contrasting with Daniel's hilarious attempt to break the news to the crowd that Robbie was stood up at the altar. Cormac Malone evoked all the unlikeability and arrogance needed to portray the cheating slime-ball Glen. He was very believable as the perfect baddie. His horrid characterisation worked well against the rest of the central cast of nice people. Here is a bizarre compliment… but he was seriously excellent at being in the freeze in the restaurant. How did he do that? He busted a few nice moves in 'All About the Green' also. A very good performance overall.

Cora Coffey Maher was absolutely brilliant as Robbie's Grandmother, Rosie. She was so cute, making all the innuendo more shocking and hilarious. She was so cute when addressing Robbie in 'A Note from Grandma', ergo taking the house down when she called his ex a "skanky whore" at the end. Her lovability meant that we were moved when she was sad and championed her when she broke out in a side-splitting rap or dance-break.

We got a scene-stealing performance by Hayley McCormack as Linda. Her change from the angelic to the rock-psycho and back again was highly comic in her solo song on the steps. She gave a no-holds- barred risqué performance on Robbie's bed that made us older members of the audience blush. Her commitment to this moment cannot be questioned, such was the massive reaction she got from the audience, in this hysterical portrayal. Gill O'Brien was very good as Julia's Mother, Angie. She got a great laugh on her "fake pregnancy" idea and how she consistently reminded her daughter that her slime-ball fiancé was rich. Rory Chadwick was highly entertaining and convincing as the drunken best man, David Fonda, who passive aggressively compares himself to his Mr Perfect brother.

There were a number of other quality cameos throughout the evening ensuring that, whether a part was big or small, no one let the side down. This committed chorus knocked the dance numbers out of the park and sang very well indeed. They looked like they were having a lot of fun and the audience had fun as a result. It was clear how much work went into this show and I congratulate them on a job well done. What a joy it must be to be a member of this group and it was a joy to watch their show.

Children of Eden is a fascinating, albeit flawed, show that sets the domestic issues of biblical characters against the epic events of the Book of Genesis. The first act centres around Adam, Eve and their two sons Cain and Abel. The first act is sort of unsettling as Eve is tempted by the fruit (that God* put there) and gets turfed out of the Garden of Eden. Much misery ensues as all human suffering, including painful childbirth, becomes Eve's fault and they both pray to a God that isn't talking to them to return them to paradise. I found myself philosophising far too much about whether we (and particularly women) deserve the suffering we have caused ourselves. God returns to get to know his grandchildren Cain and Abel, yet refuses to see Adam and Eve. Adam dies without as much as a buy your leave. Eve is spectacularly taken into Heaven by God, who is now (temporarily) in a much better mood. A woman asked me at the interval "Is it over?", and certainly there was a finality to proceedings.

The second act is essentially a brand-new story about Noah's Ark, with the slightly tenuous link that Yonah is a descendant of Cain (so God doesn't like her) and as she has been stowed away on the Ark by her lover, Noah's son Japheth. God is furious so refuses to stop the endless rain. There must be a descendant of Cain hiding out somewhere in Ireland. The lovers would rather die than live without one another but, in a shock twist, Noah refuses to sacrifice them, teaching God a thing or two about love. God comes out of his sulk and clears the clouds and the human race goes on forever more with the understanding that all you need is love. The more I think about the show, the more interesting it becomes. But does it work? I'm going to say: not really. Act One has a finality to it and it is slightly laborious to have to buy into a whole new story/ characters in Act Two. Also, there are so many lilting ballads, tinged with sadness, that an audience could potentially become desensitised. However, my job is not to adjudicate a show based on the writing but on how well a society produces that show. And, my goodness me, Tralee Musical Society put on a spectacular version. Jaw-dropping at times in its visual quality. The audience leapt out of their seats at the end in appreciation for the high standards evident in this production. It was as epic as the stories themselves.

It is a massive achievement that Oliver Hurley directed and choreographed this gorgeous production. In terms of choreography, Oliver made a strong choice that, just like the score, movement would be thematic throughout, similar in its tribal, balletic tone, with a hint of folk dancing. Sometimes it was brilliantly simple, but perfectly suitable, very well executed and effective to the point of being hypnotic. Formations around the stage (combining primary dancers, Greek choral singers, our three narrators and the named parts) beautifully finished the wonderful aesthetic.

Children were employed to appear as animals in the creation sequence, such as a unicorn or a whale and they were expertly prepared in their physicality. There were clever moments like when a train of sultry ladies in animal-print dresses and black bobs slithered on, representing the serpent, holding every s to enhance the sibilance of the character. Or when the young Cain and Abel were rough- housing and in their running around were replaced in the blink of an eye by older actors to play their grown-up versions. Later, there would be a flashback to these younger actors, which worked so well. The final moment of Act One as the family tensions rise, Adam not wanting the boys to seek out other people, built into a furious argument between Cain and Abel as the chorus drummed the floor with their hands, supporting a dramatic crescendo with Cain killing his brother in a dangerous red swash of light. This led to an epic moment when God, a hint of reverb on his voice, speaks to Eve on the brink of death (or her time "to sleep" as they put it, sending the woman beside me into inconsolable sobbing) and takes her into heaven with breath-taking visuals like a simulator in a theme park. The second Act, which is more demanding, was directed with aplomb, shaping the sides of the Ark and the deck with wood and managing the blocking of this small space effectively.

The story begins with three modern- dressed narrators, played very well by Sharon Walsh, Jerry Lynch and Jackie O'Mahony, telling stories to their young children. Elsewhere, they filled in the gaps of time in the rest of the show. This excellent trio, each with strong stage presence and excellent vocals, would be cleverly placed around the stage at just the right moments to be impactful when necessary.

At the top of the show we are introduced to Father (God) played by Mike Lynch. He had that wonderful presence required for this semi-sentient/semi-human being. He moved around the stage, sometimes observing, sometimes getting involved. As the flawed human-style God, he manoeuvred through the emotional content of his material well. As the heavenly interpretation of God, he had the presence required to actualise this. He had an impressive velvety speaking voice that evoked the idea of God. His gorgeous baritone singing was spot-on too, ensuring that he carried the demands of this omni- present role with competence.

God creates the world and the animals and finally Adam and Eve, played by Gary Murphy and Clódagh Harrington respectively. As Eve, Clódagh had a mammoth amount of material to perform. While there was the odd hard to reach high- note, she displayed a lovely voice overall. She had great character development; moving from the young wide-eyed Eve, who is eventually seduced by the forbidden fruit, to the world-weary woman who saw one of her sons kill the other, now ready for her final "sleep". She was equally matched in a lovely partnership with Gary as Adam, who also charted the journey from young wide-eyed man, happier than Eve with the simplicity of the life given to them by God. He had a great voice and a lovely naturalism to his performance.

We got excellent performances by Dylan O'Sullivan as Cain and Jamie Fitzgerald as his brother Abel. Characterisation was strong between these two actors. Dylan as Cain presented as the older more daring brother, takes after his mother Eve in that he does not want to obey the rules. He was the stubborn rebellious type, longing for adventures and the company of other humans. Jamie as Abel gave us a meeker, more obedient character, contrasting with his angry brother. Their differences become their downfall as Cain kills the tamer Abel in a furious family row.

Act Two leaves the original family behind and jumps to the story of Noah. Tim Moran firmly established himself with presence as Noah, the wise elder of his tribe charged with an onerous task. He is an excellent actor, with a Shakespearean quality to his speaking voice. His singing voice is not what might be described as "traditional musical theatre" (that is usually pitch perfect with cut-glass diction). His was a more guttural vocal performance. I imagine he would be very good at singing Irish ballads.

Laura Crowley as Noah's wife, Mama Noah, had a calming presence and mediated the family tensions well. She was responsible for giving the audience a rare treat with her show-stopping rendition of the upbeat 'Ain't it Good'. Overdue a little bit of positivity, the audience gave her a huge reaction here.

Pa Lynch was very good as Japheth, youngest son of Noah who falls in love with Yonah, a servant girl who is a daughter of Cain. Rebellious and stubborn, he is willing to sacrifice his own life rather than see her die. His duet with Yonah was gorgeous, their voices blending in beautiful harmony. Janna Foley was equally as good as Yonah. She was given a bumper amount of material in Act Two, and she delivered it excellently well. She has a superb voice for musical theatre. Despite the credibility of this performance, I also think she would make a super Elle Woods in Legally Blonde. Great performances from this pair. Jonathan Lynch as Shem, the eldest of Noah's three sons captured all of the hot-tempered and impulsivity required for the role. He was nicely matched by Aoife O'Mahony as Shem's wife Aysha, who injected lots of tension into the family circumstances on board the Ark with her paranoia. Aaron McLarnon as middle- child Ham brought a nice balance as he was not as optimistic as Japheth and not as pessimistic as Shem. His pregnant wife Aphra was played by Olive Sharp who added to the drama by worrying and praying for an end to the flood. All family members gave equally good performances, creating good drama in these domestic scenes.

Like the set, all of the costumes were created in-house. The three narrators in their modern dress contrasted nicely with the ancient look of the rest of the show. The chorus wore muted beige and browns, nothing too colourful, such was the time-period. They looked almost like clothing one might find on other planets in old Star Trek episodes, ancient and futuristic all in one. Timeless. Adam aged very well as the show went on, but it seemed as though Eve was impossible to age. It must have been all that fruit. More material would be added to Eve's outfit as she grew older, covering more and more of her head and shoulders. A definite decision was made that those performers who wore spectacles would wear them in the show, which was an interesting touch. The animal costumes were incredible. Each body was somewhat uniform, pulling them together thematically and ensuring things did not look too random, yet each of the individualised masks were striking in their presentation and detail. The giraffes were like what one experiences when they see the Lion King on the West End. Stunning work overall.

The set, stage-managed by Des Hurley, had two lovely build-outs on either side, onto which different shapes of banister- like structures appeared, creating various performance levels. These were finished off with wooden stand-alone branches, a theme that would be explored throughout the whole aesthetic. Tall rocks stood at the sides, but would be moved centre-stage in a stylised way to create new spaces later on. There was a sense of symmetry, yet it was mixed up enough for it to be subtle. A giant section of the Ark, beautifully made from sticks, came out of the wings in Act Two, and once the characters were aboard, the deck was effectively created with stand-alone wooden structures. The projections needed to be seen to be believed. Epic in their expansiveness, they appeared on the wings also, making the experience entirely immersive as though we were watching it in an IMAX cinema. The title "Children of Eden" revolved with the Planet Earth on the giant screen, like a movie. The whole stage could become a starry sky, complemented by even more stars created by lighting around the whole auditorium, like an astronomy experience. The Garden of Eden appeared in all its glory, initially looking like a stationary backdrop until a subtle butterfly would flit from set piece to set piece like magic or a flower would burst into bloom. Elsewhere, fireflies would fill the screen or rushes would gently blow in the breeze. Burning trees with billowing smoke in the more dramatic moments and the rain effect during the forty plus days of rain, as a result of God's anger, was incredible. At one point, a character released a dove and the bird flew across the screen, as though it had flown out of her hand. Let there be light. And God dramatically appeared to us at the top of the show. I cannot begin to list the lighting cues, designed by John Hurley, that took place throughout the show. They were perfectly pitched; always enhancing the mood or framing the story. From the spotlight on Adam and Eve, as they innocently prayed, to the special on the tree containing the forbidden fruit, to the ominous tones of grey during the epic storm, it was all wonderful. Lighting punctuated the ending of songs when appropriate, doing its bit to ensure that the aesthetic was never anything but wonderful.

Sound design, by Murt Whelan and Shane Murphy, was great in Act One. There was just the right amount of reverb on God's voice when necessary. One microphone was hanging off in Act Two, which was noticeable without ruining the moment too much. I am sure this did not happen at other performances. The microphones for the full-family scenes in Act Two were a little all over the place. Clearly something had gone wrong and feedback was created by the attempts to solve the issue. Could people have been fitted with the wrong mics? The hug between Noah and Japheth created feedback also. The sound of the choral singing was wonderful, however. Áíne Murray as Musical Director and Laura Crowley as Choral Director ensured amazing ensemble signing on the night. Áine played keyboards and conducted, meaning that signalling was subtle from her. There was barely a glitch, however, suggesting that all involved were very well prepared, thus requiring little for the MD on the night, leaving her to slog it out on the keyboard. Choral singing captured the enormity of this biblical piece that charters the creation of the world and the human race. The bass line in the opening sequence created a sinister foreboding to the creation of the Earth. Those old- school showgirl harmonies on the serpent were cool. The violin as Abel's dead body was carried out was haunting. The opening of Act Two was stunning. The final number built brilliantly from two people to the whole family, who were then joined by the Narrators to make a brilliant sound working towards a crescendo with the whole chorus. The origins of what we know as theatre began in Ancient Greece and it was fitting that this chorus made up of all ages would assume the role of a Greek chorus, evoking a sense of time immemorial. The movement was magical in its otherworldliness and singing was powerful. It was more than a trip to the theatre. It was a trip to the cinema, a trip to the planetarium and a trip to the art gallery. Have I used the word "epic" enough? Well that is the word that describes the choral contributions and the visual and technical quality of this production. Epic.

Director, Damien Hurley, did a good job of keeping a steady pace to this production, and in presenting a well-drilled company, comfortable in their roles, and confident in their moves. The show was visually effective, even if there were several hitches on the night, concerning the projected images on the back screen, but it was evident that a lot of thought went into varying the backgrounds in what can often be a rather dull show scenically. One or two of the younger performers needed a tad more guidance concerning their comedic timing i.e. allowing for audience reaction, but generally, there was a strong sense of comedy in the style and business of the production.

The actual structure of the set was good in design and well organised by the stage manager, Philip Somers. Thanks largely to the use of projected images, I don't think I have seen a 9 to 5 achieving so much variety in surroundings. However, the coordination between set, lighting and projections needed a lot more rehearsal to eliminate the frequent mishaps when the wrong slide appeared. Congratulations to the props team for coping so well with a prop heavy show. Apart from the problem already mentioned, the lighting was generally atmospheric and of a good standard. Sound was well-balanced and cueing was good.

As with the direction, the music of the show was well paced, with good tempi throughout. The orchestra, in the safe hands of MD, Dave McGauran, played a highly commendable accompaniment to the on-stage performers, and the balance was just right. There was evidence of good vocal preparation with the harmonies, and the principal line was well on top of its music. All-in-all, a very satisfactory musical presentation.

Kathryn Gibbons started timidly in the role of Violet Newstead, but grew in stature as her character developed throughout the show. When she was in full stride, she became strong and confident, with a good feel for her comedy, and a very good control of her vocals. Indeed, she proved herself to be the natural leader of the girls. Karen McCourt, with a perfect Dolly Parton accent, gave loads of character to the role of Doralee Rhodes. Her voice suited the style of the music and with the exception of rushing a few of her lines, she handled the comedy very well.

Nicola Smith's only problem in the role of Judy Bernly was her age, which detracted a little from the sense that Judy has lived her life as a dependant, and is facing the reality of being a woman alone for the first time. Regardless of that, Nicola had a believable nervous, naivety in her opening scenes and realised her more playful inner self as the show progressed. "Get Out and Stay Out" was forcefully delivered.

Michael Evans gave a very funny and equally distasteful sense of misogyny to the character of Franklin Hart. This character needs to be a send-up to prevent him from just being hateful, and Michael got the balance just right. His "Here For You" solo was as tasteless as a Benny Hill romp, but extremely funny. There was a stern, stiff resolve to Keeva Kavanagh's Roz that completely suited the role, and gave way to a hilariously sexual "Heart to Hart". This was a very well delivered performance, with a strong sense of comedy.

Albeit an accomplished young performer, Adam Kelly looked and sounded too young for the role of Joe, which kind of diminished the believability of his relationship with Violet. His delivery of "Let Love Grow" highlighted his talent and his potential, both as a singer and an actor, but I just feel he was, on this occasion, mis-cast.

Colette O'Beirne gave a delightful inebriated performance as Margaret and led a supporting office staff that produced impressive performances from Sinead McMullan as Maria, Sinead McCrohan as Kathy and Alex Murphy as Bob.

Richie Smith added a fine sense of authority to the role of Tinsworthy, and there was good support from Jonathan McKenna as Dwayne, Chris Bass as Josh, Fergal Sweeney as Dick and Helen Cahill as Missy.

The chorus put plenty of energy and enthusiasm into their routines, and performed confidently with their vocals. Trisha McDermott did a good job of keeping the movement of the show very fluid, despite there being a lot of furniture to negotiate. Routines were not over- complicated, which helped in keeping them tidy and precise. When she did have an opportunity to be more flamboyant, she devised good routines for the dream sequences and for "One of the Boys". She was also blessed with an enthusiastic company of dancers and movers.

The show was effectively costumed, with variety nicely added whenever the opportunity arose. (Dance of Death, Cowgirl's Revenge, Potion Notion and One of the Boys.) Hairstyles were what one would expect for the era, and there were no problems with make-up.

In most respects, this was a well- disciplined show, performed by a very enthusiastic cast, and I admire that it was a production that brought some new younger talent into the limelight. Thank you very much for a most enjoyable night of entertainment.

Among the really enjoyable aspects of this production, by Vickey Buckley-Gallagher, was the inclusion of a children's chorus, who gave 100% to all their involvement. The show was also extremely well cast, with good realisations of the various characters, and visually, placings and pictures were always attractive. While some of the costumes were very good, I did feel that others needed more definition, and on an attractively painted set, I felt that opportunities were missed to make better use of the back cyc. Either through lighting or projection, there was scope to create more magic behind Whoville, Solla Sollew and even the bath time with Jojo. Stage manager, Gerry McCann, had few problems keeping everything running smoothly back stage, with the few changes that were required being smoothly operated. Much of the lighting was colourful and effective, with perhaps a few dark spots on the periphery of the stage, and while there was little to criticise visually, I just felt that more imagination was needed to really highlight the fantasy, story-book nature of the show. The Cat in the Hat conducting the orchestra during the entr'acte was comedy gold, but I felt there were opportunities for more comedy elsewhere.

With the possible exception of Musical Director, Elizabeth Gregan, perhaps not being aware that General Schmitz hadn't put on his microphone and calming the orchestra to a sympathetic pp in response to the crisis, this was a delightful musical presentation, played by a very efficient orchestra and vocalised by a company who were obviously enjoying their music. There was plenty of evidence of well-rehearsed harmonies, and tempi throughout were spot on.

Young Matthew Nolan in the role of Jojo gave a strong and confident performance, clear in his diction, tuneful of voice, and displaying a good range of emotions. This wasn't a case of a child being good just because he was a cute child. This young man had bundles of talent.

Tim Forde was comical and animated in the central role of The Cat in the Hat. He sang very well and was a constant bundle of energy, and his mime with the orchestra during the Entr'acte was a show-stopper. It highlighted a fine comedic ability that perhaps wasn't exploited enough during other sections of the show. He was, never- the-less, extremely good.

Performance of the show came from John Conroy as Horton the Elephant, exuding charm, character, comedy and an astute sense of pathos and emotion. He was totally believable and put so much sentiment into his lyrics, with a most pleasing vocal quality.

And speaking of vocal quality, Clodagh Forde unleashed a gritty jazz instrument as she delivered her songs as The Sour Kangaroo. Her voice, and her 'ears' really stood out. This was a nicely played character, aggressive and bullying at the outset, and tender at the end, when it mattered. She was well supported by the confident and cute Maya Loughman as Young Kangaroo.

Also high on the 'cute' scale was Camilla Waters in the role of Gertrude McFuzz, with an adorably child-like quality to her vocals that added sentiment to her performance. There was a sincerity to her acting that made her an audience favourite, and she was secure in all her music.

Kelly-Marie Davy was a feisty and flirtatious Mayzie La Bird, strutting her stuff with a self-assured arrogance and disregard for responsibility. She delivered her songs with character and confidence. Mr and Mrs Mayor, portrayed convincingly by Peter DuBerry and Nichola Collier, had just the right amount of reprimand as the concerned parents of Jojo, and an equally believable love and concern for his well- being in the latter scenes. Their vocal delivery was pleasing and secure.

Poor Brian Kelly was almost inaudible in his major scene as General Schmitz, even though he did look authoritative, and in his other brief appearances, he delivered his lines effectively.

I get that Robyn Ferris, Caoimhe Murphy and Joanne Keeling, as The Wickershams, were attired as grease-monkeys, but their very competent performances would have been further enhanced had they been played, and attired, as actual monkeys. They still made a very significant contribution to the show, with Robyn Ferris being particularly expressive.

There was good support from Paula Gregan as Yurtle the Turtle, Simon Tobin as The Grinch, Jenny Sparkes as Vlad Vladikoff and great physicality from Ciara Fleming and Sarah Egan as the Things. Sharon Osborne, Molly Gordon-Boles, Emma Currid, Zara Boxall, Laura Spooner and Paula Gallagher, as The Bird Girls, made a strong impression with their harmonies and their dance throughout the show.

There was very good work from Choreographer, Yvonne Prendergast, in her use of the bird girls in particular, and much of the general chorus movement was well managed, but I did feel that the whole circus scene needed more fun and elaboration. With a piece of work that is so fantastical and fanciful, I felt that there was scope to push boundaries and be more outrageous.

Costumes were generally very acceptable and colourful, although I'm not sure that the Wickersham's costumes did much to enhance their characters. The Sour Kangaroo had a fabulous hairstyle, but she could have been dressed a little brighter. Make-up was well done, and hairstyles were fine.

To quote the beautiful theme-line of Seussical, "A person's a person, no matter how small", and in this production, right down to the last moment and that wonderful appearance of the beautiful Elephant Bird, every individual made a big contribution to the success and appeal of this most enjoyable night of musical fun. Thank you to all concerned.

Director Art McGauran got the balance of this show just perfect. There was plenty of genuine sentiment, joyous celebration and outstandingly good comedy, the latter being brought about by astute casting and some very clever gimmicks. Something as simple as having the two sections of the confessional on opposite sides of the stage, with hidden operators, opening and closing the voice shutters in perfect sync, was a touch of class and very funny. But it was the pace of the show, the tidiness of the technicals, the attention to detail and the excellent direction of the principals that made this such a smooth and thoroughly enjoyable production.

A very nice clean and tidy set, with nice insets was sufficient to create the various locations of the show, with that clever two-piece confessional working most effectively. It would have been nice to have a pulpit for the church scenes, but the little playing area beyond the orchestra was well used instead. The bits and pieces that had to be placed and removed were smoothly handled by Stage Manager, Mark Nolan, and his team and ably assisted by various nuns. Lighting was generally very acceptable with some nice ethereal effects during the church numbers and good atmospheric smaller areas for the solo or small group work. The sound was very good, with good balance and cueing, but with the exception that has occurred at just about every Sister Act that I've seen. The "nice acoustics" that Deloris remarks upon, was accompanied by a nice bit of echo/reverb, which wasn't apparent before the line, and disappeared straight after the line.

Mairead McKenna did a fine job of leading the orchestra through the racy score of the show, with good attention to tempi and maintaining a good balance with the performers on-stage. Choral numbers were well executed with good evidence of well-drilled harmonies, and the vocal presentation of the principals was top notch.

The experience of choreographer Deirdre Browne really told in the style of her routines being so appropriate to the era of the show. She had an energetic chorus who delivered her work with a good level of precision, and she worked the more frail nuns nicely into the routines with good comedic effect. There was some excellent work done on crafting the comedic routines of the gangsters.

In a role that requires comedy, sincerity, feistiness, vocal prowess and a touch of romance, Amanda Cunningham ticked all the boxes and gave a divine performance as Deloris Van Cartier. As bold as brass in the opening scenes, her transformation to a more caring and considerate "sister" was perfection, and believable at every step of the journey.

Helena Begley, with the most delightfully polite accent, was the perfect choice for the Mother Superior, as righteous in her beliefs as she was hilarious in her attitude towards Deloris. This was a crafted and genuine performance, enhanced by a quite excellent vocal display.

Aoife Small was a commendable Sister Mary Robert, combining an early innocence with a feisty realisation of her abilities, but if I'm honest, I'd have liked her to retain her shyness for longer, really only finding confidence at the point of her confrontation with the Mother Superior. Louise Moore was a giggly, loveable Sister Mary Patrick who made the most of her opportunities, but why, oh why, was she always playing with a yoyo? I found it somewhat of a distraction in an otherwise very capable performance.

Marie Kelly got into the role of Sister Mary Lazarus with rap-tastic enthusiasm, and gave plenty of laughs along the way. A stern but sincere and sympathetic performance.

And then there were the crazies! Fiona Shirran, she, who by nature is the epitome of organisation and control, had me mesmerised with her vacant, lost and befuddled expression and her aimless roaming. What an hilarious cameo performance, and right alongside her, looking like she might gasp her last breath after every energetic movement, Philippa Alford typified the dear old nuns of yesteryear who still exist, holed up in the quiet cloisters of Ireland's convents. These were two really crafted and dynamic performances.

Maeve Cunningham as Michelle and Sharon Murphy as Tina provided good secure back-up to Deloris in her opening scenes, and there were a couple of very credible Hookers in the Police station scene, in the shape of Allison Looney and Abbie O'Brien. Roisin Reddy was a believable waitress and either Lucia Connaughton or Hannah McMoreland was an impressive Young Deloris.

The male cast was led by Cárthaigh Quill almost as a cartoon characterisation of policeman Eddie Souther. He was extremely funny and likeable, although perhaps there could have been a gentler, nervous side to his character. He delivered "I Could Be That Guy" with a great sense of fun.

Andrew Docherty looked every bit the Mob leader, and acted accordingly. It was little wonder that his "boys" were so wary of him. This was a good performance with a no nonsense nastiness about his delivery of "When I Find My Baby". We were all glad to see him get his come-uppance at the end of the show.

As a team, Joey, TJ and Pablo had the audience in hysterics with their brilliant performance of "Lady in the Long Black Dress", but there was much more to the performances from Dominic Reid, James Place and Jordan Bass. Dominic, looking like a geriatric Fonz, was perfect as the "Hey, I can still be cool" dude. James Place was somewhere between "camp as a boys-scout jamboree" and "I recently had a lobotomy", and the combination was nothing short of hilarious, and Jordan Bass incessantly groped himself in a way that only a very suave latin lover can get away with. They were a class act who made the most of all their scenes.

Martin Fahy gave a rather cheesy performance as Monsignor O'Hara, although it was in keeping with the craziness going on around him all the time. He really enjoyed becoming the cool rev as the show progressed.

There were good cameo performances from Aaron Stone as Ernie and the drag Queen, Mark Nolan as the cop and Adam Norris as the Newscaster.

The chorus contributed brilliantly to the overall show, both in well-realised harmonies and in disciplined movement. The attire of the nuns started as traditional as one would expect, and progressed beautifully through sparkly enhanced robes to the excellent sequenced finale. The nightwear, from head to toe, was entirely appropriate, and the men were well costumed throughout. Costumes and wigs for the dancer numbers were dynamic looking. With no problems with hair or make-up, the overall visual presentation was very tidy and secure. This was a beautiful, funny and tidy production and a wonderful night of joyous entertainment. Thank you for the spiritual up-lift. Amen.

It's hard enough putting on a full scale musical at the best of times, but when your University tells you that you can't have use of your on-campus performance facility because of renovations in preparation for the Autumn visit of the Pope, and you're forced to put your production on in a hotel ballroom, with no height, no proper stage, and extremely limited facilities, you just have to take a big breath and try to make the best of a fairly awful situation. Such was the proposition facing Maynooth UM&DS as they began preparations for "All Shook Up". Obviously, the production suffered badly, but mostly from a technical point of view, but I have 100% respect for the production team and the performers for putting their best feet forward and striving, against the odds, to bring their show to the (very small and precarious) stage. Un-dampened by their misfortune, the cast rose to the occasion and delivered a very funny production, with much great acting, singing, comedy and dancing. So let's get rid of the awkward stuff first. I'm not even going to criticise the lack of scenery, for the scenario made dressing the stage an impossibility. The few pieces that could be used, particularly on the front edges, were sufficient to give some indication of setting and era. Well done on managing to include the motorbike in the action. It's the chorus I have to congratulate for getting props and furniture into place as quickly and quietly as possible between scenes. With so little to light, the lighting designer did at least create some atmosphere with use of colour, and made sure that everyone's faces could be seen, but his rig was minimal and with a roof only a foot or two above the heads of the tallest performers, his was an unenviable task. Sound quality was very acceptable, with good cueing. Director, Emma Thornton,did her absolute best to present her company at their best. On an awful stage, she managed to create little playing areas, with the bar crammed into stage left corner, and the garage virtually on the floor on stage right. But her most important achievement was to give life and personalities to each of the individuals in her charge. She made sure that the pace was good, and the comedy was well pointed. Forget the setting… the cast made this a highly enjoyable adventure.

On the plus side too, despite being jammed into a corner of the room, and barely visible to the cast on stage, Musical Director, Ailbhe Kehoe, managed to coordinate between the band and her singers, with a good balanced level of sound, and a well-played orchestration. I'm assuming she was also responsible for the vocal preparation of the cast, which was well done, and particularly good for "Can't Help Falling in Love".

Emma Harte, as Natalie/Ed, had a very confident stage presence and seemed to thoroughly enjoy her role, especially the comedy of becoming Ed. She delivered her songs extremely well, and was a good natural dancer. A most entertaining performance.

Sam Lee had a twinkle in his eye, and a swagger in his hips, as the roustabout Chad. He exuded confidence and made the most of those great Elvis hits, with a fine vocal quality. "I Don't Want To" was well sung, but did have the potential for more comedy, but in every other respect, this was a strongly delivered role.

While Micheál Kearney doesn't have the greatest singing voice in the world, he used it well with some lovely comical falsetto. His acting and comedy, however, came right out of the top drawer, with a hilarious realisation of the character of Dennis. He made nerdiness cool!

Niamh Kelly gave a fine performance of the agitated single Mom, Sylvia, and showed some lovely mellow acting in her relationship with Jim. There was a beautiful tenderness to her rendition of "There's Always Me", which perhaps didn't need the 'belted' ending.

Declan King 'acted' the older man very well, despite looking quite youthful as Jim Haller. This was a nicely judged character, and he got the desired comical response from the audience as he tried, in vain, to make himself 'cool'. Very well played. In the role of Miss Sandra, Nadine Conlon displayed a nice sense of superiority over Chad, which gave way to a convincing seductress when she fell for Ed. Good comedy and a strong vocal helped to give energy to her provocative "Let Yourself Go". Very well delivered.

Tobias Barry is a young actor/musician with tons of potential, and with a confidence and likeability that will see him go far in the future. He has a strong voice, a good look and is a natural mover, but, if I'm honest, he had just a tad too much swagger for the character of Dean, who needed to begin with a less confident air and gradually develop from a mommy's boy into a stronger individual.

Ailbhe Travers gave a very feisty performance as Lorraine, the hometown girl who wants to push the limits, singing with confidence and convincing in her instant affection towards Dean.

Meghan Reid strutted with self-importance as Mayor Matilda, and her height gave her the advantage of literally looked down on everyone. This was another well-realised character, and she delivered "Devil in Disguise" with good comedy and a fine vocal.

While Jordan Taylor was overly aggressive and abrupt with his dialogue at the end of the show, he was absolutely hilarious as the silenced Sheriff Earl throughout the rest of the show. His deadpan expression was brilliant, and those expressionless dance moves were a touch of genius. Elizabeth Murphy lent a strong vocal to the start of "Heartbreak Hotel" as Henrietta. God bless the chorus for achieving all that they achieved on such a ridiculous stage, and they performed their acting, singing and dancing with ever-beaming faces and bundles of energy.

Cáit Cregan did the impossible. She managed to get the entire cast dancing on a postage-stamp stage without tripping over each other, and despite the lack of space, only on a very odd occasion did the stage look overcrowded. She also managed to provide plenty of variety with everything from rock'n'roll pairs dancing to acrobatics. She also made good use of the centre aisle, and gave the audience a bit of close contact with her dancers. Given her restrictions, this was remarkably good work. Costumes generally were good and appropriate, with nice variations for the jail scene, the statues and the devils and angels in "Devil in Disguise". Hair styles fitted the era, and make-up was very satisfactory, even if Jim needed a tad more ageing. There were no real visual distractions. Good work.

It's a shame that the University didn't afford a week out from their preparations for the Papal visit to accommodate with a proper stage for this wonderful show. Thank you to all concerned for a sterling effort. Your industry was much appreciated by myself and a very responsive audience.

The St Mary's Clonmel production of "Grease" was, in my humble opinion, approached with entirely the correct amount of humour, cynicism, and joyful appreciation of the nature of the show, in order to make it a delightfully entertaining parody of the Rock'n'roll era. This joyful bubble-gum musical reflects an era when college kids believed that their small world problems were seriously major issues. It laughs in the face of propriety, and through the media of music, comedy and dance, it acknowledges that youthful angst and drama is all a delightful part of growing up. Even before the highly efficient band got to play a note of music, Director, Des Henn, set the scene and the atmosphere by having Vince Fontaine performing his WAXX radio show to the expectant audience. A great touch, but then again, the show itself was peppered with clever ideas, original interpretations, a wealth of excellent comedic episodes, like the 'nerds' being locked in lockers, and then re-appearing as the smartly dressed backing vocalists to "Magic Changes".  The "greasers" were bullies, but they never actually hurt anyone, and they poked as much fun at themselves as they did at others. The running "wedgie" gags were brilliant, and almost made an unlikely hero out of Eugene.

What a beautifully designed, painted, presented and manoeuvred set. It was a work of art, totally functional, full of colour and atmosphere and gave depth and levels to the small stage of St Mary's hall. Props were equally as good and always appropriate. Stage Manager, Kay Sheehan, and her team did a good job of keeping the pace of the show going by working efficiently at the changes. Lighting throughout was very good, capturing the mood and atmosphere of each scene, with good colour schemes and good highlighting of the focal point of the action. Sound was well cued and got the balance between stage and pit just right.

The cast, at all times, were beaming and animated by the antics that they performed throughout the show, and it was a production all about team work. . The "Jets" worked brilliantly together, the "Pink Ladies" had a strong sense of group identity, and even the nerds, led by Eugene and Patti, were a recognisable gang who took strength from each other. Emmet Donlan, freed from the shackles of being a recent reluctant Pirate, relaxed beautifully into the role of Danny Zuko, and played him with a kind of cool, but not really THAT cool, swagger. His insecurity when confronted by Sandy made the character human and believable. His vocals were very strong and he's not at all lacking in dance energy or ability.

Diarmuid Vaughan, in the role of Kenickie, led the bullying of the nerds with a mixture of aggression and glee, but without ever betraying his sense of fun. This was a nicely drawn character, full of mischief, and yet with a sensitivity that was best displayed when Rizzo tells him "you don't even know the guy". He led "Greased Lightning" with authority and a strong vocal quality.

Joe Sheehan was like a nerdy version of James Dean in the role of Doody, looking super cool, but acting like an insecure teenager. But there was nothing insecure about his performance of "Magic Changes" where he displayed a fine voice with a strong falsetto. Nicely played. James O'Donovan gave a nice "slob" quality to Roger, the one that the gang will pick on the most. He had a very good sense of comedy and always looked relaxed. As with his fellow Jets, his vocal quality was very secure.

Completing the gang, Kevin Twohig was a confident and convincing Sonny, who had a nice boyish shyness in his attempts to strike up a relationship with Frenchy, but was still 'man' enough to be one of the gang.

Despite towering over most of the rest of the cast, Jason Ryan played the ultimate nerd, Eugene, to great effect. His comedy was on point, and his sensitivity was evident in the respect and sympathy he elicited from the audience. Very well played.

James Sweeney gave good support in the sleazy role of Disc-jockey, Vince Fontaine, smarming his way around the stage and making a meal of Marty at the dance. He also put across the "Teen Angel" role with a good vocal strength.

Alan Bourke had a touch of flair and charisma as he strutted his stuff on the guitar and nailed his vocals as Johnny Casino.

Jordan Freeman had the look and the naivety for the role of Sandy, and had a very pleasant vocal quality, even if it got a little lost on occasions in her duets. I would perhaps have liked her to display a little more feistiness to balance against her shyness, which was her most comfortable emotion.

Michelle Smith reminded me a lot of my wife, a strong and domineering force, capable of scathing witticisms, and yet with a concealed vulnerability and sincerity. This was a beautifully played Rizzo, with excellent delivery of her solos. Nicole Butler was a feisty Marty, full of vanity and self-indulgence, and yet quirky and comical when the script required it. Her "Freddy My Love" was nicely delivered, and she made the most of that kiss with Vince Fontaine.

Emma Sunderland was delightfully cast in the role of food-a-holic Jan, proving that you don't have to be on the heavy side to portray a food junky. She was as slim as she was cute and perky and delivered her comedy with a relaxed and natural ease. Grace Hogan was a beautiful and unusually serene Frenchy, avoiding the tendency to play the role as an absolute ditzy-blonde. While this might has reduced her comedy potential a tad, it nevertheless made her a very believable and more real character. Eimear Hughes was a comical and nerdy Patty, who had good stage presence and plenty of confidence, but I felt she could have been more larger-than-life to make her really, really annoying. That, however, didn't prevent her from making a strong impact in the role.

Lauryn Boyle played dancer Cha-Cha Di Gregorio with nonchalance and a mighty annoying voice, which suited the character perfectly. She made a strong impression in what is a fairly minor role. Olwyn Grogan aged delightfully at the start of the show to portray the older Miss Lynch, and had an abrupt manner as her younger self that was perfect for a no- nonsense school teacher.

Barbara Meany used imagination, originality and a fine sense of comedy to give her routines a unique feel. I've already acknowledged the clever use of the backing singers for "Magic Changes" whose movement typified the style of the era, and "Greased Lightning" was simply electrifying. The opening of Act Two and a very well devised "Born To Hand Jive, Baby" were precise and delightfully executed displays of the more typical rock and roll style. The choreographic contribution to the overall performance was vital and exhilarating. Excellent work. I'm guessing somebody had a field day working on the arrangements for this show, for there were beautiful harmonies that I have never heard before, and they were performed with excellence by the cast, particularly a beautiful 4 part rendition of "Rock and Roll Party Queen". Indeed, throughout the show, the choral harmonies were superbly sung. Musical Director, Laura Cotter, had good control of an exuberant band that let-rip with the racy musical numbers but still showed consideration for the on-stage singers. A well-designed "Grease Mega-Mix" brought the show to a thundering end.
