Principal vocals were consistently good, even though during one or two of the duets there seemed to be a slight balance issue, but overall, the musical quality of the show made a powerful impact.

There was a stark contrast between the leather and jeans look of the Jets and the tidy yet nerdy outfits of Eugene and his nerdy friends. Everyone looked perfectly attired. The standard Pink Ladies jackets were very good as was their night wear and their dance dresses. I loved the nerds suits for when they were backing singers. The wigs/hairstyles for both girls and boys were very good and of-the-era, and make- up was pleasing. Miss Lynch was nicely aged for the opening scene.

For anyone who thinks of Grease as a young person's show, there was a guy sitting beside me who must have been at least ten or fifteen years my senior, and he was enthralled by the production. It was, after all, a night of heart-warming, hilarious, up-lifting musical escapism. Most significantly, it was superbly entertaining, and that is the business we're in. Thanks for such a memorable night.

When the curtain opened to reveal a beautifully designed and painted set, I knew at once that it was going to be a most enjoyable night. A live fiddle player opened the action as Tevye strode into place for his first monologue. Tevye is the adhesive that holds Fiddler on the Roof together, and in this case, it was as secure as super-glue.

There were many examples of Director Bill Stafford doing his homework on the traditions involved in this production, from the lighting of the Shabbat candles, to the breaking of bread, crushing the glass at the wedding and observing the rules that make the Jewish people unique. It's a show that deserves that attention to detail, and was all the stronger for taking that care. There were times when the pace of the dialogue was a bit rushed, giving the impression it was being recited rather than spontaneously flowing from the performers. This happened particularly between Perchik and Hodel, and a little bit during Tevye's monologues. Occasional pauses for thought give a better impression of emotional consideration of what is being said. In what was a strongly disciplined production, I did feel that more could have been done with the Dream scene, and particularly the pogrom at Tzeitel's wedding, which was a bit lame. The main set was beautifully constructed with the little "bird-houses" giving the impression of a village. Very clever. As the show progressed, I did occasionally wish that the background might change, as one or two scenes felt a little claustrophobic, but it was, nevertheless, a very tidy set, and the various props and furniture were well manoeuvred by Stage Manager, Paul Greene, and his team. The lighting was, more-often than not, beautiful in design, but there were occasions when the stage went too dark in the effort to create atmosphere. The Sabbath Prayer was delightful, but the candle light was not sufficient to allow us to clearly see Tevye and Golde's faces. Sound quality was good throughout.

There was more effective movement to music than dancing throughout the show, which is by no means a criticism. The big crowd scenes were well managed without the stage looking over-crowded. The Opening and the Wedding were well worked, and the fairly static "Anatevka" and Move Out were delightful. Choreographer, Margaret Kavanagh, did a good job on the Bottle Dance, but once Perchik had dismissed the rope separating the male and female dancers, there was scope to make more of the subsequent routine, rather than reverting straight back to boys and girls dancing separately. "To Life" had plenty of fun and energy, and the family performed a lovely dance to accompany the Chava sequence.

Musical Director, Wayne Brown had an extremely talented and sensitive orchestra well under control, keeping them restrained and disciplined during the many emotional musical sequences, and vibrant and energetic throughout the more frantic sections of the score. The violin solos were very well handled by Fiddler, Nataylia O'Neill, on stage, and equally well taken over by the pit. As chorus master, Wayne brought out good vocal quality from his chorus, with clean harmonies and excellent diction. The show was musically very strong.

Even given my comments about his monologues being a bit rushed, Ray Collins gave a beautifully crafted performance that was polite, mellow, deeply sincere and on the right occasions, extremely funny. This was a good character study and his warmth of personality made him totally appealing to the audience. He delivered his songs with conviction, and especially "Do You Love Me" which for me, was the song of the show.

Equally mellow, yet firm with her children, was Greta Rochford in the role of Golde. She was very amusing and expressive, especially during her encounters with Yente, which were delightfully played. Again, "Do You Love Me" brought out the finest moments of her performance. Trish Orpen was a delightfully busy, nosy, invasive Yente, but also had a gentle manner that made you want to forgive her for her interfering. She played her comedy extremely well.

Neil Bourke made a wonderful Lazar Wolf, adept at grovelling to Tevye, yet with a fine sense of humour. The two made a good job of "To Life", and their mutual disdain at the wedding feast was very strong.

As Tzeitel, Jennifer White was a little abrupt on occasions, but delightfully feisty with Motel, and ultimately sincere in her love of her family. Her "Matchmaker" skit of Yente was well done.

Brian Tuohy was a fine and credible Motel the Tailor, awkward with Tevye, shy with Tzeitel, but sincere in all his thoughts and actions. A very nicely played role, with good delivery of "Miracle of Miracles". I had a bit of a problem with Niamh Fennessey as Hodel and Adam O'Neill as Perchik, in so far as their dialogue together seemed rushed and lacking in warmth, with the exception of that moment where they danced and ended face to face. That was the only moment when I truly believed in them. Niamh did a fine job on "Far From The Home I Love", while Adam struggled on one or two of the higher notes in "Now I Have Everything".

Emma Walsh was a sweet Chava, who danced delightfully and played her scenes with Fyedka and Tevye with a lot of sincerity.  Beside her, Jack Cunningham was a worthy Fyedka, gentle yet determined, and likeable despite his origins.

The experience of Des Manahan shone through his cameo performance as the gentle-souled Rabbi, and good support was given by Niall Kelly as Mendel, Brian Hogan as Mordcha and Jonathan Kelly as Avram. Dermott Sullivan was a sturdy but amicable Constable, and Ben Nolan gave a fine voice to Sasha during "To Life". With quite excellent make-up which completely disguised their youthfulness, Avril Hartrey as Grandma Tzeitel and Paula Weldon as Fruma-Sarah both made a big impact in their cameo roles.

The chorus were very good for most of the show at creating ambience and atmosphere, but they did look like they were attending a funeral rather than a wedding during "Sunrise, Sunset". It was, however, beautifully sung, as was most of the choral work.

The show was beautifully and traditionally costumed, with good attention to detail. From covered heads to appropriate footwear, everyone was well turned out. The make-up of the general characters and chorus looked natural and appropriately dull, while there was a bit of a party had by the hair and make-up team in creating a superb looking Fruma-Sarah. Grandma too was given a wonderful make-over. The men's hairy faces all looked realistic too. Visually, the show was absolutely spot-on. As an overall production, this was a beautiful and well-delivered rendition of one of the finest musicals available. Thank you so much for re-kindling my passion for the show, and for a very delightful night of emotional theatre

The first thing that Director Paul Norton got right with this production of Little Shop of Horrors was making sure that it was played against a suitably impressive setting. With clever design and comic- book colouring, the audience were drawn in even before the show took off. This was a really nice set, and was super-efficiently controlled by Stage Manager, Ian Hanrahan, and his team. Props were plentiful, appropriate and well-sourced. The lighting was colourful and imaginative, with only an occasional slip-up in highlighting principals in solo spotlights, but the overall lighting effect was to enhance the show. Sound quality was generally good and well-balanced. Cueing was fine.

The casting of the show was also very impressive, with performers being very well suited to the demands of their roles. There was good attention to the visual impact also, although I might have been inclined to have some more normal people, (maybe a builder, a nurse, a milkman, etc.) among the Skid-row inhabitants, rather than all looking like down and out winos. I get that the place is impoverished, but lots of nice people are poor! I'm poor! The plant-people during the "Don't Feed The Plants" finale worked extremely well. The pace of the show was very good, and the chorus involvement, while fairly minimal, was always well considered. Perhaps it's more to do with the final few scenes being a tad repetitive that the show seemed to flag a little towards the finale, but overall, this was the strong and secure production that I would expect from this very talented Director.

This isn't a demanding show for a choreographer, but Julianne McNamara moved the chorus well, given the limitations of the small stage. More important than steps, her routines maintained an atmosphere through appropriate movement and attitude, but on the few occasions that there were dance moves, they were well executed. Good work with the three girls.

The beautiful Rose sitting front centre in Mushnik's Skid-Row Florists was Musical Director Mary-Rose McNally, who led the orchestra from the keyboard with confidence and comfort. Tempi were always secure and the balance was just right to allow the on-stage singers to shine. Vocally, she did a very good job on the harmonies of the few chorus numbers, and particularly with the Crystal, Chiffon and Ronette. Principals were secure in their music, and overall, the musical quality of the show was very pleasant. Conor O'Meara was a secure and very likeable Seymour, whose youth didn't prevent him from giving a good dramatic and comedic performance. His timing was spot on, and he had the required vocal capacity to make the most of his songs. Brid Delaney had a lot of fun with the role of Audrey, maintaining a good accent and posture throughout the show. "Somewhere that's Green" was very nicely delivered, and she displayed her belter quality during "Suddenly Seymour". Again, a nicely balanced performance. Paul Spencer was his reliable self in the comedy role of the Dentist, Orin Scrivello, DDS. His comedic ability shone through his performance, although I'm surprised that he, or maybe his director, didn't push a few boundaries in making him even more inhumane. Nevertheless, a totally comfortable performance.

Colin Hughes gave a strong caricature performance as grumpy Mr. Mushnik, with a very good accent and attitude. "Mushnik and Son" was a very well-delivered number.

Aishling Rohan, Aoife Nell and Emma O'Rourke as Crystal, Ronnette and Chiffon respectively, worked together like a well-oiled machine, all good in the delivery of their script and strong in their vocal harmonies and in their solo lines. It helped that they were also well-able for the choreography.

Audrey ll had attitude and anger issues, courtesy of a fine vocal performance from Proinnsais Loughnane, and the strong arms of Ronan Foyle as the operator. This was very good and well timed animation and very good plant props.

There was strong support offered by the very experienced Siobhan Bowe as Mrs. Luce, Colm Hogan as a delightfully sleazy Skip-Snip, John Lynch as a very capable Mr. Bernstein and Conor Harte as the business-like Patrick Martin.

As suggested elsewhere, the presence of the chorus was always appropriate, and they performed as characters, not just as dressing. Very nice work.

Apart from the suggestion already made about giving more variety to the Skid- Row chorus, the costumes were of good colour and texture. Principal costumes highlighted the personalities of the characters, and the human extensions to the plant for the finale were very good indeed. Hair and make-up were nicely in keeping with the era and the feel of the show.

How wonderful it was to be so warmly greeted at the door by 90 year old Paddy Moloney, a most charming gentleman, and one of the backbone of this warm and friendly company. Keep up the good work of filling your shows with the spirit of enjoyment and adventure that you have in abundance. Sincere thanks to everyone for a thoroughly enjoyable and nostalgic night in Roscrea.

That famous portrait of the girl from Les Misérables beamed onto the screen, as the audience took their seats, but this time she was cleverly sporting a school uniform. A subtle green gobo filled the auditorium with atmosphere before the show began. The smoke and blue lighting at the beginning, as the steps turned, set the tone for what would be a very well- staged, dramatic evening, filled with super performances from all. An instant standing ovation erupted from the audience at the end of Ballywillan Drama Group's production of Les Misérables and well deserved it was.

As producer, Brian Logan was responsible for so many aspects of this show (direction, set and lighting design) and produced a high-quality version; a show that was well- measured, epic at times, simple in parts, all placed within a well-lit atmospheric setting. The orchestra was on a level on stage-left; visible and therefore adding to the whole musical experience, without ever getting in the way or overpowering the performers, thanks to Musical Director Eric Boyd ensuring that the band played at the perfect volume, well-supported by Darren Gardiner on sound. Ensuring that the actors did more than just sing, they were enabled to mix emotive acting with their impressive vocals.

We were greeted by three separate set- pieces that blended beautifully into the stage; wooden structures with lop-sided laths of wood that had great energy in their construction while being wonderful asymmetrical, some small pieces of lonely torn fabric hanging off. The versatile steps structure enabled so many different moments of staging and different framings of space. The screen in the middle of the back wall that would be used to clarify times and places, something this work needs.

Musical Director Eric Boyd, assisted by Andrew Robinson, ensured that solo lines from all of the prisoners in the opening scene were clear and well-delivered, as were those from the labourers who refused to employ our hero. The suffering of the men in prison was very clearly acted by this group of convicts. Jean Valjean and Javert's timing in the opening sequence was very impressive and they had clearly been well tutored. There was a dramatic spotlight use on Jean Valjean after his release from prison.

The silverware on the Bishop's table really looked the part, thanks to a great job on props by Karen Hunter. The Bishop of Digne had a lovely voice and was able to capture the essence of a more aged man. The all-female 'At the End of The Day' was acted with superb conviction, as they sold the desperation of their situation. The factory girls' harmonies were excellent. That nasty one in the factory who snapped Fantine's letter out of her hand was very good. The Foreman was suitably hateful also.

The blue wash and the white special on Fantine was lovely in 'I Dreamed a Dream', growing slightly warmer when she sang about the summer. Her death scene only contained the colours black and white, capturing the sombre mood of the moment. The celestial white light that shone on her dead body was powerful. The appearance of a star-cloth on the word 'There" at the top of 'Stars' was really cool. The way in which Javert fell backwards off the upper level when ending his own life, followed by a dramatic blackout, was an impactful piece of staging. The boys belted out 'Red and Black'. The pick- pocketing in 'Master of the House' was excellently done and the chorus really knew their stuff here. The Thénardiers with their bread baby (and the silverware falling out of her dress in the wedding scene later) was a hoot. The bricked pillars and gates that were brought on for 'A Heart Full of Love' were perfect. The classic stepping back and forth on 'One Day More' worked very well as they sported the iconic red flag. The blue and red lighting in 'One Day More' enhanced the idea of national pride, and the way in which the lights shone out into the audience was a great way to finish this dramatic finale of Act One.

It was great the way the steps moved as Eponine used it to perform 'On my Own'. The three seemingly separate structures would all eventually revolve and join up to become one long awesome barricade. The girls' echoing on the "to you" and their lovely 'aaaah" backing vocals in 'Drink with Me' were lovely, bringing a fresh flavour to the number that I had not heard before. The mix of dramatic fighting, slow-motion sequences and freezes all worked very well in this sequence. The red and blue movers in the battle scene added drama and energy to this moment. A bit more shoulder action was needed in the shooting scenes in the barricades. The firing of those old-fashioned guns looked a little too easy. I might argue that there were a couple of staging moments in the barricades that could have been re-worked e.g. the pretend killing of Javert did not have a sense of privacy to it; it looked as though Jean Valjean was shooting the gun as part of the greater crowd and perhaps this could have been brought to the side. Enjolras' speech was up quite high on the barricade also and this suggested to me that he would have been an open target in this moment. The gunshot sound-effects were awesome. as was the dripping effect in the sewers. There was a really cool entrance created for the sewer scenes. The echo on the voices here nicely suggested a sense of space. The use of follow spots throughout brought excellent clarity to proceedings, drawing the eye and giving drama to intimate moments (I might argue that one or two of them were a little tardy coming in, however). They worked excellently well in 'Drink with Me' when there were a lot of people on stage and little movement possible to draw the eye to who was taking the lead. Stage Manager David Wray's crew moving the barricades with the dead bodies still strewn across them, drenched in blue light, a spotlight revealing that Enjolras was actually killed, was striking. The lads coming back on in an eerie light during 'Empty Chairs at Empty Tables' was emotive, causing sniffling throughout much of the audience.

The waltzing in the wedding scene, devised by Choreographer Sharon Logan, was very well executed; there were two groups on stage here, one doing a couples' dance on one side and another circling in a group on the other, adding nice variety to the scene. The dancer who Thénardier referred to as "queer" owned the stage during this moment, and with the whole crowd circling the Thénardier's in the end, the audience thoroughly enjoyed the whole number. The final note of the show was powerfully sung and, coupled with a blinding lighting effect at the end, caused the audience to jump out of their seats to give an instant standing ovation.

Costume Design was by Ewan Campbell and effectively captured the social stature, profession and position of each of the performers. The uniformed grey tops and trousers on the prisoners, the oversized shirts on the farmers, and the villager outfits of mop-caps, shawls and aprons all looked very well and invoked the essence of their situation. The corsets and petticoats in 'Lovely Ladies' gave a different flavour. Older Cosette wore the same dress in a bigger size, effectively achieving a sense of continuity here. Everyone in the barricade scene wore red, white and black, which was really effective. The gowns and tuxes for the wedding scene were gorgeous.

Hair and Wig design was by Choreographer Sharon Logan, with make-up supervised by Chloe Freeman. Jean Valjean had a series of wigs to chart his story; the first was scraggy, supporting the idea of the horrible conditions in prison, to a shinier slicker do to show how far he had come, and a greyer one by the time Cosette was all grown up. The ageing/sickly make-up on Jean Valjean in his final moments, those dark circles under his eyes and whitened lips, was done very well. Fantine also had two wigs, one to show a gorgeous head of golden tresses and another pixy- style after she was forced to sell her hair. Enjolras ensured he had the right look for the piece by sporting a wig also. The final appearance by the Thenardiers, both sporting comic white faces and painted on rosy cheeks, he in his white peruke and her with a head of red curls and ringlets, was hilarious.

Ross McAlister was excellent as Jean Valjean. He was nicely dramatic in his 'Soliloquy', ensuring that we understood his plight and intentions, and we began to care about his story. He captured all of the warmth he felt towards Fantine and the protectiveness of his ward Cosette. 'Bring Him Home' was emotive and beautifully sung. His final scenes, in which he was taken into heaven by Fantine, were moving. This is a mammoth role, one that requires an actor to chart so many emotions and have a singing range to match. Ross delivered very well on all scores and should be very proud of himself for conquering such an iconic role at such a young age.

Patrick Connor was really good as Javert. He was authoritative, stoic and firmly fixed on his black and white interpretation of the law. Every "villain" is the hero of their own story and it was obvious that Patrick understood that Javert is not a bad person, just very intense in his views on right and wrong and his role to do what he thinks is God's work. He and Valjean both knew the opening sequence very well and their timing was great here. His rendition of 'Stars' was very good, kneeling to pray during the instrumental. He was very emotional in the barricades as Jean Valjean released him and his suicide was tastefully performed. Very well done indeed.

Jasmine Gardiner was awesome as Eponine, giving us an outwardly tough but secretly very vulnerable character. In so many ways she is the hero of the piece, selflessly ensuring Marius' happiness, to her own detriment and tragedy. Her partnership with him was gorgeous and we could not help but wish that things had been different between the two of them. Her 'On My Own' was brilliantly performed and the song 'A Little Fall of Rain' in which she dies was excellently measured; not too over-the-top, mixing the performance of the beautiful score while the life force leaves her body. This was a star-turn. Elena Sheppard was also superb as Fantine. She is a great actress, not afraid to be a little sassy in the factory, attempting to stand up for herself against those bullying her. Her 'I Dreamed a Dream' was impactful, as she effectively moved from soft to loud. It was clear how broken her character was, having been working as a prostitute, and she acted the desperation she felt about her child very well indeed. The woman next to me was bawling her eyes out during the death scene. She looked so happy and content when she returned as a spirit at the end, showing how her face lit up with a warm smile, an emotion we had not gotten to see before in her tragic short life.

Carly Weir showed us a lovely sweet voice as Cosette, displaying gorgeous soprano notes coming towards the end of Act One. She too was adorable in her partnership with Marius. (This Marius is a lucky guy having two girls love him!) She captured all of the poise and grace required for the role as a girl who had been brought up in a setting far more fortunate than the other ladies in the show. Her love for the two men in her life was convincing. She ensured that we were saddened when her Father died, while being happy for her that she got to learn the truth, say goodbye and still be with Marius.

Jon-Lee Walker was very good as the rebellious student Marius, with clear vocals and a great ability to mix acting with singing. He captured all of the passion the young man felt about his role in improving society. His 'Empty Chairs at Empty Tables' was emotive, as he broken-heartedly recounted the loss of his friends, acting through song effectively. His respect for Jean Valjean, his love for the two females in his life, and his desire to put everything to right at the end was very clear.

Ewan Williams and Lucy McDowell as the scene-stealing Thénardiers were hilarious as they tried to get as much money as they could out of Jean Valjean (and also as they entered the wedding scene). Their highlight moment - 'Master of the House' - was excellently performed; as they expertly picked those pockets and negotiated the meat-grinder etc., teasing all the comedy out of the number. They captured the ugliness of the characters, as they mistreated both the young ladies in the show, stealing from anyone they could, while never getting anywhere in life. Fantastic performances from both actors here.

Seamus Donaghy was very good as Enjolras, invoking the passionate determination of this student to right the wrongs in his society. He was an excellent leader of the pack and manged all of the vocal demands of this part with competence. We were heartbroken when the barricade turned to reveal his corpse. Very well done.

Poppy Mairs was adorable as Little Cosette, playing her part very well indeed. She made sure that we felt really sorry for her, showing off the Thenardiers for who they really are. She sang so sweetly in 'Castle on a Cloud'.

Mathew Kirkpatrick had an excellent cockney accent as Gavroche. He had portrayed all the toughness and courage wrapped up in this little guy, his brave risk- taking proving to be his tragic downfall. His solo moments in 'Look Down' were excellent. He had such presence in the role and the West End production would be lucky to have him.

Each moment the ensemble had to belt out their rousing choral pieces, they did so in style. Couple this with excellent principal performances, nicely devised staging and an inventive set and it made for a quality evening at the theatre. All those involved should be very proud of what they have achieved. While we were moved, miserable we most certainly were not.

Ragtime, an adaptation of the E.L. Doctorow novel, is an exploration of urban America at the turn of the century; a new world full of racial tensions, social injustice, industrial growth and a little bit of romance. The show resonates as strongly today, particularly with the dire immigrant situation facing the world over.

An actual classic Ford car impressively sat outside the Premier Hall in Thurles (a different model on some nights I believe), setting the tone for the quality aesthetic that was to be enjoyed with Thurles' Musical Society's truly excellent production of this show. The venue is a fantastic resource that can house a large crowd in front of a wide stage. The striking set housed meaningful lighting that framed and punctuated the narrative. Director Christine Scarry dressed the set with human beings, in ever-changing stunning vignettes, like a series of artwork. The beautifully-clad cast sang with such power and accuracy, doing great justice to this challenging and vibrant score. Add in nineteen musicians, and this musical delight was a feast for the senses; educational, dramatic, and emotional, expertly interweaving the domestic with the historical.

Director Christine Scarry was responsible for this fine blending of interwoven narratives, played out against an epic historical backdrop. The relationships within the domestic life of the white family were very nicely observed. The arrival of the immigrants to the shores of America (against an image of the Statue of Liberty, behind that large gate that opened halfway and then fully) was dramatically impactful. The Emma Goldmann sequence was memorable, with the crowd having their backs to the audience for the first sequence, and then turning to create a variety of freezes (in bruise coloured light against an image of a crowd on the screen) and created a very nice freeze in the 3rd set-up. The riot was very frightening and brought us nicely into that contrasting tender moment with Tateh and his daughter, as he soothes her asking her "is she happy yet", the light growing warmer as he pacifies her.

Sarah's funeral was haunting, as Coalhouse placed the lid on her coffin and lowered her into the ground. The ground is a motif we associate with her and Coalhouse mirrored Sarah's blocking of 'Your Daddy's Son' at the top of Act Two, against an image of a modest tombstone. Her return in Act Two, as a ghostly figure dressed in white, was emotive, as they danced back to back. The movie within the musical was very well staged, with four ladies surrounding Houdini, all lit in an old-school cinematic crimson light. It was so interesting how the children playing on the beach, atmospherically running through the stage smoke in front of a seaside image, focused our attention away from Tateh and Mother and firmly onto the next generation. As though the parents were providing the soundtrack, this was almost filmic in how our attention was drawn to the children.

The blackout on the gunshot at the end and the silent scene change thereafter allowed us time to drink in the injustice of the moment. All this juxtaposed nicely against the next Statue of Liberty slide, that invoked the inherent optimism of the piece, despite the suffering of the characters.

The wonderful musical direction was by Mary Rose McNally. She stayed sitting at times, ensuring she did not block the action when conducting, yet managed to give very clear signalling to her large troupe of musicians. Why can't this be done more often in other societies that have no pit? The six violins not only produced a gorgeous sound but the amount of them created that lovely visual one gets when one goes to a full orchestra, as though the bows are dancing. She knew when to bring the band off the boil for more tender sequences, or to allow them to reach full gusto in the more dramatic moments. The band swelled with Tateh's emotions in the market scene, where he breaks down about his and his daughter's dire situation. Mary Rose ensured that the balance between this large band of nineteen musicians and the performers on stage was very good, no doubt in partnership with Star Systems, Thurles, on sound. The immigrant's Hebrew performance is to be highly commended. The chorus were well-trained to follow her cues and she brought them off with superb slickness, such as on the "t" at the end of "get". The finale of Act One, wonderfully complicated with its various musical motifs, was powerfully performed as the voices sung together in the final moments. The backing vocals from off-stage on 'Back to Before' were lovely. I could go on and on.

Choreographer Lea Carroll gave us a Prologue that everyone wants from that infamous 'Ragtime' opening number, with three different ethnic groups contrasting with one another on stage by costume and movement, as each character introduces themselves in the third person. The moves were minimalistic; particularly for the stoic upper class white folk, suitably stylised, enhancing the differences in nationality. The various groups encountering each other created subtle but impactful tension. The movement of the crowd in the Emma Goldmann sequence clearly complimented the narrative, with such phrases as "poor young rich boy" being particularly memorable in terms of how they were staged.

Director Christine Scarry ordered an impressive number of props to ensure that everyone in the ensemble moments, such as the street scene, had plenty of meaningful business to do. This was also evident in how Tateh gave his daughter a blanket to effectively send her to sleep. The package around her neck, containing her papers, was a stark reminder of their situation. The exciting cogs used in 'Henry Ford' all worked really well. The cog dancing was special, and the endless sequence of moves were performed excellently well by the cast. The cogs had an almost golden shimmer to them and they made the 'Henry Ford' number very special indeed. The set was also embellished with cogs, pulling this routine and the aesthetic together with style. The slow motion, as the baseball was being caught, looked really cool against the slide of the baseball stadium. Movement was simple but effective here, with the arm-swinging and spitting etc. The broadsheets, with their dirtied edges, looked just the ticket and the rolled-up newspapers were great.

Designed by John O'Donoghue, this set gave us a striking symmetrical build with two identical balconies and ramps on either side. They would be used very effectively by Christine Scarry to stage moments and frame pictures. The image of the black and white American flag, complemented by the red and blue lighting found a lovely balance between the greyscale documenting of this era, with the colour of the world in which the characters lived. The image of travellers boarding a ship established the context of Father's journey immediately. This image changed to waves as we got a silhouette of Father on the upper level, transforming the space into the deck of the ship. The five-photo collage of Evelyn Nesbitt reminded us that she is a historical character interwoven into the fictional plot.

A picket fence, draped in foliage, effectively created the flower bed in which Mother would discover the baby (complemented by a nice photo of a large house on the screen). The gorgeous leather armchair, old table with white cloth, chairs and a slide of an interior was all that was needed to create the domestic life of the white folk. The two benches in the railway station mirrored each other perfectly and created a lovely space in which to establish the relationship between Tateh and Mother. Colm Eaton ensured that the lighting changed frequently to frame each moment and punctuated the music nicely. Memorable moments include the two different shades used for Father and Tateh on the ship, Father in white and Tateh in a more crimson light, with subtle movers behind suggesting the wavy movement of the journey. There was a nice symbolism to the bright light used as the gates opened for the immigrants at Ellis Island. The striking orange backlight on Mother's 'Back to Before' was warm and dangerous simultaneously.

The lighting for the garden, in which Mother finds Sarah's baby buried in the ground caused me to pause. It was a bold choice, with an eerie green wash and menacing smoke that heralded the darkness of the moment. This and the latter blue lighting created a night time vibe, on a haunted moor, and moved away from the domesticity of the Mother gardening in the daytime. That said, it was certainly atmospheric and imbued a haunting sense of danger. This was an example of how lighting was not within the realm of realism, but in the realm of the emotional. Although, as Professor Dumbledore said to Harry Potter: "Of course it is happening inside your head Harry, but why on earth should that mean that it is not real?"

All this was overseen by Stage Manager Tommy Sweeney, who ensured that the excellent pace of the show established by the rest of the production team was not compromised. The impressive Houdini stunt involved lowering his own son Damian upside-down from the ceiling. The very slick swapping of those versatile steps was almost a moment in itself. Evelyn Nesbitt's swing was nicely actualised on stage centre.

Costumes were sourced from 'That Looks Good' (June Young) and co-ordinated by Wardrobe Mistress Eidin Sweeney. The colourful head scarves of the African American characters really established their ethnicity with the African influence. The African American cast did appear to have some heightened colour to their skin, perhaps wearing some fake tan, but nothing you might not see on someone on a night out. Evelyn Nesbitt's showgirl costume evoked that sense of the Moulin Rouge and her fur coat was fabulous. The six showgirls costumes had a wonderful tatty quality, suggesting a grubbiness behind their intended glamour. The black and monochrome costumes for Sarah's funeral, with Sarah's friend's black veil and those in white costumes at the back were striking against the image of the stained- glass window.

I wondered whether the navy boiler suits on the Henry Ford workers were a little uniform for the time, when perhaps more of their own clothing might have featured? If I am right, then perhaps theatrical licence was invoked here to establish the context of the moment with immediate clarity. Nor did these workers dance and sing with matching golden cogs, so I acknowledge that symbolism was strong here.

None of this discussion about the success of the production team would have been possible without the hard work, talent and commitment of this impressive ensemble. Some amount of work on the choral numbers must have been done to ensure this high quality within the choral singing and staging. The chorus were a tour-de- force.

Linda Ryan as Mother invoked the domestic very well with her relationship with her first husband and with her growing affection for Tateh. She showed off a lovely voice, sustaining her notes beautifully, and trailing off nicely on her first exit. Her 'Back to Before' was enthralling, evident by the lovely reaction she got from the audience.

Michael McLoughlin showed a lovely rich baritone voice as Coalhouse, singing his material beautifully. He had great breath control, sustaining his notes in 'Make Them Hear You' with style. He also had a lovely deep speaking voice. His accent might have slipped once or twice, but that could happen to a saint. His singing more than made up for that. He portrayed the conflict of a man who wants to change the world for the better with a man enraged by personnel suffering and loss very well indeed.

David McElgunn as Tateh. He was wonderfully characterful in his street scene, yet evoked the desperation underneath as he declared to Goldmann "I told you - no politics. My daughter needs to eat". His anger and aggression, as he cried "She is not for sale", turned into a nervous breakdown of sorts as he movingly laments to his daughter that he promised her America. This all contrasted nicely with a far more upbeat Tateh in the later scenes as a successful movie director. His speech to Mother, revealing that he is no baron, was moving and created a lovely moment between the two them, justifying the otherwise potentially panto-esque marriage of the two of these at the end.

Marie Therese Kirby was gorgeous as Sarah. She has a beautiful voice; both when speaking and singing, rich and emotive. We saw her trauma in her abandonment of her child, as she tortured herself with the line "buried you in the ground", reliving the moment with great passion, on her knees with her hands in the dirt.

Barry Derby gave us a Father that captured the conflict of the old and new world. He struggled to accept change, yet we liked him nonetheless, seeing him as a nice man who does not understand the world he returns to after his trip to the North Pole. His relationship with Mother was complicated, in that it was as affectionate as he knew how to be without always being able to show it.

Jack Carolan gave us an excitable, energetic and sometimes slightly hysterical Younger Brother, always in search of a cause. We got to hear some great belt from him in the Emma Goldmann sequence. His row with his Father in Act Two provided quality tension within the domestic aspects of the show.

Fiona Delaney is a highly competent performer, whether adding brilliantly to ensemble moments or taking the lead. She sang with power and emotion as Sarah's friend in the funeral scene.

Dónal Taylor as Booker T. Washington had such a nice deep voice, highly passionate and persuasive in his final speech as the man who endeavours to lead his people in their struggles against racial inequality. Maria McElgunn developed a great accent as another of our historical characters, Emma Goldmann. She was stern in her mission to create social justice for the working class. She proved to be an excellent orator; emotive and authoritative.

Damian Sweeney as Harry Houdini was confident and evoked the showman status of a man celebrating new-found success and fame. Perhaps some of those belter notes were a little strained, but I was at the final show of the run so this is understandable. His escapist stunt at the top of the show was highly commendable, as he hung upside-down from the roof. The "passionate and beautiful" Evelyn Nesbitt was played by Danielle Martin. She gave us a sultry performance that invoked her iconic sex symbol status. She caught all the showbiz pizazz required and her cartwheel deserves a special mention. In contrast, Ciaran Dunphy was suitably unlikeable as the racist and violent Willie Conklin, a performance that actualised the catalyst for Coalhouse's uprising, ensuring we sided with Coalhouse and felt the tragedy of the outcome of his rebellion.

Brendan Bailey gave us all of the enthusiasm and energy of Henry Ford, an inventor and business man of the time, injecting the economic growth that is celebrated in the show. Another extremely wealthy man of the time, J.P. Morgan, was played by Frank Tuohy who showed off a very good speaking voice. John Scott provided some light relief as the cranky old Grandfather, who showed little patience for the antics of those around him. Nina Scott as the maid Kathleen got a great laugh with her Irish accent as she declared "Oh holy Mother, it's the Master", not recognising Father with his unshaven appearance after his trek through the North Pole.

There was never a weak-link on stage. Other quality cameos were provided by Geraint Flyer as District Attorney Charles S Whiteman, Jonathan Gleeson as Architect Stanford White, Finbarr Shelly as the eccentric millionaire Harry K. Thaw, John Hayes as North Pole Explorer Admiral Peary and Peter Donnelly as First Officer Matthew Henson. Harry Keane as the Little Boy and Chloe Cahill as Little Girl were brilliant. How adorable was Éanna Hayes as Coalhouse and Sarah's son! The impressive cast of children all did very well also.

This is a lengthy show. As Variety Magazine stated "Unfortunately, by the time Ragtime reaches the end of its long fuse, after a repetitive second act that often manages to be both overwrought and dull, the musical has very nearly worn out its welcome." Thankfully, this version was brilliantly pacey, with the rhythms constantly changing, convincing me as to how the piece works - as a visceral immersive soundtrack of the time, giving us a taste of the world rather than the straightforward narrative of the well-made play. The Seattle Times said that "Ragtime should unspool like a long, seamless ribbon of song and story", and with this production of Thurles Musical Society's version, it certainly did. It was amazing.

Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street is a masterpiece, because every line and moment can be interpreted in so many ways. It's like the Macbeth of musical theatre and glorious debate can take place 'til Kingdom come about who these characters are, what their motivations are, whether they are good or evil or which shade of grey to invoke in between these two reductive extremes. There is little ability to be right or wrong with this show. Decisions must be made, in particular in terms of how the comedy lies with the tragedy in this piece (where audience members find themselves laughing when innocent strangers are murdered in cold blood). Sweeney Todd reminds me of chocolate. Some people like 50% darkness, other people would push the darkness to 80%. The latter recipe is far too sour for some folk and they'd rather have nothing at all. If the comedy is missed, it is an awful shame. If the darkness is glossed over, then the tragedy of the piece isn't fully actualised. This production of Sweeney Todd was delicious milk chocolate. With a little more milk than cocoa, the audience were rolling in the aisles watching a production that seemed to almost send itself up; as Mrs Lovett, tongue firmly in cheek, concocted the plan to use a dead body to fill her pies, we were howling at the ridiculousness of it all. The audience guffawed with glee when Sweeney disposed of the bodies down the shoot and were riotous in their laughter during 'By the Sea'.

Director/Designer Vivian J.

Coates ensured no stone was left unturned with the quality of his aesthetic, taking inspiration from Scenic Projects London. The beams of criss-crossing white light and smoke graced the stage and a lonely winding staircase sat ominously upstage- left as the audience took their seats. Lighting was designed by Alistair Kerr and was almost like a character within the show, because of how it framed each and every moment. The two beams of the light coming from the trap door set the tone of the creative lighting design that we would be treated to. Sweeney's body was dumped into a grave and the music started as the trap door slammed shut, ensuring a dramatic beginning to the show. The "he served a dark and a vengeful God" from the sopranos in the opening number was thrilling, thanks to Musical Director Fintan Cleary (and Eithne Corrigan as Chorus Mistress/Repetiture) who enabled good delivery of all the difficult choral pieces. These multi-purpose steps would create a variety of spaces, such as Johanna's balcony, which added a lovely window-box of flowers. (Later, this would transform into the Judge's pulpit.) Anthony teasing her with the birdcage was a good motivation for her to come outside. A quality truck was wheeled on for Mrs Lovett's counter and her shop backdrop was flown in. Later, the exterior of the pie shop would sport lovely brickwork, an arched door, and a chimney at the back, with the upper- section showing a cut out of the tonsorial parlour, with suggestions towards a roof window. There were moments when a sense of space was effectively created, without needing to be overly-literal; such as that gorgeous red curtain that was brought on stage-left, with an amazing chandelier, pillar and plant, to suggest the Judge's soirée.

The backdrop of London City had a pencil drawing quality to it and this ensured that it reflected different colour light very effectively, becoming warmer or cooler to match the mood of the moment. Pirelli's wagon was gorgeous, with very clear signing on the side. This was supported by two posters on sticks that displayed the suffering of those in need of a dentist back then and words on the steps such as "painless" etc. Solo lines from the ensemble in 'Pirelli's Miracle Elixir' are a curse to teach and learn, but they were well done here (with the exception of the two leads who missed their cue here). The slapstick between Tobias and Pirelli was well staged, as he gripped Pirelli with his thighs in an impressive stunt.

For me, the staging of the Judge's 'Mea Culpa' sequence was one of the most memorable of the evening, having never seen it dealt with so well before. Nuns with veils over their faces placed candles on the floor on which the Judge lay. A crucifix dripping in red material was flown in then tilted to peer down on him, as he whipped himself to convincing sound effects, in flame-coloured lighting framed in blue. In the end, he revealed disturbing red marks on his back, which matched those on the cross and in his red gown.

The music was a little behind Mrs Lovett in 'Wait' or vice-versa, depending on what was decided in rehearsals. The four funny jolly young beach-goers, dressed comically in old-school bathing suits, injected much humour into 'By the Sea', appeared at one point with seagulls on sticks, to compliment the lyrics. The audience were in hysterics. The pay- off was that we couldn't watch much of what Mrs Lovett was doing. This is a masterpiece of a song that uses humour and character to show how delusional she is, which has an undercurrent of sadness in all its enthusiasm. That was missed as a result of the injection of comedy by the additional cast members.

The quintet holding lamps on the winding stair looked amazing (and performed this difficult piece expertly). The way these performers were left in shadow captured the idea that they were merely thoughts in his head, and not characters in their own right, which worked really well.

Stage Manager Colin Murphy ensured a very slick show, where some changes appeared to happen by magic while others were executed by the cast. The moving of the trees was stylised and slickly rehearsed, successfully creating a variety of spaces, including a pathway for Anthony. The summery scene created by these trees around a park bench for 'Not While I'm Around' was most certainly successful at providing a fresh setting, like nothing that had come before, juxtaposing the tragic outcome of this song with the attempt by the pair to live out a happy life in the sunshine. The trade-off was that these characters seemed removed from their cramped claustrophobic microcosm, the darkness that can exist behind closed doors and the dingy hardship of their situation.

Mrs Lovett's "cheery wallpaper" was actually made up of giant splats of blood, which was brilliantly ironic, nicely pulling together the red chaise and the wood of the harmonium. I would argue that Mrs Lovett did not display enough panic when she discovered Beadle Bamford in her home. She is a woman who has been complicit in multiple murders, cooking these victims on the premises, and I would suggest the presence of the authorities would have her far more riled up, even if she does everything in her power to hide this.

The Beadle's death was not shown, with the scene ending with Mrs Lovett playing her harmonium, and the Asylum scene was played as silhouettes behind a gauze. The Asylum sequence had some very cool aspects, with the chorus coming on and suddenly falling to slither like snakes on the ground, as Mr Fogg's murder was played out in shadows. The cast scarpered so slickly for 'Searching' and crawled back on the Beggar Woman's "Demons are prowling". The latter entrances of the choral singing suffered from this amount of running on and off, however.

The final bakehouse scene had human limbs hanging from the ceiling like a butcher's shop. The grinder and the oven were such good quality. The echo on the voices in the bakehouse helped to establish this sense of space, as did Lovett's off-stage click of the door as she locked Tobias in. Tobias returned at the end covered in flour, re-enacting the violence, acting out the throat gagging, taking his time to contemplate the razor before doing the deed. This was highly engaging, but two seconds more of it and it could have become indulgent. While I think the arrival of the police etc. at the end is a little corny, it suggests that Tobias might well be locked up (for insanity if nothing else), enhancing the tragedy of the piece. In this production, the scene finished with Tobias alone, changing things slightly. It was nonetheless very creepy, as we imagined he might stay down there, like a creature, for a long time. The finale ensured engaging dynamics, with a whisper-like quality from the chorus at the get-go, giving it somewhere to go, allowing it to build to a dramatic crescendo. The final moment created a cyclical narrative as Sweeney climbed back down the hole he had come from. Wardrobe Mistress Anne Reck, assisted by Marie Brady and Maria Routledge, ensured quality across the board with costuming. Hair/Wigs were by Elle Doyle and Make-up Design was by Ali Murphy, continuing the quality aesthetic to be found everywhere else.

Tony Carty was intense and coarse, seething with anger, as Sweeney Todd. He captured all of the vengeful drive that the character feels, unrelenting in his mission to make those responsible pay for his tragedy. His voice is impressive, performing 'Epiphany' with style. The audience were gasping on the edge of their seats here by the time he finally cornered the Judge. This is a mammoth role and was executed very well.

Catherine Walsh was hilarious as Mrs Lovett. She did not feel the need to be obvious at every moment, knowing when to spell out certain keywords or moments, and when to use nice free rhythms to let the dialogue wash over, combing naturalism with heightened characterisation. 'Worst Pies in London' is gruelling and this was well-rehearsed, with plenty of banging of the utensils to the music and much chuckling to give character and energy to the number. There were belly laughs in the audience when she unknowingly sat on the chest containing Pirelli. This role is just as demanding as Sweeney Todd and was very well delivered by Catherine.

Michael O'Gorman as Tobias Ragg had an excellent singing voice, crystal-clear, while ensuring it was full of character. He developed an interesting physicality, complete with a pathetic limp. That 'Pirelli's Miracle Elixir' is a challenging number, but Michael performed it with accuracy. It was very interesting the way he finished Mrs Lovett's sentences, chiming in with "hardworking and obedient" as though he had learned off the rules and wanted to show off that he could say them. His final moments in the bakehouse were utterly engaging, as he showed how mad he had become as a result of having been through so much.

Ciara Cullinane showed off a gorgeous singing voice as Johanna. She had a beautiful vibrato that gave her vocal a bird-like quality, invoking the metaphor of her character's situation nicely. She represented light, in an otherwise dark show. Her partnership with Anthony was lovely and we were rooting for her every step of the way to escape her perverted "father" and live a life of innocent love. In a bleak London, Brendan Long as Anthony Hope was full of optimism; with a broad bright smile, he was the perfect foil to Sweeney's darkness and the Judge's evil. I might suggest that he used his hands a little too much, but that is a personal performing choice I suppose. His pairing with Johanna gave us hope (get it?) in a world full of sorrow and the brightness of their potential future brought balance to a show that is so tragic elsewhere.

George Lawlor established his presence immediately as an over-the-top Pirelli, appearing like the circus ringmaster to wow us with his voice. All his fussing in the shaving contest contrasted nicely with Sweeney's stillness, as he comically covered his victim's entire face with foam and was suitably cruel to Tobias. It was very interesting that he used a Northern Irish accent in quite a southern production. I think it worked very well, as using the local accent can sometimes take us way too much out of the story. This way it remained performative, which I think worked nicely. Very well done indeed. With John Crosbie's performance as Judge Turpin, there were moments of utter genius combined with moments that appeared overly-heightened, bordering on the panto villain. His moment of self- flagellation in the 'Mea Culpa' scene was seriously committed, striking at times. It might have gone a little OTT in parts, those psycho-eyes perhaps becoming a little overly performative. His first appearance in the tonsorial parlour was a little too chirpy and characterful for me. He was at his best when he was present, honest, in the zone and when he did not try to "show" us anything. But I sound very mean here about a very good performance. He has a wonderful speaking voice and superb presence on stage. It was clear that he had worked hard on his material; that 'Johanna' number is a curse to learn, and his clarity in the 'Pretty Women Reprise' kept the thing from falling apart. Overall, very well done.

Antonia Close was impressive as the Beggar Woman. Her voice was gorgeously rich but sorrowful and gaspy, pitch- perfect while never attempting to sound too pretty. Her tragic life was well acted by Antonia; her final moments moving as she physically re-lived her life in the Tonsorial Parlour, emotively hugging a towel as though it was her long-lost baby.

Michael Farrell as Beadle Bamford captured all of the low-life menace of his character, forever sucking up to the Judge. He was pathetically enamoured by his role as judge in the shaving contest and the offer of a free shave from Sweeney and Lovett. He was suitably ridiculous as he sang "one of Mother's favourites" at the harmonium.

Pat Lawlor as Mr Fogg, who appeared as a silhouette behind a screen, had a superbly rich speaking voice. Gearóid Mcauley had a characterful croaky voice and a great accent as the Bird Seller also. Lucy Caufield and Cian O'Gorman did very well as the little boy and girl.

Debbie Kiernan was responsible for choreography, assisted by Dance Captain Sinéad Reck. The chorus' appearances were always top-notch, with inventive and effective spacing and sense of movement. The ensemble was 100% committed to every scene they were in, appeared very well-rehearsed and their singing and acting were excellent. They were able to move from the menacing, to the characterful to the insane, clearly understanding their role and intention in each moment. The choral work in this show is gruelling and punishing to learn and any group who performs it to this standard should be very proud of themselves.

It was a glossy evening of spectacle, with glorious moments of lighting, superb staging and a clever high-quality set- design. Just like chocolate, the whole thing was delicious.

The Titanic experience began as soon as the audience entered the premises in Castlerea. The foyer in the venue was spectacularly decorated with endless examples of Titanic trivia and memorabilia. The box office looked like the deck of a ship, complete with a life buoy. On the walls, there were passenger lists, a Titanic jigsaw, newspaper articles, blueprints of the decks of the ship and a colouring competition. Under each person's seat was the name of a real person who had boarded the Titanic, and the audience were able to check on the way out if they had survived or perished.

For those who are wondering, the show is not based on the 1997 movie with Leo and Kate. Each character is based on a real person who actually sailed on the ship. The events form a linear narrative most of us are familiar with; the passengers board, as we are introduced to the somewhat uncomfortable class divide, those behind the scenes bicker about the fact that the ship should be sped up, the ship hits the iceberg and tragedy strikes. There are too many characters in the story for us to really care about most of them. That said, it is a moving event, and the inclusion of Irish characters stirs something in our emotional DNA. The production itself was very good, with lovely moments of direction, rousing choral singing and fine principal performances.

Director Niall Heaney used the space very well to structure a narrative that requires the enormity of the Titanic tale to be staged on one stand-alone set, with various vignettes exploring the stories of an endless selection of characters. We began with a simple set-up of a stand in the corner with blue-prints of the ship, which would be where we were introduced to ship-designer Thomas Andrews, pondering over his work as boarding action began behind the gauze.

The opening number effectively contained various character archetypes, spanning the classes and professionals impacted by the "ship of dreams". The accents here, Cockney and Scottish etc., were all very good. The smoke in the boiler room was very atmospheric, as it built and built, wafting out into the audience, giving us a taster of the choking conditions these stokers would have endured. At one point, after the collision, a tea trolley rolled across the stage. This was an excellent trick, simply but ingeniously indicating that the ship was at a slant.

'Blame' created a nice piece of drama where the three men who had a hand to play in the disaster really went for each other. The moment the slow-motion red- swashed chaos of the ship appeared behind Mr. Andrews, as he emotionally re-designed the ship in his head, was impactful. Each person did well delivering their solo dialogue that described the deaths of those at sea. Lights behind the gauze came on to reveal the lost souls and the survivors recounting the events turned to face them (with the guilt-ridden Ismay standing in the centre holding the model of the ship, creating a dramatic and emotive ending).

Set design by John O'Donoghue endeavoured to achieve simplicity in a narrative that is quite complicated. The wings were decorated in blueprints of the decks. The black material covered the stage, giving us a hint of what was behind, without giving away the whole set until the beginning of the show. A gangway for the passengers to board the ship would be easily retracted on departure.

The three regular ship doors worked so well to create various locations in the ship. They worked as general entrances and quarter doors that would be banged on in the middle of night during the panic. Red curtains were hung from them to depict an upper-class event and were replaced with bars to stage the dramatic moments when the lower classes were trapped below deck. I loved the subtle projections over the door; in a simple font, like what a telegram might use. In a world full of giant screens, this was a tasteful use of modern technology to evoke events which took place over 100 years ago.

The watch-tower was wheeled on against a glorious star-cloth. I am not always convinced of the suitability of star-cloths in some shows, particularly in scenes set in cities. It was a clear starry night, on the date Titanic foundered, and this worked excellently well here. There were lots of champagne flutes, brandy glasses, cards and cigars during the upper-class soirées. The moment everyone was waiting for would be how well the set would fall apart once the ship foundered. I think this was achieved to a good standard. Parts of the ship were askew and lopsided with railings at an angle.

Director Niall Heaney and Liam Feeney designed the lights. Lighting through the grill of the boiler room looked cool. The eerie greenish freeze, as the young boy announced the dinner sittings, effectively showed the passing of the days and the increasing pressure on the Captain to speed up the ship. The spooky light, filled with smoke, for the final moments of Act One created a sense of foreboding.

Shane Farrell, in that dashing piano tie, provided musical direction and conduction on the evening. He was positioned in the corner of the theatre with the piano player, while the rest of the musicians spilled over into an adjacent room. His instructions to the sixteen musicians were very clearly given and they provided a sound that was epic, dangerous, romantic and exciting. Principal vocals were excellent throughout and the choral singing had so much power. The chorus presented as though they were very well rehearsed. There did not appear to be as much harmony required in this show than there is in most other shows. While the chorus confidently belted out their numbers, there were times when it appeared to be more in unison than many other pieces I have seen. If that is how it is written, then absolutely fair enough.

Sound was by Liam Feeney. The hopeful hoot-hoot of the ship as it departed was well done. There was a lovely echo effect on the choral singing of 'Hymn, God Lift Me Up', which made the ensemble sound as though they were singing in a cathedral. I hate being negative. It is not my thing. But the show was so loud that at one point I thought my eardrum, the right one in particular, was going to burst. There were eighty people and sixteen musicians, so I imagine they were hard to tame. Little amplification was necessary, I would argue, but amplified they were.

Choreographer Hazel McLynn ensured energetic routines throughout, which captured the time period and the social standing of the characters taking part. The opening number cleverly grouped the various classes into separate sections, placing the officers/crew on the bridge above. The simple bobbing up and down by the maids in the upper-class soiree worked very well. 'Doing the Last Rag' was a joyful number with the four couples downstage doing different moves to those above, and everyone joining in together for the last minute.

John Griffin as Captain Edward J. Smith was suitably imposing and authoritative as he captained one last maiden voyage before his retirement. It was clear that his character understood his responsibility to all those on board. He portrayed the struggle between himself and owner J. Bruce Ismay, who pushed for more speed to get better headlines, with competence. With a heavy heart and a burdened conscience, he went against his better judgement and complied with Ismay's demands. He sang well in the trio 'Blame', when each man was pointing out the other's involvement in the disaster. His voice was powerful as he announced that the ship was lost.

David Cooke as Designer Thomas Andrews gave us a man of integrity, understated but strong, who acted as the moral compass for the show. He portrayed the anguish he felt as he learns that the compromises he made in the construction of the Titanic has contributed to its demise. It was clear from his opening scenes that he has a good voice, and he performed 'Andrew's Vision' very well.

Pat Walsh was very good as owner of the Titanic, Bruce Ismay. Factual or not, he played the villain of the show, greedy for success and manipulative in how he forces the Captain to speed up and take a colder, more Northerly route. He was excitable about his achievements, yet he could really manage to get a rise out of those around him. He, too, added nicely to the 'Blame' trio.

Brian Flanagan was striking as Coal Stoker Frederick Barrett. He did very well at balancing his function as questioner of the misguided decision to speed up the ship, trapped in a position of no influence, and a man in love with a girl back home, planning a future as he writes to her asking for her hand in marriage. He is a very good singer and captured all of the angst he felt about the ship's increasing speed in 'Barrett's Song'. His singing of 'The Proposal' was lovely.

Conor Walsh was adorable as Wireless Operator Harold Bride. His accent was excellent, and he has a very good singing voice. He was cute as a button in how he said that he had no time for romance. Vulnerable, cute and shy, he was in love with his telegraph machine but understood Frederick's need to send a message to his would-be fiancée, without paying. His solo moment ("Fair thee well…") in the finale was very nice. The counterpoint and solo vocals from Barrett, Bride and Clarke in the finale were lovely also.

Our working-class Irish contingent was made up of three Kates and a Jim. Kate McGowan (Head Kate) was played very well by Patricia Collins. Her character is escaping the fact that she fell pregnant for a married man while single in Ireland. She needs a husband and with her assertive charm, convinces a passenger, Jim Farrell to take her on and marry her, despite her condition. John McHugh was dashing as Jim. He was well able for her but could not help but be amused by Kate's confidence and self-assured beauty, eventually falling for her. While he could turn on the confident boyish charm, he was strong in the scenes when things got serious.

Kate Mullins, played by Zara Walshe, intended to live with her sister and become a maid. She was the most frightened of the Kates, overwhelmed by the scope of everything, and grateful for the companionship of her fellow Irish third- class passengers. Michelle Cooke gave us a tough, no-nonsense character as Kate Murphey. All three Kates showed off excellent vocals and ability to harmonise in 'Lady's Maid'.

Anthony Flanagan as First Officer Murdoch showed a lovely voice in his solo number 'To be a Captain'. He presented as more cautious than Ismay, bringing balance to the arguments about speed. Joey O' Flanagan was very good as Second Officer Charles Lightoller, the highest-ranking officer to survive, and it is through his accounts of the sinking that most of our knowledge of the events is gleaned. He was suitably competent and confident in his official role and sang well in his featured solo moments. Kevin Moran as Quartermaster Robert Hitchens was responsible for steering the ship and carrying out the helm orders. He did very well as the officer manning the wheel the night the ship hit the iceberg, obeying that famous "hard a' starboard" order in the climax Act One. Robert Reid showed off a good voice as Lookout, Frederick Fleet Good, the man in the crow's nest who dramatically shouted "Iceberg, right ahead!" during the final dramatic moment of the first act.

Ivan Moran as the haughty first-class steward Henry Etches, oozing in experience having served many a celeb in his time, provided some nice comic relief throughout the evening. He very good at handling that wordy 'What a Remarkable Age This is' number. Aidan Flanagan as bandmaster Wallace Hartley vocalised well and was full of character in his performance of 'Doing the Last Rag' and he treated us to some nice solos behind the piano during 'Autumn'.

Eugene Collins as poor long-suffering Edgar Beane, was funny as he put up with his equally comic wife Alice, played by Majella Flanagan. Frustrated by her lowly status as a middle-class passenger, she was forever looking to climb the social ladder whilst gossiping about all those she envies. They both provided a lot of comedy, yet their rendition of 'I Have Danced' was nicely touching.

Declan Connolly and Jackie Kenny were great as Isidor and Ida Strauss. Mrs. Strauss had a good European accent and a very lovely voice when she sang her solo bits on 'No Moon'. Both she and her husband gave us a gorgeous and powerful rendition of 'Still', their voices blending beautifully together in this adorable moment.

Jamie Mee and Janet Feeney were very nice playing "The Clarkes", a couple who are enjoying pretending to be married, because their love is forcing them to elope (and to save on accommodation fees on the ship). Born to first class, Janet exuded class as Caroline. They clearly showed that they loved one another, with Caroline willing to leave fortune behind to be with him. Filled with hope and ambition, Charles dreams of being a journalist in New York City. The adorable partnership of these actors made for highly dramatic scenes when they were parted at the lifeboats. Jamie showed off a great voice in his solo moments of 'To the Lifeboats'.

Olivia Walsh played Charlotte Cardoza, the woman who booked Titanic's most expensive suite, and travelled with fourteen trunks full of designer clothing and jewellery. Her unconventional ideas set the pulses racing of some of her first-class male counterparts, as she challenged the gender traditions onboard. Olivia had all of the charisma and charm to do this, captivating the group of men with her good humour.

The wealthy Astors (a pairing Kate Winslet points out in the movie if anyone recalls) were played with competence by Pat McDonnell and Emer Kelly, who were returning to give birth to their first child after a honeymoon, where they had been waiting out the gossip that followed their scandalous marriage (He divorced and remarried without delay, which was uncommon. Plus, she was considered terribly young and all too-quickly pregnant). The American mining tycoon, Benjamin Guggenheim, was played by Chris Duffy. He was a regular cross-Atlantic traveller, with a mistress in Paris. The mistress, Parisian singer Madame Aubart (played by Danielle Carroll), accompanied him on the Titanic. John B. Thayer, the Vice-President of the Pennsylvania Railroad, was played by John Hanley and his "old money" wife Marion was played by Caroline Madigan. Their parting at the lifeboats was a heart-breaking moment, as John tries to reassure her that they will be fine.

The Wideners, heirs to a large fortune, enjoying the Titanic for leisure purposes, were played very well by Adrian Murray and Angela Webb. Edith Corse Evans was played by Niamh O'Flanagan, a single woman who was returning to America from a funeral in England. Unfortunately, there was only one spot left, and she convinced a friend to take it, because the friend had children. Gambler and card shark J.H. Rogers was played by Cathal Tivnan, who gave us some interesting scenes where he was trying to pull the wool over the eyes of the other passengers. Micheál Ward played The Major, who provided some comic relief in the series of upper-class dining room scenes with stories of his foreign adventures and encounters with "crazed, godless savages."

It can be argued that each class is a character in itself, and within each one there is representation by principal performances. There were four primary groups of people; the three classes and the crew. Together they gave powerful performances. There was a strong sense of confidence in the powerful choral singing, suggesting that they were well-prepared by Musical Director Shane Farrell. Facial expressions etc. were top-notch. The children in the opening number were great at acting excited and their timing was excellent. Their scrambling scenes were so well-acted with each and every person on stage showing full commitment, and their slow-motion section was great too. I am happy to report that Castlerea Musical Society did not leave any stone unturned in the costume department. There are three greater ensemble casts - upper, middle and lower classes, and a variety of crew costumes to source. Not only that, but the first-class passengers, for example would need day wear, evening gowns, silk robes for the night-time panic scenes etc. These needs ran through all the other classes, with each class having appropriate attire for all occasions, suitably suggesting their caste and the context of the scenes e.g. arrival, social, night-time etc. Hair and Make-up encouraged likenesses between the actors and the real-life people they were portraying. There was a clear distinction between all of the classes on the ship.

This show is a massive undertaking, visually and chorally and I am glad to report that the society delivered a fine version. Congratulations to Castlerea Musical Society and all who sail in her on their 50th Anniversary.

A portrait of Eva Peron against an Argentinian flag was beamed onto a gauze for the set-up with the IMC Cinema in Banbridge. Behind this gauze, the actors filed into a cinema while the audience filed into a cinema. It set an atmosphere for the piece, without creating the awkwardness one can feel when actors appear onstage before a show. Sometimes that can force us to whisper or feel a little tense, but not here. It also gave us a suggestion of the set, with its lovely brickwork, columns and steps, without giving away the whole shebang too early. This action was cyclical, with the cast returning to these positions to tastefully turn in groups towards the audience, rather than bowing - a nice compromise for a sombre ending that depicted the death of a real person. In between this imaginative start and end to the show, we got some inventive directorial ideas, a committed chorus and an excellent performance from the lady herself.

Director Ian Milford ensured that there were many nice pieces of staging, such as: when the news of Eva's death resulted in an anguished cry from the crowd, watching a movie from the period in a cinema, giving me shivers, Ché slamming the coffin lid to the music and sitting atop of it during 'Oh What a Circus', the way in which the men and women sat separately in Junin, with nice pieces of business such as arm- wrestling, Magaldi coming on with his guitar in a case showing that he was leaving without needing to say it or buttoning up his shirt to suggest he had been a naughty boy, how Eva looked up at the screen at the beginning of 'Buenos Aires' (naturally bringing our attention to this information), the revolving door that perfectly illustrated how Eva was going through men on her race to the top, the bit of humour as Eva shoves away her date as she tells Peron she is alone, having children ask them both for autographs (illustrating that this was a meeting of equals), the political symbolism of a game of musical chairs with the statesman, which was genuinely fascinating as we were glued wondering which character would be bumped off next (concluding with Peron as the right-hand man, still somewhat left in the shadows as a result of a clever lighting moment), how guards blocked the crowd during the ball, Eva's determination to address the crowd after a jealous statesman says that "statesmanship is more than entertaining peasants", the slide of the plane beamed onto the gauze accompanied by nautical sound effects as the European tour sequence was being slickly set up behind, and the nurses who tried to hold her down as she writhed and ranted in her hospital bed. And breathe.

There were some nice moments in the latter part of the show when Eva directly clocked Ché as though he was acting as her conscience or at least provoking it, the trick which sneaked Eva out of her deathbed so that she could return on the height to look down on the action, 'You Must Love Me' was brilliantly re- imagined as a domestic argument/love song between Peron and Eva, with Eva disgusted as she sang "Why are you at my side?". This duet worked so well as a dramatic but intimate moment.

I would suggest that Peron's emotion in the opening sequence was overdone. It can be more moving to see someone desperately trying to hold it together than to indulge in their emotions. I think a man of great power and station would know how to find the stoicism required in these public moments. I am reminded of Princes William and Harry who talk how they couldn't cry at their mother's funeral because they were "at work".

Choreographer Lynn Gourley ensured that the narrative was fully supported by her movement choices and the ensemble appeared to be well-prepared for their task. The 'Buenos Aires' number was really cool, with varying formations and different groups doing different things. The crowds surrounded Eva here, two guys lifted her onto their shoulders, created a diamond formation and performed a stylised March under Ché's speeches. The male box-stepping worked well in 'Peron's Latest Flame'. The use of props can be really successful at enhancing the function of a number. The use of the newspapers in 'Rainbow Tour' was a great idea as was the money in the hands of those performing 'And the Money Kept Rolling in'. While the feet were not always together in 'Peron's Latest Flame', the ensemble ensured that they performed fully in character, which is what is most important.

The set made up of palatial columns, brickwork and steps was designed by Director Ian Milford and Russell Caughey and successfully managed by Andy McKnight. Three screens in total would be used throughout the evening, projecting clarifying information for the audience, such as place names and dates, but there were also lovely historical photos of the real events.
