Mark Ivory's portrayal of Professor Marvel/ The Wizard of Oz was characterful and entertaining.

These characters must establish themselves instantly when they appear on stage as they are not given a slow introduction. Mark had good presence and naturalism and managed this task nicely. He captured the balance between Professor Marvel as the chancer and as the wise man very well.

With the greatest respect, I have to say that sometimes when very young performers appear on stage, they can lack a certain polish, energy and volume, sometimes creating a lull in a show. Not with this superb troop of young stars! Clearly the ensemble had put a huge amount of work into their performances. The energy from the Munchkins was amazing. Their movement was so slick. Dressed as ballerinas, the Lullaby League gave us some brilliant ballet dancing. The solo lines in the Munchkin scenes had super energy and clarity. The Citizens of Oz had superb reactions. The Flying Monkeys (with a very good Katie Cunningham as Nico) had well- developed animal physicality. The Poppies and Snow People created a magical moment and the Jitterbugs gave us a show stopping routine. All of this added to the lovely principal performances, in a show that looked great and ran like clockwork. There was nothing boring about this version of this classic tale. It was super fun.

In this somewhat stylised production, the staging difficulties normally associated with "Sweet Charity" were significantly alleviated, which worked very well, although it did put an added pressure on the lighting designer to be highly inventive, and the lack of a structured set did, on occasions, lead to a slight lack of atmosphere. The set was minimal with only occasional free standing pieces that were essential for comedic business. The wardrobe in Vittorio's bedroom and the lift both worked well, even if more could have been done to give the illusion of the lift moving or rising before it jammed.  These pieces, plus furniture and props, were efficiently put in place by Stage Manager, Amy McCarthy and her team.

While there was plenty of colour and variety to the lighting plot, with moving heads and attractive effects on the cyc, I rarely had the feeling that the colourful display was particularly relevant to the action. The most effective states occurred when smaller areas were being focused on and there was less activity. While the recorded opening dialogue probably took pressure off the sound engineer, it did also detract from some very funny dialogue, as the audience were more concerned with trying to grasp what was going on. Apart from that, the sound quality throughout was very satisfactory. Where Director, Kevin Hynes, scored highly was in his drawing of the characteristics of the various individuals on-stage. This was a thoroughly well-rehearsed cast, each of whom had a definite and individual identity. It was easy to be sympathetic to Charity with her quirky naivety, and to see through the transparency of most of the male characters.

While she sang very well and moved with ease and comfort, it was the sincerity of her acting that made Gail McGrath so acceptable in the role of Charity. There was an almost self-effacing quirkiness to her humour, which made her a delightfully sympathetic character. Vocally, she was well up to the challenge of the role.

There was a good contrast between Sophia Daly as Nikki and Róisin Ryan as Helene, Sophia with a seen-it-all, done- it-all acceptance of her lot, coupled with a brash sense of humour, and Róisin the more reluctant and frustrated hostess, with a drier, bitter view of their station in life. Both were consistent and extremely capable in their portrayals, displaying great rhythm and vocal ability, with Sophia having that extra dimension of being a sincere, if somewhat misguided, mother hen figure. The two worked extremely well together and with Charity.

Chris O'Connor gave a stalwart performance as their seedy boss, Herman, always comfortable on the stage, albeit in a loathsome kind of way. This was an enjoyable performance, coupled with a very good delivery of "I Love to Cry at Weddings". Chris also doubled as "Daddy" to perform "The Rhythm of Life", which he did with panache, although I would have liked to see him visually more outrageous or flamboyant.

Peter O'Brien handled the claustrophobic comedy of Oscar with talent and very good timing, establishing his character from the outset. He had an infectious likeability as the quirky would-be lover, and it's a testament to his acting ability that when he suddenly refused to accept Charity's circumstances, the audience, quite vocally, turned against him. This was a well-acted and well sung role.

Aaron Tierney brought an unexpected kind of bedraggled, youthful exuberance to the role of Vittorio Vidal, with a mixture of fame induced arrogance and naïve insecurity. It did work very nicely, although I did feel that more comedy could have been squeezed out of the bedroom scene. Alicia O'Connor was suitably pouty and pretentious in the role of Ursula, full of tantrums and shallow affection.

The principal line was completed by a very worthy Laura Walsh as the not so innocent new-comer, Rosie.

The chorus performed with great credibility throughout the show, adding atmosphere and character to all their scenes, and the feeling of inclusiveness was beautifully highlighted by the performances of Alice McGrath and Mark Claffey, who made their presence felt in a most delightful manner.

In the very secure hands of Musical Director, Caitriona Ni Threasaigh, there was little to criticise in the delivery of the musical content of the show. Tempi were always on point, and the effervescence of the livelier numbers was balanced by a sympathetic rendition of the more mellow and emotional pieces. Principals were vocally well-disciplined in numbers which are rhythmically quite challenging, and the chorus performed "Rhythm of Life" and "I Love to Cry at Weddings" particularly well. There were beautiful tributes to Bob Fosse in Nicole McDonald's choreography, which was always stylish and appropriate to the show and the music. Her chorus and dancers made a very good job of executing the Frug and Rhythm of Life in particular, and she had good dancers in the principal roles, who were able to give life and energy to "Something Better Than This", and "If My Friends Could See Me Now". The small hand movements of "Big Spender" work better on camera (with close ups) than they do on stage, but this still developed into a good routine.

Costumes were of a good standard, with the dance hostesses always suitably attired. Outfits for the Frug were very good, and principals were appropriately dressed. There was good attention to hair styles and make-up, giving the overall effect of the era of the show.

I'm delighted that Glencullen took a chance on this piece of musical theatre, and did so with conviction. The 'studio' style of the production was interesting and imaginative, but perhaps because of the need for certain set pieces to give comedic effect, it did seem to fall somewhere between an abstract concept and a fully staged show. Thanks, however, to a very committed cast and some very good direction and choreography, it was still a highly entertaining night of musical theatre.

In the safe hands of the experienced Justin Parkes, I expected to see a well-drilled, thorough and entertaining production of this classic, and that's precisely what I got. While it may have been more traditional than innovative, it had polish and commitment from all on stage, and was marked by a beautifully natural sense of community, through the involvement of children in the crowd scenes. While Dunboyne weren't able to use all the pieces of their hired set exactly as designed, due to stage limitations, they very cleverly crafted the pieces they could use into an excellent background to the action. It was well painted and functional, with the smoke house being particularly impressive. Just as important as it looking good was the fact that it was seamlessly manoeuvred around the stage by Stage Managers, Elaine McLoughlin and Sean Keany, and their team. There was good flow and pace to all of the action, and very good attention to the development of characters.

The strength of Aishling Rountree's choreography in this production was that it carried through on the director's sense of inclusivity, so that instead of a stand- alone dancers routine for "Farmer and the Cowman" we got the whole community dancing as you might expect at a box- social. There were kids doing their own (choreographed) thing, oblivious to the adults around them, and there were people dancing in their own little groups and circulating to dance with others, an occasional bit of tension between a farmer and a cowboy, and there were cowboys showing off their steps and girls trying to flirt and dance with them, and it all just worked brilliantly. I'm well aware that such organised chaos is much harder to perfect than a straightforward routine. In "Kansas City" too, there was plenty of step work, but it was played with Will Parker teaching the others their steps, at which they gradually improved until they were all dancing joyfully in unison. Very clever work. The Ballet was excellent, with Jud, Curly and Laurey fronting it with some very nifty dancing. Overall, the choreography thoroughly superbly enhanced the quality of the production.

Kevin Hartnett and Keila-Ana Whelan developed an almost symbiotic relationship in the roles of Curly and Laurey, feeding off each other in the comedy of their teasing, and totally believable in their developing romance. Their voices blended beautifully together and they flowed gracefully in the execution of their dances. Individually, they created strong and believable characters and interacted very well with the rest of the cast. Keila-Ana's loathing of Jud was as convincing as her love for Curly, and both were beautifully acted.

Monica Hannigan (above) was a secure and homely Aunt Eller, well able for the antics of the men around her, and delightfully sympathetic towards her niece. She steered the auction scene with good authority and contributed well to the vocals of "The Farmer and the Cowman". Eoin O'Reilly was an animated Will Parker, enjoying his opportunities to display his dancing ability, and comfortable in his comedic encounters with Ado Annie. He made a very good job of "Kansas City". Meaghan Ebbs was a quirky and robust Ado Annie, making the most of her silliness, and putting good comedy and energy into "I Cain't Say No".

There was almost a sympathetic simplicity about the loneliness of Shane Fox's Jud Fry, until the turning point when Curly exposes the inner soul of an unsettling psychotic personality during the smoke- house scene. From then on, he was scary. This was an excellent performance, both in character development, and in the execution of his songs and dances.

Eoin Kenny sustained a very interesting accent throughout his performance, and used it to good comedic effect, playing the role of Ali Hakim with great character, confidence and comedy.

Grace McEntee's laugh was obnoxious! (That's a compliment.) She presented a good character and got plenty of fun out of the supporting role of Gertie Cummins. If I met Gerry Hannigan with a shotgun, I'd run the other way, so grumpy and gruff was he when he stepped out as Andrew Carnes, but he balanced that scariness with a fine sense of comedy, and developed into a very likeable old character. Good work in "The Farmer and The Cowman".

There was good dependable support from Ian McColgan as Ike Skidmore, Ben Hannigan as Slim, Cyril Green as Fred and Colm Woods as Mike, while Sean Whelan gave a good smug self-righteousness to Cord Elam in the ad hoc court scene. The chorus were particularly well integrated into their scenes, always having a sense of purpose and reacting to the focal point. Their vocal contributions were secure and they dance and movement were lively and well-executed.

Musical Director, Paul Strachan, led an impressive orchestra securely through the score, with good tempi and good volume control. The chorus were well-rehearsed in their music and lyrics, with well-realised harmonies and clear diction. Principals were musically very secure. The musical quality of the show was most impressive. There were no issues with the fairly traditional costuming of the show, with chorus and principals alike very well turned out. Jud looked sweaty and filthy, which I credit to a good make-up artist, and the rest of the cast looked as they should, both from a hair and make-up point of view. The lighting of the show was delightful, with the frequent beautiful blending of lavender and amber gels. The ballet gave a well-taken opportunity to be a bit inventive and artistic. It was atmospheric, picturesque and cueing was very good. Sound quality was very satisfactory with good cueing and some lovely ambient background effects.

Dunboyne Musical Society did themselves credit and were well served by their production and technical teams. Thank you for a very enjoyable evening and a very nice presentation of a popular classic.

The Backstage Theatre in Longford is a super resource, with comfortable tiered seating and a fine stage, creating the perfect setting to put on a show. This was my eighth time to adjudicate Sister Act, yet there is something about it that always seems fresh and new. It never fails to delight, and this version was no exception. With strong performers in the leading roles, supported by a great chorus of nuns, the production provided a great night's entertainment for all.

Director Seán Power gave us a solid version of this show that used the space very well. The way the nuns appeared live on stage for their backing vocals in 'Here Within These Walls' was cool (they often do these off stage) and it meant they were ready to go for the dining scene. The prayer before meals built very nicely. Mary Robert was very clearly blocked in isolation during 'How I Got the Calling'. I loved how Deloris brought the cheesesteak back from the bar and how the Mother Superior snatched it out of her hands. The business given to the bums, such as searching the bins for bottles, gave context to their appearance. The two altar boys pointing to the fundraiser thermometer was a hoot and the five altar boys wearing sunglasses on the balcony was gas.

The 'Fabulous, Baby!' reprise, in which Deloris wrestles with her conscience, was very well staged with the nuns up on the balcony with their backs to the audience, looking over their shoulders when it was their turn to interject. Mother Superior hyperventilating into a paper bag was a hoot. The moment Deloris leaves the convent was lovely; sad, sombre and touching. The moment when she told Mary Robert to "stay or go" was very nicely measured.

The chase scene combined humour and danger well. The cross-dresser came back for a cameo! The fighting in the chase scene never looked real, however. It is possible to look like contact is made between two people, without hurting anyone. The bump on the head was not in time with the music either. My friend was crying when the nuns starting to say "Take Me", which is a testament to how touching the moment was.

Set design was by Robert Belton and Stage Manager Eddie Kiernan. The lovely wings, each with its own lancet stained- glass window, stayed on for the whole show, framing the stage nicely. A series of trucks were wheeled on to form a sense of space behind the actors, such as a backdrop for Curtis' Bar and the entrance to the convent with a statue of Mary. The bar across the street from the convent looked cool with its silver bar top, dartboard, shelves with proper 3D bottles, red and white tiles on the floor, jukebox and disco-ball.

The convent set was fantastic with its series of doors, circular windows with clover-like stained glass decoration and balcony finished off with organ pipes. The working doors utilised in the chase scene were excellent and it seemed a shame that they were not used more. When Mary Patrick was eavesdropping on Mary Robert and Deloris, she might have used one of the doors, for example.

The confessional boxes looked really well. The crew were cleverly hiding behind the confessional boxes all the while so they could magically wheel themselves off at the end of that scene. This also happened behind the entrance truck with statue of Mary as it glided off like magic before the final scene. The curtains on the side solved a problem that most other societies were not able to overcome. The sofa and T.V. were all that were needed to establish Curtis' gaff. Deloris' room was nicely framed with a small backdrop with crucifix and her old school blanket and tartan bedspread on her little brown wooden bed looked the part. Eddie's dingy apartment was effectively established with the covered sofa and small set of flats behind it, framed by the Philadelphia skyline, creating a nice sense of space. The big red staircase gave great structure to the final number.

Lighting was designed by Paschal Gough. There was a nice white special on Mother Superior in the opening of Act Two when she tells God he is killing them with "the cure". The special on stage-left to cover at the top of the 'Fabulous, Baby!' reprise in Eddie's house was helpful at covering the scene change, nicely revealing the convent when it was set-up. The flickering light coming from the TV was cool. The 'Sister Act' number was great, with the slow disco-ball at the beginning, followed by a lovely rainbow effect on the floor and a final blackout, with the stained-glass windows left on.

Musical Director Alan Recks gave clear conduction to his seven musicians, while two keyboards sat in front of him also. Sound by Jody Trehy was perfectly balanced, ensuring that the seven musicians never overpowered the performers on stage, which is always an impressive achievement when the band are in the room, without a pit etc. Principal and choral vocals were all very good. The final three sentences of 'How I Got the Calling' contained noticeably well- delivered harmony lines. The high-pitched backing vocals from the three gangsters were good. The final "Heaven" in the reprise of 'Take Me to Heaven' was sung with power. The counter-point from Mother Superior and Eddie in 'Sunday Morning Fever' was clearer than I have ever heard it. The backing vocals from the bums were good. Mary Robert stayed down the octave for the ending to 'The Life I Never Led' which was the right choice. It is far better to do something simple and do it well. The 'Benedicta Tu' choral singing from the nuns and Mother Superior, after Deloris suddenly leaves them, was gorgeous. The 'Raise Your Voice' reprise bounced off the stage, sending everyone off on a high.

Choreographer Emer O'Brien impressively crammed the moves in 'When I Find my Baby', showcasing that a lot of work went into this number. All that sideways marching on the tiptoes looked great. There was a lovely organic feel to the 'Raise Your Voice' rehearsal as Deloris worked in small groups and the nuns filed in gradually. Bringing the nuns out of their pews for the final bit of 'Raise Your Voice' was impactful and while the Bible moves at the end was excellent in theory, the final 'Your Voice' was a little off, as though the nuns were slightly distracted. The choreography for the nuns' 'Take Me to Heaven' was well-rehearsed, slick, inventive, varied, never boring and never ending. 'Lady in the Long Black Dress' contained some cool moves and got a great reaction from the audience. 'Bless Our Show' was lovely as the nuns innocently danced circles around Deloris, "wooing" as they moved in and out. Their hand holding as they raised their arms at the end was lovely, showing their solidarity before Deloris has to suddenly leave. Including the Mother Superior in the movement of the final moments was gas. The bows were a moment in themselves, with Deloris coming down the impressive red staircase.  The moves for the curtain call were simple, but hugely effective when done in such a fantastic formation. Janice Gibney as Deloris was full of attitude in her opening scenes and rough around the edges when first introduced to the convent. Her facial expressions were hilarious. She was funny when she saw Ernie being shot. She showed good character development as she wrestled with her conscience in the 'Fabulous, Baby!' reprise, was bitter-sweet in her introspection during 'Sister Act' and when she defiantly stood up to Curtis in the final scenes.

Valerie Nolan was very good as Mother Superior. While dry and droll in her characterisation, she was capable of being funny also, such as her line "I take it back" when the Monsignor reminded her of her vows. She had a lovely voice, perfect for the role. She was lovely and quiet and sad in her little reprise of 'Here Within These Walls'. She was nice and sincere as she simply proclaimed that she was frightened when talking to God in her study. Her lyrics for 'I Haven't Got a Prayer' were so clear and she showed impressive soprano on her powerful high notes here. She also showed off some impressive vocals when comically repeating Deloris in the final scene.

Maryann Lynch as Sister Mary Robert was meek and shy at the beginning, barely able to talk or make eye contact. She grew in confidence nicely and acted through song very well indeed during 'The Life I Never Led', really getting to show off her singing voice in the first section of that song. Anthony Heavey was very good as Eddie. While I think he could have let go a little more in his 'I Could Be That Guy', this routine got a great reaction from the crowd. It was very cute when he sang to Deloris in his apartment, and his assurances to her that she would be a star were nicely convincing.

Dearbhaile Barrins as Sister Mary Patrick captured all the sunshine and jolliness of the character. She was very funny as she continued to interrupt Mary Robert in 'How I Got the Calling'. Michelle Kelly Conlon was good as Sister Mary Lazarus, with her no-nonsense Bronx-style accent. Her "ringer" speech was good as she accused the Mother Superior of holding a grudge of a past folk-mass. She performed her raps well.

Paul Hennessey was suitably slimy and had a great accent and scary growly voice as Curtis. He was comic in the heights of his aggression about Deloris in 'When I Find my Baby'. Lorcan O'Brien as Pablo, Dylan Murray as T.J. and Cormac Göbl as Joey formed an entertaining trio of goofball gangsters. Their moves were slick in 'When I Find my Baby' and it was clear that a lot of work had gone into the movement of this number. Their high- pitched backing vocals were good here too. Joey was gas in his solo for 'Lady in the Long Black Dress', as he rolled on the ground or his legs open towards the audience. T.J. showed off some impressive snake hips as he comically wriggled around the stage. Pablo got a great laugh with his high-pitched singing, as he rolled his r's brilliantly.

John Kelly did very well as Monsignor O'Hara. He was brilliantly excitable in his scene where he reports the news that the Pope is coming to visit.

Niamh O'Brien and Sinéad Mullally played Tina and Michelle respectively. They matched Deloris in their attitude, taking no nonsense for the deluded wannabe diva. They managed those difficult backing vocals in the opening number with aplomb and performed some sassy dance moves too. Eimear Reynolds as Sister Mary Martin of Tours was very good, with eyes that really captured the otherworldliness of the character. It was gas the way she was splayed out on the piano asleep and her quotation of Isaiah 55:12 was genuinely touching. Ríona Lynch as Mary Theresa gave us some very good old-aged acting as the nun who was apparently old enough to have known Jesus personally. Daire O'Muire as Ernie and Aaron Nelson as Cop/Taxi Driver provided quality cameo appearances.

June Belton and Yvonne Bennett headed up the costumes, which were hired by Sparkle Costumes, Dublin. Deloris wore her signature animal-print dress with a hint of a pink bra popping out and her infamous Father Mulcahy purple boots. Tina and Michelle wore spray-on psychedelic flared catsuits. The backing dancers all wore gold sequined dresses with black trim. I can't say for certain that Eddie's strip worked as well as it might have, with his sleeves already half open and the second cop uniform exposed by the low red neck. His white suit gave us a laugh, however. The gold tunics with red hearts looked super on the nuns' 'Take Me to Heaven' and the reveal was well- executed. The multicoloured robes for 'Sunday Morning Fever' were fun. Mary Lazarus' sunglasses, chains and blinged- up cap were hilarious. The head-caps and white night dresses were perfect, and always better than when productions use pyjamas. The silver and white robes on the ensemble nuns in the finale looked great as the primary nuns wore black sequined versions. The altar boys were dripping in bling here also. Deloris' dream came true, with her fabulous gown and white fur for her final appearance.

With this show, everything hangs on the chorus. Their numbers are what makes it so special. I am glad to report that we had a committed group of nuns who worked hard to learn their harmonies and ensured that the dance moves bounced off the stage. By the final number, the audience were buzzing leaving the venue.

Congratulations to St Mel's Musical Society on their 40th Anniversary (including John Kelly who has appeared in all forty productions!) and for putting on a very good show.

society_raw: St. Patrick's Hall Musical Society, Strabane
review_text:
You can always spot when the Director of a show is also a Drama School Teacher, for they have that ability and desire to encourage as much involvement as possible from all the participants in the show. That was clearly evident here, with the chorus and dancers being integrated at every possibility into the action and the musical numbers, and what a huge and talented bunch they were. The real talent of Director, Leah McCay, was that even with so many involved, the stage rarely looked over-crowded. There was good attention to characterisation, and even though there are sections of the script that are a bit tame and poorly written, everyone maintained their character very effectively. Some of the scenes could have been better highlighted with more specific lighting, but stage positions were good, and the show kept a good pace from start to finish. There was good emphasis on comedy throughout, yet very good sincerity from the leading players. Corey O'Connor (pictured with other cast members below in  rehearsal) proved himself to be the perfect choice for the role of Ren, full of angst and fire, song and dance ability, and yet, sensitive enough to become the more considerate and thoughtful Ren of the last few scenes. While he was dynamic and constantly on the verge of breaking into a dance, perhaps he could have become a bit more calm, physically, as his mind become more focused, but that's a minor criticism. This was a very well sung, danced and acted role.

Ariel, the vicar's daughter with a bit of a reputation, was charmingly played by Shonagh Forbes, with a precocious nature that never stepped over the mark, and was equally full of heart. She had a relaxed pop-style voice that suited the role, and a great rhythm and style. Her acting was very believable.

Cahir O'Neill is a young comedian/song and dance man to watch out for in the future. There was a great goofiness to his character, and a very good sense of timing about his comedy, making him perfect for the role of Willard. The scene where he admits his inability to dance, and then transforms into a dance champion, was pure gold, and his rendition of "Mama Says", backed by all the boys, was the comedic and musical highlight of the show.

Naoimh Long was a cute, quirky and radiant Rusty, with a sense of comedy that was matched by her strong vocal ability. "Let's Hear it For The Boys" highlighted her all-round ability and made her a popular favourite with the audience. Very well played.

Jamie-Lee Gallagher took on the least likeable character in the show, Chuck, a bully and a thug, and did a very convincing job of making him loathsome. It's harder to play the bad guy than the good guy, so this was a very good achievement, and he also showed his fine vocal quality in "The Girl Gets Around".

Wendy Jo and Urleen, Ariel's pals, were charmingly played by Maria Carlin and Darci Wilders, respectively, both making the most of their comedy and their song and dance support. They had some lovely moments with Lyle and Travis, two wannabes, effectively played by Matthew McLaughlin and Oran Curley.

Fronting the adult roles was Joe Harley as the Reverend Shaw Moore, the misguided vicar who couldn't let go of his past misfortunes. While Joe acted well and sang with good emotion, I had a feeling that he was not always comfortable with some of the rather contrived dialogue that was given to this lost father figure, which was almost certainly a problem with the script, rather than the performer.

Judy Duddy as Vi, his wife, had better material and a more rational character to portray and did so very admirably. If her singing sounded slightly forced, it was none-the-less performed with good emotion.

Ann Coyle, the abandoned mother of Ren, gave a solid performance, never allowing her own circumstances to distract from her concern for her son.

Stephen Bradley showed good vocal quality and a confident character at the Bar-B-Que, as Cowboy Bob. Wes and Lulu Warnicker proved themselves to be the Uncle and Aunt from hell, or at least from Bomont, and were nicely characterised by Martin McGurk and Andrea Porter. Of the many other smaller roles, Andrew McDaid was an wonderfully obnoxious Coach Roger Dunbar and fine performances were turned in by Janice McCay as Eleanor, Evan McCrea as Jeter, Tom McLaughlin as Garvin, Mark McLaughlin as Bickle, Clare Dunbar as Betty Blast, Mary-Claire McDaid as the unyielding School Principal and Jamie Bonner as the Cop.

The chorus throughout the show were filled with youthful energy, wonderful dance ability, and a good quality of vocal ability.

Emmet Stewart's choreography was funky, it was fresh and it was varied and he did wonderful work with a highly capable dance team and chorus. It was as much about creating atmosphere as it was about doing the steps right. There was also a very good awareness of the need to extend the comedy into the dance routines.

Ryan Quinn led an extremely efficient band from the keyboard, and got under the skin of this energetic and fun musical score. The tempi throughout were very good with as much sensitivity in the slower numbers as there was attack in the rock numbers. The on-stage singers didn't always finish on exactly the same beat as the band, but they were generally good at their harmonies, and sang with great enthusiasm. "Footloose", "I Need A Hero", "Let's Hear it for the Boy" were all very strong numbers, but the absolute show-stopper was the amalgamation of comedy, harmony and musicality that was "Mama Says".

The composite set, with its bridge at the rear, if not a work of art, was at least functional and practical, and with a good amount of well-sourced props and furniture, was sufficient to suggest the locations of the various scenes, and stage manager, Marie Brown, kept things going at a good pace with efficient scene changes. The members of the cast also contributed well to carry bits and pieces on and off the stage.

While the lighting was always colourful, and with some nice disco effects, it really did need to be a bit more specific with cueing. It was somewhat random, and some of the more emotional scenes would have benefitted from having smaller areas, atmospherically lit. The sound quality was very acceptable, with all lyrics clearly audible over the rock score. Costumes were well-selected, with a good distinction between Ren and the country bumpkins, and a lovely display of checked shirts and country dresses at the Bar-B-Que/Barn Dance. The adults were all suitably attired, and the change in Ariel from obedient church-goes to party girl was excellent. Hair-styles were funky and appropriate and make-up was fine throughout.

It's always nice to welcome a new Musical Society under the umbrella of AIMS, joining the 120+ societies who are bound together through a mutual love of Musical Theatre. With this production, by St Patrick's Hall Musical Society, Strabane, the positives heavily out-numbered the negatives, and I am absolutely certain that AIMS will be all the richer in the future for the involvement of this vibrant and exciting young company. Thank you so much for a very enjoyable experience, and I wish you great success with your future projects.

With so many ultra-modern productions of this show tending to be the trend, it was refreshing that Director, Liam Butler, chose to go down the more traditional route, and it was a good decision. With the costumes of the era, there was a much elevated sense of the history of the biblical epic. Played against a quite stunning set, I felt that much more could have been done, particularly in the more dramatic second act, to enhance the set with dynamic lighting, which was initially very good and atmospheric, but seemed to wain as the show progressed. With a very good cast at his disposal, Liam achieved some very strong moments of drama, but there were times when the involvement of the chorus seemed somewhat pedestrian. There wasn't enough joy and celebration as Jesus entered the square amid a profusion of palms, and the market place, despite some excellent work from the ribboned dancers, lacked a feeling of debauchery and corruption. Jesus' interruption of that scene needed much more drama and ferocity. The crowd also needed to be much more threatening to Pilate as he tried to determine how to deal with Jesus. More imagination was needed when carting Jesus from Caiaphas to Pilate to Herod and back to Pilate and when he was being beaten by the guards in slow motion, a more emphatic lighting effect would have enhanced the drama.

When the dancers were given their (all too rare) opportunities to shine, they proved themselves to be well-disciplined and energetic, and they did justice to some very effective choreography from Aisling Rountree. "Jesus Christ Superstar" was the highlight of the terpsichorean display, but there was good work too in Herod's Song and in the Market Place. I'd have liked the good tempos of "What's The Buzz" and "Christ, you know I love you" to be given a bit more expression through movement, as they tended to be a tad "stand around and mingle", but as stated, what choreography was permitted, was most attractive.

Aiden McCluskey cut a fine figure in the role of Jesus, and despite it being his first major on-stage role, he used his concert and band experience to exude a certain confidence and charisma in his acting. Vocally, there was very good quality in his lower range, but much of the score sat above his comfort zone, which resulted in several optional lower notes, and occasionally a falsetto that sounded a tad shrill and strained.

Sinead Butler brought a fine vocal quality and a warmth of character to the role of Mary Magdalene. "I Don't Know How To Love Him" was full of emotion, and the "Could We Start Again Please" duet with Peter was particularly moving.

In the narrative role of Judas, Kevin Fagan dominated the stage from the first moment to the last, relaxed and comfortable with the demands of the role, both dramatically and especially vocally. Here was a voice that is full of sublime musicality, a superb range, an amazing falsetto and capable of expressing the widest range of emotion in song. This was an outstanding performance.

Sean Flanagan had a beautiful calm in his expression of "Pilate's Dream", and then displayed a commanding presence in his early encounter with Jesus. The performance was rounded off with a very believable reluctance and lack of understanding as he eventually washed his hands of Jesus. Nicely played.

The casual, flippancy of Herod was very effectively captured by Colin Flynn, who made a strong impact with "Herod's Song" without having to resort to high camp or over-theatrical devices. Very well delivered.

There was a good superiority about Ian Rountree's Caiaphas, which balanced very well beside the more snide and aggressive nastiness of John Husband's Annas. The two worked very well together, and were ably supported by Barry Murray and Vincent Russell as the other high priests. The four performed their vocals with comfort and confidence.

Ultan Ó Cinnéide, as Peter, gave a nice vocal tone and quality to the "Could We Start Again Please" duet, and was believably frightened when confronted as an acquaintance of Jesus. Craig Regan, as Simon, led the vocal to "Poor Jerusalem" with confidence.

The chorus generally functioned very well, adding ambience to their scenes, but I did feel that they needed to be more fiery and vitriolic in the trial scenes.

Both principals and chorus were secure and well-rehearsed in their music, and well done to Chorus Director, Helen McHugh for the clear harmonies and diction. But as with the occasional pedestrian pace of the production, I felt that this was more of a "Middle-of-the-road" opera than a "Rock" opera, as the orchestra, under Musical Director, Paul Byrne, seemed a little too laid back to give the show its strong, pulsating, rock feel. There were no wrong notes and no lack of musicianship from Paul or his players, and the pace was fine for most of the songs, but the 'feel' just seemed to lack energy.

The set for the show was absolutely beautiful, both in construction and in visual impact, capturing the location perfectly. I therefore found it somewhat frustrating that technically, it was let down by a lighting plot that showed so much promise in the early scenes and then seemed to run out of steam in the most dramatic scenes. There was good use of colour and good focus to the smaller areas in act one, and the lightening flash effect in the whipping scene was quite inventive, but the hanging of Judas and the crucifixion of Jesus were underwhelming and somewhat bland. The standstill finale wasn't specific enough to work effectively. There was little for stage manager, Tracy Fitzsimons, to be concerned about as there were very few moving pieces, but the cast members who erected the cross were obviously well tutored and rehearsed. There were just enough appropriate props to meet the needs of the production. There were no problems with sound quality.

In a very traditional style, the show was beautifully costumed, and when required, there was a nice flamboyance about the "special" costumes, i.e. for Herod's Song and particularly the excellent and unusual black costumes for "Jesus Christ Superstar". Hairstyles, facial hair and make-up were all very good and appropriate.

A strong production team and a dedicated company have resulted in a production that, while I felt it needed an injection of energy at times, was nevertheless beautifully presented and most competently delivered. Thank you too all concerned for a very enjoyable night.

"Come along and listen to the lullaby of Broadway". That's exactly what we got from St Agnes' Choral Society. A pure unadulterated showbiz dream that would not look out of place on the The Great White Way itself. The costumes were glorious. There were stunning set pieces. And the dancing was unbelievable. When I go to the theatre, I want to feel something; happiness, sadness, pity, fear, shock or awe. How did I feel at this production of 42nd Street? Drop your jaw. Take a sharp intake of breath through your mouth. And stay like that for as long as you can. That's how I felt watching the choral numbers in this show.

There was very good story-telling by this director, all framed in a wonderful aesthetic. Knowing when to leave the stage sparse and when to fill it full of business, Director Laura Kerr did a wonderful job at assembling this show. The business in the opening scene, such as the work happening around the piano, the men on ladders, or the seamstresses toiling in the background brought realism, enhancing the frantic nature of a rehearsal room.  How the dance rehearsal went on behind the dressing room scene is another example of knowing when to bring the staging of a scene to its maximum potential. From the poignancy of 'About a Quarter to Nine' to the comedy of 'Shuffle Off to Buffalo' to the touching final moments between Peggy and Mr Marsh was nicely measured, expertly bringing us up and down as the narrative unfolded. The lighting trick in Dorothy's shadow- dancing was amazing, enhanced by little touches, such as the making of the birdie- shaped silhouettes. The bows were an exciting moment in themselves, with the choral girls coming down the steps and then making room for the principals to come down thereafter.

Superb musical direction was provided by Wilson Shields, who conducted an orchestra of thirteen musicians. Principal singing, overall, was excellent. The use of a pit supported the fact that levels were always appropriate and the singers on stage were never over-powered, in part thanks to the great job on sound by MK Audio. The harmonies shone through excellently well, such was the balance ensured by the sound desk. The choral work was awesome, with particular mention of the final amazing chord in 'Getting Out of Town'. Harmonies from the girls during 'Shadow Waltz' deserve a special mention also. Not everyone came off the final note of 'Dames' at the same moment, but this was the only slip-up on a night where the music was just as good as the dancing, ensuring a memorable experience.

What a job Ann Marie Morgan did on the choreography for this production; full of showgirls with feathers and tap dancing to melt your face off. The grouping in the opening number worked brilliantly. I love when props (by Maeve Gillen) are used in routines, as they so often enhance the narrative and meaning of the song and add super variety to the show. The suitcases in 'Getting Out of Town' worked great in this context and the final picture was awesome here. The ladies' tapping moves under the café table were really cool and the five male tapping waiters added even more to this moment. The giant silhouette dancing was special, and the line of female dancers did great work here. 'We're in the Money' was pure showbiz heaven, as the troupe danced on giant coins. The 'Lullaby on Broadway' routine bounced off the stage. The four couples dancing in '42nd Street' were awesome. The final routine on the steps needed to be seen to be believed. The way in which they went up the steps, row by row of dancers, was breath-taking. The dancing in this show was seriously intense. This society should release a fitness DVD.

Everyone looked smashing. Costumes were designed by Elizabeth Dennis and supplied by UK Productions Ltd. These high quality, professional costumes were overseen by a large group of wardrobe personnel, ensuring lovely colour and textures throughout the scenes. The shorts on the girls for their rehearsal moments were perfectly "of-the-time". There was great attention to detail, like how the girls all wore hats to the café on their break from rehearsals. Later on, the white pyjamas on Peggy's supportive friends before showtime would continue this attention to detail and ensure that their final costumes were not revealed too soon. The purple on Billy and Dorothy was lovely. It was amazing how the cast changed to white top hats, tails and canes for the mirror dance. The gowns on those not dancing, who came through the doors of the nightclub, looked fabulous. The coin theme was cleverly repeated in the hats for 'We're in the Money'. Annie's slutty showgirl wedding dress looked great. The various groups of costumes in '42nd Street' were just wow. Make-up design by Lisa Cunningham Black and the million wigs supplied by The Wig Centre UK ensured no stone was left unturned in this very professional show.

There is an extraordinary number of sets required for this show and so many aspects of the visual were jaw-dropping. This was no small job for Stage Manager Clare Donnelly, who ensured the whole thing ran like clock-work. While I acknowledge that money doesn't grow on trees, however, some of the backdrops were a little 2D in their presentation. While they were well- printed, and I should probably be telling myself that in the theatre we suspend disbelief, they did not create the same realism that the quality costumes did. I wonder, considering that the show is set on a stage, could the actual environment of the theatre have been used more, with some smaller 3D set pieces employed to denote the differences when they go out of town etc? I am being very picky here in this visual delight of a show, but this was the only aspect of the production that differed from a fully professional West End version and I hope that is viewed as an enormous compliment. The "Maison de Dames" backdrop worked perfectly, however, because there was a performative/theatrical context for this. The giant mirror that reflected the dance taking place on the stage floor was incredible - an example of how the society went so far in ensuring an exciting aesthetic for their audience. The nightclub backdrop was fabulous, complemented by the red tablecloths, gold chairs, piano and chaise. The enormous gold coin in the centre of a series of individual coins, on which 'We're in the Money' was performed was fantastic. The 'Pretty Lady' gauze was cool. That star-cloth at the end… those giant steps at the end… (Imagine an Italian is placing his fingertips to his lips to blow a kiss).

Lighting designed and operated was by ACK Productions added wonderfully to the overall fabulous aesthetic. The gobo on the that gorgeous red and gold curtain was lovely. The music was punctuated really well, such as when those lovely pinks and purples came in during 'Young and Healthy' or on the final moment of 'We're in the Money'. The memorable gigantic silhouette effect created for Dorothy Brockman's interpretative dance was fantastic and the final lighting moment was awesome here also. The spotlight on Peggy, as she was putting on her robe after 'Lullaby of Broadway', was excellent at drawing our eye to this moment and allowing for the dressing room to be set up. The isolation on the dressing room thereafter was lovely. Brilliant Broadway signs flew in at the end and then lit up. The actress playing Peggy Sawyer must be a triple threat; able to sing, dance and act in spades. Lorraine Jackson Brown as the leading lady did not disappoint. She invoked a lovable girl who wanted to fight for her dreams, while nervous and unsure of her own potential. Lorraine was simply lovely, with an endearing physicality to her movements. She was hilarious in those panicked last-minute rehearsals before she opened as the lead in 'Pretty Lady'. An all-round gorgeous performance. John Lindop as Julian Marsh gave us a man with the weight of the world on his shoulders. He was gruff in the beginning, hugely pressurised by his loses in the Wall Street crash. He barked his orders at those around him and was dismissive of Peggy, evoking the harsh realism of the pressures of showbiz that the younger kids don't think about so much. With a naturalism to his acting, his character had a no- nonsense approach. But he softened, however, when he realised that he needed to inspire Peggy to return to the show and his final moments were touching.

Michelle Hannaway as Dorothy Brock captured the somewhat past-it, yet gloriously difficult, diva who is famed for her rubbish dancing. She started out as selfish and mean but showed nice character development as her broken ankle made her reflect on her career, resulting in her giving Peggy some well- meant advice. Michelle showed off a powerful voice. Her inaccurate kicking in her dance routines was comical, yet the sadness she portrayed in 'About a quarter to nine' was touching, as she demonstrates to her younger replacement how to effectively take over from her. This duet with Lorraine was lovely.

Gareth McCreevy had wonderful ownership of the stage as Billy Lawlor, the leading tenor of the show within the show. He demonstrated a great speaking voice and his final note on 'I Know Now' was awesome. He danced his brains out, which was hugely impressive. Billy must also be a triple threat and Gareth was able to deliver in spades as well, ensuring a quality performance.

Fiona Keegan gave us a cheerful Maggie Jones, writer of the show-within-the-show who has much wisdom to pass on to the showgirls. She had a very good "broad" New York accent. There is no denying her awesome voice. Her joke that musicians should be kept in a pit was a hoot.

She was joined by Peter Burke as Bert Barry, the other writer of the show, who also appears in this show he is producing. He was hilarious with Anytime Annie in their comical marriage sequence in 'Shuffle off to Buffalo'. He and Fiona made a great team.

Aideen Fox as Ann Reilly (Anytime Annie) had some excellent comedy moments such as when she said "Anytime, Mr Marsh" at the top of Act Two. She is an excellent dancer. Her counterparts, played by Helen Smyth as Phyllis Dale and Cherelle Hinds as Lorraine Fleming were nicely supportive of Peggy, taking her under their wing and showing her the ropes. These gals were all fantastic. We got such an incredible dancer in Timmy Bell as Andy, the choreographer of the show-within-the-show. He socked the dance numbers to the audience in a high energy, exciting and impressive performance.

Jim McGuigan was great as Abner Dillon, Dorothy's Sugar Daddy from Texas, who is responsible for keeping her in the show because of his financial backing. The poor soul doesn't realise that she is with him for his money. He had a characterful voice, all old and southern and invoked his character with lovely convincibility. Tony Young as Pat Denning (the former vaudeville partner of diva Dorothy who is now her true lover) did very well as the man who is often side-lined by his love when she must put her career or her Sugar Daddy first. He also had a great accent. James McConnell appeared as Oscar, the onstage rehearsal pianist for the show- within-the-show, who also appeared in the nightclub scene. It was special to have a real piano player on stage for these moments, providing lovely authenticity to proceedings. Adrian Egan as Stage Manager Mac had all the authority and presence required for this role, which requires seriousness in a group of bonkers showbiz types. Other quality cameos were provided by Tom O'Kelly as Frankie/ Stagehand, Maeve McLoughlin as Diane Lorimer, Sean O'Neill and David Price as the Thugs, Stephen McQuillan as the Doctor, James Hyde as the Waiter and Felicity Rooney as the Thief.

The Riverbank Arts Centre in Newbridge was the perfect venue for The Odd Theatre Company's production of Rent. The venue has an intimate quality which really added to the enjoyment of the production. This is a show which is set in New York in the late 1980s and is overshadowed by the HIV/AIDS epidemic that was ravaging the city at the time. It is loosely based on La Boheme and revolves around the loves and losses of a group of artistic friends living in East Village, Manhattan. The show has a rollercoaster of emotions involved in it as there is much humour in the lyrics but there are also moments of tragic loss and sadness. Both aspects must appear genuine or the audience loses the impact of the story. Direction was in the hands of Cian O'Dowd who also performed in the show and was stage manager! Quite an undertaking for such a young director. The direction was taken at quite a pace but there were moments when we paused and enjoyed some beautiful singing such as 'Seasons of Love', 'Light My Candle' and 'Will I?'

Cian chose to use one set for the show. This comprised a graffitied wall at the back of the stage and a set of steps onto a platform stage right. There were two rather large tables which dominated the stage slightly and multi-coloured chairs which could be moved to create different venues. At times I felt that the furniture slightly got in the way of the action on stage.

Cian gathered together a very talented and mostly experienced cast. He obviously inspired them, as they all worked together extremely well and supported each other on stage.

One thing he could have a look at in future is how individual numbers are finished on stage. I feel that each one should have punctuation at the end so the audience knows that moment is now over. This was generally a sound and moving piece of direction, well done Cian.

Niall Mulpeter was the musical director for the show and showed a great ability to control the orchestra and balance the sound from the pit with the singing from the stage. This has been a gripe of mine for a while as in this particular show the story is told in song and to miss any words would be to miss the story. I did not miss a syllable in the show. This was very refreshing. As it turned out from further inspection the orchestra consisted of four players who were positioned backstage and linked up with the cast by video projection. This seemed to work really well for the show and the cueing and tempi of the songs was very good throughout. There were times when the accompaniment was very minimal. It was nice to have that contrast with the rock moments which really blasted and brought the house down.

Although there is very little formal dancing in the show I was looking also at the general movement that was involved. Choreographer Áine Foley gave a very naturalistic touch to the choreography. It seemed that at times the cast had been given free rein to be inventive with their own movements. This created a spontaneous feel to the show. I did like all the set pieces including the wonderful 'Tango Maureen'. The cast moved well and used the acting areas effectively. There was a lovely bit of 'tableography' for the 'La Vie Boheme' number, which was very clever and performed with such accuracy by the cast. This was when they were sitting at the table and were doing moves such as slapping the table, linking arms, putting their hands above their heads but all done at a great speed and with perfect timing.

Daniel Ryan played Mark Cohen. He is an up-and-coming filmmaker and his use of the camera pin points the events of the story, giving his audience a focus. Daniel has a beautiful tone to his singing voice and his acting was good too. He worked well with Roger and they seemed very comfortable together on stage. Chris Corroon played Roger who is the rock star with, as he put it, baggage. He is HIV positive and his girlfriend has committed suicide when she finds out that she was also. He begins a love affair with the beautiful young Mimi. There are some wonderful moments of tenderness between the two and also moments of extreme frustration when Roger can't quite tell her all about himself and how he feels about her. He is trying to protect her but in doing so chases her away. Chris made this part his own. He has a beautiful singing voice: rocky and emotional. He looked the part and he acted the part. This was a very moving portrayal. Mimi played by Seana Stenson worked really well with Roger. Seana is a beautiful mover on stage and we were always fascinated by her. She was exotic; she was frightened, she was angry. She portrayed all these emotions beautifully. When we thought she had died in the second act, we were all devastated and there were people crying in the auditorium. She sang with conviction and I particularly liked the moments of gentleness that she had when singing duets with Roger. Tom Collins is a gay activist in the show and was played by John Conroy with great conviction and style. He meets and falls in love with the transvestite, Angel, who helps him when he has been attacked. It is an unlikely match, but such is life. The initial attraction between them was electrifying. John played the part really well especially when Angel was being consumed by AIDS and he was attending to his lover in his final hours. This was very moving. John has a beautiful rich singing voice which he used to great effect throughout the show. Gerard Lyons had the difficult task of playing Angel who is the transvestite in the story. We meet Angel first of all in the guise of a man and then meet her again in the persona of the female Angel. Gerard seemed more comfortable in the former role rather than the latter role. I was impressed by the potential that Gerard has for musical theatre. He has a most unusual, stunning tone to his singing voice which was used to best effect in the number 'Contact'. When his confidence grows and he begins to relate a little more to his audience I am sure he will be a great asset to any musical theatre company. Maureen is a fascinating character for any actor to play and it was played brilliantly by Jessica Adamson. She was able to create the wacky stand-up character very well and we were all blown away by her rendition of 'Over the Moon' which was so physical, so funny and so successful. She has a great ability to relate to her audience and she has a wonderful singing voice. Those eyes were just so involving. Her partner Joanne was played by Keelin Kilduff. Keelin has a fantastic singing voice and she could reach heights that other singers might dream of. Again, she related well to the audience and we instantly became involved with her life. This was a good all-round performance. Cian O'Dowd not only directed, stage managed but also played the part of Benjamin in the show. He is the ambitious friend who owns the building in which the story is set. He also is in love with Mimi and at one stage tries to buy her love. This was a solid performance. Cian has a very pleasant singing voice and the voices of the three men blended very well together. Other players were not just chorus members each person had a part to play in the show and each person played it extremely well. I particularly liked Emma Kilduff as Alexi. Her sense of comic timing was brilliant.

The show's setting was adequate, with a graffitied wall covered in rock posters to give us the idea of Roger's profession, a functioning doorway and a platform raised at the back of the stage with a staircase leading up to it. As I have said before, there were two large tables on stage. These were at times used well as they became a bed, a sofa, and the tables in the restaurant but maybe smaller ones would have sufficed. I walked the stage after the show and there was very little space so hats off cast for how well you moved around it. The lighting was generally a little dull for my liking and that was a pity because there were wonderful moments on stage which would have benefited from a stronger pool of light to give focus to what was going on. The sound was well-balanced and each person's words could be heard loud and clear. Well done Connor Wilkins for that. The properties were of the correct time and all looked authentic. Make-up and hair were fine but it would have been nice to see a little more of a nod to the late 1980s in design. The costumes too were adequate but again it might have been nice to try and create the 1980s look. Either that or do the whole thing in just black t-shirts and black trousers.

Overall this was a good production which was thoroughly enjoyed by the full house on Saturday night, so much so that there was an instant standing ovation which went on for several minutes. This was thoroughly deserved as the heart of the show was extremely good and moved us to the core. It is hard to believe that what was then seen as the 'gay plague' has now been tamed but it is important to know what journey we had to come through to get to that point and remember those who didn't make that journey.

Many thanks to all at the Riverbank Arts Centre for your warm welcome.

show_raw: The 25Th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee
review_text:
Written in 2005, 'The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee' is a musical comedy in one act. A diverse group of six geeky adolescents, all played by adults, compete for the Putnam County spelling championship. They spell their way through a series of words, hoping never to hear the "ding" of the bell that signals a spelling mistake. But, hey, at least the losers get a juice box!

As we entered the Astra Hall, which was decked out like an American High School Gymnasium, we were greeted by Rona Lisa Peretti (Anna Bergin) - moderator of the Bee. So, straight away the fourth wall was broken and we were endowed with a collective character, that of spectators of the Bee and not audience to a musical. This was a clever device that worked really well later on.

The band, set at stage left, was tuning up and there was a palpable sense of excitement in the audience. This was the second performance of the show for UCD Musical Society and it was a packed house. The audience consisted of 80% students, with a few proud Moms and Dads and younger siblings of the actors in attendance.

To kick things off, each character came on and introduced themselves in song. Anna Bergin, as moderator Rona, immediately impressed with a fine soprano voice. We met Chip Tolentino (Morgan Moore) last year's winner, dressed as a boy scout, Logainne Schwartzandgrubenierre (Louise O'Connor), the youngest competitor with Pippi Longstocking pigtails and irritatingly high voice, Leaf Coneybear (Peter Richardson) with Superman cape and dungarees, William Barfée (James Bergin), whose name is mispronounced constantly during the show, Marcy Park (Lauren Dooley), who has just transferred from another school and Olive Ostrovsky (Niamh McGowan) with her massive glasses.

Each performer sang well in the opening number 'The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee' and we got a sense of their characters. They all played considerably younger (12 - 14yrs), it was written for adults to play children, but this did grate a bit during the show as sometimes they played it too young.

However, that was not all of the contestants, Rona called out four names to the audience. Turned out these were real audience members and they were invited up on stage to participate. Strangely, she only chose men on the night I attended, however I'm informed that it varies considerably from performance to performance. The four were suitably game and when called up to spell, they initially got easy words. The words became progressively more difficult in order to clear the stage of the non-actors.

We then met Vice Principal Douglas Panch (Malachy Conlon) who had a sinister past he would not discuss. Panch called out the words and when asked to place them in a sentence created very funny juxtapositions "Spell phylactery." "Can you put that in a sentence?" "Billy put down that phylactery - we're Episcopalian." The final character was Mitch Mahoney (Pádraic O'Brolcáin), the school counselor.

The band led by Musical Director, William Le Bas, consisted of Piano, Synth, Flute Alto Sax and Clarinet, Cello, Drums & Percussion. They were very tight but the balance was a bit too much to the audience right as that was where they were placed. Sound design and engineering was un- credited and whilst the cast was well mic'ed and sounded great the band was at times overwhelming.

Choreography by Mairead Bond, was simple as befitting the style of the show and mostly culled from other productions. There was a great slo-mo section, which worked very well, mostly thanks to Malachy Conlon's accompanying slowed down vocal.

Lighting design by Camille Lombard, was a bit hit and miss, the cross fades were a bit sudden and operation seemed to be improvised. The three par cans utilised as house lights were too bright and flattened the visuals. Set was simple, some steps, a table and a few pennants and flags attached to a red tab. A nice touch was the pyramid of large kindergarten style lettered building blocks up stage left, some of which were internally lit.

Stage management by Eoghan Walsh was relatively easy on this show, I suspect as once it starts it doesn't really stop as we are in the same location and it's mostly in real time. However all actors seemed to have everything they needed when they needed it. Costumes and props by Kelly Nic Chumascaigh, were perfect for the characters and added to their 'youth'. The props were functional and suitable.

Anna Bergin as Rona, is a fabulous vocalist, her work on all of the numbers was splendid. She controlled the whole show like a cross between a presenter and a judge. Her delivery of seemingly improvised comments on the audience spellers was perfectly insouciant. She also played Olive's mother with great internal emotion.

Malachy Conlon played V.P. Douglas Panch with an exquisite inner energy. His deadpan delivery of the words and their meanings was perfect and his comic timing excellent.

As Mitch Mahoney, Pádraic O'Brolcáin was well cast. Looking like an undercover cop, his looming presence was counterpointed by his character's obvious care for the contestants, hugging and kissing them when they failed. He also played Olive's Dad and at one point, a highly irreverent but hilarious Jesus tied to a huge cross. The six contestants were very individual. Clearly, much work went into their characterisations. Director, Ruairi Nicholl, ensured that his cast was constantly alert, in character and responding to every situation.

Morgan Moore played Chip Tolentino, a boy scout who won last year's Bee. Mr Moore played him as a nervous but likable lothario as he fantasises about Leaf's sister, Marigold who is presumably in the audience. His song 'My Unfortunate Erection' during the 'Snack Break' is a highlight of the show. He also played one of Logainne's Dads in a delightful vingnette.

Logainne Schwartzandgrubenierre as played by Louise O'Connor, the youngest competitor and spoke with a superbly delivered lisp. Her vocal was strangely off key at times, but I suspect it was deliberate. Ms O'Connor was perfectly cast in the role.

Leaf Coneybear was played by Peter Richardson and he stole the audience's hearts with a beautiful performance full of childlike vulnerability.  His vocal was patchy at times but full of character. Mr Richardson also hilariously played the other of Logainne's Dads.

James Bergin played William Barfée as a repulsive, nose picking, irritatingly clever, know all. (That's a compliment!). His characterisation was brilliant. From the 'interesting' choreography with his 'Magic Foot' to his sweet puppy love scene with Olive, Mr Bergin embodied William Barfée. Marcy Park, who speaks six languages, was well played by Lauren Dooley. Ms Dooley played the piano at one point and her scene with Jesus was skilfully timed. Her portrayal of Marcy, the poster child of the Over Achievers was excellent, particularly when she decided to purposely fail.

Niamh McGowan delivered a near perfect performance as Olive Ostrovsky. She was the youngest looking actor and she radiated youth and a shy energy. Ms McGowan depicted Olive's journey from introverted, over looked child to self- reliant teen remarkably well. Her singing on 'The I love You Song', was the finest vocal of the evening. Outstanding work. "The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee" is a quirky little musical. It's funny, has a few good songs, a great script and was a perfect choice for the Society who gave it a very 'syzygy' production. UCD Musical Society is a group who know who their audience is and what they want and are experienced and talented enough to give it to them, and more.

This lively and energetic musical is not all hairspray and bubble gum. Underneath its glossy coiffed exterior there are themes of fat-shaming, racism and discrimination. It is a show full of the joy of life but the sadness of being not accepted. It therefore needs to be handled with care on both these levels. Set in 1960s Baltimore our hero Tracy Turnblad takes us through her own personal journey of acceptance and reveals other discrimination, especially at the local TV station where black people are not allowed on the show except on the monthly 'Negro Day'. Tracy rallies her friends to protest and change how they are treated.

I was made most welcome at the Scouts' Hall in Nenagh and was so pleased to meet the team who created such a good production of Hairspray.

Stephanie Browne directed the show and choreographed it too, with style and great attention to detail. The young cast were obviously very well-rehearsed and also enjoyed every moment on stage.

Stephanie chose an excellent cast of leading players who were backed up by an enthusiastic and talented chorus. They were always involved in the action on stage.

She created, with the help of producer Greg Browne, an interesting and innovative setting for the show with two stage extensions which were used to good effect throughout the show.

I had concerns as to how the Afro Americans would be portrayed in the show. Stephanie decided that she would use a darker base for their make-up and added touches such as black tights and black shoes. This created the difference between the two groups without being offensive. The show had a great sense of energy and pace throughout, giving us as the audience a roller-coaster of fun and reflection.

The musical director William Cullagh created some wonderful moments with his nine-piece orchestra. There was a great sense of the era in the playing. The sound cues were all very good and the pace of the show musically was excellent. The individual singers sang with confidence and emotion throughout the show and there were some amazing voices on the stage. Occasionally the sound of the orchestra was a little loud and we could not hear all the words sung by the principals which was a pity.

Stephanie's choreography was slick and reflected the time in which the show was set. All the cast and chorus looked comfortable with their movements and the routines were delivered with verve and gusto. There were some very talented dancers on the stage who were supported by a well-rehearsed chorus. Nice to see boy dancers who can really dance and can work with their partners to produce beautiful patterns and routines. The duets and group numbers were moved very well throughout the show. The 'You Can't Stop the Beat' number as a real show-stopper with the audience clapping along and most of us wanting to join in.

Jayde Ryan was an excellent Tracy Turnblad. She looked right, she sounded right and she moved and acted the part excellently. The audience liked her from our first meeting in 'Good Morning Baltimore'. Edna, her mother, played by Colin Dillon was a real source of humour throughout the show. Although not feminised too much, Colin played the part with excellent comic timing and his 'Timeless to Me' duet caused great hilarity. Lara Smyth played Velma, the scheming TV producer, with all the charm of a rattlesnake which was perfect for the role. She appeared older than her years, sang well and moved elegantly round the stage. The smarmy ever popular TV presenter Corny was played by Shane Killilea-Curran with the style of the stars of the time. One of the highlights of the show was the performance of Caroline Browne as Motormouth Maybelle. She had real stage presence, a wonderful singing voice and knew how to move around a stage to perfection. Her 'Big Blonde and Beautiful' number got a huge round of applause from the audience. Calvin Coleman charmed us with his performance as Link. He was always in character and made a lot out of his role. Tracy's friend Penny is a part which is sometimes not made the most of. Not so in this show as Joanne McDonnell was able to get every laugh out of the script. This was an intelligent and endearing performance. Velma's daughter Amber was played by Megan Maher. She is the ambitious over-indulged child who is determined to win her slot on the TV programme. Megan gave us a really good portrayal of this role. Wilbur who is Tracy's father was gently played by Jack McGrath. It was not until his big number with Edna that we realised what comic ability Jack had. He and Edna worked together so well and gave us so many laughs. Justin Heaney who played Seaweed gave us just the right amount of swagger and attitude. He moved well, always keeping the Afro-American feel in his movements. There were lots of other roles in the show such as Rachel Brown as Prudy Pingleton who gave us a frightening mother to Penny. Other roles such as Little Inez was played by Indya Higgins with style and commitment. Ciara Sherlock was the prison matron who really rattled our cages. Dillon Noonan-Kelly was beautifully dressed as Mr Pinky and Liam Daly was a cut throat business man as Harriman F Spritzer. The Dynamites were wonderful to look at in their purple sparkly dresses and they danced and sang with real Supremes' charm.

I was very impressed by the chorus in the show as they had a large part to play in its success. They sang and danced well but they also were able to listen to what was going on around them, which focused our attention onto the main action on stage. The set itself was a bit of a masterpiece. As I have said there was use of LED lighting around the proscenium arch but on stage there were banks of television sets. Each one had a colour changing screen so that the atmosphere on stage could be altered at the press of a button. This was very effective. At the back of the stage projections such as rooms, walls and patterns were shown, creating scenes very quickly. Larger pieces of scenery were wheeled into place by a very experienced stage team. These were items which were well made and well painted, such as the Har de Har shop counter and the large can of hairspray which had smoke coming out from the nozzle. The lighting on stage was usually of a very good standard with very few dead areas and was excellently cued. The microphones worked very well and on most occasions the sound was excellent with a well-balanced tone, though at times it was difficult to make out the words being sung during some of the songs as the orchestra appeared to be a little loud. The show looked beautiful and one of the reasons was the wonderful costumes on stage. These were well chosen, beautiful colours and all fitted the cast very well. I was impressed by the attention to detail, for example in the choice of shoes: the boys all wore black patent shoes when they wore their white and black suits. The girls' shoes were all the same type and matched their costumes which were beautiful. There was a range of pastel colours used for both the boys and the girls. Mr Pinky's outfit was stunning as were the outfits worn by the Dynamites, who wowed us with their purple sparkly outfits. The makeup was right for the era and the Afro-American cast who had a darker base make-up had darkened eyebrows and heavier eyeliner. This looked effective without being offensive. The wigs were generally very good though I still think that we could have had even more exaggerated beehives.

There were a great many people helping with the show. There was a team of very enthusiastic folk working in front of house. They made everyone so welcome and helped to create the real buzz before the show began. Nenagh Choral Society Ltd is a very family friendly group and it is obvious that the older members really want to support the up-and-coming younger members. This is a wonderful ethos and in no small way a reason why this show was such a success.

The Helix is a wonderful modern theatre in leafy Dublin City University. It has a large front of house area with a bar and coffee shop and tucked away in a corner, a small tuck-shop. Having directed and lit a show there a few years ago, I can attest to the excellence of the staff and the facilities. I arrived to see 'Legally Blonde', which I had seen a number of years earlier on the West End, and was greeted by the venue's manager and the company's Front of House Manager. Both made me feel most welcome.

The original 'Legally Blonde - The Musical' has been described as "high- energy, empty-calories, and expensive- looking hymn to the glories of girlishness", an "ingratiating trifle" and "it should be entitled 'Irredeemably Bland'". It is true that the plot is not exactly Shakespearean in its' complexity (girl loves boy, girl loses boy, boy wants girl back, girl has moved on) nor are the characters anything more than two-dimensional. However, one knows this in advance of attending and indeed, I would argue that this is part of its charm.

Based on the book and MGM film, 'Legally Blonde' is about the lovelorn Elle Woods whose boyfriend, Warner, dumps her and attends Harvard. Elle follows him to college and whilst there grows up, gets an education and ultimately finds her true vocation whilst staying true to herself. She also falls in love again.

Sean Gilligan's production was fairly slick. The set, designed by Mr Gilligan, was cleverly rendered through projections of images, designs, text and colour onto various drapes, which were flown in and a solid twin stair-cased platform set upstage. A door truck was on and off for various scenes and served as a great entrance and exit for different locations. Unfortunately, on the night I saw the production, opening night, the cast and crew seemed to be still getting to grips with the scene changes, but this didn't take from the overall pace of the piece. This was all lit well by Damo O'Connor, there were a few glitches but nothing serious. The house light preset included two very bright lanterns, with pink beams, shining into the audience. The tab warmers were in the shape of a heart. All very appropriate, given the nature of the show. The crisp and clear sound was by Vinny Osborne, again very professionally done, a little bit of feedback and mic drops here and there but nothing to spoil the night.

Superb Musical Direction by David Hayes who conducted a reasonably large orchestra, strangely there was no band credits in the programme so I can't comment on individuals, and a large chorus from the pit. His direction was precise and on-target, eliciting impressive harmonies particularly from the 'Delta Nu' ensemble on 'Omigod You Guys' and the Greek Chorus on 'So Much Better', which opened and closed the first act. The choreography, credits were shared by Aoibheann Cooke and Sean Gilligan assisted by Rebekah Byrne, varied from huge high-stepping parade like numbers like 'What You Want' to concise routines like 'Gay or European' was suitably Broadway in its scale as it should be as it is predominantly a dance-driven show. The dancers were well drilled, effortlessly segueing from one style to another, hip-hop to dance exercise videos to Riverdance, but again it was the 'Delta Nu' ensemble who really excelled here, their characters shining out through the complicated routines. 'Bend and Snap' was particularly memorable as was 'Positive', where they really gelled as an ensemble.

Hair and Make-up by Ali Murphy and Sinead Judd was suitable and varied enough to show individual character. Costuming by Sparkle Costumes was absolutely perfect; from the Harvard preppy look right up to the heavenly Greek Chorus ensemble. It was flashy, full of sequins and with, of course, lots of pink. Stage management by Sarah Hall, seemed smooth enough but I would have liked the stagehands/arms dressed in black.

The success of 'Legally Blonde' rests firmly on the casting of Elle Woods. She has to be blonde, feisty, be a superb singer, good dancer and a great actor.
