Elle's journey from Marilyn M to Jackie O is peppered with cringy dialogue and cartoonish characters, so she must rise above this to make us care about her. Ciara Lyons was Elle Woods. She sang and danced faultlessly and delivered the somewhat silly dialogue with just the right amount of dramatic irony. Her voice was crystal clear, her range impressive and she displayed an inner energy and vivaciousness that burst out when required.

Her 'Delta Nu' ensemble, who were mostly her Greek Chorus, complemented her talents. Hannah Brady as Margot, Aly Coyne as Serena, Shona Carroll as Pilar and Caoimhe Donnelly as Chutney lit up the stage at each visitation. They had a wonderful grasp of their roles with impeccable singing, sensational dancing and a delicious tongue in cheek humour. Less assured was Kevin Hartnett who played Warner, he sang well on 'Serious', but struggled with the character I felt. James Deegan's Emmett was an excellent dramatic performance full of poignancy and nuance. His singing on 'Chip On My Shoulder 'was heartfelt, although the higher notes were a strain on his range. Inga Bourke Mullaney acted Vivienne to a tee. Her spat with Elle at the party scene was hilarious. Her accent and singing were a bit patchy, but she did redeem herself during the 'Legally Blonde: Remix' in the second act.

Professor Callahan was played by Sean Hendley, a confident solid performance with just the right amount of imperious sleaziness. A special mention must go to Conor Clear who played four different characters; Prof Winthrop, Carlos, Elle's Dad and the slovenly Dewey. Mr Clear's performance was a textbook example of multi-characterisation, he was funny and totally owned every scene he was in with his stage presence.

Sarah Gordon excelled as Paulette. Her characterisation, her singing, her dance and her sub-text and comic timing were a joy to watch. Marco McVey played Kyle with a beautiful swagger, which had the audience wolf-whistling. Brooke Wyndham was played by Serena Salmon. A confident assured performance, her dancing was superb, her rope skipping excellent. Of the two dogs featured, sadly we only saw Elle's dog, 'Bruiser', happily relaxed in her handbag. Paulette's dog got stage fright and refused to exit his trailer. This was a very entertaining evening; the sets, costumes, sound and performers gelled together to create a very good Legally Blonde. The absolute star of the show was Ciara Lyons, her entire performance consolidated the show under Sean Gilligan's first-class direction.

society_raw: North East Musical and Dramatic Society
review_text:
The Belvoir Studio Theatre is a 200-seat venue tucked away behind a Community Activity Centre in Belfast. A small foyer leads to a traditional end on auditorium with raked seating. This was my first visit and it took some time to find, as it was poorly signposted. Belfast Music and Drama Society (BMDS), the Society staging this outing of 'The Producers', was formed in 2015 and has produced a rake of shows, both traditional and contemporary in the last three years. They have garnered a good number of nominations and wins thus far from AIMS and have a very busy schedule for this and next year.

Mel Brook's 'The Producers', is one of my favourite musicals. The story of Max Bialystock and his quest to produce the worst show on Broadway, aided by his reluctant OCD accountant Leo Bloom, in order to keep all of the investor's money, was originally a very successful film made by Brooks in 1967. In 2001, he wrote a stage musical version, which also became a big hit. The plot is simple, the songs are catchy and the show is risqué but very, very funny.

Once inside, I joined the small audience and was treated to the 8-piece band soundchecking. They were located at audience left beside us in the auditorium. The front tabs were drawn, concealing the show to come. We could hear cast running around and whispering behind the tabs, which was quite amusing for the audience. I suspect, however, it was not intentional noise. Over the PA system, there was a selection of show tunes (Les Mis, Moulin Rouge etc.) playing as house music. I kept my coat on as the building was freezing. There were less than 50 in the audience, so we couldn't generate much warmth.

Finally the house lights dimmed and the small orchestra went into the Overture. I immediately realised that there was going to be sound issues as the balance of the music was mostly to the left, which was to be expected, as that was where they were sited. However, I assumed the front of house mix would have addressed this, but sadly it didn't. But that was just the start of the evening's audio problems. Four usherettes; Chloe Bell, Amy Blackshaw, Cherelle Hinds and Sarah McFarlane, opened the show with 'Opening Night', setting the Broadwayesque tone of the show to come. They sang and danced well, dressed in tails and tights but were dreadfully under lit. Paddy McGennity as Max sang 'The King of Broadway' well, but was let down by loud sound issues and again was in and out of shadow. The ensemble backed him up and sang really well, with complementing harmonies and, despite the small stage, good movement. The staging of the show was somewhat hampered by a very solid set, designed by Vincent Vyce, upstage consisting of two small staircases leading up to a platform, whilst downstage left and right we had two doorways which were trucked on and off. As the main set was so unyielding, it had to remain for all of the show. This compromised not only subsequent scenes but reduced the playing area available to the choreographer and ultimately the actors. The set remained dressed as Max's office throughout.

The choreography, by Alex McFarlane was good, with some lovely sequences executed by a well-rehearsed cast. It was great to see some good tap routines and these were relished by the dancers and appreciated by the audience.

Costuming was un-credited but was very germane where needed; the Third Reich brown shirts and swastika armbands gave a real sense of menace, whilst Roger DeBris's dress was very becoming! I missed the opulence and couture of the Broadway the show was lampooning though, it would have been delightful to see some glitz and glamour. Hair and make up was un-credited but worked well given the intimacy of the venue.

Sadly, much of the show was under lit by Robbie Irwin and Gary Redpath. The LED pars on stage and four or five generic profiles out front were insufficient to light what is essentially a large scale musical. A followspot was used once, that I could see, on Max as he was singing 'Along Came Bialy', but I think this was to try and isolate him as ASM's moved set, rather than as an artistic decision. There was no big difference in the look of the show once we got to the Broadway staging of 'Springtime For Hitler', which was a pity as the sumptuousness of the musical within a musical is an important plot point in the main show. That said, some of the blue states were effective. Stage Management by Andy McKnight was reasonably well achieved but we could see ASM's behind the flats, holding doors shut from the audience's gaze.

Sound by Diarmuid Rankin was not perfect by any means. To be fair to the Society, the Director, Jordan Walsh, informed me prior to the show that their Sound Engineer was taken ill and they had to hire a replacement at short notice. But I can only judge on what I heard, or didn't hear. There was a very unbalanced front mix, which meant that most of the sound came from stage right. Sometimes mics were left on when actors exited into the wings, so we could hear them speaking to each other or stage management. There were many incidents of loud electrical buzzes and crackles and pops. Ulla's mic cut out during When You Got It, Flaunt It. On the bigger ensemble numbers, it was very hard to actually hear what the cast were singing as the mix was so cacophonous.

Musical Direction was by Wilson Shields. Mr Shield's players were well rehearsed but let down by the poor sound quality. The brass were strident and had a nice big band quality at times, the violin was gentle and always present, drums and bass kept everyone in line and the reeds were earthy and subtle.  However, the sound mix did mean that the band were overwhelming at times, particularly during solos.

Max played by Paddy McGennity was an interesting casting choice, as he seemed a little young for the role. His Max was full of nervous tics and peculiar facial expressions. He had a great energy and put every ounce into his performance, and while not note perfect his singing was full of emotion, exasperation and character. Timothy Bell played Leo as an OCD ridden, lovelorn Mammy's Boy. His comic timing was excellent, his singing very good and his dancing superb. Mr Bell stole every scene he was in with subtlety and attention to character detail.

Both Karl Dawson as Roger DeBris and Matthew Watson as his live in lover, Carmen were brilliantly portrayed. Their singing was flawless and their onstage relationship hilarious.

Mr Dawson's depiction of Adolf Hitler during 'Springtime For Hitler' was sublime and a highlight of the show.

Simon Pyper as Franz and Kathryn O'Neill as Ulla did wonders with their roles and whilst neither sang brilliantly their acting was first class. Sean Harkin, who sang the opening of 'Springtime For Hitler', has a beautiful tenor voice and was another stand out. The ensemble worked very hard with multiple costume changes, difficult choreography and tricky choral work, their youth and energy drove the show.

As directed by Jordan Walsh, this production clearly lacked budget, suffered from poor production values and was possibly not a great choice of show for the society. However, the cast saved it. Their commitment, talent and sheer doggedness made it an entertaining evening. I look forward to visiting with them again.

Originally written as a stage play based on real life events in 1924 by Maurine Dallas Watkins, Chicago was turned into a musical by Bob Fosse, John Kander and Fred Ebb in the early 1970s. It has been revived many times since and became a very successful film in 2002.

Bravo Theatre Group's production was staged in a provincial hall in a small town outside of Galway, but on entering the venue we were transported back to 1920s Chicago. Set dressing was extended right out into the auditorium, where the orchestra was set up around a grand piano. Haze in place of cigarette smoke hung in the air and there was a tangible sense of seedy intemperance in the Temperance Hall.

The show opened with a charmingly played overture by the seventeen-piece orchestra under the assured musical direction of Shane Farrell. The band was confidant, vibrant and perfectly in accord. Mr Farrell conducted from the grand piano and his arrangements of the score were suitably sleazy, with the trumpets muted and the percussion hopping.

Since the film, many non-professional productions strive to imitate the look of that movie by casting Zeta Jones and Zellweger lookalikes, and Bravo's production was no exception.

Velma, played by Emily Lohan looked exactly like Catherine Zeta Jones, with her dark bobbed hair and red slash of lippy; Roxie, played by Hannah Wright was a dead ringer for Rene Zellweger with her blonde locks and surprised facial expressions. However, both actors played their parts so well, that one forgot about the movie stars and became transported away with their interpretation of the characters.

However, this lookalike casting didn't extend to Mama Morton (Jessica Bray), Billy Flynn (Michael Coen) or Amos Harte (Chris Coroon). All three performers were exceptionally well rehearsed in terms of their acting and singing and created unique interpretations of their characters. Jessica Bray had a fine commanding presence and a great jazzy vocal, her duet with Velma, 'Class', was, well… class. Michael Coen's portrayal of the shyster lawyer, Billy Flynn, was one of the best I've seen. His true phoniness was revealed brilliantly in 'All I Care About' and his duet with Roxie, 'We Both Reached for the Gun' was a stand out moment in the show. Poor Amos Hart, the true victim of the scheming shenanigans of Roxie and Flynn, was poignantly played by Chris Coroon, his 'Mister Cellophane' was charming in its simplicity.

The director, Aoife McClafferty, also choreographed the show, and whilst the ideas behind the choreography were sound enough, I'm afraid the execution left a lot to be desired. Bob Fosse, the original choreographer, created a style of dance, which is evident in Cabaret, Sweet Charity and many films of the 50s, 60s and 70s. His style, famously 'adapted' by Michael Jackson, was all about insolence, attitude and perfectly executed meticulous movements. The choreography in this production, rightly attempted to recreate some of the routines created by Fosse, but sadly, failed to live up to the exactness required. That said, some of the individual dancers did impress, notably the (un- credited) lead male in 'All That Jazz' and 'Cell Block Tango'. The choreography of the 'jury' in the courtroom scene was, whilst not sharp enough, very creative. Overall, the choreography in Chicago is all about the technique, the attitude of the performers/characters and the precision of the moves. It didn't really have that Burlesque decadence that it should. I feel that the dancers did let the choreographer and the show down a little by their lack of finesse.

Some of the choral work on this show by Shane Farrell was superb, his work on the duets was particularly fine as noted above. However, we did miss the power of choral voices from the stage. The ensemble was not punchy enough in their vocal. As I was watching 'Cell Block Tango' I was waiting for the big vocal on the chorus, but it was sadly fairly weak. I don't think this was a PA problem as the sound by Derek Recks was near perfect throughout. The same issue arose with 'We Both Reached for the Gun', a lack of power from the vocal ensemble. These numbers are meant to pretty much nail you to your seat with their intensity and intention, but they didn't. Set, props and lighting worked perfectly in harmony on this production. Paul Kelly's sparse but effective lighting design, with festoons and little LED's everywhere and his clever footlights during the trial and vaudeville ventriloquist scenes, worked really well. Aoife McClafferty and John Wright's set was very simple; the main set piece a hydraulic bridge spanning the width of the upstage was used very ingeniously to create different playing levels. The jail cell doors on castors worked well, but were a bit cumbersome and probably not really needed. However, I really like the festoon-rigged frame that angled upstage during the trail scene. The bentwood chairs were perfectly in era and the mocked-up newspapers were a nice touch. Hair and Make up were good and costumes by Utopia Costumes were also on point.

Of course, the real success of Chicago rests firmly on the casting of the two female leads. Emily Lohan's interpretation of Velma Kelly was a delight. Her singing was near flawless, her dancing very impressive. She seemed to run out of steam a little toward the end of the show but her characterisation of the murderess was striking. Her vocal work on 'Nowadays' with Roxie and 'Class' with Mama Morton was lovely.

However, as good as Ms Lohan was as Velma Kelly (and she was very good), she was totally eclipsed by the performance of Hannah Wright as Roxie Hart.  This was an outstanding performance from an accomplished actor, singer and dancer. For one so young (she's twenty- one), her command of her craft was very impressive. Her accent was perfect, not just in terms of location but in terms of the era (or what we know of it). She played the innocent equally as well as she played the hard-nosed vixen, effortlessly switching between the two sides of Roxie. Her dancing was super, her comic timing superb and her singing, particularly on 'Roxie' and 'Nowadays', impeccable. Her portrayal of the ventriloquist puppet on 'We Both Reached for the Gun' was perfect.

Direction by Aoife McClafferty was excellent. It was obvious that she exerted total control over all of her departments, drawing them all together to service her vision of the piece. Her work with the leads created super living and breathing characters, most of whom we cared about. Ms McClafferty's attention to detail on the setting of the show, involved us in the audience, completely and for a couple of hours on a rainy September evening in County Galway we were transported back to the roaring twenties of Chicago.

'Pajama Game' was based on the 1953 novel '7 ½ Cents.' With music and lyrics by Richard Adler and Jerry Ross this is the story of workers in the Sleep Tite pyjama factory who campaign for a seven and half cent pay rise. Love blossoms along the way between Sid and Babe. The show opened on Broadway in 1954 and there have been numerous revivals since. The score is glorious with some classics of the musical theatre genre, such as 'I'm Not In Love At All' and 'Hernando's Hideaway'. The show was directed with pace and energy by Philippa Alford. Philippa chose to use an adaptable set with a range of large pieces brought on as appropriate. There was clever use of lighting at times to make acting spaces more intimate and to create atmosphere. The characters of the cast were broadly painted and well defined. In shows such as this there is a tendency to go slightly 'over the top', this was not the case here as we really felt we knew these people. The movement around the acting areas was good throughout, though there were a few times when masking of players occurred. A solid piece of direction which brought out the humour of the piece.

Barry Power created a lovely balanced sound with his twelve-piece orchestra. There was always a steady tempo to the music and a great balance of the instruments. The cast were very comfortable in all their singing roles and the ladies' chorus in particular were outstanding, giving us that fifties sound. There were good harmonies throughout. A couple of characters however did just push their voices at times into a pop range which didn't quite work. Cueing was generally sound and the balance between voice and pit was very good. The 'There Once was a Man' number was a highlight of the show.

Laura Macken-Posavitz's choreography was very much in the style of the show. There were many memorable dance moments such as 'Steam Heat', with the girls in their sparkly dresses. I loved the clock like movements used in 'Think of the Time I Save' and my favourite was the joyful 'Once A Year Day'. There was a good use of the whole stage area and the changing moods and patterns added so much to our enjoyment. It might have been nice to see a little more movement in the duets and solos which could have added to the fun.

Philippa had gathered a very strong cast for this production. Sophia Daly gave us a feisty performance as Babe. This is the union woman who fights for the increase in pay. She sang really well though at times added a wee pop element to her voice which didn't really fit. I loved her singing of 'Hey There' which was a magical moment. Her acting was good and she reacted well to most of the players on stage. This was a strong performance. Her love interest was Sid Sorokin played by Kevin Macken. Kevin seemed a little nervous to begin with but soon settled into the part and gave us a nice portrayal of Sid. Kevin has a glorious singing voice which soared at the end of each number. He became a very likeable and watchable character. Aaron Tierney was Hines. This was a great performance which gave us plenty of laughs along the way. I loved his 'drunk man' act which was very realistic. He also had to do a knife throwing act which was very convincing. He moved around the stage so well with very fluid movements. His partner was Freda Quinlan as Gladys. Gladys is the dipsy secretary of boss Mr Hasler. Freda created a wonderfully rounded character from the way she walked to her screeching Bronx accent. Freda has a great sense of comic timing and we were in hysterics at her antics at times. She is also an excellent mover which she really showed us in 'Steam Heat' and 'Hernando's Hideaway'.

Prez who is the factory's lothario was played by Brian Dennison. He tries to work his way round all the girls in the factory who can't resist his charm. He played this role well. He looked the part and acted it well too. His singing voice became stronger as the show progressed. His rendition of 'Seven and a Half Years' was great. Jackie Carroll was the long- suffering secretary with attitude. Where Gladys was always in a turmoil, Mabel was just the opposite, she had seen it all before. This was a nicely characterised role, though just watch the pace.

Terry Martin played the frazzled boss Mr Hasler. The hall echoed when he shouted, 'Gladys!' and poor Gladys came scurrying on after him. He was all bluster and shouting which was perfect for this role. He looked so ill at ease in his casual checked shirt, rather than his usual suit, at the picnic which was very convincing. Yvonne Coyne gave a really strong performance as Mae. She looked as if she had stepped straight out of a 1950s movie. I loved the tone of her speaking and singing voice. At one point she was talking about potato salad and she even made that sound sexy! Brenda was played with real style and charm by Laura Geoghegan, Jen Keane made a lovely Virginia and Nikki Johnson was a most convincing Poopsie. What I liked most about these three players was that they worked selflessly as a team. They sang really well individually and as a group and really supported Babe in her big numbers.

Darragh Carroll was a handsome and at time panic-stricken Max. As the boss's aide he discovers that the pyjamas have been tampered with, with hilarious consequences. Daire Kelly has the most glorious tenor voice. I hope we hear more of it in the next show. Pop was played by Paul Johnston who captured the hardworking man so well.

The chorus in this show added so much to its success. They never stopped acting and reacting on stage. They sang well together and those with individual lines to say or sing did so with great clarity. The harmonies were good too. Well done chorus.

The stage had a raised platform at the back and above this there were the factory windows. This was clever as with a lighting change they became lit panels in Hernando's Hideaway. They were covered over for the picnic with panels painted with trees. The rail of the raised area was used to hang a union badge, festooned material etc. Pieces were brought onto the stage such as desks, chairs and the sewing machine stations. This was all very slickly executed and didn't interrupt the flow. The lighting was good, creating moods and more intimate areas. I loved the red moody light used in the night club. The properties were well chosen and looked correct for the period, adding much to the feel of the production. I would have loved a filing cabinet in the office which would have given a wee bit of business for the secretaries to do and would have made the scene with Mabel less static. That box file with the lock was wonderful, we were all dying to know what secrets were stashed in there!

The costumes were generally in the correct style for the era. The wide skirts worn by some, complete with layers of underskirts, Gladys' tight and tailored look. The men in their rolled-up sleeves, bowling shirts even the orange dungarees, all looked correct. Babe had quite a range of dresses. I liked the purple spotted one and some of the darker floral ones. This actress really seemed to suit the stronger colours. Make-up and hair were appropriate for the time and place with nice bright red lips and matt foundations. The girls had a consistent look. Their hair looked good too, though some of the men might have needed a wee trim to make their look more period.

I was made most welcome and I loved the fact that the front of house staff were wearing little 1950s neckties made from colourful material. The pyjama bunting in the foyer was most effective.

This was a great night's entertainment and fun. It is now very obvious why this show has been revived so many times. Well done Philippa and team for choosing this classic and bringing it to life for us to enjoy.

The fictitious household created by cartoonist Charles Addams is a satirical version of the ideal 20th century American family. They are a clan who delight in the macabre and seem to be unaware or don't care that other people find them frightening. Following on from the television series and the movies comes The Addams Family Musical. The An Táin Arts Centre in Dundalk was the venue for the show produced by Dundalk Musical Society. A show such as this needs a perfect sense of comic timing and excellent lead players. We had both in this production and we had a wonderful chorus who worked so hard during the whole show adding much to our enjoyment. Director Bernard Lynch managed to bring out the humour of the show very well. The audience of all ages enjoyed the humour throughout the production.

Bernard chose to use beautifully painted cloths as the setting for the show with a feature sweeping staircase. The show was well paced and scene changes were planned to not interrupt the flow of the show. The musical director was Ronan Dennedy who gathered a strong team of players for his orchestra. The tempo of the show was excellent throughout as was the cueing of the cast and the balance between stage and orchestra was as it should be. The cast were all very capable singers and thanks must go to Ann McCabe for her efforts as chorus mistress as we were treated to some great musical moments. There was some inventive choreography from Lea Carroll who had obviously worked extremely hard rehearsing the group as there was great attention to detail in the movement. I particularly liked the scene at the table when we had bit of 'handography' which was well timed and extremely funny. Paudie Breen as Gomez gave us a charming South American characterisation. We loved his eccentric nature and enjoyed his beautiful rich singing voice. He pointed his comedy lines extremely well to get the most laughter from them. His wife Morticia was played with scary charm and elegance by Carol McCourt. She was the epitome of our image of the character. She could act, dance and sing. What more could we have asked for as our Morticia? Wednesday was played by Hannah Mullen in a tomboyish and slightly frightening style. She shocked us when she crushed the budgie and fed it to the cat but we could see there was a softer side underneath especially in her romance with Lucas. Her brother Pugsley was played by E.J. Dunne. Although only eleven years old E.J. gave us a great comedy performance with some lovely nuances throughout the show. He looked appropriate and sang really well. Wednesday's love interest was played by Alan Doherty as Lucas Beineke. He and Wednesday made a good on- stage couple and he sang and acted the role very well. His mother Alice Beineke was played by Karyn McCooey. This was a standout performance with comic timing at its best. Karen never stopped acting on stage and we got to see two or more sides of her personality. The audience were in stitches at her 'Full Disclosure' at the red table. This was a hilarious and memorable performance. Her husband was played by Brian Halpin. Mal starts off as quite a boring businessman but revisits his youth in the 'Greater Than You' number which was a memorable part of the show. Grandma played by Marie McSorley was a great little character, so self-contained and quirky. Uncle Fester was in the capable hands of Gerry O'Hara. This was a wonderful comic performance. Gerry looked, moved and acted so well, always in character and always entertaining. His love affair with the moon was intriguing for us all and the final picture of him hugging the moon was a fitting farewell to his character. Andrew Sansom as Lurch gave us a very strong and controlled performance. It was a delight at the end to see him come to life and sing with such a rich, dark tone.

The chorus (pictured right in a pre-show pose) in this show played a very important role. They were on stage for most of the production, watching, listening and focusing the audience's attention on the action. They never distracted, they always added to the production. They sang well, they moved well and their costumes were wonderful looking. They all had individual personalities and it was obvious that they had worked out exactly what character they were meant to be and what period they were from.

The lighting in the show was an important part of its success. There was a complicated lighting plot with all sorts of gobos; including trees, moon etc. There were specials which created beautiful pools of light on the stage and there were lights behind scrims which magically revealed their secrets. There were functioning candles on the staircase and even some suspended above it. I was impressed how smoothly the lighting plot ran during the production. Praise indeed must go to Peter McDonnell.

The sets in this show were mostly beautifully painted cloths which could be flown in or pulled across the stage. This added quite a professional touch to the show. The feature staircase was solid and looked stunning on the stage. I walked over the stage after the show and the staircase hardly moved when my considerable weight climbed up it. It was painted in black with rich red curtains. The properties in the show were also of a very high standard. We had big props such as the torture rack, the stocks, a huge throne like chair, dressing tables, a cart laden with bottles of potions. There was quite an array of properties evocative of the period and they all looked in keeping with the feel of the show. Overall the costumes in the show were excellent. The chorus who appeared from the family crypt were all dressed in the same cream toned costumes. This gave unity to the group. What was nice was that the costumes were all of different eras but the material colour palette was the same, very uniting. The principal costumes were either colourful (like Alice's yellow dress) or monochrome. Either way the costumes were a very good fit and completed with the correct footwear on all occasions. The costumes were finished off with a set of excellent wigs. The chorus ones were all shades of grey and the principal ones were a variety of styles such as Wednesday's plaits. They all looked correct, they all looked professional. The make-up also was carefully planned and executed and always in character with the production. I commend the hair, makeup and costume teams who must have worked together so closely to produce the look of the show which worked so well.

Overall this was a most entertaining evening. There was much laughter, maybe a couple of tears in places but what impressed me most was the team work on stage and around the stage. It was obvious that the cast were all having a ball and because of that we enjoyed every moment of The Addams Family. Well done Dundalk Musical Society.

There was a real buzz of expectancy around the St George's Hall in Tuam for the Irish premiere of the musical Made in Dagenham. This charts the struggle that the female workers supported by their male counterparts had in the late 1960s when their status was reduced and hence their wages cut. It is set in the Ford car factory in Dagenham. The said ladies are on the conveyor belt making the leather upholstery for the cars. What was quite interesting was during the show a new exciting car is being premiered, it was a Ford Cortina. Frighteningly I remember the first Cortinas so well.

As we entered the hall there was a large and interesting display of Ford memorabilia such as dungarees, car tyres and press cuttings from the time. I, like most of the audience that night, had really never seen the show in its entirety before. I had googled a few numbers to familiarise myself but the evening's entertainment was a complete surprise and a very enjoyable one at that. The hall is a good size with a raised platform midway so that there is a good view of the staging. There was no curtain and the stage was open displaying an interesting blue light. An extension had been added to the stage which gave a large acting area and two more intimate spaces in front of the proscenium arch on either side.

The show, directed by Enda Burke and assisted by Aoife McClafferty, moved very well. The dialogue on most occasions was slick and the pace of dialogue was good, particularly with the female cast. There was great attention to detail shown with the staging of this show. Upstage right we had a room which was one of the worker's homes. It was the usual chaos of a kitchen with a young family. There was washing, table, chairs etc. which were all in keeping with the era. Even the wallpaper felt authentic.

The directors had established individual characters for the workers in the car factory and they had an expert touch at bringing out the humour in the show which was hilarious at times. When the story was being told it was hard to believe that women were treated in such a poor way in the workplace and interestingly enough still are as there is still not always parity of salary in every job. The main acting area was the shop floor of the factory and we saw the cleverly made sewing machines of the workers with conveyor belt for their finished products moving in the background which was very authentic looking. Various pieces of furniture including tables, coat-stands and benches were brought on in a very organised manner so that the flow of the show never faltered. Properties used were authentic and all were in good condition such as the beautiful decanter and sherry glasses that the ladies tried to sip from as they visited Barbara Castle in Westminster. We even had the epitome of 1960s chic, a fondue set in the boss's house which was so appropriate.

Shane Farrell who modestly praised his team of players in the orchestra, but took no praise himself, played keyboard throughout the show but led the orchestra from his seat. There was nice playing from the orchestra throughout with reeds, trumpet, guitars, bass, drums all blending so well and adding so much to the production. The instruments never overpowered the actors as we could hear every word of every song. The sound team from Dervan Sound, Loughrea did a great job on the show as there were many body microphones used, the dialogue was clear and cues were accurate.

As I said earlier there were interesting lighting effects created with coloured lighting but there were also moments where we had intimate lighting areas which created a great atmosphere for the scene. A well-lit show Indigo Lighting. The cast were excellent throughout. Suzanne Garvey-Brennan was excellent in the role of Rita O'Grady. We watch Rita develop from the under-pressure mother trying to keep all the balls in the air, including her job at the factory, looking after two children, wife to Eddie O'Grady played by real life husband Louis Brennan. She takes on the fight that Connie Riley begins and ends up speaking at the Trade Union Conference, which was quite a moment in her life. She sang well, she moved well and she was very convincing particularly in her relationships with her fellow workers, Connie and of course her husband. This was a well-studied and three-dimensional performance, well done Suzanne. Her husband Eddie fitted with her like a glove. We could see his frustration when the women were on strike and he had to move away with his two children for his own peace of mind, this was a very moving performance. Trade Union leader Connie was played by Frieda McGrath with a sincerity and honesty. Frieda was able to capture the strength of character of the real person. There were some beautifully touching moments which were gently played. Martha O'Toole had us in stitches as Beryl with her strong language and strong emotions. She created a wonderful character on stage. Emer Kelly was Clare who was a slightly eccentric character and give us lots of laughs along the way. Mary Newell as Sandra was a breath of fresh air with her wonderful singing and dancing, particularly in the Cortina number. She also acted very well her uncertainties as she is tempted off the strike to take part in a bit of advertising.

Lisa Hopkins was played by Clodagh Ruane. This is the rather posh wife of the boss of the Ford factory. It seemed that she was worlds apart from Rita but in actual fact they were able to strike up a wonderful friendship which was a very heart-warming thing to see.

Alisha Garvey was appearing on stage with her mother and stepfather as Cass and she did them both proud, as she moved, danced and acted extremely well through the whole show. Norman Quinn's Harold Wilson was absolutely wonderful. He took the stage by storm and his wacky interpretation of the part. It was so funny, we laughed out loud on so many occasions. This was a real tour de force of comic genius. Well done Norman! Beside him was Barbara Castle played by Eileen Newell with great dignity. Barbara Castle was a tough politician in the 1960s and Eileen captured the essence of her quite well. Stuart Barrows was jetted in as Mr Tooley who came from America to sort out the dispute. He was all chat and all bluster and reminded us of some modern American politicians!

Patrick Cummins played this sexist supervisor in the factory and it was interesting just to see how his approach then compared to what it would actually be now. Mr Hopkins was played by Declan Carroll. He achieved the feel of the period in his relationships with his workers and also his long-suffering wife. The rest of the male players worked hard to give us balance in the show. They all had the correct look and acted the part of factory workers very well. They all had the required 'blokishness'. The Cortina man was played by Owen Mullins in a 1960s pop star way which was just right for his 'Cortina' number. This was well choreographed and well portrayed.

The two children in the show Jack Blake Cleary and Taillte O'Callaghan as Graham and Sharon did a great job. They were under her feet when she and her husband were getting ready to go to work in the morning but they also showed great attachment to their mother when she was going off and leaving them.

The look of the show was achieved well with particular attention to hair and make- up, though the old-fashioned drawing on of lines to age people didn't really work for me and I think wasn't necessary. There was also great attention to detail with the costumes and I'm not sure where they got all those overalls from but they all looked like authentic Ford factory outfits. The girls' dresses were all in keeping with the period and the American cheerleader costumes sparkled and they added pizzazz to the number. The silver outfits which were used in 'Cortina' added more sparkle particularly with the shocking bright pink gloves which floated around the stage. The costumes were a good fit and they looked as if they had actually been bought by the people wearing them, they seemed to match their personality. On the whole this was a really memorable performance of the Irish premier of Made in Dagenham. There was a serious story to be told but it was told in a very fun and interesting way. This was a wonderful night's entertainment and we all left St Jarlath's Hall feeling we really had had a great night out. Thank you to The Marian Choral Society for a night of fun.

Originally written in 1971 as a gritty, violent slice of life about working-class Chicago youngsters in William Taft High School, Grease has been sanitised down through the years from a raw adult show into a the pasteurised, PG version we all know and love today.

The Ulster Operatic Company, who staged the show in the Grand Opera House in Belfast, has been around for about 108 years and has a huge number of productions in their canon. Following on from last year's Spamalot, they returned to a fan favourite, Grease and were rewarded by seven sold out shows.

This year is the fortieth anniversary of the hit 1978 film, which starred, a 23 year- old, John Travolta and, the then more established, Olivia Newton-John. In the Ulster Operatic Company's programme for the show, they dedicate a whole page to trivia from that film, so we could see the massive influence that movie has had on the creation of this version of Grease, from the costumes to the choreography and even the casting to a degree. But it's de rigueur now to try and emulate the 'movie versions' because that's what the audience want and expect.

The show opened with a unique and refreshing version of 'Alma Mater' by the Musical Director, Wilson Shields. No stranger to the Belfast stage, Mr Shields' interpretation of the score; his sterling work with the singers and his deft touch with his nine piece band brought a joie de vivre to the show.

The large ensemble on this production was admirable; their voices blended beautifully and exuded a palpable energy. They female voices particularly shone on 'Beauty School Dropout' with delicacy whilst the male voices on 'Greased Lightnin' were muscular and energetic. Of the male characters one stood head and shoulders above the rest vocally; Matthew Campbell's Doody was note perfect and commanded the stage like a young Ed Sheeran. His duet with Roger, played extremely well by Jordan Walsh (who soldiered on with his arm in a sling), 'Rock and Roll Party Queen' was effortlessly performed. They both shone over the other T-Birds in their sense of comic timing and general consistency of character. With 'Those Magic Changes', Mr Campbell gave us a masterclass in pitch, tempo and faultless delivery. He's definitely a performer to watch out for in the future. Joel Johnston's Kenickie rocked out well on 'Greased Lightnin'' as did Sonny as played by Rory Jeffers. Laura Livingstone's Jan and Rachel McAdam's Marty were also excellent as were Jordan Rosborough's Patty and Courtney Burns' Frenchy. But Ciara Mackey stole hearts with her rendition of 'There Are Worse Things I Could Do'. Her pathos in delivery and her emotional investment in her characterisation of Rizzo were superb. She really made the character her own. The stand out comedic performance on the night was Laura Kerr's Miss Lynch. Like a 1950's Bette Midler, her sense of timing was superb and her delivery spot on. A close runner-up was Jay Walsh's Vince Fontaine, his characterisation of the sleazy radio jockey was suitably cringeworthy as he oiled around the stage. Johnny Casino was brilliantly played by Vijay Sharma. His singing on 'Born to Hand Jive' was reminiscent of Prince in his heyday.

Vocal performance of the night was by Matthew Cavan who played Teen Angel, Frenchy's guardian angel. His drag performance of 'Beauty School Dropout' was perfection. His range was very impressive and he had a thrilling 'growl' in his voice, which he used to great effect. He also looked fabulous, with his big hair, skin-tight dress and huge heels. This scene was brilliantly directed. It looked like a colourised 1930s Hollywood movie scene, all smoke and sharp lighting and a vampy Guardian Angel striding up and down a staircase to convince the hapless Frenchy to go back to High School.

Jamie Johnston was cast as Danny and his vocal was quite good, and though his singing of 'Sandy' lacked a bit of emotion, he got through it. Caitlin McClurg as Sandy however, brought the house down with 'Hopelessly Devoted to You'. This was faultless as was her reprise of 'Look at Me, I'm Sandra Dee'.

Sadly, the dynamic between Jamie Johnston's Danny and Caitlin McClurg's Sandy wasn't as electrifying as I would have expected. They just didn't gel on the night I attended. The scene at the drive- in didn't land at all. There didn't seem to be any real chemistry between them. Mr Johnston's Danny was presented as a wise cracking class clown, full of tics and stutters. He didn't portray the charisma needed to be leader of the pack and mugged a lot at the audience. Ms McClurg, in the admittedly underwritten role of Sandy, didn't convince in her scenes with Danny but worked well in her scenes with the Pink Ladies. As the T-Birds were presented as so incompetent and frankly harmless, one wondered why Sandy would be attracted to their lifestyle or to Danny, who was played as being quite low status within the gang.

The staging was splendid; the set by Scenic Projects was a big help here as the design made for quick transitions between scenes. Production Manager, Gareth Maxwell, did a good job on keeping all of the elements working together as did Director, Neil Kerry. His work with the ensemble was commendable, as they seemed fully invested in the piece.

Timmy Bell's choreography was of high quality. Two memorable routines were 'We Go Together', where the entire ensemble was on stage in perfect sync and 'Born To Hand Jive' for his innovation. Overall the standard of choreography and the execution was very good. His integration of 1950s classic dances into the routines was clever and implemented well by the ensemble.

His work on 'Greased Lightnin' with the male ensemble was superb, their timing and physicality was frantic and rousing. But it was Beauty School Dropout where his work really shone. The quasi-1930s fashioning and feel on this number, really worked well. Teen Angel and her dancers (angels) evoked a past era but yet, also a 1970s Diana Ross like styling, it was a standout moment in the production.

Stage Management by Andy McKnight and his crew was good. The transitions were clearly well rehearsed, props by Valerie Greenlees and Ann Browne, were of the era (I liked the album covers, nice touch) and seemed solid.

The sound by Geoff Clarke was quite full and well balanced throughout the show, with little or no feedback and a good harmony between band and singers. There were some lovely evocative lighting states by Declan Anthony; the drive-in (the restrained use of the star cloth was pretty) and Teen Angel, come to mind.

The costumes by Jennifer Johnston, Martine Vitty and Margaret McAlister were just about perfect. They were totally authentic and evoked the era very well. The colours were vibrant and popped out at us. Teen Angel's dress and the silver capes of her entourage were suitably ethereal and otherworldly and a direct contrast to Frenchy's drab costume during the scene.

On the night I attended, the audience became part of the show. Singing along and clapping with the more popular numbers. I think this threw the cast somewhat, although they behaved impeccably throughout these interruptions, didn't reference them, and strove on bravely. This was a superbly entertaining production by Ulster Operatic, showcasing some fine new and established talent and adding new ideas, musically and in terms of production, to a tired, at this stage, formulaic musical. Their injection of energy, innovation and sheer fun into the show made us see and hear it anew. On the way out of the theatre I overheard one of the audience exclaim; "That was better than the film!" I totally agree.

It was a pleasure to attend the opening night of Jesus Christ Superstar in The Feohanagh, Castlemahon Community Hall.

This production marked the company's tenth anniversary and it was obvious that they are going from strength to strength.

There was a very family feel to the evening with a wide range of ages involved on and off stage. I was royally welcomed by the Chairperson and found out a lot about the history of the society.

The show was directed by Susan Browne who has worked tirelessly to train the cast for a polished first night performance. Susan was also the choreographer of the show and appeared on stage too. I commend Susan for all she does voluntarily for this young society. She chose a simple but quite effective stage setting with feature moving scenery pieces. There was a raised area front right which was occasionally used as Caiaphas's base. There was a television screen which showed us names of characters, settings, plot details through the show. I wasn't too sure about this initially but it did work well. The pace of the show was good with prompt scene changes and a good pacing of music and action. Susan had gathered a cast with a range of experience and it was good to see some of the less experienced rising to the challenge that this difficult show provides. Generally, there was good positioning of the principals throughout the show with limited masking of characters. There was a good flow to the production and I was impressed how well the story- telling was managed.

Choreography was a bit restricted due to the size of the stage and the huge cast involved. It would have been nice to see more patterns being created with movements which would have added more interest for the audience. The hand and arm movements were well rehearsed and executed. The chorus were always actively involved in all their routines. They moved on and off the stage with ease and I was very surprised to see the limited area they had in the wings.

Michael Young was Musical Director and made a well-rounded sound from a fairly small orchestra. The principals showed a wide range of talent and coped really well with this demanding piece. The tempo of the show was steady throughout and Michael showed great control over the players in the pit. The rendition of 'Herod's Song' was lively and 'I Don't Know How to love Him' was gently accompanied and created a memorable moment.

Jesus was played with passion by Jamie Herlihy. He coped well with the demanding score. He related well to the cast on stage but I would have liked him to angle his body a bit more towards the audience so we were included in his emotions. He moved with ease around the acting area and with his slightly retro flower power image we were transported back to the late 1960s which worked really well. He has some explosive moments particularly with Judas which he handled well. He also has to show a complicated love of Mary Magdalene which he carried through convincingly. A solid performance Jamie. Shane Walshe gave a strong portrayal of Judas. His frustrations were clear and the decision to betray Jesus was not taken lightly, this turmoil was very well acted. His singing was strong, particularly in his lower and mid vocal range.

Mary was performed by Grainne Aherne with genuine warmth. We were convinced by her feelings toward Jesus and her uncertainty of what those feelings really meant. Her singing was beautiful and 'I Don't Know How to Love Him' was a beautiful moment. Grainne was extremely watchable and moved elegantly around the acting areas. Dave Wrenne wowed us with his deep, rich voice. He created a menacing role as Caiaphas. He looked good in his dark robes and showed great stage presence. Annas played by Padraig O'Shea was a good second in command, a character to listen and comment on the action. He added much to the scenes he appeared in. Young Robbie Moriarty gave us a focused and committed younger priest and he shows potential for the future. Peter was sensitively played by Diarmuid Curtin and he gave a super rendition of 'Peter's Denial.' Shane Prior was a believable Simon who wowed us with his singing throughout the show. Tom Madigan was a slightly camp Herod. He sang and danced his way through a great rendition of 'Herod's Song'. This was poignant and hilarious at the same time. The dancing in this number with Tom and the glamorous girls was great and it was one of the highlights of the show. As I said earlier there was a huge cast of all ages, in fact there was a chorus of nearly sixty. They all acted and sang their socks off and contributed so much to the success of the evening.

Siobhan Hennessy and her extensive stage team who created, built and moved the set did a great job throughout the show. We had a pair of huge triangular trucks which when revolved lit up to show intricate designs. There was a suspended Star of David which shone down on proceedings from the back of the stage. Large blocks of polystyrene rocks were quickly moved into place as the base for our pole dancers outside the temple. A wall of greenery and potted trees might not really have been needed to create the Garden of Gethsemane as a lighting change would have been more effective. The lighting through the show supported the action most of the time and there were some very pleasing touches. It might be good in future productions to investigate how to create intimate scenes with lighting effects. There were limited properties used in this production but those used added to the intended style of the piece.

Hair was mostly in a hippy chic style and looked appropriate. I didn't particularly like Jesus' wig as in Act Two it hid his face from us. I really loved his white flowing top which gave a nod to the Middle East. Judas looked great as the rocker and the rest of the principals had simple costumes which had a real feel of the desert setting. Herod and his harem were in red sparkly outfits which added a perfect incongruous touch. The chorus looked great in a complete mixture of costumes adding a hippy commune look their numbers. This was a very sincere and honest interpretation of the script. The story telling was excellent throughout and the audience were captivated throughout the show. There was a well-deserved standing ovation at the end. I wish the society happy anniversary and good luck for the next ten years and beyond. Susan you should be proud of all you have achieved with such a large and talented cast.

I have looked forward to seeing this new musical conceived and written by the late Bryan Flynn. It is a great legacy to leave the world of Irish amateur theatre and a wonderful symbol of Bryan's passion for the stage. I was not disappointed by the moving and detailed production of the show performed by Oyster Lane Theatre Group. There was a buzz around Wexford and in the foyer of the Dún Mhuire Theatre on the final night of the show. The theatre which had been a cinema was a good setting for the musical. The tiered balcony seating gave a great view of the stage and the acoustics for the most part were very good.

The open stage was beautifully lit to reveal a raised platform, ramparts and intimate areas in front of the proscenium. The set seemed well painted with images of the Custom House on either side of the acting area. I was later to discover that this represented the fragmentation of British imperialism making way for the resurgence of the Irish Nation. An image of 'The Big Fellow' was projected onto the cyc. A hazer helped to create shafts of light on this scene. It was evident from the start that there would be great attention to detail and indeed there was.

Director Imelda McDonagh and Choreographer Suzanne O'Leary gave us exquisite movement of cast and chorus throughout the show. From that first moment when Mother Ireland opened her cape to give birth to a new Ireland right through to the end of the show, there were stunning tableaux, gentle choreography such as the waltzing when Kitty first meets Collins and strong aggressive positioning of the men at Frongoch. The show was a delight to the eye and a challenge to the senses.

There is a play within a play as throughout the musical we revert back to the Abbey Theatre's production of WB Yeats' 'Kathleen Ní Houlihan'. The extremely well-chosen cast carried this off to perfection, right down to the slightly over staged voices they used when in the play. The character of Mother Ireland was used to weave through the story giving a poignancy to each scene. There was careful thought given to every detail of this production and it showed. I loved the way Imelda teased every last meaning from the text which in the hands of our admirable cast came to life with a natural realism. The movement of the large chorus was great too and scenes were speedily changed using the cast to bring on chairs etc. This was a thoughtful and slick piece of direction.

The music was in the most capable hands of Patrick Clancy. He controlled the eight musicians in the pit as well as leading the cast and chorus, pit singers and pre- production Celtic ensemble. The sound was glorious with some very rousing music which reminded me of current West End shows. The tempo of the music was nicely judged throughout the show. There were lovely quiet moments when the orchestra almost vanished and rousing patriotic numbers which moved the soul. Our MD and our orchestra coped wonderfully with this complex score.

Of course, to even contemplate this show you must have a leading man of the highest calibre. A man who can act, convincing us of his passion for his country, he must show the fire in his belly and the gentler love in his heart for Kitty. We had this in Chris Currid who gave us a stunning performance as Michael Collins. Chris must have worked hard to find the very essence of the character. How he thought, how he moved, how he acted and reacted. Chris also has a superb singing voice. This part demands a singer with a wide vocal range and this we had in the effortless singing of Chris. He looked, sang and acted superbly well. Denise Brennan was equally as good as Kitty Kiernan. She shone out from the rest of the cast with her striking looks, stage presence, perfect diction and beautiful singing. This was a very convincing performance. Completing the love triangle was James McDermott's Harry Boland. This character not only helps to create a domestic conflict with Kitty and Collins but also becomes a political commentator and hence some of the show revolves around his political aspirations. This was a well-balanced portrayal of a complex character.

De Valera is a very difficult role to play. He is probably a personality in Irish politics which some of us can remember as he was third president of Ireland until 1973. Sean Hendley not only looked like him but also captured his mannerisms, giving us the soul of the man. Sean created some wonderful moments such as his stay in gaol which gave us another gentler facet of his personality. This was a well-rounded and well sung characterisation.

Joe Emmett was played by James Hobbs. James gave us an energetic and optimistic interpretation. He moved well around the acting areas and became a good sounding board for the rest of the cast. Mother Ireland was expertly portrayed by Louise Dillon. From that first moment with the cape, we were intrigued by the strange, mysterious woman. She came to life in the Abbey Theatre play. A chilling performance Louise. The rest of the Abbey Theatre troupe were extremely believable. The interplay between this group was excellent. Well done Yvette, Neal, Niamh and Gearoid you were all wonderful, as were Brian Kelly and Andy Fanning who played Cathal Brugha and Arthur Griffith. These were strong political leaders, and you gave them a voice, well done both of you. Eilish Coady, Dara Cullen and April Roche-Kelly you all played Kitty's sisters with style. You all danced beautifully too. Jonathan Blake gave us a very upset young soldier and Greg Currid was just perfect as the British Viceroy.

The chorus were the very backbone of the show. They created such memorable moments of such deep meaning. The unforgettable image of 'The Killings' when indiscriminate killings were carried out. It was the sound of the gun and the thud when each character hit the floor, this was so thought provoking. There really was not very much wing space but the chorus never showed the limitations as they dragged their executed countrymen off stage.

The staging of this show added much to its success. The stage as described earlier was solidly constructed and well painted. The were also hidden surprises such as the gangplank which lowered so poignantly indicating the leaving and returning to the native land and the door of the gaol which pulled out of the scenery stage left. The painting of the set and of course the stunning lighting plot which included historical back projections created a very professional look. Throughout the show the lighting was used to great effect to create atmospheric moments and was adapted as the show progressed to create a continuous flow on stage. Expertly done Mark Redmond. The sound was also very well managed as cueing was perfect and effects such as gunfire were always well- timed. A good job I -Tech Productions. Personal props were always of the correct period and I was impressed to see an array of different chairs appear on stage depending on the scene. Nice touches Clara McDonald.

Costumes, hair and makeup were all natural looking and with the odd exception costumes fitted and were of the correct era. The black, white, grey palette unified the look of clothes on stage. There was real attention to detail throughout.

This was an extremely moving show which was particularly successful in the First Act. The performances were all of an extremely high standard and the essence of the story came through loud and clear. There was great attention to detail throughout the whole show and I absolutely loved how groupings of people were placed. Imelda and team you produced a memorable evening of amateur theatre.

The foyer of St Patrick's Comprehensive School in Shannon was decorated as a New York subway station, complete with hairdressing salon, ticket desk and buskers, to create the atmosphere for Muse Productions interpretation of In the Heights. The audience were brought in through a side door past posters of the New York underground system, so we really felt that we had gone on a journey to get into the auditorium. The show is set in 2008 and deals with three days in the life of a Latin American community in New York, struggling from day to day with that ever-present desire to return to their homeland.

We were greeted by an open stage with a stunning set created by Ted Germaine and his wonderful team. This was a New York street scene with hairdresser, car rental shop, the bodega and in the distance, there was the Washington Bridge which was accurately created and was lit in many different ways during the show. The set which was solid and looked as if it has been built out of bricks extended from the stage into the auditorium. It was aligned at a sharp angle which gave an illusion of depth to the stage making it appear much bigger than it actually was. In a show such as this the characterisation is actually more important than the storyline itself. Director Martin McNelis had obviously worked hard with the cast to investigate the characters in the show with very pleasing results. Martin also expertly created different moods for different events and also for different times of day. So clever was this that we really felt that we were on a journey with the cast of this show. The pace of the production was very good with rattling dialogue and then pauses to appreciate more tender moments.

Martin was supported by a wonderful team of choreographers: Pamela McGlynn and Edina Erdei. There were all sorts of dance routines in the show from Latin American jive, salsa and mambo to hip-hop. These were all carried out with great conviction by the cast who moved effortlessly around the stage giving us wonderful patterns and dance moments. I particularly liked the moment in the club when we were treated to some wonderful cha-cha-cha dancing. One of the highlights for me was the 'Carnaval del Barrio' which nearly brought the house down. This number started slowly and then build up to a frenzy. The music was from an orchestra of ten pieces with Mary Rose McNally playing keyboard and conducting.

For the most part this was a very tight sound with wonderful Latin American rhythms and brassy touches. The rap moments were well attempted but sometimes difficult to make out the words due to a lack of balance between the pit and the stage. There were some glorious harmonies in the show with the singing of such numbers as 'No Me Diga' with Carla, Nina, Vanessa and Daniela. There were some lovely tender moments of song too such as Kevin's 'Atención', Claudia and Usnavi's 'Hundreds of Stories'. The orchestra provided such wonderful energy for Pamela and Edina's stunning dance routines, which were carried out with such vigour by this young and enthusiastic cast.

Usnavi was portrayed by Eoghan Rice. He is the central character in the show and narrates the events going on in street. So called as his father named him after the first ship he saw when entering New York, unfortunately for him it was a US Navy ship!! He runs the bodega which is the focus for the social life of the area. We see his frustration at being away from his home and the tragedies that befall him during these few short days. Much of Eoghan's singing was in the form of rap which is a difficult thing to master and he did a great job at doing so. Eoghan showed great emotion in his relationship with Abuela Claudia and his relationship with Vanessa played by Lauren Rice. Lauren created a three-dimensional character as Vanessa, we could see her frustrations in her relationship with Usnavi and her desire to move away from The Heights and yet there was something holding her there. Clíodhna McNelis played Nina with an easy charm and showed wonderful interpretation of the script and the music. She has a super stage presence and singing voice. She really made the character of Nina her own. Her love interest is Benny played by Tom Barrett. Tom is a gentle character in the show who falls in love with Nina and much to their parents' disgust, begin a relationship together. Aodan Fox played Kevin who was Nina's father and Camilla who was her mother was played by Anna Marie Barrett. These two worked together brilliantly to create a convincing married couple. There were highs and lows, there were fights and reconciliations, there was tenderness. A very well-rounded performance from both. Sonny played by Cillian Fahy had a love of life which was contagious. Sonny is Usnavi's cousin and someone who hasn't really settled down to the responsibilities of life. This was an energetic and fun-loving portrayal. The part of Graffiti Pete was played by Conor McNelis. He gave us a character for Sonny and Usnavi to bounce off but also creates a memorable moment with his graffiti for Abuela at the end of the show.

Daniela who runs the hairdressers was played by Clare McNelis (this is really a family affair). She looked stunning on stage and created a wonderful rounded character. Daniella is moving from the street to somewhere she considers better, closing her hairdressing salon and leaving the street behind. It was a very emotional and charming performance. I also liked how she sang in her various songs such as the beginning of 'Carnaval del Barrio'. Working in the shop is Carla who is played by Hazel Park. Carla is the junior in the hairdressers. This was well-acted and her innocence was very endearing. I really enjoyed the performance by Edel McFadden as Abuela Claudia. This is someone who knows how a stage works. She really knows how to relate to the audience. She knew how to use the light so that it glistened in her eyes. She could sing to perfection in this role. She knew how to get us on her side, this was a most memorable performance, well done Edel. The Piragua guy was played by Ronan Mitchell who appears pushing his cart selling his shaved ices. He looked well and acted his part well too. Chorus members were super with really good male and female dancers. Nice to see men on stage who can really dance too and a few characters who really brought a warm smile to our faces as they were so involved in all the action. I would like to thank Cormac for his lovely portrayal of assistant to the Piragua Man.

Everyone looked right on stage for the part they were playing and right for the period in which the show was set. The costumes were varied and ranged from Claudia's crossover house coats, to the street wear and baseball hats of the chorus. I particularly liked Usnavi's bowling shirt which really added a New York feel to the stage but all the costumes worked really well. They moved well and they did not inhibit movement round stage. Properties such as chairs, tables, various cans, litter, hairdressing supplies, hairdressing stools were all in keeping and correct with the period of the show.

The lighting was stunning as supplied by Star Systems Thurles. There were beautiful moments of sunrises and sunsets. There were mood making moments like the light in the club and the bridge at the back was often delightfully highlighted by coloured light. I particularly liked the scene after Abuela Claudia had died and the cast came on with various candles creating a magical tribute to her. The sound was good except for that little problem with the balance during the rap numbers, the rest of it was spot on. The cast make-up and hair were appropriate to the time and were often accompanied by the correct baseball hats and other accessories of the time.

This was a very interesting show, one that I had not seen before but I am delighted that I have now seen it in its entirety. It is a very emotional and a very funny piece of musical theatre too. Our evening in Shannon with Muse Productions was most enjoyable. A huge thank you to all the cast and crew for inviting me to your show and for the faultless hospitality I received when I was there.

Does somebody need a hug?

One of the most popular Christmas films in recent years is Jon Favreau's Elf starring Will Ferrell. It's a perfect family film, with goofiness for the kids and hilarious innuendo aimed at Mum and Dad. The musical loses some of the wicked humour, but has a few very good songs and is narrated by none other than Santa Claus. Staging a show aimed at an audience of children is somewhat daunting as you have to keep their attention through spectacle, energy and a kind of magical realism. Unfortunately, Belfast Operatic Company decided to stage Elf - The Musical in the vast Waterfront Hall but didn't size the production to fit the venue, so whilst the Hall is spectacular and the cast had great energy, the magic was just not there. Except for Buddy.

Playing Buddy the Elf of the title was Paddy McGennity. His energy onstage as Buddy was intensely maniacal and he had great comic timing. His portrayal of the man-child was very good and more reminiscent of Tom Hanks in Big rather than a direct copy of Will Ferrell in the film version of Elf. This was a good decision by him and his director, Wilfie Pyper, as he made the part his own and not an impersonation. Complete with elf suit and afro wig, Mr McGennity bounced around the stage like a small child on Christmas morning. His singing was quite sweet and at times emotional. Mr McGennity was especially moving on the 'World's Greatest Dad' where he imagines what his actual father may be like. Buddy's duet with Jovie, his love interest, on 'A Christmas Song', where he convinced her to sing, was really heart-warming.

As the underwritten Jovie, Aideen Fox, did well and was quite believable. I preferred her early scenes when she was a bit grouchy as her comic timing was very good. She had a wonderful musical theatre voice and a good range. Her solo song in Act Two, the jazzy 'Never Fall in Love With An Elf' was touching and one of the best performances of the evening. However, the best vocal performance of the evening was by 12-year-old Andrew Montgomery who played Michael Hobbs, Buddy's half brother. His two duets with his onstage Mom, Emily Hobbs played by Laura Kerr, were impressive. His voice was amazingly controlled for one so young and he handled all of his songs like a true professional. He soared to impressive heights whilst retaining the emotions and intentions of the songs. He had good comic timing and he played him as a likeable kid influenced by his kind mother rather than his often-absent father. Laura Kerr had a marvellous warm tone to her voice and she also excelled when she sang with Mr Montgomery on 'I'll Believe in You' and again on 'There is a Santa Clause'. She exuded a sincere maternal nature and her scenes with her onstage son were very realistic. As Buddy's father, Walter, Colin Boyd played him perfectly, a workaholic businessman rather than a bad guy. His performance was consistent and he sang rather well too. As Santa Claus, Eric Miller definitely looked the part but he changed accents at the start of Act Two, which kind of worked for the local references but was in danger of straying into Panto territory, however he got it back towards the end of the show.

A special mention must go to Shirley Adair who played Deb and sang superbly on 'In The Way' and 'Just Like Him'. She told a hilarious story of Polko, the one legged Hungarian boy, who got a leg for Christmas. Her comic delivery was perfect and her New York accent was spot on. Keith Pyper as the Store Manager was also very good as was Kerry Cooper as Mrs Claus. The evil Mr Greenaway was played with confident assurance by Jeff Manning. Gary Redpath and Ian McMaster played Chadwick and Matthews, two office workers, with glee and fine comedy. Josh Kelso and Alice Johnston played Charlie and Shawanda very well as did Liz Boyd as Charlotte Dennon the T.V. Reporter. Colin Scott was Musical Director on this show and his arrangements and interpretation of the score was quite faithful. Mr Scott also conducted the medium sized orchestra and acted as Chorus Master on the show. A twelve- piece band gave us a big tinselled full sound. The band's tempo and pace were just right and their tone and balance were superb. I loved the percussion, especially the sleigh bells!

Choreographer Timothy Bell created some great routines for this show. Christmastime with Buddy and the elves was very well executed, and despite the elves being on their knees, it was full of energy and dynamism. The scene when Buddy gets to New York during 'World's Greatest Dad' and is amongst the commuters was also very good, each actor had moves specific to their situation, waiting for a cab, on the subway and so on.

In 'Sparklejollytwinklejingley' the Store Manager and his staff along with Buddy did a great routine involving Christmas presents and decorations. Again they had a great energy, unison and connected well together. The scene with the ice skates (actually roller blades) was also well choreographed.

The sound by McCusker Audio was well- balanced and filled the vast auditorium well. There was a good mix between band and singers and it was a nice full sound. Lighting by ACK Productions was well- designed and operated with a good use of two follow spots allowing for some nice saturated states on stage. The lights on the Christmas trees should have been dimmable as they just snapped on and off during crossfades. But generally it was a brightly lit show and we could see everything we were meant to see.

Set design was accredited to Alan Marshall and he produced a good array of Christmas trees. All of the specific areas and locations were created by furniture and by projecting images onto the BP Screen. There was very little in the way of traditional flats or set dressing apart from Christmas decorations. The company used a snow machine at one point but it was very noisy and only produced a small amount of 'snow'.

Projection design was by Paul Young Scenery Projection and was very sharp and bright. Some of the animations looked a little laggy and some of the images didn't really convey location well enough. But generally it was good of quality.

The costumes were bright and colourful and seemed to fit well. Buddy's elf costume was perfect and the office workers all had red ties or scarves, which showed a good uniformity. The department store elves had lovely, festive sparkly costumes during 'Sparklejollytwinklejingley' and the scene with all of the fake Santas, 'Nobody Cares About Santa' was resplendent with Santa suits. I liked all of the white costumes at the 'Finale' too. Hair and Make-Up were unaccredited in the programme but looked fine.

Stage Management by Marie Cusack and her team was a bit slow on the setting but quite quick on the strikes. Props were a bit sparse for a show that's set in the Elves Workshop, a Department Store, an Office and other locations, but what was there worked fine. I liked that Santa's Book of Names was an iPad.

The pacing on the show was very staccato. The transitions between scenes seemed to take longer than they should have, as there wasn't much to bring on or strike. The pacing within scenes was better as most of them were driven by the high energy Buddy.

It wasn't a bad interpretation by director, Wilfie Pyper, but I did feel the whole show was too small for the venue. The pieces of set looked tiny on the big Waterfront Hall stage, the actor's energy did help fill it out a bit, but ultimately they looked a bit lost. Too much focus was placed on the projection screen images, which I think distanced the audience more from the live action and so we lost that 'liveness' and immediacy that is essential for the audience to empathise with the characters.

The whole show was driven by the frenetic performance of Paddy McGennity. His Buddy elevated the production. He had great presence and his energy and commitment to character was admirable. Clearly fuelled by the four main food groups: candy, candy canes, candy corns and syrup, Mr McGennity was magical.

A smiling dummy nun at the roadside welcomed us to the Tullyvin Community Centre. Tullyvin Musical Society were to perform their version of Sister Act. Tullyvin is a small society which has only formed within the last few years but seems to be going from strength to strength. The foyer of the hall was decorated with church candles and the smell of incense burning. It created the atmosphere of the show. The hall itself is a good size and seats around 300 on two separate levels. The stage was open as I entered and the set looked solid with a large extension built to the front of the stage which created a huge acting area. In the centre of the stage there was an altar with a candle burning and a cross, this was lit by very strong white beams which you could see in the shafts of light created by a hazer. The walls of the stage were very convincingly made to look like brick and had a three-dimensional quality about them.

I was interested to see that the musical direction was by Barry Power whom I had seen the previous week in Dublin. This time Barry was dressed as Bishop Power which was a very effective beginning to the show and the chaos he created going up and down the aisle made a diversion so the set could be changed to the nightclub. Barry gathered a strong team of players and there were some nice moments such as the balance in 'I Haven't Got A Prayer' which was enhanced by beautiful clarinet playing. The show started with a real bang musically but settled down to a more rounded sound as the show went on. The show was directed by Paul Norton who gave us a thoughtful well-paced production. From the opening with the clever use of Monsignor O'Hara as the announcer of fire regulations there were wonderful entertaining moments through the show. The cast was made up of so many well-developed characters, who gave us much fun throughout the evening. Each one of the nuns had an individual charm and personality. Each one even funnier than the one before!

Paul had chosen to have the back panels of the stage revolve to change scene and also a fold out panel stage left which turned into the police station.
