This was very effective and did not detract too much from the pace of the show. The set created by Brian Feerick and team looked great and worked well. Large pieces were brought onto the stage to create a scene such as chairs and even a jukebox. These items were usually well-managed. Properties were all very much in keeping such as the lectern, guns etc. The lighting added much to the show with some nice touches. I particularly liked the roving blue and red spots which were teamed with the police siren, very effective. It might have been nice to have a few atmospheric gobos, maybe of church windows, casting interesting shadows.

There were a few things in the setting of the piece which jarred with me. Nearly all the solos and a few duets were played downstage centre. They also tended to be static. This worked for some such as the magical Sister Mary Robert solo, but to be honest it became a little too static for some of the other numbers. I really enjoyed the joy that the cast showed when moving but I would have loved to see more changing patterns in the choreography rather than the excellent but usually static 'armography' on stage. We need to be visually challenged when watching a show so changing patterns are essential. The moves on stage were in keeping with the 1970's and all the cast managed to carry them out really well with huge smiles on their faces.

Andrea Fitzpatrick headed the female cast as the soul singing diva Deloris. This was a good performance and Andrea grew in confidence as the show progressed. She created a believable character whom the audience supported throughout. The lady can sing too! She really blew us away in those big numbers such as 'Raise Your Voice'.

Mother Superior was played with just the right amount of severity by Fiona Lynch. She captured the inflexible head nun beautifully. There were lovely moments of comedy brought out in the performance too especially with those confidential chats to God. Tomasina McGinnity, who also choreographed the show, played Sister Mary Robert with such realism we were totally convinced. Her character grew from the timid postulant to the strong woman at the end of the show. Her singing was wonderful throughout. A great performance. Sister Mary Patrick was played hilariously by Sandra McCormack. She had such an expressive face and captured those outbursts so well.

The reluctant policeman who comes up trumps in the end was played by Jack Carolan. Poor Sweaty Eddie as he was known has a fear of guns which he manages to overcome at the end of the show. This was a lovely performance by Jack who looked so natural in the role. He coped well with his big number while doing a speedy costume change, quite a feat!

Sister Mary Lazarus was a delight as played by Pamela McCormack. She had this booming voice and wore heavy dark rimmed spectacles which gave her such a comedic appearance. Seamus Smith was a sparkly and enthusiastic Monsignor O'Hara. From that first announcement we knew we were going to love the character and we really did. He was such fun in all those glittery costumes. He also dealt well with the more serious moments he had with Mother Superior too. His two altar boys Odhrán and Donnchadh were great wee characters too and added to the scenes in which they appeared.

Liam Wallace was a very threatening Curtis. He sported a gun which had a horrible clunk and when he actually pulled that trigger at the start of the show it put the fear of God into all of us. Liam really played the controlling psycho so well. He can also sing well and performed 'When I Find My Baby 'really well. The rest of the gang comprised John Grogan as TJ, the gangly sidekick who kept getting it wrong and getting in trouble with the boss, Eddie Hall as the man of few words Pablo, who was always threatening and Joey played by Dermot Carragher. Dermot looked a bit like a seventies pop star in his long wig. The audience loved their sexy moves in 'Lady in The Long Black Dress'. Sister Mary Martin of Tours was a brilliant cameo performance by Finuala Duffy who really made the part her own. She was just an 'over the top 'character we couldn't help loving. Jackie McQuillan really aged up to be a convincing Sister Mary Theresa with hilarious moves and a great delivery of her lines. His Holiness who appeared in his push along Popemobile gave us all a great moment.

Other smaller roles, which are too numerous to mention were well performed. The chorus in this show worked their socks off and assisted by the pit singers they produced some very nice singing with beautiful harmonies at times.

Gemma and Claire looked great in those Farrah Fawcett wigs as Deloris' backing singers. The hair and makeup were pleasing, on the whole, and a good effort had been made to capture the feel of 1970's, even with the men's hair. The costumes were at times stunning, especially those glittery nuns' habits. Most of the costumes were a good fit and the cast appeared comfortable in them. Sister Mary Robert those boots were something else! How you were able to walk in them, I will never know. The transformation costumes were good too.

There was a wonderful community feel about this show. It was obvious that several generations of a family were taking part and everyone was having a ball. That's what our wonderful hobby is all about, us having a great time while making others happy too. This was a great effort by Tullyvin Musical Society who gave us an evening of such enjoyment. Well done everyone.

Back Of The Net!

Now I'll be the first to admit that I never understood the attraction of soccer. In school, I'd always be last to be picked for teams and I don't understand the offside rule. However, having seen South Eastern Theatre Group's version of 'The Beautiful Game' in the beautiful Theatre Royal in Waterford, I'm almost convinced to watch a match or two.

Written by Ben Elton, one of the stars of '80's 'alternative' T.V. comedy, and with music by Andrew Lloyd Webber, this thinly veiled allegorical tale of two halves is set in Belfast in 1969 and follows the trials and tribulations of a local football team. Using the troubles as a backdrop, quite literally as we see projections of war-torn Belfast quite frequently, the story revolves around the team members, their love lives and paramilitary groups vying for the hearts and minds of the citizens. This was a bit of a departure for Lloyd Webber as the whole show is rooted in naturalism, but when Elton approached him with a treatment of the script, he immediately set to work.

The music, helmed by the ubiquitous David Hayes, was a mixture of rousing anthems, sweet mournful ballads and even included a glorious fife and drum band. His arrangements of the score were first class and he added charming little 'celtic' touches. He clearly worked hard with the ensemble as they were dynamic, harmonious and robust in their delivery of the, sometimes rousing, choruses. His work with the fife and drum band was excellent and they clicked seamlessly into the production.

The orchestra of nine was cloistered under the stage with a trap open for Mr Hayes to conduct both the singers and the band. Apart from the keys, the flute and percussion really sparkled in this production. There was an exquisite warm tone achieved for some of the softer numbers and great attack on the more energetic songs. During the funeral scene at the end of Act One, we had an evocatively effective solo drummer, Johnny Farrell Doyle, playing on stage. This was a wonderful arrangement by the MD and a poignant way to end the Act. The ensemble sang well on the choral numbers. I was particularly impressed by their impassioned work on The Beautiful Game, The Final and The Craic. Their harmonies on The Happiest Day were beautiful and I really liked the power of the male ensemble on Dead Zone. They could also dance quite well.

Working with untrained dancers is always difficult for a choreographer, however Michelle Condon did wonders with her young ensemble and created some brilliant football inspired routines. During the main match the players circled each other, going through a series of choreographed swerves, skids, deflections, fouls and mimed goal scoring in slow motion. This was very effective and was helped by the swirling lighting. Other routines consisted of much simultaneous movement by the ensemble, mimicking supporters loudly cheering on their teams. Sound by 'All Around Sound' was reasonable. A full range was achieved with no feedback or signal drops to the many mics during the songs and band numbers. However, I felt that the pure dialogue sections were badly equalised and many actors sounded muffled; especially John and Ginger. Also, all of the dialogue came from all of the speakers rather than being panned to left or right depending on where the actor was on the stage. This resulted in a very artificial sound, as these sections were also quite unnaturally loud. But the music and singers were blended quite well and a nice balance was restored during the songs and musical interludes.

The show featured some of the best lighting I've seen in quite a while. It was pin sharp with a great use of movers, which mixed well with the generics. The prison scene was very effective as was the football match and the training scenes. Designer Eoin Sheridan also lit the set very well and created a tense dangerous mood during the rioting scenes. Full points to him for a sympathetic, considered and faultless design and plot.

Set design by Dermot Quinn was very good with many flats and set pieces trucked on and off. The corrugated look was very striking as was the brick effect on the side flats. Sadly, we could barely see the projections from where I was seated, which was a shame as they looked interesting and clearly added context to the show. The locker room and football stands were very authentic looking, as were the house interiors with de rigueur Sacred Heart pictures. Hair and make-up by Christine Hennessy was expertly applied and well researched, as was costume by Avril Musgrave and Elaine Tighe.

Mary, played by Phoebe Dipple, sang well on the duet God's Own Country but it was Niamh Fennessy as the Protestant Girl who really excelled here. Her voice had a beautiful ethereal quality on the song and we wanted to hear more from her. However, Ms Dipple really came into her own on the highly emotional If This Is What We Are Fighting For and the memorable Our Kind Of Love. She had a fabulous sensitive voice, full of character and empathy and sang and played Mary exceedingly well. Mary's beau, John, as played by Adam O'Brien, sang well throughout the show. He didn't have a lot of power in his voice, but his tuning was good and he sang with passion. His acting was very believable and he had a good dynamic with Ms Dipple.

Thomas, John's friend and later enemy, played by Danny Brockie, had a very strong vocal. His singing of I'd Rather Die On My Feet Than Live On My Knees was full of anger and frustration and really encapsulated the feelings of those under duress. His was a multi-layered performance, and he played the sub-text splendidly. Fr O'Donnell, the genial man of God and part-time football trainer, was played by Paul Corcoran. He was quite charismatic, in a Spencer Tracy - Father Flanagan way, and played it well.

The camaraderie of the team was very palpable, they had clearly worked hard with their director and he built up a fine, credible ensemble. Both Daniel, played by Cathal Moran and Gregory 'Ginger' as played by Ben Nolan were particularly effective and portrayed their close friendship very well. Mr Nolan played Bernadette's (Carrie Mullane) new lover who reached a sticky end and his duet with her was sweet. Ms Mullane had an exquisite tone, delicate and full of sorrow when she sang a short reprise of Let Us Love In Peace.

Padraic Di Fusco's, Del, the protestant team member who was dropped from the team, was sublimely played as an intelligent young man who saw the writing on the wall for what it was and escaped to the USA with Christine, his Catholic girlfriend played by Aisling Larkin. She brought the audience to their feet mid- show when she sang the main parts of Let Us Love In Peace. Her performance of that song in particular made us remember we were at a Lloyd Webber musical. She had a brilliant range, with her soaring top notes and her emotional investment in the song was intense.  Ms Larkin was definitely the stand out performer, vocally, of the evening.

This was a great production full of youthful energy and edgy emotion. Some scenes were extremely well produced. I loved the funeral scene where sections of the stage were removed to create a grave and the coffin was lowered into it, accompanied by a solo drummer and a video rain effect. The pacing of each scene was perfect, with the exception of the wedding night scene, which dragged a bit. The prison section was also cleverly staged with a flown in fence and sharp lighting. It was a very good interpretation by director, David Hennessy, which certainly ranked high in terms of emotional intensity and production values. Now, what time is the match on?

society_raw: St Michael's Theatre MS, New Ross
review_text:
St Michael's Theatre was the interesting venue for this production of the Dolly Parton musical '9 to 5'. Interesting in that the once church building now doubles as a cinema and theatre. It is a pleasant auditorium with a good feel from the stage of the tiered space below. There is a pit for the orchestra which in my book creates a better more balanced sound for any production. It is ambitious for the company to maintain and run this great facility which also has a little restaurant which can provide pre-theatre meals. Dolly Parton herself introduces the show by video projection. The setting for the show was a slightly abstractly painted set on moveable trucks. This was clever as the trucks were quickly moved and scene changes were pretty slick throughout. It would have been nice if these flats had been a bit sharper in their construction and painting which didn't quite work for me. There were however some effective touches on the set and the bathroom scene was well appointed with taps and sink. Great effort had also gone into making the rear of the car (pictured above) where poor Hart was flung. The desks and all the props thereon looked very authentic. These were speedily carried into place. The boss's desk was on a wheeled truck. There was an unusual peachy/orange colour palette used for the scenery and the city skyscraper backcloth.

Director Kevin Kennedy used the available space quite well adding in some action on an extension stage left and also a room in the stage right area. The direction was neat and the production moved at a steady pace throughout. The movement of a large chorus is quite a daunting thing to choreograph and the general office scenes could have had more passing through movement with chorus entering and exiting the space for some logical reason otherwise we have slightly distracting action behind the principals. The clip boards were great in one of the dance routines but were a bit overused at other times. Kevin chose his cast very well and everyone seemed most suited to their role. He must have worked hard to develop the individual characters and the various American accents were sustained well by the cast. He managed to tease out all the humour from this quite straightforward script. I would however have liked Hart's sexy moves to have been toned down as I think it might have been more in keeping with the character and would have led to more laughs. Overall a competent, slick production.

Musical Director Philip Kennedy created a very rounded and usually balanced sound from the ten-piece orchestra. There was the lovely brassy sound which the show demands as well as that Country and Western lilt. There were a few times in the big Country numbers when the singers on stage were overwhelmed by the sound of the accompaniment. The cast were well rehearsed and, on most occasions, sang really well, in character. There were some beautiful harmonies with the chorus and the three principal ladies made a gorgeous sound together. The choreographer Claire Kickham created some wonderfully memorable moments. I particularly loved Roz and her lookalikes' 'Heart to Hart'. This was an hilarious routine which really used the words of the number to create the moves. 'The Dance of Death', 'Cowgirl's Revenge' and 'Potion Notion' were all such well-constructed and executed routines. I would have liked to see a bit more interpretation of the words of some of the big group numbers, which though well danced were a little static and didn't push the story telling along.

Violet who is the divorced, hard-working mother was played superbly by Teresa Buckley. She has wonderful comic timing and delivered all her lines with great punch. She captured that 'Bronx' feel very well with her sharp movements and impeccable accent. She sang really well and I particularly loved her emotional duet with Joe, 'Let Love Grow'. Doralee was played by Jennifer White. She really looked the part in her beautiful blonde wig and fitted costumes. She had a nice Country tone to her voice when delivering dialogue and sang quite well. This is a difficult sing as the part builds to the end of the big musical numbers and the singer has to compete with a building accompaniment. Judy was delightfully portrayed by Ashley Doran who first appears in an oversized hat. Ashley was perfect for this role and we were carried along on her journey from a shy 'I will not cry!' novice in the office to the beautiful and confident business woman at the end of the show. She moved elegantly around the acting areas. What a delightful tone Ashley has to her singing voice too. The womanising boss, Franklin Hart Jr was played with great swagger by Keith Flanagan. He really got the audience to dislike his wicked ways. He moved and sang well and was able to deliver his lines with aplomb. He was too easily tied up and didn't seem to mind being hoisted in that harness either!! Joe was gently played by Michael Benson. This is Violet's accountant suitor. Michael created a really lovely character which was in complete contrast to his lecherous boss. He sang his duet with Violet very emotionally. Roz was the wonderful creation of Julie Kinsella. This was a fantastic performance which had the whole theatre in hysterics. Her love for Franklin was almost tangible. She slightly underplayed the role which was a great idea but Julie was never afraid to let herself go and her moves in her solo with the 'mini me's ' were absolutely brilliant. Dwayne was nicely played by Phil Erskine. He is Doralee's supportive husband. Phil gave the role a sincerity and old world charm. Owen Cullinan was Dick in the production. He played the angst- ridden estranged husband of Judy with a sense of awkwardness, no doubt regretful having walked out on his beautiful wife. Edward O'Dowd was violet's son Josh. Edward created a great rapport with Teresa on stage. We were totally convinced by his portrayal. There were a few great moments of comedy from the drinking antics of Margaret played by Bríd Maloney. We were so surprised to see the reformed Margaret at the end of the show, who was almost like a different person. A nice wee character performance Bríd. The Chairman of the Board Mr Tinsworthy was played with great style by Lorcan Dunne. He injected a bit of energy into the plot towards the end of the show. This was a small but memorable performance. Hart's wife Missy was portrayed by Caoimhe Doyle who really captured this tortured but at the same time defiant woman. She added much to the scenes in which she appeared. Other parts were well played and contributed much to the show's success. The chorus were of all ages from office lads to more senior staff members. Everyone on stage created a wee character of their own and shared that with us the audience. I just wish the chorus ad lib moves had been choreographed, as at times it did look like they were moving in circles with no set purpose. The chorus sang and danced well and were always reacting to everything happening on stage.

One problem I had with this show was the rather dull lighting. Looking around, I could see a huge array of lights but at times feet were being brightly lit while faces were shadowed. It didn't help that there were overhead stage lights which shone directly down plunging faces into semi darkness. We were always told, 'If they can't see you, they can't hear you!' this might be old hat but at times this was true as we were not focussed on who we should look at. There was possibly a technical glitch on the night I attended and I hope it was resolved. There were however some nice lighting moments such as the spotlight at end of 'Here For You'. The sound was generally well executed and sound cues were accurately carried through. There was a slightly tinny feel to the sound for some of the characters. I loved most of the properties used on stage, the desks with their painted panels worked well, I loved the typewriters, very in keeping with the show, the desk phones, all the smaller details such as the revolving phone book. I think though that flashy Franklin might have had a trendy new desk. Overall good attention to detail with the props.

This was a huge costume plot and I congratulate the team for a job well done. The chorus women had a great mixture of appropriate styles and colours of dresses and two pieces. Our principal women were carefully differentiated by very different clothes which quickly helped us to recognise them. I loved all of Judy's outfits, most of Violet's and all of Doralee's, especially the lovely red blouse. Killer heels were in evidence, just not sure how anyone can walk, let alone dance in those. The hospital uniforms were authentic. I loved those purple blouses in Roz's big number though I thought identical skirts would have been better. Roz appeared back from her French lessons in great style, red scarf, beret and shoes. She looked wonderful.

Hair and makeup were all fine. Jennifer's nice Dolly wig was stunning.

The hairstyles all looked very much of the era. A few characters might have needed a wee touch more make-up. The eighties were times of excess and the clothes, hair and makeup created that effectively in this production.

To sum up, this was a most entertaining show with some great performances. There were a few things to do with the presentation of the show on stage which could be easily resolved. Thank you to everyone who greeted us so warmly to St Michael'sTheatre, I hope the rest of the run went well.

Released on Broadway in 1997, coincidently the same year as James Cameron's blockbuster film, 'Titanic - The Musical' won public and critical acclaim garnering five Tony awards.

The well-documented, ill-fated Titanic, pride of the White Star Line, sadly sank during its maiden voyage in 1912. On board were over two thousand, two hundred and twenty-seven people. To maximise space in the first class areas of the ship, which was where the lifeboats were stored, there were only enough lifeboats for half that number. During the pandemonium of evacuation, none of these lifeboats were at capacity. Only seven hundred were saved. Most of these were first and second-class passengers. The majority of the drowned were from third class.

Titanic - The Musical was quite a political piece, focusing on the class divide, the well healed embarking on a holiday experience and the poorer hoping to seek their fortune in America, where the streets were paved with gold. It also highlighted the greed of the owner and pride of the designer. It also called into question the professionalism of the Captain and crew. Dunamaise Arts Centre, whilst a fabulous and well-regarded community resource, doesn't have a very large stage. So, when I arrived I wondered how they would stage such a huge piece of contemporary theatre. Although Titanic - The Musical is not a traditional popular musical, and there have been chamber versions done in the past, it has a huge score, is mostly sung through and requires a large ensemble to do the choral pieces justice. Massive challenges for cast and creatives and how daring for Portlaoise Musical Society and director Paul Norton for attempting it. The Dunamaise foyer was awash with Titanic memorabilia and an exhibition mounted on the walls by local schoolchildren. A children's string quartet was playing live as background music and a huge poster detailing the names of all who were on board the ship was hung on one of the walls, as was done on the original Broadway production. When we received our tickets we were also given a small piece of paper with a passenger name and encouraged to see if our person lived or died. A bit ghoulish, but it did provoke us to read through the big list. Sadly, my passenger never made it.

The set, designed by the reputable John Wright was basically a representation of an area of the ship. It was beautifully finished, with clean lines, portholes, two levels and side flats dressed as bulkheads. Two doors were set upstage under the bridge and they became cabin doors, a cleverly pulled out radio room and access to the third-class decks. A small boat was suspended from the setting line bar and information such as location, date and time was regularly projected onto its surface. Later in the piece, the boat was flown in and some of the survivors boarded it to escape the sinking vessel. During the final moments of the production the upstage platform started to list quite effectively and passengers and crew could be seen to slide off it into the abyss. During the scenes in the boiler room, the actors lifted four traps in the stage, which vividly represented the engine room, lit in an intense red. This was an absolutely brilliant set, the attention to detail, the cleverness of multi-function and the pristine look of it all was marvellous. To cap it off they even had a small hydraulic platform dressed as a crow's nest from which Crewman Fleet first spotted the iceberg.

Lighting by Nick Anton was very atmospheric, with good use of haze and dry ice. Some lovely tight focusing on the portholes, a range of blues, a practical chandelier and effective use of floor lights blended well into the production. Vinny Osborne's sound was perfectly balanced; the singers were crystal clear and the band powerful. His sound effects were also very good, the sound of the sea and waves were evocative and the sound of the ship hitting the iceberg at the end of Act One was terrifyingly deeply effective as was the groaning and metal rending of a ship falling apart. Bob O'Kelly and his team handled stage management very efficiently and successfully on such a huge show.

Costuming by the Theatrical Costume Company was perfect. Showing the class differences between the passengers through dress was well done and the crew uniforms were simple yet accurate. Make up and wigs by Maria Corcoran was elaborate where needed and inconspicuously subtle given how close the audience was to the stage. Props by Eva Fairbrother were very authentic. I really liked the large scale of the ships blueprints and the maritime paraphernalia and a brilliant touch was the blankets the survivors were wrapped in. They were printed with the word Carpathia, which was the name of the rescue ship.

Musical director/Chorus Mistress and Conductor on this show was Emer Hartnett. Her work with the ensemble was impressive. Their harmonies, pace and timing were perfect and very powerfully emotional. Ms Hartnett's band of ten sounded much larger than their number. The lush orchestral sound really did justice to the swirling symphonic score. Some of the music is written as swells, peaks and troughs mimicking the sea and Ms Hartnett's arrangements captured this perfectly.

This is not a conventional production in that there is no central love story, no boy meets girl, loses girl, gets girl back kind of plot. Instead it centres on two issues; mankind's technological aspirations and mankind's aspiration to better themselves socially or in the case of the Upper Class, retain their status. This and the quality of the score is what separates it from many recent 'jukebox musicals'. It also has a huge cast of characters.

Some of the actors were preset on stage when we entered the auditorium, the projection told us we were in the iconic Harland and Wolff Shipyard and here we met the ship's designer, Thomas Andrews, wonderfully played by Eoghan Fingleton. He sang In Every Age and played the character of the designer with a naive simplicity, believing global transportation is the future for all of mankind. Later, as the ship is going down he remained, obsessing as to how he could redesign it in Mr Andrew's Vision. He had a wonderful duet with Ismay, The Blame, where they argued over whose fault it was that the ship was sinking. The ship's owner, J. Bruce Ismay was portrayed by Alex Cathcart. Written as the only antagonist in the piece, Mr Cathcart played him as a highly strung, cowardly bully, ordering the Captain to go faster to enhance the ship's reputation despite being advised by Andrews and Smith that it would be unwise. Captain E.J. Smith was sympathetically played by Paul Spencer. He exuded a commanding presence but also showed a distinct vulnerability. All three sang The Largest Floating Object In The World, where they had superb complementary voices and really delivered the excitement they felt of being a part of history.

Gradually we were introduced to more crew, Daniel Whelan as the young radio officer Harold Bride really impressed with his characterisation and sang well on a number of songs most notably The Proposal/The Night Was Alive which he shared with Barrett perfectly played by Shane Kelly who also excelled on How Did They Build Titanic and Barrett's Song (The Screws Are Turning). Similarly, David Walshe as Frederick Fleet was impressive particularly on No Moon, where he is in the Crow's Nest and sees the iceberg looming. Mr Walshe has a wonderful rich voice, which cut through the intense Finale in Act One. Cian Mac Gearailt as 1st Officer Murdoch, who was at the helm when the ship crashed played his mind-numbing guilt brilliantly and Donal Brennan as 2nd Officer Lightoller performed well as did Sean O'Neill who played two characters; Quartermaster Hitchens and Bandsman Bricoux. Colm O'Toole also skilfully played two characters; 3rd Officer Pitman and the cantankerous, long-winded Major, one of the few comic characters in the piece. Further crew members included a lovely delicate performance from Charlene Duff as the Bellboy, an emotional and stoic performance from Jason O'Reilly as the Steward who really cares about the passengers, particularly the older ones. The Stevedore was strongly played by Jamie O'Callahan, who sang well on There She Is and John Coss portrayed a wonderfully camp but officious Harry Etches and sang well on What A Remarkable Age This Is. Paul Kenna also played two characters; Bandmaster Wallace Hartley, who sang Autumn quite well and Chief Engineer Joseph Bell. The three Irish girls, all named Kate, who meet for the first time in line to board the ship were all excellently portrayed, they embodied the hopes and dreams of the poor Europeans wishing to better themselves in the New World. Aishling Rohan, who played the pregnant Kate McGowan, sets her sights on Jim Farrell, solidly played by J.J. Tynan, as a potential father for her child. Their scene during the long Finale of Act One was very touching. The two other Kate's, Zeta O'Reilly as Murphy and Jayne Louise Kelly as Mullins, also did wonderfully well particularly during Lady's Maid.

Ida and Isidor Strauss, the older couple, were played movingly by Dawn Kavanagh and Aidan Delaney. Their duet Still, where Ida decided to stay with her husband rather than taking to the lifeboats brought a tear to many an eye in the audience. Michael Lillis played the millionaire Astor who, with his pregnant young bride, Madeleine played with child-like vulnerability by Aishling Kelly, epitomised the privilege of the Upper Class as did Frank Egan as Guggenheim and Julia Cahill as Madame Aubert. Hilary Treacy as Edith Corse Evans and Joan White as Charlotte Cardoza were very believable in their portrayals as was Angi McNulty and John Lynch as the well- off Widener couple whose stage son was unaccredited on the programme. Brian Rohan played J.H. Rogers, the swindler very satisfactorily. Conor Harte and Teresa Lynch as the Thayers performed well as did Claire Carroll.

In second class the piece focused on two couples specifically. Charles Clarke played by David Wrest and Caroline Neville played by Suzanne Lillis as the eloping couple, off to find a new life away from family influence. They played it elegantly, their relationship finely honed and quite sweet. Alice and Edgar Beane were brilliantly played by Louise Moore and Rory Chadwick. Their comic timing was faultless as were their accents. Ms Moore sang wonderfully, she has a beautiful voice and amazing articulation particularly evident on The First Class Roster. A special mention must go the wonderful child performers featured in this production, many of them played 3rd Class passengers trapped during the sinking which had a devastating effect on the audience, others played more well- heeled passengers of privilege with gusto. Choreography on the production was by Grace McGrath. Her work on the traditional 'Irish' dances in third class was uplifting and her choreography on the upper-class deck ball was elegant. However, it was her innovative addition of three white clad superb contemporary dancers during the finale of Act One that was a standout moment of this production for me. Representing the iceberg, the three wraith-like dancers interwove around all of the passengers during the lead up to the crash, contacting with each and every passenger and crew member. Their dance became more and more frenetic and emotional as the ship came closer to disaster, almost as if nature itself was trying to intervene and halt the course of fate. A wonderfully evocative end to a first act as ever I've seen.

Director Paul Norton created a fabulous production, his attention to detail and mentorship of his cast was exemplary. His artistic vision for the piece was lucidly delivered to the other creatives and he clearly inspired all involved to produce their best work. This production was a fitting tribute, not just to the writers of the show, but to those brave souls who lost their lives and to those who survived. Portlaoise Musical Society is to be lauded for creating a truly civic production, the involvement of the wider community of crafts people and in particular children and young people, onstage and offstage, created not just a local show but an exceptional event to remember by all involved and those who were lucky enough to see it.

What a way to make a living!

Dolly Parton (on video) opened this show by Harold's Cross and Tallaght Musical Society at the Civic Theatre by telling the audience it was watching a musical set back when there was no cell phones and when women couldn't be promoted to positions of power. She popped up again at the end wishing us well and singing a bar or two of the titular number. The audience lapped it up but I must admit I found this very odd and couldn't see Mr Lloyd-Webber doing it. But this is an odd show, written in 2009 and based on a film made and set in the late '70s/ early '80s about office politics and a misogynist boss (Franklin Hart Jnr.) vs his rebelling staff (Violet, Judy and Doralee). It is an engagingly old-fashioned, simple story full of Dolly songs and lewd slapstick, with a Scooby Doo thin plot and, in this version, some wonderful performances.

It started out with the ensemble asleep on the stage floor under blankets and duvets. I think beds would have been more appropriate as it looked like a teenager's sleepover, but the Civic stage is not that big, so perhaps they ditched the beds in favour of a bigger ensemble being onstage. They all woke up to and sang the opening number '9 to 5' and quite literally performed the actions of the song. This segued into a very well- choreographed, by Lea Carroll, dance routine. Ms Carroll's work on the show was very accomplished, particularly on the fantasy sequences; 'Dance of Death', 'Cowgirl's Revenge' (pictured overleaf) and 'Potion Notion' where three different styles of choreography were on show. However, her work with Violet and the Male Ensemble on 'One of The Boys' in Act Two was outstanding. Reminiscent of a Busby Berkeley musical of the '30s, Violet and the boys danced some very complex and decorative patterns that would challenge some professional dancers.

In the opening scene, most of the cast were under lit or not lit at all. This continued into the show, with some states so dark that we could not discern who was on stage. It did settle after a while and I suspect that some of the front of house was tweaked in and out manually. That said there was the most exciting use of movers, by designer Darren Kelleher, I've seen in a while, swirling with the music on some numbers and they came into their own during Judy's fantasy sequence 'Dance of Death'.

Musical direction on this shown was by Dermot O'Callahan. His musical arrangements added a certain home- spun country and western feel to the majority of the show, not surprising as all the tunes were written by Dolly. His work with the offstage chorus in particular shone through. There were a couple of musical genres explored in the score, from jazz to hoedown to big brassy Broadway numbers, but Mr O'Callaghan worked well with his band to authentically deliver each style. As the Civic does not have a pit, the band was sequestered way upstage but out of sight. I have no idea how many were in the band as there was no band credits in the programme. But I liked the guitar work and the percussion was resonant. As mentioned, I thought the ensemble was top notch on this show. They had some lovely harmonies on 'Nine to Five Finale' and 'Shine Like the Sun' and provided powerful backing to some of the other numbers.

A very clever set design by Marie Cusack, who also stage managed, saw the office desks connected to the chairs on castors, making scene changes very easy. A large cut out skyline upstage showed the city. Hart's office was beautifully finished, with bookshelves, a large desk and chairs. His bedroom was also very well done, with him being trussed and trucked on and off very effectively. The hospital scene was well represented by hospital screens on castors, and the bathroom scene with the two toilets worked quite well.

Costumes by Martina Foreman, Joan Kelly, Rosaleen Nolan and Martin Heffernan were suitable for the era and well fitted. I particularly liked Judy's fantasy scene dress, sparkly and form fitting and Violet's 'One of the Boys' costume. Doralee's country and western outfits were great as was Hart's suit. Wigs by Ali Murphy were super and looked real and make-up by Catherine Coventry was well applied and suited the characters.

Damien Hurley as Franklin Hart Jnr, really grasped his role with both hands in this production. He relished every scenery chewing, cartoonish moment, with his Tom Selleck mustache and a fierce misogyny, he epitomised male privilege in business with gusto. His comic timing was excellent as was his physicality in the more slapstick moments. Vocally he was super too, his 'Here for You' is probably the most sexist song ever written and he hammed it up perfectly.

As Violet Newstead, Julie Donnelly commanded the stage in every scene she was in. Playing the hard-working widow, she was totally believable. Her scenes with the younger office worker, Joe - nicely played by Stephen Fagan, were tender and they had a good chemistry. Similarly, her scenes with her stage son, Josh well played by Jordan Bass, were believable and conveyed her sweet maternal nature. Ms Donnelly's stand out moment was on 'One of the Boys', where she sang and danced brilliantly with the male ensemble. Serena Salmon performed Doralee Rhodes with an exuberant good ol' girl energy. Ms Salmon played her sub-text very well and really projected the character's life-long problem of being misunderstood with a fine touch. Her singing was particularly memorable on 'Cowgirl's Revenge' and 'Backwoods Barbie'. James Pierce as her husband, Dwayne with his ever-present bandana, gave a solid performance as the supporting partner.

As Roz Keith, Kelly-Marie Davy really radiated competence and bitchiness in equal measure. Her love for Hart, although bizarre as he was such a monster, was well played and surprisingly convincing. She performed a wonderful '5 to 9', showcasing a fabulous voice coupled with an amazing energy.

Gavin O'Reilly as Dick, Judy's ex, did what he could with a drastically underwritten role but he didn't have much to work with. Stand out performance on the night was Jaqueline Brunton as Judy Bernly. Ms Brunton's comic timing was excellent, she played the character as physically awkward and innocent, Judy's reactions were always a second later than everyone else. Her pathos was also brilliantly executed, we genuinely felt sorry for her and were willing her to succeed. Her performance of 'Get Out and Stay Out', brought the house down. Ms Brunton's masterful control and emotional investment during this song was stunning. In this fluffy, feel-good, yet divisive show, her performance of the song brought the whole show to another, higher, level. Her characterisation of Judy was peerless. Director Art McGauran did a good job on this show. Yes, it is hammy and creaky and out of date already, but he had such a light touch with the comedy, it worked. The staging was quite good in places; the fantasy sequences were well handled and the office scenes were well rendered. The pacing of the production was quite fast as it should be, and there were some lovely set pieces.

His casting of the principals was excellent, particularly Mr Hurley and Ms Brunton and his work with the ensemble, together with the MD and choreographer, raised the show to a higher level. However, the Dolly videos brought it all back down to a crassness he was clearly trying to conquer! But, I suspect one has to show them as part of the licence. Which is a shame as the production was better than that.

Every Heart Awaken Michael Collins - A Musical Drama, was a real labour of love for its' creator Bryan Flynn. Many years in the making in collaboration with different venues and numerous creatives, the show centres on the years and activists during and following the Easter Rising in 1916. Like a cross between Les Miserables and Evita with a W.B. Yeats play at its centre, this is a complex piece of theatre that requires many talents and abilities to do it justice. Coolmine Musical Society has been in operation for a long time and have won many accolades for their productions, so when I made my way to Draíocht, I knew that they would certainly have the experience to stage it well, but would they have the passion that's required to deliver the pathos.

I need not have been concerned as from the outset, with the Players preparing for their roles in simple mimic gesture on the apron in front of a black gauze, I knew we were in for a treat. Opening with such mesmerising theatricality, whilst the audience were still entering the auditorium was a superb device that set the stage for what was to come.

High production values by Coolmine ensured that this biographical show where we followed the life and times and eventual martyrdom of Cork's most famous son was given the respect it deserved.

Collins was played by Kevin Fagan and whilst smaller in stature than the Big Fella, he delivered a very fine performance. His acting was nuanced and strong, his rock tenor singing was well modulated, dramatic and articulate. His stand out songs were; 'Survival of the Fittest and his duet with De Valera 'Confrontation'.

Kitty Kiernan, the woman at the centre of the love triangle involving Collins and Harry Boland, was played by Nicole Lamb. She had a wonderful musical theatre voice, her belt was exceptionally smooth and she poured great emotion into her singing. I particularly liked her work with Harry on 'For Nothing Else I Cared' and her duet with Collins 'Our Love Will Never End'. Her performance was imbued with an elegant delicacy and she was an excellent casting choice. Equally, Liam Egan as Harry Boland was very well cast. Showing a naked vulnerability beneath the fervour, he played the role with self- possession and a fine balance. He sang well throughout but especially well on 'Not That Man', where he held that last note perfectly for its' duration.

De Valera was played by Seamus Sullivan. His singing was strong and his parlando was good. His characterisation of Dev was however a trifle strange. He played him as very stiff and wooden and whilst De Valera was a formal character, I felt that Mr Sullivan's interpretation of this stoicism was too villainous.

I was very taken with Colin Flynn's performance as Joe Emmet (pictured top right surrounded by "the players"), from the first scene he radiated a youthful warmth and eager intensity to help Collins. His character's journey from innocence to terrorism was subtly executed and on point.

The Players were outstanding in their character(s). Bouncing from Greek Chorus to the Abbey Players, they spanned genres effortlessly. Kathy Kelly and Jim Walsh as the older Players exuded experienced stagecraft and morphed from poor rural peasants to the higher status of narrators with ease. Matthew Williams and Orla Walsh as the younger Players, had a tangible vitality and were equally adept at this dual characterisation. As Player5/Mother Ireland, the relatively young Niamh Carroll convinced as a much older character and her sean nós singing was eerily memorable. Her stillness and presence were fascinating to watch. With the exception of Collins, this quartet had the lion's share of singing in the musical as they narrate, perform characters in the play within the play and sing with most of the principals. Their precision, unity and individual distinctive voices were a most welcome and elegant respite from the sometimes full-on emotional expressiveness of the ensemble.

Other notable mentions were, Michael Flynn as Arthur Griffith and Ciaran Lenehan as Cathal Brugha, both showed great musical timing in 'Treaty Debates'. Despite Mr Flynn's mic not working, he projected brilliantly and we didn't miss a word.

Michael Collins is obviously not a Broadway dance show and doesn't have many routines or dance numbers for a choreographer to get their teeth into. However I'm sure choreographer Nicole McDonald was an enormous help with the fight, group and battle scenes as they looked very well-rehearsed and more importantly, safe. The use of freezes and slow-motion was very effective too. The prison scene, where the male chorus sang 'Frongoch Prison Song', was very well staged with the choreography physicalising their powerlessness.

The opening scene with the Isadora Duncan'esque scarves dance was quite ethereal and worked well.

This set was quite sympathetically designed. Upstage we had a platform, mostly used by Mother Ireland, flanked by sections of two story houses. The Abbey stage was cleverly built in two sections and trucked in from left and right to join at centre. Some scenes were created by simply bringing on furniture and there was great use of the downstage left and right pros by the Players and to isolate characters. During the street battle scenes a barricade was trucked on where the actors could hide behind and this was particularly effective.

Clearly a lot of imagination went into this set by designer Dave Benson and the build quality was very good. It really captured the mood of the piece as most of the set dressing was distressed, looking like a war zone or at times an area suffering great deprivation. Collin's mobile podium was trucked on and off and even used by Dev at one point. It could spin 360 degrees and looked perfectly in period. The flying in of the tattered tricolour was cleverly divisive and the downstage black gauze was used very well, particularly at the start of the show.

Projections by Donal Cantwell were splendidly designed and constructed, showing newspaper headlines and time and place, reducing the need for exposition.

Lighting by Denis Twomey was quite good, however I felt the sound was a tad too loud and we missed some of the lyrics on the bigger numbers as they became quite muddy. Costumes by Nomac were of the era and hair and make-up by Ali Murphy was very good, particularly the ageing make up on Mother Ireland.

The eight-piece band, lined up across the front of the stage on the auditorium floor, was comprised of violin, two keyboards, clarinet, French horn, drums & percussion, guitar and electric bass. They played accurately, were tight and their tempo was good. Musical Direction by Dave McGauran was excellent. His mastery and clear admiration of the music enhanced the delivery, by a committed band, of this emotional production. Mr McGauran's excellent work as Chorus Master ensured that even the weaker singers, and there weren't many of them, blended well. The tracking was very effective too, particularly the uilleann pipes and additional percussion. The live band blended well with the tracks and we couldn't discern any joints.

This was a very good show, the Director, Pat McElwain, did a fine job in bringing the story and all of the themes and passion to the stage. The pace was perfect, it never lagged, which is quite good for such a long show. The settings were professionally rendered and expertly placed, the blocking of the actors was natural and the sheer emotion rolling off the stage was palpable. Mr McElwain clearly infected the cast with his passion and enthusiasm for the work and it showed in their performances and their tears during the curtain call. A well-deserved standing ovation by an emotionally wrung out audience, told Coolmine that yes, they did awaken our hearts and definitely projected the pathos and also that terrible beauty of a turbulent era in Irish history.

The Siamsa Tíre in Tralee is quite an imposing sight, set back from the road just a short walk away from the bustling town centre. The foyer is a wonderful space with curved stone wall, pleasant sitting area and bar. We were warmly greeted by the beautifully attired Ena, who was a great help throughout the evening. The auditorium has wide curved and tiered seating areas and the most comfortable seats.

There was a scrim about midway across an open stage, through this we got the impression of the staging behind. There were illuminated fairground signs which set the scene and created interest. The side flats were of a slightly three- dimensional quality which lit well during the show, adding texture to the panel. There was no music playing which was a pity, as I think this adds a bit of a buzz and gives an opportunity for the audience to be familiarised with an unknown score. This production was accompanied by a recorded track which was a good sound quality and created a nice balance between singing and music throughout. The settings for this show were produced by John Hurley. WOW! This was a touch of genius. The settings were projected onto the flats on stage creating wonderful surrealistic scenes which were ever- changing. The time, effort and expertise that John showed in his design were quite staggering. We had butterflies flying, a stunning Emerald City scene, balloons taking off - you name it. The stage became alive with all this movement and wonderful colourful. I would have one criticism about this effect. Because it was projected from the back of the auditorium and not from above the acting area as it is usually done, the images also projected on our cast. Due to this we at times lost the clarity of these figures on stage, and most importantly facial expressions. This needed to be counter-balanced by some more front lighting on the cast. This was a very exciting and innovative way of creating scenery, not one that would suit every show, but in the Oz fantasy world it was stunning.

There was a huge cast of enthusiastic and talented young people involved in this show. You can't force a genuine sparkle from the eyes of everyone on stage unless they are all really having a great time. This group showed us that they were enjoying every moment. A huge part of this must be the excellent way in which they were directed by Oliver Hurley. Oliver grabbed every opportunity to involve as many of the cast into the production as possible. He created a 'waistcoated' backing group who appeared from time to time throughout the production, adding visual and vocal backing to many of the big musical numbers. The Munchkins were played by the youngest members of the troupe, who were all so involved in the production. There were huge dance sequences.

These were so neatly executed by the team. There were great arm movements with super extension to the tips of fingers. The routines involving Dorothy and 'the boys' were slick and fun. The 'Tornado Ballet' was a riot of twirling moves in some very voluminous costumes. The show was moved well and dance routines seamlessly segued from dialogue.

Oliver had gathered together a very talented cast of principals for this show. Originally a vehicle for the vocal talents of Michael Jackson and Diana Ross, there are some difficult 'RnB' songs for the leading players, demanding a lot vocally from this young group. They managed superbly with the challenge, Laura Crowley had obviously worked hard with the cast, especially the principals. Clodagh Harrington blew us away with the opening number 'The Feeling We Once Had'. Sarah Cleary sang powerfully throughout. I loved Matthew Dineen's tone, especially in 'I Was Born On The Day Before Yesterday'. Padraig Harrington gave us a really soulful 'Slide Some Oil On Me' and Marcus Nolan had touches of Barry White in 'Mean Ole Lion'. Laura created some lovely harmonies between the principals such as in 'Be A Lion' when the two voices blended delightfully. The chorus also created some harmonious moments when singing on stage or in the wings.

The sound system was in the capable hands of Murt Whelan Sound Ltd. The backing track was always on cue and there was good balance between the accompaniment and the singers on stage - and thanks too for those occasional sound effects such as the dog barking at the beginning of the show.

The cast worked their socks off throughout the show, always keeping in character, always convincing in their various roles and maintaining their accents so well. Dorothy was played with so much fire by Sarah Cleary. Not only could Sarah deliver some of these very difficult songs, but she acted through the whole range of emotions in this show. She built up very believable relationships with 'the boys'. This was a nicely judged and acted performance. 'The boys' in question made a great on stage team. Matthew Dineen surprised us all with his rich deep southern tones. He captured the essence of Scarecrow with his floppy body moves and turning, twisting and falling at the drop of a hat. Matthew entertained us with the characterisation from his first appearance on the helter-skelter to the end of the show. Padraig Harrington was a great Tinman. He moved so well on his first appearance, slowly coming to life limb by limb. He too acted and sang in a style which fitted the part so well. Lion was portrayed with so much macho charm by Marcus Nolan. His rich voice and great movements using the whole stage area created a wonderful persona. He really provided so much humour in his performance with his easy delivery of lines. Pierse O'Brien was very mature in his performance as The Wiz. He managed to capture the overpowering 'Great Wiz' and also the discovered 'fake' equally as well. He moved around the stage with great 'watchability'. Aunt Em was beautifully sung and sympathetically acted by Clodagh Harrington. She gave the role the maturity which it needed and we were convinced that she was much older than Dorothy. Katie-Anne Harris made Addaperle into a wonderfully colourful comedic character with real 'attitude', very in the style of 'Legally Blonde'. Aoife O'Mahony gave us a powerful and strong rock chick performance as the nasty Evillene. She blasted her way through her dialogue and belted out her musical numbers with great venom. I felt sorry for Dominick Hurley as Monkey, Eoin Griffin as Lord Underling and particularly Jordan Tearle as Messenger, who all caught the terror of Evillene. Well played boys for your portrayals of these smaller yet important roles. I feel I have to mention Sorcha Ringland as Glinda. She entered in semi-darkness sitting on a carousel horse which was lit by fairy lights. The horse miraculously rose and fell as it galloped across the stage. The effect was wonderful. Also wonderful was the singing of the rider. This was such a magical moment when vocal, performance and staging combined to produce one special and unforgettable picture on stage.

The chorus of 'The Wiz' made a huge contribution to the show's success. They were always there supporting the action, listening, focusing our attention. They all sang out, there wasn't one person who wasn't committed on stage, not one who wasn't giving their all in their singing and dance routines. The future of musical theatre is safe, keep acting and singing everyone!

The look of the show was enhanced by great costumes. With the number of cast involved on stage, this was a huge costuming challenge, so well done to the costume team who obviously went that extra mile. Some of the creations on stage were extraordinary, such as the wonderful 'space invaders' costume in 'Kalidah Battle'.

The principals' costumes all worked really well. Dorothy in her red checked short skirt, T-shirt with touches of gingham, leather jacket and sneakers (later to be replaced by a beautiful pair of glittery silver court shoes) The Witches all had a different identity due to some wonderful fantasy outfits. Addaperle's dress was particularly extraordinary with a sort of crinoline effect. I loved the simplicity but effectiveness of the Munchkins' costumes. Pastel colours of T-shirts teamed with matching jeans and trainers looked very striking on stage. The principal men in their interpretation of the original Scarecrow costume, in this case a pinstripe suit with patches, a leather look silver Tinman's suit and glorious Lion costume, completed by a stunning Rasta wig. The wigs throughout, such as Evillene's black and red creation, were wonderful. The make-up was appropriate. The principal men had character make- up which was beautifully applied. The rest of the make-up for chorus was quite naturalistic but consistent.

The staging was not just created by the use of projections, there were also moving trucked panels which became the onstage screens for the projections. These were moved seemingly effortlessly into place by a well-drilled stage team. There were also big pieces such as the fairground helter-skelter which later became the hillside on which we discover Scarecrow, a roller-coaster car which appeared carrying Lion into the scene, and of course that magical bobbing horse which was cleverly operated with a bit of brute force but looked so entrancing on stage. Smaller props were few but were in character with the show such as the green Ozian sunglasses.

This was a polished and visually stunning show, with great commitment shown by everyone on stage and a huge support given to the Tralee Musical Society's Youth by the more senior members of the company. I know that many of The Wiz's cast will be leading players in the adult society. I wish them all future success.

Lime Tree Theatre in Mary Immaculate College in Limerick is a most interesting space. It obviously doubles as a lecture hall during the day but can be used as an excellent theatre space in the evenings. The steeply tiered auditorium gives each seat an excellent view of the stage and creates an excellent acoustic from the stage area. From my seat in row G I had a perfect view of the action. The rich velvet curtains were drawn at the beginning of the show and the sound of Michael Young's Orchestra tuning up could be heard. Michael had gathered together a group of ten musicians who worked excellently together to interpret this tricky fast paced score. This was musical direction and playing to the highest level. There was a wonderful blend of sound and the tempo of all the musical numbers was excellent throughout. The balance between stage and orchestra was perfect and we could hear every word of every song which is so important in this show as there is so much humour in each musical piece. The cast all sang their parts excellently and had all clearly been rehearsed extremely thoroughly. There was an unfortunate glitch in the microphone system in the second half of the show which was sorted quite quickly but did cause a lack of pace at one point.

The director of this production was Des Henn who added wonderful nuances into the production. The humour of the piece was extracted to perfection and delivered so well by a most talented cast. The movement of principles and chorus was excellent throughout the show. Everyone was so well chosen for the role they played and they played it very convincingly maintaining the correct accent throughout in most cases. The choreographer of this show was Barbara Meany who created some stunning and inventive choreography for the show. From the beginning with the four usherettes whose detailed movements were perfectly in time with each other, to the huge finale, this was a delightfully choreographed production and one of which Barbara should be most proud. She was working with a fantastic team of dancers and a strong chorus. One number that I particularly enjoyed was 'I Wanna Be A Producer' which had a team of girls in smart silver dresses creating all sorts of patterns on stage. Barbara's choreography rose to crescendos paused and then rose again, this really is to me what good choreography is it all about. She also used the words of the songs so well to create storytelling through her dance movements. A job well done Barbara.

There was a very talented cast in the show who played each role so extraordinarily well. Dickie Donnelly made a great Max Bialystock. His adventures with the older women were hilarious and he managed to get a wonderful mix of panic and humour into his portrayal. Dickie has a great singing voice and the tone of his voice really suited the character he was playing. Leo Bloom was played beautifully by Jason Ronan. We loved watching Jason hugging his little blue blankie. I loved his optimism about the world, willing him to leave his job in the boring office to become a Broadway producer. He has a very pleasing singing voice and showed it off to good effect in all of his musical numbers. Wow! Tara Downes was a wonderful Ulla. She looked the part, she acted the part and she sang the part, always in character. She had us all entranced with her Swedish accent and her impeccable comic timing. This is an actress who can move extraordinarily well around the stage using the whole stage area to create memorable dance moments. Well done Tara.

James Malone was an over the top Carmen and his on-stage partner Roger played by Brian Henry were both great creators of sublimely hilarious moments. There was no shortage of camping it up for these two. I loved the bitter sweet relationship they had together. They delivered their rendition of 'Springtime For Hitler' with great style, producing a great wee moment of musical theatre. 'Keep It Gay' was another highlight with the gathering of all sorts of artsy characters. Franz Liebkind was played well with a lack of Germanic charm by Barry Danaher. Barry created a totally wacky Nazi-loving character. He sang well and moved well around the stage, always in character. We all loved his dancing pigeons and those lederhosen!

There was a wonderful group of dancers and chorus who for me really added the professional gloss to this production. They showed commitment to every scene they were in and those brilliant, expressive faces always added just the right amount of showbiz in their smiling eyes that gave the show a real class. There were so many beautifully played cameo roles in this show. Well done Hold Me, Touch Me played by Clíodhna de Paor and Lick Me, Bite Me portrayed by Gráinne Hartnett, hilarious. Roger's Team gave us a real mix of brilliant characters of all shapes and sizes! Other parts, mostly played by Glen Carr, contributed much to the success of the evening.

The staging of the show, cleverly managed by Ray Burke, was fascinating. There was a pair of box-like trucks which could be moved and opened to reveal different scenes. We had nicely painted and functioning doors of the theatre, the stage walls and doors for the auditioning scene, then the panels opened to reveal a detailed office scene with windows, functioning doors, painted wainscot and book shelves. The whole thing revolved again to become Roger's apartment. This was a substantial piece of scenery and it did take a little while to set up but we were captivated as to what was going to happen next so it didn't really distract from the flow of this production. Everyone quite obviously had their job to do so scene changes were sharp. The props used to finish the sets were all in keeping and looked authentic, such as the step ladder, adding machines and work stations. I was however disappointed with the lighting in the show. At times this was excellent and created wonderful effects such as when the posters at the sides of the stage were correctly lit, either from behind or with bulbs encircling them. The general lighting was quite dull at times which slightly cut us off from the action. Cues were a bit tardy at times. There was also a roving lighting effect which really had no place in this production. This was just confusing and really made no sense. Overall the sound plot was well managed and there was a good sound quality with a nice balance between stage and pit. A pity we had a wee blip with a microphone in Act Two, it happens.

The costumes throughout were stunning with great attention to detail. The principals' costumes were all great fitting, especially Ulla's which looked as though she had been sewn into them, a perfect fit. The chorus costumes were many and varied. I loved the red usherette costumes, the silver show girls' outfits, the wonderful 'Springtime For Hitler' set of costumes. The old lady dresses and hats were great. Where appropriate there were matching shoes though I would ask that sets, such has these should be double checked in future as a wee difference in shoes or socks doesn't seem important but it really catches the audience's eye on stage. The make-up was very cleverly applied in the show as it was strong enough, especially the girls' eyes and lips, to appear to be show makeup from a different era. The hairs were all in appropriate styles and the wigs were well set. There was an almost 1950's style created. This worked well with the overall feel of the show which didn't really have a set time zone.

This was a wonderful evening of Broadway glamour and just great fun. It was a slickly directed show which was very well cast. The choreography was intricate and well- rehearsed. We had a great team of dancers and chorus. Musically it was a delight. This was a good show from a great team. Well done The Cecilian Musical Society.

Based on the true story of the Von Trapp family, 'The Sound of Music' is undoubtedly the epitome of the classic stage and movie musical. Based on the blossoming love affair of Georg Von Trapp and Maria, the origins of the Anschluss in Austria and the family's exit to a brighter life in the United States. Obviously, there was a bit of poetic licence in the final Broadway production which opened in 1959 with the then forty-six-year-old Mary Martin as Maria. It was an instant hit and is still popular with audiences today. It was a pleasure to be back in Galway's Town Hall Theatre to see 9 Arch Claregalway Musical Society's production of the show. I attended on the opening night of the society's short four performance run. There were a few wee first night nerves which I am sure were sorted out during the rest of the run.

The show was gently directed by Jay Molyneux who explored the script to tease out as much humour as possible from it. There were some lovely touches in the direction such as how certain lines were delivered, how and when pauses were taken to maximum effect and some of the disapproving facial expressions were great. There were a few wee pieces which I would have directed differently and would have held a moment a little longer for dramatic effect. This is an important story which really shows how Hitler was able to manipulate minds such as Rolf and Franz, turning neighbour against neighbour and family against themselves. The horror of what was to come after the family left Austria should always be at the back of our minds.

Jay was also choreographer of this show. Although there is not much dancing as such in the show the stage movement was on the whole well thought through and executed, though there were opportunities for even more movement in the production. There was obviously a wide range of talent which I am sure could have risen to further challenges.

Shane Farrell conducted the nine-piece orchestra. This was a beautifully melodic interpretation of the score. The singing throughout the show was of a high standard. The chorus, particularly the huge chorus of nuns, at times created a wonderful depth of sound. The principals and those with just one or two lines in the show sang with conviction in a very tuneful and pleasing manner. The children had all great voices which made a beautiful blend together and sounded very good in their individual roles. Maria and the Captain's voices sounded very strong individually and harmonised well together.

Maria was beautifully played by Megan Lohan.

There was a well-scrubbed innocence in this portrayal. Megan looked the part, sang with a gorgeous tone and acted so well too. There were some lovely moments such as her confrontation with Von Trapp, the first meeting with the children and her subsequent winning them over and a nice scene in the bedroom with Frau Schmidt. She related well to the Captain and their love affair seemed very natural. Alan Greaney (above) gave us a slightly wittier Captain than usual, with a natural flair for comedy shown in some excellent delivery of his lines. He too had a beautiful tone to his singing voice and gave us a pleasing 'Edelweiss'.

Elsa was played with class by Anne O'Donnell. She moved so elegantly around the stage creating beautiful poses as she went. Her acting throughout was in keeping with the part and she has a stunning singing voice. Max who looked a bit like Georg's brother with the same body type, hair and beard differentiated himself with great comedy timing and a convincing American accent. This was a gentle and nicely paced performance. Annette Cavanagh who played the Mother Abbess did so with a great deal of dignity and gave us a wonderful version of 'Climb Every Mountain'.

Cian O Ceallaigh as Rolf and Saoirse McCarthy as Liesl worked well together as the ill-fated young lovers. Cian created a character who grew from a nervous young man to a determined Nazi who almost betrays the family. Cian moved round the stage well and I think I would have stretched his dancing skills much more than in the slightly lack lustre routine for 'Sixteen Going On Seventeen'. Liesl too looked as if she could have risen too much more of a challenge. As the eldest child in the family, Saoirse was most convincing, particularly in her growing friendship with Maria. This was a great performance with Saoirse showing a lovely maternal quality towards the other children. She sang well in all her musical numbers.

Franz, played by Michael Cooney, made an efficient butler who really can't be trusted. He was always there in a scene bringing information and pushing the story on. Olibhia Donnelly played a warm Frau Schmidt and I really didn't mind her using her own accent. David Alexander was a threatening Herr Zeller. Feargal Cavanagh played the Admiral von Schreiber with an experience and menace in his voice. The three principal nuns: Sister Bertha (Sonja Stevens), Sister Margaretta (Eve Garavan) and Sister Sophia (Katie Bebbington) were all excellent in their very individual roles. Each one created a particular stage character but they all worked so well together. The singing was great and we had a lovely version of 'Maria'. I particularly liked some of the looks of disgust poor Maria was given. The team of children did a great job right through the show. This is quite a long show and they never seemed to tire as the night progressed. Friedrich was the young man of the group. He delivered his lines really well, moved well round the stage and sang with a rich but very tuneful tone. Well done Keith Hanley for your interpretation of Friedrich and thanks for the laughs you gave us in 'Lonely Goatherd'. Louisa played by Alana Mullins had wonderful posture on stage. Her accent was impeccable and she managed to maintain it throughout the show. She sang gloriously and moved with such ease around the acting areas. Cameron Heneghan created a very believable Kurt. I loved his dancing with Maria at the ball. He sang brilliantly, how can we ever forget that last note in 'So Long Farewell'. Katie Larkin gave us quite a few belly laughs as the slightly outspoken Brigitta. Her delivery of lines was faultless. She too sang strongly and moved well also. Lucy Keenan made a lovely Marta. She had a wonderful stance on stage and she lit up the auditorium with that radiant smile. The youngest member of the family was Faye Greaney as little Gretl. Well done Faye you played your part so well. There were lovely moments with this character, like when she steps forward to bow but doesn't, Faye played this with such great comic timing. She also sang her solo line in 'So Long Farewell' so beautifully.

The setting of the show caused all sorts of problems which I hope were resolved after the opening night. The society had decided to use a series of painted cloths, some of which were beautifully painted. Cloths of this type then set a standard for all the properties, furniture etc which appears in front of them. I was very disappointed in the look that was created and also by the impracticality of giving so much of the stage area to a permanent hillside which was really only used at the start and end of the show.

This caused great congestion on the stage which was a big area and problems of this type with more creative planning just wouldn't have happened. I have seen quite a few shows recently which have used rotating trucks to give a seamless change, maybe an idea for next time. I would also advise that the stage team should constantly check that that black tabs are positioned so that they cover activity in the wings, unfortunately this was not the case in this show. The props were a mixed bag with some nice pieces of furniture, tea set etc. I really missed the tombstones or grille in the penultimate scene which was a bit flat with the family hiding behind one lectern.

The stage was quite well lit through the show, though I think a few tree gobos would have added a lot to the evening scenes. The penultimate scene in the Abbey really didn't work as the stage light was too bright and Rolf's torch was too tiny. Pity as this can be one of the most dramatic moments in the production. The final picture however was absolutely stunning with the nuns silhouetted and the family at a height behind them. The quality of the sound was great throughout the show. A lovely tone was created and the stage/pit balance was perfect.

The costumes were generally of a pleasing standard but a few modern shoes and a selection of coloured stockings on the nuns did jar a little. The children looked pristine in their beautiful costumes and Maria had a good range of outfits. The nuns' habits were all very authentic looking. Hair and make-up were generally sound but I would aim for less colour on the nuns whose makeup should be very nondescript. There were nice touches with hairstyles at the ball.

The huge chorus in this show added much to the production. This is a bit of a thankless task for the chorus who aren't on stage too much but this cast gave heart and soul when they were on. Well done.

There were some fine performances in this production of 'The Sound Of Music'. The bones were here for a great show. I would hope that in future this company would think about the show's staging, as sets, props etc should enhance a show and not detract from it.

This was a hugely entertaining night of a heartfelt production which was lyrical, witty and at times poignant. Well done to all involved in 9 Arch Claregalway Musical Society's The Sound of Music.

Carrigaline Musical Society is a community-based project which involves a wide range of ages and talents from the local area just outside Cork city. It produces a musical each year, this year they chose the classic Oliver! Based, of course, on the novel Oliver Twist by Charles Dickens this show is jam packed with memorable tunes. There are of course many children's parts in the show so it is a firm favourite with groups such as this. There was a real buzz around Carrigaline Community Complex for the Sunday afternoon matinee of the show. The hall is a good size though to stage this performance a stage had to be created at the front which did take up quite a sizeable space. An orchestra of just six players was placed in front of the stage under the musical direction of Denise Crowley, who created a very pleasant sound throughout the show with this limited orchestra. There was beautiful violin playing especially in 'Reviewing the Situation'. The casts' singing had obviously been rehearsed well and the chorus also created a good sound on stage with some pleasant harmonies at times. Nancy's 'Oom-Pah-Pah' was one of the show's many musical highlights. The director, Jacinta McBride chose an adaptable set and used trucked on pieces to create changes of scene. A black curtain was also pulled across and was acted in front of and at times this covered scene changes though I would advise a better-looking cloth for future shows. The cast of young and not so young players were totally committed to performing to their very best standard in their production of Oliver! One could feel the pride they all had in working together as a team. Jacinta moved the cast well around the stage and there were some nice moments of tension and humour created through the whole show such as Bill's chilling arrival at the bar. The Cockney accents had obviously been drilled well into most of the cast and the majority of the performances were very convincing. There were just a few moments of people being masked on stage especially when there were entrances at the back of the stage. Overall a steady piece of direction.

Choreographer Tara O'Connor set her choreography within the limits of the cast and created some interesting pictures and movements for some of the set pieces such as 'Food Glorious Food' and the shortened version of 'Who Will Buy?'
