Tara used marching movements which were very effective with the children. There was a lovely moment with white umbrellas in Fagin's Den. The movement was neat and of the period.

The set was very interesting and looked very realistic. Rough wood and brick effect had been used to create a multi- purpose stage which would change from Fagin's lair to the street, to the bridge. The brickwork was well painted and the addition of practical candles added a very Victorian touch to the show. Properties also were realistic looking and of the time. There was a beautiful metal bed brought on for Mr Brownlow's house. There were tables and benches which looked appropriate for the pub, there were bottles mugs etc which were in keeping. Shay Gilley played Oliver with a gentle and thoughtful style. He sang really well and acted well too especially in his scene in the undertaker's where he has a real fight with Noah. He worked well with Fagin and he and Dodger were very believable as a couple of unlikely friends. Sam Tanner played the part of Dodger with just the right amount of swagger and charm. He worked well with Nancy and the rest of the boys in Fagin's lair. Ava Costin looked and sounded great as Nancy. She broke down the fourth wall, challenged us as the audience and brought us into her world. We could see the pain in her soul as she sings 'As Long as He Needs Me' and knew that she really loved Bill Sykes and though she shouldn't she just can't help herself. This was a very strong performance. Bill Sykes was played with much menace by Dec Kiely. He threatened the cast and was even threatening to us as an audience as he prowled the stage. He had a very gravelly voice which was perfect for the part. Surprisingly Fagin was played by a female, in this case the wonderful Lorna Hughes. I was sceptical that this would work when I read the program but was instantly caught up in Lorna's performance and forgot all about gender. Lorna weaved her way in and out of the story with such style and captured the essence of the character brilliantly. She also sang very well too and though some of the music may have to have been transposed, most of it she was able to perform as written. I particularly enjoyed her rendition of 'Reviewing the Situation' which was one of the highlights of the show.

Laura Reddy played Nancy's sister Bet. This was a very polished performance as she sang, moved and acted really well. She and Nancy had a great relationship together on stage. The idea that they were sisters was very convincing. Mr Bumble was played by Kevin O'Keefe in an energetic way. This Mr Bumble moved well around the stage and danced about with ease. He and Widow Corney, Angela Tanner worked well together as a couple and sang and acted their song 'I Could Scream' with great style.

Mr Brownlow and Mr Sowerberry were played by Aidan Hurley who give us a gently paced performance. Possibly a little more pace was needed in the scene with Dr Grimwig who was played by Brian O'Keeffe. Brian looked well on stage but needs to watch his pace of dialogue. This is not how quickly you say the lines but the lack of gaps between people speaking. We naturally slightly overlap or come straight in when we are chatting to a friend, it is really the same on stage. Mrs Sowerberry, Mary O'Sullivan, was a nice fussy character with a voice which would have cut corn as she entered the stage. Liz Hesse-O'Sullivan was on stage as the old woman in a wheelchair. We didn't actually see her face but she told her story well.

Charlotte was played by Clodagh Tanner and Noah by Fionn Mehigan. Again, they were well developed characters and made us not like them too much, as they were so nasty to Oliver. Mrs Bedwin, the nurse was played by Helen Hunter and she had a lovely moment with Oliver in the bedroom where he is sick in bed. The chorus in the show worked very hard, both adults and children, particularly in the first half of the show when they were involved in so much of the action. They were all committed and they all sang very well. They moved well too and everyone seemed to be able to remember the tricky choreography that they were given - well done!

The costumes were a bit of a mix in the show there were some beautifully made costumes which were right for the era, though many of the costumes were just too clean for Victorian London. I particularly liked Bill Sykes' costume which was very authentic, right from the top of his perfectly fitting top hat to the bottom of his perfectly chosen boots. Nancy looked good too and her red dress with lace-up boots, nice new lace-up boots, but in some cases more attention to detail could have been made to the costumes as there was a bit of a mixture of particularly footwear which can be distracting whenever you are looking at a period piece such as this. The hair, in particular the girls' long hair, was caught back into ribbons occasionally and looked very good. There were some hair styles of the ladies which were too short for the period and I would suggest that in future you should be able to gather up some wigs and hair pieces for these ladies. Eye make-up too should be in character with the time so I would avoid coloured eyeshadows like greens and blues and instead use a brown and cream palette which would be more in keeping with the period.

Overall this was a great afternoon's entertainment. The hall was filled with an audience of all ages and as I entered, quite a few of the children were on iPads and phones but from the second the show started these were put away and they never appeared again, which goes to show how involved the children were with the show. They were watching and living it. This is what it is all about!

Well done Carrigaline for a great effort. There are a few things which are small details with costumes etc which could be worked on for next time but your young society has the heart and soul to produce a great show. Well done everyone involved. P.S. I am sorry I didn't see the other group of players perform too, (some parts had alternating cast) time would never allow me to do that, but I am sure they all did a great job too.

The Hawk's Well Theatre in Sligo was the venue for Sligo Fun Company's production of Sister Act. The intimate theatre was packed with an audience of various ages. There was quite a buzz of expectancy before the show and we weren't disappointed. Based on the movie starring Whoopie Goldberg, Sister Act is a feel-good show which revolves around the cabaret singer Deloris, originally Doris, and her escape for protection into a struggling convent. There is a wonderful sense of fun throughout the show and it is a great vehicle for a company with a large number of women in the cast.

The characters have all to be well-formed and the pace at times needs to really rattle along. There are also other moments of tenderness and self-doubt which have to be brought out too. Mary MacDonagh was the Director and Choreographer for this busy show. There were some wonderful pieces of direction on stage backed by glorious dance moments. The show moved at a great pace with quick changes of scene. Steffen Jorgensen created two large revolving pieces which had three different scenes on each one. These, with the exception of one which I didn't like the painting of, were very effective, especially the convent scene which had a three- dimensional quality.

Mary took a few risks with the casting of the show and chose several principals who hadn't played a major role before. Well done, this really did work as everyone on stage was excellent. She also managed to really bring out a great performance in each player and created some wonderful on-stage personalities. Mary's eye for detail was wonderful, especially in the placing and moving of the cast. There was wonderful grouping of cast on stage. Clever reactions with each other like poor old TJ being constantly hit on the head. There were good relationships shown between the cast such as the gang and how well they all worked together and also between the nuns and Deloris. I particularly liked the friendship between Mother Superior and Deloris at the end. The movement during acting scenes was well thought through and always made sense with the dialogue. The movement during the dance routines was just my kind of thing. There were constantly changing patterns, building up to a crescendo, holding and building again. This always left us as an audience wanting more. The solos were nicely moved too, in a way that did not take away from the feel of the moment. She even had Deloris dance with her bottom to us in 'twerky' fashion and it was fantastic! This was an interesting, ever changing piece of choreography. I loved the way the six altar boys were incorporated into the final number, they had a ball.

Musical Director Niamh Crowley gave us a wonderfully energetic and balanced sound from the pit. What was interesting to see was the variety of ages playing, from more experienced to teenagers. There was a glorious accompaniment throughout and I particularly enjoyed the delicacy of the playing for solos and duets. The cast had been very well rehearsed musically and everyone was singing strongly within their own vocal range. Diction in the singing was excellent and every syllable was as clear as a bell.

Niamh and Mary did have a wonderful cast to work with of course. Sinéad Conway made a great Deloris Van Cartier. That first 'Take Me to Heaven' number nearly blew us away and at times Sinéad's singing was so good, it felt that we were watching her in concert. (She was backed by the wonderfully dressed backing singers played by Holly and Kerry - well done ladies). Sinéad's acting became stronger as the show developed and she managed to get great moments of humour out of the role. This was a great first major part in a musical. Well done! Her love interest Eddie was played by Kieran Cunnane. Poor mocked Sweaty Eddie begins as the gun-shy cop and becomes the hero. This was a nicely judged performance. He carried off the instant costume change into John Travolta very well. The other bad boy, that Deloris had a thing for, Curtis was played with comedic menace by Franny Curley. He looked good in his leather jacket, with the gangster swagger. This was a frightening performance at times but he was able to have humorous moments especially in his dealings with his gang. He sang well and gave a great rendition of 'When I Find My Baby'.

The characters of the nuns were all different and all brilliantly portrayed. Mother Superior was played by Angela McGuire with just the right amount of coolness and yet showing a great heart at the end of the show. Angela brought out humour in the lines I hadn't even thought of before. She has a soaring voice and gave an emotional but witty 'Here Within These Walls'. Fiona Hiney played Sister Mary Robert and took us on a journey with the character from a timid postulant to a forceful woman. Fiona sang beautifully and her solo was a lovely moment.

Sister Mary Patrick was portrayed wonderfully by Rebecca McGillen.

Rebecca was just so involved in all that was going on on stage. She was a great listener and those facial expressions were super. Pam Lindey was Sister Mary Lazarus, whose gruff exterior hid a really comic side, especially in the rap number. Sister Mary Martin of Tours was a statuesque and commanding nun, as played by Maureen Howley, with some great well delivered comic lines. Siobhan Terry gave us a prickly Sister Mary Theresa who added a spark to all the scenes she was in.

Curtis' three henchmen were hilarious; there was TJ who was constantly battered for his stupidity played by Luke Devaney, Pablo (Brian McGauran) who was a silent but deadly type and Joey played with great style by Micki Murray. These three had us in hysterics, especially in their 'Long Black Dress' number. They gave us their best pumping and grinding moves and created a magical comedy moment. Robert Fitzpatrick was a wonderfully fussy Monsignor O'Hara. He related well to both Mother Superior and Deloris. He was like a breath of fresh air each time he entered. He kept the story telling rolling along by telling how 'the two antique dealers' were progressing with their negotiations. Other roles were captured well by Mark, Darren, Killian, Lloyd and Hugh. Hugh you were a very humble Pope to join us in the stalls! The chorus very so involved and everyone knew exactly what they were doing in all those complicated dance routines.

The lighting in this show was pleasing throughout with some lovely gobos being used. There were nice effects made with coloured lights, particularly against the back arches. Intimacy was achieved by giving us pools of light as appropriate. I must say increasingly I like the 'shaft of light' effect a hazer can produce in a show. We had some smoke when Deloris was in the confessional (those confessionals were stunning props with their red velvet curtains) this smoke gave a great atmosphere on stage. I hope the problems with the sound system were resolved. The costumes all looked in keeping with the feel of the show. They were a good fit and appeared to represent the 1970s very well. The sudden change costumes worked well. I loved the white and silver finale costumes. The sparkly coloured habits were quite nice but could have been even more over the top. I loved Curtis' leather jacket and the boys' flared trousers took me back! The nuns' basic habits were a good fit. Our drag queen was a treat in that great outfit. The Pope looked wonderful as he entered and sat among us.

The women's wigs were well presented and I thought the men's wigs gave a nice 1970 touch. Make up was subtle for the nuns. I did love Kerry and Holly's makeup which was stunning. Deloris' wig moved really well but I am glad to say never covered her face, it looked pretty realistic. This was a great night of comedy musical theatre. It was a thoughtfully directed show which teased out all the comedy of the writing. The music was a glorious balance between voice and instrument. The choreography interpreted not only the music but also the words of each song. This was an evening we just didn't want to end. Congratulations to all the cast and crew for a job well done.

Despite countless requests, George Bernard Shaw resisted releasing the rights of his most famous play Pygmalion to be turned into a musical, a genre Shaw believed to be frivolous. However after his death in 1950, Alan Jay Lerner and Frederick Loewe embarked on the long journey to turn it into a musical. Despite many rewrites, as they felt the story didn't follow the conventions of the 'musical' at the time in that there is no central love story, they managed to create the immensely popular My Fair Lady.

One of the most prominent reasons for the musical's popularity lies in the retelling of the Greek myth of Pygmalion, the sculptor who created a statue of Galatea, the perfect woman, brought to life for him by Aphrodite. In Pygmalion, Higgins is the sculptor and Eliza the clay which he moulds from a simple lower-class flower girl into a Lady. However, the Eliza of My Fair Lady takes a more active role in her own transformation and at play's end becomes a necessity for Higgins, who has "grown accustomed to her face." Shaw didn't want a romantic ending to Pygmalion. He said in a postscript to Pygmalion in later editions, "She will, if she marries either of them, marry Freddy…" Lerner and Loewe retained an ambiguity in their script and it could be argued that Eliza had nowhere else to go because even though her speech had improved, she didn't have the wherewithal to improve her station or class. In Shaw's revised play, Pickering helps her and Freddy open a flower shop and they both live happily ever after. In the musical we are left wondering what her role will be in the Higgins household.

Carnew Musical Society under the assured direction of Michael Dunbar presented a mostly traditional telling of this joyful musical. In the foyer, the staff were dressed in Edwardian costumes and in the auditorium the company had affixed silhouetted scenes from the show to the walls, in particular Ascot, which immediately gave a sense of place. The stage was open with a set of side flats fashioned to resemble old hardback book spines, akin to a giant's library. A stage wide platform upstage was also dressed as books stacked on their sides. A wraparound cyclorama on the back wall doubled as a projection screen. A very well stocked flower barrow was set centre stage and lit in preset.

The twelve piece orchestra were situated in front of the stage and screened from the audience. The Overture was sumptuously full, the viola, violins, cello and bass giving that lush string sound with the woodwind and brass cutting through backed by the drums and percussion. The keyboard added another pleasing layer to the resonance. Musical director and conductor Lar Duffy conducted with deftness and his timing and pace with the band was perfect. Mr Duffy also doubled as Chorus Master and his work with the ensemble was excellent, producing lovely tones and wonderfully, powerful and joyous harmonies.

Eliza as played by Joanne Logue, looked and sounded a lot older than the traditional portrayal of the character, her physicality and throaty cackle was more akin to an older woman. During her initial scene with Pickering and Higgins, she was less the waif like urchin and more an older hard- bitten Dickensian Nancy in Oliver Twist, had she lived. Ms Logue's singing however was superb, her soprano was crystal clear and note perfect. When she sang "I Could Have Danced All Night", we knew we were in the presence of a first-class soprano. As she became educated, we started to see her character's intelligence shine through, her speech whilst not quite received pronunciation, did convince. Interestingly her posture did not change. She still carried the world weary furtiveness, which was odd as one would have expected her to have the aloofness and bearing of one to the manor born needed to convince, yet it somehow worked and was quite realistic. Ms Logue's scene with Higgins when she asks what is to become of her, now she has won him his wager was quite heartbreaking. Her portrayal of anger and helplessness brought a sense of tragedy to the story, which was very refreshing as it is not often played as realism.

As Professor Higgins, Rory Robinson channeled the voice of Rex Harrison, his cadence was uncannily similar, particularly during his singing/parlando. However his physicality was much more energetic. His performance was a highlight of the show, he became Higgins. Mr Robinson played the privileged misogynist extremely well and his insouciance towards Eliza gleefully incensed the audience.

Colonel Pickering, with whom Higgins makes the wager to turn Eliza into a lady within three months, was played by Sean Hallahan. The Colonel was also a linguist, having spent some time in India and Mr Hallahan played him as a genial gentleman. He was more attuned to Eliza's plight and tried to soften Higgins more outlandish demands. As Freddy, the young man who was besotted with Eliza, Padraig D'Arcy sang "On The Street Where You Live" rather well and was quite believable as the simpering Mummy's boy. One could never see Eliza being in any way attracted to him and she practically tells him so during "Show Me".

John Young played Eliza's father with a cheeky cockney charm. Mr Young was a very physical Alfred Doolittle, animated and dynamic - particularly when being repeatedly thrown out of the Pub. His sidekicks, Jamie played by Jimmy Spellacy and Harry played by Paul Doran were perfectly cast and all three sang "With A Little Bit of Luck" with great energy and zeal. His "Get Me to the Church on Time" showed off his clowning prowess and his fine baritone.

Higgins Housekeeper, Mrs Pearce was played by Mandie O'Keefe. Although written as an English servant, Ms O'Keefe retained her own accent, which was a good decision as it gave her a softer edge, particularly when dealing with the distraught Eliza. A kindly portrayal, her Mrs Pearce was quite endearing. Also present in the Higgins household were the servants; played by Anna Furlong, Cathy Tighe, Catherine Stafford, Ellen Kinsella, Paul Doran and Richard O'Toole. Their choral work was top notch, particularly on the quite difficult harmonies.

As Higgins' Mother, Jennifer Byrne excelled at playing the subtext. Although concerned with propriety, Ms Byrne played her as quite feisty and ultimately benevolent.

Eileen McCabe, as Freddy's mother Mrs Eynsford-Hill, played her well. She perfectly embodied the upper-class sense of entitlement Shaw despised. Professor Zoltan Karpathy, who Eliza must convince that she is a Lady at the Embassy Ball, was played with a delightful over the top performance by Malcolm Byrne. Mr Byrne, complete with incredibly coiffed facial hair and impeccable Hungarian accent, flounced around the stage in a welcome cameo performance.

Choreography on the show was looked after by Frances Ryan and she did a great job. Stand out routines were the broomstick work in "Wouldn't It Be Lovely", the slapstick of "With a Little Bit of Luck" and the fabulous synchronicity of the "Ascot Gavotte". The Embassy Ball was well staged and the group energy of "Get Me to the Church on Time" leaped off the stage.

The set by Tony Barry worked well, basic trucked flats and furniture against a white Cyc and the stylised book end flats and platforms. There was some projection on the cyc, but it was underpowered and frankly looked badly skewed. Ultimately it was not required, as it did not add anything in terms of setting, location or time. Props by Grace Dunbar, Lar Duffy and Cathy Tighe were very authentic and well sourced.

Costume was mostly supplied by Nomac in Waterford and was of the Edwardian period. The Ball gowns looked great and I liked the smoking jackets and the men's attire. Make-up and hair was looked after by a team of eight and looked well.

Lighting was by Kevin McEvoy and was perfectly fine, mostly general washes with little specials and some practicals as befitting the show. But the LED lights didn't fade smoothly with the generics, so the cross fades were bit jerky. Sound by Joe Murphy, Itec Productions was full and well balanced but Higgins mic didn't work in the first scene, his "Why Can't The English" was a bit lost against the full band, but he managed to keep getting close to other actors and used their mics, which sporadically worked. Stage management by Tommy Kavanagh and his crew was very good. Transitions were swift with the cast doing some of the work.

Director Michael Dunbar produced a fairly traditional take on what is now known as 'the perfect musical' but he also added a great deal of pathos to the playing, particularly of the role of Eliza, which is not often done.

As a revisionist viewing through a contemporary lens, My Fair Lady could be seen as a celebration of sexism and misogyny. Directing this musical today, one must be aware of how far society has progressed in terms of equality and the class system. Mr Dunbar clearly addressed these issues in this production by highlighting Eliza's plight at being used as an experiment in social conditioning. Joanne Logue as Eliza brought a modern sensitivity to her playing and an innate sadness in that she had to return to her creator, as she had nowhere else to go. Interestingly, the casting of a seemingly older Eliza does make the relationship between her and Higgins more viable, although Mr Shaw would I imagine vehemently disagree!

This production took risks, and whilst playing it as a light comedy it did not shy away from the conflicts and the injustices that women experienced in Edwardian England and are still experiencing today. Well played Carnew, well played.

There was a warm welcome on a cold winter's night in Claremorris Town Hall which had been decorated with a balloon archway to greet an enthusiastic Friday night audience. BIG THE MUSICAL was a new experience for me and apart from the research I had made online I really was open-minded about the show. I had seen the movie starring Tom Hanks in the late eighties and I was looking forward to seeing how the story transferred to the stage as a musical.

Director Donna Ruane had taken on this show at relatively short notice and in doing so took on a show that involved a cast of various ages. The basic premise for the show is that young Josh who gets tongue- tied when he meets the love of his life, visits a fair and at the 'I Grant Your Wish' machine he wishes to be suddenly 'big'. His wish is granted with some hilarious consequences, as he has the heart and mind of young Josh captured inside Adult Josh's body. He comes to realise that being a grown-up isn't all he thought it would be, as with age comes baggage and responsibility. So, he eventually finds the machine and reverses the wish/ curse. To be very honest there are some nice musical moments in the show with a couple of lively dance numbers and a few beautiful ballads but the script could be wittier. That being said Donna made a good job of directing the show and the story was nicely told. The production was set at a good pace but there were pauses for the more poignant moments too. Donna and the stage team used an open set for the show with raised platforms at the back of the stage. This was topped with a cut out of the city skyline which was detailed and looked effective. Behind this was a black syce which later during the 'Stars' song sparkled with stars. The side flats were on a rotational pivot and on one side there was a realistic brick wall while the reverse had a collage of photographs of various toys and games. The two front stage extensions housed the boys' bedrooms. These were detailed in their dressing but were not utilised very much during the show which was a shame. The audience will always look for that big floor piano moment. The keyboard had been created at the front of the stage and it lit up effectively when Josh and George danced out 'Chopsticks' on it. This was a difficult thing to time properly and to synchronise movement with lights, it nearly worked. The large pieces of scenery such as the wonderful Zoltar's cabinet were quickly moved into place, though a couple of things did take more time as the crew were working in a very confined wing space. David Keane, I don't envy your job trying to make a set of bunk beds disappear in this limited space. Most scenery was nicely painted though the style and quality of these was not always consistent.

There was a pleasant blended sound from the orchestra under the direction of Deirdre Lee. Deirdre directed with great control and precision from behind the keyboard. There was a good balance between the singers and the accompaniment so we could hear every word. There were pleasant harmonies and the ladies' chorus really created a powerful sound. Principals were secure with their songs though the vocal range of some of the numbers did prove quite challenging.

The choreography from Jay Molyneux was in character with the general era and added to the feel of the show. There were some good lively numbers for the younger cast when they could show real 'attitude' by moving sharply from one pose to another. Arm movements were big, extended well, in time and in sync with each other. I would have liked to see more changing patterns on stage to add further interest. I did however love the angles and move of the smartly dressed secretaries in 'Coffee Break'. The ballet with young and adult Josh, Susan and Cynthia was very moving. Everyone looked like they knew exactly what they were doing and most important everyone was having a ball. Young Josh was played by Jack Mannix. He gave us a sensitive performance as the boy who struggles to express his feelings to Cynthia. The older Josh of Cairán Hennelly was most convincing. He managed to maintain that wide eyed innocence of youth throughout and gave us some humorous moments.

Josh's pal Billy Kopecki was intelligently played by James Fletcher who showed great comic timing for a young man. Josh's mum was portrayed by Karen Ronane. She emoted well from nagging mother to heartbroken parent. She sang well too and her wee moment at the table singing 'Stop Time' was beautifully done. Sonja Stevens was Susan Lawrence. Sonja has one of those show voices which can really affect the listener. The 'Little Susan Lawrence' number was a wonderful moment. I also enjoyed her awkwardness when having to sit on those huge bean bags.

Ronan Egan made a strong boss of the toy shop, George MacMillan. He moved easily around the stage and acted with conviction. Ronan showed us what a strong, rich singing voice he has. His office manager was the highly efficient Miss Watson played by Aishling Costello. She moved round the acting areas with great style and her frustrations at Josh's ideas and demands were clearly shown in her facial expressions. Michael Goulding was the upwardly mobile Paul Seymour who tries to control Susan and hates the boss's new favourite. We believed in this character and I am sure many of us have worked with a Paul who would climb over everyone to get to the top.

Cairán Kelly was busy as Zoltar and also as the BMW owning sophisticate in the roof top apartment scene. He played both roles very well and created the magic required for the wish-granting automaton. The pairing of Abigail (Vivienne Lee) and Diane (Mary Dempsey) was wonderful. They added a well needed burst of energy and sang really well together giving us great harmonies. I loved the sophistication these two added - two polished and experienced performers. Mrs Kopecki had just the right blend of bossiness and frustration that all parents of thirteen-year olds have. Nicely acted Tara Niland. Young Josh's love interest Cynthia was played by Ciara Farrell. She was just right in the role and the support she got on stage from her group of friends was effective.

The chorus contributed much to the production. I would ask that in future any 'business' the chorus have to do is thought out a bit more. I always feel that their movements in the background should be 'choreographed' too as sometimes when less experienced chorus are left to their own devices, they are just not too sure how to improvise in character. The freezes in the show were held very well.

Some of the costumes, particularly the ladies' costumes gave us a real sense of 1980's. Hairstyles were sometimes in keeping with the era. The make-up was a little restrained and could have been stronger on the ladies. Small personal props were in good condition and appropriate to the period.

The sound was excellent in this show. The tone and cueing were exemplary. The smoke machine was a bit heavy handed and left such a cloud during the following scene that we couldn't see the action which spoiled the momentum. Lighting created different moods throughout and the team were not afraid to give us good bright light on the stage. (One of my pet hates is unnecessary dullness on stage unless for a special effect). The light up piano was effective though difficult to co-ordinate the foot stamp to the flash of light. There were some nice pools of light which gave intimate moments.

In summary, this was a competent show. One which cast and audience thoroughly enjoyed. A really good night out.

When we think of the portfolio of songs made famous by the wonderful Elvis Presley, it is hard to imagine why a show such as 'All Shook Up' didn't happen much sooner. This story tells of a roustabout Chad who gets out of jail and comes to town. His hip-swinging ways make him popular with the women of the town. A comedy of errors follows against the musical backing of the songs of Elvis. This is a clever and funny script which needs good comic timing and breakneck pace. We had this in spades in the production staged by Birr Stage Guild. The red velvet stage curtains were closed at the beginning of the show in Marian Hall when we entered and found our seats. These opened to reveal a desert landscape, painted cloth (I think it might actually have been painted onto the back wall) with neck and headstocks of guitars as telegraph poles disappearing into the distance. This effect created an illusion of depth to the stage. The guitar theme was carried out to the proscenium arch where there were two huge guitar cut outs mounted.

The opening scene had free standing cell bars for the first number 'Jailhouse Rock'. As the show continued various items such as the bar, complete with quite an array of bottles and props were wheeled on. Tables and chairs appeared and disappeared quickly. A petrol pump and sign represented the garage, the motor bike providing an authentic touch. Human exhibits represented statues standing on box plinths in the museum. There was a detailed and well-painted Tunnel of Love car. Props and set worked together well and one of the highlights of the show was the Greyhound bus which miraculously revealed itself when suitcases carried on by the passengers opened and placed side by side formed the side of the bus, very clever and very effective.

The orchestra was under the direction of Enda O'Connor. I was initially puzzled that I couldn't actually see the orchestra in the auditorium. It turned out that they were in a side room and their sound was played out over speakers into the hall. There was a video link with the MD to screens which were on either side of the stage. It worked perfectly and we had a glorious balanced sound between the stage and the orchestra. This is a lively show with some real rock 'n roll belters such as 'C'mon Everybody' and melodic ballads such as 'There's Always Me'. Both genres were played well. The orchestration never overpowered and cues were excellent throughout.

Every ounce of humour was brought out of the script by experienced director Paul Norton. He added those magical nuances which make a simple, though witty script into a rollercoaster of laughter.

There were clever moves, gestures, facial expressions, moments held, breakneck pace, all the ingredients of great comic timing. His choice of set which was followed through by the work of an excellent stage team meant that the show never stopped rolling, carrying the audience along with it. Paul's choice of cast was so important too as they not only rose to his challenge of attention to detail and timing but they all looked like they were having a great time on stage. The characterisations were broadly drawn but also nicely developed as the show continued. We felt real empathy for every principal character and really willed there to be a happy ending for each one.

The casting of this show really came in pairs and each of the pairings in this production worked well, with a natural connection established between them. David Sheils who played Chad had a bit of the Elvis swagger but also an innocence of youth. He sang well throughout the show and his pumping and grinding brought colour to one or two cheeks in the audience! He worked with the many characters he built up relationships with but we all loved watching his on-stage relationship flourish (with twists and turns of course) with the stunning Sarahgene Loughnane who played Natalie, or was it Ed? In both roles Sarahgene gave her heart and soul. Her blokeish moves and sound effects (how did she burp on cue?) were great and when she, as Ed, and Chad kiss we are quite shocked. There is a great deal of comedy in the writing of these two parts and these two got as many laughs from the script as they could.

Jim (Natalie's father and owner of the garage) was played by Patrick Byrne. We were in stitches when Jim tries to tell Sandra that he fancies her, we were willing him on from the auditorium. Jim's character develops as the show progresses and Patrick did a great job throughout. We had great humour but some tender moments such as when Jim comments on Natalie's red dress. He gradually falls in love with Sylvia and we could see this love blossom before our eyes. Barbara Hanamy was the hard-working bar owner Sylvia. She tries to be dogmatic with her daughter but realises she has to let go and leave her to follow her dreams with Dean. Barbara has a beautiful tone to her singing voice. We were delighted when she and Jim finally did get together.

We couldn't take our eyes off the attractive Miss Sandra (Bríd Delaney). We loved seeing her transformation from museum manager to vamp. She played both roles very well. She made great use of the side flats as a place to gyrate and her stage exits were always fascinating. We weren't sure who Miss Sandra was going to end up with but we wouldn't have guessed the geeky Dennis played by Patrick Kelly would have stood a chance. When Patrick appeared initially, I thought I wasn't going to like the performance. He had an exaggerated voice and movements, but after the first scene I was bowled over by his total commitment to the part. This is an actor who has that something you really can't teach, perfect comic timing. He can make a word or a line funny by timing, facial expression and delivery. The man can sing too and he is not a bad mover either! Well done Patrick you gave us so much joy as Dennis.

Sylvia's daughter Lorraine (Robyn Luttrell) is the feisty young woman who meets GI Dean played by Gerry Clarke. Their love affair is the most straight-forward and sweet pairing in the show. They worked well together and the 'It's Now or Never' number was a real blockbuster moment. Both players were convincing in their roles.

Heather Colohan as Mayor Matilda I enjoyed your tough no nonsense character. Again, Heather has wonderful comic timing and I loved how she asked poor Earl (Kevin Murphy) a question but never gave him a chance to answer it. That walk was wonderful. Many actors begin building a character from the feet up and I got the impression that is what Heather had done. A great piece of comic theatre. Earl was the lap dog who appeared to follow her everywhere, never objecting but adding little gestures to others as he left the stage. What a joy to see Earl stand up for himself and to wow Matilda not with aggression but with love. There is a lesson for men here in how he managed to re-establish a relationship in the nicest possible way. This was a great on-stage partnership.

The chorus backed up the principal cast well. They sang strongly and moved with great co-ordination during the big dance numbers. Nice to see a wee troupe of dancers. Aideen Leacy, the choreographer had ten ladies who moved really well throughout the show. They first appeared coming down the aisle for the opening number and appeared regularly during the show. I always look at feet, body extensions and faces. Faces are so important and the joy from these dancers was so obvious. The routines were tight, neatly carried out with sharp arm movements.

Though space was limited when chorus and dancers were on together, I would have liked to see more changing of patterns and pictures on stage. The use of torches was a lovely touch in one of the numbers and created a magical effect. The movement of couples and small groups was gentle and at times added to the story telling.

The quality of the sound was very good and the tone of the orchestra and voice were well blended. I would have liked a bit brighter stage lighting at times but there were some nice moments when 'specials' created great atmosphere.

Well done stage team for moving the scenery on and off with so little room in the wings. The scenery was on the whole nicely painted and looked effective. The costumes were smart and sets of costumes such as the striped prison outfits worked very well. Neckties etc gave a 1950's feel. The blue suede shoes were smart and the court shoe version on Sylvia were great. The red and white spotted dresses were very effective. The hairstyles gave a nod to the period, with pigtails and of course Miss Sandra's flowing Marilyn Monroe golden locks. Make up was sensitively handled and at times maybe a bit more blusher and redder lipstick could have worked. The men's look, especially the slicked hair, looked good.

This show is not trying to be anything more than a good two hours of fun with some brilliant music. We had fun in bucket loads from this talented group. The audience came out smiling and humming tunes having had a great night at the theatre. Thanks to all in Birr for making me feel so welcome.

A Tale as old as Time 'Beauty and the Beast' like all good fairy tales, has it's roots in old European folklore. This one is from France and was written down in the 18th Century by Jeanne-Marie Leprince de Beaumontas and called 'La Belle et la Bête'. It tells the story of a sadistic prince who has been magically turned into an ugly Beast as punishment for his evil ways. In order to become human again, the Beast must first learn to love a bright, radical young woman (Belle) whom he holds captive in his decaying castle and more importantly, she must love him in return. 'Beauty and the Beast' is an allegorical tale, which touches on two essentially human attributes: being different and finding inner beauty.

Disney turned it into an animated musical film in 1991 and this is what the stage musical we saw in Newry Town Hall and presented by Bosco Drama Group, is based upon. Bosco Drama Group is a Community Youth Group, which provides a creative outlet for the young people of Newry in the form of theatre activities and specifically musical theatre. Adults are also involved and encouraged to share their skills and experience with the young performers.

The show opened with a fabulous choreographed sequence where we saw the evil Prince being beastly to an old crone who became a young preternatural being and transfigured him into a hideous creature and his castle servants into household objects. The choreography in this show was excellent throughout. Choreographer Ann-Marie Morgan really created some marvellous routines and scenes ably supported by Assistant Choreographer, Donna King. Be Our Guest had a spectacular Broadway quality, Gaston was deliciously violent and their contemporary dance work with the 'wolves' was superb.

Musical direction on the show was by Aislinn Mulholland, her work with the ensemble was great. Their harmonies on the bigger numbers were very accurate and soaring. The orchestra of twelve included a beautifully present Grand Piano and wonderful woodwind and horn sections. The flutes and clarinets in particular were noticeably transcendent. Her interpretation of the score was perfect. Belle, here played wonderfully well by Calla Hughes, was very different from the rest of the young people in her small provincial town, in that she loved to read and tried to see the good in people. Ms. Hughes played her with a fine received pronunciation and her diction was particularly clear. Her singing on Belle was full of aspiration and joy. Less assured on A Change In Me, but overall she sang well. Her scenes with Gaston really worked and they had a well-seasoned antagonism. There was less of a dynamic with the Beast, as he was so heavily made up I suspect, but they still worked well together notably towards the end of the show when they start to fall for each other. Belle lived with her dotty inventor father, Maurice, played by the show's co-director Jim McGuigan, who was the laughing stock of the village as his inventions invariably failed. These two characters were the real heart of the story and their relationship was very believable. Mr McGuigan was the epitome of the nutty professor type and sang well on both versions of No Matter What.

Gaston, the village Lothario who hankered after Belle as if she was a trophy, was brilliantly played by James McGinn. His Gaston was a narcissistic, violent, ignorant bully, petulant and ready to use his fists rather than talk. A charismatic performance, his singing was powerful, his slapstick work with LeFou was first class and his presence on stage was wholly intimidating.

His sidekick, James McLoughlin as Le Fou, also had a superb physicality and bounced well off Gaston - literally! I did have an issue with Mr McLoughlin's accent, his was the only American accent in the show, which was a bit odd as everyone else used a French or English dialect. But he did have very good comic timing and sang well on Gaston.

In the village there were Three Silly Girls, a bit like the Ugly Sisters (although they weren't ugly I hasten to add) who were vying for the attention of the gigolo Gaston. Simpering and fawningly played by Niamh Walsh, Aimee McDonald and Catherine McLoughlin, they were hilarious. Their comic timing and vocal work on Belle and Gaston was delightful as was their swooning dramatics.

Once Belle arrived at the castle in search for her father who had gone missing, she encountered some of the household objects that had come to life. She first met Lumiere, an animated candelabra, strikingly played as a suave maître d' by Ronan Sharkey. Mr Sharkey's performance, with a strong Parisienne dialect and attitude, was très charmant. He had a wonderful physicality, his elastic upper body movements bending him into flexible elegant postures. He sang really commandingly on Be Our Guest and his onstage relationship with Cogsworth, a Grandfather Clock and formally Head of the Castle, was delightful. Impressively played by Dennis Walsh, Cogsworth was a stuffy, nervous character, fearful of the Beast's wrath but with a tender geniality towards Belle.

Of the other animated objects, Mrs Potts (a teapot) the Head Cook, was played by Helena Hughes and sang the title song very well. Her motherly attentions towards Chip (a cup) played endearingly by the young Ronan Caldwell, were convincing. Annette Ward played Babette, a flirty feather duster, well as did Anne-Marie Campbell as Madame de la Grande Bouche - an Opera singer transformed into a wardrobe. I felt that the actor playing the character of the Gargoyle was underused as was actor playing the Rug, she was particularly good with a great acrobatic performance. They all sang very well and as an ensemble worked very effectively together.

Gaston had an idea to incarcerate Maurice thinking him insane as he spoke of the ferocious Beast and the talking inanimate objects he witnessed whilst at the Castle. Once Maurice is confined, Gaston's plan was that he could have his wicked way with the beautiful Belle. He arranged for the Governor of the town Asylum, the aptly named Monsieur D'Arque, gloweringly well played by Lowry Hodgett to assess Maurice's soundness of mind. Meanwhile, Belle returned having been released by the Beast to help her father. She corroborated his story and both were locked up whilst Gaston and the village folk light torches and decided to storm the Castle. Gaston and Beast fought and as the Beast lay dying Belle proclaimed her love for him and he became a Prince again and his servants returned to human form. Ruairi McAlinden played the Beast with a domineering presence. It's always a difficult task for an actor to convey emotion and intention when heavily made up as Mr McAlinden was during the show, but he did succeed. His Beast was a heartfelt performance and his growl, whilst quite menacing, was full of pain and longing. His singing was quite good and although a bit off key in places his rendition of If I Can't Love Her was sweetly plaintive. The set by Anne-Marie Campbell and Dennis Walsh was partially based on pop up fairy tale books, especially the village. The Castle was also well designed with steps leading up to a higher level. A star cloth and other painted cloths gave a good sense of place and I particularly liked the framed portrait of Gaston in the village inn. Lighting by Rodney Ellis was very good and there were some nice dark states achieved, helped by the two follow spots highlighting the actors. Sound by McCusker Audio and Sean Keenan was well balanced and full and Stage Management by Aimee Yates and her crew was really well done, managing many props and a large ensemble.

Costume and Wardrobe were of the period and the household items were particularly good, especially Lumiere's lit up hands, Chip's tea cup and the Beast's costume. Belle's ball gown was very well made and blended well into the production. Make Up and Wigs were also particularly well done, again the Beast's make-up was especially fine work.

Directors Jim McGuigan and Corinna Cunningham did a fine job on this production, the pace rarely let up, the blocking was very well thought through, the music and singing first class, the choreography original and the onstage relationships were quite believable. Bosco are to be commended on this achievement and indeed on the sterling work they do with the young people in Newry. They are the ultimate embodiment of community theatre, bringing together experienced performers with up and coming talents and producing superbly entertaining musical theatre. To paraphrase one of the most popular songs in the show Be Our Guest, we did put their service to the test and found it to be A+.

A clever story of loves won and loves lost, mistaken identity and the music of Elvis Presley how can we fail to have a great night at All Shook Up. We certainly had a wonderful night in the company of the cast and crew of the team from Malahide. The foyer and hall had been decorated with 1950's memorabilia, the ticket desk resembling the front of a car. There were records, juke boxes and of course a popcorn machine. This really added a bit of period atmosphere as we entered the Malahide Community School Hall. It is a good-sized hall and the acoustic seemed quite good. As we entered there was a huge screen at the back of the stage showing images and newsreels of Elvis' life. The 1950's movies added a lot to the setting of tonight's show, though 1970's footage did jar somewhat. These images were not projected but the whole back of the stage was like a huge computer screen so images were in focus, and there was no worry that stage lighting would affect the images. There was no sign of an orchestra but two large speakers were set up at the front of the stage. I later discovered that the orchestra was in a room off the foyer and the music was broadcast to us through these speakers. The stage was open with a wide set of steps from hall level leading to the stage, though these were not used very much, and another set of steps at the back of the stage which were.

I have seen quite a few shows using images as a show setting but it has to be said that this was in a different league as there was total clarity of the image and no spill from a projector. I imagine this was a very expensive machine to hire. We had all sorts of backgrounds from sparkling stars to the disused fairground. The only problem being that the rest of the scenery used looked a bit shabby in comparison, something to think about in the future as we needed a consistent look.

The musical direction in this show was exquisite. There was a wonderful sound from the orchestra throughout the show with some glorious moments created by Dave McGauran and his orchestra. Nice that there was a vision of them in their room on the screen for the play off at the end of the show. The singing was stunning, particularly the great work done by the chorus who delighted us with some wonderful harmonies. Unfortunately, there is a 'but', but it was painfully loud. Such a real shame that the sound broadcast especially when singing was so loud and so bassy that the floor of the hall actually vibrated and my ears were buzzing long after the show ended. The quality of the music in the show was exceptional but the volume was just too high.

Director Damien Hurley gathered a very confident cast who worked together very well. The show is really about pairing of the cast and he had chosen each pair with care. The pace of the piece was pretty frantic with us having hardly a chance to catch our breath before we were laughing at the next scene. Undoubtedly everyone in the hall that night had a great night of fun and laughter. He moved the cast and chorus round the acting area in a very natural way and I particularly liked how he grouped the cast on stage. The personalities of the principals had been well drawn and the story was very eloquently told by them all, with some nice wee nuances in their movement and delivery of lines.

The show was beautifully lit and there was obviously a very detailed lighting plot. There were subtleties in the lighting but we could see the characters and their emotions clearly. One thing I have noticed in a few shows is a swirling snowflake type gobo. This really only works as distraction in most shows and I hate it. It was the only fly in the ointment in the lighting of this show.

Jean Gill gave us a very exciting choreography plot for the piece. In fact, I think there was actually extra dance added in, so the whole show moved and sparkled along. Nice to see a group of male dancers who added a depth to the routines. The dance off between the angels and devils was clever and really well executed. The huge chorus numbers were well moved, creating good stage patterns and building routines to a climax. The leading players could all move well and there were great hip pumps and gyrating throughout. All the routines had a feel of the period of the piece. A job well done.

Chad, the roustabout was played with great charm and machismo by Jordan Bass. Jordan really looked the part and there was a sigh from the girls beside me when that skin-tight t-shirt was removed! He had all the hip swaying moves and a great voice which sounded really good through the show. He acted well from the 'Fonzie' macho man to the confusion of his love for Ed/Natalie, played by Orla Connolly. She was convincing as the Tomboy even when she was in that oily flowery dress. Then as Ed we had a great bloke who looked and sounded 100% male. It was a clever transformation from man to woman and one which Orla was able to switch on and off with ease. She sang really well but I really loved when she sang as Ed as she had a great tone to her voice in that role.

Dennis is the love-struck geek who adores Natalie. We all loved his performance which gave us so many laughs along the way with his great comic timing. David Latham has the most dazzling smile which he used brilliantly in the role. He looked great as the side kick to Chad and we were blown away by his great singing voice. Who would have thought he would end up with the glamorous Miss Sandra? Irina Pilos added a European sophistication to the role. We were mesmerised  when she let her hair down and changed into that dramatic red dress, quite a transformation. Irina moved around the stage with such determination like a huntress searching for her prey.

Kirstin Keegan gave us a very natural and heartfelt interpretation of the role of Sylvia. She was every part the 'hard done by' bar owner trying to bring up her daughter on her own. She sang very movingly and we were always on her side. Her love developed for Jim played by Vincent Oliver as we watched. They made a good on-stage team. Vincent gave a gentleness to the character of the widowed garage owner. He has a beautiful tone to his singing voice which was showcased in 'I Can't Help Falling In Love'. He could have made a little bit more of the comedy associated with the role especially when he tries to talk to Sandra.

Daire Kelly as Dean and Nicole Kennedy as Lorraine gave us the two love sick teenagers. Theirs is the sweetest of love affairs and they acted and sang their parts really well. The bicycle chase which had the moving background looked brilliant. These two made a great couple. We were so glad when they stood up for themselves particularly against Mayor Matilda.

This was played with great style by Emma Jane Reilly. This actor was dressed and styled to perfection for this role and she acted and sang the part so well too. We had that quick talking, puritanical matriarch in spades. Always cutting off poor Earl before he has a chance to open his mouth though we cheered when Earl, as played by Lorcan White, stood up for himself. His speech was sensitively played.

The costumes added much to the look and feel of the show with lovely attention to detail. I always checkout the shoes first and they all were in harmony with the era and matched each other. We had nice sets of costumes such as the angels and devils, the chorus looked good, though there were a few men whose look just appeared a little modern. The principals were dressed well with a definite period look, for example Dean's orange shirt and Miss Sandra's red ruched dress. Nice accessories like shoes to match outfits which makes such a difference to the overall look. Hair was good for some of the cast but might have been a little more in period. Sylvia's and Matilda's wigs were the right style for the older women. I wanted to see a bit more shiny product on the men's hair. The make-up really made the eyes of the ladies stand out and foundations and blusher gave quite a natural look. Props were well chosen and in keeping with the era.

This was a great, slick, beautifully sung show. There was great humour throughout and a quick-fire pace which left us wanting more. It was such a shame that the sound was just too loud, I hope that this was something which was resolved for the Saturday night. Well done to all in Malahide Musical and Dramatic Society. PS Thank you to the member of house staff who came down and removed the camera from the man in front of me who was taking photos all through the show. There were several people with phones recording scenes from the show, even sending texts, it must be very distracting for the cast as it is certainly very distracting for the audience.

Based on the comic strip of Little Orphan Annie, the musical opened on Broadway in 1977 and ran there for nearly six years. The show appeals to children and adults who enjoy the defiance of the children and the tender heart-rendering moments. It is a popular show for amateur companies to perform and as there is a great mix of ages with a large chorus of girls who are always well supported by relatives.

I was welcomed to An Táin Arts Centre in Dundalk by Ann. Our seats were in the upper tiered area with a great view of the stage. There was a wonderful family feel in the theatre which became like a meeting place for old friends. The safety and no mobile phone announcements were done by young members of the cast and must have hit home as phones were not used in the auditorium which was a very pleasant change.

The curtain opened to quite a simple set with a series of large windows at the back, these turned out to be a projected image. In the foreground the stage was strewn with bodies sleeping on the floor or in one of the three authentic looking beds. This back projection created all sorts of stunning effects such as Brooklyn Bridge, the library inside the Warbucks' mansion, the hallway with crackling fire etc. These all looked great though due to the projection nature of the image there was a slight blurring of the image and it also meant that the lights at the back of the stage in particular had to be dimmer to see the effect which did cause problems through the show as the stage was often underlit to the detriment of the action. It was a shame that the lighting plot was not thought through fully as there were some lovely moments. That opening scene was quite well lit as an eerie night-time but as Miss Hannigan came on, she would have switched the lights on suddenly which would have had a great sudden effect. For the audience to really be in touch with the actors' emotions, we really have to see their faces. At times the light was so gloomy this became impossible and we lost touch with the show. The projected scenery did however mean that scene changes were done very quickly. We had some lovely pieces of furniture brought on and set in place by a highly efficient team under the direction of Moya Hodgers. The beautiful red leather winged chair in particular looked great on stage.

The orchestra of seven players, including Musical Director Patrick Dunne gave us a well-rounded sound throughout and actually sounded like there were far more in the pit. Music was played at a nice steady pace which never dragged. There are a couple of numbers which can slow the pace of this show such as 'Something was Missing' but there was a nice steady tempo which moved it nicely along creating a gentle and beautiful moment. A few times diction with the younger cast was a bit careless with the end of words not quite finished off. The younger cast did however sing out really well and they had great energy during 'Hard Knock Life'. I loved the fun they gave us with their 'Never Fully Dressed Without A Smile'. The adult chorus really lifted the roof with their singing of 'We'd Like To Thank You Herbert Hoover'. The individual voices in ' I Think I'm Gonna Like It Here' worked well. All the hard work put in by Irene Dunne really paid off.

The show was double directed by Terese Dunne, who also choreographed most of the show, and Rosemary Winkless. They produced a well-moved production which flowed well. The characters were well defined and most really suited their roles. There was great humour brought out by the interpretation of lines and movements. I loved the radio studio scene which was wacky and good fun. There were however problems with the pace of the show which did drag at times particularly in the second half, I hope that this improved as the week continued. I really enjoyed the choreography of the show. We had an exciting 'Hard Knock Life' with so much going on it was hard to know where to look, a great and aggressive Hooverville routine and the scenes with the staff in the mansion were nicely moved. The little dance moment with Annie and Warbucks was gently moved and I thought the 'Easy Street' routine was full of life. 'NYC' was moved by Tara Gill and looked very colourful.

The show relies on the magic created by our Annie. We were in the capable hands of Sarah Dunne. She gave us a nicely rounded character with just the right mix of feistiness and warmth. I loved her maternal relationship with some of the younger orphans. She also stood up for herself really well too. She really sang out her songs too. I am interested in seeing her develop in future roles. One of the hardest things in any show is getting the 'Sandy' to answer to the name 'Sandy' and to come to Annie on cue. This worked brilliantly and we were so convinced by the bond these two lost souls had with each other. Well done Toby too! I heard great praise for Caragh Mailley who was performing the role on alternate nights, I hope she enjoyed playing the role too. Jane Stanley made a totally out of control matron of the orphanage. Always with a wee bottle of something close at hand she staggered her way round the stage giving us many laughs along the way. Jane underplayed the role instead of the usual shouted version, this was very effective most of the time and made a nice change. Tom Maher didn't make the ultimate sacrifice of going bald for the part and looked tall and serious as Daddy Warbucks. This was a slightly gentler Warbucks with some nice moments such as his giving the new pendant to Annie. Just a bit more pace needed to rattle the story along.

Sheena Duffy gave us a professional and controlled performance of Grace. She moved elegantly and always with great purpose around the stage. She appeared that she had stepped out of a magazine of the time. A most convincing portrayal. Drake, played by James Brennan was a nice foil to Grace. The sensible butler was well acted and the little touches of humour were appropriate.

I loved the tone of Tom Doonan's voice either talking or singing. It was rich and deep creating a very strong character of Rooster. He had all the swagger needed for the lovable rogue Rooster but also created the ever so humble farmer Mr Mudge extremely well. I loved how his movements and in particular his walk changed from one character to the other. His side kick Lily was played well by Lucie Robinson. She had some great moves which really added to her portrayal. She and Tom made a great on-stage team and gave us many laughs along the way. Well done to all the other characters in this production with special mention to the President himself played well by Andrew Browne who has the most wonderful singing voice, his cabinet all did a great job in their scene. The staff in the Warbucks' mansion looked and sounded good. The scene in the radio studio was hilarious, well done Bert Healy aka Kevin Stanley and team.

Congratulations to all the children on stage, your energy and enthusiasm was fantastic and also the adult chorus who really acted and sang their socks off too. A general comment for all on stage, don't forget about the audience in the balcony. It seems really unnatural but you must keep your heads up and look up towards us. In so doing the lower level will still be able to see your faces but so then will we in the balcony. For most of the production we were looking at the tops of your heads. Those with hats wear them back so the shadow on your face is reduced, there was one character we couldn't make out at all. This was a shame.

The costumes through the show were many and varied. There was great attention to detail with a real period feel to everything. I particularly liked the sets of costumes used at the end of 'NYC' which really added a splash of colour. The principals' outfits all added to their characters and accessories such as shoes and gloves were generally in keeping though two sets of staff shoes were not quite a match which sounds trite but really stands out on stage. The Hooverville folk had all really wrapped up well against the cold.

Hair was generally in keeping but it is important that everyone's hair is appropriate as those who decide to do their own thing really spoil the illusion we are trying to create. Make up was restrained but I loved Miss Hannigan's lipstick which looked it had been applied in the back seat of a bumpy New York cab! Perfect.

This was a slick and well-rehearsed show. There were some nice moments but at times these were hard to see in the dull lighting on stage. The pace tended to slow periodically which was a pity. There was great talent vocally and acting wise on stage. The audience really enjoyed their trip to NYC courtesy of SONG!

show_raw: Sugar The Musical - Some Like It Hot
review_text:
Based on the 1959 Billy Wilder movie starring Marilyn Monroe, Tony Curtis and Jack Lemmon, 'Sugar - The Musical' is actually quite true to the original script. The movie is perhaps the funniest movie of all time so with that script to work with Sugar should be a wonderful show. I really enjoyed the show as a film to stage experience and the audience in CBS Auditorium in Mitchelstown came out with wide smiles after a night of great fun. There were things which the company need to address but the general experience was one of laughter and joy.

I was very surprised as I entered the auditorium having been nicely welcomed by one of the house managers. I expected an austere hall with folding seats but was shocked to see tiered theatre seating which it turned out had been hired for the performances. Some of the walls had been covered with heavy black material which must have helped the acoustics. The set up was all done the weekend before the show which was quite a task as a high raised area to accommodate the orchestra was also constructed. This mammoth task might have been why the presentation of the stage suffered as we had a very simple and a bit untidy looking stage set. I would advise that an even simpler 'black box' with interesting pieces brought on would have been more effective. The stage was managed by Rachael Lawton and Paul Seymour who quickly brought some nice pieces of furniture onto the stage such as a beautiful chaise longue, side tables, beds and even a set of double bunk sleeper beds. When I examined the stage area after the show, I was intrigued how this was possible with such space restrictions. Well done stage team.

Director Killian Collins had obviously worked very hard to tease out all the humour from the script. There was good comic timing shown from the principals. He set a rattling pace with the show though there were some nice moments of pausing before delivering a line which really pointed it. Overall, he created the feel of the piece with some good performances, with most of the cast maintaining the American accents. We maybe needed more differentiation from the cold Chicago streets to Florida with dress and movements. What really did come across was that the entire cast must have enjoyed the rehearsal process as they were having a ball on stage too. The Musical Director Sarah Chamberlain Dewhurst created a nice period, jazz, rag-time sound with her eleven players. Apart from a few wee glitches the music sounded authentic and with a good steady tempo in each number. The sound of the singing was well balanced to the orchestra and the diction was pretty good. The chorus really belted out their big numbers and raised the roof. Well done Chorus Mistress Noreen Hellen who had a good cast to work with. The singing was fairly strong throughout, with some superb male voices in the principal line-up.

The girls in the band doubled as the dance troupe for the show. There was great dancing talent with this group who lit up the stage with their winning smiles each time they came on, but also performed their routines with agility and accuracy. Well done Aileen McMurtry for some detailed routines which filled the stage but gave us attractive developing patterns. Just watch all the big numbers don't end in the same position on stage. Aileen managed to move dancers and a large chorus with ease and it was heart- warming to see the chorus helping each other.

One major criticism with the show was the lighting plot. I am all in favour of a clever and moody plot but we must be able to see the action. There were so many moments lost to us as cast walked into a dimly lit area and even at times a dark stage. Maybe there were problems the night I was there but this is an issue which must be addressed in future shows. The use of the torches for the gangsters searching for Jerry and Joe was very effective but we really lacked a bit of Florida sparkle later in the show. Such a pity.

Sugar Kane was played elegantly by Sarah O'Shea. Sarah was nicely styled for the part and didn't try to emulate Marilyn Monroe but created a part of her own. She moved well around the stage and sang well. She and Joe gave us many laughs particularly on board the boat. Declan Herlihy played Joe/Josephine. Declan seemed a bit shy at the start of the show and he took a while to fully include us into his world. However, as the show developed, we got some wonderful moments of comedy. The seduction of Sugar was hilarious and that ever-raising left leg when they kissed was a great piece of comedy. Declan looked the correct amount of ill at ease and total enjoyment when he appeared as the dancing girl in shorts and black tails. I was glad Declan gave us a posh accent rather than copy the Cary Grant tone used in the movie for the millionaire. Jerry/Daphne was played with such comedic timing and a real understanding of the lines by Paul Finn. This was an exceptional piece of camp, but not too camp comedy. We were enthralled by his transformation into Daphne and his interplay with Osgood was superb. Michael Murphy was a wonderful foil to Daphne as Osgood. This was team work at its best with a very believable love affair developing with Daphne. Michael delivered all his lines with real style and punch, particularly that very last line which brought the house down.

Siobhán Barry was the strong band leader Sweet Sue. Siobhán gave a controlled performance and was obviously in charge of her girls. Not too shouty which was nice. She sang well and gave us a nice solo which was beautifully lit. Her henchman/ manager was poor Bienstock who fussed around trying to organise the team. This was nicely played by James Sherlock. He was very much the hen-pecked man trying to look in control. Jimmy Hennessy as Spats Palazzo created the baddie we loved to hate. He worked well with his on- stage gang. He delivered his lines well and sang well too, keeping in character.

The chorus worked well throughout the show with some great singing. Everyone had made a good effort to look the part but I would ask that the young men always check that they are correctly dressed as undone top buttons etc just jar on stage and although it sounds petty it takes away from the overall look.

The costumes were generally good and created a feel of the era. There were period hats worn by the girls on the station platform, a great set of bathing suits in monochrome and Sue always looked sparkly and showbiz. I liked the look of the old millionaires with their striped jackets and flannels. I would advise that the sense of place is brought out more in costumes with more wrapping up in 'The Windy City'. I would also advise that when trying on a set of costumes such as the black fringed flapper dresses that the hem lines all be set at the one length, some were very short and didn't look right.

Hair was mostly a styling of the cast's own hair and as a result there were some contemporary styles.

Perhaps more wigs might have been the answer. I liked Josephine's straight black bob and Daphne's curly wig. Make-up was mostly in keeping with nice red lips and the two boys had just the right amount on to create the change.

This was an entertaining evening. There was a wonderful community spirit about the event. The society is really well supported by wonderful sponsorship which proves how much the local businesses value the contribution of Mitchelstown Musical Society to the life of the town. I hope this young group will go from strength to strength in future productions.

Who Says That Murder Is Not An Art? Shannon Musical Society first sashayed onto the stage with Oklahoma! in 1979 and have been entertaining the good people of Shannon and its environs ever since with annual musicals, Cabarets and Christmas concerts. Last year they tackled The Wiz and won the coveted Best House Management gong at the AIMS Awards. This year they brushed up their Fosse and gave us a super rendition of Chicago. Chicago was originally written as a stage play based on real life events in 1924 by Maurine Dallas Watkins, the play was turned into a musical by Bob Fosse, John Kander and Fred Ebb in the early 1970s and it's been revived many times since and became a very successful Hollywood film in 2002.

Staging a musical in a school hall is, as I've said in the past, no easy feat. School halls are designed to be multi-purpose and they are used for sporting events mostly so the usual facilities we need to make good theatre are largely absent. Which means we have to bring them in, set them up and all within a tight time-frame. This is what Shannon Musical Society had to do this year. St Patrick's Comprehensive School does however have quite a large space, so at least there was room to extend the stage. Out front we were treated to living sculptures of inmates behind bars, a clever nod to the Cook County Jail where much of the show takes place.

In the auditorium, the stage was framed with flats and a hanging sign with the Chicago logo spelled out in light bulbs. The light bulb motif continued around the side flats where they were recessed. The band were placed up stage behind a low narrow platform, with a flown in gauze on hinges as there was no height to fly. Centre stage was back lit two Bentwood chairs in a light haze. The stage was set, the band tuned up and we were in 1920's Chicago.

The plot is quite simple really and reads like a 1940's film script. Velma Kelly is on remand in prison awaiting her trial for murdering her husband and her sister. Her lawyer, Billy Flynn is a celebrity showman and for a fee will get anyone off because he has the ear of the press and is good copy. Roxie Hart shoots her lover and ends up in prison with Velma, she persuades Flynn to take her case too. Velma now hates Roxie as she feels that Roxie will get more coverage than her and knows that Flynn also believes this. The more public the case the better chances of being found not guilty. The show is mainly all about these three characters, with minuscule sub plots, and about the power of celebrity and how the press is easily manipulated and as Mama Morton, the prison Matron, says "In this town, murder is a form of entertainment." Derek Barrett opened proceedings as the Announcer/ MC. He played him with authority in Black Tie and kept popping up to introduce performers and really looked elegant and refined. He also played the Judge with a quiet command.

As Velma Kelly, Louise Cormack was superb. Her singing was strong, jazzy and powerful. She set the bar quite high with her opening number 'All That Jazz', where she performed with the ensemble some lovely Fosse moves and sang it extremely well. Ms Cormack's duet with Mama Morton, 'Class', was perfect, they effortlessly hit the tricky harmonies and her solo number the difficult 'I Can't Do It Alone' was a triumph of song and dance. 'My Own Best Friend', her duet with Roxie was also a stand out number as was their final number 'Nowadays/Hot Honey Rag'. But of course, Chicago is not a concert. It's has a plot and Ms Cormack proved to be quite an accomplished actor too in the role of Velma Kelly. She is a triple threat, as we say, and I felt her performance was exceptional.

Velma's nemesis, Roxie Hart was well played by Lauren Rice, who also has a wonderful voice and really showed it off on 'Roxie' and 'Me and My Baby'. The slower number 'Funny Honey' showed her control of her vocal and as mentioned 'My Own Best Friend' and 'Nowadays' with Velma was great. Ms Rice seemed less assured in showing Roxie's vulnerability however, and her dance wasn't as polished as others, however she did perform well generally and I quite liked her characterisation of Roxie.

Their lawyer, Billy Flynn was played by Brian Roche. This was a different portrayal of the attention seeking shyster to the norm. Coming across more like a 1920's gangster as opposed to a suave, sophisticated ladies man, Mr Roche played him quite hard. This worked quite well on the scenes with Amos and when he was fobbing off Velma, but not as well on his musical numbers which celebrated Flynn's elegance. On 'All I Care About' he seemed a little lost in the dance number as he did in 'Razzle Dazzle', but on 'We Both Reached For The Gun' he did particularly well as it suited his voice and he managed that penultimate long note. He also convinced in the Courtroom scene where they re-enacted Roxie's crime.

The role of Matron Mama Morton was taken by Grace Collins and she sang and acted it well, her 'When You're Good To Mama' was quite good but her stand out number was with Velma on 'Class', where they gelled really well together vocally. Her acting was quite good and she played high status very effectively.

Amos, Roxie's long suffering husband, was subtly played by Stephen Byrne in a very understated performance which was perfect for the character. He had the audience in the palm of his hand when he sang 'Mr Cellophane' as he elicited empathy and sympathy in equal measures. As Roxie's lover, Fred Casely, Colm McGuinness was physically the opposite of Amos, strutting powerfully around the stage, he really looked the part.

Mary Sunshine is an interesting character as she is written as a man in drag by the writers as a nod to Vaudeville which they admired so much.
