However, the actor cast must be able to sing the song 'A Little Bit Of Good', which is written for a countertenor. R.B Mitchell was cast as Mary and I'm happy to say he performed it very well, he kept the humour and had no problem singing it. R.B was also great in 'They Both Reached For The Gun' and reporting the trial on the radio.

One of the most difficult numbers in Chicago is 'Cell Block Tango'. This was staged quite simply with chairs and whilst it didn't quite have the power in the chorus it should have, individually each 'merry murderess' performed extremely well in their respective roles; Louise Cormack as Velma, Michelle Drysdale as June, Laura Gough as Mona, Hazel Park as Hunyak, Claire Heffernan as Annie and Karen Barrett as Liz were all gloriously strong. The ensemble in this show were really very good; Rachel McIntyre, Joe Bracken, Dara O'Callaghan and Lorcan McAuliffe were particularly good.

Chicago is all about the dance and director/choreographer Oliver Hurley really captured the Fosse style here, especially in 'All That Jazz', 'Tap Dance', 'Hot Honey Rag' and the 'Finale: Act II'. His ensemble were very well drilled and they had all of the little touches quite well synchronised. It wasn't perfect and at times seemed a little jaded, but it did read very well from the audience.

Musical Director Carmel Griffin also conducted and was Chorus Mistress on the show. Her band played buoyantly and she could be seen dancing away with the music. We had piano, reeds, brass, bass, drums and a very present banjo, which was great to hear in her clever arrangements. Vocally the ensemble were very well directed by Ms Griffin and we had a nice burst of harmonies at times. Lighting by Indigo Lighting was very subtle. A good mix of generics with LED Pars, gave a nice warm tone to actors skin. Birdies hidden behind Art Deco sconces, acted as footlights for some scenes and were very effective in the trial scene. Sound by Star Systems was well balanced with a nice mix out front, but I felt it could have been raised in volume to match the vocals. As the band were so far upstage, they were quite removed from the action and the relatively low volume accentuated their distance.

Hair by Ronan Mitchell and Pamela McGlynn was very well styled as were the wigs by Jean McGlynn. Make up by Rachel McIntyre and her team was quite good and of the style. Costumes by Karen Barrett were great, the black and red theme really worked and I particularly like the girl's costumes in 'Razzle Dazzle', however I felt that Flynn's suits were too big for him! Stage Management by Francis Maloney and his crew was fast, efficient and the transitions were speedy.

Oliver Hurley and his cast and creatives created a very good production of Chicago, all of their hard work was there on the stage for us to enjoy and we did enjoy it immensely. I had some issues with some of the casting but I think overall it was an admirable achievement.

Mr Hyde and Mr Seek Tullamore Musical Society has been around since 1955 and in that time has garnered many awards and accolades. Last year they staged Sister Act and in 2017 they won many nominations with Sweeney Todd. This year, 2019, they return to the dark side with Bricusse and Windhorn's musical take on Stevenson's gothic horror story.

Robert Louis Stevenson wrote the novella The Strange Case Of Dr Jekyll And Mr Hyde as he was fascinated with the 'duality of man' and wrote, quite quickly, the first draft of the book. Dissatisfied with it, he burnt it and immediately started on the next draft. Stevenson was quite ill and practically bedridden at the time but believed the cathartic action of writing the book was conducive to his recovery. It was published in 1886 and sealed his reputation as a serious novelist.

Jekyll And Hyde, the musical was written in 1986 and took almost ten years to make it to Broadway where it opened in 1997. It ran for four years and won a number of Tony nominations and a few Drama Desk Awards.

Tullamore Musical Society staged the piece in the local GAA Centre, directed by Paul Norton with Musical Direction by Shane Farrell and Choreography by Graham Finnerty. Tullamore GAA Centre is an atypical GAA venue with rudimentary facilities, a platform stage and loose seating. The Society lined the walls with black drapes to deaden the sound and to add to the grotesque undertone they needed to pull off such a dark piece of musical theatre.

As the audience entered the space we were intimidated by three scantly clad, heavily made up young women who wandered the aisles with a passive aggressiveness that dared us to engage with them. Some did, to be met with accusatory dead-eyed stares. This was a wonderful display of immersive theatre, which was topped off by other actors playing lunatics howling and gibbering across the stage, where a raised hospital bed containing a dying old man was placed. Dark ambient sounds were played and the haze was abundant and this pre-show exhibition really set the mise en scene for the eerieness that was to come.

In the title role(s), Chris Corroon embodied the angst of the helpless medical doctor and scientist, who wanted to make a difference. He believed he could eradicate man's evil nature, thus leaving only the benign and good. Prevented by the Governors of the hospital where he works from experimenting on live subjects he uses himself as a guinea pig, injecting a potion designed to expose the duality. This potion turned the gentle doctor into the evil Mr Hyde. As Hyde, Chris Corroon stalked and growled about the stage, his face masked by his long lank hair. His singing was first-rate, 'This Is The Moment', the most well-known number, was performed very well as was 'The Transformation' and 'I Need to Know', which sets up the whole premise of the show. However, he was outstanding on 'Confrontation' where he plays both characters during the one number. His transformation, helped by Ronan Kenny's lighting, between both characters was very impressive. Mr Corroon's performance was very physical as Hyde and more cerebral and still as Jekyll, which I feel was the right direction for the actor.

Henry Jekyll had two love interests; Emma a young lady of society and Lucy a young lady of the night. As Emma, an innocent alluring homely character, Yvonne O'Toole played her to perfection. Ms O'Toole's voice, clearly a trained soprano, was captivating particularly on 'Once Upon A Dream' and the duet 'Take Me As I Am'. Her performance was a well-honed contrast to Linda Murray who played the kind-hearted prostitute Lucy, who Jekyll befriends. Ms Murray, had a powerful mezzo which really shone on the plaintive 'Someone Like You' and the power ballad, 'A New Life'. Her performance was nuanced and layered and we had great empathy with her plight. A fearless actor, Ms Murray really captured the essence of Lucy and her performance of 'Bring on the Men' with the girls of the Red Rat was a stand out moment of squalid theatre. As Spider, the ubiquitous pimp, choreographer Graham Finnerty, oozed menace as he controlled his stable in the Red Rat, which was like an X-rated Kit Kat Klub.

John Utterson, Jekyll's good friend and narrator of the piece was played solidly by Stephen Rabbette. Tomas Glynn played the sneering Simon Stride, secretary for the Hospital Governors and Jekyll's rival for Emma's affections, with an aloof superiority - delighting in thwarting Henry's requests. The Governors of the hospital were played by a wonderful selection of talented actors. The ghastly foppish Lord Savage was played with relish by Rian Fitzmaurice Condron. When Mr Hyde dispatched him, the audience almost cheered, such was Mr Fitzmaurice Condron's masterful characterisation. The Bishop of Basingstoke, a slimy pederast was played by Malcolm Whelan. The audience gasped in revulsion when a very young girl was presented to him for his delectation and again almost cheered when he was stabbed by Hyde. Joan White as Lady Beaconsfield was superb with pursed lips and disapproving haughtiness and Paul Spencer as General Lord Glossop was also rather good. Sir Archibald Proops was well played by Colin Hughes. Emma's father, Sir Danvers Carew was played with a assured geniality by Seamus Feerick. As Chairman of the Board of Governors, he favoured Jekyll's experiments, looking on him as a son, but abstained from voting for him. Mr Ferrick exuded an 18th century upper class attitude but with an endearing humanity. Choreographer Graham Finnerty, was also responsible for the make-up and working with the director and set designer, I suspect helped shape the styling of the production. His choreography on 'Façade' and the stunning 'Bring On The Men' was inventive, innovative and very well executed by the cast. The ensemble in this show were really well drilled both in movement and singing. They owned the stage and were a forceful entity. Particular praise goes to the young actors of the Red Rat, they were bold, graceful and sang as well as they danced.

Shane Farrell as Musical Director and Chorus Master, conducted an orchestra of keys, strings, woodwind, brass and percussion with a deftness and lightness of touch. Heather Shine's piano was the backbone of the production, her playing was delicate and beautiful. Mr Farrell's pacing and timing were really good as was his work with the chorus, who were excellent.

The set was designed by John O'Donoghue and built by Wayne Handy, the Stage Manager. A steampunk design throughout, with pipes spouting smoke and haze, platforms and a wonderfully realistic laboratory, this set was perfectly complementary to the era and gothic atmosphere of the musical. Numerous clock faces were attached to the flats and there was a good use of levels. Costume design, by Andrew Reddy and Pat McGann Costumes, was also of the steampunk era, with accessories of round sunglasses and bespoke hat wear. Props co-ordinator, Nathalie Watts, assembled a remarkable array of laboratory gear and general props to accentuate the style. Make-up Artist, Yvonne O'Toole, co-ordinated a superb look for the cast, designed by Graham Finnerty.

Wayne Handy stage managed the entire show with his crew of nine asms and showed great innovation on settings. The cast also set up and struck some of the scenes, which was effective and made transitions quick and simple. Sound by Jody Trehy was full, well-balanced and they achieved a good mix between band and singers. Jekyll's pre-recorded voice when writing his notes was cleverly done. Lighting by Roken Lighting and Ronan Kenny was atmospheric with a good use of greens and reds. Strobe use was restrained and effective as was the LED footlights.

Jekyll And Hyde is full of power ballads, which whilst really well sung by the principals, certainly dates it a bit. That said, it has a good solid script and interesting characters. As a blueprint for a director it is quite appealing I suspect as the provenance of the source material is so interesting. But, it can fail miserably if badly handled. The creatives need to share a definite artistic vision on how to stage the piece. Thankfully, director Paul Norton had a great vision for the show and together with his formidable team of creatives and a dedicated and talented cast managed to create a show that was more than the sum of its parts. Tullamore Musical Society brought a taste of bawdy gothic Victoriana, underpinned with philosophical and physiological horror, to a surprised and appreciative audience who luxuriated in the seediness.

Pippin the musical has slightly gone out of fashion in recent years. Some find the theme and the music in the show dated. It was therefore great to see the show reinvented and given the enthusiasm and commitment it deserves. Indeed, the themes of the show are all too current. The themes of dictatorship, governmental control, territory, ambition and self- fulfilment are actually all too relevant today.

This production by Galway University Musical Society had a real fire in its belly which electrified the audience of The Black Box Theatre on the final night of its run. The Black Box is an intimate space with staging set at floor level and tiered seating accommodating around 300 in three seating blocks. There is therefore a great intimacy between the actors and their audience which worked particularly well in this show which very much breaks down the 'fourth wall'.

This was an entirely student production. By this I mean that everyone involved in the show was a student, from the orchestra to each member of the stage team, production, actors. I am delighted to report that if this is the talent we have standing waiting in the wings, the future of musical theatre in Ireland is secure.

Heading the team was Director Kevin Murphy. It was so obvious by the intelligent, fast-moving show we were given that Kevin had put so much thought and planning into each aspect of the show. He and the stage team, under the management of Emily Aherne, created an open set with two raised areas upstage. One was used to house the fourteen- piece orchestra, the other was periodically used by the actors and created a castle ramparts effect. Below this was an entrance through smart red velvet curtains which echoed the red ruched drapes on the back wall. This seemed to create a circus- like setting. There were painted panels on the front of the raised area. These were painted in images which were probably significant historically but I am afraid my knowledge doesn't extend to that. I found them to be slightly distracting and a plainer background might have defined the action downstage better. There were cubes in the form of dice, luck playing such an important in our lives. These cubes were turned to reveal ideas such a love, war, flesh etc. written on them. Big set pieces such as the throne, which had the King of Hearts painted on it carried the magic, luck of the draw idea through. By the way, the foyer of the theatre had been decorated with cards and balloons everywhere. The toilets even had King and Queen of Hearts cards on the doors. The scene changes became very much part of the action as pieces such as a gingham clad kitchen table came sashaying onto the set making every scene change a piece of choreography. This was always in character, nicely moved and must have taken a lot of practice, but it was so, so effective.

There was an accompanying intricate lighting plot, which, for the most part worked really well. There were lovely pools of light on the stage which brightened and dulled as principals entered and exited the area. There were moments when coloured lights were used to good effect, for example when King Charles was murdered the lights reddened dramatically. However, towards the end of the show only one follow spot tried to cover a battling duet with the result that we lost one of the players, which was a shame. Also, there was the beautiful 'Love Song' with Pippin and Catherine which would have been more intimate if it had been enclosed in a narrower pool of lighting.

The Musical Director Eoin Corcoran and Assistant MD Laura Shivnan created a wonderful sound from the orchestra. From jazzy numbers, Charleston rhythms, to beautiful ballads, there was a rounded and well-balanced accompaniment.

Having the orchestra upstage can cause problems with cueing but that was not evident here. It also meant that the cast were not singing out over the orchestra and we could hear every word loud and very clear. (Diction was excellent throughout in speech and singing). The principals were obviously well rehearsed and they were all comfortable in their singing roles. The chorus too sang really well, blowing us away in those big numbers with some nice moments of harmony dotted through the show. This was a nice piece of secure well-rehearsed musical direction.

The chorus actually played a huge part in the success of the show. The Director let each individual develop as a real person so we didn't just see a group but a collection of individuals working together. Each had a very distinct and unique personality. The entire chorus could rise to the challenges of one of the most stunning pieces of choreography I have seen on my travels. I commend Meadhbh Lyons and Anna Campbell for some wonderful theatrical moments. We had superb body lines, angles, detailed gestures and my 'thing': ever changing patterns on stage. These were dance numbers which didn't stand still, patterns, groupings changed, other characters came on stage, others left, as the music developed so did the movement. Choreography which always related to the words and feel of a song, added to the moment, helped in the overall storytelling, leaving us wanting more. Nice 'nods' to the choreography of Bob Fosse, those 'Frug' boxing punches, the 'Cabaret' raised foot rotations, clever and detailed touches. The smaller groups moved really well too. I particularly loved the routine with Leading Player and two guys, magical wee moment. I had the feeling that the whole show was choreographed in that the acting moves and the dance moves married together so very well.

The principal line up was excellent. Everyone fitted their role so well. Kevin must have worked really hard with the cast in developing the individual characters, all of whom were convincing. Of course, Pippin himself has to hold the whole show together. We need an actor who can run through a whole gamut of emotions, we need to have empathy with him in his search for contentment. He has to be able to sing, act and move. Eoin Mullins gave us a strong performance in the title role. He created some very memorable moments. I particularly liked his rendition of 'Corner of the Sky' and his duet with Catherine was moving. Leading Player was given a slight 'Greatest Showman' feel as Rachel Gaughan was dressed in a ringmaster style. This is the observer, the MC, always guiding the story and finally trying to control it. Rachel was always watchable, pulling us into her world. She sang well and she moved beautifully around the stage. (Great hip movements too). She really related to us in the audience with her direct eye contact.

King Charles was played by Shane McCormick. Shane managed to capture the blustering eccentric but also created sensitive moments too. He injected wonderful comic timing into the role and gave us many laughs along the way. The patter beginning to 'War is a Science' is very difficult and perfect diction is demanded for its success. His glamorous second wife Fastrada was in the capable hands of Kate O'Mahony. Kate stunned us with her quick changes and totally skimpy gowns. This is an actor who just loves being on stage and in return we loved watching her. The stage came alive when she stepped elegantly on. She didn't shy away from difficult choreography. There was a leap of faith into the arms of the chorus, there's trust indeed. Marc O'Connor made a wonderful creation as Pippin's step brother Lewis. This was a gung-ho, macho man at his best. We were thoroughly entertained with his swashbuckling antics.

Taz Spellman's song was like a show in its own right. This is an actor who gives 150% to the role and certainly the energy needed for her solo was huge. Berthe is the grandmother of the King who readily passes on her theory of life to her grandson. This was a frenetic, hilarious tour de force performance. Every ounce of energy was put into the delivery of her lines and she related brilliantly to her audience even getting us to sing and move with her.

Catherine, as played by Ailbhe Lohan, is Pippin's lover. Ailbhe gave the role her own twist with some moments of perfect comic timing. She has a glorious singing voice which blended beautifully with Pippin's voice. Danielle McElroy was her daughter Thea. Danielle maintained the body language and 'attitude' of a child throughout. She gave us a very moving moment at the very end of the show as she tries to re-enact moments from the show on the empty stage.

I loved the pale base make up and the bright red lipstick. Eyes were well lined and really made the eyes pop out to us. Costumes were colourful and I loved the sheen off the chorus shirts. It is difficult with a budget to get perfectly fitting costumes for everyone but by and large the costumes fitted well and added a circus feel to the production with details such as the Leading Player's hat, Fastrada's wonderful outfits and Bertha's revealing skimpy top. There was clever self-costuming such as black jeans, boots etc. this actually added a 'review' quality to the production which I liked for this show.

Well done GUMS this was a thoroughly entertaining, humorous and thought- provoking show. There was good attention to detail, some great performances, wonderful choreography, superb music and total commitment from all involved. A joyous and colourful night in The Black Box. Well done one and all.

Fantastmagorical Ballinrobe Musical Society first staged a musical, The Mikado, back in 1944 almost twenty years before Ian Fleming wrote the short novel on which Chitty Chitty Bang Bang is loosely based. They took a break between 1949 and 1974 when they returned to the stage with another Gilbert & Sullivan classic The Pirates Of Penzance and have been consistently producing shows every year since. This year they staged the family favourite Chitty Chitty Bang Bang, directed by Peter Kennedy, for eight performances in the school hall of Ballinrobe Community School during the school's mid-term break.

Turning a school hall into a theatre takes a lot of work. The society had to extend the stage, bring in raked seating, lighting and sound equipment and try and fit a full-sized car onto a relatively small platform stage. They also had to build two additional cars in addition to the Chitty they hired in from Sound Ideas Theatre in Norfolk.

As we entered the 430 seat venue we were delighted to see a full-house. On the stage was an old car, which the society had rescued from a shed in Roscommon. Upstage was a giant BP screen with the Chitty logo proudly displayed and giant barn door style flats. On stage left was a two story house with a small windmill perched above it, clearly the Potts residence as we saw later when it opened onto a kitchen and the children's bedroom. On stage right was the Vulgarian Toymaker's shop and above it a small living room with a chaise. Set design was by David Nevin, John O'Shea, Kenneth McCarthy and Mick Harte and looked very solidly built by their large set construction team.

The plot of the musical reads like a junior James Bond adventure by way of Lewis Carroll in that the hero, whacky inventor Caractacus Potts, his girlfriend, Truly Scrumptious and his children, Jeremy and Jemima, go on a big adventure to a fictional European country, Vulgaria, which is populated by very odd characters to rescue his father who is being held captive by the dictator Baron Bomburst.

As Caractacus Potts, Dave Langan gave us a gentle widower who shines with love for his two children but worries about their future because as an inventor, he's not very good and does not earn very much money. Mr Langan had a sweet voice, most notable on 'You Two', where he sings with Jeremy and Jemima. His dancing was also quite good on 'Me Ol' Bamboo' and when he became the rag doll on 'Doll On A Music Box/Truly Scrumptious'. His was a solid, believable performance and where required, on 'Teamwork' for instance, he commanded the stage well. One little niggle I had with his direction was that he masked himself totally for most of 'Hushabye Mountain' by facing upstage. I know he was singing upstage to the children but this could have been cheated out earlier. This was a pity as he sang it very well.

Playing his father, Grandpa Potts, was Richard Crumlish. He played him as a smaller character than is usual and didn't have the Sergeant Major roughness to his character. However, Mr Crumlish was very similar to Potts Junior in his gentleness towards the children, which did work quite well on his song, ''Posh!' with Jeremy and Jemima. His solo 'Them Three' was also quite good. He also sang well on the big farcical number 'The Roses Of Success' in Act Two with the inventors.

Jeremy and Jemima were played by Paddy O'Brien and Rachel Gallagher. They were rather good, their accents were perfect and their singing was sweet and tuneful. Their onstage relationship was quite believable, in that we could see Jeremy sometimes getting irritated with Jemima's antics, just like a real brother and sister. They sang very well with Truly on her eponymous song 'Truly Scrumptious' and danced quite well throughout.

As Truly, Stephanie Cassol gave a very good performance. Her diction and RP were perfect. She also sang very well on 'Truly Scrumptious', 'Doll On A Music Box' and on the title song. Ms Cassol had a great onstage relationship with the children, particularly Jemima, where they quickly formed a mother/daughter bond. Her scenes with Caractacus were delightful and they had a good dynamic. Playing her father, Lord Scrumptious was Gerry Hayes who oozed gravitas but good humour.

In Vulgaria, we had an odd assortment of weird characters headed up by the child-like Baron Bomburst. Niall Conway was absolutely superb as the Baron. Showing his inner child and in contrast his psychopathic self often within one line of dialogue. Mr Conway's performance was masterful, his comic timing impeccable, his slapstick sharp and his singing on 'Chu-Chi Face' with his Baroness was memorable. As the Baroness, Angela Staunton matched Mr Conway in terms of comic timing however her singing and dance on 'The Bombie Samba' was excellent. They also clearly added their own small routines to the roles and had a wonderful chemistry and absolute trust in each other, which was heartening to see. The Vulgarian Toymaker was played by Ronan Egan, a rather small role but an important one as he is the character who conceals the children from the Baron and Baroness. Mr Egan performed well, had a wonderful Germanic accent and sang 'Teamwork' nicely with Potts and the hidden children. The children were also hiding from the Childcatcher. This character is not in the original novel, but was created by Roald Dahl for the film and was kept in for the musical. John Byrne played him very well, he was quite balletic and graceful in a scary 'I'm coming to get you' way with his sing-song voice, long nose and white face. The spies Goran and Boris who are sent by the Baron to kidnap Potts were played by Tom Byrne and Mike Ansbro. They interacted with the audience and had a couple of good routines including 'Act English' where they were teaching themselves typical English phrases so they could integrate seamlessly into English society.

Director, Peter Kennedy, did a wonderful job controlling the sheer amount of creatives and cast on this show. He really brought out the humour of the Vulgarian section and its despotic leaders and the pathos of the children having to hide from the monstrous Child Catcher.

Choreograph was by Aoife McClafferty and she did a good job with 'Me 'Ol Bamboo' and the Fair scene with the acrobats. Her work with Truly on the music box was also very good as was 'Teamwork' with the children and 'Toot Sweets'.  'The Roses of Success' was also done quite well and she clearly matched the routines to the abilities of her cast.

Musical direction was handled by Finola Higgins who also acted as chorus mistress and conductor. The horn and piano were lovely on 'Hushabye Mountain' and the offstage chorus on the title song was powerful with a great presence of the sopranos. Percussion on 'The Bombie Samba' was also very powerful and the horns greatly added to the Latin American vibe.

Lighting by Dirk Beauman DBL Lighting was a bit hit and miss I felt. Some states were very nice, the underground scene worked well but could have done with follow spots. The people in Chitty were sporadically lit but mostly in shadow when aboard and as the children's bedroom was lit mostly with lilacs, Potts's face when he turned out was a strange shade of violet, again a follow spot would have helped here. 'The Bombie Samba' was really well lit and there was a great use of colour and movers in this number. Sound was well balanced and full range by Derek Recks and he achieved a great mix between stage and band.  However, the projections were a bit laggy and the audience could see the video controls on screen.

It's a huge show and good stage management is vital on the smooth running of it. Thankfully Stage Manager Kenneth McCarthy was on hand to ensure cars, people and set went on and off without a hitch. Well done to him and his crew. Make up was done by a large crew as there was so many cast onstage. This was done well and suited the actors, with the exception of the bright red lipstick on Jeremy and Jemima. Hair and wigs was also looked after by a large crew and worked very well, particularly the 'Inventors' wigs. Sadly, I don't think the hired car worked as well as one would expect, the scissors lift underneath was very visible and the four wheels were about a foot off the floor. Dry ice to conceal the machinery would have worked wonders and preserved the magic.

This was a good production by director Peter Kennedy of Chitty Chitty Bang Bang and the audience absolutely loved it. It had only opened when I saw it and I'm sure the little niggles I experienced, which didn't take from my enjoyment, were remedied for the rest of the run.

Viva La Vie Bohème Produced by CIT Musical Society and directed by Dan Coughlan, Rent ran on the Curtis stage in Cork's School of Music for three performances in February. Established eight years ago, when they staged Jonathan Larson's Tick, Tick… Boom!, the Society has won a slew of awards for their, mostly, contemporary musicals.

This year's outing was also written by Jonathan Larson in the early 90's and based on Puccini's opera La Bohème. Rent is about a year in the life of a group of friends living in a building in New York City. Like La Bohème, these friends are all struggling artists, but some are HIV Positive. The title refers to their inability to pay the rent as the area becomes more gentrified. As the show's creator sadly died just before the Off-Broadway premiere, Rent  has become a homage to his memory and spawned Rent-heads, fans who queued up for cut-price tickets when it played on Broadway.

There was no set designer credited but the set was very simple as the Curtis is more of a concert hall and there are restrictions on what creatives can do in the space; a fairly large platform stage with no masking or drapes. The band and conductor were placed upstage right, behind the stage alongside a massive organ. On stage were a series of trestle tables and far left a small Christmas Tree. The platform was like an island in the middle of the room, with the audience in front on chairs and on a raked seating bank.

The whole show is sung-through and narrated by Mark, an aspiring filmmaker. He was played by Michael Moone in a considered performance. His scenes with Roger, his roommate, were quite good and they had a good chemistry. Mr Moone's singing was stable on "Rent" with Roger and ensemble, "Tango: Maureen"- a duet with Joanne, and generally throughout the show, however he had tuning issues on a couple of numbers. I liked his Mark, though - he focused on the character's strengths rather than his indecisions. Roger, Marks's roommate, was played by Pearse O'Donoghue, who also played electric guitar onstage as Roger was a musician. Roger was HIV positive and trying to write that one great love song. Mr O'Donoghue did have the pretty boy frontman swagger alluded to in the show but his singing was a little forced on "One Song Glory" and he had tuning issues on "Without You" and "Living In America". His acting was good though, he expressed Roger's brooding pessimism very well and his scenes with Mimi, his love interest, were quite convincing.

As Mimi, an HIV positive, drug addicted club dancer and Roger's love interest, Dannielle Hoban Maguire acted and danced well but her singing let her down at the performance I attended. Her energy flagged on "Out Tonight" and she was very off key on "Without You", especially when Roger joined her at the end of the song, although her earlier duet with Roger, "Light My Candle" was nicely performed. Ms Hoban Maguire did portray Mimi's addiction very well however and her brief scene with The Man convinced.

Mimi's ex-partner and former roommate of Mark's, Benny, who married into money and now owns a lot of real estate in the neighbourhood including the building where Mark, Mimi and Roger live, was very well played by Sean MacGearailt. He captured the conflict of being a landlord to his friends. His singing was good too on "You'll See" and his sections of "La Vie Bohème A".

Another ex-roommate, Tom Collins was played by Darragh Johnson. As the anarchic university professor, Mr Johnson really convinced particularly in his relationship with Angel. His voice was exquisite, a fine baritone, he handled "Santa Fe" and "I'll Cover You" with ease but it was on the slow-tempo "I'll Cover You (Reprise)" with the ensemble where he shone. His emotional connection with this song was palpable. A very fine performance.

Collins's love interest was Angel, a young drag queen with AIDS, who tended to him when he was mugged, here performed by Ryan O'Sullivan. Mr O'Sullivan's performance was quite heartfelt, he played Angel with a delightful delicacy. His singing on "Today 4 U" was good as was his duet with Collins "I'll Cover You" and his sections in "La Vie Bohème". The final two friends, who are also in a relationship were Joanne, played by Christine Caldbeck and Maureen (Mark's ex) here played by Kayme O'Callaghan. Both were very believable in their onstage relationship and were dazzling when they sang the duet "Take Me or Leave Me". Ms Calbeck's "We're Okay" as Joanne was also good as was her duet with Mark, "Tango: Maureen". But it was Ms O'Callaghan who brought the house down with a very well performed solo 'performance piece' "Over The Moon". This song included the audience mooing, two very funny deadpan reluctant backing singers and a cowbell! This song was the highlight of the show.

Katie Taylor and Andrew Lane were two featured soloists on "Seasons Of Love" and they had perfect voices for the song, Ms Taylor also soloed on the beautiful reprise of "I'll Cover You", where she sang from the centre aisle.

There was no choreographer credited, however there was some movement on stage. "Contact", performed to a very poor quality backing track, was really well directed by Dance Captain Ciara O'Neill. The group movements in "La Vie Bohème", were also good, but not as sharp as needed. Angel's little routine in his Santa costume "Today 4 U", was performed well but again the backing track was substandard.

Musical direction was by Keith Greene and whilst it was quite faithful to the score, there was a lot of tuning issues with the singers and ensemble. Conductor/ Keyboard 1, was by Jimmy Brockie but he was sited upstage right, out of view of the cast. There was no camera/monitor set up, so it appeared that the cast were not conducted, which may explain some of the vocal issues on the night. However, they were really balanced on "Seasons Of Love", which opened the second act and there was some lovely guitar work on "One Song Glory" and "Rent".

Sound by Declan O'Sullivan and Downey Brogan was quite well-balanced and full, with the exception of the backing tracks, which sounded very shrill and lacked any bottom end and the song "Christmas Bells" which was really muddled. Mr O'Sullivan also designed the lighting for the show, but as he was hampered by what he could adjust in the venue, the design failed to sufficiently light the actors - but for some of the numbers it looked like a rock gig, which worked well.

Hair and make-up by Aoife Marie Healy was good and eclectic, which suited the show. I particularly liked Maureen and Angel's make up, it was very distinctive. Costume design was unaccredited but was also suitable for the era and the style of show. Stage management was handled by Christopher Hopcraft, who also operated the lighting. The back stage crew and cast organised the transitions, which were a bit laboured and slow in places.

Rent is a fabulous musical, which I really liked and indeed everything it stood for, being old enough to have experienced the effects of the Aids epidemic on friends and acquaintances. I think director, Dan Coughlan did a satisfactory job in bringing it to the Curtis stage, given the inherent problems the society faced and I look forward to re-visiting the society in the future.

A Drop Of Golden Sun Killarney Musical Society took over the INEC for a few nights in February to bring us Rogers and Hammerstein's masterpiece The Sound Of Music. The show was originally staged on Broadway in 1959 and won 5 Tony Awards. Of course, most people know it from the 1965 film version starring Julie Andrews, which won 5 Oscars and is required viewing for all children everywhere.

Killarney Musical Society was revived in 1985, staging H.M.S. Pinafore, following a twenty year hiatus. Their home since 2001 has been the INEC, a vast modern theatre complex in Killarney. The plot of the show is based on Maria von Trapp's autobiography The Story Of The Trapp Family Singers and revolves around a postulant, Maria Rainer, and her struggle with her faith. She leaves the Austrian Abbey and meets and eventually marries widower Georg von Trapp and becomes mother to his seven musically talented children. This is all played out against a backdrop of the rise of the Nazi s and their eventual annexation of Austria.

Directed and choreographed by Peter Kennedy with musical direction by Noël Lennon, Killarney's Sound Of Music opened with a large cast of children performing "The Lonely Goatherd" accompanied by Nuns of the Nonnberg Abbey. An unconventional opening which did work as the children were in fine voice. The children were ushered off by the nuns and we were introduced to Maria, played by Siobháin Bustin who sang the title song.

Ms Bustin had quite a contemporary musical theatre voice with small modern nuances and inflections which lifted the song in places. Ms Bustin played Maria with a largely accurate English accent as most actors do since the original, hers was a gentle portrayal of Maria, coming across more as a caring motherly figure rather than a maverick, which suited the production. Her singing was sensitive and at times hearty. On "My Favourite Things" with the Mother Abbess and the reprise with the children, her diction and articulation was superb; on "Do-Re-Mi", she injected a lovely humour; on "I Have Confidence" she was strong and full of vitality and on "Something Good" with Georg, tender and warm. Ms Bustin had a superb range and marvellous control of her vocal and was a pleasure to hear. Her acting was also quite accomplished, especially when working with the children. As Captain von Trapp, Derek O'Leary gave us a stoic, humourless Georg. A nationalist gradually realising his nation was being overrun by fascists, helming his household like a battleship and his children like his crew, he gradually softened due to Maria's efforts to cultivate him. Mr O'Leary had a fine voice, most notable on "Something Good" with Maria and on "No Way To Stop It" with Max and Elsa and his solo "Edelweiss", which he sang with great emotion. His performance was very austere, he rarely if ever smiled, but he did capture the fierce loyalty the Captain had for his country and the revulsion he felt for the Nazis.

Georg's friend Max Detweiler, a music agent and concert promoter, was played by Pádraig Creedon. His voice was robust on "No Way To Stop It" and his comic timing was quite good. Mr Creedon played Max as an equivocal, selfish character, determined to retain his position in society and business despite the Anschluss. However, he didn't resort to sieg-heiling Rolf as is often done in other productions. Max is the comic relief in the show and the eventual hero of the hour as he enables the von Trapp's to escape and Mr Creedon played him well. Playing the local Gauleiter, local Nazi Party leader Herr Zeller, was Des Furlong. Mr Furlong played him with a zealousness that was quite frightening. He strode across the stage and even into the auditorium with goose stepped fascist fanaticism and really embodied all that Georg was railing against. A chilling performance that reminded us of the injustices that extreme fundamentalism can perpetrate.

Von Trapp's initial love interest was Baroness Elsa Schraeder, played by Harriet McGuigan, a wealthy widow who became his fiancé. Elsa is often demonised in productions of the musical, but the reality was that she was just of a totally different class and could not relate to children or indeed servants, which Maria was, as being in any way equal to her status. Ms McGuigan played her as aloof and imperious and her performance was quite faithful to the original. She broke off the engagement due to a difference in politics and not because of Maria's presence, which Ms McGuigan played this very well. She also sang well on "No Way To Stop It" and "How Can Love Survive". Playing Georg's servants were Orna Cleary-O'Shea as Frau Schmidt, who gave a fine nuanced and subtle portrayal of the Housekeeper and Peter Cook as the butler with fascist leanings. Mr Cook's performance was quite good, but some of his lines were lost or mixed up so that sometimes they didn't make sense.

As the Mother Abbess, Bríd Mills, gave a wonderful performance. Her singing was absolutely exceptional on "Climb Ev'ry Mountain", where she soared with the high notes and her characterisation was warm, benign and wonderfully accomplished. She showed a lovely hesitation on "My Favourite Things" with Maria, but we could see the character gradually savouring the joy of the song. Ms Mills gave us an exquisite and consummate Mother Abbess, which will be long remembered. At the Abbey we also met Claire Sheehan as Sr Sophia, Brónagh Murphy as Sr Margaretta and Judy Rezin as Sr Berthe. All three excelled with Ms Mills on "Maria", where they sang of her virtues and her  imperfections and again on the "Nun's Processional" and "The Wedding Processional" with the Nun's ensemble. Their performances were idiosyncratic and quite believable.

As the young Rolf, the local delivery boy, Jonathan O'Keeffe sang quite well on "Sixteen Going On Seventeen" with Liesl and he handled the dance sections with great precision. Mr O'Keefe performed the role of Rolf, who eventually became a Nazi, enthusiasm and spirit.

Captain von Trapp's seven children were performed by two casts, given the demands of the roles. On the performance I attended Liesl was performed by Lillie Foley. Ms Foley had a lovely voice on "Sixteen Going On Seventeen" with Rolf and the reprise with Maria and played Liesl with a well-pitched emotion. In the roles of the other children we had; Brayden Slattery as Friedrich, Saoirse O'Sullivan as Louisa, Denis Moroney as Kurt, Clodagh O'Sullivan as Marta, Caoimhe Murray as Brigitta and Emily O'Shea as Gretl. All were rather good, well drilled in the choreography and had excellent harmonies.

Musical Direction was by Noël Lennon and he did a fabulous job. The "Nun's Processional" and "The Wedding Processional" were outstanding and the von Trapp Children's harmonies were also very good. His work with the band was also quite notable. The brass and keys were resplendent in the Wedding scene and the woodwinds were lovely throughout.

Stage management by Phil Edmonds and crew was quite good but there were too many long transitions I felt which negatively affected the pace of the production. Set was by Wayne Handy and worked quite well but seemed a little small for the stage. That said the Abbey looked good with the altar and the columns. Some of the furniture was a tad contemporary, such as Maria's bed which was a modern divan but generally worked quite well. Lighting and projection was by Kieran Sommers was quite good but seemed a little flat at times, with too much front lighting and not enough sculpting and was too bright in the graveyard scene where Rolf's torch was hardly discerned. However the Abbey was nicely lit with gobos and this gave a pleasing look to those scenes. Sound was by Star Systems and was quite full and well mixed. Costumes by Pat McGann were very accurate to the period and the Nun's habits were in keeping with the era. The children's 'play clothes' made from curtain material were super. Make up by Ann Elizabeth Rohan was also quite good and suited the look of the production.

Peter Kennedy gave us a nice solid production of the Rogers and Hammerstein musical and although I would have liked a bit more attention to detail, I thought that the performances more than made up for this.

First staged in 1975, the Kander, Ebb and Fosse musical Chicago has broken all sorts of box office records and deservedly so. The idea behind adapting the play by the same name by Maurine Dallas Watkins was the brain child of Gwen Verdon and husband Bob Fosse. Watkins had written the play based on real life trials in 1924 of accused murderers Beulah Annan and Belva Gaertner.

Lawyers William Scott Stewart and W.W. O'Brien were the inspiration for the fast- talking Billy Flynn. Why is the show the longest running American musical on Broadway and in the West End? The clever story-line is as relevant today as it was when first conceived in 1926. The musical score is stunning, the mix of characters outstanding and the potential for wonderful choreography makes it a modern-day classic. It mixes story with dance, drama with vaudeville, a wonderful piece of theatre, but one which shouldn't be attempted by the faint-hearted as our expectations are high for any production of the show.

The O'Reilly Theatre near Parnell Square was the venue for the opening night performance which I attended. This is a great venue as the auditorium is a surprisingly good size with tiered seating for nearly five hundred. A nice mix of jazz and ragtime music was playing as we entered which created the mood of the piece. The stage is vast, very wide with loads of space in the wings and deep enough for most stage settings. The open curtain revealed a set with a raised platform at the back accessed by two sets of stairs. Brick buildings flanked either side with a further balcony effect on each side. There was a set of doors at the back of the stage, very plainly painted (might have been nice to make more use of these during the show) and the word Chicago with cut out letters inset with lights which functioned well at the end of the show, changing colours for a great effect. An Art Deco piece stood centre stage to break up the line of the raised platform. The staging looked fine throughout but it might have been nice to see the stairs light up, have a bit more glitz and glamour for some of the numbers. During the show, scene changes were just pieces brought on such as the black chairs and tables and prison bars for 'Cell Block Tango'. These were deftly positioned on stage by a well-trained cast. The changes of scene never affected the rattling pace of the show.

Director Eoin Hannaway had obviously worked extremely hard with his cast and crew of students to produce a really entertaining evening of theatre. I attended on the opening night and although there were a few wee glitches, it was obvious that the show had 'great bones'. Eoin created nicely rounded characterisations of the main players. He chose to have Mary Sunshine played by a female. This is optional but in many shows I have seen it is played by a man in drag. Of course, there must be a shock reveal and it is hard to get a man who convincingly sings counter tenor.

The stage design gave Eoin seven entrances onto the stage. This led to some interesting moments, such as the staging of 'Class' which was stripped down and played seated in a nice pool of light and hence created a bit of magic. On the whole Eoin gave us a classy, polished piece of theatre.

Of course, with the pedigree of Bob Fosse behind the show, the dancing in Chicago is something we all look forward to. The choreography was in the very capable hands of Cian O'Sullivan. In the opening number cast kept pouring out onto the stage, but thanks to well planned movements and rehearsals, everyone knew exactly where they should be and what they should be doing. My old bug- bear, changing patterns on the stage, delighted to say we had lovely detailed, intricate moves with great ever-changing patterns on stage. There was a light touch at times too, such as in 'Me and My Baby' when Roxie and two girl dancers in bowler hats gave us a delightful soft shoe type routine. Nice period moves and patterns. 'All I Care About' was good, though it would have been nice to see something new in the staging of this number. 'Razzle Dazzle' was nicely set and the last few moments of the whole show with the full cast were stunning. This was a competent and intelligent piece of stage choreography.

There were fifteen in the orchestra, again all students. This created a glorious rounded sound. We had lovely touches of jazz and ragtime with a rich brassy sound. The cueing was a bit problematic at times but when that was sorted, Molly Burke had a good control over the orchestra and there were good tempi in most of the numbers. Emily Hogarty had obviously trained the cast well and I enjoyed the harmonies between two players. ('Class' with Mama and Velma was particularly good). Again, at times the cast were not always too sure when to come in with the music, but I am sure this improved as the run continued.

Before I move on to individual performances one thing I would advise as a general rule, be careful with shouting on stage. If you let yourself go to a scream too soon you have nowhere else to go but higher and more hysterical. We lose diction and to be honest it becomes unreal (just something to watch, sometimes held back and quiet can be more effective). Wow what a strong line up of principals we had for this show. Really there are just six principal players who have to totally convince us and carry the show. Rua Barron made a great Roxie with a nod to 1920's hairstyle she looked right for the role, sang really well, giving us great moments of comedy in her singing. She acted her role well too and moved well in all her dance numbers. Rachel Galvin built a great character as Velma and the on/off friendship with Roxie was nicely told. She has a real belter of a voice but also can hold an audience in those softer, gentle moments too. She commanded the stage in in her many solos and her dancing had the right amount of vaudeville feel. There were lovely harmonies created between the two leading ladies who both told the story very eloquently. The smooth-talking Billy Flynn was played by Joshua Hurley. He did a great job with the part (though I wanted to see him in a beautiful suit and Oxford shoes). He sang really well and his ending notes of 'All I Care About' and 'We Both Reached for The Gun' were excellent. He had the right stature for the part but might have needed signs of his success such as nice gold cufflinks, tie- clip etc. A good performance Joshua. Joseph Ó Baoill played poor Amos really well. He gave us a heartfelt performance of 'Mr Cellophane' and showed at the end what a rich and beautiful tone he has to his singing voice. Máirín Hayes was a very glamorous and striking figure as Mama Morton. Máirín was very at ease in the role. She moved well around the stage convincing us that we were in her world. She sang well too, giving us a great solo, 'When You're Good To Mama' and a lovely duet with Velma in 'Class'. She managed to capture the money-grabbing prison warder without giving the part the usual sexual undertone. Jenny Kearns did a great job as Mary Sunshine. I think when you cast a woman in this role that the actor has to work twice as hard to develop the character. I loved the way Jenny at times used her voice. On those occasions when we thought her voice was going to keep soaring, she would drop an octave or two! Very funny portrayal of the part.

The girls of 'Cell Block Tango' were all so different and so talented. They carried out their song with great style, super singing and brilliantly choreographed moves. A very slick moment of theatre. I also loved the male dancer being added in to do the tango of life and death with each girl, this was very effective. Well done Ina Caul, Katie Clarke, Jill Montgomery, Sarah McAleer and Lainey O'Sullivan. Oh, and Jill that walk to the gallows was so very moving. Dave Quane made a convincing Fred Casely. I particularly loved the interplay with Roxie in the courtroom scene. Sean Cassidy and Jack Farrell, I was keeping a careful eye on you as I had played the Master of Ceremonies a million years ago. It is a nice wee role and fun to do, you both gave it real gusto. Pity the lighting cues weren't on your side each time you appeared. Well done too Matthew Coalter as Officer Fogarty and Sarah Curran as the Socialite Kitty.

That huge chorus was a wonderful team of enthusiastic and committed players. There was obviously great teamwork and rapport between the group. Each person knew their own moves and carried them out really well. The individual pieces came together so well to complete the intricate jig saw.

One thing I wasn't too keen on was the lighting for the show. There were some nice moments when we had a pool of light and in particular, I loved the way 'Class' was set and lit. However, there were far too many times when cues were late and the overall feel of the lighting was just dull. The old adage. 'If you can't see them you can't hear them,' still holds true for me. To be honest there were times when we lost characters on stage. Maybe think about having light coming onto the stage from off stage 'rooms', or creating pools of light on stage, or possibly follow-spot more. Maybe the lighting was mostly from directly above the stage which of course will tend to plunge a face into shadow, hard to work around that but it does need to be addressed. I hope the lighting of the show improves as the week progresses. The twenty-four microphones gave our characters a great sound and we could hear everyone very well above the sound of the orchestra.

The costumes were a mixed bag for me, some nice black gear, with the black leotards and touches of lace, men in black waistcoats, see-through shirts. There were black trousers and white shirts for the reporters. I liked the grey overshirts for the prison girls. The 'Cell Block Tango' outfits were great. I thought Billy needed a much better cut suit, maybe a dark suit with a broad pinstripe. We should see Billy as a sharp dresser. I know the effect that the over-large jacket was meant to have on Amos but not sure it worked for me. The Roxie and Velma outfits at the end of the show added the sparkle we needed. Hairs were generally in the cast's own style though the up-pinning of Roxie's own hair gave it a 1920's feel. Velma's wig was a good shape and moved well. It would have been nice to see more of a nod to the period with touches such as waves and kiss curls for the girls' hair. Make up was quite restrained, very nicely applied but I would have gone for a lighter base and really accentuated the eyes, darker greys for eyeshadow and an even heavier colour on the lips, maybe a mulberry colour. The make up was however very consistent and looked for the most part in period. Overall, props were in the style of the piece with simple black tables and chairs, good 'Cell Block' cell bars etc. It is worthwhile to copy the originals of newspapers of the time as modern papers tend to have colour pictures which stick out a mile. In conclusion this was a very competent and entertaining show. There was good attention to detail in the direction, though I would have liked a little more 'razzle and dazzle' in some of the presentation. Some super performances and theatrical moments. Well-done all in Trinity Musical Theatre and good luck to those with their finals this year.

It's a Hard Cold Tumble Of A Journey Urinetown is a hidden gem of a satirical musical written by Mark Hollmann and Greg Kotis in 2001. It is set in a weird future where water shortages are the norm and the government has restricted human urination to public toilets controlled by the UGC (Urine Good Company). The musical satirises politics, capitalism, bureaucracy, justice and social responsibility. It is also a parody of other musicals such as Les Mis, The Threepenny Opera and cleverly the musical form itself as well as certain films and even Shakespeare. Urinetown is one of those shows that seems light and easy enough to stage but it is very demanding of its cast, both vocally and physically. Oh, and of course it's a comedy, so it has to be funny.

Trim Musical Society, engaged Liam Butler to direct the piece and it was staged in Scoil Mhuire during the mid-term break. The venue was a school hall, where the society had to bring everything in. As a venue, it was limited in its facilities and the society had to work hard to stage the show. But it really paid off and we were treated to a tight, hilarious, beautifully theatrical piece of work.

The set, designed by Liam Butler, was really clever, with two staircases leading up to a platform upstage and a series of louvred flats stage left and right on the apron and upstage. Lights were built into the flattage and gave a three dimensional feel to the set. The set was glowing when we entered the auditorium and we watched the band, in front of the raised stage, tune up.

The entire show is narrated by a policeman Officer Lockstock assisted by a young girl, Little Sally. These two characters would pop out and speak with the audience, telling us what was going on, what was going to happen and what we should feel about certain characters in a lovely parody on Brecht's Epic Theatre conventions. The Brecht link continues into the orchestra where, like in his Threepenny Opera (which is itself a socialist critique of capitalism), musicians double and triple up on instruments. Urinetown's band, conducted by the Musical Director Dermot O'Callaghan, had five musicians playing about eleven instruments. Mr O'Callaghan's musical direction was very faithful to the original score and he managed to get a great big sound from relatively few players. I must mention the two horn and wind players, who expertly played many instruments between them throughout the piece. Helen McHugh as Chorus Mistress did a wonderful job with the ensemble, their harmonies rang out and the solos were perfect.

Choreographer, Aisling Rountree clearly worked very hard on this show. The ensemble were all very well drilled and it seemed relatively effortless for them. I really liked the intricate choreography on 'Cop Song' and the slo-mo sequences were very well handled. Ms Rountree put great humour into the routines too; 'Don't Be A Bunny' and the title song were hilarious.

Every story needs a hero or a heroine and the hero of this piece was the dashing Bobby Strong, played by James Branagan. Mr Branagan sang really well on 'Follow Your Heart', a duet with Hope and on 'Look At The Sky' with the poor people of the town. His voice was sweet and gentle but full of character. He played Bobby as an innocent happy go lucky kind of guy until his father, Old Man Strong played with red-faced earnestness by Sean Fox, gets sent to Urinetown. Urinetown is a place where folk get banished to for breaking the rules and Old Man Strong broke the rules because he urinated in the street as he couldn't afford the fee to pee in Public Amenity #9. Bobby leads a revolution and falls in love with Hope Caldwell, the daughter of the President of the evil UGC. Mr Branagan's timing and physicality was spot-on and he had a lovely energy in the role.

Public Amenity #9 was overseen by Penelope Pennywise, played by Helen McHugh. Ms McHugh had a super range and handled the very demanding 'It's a Privilege To Pee' with great vocal dexterity. Her comic timing was also excellent and her duet with Caldwell, 'I'm Not Sorry (Reprise)' was heartfelt. As Caldwell, the exploiter of the poor and Head of UGC, Ian Rountree played him with a cold callousness. Like a cross between a certain US President and Will Ferrell's Mr Mugatu, he embodied the evil capitalist with cartoon-like glee. His singing was also rather good, particularly on 'Mr Caldwell', 'Don't Be A Bunny' and the 'Act One Finale'. Caldwell's side-kick (all villains have side-kicks!), was the delightfully camp Mr. McQueen, a self- serving sycophant brilliantly played by Sean Brown. His physicality, mimicking Caldwell's every action, was sublime. Shane Fox played a crooked Senator Fipp as a cigar chewing Texan, who just wants to fly to Rio. Mr Fox was excellent in the role, his lasciviousness towards Caldwell's daughter, many years his junior, was cringe worthy.

Bobby fell in love with Hope Caldwell, the baddie's daughter, who having just returned from the Most Expensive University in the World to learn the family business, eventually joins Bobby as part of the Revolution. Played beautifully by Megan Pottinger, she exuded a delicate innocence and naïveté that was very funny. Her voice was lovely as she sang 'Follow Your Heart' with Bobby and later the reprise, solo.

Officer Lockstock, the narrator, was played by Ronan Walsh and he absolutely nailed the role. His timing, choreography and singing were near perfect. Mr Walsh's presence and stage craft was superb, reminiscent of Jim Carrey in his early films, he totally immersed himself in the role. His rap style duet, 'Cop Song' with his foil, Officer Barrell - played wonderfully by Eoin Kenny, was laugh out loud funny. Little Sally, Lockstock's co-narrator who constantly questions the validity of the show, was played by Áine Fox. She sang quite well on 'Too Much Exposition' with Lockstock and on 'Tell Her I Love Her' with Bobby and Co. But it was her comic timing and precociousness that made her shine for me. She was cheeky and mocking but with a tongue-in-cheek knowing intelligence that belied her years. Sally's friends, who joined the revolution were played by an ensemble that was well-rehearsed, vocally excellent and showed great movement and attention to detail. Little Becky Two Shoes, a girl with a leg-brace, was wonderfully played by Jenny Seery; Colin Flynn played the unhinged Two Blades Harry, who really shone on 'Snuff That Girl'; as one of the bigger actors on the stage it was only fitting that Paddy O'Sullivan played Tiny Tom; Gwen Bagnall really impressed with her playing of Bobby's mother Josephine, one of the few characters allowed to play the pathos of the piece, she was perfectly cast. The ensemble really seemed to 'get' this piece, they relished every scene, knew when to pull back and when to go full on and generally just enjoyed being in it! Costumes by Miriam Donnelly were perfectly pitched, Les Mis rags for the poor and sharp suits for the rich. Make-up by Ali Murphy also suited the characters, I really liked Mr McQueen's overall styling and Fipp's aged make-up. Lighting was by Denis Twomey and was just right for the show, naturalistic and not flashy and everyone was perfectly lit. Sound by Alan White was just the right mix for the hall, good balance between band and singers and a lovely warm tone was achieved. Stage management by Frank Connolly assisted by Elaine McLoughlin, was slick and timely. Transitions were quick and accurate and the show didn't lag at all. Director Liam Butler did a marvellous job on this show. He wrung all of the classical and contemporary references and jokes out of the script and gifted them to his actors. His pacing of the piece was just right, his comic timing of the set pieces was perfect. Mr Butler clearly has a well- developed sense of humour as a director would need this to stage Urinetown. It is a piece of musical theatre in the Absurd tradition, it could have been written by Ionesco or Beckett, and Mr Butler's instinct and intuitive direction absolutely captured the nature of the absurdity. He shared and developed it with his actors and creatives and we in the audience were lucky to have borne witness to this wonderful production.

Where's the Buzz?

Like Chess and Evita, Jesus Christ Superstar, started out as a concept album, ostensibly to raise the funds to stage it as a show and to generate interest in the notion in 1970. It opened on Broadway a year later to mixed reviews and some controversy as did Stephen Schwartz's Godspell, which opened the same year. They both have similar themes but whereas Godspell focuses on the effects of the teachings of Jesus, Superstar spotlights Jesus and his disciples, especially Judas. The controversy was that neither musical concentrated on the resurrection, and in the case of Superstar, that the character of Judas was written sympathetically. Over the years, the controversy died down and there have been many different styles of production staged of Superstar; ultra- modern, futuristic, contemporary and so on and also versions rooted in the time Jesus is said to have walked the Earth. Which is what director, Bill Stafford and Tipperary Musical Society decided to do in the Excel Theatre in Tipperary in February.

Using an open staging with no tabs drawn, the audience were immediately treated to a massive set, impressively designed by Ben Hennessy, based on a Syrian landscape with a large hill-like structure and what appeared to be caves cut into the pink sun-drenched rock and built- in mesas. At the base there was a large fabric sheet with an image taken from the Turin Shroud. At rise this was removed to show a wooden trunk, which initially looked incongruous, but once a bunch of children in modern-day costumes entered (eventually followed by some of the show's characters) to the overture and started to play hide and seek, it made sense as it contained accessories for these characters. The children offered the accessories, in a ritual, to the players and the show began with 'Heaven On Their Minds' wonderfully sung by Judas.

From here on in it was quite a traditional version of the musical. As most audience members already know the story, exposition and dialogue was seen by the writers as superfluous, so all words were written to be sung. Relying on non-verbal communication and the score only, this show needs very skilled actors/singers to pull it off.

Musical direction was by Helen Colbert who was also chorus mistress and conducted an orchestra of twelve players. The three keyboards and two guitars were very present in the score, as one would expect in a rock musical. The brass and woodwind section allowed a more organic sound and integrated well with the electric instruments. Ms Colbert's work with the large male and female chorus was very good, harmonies were melodic and there was a great big choral sound in some numbers, particularly; 'Hosanna', 'Damned For All/Blood Money' and 'The Arrest'.

Choreography was by Miriam Ball and whilst the show is not a typical song and dance Broadway musical, she managed to create some very interesting routines. I really liked the Marionettes on 'King Herod's Song' and the choreography on 'Superstar' was superb.

Thomas Grogan gave a good performance as Jesus but his characterisation was quite internal. Dressed in white, to stand out from others, he gave us a very subdued Jesus throughout, apart from smashing through the moneylenders in 'The Temple' and in his altercation with Judas during 'The Last Supper'. Of course, Lloyd Webber and Rice did write Jesus as an angst-ridden prophet so it's rather difficult to portray him as a charismatic Superstar who enthrals all at this point in his story. But Mr Grogan's singing was pleasing, particularly on the melancholic 'Gethsemane' and the lead in 'Everything's Alright'. His voice really suited the role and his falsetto was very good, however, we never really got any flash of his magnetism in this production. It is an aphorism that the baddies get all the good lines and Superstar is no exception. Judas the betrayer was played by Emmet Donlan with a scenery-chewing intensity. His performance was very good, if a little over overplayed at times. 'Judas' Death' was very melodramatic and badly paced, the emotion hit its peak too early and he had nowhere to go for some time, despite this he certainly convinced for the most part due to his marvellous singing and brooding inner tension and presence. Mr Donlan had a wonderfully expressive voice and he controlled it very effectively. On 'Heaven On Their Minds' where he voices his doubt that Jesus is the Son of God, he displayed a fine rock vocal and on 'Superstar' he excelled.

As Mary Magdalene, one of Jesus' followers who was considered a prostitute, Deirdre Ryan was also quite good. She played Magdalene as an infatuated believer, in love with Jesus as revealed in her very good rendition of 'I Don't Know How To Love Him'. Dressed down with head covered, Ms Ryan underplayed the role but her performance did suit this production's portrayal of Jesus in that she emanated a quiet devout belief in him and matched his internal characterisation. Her duet with the disciple Peter, the pop ballad 'Could We Start Again Please?' was really well-sung by both and the ensemble and she really stood out vocally on 'Everything's Alright'.

Jack Sharpe as Peter gave a fine performance, he portrayed Peter, the denier, exceptionally well.

From an excited, exuberant larger-than-life character to a self-loathing coward; his journey through the show was carefully plotted. The other featured apostle in the show was Simon, effectively played by Alan Kennedy. Mr Kennedy had just the right amount of pathos for the role. Both actors sang strongly too.

As Caiaphas, the high priest who regards Jesus as a revolutionary, Derek Ryan played him with very high status, his remarkable bass voice resounded around the auditorium. His acolyte, Annas, played by James O'Donovan also acquitted himself well, his voice an imposing contrast to Caiaphas. Liam Hunter and David Hughes, both as High Priests, completed this impressive quartet of conspiring clergy. All sang 'This Jesus Must Die' with conviction and brevity, and working with Judas, had Jesus arrested and brought before Pilate.

Pontius Pilate, capably portrayed by Aidan O'Connell, sang the prophetic 'Pilate's Dream' about how he will be complicit in Jesus' death thus heralding the rise of Christianity. Mr O'Connell sang extremely well on this and on 'Pilate and Christ', where he showed his exasperation with Jesus' failure to defend himself. He played the subtext with finesse as he sent Jesus to Herod and, fulfilling his own prophecy, ultimately to his death. Mr O'Connell gave a very powerful performance and I look forward to seeing his next role.

'King Herod's Song' was written in a camp Ragtime style, as a sarcastic mocking of Jesus by Herod, here played by Martin Cosgrave. However, Mr Cosgrave, whilst embodying the regal power of Herod, practically shouted his way through the song and lost the satire by hitting it too hard.

The ensemble sang exceptionally well on this show, the large male and female chorus were very powerful and I heard some harmonies here I'd not heard in previous versions of Superstar.

Stage management on the show was well controlled by Denis Fitzgerald, who had a very large cast to manage. Costume design was unaccredited but was provided by a range of costume hire shops. I liked the High Priest's robes, Herod's sparkles and the apostles were clad in earthy colours as a contrast to the whites of Jesus' costume, which worked well.

Make-up and hair were very well done by a team of six. I liked the eye make- up on the High Priests, this was very effective and quite scary. Unfortunately, Jesus's wig came off during the arrest, but thankfully divinely reappeared in the next scene. Sound by Star Systems was perfectly balanced and full range, I would have liked a touch more reverb on all the lead vocals to give more presence. Lighting by Paul Browne was good with some nice sculpting of the set (particularly the crucifix) and efficient use of the follow spot, though the show could have done with two spots. Cuing was a little lazy on some states though, Judas death by hanging scene was a fraction late, which spoilt the pathos.

Director, Bill Stafford produced a fairly solid, uncontroversial traditional staging of Superstar. He didn't re-imagine it or stress any one specific theme, nor did he really add any superfluous events or scenes. Some scenes were very powerful; the flogging where Jesus was held by ropes from the pros, whilst a soldier whipped him relentlessly; the actual crucifixion scene was quite emotionally staged and the High Priests were frighteningly dominant. It was a simple re-telling, where the music was front and centre against a splendid set, populated by a good cast and a fabulous ensemble and chorus.

Tomorrow Belongs To Them There is such a thing as a perfect storm in theatre, it happens when all of the elements that make up a show are perfectly aligned. It doesn't happen very often, but when it does it stays with you for a long time. It happened on the night I attended UCD Musical Society's Cabaret, the audience were enthralled from start to finish with the inventiveness, uniqueness and sheer virtuosity of their production. Most people know Cabaret from the Bob Fosse directed film starring Liza Minnelli made in 1972. It's based on Christopher Isherwood's 1939 book, Farewell To Berlin, a sort of biographical novel about his time spent in Berlin in the 1930's, a time when the decadence of the Weimar Republic was transitioning to Hitler's Germany. The plot is about an aspiring young American writer who arrives in Berlin and meets a young English Cabaret artist, Sally Bowles. They fall in love but outside forces tear them apart.

UCD's Astra Hall is on campus and is a very flexible space. For this show, directed by Cian Gallagher, they constructed a large raised stage with three solid doors and a pair of staircases leading up to two platforms upstage, over which a sign reading 'Kit Kat Klub' was placed. Around the stage they placed festoon lights and furniture and props were brought on and off to denote locations. Set design was clever and designers, Kellie Comerford and Kieran Sheehy did well to create the seedy club atmosphere.

1930's German music was playing in the pre-set and when the show started, a young man, bruised and in rags entered through the middle upstage door and switched on a pre-set gramophone. The song "Tomorrow Belongs To Me" played, after a while he switched it off and exited. Then the Emcee, a wonderful Ruairí Nicholl, entered with the Kit Kat Klub dancers and playfully sang "Wilkommen", complete with ad-libbing and improv with the audience. This playfulness continued into all of his songs with the exception of "I Don't Care Much", where he sang it straight and very well. His singing on "Money", "Two Ladies" and "If You Could See Her" was sublime. He played the Emcee as an androgynous libertine, salacious with his fellow characters and in his repartee with the audience, but he also projected pain. Mr Nicholl's performance was layered and exquisite with a delicious topping of sleaze. He was present in most scenes, lurking, watching. This show had some very competent actors, oozing talent and commitment to the piece. Caoilfhionn Ní Dhúlaing's portrayal of Sally Bowles was nuanced, at times brash and bold, other times thoughtful and desperate. She developed this 'thousand yard stare', an unfocused gaze to inoculate or distance herself from the impending horrors of what was starting to happen and also to distance herself from her own life and what it had become. Ms Ní Dhúlaing gave an extraordinary performance and captured the essence of the character. She sang Sally Bowles' songs perfectly. More Jane Horrocks than Liza Minnelli, which was the right choice of character as Sally was a young English girl out of her depth in Berlin. Her singing went from seductive and alluring to audacious and at times wasted. On "Mein Herr", she had a lovely command of her vocal and on "Cabaret", which was slowed right down at the beginning, she paced the song beautifully. She was note perfect and imbued each number with intention.

As Cliff, Andrew Murray only had a couple of songs - his duet with Sally, "Perfectly Marvellous" and on the "Finale". Mr Murray had a nice voice and sang well. Playing him as a genial, sensitive artist who falls head over heels for the ingenue Sally, his performance was finely pitched. He transmitted Cliff's sexual curiosity well in his brave scenes with Bobby and Victor and the audience really empathised with him.

Ernst Ludwig, who befriends Cliff on the way to Berlin was very well played by Colin Gilligan. He handled his sub-text really expertly and gave us affability masking his fervent dedication to the National Socialist German Workers' Party. When he revealed his swastika armband, the audience were quite shocked.

As an actor, it's very difficult to portray a character that is decades older than yourself and generally a director will always cast an actor closer in age to the character. But in a student society such as UCD's, that is not always possible. Thankfully this show was served with two superb performances by actors, who on paper, are for too young to effectively play the septuagenarians; Fraulein Schneider and Herr Schultz. As the convivial Jewish Herr Schultz, Pádraic Ó Brolcháin used his physicality and voice to great effect to create the older character. What I liked is that he didn't give us a stereotypical playing, but played him as a quiet gentleman, who prides himself on being a German. Similarly, Taylor Fewer played Schultz's love interest, Fraulein Schneider in a non-traditional manner. Her gestures and lower voice gave her the age she needed to convince. Ms Fewer played the character's anguish very well and we really felt for her.

Cliff moved into Fraulein Schneider's boarding house and eventually Sally moved in with him. Fraulein Kost, a prostitute who lives in the house was comically played initially by Eimear Finnegan, however she gradually revealed Kost's dark side as she sang "Tomorrow Belongs To Me" a Nazi anthem with Herr Ludwig. As Sally's employer at the Club, Max was played with menace and repressed violence by John Felton.

Like all of Kander and Ebb's work, particularly when Bob Fosse was involved, dance and choreography is another character and must be performed well. Using the Bob Fosse style throughout, choreographer Leah Meagher's work with the cast was fantastic. Each routine became more daring and adventurous. Sexy, confident and very on point, the dancers were shameless and gave off tons of attitude to complement their superb dance work.

Whilst, the early numbers "Wilkommen", "Mein Herr", "Don't Tell Mama", "Two Ladies" (where she added another six dancers) and 'Money" were perfectly choreographed and executed, it was the "Entr'acte" / "Kickline"  that opened Act Two that really showcased her talents. This section featured a series of very well- choreographed dance sequences, led for the most part by the Emcee, and lasted about ten minutes. The final kickline was perfectly done and the audience were on their feet at the end of it. There was also a really funny dance sequence between the Emcee and the Gorilla during "If You Could See Her".

Musical direction was by Ben Duffy with chorus work being looked after by Hilary Murnane.
