Not a likeable character, Mr Jeffers played him as a shallow, narcissistic and self-serving buffoon. His relationship with Florence was well-drawn and he really convinced as the spoilt American.

Freddie's lover, Florence, who eventually defects to Anatoly, was played by Caroline Naughton. Ms Naughton, a mezzo, had a very pure voice on "Nobody's Side" and the "Mountain Duet" with Anatoly, where he steals her away from Freddie. She also sang "Heaven Help My Heart" with a real depth of emotion and her duet with Anatoly's ex-wife, Svetlana, "I Know Him So Well" was lovely. Ms Naughton played Florence quite well and convinced as the character. Anatoly's abandoned wife, Svetlana, was sensitively played by Abbie Watson. Ms Watson brought an internal emotional contrast to a dreadfully underwritten role, which mainly required her to stare into the audience and look depressed. But it was in those stares that we could see the despair and loneliness she was battling. Although appearing only in Act Two, she stole the show with a riveting performance of "Someone Else's Story". Her emotional investment in the song was palpable. On the duet "I Know Him So Well"; whilst Florence was strong and note perfect, Ms Watson really captured the pathos of the song, as she realised that Florence had plucked Anatoly away from her and intended to keep him. A poignant performance from Ms Watson. The show had a narrator, The Arbiter played by Evan Keating. He had a good voice and sang well on "The Story Of Chess" with the Ensemble and "The Arbiter". However, I felt he was a little overwhelmed by the role, which is meant to be played in a relaxed manner, he was so serious and earnest! Walter, a CIA agent in Freddie's retinue, was played by Jason Tsoutsas. Whilst not as accomplished vocally as some of the other actors, he did sing well on a couple of numbers, notably "Quartet" and looking like a young Matthew McConaughey in a cowboy hat, he became the light relief and his performance was very enjoyable to watch. As Molokov, Anatoly's second, Jordan Kelly - who had a superb bass-baritone, sang "Anatoly & Molokov" / "Where I Want to Be" with Anatoly and "Diplomats" with Walter and the Ensemble among others. Mr Kelly had a very strong, commanding voice with a superb range and it was really evident when he sang "Quartet" with Anatoly, Florence and The Arbiter. This was a consummate rendition from all four, but Mr Kelly's voice was certainly the more assertive. He gave us a well-rounded character who oozed a Slavic menace and used his physicality to dominate other characters very effectively.

Ian Milford also looked after all of the music on this show. He did a sterling job especially as he was working with, mostly, untrained voices on a fairly demanding score. His interpretation of the score was admirable, although I missed the "Golden Bangkok" opening of "One Night In Bangkok". He amassed a fairly big band of about a dozen players, some doubling up on woodwind/brass and guitar/cello. Keyboard 1 was exceptional throughout and the violin and flute also impressed. The playing on the instrumentals, "Chess #1" and "Chess #2" was glorious.

Jillian Liggett's choreographic structures were quite simple on this production. The ensemble were very well-drilled in their simultaneous movement and at times quite militaristic particularly on the comic Soviet style dances and quite impressive on "Hungarian Folk Song". "One Night In Bangkok" was complicated and multi-layered and filled the stage with many different routines. The US-style cheerleader dance was also quite good as was the movement of the 'chess pieces' during the games.

Set design was by the director, Ian Milford. It worked quite well with a square chequered chess board design on the floor centre stage, steps up to a platform upstage and a series of locations denoted by furniture brought on. There was also a video screen on the upstage wall where various images and film were displayed. The show was well-lit by Paul Hinchcliffe and he achieved some really nice states on stage, particularly on the chess games where the ensemble played chess pieces. They were well sculpted with light and it suited the style of these scenes. Sound by Jody Trehy did not find a good balance initially, causing many lyrics to be lost in some of the songs and the band sometimes outpowered the vocalists, but as the show went on it improved quite a lot and by the second act it had settled and became quite even.

Costume by Rosemary Kelly was well designed. The black and white monochromatic palette suited the themes of the show. I liked the men's suits and Florence's costumes. Freddie's white suit and Walter's fringed jacket and hat really contrasted with the darker colours of Anatoly's team. The Soviet and US tee- shirts on the ensemble also really worked, as did the colour in the Bangkok scenes. Make up was unaccredited but was quite natural and Florence's make up looked great.

Mr Milford's interpretation of what is frankly, Mr Rice's naive view of East/West relations, was quite good. He managed to bring out the differences in culture without resorting to too much caricature and injected some humour through the advertising material in the projections. I really liked the prologue where we saw Florence as a child in Hungary, where her father is taken away leaving her with a music box. This music box became a reoccurring motif through the show reminding us of the harshness of the Soviet regime. Mr Milford did well to assemble some excellent pieces on his board for this production, his opening, midgame and endgame were all exemplary. Otlichno srabotano!

This is a musical which is good to see at any time of year because it is full of fun, full of great comedy roles and contains some good up-tempo musical numbers. Based on the 1960's TV series and subsequent movies, the emphasis of the whole evening was on humour and that is exactly what we had at The Addams Family - A New Musical produced by Ennis Musical Society in Glór.

I was very impressed by the venue for the show and its interestingly shaped auditorium, which is very wide but not very deep as in fact is the stage. This could cause all sorts of problems but the setting was beautifully achieved by stage manager Alan Jackson and his well- organised team. The main set which was the interior of The Addams' house had textured stone walls and two sets of stairs onto raised areas. The side flats were also of stone with three arches on each side, meaning we had so many entrances onto the stage. This contributed to the pacey feel of the show which rattled along at a great rate. This set was beautifully adorned with all sorts of macabre pieces such as antler heads, stuffed animals, skulls etc. Of course this was beautifully lit with the use of up lighting against the textured wall in tones of greens and purples and also in rich reds which created all sorts of interesting pictures during the course of the production. A black curtain was used for variety. This was lit with a tree gobo and dressed at times with a nice set of metal gates. The cast moved much of the scenery, by 'cast' I mean the ancestors who played a lovely role as observers in this production. The props used through the show were great, from the torturous rack to Granny's little store of lotions and potions on the trolley.

The conductor Shane Farrell had set up an orchestra of ten pieces. This well controlled team created a wonderfully complete sound during the course of the production and the balance between the orchestra and the voice were in perfect harmony throughout. Thanks to the team working the microphones for a job well done too. The singing in this production was very good, especially from the talented principals and the chorus also contributed much to the sound and feel of the music. The music in the show is not too challenging but it was very pleasantly carried out and it was obvious that Shane and Eilís O'Neill the Choral Director had spent a long time working with the cast, particularly on their diction, which was excellent.

Director Jessica Bray brought out all of the humour in the piece and added her own little touches in as well. This was a very funny show. The characters were well drawn, they were always committed to their roles, the dedication of the cast throughout was very good. Jessica had thought about the setting of the show and about the movement of the cast around this set. I particularly liked how she used the ancestors draped and posed around the acting areas, never taking away from the action in front of them, but always adding to our fascination by focusing us on what was going on with the principals. This was a well-conceived and directed production.

There was nice movement in the show too, thank you to choreographers Pamela McGlynn and Edina Erdei for all their hard work with the cast. Pamela moved most of the bigger numbers with a large group of chorus players. They all seemed very confident with their movements and carried them out extremely well. There were some nice numbers where the patterns changed in an interesting way and others where they were mostly on the one spot but carried out well synchronised arm movements through the number. Edina had worked hard on the Tango number which was very authentic, though I would have liked a little more time with just Morticia and Gomez dancing so we could have brought out more of the humour of the piece.

The casting of the show was extremely well done as everyone seemed to fit the roles so well. Ailish Sarah Flaherty played the role of the cool, calm and collected mother Morticia Addams. She had a wonderful elegance and sense of style on stage. She moved well, she sang well and delivered her lines with wonderful admissive quality. She also worked well with her husband Gomez played by Alan Greaney. This was a standout performance of great quality as we were always convinced by Alan in the role. He captured the wacky charm which was perfect for the part he was playing. He also had charisma, a good singing voice and he could move too! I would love to see him playing Harold Hill in The Music Man. I think it would be a perfect part for him.

The daughter of the house, Wednesday was played by Aoibheann Malone. She gave us the feisty teenager who got such pleasure from torturing her little brother. Her love affair with Lucas was also very believable. She sang well and moved well. Tiernan Kilroy was the little brother Pugsley who blew us away with his beautiful rendition of 'What if?' He acted so well, sang brilliantly and gave us many moments of comedy in his portrayal. I hope this young man goes on to play more parts in future productions.

Uncle Fester was played by Patrick Kelly. This was a mesmerising performance as we met a madcap, moon-loving character with whom we all fell in love. He was funny, a little bit sad and totally committed to his role on stage. I loved the song to the Moon, 'Moon and Me' which was a very effective moment. Lurch who is the butler in the house gave us a totally vacant, slow-moving servant who surprised us with his voice at the very end of the show, something that most of the audience were not expecting. Well done Joe Moran for your self-control throughout the production.

Granny Addams played by Rachel Culligan was another madcap character of the household. I would have liked a little bit more ageing makeup on her, but she acted the part extraordinarily well giving us such laughter in her scenes, particularly when she was playing opposite little Pugsley, a wonderful moment of theatre.

Mal Beineke was played by Patrick Woulfe, who is younger than the part is normally played. He gave it great depth by his portrayal of Mal who is Mr Sensible and then is reignited into Mr Loverboy yet again by his wonderful wife Alice played by Sarah Kenny. Alice has that wonderful moment of breakdown and Sarah played that part brilliantly. The audience were laughing hysterically when she climbed up onto the table and after gyrating, collapsed in a heap. What a wonderful moment of fun. The son, Lucas Beineke was played by Daniel Lynch who looked every bit the young matinee idol for whom Wednesday has fallen. He acted really well and he has a really nice tone to his singing voice which I hope he will use more in future productions.

There was a huge chorus to the show, only six men who did their parts really well and a large number of equally talented female chorus members. The singing was excellent, the diction was superb and they all moved, acted and reacted really well to the action going on in front of them. The costumes for the chorus were excellent in tones of cream, as was the makeup and on the whole the hair and wigs were of a high standard.

The welcome was warm from Rosaleene O'Sullivan and her team. They had gone to town with the decoration of the foyer for this show. There were three or four displays with gravestones, coffins and ivy. There were even her own children dressed up as the characters who stood there motionless as the audience entered. They were like zombies (apparently not as quiet all the time). All the tables in the coffee area had some form of strange object on it such as a cut off hand or skull, very, very effective and all created such a fantastic atmosphere as we entered the building, we knew we were in for a treat and indeed we were.

This was a well-directed, well moved, well-acted and most enjoyable production of The Addams Family. The audience were blown away by the professionalism of the production and the humour the cast got from the show. It was a great night out at the Glór Theatre and Ennis.

Oh, What a Circus!

Yes, I know that quote is from Evita, but it is particularly apt for director Alan Recks' version of Chicago produced by Clara Musical Society in Clara, County Offaly, as the circus motif was used quite a lot in this production. Clara Musical Society have been going strong since 1971, when they hit the stage with Oliver!. Last year they produced All Shook Up and this year they tackled Kander, Ebb and Fosse's iconic Chicago.

Set in the legendary city during the roaring 20s, Chicago tells the story of two rival vaudevillian murderesses locked up in Cook County Jail. Nightclub star Velma's serving time for killing her husband and sister after finding the two in bed together. Wannabe chorus girl Roxie's been tossed in the joint for bumping off the lover she's been cheating on her husband with. Velma enlists the help of prison matron Mama Morton and shyster lawyer Billy Flynn, who turn Velma's incarceration into a murder-of-the-week media frenzy, thus preparing the world for a splashy showbiz comeback. But Roxie wants a piece of that action and usurps Velma's status as celebrity slayer. Both crash and burn due to their greed, but eventually team up, get their names in lights and all that jazz. Amanda Cunningham was super in the role of Velma. She had a world-weary attitude and a fervent desire to get out and back on the road. Her dance was energetic, and her singing was especially good on 'All That Jazz', 'Nowadays', I Know A Girl' and 'Class'. Ms Cunningham portrayed the character quite well, her Velma went from weary to whacky in a heartbeat and this was particularly exampled in the crazy 'I Can't Do It Alone', where her desperation was a tidal wave of relentless energy. As Roxie Hart, Sinead Handy played her as quite dumb but hard as nails, which really worked. A superb dancer, her work with the ensemble on 'Roxie' and 'Me and My Baby' was very accomplished. As foxy Roxie used to getting what she wanted using her feminine charms, her horizons were opened wider by her notoriety as a murderess. Ms Handy's singing was excellent. She had a palpable energy and sang well on all of her songs but stand- outs were her eponymous song and 'Funny Honey' where she transitioned it from a gentle love song to a tirade against Amos perfectly, 'Me and My Baby', where her timing was superb and 'Nowadays' with Velma, which was melodious and strong. A spirited performance full of vivacity and moxie.

Chris Coroon was superb as debonair Billy Flynn, with exquisite comic timing, and excellent singing. His Flynn was the epitome of a shyster lawyer, smarmy with the press and blunt and ruthless with his clients. Mr Coroon played Billy as a walking phoney, revelling in his lies in the marvellously entertaining 'All I Care About' and sleazy on 'Razzle Dazzle'. On 'We Both Reached for The Gun', he bamboozled the press and Roxie with equanimity and a fierce control. His performance was musical in every way, playing not only the songs but the other characters as well. Jay Origan played Mama Morton, the prison overseer, as a predatory high- status libertine, who reveled in her corruption. Her singing was first-rate. On 'When You're Good to Mama', she was quite carnivorous, voracious for money and whatever else she could squeeze out of 'her girls'. Her duet with Velma, 'Class' was quite paradoxical, given she was such a rapacious character. Ms Origan's portrayal of Morton was a superb characterisation; funny, sinister and a joy to watch.

Five of The Six Merry Murderesses of the Cook County Jail were played with a shameless intensity by Seana Slenson (Liz), Ruth Maher (Annie), Ruth Kelly (Mona), Grainne Donoghue (June) and the wonderful Eimear Doolin (Hunyak). The sixth was of course Velma, who was equally as good. Their 'Cell Block Tango' exploded off the stage into the audience and each was a good as the next in their monologues and collectively in their powerful singing and dancing. When Eimear Doolin's Hunyak dangled dangerously from red material during her circus inspired 'hanging' scene, the audience held their breath, and when she fell, they gasped and applauded wildly. This scene was theatre gold: unexpected, emotional and dangerous.

As Amos, Roxie's cuckolded husband, Malcolm Whelan really pulled the audience's heartstrings. Playing him as a sad circus clown, even donning white gloves and face paint at one point during 'Mr Cellophane' - which he sang with feeling and superb timing, the audience felt great empathy for him. Mr Whelan portrayed him with such a fine delicacy but wince inducing gullibility that we feared for the character's safety if not sanity. Amos' love rival, Fred Casely was very well played by Jared Madden. He was excellent in the re-creation of his own death in the Courtroom scene, channeling the fabulous Bela Lugosi's Dracula in his expressions and physicality. Mary Sunshine was played by Eleanor Mac Donagh. She was perfect in the role and her song 'A Little Bit of Good' was funny and she sang it well.

Alan Recks was not only the director of the production but also musical director, conductor and chorus master on this very well put together show. His work with the ensemble as Chorus Master was great, getting some super harmonies and very powerful singing from them. Mr Recks conducted the excellent twelve-piece laid back band from the piano with brio and accuracy. His interpretation of the score was authoritative, dynamic and at times quite sensual.

Lea Carroll's choreography was quite innovative. She managed to not only include plenty of Fosse work into the routines but created new dances which the dancers executed quite well. The most impressive piece of choreography was on 'Me and My Baby', where Roxie and the ensemble sat on large children's alphabet cubes and did an incredible non- locomotor upper body routine perfectly in sync. This was not only crisp and well- rehearsed but funny as well as they also had giant pacifiers in their mouths. Her interpretation of the dance of Chicago, took in to account a few different styles of the era; ragtime, flappers, jazz ballet etc. and she clearly worked her ensemble hard as they were very confident.

The set and stage design accreditation were shared by Stephen Rabbette and stage manager, Wayne Handy. It was quite simple; an upstage platform with two sets of treads, where the band were set, below this was a squared off red curtained archway, from which set pieces and cast could enter and exit. Furniture was brought on and off to represent locations and that was pretty much all. However, the show did not need anything else. It was a compact, well realised design that worked marvellously. Mr Handy, who also had a cameo role as the judge, and his crew managed this stage very well. Transitions were slick and I loved how scenes were set up whilst others were still in progress, which enabled scenes to segue into each other.

Lighting was designed by Ronan Kenny and was perfect for the show. Good use was made of the two follow spots and a mixture of red and blue gels. Derek Recks' sound was very full on this show. The band was nice and punchy and loud as was the ensemble, with a good use of off-stage mics for the off-stage chorus, particularly on 'My Own Best Friend'. Pat McGann and the Society furnished the costumes and they were super. Mama's big vulgar leopard skin coat looked outrageously déclassé and Billy Flynn's suits and sparkly waistcoats elegant. Roxie and Velma's costumes were great, particularly their big coats in 'Nowadays' and their dresses and hats in 'Hot Honey Rag'. This cast were totally in sync with each other and the substance and style of the show. The ensemble sang wonderfully, finding harmonies I'd not heard in the past. Collectively, they all worked so well together, were clearly well-rehearsed and most importantly seemed to thoroughly enjoy what they were doing! Director, Alan Recks is to be lauded for giving us a super production of Chicago. He paced the show very well. Segueing scenes was a really clever idea and helped keep it rolling. His interpretation of the show was quite individual and clever, and his staging really suited the venue. What a show!

Hear My Song Jason Robert Brown's first foray into musical theatre back in 1995, directed by Daisy Prince, daughter of the legendary Broadway director Hal Prince was Songs For A New World. An abstract musical, which doesn't at first appear to have a plot and seems more like a song cycle. Brown went on to great critical and public acclaim with The Last Five Years, Parade and 13. First staged Off-Broadway, the show is a compendium of, mostly, previously written songs Brown composed for different projects. However, the songs are connected by a theme, as Brown says, it's 'about one moment. It's about hitting the wall and having to make a choice, or take a stand, or turn around and go back.' The decisions in the show are often life altering and sometimes characters are compelled into taking them and entering a new world. It's a very American musical and all characters are firmly rooted in the US.

BRAVO, under the direction of Aoife McClafferty and under the baton of Musical Director Shane Farrell staged the production in the Mall Theatre in Tuam for two performances in early March. The venue is a small theatre, with a tiny stage and little or no backstage facilities, but was perfect for this show as it demands intimacy. Each of the sixteen songs were sung by a different character, although all characters were played by only four performers. Alongside the four main singers, there was also an ensemble of ten performers who sometimes provided context and sang on some of the numbers. The atmosphere in the venue was akin to a cabaret, with red painted walls, smoky haze and some soft jazz playing on the sound system. The band were chatting with the punters and it felt like a private concert, where everybody knew everybody else and there was a cosy relaxed feel in the air. On stage there were thirteen chairs placed at odd angles around the space, lit in red and blue. The band were placed along the front of the stage in a make-shift pit.

The opening number, which was the last song to be written in the cycle, 'A New World' was sung by all, with each soloist taking sections of it and the ensemble building the chorus. It was a superb beginning, the violin and piano driving the song with the ensemble picking up the chairs in slow motion against a projection of cloud gobos on the upstage wall. All soloists were superb on this song but Woman #2, played by Jessica Bray had fabulous phrasing and really delivered the song to us.

Brown inserted 'Transitions', which were really a refrain from the 'A New World' song, between some of the numbers. These were sung mostly by Woman #1, Sarah Corcoran and Man #1, Eoin Mullins. The second song 'On The Deck Of A Spanish Sailing Ship' was mostly performed by Eoin Mullins. There was a lovely reverb on his voice and some powerful cello and bass contrasting with Mr Mullins tenor. The percussion and voices were quite haunting on the repetitions of the line, 'Lord take my hand, I am not strong enough' as it built to a climax, then softened as the refrain from 'A New World' came in again.

Jessica Bray, sang the comedic 'Just One Step' about a woman threatening to throw herself off a ledge high above a New York street if her husband didn't pay her more attention. This song requires fabulous breathing technique, comic timing and expression and good characterisation to carry it off. Thankfully Ms Bray had all of this and more. It was perfectly sung, funny and sad. Sarah Corcoran sang the hauntingly beautiful 'I'm Not Afraid Of Anything' extremely well. She had consummate control of her vocal and sitting alone in the centre of the stage surrounded by chairs, came across as initially lonely but determined to face and conquer her fears.

On 'The River Won't Flow' Stephen Macken (Man #2) and Eoin Mullins took turns in a fabulously jazzy upbeat song. They were eventually joined by the two women as they all sang well about bad luck being just fate. The piano was front and central for this one. 'Stars and the Moon' was sung by Jessica Bray. It was about a woman rejecting poor suitors in favour of a rich man and regretting her decision years later. Ms Bray lived the song for us, she inhabited the character fully and her singing was first class.

Stephen Macken, sang 'She Cries', a piano-driven love song against a tableaux of the ensemble supposedly in a bar. Mr Macken's voice was very expressive and he handled the high notes with aplomb. Lovely use of percussion throughout the song gave it a pulsing energy. 'You don't know me but you will' speaks Eoin Mullins at the top and end of 'The Steam Train' a Quincy Jones like number where he is joined by the full company. The ensemble arranged the chairs to resemble a train carriage and shuffle them around the stage, which worked. This song was about a disadvantaged youth and included the 'New World' theme cleverly stitched into it. Mr Mullins voice was warm and melodic and the song was quite funky, which the cast and audience both enjoyed. A great song to end Act One.

Act Two began with 'The World Was Dancing' sung by Stephen Macken, set in an unknown location where the ensemble were all reading books. Mr Macken sang of his relationship with Lisa, here represented by Ms Corcoran, who doesn't sing. The song was wistful, with the chorus dancing with the books and joining in at the end. Mr Macken had a very expressive voice similar to Ms Bray, in that he became each character as he sang their stories. In this case he became the character who was heavily influenced by his father's failed life, determined to not follow in his footsteps, regardless of who he harmed. The violin was particularly fine on this song.

Jessica Bray played Santa's betrothed, Mrs Claus in a pastiche of a Kurt Weill song, German accent and all, in 'Surabaya Santa'. She was tired of being the stay at home wife, whilst he's off around the world, so the song is a farewell to their marriage. Ms Bray, in a Lotte Lenya'esque torch song, again nailed the genre with a funny and well phrased performance. The cello and snare drum were very present and we even had a bit of 'Jingle Bells' though it. Staying with the Christmas theme, Sarah Corcoran sang 'Christmas Lullaby'. A song about a pregnant woman who muses that her baby may be the Saviour of the World and that she's the Virgin Mary. Set in an obstetrician's waiting room with other expectant mums, some reading magazines, some just sitting with their hands across their 'bumps', the song was well performed by Ms Corcoran with a lovely piano accompaniment.

'King Of The World' was sung very emotionally by Eoin Mullins as he was clearly incarcerated and demanded to be released to continue in his position as an officer in the armed forces. Costumed in an Army uniform, Mr Mullins sang it well and projected his helplessness perfectly. Mr Macken and Ms Corcoran sang a lovely duet 'I'd Give It All For You', which vaguely linked to an earlier song 'The World Was Dancing' in that they seemed to play similar characters to those they played in the earlier song, except Ms Corcoran sang on this one. Superbly accompanied mostly by piano, synth and violin, the song was a sort of reconciliation number and both sang it very well.

Ms Bray returned with a poignant song about her husband and son who were away at war as she sews a US flag. Aptly titled 'The Flagmaker, 1775', she gave a very emotional performance. During the song, Mr Mullins, still in his US Army uniform, was shot and died in slow motion and lay down on chairs behind her, as if in a coffin. This added to the pathos of the song wonderfully and gave it a physical context. The military snare was eerie in the song. Mr Mullins segued into 'Flying Home' from the chairs, a song about a dead soldier being flown home to his family and crossing over to a new world. Mr Mullins performed it marvellously and the chorus joined giving a spiritual feel. The 'Final Transition' segued into 'Hear My Song', the final number of the show, sung by the whole company. The song was about how experience can change one for the better and the new world is what you make it. All sang well on this and there were some lovely harmonies and marvellous percussion. An encore was called for from the audience, so they sang the title song one more time.

Sound by Jody Trehy was perfect throughout with lovely clear and bright vocals and a nice mix from the band. Lighting was perfectly judged by Paul Kelly with interesting projections on the upstage wall. Aoife McClafferty directed well on the show, adding some context to some of the songs with the ensemble, some of the links were tenuous at best but Ms McClafferty knew when to just let the singers sing the song. Ultimately it was Shane Farrell's musical direction of the principals, ensemble and band that made the production a success. Well done and thank you for airing a rarely produced masterpiece.

Reciprocity!

Subtitled 'A Musical Vaudeville', Chicago premiered on Broadway in 1975 with music by John Kander and book by Fred Ebb and Bob Fosse. Fosse also directed and choreographed the original show and it was through this initial production, and not necessarily the writing, that many of the 'traditional' Chicago staging conventions were created.

Carrick-on-Suir Musical Society, under the direction of Liam Butler with the choreography of Edel Quinlan, staged the musical in their venue, The Strand Theatre in Carrick-on-Suir, in March this year to sold out houses. The plot of this musical is really quite simple and still relevant as it looks at the fickleness of fame and how some celebrities believe they can get away with anything. In this case, murder. Set in 1920's prohibition era Chicago and based on real-life trials, the show follows Roxie Hart, a hopeful showgirl who murders her lover and is arrested, despite trying to convince her husband, Amos, to lie for her. On remand in the Cook County Jail, Roxie meets her hero, double-murderess and nightclub performer Velma Kelly. When both procure the same lawyer, media darling Billy Flynn, tensions come to a head as they fight for press attention, believing publicity will get them off. The show was partially narrated by an MC, here very well played by Chris Hanlon, who introduced the acts and gave the audience a bit of exposition.

We first met Velma as she sang 'All The Jazz' with some of the ensemble and played by Sandra Power. She sang it well, but I was a bit disappointed in the dance as the dancers wore elbow-length gloves, so we couldn't see their hands, and they didn't really have that Fosse precision one expects. Ms Power did impress with her singing though and sounded great on 'I Know a Girl' and her duets with Mama Morton ('Class') and Roxie ('My Own Best Friend'). However, on 'I Can't Do It Alone', she didn't perform the choreography and two young gymnasts were brought on to show Velma & Veronica's act. I don't think this worked because the point of the song is for Velma to attempt the double- act on her own to convince Roxie to join her! Ms Power played Velma with quite a low energy insouciance and whilst that worked for some scenes, those with Mama Morton for example, she didn't give us that arrogant, vivacious Velma that we expected.

As Roxie, Louise Mulcahy sang and acted the role well, but her dance was rudimentary at best. Her singing was good on 'Funny Honey' from atop a piano, 'Roxie' and 'Me and My Baby' were also enjoyable and she performed Billy's penultimate note on 'We Both Reached For The Gun'. Whilst her dancing wasn't perfect, her acting was super and she convinced as the conniving Roxie. However, similar to Ms Power, I found her a tad undynamic.

Their shrewd unscrupulous lawyer, Billy Flynn was suavely played by Neill Bourke. His 'I Don't Care About' was sung very well as was 'Razzle Dazzle' and he presented the sophistication of a born hustler. Mr Bourke performed 'They Both Reached For The Gun' smoothly in a great choreographed sequence with Roxie and the marionetted reporters. One of the reporters, Mary Sunshine, traditionally played by a man in drag, was played by David O'Donovan. He sang 'A Little Bit Of Good', which was written for a countertenor, quite well and the reveal that she was a he was done effectively at the trial.

Mama Morton, the crooked matron of the Cook County Jail where Roxie and Velma are incarcerated, was here played by Irene Malone. In a change to the conventions of the show, Mr Butler had Ms Malone downplay Morton's status from an imposing, imperial character to an unkempt, Mme Thenardier like character. This worked to a point, especially when she sang 'Class' with Velma, which was deliciously ironic. But a character with such low status cannot command respect, even with cons, so ultimately it didn't really land. Nevertheless, Ms Malone's character was very funny, in a coarse way and she had a powerful voice. When she sang 'When You're Good To Mama', she channelled the great Ethel Merman and this even extended to her accent, which was pure New York.

In Morton's jail, Velma and some of the other inmates 'the six merry murderesses of the Cook County Jail' sang 'Cell Block Tango', one of musical theatre's most famous and favourite numbers. Along with Ms Power as Velma, we had Tarryn Attlee as June, Aisling Healy as Mona, Siobhan Grace-Regan as Hunyak, Sarah Power as Annie and Sheridan Brady as Liz. All were adroit in their roles and displayed sneering attitude. Performing on bentwood chairs, they were joined by the dance ensemble, six who had prison bars on castors in a very powerfully sung number. The choreography was quite complicated and quite well delivered by all, but it was the vocals which really shone through on this one. Hunyak's execution later on was a bit of a let-down though, she just put her foot in the noose from the platform and it slowly lowered then blacked out.

Hapless Amos, Roxie's husband, was played by Caolán Deehy-Power in a convincing portrayal of a character who is invisible to all, including the Musical Director! Mr Deehy-Power's episodes with Billy were snappy and believable and his grovelling scenes with Roxie, made us want to either throttle her or kick him for being so naïve. His song 'Mr Cellophane' was perfectly pitched and expressed to gain the most pathos and empathy. A most impressive performance. Roxie's lover, Fred Casely was strongly played by Dennis Barry, his bed scene with Roxie was brave and their re-enactment of the murder was well-paced.

In Chicago good choreography and execution is essential as the show is about two vaudevillian performers and, of course, because of the heavy involvement of famous choreographer Bob Fosse in its' creation. On this show choreographer Edel Quinlan, clearly worked hard on the choreography, there were some really great original routines created. However, her dancers were just not sharp enough to carry out some of the moves. There was a distinct lack of sensuality, very few males (so there was no sexual tension) and little or no isolated movements or sharp angles from the dancers. However, some of it worked really well; 'We Both Reached For The Gun' was really well performed as were both of Billy's numbers, 'Tap Dance' was excellent and the 'Hot Honey Rag' was quite good, though a little low on energy. Musical Direction was by Fergal Carroll with Eamon O'Malley looking after chorus master duties. The band were very tight, lovely work from the boisterous brass and the reeds and violin gave a warmth. Chorus work was gorgeous, lovely harmonies and power.

A splendid set design by John O'Donoghue, really brought us back to the roaring 20's with an Art Deco proscenium and flats. I liked the way some of the furniture emerged from the upstage platform and the festooned side flats completed an exquisite stage picture. Lighting design by Dirk Baumann, Liam Butler and Eoin Sheridan was very nice, with effectively operated follow spots from perches on stage left and right and footlights on the stage line. Colour was from LED pars and worked quite well to give different atmospheres to the show. Sound design was by Star Systems and was punchy, full range and had a good balance. Hair/ wigs by Ashley Cooke and make up by Denise Hunt was perfectly suitable for the era as were the costumes, supplied by NoMac and the society and co-ordinated by Breda Butler. Stage management by Michael O'Hara, who deserves a medal for operating from under the platform which was like being in a drum, was excellent and all performers, props and set came on and were struck quickly and with precision making transitions very rapid, though a little over lit.

Liam Butler produced a quirky version of Chicago, it wasn't a 'cookie cutter' copy of the original or the numerous revivals. His casting was unconventional and he managed to stress the comedic elements of the show quite effectively. However the pacing was quite sluggish and many scenes were a bit languid, due I suspect to some of the cast being a bit enervated. Unfortunately this passivity carried over into many of the dance sections, which was a shame as they should have popped as the direction was there. Mr Butler's staging was very good, the production elements worked very well together and the show looked lavish, skilful and efficiently run. But, some of the performances just were not theatrical or sharp enough for a Bob Fosse musical and it didn't have that steamy sexy aggressive dynamic it should have.

Reciprocity!

Rush Musical Society have been around since 1989 and have a great track record in producing comedy, as well as traditional fare. So, it's no surprise to their fans that they would attempt Greg Kotis and Mark Hollmann's satirical romp, Urinetown. Enthusiastically directed by Tony Finnegan, with musical direction by Gay Kirwan and choreography by Sinead Lightly, this was a show that was so funny the audience almost wet themselves, which was a problem as we were only permitted one visit to the facilities during the evening(!)

Urinetown is a sharp, smart, funny and disturbing Brechtian fable set in a dystopian future when years of drought have led to the banning of private toilets, so everyone must pay for the privilege to pee in public amenities controlled by the UGC, the Urine Good Company, headed up by Bond villain, Mr Caldwell Cladwell, a sinister Mr Big, who has the police and politicians in his pocket. But the whole show is also a gleeful parody of musicals, ranging from Les Miserables to Chigago And Guys and Dolls and even of itself. Narrated by local cop Officer Lockstock and Little Sally, a poor waif, this story relates a tale of revolution by the rebel poor and what happens when the civilians refuse to pay and take over the utilities. This show is mad, quite mad and Rush Musical Society staged it in the Millbank Theatre in April of this year.

The show is narrated by Officer Lockstock, played here by Seamus Griffin. Mr Griffin's comic timing was really excellent, as he interacted with the audience and the characters. His singing on 'Cop Song' was particularly good and he formed a very funny comedy duo with Officer Barrel, a nice physical performance from Jim Walsh, with his little kid 'gun fingers' always drawn. Questioning his motives and the reason for the shows' existence was Little Sally, a precocious child played by an adult, who had a wise-beyond-her- years demeanour. As Little Sally, Caoimhe McGowan gave a stand out performance. Her comic timing and deadpan delivery were superb, and she sang really well with the ensemble. Trying to be the voice of reason during the revolution, Ms McGowan played the enfant terrible exceptionally well.

Bobby Strong, the toilet attendant at Public Amenity #9 and heroic leader of the revolution, was played by Adam McGealy. He personified the ordinary man who couldn't take anymore once his father had been sent to Urinetown. (Urinetown is a mythical place where miscreants are sent, never to return). His scenes with Hope, Cladwell's ill-informed daughter, were hilarious. They fell in love and sang a brilliant pastiche of a love song, 'Follow Your Heart'. As leader of the rebellion, Mr McGealy's Bobby Strong was strong and charismatic, even conducting the rebel poor in the a cappella section of Spiritual music inspired 'Run Freedom Run' from atop a cheery picker. His performance was perfectly in tune with the humour of the show and he had a fine voice.

Bobby's boss at the Public Amenity #9, was Ms Pennywise played by the brilliantly physical Mags Kirk. An employee of the UGC, Ms Kirk projected a no-nonsense, tough exterior for Ms Pennywise, but also hinted at a softer secret past which was eventually revealed. She sang the rather tricky 'Privilege to Pee' very well and literally walked all over the poor citizens of the town and her bittersweet duet with Cladwell 'I'm Not Sorry' was very well performed.

As Hope Cladwell, Niamh Kavanagh was hilarious. She sang beautifully on 'Follow Your Heart' with Bobby and with the Ensemble in act two on 'I See A River' But it was her nuanced acting performance that really worked, at one point she sang through a gag, having scooted across the stage on a wheelie chair to find her light. Ms Kavanagh gave just the right amount of faux pathos and innocence to underpin the humour.

As her father, Caldwell B. Cladwell, Barry Kavanagh played the Bond baddie really well. With his penchant for bunnies rather than cats, Mr Kavanagh sang 'Don't Be a Bunny' accompanied by a plethora of children dressed as rabbits, which he summarily killed. He initially played the evil industrialist as quite genial, but by the end of the first act, the mask had slipped and he went full despot. An enjoyable performance. Colm Heaney played his simpering flamboyant assistant, Mr McQueen superbly, barking orders at the staff and being as obnoxious as possible - just because he could. Gary Finnegan played the local Senator, who is in the pay of Cladwell. Dreaming of the beaches of Rio, with a suitcase full of cash, Mr Finnegan played him as cowardly and quite salacious towards Hope. Out of his depth once the peasants revolted, he gibbered and protested his innocence. His was a fine performance reminiscent of a certain US capitalist who recently became a politician.

The rebel poor were a rag tag assortment of post punk townsfolk, with a sort of Les Miserables meets Mad Max styling in their costumes and make-up. Hot Blades Harry a psychotic hot-headed, loose cannon of a character was played by Nathan Durkin. He had a very imposing presence and was quite scary but very funny especially on 'Snuff That Girl', where he wanted to kill the bound Hope. As Little Becky Two Shoes, Kate Motherway was brilliantly physical, pregnancy bump and all. Her vocal on 'Snuff That Girl' and the other ensemble numbers was great. The excitable Soupy Sue was nicely played by Jen Browne. Young Mattie Scott gave a great performance as Tiny Tom, and Helen Kavanagh played Bobby's mother with a perfectly judged performance. Peter O'Brien's Old Man Strong was very funny, especially when he was taken short and his Shakespearian returns as a ghost were joyfully cheesy.

Musical Direction was perfect, with a five- piece band of multi-instrumentalists, Gay Kirwan really nailed the Kurt Weill'esque score. It was frenetic and fun, quirky and just plain bonkers at times, but always really well paced and timed. The ensemble's harmonies were rather excellent, especially 'Urinetown', 'Run Freedom Run' and 'I See A River'. 'Why Did I Listen To That Man' was superbly sung by Lockstock, Pennywise, Hope, Fipp and Barrel; who sound like a law firm. The choreography by Sinead Lightly, was quite simple but very well executed by the cast. Set design by Tony Finnegan was really clever, with an upstage platform accessed by two sets of treads and gatefold flats to denote different locations and a tunnel up stage right to facilitate entrances and exits. Stage left and right there was a series of doors into the wings. Stage manager John Foley and his team, including the ensemble, managed the transitions quite swiftly and accurately. Costume was hired from Theatrical Costume Hire in Newry. Hair and make- up was designed by Ali Murphy. Lighting by Colm Eaton was a little sparse during the first scene, it looked good in terms of colour and gobos but we couldn't really see the actors! Thankfully it improved hugely later on. Sound by Jody Trehy was excellent, lovely clear vocals and a full beefy sound from the band. Director Tony Finnegan gave us a marvellous interpretation of this show. All of the pastiche and all of the references were laid out for the audience to appreciate, and most of them hit home. His pacing was spot-on and the staging was really good, particularly given the small playing area they had to work with. But most importantly it was funny, so funny that there wasn't a dry seat in the house at the end!

Well I stumbled out of bed and took a cup of ambition and got down to Dundrum to the DLR Mill Theatre to see the hilarious Dolly Parton stage musical 9 To 5, based on the 1980s movie. Recently on stage in the West End starring Louise Redknapp and Brian Connolly amongst others. As always Dolly Parton welcomes us to the theatre and as she says in her own blurb that 'this is a stage show inspired by the cult film and brought to you by Dolly herself'. 'It is about teaming up, standing up and taking care of business.' The business for Kilmacud Musical Society was taken care of by production team Paul Laycock who directed, Audrey Nolan, Choreographer and Musical Director Geoff Woods. This experienced and talented team brought us a fun evening of entertainment with great humour, good dancing and super singing.

Geoff Woods and his orchestra were set on floor level stage right. It is a tight space to put in seven players and all their gear but they managed and didn't really block the action on stage too much. There was a good sound throughout the show. There are some nice numbers and Geoff and his orchestra sounded good with a lovely brassy sound. There was a steady beat to the accompaniment of the show with of course that typewriter beat coming through loud and clear.

The use of the chorus singing off stage added a pleasant sound supporting those on stage. The chorus had been well rehearsed in their songs and there were very pleasant harmonies dotted through the production. The leading players all sang well and gave us some wonderful musical moments.

This was well planned and careful direction from Director Paul Laycock. What I particularly enjoyed was how well the story was told. There were quite a few in the audience who obviously had not seen the show or heard the music before and each of them had a ball and went out singing the tunes at the end. Paul had decided to use a back projection for the scenery at the back cyc and then bring larger pieces onto the stage to create different scenes. This all worked well to give us rooms in the office block, the Hart bedroom etc. The pieces brought on such as the rather complicated scenery for Hart's office looked really good and were beautifully dressed with photographs of Hart with a young Donald Trump, a baseball bat, American football, all nice touches to create time and place. All these pieces were quickly moved into place though as there is so little storage space stage right, most had to come on from stage left which caused a bit of a traffic jam at times. I would suggest a bit of music from the orchestra to help cover that. Well done to Aoife Ryan who led a well-trained stage team.

The main characters were nicely constructed especially the three ladies, who were very different in personality but developed a common bond. There were some lovely comic touches such as the characters in the hospital scene which somehow really appealed to my sense of humour. The scene with Hart and Doralee in his office was actually quite shocking and thank God we have moved on a bit in our treatment of each other in the workplace since 1970s! Paul made sure that the dialogue moved on at a good pace. I attended the show early in the run due to a very busy schedule and I am sure that any wee pauses in pace were improved as the week rolled on. This was a thoughtful and neat piece of stage direction.

The choreography in this show was quite a challenge for the abilities of the group. Many on stage mastered the complex '9 to 5' movement with the arms moving like clock arms. The big group numbers I am sure settled as the week continued as there was a wee bit of hesitancy at times. There were some wonderful moments such as the great routine when Roz really let her hair down. This was backed up with four other dancers nicely attired in the same outfit as hers, very funny and very effective. The triple song moment of the girls' fantasies were all hilarious and well moved. Judy gave us a great 'Dance of Death', Doralee looked good and sang even better. 'Cowgirl's Revenge' and Violet's Snow White look backed by all her nursery rhyme princesses in 'Potion Notion' was superb. Of course, one of the highlights of the show has to be Violet and the boys singing 'One Of The Boys'. This was a great moment of the show nicely moved and beautifully styled.

Of course, you can't take on this show without a strong cast and that we surely had. There was a very strong principal cast supported by an enthusiastic chorus. Violet is perhaps the most worldly wise of the three leading ladies. Gillian Lynch gave us a strong and often impassioned performance of Violet.

Her acting subtleties were much appreciated as was the powerful delivery of all her musical numbers. She moved very naturally around the acting area and as she engaged with us so we were drawn into her life and struggles. Her singing tone developed as she settled into the role. Sarah Lawlor gave us some magical moments of singing in the show. We could see a butterfly emerge as the story unfolded and she was able to stand up for herself. I wasn't wild about the way this character was styled and think that it actually took away from her excellent performance. For the first time in a principal role, Laura Murphy was a wonder in what is really the Dolly Parton role of Doralee. She maintained the accent really well throughout and gave us a lovely Country and Western twang to her singing voice. She really looked the part as very article of clothing looked as if it had been made for her. She moved around the acting area with graceful ease. How she acted that scene at the start with lecherous Franklin pawing all over her I will never know. Well done our three kidnappers you were an unlikely gang but you worked so well together.

Franklin Hart Jnr was played with misogyny smarm by Ray Bissett. His antics with the ladies who worked for him guaranteed that we wanted him to get taken down a peg or two by the end of the show. Difficult to play the bad guy but still keep a smile of defiance on his face, well done Ray for a well-interpreted role. I loved how his charm worked on the one he didn't actually want in the office, the frustrated Roz. Nikki Johnston gave a hilarious performance of the office bossy boots who is head over heels in love with Franklin. We laughed so much at her kissing his picture, her antics when she let her hair down. This is an actor with great ability to point lines and get wonderful humour from them.

Joe played Violet's suitor with great conviction and the 'Let Love Grow' number was beautifully sung. Some great moments created between him and Violet. Doralee's husband Dwayne was played by Carl Mageean in a very natural way. He was always there to support his wife and their scenes together worked really well. Judy's ex was played by Sean Riddick who was straight out of the Franklin mould and it was great to see Judy stand up for herself against him so that history did not repeat itself. Other cast members contributed much to the evening including Alison Gill as Margaret, Lesley Cosgrove as Kathy and Rhona Gleeson as Maria, well done.

There were some wonderful outfits on stage which were a nice fit and reflected the era. There were others which could have reflected the character a little more. I loved the black and silver set for Violet's big number. Well done Sophia Arkelid. Hair styles and wigs might need a bit more attention in future shows. There were a couple of wigs in the show which I wasn't too keen on. Also, if I was going to put wigs on my three leading ladies it is an idea to scatter a few wigs among other members of the cast otherwise it all looks far too contrived. Make up was generally sound but for some that very pale base needed a bit of warming up.

There were some nice scenes created with clever use of props such as those great office workstations complete with period typewriters. The bits and pieces on the office desk looked so right too. There was obvious potential for some great effects with the lighting and sound in the show which I am sure will be fully achieved as the show continues its run. It was a great idea to set up the microphones backstage so the chorus could back the principals periodically. This gave a glorious effect at times.

Overall this was a great fun show. It was nicely staged, acted and sung. It is an entertaining show and Paul and this talented group gave us all a most enjoyable evening.

The first production of Calamity Jane on stage was in 1961 at the Casa Manana in Fort Worth Texas. The show has been a favourite with audiences around the world ever since. It has been a great vehicle for some of the world's most talented leading actresses to play the part of Calamity, such as Carol Burnett and Ginger Rogers. In a UK tour the one and only Barbara Windsor and singing star Toyah Willcox have donned the deerskins.

The story is based on historical figure of frontierswoman Martha Jane Cannary who was a professional scout, known for her claims of being an acquaintance of Wild Bill Hickock and fighting against Native Americans. The story made famous in the 1953 movie with Doris Day and singing legend Howard Keel as Wild Bill was a huge success and still is watched by millions today. It is a light and fun show with some great music and opportunities for comedic playing.

It was produced by Gorey Musical Society and staged in Gorey Little Theatre. This has tiered seating of over three hundred places in a pleasant auditorium. The orchestra was nicely placed centre in front of the stage and was under the direction of Conor McCarthy. The show was directed by Chris Currid, who certainly has been a busy man recently on and off stage. Conor directed the orchestra beautifully through the show giving a very pleasant rounded sound to the classic numbers such as 'The Deadwood Stage', 'Secret Love' etc. At times there sounded as if there were more players in the orchestra than was the reality with some players doubling up on instruments. The principals sang well throughout and the chorus managed to sing and keep up with the challenging dance routines set by choreographer Clodagh Leacy. There were some beautiful moments of singing particularly the scene with distant moonlight of the 'Black Hills of Dakota'. The principals sang their parts well throughout the production giving us many moments of humour and sentiment. Director Chris Currid had nicely established the characters of the players on stage, each of whom was distinct from the other and sounded comfortable in their role. There were nice moments of humour through the show which charmed the audience - the show moved at a good steady pace and humour was nicely teased out of the dialogue.

Chris had chosen a fairly simple set with a nicely lit cyc at the back and a kickboard of black silhouetted against the back wall. Then pieces were brought on such as the bar and the inside of the cabin These looked very three-dimensional. There were some nice props used during the show particularly in the cabin. Though I would have liked a more transformation scene for the 'Woman's Touch' number. The stage team led by Paul Doran and Frank Byrne changed sets quickly so that the movement in the show was not slowed. At times the lighting and staging combined to create a lovely atmosphere in a scene such as the open spaces during the 'Black Hills' song. There were other good lighting ideas through the show which added colour and mood. The use of sound equipment was generally good and well cued. The principal's dialogue and singing could be well heard through the show. There were some good sound effects too though one character appeared on stage as the sound of his horse's hooves were still rattling off stage. The title role was played by Lindsey Tindall who gave us a strong performance as Calamity. She had obviously started creating the role with her movements which were strong and tomboyish. She sang well and I was particularly impressed by her 'Secret Love' which she sang particularly well. She worked well with all of the cast around her and she and Katie built up a good but unlikely friendship. Wild Bill Hickock was played by John Young who gave us a controlled and relatively gentle portrayal of the character. He looked well in the part and sang the role well too. There were some nice moments of acting from John who established that banter and spark with Calamity but also had some gentle romantic moments with her too. Lily Cullen was the stand in star who arrived at the Golden Garter as Adelaide Adams and wowed the men of the town as herself Katie Brown. This was a superb performance of the part. Lily Cullen has a certain something which means that you just can't take your eyes off her. She acts really well and sang well too but it's how she reacted to those around her which impressed me most. Every gesture carefully planned and beautifully executed. A delightful performance Lily. Brian Harty played dashing Lieutenant Danny Gilmartin in a very no-nonsense way. He looked good in the role and acted the part well. Niece of Henry Miller, Susan was played with great sincerity by Ciara Spellman. This was a gentle and nicely moved performance. We got great humour from Francis Fryer aka Brendan Kenny, particularly when he dressed as the female singing star and looked hilarious in red and black basque. He danced well and delivered his songs well too.

Singing star Adelaide Adams was portrayed by Erin Hogan. She sang well and looked good as the star of the show. Vincent Kilroy was Henry Miller who had us all on edge worrying about the success of the Golden Garter shows.

There was an involved and hard-working chorus through the show who added much to the success of the production. There were some nice dance routines performed particularly by a set of dancers who stepped out of the chorus. Everyone was well costumed in outfits which were appropriate to the time and place. Cloaks added a nice touch to the 'Black Hills' number though I would have left the showgirls out of this one or cover them up somehow. There were some good dance routines through the show performed by a dancing troupe and the chorus who were all greatly involved with the action in the show. There was good interplay behind the principals acting which did not distract from the action in front of it. Well done choreographer Clodagh Leacy for some nice touches with the dance routines in the show though some of it did leave me breathless as it went at breakneck speed. There were good patterns created on stage and some interesting touches though I would have liked to have seen a little more done with Katie's 'Keep It Under Your Hat' number. On the whole an interesting and nicely moved piece of choreography.

As I mentioned earlier everyone on stage looked well costumed with some good choice of footwear. There were nice colours in the dresses and the men looked good too in their cowboy gear. The showgirl outfits are not for everyone and I think a little over skirt might have been more appropriate. Calamity looked good in the cabin scene and her dress was adequately ruined by her fall into the crick. I wanted to see a total transformation in her when she arrived at the ball unfortunately her dress in this was lacking and we missed that wow moment when she took her cloak off at the ball. The men were nicely kitted out in formal wear when needed and throughout there were interesting touches of colour in the costumes which brought life to the scenes.

The scenes themselves were nicely painted. We had the bar scene with pieces such as the gold swinging doors, the interesting little theatre stage and the bar area. Difficult whenever you have all of these things on stage to place them so that masking doesn't occur, not sure exactly how to get around that but possibly the bar would have been better at an angle at the side of the stage rather than at the back. The inside of the cabin looked great with textured walls and interesting props to decorate. The props team had obviously worked hard to gather the bits and pieces together to finish off the sets and by and large these looked really well. The makeup team had gone to the trouble of making the characters look quite natural on stage which was wonderful though I wanted a little bit more rouge on the Golden Garter girls to set them apart from the rest of the locals.

It was so lovely just to see this show again and to hear that wonderful Sammy Fain and Paul Francis Webster music again. It is a classic, it is nostalgic but it is great fun and the audience in Gorey Little Theatre were given a great evening's entertainment on the opening night of the production.

I'm sure the show went from success to success in their week's run. Thank you for making me feel so welcome, it was a pleasure to come and visit Gorey for the first time.

The Pavilion Theatre is nicely positioned in the centre of Dun Laoghaire. There is a welcoming bright foyer which was full of life when I arrived on the Friday night of the show. The auditorium has steeply tiered seating which accommodates around two hundred with further seats at the sides on a raised level. In this show a couple of rows of seating had to be removed to make room for the orchestra. The front of house curtain was open revealing a stepped stage area with a projection of the show title on the cyc. The box like setting was of grey stone painted walls with arched entrances onto the stage on each side. These were perpendicular to the back wall and actually worked well. The scene changes for the show were really in the form of pieces being brought on to this acting area and lighting framing an area to indicate different places with of course some beautiful back projections of London street scenes, windows etc. These were very atmospheric projections which worked really well with the setting of the show. The scenery brought on in the form of props was very slickly moved, such as a beautiful antique desk and chair to indicate his study, shelved area with bottles and a desk covered with all sorts of test tubes, Bunsen burner etc. to indicate his laboratory. An area of the back of the stage was used to house Lucy's bed towards the end of the show which looked very effective with the window and full moon behind it. All of the scenes created the correct atmosphere for this piece. Of course, the stage was beautifully lit throughout with moody lighting.

This is a show which should not be taken on by the faint-hearted as it is a dark, difficult piece. So important when you are directing this that you do get some sort of light and shade in the direction otherwise it can be very gloomy from beginning to end. What must happen is we must have great pace to the show and certainly that is what director Paul Laycock had planned. The pace of the show moved along very well so that we never really paused for long between scenes or between musical numbers. It is quite a wordy script but the dialogue was also taken at a good pace so it did not seem too drawn out. Paul moved the cast nicely around the stage, creating pleasing groupings when needed which again were interestingly lit. One thing I would have done a little differently would be to really dirty up the prostitutes and street folk as they just looked too clean and there should have been more of a contrast between them and the rich decision makers.

Choreography was nicely handled with some nods to movements of the era. Well done Denise Donoghue for your routines, particularly the 'Murder, Murder' and the 'Bring on the Men' number, using the chairs in a slightly 'Cabaret' Victorian style.

The chorus and principals were moved nicely in the musical numbers, there is not a great scope for dance as such in the show but the movement was natural and effective throughout.

The orchestra was of a well-chosen small number of players who created a very together, rounded sound. I particularly liked the brass section including the trombone and the lightness of the flute and piano worked well in some of the gentler musical pieces. Well done Des Cox for your musical direction in the show. Some of the numbers build and it was so good to have Vinny Osborne balancing the sound of the orchestra against the onstage voices. We could hear every word of every song which in a story telling musical like this is so important.

Some great singing by our principals and some wonderful singing from the chorus with great harmonies dotted through the show. Lots of individual lines for members of the chorus to shine through. So, who was the leading man in the show? Well Kevin Hartnett made a fantastic Jekyll and Hyde. He radiated the passion of Jekyll to try and make the world a better place but also gave us the spine-chilling horror of Hyde as well. Clever use of an adaptable wig changed him from one into the other. But it was really his acting which convinced us that this was like two separate people, very effective. This is a man who can really sing too and sang really well as both characters making them sound slightly different as well. Overall this was a superb performance though I would have liked to have seen more glimpses of his face and expressions as Hyde, as the wig did tend to completely cover his face which was a pity. The duet that he has with himself was incredible. Well done Kevin. The two very different loves in his life were played by Clodagh Lalor as Emma and Lauren McMahon as Lucy. Clodagh has a beautiful vocal tone and delivered her 'Once Upon a Dream' and duet with Jekyll 'Take Me As I Am' excellently. She has a dignity on stage which worked really well for the part. Lauren has also a great voice. She was in contrast to Clodagh. She really rocked us with her singing of 'Bring on the Men' and then was able to bring us to tears with 'No One Knows Who I Am'. This was a very well-judged performance with a wonderful use of the stage light in her eyes. She really related to us as the audience and let us into her world. She moved well round the stage but also held us on the edge of our seats when she was still being half strangled and seduced by Hyde. Well done to our two leading ladies. Jekyll's best friend, John Utterson was played by Tom Delahunty. This was a considered role played well. He is the Voice of Reason trying to convince Jekyll to give up his experiment, he was most convincing in the part. Sir Danvers Carew was played by Eamonn Murphy who had a great stage presence as Emma's father and sang well. Simon Stride was played by Brian Dennison who was authentic and strong in the part. Lady Beaconsfield was played elegantly by Ciara Kelly. She captured the forceful and determined member of the committee very well. I believe this is her first performance with the society and I am sure it will be the first of many. Denis Sherlock gave us a terrifying character as Spider whom all the working girls feared. Lord Glossop was played by Tom Fitzgerald who added real gravitas to the part. Sir Archibald Proops was played by Hugh Beckett who is the sensible Queen's Counsel at the hospital and the Bishop of Basingstoke was Derek Scott who looked and sounded the part. Well done to Jenny Melvin as Nellie. Jim Ryan as Poole the butler played his part very well and the minister was played sanctimoniously by John Freeman.

The ensemble worked really well together. They sang and moved well and they were convincing as people from the period in their movements and attitude. The costumes differentiated the cast well, though again I would have liked to see the poor much dirtier. The attention to detail with shoes etc. was very good and I particularly liked the touch with Lucy's red gloves in the Red Rat as it set her apart from the crowd.

Make-up was a little bit of a mixed bag for me and I would have liked to see a more Victorian look, with the prostitutes really standing out as different from the rest of the cast. Hair was generally good although it might have been nice to have one of the other men with the long hair so that it didn't seem so contrived when Jekyll lets his wig down.

In conclusion this was a well-staged production which looked good because of the attention to detail of the props team, the scenery team, lighting and costumes. The sound was good with a nicely balanced musical direction and a cast who really could sing these challenging numbers. The use of radio mics was handled well and gave a complete rounded sound to the production. The characters moved well in their roles on stage and any movement with music and dance was well handled and in period. The show was thoughtfully directed and moved at a good pace but also took time to pause for some meaningful moments. I commend all on stage for their efforts in bringing this rather dark story to life. It certainly was a most exciting and memorable evening. Thank you all in Dun Laoghaire for your production of Jekyll And Hyde.

Swing Out Sister Ballinasloe Musical Society has been around since 1988 when they staged their first production Viva Mexico. They have been going strong ever since producing a show a year and winning many AIMS awards and nominations for their trophy cabinet. This year they tackled the cheerfully entertaining Sister Act, directed by Paul Norton with musical direction by Shane Farrell and choreography by Aoife McClafferty.

Sister Act tells the story of Deloris Van Cartier, played here by the talented Emily Lohan, an aspiring singer who witnesses a murder committed by Curtis, Paul Drysdale, a gangster who she is dating. Deloris is thereafter placed into a witness protection program where she poses as a nun in a convent, going by the name Sister Mary Clarence. Bored and disruptive, Deloris takes over leading the choir, and dramatically changes their musical style, and they through their unconditional love for her, change her life for the better. Raising their voices they also managed to raise the money needed to save the Queen Of Angels Church and Convent from greedy yuppie developers. Originally a star vehicle for Whoppi Goldberg, the 1992 film was then turned into a musical in 2006. The show has great original tunes by songwriter Alan Menken and lyricist Glenn Slater that moves from Motown, to soul and funk, to disco and even a little pastiche on Barry White, for those of us old enough to remember Barry White, with a subtle tribute to his own Beauty And The Beast and the Master, Sondheim.

Emily Lohan, a natural and dynamic performer, played the nun on the run, Deloris, with a great energy. Her scenes with Curtis were well-timed and she had a good chemistry with Mother Superior. She played the mentor to Mary Robert with tenderness and developed a good camaraderie with her 'sisters'. Ms Lohan's voice suited Deloris' songs and she was most impressive. 'Take Me To Heaven' and 'Fabulous Baby!' were delivered with a high energy and were note perfect. Her phrasing of 'Sister Act' was super, building from mournful to determined. Most of her numbers were big, and at times soulful, songs and she handled them all with apparent consummate ease. I particularly liked her work on 'Bless Our Show', with its Sound Of Music homage.

As the beleaguered Mother Superior, Madeleine Fleming channelled her Mother Abyss from the aforementioned musical, and although the role is wispy at best, managed to convey a Catholic stoicism. She sang well too. 'Here Within These Walls', a song that would be well-placed in Beauty And The Beast, was delivered with a fine touch, her voice effortlessly singing of the joy of convent life. On 'I Haven't Got A Prayer', a nod to Sondheim, she bemoaned Deloris' modern influence on the lives of the nuns within her walls. Ms Fleming was a good casting choice for the character as she exuded high status but yet an adaptability to the mysterious ways her God worked to preserve the failing convent. As the local Monsignor O'Hara, her confidant, Seamus Feerick opened proceedings with a clever house announcement about fire exits and raffles. He was larger than life and he seemed to relish talking with the audience during the show, which they loved.

Nicky Lawless was excellent as Eddie, a cop and former high school classmate of Deloris who helps get her into hiding. He played the lovelorn nervous, sweaty wannabe hero with a fine touch. His big song, the fantasy 'I Could Be That Guy' was a nice big Broadway number. Deloris' nemesis, Curtis was played by Paul Drysdale who sang 'When I Find My Baby' and the reprise. He struggled with some of the notes, but certainly delivered the intention quite well. Mr Drysdale had an amazing stage presence and created a character who was genuinely quite scary. His henchmen, the Three Stooges, although they'd rather be seen as Three Musketeers, were comically played by Ciaran Smyth as his daft nephew, TJ, Mike O'Reilly as the laid-back Joey and Barry Dunne as the Spanish-speaking Pablo. On the Barry White inspired song, 'The Lady In The Long Black Dress', they really battled with the high notes, but got away with it as they were so funny. These three had good chemistry, and what they lacked in vocal ability they more than made up for in high farce and good characterisations. The postulant in the convent that Deloris tries to help, Sr Mary Robert, was played by Cherise O'Moore and she sang the emotive 'The Life I Never Led' and its Reprise splendidly, and seemed very comfortable with the higher octane and faster numbers too. She really looked the part, open-faced with a striking fringe, and developed her character's journey with skill, from a quiet mousey nun to a confident independent young woman. As Sr Mary Patrick, Catherine Dempsey embodied a fun-loving generously spirited character. She really shone in the portrayal. Margaret Mulligan-Murphy developed the role of Sr Mary Lazarus with a comic finesse. Like a character from The Simpsons, she had a gravelly voice and taciturn nature that really entertained. Frances Leahy as Sr Mary Martin was hilarious with her out-of- sync reactions and Gretel Sullivan played the decrepit but feisty Sr Mary Theresa very well. They all sang particularly well on 'Raise Your Voice' and 'Bless Our Show' together with the rest of the nuns.

Gerry Sweeney had a busy show as he played three characters, Ernie - the undercover police informant, a Pool Player and a Cab Driver. All three were good characterisations. Brian Derrane played Eddie's colleague, a cop at the police station quite well. Lisa Whyte's Michelle and Emma Greally's Tina were quite convincing as Deloris' backing dancers with their Afro's and attitude.

Shane Farrell gave us nice bouncy disco- inspired arrangements of the score and a great big Philly sound. His vocal arrangements were deft, the nuns had lovely harmonies and the leads were pretty good too. His pace suited the comedy of the piece, at times really driving the slapstick and at other times slowing it down for a poignant ballad. Mr Farrell conducted while playing piano, as is his wont, and commanded band and singers well. The players looked well in their nun's costumes and the conductor resplendent in his Bishop's garb.

His frequent collaborator, Aoife McClafferty, choreographed the show with good skill. The opening numbers with Deloris, Tina and Michelle were perfectly done with 1970's dance moves in the sleazy club. The big numbers with the nuns were also quite intricate, and her ensemble definitely didn't let her down. Eddie's 'I Could Be That Guy' was well paced with the homeless people joining in a perfectly syncopated routine. Elements of Saturday Night Fever and line dancing were incorporated into the basic 'disco' dancing routines, which worked well. Stage Wright provided the set for the production. As the locations bounce between a nightclub, a bar, the convent/ church, the street, an apartment and a police station it required quite a few trucks and cloths. The Queen of Angels church location, looked good with internally lit stained glass detail on the upstage structure and a couple of flown in panels. A sparkly red and silver drape was dropped for the club scenes which looked suitably gaudy. The Pope on a rope swing was a nice touch! Pat McGovern and his crew managed the stage very well, but some transitions were a bit laboured. That said, it was fairly smooth and unobtrusive. Lighting was designed by Pascal Gough and Ken O'Carroll and worked very well. I liked the use of movers on the dance numbers and Mirror ball and LED Crucifix lights were a nice touch. There were some nice states achieved in the church settings too. Good sound by Derek Recks was marred a little by the volume of the orchestra over the singers. Sometimes it was hard to make out the lyrics of the songs over the band. This happened a few times early on in the show, particularly the lower notes of Deloris' opening songs and on Curtis' song. Sound did improve as the show went on though and it was certainly beefy enough for the disco numbers later on.

Paul Norton's direction rightly centred on developing realistic characters then placing them in a ludicrous situation.
