His slapstick on the chase scenes at the start of the show, when the hoods chase Deloris and at the end when the hoods infiltrate the Queen Of Angels was pure Scooby Doo, but worked. His pacing of the production was good and his interpretation was also accurate. He clearly worked hard on authenticating the era through dialogue, costumes and props. Sister Act was energetic, hilarious and thoroughly enjoyable.

Cecilian Theatre Arts is a wonderful scheme for a holistic training of young people in the joys of theatre arts. It encourages each child to become more confident and to be the best they can be on and off the stage. The energy behind all this is the mother and daughter team of Rosalind and Jennifer O'Dowd. They work tirelessly to give the folk in their care the very best experiences possible. With this in mind this production of Grease was not just a staging of the show but an opportunity for as many as possible to perform for their relatives and friends. This was not the show as I had ever imagined before. There were children of all ages brought on during many of the musical numbers, all immaculately dressed and made up. They did however take away from the performances of the older cast and created a slightly strange but highly entertaining show. So, this was a showcase rather than a musical in the true sense of the word.

It was a no holds barred production too with obviously a great deal of money spent on hiring the venue (Draíocht Theatre Blanchardstown), the stunning set which was the original West End staging, Orchestra, sound, lighting and of course all those hundreds of beautifully fitted costumes. The young cast were well and truly given the star treatment. The expertise of the two directors was evident through the show. The curtain opened to reveal the set which had a raised platform accessed from the stage level by stairs right and left. The whole piece resembled a juke box which tied in very nicely with 1950's music which was playing as we entered the auditorium. The area under this platform had pieces which pulled out and created the diner, drug store and bedroom which were all nicely painted and effective looking. These fold outs looked good but I wouldn't have liked the pressure of moving them so well done stage team under the guidance of Joe Sinclair. Well done too to the props team who had gathered a collection of very appropriate items from the cafeteria trays and cups to the burgers. Such great attention to detail which I really appreciated. The clear sound quality for the dialogue meant we could hear every word spoken. The show started off with great pace obviously encouraged by the production team, occasionally this pace flagged, but picked up again towards the end. The story was well told though at times our eyes were taken off the ball when a couple of cute wee ones came on stage and danced beautifully. Masking was not too bad in the dialogue sequences and the principal cast all looked and acted well in their roles.

Rehearsing the music for the show must have been quite a challenge for Ivan McKenna and Dave McGauran. They had a great line up of young principals to work with and there were some nice moments with the younger chorus group too. Ivan had chosen eight players, quite a lot of electric instruments in a line under the fairly high stage. This is one of the widest stages I have seen on my travels and must have taken quite a job for Choreographer Jules McNamara to fill, in those reduced chorus moments and then try to tone down the movement when all the wee ones were on stage. When the stage was swamped, we had quite simple, on the spot movements but there were glorious moments such as Colm Lombard's 'Beauty School Dropout' when the dancers mesmerised us with great synchronised movement and good use of the fans. There were those wonderful moments when that huge younger chorus burst onto the stage with such enthusiasm though by the end of the evening the lateness of the hour took its toll on their energy. The 'Greased Lightning' number was great and the addition of the girls in orange dungarees actually didn't take away from it. The fact that they were dancing around an over a full-sized red car really added to the impact of the moment. Throughout the show there were some lovely touches with the choreography which the principals and chorus executed very well.

There were some great young voices on stage. This is a tricky score because we come as an audience with high expectations and we weren't disappointed by the voices of the main characters and the support they received from the chorus. Danny had a commanding voice and seemed to hit those high final notes with ease. Sandy had a real show voice, strong and punchy and always in key. The amplification of the music and singing was too strong for most of the show and really wasn't necessary as this group could have held their own with much less assistance. There was wonderful diction from the cast either in dialogue or when singing.

Denis Twomey had created an interesting and ever-changing lighting plot which gave us some memorable moments. This is lively and bright show and the lighting was light and bright too with some nice areas of the stage where we had a great sparkle which opened up the casts faces to us. Our leading man Danny was played with such style and total cheeky charm by Callum Martin. He had all the Danny attitude in his movements and how he delivered his lines. I loved the rapport he built up with the rest of the T Birds; there were lots of interplay moments between the lads which looked very authentic. Callum related so well to the audience pulling us into his world and into the story. A very energetic and well sung portrayal Callum. Erin Dunne made an excellent foil for him. I just loved the joy of performing in this young woman's eyes, she obviously enjoyed every moment on stage and in turn we enjoyed her too. This was a delightful Sandy, powerfully sung, I particularly loved her 'Hopelessly Devoted' number. She looked the part, moved well and wow what a transformation into the raunchy Sandy. Olivia Newton John was sewn into her outfit for the movie and it looked like Erin had been too. She built up a great on- stage partnership with Callum.

A beautiful short dark wig transformed Sophie Roche into an assertive Rizzo. This character's storyline has changed over the years but we still had that difference with this performance which appeared more mature than the other Pink Ladies. Dan O'Neill was the wise-cracking Kenickie who acted, moved and sang well. Frenchy was played by Emily Harkin in a very sincere and natural way. We felt sympathy for her when her beauty school career came crashing down. Ryan Sinnott created a natural looking gang member Sonny who moved well in all the musical numbers. Conor Swan gave a lively but also, very sincere performance as Doody. He was able to engage us in the lively routines and the gentler moment when he was on stage, guitar in hand. Roger played by Karl Nolan gave us some moments of laughter but I was also very impressed by the tone of this young man's speaking and singing voice, delightful. Jan played by Kate Halpenny brought a great energy and sensitivity to the stage. We loved to see the blossoming of romance between Roger and her, giving us hope that there is someone for everyone in life. Pink Ladies Marty and Patty were played effectively by Lyndsey Dennehy and Maria Power, adding so much to the feel and sound of the piece. Marty's suitor Vince Fontaine was played with real showbiz smarm by Kyle Laing. Nice use of that top platform area for his radio interjections. Daniel Reilly gave us an efficient and commanding Coach Calhoun, showing a maturity in the acting of this role. Cha Cha was played with great Puerto Rican flamboyance by Laura Behan. Well danced too Laura. Bronwyn Andrews was a wonderful creation of Miss Lynch. There was total commitment to the role with such stylish movements and pointed delivery of lines. A real tour de force performance. Andrew Hayes looked striking in that beautiful red velvet jacket as Johnny Casino. Nicely sung and acted too Andrew. I don't know how Isabelle Brennan managed to maintain that unusual voice and movements as Blanche, very entertaining. Colm Lombard was a striking Teen Angel who sang and moved the song really well. Eugene was portrayed by Cian Mulligan. We all were touched by this performance, well done Cian. All the other parts were well played by a young and talented cast. Great job everyone.

Thank you too to all those chorus members who burst onto the stage, they all looked, danced and sang so well. The costumes in this production were many and all were of a wonderfully high standard. The chorus looked great in sets of cheerleader costumes, mini silver leather jackets, polka dot dresses to name a few. The main characters all looked great with wonderful attention to detail right down to appropriate footwear. A huge job for the costume team to gather the costumes and another huge job to change so many backstage during the show. The makeup was stunning throughout. It was consistent, period correct and added a real 1950s feel to the show, as did the clever use of some wigs on stage. Again, a huge job well carried out.

Wow, this was quite an evening. So many on stage showing off their talents. There was great charm from all the younger players on stage and a super line up of older chorus and principals who gave us an interesting and entertaining version of Grease.

I have seen quite a few versions of this show now, I loved it the first time I saw it and you know I always look forward to seeing it again. It is a show which celebrates our differences, friendships and offers hope. It is full of great music, memorable moments and some super roles for men but more importantly excellent rounded character roles for a large number of women. That in mind I headed off to Mermaid Arts Theatre in Bray to see Bray Musical Society's production. Nice touch to be welcomed by some of the cast in full costume. They never let the persona drop for a second. It was a bright and cheery night as was the welcome in the airy foyer. The auditorium itself is a tiered seating area which comfortably seats two hundred and forty. I was delighted to see that there was a pit for the orchestra. Maybe it is psychological but I always feel that the sound it more blended and rounded when coming from a pit, also there is no intrusion into the acting area. Elizabeth Gregan and her orchestra of nine gave us a great balanced sound. There was that big brass and electric guitar feel of 1970s and then much more sensitive moments of accompaniment too in some of the tender songs such as the gloriously sung 'Sister Act'. One thing that the combination of voice and instrument did in this show is that it had the power to move us emotionally. There were those wonderfully joyous songs which elated us and then ballads which really affected us. Not sure how the connection is made from the stage to the audience but when it happens it is a beautiful thing. Of course, Elizabeth had a great cast to work with but it was obvious the songs had been thought through so that when they were sung their full meaning and emotion was released. A perfect volume and balance between stage and pit. Spoken and sung words were all as clear as a bell courtesy of Derek Nangle.

Chris Currid and I have met on quite a few occasions; indeed, he directed the show I saw earlier in the week in Gorey. He had decided to go with a black box staging for the piece. There was a raised platform running the width of the acting area up stage. Health and safety meant that a hand rail had to be installed between it and the black back curtain. This looked a bit untidy and took away from the intended sharpness of the look. There were some gobos projected on the black upstage curtain which gave the impression of place though it might have been good to add a bit of colour into the setting. There were some nice big pieces of scenery which were trucked on such as the night club stage, confessional boxes etc. These stood out well against the black background. I might have cut the two pillars at the back which were a bit too thin looking. Did the black box idea work? Mostly yes as it focussed us on the acting of the cast but it really needs to be sharp and has to be beautifully lit. There was a detailed lighting plot in the show with some nice touches though a few areas of the stage tended to be dull and we lost the faces of the cast which was a shame. I would also ask that casts think about how they look to us, particularly how to use the stage lighting, try to move into these lighting 'hot spots'. Lighting cues in this show could have been more precise, again because we are so dependent on lighting to create our sets we notice every detail.

Chris had set an easy pace for the show. There was a natural quality to it with the scenes with the nuns initially having a more gentle pace, of course when Deloris comes on stage the energy and pace really kicked in as it should have. Chris added in some beautiful moments of grouping of the cast. I loved that wee moment when in Eddie's flat he is on his knees at the side of the bed telling Deloris how he feels about her. This was so tender. There were a couple of times when our focus was distracted from what we should have been listening to or watching, by other stage action. Just be careful of that in future shows. Also there was a scene when only the stage left side was used but the whole stage was lit which looked a bit unbalanced. Chris did however bring out the humour of the script. There were some clever moments of dialogue which rang out loud and clear due to excellent comic timing and good delivery of lines. The choreography was neat and very well-rehearsed. The nuns in particular had wonderfully synchronised moves. There were some pleasant changes of patterns on stage. Good use of arm movements and great interpretation of the words and beat of each song. The initial 'Take Me To Heaven' was a bit limited due to the lack of space on the little stage platform but the cast made the best of the moment. The boys gave a good 'Lady In The Long Black Dress' but I would have liked them to have let themselves go. This was a moment for great visual comedy to come to the fore. On the whole though this was a well-moved show with a cast who obviously loved performing all the dance moves. Nice too to see the restraint when some numbers were kept fairly static so the voices had a chance to shine.

Of course, to carry this show off we need a brilliant cast. This we had in Bray. Joanne Keeling was a great stand offish, unchanging Mother Superior. What was lovely were the little chinks in her armour which were so cleverly shown and how her affection for Deloris grew. Her stubbornness to change but her over- riding love for the other nuns, beautifully played Joanne and nicely sung too. Sr Mary Robert has to be younger, has to be able to act her way through some very moving scenes and has the wonderful 'The Life I Never Led' number to sing. This part was beautifully played by Hannah Salmon who achieved all of the above and more.

Eddie was played with great honesty by Tim Forde. Sometimes this character is portrayed as the village idiot, we had a gentler approach in this show which worked very well. The transformation song worked well and was well costumed. Kevin Hoey was a very genuine looking and sounding priest. He gave us some lovely moments of gentle comedy. Sarne Lightman is relatively new to musical theatre and this was a good early effort, just make sure that you angle towards the audience so we can see you properly. I actually thought the English accent worked well and gave a ' Lock Stock and Two Smoking Barrels' feel to the part. Kelly-Marie Davy had such energy as the madcap Sr Mary Patrick. She created a wonderful character whom we instantly loved. Lyndsay Tracey transformed into Sr Mary Lazarus. Her movements and gestures were wonderful and her rap persona was hilarious. Well done Aishling Uí Laoire And Ali Logue as Michelle and Tina. They moved and reacted well to events around them. Good work too from Cecily Napier as Sr Mary Theresa, Jackie Fisher as Sr Martin de Tours, both nicely constructed characters bringing much humour to the evening.

Cian Gallagher as Joey, Conor Martin as Pablo, Darcy Potts as TJ worked really well as Curtis' gang. They were very individual in their roles. They acted and reacted well together and gave us lots of fun along the way. They sang that 1970s pastiche based on The Floaters 'Float On' very well but as I said earlier, I would have liked this number's choreography to be pushed a bit further. Eoin Martin made a nervous Ernie.

Is there someone I have left out? Deloris Van Cartier played by Clodagh Forde. Why was this such an affecting performance? I think because the actress opened her heart and soul to us for those two hours on stage. This was quite an extraordinary portrayal. No use of ethnic make-up, wigs, tricks, just pure talent and total commitment. Great singing throughout but that 'Sister Act' song was simply stunning and so, so emotional. This character can sometimes be one or two dimensional, Clodagh added so many layers to the character that we felt we really knew her. Perfect comic timing too. This is how it is done, I felt privileged to see this performance.

The chorus were fantastic, the singing was super and their movements were very together. They were nicely turned out though I really didn't like the pyjamas and I really hated the sensible ones Deloris was in, she just wouldn't have worn them. The men looked good in their 1970s look though in a black box stage set it is best to have contrasting colours or the eye gets a bit confused.

Make-up was generally underplayed though some of the characters could have had the nightclub greens and blues eye shadows to evoke the era.

So, this was a great night with some wonderful well measured acting. I wasn't wild about the staging and think it could have looked a bit sharper. It did mean that the performances were given a space to shine through. Nicely sung with great involvement from the chorus. There were some memorable moments created by Chris Currid and a talented cast.

society_raw: North East Musical and Dramatic Society
review_text:
Kick Off Your Sunday Shoes Written by Tom Snow, Dean Pitchford & Walter Bobbie and based on the hit film from 1984, Footloose The Musical was originally penned in 1998, one of a number of classic films that were made into stage shows like Flashdance, Fame, The Producers, Hairspray and Disney's Beauty And The Beast And Aladdin thus proving that nostalgia never goes out of style. It received a mixed critical reception, but the script was tweaked in 2005 to allow for more naturalism, which improved it considerably. The audience at the Grand Opera House where Belfast Music and Drama Society staged the show was a mixture of those who would have remembered seeing the film when it came out and a younger cohort who came along because they clearly love musical theatre! An open staging with the neon Footloose logo suspended centre stage was soon filled with the young ensemble dancing and singing the title song.

The story is quite simple: Ren McCormack, a high school student from Chicago, moves with his mother to a small conservative rural town after his father walks out on them. However, Ren finds himself clashing with most of the town, including the Reverend Shaw Moore who has convinced the town to prohibit dancing. This, Ren finds preposterous and upsetting as it's the only thing he's good at. With the help of Ariel (the Reverend's daughter) and her school chums, Ren convinces the Reverend and the Town Council to let the teenagers be teenagers and dance.

Ren was well played by Sean O'Neill, he captured the frustration of a city boy being relocated to rural America. His singing was strong and vibrant on 'Footloose' and on 'I Can't Stand Still'. Mr O'Neill had good vocal control on 'Dancing Is Not A Crime' and produced a fine falsetto in his duet with Ariel at the bridge on 'Almost Paradise'. His scenes with Ariel were quite sweetly done but it was his scene with the Reverend Shaw Moore in the second act where he really impressed. His emotional connection to the character was solid and his relationship with Shaw was quite moving. As Moore, Fergal White portrayed the inner torment of a father who has lost a child quite movingly. He had a wonderful stage presence and control and sang 'Can You Find It In Your Heart (Reprise)' and on 'Heaven Help Me' with a delicate tenderness.

Ariel, Shaw's daughter and Ren's love interest, was played by Courtney Burns. Ms Burns sang well and her scenes with Shaw were quite powerful and she had a nice chemistry with Ren. Ariel's mother, Vi, here played by Ceara Gallagher was stunning on 'Can You Find It In Your Heart', her voice was beautifully pitched and full of anguish. She was also extremely convincing and gave a deeply engaging performance. The role of Ren's mother, Ethel, was taken by Julie Bell. It was a rather underwritten role, but she did well with what she was given.

Wendy-Jo, a ditzy friend of Ariel's was perfectly played by Calla Hughes. Her attention to character was excellent and she had great comic timing. Leah Henderson played Urleen, the sensible one, quite well and Niamh Long's Rusty really impressed with her energetic performance and her singing on 'Let's Hear It For The Boy'. The trio all sang brightly on 'Holding Out For a Hero' and softly on 'Somebody's Eyes' Travis played by Louis Fitzpatrick and Lyle played by James McLoughlin were great foils for Matthew Watson's Chuck, who played the misogynist very effectively. All three sang well on 'The Girl Gets Around' and Ren's friend Willard, a typical hick in dungarees and cowboy hat, was nicely played with genial comedy by Jordan Walsh.

As it is a 'dance musical' Footloose has to be well-choreographed and executed. Thankfully the production was very well served by choreographer Ann Marie Morgan. The ensemble were athletic, accurate, daring and showed us many different styles. From the line-dancing of 'Still Rockin'' to the contemporary of 'Somebody's Eyes', the Rock 'n' Roll of 'The Girl Gets Around' and the energetic and complex 'Footloose', Ms Morgan directed and created some superb routines which the fabulous cast performed with gusto and obvious enjoyment.

Andy McKnight and his team directed the stage very well. Transitions were quick and accurate. The set was designed by Scenic Projects fit perfectly onto the Opera House stage. The church was most impressive, with the wood planking on the pews and lectern, it looked very natural and the bridge where Ren and Ariel fall for each other was very well rendered and impressively big.

Declan Anthony's design perfectly complemented the show. His use of movers really enlivened the dance sections. Michael Kielty looked after the sound design on the show and did a good job. Voices were clear and nicely reverbed on the songs. The band sounded very full and beefy and MD Wilson Shields gave a good interpretation of the keyboard driven eclectic score. From rock to c/w to gospel to the odd mournful power ballad, his pace and timing was faithful to the original. Sterling work with the ensemble's voices gave us lovely defined harmonies, particularly in the church scenes, and the principals were powerful.

The pace of this feel-good production well directed by Jordan Walsh was quite good, and transitions were speedy and accurate. His interpretation of the piece was authoritative and they used the revised script which made the show more rounded. The casting of the principals was agreeable and the ensemble were super. I enjoyed the energy of the production, it was infectious and during the 'Megamix' at the end, some of the audience were dancing in the aisles! Belfast Music and Drama Society are to be commended for producing a show that featured so many talented young performers.

At this stage of the year Sister Act is like a very old and dear friend whose company you always enjoy when you meet up. Someone you can sit with and enjoy being in their company, listen to their latest adventure and most of all laugh together. This old friend was brought to life so well by Enniscorthy Musical Society in Coláiste Bríde in the town. Interestingly I had brought my other dear friend Des O'Keefe from Waterford to see the show for the first time and it was so interesting seeing his reactions to the show too. The hall is pretty impressive in size with an upstairs area used for tea and coffee in the interval. It was obvious that the walls had all been covered in heavy black material to help the acoustic. The stage had been added to at either side and indeed a walk around had been built which enclosed the orchestra. More on the set later. The show was directed with great attention to detail by Imelda McDonagh who had injected a great sense of pace into the production. The delivery of lines was good from some and basically outstanding from others. There was a huge sense of fun in the production and some of the characters you would think of as being the straight ones were absolutely hilarious. The cast were obviously well rehearsed as they were comfortable with their moves and dialogue. She had broken down the fourth wall at times with the characters running off stage and through the audience. There were some very gentle and poignant moments which contrasted well with the hilarious ones. His Holiness appeared in a spotlight on the balcony which contained the moment nicely.

Musical Director, Kevin Kennedy did a beautiful job with the music in the show. The standard of musical direction in Ireland is wonderful and Kevin's intelligent and sympathetic direction was really up to the high standard I have come to expect. The nine-piece orchestra gave us some great moments of dance and soul but quietly let us enjoy the beauty of some of the ballads such as the title song. The principals all had great voices. Deloris really sang her heart out and Eddie has a stunning spine-tingling tone. Mother Superior has a crystal-clear voice which so suited the part.

The three boys who are in hot pursuit of Deloris have the great 'Lady In A Long Black Dress' to perform and let me tell you perform it they did. The audience were in hysterics especially watching Joey. This was a great piece of Anne-Marie Cooney's dance plot. The movement in the show was pretty well executed and was set at a level which most of the cast could achieve. Deloris and her two backing singers gave us 'in period' moves.

This was a strong cast led by Ashley Doran as Deloris. I had seen her earlier in the season in 9 To 5 and am impressed by the range of parts this actor can play. She sang the role brilliantly and created a very believable character. She related well to others on stage, building a strong rapport with the nuns, a romance with Eddie and a respect for Mother Superior. Jennifer Byrne gave a stunning comedy performance as Mother Superior. I have seen this role played in many ways, this time it was comedic timing at its very best. There was a glorious slightly cynical edge to her lines but we also saw that softness and care for those in her care too, a very balanced portrayal. She sang 'Here Within These Walls' beautifully too. Chris Currid captured the awkward charm of Eddie really well. We warmed to the character straightaway and we were willing that the love affair with Deloris would develop. Chris has a wonderful tone to his singing voice and his John Travolta moment in the white trousers, red shirt and waistcoat was a lovely moment in the show.

Monsignor O'Hara was portrayed by the humorous Andy Fanning who gave us many laughs, but particularly when he adopted his cool, hip voice. Curtis was quite frightening as played by Brian Kelly. The first gun shot was really realistic and although I was expecting it, I still jumped. He sang his 'When I find My Baby' well. The three Musketeers who form his gang were hilarious especially when it came to their dance routine. When David Cox as Joey let down his long hair, shook it out and then lying on his back let it tumble into the orchestra pit the audience reaction was wonderful. James Dobbs had all the attitude and Latin moves (those hips had a life of their own!). Murt Murphy gave us the slightly thick nephew really well though was a little more mature than the way the part is usually played. Well done guys you worked together well as a team. Michella White created the innocence of the postulant Sr Mary Robert. She has to appear younger than the rest and yet there has to be a fire in her belly too. 'The Life I Never Led' was beautifully sung. This was a good portrayal. Sr Mary Patrick was courtesy of Majella Londra. There was real energy and drive with her delivery. We probably all know a Mary Patrick, always volunteering, diving straight in. She also sang strongly. I had to look twice in the programme to find Sr Mary Lazarus, quite a transformation for Teresa Buckley. She managed the difficult rap very well. Teresa captured the off the wall character. Joan Duignan and Carmel Monaghan gave good character performances of eccentrics Sr Mary Martin of Tours and Sr Mary Theresa. Other roles were played with style.

The chorus were great appearing as nuns, dancers, bar goers, even the Village People. They all added to the enjoyment of the evening. All were nicely dressed with good well-presented nuns' costumes, the costumes of the baddies and the folk in the bar gave a real feel of the era. Make up was as it should have been. Light enough for the nuns, though the eyes were well highlighted. Deloris and her two backing dancers, Tina (Debbie Marchese) and Michelle (Julie Kinsella) who acted and danced well, had more make up around the eyes which looked correct.

The staging was quite ingenious. There were two huge revolves which silently spun round. This meant that the next scene could be set and then spun back again with no hesitation. It seems simple but was probably more complicated, but it worked, and worked so well. These scenes were really well dressed too so we never felt short changed by the revealing scene. The confessional was beautifully made and seemed to float in from nowhere. The tables for the meal and those wooden folding chairs which the nuns carried in themselves were so authentic. The back arches and the side windows looked really solid as did the window down stage right which had a glorious light shining through it at times. This was a well-constructed set which just worked. It was for the most part well lit, though there were so many areas including the walk around to light, it must have been a bit of a nightmare! A good sound system with great balance between the voice and the orchestra. A really great evening of fun in Enniscorthy. There was a great buzz before the show from the loyal fans. Everyone was still buzzing as they left after seeing a great production of Sister Act. Oh, by the way Des loved the show too!

I first saw this show in the much-missed N Ireland Festival of Light Opera staged each year in Bangor Co Down, performed by a group from Glasgow. We were all quite shocked by the graphic nature of the storyline and the language. Even today the show still maintains that slightly risqué feel. The production by Pop-Up Theatre gave us a contemporary feel to the show. The styling of the 1996 Revival was used and pushed even a little further. Director Karen Gordon decided to have the curtains open to reveal a huge metal staircase. This created some lovely pictures but caused a few problems too. One great aspect of the stairs was that when the cast were on them everyone could be easily seen. However, getting into position took a little longer and this extended moments which led to the show dragging its heels a few times. The orchestra under the leadership of Niamh Crowley was divided and placed on either side of the stage tucked in close to this staircase. Herta Kelly was Chorus Mistress for the Show. The orchestra of young talented players were all dressed for the occasion with caps braces etc and at the opening of Act Two they were discovered strewn over the staircase when the curtain opened. This was a very clever touch which really integrated them into the show. The cast on the whole sang really well but there were a few occasions when it seemed that they couldn't quite hear the tune and there were the occasional problems with pitch. That aside there were some moments of great singing both from the principals and the chorus. I loved the selection of period music which was being played in the theatre as we entered the auditorium which really set the mood and the scene.

Karen Gordon's direction gave us some mesmerising visual moments. I was intrigued by the stylised movements of, in particular, the MC who contorted his body into all sorts of shapes as he entered and left the stage. The characters were neatly drawn and everyone on stage looked very comfortable in their chosen role. The two leading actors worked well when opposed to each other and together as a partnership at the end of the show. As is more often the case, Mary Sunshine was played by a female. Though the reveal at the end removed a wig rather than the now usual outer costume to reveal that she was dressed in the fishnets and basque like everyone else. Props and furniture were limited and that worked well as we really focussed on just the action. The pace was a bit hesitant at times and it appeared that rhythms were repeated so that cast could get into place etc. which caused further gaps. There were a few of the numbers which I would have liked moved a little more such as 'Funny Honey', not a dance routine just acted out moves. What really did impress was how the Cell Block Tango ladies all delivered the punchline, not sure who was behind training the ladies but it was one of the highlights of the show. I missed the actual tap dance which is meant to re-emphasise the forward and back interplay dialogue between Roxie and Amos. The use of the chorus throughout was interesting with just the addition of sunglasses they became reporters. The audience were automatically accepting of that subtle change. Although I have suggested that magic tricks are incorporated in the 'Razzle Dazzle' number, the time taken up of the song to perform that sawing in half trick was too long and Billy would have been better to start with small tricks and get increasingly more flamboyant and showy. The action was nicely directed and the story telling was good.

This is very much a dance show and creating the choreography plot was Ingrid McLoughlin. This was very much in the style of the period with some very energetic and well carried out routines. The flat area in front of that huge staircase was limited so at times that restricted the type of movement which was possible. There were moments when the cast moved through a series of complicated, exaggerated poses, which looked very effective. The chorus gave some very enthusiastic movement sequences. I particularly loved 'We Both Reached For The Gun' which was well acted by Billy and Roxie but the chorus moves really worked well too. Overall some good moments of choreography.

This was a strong cast with the two ladies playing Roxie and Velma pushing the story along and singing the roles really well too. Maggie Villarini made a very convincing edgey Velma Kelly. She was wonderfully styled with a great slicked back hairstyle. Maggie really punched out that dialogue with a most convincing American accent. She moved well and I was very impressed by her stamina in 'I Can't Do It Alone'. She sang most of the difficult score really well. Laura Kelly settled quickly into the character of Roxie Hart. A nice contrast in looks to Velma with finger waved hair which looked great. She delivered the lines really well with a punchy delivery and excellent comedy timing. She made an excellent ventriloquist's dummy. Laura had wonderfully expressive eyes as Roxie and used great facial expressions to point her comedy lines. The two 'Thriller Dillers' worked well together in that final sequence though I think the number needed more razzle dazzle. Which neatly brings me to Billy Flynn played by Conor White. He wore this part like a perfectly fitting kid glove. His look with that immaculately cut hair, those perfectly fitting suits and velvet jacket and of course the correspondent shoes all added to the impact of the character. This was a very slick piece of acting. He too punched out his lines of dialogue and we all were entranced by his hocus pocus. Nicely sung too Conor, a well-judged portrayal.

Mr Cellophane, Amos was played with a gentle charm by Brendan Reid. There were some lovely little touches in this performance and we all loved and felt so sorry for poor Amos. He delivered his lines well particularly in the 'Funny Honey' when he must keep time with Roxie's singing. Rachel Patenande gave us quite a glamorous Mama Morton. This was a very stylised performance with some nice delivery of comedy lines. She sang well too and 'When You're Good To Mama' was a memorable moment. Mary Sunshine was played with a classy elegance by Laura Coulter-Low. The 'A Little Bit Of Good' number sounded great, just a pity the lighting wasn't picking up her face until the end of the number.

Matthew Whitehead created a most unusual and fascinating character as the MC. His movements and expression of his words were quite unusual and helped to create an individual personality on stage. The 'Cell Block Tango' girls really blasted us away. Elissa O'Dowd looked wonderful and convincingly Eastern European as Hunyak. Liz (Lauren McKenna) would definitely have fired that shot into his head. June (Karen Lynch) sounded great as the Puerto Rican murderess. Aoibhín Buckley was a really powerful and threatening Mona. Cliona Dowd completed the group as Alvin's wife Annie. Well done ladies for a really well staged and sung moment. All the many other characters such as Fred (Michael Bonner), Kitty (Karen Kane), Harrison (Darren Jenkins) Aaron (David Church), the Clerk (Sean McInerney) all added so much to the production.

There was a lively chorus who coped with the choreography given to them. I loved the enthusiasm in every face which really put the audience at ease.

There were some stunning costumes from the set of black cropped tops, basques, suspenders, etc to Billy's perfectly cut suits. They all worked well together though I wasn't wild about Mama's tweeds, I never thought of Mama Morton in tweeds. The two black sparkly coat dresses at the end were alright but should have been the same length. Make up was superb with so many novel ideas which all worked so well. Hair and wigs were so in keeping and gave a real unifying appearance to the folk on stage.

The show's sound was nicely balanced and sound cues were good. Lighting had its moments. At times there were some stunning effects and at others, faces were in semi darkness, which cut the character off from us. I liked the use of lighting on the edges of the stairs, which gave a Hollywood glamour to events.

This was a most interesting, highly-stylised version of the multi- award winning show. The cast and crew gave us a very polished performance. The story-telling was good, some great singing and dancing. An entertaining evening. Thank you all at Pop Up Theatre, Sligo for Chicago.

The Slave of Duty This was the only Gilbert and Sullivan work I got to adjudicate this year, as they are not performed as often as in the past. One would have to wonder why as this was a brilliantly anarchic production with fabulous singing and tongue-in- cheek performances of a classic which myself and the audience felt privileged to attend and enjoy. So, if you missed it, your loss but let me tell you why it was so good. First off, it has a very cleverly written libretto by Mr Gilbert, which revels in wordplay and innuendo and some of the most beautiful tunes Mr Sullivan has ever written. To top it all it was performed by a company of superb performers and creatives who knew exactly what they were doing. Directed and choreographed by Mr Peter Kennedy with great attention to detail and with sublime musical direction by Mr Andrew Tubman, this was a perfectly articulated, well-paced, and modulated production of The Pirates Of Penzance, a far superior operetta to that infernal Pinafore.

On the coast of Cornwall, a band of tender- hearted pirates, led by the braggart Pirate King, celebrates the coming of age of Frederic, who was mistakenly apprenticed to the pirates (he was meant to be an apprentice pilot not pirate) until his 21st birthday. Now, Frederic has vowed to devote his life to the extermination of piracy - until a preposterous leap year snag threatens to keep him chained to the pirates for life! He meets Mabel, daughter to Major General Stanley, falls in love and contrives to unravel the paradox his life has become.

As Frederic, John Lindop played just the right amount of naivety as the innocent hero. His scenes with the Pirate King, Kerry Rooney, were hilariously funny particularly when they were arguing over who got to keep Ruth, Ditanya McKinty, the maid-of- all-work as neither of them wanted her. Mr Lindop had very good comic timing and his voice was quite good on 'Oh! false one, you have deceiv'd me' with Ruth and the very funny 'All is prepar'd; your gallant crew await you' with Mabel.

As Mabel, Megan Jane Mooney, was spectacular. Her voice soared around the theatre on every song she sang. Her range was impressive as was her control, her bel canto parodies in her arias were sublime. 'Poor wand'ring one' was a triumph. Ms Mooney was very funny too, her timing within the songs and her expressions, particularly barking at her sisters as she stole Frederic away from them. A superlative performance.

As poor Ruth, who is discarded by Frederic for Mabel, Ditanya McKinty really impressed with her comedy skills as well as her vocal. 'When you had left our pirate fold' which she sang with the Pirate King and Frederic was a brilliantly executed comedy scene, where she became a fully- fledged pirate and her character became strong.

The Pirate King was played by Kerry Rooney with great energy and incisive comic timing. His characterisation was full of proud bravado masking a gentle soul which Mr Rooney really carried off with ease. We could see the character's thought processes in full flight, written on Mr Rooney's face. His singing was also superb on all of his songs and his wonderful swashbuckling routine on the hidden trampoline was masterfully done as he sang 'Oh, better far to live and die'. 'When you had left our pirate fold', the paradox song was also very well performed with Ruth and Frederic.

As Mabel's father, the Major General, Drew Reid gave a wonderful performance. His status commanded the stage in the scenes with the Pirates and he showed vulnerability when with his daughters in his ruined chapel as he pined for his late wife 'Oh, dry thy glistening tear' was sung to him by the girls as he held his teddy bear. But it was on one of G&S's most famous patter-songs, 'I am the very model of a modern Major-General', where Mr Reid excelled. His diction was outstanding and we could understand every word and when the Pirate King asked him to do it one more time and to do it fast - he did and it was even better. This was a very funny scene and he was supported by the ensemble as they physically inhaled with him, urging him on.

Once Frederic decides to fight off the pirates, he enlists the help of the Police Sergeant and his men. Like the Keystone cops of the old Mack Sennett silent films, the policemen were incompetent and cowardly. Aaron Butler played the Sergeant and took the lead on 'When a felon's not engaged in his employment', a wonderfully funny song. His performance and curious movements were laugh-out- loud funny and a highlight of the show. One of the principal pirates was Samuel as played by Stephen McQuillan, he sang well on 'Pour, oh pour, the pirate sherry' and 'Hold Monsters' and had a good presence on stage. Edith, Mabel's older sister who is the de facto leader of the girls, was played by Helena Hendron with great control; another sister, Kate was played by Ella Taylor Campbell with a mischievous pep and Isabel, the youngest and shy sister was played with a lovely gentleness by Megan Paul.

Peter Kennedy's choreography was simple, unfussy and fitted the style of the show. His performers were well-drilled and the female ensemble were particularly elegant. Musical direction by Andrew Tubman was very tight and bright. A small orchestra of keyboard, violin, viola, flute, clarinet, percussion and occasional trumpet managed to sound more than the sum of its parts thanks to Mr Tubman's arrangements.

Stage management by Andy McKnight was efficient and although there were few transitions, they were done speedily and with accuracy. Set design by John McConnell and Seamus Hughes was perfect for the show, a pirate ship on a track upstage in front of a tight cyc and some boulders, boxes and barrels downstage and for the chapel, a simple widow upstage. Classic, clean and uncomplicated, in the Victorian toy- theatre style. Lighting and sound were looked after by A Show in a Box. The lighting design was simple, lights up at the beginning and down at the end, the rig was mostly pars and it was pleasing to see a show so well-lit, bright and full of depth. Sound was also very good, with sharp vocals from the performers and a full- range from the band. Costumes by Utopia were suitable for the show, a great range of dress and night ware colours on the ladies and nicely fitted pirate and police costumes for the men with the Major- General's de rigure pith helmet and khaki uniform. Make-up by Jordan Humphries was great, slightly too much eye make- up on the Pirates - which was perfect and similar on the ladies. Mr Humphries gave everyone a tad too much, which made it all seem perfectly within the style of the show.

Director Mr Peter Kennedy controlled the pace expertly, his staging was perfect and his interpretation of a 140 year-old show made it timeless. He delivered all the jokes and puns and his cast luxuriated in the word play. It was light, bright entertainment and the audience loved it.

The Scouts' Hall in Nenagh was the venue for Nenagh Choral Society's production of Sister Act. The folk of the town always give a great support to the society and tonight was no exception with a full house and a whole variety of ages attending. Everyone in the hall was transfixed by this lively and well-produced show. The welcome was great and the hospitality was genuine. The open curtain revealed a wonderful set with projected church stained glass windows in the background and in the foreground there was an altar with a cross and candles burning. On further inspection the light up panels I had seen on my last journey to the town were being used again, this time with attachable flats over them which transformed them into arched windows, city windows and nightclub effect. The lighting was very atmospheric to begin.

Once again the direction was from Greg Browne who produced a fast-moving production with great pace which was only hampered by the changing of the side flats. The integration of the musical numbers and dance sections into the production worked very well and seemed well considered. Greg had added a few interesting touches into the production some of which I enjoyed and some others I wasn't so keen on. The characters were all well-rehearsed, well-moved and they all suited the role they were playing. There were good relationships between characters and everyone was given a moment to shine. The musical direction was carried out with great ease and expertise by William Cullagh who gave us nice beat to the big dance numbers and also beautiful backing to some of the more tender ballads. The sound system was nicely balanced.

Stephanie Browne not only played the lead in the show but she was also choreographer. The dance numbers were extremely energetic, fast-moving showing a good use of changing patterns. On the spot moments were all well synchronised. One thing I would ask is to just watch the masking of dancers when there is a raised platform on stage. There were nice nods to the disco moves of the 1970s but with some modern dance moves added as well. There was humour brought out particularly in some of the boys' numbers and there was a huge amount of energy from the chorus and nuns. There was a wonderful 'Raise Your Voice' and 'Take Me To Heaven' which seemed to soar into a different dimension.

Stephanie, well done as Deloris Van Cartier, you gave us a strong and powerful creation of the character. Her bouncy, no nonsense walk added much to the attitude of the character. She sang well and of course danced brilliantly. Niamh Chadwick was a strong and resolute Mother Superior who sang beautifully and built up a good relationship with Dolores at the end of the show. Sister Mary Robert played by Máire Long was the timid postulant who builds in confidence to stand up for herself. This was a nicely acted and sung portrayal. Sister Mary Patrick was played by Vivienne Mulcahy. She blew us away with her enthusiasm in the role.

Sister Mary Lazarus was given a cross and edgy character by Karen Ryan but softened as the show continued, her rap moment was hilarious. The role of Monsignor O'Hara was played by Alan O'Brien who gave us an 'in character' safety announcement at the beginning of the show which was very effective and funny. Needless to say, not one mobile phone appeared after his scowl! Eoin Byrne played the character of Curtis who is a real baddy. He played the role with quiet menace in contrast to Eddie played by Pádraic Walsh who gave us a gentle and sincere policeman. Jack McGrath played TJ, Colin Dillon, Joey and Paddy Rohan played Pablo. These are Curtis's gang. They gave us great moments of humour, chase routines, dance routines and some funny dialogue. They certainly looked the part in their 1970s gear and they acted their parts really well too. We will never forget that pelvic thrusting! Marese Dolan-Hutchinson played Sister Mary Theresa who looked hilarious when she was running backwards and forwards across the stage shaking her walking stick chasing the baddies. Claire Loughnane and Sharon Kelly were two nuns who were kept busy during the show, putting a great deal of effort into their roles. Nuala Woulfe gave us a sincere and convincing Sr Mary Martin de Tours and created a real 'one off' character. What I particularly liked about the group of nuns supporting this principal cast was the fact that whenever they were on stage each one of them seemed to have their own individual personality. They just didn't fit into the background but they actually became characters in their own right which was wonderful and must have taken a lot of rehearsal to plan.

Of course, the chorus could really sing and we had wonderful moments of harmony and wonderful moments of total lack of harmony before Deloris teaches them, which is a very difficult thing to actually achieve for ladies who can sing. Their initial singing was hilarious. I was blown away by their energy. The dance routines were well rehearsed and well delivered. There were quite a few men who appeared from time-to-time on stage, sometimes as drunks, sometimes as men of the cloth and each one of them did a great job. We all particularly loved when the older men got their own back on Curtis's gang and beat them up in the middle of the street. The costumes were good with a wonderful set of nuns' habits and nicely chosen stockings and shoes. Also the nice touches such as slippers which were very effective. The night dresses were very sharp and looked very appropriate. The glitzy tabards added to the habits and gave a sparkle. The white sequined habits looked super with of course Mother Superior in a black sequin habit. The men's costumes evoked the 1970s very well with baggy trousers, wide lapels and lots of blingy jewellery (very Mr T!). The dresses worn by Dolores' Divas were appropriate especially with those silver sparkly boots. The makeup was generally good, though some of the cast who had to double up between being dancers and nuns might have needed to tone down the makeup between roles. The hair styles were good, the wigs used didn't hide the faces of the cast. Also, I liked how some of the men had made an effort with their hair and particularly with the growing of sideburns which created the look of the period. The back projections were fantastic and added much to the whole feel of the production. I particularly liked the inside of chapel and the inside of the club which actually looked familiar to me (memories of my youth). The lighting was quite good throughout although at times I would have liked a little bit more light on the principal actors' faces. When they did walk into the strong light at the front of the stage, we suddenly got a real sparkle from the eyes of the cast.

The props used such as the furniture, bentwood chairs, tables, desk etc. looked all quite appropriate as did the altar.

This was a well-polished, well-rehearsed and well thought through production. It moved well, it looked well and sounded good throughout. The cast were well chosen for their roles and the most important thing was that everyone on stage was having a ball and in doing so the audience thoroughly enjoyed their trip to Sister Act.

When we see that the music in a show is by Alan Menken we know we are in for a treat. The composer is winner of eight Academy Awards and eleven Grammies. With scores such as Sister Act and Beauty And The Beast to his credit, Little Shop Of Horrors premiered off-off Broadway in 1982 and then moved to the Orpheum Theatre off-Broadway for a five year run. This horror, comedy rock musical tells the story of Seymour and his human flesh- eating plant. It is a great wee musical with some wonderful moments and songs dotted through it.

It was a pleasure to finally enter the campus of Maynooth University to see their production of this fun show. Much rehearsal had obviously taken place to bring it to production standard for a very short three show run. As with many of these university shows this was very much a student led production with players, crew and production by either present students or recently qualified students. Because of this there was a natural youthful energy about the production. The Aula Maxima is a large theatrical space. The open curtain revealed a solid looking set with a crazy perspective which set the tone of the show. This set was nicely lit with blue spots. The musical direction for the show was in the relatively inexperienced hands of Ailbhe Travers and Chris Carew. Ailbhe conducted the show and Chris was on keyboards. There were eight players who were also students. They worked together well to give us a well-paced and melodic sound. The big soul/rock numbers were given plenty of oomph (technical term!) and we had some real rock blasting moments. A couple of times the sound from the orchestra overpowered the singers and we lost the clarity of the words. The singing was good. The three girl backing singers did a good job and gave us some nice moments of harmony. The principals sang their roles well and the chorus proved some great vocals even when they were moving flat out dancing. Rachel Bermingham directed the show with a deft touch for the most part. The show was set at an undetermined time which gave a bit more free hand with the design of costumes etc. This worked well as themes such as tartan were introduced for costumes. The cast seemed very at ease with their movements in all the acting areas. I would just ask that the cast would punch out the dialogue a little more as word endings were not complete and so diction suffered at times. There were some lovely sensitive moments created such as the 'Somewhere That's Green' song. The decision to have the full sized Audrey II as a manipulated plant and also at the same time have the voice of the plant personified by Adam Kelso moving round the stage was an unusual choice and I am not sure the double image totally worked for me. Maybe if the singer had emerged from the centre of the flower each time it might have worked better. The tendrils however were amazing, never stopping, always gesturing always focussing our attention on the action, a great idea I had never seen before. So overall a nicely directed production with some interesting novel touches.

Gavin Murphy devised a detailed and very fast-moving choreography plot. What I liked was the energy of the cast and chorus as they hit the stage, carrying us along with their enthusiasm. There were clever nods to the days of Motown and the early sixties with some of the hand and arm movements. The tendrils were simply amazing, they constantly moved with great arm and hand contortions, creating all sorts of interesting angles. The chorus were very committed and had obviously put in a great of effort into perfecting their routines. The final moments of the show were a real extravaganza of balloons, ribbons and dancing on stage and through the audience.

The set which was mostly brought in for the show worked really well and looked very professional. This was well dressed with props such as plants and flowers. I wanted to see a more crazy source for Orin's gas such as a heavy cylinder, think of the fun he could have had wheeling a large gas cylinder round the surgery! I also wanted to see a bit more blood splattered and a working drill would have created that awful grinding sound we all hate. The stage was quite well lit through the show with the use of interesting colours. A follow spot or a special focussed on faces would have helped pop the facial expressions out to us, this was used at times and made a great difference. There were some wonderful moments created with the use of focussed lighting through the piece. The sound was generally good with some moments when the orchestra overwhelmed the principal voices. I always much preferred the headset microphone which fits over the ear to the ones which are taped to the cheek and look a bit untidy. Also, when the actors sweat the tape peels off as happened in the show, well done Seymour for carrying on so well. This role was nicely played by Joe Jennings who gave the part a freshness and innocence which worked really well. I liked how he delivered some of his lines out to us. He related well to the others on stage and he looked very comfortable with his movement. He built a cute love affair with Audrey played beautifully by Laoise Fleming. She has a sweet voice and gave us a magical 'Somewhere that's Green'. Laoise has also a rock quality to her voice which worked well in the up- tempo numbers. She acted the part well and was convincing in the role.

Mushnik, the owner of the florist's was played by Cormac Dredge who looked older that the others but I would have liked more tired, older movements as Mushnik. Good delivery of lines and a good relationship with Seymour was created. Adam Kelso, rather than just providing the voice of the plant actually became the plant. He appeared in a leaf clad jacket and trousers, he dominated the stage, we couldn't take our eyes off him. It did confuse the eye as we were torn as to where we should look, at Adam or at the Audrey II. Adam performed really well, moving with great energy around the stage and he has a wonderful tone to his singing and speaking voice. The role of Orin the Dentist was played by Adam Lau. This is a very demanding role physically and emotionally. Adam did well but there is room to go even more over the top with the part.

The backing singers who also work as sounding boards for the principals were played by Niamh Kelly, Emily Carrick and Nadine Conlon. Hard to separate this great team as they were super individually but really worked well together too with some good dance moves and lovely harmonies. They added much to the look and feel of the show. Well done ladies.

The chorus really burst onto stage with such energy and backed the principals well. Cast with a few lines to say did a good job such as the first customer. The dancing was generally good though some of the tricky lifts didn't look quite right. The 'Mushnik and Son' red and black tango routine added to the number.

Costumes were interestingly themed with one theme of plaid which actually worked well to create a look. Those tango dresses were great. The Skid Row beggars looked good but a time of year needed to be shown by the costumes of everyone on stage. The Tendrils were given an almost 'Midsummer Night's Dream' look. The human plant had a jacket decorated with leaves but more could have been added. Hairs were very much the actor's own which was fine up to a point though I would have liked Audrey to have stood out a little from the crowd with her styling. Make up seemed to have a 1950's feel to it.

Properties were generally good with the shop nicely dressed. There were loads of balloons and ribbons for the finale which gave a great look to the last number. Personal props such as the camera looked authentic. Be careful laminating wall posters as when the stage lights hit them we can't see the picture.

This was a confident and energetic show with some great moments of comedy and also some tender moments too. I commend this group for all the hard work they put into producing Little Shop Of Horrors and I wish all the students best wishes for their forth-coming exams.

The Country Girls St Mel's Musical Society has been around a while, starting during the second world war in 1944, when everyone needed a bit of cheer. Taking an eighteen-year hiatus in 1960, they bounced back in 1978 with a series of revues. Staging South Pacific in 1983, the group were on a roll and have been going strong ever since, producing Sister Act last year and in April of this year, Dolly Parton's feminist revenge musical 9 To 5.

The musical was written in 2008 by Dolly Parton and Patricia Resnick and based on the 1980 film of the same name. It's a satirical take on office politics and feminism about three female secretaries who decide to get revenge on their dictatorial, chauvinist boss by abducting him and running the business themselves. Dolly herself appears in the musical via two film clips; one at the beginning contextualising the show and one at the end thanking everyone for attending. Sean Power deftly directed this slick and spirited production for St Mel's at the Backstage Theatre in Longford. Vince Tully was chorus master and musical director and conducted a seven-piece band called The Urban Day Spa Orchestra for the show and the choreography was skilfully looked after by Tracey Carty. Paul Hennessy played Franklin Hart Jr, committed misogynist and CEO of Consolidated Industries, promoted because he was one of the boys and not because he earned it through hard work. He did what he could with the role, but as the character is so one dimensional and his lines so puerile, he couldn't help but come across as a cartoon villain. That said his comic timing was excellent and he added a nice flexible physicality to the character. His singing was good too, 'Here for You', whilst cringe inducing in its lyrics, was well sung by Mr Hennessy as was the highly sexist 'Always A Woman' in act two. Clearly a fine performer, Paul Hennessy played the farce and slapstick quite well and in his final scene we almost felt sorry for Hart.

Hart's nemesis and leader of the office revolution was Violet Newstead played by Valerie Nolan. Ms Nolan had a very good grasp of Violet's character. She was witty and sharp in her dialogue and had a nice stillness at times. Her singing on 'Around Here' was authoritative and 'Potion Notion' was fun. But it was on 'One of the Boys' early in act two, where she really stood out. She sang and danced it really well accompanied by the male ensemble and some excellent dancers. Ms Nolan projected the difficulties of the harassed widow bringing up her teenage son on her own, whilst holding down a full-time job in a glass-ceilinged company with a convincing naturalism.

Judy Bernly, the newbie in the office who became empowered through the ousting of Hart, was delicately played by Natasha Brady. Her journey from meek housewife to self-sufficient manager was well conceived and performed. Ms Brady had a super voice and the showstopper 'Get Out and Stay Out' really showcased it. It's by far the best song in the show and Ms Brady performed it brilliantly. She also sang well on the intriguing 'Dance of Death'.

Hart's personal assistant, Dolly clone Doralee, was played by Eimear Reynolds. Assumed by all to be having an affair with Hart but happily married, Ms Reynolds played her frustration at being misunderstood very well and with a no- nonsense humour. She sang 'Backwoods Barbie', a sad song bemoaning her life with passion and on the rather sadistic 'Cowgirl's Revenge', with verve. Ms Reynolds played Doralee with a light touch and it worked.

As Roz, an office worker who was in love with Hart, Grainne Fox gave a superb comic performance. Roz tried to undermine anyone she felt may be more efficient than her and Ms Fox played her exquisitely. Her singing on the fantasy song 'Heart to Hart' revealed an outstanding voice, full of longing and heartache and she revealed a vulnerability which was quite endearing. Another office worker, Joe, who helps in the overthrow of the Hart regime and has designs on Violet, was played by Conor Lynn-McLoughlin. Joe, although considerably younger than Violet, kept declaring his affection for her and eventually won her over. Mr Lynn- McLoughlin played Joe's tenacity with doggedness and sang a lovely duet with Violet 'Let Love Grow'. Doralee's husband, Dwayne was pleasantly played by Cormac Gobl, his was a laid-back character which contrasted well with Doralee. Judy's ex-husband, Dick, was portrayed by Oisin O'Reilly who encapsulated Dick's dastardliness with aplomb. Iarlath O'Rourke played the role of Josh, Violet's son. He had a warm relationship with Violet, and they worked well together. Michelle Kelly Conlon played Hart's clueless wife, Missy and was quite funny in her ignorance of Hart's true nature. Amy Oates as Maria and Cathy Lenehan as Cathy played well as office workers, but Maria Dunne as Margaret was extremely funny and had good comic timing. Dylan Murray played the young doctor in the hospital with vigour and Kim Phillips as the Candy Striper was droll. As the young police detective, Lorcan O'Brien was amusing and Daniel Penrose played Bob Enright with assurance. As the Chairman of the Board of the company, Russell Tinsworthy, John Kelly had good comic timing and played high status well.

Choreography by Tracey Carty was excellent.

The drug-fuelled fantasy sequences were well moved, particularly 'Cowgirl's Revenge' with the faux line dancing. 'One of the Boys' was extremely well choreographed, especially the tap dancing which was super. The opening number '9 to 5' was a little unstructured and the cast seemed a little unsure, but 'Around Here' was very well done. There was a small troupe of excellent young dancers who kept appearing in different guises throughout the show, these were very confident and very well-rehearsed and really lifted the dance numbers.

Musical direction and chorus master, Vince Tully, conducted a smashing little band. The bass and drums were superb, as was the sax/clarinet. His choral work with the ensemble was also great, lovely strong harmonies and power.  Sound by Vinny Osborne was excellent, really clear vocals and a nice mix on the band. Lighting design by Shane Byrne, was rather good. The set was designed by Robert Belton and stage manager, Eddie Kiernan and worked very well, with a large cloth upstage depicting a cityscape and a series of flats, furniture and trucks rolled on to denote location. The set was very well dressed and finished with some nice attention to detail. Costumes by Sparkle and Pat McGann were accomplished and suited the production and make-up by Fiona Fenelon and her team was well- applied.

Although a sleek and energetic production, the show feels a bit dated already though, and that's not just the jokes, but the entire premise. Some of the music is rather good however and very hummable and the society produced a very good interpretation of the musical. Director, Sean Power paced the production well and his staging was clever and well managed by stage manager, Eddie Kiernan and his crew.

Sisters Standing Strong Limerick Musical Society was formed in the year 2000 and started out with a production of Jesus Christ Superstar, which they restaged last year. This year they produced the musical-comedy Sister Act for three performances in the University of Limerick's Concert Hall. The show is based on the 1992 successful film of the same name, but the music score is expanded and different to the original film. The plot however remains largely the same. Wannabe singer and gangster's moll, Deloris Van Cartier, sees her boyfriend, Curtis Jackson, kill a police informer. She goes to the cops, and meets Officer Eddie an old school acquaintance, who harbours a secret crush on her. Eddie places her in a convent for her safety until they bring the baddie to trial. Whilst secreted in the convent she teaches the nuns how to sing, they become famous. Curtis and his incompetent acolytes try to infiltrate the convent to kill the witness but the sisters protect our heroine, Curtis gets arrested and Eddie gets Deloris. Sounds like the plot of a film noir from the 40's, but this one has singing nuns. A lot of singing nuns.

Alison Kearney played Deloris as quite a sassy but shallow chanteuse. Deloris' transformation from an uncaring selfish impetuous character to a benevolent, altruistic 'sister' is implausible to be fair, but Ms Kearney managed to hold onto the truth of the character and it worked. She sang very well throughout the show. Her 'Raise Your Voice' was excellently paced and her voice on the higher octane numbers such as 'Take Me To Heaven' and 'Fabulous, Baby!' soared out to us. She sang the title song very well too, her phrasing showing her emotions. A very fine performance indeed. Deloris faced tough opposition from the Mother Superior, played here by Hilary Phayer, as she tried to modernise the nun's repertoire. Ms Phayer sang 'Here Within These Walls' beautifully and with the ensemble joining in at the end - it sounded heavenly. On 'I Haven't Got A Prayer", her articulation was marvellous and she had a fabulous Julie Andrews quality to her voice. She played her as quite maternal and gracious with a sarcastic bent, which really worked for this production.

Deloris met loads of nuns in the convent but had a special chemistry with a young postulant, Sr Mary Robert, who grew up in Queen of Angels and had never been outside. Hannah Doogan played her with an endearing innocence and sang 'The Life I Never Had' with a lovely emotion. She had a fine voice which sounded wonderful throughout the show and possessed a great range. Danielle Farrell's Sr Mary Lazarus was very strong, with a deadpan delivery. She presented a no-nonsense character who eventually bowed to Deloris' musical talents. Kate McBrearty's rather annoyingly perky Sr Mary Patrick radiated enthusiasm for everything from fasting to funking-out in a wonderful uplifting performance. Áine Hogan's Sr Mary Martin de Tours, who was in her own world, was a great characterisation as was her performance of Tina, the sassy showgirl. Similarly, Kim Burke played two roles; Sr Mary Theresa, the old gritty nun and Michelle, Deloris's friend with well contrasting characterisations. All the nuns sang with great gusto and displayed wonderful harmonies and joy!

Barry Danaher as Eddie, the lovelorn wannabe hero, sang well on 'I Could Be That Guy' and displayed a very fine falsetto at one point, which I didn't expect. Jason Ronan, in a hideous shiny suit, played baddie Curtis. But I didn't get any real sense of unbridled menace from him. This Curtis was a small-time crook, rather than the entrepreneurial notorious gangster, who kills with impunity. He sang 'When I Find My Baby' and struggled with some of the notes, but delivered it quite well. His acolytes; TJ played by Adam Skeffington, Joey here played by Patrick Woulfe, Pablo played by James Malone and an additional character Tiny played by Glen Carr all had difficulty singing 'The Lady In The Long Black Dress', but their comic antics, especially Pablo's not quite 'Full Monty' were amusing.

Brian Henry's Monsignor O'Hara, who embraced change, was an interesting portrayal as he came across as quite low status until the money started rolling in. He had a good presence on stage and there was nice sub-text between him and Deloris. Martin Pierce's Ernie, the informer was also a good performance.

Choreographer Amanda Kearns best work on this show was during Eddie's song 'I Could Be That Guy'. Her choreography on this number with the 'homeless' dancers was excellent, they had lovely lines and were perfectly synchronised. The nun's dances were not as polished but still looked very good as there were so many of them! Her 'boyband' work with the four henchmen was very 'Westlife' and they did their routine quite well.

Musical Director, Elaine Davern's arrangement of the score was rather masterful. It's mostly a bouncing disco- infused series of numbers but Ms Davern managed to uncover many lovely melodies I'd not heard in the past. Her work on the ballads had a delicacy which really added nuance to the songs. The bigger numbers, whilst sometimes a little thin, were punchy and well-paced. Orla McEvoy along with Elaine Davern did an amazing job with the ensemble on this show. 'Gloria in Excelsis Deo' was excellent as was 'Raise Your Voice'. All of the nun's harmonies were highlighted well during each of the songs and they managed to get a real 'gospel' feel from the singers.

Set design was co-ordinated by Production Manager Jacinta Flourish and construction by Tom Lynch, stage manager was Ray Burke. Repurposing an old set from Chess, the pillars and archways looked really good in the Queen of Angels scenes. The two big trucks upstage centre were rotated and opened to reveal the Police Station, Club and Bar. The scene transitions were quite time- consuming due to the large set pieces being manipulated, but stage hands all wore priestly garb, so they actually looked like part of the play. Sound design was very well mixed by Declan O'Sullivan and full-range on this show. There was a good balance achieved between band and singers and it was just perfect for the room.

Costume was accredited to Jacinta Flourish, Mags Naughton, Rachel Le Gear and Rachel O'Brien. The nun's habits were great and in every number they became progressively more garish and showbizzy. Make-up on Deloris and her dancers was perfect for the club scene and although the nuns make up was subtle, it worked as we could see eyes and faces well and the wigs were fabulous!

Director Des Henn kept the pace rolling on the show, he pushed the comedy and his work with the ensemble and principals was quite original. The interpretation was fairly faithful and the humour was raucous and quite well-timed. The musical direction was really excellent and the cast were well-drilled and all this added up to a fun-filled, blessed event!

Based on the play by George Bernard Shaw, My Fair Lady with lyrics by Alan Jay Lerner and music by Frederick Loewe is the rags to riches story of Eliza Doolittle, flower girl, who is befriended by Professor Henry Higgins and as part of an experiment is given speech lessons so that she can pass as a lady. The original play Pygmalion created a way to understand the breakdown of the class system in Edwardian England.

The musical opened on Broadway in 1956 and has continued to be one of the world's most popular and best loved musicals ever since. The lavish movie starring Rex Harrison and Audrey Hepburn set a high standard for what we expect in the stage show. In particular the styling of the movie gives us expectations of the glamour we should expect on stage and of course those black and white Ascot costumes. Glencullen Dundrum Musical and Dramatic Society staged their version of the show in Dlr Mill Theatre in Dundrum. This is an interesting space set on different levels with a pleasant bar area and foyer. The front of house curtain was closed as we entered the auditorium and classical music was playing. Róisín Ryan had gathered six players to form the orchestra, and presented us with a well-rounded accompaniment throughout the show which actually sounded as if there were more pieces in the pit. The standard of singing was good with the chorus giving us some very well harmonised and enthusiastic singing.

The setting was in the form of various panels of material, books etc which did not altogether work for me as I found the concept a little confusing to the eye. There was quite a nice staircase which led onto the stage in the centre and the cast could enter the stage easily through the spaces between the side flats. Changes of scene were achieved by carrying on pieces of furniture such as a beautiful leather chair, satisfactory desk on a truck and trolley for the cups and glasses, though this would be something that might need to be given a little more thought in future productions. I did like however the setting for Mrs Higgins' garden which was created by the beautifully dressed maids bringing on some white fencing, plants and white wrought iron furniture which looked very in keeping with the period of the show. The scene changes did cause a little moment of hesitation to the pace of the production, though they were done as quickly as humanly possible by a well-trained and rehearsed stage team under the guidance of Stage Manager Tom Ronayne. I liked the lighting through the show, with some good use of colours and good 'specials' set to create intimate moments for the cast.

The director of the piece was Helen McCann who moved the large chorus and cast quite well, giving us some pleasant groupings. This is, by modern standards, a long show with a fair amount of dialogue, suffice to say that the pace of the dialogue was good and the show moved neatly along. Helen had gathered together a very strong cast and had built good relationships between the cast on stage. The friendship between Higgins and Pickering was natural and the love/ hate relationship between Eliza and Higgins worked really well.

There were some exciting and fun dance routines in the show involving a large and enthusiastic chorus. Some of the highlights for me were 'I'm Getting Married in the Morning' and 'Wouldn't It Be Loverly'. Well done choreographer Laura Macken who had obviously worked hard to put the cast through their paces. There were some nice patterns and pictures created with the dance in the show.

Kate Canning give us a forceful performance as Eliza. She looked good in her various costumes, though I didn't particularly like her first ripped costume. She transformed so well into the posh Elisa with a crystal-clear accent. The tone of her singing voice was delightful but particularly in the second half of her role. Brendan O'Sullivan looked and acted the part of Henry Higgins extremely well. This is a very demanding role and Brendan appeared to make the lines sound very natural as if he was saying them for the very first time. It was a convincing and strong performance of a difficult role.
