Brian Carroll gave us a different slant on Colonel Pickering, a slightly more nervous and fumbling character, which at times worked well. I did miss however the military bearing of an old colonel. In this production Niall McCarthy was a tall and handsome Freddie Eynsford Hill. He looked well with Kate and sang very well. This was a slightly more mature and less wide-eyed version of Freddie.

Louise Culleton was Mrs Pearce with a clipped walk and manner, but also showing that she had a warm heart. She and her team of maids looked smart and gave a beautiful rendition of 'I Could Have Danced All Night'. The Cockney charmer himself, Alfred P Doolittle was played by Barry Donaldson. Barry gave us a robust and warm-hearted Doolittle. I would encourage Barry to watch closing his eyes to the audience which can cut us out of his emotions. Shona Ashmore transformed into Mrs Higgins. This was a standout performance for me. Shona created so much class and dignity in the role with a wonderful cut-glass accent and fantastic body language very much in keeping with the show and the era of the show. Mark O'Leary gave us a strong cameo performance as Zoltan Karpathy. He looked the part and also sounded good too. There were other members of the cast with some lines to say who delivered them very well such as Imelda O'Sullivan as Mrs Eynsford-Hill who created quite an interesting little character. Michelle Kennedy as Lady Boxington, Fiona Doyle as a hilarious Mrs Hopkins. Sherry Perreault as Queen of Transylvania, Liam Ryan as Charles, Padraic Brady as Jamie, Daragh O'Duffy as the Barman, Garreth Grimes as the policeman, Darren Molloy as Harry and Tony Matthews as a footman. Of course, the chorus were one of the greatest attributes in the show and they all delivered so well and so energetically to the overall success of the production. Some of the costumes were wonderful. We had the traditional black and white costumes for Ascot and the men in grey tails which looked very smart, particularly when we added nice sharp white parasols used to form part of the routine which was very effective. Some of the other costumes were good too, such as Mrs Higgins dresses and indeed all the professor's costumes. As I said before I didn't particularly like Eliza's ripped skirt and I would have liked to have seen her in another outfit whenever she came to visit Higgins initially, (she probably would have been wearing what she considered her Sunday Best). The ballroom dresses added colour to the scene and there was the nice addition of sparkling jewels to finish off the look. I would have liked the butler to have been in the correct costume as I think this was done by Mrs Higgins Chauffeur.

One thing to keep an eye on in the future would be the balance of stage makeup. It's very important if people are doing their own make-up that there is a formula so that they all appear similar. The street folk needed to be slightly dirtier or maybe just a few marks on their faces just to give the impression of a difference between the two classes.

The furniture as I have said by and large looked good on stage and the smaller personal props such as the decanter and glasses were appropriate. I particularly liked the scene in Mrs Higgins' house where we had a pretty tea set and white wrought iron furniture. It would have been nice to see more bits and pieces around Higgins study to create the feel of a man obsessed with the sound of the human voice, maybe posters of vowels, more recording machines, metronome etc. Overall this was a good evening, thoroughly enjoyed by the audience around me who were very vocal, particularly when a lady behind me turned to her friend and said, 'Come on Eliza we know you can do it!' when she was about to utter her 'Rain in Spain'. There were some lovely performances but a little bit of pity that wasn't more detail with the setting which might need more thought in subsequent productions.

Karaoke Grease Dunboyne Musical Society produced Jim Jacobs and Warren Casey's classic homage to Americana, Grease, at Dunboyne Community Centre in April, directed by Colin Flynn with musical direction by Paul Strachan and choreography by Aisling Rountree. It was an odd little show, that didn't really work despite the very good performances of the cast as it was let down by poor production values and synthetic backing tracks.

It didn't open with the Rydell Reunion or with 'Rydell Alma Matter', even though this was written in the programme under 'Synopsis of Scenes' and 'Musical Numbers' and it must have been confusing for the audience as it looked like they skipped a scene, which indeed they did. The Reunion scene serves to contextualise the musical on stage, however in the 1978 film they dispensed with this conceit, instead opening with the beach scene between Danny and Sandy. Which is sort of what Dunboyne did as it all started off with Danny Zucko, nicely played by Conor McQuaid, sitting on the stage singing 'Sandy'. Sandy, delicately played by Jane Brogan, eventually entered and joined in on the song. It was pleasant and a bit different but didn't really work as the lyrics of the song relate to her running away from him at the drive-in and it's not a duet as she wouldn't sing this song about herself and it was not well-staged enough to convince. From then on it ran quite conventionally, with a lovely energy from the principals and ensemble but was frequently let down by the clunkiness of the technical and production elements. In Rydell High School we met two groups of students, both in gangs; the male 'T-Birds' and the female 'Pink Ladies'. Danny was the leader of the T-Birds and Betty Rizzo the leader of the 'Pink Ladies'. The story is that, new student, Sandy turns up at the school and is surprised to see Danny, who she had a Summer fling with at the beach. He considers himself too cool for school or romance and brushes her off in front of his friends, while secretly adoring her. She joins the 'Pink Ladies', discovers her sexuality and they all live happily ever after.

The T-Birds were led by Danny who was engagingly played by Conor McQuaid.His singing was really good on all his songs but particularly 'Sandy', which he reprised as a solo in Act Two, 'Summer Nights' the first big number and 'You're the One That I Want' at the end of the show. His characterisation of Danny was thoughtful, he didn't play him as stupid as some do, but actually as quite sensitive throughout, seemingly uncomfortable with the bravado the T-Birds expected of him. An amiable performance and his dance skills were quite good. As Kenickie, the more-wild T-Bird and second in command, Shane Fox played him as quite moronic, which was quite funny. He sang well on 'Greased Lightin'' and his on/off relationship with Rizzo was quite nicely progressed throughout the show. Ben Hannigan played Doody, a rather girl-shy T-Bird who fancies himself as a Rock 'n' Roll star. He also fancied Frenchie, a Pink Lady, but was too bashful to tell her. He performed two numbers, the first 'Those Magic Changes' with the ensemble and 'Rock 'n' Roll Party Queen' with Roger. These were very well performed, particularly the second number as he seemed to be playing the guitar live with no track backing them. Eoin O'Reilly played Roger, who had a tendency to 'moon' and performed well on the duet with Mr Hannigan. He also sang 'Mooning' with Jan, who he ended up with romantically. As Sonny, the self- styled ladies-man of the T-Birds, Eoin Kenny was quite good. He sang well on the ensemble numbers and had a wacky energy.

The 'Pink Ladies' were helmed by Betty Rizzo, played by Grace McEntee. She showed Rizzo's high status very well and her singing was excellent on 'There are Worse Things I Could Do' where she defended her lifestyle and quite funny on 'Look at me I'm Sandra Dee'. New girl, Sandy Dumbrowski was played by Jane Brogan as a 'girl next door' type, who has landed in a hormone-infused land of alcohol, cigarettes and sex. In love with Danny but unsure how to snag him, Ms Brogan played her as quite demure. Her singing on 'Summer Nights' and 'You're the One that I Want' was great and on the ballads; 'Hopelessly Devoted to You' and the split-stage duet with Jan 'It's Raining on Prom Night' were warm and gentle. Jan, the voracious one, was played by Aine Fox with great comic timing and really shone on stage. She sang 'It's Raining on Prom Night' very well during the dance scene and her relationship with Roger was quite sweet. Marty, who was having a fling with a Marine overseas, was nicely played by Kiera Judge. Her singing on 'Freddy, My Love' was really good and she portrayed the character's maturity and experience with relish. As Frenchie, Ailbhe Clancy almost stole the show. Her accent and comic timing were superb. Her partial duet with Teen Angel was really funny and she sang it with fervour.

As Teen Angel, Frenchie's guardian angel, Caolan Reilly really impressed with his singing on 'Beauty School Dropout' and its comic reprise. Wearing big white wings, which he frequently hit Frenchie with, this was a stand-out scene in the show. The two more conventional Rydell students highlighted in the show were; Patty, a high achieving cheerleader who befriends Sandy, yet has designs on Danny was played with conviction by Chloe Kinch and her focus was great, and Eugene, the blundering nerd was played well by Colm Woods who showed just the right amount of social awkwardness to be convincing. The choreography, by Aisling Rountree, in the show was good and quite well- rehearsed.

'We Go Together' was particularly good as was the athletic 'Greased Lightin'. 'The Rydell Fight Song' cleverly added a small marching band into the choreography which looked great. Danny and Cha Cha's dance was excellent, and I really liked the girl's choreography on 'Freddy My Love' as they performed a mock wedding.

Musical Direction by Paul Strachan was good in terms of the choral and individual voices with some nice big choruses on the bigger numbers. Not so much harmony on these songs that I could discern but they were vigorous and energetic and the a cappella sections of 'We Go Together' were tight. The backing tracks were not so good, sounding a bit synthetic at times. Set design was unaccredited, and I believe the Society rented some of the set from Banbridge Musical Society, the upstage platform looked good and was utilised well for the High School Hop, but the car looked a bit modern.

C a l e n d a r Michael Collins - A Musical Drama Bravo Theatre Group 24/09/2019 to 28/09/2019 July 2019 West Side Story Sheevawn M. Youth Theatre Mermaid Arts Centre, Bray 25/07/2019 to 28/07/2019 October 2019 Chitty Chitty Bang Bang Dundalk Musical Society An Tain Arts Centre 08/10/2019 to 13/10/2019 September 2019 Chitty Chitty Bang Bang Fusion Theatre Group Island Hall, Lisburn 04/09/2019 to 07/09/2019 Lighting design by Shane Byrne was passable, but the follow spot was very haphazard, not picking up the right performer, lighting the pros, changing colour mid-song etc., and the cuing was also a bit hit and miss, lights coming up to full whilst the assistant stage managers were still on stage moving set and the general cover was uneven. Sound design was unaccredited in the programme but was good. The vocals were nice and sharp the playback of the tracks seemed well-cued. Costume design by Rita Tighe, Brendan Brady and Sparkle Costumes were perfect for the era and I liked Teen Angel, costume and wings and his backing dancer's silver costumes were nice. Make-up and hair design were also unaccredited but looked good. I liked Frenchie's wigs and Teen Angel's styling. Stage management by Aoife O'Rourke seemed a bit under-rehearsed, there were long delays during transitions and some props were not set correctly.

Generally, it was a clunky version of the musical saved by a talented cast. Their energy and commitment to the show was to be applauded. Director, Colin Flynn paced the scenes well, but the transitions kept slowing it down. The staging of the performers was quite good, and the interpretation of the source material was, whilst uninventive apart from the ill- advised opening, quite competent.

Good production values and performances save this rather contrived show, helmed by Stephen Acton with choreography by Martina Lynch and musical direction by Naoimh Penston and vocal direction by Amy Penston for Avonmore Musical Society, about office politics in the late 1970s. Although written only eleven years ago, 9 to 5 The Musical already feels incredibly dated. The central message that kidnapping and physical violence is a suitable riposte for inequality is a bit dubious, but none-the-less, the message was delivered with confidence by a cracking cast and some lovely voices. 9 to 5  The Musical is based on the 1980 popular film. It's a story of friendship and revenge and the old boy's network that ensured women didn't advance beyond the typing pool. Pushed to boiling point by his discrimination, three female co- workers concoct a plan to get even with the sexist, misogynist manager. There's a big drug-induced fantasy sequence in the middle of the show where the heroines Violet, Judy, and Doralee live out their wildest dreams: killing their boss. Whilst they don't quite kill him, they do kidnap him and incarcerate him and take control of the company much to the delight of their co-workers.

Office supervisor, Violet Newstead, was solidly played by Jennifer Lee who sang well on 'One of The Boys' and on her fantasy sequence section 'Potion Notion'. Ms Lee's character had a convincing relationship with her onstage son Josh, played by Pádraig O'Leary and her love interest Joe, played here by John Hughes. But it was the camaraderie with her two co-workers Doralee and Judy, where she really shone.

Doralee (written as a thinly disguised version of Ms Parton) was played by Eimear Harper as more of a Marilyn Monroe figure rather than a Dolly clone, which was refreshing. Although adopting a country and western twang, Ms Harper skilfully managed to steer away from the Dolly comparison through her considered and intelligent performance. She sang with passion on 'Backwoods Barbie' and 'Cowgirl's Revenge' and 'Shine Like the Sun' with her co-workers, and her scenes with husband Dwayne, strongly played by Brian Harty were natural and believable. As Judy Bernly, the third woman pushed into action against the boss, Denise Brennan played her as a ditzy helpless divorcée going through a mid-life crisis, and learning how to cope with Dick (her husband). Her arrival at the firm completed the trio and she worked very well with Violet and Doralee. Her singing on 'Get Out and Stay Out' was powerful and she performed 'The Dance of Death' and 'Shine Like the Sun' very competently. All three performers acquitted themselves admirably and were quite believable in their respective roles.

The baddie of the piece was Franklin Hart Jnr, the misogynist boss played with gusto by Gary Finnegan. His vocal on 'Here for You', a perverse 'lustsong', which he sang to Doralee was a bit strained but he carried it off by acting it quite well, eliciting boos and laughter in equal measure from the audience. This production didn't follow the action to the bedroom of his house where he is held captive for most of the second act, so at least we were spared the sight of him being trussed up in S&M gear, which is a rather distasteful section of this show. Mr Finnegan was rather good as Hart and had great comic timing in the role. His scenes with another office worker, Roz, who inexplicably loves him were really well staged and hilarious. As Roz, Elaine Sweeney stole the show for me. She had fabulous comic timing and a great voice. Her love song to Hart, 'Hart to Hart' was brilliantly performed, full of yearning and sensuality, and Hart even made a cameo appearance in it! Ms Sweeney had a fabulous voice and her performance brought the house down. Other performers that impressed were: Genevieve Molloy as Kathy another office worker who was quite straight- laced; Joanne Logue as Margaret, the office lush, really well-performed by Ms Logue; Maria the Spanish co-worker also well performed by Tara Boukhima; John Hughes as Joe, Violet's love interest, who sang very nicely on 'Let Love Grow' with Violet; Dick, Judy's ex-husband played well by Gary Joyce and Rob Donnelly was very strong as Mr Tinsworthy.

Naoimh Penston was musical director on the show and she and her choral director Amy Penston got some lovely harmonious work from the ensemble. Their voices soared offstage on 'I Just Might', which had lovely flute and guitar, and the slide guitar led 'Backwoods Barbie' and onstage on 'Shine Like the Sun' and 'Joy to the Girls'. Ms Penston's arrangements of the score and underscore were superb. Choreography by Martina Lynch was good all round but specifically on 'One of the Boys' and the whole fantasy section. Her routines with the office workers was great on 'Around Here' and 'Fix It'.

Stage design by Stephen Acton was clever. Office paraphernalia was affixed to the upstage all and pros with a projection of a clock also on the upstage wall. Two staircases dressed as piles of cardboard boxes led to a platform upstage which allowed for different playing levels. Office furniture on castors and Harts office on trucks created locations. It was a great set and was used well by the performers. Lighting design by Pádraig Reid was interesting as he used very old Rank Strand lights mixed in with more modern instruments. This gave a nice warmth to the show and worked well. Sound by All Around Sound was super, nice lively vocals with a good band mix. Costumes by Utopia and Wexford Light Opera Society co-ordinated by Els Penston and Elaine Sweeney worked well for the era of the show, Violet's white garb was great on 'One of the Boys' and I liked the whole clandestine look for the trio when they went to the hospital. The costumes in the fantasy scene worked too. Hair and make-up were designed by Sharon Kavanagh and suited the show, the wigs were great. Stage management by Barry Ryan and his crew was excellent, lovely smooth transitions from scene to scene and quick too.

A good production by director Stephen Acton, very well staged and produced. Mr Acton generated a lively pace for the show and the cast were energetic and engaging. The staging and set design were good and I think the society gave a good interpretation of the source material and delivered Ms Parton's message loud and clear.

Girl Crazy A banker, Bobby Child, with show business aspirations is sent to impound a property in Deadrock, a small town in the Nevada desert, by his over-bearing mother, Lottie, who is also his boss. She wants to get him out of New York, so he can focus on his job and not the Zangler Follies where he really wants to work as a song-and-dance-man. However, the property turns out to be the derelict Gaiety Theatre. After falling in love with the local postmistress, Polly Baker a sweet but rugged country lass whose father owns the theatre, he decides to put on a show to save the venue. This is a synthetic musical featuring classic Gershwin songs and a Ken Ludwig libretto inspired by the 1930 musical Girl Crazy and St Mary's Musical Society successfully staged it in Solstice Arts Centre in April of this year. The book is quite well-written but the songs, only five of the original Girl Crazy songs remain - the rest are taken liberally from the Gershwin canon, are shoehorned in and at times just don't make sense in the context of the plot. That said, the choreography by Sinéad Lightley and musical direction by Sarah Lynch Barrett were first-class and Ray O'Hare's astute direction made for an entertaining night out and a homage to the classic optimistic musicals of the 1930's. Bobby Child was played by Craig Regan and he really convinced as the city boy who turns rural. His acting harked back to the classical style of early Hollywood and he had a fine voice and great dance skills. His dancing on "I Can't Be Bothered Now" where he used the whole stage, including on top of a car, was excellent. His duet with Polly, 'Could You Use Me' was sweet as was 'Shall We Dance' but it was the extended scene with Zangler 'What Causes That?', where Bobby is dressed as Zangler and they mirror each other's actions, that really showcased his talents as it was a perfect little piece of comedy gold.

Bobby, who was initially promised to socialite Irene Roth, becomes infatuated with Polly Baker, local postmistress in Deadrock. Meaghan Ebbs played her as a spunky no-nonsense country lass, fiercely protective of her father, Everett as she fended off the amorous advances of local saloon owner, the lascivious Lank Hawkins. Ms Ebbs gave a great performance, her acting, like Mr Regan's, was quite classical and her song and dance was quite accomplished. On 'Someone Who'll Watch Over Me', she expressed her desire to be looked after for a change, finishing the song on top of her post office. This was a lovely gentle scene and she revealed a sensual side to the character when she sang 'Embraceable You' with Bobby (dressed as Zangler). Her dances with Bobby were also quite good, especially 'Shall We Dance?'. This was a fine considered performance from Ms Ebbs, who managed to make her quite stereotyped character into one with charm and gusto.

As Polly's father, Everett, Des Lynch portrayed him as a strong-willed man reluctant to sell the theatre to local entrepreneur Lank, where his late wife, Polly's mother, was the star of the many shows staged when the mining town was wealthy. His characterisation was one of a man hankering for past times, not fully in the present, but Bobby's ideas ignited a spark and he played Everett's journey very well. His relationship with Polly was very believable, and they had a lovely dynamic. Bobby's mother, Lottie, a wealthy banker, was very well-played by Caithriona Madden. She exuded class and frustration with Bobby's lack of real ambition with surety. She also had very good chemistry with Everett in their brief scenes together.

Every story needs an antagonist and here we are given, Lank Hawkins, local saloon owner with ambitions to take over the town completely. He was gleefully played by Barry Murray as a covetous, predatory gun-slinging creep. Mr Murray, challenged by Bobby for Polly's affections and by his big-city ways, played him very well. His sadistic and masochistic nature was however tamed by Irene, Bobby's ex-fiancé when she arrived. Their scenes were very funny and the scene where Katie Crosby as Irene sang 'Naughty Baby' with Lank on his knees was uncomfortably pleasurable, eliciting applause from the audience. Ms Crosby played Irene's shift from poor little rich girl to dominatrix very well.

As the Hungarian Bela Zangler, Ronan Walsh was superb. His vaudeville 'mirror' scene with Bobby as mentioned above was exquisite and he was quite funny as he chased after his Dance Director, Tess, whom he was in love with. Mr Walsh captured the spirit of the 1930's impresario to a tee. In his early scenes in New York, where Bobby tries to audition for him, he expressed delicious exasperation and haughty high status. Tess was played by Sarah Uí Cinnéide. Her dance was superb and she really commanded the stage with her focus. Her portrayal of Tess had great attitude yet was warm. Her fellow Zangler Folly, Patsy was played by Maeve Forry. Ms Forry really impressed with her comic timing, dance and stagecraft. There are two sorts of cameo roles in the show; a pair of English tourists who are writing a guide book.  Eugene Fodor and his sister Patricia were brilliantly played by Patrick Fox and Mary Murphy. Their accents were suitably received pronunciation, and their comic timing and singing on 'Stiff Upper Lip' was excellent. Sadly, not everyone got the 'Fodor' gag as the guide book seems to have now fallen out of fashion in this Tripadvisor age.

Choreography was well directed by Sinéad Lightley. Some of the Follies routines were outstanding and I really liked the tap routines on 'I Can't Be Bothered Now', 'I Got Rhythm' was a great closer of the first act and 'Slap The Bass' was a triumph. Overall, a very well-choreographed show. Musical direction by Sarah Lynch-Barrett was also top notch. Her arrangements of the classic Gershwin tunes were excellent. We got that big Broadway sound from the thirteen-piece orchestra, where the brass was dazzled and I really liked the ragtime piano and violin on 'The Real American Folk Song' and the accordion on some of the numbers was a touch of authenticity. Ensemble vocals were really harmonious on 'Bidin' My Time' and 'Tonight's the Night' with lovely work on show for 'Finale'.

Set design was unaccredited in the programme but looked sumptuous, with a wooden clad pros and trucks onstage representing the Zangler Theatre, the streets of Deadrock, the interior of the Gaiety Theatre, the saloon and a lovely art deco dressed finale. Props by Jenny D'Arcy were of the era and plentiful, hair by Leah Fitzsimons and wigs by Ali Murphy and SMMS Wigs were super and make- up by Aishling Quinn was particularly good on Zangler and Bobby. Costumes were looked after by Miriam Donnelly and Rita Monaghan and were great especially on the Zangler Follies and the cowboys. Lighting design by Derek O'Neill was super and he got a nice separation between the fantasy dance numbers and the realism of the action, follow spot use was also very accurate. Sound by Alan White was pin-sharp, with good full frequencies from the band and nice clarity in the vocals. All stage managed with efficiency by Tracy Fitzsimons, her assistant Chris Murphy and their skilful crew.

Whilst the show made little sense, particularly the writer's choice of songs to include, it was very charming, entertaining and well put together with tight direction by Mr O'Hare. Excellent pacing and clever staging, gave us a truly buoyant homage to the classic pre-war happy musicals of George and Ira Gershwin.

From Vulgaria With Love A rousing production of Ian Fleming's Chitty Chitty Bang Bang by Wexford Light Opera, with terrific musical direction by Fintan Cleary, wondrous choral direction by Eithne Corrigan, creative choreography by Nicole McDonald and efficient direction by Thomas O'Leary.

Written longhand by James Bond author, Ian Fleming for his then twelve-year old son, The Magic Car, was a sort of James Bond for kids. Sadly, Fleming died before the stories were published as Chitty Chitty Bang Bang, named after a series of real cars, invented by Louis Zborowski in the 1920s, which is when the musical is set. Apparently, Roald Dahl who co-wrote the screenplay for the 1968 film, invented the character of the Child Catcher and the country Vulgaria, where the second act takes place - they were not in the original stories. The plot reads like a pantomime version of a James Bond story!

Widower, Caractacus Potts, an inventor, and his two children Jeremy and Jemima join up with Sweet Factory heiress Truly Scrumptious aboard Chitty Chitty Bang Bang, a resourcefully sentient car, to rescue Grandpa Potts from the nasty Baron Bomburst, who rules Vulgaria with his wife who hates children.

Caractacus Potts, a self-styled inventor, was played by Pete McCamley as an amiable character who clearly missed his late wife but was doing his best for his children. However, it was clearly not good enough as his inventions always malfunctioned, and the children played truant with his knowledge. Mr McCamley gave a good performance and was quite believable in the role, his onstage relationship with Jeremy and Jemima was quite credible and natural. His singing, however, was a bit laboured and he seemed to struggle with some of the songs. 'You Two', his first song was a little underpowered, and on 'Toot Sweets', we could hardly hear his contribution but on 'Hushabye Mountain', he paced the song well and sang it with a nice warmth and sentiment. His Caractacus was a nice genial character and his relationship with Truly was quite finely drawn.

As Truly Scrumptious, who happens along on a motorbike and accidentally invades the Potts family, Aileen Donohoe's Truly was like a character out of a Famous Five novel, she was feisty, courageous and yet quite maternal to Potts' children. Her performance of 'Lovely Lonely Man' demonstrated a fabulous voice and was a showstopper. 'Truly Scrumptious' with Jeremy and Jemima was absolutely charming and Ms Donohoe's voice blended beautifully with the children's singing. Her diction and enunciation were splendid as was her accent. A truly wonderful interpretation which made the character very engaging.

Jeremy and Jemima were played by Hugh O'Brien and Grace Goggins. They both captured the essence of these pre-war children. Their opening scene in the old Chitty was excellent and they established an endearing relationship with Caractacus and Grandpa. Their singing was harmonious and very confident on all of their songs, particularly 'You Two' with Caractacus and 'Posh' with Grandpa. As Grandpa, Pat Lawlor commanded the stage. He showed the character's warmth with Caractacus and the children and his sense of humour with the Baron. His song 'Posh' with Jeremy and Jemima was perfectly presented, strident yet humorous. On 'The Roses of Success' with the Inventors, who were hilarious, his slapstick was excellent as was his singing. A fine, funny and at times, subtle, performance.

Des Whelan played two characters in this show; Lord Scrumptious and Baron Bomburst. As Lord Scrumptious, Truly's father and owner of Toot Sweets a sweet factory, he was dismissive of Potts and quite sarcastic but showed a boyish delight when Caractacus's invention (a whistling sweet) sang. As the Baron, he played him as a spoilt child, demanding toys and parties. Mr Whelan had a very strong stage presence and sang well on 'Chu-Chi Face' with his Baroness, played with child-hating hysteria by Elisabeth Rose Browne. Ms Brown played the Baroness as the polar opposite of the Baron. She was quick tempered, flirtatious and smart. She had a fine voice on 'Chu- Chi Face' and was quite good on 'The Bombie Samba' where she also danced quite well. Ms Browne also played Lord Scrumptious' secretary, Mrs Higgins, with a fine officious and snooty demeanour. The Baron's henchmen, who were charged with kidnapping Caractacus so he could build a fancy car for the Baron, were so incompetent that they snatched Grandpa instead.

Played with an unmitigated glee; Gearóid McCauley as Boris and George Lawlor as Goran made a fine comedy duo and were very funny. Disguising themselves to pass as proper Englishmen they sang 'Act English' with great comic timing and verve. Popping up throughout the show in various disguises the two actors clearly had a lot of fun with their roles, which was infectious for the audience.

On arriving in Vulgaria, Grandpa's rescuers met The Toymaker, a maker of toys (!), but not for kids, as children were banned in this country, but for the Baron. Played with a geniality by Brian O'Gorman, who portrayed the character as the most-sane person in Vulgaria. Secreting the Vulgarian children underground in the sewers, he fed and looked after them. Mr O'Gorman's Toymaker had a genuine kindness and also sang quite well on 'Teamwork'. He also played Mr Goggins, the garage owner where Chitty was stored. Again, a good characterisation of the benevolent mechanic.

The Baroness employed a scarecrow- like character, the Child Catcher, to round up and imprison all of the children in this horrid land. This character was a black-clad, hook-nosed, spider-like man who engendered fear into everybody in Vulgaria. Played by John Crosbie, who stalked about the stage like a preternatural demon, this was a very fine performance. Mr Crosbie intimidated the Toymaker and tricked Jeremy and Jemima by offering free sweets. He also played the Junkman early on in the show, who offered thirty shillings to Goggins for the wrecked Chitty car. As the Junkman, he was equally as convincing, unsettling Jeremy and Jemima as he shouted at them. A strong performance from Mr Crosbie.

The ensemble played many different roles, all with a lovely energy. They also demonstrated wonderful stagecraft, the Turkey Farmer's spirit-gummed beard came loose as he mentioned that he was going to make a fortune from Caractacus' hair cutting machine and quickly declared that he was going to buy a new beard with some of the money he'd make! Choreography was looked after by Nicole McDonald and she created some lovely moments on stage. 'Toot Sweets' was nicely moved with a huge dance ensemble as was 'The Bombie Samba' and the opening, with some of the ensemble moving in harmony behind a gauze that looked splendid. 'Me Ol' Bamboo' was a spectacular feast for the eyes and even had a bit of Morris dancing. Aileen Donohoe's robotic doll-like moves in 'Doll on A Music Box' were brilliantly choreographed too.

The music in Chitty Chitty Bang Bang is quite infectious, with ear-worming tunes and some great orchestrations. Fintan Cleary's arrangements of the score were quite uplifting, evocative of the famous English composers of old. Big brass and percussion sound with warm woodwind and keyboard fills, the twelve-piece orchestra resonated around the perfect acoustic of the Opera House. Chorus mistress/répétiteur, Eithne Corrigan's work with the ensemble and off-stage chorus was stunning.

Ms Corrigan managed to elicit harmonies on some of the songs I didn't realise were there! The performances of title song, 'Chitty Chitty Bang Bang' became bigger and more harmonious on each reprise. The children's chorus on 'Teamwork' was fabulous and even the comic ditty 'The Rose of Success' was superbly drilled. 'The Vulgarian National Anthem' sounded authentic, like a Roger Wagner Chorale. Outstanding work from Ms Corrigan and Mr Cleary.

Set design by Ben Hennessy was quite elaborate and very well finished and dressed. The Pott's house in particular was very well rendered. Lighting by Aidan McGrath was well-designed and cued and sound by Jason Fallon was excellent with some nice high-quality sound effects. Costumes were co-ordinated by Anne Reck and were suitable for the show as was make-up by Elle Doyle, which looked great on the Child Catcher especially. Stage manager Colin Murphy controlled everything with finesse and the transitions were good.

Wexford Light Opera's Chitty Chitty Bang Bang was a show full of fun and the audience loved it. The car, hired from Blue Chill in the U.K. was perfect and drove, floated and flew with impeccable mechanical elegance. Thomas O'Leary's direction was good, with some nice little touches and there were some dazzling performances from the principals and ensemble. A very good production of a feel-good show.

Leixlip Laid Bare The Full Monty, a musical about a group of unemployed average men who decide to put on a one-night-only strip show to make big money, was staged by Leixlip Musical and Variety Group at St Mary's GAA Club in April. Directed and choreographed by Claire Tighe with Musical Direction by David Hayes, the show is based on the 1997 British movie of the same title. The stage show relocated the story to America and focused on relationships, friendship, sexuality, marriage and how unemployment can have an emasculating effect on the male psyche.

Jerry Lukowski, the fast-talking ringleader of the men was played by Ian Tighe with a frenetic energy. He sang well on the opening number 'Scrap', with some of the other men and on 'Man' with his best friend Dave, played by Kevin Sherwin. His performance of the moving 'Breeze Off the River', one of the better songs in the show, was very good and captured a father's love for his son. His relationship with his son Nathan, played very naturally by Max Rochford, was good and they played the almost role reversal well as Nathan was clearly better adjusted to deal with life. Mr Tighe played Jerry as a likeable character, although immature and self-serving, and his relationship with his ex-wife Pam, played by Jennifer Dawson, was quite believable.

Jennifer Dawson, the show's assistant choreographer, stepped in at the last moment due to the original performer suffering a bereavement to play Pam. She played her as a woman who just wants what's best for her son, and knows that Jerry is not a great role model. Ms Dawson showed the character's frustration well and also her compassion towards Jerry and gave a very strong performance. Jerry's self-conscious best friend, Dave was played by Kevin Sherwin. He sang well on 'Scrap' and 'Big-Ass Rock'. Mr Sherwin gave a deeply considered performance, more cerebral and proud than Jerry but plagued with self-doubt. He brought the house down when he sang on 'You Rule My World' a love song about his stomach. His wife, Georgie, was played by Orla Jennings. Ms Jennings played her as loud and audacious and was quite funny. Her singing on 'It's a Woman's World' was powerful and the reprise of 'You Rule My World' was touching and sweet.

Another member of the 'Hot Metal' troupe of wannabe Chippendales was Harold, the former boss of Jerry and the men, now unemployed too. Ross Murray gave a fine performance as the stiff ballroom dancer, who was hiding his redundancy from his wife, Vicki. He performed a split-stage duet with Dave on 'You Rule My World' and was equally as poignant. Harold's wife, Vicki was played by Jacqueline Brunton, who had great comic timing and expression and sang very well on 'Life with Harold' and the reprise of 'You Rule my World' with Georgie. Ms Brunton had great articulation, a perfect accent and was very impressive.

As Malcolm, the shy, bespectacled friend who joins the new team, Jamie Hennessey was perfectly cast. His characterisation showed awkwardness and unsureness, and Mr Hennessey played him perfectly. His duet with Ethan 'You Walk with Me' was delightful and quite mushy, in a good way and on 'Big-Ass Rock' with Jerry and Dave when they rescue him from his suicide attempt he really showed the vulnerability of the character. As Ethan, who falls in love with Malcolm, Ciaran Tighe gave a lovely naturalistic performance as a character with a quiet determination to change his life. His singing on 'You Walk with Me', with Malcolm after his mother's funeral was tender and heartfelt. Reg, another 'Hot Metal' head, was played by Justin Parkes in a very funny performance, his first attempt at stripping was so funny, even some of the cast broke character and laughed. Horse was played by Mark Asante, reprising the role from previous productions elsewhere, and he was just great. His patter was very funny and his moves had a natural grace. His song 'Big Black Man' was a stand-out moment in the show.

The piano player, Jeanette, who just showed up at rehearsals was brilliantly played by Jenny McCabe. Her comic timing was superb and her characterisation was faultless, her delivery was quick, witty and perfectly enunciated. She opened the second act with 'Jeanette's Showbiz Number', which had a sort of Elaine Stritch meets Joan Rivers vibe and ended up on top of the piano surrounded by the guys. Perfection.

Choreography on this show is quite important as you can imagine and Claire Tighe and her assistant Jennifer Dawson created some very simple yet effective routines. As the characters were not supposed to be professional dancers, their routines were quite basic, but their attitudes sold the dances. A nice routine at the start of the show on the upstage platform was well moved and on 'It's a Woman's World' the addition of the male dancers really added to the intent of the song. The ballroom dance scene featuring Vicki and Malcolm was well choreographed and funny.

Musical Director David Hayes produced some great arrangements of the score and there was great synergy between keys, brass and reeds. The drums and percussion were very prominent on many of the up tempo numbers particularly the Girl's Night out opening and the disco inspired 'Michael Jordan's Ball'. Vocals were quite good all around, with some nice choral work on some numbers, especially 'It's a Woman's World' and 'Let It Go' and the funny 'The Goods' was great.

Set design by Claire Tighe, Aidan Mannion and Eileen Fagan was clever; a series of rolling flats went from stage left to right, creating various backdrops, a platform upstage allowed for different levels and the overall style was like a musical instrument flight case. Lighting design by Darren Kelleher was good, nice use of colour and movers with festoons built into the set. He used the audience blinders well at the end of the show, so even if 'Hot Metal' did indeed go 'Full Monty', the audience were spared the sight as they were blinded by the light! Sound by Jason Fallon was big, beefy and bassy as it should have been. Vocals were sharp and there was a good mix out front. Costuming by Rita Tighe, Bern Dawson, Judy Miller and Kevin Hynes was of the era and class of the characters. The 'Hot Metal' costumes were great, uniforms, hats and red posing pouches! Hair and Make-up by Bern Dawson was suitable for the show as was the good array of props by Louise Kenny and Seamus Kenny. Stage Manager, Mary Purcell kept a tight rein on everything and transitions were quick and precise.

The audience were made to feel part of the story on the show and certainly showed their appreciation in their reactions. During the final section 'Let it Go', female cast members infiltrated the audience and encouraged them to whoop and holler at the males on stage, I suspect a lot of this was improvised and rightly so. It was a tight production with good pace and good staging. Director, Claire Tighe managed to highlight the social issues of the so-called 'rust belt', where unemployment became rife as industry dried up and corporations moved to Mexico and the Far East because of the cheaper labour leaving behind a generation of disenfranchised workers. A thought provoking yet highly entertaining production from Leixlip.

Shakespeare Shook Up Sticking with the rock 'n' roll theme after last year's highly successful production of Grease, this year's presentation All Shook Up was produced by St Mary's Choral Society at the White Memorial Theatre in Clonmel was directed by Des Henn with musical direction by Laura Cotter, choral work by Mary Rose McNally and choreography by Barbara Meany.

All Shook Up, is a jukebox musical, written by Joe DiPietro, which opened on Broadway in 2005. The plot is a mash- up of; Footloose, Shakespeare's Twelfth Night and A Midsummer Night's Dream, Edmond Rostand's Cyrano de Bergerac and Benedek's outlaw biker film The Wild One, starring a leather jacketed Marlon Brando; all to a soundtrack of songs made popular by Elvis Presley. It tells the story of a small-town girl, Natalie, who dreams of hitting the open road, and the guitar-playing roustabout, Chad, who brings romance, rebellion and rock 'n' roll not only in to her life, but into the lives of everybody in the puritanical town.

We first met Chad, the cool but intellectually challenged hero of the show, as he was released from jail. He was played by Emmet Donlon, who had a fabulous grasp of the role. His singing of 'Jailhouse Rock' introduced us to a superb vocal, his Chad was not an Elvis impersonation but a character in his own right. He had a swagger, a vanity and a shallowness where Mr Donlon's excellent comic timing was showcased. He sang on pretty much every song in the first act and quite a few in act two, stand-out numbers were; 'Don't Be Cruel' with Natalie's Dad, Jim and the solo 'I Don't Want To'. A fine performance by Mr Donlon. As Natalie, Emma Sunderland lit up the stage each time she entered. She exuded a radiance and stage presence as the frustrated car mechanic who fell for Chad but sadly Chad only had eyes for another. Ms Sunderland's singing was exquisite. Her vocal soared on 'One Night with You' and as Ed, who she became to impress Chad, sang 'A Little Less Conversation' and 'Blue Suede Shoes' really well. Natalie's dad, Jim, was played by Diarmuid Vaughan. His characterisation was solid and he really convinced as the widower trying to bring up his daughter. His scenes with Natalie were emotional at times and he had a fine voice on 'The Power of My Love' and 'Don't Be Cruel'.

Michelle Smith played Sylvia, a hard- bitten mother to Lorraine (Natalie's friend) who ran the local bar and eventually fell for Jim. Her solo 'There's Always Me' was well performed and she had a great onstage relationship with her daughter. Lorraine was well played by Sadhbh Treacy, who sang 'It's Now or Never' with Dean, the Mayor's son she falls for. As Dean, Luke Condon's characterisation of the Mummy's boy who rebels was quite good. Playing his mother, Mayor Matilda, Olwyn Grogan radiated small-town bigotry with a high-status performance. As her henchman, Sheriff Earl, George Barry had a strong presence, only speaking towards the end of the show as he was cowed by the Mayor's big personality. Natalie's lovelorn friend, Dennis was played by Joe Sheehan, his scenes with Chad were good and his solo with the ensemble 'It Hurts Me' was well sung. As Miss Sandra, Sinead O'Donovan captured the nuances of an academic, who falls head over heels for Ed, whilst spurning the advances of Chad. The scene in the museum with the statues was excellent, where she sang 'Let Yourself Go'. She also sang on 'Teddy Bear/Hound Dog' with Chad, Dennis and Natalie which was very funny.

Musical director Laura Cotter and chorus mistress Mary Rose McNally clearly did some sterling work with the ensemble to produce some beautiful and powerful harmonies. 'Heartbreak Hotel' had fabulous harmonies as did 'Can't Help Falling in Love'. The guitar work on 'Roustabout' was also super as was the Bass on 'There's Always Me'. Choreography by Barbara Meany was quite good on 'Jailhouse Rock' and great on 'C'mon Everybody'. The performers were well drilled and made the often- complicated moves, look effortless. Diarmuid Vaughan, who played Jim, also designed the complex set, a series of large trucks that were rolled around the stage depicting different locations. Upstage was what looked like a large set of municipal doors, but opened and rotated to become the bar, garage etc. The side walls of the stage area were painted mural-style depicting oil wells and a sort of desert landscape. It was a very clever use of the space, well- designed and well-built. Stage Manager Kay Sheehan and her team handled the transitions well, sometimes they were a little slow but generally it was quite tidy. Lighting design by Alan McCormack was good throughout, but the bar scenes were very flat and seemed to be lit entirely from the front giving a washed out look. But the 'Jailhouse Rock' scene was very effectively lit as was 'Can't Help Falling in Love' where each character was spot lit, which closed the first act. Sound by Pat Marnane was generally quite full and the ensemble vocals were particularly sharp. However, I felt it was a tad too loud and the band sometimes drowned out the solo vocals.

Costume was hired in from Pat McGann, NoMac and Cecilan Musical Society and was perfect for the era. Make-up was looked after by Jennifer Lynch and looked very effective, particularly on Natalie/Ed. Director Des Henn produced a well-paced show, his interpretation was quite faithful and it was well-staged. Mr Henn's casting was spot-on, Chad, Natalie and Jim gave extremely good performances and were fully invested in their characters.

Distinctive and Distinguished Roscrea Musical Society staged their 79th annual production in the Abbey Hall, Roscrea from 27 April to 4 May and chose Lerner and Loewe's musical My Fair Lady as this year's offering. Originally staged sixty-three years ago on Broadway, starring Rex Harrison and Julie Andrews, the musical stands the test of time as it's very witty and essentially about transformation, patronage, gender politics and class, all of which remain relevant today, and it has some great songs. Based on the George Bernard Shaw play Pygmalion written in 1913, the story is about Cockney flower girl Eliza Doolittle and her quest to become a lady, with the help of phonics Professor, Henry Higgins and his friend Col. Pickering.

The musical was staged in the Abbey Hall, an old parish hall style venue with a platform stage and balcony. There was very little room backstage for the performers, and they shared facilities with the audience, which made for an old school theatrical experience, where the audience mingled with the acts. The show opened with a downtrodden Eliza entering the auditorium and walking up the centre aisle, offering flowers to the bemused audience members, eventually climbing treads to sit on the stage. Straight away, with this bit of direction by Paul Norton we knew we were in for a unique version of this classic musical.

Eliza was played by Audrey O'Meara with a faultless cockney accent and an incredible vocal range. Her transformation from working-class flower seller to high society lady was expertly plotted and paced by Mr Norton. Ms O'Meara's acting skills were well demonstrated too as realisations started to dawn that she may speak like a lady and have a lady's manners, but she will never have the money to become one. This sad paradox was very well performed by her and by Paul Spencer as Higgins. Her singing was superb on 'Wouldn't it be Loverly', 'I Could Have Danced All Night' and 'Just You Wait'. However, 'The Rain in Spain' with Higgins and Pickering really showcased Ms O'Meara's range and was very funny too.

Paul Spencer did something with Higgins I've never experienced before on this show. Through his faultless diction and impeccable accent, I forgot I was watching a musical and instead engaged with the show as Pygmalion. Mr Spencer brought a high drama sensibility to the show through his delivery and characterisation. Every epigrammatical line was superbly placed. His singing obviously brought me back to Lerner and Loewe's adaptation. 'Why Can't the English', 'I'm an Ordinary Man' and 'I've Grown Accustomed to her Face' were brilliantly sung with a smooth transition from dialogue to song. On 'The Rain in Spain' he was very strong and displayed a youthful excitement at having succeeded in teaching Eliza. When Eliza rejects him at the end of the show his face showed the realisation that he had gone too far and was to end up a lonely old man. A wonderful heartfelt performance of a normally facilely played character. As the loveable Colonel Pickering, John Lynch also excelled in the role. His was a genial Pickering, warm and caring towards Eliza and the servants and more than a match for Higgins' bluster. Mr Lynch's characterisation of the arthritic soldier was quite endearing, and his singing was also quite good on 'The Rain in Spain' and 'You did It', where he became quite athletic. The other main member of Higgin's household was Mrs Pearce, here played by Brid Delaney with a rather good Scottish accent. She was perfectly cast and showed a caring attitude towards Eliza and her plight. Ms Delaney also joined in with the Servant's Chorus and Eliza on 'I Could Have Danced All Night'. Eliza's father, Alfred, who tried to squeeze money out of Higgins as he believed Eliza was being taken advantage of, was played wonderfully by Colin Williams. It's a difficult role to portray as he is such a scoundrel and the performer must have the charisma to carry it off or he'll be booed off! Happily, Mr Williams had charisma to spare. Higgins managed to hook him up with a wealthy American, who left him very well off when he died, so Alfred became 'middle class' and was not happy about it. His singing on 'With a Little Bit of Luck' with his mates, Jamie and Harry was great as was 'Get Me to the Church on Time'. Harry was played by Conor Harte and was a cheeky chirpy cockney with good song and dance skills and Jamie was portrayed by Andrew Walsh as an older more avuncular chap but was equally as good in the singing and hoofing department. Another of Alfred's small tribe of confidants was Mrs Hopkins a gossiping busybody who was very well played by Maeve Conlon with great comic timing.

Professor Higgins' mother, Mrs Higgins was played by Siobhán Bowe. She exuded class and a finely tuned sense of humour and befriended Eliza, despite Higgins' protestations. Ms Bowe impressed with her gracious portrayal of an upper-class woman by making her quite affable and pleasant, the polar opposite to her son. Her friend, the supercilious Mrs Eynsford- Hill, was nicely played by Niamh O'Donnell who had a haughtiness and was aghast at Eliza's working-class roots showing at Ascot. Her son, Freddy, was played by Tadhg Maher. Mr Maher played him as a loud insufferable buffoon. His singing was equally as loud on 'On the Street Where You Live' and his vocal seemed a little forced and when Eliza exited the house and lambasted him with 'Show Me', he wilted under her fiery temper.

The acting in this production was very good, Mr Spencer, Ms O'Meara and Mr Lynch were superb and had a brilliant chemistry together. Mr Williams was a revelation and brought a freshness to the role of Alfred and all four were consistently good throughout.

Musical direction by Mary Rose McNally was excellent, the ensemble sang well with nice harmonies and the Servants Chorus were especially good. The band were also marvellous particularly the piano and violins.

Choreography by Julianne McNamara worked very well on Alfred's numbers 'With a little Bit' and 'Get Me to the Church on Time', which was full of fun and energy. 'The Rain in Spain' was also quite well- moved in the small space allotted to it as it was in Higgins' house.

Set design by Ian Hanrahan and Paul Norton was clever and worked well for the stage. Higgin's house with the upper library floor was very well rendered and quite lavish with gentleman's club styling. Furniture and décor by Anne Louise Mitchell were perfect and authentic. The exterior scenes were also quite good, particularly the Covent Garden scenes. Lighting by Seamus Reck was good as was Joe Murphy's sound. Costume was hired from Pat McGann and was perfect for the show, the Ascot costumes were perfect as was Eliza's Embassy Ballgown. Hair by Heather Colohan and make-up by Margaret Mulvey and Clodagh Mulvey were perfectly in era and worked well. Stage manager Ian Hanrahan and his crew ensured transitions were quick and accurate and despite the limited facilities available to him, ran a very tight show. There were some lovely moments in this show; Eliza and Higgins fractious relationship; the camaraderie between Higgins and Pickering; the wonderfully kooky Servants Chorus who popped out from doorways to sing 'Poor Professor Higgins'; the fabulous ending where Eliza comes back to Higgins house and he believes she's returned to him, but she retrieves her bird cage and fan, touches his face and exits back down the centre aisle and out of the auditorium, exactly the way she entered but with her head held high this time. A lovely re-imaging of a classic musical by Paul Norton and Roscrea Musical Society. Well done.

This wonderful musical which has been revived in the Donmar Warehouse in London recently is still proving to be one of the hottest tickets in the city. With Anne-Marie Duff in the title role and lots of celebrities checking in as Daddy Brubeck such as Beverley Knight and Adrian Lester. So, the show is very much alive as indeed it was in St Mary's Secondary School in Baldoyle. I have happy memories of seeing the same show in the town many years ago and it was great to be back again. This is a story of optimism and hope. Despite the rather seedy setting of the show our central character seems like an innocent abroad, she brushes herself down and sets herself up for yet another disappointment, 'runs her heart like a hotel - you've got men checking in and out all the time'. As with all the movie musicals we have high expectations for the acting, singing and dance routines in the staged versions.

Kathryn Gibbons played the title role with great dignity and charm. This is a very emotionally demanding role and of course culminates with that awful moment in the park when Oscar calls off the proposed wedding. This was well acted and brought a tear to many eyes in the audience. We warmed to the character through the show. This was a slightly more reserved Charity but she delivered her lines well, sang well and built up a great relationship with Oscar on stage. I would have liked that coat to have been wet somehow when she climbed back on stage after her soaking as it is hard to act something that just isn't there. How nice to meet up with a more relaxed Kathryn the following week at another show and have a good chat. Her almost husband, Oscar was played by Anthony Ennis. This is also a role that demands that the actor digs deep. I know that the delivery of the line that he can't marry her really hits home with the audience and I believe one lady in the audience got carried away and called him all sorts! The timing of the dialogue between these two players was excellent and the relationship appeared very real. I particularly loved that moment in the diner when they communicated back to back. The range in those songs can be a bit challenging too, a good effort with these Anthony.

The Italian screen legend Vittorio was played by an immaculately dressed and groomed Karl Hoffman. He maintained the character throughout and was very believable in the role as was his beautiful love interest Ursula, played by Colette O'Beirne. They both glided elegantly around the stage and they too built up a great on stage partnership.

Charity's work best friends were Nickie (Kate Headon) and Helene (Helen Cahill). They were very convincing as the worldly- wise dance hall girls. Nicely acted and sung with a good 'Baby Dream Your Dream' number. Herman, the dance hall boss was brought to life by Richie Smith. He gave us a crotchety but warm-hearted character. He sang the 'I Always Cry At Weddings' number really well. Probably one of the highlights in the show is 'Rhythm of Life'. One of Sammy Davis Jr much played tunes it epitomised the 1960's Flower Power Era. Stephen Rixon took on the role of Daddy Brubeck and did a memorable job.

The main cast was well supported by the energetic chorus and other players too numerous to mention here but I have written about them in the Private Review. They all contributed so much to the success of the show. Well done Everyone. The hall itself was a good size and my view of the stage was excellent. The open curtain revealed a scrim cloth which had the log projected onto it and behind this were cut outs of the New York skyline. The two stage extensions were backed with pictures of Manhattan Bridge which served to spell out a sense of place. The orchestra were located on the hall floor below the stage, as was a bridge indicating the water in Central Park. There was a set of steps from the pit to the stage which Charity used to clamber out of the river. Philip Somers and his stage team changed scenes quite quickly and very efficiently. There were large pieces brought on such as the lift, which was also cleverly used as the wardrobe though might have looked smarter in Vittorio's apartment. I feel that this scene should have been space age modern in its look so that she was believably overcome by her surroundings and so 'If They Could See Me Now' would have resonated with us more. The large props were mostly good though at times I wanted to see a bit more opulence. I loved the barre which was nicely covered in velvet and fringing and the raised fairground car was most effective. Smaller props such as the phones, balloons, ice bucket, glasses all looked in keeping. I would have liked better clothes in the closet and a fur throw over the bed.

On the whole the show was well lit though there were times when faces were a little dull. Occasionally a spot filled in these gaps and the sparkle returned. However, 'Big Spender' was stunningly lit and the final silhouette of the girls was wonderful. The back projections were well chosen though they tended to get bleached out when the stage lights were brought in fully. The sound was also quite good though with so many body mics it is difficult to ensure they are all cued correctly. The balance between voice and orchestra was good.

The show was well directed by Paul Fay. There are quite a few moments of difficult dialogue which need to be sensitively handled. This Paul did well and we had had some lovely touching moments. One thing I hadn't seen before, and I am assuming Paul or possibly Catherine moved it, was the New York scene played out in the park during the overture. To be honest I have seen things like this before which didn't work half as well as this did. Also, there is not a wild amount for the chorus to do in the show and this really pulled everyone in from the start of the show. Paul set a good pace for the production which moved slickly on, aided by that great stage team. The characters were well-defined and it was obvious that everyone was comfortable in their role. The Musical Director Carmel Whelan gathered together a nine-piece orchestra which provided excellent accompaniment through the show. There was a wonderful brassy sound which really came into its own in the 'I'm a Brass Band Number' but some sensitive playing in 'Where Am I Going?'. The principal cast sang well with each player singing well within their range. The chorus gave us some great harmonies especially in 'Rhythm Of Life' and 'I Always Cry At Weddings'.

Some of the choreography created by Catherine McCourt was great with original moves being added, while other sections seemed to play close to the original Fosse movement, such as the very stylised 'Rich Man's Frug'. 'Big Spender' was pushed out well vocally and in the ladies' moves. 'I Love To Cry At Weddings' was excellent with ever changing movements and stage patterns. 'Baby Dream Your Dream' was nicely constructed and gently moved and 'Rhythm Of Life' was a hippy fest of 1960s movement. The chorus in this number had really gone to town with their costumes as we had a whole array of flowery outfits which combined with Daddy's long-haired hip look worked really well to capture a moment in style history. The rest of the show was well costumed with the girls in the dance hall all having their own look but still managing to look unified as a group. The 'Rich Man's Frug' costumes added class to the club scene with gloves which accentuated the moves. Vittorio had a good suit though the scarf was a little short. The red and blue band uniform added a spark of dramatic colour. As I said earlier, I would have had a second wet trench coat for Charity pre placed in the pit for her fall.

Hair was well back-combed and teased into mini-beehives which really epitomised the period. The men's hair was good too. Great make-up on the ladies giving a Dusty Springfield look with smoky eyes. There was an appropriate light touch with the men's make-up. Charity had a very clear and authentic looking tattoo.

This is a great musical with some wonderful songs and great opportunities for the dancers in the show to shine. First and foremost, this is a show for good acting technique and the society are lucky to have such a wide range of talent to choose from. Well done to everyone involved in the show and to the committee, a well chosen show which worked well for your members and actually stretched them a little out of their comfort zone. Delighted that they rose to the challenge.

Love Island Waterford Musical Society staged Rodgers and Hammerstein's South Pacific in Waterford's Theatre Royal this May, directed by Bill Stafford with choreography by Donna Murphy and musical direction by Wayne Brown.

Based on a series of stories by James A. Michener, South Pacific was a huge hit when released on Broadway in 1949 and won ten Tony awards and the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 1950. The musical focuses on a group of American sailors and Navy nurses stationed in the South Pacific during World War II. Ensign Nellie Forbush, a nurse, befriends and quickly falls for Emile de Becque, a French expatriate and plantation owner who has mixed-race children, and Lt. Joe Cable finds himself in a passionate affair with Liat, the young daughter of Bloody Mary, a local grass-skirt wheeler-dealer. As the war against Japan escalates, reality sets in for both Forbush and Cable, who struggle to reconcile their unconventional love affairs with their own inherent racism. Nellie Forbush was played by Susan Boyce who had a really lovely Doris Day quality to her voice. Ms Boyce played Forbush as a confident, outgoing happy-go-lucky young nurse who fell for an older man. Her singing on 'I'm Gonna Wash That Man Right Out-a My Hair' one of the show's enduring numbers, with her colleagues was excellent; on 'A Cockeyed Optimist' she gave a jauntiness to her singing and the duet with Emile 'Twin Soliloquies' was quite divine. Her reprise of 'Some Enchanted Evening' was performed with a sad longing in her voice but 'I'm in Love With a Wonderful Guy', with its impossibly long end phrase, was full of elation and lightness.  Ms Boyce had a fabulous voice full of expression and depth of feeling and was a joy to listen to.

As her lover, Emile, Dermot Keyes demonstrated a terrific baritone in the role and played Emile with sensitivity, showing his disappointment in Nellie's fickleness and racism. 'Some Enchanted Evening' is one of Rodgers and Hammerstein's more famous songs and is reprised three times in the musical after its first outing by Emile. He sang it extremely well, and the audience were most appreciative. His duets with Nellie, 'Twin Soliloquies' and 'Some Enchanted Evening' were beautiful. Mr Keyes had a sensational voice which suited the music in this show. His Polynesian servant Henri, played by Thomas Rogers, was suitably subservient and had a very authentic look and accent. Lt. Cable was played by Adam O'Neill. He struggled a little with his singing on 'Bali Ha'i' and a lot on 'Younger than Springtime' but sang 'You've Got to be Taught' quite well. His scenes with Liat were slightly awkward and they didn't seem to really gel on stage. Emma Walsh played Liat as a very young girl. She did not really have any lines or songs, but her sign language and focus were good. Liat's mother, Bloody Mary, was played by Lynsey Penkert. Ms Penkert had good comic timing and she sang 'Happy Talk' and 'Bali Ha'i' quite well, but did come across as a bit of a racial stereotype. The comic relief in this show came in the form of sailor Luther Billis, here played by Jonathan Kelly. Mr Kelly gave a charming performance and was easily the most natural player on the stage. He didn't seem to act the role, he became Billis. Impressive in his dance and singing, Mr Kelly brought a freshness and truth to the show. He took the lead on 'There is Nothing like a Dame' and was eminently watchable as the small-time swindler. His fellow Seabee, Quale was nicely played by Killian Delahunty.

Damien McDonnell played Commander Harbison, who had a good presence and showed the character's lighter side well as being the side-kick and foil of Paul Dillon's Captain Brackett. Mr Dillon gave a gravitas and an avuncular and quite wistful quality to the character. His scenes with Nellie were quite well done and his scene with Billis enjoyably funny as Billis frustrated him. As Pilot Buzz Adams, Jack Cunningham presented a gung-ho 'fly- boy' demeanour, which really suited the character. Radio Operator, McCaffrey was well-played by Tom Rodgers.

Donna Murphy's choreography was quite interesting in that some motifs were repeated throughout the show. 'There is Nothing Like a Dame' was excellent, the dancers were faultless and used the stage very well. 'Bali H'i' was quite simply directed and had a nice wave-like quality to it, and a similar choreography was used on 'I'm in Love with a Wonderful Guy' with the nurses. 'I'm Gonna Wash That Man Right Out-a My Hair' was nicely moved and quite delicately performed on the towels.

Musical direction by Wayne Brown was quite nice but I would have liked more harmonies on some of the bigger songs. However, his work with Emile and Nellie was excellent. A thirteen-piece orchestra ensured we experienced the big Richard Rodgers score fully. Strings were lush and the woodwind earthy with the brass cutting through to give an almost symphonic sound.

Set design by Ben Hennessy followed the island theme, with grass huts and wooden and bamboo beech style cabanas. Flowers were spread liberally around, a small stage with a red drape backdrop was trucked on in the second act. Lighting design by Paul Browne was generally quite well designed for the show, but there was an odd use of colour at times. Sound by Jody Trehy was good, but a little more bass would have been nice.

Costumes were hired from Nomac and Theatrical Costume Hire and co- ordinated by Avril Musgrave and Elaine Tighe. They were of the era, except for Bloody Mary's leggings! Hair and make- up design by Marina Murphy and Derek Harvey was good, but the eye make-up on some performers looked very heavy. Paul Greene stage managed the show and did a good job.

The show was quite well blocked by Bill Stafford. The pacing was very slow at times and although some of the staging was very well-thought out, some scenes didn't work as well as they were set too far upstage. It was good interpretation with some excellent performances.

You Will Believe a Car Can Fly!

Tralee Musical Society was founded in 1986 and has been active ever since with musicals and pantomimes. From their first musical Annie Get Your Gun to last year's multiple AIMS award nominated Children Of Eden, winning Best Visual, the society has consistently staged high quality productions. This year was no exception with a scrumptiously engineered version of Ian Fleming's Chitty Chitty Bang Bang. Directed and choreographed by Oliver Hurley with musical direction by Aine Murray, this Chitty flew off the stage. Most people know the story from their childhood, and it's basically about a widower, Caractacus Potts; his kids, Jeremy and Jemima; and a lady friend, Truly Scrumptious (with a name like that you'd know Bond author, Fleming wrote it!), embarking on a quest to rescue their kidnapped Grandpa Potts, with the help of the sentient car of the title. The baddies, there has to be baddies - it's an Ian Fleming story, are the Baron and Baroness of the mythical Teutonic Republic of Vulgaria, where the second act takes place. The musical is based more on the 1968 film than the small novel and features the Child Catcher, the art direction and of course the songs from the movie and a few new ones written especially for the stage show. It also features the car, and it must be driven around the set, and it must float on water, and it must fly.

Caractacus Potts, the somewhat failed inventor, was played by Mike Lynch. He gave a good performance but was a little hoarse on the night I attended which impacted slightly on his singing of 'Hushabye Mountain' but he carried it off well. His dance was very good on 'Me Ol' Bamboo' and 'Toot Sweets'. 'Teamwork' was great though, he really energised the hidden children into rebellion. His relationship with his love interest, Truly, was quite believable and they sang well together on the title song and on the 'Doll on A Music Box/Truly Scrumptious' number.

As Truly Scrumptious, Janna Foley was impressive. Her accent and diction were very BBC c.1950 and her singing was heavenly. Her eponymous song, 'Truly Scrumptious' with Jeremy and Jemima was delicate and they blended well together. 'Lovely, Lonely Man', her declaration of love for Potts simply soared powerfully around the theatre. Her robotic movement on 'Doll on a Music Box' was exceptionally well done as was her dance throughout. Ms Foley gave us quite a chipper and plucky Truly, who kept calm and carried on!

Jeremy and Jemima were played with a great controlled energy by David Lynch and Fiona O'Connor. Their singing was perfect on all of their numbers, especially 'Truly Scrumptious' and 'You Two' and they harmonised wonderfully on the title song and its' numerous reprises. They had a great onstage relationship with Potts and Truly and were a pleasure to watch. As Grandpa Potts, Tim Moran gave quite a relaxed performance. His Grandpa was not the normal loud brash colonial Sergeant Major type but more congenial, which worked in his scenes with Potts but not as much on the song 'Posh!' with Jeremy and Jemima. However, he was great with the inventors on 'The Roses of Success' where he became a lot more energised.

In Vulgaria, where all the baddies lived, we met the Baron and Baroness. As the Baron, Tim Landers played him as a big child. He sang well on 'Chu-Chi Face' but he never really came across as a serious bad guy, easily distracted by toys or sweets! The Baroness was played by Jackie O'Mahoney who portrayed her as quite a sensual despot. She struggled a bit vocally with 'The Bombie Samba' but danced it well. Strangely, a group of ladies in the audience whooped repeatedly whenever she entered, which was odd as it was a kid's show and it must have thrown her a bit, but she remained unruffled and ignored the catcalls.

The Baron and Baroness's henchmen, Boris and Goran were played with great comic timing by Marcus Nolan and Matthew Dineen. As a pair of incompetent spies tasked with kidnapping Caratacus Potts for the Baron so he could enslave him and force him to build him a car, they played it as a Vaudevillian double-act. Both sang 'Act English' very well and quite inventively appeared when we least expected them. Of course, they snatched the wrong Potts, attaching the outhouse where Grandpa was ensconced to a zeppelin and flying it to Vulgaria. Hence the rescue mission by his family and Truly. Also, in Vulgaria we met The Toymaker, who makes children's toys in his shop, not for children but for the Baron as children have been banished from the Kingdom. Played with a gentleness by Aaron Mclarnon, the Toymaker hid the children in the sewers of Vulgaria, away from the Baron and Baroness. Mr Mclarnon had a delicacy to his playing that really worked, and he sang well on 'Teamwork'. The other henchman of the Royal duo was The Child Catcher, a hideous long-nosed, black clad monster, played with lovely malice by Padraig Harrington. His scenes were quite scary, especially when he lured Jeremy and Jemima into a mobile cage to be taken away and imprisoned for the crime of being young.

The show started well with the children in the old car and the ensemble behind a gauze singing the 'Prologue' and the film and sound effects were very good here. However, once we opened out into Goggin's Garage and then into the Potts house the energy seemed to flag a bit and the pace was very slow. It did start to flow better once the restored Chitty arrived on the scene and picked up from there to the finish line.

The music in Chitty Chitty Bang Bang is quite good in places and musical director Aine Murray gave us some lovely arrangements of the score. Her work with the principals was excellent, particularly the children. Kudos must go to Choral Director, Laura Crowley for the fine harmonies in some of the songs, particularly the reprises of the title song, 'Teamwork' and 'The Roses of Success'. The orchestra impressed throughout, with super percussion and bass on 'The Bombie Samba' and gorgeous piano and violin on 'Hushabye Mountain'.

Mr Hurley's choreography was also quite inventive, I liked the South American dances on 'The Bombie Samba' which were very tight and filled the stage with movement and colour. Truly's doll-like movement was very well directed and executed and the children in 'Teamwork' were perfectly drilled. 'Me Ol'Bamboo' was also good, frenetic and accurately achieved.

Polymath, Mr Hurley also designed the set, which was excellently rendered and utilised. It was quite an industrial/ steampunk design with cogs and gears on the pros framing the action on the stage. Potts' inventions were also quite quirky, and he made great use of projections. The props were all good too, Truly's bike was very realistic and I liked the house set. But the star of the show was the Chitty car, which the society built themselves. It drove around the stage, apparently floated and when it rose up and banked it really looked like it was flying. Costumes were designed and created locally too by a large team and looked great, the 'Toot Sweet' costumes were colourful and bright and the Vulgarian traditional costumes looked quite Austrian, which was perfect for the Teutonic state. The Child Catcher's layered look added to his menace. Make- up and hair were looked after by Emma Quirke Hair and Una Sheehy and was totally suitable for the era.

Lighting and Projection design was done by John Hurley and worked very well. Mr Hurley's use of colour and follow spots was fabulous and he lit the set equally as well as the cast. The projections were of high quality, were sharp, bright and cleverly designed. Sound by Murt Whelan was suitably loud and sharp and the sound effects by Nicola O'Flynn were of good quality and very well cued. Stage manager, Des Hurley kept everyone and everything in line and his transitions were smooth.

This was a great show by Oliver Hurley and Tralee Musical Society, there was lots of colour, great sets, good acting, super singing and it really delivered the magic for the children and their adults and we truly did believe that that car actually flew!

Why do we love going to the theatre and why do we love musical comedies? Escapism, for a few hours the mundane is forgotten and we get transported off into a different world. We meet new friends and see their struggles, celebrate their successes. This was definitely the fact when I went to see the phoenix arise from the ashes in Carlow. This was the first full length musical to be performed by the town in over twenty years. A huge effort had gone into making this show the joyous night out it surely was. Well done to the enthusiastic team who worked so hard to re-establish this form of entertainment in Carlow.

The centre for Contemporary Art and George Bernard Shaw Theatre certainly lives up to the grandeur of its name. This is striking modern building in the midst of striking ancient buildings so was the perfect location for Striking Productions to perform the show.

The set was cleverly designed with a raised area at the back of the stage accessed on either side by a set of steps. This was used well through the show, particularly by the nuns. There were flats of stained glass on each side and some realistically painted stonework. A huge circular window dominated the back wall with two other arched windows which unfortunately didn't let light shine through. The props brought on added to the scenes. Changes were usually pretty slick and didn't interrupt the flow too much. Lighting created some very pleasing effects though a set of moving lights, such as at the start of the show, benefits from having a steady beam on faces as we lose focus. I hope the glitterball worked better later in the week as it is such a magical moment in the script.

Under the raised area at stage level was the quite large orchestra who were facing towards Musical Director Joan Butler located stage left. This very much in the central location didn't actually detract from the unravelling story as I thought it might. Joan led the players very well creating a lively and interesting accompaniment.
