Those images we all left with in our minds: of prisoners in jail, Vegas Showgirls, school kids - all little scenarios in the story. The staging was clever with a raised platform reached by pretty steep steps on either side, some brick flats on wheeled trucks which could be easily moved around the acting area. No pit here (the orchestra was set down stage right) and the stage surface is at floor level for the first row of seats.

Wee rant coming up … why did a member of the audience wait until half way through a musical number to walk right across in front of the cast to presumably go to the loo? However, well done cast you kept going when others would have been thrown!

There were interesting and quite realistic projections on the back cyc and also there was a super effect of flames on the house flats towards the end of the show. The space under the platform had a pair of checkered swinging doors. At times this became an entrance/exit with strong back lighting and a great puff of stage smoke to add to the effect. Paul had obviously thought about how to portray the passage of time for the characters. Sarah in particular grew into an independent woman before our eyes from the shy schoolgirl. All the dialogue was very naturally moved and I didn't spot any masking. There were some glorious romantic moments and some touching moments especially with Joe's mum. Full marks right to the end Paul, who gave us a clever use of the scenery flats to bring on the cast for their bows. I really liked that idea.

The choreography in the show flowed very easily from the dialogue. Jay Molyneux gave us a plot which really made full use of the beat and words of the music. The 'Baggy Trousers' routine was a triumph with wonderful white chairs being used as props, we had girls running up guys' backs, diving into the unknown hoping that three other guys would be there to catch them. The signature moves of Madness appeared from time to time but were never overused. The Las Vegas routine was exciting. The finale was a real dance of pure joy for the cast and the audience.

These modern shows have a much greater number of central characters than traditional shows and this is no exception. Eoin Corcoran played Joe. This is a very demanding role as he has to play two sides of the same person. This was a very energetic and sincere portrayal. He moved well around the stage, used the rhythms of the accent well in his speech. He sang well too. Good relationships were shown between him and Sarah, his mum, friends. Claudia Glavey started out looking so young but it was amazing how she matured during the show. This was a nice piece of acting. Her voice also seemed to suit the songs she was required to sing. Her lonely figure on that raised area was a very moving moment.

Anne O'Donnell was a very grounded Kath. I liked the Donegal accent she used. It created an earthiness for the character. She portrayed the hurt of losing very well. A shame that the part doesn't demand more singing as she has a stunning singing voice. Dave Langan was Joe's Dad. Nice touch that we don't ever find his name, always Joe's Dad. This performance of the broken soul grew on me as the show progressed. Joe's mates who were on their own life journeys were played by Cian Elwood and Marc O'Connor. They had just the right mix of swagger, bravado and insecurity. Sarah's mates were Róisín Nic Aodhgáin as Billie and Shifra Tobin as Angie. They added great energy to the stage with their 'wide girl' delivery of lines. Not content with all the choreography to design and teach, Jay Molyneux also played the bad boy Reecy. He used a great gruff speaking voice and Cockney accent. Mervyn Fahy was the posh Mr Pressman who wants to develop the street. There was a cool delivery of this role from Mervyn which worked well. Kevin Murphy played five roles in the production though will probably be remembered as the kilt wearing Callum who would have been Sarah's love interest. This was a nice part, well played.

Cian O'Ceallaigh was just the right shape and size to be Joe's body double. Eoin has so many quick changes that Cian facilitated the change without the audience realising what was going on. Other roles played in the show were well delivered by Meadhbh Lyons, Linsey Cant, Orla Nugent, Grainne Curtin, Jay Hall, Mike Flaherty, Mike Cooney, Deirdre Heneghan and Stephen Long. The chorus were wonderful too, they were given some really tricky choreography and they really did well with it. Just always remember that on stage the life in your eyes is the most important thing of all.

The costumes were many and varied and apart from a few wee gripes to do with trouser length this was a well costumed show with a nod to the era but not slavishly trying to emulate it. I loved the black and white prison vests, the school uniforms, the red hats and all those dresses in Vegas were great. Props too, although not huge in number were well presented. Make up and hair added to the look of the piece with nice eye definition.

In conclusion I was delighted to see this show handled in such a sympathetic way. It would be easy to make a bit of a pantomime of the piece, but here it was treated sincerely and we ended up with a fantastic night of theatre.

Sweet as Pie This bio-musical based on the life of Vaudeville star Fanny Brice is a big show, with Broadway Ziegfeld Follies song and dance numbers liberally scattered throughout, and really needs a big stage and high production values to do it justice. Renowned for its 'problematic' book, which runs out of steam by the interval and the one dimensionality of some of the characters, it's really a star vehicle for the performer playing Fanny Brice. Famously played by Barbara Streisand on stage and screen originally and Sheridan Smith in the more recent revival, Fanny Brice was a comedienne ahead of her time, who told risqué jokes on radio and revelled in physical comedy and slapstick in her theatre work.

Clane Musical Society staged it in The Abbey venue in April this year. Directed by Arthur McGauran with choreography by Gráinne Gorman and musical direction by Michael Fay. The venue was quite small and a little cold on the night I attended, but as it was a full-house it soon warmed up a bit. The stage was also on the small side and I wondered as I sat before the show started, listening to country and western music on the sound system as pre-show music, how they would stage the big Follies dance numbers. The band were sequestered backstage somewhere as there was no room front of stage for them to set up.

A gauze hung on the stage line served as a projection screen for an image of red tabs, once opened revealed Fanny, played by Ellen Stapleton, dressed in leopard skin coat and matching scarf who sat at her backstage dressing table and we were off. The book is a 'memory play', in that as Fanny sat in her dressing room awaiting the return of her husband, Nicky Arnstein, from prison, she reflected on their life together, and their story is told as a flashback.

As Fanny, Ellen Stapleton had very good comic timing and wasn't afraid to mug and grimace. Her relationship with Nick, her eventual husband, played by Robert Gallagher, was well-developed and there was a spark between the actors. Ms Stapleton played Fanny as a happy-go- lucky, wise-cracking optimist, always seeing the best in people. But we could see her vulnerability and really felt for her as she became a doormat for Nick. Her voice was well-modulated on 'People', where she sang it with subtlety and on 'Rat-tat-tat-tat' which was fast and funny. Her performance of 'The Music That Makes Me Dance' was quite emotional and on the duet with Nick, 'I Want to Be Seen with You Tonight', she played the excitement of infatuation very well. Of course, the big number and most famous song in the show is 'Don't Rain on My Parade', which had two reprises and is also cleverly stitched into 'I'm the Greatest Star'. The song ends the first act and should be a belter, sadly it didn't reach the heights vocally on this performance. However, Ms Stapleton did give a smashing portrayal, her scene with Nick when he returned from prison at the end of the show was heartfelt and emotional and she really gave us the pathos and sadness of Fanny's disappointment and heart break that her love for him was unreciprocated and that he was and always would be a small-time self-serving gangster.

Robert Gallagher played Nick Arnstein. He seemed at first a little young for the part, but his performance was energetic, and he was quite suave. Arnstein was in reality a cad, he had a steak in a lot of dodgy dealings, was a gambler and was, reportedly, involved in organised crime. However, the script of Funny Girl, barely touches on his real nature. It paints him as unlucky in business but lucky in love. Mr Gallagher valiantly tried to flesh the character out a bit by laying on the sub- text and it worked to a point. He played the sophisticated man-about-town aspect of Nick very well and one could see why Fanny would fall for him. Their relationship was well-honed and there was a nice chemistry between the actors. He sang well too, the awfully titled but good song, 'You are Woman, I am Man' was well timed but it was in his reprise of 'Don't Rain on my Parade' where we caught a glimpse of the inner cad.

Fanny hooked up with a dance director early in her career by the name of Eddie Ryan. Eddie was played here by Paul Dicker and he had a good grasp on the character. His dancing and singing were good on 'Who Taught Her Everything?' with Fanny's mother, Mrs Brice. He led the number 'Rat-tat-tat-tat' and worked well with Mrs Brice again on 'Find Yourself A Man'.

As Mrs Brice, Elaine Moore O'Donohue played the Jewish New York Mama to a tee. Her singing on 'If a Girl Isn't Pretty' with her cronies and Eddie was excellent as it was on 'Find Yourself A Man'. Her dancing was also quite good throughout, but her acting was great, she had good comic timing and a nice dynamic with Fanny.

Mrs Brice's friend, the nosy neighbour Mrs Strakosh was excellently played by Edel Marron. Ms Marron had a wonderfully authentic New York accent and a great grasp of her character. She had some great one-liners and delivered them with superb comic timing.

Florenz Ziegfeld, creator of the Ziegfeld Follies where Fanny worked for some time, was played by Brian Patrick Gallagher. He first appeared in the centre aisle in the audience where he had an argument with Fanny, which really worked as it showed his status straight away. His scene with Nick was very well timed and Mr Gallagher had the gravitas yet softness of this famous impresario, which gave us a well-rounded characterisation.

The ensemble played dancers, singers, party guests, train passengers etc. and were well utilised. Choreography by Gráinne Gorman was quite good in places, but a bit hampered by lack of space on stage. 'Who Taught Her Everything?' with Eddie and Mrs Brice was nicely moved as was 'Rat-tat-tat-tat', with the military precision. 'Henry Street' showcased almost the entire ensemble in a fabulous waltz section and there was a clever lateral dance on 'Sadie'. The reveal within the choreography of the bump in 'His Love Makes Me Beautiful' was very well done as was the Finale.

Musical direction by Michael Fay was good, a nice jazz band feel to his arrangements. 'Cornet Man', was particularly good (although it was played offstage with the onstage performer miming it) as was 'Downtown Rag' which really bounced along. 'Don't Rain on My Parade' had a big Broadway sound as did 'The Music That Makes Me Dance'. Vocally, the ensemble was tight with nice harmonies.

Stage Management by Alan Maleady, who also performed as the Ziegfeld Tenor, was excellent, Mr Maleady and his crew had to quickly transition many different scenes and locations. This was helped by Arthur McGauran's clever set, which included projections of different locations and symbols such as the US flag. It was a box set, becoming a saloon, backstage areas, a street, a train station and Fanny's new house among other areas. Lighting by Cathal Donoghue was very good with a nice range of colours, cuing was excellent on Fanny's funny 'Nick Arnstein' internal moments and I loved the 'love heart' gobos. Sound was looked after by Wilkins Sound Systems and was perfectly suited to the venue. There was a good range of sound effects and I particularly liked the train station ambience. The costumes were hired from That Looks Good, Kilmore Variety Group, the society and designed and overseen by Joanne Cribbin and worked well for the show. I liked the feathered look on the ensemble. Make-up by Jordan Marron and Cian McKeon was well designed and applied.

Arthur McGauran's direction for Clane Musical and Dramatic Society was fast-paced and his interpretation of the show was quite traditional, as befitting the writing. The staging was clearly a challenge - particularly the choreography - as the stage was so small, but they managed to produce a well-thought out, cleverly designed production.

I have seen this wonderful Tim Rice, Andrew Lloyd Webber in all sorts of styles and settings. Director Peter Kennedy had chosen the traditional look to the show with authentic looking settings and costuming (for the most part). It was a very good piece of very emotional story telling with some great performances. The Hub is a multi-functional space which doubles as a sporting venue. The addition of special flooring and heavy black lining material round the walls gave it a good acoustic.

Shane Farrell whom I have met on many occasions was Musical Director. He had gathered a team of twelve players who gave us a beautifully judged accompaniment through the show. There can be a tendency in a rock musical such as this to blast out the music to the detriment of the story-telling, not here, we had a subtle and melodic backing which at times burst into robust rock but never overpowered the singing. The 'Overture' set the tone for the show, interestingly Peter had decided to act out the main moments in Jesus' life. Mary and Joseph coming down the aisle of the theatre, Jesus' birth, the miracles, turning the water to wine, the blind made to see. This was gently and effectively done. There was an easy flow with the direction and hence the movement through the show was very natural. There were some nice placings of cast though at one stage Jesus was lying down stage and those addressing him kept looking straight down at Him which cut them out of eye contact with us. There were beautiful and poignant moments such as the sound of the bag of coins hitting the stage. There were some quite disturbing images like when the followers turned on Jesus, very much like a group of wild animals turning on one of their own. The characters had all been thought through well and the cast delivered good performances.

The staging was very realistic with nicely constructed and painted gables of buildings, staircases and arch ways. Some of these had interesting lights coming through from off stage which really added to the look of the show, well done to the stage team. The show was nicely lit with some wonderful effects in a complicated lighting plot. There was a wide range of colours used which added to the drama of the piece. The movement/dance in the show was well handled though there were some movements which didn't seem to totally fit in. I did however like the touches of traditional Jewish moves and turns with raised arms. The end of 'The Temple' number with the crowds crawling over the stage in pursuit of cures from Jesus was hauntingly memorable. 'Herod's Song' was set as a 1920s moment of escapism though there was quite an edge to that scene which gave a different dimension to it.

The sound throughout the show was nicely balanced with good cueing of the microphones and a very pleasant sound. In a hall like this that is no mean achievement. Perfect volume too. Well done sound team.

There was a strong cast of actors in principal roles in the show. In the title role was Brian Flanagan. This is perhaps one of the most challenging roles in modern musicals as we run through the last emotional days of Jesus' life. This portrayal was well developed with instances of frustration and even self- doubt shown very well. There were gentle moments when we saw the developing friendship and love for Mary Magdalene. Brian sang really well, giving us a powerful rendition of 'Gethsemane'. Louis Brennan had an interesting shaved head look for Judas. Not here the obvious black but a shade of grey. Louis used all the acting areas well, moving effortlessly around the stage. This was an emotional performance, with some good singing, I thought he was particularly at his best singing 'Judas' Death'. I would just watch that the emotion of the moment doesn't take away the clarity of the diction.

Mary was tenderly played by Sonja Stephens. There was a beautiful subtle difference between her costume and the others which meant that she could stand out but at other times she blended in with the crowd. She acted the role with great dignity and sang well throughout the production. This was a gentle portrayal of the role. Pilate was very intelligently played by David Cooke. This role really developed through the production because of David's interpretation. The way he reacted to the unfolding story was great, making a memorable character. Niall Heaney made a real impact in the role of Caiaphas. He began with the most wonderful deep rich voice which seemed to resonate around the auditorium. He acted and sang this role well. Niall was well supported by Declan Carroll as Annas who had good stage presence in the part. This was a well sung and sincere performance. The High Priests were played by David Alexander and Pat McDonnell. They helped to create a good on stage grouping with Caiaphas and Annas. This team of four players looked correct on stage and acted well together. They created some very pleasing tableaux, especially when they used the raised area at the temple.

'Herod's Song' was nicely sung (though I feel we could have made a little more of the staging of the number) by Anthony Flanaghan. The OTT dressed Herod brings a moment of levity to Act 2. I really liked the edge that Anthony gave the number, giving it more of a threatening quality. Simon played by Jamie Mee really blew me away by the glorious tone of his voice. He gave a thoughtful and highly moving performance of his song. Ivan Moran was a troubled Peter who really showed us his pain when he felt he had to deny Christ. One thing that several actors had a tendency to do was to always look directly to the person they are addressing. This means that their contact is broken with us. Several times Jesus is lying on the floor which meant the actors looked down at him cutting us out completely. This is something which needs worked at for your next production.

The chorus gave us some incredibly moving and dramatic moments. They really became like a pack of animals when they were chanting for Christ's blood. They looked incredibly eerie when they sought Jesus' miracles outside the temple. A totally memorably acted and lit moment of musical theatre. There was great singing from this chorus who gave us gorgeous harmonies and of course there were those wee Shane Farrell singing touches which added that little bit extra.

The look of the piece was one of sandy desert colours. This was seen in the wonderful set and of course the costumes. These were in shades of creams and burnt orange, almost like the colours in old faded photographs. This created a kind of consistency to the look which was punctuated by the 'Herod's Song' and the final sparkly build up to the crucifixion. Other costumes such as the Roman soldiers, Pilate and the High Priests were beautifully attired. One thing I really did appreciate was the attention to detail with the footwear. There was a great mix of really authentic looking sandals which looked so good.

Make up was very natural but worked well. Character make up was in keeping. Hair was again very natural but please if actors have to have a beard, either grow one, which is preferable, but make sure the beard colour is a match of the hair colour. This was not the case and it just didn't look right.

Props were by and large in keeping and in good condition. We had nice items to dress the Temple set and for the Last Supper. The benches and carts looked well on stage. An overall harmonious look to the production of setting, props and lighting.

In conclusion Castlerea Musical Society really dug deep to give us a memorable production of Jesus Christ Superstar. I commend the society for all their hard work and the attention to detail from production team, cast and everyone working backstage.

Grease is a very popular musical, due in no small part to the 1978 film starring John Travolta and Olivia Newton John, but I suspect it's more because of the eminently hummable tunes and the nostalgia for 1950's Americana. It started out as a much more risqué musical commentary of gang culture and the social problems facing teenagers in Chicago. However, down through the years it has become more sanitised through countless rewrites and become a more family-friendly show. New songs were added and most producers follow the stylings of the film, especially in the costuming.

Banbridge Musical Society have been around since the early 1980s, staging an annual Spring production. Since 1997, they upped their output to at least two productions per year and this year they will be staging The Wizard Of Oz in November, hot on the heels of Grease, which I had the pleasure of seeing in April at the IMC Cinema Theatre. The IMC Cinema is an actual modern cinema multiplex and nestled in the middle is a fully functional theatre space complete with super- comfy cinema seats. The sight-lines are excellent and there's even a place to put your popcorn and soda!

Grease tells the story of two love-struck high school seniors, Sandy Dumbrowski and Danny Zuko. Sandy has a fling with Danny at a beach during the summer and is surprised to run into him when she moves to Chicago and attends his school, Rydell High. Their love manages to survive several misunderstandings.

However, in the end Sandy realises that she must change herself to truly be accepted by Danny and his friends.

Ian Milford confidently directed a charming, youthful production of this well- written musical. The predominantly young cast were lively, energetic and clearly passionate about the show. Musical Director Niall O'Flaherty arranged the score and conducted a very tight seven- piece band and well-rehearsed chorus and ensemble. Choreography by Lynn Gourley was simple and very effective as the ensemble were totally syncopated especially the 'Hand Jive', which was an outstanding dance number. Mr Milford didn't sanitise the show, swear words were kept in and he didn't shy away from highlighting the social issues, which gave it a touch of realism, often missing in productions of Grease.

As Danny, Ethan Haddock captured the essence of the dumb hoodlum, leader of the T-Birds gang. His singing was great, 'Summer Nights' a bi-located duet with Sandy where they give their own version of their fling to their friends, was full of energy and passion. 'Sandy' his love song to his true love was also well performed, showcasing a fine falsetto and 'You're the One That I Want' was full of joy. Mr Haddock played his internal conflict well, being macho and pretending not to care about Sandy, whilst falling hopelessly in love with her.

Lauren Hill played Sandy as a shy, somewhat innocent, teen compelled to grow up fast as her friends, the Pink Ladies, were socially well ahead of her, a common situation even today. We had great empathy with her as she was thrown into this maelstrom of raging hormones. Her singing was very soulful at times. On 'Hopelessly Devoted to You' she epitomised puppy love as she gazed at a photo of Danny. Her 'Summer Nights', was full of romance, whereas Danny's was more sexual, and on 'You're the One That I Want', she became a female version of Danny.

The self-declared leader of the Pink Ladies was Betty Rizzo, here played by Maille Connolly. Ms Connolly's Rizzo was tough-as-nails, sarcastic and ultimately a sad and lonely character. By underplaying her, she brought a realism to the show which we didn't see in most of the other characters. Her song 'Look at Me I'm Sandra Dee' was biting in its criticism of Sandy and on 'There Are Worse Things I Could Do', where she defends her promiscuity, she brought the house down it was so emotional. An excellent performance from Ms Connolly.

Rizzo's on off relationship with Kenickie was the secondary love story in the show. Kenickie, a T-Bird gang member, was played by Colm McBrien. His performance was quietly seething at times, at other times his character was quite aggressive. This was a well layered portrayal and like Ms Connolly, steeped in realism. His performance of 'Greased Lightnin' with the other T-Birds was a highlight of the show, it was fast and furious and full of fun.

The other T-Birds and Pink Ladies were perfectly cast for this production, their singing and dance was excellent as was their comic timing. Doody, played by Kyle Emerson and Roger, played by Ronan Sharkey really impressed on their duet 'Rock 'N' Roll Party Queen' and Dáirine McCaughley as Marty sang 'Freddy, My Love' superbly with the Pink Ladies. The set was designed by Russell Caughley and resembled a High School musical set in a gymnasium, which was very clever. An empty stage with two sets of treads leading up to a platform upstage and a larger 'RYDELL' sign up stage centre. Furniture and props were brought on by stage manager Andy McKnight's efficient crew, to denote other locations. A series of set pieces should have been flown in but unfortunately the motorised winches packed up on the Dress, so they remained in the flies. This didn't take away from the show too much though as the style of the show was quite 'let's put a show on in the gym', so it still worked!

Lighting by Rodney Ellis was quite good using LED pars and movers during the dance numbers and the Hop. Sound was provided by Enda and Barry McCusker and was very clear with a lovely sonic quality. Costumes were provided by the society with the help of Bangor Operatic Society and were perfect for the era. I particularly liked Teen Angel's silver get up, especially his silver jacket with the wings on the back. Make-up was unaccredited but was fine, again Teen Angel's pink wig and silver body paint were particularly effective.

Ian Milford directed with an even hand here, he stressed the social issues with Rizzo's plight but didn't let it overshadow the lightness of the musical. His casting was very good and he paced the production well. Mr Milford's staging was excellent, making good use of the space. His interpretation of Jacobs and Casey's script was thoughtful and he and his creatives and cast did justice to this iconic show.

Portadown Phoenix Players gather together a group of over fifty young people each Summer to rehearse and perform a musical. This year they had chosen the ageless classic Oliver! There was a wide range of talented young folk coming from a total of thirty-three different schools and colleges on stage on the opening night in Portadown Town Hall. There are a few roles which are played by two actors on alternate shows.

The formality of the building, the plasterwork and light fittings etc added a Victorian feel to the space. As I entered the theatre there was the pleasing sound of the nine-piece orchestra tuning up. Pity the generic 1980s taped music playing hadn't been replaced by something which might have helped to set the time and place of the production. The rich red velvet curtains were closed and beautifully lit to create a rich look. The Musical Director and players were warmly greeted by the capacity audience as they entered down the steps of the auditorium.

As the opening number was being played the curtain opened to reveal a cleverly painted monochrome set. There was a panelled bridge at the back of the stage, a white and black trestle table with matching chairs and one of my favourite things, especially when the audience are looking down onto the stage, the stage floor area was covered with painted boards which really added so much to the overall appearance of the stage, giving a very sharp look. This stage set was only changed by the slick movement of pieces of furniture carried out by the cast. There was an etching look created, reminiscent of the sketches in Victorian books. This open stage worked well for the huge number of cast involved but a tightening of lighting spots and specials would have helped take away the starkness that was created at times. This could have been further softened by use of occasional smoke.

Director David O'Toole, assisted by Megan Henry added some interesting novel touches to the production. There were some themes of; the past linked with the present and the Victorian obsession with death, by creating five ghosts. Jacob Marley with the chains of his ill doings around his neck and the Miss Havisham among others appeared periodically. Some of the characters were restyled in the look of a much earlier era, which jarred initially but actually worked well. Fagin's character went through all sorts of metamorphoses before our eyes, ending as a well-dressed banker off to have a future of robbing folk of their money in a slightly more socially acceptable way. The show moved, for the most part, at a good steady pace with very snappy changes of mood and scene, though sometimes the pace in dialogue dipped slightly. Raised voices can cause diction to get distorted so I really liked those occasional moments especially with Nancy, Bill and Fagin when they controlled their voices to almost a whisper, which was so chilling. There was a good balance of the dramatic with humour.

The orchestra were under the capable baton of Musical Director Dennis McKeever. There was a generous rounded sound to the accompaniment throughout. The tenderness of the orchestration for songs like 'Where Is Love' contrasted nicely with the blasting beat of 'Oom Pah Pah'. Always accompanying and never overpowering. Well done to the sound crew for your cueing and balance of microphones. The principals who all showed such singing talent and future potential were generally very secure in their singing, indeed there were some wonderful singing voices on stage. The chorus really gave it all they had in those wonderful showstopping numbers.

Some lovely ideas for the movement in the show came from choreographer Lynda Wright. There was a huge cast to move at times and so the dance was restricted, but at other times the cast were able to really showcase their talents with intricate and involved routines. Everyone really shone with bright smiling faces really delivering the story danced out for us.

I can only comment on the cast I saw for the opening night show but I am sure the alternate cast did a wonderful job too. Kiyan Telford made a very well-balanced Oliver. Sometimes this character can be a little one dimensional but not here as we had a strength shown in his acting especially when dealing with the threatening Bill. Kiyan sang with a clear, though rich voice which was a delight. Nancy is perhaps one of the most coveted roles for a young woman in musical theatre. It demands an actress who can run the whole range of emotions. She also has the difficult task of explaining to her audience why she stands by Bill right to the bitter end. She must sing well and emotionally move us. This is a real challenge, but a challenge which Dion DiMaio took in her stride. This accomplished actress burst onto the stage and held her audience through her journey. She sang well and reacted well to those around her establishing a good rapport with Oliver and her fiend Bet. This role was sensitively portrayed by Meadhbh McGrail. She moved well around the stage and wowed us with the clarity of her delightful singing voice. Donal MacAuley interpreted the reinvention of the Fagin character as created by the Director. This was a complex, involved concept for the audience with Donal changing from a woman, adding a beard, removing the beard, becoming a range of Dickensian characters before our eyes. My interpretation was that he represented self-obsessed personae who had only the idea of gathering up worldly goods on their minds. His exit dressed as a smart banker, off to make another fortune was poignant. Donal managed this difficult role well and built up very different but believable relationships with his fellow actors. We were chilled at the entrance of Forrest Campbell as Bill Sikes. He gave us a frightening, violent villain. He worked well with Nancy to create a convincing destructive relationship.

Dodger was played by Shane Curran who looked the part and moved well around the acting areas. He related well to his new friend and showed a mature friendship with his mentor Fagin.

Oliver looking suitably terrified in the Sowerberry's funeral parlour When I first saw the styling of Widow Corney and Mr Bumble I was quite shocked. Their clothes and make up appeared from an earlier era and had a look of the Les Misérables innkeepers with white face make up, red lips, and blushed cheeks. However, these characters grew on me almost instantly. The interaction between them and their comic timing really created something special for the audience. Lily McClatchey showed wonderful comic timing in the delivery of her lines, facial expressions and of course the swish of the fan. She really surprised us with those operatic notes which were hit with such ease in 'I Shall Scream!'.

This was a memorable performance from a talented actor. Michael Morrow was a great Mr Bumble who worked so well with Lily. His beautiful tone in his singing sounded so mature and just right for the role. I enjoyed the scene with Mrs Sowerberry, played with such flirtation by Grace Glasgow, when she was making eyes at him and he didn't quite know how to react. The Sowerberrys too made a good team with Jonathan Reid creating a most disturbingly creepy husband. It is a difficult thing to create a nasty character who also makes us laugh, so well done. Holly Coulter was a lovestruck Charlotte, pampering to every whim of Morgan Shuttleworth's Noah.

They were a convincing couple too. Other support roles were played with great conviction and I particularly commend those on stage who actually played two parts. The chorus burst on with such energy and were all really involved in what was going on. They all sang really well and those with individual lines to sing did a wonderful job. They were on the whole nicely costumed in the style of the time but they were all impeccably clean. Maybe a dirty up and an untidy of some of the hairs would have help differentiate the social classes. Make up was at times quite creative such as Fagin and the Corney/Bumbles. There were some grubby faces but we really needed much more to create the impoverished feel of the period.

This was an interesting version of a classic. There were aspects of the styling which were innovative, most of which worked well. What I really loved was the joy on each one of the cast's faces - they were having a ball. We laughed, maybe the odd tear and we were certainly entertained by Portadown Phoenix Players' production of Oliver!

You Gotta Believe The London and New York theatre publishers, Samuel French Ltd, first published Piers Chater Robinson's Peter Pan musical in the UK in 1985. It is now in its third edition and fourth reprint and has sold thousands of copies in most English speaking countries. Since then, in addition to ongoing international professional productions, the work has been translated into seven further languages and is now also a global favourite with schools and amateur societies and this is the Peter Pan that Twin Productions staged in August at the Town Hall Theatre in Galway.

Twin Productions is a company run by Seán and Brian Power who have also run the Power Performance Academy since 2005. Staging a number of shows every year, Peter Pan was their Summer production this year.

Generations of children and parents are familiar with J.M. Barrie's story. Peter Pan, the boy who won't grow up, visits the Darling children in their nursery and whisks them off to Neverland, where they befriend the Lost Boys and join the battle against the nefarious Captain Hook.

The show opened in the Darling household where Mrs Darling, played by Síofra Níchunluain (who stepped in at the last moment from the wings where she was assistant stage manager to play the role as the original Mrs Darling had to play Peter Pan due to a cast injury) recounts the tale of how she captured a boy's shadow. Ms Níchunluain played her as a kind maternal figure, mother to Wendy, John and the youngest, Michael. Her husband, Mr Darling, played by Jay Hannon who also popped up as an Indian Chief later in the show, was a pompous, self-important character very well portrayed by Mr Hannon. Both sang quite well on the 'family song' "The Darlings". Wendy, their teenage daughter, tells of a recurring dream she's been having about a boy who keeps visiting her room at night. Instead of calling Dr Freud or a constable, her parents dismiss her fancies and send the kids off to bed whilst they go out on the town. In the middle of the night, Peter Pan arrives with his fairy Tinkerbell to retrieve his shadow and kidnaps all three children, who go willingly to escape their father I suspect, to join his Lost Boys in Neverland. As Wendy, Jessica McDonagh was a revelation. Her performance was superb, her singing sublime and her commitment to character and her character's underlying conflicts remarkable in one so young. Her duet with Peter "Come Away, Come Away" was the stand-out musical moment of the show. Her solo "Peter" was also terrific. As Pan, the brave Amy O'Hehir had only a few hours to learn the part but she was faultless. Her singing was excellent and heart-felt on "Don't Say Goodbye" and the duets with Wendy and she gave a lovely gentle soul-searching aspect to Pan I'd not seen before. This internal conflict, to stay a boy forever or to go back to the real world and grow up was to the forefront of her performance, giving her reading of Pan a marvellous depth. And I feel that the audience picked up on this, attending what they imagined was to be a panto but being moved by Pan's plight.

Wendy's brothers, John the older clever top hat wearing one was quietly played by Jason Harney and Michael the younger more mischievous one was nicely played by Cian Power, enthusiastically embraced the Lost Boys way of life and became part of the band of merry miscreants. Some of the Lost Boys, and there was about twenty of them, really shone out from the stage; Katie Larkin's Nibs and the twins Lauren and Emily Egan, whose choral speaking was eerily reminiscent of the girls in the Shining film it was so good, were stand- outs. Wendy however was cast in the role of Mother to the Boys, which she gamely tried to fulfil.

Of course, the enemy of Pan and the Lost ones was Captain Hook and his ragged pirates. As Hook, Keith Hanley played him quite straight, he didn't pander to the audience, he was what he unapologetically was. Mr Hanley's singing was great, he had a lovely tone to his voice. His "Rich Damp Cake" was another stand-out moment! Hook's lead acolytes Smee, intelligently played by Luke Dennigan who brought a modern geekiness to the role, and Starkey, here played by Seán Steede in a considered performance, were lieutenants who led a rag-tag bunch of sadistic dreadlocked pirates eager to make the Lost Boys permanently lost. All were very well costumed by Tara Kinsella and I especially liked the nods to films like Pirates Of The Caribbean with the pirate's costumes and Hooks' red and black uniform from the Disney film and the Lost Boys Lord Of The Flies styling. Make up was looked after by Fiona Lawless and Áine Lawless and worked particularly well on the two opposing tribes of children, punk-like for the pirates and Les Mis for the Lost Boys.

In addition to the two tribes of warring children, we also met a Native American Indian tribe. An unexplained incongruity in both the book, films and stage shows, that seen though contemporary lens is clearly racist. In a land of childish savages, of civilisation rejected, the Indians are the most degenerate. Even the children treat them as other, and even the (all-white) children are seen as superior to them. That aside, the character of Tiger Lily, the Chief's daughter is rescued from certain death by Peter. Tiger Lily, played by Aisling Carroll convinces her father the Indian Chief, played by Jay Hannon to go to war with the Pirates to save the Lost Boys. In "Braves to War" choreographer Declan J. Gardiner excels himself in a wonderful piece of contemporary choreography with some tribal overtones in another great moment of the show.

Peter, Wendy et al are captured and held as prisoners on the Jolly Roger, Hook's ship, and in a big fight sequence overcome their adversaries and Hook is fed to a crocodile. Wendy persuades the Lost Boys to come home with her and her brothers where her parents will adopt them. She begs Peter to join them, but he declines saying he will visit them often. The show was stage managed well by Gerry McCann who lost his assistant to the stage but nonetheless soldiered on and controlled the production very well. Eoin Corcoran's musical direction was very good. It's not easy working with backing tracks in a live show and he managed to get some nice harmonies from the ensemble and some lovely principal work from Wendy, Peter and Hook. Lighting by Paul Kelly and sound by Fintan Higgins complemented perfectly the versatile set by Aidan Mannion. Projections were looked after by Mattie Burns and were of high quality.

It was intelligently directed by Mr Power; the staging was at times inspired and the pace was pretty fast throughout with very little flagging. As a contemporary interpretation of J.M. Barrie's classic it worked, the score is quite modern and mostly up-tempo, and the power ballads are memorable. What I liked about this production though was that it didn't veer into Panto territory, which it could so easily have done, but remained true to the spirit of the story and the musical. It's a big ask for your audience to believe that Peter Pan is flying, when really he isn't as the budget won't allow it, but I do think that this production got around that anomaly by the sheer application of talent and the commitment of a fine group of creatives and the indomitable spirit of the cast.

Undoubtedly Séimí Campbell and his team enjoy taking risks when they produce the annual show for Donegal Youth Musical Theatre. The group gathers talented young people from all over the country and there follows an intensive three-week rehearsal period before staging the show in An Grianán Theatre in Letterkenny. What has impressed me is the fearless way the team choose to reinvent their productions giving them a very contemporary edge and giving the audience a thought-provoking evening of musical theatre.

This year the company decided to stage Lionel Bart's classic 'Oliver!'. The cobbled streets of Victorian London were however left far behind and the show was portrayed in modern day Dublin. The attention to detail with this resetting was excellent and the finished piece became a very much darker theatrical experience than the original. There were many aspects of this newly invented show which were exciting and challenging and really provided food for thought about urban life in contemporary Ireland.

The open curtain as we entered allowed us to examine the set and the acting areas. A long white table was being set by a smartly dressed host. The scene was stunningly lit in a pool of frosty white light. Cutlery, glasses, cakes were brought out. Guests arrived, and even over the buzz of the excited audience, we could hear their animated conversation. A birthday cake appeared and celebrations of this middle- class group, (beautifully attired in tones of black, white and grey) could be observed. As the show proper started the uneaten food was unceremoniously dumped into black plastic bags. A change of lighting, the setting up of a charity street soup kitchen and our impoverished homeless cast entered for the 'Food Glorious Food' number. This was an effective and chilling start.

The stage was divided into three main acting areas. Stage right there was a cube similar to the design of the TV programme with just the framework. It contained a set of stairs and rotated to evolve into various scenes. The main stage area to the left of this was left fairly clear and provided a good acting space which gave the cast a chance to really relate to us. Behind that, quite set back was the frame of a block of flats, the two upper stories being linked by means of sets of metal stairs. This created a wonderful sound as the cast thumped up and down these. On the first floor was Fagin's compact bedroom and an outside landing. Above on the second floor is where the orchestra were positioned. At times the positioning of cast on the first floor meant that we were slightly emotionally cut off from them. There were a few issues with masking and positioning of cast which did take away from the effectiveness of the dramatic moment. However, there were many very clever ideas of reinvention from the Director. Mr Bumble became two characters, one a Fine Gáil TD seeking re-election (nice touch to put a 'Vote Bumble' flyer in each programme) and one who was really trafficking Oliver but looked and acted like a social worker. Bill Sykes was a drug gang leader out of control and showing that a gun would earn him respect. 'Who Will Buy?' was set at Dublin street market stalls. A back reference to the London hansom cab was made by using a bicycle rickshaw. The dreamlike appearance of Oliver's mother when he was singing 'Where Is Love' and the use of the shawl to indicate the child she had died delivering, floating down to him to wrap in comfort around him, was very moving.

Some fine work from the principals and chorus but I felt that the gentle balance of humour in the original was missing and though well intentioned the story telling became a little self-conscious. The pace of the dialogue was particularly good in the Second Act. The actors worked hard to establish the new roles that the resetting created. Most of the dialogue diction was good. There was a slightly different approach to some of the music in the show too, under the direction of Herta Kelly. It sounds improbable but during the interval there were podium dancers moving to an up-tempo version of 'Boy For Sale'. With light up soles to their shoes and provocative gyrations, this was a haunting sight. The 'Oomp-Pah- Pah' number which opened the second half was also given a modern dance edge, which actually worked really well in this context. Some of the other numbers kept a very traditional feel which seemed juxtaposed to the time and setting. There was strong and aggressive singing from the principal cast and a good rich vocal was produced when the whole ensemble sang those wonderful big production numbers.

Young Ethan Barron gave us a charming but strong-willed Oliver. He sang and acted well and reacted to those around him with a maturity beyond his years. Sadbh Breathnach gave us a feisty and street wise Dodger. She had a wonderful clarity to her voice. She moved well around the acting areas.

Cian Judd's Fagin became a cocaine addicted wheeler dealer, always on the edge of the dangerous criminal world that Bill inhabited. His 'Reviewing The Situation' gave him an opportunity to break down that fourth wall and really relate to us in the audience. Conor White's Bill Sikes was a threatening drug dealer. A loner in the city prowling the streets and hallways, always threatening but also with that sexual edge which attracted the ill- fated Nancy.

Anna Gallagher gave a very strong performance as Nancy. The girl with a past but also with a heart. She was powerful but fragile at the same time. Her styling really suited the modern character she had created. Her friend Bet was played naturalistically by Niamh Anna Doherty and the two female characters appeared to work together with great ease.

Mr Bumble was actually portrayed by two actors. Michael Greene was the formal, proud Fine Gail TD. Seen in the streets as a 'do-gooder' trying to drum up election votes. Suited and with shirt and tie he appeared a strait-laced candidate. That is until his encounters with Widow Corney played by Siofra Harvey. We had some well needed moments of levity when they both frolicked in the bicycle driven rickshaw. Siofra was styled as an efficient secretary in black and white dress. There was good chemistry between these two. The other Mr Bumble had the appearance of a social worker. There were however implications by his actions that he was in cahoots with the Sowerberrys and child trafficking was insinuated. Declan King was a believable second Mr Bumble. Mr Sowerberry was played with menace and sung well by Colin Flynn. Georgiana Taylor was his aloof and uncompromising wife. Dressed in severe black both characters looked current and worked well together. Their daughter Charlotte was nicely played by Caitlin Rose James and Diarmud Doherty was the bullying Noah, creating a good threatening scene with Oliver.

Residents of the Brownlow house which was nicely represented by a beautiful red velvet chair (The use of touches of red through the production was very effective) included Mr Brownlow as played with commitment by Aodhan Gavigan, Amy Cassidy as Mrs Bedwin, who gave us a gentle yet memorable performance. Other parts were played well by members of the cast and helped to create a slick piece of theatre.

The 'Gang', 'Children's Ensemble' and the 'Core Ensemble' were all really put through their paces by choreographer Jennifer Rooney assisted by Amy Jordan. At times space did limit the finished product but there were some innovative ideas and movements on stage. I particularly loved that 'Oomp-Pah-Pah' sequence which had so much aggression and drive.

The costuming throughout was modern urban with a lot of greys and blacks being used with touches of white and red. This on the whole created a unified look with the staging and settings, something Sinead O'Donnell Carey does so well. Make-up and hair really were in a very unobtrusive modern style and did not dominate the look on stage but worked well with the costuming and surroundings. In conclusion this was a brave and honest attempt to use the vehicle of the Lionel Bart classic to make us think about society today in Ireland, raising issues such as homelessness, poverty, domestic violence, gang rule, rising crime statistics, trafficking. These messages did come across in a much darker than usual world for 'Oliver!'.

Creative Minds Productions based in Clonmel chose the Chad Beguelin, Matthew Skylar, Tim Herlihy musical 'The Wedding Singer' as their first show to be adjudicated under the AIMS scheme. It was a pleasure to attend this inaugural AIMS show in the charming White Memorial Theatre in Clonmel. This building had once been a church and was nicely decorated with lanterns and flowers as if a wedding was taking place inside. In fact, we were guests at a few weddings during the evening, all set in the flamboyant 1980s. Based on the movie of the same name starring Adam Sandler and Drew Barrymore, the plot is simple but the storytelling is sincere and the music in the show covers a great range of 1980s genres. The sell out audience on the Thursday night were of all ages and everyone in the audience was drawn into the story.

The auditorium's aisles had been decorated with flowers when the audience entered. This combined with a sound track of the time playing really helped to create the mood. The open curtain revealed a compact stage with a raised upper area accessed by a central staircase.

There were guitars and keyboard in situ ready for the wedding band. This raised area would also be used for the airport scene and the stairs as an entrance to the basement bedroom. There was a curtained doorway stage left and a window stage right. The set was painted in a pinky peach tone accented by a peppermint colour. These colours were carried on to the abstract paintings on the walls. Scene changes were achieved by bringing on large pieces such as the bed in the basement. The weddings were very cleverly handled, with the simple addition of white covered tables and chairs, but each one had a different colour tones used, for example Shane and Donatella used touches of red. There were some red flowers in the bouquet, the groom wore a red jacket, the chairs had a red bow on them. This was very effective. The properties were well chosen and added to the feel of the era, such as the mobile phone 'brick', the bouquets, wedding cakes etc I commend Jenny Sheehan, Anne Sheehan and team for their slick stagecraft. The lighting plot was intricate with a variety of specials and gobos which were perfectly cued, creating some magical moments and adding much to the overall feel of the show. The sound too was wonderfully balanced and all the many body microphones were carefully cued. Well done everyone backstage for your attention to detail.

Director Jennifer Williams set a very steady pace with the dialogue. The cast moved with great ease around the acting areas. Their lines were well known and were, for the most part, delivered with expression and meaning, though I would ask that some cast just slow their dialogue slightly as words seemed to run into each other at times. The humour of the piece was nicely teased from the script and there were some touching and romantic moments. A couple of times I just wanted a few seconds more in a pause to point the lines and create more intensity in the scene. This was a confident and well thought through direction. The choreography always seemed a natural fit in the show. Quite a few scenes began with the guests dancing at a wedding. This always seemed very realistic and natural. Then there were those really big dance routines which showed great invention. Praise must go to Choreographer Henry James Fitzgerald for his exciting movement ideas, which had so many novel moves but also paid homage to 1980s and Dance Captain Grace Hogan for her work in perfecting the dance numbers. This was a very talented team of dancers who made the complex seem very natural.

The music of the show was in the capable hands of Musical Director Eamon O'Malley. He had gathered six players to form the orchestra. With Eamon also playing keyboards, he created a very balanced sound. There were huge power ballads, rock numbers and tender love songs. Each one sounded right with lovely tone in the playing and a sensitivity for the singers shown. The cast were well drilled and delivered their songs well. There were some very pleasing harmonies from principals and chorus. I particularly loved the blend of Emma and Omar's voices at the end of 'If I Told You' - gorgeous. A job well done Eamon.

The title role was played by Omar Sallam. Omar showed a good range in his singing voice and coped well with the challenges of the demanding score. He went through a wide range in emotions, but I particularly loved his outbursts at Donatella and Shane's wedding which created an hilarious scene. He worked well with Emma Sunderland who played waitress Julia. This was a very sincere and dignified performance. This actor really wore her heart on her sleeve throughout and we could really see her pain and frustration. Well sung too Emma, who gave us some beautiful tender moments.

Marie Kelly was convincing as Holly. This is quite a pivotal character as she adds energy to the narrative and moves the story along. Marie looked very 'of the time'. She used body movement and gestures to good effect to establish the feisty character. Her relationship with jilted lover Sammy was realistic. Sammy played by Conor McGuigan sported a long rock star wig which he swished to create the image. He acted the heartbreak of youth very well and had us all on his side in his pursuit of Holly. George played by David O'Donovan was the flamboyant third member of the band. This role was played with conviction and David added a good vocal to his big numbers such as 'George's Prayer'.

Glen is the upwardly mobile, manipulative boyfriend of Julia. Very much in the mould of the 1980s yuppie he tries to control her until 'the worm turns'. Neill Bourke looked and acted the part very well. The awkward 'Pop!' number worked really well with excellent comic timing from principals and the ensemble.

Robbie's former lover, Linda, was played with great energy and sensuality by Tarryn Attlee. Her wonderful, very revealing costumes added much to the vampish character she created. Great humour was added to this production by Mary Condon O'Connor as Grandma Rosie. There was her first appearance as the announcer of safety information and she gave a very definite instruction about mobile phones which the audience really heeded. I really appreciated this as the use of phones is quite shocking and distracting. Indeed, I sat behind a man who watched a football match during the first half of another show. Keep insisting about this everyone. I hope other societies are as emphatic as Grandma Rosie! This was a young actor who aged quite well to give us a most entertaining piece of comedy. Her scene in the garden in that wonderful multicoloured tracksuit was so funny. Grace Hogan played Julia's protective mother.

This was a very genuine performance and a lovely relationship between the two was created.

This cast of principals was well supported by a strong and committed chorus. What impressed me was how well each member moved in those complicated dance routines. There was a strong vocal from this team who added some nice touches of harmony to the production.

There was a great array of 1980s 'over the top' outfits on stage, from those sateen bridesmaid dresses to the boys' multicoloured suits. Accessories were generally complimentary though I would have changed some of the footwear to match dresses. I also would have liked a bit more emphasis on the eyeshadows used. Eighties to me is more blues and greens with strong blusher and not quite so much highlighter which the stage lighting overemphasises. The wigs were quite a mixture, from Angie's huge perm to the long wig sported by Sammy. The 'fake' stars all had great wigs, I particularly liked Fake Tina's spiky wig which moved so well as she attacked Glen! Many of the cast had curled and backcombed their own hair which looked great too.

This young company should be most proud of the wonderful evening's entertainment they gave an enthusiastic audience in The White Memorial Theatre. There was some great attention to detail in the direction and presentation of the show, with some good performances and singing throughout. Thank you for the privilege of letting me adjudicate this, their first AIMS show.

A Road Trip to Oz Fusion Theatre has been around in Lisburn since 2002, when they launched with Peter Pan.  This year their production of Ian Fleming's Chitty Chitty Bang Bang ran for eight performances in early September in the Island Hall, in Lisburn. It was a good show marred by some production issues, most notably the absence of some crucial set elements. James Huish directed the cast of young performers whilst Matthew Milford and Jillian Liggett looked after the musical and choreographic direction respectively.

The plot of the musical is that the hero, failed inventor Caractacus Potts, his girlfriend, Truly Scrumptious, his children Jeremy and Jemima and their old refurbished car go on a big adventure to a fictional European country, Vulgaria, which is populated by very odd characters to rescue his father, Grandpa Potts, who is being held captive by the toy-loving despot Baron Bombrust. Along the way they meet two incompetent spies, a Childcatcher, a genial Toymaker and some incarcerated children. The car reveals itself to be quite sentient, can sail on the sea and even fly, and ultimately saves the day.

The opening was super, with a giant projection of a vintage car race and Jeremy and Jemima sitting centre stage in an old, wreck of a car. The ensemble surrounded them and sang along with them through the opening number. Musical Director Matthew Milford's interpretation of the choral here was excellent, Jeremy and Jemima were superb, the projection super-bright and imposing, and the scene boasted really high-quality production values. Sadly, the rest of the show didn't quite live up to this opening promise. In Goggins' Garage stood an old racing car which Jeremy and Jemima had fallen in love with and they tried to persuade their father, Caractacus Potts, to buy. But at thirty shillings, it was beyond the family's means. Goggins, played with assurance by Paddy Adair who also played the Toy Maker in Act Two, promised to keep it for them if Potts can find the money rather than selling it to an unpleasant Junkman, played with vileness by Theo Traynor who also played the Childcatcher in Act Two. By casting these actors as other characters in the second act, director James Huish gave a knowing nod to that other children's classic, The Wizard of Oz. Caractacus Potts was played with a contemporary comedic spin by Rory Jeffers, whose comic timing was excellent. He struggled a little with some of the songs, but his characterisation was so good, that it didn't matter. "Hushabye Mountain" whilst not faultless musically, was perfect in terms of intention and phrasing. Mr Jeffers also danced very well, particularly on "Me Ol' Bamboo", where he was quite acrobatic, but it was in his scenes with Jeremy and Jemima where he really sparkled. They had a wonderful dynamic, full of love and humour and good chemistry. As Jeremy, Daniel Boylan was a well-scrubbed typical boy, fascinated with cars and adventure. His accent and general performance were straight out of an Enid Blyton novel. Jemima, beautifully played by Matilda Gibson, was a bossy and curious girl with a great wit and fierce intelligence, clearly the leader of the two. Ms Gibson and Master Boylan displayed great command of their stagecraft, had fine voices which blended beautifully together and stole each scene they were in. They all lived together with Grandpa Potts; a retired Sergeant Major played by Stefan McVeigh. Mr McVeigh gave us a quiet Grandpa, seemingly lost in his own head, but his singing and physicality twinkled through in the second act when he sang "The Roses of Success" with the barmy inventors.

Into this loving family came Truly Scrumptious, daughter of Industrialist, Lord Scrumptious. Played by Abi Dynan as a jolly hockey sticks kind of gal, she falls for Caractacus and has maternal instincts towards his kids. Ms Dynan had a wonderfully clear voice and demonstrated this when singing "Truly Scrumptious" with the children and later on with "Lovely, Lonely Man", her love song to their Dad. Meanwhile, over across the pond in Vulgaria, a thinly disguised Soviet influenced country in the midst of Europe, a certain dictator and his wife were plotting to steal the car from the first scene as the dictator, Baron Bombrust, wanted it for his birthday. They had dispatched two incompetent spies to England to retrieve it.

As the Baron, Jordan Kelly clearly enjoyed being t a c i t u r n , t h r o w i n g tantrums and g e n e r a l l y unleashing his inner brat. He sang on "Chu- Chi Face" with his Baroness, played by Megan Husband in Bond Villainess mode. This was a weird and rather distasteful performance by the two actors as they repeatedly hit, bit and scratched each other ending up in a physical fight on the ground during the song. Clearly, it was meant to be funny, but it was just unpleasant and rather inappropriate, give that this is a kid's show. Ms Husband also sang on "The Bombie Samba" and had some amusing interaction with the musical director as her character couldn't reach the notes. The Baroness, clearly the power behind the throne, hated children and couldn't have them near her or even have the word 'children' uttered in her presence.

The spies; Goran played by Evan Keating and Boris, played by Rory Maguire were a sort of vaudevillian double- act, incompetent and ignorant. Both performers played with energy and their song "Act English" went down well, particularly the innuendo. But they didn't quite have the chemistry together or the comic timing needed to truly pull it off. That said, they were quite good and amusing at times. These two kidnapped Grandpa Potts, believing him to be the inventor, and so began the rescue operation.

When the Famous Five (Caractacus, Truly, Jeremy, Jemima & Chitty) arrived in Vulgaria they stashed the car and ran into the Toy maker, played with a lovely gentleness by Paddy Adair, who tells them that he only made toys for the Barron as all children had been banished from the country. When the Childcatcher arrived, as he smelled children, the Toymaker took Caractacus to the sewers as he had stashed the kids there. The Childcatcher returned and captured Jeremy and Jemima. In the sewers Caractacus revealed a plan to thwart the Baron and lead the kids in a rousing song "Teamwork". Choreographer, Jillian Liggett's work here was rather good, with the children marching in perfect time. Ms Liggett's work on the show was generally rather good, with "The Bombie Samba" and "Me Ol' Bamboo" being the stand- out numbers.

Meanwhile, the Baron hooked Grandpa up with his resident Inventors to turn his old car into a Chitty clone. Thus, ensued one of the best songs of the show "The Roses of Success" sung by Grandpa and the dishevelled ancient white-coated inventors. This scene was quite funny and choreographically acrobatic as the Inventors attempted to fix up the car, failing miserably of course.

At the Baron's birthday party, the Toymaker revealed two dolls he had supposedly made for the Baron; one a doll on a music box, the other a life-sized rag doll. "Doll on a Music Box" was really well-sung by Ms Dynan but was let down as she didn't revolve in the box, making nonsense of her lyric "turning around and around", nonetheless she performed the robotic actions very well. Mr Jeffers played the rag doll, but didn't act it at all, which was a pity. Eventually the children invaded the party and captured the Childcatcher, the Baron and Baroness. Oh, and Chitty arrived with Grandpa, Jeremy and Jemima. This scene was very well directed by Mr Huish, as it all looked like improvised mayhem, but obviously was well-blocked. It was all happy ever after from then on with Grandpa staying in Vulgaria to colonise the natives with Boris and Goran's help; the Baron and possibly pregnant Baroness being banished; the Vulgarian children reunited with their families and the Famous Five flying off to another adventure.

Musical Director Matthew Milford did a fine job on this show. We didn't quite get the big lush sound from the orchestra or the harmonic layers from the chorus, but the band were accurate and very tight. The children's chorus was excellent though, lovely power and great diction. Stage Manager, Andy McKnight marshalled it all with finesse and fairly quick transitions. Set design by Vincent Vyce was a let down though, nothing appeared finished or well-dressed. Projections by the director, James Huish saved the day in terms of showing locations and the movement of the car through the countryside and at sea. Lighting by Paul Hinchcliffe and sound by Jody Trehy was spot-on, particularly Mr Hinchcliffe's movers and Mr Trehy's use of surround sound. Costumes by Rosemary Kelly were perfect for "Toot Sweets" and the imprisoned children, whilst make up by Colleen Sesay and Katie Sesay suited the production. The car was hired from LD Productions and worked perfectly but was a little big for this stage.

Director James Huish did some delightful work on the show, it was quite well- paced, and the staging was good despite the set issues. His interpretation of the material was also respectable. His work with the principal characters was first-rate and they gave a great show, particularly Caractacus, Jeremy and Jemima.

Fusion's Chitty Chitty Bang Bang was a feel-good production with some really superb performances, good choreography, delightful music and a flying car. A road trip through a mythical, dystopian Eastern European Land of Oz with a superb soundtrack on the stereo! Sounds great? It was.

show_raw: Joseph And The Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat
review_text:
What's not to love about Joseph? It has great music, an array of character roles, plenty of opportunities for dance and interpretation, a good smattering of comedy… and it's short! On a wintry night, with a long drive ahead of me after the show, it was great to be on the road at 10.15pm, thoroughly entertained, humming the familiar songs and remembering the key moments of a delightfully uplifting production.

This was a very tidy, by-the-book production by Director, Kevin Kennedy, enhanced by some lovely comedy touches, and nicely directed principal action. The simple but effective set meant few delays throughout, and the selection of props and furniture added greatly to the fun. The pace throughout was very good, and the principals had well-established character. There was good attention to atmospheric lighting, and sound quality allowed for every line to be clearly heard. Perhaps the Narrator could have had a change of costume for the second act but costuming throughout was very good. My only niggle was that on a few occasions, when Joseph and the narrator were dancing with the chorus, they were the only ones not singing, and while the Narrator was strong and secure, I did feel she needed a confidence boost to be more exaggerated in some of her comedy. These are, however, minor criticisms of an otherwise very strong and secure production.

Choreographer, James Dobbs, kept the pace and action on stage varied, creative and well-disciplined. The wives and brothers performed their routines with panache, and the bigger chorus numbers were alive with energy and enthusiasm. There were nice comedic touches too, with a fun routine during Those Canaan Days, and maybe a slightly less successful dance for Mrs. Potiphar, but the overall choreographic contribution to the show was extremely positive.

Definitely a highlight of the show was the quality of the music, both from the pit, under the leadership of Musical Director, Phillip Kennedy, and from the stage. All of the singing principals made a strong impact, but it was the chorus, and particularly the male chorus, that really lifted the show. The band of Brothers achieved great harmony and character in all their songs, and when they combined with the ladies, the harmonies were excellent, and the vocal strength was awesome.

Timmy Moloney had a relaxed, easy- listening vocal quality and chanted his way through the central role of Joseph with confidence. His acting was commendable throughout, growing in stature as the story progressed. I did feel that his modelling of the Technicolored coat in the finale became a tad exaggerated and flamboyant, nevertheless, this was a very well-played role.

Sophie Blaney Parslow carried the exhausting role of The Narrator with a most genial manner. Her vocals were extremely secure with a good, rounded tone, occasionally giving vent to a bit of quality belting. While many of her facial expressions captured the comedy of her situations, there were a few times when she looked a little bit self-conscious, but given her obvious talent, she should have more self-belief. She is a lovely performer. David Burke was a convincing Jacob, who beautifully over-acted his sadness, wailing almost in tune, and when he sang, he displayed a strong and articulate baritone voice. A nice balanced performance.Keith Flanagan played Pharaoh with secure comedic timing and a lot of swagger. Clearly, he enjoyed the freedom of milking the comedy of the Song of the King, and the audiences thoroughly enjoyed his antics. His singing was in keeping with the Elvis styled number.

James Dobbs, not contented with doing the choreography for the show, popped up not only as a very convincing Naphtali, with a splendidly pigeon-French rendition of Those Canaan Days, but also as the delightfully comical, high-camp Butler to Pharoah. He played each part with individuality and aplomb. Anthony Finn, as Asher, did a very good job of leading the brothers in One More Angel in Heaven, and Phil Erskine gave a flamboyant charm to the Benjamin Calypso. Individually, and as a group, the brothers were a strong and secure presence throughout the show. Martin Conway and Brid Moloney worked nicely together and fulfilled the roles of Potiphar and Mrs. Potiphar most credibly, and Ger O'Riordan did all that was required of him as the unfortunate Baker.

The Brothers, The Wives, Maid-Servants, Hairy Ishmaelites, Guards and Dancers all contributed to the overall success of the show with committed performances, displaying good acting, great movement, some inspired dancing and above all, a very strong vocal ability. When the full chorus were on the stage, not just the volume but also the quality of the singing was of the highest order. And then of course there were the children, who looked and sounded so good, and if some of them couldn't resist spotting and waving to their parents in the audience, well, it only added to their cuteness and my enjoyment. Very well done, kids.

The stage was very nicely designed, with colourful, neutral flats and very effective set and furniture pieces, like the well that doubled as Mrs. Potiphar's bed. Palms added a nice atmosphere, and the Sphynx was excellent, as was the Chariot of Gold in the final scene, and the prison bars were very good. The stage crew, under Stage Manager Lizzy Heffernan, kept things moving at a brisk and efficient pace.

Lighting was well-plotted to enhance the action, and created beautiful atmospheres, most notably when Joseph was imprisoned. Not a word was lost, thanks to a very good and well-operated sound system.

This was a vivid and colourful production that benefitted strongly from well-selected costumes and good accessories. Wigs and beards were very good, Joseph's coat was very effective and the final effect of the coat taking over the whole stage at the end was wonderful. But it was the attention to detail that added so much to the show, like the very realistic goat that got torn limb from limb, the 'very last sheep', the comical glove-puppet snake, and top marks go to the amazing nodding, singing, fur-coated camel which almost stole the show. There was always something interesting and comical or colourful to draw one's attention and to add another level to the visual impact of the production. There was an abundance of wigs and beards and they all looked very effective, as was the standard of make-up.

Having recently directed Joseph myself, it was a humbling experience to see how different, and creative and beautiful the show can be, in the hands of a different director, and from one Mr Kennedy to two other Mr Kennedys, congratulations on achieving such a wonderful standard with this highly entertaining production.

Thankfully, as it seems to be extremely popular of late, All Shook Up is one of those shows that I don't mind sitting through several times in a season. It has a good comedic book, a plethora of zany and identifiable characters and above all else, the wonderful music of Elvis. For an old guy who grew up in awe of "The King", such a musical tribute is always a pleasure to savour, and when it is presented with such striking choreography and such a high standard of direction, production and performance, there aren't really many better ways to spend an evening.

Director Stephanie Browne ensured that her production of this show was vibrant and fast-paced, colourful and creative in design, and captured the essence of the rock and roll era. With a very strongly cast show, the direction and movement throughout made sense and her cast always looked comfortable on the stage. Characters were all very clearly established, and with the exception of a few laugh lines being skipped over, and an occasional over-the-top comedic reaction, all gave believable and commendable performances. But it was her choreographic achievements for which Stephanie deserves the greatest plaudits. The energy level was ultra-high throughout, and the dance routines varied from graceful and genteel, to raucous and outrageous, with smatterings of gymnastics, acrobatics and jazz-hot gyrations. She was, of course, assisted in her task by a very fine and dedicated troupe of dancers who seemed to enjoy every second of their performances. Excellent work.

Congratulations to the production and technical team for creating a show that was so colourful and varied, visually, that one was scared to blink for fear of missing something. The lighting was generally top-notch, with great use of special effects, including a projection screen which created some beautiful effects, although in some of the gentler moments of the show, it was a tad distracting. Good atmospheres were created with strong use of colour and moving lights, but the down-stage right and left areas did have a couple of dark spots. Stage managers, Rachel Browne and Máire Long and their team executed the scene changes efficiently, preventing the excellent pace of the production from being interrupted. Sound quality was generally very good, with the minor faux pas of a mic being kept alive on one of the off-stage performers. Well done, also, to the props team, for a wonderful array of appropriate and well- selected items to enhance the ambience and period of the piece.

Musical Director, Laura Kearney, got good results from her chorus and principals, with well-rehearsed harmonies and an abundance of vocal talent on display. The orchestra were tuneful, rhythmic and energetic, if on occasions, a tad over- exuberant. The chorus, singing while executing quite intricate dance routines, were once or twice slightly over-powered by the pit. Nevertheless, this was a production with a high-quality musical accompaniment.

Gráinne Scullane brought a good balance of femininity and tom-boyish comedy to the role of Natalie, especially amusing in her assumed role of Ed. Here is a young lady with good vocal quality, fine stage presence and a very capable sense of comedic timing. This was a well-judged performance.

Joe Keyes had all the swagger and bravado required for the role of Chad, enjoying the hip-swivelling and outrageous flirting and cutting a fine figure on the stage. If not the most powerful singer, he certainly had a secure vocal quality and enough charisma to carry off the Elvis numbers with confidence.

As Miss Sandra, Caroline Browne dominated the stage from the outset, oozing confidence, sexuality and excellent comedy and combining it with powerful vocals. This was a wonderful piece of casting and a most note-worthy performance from a very talented actress. Dylan Noonan made a very convincing Dennis, almost pantomimic in his nerdiness, and very secure vocally throughout. He was believable in his love for Natalie and provided a good contrast to Chad in their scenes together.
