Musical director Killian Cogan gave us some beautiful arrangements of "Heartbreak Hotel" and "Can't Help Falling in Love" and his band were quite tight, especially the electric guitar which was the backbone of the production. Dance duties were looked after by choreographer Aoibh Tully. Ms Tully devised some intricate and pleasing routines, at times the ensemble was not quite in sync, so some of the routines looked untidy.

Lighting by Mick Byrne and sound by Fintan Higgins were good if not remarkable and stage management by Kate O'Dowd was solid. There was no set as such just some set pieces brought on and off to set scene locations. The bar, tables and chairs worked in Sylvia's and the 'tunnel of love' upstage in Act 2, looked suitably garish. However, the Garage scenes could have been better dressed and Chad's Honda 50 motorcycle didn't work! Some of the costumes were of the era and very colourful. The angels and devil's costumes looked okay. The gowns and men's suits at the end added to the atmosphere of love being strengthened after all the chaos. However, Chad's and 'Ed's' costumes were too modern, but the band's striped tops looked great!

'All Shook Up' is written as a farcical comedy of errors, mistaken identity, and subterfuge. It holds a mirror up to small town America of the fifties and its evangelical draconian rules and celebrates the birth of the 'teenager' through Chad's rebellion against authority.  But first and foremost, it's a comedy that should be played tongue in cheek. GUMS production didn't feel like a parody or a farce, it was too loose and most of the 'jokes' fell flat. The pace was good though and it did rattle and roll along quite fast, as it should. More attention to detail on costumes would have made a huge difference, especially Chad's jacket, it was a glaring error and diminished Chad's character which made his character less effective on stage. Chad represents the 'new' America and as he says he travels around spreading his 'love', but this is an allegory of Chad as a prophet disseminating the news that the old ways no longer cut it. He is a rebel with a definite cause and should be charismatic, charming, larger than life and very different to the young people he encounters.

A few years ago, Mel Brooks and Thomas Meehan decided to write a musical based on Brooks' 1974 film about Mary Shelley's Frankenstein. This was kind of in response to the success he had with 'The Producers'. 'Young Frankenstein' was a big hit for Brooks and his co-writer Gene Wilder who also starred in the title role. The making of the film is now the stuff of legend as much of it was improvised and workshopped, showing a cast and director at the height of their powers. The musical uses a lot of the same script plus some of the songs are sort of based on the original actors' interpretations of their characters. So, it's not an easy show to produce because it will rise or fall based on the success of the casting.

And so, it came to be that I was in Solstice Arts Centre on 17 February this year to see Trim Musical Theatre Society's version of the musical praying that it would be good as it's one of my favorite films. It's an eminently quotable iconic film, like 'Withnail & I', 'The Princess Bride' or 'The Rocky Horror Picture Show' and many other similar relatively low-budget movies, so it was important that they got it right! Well, dear reader I should tell you straight away that they did. It was marvelous, funny, fast and accurate with a stunning cast, a creepy set, great band and crazy choreography - all drawn together by director Pat McElwain and his creatives.

Musical director Dermot O'Callaghan conducted an eleven-piece band that appeared to enjoy the show as much as we did! Their playing was light and bouncy, hitting the different styles just right. Jazzy, bluesy with a hint of Vaudeville plus the underscore straight out of a 1930's horror film - all was interpreted to perfection. Laura Douglas choreography was full of energy and madcap fun, with the "Puttin' on the Ritz" shadow dancing sequence being a standout. There's not a lot of big dance numbers in the show but I loved "Don't Touch Me" with the passengers and "Welcome to Transylvania" was well blocked and moved and very funny. John O'Donoghue's set design looked fabulous, it was not a replica of the film set but had its own quirkiness. The lights and huge switches on the lab machines, the fireworks upstage on the bed all added to that old school 1930's feel. The revolving bookshelf was great and allowed for some slapstick fun. But the best bit was the carriage with the actors' playing horses, that really worked. Constructed and dressed by Ben Hennessey and Jim Whelan, the set was not meant to be perfect, more like a movie set on an Ed Wood film; quirky, wobbly and a bit cheap looking. In other words, ideal!

The performers acted their socks off in this show and seemed to be having great fun doing it, which transferred to the audience who loved every minute. Each cast member clearly understood the genre, the humour and how to play it. The physical comedy was great, the double takes, the madcap moments of pure mayhem all worked. Some scenes seemed to have been workshopped and played with as they gave off a lovely immediacy and freshness. The actors seemed to enjoy the script, the faux German accents, rolling it around their mouths before expelling it in moments of great comic timing.

So, for those of you unlucky to have missed the film and especially Trim's musical take on it, here's the plot: In Transylvania, Dr Victor Frankenstein (maker of monsters) has just died, and his estate is left to his grandson Frederick, a surgeon in New York. He travels there to sell the castle and meets Inga, Igor and a host of other characters who convince him to carry on his grandfather's work. He creates his own monster and raises the ire of the local villagers who want to burn him out. It's a silly plot and clearly parodies the James Whale 1931 film, but it's the characters that make it funny rather than the situation, although that becomes hilarious once they veer away from the original.

Leading the cast was Colin Flynn as Frederick Frankenstein (or Fronkenstein as he insisted on being called early in the show). Mr Flynn had great comic timing and a frenetic physicality that was so energetic it was tiring to watch! His singing was good on "Together Again" with Igor and "Man About Town" & "Puttin' on the Ritz". But it was his clear love for the character that came over to us the audience. He seemed to embrace the madness of Frederick and played it to the hilt without hamming it up, difficult in a show that is all ham! Playing his servant, Igor, was Damien Douglas. His mannerisms, his timing, his accent was all perfect in an idiosyncratic performance where he made the character his own. Frederick's lab assistant, Inga, was played by Louise Cassidy. She was super in the role, just the right amount of innocence and seduction. Frederick's fiancé, who he leaves behind in New York, was played by Jenny McCabe who's timing and singing were flawless. I loved "Please Don't Touch Me", where the timing is everything and she nailed it. She transformed into the Bride of Frankenstein quite well too, with the Elsa Lanchester hairdo and unbridled sensuality.

As the monster we had Chris Corroon. He was so tall in the massive platform boots yet managed to run and dance with much energy risking an ankle injury at least! His timing was also excellent, and his range of monosyllabic grunts was quite impressive. His scene with the Kevin Hartnett's Hermit was a highlight of the show. Mr Hartnett's Hermit was so sad, much more so than the film and his singing on "Please Send Me Someone" was excellent. Playing the Housekeeper, Frau Blücher, we had Siobhan Fawsitt. Her timing on the Ovaltine scene with Frederick was flawless as was her singing on "He Vas My Boyfriend". Whenever her name was mentioned in the show, a sound effect of horses neighing was heard. We also had Sean Fox as the local Police Inspector, Hans Kemp, who had lost an arm and a leg to the original (Victor's) monster. The limp was great, as was the arm business. His accent was good too and he never dropped it. Mr Fox's comic timing was good, and he sang well on "Law" with the villagers. He was often accompanied by the Village Idiot, Ziggy who was played by Eoin Kenny. Mr Kenny adopted a hilarious gormless expression and his antics with the gun, where he always pointed it backwards, were great. Again, great comic timing and super delivery. Finally, we had a surprise appearance by Frederick's Grandfather, Victor, in a dream-like sequence. Played by Ronan Walsh, he gave us a super character, quite the dad figure with Frederick encouraging him to continue his work. There was an ensemble cast too, playing villagers and New York citizens and others, who sang and danced throughout with great energy. This cast were marvellous. United in their appreciation for the show, they worked together to get the humour across, and it did. The audience loved it. It looked like a B-movie, with Ali Murphy's fabulous make-up and wigs, Miriam Donnelly's great costumes, Darren Kelleher's spooky lighting and Alan White's full band sound and great sound effects all held together by stage manager Frank Connolly.

Pat McElwain directed this show with a light and delicate touch, allowing the comedy to flow without forcing it. His interpretation was excellent, and it rattled along like a horse and carriage on the way up to the Castle. I loved his little touches like the horses and the werewolf and the Jenga and fireworks on the table. The production looked good, with minimum fuss in the transitions keeping it fast paced yet he allowed it to breathe at times. Excellent work.

Les Mis meets Phantom Produced by Tipperary Musical Society with choreography by Stephanie Browne, musical direction by Mary Rose McNally and direction by Paul Norton; 'The Hunchback of Notre Dame' was staged in the Simon Ryan Theatre in Tipperary from 13th to 18th February. It is an odd musical, it's like a cross between 'Les Miserables' and 'The Phantom of the Opera' scored by Disney regulars Alan Menken and Stephen Schwartz. Originally written as a novel by Victor Hugo in 1831, the stage production of the 1996 animated Disney film has been around since it was first produced in Germany in 1999. Although there have been changes from the film, some of that American 'Disneyness' remains in some of the characters and in some of the text. That said, large swathes of Hugo's novel remain, and these are to my ears the more successful servings of the show.

The story explores love, lust and faith in 15th century Paris and focuses on Quasimodo, a deformed bellringer, his uncle the Archdeacon Frollo and a Romani girl called Esmerelda with whom they both fall in love and is set in and around the Notre Dame cathedral. The opening of the show blew everyone away; the set, lighting and most of all the choral singing on "Olim" was fabulous.

Musical director, Mary Rose McNally conducted a sixteen-piece orchestra to bring us the big, sumptuous sound demanded of the score. Her interpretation was excellent, and I particularly liked the strings which were lush and full. The ever-present choir sited upstage on the platform and below nailed the complex harmonies and were powerful. Most of the leads were very well cast and the 'Gypsy' numbers were particularly vibrant mostly due to choreographer Stephanie Browne's work. It was full of energy, especially on "Tavern Song", "Rhythm of the Tambourine" and "The Court of Miracles". The crowd scenes were nicely blocked and looked natural, and the ensemble were meticulously rehearsed. Most of the actors in this show really engaged with the style set by the creatives and there were some stand- out performances on the night I saw it. Emmet Donlon played the title role and had a great physicality as Quasimodo. He dropped his head and trunk down and rounded his back to create the effect of his kyphosis. This was particularly effective and lowered his status among the other performers. His singing was also very good, especially on "Heaven's Light" and "Out There". He had a great chemistry with Frollo and his portrayal of the character's attraction to Esmerelda was subtle and heart-breaking. As Frollo, Derek Ryan was quite mesmerising to watch, his wonderful voice brought out all the character's emotion particularly on "Hellfire". His acting portrayed Frollo's devotion to God, his reluctant care for Quasimodo and his inner conflict with his desire for Esmerelda and his hatred for the Gypsies. As Esmerelda, Madeline Blackwell stole every scene she was in and did it effortlessly and, I suspect, unconsciously. Her portrayal of Esmerelda was complete; her singing was sublime, and she had a beautiful tone and a wonderful presence. Her dance was excellent and full of character and her acting, particularly the scenes with Frollo, was heartfelt and luminous. Ms Blackwell is a performer to watch. These three performers were ably supported by a great ensemble, who played multiple roles including gargoyles! These gargoyle characters should not have worked - they are quite contemporary in their text, like a leftover form the animated film and seem out of balance with the style of the production. However, their stillness and vocals and empathy with Quasimodo was excellent and it is a testament to their skills that they integrated flawlessly into the story.

Another potential suitor for Esmerelda was Captain Phoebus de Martin as played by Adam Skeffington. He played him more like a Disney Prince rather than a Hugo character, which seemed to be at odds with the rest of the cast and the director's intention. However, once the character was injured and less the Alpha Male, his acting improved immensely, and we could see why Esmerelda was attracted to him. His singing on "Someday" with Esmerelda was lovely. Another character worthy of mention was that of James O'Donovan's Clopin, the King of the Gypsies. He strode around the stage with high status and like a ring master orchestrated much of the action. Mr O'Donovan's accent and mannerisms whilst playful and grandstanding, belied the darker nature of the character, which he revealed at poignant points during the show. His singing was excellent on "Topsy Turvey" and during The Court of Miracles scene. He also had a magician quality where he would disappear in a puff of smoke!

Other performances to included Cormac Maher as Jehan, Frollo's brother and father to Quasimodo, who played his death scene very well; Kevin Reade as St Aphrodisius who had the skills and gravitas of making a headless character work and he sang with passion; Lorraine Cormack as Florika, Quasimodo's mother a feisty, free-spirited character; Conor Ryan as Father Dupin, a lovely performance as the guardian of Frollo and Jehan. Jason Ryan as Frederick, Cole Flanagan as King Louis, Lena Hally as Madame, Tadgh O'Connor as Gypsy Singer and Dave Condon as Gentleman all played with energy, passion and were totally on point.

Aidan O'Connell's set design was super. The platforms were at a good height and the chess board-like floor added a nice detail. The moving platform was used with restraint, and I liked how the performers could climb up the upstage corner uprights. The festoon bunting and clothing really changed the space for the outdoor scenes and the bell rope looked great as did the brought on wooden rails to create the top of the church. The platform for the Fool and burning scenes worked well too. Lovely attention to detail and clever use and re-use of materials created a set with depth and purpose. Stage manager Alma Quinn marshalled everything with an enviable tightness. Transitions and scene changes were quick and faultless. Excellent work. Costume and make-up were flawless and with excellent lighting by Alan McCormack and lovely sound by Star Systems, it really was a feast for the ears and eyes.

Paul Norton directed with a lot of sensitivity and managed to wrestle the work into a moving spectacle. It's not a perfect stage musical in that there are still some hangovers from the Disney animated film, which do not work on stage, but the music is great, and Mr Norton elicited some superb performances from the cast. The whole production looked very high quality from the set to the costumes, we felt like we were in Paris in 1482. Mr Norton paced the show very well and we felt empathy with some of the characters. The addition of sign- language towards the end of the show was a nice touch as Quasimodo was deaf from the bells and there was a palpable energy during the more rousing scenes. The transformations of actor to Quasimodo and back again at the start and end of the show was an interesting device that highlighted one of the themes of the piece, that of inner beauty trumping outer attractiveness. It was very enjoyable by all, the audience gave the company a well-deserved lengthy standing ovation.

En Passant Tim Rice and the two lads from Abba (Björn Ulvaeus and Benny Andersson) wrote 'Chess' in 1984 and it's one of those marmite musicals that you either love or loath. It has some great tunes and a good story but when you listen to the original recording it sounds awfully dated. It was first released as a concept album, like 'Evita' and 'Jesus Christ Superstar' - two of Rice's earlier collaborations with Andrew Lloyd-Webber, and was eventually made into a stage show in 1986. Maybe it's the synth infused score mixed with the OTT orchestrations that date it, but it's not an easy listen. So, it's a real challenge for a production company to make it work in 2023.

Athlone Musical Society took up the challenge and staged it in the Dean Crowe Theatre in March of this year. Directed by Alfie Kilduff with musical direction by Ger Madden and choreography by Jay Molyneux, this was a sumptuous looking production, colour coordinated in black and white with dashes of reds and blues and an MTV staging, good sound, and brilliant vocals from committed singers, especially the onstage choir and a cast of well-known musical theatre performers. The story takes place at the World Chess Championships in Merano, Italy and Bangkok, Thailand one year apart at the height of the Cold War between the Soviet Union and the USA. The Russian, Anatoly, and the American, Freddie, compete, not just at chess, but for the affections of Freddie's assistant and second, Florence. Conspiratorial mind games by Anatoly's compatriot Molokov, and the journalist/ CIA informant Walter, play out as Anatoly's wife Svetlana arrives adding to the difficulties. The Arbiter, basically a referee, acts as a narrator, so that we don't get too lost in the politics of the post-World War II superpowers.

It was an open staging, so we could see the set when we sat down at the start, with a video screen and benches for the choir, it was quite modern looking. I liked the big chess pieces framing the space and the chess board patterns on the floor and on some of the props e.g. the drinks trays. The brick effect flats looked good and added depth and texture to the stage and the black upstage doors were a great addition, particularly as the performers had to climb treads to the chessboard. Kudos to scenic artist Anna Boles too, whose paint work was admirable. It was lit by Ronan Kenny who went all out with "One Night in Bangkok", using every light in the rig to great effect yet brought it down beautifully though the use of sharp specials. The sound by Derek Recks was also superb, lovely balance between band and singers and he managed to get a full, rich sound across to the audience with subtle reverb on the mics.

Musical director and conductor Ger Madden made what is frankly a tired score sound new and fresh. The music is rooted in overblown orchestrations and '80's synths complete with syn drums and the odd electric guitar lick as a throwback to the 70's, but Mr Madden wisely eschewed the Abba sound and gave us a very contemporary sounding score. His band of ten players at times sounded like a full orchestra, such was his and their skill. Flute and horns were great as was the guitar, particularly in Freddie's songs. The rhythm section of percussion and bass drove the whole show with a relentless beat, and I loved the odd bit of xylophone. The choir were superb, their harmonies on "Merano", "Hymn to Chess" and "Anthem" were beautiful and as we could always see them, we connected with them throughout. Having the choir visible and invested in the action of the piece was one of the high points of the show. Not only was their singing most excellent but they doubled as ensemble at times; cheering on Freddie; waving flags for Anatoly and generally providing crown noise for the bigger scenes. They also looked great and sported several hand-held props and simple costumes. They were arranged in their black or white shirts diagonally across the benches upstage and looked and sounded fantastic.

Choreography was handled by the ubiquitous Jay Molyneux who gave us a great selection of styles on this show. There was much to like in the show, I loved the white gloves and the 'Durga' routine, which was repeated. I also liked some of the choreography during the chess games and "Golden Bangkok / One Night in Bangkok" was very well moved and a great second act opener with lots of energy and sexual tension.

Director Alfie Kilduff seemed to focus most of his energies on the presentation of the songs and at times it was like watching a 'Concert' version of 'Chess'. Florence and Molotov were the notable exceptions here. A lot of the cool looking visuals were kept for the song performances too, so that when the actor was singing it looked like they were in a concert or an MTV video. Almost every song was performed downstage and out to the audience and not in the location where it was meant to be set or to another performer.

Playing Freddie was Derek Collins who looked great in his white suit and relaxed attitude, he was every inch the brash American. He had a good relationship with Florence during the newspaper scene and his scene with Anatoly in Act II, when he is trying to help him was good. His singing was good and "One Night in Bangkok" was powerful, with loads of energy and a great vocal. As Florence we were fortunate to have Lucia Evans. She was absolutely the star of this production. Her vocal was incredibly poignant at times, full of expression, angst and feeling and at others just showstopping in its range. Her duet with Svetlana "I Know him so Well", was excellent and they bounced well off each other, and she brought the house down with her solos. Her acting was also good, she was invested in her fellow performers and had a great chemistry with Molotov in particular. Ms Evans owned the role gave us the most three- dimensional and rounded character in the show. As the third wheel in the love triangle, we had Anatoly, the Russian, played by Shane Kelly in a soft brooding performance. He sang well throughout but especially on "Anthem", where he was backed by the fabulous choir and gave a fitting lift to the end of Act I.

Emily Lohan played Svetlana, Anatoly's abandoned wife. Ms Lohan can turn her hand to any role and here she perfected the accent and showed the character's pain and anguish and sang well on "I Know him so Well" with Florence and on "Someone Else's Story" which is not often performed in productions of the show, but Athlone got permission. Kori Kilduff played the Arbiter with fierce focus and control. She held the stage with her presence and had a passivity in her performance that was quite riveting to watch. She sang very well throughout, and exuded confidence. As Walter, a TV presenter for Global News but also possibly in league with the CIA, Kieran Kilduff gave off a quiet confidence and was often seen on stage just observing. He played his sub- text quite subtly and sang quite well on the few songs he was in. Joe Steiner was brilliant as Molokov. He had great accent both in song and in dialogue and a wonderful energy as the devious Russian. He eclipsed others in every scene such was his focus, except Florence where he had a wonderful dynamic and they were equal. His singing was great especially on "The Soviet Machine". Paul Holloway played The Mayor. Mr Holloway had a fine presence on stage and sang well on "Merano". I also believe that I spotted him in other roles during the show...

The ensemble was very adaptable, becoming many different characters from Russian Embassy Staff to dancers to guests, they were aided and abetted by the ever-present choir and populated certain scenes with energy and presence. Cherise O'Moore's costumes looked very natural. Great range of costumes for the dancers especially the Thai look in "Golden Bangkok' and the black and white clad dancers and a great range of masks. The suits looked super, and I loved Molotov's red leather coat. Make- up was unaccredited but looked good. Hair by Rosaleen West was perfect, with Freddie looking dishevelled and Anatoly looking pristine. Stage manager Jonathan O'Brien and his crew were very stealthy, we hardly saw them. The transitions were quick and accurate, and he organised and assembled his cast and ensemble very well.

There was a lot to admire here, it just didn't gel as a musical theatre production. So, yes Athlone certainly did rise to the challenge and were successful in bringing 'Chess' to the audience, just not in the form expected.

show_raw: Joseph And The Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat
review_text:
The impressive INEC in Killarney was the venue for Killarney Musical Society's production of Joseph And The Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat. A huge bank of tiered seating had been placed in front of the stage stretching up to the back- balcony area. On the final night of their four-show run, this auditorium was well filled with a lively audience of all ages. On Tuesday, a daytime matinee had been attended by school groups who filled the auditorium. This early Tim Rice, Andrew Lloyd Webber collaboration is jammed packed with a huge range of musical genre and the piece is open to all sorts of styling and interpretation, giving the artistic team free rein with how this musical is staged and how the story is told.

In charge of the direction of the show was seasoned and talented director, Peter Kennedy who I am sure is no stranger to the piece. He made great use of the vast space of the INEC stage creating a raised level upstage which gave interesting acting areas. The cast of over seventy young and more mature players all seemed well rehearsed and very comfortable with their singing, acting and dancing roles. Peter had selected his cast well as each principal player related to the audience with some very pleasing singing voices on stage. The pace of the show never faltered with smooth links between scenes and musical numbers. There were super moments of comedy added, with hilarious nuances in some of the songs This is an exhausting show for any director. As there is no dialogue but with each word is sung, it means each moment has to be choreographed too. I salute Peter's stamina as choreographer for giving us an exciting and indeed challenging set of intricate routines which really pushed the abilities of the cast and chorus. There were changing patterns and then more synchronised movements with ample opportunities taken for movement in pairs such as in the upbeat jive influenced routines. The 'Hoedown' dance was a real celebration of the American West with energetic moves and detailed footwork. The Parisienne Tango in 'Those Canaan Days' was given an almost daredevil performance as the waitress was lifted, dived into the men's arms and spun around the stage. A great effort from all on stage who looked like they were really concentrating during each number.

Musical Director Noël Lennon took full charge of an orchestra of eleven players. There was a great drive in the accompaniment for the show with the changes in mood from one genre to another so well handled. The sound of the orchestra combined with a very well operated sound system meant that the words of songs were clear and harmonies were allowed to come through. The principals were all secure in their singing roles. The two narrators in the production sang in unison for most of the show and it might have been nice to vary that, possibly taking alternate lines at times. Joseph gave us some great moments of singing gymnastics when his voice really soared. The chorus work was great with strong voices creating some wonderful moments of harmony.

Orna Cleary O'Shea and Fiona Crowley made a great team as the two narrators. At times they gathered groups of children in front of them and addressed them as if they were teachers telling their class a story. They flowed around the acting areas helping to focus our attention on the action.

Rory Ward should be very proud of his portrayal of Joseph. He captured the youthfulness of the character at the start of the story and then the fall into slavery with some beautiful singing such as 'Close Every Door' in which he really excelled. Then the rise to fame and fortune to the prince-like figure whom the brothers did not recognise. Each aspect of the show was well acted and he quickly endeared himself to the audience. His Father, Jacob was nicely played by Gerry Adams  who gave the role a certain sincerity. He sang the part well and his facial reactions gave us a few laughs.

The Potiphars were courtesy of Johnny Courtney as Potiphar and Shinann Buckley-O'Sullivan as his wife. Very much in a 1920s style the husband dressed in black looked and acted like an old Lothario while his wife in heavily fringed dress was a flapper of the time. The 'Potiphar' number was quite racy and Shinann really let her hair down on that bed silhouetted against the curtain.

We had a strong family of brothers who worked well together in their dance routines and vocally too. There was plenty of the rough and tumble body contact which brothers usually have. They all really let themselves go in the big comedy numbers especially 'Canaan Days'.

Padraig Creedon led this number with great attack as Simeon pushing them into those long, long held notes which were funnier each time they were sung. Then Ben Quinlan, who also doubled up as the Baker, gave us a rhythmic 'Benjamin Calypso' in the role of Judah. He really delivers a song strongly with wonderful facial expressions and a natural easy body movement. Finally, Derek O'Leary created the Western feel of 'One More Angel In Heaven' as Reuben. Conor O'Leary was a very elegant Butler who sang his lines well.

The larger than life character of the Pharoah was played by Derry Healy with great style. The Elvis moves and hairstyle were all there for his big number.

Congratulations to a committed chorus who added so much to the look and feel of the production. Hopefully the younger generation will become the adult members of the future, some wee stars on stage to be sure.

The visual impact of the setting for the show was strong with two well painted and striking backcloths. One had sky, dunes and palm trees while the 'Egyptian' one was painted with a huge Pharaoh's head in golds and blue. The raised walkway upstage meant that the cast could vary their entrances onto the main acting stage area. It helped to create more interesting pictures on stage too. This raised area was edged with a castle wall which helped create the look of the Pharaoh's Palace.

Changes of scene were then created by the addition of set pieces such as the circular well, painted to appear like stone. Tables, chairs etc were brought on which helped to create a different scene on stage. These pieces were generally interestingly lit to create atmosphere and give depth to the stage. Props like the array of coloured flags were all in good condition and added to the show.

The costumes, particularly in the finale were quite stunning with sets of multi- coloured patchwork dresses for the ladies and patterned suits for the men. The result was a total riot of colour which made the 'Megamix' number something very special. There was a much more restrained colour palette used for the wives and the brothers' outfits during the rest of the show with the use of sepia tones.  The children had black trousers and brightly coloured t-shirts which looked particularly well when they were carefully placed on stage. The 'Egyptian' chorus looked splendid in black and silver with a set of black wigs. The coat itself was a wonderful patchwork of colours and sparkle. The coat was extended towards the end of the show by the addition of a huge cloak which flew in and was attached to Joseph. His gold collar and head gear in the Egyptian scenes were eye catching on stage. All the costumes were well fitted and well accessorised with jewellery and appropriate footwear. There was good attention to detail with the use of head-dresses and wigs. Make up had been gently applied and possibly the Egyptian scene might have benefitted from even stronger eye outlining. Joseph's eyes were particularly well defined which meant that his emotions punched out to us loud and clear.

This certainly was a huge undertaking in a huge auditorium but one which was successful, as the audience certainly had a wonderful time. The show moves along with a great pace and there really is no dead time on stage as the review nature of the production means we rattle on from one number to the next. But what a great journey we had, when watching Joseph And The Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat. We were totally entertained by this production courtesy of Killarney Musical Society. A slick, pacy and highly humorous show which was well moved and sung. Well done to all involved.

Up the People!

Trim Musical Society staged Michael Collins: A Musical Drama at Scoil Mhuire in Trim in February, and it was a very strange feeling going to see this show in the aftermath of the recent General Election where at the time of writing we do not have a new Government. Yet this show is all about sovereignty and the sacrifice of many for the future of the free-state and the right to self-govern. I'm sure the irony was not lost on the very appreciative audience who shared the room with me that night.

The foyer was bedecked in tricolours and army memorabilia and the front of house staff were costumed in Irish Army uniforms. First time director, but experienced musical director, Dermot O'Callaghan was at the helm relinquishing his baton to Mairéad McKenna on musical direction with Grace McGrath on choreography. This was a big change in tone from last year's successful comedy parody Urinetown but Trim Musical Society pride themselves on their versatility since 1987, producing thirty-three shows from the musical theatre canon; from G&S to Lloyd-Webber right up to this year's revolutionary Irish musical.

Michael Collins is a biographical show where we follow the life and times and eventual martyrdom of Cork's most famous son. The show concentrates on the years and the militants during and following the Easter Rising in 1916. Theatrically styled like Les Misérables and Evita with a W.B. Yeats play at its' core, this is a multifaceted piece of musical theatre that requires many talents and abilities to do it justice. The show's creator, the late Bryan Flynn, worked for years to perfect it and it is truly his magnum opus.

A very challenging show for a society to produce as it requires exceptional talents in singing and acting from all performers. It has a tricky and evocative score, some of which is tracked; multiple locations for the set designer to create and, probably most importantly, it requires empathy. It requires all involved to understand the feelings and passions of the characters and to share these with the audience. Similar to Schönberg and Boublil's Les Misérables, Michael Collins: A Musical Dramais a rousing, emotional rollercoaster of a show. Haunting, thrilling and very poignant as it's based on real life events. The first thing that struck us when we entered the auditorium was the set. Designed by the director and Aidan Mannion's company, Set 4 Stage, it was a basically a recreation of the façade of Dublin's GPO, with its massive Doric columns and broken windows. It loomed over the audience. On the apron were two projection screens one stage left, the other stage right, which were surrounded by block work and keyed into the whole art direction of the production. An empty stage was broken at the centre where it stepped down onto a lower platform, with treads leading into the auditorium. Either side was the band, sited on the floor in front of the stage. Lit in a preset of theatrical blue by lighting designer Darren Kelleher, who created very evocative and dramatic lighting states for this show. It all looked very striking and imposing. This windows in this clever set had sills which allowed performers, particularly the Chorus to dwell upstage, backlit at height overseeing proceedings and a mobile platform was very effectively wheeled on and off, which was used by Collins and Dev to speak to the people.

Costumes by Miriam Donnelly added to the realism of the piece and I really liked the distressed Prison garb! Ali Murphy's hair and make-up dovetailed nicely to create a fabulous looking show, complemented by Dónal Cantwell's bright and well-sourced projections. Alan White's sound design was excellent; bright vocals, violin and uilleann pipes, a sharpness to the snare, and an ominous depth in the bass and drones added to the dramatic tension of the production.

Director Dermot O'Callaghan really pushed this dramatic tension throughout; from the love triangle between Kitty, Harry and Collins to the Treaty Debates and the final shootout, the production had a tautness and air of impending doom. The entire plot was foreshadowed in a prologue where Collins lay supine with Joe Emmet over him whilst Mother Ireland watched. This was a marvellous opening and worked dramatically as Collins eventual death was not a dénouement as most of the viewers knew the story.

The acting and singing in this production was excellent. Michael Collins was played by Ray O'Hare who had the swagger and self-confidence of the Big Fella' and also displayed his passion and self-belief. Mr O'Hare had a great stage presence and well-honed stage craft and his voice was perfectly pitched for the character's songs. From the rousing "Every Heart Awaken" to the more intimate "Our Love Will Never End" with Kitty, Mr O'Hare's voice was full of expression, passion and conviction. As Kitty, the apex of the love triangle, Jenny McCabe was perfectly cast. She had an endearing quality as Kitty, alluring yet quite spirited. Her 'breakup' scene with Harry was beautifully played and her relationship with Collins was nicely paced. Ms McCabe had a fine voice on "Collins & Kitty" and the beautiful "Our Love Will Never End" with Collins. As betrayed Harry Boland, Kevin Hartnett brought a fervent thirst for the cause. He played his love for Kitty and her eventual betrayal of this love exceptionally well with high emotion. His singing on "Not That Man" was full of fury and superbly paced whilst on "Toast to the Host" it was sweet and delicate. Mr Hartnett captured Harry's character admirably; his admiration for Collins shattered by Collins' treachery influencing his politics.

Collins' young acolyte Joe Emmett was intensely played by Colin Flynn. This was a performance full of youthful energy and idealism, perfectly illustrating the disenfranchised young men of the time. Mr Flynn had a marvellous well- controlled voice too, noticeable on "Joe Interrogation" and "Prison Song". As Collins' opponent Eamon De Valera, Seán Hendley gave the character a gravitas and power that leapt off the stage. Portraying a quiet charisma, Mr Hendley showed De Valera's high intelligence and duplicitousness as he used Collins' enthusiasm to his own ends. He sang "Stepping Stone" and "Confrontation" with Collins very convincingly and with great diction and intensity.

With a nod to classical Greek theatre, Bryan Flynn created Chorus characters who narrated the show but also starred in the Yeats' play Kathleen Ni Houlihan, which is shown as an allegory to Ireland's struggle for independence. These five characters are mystical, otherworldly spirits that act as our guides; dressers and stage hands; Abbey Theatre actors and ethereal press reporters. Requiring prodigious singing voices as their music is so full of difficult harmonies and timing as well as good acting skills as they also play characters in Kathleen Ni Houlihan, Trim Musical Society struck gold with: Helen McHugh (Player 1/Bridget), Sean Flanagan (Player 2/Peter), Jane Brogan (Player 2/ Delia), Jordan Bass (Player 4/Michael) and Gwen Bagnall (Player 5/Mother Ireland). Individually all five had quite distinctively fine voices but when singing together, their chorale was electric. Ms Bagnall's sean nós was haunting and her physicality and stillness as Mother Ireland, captivating. Ms Brogan and Mr Bass gave fine performances as Michael and Delia, and were very strong as the Players. Ms McHugh and Mr Flanagan were perfect as Bridget and Peter, very Stage Irish in their playing, and commanding as the chorus. Excellent casting and performances. Other featured performers who impressed were: Shane Fox as a convincing Cathal Brugha; Séan Fox as a passionate Arthur Griffith, complete with moustache; Eoin Kenny as a Volunteer who really captivated in his debriefing scene with Collins.

Kitty's sisters were played by Jenny Seery, Louise Cassidy and Joanne King. All sang very well on "Toast to the Host" and had a lovely warm sisterly dynamic together. These performers also played as ensemble and were very strong in their singing and commitment to character. Generally, the whole ensemble on this show were very good, they exuded a passion for the work and clearly loved it. Their singing was exceptional under the direction of Mairéad McKenna, multiple harmonies and a raw but well-placed power in the delivery of the bigger rousing numbers created a wave of pride in the audience, where many who knew the piece felt compelled to sing with them.

Ms McKenna's interpretation of the score, although slightly hampered by the required tracking, was very good. Her work with the violin and clarinet was excellent as was the pounding drums and percussion. She conducted the band and singers and could be seen mouthing the songs along with the singers, which was lovely to see. The pace was relentless only slowing for the ballads and drones then it was back to the Celtic inspired rock-infused anthems. Grace McGrath's choreography was also great. It's not a big dance show, except for one or two traditional set pieces, but "Prison Song" with the men pounding the beat on the floor and with arms raised was good as was the staging of the bigger ensemble pieces. Stage manager, Frank Connolly and his crew kept these bigger scenes in check and the show rolled along with very swift transitions and cast wrangling.

Directing one's first show is often a baptism of fire and most directors would only remember the disasters. Jumping from being a musical director to a production director is not easy, all of a sudden you are the one everybody is looking at to make decisions because you are the one with the overall artistic vision for the production. If you don't have a cogent vision you cannot answer many of the questions. Luckily for Trim Musical Society their director, Dermot O'Callaghan did have a clear and lucid concept for this show and he effectively communicated it to his cast, crew and creatives. I suspect that his vision was rooted in sharing Bryan Flynn's desire to tell the story of Michael Collins' passion for his country but also, I think he wanted to share Mr Flynn's wonderful score and dramatic talents. Dermot O'Callaghan can look back on this show and consider it a triumph as I feel the audience did each night as they left the venue, feeling alive and grateful to their ancestors and humming the songs.

The Bardic Theatre is in a whole huge complex with the theatre as an integral part but also housing gymnasium and sports' training grounds. The theatre is very much a focal point for the community and it was obvious that the local community give their full support to the shows performed by this thriving company. This year the group had chosen Annie - The Musical. as their Spring show. This is a great way to introduce new talent to the stage but also the show provides some wonderful parts for the adult principal cast and there is plenty for the chorus to get their teeth into too.

The stage setting was quite stylish and simple in appearance with nicely painted Art Deco side panels and the Warbucks' mansion being created by the addition of smart French doors which had the Warbucks 'W' set on top. This was all set against a 3Dimensional effect of the New York skyline. Miss Hannigan's office was trucked on and was nicely dressed. The White House scene may have benefitted from the addition of two flags in stands at the back of the stage to add a little more colour, though the flag on the table worked well. The scene changes such as the removal of the orphanage beds were carried out with slick precision by a well- trained stage team. The result was that there weren't any long moments waiting for the next scene to start and the flow of the story telling was not interrupted. Indeed, the pace of the whole show was impressive throughout. The delivery of dialogue and the setting of the pace in this show is down to the orphans in that first scene. This was a wonderful team of girls. Each with great delivery of lines and each developing their own wee character in the role. Director Declan McGrath, who also played Daddy Warbucks, assisted by Claire Quinn must have worked hard with this talented group and they must have had fun too as the children were also having the time of their lives. I saw the group led by Aoife O'Neill as Annie but I believe the alternate group with Eva Donaghy in the title role was equally as talented.

The direction of the show added some lovely moments. We have to have that Bronxy humour but we also need the touching moments too. Some beautiful groupings of cast. The principals were all secure in their roles and at ease on stage, moving fluidly around the acting areas. The decision to change from the usual visual of the two main characters, (Warbucks was not bald headed and Annie was not in a red curly wig) was an interesting one but actually after that initial disappointment we really got so caught up in the acting that it ceased to matter. Damian Cullen who was Musical Director for the show added a slightly modern sound to the accompaniment of the show. He conducted from behind a keyboard with a further six players in the orchestra. Good tempi for the music with a driving rhythm for 'Hard Knock Life', building the beat in 'Easy Street' and a powerful 'Tomorrow' with a stunning harmony in 'Cabinet Reprise of Tomorrow'. The Boylans managed to capture that very tricky 1920s close harmony too. Good delivery of the songs with excellent diction.

Jamie-Lee Meneely was certainly a busy woman as not only was she Choreographer of the show but she also played the demanding role of Miss Hannigan. She gave us a set of interpretive and well-rehearsed dance routines. Some really novel moods and images such as the moves of the stylised businessmen in cream coats at the beginning of 'NYC'. The orphans' dances had lots of 'attitude' and punch and one thing which was impressive were all the dance endings with great positioning of cast for that final pose. Great energy from everyone, young and not so young on stage with facial expressions adding so much to those dance moments.

Aoife O'Neill acted and danced her socks off in the title role. She showed a real depth of emotion in the part and very soon had us captivated by her story-telling. She added so much gentle and not so gentle humour into the role, but there were those great moments of sadness and rejection which she played so well too, bringing a tear to many eyes. She even managed to tame Sandy the lovely Golden Retriever who came so easily to her. We need a great Annie for our show to work and we had one here. Declan McGrath who played Oliver Warbucks worked so well with Aoife. They built up a gradual love and respect for each other in front of our eyes. We had the driven businessman at the start changing into the doting daddy. Romance blossoming along the way with some well-played awkward moments with Grace. Nicely played and sung Declan. Jamie-Lee Meneely was the out of control head of the orphanage. This is a wonderful comic role and of late many women and men including Lesley Joseph and Paul O'Grady have brought the acid tongued character to life. We had all the aggression and sharp delivery of lines that we expect in the part. Good singing and delivery of the 'Little Girls' number with a well moved series of 'Easy Streets'.

There was something very authentic in the styling of Lauren McCrory as Warbucks' Secretary Grace Farrell.

This can sometimes be a thankless role but Lauren gave it a touch of class. She added an important part of the narrative and really helped to set scenes and move the story along. Wow, that green dress really gave a new dimension to the character and made Warbucks look at her in a totally different way. A stylish and convincing piece of acting.

Conor Begley had some of us in tears of laughter as Ralph Mudge. Earlier he was the 'Flash Harry' Rooster dressed to impress with all the strutting of a rooster in the farmyard. He really excelled though as Ralph which was a wonderful invention and hugely funny. The partner in crime Lily St Regis was played by Holly Foy McCann who was the dipsy side kick, always there to force Rooster on if he ever got off track. Conor, Holly and Jamie-Lee made a great team of baddies.

This core of principal players was extremely well supported by a talented and committed supporting cast of players. Brian Mills was strong as President Roosevelt, Bundles and Eddie. Sean O'Neill was a great Bert Healy and Ickes. Fergal Marshall took control as Drake. The Boylan Sisters sang into our hearts with great style. Dion Di Maio blowing us away with her performance of Star To Be too. Shane Coleman was Lt Ward, Malachy Quinn acted Judge Brandeis with authority and Alex Wimberley was the Radio Announcer. Other members of the company stepped forward to play other individual roles too.

The lighting in the show gave some interesting effects which really added to the piece. Nicely positioned 'specials' gave interesting pools of light. The moving lights have to be used sparingly as in a show set in the 1920s, they can seem out of place.

Clever use of the fade button for the stand microphones which gave the effect that the speaker's voice got louder as they approached the microphone. The sound team did a great job with great clarity of voice and a super voice/orchestra balance. Oh, and did I notice a clever use of songs with 'New York' in their titles playing as we came into the hall? - nice touch.

Some beautiful period costuming in the show. Lovely maroon set of staff costumes with white detailing. Well accessorised too. Some of the men's outfits were not quite right for the era and watch footwear as men really should have all been in black Oxfords with black soles. Annie really looked the part in her costumes which recreated the comic images. All the costumes were neat and fitted well.

Hair and make-up were generally in keeping with the era and style of the show. Grace looked so right with the hair styled to balance the lovely hat in which she first appeared.

It was a pleasure to be with this company who give so much back to the local community and in return get great support for their shows. This was a warm and gentle retelling of the Annie story. It looked good, it sounded good and I think the audience all felt the better for our experiences in New York in 1920s. Well done all in Bardic Theatre for a super night of Annie - The Musical.

This was a very interesting night on all sorts of levels in Glór in Ennis. I had stayed in the town for several days before the show on Wednesday night and there was a great buzz around the town about the production. The company had opened the show that Wednesday afternoon with a matinee for local school children. As we entered the foyer there were living statues of some of the actors in the production. The children posed motionless and were not going to be distracted into movement. The enthusiastic audience with representatives from other local societies more than made up with their applause for the reduced number in the auditorium. It is a confusing story on paper but as told by Ennis Musical Society, 'Seussical - The Musical' captivated us with detailed and clear story-telling. It is a story in which despite all odds Horton and Gertrude band together to save the Whos, free Horton, restore peace and unity to the Jungle of Nool. It is a story of friendship, loyalty and love which teaches us the power of being unique and the importance of fighting for your beliefs. It also tells how something so microscopic can have a huge impact, which has a real resonance in our world today.

Director Aódan Fox had his work cut out to manage the plot and make it totally believable while working with a large cast on stage. There are certain images that the audience have which are based on the illustrations in the Dr Seuss books and he held quite true to these. This was a pacy piece of direction with seamless changes from scene to scene thanks to clever planning and a well-organised stage team. The characters were all so well developed that we really related to their pain and their triumphs. Various underlying messages such as accepting difference were nicely teased out but not forced. We were entertained, at times we were moved by this production.

Some super up-tempo music in the show which talented Musical Director Shane Farrell brought beautifully to life for us. He had eleven players in the pit and there was a wonderfully balanced and rounded sound with the depth of brass and reeds balanced with strings. The cast microphones created a clear sound which was just at the right level for the accompaniment. Singing throughout was well performed from a talented cast and chorus work added some very pleasant moments of harmony.

So much scope for a choreographer in this piece and Edina Erdei rose to the challenge. From the young army's marching patterns, to the detailed and ever-changing formations of the chorus and the stunning individual dance moves of our Cat In The Hat. The show had commitment from the dancers and loads of sparkle. Very entertaining throughout. Brian Roche was the iconic Cat In The Hat. I suppose if we were to mention Dr Seuss that is the first character we think of. Brian gave us an engaging, energetic and fun persona, always suddenly appearing on stage in different guises. He impressed us by his acting of the role with a whole kaleidoscope of accents and looks. His dancing was wonderful, graceful and masculine, expressing the rhythms and lyrics in the music. Young Daniel Murphy is a real natural on stage. He obviously loved every second as Jojo and we all loved watching him in the role. He really played the part out to us in the audience with a real 'wee man' stance, relating so well to us and bringing us into his world. Well moved, acted and sung Daniel.

Patrick Kelly created a wonderful character as Horton the elephant. He slightly underplayed the role which worked so well. The result was a gentle giant whom we all loved and wanted the best for. He was the shoulder to cry on, the dependable friend and ultimately the great husband and father. Nicely acted and sung Patrick. His love interest was in the form of Gertrude McFuzz the beautiful bird with only one tail feather who goes to such lengths to have more feathers, only to discover that that is really not what makes her happy. A message to all those who try to change their looks. A super speaking and singing vocal tone for this part. Her singing was at times deeply moving and poignant. Well done Hazel Park.

Vampy Mayzie La Bird was played with great style by Lauren Rice. She really inhabited the role giving us that laisse faire attitude of one so beautiful she does even have to try. Lauren and her 'brood' gave us some memorable moments of high camp such as 'Amayzing Mayzie' and 'Mayzie In Palm Beach'.

Mr Mayor (Stephen Byrne) and Mrs Mayor (Vanessa Kirwan) were a good double act and bounced well off each other, particularly in those spoken rhyming moments when as an audience we are almost predicting what the last rhyming word will be. Some good comic timing from this pair. Looking every part the General was Rachael Culligan as General Gengus Khan Schmitz. This was a totally over the top military type with a wild marching gait. She brought many laughs as she tried to keep her ill-fated army under control. Olivia Parkinson played Sour Kangaroo who looked splendid with purple hair. Her offspring was in the form of a hand puppet with which she interacted well.

The Bird Girls who had a 'showgirls' appearance with corseted dresses and elaborate feather head gear, strutted around, very much looking and acting the part of support act for Mayzie. Elaine Gavin, Ciara Lynch and Fiona Coughlan looked appropriate and sang well together. Bursting aggressively onto the stage were the Wickersham Brothers who 'monkeyed' around the stage with good animal movements. They were colourfully styled with flashes of orange which suited their vibrant personalities. Nicely moved and acted Séan McInerney, Robert Sullivan and Declan Honan.

Des Sullivan gave us a strong portrayal of Judge Yertle The Turtle, forcefully taking charge of the courtroom. Cormac Ross was impressive in his role of Vlad Vladikoff. Other parts were played by members of the chorus.

Everyone worked together well as a team following the moves of both Choreographer and Director very well with drive and involvement.

There was a good overall look to the staging of the show with great use of primary colours. Initially there was a huge cut out of a red and white striped top hat in the centre of the stage, this was echoed by red and white stripes for side flats. An elaborately painted, and colourful piece of scenery was positioned up stage, this at times opened out to reveal the land of the Whos, complete with functioning door. Various other bright and colourful objects appeared such as the Big Top, the truck with Mayzie's nest on the top, that piano with the effective drips of paint on the back of it and many more. All these gave a magical, 'other world' feel to the show. The flooding of the back cyc with interesting colours meant that we had dramatic changes of mood. Nice to see the scrim cloth being used, it was effective for the underwater scene.

The various properties used and the dressing of trucks etc really added to the feel of the piece, from the twiggy nest to the foaming bath, all were colourful and appropriate for the show. The illuminated jellyfish and fluorescing fish were dramatic touches in the submarine scene. A field of clover pompoms was unfurled and really looked good. Lighting was good when it was good. Some nice touches. Sound was well balanced and well cued.

The costumes were a wonderful mix of ideas and colours. The costume team really should be praised for the attention to detail and the subtlety of colours and tones used. I particularly liked the army's yellow and cream outfits. The bird costumes were super especially Mayzie in her fiery red with feathery headpiece. The monkeys were brightly dressed in black with touches of orange. I loved the concept of Horton's grey dungarees, peaked cap with side pieces which looked like ears, very clever. The Cat's costumes were varied with sparkling waistcoats which added to the showman look.

The styling was completed with a good array of wigs. The Cat seemed to reinvent himself with a variety of styles and the judge looked very important in his long curls. Make up was strong when needed to create a character such as the birds in the group especially Mayzie who had a wonderfully dramatic look. Good eye shadows used to make the eyes really stand out.

This was a thoroughly enjoyable flight of fantasy. The cast gave it their all and the audience really appreciated their efforts. My heart goes out to the society who like so many had to cut their run short. I appreciate all those hours of planning, making, rehearsing and I feel a huge and heavy sadness for the performances which did not go ahead. Ennis Musical Society be assured that though your run was short we all enjoyed our magical trip to Seussical - The Musical.

show_raw: Joseph And The Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat
review_text:
Why do we go to see a musical? To be entertained, to see our friends and family, to escape, to laugh and occasionally to have a cry. Rarely do we attend a musical and our values are challenged, rarely do we come out after a show and think 'what was that all really about?' This was certainly the case with this clever and thought-provoking retelling of the Joseph story by Athlone Musical Society. Especially at this time of illness and flooding to near biblical proportions, ideas such as ignorance, greed, envy, care for others, are paramount in our minds and were central themes for this production of the now classic Joseph And The Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat.

Our first view of the stage as we entered was confusing. No palm trees here, no blue skies and pyramids but instead we are looking at a peaceful city park scene with distant skyscrapers. A raised area is accessed by tapering steps stage left and right from the main stage area. A park bench was placed right of centre with a large street waste bin beside it. Onto this urban scene wandered children all in anoraks with rucksacks and carrying posters calling for change. They were then followed by a whole group of out of control adults. Drunks urinating against trees, throwing waste newspapers and coffee cups and beer cans, a hen party drunk and noisy, someone being pushed around in a shopping trolley, smoking. When they left the scene, the stage was a mess and it was the children who had looked at the destruction created by their elders due to greed and excess, who ended cleaning up the mess. That was a powerful moment and in the middle of this was the Greta Thunberg figure, serious and taking it all in, making us see the world through her eyes. As the music for the show started a geeky looking Joseph appeared in the melee and gathered the group of children around him. The Narrator, stunning in winter white trousers and top introduced the show and in particular Joseph who didn't at this stage look like the leader of men. A great start to this absorbing production.

Alfie Kilduff directed the show at a cracking pace but allowing the show to breathe at times too. The story telling was paramount and this was expertly handled. The production was full to the brim with clever ideas and nuances which totally captivated the audience. The energy flaming out to us was electric. The commitment, remarkable from every person on stage.

Ger Madden did a wonderful job with the music in the show. The playing of the orchestra was en pointe but what I was really impressed with was the singing throughout the piece. The individuals not only could sing but they could really deliver those songs. When they sang, we were affected by them. The harmonies created in smaller groups but more especially by the chorus were just stunning and gave this score a whole new edge. At times the audience were almost on their feet half way through a number. Great diction in the singing and the humour of the songs was well pointed.

As I said after the show, forget the diets just do a night of Lea Carroll's choreography to lose the pounds! This was high octane dance. Fast moving, energetic dancing with precise steps and arm/hand placements. Cast were well positioned on stage, patterns were complex and many. There was great interpretation of the lyrics in a song which meant that the dance was an essential part of the story-telling. Tight and detailed movement throughout which kept building in each number until the cleverly placed final pose.

Initially Daniel Ryan looked like an unlikely hero. Dull overcoat, heavy rimmed glasses, checked tank top, not our usual vision of Joseph. In fact, when he first appeared, I wasn't sure if he was indeed our Joseph or one of the crowd, but that is exactly what the Director and he wanted us to think. Daniel grew and grew through the performance in strength of character as Joseph and vocally too, giving us a really well sung portrayal. This was an emotional rollercoaster which was a pleasure to see. Often the part of Narrator is played by two or more players, this time the weight of this huge linking role was in the more than capable hands of Cherise O'Moore. Always so much a focal point when on stage our eye was drawn to her. She moved effortlessly around the stage. Wonderful facial expressions and an ability to draw us into her world with all those songs so well sung. Paul Holloway brought the part of Jacob to life in a most realistic manner. We could see his pain when Joseph was lost but his flirtation with the French maid seemed to cheer him up.

Darren O'Hara really looked the part of a sun kissed Pharaoh straight from Las Vegas. He had the moves, the attitude and delivered the 'Song of The King' well. The direction of the Potiphar sequence made the Potiphar character into a computer magnate with an 'Apple' styling to the scene. Tomás Glynn made a Silicone Valley billionaire with cool, aloof delivery surrounded by his cool, aloof secretaries. A very stylish moment. Of course, his wife who was also …. you've got it…cool and aloof! played so well by Heather Doyle, seduced young Joseph. It was a racy moment which raised a few eyebrows in the audience.

Angela Bannon played the Baker in a very gentle way and made a good partnership with Mary Helen Hensley who was the Butler. Around this core of principal players was a superb team of wives and brothers. They sang and danced so well, even doing both together which was always a challenge for me on stage! Fantastic energy and drive in each number. Great interpretation of the feel of each genre of music shown in their body language. Of the brilliant band of brothers, Joe Steiner stepped forward to give us a husky Country and Western version of 'One More Angel in Heaven'. He also led that thigh-slapping 'Hoedown' which really blew us away. Jonathan Kilduff gyrated to the Caribbean rhythms of 'Benjamin Calypso'. This was a joyous number. Paul McCarrick really entertained with a real tongue in cheek version of 'Those Canaan Days', the sustained notes held for an impossibly long time!

The set very much added to the modern nature of the piece as the traditional Egyptian feel had been replaced by a cityscape and then a Caesar's Palace type set. With a carefully designed lighting plot and the addition of strings of lights edging the set, this was an evolving and adaptable staging. A raised upper level was accessed by nicely tapering steps right and left, which gave that pyramid shape. It was a well-lit show with good atmospheres created with lighting. Any changes were quickly completed such as the chairs and gingham covered tables brought on and set in front of a truck with a Parisienne Café painted on it. Great props such as the brazier with flickering light inside.

Every word as clear as a bell with the sound system creating a really good balance between the voice and instruments.

Costumes were many and were a total kaleidoscope of colour. The modern idea of Joseph's multicoloured hoodie actually worked well and the mini padded rainbow- coloured jacket given to our Greta character added such a moment of colour to the stage. The hairstyles all worked well with the themes of the show and make up was varied such as the strong eyes and tight hairstyling for Potiphar's secretaries. This was a detailed production which really did make an impact with the audience. A new approach was taken which really worked and added a certain resonance about modern life. Greed, envy at this time are ideals which might have been resting but have burst again into modern life. I always look forward to my arrival at The Dean Crowe Theatre as the Front of House team put in such a huge effort into making the outside of the theatre reflect the production. Multicoloured patterns covered the windows, wishing trees with coloured ribbons at the entrance. Then in the foyer, Chinese lanterns of every hue hanging from the ceiling. Even the bar area had had a makeover with coloured pillars everywhere. I thank Michael and Joan for making me feel so welcome. Our trip to Joseph And The Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat was amazing, it was definitely colourful and it was a bit of a dream of a show. Thanks to all involved but particularly the vision of Alfie Kilduff at Athlone Musical Society.

I was back in Firkin Crane Theatre to see UCC Musical Theatre Society's second full show of the season. This time the company had chosen the very age appropriate musical based on the Reece Witherspoon movie released in 2001, Legally Blonde - The Musical. With themes such as how women are treated in the workplace and indeed in society it was appropriate that I was there to see the show on International Women's Day. This is a performance with the production team of students from the university, the orchestra of students and yes, all those on-stage, students, indeed many of them First Years too. Such talent and commitment for their age and I do not mean that in any way to be patronising, but I am sort of jealous that I didn't do more when I was their age.

The direction was in the capable hands of Mary Condon O'Connor who quite unbelievably was directing a musical for the first time. She had obviously put in the hours and hours of work preparing and rehearsing the show, as this was a slick, fun production. She cut down on all the distraction that moving solid sets can produce and instead used lighting and well-chosen pieces to create the scenery. The movement of cast was generally well handled, though I would advise that straight lines are limited as they can be a little flat to the eye, better to create small groups instead. The story was well told and the characterisations were nicely developed through the production as at the end we really felt we knew everyone on stage.

This show is full of up-tempo music. The humour also has to come out during the songs and indeed this was achieved by our musical double act. Alina Whitla took great charge of the 12-piece orchestra, at times playing keyboards at other times with baton in hand. Cues were good and she created a well-balanced, rounded sound with lots of brass and beat. Anna Healy García had worked with the cast on their singing and overall, the principal cast were strong with great delivery of musical numbers even when they were dancing flat out. The chorus sang well too with good moments of harmony mixed in. There were lots of fast dance numbers which were danced flat out by an enthusiastic and obviously very fit cast. Emily Byrne and Kirsty Keating planned and rehearsed some really intricate routines, with clever footwork and explosive arm movements. There were some interesting patterns created but possibly this might be an area of choreography the team might think about developing in future productions.

Elle was well portrayed by great all- rounder Caoileann Nic A Bháird who sang, danced and acted the lead role with real energy and commitment. From that first number 'Omigod you Guys' she had the character established. She did however develop the role as the show progressed and we could see Elle grow into the confident attorney making her own life choices. One of which was her choice of man ending up with that wonderful kiss with former geeky student Emmet Forest played so well by Luke Maziarek. He too grew in confidence through the show and we all wished the love affair with Elle wold succeed. Warner was undoubtedly confident throughout! The 'Ivy League' student with a desire to be a success at whatever cost was played with just the right 'attitude' by Omar Sallam. There was good contrast between his look and manner compared to Emmett. He played the scene so well in the restaurant when he dumps Elle for the sake of his career. His university girlfriend Vivienne was courtesy of Hayley O'Connell Vaughan. She had all those wonderful cutting lines of dialogue and distain aimed at Elle. Eleanor Feeley was Brooke. This is the aerobics teaching defendant whom we first meet performing a flat-out aerobics class in prison. How she managed to talk and sing while doing that exercise was remarkable. She really created a very believable character, very much in the same vein as Elle herself. This was a strong performance.

Appearing older and initially more mature was Patrick Cleary as Prof. Callahan. His stiff delivery of lines suited the role he was playing. We were all a bit shocked when he made that move on Elle as we certainly didn't see it coming. A solid portrayal. Elle's best friends were a great team created by Kimberley Harris as Pilar, Aoibheann Malone as Margot and Allex Keily as Serena. We meet them first as the enthusiastic cheer team who came on before the show started to really point out that phones shouldn't be used, no photography and where the exits were. They made this witty but at the same time, they really got the message over and their advice was well heeded. Each one had very much their own personality and idiosyncrasies but they blended so well as a team too. They brought us humour, they helped push the story telling on, they all sang strongly and were all super movers too. Enid Hoops is the feisty student always prepared to put herself out there to stand up for her rights and those of others. This role was bought to life by Eileen O'Farrell who gave us a very forceful portrayal.

Playing Chad who is Paulette's love interest was Dillon English. He gyrated his way around the stage while delivering the mail. We all loved his cheeky, flirtatious manner and his punchy delivery of lines. He built up a brilliant on-stage partnership with Hairdresser and Beautician, Paulette. This was quite an extraordinary portrayal by Jude Donegan. Paulette at one moment had us all in tears of laughter but then was able to switch the emotion to pain and regret especially over the loss of her dog to her ex-husband. A wonderful creation of a character whom we all warmed to instantly. Those movements, tottering on heels and that giggle which made us all smile with her made Paulette our best friend. She was a great confidante of Elle and the two actors created a very believable friendship.

From a society's point of view one of the plus points for performing this show is that there are lots of supporting roles. These were all nicely played by cast who stepped out from the chorus. This chorus were all energetic and added much to the whole feel of the piece by their involvement. The show took place in what one would call 'a black box' with black cyc and black tabs. Into this box, pieces of set such as the bathroom scene with toilet and the versatile folding screen were speedily put into place. Some pieces moved by the well organised stage team and others brought on and struck by members of the cast. The flow of the show was rarely halted. One quirky piece of scenery was the impression of a caravan which added a sense of 'trailer trash' to the scene with Paulette's husband. Of course, the lighting has to be really good for this type of stripped-down staging to work and for the most part it did, with atmospheric shafts of light, though at times the faces needed a bit more warmth so we could see the expressions more clearly. The sound soon settled to a good level with a fine balance in the second half between voice and instruments.

Cleverly the costume team decided to make the costumes with a present day feel. There was of course every shade under the sun of pink for Elle who accessorised with an array of stylish shoes. The suits looked good especially the second one worn by Emmet. Some good cheerleader looks. The Greek Chorus looked different enough to really stand out. I was convinced that Elle's hair was the actor's own hair, dyed. It was a super wig which really moved well on stage. Paulette had loads of curls which seemed to suit her personality. The make-up was good though maybe Paulette could have been a little more natural looking. I liked how both Elle and Brooke were made up, particularly their eyes which were so well outlined.

This is a heart-warming story. One where we really can't take people for granted and we can't judge someone by how they look or talk. We will the leading lady to succeed and cheer when she does. There is probably a bit of Elle in us all, wanting to be taken seriously for who we are.

Well done to the cast and crew of UCC Musical Theatre Society's second show of the season and thank you for our journey in the world of Legally Blonde - The Musical.

The touching story based on the comic strip, which first appeared in 1924 and then became a staple on American radio in 1930s, involves the unusual friendship and respect created between Little Orphan Annie and billionaire Oliver Warbucks. They are from two different worlds, but maybe not, as towards the end of the show Warbucks confides in Annie that he too did not start life with a silver spoon in his mouth. Along the way we see both sides of the Great Depression and the show needs to clearly differentiate between the haves and have nots. Traditionally set in the 1920s era the details of costume, set etc should all reflect time and place. This is quite a challenge for any society as it usually involves a large cast with many 'little girls' needed to play the orphans and a team of staff to run the Warbucks' mansion.

Castlebar Musical and Dramatic Society staged this musical in St Mary's Hall, GMIT in the town. That alone is quite an achievement as everything has to be built from scratch. Stage has to be built, lighting bars secured, seating moved into place, all before any set or prop can be put in position. I am sure this is a huge task for the stage team who deserve great credit for their efforts.

In charge of the direction of the show was busy Director Donna Ruane. I was impressed by the obvious amount of work she had done with the cast, particularly the young cast, who really burst onto the stage and set a rip-roaring pace for their scenes. I was at the show on the opening night so I am sure the pace of the other scenes which did drag slightly will have picked up during the run. Donna grouped the company nicely at times creating some very pleasing pictures on stage. There was quite a lot of humour teased out of the script especially in those scenes with Hannigan, Rooster and Lily. She had decided that Warbucks should keep his hair but Annie was in a good curly red wig. I sort of missed Sandy the dog. Its never quite the same acting to an imaginary one off stage and a real one can be testing to say the least, but Sandy running to her is such a magical moment.

That said Donna chose her cast well as everyone gave their role great commitment.

There were wonderful American accents through the show, I can be a bit of a stickler for that 'th' sound but all was spot on here.
