The story was nicely told with some moments of charm and sentiment and the audience loved it. Deirdre Lee created that authentic twenties' sound with her seven-piece orchestra. It was, at times a punchy piece of playing with well driven rhythms and then beautifully melodic with some of the softer numbers. Again, I am sure that the principal cast will grow in confidence in their singing as the show runs. Leading players were at times very impressive singing clearly and always in character. The harmonies in ensemble pieces were very well practised and the men's voices added a wonderful background depth. Elly Cazabon Reagan created some interesting moments of dance and movement in the show. She was a little restricted by the size of the stage and I am sure she wanted to extend some of the numbers even more. We had a great 'Hard Knock Life' performed so well by a really enthusiastic group of girls and a well told story in 'A New Deal For Christmas'. This show centres around the trials and tribulations of Annie, from orphanage to mansion and a few other places besides. We need a young lady who can really act a range of emotions and really sing too. Rachel Gallagher played the part extremely well, getting all the emotion and comedy from the lines. She has a wonderful control of her singing voice for her age with a stunning tone. She built up great relationships on stage which seemed very natural. Ronan Egan went from bullish businessman to a bit of a softy, at least as far as Annie was concerned, in a well delivered portrayal of Oliver Warbucks. Ronan has a strong rich vocal tone which suited the role.

Grace Farrell, Warbucks' Secretary was gently played by Mary Dempsey. She was nicely styled for the part with a period hairstyle. She was elegant and classy in the role. Everything that her Nemesis, Miss Hannigan isn't! Vivienne Lee created the monster that is Miss Hannigan. She gave us some good comedic moments as she swigged the booze and staggered around the stage. Her scheming brother Rooster was brought to us by Gearóid Herraghty who acted the money grabber with great charm. He was well supported in his crimes by the glamorous Lily St Regis played with real flapper style by the talented Sonja Stevens. She never stopped acting for a second in the role, fixing a seam, sorting the curls, checking her make-up. Great facial expressions too.

President Roosevelt was portrayed with great strength by Richard Heneghan. He impressed with the delivery of his lines and the way he commanded the stage. He has a beautiful 'dark chocolate' richness to his singing voice which worked well in the role.

Andy Hannon was busy as Bundles fighting off Miss Hannigan's advances with a nicely delivered put down and then as the authoritative butler, Drake. He played both roles well. Liam Connell was the announcer Bert Healy in a slick Radio Station scene which also included the all singing Boylan sisters who gave good harmonious singing of 'Never Fully Dressed'.

Annie was well supported by a team of orphans including Louise Ward as Duffy, Emily Prendergast as Pepper, Ciara-May Ball as July, Cara Caufield as Kate, Anna Barry as Tessie and Lucy McDermott as Molly. Well played girls you and the rest of the group must be very proud of how you came across on stage.

There was a super chorus from whom players stepped forward to perform incidental parts. Well done everyone on a great effort.

As I said earlier this was a difficult piece to stage and some of the sets used did take up valuable stage space. I would possibly rethink what is really needed to give the effect and maybe cut down on solid walls etc. Sometimes a black box with well chosen pieces can give the impression of a solid set. There was a good staircase in the Warbucks' mansion and nice book effect for the library. The orphanage window looked effective with reversed writing on it. Interesting props such as Christmas tree appeared in place very quickly and indeed, I commend the stage team for their speed of changes. Props often added to the authentic feel of the piece with good grey blankets in the orphanage, super ventriloquist's dummy, microphones etc There were some good lighting effects through the show with nicely defined 'specials' which created good pools of light. I wasn't wild about those moving lights during some numbers as they can distract. The sound was good throughout with excellent balance.

The costumes were a bit of a mixed bag. A little more attention to detail might be needed in future productions to really capture the look of the era and the season of the year. But I give credit to the hard- working costume department who had a great number of outfits to prepare. Grace looked stunning in her clothes and Miss Hannigan had a glamorous styling. The orphans all looked just right.

Some good wigs on stage and some neat hairstyles for the servants. Rooster had a real spiv moustache and Lily's hair was a mass of waves.

There was such a wonderful buzz around the auditorium for the opening night of the show. Friends and family were out in force to cheer on the actors. They were given an entertaining show which although there were a few teething problems, I am sure will settle into a more pacy piece of musical theatre. Thank you all in Castlebar Musical and Dramatic Society for our trip to NYC for your production of Annie -The Musical. As I type this review with the rain pelting against the window, I too hope that 'The Sun'll Come Out Tomorrow.'

This way, Madness lies… UCD Musical Society staged Our House, the musical by Tim Firth based on the songs of London ska group Madness, in the Astra Hall in February this year. Self- confessed musical theatre novice, Suggs - the main signer with the band, agreed for the band's music to be raided by Mr Firth to create the show in 2002 and even starred in a few productions as the hero/ anti-hero's Dad. It's a peculiar show, with elements of the film Sliding Doors, where we follow the lead character, Joe, and the two diverging paths he takes in life; one honest the other, dishonest.

Directed by Roy Geary, assisted by Caoilfhionn Ní Dhúlaing, who was also Chorus Mistress with musical direction by Hannah Reilly and choreography by Lauren Dooley; this was a fun-filled show with a talented bunch of performers and some clever quick-change effects. The set was a platform stage with three doors upstage and two smaller platforms downstage right and left. A further narrow platform upstage overlooking the stage was effectively used as a higher playing area and furniture and props were brought on and off as needed. Jody Trehy's sound was excellent with good balance between band, situated at stage right, and singers. Lighting by Tim Coyne was a bit haphazard and not well-cued but well done to the cast who found their light when needed. Stage management by Ada McDonagh was very good with very quick transitions thanks to the crew and it was a very slick show.

In the lead was Peter Richardson who played Joe. This was a very difficult role necessitating very quick changes not just of costume but character. Joe is out on a date with his new girlfriend, Sarah, when he takes her into a building site. Romantic eh? But as he's only sixteen, forgivable. The cops arrive to investigate and this is where the split occurs. One Joe stays and takes his medicine, the other runs away. Thus, the diverging storylines, as we follow one Joe who falls into criminality and the other who ends up in prison and struggles to get a career hampered by a criminal record, over a period of seven years. Mr Richardson excelled as both sides of the same character. As 'bad' Joe, he had a sneering obnoxious quality, not believing in anything but his own pleasure and invulnerability; as 'good' Joe, he showed a caring side, particularly for his mother and Sarah and a willingness to right the wrongs of his past. Mr Richardson also sang exceedingly well on "Rise and Fall" and "It Must Be Love" with Sarah and "Simple Equation" with Dad.

Rory Sheehy played Dad in a superb performance full of regret and longing and desperation to help Joe and his mother. His opening number "Simple Equation" and its subsequent reprises were beautiful and heartbreakingly sung by Mr Sheehy. He loomed over a lot of the action like a flawed guardian angel, full of angst and sorrow. He sang with a few characters, most notably Sarah on "N.W. 5". Sarah was played by Niamh McGowan and she was perfectly cast in the role. Her Sarah had a very mercurial morality, standing by 'good' Joe as best she could but also marrying 'bad' Joe, seduced by wealth and status. She sang well on "It Must Be Love" and "Tomorrow's Just Another Day" with Joe and "N.W. 5" with Dad. As Joe's Mum, Kath, Laura Fleming was great. She had a gentleness befitting the maternal nature of Kath and sang and danced with effectiveness and good ability. Ms Fleming had a strong presence in the role and the audience were visibly upset when she came to a sticky end in one of Joe's realities.

'Bad' Joe hooked up with local gangster, Reecey, who was played by Aisling Benson in a role usually played by a guy. Ms Benson had a fine alto and sang Reecey's songs with ease, particularly "Shut Up" and "Baggy Trousers" with the Joes. Her strong physicality and pointed stare added to the character's danger. Joe also worked with an unscrupulous property developer Mr Pressman, played with an unconscious menace by Pádraic Ó'Brolcháin in a fine, still performance. We also followed the fortunes of Joe's school fiends, Emmo and Lewis; played respectively by Michael Bergin and Cormac Gilligan. Mr Bergin developed a great character, his Emmo was clearly intellectually wanting but with a bright sense of comedy and a quirky physicality. Mr Gilligan's Lewis was equally adept at comedy and his timing was excellent. Both also sang with gusto on "Driving in my Car" with Joe, Sarah, and Sarah's friends Billie and Angie. As Billie, Alice O'Loughlin Kennedy was hilarious. She had superb comic timing and sang well as did Clíona Nic Shuibhne's Angie. All four character's journey's over the seven years were well plotted and quite believable. The music of Madness is very danceable and it was no surprise that there was extensive choreography in this show. Directed and created by the show's choreographer Lauren Dooley, most of the routines were extremely well-drilled and executed with a high-spirited panache. The big opening number "Our House" was excellent as was the Las Vagas sections and the smaller numbers were super. I liked the opening pas de deux and that the show closed with Joe and Sarah and his Mum and Dad waltzing on the small platforms. Intelligent, fun, high energy and at times poignant choreography from Ms Dooley.

Musical director, Hannah Reilly's band were very visibly moved by the music, we could see them at stage left, almost dancing as they played the infectious tunes. Ms Reilly's arrangements were great, the brass was very present, particularly Chloe McNamara's sax and Henry Start's trumpet especially on the more ska-oriented numbers like "Night Boat to Cairo". Drums and bass kept everything pulsing along and the keys and guitar added melody to a very fine interpretation of the score. Caoilfhionn Ní Dhúlaing's choral work with the ensemble was also exceptional. She managed to get some beautiful harmonies on "Wings of a Dove" and "The Sun and the Rain" and "Our House" rang out with power and delicacy.

Costuming on this show, even though most of it is contemporary, is quite tricky. The actor playing Joe must have some very quick changes between characters. Bebhinn Hunt-Sheridan created two very different looks for Joe, one black-clad the other white. The 'good' Joe costume tore away offstage to become 'bad' Joe very quickly and vice versa. Excellent work. Make-up by Nino Tsereteli and Sadhbh Geoghegan was suitable for the era and well-applied. Director Roy Geary created a very good version of this somewhat difficult musical. The splitting of the two Joes and their re-uniting was brilliantly done and his staging of the whole show on the platform with very little set was excellent. His work with the actor's intentions was also admirable; Dad's frustration and helplessness was palpable; Joe's duel personality was expertly directed and Sarah's realisation of what 'bad' Joe had become was emotional. His work with the ensemble was also really effective, the performers were fully invested in the show and their energy and commitment to character and to telling the story jumped off the stage. The vocals and band were beautifully harmonised and we all left the theatre singing snatches of various Madness songs. A great show, wonderfully produced.

Retro Overkill Tipperary Musical Society presented The Wedding Singer at the Excel in February of this year. Directed by Bill Stafford with musical direction by Helen Colbert and choreography by Miriam Ball. It's the '80s and wedding band singer, Robbie Hart lives in his grandmother's basement. His dreams of being a singer/songwriter are long faded, replaced now by a simple desire to find the right girl and settle down. When his fiancée leaves him, he takes out his cynicism about romance on stage at the various weddings they play at until he gets to know and fall for Julia, a waitress. But she's engaged to a greedy Wall Street hot-shot who unbeknown to her, cheats on her. Robbie decides to embrace this 'greed is good' lifestyle and woo Julia away. It's a humble little story full of caricatures, clichés and retro trappings, typical of the American films of the nineties, where indeed it started out as a star vehicle for Adam Sandler and Drew Barrymore. The music doesn't have any real ear worming songs, but Helen Colbert's musical direction was quite good. Her keyboard heavy band of ten musicians were very tight and a special mention must go to the guitar players, who rocked it out of the venue at times. There was little room for intricate harmonies in the score but the chorus was good and strong. Miriam Ball's choreography was also quite good, especially on the bigger numbers, with more than a nod to Flashdance, Material Girl, Thriller and many other routines made famous by MTV.

Tipperary Musical Society recruited Ben Hennessey to design the set and this was a great choice as it was big, bold and beautiful, with integrated projection screens so we could watch MTV Music videos on a pre-show loop. Blocks of colour on the back wall were mirrored with floor painting and there were treads up to an upstage platform. Robbie's bedroom and a small stage complete with Billie Jean floor lights on stage level made for a very clever utilitarian playing area. A trucked bathroom, some tables and chairs and grey DeLorean car added interest to this very well-designed and painted stage set.

It was quite a well-cast show, with our eponymous hero, Robbie Hart being played with a youthful vigour by the fabulously named Edmund Gubbins. He had an incandescent energy which shone from the stage out into the audience. Eminently watchable, Mr Hart had a good dynamic with his fellow bandmates and a nice chemistry with Julia. His singing was excellent, particularly "Awesome" and "If I Told You" with Julia. As Julia, Amy Cummins, also had a nice energy. She held the stage well and worked very well with Robbie and whilst she seemed to struggle on some of the higher notes on her songs, she had a lovely tone and I liked her timing on "Come Out of the Dumpster" and her other duets with Robbie, especially "Grow Old With You" which was sweet. Ms Cummins played Julia's naiveite and purity with skill, while showing her inner conflict as to who to choose: lovely but poor Robbie or shallow but rich Glen, who was played by Jason Ryan. Mr Ryan had a striking presence, looming over most of the cast he used his physicality to great advantage, denoting Glen's higher status. His voice was good, but not as powerful as one would like. However, his performance of "All About the Green" with Robbie and the ensemble was excellently delivered. His character was very different to the others and he made the most of this with his sneering "Gordon Gekko" like proclamations about money and the acquisition of wealth making him invincible and irresistible. Robbie's ex-fiancé, Linda, who jilted him at the altar by sending him a note, was played by Claire O'Dwyer. Ms Dwyer had a great rock voice on "A Note from Linda" and superb dance moves on "Let Me Come Home". Her characterisation had a quiet sensuality yet sadness, which Ms O'Dwyer played very well.

Robbie's Grandmother, Rosie, was played with a delicious boldness and cracking energy by Michele Foley. Ms Foley went full-on Mrs Brown, minus the bad language, for the role and really impressed with her characterisation. Her rap song "Move That Thang" with George was a highlight of the show. George was one of Robbie's bandmates and played keyboards and sang in the wedding band. Portrayed by Richie Crowe, and styled after Boy George the eighties singer, he had a nice understated naturalism on stage. His singing was quite good and he had a lovely tone to his voice. The other bandmate was Sammy as played by Adam Skeffington. Mr Skeffington was very energetic on stage, styled like an extra from Grease, he had a good presence and excellent comic timing. He sang a nice duet, "Right in Front of Your Eyes", with Holly and demonstrated a good voice. As Holly, Julia's friend, Rachel Breen stole the show. She was constantly 'on', reacting to everything with a shrug, a yell or a raised eyebrow as she examined her nails. This was a super performance from Ms Breen and her singing with Sammy was delightful. Sammy and Holly had a great chemistry on stage and the audience were willing them to re-unite. The ensemble was rather good too. Playing wedding guests, workers in Wall Street and many other roles including celebrity impersonators; Mr T, Billy Idol, Tina Turner etc. The costuming and make up on these characters was excellent. They really looked their parts and were a testament to the designers. Hair and make-up duties were proficiently looked after by a large team of people who cleverly recreated the 1980's look. Costuming was supervised by by Aileen Ryan and Siobhan O'Donoghue and hired from Nomac, Pat McGann and TMS and suited the era. Rosie's shell suit was especially accurate! Sound by Star Systems was full and there was good balance between singers and band and lighting design by Paul Browne worked well for the show, especially the mirror ball. It was all stage managed by Denis Fitzgerald and his crew whose transitions and scene changes were quick but a bit over lit!

The Wedding Singer is not the most exciting musical in the world. But it's a nice little story, and has some clever eighties references in the writing and some very personable characters. But it requires a director with a very unique vision to give it the energy and pace it needs. Unfortunately, I don't think the required vision to make it work was realised. There was a peculiar hollowness to this production and I was trying to figure out what caused it. I mean, the leads were very good as was the ensemble. The band were spot-on and it had great visuals with Mr Hennessy's set and the costume and make-up and so on. But I feel it was the direction. There were times when the cast seemed almost afraid to interact with each other, delivering everything out to the audience. In some of the earlier scenes when Robbie was speaking at the weddings, he directed the speeches out to the audience. The cast, meanwhile, were just mouthing to each other silently when they should have been loudly protesting at him ruining their celebrations. This created a vacuum on stage, which was very difficult for the cast, especially Robbie, to fill, when they couldn't speak aloud or improv or ad lib. This happened a lot during the show, vacuums on stage. It was a pity because the cast were great when they were allowed to be loud. Rhubarbing is an important device all directors use, but we must hear it. We must be able to hear the babble of voices, even with their mics off, it adds life to the world of the show. Theatre is a reflection of real life, as Shakespeare sort of said, but it has to be played out larger than life and Opera and Musical Theatre is even bigger, it must leap off the stage and grab the audience and make them laugh and cry and sing and empathise with the

American Dreams Carrick-on-Suir Musical Society staged Rogers and Hammerstein's 1943 musical, Oklahoma! in the Strand Theatre in Carrick- on-Suir in March of this year. Directed by Liam Butler with musical direction by Fergal Carroll and choreography by Edel Quinlan, this was a fairly traditional telling of the story with a wonderful set designed and painted by John O'Donoghue and exquisite lighting by Eoin Sheridan. It all looked very clean and picture-perfect with well-pressed costumes and highly polished boots. This was a beautiful looking production and the third outing by the Society for this classic musical, having previously staged it in 1966 and 1980. But, of course the success of this show rests, like most shows, on the shoulders of the lead characters and not just how it looks. In the lead role of cowboy Curly McLain, we had a very animated Michael Raggett vying for the attentions of local woman, Laurey Williams, who lived on a farm with her aunt. Mr Raggett's Curly opened the show with a spirited and perfectly sung "Oh What a Beautiful Morning". His characterisation of Curly was interesting in that he initially came across as quite creepily stalkerish but this was clearly because he wasn't very good at courting. He showed Curly's ruthlessness when he tried to get Jud, a farmhand who worked on Laurey's farm, to commit suicide. Mr Raggett played this scene very well, jokingly but with a malicious undercurrent. His singing was excellent, "The Surrey with the Fringe on Top" and "People Will Say We're in Love", with Laurey. Sandra Power played Laurey as cossetted and quite aloof with a lethargic disposition, in a sense the polar opposite of Curly, except when she was in trouble and ran to Curly for protection. But opposites attract so the characterisation did make sense. Ms Power sang with evident skill on all of Laurey's songs but most notably on "People Will Say We're in Love" with Curly and on "Many a New Day" with the chorus, where the character really came alive. She had a good chemistry with Curly and a great dynamic with her onstage aunt, Eller.

As Aunt Eller, Irene Malone really shone in this show. Her Eller was feisty, brave, independent and yet quite thoughtful. The matriarch of the town, she ruled the roost and Ms Malone exuded high status and control in the role. Her singing was excellent although she did not have any solo numbers, she led in some of the bigger chorus songs and her voice was very prominent. A very intricate characterisation, full of warmth yet quite dangerous to cross. Her farmhand, Jud Fry, was played by Derek Ryan in a bravura performance that all but eclipsed everybody else on stage. Mr Ryan's deep characterisation of Jud; from his stutter to his stooped physicality and penetrating gaze was electrifying to watch. He oozed menace and danger but Mr Ryan also portrayed a troubled, clearly damaged man where one can only imagine the atrocities he witnessed and possibly committed in his childhood. His singing was also superb, "Poor Judd in Daid" with Curly was quite sad as we knew he didn't realise what Curly was trying to do. The song of the evening for me was Mr Ryan's rendition of "Lonely Room" where he sang of his unrequited love for Laurey and poured all of the slights he bore and the bitterness he felt into this showstopping song.

The love triangle between Curly, Jud and Laurey was very effectively performed by all three. The relationships of these characters were most markedly illustrated in the prescient dream dance sequence towards the end of Act One where dream Curly (Brian Cahill) and dream Laurey (Katie O'Shea & Leah Dunphy) and Jud (Derek Ryan) played out a future alternate reality with great skill. Choreographed by Edel Quinlan, this dream sequence was excellently directed and executed by all of the dancers and Mr Ryan integrated well into the routine. Ms Quinlan's other work on the show was also really good "The Farmer and the Cowman" scene was quite intricate and fun as was "All Er Nothin'" with Ado Annie Carnes and Will Parker.

As Ado Annie, Ruthie Raggett was really well cast. She showed the coquettish charm, yet fickleness and had the comic timing that this character requires. Her song "I Cain't Say No" was extremely well sung and she had a good chemistry with Will, who was played by James O'Donovan. He had a super energy on stage and portrayed Will's foolishness with a nice comedy. He led "Kansas City" with a fine voice and gave us a very likeable Will Parker. Annie's other suitor was Ali Hakim, a Persian peddler played by Neill Bourke. Mr Bourke's accent was perfect and I really liked his manic, slapstick liveliness. This was another love triangle, albeit a more light-hearted one and the three performers had a lovely buoyancy to their playing, their comedy almost vaudevillian, particularly Mr Bourke and Ms Raggett who had a great comic chemistry.

Surrounding these two rather complicated love stories, we had the townsfolk: Gertie Cummings, whom Ali eventually ends up with, was played by Siobhán Grace- Regan in a very funny performance. Her laugh will haunt me forever. Ike Skidmore, a farmer who owns the land where the box social took place, was solidly played by Chris Hanlon and Slim, another farmer, was soundly portrayed by Declan Smith Robinson. Jim Kennedy played Local Marshall, Cord Elam with a capricious authority. I liked how he played Cord's indecision, bowing to public pressure. Ado Annie's shotgun wielding father, and local Judge, Andrew Carnes was played with assurance by Seamus Power, who was back treading the boards after his two-year diplomatic absence.

Musical director, Fergal Carroll and chorus master, Eamon O'Malley did a great job on the show. The arrangements were sumptuous, beautiful lush strings and pitch perfect woodwind and horns backed by a solid bass and percussion and permeating piano. Mr O'Malley's choral work was also excellent. The male chorus on "It's a Scandal! It's an Outrage!" were particularly fine and the female chorus on "Many a New Day" were quite good. But it was on the title song "Oklahoma!", where we could really appreciate the harmonic power of the ensemble.

Michael O'Hara stage managed the show with skill and the help of his very good crew. Star Systems helmed a nicely balanced sound and Eoin Sheridan's lighting design showed off not just the actors but John O'Donoghue's fabulous scene painting. This was on the upstage wall, lit by a ground-row, and extended out around the proscenium arch. A fence upstage and some home-made cornstalks were very rural, with Eller's house hinted at on stage right. Cleverly leaving a large playing area centre stage, there were ramps on the left and right apron and working ladders affixed to the proscenium, the large ensemble had oodles of space. Costumes and hair were of the period (1908) and the make-up was fine.

This was a very well-cast and directed show by Liam Butler. He had a light touch with most of the scenes as required and really brought out the pathos of Laurey's Jud Fry predicament. The show is renowned for its over-long first act, but I felt that it zipped along and Edel Quinlan's excellent dream sequence added so much to the story, that I didn't want it to end! A nice, tight, charming production from Carrick-on-Suir that had the audience on their feet at the end wanting more and that says it all really!!

Festive Fun!

It was a real pleasure to see Belfast Operatic Company back in a beautifully refurbished Grand Opera House for this festive show. The atmosphere certainly confirmed the anticipation of everyone welcoming back live musical theatre after a difficult time. The whole production team gave the audience an excellent example of what has been missed for so long, in a very fine show with an excellent large cast and orchestra.

A Christmas Carol: The Musical is a 1994 American musical, based on the 1843 novella by Charles Dickens with music and lyrics by Alan Menken and Lynn Ahrens. The book is by Mike Ockrent and Lynn Ahrens. It also inspired the American televised film of the same name in 2004 which starred Kelsey Grammer as Scrooge. It was first performed at the Paramount Theatre in Madison Square Garden, and then annually from Dec 1st 1994 until 2003, with Tony Randall, Roger Daltrey, Tim Curry, Jim Dale and Frank Langella as notable Scrooges. Concert performances have been produced in London every December from 2016 to the present with Robert Lindsay, Griff Rhys Jones and Brian Conley amongst the actors to have played Scrooge.

Director Wilfie Pyper directed and oversaw a large company of somewhere in the region of 80 adults and children, with wonderful skill in this admirable production. The sumptuous setting of the Grand Opera House refurbishment fitted perfectly with the Dickensian theme and housed the large audience magnificently. Using all of the large Opera House stage very effectively, he moved his chorus with flair and effortless pace from the first scene to the last, keeping the audience enthralled throughout, and producing a magnificent festive feast with all his production team, especially Production Manager Carole McClure and Stage Manager Marie Cusack, who, with all the performers and stage crew, ensured a seamless production. Castors on most of the larger furniture ensured very fast transitions between scenes, which benefitted the overall tempo of the production. Continuity was excellent throughout. Instead of a large cumbersome set, which would have proved difficult for continuity, large projections by Chris Thompson depicted the scenes beautifully and also combined with the very effective lighting by ACK Productions, to create the necessary, and at times, outstanding atmosphere. This was especially so in undoubtedly the visual moment of the entire show, which featured the children all in white, with the Ghost of Christmas Yet To Come, all of them acting as a final warning to Scrooge. Musical Director Adam Darcy brilliantly led the singers and large orchestra of 18, which produced a thrilling sound helping create energy and pathos in equal measure. Sometimes the balance in sound between the orchestra and individual singers was a little lopsided, but the choral singing, in particular, was of a very high quality and Alan Menken's music was beautifully served. Choreography by Timothy Bell was synchronised and innovative, especially when using the excellent female dancers, who showed precision as well as flair. His choreography for 'Link By Link' was also very notable with Jacob Marley and his scary entourage.

Colin Boyd as Scrooge led Dickens' famous story as the miser, who is warned from his selfish ways to the happy ending we all know and love. His reactions throughout admirably helped build the storyline. Jacob Marley (Matthew Campbell) stole the show with his wonderful and ghoulish characterisation. 'Link by Link', which he sang with his ghostly companions, was most definitely a highlight of the show. All of the ghosts were 'flown' with great expertise, especially when it must have been difficult to rehearse in the theatre with Covid restrictions. Duarte Silva Moreira as Tiny Tim managed to steal the audience's hearts in a beautifully judged performance.  Naomi Smyth as Emily looked and sang stunningly in her small role. The Fezziwigs were the comic highlight of the production with Laura Kerr as Mrs Fezziwig standing out with her characterisation, a mixture of Dickensian parody and a touch of Madame Thenardier from Les Miserables.

This was a very fine production with a very large group of performers, musicians, creatives, production team and front of house. Belfast Operatic Company should be justifiably proud of their first production after emerging from the restrictions of the Covid pandemic. If they carry on as well as this in future productions, they will have no trouble filling the magnificent, newly refurbished Grand Opera House  and entertaining all their followers and patrons.

Superpowers, CIA and KGB manipulating an International Chess Championship, two grandmasters embroiled in a love triangle with a Hungarian refugee, absentee parents, the height of the Cold War, trapped in the 80's with some questionable scoring from Ulvaeus and Rice and there you have it 'Chess' the Musical. Like it or loathe it, it's still going strong since its release in 1984. With music by Benny Anderson and Bjorn Ulvaeus, from the famous pop quartet Abba and lyrics by Tim Rice and Ulvaeus, it lasted a mere two weeks on Broadway in 1988. On saying that, Chess did produce the international hit single 'I Know Him So Well' made famous by Elaine Paige and Barbara Dickson and has some show stopping tunes such as 'One Night in Bangkok' and the fabulous 'Anthem'.

dlr Mill Theatre was a hive of excitement as we approached. People were happily chatting, purchasing programmes and enjoying a drink in the downstairs bar, it was such a lovely atmosphere to enter. I was greeted by Ray and shortly after we were seated, admiring the open stage, which was beautifully lit. The set was constructed of cubes, these were back lit to give an impressive 80's vibe. The steps and riser were cleverly built into the set and a projection was positioned centre back. The Orchestra were situated across the back, behind the set and their silhouettes were visible, this gave another interesting element to the overall design. So here we sat waiting for the eagerly anticipated production from KMS, that had taken two and a half years to finally make it to the stage!

E.J Reilly gave us a well thought out and inventive production. The visuals were powerful and the thinking behind the plot strong. E.J utilised a relatively small space and transformed it into a multifaceted hive of high drama. Ms Reilly's principles embraced their roles, as they wove their way through the intertwining narrative, and the chorus showed fierce commitment, making a huge impact on the overall production.

Behind the baton was Mr Geoff Woods, Geoff and his orchestra, who in my opinion, were the backbone of this production provided us with wonderful full-bodied sounds, which emanated from the pit. Number after number was propelled with power, keeping the momentum of the production at an all-time high. Great work was also achieved with the singers who delivered some fabulous choral harmonies and solo work.

The choreography in 'Chess' has many challenges, demanding many different dance genres, starting with national folk, then a little ballet/contemporary, the Arbiter's dancers are usually of a commercial/hip hop vein, some Russian traditional dancing and there are many large ensemble numbers to tackle also, all in all quite the workload! Rachel did a good job and provided some highly energetic and well-rehearsed routines. As a production team E.J, Geoff and Rachel gelled well, providing a well-balanced production.

When you get into this show, you find it quite captivating to watch, and certainly to listen to, with its explosive musical score, pulsing heavy drums and electrifying guitars.

American, Fredrick Trumper played by Dónal Lynch certainly made the music his own, firing on all cylinders, he relived the story of his debauched childhood in 'Pity the Child' and had many heated altercations with Florence Vassy, his on- stage lover played by Sarah Riddick. Sarah gave us an honest and calm Florence with excellent vocals, particularly in 'Nobody's Side' and 'You and I'. The third part of the love triangle was the Russian chess grandmaster Anatoly Sergievsky, played by Ciarán McLoughlin. Sarah and Ciarán had a believable chemistry and 'The Mountain Duet', was beautifully construed. Ciarán brought something real to Anatoly, delivering a well-rounded character with fine vocals. The obvious standout moment being, 'Anthem' which he delivered with sublime sincerity.

The Arbiter is the person who pulls the story together, appearing here, there and everywhere. This is quite an intricate part, calling for an emotionless character, but one that still has texture. Nikki Johnston in a matrix like fashion delivered the part with style and efficiency, always on cue and in character with solid vocals and clean well-rehearsed movement.

The Fixers - Walter De Courcey, played by Chris O'Connor and Alexander Molokov, played by Brian Dennison. Great parts with plenty to do, and these guys did it so well. Chris gave us a convincing De Courcey, with strong acting and vocals. Brian Dennison for me, was one of the main players in this production. With his impressive Russian accent, he commanded each scene he visited with his imposing presence. Delivering robust vocals and strong and authoritative acting. A woman scorned; Svetlana Sergievskaya played by Kristy McDougall. Feeling rejected and bitter, Kristy portrayed this part with fierce emotion, there was some lovely acting in quiet movements and also some highflying scenes with lots of drama, not so quiet moments! A talented actress with great vocals.

The Chess Chorus - Wow! What a group of enthusiastic and hard-working people. You should all be commended on your proportionate contribution to this production. From the very first musical number to the last you gave 110%. Choral singing and harmonies were beautiful to the ear and choreography and acting in crowd scenes well-rehearsed and generously embraced. A big' Well Done' to the KMS Chorus.

Production Manager Gillian Lynch was on the ball with this production, as was Stage Manager Colum McDaid. Colum and his crew worked efficiently behind the scenes ensuring set pieces moved on and off with ease. I stood on the stage after the show and noted how tight the wing space was, so I can only imagine the precise planning this took. Good job everyone.

The Set, again, down to the hard work and talent of Colum McDaid, was highly impressive. Constructed of many cubed squares pieced together and backlit giving the audience a stunning visual. Clever use of a relatively small space was utilised with the side steps and riser built into the set; this use of levels added greatly to the over-all practicality of the production. The chess table and chairs for the games were neatly mounted on a truck which was rolled on and off when required. The attention to detail was of a high standard, with the chess board on the truck even lighting up when the players started the game.

The Lighting on this production was a highlight for me. Kris Mooney treated us to some spectacular pictures. At times it felt like the lights controlled the music. Deep reds and blues washed over the stage. Different sections of the cubed set reflecting different colours to suit the mood at hand. Intimate moments were captured beautifully and 'Anthem' and 'Anthem Reprise' had the hair standing on the back of my neck, it was such a powerful visual to finish with, Florence centre stage surrounded by the main players. Stunning.

Sound was clear and aided the singers and chorus well. Levels were balanced well and there was good separation between singers and orchestra, on saying that the orchestra did over power slightly once or twice, but over-all, it rocked along as you'd expect a musical of this calibre to.

The costumes and styling by Rhona Gleeson were quirky and inventive. The British Consulate with their red dickie bows, braces and top hats was jovial, 'One Night in Bangkok' was adequately costumed, with black sequenced dancers, a lovely Lady boy and typical tourists, I must mention at this point, I spotted the tourist with the 'I love Freddie' t-shirt in the first scene and it made me laugh! Black and white striped costumes, Merano national folk costumes, black and white lace ballet costumes and the black capes for the choral chorus, were all well envisaged. Principals' costumes were all in keeping, I particularly liked Svetlana's red suit and the matrix styled Arbiter. Hair and makeup design were also to a high standard.

Props for this production were all well sourced and efficiently coordinated into the production.

The KMS programme, by Marianne Lambert was to a high standard and I particularly liked the art work on the cover. Photography by Hazel Button was nicely done.

The graphic work on this show had a powerful resonance on the over-all picture. This was carefully distilled by director E.J Reilly. Projections ran throughout the complete production, aiding the narrative greatly. We were never in any doubt where we were or what was happening. Some fabulous visuals carried us along on the journey, until the last chess piece fell on the final note of the score. Poignant and uplifting.

E.J, Geoff, Rachel, Gillian and everyone at KMS, I enjoyed a wonderful night's entertainment and I wish you many more successful productions, hopefully your next one won't take two and a half years to hit the boards!

The premiere amateur production of ONCE in UK and Ireland. What a prospect for UCD Musical Society after a bleak eighteen months or so without a production, because of the restrictions associated with the Covid virus! They deserve a big feather in their cap for having been the first Irish company to acquire the rights. However, could they do justice to this multi award-winning show - it won multiple awards - Oscars, Tonys, Grammys, Drama Desk and Olivier! It has also played professionally at Broadway and the West End as well as tours abroad. This is the story of a guy who gave up on love and music, and the girl who inspired him to dream again. Guy falls for Girl from the very start but she, although also enamoured with him, has her head very firmly on her shoulders. She knows that she has a young daughter and her mother to look after, with very little money coming in. She also knows she would be better getting her husband to come to Ireland and help his family. So, she helps Guy get a loan from the bank to record some of his songs, but without the getting together at the end! Instead, after telling him that her husband is joining her in Dublin, Guy leaves for London hoping to fulfil his music's dream, and perhaps start again with his old girlfriend, who had left him earlier in the story. Having enjoyed the film, and seen excerpts of the professionally staged version, I was looking forward to seeing this musical at UCD. I was not disappointed!

From the very start a great impact was made with the very first number 'Leave'. Alone onstage with some smoke and a single backlight, Peter Richardson as Guy showed everyone what a fabulous guitarist and fine singer he was. Then as the lights came up, we saw he was being watched by a single female, Girl (played so well by Sorcha McGlynn) and immediately we, as an audience, were caught up in the chemistry of this couple that was to last and, indeed, develop throughout the storyline. Then the action moved to the music shop, where Girl was allowed by the owner Billy to practise on a piano. Cue the big song - Guy and Girl accompanying the Oscar winning 'Falling Slowly'. What an opening!

Peter Richardson was very comfortable and easy on stage as Guy. Very natural and subtle acting the part, he never tried to impose his character, creating great believability. He is the perfect foil for the more pragmatic yet outgoing character of Girl, and thus creates a very interesting couple. Sorcha McGlynn as Girl, gave us an excellent, ebullient portrayal. Always the naturally dominant person in the twosome, with her cheeky smiles and pragmatism, she never failed to both intrigue and amuse the audience. She also showed fine skills as a pianist.

Next, we were introduced to the motley assembly of other characters in the show.  Billy the music shop owner (Owen Finnegan) was funny, fiery and had the hots for Reza (Nino Tsereteli) a Czech friend of Girl's, who showed wonderful sensuality in her physicality, especially in her dancing. She was certainly a match for Billy in more ways than one, being able to stand up to him when he tried to take the upper hand. Baruska (Girl's mum), very nicely played with lots of comedy and yet sympathetic, and her young toddler daughter (not named or credited, but beautifully played by a student who was probably four or five times her age) also gave very credible characters. John Higgins was very good as the bank manager who gave them the loan, producing his guitar to impress them enough to be added to the band in the recording studio. Guy's Da (Oisin Horne) although drafted in late to the part, gave another convincing portrayal, and the last two roles of Czech men, Svec (Cormac Gilligan) and Andrej (Eoin Harrington) gave good performances, demonstrating, like all the Czech characters, excellent accents throughout, showing how worthwhile it was to have Vocal Director Amber Dixon. The storyline developed with a great deal of comedy and sensitivity, which showed the excellent direction by Jess Goodbody, assisted by Hannah Breen. I cared so much for the two main characters of Guy and Girl and the feeling between these two was pitched very carefully and sympathetically. Although this was very much a huge team effort, with some outstanding individual performances, her directorial hand was what I saw throughout the production. The true essence of this musical is sensitivity, and that was always very evident. A very fine band of eleven provided an excellent background for all of the music, often joining in with numbers that started with one or a few instruments played by the cast, but it was always unobtrusive yet effective in underscoring all of the action, from high spirited jigs and reels, to more contemplative solos and duets. The musicians were so good that they were hardly noticeable under the expert direction of Aishling Byrne, who also doubled on accordion, and ensured a very impressive soundscape for all of the action. All twelve girls of the ensemble excelled as dancers in the wonderful choreography by Jess Goodbody again, which featured ballet (from her own background) as well as ethnic, and Irish dancing. So at times it resembled Riverdance, or Swan Lake, but was always wonderfully sympathetic to the action, just like her direction. The Stage Manager was Ada McDonagh, assisted by Irina Agotha, had little or no scene changing to do, because they used a wide stage, split into three separate settings - (Stage right) Girl and her family's Dublin flat, (Stage left) the music shop/recording studio (with a bed above to denote Guy's bed/Da's shop), and (Centre stage) the bar/outside area. Sadhbh Geoghegan was props manager and did a great job providing the many props and getting them onstage and off, from a hoover to a piano! The lighting by Gav Coll and sound by Jody Trehy was always sympathetic to the action, the backlighting in particular creating much needed atmosphere.

The ending which was neither happy nor sad, but a bit of both was handled very well by Guy, Girl and everyone else. Sympathetic, but merely a lump in the throat rather than a three hankie job! This was a performance of all-round excellence and all the team of performers, musicians, dancers and offstage (back and front) should be justifiably delighted with their part, in what was an excellent amateur premiere in Ireland and the UK, of Once. I'm quite sure other groups will be clambering for this wonderful Irish show!

The audience were lined up outside the Tullyvin Community Centre on a chilly but dry Autumn evening. There was a great feeling of anticipation for the friends of the society who knew they would be well entertained by Tullyvin Musical Society's production of the 'Elvis' musical All Shook Up. We certainly were entertained as we waited, by Sandra McCormack who gave an impromptu stand-up comedy routine. The foyer was nicely decorated for the show with an exhibition of vintage motorbike, guitars, posters of the era and even the ticket desk was behind the bars of 'Jailhouse Rock'. Nice to see all the front of house staff wearing the prison black and white stripes and black jeans. As we entered the hall there was 1950s music playing, which created the mood of the piece. The guitar motif was used to great effect around the stage with huge solid guitar bodies placed in front of the orchestra and necks of guitars placed around the stage. In the centre of the open stage was placed a white guitar which was caught in a criss-cross of bright shafts of white light.

The announcements were from the prison warder Brian Feerick who shouted at us like we were prisoners, warned us not to use mobile phones and told us what the fire evacuation drill was. Hilarious, but he really got the message across as very few phones appeared. He really set the scene for the beginning of the show.

It was a nicely paced and well directed production. The Director Paul Norton added some nice touches with movement and comedy was very much to the fore. There were some pleasing groupings and positioning of the principals on stage which all seemed very natural. He had drawn the characters very nicely and realistically and had chosen his cast well as they all seemed most suited to their roles. There were some beautiful, sensitive moments which were handled well by the cast. His setting gave us different levels to the stage which were used quite well and many exits from the stage which meant that scene changes could be speedy and didn't slow the pace.

Noel Lennon and just four other players made up the orchestra. It was quite a revelation to discover that as the finished sound was of a great quality. Good rock and roll band sound for those production numbers, but also a light touch given to some of the melodic ballads. Always accompanying and never overpowering the cast's singing. They all sang well and the voices of each romantic pairing blended well together. The chorus added much to the overall sound of the show, well supported by some pit singers.

The choreography was at times interesting and inventive. There were nice references to the jive moves of the 1950s. Some routines had constantly moving patterns which really challenged the eye. Full cast numbers tended to be slightly more on the spot with clever and well-rehearsed arm movements. Pairs and individuals 'sold' their songs well with gentle movement which reflected the mood of the number. Chad (Liam Wallace) of course had the ladies in the audience swooning with his gyrating pelvic movements and his Elvis poses which he struck so well. He related well to the audience talking out to us for approval at times. Chad has a lion's share of the singing in the show and Liam delivered the rock and roll numbers and ballads with style. He worked well with the array of women whom he met on his journey. Finally, 'falling in love' with Natalie/Ed. Aoife Shalvey did a great job as the girl in the garage. She was a great Tomboy and transformed really well into sidekick Ed. Her deeper voice and masculine mannerisms were very convincing. Aoife sang the part well with a powerful and very musical tone to her voice.

Dennis, the geek in the town was played by Colm Shalvey. Colm didn't go too pantomime with the character and made him believable. He gave us some moments of comedy when we laughed with him rather than at him. He impressed when he was singing and 'It Hurts Me' proved to be one of the highlights in the show. Miss Sandra was played with appropriate aloofness and then vampiness by Andrea Fitzpatrick. This is an actor who really knows how to move around the stage, she glided and posed her way through the show. She also has a strong and tuneful vocal tone.

There was a pureness, a realism in the performance of Finuala Duffy as Sylvia. She is the hardworking, hard edged bar owner who really just wants to be loved. Finuala got all the raw hurt from the part and delivered 'There's Always Me' with such touching honesty. A very moving performance. Her love interest in the show was Jim courtesy of Dermot Carragher. This was a portrayal which seemed to grow and develop as the show ran. He related well to his hero Chad even copying 'the look' and his 'will they, won't they?' relationship with Sylvia was nicely played. Our innocent youths were Emma McKeown as Lorraine and Jason McNulty as Dean. They created a very sweet young relationship which worked well in the show. There was the awkwardness of youth but also the strength when they stood up for their love at the end of the show. Nicely played and both were particularly well styled for their roles. Some great singing from the pair with Emma blowing us away with her voice.

Our last couple were Mayor Matilda, Pamela McCormack and Seamus Smyth as Sheriff Earl. Matilda reminded me of some of the less liberal politicians we have in the news at the moment. Pamela got much humour from the lines and developed a strong character through the show. The vocal dual with Chad was great fun. The henpecked Earl nearly brought the house down when the worm turned. This was a great acting moment in the show.

The Chorus and pit singers worked very hard with the singing of those big rock and roll classics. Some nice harmonies along the way. They all moved quite well and will impress further in the future with more expressive facial expressions. The camaraderie within the group was very obvious.

This was a thematic staging with the impression of desert landscape and blue skies. The guitar symbol was used to great effect. With a multi-purpose hall, the original stage was limited so the team had done much to increase the stage area and added a huge front stage extension. Wings had been added and my customary walk around revealed clever areas created for quick costume changes. The raised area at the back of the stage added another useful level which helped to vary the action.

Large pieces of scenery were wheeled quite speedily into place such as the bar, garage flat, gas pump etc. These were all carefully painted, with some being battered to show wear and tear. Pieces such as tables and stools were suitable. Smaller props such as the suitcases which transformed into the Greyhound worked nicely. Personal props, including books, bottles etc all looked good.

There were some great touches in the lighting plot but a couple of times when only coloured spots were used, the effect was a little gloomy. The fairground scene which is meant to be in the evening is difficult to light. The torches used to cut through the blue lighting created an atmospheric effect. There was a glorious moment when Dennis was singing and the lights changed to focus our attention. The sound throughout was well balanced and cued.

There were some great authentic costumes on stage and others which could be made more period by adding a belt or scarf. The polka dot wide skirts looked good and moved really well especially in the spins. The array of very different wedding dresses added much to the final scene. Teaming shoes with the outfit can really add a professional look to a show.

Some of the hairs, particularly the swept back single pony tail looked just right for the production. Possibly a few more wigs would have helped create the image of the period. The boys had brushed their hair back and had added 'product' which helped give an Elvis look.

This was a great night's entertainment which the large audience really enjoyed. Tullyvin Musical Society is very much an important part of community life in the area. The society were so blown away by all the support they receive in the form of sponsorship, ticket sales and just folk arriving and volunteering to help with the car parking. From the car park attendants to the front of house to the warmth of the audience and cast, Tullyvin welcomes one and all.

I congratulate the Tullyvin community for giving us a fun night of All Shook Up.

Magic Changes There have been many versions of Warren Casey and Jim Jacobs' musical about the struggles of teenagers in the atomic age of 1950's Chicago produced in the past forty eight years. From the edgy to the saccharine to almost direct copies of the corny 1978 film; Grease is a firm favourite of regional, community and school groups around the world. The original show was quite earthy, reflecting the working class society where it was set, where there was a sense of impending doom because of the Cold War and anti-communism was rife. Post World War II America was not all white picket fences and rampant consumerism and whilst the middle classes certainly expanded into the new suburbs, the working class inner city citizens were left behind with little employment and little hope. These were the teens that Casey and Jacobs were writing about, highlighting real issues like teenage pregnancy, gang warfare, delinquency and rebellion against conformity. Some of these issues remained in subsequent versions of Grease, but unlike the original where the show was a social commentary of the era and not for the kiddies because of the subject matter and bad language, the musical became primarily a rather sexist, slushy love story between Sandy and Danny with a secondary, albeit more authentic and realistic, love story between Rizzo and Kenickie and was firmly aimed at a young audience.

Fresh from last year's triumph on winning best show with Michael Collins in the AIMS Sullivan category, Wexford's Oyster Lane Theatre Group went back to basics and staged Grease, which was their first production twenty-five years ago, in the Dun Mhuire Theatre in October of this year. Directed by Suzanne O'Leary with choreography by Jonny Smith and musical direction by Patrick Clancy, this was an uncomplicated and energetic adaptation of Casey and Jacobs' 1950's teen musical and as far from the caliber and aesthetics of Bryan Flynn's brilliantly moving Collins as one could get!

Featuring a relatively young cast, this Grease was very animated and full of pizazz. Sticking with the decontaminated version, the director opened with the "Sandy Duet" rather than the "Alma Mater". Danny and Sandy sang about their blissful encounter on the beach during the summer holidays. This was well sung by both performers and their reveal was nicely done as they were rotated onto stage, framed in the upstage edge of the bleachers. From here on the show galloped along with few surprises as it was a fairly conventional take on the musical. Thomas Furlong played Danny, leader of the T-Birds, as a lively lad full of kinetic energy. His characterisation was quite believable, particularly in his scenes with Sandy with whom he had a nice chemistry. His singing was peppy especially on "Summer Nights" and "You're the One that I Want" and quite poignant on "Alone at the Drive-In (Sandy)". As Danny's love interest, Niamh Cullen gave us a pleasant and winning Sandy. Her on-off relationship with Danny was performed quite credibly and her singing was delightful at times. "Hopelessly Devoted To You" was solid and she gave us a nicely sustained final note I'd not heard done before. Her singing on the other numbers was also good, particularly on the reprise of "Sandra Dee" and her opening song with Danny "Sandy Duet". Both performers assuredly captured the delicate emotional roller-coater of hormonal first love and pitched their performances perfectly to this production.

Danny's gang, the T-Birds, was made up of a rag-tag collection of clowning testosterone fuelled boys, who clearly took 'shop' courses at Rydell High School, and were behind the door when intelligence was bestowed. Michael McKenny, played Kenickie, Danny's second in command, with a reasonably high status, taking control of the gang when Danny was otherwise engaged with trying to impress Sandy. His stand-out moment was when he sang "Greased Lightning" where he led the song with a fine rock voice. Kenickie's girlfriend Rizzo was played by Ruth Donegan in a mature performance. Leader of the 'Pink Ladies', Rizzo's relationship with Kenickie was fairly fractious. Ms Donegan's characterisation of Rizzo was relatively nuanced, actively removing herself from some scenes, observing rather than participating in some of the Pink Ladies more immature moments. This worked to a degree, especially when she announced she was possibly with child. Her scene with Sandy, when she sang "There Are Worse Things I Could Do", where she berates Sandy's goodie two shoes persona was particularly good as was her vocal on the acerbic "Look At Me I'm Sandra Dee".

The other T-Birds were all very energetic, engaging in constant slapstick. They bounced around the stage hitting each other and generally goofing off like chimps on a sugar rush. Michael Carroll's Sonny, Michael O'Gorman's Roger and Dylan Walsh's Doody all acquitted themselves well and ingratiated their characters to the audience's delight. Mr O'Gorman had good comic timing with Jan, particularly on "Mooning" and Mr Walsh demonstrated a good singing voice on "Those Magic Changes" and "Rock and Roll Party Queen". The characters of the Pink Ladies in Grease are better developed that the T-Birds, who are written as caricatures. As Jan, Aileen Sutherland had some issues with the accent but her characterisation of the kooky food-loving girl was largely well-drawn. Emma O'Leary's Marty was truly endearing, she carried the song "Freddy My Love" with assurance and a nice vibrato, and hinted at a sub-text of whether she was really going out with a Marine. However the Pink Lady who really eclipsed all others on the night I attended was Dara Cullen's Frenchy. With her cartoon like voice and delicate characterisation, Ms Cullen gave Frenchy an open innocence and she was quite beguiling in the role. Her scene with Teen Angel was funny and she sang with relish and in character on all of the ensemble numbers.

Eilish Coady's Patty Simcox, lead cheerleader who has a serious crush on Danny, was a great character. Ms Coady nailed Patty's social ineptness and total ignorance of what was really going on around her. Her equally nerdish friend, Eugene was played by Brandon Cogley who also did well with this underwritten character. The Society's excising of the "Alma Mater" at the start of the show, where the audience are properly introduced to Patty and Eugene, meant that Eugene's character in particular was not as well developed as others. Other characters that shone for me were Adrienne Meyler's Ms Lynch, who was scary; Neal O'Leary's Vince Fontaine who was also scary, but for a different reason as he was so monstrously pervy; Mick Farrell had a fine voice as Johnny Casino and Tony Carty's Teen Angel, dressed as a game show host, crooned brilliantly and had a great falsetto.

Grease has some great musical ear worms. Most audience members would know many of the songs and it was a testament to Musical Director, Patrick Clancy, that the music in this production had a freshness because of his clever arrangements of the score. There was a hard rock edge to many of the songs and some were extended. "Greased Lightning" had a wonderful Jimmy Page-esque guitar solo towards the end of the song and there was a beautiful introduction to "Alone at the Drive-In (Sandy)" on acoustic guitar and keys. Nick Bailey's drums were heavy and powerful and at times it was like being at a rock gig! Mr Clancy's work with the ensemble produced some lovely harmonies and some of the solos had a pleasing contemporary resonance. Jonny Smith's choreography was also very innovative. "Hand Jive" was pin sharp and "Greased Lightning" wonderfully energetic and exhausting to watch! Mr Smith's impressively vigorous and spirited work was dynamically demonstrated by a strongly drilled ensemble.

Set and Lighting was looked after by Mark Redmond. Mr Redmond's set was quite simple. Upstage sliding doors under a platform to facilitate setting and striking of set pieces; some simple flying and two sets of treads that could move to centre or out to stage left and right. Set dressing by David Redmond was suitably garish. Mr Redmond's lighting was excellent, restrained use of movers and LED's meant that the lion's share of the illumination was done by generics, which was suitable for the era of the show. Eschewing follow spots, his actors had to find their light and they did every time.

Sound by I-Tech Productions was good. It wasn't too loud, which was a blessed relief as the norm over the past couple of years has been to push it to eleven! They got good separation between band and singers and a warm full range sound. Stage manager Greg O'Leary also designed and operated the projections. His transitions on stage were quick and seamless and the projections well-timed and quite bright. Costumes by Elaine Murphy and Nomac were suitable for the time and hair and make-up was good too. Director Suzanne O'Leary clearly created a good atmosphere in the rehearsal room and it definitely showed on stage. The cast were obviously enjoying themselves and this enjoyment infected the audience. Her pacing of the show was good and her interpretation of the source material quite faithful. Leaving it to her musical director and choreographer to re-imagine and artistically play with the material, Ms O'Leary helmed a solid production that took us away from rainy multi-cultural, woke Wexford in 2019 on a wave of nostalgia to the halcyon days when misogynist white, heterosexual Protestants ruled America and social problems were glossed over by a culture aimed at its' creators.

Set amid the shoulder pads and perms of the 1980s, The Wedding Singer follows the fortunes of Robbie and his pursuit of love, finding it eventually in waitress Julia. It is a gentle comedy with some very pleasant musical numbers and gives plenty of scope for how the show could be portrayed visually.

Colourful posters pointed us in the right direction for the show, namely Inchicore College of Further Education, where the entrance hall had been decorated with items in the form of an impromptu Wedding Show. Music of the era was playing as my friend and I entered the hall, which really helped to set the scene. The show was confidently directed by experienced director Philippa Alford. The characters had been well constructed with the actors and indeed there was a feeling of realism from the cast. The pace of dialogue was steady and the story- telling was good. Occasionally I wanted a little full stop in a scene so we could have a few seconds to consider what had just been done or said. Grouping was generally good though there was the odd bit of masking, some of which could have been solved by making the raised stage area just a little higher. There were some lovely moments of comedy, sentimentality and affection brought out from what is at times, a rather simplistic script.

Barry Power was obviously enjoying every moment of being the show's Musical Director. The orchestra worked well together to create quite an authentic sound which was so reminiscent of the era. The cast, principals and chorus, all sang really well, with a fair smattering of beautiful harmonies within groups and pairs. Always more difficult to get the audience involved when they don't really know the music in a show but well done Barry, at the end the audience were leaving singing.

Dance is a very important aspect of this show and there should be some references made in the choreography back to the era in which it is set. Laura Macken-Posavitz devised a wide range of quite complicated numbers. There was good footwork, arm extensions and ever-changing patterns on stage. A nod was made to dance classics of the time which worked so well. Even a lovely wee balletic moment with some great lifts.

Jordan Bass gave us a very endearing Robbie. He had us on his side from his first appearance. He ran the whole gamut of emotions on his journey and of course in his heartache he made a great unpredictable drunk. His voice sounded good singing these numbers and often affected us emotionally by his delivery of some of the songs. He can really let himself go on stage, which he did, but still took time to register out to us.

Julia was played by Laura Geoghegan. She established a very honest and believable relationship with Robbie. Some of their duets were fantastic. 'If I Told You' was a triumph with excellent harmonising. She played the down-trodden girlfriend very well to Glen. He was played with money grabbing smarm by Chris Bass. We all very much hoped that Julia would come to her senses and ditch the two timer.

Guiding Julia along the way was best friend Holly who was played with such strength by Jen Keane. This is an actor who really demands our attention when she comes to the stage. The role also asks for a strong singing voice and Jen rose well to that challenge. This was a very believable and multi-layered character created by someone who can act, sing and dance. In hot pursuit of her was Daire Kelly as Sammy. He acted the band member with the broken heart really well and delivered some hilarious dry humour comedy lines. George the most flamboyant member of the band was played with the campest of touches by Aaron Tierney. He impressed in his singing of 'George's Prayer' in which he delivered a wide vocal range.

Nikki Johnston was Linda, Robbie's first love. Her reconciliation seduction of a drunk Robbie was determined and energetic. The role was well sung too. Jackie Carroll's Granny Rosie provided us with many moments of comedy and also some touching moments. The actor was not afraid to really let herself go in the part and the rap section was a surprise to the audience and well delivered. Frank Foley gave us a very genuine and sensitive moment as her long- suffering husband. Deirdre Gillespie portrayed Julia's mother Angie. Deirdre had really developed the character from how she was styled to the stance and that grating accent. There were some nice moments of tenderness in there too which really made the character live on stage.

There was great support given to the principal cast from a very involved chorus. There was good singing from the group with some very pleasing harmonies along the way. They coped well with the intricate choreography they had been given and it was good to see that there were quite a few opportunities for individuals to step forward to give us cameo roles. Well done Rachel Johnston who added facial hair to be Sideburns Lady, Alan Lau as Bad Haircut Guy, Lisa Younge as the Sales Clerk who sang so well. Kevin Macken seemed to be everywhere on stage supporting the action so well as Ricky as did Brian Dennison who kept appearing the worst for wear as Bum. The 'Pop' number is one of my favourites in the show as the story really progresses through the number. The couples who all had their moment to shine in their proposals really worked well together. Leah Kilcullen as Tiffany, Jack Halpin as Donny, Emily Deasy as Crystal and Kevin Johnston as Mookie all did a great job. Impressive too was the expert popping of champagne by waiter Mikey Flynn and his surprise proposal from fellow waiter Graham Dunne.

The fake players give a huge amount of fun, especially when they are always called 'Fake…..'. We had Nyree Blackhall as a pointy bra wearing Fake Madonna, Darragh Carroll as the dyed haired Fake Tom Jones and my goodness the stunning Fake Tina Turner, played by Tony O Brien, who really blew us away with her star attitude and strutting walk. The rest of the chorus acted and reacted in all their scenes and added so much to the overall look of the show.

The staging of the show looked deceptively simple with side panels decorated in blocks of colour. The back wall had panels which lit up in various sequences. There was a wonderful effect which had deep yellow panels and strong red spot lights which looked particularly good. The raised area upstage was useful but if it had been higher some masking would have been avoided. Large pieces were brought quickly into place by a well- trained stage team. There was a stunning wedding bower and arch, bar, bed (onto which the cast could confidently throw themselves) all of which looked effective. Smaller items such as desks, chairs and office paraphernalia all added to the authentic feel of the piece. Personal props such as bottles, mobile (brick) phones and the cellar bedding all fitted in well with the look of the production.

The lighting plot was generally sound though I do miss the smokiness that a hazer produces and, in the dance, /club sequences the shafts of light would have really added to the look. The sound settled well and there was a good balance with the voice and the orchestra. The sound effects used were really well cued and added an extra dimension to the show. How did we wear that gear in the 1980s and think we were cool? A good selection of outfits from the period appeared on stage with some very interesting bridal party outfits. Some of the men's costumes gave a nod to the business men of the time and the 'Fake' team were all just right for their roles.

Some of the ladies' hair was backcombed, teased and curled to give us that 'big hair' look. The wigs used were appropriate. Possibly some of the men needed longer wigs as I can remember being very fussy about my long locks at that time.

Eyes were well made up in a range of appropriate colours such as reds and browns, with good eye definition. Plenty of strong lip colour and glosses adding to the look. George was given a good 'Boy George' make over.

This was a most entertaining show from a well-rehearsed and talented cast and crew. One thing which really came across was just how much fun everyone on stage was having. Like all good weddings. the evening really flew by but left us with such happy memories of our night in the company of Kilmainham Inchicore Musical Society and their production of the Chad Beguelin, Tim Herlihy and Matthew Sklar stage musical The Wedding Singer.

Mel Brooks once said in an interview, "If you stand on a soapbox and trade rhetoric with a dictator you never win, … but if you ridicule them, bring them down with laughter, they can't win. You show how crazy they are." This really is the ethos behind one of the most outrageous and cynical stage musicals The Producers. Cynical, yes but hilarious too.

Marian Choral Society had us rolling in the aisles with their production. The humour had been really well extracted from the script by Directors Enda Burke and Aoife McClafferty and of course by the talented cast of players.

We entered the St Jarlath's College Hall on a damp October evening and were greeted into a nicely decorated outside foyer. The hall itself had 1920s jazz playing which gave a feel of the show to come. The open curtain revealed side flats covered in authentic posters from 1930s to 1970s movies. The hazy blue lighting revealed a double doorway leading into the theatre. This central area would transform into the office and the apartment. (More details later).

It is still a risky choice for a society as the content of the show can at times shock as some of the dialogue is a little racy and the Nazi mockery could appear bad taste. So well done to the society for this choice as there are some wonderful parts for principal players and plenty for the chorus, particularly the ladies' chorus. The directors have to negotiate with the stage team how to easily capture all those scenes. Then with the direction of the piece much of the humour is only really funny if it is underplayed. The most important thing is the pace of the show. This was all really well achieved by the directors who had generally set a great pace with a well-rehearsed cast. Obviously, there is a tendency with this show to almost pantomime the characters. What I liked here was that the characterisations seemed very real so we became involved with the cast's journey. Movement and flow around the stage was good with very little masking. I felt that a couple of the individual and small group numbers, though moved well, had an opportunity for even further movement. The story telling was well handled and it was very obvious that all the cast were having a great time on stage. I remember many years ago the shows in which I first appeared that a director would arrive from usually England and rehearse very intensely for a five or six week period and the show was put on for a fortnight usually. It was a huge commitment for that period of time. There is a similar rehearsal period for this company so I take my hat off to how polished the end product was in such a limited rehearsal time.

Musical Director Shane Farrell controlled the eleven-piece orchestra with precision to bring us a rich and rounded accompaniment to the production. Most of the singing from the principals and chorus was of a very high standard. The chorus really did sing out very strongly in those highly energetic dance routines. These were the brainchild of Choreographer Aoife McClafferty who gave us a varied and exciting choreography plot. The cast appeared well rehearsed and the energy levels of presentation were excellent. The old ladies with the Zimmer frames really brought the house down in a routine which seemed to just grow and grow. The big production numbers had great flow, storytelling and ever-changing stage patterns.

Of course, this show demands a cast who really can deliver the comedy by actually playing it all quite straight. Timing, comic timing, is hard to describe but impossible to miss when we see it. Niall Conway made the ultimate Max Bialystock. His timing was superb. Never labouring over a line but throwing lines away and getting a huge laugh each time. I have seen this show many times and Niall made the lines and humour feel so fresh for me. A real masterclass in comedy here. A good singing voice matched the rich tone of his speaking voice too. Michael Coen was very much his straight man with a totally different look from the wild haired Max, much more sedate, jacket always correctly buttoned, hair always in place and shoes polished. We watched as the character gained confidence before our eyes, running off to South America with the lovely Ulla. Michael has a delightful tone to his singing voice too and delivered a powerful rendition of 'I Want To Be A Producer'.

Ulla is a great comedy role which Angela Staunton obviously so relished. Angela really owned the stage with every entrance as our eyes were always drawn to her. She moved so purposefully around that acting area. She had a wonderful accent from which emanated a great deal of comedy. Bavarian born Steffen Knauer was the ideal choice for madcap character Franz. The scene on the roof top with the pigeons was hilarious. He also gave us some great moments when the 'Springtime ..' show was in rehearsals.

Faded director, Roger was given a real OTT persona by Nicky Lawless. The initial appearance in the wonderful 'Chrysler Building' dress and subsequent sparkling headgear added so much 'camp' to the character. He has a great singing voice which suddenly came to the fore in 'Springtime For Hitler'. His partner Carmen, Eoin Mullins, was nicely styled in black. This is his assistant who is very precious and was well created by Eoin. The gaggle of elderly rich ladies worked their socks off throughout the show. Their ''Til Him' worked so well as each person never let their character slip for a second. Leading this group was 'Hold Me Touch Me' played by Suzanne Garvey. Glamour had definitely been put aside, false teeth added and a super costume. Her seduction of poor Max on the sofa was breath-taking! Another great comic performance.
