The principal cast were really well supported by a huge range of cameo players (too numerous to mention individually) who added so much to the feel of the finished show. From Norman Quinn who sang the role of the Stormtrooper so well, the 'Production Team' in Roger's apartment, to the auditionees in the theatre. Job well done!

The initial set of the double doors, adapted to become the office by means of a fold out design. The office produced looked good, it was naively painted with rows of books etc and appeared quite solid too. This then could be rotated to make the pink and gold apartment. A scrim was also used in the production which helped to camouflage some of the screen changes. The team were efficient and obviously well drilled as everyone knew exactly their role which made the quite speedy changes work. The properties in most cases added to the look of the scene with touches such as the adding machines on the desks. There were more opportunities for the use of clever lighting ideas though some of the effects were good and the prison cell in particular was very effectively lit.

Some of the costumes used worked really well. The blue/green set which the female dancers wore looked glamorous and colourful. The khaki shirts for the lady dancers in the big production number were a novel and interesting look. The actual 'Springtime' speciality dresses were in gold as were the headdresses and they didn't work quite as well for me as some I have seen. Roger's Hitler uniform with glittery edges was great. The two main characters were nicely contrasting in their styling as was appropriate for the story. It was a good touch to bring Leo back from South America in a pale suit, buttoned right up of course. Ulla had a wide range of costumes but the red velvet was stunning and I wish it had reappeared for the finale. The old ladies looked good in their royal blue dresses which were trimmed in white. Accessories were generally very good.

Wigs were of a good quality such as those grey wigs worn by the ladies. Most others wore their own hair slightly styled which worked well. Make up complemented the look. This was quite subtle with eyes well outlined and good lipstick. Roger and Co. all looked slightly more made up which was appropriate.

The loyal followers were not disappointed when they travelled to see Marian Choral Society's version of The Producers. This was a fun packed evening from beginning to end. It was full of life, with great performances. The pace was good and I know everyone in the hall was moved in some way by the acting and singing. Laughter is a wonderful thing and needless to say we all had a great laugh at this hilarious musical.

The Strange case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde by Robert Louis Stevenson was first published in 1886. Set in the grimy and murky streets of London this gothic tale still intrigues today as it investigates the duplicity of the human psyche. Stevenson had gained inspiration for the story from the real-life murder by French teacher Eugene Chantrelle of his wife by Opium poisoning. This being totally out of character with his normal behaviour. Stevenson became obsessed by the idea. Hence a legendary story was born. Of course, there have been many plays and countless movies based on the story and now Jekyll And Hyde The Musical.

This was the ambitious choice for Newcastle West Musical Society directed by Tom Madigan and Susan Browne who also choreographed the show, oh and played the leading role of Lucy, a busy woman indeed! What is so wonderful about this society is the community feel of their productions which involve a wide age range and also the local support they get in the form of mostly sell out audiences. The setting and stylising of the show was a little confusing as there were touches of modern clothes, scenery etc mixed in with the more traditional Victorian style, so there wasn't always a cohesive look. That being said this was an engaging show with much of which to be proud. The simple yet effective setting meant that scene changes were speedy and the action of this rather long piece rarely faltered so the pace was pretty good throughout. The story was well told, okay it is one that nearly everyone knows but the reasons for and consequences of Jekyll's actions were explained well. There was a great team effort from the cast who all worked their socks off, from the main principal line up to every member of the chorus. They all moved with ease around the stage and apart from the odd wee moment, masking of cast was rare. The principals had been well chosen for their roles and they had obviously been really well rehearsed. Good to see that the directors were prepared to take the odd risk when casting as some quite inexperienced people had a chance to shine.

Michael Young and seven players gave us a very controlled orchestration. There is some stunning music in this show. I remember many years ago buying the concept album CD from Dress Circle and I played it constantly in the car. There was a great steady tempi throughout and those big chorus production numbers really soared. There was a gentle feel to some of those beautiful ballads which gave the singer the chance to really show their talents.

The movement in the show was dramatic such as the powerful 'Murder, Murder'. The cast all looked confident with the routines they had been given. There were good changes of mood and focus in the routines and the on-stage patterns changed so it was always visually interesting. There were some nicely placed moments in the duets and with smaller groups of principals. Michael Anthony Greene had the mammoth task of bringing Jekyll and Hyde to life for us. He was smartly dressed in a dark suit with a good black wig which was held back in a ponytail for Jekyll and released for Hyde. He did a great job in both roles, though at times as Hyde that wig totally obstructed his face so we lost all his acting and facial expressions. He has a stunning tone to his singing voice and he added a slight pop vibe to the singing of the role which worked well. The highly anticipated transformation scene did not disappoint. He related well to Emma and there was a real sexual chemistry as Hyde with Lucy. Lucy was played by Susan Browne who brought her rich experience to the role. There was a strength in the character she created but also the vulnerability too. She delivered those huge emotional songs with great power and commitment.

Emma was played in lovely contrast by Katelyn Davis. There was such a fragility in her look and her character which was really endearing. A beautiful tone to her singing voice. Her character dealt with all the emotional bows that Jekyll gave her and she kept a great dignity in the part. All this at just seventeen. I am sure she will continue to grow as an actor and I wish her future success. Paul Moriarty who played her father Sir Danvers established a great on-stage rapport with Emma. He had some moving emotional moments in the show which he handled well.

Dave Wrenn has a beautiful tone to his speaking and singing voice. He played John Utterson in a very sincere manner. The relationship he established with his friend Dr Jekyll was always very believable and we always willed him to get Jekyll to cease those experiments. Caroline Walsh looked and acted every part the English lady. Very in the 'Let them eat cake' mould she added much to the scenes in which she appeared. She worked well with the rather strangely attired Archibald Proops played by Dinny Aherne. He maintained the aristocratic accent throughout and developed the foppish character quite well.

As if he too didn't have enough to do, Director Tom Madigan was the Bishop. Tom has a great stage presence and a delicious rich voice. He captured the slightly lecherous clergyman well and the hypocrisy of Victorian society was nicely told in his storyline. Military man Lord Savage was authentically styled and enacted by Paul Keyes who gave a great military bearing to the role. Molly Giltenane was a Cockney treat as Nellie. This is one of the ladies in the Red Rat. The character has to help create the feel of that underground world inhabited periodically by the holier-than-thou wealthy clientele. She moved and sang so well, always in character.

Padraig O'Shea added much to the performance with his strong acting as General Glossop. What I particularly noticed was that he is a wonderful listener on stage and reacted to what was going on around him. Shane Walsh was a slightly intimidating Spider and also played Simon Stride. He moved and sang well in both roles. Well done for the cameo roles of Jamie Herlihy as the Priest and Robbie Moriarty as the Newspaper Boy as they added to the whole feel of the production. This was a really involved chorus too. Everyone on stage really gave their all in those big production numbers. Nice to see a wide age range too as the future of any society lies in the youth of today. The set was rather puzzling in its design and styling. There were two panels about three quarters of the way back which were divided into crazy angular shapes with some cut out and others filled with orange card. The back wall had several cubby holes cut out and there were large battery powered candles in each one. The side panels were painted more traditionally with chimneys smoking. This did seem initially very strange but actually I got used to it and focussed my attention on the acting instead. The scene changes were speedy and the change to the laboratory was ingenious as two shelf panels were attached to the curtain rail and could be 'drawn' into place. With the candles all over the 'bench' and shelves a magical world was created. I wasn't too sure about the look of Lucy's room, but the space worked well to create some good pictures for the ladies. Lighting at times was used well to create effects, however at other times we lost some of the faces which was a shame. The initial light in the bedroom was stunning. A strobe was used when a murder was taking place and this worked really well to highlight the actions. The quality of the sound system was good throughout with good clarity for spoken and sung words.

As I said earlier, I wasn't too sure about the styling of the production. If the show is to be set in a particular era either Victorian London or even updated to say 1980s New York, whatever, there has to be a consistency and a real attention to detail. Many of the societies in AIMS have built up a great knowledge of costumes and would be only too willing to share ideas. There are also many very experienced costumiers who have a wide range of stock for hire. So, there is help there when choosing a period piece.

In conclusion this is a difficult show to stage and perform. There were some good ideas in the staging of this production and some excellent performances on stage. It was moving, emotional and the audience were entranced by the unfolding story which was so well told. I commend the society for their bravery in undertaking Jekyll And Hyde.

Originally written for television, this sometimes-forgotten Rodgers and Hammerstein musical was an early vehicle for Julie Andrews who amassed a viewing audience in 1957 of over one hundred million viewers. Subsequently it has been remade for television twice, most recently starring Whitney Houston as the Fairy Godmother. It has been adapted for the stage and the content of the show varies with some songs added and others removed. It has a very gentle charm with witty roles for the step family and some beautiful romantic musical moments. There was a great buzz in the Carrigaline Community Complex, quite a few younger members of the audience equipped with copious amounts of crisps and sweets to get them through the evening. Jacinta McBride directed the show and added in some nice touches along the way. She set a good pace for the show and apart from the odd awkward scene change the show moved along at quite a lick. This is not a pantomime and the characters should be played as real as in any other stage musical. This indeed was the case with this production as for example the step family were not too caricatured and actually their scenes were all the more enjoyable for that. The chorus were well integrated through the show, with a clever trick of bringing them on and off which made it appear that there were many more than was the actual case. The characters were well chosen for the part and especially the Cinderella body double who had quite a few fooled judging by the 'Oohs and Ahhhs' when the dress finally appeared. Dialogue sequences were on the whole nicely moved and lines delivered clearly and with clear expression of the meaning. A couple of comedy opportunities could have been further developed.

Denise Crowley gave a relaxed and gentle accompaniment for the show. She directed five other players in the orchestra and played keyboard herself. The principal cast and chorus were all confident with their musical contributions. The principals all sang well (possibly one or two a little nervous initially but settling down quickly into their roles) and the chorus really blew us away with some of their big numbers. A shame that there weren't more men in this production as their voices would have added a certain depth to some of the harmonies.

Tara O'Connor gave us a neat and well- practised choreography plot. I loved the way she brought some chorus on, let them have a wee moment to shine and then exited to be replaced by another group. Sometimes a choreographer feels that everyone must be on from the beginning of every dance and stay on until the bitter end, the on/off idea works really well occasionally as it refocuses the attention and makes the whole number so much more interesting. Again, I felt sorry for Tara that she didn't have the men for the ball scene which I might have rethought. Our Cinderella was played with elegance by Aisling Kelly. She was every little girls' dream of the role. What impressed me about Aisling as a person was that she went down into the auditorium after the show and posed for hugs and photos with some of the younger members of the audience who were just starstruck. They loved that and so did I. At the start of the show she was a little nervous but as her confidence grew, we got a lovely performance with a wonderful 'When You're Driving Through The Moonlight' and 'A Lovely Night'. Her body double must be congratulated too for making that swap so convincing. And of course, that dress! Quite simply stunning on her. She sang nicely and gave us a lovely, well-acted 'In My Own Little Corner'. Her Prince Christopher was played by Cathal Broderick. He looked dashing in a superb set of costumes, especially that white suit. He added touches of humour to the part which is usually played very straight. He moved with ease around the stage and sang with a very pleasing tone. His love for Cinderella seemed very genuine and we were very convinced by the romance. Ava Costin as Fairy Godmother has the difficult job of opening the whole show so no wonder she was a bit nervous. By the time we reached the 'Transformation' the nerves had gone and she really took charge of proceedings. She sang well throughout the production.

Angela Turner burst onto the stage as the Stepmother. This was such a well- judged performance. She looked great and was exceptionally well groomed in a few beautiful dresses. She seemed to dominate every scene she was in due to a very charismatic stage presence. Her little flirtatious moment with Lionel was very funny.

The Stepsisters were nicely in contrast with each other in looks, mannerisms and personalities. Sharon Wynman's Grace was fond of her food, awkward and had been smitten by a rash which needed constant scratching. Lorna Hughes' Joy was angular, had the most bizarre walk (by the way I worked with a woman who always insisted in wearing the same sort of impossibly high shoes and walked in a similar manner). Individually they were good but together they made a super team.

The King and Queen were played by Nick Cotter and Liz Hesse O'Sullivan respectively. They too made a good team though it might have been fun to make the King even more hen-pecked. They both moved well around the stage and settled well into their regal roles.

Lionel is the manservant who virtually runs the kingdom singlehanded. This was created for us by Glen Barton. He added that urgency to scenes and very much helped to push the story telling on in the show. He was nicely styled with those elaborate kiss curls. He made a good foil to the Prince when on their search with the slipper.

The chorus were of a wide age range but gelled together well to create some touching and entertaining moments on stage. Such a shame there were not more men but really all anyone can do is make the most of the wonderful talent you have. The chorus all sang so enthusiastically and all worked so hard to master those complicated dance routines.

The costumes added a great deal to the show. Cinderella looked good as the poor servant girl and wonderful in the blue dress which really could grace any professional production. Made by Betty Brosnan (every society needs a powerhouse like Betty) some of the costumes were simply wonderful and those hired were of an extremely high standard too. Footwear needs a wee bit of attention in future so there is a cohesive look on stage. Though those glass slippers were perfect. The slightly medieval look worked well though some of the chorus dresses at the ball were a little too modern.

Hair was generally the actor's own, restyled. This worked in some cases but it might be something to investigate for the production of period shows in the future. The wigs used were generally of good quality and I particularly liked Cinderella's hair in the Ballroom scenes. A set of powdered wigs for the chorus at the ball would have added much to the scene. Make up was beautifully applied and eyes were particularly well defined.

The setting looked good with quite a lavish looking ballroom at the castle complete with two rather attractive red velvet chairs. The stepmother's house was formed from movable trucks with wall, fireplace and door on them. Not sure all this was needed. The reverse of these were the shop fronts for the street scenes, they were quite well painted. The sets were usually well dressed with objects such as old kettles, bellows, authentic tea sets etc, all appropriate with the overall look and feel of the production. The lighting was good throughout. The faces were clear, the focus of attention maintained though I might have tried something a little different for the trying on of the slipper by the villagers as the cast were hidden behind the orchestra and the lighting might have been better as a tight spot on the slipper. So, this is a show which transports us off to other worlds, other times. It is purely a piece of unashamed romance. There are some moments of gentle humour in the script but thereafter the Director must tease out comedy from the libretto. Is it one of Rodgers and Hammerstein's best shows? Probably not but it does give us an escapism for a few hours when we can relax and enjoy some wonderful music from the musical Cinderella. Thank you Carrigaline Musical Society for reviving this almost forgotten classic.

The Addams Family is all about fun and ridiculous comedy, and these are the elements that the St.Patrick's production rightly focused on. With a talented front- line at his disposal, Director, Simon Pyper, provided a no-nonsense approach to the show, making sure the story was told at a brisk pace and with plenty of activity to keep the audience interested. I liked his use of living photo frames throughout the show, which worked particularly well when Morticia discussed her family album. The chorus of dead ancestors were a nice addition to virtually every scene, as if they had a right to be there, but they needed to take care not to pull focus from the dialogue. Good attention was given to characterisation throughout the cast, each having a definite individuality, and most achieving a high level of performance. Having a good grounding in pantomime, I was delighted to see Simon putting good emphasis on the slap-stick, visual comedy aspects of the show. Overall, a very nice package.

While the set was well painted, well designed and very functional, the front areas were perhaps less effective in detail, Pugsley's torture "rack" could have been a tad more inventive, and the chair might have been a bit more terrifying. The available space was, however, well used. The use of laurel branches as the forest was very effective. Lighting was generally quite good, although on occasions, the follow spot could have been intensified. Also, the monster in Pugsley's bedroom was almost lost in darkness. There were issues with Mal's microphone which took some time to resolve, but the sound and effects were generally good.

Alex McFarlane did a good job of creating exciting dance routines, and of highlighting her best dancers. The front line were very capable and precise, but the full chorus also proved to be high achievers in their movement. They were also very accomplished vocally.

With a tight six piece band under him, Musical Director, Wilson Shields, controlled both the musicians and the on-stage singers with precision and good balance. Principals and Chorus seemed well-rehearsed and all made a most pleasing sound. Musically, the show was extremely secure.

I'm starting to suspect that Sean Harkin has a double, for he seems to be popping up everywhere. Last week he starred in 9 to 5 in Co. Monaghan, and now he's playing the lead in The Addams Family in Downpatrick. Such energy and enthusiasm are undoubtedly the reason why he performs like a Duracell Bunny, always animated and always on top of his game. His Gomez had pace and a wacky personality that gave it a cartoon quality, and yet he handled his sympathetic scenes with Wednesday and Morticia most sincerely. A nicely balanced performance with impressive vocals thrown in for good measure.

Jordan Rosborough was the definitive Morticia.

Venomous when crossed, vampish and vivacious when inspired, she commanded the stage with her very appearance. Her singing was as strong on interpretation of the lyrics as it was on vocal quality, making 'Death is Just Around The Corner' a divine performance piece. Her comedy was of the finest quality.

Truly her mother's daughter, there were similar qualities on display from Fiona Rice as Wednesday. This was a young performer full of promise, who looked, reacted and sang most impressively throughout. It was hard to believe that this was her first principal role.

Uncle Fester was well played by an energetic Andrew Devonshire, who, as narrator, made a good connection with the audience. What he lacked in vocal quality, he made up for with good interpretation, although 'The Moon and Me', while nicely danced, was a little disjointed. His comedic timing was on point.

Maya Kelly was a feisty Pugsley, full of outward attitude, yet soft in the centre, and we loved that under the bravado, she just wanted to be loved/tortured by her sister. Nicely played.

Kathryn Anne Simpson's Grandma was quite a gentle soul, which made her moments of ribald humour all the more comical and unexpected. A better wig would have enhanced her appearance and aged her more convincingly.

Aaron McElroy's Lurch possibly needed to be more visually intimidating to create a stronger impact, but he did all that was asked of him with good confidence and security.

Laoise Carney was a rather reserved Alice Beineke, which served her well in her early scenes, but she needed to be slightly more 'unrestrained' in her 'disclosure' scenes. But she and her husband combined beautifully with Wednesday and Lucas in a fine rendition of the musically tricky "Crazier Than You" number.

Tim Pentland was most impressive as Mal Beineke, a suitable stuffed-shirt in his early scenes and convincingly 'hip' when he rediscovered his former self. Very nicely played.

Adam Madine captured the character of Lucas extremely well, proving to be a worthy partner for Wednesday and singing with confidence throughout.

The variety of characters among the ancestors was excellent, each with a very eye-catching costume to suit. Lovely detail. Chorus were really well dressed, their make-up was creative and their hairstyles and wigs were appropriate and well worn. The show was visually interesting and well-designed.

This was a production that tickled me in so many places, and while it's easy to nit-pick a production that is generally of a high standard, the most important feature of any show is the impact it has on the audience. The Downpatrick audiences loved it, so congratulations to one and all for a ridiculous and highly entertaining night of ghoulish fun. Thanks also to Anne Millar and the front of house team for the warm hospitality and refreshments.

For those who may not have seen the movie upon which this new musical is based, Nativity, not surprisingly, tells the story of a reluctant primary teacher's attempts to put on a nativity show, haunted by the fact that his previous effort, some years earlier, had been a total disaster. When he is pressured into it, he has a new employee, Mr Poppy, thrust upon him as an assistant. But Mr Poppy is not your conventional classroom assistant. To say that he is child-like and unpredictable would be an understatement, but he is the catalyst for the mayhem and madness that brings about a happy ending for all concerned. The movie was great fun, and I'm happy to report that it translates pretty well to the stage too.

Doubtless conscious of being a premiere and therefore setting a standard, directors Terese Dunne and Rosemary Winkless didn't hold back on making this show as spectacular as possible, and in most respects, their enthusiasm paid dividends. Their casting was strong, their direction of principals and the use of space for both principals and chorus was extremely impressive. The children, who obviously play a major role in the success of the show, were meticulously drilled yet still so full of energy and natural flow. They shone like little stars.

Played on an empty stage, with neutral flats and a massive, and well-utilised, projection screen, the technical and visual aspect of the show was ever- so-slightly two-dimensional and might have benefitted from some solid scenery pieces. That said, the projections were excellent and varied, giving a good sense of location and atmosphere. Use of more different levels might have enhanced some of the pictures when a full chorus were on the stage. But the good choreography and very secure lighting plot did ensure that there was plenty of variety to savour. Lighting was generally very good and colourful, and only on one occasion was the main lighting at a level where it partially washed out the lower level of the projections. Good use of isolated spots and special area lighting. The sound was very good and nicely balanced, and with so many radio mics I'm delighted that none of the children's lines were missed. Mr Poppy possibly needed to be slightly boosted at the start of the show, but once he settled, the sound was fine.

I love a keyboard that does the work of half an orchestra, and in the creative hands of Musical Director, Patrick Dunne, that's exactly what I got. With only himself and guitar and percussion, there was a full and robust output from the pit, which beautifully enhanced the on-stage activity. Vocal coach, Irene Dunne, had obviously done excellent preparation, with all her choruses making a tuneful, precise and secure vocal contribution to the musical success of the show. Great work was especially noted on the youngest stars, who performed their music most delightfully, even the rapper!

The choreography of Terese Dunne, Tara Gill and Aoife Kerley, assisted by Nik Parks, Zoe Parks and Ellen Hodgers, was vibrant and varied. Good precise military movement for the Oakmoor kids, and flamboyant, energetic routines for the St Bernadette's mob. The adults too contributed to the spectacle, always on point and full of energy. The children's Nativity show numbers were so much fun. Taking the central role of Paul Maddens, was Brendan Cleary who captured the essence of the Grinch-like, rather sullen 'I don't really want to be here' teacher. He had delightful and emotional moments of hope and romance, but for the most part, his grumpiness was his defining feature and he played it with conviction. His timing was excellent, and his grumpy rapport with the school children was very natural. He also had a very good vocal quality.

Mr Poppy is a role that gives a grown man the chance to become a big kid again, and the opportunity was grasped firmly by Tom Doonan in a fantastically funny manner. Basically, he's as silly as Mr Blobby, but without the costume to hide behind. The kids on stage loved him and so did the audience. As the catalyst for mayhem and madness, but also for the progression of the central love story, he played his role with total conviction, great comedy and good vocal security. Playing the female lead, Jennifer Love, Sheena Duffy had the warmth and sincerity required to be focus of Mr Maddens' affection. Brimming with expectations in her early scenes, she transformed nicely into the 'didn't quite make it' character, reflecting on how different things might have been. Sympathetically played, and with very nice vocals. Head teacher, Mrs. Bevan, was played with assurance and authority by Jane Stanley, yet vulnerable enough to be gently seduced by the attentions of the opportunistic Lord Mayor, played with good smarmy charm by Kevin Stanley. The wannabe Lord Olivier was perfectly captured by Andrew Brown as Gordon Shakespeare, with all the charm of a pantomime baddie. He was forthright, robust and appropriately sulky at ending up as a primary school teacher, instead of finding fame in Hollywood. With a fine singing voice, he made a hilarious impression playing 'Herod' in his own school's rock opera. Very good character performance. Lucie Robinson packed several punches as the acidic theatre critic, Pamela Burns, making the most of her opportunities to be a perfectly nasty piece of work, while Aoife Curran-Butler gave a convincing performance as the icy, high-powered Hollywood executive, Ms Parker. There was good support too from Siobhan Jordan, Tony Dolan, Aaron Duffy and EJ Dunne, in a variety of cameo roles, all performed with confidence and competence.

And then there were the kids! The snotty- nosed posh kids from Oakmoor School were delightfully led by Arden Oakes as Sebastian, Mia Gogarty as Malificent and Noa Goss as Thomasina. As a group, they perfectly performed in a smug, superior manner, giving great expression to "Better Than You" and "Herod, the Rock Opera". Leading the way in St Bernadette's were dynamic performances from Tess Kierans, Noah Cotter, Brendan Carolan, Elliott McLoughlin, Brianna Little, Dearbhla Tuite, Emily Morgan, Clodagh Maloney and Alan McIntyre, each displaying excellent individual personalities, and giving 100% commitment to their roles. Their entire team were effervescent and adorable, with little Tess Kierans being especially cute in her solo work. Well done to each and every one of you.  And if two choruses of children weren't enough, there was also an adult chorus, whose contribution was always enthusiastic, and well-rehearsed. They also made a good vocal impression in their big musical numbers.

Congratulations on a great display of costumes throughout the show. Principals were all dressed appropriate to their status; Mr Poppy wild and unkempt, Mr Maddens suitably square, Mrs. Bevan and Ms Parker suitably austere. The children's outfits were spic and span for Oakmoor, and nicely scruffier and more random for St Bernadette's. But the hard work was done on a great array of fancy outfits for the school shows, and for the early Christmas songs. Excellent work in these areas. Wigs, hair and make-up were all spot-on. I loved Mr Shakespeare's 'hard- rock' image for 'Herod'.

I wouldn't be at all surprised if this show became a highly popular choice for companies that have a good youth section, and who like to present Christmas entertainment. It really is great fun. This production by SONG offered so much energy, presented so much talent, and delivered an excellent standard of entertainment to a very appreciative audience. SONG is a company that thrives and benefits from a perfect amalgamation of youthful energy and focused learning, and a wealth of experienced mentors. Their strength in depth is a sure guarantee that they will flourish in the future as well as the present. Thank you to all concerned for this thoroughly entertaining first taste of Christmas spirit this year.

Sister Act is a show that, with only a few characters on-stage for the first ten minutes, can take a while to warm up and get going, but once Deloris Van Cartier dons her habit and enters the convent, the fun and frolics and the fast-flowing sequence of joyful choruses never cease until the final curtain. Add to that some nice emotional moments and some outrageously silly gangsters, and this show is always going to entertain. In this production, a high standard of performers ensured that the slightly less successful technical aspects of the show didn't detract too significantly from the audience enjoyment. I did feel that attention to the technical side of the show was a bit disappointing. While the concept of the two revolving set pieces on stage was a good one, the artwork didn't really enhance them, being a bit untidy and abstract, with the notable exception of the abbey, which was nicely created, along with the good arches at the back of the stage. Good props did help to give each scene an identity of its own, but those revolves added little warmth to any of the settings. Neither was there much warmth created by the lighting, which was initially a little bland, but did improve significantly during the more joyous Abbey scenes. Stage manager, Clare Campbell, did, however, manage to keep the scene changes rolling fairly swiftly and smoothly. Sound quality was good, and the singers had no difficulty in being heard above the band.

In all other respects, however, director/ choreographer, Mary McDonagh, presented us with a show that rattled along at a very good pace, had good emphasis on comedy and the realization of characters, was musically strong and was bright and breezy, choreographically. Her performers were never short on confidence or ability, and her chorus and dancers approached all their routines with good energy and a very impressive level of competence. The comedy of 'Lady in the Long Black Dress' was a high point of comedy, and a particularly good job was done on the second act reprise of 'Fabulous Baby', leading into a beautiful shaped and sung 'Sister Act'.

Musical Director, Niamh Crowley, gave good leadership to a very accomplished orchestra, who maintained a strong and rhythmic accompaniment throughout the show. She had obviously prepared her chorus thoroughly, as evidenced by their good vocal contribution to the show. Likewise, all of the principals were in fine voice and secure in their music.

It takes a formidable woman with a good set of lungs to fulfill the credentials of the leading role of Deloris Van Cartier, and in Sinead Conway, Sligo found such a woman. She had a commanding voice and presence and was a natural leader among the nuns. Her comedy was secure, and she had fun with her romantic encounters with Sweaty Eddie.

Equally secure and confident was the austere and sometimes unorthodox Mother Superior, delightfully portrayed by Angela McGuire. A wealth of experience gifted her with very good comedic timing, and she really sold her 'I Haven't Got a Prayer' number.

Fiona Hiney, in the role of Mary Roberts, got a very good contrast between her early shy and naïve scenes and her later determined and loyal friend, giving a strong rendition of 'The Life I Never Led'. Rebecca McGillen provided lots of laughs as the delightfully over-the-top cheerful nun, Sister Mary Patrick, and she blended well with the straight-talking, severe, but ultimately pleasant and comedic Sister Mary Lazarus, a role thoroughly enjoyed by Maureen Howley.

Good support in the convent came from Siobhan Terry as Sr Mary Theresa, and Cath Rahilly as Sr Mary Martin of Tours. If Niamh Keaveney as Michelle and Aoibhinn Dooner as Tina seemed at tad young to be giving advice to Deloris, they nevertheless performed with confidence and credibility, secure in their vocals and light on their feet.

The male cast was led by a very likeable and endearing Eddie Souther, played by Kieran Cunnane. With strong comic ability, and a pleasant voice, it was his sympathetic acting that made him a firm favourite with the audience. 'I Could Be That Guy' was nicely sung.

Franny Curley was possibly a bit gentle as thug gang leader, Curtis Jackson, but he maintained his character well throughout and made a good job of 'When I Find My Baby'.

The comedic trio of Joey, TJ and Pablo, played respectively by Killian Oates, Luke Devaney and Brian McGauran, gained many belly laughs from the audience, especially for their ridiculous antics during 'Lady in the Long Black Dress', which, for me, was the comedy highlight of the show.

Joe Shannon gave a good account of himself as Monsignor O'Hara, although I did feel that he played his punch lines a tad too deliberately towards the audience. Ben O'Loughlin and Darren Jones gave good support in a few cameo roles, each of which had a good individuality.

A good solid performance was given by the nun's chorus, who seemed to enjoy transitioning from a tuneless mob into a very tuneful and pleasing choir of angelic quality. Their robust vocals as the show progressed were most impressive. Neither did they lack energy in the execution of their routines, as they made the most of the rock and rap rhythms. They were enhanced on a few occasions by an enjoyable contribution from the altar boys, who also performed with gusto.

While the nuns' habits were sufficient to represent that they were nuns, the chorus needed to take more care with how they presented themselves, some having their veil too far back, some with wimples tucked in, some visible. More uniformity would have advanced their visual appeal. As glitz and glamour was added, however, they became much tidier. Deloris, Michelle and Tina's outfits looked fabulous, baby! The gents were all suitably attired, with Sweaty Eddie's peel-off outfits working well during 'I Could Be That Guy'.

This was a show with lively and energetic dances, some wonderful vocal displays, from principals and chorus, and some really excellent comedy sequences, all of which sent the audience, and this adjudicator, home with smiles on their faces and songs in their hearts. Thank you for the uplifting religious experience!

For those who, like myself, may be unfamiliar with the show, "First Date" is just that, a couple of hours in the company of a seemingly mismatched couple, on a blind date organised by a relative of the female. The couple and the barman are the only real characters on stage, while the remainder of the cast are a physical representation of the voices in the heads of the central couple. A sister, a mother, an ex-girlfriend, the voice of conscience, a bailout friend, contribute to the story in a series of often hilarious freezes, and occasionally perform together as commentators on the risks of blind dating. It really is a simple formula, but one that is very cleverly put together, and features some great musical numbers and quite brilliant comedic opportunities. On this occasion, all of those opportunities were taken in presenting a riveting night of rib- tickling hilarity.

Any director taking on a premiere of an unknown show is putting themselves on the parapet, risking a hammering if the goods aren't delivered in a manor to encourage others to take up the challenge, but I'm very happy to acknowledge that Director Cian O'Dowd need have no worries of being chastised for his courage. In every respect, he realised the potential of this piece, with a no-nonsense, clean and simple set, effective and atmospheric lighting, and above all, eliciting comedic performances of the highest standard with a production that used verbal and the physical technique to make this a sparklingly dynamic vehicle.

The show was played on basically a black box set, with nice overhead restaurant lights, ample appropriate furniture and good props, including consumable food and drinks. With the entire action occurring in the one space, there was little to trouble stage manager, Conor Kilduff, bar having props on stand-by and calling the lighting cues. There were no awkward moments at all in a seamless easy flowing presentation. One could, I suppose, have had a more detailed and 3-dimensional set for the restaurant, but I honestly doubt that it would have enhanced the show, the benefit of the black box being to focus attention on the performers rather than their surroundings.

The lighting, as mentioned above was atmospheric and colourful, but also very disciplined, as much of the action centered around freezes, during which the 'voices in their heads' came to life. These freezes were beautifully timed and managed and were extremely effective. In such an intimate performance space, sound quality was of a high standard and perfectly balanced.

This isn't a show that's big on choreography, but when the opportunity arose, choreographer Ainé Foley gave shape and style to her performers, adding some nice touches to the visual quality of the action. She was also blessed to have a group who were all very capable of good movement.

I'm not a big fan of backing tracks, as they tend to be merciless and do not take into account faults, pauses, fluctuating tempos from singers. Therefore, the central task for Musical Director, Keelin Kilduff, was to have her performers so meticulously rehearsed that they would never falter. This, she achieved most successfully. All of her singers were well-drilled, beautifully harmonious and articulate with their diction.

Each person on stage was appropriately attired to suit their personality, with the 'voices' being established in their different characters by the simple addition of a hat, or glasses or a scarf. Simple and effective costuming is one of the joys of a small cast show, I suppose.

And as for the performers, Stuart Pollock, as Aaron, had enough nerdiness at the outset to suggest that he might not be the Mr Right that Casey was hoping to meet, but with great acting, excellent comedy and a fabulous vocal display, he became more appealing as the night progressed. This was a very disciplined and well-judged performance, with many outstanding moments, most notably when he eventually confronts his ex-girlfriend, and as he reacts to the letter that he was left by his mother. An excellent performance.

Likewise, there was a great range of emotion expressed by a totally convincing Casey, expertly played by Jessie Woods. She had the perfect sharpness and wit for one who had played the field with the bad boys in the past, yet there was great heart and sentiment in her realisation that Aaron might just be what she needed to change her ways. Her singing was also top-notch. But it was the great balance between these two that was the cement that held the whole show together.

Robust support came in the shape of Adam Trundle as the voice of Aaron's conscience, a role played with great comedic prowess and secure vocal quality. His timing was impeccable, and he was as physically funny as his delivery of lines. This was very good work, as was the contribution of Robert Gallagher, who, among his characterisations, shone at his brightest as Reggie, the deliciously over-the-top bail-out friend of Casey. He handled the 'you're either having a really good time, or you're dead in the back of a van' monologue with perfect delivery and sublime comedy.

Shauna Maguire greatly impressed as Casey's pushy and impatient sister, but perhaps it was her role as Aaron's mother that was the most affecting. As with the other cast members, her versatility was wonderful, in acting, comedy and vocally. Aine Winter's greatest triumph was as Allison, Aaron's ex-girlfriend, which afforded her opportunities to display lust, passion, comedy and anguish and she performed each emotion with panache and yet another powerful vocal ability. Completing the cast was Philip Emmet as the waiter, a role that benefitted from his dry, wry delivery of his comedic lines. This was another wonderful performance that peaked with his compelling delivery of the very funny 'I'd Order Love'.

But perhaps the greatest strength of this show was the combined efforts of the group, that infused the ensemble pieces with raw energy, perfect harmony and an overwhelming sense of camaraderie. Thank you to everyone involved for the top-notch production and for the belly laughs. This was what entertainment is all about. Thoroughly entertaining. Thank you also for the warm hospitality in the beautiful Riverbank Arts Centre.

It's been quite a while since I've had the pleasure of attending 'The Sound of Music', a show very close to my heart, having begun my theatrical involvement (a long time ago), playing Kurt in the Opera House in Belfast, while my father played Uncle Max. In Newcastle West, the memories came flooding back, as I enjoyed the wonderful musical score and the ever-popular story of Maria Reiner and the Von Trapp Family.

The strength of this production lay in good performances from the central characters, and in a very capable and tuneful female chorus. While the technical side of the show was by no means a disaster, it is the area where, in future productions, perhaps more creativity in design would make better use of the available space. While the mountain back-drop created an impressive focal point, there was just too little scenery available to make a good distinction between the indoor and outdoor scenes at the Von Trapp home, and on occasions, the movement of some pieces seemed superfluous. The trellised flats either side of the stage were quite effective, except that they moved a lot, and seemed to impede the smooth entrance and exit of people and of other pieces. I do appreciate the lack of space that you had backstage, and the hard work the stage team did to keep everything moving, and to attempt to make the scenes as varied as possible.

Directors Tom Madigan and Susan Brown kept very true to the book with this production, adding only the "I Have Confidence" solo for Maria, and swapping "Something Good" in place of "An Ordinary Couple", both changes of which I strongly approve. If there was a weakness in performance, it was perhaps that some of the principals needed to assimilate their reactions and tone of voice with what they were saying or singing, as on occasions, the dialogue came across as 'reading from a script' rather than coming from the heart. The notable exceptions to this were Maria and the Mother Superior, who flowed with a natural ability and with great confidence. The children were beautifully directed in their action and their delivery. Tara Downes proved to be the perfect choice for the role of Maria, with just enough mischief to accentuate her youthfulness, a bundle of compassion towards the children, a confident boldness to confront the Captain, and a very convincing inner conflict as she came to terms with discovering love for the first time. This was a very good complete performance, combined with a most pleasing vocal quality.

Co-director, Susan Browne, led by example by giving a splendid performance as the Mother Abbess, filled with a religious devotion and a heart full of compassion. While her "Favourite Things" duet with Maria was of great quality, it was her "Climb Every Mountain" that really made a powerful impact. Very nicely delivered. Charlie O'Connell had the strong physical presence to present himself as a disciplinarian Captain, but was perhaps a little less comfortable with his relationships with Elsa and Maria. There was good sincerity in his anger at the intrusion of Nazi-Germany into his Austrian lifestyle, and also a nice warmth in his rendition of Edelweiss.

Paul Moriarty was an amusing Uncle Max, trying to make the most of his comedy, if on occasions a tad too deliberate in his delivery. Molly Giltenane was similarly too exaggerated in her movement as Baroness Elsa, and while she looked and sounded perfect for the role, she needed to be a little less mobile and a little more relaxed. Their musical numbers together, however, were well-delivered and well received.

A young Domhnall O'Connor gave good account of himself in creating the character of Rolf Gruber, sincere in his affections for Liesl, and conflicted in his acceptance of Nazism. "Sixteen Going on Seventeen" was very nicely presented. He was helped by an equally splendid performance from Keelan Fahy as Liesl, played with just enough attitude to capture the mischief of a teenager, but also with a bucket load of affection for her family.

The children, from Friedrich through to Gretl, performed beautifully throughout the show. Joseph O'Connor and Padraig Doherty were delightfully pleasant young men, while Leah Walsh as Louisa, was convincingly precocious. Jade Massey's Brigitta was amusingly wise beyond her years, and Molly Sparling and Anna O'Sullivan added much cuteness to the junior roles of Marta and Gretl.

The trio of nuns, Evelyn Shanahan as Sister Bertha, Caroline Daly as Sister Margareta and Ann Marie Murphy as Sister Sophia, gave good account of themselves in a nicely delivered "Maria" and maintained their characters well throughout the show. Dinny Ahern was a suitably treacherous Franz, the butler, and Caroline Walsh, was a very capable Frau Schmidt. Tom Madigan had the stature and menace to be a convincing Herr Zeller.

Other minor roles were comfortably portrayed by Padraig O'Shea, Marie Hestor, Helen Ahern and Lisa Kelly.

The Nuns Choruses were all very nicely sung, and they presented themselves well, if only they had looked a little more joyous, particularly when singing the celebratory Alleluia at the wedding. I was delighted that all the nuns pieces were sung in full, as the vocal quality was most satisfactory. They contributed well to the overall production.

A more creative lighting plot might have enhanced the settings, like using break- up or leaf gobos for the garden scenes. As it was, the lighting succeeded in making sure that everyone was well-illuminated, and colour variations did help to change the atmosphere.

Sound quality was generally good, although sound effects (Abbey bells, etc) needed to be faded down, rather than cutting off abruptly.

Much more successful was the visual presentation, with very nice costumes for the children and the principals, and the nuns all looking proper and correct. The only glaring error, costume wise, is that Von Schreiber, as a high ranking Naval Officer, would most definitely not have been wearing a Nazi uniform. The children presented themselves very well at all times. The curtain outfits were very good. With a small band at his disposal, Musical Director, Michael Young, was perhaps a little heavy-handed on his keyboard, which occasionally competed with the singers on stage, but tempi were good and steady throughout the show. The principals all seemed to be musically well-rehearsed, with the Nuns Chorus sounding articulate and harmonious, and the children making a splendid job of their harmony pieces. There are very few opportunities for choreography in this show, but the children's numbers were kept interesting and well-devised, and they were performed with confidence and enthusiasm.

The Sound of Music boasts a wonderful musical score, endearing characters and a great story of family and National pride in the face of adversity, and all of those elements were given such good treatment by a most enthusiastic and hardworking cast. I am grateful to have been there to have so many happy memories brought back to me. Thank you all for a most enjoyable and entertaining evening.

It never ceases to amaze me that the wonderful old chestnut, that is "Oklahoma!", still continues to captivate audiences and more significantly, that directors still manage to find novel ways to keep it fresh and individual. Such was the case with this beautiful production by Naas Musical Society. It says a lot about the class and talent of esteemed Director, Mona Conroy, that even on this, her swan song as a director, (such a sad revelation) she has infused this production with so many wonderful and original touches. The choreographed overture was delightful and nicely introduced the chorus and some of the principal characters even before a word had been spoken, which made a pleasant change from the usual opening scene with just three characters on stage for the first 10 or 15 minutes. The use of little children in this scene was also charming. Then there was the excellent strengthening of the relationship between Laurey and Gertie which gave a new dynamic to both of their characters and added some lovely comedic moments. The whole production had a feeling of inclusivity, with chorus introduced as observers and by-standers in several scenes, which I'm quite sure gave the chorus a greater sense of involvement. The pace of the show was well judged and there was good focus on the important pieces of action, although I did feel that Jud's death happened just a tad too swiftly. A bit more of a tussle might have intensified the drama before he fell on his own knife. But it has to be said that the overall production had the stamp of a lady who continues to inspire and encourage, whose positive influence will endure even in her absence and whose talent and expertise will be sadly missed if those very experienced boots are finally hung up. Thank you, Mona Conroy, not just for this production, but for your legacy. The set was well-designed and beautifully painted and presented. The backdrop was attractive, while the set pieces were securely constructed and nicely detailed, Aunt Eller's House and the Smoke-house making a fine impact. My only grumble was that there was no way to alter the appearance of the stage for the Box Social, which appeared to be held in Aunt Eller's yard. In every other respect, staging was visually strong and managed with comfort and precision by a well-drilled stage crew under the leadership of Stage Manager, Tom Kavanagh. There were some very authentic and appropriate props and furniture, although the hot-water bag and some of the... (ahem!) rather scant underwear items in Ali Hakim's bag were rather obviously a bit too modern. Lighting, throughout, was splendid, with good use of colour, nice atmospheres, and a fine level of surrealism for the dream ballet. The quality of sound was excellent, especially given that the orchestra were behind the stage. Balance and clarity were of the highest order. Curly was lucky not to lose a few fingers when his gun-shot was let off just a tad too prematurely in the smoke-house, but that's a very minor issue and was actually quite amusing. The choreography of Grace McGrath is consistently clean, precise and designed to suit and accentuate the talent of her choruses and dancers, which is why it achieves a high level of success. As with Mona Conroy's work, there is a sense of inclusivity, giving everyone their moment in the limelight, and saving her best work for those most capable of a challenge. The Dream Ballet was very well worked and featured good moments of fun combined with strong moments of drama. The Farmer and the Cowman was energetic and fluent and very well danced. Kansas City, as the opening choreographed number, was fun-filled and got things off to a confident start. Very good work. Hidden behind the set, the orchestra for this production were disciplined and precise and expertly led by Musical Director, Mairead McKenna. That the balance of sound was perfect and that entrances and exits, musically, were tight and accurately observed is testament to good preparation and thorough rehearsal. Chorus vocals were wonderful, and all of her principals were on cue and on point in their delivery. The show was musically delicious, and the familiar tunes were greatly enjoyed by the audience.

Rory Dignam offered us a cocky, secure and very believable Curly, but also good in his sentimental romance with Laurey. He had good appearance, good confidence and a very pleasant voice. Beside him, Sarah O'Driscoll made an absolutely delightful Laurey. She gave us all you would expect from Laurey, but with added vim, thanks to the nicely developed relationship between herself and Gertie. Her vocals were very secure, and her dancing was charming.

Gill O'Brien was a force to be reckoned with in the role of Aunt Ellen. No mellow old woman here, but a wily, street-wise matron, with a rambunctious sense of humour and commanding voice and presence, and frankly, much more personality than we might normally expect from Aunt Eller. I liked her, a lot.

Shane Byrne was a very credible and very likeable Will Parker, with a good voice and an even better sense of comedy. He was well able to lead the Kansas City dance and worked delightfully well alongside Ado Annie.

Lynn Carter gave a petite, perky, powerhouse of a performance as Ado Annie. Her acting and comedy were very strong, but it was her facial expressions that made her stand out, always beaming, always mischievous and always alert. She compelled the audience to take notice of her. She also put so much energy and a very fine voice into her musical numbers. As the roguish, philandering peddler, Ali Hakim, Paul Dicker relished the opportunity to milk the comedy to the full, and he did so with charm and character. Only occasionally did he need to slow the pace of his dialogue and emphasize his comedic reactions, but this was a very commendable performance.

Rory Dunne had a strong stature and a good growly look for Jud Fry, which was complemented by his strong acting and delivery of lines, but without a shadow of a doubt, his vocal delivery of Poor Jud is Dead, and particularly Lonely Room, was the musical highlight of the show. The power, the tone and the quality of his singing was awesome, so much so that I almost wished him to win the knife fight with Curly on the off-chance that he might burst into song again. (No offence at all to Curly!) A remarkably fine performance. Hayley Campbell proved to be hilariously obnoxious in the role of Gertie Cummings, with a laugh that would put years on you. A very nicely developed and performed character.

Arthur McGauran provided gravitas and excellent character comedy to the role of Andrew Carnes, comfortably in control of all his scenes, and a strong leader in The Farmer and The Cowman.

As previously mentioned, there was excellent and creative use of the chorus throughout the show, particularly as peripheral dressing to many of the scenes. There were all business and well- disciplined in the choreographed overture, and if one or two of the tiny performers didn't quite achieve their 'freezes', their cuteness only added to the delight of the audience. Vocally, the chorus were excellent, with ever-consistent tone and harmony. The Farmer and the Cowman was vibrant and uplifting and the Oklahoma Chorus was exquisite. The ladies in Out of My Dreams and Many a New Day were articulate and easy on the ear. Physically, everyone gave 100% to their acting and provided so much atmosphere to the box social and to the auction scene. Dancing throughout was precise, efficient and gleefully performed.

There was very good attention to detail in the costuming of the show, from head to toe, with footwear being notably appropriate at all times. I did wonder if one or two of the hats on some of the ladies were a bit more 'My Fair Lady' than 'Oklahoma!', but they were beautifully made and presented. The ladies' dresses were colourful and authentic, and the men were well turned out. Ballet costumes were attractive and in keeping with the various moods of the piece, and I liked the smartness of some of the men in the wedding scene. Hair styles were consistently good, as was make-up. Visually, the show was very successful. Sincere thanks to Dave Smyth in particular and to all the front of house staff for their courtesy and efficiency. It is always a bonus to see the staff dressed for the occasion. Dave, (who has always been a bit of a cowboy!) looked wonderful, as did the other cowboys and cowgirls.

The boots of the dynamic Mona Conroy will be difficult to fill in future productions, but as she retires from direction, she leaves Naas with a legacy of excellence, involvement and community pride that will not be extinguished. While thanking you all for a most enjoyable night of entertainment in Naas, I wish you future success in all your endeavours and I would like to wish Mona a long and happy retirement.

If anyone ever doubted the old saying 'the apple doesn't fall far from the tree', they should have seen the Muse production of "Our House" where a new generation of young thespians was led by a dynamic couple who performed out of their skins to make this a most memorable and highly talented experience. Following in the footsteps of their extremely skilled and experienced parents, Conor McNelis, as Joe Casey, and Julita Fox, as Sarah, displayed talents that went far beyond what one would expect, given their tender years. They were quite remarkable, and they were supported by a cast that brimmed with talent, energy and enthusiasm in every aspect of their performances.

Director Martin McNellis really did his homework to ensure that "Our House" was as authentic to its era as possible, and to stretch the talents of his young principals to the max. In both of these tasks, he succeeded most assuredly. Furthermore, he stretched himself, taking on a very modern piece with demanding stage requirements. With a beautifully crafted set, on a tight and unforgiving stage, he achieved something of a technical miracle. The 'Driving in my Car' number, a combination of classy direction and technical genius, was quite brilliant. The staging of the show was clever, concise, and ran like clockwork. The design was excellent and the management of all the moving pieces was a tribute not only to the industrious stage manager, Ted Germaine, but also to his team and the cast members who worked together in perfect harmony. The upper platform was well used, especially for the presence of the 'ghost' father, and props and furniture were always authentic and moved in and out efficiently. Astute direction also contributed to perfectly timed costume changes for the central character, which played an essential role in the continuity of the piece. Likewise, choreography played an important role in the transitions, highlighting choreographer Pamela Glynn's astute appreciation of the drama as much as the dance. She also perfectly recreated the 'Madness' era, with wonderfully nostalgic and highly energetic dance routines, which were performed with dynamic enthusiasm and precision. Lighting was an important part of the drama, requiring very well-timed lightning flashes at every transition. These were achieved to perfection. The lighting of ghostly Dad was delightfully cold throughout, if once or twice, slightly too dimly lit. The rest of the lighting plot was colourful and atmospheric. Sound quality was generally good, even if Dad was a little under-amplified in the early scenes. Between sound engineers and musical director, a very careful balance was maintained so that the hidden band never overwhelmed the singers.

The ever youthful and dynamic Mary-Rose McNally was the leader of that hidden band, kept under-stage for the performance, visible only to the cast by video-link, but even from her darkened abode, she kept a tight rein on the musical quality of the show, with assured entrances and cut- offs. She also produced balanced sound and an astoundingly authentic 'Madness' feel from her excellent musicians. So much so that I initially wondered were they using original backing tracks, but no, they were just that good.

But the night belonged to the dynamism that was abundantly evident on the stage. Conor McNelis, as Joe, displayed a level of maturity in his performance that is uncommon for someone so young. He understood his character and the juxtapositions that he faced and played both versions of himself with good contrast and much intensity. His love for Sarah was very well-delivered, and his guilt and emotion in the final scenes was spine-tinglingly sincere. Such a strong and assured performance.

It was the equally mature, sensitive and balanced performance from Julita Fox as Sarah that made this central relationship so powerful. Here is a young lady who understands vulnerability and heartache as convincingly as she displays the confident and capable modern woman who is prepared to go it alone when required. Again, she handled the emotional scenes with great sensitivity. Added to the strong acting, both performers showed excellent comedic timing and strong vocals throughout.

As Dad, first time performer, Colm McGuinness showed few signs of nervousness, giving a ghostly performance that grew in intensity and emotion as the show progressed. He is also in possession of a fine set of vocal chords.

Olivia Parkinson gave a warm and resolute performance as Kath, Joe's widowed mother. There was great strength in her determination to survive her hardships and great passion in her relationship with Joe. Her songs were delivered with clarity and sincerity.

Sally Fox as Billie, and Alanna Willets as Angie provided the comedic back-up to Sarah, and did so with a great sense of fun, and often a caustic sense of humour. These were strong performers who, given that the show is very much a drama with music, perhaps played just a little too obviously to the audience rather than to their fellow performers. They were, nonetheless, delightfully funny and crass, and both were very capable of belting out their lyrics. On Joe's side of the table, comedy support came from Cillian Fahy as Emmo and Ciarán O'Keefe as Lewis. Both made the most of their opportunities, with Cillian in particular, acting out the required immaturity to present himself as the twit of the group.

As the bad apple, irresponsible delinquent of the piece, Sean McInerney was a strong and repugnant Reecey, as was required of him. It's not always easy to play the bully, but he did so with conviction.

There was a note-worthy performance from old-timer, Aodan Fox, as the corrupt businessman, Mr Pressman, and it's fair to assume that the many younger performers on the stage have learned a lot from his self-assured, always considered and highly professional approach to every part he plays. Completing the younger cast were good solid performances from Tara Monaghan as Julie and Richard Germaine as Callum, while Dara O'Callaghan, Ian Collins, Laura O'Brien, Michelle Kelly, Sarah Allen and Kim O'Dea filled a vast array of supporting cameo roles with credibility and confidence. A special mention too, for the delightful cameo performances of Cormac Ross as Elvis and Cooper.

Sheer energy was the key to the success of the chorus, whether it was the vocal energy of their strong choral contributions, or the physical energy of their wonderfully performed dance routines. They were never on stage looking lost or being passive. They always contributed to the atmosphere and ambiance of their scenes. Visually, the show was also most successful. The black suit and white track-suit of Joe worked brilliantly in facilitating those numerous and essential fast changes. Similarly, Sarah's costumes were well selected to blend with each scene.

Costumes generally were attractive, era-appropriate and worn well by the company. From hairstyles, to make up, to footwear, the cast looked correct from head to toe. The extra-speedy on-stage costume change for Joe was amazingly slick!

There's no such thing as a flawless or perfect production, but it's an awesome experience when a show comes close. Not for the first time this season, I'm feeling that awe. Well done, Muse, on something pretty spectacular.

There was something nostalgic and wonderful about seeing Director Ronan Lardner and Musical Director, Shane Farrell working side-by-side in the very venue where they both cut their musical teeth, under the guidance of the late, great Joe O'Donoghue and the late, great Noel Kirrane. How proud their past masters would have been to see how both of their students have established themselves in musical theatre. They would most certainly have been impressed with this wonderfully joyful production of Sister Act. Boasting a highly talented front line and an energetic and enthusiastic chorus, this was entertainment of the highest order. An excellent comedian himself, director Ronan Lardner managed to wring every ounce of comedy out of the very funny script, and added many little individual touches, but he was just as thorough about playing up the sentimental side of the story.

The set for the show was as simple as possible, given a stage that has no room at all for massive pieces or storage, but it was clean, effective and well-painted. Only essential items of props and furniture were apparent, and it was more than enough. The centre piece of the set was an excellent circular stained-glass window, which, combined with really effective lighting, looked superb. The confessional boxes were very good, and the rest of the props were appropriate and acceptable. A centre stage black gauze was well used both for isolating the forward scenes but also as a bleed-through to create some nice effects. Lighting was generally very good, with atmospheric use of colours and back light. Sound quality throughout was just about perfect.

The band, under the direction of Shane Farrell, obviously enjoyed every note of this excellent musical score, playing with a vibrant and precise energy, always on point, and always sympathetic to the vocalists on stage. Tempi throughout were just perfect. Shane had gone to town on the choral vocals, as evidenced by secure harmonies, excellent diction and a certain joie de vivre in performance. This was a top drawer choral display. Musically and physically, they performed out of their skins, adding a secure backbone to the whole production. Their sheer sense of enjoyment was contagious.

Commanding the stage from the get-go, Emma Brady proved to be the perfect casting for the demanding role of Deloris Van Cartier. Her acting and her comedy were on point, her movement was fluid, and when she sang… Wow! With a voice like a finely tuned instrument, she raised the roof in every number. Whether with the gentle, dulcet and emotional tones of 'Sister Act' or unleashing the inner beast in 'Take Me to Heaven' and 'Raise Your Voice', the vocal quality was simply awesome. It almost converted me!

There was a sublime quality to the voice and performance of Frieda McGrath as the Mother Superior, dignity and decorum epitomized, until the strain of coping with Deloris eventually cracked her outer shell. Then she delighted us with a very funny and slightly demented rendition of 'I Haven't Got A Prayer'. Frieda and Emma played off each other absolutely beautifully.

A young and endearing Alana Mullins made a big impact as the shy and reserved Sr Mary Robert, then floored us all with her feisty power when she unleashed 'The Life I Never Led'. Such talent from one so young, and a very well-played role.

Who can resist a nun with attitude? With a voice that could shatter concrete, a presence that would ward of the devil, and an abundance of comedic talent, Clodagh Ruane rocked and rapped her way into our hearts with a superb performance as Sr Mary Lazarus.

Olivia McNama was filled with fun and religious fervour as the highly animated and extremely funny Sr Mary Patrick, making the most of all her opportunities to shine. There were equally accomplished performances from Eimear McGovern as Sr Mary Theresa and Sinead Whelan as Sr Mary Martin-of-Tours.

Congratulations to the very talented Declan Kelly for playing Monsignor O'Hara with great empathy, understanding, excellent comedic timing and a modicum of irreverent humour.

Norman Quinn presented us with a very sweaty and very loveable Eddie, playing the love-struck, weak-willed cop to perfection. He realised his comedy most effectively and sang like a nervous bird until he found himself being suddenly manly. A lovely performance.

Niall Conway was a strong and believable gang-leader in the role of mafia-style hoodlum, Curtis.

His stature made him imposing but it was his menacing demeanour and his confident acting that made him such a convincing character. The man can sing a bit too. He was ably assisted in his nefarious endeavours by a trio of comically inept bad-guys, Stuart Barrows as Joey, as smooth as he was stylish, Thomas Edwards, as TJ, the very funny idiot relation that everyone denies knowing, and Michael Cooney, the ludicrous Latino who represents the strongest argument for tighter border controls. Very good performances from this whole team of desperados.

As Deloris's night-club sidekicks, Michelle and Tina, Emer Kelly and Sinead Murphy sang and danced delightfully and handled their dialogue with assured comedic ability. It's a pity these parts aren't bigger, but very nicely played.

There was good support, too, from Sean King as the 'disposable' Ernie, who also doubled as an altar boy alongside Ruadhan Gormally. Feargal MacMeanmain made a delightful cameo appearance as the Pope, even kneeling down to kiss the floor of the school hall. A nice touch.

From a visual point of view, you can't go too far wrong with nuns habits, and in this case, they were worn well, and increased delightfully in glitz and glamour as the show progressed through to a dazzling finale. Principal costumes were all appropriate, although you could have been a little more flamboyant with the hoodlums outfits. Curtis was delightfully dapper as the gang-leader. Eddie's triple costume was very good, and not at all obvious before he was disrobed. Wigs/ hairstyles were fine, although Deloris might have had a slightly tidier corkscrew, but it didn't impede the quality of her performance. Make up seemed natural, with no glaring eye-liners or polished nails on the nuns. Good work.

Sister Act isn't the most challenging show to stage or to perform, but it is most certainly one of the best feel-good shows of the modern era, and when it is performed to such a high standard, it is easy to get carried along by the euphoria and the heavenly goodness of the piece. This wasn't a very good production, it was a very excellent production, and it was a privilege to see Marian Choral Society reaching such heights of achievement. Thank you for a truly wonderful night.

Tralee's Siamsa Tíre is a beautiful venue, and one that I always enjoy visiting, and when the standard of production and performance is as high as was presented by LOST, it makes the journey south seem somehow shorter and so worthwhile. "Evita" is a wonderful biographical musical, with a superb score and an intriguing story, but it can be very demanding, which makes the success of this production all the sweeter. From sets and costumes to direction and choreography and magical musicianship, all the elements came together beautifully to frame and accentuate a cast of excellent performers. Director Grainne O'Carroll's passion for this show was clearly evident in her disciplined and beautifully stylised production. The attention to detail was excellent, from the eye-catching set to the costumes, the lighting, the groupings on stage and the right tone and mood of each scene. With a very well-constructed and painted set, featuring nice little playing areas on the front aprons, and a stunning Casa Rosada centrepiece, the stage was beautifully and atmospherically lit throughout, with good use of colours and nicely defined special areas. Props were generally very good, although I'd like to have seen maybe more bunting or national flags for the countries on the Rainbow Tour. The projected footage of the cinema, and then the newsreel of the actual Eva Peron funeral was of very good quality. The production was streamlined, with little or no superfluous dressing or action, which saw the focal point of the action always clearly apparent, and it helped to maintain a very good pace. If she had felt so inclined, Grainne might have added another dimension visually by being a bit more flamboyant and carnival minded in the costuming of the 'Buenos Aires' number. However, chorus costumes had good variety between the street people and the sophisticates, and the men's uniforms were, by and large, appropriate and well-worn. Eva Peron's gowns were fabulous and flattering, her red outfit being wonderful in allowing her the freedom for the stylised dancing, and the white balcony dress was exquisite. Peron was sharp and elegant, and Che was cool and casual.

Ranging from precise military style routines to flamboyant street dances, including very well-devised choreographed fights and an elegant tango and waltz, a great amount of thought and care went into the work of choreographer, Tara Dore. It was vibrant, fluent and mostly extremely well executed by the chorus and dancers. Dancing on chairs is never easy, but in the 'Art of the Possible' routine, the cast were meticulously well-drilled. This was a most varied and exciting dance show.

A very strong orchestra, under the guidance and leadership of Musical Director, Anna Connolly, played the beautiful musical score with tone, balance and wonderful expression. Rhythms and pace were pretty much perfect. Chorus Mistress, Caitriona Fitzmaurice, had her singers well-drilled and full of expression and articulation. The quality of the music, throughout, was extremely high.

There can be few female roles as demanding as that of Eva Peron, requiring powerful vocals and a wide range of emotions, and in Clodagh Harrington, this production has found the perfect performer for the role. From the flirtatious social climber to the manipulative power behind Peron, she infused her character with style and dynamism, most often expressed through a pitch perfect and commanding vocal display.

Clodagh played this role several years ago as a very promising up-and-coming artiste, but now she has come of age with a quite brilliant performance.

There was a stirring performance too from Marcus Nolan as Peron, strong in stature, secure in his vocals, highly believable in his acting and also fleet of foot as he fought his way into power. This was a sincere and well-rounded characterisation.

Sean McElligot, as the narrator, Che, despite the annoyance of a dodgy radio- mic for his early scenes, never lost his composure and kept the story moving with a strong and confident personality, and an excellent voice.

Owen Rua Herlihy established himself as the crooner Magaldi with a fine rendition of 'On This Night of a Thousand Stars'. Perhaps we needed to see more obviously his flirting with Eva at the start, but his frustration at her behaviour as the show progressed was well-registered.

In the most thankless role of the Mistress, Lauren Glennon did all you really can do, which is to sell the beautiful 'Another Suitcase in Another Hall' with conviction. She displayed nice vocal quality and expression.
