Characters stepped out of the chorus to give us some nice cameo moments, such as Shea Brady, Malachy Quinn, Canice McIlvenna and Holly as Mrs Luce. All gave a depth to the show. The chorus were included as much as possible and all knew what was expected from them and delivered in spades. A well moved and sung piece of chorus work.

This was a fantastically designed and presented set. So so simple but so effective. A raised central area was the shop with a doorway to the cellar stage right and a door to the street stage left. This was then hidden from view by two trucks painted with shop frontage which simply slid into place. The changes were then virtually instant. There was a doorway with steps leading to it downstage right. This was a good place to group the girls. There was an interesting effect of further distant buildings behind the scene. The painting of the set was superbly done with a real feel of comic book style. The stage floor was painted in the similar off white/ taupe tones. This always adds a certain unity and especially in theatres where the audience is looking down at the stage gives a very professional finish to a set. Mushnik's shop was sharply painted and might have appeared a little more down at heel initially. It had a wonderful black and white tiled floor.

Scenes such as the Dentist Surgery were quickly established with cleverly chosen and authentic props such as the green hospital screen and the wonderful dentist's chair. The four Audrey 2 plants were incredibly detailed and were painted really well. The final huge one looked wonderful and moved really well too. I was surprised when I asked where it had been hired from that it had been made by the team. I am sure they will be in great demand from societies staging the show. Properties were in the style of the piece and in good condition, though I would have liked the shop to have been dressed a little more to show a contrast from rags to riches.

The lighting plot was detailed and very effective, creating all sorts of interesting pictures such as the back lit windows. This was a lighting scheme which was not rigid but adapted to the movements of the cast, areas being gently lit as the cast moved out of one well lit area into another. Our attention was nicely focussed on the action with well placed specials. There was excellent sound quality to the production for most of the show with good balance between the performers to produce those perfect harmonies.

There was a modern urban theme to the chorus costumes. Audrey wore figure hugging dresses and those great high shoes. The costumes were all in keeping with the look and feel of the show and the era in which it was set. The hair was well set and make up was all well applied with a very naturalistic look. Audrey's wig was good and moved well as she teetered around but didn't obstruct her face.

We were given a very warm welcome to the theatre and enjoyed our chat with Sean O'Neill. The soul music playing as we entered the auditorium helped to set the atmosphere.

This was a show directed with real heart, real thought and wonderful attention to detail. I know that this society will be an integral part of the AIMS movement and I wish them future success. I really enjoyed the craic in Little Shop Of Horrors.

Better known now as the Dolly Parton musical, the stage show based on the movie which was released back in 1980 is quite true to that story. The story of sexism and exploitation in the workplace seems quite hard to believe but was very real at the time and one which is useful to remember so it never happens again. It is a great vehicle for some fun packed and also moving performances and Sligo Fun Company gave us a really sparkling version of the show in The Hawk's Well Theatre in the town.

The show was directed and choreographed by the highly experienced Mary MacDonagh. She decided that it should be set in a 1970s world and there were many references to the era with costuming, props and styling. She had chosen her principal players very well and everyone on stage really suited their roles. There was also good pairing of couples with believable relationships formed between them. The three main female characters of Violet, Judy and Doralee established a good though initially unlikely partnership. Humour was very much to the fore and the audience were guaranteed to have a really good laugh. The settings chosen were solid looking and elaborate. The cast all moved well though a few of the solo numbers offered a little more scope for movement. Production numbers were exciting with a well-trained cast giving us routines with good changing patterns but also neatly executed dance steps and great positioning of arms. The office dances were great with the men really adding an authentic touch to the routines. The three speciality dances of 'Dance of Death', 'Cowgirl's Revenge' and 'Potion Notion' were all really well executed and terrific fun.

Musical Director, Niamh Crowley was blessed with a cast who could all sing to such a high standard. Principal players all had great singing voices and delivered Dolly's songs with style. The eight-piece orchestra gave a vibrant accompaniment to the piece, mostly nicely balanced to the voices of the cast but a few occasions when a little restraint might have been needed volume wise. A nice rounded sound and good tempi in the ensemble numbers. The chorus gave us some memorable moments with strong singing. The three ladies at the centre of our story gave us some wonderful sensitive acting, much comedy and great singing in their roles. Judy was strongly portrayed by Sinead Conway. This is the hard-working single mum striving to take care of her son and getting knocked back from promotions because of her gender. Sinead captured the essence of the role very well but really came into own when she was acting in the hospital where she showed exceptional comic timing. 'The Potion Notion' routine was very well staged and really funny too.

Sinead sang well and moved around the stage with purpose and confidence. The developing love affair with Joe was nicely handled. Sinead Conway blew us away with her wonderful performance of 'Get Out, Stay Out' as Judy. She played the 'unsure of herself' well and the defiance in this last number had great resonance. Her 'Dance Of Death' certainly showed what a performer she is, well sung and nicely moved. Doralee was portrayed by Fiona Hiney. This part holds great expectations as this is the part Dolly herself played in the movie. We weren't disappointed. Fiona captured the character well.

There was a lovely vulnerability in her performance which was so right for the role. She showed a sensitive side in her relationship with husband Dwayne. Individually good, together they of course caused such mayhem such as the scene with the dodgy cigarette!

Franny Curley played the part of Franklin Hart in quite a gentlemanly manner not becoming too tactile with the staff. This can often be the case for this role and it can become a little offensive to the audience. He did however seem very at ease on stage and was a good foil to the three secretaries. The final scene when he discovers his promotion involves a move to Bolivia was hilarious. This number one fan Roz was played with such commitment to the role by Rebecca McGillen. Her love for him was tangible. Her delivery of 'Heart to Hart' was so funny especially those wee side glances and the tracing of her toe on the stage. I wasn't wild about her outfit at the end as I could have seen her in something much sexier but it was a great piece of comic acting Rebecca. Judy's 'toy boy' Joe was nicely played by Luke Devaney. This was a role which really grew through the production. He doesn't give up on his pursuit of Judy and in the end his dedication pays off. He showed what a stunning tone he has to his singing voice in 'Let Love Grow' which was a beautiful romantic moment in the show. Kieran Cunnane was a very real Dwayne and his relationship with Doralee very strong. There was a lovely image of him sitting strumming his guitar which really established the character for us. Dick who had left the lovely violet to be with a much younger model was played by Brian McGaurin. He captured the cheating weasel really well and almost got the audience to take pity on him. We all celebrated when Violet told him to 'get out and stay out'.

Judy's teenage son Josh was played by Matthew Eglinton. He created an interesting character with very little dialogue. The scene with him chatting to Judy as he sat on his skateboard seemed relaxed and their relationship grew from that through the show. The appearance of Russell Tinsworthy, the Chairman Of The Board brought an extra spark of life towards the end of the show. Hugh O'Neill is obviously a seasoned performer as he seemed so comfortable in the role. He tied up all the loose ends of the plot so well. A team of talented cameo players supported the principal cast with great conviction.

Siobhan Terry was the reformed drinker Margaret, Terri Brennan as the idealistic Mrs Hart (Missy), Eva Hamilton as the hard done by Maria, Eva Devaney as Kathy, Declan Flavin as Bob Enright and the Doctor, Darren Ker as the Detective, Niamh Noonan as the Candy Striper and Daeneara McGowan as the New Intern. All of them added so much to the show. The chorus very much dressed the set but they all looked as if they really were working in the office. There was good acting and reacting to the story being told. The set looked good when each set was placed but the pieces used were quite cumbersome to move even by this hard- working stage team. It might have been better to really strip this right back and use tighter spot lit areas to denote place. One scene which for me worked so well was in Judy's apartment when the room was created with a few well-chosen pieces which were well placed and interestingly lit. However, the bedroom when in place looked very opulent with carved gold mirror against the wall behind the bed. The desks in the office worked well though to incorporate the moving of scenery as part of the show might be something to try next time as it means we don't have to pause the action while scenery is being moved into place. Lighting was used quite effectively through the show with some snappy cues. There were possibilities to develop the lighting plot even further to create more interesting effects. The microphones were well cued and for the majority of the show the orchestral backing was nicely balanced with the vocals.

The colours of the 1970s inspired clothes brightened from mostly earthy browns and creams to vibrate colours, as colour was brought back into everyone's life. This was a very clever visual touch. As there should be, there was a good mix of styles from the era which worked well together. The three principal ladies all looked quite appropriate and the dresses for their fantasy number looked super. The cast's own hair was curled into flicks which gave the feel of the time. Make up was quite restrained but looked quite natural. The longer hair of some of the men helped capture the feel of the time.

The Hawk's Well Theatre is always a joy to visit. We were welcomed and looked after by Fintan who is a great source of local knowledge. He was rightly very proud of the efforts of everyone involved with the show. It was plainly obvious to me that the cast and crew had been working beyond the hours of 9 To 5 to perfect all that was involved in this production. To all involved, well done and particularly to those many folk in the cast who Mary told me were new to the stage, stick with it, you will gain so much pleasure from all those future shows.

The story of Tevye and the folk of the Jewish village of Anatevka still has a certain resonance today. Thrown off their lands in a pogrom by the Russian authorities, forced to move all around the world seeking a new home. It is a sad story but a story of humour and hope in adversity. It portrays a whole community and is a great vehicle for an amateur society as so many people of all ages can get involved. It gives us some of the most enduring and popular characters in musical theatre with a truly memorable score. 9 Arch Claregalway Musical Society gave us a most enjoyable evening with good story telling of this classic musical. Director David Harkin produced a very sincere version of the story. He had obviously decided to slightly underplay some of the dialogue to achieve a very realistic feel. This for the most part worked well. There was good natural movement on stage during dialogue with very little masking. Some of the most dramatic moments in the show such as Hodel's leaving at the railway station were sensitively handled. The gentle humour was quite well teased out of the script. The pace between principals was good but did go out of gear a few times due to settling in nerves. The Second Act had a much steadier pace overall. The characters were nicely developed and the relationships between players were clear. There was a good choice of actor for each pairing, all of which seemed well suited. There is some glorious music in the show and experienced Musical Director Shane Farrell gave us a very charming and melodic accompaniment. There were some wonderful voices to train for this show with a strong principal line up. The chorus were all very comfortable with their parts too. The show needs a rousing opening number and that is what we got for 'Tradition'. Some lovely 'Yiddish' moments which were hauntingly played by members of the eight-piece orchestra. A most memorable song was the beautiful 'Little Bird' which was given the lightest of touches.

Some of the choreography in the show was intricate, detailed and quite novel. Choreographer Jay Molyneux interpreted the opening number well with the story building as characters were introduced. Some good moments later in the show working with pairs and groups. 'Matchmaker, Matchmaker' was lively vocally and the three sisters moved well as they told of their marriage ambitions. 'To Life' was exciting and very energetic. The 'Bottle Dance' needed a little more. Tevye is perhaps one of the most difficult of men's roles in a musical. He is very much the linchpin of the show, we see the world through his eyes. It is a responsibility to play this role and one which shouldn't be taken lightly. Alan gave us a very sincere and quite calm Tevye. This was a very naturalistic version of the role and we all felt very comfortable in his company. He managed to get good moments of humour from the script, some of the lines which I had heard many times being given new life. When he pushes his singing voice out to us, wow what a delicious rich tone he has! I would have loved a special place for him to talk to God maybe with a special light which would have highlighted those moments even further. There were some very moving moments with the three daughters and their spouses. His own relationship with Golde was realistically played. Golde was performed with great inner strength by Roisin Egerton-Lawless. She built up a good relationship with Tevye and related well to the daughters who she desperately tried to keep in order. There were some good moments of beautiful singing such as a delightful 'Sunrise, Sunset' and 'Sabbath Prayer' and great comic timing, especially in the 'Tevye's Dream' sequence. 'Do I Love You' was thoughtfully portrayed.

Eldest daughter Tzeitel was performed by Anne O'Donnell. She acted the interplay scenes with Motel very well. There was great humour from her moments when she was trying to get Motel to talk to her father about their plans. She gave a heart-breaking moment when she told Tevye she couldn't marry Lazar Wolfe. She and Motel, played by Kevin Murphy gave us a good rendition of 'Miracle of Miracles'. Kevin was a super foil for her. He delivered a committed performance with lovely moments of dignity, anger and joy. The pride on his face as he uncovered that sewing machine was wonderful and when he stood up to his father in law, we all nearly cheered aloud.

Hodel was beautifully played by Megan Lohan. She always related to us in the audience and we could always see what she was feeling and thinking. The little scene on the railway platform was sensitively played and the song delightfully sung. Her love interest, Perchik was performed by Niall Caulfield. The young revolutionary was given a real sense of purpose in this performance. His acting was strong and his relationship with the family convincing. His growing love was well portrayed and his clumsy proposal nicely played.

The 'Little Bird', Chava was played by Emily Macken. Her family were sitting in front of me in the theatre and were understandably proud. She played the most difficult of marriage partnerships so well, we watched as she is taken from her faith by the love of a good man. There was a lovely innocence in this performance. An elegant dance routine during the song was executed well. Fyedka was played with a sincerity by Keith Hanley who looked just right in the role. Good interplay with Chava in the courtship and a moving final scene. The other youngest daughters were brought to life so well by Katie Larkin as Shprintze and Aoife Warner as Bielke. Well done girls.

Lazar Wolfe the butcher who was originally intended to marry Tzeitel was played by Jay Hall. Jay has the deepest of speaking voices and a wonderful rich singing tone. He acted the jilted lover very well and showed great dignity in his little farewell scene with Tevye at the end of the show. Marsha Maly gave us a very animated and conniving Yente, The Matchmaker. This was a totally committed and endearing performance. Acting well beyond her years, Marsha was very convincing in the role and brought much fun to the scenes in which she appeared.

Grandmother Tzeitel was brought back to life with a powerful performance of the role by Annette Cavanagh. Her vocal tone was just right for the part and the character was hauntingly styled.

Lazar Wolfe's first wife Fruma Sarah was hypnotically played by Sonja Stephens. That wonderful red dress and those sweeping arm movements combined with a strong delivery of a very difficult song, worked so well to create the moment. Feargal Cavanagh made a believable Rabbi. He evoked the feel of the piece in his movements and delivery of his wise words and blessings.

There were a whole host of other cameo players who contributed much to the overall look and feel of the show. The chorus were also an integral part of the production and captured the essence of the piece.

The set was very sharp looking with the impression of the wooden buildings of the village. To this, smaller items such as tables, chairs, benches etc were added to create scenes such as the wedding. These all worked well. I have suggested that the stage team could dress in costume and actually be integrated into the production so there wouldn't be a small gap between scenes. Well done to all concerned for an authentic looking village which was nicely dressed with appropriate properties such as a super Singer sewing machine.

The cyc was nicely flooded with various colours during the performance which created changing atmospheres. Overall the lighting was effective, though a 'God Spot' as I always called it, which gives that reverence when Tevye talks to God was missed. The scene at the station was particularly well lit.

The sound balance was good throughout. There were quite a number of body microphones used which were cued with accuracy.

Costumes on the whole were good, creating the feel of the era and the religious aspect of the show, but there were a few wee attention to detail issues which would need resolved in future productions to fully capture the look. The make up was generally as it should be, very lightly applied. In most cases the cast restyled their own hair though there a few well-groomed wigs such as Grandmother Tzeitel's which looked great.

As always there is a warm welcome in the foyer of The Town Hall Theatre. After the show this is quite a meeting place too. There was great excitement from the supportive audience who were all carried away with the story told of Tevye, his family and of course the Fiddler On The Roof.

Cecilian Musical Society celebrated its 100th birthday in November of this year by staging Ian Fleming's Chitty Chitty Bang Bang at the Lime Tree Theatre in Limerick. The Society's first show in 1919 was A Greek Slave, a popular musical about tangled love lives in a Roman household, written in 1898. Over the past century the Society have won many accolades and AIMS nominations and awards and last year they garnered four AIMS nominations including a win for Best Chorus.

Chitty Chitty Bang Bang is a sort of Enid Blyton version of James Bond with cartoon villains, mad inventors, a struggling upper middle class family and a flying car. The story was made popular in the 1960's via the film and the musical premiered in 2002 on the West End and spawned a mini industry of Chitty car makers around the world. In Cecilian's production they used one of the better Chittys, that made by Blue Chilli in the UK.

The show features a bunch of well-known tunes from the film and a couple of new ones written especially for the musical. It can be quite tricky to stage, some scenes are written more like film scenes requiring quick changes from location to location and of course there is the car that must drive around the stage, float on the sea and fly around Europe, which requires a considerable amount of audience disbelief and technical skill to pull off.

The plot of the musical uses the tropes of a quest in that the hero, whacky inventor Caractacus Potts, his girlfriend, Truly Scrumptious and his children, Jeremy and Jemima, go on a big adventure to a fictional European country, Vulgaria, which is populated by very odd characters to rescue his father who is being held captive by the dictator Baron Bomburst. Director Des Henn gathered together a very competent cast for this show, who with musical director Michael Young and choreographer Barbara Meany gifted the audience with a fine night of entertainment. As Caractacus, Jason Ronan was excellent. He sang well, particularly on "Hushabye Mountain" and his dance skills on "Me 'Ol Bamboo" were quite agile. Mr Ronan was quite believable as the kids father and his tentative relationship with Truly was quite sweet. Truly was played by Kim Burke, who had a fine voice on "Lovely, Lonely Man" and her eponymous song. She was quite maternal to the children and had great robotic moves on the "Doll On A Music Box" section. Potts' children Jeremy and Jemima were played with assurance by William Shields and Holly Purtill and both demonstrated fine voices on "You Two" and "Posh!" which they sang with Grandpa. He was played by Paul Cable as a Carry On Sergeant Major type and sang "Them Three" and "The Roses of Success" quite well. As a family unit, with the addition of Truly, these performers really gelled well. They had a great chemistry together and were quite natural and quintessentially English. Meanwhile, in the fictional country of Vulgaria, the despotic Baron and Baroness - here played by Brian Henry and Gráinne Hartnett - send their spies, Boris and Goran - played by Brian Roche and Barry Danaher - to England to capture Caractacus, bring him to Vulgaria and get him to invent a magical car.

Brian Henry's Baron avoided the infantilism often attributed to this character and concentrated on his avarice and tyranny. He sang well with his Baroness, Gráinne Hartnett, who played the melodrama of the child-hating fascist. Together they made a formidable team. Their "Chu Chi Face" song was hilarious full of slapstick and innuendo and their "Bombie Samba" full of energy and life. Their two spies, Boris and Goran had great comic timing. Boris, played by Brian Roche was the smaller of the two was a master of the double-take. Barry Danaher's Goran, who was at least two foot taller than Boris, was played as being a little slow. They were a great comic double-act and sang "Act English" with superb comic timing and pace, the height difference provided some excellent physical comedy. In Vulgaria, Potts and Co also met the Toymaker, played with a geniality by Brian Curtin whose Germanic dialect was excellent.

The Childcatcher does not appear in the original novel. He was added to the story by Roald Dahl who wrote the screenplay for the film. He's the character that the Baroness employs to capture all children as she is allergic and doesn't want them in her country. James Malone gave us a wonderfully creepy Childcatcher, black clad with long fingers and Commedia de Arte make-up.

Musical director, Michael Young gave us some very nice and pleasant arrangements of the score. The band were very tight and whilst there was no string section the brass and woodwind were excellent. Mr Young's work with the chorus and ensemble was really good and we heard some very good harmonies, especially on the title song and on the "Vulgarian National Anthem". Choreography by Barbara Meany was truly scrumptiously performed by a talented bunch of dancers. Stand out routines were "Bombie Samba" and "Me 'Ol Bamboo" both executed flawlessly. Set design by Dermot Quinn was good as he used a steampunk styling for the framing and quite intricate Heath Robinson contraptions for Potts' inventions. Matty Moran's lighting was well focused with a good colour palette and Star Systems sound was perfect. Costumes were hired in from elsewhere and were clearly made for the show and make-up and hair was well applied. Ray Burke stage-managed everything competently with his crew of assistants.

Director Des Henn did a fine job on this show. It was funny, with some stand- out performances and the car amazed everyone when it started to rise up. All in all Cecilian should be proud of themselves for staging a difficult show very well.

Compelling Calamity Calamity Jane - A Musical Western was adapted by Ronald Hanmer and Phil Park from the stage play by Charles K. Freeman after the Warner Bros. film written by James O'Hanlon. The lyrics are by Paul Francis Webster and the music by Sammy Fain. The musical tells the story of Calamity Jane, a sharp shooter from the American Midwest. The character is based on the real life figure Martha Jane Cannary who lived in the second half of the 19th century. It was first produced in 1961 and has been running all over the world since. Produced mostly on the non-professional stage, the show features additional songs not in the film, but pretty much shares the same plot.

The action of the musical takes place mostly in the Golden Garter Saloon in Deadwood, South Dakota. Calamity Jane, along with Wild Bill Hickock, comes to the rescue of the proprietor of the local saloon, Henry Miller, when the actress Frances Fryer (who Miller has been promoting as a headline act at the saloon) turns out to be Francis Fryer, a man. To quell the patrons' anger, Calamity Jane undertakes to travel to Chicago and bring back the actress Adelaide Adams to perform at the saloon. However, instead of Adelaide she brings back her maid, Katie Brown. Chaos ensues as Katie falls for Jane's crush, Lt Danny Gilmartin. However, Calamity overcomes her anger over losing Danny and discovers her true love for Wild Bill. The first thing we noticed on turning up at the Annesley Hall was that there were tables and chairs in the auditorium instead of the usual rows of seats and a bar placed just below the stage at audience left. The audience were offered shots of Sarsaparilla, a soft drink popular in the Wild West, which many partook. It looked like his was going to be a cabaret performance, possibly with audience interaction.

In a very unusual move, the director, Laura Kerr, took to the stage to deliver the fire speech. She was in costume and sported a flawless Midwest accent. What followed was an incredibly immersive production where the audience were in the centre of the action, where the actors related to us as if we were their friends and where not only was the fourth wall broken, but all the walls came tumbling down.

The whole show was driven by the exceptional performance of Emma Nugent as Jane. She played her as larger than life and we could really see why Calamity Jane was so revered in the US. Ms Nugent had a wonderful charisma, she was absolutely transformed into the character. In a show like this, in this staging, there is nowhere to hide. Every nuance is visible, every breath is heard. It's a real challenge for an actor and Ms Nugent really stepped up and conquered that challenge. He singing was excellent as was her characterisation, she was feisty, violent and very funny at times. She also showed the character's vulnerability and sentimental side, particularly when Jane realised she had fallen for Bill. As Wild Bill Hickock, Tim Reynolds played him as slightly aloof, as a man with nothing to prove. He was relaxed and each line was considered before delivery and as we were so close to the performer we could almost see his thought processes. He sang very well too, demonstrating a pleasant modulated voice. These two performers had a great chemistry together, often communicating across the playing area with just a gaze or a shared chuckle. Great casting.

But Jane didn't fall for Bill straightaway. She was besotted with an army officer, Lt Danny Gilmartin who didn't reciprocate her adoration. He was played by James Cooper who played him as the opposite of Bill; big, gung ho and full of energy, wanting to get back to fight the good fight against the Indians. Eventually Danny fell for Katie Brown, the maid Jane brought back from Chicago, thinking her a famous singer. Suzanne Smyth played Katie and she was mesmerising in her character work. When she got up to sing in the Golden Garter, her fear was palpable. She stumbled and twitched through the song in one of the funniest pieces of theatre I seen in a long time. Ms Smyth had incredible comic timing, instinctively knowing how far to take the gag. Her scenes with Jane in Jane's cabin in Act II were really natural and we were drawn into her world. A wonderful and quirky performance from Ms Smyth. Just before Jane arrived in Chicago, we met Adelaide Adams, the famous Vaudeville star as played by Orla Russell. Ms Russell's rendition of "It's Harry I'm Planning to Marry" was excellent and she really showed Adelaide's selfishness and self-centred personality in her scene with Katie.

The proprietor of the Golden Garter was the highly strung Henry Miller, superbly played by Andrew Hill. He had a great stage presence and good comic timing. Mr Hill played Miller's despair with a great comic nervousness, his panic at booking the wrong act almost cataclysmic for him. His niece Susan, was played with conviction by Fiona Keane. Susan looked after Francis and convinced him to drag up as Frances and eventually they paired up romantically. Ms Keane played the role very well and had a nice stillness on stage. As Francis Fryer, Francis McKinney really captured the essence of the character; that of a fairly cultured performer ending up in the Wild West on a two-bit stage. He played Frances really well, apart from the heels, but was more at home as the song and dance man as shown in his performance of "Hive Full of Honey" The stagecoach driver of Deadwood was an older guy called Rattlesnake played here by Dessie Murphy. Mr Murphy had a great physicality and voice and reminded me of the old timers in the John Ford westerns of the 30's. 'Doc' Pierce was played with a dubious authority by Eamon McMullan. He showed good high status in the role. Bartender of the Golden Garter, Joe, was played by Daniel McCormack. He was the quintessential saloon bartender, polishing glasses and lining up the drinks. A nice solid performance. Lt Danny Gilmartin's friends and scouts Hank and Pete were played by Jack Reilly and Gordon Donaldson. They had a youthful energy and good physicality.

Musical direction by Mark Tilley was very good. His arrangements of the familiar score were superb. The band were sited on a platform upstage but the cast didn't really interact with them, which is a pity as this would have worked quite well within the world they created. Mr Tilley's work with the ensemble was excellent, they had some lovely harmonies particularly on "The Black Hills of Dakota", where the Chorus sang in and around the audience. Choreography by Clare Donnelly made the most of the unusual staging, bringing the routines into the audience. It's not a particularly dance driven show, but Ms Donnelly created some nice routines, particularly to the more C&W songs. Set design by Laura Kerr and Seamus O'Grady used the main stage area as the saloon of the Golden Garter with a platform upstage. Tables and chairs on the stage left and right apron were used effectively and the bar in the audience was inspired. Lighting by Sean Keenan worked well considering he had to light the entire auditorium and sound by Jody Trehy was full and sharp. Paula Young brilliantly stage managed what was actually a very complicated show with multiple entrance and exit points.

Director Laura Kerr, through her imaginative staging breathed new life into this classic musical. She didn't attempt to update it in any way, but definitely thought outside the box on the presentation. She was blessed with a talented cast who committed fully to her vision and a team of creatives who helped realise this vision.

society_raw: St Michael's Theatre MS, New Ross
review_text:
Putting this wonderful musical in context, when it premiered in 1957 it was nominated for six Tony Awards but was beaten for the title of Best Musical by The Music Man, a great musical too but one which appears to be of a completely different era. What I am trying to say in rather a clumsy way is that this masterpiece was ground-breaking and still has a resonance today. The story of two rival teenage gangs set against the urban backdrop of the deprived Upper West Side in New York city developed from the original idea of anti-Semitic conflict between Irish Catholic Jets and a Jewish gang. The story metamorphosed into the musical which still has a huge impact today between The Sharks, a gang of Puerto Rican immigrants and The Jets, a so called 'white' gang. The theme of racism set in a very violent context being offset by love, acceptance, hope for the future. All seen through the Romeo and Juliet eyes of our lovers Tony and Maria who really represent the purity of true love and how those around us can destroy even that.

The show must echo those feelings of hate, distrust, violence but we must see a genuine and pure love develop and grow like a beautiful flower set against a barren landscape. It must be real. We must believe these characters and all they stand for. This is a huge ask of any amateur society and a real challenge for any director. Taking on this task for St Michael's Theatre Musical Society was Kevin Kennedy. He gathered together a cast of varying ages some of whom really looked so right in their designated roles. The pace of the production was good with well organised staging which meant that the action rarely halted. The two gangs were visually different from each other and most of the accents used sounded authentic and were well sustained by the cast through the show. He had tried some inventive movement on stage some of which worked well. There is a tendency in aggressive moments to have dialogue shouted and it might be an idea to explore the idea of quiet internalised anger at times to give a little more light and shade. The scene with Anita in the Drugstore was chilling with excellent committed acting from all on stage.

This is quite a score of classic proportions and really must have that rounded depth of operatic sound. Musical Director Philip Kennedy assisted by Kevin Kennedy who conducted the orchestra created a pleasant accompaniment for the production with some beautiful moments and those haunting tritones coming through binding the music of the show together. The musical layering in the 'Tonight (quintet)' was well handled with good emotional build up. The chorus work in the 'Somewhere' gave us some delightful harmonies. The principal cast gave a good account of the songs in the show with some beautiful solos and harmonious duets. The feisty 'America' number and 'Gee Officer Krupke' were lively and really well sung. Tony, Maria and Anita all gave us powerful and emotional singing moments in the show.

Set in a time of violent battles between gangs of different races the dance in this show has to show this aggression but in a balletic way. Choreographer Claire Kickham captured this well in 'The Rumble' number which was energetic and aggressive. Possibly this aggression could have been more evident in some of the earlier numbers. 'America' was given all the correct Latin-American attitude and body angles. 'I Feel Pretty' was very interestingly moved and seemed natural for the performers. 'The Mambo' sequence was exciting though slightly staggering the position of the pairs on stage would have avoided masking.

Keith Flanagan played Tony, adding his experience on stage to the role to capture some very tender moments. He built up a good relationship with Doc who very much became a father figure for him. He sang well throughout and created some beautiful harmonies with Maria. Ashley Doran was a graceful and ever hopeful Maria. She looked very right with a simple restyling of her own hair and natural make up. She was totally believable in the role, singing those operatic phrases so very well. The part is very much a rollercoaster of emotions from first love to the loss of Bernardo and then Tony's death. She coped well with portraying this kaleidoscope of emotions.

Anita was played with great class by Jennifer White. She oozed Puerto Rican feisty charm. One of the most difficult scenes in any stage musical is that alarming moment in The Drugstore when even Anybodys turns on her, this Jennifer handled so well creating a very real and shocking scene. She sang the role and acted this part extremely well. No trace at all of his native Australian accent for Patrick Dower as Riff. This was a lively, aggressive and sincere portrayal. His fight with Bernardo at 'The Rumble' was realistic. He controlled the gang well with his singing at the beginning of the 'Cool' number. Bernardo was forcefully played by Phil Erskine. He gave some style and dominance as the leader of the Sharks. He moved with ease around the acting area and his relationship with Anita was fiery and believable.

Action was played with bundles of nervous energy by James Dobbs. This is Riff's right-hand man who is always trying to prove himself as the gang leader in the future. This really came across in his acting and mannerisms. He gave a good account of himself in the 'Gee Officer Krupke' number. Eryn Buckley as Anybobys had a strangely moving scene with Riff when finally she is accepted into the gang, well played by both actors. Anthony Finn gave a moving portrayal of Chino. The other gang members added to the look and feel of the show such as Arab who presented a disturbed young man, damaged by life. Kerrie Campbell was impressive in her role as Rosalia, singing and acting her part in 'America' with great energy and naivety. Claire Kickham was Francisca and Nicola Roche captured the blonde bombshell look as Consuela. Both moved and sang so well during the show but particularly in the 'I Feel Pretty' number.

Brian Kelly was a battle worn Lieutenant Schrank, his job to keep the gangs in line making him uncompromising. This was a well-developed character and he was ably assisted by Ger O'Riordan as Krupke. David Burke built a good relationship with Tony in his role as Doc. There was a large chorus of young players who were joined by some more senior members who added depth to the singing, notably in 'Somewhere' when they helped to create some great harmonies.

The stage design added much to the pace of the show as the well drilled stage team under the leadership of Mark Hayden quickly moved the set pieces, namely some nicely painted and graffitied walls on trucks plus some room interiors such as the dress shop and the drugstore, into place. The theatre is blessed with a huge area at the rear of the stage to store things. Larger items of furniture i.e. chairs, tables etc were on the trucks and were simply lifted off and into place. The silhouettes of a New York skyline finished the setting and gave a real sense of place. This was all nicely lit for the most part with some nice touches such as the tight special on the two lovers on the balcony. The opening number could have had a little more atmospheric lighting to heighten the initial tension. The faces were clear and we could see the emotions which is the most important thing in a show of this type. The sound was good throughout and well cued. There was excellent balance with the orchestra which in some of those hugely dramatic numbers like 'A Boy Like That/I Have A Love' was quite an achievement.

The costuming very much captured the feel of the era. A complete mix of wide skirts in a variety of colours though the Shark girls tended to be in red, black and white which nicely separated them from the Jets. The boys had blue jeans, white T shirts and leather jackets which looked good and the Shark men in black with touches of red and a deep plum colour. Shoes were excellent throughout with a great range of baseball shoes. I like Tony's green jacket but the grey one at the gym didn't work for me. Maria had a set of costumes which were a wonderful fit for her.

The black wigs were well set and styled. When the cast used their own hair, it was quite evocative of the period. The boys' hairstyles gave a nod to the era. The Sharks had a slightly darker foundation and more defined eyes. The Jet ladies were appropriately made up.

The welcome was great and the ride in the new state of the art lift to the upper floor made me feel very important. The safety warnings were clear and the seating most comfortable.

This show has been called the greatest stage musical ever. It has all the correct ingredients to live up to that title. This was a sincere production with some excellent dramatic moments, possibly a few things which could be tweaked in future productions but the story in West Side Story was well told and enjoyed by the audience in New Ross.

This is such an uplifting and fun show and it is a fresh experience to see it each time. Full of great comedy roles for women and men it gives the audience a few hours of innocent escapism with plenty of laughs with some great tunes to hum on the way home. Boyle Musical Society was well supported by an audience of all ages who thoroughly enjoyed themselves.

The show was directed by Vivienne Moran who not only directed but also choreographed too. With the Whoopi Goldberg movie at the back of our minds some directors have given an ethnic look to the leading lady, not so here and really it was not needed as Deloris Van Cartier is really just a woman with attitude regardless of race. The setting for the show was traditionally set in the 1970s which of course gives scope for the stylising of the piece. The cast were well rehearsed though the pace did occasionally falter, possibly due to nerves. The stage design and the speed of the changes helped to rattle the show on. Much of the humour was brought out of the script with some good comic timing on display. The principal characters were well created and relationships between characters looked quite natural. The story was clearly and interestingly told.

Musical Director Anne Kielty created some good moments of accompaniment. Some of the numbers are quite a vocal challenge but in most cases the cast managed well. There was a good balance between the pit and the stage, with some rousing disco beat backing but also gentler more romantic playing. The cues were good and the contribution of the chorus was pivotal to the show's success.

Vivienne produced a neat and well synchronised choreography plot. The movement of arms tended to be slightly more on the spot and of a linear format but those moves related well to the tune and words in a song. There were opportunities with this talented lot for further movement, maybe with a greater variety of pattern changes. The boys gave us a funny 'Lady In The Long Black Dress' number.

I was surprised to hear that the role of Deloris was the biggest role Janet Feeney had played. Originally from New Ross Janet is now well established in the area and proved in this show that she is a great asset to the society. She captured the character of the brash ambitious singer with a heart very well. Her singing was good and she was very natural in dialogue scenes. She created a believable love/ hate relationship with the Mother Superior. This was played with coolness and dignity by Catherine Bolger. Catherine gave us some beautiful moments of song as she has a delightful and distinctive tone to her singing voice. I particularly enjoyed her two thoughtful solos 'Here Within These Walls' and 'I Haven't Got A Prayer' which were so very moving.

Eddie Souther, the awkward policeman who falls in love with Deloris was brought to life by Robert Reid. He relaxed into the role as the show ran giving us some good comic moments and also that great scene towards the end of the show when he defends Deloris from scheming gangster Curtis.

The enthusiasm for life from Sister Mary Patrick was tangible. Karen Gordon was obviously having a great time playing this role. She delivered those comedic lines so well with a great sense of timing. Laura Kiely was a convincing Sister Mary Robert whose doubts were well acted in the scene with Deloris. Her acting was good portraying well the innocent, uncertain nun in training. She sang her songs with emotion. Sister Mary Lazarus, the crotchety choir mistress was given life by Daniela Beadnall. Her movements around the stage were sharp and her lines delivered quick fire as was appropriate. A good rapper sequence too. Gerry Wade tried to keep order as Monsignor O'Hara. He developed the personality of the priest well as the show progressed. His 'street' edge was very funny.

The villain of the piece Curtis Jackson was played by Darragh Beirne. He managed to not only get the scary psychopathic feel but also added some humour into the character too. He delivered his songs with style and had great interaction with the three boys in his gang. They were nicely different from each other both in looks and character. Diarmuid Beirne played wide-eyed innocent TJ. Not exactly the sharpest knife in the drawer, TJ interjects with 'off the wall' comments throughout the show, usually at totally the wrong times. These were all well delivered By Diarmuid who gave us many laughs along the way. Joey made his presence felt in each scene. Played well by Enda Regan his gyrations in the number 'Lady In A Long Black Dress ' were mesmerising and hilarious at the same time. Completing the gang was Cathal Tivnan as Pablo. He gave us that great scene at the end of the show when his words are being translated. The 'Three Musketeers' worked well together and created great chaos and fun particularly when each one is knocked out and wheeled off stage in the wheelchair. Other cameo parts were filled by members of the chorus. Ceara Conlon and Colette Noone were good backing singers, Ruth O'Dowd was a scatty Sister Mary Martin of Tours while Majella Gaffney aged to become the old Sister Mary Theresa. The other nuns added much to the authentic feel of the show in their acting, reacting and the harmonies they created. There were male and female disco dancers and many more, all working hard maintaining their chosen character and reacting to the unravelling story.

St Joseph's Hall provides a comfortable audience space but alas as with many such halls there is very little space in the wings. The stage team in this show therefore had to be quite ingenious as how they moved and stored large props and scenery. The basic set had an interesting large semi-circular stained-glass window upstage. The arched doorway flats were on hinges and could be swung back out of the way when necessary. The walls were realistically painted and embossed to give a solid effect. Trucks with various scenes such as the bar and the bedroom appeared and were placed speedily. There was a wonderfully realistic looking pipe organ and solid juke box which added the detail to some of the scenes. Furniture was authentic looking such as Mother Superior's desk and chair which were nicely chosen antiques. Other properties were in style with the time and place of the show. The stage team did a great job to place and strike these so efficiently under the leadership of Enda Commons.

This show was beautifully lit. What was particularly good was we could always see the faces so we always felt connected to the actors. There were some interesting effects created with the stage lighting, with the occasional use of hazer to create those shafts of light. Scenes such as the Mother Superior's office were neatly created by the use of tight spotlights. The sound quality was also good. It was well balanced and cued.

There was a great feel of the era created with the costumes. Deloris and the dancers were 'fab' in skin tight jump suits and leopard prints. The men had good shirts though the trouser legs could have been flared. The nuns' costumes were all in good condition and a good fit. The over tabards were sparkly and colourful. A great set of white sequined costumes for the finale with the Mother Superior resplendent in black sequins.

The wigs used had been appropriately styled, the men could have had either slightly longer hair or appropriate wigs to evoke the period. Make up was good though actually for some characters a little retrained. Some of the nuns needed to tone down a little to stay in character. The welcome was very genuine and there was very much a feel of family as the audience entered. The hall was packed to capacity for the welcome announcements which helped ensure that few mobile phones appeared during the performance. The adults in the audience all had a great evening and the many young folk in attendance were really fascinated by the show too.

This was a fun few hours of escapism. Nicely played and staged by members of Boyle Musical Society.

Initially I thought that this Dolly Parton musical was an unusual choice for this young society. Often thought of as slightly dated in its theme, the story of the lecherous boss in a 1970/80s office getting his comeuppance still entertains and actually reminds us of the journey equality has come in the last thirty years. I also wasn't too sure how the ageing of the University College Cork students to get them to appear like work-worn employees would be achieved. My fears disappeared in the first scene as this cast were so committed in their acting that we were instantly convinced by their characterisations and could just sit back and enjoy the story.

Director, Second Year student, Gearóid Treacy had obviously a clear vision of how he wanted the show to look and how the story was to be told. I have eluded to the characterisations in this production. I was very impressed as each person was clearly created and the personality shown in movement, delivery of dialogue and song. There was a great maturity of direction with a very visually flowing production, with just a couple of masking issues which could be easily sorted. The use of the cast to move the scenery is something I have suggested to others, used here that awkward first scene in the office was just choreographed into place with so much ease and actually became part of the show. The pace of the show was good though a few scene changes in black out later in the production did cause a hiccup. He managed to guide the delivery of the lines to bring out as much humour as possible from the piece.

Though there was a feel of the time there wasn't a great obsession with this, neither was there too much looking out of place. One thing which was evident from the show was every single person was having the best time of their albeit young lives and it was clear how much respect they all had for Gearóid. The principal cast were all well chosen for their roles and looked comfortable on stage. The chorus were purposeful in all their movements and we really felt that actual office work was being carried out.

Final Year Student, Claire McHugh took on the role of Musical Director. She played keyboards and conducted an orchestra of eight. There was a great ease with the sound she created and a good marriage between the instruments and the voices on stage. Good cues and tempi throughout. This was a confident piece of work with a talented cast who tried very hard with this quite 'rangey' score. There were some powerful individual voices and pleasant harmonies in duets and production numbers.

Second Year Student, Gráinne Fleming created a wonderfully detailed and captivating choreography plot. The first moments of the show made us all sit up as she used lots of freeze frame with individual poses frozen temporarily then bursting back to life again. There can be a tendency to move cast and chorus around a stage without specific dance steps, not in this case as she had jam packed the show with dance steps. She had obviously pushed the cast to new heights and the majority of the steps were well executed by the majority of the cast, with neat footwork, good arm extensions and nicely held frozen poses. Great use of the stage area too with a whole range of interesting and evolving patterns. Impressive work Gráinne.

There were some great performances from this relatively young cast. Molly May Powell was a strident driving force as Violet. This is the recently widowed office worker who is constantly being passed over when promotions go to the men in the company. She was played with just the right amount of edge and also a little hysteria when we were in the hospital scene. She related so well to the other two ladies and the scene with the spliff was hilarious. The developing love affair with Joe was nicely played and the singing throughout was good but in 'Let Love Grow' was superb with beautiful harmony. Newcomer to the office, Judy who had just been dumped for a younger model was sensitively played by Katie Bradley. We watched her grow in confidence from the awkward 'newbie' in the office to standing up for herself against husband, Dick with a moving rendition of 'Get Out And Stay Out'. She surprised us with a slinky and sexy version of 'The Dance Of Death'. Doralee who is very much in the mould of Ms Parton was nicely portrayed by Éabha Griffen Kelly. She captured the vulnerability of the character well and entertained us with those quick-fire comedy lines showing a good sense of comedic timing.

Franklin Hart the lecherous office manager was brought to life by Máirtín Ó Cathasaigh who really put such energy into the role. He has a wonderful tone to his speaking voice and a dark, rich singing voice too. He moved really well around the stage and developed a very believable character. Roz, his devoted secretary was courtesy of Susan Burke. This was a 'no holds barred' hilarious performance of the secretary infatuated by the boss. Great presence on stage and good comic timing.

Luke Maziarek who played Violet's pursuer was steady in his affection towards her and eventually endeared himself to her at the end of the show. Luke has a stunning singing voice and one of the show's highlights was the duet with Violet, 'Let Love Grow'. Dwayne who is Doralee's other half, was well played by Jack McEnery. There was a simplicity in their relationship which worked. Two timing Dick was brought to us by Kevin O'Connor. He played the role convincingly. This main principal line up was supported well by talented acting from a whole range of cameo performers who gave a depth to the show and also created much humour. Particular mention to Esha Hourihane Clancy as the ever-optimistic Missy, Danica Gaffney as Maria, Anna Healy as Kathy, Katie O'Brien who was an hilarious Margaret and Cormac Noonan as Violet's son Josh. Well done one and all.

The Firkin Crane Theatre is a hidden gem, interestingly rotund on the outside the interior provides all sorts of rehearsal and meeting places. The stage is quite wide and fairly deep, not much space in the wings but a good storage space behind the back curtain. The set used here was really in the form of large pieces brought swiftly on, sometimes by the cast which worked brilliantly; the sofa, the desk, the cabinet box on wheels, chairs, office desks, plants. All these were appropriate looking and added to the feel of the show. The curtains which were on a wheeled stand were not needed, otherwise the look was good. The stage team worked smoothly together and scene changes were speedy. The whole look and feel of this production did however benefit from a wonderful lighting plot. Shafts of lights caught the swirling mists created by a hazer and gave us all sorts of wonderful effects and atmospheres. At one point the three ladies were caught in downspots, but there was still enough front lighting that we could see their expressions.

The sound quality throughout was very good. Always tricky when there aren't enough body microphones for everyone but those cast members without one, really pushed their voices out to us so we didn't miss a word.

The costumes all looked appropriate for the place. Duller colours used at the beginning of the show, then when there was a less caustic atmosphere in the office touches of red and emerald green were subtly introduced. The principals all looked good, Doralee in her 'Pretty Woman' dress, Violet in skirt, blouse and jacket and Judy arriving with that great wide brimmed hat. The fantasy dance numbers looked great with sets of skirts and blouses, the boys in black tails and ruby waistcoats. The ladies' shoes were good but a few socks and shoes were not so good in the men's chorus (unfortunately against the black stage they really show up).

Hair and make-up were given a fairly natural look which really worked well. Good eye liner and eye shadows which brought great expression from the eyes and strong statement lipsticks.

It was a pleasure to meet the team after the show and have a chat outside overlooking one of the most picturesque urban scenes I have seen outside a theatre, twisting streets, pillared buildings and distant church spires.

This was a fine night of quality musical theatre entertainment. What came across to me was the joy that each person on and behind stage was having during this run of 9 To 5 The Musical brought to us by UCC Musical Theatre Society. I hope everyone here continues with this mad but wonderful hobby after they graduate.

This wonderful pastiche of 1950s/60s B movies first opened 'off Broadway' in 1982. Winning many awards along the way, the original show ran for five years and became the highest grossing 'off Broadway' show in history. One of the charms of the original production was the small cast size. This was recreated by The Odd Theatre Company for their all too brief three performance run of the show. There was added poignancy given to the underlying themes in the story by the detailed and thoughtful direction of Cian O'Dowd. He decided to reset the show in the upwardly mobile 1980s, with nods given to the sharks on Wall Street, Ronald Reagan in the White House, poverty in 'The Big Apple'. This wasn't slavish styling and didn't actually get the way of the strong characterisations and story- telling. The use of a static setting on this rather tight stage meant that the action never paused and we were totally caught up in the unravelling narrative. However, it might have been possible to do the biggest scene change slightly differently as it detracted from the 'Somewhere That's Green' number. Lovely thoughtful touches with the 'green' idea from some of the costumes, to the dollar bill framed on the wall and of course a huge array of flowers and plants.

Keelin Kilduff, who also played Audrey, was the show's Musical Director. The orchestral accompaniment, courtesy of Dave McGauran blended effortlessly with the talented singers on stage. The big production numbers were mostly given just the right amount of 'welly' without overwhelming the cast. Then numbers such as 'Suddenly Seymour' began gently and built to a great climax. This cast could all really sing too. Obviously well- rehearsed by Keelin we had a great depth of emotional singing. The three backing singers could each have played leads in any show, together their voices were 'supreme'. Such stunning harmonies and such wonderful clear as bell diction. Solo voices all sounded en pointe and duets all really worked. It is difficult for the Voice of the Plant as the audience's perception is based totally on the vocal. This was handled really well with a gorgeous rich tone from Mark Trundle. To be honest at times it was hard to believe that the sound bouncing from the stage came from so few. Great work musically.

Ainé Foley worked wonders with the limited number on stage to create a really interesting and totally slick piece of choreography. The three girls were brilliant together. They seemed to nearly predict each other's moves so they constantly made beautifully framed pictures and little moments. Their 'armography' through the shop window created a magical scene. Somehow even with just these three for most of the dance numbers we were always entertained by the moves and patterns they created. Other numbers when the whole ensemble were involved were also slickly moved and intricate. In a show with such a reduced number on stage there is even more pressure on the cast to give a great performance. That is certainly what we had here, each actor supporting each other on stage. Seymour the nerdy flower shop assistant was beautifully played by Daniel Ryan. He related well to his audience and brought us into his world. He almost convinced us that he had no other alternative but to kill the dentist and feed him to that plant. He delivered his songs with great conviction and a natural relationship was developed with Audrey. The other flower shop assistant was the much-battered Audrey played by Keelin Kilduff. Keelin gave the part her own spin rather than just copy the movie version. We had a slightly more centred character which worked well. She sang with a beautiful clear tone and harmonised easily with Seymour. Nicely acted and moved throughout.

Shop owner Mushnik was played with great energy by Con Kilduff. His financial frustrations were very much played out to us in the audience. He moved extremely well around all the acting areas using the space and creating excellent pictures with the others in the cast. The adoption song 'Mushnik and Son' was one of the highlights of the show, bringing great tongue in cheek humour to the moment. Cormac Malone was like a one-man theatre company as not only did he play the sadomasochistic Dentist, Orin but also a whole gamut of other roles too. Orin was always short tempered and domineering. A good rendition of the 'Dentist' number, with it played so well to us in the audience that we all joined in too! He played the relationship with Audrey well always pushing her for that, 'Yes, Doctor!' line. Other cameo roles like the purchaser of the hundred dollars of roses, the various men and woman who were trying to get him to sign their contracts etc were all well played for maximum fun value. There was a whole array of costumes which Cormac seemed to take no time at all changing into.

The three backing singers were just great. They were so very individual in their look and mannerisms but they also worked so well together. They gathered on the steps, near the bins, through the window, dressed in an ever-changing set of good costumes. They moved well, sang well, reacted and acted well too. Each had a strong enough voice to play a lead in further shows, in this show their voices blended effortlessly to give us some very subtle harmonies. What I particularly liked was how well they related out to us in the audience. Excellent work Cherise O'Moore, Emma Kilduff and Lynn Carter. Of course, the show is all about the man- eating plant Audrey II. The four plants representing this 'character' were quite good visually and the final one which swallowed half the cast moved really well. It is quite a task to co-ordinate the movement of the plant to the speaking and singing of the character. This was well achieved by Mark Trundle as The Voice and Adam Trundle as the puppeteer of the huge plant. I had a look at the mechanism of it after the show and was even more impressed by how well this was done as the system really takes a huge effort to move it and strength to keep the plant shut. Adam's voice was a rich delight and always in key and on cue. It must be a difficult thing to react only verbally without any other means of communicating to the audience. This was realistically achieved. Rory Dignam was the puppeteer to the smaller plant which also worked successfully. Good to see these three on stage playing winos and adding to the vocals of songs such as 'Skid Row'. This was a static set with very few things apart from plants, 'Audreys' and the dentist chair being brought onto the stage. This lack of scenery change meant that the story could rattle along unhindered. The upstage left area of the stage was the location of the flower shop. Just a simply painted back wall, plain shelves with weary looking plants for this to work. I must say I loved the fact that the floor of the shop area appeared tiled. This really denoted the boundaries of the shop. I have seen a few shows now with floors painted and when you are in tiered seating looking down this has a wonderful effect, as it certainly did here. There was the barred doorway and steps downstage right which was a useful area for cast to gather on. A central cash desk was in the shop and the Audrey plants when they were full size were placed upstage left running into the wings so that the swallowed unfortunates could slide easily off stage. It was a sharp and effective setting. My only grouse was that move on of plants etc during such a sensitive song as a 'moment' was lost. The lighting really added to the show. There was a great spacey effect with rotating white light at the start of the show. Moving spots created energy at times. Backlighting was used effectively but we could always see the faces. Red light was used when one of the 'horrors' was taking place.

The sound was well cued and nicely balanced throughout. It must be a difficult thing to achieve this as the orchestra are located backstage.

As I said earlier the show was reset in money grabbing, shoulder pad wearing 1980s. There was quite a costume plot for the show with the backing singers alone having (I think) five sets of costumes. These varied from interesting Madonna inspired outfits to a set of sparkly copper coloured dresses. (Good footwear too) The principals were all well attired and the increase in wealth of those involved in the shop was evident in their clothes such as Mr Mushnik's smart suit. Hair and make up was all in keeping with good eye shadows and eyeliners used. This is a very intimate theatre and the audience are close to the action so the subtle touch that was given looked really well.

Divorced, Beheaded, Died, Divorced, Beheaded, Survived. The famous rhyme takes on a new life as the basis of "Six," a musical reimagining of the six wives of King Henry VIII as they battle to emerge as the leader of a new pop girl group. While the show is really more of an 80-minute concert piece, it certainly packs a punch. The performers immediately break the fourth wall, informing the audience that they will be tasked with determining which one of them has the most tragic backstory and will therefore be named leader of the new girl group. From there, they take turns performing musical numbers telling their tragic backstories and making their case to become the group's star. Many esteemed critics of professional theatre were harsh in their estimation of this show, branding it, "a pale attempt to do for British history what Hamilton had done for American history", and "a vacuous attempt at feminism, which fails miserably because the whole central concept, (women competing against each other to win a popularity contest) was, in itself, a total contradiction of feminism."  Well frankly, I don't know what they were talking about. I viewed it purely as a creative piece of fun and entertainment based on a popular period of history, with identifiable and well-drawn characters. As such, in my own humble opinion, this production was a resounding and highly entertaining success.

Putting this piece together required a good awareness of aesthetic content on the part of director, Martina Lynch. With very little script to play with, the focus had to be on the costumes, the lights, the setting and of course, presenting six unique and individual characters. In most respects, all of this was achieved successfully. Lighting was excellent and costumes were good and inventive, and the establishment of individual characterisations was achieved through a strong opening number, "Ex- Wives", in a style reminiscent of Cell Block Tango from 'Chicago', where the ladies introduce themselves and recount their demise; hence, Divorced, Beheaded, Died, Divorced, Beheaded, Survived. Where Martina really made her mark was in the choreography of this, and indeed every number in the show. In an amazingly tight, disciplined and high-energy display, with a range of rock, pop, hip-hop and funk, this was an outstanding achievement of non- stop gyrations and gesticulations that left the audience even more breathless than the dancers themselves.

With no band to direct, Amy Penston's entire focus, as Musical Director, was to ensure that her charges were note perfect, tight in their harmonies, accurate in their timing and totally tuned into the backing tracks and filled with vocal energy. She did not fail them. This was a job extremely well done.

Roisin Vigors, as Catherine of Aragon, Henry's first wife, made great arrogant play of the fact that she was the wife who kept the King's interest the longest. Strong on vocal quality, excellent in "No Way", and a great mover, her whole performance had a wonderful air of smug superiority.

Leah O'Hare, as Anne Boleyn, initially worried me, with a couple of fragile notes in the opening number, but my worry soon dissipated when she gave vent to "Don't Lose Your Head" with vim and vigor and a very strong sense of comedy. Indeed, her frequent whinging that "I had my head chopped off" became a central running joke of the show. Very well-portrayed. Leah Byrne played Jane Seymour, arguably the most sedate and dignified wife of Henry. Her tragedy was that having given the King his much-desired son, she died shortly after his birth. Leah's portrayal captured that dignity, with a touch of gloating at being the provider of a son, and her vocal delivery of "Heart of Stone" was beautiful and sincere.

Doireann Hurley, as Anne of Cleves, brought the house down with her witty, quirky rendition of "Get Down". This was a combination of vocal dexterity, superb body language and a wink and a smile that couldn't help but woo the audience. Her charm and all-round ability were remarkably fine.

Holly Prestage, as Katherine Howard, despite her youth, gave a super- convincing sensuality to the most flirtatious and provocative of the King's wives, and her rendition of the "All You Wanna Do" number, captured the essence of her character perfectly. Very well sung and acted.

Last but not least, Bri-Elle Finn, as Catherine Parr, performed "I Don't Need Your Love" (seen as the feminist anthem of the show) with a stirring passion and beautiful vocal quality, but she was equally as accomplished in her funkier contributions.

But it was when the six girls performed as a unit that the magic really occurred, perfectly in sync in all their routines and perfectly in tune with all their harmonies. What a team!

Costumes were cute and quirky, modern in design but with a few appropriate hints of historical garb. Wigs and/or hairstyles were funky and fun, and make-up was great, giving the girls a super overall appearance. Loved the mock mics as well.

The set for the show was the only aspect of the production that could have been more elaborate. While the flats containing portraits of the six wives were fine, and the cyc at the rear of the stage allowed for nice lighting effects, it was a tad empty. Maybe a period, palace décor would have suited the historical nature of the story, or a modern studio set, to capture the contest element of the whole scenario. (Or maybe six large gilt-edged portrait frames, each with a throne, and the wives in frozen poses as the audience enter?) Thankfully, though, an excellent pop-concert style of lighting design meant that the background was never that important. And while the effects and flashing, moving lights were awesome, care was taken that focus was always on the right person at the right time, which showed great attention to detail. Sound quality was excellent throughout.

I was delighted and excited when this show popped onto my adjudication list, and I travelled to Arklow filled with anticipation. I was not to be disappointed. Studio 55 didn't just meet my expectations, they surpassed them, with a sparkling and scintillating show. Thank you, ladies, for a fabulous night.

Co-directors, Elizabeth Gregan and Yvonne Prendergast, on behalf of Bray Musical Society, presented us with an Oklahoma that was note perfect, word perfect and appeared to be very thoroughly rehearsed. An orchestra of very capable musicians, under Musical Director Elizabeth Gregan, treated us to an overture played to perfection. The choreography of Yvonne Prendergast gave us a good, lively Farmer and the Cowman and a well-presented Dream Ballet, and the females were tidy in their execution of Many a new day and Out of my Dreams. Kansas City, while fairly uncomplicated, was well performed. The costumes for the show were colourful and well selected, particularly the female dresses, and completing the overall look of the performers, hairstyles and make- up, with the exception of a couple of characters who needed to be better aged, were appropriate and pretty good.

The staging, while fairly simple in design, was effective enough in providing a good framework for the action, and while the lighting was straightforward in design, good use of colours and effective pools of light allowed for variety in the look and atmosphere of the different scenes. Scene changes, under the guidance of Greg Egan, were carried out with a minimum of fuss, and there was a very decent display of props appropriate to the show.

Performance wise, there was a very good characterization of Ado Annie, played with a delightful deadpan comedic style by Sarah O'Hanlon, with a nicely rendered Cain't Say No. Aunt Eller, played by Bairbre Murphy was the most comfortable and relaxed performer on stage and supported her good acting with safe and secure singing.

Stephen Carvill had a good look and a good voice for Will Parker, and he worked very hard, especially in his scenes with Ado Annie. He did need more direction to fully realize the comedy potential of his role. The same would have to be said for Nick Russell as Ali Hakim, who despite some good character acting, needed to be much larger than life to exploit the good comedy of the script.

Eoin Martin was very young to play Ado Annie's father, Andrew Carnes, despite making a good job of the character. Had he been more successfully aged with good make-up; he might have been more believable. Gertie Cummins was well- played by Grainne Shortt, with a laugh and a grunt that were very amusing. The Jud Fry of Peter Manning was quite menacing, but not really in a subtle manner. He did play the smoke house scene with Curly very well and delivered "Poor Jud is Dead" and "Lonely Room" in a satisfactory manner.

There were decent supporting performances from Kevin Rockett as Cord Elam, Tom Gallagher as Ike Skidmore, Dylan Anderson as Slim and Raven Gabriel as Fred.

Michelle Murray as Ellen, Catherine Gregan as Kate and Niamh Webbley- O'Gorman as Vivienne, led the female chorus in the very nicely sung "Out of My Dreams" and "Many a New Day".

The chorus generally brightened the atmosphere of all their scenes and impressed with their harmonies. They also moved well and were probably capable of much more than they were given.

Laurey, played by Orlaith Dunne, had a most delightful operatic quality and excellent diction, and some of her scenes were strongly acted, especially the confrontation with Jud, but a lack of chemistry between herself and Curly, played by Conor Martin, diminished the central romantic story line. With a very pleasant tenor voice, Curly seemed to lack the confidence to fully realize the lighter side of his character, and perhaps needed more direction to achieve his full potential. The overall tone and atmosphere of the show didn't seem to sparkle and was somewhat uninspired. Principals generally needed much more guidance in the development and delivery of their lines, and in achieving a more natural presence on the stage.

Romance was lacking, and verbal and visual comedy was missed on many occasions. While the music was note perfect, constant pedantic rhythms did little to inspire flair or flow in the delivery of the lyrics. Despite some very good voices and a hard-working chorus, many of the songs needed more joy and expression. I do appreciate that the whole company worked hard in presenting a show that was very clean and tidy and musically well-rehearsed, but I just longed for more natural flow and spontaneity. I'm inclined to think that, despite the obvious talent and experience of Elizabeth Gregan, the roles of Director and Musical Director, both of which are demanding and time- consuming, might benefit from being under separate control.

It was still a great pleasure to hear the beautiful songs of Rodgers and Hammerstein, and to enjoy some of the brighter routines. I'm quite sure that both the production team and the performers on stage are capable of so much more, and I do genuinely wish them all success with their future endeavours.

Once Director Karen Gordon had set her mind on the style that she wanted to employ for this Pop-Up Theatre production of "Hairspray", she relentlessly went about ensuring that the style was incorporated into absolutely every aspect of the production. Her chosen style was Comic Book Cartoon, and from eye- dazzlingly bright, multi-coloured, sharp and angular scenery, to outlandish, multi-coloured, but perfectly in period, costumes, to outrageously styled and multi-coloured wigs, to make-up that made the characters look as if they had been hand-drawn, to movement that was stylied like an animated movie, to dance routines that were quirky, slightly surreal and buzzing with energy, everything about this production gave you the feeling that you were watching a Disney or DreamWorks animation, or reading a brightly coloured comic book straight off the shelf. From a design perspective, it was quite simply stunning. Principals had doubtless been well-tutored in creating virtual animated caricatures of their roles. Nothing was bland or normal, and everyone played their part in creating a surreal musical adventure. This was an amazing achievement in Direction.

The set for this show was remarkable.
