Large, brilliantly vibrant painted flats with all manner of abstract patterns and often location signs, were moved about with the greatest of ease by a very efficient crew under stage manager, Jemma Gordon. The area stage left that contained a giant television screen, which played live action of the numbers on stage, (in black and white, of course) was a marvelous piece of crafting. Every set looked like a page from a Comic Book. Lighting was handled with much the same level of madness as everything else, but there was also nice subtlety in the lighting of the more mellow and emotional scenes. Sound was good, though perhaps, given an occasional heaviness from the band, some principals might have occasionally needed a slight boost. Sound effects were very good as were all the visual effects.

I'm in danger of running out of superlatives, trying to describe to those who didn't see it, just how all-consuming the visual impact of this show was. Costumes were all appropriate to the design of the era, but instead of normal tones and shades, it was as if they'd all been dipped in a vat of rainbow paint. Vivid, loud, exaggerated, and stunning. The wigs alone were a work of art, not just that they were in every conceivable colour, but the styles were enormous or exaggerated, and totally, outrageously, wonderful. And if all that wasn't enough, every character was made-up as if they had been pencil drawn by a cartoonist, with lines defining the shape of a nose, the height of a cheek- bone, the intensity of the eyes. Again, it had a perfect comic-book effect, achieved through a touch of creative and artistic genius.

Thomas Spratt's choreography, in keeping with the director's vision of the show, was pretty crazy with inventive and exaggerated movement. It was so much fun to watch, as it never stopped moving. Was everyone perfectly in step and in time? No, but the frenetic nature of the routines meant that it didn't really matter. It was a feast for the eyes, with ever changing patterns, high, high, energy and wonderful imagination.

The beautifully costumed orchestra, under Musical Director, Niamh Crowley, nailed the score with great rhythms, good accuracy and, for the most part, decent balance. The percussionist did have a tendency to drown out some of the singing in the more animated numbers, and perhaps the brass section could have pulled back a little, but the overall quality of the music was very good indeed. Good work had also been done on vocals, with the chorus making some lovely sounds and the principals being strong and secure.

Jaidyn Gieni, in the role of Tracy Turnblad, was bubbly and energetic, full of positive attitude and delivered her musical numbers with a strong and confident voice. A very nicely created central character.

Megan Kilcawley gave quirky, cartoon character and comedy to the role of Penny Pingleton, visually delightful and also possessing a good, secure vocal ability. Maggie Villarini was a show-stealer as the feline and ferocious Velma Von Tussle. Her appearance, her tone of voice, her gesticulations, her comedy timing and her amazing vocals made this such a powerful performance.

Not far behind her, and almost as catty and obnoxious, was daughter, Amber Von Tussle, comically portrayed by a very capable Leanne Syron.

With genuine Gospel in her soul, Mabel Chan gave a wonderful performance as Motormouth Maybelle, selling her songs with passion and presenting a warm but determined personality. Her "I know Where I've Been" had a most affecting sincerity.

Likewise, Mimi Lee gave energy to a fun and feisty characteriation to Little Inez. Suzanne Harvey made a good comical impact as Penny's pretentiously pious mother, Prudy Pingleton.

I hope he won't be offended, but Micheál Kearney portrayal of Link Larkin, looked, walked and behaved like TinTin on speed. This was a wonderfully funny and yet sincere performance, truly getting into the spirit of the production, and crooning with a most pleasing vocal quality.

Gerry Ryan, as Edna Turnblad, certainly displayed a very strong comedic ability, but he was a tad too much pantomime Dame for me, with a poor opening costume and wig that didn't quite fit in with anything around him. Having said that, I did warm to him as the evening progressed, and his duet, with Wilber, "Timeless To Me" was a bit of a show-stopper.

Wilber Turnblad, played by Brendan Reid, was cheesy, cheerful and delightfully more in keeping with the style of the show. These two were a very good team.

Tom Nolan's Corny Collins looked and sounded perfect as the host of the show, and he played his scenes, particularly with Velma, with confidence and control. It took me a few minutes to tune into Donovan Siziba's strong accent, (my fault, not his) but once I did, I was strongly impressed by his plucky, playful and rhythmic interpretation of Seaweed J. Stubbs. He and Penny made a cute and comical pairing.

Kieran Cunnane was a highly amusing hyper-thyroid as Spritzer, and Franny Curley gave a good over the top character to Mr Pinky.

The chorus did a wonderful job in terms of sheer energy. They had so much dance and movement, much of it fast and furious, and most of it also accompanied by singing. Their skill level was good, but their enthusiasm level was sky-high and beyond. Foot work wasn't flawless, but the frenetic patterns and the style of routines allowed for small errors to be swept away in the delightful chaos. What impressed me most was that everyone on stage looked to be having an absolute ball. That kind of energy is infectious, and as a member of the audience, I was carried along on that wave of exhilarating, intoxicating, colourful, charismatic craziness. Thank you for that journey into another realm.

Sweet Charity was energetic, imaginative, a step away from the norm, and overflowing with joie de vivre. It was a great achievement to take an old favourite and infuse it with a modern approach and an inventive eye. From a performance point of view, the company delivered a high standard of competence and confidence, with notable individual performances, strong chorus contributions and a lighting display that was almost a show in itself. There were occasions, however, when innovation came at the expense of comedy and clarity. Sweet Charity, at its core, is the story of a dysfunctional girl, trying hard to become a part of the real, dare I say, normal world. Her failure is a consequence of simply replacing her downbeat existence with surreal alternatives. Fosse achieved the distinction between Charity's real life and her expectations of a better life by using the surrealism of the Pompeii Club and its stylized clientele, and the outrageously flamboyant 'hippies' of the Rhythm of Life Church. I did feel that Director, Beth Strahan, obscured the divide between real and surreal by stylizing every aspect of the show. It's no accident that when Charity is actually face to face with the normal life that she so desires, it's in a situation where she feels trapped. The pond, the lift, the bathroom/closet of Vidal's apartment, the fairground ride. She simply seems unable to function in normality, which pre-empts the tragedy of her lost finale.

In so many respects, Beth's direction of this production paid homage to a master- craftsman, (Fosse) and did so with a remarkably accomplished degree of success, but just as tragedy needs comedy, and love needs hate for comparison, in Sweet Charity, real life and the surreal alternatives depend upon one another.

More positively, Beth infused her chorus and principals with a belief in her vision for the show, and they responded by being energetic, disciplined and totally immersed in their commitment to the vision. She also made very good use of mime in this production, as in the elevator that wasn't there, and the subway ride, which was super-effective.

Minimalist would best describe the scenic presentation of this show, which can most effectively assist the pace of the action, even if, on occasions, location was not always apparent. With lighting that followed the director's vision of surrealism, there was not always a clear distinction between indoor and outdoor scenes, daytime and night-time. There was most certainly a dazzling lighting display of ever-changing tone and atmosphere, employing every lamp that the lighting director had at his disposal, and I applaud him for wonderful pictures and creativity. For me personally, though, it was the emotional moments between Charity and Oscar, with minimal activity, and subtle but highly effective pools of light, that made the strongest impact and allowed the audience to focus entirely on the actors, the drama and the sentiment of the story, asserting the principle that sometimes less is more. Props were generally appropriate, if somewhat scarce, and what movement of furniture and set-pieces there was, was efficiently carried out by the stage team, under the direction of Shona Carey and Amelia Hemmings. Sound quality was very good and well-balanced throughout, with the use of some good sound effects. Hats off (and very little left-on!) to the dance hall girls for appearing scantily- clad, in a delightful array of appropriate outfits, without ever appearing self- conscious or embarrassed.

Costuming throughout was very good, with the exception of the Brass Band number, which was a tad piecemeal and untidy. Hairstyles/hairpieces were good and era- appropriate, and there were no problems with make-up, even if Daddy Brubeck could have been presented as a little larger than life.

An accomplished orchestra, under the direction of Hayden Kline and Assistant MD, Erica O'Reilly, managed a very tricky musical score with good accuracy and plenty of energy, even if the exaggerated, accentuated rhythm of the sixties-swing wasn't always fully realised. Accompaniment was, however, always good in tone and balance, and sympathetic to the singers onstage. Chorus Mistresses, Laura Roantree and Grace Doyle Flaherty, did a wonderful preparation job on the vocals for the show, with very secure principals and a strong and accomplished choral presentation. The shows iconic numbers were performed with vocal prowess and well-realised harmonies. Rhythm of Life brought the house down.

The high points of Conor Lawlor's choreography were an excellent and inventive Rhythm of Life and a faithfully recreated Fosse-style Frug, the former being a credit to his own imagination and creativity, and the latter delightfully paying homage to a master craftsman. In both of these, and indeed throughout the show, Conor was blessed with a high-energy, extremely capable chorus of dancers, who worked so hard all night. The dance hall girls were very well moved in Big Spender and throughout the show.

In Lily-Kate Hearns was extremely well cast in the central role of Charity Hope Valentine. She exuded confidence, always looking and sounding at ease being centre stage. Her vocal quality and range were perfect for the role, her comedic timing was good, and she earned the warmth and sympathy of the audience in her more emotional moments. In Something Better Than This, she also displayed good dancing ability. Such an enjoyable performance.

She was very ably supported in her Fandango Dance Hall settings by Anabel Sweeney as Nicki and Sadhbh Murphy as Helene. Both of these ladies achieved the sometimes brash, sometimes sympathetic, world-weary acceptance of their station in life, with good humour, good vocals and very good movement. Their Baby Dream Your Dream was beautifully performed, and Something Better Than This was feisty and thrilling. In the role of Carmen, Lucy Jamison proved that there is no such thing as a minor role, as she made an immense impression with her bawdy and brash countenance and her excellent line- delivery. Katie McCormack made a good job of Rosie, but perhaps being a little more insecure on arrival might have made her early success even funnier.

Completing the female line-up was Laura Cole who played Ursula with the right amount of Diva quality.

An exceptionally good comedic performance was given by Dan Whelan as the neurotic Oscar Lindquist. His timing was great and his physicality was excellent. He moved convincingly from claustrophobic nerd to charming love- interest and returned delightfully to his neurotic self for the climax of the story. Vocally, he was both tuneful and robust. A super performance.

Tom Dwan looked and sounded great as Vittorio Vidal. I've expressed my opinion about the over-stylised interpretation of some of the characters, but Tom did all that was asked of him, and did it with panache and vocal quality.

Owen Henry's Daddy Brubeck used his only scene to create a very good impact, vocally strong and comfortable holding centre stage. This scene was a highlight of the show and he led it with charisma and authority.

Conor Finlay, as Hermin, was suitably sleazy and insincere, and while Cry at Weddings was slightly outside of his vocal range, he did perform it with enthusiasm and energy. In the earlier scenes, I did feel that he got lost slightly amid the stylized goings-on.

Energy was in abundance in every aspect of the chorus performance from excellent dance and movement to secure and expressive vocal delivery. Everyone did as they were asked and did it with confidence and belief.

I have a passion for the energy of youth, and a love of innovation, and with this production, I found both in abundance. Some of the best and most compelling work I have seen this season has come from the minds and the performances of a new generation of thespians, and it augers well for the future of musical theatre. You should be very proud of all you have achieved. We all build our successes on the shoulders of giants, learning, as in this case, from the comedy genius of Neil Simon, and the unique and brilliant talent of Bob Fosse, and it is a credit to you that you paid homage so effectively to their inspiration. Just keep in mind, though, that change for change's sake is not always a step forward.

I sincerely thank you all for a most enjoyable and energy-filled production.

Newry Musical Society took a bold step in presenting the recently released stage version of the 2003 Movie musical, School of Rock, and judging from the audience reaction, it was definitely a step worth taking. This is the story of a failing rock band front man, Dewey, who, trying to recover from being dropped by his band, seizes an unlawful opportunity to earn some cash by posing as his mate, Ned Schneebly, and taking on a supply teacher role in a prestigious Prep School. Before his complete lack of teaching ability can be discovered, he realized that the children in his care are musically gifted, and he sets about crafting them into a young Rock band. They manage to bluff their way into Battle of the Bands (when the kids pretend that they are all terminally ill) and make it to the finals. At about this time, the headmistress and the parents learn the truth about Dewey, and in rushing to have him arrested, they discover that their children are incredibly talented. Of course, it all ends happily ever after, and along the way, we are treated to great comedy, vibrant rock music and an amazing array of young talent.

In this Newry production, that talent came in the shape of 12-year-old Conrad O'Connor, as lead guitarist, Zach, 12-year-old Isabella Quigley, as bassist, Katie, 12- year-old Molly O'Neill, as keyboard genius, Lauren, and 16-year- old Lauren Agnes Brannigan, as drummer extraordinaire, Freddie. Not only did these four superbly play half the show live on stage, but each was also a gifted actor/ performer. And they weren't alone in that respect. The acting and singing of 12-year-old Clare Keeley, as Summer, and 12-year-old Emilia Quinn, as Tomika, were outstandingly consistent, with superb back-up from John McCaffrey as Billy, Stella Magill as Marcy, Conor Downey as Mason, James Hollywood as James, Ellie Lavery as Madison, Éadaoin Walsh as Sophie, Lily Maher as Alicia, Katie Rafferty as Frankie, Catherine Convery as Michelle, and the exceptionally animated and energetic Robyn Cunningham making her mark as Shonelle. Then there were choruses of more kids and senior students, all of whom contributed to a wonderful display of disciplined routines, great acting and most impressive singing. If this was the showcase upon which to judge, the future of musical theatre in Newry is in very secure hands.

Leadership of this group, and indeed the whole production, came from the experienced hands of Director, David Cunningham who, not unlike me, is old enough to have witnessed the Rock era first hand, and it showed in his creation of something that was as chaotically random as it was precise and disciplined in the 'normal school' scenes. It was that appreciation of and interweaving of the two cultures that provided the backbone to the whole show. The use of the stage space was well- managed, on what was for the most part, a black box set, and perhaps it might have been worth considering going even more minimal with settings, as some of the roll- in set pieces were a tad cumbersome for the stage crew, under William MacLennan, and not entirely necessary. Locations could have been suggested with just furniture props and more specific area lighting, but that's just a suggestion. As it was, the set pieces, if a little awkward, were at least well presented. Lighting, generally, contributed to the randomness of the unfolding events, although I felt it could have been more spectacular for the concert pieces, and occasionally during dialogue, principals were moving through shadowed areas. There were a few problems, too, with the sound system, with a few late cues and some imbalance during choral numbers.

Regardless of that, the contribution made by the various choruses was remarkably good, with powerful vocals and excellent harmonies. Musical Director, Fiona Flynn, assisted by Jonathan Reynolds, had done great preparation work on vocal quality, particularly obvious from the great achievements of the kids. She also kept the band, and on-stage musicians, in good control, never allowing the rock score to run away with itself.

Likewise, there was good attention to costumes. School uniforms were neat and tidy throughout, and then brilliantly funked- up for the Battle of the Bands. Teachers and parents were appropriately dressed, and Dewey was delightfully scruffy and unkempt. Make-up looked natural, while hairstyles were varied but appropriate. Though not a particularly glamorous show, this was most satisfactory from a visual perspective.

In the leading role of Dewey, Jordan Walsh gave an outstanding performance, capturing the arrogance, immaturity and complete lack of responsibility required by the role, but he also played it with warmth and appreciation of the children in his charge, and successfully achieved good moments of self-realization as the story progressed. With more than a hint of a nod to Jack Black in his moves and interpretation, he looked totally at home and in control of all his scenes. Despite occasional issues with his mic balance, he performed his rock numbers with energy and commitment. All in all, an excellent performance.

In contrast to his brashness, Maille Connolly played School Principal, Rosalie Mullins, with dignity and decorum, until her inner rock-chick was revealed later in the story. This was a lovely performance combining good acting and a wonderful voice. When she eventually unraveled, she did so with good comedic effect. Dewey's best buddy, Ned, was comically portrayed by Eoin Sands, who was a believable hen-pecked nerd for most of the show. His frustration at the antics of Dewey was perhaps a little over exaggerated, but when he eventually snapped back at his girlfriend, the comedy was marvelous. Anna-Maria Boyle, as the afore- mentioned girlfriend, Patty, was delightfully severe and intolerant, and it was good to see her getting her come- uppance. Veronica Barr turned in a quirky and consistent performance as school secretary, Ms. Sheinkopf, and was well supported by the various members of the school staff. There were also many accomplished performances from a wide range of parents with Damien Lavery as Mr. Mooneyham, Helena Hughes as Mrs. Hathaway, Daryll Galloghly as Mr. Williams and Brian Reavey as Mr. Spencer, making a particularly good impact.

Neil Heaney made the most of hosting the Battle of the Bands, as Jeff, and the members of the band No Vacancy, gave credible performances, but there is no question about it, the real stars of this production were the school kids.

Whether parents, teachers or school children, the chorus were immersed in the story and contributed strongly to the atmosphere of each scene and to the vocal quality of the musical numbers. A very good job was done by choreographer, Lisa Irvine, in recreating the randomly abstract, energy-driven feel of the rock era with her choreography. There was just the right balance of wild-abandonment, without ever looking untidy or undisciplined. There was good contrast, too, with tidy and effective routines for the children and staff under the more formal eye of their head- mistress. Stick It to the Man and School of Rock were both the visual and musical highlights of the show.

It was a pleasure to be greeted and so well looked after by old friend, and company Chairman, Donal Fegan. Front of House staff were polite and efficient, and it was enjoyable to meet the musical director and musicians for refreshments during the interval. How wonderful it is to see Newry Musical Society moving with the times and bringing on the next generation of musical theatre stars. The progression has certainly paid off, as they continue to shine and to inspire their new young membership. Perhaps it all worked so well because the 'old' and the new appear side by side and work so well in tandem. Thank you to all concerned for an uplifting and entertaining performance.

Written longhand by James Bond author, Ian Fleming for his then twelve-year old son, 'The Magic Car', was a sort of James Bond for kids. Sadly, Fleming died before the stories were published as 'Chitty Chitty Bang Bang', named after a series of real cars, invented by Louis Zborowski in the 1920's, which is when the musical is set. Apparently, Roald Dahl who co-wrote the screenplay for the 1968 film, invented the character of the Child Catcher and the country Vulgaria, where the second act takes place - they were not in the original stories. The plot reads like a pantomime version of a James Bond story!

Widower, Caractacus Potts, an inventor, and his two children Jeremy and Jemima join up with Sweet Factory heiress Truly Scrumptious aboard Chitty Chitty Bang Bang, a resourcefully sentient car, to rescue Grandpa Potts from the nasty Baron Bomburst, who rules Vulgaria with his wife who hates children. Add in two bungling spies, Boris and Goran, a terrifying creature called the Child Catcher, a Toymaker, quirky catchy music, and you have all the ingredients to make a fabulous show.

Produced by Nenagh Choral Society and directed by Greg Browne, with musical direction by Laura Kearney and choreography by Stephanie Browne, the show was funny and big, and featured some standout performances. A clever set designed by the director was perfectly in keeping with the style of the show. The windmill on the stage right apron worked a treat and the trompe-l'oeil effect on the wall of the stage left apron added a depth to the stage picture. The car was excellent and well done on the build! Create Scenes Productions provided the costumes. The samba costumes were super, very authentic. I loved the peasant look on the Vulgarian outfits and Boris and Goran's uniform. Grandpa's khaki look worked, and Truly's Doll costume was good, and Caractacus' plaid suit looked suitably eccentric. Excellent make-up throughout and the inventors' bad wigs were perfect. Alan McCormack and Greg Browne designed the lighting, with the underground scene being suitably dark and moody with the wall sconces, and the projections and mirror ball worked a treat. Star Systems sound design was excellent. Nice balance between band and singers and some good sound effects of cars and dogs! It was a well-produced show that highlighted theatrical ingenuity and a dedication to excel.

Playing the lead, Caractacus Potts, was James O'Donovan who at times looked like comedian Peter Kaye! It was a lovely avuncular performance from Mr O'Donovan, who also sang well especially on "Hushabye Mountain". He had a good stage presence and I liked how he showed zero interest in Truly until she sang with the children on the picnic, and he danced with vigour and some skill on "Me Ol' Bamboo". Playing Truly was Louise Cormack, who had an excellent RP accent and even better singing. Nice diction and a very pleasant tone on "Lovely Lonely Man", and she sounded great with Jeremy and Jemima on her eponymous song. Ms Cormack had a good chemistry with Mr O'Donovan, they made a lovely couple! Playing the Potts children, we had Jayden Guilfoyle as Jeremy and Roisín Galvin as Jemima. Sometimes, in doing this adjudicating job one gets bowled over by a performance. That happened here, both of these young actors were perfect; great acting, singing, dancing and the lived their characters and stole the show. Playing Grandpa Potts with Sargent Major bluster was Greg Starr. His mutton chop whiskers and Khaki styling really defined the character. He had good comic timing and was especially good in the Vulgaria scenes. He had a nice dynamic with Jeremy and Jemima and sang well on all of his songs, particularly "Posh". They all owned their characters and with their excellent accents, really convinced us they were living in a small town in the English countryside.

Meanwhile in the fictious European country of Vulgaria, ruled by Baron and Baroness Bombast, it was the Baron's birthday, and he wanted a Chitty car. A lover of toys, the Baron was played with childish petulance by Pat Kelly who sang well on "Chu-Chi Face" and had a good chemistry with Claire Loughnane, who played his child- hating wife. Her over-the-top reactions to the 'c' word were very funny. I loved her accent, a kind of faux German "Ve Vant Ze Car!" she shouted, and she sang well on "The Bombie Samba". They tasked their two incompetent spies, Boris and Goran to kidnap Caractacus so he could build the Baron his own Chitty. Boris was played by Colin Dillon who was clearly the less idiotic of the two, he controlled Goran and was the ideas man. He performed "Act English" with good comic timing. His accomplice, Goran was played with goofiness by Dylan Noonan who had a good physicality. They kidnapped the wrong Potts and Grandpa ended up in Vulgaria. Caractacus and Co followed them on a rescue mission.

Vulgaria was a country where being a child was an offence. They employed a Child Catcher, whose job was to rid the country of these pesky creatures. He was scarily played by Paul Shesgreen with a melodious voice that lured children to their doom. He also played the Junk Man in Act I. The children's hero was the Toymaker, played by Alan O'Brien who also played the Garage owner in the first Act. As the Toymaker, he presented a character who was frightened out of his wits but rescued the children and hid them in the sewers. Suffice to say that Caractacus empowered the children to rise up and beat their oppressors and they all lived happily ever after.

It was an all singing all dancing show and perfect family fare, with Stephanie Browne's great choreography that was quite acrobatic at times which was exhilarating. Laura Kearney's musical direction was good too. Her work with the chorus was excellent with some lovely harmonies on the "Opening", "Me Ol' Bamboo" and "The Bombie Samba". "Toot Sweets" had a huge choral sound and was one of the best sequences in the show.

Greg Browne should be proud of this production. His pacing on the show was excellent, it flew along. Mr Browne's work with the actors was terrific, especially with Jeremy and Jemima who stole the show with their performances. The set looked good as did the costumes and make- up, and the car was nice. All together it was good evening's entertainment and a distraction from real life for the appreciative audience who gave it a well- deserved standing ovation.

show_raw: The 25Th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee
review_text:
What a Buzz!

Created in 2005 by Rachel Sheinkin, William Finn and Jay Reiss from a series of improvisations, 'The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee' is a musical comedy in one act. A diverse group of six geeky adolescents, all played by adults, compete for the Putnam County spelling championship. They spell their way through a series of words, hoping never to hear the 'ding' of the bell that signals a spelling mistake. Four audience members are added to the competition each performance and they too are eventually 'dinged' off.

The show started the second we entered the Rory Gallagher Theatre as two ushers showed the audience to their seats whilst calling each other 'Honey'. These were, as we found out later, one of the contestants' two dads, Carl and Dan who later went up on stage. These were funny, commenting on audience members and being over the top in their campness. The sound of bees was played, house lights were dimmed and two actors in beekeepers' costumes opened a spot lit box to reveal, not bees but the Spelling Bee trophy.

Thereafter each character came on and introduced themselves, some in song. Alison Fleming, as moderator Rona, started and showed high status and a good singing voice which we heard more of later. We met Chip Tolentino, last year's winner, played by Dominick Hurley dressed as a boy scout, Logainne Schwartzandgrubenierre, the youngest competitor with very tight pigtails and a lisp was played by Katie Anne Harris, Leaf Coneybear with his ever present hat with ears, played by Bobby Ho, William Barfée whose name is mispronounced constantly during the show, was played by Rian Fitzmaurice Condron, Marcy Park, who has just transferred from another school was played by Julia Cahill and Rebecca Hill played Olive Ostrovsky a shy vulnerable kid.

Each performer sang with energy and commitment in the opening number "The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee" and we got a feel for their characters. They all played considerably younger (12 - 14yrs) as the show was written for adults to play children, and this worked especially with William Barfée and Logainne Schwartzandgrubenierre. We also met Vice Principal Douglas Panch, played by Andy Armitage, who had a sinister past he would not discuss. Panch called out the words and when asked to place them in a sentence created very funny juxtapositions "Spell phylactery." "Can you put that in a sentence?" "Billy put down that phylactery - we're Episcopalian." Two other Officials were seated at a table upstage and were played by Eve Fitzsimons and Jacinta Hegarty. The final character was Mahoney, the school counsellor played by Precious Abimbola.

The band led by Musical Director, Michael Young, consisted of Piano, Keyboard, Flute Sax and Clarinet, Cello, and Percussion and were sited upstage of the action where we could see them allowing some interaction with the cast. They were very tight and sounded great. Sound design and engineering was by Shane Healy with lovely reverb on the songs and a fine balance between band and singer. Eimear James choreographed, and even though there is not much in the way of dance numbers here, her work with the cast on movement was good. The choreography worked best on the syncopated movements.

John Hurley gave us a great lighting design. Static for the most part but he let loose during the songs and/or fantasy/ backstory scenes. Nice focus and choice of colours - mixing blues and greens together always looks great as he did here. Also, I liked his use of side lighting, it made everything more three dimensional. Hannah Lane's set design used the motifs of Bees and Honeycombs. The honeycombs on the pros looked good. The simple tiered platforms for the contestants' chairs worked as did the Official's tables at stage left. I liked the printed wooden letter signs too and the stars and stripes treads leading up to the stage. The confetti was great at the end too.

Ciara O'Neill stage managed the show. There's not a lot of scene moving or transitions so, it was more managing people and props, which she did quite well. Gillian Roberts costume design was perfect, Leaf's hat, Logainne's jacket, William's tie - it was all perfect.

The cast were excellent and fully invested in their roles. Heading up the 'adults' was Alison Fleming, who played Rona the moderator of the Bee. She portrayed Rona's love for the competition and the syzygy of the Bee. Her singing was good on "My Favourite Moment of the Bee" and she showed high status as being the one who is really in control. Playing the school Vice Principal Panch as well as Olive's dad, Andy Armitage had a great presence on stage. His pronunciations of the spelling words showed very good diction. Nice performance with great comic timing. Precious Abimbola was brilliant as Mahoney. Her comforting of the losers was awkward, showing us that Mahoney was not really the right person for the job as she seemed to lack empathy! Amazing vocal performance on the "Prayer of the Comfort Counsellor", she blew us all away with her performance of this song. Lovely, focused performance from Eve Fitzsimons as the Official. She portrayed Jesus too with a funny reluctance and had a good voice, as did Jacinta Hegarty who was stoic as the Official, but she really shone as Olive's hippy mother. Her singing on "The I Love You Song" was excellent. The contestants were a weird bunch of high achieving but socially awkward kids who were individually very quirky. Rebecca Hill played Olive in orange dungarees and exuding sadness. Her singing was good on "My Friend the Dictionary" and particularly on "The I Love You Song" with her onstage mum and dad. She deftly exposed the character's vulnerability through her performance. The nervy William Barfée was played by Rian Fitzmaurice Condron with a juvenile antagonism. His 'magic foot' routine was very detailed as was his subtext of being attracted to Olive and his contestant number was Pi. Katie Anne Harris played Logainne, her voice, complete with lisp, was superb as was her dynamic with Carl and Dan. Their "Woe is Me" was fabulous. Defending his title, Dominick Hurley's Chip Tolentino was very funny. His solo, "My Unfortunate Erection" was a great moment of theatre, particularly as he started it in the audience during the tail end of the interval. One of the more interesting characters was Marcy as she was an example of total over achievement and what it can do to a child. Julia Cahill played her as very strait-laced, and we could see Marcy's glee as she messed up. Her scene with Ms Fitzsimons's Jesus was very funny. She had a superb voice on "I Speak Six Languages" and "Jesus". The final contestant was Leaf Coneybear, played by Bobby Ho. His general relaxed air of 'whatever' was great in that he didn't have as much invested in the competition as others. His song "I'm Not That Smart" was excellently performed.

During the show we gradually got to know them all very well, including their homelife. It was all very American as you can imagine and gave a good insight on how such intense competition can negatively affect children. We ended up feeling that they shouldn't be doing this but out and about being kids, but parental pressure seemed to force them to compete.

'The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee' is a quirky little musical. It's funny, has a few good songs, a great script and was a perfect choice for the Society who gave it a unique production full of energy and humour. Director Michael-Anthony Greene clearly worked hard with his actors to produce superb characterisations. Their comic timing was excellent, and it zipped along at a good pace, we were never bored, nor did we drift. We cared what happened to the characters as they experienced some of the underlying issues facing young people today, including absent parents, the pressure to excel, the pressure to fit in, the angst of first love and the difficulty of navigating an adult world. This production by MTU Musical Society opened a window into the world, not just of competition, but of the unfair high expectations and we have for our children and what that can do to them.

I have the greatest admiration for the courage shown by Director, Cora Tyrell, in tackling this extremely challenging piece of musical theatre, and in many of the clever devices she employed in trying to achieve a believably sinister atmosphere with the content. As one might expect from a musical based on a novel by Stephen King, "Carrie" is not a musical for the faint-hearted, dealing, as it does, with issues of abuse, peer-pressure, bullying and dangerously warped religious fervor. In so doing, it throws up an array of interesting and unusual characters, from Carrie herself, the telekinetically gifted victim of abuse, and her mother, a psychotic religious zealot, to a range of unruly and confused teenagers, and adults unable to deal with the challenges of confronting an unhealthy youth-culture. The dark undertones of religious fervour and supernatural powers make it a challenging piece to fully realize on-stage, without the benefit of cinematic gimmicks. While ULMTS gave it their best shot, including some excellent performances and strong vocals, they were perhaps too limited by financial constraints and available facilities to visually recreate what was a multi-layered special effects movie and a dark and psychologically intense novel. The show was very well costumed and the make-up, especially the scenes involving a lot of blood, was very visually effective. The pouring of pig's blood over Carrie in the penultimate scene was most successfully achieved, as were the moments when she displayed her telekinetic powers.

Block pink was not an ideal colour for a neutral set that had to function as various locations.

An empty, black box stage, with varied levels, might have been more functional, and would most certainly have made lighting effects more possible and more effective. I did appreciate how the lighting designer tried to create atmosphere with strong colours and over-head spots, but on occasions, particularly in solo numbers, this caused facial expressions to be poorly lit. Sound was good and well-balanced throughout the show, but perhaps the sound effects when the telekinetic events were occurring could have been more sharply amplified to startle the audience. The stage team, under stage manager, Brian Dowling, managed to keep scene changes moving at a slick pace, but I did feel that more dressing was needed in several scenes to suggest location more emphatically.

In the title role of Carrie White, Caitlin McVicker strongly portrayed a victim, not just of school bullying, but of abuse at the hands of her psychotic mother. Her body language was very convincing, stooped and unable to look anyone in the eye, and it was enhanced by a fragility in her dialogue that only grew in intensity when she was provoked. When the fire within her was ignited, her attitude, physically and vocally, became powerful and intense. She presented herself as a very capable actress with a most pleasing (if somewhat scary) vocal quality. A very good performance.

As her religiously zealous mother, Margaret, Katelyn Carson displayed very good singing and an awareness of the instability of her character. She was at her best when she had a lot of physical activity to keep her hands occupied and when she interacted with Carrie, while perhaps she needed more guidance or confidence to fully realise the psychotic nature of her monologues.

There was sincerity in Sarah Meaney's portrayal of Sue Snell, the one who reaches out to befriend Carrie. She was believably ashamed of her bullying, and totally convincing both in her feelings for Tommy and her concern for Carrie. Her vocals were also strong and secure.

It's a credit to Sally Fox that, by the end of the show, I had an intense dislike for her character, Chris, such was the venom and viciousness of her attitude and bullying. She perfectly captured the sense of entitlement of a brat with no moral compass. Very well played and sung. As Tommy Ross, Mark Langtry was the most believable of the male performers, with a good self-assured confidence, but also a genuine nicer side to his character. This was well-played and well-delivered, with the added bonus of good and clear vocals.

Makayla Palmer gave good character to the role of Miss Gardener, believable in her concern for Carrie and resolute in her determination to end the bullying. Her vocal contributions were note- worthy.  Rania Ahmed perhaps needed to be a bit more authoritative to establish her position as Principal Stephens, but she did get across the frustration of a teacher with control issues and unruly students. As Billy Nolan, Marc Jones was a believable bad-attitude kid, and indeed, he portrayed his asinine character without the need for such frequent crotch-focused gestures. He also managed his vocals very comfortably.

Competent support was given by Alex Szware as Freddy and Daniel Tuohy as George, both displaying good teenager attitude and immaturity.

Cayla O'Neill Ruane made a good impression as the devious and easily corrupted Norma, and she was ably supported by Khayla Timothy as Liz, Caoímhe Tuohy as Frieda, Silver Chuks as Helen, Zahraa El-Hassany as Tina, Jess Madden as Laura and Kara Madden as Lucy. As an ensemble, this group played well together in establishing the gang mentality of the school yard, but also in having enough redeeming features to warm to Carrie when she turned up at the ball.

Although a small group, the cast still managed to produce some fine vocal harmony and quality, and although choreography was limited, each one entered into the spirit of all their movement and routines.

Costuming was good throughout the show and the blood-stained clothes for Carrie were very impressive and disturbing. She always looked frumpy and at odds with her fellow students but blossomed in her party dress. Her hair was also nicely altered to enhance her appearance at the dance.

While choreography was not a major feature of this show, choreographer, Avril Healy, contributed to the attitude of the school kids with good funky movement and as much activity as the space would allow. The mimed volley-ball game was a nice piece of theatre.

In conclusion, a Director with a willingness to be adventurous and experimental, a talented and enthusiastic cast of performers and a wonderful team spirit, made this a production of note, and provided a very good standard of performance and entertainment to a most appreciative audience. Sincere thanks for a most enjoyable experience.

Anything Goes is a playful romp, set at sea, aboard the SS American. The story-line is zany and very amusing, and the Cole Porter score features many of his best-known songs. As a package, it's what I would call a safe show, good comedy, cheesy romance, nicely written characters, and all those wonderful tunes. This production, from Director, Paul Fay, was a clean and comfortable one, nicely played on a good, fresh and well painted standard set for this show. Most of the action takes place on-deck, but the areas opening up into the various berths were tidy and effective. Stage Manager, Colum McDaid, and his team, had no problems at all with achieving scene changes with a minimum of fuss. The upper deck and steps were well used for pictures and entrances. Aided by a very capable cast, characters were well-developed, and while some of the comedy could have been more pointed or exaggerated, everyone gave a very good account of themselves.

Sarah Riddick as Reno Sweeney played her role with a reassuring confidence and a chilled persona. She handled her comedy with a fine sense of timing and good physical reactions, and she was well-able for her big show-stopper musical numbers. A very pleasing all- round performance.

Billy Crocker was played to a T by Niall Gallagher. He was as quirky as he was charming, with very good facial expressions that enhanced his comedy, but most impressive for me was his velvety tenor tone and the perfect diction of all his vocals. Easy listening at its finest. I've always felt that Hope Harcourt is an under-written role, but in fairness to Tara Doherty-Eagles, she injected her with a bit of character and was warm and impressive in both her acting and her delightful vocals.

David Supple was extremely enjoyable as Moonface Martin, making the most of every ridiculous situation in which he found himself. His comedy timing was excellent and his delivery of Be Like The Bluebird was spot-on, likewise his Friendship duet with Reno.

Initially, I thought that James Twomey's dead-pan portrayal of Lord Evelyn Oakleigh was a tad too laid back, but I quickly changed my mind, and ended up finding his portrayal quite hilarious. The Gypsy in Me was a delightful romp.

Aisling Cuffe was very brash and amusing as Erma, delivering all her material very successfully. I just wished she had more to do. Very impressive.

Zarah Doyle brought a rasping resonance to the voice of Evangeline Harcourt, and a bundle of character to the role. Again, this was an assured and relaxed performance and very enjoyable. Ray Bissett gave good comical account of himself as the short-sighted tycoon, Elisha Whitney, and enjoyed the journey, as did the audience. Alison Gill, as Spit, and Mary B. Dunphy, as Dippy, played the two small time gangsters, who seem to change identity with every production of Anything Goes that I've seen. The original Chinese characters were replaced, presumably due to political correctness. On this occasion, they were both very amusing and very effective.

Good support can from Malcolm Bolton as a very jolly Captain, and a Mitchell Pritchett (Modern Family) doppelganger. Reno's Angels, Chastity, Charity, Purity and Virtue, were confident and competently played by Lauren Murphy, Amy Behan, Ava Blythe Duggan and Nikki Johnston. Other cameo roles were played by members of the ensemble and were all commendable.

The chorus had a fine vocal quality, the men having a good barbershop quality in No Place Like Travel/ Bon Voyage and There'll Always Be A Lady Fair. Harmonies were very good in the title song, Blow Gabrielle Blow and Public Enemy Number One. Physically, the movement and dancing was clean and tidy, and when in the background, they contributed to their scenes with good focus and reactions. As with the direction of the show, Musical Direction, under Kevin O'Sullivan, was very shipshape and Bristol fashion. Tone and tempi throughout were very good, and the musicians played with consideration for the singers on stage. Judging from the clarity of the vocals and the well-realized harmonies, good preparation had gone into the vocal work, and principals were all very vocally secure. A good job all round. The Anything Goes finale of Act One was the best presented and performed number, from choreographer, Rachel Sheahan, closely followed by a good energetic Blow, Gabrielle Blow.

Perhaps more could have been made of Erma's Buddy Beware, but there was good work in the duets between Booby and Reno and Hope. The other chorus numbers, while a little unimaginative, were tidy in execution and allowed the chorus to focus on their vocals.

Lighting was good insofar as everyone could always be clearly seen, but it was perhaps a little bland at times and maybe wanted more magic for those bigger chorus numbers. There were no problems with the sound system, which included good sound effects and was always well- balanced.

Costumes throughout were tasteful and appropriate for both passengers and crew, with Billy's 'acquired' sailor suit being delightfully under-sized. The Angels looked good, but maybe wanted more flamboyant Cabaret costumes. Reno was always beautifully attired. There was nice attention to ladies' hairstyles too, and make-up was natural and most satisfactory.

Overall, this was a very tidy, well-delivered and enjoyable production, and I sincerely thank all concerned for a most pleasant and entertaining evening.

Bonnie and Clyde, composed by  Frank Wildhorn, (Jekyll & Hyde, The Scarlett Pimpernell) with lyrics by Don Black and a book by Ivan Menchell, was first presented in San Diego in 2009. This gritty and passionate love story between gun-totin' ganster, Clyde Barrow and his wannabe Hollywood actress girlfriend, Bonnie Parker, provides a story-line that is sometimes vicious, often intense and yet delightfully romantic and comical. The morality theme is represented musically by a gospel score, while the seedier lifestyles of the shows protagonists are captured by rockabilly country styles and smouldering gospel and blues ballads. It's very well put together, and for those who may not know, it is also a true story. As for this particular production, I think it's safe to say that it got all the ingredients right to serve up a very tasty treat for Waterford audiences. David Hennessy's attention to detail was absolutely top-notch, from the well-structured set to a lighting plot that captured the right tone and atmosphere, to very good costumes and make-up and perfect hairstyles. It all looked and felt just perfect. The pace of the show was very good, and the stage space was, mostly, well-used.

Characters were strongly established, and accents were good. Being a historical piece, there were also plenty of visual references to the era and the details of the story.

The set was a very good combination of a three-door physical structure and emotive projections, which, when projected onto the wood-work of the doors, gave an excellent ageing effect to the well-selected images. While the centre door was needed to conceal Clyde's car, the doors either side could probably have been done without as the areas behind them were really too tight to allow much action within. Regardless of that, stage manager, Brian Collins, and his team keeping things running very efficiently. Everything else was achieved with a great variety of era appropriate props and furniture, including the impressive car. (Those large wooden doors, while very well constructed, had motors that were a bit noisy and annoying, but not to the extent that it seriously intruded into the action.)

So much hard work went into making this a classic visual treat, with super props, as already mentioned, quite excellent and appropriate costumes and a quite stunning display of detail with wigs, hair- pieces and make-up. The application of blood and bruises, when required, was handled with sensible restraint and was always effective.

It was, however, the principal actors that made this production explode of the page and into the hard-hitting on-stage action. Jordan Bass in the central role of Clyde Barrow, gave a performance that was as crazy and comical as it was vicious and vindictive. Clyde was not really a very nice character. His love for Bonnie was beautifully portrayed, as was his affection, albeit selfish in nature, for his brother. The role requires much physicality and an abundant range of emotion, and in every respect, Jordan hit the target. His vocals were also rock solid.

Not to be out-done by him, Emma Sunderland was radiant, sexy, flirty, and passionate in her portrayal of Bonnie Parker. The sensuality of their relationship was steamy yet very tastefully realized, and Emma excelled in her emotional scenes. What impressed me most of all was her strong and passionate vocal delivery, making the most of some really great musical numbers.

And then there was Blanche Barrow, superbly portrayed by April Kelly, hilarious in her Bible-thumping control over her husband, full of self-righteous indignation and yet never lacking a fierce sensual passion. As with Emma, her singing was sensational, and her comedy was priceless.  Her husband, and Clyde's brother, Buck, was given top-notch treatment by Eoghan Fingleton, playing his comedy to perfection in trying to appease both his wife and brother in their conflicting moral standards. Strong in his drama and totally secure musically, he even died with panache.

There was a good strong development of character from Simon Broderick, in the role of Ted Hinton, starting out as the good cop, with a good work ethic and a sincere love for Bonnie, and morphing into a hard-nosed bullying loser-in-love. Very well played and very pleasing vocal quality too.

Caoimhe Scanlon as Young Bonnie and James Lyons Power as Young Clyde got the show off to a cracking and confident start, both full of energy and talent. As scene-setters, they beautifully captured the characteristics of their older selves, making the transitions very believable. Jamie Murphy made a big impact, particularly with his vocals, in the role of the Preacher. Edwina Cummins, as Cumie Barrow, very nicely captured the dilemma of a mother who loves her son unconditionally but can't cope with the reality of him being a rotten egg. Similarly, Bill Stafford as Henry Barrow, nicely registered the heart ache of a father finding it difficult to respect his son. Possibly he needed a more striking change of physical appearance when he became Deputy Johnston. (For a second, I was confused into thinking that Clyde's dad was a copper!) Completing the parental line-up, Delia Lowery as Emma Parker displayed valiant efforts to keep her daughter on the straight and narrow in a very well-played and well- sung performance. Keith Flanagan had an aura of hard-nosed authority about his no-nonsense Sheriff Schmid and Darren Malone impressed as Capt. Frank Hamer. Good support came from Leon Sheehan, Lauren Cardiff, Samantha O'Regan and Kayleigh Grant and the ensemble who doubled up in cameo roles. As a chorus, they were well involved in the action, and although small in number, they made an excellent vocal contribution to the show, especially in the gospel-style numbers. The band, half of them side stage and half of them in the rafters, and all dressed in period costume, under the watchful eye of MD, Jimmy Brockie, made a brilliant contribution to the show, with excellent playing and a strong 'feel' for the gospel and country style of much of the music. Indeed, the whole experience was musically dynamic, with powerful principal vocals, a vibrant and well-tuned ensemble and beautifully realised harmonies throughout. This was my first time to hear this excellent musical score, and what a delight to enjoy it with such accomplished performances.

Choreographer, Michelle Condon wasn't over-challenged with this production, as choreographic opportunities are quite limited, but what dance and movement there was, was tidy, varied and always fitting with the mood, tone and atmosphere of the music.

Lighting throughout was extremely atmospheric, with good special areas, emotive colour filters, and well-timed cueing. Only a few times, the upper level could have used a bit more lighting to eliminate shadows in those covered areas. Sound quality, including voice overs and effects, was all very secure and balanced. There were quite a few members of other musical societies in the audience on the night I attended, and I wouldn't be at all surprised if this quite brilliant show makes it onto their "to-do" lists for the future. Congratulations to David and his whole company on a super night of engaging entertainment.

Wexford Light Opera Society produced 'The Hunchback of Notre Dame' in April at the National Opera House. Based on a novel written by Victor Hugo in 1831, the stage production of the 1996 animated Disney film was first produced in Germany in 1999. There have been many changes from the film, it's darker and concentrates more on the relationship between Quasimodo and his uncle Frollo.

Set in 15th Century Paris, the story explores ableism, racism, love, and faith and focuses on Quasimodo, a deformed bellringer, his uncle the Archdeacon Frollo and a Roma girl called Esmerelda with whom they both fall in love and is set in and around the Notre Dame cathedral. The Captain of the Paris guard, Phoebus, also falls for Esmerelda, who is part of a band of travelling Roma that the Church wants to exile. The musical was written by James Lapine and Peter Parnell with music and lyrics by Alan Menken and Stephen Schwartz. The WLO production was directed by Thomas O'Leary with musical direction by Fintan Cleary and David Hayes, choral direction by Eithne Corrigan and choreography by Aisling Doyle.

Thomas O'Leary directed this poignant journey through Quasimodo's life with sensitivity. He didn't shy away from the emotional content of the book but embraced the melodrama of the love quartet between Esmerelda, Quasimodo, Frollo and Phoebus. The performances of these actors lifted the production as did Eithne Corrigan's choral work and the stunning orchestrations of Fintan Cleary and David Hayes. There was still a vestige of the Disney film in the presence of the speaking gargoyles and statues, however in this production they came across more like Quasimodo's inner thoughts rather than quirky friends, which worked. Mr O'Leary decided to lose the metatheatre device in the book where the actor becomes Quasimodo in front of the audience by putting on the character's make-up and costume and then reversing the process at the end of the show and becoming the actor again. Instead, we were introduced to adult Quasimodo fully costumed and in his special effects make-up. Which was a pity as the device highlights the "What makes a monster? What makes a man?" theme and is consistent with the theatrical style of the piece.

David Hayes & Fintan Cleary & Eithne Corrigan directed the cast musically and the band on this show. Mr Hayes stepped in when Mr Cleary became ill and worked with the orchestra and with the cast. Ms Corrigan directed a magnificent choir who delivered every note and harmony with confidence and beauty beginning with "Olim" and continuing up to the "Finale Ultimo". The orchestra of fifteen players were brilliant as they played the hauntingly beautiful music, the strings, brass, woodwind, and percussion were augmented by two keyboards to give us a practically symphonic sound which soared around the auditorium. Aisling Doyle directed the choreography, which was mostly featured within the Roma scenes, and was full of energy, especially on "Tavern Song", "Rhythm of the Tambourine" and "The Court of Miracles". "Rest and Recreation" was particularly good too and the Feast of Fools scene was very well moved. But this show is all about the characters and their fractured desires and relationships.

Leading the pack, we had a riveting Michael O'Gorman playing Quasimodo. Mr O'Gorman's physicality was excellent, he hunched down to make himself shorter and dragged one leg for most of the time. His make-up gave him a pronounced forehead and he squinted from beneath. His voice was high pitched like a pre- pubescent child's and was quite melodic in speech but staccato too and his singing was full of expression, longing, hope and despair on "Out There" and "Heaven's Light" . He got to the emotional core of Quasimodo and we, the audience, felt a great empathy towards him. Mr O'Gorman had a very good dynamic with Tony Carty's Frollo, they worked very well together and had almost a father/son relationship. Mr Carty had a wonderful stage presence on this show and his Frollo was thrilling. His multi-layered performance portrayed Frollo's commitment to God, his hesitant care and cruelty of Quasimodo and his inner conflict with his yearning for Esmerelda and his hatred for the Roma. His singing was good throughout but especially on "Hellfire", I can still hear that final long note.

Some of the best scenes in the show were between Mr Carty and Niamh Cullen's Esmerelda, their scenes jumped off the stage. Her portrayal of Esmerelda was thorough; her singing was great, "God Help the Outcasts" was divine, and her acting was moving. Her dance was first- rate and full of character, and she really got under the skin of the character. Esmerelda, despite being wanted by both Quasimodo and Frollo albeit for different reasons, only had eyes for Captain Phoebus De Martin. Played with assurance by Thomas Furlong, his Phoebus was initially all swash and buckle but once he defied Frollo and sided with the Roma, his characterisation came alive and more three dimensional. His singing was superb, particularly "Someday" with Esmerelda and their onstage relationship convinced. There was a very strong performance from Eric Hayes as the King of the Roma. Quite the trickster, a magical character with the harlequin costume. He owned his scenes, and his singing was excellent on "Topsy Turvey" and during Act II, Sc II in The Court of Miracles. Reminiscent of a Ring Master, he controlled a lot of the action in the show and impressed.

The ensemble were excellent in this production and played a range of characters from Roma to priests to gargoyles etc. Most notable for me were: Florika, especially her singing at the end of the show, Jehan's acting in the early scenes, Fr Dupin and the Madame were good as was St. Aphrodisius who sang with passion on "Flight into Egypt".

Visually, this show was a treat. Scenic Productions set was made especially for this show and featured a series of platforms and most notably a flown in stained glass window up stage. Set dressing was excellent and the up stage centre doors were brilliantly used by the production. The treads at stage left and ladder at stage right were also well utilised, especially the ladder by Quasimodo and the red material as burning metal looked great.

Thespis Theatrical Costumes Ltd. supplied the costumes, and they were perfect. The Roma costumes were colourful and had great texture, Frollo's range of priestly costumes were excellent, and the guards looked good, especially their helmets. Stephen Byrne, Emma Carty, and Elle Doyle looked after make- up and wigs. Everything looked great and of the era. Quasimodo's make up was good as was the range of dark wigs on some of the ensemble. Aidan McGrath's lighting was excellent. I loved his use of gobos, especially in the prison scene. His deep reds and blues were very moody and nicely saturated and Jason Fallon's sound design was terrific. It was loud and beefy as it should be. Lovely balance between band and singers, with amazing reverb and deep booming bells.

This was a moving interpretation of the musical where the actors inhabited their roles and together with the ensemble told the story. The direction was thoughtful and there was a good synergy between the creatives and the cast. Sadly, the original musical director, Fintan Cleary, passed away not long after the production run so this beautiful production was his swan song. Rest in Peace Fintan.

Waterford Musical Society presented a lovely production of Lionel Bart's 'Oliver!' at the end of April this year at the quaint Theatre Royal in Waterford. Directed by Andrew Holden with choreography by Ali Reville and musical direction by Wayne Brown, this was a deliciously dark version of 'Oliver!' more in keeping with the novel than the countless saccharine versions one is used to seeing. It was thrillingly original with excellent performances all around.

Lionel Bart's musical is based on Dicken's 'Oliver Twist', a novel published in serial form from 1837-39 about the trials and tribulations of an orphan boy growing up in Victorian London. The musical premiered in 1960 and went on to be adapted into a very successful film in 1968, directed by Carol Reid, which won six Academy Awards.

Oliver, a malnourished orphan in a workhouse, is sold as the apprentice to an undertaker, whose daughter's fella he beats up for insulting his late mother. Oliver escapes and meets Dodger, a young pickpocket who lives with a group of thieving children under the care of the charismatic Fagin, a fence for stolen goods. When Oliver is captured for a theft that he did not commit, the victim, Mr. Brownlow takes him in. Fearing for his livelihood if Oliver talks, Fagin employs the malevolent Bill Sikes and his girlfriend Nancy to get him back, however things don't go according to plan; Sikes kills Nancy and is in turn shot by the police and Oliver is returned to Brownlow, who through a series of 'Dickensian' coincidences, happens to be his grandfather. Fagin and the children flee together most likely to another part of London to continue the lucrative business.

Most productions concentrate on the song and dance, and the songs are great, and everybody knows them at this stage. But this production was different. The songs and dance numbers were present and excellently done but director Andrew Holden seemed to direct this show as a play with musical interludes rather than a musical theatre piece, which was wonderfully refreshing and ensured that the drama of the story took centre stage. It is a dark story, as are most of Dicken's works, populated by hideous characters with less than good intentions. Bumble and the Sowerberry family were repugnant as were Corney and Sikes. Fagin and Nancy were very much the hero and heroine of this version, and both were wonderfully and empathically played. The beginning of the show was quite compelling as we were introduced to a series of repugnant self-serving characters who meant our hero harm. Ray Collins played Mr Bumble, the workhouse overseer, with a wonderful Northern English accent. Mr Collins gave us a corpulent, revolting Bumble. Less bumbling and more salacious towards Corney, their bizarre courting scene was brilliantly performed, full of suggestive sub-text and desire. The scheming Widow Corney was given a true Dickensian interpretation by Avril Hartrey. Her voice was from 'up North' like Bumble, but she had a cunning edge and sharpness to it that could cut glass. Her seduction scene with Bumble was great as was her singing on "Oliver!" and "I Shall Scream". When Oliver disobeyed them, he was sold on to funeral directors Mr and Mrs Sowerberry. Played with creepy intensity by Jonathan Kelly and Olga Greene, they sang "That's Your Funeral" with excellent timing and devious intent. Their slovenly daughter, Charlotte, was played with a lazy petulance by Devlyn Lonergan who was more interested in coupling with the other apprentice, Noah Claypole, here played with jack-the-lad cockiness by Patrick Brennan. All of these characters were straight out of Dickens, they had the narcissistic, egotistical cruel streak he wrote about so well. Lovely strong performances.

Conor Lyons played Fagin and did something with his character I'd not seen in the past. He performed him with a distinct vulnerability, quite fearful of Bill whom he'd trained and scared of change and his little Kingdom being destroyed. He was also quite kind towards the kids in the gang and one could see the affection he had for them, particularly Charles Ware- Murphy's Charley, who really impressed. Mr Lyons singing on "You've Got to Pick a Pocket or Two" was excellent but he excelled on "Reviewing the Situation", where he commanded the stage. His Fagin was quite camp and mannered, which really worked. He'd taken in Nancy when she was a child and she remained faithful to him as an adult. Played by Megan DeCourcey, who was full of energy and naughty fun on "Oom-Pah-Pah" and superb on "It's a Fine Life". Her Nancy was a wonderfully grounded character, with a soft heart and a firm sense of responsibility and her interpretation of "As Long as he Needs Me" about boyfriend Bill was heartrending, she lived the song not just sang it. Bill Sikes was played with barely repressed violence by Kieran Walsh. Entering on "My Name", where he set out who he was and what he does, Mr Walsh sang with menace. His stage presence was palpably strong, and he was particularly vicious with Nancy. Nancy's sister, Bet, was played by Emma Walsh who had a lovely energy especially on "Oom-Pah-Pah". She showed her devotion to Nancy and Fagin's gang and had a good characterisation and physicality.

Oliver was played by James Lyons Power, and he looked and acted differently to the other urchins in the show. He had a gentle relaxed inquisitiveness and stillness that seemed to indicate an inborn privilege. His singing on "Where is Love?" was excellent as was his parts of "Who Will Buy?" He had a good dynamic with Dodger and Nancy and an engaging wide-eyed fascination with Fagin. He was befriended by the Artful Dodger, played by Alex Brophy with good singing and dance skills. He had a good chemistry with Oliver and Nancy and an excellent dynamic with Fagin. He led "Consider Yourself" with assurance and convinced as the number two of Fagin's gang.

Oliver was rescued from a life on the streets by Mr Brownlow, played by Paul Corcoran in a genial and avuncular manner. Clearly upper-class, he was strong with Bumble and Corney when they came sniffing around and gentle with Oliver. Socially the opposite of Fagin, but one couldn't help feeling that Oliver would have had more fun with Fagin and his gang! His housekeeper, Mrs Bedwin, was played with a nice maternalism by Karen Hearne, who sang the reprise of "Where is Love?" sweetly and had a kind demeanour. The local doctor and friend of Brownlow who looks over Oliver for signs of disease was Brian Hogan's Dr Grimwig. With his repeated "...I'll eat my head." Mr Hogan's Grimwig was dryly funny. He had a good chemistry with Mr Brownlow and a nice presence.

Ben Hennessey's set design was perfect for the small stage in the Theatre Royal, a series of wheeled reversable flats that showed different locations including Fagin's den, the Workhouse, the Sowerberry's Funeral parlour and even London Bridge. The stage was managed with skill by Paul Greene. Paul Browne's lighting was good, but the movers were often on when moving, which gave a contemporary look to the show that didn't work, and the follow spots didn't seem to have sights as they were often hastily moved from the set to the performer. One Louder Sound Ltd designed the sound and it was good. Nice balance between band and singer, especially on the underscore. Some good weather sound effects too. Rita Loncke-Drohan and Nomac provided the costumes which were of the period. Bumble's costume was great as was the Sowerberrys, but the children's and Fagin's costumes were excellent; dirty and torn, with little accessories. Carol Knox's make-up was perfect, particularly the greasy filthy look on the children and Fagin. Mr Sowerberry's make-up was great too. Aidan O'Dwyer looked after the hair and wigs and they worked, especially Fagin's bald look with the straggly hair hanging down.

The Big Fella' Tullamore Musical Society produced Bryan Flynn's 'Michael Collins - A Musical Drama' in the new Esker Arts Centre in May of this year. Commissioned by Cork Opera House and written in 2005 when Cork was European Capital of Culture, the musical follows an important period in Collins' life, leading up to his death in 1922. Directed by Pat McElwain with musical direction by Enda O'Connor and choreography by Deirdre Browne, the production was a superb interpretation of the work with an excellent cast and high- quality production values.

The show focuses on the Civil War, and specifically Collins, during and following the Easter Rising. Heavily influenced by 'Les Misérables' and 'Evita' in structure, with a play-within-a-play, W B Yeats' 'Kathleen Ni Houlihan', as an allegorical nucleus and four narrators; it's an elaborate piece of theatre, a massive production that utilises many theatrical tropes with a huge chorus and carries with it an obligation to do it justice.

This was not Mr McElwain's first rodeo with this show, having previously directed a wonderful version which I saw a few years back. This iteration was an even more heartfelt production of Bryan Flynn's musical swan song. I've seen quite a few versions of the piece over the years and here Mr McElwain's interpretation of the book was exceptional: sharp and emotive. A strong focus was put on Collins' friendship with Harry and how that disintegrated and on his fractious relationship with De Valera. These scenes were electric and really bounced off the stage as did many others. The barricade scene with the gunmen at the windows early in the show was outstanding in its scale and noise and in showing the horror of battle and the fear in those engaged in and affected by it. The prison scene was excellent too as was the Dail scene moderated by Player 1. The more mystical scenes and the play within the play were also superbly portrayed. The production was very high quality with an excellent set, costumes, and lighting all combining to awaken the audience's hearts to this fabulous work.

The music in this show is rousing and musical director Enda O'Connor's chorus were splendid. Fantastic harmonies and power from the ensemble on the bigger numbers "Every Heart Awaken" and "Fly the Flag of Freedom". The male chorus on "Prison Song" were excellent too. The individual singers really impressed as well, particularly Jordan Bass as Collins and Liam Egan's Boland. Mr O'Connor's band of seven sounded much bigger than their number would suggest with, for me, the reed being the most prevalently gorgeous. The pre- recorded uilleann pipes sounded powerful as did the various drones. His interpretation of the score was wonderful and it had an immediacy and dominance, especially with the two percussionists. It's not a big dance show but choreographer Deirdre Browne did work a bit of magic on a couple of dances that were nicely moved. The majority of the choreography is ensemble movement, and this was very efficiently directed, particularly the scenes with the newspapers. The slow motion, living tableaux and freezes were all expertly led and accomplished and added a contemporary theatricality to the production.

Playing the big fella we had Jordan Bass, who gave us an impeccable characterisation and a giant presence on stage where Mr Bass really convinced as a Corkonian. Collins has the lion's share of songs in the show, and Mr Bass excelled on each one of them. He had a great dynamic with both Harry and Joe and his scenes with De Valera were full of tension and conflicting passions. I liked his gentle scenes with Kitty too, their duet "Our Love Will Never End" was sweet. Audrey O'Meara played Kitty as a sad character who has some happiness early in the show but ultimately ends up alone. She had a good chemistry with Collins, and I'd suggest a better one with Boland in Act I, they did seem to gel and were believable. Her singing was lovely with a nice tone on "Our Love will Never End" with Collins and she was touching on "For Nothing Else I Cared" with Boland. Harry Boland, Collins' friend until he stole his girl, was played by Liam Egan who impressed. He charted his journey from idealist to bitter realist with some skill. He had a good chemistry with Collins and initially with Kitty, their break-up scene was excellent, full of resentment and emotion. His singing on "Not That Man" was honest and full of acrimony. In an earlier scene at the party when he proposed to Kitty, he endeared the audience to him. He played the character so well that there was a gasp from the audience when he was killed, a testimony to Mr Egan's admirable performance. It was at this party that we also met Kitty's unnamed sisters played by Aisling Geoghan, Ruth Kelly and Sinéad Handy. All three were very good in "A Toast to the Host". They had an easy camaraderie with Kitty and sang and danced with enthusiasm.

The main protagonist in the show is actually De Valera, who was played by George Ross. Mr Ross is fairly new to the boards but did a good job here. He portrayed De Valera's stoicism and coldness with a fierce concentration. His scenes with Collins were good, there was a palpable tension between them. His singing on "Confrontation" and "Stepping Stone" hit the mark and his acting was full of sub-text. He was present during the treaty debates along with the characters Cathal Brugha and Arthur Griffith, who were played by Brian Gunning and Simon Byrne. Both performers were forceful, articulate, and strong with great expressive energy. Equally as strong was Stephen Keegan's young volunteer who appeared in many scenes and had a great focus. One of the most interesting actors on stage was Colin Hughes who played Collins' acolyte Joe Emmett. He epitomised the excitement of working with Collins to build a new country. His emotional connection to the role was intense, especially when Collins was killed as he let out a loud primitive cry that sent shivers around the audience. Mr Hughes had great timing too, and his repeated "Mr Collins" instead of Michael was great. A very fine and naturalistic performance that gave us an insight into how Collins inspired.

The four narrators of the show, the Greek Chorus if you like, also played characters in the 'Kathleen Ni Houlihan' play. These four owned the stage, appearing and disappearing, interviewing other characters, and moving set around. They were made up of two older and two younger actors: Jay Origan as Player 1 and Bridget, Tom Maher as Player 2 and Peter, Valene Greer as Player 3 and Delia and finally John Doyle Peredo as Player 4 and Michael. These performers were the backbone of the production and effortlessly switched from role to role and sang brilliantly on the intricate harmonies. Mother Ireland was another mystical character, played by Joan White, she was the embodiment of Ireland. Her singing was excellent, and she had a good grasp of this unusual character. She worked well with the Players in the 'Kathleen Ni Houlihan' play within the play predicting doom and peril and generally 'haunted' the set, urging the young men to rebel against their oppressors.

This was a significant production in that all of the elements worked in tandem and complimented each other; from Wayne Handy's marvellous stage management and set design to Ronan Kenny's super lighting design to Derek Reck's powerful sound aided by Ultan Keena's costuming, hair and make-up designs. Everything dovetailed beautifully within Pat McElwain's artistic vision. But above all the production showed us the heart and soul of the show, it gave us what Mr Flynn wanted us to experience and for that it more than deserved its standing ovations.

Back to the '80's Leixlip Musical and Variety Group produced the comedy retro musical 'The Wedding Singer' written in 2006, with music by Mathew Sklar, lyrics by Chad Beguein and book by Tim Herlihy and based on the 1998 Adam Sandler / Drew Barrymore film of the same name. Directed and choreographed by Claire Tighe, with musical direction by Dermot O'Callaghan this was a fabulous high camp version of this ode to the '80's. It was fast and furious with great tongue in cheekiness and marvellous singing.

The plot is thin but fun. Wedding singer Robbie Hart and waitress Julia Sullivan have a DMC and bond the night before Robbie is jilted at the altar by Linda, his fiancée. Julia gets engaged to her Wall Street boyfriend Glen, who cheats on her, reveres money, and becomes the antagonist. But Robbie and Julia's bond becomes stronger, and this puts her wedding in jeopardy. Throw in a funny best friend, a rapping granny, frustrated bandmates, a synthy derivative score, a bunch of look-a-like performers in Vegas into the mix and you have a sure-fire formula for a hit show, which this was.
