Che analyses her price for fame in 'High Flying, Adored'. Then Eva, very cleverly and well-rehearsed, changes her costume (assisted by her fashion consultants) during her singing of ' Rainbow High'. After the highs and lows of her Rainbow Tour, Che asks her to keep her promise to help the poor, and she forms her Foundation, which Che critically illudes to as a possible money laundering operation. In front of her adoring supporters Eva passes out suddenly, denoting her fight with cancer. For health reasons, she decides not to run for Vice President and speaks to the nation in her final broadcast, and shortly after we are where the show started, at her funeral and her embalming.

With only five principal roles and no dialogue, the onus is very much on keeping the storyline alive with great articulation in the singing, physicality and believability in the acting, as well as much expression in the choreography. The chorus were the mortar between these five bricks and added greatly to the production with their dancing and singing. I also noticed that each of the principal roles were understudied, presumably because of covid, showing, as if we needed it, how a production could be decimated because of a few succumbing to the pandemic. I am so happy to see this and am fully aware of its necessity. Well done to Newbridge Musical Theatre for having the forethought to implement it. Directed by Sharon McNamara, this opera, liked most others, needs to be visually stunning, with very good movement and grouping. And in many ways it was. She, with Production Manager Phil Jennings, gave us a fine production which used placing that was always very interesting and provided lovely groupings. Musical Director Dave McGauran, who I've already come across in a few other shows in the area, did an excellent job in the pit with both orchestra and performers. It's no wonder he is so popular as an MD for societies. Working wonders in many of the standout numbers of the show such as 'Peron's Latest Flame' with the fine singing of the aristocracy and its excellent drums, to the exhilarating money, money, money' of 'And the Money kept Rolling In', contrasted with the beautiful violin in the reprise of 'Don't Cry For Me Argentina'. The movement and choreography by Julianne McNamara was also very visual, with lovely contrasts. I especially loved the slow hands I've already mentioned in the 'Requiem for Evita' at the start of the show. This was even improved on at the very end, as the hand choreography moved slower and slower until it and the music stopped instantaneously. All of this was excellently contrasted with the goose-stepping Fascist soldiers, and in big numbers like 'And the Money Kept Rolling in' which really moved along and gave that necessary contrast with exuberant movement.

Good costumes by Andrew Reddy, especially Eva's stunning black dresses and red and black checked suit, which even outdid her usual white diva outfit with silver and blonde hair. I wasn't quite sure why the chorus, at the opening cinema scene, were dressed chiefly in black, pre- empting the announcement. Also, I had a problem with the aristocracy dresses, despite the furs, gloves and stoles. They were too mundane with dark, muddy shades and were ill-fitting on the ladies of the chorus.

The set, built by Bob O'Kelly, and consisting mainly of a large black wall upstage, with a high grey balcony (later to be decked by a very large Argentina flag) and with only quick changes for other scenes, suited this production admirably. However, I'm not sure black works as a colour for the whole back of the stage, and for me the balcony was too high, removing especially Eva from the audience. 'Don't Cry for Me Argentina' the big number of the show, made it very difficult, if not impossible for Ms Williams to emotionally involve the audience in this huge number, and that was a great pity, because that's what it's there for. Also the large grey balcony, unless it was covered by the huge Argentina flag, looked wrong. Maybe it was there for holding the large flag, which looked good.

Stage Manager Tom Kavanagh and his deputy Orla Kavanagh provided good continuity and set changes, while props were good throughout also. Jody Trehy's Sound Design was a little unbalanced, in that I didn't always hear every word (except with Che whose articulation was exemplary) with the orchestra overpowering at times. Lighting by Stage Lighting Centre produced some nice effects, for example the colours of the Argentinian flag, brought out in the legs to either side and the stunning blue scene of 'Another Suitcase' but other scenes passed me by without the excitement of these scenes and I felt more could have been done.

I enjoyed tremendously my trip to Newbridge to see 'Evita', which although a very testing musical for any company to perform, is another great addition to the works of Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice. I thoroughly enjoyed the production and extend to Newbridge Musical Theatre my best wishes for the future.

Not everything is black or white.

I think I expected the Scouts Hall in Nenagh to maybe be small and dilapidated, but I couldn't have been further wrong. Instead, it turned out to be a modernised, spacious and well-equipped venue with plenty of room for a sizeable audience, a generous stage and able to accommodate an orchestra of fifteen.

The musical chess was the idea of Tim Rice, who after being unable to get his friend and colleague Andrew Lloyd Weber on board, worked with Abba twosome Benny Andersson and Bjorn Ulvaeus. They made a concept album to start the project in 1984, followed by a West End opening in 1986 and a revised version for Broadway in 1988.

The set, designed by director Greg Browne, constructed by Alan Hogan and team of five others, worked by Star Systems, and stage managed by Derek Cunneen and Philip Talbot was very visually appealing, with twenty-four large, individually lit perspex boxes, forming the proscenium, two aprons to the stage and three legs on either side of the stage. Each of these boxes was capable of being lit separately, so we had an immediate change of colours and patterns throughout the show. Projections on the back wall, by Greg, provided changes of locations and other info that helped the audience. Particularly effective was the video of the chess game that was projected when Florence and Svetlana were singing 'I Know Him So Well', as it honed in on Anatoly, thus showing enlarged on the screen behind them, the subject of their song. This was a great idea! The stage itself had good depth, with two levels onstage - upstage slightly higher than downstage, ensuring that the full cast could be seen. The preset lighting featured alternate blue and yellow squares surrounding the projected title and a chessboard with pieces.

The orchestra consisted of four keyboards (including MD William Cullagh), three strings, three brass, two woodwind and drums with bass or guitar. The strings soared on occasions to heighten the emotional element of many of the songs ('You And I'), with the brass and drums beefing up many of the more upbeat numbers from the well-known score ('One Night in Bangkok'). Mr Cullagh oversaw this excellent orchestra from his keyboard and gave us many lovely interpretations of all the fine music from the two Abba composers.

Director and Producer Greg Browne was justifiably proud of all the technology that was used with the backdrop lighting to stage the show. He oversaw a very fine production through his work, highlighting principals and chorus throughout the story as they played out the emotions and goings on of the international chess competitions and surrounding circus. Much drama, including the love/hate relationships as well as the backdrop politics between Russians and Americans, was skilfully developed by Mr Browne. His daughter Stephanie choreographed and danced with the Dance Troupe. Her excellent work included the American and Russian chorus, Merchandisers and Reporters as well as the specialist dancers. The general movement of all these groups was always purposeful, well grouped and very interesting, but it was in her choreography with the dancers that she really shone. In particular, the balletic dance and movement that she created in front of the chess games was extremely highly skilled with excellent lifts and use of various levels.

The Lighting and Sound Design was (again) by Greg Browne and Star Systems and both elements were excellent throughout the show. One particularly visually stunning moment was for the scene involving the song 'The Deal' which was bathed in green light. Another, was that amazing shimmering light around Florence at the very end of the show as she reprised 'Anthem'. Visually stunning! However, there are two provisos - I would have liked to have seen more flashing lights and visuals in 'One Night in Bangkok' and my only worry concerning sound was that the orchestra overpowered some of the solo singing. My theory for this is that it is very difficult for an MD to achieve a balance, and that it can be difficult also for a sound engineer because of bouncing acoustics from the walls (and in this case the high ceilings of the hall).

Costumes by Creative Scene Productions, Nomac and the society were very fine, from the national costumes of the Merano people, the photographers, the merchandisers, the retinues from Russia and America, the dancers and the principals, with individually stunning costumes for Florence in her more glittery dresses and Svetlana, with that very striking dress that she wore towards the end of act two (very strong, striking colours). Was it a conscious decision for the ballet dancers in white to wear black undergarments?

The cast was fronted by four main singing principals (Freddy, Anatoly, Florence and Svetlana), the narrator (the Arbiter), and two seconds (Molokov and Walter). The singing was of a very high standard.

Freddy (Shane Kelly) showed his temperament from his first entrance and sang very strongly throughout, especially in 'Pity the Child' with its very high register which suited his voice admirably. He was always fiery, self-assured, even cocky and made an excellent foil for both Anatoly and Florence.

Anatoly (Paul Browne) has a very fine voice and his singing of the big number of the show 'Anthem' was spectacular, not only for the purity of his voice, but also for the great drama that it transmitted. He developed a very believable love story with Florence, while his acting was suitably quieter than his American opponent. Florence (Kirsty Ryan) gave a really lovely performance as Anatoly's doomed lover, while her singing was magnificently varied in songs like 'Heaven Help My Heart', 'Nobody's Side' as well as 'I Know Him So Well' and 'Anthem' with which she finished the show on such a huge high.

Finishing the quartet, we had Svetlana (Niamh Chadwick) with a beautifully pitched and sensitive performance as Anatoly's Russian wife. Her singing was superb, showing great strength and character as well as beautifully tuned tender moments. I particularly enjoyed her in 'I Know Him So Well' and especially her interpretation of 'Someone Else's Story' which was so well acted and so convincing.

The Arbiter (Paul Shesgreen) was excellent narrating the show, with very fine diction and singing to open the show with 'The Story of Chess' and 'Quartet'. He created his character wonderfully well.

The same could also be said of the diction from Molokov (Andrew Whelan), who managed his Russian accent capably and gave a very well understated performance that was crucial for the role.

Walter (Alan O'Brien) as Freddy's second and later manager, gave a nice performance and sang well also, although I would have liked to have seen more guile and scheming from his portrayal.

The show was very enthusiastically received by the Nenagh audience and myself. It was visually stunning, with marvellous singing, especially the four main principals and with an excellent orchestra and very special choreography. The music in 'Chess' is so magnificent and it was highly served by all the company from Nenagh Choral Society. Congratulations on a great show!

A very colourful and nicely dressed stage caught the eye the moment one entered the St.Mary's GAA hall in Leixlip, for the LMVG production of The Addams Family. A well-painted composite set provided enough variety to suggest various locations, with the aid of sliding gauze screens, a moving centre piece and a variety of trap door entrances and exits. The clever design allowed for a smooth flow to the proceedings, assisted by cast members and crew in costumes. Technically, the show was presented with a strong emphasis on enhancing the horror-genre atmosphere of the piece, with often surreal lighting effects and sound that was amplified to a level that demanded attention. There was little chance of anyone dozing off during this production. It's a tribute to all concerned that the show appeared to fly from start to finish, such was the cracking pace, the level of energy and the high, high quality of the performers. After the long, quiet months of Covid isolation, we didn't slip gently back into the world of musical theatre, we were thrown straight into the fiery heart of a vibrant, explosive and high energy experience that was most exhilarating for the entire audience.

Director/Choreographer, Claire Tighe, must have relished getting back to work with such an enjoyable piece of musical comedy. She didn't miss a trick in assaulting the funny bones of the audience, with visual comedy given as much emphasis as the verbal comedy provided by a clever script, and many added gags that gave the piece a breath of fresh air. She ensured that the cracking pace never faltered, and even the slow- motion exploits of Lurch were always accompanied by hilarious reactions and distractions. But the greatest strength of Claire's work was in her casting, surrounding herself with a top-drawer line-up, who had the energy and the talent to realise her vision of the show. With a script that is heavy with sexual innuendo, it's a tribute to her diligence that it was never represented in a crass or tasteless manner, and yet none of the innuendo was lost on the audience.

Claire's choreography usually takes centre-stage, but it was correctly more of a side-salad in a production where the focal point is really comedy. That said, as side-salads go, it was delicious, varied and presented with energy and precision, and a perfect accompaniment to the main course.

Musical Direction, by Dermot O'Callaghan, was energised and relentless, and capitalized on the fine band of musicians under his incisive control. A cracking pace was maintained throughout the show, yet it never lacked the tenderness or nuances required for some of the less explosive pieces. As a Chorus Master, he produced a disciplined, tuneful and extremely full sound from a relatively small group of singers. Principals were rehearsed to all be very much on top of their music, both in pitch and in tempo, and dramatic (comedic) pauses, of which there were many, were always well realised.

In terms of costumes, the show was very effectively designed, the selections allowing chorus members to have individual personalities.

Principal costumes throughout were well-chosen and well worn. But it was the quality and detail of the wigs and make-up that really created the living-dead appearance of the ensemble and enhanced the visual spectacle of the production.

Stage Manager, Mary Purcell, was no doubt delighted that the clever set design of Claire Tighe, Aidan Mannion and Eileen Fagan facilitated a very smooth running technical effort in terms of scene changes, and her crew and various cast members worked flawlessly to keep the action of the show uninterrupted. Louise Kenny and Seamus Kenny gathered an impressive range and variety of appropriate props and furniture pieces. The vertical "rack" on which Pugsley was stretched during "Pulled in a New Direction" was a work of art, well-conceived and brilliantly used. Lighting for the show was of a high standard, creating very good atmospheres, highlighting the focal point of each scene, and providing enough variety to keep the audience interested. The lighting for Fester's encounter with the Moon was particularly effective. It's a minor point, by a second of anticipation was needed on a few occasions when principals moved from a highlighted spot and were temporarily in shadow before a full state was employed. The quality of sound throughout was excellent with every word and lyric clearly heard, indeed such was the volume that I'm quite sure the living dead might have been catching the show in neighbouring graveyards. This is not a criticism. The robust sound and the strong orchestra made you sit up and pay attention and added significantly to the horror-impact of the piece.

But it was truthfully the overall standard of the performers that set the stage alight in Leixlip.

Ian Tighe in the role of Gomez Addams gave a powerhouse performance, vocally sound, commanding the stage and delivering his comedy with perfect timing and expression. He captured the essence of the patriarch who believes he is in charge, but is really the puppet of his dominant wife, and his abundant love, for both wife and daughter, was managed with sincerity and sentiment. Jenny McCabe brought a wealth of experience to the role of Morticia. She was vampy, sombre, sulky, and superior in equal measures, serenely deadpan, and always sensual. Her musical numbers were excellent, especially the brilliant comedic delivery of Death is Just Around The Corner.

James Deegan was a spooky, but gentle and entirely loveable Uncle Fester, serving the role of narrator with aplomb, and displaying a top notch comedic ability. I loved his business with the ukulele, and his "floating" with the moon was a perfectly presented and show-stealing moment.

Lauren Dooley gave a feisty interpretation of Wednesday Addams, possibly showing a little too much emotion for a character whose strength lies in her dead-pan countenance. Regardless of that, there was no doubting her vocal delivery and her complete confidence on the stage. Her love interest, Lucas Beineke, was given a youthful and exuberant interpretation by Brian Dalton, who fell delightfully between the wannabe cool young romantic and the geek. He was well matched with Lauren, and their scenes together, in particular, showed very good timing and sincerity. I happen to know what age Chris McDonald is, and believe me, he is way, WAY older than the character he was inhabiting, as Pugsley Addams, and yet he was entirely believable as the sulky, masochistic young adolescent. This was so very well played and enhanced also by a strong and effective falsetto voice. Adam Lynch maintained his dour, grunting, slow-moving caricature of Lurch very successfully throughout the show, and then impressed significantly with a rounded bass solo for Move Towards the Darkness. Judy Millar was very well cast in the role of Grandma, creating an eccentric and delightfully funny old crone, who seemed to thoroughly enjoy peeing herself during her full disclosure.

Aoife Masterson beautifully showed us the two sides of Alice Beineke, starting as the timid and subdued wife, living on her nerves, and then bursting forth with wild abandon as the hot, passionate vamp, in need of fulfilment. The transition from one to the other displayed great versatility, coupled with a very confident vocal ability. Completing the principal line-up, Ross Murray gave a stalwart performance as the rather fusty Mal Beineke, suitably stern and severe. But he certainly seemed to enjoy his transition, recreating his younger, wilder self, and rediscovering his passion for his wife. Very nicely played. The chorus were small in number, but enormous in energy and commitment, contributing strongly to the show with precise and confident dances and well prepared and executed vocals. They were also visually delightful, not just in costume and make-up, but through their awareness of the atmosphere and tone of each scene. Great team work.

The front of house team, under the leadership of Carol Byrne, did a splendid job of ushering the audience to their places in a courteous and orderly manner. I was shown wonderful hospitality before, during and after the performance, for which I was extremely grateful.

All in all, I'm delighted to say that the Covid-enforced interruption to their normal schedule has done nothing to dampen or diminish the energy, enthusiasm and performance standard of this most accomplished musical society. Thank you to everyone for a super-enjoyable night.. Dunboyne Musical Society ALL SHOOK UP All Shook Up is a musical based on the songs of Elvis Presley opening on Broadway 2005, touring 35 American cities in 2006-7 and touring the UK as 'Love Me Tender' in 2015. The show is set in a small Midwestern town that is thrown into a frenzy with the arrival of Chad, a good-looking, motorcycle-riding roustabout, who rides from town to town with a guitar on his back, blue suede shoes on his feet, and a song in his heart. Repressed by their conservative mayor, the town begins to come alive once more under Chad's influence. Lovers meet, woo, pursue, and more, all in one zany night that will change the town forever. All Shook Up is a rocking, heartwarming tale about following dreams, opening up to love, and the power of music.

When I arrived, there was an eye-catching set open to the audience, with a selection of Elvis songs playing until the start of the show.

Chad (Ryan Flanagan) had a nice easy presence onstage but I'd like to have seen him as more of a snarling roustabout, remember he's just been in jail. He loves himself more than any girl. Yes, he has to be appealing, but that other side to him is very important. Even his costumes were a bit too much nice guy, instead of anti- establishment rock and roller.

However, Sylvia (Kiera Judge) the honky tonk owner and mother of Lorraine really struck a note with her characterisation. This was a strong portrayal with a good singing voice and very good at playing comedy. Her character grew through the show until the writing let her down by making her settle as Jim's second choice in the marriage stakes.

Natalie (Tara Brazil) was extremely strong in her role as the tomboyish mechanic, who can't get Chad to notice her, so changes her identity to Ed, only to find Sandra falls for her. Her powerful singing voice in particular made her stand out in numbers such as 'One Night with You', 'Follow That Dream' and 'Fools Fall in Love'. She really could belt out a song as well as come up to the mark as an actor. Jim (Mark White), who played Natalie's dad, was another character who grew well through the show with good acting ability and a fine voice. He also handled his comedy very well.

Dennis (Turlough Malone) was one of the foremost characters and gave a very convincing and likeable characterisation of yet another person who didn't end up with who he wanted. He sang, danced and in particular gave a strong acting performance as the nerdish Shakespeare- loving Dennis.

His eventual bride is Sandra the museum curator (Ailbhe Travers) who doesn't look twice at him until she realises he likes Shakespeare! She looked great in the part and sang, acted and danced well throughout. However, she did know who she didn't want (unlike most of the others) as she continuously saw off Chad and Jim. I'm not sure that her tight dresses were very 50s but she looked well in them throughout.

Another with a dodgy costume was Dean (Jonathan Murphy) in an army costume that didn't fit very well. In fact, I barely recognised him in the second act when he wore a much better fitting costume and provided a much better partner for Lorraine (Deirbhile Travers), and the young couple proved a good match for each other, although Dean managed to drop her when he took her in his arms (just a slip). She gave a lovely high-spirited performance and they worked well as a couple.

His stage mother Mayor Mathilda (Caoimhe Cullen) gave a powerful performance of the highly irritating, talkative bully who eventually marries her taciturn sidekick Sheriff Earl (Olivier Carey) who, when he eventually says something, puts her in her place. He showed that you don't need lots of lines to achieve good characterisation, as he relied on excellent reactions.

Director Richie Hayes oversaw a good cast, even if the storyline was largely implausible, and in any case the story really doesn't matter in this jukebox musical of Elvis Presley songs. The audience were there to hear the songs, watch the dancing and enjoy the many comic elements within the show. He certainly did that and more in a highly entertaining and visual feast of a show.

Choreographer Aisling Rountree delighted us with lovely energetic and synchronised dances that sat so well with Elvis' many hits, while Musical Director Orla Mulreid Deane and Chorus Mistress Helen McHugh enthralled us with a catalogue of Elvis' famous hits. Indeed, they really gave the treatment to 'Can't Help Falling in Love' by harmonising it and reprising it at the show's end as well as the finale of the first act. Great choice, as it's mine, as well as many others, I expect.

Aoife O'Rourke was Stage Manager, but nobody else was mentioned in the programme for Set Design and all the other creatives. One of the big features of the show was the great continuity and the scene changes. This kept the whole production flowing effortlessly and maintained great energy and continuity. The eye-catching set featured a large illuminated blue arch, with a juke box in front of it. In fact, this resembled a large juke box also and was very much in keeping with the theme of the production. There were steps on either side of this large arch that led to platforms on either side of the huge jukebox. Further steps from these led to a central platform higher still and just under the illuminated arch. This gave excellent levels at different heights. The stage area had been extended greatly and two aprons added for extra scenes on either side. On stage right was the garage where Natalie worked, while the other side featured a bench which was useful for many locations. None of this needed changing throughout, which contributed to the great continuity. A very clever set, with lots of very useful levels. Props, too, were generally good but I have to criticise the lovely looking scooter rather than a motorbike, which was completely unsuitable for roustabout and ex-jailbird Chad. However, on the plus side, I loved the large Greek statue that was used in the museum.

Lighting was excellent, with lovely colours throughout, and with very good combinations. There was that lovely blue lit scene where Dennis sang with the chorus in Act Two 'It Hurts Me'. Also, the very quick change to purple just after Chad sings 'I Don't Want To'. One of the best scenes in the production was in Sandra's museum with the beautiful Greek statue, as she sings 'Teddy Bear /Hound Dog' with Chad, Dennis and Natalie. I also liked, while Natalie was singing 'One Night with You', her short interludes that created such drama and atmosphere. These scenes really stood out because of the fantastic lighting, which really was magnificent throughout the show Once again, no mention of a credit in the programme, but costumes generally lived up to their brief, with a few exceptions. Chad's image was wrong. He was supposed to be a dangerous rock and roller, troublemaker, just out of jail but he had a very clean-cut image. He could have been a chorus member, so anonymous were his costumes. There were some costumes that didn't shout 1950s to me, especially Sandra's tight dresses, and Lorraine's costume with a bare midriff. One poor dancer lost her yellow skirt during a dance number and had to work hard to try to hide the fact. Also, I'm going to talk about hair and make-up here. Ladies were fine in this area, but the men's hair certainly didn't suit this period. It needed Brylcreem, but if too short then wigs were needed.

No credit again for Sound in the programme, but there certainly didn't seem to be any problems and the balance with the backing tracks was always good. To sum up, the production was pacey, highlighting comedy and energetic dancing, with the very impressive lighting giving it lots of visual appeal, to create a lovely easy feel to the whole show. I was highly impressed with the real feel-good factor that emanated from all onstage, and congratulate Dunboyne Musical Society on a great show. Many good wishes for your future productions!

Wondrous fairy-tale.

Based on the 2001 DreamWorks animation film, Shrek the musical opened on Broadway, after a trial run in Seattle, in 2008 with a revamped West End version in 2011 and a four year UK tour starting in 2014. It's a big cast show with the emphasis firmly on visuals - Set, costumes and, of course, the dragon. The GAA Centre in Clara provided an excellent setting for the show, with raked seating looking down on a large stage area. The set featured a large proscenium and legs of trees twisted and tangled together that was very effective, although I would have preferred to have seen these painted more prominently, like a cartoon, rather than the subtle tones they decided on. Nevertheless, it still created the desired effect of the fairy-tale we were about to witness. Upstage there was a projection screen that featured the Music Theatre International animated backdrop to the whole show, with very professional and highly delightful settings, helping create just the right ambience for the whole production. I also liked the moving trees, which were used well to differentiate the various woodland scenes, which blended very well with the rest of the set. The floor rope lights underneath the back projections also helped immensely to create atmosphere. All in all a very fine set which provided an excellent backdrop for the show.

The introductory narration featured the young Shrek being advised by his two caring parents Mama and Papa Ogre (played excellently by Ruth Kelly and Stephen Rabbette) and young Shrek, nicely played by Oscar Handy. All three, like many other minor roles, turned up as other characters in the storyline. Then Shrek (Chris Corroon) makes his first entrance on to the scene. And what an entrance! He bursts on to the stage with great physicality, booming voice and characterisation. From then, I knew we were in safe hands. And as the story enfolded, I realised that this was a very fine production with every role showing the same detail in performance.

Joining Shrek as the four principals we had Fiona (Amanda Cunningham), Donkey (Colin Hughes) and Lord Farquaad (Malcolm Whelan). They made up a very strong line-up of principals, sustaining the storyline whilst acting, singing and dancing with a huge amount of talent. Fiona and Donkey and Shrek made such a formidable trio throughout the show on their travels, while Lord Farquaad acting on his knees throughout, with little dummy legs, always looked easy in the uncomfortable role and was hilariously funny on every appearance. Linda Murray, who played the Dragon's voice, sang expertly in her wonderful costume and her soul singing was so absolutely right for the role, as well as staying close to the very fine huge Dragon puppet throughout, that was built and operated by the stage team, with marvellous large eyes that changed colour.

With such a huge cast it is very difficult to comment on everyone involved, but I'll do my best to mention all that took my eye. After the great opening we had a scene with the Captain of the Guards (Bernard Coyle) and the Big Bad Wolf (Ger Dunne) which showed their very good acting ability. The Fairy-tale Creatures were a large company, splendidly costumed and bringing such tremendous detail to their roles. From their midst quite a few stood out. Gingy (played by Natalee Connolly) had a wonderful high, squeaky voice, just right for the part and her puppetry skills brought the gingerbread man to life. Pinocchio (Barry Dunne) once again had a fabulous squeaky voice which he used to good effect in his songs, and of course his nose, that grew as he told lies, was always very funny. Mama and Papa Bear (Jay Origan and Ruth Kelly) were delightful with two excellent voices. There were so many and they were so well represented by their colourful and charming costumes. Other notable ones were the Three Little Pigs (more like three hairy bikers) played by Liam Cushen, Ethan Fox and Eoin Handy, the beautifully costumed Sugar Plum Fairy (Aoife Fitzsimons) and the Wicked Witch (Janet Coss) with her added prosthetic chin and nose to make her even more gruesome. The two other Fionas ('Young' played by Eabha Mai Tierney, and 'Teen' by Therese McCormack) performed with Princess Fiona in a lovely trio for 'I Know It's Today' and this was delightful by all three performers, especially Therese. To think that this huge show was directed by Alan Recks, who also did Musical Director and Chorus Master. This showed huge commitment and fantastic skill, because there really were no weak links in this production. The choreography (Lea Carroll) was always beautifully synchronised, with everyone onstage, from principals, Fairy-tale Creatures, Duloc dancers, rats, three blind mice and guards dancing delightfully throughout. Backstage we had the talents of Wayne Handy, his construction crew and his backstage crew, while Costumes, Make- up and even design of Gingy and the Dragon were led by Liz Rickard and Mary Cornally and their team superbly. Lighting Design and operation were in the very capable hands of Ronan Kenny, while Recks Audio did the sound which was excellently mixed with the hidden offstage orchestra.

The show rocked on with many treasures along the way. The Magic Mirror (voiced by Stephen Rabette) was excellent, followed by a very good scene with Lord Farquaad, This Is Your Wife (tv style scene), lovely colourful Duloc dancers in red and blue, with yellow plastic hair, the very good scene with the hairy men in the stocks, The Dragon, its wonderful singing voice and her backing singers and dancers, and then Shrek, Donkey and Fiona gave us a terrific ending to Act one with 'Who I'd Be'. Highlights of the second act were the exploding bird in 'Morning Person' with Fiona, who was then joined by the rats for a delightful tap dance in their top hats. Then we had the farting and burping contest between Fiona and Shrek in 'I Think I Got You Beat'. Lord Farquaad's big number, with delicious brass accompaniment from the band, then took us through to the three blind mice's excellent dance. After this Shrek and Fiona fall out and he shuns her. Then we have probably the best song of the show in 'Freak Flag' with the Fairy-tale Creatures led capably by Pinocchio and Gingy, before Lord Farquaad and Fiona's wedding scene, which is gate-crashed up through the audience, first by Shrek and then the Fairy-tale Creatures. Finally we had Fiona's stunning transformation into an ogress, which I still haven't worked out. I didn't see her leave the stage, but when she walked up on a height upstage I swear she transformed magically into an ogress, finishing in a real big ending with 'This Is Our Story'. What a truly wonderful show!

I can only congratulate Clara Musical Society on a fabulous production of a show that certainly wouldn't be one of my favourites. However, I can only adjudicate what is before me, and this was top quality right throughout every area of the production and performance! Well done everyone in Clara Musical Society!

Legally Blonde the musical, with music and lyrics by Laurence O'Keefe and Nell Benjamin, and with a book by Heather Hach, is taken from both the novel by Amanda Brown and the 2001film of the same name. The show premiered in San Francisco before moving to Broadway in 2007. It fared much better critically in the West End, where it garnered three main awards including the Olivier award for Best New Musical in 2009.

Clane Musical and Dramatic Society's 2022 production of Legally Blonde was staged in the beautiful, old and atmospheric Abbey, which has become home to the Society. The old stone walls and high ceiling I'm sure gives it good acoustics. However, as is increasingly the case with many societies that have issues with the amount of space available, more and more now seem to house the band or orchestra in another room, freeing up space for more audience. Each instrument can then be miked up, with the sound coming through the speakers in the venue along with the performers' voices. It's then much easier for the sound engineer to balance the sounds together, with no acoustics in the auditorium to worry about, Director Olivia Smith rightly made the decision that because the musical was light, frothy, frivolous and funny, the way to play it would be with the accent on comedy, high pace and keeping scene changing to a minimum. The show is a bright, breezy comedy that can require lots of changes of scenes, so with the emphasis on high tempo the correct decision was made. The only small blemish I noticed with the set was the flimsiness of the caravan, which quivered when touched by the actors, especially opening the door. However, the continuity of the performance more than made up for this slight flaw. Ms Smith's work with the performers, with the emphasis on tempo and the production always light hearted and breezy, meant that there was always interest for the audience.

Likewise, MD Dave McGauran, kept the pace lively throughout for band and singers, with an exuberant and highly charged tempo that never seemed to stop for breath. He always had tight control over his band of instrumentalists throughout this pacy show. Numbers that stood out included a breathless opening with 'Omigod You Guys', the parodied Riverdance-like 'Ireland', the extremely comic 'Gay or European' and the magnificent 'Finale'. The whole show flew from beginning to end and was due in no small way to the band and their conductor/musical director.

Choreographers Marie Cashin and Olivia Smith followed the same principles and values, and the choreography was always energetic, lively, enthusiastic and high octane throughout. The opening number "Omigod You Guys' was highly comic and enthusiastic and the show never eased off throughout. Brooke led the singing and dancing in 'Whipped Into Shape' at the start of the second act, and it was just a rollercoaster from then until the finale. Another dancing highlight was 'What You Want' complete with cheerleaders brandishing tinsel pom-poms.

Looking at the backstage and front-of- stage creatives, Olivia Smith designed the set, which was constructed by Pro Staging - Marie Cusack, who was assisted by Eilis Browne, Catriona Browne and Fran Styles. The gauze curtain was often used as a backdrop for front of stage scenes, while changes were made behind, thus ensuring great continuity. The stage was framed below and on either side by a pale brick wall throughout. The design centred on the fact that everything had to be easily set and changed. When it's considered that scenes included the Delta Nu's residence (upstairs, downstairs, inside and out), Harvard lectures, Paulette's hair salon, the courtroom for the trial, the jail, the caravan and various other locations, then it's easy to see this was no small task. However, the continuity and breakneck pace of the whole show never eased throughout. Credit for this should also firmly lie with Continuity by Elaine Moore O'Donohoe and the props which were provided by Ellen Stapleton, Grainne Ui Luing Jennifer O'Brien, Brid Murphy and Jane Eustace. Lighting and Sound were both operated and designed by Cathal Donohoe and Wilkins Sound Systems. The action was well lit by a combination of LEDs and movers that definitively helped the pace of the show, as well as providing beautifully lit moments (the two simultaneous scenes at the start of act two, where Brooke does her dance with her exercise gang in the video ('Whipped Into Shape') using all of the upstage, while simultaneously Professor Calahan watches with his students on the steps at the front.

Costumes by CDMS Wardrobe, Kevin Hynes, Nomac and Orla Reidy, assisted by Sadie O'Reilly, and with Make Up and Hair provided by Jordon Marron and Cian McKeon also greatly helped with the overall look of the show. Pink, of course, was the chief element for Elle, with her bedroom, while the Greek Chorus looked very striking in their white.

The cast, which listed seventy one roles (although I realise many people doubled up) was still a large company for such a small stage, yet it never appeared to be over congested or difficult for all onstage to move, such was the organisation of the director and choreographer.

Aideen Leacy gave a great performance as the essential Delta Nu girl, who is dumped by her boyfriend Warner, because he doesn't think she is serious enough for his ambitions in politics after Harvard. This leads her on the road to self-discovery and the realisation she doesn't need Warner, or his type, to fulfil her dreams. Very assured onstage, her reactions and facial expressions underpin her very good work as this girly character-come- good. Her very good singing voice underlines her credentials (illustrated in 'Serious' a duet with Warner, 'So Much better' at the end of the first act, 'Legally Blonde' with Emmett, and 'Find My Way' just before the finale).

At the opening we were introduced to all the girls from the Delta Nu sorority, including Elle's three close friends Margot (Laoise Burke), Serena (Sophianne Horgan) and Pilar (Sarah O'Flaherty, who also understudied Elle). From the word go the dialogue of these three characters was delightful and their movement and dancing was so energetic and lively. This was, of course, typified by the opening number "Omigod You Guys'.  Emmett (Robert Gallagher) as the down-to earth young man who appreciates Elle's qualities and helps her in her quest, gives a very centred, sensible and sensitive portrayal, and eventually realises he loves her. Grainne Ui Luing as Paulette, really excelled in her role as the hairdresser with a love of all things Irish. Her sense of comedy was always to the fore in her portrayal and she danced and sang so well ('Ireland'). Professor Calahan (Martin Fahy) is such a misogynist and abuser of his position over his students and this was a very assured performance, nailing his character, especially when he comes on to Elle. Warner played by Maurice Treacy, gets his character just right in his portrayal of Elle's erstwhile boyfriend, when he ditches her because she isn't serious enough to help him in his quest to reach the Senate. He loves nobody half as much as himself and because he succeeds in his portrayal, the audience love when he gets his comeuppance. His new girlfriend Vivienne (Sarah McGauran) once again caught my eye, because of how she handled both sides of her character. To begin with she sided with her new boyfriend Warner and was nastiness personified with Elle, but when she sees how wrongly Elle is treated by Calahan and Warner she changes her tune, with a lovely characterisation of the woman who got her adversary wrong. Brooke, (Sinead Byrne) as the jailed fitness queen who is on trial for the murder of her husband is so well cast, with her great dancing skills to the fore. She can't divulge her alibi, because telling everyone she was having liposuction, would ruin her business. Enid Hoopes (Pauline Hoban) is another high flying student who, with Warner, Vivienne and Elle wins internships from Calahan. She fits in so well with all the other friends of Elle in this show that never takes itself too seriously and provides lots of dancing, singing and character. The only other characters that haven't had a mention, yet fully deserve one, are the two excellent dogs Bruiser and Rufus played by Rocky and George.

The rest of the cast were tremendous in a very fine show, backing up all the principals with great singing, dancing and acting/reacting, with Nicos (Cian McKeon) and Carlos (Art McGauran) stealing the limelight for their performances in the big number 'Gay or European'.

I really enjoyed this show, even though it is so girly and pink. Because, certainly in Clane's production, the essence was very much of a show that didn't take itself at all seriously, yet committed totally to a fast- paced, energetic and hilarious comedy with lots of slick, high energy dancing and vivacious songs and music, that left the audience loving every minute of this refreshing musical. Well done Clane Musical and Dramatic Society for your production of Legally Blonde.

Nuns on the Run.

Sister Act is a musical taken from the 1992 film of the same name, with music by Alan Menken, lyrics by Glenn Slater, book by Cheri and Bill Steinkellner and additional material by Douglas carter Beane.

Originally opening in the West End in 2009 and Broadway 2011, it subsequently had tours in both UK, USA and internationally. Sister Act tells the hilarious story of Deloris, whose life is changed when she witnesses a murder. Under protective custody she is hidden in the one place she won't be found - a convent. Disguised as a nun and under the suspicious watch of the Mother Superior, Deloris helps her fellow sisters find their voices as she unexpectedly rediscovers her own.

I found my way to St. Mary's College, Arklow with AIMS President Rob Donnelly and we were seated together. At least for the first act. However, he didn't reappear for the second and I wondered what had happened to him, only to find he was getting dressed for a small walk-on role in the final scene. When he made his entrance I didn't recognise him at first, until he turned around to the audience as the Pope, albeit the first bearded Pope I had ever seen. It brought the house down of course.

Director Stephen Acton, Musical Director Naoimh Penston and Choreographer Martina Lynch were obviously of the same opinion that the most important element of the production should be the feel- good factor, with the utmost energy and vitality, emphasising the whacky nuns' chorus in singing, dancing and especially comedy. Every single nun in the chorus was completely individual. All had quite different personalities and each one was unique.

I particularly noticed one very small, older sister, who commanded my attention a lot of the time she was onstage. I found her so intriguing and charismatic and think she was Sister Mary Theresa, who used a walking stick and was played by Joanne Logue. Apologies if I got this wrong, because I couldn't make out faces too well, with the wimples that were worn disguising their faces. But all of them deserve great credit for bringing so much to their portrayals, whether it be singing, or dancing or general movement/physicality. Deloris (Ellie Willoughby) was so good with her hilarious Bronx accent and her comic timing was excellent as she wove so much of the action together, whether it be with the nuns or with the gangsters. She has great stage presence, a strong voice that was entirely suited to her role and she got so much vitality from her character.

Mother Superior was played by Elaine Sweeney and she was the antithesis of Deloris, very correct in everything she did so seriously as befitting the sister at the head of the convent. However, even she in the later scenes lost her officious manner, smiled and became as enthusiastic as her fellow sisters.

The other named principal sisters were led by Sister Mary Patrick (Lisa Buckley) the perky, dizzy, always laughing and never serious nun. Sister Mary Robert (Connie Tobin) is quite the opposite, in that she is very timid and uncertain of herself but, of course, finds her personality and singing voice to help change her personality totally around. Sister Mary Lazarus (Isabella Wong), Sister Mary Martin-of- Tours (Rachel Kealy) and my favourite, Sister Mary Theresa (Joanne Logue) were all sisters from the chorus, who had small speaking roles, but otherwise were part of this very fine chorus.

Sweaty Eddie (Richard O'Toole) is the cop and ex-boyfriend of Deloris who still holds a flame for her, and Curtis (Tomas Byrne) is her current boyfriend and sadistic gangster, who murders in front of Deloris and she goes on the run from him. His fellow gang of gangsters include Joey (Patrick Bracken), TJ (Daniel Codd) and Pablo (Brian Harty) and all are less fierce than their boss Curtis, even comic on many occasions.

Monsignor O'Hara (James Kearon) is the only male in the convent and acts as a buffer between the nuns and their Mother Superior, with much dedication and plenty of fun.

Deloris' backing group of singers and dancers, played by Genevieve Molloy, Fiona Walker, Niamh Harper and K-Lou Murray, were excellent as the backing group to Deloris the lead singer.

Stephen Acton oversaw a vibrant production with the emphasis firmly on comedy, high energy dancing and singing and with an overall feel-good factor. Quite rightly, he made the decision with the emphasis on great continuity and fun. The music was well sung by all the performers, with great help from the band and MD Naoimh Penston, who conducted everything energetically and with great drive, especially in the big important numbers.

Choreography played a large role in this show and was gloriously danced with endless energy in all the dances arranged and invented by choreographer Martina Lynch. All the big numbers were such a huge hit not just because of the great singing of the full company but also because of the boundless vivacity of all the dances.

The set design was good and not too involved so that scene changes could be kept speedy and let the show run as fluidly as possible. I liked the mahogany items in the convent which were very correct, but they were compromised by the upstage grey platform with stairs to either side. They should also have been in matching mahogany. I also loved the round stain glass window which was very effective but the stain glass legs were not as effective because they weren't lit from behind.

The costumes were at times wonderful (the nuns, the gangsters with more colourful contrasting colours) but at times out of period. This is firmly set in the 70s or early 80s, but drainpipe jeans or patched and ripped jeans were wrong for the period. Similarly the Monsignor's costume was a puzzle with a surplice worn inside a tunic top. The nun's night attire was interrupted by one in striking striped pajamas! Eddie's police uniform looked more suitable for a security guard although I loved his double change during a song. Lighting was fairly traditional, although in this visual show I would have liked to have seen a bit more innovation and there were some missed cues, albeit on the first night.

Nevertheless, in spite of these small shortcomings, the show fairly ripped along and the action was breathless in its vitality, energy, humour, movement and colour.

I thoroughly enjoyed it and I'm sure many of these small criticisms disappeared on subsequent evenings. Please realise that these criticisms are very small in comparison to the great joy you brought to tonight's and, I'm sure, subsequent performances. Well done on a very good show! Nuns on the Run.

I thoroughly enjoyed it and I'm sure many of these small criticisms disappeared on subsequent evenings. Please realise that these criticisms are very small in comparison to the great joy you brought to tonight's and, I'm sure, subsequent performances. Well done on a very good show!

Spring Awakening, a coming-of-age rock musical focusing on adolescent anarchy and the trials and tribulations of growing up. This award-winning musical tells the story of how young people struggled when controlled by repressive social and sexual rules in a provincial German town dominated by Lutheranism. As they try to navigate their way through this teenage anxiety, they deal with homosexuality, rape, suicide, abortion and sexual desire. Their stories unfold in this bygone world of draconian religious beliefs as we witness them journey through adolescence into adulthood with poignancy and passion. Music by Duncan Sheik and book and lyrics by Steven Sater, Spring Awakening opened on Broadway at the Eugene O'Neill Theatre on December 10th 2006, winning eight Tony Awards, four Drama Desk Awards and a Grammy. This landmark production, based on the 1891 play of the same name by Frank Wedekind, is an angsty rock musical, which explores the lives of a group of young adults as they try to find themselves.

UL Musical Theatre Society, a relatively newly formed Society, finally got to showcase their very first musical since their inception in 2019, and what a showcase it was. The atmosphere certainly confirmed the anticipation, as it was just electric, with production team buzzing around and friends and family settling into their seats in the Belltable Theatre. To be honest, I didn't know what to expect, but I can now ratify, I was pleasantly surprised and quite overwhelmed by some of the young talent I witnessed. The set was dimly lit on a dressed stage, with a loft structure centre hosting a back lit diamond shaped window.  At either side, there were two large tree flats with branches sprouting from the top and four flats, two either side painted similarly and giving continuity. Later in the production we would see the two back set pieces turn and move down stage to cleverly double as house interiors and a doctor's surgery. Although the set was simple, it was very well utilised and the lighting was terrific, with pools of lights only used were necessary, pin pointing faces and actors and aiding the ongoing narrative. Cueing was also sharp and they were some fabulous shafts of light from upstage left that almost gave a heavenly concept to certain scenes. There was nothing static about this production, directed by Cora Tyrell, even the slower songs had great pathos and held the audience. The ensemble was in constant motion and we witnessed some rigorously and artful staging. A vivid version of the narrative was delivered, digging deeper and getting darker. The singing was to a high standard and the musical director, Michael Young, produced some great work here, as it was full of sensory overload and fabulous harmonies.

Choreographer, Pam McGlynn, was certainly up to the challenge and this show was a fine specimen of compelling choreography. Chorus work was inventive and well-integrated into the scenes keeping all the action fluid and forcing the narrative forward with a propulsive drive. It is a rocking good musical score and this was certainly  matched by the ferocious performance from Conor McNelis, playing Melchoir.  His elaborately textured performance constantly pushed boundaries. He had real passion for the role and his energy was off the scale, at one point propelling himself onto the loft structure without the use of the ladder, just a leg up from the lads. Athletic and fearless, yet capable of truthful intimacy and intense sincerity. Great work from Mr. McNelis. Wendla, played by Avril Healy was sublimely beautiful to watch and I really felt for poor Moritz, played by Cillian Fahy, with his nervous ticks and his fine portrayal of a young man traumatised by puberty. Colm Hogan was a dominant figure in this production, with excellent comic timing and fine acting and vocals. It was unashamedly silly and gloriously funny to watch. Angia McCarthy shone out with beautiful vocals as Ilse and Ciaran O'Keeffe was just hilarious to observe as Ernst, demonstrating a fine capacity for comedy. Other characters also to high standard were, Otto, Georg, Martha, Anna and Thea this tightknit group of friends were well integrated into the production, and gave rich support to the principals with a high emphasis on performance and great delivery of vocals and choreography. The crew behind the scenes, led by Stage Manager, Eimear Callaghan, did a stellar job. There was nothing lacklustre about this production of rebellious youths, unfortunate events and lost souls. Firing on all cylinders, this talented group of young visionaries brought us the rapturous act of story-telling and in no uncertain terms put their stamp on this performance. It would be no surprise to me, if I heard some of the names from this production pop up in musical theatre circles in the future. UL Musical Theatre Society, without a doubt, have some stars of the future in their presence.

The very best of luck with your next endeavour and please keep doing what you so obviously love, and are undeniably talented at, making wonderful musical theatre.

Little Shop of Horrors, a musical telling the tale of Seymour, a down on his luck plant store attendant, his convoluted relationship with a voracious plant (who he ironically named Audrey II and who ultimately gets its way, which unfortunately, for the human race, is world domination!), the beautiful Audrey, Seymour's work colleague, who is burdened with zero self- esteem and has a history of making bad relationship choices, but who Seymour has a massive crush on and finally Audrey's boyfriend, Orin, the sadistic dentist, who is most definitely, a nasty piece of work. Based on a low- budget 1960's comedy, sci- fi movie of the same name by Roger Corman, Little Shop of Horrors, with book by Howard Ashman and music by Alan Menken premiered Off-Off Broadway in 1982. It then transferred to the Orpheum Theatre Off Broadway, where it enjoyed a five- year run before closing in 1987, with an impressive 2,209 performances. This Rock/Motown musical is famous for well-known songs such as 'Suddenly Seymour' and 'Down-town' (Skid Row). As you've probably figured out by now, this one doesn't have a happy ever after ending, nevertheless it provides an hour and a half of retro irony, toe-tapping and catchy tunes and freaky nonsense that I personally was quite happy to indulge in! Making his Directorial debut Dillon English gave the audience what they wanted, an energetic two hours of song and dance, with many laughs provided along the way. The ecstatically happy cast were joyous as I spoke with them after their well- deserved standing ovation from friends and family. Dillon directed well, assisted by Isabella Dogliani, and the show had good pace and lots of innovative ideas and delicious humour. I really liked the take on the plant not being a prop with a voice over, but an actual person. And Máirtín Ó Cathasaigh was perfectly cast as Audrey II, the Venus flytrap intent on world domination. The music for this show was very impressive, under the baton of Rachel Rentz and assisted by Iona Ritchie. The band were just super, so tight, producing some fine sounds. I was particularly impressed by Tom Pickles on the flute and tenor sax. Choreography was by Henry Fitzgerald and assisted by Charlotte Troy. This is not a chorus heavy show but what Henry produced was clean, well-rehearsed and we witnessed lots of exciting movement between the three Ronette's and some very well thought out choreography in the Skid Row number with good placing and co-ordination. Dara Keane played Seymour, the soft-hearted geek whose love for plants lands him in a very sticky situation indeed. I found Dara's performance compelling, he got Seymour just right. When you first met him, you were instantly drawn in and felt for him, right up until his dismal end. Dara played the part with sensitivity and had great characterisation. Vocals were also strong and chemistry with Audrey convincing. The scene where he gave Audrey to the plant was particularly moving. Audrey who sadly meets her demise in the jaws of the blood thirsty carnivorous plant was played by Sarah Cleary. Sarah gave a sincere Audrey and didn't over act the part, which is often the case. She kept Audrey real but still added a touch of quirky and dizzy to the mix. Miss Cleary's 'Somewhere that's Green' was fabulous, as was her 'Suddenly Seymour' duet with Dara and her dying scene was beautifully measured. The reason for poor Audrey's brutal end was down to Máirtín Ó Cathasaigh who played the part of the blood thirsty plant Audrey II. This was a great fit with Máirtín suiting the role perfectly. His first appearance was intense as he appeared from behind the red curtains, where the plant took residence. His tall and broad stature with his green shirt and eye makeup worked really well and he actually looked quite intimidating as he roared at poor Seymour to feed him. Mr. Cathasaigh had a powerful singing voice and this added to his threatening superiority. Mrs. Mushnick, is usually Mr. Mushnick, so it was refreshing to witness this role taken on by a female player. Rosie Byrne governed this role with a formidable force. Miss Byrne didn't let up once, always dominant and commanding.  Rosie delivered Mrs. Mushnick with high energy, vigour and excellent characterisation.

The three Ronettes were like three firecrackers, dispelling oodles of explosive energy and style whenever they entered the scene. I must highlight the excellence of the vocals here; the harmonies were sublimely beautiful and the individual singing exquisite. Acting was strong, as was movement and I thought some of Rachel Fox's expressions were priceless. Hayley O' Connell Vaughan played Crystal and was in fine voice, Caoimhe Dunne gave us an energised and fiery Ronette, delivering some stunning vocals. The final part of the trio was Rachel Fox playing Chiffon. Rachel gave us a dynamic Chiffon with great stage presence. The weird and wonderful Orin, the dentist was played by Luke Maziarek. Mr. Maziarek slid into his skin-tight leathers and white coat for the part of the dentist. Strutting around the stage and owning every part of it, with his crude and grinding shapes, he dominated, delivering a sensory overload. Chloe Leahy played the dentists patient or should I say victim! This scene was highly humours. Playing Mrs. Bernstein we had April Keeling. April's delivery was excellent and her vocals strong. Conor Walsh brought Mr. Martin to the stage with great enthusiasm and even though he stated in the programme he was somewhat out of his comfort zone Mr. Walsh seemed very much at home up there. David Quinn caught my eye from the very start, the costume and characterisation of the wino was brilliant and highly entertaining. Ms. Luce was well played by Thérése Keniry, Skip Snip by Joseph Dorgan and DJ by Eimear Hughes. All ensemble parts by Deirbhile Herron, Sean Casey, Sam Anderson and Lauran Murphy aided the narrative and were all key players. The enthusiastic and well drilled chorus added greatly to the larger scenes and the choral singing was to a high standard. Ciara Powell did a fine job as production manager ably assisted by Eimear Hughes as did Katie O'Brien as Stage manager assisted by Dean Hayes and their crew Katie O'Brien, Dean Hayes, Cliodhna O' Readron and Ellie Hession. The lighting was vibrant and impressive with good use of light stacks, set on stage, plus additional lights overhead. The sound was clear and there was good balance between the singers on the stage and the orchestra in the pit, this was down to the good work of Shane Healy from Healy Lighting and sound. Costumes, hair, makeup and styling were all also to a good standard and the set was adequate and functional. A shout out to the understudies who I believe performed on the first night, which I thought, personally was a lovely idea, giving everyone a chance to shine after all their hard work. Fergal Crowley- Seymour, Zoe Allman Walsh - Audrey, Susan Burke - Audrey II, Cormac Noonan - Dentist. Well done everyone.

Thank you for a wonderful night's entertainment and I wish each and every one of you every success going forward. Remember, keep Musical Theatre in your life and you're sure to find like-minded friends and lots of happiness.

The Producers with music and lyrics by Mel Brooks and book by Thomas Meehan and Brooks, hit Broadway with a bang in 2001, running for an outstanding 2,502 performances and winning a ground breaking twelve Tony Awards. This satire musical was an adaptation of the Brooks hit movie from 1967, of the same name. It tells the story of Max Bialystock,   Broadway's most consistently unsuccessful producer and Leo Bloom, a miserable and nervy accountant who, after much persuasion from Max agrees to fraudulently oversell a Broadway flop. Bialystock, who was once the King of Broadway, proceeds to lead the wide-eyed Leo into a life of utter chaos after convincing him to do some creative accounting with the books. They then set out to find the worst production team possible for their musical 'Springtime for Hitler', an unapologetic musical comedy that radiates bad taste. On saying that, when you witness Max and Leo with the cross-dressing Roger, the pigeon- loving Franz, the temperature-raising Ulla and the goose stepping, bespangled chorus, sporting sausage and eagle crested costumes and headdresses, you suddenly find yourself celebrating the compulsively funny exploitation of cynicism and leave political correctness at the door, giving yourself permission to laugh.

Pop-Up Theatre, Sligo, at the Hawks Well Theatre was the venue for 'The Producers', directed by Karen Gordan. We were welcomed by the lovely, bubbly Karen herself and after a nice chat, went on into the auditorium and settled into our seats. The thirteen-strong orchestra were tuning up and the open stage displayed a backcloth of the exterior of a Theatre brandishing an 'Opening Night' poster. Hollywood spot- lights swooped over the stage and as the show kicked off, we had an impressive rim of LED's, which framed the  proscenium arch, light up in sequences of greens, blues and reds, this gave a real Broadway feel to the proceedings. The cast bounced onto the stage for the 'Opening Night' number. We had two beautiful Ushers, who danced and sang with great gusto, followed by the introduction of Max Bialystock and a mixture of very interesting characters, from a blind fiddle player, a drunk man, a bag lady and we even had a couple of Nuns at one point, a very eclectic mix indeed!

The overture boomed through the building and when the lively number finished the two Ushers, accompanied by the fiddler pulled across the hanging Theatre backdrop to reveal Max Bialystock's Office. Karen gave us a great insight from the first scene how things would unfold in this production. The performances were fast paced and energetic, and the cast and chorus were very obviously enjoying every minute of it, which at the end of the day, I feel, is what matters most.  Set changes were well plotted, scenes were well-rehearsed and characterisation was strong, as was continuity. The Orchestra were in the capable hands of Niamh Crowley. Niamh and her thirteen musicians propelled one excellent piece after another.  With up tempo pacing, combined with well- rehearsed singers, the show took off with a bang. A little shout out to the young violinists, Leo Tarrant, Leah Higgins and Conor Cannon for some superb playing and also the brilliant, booming brass by Martin Moser and Johannes Kavanagh, which was highly impressive. The Choreographer for Pop-Up Theatre was Thomas Spratt. Thomas did a fine and thorough job. All principals and chorus were well drilled in their choreography and a nice touch of flair and style was demonstrated throughout. A good facility for comedy in the movement was also adhered to and the tap numbers were hopping. This is a high energy show, in fact, it's exhausting to observe, and in that respect, Thomas delivered on all fronts.  Jemma Gordan was stage manager for this production and had her work cut out for her. It is a massive production with numerous set changes. I was informed there is no flying facilities in the Hawks Well Theatre and I saw myself how tight wing space was, so I commend you on a slick operation Jemma. It ran very smoothly, or that's what it looked like from the front, but I know from years of personal experience, that's not always the case behind the scenes!  Good job Miss Gordon.

Max Bialystock was played by Robert Fitzpatrick.

Robert is obviously no stranger to the stage, feeling quite at home up there. He delivered a fast paced and frantic Max, with many fine comedic moments. Roberts on-stage relationship with Leo Bloom, his partner in crime, was wonderfully humorous. Mr. Fitzpatrick generously embraced this part, a part I believe was a dream of his to play for some time now. Éanna O'Donnell played Leo Bloom, the nervous accountant, with the secret dream of one day becoming a Broadway producer. The problem with this particular character is, unfortunately people tend to get a little too enthusiastic with it, and so, often over animate the role, thankfully for us, this was not the case and Mr. O 'Donnell  measured Blooms character just right.  Robert and Éanna were both fine singers and numbers such as 'We Can Do It' and 'Where Did We Go Right' were real show stoppers. Add Ulla to the mix and the plot thickens! Laura Kiely was the lovely lady sandwiched in between these two priceless characters, playing Ulla, the evocative and passionate assistant. Laura wrapped the audience in swathes of sumptuous and flirtatious fun. Miss Kiely's vocals soared across the auditorium, delivered with effervescence, and the attention to detail with body mannerisms and choreography were everything you'd expect from the blonde bombshell. The pigeon loving Franz Liebkind was played by the vibrant Kieran Cunnane. Kieran had a dominant presence and a robust take on the character Franz. He was in fine voice and undeniably hilarious in ' In Old Bavaria' with his chorus of pigeons and 'Der Guten Tag Hop-Clop'. So once Max and Leo had secured the musical rights from Franz, they set out to find the worst director in the business, as so we are introduced to the cross-dressing Roger De Bris, played by Brendan Reid. Brendan smothered this role in finesse and delivered a gloriously funny De Bris. I particularly liked ' Keep It Gay', this was a steamroller of comic delights and a real crowd pleaser. Rogers loyal sidekick, Carmen Ghia, played by Jason Kenny, provided us with enough melo-dramatic hysteria to last us a year. De Bris and Ghia worked well together, then add De Bris's weird and wonderful production team to the mix and we were in comedy heaven. And just when you think you can't laugh any more, an army of little old Grannies burst onto stage with the ingenious number 'Along Came Bialy' closing Act One with a bang. Hold Me - Touch Me, the leader of the highly aroused Grannies was ably played by Emily Tansey. Emily's first scene with Robert was sublimely funny and her construal of the aging nymphomaniac was very well characterised.

The Chorus of this performance were a great asset to the overall production. They were responsible not only for, the necessary all singing, all dancing, production numbers but also for set changes. The use of backdrops throughout gave continuity to the overall presentation and the lighting by Barry Mc Kinney was suitably glitzy for the large chorus numbers such as 'I want to be a Producer' and 'Springtime for Hitler' and then subtle, mood  lighting was provided for the more intimate numbers. All in all, good use of movers, follow spots and LEDs gave a picturesque, impression of  bustling old Broadway. The sound by Vinnie Higgins was well balanced and cues were tight. The costume team of Karen Gordon, Liz Gilligan and David Church, with hire from Triple C  Company, London were impressive and the hair and makeup by Niamh Noonan and Siobhan Kelly, also in keeping with the era and well groomed. The set was built by Tommy Sheridan, painted by Bridie Garvey and ably set and struck by Orianne Gordon, David Church and Meadbh Fitzpatrick, under the guidance of stage manager, Jemma Gordan.

Judging from the reputation of some of the names above, I'm guessing this was a tight group of family and friends, all pulling together to do what they love, produce musical theatre. The tremendous team work was transparently evident here and this resulted in a great production.

Karen & Company, wishing you every success with future productions and thank you for a great night of entertainment.

Better have a phone charger backstage! Jesus Christ Superstar An adrenaline pumping musical with edgy and revolutionary vibes, partnered with a legendary score that rocks the roof. JCS, the musical captures the last few days in the life of Jesus Christ, seen and translated through the eyes of  Judas Iscariot. It premiered at The Hellinger Theatre, New York, in October 1971 and a year later in the Palace Theatre, West End London, in August 1972 and has since become a global phenomenon gathering a world-wide fan base. With award winning music by Andrew Llyod Webber and lyrics by Tim Rice, this infectiously melodic rock opera is loved by musical theatre enthusiasts across the universe.

As we entered the Phoenix Building, the home of Maynooth University Musical Society, the atmosphere was jovial with friends meeting and committee members making last minute preparations to open the doors and lead the audience into their final performance of 'Jesus Christ Superstar'.  Every show we have attended has had a great buzz surrounding it, obviously because people are so happy to have returned after such an agonising absence and are now finally back doing what they truly love. Regardless, MUMS were certainly raring to go and couldn't wait for the audience to become seated so that their talented cast could display what an admirable job they had done. The stage was all on the one level with three risers, two backstage right and left and one centre front. These risers were cleverly painted the same colour as the stage floor and so camouflaged nicely, giving us a blank canvas, which the cast would dress with choreography, clever vignettes and basic stage furniture. A large scaffolding surround, with a well- supplied lighting rig housing many moving heads and down lighters was on show as you entered the auditorium and aided by the use of smoke, these lights would later create some impressive pictures. The overall vibe was more rock concert with a story thread.

Gavin Murphy gave us a modernistic fabrication of this visual. Everything about this production was current, from the movement, to the costumes and the staging was radical and had a pulsive drive. The music was in the very capable hands of Michael Young and his band of musicians, who were all students from Maynooth University and the singing had been well-drilled by Elizabeth Murphy and was performed with even servings of passion and pathos.

The overture began, and amid the helter-skelter of music and movement choreographed by, Mark Lehane, we witnessed the chorus, dressed in modern day costumes, walking around the set absorbed by only one thing, their mobile phones! With their phone's beaming light onto their faces and the shadowy and smoky lighting, the setting was quite eery and sinister. Jesus, played by Eoin McGlynn, then appeared in a beam of white light centre stage, wearing white jeans, t-shirt and jacket. Eoin had an aura of calmness around him but he would later show us in no uncertainty, he also had all the requirements for this demanding role. The chorus surrounded Jesus, shining their phone torches towards his face and forming a circle of light around him, creating a glowing and ethereal picture. They then took selfies with Jesus and dispersed, as Judas lingered and an uneasy atmosphere enveloped the stage. Judas, was  played by a female, which I found refreshing. Colleen Doyle took no prisoners with her portrayal of the disloyal apostle, who lives in a state of personal panic and relentless guilt. Dressed in a long leather coat and big black boots, Colleen looked fierce and as we would soon find out Miss Doyle had the temperament and voice to match.  As the narrative travelled on, we were introduced to Anna Kenny, playing Mary Magdalene. Dressed in a red outfit and accessorised with a black waist bag, for her oils and cloth to sooth Jesus. Anna had a liquid tone to her voice and bathed in a beautiful pool of light she sang ' Everything's Alright' with  solace and compassion.

The High priests had a dominant power in their scenes, commanding them well as they played the cold, corporate sharks. James Sheridan, playing Caiaphas, blew me away with his rich bass vocal and Dan Lavelle provided fine characterisation in the role of Annas. Next to take to the stage was Cian Murray, playing Simon with an infused playful energy. Mr. Murray, wearing  black lace underwear and red jeans imploded into the song and aided by backing dancers delivered an unstoppable Simon Zealots' number. Things took a more serious turn when were then introduced to Ellie-Anne Smith who played Pontius Pilate. This was the second gender swap of the night, which again I applaud. Miss Smith was in fine voice and had a troubled look as she sang 'Pilates Dream' and later in Act Two in 'Trial before Pilate', we witnessed a far rawer piece, which indelibly determined the hopeless result of this tragic tale. Peter, played by David McDonnell, the young apostle shrinking inside himself with the guilt of his denial. This was beautifully nuanced with sincere acting and a sublime vocal. King Herod was brought to the stage by Lar Bathe. Mr. Bathe was like a glitter bomb of opulent showmanship, assisted by Charleston dancers, this was a dynamic and exuberant number.  Suddenly the pace ground to a halt and the playful spirit disintegrated as roman guards, Lars Foossen and Darragh McDonnell, dressed in all black and carrying machine guns took control of the scene, unstoppable and unforgiving they threw Jesus around the stage like a puppet, cruelly lashing him and finally nailing him to the cross. The hairs stood up on the back of my neck when the young orchestra played John Nineteen: Forty-One and a sobbing cast surrounded Jesus, as his limp body fell from the crucifix and they carried him away, leaving a distraught and desolate Judas clinging to the empty cross.

Costumes and props were rural and edgy, with phones being the main prop! Costumes were layered and changed regularly which made for an exciting visual. Standout numbers were, 'Herod' with the bit of bling and 'Superstar' with Colleen Doyle rocking rather large but wicked black angel wings. Lighting was in keeping with the modernistic approach and some beautiful atmospheric moments were created with heavenly shafts of lights pouring onto the stage. Up tempo numbers were also sufficiently lit with flushes of colour and the use of strobe was effective and cueing tight.  Sound was well managed and levels between the orchestra and singers well measured. The set was minimalistic, but effective, and the crucifix was intelligently designed with the nails pre-set for Jesus to lace his fingers through making the whole manoeuvre flow with ease. On saying that, Eoin Mc Glynn's physicality in the movement was impeccably real. Maynooth University Musical Society with an ensemble of eight on top of the forementioned adds up a relatively small cast of just nineteen players. The energy and momentum radiating from this stage was so impressive, with strong and polished vocals full of sensory overload. There was nothing static about this production. Well done to everyone involved, please keep using your fabulous talents to continue doing what you so obviously love, making musical theatre.

Thank you for a wonderful night's entertainment.

The Sound of Music, the worlds most beloved musical, was the genius of well- known team Rodgers and Hammerstein. The pair started the collaboration after the discovery of the memoirs of Maria von Trapp in 1958.
