Music, by Rodgers, lyrics by Hammerstein and book by Howard Lindsay and Russel Crouse, were all inspired by the 1956 German film 'Die Trappe Familie'. It tells the tale of the exuberant and strong-willed postulant, Maria Rainer, who resides at Noonberg Abbey. She is very unsure of which direction her life is travelling, and while deliberating, she is sent to act as a governess for the seven Von Trapp siblings, who are, sadly, starved of their Fathers affections. Captain Von Trapp is a highly decorated naval officer and runs his home like he did his battleship, much to the destress of his children and staff. Maria, finds a way to bring happiness and music back into the Von Trapp home, while unknown to herself, falls in love with the captain. This is ultimately a love story, set in Austria in 1938, it opened on Broadway in 1959 and won five Tony Awards. The first London production was at the Palace Theatre in 1961 and it has since enjoyed numerous revivals. In 1965, it was adapted into a movie, starring Julie Andrews and Christopher Plummer, this won five Academy Awards, and to this day people worldwide are still enjoying The Sound of Music.

Back to The Millennium Forum for the second production from Londonderry Musical Society, after last visiting in October '21 for 'Calamity Jane'. Also, my second 'Sound of Music' of the week, a week full of Nuns and Nazi's, as I also attended 'The Producers'. This impressive Theatre never disappoints, with its large and imposing dome front foyer and its 1,000-seater auditorium. The stage is of a generous scale and so the set was impressive in size and the facilities for lighting excellent. As usual, the wonderful Valerie Haslett, LMS Honorary Secretary, was just inside the door waiting to greet us. We mulled through the large crowds and there was a jovial spirit in the Millennium Forum Foyer and that increased when Donald Hill, the LMS President greeted us, always so warm and welcoming. After a nice catch up, we headed to our seats and the LMS production of' The Sound of Music began.

The curtain lifted and a large Nuns chorus stood solemnly in position, candles in hands, singing the celestial and haunting 'Preludium'. The set surrounding them consisted of three arches one large in the centre and two smaller ones framing them on either side, there were also large, impressive double pillars on stage right and left. Heavenly light shone through the arches and pillars reflecting beautifully onto the stage. The choreography was constructed of simple formations which set a sacred and devout atmosphere. We then had the young postulants searching for Maria and immediately the beautiful Caitlyn McCrea who played Maria appeared singing the well- known classic 'The Sound of Music' with an impressive backdrop of the Swiss forests and mountains behind her. Caitlyn's fabulous voice rose and soared out over the auditorium. Miss McCrea portrayed the innocent girl with her head in the clouds, who we later witness, flourish into an astute young woman. Maria appears in nearly every scene in this show and that requires great stamina and consistency, which Caitlyn had in abundance. Her chemistry with the children was very special, particularly Liesel and the reprise of 'Sixteen Going on Seventeen' was thoughtful and compelling.

The same production team were in place for this;  Director Michel Poole, Musical Director Peter Doherty and Choreographer Vanessa Chapman. This team of three seem to work well together, delivering well- rehearsed and polished material. The direction was clean and there was excellent continuity throughout. Michael ensured good attention was paid to characterisation, even down to the youngest cast members. Principal and Chorus vocals were all well drilled and to a fine standard, particularly Caitlyn McCrea, playing Maria Rainer and Susan Wilson, playing Mother Abbess. The fine orchestra of seventeen produced some fabulous sounds under the expert guidance of Mr. Doherty. Choreography by Vanessa Chapman was effective and the children were delightful to watch in their groupings with good attention paid to the solo's, duets and pas de deux arrangements.

Mother Abbess, played by Susan Wilson, was a dominant force in this role, and her rendition of 'Climb Every Mountain' was sublimely beautiful. Sr. Berthe, Sr. Margaretta and Sr. Sophia, all contributed greatly to the Abbey scenes, adding a nice splash of humour. The arrival of Maria Rainer to the Von Trapp Home brought great excitement, as we meet the seven beautiful children. Liesel, played by Holly Deane, delivered an astute and independent young woman, experiencing her first flush of love. Her love interest was Rolf Gruber, played by Simon Quigg. The two matched up well and gave a believable portrayal of loves young dream, Holly is a beautiful ballet dancer, classically trained no doubt, and this added tremendously to the pas de deux choreographed into 'Sixteen Going on Seventeen'. In fact, I believe I would be correct in saying, we had a few ballet dancers in the Von Trapp family, a trained dancer always shines through.  And so, we were introduced to, Louisa, Friedrich, Kurt, Brigitta, Marta and last but certainly not least, Gretl, played by the adorable Lilymay Tolley. All the Von Trapp children from the tallest to the smallest did a superb job, finding their character and filling the stage with exuberant energy.

Their father, Georg Von Trapp, was capably construed by David Keown, delivering an authoritative and cold character. We later saw a gentle thawing of the brittle and anguished Captain as he softened to the irresistible charms of the young governess. Elsa Schraeder, the sophisticated and worldly Baroness, who is very obviously lacking in moral balance was played by the talented Natalie Armstrong. 'How Can Love Survive' and 'No Way to Stop It' were well performed, assisted by Brendan Brady, playing the dapper Max Detweiler, the cynical and unscrupulous musical impresario. The Von trap butler, Franz, was played by the straight faced, Matthew McLaughlin, who made brief, but plentiful appearances throughout the night and Frau Schmidt, the housekeeper was humorously played by Maureen Tolley, with a quirky twist, which I found original. I believe it was Maureen's first role, so hopefully the stage bug has bitten and it will be the first of many enjoyable shows. The Nazi regime, Herr Zeller, was strongly delivered by Colin Ash as was Admiral Von Schreiber, by Dan Mc Caffrey, I did feel for you both on the bows when you got booed, but that means your callous and intimidating characters were effective. Baron Elberfeld was played by Robert Blair and Ursula by Anne Pollock, all suitably aiding the narrative to unfold. A big shout out to Donald Hill, the President of LMS, who has dedicated 60 years to this Society. Donald, played the Wedding Celebrant in this 60th Anniversary show and how poignant and fitting it was. Congratulations Donald, it was very emotional to watch you take centre stage, with reverence and undeniable pride for this company you have called your second family for so long. I'm sure your daughter Christine, the production stage manager was proudly watching from the wings and your beautiful Granddaughter Holly, who played Liesel, was also honoured to share the stage with her legendary Granddad. What a fabulously talented family, wishing you all many more years of happiness shared on the stage.

The Nuns Chorus and Men's Chorus both had good momentum, were very well- rehearsed with some beautiful choral harmonies emanating from the stage. We had some picturesque settings against a stunning set from Proscenium Hire and superb lighting from Martin McDonald. All of this was in the capable hands of stage manager Christine Deane and her deputy stage manager Gavin Webb and their crew of five. The sets were of a large scale and there were frequent sets and strikes, so it took an experienced crew to seamlessly make this production flow effortlessly, which it did. I have personally survived many a torrid tech rehearsal, so all I can say is 'respect'. Sound was clear and well balanced, by Michael Kielty, not an easy task with so many head mics, especially on younger members, so impeccable work. It was actually like watching the movie when it came to the costumes from Utopia,  there was great attention to detail by Joanne Palmer and her team, keeping everyone looking ship-shape. Props by Julie Faulkner and Sara Polley were well sourced, in keeping and provided on cue. Its deceiving just how many props are actually in this musical, so, great job Ladies.

Thank you once again LMS for a wonderful night and heartfelt congratulations on your 60th Anniversary, an outstanding achievement. I wish you all the very best of luck going forward, but somehow, I feel, judging from what I've seen to date, you'll be just fine with the next 60.

Sunshine On Laois!

Portlaoise Musical Society have been around since 1999, when they first hit the stage with 'Oklahoma' and since then have given the people of Portlaoise offerings such as 'Fiddler on the Roof', 'Singin' in the Rain' and other classics right up to their award winning 'Titanic' and in 2019, 'Ragtime'. Starring as Jud Fry in their first production was Paul Norton, who has gone on to direct many of their shows and he helmed their latest production, the Irish Premiere of 'Sunshine on Leith' in November at the Dunamaise Arts Centre. Many of you won't know much about this show, it being an Irish Premiere, so a few words on the origins I feel is needed. This Jukebox musical started out as a project by Dundee Rep in Scotland and was staged by them in 2007 and was made into a film in 2013. Playwright Stephen Greenhorn, who created the Scottish soap opera 'River City', wrote the book which is woven around songs written by Craig and Charlie Reid, known as The Proclaimers. Named after the band's second multi- selling album, the musical also contains songs from some of their other albums. It seemed like a winner when first mooted as their music, and there is a lot of it, is so catchy and the band rarely strayed far from their Scottish roots, so that would give the book provenance.

The plot centres around three couples. Army buddies Davy and Ally are back from the war in Afghanistan and trying to settle into civilian life. Ally takes up again with nurse girlfriend Liz while Davy, her brother, embarks on a relationship with Yvonne, her co-worker. Davy and Liz's parents, Rab and Jean, are about to celebrate their 30th wedding anniversary when an unknown blast from the past steps into their lives. That's it. There is little exploration of PTSD, which one would expect with soldiers returning home nor is there any meaningful consideration given to the nature of family. It's a soap opera plot with a hint of rom-com.

'Sunshine on Leith' seems to fall into the Jukebox Musical trap that has snared many other contrived shows. What suffers is not the music but the veracity of the story. None of the three love stories in the plot rise above a soap opera depth. The cliff-hanger at the end of Act I, where all three relationships are in danger of fracturing at the same time is pure melodrama and shamelessly contrived. The characters, except for Rab, are mundane and paper thin. But I suspect that Mr Norton knew this, and it is to his credit that he managed to integrate his vision for the piece and create a feel-good love letter to Edinburgh, shown by the projection of countless photographs of the Athens of the North. His use of projections and the mobile treads to denote locations helped to ground the piece. However, the constant moving of the set pieces during the many scene transitions became tiresome to watch, and I suspect execute, and adversely affected the pace of the show.

It came alive during the big well-known songs, which often started out with just one or two singers and then the whole ensemble would enter, creating a big overblown version of the song, thereby entering concert mode. This happened a lot throughout the show. That said, Musical Director Emer Hartnett did wonderful work with the chorus, their harmonies and power were superb. Her band were sited up stage left under a platform and in full view of the audience. They were excellent and were often augmented by musicians on the main part of the stage, which helped integrate the music into the plot. Choreographer, Stephanie Browne also managed to incorporate the choreography into the story and at times there was a lot of performers on stage, but they were well drilled and rehearsed. The addition of some traditional Scottish dance was sweet and the Call Centre scene, "Throw the 'R' Away", was particularly effective as the performers made great use of the treads and the A4 laminates. However, I found the Hibs scene choreography very unfocused.

With an ensemble of about seventy performers on the Dunamaise stage, all singing and dancing, sound designer and operator Vinny Osborne had his work cut out for him! But he nailed it, lovely deep bass and delicate highs from the band and every voice was crystal clear. Lighting all of this was Nick Anton's wonderful design, although it was hampered somewhat by the projections. Many scenes were set upstage against the cyc on the platform but weren't lit because of potential spill onto the projection screen. This was a pity, because I think we would have preferred to see the actors rather than a nice projection. The audience blinders via open white pars on the explosion as we moved from Afghanistan to Edinburgh was an excellent effect as was the mirror ball during "Oh Jean".

Set design by Paul Norton was clever. The main set pieces were the treads upstage which were moved around the stage to create different locations. The boxes at the beginning of the show were great and created a contemporary look to the show as the audience entered. The projections, of which there were many, helped to set the locations as they were mostly photographs. But I couldn't help wondering if they were needed. They were quite distracting at times and some of the shots were of the interiors of rooms, which we didn't need to see as we can use our imagination!

The lead performers were all very good. Their acting was uniformly excellent, their accents impeccable and they really gelled as a 'family' group. Shane Kelly's Davy was quiet and thoughtful, and his singing was admirable especially with Aishling Rohan's Yvonne, who's acting, and singing was faultless. Ally was played by Eoghan Fingleton, who really captured the essence of a character who was lost. His singing was also first-rate and his onstage relationship with Sarah Troy's Liz was the most naturalistic of all. Ms Troy played Liz as a character with intelligence and great self-control. I was particularly impressed with her journey from 'hometown girl' to 'wanderer', determined to better herself no matter what the cost.

Davy and Liz's parents, Rab and Jean, were played by Andrew Docherty and Hillary Treacy. Mr Docherty stole the show for me. His languid style of performance helped to bring life to Rab more than any other character. Rab is a well-written role in comparison to the others as his backstory is explored and developed. When he first meets Eilidh, his daughter from a previous brief affair, his confusion, fear, and surreptitious delight was written on his face. Mr Docherty's performance of "Oh Jean" was perfect as was his fronting the 'band' that opened Act II as they sang "Sky Takes My Soul". His accent and character were steeped in naturalism, and he was a joy to watch. Ms. Treacy's acting was superb. She embodied the character of Jean, a hard-working woman who has been deceived and feels like she has been living a lie for 25years. Her scene with Rab where they argue over his long- ago affair was outstanding. Aoife Digan's Eilidh was the result of Rab's affair, and she gave very moving performance. Her first scene with Rab was a tour-de- force of an emotional performance as she gradually revealed who she was and spoke of the death of her mother. All of these performers really made the best of the material, they managed through their skill and Mr Norton's direction to flesh out the characters.

Bob O'Kelly stage managed the show with some skill and although the transitions were somewhat laboured and clunky, I'm sure they improved during the run. Andrew Reddy oversaw the costuming and assembled some nice pieces for the show. I liked Rab's kilt and the soldier's uniforms at the beginning looked perfect. The NHS outfits were great as was the cleaners' costumes and the Hibs jerseys and scarves.

I did enjoy what Portlaoise Musical Society tried to do with the material. Their primary research of traveling to Edinburgh to understand Leith and where the show emanated from stood to them as they took many photographs, many of which were projected during the show, and immersed themselves in the culture. However, the story is utterly deferential to the presentation of the songs, which is always a problem with Jukebox Musicals. I wanted to know more about the characters, I wanted to feel empathy with them, but that's not in the book and despite the skill of the creatives and the cast, and the rousing choruses, something was missing for me.

Guts is All Newcastle Glees Musical Society presented the Northern Irish Premiere of this riotous musical based on the infamous sewing machinists strike in the Ford factory in London in the 1968. The musical, spawned from Nigel Cole's 2010 film, was first staged in 2014 in Adelphi Theatre starring Gemma Arterton. It's a super piece, full of rousing choruses and poignant solos with a dramatic book that takes some liberties but is somewhat faithful to the historical events. The story follows factory worker, Rita who becomes a reluctant heroine and labour activist who fights for equal pay for women. This has some negative impacts on her family life as well as on the men who work in the plant. However, her actions and those of her fellow co-workers led to the creation of the Equal Pay Act in 1970.

The Society has been around since 1957, when they launched with 'Trial by Jury'. Since then, they have produced a mixture of classic and contemporary shows to great acclaim. I first saw them perform when I adjudicated their superb 'Curtains' in 2019 and then again in 2020 with their immersive 'Calamity Jane'. Like many other societies, they took a forced break due to Covid-19 but bounced back in 2022 with this London-based musical. They own and operate the Annesley Hall on the seafront in Newcastle and run workshops for kids and teens plus stage the occasional concert series, and this is where I saw 'Made in Dagenham' in November 2022.

The show's director, Laura Kerr, gave us something very special with this production. Unlike many other musicals 'Made in Dagenham' is written like a play. The characters are three dimensional, the plot has many layers and there is a sense of watching history unfold in real time as it's based on real events. I'm sure that Ms Kerr was aware of the very dramatic origins of the story, but she wisely eschewed melodrama, instead working with her cast on naturalism, realism, and character development. This paid dividends as the acting was very natural and the character's objectives were extremely clear, and their onstage relationships were fully realised. Ms Kerr also pushed the comedy and the performer's comic timing was excellent. Choreography by Clare Donnelly was superb, especially the second act opener "This is America". Musical Direction by Mark Tilley was spot-on, and his 'hidden' orchestra were impressive as was the imaginative set. The overall interpretation of the source material was admirable in this production, funny and poignant in equal measure.

The production values were set very high on this show. The production team managed to build a brilliantly representative set reminiscent of a factory, complete with realistic machinery and even a time clock that the workers clocked in and out of. Costumes were excellent as were the 1960s wigs and make-up. Sound and lighting by Geoff Clark were good and suited the show. Annesley Hall does not have a big stage, but the Society managed to fit everything in; from a house to a factory to an office, everything looked like it belonged, all competently marshalled by stage manager Clair Williams. But it was the performances that really shone in this production, and I would argue that they could have staged it on a bus, and it would have been just as good! Playing our protagonist Rita O'Grady, the busy working mother who is thrust into the spotlight to become the voice of disenfranchised women in the workplace, we had Orla Russell who was perfectly cast. Ms Russell handled the pathos very well and her singing on "I'm Sorry, I Love You" with Eddie and "Busy Woman" was lovely. Her husband, Eddie, was played by Allen Gordon who played him with a relaxed confidence. His main song, "The Letter" was a showstopper of emotional intensity and they had a lovely chemistry together, especially when paired with their two onstage children, Graham, nicely played by Caden Curran and Sharon played by a very focused Martha Pryce. In the Ford factory were they both work, Rita's friend group were played by a group of very talented and well directed performers. Mia Pobloth played Sandra, a tall aspiring model. She owned the stage in all her scenes. Her singing was exceptional, displaying a wonderful range and power, particularly on the opening of "This is What We Want". Her acting was also great, inhabiting the role as if born to it. Katy Keaveney played the well- meaning but totally inarticulate Clare. This was a perfect comedy performance. Ms Keaveney was always 'on', when she was onstage, with little gestures and reactions to other characters, she presented a highly nuanced character. Her singing of "Wossname" was brilliant, with a good voice and outstanding comic timing. The wonderful Orla McCrickard played the foul-mouthed Beryl, with just the right amount of funny lewdness. She didn't go over the top into 'Carry On" territory but was quite subtle with the coarseness! Her singing and dancing were first-rate, and finally Cass, the sensible one who wants to be a pilot, was played with consummate ease by Melissa Poland. These four actors (Ms McCrickard, Ms Pobloth, Ms Poland & Ms Keaveney) benefitted from a good well-written script, which gave them room to develop their quirky characters. They all had perfect comic timing and East End accents. They had a great collective dynamic and were the backbone of this production.

The shop steward, Monty, was a marvellous characterisation created by Dean Richman. A wonderful spiv-like invention, with his ever-present cigarette and quickness of gesture and walk, he was perfectly cast. Monty's old friend and fellow activist Connie Riley, who was the Labour Party representative, was delicately played by Fiona Keegan. Ms Keegan nailed Connie's passion for worker's rights and her disillusion that she hadn't done everything she wanted. She had a lovely sub-text with Monty, which she played extremely well and sang beautifully on "Connie's Song" and shone as Rita's mentor as she passed the baton to her due to her declining health. These two characters played their fondness for each other and past romantic liaison with skilful elegance that was a joy to watch. Factory boss, Mr Hopkins was played by Lowry Hodgett with a supercilious old-school-tie charm and his wife, Fiona Keane's Lisa Hopkins, was excellent as the Upper-Class turncoat who sided with the factory workers. Brian McElroy played Mr Tooley, a head honcho from the USA division of the Ford organisation who visits Dagenham in a blaze of pure Americana to sort them out. Mr McElroy encapsulated the ignorant, forceful executive with much pizzaz. His accent and mannerisms were spot-on and, with a knowing contemporary nod to a famous ex-President with difficult financial issues, he revelled in the character's crassness. His singing was also quite good on "This is America", a huge overblown number that was a highlight of the show.

A large ensemble played multiple roles throughout this production. They were energetic, tuneful and one hundred per cent committed. Notable performers playing named characters included: Josh Clarke as Sid, who had good comic timing and was quite forceful with Monty as was Francis McKinney's Bill. Mr McKinney also played and sang as the Cortina Man with just the right amount of cheese! Finbar Finnegan played Stan with a nice presence and Jacob Blue as Barry was notable. Diarmuid Taggart played Mr Buckton with authority, Campbell Evans as Hubble was perfect, and Gordon Donaldson as Macer was spot-on. Bethany McKinney and Louise Warnock who played Emma and Jo were also well-cast.

Politicians of the day were represented in the show, specifically the Prime Minister, Harold Wilson. Here, played by Tim Reynolds, the character is written as something of a caricature and Mr Reynolds embraced this and showed no vestige of the real person, apart from the accent and pipe smoking. He elicited a lot of laughs from the audience and sang with gusto on "Always A Problem". The other politician was Barbara Castle, played here by Emma Nugent. Ms Nugent gave lovely performance and portrayed the politician's dilemma extremely well. Her singing on "In an Ideal World" was excellent and she dominated the scene with the factory workers in her office. This wasn't an impersonation, but more of an interpretation of the character's conflict of being true to her working-class origins yet having to work within the Government to balance the books.

Newcastle Glees Musical Theatre Society represent a benchmark in nonprofessional musical theatre production. They seem to choose work only if they can bring something new to it. In this case they brought a delightful realism to the characters and their situations, which resounded with their audience. This success was due in no small part to the vision and hard work of their director, Laura Kerr, who should be proud of her cast and creatives for giving us an exceptional production.

Yippy-Kay-A Rogers and Hammerstein's 'Oklahoma!' is set in near Kansas in 1909. A dust bowl state newly forged by settlers with the occasional farm and not much else. It's a horse opera, a romantic comedy where Native Americans have been killed off and so don't appear and everyone is bored to death with their lives, looking forward to their next drunken dance so they can hook up with someone, anyone. There's a jealous rivalry between the settled farmers and the cowhands they employ; the farmers envying the cowhand's freedom and the cowhands envying the farmer's wealth. It's an interesting story with plenty for a director to get their teeth into - jealousy, mental illness, misogyny, and murder.

I've seen many versions of this show down through the years and most of them have been identical to each other; the same dances, same musical arrangements, same direction, with very few exploring the actual drama unfolding between the characters, focusing instead on the well- known music, and burying or ignoring the tragedy within the story. So, it was with anticipation that I attended a performance of The Cecilian Musical Society's production at The Lime Tree Theatre in Limerick in November 2022.

Directed by Des Henn with musical direction by Michael Young and choreography by Barbara Meany, this was a very clean-looking production where everyone looked immaculate and there was not a speck of dust or dirt on Wayne Handy's pristine set to mar the presentation.

On the surface, very little happens in 'Oklahoma!', but that's okay because there is an underlying sexual tension among the characters, that nourishes the story. The director's role here, I would argue, is to focus on building this tension among them, until it explodes towards the end of Act II with the murder of Jud Fry, which should have a huge effect on everyone. Sadly, we didn't get this in Cecilian's production. Scenes that should have leapt off the stage in nail biting suspense were played too lightly, which was a missed opportunity to inject that much needed tension. That said, we did get a glimpse of anticipation, thanks to Jud, during the highly dodgy auction scene, which was nicely paced, but it wasn't sustained and evaporated quickly. We didn't feel any empathy for any of the characters, apart from Ali Hakim, whose dilemmas were effectively played by Jason Ronan and Ado Annie, brilliantly played by Ailish O'Donovan. Their relationship was the most adult and there was a real sexual tension between them.

However, production values were high on this show, with fabulous lighting by Michael O'Brien and Star System's superb sound. The simple representative set worked, and the costumes and make-up were of the era, and it was all competently stage managed by Ray Burke. So, it looked good (apart from being too clean) and sounded great. The performers were individually splendid, but they didn't gel as a collective. It seemed that each scene was directed in isolation without any reference to other scenes or a super objective. So, when they were assembled, they didn't quite dovetail together into a whole. At times it went into concert mode when the ensemble stood facing out like a choir, which affected the pace and the continuity of the story and the character relationships.

Musical director, Michael Young's work with the large ensemble, was great. The harmonies on "Kansas City" and "Oklahoma" were excellent. The band were lavish, the violin was especially expertly played and beautiful, and the horns and winds were at times gentle and at others aggressive and bold. Dance throughout this production was exquisitely performed and developed the story thanks to Barbara Meany's lovely choreography. It was quite intricate and delicate at times and it's a credit to her that the performers executed it all with such skill. Of course, the big dance number is the "Dream Ballet", which foreshadowed the events to come, and I'm happy to say that this was the highlight of the show for me. It was just mesmerising to watch; I didn't want it to end. And it was here, during this dark dream fantasy, that the characters started to live for me; they had objectives, passion, and connection.

The performers were, as I mentioned, uniformly quite adept. Barry Danaher's Curly had a great presence on stage, he towered above others as he strode around like a lovesick puppy. His Curly was curious as he came across as quite dim and one dimensional most of the time, yet when he was with Jud trying to cajole him into committing suicide, he showed a cunning maliciousness, but sadly this more interesting side of the character wasn't carried through into other scenes. His singing was excellent, he had a wonderfully expressive voice on the opening song "Oh What a Beautiful Morning" and on his duet with Laurey on "People Will Say We're in Love". Hilary Phayer's Laurey had a good dynamic with Aunt Eller and their scenes were good. Her scenes with Curly were a bit cloying but her scenes with Jud were quite dramatic. Ms Phayer's singing was excellent on "People Will Say We're in Love" with Curly and with the ensemble on "Many a New Day".

Probably one of the more interesting characters in the musical theatre canon is Jud Fry, the ranch hand on Laurey's farm who lusts after her. He is unique and should be played as an outsider which Aidan O'Connell did quite well. His physicality, hunched over as if he had the weight of his crimes on his shoulders, was marvellous as was his voice, a gruff curt growl. He sang "Lonely Room" with a fantastic, repressed anger, full of longing and fretfulness and we saw through this scene that he was suffering. Laurey lived on the farm with her Aunt Eller played by Gráinne Hartnett. Her portrayal made her quite soft and maternal but with a will of iron. Her affectionate and tender relationship with Laurey convinced and her faux flirting with Curly was charming. She sang well with the others and her control of both the dance and the auction was terrific, showing her character's high status.

The secondary romantic storyline concerned the love triangle of Will Parker, Ado Annie, and Ali Hakim. Adam Stapleton gave us a young, fresh-faced Will. His sojourn in the big city did little to mature him and his Will Parker was quite funny in his ineptitude. His quest to hook back up with Ado Annie, was effectively journeyed and he had a good chemistry with her, although he was a child compared to her. His singing was good on "Kansas City", and he bounced well off Ali. Ailish O'Donovan played Ado Annie, the girl who can't say no, dangling Will and Ali, she was caught between two lovers. Ms O'Donovan's Annie was full of energy and lit up the stage each time she entered. Her singing on "I Cain't Say No" was full of expression and fun and she had a great dynamic with Ali, played by Jason Ronan. Mr Ronan's accent as Ali Hakim was faultless. He didn't go over the top into caricature, which often happens with this role, but played him as a real character. His comic timing was a highlight of the show, and the audience loved him. His relationship with Annie was very funny yet quite mature and his singing on the slightly misogynistic "It's a Scandal! It's An Outrage" with the ensemble was full of indignation and incredulity. Ultimately, Annie chose Will over Ali as dictated by her father as Will paid him off. The father, Andrew, was played by Brian Henry. His scenes with Ali were very funny and believable. Although he is a hideous character, demanding money from Will or anyone, for his daughter's hand in marriage, Mr Henry played him as more of a buffoon, which worked in the context of this production.

The other named characters in the show were all quite well cast and helped create the world of the musical: Jane Henry's Gertie nailed that awful laugh; Martin Pierce's Marshall Cord Elam played the character's frustration with the townsfolks disregard for justice and the rule of law very well; Brian Quinlivan's Ike was solid as the rancher and Amanda Leddin's Vivian had a good stage presence as Laurey's friend who told the girl's fortunes. Brian Curtin's Slim and Caoimhe Síochrú's Ellen were also notable.

I enjoyed Michael Young and Barbara Meany's work immensely and some of the performers were excellent, especially Ms O'Donovan, Mr Ronan, and Mr O'Connell. But this production didn't hang together for me, the sum of the parts didn't add up to a cohesive production.

in Claregalway produced 'The Addams Family' at the town Hall Theatre in Galway in November of this year. Hot on the heels of their award-winning 'Little Shop of Horrors' last year, director Alan Greaney reunited with musical director Shane Farrell and choreographer Jay Molyneux to put their own spin on the popular musical.

'The Addams Family' is a black comedy musical, quite well written with some witty one-liners and some excellent songs. The whole premise is of course ludicrous and sort of goes against what made the Addams Family so popular for Charles Addams when he wrote about them as he celebrated their weirdness. But, hey it's a musical so we leave our intellectual reservations at the door on the way in. The show opened with Thing (the hand) in a box on stage and a man in a dress suit telling us where the fire exits were located and urging us to buy raffle tickets. The man exited the stage, and the overture began, conducted by Thing with a baton, from his box.

The overture sounded great though, as Musical Director Shane Farrell took his band through some of the tunes foreshadowing the songs to come. Musically, this show is quite good with lots of songs with great hooks so that even if you didn't know them before you came, your guaranteed to be humming them as you leave the theatre. Mr Farrell clearly worked his magic on this show, and it paid off as his chorus were marvellous, particularly on "When You're an Addams", and "Move Towards the Darkness" and the harmonies on "Full Disclosure" were riotously good.

So, a quick synopsis of the plot: The Addams family, led by the elegantly black-clad Morticia with the never- ending cleavage and her ever-devoted Latino husband Gomez is troubled. Their daughter Wednesday, now eighteen, has fallen in love and is engaged, which she is keeping from her mother but confesses to Gomez. When she invites her fiancé, Lucas Beineke and his family over for dinner, it turns out that the 'normal' family are even more disturbed than the Addams. As Gomez, Jay Hall played him rather low- key, playing the pathos sweetly which, I couldn't help feeling, masked an innate sadness in the character. His singing was heartfelt on "Happy / Sad" and strong on "Not Today". Mr Hall was a wonderful foil for Suzanne Garvey's vampiric Morticia. Ms Garvey's singing was excellent, especially on "Just Around the Corner" and "Secrets" with Alice and she had a sparky chemistry with Gomez. They both convinced as their characters, embracing the dark side yet showing their love for their kids as any parent would do. This relationship was the fulcrum of the show, and they played it with adroitness.

Playing their troubled daughter, Wednesday, was Síofra Ni Chonluain, whose make-up was so strongly applied that she looked a lot older than Morticia! This aside, Ms Ni Chonluain played the moody teenager with foot stomping petulance. She sang fabulously with Pugsley on "Pulled" and with Lucas on "Crazier than You" and generally embodied the rebellious teen with confidence. Wednesday's brother Pugsley was played by Sarah Brennan in a stand- out performance for one so young. Her singing was excellent, and she totally nailed the irascible Pugsley and was fully immersed in the role. Displaying nice emotion on "What if", she had a great chemistry with Grandma and Morticia and an infectious inner energy, which permeated all her scenes.

Another member of the Addams clan was Uncle Fester, brother of Gomez. Played by Richard Brown in a quietly confident performance, Mr Brown accentuated Fester's gentler nature rather than the zombie wrangling wisecracking narrator we often see. It worked to a point, especially on "The Moon and Me", where he declares his love for Luna, but I think we missed the madcap elements that make Fester so appealing. His relationship with Grandma, played by Ailbhe Slevin, is clearly a match made in hell and we didn't really see this played out. That said Ms Slevin also gave us a gentler Grandma, accentuating the maternal with Pugsley which worked. And then there was Lurch. Mervyn Fahy played him on stilts, so that he looked about 10ft tall, which necessitated slow walking - ideal for the character.

Into this zany, chaotic family came the Beineke's: Lucas and his mother Alice, a frustrated housewife and his father Mal, a stuffy accountant. Keith Hanley's Lucas, an all-American guy, was probably the most 'normal' character on stage. His singing with Wednesday on "Crazier than You" was great and kind of explained why he was so into her. Mal was played with a dour manner initially by David Alexander and his transformation to ageing hippy really worked. He had a great chemistry with Alice, who was played with serious skill by Roisín Lawless. Ms Lawless sang "Waiting", the song of the night for me, with wonderful theatricality, displaying a superb range of movement and vocal dexterity.

All the front line were supported by the Ancestors, who were called from the grave by Fester at the top of the show to celebrate being an Addams. These characters are historical versions of the Addams Family going right back to Europe, and were costumed, by the fabulously talented Andrew Reddy, accordingly. They lounged around the stage, moved stuff and were the dancers and chorus during the show. I think they may have needed a little more direction really as they came across as quite contemporary and not at all spectral or, you know, the risen dead. But they sang and danced well and added a griminess to the proceedings.

Jay Molyneux managed to create some interesting choreography with these performers in the space. I liked the intricate hand gestures during "When You're an Addams", the couples joining Morticia and Gomez on the "Tango de Amor" and the use of scarves on "Secrets". "Just Around the Corner" was a showstopper for Morticia and the Ancestors, like an old MGM musical with the hats and the canes. Lovely work from Mr Molyneux. The show was joint stage managed by Chontelle Kenny and Jacqlyn Cronin and together they did a fine job and Fintan Higgins looked after the sound. I thought the overall sound could have been bigger and louder - it's huge show demanding a big sound which we didn't really get. Lighting by Paul Kelly showcased some nice states, and his cuing was perfect. Marsha Fleming and Alan Greaney designed the set, which was a gothic house with a balcony and a chaise lounge which got so much stage time it should have an Equity Card as it was on and off so much.

Director Alan Greaney seemed to concentrate on the more salacious and base elements of the show, the ribald jokes were front and centre like a 1970s Carry On film. It is of course a comedy and a dark one at that. But black comedy is best played subtly and not forced, if its well-written (and this is) it sells itself. The pace of the show was good and the transitions quite smooth, but there was a distinct lack of energy from the performers on stage at the show I saw. They didn't bring that vitality and liveliness that makes a show bounce off the stage.

Of course, it could have been an off-night, I saw the final performance so perhaps exhaustion had set in…

If you grew up, as I did, listening to the music of Madness, you can't help but love Our House, the musical, featuring all the best of their hits, but it's much more than the music that makes the show appealing. Those songs have been cleverly woven together in a very real dramatic piece that tells of teen angst, broken homes, and trying to survive in a world where nothing comes easy. The play is strong, with well created characters and contains a nice balance of fortune and misfortune, peppered with plenty of humour and a core story of romance. It uses a kind of 'Sliding Doors' device to show the two possible outcomes of Joe Casey's actions, which can be challenging for the audience, but when handled with an appreciation of the direction that the show takes, as this production was, it really is an excellent piece of theatre.

Director, Sean O'Neill showed a good understanding of the subject matter of this show, putting strong emphasis on the dramatic storyline, and keeping the comedy at a level that didn't take away from the more serious aspects of the drama. It was well-pitched and very balanced. He did possibly need to rein- in one or two of the supporting cast who had a slight tendency to break the fourth wall and play specifically to the audience rather than to each other. In such a dramatic piece, the only one who should play out front is Dad, who is basically a narrator, unseen by the other players. As choreographer, Sean captured the era and the moves associated with the string of great Madness hit songs and his cast delivered the goods with energetic effect. I wasn't quite sure of the relevance of the roller-coaster video behind Driving in My Car, but aside from that, all the musical numbers were creative and interesting to view.

The set for the show was simple but effective and was painted in a nice, surreal manner, which suited the tone of the drama. There was also a very effective screen centre stage that the director used most efficiently to provide location titles and also some lovely effects, particularly the fire at the start of the finale. In keeping with the black/white theme within the script, props consisted mostly of black and white boxes that became, tables, chairs, car seats, et al. They were very efficiently moved about the stage by the busy chorus or costumed backstage crew. Lighting was effective throughout, highlighting the main acting areas and adding atmosphere to the scenes through good use of colours. The switch from Joe's Black life to his White life was effectively accompanied by a flash of lightning in the early stages, and it might have been a good idea to continue that trend throughout the show, as it did, initially, make the story easier to follow. From her vantage point centre-stage behind the set and below the screen, Musical Director, Roisin Corr, kept a tight rein on a disciplined orchestra and maintained contact with her on-stage performers, keeping entrances and exits from the musical numbers clean and crisp. The band created a pretty authentic 'Madness' feel to the music, and their tempi were just about perfect throughout. When everyone could be heard, the quality of singing from those on-stage was very good and Roisin gave consistently good leadership, and seemed to really enjoy her music, even donning a Fez for the opening of act two. A nice touch.

The sound system caused some serious problems. There were some cameo roles who didn't appear to be mic'ed at all, hence several lines were lost, and while the central principals were always clear and articulate, spoken and sung lines from some of the supporting cast were not clearly amplified, sometimes even to the point of being lost. I'm inclined to think this was a sound system fault, as the orchestra didn't appear to be over- amplified. Sound issues aside, the rest of the technical aspects of the show were all good. The costuming of the show was good in so far as they related to the individuals wearing them, like Sarah always being tidier than Joe, the Dad and Reecey looking somewhat thuggish. Pressman could perhaps have looked a tad sharper and more pretentious to set him above the common throng. Joe's quick changes were well handled. The cameo roles were all suitably attired to give a clear indication of their varied roles. Make-up looked natural throughout and the girl's hair seemed entirely appropriate. Taking the leading role of Joe Casey, Liam McIlvenna captured the innocence and confusion of youth, and there was a sincere passion in his struggle to come to terms with the loss of his father. Equally convincing was his love both for Sarah and for his mother. With a very capable singing voice and a very competent handling of his comedic moments, this was a delightfully rounded and accomplished performance. Holly McCann started inconspicuously in the role of Sarah but as the night progressed, so did her presence, her emotions and her strong acting ability. She was particularly strong in registering her unfailing love for Joe, through good times or bad. This was also a well-sung role.

Tony Girvan gave a strong and assured performance as Joe's ghostly Dad, and while he did not possess the most musical voice, the emotion of his musical contributions was quite superbly achieved through quality acting and delivery. Physically he was perfect for the role. When it comes to being a vile and loathsome reprobate, Conor Begley hit the nail on the head with an outstanding performance as bad guy, Reecey, as strong vocally as he was as an actor, and still managing to wring some comedy out of his performance. Excellent work.

Cathair Brady and Canice McIlvenna provided strong character comedy in the roles of Emmo and Lewis, capturing the essence of harmless, miscreant, adolescents with well-judged naivety and charm. And their female counterparts, Lisa O'Neill as Angie and Maire Coyle as Billie, were delightfully comical and bitchy as Sarah's best friends. These four also had good competent vocal quality.

Rosaleen Rea Wardell played the mother, Kath Casey, with a fine sense of motherly love for her boy and a stoic stubbornness regarding the possible loss of her home. She sang well and made a worthy contribution to the success of the show. Mr Pressman came across as a nouveau- riche, sleaze-bag, with very few redeeming qualities, which was the result of a good interpretation by actor, Malachy Quinn. Among the supporting roles, a most worthy performance came from Aoife Corr, as an aggressive bartender, and as a sometimes-man-eating secretary. Each cameo that she created had strong comedy (if occasionally pantomimic,) and very good individuality. Similarly, Decky Kelly played Mr Jesmond and various other cameos with assurance and good solid acting ability, and Rebecca Hanna gave a competent performance as Heather.

The chorus functioned as supporting actors too, taking on a plethora of one or two liner roles, as well as functioning together as a cohesive unit. They were good in their vocals and very good in their dance and movement. They were always very much a part of the action and performed with energy and confidence. I had to admire their industry in moving and rearranging the props as part of the action.

Thank you to director, Sean O'Neill and the staff of the theatre for the hospitality and for much information about the theatre and the company. Thank you so much for making the trek from Galway to Coalisland so worthwhile, and congratulations on a truly entertaining production. Everyone on the stage did themselves proud, and I sincerely wish you continued success as a company.

produced a wonderfully emotional Michael Collins last year, has been around since 1981 and in that time has staged many shows from G&S to Lloyd Webber and Sondheim alongside many contemporary works and Christmas offerings. Made in Dagenham was succinctly directed by Sharon McNamara with the talented Dave McGauran as musical director, chorus master and conductor and Nicole McDonald looking after the extensive choreography.

Based on the 2010 film directed by Nigel Cole, Made in Dagenham the musical, was premiered in 2014 to good reviews but failed to set the box office alight and closed after six months. Set in 1968, the plot revolved around the striking sewing machinists at the Ford motor factory in Dagenham in the U.K. and how their demand for equal pay with the male workers was instrumental in ushering in the Equal Pay Act of 1970. Produced by Coolmine Musical Society on the wonderful Draíocht stage during November, this show had the audience firmly on the side of the proletariat - represented by the factory workers, in their fight against the bourgeoisie - here represented by the owners of the Ford Motor Company and the Government of the day, which was, curiously, Labour. Marxist doctrine would not normally be top of the list of issues when considering creating a musical I suspect. However, as a subject the real-life history of the Ford strikers contained some great elements for dramatic exposition: the emancipation and empowerment of women; the rise of the oppressed against their well-heeled oppressors and the toll the struggle took on the protagonists and their families. All of this and more made up the plot of Made in Dagenham, with a rousing score and fabulous dance numbers and a bit of pathos thrown in, Coolmine gave us a wonderful night's entertainment.

The central character of the drama was Rita, Bronwyn Andrews, who was persuaded to be the mouthpiece of the disgruntled workers and take on the Unions, the Ford Corporation and the Government in a quest for equal pay. Ms Andrews' charting of Rita's journey from working housewife to revolutionary didn't really convince as she appeared no different at the end as she was at the beginning. Her singing was superb however, leading the big numbers "Everybody Out" and "Stand Up" with confidence and her duet with husband Eddie, "We Nearly Had It All" was beautifully sung. Ian Rountree played Eddie as a stereotypical working class man who was distressed that his wife would dare have an opinion. Mr Rountree's everyman portrayal was good, his singing less so as he struggled with some of the songs. Rita's mentor in all things Trade Union was Connie, delicately played by Niamh Carroll. Ms Carroll's characterisation of the older experienced shop steward was super, she gave her a gravitas and matronly warmth and sang powerfully on "Connie's Song" about equality and smashing the glass ceiling. Connie's story also included a one-night- stand with Monty, another shop steward played by Robbie Kennedy. Mr Kennedy had a good stage presence and performed the go-between very well.

Rita had a great dynamic with her colleagues in the factory. Each one was very distinctive and we got to know them quite quickly, due in no small part to the director's excellent character work. The stand-out character was Beryl, a foul- mouthed firebrand played by Michelle Harris with impeccable timing; Claire, the ditzy one, was hilariously played by Niamh Kiernan who gave a fabulous rendition of her solo song, "Wossname"; Kathryn Gibbons' Cass was deliciously sarcastic and had a good presence and Karen McCourt's Sandra, who defects to work in Marketing i.e.dancing at the launch of the new Cortina, was impressive in showing the financial hardship caused by the strike. Eddie's fellow workmates were less well-written but convinced as stereotypical 'Essex Boys'.

The manager of the factory, Mr Hopkins, was played by Ciaran Lenehan. He didn't quite portray the high status one would imagine he should have but was convincing all the same. Amie Preston played his wife, Lisa, with a haughty superiority that softened when she joined Rita and the gang in their fight for equality. Hopkins' lapdog, Gregory Hubble, was simperingly played by Nathan Everett Patterson in a superbly timed performance. The Ford Executive from Texas who visits to quell the strike and restore order, Mr Tooley, was played with a Trump-like glee by Eddie Brady. His song "This is America" was brilliantly staged, choreographed and sung. Mr Brady's characterisation of the risible Texan was first-class. The UK Government was represented by Harold Wilson and Barbara Castle, here played by Justin Parkes and Delores Hughes. Mr Parkes was the spitting image of the Prime Minister and his song, "Always a Problem" was very funny. Ms Hughes captured the socialist minister perfectly, with just the right amount of ministerial swagger yet with a Marxist heart. Her song "Ideal World" brought the house down, she performed it so well. A lovely engaging performance.

The entire ensemble on this show were spot on, they had a great cohesion and unity. Special mention must, however go to Stuart Pollock who played numerous characters throughout from an Aide to the PM, to a Union Rep, a reporter and most amusingly Buddy Cortina. Mr Pollock's swing roles were a joy to watch for his commitment to character, versatility and his Lee Evans like energy!

The tunes in the show were not really that memorable, but musical director Dave McGauran managed to make each one hop of the stage. His arrangements with three keyboards, two guitars, bass, drums and three horns was full and more than the sum of its parts. The lead guitar player was excellent, relishing in his frequent solos. Mr McGauran's work with the chorus, both offstage and on, was super - eliciting some lovely harmonies and power from his ensemble. Nicole McDonald's choreography was rooted in late sixties dance moves and her dancers were well- drilled. Set design by Aidan Mannion consisted of a high platform upstage, accessed by a mobile metal staircase, with sliding doors revealing Rita's kitchen and bedroom. Factory style windows above the platform doubled as projection screens and trucks and flats were trucked on to represent other locations. A large Ford logo was flown in and out when in the factory and sewing machines on tables rolled on and off. The set was very well constructed and designed as were the props, which really set the 1960's vibe. Lighting by Denis Twomey was unfussy and nicely blended, lighting the actors throughout and sculpting the set. Sound by Jody Trehy was perfect, some small well-cued sound effects and a good balance between singers and band. Ali Murphy's make-up and hair styles were consistent with the era as were the costumes co-ordinated by Gráinne Ui Chaomhánaigh. Gerry McCann expertly stage managed the entire operation with swiftness and accuracy.

Director Sharon McNamara wisely set a fairly fast pace with this show, it's quite long!, and marshalled her cast and creatives well. Her interpretation of the material was quite faithful and very similar to the original. The bigger crowd pleasing numbers were well received by the audience but the pathos was less well realised I felt. Whilst we connected with some characters, Connie in particular, the main domestic story didn't really land. This may be the fault of the writing, or that Rita and Eddie were just not played big enough for this production.

Murder in the Theatre!

There is a rather sad history to this show. Three years in development by the original writer, Peter Stone, who died before completing the book, it opened in Los Angeles in 2006 not long after Fred Ebb's death. It was not an instant success and received mixed critical reviews, partially due to the comparisons drawn to Kander & Ebbs earlier works; Cabaret, Chicago etc. However, it did go on to garner eight Tony nominations with one win and two Drama Desk awards and audiences loved it.

It's basically a musical murder mystery whodunit, a cross between Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None and Cluedo, with more than a passing nod to Stoppard's The Real Inspector Hound and set in a Boston Theatre in 1959. During a performance of the less than inspiring new musical comedy Robin Hood, the supremely untalented leading lady, Jessica Cranshaw, is murdered. The entire production team are suspects and a plain-clothes detective, Lt. Cioffi, locks down the theatre keeping everyone inside whilst he attempts to solve the case.

Produced by Harolds Cross/ Tallaght Musical Society at the Civic Theatre, with direction by Ciaran Mooney, choreography by Lea Carroll and musical direction by Dermot O'Callaghan it was a clever pastiche of a pastiche featuring some great dance numbers and lots of overacting.

As Lt Cioffi, Damien Hurley gave a nice understated performance. His deadpan delivery, fast and earnest throughout, of the very witty script full of murder mystery tropes was faultless. Personifying the plodding meticulous detective à la Columbo, complete with trench coat, only becoming energised when talking about the show as he was a star-struck amateur actor. He also had a good singing voice on "Coffee Shop Nights" where he sang of his loneliness and the fantasy duet with Niki (an actor he was falling for) "A Tough Act to Follow".  Niki, his new found love interest, was played by Serena Salmon with a wide-eyed innocence which masked a cunning deviousness. Cleverly playing the sub-text as dramatic irony, Ms Salmon had good comic timing and a fabulous voice, wonderfully showcased on her duet with Cioffi. Their Fred and Ginger slapstick routine to this song was very well choreographed by Lea Carroll and quite funny.

Ms Carroll's choreography was very accomplished throughout the show and spanned a few styles. Going from the C&W, line dancing and hilariously awful "In The Same Boat - Completed" of the Robin Hood show within the show to the old MGM Musical stylings of "A Tough Act To Follow", to the funny slo-mo syncopated movement on "The Woman's Dead", her ensemble were well-drilled and quite acrobatic at times, but always with tongue firmly in cheek, especially Bambi's cartwheeling around the male ensemble, one of whom almost dropped her!

Bambi, or Elaine the show's producer's daughter, was played by Laura Kelly, complete with petulant child-like voice and manic effervescence. Ms Kelly played the love-hate relationship with her onstage mother, Carmen, quite well. Julie Donnelly gave a compelling portrayal of Carmen, the show's producer. Showcasing a wonderfully strong voice, she also had great comic timing. Carmen's husband and co-producer, Sidney, was played with a fierceness by gravel-voiced Matthew Carpenter. Coming across like a Mafia extra from Goodfellas, Mr Carpenter was riveting to watch, exuding danger and salaciousness towards his step-daughter Bambi, his performance was super.

The director of the show within the show, Christopher Belling, was played by Gearóid McGauran. Mr McGauran played him as a stereotypical British Theatre director, all camp swishing and biting acerbic comments. His timing was very good as was his perfect diction and physicality. Robin Hood's financial backer, Oscar Shapiro, was brilliantly played by Gary Finegan. His stage presence was excellent as was his singing. Local newspaper theatre critic Daryl Grady was played by Robbie Keogh. His portrayal was great as a jaded newspaper hack, he played his intention and subtext particularly well.

Robin Hood's choreographer and leading man, Bobby, was played by James Place. His was a rather quiet Bobby, engaging but not overbearing. Jessica Cranshaw, who comes to a sticky end quite early on, was portrayed by Kelly-Marie Davy. A difficult role as the actor has to sing and dance dreadfully, but Ms Davy managed with good timing and awful dancing! The show's stage manager, Johnny, was nicely played by Eamonn Murphy and the character of Randy, one of the Robin Hood ensemble, was played by Adam McGealy, who had a marvellous stage presence, leading man demeanour and great stagecraft.

The Robin Hood writers, Aaron Fox and his ex-wife Georgia Hendricks were played by Eoin Salley and Aoife Small. These two actors stole the show with their wonderful performances. Mr Salley sang beautifully and with passion on "I Miss the Music", Ms Small gave a complete performance with her acting, singing and terrific dancing. They had a great chemistry together and were the most believable characters on stage.

Musical direction was by Dermot O'Callaghan, who did a good job on the jazzy arrangements of the score, even taking centre stage and singing "The Man is Dead" just after the Entr'acte. The set design by Ciaran Mooney and Wayne Handy was very simple as the show is set in a theatre; a raised platform upstage for the band, mobile staircases and a series of 'school play' style flats for the show within the show, and worked a treat. Lighting by Derek O'Neill was naturalistic and suitable and sound by Vinny Osborne was punchy and full. Andrew Reddy's costumes were great for Robin Hood and suitable for the main show. Wigs by Ali Murphy were ok, but Bambi's wig was too stiff and we could see beneath it. Stage Manager Marie Cusack controlled the show well, transitions were done by assistant stage managers in costume and were quite swift.

This was a very funny, fast and madcap show with some lovely clever staging. The scene at night, "He Did It", where the cast have to sleep in the theatre was inspired as they used torches to light the scene. The Robin Hood sequences were funny as the style of acting became more 'amateur' and hammy. Director Ciaran Mooney had a very deft touch with this show, he managed to get the pathos of Aaron and Georgia's relationship across whilst also lampooning the relationship. Curtains was like a love letter to regional theatre and murder mystery aficionados and although musically it is not exactly Kander & Ebb's best work, the tunes are quite forgettable, it did have a charm all of its own. It is an actor's show, like The Producers and Urinetown, where the performers are encouraged to indulge themselves as their characters are so clichéd, and overact. Wallowing in the melodrama of it all. Mr Mooney successfully directed a great evening of theatrical excess and we, the audience, enjoyed it immensely.

I first discovered this show many years ago when I was lucky enough and fit enough to play the dentist. It seemed to have dipped in popularity for a while but I am delighted that it has become popular with companies all over Ireland more recently. It is a charming, witty and endearing show which appeals to all ages on many different levels. The original early 1960's setting is now often changed to a more modern setting. This indeed was the case with this production which was neatly directed by Donna Ruane, indeed as she explained to me after the show, it was set in an abstract time, rather than follow slavishly the styles of one particular era. This actually worked well and the focus became very much on the story telling, though I did miss the sixties setting at times, especially as a backdrop for some of the musical numbers.

Donna had chosen her cast well and had made the decision to have the Mushnik character played by a female. The final Audrey ll was brought to life by a wonderfully created and operated plant but also by the personification of the plant by an actor. The story was well told and apart from a few wee issues of masking, the action on stage was nicely moved. The characters were well drawn, though a couple of times they could have gone a bit further with the humour. The pace was generally sound and the staging helped to keep the show rattling along. Donna looked for every opportunity to involve as many of the chorus as possible in the show in quite inventive ways. The 'Ronnettes' were used as observers and were nicely placed in poses around the stage during the action, always adding to the moment and never detracting from it. This was beautifully balanced musical direction from Deirdre Lee. There were those belting rock moments such as the rousing 'Finale' but there was such tenderness of accompaniment with the moving 'Somewhere That's Green'. The seven-piece orchestra worked wonderfully together, great tempi throughout, subtlety of balance between the stage and the pit and well cued. The cast had been obviously put through their paces as everyone on stage was more than comfortable with their singing roles. There were good harmonies from the chorus and the three 'Ronnettes'.

Jay Molyneux's choreography was inventive, at times creating great moments of drama such as the entrance of the chorus with their zombie movements. The three 'Ronnettes' worked together so well as a synchronised team with slick steps and arm movements. The final number in which the cast were adorned with sparkly tinsel tendrils was good with cast staggered in their positioning on stage so everyone could be so well seen and have their own moment of glory.

Stuart Barrows gave a very sincere and believable performance as Seymour. He captured that youthful awkwardness in his movements and delivery of lines. He sang the role very much in character too. He gave us some well-judged moments of both comedy and pathos. Stephanie Cassol was well cast as the hard done by and ever hopeful Audrey. This was a moving and also humorous portrayal of the wacky character. She got many laughs from those lines about handcuffs and 'Doctor' Scrivello. A simple staging for the 'Somewhere That's Green' number gave us a memorable moment of tragedy. Kevin Murphy not only provided the rocky voice of Audrey ll but also appeared as the plant in human form. This personification of the plant worked particularly well when he was actually in the plant's 'mouth', which was quite a magical moment on stage. Well sung and acted Kevin.

In a break with tradition Mushnik was Mrs Mushnik in this show. It is not such an unusual concept now and many local companies cast in a gender neutral way, indeed the recent West End production of Stephen Sondheim's 'Company' changed the gender of several of the roles. Vivienne Lee gave us a strong, almost 'Judge Judy' sounding character as Mushnik. She built up good relationships with Seymour and Audrey. She moved purposefully around the stage always grabbing our attention. The man we love to hate, Orin The Dentist was courtesy of David Alexander who has just joined the society. He gave a controlled and strong portrayal of the masochistic baddy. The relationship with Audrey was nicely played and his aggression towards her gave us goose bumps at times.

The three Ronnettes are the Greek chorus of the piece. They observe, focus our attention on the story being told and their comments get us to think more deeply about the plot and characters. This certainly was the case with this very talented trio. Firstly, they could all sing, both strong in their individual lines and together gave us great harmonies, they could act and react to what was going on around them and they moved so well too. What also was impressive was that each one had a very individual on-stage personality but also blended to work as one unit when required. Mary Dempsey was the street cred Chiffon, Sonja Stevens the feisty Crystal and Karen Ronane the strong Ronnette. Great use of eye contact with the audience with wonderful use of the lights to make the eyes sparkle.

Another trio which worked well individually and together were Gearóid Herraghty as Bernstein, Ciaran Kiely as Mrs Luce and Brian Fogarty as Skip Snip. Each one had very much their own look and personality. Gearóid dominated the stage with his presence and impressed with a good vocal tone as the smartly suited Bernstein. (Nice touch to give him a set of secretaries to complete the scene). Then Ciaran dressed in sombre black with a wonderful wide brimmed hat and black parasol as Mrs Luce. The black beard really added an 'another world' look to the character. Finally, Brian Fogarty sounded impressive with a chocolatey rich tone to his singing and speaking voice as Snip. The chorus really added to the scene both visually and vocally. They were kept involved through the show, appearing in the renovation scene, 'Skid Row' etc. They all showed good commitment to their role in the production.

The setting of the show was smart and added much to the whole feel of the piece. A raised area Upstage Left added depth to the stage, the textured bricks giving a great effect when lit. The doorway and steps were free standing Downstage Left and upstage right was the shop which revolved so we could see the interior and then exterior. Also, a wall which represented the Dentist Surgery appeared. This is a particularly awkward stage to work on with really no backstage space so this set worked really well for the company. The stage team ensured that the changes were relatively prompt. Good attention to detail was shown with the properties used in the show such as great flower arrangements, dentist chair, shop bags, telephones etc. All in great condition and helping to create the look of Skid Row. The plants were very real looking and I must congratulate the operators for the co-ordination with the voice of Audrey ll.

The lighting really added atmosphere to moments giving an eerie feel with strong reds and greens when required. The faces were all clear throughout and I was impressed by how the lighting adapted to the movements of the cast on stage, meaning that we never missed a facial expression. The sound was beautifully balanced with the microphones working so well with the accompaniment so we could hear nearly every word.

The costumes were a whole mix with no particular era defined but they all worked together to give an urban look. The Ronnettes appeared first in denim and checked shirts, then in oriental dresses and finally those stunning slightly Grecian long dresses. Audrey was in leopard skin and pink mostly and possibly could have been a little more as Orin would have dressed her. Mushnik had smart frocks which gave a feel of 1960/70s. The other characters were neatly dressed with good attention to detail, the chorus surprised us at the end of the show with red and green tights and glittery steamers tied to their wrists which added much to Jay's clever dance moves.

The wigs such as Audrey's blonde bob were all neatly set and helped to establish the character. The other hairstyles evoked the original setting of the show. Make up was carefully applied and eyes in particular were emphasised with lips colourfully outlined. Kevin's make up was a real triumph with great use of greens and reds for maximum visual effect. From the moment I entered the theatre and was greeted by June beside that super space-age balloon sculpture, until I left, I was made so welcome and as always it was great to chat to the cast after the show. An enjoyable evening with a well-acted, sung and presented show. Thanks to all in the Little Shop Of Horrors in Claremorris.

Heaven Can Wait Following on from last year's excellent Chitty Chitty Bang Bang, Ballywillan Drama Group returned this year with Whistle Down The Wind. The show was written by Andrew Lloyd Webber and Jim Steinman with additional book by Patricia Knop and Gale Edwards in 1996 and is based on the 1961 film starring Hayley Mills which in turn, was based on the novel of the same title written in 1959 by Mills' mother Mary Hayley Bell and set in rural Lancashire. The musical setting has been moved from England to rural Louisiana in 1959. Three siblings; Swallow, Brat and Poor Baby who have just lost their mother, discover a man in their barn. He is injured and before he passes out, they ask his name: "Jesus Christ" he says, and they believe him and so decide to hide him. In fact, he is an escaped prisoner, convicted of killing his wife. Swallow wants him to be Jesus in the hope he can bring her dead mother back to life and together with many of the local children, secretly feed and care for him. But a secret shared is a secret revealed, especially in small towns and a mob gathers to capture the man. Directed by Brian Logan with musical direction by Eric Boyd and choreography by Sharon Logan, this colourful production was unfortunately slightly marred by low energy, weak vocals and nervous acting from the adult cast however the children were superb.

I attended the fourth performance of the sixteen show run at the wonderful Riverside Theatre in Coleraine. Director, Brian Logan, clearly did very good work with the children's chorus and ensemble and they shone out with well- scrubbed innocence and spirit. Mia McConaghie as Brat, the middle sibling, was particularly good both vocally and in her naturalistic performance and John Mullan's Poor Baby, or Robin as he was christened, presented an inquisitive intelligent character. Both actors had a lovely youthful energy in their roles and sang splendidly. Older sibling, Swallow is supposedly aged about sixteen but with the innocence of a much younger girl. In this production I felt the actor playing Swallow, Claire Campbell, came across as far too mature for the role. Ms Campbell did work well with Alan McClarty's character of The Man and her singing was pleasant but she did have breathing issues on some of her songs.  However, Ms Campbell didn't really convince as she didn't demonstrate Swallow's innocence and naïveté to convey and make credible her unshakeable belief that The Man was Jesus. As the children's father, Boone, Richard Mairs gave a solid performance, a little spoiled by vocal issues on the night I attended, but I really liked his emotional intensity in the role as the grieving widower trying to do what he feels is right for his children. There was a lovely profound father/daughter moment between Boone and Swallow as he started to sing "Whistle Down the Wind" and broke down but Swallow joined in showing fortitude and appreciation for all he was doing for them. Mr Mairs had a quiet stillness in the role, which contrasted nicely with the more mercurial characters resident in the town. As The Man, Alan McClarty gave a very good performance. His attention to character detail was excellent and he played The Man's journey with subtlety. His relationship with Swallow was quite complex as she started out as his 'apostle' but gradually wormed her way into his heart. His character only engaged with the children throughout the show, none of the adults ever see or speak with him and his rapport with the children was excellent, especially during his song story "Annie Christmas", where he playacted with them. I felt that he struggled with some of the songs, they were perhaps a little high for his range, but his duets with Swallow were good and "A Kiss is a Terrible Thing to Waste' with Swallow and Amos was quite proficiently performed. The townspeople, played by the, mostly, female ensemble and children's chorus, were a God-fearing bunch, living their lives according to the fire and brimstone of orthodox religion. The rebellious ones were characterised by Amos and Candy. A multi-racial couple; he's white, she's African American, who planned to leave and travel the highways on his motorcycle, to chase the American Dream. Matt Suddaby played Amos as an indecisive, slightly dim character who secretly yearned after Swallow, captivated by her innocence. This is often played as a perverse, almost grooming relationship as he's clearly written as much older than Swallow's sixteen years. However, in this production both actors were obviously much older, so it scanned as a more traditional relationship. Mr Suddaby gave a good performance, more Danny Zuko than James Dean, of the rebel without a clue and although he didn't quite have the rock tenor required for some of Amos' songs, he  sang it well. However, his duet with Candy, "Tire Tracks and Broken Hearts" was staged more like a song from Grease rather than the big dirty rock number it should have been. Megan Cunning played Candy as a sassy rebel who didn't fit in. Her acting was rather good and she really projected her frustration with Amos' reticence to leave and the bigotry of the town that she was forced to endure. Ms Cunning had good vocal expression and delivered her solo numbers well.

Candy's father, Edward, was played by Patrick Connor. The character was a family retainer or servant who had been with the Boone family for a long time. Normally played by a black actor, Mr Connor's dialect was African-American Vernacular English. He was a strong performer and had a substantial stage presence. His relationship with Candy was well developed and his geniality and care for the family was tangible, particularly his relationship with the three children. There were a few altercations during the show with the local Sheriff, played with menace by Paul Sleet, particularly with the Snake Preacher, leader of the revival meetings. Played with a strong presence by Adam Goudy, this travelling preacher used his handling of poisonous snakes to gain religious recruits. He led the ensemble on a vigorous rendition of "Wrestle with the Devil", which had some nice harmonies. Musical direction on the show was by Eric Boyd, who also conducted a thirteen piece band situated at stage left. The band were good, but the flute was quite discordant and off-key at times, which I think threw some of the singers, and the guitar was not as grungy as needed on some of the numbers. Mr Boyd did some commendable work with the ensemble, stand-out numbers were the songs at the end of each act; "No Matter What" and "Whistle Down the Wind". Both songs had finely layered harmonies. The Children's Chorus impressed with their tuning and power on "When Children Rule the World" and "No Matter What". Some of the lead vocals were a bit weak and I think more work could have been done here by Mr Boyd.

Choreography by Sharon Logan and Laura Fisher was sparse, it's not a big dance show, but effective on a couple of numbers, notably "Cold", which had a well-rehearsed line-dance routine.

Ms Logan also looked after the musical staging of the songs which made good use of the set and floor space available on stage. Set design was by the director, Brian Logan, and consisted of platforms stage left, a trucked barn stage right and a square arch upstage. Set dressing was faux wood and looked great.
