A set of white tabs downstage were pulled for some projections and there were a number of very authentic looking props including a motorbike. Lighting was designed and operated also by the director but was less effective. Lighting instruments scrolled colours and gobos on to the set during some of the more intimate scenes and was quite off putting and most of the scenes looked very flat. However, there was good use made of the follow spots during the show. The projection worked well for the train sequence but not as well for the road scenes where it just looked weirdly psychedelic. Sound design by Darren Gardiner was reasonably punchy but the mix between band and vocals was very unbalanced and we didn't hear a lot of instruments as the drums were so loud. Stage manager, David Wray's transitions were quite swift but very visible, with stage hands in contemporary blacks and talkback systems mingling with the cast to reset and strike scenes, which took from the world of the show.

Ewan Campbell's costume design was excellent. I liked the 1950's dresses and the different coloured berets were a nice touch on the girls. Make up was co-ordinated by Chloe Freeman and worked particularly well on The Man, who was effectively dirty and blood-stained. Edward's make-up was very dark, especially around the eyes, which gave him a furtive and menacing look contrary to his character and Swallow's make- up was quite heavy which took from the innocence of the character.

Brian Logan directed a fairly solid interpretation of one of Lloyd Webber's lesser musicals. The pace of the show was quite lively and his staging was good. There were a lot of entrances and exits through the audience which worked well on some scenes; the church, the bar, but a bit strange on others. His direction of The Man and his relationship with Swallow was delicate and nuanced as was his work with the younger members of the cast, yet there was a lack of emotional connection by some of the actors with their characters and ostensibly with the piece. It didn't really move the audience as much as perhaps it should have and we didn't really get a sense of place or time despite the good set and costumes, or a sense that the issues in the musical were being explored or highlighted. That said, I did see it early on in the run, so perhaps it will get better and that connection will be established.

Apart from the very obvious energy and pace that Director, Sean McMahon, brought to this GDMDS production of Footloose, he scored highly in also showing deference to the genuine religious theme that underlines the attitudes of the parents, highlighted by the Rev. Shaw Moore. He was very respectful, too, to the heavier topics of grief through loss and of broken homes and families, without it ever becoming dreary or maudlin. It was the very good balance between this dramatic story line and the mad-cap fun and craziness of the younger generation that glued this production together as a complete package.

The fairly minimal, but simple and effective set, met the requirements of the script, and locations were never in doubt. Scene changes we more about movement of props and furniture than set pieces, and were unobtrusively handled by stage manager, Rob Coventry, and his team. The use of projections was equally unobtrusive and helped in giving a sense of location, but it would probably all have worked just as well without them. In a technically pleasing show, lighting was of a good general standard, capturing the tone and atmosphere of each scene, but could possibly have been ever more exuberant in the up-beat numbers. Strong pools of light defined some of the most tender moments in the script. Sound quality throughout was most satisfactory. While this isn't a glamorous show to costume, there was a good distinction between the contemporary and colourful outfits of the younger cast and the somewhat stuffier and severe look of the religiously inclined adults. A nice infusion of cowboy classics enhanced the line-dancing scene. With its contemporary setting, hairstyles were varied and entirely appropriate and make- up was natural.

What contributed enormously to the success of the show was a finely tuned band, a strong vocal chorus and an abundance of excellent principal vocalists. Harmonies throughout were very well-realised. With much credit due to the balance between stage and pit, Musical Director, Barry Power, can be extremely proud of the musical quality of this production.

That strong vocal chorus also needed to be fit and energetic, as Nicole McDonald's choreography was vibrant and sometimes exhausting. With plenty of pacy musical numbers, she showed good variety and invention in her routines. Holding Out For A Hero topped the list for me, but there were plenty of others that rocked the house, and she also displayed a good awareness of comedy in some of the pieces. I didn't love the line-dancing number, but that is a mere blip in the overall high quality terpsichorean treat.

Sean McMahon also did a great job with his direction and characterisation of principals, assisted, no doubt, by the very good level of talent with which he had to work.

Playing the central role of Ren McCormack, and enjoying the range of the character, was Gavin Molony. From the protagonist who challenges the warped mores of his new, unjust community, to the romantic who handles his wooing of the Reverend's daughter with sincerity and dignity, and then to the grieving son who struggles to understand why his father abandoned him and his mother, Gavin got under the skin of his character and brought out the best of emotions in each scenario. Very well played, with the added bonus of a most pleasant vocal quality. Ariel Moore, the wayward daughter of the Reverent, was played with vim and verve by a spirited Aly Coyne, whose singing was most impressive. While much of her character is centered around being rebellious, it was her more emotional scenes with Ren that displayed her best acting ability. The Reverent Shaw Moore displayed indignant moments of hellfire and brimstone in his monologues and moments of thought- provoking religious reflection, both of which were strongly delivered by Eamonn Murphy, but it was perhaps in his more emotional moments of self-reflection, and in his heartfelt duologues with his wife, Vi, that our hearts were won over by his sincerity. As his wife, Vi, a most understated and beautifully delivered personification of tolerance and empathy was given by Marion Holohan. Her vocal contribution, particularly in "Can You Find it in Your Heart", was sublime.

And from the sublime to the ridiculous! Éanna O'Donnell as Willard, the muscle- bound, tell-it-like-it-is, country bumpkin with a temper and a heart of gold, was nothing short of hilarious. He could kind of sing, and kind of dance, but his comedy was pure gold. Excellent performance. The quality of the female vocalists was so abundant that it's hard to know where to begin, but Lauren Dooley as Rusty was front and centre of the shows outstanding numbers, especially "Holding Out For a Hero". But right up alongside her were Louise O'Connor as Wendy Jo, and Maria O'Loughlin as Urleen, and when they joined forces, as in "Somebody's Eyes" and "Let's Hear it For The Boy", they were superb. Lauren Dooley's Rusty also delivered great comedy alongside Willard. As the bad boy of the piece, Maurice Treacy delivered a highly dislikeable Chuck Cranston with conviction (and convictions!) in a very well-played role. Strong support came from David O'Hare who doubled as Travis and Jeter, and Conor Delahunty who doubled as Lyle and Bickle. In the more mature roles, Ethel McCormack was tenderly played by Niamh Cartwright, whose vocals were also of a high standard. Peter O'Brien made a nasty and obdurate Coach and gave a good country feel to Cowboy Joe. Peter Dillon as Wes, Michelle Kennedy as Lulu, Megan Moriarty as Eleanor, Fiona Doyle as Principal Clark, William Anglim as both the cop and Garvin, and Niamh Thornton as Betty Blast all made worthy contributions to the story.

As already stated, the cowboys, cowgirls, townsfolk and the youth of the town all combined to produce some excellent vocal quality, loads of energetic and well- executed movement, and very good acting and reacting to the events of the show. Really very impressive.

I confess that I had always seen Footloose as a poor man's All Shook Up. They have remarkably similar themes and scenarios, but perhaps my view is changing. While All Shook Up is a tad frivolous, Footloose, when well-directed, as this most certainly was, has a quite passionate and dramatic core. I enjoyed this so thoroughly because of that combination of high-energy antics and the more poignant moments of drama. Congratulations to cast, crew and the production team for getting it so right.

Sunshine on Leith, at its heart, is a drama with music, as opposed to a full-blown musical show, and with this particular production, it was the drama that really touched the heart, especially the damaged relationship between parents, Rab and Jean. Musically, a massive impact was made by a particularly strong vocal chorus. Not all the music in the show is outstanding, but the delivery of the music was top- notch. Credit for that must lie with Musical Director, Enda O'Connor, who did an excellent job both as the leader of a well-tuned and precise orchestra, and as chorus master. Tempi and tone were just about perfect, as was the balance between stage and pit. The quality of the chorus vocals was of a very high standard, and the principals throughout were very vocally secure. I know that aspects of Paul Norton's direction were affected by the limitations of the performance area. Played against a cyclorama that showed an excellent panoramic view of Edinburgh and it's outlying regions, the never changing set made a good initial impact, but became a tad monotonous as the show progressed, as its sheer expanse made scenes or moments of intimacy less focused. The lighting, which was by no means bad, wasn't creative enough to narrow scenes down and isolate the focal point. Consequently, the show had more of a concert feel about it, than a drama. The other misfortune of minimal technicals was that people seemed to stand around a lot, sometimes illuminated even when they weren't the focal point of the action. Paul's production was very tidy in presentation, if occasionally static. What worked extremely well were the relationships between Ally and Liz and between Rab and Jean. The drama and pathos of their story-lines was very well- realised, as were the very moving scenes involving Rab's daughter from another mother, Eilidh. Perhaps there needed to be a bit more fire and passion in the early scenes between Davy and Yvonne. They seemed to meander rather placidly towards their explosive confrontation at the end of Act One.

There aren't too many opportunities for choreography in this show, but Choreographer, Lisa Hogan, moved the chorus effectively in the more animated numbers, incorporating a bit of set dancing into the anniversary party scene. There was good acting/reacting from the chorus in the soccer-match scene and that party scene. Their other entrances seemed a bit formulaic, as in enter-sing- exit, but they get top marks for their vocal presentation, which was exceptionally impressive, especially in I'm On My Way, Oh Jean, Letter from America and of course 500 Miles. A combination of well- realised harmonies and powerful singing made this a wonderful vocal experience. The character of Davy was well-realised by Dave McArdle, instantly likeable and sincere. There was an element of discomfort in his hand movements, but verbally, he always conveyed his emotions most successfully. His vocals were also very secure. Perhaps he and Yvonne needed to be a bit more convincing in their affection for each other.

Robyn Luttrell, as Yvonne, was likewise, instantly likeable, with a radiant warmth. but there needed to be more evidence of her obviously fragile or scarred persona as a result of past relationships. Her relationship with Davy, for the most part, seemed a little too tame to justify the drama that almost tore them apart. Much more believable was her friendship with Liz, and her concern for Rab in the hospital. Her vocals were most pleasing throughout, as was her accent.

Conor O'Meara gave an excellent performance as Ally, a cheeky chap with a great sense of humour. His love for Liz was abundant, despite his inability to read his situation. We truly felt for him when Liz turned down his proposal. He displayed affection as comfortably as he displayed anger and frustration. A nicely balanced performance, combined with assured vocal quality. Aoife Digan was a most sincere Liz, expressing well her inner conflict between being a bird in a cage and wanting to fly free. Most affecting was her love for her parents and her strong friendship with Yvonne. Again, a most convincing performance complemented by a lovely singing voice.

Heather Colohan played the wife, Jean, with a great combination of tolerance and affection, and ultimately with dignity, as she learns of her husband's betrayal. Her acting was poignant but never exaggerated, and her vocal contributions were very strong.

Performance of the night came from Patrick Byrne as Rab, from his fine and well- judged comedic drunk scene to his heart attack, and in coping with the realisation of the consequences of his past indiscretions. This was a performance that pulled at the heart-strings, sincere in his regrets and passionate in his love of wife and family. His accent was absolutely rock solid, as was his vocal security.

Lauren Doonan gave a warm and believable performance as Eilidh, sincere in her grief for her mother's passing and genuine in her insecurity at meeting her father for the first time.

There were good performances too, both vocally and in their acting, from a range of featured supporting roles.

What props and furniture there were, were efficiently moved in and out by the stage team, under Charlie Brophy, and by the cast themselves. Sound quality throughout was very good, including sound effects and voice overs. There were very good uniforms for the boys in Afghanistan at the opening, and a varied and appropriate selection of costumes for the different scenes in the show. In the relatively modern setting of the show, hairstyles and make-up were natural and totally acceptable.

Criticisms aside, Sunshine on Leith is a challenging show, and for the most part, one that was very well done on this occasion. I'm grateful for the hospitality shown during my visit, and it was a pleasure to meet such a warm and engaging cast after the performance. Sincere thanks for a most enjoyable night in Birr.

Well, here we are again. Yet another production of the ever popular and entrancing musical, The Sound of Music. Thank goodness it's a show I never tire of watching.

In the hands of Director, David McEvoy, this was a very thoroughly rehearsed and a meticulously performed presentation, from beginning to end. Everyone knew their place and were word and note perfect. Characters were well-established and the level of talent was of a high order throughout, and yet, I did feel that it was all slightly mechanical in feel, rather than flowing and natural. I had a strong sense of performers acting, rather than feeling their emotions. There were exceptions to this; most notably, the Von Trapp children who were a sheer delight in everything they did. I believed in Bethany McLoughlin's Liesl, precocious yet vulnerable, boldly flirtatious with Rolf, yet a child at heart. This was delightfully played and her singing and dancing were very good. Gavin Gilligan as Frederich was strong and confident in his vocals and in his character. Catherine Tsvikovych as Louisa, Brendan O'Connor as Kurt, Annelies Rooney as Brigitta and Robyn McCorry as Marta each had great individuality, super voices and great discipline, and little Lily Tansey as Gretl was simply adorable. Together, they performed perfectly as a believable family of siblings, natural and comfortable on the stage, and vocally very secure indeed. Emily Tansey acted the central role of Maria with great versatility and ability, moving from the somewhat scatter-brained and out-spoken innocence of a postulant to a believable mother-figure with the Von Trapp children, and maturing into a loving and supportive wife, courageous in the face of adversity. Though sometimes predictable in how she delivered her emotions, she was never lacking in sincerity, and her vocal contribution was extremely good.

Iain Howard was as debonair a Captain Von Trapp as I've ever seen, comfortable in his own skin, whether as the icy disciplinarian or when discovering love for the second time. He was particularly impressive in his indignation towards the rising threat of Nazi-German, but there was also great sincerity in his emotions for Maria. His rendition of Edelweiss was extremely good.

Michele Feeney had the required poise and posture for the role of Elsa, if a little deliberate in the delivery of her lines and emotions, but she certainly looked the part and managed her comedic contributions with charm and ease. She paired up well with Uncle Max in their musical ability, with How Can Love Survive being very well- delivered.

Franny Curley, as Uncle Max, was probably the most natural performer in the cast, strong in his characterisation and his comedy and always at ease on the stage. A very good performance.

Also delightfully natural and sincere was the performance of The Mother Abbess by Margaret Curley, authoritative without ever losing her warmth and humanity, and believable in her religious devotion, exemplified by her beautiful rendition of Climb Every Mountain.

The supporting nuns, Colette Furlong as Sr Bertha, Joanne Cullen as Sr Margaretta, Reichelle Celine as Sr Sophia, Catherine Gaffney as Sr Catherine and Emer Henderson as Sr Agatha, each displayed good individual identities while working very well together as a team.

Occasionally, their delivery was a tad mechanical, but there was no doubt about their commitment, nor indeed of their vocal acumen.

There was a lovely performance from Pam Lindey, as housekeeper, Frau Schmidt, mature, frustrated and yet homely, and Adam Norris made an impression as nazi- inclined Butler, Franz. Jonathan Flynn made a convincing Rolf Gruber, youthful and easily misguided, and he transitioned well into the Nazi-youth of the final scenes. His movement was good, and he has a voice that, with a bit of work, should mature into a fine baritone.

Trevor Gorman gave us a creepy, and somewhat stereotypical Herr Zeller, but he was secure in his delivery of lines, and there was good support from Kevin Sheridan as Baron Elberfeld, Enya Kilfeather as Baroness Elberfeld, Garrett Crowley as Admiral Von Schreiber and Norah McLoughlin as the maid, Ursula. Discipline was the key to the success of the Nuns Chorus, extremely tidy in their entrances, exits, movement and vocals. They never put a foot, nor a note, wrong. The few opportunities that existed for the men to be involved were well taken.

A good orchestra, under the direction of Charles O'Connor, played a very secure and accomplished accompaniment to the show, although perhaps one or two numbers would have benefitted from a slightly less pedantic tempo. However, orchestra, chorus and principals all seemed very well-rehearsed musically, and the quality of the vocals throughout was extremely good. Great attention had been given to the children's harmonies, and the unaccompanied nuns choruses were delightful.

In a show that offers very few opportunities for choreography, Jennifer Heavey managed to add variety and colour to the children's routines and made the most of the Landler with Maria and the Captain. The scenic variations for the show were achieved through the combination of vivid projections thrown onto large cut-outs of mountains. It all had a slightly surreal feel to it, with Picasso-esque Abbey windows appearing on the hillsides, but I have to say it worked quite effectively, particularly for the outdoor scenes. Some of the indoor projections were distorted by being thrown onto two surfaces, but the concept was admirable. It also assisted with swift changes, under the direction of Stage Manager Lorna Davey. The other element of the set was a walk-way and steps up- centre stage. These were well used and effective but might have blended better if they hadn't been pure white.

With the strong light of the projections upstage, a good job was done by the lighting team to create good atmospheres downstage. Sound quality was a little uneven at times, with solo voices within a chorus occasionally over-amplified. Apart from a couple of late entrances, the principals' mics were well-managed and sound effects were well-selected.

The costumes for the show were very good, with all the children's sets clean and tidy, and a good uniformity amongst the nuns. Principal costumes were excellent, elegant and rich for the Baroness and the party guests, and the military attire was always appropriate. The Captain had impressive outfits, including a good naval suit for his wedding. The ladies' hairstyles were all proper and correct and make-up throughout looked natural.

I'm extremely appreciative of David McEvoy for his courtesy throughout the evening, and while I did find some performances mechanical rather than natural, this was most certainly a well- drilled, well-rehearsed and very talented display, and one that I thoroughly enjoyed. Sincere thanks to you all for a very memorable evening.

Two events led to Fiddler on the Roof being an excellent choice of show for Rush to present this year. Firstly, its poignancy and relevance to the current on-going political crisis in the Ukraine, and secondly, the sad passing of Chaim Topol in March. The definitive Tevye, Topol has inspired and influenced not just those of us who have had the honour of playing the role, but everyone who has seen and enjoyed his remarkably passionate performance. To quote director Tony Finnegan's programme tribute to the man, "you have given us an incredible legacy, and we are forever grateful."

As evidence of that inspiration, Rush have presented a show that was as passionate and heartfelt as it was talented and accomplished. From outstanding performances to top-notch technical and production standards, they sent their audiences home both moved and highly entertained.

The set by John O'Donoghue was exquisite. Simple yet so effective, with its sliding panels, multi-purpose boxes, different levels, and creatively beautiful painting, and all in such a tight space. It was also very practical, allowing for quick and efficient scene changes, so very well handled by Connie Murray and her team. Props were excellent with great attention to detail. Lighting was atmospheric and enhanced the set beautifully, with good focus on the main acting areas and sound quality was generally very good. All these elements combined led to a most impressive technical display which fully captured the tone and atmosphere of the story.

One of Director Tony Finnegan's trademarks is attention to detail and where it was most notably evident was in the immaculate costuming of the show, from head-dresses, hats and caps through to appropriate footwear, from wedding and prayer attire to uniforms and everyday clothes. Make-up, too, was appropriate, keeping to good earth-tones, the exception being the very effective 'horror' make-up for the three incarnations of Fruma-Sarah. Grandma was delightfully aged and 'dead' looking. In the case of Fiddler, whose core is 'tradition', Tony set the tone and the atmosphere of the piece from the get-go and maintained a terrific standard throughout. He also captured and presented an awareness of how relevant the piece is to the current political landscape of the Ukraine, particularly with a beautifully crafted finale. Choreographer, Sinéad Lightley, showed the same respect for tradition with a well-crafted opening, captured the sense of 'the circle of our village' and the wedding dance adhered to the tradition of men and women dancing separately until Perchik upsets the applecart. There was good inventive work in Matchmaker and the Chavalet number, and the bottle dance (real bottles, thank you) was well designed and executed. To Life was perhaps the only number that might have been more adventurous, but the overall effect of the choreography was to enhance the show.

Musical Director, Gay Kirwan, had his chorus and principals well-disciplined both in their cueing and their harmonies, an essential discipline, given that the orchestra and conductor were in a room backstage. Said orchestra, under guest conductor, Aidan Faughey, played the score with assurance and sensitivity. This was a very well-sung show, with the principals being particularly impressive. Shay Griffin exuded confidence and security from the moment his Tevye set foot on the stage. As a story-teller, he captured the beautifully crafted comedy of his character with aplomb. His relationship with wife, Golde was quirky and sentimental in equal measures, and his abundant love for his daughters was apparent from the outset. His vocal prowess was displayed in If I Were a Rich Man and To Life, but for me, his musical highlight was a brilliantly performed "Do You Love Me" with Golde. He handled the relationships of Tzeitel and Hodel with well-moderated anger, strong comical logic and eventually, humble acceptance. In the case of Chava, his breakdown was perhaps more visible than a broken man, too proud to change his course, and too proud to show the hurt of her actions, would have permitted himself. Nevertheless, this was an emotional performance.

As Golde, Kathy Kelly was quite simply perfectly cast.

Her wit, her visual expression of her emotions, her vocal quality, her tenderness, her passion and her heartache, every detail was just as it should have been. A wonderful performance, and perhaps the best Golde I've seen in a lifetime of loving Fiddler on the Roof.

Had I been this particular Teyve, I think I might have given up being a milkman, moved to America, and become the theatrical agent for my incredibly talented daughters. Doireann McAuley, as Chava, was full of mischief, passion and musicality, and played her separation scene most effectively. Rebecca Leonard, as Hodel, was as fiery and stubborn as her father and as devoted as her mother. Perhaps she was a tad over-aggressive towards Perchik initially, but when she finally fell for him, it was genuine and heart-felt. Far From the Home I Love was well-delivered. But it was Amber Dixon, as Tzeitel, who made the biggest impression on me, with a wonderful voice and a strong command of her comedy and her emotional displays. When the three together sang Matchmaker, the result was a tour de force. Not to be outdone, Ava O'Connor, as Sphrintze, and Abigail Hickey, as Bielke, made very worthy contributions to every scene they were in. As the woman who introduced twerking to the Shtetl, Niamh Carroll gave great physical comedy to the role of Yente, the matchmaker, but she was also sincere in her emotions, and expert in the non-stop- babbling nature of her monologues.

A good character performance came from Martin Gallagher in the role of Lazar Wolf, with good comedic touches, and the stubbornness that made him a most unsuitable husband for Tzeitel.

Alex Mahon had good stage presence and a very pleasant voice, and while he was a likeable and believable Motel, I did think he could have squeezed more physical and vocal comedy from the character. Shane Aherne's Perchik was suitably revolutionary in attitude and strong in his presence. Perhaps he had room for a little more warmth and charm to merit the affections of Hodel.

Gary Finnegan impressed in the role of Mordcha, the Innkeeper, making a good impact with his lines and a strong presence even when he wasn't the focal point of the action. Likewise, Barry Kavanagh was consistently befuddled and confused as he gave confidence and conviction to the role of the Rabbi. Declan Costello, in his first ever show, made a very confident debut as Avram, and Brian Magennis had a smug yet sincere presence as Mendel, the Rabbi's son. Cian Plant brought a youthful sincerity to the role of Fyedka and played his romance with Chava at just the right level.

Poor Lazar Wolf was lucky to be a widower, judging from the ferocious nature of his ghostly deceased wife, Fruma Sarah, who, by the miracles of theatrical license, was presented, most effectively, as an unholy trinity of ghastly women. Aoife Parkes, Maria Kavanagh and Niamh Parkes are, I'm quite sure, lovely ladies, underneath the garish make-up, and they all performed with confidence and competence.

Peter O'Brien gave a good performance as the Russian Constable, affable to a point but ultimately the harbinger of the anti-Semitic reign of terror.

Good support came from Catherine Foley as Shandel, Mattie Scott as Sasha, Daniel Farrell as the Russian Tenor (nicely sung), Bob Crowther as Nachum the beggar, Richard Kenny as Yussel, and a strong cameo performance from Helen Kavanagh as Grandma Tzeitel. John Cleere made a good impact as the Fiddler.

Both vocally and visually, the chorus made a strong contribution to the overall strength of this production, good in their acting and reacting, and very competent in the movement and dancing that they were given.

In a season that has been liberally peppered with juke-box musicals, young shows that focus on teenage angst, and comical romps to welcome back the audiences after lockdown, how wonderful to see an old favourite like Fiddler on the Roof being presented to a standard that affirms its rightful reputation as a timeless masterpiece. Thank you, from the heart, for such an accomplished and moving night of emotional musical theatre.

The premise for Disco Inferno was to take the popular Faustian theme, centre it around a wannabe pop star, willing to sell his soul for fame and fortune, and embellish it with a string of hits from the disco era of the 1970's, and Mitchelstown Musical Society went all out to present it with as much style, energy and enthusiasm as was humanly possible. Director, Killian Collins, devised a clever stage that employed several levels, and an apron and podiums out front of the main stage that were well used to facilitate scene changes even while the action continued and having the band constantly on-stage, appropriately attired for the era, was a good touch. There was particularly good attention to detail in the costuming of the show, and despite the always-on-the-move style of direction, principals and chorus alike were always in the right place at the right time. The use of projection screens to name locations, but also to provide further lighting and design effects, was very good. Indeed, there were so many good aspects to this production that I just wish Killian had had the courage to take a pair of scissors to the script. Despite the company's best efforts, strong performances and much musical magic, with a vacuous, meandering script that ran the show to well over 3 hours, and at least half a dozen songs too many, judicious pruning was needed. It was, quite simply, far, far too long.

Setting that fact aside, the show was musically delightful, with songs by Elton John, David Bowie, Queen, Sweet, Gloria Gaynor, Val McCoy, Arthur Brown, David Soul, the Tramps and many more besides, which made the whole event a bit of a familiar sing-along experience. Under the guidance of Musical Director, Robbie Pender, the band contributed not only with perfect feel and tempi throughout, but also in their involvement in the action, adorned with excellent wigs and hairpieces and costumes, Great work was also done on the vocal quality of the show, with secure and well- rehearsed principals, and a chorus who, despite the demands of the choreography, still managed to realise good harmony and strength.

Aileen McMurtry was charged with the unenviable task of having to present varied and high energy choreography for an unreasonable number of disco routines, but she has my admiration for a job well done. She catered for the older cast members with enthusiastic routines that wouldn't have looked out of place at a family wedding, and she saved her best work for the younger team of accomplished and energetic dancers. The dancing never seemed to stop, and her work load was immense.

With hardly a moment off the stage from the start to the finish of the show, Jack Fitzgerald, in the leading role, Jack, deserves an award just for energy and durability. Here was a young man with good presence, very capable acting ability and a fabulous voice, which he had so many opportunities to display during this show. His energy level knew no bounds in this extremely good performance. His main support came from Rory Ward in the role of best friend, Tom, a not so cool, comedic nerd, uncomfortable with women and with dancing, but always willing to give it a go. This was delightfully played, with much visual comedy that compensated for a fairly poor script. Rory's singing was also bang-on.

Paul Finn took on the role of Duke, the nightclub owner, with an accent that tended to float a bit in the mid-Atlantic, but with a confidence that presented him as a strong authoritative figure. He also assumed satanic qualities and gave a strong vocal performance of "Fire" towards the show's climax.

Diarmuid Hanley impressed as Heathcliffe, the somewhat psycho, regular front man in the nightclub, full of angst and anger, and abusive to his girlfriend. That he made himself decidedly dislikeable to the audience was a tribute to his good acting, and he was vocally secure.

Completing the male line-up was Gabriel Casey as Disco Inferno's smooth-talking DJ, Terry, who eventually becomes the new boyfriend of Jack's rejected girlfriend. His DJ was delightfully cheesy, and there was good sincerity in his respect for Jane and for the loss of Tom.

In a role that I felt was very under- written, Lisa Feerick did all in her power to impress as the leading lady, Jane. Her acting, as the much-neglected girlfriend of Jack, was always believable, and we felt the depth of sense of betrayal. Good in all her musical contributions, she particularly made a powerful impact with "I Will Survive". Similarly, the role of Maggie, Tom's reluctant girlfriend, never seems to rise above the rank of an 'also- ran', which is a great pity, as Julie Buckley demonstrated that she was certainly capable of a meatier role, confident and adept in her acting, singing and dancing. Colette Daly, as Kathy, the much-abused girlfriend of Heathcliffe, became more relevant to the story when she switched her attentions from Heathcliffe to Jack, and she played the victim extremely well. Again, she made the absolute most of a script that didn't really provide her the opportunity to show off her full potential. The meatiest female role was unquestionably Lady Marmalade, the embodiment of evil, deliciously and deviously portrayed by Alison McCormack. She was strident in her disregard for emotions and sentiment, and delightful in her comical representation of her devilish character. Her stage presence was excellent, and she performed her vocal pieces with confidence. Highly amusing, too, was Mary O'Callaghan, in the flamboyant and exaggerated supporting role of fashion consultant, Nicky Diablo. With a succession of song after song after song, all set in the Disco, with pumping rhythms, the chorus had little time to twiddle their thumbs during this high energy show, and fair play to them for keeping going for so long. As one would expect in a Disco setting, the variety of styles, fashions, dance ability and age were wide ranging and appropriate, but the constant was that everyone gave full commitment to the scenes in which they were involved. The younger element displayed so much energy and dance ability, and added to all of that, the chorus vocals were also extremely impressive. Fair play to the whole ensemble.

The greatest success of this production was its visual impact, from the creative and versatile staging to the vast array of colourful costumes and designs. It was a feast for the eyes.

I'm sorry for laboring the point about the poor script and the over-long running time of the show, but I had to mention it, insofar as it did have an effect on my enjoyment of the evening. That said, the company can take much pride in the commitment they gave to every aspect of their performance. Thank you sincerely to all concerned.

A Times review of Legally Blonde in the West End summed up my own opinion of the show perfectly, when Benedict Nightingale wrote, "Let's agree that Legally Blonde is, well, fun!" and "ridiculously enjoyable from start to finish!"

The character of Elle Woods is a wonderful creation, and Ennis were fortunate to have a performer so capable of carrying the show on her shoulders. While some of the technical aspects of the show could have been more adventurous, there was little to criticise about the performances, which were universally good. A strong production team had all done their work very thoroughly, and the result was a night of great fun, that sent the audience home with toes tapping and smiles beaming. Jessica Bray's direction of this show set a cracking pace from the outset that was maintained right through the show. Her casting was very strong, and perhaps, most importantly of all, was the sense of fun and nonsense that permeated her entire production. A couple of dramatic moments maybe needed to be more sharply focused upon. Callahan's inappropriate advances to Elle happened a tad too quickly, and her response, likewise, needed a moment of suspended animation to allow the audience to emphasise with the creepiness of the situation. Similarly, Elle's triumph in retrieving Rufus for Paulette was gone in a flash and needed that frozen moment of realisation. But it's fair to say that this was a production that hopped off the stage, focused strongly on comedy and fun, and left the audience wanting more. That, to me, is a job well done.

Equally fast-paced and energetic was Laura Jane Allis's choreography. The faux Riverdance routine was fun, as was the Bend and Snap, but I felt that Elle's presentation to the board of Harvard could have been more flamboyant, in the over- the-top manner of American cheer- leaders, and while Whipped into Shape was tidy in its execution, it didn't quite have the awe factor of an intricate skipping routine. Those aside, everything from "Oh My God" through to the conclusion of the show, was an energy rush that was very well-executed by a dedicated and diligent cast of chorus and dancers.

Not to be left out of the high-energy equation, Musical Director, Shane Farrell, drove the musical content of the show like a finely tuned sports car. The band were dynamic and always under good control, and the vocalists on stage kept time and tempo with energy and accuracy. Great work had been done in preparing the chorus in their harmonies by Chorus Mistress, Eilís O'Neill.

In the demanding role of Elle, Julita Fox carried the entire production. I've already witnessed her acting ability this season, but it was the additional element of comedy that really made this a stand-out performance. Her timing was excellent, and her delivery of lines was as carefree and casual as it was pointed and poignant. She perfectly captured the intellect and intelligence of her character. And if that wasn't enough, her dancing was dynamic, and her vocals were vociferous and volatile. An excellent all- round performance.

Sarah Kenny was a confident and convincing Paulette, very laid back and very comical, especially in her advances towards Kyle. She was vocally strong and assured in her routines. Pa Woulfe created an arrogant, not-as-cool-as-he-thinks-he- is, jock with the role of Warner, and did so with good comedic effect and secure vocals. There was warmth and sincerity in Cian McKeon's portrayal of Emmet, combined with a most pleasing vocal quality and a very good sense of comedy. He and Elle together had a chemistry that made their eventual romance inevitable and very believable.

It was nice to see an old friend, Aidan O'Gara, taking on the role of Callahan, and doing so with conviction, even if it was of the callous and misogynistic kind. He made a very good job of Blood in the Water. Elaine Brennan was delightfully cold and condescending as Vivienne, but also totally believable in her acknowledgement of how she had unfairly judged Elle. Very nicely played.

Adding spice, sparkle and quirky characterisation to the Delta Nu sorority were the mad-cap Margot of Holly Dunphy, the pert and playful Pilar of Clíodhna McNelis, the scintillating Serena of Saoirse Daly and the capricious Kate of Rachel Hunt. Like Duracell bunnies, they never ran out of energy, and their comedy was as delightful and accomplished as their singing and dancing. A fit and physical Natasha Coughlan gave energy and character to the role of Brooke, leading the Whipped into Shape number with great confidence. Claire Curtin added butch charm and much good humour to the role of Enid. A myriad of supporting roles were all played with clarity and confidence, led by Lorcan McAuliffe and Sean McInerney as the very funny Nikos and Chad, Carole Murphy as a quirky Chutney, Vanessa Kirwan as a believable Whitney, Brian Dowling as the slob, Dewey, Richard Donnellan and Michelle Vaughan as Elle's somewhat ridiculous Dad and Mom, Carol Hackett as the Judge, and of course the heart-throb, beef-cake known as Kyle, delightfully delivery (see what I did there?) by Ruan Kent.

I suppose I should also mention Bruiser Woods and Rufus Buonofuonte, doggedly portrayed by Missy Hassett and Izzy Murphy. Such natural and disciplined performers!

As already mentioned, but also worth repeating, the chorus did all that was asked of them with great style, energy and a good awareness of their surroundings. What's more, they achieved amazingly good vocal quality, considering the amount of activity that accompanied most of it. A highly impressive contribution to the show.

Technically, it was a good array of props, furniture and set pieces than gave location throughout the show, rather than a solid and realistic set. The set itself was fairly minimal, but tidy and functional, facilitating smooth transitions from one scene to the next for Alan Jackson and the stage crew. Lighting, while adding atmosphere to many of the musical numbers, was occasionally a tad bland, and tighter area lighting might have given some scenes more specific focus. The sound quality throughout was well-balanced, with tidy cueing. For the most part, costumes were very good and appropriate to the characters of those wearing them. When Elle made her presentation to the board of Harvard, her Majorette costume was outstanding, but it did make those around her a tad tawdry by comparison.

There was good attention to hairstyles and make-up, both being tidy and appropriate. I try not to pay too much heed to what the audience are saying as they exit a production. We're all used to hearing our locals telling us, every year, 'That's the best show you've ever done', and sometimes it might be true, and sometimes it's nonsense, but as I exited this show, I couldn't help but hear the oft repeated observation, "My God, wasn't she brilliant?", and they were ALL talking about Elle. I can't and won't argue with that.

This is a show of which I never grow tired, with its zany script, its colourful array of characters and of course, the magical music of Elvis. It's such an audience pleaser because of the combination of comedy and the very familiar musical score. Perhaps what it relies on, above all else, is high energy, and while this production was very impressive, I did feel that the energy level could have been pitched a tad higher, particularly in the staging of the big chorus numbers. Director, Donna Ruane, presented a show that was well- rehearsed, very capably performed by a talented cast, and made good use of a tidy set. The individual characterisations of her cast were generally very secure, and they were well-supported by a hard-working ensemble. I felt that perhaps more could have been done with the lighting of the show, which on occasions seemed rather flat. That aside, Donna's attention to detail and her appreciation of character and comedy were clearly on display.

Choreographer, Claudia O'Sullivan, did a good job of presenting routines that were polished, had good shape and were very competently performed. I did feel that perhaps she could have challenged her dancers a bit more, particularly in the livelier chorus dances. Numbers like Can't Help Falling, and Fools Fall in Love were well presented with good pictures and poses, and as mentioned, everything was very tidy and well-rehearsed.

With a very competent orchestra in the pit, and a group of vocally secure principals on stage, the show was musically delightful, and well-controlled by Musical Director, Deirdre Lee. Tempi were secure throughout and the balance between stage and pit was just right. Both chorus and principals seemed secure and well- rehearsed in their vocals and harmonies. An endearing performance from Nicole Scott, as Natalie/Ed, was the strong and assured backbone of this production. She seemed completely at home in both her personas, maximising her comedic business both vocally and visually, and her singing throughout was of an excellent standard.

Towering above the rest of the cast, Enda Mulchrone certainly had the stature to impress as Chad, and he made a good job of his vocals. While I didn't feel that he was totally comfortable presenting his 'stud' image, he did make a strong impact with the comedic side of his character. Jim Haller was played with good emotion and sentiment by Brendan Mullins, but he also managed to play his comical awkwardness with good confidence, and he performed his musical numbers very well. Ewa Cieslak, with her alluring Polish accent, made a very good job of Sylvia, sassy and assertive, yet wonderfully warm and empathetic towards Jim. Her There's Always Me was sung with good sincerity and emotion.

Matthew Largent was a quirky and comedic Dennis, using his physicality as effectively as his voice to create his nerdish character. I'm not sure what was going on with his hair, but it didn't detract from a very good and sincere performance, and his singing was very secure.

Emma Daly gave good character to Lorraine, as pleasant as she was precocious, and well able to belt out her vocals. She also created a good partnership with a confident John Morley, who impressed greatly in the role of Dean Hyde. Their voices blended well in It's Now or Never. As Miss Sandra, Vivienne Lee captured the aloof composure of her early encounters perfectly, then transformed, with good comedic effect, into the vamp of the story, oozing confidence and sex- appeal.

Eithne McGreal was a strongly prim and proper Mayor Matilda, who also transformed delightfully into a bit of a giggly school-girl when she realised that Sheriff Earl was in love with her. Ronan Egan, as the Sheriff, made the required comedy impact when he eventually opened his mouth, and with only a verse to show it off, displayed a strong and most pleasing baritone voice. There was a neat cameo performance, too, from Aoife Halligan as the gin-soaked barfly, Henrietta.

There was good musicality from the chorus who seemed well rehearsed in their vocals and harmonies. As actors and dancers, they tidily performed all that was asked of them, although I did feel that more could have been asked of them by the choreographer. They did, however, make a very good contribution to the show.

A simple but effective set nicely painted and presented, and the use of good props and furniture meant that the show had a clean and efficient appearance. Scene changes, under Brian Murphy's guidance, were tidily executed. The quality of sound throughout was good and well-balanced. Lighting was acceptable, if on occasions, a little unadventurous. Once or twice principals had to walk through shadow to get to the next special, and perhaps some of the faster numbers would have benefitted from a bit more variety. All in all, however, the technical aspects of the show were clean and efficient.

Principals were well-costumed, with outfits depicting the social standing of each character; Dennis, nerdy and educated, Natalie and Jim, working clothes, Matilda, Earl, Dean and Miss Sandra a cut above the rest. Chorus costumes were generally very good and era-appropriate, and hairstyles and make- up had a good natural feel.

House Manager, Noreen McNamee, led a polite and efficient team in meeting and greeting the audience. I very much appreciated the hospitality, and indeed the effort put in by all concerned in making this a very entertaining and audience pleasing production.

Into Our Hearts First staged in San Diego in 1986 and transferred to Broadway a year later, 'Into the Woods' is a musical about fairy tale characters with music and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim and book by James Lapine. Back in the late 1980's it was unusual to see a musical that explored the darker side of the Brothers Grimm, however since then a whole new genre has sprung up with the Shrek franchise and films like 'Enchanted', 'Maleficent' and even 'Frozen' getting in on the nostalgist bandwagon.

The story centres around a Baker and his wife who learn they've been cursed with childlessness by the Witch next door. They embark on a quest for the unusual objects required to break the spell by swindling, lying to and stealing from Cinderella, Little Red Riding Hood, Rapunzel, and Jack (the beanstalk guy). Everyone's wish is granted at the end of Act I, but the consequences of their actions return to haunt them in Act II, with devastating results.

Directed by Eoghan Funge and Lyndsey McKiernan with musical direction by Luke Shiels, with Ciara McKenna and Aimee O'Neil looking after the Chorus and Becca Lennon on choreography duty, this was a smashing show that leaped off the Astra Hall stage and into our hearts. It was a wonderfully energetic homage to Mr Sondheim that I'm sure he would have loved. It was fast yet dwelled on the pathos where needed and was technically a triumph.

Musical direction in a Sondheim is so important and here we had Luke Shiels, Ciara McKenna & Aimee O'Neil. Mr Shiel's conducted an eighteen-piece orchestra, with Ciara McKenna and Aimee O'Neil as looking after the Chorus. The orchestra gave us a very lush sound where strings, woodwind and horns blended beautifully together. The synth was subtle and yet present, and the tempi was perfect throughout, thanks to the percussion and double bass. There are so many songs in this show and pretty much all of them were delivered with skill, delicacy, and panache. The Chorus was full of intricate harmony and great power at times, the repeated "Into the Woods" was especially good as was the tricky but perfectly timed "Your Fault". But there were some standout musical performances within the show; especially the Baker's Wife, Witch, and Cinderella who all excelled. These three performers would easily grace a West End stage. Choreographer Becca Lennon created some very visually exciting choreography in the production. There are not a lot of dances per se in the show, but the opening and closing were brilliantly devised and performed with great attention to detail from the ensemble. Timing is everything in choreography and this ensemble were extremely accurate in their skilful dance moves. From the Princes' quirky faux posturing in "Agony" to the "Finale" numbers the performers owned the movement.

The ensemble on this show was super. Playing incidental characters, acting as chorus, and populating various scenes - they were electric. Performers of note included: Sorcha McGlynn as Cinderella's Mother; Maya Gaul as an empathetic Milky White; Robert Hogan as the world-weary Cinderella's Father; Neo O'Herlihy as the put-upon Steward and Lia Mullan as the crazy Granny and voice of the Giant. All created excellent characters, added much to the production, and supported the principals of which there were many! John Higgins played the Baker as a quiet, dependable character who disliked change but was willing to do anything for his wife. Mr Higgins sang with a wistfulness on "Maybe There're Magic" with his stage wife and with lovely emotion on "No One is Alone". His Baker was the epitome of the reluctant hero and the Baker's Wife, played by Alice Morgan who played her character's journey from submissive to assertive, with super believability. Ms Morgan had a splendid dynamic with Mr Higgins, and they were very credible as a couple. She was a joy to listen to as she had a beautiful tone to her voice, especially on "Moments in the Woods". Playing Cinderella, we were lucky to have Chloe Burke. I last saw Ms Burke as Judy in UCD's '9 to 5' last year, where she blew everyone away with her splendid characterisation and exquisite voice. She did not disappoint this time around either, as her Cinderella was thoughtful, intelligent, and feisty. Her singing was an absolute delight, and I loved her interactions with her stepmother and stepsisters. She also portrayed Cinderella as an innocent, and her scenes with the Prince were very funny and natural. "On the Steps of the Palace" was lovely as was "Cinderella at the Grave" with Ms McGlynn's character, Cinderella's Mother. As the Stepmother we had Laura Shivnan, she bustled and powered her way through scenes with a strong energy. Her singing was good on "Careful My Toe" and "So Happy" and she had a wonderful chemistry with stepsisters Florinda, Alice O'Loughlin Kennedy, and Lucinda, played by Sarah Melvin, both of whom were hilarious. Jack, of Beanstalk fame, was played by Darragh MacLachlan. Written for a younger actor but more often played by an adult, Mr MacLachlan's Jack had that youthful energy that defined Jack. His onstage relationship with his mother was very natural but it was his chemistry with Milky White, the cow played by the wonderfully expressive Maya Gaul, that won over the audience. His singing was Alice O'Loughlin Kennedy and Sarah Melvin as Florinda and Lucinda, as well as Laura Shivnan as the Stepmother good as was his tuning and I liked how his character developed in Act II. As Jack's mother Julie Bowell exploded onto the stage each entrance and the stage came alive with her entry. Her singing was perfect too. Wonderful work with Mr MacLachlan, she was very believable as his domineering mother.

Obviously, 'Into the Woods' 'borrows' from a few Fairy Tales to tell its own story about what happens after the happily ever after, it shamelessly twists the tale to give a twist in the tail. Red Riding Hood for example is not at all sweet, she is violent, sassy, spoilt and not very nice! Perfectly played here by Brianna Kelly with an imperious air and a fabulous voice, she sang beautifully on "I Know Things Now" and charted Little Red's journey from impudent teen to responsible adult with some skill. Her nemesis, the Wolf, was played as an unctuous predator by Colm Fagan, who also played the Mysterious Man with assurance and coolness. His Wolf sang and oiled around the stage with glee but got his comeuppance from Red and Lia Mullan's cantankerous Granny. Aoife Blake's Witch was quite a sad thing really. She imprisoned Rapunzel and wanted more than anything to be a good mother and to be beautiful again. Her singing was excellent, "Stay with Me" was a highlight of the show. When she changed, I liked her high status and how she tried to continue to want the mere mortals to be afraid of her, even though her power had waned. "Lament" was a showstopper that she sang with marvellous skill. Hilariously, Amber Dixon's Rapunzel spent the show either in tears or singing very operatically into her hair, she looked great with her eye make-up streaming down her face. The two princes, Cinderella's Prince, Adam Schmitz, and Rapunzel's Prince, Liam Cotter, were like an alternate universe version of Jedward. Just the right side of Panto; this double act was a highlight of the show, their hand slaps, poses, comic timing and energy was tremendously engaging and charming. Some Fairy Tales use a Storyteller and here we had Eoin Ó' Dúinín, who was perfectly cast as the Narrator. He had the look of an academic at his desk as he wrote and related the story. His voice was melliferous, and he had a confident tone in that we believed that what he was saying was the truth as he knew it.

This was an exceptional front line here, their talents made the work look easy, which it's not, and they were fully invested in their characters and totally understood the style and delivered it with energy, fun and impeccable timing. They were supported by a great production team too. Jody Trehy's sound was excellent, and Gavin Coll's fabulous lighting and projections helped create this strange underworld. Costumes and make-up were perfect as was the set. Stage managers Esther Campbell and Paddy MacFhionnlaoich did a marvellous job of keeping everything running smoothly. Transitions were quick and accurate, and helped keep the pace of the show on track.

It's not often we see shows that don't have any weak links - but this was one of them. Everything dovetailed just perfectly from performances to set to technical - it all just worked. The artistic vision for the production was front and centre and everyone bought into it, including the audience. It was stylised, tongue-in- cheek, irreverent at times, and very post- modern in its referential nature. It didn't pull back from the heartbreak either, we really felt for various characters and those that were left behind. Tugging at the heartstrings and the funny bones in the audience, the production breathed new life into what is Sondheim's most well- worn work. I wish I had seen it earlier in the run so that I could go back and see it again!

Made in Thurles!

The last time I was in Thurles was to see Thurles Musical Society's 'Michael Collins' at the Premiere Hall back in 2019. It was a great show, and I was looking forward to seeing what they would do with 'Made in Dagenham' when I visited again at the end of March this year. 'Made in Dagenham' is based on the famous sewing machinists strike in the Ford factory in London in 1968. The musical, germinated from Nigel Cole's 2010 film, was first staged in 2014 in the Adelphi Theatre. It's a fabulous show, full of rousing choruses and poignant solos with a dramatic book that takes some liberties but is somewhat faithful to the historical events. The story follows factory worker, Rita who becomes a reluctant heroine and labour activist who fights for equal pay for women. This has some negative impacts on her family life as well as on the men who work in the plant. However, her actions and those of her fellow co-workers led to the creation of the Equal Pay Act in 1970.

This is an unusual musical in that it's written like a play or a film, where the dialogue allows for deep character development and the plot is multi-layered and of course it's all based on a true story. Because of the veracity of the story, it becomes even more important for the production to do it justice. That's always the challenge when choosing to stage historical work, that you get it right! Directed and choreographed by Oliver Hurley with musical direction by Mary Rose McNally, with a magnificent set, a recreation of a Ford Motor Factory, looming over the action, almost overshadowing it, this production almost worked.

Mr Hurley's production suffered a little from his cast's delivery, the comic timing was off a bit too and some of lines fell flat. The onstage relationships were quite well drawn though, particularly the relationship between Eddie and the children and the misogynist camaraderie between the shop stewards. The overall pace of the show was quite slow, although enlivened by Mary Rose McNally's superb band. The set was quite stunning, with lots of attention to detail and two half- revolves. Costume and make-up were good, particularly the uniforms and the costumes in the Cortina sequence. But I think the low energy of the cast made the show feel laboured and their intentions seemed to become lost at times. Which is a pity as the script is quite good in a 1970's soap opera meets sitcom kind of way, and the story is poignant and very important historically.

Mary Rose McNally conducted a superb band of nine players. Her exceptional efforts helped enliven the production, which was at times a little inert. Ms McNally's work with the chorus was also splendid, eliciting nice harmonies and power from her singers, particularly on the Act I closer "Everybody Out" and "Stand Up". It's not a big dance show as such but there are a few moments where it moves. Choreographer Oliver Hurley worked within the abilities of his cast and created some interesting and well-executed sequences. Mostly, it was simple steps and hand/arm gestures, which worked well. The two big dance numbers; "This is America" and "Cortina!" looked great, again relatively simple moves but done with pizzazz!

Heading up the cast and playing the heroine of the hour was Fiona Delaney who played Rita. Her journey from working mum to Labour activist is well written and although Ms Delaney did underplay her a bit, she did convince. Her singing was good, especially on "Stand Up" at the end of the show and her delivery of Connie's speech was moving. Playing her husband, Eddie, was John Hayes who's singing on "The Letter" was full of emotion. His onstage relationship with the kids, a very confident Éanna Hayes as Graham and Fladh Hayes as Sharon, was excellent. They had a natural chemistry together and the father/children dynamic was brilliant played as was their naturalistic relationship with Rita. Mr Hayes and Ms Delaney worked well together, they showed a realism in their relationship and were quite believable. I really liked their scene in Act II where they meet in the park with the kids and agree to disagree, it was very touching.

Back at the factory, Rita was surrounded by a group of wise-cracking friends headed up by the foul-mouthed Beryl played with assurance by Mary Callanan. Cass, the wannabe pilot was played by Siobhan King and Sandra the aspiring model was played by Therese Murphy. Denise King played the totally inarticulate Clare, whose song "Wossname" was brilliantly delivered, and her comic timing was spot-on. For me, this was possibly the best performance in the show. This friend group accompanied Rita on her journey peppering it with lewd humour and good intentions. Another of Rita's friends was Shop Steward Connie played by Nina Scott, who sang "Same Old Story" with a restrained passion. She had a gentleness but yet was fierce in her commitment. Connie became Rita's mentor and encouraged her to fight for equal pay. Connie's one time lover Monty, played by a self-possessed Barry Derby, joined them in their fight for justice against the bosses.

Heading up the bosses was Mr Hopkins, played by a very prim and proper John Butler. His management staff, Production Manager Ron Macer, played by Gerry O'Hagan and HR Director Mr Hubble played by Geraint Flyer were old school sexists who feared the top dog Mr Tooley, an American flown over to "sort out the Brits". Mr Tooley made a great entrance in Act II, he was played by Frank Tuohy who sang "This is America" complete with a large cast of stereotypically dressed US Citizens. This was a very strange sequence in an otherwise quite naturalistic show, but it was fun, and Mr Tuohy nailed the song.

Mr Hopkins long-suffering wife Lisa was wonderfully played by Deirdre Hayes complete with RP accent and upper-class mannerisms. She rebelled against the bosses and helped Rita and Co in their fight for equal rights. This fight went all the way up to parliament and involved the Prime Minister, Harold Wilson delightfully played by Brendan Bailey, who gave us just the right amount of buffoonery and sang hilariously on "Always a Problem". His Transport Secretary, Barbara Castle was here played by Linda Ryan who invited Rita and Co into her office where she regaled them with a perfectly sung "An Ideal World", definitely the song of this production. Suffice to say Rita with the help of Barbara and indeed Mr Wilson, did manage to change how women were treated in the work force with the instigation of the Equal Pay Act 1970. This production was good, it told the story very well and whilst some of the gags fell flat and there was a low energy running through the show, it did often engage us. It just didn't have the chutzpah, the boldness that it deserved. Costumes and make-up were good, and lighting and sound were excellent, and the set was almost like another character, it was so expressive and expertly stage managed by Anthony Kirby. Mr Hurley did some great work with the ensemble; they were on point and thanks to Ms McNally they sounded marvellous. But I think some of the principals may have struggled to fully engage with character and appeared a bit lost at times and this had knock-on effect which stymied others. That said, the final song "Stand Up" was rousing with superb harmonies and pace that raised the roof. It's just a pity it didn't happen at the beginning, it may have permeated through the whole show.

The last time I was in Ballinasloe was to see 'Sister Act' produced by Ballinasloe Musical Society back in 2019. The Society continued their love of nuns with this year's offering of 'The Sound of Music' staged in the Town Hall Theatre in March of this year. It was directed by Declan Kelly with Shane Farrell on musical direction duties and choreographed by Aoife McClafferty. This is probably the world's best-known musical, mostly thanks to Robert Wise's 1965 film starring Julie Andrews and Christopher Plummer. The musical tells the story of Maria, who takes a job as a governess to a large family of seven children while she decides whether to become a nun. She falls in love with the children and their widowed father, Captain von Trapp. He is ordered to accept a commission in the German navy, but he opposes the Nazis, so they flee to Switzerland leaving their privileged life behind.

One of the challenges of staging 'The Sound of Music' is not falling into the film to stage trap, that is; trying to recreate the film on stage with your actors emulating the screen actor's interpretation of the characters. Most productions do fall into the trap. Of course, it's not necessarily a bad thing because the film was so successful and the characterisations were excellent, so 'if it worked for them it'll work for us' seems most often the case in staging the musical.

The character of Maria is central to this show, she must be playful, charismatic, wilful, and warm with a hint of piety. Most interpretations of Maria choose to play her with received pronunciation, like Ms Andrews used, and this one was no exception. Playing Maria, we had Emer Kelly who sounded like Julie Andrews, from her RP accent right up to her singing. Ms Kelly didn't show the tomboyish side of the character much, which was a pity as she is meant to arrive in the Von Trapp household like a 'whirling dervish'. Her singing was excellent on all of her songs from the title number right up to the concert. Her duets with Liesl and the Mother Abbess were superb and her duet with Georg was good. So, it was a different interpretation of Maria, which is to be applauded, in that she was more serious, more 'grown up'. This characterisation made the love affair with the strait-laced Georg more realistic. Padraic McDonagh's Captain Von Trapp was stiff and authoritarian, yet he showed the character's morality and ethics with passion. His chemistry with the children was excellent and he worked well with Max in particular. They had a very natural onstage relationship. His singing was good especially on "Edelweiss", where the emotion of the song overtook him and his dynamic with Maria was quite realistic. The Von Trapp children always steal the show in every version I've seen, especially Gretl. This production was no different in that regard, the children were uniformly excellent. Whilst their ages were slightly different in real life and they didn't quite have the 'steps of the stairs' look, it didn't matter as they had a lovely energy and great voices. Liesl, the oldest, was played by Izzy Tuohy who was a lovely charismatic performer. She lit up the stage when she entered. Her dynamic with the other children was good as were her scenes with Rolf and Maria. Her singing was sweet, and she had a gorgeous tone to her voice, especially on "Sixteen Going on Seventeen (Reprise)" with Maria - they blended beautifully. Harry Greaney's Friedrich was also very good, he sang with passion and accuracy and had a good chemistry with Kurt and the other children. Eva Bergin's Louisa never wavered, when she was on, she was 'on'. Her singing and dancing were excellent, and she really impressed. Ronan Harney's Kurt had an excellent voice, even eliciting well-deserved applause when he sang the high notes in "goodbye' during "So Long, Farewell". His Kurt was cheeky and like Ms Bergin, one hundred percent 'on'. Teagan Farrell's Brigitta had good timing as an actor especially in the scene with Maria, where she tells her that Georg is in love with her. That scene can be quite difficult, but she nailed it. Eve McCourt's Marta was also good and nicely played as was Anna Morrissey's Gretl who had a great focus and was the audience's favourite. All the Von Trapp children were well directed, and each character was nicely defined.

The nuns in the Abbey were plentiful and we got to know a few during the show. The Mother Abbess was played by Sarah Corcoran who had a smoky jazzy voice, which gave a freshness to her character's songs. The duet with Maria, with a bit of a sing off at the end of "My Favourite Things" I loved as I did "Climb Ev'ry Mountain", a showstopper at the end of Act I. Her Mother Abbess was kind and understanding and clearly in Maria's corner. The three nuns who sang "How Do You Solve a Problem Like Maria"; Sisters Margaretta, Bertha and Sophia were also fine. Rachel Walker as Sister Margaretta stepped into the role at the last minute and had a feistiness and energy; Lisa Whyte as Sister Berthe was stern and prudish, and Fiona Scerri was a calm Sister Sophia. They bounced well off each other and had a nice dynamic.

Back in the Von Trapp mansion, the captain's fiancé, Elsa, was played by an imperious Megan Lohan. She was every inch the high-born Baroness, who wanted to appease the Nazis rather than fight for freedom. Her relationship with Georg was natural and she had a lovely elegance and sophistication. Her comrade in arms was Max, Georg's friend, and organiser of the choral concert. Played by an avuncular Seamus Feerick, who sang with gusto on "How Can Love Survive" and "No Way to Stop It" and was great at the opening of Act II with the children. He also held the stage well in the concert scene, as the MC. Servants, Frau Schmitt and Franz were played by Gretl Sullivan and Patrick Hanrahan. Both performers were good and held the stage well. Finally, we had Rolf, Liesl's paramour, played by David O'Grady who was great at the beginning when he was courting Liesl, he was gentle and was clearly besotted with her and sang well on "Sixteen Going on Seventeen" with her.

Musical direction by Shane Farrell was excellent. It was bouncy and full of life thanks to his interpretation and conducting. The nun's chorus sounded good on "Preludium" and his work with the children was superb. Aoife McClafferty gave us the dance routines on this show, however on "Sixteen Going on Seventeen" the dance between Rolf and Liesl seemed to be very short. "So Long, Farewell" was cute and nicely performed by the young performers as was "Do-Re-Mi", a highlight of the show. The Ländler was another nice bit of choreography, particularly between Maria and the Captain as they got physically closer. Set was provided by Tony Finnegan, Festival Productions. It was a simple affair; a permanent raised platform upstage with three sets of threads leading up to it. It was changed from the Abbey to the Von Trapp mansion quite quickly. Derek Recks looked after the sound on the show. It was good and we could hear everything quite well. Ronan Kenny from Roken Lighting designed the lighting, which was okay. The stage was well lit and there were some nice states. However, the wedding procession through the centre aisle in the auditorium wasn't lit at all, which was a shame. Pat McGann Productions provided the costumes overseen by Eithne Blackwell. The nun's habits were good and the adults in the Von Trapp house looked great. I liked Elsa's costumes, very elegant, and Georg's suit looked good. The kid's uniforms and play clothes looked perfect. Jacinta Keane looked after hair and make-up and did a splendid job here. The make-up was perfect throughout and the kid's hair was flawless - great plaits!

Director Declan Kelly's tight production was light and fluffy, focusing on the development of the romantic relationship between Maria and Georg - everything else in the show was delegated to a sub- plot. There was no sense of drama from Herr Zeller, or the Admiral or the few Hitler Youth in the audience. The Hitler salutes were more like Black Power salutes as they used a fist rather than the hand outstretched, this was not only inaccurate but diluted the impact of Franz and Rolf being turned towards fascism. We never felt fearful for the family, and we didn't get that contrast between good and evil. The scene in the garden when Rolf arrives looking for the family was very swift so there was no anxiety built in what is written as a very tense scene. That said, it was a very bouncy production with lovely vocals from most of the cast and it was different from the film, and I think that the good reaction of the audience on the night I attended attested to the success of the production.

show_raw: Joseph And The Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat
review_text:
Go, Go, Go Banbridge!

Banbridge Musical Society prides itself on nurturing new talent and giving every member a place in their shows. Their production of Lloyd-Webber's Joseph... was no exception. With a cast of over fifty performers on stage at the Market Place Theatre, the cast rocked the place, and their infectious energy made the audience dance, sing, clap, and cheer. It was a unique take on the biblical tale of Jacob and his many sons that shunned the fourth wall and the drama of the story in favour of showcasing the cast and their love for the music. It was a good choice from director Ian Milford, who was also musical director on the show, to play it for laughs and add in contemporary references and expose the absurdity of the book.

Mr Milford's musical direction was great. His band of ten players clearly enjoyed providing accompaniment to the singing and were clapping along and were really engaged with the music. Mr Milford's conducting was top notch, he even at times spoke and argued with the cast on stage. The children's choir were super and managed some tricky harmonies on "Close Every Door". Highlights for me included the three degree-like presentation of "A Pharaoh's Story" with the three narrators, "Benjamin Calypso" with the brothers, the Elvis inspired "Song of the King" and "Go, Go, Go Joseph" which was full of disco motivated energy that had the audience singing and clapping along into the interval. I could even hear some of the audience singing this during the interval as they snacked out on sugary drinks! Jordan Rosborough's choreography was very simple for the most part but managed to include a number of different styles. From the French Café tango-esque of "Those Canaan Days" to the Country and Western hoedown/line dancing of "One More Angel in Heaven" to the pure disco of "Go, Go, Go Joseph". Each dance was infused with a youthful energy and was brilliantly rehearsed, and I loved the simple hand gestures of the children's chorus during the songs.

Like many eponymously titled shows, the success of a show often rests on the portrayal of the hero. Daniel May is a very versatile performer as proven here in his portrayal of Joseph. He is the epitome of a triple-threat, good dance, singing and acting plus a winning charisma that shines out to the audience. His performance of Joseph was in keeping with the lampooned nature of the show and he never took it too seriously, which was perfect. His singing on "Close Every Door" was masterful, with a pristine final high note that soared around the theatre. But it was his charming smile and how he made everything he did look easy that made the audience empathise with his Joseph, despite the parodic nature of the show. Playing the narrators, we had Kayla Lennon and Claire Costello. Both performers sang with great passion and talent and owned the stage, as did Aimee McVeigh, who joined them in a Three Degrees like presentation of "A Pharoah's Story". This was the song of the night as all three are brilliant singers and know how to deliver a song. Classy stuff. Ms McVeigh also played the lustful Mrs Potiphar with a lovely abandon! Daryll Galloghly played her cuckold husband, Mr Potiphar, like a Wall Street banker, all sharp suit and tech savvy with his MacBook and as Gad, another of Joseph's brothers, he was a vital part of the ensemble.

Playing the above-mentioned Pharoah, who is written as an Elvis like character (this is early Lloyd-Webber, where he chucked all of his ideas into each show!), we had Ruairi McAlinden. Mr McAlinden is that rare breed of actor in that he is a chameleon and literally becomes the character as theatregoers in this area of the country know. He could easily take up a side line as an Elvis Presley impersonator as he absolutely nailed his portrayal of the Pharoah. His singing and movement during "Song of the King" was pure Elvis, even down to the arthritic knee and the white jumpsuit! As one of Joseph's brothers, Ruben he was notable for his stagecraft - he was always on point - and his singing. Great performance. Playing Joseph's father, Jacob, we had Jim McGuigan. Mr McGuigan had a gravitas as Jacob. He was just as mischievous as his sons early in the show, taking selfies and larking about with them. Then mourning the loss of Joseph, he showed a poignant sadness in the character. A nicely pitched performance from Mr McGuigan and very well cast.

An exuberant ensemble made up of adults, teenagers and children gave this production a vitality that bounced it off the stage. They were totally on point with their movement and singing and were exhausting to watch, but also a joy to behold! There was a wonderful sense of community about this show, everybody seemed to be having a great time on stage and this permeated into the audience. A big congratulations must go to stage manager, Andrew McKnight for his crowd control on such a large cast of all ages. Also, he and his crew were invisible on the transitions, which were quick and accurate as were the many fly cues. Both Mr McKnight and Ian Milford designed the set, which was great. Because of the large cast it wasn't a big production in terms of scenery, but I liked the painted floor and the various drops of pyramids, camels, jail bars etc and the nightclub sign 'PHAROAHS' was brilliant as a backdrop to "Song of the King". The treads upstage worked well for the children, who were always on stage, and to create another level when needed.
