A fake psychic medium, Oda Mae, can hear him, much to her surprise and he convinces her that Molly is in danger from the man who attacked them. So begins his quest to save Molly from the attacker and the man who employed him. The licence to produce this show includes projection files, so that it will look similar to the original show, but director Derek Shannon decided to not use them and to try, with set designer Ray Shannon, to create the spectral special effects live in real time. I applaud this decision as it really made this production quite magical and unique, and not a direct visual copy of the original. Ray Shannon's set design was quite imposing; a series of vertical stanchions with louver dressing and huge cross-pieces bisecting the playing area. Upstage was mostly in darkness throughout the show allowing performers to almost materialise on stage. A cross- section of a subway train was used for the important station scenes and Molly's apartment was set and struck by stage hands dressed as removal men in brown coats. A small bedroom was built on the stage right apron with a ramp leading into the 'apartment'. Oda Mae's consulting room was cleverly created by affixing a heavy drape across the up-stage centre exit. This was a very cleverly designed set, which made good use of the stage depth. However, the real surprise was when Sam apparently walked through the solid door, parts of him disappearing as he pushed through. This got gasps and a round of applause from the audience.

As Sam, Cormac Malone gave us a warm, likeable character with commitment issues. Refusing to say the three little words Molly longed to hear, he nonetheless portrayed the character's protective nature, in life and as a spirit, with a strong assurance. Mr Malone played his spirit's anguish and helplessness with palpable emotional intensity and channelled this poignancy into his singing. The ubiquitous "Unchained Melody" was sung by Sam a number of times, most effectively when he lampooned it on acoustic guitar. "Here Right Now", the opening number was nicely sung by Sam and Molly with Carl and "Three Little Words" was excellent. Molly was played by Ashley Doran in a highly emotional performance. She portrayed Molly's journey from a happy young woman in love with life and her art to a grieving, frightened nervous wreck with a fine proficiency. Her singing was also very emotive, particularly on "With You", where the free tissues certainly came in handy as she brought the house down in a beautiful rendition of this, the song of the show. Sam's colleague Carl was played by Cian O'Dowd in another super performance. He played Carl's guilt and desperation with a high tension and his fear of Sam's spirit was tangible. He sang with passion on "More" and really personified the high achieving businessman with an obvious drug problem.

After Sam was fatally injured, he travelled to the hospital, where we saw the mortal remains of Sam on a gurney. He met a ghost in the hospital, played by Declan Taylor who told him that he was indeed dead. Mr Taylor sang "You Gotta Let Go", with the ensemble as grey-clad spirits, a song imploring Sam to pass on. Mr Taylor really looked the part in his three-piece suit, hat and cane, like a New Orleans gentleman. He had a fine voice and performed with a lovely refined dignity and I felt I wanted to know his backstory. Sam spotted his assailant, Willie, and followed him to his apartment. Played by Nicholas Flynn as a Latino character, Willie was hired by Carl to assault Sam and get his computer pass-codes not to kill him. Not having the codes Willie planned to visit Molly to get them from the apartment. Mr Flynn played him with a menace but also as a weak-willed small-time crook. Frustrated with being unable to interject or interact with Molly to save her from Willie, Sam called upon a psychic medium called Oda Mae to help him.

Joanne McCabe's comedic portrayal of Oda Mae was fantastic. Bearing in mind Whoopi Goldberg's iconic performance in the film, Ms McCabe did well to fill her shoes and her performances of "Are You a Believer?" and "I'm Outta Here" were the real showstoppers of the production. Attended on by her 'minders', Louise and Clara; hilariously played by Kerrie Campbell and Bronagh Hogan respectively, and Ortisha played by Carmel Rowe, Ms McCabe embraced the African American idioms of the character's speech and her timing was razor sharp. When she realised that she could actually commune with the dead, her reactions were comic gold. A stand-out performance from Ms McCabe. A special mention must go to the client Oda Mae was fleecing, Mrs Santiago as played by Niamh Bolger. Ms Bolger's characterisation was full of nervous tics and broken-English, barely holding it together as she tried to commune with the dead through Oda Mae. At the end of "Are You a Believer?", she released this amazing voice that soared around the theatre!  Sam also met a Subway Ghost and convinced him to teach him how to move corporal objects. This ghost was played by Seán O'Brien in a physically powerful performance, quite scary and clearly deranged. His song "Focus" was brilliantly performed, full of anger and bitterness.  Edward Hayden played the soft-spoken minister at Sam's funeral in a nicely judged performance.

This was a strangely uplifting production, give the subject matter. It celebrated everlasting love and, in a sense was a morality tale of good vs evil. When the bad characters died, they were taken down into the orchestra pit (standing in for Hell, I assume) by black clad demon dancers, whereas Sam eventually walked into bright light. The musical direction by Philip Kennedy was exquisite, lovely interpretations of the score. The band of nine were superb, particularly Kevin Kennedy's piano and Tomás Kavanagh's trumpet and the reeds and strings were gorgeous. Mr Kennedy's chorus work was also quite good, particularly on "Are You a Believer?", "I'm Outta Here", "Talkin' 'Bout A Miracle" and "More". Anne-Marie Cooney's choreography was very suitable for the production, the scary demons were very reptilian and the bigger numbers: "Are You a Believer?", "I'm Outta Here" and "More" were well-drilled and fun. Stage manager, Mark Hayden and his crew kept everything moving along nicely. Lighting by Anthony Quinn was excellent and sound by Abe Scheele, whilst a little underpowered and slightly off-balanced at times, was quite good.

Director Derek Shannon created a fairly unique version of Ghost. His flair for comedy was very evident in Oda Mae's scenes but he also had a fine touch with Sam and Molly's relationship. The pace was quite slow because of the many transitions, but it certainly picked up at the end. The special effects and set design were seamlessly integrated into what was a magical night at the theatre.

produced Sister Act in DCU in March. Government restrictions because of the Covid-19 virus meant that sadly the show had to close after just two performances. I attended the second and final show. The musical was adapted from the 1992 film of the same name in 2006 and has become a firm favourite of societies all over the world. If one were to sit down and brainstorm what elements make up a perfect musical, Sister Act would score quite highly I suspect, with singing nuns, a contrived love story, sweaty cops, incompetent gangsters and a singer who dreams of Broadway stardom. The only things missing are kids and a small dog with a cute name.

Set in 1978 at the height of the Disco explosion, the score, by Disney regular Alan Menken, is awash with synths and pounding disco beats and also, as it mostly all takes place in a nunnery, some ecclesiastical mashed up hymns and a couple of power ballads. The plot centres around singer Deloris Van Cartier, who when auditioning to perform in a gangster's club witnesses a murder. She runs to the cops who hide her away in a local convent. Whilst here she takes charge of the nun's choir, injecting some 1970's attitude into their performances. They become famous, appear on television where the gangsters see her and break into the convent to kill her. The characters are all very one dimensional, almost cartoons, but that doesn't matter as the music is great with jiving nuns singing euphorically.

Superbly directed by Ciarán Mooney (above)with upbeat musical direction from Dermot O'Callaghan and wonderful choreography by Serena Salmon, this was a feelgood show that had the audience dancing in their seats. It looked great with fabulous costumes and stand-out performances from Bronwyn Andrews as Deloris and Emma Stack as Sr Mary Robert. Dermot O'Callaghan's musical arrangements of the score were super. It was funky and loud and brash with thumping disco beats from bass and percussion and sharp and powerful brass. His work with the chorus was excellent, power and intricate harmonies on all of the bigger numbers and delicacy on the ballads. Serena Salmon's choreography was also very good, the nun's routines were well drilled and accurate. However, the choreography with the homeless people on "I Could Be That Guy" was really excellent, it was sharp and perfectly performed.

As Deloris, Bronwyn Andrews really impressed. Her voice was perfectly suited to the songs and she performed them with an apparent ease. Most of her numbers were fast disco-diva songs, which she did really well but the title song, "Sister Act" was a slowed down ballad where she really shone. It was beautifully performed and quite poignant. Ms Andrew's Deloris was very likeable, her voice reminiscent of Ms Streisand at times, and she had great empathy with the character. Her onstage relationships were well- developed, particularly with Eddie and Sr Mary Robert and she had a good love/hate dynamic with Aisling Green Madden's Mother Superior. Ms Green Madden gave us a very compassionate Mother Superior. She played the comedy quite well but it was in the character's inner conflict where she really excelled; despairing of the changes Deloris made in the convent, yet knowing they were necessary for it to continue. Her singing on the Sondheim inspired "I Haven't Got A Prayer" and the Disneyesque "Here Within These Walls" was excellent, full of intent and expression. Deloris' backing singers; Michelle and Tina were played by Nicole Kelly and Eva Kelly respectively. They had really good dance skills and fine vocals and looked the part in their wigs and perfect Abba'esque costumes.

When Deloris went to the police to report the murder she witnessed, she was surprised to meet Eddie Souther, a classmate from her youth. He was now a police lieutenant and promised to help her by putting her in a witness protection programme and placing her in the sanctuary of a local convent The Queen of Angels. I really liked Seán McMahon's Eddie. He was an accident prone, bumbling, nervous character who was clearly besotted with Deloris. His slapstick was well played and he had a nice voice on "I Could Be That Guy" and "Fabulous Baby (reprise)". Curtis Jackson, the gangster who wanted to kill Deloris, was played by Eddie Brady who had a very strong stage presence and sang well on "When I Find My Baby" with his henchmen. These guys were hilarious, with bad wigs and moustaches, jewellery and tight pants - they were everything bad about the 70's and the performers knew it and milked it. TJ, the more stupid one and Curtis' nephew, was played by Maurice Treacy with big rings and a bigger gormless smile, his timing was brilliant; Art McGauran played Joey, a wannabe lady's man and Curtis' lieutenant who also had good timing and a strutting physicality and the lithe Paolo Garau who played Pablo with a sensuous reptilian oiliness that really worked. All three sang brilliantly on "Lady in the Long Black Dress", a pastiche on bands like Tavares, Kool and the Gang and Barry White. This was a highlight of the show as it was so self-depreciatingly funny. They had great comic timing and were like a 70's version of the Three Stooges, complete with prat falls and misplaced macho posturing. At the convent, Deloris lived and sang with the nuns who, before she arrived had appalling voices but were devoted to God and the church. Deloris took over musical direction of the choir from Sr Mary Lazarus, played by Ruth Slattery who had great frowning facial expressions and a sarcastic lilt to every line she uttered. Ms Slattery was great and had a subtle comedy. The highly excitable Sr Mary Patrick was played by Niamh Walsh in a performance that was exhausting to watch. She never sat still, bobbing up and down in her seat and jiggling about when standing. A wonderfully comic performance from Ms Walsh. Deloris took a particular interest in the postulant Sr Mary Robert as she couldn't understand why one so young would choose such a life. Emma Stack gave a superb performance as Sr Mary Robert, full of innocence and devotion yet curious about Deloris' life on the outside. She sang "The Life I Never Led" with such stunning emotion and beautiful expression that it had the audience in tears and on their feet. A showstopping moment that illustrated Ms Stack's wonderful singing voice and acting talent.  Pat McElwain stepped out from behind his well-worn director's chair to take on the role of Monsignor O'Hara and actually gave the fire speech at the top of the show. His O'Hara was very Spencer Treacy, pure Irish-American with a knowing twinkle in the eye and a firm grasp of the lucrative financial possibilities that the public interest in his nuns may bring. Mr McElwain had a light touch in his characterisation and was very funny as the nun's MC.

Stage management by Gerry McCann was good, with relatively quick transitions and accurate setting. The set was hired in from Scenic Projects and looked great, especially the stained-glass cloths and enormous holy statue. Lighting by Denis Twomey was good and sound by Jason Fallon very full, well-balanced and disco- loud. Costume, hair and make-up design was perfect, like watching an old Scorsese film; big hair, garish make-up, flares and moustaches.

Director Ciarán Mooney really got to the heart of this show and laid it all out for his audience to enjoy. It was funny and at times, poignant. The music and singing was first-class and the choreography was excellent. It looked good and had some great performances. It's a pity it only ran for two performances because it deserved a much longer run and would have only got better.

The Sounds of the Earth are Like Music Rogers and Hammerstein's Oklahoma! is said to have been one of the first successful book musicals, that is where the music, songs and dance are fully integrated into the drama of the story and help progress the plot. It opened on Broadway in 1943 to universal critical and public acclaim and ran for over two thousand performances, a feat unheard of in its day.  The musical is based on Lynn Riggs' 1931 play, Green Grow the Lilacs. Set in farm country outside the town of Claremore, it tells the story of farm girl Laurey Williams and her courtship by two rival suitors, nice guy Curly McLain and the sinister, Jud Fry.

This November, Carnew Musical Society presented Oklahoma!

as their 53rd production since they formed, at St Bridget's Hall in Carnew. The Hall was dressed with Americana and the ushers wore costumes of the period (1906), complete with Stetsons. This was the third time the society have presented the show. Previous productions were staged in 1978 and 1996 and some of those casts were in the 2019 version we saw this year.

Oklahoma! was considered a modernist piece when it was first staged, the inclusion of a 15 minute dream ballet was very daring at the time as was the love triangle between the Persian (Iranian) Ali, the seductive Ado and lovesick Will. There are any number of ways a director can approach a classic musical, but they can be distilled down to two basic concepts: either you play it as written with no contemporary intervention, as if the intervening years and social advances have not occurred or you can stage a revisionist production, where a modern sensibility can be applied. Director Michael Dunbar, went with the traditional telling of the show, but he definitely increased the dramatic tension and underlying violence of the other love triangle between Curly, Jud and Laurey. He created a sense of palpable menace on stage whenever Jud entered and even those who knew the show quite well were on the edge of their seats when he appeared.

Farmgirl Laurey Williams was played with confidence and assurance by Erin Hogan. She had an elegance coupled with a down to earth quality to her performance that was quite engaging. She also had good stillness in her performance that hinted that all was not as it seemed. Her singing was admirable, particularly on "Many a New Day" and "People Will Say We're in Love". She played Laurey as quite disengaged, seemingly relatively indifferent to Curly's advances initially and we were left wondering if she only chose him to get away from Jud. Ms Hogan's performance differed to that of the rest of the cast in that she, even more than Jud, was like an outsider in the community. She seemed to be playing a role within a role, which made her fascinating to watch. Laurey's aunt, Aunt Eller, had brought up her niece by herself, and with her (and a series of itinerant farmhands, of which Jud was the latest) had run her farm successfully in 'a man's world'.  She was played by Jennifer Byrne as a tough, no nonsense frontierswoman, handy with a gun but yet good-hearted. Ms Byrne showed probably the highest status on stage, demonstrated when she fired a gun to quell the distrust between "The Farmer and the Cowman" and railroaded the Federal Marshall in Act Two.

As Curly, Padraig D'Arcy played him as cocky and smart but also with an extreme cruel streak. His scenes with Laurey were quite soppy but sweet but his scenes with Jud, particularly the "Pore Jud is Daid" scene, showed an unpleasant side to his nature. This was an excellently paced scene by Mr Dunbar, full of tension and threatened violence, and both actors played it brilliantly. Mr D'Arcy opened the show with a fine rendition of "Oh, What a Beautiful Morning" his voice spiralling over the auditorium in perfect pitch. A very good performance.

The final character in this tragic love triangle was Jud Fry, played by John Young.

Mr Young's characterisation of Jud was mesmerising. He brought a real danger to the stage, a tangible undercurrent of violence under a cloud of psychosis. He gave a chilling performance of "Lonely Room" where he outlined his intentions towards Laurey. But Mr Young also skilfully managed to create empathy for Jud, we felt that he was possibly misunderstood a bit even though he all but admitted to a previous murder he may have committed, by showing a vulnerability and possible mental disability. A multi-layered performance of some note.

Choreographer Frances Ryan did a marvellous job in re-creating Agnes De Mille's original choreography for the Dream Dance sequence, it was quite amazingly danced, predominantly by Lauren Byrne and Richard O'Toole. Other more traditional dances were also well choreographed by Ms Ryan. Musical director Lar Duffy conducted a very good twelve-piece orchestra of brass, reeds and strings, giving the music a lushness. The more comic love story was between a travelling peddler Ali, the playful Ado Annie and cowboy Will. These scenes were played with a light touch, fitting the more traditional nature of the sub plot. Ali Hakim, a kind of snake oil salesman, was played by Rónán P. Byrne in a delightfully funny sleazy performance. He was quite endearing in the role, and didn't overdo the accent or mannerisms. His performance of "It's a Scandal, it's an Outrage" was very funny and I liked his physical comedy and timing. He fell for Ado Annie, an innocent naïve flirty young girl played with great energy by Ellie Willoughby. Her performance of "I Can't Say No" was excellent. Her Father, Andrew, was nicely played by Sean Hallahan, who excelled at shotgun brandishing. The final side of this triangle was Will Parker, a non-too bright cowboy, played by Graham Finnerty. Mr Finnerty had great comic timing and duetted with Ado on "All 'er Nothing", where he sang quite well.

Laurey ended up with Curly, Ado ended up with Will and Ali ended up married to daft Gertie Cummings, excellently played by Miriam Murphy, who's laugh was piercing and all too frequent! Sadly, Jud ended up dead. Killed by Curly in defence of Laurey at their wedding reception. Local Federal Marshall Cord Elam, strongly played by Jimmy Spellacy, suggested that a proper trial should be held but the townsfolk, led With the cancellation of many shows the following are the ones that have been adjudicated and eligible for nomination Gilbert Section Ballinrobe Musical Society Pirates Of Penzance Ballywillan Drama Group, Portrush Whistle Down The Wind Banbridge Musical Society The Wizard Of Oz Bravo Musical Theatre, Loughrea Michael Collins - A Musical Drama Carnew Musical Society Oklahoma!

Carrick-On-Suir Musical Society by Aunt Eller decided to hold the trial there and then as they didn't wish to disrupt the honeymoon! Curly is found innocent and they all celebrated. Justice was served. Indeed.

This production looked gorgeous, mainly thanks to lighting designer Kevin McEvoy who used a range of warm colours both onstage and on the back wall to evoke the sun-soaked prairie lands. Set by Tony Barry was simple, a cabin stage left and a smokehouse stage right, with bits and bobs brought on and off. Costumes were hired from NoMac and there was a formidable team of make-up artists and hairstylists involved in the creation of the characters.  Sound by Joe Murphy was a little too full of reverb on the dialogue scenes I felt but the band sounded full and powerful.

This was a very good production by director Michael Dunbar and his creatives, enlivened by some stand-out performances and a solid ensemble. It looked sumptuous, the orchestrations were lavish and the chorus big and strong. The dramatic intention of the story was also well-realised and the comedy landed just right.

I have worked on the production team for this musical on several occasions and can honestly say, I've never tired of it. Guys & Dolls for me, was what I've never classed as work, it was simply fun. You could go into the rehearsal room feeling deflated and tired, yet two hours later, bound out the door humming the show tunes. This timeless classic set in Old New York has held its popularity for over 50 years with generations of theatre-goers. It has what is referred to as the 'feel-good factor', with catchy songs and likeable characters. It provides a perfect two hours of escapism delivering infectious toe-tapping tunes and many fine comedic moments, all partnered with beautiful heart-warming ballads such as, 'I've Never Been in Love Before', and big band numbers such as 'Sit Down You're Rockin' the Boat'.

Guys & Dolls opened at the 46th Street Theatre in New York on November, 24th 1950 and proceeded to sell a staggering 1,200 performances. To this day it is claimed to be one of the most produced musicals by amateur theatre societies around the world and the fifth longest running Broadway musical. With music and lyrics by Frank Loesser and book by Jo Swerling and Abe Burrows, this Tony Award winning musical was also adapted into a film in 1955 starring Marlon Brando, Jean Simmons, Frank Sinatra and Vivian Blaine. 'Sit Down You're Rocking the Boat' is certainly a  show stopper but I would have paid dearly to have witnessed Ewan McGregor sing 'Luck Be a Lady Tonight' when he played Sky Masterson in the 2005 production in the Piccadilly Theatre Production!

The cast and crew of Trinity Musical Theatre certainly know how to make an audience feel good! As we were ushered to our seats by the TMT Chairperson Hugh Kelly, the buzz in the theatre was jovial. Trinity students, friends and family members all gathered to support these amazing young people, who were eagerly prepping backstage. As we settled, we had the visual of a plush red curtain and in front of that, sixteen young orchestra members, all tuning their chosen instruments. The energy in the room was simply amazing.

The overture kicked off with a bang and as the curtain opened, we were greeted by a busy street scene of bustling New Yorkers. The stage was aflutter with young, vibrant actors. Trumpets loudly sounded as if a horse race was about to commence and Nicely Nicely, Benny Southstreet and Rusty Charlie took centre stage to sing the opening number 'Fugue for Tinhorn'. And so, the story of Guys & Dolls began, introducing us to Nathan Detroit, who runs the illegal crap games in New York, his misfit gambling buddies and his ever-devoted finance of fourteen years Adelaide, a show girl in the Hot Box Club. We also meet Sky Masterson, a high roller and the unexpected girl he falls for, strait- laced missionary worker, Sarah Brown. There are lots of twists and turns in the plot, lots of comedy, beautiful ballads and show stopping musical numbers lending themselves to fine choreography.

Director Colm Lombard helmed a tight production. He distilled an element of realism in his characters which made them very believable and extremely likeable. The production as a whole was fast and furious and travelled along at a great pace. Colm was ably assisted by Erica O'Reilly who, not only professionally commanded her sixteen-piece orchestra but also assisted with the direction on the final run up. The orchestra had a fine string section and the four violinists played beautifully and I must also mention the excellent playing from Rachel Nolan and Martina Rosaria O'Connell on flute. The brass section had a few little wobbles, but overall, good work. The singing from principals and chorus was also to a high standard, in fact there were one or two show stopping moments vocally.

Niamh McDermot was the show choreographer. It was obvious to me from the off Niamh had been trained in this genre. The routines were cleverly assembled with great use of gravity for the crapshooters and male dominated numbers and sweetness and light for the Hot Box Cub dancers with cheeky hips and playful acting. The 'Crapshooters Dance' was the highlight for me, as I watched the cast leap and bound across the stage, in and out of wings at a ferocious speed, exciting and inventive, with fast foot work and energy levels off the scale.

Ashley Cantwell the stage manager probably took cover against a wall or under a table for the Crapshooters dance, but certainly for the rest of the production she was very present and efficiently running the backstage. Sets rotated, opened, reversed and closed with ease never once infringing on the smooth and seamless run of the performance. Ashley also wore the Production Manager's hat, multitasking as a lot of this enthusiastic group of young people seemed to be doing! You really got the feeling of an 'All for One' vibe with this terrific young group. Each and every one gave 110%, moving sets, setting props, acting in quiet moments, singing, dancing and smiling their way through the two hours of highly entertaining theatre.

Playing Adelaide Adams was the fabulous Rachel Galvin. I always say with characters like Adelaide, it lies on a knife's edge, it can be never enough or just way too much, it's hitting the right balance that proves problematic sometimes. I have seen the 'way too much' version a few times and have seriously regretted not packing my ear plugs! Rachel needless to say, got this character spot on. Her comic timing and pairing with Nathan, her long standing finance, was comedy gold. Miss Galvin didn't have to speak, her facial expressions and body mannerisms said it all. Then top that off with fine acting and impressive vocals and you've got Adelaide Adams in the bag. 'A Bushel and A Peck' and 'Take Back Your Mink' were high energy and well-polished fun numbers, but the show highlight for me was 'Adelaide's Lament' particularly the reprise which really tugged at the heart strings, as we witnessed poor Adelaide's despair as Nathan once again disappoints her.

Daniel Whelan played the part of Nathan Detroit, a ball of energy flying around the stage, he was unashamedly silly! It takes a lot to make me laugh, but boy did I laugh! Nathan had a telephone conversation with Joey in Act One, trying to convince Joey to let him use his garage for an illegal crap game and I have to say it was one of the funniest scenes I've ever had the pleasure of watching. Mr Whelan's comic timing was sublime, as was his performance in general. The stage chemistry with Adelaide was wonderful and 'Sue Me' was unstoppable! Daniel did not oversell his character; he simply demonstrated his great facility for comedy. Vocals and choreography were also to a high standard. Thank you for the laughs and a big shout out to Joey.

When the Mission band marched onto stage singing ''Follow the Fold' I knew we were in for a treat as we heard the powerful vocals emanating from Hannah McNicholas Roche who played Sarah Brown. Her magnificent soprano voice bounced off the auditorium walls, much to the delight and appreciation of the audience. Hannah with sublime grace delivered a true portrayal of a young woman falling in love, of course the problem was she was falling in love with a notorious gambler, namely Sky Masterson. David Hannafin was every bit that notorious gambler with a cool and calculated persona and a true gamblers approach to resolving every problem, with a bet! What he didn't bet on was falling in love with Mission Doll, Sarah Brown! David provided rich vocals and a solid performance of Masterson.

Nathans two side-kicks, Nicely Nicely Johnston and Benny Southstreet were played by George Rohan and Callum Byrne. These guys were the glue, they appeared everywhere and anywhere, always lending great support and in true comic fashion. Nicely Nicely's song 'Sit Down You're Rockin' the Boat' is one of the best-known numbers in this show and George delivered a standout performance here. Together, with their witty one-liners, they generously embraced their roles and provided scene after scene of crowd- pleasing theatre. Callum's running gag of not having his own hat and persistently taking other cast members hats continually provided laughs and both George and Callum were fine singers and dancers, bringing energy and impact to the musical numbers they participated in. A job well done lads. Arvide Abernathy was played by Anabel Sweeney. This performance was embedded with richness. Stunning vocals and poignant acting giving us a sophisticated and sympathetic Abernathy. Gloria Robberto played General Matilda Cartwright in a strong and governed style. She set out in an orderly fashion, but after 'Rockin' the Boat' she too was rocking the rafters in fine voice and spirit. A quirky and uninhibited performance.

Grace Doyle Flaherty took on Big Jule, the terrifying and threatening card shark, that you do not dare mess with! It was so refreshing to see this role played by a female. Grace was well able, looking stunning in a red suit, she commanded her scenes. Miss Doyle's dancing and pure attack was to also be commended, super stuff. Harry the Horse was well characterised by Tom Dawn. A talented team player and a great asset to the crapshooter's crew. Rusty Charlie was played by another capable young lady, Miss Alba Walsh Subiran. Alba generously embraced the role of Rusty Charlie. 'Fugue for Tinhorn' with Nicely and Benny was a great show opener. I'd like to give a mention to the beautiful air hostess on the flight to Havana, Cuba who delivered the safety flight instructions not only in English but also in Spanish. Excellent. The TMT Chorus, what a gang of enthusiastic, likeminded, young people all pulling together to create this fabulous night's entertainment. TMT generously embraced this production and their pure love of theatre shone from the stage. Vocals and choreography were tight, well- rehearsed and a joy to watch. I commented to Hugh the Society Chairman, that the after-show party would probably resemble the 'Havana' number, which literally was an explosion of wild happiness, fun and enjoyment. But the night's highlight for me personally was the 'Crapshooters Dance'. As a choreographer, I could see the amount of work and planning that went in here. It was exciting and pulsated energy from every pore. Fabulous work.

Lighting was adequate. We had the use of coloured gels which gave the scenes a nice atmosphere. The Havana scene was bright and awash with colour and all set change cues were spot on and tidy. Sound was well balanced between the orchestra and stage. Mics were clear, with no feedback. I did feel the percussion was a little loud at times but overall, a very efficient job, with principals and ensemble receiving satisfactory support.

Set Design by Jordan Brown, assisted by Rachel Sherry Robinson was good. We had the black and white set for New York that later opened up into a colourful Havana set. All pieces rotated, opened and reversed with ease. The sets were moved efficiently by cast members and never infringed on the smooth running of the production. I also liked the way the cast stayed in character, particularly the Hot Box Girls, when striking and setting. Costumes were basic, but well plotted. We had black and white for all the New Yorkers, except principals, who all added a splash of colour. Sky wore blue, Sarah - brown, Nicely - yellow, Benny - orange, Big Jule - red and so on. This was a nice touch. Then when we hit Havana Cuba, we had dancers in multi-coloured Cuban dresses and tourists all colourfully clad. Hair and Makeup could have been more unified. A little more attention to detail was needed in certain areas of this department. On saying that, Adelaide, Abernathy and some of the girls looked stunning.

Props managed by Lindsay Duet were basic, but nevertheless provided efficiently and on cue. I have to mention a very clever ad lib by Daniel Whelan playing Nathan, when Adelaide found herself without the prop which was a letter from her mother, so she handed him the newspaper and he said 'So your mother's writing letters to me in the newspaper now' it was priceless! TMT should be incredibly proud of their Guys & Dolls production. The high level of commitment was obvious and the energy and sheer enjoyment being propelled from the stage was infectious. Delicious humour, striking choreography and sensational singing wrapped up in a youthful perspective. I have lots of lovely memorable moments from this show, thank you TMT and the very best of luck with your next venture.

Fiddler raises the Roof!

Do you honour the traditions of the past or accept the progress of the future? Tevye's line echoes in my head "On one hand" and "On the other hand". He certainly had a fine ability to see both sides of the situation! As for me, there is no decision to ponder on, this was most definitely a fine production. But this musical's narrative hits home with unusual sadness and poignancy, due to the resurgence of recent discord, shadowed by genocide in Ukraine. My eyes filled as I watched the chorus of TMS sing the closing number 'Anatevka'. Men and women, girls and boys, age nine to ninety stood feet planted, heads high, starring out over the audience and the line that sticks with me still is "Soon I'll be a stranger in a strange new place, searching for an old familiar face". Chilling, and a subtle salute, as blue and yellow lights filled the stage on the closing lines of this stunning production. Set in the Pale of Settlement, a region designated for Jews by Russia's Catherine II. Imperial Russia 1905, in a little village named Anatevka lived Tevye, a milkman, his wife Golde and their five beautiful, but strong-willed daughters. We see how modern love struggles with ancient customs and how Tzeitel, Hodel and Chava, Tevye's three eldest daughters, all fall in love with suiters deemed unsuitable. These choices, mixed with the endless suffering of the Jewish community in Anatevka under Russian Imperialism, leads to the gradual disintegration of Tevye and Golde's poor but once happy family.

Featuring a cast of 57, the mix of youth and experience on the stage was a beauty to behold. Directed by the talented Paul Norton, who is no stranger to this musical, being nominated in 2003 and winning the Aims Best Actor Award in 2007 for the role of Tevye. The production had been very obviously thought through and this was evident in the attention to detail. The set, lighting and special effects were mesmerising, the music and vocals immaculate, the choreography energetic and creative and the comedy and tragedy both equally in abundance. Mr Norton had a strong team behind him and a strong front line in front of him and this certainly made for a winning combination. The set, designed by John O'Donoghue, constructed by Kenny Ryan and painted by Neil Dwyer was an impressive two- storey fixture with upper windows which were back-lit, lending atmosphere and depth to the space. This wrapped around the stage and blended well into the wings. There was a large barn like building centre back, which the Fiddler perched on top of for the majority of the performance, Miss O'Brien was obviously not afraid of heights! Six tall trees were set on either side and up-lit giving a stark and cold reflection and there were also six Jewish star posts, made out of wood, which were used in different positions, aiding with the scene location. It was an impressive set with multifaceted uses, which were cleverly incorporated into the narrative. 'Tevye's Dream' was very exciting to witness, with Lazar Wolf's dead wife, Fruma Sarah played by Missy Cleary flying above Tevye and Golde in their bed and two separate sets of dancers performing conflicting choreography around them. The lighting, designed by Alan McCormack and operated by Jimmy Spillane was excellent and the standout scene of the night for me was 'Far from the Home I Love', this was sublimely beautiful. Set with Hodel sitting at the train stop, the snow falling, the sound effects of the wind and the steely cold blue lighting. Magical.

The twelve-piece orchestra lead by Mary Rose McNally was exquisite. The brass was particularly strong and I must give a special mention to Margaret Butler and Eva McNally on Violins and Etain McCooey on Oboe, beautiful. Also, a little shout out to the on-stage Fiddler, Anna O'Brien, who actually played her instrument live, while interacting throughout with Tevye's story. The sound for the production was well balanced and clear, with tight cueing and this was down to the Star Systems team. The Stage Manager for the production was Alma Quinn and her team David, Marguerite, Martin and Conor worked efficiently behind the scenes. The hair and makeup were taken care of by Geraldine, Fionnula, Karyn, Aoife and Nora, all these hard-working people insured the cast were well groomed. The costumes were all well presented by Creative Scene Productions and props by Lynda Breen, Denis Fitzgerald and Eileen O'Connor were all well sourced and fitting to the era. The hard-working choreographer for this production was Stephanie Browne. I have worn these shoes for many years, so I am fully aware of the hours of blood, sweat and tears that go into making 57 people move, not just together, but simply in the same direction! So, I say, well done Stephanie, it was obvious from the off the amount of work that went in here. Favourite pieces of choreography had to be 'Chavaleh', and also the fierce Russian dancers with their intricate and fast footwork and fabulous flips. Tremendously energetic work and refreshing to see men embracing such full-bodied choreography.

A show of this calibre requires an accomplished actor for the role of Tevye and that is what we found in Derek Ryan. The work load is immense for this particular character, with Tevye leaving the stage on the rare occasion. Luckily for us, Mr Ryan did not roar his way through the performance, but tastefully juggled comedy and tragedy with style. The show piece of the musical 'If I Were a Rich Man' where Tevye taps into all his hopes and dreams was delicious with humour and masterfully sung. The drama in the scene with Golde where he disowns Chava was piercingly powerful and the scene where he bids Chava farewell, by prompting Tzeitel to tell her "God be with You", was beautifully moving. Derek Ryan with his superb singing and fine acting found the very essence of Tevye, the God-fearing Milkman from Anatevka.

Playing his long-suffering wife was Deirdre Ryan. Deirdre had Golde down, with her dry wit and sarcastic sense of humour, she was an even match for Tevye's constant banter. Deirdre is a fine actor and the delivery of her despair and devastation when Tevye claimed Chava was dead to him was heart-breaking to watch. On a lighter note, favourite of the night had to be 'Do You Love Me' this was charming to observe and a wonderful pairing vocally. The eldest daughter, Tzeitel, was played by Sarah Gillman Gallahue. "Matchmaker, Matchmaker" was a lovely combination of the three sisters singing about what kind of husband they wish for and then the dreaded thought of an old, drunk one was very cleverly acted out. Sarah's chemistry with Motel, the poor tailor, played by James O'Donovan was believable and Mr O'Donovan's interaction with Tevye was highly humorous. The song 'Miracle of Miracles' was very well delivered as was the comic scene when the village came to see the new arrival, the sewing machine! Hodel played by Emma Sunderland gave a convincing performance. With a strong stage presence and a beautiful singing voice, she blended well with Aidan O'Connell, as Perchik. Aidan delivered a commanding character with forte and a will to change the world. 'Now I Have Everything' was a beautiful duet from Emma and Aidan, sincere and truthful. Chava the final sister to fly the nest, was played by Muireann Slattery. Muireann's dance to 'Chavaleh' was spellbinding and she generously embraced her character. A heartfelt moment was when she fell to her knees screaming for her Papa's forgiveness. Miss Slattery's love interest was Russian guard Fyedka. They created a unified pair, very much in love and desperately searching for acceptance.

Yente the matchmaker, what a fun character, played by Siobhan O'Donoghue. The audience really enjoyed this performance from Siobhan, the village gossip, with light fingers. The wealthy butcher Lazar Wolf, who wished to marry Tzeitel was played by Cathal O'Donoghue. Cathal is a fine actor and singer. The musical number 'To Life' with Tevye and the Villagers was a highlight of the production and the drunk scene after, was so believable and hilariously funny to observe. Mai O'Donoghue and Fai Sexton were the two younger daughters, Sprintze and Bielke. These two pretty little ladies were right at home on the stage and I particularly liked the scene where Yente was trying to matchmake them with two younger boys and they spent their time making funny faces at them. Very entertaining. Mordcha played by Jason Ryan and Rabbi played by Kieran Hickey, both contributed greatly as key players and raised quite a few laughs throughout the night. Aaron O'Donoghue gave us a confident Mendel. Caroline Brahan as Grandma Tzeitel and Missy Cleary as Fruma Sarah were both responsible for a stunningly visual dream scene, delivered with fierce impact and transporting us to the other side! Conor Ryan as Avram, had good characterisation and David Hughes delivered a stern and straight- talking Constable. The Russian tenor Eimhin O'Meara was impressive and Fiona O'Connor and Ned Lonergan both contributed greatly.

To the amazing TMS chorus, the backbone of the show, you were terrific.

Lastly to the children of the chorus, you are the stars of the future. You were amazing, keep it up.  And a shout out to the twins, Matthew and Luke who missed the show week. Chin up, I'm sure the committee are already planning the next one!

Thank you TMS for a very special night and I wish you all the very best for the future.

St Agnes' Choral Society, Belfast SHREK 'Fairy-tale Spectacle' It's always lovely to visit the splendour of the newly refurbished Grand Opera House, Belfast and especially to witness this spectacular and very large production of Shrek the musical, involving some 77 actors/singers/dancers onstage.

The society obviously decided to go big with this production hiring lavish sets, costumes, props, wigs, prosthetics and make-up. Even with all of this hired, they still had to have a legion of backstage workers to deliver it all for each performance. I counted at least 36 mentioned in the programme.

This was a monumental achievement and I congratulate director Laura Kerr and her huge team. The organisation of all this backstage work was huge, yet at all times worked extremely efficiently throughout the production.

Shrek the musical was based on DreamWorks' animation film of 2001 and opened on Broadway late 2008. A greatly changed version opened in the West End in the summer of 2011, with a UK and Ireland tour succeeding that in 2013. I attended the final night's performance, which was their sixth including two matinees, to a packed audience in this large theatre and was met by honorary Vice President Pat Smyth for some hospitality before taking my seat in the circle with a very good view of the production.

Director Laura Kerr and Production Manager Gareth McGreevy had to manage a huge production and their organisational skills were there for all to see in this massive production. It was swan-like, in that everything out front was calm and precise, yet backstage with costume changes aplenty, as well as sets and props constantly changing for the numerous scenes, it must surely have been all action. Ms Kerr's unflappability must surely have been tested, but even when I met her she was calmness personified, answering all my questions inimitably, concerning the huge organising of the whole production. Her work with all the principals, minor featured roles and choruses of fairy-tale characters, guards and Lord Farquaad minions was exemplary with absolutely nobody onstage showing indecision or unease at any time. All of the action onstage was well worked and purposeful throughout.

Musical Director Colin Scott and his assistant Andrew Robinson had worked hard with all the cast to deliver all the songs and both were evident with a very fine orchestra, achieving a great sound both onstage and in the pit. In particular, that wonderful scene with the three Fionas - Young Fiona, Teenage Fiona and Princess Fiona - gave us the very fine singing of all three Fionas. The musical highlight of the show!

Anne Marie Morgan worked her magic not only with her fine dancers but also with all the other choreographed numbers from the three blind mice, the tap dancing routine of the Pied Pipers' rats, the fairy- tale characters' choreography (especially in 'Freak Flag') to Farquaad's chorus of vivid reds and blues with yellow hairstyles and their precise, inventive dancing. There was so much wonderful choreography throughout, especially in the scene with the long-haired stocks prisoners, the Dragon with puppeteers/red costumed dragonettes/beautifully red costumed voice, and the weaving and undulating skeletons. There was so much involved here simultaneously, that it was difficult to take it all in. Perhaps if it was broken up into staggered sections? Nevertheless, the choreography was a delight from beginning to end!

The set, hired from UK Productions and under stage manager Andy McKnight, assisted by his deputy Clare Donnelly, assistant managers Malachy Hanna and Andrew Devonshire and a large stage crew, was proficiently put into position and struck for the numerous scenes, always looking splendid, in particular the wedding scene with the massive stain-glassed window and the wonderful proscenium with full three-dimensional effect in the intertwining branches and trunks of the trees.

The Wardrobe team of nine (too many to mention) had plenty on their hands, not only with many costumes, but also with wigs and prosthetics. I don't think there were many performers who had only one costume and some of the changes must have been ultra-quick. In particular I noticed that Fiona was offstage for the briefest of moments in the final scene when she transformed into an ogress, including green skin, prosthetic nose, wig and new costume. Well done for all of this! The props team of at least ten and led by Maeve Gillen had a great deal of work also. There were so many props that I would just love to have seen them all set out on a table backstage. I particularly liked the destructing bird in the scene with Fiona, at the start of the second act, which got a big laugh from the audience (with maybe a few sighs!).

Lighting by ACK Productions was always good, with colours changing in the ever- present proscenium arch. I particularly liked the purple you used for the pre- set and at other times. I would perhaps have liked to have seen ultraviolet lights for the skeletons to bring out the lovely white bones. However, I liked the clever shadow scene in the cabin when Fiona was showing Donkey how she changed at night to an ogress. This meant it was still a secret from the audience until seen in all her glory at the very end.

The sound was handled by Jody Trehy and once again this must have been a huge undertaking with so many people onstage needing miked. I did feel that the balance between orchestra and singers was, at times, uneven, with the orchestra drowning some principals, in particular Donkey in some of his songs and occasionally Shrek also.

The line-up of cast members showed a very good consistency right across the board, were well cast and all of them sang, acted, moved and danced well. Shrek, played by Fergal White, had the perfect stature for the character. His Scots accent, which was very good and not overdone, was suitably underlined by his red tartan pants. He spoke well, showing his ogre-like qualities, and mostly remained sensitively even-tempered throughout, with his dry Scots humour, which occasionally spilt into moments of anger and frustration, mainly with his friend Donkey. His singing, demeanour and general reactions, combined with his general movement were again of a high standard. Just be careful, that when you are heavily made up, it's more difficult for the audience to see facial reactions, so perhaps improvement here would pay high dividends, but this was a lovely characterisation.

Of the principals, I felt that Fiona (Blaithnaid Scullion) stood out for her very fine voice and her strong acting. An innately good comic actress, she had that magnetic quality when onstage, building up and maintaining a very interesting character. Her singing in her scene with the other two Fionas, and in 'This is how a dream comes true' was particularly good. Donkey (Gareth McGreevy) had tremendous physicality for the role, putting himself about the stage very well and this added greatly to his portrayal, with his singing and irrepressibility. With Shrek he made up an excellent couple throughout their adventures.

Lord Farquaad, played by Tony Young, was the undoubted star comedian of the piece, with excellent comic delivery and timing, a master of both. His movement, although on his knees throughout, was never laboured, as he seemed effortless across the stage, and his manipulation of his small dummy legs was always entertaining. Unfortunately, in the final scene he upstaged poor Shrek by having a personal joke with his henchman. Shrek was pouring his heart out to Fiona in his song, but was largely unheard because of the audience laughing with Lord Farquaad. Please be aware when others have key dramatic moments and when comic reactions should be restrained. These were the four big characters of the show, but that certainly didn't mean they carried the rest. In fact, quite the opposite, because the whole company were the stars, constantly singing, dancing, reacting and thoroughly amusing and entertaining the audience. Whether it was the fairy-tale creatures, Lord Farquaad's guards and minions or the dancers in their many forms. Here are some that deserve at least a mention. Pinocchio (Aideen Fox), the ringleader for the fairy-tale creatures, had a fine voice (if a little squeaky), but she shone in her role as the naughty boy who continually tells lies, with her nose lengthening each time we saw her. Dragon (Michelle Hannaway) looked wonderful in her sparkly red dress and sang beautifully in her scenes, even if she was distanced from the actual dragon. Gingy, sung, spoken and puppeteered by Helen Smyth, was excellent in her puppetry and high pitched voice, while the White Rabbit (Felicity Rooney) constantly dazzled with her movement and dancing skills. Fiona in her scene with her two younger selves, played by Sophie Lennon and Lucy McNally, produced for me the lasting and takeaway moment from the whole show - 'I know it's today'. I must mention here in particular young twelve-year-old Sophie Lennon, with her marvellous voice in 'True love's first kiss' and her bright-eyed expressive face. Certainly, a star in the making!

This was a marvellous spectacle from beginning to end with sets and costumes giving us a memorable presentation. Add to that the organisation and control of a huge ensemble onstage, under the imaginative and careful direction of all the creatives and overseen by director Laura Kerr, and it's very easy to see why audiences were enthralled by this production. Very well done St Agnes Choral Society!

'Puppets, but for adults!'

St Michael's Theatre, New Ross is an older venue situated in the centre of the town, with an imposing entrance from the street. Once inside, I found a welcoming front of house lady, who kindly showed me to my seat. Not a long narrow auditorium, but a shorter and wide one with a similar sized balcony. The proscenium was painted completely black for best effect for the lighting, costumes and set.

Avenue Q was based on an original idea by Robert Lopez and Jeff Marx, who also wrote the music and lyrics, with the book by Jeff Whitty. They had seen the great success of Sesame Street and The Muppet Show and realised the idea could be equally successful as a musical. First produced on Broadway in 2003 it has had enormous success and appeal throughout the world, in various languages. The show's format is a parody of Sesame Street, but its content is very much for adult audiences with themes of romance, sexuality and racism.

Eleven performers and thirteen puppets make up the cast, with two people playing only as humans (Brian and his fiancé, Christmas Eve) and many others playing several roles (including two who share the role of Trekkie Monster's right hand!) All the puppeteers are in black, while the puppets, as well as characters Brian and Christmas Eve, are very colourful in comparison for obvious reasons.

One clever difference in this production is the role of Gary Coleman, who is played by an African-American in professional and many amateur productions, when there is a multi-racial mix of talented performers, but as a black puppet here, because of difficulty with casting. This worked a treat, as well as being politically correct in this very modern show, which addresses homosexuality, internet porn and other issues.

Director and Production Manager Derek Shannon had a very clear vision of what was required for this show to work. A very clever, funny script would only truly work if the puppets 'came to life'. To achieve this is no small feat, because the cast had to become very proficient puppeteers to achieve real success with the script and songs. So, as well as acting, singing and dancing, the cast had to deliver yet another skill that must have taken a lot of work. And the audience loved it! And so did I! The way Mr. Shannon integrated all this work showed great dedication and understanding. None of the puppets lacked believability or precision in the whole show. To say the performance lived up to the standard that we normally see when we watch 'The Muppets' or 'Sesame Street', shows just how good it was. MD Phillip Kennedy managed to give effervescence to the music, matching the essence of the onstage action to the songs and orchestrations. Although hidden in the orchestra pit, I could clearly see his raised hands at times cueing the singers onstage. The songs were so catchy, I found myself humming the tunes a week later and, of course the lyrics were so funny that the audience was constantly creased with laughter. My favourites were 'It Sucks to be Me' (which gave a great start to the show by highlighting each in turn), 'The Internet is for Porn' (hilarious), 'There's a Fine, Fine Line' (contrasting the humour with great pathos) and 'The Money Song' (hilariously funny as the audience felt badgered by the cast).

The Set Design by Ray Shannon, and helped put together and painted by Alex Shannon and Noel Bennett, showed a rundown, ramshackle street in America, with good levels produced from windows, steps (stage right), and even up in front of the skyline, for the Empire State Building scene with Kate Monster. Also, to either side of the stage there were large TV monitors, which from time to time showed short cartoon episodes to enhance the action. These were informative, very amusing and an integral part of the stage action. The buildings all had a real three dimensional feel to them with prominent bricks, windows and doors, rather than just painted on a flat screen, while the lighting by Anthony Quinn certainly helped highlight all areas of the stage, both used in spots for individuals, as well as for full cast numbers downstage. This was achieved without a bar for profiles in front of the stage, like most theatres have. Here, the much needed profiles were mounted to either side of front-of-stage. The show was always well lit but in an unobtrusive way. Sound, also by Mr Quinn, was always sensitively balanced so that band and performers could clearly be heard, both in sensitive solo numbers and raucous, high energy full cast numbers. Never shouting out "look what's happening here!" the Lighting and Sound, nevertheless, did a very fine job in an essential area for the success of the show.

Choreographer Anne-Marie Cooney had the unenviable task of choreographing puppets as well as humans, but the dancing was always buoyant and fun, especially in 'The internet is for Porn' and 'The Money Song' with lots of impressive movement by actors and puppets.

Costumes too, by Susan Synott and helped by Eileen St Ledger and Donna Bradley, never failed to impress. The actors working the puppets were all in black, but not nondescript or exactly the same. In fact Therese Canavan Bolger managed to convey some of Lucy the Slut's character in her own costume. But it was in the costuming of the puppets that the real success was found. Fantastic colourful faces and costumes that were so right for each puppet's character, whether it be Trekkie Monster, the Bad Idea Bears, Lucy the Slut or Kate Monster.

Of the cast, everyone handled the puppets very proficiently and succeeded in portraying rounded and highly entertaining characters. Princeton was expertly puppeteered by Keith Flanagan. So much so that he managed to bring the puppet to life, with lots of detail in his reactions and very often I had to tell myself that it was only a puppet and not a person. Fabulous puppetry here! I also particularly liked the Bad Idea Bears (Bronagh Hogan and Anthony Finn) who were absolutely vivacious and naughty. I loved Anthony's falsetto voice, perfectly matched by Bronagh's. Rod and Nicky (Graham Finnerty and James Dobbs) gave lovely masterful performances as the closet gay and his friend, while Trekkie Monster, the internet porn character (Sean O'Brien) was greatly helped by having an extra arm worked in turn by two others (Therese Canavan Bolger and Anthony Finn) when they weren't operating their main puppets. Kate Monster (Ashley Doran) who becomes Princeton's girlfriend, Gary Coleman (Jennifer White) the caretaker and Lucy the Slut (Therese Canavan Bolger) whose name says it all, played the other three wonderful characters in the amazing line-up of puppets. Henpecked Brian (Phil Erskine) and his fiancé Christmas Eve (Lynsey Penkert) as the only humans in the cast had to deliver very fine performances to match the puppets, and they did, with Ms Penkert in particular never being outdone by the puppets.

Although this was an extremely hilarious show, especially for the audience on the night I attended, the greatest plaudits must go to the huge amount of creative work necessary to stage this production. All the creative talents of New Ross Musical Society - in Costumes, Set, Choreography, Musical Direction, Lighting and Sound and Stage Management, but especially the Puppeteers and Director - should be heartily congratulated on a very fine show.

'Ghoulish Fun!'

The entrance to the Community School, Malahide was bedecked in black with many references to the Addams family and with many front of stage staff in ghoulish costumes and make-up to give the audience an immediate feel for what was in store. This continued in the auditorium and had mover lights from the stage focused on the back wall to give a really great atmosphere ahead of what was in store. Then, in 'Strictly Come Dancing' mode, the lights from the back wall of the auditorium slid across everyone to reside once more on the stage and the show started with the whole company onstage performing the opening number, 'When You're an Addams', and everyone knew we were in for a great night of theatre and music.

Director Damien Hurley started with a bang, a great line-up of principals and a sensational ensemble depicting the Addams ancestors, resplendent in costumes of many eras and periods in various shades of white and grey and with phenomenal detail. The opening of the show had so much to see, hear and take in, that I was constantly trying to notice as much detail as I possibly could, whilst enjoying everything onstage - the singing, choreography, costumes and wigs, lighting, set and the band (very much heard but totally invisible) - and there was so much to enjoy!  Musical Director Dave McGauran very capably led the invisible band, that sounded like a full orchestra of 30, but was in fact just 10. I only realised this fact when I saw them in their little room at the back of the auditorium and was even more astounded that they were not mentioned on the programme. There was a great richness to the sound, which belied the number of members, and with Mr McGauran televised to the stage, the performers were able to follow his every cue (like myself from time to time).

Stuart Bourke with director Damien Hurley created the necessary atmosphere in the Set Design, especially with the very fine castle gates, which covered the full width of the stage, and Caoimhe Farrell's family portraits added a nice touch. But I thought many of the projected backgrounds and some of the sets were a little too ordinary and commonplace, not providing enough atmosphere as an ancient ghoulish castle. Choreographer Julianne McNamara shone, especially in her movement of the Ancestors, with their deformities and anguished movements that I found spellbinding. Some members at the back perhaps didn't always fulfil this quite as well, but the overall effect was wonderful. Ms McNamara's dances and movement were always interesting, cohesive and absolutely in keeping with the characters, especially The Tango, which was absolutely terrific.

Costumes by Susan Talbot, and co- ordinated by Andrew Reddy were absolutely incredible. Especially for the Ancestors, which was just fantastic. The amount of detail here, along with excellent wigs and very fine make-up (by Caoimhe Farrell), was astounding. The phenomenal detail to different periods, with shades of white and grey was very professional. I spotted a ballet dancer in tutu, a pirate, a flapper of the 20s and even one who looked like Miss Havisham from Dickens' Great Expectations. There were too many fabulous individuals to mention them all. Lighting by Cathal O'Donoghue was brilliant from pre-show right throughout. Most of this centred around his use of overhead, colour changing, LEDs coupled with multi beam movers that sensationally provided all the necessary atmosphere for the show.

The principal couple of Gomez (Stuart Pollock) and Morticia (Yasmine Missaoui) effortlessly carried the show throughout. Stuart gave a very assured performance with excellent physicality and delivery of lines. Suave and flamboyant, he also provided endless energy and pace. So much so, that sweat and make-up could be seen running down his face after the wonderful tango with Morticia. Yasmine, always totally unflappable, acted and danced her part beautifully. Her diction was exemplary.

Always composed and effortless, she lit up every scene. Wednesday (Rebecca Gamble) gave a very assured portrayal of the rebellious teenage daughter. Her singing, especially, was expertly and beautifully achieved. Her acting and movement/dancing were also of a very high quality, and she shows very high promise for the future. Lucas (Daire Kelly) provided a lovely foil for Wednesday and I particularly liked his geekish wig! Uncle Fester (Phillip Emmett) gave us a nicely judged performance as the sensitive uncle who also confides with the audience. His number with the ancestors was particularly memorable complete with a large global moon. Pugsley (Cillian Waldron) has a very fine young voice, that he used very well in the show and exhibits enough in his acting to prove that he can learn with experience. His Grandma (Mary Gamble) gave an excellent characterisation.

Bombastic yet sympathetic in turn, she was always hilariously funny. I loved her costume and wig which helped her enormously in achieving a memorable and funny portrayal. Lurch (Gearoid McGauran) had a lot less to say than the others, but this was nevertheless a very eye-catching performance. His reactions to others, and what they said, spoke volumes, as he constantly upstaged everyone else with the slightest smile, sneer or whatever. When he did utter sounds they showed a very fine bass voice and proved that he was very much an important character in a very fine line-up.

Alice (Jennifer McGuire Noirant) and Mal (Dominic Reid), the normal (?) parents of Lucas, both gave portrayals that showed they were nothing of the sort! Their manic qualities were very capably demonstrated by Alice's physical antics crawling over the dining table etc; and by Mal's transformation from wife-hating to wife- loving-once-more.

Finally, the ensemble was in many respects the stars of this show, completely demanding attention from the audience on their every appearance. For much of this they should thank those that provided their costumes, wigs, make-up, their dance and movement by the choreographer and their personalities from the director. Nevertheless, they themselves brought this weird collection of characters to life and I thank them all, with the principals, for providing a great night's entertainment.

''Scary Musical!'

Musical theatre is back in Galway! Stephen King's famous novel and film Carrie, with the book by Lawrence D. Cohen, Music by Michael Gore and lyrics Dean Pitchford (Fame) took to the stage at the Black Box Theatre to entertain, thrill and scare audiences in equal measure. On its first appearance on Broadway in 1988 it was a flop that only lasted a few performances. After a considerable rewrite the revival on Broadway was 24 years later in 2012, where it received much better reviews from critics and audiences alike. Very much made to measure for GUMS with a youthful cast, it won over Galway audiences with this riveting story of adolescent Carrie starting as the butt of school bullying as well as having a religious fanatic of a mother to cope with. However, with her telekinetic powers increasing, she brings an overwhelming conclusion to all of this in a stunning, violent climax that must be the most horrific in musical history.

Director Caolan Moriarty did an excellent job in his production, not only with his cast of principals, but also by the way he encouraged the ensemble to show us their own individual stories, mainly through reactions. This meant that there were so many other minor stories to be told, of each and every member of the chorus. Just be careful not to upstage main characters' dialogue at the same time. Relationships between characters were always to the fore and this rightly gave much more depth to characterisations, which made it all the more perplexing that the chief relationship in the piece should have been more fully developed. I'm talking of young insecure and naive Carrie and her mother Margaret, the religious fanatic and zealot.

MD Maeve O'Callaghan was assisted by Tara Mackin and they oversaw a very small but tight band, behind the rostra and upstage of the action. Maeve's conducting ensured a great pace throughout, creating excellent continuity but also relaxed into the quieter numbers such as 'Unsuspecting Hearts' and 'Dreamer in Disguise'. Much of the time the music melted into the background and was unobtrusive, yet when a statement needed to be made, it was powerful and compelling in numbers such as - In 'A Night We'll Never Forget', 'Why Not Me', 'Carrie' and 'Destruction'.

Stage Manager Lucy Birmingham and set designer Cormac O'Leime (assisted by Dan O'Connell) decided on minimal sets and furniture, which proved very clever, because this gave excellent continuity so that there were no signs of flagging and this kept the audience riveted throughout. Michael Healy and assistant Mary Egan, helped onstage by their three dance captains Killian Cohan, Abbie Lane and Aoibh Tully, combined to devise and execute choreography that was so exhilarating, synchronised and at the same time innovative. At times it was breath taking, especially the wedge shape they created, on a few occasions, with all of the ensemble moving as one inside a large triangle. The youthful exuberance that was so well controlled and disciplined, produced choreography that would have graced any professional performance. Costuming the show was in the safe hands of Aine Ni Mhorda and her assistant Hannah Schmidt. Aine confidently stated, and rightly so, in the programme that the 'costumes enhance the characters' personalities and can help the actors get into their roles'. This struck a chord with me, and with so many individual personalities onstage, it added great variety to the spectacle, with a few 70s costumes to the fore - the short plaid dresses of Sue and Chris as well as the baseball jackets of a few men.

Lighting and sound are not accredited in the programme, but they were a major influence on the show's success. Because there was so little in the way of scenery, the lighting, in particular, helped achieve the very necessary atmosphere. Not just in big numbers like the 'Destruction' or 'A Night We'll Never Forget', where it was all guns blazing, but also 'Once You See', 'When There's No One' and 'Carrie', where we needed a softer, quieter or singular atmosphere.

With little scenery the lighting created a very necessary atmosphere and dynamic, often lighting individual areas rather than all the stage. The cyclorama was used very effectively on which to project abstract backdrops to the action. Colours were used selectively and I liked the use of side lighting from the wings which added a three dimensional effect. The lighting for the finale of the 'Destruction' number was truly devastating. Very good sound effects and very well balanced mics added greatly to both speech and singing throughout the show.

Carrie, played by Katie Feeney looked just right for the role with her long auburn hair. She delivered all her songs, but notably 'Carrie', 'Unsuspecting Hearts' and 'Why Not Me' through to the show stopping 'Destruction', with a wonderful voice that stated all of Carrie's personality - innocent, girlish through to demonic and powerful. In a riveting performance she showed all facets of this very demanding role from pitiful victim to commanding, evil destroyer.

Margaret played by Aisling Fox has a lovely voice and showed great delicacy as the worried, caring mother, but lacked the immense power and intensity of the religious fanatic.

Sue played by Hannah Cogan, is the narrator of the piece, being the only survivor from the fateful prom night. As the bully then friend, her transformation was believable and sensitive.

She also interacted well with all the other characters, notably so with Tommy, her boyfriend and Chris who mercilessly bullied Carrie to her bitter end. Her lovely singing in 'Once You See' summed up all her qualities beautifully.

Tommy, played by Adam O'Connor, looked very easy in the role as the most mature of the boys. Always looking extremely comfortable in this portrayal, he gave a very fine performance allied to a very fine voice in his singing.

Chris (Anna Doherty) was a real nasty piece of work as she incessantly bullied poor Carrie, aided by Billy (Andrew Richardson). We never got to see a better side of both throughout the show, right until they covered Carrie with pig's blood and certainly paid dearly with their lives in the final destruction.

Miss Gardner (Lorna Collins) and Mr Stephens (Mark Heffernan) were the two teachers who tried but failed to stop the bullying of Carrie. Both gave convincing performances, especially Lorna who grabbed her chance when she stood in late on. She was very believable as the gym teacher, both punishing the bullies and befriending Carrie.

Her voice also displayed great sensitivity in 'Unsuspecting Hearts' with Carrie.

All others in the ensemble contributed in no small way towards the high standard of acting, singing and dancing throughout the show.

What a great way to come back, after two years of a pandemic, with a great show, that was a perfect fit for this group of young performers. I wish you luck in your future shows!

'Women's Rights' 9 to 5 is very much Dolly Parton's show. She decided to make a musical of the very popular film and accordingly wrote all the music and lyrics, with her friend and associate Patricia Resnick, who was screenwriter for the film, providing the book for the musical. The show opened on Broadway in 2009 after a premiere in Los Angeles, with further productions around the world. A UK tour began late 2021 when Covid restrictions eased. This was my first visit to the Craic Theatre, a small theatre modernly adapted in the Tyrone countryside just outside Coalisland, but it certainly won't be my last. Seating no more than 200, with the audience raked down to a good size stage, it was very comfortable with good stage facilities, a lighting and sound box and a bar for patrons.

Quite honestly, I was taken aback by the quality of everything on offer in the Craic Theatre on 4th March. The show was very slick in every respect, especially the creative departments - Direction, Set Design, Lighting and Musical Direction Direction by Sean O'Neill was excellent. There were well formed characters throughout the cast, with the ensemble showing marvellous reactions and developing their own personal and group storylines. Very good evenness right across the board of principals ensured absolutely no weak links. Mr O'Neill combined his role of director with choreographing the show most capably. This was done with great verve and imagination, and the integration of the dancing and movement throughout the show bore testament to his excellent production values.

Set design by Fiona McNaney and Tony Donnelly was impeccable, with all the action framed by chests of drawers topped by blinds. Two illuminated clocks upstage right and left where two clocks proclaimed nine o'clock and five o'clock. Centre upstage changed between the Hart office, Judy's Joint and other venues that were eye-catching yet evocative and extremely utilitarian. Stage management by Dylan Fox and Daniel Taaffe kept the action flowing beautifully, with the cast choreographed to maximise the efficient changes of scenes. The office work floor desks on castors were smoothly taken offstage through chests of drawers to provide seamless transitions. Once again, excellent work in this department with brilliant design.

The seven-piece band under MD Roisin Corr were placed over the upstage area and provided perfect accompaniment for all songs and action. Even though small in numbers, we had keyboards, guitars, brass, woodwind and percussion that ticked all boxes with great aplomb.

The lighting by James McFetridge was delightful, yet never 'in-yer-face', with overhead LEDs constantly changing colours that were echoed in the six sets of blinds on either side of the set. All the action was very sympathetically lit, with great subtlety dimming the ensemble and highlighting principals when the need arose. Sound by Gerard Wilkinson was very good also, with a very nice balance between singers and orchestra and amongst singers in duets, trios, and indeed any combination. Costumes, not accredited in the programme, were always suitable and usually from the 80s, which is necessary for Hart's believability as an out and out chauvinist, but there were issues with costumes fitting at times.

All three leading women created a super- strong team in the acting and singing departments with great sensitivity for one another. This was so apparent in their big number together 'Shine Like the Sun', to finish the first Act. Violet, played by Claire McCrory, was so believable and sympathetic to all members of the cast around her, yet she was so capable of rising to great heights of stardom when required, especially in her big numbers, both in singing and dancing. Her duet with Joe in the second act 'Let Love Grow' was absolutely delightful and showed the great depth of feeling that developed so well between the couple. Judy (Lauren McCrory) developed her character so convincingly throughout the piece, from giddy and extremely nervous newcomer, right through to her tour de force big number 'Get Out and Stay Out", when she showed her character to now be a very strong minded and extremely capable woman. This was definitely the big number of the show as she gave it everything she had. Doralee (Lisa Ryan) was the delightful Dolly Parton character, and this lady certainly didn't hold back in her very strong singing and inimitable character. Looking and sounding just right, she gave a very convincing performance of the Dolly lookalike. Hart, the big bad boss (Dec McGrath), was suitably lecherous and chauvinistic in all his dealings with the three ladies, especially Doralee, who suffered his repeated onslaughts. His physicality was a delight as he drew laughs from the audience throughout the storyline. Roz (Aoibh Johnson), his completely devoted yet zany secretary, revelled in her situation and was totally convincing as Hart's doormat, showing the very high skills required to extract every ounce of humour from her role and succeeding very capably. Joe was the love interest for Violet, and this could so easily have been a two-dimensional caricature of a role. But instead, he made this character in turn highly believable, sensitive and very engaging. He developed a great rapport with the hard-to-get Violet and both of them were extremely easy together and authentic as a couple. The minor principals and ensemble did much more than back up the top of the billers. Instead, through their wonderful reactions and developed storylines, they helped in no small way ensure the great success of the show.
