This society is a fairly new addition to the AIMS ranks, but if the professionalism exhibited in this show continues, then they are going to be a force to be reckoned with. I thoroughly enjoyed my visit to Coalisland and wish the Craic Theatre all the luck they deserve in their future shows.

Given the limitations of their performance venue, the technical presentation of Tullyvin Musical Society's production of 'The Addams Family' was nothing short of a minor miracle. To say there was a lack of space and facilities on and behind the stage would be an understatement, yet with good fore-thought, excellent stage management and a very capable building team, Tullyvin managed to extend their wing space, store a plethora of sizeable props and furniture, and present a stage that looked absolutely wonderful. The attention to detail in the house interior was unbelievable, with cobwebs, skulls, potions and abstract art, bannisters made of bones, candle-light, rickety stairs, portraits of the family and a collapsible wall with door frames and windows which then became the stage floor. It was all done in the worst possible taste and created the best possible effect. Simply ingenious. Visually spectacular.  Stage manager, Brian Feerick, had his work done in advance, and used cast members and costumed minions to carry out the furniture movement, and it all ran so smoothly. Whoever assembled the props for the show deserves a medal. They were plentiful and perfectly selected. The centre-stage trap door was well used, and the fold-down headstones were a clever touch. Gates and trees were enough to suggest different locations around the house.

Having had the pleasure of visiting Tullyvin in the past, I am happy to report that this is a company very much in the ascendance, honing their skills, pushing themselves to higher levels of competence and confidence.

'The Addams Family' is pretty close to pantomime, with its surreal characters, un-likely plot, and abundantly ridiculous script, and it consequently takes a director with a zany, often outrageous, sense of humour to bring out the best in it. Such a director is Paul Norton who, from the get-go, used every conceivable gimmick, verbal and visual comedic device to enhance this piece to its fullness. From the highly amusing headstones that were on- stage as the audience entered, to the final note of the show, when Lurch managed, at last, to click his fingers in time with the rest of the cast, so much thought was put into the production. There was The Grim Reaper, who eerily ambled on stage, scythe in hand, to brief the audience on the emergency exits, and then assured them that they would be here for eternity. The audience were in the palm of their hands from that point onwards. Equally in tune with the production standards, Musical Director, John Roe, got us off to a rollicking good start with a lively and precisely played Overture, leading a very efficient six-piece band from the piano. He also maintained good contact with his on- stage performers throughout the show. If there were moments when one longed for more flamboyant dance routines, it was not the fault of choreographer, Julianne McNamara, but due to the absence of a male chorus. With what she had, Julianne worked hard to use the limited space effectively and with creativity, and the opening number, "When You're an Addams" was particularly impressive, and in fairness to the female chorus, they did all that was asked of them with a great sense of fun and an abundance of energy. Paul Norton not only directed, but also took on the role of Gomez, and led from the front, giving an inspirational performance. His comedy was of the highest order, but it was the sentiment and sincerity that he put into his relationships with Wednesday and Morticia that really made an impact, with "Happy, Sad" and "Live Before We Die" providing the emotional high-points of the show. Excellent work.

Andrea Fitzpatrick was a confident and convincing Morticia, with good vocal quality and a fine sense of comic timing. She had the strength of character to keep Gomez on his toes, but also the grace and gentleness to see the errors of her stubbornness.

A powerful vocal quality was the highlight of a very assured performance from Emily Smith as Wednesday Addams. She maintained a delightful dead-pan throughout the show, which contrasted brilliantly with the joy in her vocals.

Sean Slowey had attitude and presence as the masochistic young Pugsley. He looked the part, nailed his comedy, and delivered his vocals with confidence. Standing at approximately 8', Jason Nulty was certainly the tallest Lurch I've ever encountered, and fair play to him for his relaxed confidence on those stilts, but his height was overshadowed by his equally enormous personality, which shone through a wonderful comedic performance.

In contrast, it was the amiable, somewhat demented smile of Liam Wallace's Fester that made him so appealing. He flirted delightfully with the audience and made the most of his musical numbers, especially "The Moon and Me". This was a most note-worthy comedic performance. Emma McKeown worked hard and was impressive in the role of Grandma, but even with good make-up and wig, she couldn't completely disguise that she was a bit too young for the role.

John Grogan, as Mal Beineke, probably needed to be more authoritative in his early scenes, but he came good when he relaxed into his old self as the show progressed. Pamela McCormack got a good contrast between her nervous wife of the early scenes and her more provocative vamp of the Full Disclosure scene. The Beinekes were a little pitchy vocally in the difficult "Crazier Than You" number, but they were a capable and entertaining couple nevertheless.

As their son, Lucas, Colm Shalvey was well partnered with Wednesday, nerdy enough to frustrate her, and yet confident enough to win her over in the end. A well- judged performance with a good confident singing voice.

An uncredited Grim Reaper brought a captivating start to the show and was useful throughout in assisting with furniture moves.

The vocal quality of the female chorus was good and their actions and reactions were a good contributing factor to the flow and ambiance of their many scenes.

Costumes throughout were entirely appropriate and well presented. Chorus greys were effective, combined with good ghostly make-up and an assortment of very good wigs and hairstyles. Lurch's extended physique (approx. 8' high) was very well achieved, looked proportioned, and was excellently used by the actor. It was the combination of all the above with the superbly dressed set that made this show an absolute visual treat, and all comments made about the effort made on presenting a visually exceptional set can be extended to include the effort that went into the dressing of the front of house area. A lovely Halloween atmosphere was created, and front of house staff were delightful, helpful and most welcoming. I think the most evident characteristic of this production was the sheer sense of fun and enjoyment that emanated from the stage, which I have little doubt was contributed to by the influence and personality of their Director. The overall performance level was high, often hilarious, and always thoroughly entertaining. Congratulations on a most enjoyable experience. It was a very great pleasure to be with you.

society_raw: North East Musical and Dramatic Society
review_text:
9 TO 5 Whether It's always exciting to see a new musical society pop on to the radar, but it's uncommon for them to explode onto the radar to such an extent that one has to adjust all the settings and brace oneself for a veritable roller-coaster ride from the opening chorus to the final curtain. But this was exactly the impact created by the highly talented cast and production team of the North East Musical and Dramatic Society's production of "9 to 5".

Attention to detail was the key to the high sheen that made this such a polished production. Director, Gavin Quigley, had a talented cast to work with, and he complemented them by providing well- paced, easy-flowing action, with a strong focus on comedy. Principals were always comfortable on the stage, and there was good attention to the smaller character roles, making their performances stand out and relevant. Excellent work.

I was blown away by the energy and the precision of the dance routines throughout the show. Moreover, they weren't just dances. They always had a purpose and contributed to the story line. The opening chorus was a masterpiece of non-stop, stylised, scene-setting, performed by a dynamic and extremely energetic ensemble, which led almost seamlessly into an equally exciting "Around Here." The entire Dream sequence, from "Dance of Death" through to "Joy to the Girls" was meticulous, creative, inspirational and thoroughly engaging, as was the "Shine Like The Sun" finale to Act One. "One of the Boys" set the second act alight, and the terpsichorean treat never waned until the rousing finale. This was top notch choreography, brought to life by a skilled and spirited group of performers. Choreographer, Leah Meagher, take a bow.

The show was very well costumed, and I noted the lovely change, when Violet and the girls took over the running of the office, to brighter and more colourful outfits. Good costumes for the Dream sequence dance routines and for One of the Boys. Wigs and Hairstyles were always appropriate, and make-up looked natural throughout.

Carol McCourt was a worthy Violet Newstead, brimming with confidence, displaying great leadership quality, and as strong in her vocals as she was in her acting. Her comedy was very well timed, and she fronted her musical numbers with a reassuring ease.

Louise Steele was a robust Doralee, delightfully voluptuous and self-assured, yet soft and gentle when it was required. Her delivery of Backwoods Barbie was particularly endearing.

As with Carol, her vocal quality matched her acting skills.

Completing the main trio, Paige Kelly was a perfect choice for the role of Judy, vulnerable and insecure, yet when it was required, thoroughly capable of making a powerful impact. Her "Get Out and Stay Out" was one of the musical highlights of the show.

Sean Harkin gave a top-drawer performance as the misogynist boss, Franklin Hart Jnr, enjoying every moment of the comedy, and performing his songs with great energy. He was delightfully loathsome in all his dealings with his female staff, and we were truly delighted to see him getting his come-uppance at the end.

Lorraine Cotter was obnoxiously authoritative as Roz Keith, and divinely comedic in her lust for Franklin. "Heart to Hart" was very well performed, and I think we all felt a little sorry for her when she was sent away to learn French.

James Brennan was a very likeable and sympathetic Joe, firm but gentle in his love for Violet, and his singing in "Let Love Grow" was very pleasant indeed.

Orla Sheridan made an excellent comedic contribution to the show as the office lush, Margaret, growling through her drunken haze and ultimately returning from rehab as an articulate and sophisticated lady. Strong support came from Sinead Walshe as Maria, Fiona Longmuir as Missy and Lauren Murphy as Kathy, all of whom established themselves as individuals. Calum Duffy played teenage son, Josh, with a relaxed confidence, while Adam Lynagh as Dwayne and Thomas Whyte as Dick gave solid support in their respective roles.

There were good performances too from Aoibheann Byrne, Emma Kerley, Kerrie Gorman, Issac John, and new-comer Peter Phillips made an excellent job of his maiden performance as Tinsworthy.

In their vocal contributions, in the execution of their numerous dance routines and in their top-notch reacting to the focal point of the action, the chorus were the backbone of this production. They were meticulously attired, energetic and brimming with expression and confidence.

With four people credited as Musical Director, Chorus Mistress/Mister, it's hard to know who did what in preparation of the musical content of the show, but it's safe to say that a mountain of work was done on achieving a strong and harmonious choral sound. Musical entrances and cut- offs were all precisely timed, which was a good achievement without the benefit of a conductor out front to keep control. This brings me appropriately to the drawbacks of using backing tracks. There were a few occasions when the stage team were so efficient with their scene changes that there was a surplus of music that we had to endure in darkness before the lights took us into the next scene. There was one obvious and a couple of minor incidents when principals got through their dialogue briskly and were left with a lengthy pause of inactivity before their vocal cue. I acknowledge that these flaws were highlighted by the fact that the rest of the show was so perfectly paced. Setting the level of the backing tracks can also cause concern, and while volume wasn't a problem, there was a pounding bass throughout the show that made the output unnecessarily heavy and rattled the eardrums a little. That said, it was most enjoyable to hear a full orchestra sound at an affordable cost.

Lighting was varied and atmospheric, with excellent use of the louvered light boxes. Lighting cues were crisp and precise, and only on a few occasions were the chorus a tad too dimly lit behind a highlighted principal.

Sound quality throughout, (apart from that bass line) was very good, including the video voice-overs.

As already mentioned, the stage sets were clean and beautifully presented, with very good props and furniture, and all managed and moved by cast and crew with mega-efficiency, under the guidance of the director, who also doubled as stage manager.

After an arduous journey from Galway to Castleblayney, it was lovely to receive such a warm welcome to the beautiful Iontas Theatre. Front of House manager, Monica Marron, and her staff were delightful and efficient and their hospitality was generous.

This really was an excellent night of entertainment from a fresh and exciting new musical group. My sincere thanks to you all for a most uplifting and thoroughly enjoyable experience. I hope you continue to produce and present such a high calibre of musical entertainment.

As I left An Tain Arts Centre in Dundalk last night, I overheard a conversation between two teenagers.

"That was pretty good," said one, "but I didn't know any of the songs."

"I knew the one that the girl who sounded like Forest Gump sang," said the other. "I can't say No. I think I've heard Ma singin' that to me Da."

Lucky man, thinks myself. My wife says no to me all the time, but that's neither here nor there. The point is that Oklahoma despite its age, still has an appeal to a generation who have never seen nor heard of it before, which is probably why it remains such a popular choice for musical societies throughout the country. And when a production is as well manicured as this one was, it's easy to understand its popularity.

Trimming the fat, would be an apt description of Director, Tony Finnegan's approach to the show. "It's a Scandal" was gone (no great loss) and some irrelevant dialogue as the show reached its climax, resulting in a more fluid journey to the final rousing chorus. Tony's trademark is to include children in his productions, and whether they are needed or not, it does add authenticity to crowd scenes to see family units enjoying themselves. Moreover, he also used them in this production to create a beautiful ballet scene that saw Curly and Laurey playing together as children. This was a lovely detail. The pace throughout the show was very good, and relationships were all very believable. There was good chemistry between Curly and Laurey, and between Ado Annie and both Will and Ali. Good tension was created in the scenes involving Jud Fry, and there were nicely added comedic touches that added a freshness to the well tried and tested script. What the show definitely had was confidence, engagement and great attention to detail, all of which suggest a thoroughly rehearsed and well-thought out production.

Musically, the show was a treat. In the safe hands of Musical Director, Ronan Dennedy, we were treated to a nicely balanced and precisely performed accompaniment from the orchestra throughout the show, and an equally accomplished vocal performance from the entire cast. Credit goes to Chorus Mistress, Ann McCabe for a well-drilled and thoroughly rehearsed chorus.

As Curly McClain, Ray O'Hare sang in the most delightful tones, and proved to be a confident and capable actor. His relationship with Laurey was always playful, romantic and sincere, and he showed no fear when standing up to the ogre-ish Jud. This was a well-judged performance.

Clara Quigley, as Laurey, had an equally pleasant singing voice, and a delightful coquettishness in her flirting with Curly. She handled her fear of Jud extremely well up to the point where she eventually admonishes his behaviour, when she was, perhaps, almost too strong. Nevertheless, this was a very capable all-round performance.

As Ado Annie, Chloe Copas managed to wring every ounce of comedy out of her character. He vocal delivery, her facial expressions and her body language all came together to create an engaging and loveable caricature to which the audience certainly warmed very quickly. As for her accent, well, it certainly made me laugh, even if it jarred slightly with all around her. It was the exuberance of youth that made Max Valentine's Will Parker so likeable. His comedy was perhaps a little over-emphasised, but his energy was infectious, and this is a young comedian to watch out for in the future. His singing was very good and his dancing was, well…enthusiastic and very entertaining. I enjoyed the performance of David McArdle as Ali Hakim, who had more than a touch of Benny Hill about both his physical and vocal comedy. His timing was very good and he handled the added "Hakim v Hakeeeem" gag with accomplishment. He was a very enjoyable likeable-rogue.

Confidence and security under-pinned the delightful performance of Patricia Savage in the role of Aunt Eller. There was the warmth of her care and concern for Laurey, and humorous teasing of Curly in his romantic endeavours. She also fronted "The Farmer and the Cowman" and the auction scene with authority.

James McGinn's Jud Fry was menacing, but showed signs of a psychopathic nature with his almost childlike tantrums and explosive temperament. His scene with Curly in the smoke-house was particularly well-judged. This was a strong performance and his passionate deliver of "Lonely Room" completely validated his vocal credibility after a slight hiccup at the end of "Poor Jud".

Tim Ahern was an amusing and very credible Andrew Carnes, clear and sharp in his delivery of dialogue. He was well supported by Aaron Matthews as Cord Elam, Eoghan Weldon as Slim and Stephen Clarke as Ike Skidmore, who all gave individuality to their characters. As Gertie Cummings, Caoimhe McBride was suitably pert and pretentious, and enhanced her performance with a truly irritating laugh/giggle. Nicely played. A special mention for Josh Murphy, Aoife O'Connor, Eoghan Weldon (again) and Leah Kearney, as the Younger Curlys and Laureys, who delightfully contributed to the show, particularly during the ballet. And speaking of the ballet, choreographer, Sinéad Lightley-Collins, broke with tradition here by introducing young Curly and young Laurey, playing together as children, and then progressing through generations up to the characters of the present. It was a delightful distraction and enhanced the usual nightmare scenario. "The Farmer and the Cowman" had a good natural flow to it, with good patterns and precise movement, even if it wasn't as rambunctious as one might have expected. Kansas City was not overly ambitious, but was enthusiastically performed. The ensemble were clearly well-rehearsed in their musical pieces, showing good strength and wonderful harmonies. The picture finish of "The Farmer and the Cowman" allowed the vocal quality to shine, and it certainly did. The Oklahoma Chorus was equally pleasant to listen to, and the ladies made a very good job of "Many A New Day" and "Out of My Dreams". Chorus action and reaction throughout the show was very believable and dances were always tidy and precise, thanks to good choreography that took heed of the performers' capabilities. Played on a well-designed and wood- stained set, incorporating an attractive gauze curtain, scene changes, in the capable hands of Stage Manager, Niall McCooey, were managed with a minimum of fuss. There were plenty of well-selected props and furniture pieces, including a decidedly grubby and effective smoke- house for Jud. The symbolic creation of a surrey, using bales of hay, cartwheels and a canopy, was a clever device to negate the need for a full surrey on stage for the finale. Lighting was often atmospheric and generally well-illuminated, but there were a few instances of lights flickering on and off, which occasionally distracted from the action. The end of the ballet, with highlights on the young couple and the dropped Rose, was reminiscent of Beauty and the Beast, but nonetheless, very effective. Sound quality was very good, and apart from an occasional moment of feed-back, every word was clearly heard. Sound effects, especially the gun-shots, were very well timed.

Costumes for the show were appropriate and utilitarian, as opposed to over-stylised, which is a break from the abundance of ginghams and bright colours that we so often see in this musical, but all the more authentic for that. There was a bit of variation in hem lengths for the ladies dresses, and indeed, one or two modern fringes in hairstyles, but aside from those minor indiscretions, the show was visually very tidily presented. Wigs were appropriate and worn well, and make-up was natural and very satisfactory. Principal costumes were very good, particularly the ladies, and Ali Hakim was appropriately more garish and gaudy than those around him.

In safe hands, Oklahoma! will always be an entertaining show, but in creative hands, it can be enhanced and delivered with a freshness that draws in a new generation to appreciate the genius of this Rogers and Hammerstein classic. Congratulations to Tony and to all in Dundalk for achieving that goal, and for a thoroughly enjoyable night of musical theatre.

One Normal Night Full disclosure: this musical totally undermines the whole concept of the Addams Family being weird by making them aspire to normality. Morticia doesn't want to grow old, Wednesday wants to get married, Gomez wants peace and harmony in his family and even the ghosts and ghouls, the family's ancestors, want normality for their descendants. The only characters who in any way remain true to the original conceit are Grandma Addams and Pugsley who misses his sister torturing him. Even Fester wants to live happily ever after, albeit with the moon as his significant other. So, if you are a fan of Charles Addams' work, you will be confused.

The Addams family, led by the elegantly black-clad Morticia, a wonderfully still Leah Penston, and her ever-devoted amorous husband Gomez, an ebullient Fergal Millar, is unsettled. Their daughter Wednesday, a bob-haired Leah Comerford, now eighteen, finds herself falling in love and considering marriage, which she is keeping from her mother but confesses to her Dad. When she invites her new boyfriend, Lucas Beineke, the wonderful Simon Broderick, and his family over for dinner to their gothic house of horrors, it turns out that the 'normal' family are even more messed up than the Addams. It's quite a simple plot worthy of an American rom-com, but the jokes are good, and the performances fresh and narrator Fester ensures that it we don't take it too seriously as he constantly reminds us that we are watching a musical.

Director Christine Scarry pulled out all the stops together with Musical Director, David Hayes and Choreographer Nicole McDonald and gave us a physically reduced version of the show due to the limitations of the stage, but a production full of talent and a few surprises! This is a huge musical and the challenge was considerable to fit it all in on the Watergate stage. The Addams' house should be massive with hidden and secret passages and doors and picture frames for the Ancestors to pop out of, and we did get some of this in John O'Donoghue's clever set. Most notable was the internally lit trap up stage right, which was very effective, especially when Pugsley used it, and the stairs leading up to an impressively high landing. The projections of skeletal tree branches added a menace to a show that isn't very scary and Terry Heron's sound effects were brilliant, lots of loud thunder and crash, bangs and wallops which created jump scares for the audience. Colm Eaton's lighting was hauntingly beautiful at times with some lovely blues. The father of the snap-happy Addams Family is Gomez, here played by Fergal Simon Broderick as the loved-up Lucas and Leah Comerford as the crazy Wednesday Addams fabulous as he sashayed around the stage wooing his deadpan wife. Leah Penston's Morticia was an exercise in less is more. Communicating her thoughts or contempt or pleasure with an elegant flick of her wrist, Ms Penston didn't have to try. Her voice was exquisite on all her numbers but particularly on "Just Around the Corner" and her duet with Gomez "Live Before we Die" and her dancing was equally adept. Their daughter, Wednesday, was played by Leah Comerford with a goth- like sensibility, slamming around the stage moaning that her parents didn't understand her. She had this thousand- yard stare throughout the show that hinted at her being slightly unhinged, a trait that clearly attracted Lucas her fiancé, who was wonderfully played by Simon Broderick with a boy-next-door ambiance. Mr Broderick has a sweet voice, which he used to great effect on "Crazier Than You" with Ms Comerford. She also sang well on "Pulled" accompanied by her brother Pugsley's ecstatic groans as she tortured him. Ms Comerford had a good chemistry with Ciarán O'Dwyer's Pugsley, who was just the perfect evil little brother. Mischievous and conniving, he steals a truth potion from his Grandma, a hilarious Claire Henriques who resembled Brenda Fricker from Home Alone 2, to administer to Wednesday but inadvertently it is given to Lucas' Mother, Alice during the family game "Full Disclosure" and all hell breaks loose.

Alice, here played wonderfully by Sarah Brennan, a typical suburban Mom in a loveless marriage devotes her life to her son, Lucas. Ms Brennan captured her essence perfectly, when her rhyming couplets and forced laughter exploded into a rant about her life in the stunning "Waiting", which brought the house down. Her self-absorbed husband, Mal was played by Jody Ridgwell with a delicious cynicism. Both sang well on "Crazier Than You" with Wednesday and Lucas. The Addams butler, Lurch, was played by Mark Duffy. I loved Mr Duffy's physical comedy. His slowness as Lurch really worked for the character as did his moans and groans. Non-verbal characters are difficult to do in a show, but he did it very well.

However, the star of the show was David Doyle's Uncle Fester, brother to Gomez. This performance was at another level. From his aggressive gaze out to the audience at the start to his playfulness with the Ancestors and the audience, Mr Doyle owned the stage. This was not the Fester we are used to. Ms Scarry and Mr Doyle took a chance in contemporising the character and it worked brilliantly. He had the audience in the palm of his hand, and they perked up whenever he entered. His energy and stagecraft were exceptional as he swaggered across the stage throughout. "The Moon and Me", where he declared his love for Luna, was ridiculously sweet but he made it work as we wanted him to find love. The audience crooned "Ahh…", when he set off on his journey to his paramour strapped to some very hazardous looking rockets at the end of the show.

Everyone was on the same page in this show, which is sadly not often the case in some productions. They clearly understood the genre and the director's vision. When they broke the fourth wall (particularly Fester & Gomez), they did it within the spirit of the show and did not pantomime it - they were always in control. As a cohesive ensemble, the Ancestors were always attentive to the 'Family' and did not stray their focus. Christine Scarry directed a slick, fast paced show which was loud and proud and took no prisoners. Some lovely moments of theatre during the show; like Fester's use and abuse of the exercise ball, the penetrating gaze of the Family during "When You're an Addams", the inventive set and exquisite lighting. Her work with the cast, and especially the principals was clever and delicate, which I think, made them feel invested in the production. Her Ancestors were always on point and never wavered. Ms Scarry's interpretation of the work was measured and accurate with a few adroit little changes and she also took risks, which made it a very good show.

Lost in the Darkness It may seem an odd choice to create a musical based on Robert Louis Stevenson's gothic horror novella written in 1886. But Frank Wildhorn did just that in 1990 and like most musicals it went through a series of re-writes until it hit Broadway in 1997 and with another re-write, on tour in the UK in 2004. Wildhorn is clearly attracted to the dark side of human nature having also written musicals based on Dracula and The Count of Monte Cristo among many others. Jekyll and Hyde has quite a dense and overblown operatic score and seems heavily influenced by Les Miserables and especially The Phantom of the Opera. But, it also has a charm of its own and features some great tunes.

Bravo Theatre Group, based in Loughrea in Galway, staged the show in the Temperance Hall in late September, early October this year. Directed and choreographed by long-time Bravo collaborator, Aoife McClafferty, with musical direction by the ubiquitous Shane Farrell, this was on the surface, the ideal production for the talented Bravo team, who often tackle difficult shows.

The plot follows Dr Henry Jekyll, who vows to explore and excise the darkness within man through chemical means by experimenting on human subjects. The Board of Governors in the hospital where he practices won't allow this, so he experiments on himself by drinking a serum he's concocted. This has disastrous consequences as he releases his alter ego, Mr Hyde who rampages ripper-like through Victorian London. Interestingly, Jekyll is a not a very nice character, being self-obsessed and narcissistic but also a bit simpering. Hyde, in contrast was written as a charming psychopathic murderer and it could be argued that his killing of certain characters was vigilantism (the pederast bishop for instance).

Leading the cast was Stephen Rabbette as Jekyll/Hyde in a role that is not for the faint-hearted or the novice. It requires enormous stamina, a powerful voice and serious acting chops to pull it off. Mr Rabbette is certainly no novice having been in plenty of productions down through the years and it showed. His stagecraft was excellent as was his vocal. He effortlessly switched between roles, often quite quickly like during 'Transformation' where he sings as both characters.

Lucy, a prostitute Jekyll befriends at the notorious Red Rat underground club/ brothel, where she is the main attraction was played with self-confidence by Sarah Corcoran. Ms Corcoran's portrayal of Lucy was interesting in that her Lucy yearns for something better in her life and fantasises about Jekyll possibly 'taking her away from all of this' yet is attracted to Hyde. Hyde visited Lucy many times at the Red Rat eventually killing her as she intended to leave him and London. Ms Corcoran sang exquisitely on 'Bring on the Men' and her duets with both Emma (Jekyll's fiancé) and Nellie (another Red Rat employee) were highlights of the show. Nellie was played beautifully by Emily Lohan in a stand-out performance full of character and distinction and one of the few characters who sang in dialect. The illicit drinking den was run by a sleezy pimp called Spider, performed by Fergal D'Arcy in long coat and faux dreads, who exuded menace and viciousness particularly in his violent scene with Lucy. Emma Danvers, Jekyll's clueless fiancé, was played by Emer Kelly who had a fine classical voice. Her duet with Jekyll 'Take Me as I am' was lovely as was her solo 'Once Upon a Dream'. However, it was her duet with Lucy 'In His Eyes' where she could really let go and she was fabulous. Her father, Sir Danvers, Chair of the Board of Governors - a nice performance by Declan Kelly - believes in Jekyll and wants to help him but is also concerned about whether he's the right man for his daughter. Other members of the Board, who rejected Jekyll's experiments were: Tomás Glynn, very strong as Simon Fergal D'Arcy playing the creepy Spider and Sarah Corcoran playing Lucy in Bravo Theatre Group's Jekyll and Hyde Stride who disliked Jekyll and had designs on Emma; Michelle Drysdale as Lady Beaconsfield in a superbly notable performance; Cian O'Ceallaigh suitably boorish as Sir Archibald Proops; Declan Finn as General Lord Glossop; Jonathan Hopper as the lascivious Bishop of Basingstoke and David O'Grady in a finely judged performance as Lord Savage. All were perfectly cast and excelled in 'Bitch, Bitch, Bitch' which some were in and 'Board of Governors' where they worked wonderfully well together.

Jekyll's long-suffering lawyer friend, John Utterson, who narrates the novella, and the opening of this show was played by Norman Quinn with a geniality and showed great emotion at his friend's descent to what he assumes is madness. Jekyll's servant, Poole, was nicely played by Oisin Dowling and the apothecary, Bisset by a laconic Larry Morgan. In the final scene, the wedding, officiated by a very funny John Hayes as the Priest, when Jekyll finally seemed to have shaken off the demon, Hyde returned and rather than have Emma suffer in his hands, commits suicide.

The ensemble voices and movement on the various 'Façade', 'Bitch, Bitch, Bitch' and 'Murder, Murder' were fabulous. Really strong, with great harmonies and especially fine sopranos. These scenes were a joy to hear and a special mention must go to Megan Lohan, who never lost character throughout these scenes.

It's not a big dance show, but there are some movement scenes like the ones above and a Fosse style 'Bring on the Men' led by Lucy, which was like a Kit Kat Klub number from Cabaret but very well danced by the ensemble. Choreographer, Aoife McClafferty clearly spent a lot of time on all these scenes because they were quite flawlessly executed and worked. Shane Farrell's musical direction was also faultless. His work with the ensemble voices was gorgeous, we could hear every harmony and his band were super. Derek Reck's sound helped here, pushing the sound out to us, delicate and at times booming, particularly Hyde's reverbed Phantomesque laugh.

Paul Kelly's lighting was so good it seemed organic in that it seemed to grow with the scenes, out of John Wright's super moody set. Nomac's costumes were of good quality and Ali Murphy's wigs suitable, particularly Jekyll's wig. Clodagh Farrell stage managed this big show on a small stage with professionalism and her transitions were smooth.

Jekyll and Hyde is a flawed work, the lib is a bit creaky and it doesn't always make sense. Some of the music can be mawkish and the ending is awful. However, Aoife McClafferty and Bravo brought a freshness to the piece helped by a superb cast, orchestra and dedicated creatives that made it work. A well- deserved standing ovation by the audience capped off a very entertaining evening of theatre.

Rebel Without a Crew Originally called 'Can't Help Falling in Love', the title was changed by the writer to 'All Shook Up' because it was apparently easier to remember which helps with marketing. Written by Joe DiPietro, who borrowed shamelessly from William Shakespeare and featuring music made popular by Elvis Presley, 'All Shook Up' is a true jukebox musical set in a small-town in USA in the fifties. It even had a jukebox spot lit in pre- set on the stage of the Market Place Theatre in Armagh where I saw it in early October. Produced by Banbridge Musical Society and directed by Ian Milford, this post-modern show also borrows from 'Footloose' and 'Grease' as we follow the citizens of 'nowhereville' as they try to come to grips with their feelings of love and romance awakened by a highly sexed stranger who rides into town.

Chad, played brilliantly by Daniel May, arrives in town on his malfunctioning motorbike looking for a mechanic, having just been released from prison in another state. He meets Natalie, winningly played by Emma McGuckin, the local grease monkey, and she becomes smitten. Chad however only has eyes for Miss Sandra, a feisty Claire Costello, the intellectual caretaker of the local museum. Natalie dresses as a guy to get her guy a la 'Twelfth Night' and the other townsfolk all fall for each other. That's the plot. I Emma McGuckin as the smitten Natalie and Daniel May as the handsome Chad in Banbridge Mus. Society's All Shook Up mean it's hardly Shakespeare...oh hang on, it is! However, in some ways the plot is unimportant as it's merely there to showcase the songs. The story is wafer thin, but it can be very funny when executed properly. Basically, this is a farce, and each joke or situation should be milked for all it's worth for it to work. It shouldn't be taken seriously and indeed relishes in its own self-parody.

Thankfully, director Ian Milford and his talented cast and creatives knew this and what we got was a hilarious rom-com set to some great tunes, orchestrated by Niall O'Flaherty, and interspersed with a lot of high-energy dance numbers choreographed by Jordan Rosborough. The set, by Theatrical Sets Ireland, was bright and cheery, with an almost high- school musical vibe in its celebration of kitsch. Rosemary Kelly's costumes included typical 1950's garb but also featured some abundant angels and devils (in disguise) and a plethora of blue suede shoes and wedding gowns. Lighting by Rodney Ellis was suitably garish and sound by Enda McClusker was full range with lots of sound effects. Stage Manager Andrew McKnight marshalled his crew and cast with a firm hand on the hi-jinks so that everything went where it should, when it should.

Mr Milford's cast were full of energy and drew the audience into this weird and wonderful cartoon world. Everyone on the stage shone with excitement, high on the adrenaline rush of performance, infecting the audience with glee. Mr May's Chad sang with passion and danced with hip- thrusting abandon throughout the show, Ms McGuckin's Natalie also sang with, at times, poignancy and joy and her alter- ego 'Ed' was perfectly judged. Their duet "Follow That Dream" was very sweet. Jordan Walsh played Natalie's friend, Dennis, who is secretly in love with her. Mr Walsh made this role his own, a bumbling, nerdy character who yearns to be like Chad but physically just can't compete. His performance was a masterclass in comic timing and his voice on "It Hurts Me" was quite moving.

The local honky-tonk, 'Sylvia's' is where much of the action in Act 1 takes place. This is run by, you've guessed it, Sylvia who was played by Maille Connolly. She is a single parent bringing up her daughter Lorraine, a 16 year-old bobby soxer played wonderfully by Aimee McVeigh. Both performers had a nice harmony together and were quite believable as mother and daughter. Ms Connolly sang with a lot of jazz/blues emotion on "There's Always Me" a song about her unrequited love for Jim, Natalie's father whilst Ms McVeigh sang with gusto on "It's Now or Never" with Dean, her soon to be boyfriend played with a smart Mummy's boy air by Shane Curran. Sylvia's crush and Natalie's father, Jim, was played Ruairi McAlinden. This was the performance of the show for me. He not only sang brilliantly but had a magnificent naturalism on stage, was totally convincing as the widower, full of sorrow yet wanted to move on with his life. Lovely work and all hidden, as it should be.

This odd little town was full of offbeat, weird characters. The town's mayor, Mayor Matilda Hyde was indeed a monstrous Hyde-like character, outlawing "loud music, public necking, and tight pants." Magnificently played by Jacqueline Mathews, she chewed the scenery and spat it out at everyone, especially her sidekick the silent Sheriff Earl, played with mute fury by David McClelland. Ms Mathews was a Scooby- Doo baddie, singing "(You're the) Devil in Disguise" about her arch nemesis Chad, with a chorus of Angels and Devils accompanying her. A perfectly pitched comic performance.

Another pivotal character was Miss Sandra, curator of the town's museum, and a rural Miss Moneypenny, all glasses and tight-fitting dress. She sang well on "Let Yourself Go" accompanied by her moving statues, in a surreal scene with Natalie.

In Act 2, the action moved to the abandoned funfair on the outskirts of town. This was where it became really farcical, with lots of entrances and exits, falling down, Chad questioning his sexuality when he kissed 'Ed', Matilda wanting Earl to shoot everyone, her son defying her and so on. It was pure madcap and slapstick. But it worked as it was so well choreographed. Director, Ian Milford let loose, and the tongues became firmly embedded in each character's cheek. Of course, all's well that ends well, and everyone got the one that they wanted and deserved. Natalie found her feministic side and Chad, relieved that 'Ed' was a girl, became her sidekick. Dennis and Miss Sandra discovered they had a mutual love for poetry, particularly Shakespeare's sonnets, Lorraine and Dean hooked up with his mother's blessing and Jim and Sylvia also tied the knot. Earl finally spoke up and proposed to Matilda and they all lived happily ever after.

Comedy is very difficult to do well. Farce is even more demanding as it is mostly physical and is totally reliant on timing, and each performer must play everything totally seriously.

Banbridge Musical Society under Ian Milford's astute direction nailed the comedy in this show whilst showcasing some delightful voices and clever choreography that went beyond the usual for a 1950's set show.

Fly the Flag One can count on the fingers of one hand the number of homegrown Irish musicals available for production. It seems to be a genre of theatre that we have shied away from in Ireland. Which is surprising when you think about it; the land of saints and scholars renowned internationally for our literature and our music has failed to produce many works in the musical theatre canon. Stage plays by Yeats, O'Casey, Wilde and more recently O'Rowe and Walsh are produced globally to great critical and public acclaim, and we are definitely punching above our weight with the popularity of our music, both traditional and contemporary, on the world stage. But societies are reduced to scrabbling around for, at times sub-standard, works from the US and, less often, the UK. Homogenous works derived from popular Hollywood films of the '80's with paper- thin plots and cardboard characters have, sadly, been elevated to an esteem never afforded to their source material. So, who's writing the Irish musicals? Do they exist?

Waterford man, Bryan Flynn had a voracious appetite for theatre, literature and music like no other. He directed and produced many musicals in his career with a great attention to detail and an original vision. Working on his seminal biographical work about Michael Collins over a number of years, honing, writing and rewriting, workshopping and progressing it until he was satisfied, took a tenacity and passion rarely seen in Irish theatre. The result was Michael Collins - A Musical Drama, commissioned by Cork 2005 and staged to great acclaim in Cork, Dublin and his hometown. It's, by far one of the most accomplished musicals written in in Ireland in the last twenty years.

Bravo Theatre Group staged the musical over one week in late September in the Temperance Hall in Loughrea. Directed and choreographed by Aoife McClafferty with musical direction by Shane O'Farrell, this was a rather subdued version of the show. Musically very accomplished with some excellent performances but on the whole, it felt a bit flat in terms of emotion and didn't seem to connect with the spirit of the work as much as one would hope. The set, by Aoife McClafferty and John Wright, was quite a simple affair, with some raised platforms and a hinged barricade which made a brief appearance framed by black flats covered in enlarged printed pages from, I assume, the Proclamation and Treaty. Tables and chairs and a prop car populated various scenes to add depth and denote location. A projection screen showed various headlines and images from the period, giving the audience some exposition and showing the passage of time. Lighting by Paul Kelly was very uneven with little or no blending of instruments and the movers scrolling colour and beams within scenes was quite off-putting. Sound by Derek Recks was very good, with a nice range of sound effects but sometimes the underscore drowned out the voices, particularly the drone underscoring the Cathleen Ni Houlihan Abbey scenes. However, the vocals were sharp and the music quite powerfully rumbustious where needed.

Make-up was unaccredited in the programme and was quite good on some characters but a bit patchy on Mother Ireland. Costume, co-ordinated by Clodagh Farrell, Michael O'Flanagan and Caroline Kelly and supplied by NOMAC, was perfect for the era but I would have liked something more ethereal on Mother Ireland to detach her from the naturalism of the show. Bronagh McLoughney's stage management skills kept everything moving along nicely, with quick transitions and timely entrances.

Bravo had a fine band to do justice to the score with keyboards, guitar, violin, reeds, horn, bass and drums/percussion; all conducted by Shane Farrell who also acted as chorus master and overall musical director. The show was partially tracked with some uilleann pipes and orchestration, as per the requirements of the licence, which added a layer of mysticism and some beef to the more rousing songs. Mr Farrell's work with the ensemble was quite good, but we didn't get all of Mr Flynn's beautiful harmonies on some of the bigger numbers and some of the ensemble were a little off-key at times. His work with the principals was more successful, particularly Kitty, Joe and Dev. The Players, whilst individually rather good - especially Players 1 and 4, didn't blend as well together on the somewhat tricky harmonies. This was a shame as their chorale as the unemotional Greek Chorus is exquisitely composed. As Michael Collins, Brian Flanagan sang well and gave us a thoughtful Collins. He wasn't overly forceful and played the, albeit sparse, humour of the role with a light touch. His duet with Harry during "Fly the Flag of Freedom", was excellent as was his duet with Kitty, "Our Love Will Never End". Mr Flanagan had a good stage presence and played the role with a quiet determination. As Kitty Kiernan, Emily Lohan stole the show. Her characterisation in this slightly under- written role was excellent. She was a feisty Kitty, full of vigour and yet showing a depth of emotion in the later scenes. Her voice was first-class, clear and effortless and a pleasure to hear. Inhabiting the role rather than just playing it, Ms Lohan was most believable in her scenes with Harry and Collins. Her small scene with her onstage sisters was a delight and her scene with the Greek Chorus "Kitty Interrogation" one of the stand-out moments in the show. Her stagecraft and command of her voice was on par with any professional musical theatre actor.

Harry Boland, who lost Kitty's heart to Collins, was nicely played by Patrick Woulfe. He captured Harry's enthusiasm for rebellion and charted his journey from a happy-go-lucky uncomplicated character to a betrayed, brooding and spurned man with finesse. Mr Woulfe's singing was quite good although he seemed to struggle a little on "I'm Not That Man", where his vocal was a bit inconsistent. As Joe Emmet, Eoin Mullins played the young, impressionable recruit with impressive attention to detail and a faultless vocal. He was constantly 'on'. Always listening and reacting, in character, to what was going on around him, Mr Mullins' performance was exceptional.

Remarkable focus and an intrinsic and natural connection with his fellow actors made Mr Mullin's performance a joy to watch.

Collins' nemesis Éamon De Valera was ascetically portrayed by Dave Langan. Written as a rather unappealing character, Mr Langan gave us a stoic and forceful Dev. His performance was very strong, in contrast to Mr Flanagan's more-gentle Collins. Their scenes together were a highlight of the show and they sang "Confrontation" with great fervour and commitment. During the Treaty Debates, we met another two of Ireland's famous statesmen; Cathal Brugha and Arthur Griffith. As Brugha, Fergal D'Arcy was quite good, his passionate speech and vocal was strong but I felt his timing was a tad off. As Griffith, Norman Quinn was more successful, in his characterisation but his timing with the music was also a little off.

Michael Collins was narrated by four players, a kind of Greek Chorus, who also performed in the Yeats play, Cathleen Ni Houlihan, which ran in tandem within the show. Player Five was the personification of Ireland in the shape of Mother Ireland, a banshee-like character, played by Majella Flanagan. This character is written as an ethereal life-force who is affected by the actions of the main characters and presumably the actions of the Irish and British. Sadly, the character seemed a little lost, reverting to silent emoting which frankly upstaged a lot of the scenes in which she featured. The four players however were more effective. They were played by Jessica Bray, Patrick Kelly, Megan Lohan and Kevin Murphy. All four were quite good as the Abbey Players but seemed to struggle with the vocal as the Chorus, particularly when singing together. However, Player One, Ms Bray and Player Four, Mr Murphy sang well. This was a fairly good interpretation of this modern Irish classic, there was nothing physically wrong with it. Choreography by the director, Aoife McClafferty was solid, the few set piece dances were well drilled and her staging was quite good, but I feel her direction was quite uninspiring. There was a lack of fury coming from the stage, an absence of a relationship to the work and it never really took off. The death scenes of Boland and Collins didn't seem to elicit much empathy from the audience and the big numbers, whilst well-sung for the most part didn't really connect with us on the night I attended. Michael Collins is a very emotional piece of theatre when all of the pieces are working together, and the passion and pathos are highlighted. Bravo did a good job in the staging of the show but ultimately failed to connect to the emotional core of the piece.

Jesus Christ In Gaza Sean Gilligan's company is one of the busiest in Dublin, turning out numerous shows each year. Some are showcases of young upcoming talent, some mix seasoned with novice performers and some are a wonderful combination of old and new faces coupled with professional creatives to produce exhilarating theatre. This was the case in September of this year when they staged Jesus Christ Superstar at the Helix in Dublin.

An early Lloyd Webber and Rice musical, Superstar, the story of Jesus Christ from Palm Sunday through to the crucifixion, started out as a concept album, like Evita, before it debuted on Broadway in 1971. The libretto takes liberties with the Bible and focuses on Judas and his dispute with Jesus' teachings. As a 'Gospel According to Judas', it certainly was quite controversial when it came out, but the hoo-hah has died down over time and contemporary audiences see it as a slightly alternative telling of the Jesus chronicle. Featuring a 1970's rock opera score, the music, with the exception of one or two numbers - "Everything's Alright" and the title song which remain firmly rooted in the late sixties, has stood the test of time and sounds quite contemporary even now forty years later, though admittedly firmly ensconced in the prog rock genre.

The production's director and musical director, Sean Gilligan, clearly had a very strong artistic vision for this show. Damien O'Connor's stage design of six 3m high crosses made from box trusses and internally lit by small led lights gave a sense of a post-apocalyptic world as imagined by a 1980's film. These crosses, on castors, were moved around the stage throughout the show creating interesting framing. Costumes by Sparkle Costume tended toward fascism, in the form of sharp uniforms and combat gear for the rulers and their minions and refugee chic and PLO scarves for the rest of the cast. Two large TV screens were often flown in showing scenes of war and also mockumentary footage of the ruling classes and television news segments about Jesus and his teachings.

Of course, we all know the plot and how the story ended but it's the journey and the folk that we met on the way that made this version quite interesting and quite unique. The concept of a war-ravaged future is not new, however suggesting that a saviour will appear and save us all from our own conceit was quite original I feel, particularly in relation to this Lloyd Webber show. The Nazi symbolism of the Eagle on the screens and flown in upstage, the news footage, the costume; was not only reminiscent of 1930/40's Germany but was also quite suggestive of the Israeli Palestinian conflict. Into this well-imagined world came a simple man bearing the name of Jesus.

He was played with high emotion and a fierce steadfastness by James Deegan, who had a marvellous rock voice and a gentle yet at times, ferocious quality to his performance. His singing on "Gethsemane" was his stand-out moment, emotional, powerful with the audience applauding during it! His scenes with Mary Magdalene were tender and his fractious relationship with Judas quite believable and very high octane. Sparks flew when they clashed as they fought through song and tried to out-maneuver each other vocally.

Chris Currid's Judas was commanding and formidable. His singing was pitch perfect and powerful, and he dominated most of the songs involving him. Mr Currid had a good grasp of Judas' character, his realisation that he was a pawn in God's plan was extremely well drawn. His frequent visions of the dead, represented here by white-faced children in hoodies - one of who was fashioning a noose from rope - was quite chillingly done and he sang "Judas' Death" with a painful desperation. His return in Jesus' vision, "Superstar" with angel wings was a tad comical but he sang it with conviction. As Mary Magdalene, Lisa Rose McMahon portrayed a quiet and placid follower rather than a forceful rough character. This worked in her favour, particularly as Mary's songs were quite soft and gentle. She sang delightfully on "I Don't Know How to Love Him" one of the show's most popular and well-known songs and skilfully with Peter on "Could We Start Again Please?". Ms McMahon's characterisation of Mary Magdalene was embodied in her vocal on "Everything's Alright", optimistic and full of self-belief, thankful to Jesus for saving her from herself and her previous situation.

As Peter, one of Jesus' apostles, Maurice Treacy played him with a firm assurance. His vocal was very strong on "Could We Start Again Please?" with Mary and he gave a fine sense of guilt during "Peter's Denial", where he denied knowing Jesus three times as per Jesus' prophecy. Simon, another of Jesus' apostles, was played by Sean Flanagan who sang well on "Simon Zealotes/Poor Jerusalem" with a fine rock voice and was quite believable as he urged Jesus to take up arms against the oppressors.

Jesus and his disciples along with the regular people of the area; lepers, children, ordinary folk, were noticeably under the jackboot of the privileged. Dressed in 'found costumes' with scarves made popular by the Palestine Liberation Organisation in the 70's, the ensemble was quite convincing. The privileged few were well-dressed, opulent and single- minded in their tyranny. Fearing that Jesus would unshackle the masses, the high priests, Ciaphas and Annas arranged for Jesus to be brought before the Governor of the area, Pilate.

Ciaphas was played by John Ryan, who had a marvellous bass voice which rumbled throughout the theatre. He played his high status very convincingly particularly when dealing with the lowly Judas. Annas, played by Tara Brazil, was equally as domineering and had a very smooth vocal. The role of Pilate is an interesting one, an eminent figure but plagued with visions. When Jesus is brought before her, she is clearly frightened as she had dreamed this situation. Played with brilliant menace by Amy Fidgeon, dressed like a Nazi Oberbefehlsleiter, she strode around the stage, totally in control yet we could see the fear in her eyes. Her singing on "Pilate's Dream" in Act One was gentle, but once she was in front of her men, she demonstrated malice and high drama particularly on "Pilate and Christ". Unwilling to kill Jesus she sent him to Herod, here played with a dangerous campiness by Conor Clear, to be tried. Mr Clear played Herod, the King, with a deliciously threatening nonchalance. The song "King Herod's Song (Try it and See)" was brilliantly choreographed and performed despite mic issues. A stand- out moment, and frankly the only 'light- hearted' moment in the show, totally owned by Mr Clear. Herod couldn't  get Jesus to speak, deemed him a phoney messiah and sent him back to Pilate. Still unsure of his guilt, Pilate asked the people to decide. Jesus is whipped, and eventually crucified. Ms Fidgeon played this scene with a great command, showing Pilate's fear that she would be responsible for the rise of Christianity if she put him to death thus fulfilling her dreamed prophecy. The crowd, sequestered behind hurricane fencing, bayed for blood and eventually got it. The crucifixion scene was excellently done here, with Jesus high up on a wooden cross with the other crosses lit up in the background. The last image was of Mary and the remaining apostles bathed in a bright light from offstage where the body of Christ had been laid to rest.  Emotional stuff.

Mr Gilligan's musical direction was excellent on this show, his band was very tight and full, and the guitar work was especially fine. His work with the ensemble produced some beautiful harmonies and his principals were all on point. Lighting by Damien O'Connor was excellent, great use of colour and the star cloth and his lights within the crosses was genius.  Sound by Derek Nangle was spot on, a lovely warm sound where the vocals rose over the band. Stage manager, Sarah Hall did a wonderful job; transitions were accurate and fast, the movement of the crosses was smooth, and her operation of the video elements was well-cued. Choreography by Aoibheann Cooke was an interesting mix of what looked like 1980's music video routines; from the S&M club of Frankie's Relax to the lepers as zombies of Thriller but it worked. We had nice 1960's moves too along with very contemporary work on "Judas' Death". Sean Gilligan and his team created a wonderful version of Lloyd-Webber's classic musical. His vision, his casting and his obvious enthusiasm and love for the show was evident in every scene, in every song. An emotional and elegant telling with a contemporary and political edge.

In Good Company Stephen Sondheim and George Furth's Company, written in and around 1970, tells the story of New York bachelor Bobby who learns about the perils and pleasures of love, marriage, dating and divorce from his married friends. A recently revived gender-reversed production with a female lead, Bobbie, had fared very well on Broadway and the West End so it was timely for UCD to re-visit the original at the Astra Hall in UCD last September.

UCD Musical Society is one of the most ubiquitous societies on campus staging approximately three main stage productions a year. It has been around for 10 years and in that time has staged over 25 productions and garnered 30 AIMS nominations and 9 awards. Not bad going for such a young society with very little funding and whilst they are the epitome of 'poor theatre', they are rich in talent and innovation. Most shows are produced in the Astra Hall, a fairly basic big lecture room with raked seating but no theatre production facilities and it was here I saw a most engaging, well-produced and intelligent staging of Sondheim's concept musical.

The show boasted two directors, Cian Gallagher and Colin Gilligan, who set a furious pace throughout and elicited some amazing performances from the cast of twenty young actors. Niamh McGowan took care of the quite extensive choreography and a twenty-seven piece orchestra under the baton of musical director Roisin Heenan more than did justice to Sondheim's intricate score. Prostups by Bebhinn Hunt-Sheridan were perfect, with simple costume changes and an uncomplicated set, comprising of a circular stage with high platforms either side and three sofas downstage, and an enormous internally-lit clock on the back wall above two exits, left and right. The performers stayed in view on the sofas or platforms throughout the show, jumping in and out of scenes where required and singing from the sides and front. Stage manager Earl Echivarre controlled the stage very well, the numerous scene and location changes done by a small team of assistants and the cast themselves. Marco McVey produced with Luke Corish and assistants Peter Richardson and Kellie Comerford on production management duties. This was a very tightly controlled production, with excellent sound by Jody Thehy, operated by Cian Murphy but was let down by the unsympathetic lighting helmed by Henry Cahill.

The whole show revolved around Bobby, played superbly by Ruairí Nicholl, a single man unable to commit fully to a steady relationship or marriage. The show began on his 35th birthday where we saw his interactions with his best friends, five married couples and three girlfriends. The musical explored his relationships through a series of short vignettes, daringly breaking the traditional mould of a book musical and enabling the directors and performers a freedom to experiment with form and even content, which they brilliantly did.

Mr Nicholl owned the stage from the moment the lights hit his early Hugh Grant locks in the first scene to the strains of the Overture sung by the ensemble in a sophisticated harmonic canon, the fabulous vocal continued onto the title song, where it was supported by a super dance sequence. A marvellous opening, introducing the various couples, all colour-coded, and our hero stuck in the middle of this alleged matrimonial bliss. Ruairí Nicholl's performance was superb throughout, his acting and singing were perfect. He owned the role and his vocal on all of his numbers was confident, clear and full of character. His final show- stopping number, "Being Alive" was a masterclass in emotional expression through song, the audience were in tears such was the empathy he elicited from them over the course of the show. A complex role, where playing the reactions of the character and his subtext was just as important as the action and text, Mr Nicholl demonstrated a highly developed proficiency and likeability as Bobby, we were with him all the way.

During the course of the show Bobby visited his married/engaged friends, who were divided into five couples. These performers were equally adept in their characterisations. Sarah (Caoilfhionn Ní Dhúlaing) and Harry (Peter Richardson), both had addiction issues; she with food - he with alcohol, were hilarious especially when they physically fought under the guise of a 'kar-a-te' lesson. Both actors had great timing and were very believable. Susan (Laura Fleming) and Peter (Jack Hanrahan) played a couple from the Deep South, with incredibly realistic almost impenetrable accents. Ms Fleming had a great range of nervous ticks and a super focus. Mr Hanrahan's closeted Peter was perfect in the scene with Bobby where he suggested that they 'get together' in a manly way. Bobby visited Jenny (Sorcha Lynch) and David (Roy Geary) in their apartment in a very funny scene where they all got stoned. This was a brilliant scene, with a delicious slowness and was one of the better scripted scenes by George Furth. He also visited Joanne (Taylor Fewer) and Larry (Robert Stubbs) an older couple. Ms Fewer had a fabulous voice on "The Ladies Who Lunch" and earlier on "The Little Things You Do Together" an acerbic wit and wonderful stillness. Mr Stubbs played Larry, Joanne's third husband, with a lovely self-possession and confidence.

The final couple were Jamie (Jack Carey) and Paul (Ciarán Ó'Donnabháin). Originally written as Amy and Paul, the directors decided to make the couple gay, as is often done in recent versions of the show. Mr Carey as Jamie was absolutely superb in the role, full of indecision as to whether he should marry Paul, which was brilliantly highlighted in the song "Getting Married Today" one of musical theatre's most difficult comedic songs as it's so fast. It was perfectly done with slapstick and great timing and was hilariously funny. He was joined on the song by Mr Ó'Donnabháin and Sarah Moran Nolan who sang as the choirgirl. Well-deserved sustained applause followed this tour- de-force. All of the couples had great attention to detail in their characterisations and each couple wore similar coloured costumes to each other. Their vocals were terrific and their acting first-class.

Bobby also hooked up with his three girlfriends during the show. Marta (Ciara Devaney), the vulgar New Yorker who splendidly sang "Another Hundred People"; Kathy (Clodagh Smullen) the small-town girl who hated New York and played the role beautifully as an innocent and April (Orlagh McDonald) the naïve air hostess who duetted with Bobby brilliantly on "Barcelona". All three sang "You Could Drive a Person Crazy" with outstanding harmonies and great verve and performed their roles with delicacy and elegance. Each character was meticulously developed and displayed very different relationships with the dithering Bobby, who clearly loved them all but couldn't commit to any of them.

This was a marvellous show, full of energy and life. The singing was excellent; Ms Fewer and Mr Nicholl solos were outstanding and the ensemble's harmonies exquisite and strong.

Choreography by Niamh McGowan was perfectly staged and executed by a committed cast, her work on "Another Hundred People", where the cast travelled all over the auditorium was super and on "Side by Side by Side"/"What Would We Do Without You?" a big Broadway dance fest that had the audience wanting to join in. Roisin Heenan's musical direction was flawless, excellent work with the ensemble and superb conducting of a fairly large orchestra brought a fresh vigour to Sondheim's music.

Directors Cian Gallagher and Colin Gilligan breathed new life into Company. Consciously postmodern, revelling in 1970's social and psychological introspection, with an intentional nod to the present by the use of mobile phones, which shouldn't work but did, this production retained the relevance of the original. A relaxed staging put the focus on the characters, story and the music, which is where the focus should be. Their admirable work with the cast on characterisation, onstage relationships and intentions gave the show an immediacy that eschewed nostalgia and brought it into the twenty-first century, where much of our life is spent online but where we still crave company.

The Addams Family was a most appropriate show for this company to perform as 'family' is definitely the word I connect with Nenagh Choral Society. The Youth Academy section of the society are a credit to themselves but also to the huge team of senior members who work tirelessly behind the scenes to support their efforts. These are the leading players of the future and the future is in safe hands.

I have seen this show many times but I still enjoy the mad cap humour and music. This was a lively and detailed production which was given some clever touches by Director/Choreographer Stephanie Browne. It was funny, fast-moving, slick dialogue with speedy scene changes. For the most part movement around the stage was natural and the cast all fitted into their roles with ease. Stephanie had obviously worked hard to make each on-stage pair gel well together and tricky things such as the oft dreaded stage kisses looked very realistic. She had also conceptualised the rather magnificent stage setting which had side flats with sliding arched doors and a raised area accessed by a central sweeping staircase. This stage design was made reality by an ingenious stage team who created the adaptable staircase which transformed into a tomb which was topped by a magnificent mythical flying creature. The gravestones which magically rose from the stage surface complete with red mood lighting and smoke, were a triumph. The family portraits on the very back wall were actually cut out, framed and underlit so that each member of the chorus could pose behind them and become a living portrait, each young person having their own moment of glory. Large pieces which were added to this setting were well made such as Granny's potion cart, the effective rack which Pugsley so much enjoyed and the torture chair. Smaller props were all appropriate to the production and I particularly liked that beautifully draped table which was used for the 'Full Disclosure' number. The set was well painted and the stage team had even gone to the trouble of applying papier mâché to make the stone columns really stand out. The lighting was used to good effect throughout with some great use of blues, greens and reds to create atmosphere. The up lighters at the base of the columns gave a wonderful eerie moment. The hazer was really needed to create the shafts of lighting through the show and the stark white spots which cut through the smokiness at the end of each number did look well but it might have been an idea to vary these.

The stage in The Scout's Hall, Nenagh is a good size but not huge so it was a challenge for Stephanie, with her choreographer's hat on, to try to create a dance plot which got everyone involved but didn't look messy on stage. There were some very 'together' dances with the whole cast performing well synchronised moves. 'When You're An Addams' and 'Full Disclosure' worked particularly well in this regard. Some wonderful staring faces too accentuated by nicely applied make up. Everyone keeping very much in character during the dances. The 'Tango De Amor' was wonderful with some moments of true Argentine Tango dotted through the number. The three couples could really dance and the pairs gave us some great lifts too. A magic moment of the production as it should be.

The sound throughout the show was beautifully balanced.

The orchestra under the talented leadership of William Cullagh gave us a rich and rounded sound throughout. The tempi were all nicely set and I particularly liked how the change of mood of each piece in the overture was handled. The chorus had been well trained and there were some nice harmonies including a couple of tricky discordant harmonies which are so difficult to achieve. The principals all blew us away with the maturity of their singing voices. Their voices worked really well together when they were singing duets and again the harmonies were delightful.

The costuming of the show was excellent. Often with this age group it is so difficult to get costumes which fit well. This set of costumes looked as if they had been made for each player. Morticia's dress had a red under dress with a black lace over it so that when she moved, we had a nice touch of colour. Wednesday's dresses looked good and the yellow party outfit was a vibrant yellow which really stood out. Gomez had a well-tailored suit and the rest of the family and visitors looked appropriately attired. The chorus were in a set of cream and taupe tones which all looked great, styled from Marie Antoinette to 1920s flappers. Their make up and well-maintained wigs all added to the overall look.

Caroline Browne gave us an energetic yet classy portrayal of Morticia. Her smouldering good looks added to this polished performance. Caroline has a great tone to her speaking voice with a slight huskiness and perfect diction. She sang really well and there were good harmonies with Gomez. This is a young lady who can really dance too as she demonstrated in her tango routine.

Lorcan McDonnell was a dashing and charismatic Gomez. He added much humour to the lines with a good sense of comic timing. He moved well around the stage and supported many of the scenes in which he appeared. He has a pleasant tone to his speaking voice, maintaining that difficult accent really well. His singing voice is rich and melodic. I particularly liked how he related to his audience. Wednesday was played really well by Joanne McDonnell. Wednesday has some wonderful wacky lines to deliver and Joanne was able to really get the humour from them. She created a very believable Wednesday who moved well and really blew us away with that powerful singing voice. She built up some strong on- stage relationships. I thought she worked particularly well with Pugsley and the little father/ daughter scene with Gomez was charmingly done.

The crazy persona of Uncle Fester was energetically played by Dylan Noonan Kelly. He captured the lovestruck Fester and his relationship with the Moon seemed almost plausible! He gave us many laughs in the role but also a few touching moments too.

Áine Tuohy was Alice Beineke. We watched as her prim character was torn away to reveal the frustrated woman hankering for the joys of the past. This was a very mature interpretation of the role. Starting of with a 'Snow White' character and revealing the vamp within. 'Full Disclosure' was a memorable moment. Her equally prudish husband Mal was nicely performed by Cuan Culliton. He gave us the starch-collared businessman who secretly was the rocker he had been when they first met. His little scene with Gomez at the torture chair was intelligently played. Jason Quigley completed the Beineke family as Lucas. There was a very believable relationship created with Wednesday. A nicely acted and sung role and Jason shows a great deal of potential for future productions.

Jayde Ryan made a great wise cracking Granny. She delivered some of the funniest lines in the show to maximum comic effect. She had a really touching scene with Pugsley. Young Pugsley was played by Jayden Guilfoyle. He was a great foil to Wednesday and how can we forget that scream/mad laugh as he was being tortured. What a stunning tone this young man has to his singing voice.

Killian Forde had all the correct stature and presence as Lurch. His mutterings when he was 'talking' to the Beinekes on their arrival were hilarious. Such a rich deep singing voice at the end of the show which was such a wonderful surprise. Milo McGee must be commended as the Conquistador. He was very much one of the focal points and appeared as the leader of the assembled ancestors. There was a good team of ancestors who worked well together. They all worked very hard in their complicated dance moves. Their singing was good throughout. As the show progressed their individual characters began to emerge which added to the feel of the whole piece.

This was a great evening' s entertainment. Well-acted and sung with humour as very much the common denominator. The senior members such as driving force Greg Browne, who produced the show supported this young cast so well. There was great attention to detail in the presentation such as the clever set and a beautiful range of costumes. There were a few things which could be worked on in future productions such as placing of cast on stage. However, the finished product brought much pleasure to the audience which braved Hurricane Lorenzo to attend Nenagh Choral Society Youth Academy production of The Addams Family.

The stage musical based on the 1960s movie is a brave choice for any society as it is a difficult one to stage. Expectations are high for the special effects of the flying car and the settings involved in the show. Dundalk Musical Society gave us an evening of laughter, sentiment and good old-fashioned entertainment with their production in An Táin Arts Centre. The show, which was directed by highly experienced Director Tony Finnegan, was very much in the traditional style of the original. He captured the feel of the early 1900s with the styling of the piece and the characterisations of each principal player. There were convincing English and Eastern European, Vulgarian accents throughout the show. The children in particular giving the dialogue such energy. The on-stage relationships were well constructed and very real. This show depends on a series of pairings in the cast which must work well together and they did. The pace was fast-moving but steady throughout. The setting though simple worked quite well, so speedy changes did not slow the flow. Movement during dialogue was purposeful and looked most natural. There were some very clever touches with the direction of sequences, particularly when the car was travelling along the road to the picnic as overtaking two girls running was achieved by them running backwards into the wings.

Musical Director Ronan Dennedy gathered together an orchestra of nine players and played the keyboards himself. A rounded sound was created for the many different moods in the show. We had nice brassy marching rhythms but also sensitive playing for the 'Hushabye Mountain' sequence, which was a delightful moment in the show. Good tempi and cueing throughout and a great balance with the voices on stage, always accompanying and never over-powering. The chorus under the tutelage of Ann McCabe gave us some rousing singing, though a few more male voices would have added more depth, unfortunately a problem all too frequent in operatic societies throughout the country. The principals were all 'en pointe' with voices which really suited the character and the song. There was a good range of voices, from the youthful energy of the children to the rich vocals of the Baron. All nicely in tune and with good diction.

Lea Carroll's choreography was at times inventive and exciting with changing patterns, build-up of tension, breaks and then further build up reaching an exciting climax. 'Me Ol' Bamboo' was full of novel ways to make use of those sticks as props, all of which worked well. Chorus numbers were lively and generally everyone kept up with the tricky routines. Pairs and groups of principals worked together well in uncomplicated but well synchronised movements. I am not sure if Lea worked out the 'Chu-Chi-Face' number which was one of the highlights of the show and an hilarious moment of theatre.

The audience could sit back and relax in the capable hands of a well-rehearsed and talented cast of principal players.
