Paudie Breen made a very believable Caractacus Potts, the energetic hero of our story. He related so well to those with whom he was acting but most importantly he never forgot to include us into his World too. Well sung and very naturally moved. He created a convincing blossoming romance with Truly as played by Orla Sheridan. This character was played as the sweet girl she was (no pun intended!) but not too sweet so there seemed to be an inner strength to the character which I particularly liked. Beautifully sung too with a delightful moment as 'The Doll On The Music Box'. Orla used the stage well and seemed to glide effortlessly around the acting areas and in and out of that wonderful looking car with such grace which is no mean feat, as I discovered at the end of the show. Tim Aherne was the retired Sergeant Major Grandpa Potts who had some of the military bearing in his movements and his dialogue. He sang well and somehow survived the journey to Vulgaria in that rather splendid outside toilet. He built up a good relationship with the two children. On Thursday night Daragh White played Jeremy and Mia Gogarty was Jemima. These two young actors started the show with such push and energy that they captivated us immediately. Daragh played very much out to us in the audience with a wonderful joy of life. Mia too had that energy which never flagged during the whole show. They made a great partnership, singing and dancing so well, great diction and a super accent maintained. Alternate shows had Brendan Carolan and Doíreann McNally in the roles and I heard many reports about how great they were too.

The Toymaker has to be played as a very sincere man and indeed this was the case with Dominic Keating's sensitive portrayal. Mr Coggins, the garage owner trying to sell the said car was nicely played by Brian Halpin who gave the character a certain charm. Alan Doherty played the charmless Junkman wanting the car for scrap and becoming the villain in the England setting and then later transforming into the epitome of a villain as the Childcatcher. The false nose and straggly wig made him into the loathsome creature.

Great characterisation and gesturing in the role as he really did scare the living daylights out of each child and adult in the audience.

The hapless spy partnership was courtesy of Gerry O'Hara as Boris and Paul McGee as Goran. We waited with anticipation to see what crazy outfit they would appear in next, from petrol pumps to pine trees, they never disappointed! A good slapstick couple who managed to stop short of becoming pantomimey.

James McGinn and Carol McCourt worked so well together as Baron and Baroness Bomburst. James created a spoilt boy always on the lookout for his next treat. He has great stage presence and a strong, deep singing voice. Carol oozed sensuality as the Baroness. Nicely styled for the part with glamorous dresses, she moved with ease during dialogue scenes. 'Chu-Chi- Face' was a real tour de force for them both. The Samba number was given real gusto too. This was a great pairing who brought us so many laughs along the way. Well done also James for a pompous Lord Scrumptious!

Praise also to Paula Murray as Violet, David McArdle as Sid, Deidre Kenny as Miss Philips and to our Turkey Farmer nicknamed 'Bernard Matthews'.

All contributed to the fun.

There was strong chorus involvement in the show with much for the group to do. They managed well with the challenging dancing, movement and singing.

Obviously, the car is the highlight of the show and it did look impressive as it appeared through the double garage doors which remained at the backstage right through the show. The flight itself must be very difficult to achieve, after all, it took fourteen people to lift the car onto the stage when it first arrived in Dundalk. Smoke was used to build the excitement, though extra waist high smoke would have helped cover the mechanisms and enhance the effect. The driving sequence worked quite well with moving images projected which made car appear to drive along country lanes. The back projections were in a naïve style but the stage lighting did wash them out especially in comparison to the vivid colours of the pull across painted cloths and the inside of those doors as the shelves in the toy shop. Other pieces such as the music box, which rotated beautifully, and the red Jack in the Box added a splash of colour to the stage. The stage team had a lot to do and worked well together to create each setting. The final flight set up was very challenging and a bit too visible from the balcony.

The lighting was quite good with some interesting visual effects such as the swirling lights which gave a sense of the sea when the car appeared to float. The starry sky backcloth worked well. It is very tricky to balance lighting with projection. Some nice spot lit moments when the principal cast were given that wee extra sparkle.

The body mikes were nicely balanced with both singing and dialogue loud and clear. There were some further opportunities for sound effects such as a sound fade of the motor bike engine as it drove off.

There was a huge costume plot for this show with the chorus alone having three or four full changes. Phyllis Woods and her team must have been busy to sort out these well-fitted sets of clothes, from Edwardian dresses with huge hats to Vulgarian national dress and striking red and black Samba ensembles, all nicely accessorised.

Hair was well styled with a range of wigs used which helped to create an authentic period look. Make up was strong with good use of well-lined eyes and bright lipsticks. I liked the Baroness' make up which had just the right amount of vampishness. The welcome was warm and sincere and the Toot Sweet candy store in the foyer was a great temptation which I just managed to resist. Delighted to see that the majority of the audience heeded the 'no mobile phone' announcement. (One of my pet hates!)

This was a good show which threw down all sorts of technical challenges which the team did well to try to resolve. The capacity audience left humming the familiar songs, I know I did as I drove to my hotel in my own 'Chitty Chitty Bang Bang'.

A show that cries out for an exciting and dynamic choreographer, "Anything Goes" was the perfect vehicle for Jack Cunningham to display his terpsichorean skills, and to transport the audience back to the golden age of Musical Theatre. Boasting a superb Cole Porter score, the  music combines with a rip-roaring, slap-stick comedic script to offer a wonderful example of entertainment for entertainment's sake, free from pretentiousness, morality or deep-rooted societal messages. Some may call it old- fashioned, but I loved it, and based on their reaction, so did the capacity audience in Waterford's beautiful Theatre Royal.

Both Direction and Choreography were in the very capable hands of the highly talented Jack Cunningham. I really cannot speak highly enough of his talents as a choreographer, infusing the show, as he did, with energy, originality, variety and well-rehearsed and delivered routines. The title song was the highlight of the show, with a standard of tap-dancing that I haven't seen in a long time, superbly executed by Reno in the front line, but featuring virtually the entire company, every one of whom displayed a high level of accuracy, discipline, energy and enthusiasm. "Blow Gabriel Blow" was another well-conceived routine, varied and interesting in structure and again, beautifully performed. But it was the attention to the duets that captivated me, with "Friendship", "You're The Top" and "De-Lovely" all given so much thought and form, and performed with commitment and consummate ease.

From a direction point-of-view, the show was smooth running and extremely well- rehearsed, with a line-up of principals who did all that was asked of them, although I did feel that more could have been asked of a few, to emphasise and exaggerate the slap-stick comedy nature of the script. Nonetheless, this was a very well- conceived show.

Played against a fairly simple and well painted set, there was sufficient use of good props and furniture to suggest the various locations on-board the ship, and all was unobtrusively handled by stage management under Darajane O'Sullivan. A decent lighting plot allowed for good atmosphere and plenty of variety. On one or two occasions, spotlights missed their intended targets, but not to the point where it became a serious distraction. Sound quality and balance were generally very good, with the exception of an occasional late cue. The balance between the backing tracks and the vocals on stage was beautifully maintained throughout.

The other drawback with backing tracks is that the Musical Director needs to have the singers very well-rehearsed in their cueing and timing, which Musical Director, Emma Walsh, certainly achieved, producing quality choral singing and a very secure vocal performance from all her principals. So confident was she of her fellow cast members that it also gave her freedom to take on the role of Erma, which she did to great effect, displaying dancing and comedic abilities to match her very secure musicality.

Jennifer White, as Reno Sweeney, dominated the stage from curtain up to curtain down. Her voice was the perfect tone and quality for a night-club singer, her dancing was excellent and her acting was straight out of the top drawer. She was totally believable in her romantic encounters and her confidence and security in her duets was what made them work superbly. Of course, it helps that she was aided and abetted by a charismatic crooner, a dazzling dancer and an amiable and animated actor, in the shape of Billy Crocker, played perfectly by Conor Lyons. These two performers were perfectly synchronised in their vocals, their steps and their characterisations. Excellent work.

Also perfect, in his comedic delivery of his lines, was Fionnan "Fatz" Dunphy as the misguided Moonface Martin. As mentioned above, I would have liked him to have been given more physical "slap- stick" comedy, but that didn't detract from his obvious talent as a comedian. "Be Like The Bluebird" was delightful.

A tad more physicality would similarly have benefitted Jonathan Kelly, in an otherwise marvellous portrayal of Lord Evelyn Oakleigh. His accent and his facial reactions were excellent, and when he let rip with "The Gypsy in Me", goodness gracious…. What an amazing voice! Easy on the eyes and the ears was the delightful Chloe McGrath in the thankless role of Hope Harcourt. As a character, she is given little opportunity to shine, but she made the most of her "De-Lovely" duet with Billy, and she sounded appropriately moody and melodious in "Goodbye Little Dream" and "All Through The Night". The somewhat ridiculous characters of Elisha Whitney and Evangeline Harcourt were played with confidence by Brian Hogan and Anne-Marie Collins, while Ivan Kiely and Thomas Rogers Jnr had a lot of fun with small-time criminals, Luke and John. Jenna Dunphy, Ciara Burns, Emma Murphy and Anne-Marie Cooper got enthusiastically into the characters of Purity, Chastity, Charity and Virtue, with Malcolm Byrne proving to be a suitably austere Ship's Captain, and Mark Rellis gave him good support as the Purser. There were a plethora of smaller cameo roles, all handled with efficiency and as already mentioned, the chorus and dancers made an invaluable contribution to the show with their energy and enthusiasm, excellent dancing and very good vocals throughout.

Costumes for the show were generally excellent, with the exception of the sailors uniforms, which would have looked smarter with crisp white tops rather than white t-shirts with collarettes, but they didn't detract too much from the glamour of most of the wardrobe. Hairstyles, wigs and make-up were of the highest standard, adding significantly to the quality of a very visually stimulating show.

Thank you sincerely to Mary Dower- Cunningham and the Front of House staff for the warm and friendly hospitality in the Theatre Royal, Waterford. This was a wonderfully entertaining show, wanting only to have more emphasis put on the comedic ridiculousness of the script. That said, I thoroughly enjoyed every minute of it. Thank you so much for a nostalgic trip back to the hazy days of musical theatre gold, and particularly for reminding me why I have always been a lover of tap!

show_raw: I Love You, You'Re Perfect, Now Change
review_text:
Whether we laugh because the situations are really funny, or because we feel embarrassed to acknowledge that we have shared these experiences, is debatable, but what is beyond question is that "I Love You, You're Perfect, Now Change" is a masterful piece of musical theatre that takes a very light hearted look at the institution of marriage.

Director Stephen Acton took a no nonsense approach to the staging of the piece, playing in a black box, broken only by the permanent presence of the Musical Director, Conor McCarthy, and violinist Maria Ryan, in a pool of light up stage centre. The two very fine musicians blended perfectly into the on- stage action and even had moments of comedy themselves, which they relished. A suitable array of props and furniture were all that was needed to suggest different locations throughout the show, all of which were moved and placed by the cast themselves, often with great comedic effect, visible thanks to a dim blue light that replaced the blackouts. This was very well done.

Being placed behind the actors on-stage required Conor McCarthy to have great faith in his performers, and happily, that faith was reciprocated by a cast who were very secure in all their musical endeavours. The show was vocally delightful, and mention must be made of a superb piece of playing by Maria Ryan, who entered into the spirit of the show with her ad- libbed solo during the Entr'acte.

Lighting and sound were both of a very good quality, and visually, the show was appropriately dressed, and sometimes undressed, to very good effect. The minimal choreography was more than sufficient for the needs of the show, and was tidily executed by the performers. And talking of performers, this is a show that asks much of its cast, with each player needing to be multi-disciplined, as they skip through a diverse range of characters, from the ridiculous to the sentimental. North Wexford was blessed to have six top calibre performers, who individually and as an ensemble, worked brilliantly together to keep the audience rolling in the aisles.

Chris Currid, as Man 3, was as funny as he was sentimental, as the script required, but his golden moment for me was his superb vocal rendition of "Shouldn't I Be Less in Love With you."  James Dobbs (Man 1) put as much comedy into his mimed scene changes as he did into his characterisations, some of which verged on slap-stick pantomime, and he excelled as the nerd of the piece. But when it came to pure comic genius, Rónán Byrne's performance (Man 2) was nothing short of a masterclass in combining physical and verbal dexterity, with a sense of the ridiculous that completely absorbed the audience. This was a dynamic performance.

The females were equally adept. Caoimhe Boyle (Woman 1) was a particularly good foil to the antic of James in his nerd roles, and she made her strongest impact in a hilarious monologue about losing control of her bowels. Maria Forrest (Woman 3) was very strong on visual comedy, and delivered her lines with abundant energy. At her best during "He Called Me", she displayed sentimentality and ridiculous antics in equal measure and with dynamic Ronan Byrne, James Dobbs, Chris Currid, Caoimhe Boyle, Maria Forrest and Joanne Logue - the cast of I Love You, You're Perfect, Now Change during rehearsals effect.  And finally, there was Joanne Logue (Woman 2) whose "Always A Bridesmaid" was hysterical, but who melted my heart, alongside Rónán, in the beautifully scripted "I Can Live With That". Her voice, her facial reactions and her comedy timing were all top-notch.

But it was the interactions within the group and the perfect balance between all involved that made this such a fast moving, exhilarating experience. The "Wedding Vows" finale of Act One was the finest example of ensemble playing, each character so individual and outrageous, and yet perfectly in sync with each other. Ever tuneful, thoroughly engaging and ridiculously hilarious, I Love You, You're Perfect, Now Change is a masterful piece of theatre, and on this occasion, performed and presented by a masterful team. Thank you all for such an enjoyable evening. very

In the beautiful lakeside setting of Enniskillen's Ardhowen Theatre, with the early evening sun still glistening on the water, it was in a mood of mellow relaxation that I started the autumn season, anticipating a night of fun and laughter in the hands of Fermanagh Musical Theatre, with their production of "9 to 5". I'm delighted to say that I was not disappointed.

In a show that could almost be subtitled "Me Too, the Musical", the not-so-funny problems of sexism and harassment in the workplace were handled with delightfully amusing effect by a cast appropriately led by three feisty and worthy female leads. Nadia Stenson, in the demanding leading role of Violet Newstead, gave a commanding and highly competent performance. Her comic delivery of lines was excellent, and there was strength and sincerity in the deliverance of her final feminist rant to the Chairman of the Board. Combined with a strong vocal quality, she was a most believable and enchanting character.

Niamh Carney was perfectly cast as the blond bombshell, Doralee Rhodes, achieving a truly Parton-esque appearance and delivery. Her vocals were equally strong and assured. Her well-maintained regional accent did give rise to one or two moments when diction wasn't as clear as it could have been, but this was still a very good performance.

Gráinne Kennedy (no relation) was a most delightful Judy Bernly, full of hurt and vulnerability in her early scenes and quirky and comedic as she progressed into the story. She had good vocal ability, and gave a very splendid rendition of 'Get Out and Stay Out'. As a team, these three ladies worked extremely well together. Odhrán Sweeney would make an excellent Pantomime baddy, judging from his highly comical and animated portrayal of Franklin Hart, Jnr. His comic delivery was both physically and verbally strong and he was very secure vocally. It's a compliment to say that the audience really loved to hate him.

Amy Hughes gave a terrific comedic performance in the role of Roz Keith. She is a highly capable actress, an excellent comedienne, and a lovely singer, who was perhaps, on this occasion, a tad too young and glamorous for a character that is written as frumpy and dull. Yet, so very entertaining.

Rhys Hopkins, who also directed the show, gave heart and soul to the character of Joe, believable in his love for Violet, and with a most tuneful, easy-listening vocal quality. Nicely performed.

There was good support too from Josiah Johnston as Dwayne, Aidan Simpson as Josh, Aoibheann King as Maria, April McGuigan as Missy, Aoife Cleary as Kathy, Méabh Mackin as Margaret, and an assured stand-in performance from Jonny Cameron as Dick, when the original Dick could not appear due to injury.

The ensemble was small in number, but big in energy and enthusiasm, creating a very pleasing vocal quality, good stage presence and loads of ability to move and dance as required. Choreographer, Clodagh Sweeney, ably assisted by Áine Leonard, gave good account of themselves, devising interesting and appropriate routines, particularly for '9 to 5', 'Dance of Death', 'Cowgirl's Revenge' and 'One of The Boys' and there was good variety and movement in the ensemble pieces. I would have liked to see what they might have done with the full ensemble performing 'Shine Like the Sun', but what they presented was tidy and efficient, and well performed by an enthusiastic cast. Nice work.

Rhys Hopkins, directing a major production for the first time, should feel very proud of all he achieved, serving up a production that had good pace, well realised comedy, an abundance of talent and very few hitches along the way. I have no doubt that, with a couple of shows under his belt, he will become a force to be reckoned with.

Assisted by Eoin McCaffrey, Musical Director, Moya Sweeney got the best out of her performers and her musicians, striking a good balance between pit and stage. Vocals were well rehearsed and most tuneful, even when sung from off- stage. There were a few occasions when scene change cover music could have been edited to reduce black-out time when the changes were completed, but overall, the show was quite musically delightful.

The show was played against a colourful and well-painted set, incorporating Venetian blinded window sections with lights within them that changed colour to indicate changes in setting. These were effectively used, even creating a French flag when Roz was being shipped off to learn the French language. The stage crew, under stage manager Eoin McCaffrey, went about their business most efficiently. Lighting was generally acceptable and atmospheric, but perhaps more could have been done with the dream sequences to make them more evidently surreal. Sound quality was very good throughout the show, including gunshots, and the well-timed and delivered voice-overs. Some of the props were excellent, especially the mal-functioning photocopier, while others perhaps needed to be more substantial, particularly the shackles, ropes, etc; for restraining Hart. Costumes were fitting and appropriate to the era of the show, my only reservation being that the 'Potion Notion' number could have been more flamboyantly dressed. Wigs and make-up were good throughout.

Thank you to Áine Leonard for the warm welcome to the Ardhowen, and thank you so much to the entire cast and crew of Fermanagh Musical Theatre for a most enjoyable presentation and for getting my autumn season off to such a bright and bubbly start. It was a very great pleasure to be with you.

Sean Gilligan's direction of this stage version of the 1984 film, 'Footloose', was crisp, tight, and very entertaining when I saw it on Sunday afternoon in late September at the Helix.  Plot-wise, 'Footloose' is pretty much a direct copy of the film; boy from the suburbs goes to the sticks where fun is outlawed and brings his big-city ways to enlighten the hicks. In the process, he meets and falls in love with the Preacher's daughter and re-unites the elders of the community with the kids.

The film was a star vehicle for a young Kevin Bacon back in the days of Ferris Bueller, the Outsiders, and the Karate Kid, when the young guns of Hollywood were creating their own genre of teen flicks. Bacon played Ren, the stranger, with a wise-cracking incredulity which cemented his place in the new brat pack. Creating the stage version was a no-brainer really for main originator Tom Snow as it would be easy to stage and he had good songs co-written by Kenny Loggins and Dean Pitchford and of course he had the provenance of the popular film.

Sean Gilligan's take on the musical was to concentrate on the spectacle and the choreography, which was excellently directed by Mr Gilligan and Emma Gannon. A brilliant opening scene grew from one performer to dozens as they rocked out to the titular song, within the choreographic melee we were introduced to Ren and his mother, Ethel nicely played by Siobhan McNamara, as they were leaving Chicago for the rural wastelands and the town of Bomont, where much to Ren's disgust they were to now live.

Matthew Nolan played Ren more winsome and thoughtful rather than the wise- cracking city slicker suffering from culture shock. This worked at times, particularly during the quieter scenes, but ultimately the characterisation lacked any bite, and it was difficult to square Ariel preferring Ren to Chuck, her bad boy squeeze. That said, Mr. Nolan had a wonderfully expressive voice and impressive range, most notable on 'I Can't Stand Still'. Ren discovers that dancing has been outlawed by the town minister, Reverend Moore, who seems to be the moral heart of Bomont. Moore, played with a fine delicacy by Sean Hendley, is troubled by the actions of his wayward daughter, Ariel and his draconian attitudes drive her into the arms of local roustabout, Chuck Cranston, wonderfully played and sung by Mark Travers who exuded menace and danger topped off by a strong rock vocal. Ariel's mother, the long-suffering Vi was beautifully played by Emmagene Cooke. Her onstage chemistry with the Reverend was palpable. Ms. Cooke sang stunningly on 'Learning to be Silent' and with heart- breaking honesty on 'Can You find it in your Heart'.

Ariel was played by Saoirse Dunne. Vocally, she was first-rate, especially on 'Learning to be Silent' with Vi and Ethel and 'Holding Out for a Hero', which she nailed. Her dialogue scenes with her father and mother were very realistic and steeped in naturalism as were her scenes with Chuck. But there was a disconnect in her scenes with Ren, they never really gelled as a romantic couple. However, Ms Dunne had great chemistry with her close friend group; Rusty, Wendy Jo and Urleen. Channelling their Diana Ross and the Supremes on 'Holding Out for a Hero', with Ariel leading and the three girls as her backing singers - this was a highlight of the show.

Wendy Jo was played with spark by Caoimhe Donnelly, aided and abetted by the superb Jennifer Byrne as Urleen both had good comic timing, great vocals and excellent dance skills. But it was Arabella Dolan as Rusty who really shone out. Ms Dolan was clearly born for the stage. She sang divinely on all her numbers but especially on 'Let's Hear it for the Boy', which was a showstopper and the song of the production. Her performance was near perfect, and she owned the stage. All three sang with great harmony on 'Somebody's Eyes' and almost like the Delta Nu in 'Legally Blonde', came back on the reprise like a Greek Chorus.

Rusty's love interest Willard, a Forrest Gump like performance by Mark Kilcawley, all wide-eyed and stuttering with an 'ah shucks' homely manner, inadvertently suggests to Ren that they should just hold a dance and defy authority. Mr Kilcawley's rendition of 'Mama Says' was charmingly funny, especially when joined by the eponymous drunken Mama.

Act 2 opened in a bar with a big dance hall in a neighbouring town. Cowboy Bob and Cowgirl, played by Filip Klubicka and Lauren McLeod were the singers in a country and western band and sang 'Still Rockin' to some great hoedown choreography. Back home, it is decided that Ren will speak up at the Town Council meeting demanding that the kids be allowed to hold the dance. This is shot down and all seems lost until Ren goes to plead with the Reverend. This was a great scene as it is revealed that the Reverend banned dancing because of a car accident after a dance had killed his son. Both bond over their losses and the dance is let go ahead.

There were some lovely little cameos in this production Sandra Harding was a hilarious Principal Clarke, shouting her lines like an army Major; Oisin Dunne's Coach Dunbar was suitably sadistic, and a special mention must go to Corinna O'Brien as Betty. Her scene on roller skates was pure slapstick. Ren's Aunt Lulu and Uncle Wes were played by Lisa Buckley and John Ryan. They personified small- town America in their narrow views and attitudes. Mr Ryan's scene admonishing and slapping Ren was particularly well done.

Unfortunately, the company decided to use backing tracks on this production, which took from the immediacy of the piece and whilst the tracks were quite good quality, there were often periods of disjointedness as the performers waited for their music cues. A live band would have given the show a liveliness that was missing.

The set by Theatrical Sets Newry wasn't of the highest production value. The upstage platform was well designed and used for a variety of locations, but the trucks were poorly dressed. Very little in the kitchen or Betty's Café and the stained-glass panels didn't convince. But the drapes and signage by Sparkle added a much- needed detail to the locations.

Sound by Derek Nangle was good, with a nice range of sound effects to set the scenes. Musical direction was by Shauna Carrick and she coached the performers well, particularly in the bigger numbers. Lighting by Damo O'Connor was bright and colourful, with a good blend of movers and generics and costumes by Sparkle were superb, particularly on the dance ensemble and I loved the colourful suits in the finale. Ali Murphy's make- up and hair were spot on, and it was all perfectly drawn together by Stage Manager, Grainne McKnight.

Director, Sean Gilligan, did the musical justice. He had some superb performers on stage, a good mix of the experienced and the emerging. His choreography, with Emma Gannon, was top-notch as were the costumes. The addition of a live band instead of tracks would have elevated the production to a higher level as would more attention to dressing the sets. However, his pacing was fast, and his little additions of humour were really appreciated by the audience who loved the show.

Under the Sea.

I arrived in Galway on what must have been one of the hottest days of the year, the streets were alive with tourists and the city had a wonderful vibrancy. It was great to be there in daylight hours as I had been booked in to review the Saturday matinee of 'The Little Mermaid' at 2pm. I was seated in the midst of a very excited family who were attending to see their daughter in her Town Hall debut. There was a palpable excitement in the auditorium, which was thronged with Mums and Dads and small children all waiting to see a live version of one of their favourite Disney films.

Hans Christian Anderson, the Danish author best known for his fairytales, wrote 'The Little Mermaid' in and around 1837. Disney got hold of it in the 1930's with the intention of creating a feature-length animation, however it took until the late 1980's for them to create the film. The film was a success and subsequently adapted into a stage musical in 2007 and modified in 2012. This is the version we were all waiting to see.

The plot is basically about a teenager's identity crisis. Feeling trapped in her underwater patriarchal world, mermaid Ariel yearns to be human and to be free to follow her heart and marry a human prince, Eric, who she spotted and fell for on one of her forbidden trips up top to dry land. Tricked by her evil aunt, Ursula, she trades her voice and unbeknownst to her - her soul, for legs. In the original tale, Ariel ends up killing herself to save the prince and ascends into heaven as a 'daughter of the air'. But hey, this is Disney so they changed the ending and she gets her prince and they all live happily ever after. Like most fairy tales, the plot is simple, but the genius of Disney is in their character creation and 'The Little Mermaid' has some brilliant characters.

Director Seán Power, drove the narrative along with good pace aided by his young cast, mostly comprised of students from his 'Power Performance Academy'. They gave a spirited and brightly energetic performance to an audience of young children and their parents at the Saturday Matinee I attended. I found the comments from the younger members of the audience quite hilarious at times, for instance when Ariel states that she doesn't have legs a child shouted out 'I can see her feet' and later on another asked 'how can she sing when she has no voice?' However, they really seemed to enjoy the spectacle and sang along with some of the songs. Mr Power's direction strayed into panto territory on this show and to be honest, given the audience he aimed it at (6-10 year olds), it was a good call.

Ariel was played by Aisling Carroll with a lovely energy and fine singing voice, particularly on the well-known 'Part of Your World' and the beautiful 'If Only' with Eric, Triton and Sebastian. Her physical comedy was sharp, particularly when Ariel was learning how to use her new legs and she danced well. Ms. Carroll had good chemistry with her two comic relief sidekicks; Scuttle (a seagull), played by Luke Dennigan and Flounder (a fish) played with loads of camp by Cameron Heneghan on heelies (shoes with wheels, which featured heavily in the first production back in 2007). Heneghan and Dennigan had excellent comic timing with the latter exhibiting a good voice on 'Positoovity', where he was joined by another dozen seagulls on stage! They really embraced their well-drawn characters and squeezed every ounce of comedy in each scene. Ariel's sisters, known as the mersisters, were played by; Katie Larkin, Heather, Emily and Lauren Egan, Lucy Keenan and Sarah Harnett. They had great timing and were hilariously obsequious to Triton, yet when he wasn't around, really horrible to Ariel. Their voices on She's in Love blended very pleasantly and their dancing was first class. Their speaking voices were rooted somewhere in California, which clashed a bit with Triton and Ariel's more natural dialects, but helped with their characterisations.

Ariel's father, King Triton, who hated change, humans and dry land was played by Darren Shine. Mr Shine cut a rather Gandalfian figure across the stage, had great presence and gravitas and a gentle Irish brogue like Ariel. However, Ursula (Triton's sister and the antagonist in the show) had a sort of English RP, Sebastian had a Caribbean accent and everyone else had American accents, which was very odd.  Anyway, Mr Shine did indeed shine in the role and owned every scene he was in. Triton's sister, Ursula the Sea Witch, was played by Amy Hehir Curley in a scenery chewing larger than life performance, resplendent in what can only be described as an octopus dress, Ms Curley has an amazing jazzy bluesy voice, particularly on 'Unfortunate Souls' and 'The Good Times Back'. Channelling her best Panto-baddie, Ms Curley cackled at and at times terrified the young audience who loved her. Her leather-clad henchfish, Flotsam (Cian Power) and Jetsam (Shane Hanley) swam around the stage looking menacing and sang 'Sweet Child' with a casual louche dispassion.

Sebastian, King Triton's advisor and Ariel's good friend, was played by Declan J. Gardiner. Mr. Gardiner imitated the late Samuel E. Wright's (the voice actor who played Sebastian in the 1989 film) voice, complete with heavy Caribbean accent and idioms. Mr. Gardiner was front and centre on 'Under the Sea', a big production number, which he also choreographed. His choreography was very good throughout the show, most notably on 'Les Poissons' which included a great chase sequence on the reprise. Ariel's crush and the reason she wished to become human was Prince Eric, played by Keith Hanley. Mr. Hanley played him as a dashing heroic type, full of self- importance and privilege, yet yearning for true love and purpose. His voice was velvet smooth and complimented Ms Carroll's. His manservant, Grimsby, was nicely played by Seán Steede in a performance that reminded me of Hugh Laurie's Prince Regent in Blackadder. Early on in the show, he had a great scene with the Pilot of the ship, Michael Cooney, who also played the French Chef Louis, where he was constantly being seasick. Mr. Cooney played both of his roles with great fervour.

This was a colourful, simple production. Scene locations were projected on the upstage screen and the odd set piece was brought on and off by ASMs and sometimes the cast. The show ran to a backing track, there was no live orchestra or band, which was fine and of good quality. Costumes and make-up were excellent throughout, brightly coloured and well-applied and it all ended with a reprise of 'Under the Sea' by the company which the audience sang along to, followed by two confetti canons signalling curtain down. Listening to the audience comments as I left, the overwhelming verdict was positive, particularly from the young people and one little girl said, "I want to go again!!" Well done Twin Productions. .

Modern Romeo and Juliet.

West Side Story was conceived by Jerome Robbins, with music by Leonard Bernstein, lyrics by Stephen Sondheim, and a book by Arthur Laurents. Inspired by Shakespeare's Romeo & Juliet, the story is set in the mid-1950s in the upper West Side of Manhattan in New York City, then a multi-racial working class neighbourhood. The musical explores the rivalry between the Jets and the Sharks, two teenage street gangs of different ethnic backgrounds. The members of the Sharks, from Puerto Rico, are taunted by the Jets, a white gang. The young protagonist, Tony, a former member of the Jets and best friend of the gang's leader, Riff, falls in love with Maria, the sister of Bernardo, the leader of the Sharks. The dark theme, sophisticated music, extended dance scenes, and focus on social problems marked a turning point in musical theatre.

The original 1957 Broadway production, directed and choreographed by Robbins, marked Sondheim's Broadway debut. The production was nominated for six Tony awards, including best Musical, in 1958, winning two. The show had an even longer- running West End production, a number of revivals, and international productions. A 1961 film, co-directed by Robert Wise and Robbins, starred Natalie Wood and Richard Beymer. The film was nominated for eleven Academy awards and won ten, including Best Picture. A recent film, directed by Steven Spielberg was also nominated for the Academy Award for Best Picture, along with six additional nominations, winning one Oscar.

Unlike earlier productions of musicals in the Grand Opera House Belfast, it was lovely to see, not the heavy drapes, but an open set, where I could take in all the detail. On view, the set by Scenic Projects, were the high tenement slum buildings of 1950s New York, dilapidated with tall matching legs. It was all a fairly neutral colour, much like the original poster for the film with lots of balconies and fire escape metal stairs. There were plenty of different levels to create contrasts, while above, all the hanging washing was silhouetted against the skyline of changing colours. Centre upstage we had a gated fence to suggest the outdoor common play areas, with rusted corrugated iron. All of this was accentuated by the dappled light on the floor, which comes together to very effectively recreate the backdrop for this tragedy. The different scenes of the musical were simple but all the better for that, with great attention to detail, such as the metal framed bed, and always suitable.

For the overture (the very fine orchestra led by MD Wilson Shields), we had gangs of very small kids mimicking the antics of their teenage brothers, fighting and bullying their weaker members. Unfortunately, the inexperience in acting of these younger children didn't get the production off to the very high standards of the rest of the production. Nevertheless, I saw the reason for their inclusion when they featured prominently towards the end. Indeed, the image of the small boy between Tony and Maria in the finale suggested the child the couple might have had, had they married without tragedy in their young lives. This resonated strongly and emotionally, essential elements throughout, which was always foremost in the production, thereby accentuating and ensuring its very strong impact.

Detective Shrank (David Gray) and his sidekick officer Krupke (Andrew Devonshire) break up the warring factions, and straightaway we see they are no more moral than these delinquent kids. Very strong acting here from the two police, especially Shrank with his excellent accent and demeanour. Riff (Matthew Watson) speaks to his gang the Jets from a balcony and immediately we are enveloped in the storyline of the warring gangs with their vicious, joking put downs and banter, as they strive for supremacy on the streets. The dialogue is fast and furious as they go into 'When You're A Jet' with terrific athletic and energetic choreography (Choreographer Ann Marie Morgan). The wonderful eye-catching patterns of light on the stage floor cleverly move and change to bring the audience's eye to exactly where it's wanted (Lighting designed by Declan Anthony).

Accents, be they New York or Spanish are always top class by everyone throughout the show and the eye for detail is so fine and exacting at all times in every area of the production. The Sound (McCusker Pro Audio Ltd) was always beautifully balanced and clearly picked up the great accents. Costumes (Triple C, Alison MCCalister and Jennifer Tumilty) are so precisely right all the way through the production, especially in the finer detail. Bobby soxers and stilettos for the girls, baseball shoes and turned up jeans for the boys. There was absolutely nothing I could see that jarred, with lovely authentic looking frocks for the girls with contrasting styles and colours for both Jets and Sharks. Once again, the costumes of all the principals were of a high standard.

Glad Hand (Richard Gaston) was very strong as the well-meaning but essentially ineffectual organiser at the social dancing, which looked resplendent with a red, full length and very wide glitter curtain. The Mambo choreography and orchestra was fabulous with tremendous speed and vitality. Excellent scene! This is when Tony (Matthew Quinn) and Maria (Lucia McLaughlin) first meet as the clever lighting singles them out from the others, and the union of their lovely singing voices was a treat. This was then followed up by their beautiful duet of Tonight. Absolutely lovely singing from them both.

'America' by Anita (Karen Hawthorne) and the Shark girls (led by Rosalia, Alice Johnston and Consuela, Lauren Toner) was so evocatively Latin and funny with excellent dancing. Indeed, just the way the Puerto Rican girls moved in comparison to the Jet girls (led by Velma, Niamh Doherty and Graziella, Marie-Claire O'Connor) was so definitively flamboyant and contrasting. Their whole being told us they were much more exotic and Latin, by the way they moved onstage. Physicality is so important and expressive as a tool of acting.

I must mention the continuity and transitions (Stage manager Andrew McKnight, with performers acting as stage crew) from one scene to the next. Lightning fast and so smoothly done, so that we didn't have time to settle between scenes. This added fantastic pace to the whole production.

'Cool' was another wonderful number with an amazing orchestra and fabulous choreography from the Jets. Fantastic fully extended bodies from all dancers as they used all of the considerable space of the GOH stage.

A small point about the shop spaces, both Anita's dressmaking shop and Doc's (Paddy McNally). I felt both were much too spacious. Yes, we need the full stage for the dances but I would prefer more enclosed spaces for the location which could then artistically expand for choreography. I particularly liked the old sewing machine included in this scene. Also the huge veil that kept coming as Maria put it on and moved downstage for the 'wedding'. Beautifully sung, but why was it sung completely to the audience? Surely the two lovers wouldn't be able to look away from each other all the way through this intense love duet?

What a finale to the first act with the fabulous Bernstein quintet 'Tonight'. I don't think there's a more sublime and intricate song in any musical that beats this, with its marvellous syncopated rhythms and musical texture that builds and builds to climax in 'The Rumble' where Bernardo (Patrick D'Arcy) is stabbed by Tony, who is only there to stop the violence. This was truly excellent, really well worked and executed with great lighting and orchestra. 'I Feel Pretty' gave a great start to the second act with Maria's lovely voice and very charming choreography, which was then exceeded by that marvellous ballet sequence that was so beautifully executed. Then we had another fantastic highlight to the show with 'Somewhere'. Beautifully sung with such composure by 16 year old Rebekah Devlin, it was so emotional and it was followed by the marvellous procession and nightmare using Tony, Maria and the ensemble. 'Gee Officer Krupke' gave us much needed comical relief with Sondheim's very clever lyrics in a great number by the Jets with A-Rab (Adam Quinn), Action (Aaron Butler) and Diesel (Joshua Martin) all prominent in the song.

'A Boy Like That/I Have A Love' duet with Anita and Maria is undoubtedly another highlight of Bernstein's score with its fantastic rhythms and soaring melody, and it proved so here in this production with great tour de force singing and acting by both Anita and Maria.

Anita's terrible ordeal then with the Jets in Doc's shop was truly compelling and uneasy for an audience to experience. All of this was accomplished with great drama, especially in an emotive performance by Anita.

Inevitably getting closer to the final tragedy, the shooting of Tony by Chino (Eoin Hannaway) came all too soon, as Maria showed great effort at composure, while experiencing absolute hell at losing her beloved Tony. The drama here was beautifully paced as everything calmed and slowed considerably. An undoubted hallmark of the show was the way in which Director Tony Finnegan used pace. From high speed movement, choreography and fight direction to the very slow, elongated, dramatic pauses of real sorrow and tragedy.

Having watched Spielberg's much acclaimed film recently I can honestly say this production didn't pale in comparison, with great drama, music and choreography.

Exotic Tale Macabre.

We were very privileged in Ireland to have had three productions of The Addams Family by AIMS affiliated amateur musical societies, at virtually the same time as the current UK tour of the musical, which ended just a couple of weeks ago. Doubtless, others will be vying to do similar productions in the next few years. Tullamore Musical Society performed their production at the local GAA Centre, where I went to adjudicate. The front of house team looked after me exceedingly well, showing me to my seat and providing an intimate and appropriately macabre table for refreshment with front of house manager Ken Keena-Robinson at the interval. Thank you for your gracious welcome!

The stage curtains were closed when I took my seat, but I was still able to see the ornate proscenium. Directly over it, we had The Addams Family sign, which like the proscenium was detailed and ghoulish. There were two aprons one to either side, backed by stage stone walls. The orchestra consisted of nine players - two keyboards, percussion and bass, 2 brass, 2 reeds and violin, which gave an excellent full sound and sympathetic accompaniment for all the songs. There was also technology all across the front of the stage. I presume the six units were mic monitors or something similar, but they never interfered in any way with the performance.

During the overture we had a single white hand appear through the curtains to conduct the orchestra and other devilment! So the fun started immediately. When the overture ended and the curtains opened we found all the family behind the house gates with a star curtain behind and gravestones to either side.

This was a very pleasing opening. However, I didn't like the inside of the house so much, feeling the colours were too muted and the cobwebs on the stairs were too uniformly distanced. They needed to be much more random.

Immediately, we were aware of the large height difference between diminutive Gomez (Colin Hughes) and very tall Morticia (Aoife Fitzsimons). This was used to good effect throughout the show, and both of these two fine actors never failed to use its great comedy potential. Likewise, they contrasted also with their voices as well as their heights. He, high tenor, she with that sultry contralto. I missed the usual Gomez phoney Spanish accent but he was energetic and with great physicality. Morticia was wonderfully deadpan and excelled in her fine comic timing and delivery.

As the gates were cleared, the ancestors, all in white, appeared, through the trapdoor on the stage floor. This provided an especially grand entrance and allowed the audience to quickly study each in turn, as they appeared. All in white, they provided a great contrast with the family who were chiefly in black and dark colours, giving a very striking start to the show.  Add to this the very evocative choreography, and it created a fabulous ensemble.

When all disappeared, we were introduced to Uncle Fester and his ukulele. John Conroy has a very expressive face and is a lovely, sympathetic actor, with a very winning smile, and because of all this he became an instant audience favourite. This was followed by Wednesday (Valene Greer) telling her father out of the blue she was in love with Lucas (a 'normal' boy). She gave a lovely performance as the petulant and determined teenager, but it was in her singing that she really made her mark with a very fine and highly distinctive, tuneful voice.

Annoyingly, there were ropes high above, moving about during much of their dialogue and unfortunately not just in this scene. The ropes seemed to be from the curtain above the back of the stage and danced up and down very distractingly on many occasions. Nevertheless the dialogue onstage was riveting, as the action, frozen by excellent lighting, let Gomez come out of his dialogue with first Wednesday and then Morticia to talk to the audience mid conversation. This device was used on other occasions also and was always highly effective. Morticia's movement was excellent as she played up their different sizes for great comedy, while Gomez too was excellent with his stylised playing in his lovely suit and very good wig.

Next we were introduced to Pugsley (Rory Byrne) as he enjoys being tortured by his sister Wednesday on the rack. His screams were very realistic as was Wednesday's singing. What a voice! In the next scene we are introduced to Grandma (Nikki Burke) with her fantastic long wig, great costume and make-up. She looked terrific in both senses of the word as she talked with Pugsley.

The ancestors appeared again with tree trunks to denote the forest the Beineke family were coming through on their way to visit the Addams' house. This was very simply and cleverly done to create the desired effect. There were so many personalities to admire and work out in the ancestors. Cowgirl, a flapper in fringe dress, an ancient Egyptian, a ballerina, Marilyn Monroe in her famous white dress, and a pirate to name just a few. I loved the way Fester, as master of ceremonies for most scenes, opened and closed the various curtains with a wave of his hand. He also organised the setting up of the dinner table sublimely. This was very cleverly done and helped enormously with continuity.

We were then served with some of Lurch's ridiculous jibberish as he (Chris Corroon), addressed Alice (Jay Origan) and Mal (Paul Spencer) on their arrival inside the Addams' house. The comparison between his and their speech couldn't have been more contrasting as their articulation was crystal clear.

The comedy continued with Gomez telling Wednesday her yellow dress was awful just as Alice takes off her coat to reveal a similar coloured dress. We also enjoyed great physicality from Lucas (Stephen Keegan) and Wednesday as they snogged on the bench. The pace and continuity was so good here with so many good scenes to admire, while in 'Secrets' Morticia and Alice certainly highlighted the very good orchestra with their lovely singing.

After dinner, we had 'the game' which entailed drinking a truth potion and then telling a secret. During this, I loved the ancestors on the stairs brandishing candelabras, whilst Alice's disclosure was fabulously funny as she crawled across the table and passed out. All this mayhem closed the first act uproariously.

Morticia's solo on 'Death is Just Around The Corner' was fabulous with a line-up of ancestors and herself doing a high kicking routine. Each scene was so memorable, as we next saw Fester sing to the moon with the help of the ancestors and their parasols, which was then capped as we saw a 'mini' Fester magically dance with them. The special effects here were fantastic and I wasn't sure how it was done. It seemed to be ultra violet light showing up only Fester's head and small body while hiding his full body. Anyway, the effect was magical with a hidden person holding a balloon on a stick as the moon. Very well done!

I must admit to being a little disappointed by the treatment for the tango between Gomez and Morticia. I felt it never reached the heights of the other big numbers and couldn't understand the bull fighting episode? Surely that's the Paso Doble rather than the Tango? A special mention for Lurch's solo, which was beautifully sung with a rich deep bass voice. Another special mention for the magnificent and splendidly costumed performers of the chorus as the ancestors, who excelled in everything they did.

Director Pat McElwain delivered many very innovative elements, notably uncle Fester's scene with 'But Love', which was extremely clever and in his deployment of the ancestors throughout, which added so much to the overall production. His comedic touch was always to the fore and helped make this such a highly enjoyable show.

Deirdre Browne's choreography was very finely enacted by both principals and ancestors, as she combined many lovely elements in her beautifully moved dance numbers, especially the magical opening to the show.

Musical Director Enda O'Connor excelled with his nine piece band that delivered an excellent accompaniment to all onstage throughout with a rich sound.

Stage Management by Wayne Handy and his team was very good with smooth transitions and slick continuity. Likewise, Props by Nathalie Watts and Chris Corroon never failed to impress. Lighting by Roken Lighting and worked by Ronan Kenny provided many excellent moments, especially diminutive Fester, and Sound by Jody Trehy as usual was well balanced with great clarity. Costume Design, so important in this show, was expertly designed by Blathnaid Fitzsimons and Graham Finnerty and put together by a large band of workers. Similarly Make- up by Ali Murphy and team, and Hair and Wigs by Ali again, with Ultan Keena Robinson were all beautifully created. To finish the show triumphantly, I loved the way the ancestors, after their bow, used their parasols to hide and then reveal all the principals in turn for their bows.

This show, despite a few slight disappointments, delivered a very innovative production with many wonderful highlights, and provided an extremely good night's entertainment. Congratulations to all of you and it was so lovely to see everyone enjoy live theatre once again, both audience and performers.

A time to learn. A time to rebel. A time to love. A time to burn.

Spring Awakening is a coming-of-age rock musical with music by Duncan Sheik and book and lyrics by Steven Sater. It is based on the 1891 German play Spring Awakening by Frank Wedekind. The original Broadway production in 2006 won eight Tony awards, including for Best Musical, Direction, Book, Score and Featured Actor.

It also premiered in the West End, 2009. The show had a revival on Broadway in 2015 and played London again in 2021, although off West End.

Set in a provincial German town dominated by cheerless Lutheran religion, the story of Spring Awakening revolves around adolescents dealing with sexual desire, homosexuality, rape, and suicide and back-street abortions. But at its heart, Spring Awakening is about something simple: the way that if you deny teenage sexuality and individuality an outlet, the consequences are disastrous.

When I was kindly and graciously welcomed and shown to my seat by Chairperson Karen Hennessy, I found an open set, with ten rows of seats in the intimate Garter Lane Theatre, which was ideal for this type of show. We sat in the back row, with a very good view, and only had trouble seeing performers who were sitting right at the front of the stage, sitting on the ground.

Director David Hennessy decided on a pacy, energetic style from the cast which was always simplistic and natural, to create a serious look at how nineteenth century German Lutheran society was failing its young through a blinkered approach to sexual education. He gave us a production of great insight and sensitivity, with some moments of humour and a great deal of joy, especially through song and dance.

The band of seven were situated onstage in separate frames - three to stage right (Musical Director Jimmy Brockie on keyboard, with a guitar and bass) three to stage left (violin, viola and cello) with drums at the back of the stage just in front of the ruined and dilapidated stone wall. Hanging above this was a huge blackboard with the musical numbers written on it. This meant the band were all prominent throughout the production, which I loved because, for me, it really brought the music to life. The composition of the band too was ideal for this show, with the rhythm section highlighting the rock numbers and the strings adding great pathos for the highly emotional songs, and extracting the subtle complexity that lies beneath the music.

Choreography by Michelle Condon was very nicely judged, when it's considered this was a rock musical set in the late 19th century. So no brash, in-your-face dancing. Instead we had thoughtful, sensitively and beautifully controlled choreography that was at times balletic and always so expressive. I particularly liked the cast dancing to 'Touch Me' which was so effective and there was a great deal of hand choreography that was beautifully conceived and achieved.

The chief design element in the set (Paul Barry) was frames, picture frames to be precise, many of them broken or damaged. To my mind the picture frames, especially those hanging broken, highlighted the lives of all those involved, the broken frames representing incomplete lives. So, too, is the image of the tree of life central to the meaning of the show. When Wendla moves the tree to a central position for the ending, she is telling us this is the tree of life, constantly changing through the seasons and the generations alike. There are wooden chairs used by the cast to sit onstage and also used during the production, at school and other locations. The set I've already explained (complete with ruined wall, giant blackboard, various frames including the frames around the band and the large bare tree) is used throughout with simple pieces of furniture and other props added and removed by actors and just one stagehand, Jason Fitzpatrick.  These included the hayloft where Melchior and Wendla had their love-making scene and various house furniture. The Stage Manager was Brian Collins, assisted by Paul White, with Props by David Hennessy and Paul Barry and the action was seamless, with very good continuity and excellent transitions. Costumes (designed by Avril Musgrave and assisted by Elaine Tighe) were historically accurate, be it for the boys and men, or for the teenage girls and women. The teenage boys mainly wore school uniforms of jackets, shirts and ties with short knee length trousers and long socks. Strong shoes that don't shout modernity were essential and hats are also worn on occasion, while the girls are dressed chiefly in long frocks. Hair and Make-up (designed by Christine Hennessy and helped by Tori Browne, Sarah Corcoran and Audrey Glendon) catered mainly for the women and was excellent. However, watch out for hair braiding. Pigtails were indeed historically correct but I'm not sure if the same could be said for some of the modern looking braiding that was braided right up on the skull. All the adult roles are taken by just two in the cast, so they have frequent changes and don't sit on the stage for all the action as the teenagers do. All costumes were very good and hairstyles also fitted the period.

The Sound (designed by One Louder Sound Ltd and operated by Sean O'Sullivan) was always very clear with a good balance between performers and band, while Lighting (designed by Craig Cunningham) was at all times highly atmospheric and dramatic with strong cueing, when needed. Indeed, the lighting greatly contributed to the excellent continuity between scenes. Very much a team effort in the performance section, all the cast are valuable components in drama, singing and choreography. I mention this because if there had been one weaker role onstage it would have impinged on the whole performance. I am very glad to say this was a great team effort with absolutely no weaknesses in performance, with all in absolute character throughout.

The cast is made up of three groups of characters - six boys, five girls and all the adult roles played by two performers. The boys consisted of Melchior (Danny Brockie), an intelligent schoolboy with radical ideals who falls in love with Wendla. He is looked up to by both the girls and the other boys as a natural leader and level headed young man, who is very much the young male protagonist of the storyline. He gave a very nice understated performance that maximised his portrayal, and always looked completely in control of this difficult role. Moritz (Padraig Di Fusco), is Melchior's best friend. He is tormented by growing up and feelings of failure. This deeply troubled character was well presented by this young actor, who convincingly conveyed his inner turmoil that led to his death. I loved the way he burst through the scene at the start of the second act, to speak with Ilse. Hänschen (Shane Downey) is an intelligent and bisexual schoolboy, Ernst's love interest. Ernst (Conor Lyons), a closeted classmate who is ashamed of his sexuality, is Hänschen's love interest. Together they tell us of their love in a very well-produced vignette that was very well acted. Georg (Brian Tuohy), a classmate who lusts after his older, busty piano teacher, brings a little humour and light relief to the play's very serious subject, as he relates his fantasy. Otto (Adam O'Neill), a classmate who has a disturbing dream about his mother, is the final member of this very convincing line-up of teenage boys, who convey all their emotions so very well in this fine production.

The girls start with Wendla (Sarah Corcoran), an innocent, curious girl who has a sexual relationship with Melchior. Very convincingly portrayed, this was once again another top performance, manifesting all her anguish and indeed tragedy.

Ilse (Katie O'Shea), is a friend of the other children, who was kicked out of an abusive home and now lives unhappily in an artists' colony. Another lovely portrayal of this wrongly persecuted young woman who fails to stop her friend Moritz from committing suicide.

Martha (Megan DeCourcey), a friend of Wendla's who is abused by her father. She has a crush on Moritz. Thea (Caoimhe O'Connor), Wendla's best friend. She has a crush on Melchior. Anna (Tori Browne), Martha's best friend. These three young ladies were part of a very strong cast that exhibited very fine acting skills, as well as singing and dancing in this very fine production. The other two actors (Greta Rochford and Kevin Reade) involved in the production, played all the adult roles in the storyline, which demanded much skill to play some fourteen roles. Many of these roles were parents of the teenagers, but they also portrayed teachers, doctor, priest, piano teacher and an abortionist. The contrasts in such acting gave them both the chance to exhibit their great acting skills, which were very much to the fore throughout. There was a wonderful unity about this production, with very high production levels added to highly energetic and dramatic playing from all onstage that truly transmitted all this to their delighted audience. A great piece of theatre, with excellent team playing throughout.

Warmest congratulations to South Eastern Theatre Group!

The girl who wanted to be loved.

Sweet Charity is a musical with music by Cy Coleman, lyrics by Dorothy Fields and book by Neil Simon. It was directed and choreographed for Broadway by Bob Fosse starring his wife and muse Gwen Verdon. It is based on the screenplay for the 1957 Italian film Nights of Cabiria. However, whereas Federico Fellini's black- and-white film concerns the romantic ups- and-downs of an ever-hopeful prostitute, in the musical the central character is a dancer-for-hire at a Times Square dance hall.

The musical premiered on Broadway in 1966, where it was nominated for nine Tony Awards, winning Best Choreography. The production also ran in the West End as well as having revivals and international productions. Charity Hope Valentine, a lovelorn dance hall hostess at the Fan- Dango Ballroom, is in search of one thing - happiness. But the harder she searches, the more difficult it is to find. Gullible and guileless Charity is a woman who always gives her heart and her dreams to the wrong man. Featuring favourite hits such as 'Hey, Big Spender'; 'The Rhythm of Life'; 'I'm A Brass Band'; and 'If My Friends Could See Me Now'. This show is packed with fantastic songs as well as a very funny script by the American master of comedy, Neil Simon. I don't know why more societies aren't clamouring to do this wonderful show. For me it's a classic! It also kick-started the career of the great and talented Bob Fosse, now widely acknowledged as one of the choreographers of the twentieth century. Belvoir Studio theatre is a black box and that's how Fortwilliam Musical Society used it, with very little in the way of Scenery and Set. In fact the Set never changed throughout, but brought on different scene elements when needed, creating very good continuity.  The Set consisted of four nude female shop models along the back of upstage on slightly different levels. Speaking with Kerry Rooney, the director, afterwards, he explained to me that they represented the soulless characters in the musical - all the taxi-dancers, their customers and other, various characters depicted in the seedy New York of the sixties. The backcloth and legs were all black. However, the very colourful costumes more than compensated for this. Not all societies can afford to use the Grand Opera House in Belfast, and because this was their second show within a matter of months, they rightly made it a budget production. Don't get me wrong, the other side of this coin was a very strong, pacy production with lots of visual appeal and very good music, dancing and acting. As I've said, all other scenery and props were brought on/ off by the hard working cast. This included the lift, the girls dancing bar, the cafe, restaurant tables and chairs etc.

For the first scene in the park, a blue cloth worked well as the lake that Charity is pushed into by her boyfriend. The rest of the cast walk by in the park and freeze, while Charity and her boyfriend have a conversation before Charity finds herself pushed into the lake, so he can make his escape. She first disappears under the sheet as the bystanders look on wondering what to do, before she is helped by the police. This worked very well, but unfortunately we had some sound problems here, with very strange noises coming through the speakers. They quickly subsided and all onstage coped admirably.

From this scene we had a very good transition to the Fandango ballroom, where Charity works as a taxi dancer, that is the men pay for a ticket which they hand over to their choice of dancer, from all the delightful ladies standing along the dance bar. The girls were excellent here as they slouched on the rail in a lovely and suitable red light. The New York accents and lovely bored expressions, as they sang 'Big Spender', were exactly right for an excellent rendition of this great song, with a very fine orchestra, especially the brass section. We also had very good costumes here, reflecting the sixties, particularly the short miniskirts and a lot of the shoes and boots in white. (I should know I was a teenager then!)

On each side of the stage there was a table with two guys eying up the girls, basically dirty old men! There was also good interaction after the song, between girls and guys, as Charity talks to the audience. In the next scene, we are introduced to Vittorio, an Italian film star, and his girlfriend Ursula, quarrelling while the chorus, all in black and white, are frozen. This worked very well, probably because of the lovely stylisation, with all the very Mary Quant-like costumes. Once again Charity was irrepressibly good with her appealing yet comic performance. Perhaps, I'd like to see more of her vulnerable side, contrasting with her effervescence.

There was another swift transition to V's apartment with just a sofa with adequate space under, for Charity to hide when Ursula comes back. Vittorio's Italian accent was very good as they discuss the Fickle Finger of Fate - Charity can't believe her luck to be with film star Vittorio as she sings 'If They Could See Me Now'. Both have very fine voices, but Ursula returns, Charity hides under the sofa as they make love above her.

So, Charity is back with the girls from the Fandango ballroom as they all sing 'There's Gotta Be Something Better Than This'. This was a really great number, with lovely choreography and the orchestra excellent again. Following this, we are introduced to Oscar, a very timid, uptight and manic male, who panics when they get stuck in the lift.

I thought it was a very good and suitable idea for this production to have a simple lift with three panel flats hinged together in a three quarter box shape. But quivering sides didn't help the illusion, and could so easily be fixed with one or both of the following ideas. Don't let the actors touch the sides. Use stronger, thicker wood that doesn't quiver when touched. Notwithstanding this fault, the scene was beautifully acted by both Charity and Oscar to finish a very fine first act.

Act two starts in the lift again, but it starts working so they get out and go to church for 'The Rhythm Of Life' which is a fantastic song. Lovely, bright, flower power costumes with good choreography here, although I think if everyone involved moved around changing positions, this would have added the vital ingredient to make it show stopping. Big Daddy was especially static. I would like to have seen him much more prominent and with greater physicality. However, everyone kept their same stage positions for their movement, except for the ladies who dooby do'd as they wove in and out of the central circle. This was another great number with all the lovely, colourful flower power costumes, although maybe differences in volume would have helped contrast it more. The orchestra was excellent yet again in this marvellous number.

There were a few slow lighting cues and lack of focussed lighting in these next few scenes as Charity sang 'Where Am I Going'? The busy street scene that came before 'I'm A Brass Band' was transformed when everyone donned gold top hats, although not enough in my opinion for the desired effect, with their everyday costumes not helping. It might have worked better in a completely drenched lit stage all one colour. It certainly needed some pizazz to match the great work in yet another great song from this show. Back at the Fandango all are getting ready to celebrate Charity leaving, to marry Oscar, with Herman procuring a cake. Unfortunately it said "Happy birthday Angelo" rather than "Congrats Charity". Nevertheless, Oscar made up for it with a great rendition of 'I Love To Cry At Weddings'. However, poor Charity is once again disappointed by an apologetic but weak Oscar, who couldn't go through with marrying her. So, just like the start, poor Charity ends up in the lake. And so to the big finale and walk ons as the show finishes with a great rendition of 'If My Friends Could See Me Now'.

This was a really good show with strong acting by everyone on stage, especially Charity, Vittorio, Oscar, Herman, Nicki, Helene, Charlie, and Ursula. In fact all the principals. A minimalist approach in this production very nearly came off but top hats alone didn't work for the great big number that 'I'm A Brass Band' needed. In fact, it lacked that extra glitz and glamour for the really big numbers. Your infectious enthusiasm for amateur musicals is there for all to see. I really admire all the good work I saw in this production and I look forward to a really bright future for Fortwilliam Musical Society.

Chess is a musical with music by Benny Andersson and Bjorn Ulvaeus of the pop group ABBA, lyrics by Ulvaeus and Tim Rice, and book by Rice. The story involves a politically driven, Cold War- era chess tournament between two grandmasters, one American and the other Soviet, and their fight over a woman who manages one and falls in love with the other. Although the protagonists were not intended to represent any real individuals, the character of the American grandmaster (named Freddie Trumper in the stage version) was loosely based on Bobby Fischer, while elements of the story may have been inspired by the chess careers of Russian grandmasters Viktor Korchnoi and Anatoly Karpov.

As with other productions such as 'Jesus Christ Superstar' and 'Evita', a highly successful concept album was released prior to the first theatrical production in order to raise money. In the case of Chess, the concept album was released in the autumn of 1984 while the show opened in London's West End in 1986 where it played for three years. A much-altered US version premiered on Broadway in 1988 with a book by Richard Nelson, but survived only for two months. Chess is frequently revised for new productions, many of which try to merge elements from both the British and American versions, but was not revived in the West End until 2018.

The Strand theatre, Carrick-on-Suir has an impressively large auditorium seating more than 500. I was welcomed by Front of House and shown to my seat, with a nice cup of tea in the interval. When seated, I found an open set ready for the first act.

There was a back projection showing the title, with legs on both sides depicting chess squares black on white and the reverse. Uniformly spaced at the top, they scattered as they got lower. This was mirrored by the two flags, American and Soviet, on the two aprons that seemed to bleed as they reached the floor. Both images, flags and chess boards, seemed to suggest everything seemingly fine but ending in final chaos and disruption. A simple, but very clever device, that commented on the action. On the stage right apron, there was a bed beneath the US flag, while there was a buttoned leather armchair and chess table beneath the Russian flag. Stage manager Michael O'Hara kept the whole show moving well, with good changing of scenery. I especially liked the Championship chess table with its two players that were raised hydraulically for each match. An extensive array of lights were out front with profiles and LEDs and a few large movers, so I expected lots of interesting lighting. As the orchestra started the overture, an onstage chorus of singers took their seats upstage. They greatly enhanced much of the singing in the show and played a vital role.

The director of the show, Martin McNelis, assisted by Chloe O'Sullivan, had a clear vision of what he wanted his production to be and he mostly achieved that with, at times, stunning visual appeal, mixed with good characterisations from his cast of talented singers, actors and dancers. I especially liked the scenes with the press that were handled so well, including live projections onto the onstage screen, showing close up images of soloists and duets (Camera-men, James Jimsy Dowley and Bobby Landers). This worked particularly well. The storyline is at times complicated but Mr McNelis managed to sail a steady ship throughout with good portrayals from all his cast.

Musical Director, Fergal Carroll, assisted by Chorus Master Eamon O'Malley, led a fine orchestra, with strong principal singers and a good chorus, augmented by the aforementioned extra chorus singers, behind all the action.  The big numbers all worked very admirably. 'Anthem', 'I Know Him So Well', 'One Night In Bangkok', 'Someone Else's Story', 'Heaven Help My Heart' and 'You And I' all shone. But, Chess is a strange musical, with magnificent tunes and lyrics in its big numbers, but so much of the other music, for me, is instantly forgettable, trying to be too operatic and not hitting the mark. Freddie (Emmet Donlan), the arrogant and fiery American, starred, for me, with his volatile moods and temperament and he sang well also, especially in his upper register. Anatoly (Michael Raggett), of course stole the show with his wonderful highly emotional 'Anthem' at the end of Act One, while both ladies, Florence (Sandra Power) and Svetlana (Louise Russell), gave very good performances in both singing and acting with their portrayals. The Arbiter (Tarryn Attlee) was suitably unemotional and religiously fair in all her doings. I liked the scene where she fronted a female chorus of women dressed in black trouser suits with white shirts and black/white chequered ties. The two seconds, Walter (Seamus Power) and Molokov (Neill Bourke) gave nicely contrasting roles, the Russian more passionate and flamboyant, with the American quieter but equally devious. The new Soviet challenger, Viigand, to defected Anatoly's throne, said very little but certainly looked the part with shaved head and large beard.

During the overture, Anatoly talked with his children at the chessboard, and as the show proceeded I initially found it difficult at times to hear individual voices against the orchestra. When Freddie sang 'Pity The Child', I could barely hear him in his quieter first verse but when he increased his volume in verse two, it was fine. Unfortunately this was apparent at times throughout the production too, and I thought the volume of the orchestra was often too loud for the singers unless they were singing in a high register. This was especially the case with the keyboard that had a very clunky sound to it. When I realised Jimmy Brockie was on keyboard, that I heard and admired the previous week in Waterford, I came to the conclusion that it was the sound engineer (DBL, Dungarvan) that was having difficulties with the balance. The balance and quality of sound certainly disappointed me, and didn't do justice to the singers nor the orchestra. Whether this was the case only on the last night, or it was like this for the entire run of the show, I don't know.

Costuming however was an absolute delight. Everyone was in black and white, like a chessboard, except for the Merano dancers and Bangkok traditional and modern sleazy dancers. 'One Night in Bangkok' was a standout number because of costuming. The contrast of lovely traditional costumed dancers with the bang up-to-date, sleazy yet colourful gang of girls accompanying Freddie all in white, looked terrific. I particularly liked the ballet dancers and human chess pieces that were used during the championship games, especially the game that Freddie ended by scattering the chess pieces, which was reflected by the human chess pieces prostrate on the floor. I also very much liked the striking Russian guards' costumes with large heavy overcoats and fur hats and of course the well grown beards!

The choreography (Edel Quinlan), was nicely innovative with much invention in the movement of the dances. Once again, I particularly liked the ballet with their beautifully graceful movement.
