However, not all dances were perfectly synchronised and there were a few examples of individual dancers not always in time with the others.

Lighting by DBL Dungarvan, promised much with the large array of lights and certainly had lovely moments, either of saturated colours onstage or individuals picked out with small movers that were excellent. My favourite was in Anatoly's suite with 'Where I Want To Be', with the picking up of the delegation with small individual blue and then red movers. This was very slickly done here. But, sometimes the lights in other numbers were not completely accurate in picking out individuals in a highly detailed lighting plot. Often, the intricate lighting slightly missed its targets, with parts of faces unlit. Despite technical issues, there was much to admire in this production of Chess, with excellent costumes and the filming of live projections shown onstage, on the screen, by the very good camera crew, as well as good performances from all onstage and a fine production. Very well done by Carrick-on-Suir Musical Society and I wish you well for your future shows.

Hip Swinging Action and Songs.

'All Shook Up' is a 2004 American jukebox musical with music from the Elvis Presley songbook and with a book by Joe DiPietro. The musical premiered on Broadway in 2005 followed by an American tour and a subsequent UK tour.

Inspired by Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, All Shook Up follows a small Midwestern town that is thrown into a frenzy with the arrival of Chad, a good-looking, motorcycle-riding roustabout, who rides from town to town with a guitar on his back, blue suede shoes on his feet, and a song in his heart.

And so to my final musical adjudication at Athlone's Dean Crowe Theatre for 'All Shook Up' by Athlone Musical Society. I had a very warm welcome from all the ladies of the front of house team, especially their Chairperson Joan Larkin, who assisted me throughout my stay, telling me all I needed to know. Unfortunately, as with many musical societies, they lost many members to the Covid pandemic, seven in all, as Joan mentioned this to the audience in her short introduction to the show on its opening night.

I remember the Dean Crowe very well from the few times I have attended the All-Ireland Drama Festival, as having a difficult acoustic, however this wasn't the case with good sound and mics for the cast (Derek Recks and Niamh Gough) and the small, but very tight band under the inspired musical direction of Ger Madden. The setting is a small town in the American midwest of the fifties, with costumes and props of that era well served by turned- up jeans and t-shirts for the men, while the ladies are best turned out in bobby socks and flared skirts. Ladies' hairstyles are very suitable with lots of ribbons and headbands. However, for the men this is very much the Brylcreme era and that was in short supply with too many modern hairstyles.

When the red curtains are opened, we find ourselves in jail, complete with prison bars on casters for the opening number 'Jailhouse Rock', as Chad, the Elvis- like roustabout is being freed. The set consists of two legs each side that denote Jim's Garage, Sylvia's Honky Tonk, Miss Sandra's Museum and Mayor Matilda's Office. They are there throughout, which works well for the first act but not so well for the second which takes place in the abandoned fairgrounds over one night. This is unfortunately only signified by an added leg for the old deserted Tunnel of Love.

From the opening number, it's obvious that the show is going to be high energy singing and dancing with the emphasis on comedy and lots of movement. In fact, the infectious, total commitment of all the cast really grabs the audience from the very start and never lets go throughout. The cast and chorus are so appealingly wholehearted in their singing and dancing that it is difficult not to continuously tap your feet or join in with the many well-known Elvis Presley songs. Because the storyline is so superficial and improbable, the only way to play it, as they rightly do, is over the top with larger than life performances. This works a treat and, combined with high comedy and breakneck pace, carries the audience on a high that never relents until the final bows and encore.

Sylvia, Dennis, Lorraine and Natalie lead the townsfolk in 'Heartbreak Hotel', which is a great number with everyone so strong, especially the front line, and sets the standard for the rest of a very fine show. Chad's entrance to the town folk is dramatic with good backlighting and the motorbike is great, suitably well-worn and totally in period. Another great number! Then we have a lovely freeze for Natalie's rendition of 'One Night With You' with various interesting poses from the cast as well as great dancing from all. Excellent detail in props include the motorbike, the lovely Route 66 petrol pump, the very eye-catching Greyhound bus (complete with driver and passengers). All of these are great additions to the show. Chad's double breasted period leather jacket and Natalie's very good headband and dungarees underline the period very well, but I didn't like Jim's orange dungarees that were too pristine. He is the garage proprietor so presumably these were his working clothes. They needed to be much more used, worn out and perhaps grubby. I also noticed admiringly, the short pieces of action downstage, when the scene changing was a little longer, needing to be covered, but nicely picked up by parcans on either side, so hiding the transitions, and keeping the audience interested. On Miss Sandra's entrance we have excellent physicality from Chad, who is instantly smitten by her. They go into a clever two hander with Chad singing 'Teddy Bear' to Sandra, while she replies with 'Hound Dog' to him with very fine and strong vocals.

I noticed lots of individual stories from chorus members which worked a treat. However, be careful not to steal the limelight from principals who are in dialogue simultaneously. Dean and Lorraine contrast very nicely as the 'younger teenage love' couple as mum Sylvia stops Lorraine getting too close in 'That's Alright'. Now, a transformed Natalie, posing as Ed, arrives on a motorbike for the singing of 'Blue Suede Shoes'. Chad and Jim both move very well during their next dialogue with terrific comic physicality from Jim, especially here. This in turn leads on to probably the best scene of the show at Miss Sandra's museum with many of the chorus dressed as museum pieces, in blotchy white costumes and blank masks. Excellent choreography with the moving statues here, as Sandra then comes on very strongly to Ed. Great physicality again and very comic. This moves on swiftly to a fine first act finale with 'Can't Help Falling' that includes all the cast, with beautiful harmonies. A lot of the music benefits from very fine arrangements, which are presumably by MD Ger Madden, and this certainly improves the score tremendously. The second act gets off to a flyer with a high energy 'All Shook Up'. It's now night time, with the action moving outside to the abandoned old fairgrounds to further develop the amorous attractions of the entire company. The lighting changes nicely to suggest night time and we see a moon projected onto the backcloth. Also torches are used, at times very effectively, with the general lighting dimming. At times also, backlighting through the legs helps diminish these pieces, but more was needed to be done to convince that we were in the abandoned fairgrounds.

'Look at that moon' says Chad, as he points out over the audience, yet the moon is behind him? But we soon forget this, as the female chorus join Ed, well dressed all in black with red neckties, for another great dance. Chad's reaction to Ed kissing him is excellent and very funny. His movement is also exemplary as is Jim's comedy throughout with his great physicality. Sandra then joins them in 'Power Of My Love' to show her very fine voice and what a great mover she is. Another clever scene follows with Matilda fronting a church choir and congregation as they sing and dance to 'Devil In Disguise' once again very strongly. Jim and Sylvia's mutual attraction is then affirmed as she sings 'There's Always Me' very convincingly and well. This is followed by her daughter Lorraine and her boyfriend Dean, as well as Chad, fronting the chorus with a great rendition of 'If I Can Dream'.

Now, we have a big moment in the show, when Sheriff Earl finally speaks. He has been admirable as the downtrodden, can't-get-in-a-word-edgeways, constant companion of Matilda. Taking no more nonsense, he becomes the worm who has turned. Listening to no more put downs, he asserts himself and tells her he loves her! He then leads the whole company into the final number of the show in 'Burning Love'. Once again a totally committed performance of high energy to end a very memorable production.

This was a top notch show with excellent direction by Alfie Kilduff, maintaining such endless high energy throughout. MD Ger Madden, with his lovely arrangements throughout, dazzled with his musical interpretation, and the high energy of the choreography (Jay Molyneux) was breath-taking. Plaudits too to all the other creatives. Props Manager Camilla Flanagan and her assistants provided lovely props, with the motorbike, jukebox, and petrol pump and greyhound bus all outstanding. Stage manager Jonathan O'Brien and his crew kept the show moving well between scenes, helped in no small way by clever pieces of acting (usually necking) to hide any longer changes. The set design for the first act worked well, but maybe came up a little short for the second. Lighting by Ronan Kenny had some memorable moments (Chad arriving on his bike, and the Museum statues scene). Costumes (Cherise O'Moore) was much better for the ladies than the men, with greater detail needed, whilst it was a similar story in Make-up (Heather Doyle, Ella Powell and Lisa Holloway) and Hair (Rosaleen West) with more detail needed with the men of the chorus.

What a way to end my stay as Gilbert adjudicator 2021-2022! A very high energy performance of a musical that certainly wasn't one of my favourites before this production. I can't speak highly enough of the work needed to achieve such a wonderful standard, by all the cast and production team! Best hopes for all your future productions.

The Sound of Music, the world's most beloved musical, was the genius of the well- known team Rodgers and Hammerstein. The two started the collaboration after discovering the memoirs of Maria Von Trapp in 1958. Music by Rodgers, inspired by the 1956 German film 'Die Trappe Familie', lyrics by Hammerstein and book by Howard Lindsay and Russel Crouse. It tells the story of Maria, the tomboyish and exuberant young postulant who resides at Nonnberg Abbey and who is extremely uncertain in which direction her life is travelling. While deliberating, she is sent to act as a governess, for the seven high spirited Von Trapp siblings, who sadly, are starved of their father's affection. Captain Von Trapp is a decorated Naval Officer and since widowed, runs his home like a naval battleship, much to the distress of his staff and children. However, Maria finds a way to bring love and music back into the Von Trapp Family Home. This is ultimately a love story, set in Austria in 1938, it opened on Broadway in 1959 and won five Tony Awards. The first London production was at the Palace Theatre in 1961 and it has since enjoyed numerous revivals. In 1965, it was adapted into a movie starring Julie Andrews and Christopher Plummer, which won five Academy Awards and still to this day thousands of people worldwide enjoy The Sound of Music.

We entered Gorey Little Theatre where we were warmly greeted by Carmel Byrne, the GMS Vice Chairperson; Carmel was the perfect hostess and took great care of us for the night. The Theatre was buzzing, as the seats in the auditorium quickly filled. As we settled in, we were presented with a beautiful visual of a neo-gothic, antique candelabra situated centre stage. This reflected miniature shadows of meditative light, which were beautifully effective when partnered with Mark Redmond's solemn blue and purple mood lighting on the beautifully atmospheric open stage, also displaying with floor patterns which to me symbolised a stained-glass window. Director Stephen Acton gave us a polished and well-rehearsed production with great attention to detail and many fine dramatic moments. This production was well thought out and there were many nice additions providing a feeling of freshness to this tale as old as time. The dynamism was infectious between the characters, leading to an interesting and well- paced portrayal of the narrative. In other words, it was inventive, had an exquisite charm, and I found my- self quite beguiled and captivated by it.

Musical Direction was in the capable hands of Conor McCarthy.  Conor not only conducted, but played keys also, assisted by Caoimhe Comiskey. The music for this particular show is exquisite and Conor ensured it stayed in that category. All Principals, Chorus and Younger Members were well drilled and beautiful harmonies, solos and choral work emanated from the stage. The orchestra were all on top-form with well-known musicians such as Nicky Bailey on percussion, Colette Cleary on double bass and Ann Wickham on flute, all adding their professionalism to the ten strong players in the pit. A special mention for the work with the Children, they were perfect.

Choreography was by Megan McEvoy and a magnificent job was done here, particularly with the Children. What I loved was none of the choreography looked set, when it came to the kids, it was so natural and very endearing to watch.  This led to their characters becoming believable and so the whole story took on a realism and had a harmonious balance. Larger chorus numbers were well thought out and rehearsed and more intimate moments were sufficiently handled with delicate care.

The backstage was in the capable hands of Paul Doran, assisted by Frank Byrne, Nigel May and the crew. Several large set fixtures were set and struck on multiple occasions with ease, and good coordination between crew members, ensuring no disruption to the slick running of the production.

As the opening announcements were played two cast members dressed as priests carried the impressive set piece off stage and an army of chorus dressed as Nuns took position with their backs to the audience for the 'Preludium', with a postulant kneeling centre and the Mother Abbess standing over her. The impressive chorus of operatic Nuns turned on the 'Amen' and the small candles which the Nuns held and the candles used for the anointment were also visually effective and added greatly to the sanctified feel of the scene.  Overhead we had a beautiful section of scenery which symbolised the green of the fields, the grey of the mountains and the blue of the sky. This was a highly functional and an effective addition, as it worked perfectly for every scene.

We were introduced to Maria played by Laura Carroll as she performed the iconic song 'The Sound of Music' covering the stage with natural ease of movement and in fine voice.  Laura delivered a sincere and believable Maria Rainer. This role can be construed as sickly sweet sometimes, but in reality, it needs a young woman with fire in her belly and a quirky charm about her. Luckily for us, Miss Carroll found this harmonious balance. As Maria ran off stage, realising she was once again late, the scene changed to the office of the Mother Abbess, played by Jennifer Lee, with Sister Berthe, played by Tracey Brogan, Sister Sophia, played by Tee Corkish and Sister Margaretta, played by Maria Forrest. The song 'Maria' ensued, this was well characterised and the vocals excellent.  Jennifer Lee, left us in no doubt she was a dominant force in this role, her vocals were sublimely beautiful and her connection with Maria very well conveyed, 'Climb Ev'ry Mountain' being the obvious standout song. Playing Georg Von Trapp, the whistle blowing Captain, was Rónán P. Byrne. Mr. Byrne is very obviously an accomplished actor and generously shared his many emotions with the audience easily and often. We saw the gentle thawing of the brittle and anguished Captain Von Trapp, as he softened slowly to the irresistible charms of the young governess, Maria. We also saw a resilient and patriotic man fight for his beliefs and carry his family over the Swiss mountains to a new life of safety and freedom. But the standout moment for me was 'Edelweiss', this was remarkably moving, particularly when Von Trapp broke down and his son Fredrich, played by Taylor Dench, lifted his violin and walked to his side playing, showing his father honourable support, it was just beautiful.

Captain Von Trapp's Butler, Franz was played by James Dobbs. James gave us a physically rigid character with zero tolerance and unyielding humour. Personally, I liked that Franz had a definite identity, as I've seen this part played insipidly on many occasions. So, thank you James, for the fine characterisation. Frau Schmidt, the Housekeeper was played by Jazz Stynes. Jazz gave a solid Frau Schmidt with clear diction and good delivery.

The Von Trapp Children - Playing the eldest daughter, Liesel, was Eimear Wolohan. Eimear gave a sincere depiction of Liesel. She danced and sang very well and her chemistry with Rolf was convincing, as was her relationship with Maria. Friedrich, played by Taylor Dench, gave us a smart and astute young man who contributed greatly to the production. Louisa Von Trapp, played by the lovely Sofia Church. Diction was natural and clear and choreography to a high standard. Charlie Church brought Kurt Von Trapp to the stage with a charming and youthful take, vocals and choreography were also good. Brigitta, the truth teller, played by Emily Hogan, this little lady is made for the stage, her natural acting and formidable mannerisms made me smile, as she questioned and queried each situation, never missing a trick! Marta was played by the enthusiastic Lyla Keane. Lyla was lovely in this part with great energy and well- rehearsed songs and choreography. Lastly, we had Gretl, played by the little Ellie O' Donohoe. Ellie did an amazing job, at just age seven, she was so at ease up on the stage, dancing and singing her heart out. I'm sure we will see these young people for many years to come, as they progress in the world of Theatre, such a talented bunch of astute young performers, with very bright futures ahead. Well done to each and everyone. 'Bravo'. Richard O'Toole played Rolf Gruber. Richard had great characterisation in this part and played both sides of Rolf well. First, we had the innocent, young telegraph boy who worries about nothing but when he will see his girl, Liesel, again. Then later, it's the darker Rolf who has converted to the Nazi regime and now follows the orders of the Fuhrer. The scene in the Abbey graveyard was played particularly well and with great restraint. Elsa Schraeder, the elegant and worldly baroness, who is obviously lacking in moral balance was played by the talented Erin Hogan. 'How Can Love Survive' and 'No Way to Stop It' were both generously embraced as were scenes with Georg and Max. Max Detweiler the cynical, yet dapper, music impresario was ably played by John Young. Mr. Young's take on this character was appealing and quite humorous, as he delivered the unscrupulous Max with flair. Well in command of proceedings was Marc Bolton Lee as Herr Zeller. This part demanded a forceful approach and Marc delivered this very well. His commander in arms was Admiral Von Schreiber played by Malcom Byrne, again this part was played with a dominant and well- structured approach with believable characterisation. The New Postulant was played with serenity and grace by Ciara Doyle. Baron and Baroness Elberfeld were regal and well characterised. Ursula played by Nessa Last and Méabh Ní Dhubhlaing all contributed greatly. Always remember, there are no minor characters, because they are in fact major characters in a small section of the production. The Chorus for this production were well- rehearsed and enthusiastic.

The Lighting by Mark Redmond, from Stage It, was creative and captured the settings perfectly.  Sound by I-Tech, was well measured and levels between orchestra and stage were of good quality. The Set, which was very impressive was designed by Stephen Acton, Paul Doran, Nigel May and Gabrielle Brickley, with Art Work also by Gabrielle Brickley, was dressed by Adrienne Casey, painted by; Greg Smith, Gabrielle Smith and Gabrielle Brickley and built by Kevin O'Leary. These hardworking people behind the scenes are the ones responsible for the final picture which then transports the audience into the magic.

The Costumes by Concepta Church, Angela Macken and Adrienne Casey were all well sourced and well -presented. The Puppets for the 'Goatherd' song, made by Gabrielle Brickley, were excellent and all props by Romayne Farrell, Carmel Byrne and Steacy O' Donohue were correct and in keeping with the era. Good attention to hair by Marion O'Toole, assisted by Maria Forrest and Mairead Kinsella and finally, makeup by Concepta Church and Angela Macken. Well done, ladies. Great job. Congratulations GMS, you should be so very proud of your 2022 production 'The Sound of Music'. I really enjoyed watching the vision and hard work of your talented Production Team and Cast unfold on the Gorey Little Theatre Stage, to a thrilled and appreciative audience. I have been involved in every aspect of this business for 50 years now, and I have to say, it is so refreshing and heartening to witness great visualisation flourish. It was a fabulous night's entertainment. Thank you.

Rocking the rafters! What an exuberant show Claremorris bestowed on audiences, lifting the spirits, and spreading the heavenly happiness. People danced out of the Town Hall Theatre on Saturday the 28th ,singing the show tunes with a spring in their step. Well done, Claremorris Musical Society. Mission most accomplished. 'Sister Act', the musical based on the movie of the same name starring Whoopi Goldberg shot to fame in 1992. With music by Alan Menken, lyrics by Glenn Slater and book by Bill and Cheri Steinkellner, this is the story of mobbed up nightclub singer, Deloris Van Cartier, who inadvertently witnesses a murder. She is subsequently forced into hiding in the most unsuitable of surroundings, a Philadelphian convent, but not just any convent, one that is pending closure. And so, the narrative begins to grow legs and run, as Deloris is put in charge of the Nuns choir and not only succeeds in filling the church with harmonious song but also crowds of music loving parishioners. This show boasts some unstoppable songs engaging in 70's styles, and a funky soul sound that launches you with full throttle into disco/ Motown heaven. We even witness a vibe of the smooth Barry White mixed in for effect. A blessed event, excuse the pun, and a real crowd pleaser, filled with joyful noise and irresistible glee. Packed with glitz and glamour, with a few happy surprises along the way, two words describe this production, Infectious Fun. On meeting the director Donna Ruane, I immediately saw where this society acquires its enthusiasm and energy. Donna's jovial and generous personality shines through. I would imagine she is a woman who is not afraid of hard work and manages to see the positives in everything, and this was very evident in Donna Ruane's direction. The characters had strong guidance, with characterisation well visualised and adapted to their roles, which they delivered with fine confidence and style.  Good attention was also paid to the overall staging and technical aspects of the production, pulling it together solidly. The Musical Director and Chorus Mistress, Deirdre Lee did a fine job with this upbeat musical and was fortunate to have the fabulously talented leading lady, Miss Marilyn Bane, in the role of Deloris. The Nuns chorus harmonies were excellent, and the overall choral work was to a high standard. Deirdre had an orchestra of eight, including herself on keys and the uplifting score was seamlessly integrated into the narrative with ease providing some show-stopping moments. Choreographer Claudia O'Sullivan delivered well-polished and clean work. The chorus had a wealth of raucous energy and with sunbeam smiles they made the choreography highly entertaining and enjoyable to observe. A highlight of the night for me was the unashamedly silly 'When I Find My Baby' with Curtis, T.J and Pablo, the use of isolations and the acting in movement was comedy gold. The production was capably run by Stage Manager, Ken McCarthy. We had a glitzy curtain as our nightclub backdrop which was sufficient for the first two numbers and then this disappeared to reveal the convent/church interior. This was well done, with arch windows and wings displaying beautiful stone effect finish which were also up lit, giving a sanctified feel to the setting. There was a large, arch shaped stained glass window centre back and a raised two step platform, which the Nuns utilised well. Additional scenes called for the setting and striking of tables, chairs, duke box, bar, fire barrels and whatever other pieces of stage furniture the scene required. I thought the confessional box and the organ were two stunning antique pieces of set furniture and certainly added to the authenticity of the scenes. This was all efficiently manoeuvred by Ken McCarthy, David Keane and the CMS cast members. Again, I must mention T.J and Pablo for their highly entertaining choreography as they moved the tables and chairs in the bar scene change.

And now to the lady of the night, Deloris Van Cartier, played by Marilyn Bane. I last saw Marilyn in 'Little Shop of Horrors' with Claregalway Musical Society back in November and remember thinking then, "what a talent". This diva on the run brought it all to the stage, she started high and just continued to raise the bar as the production evolved. Her powerhouse vocal was superb, and her energy was off the scale, never once taking her foot off the accelerator. Miss Banes acting was also excellent and she brought the crass and unpolished character, who certainly lacked in etiquette, to the fore with sensational effect. Her arch- nemesis of the tale was Mother Superior, played by Vivienne Lee. The unapproving Convent Head despaired at the vulgar and untoward behaviour of Deloris, praying to God to save her from this, her latest challenge. Vivienne Lee had great comic timing in this role, her laugh lines landed just right, and her overall performance was convincing and a highlight of the production. Her body mannerisms and reactions were suitably humorous and her rendition of 'Here Within These Walls' poignant. A job very well done by Vivienne Lee. Deloris had three loyal allies, Sr Mary Roberts, played by Nicole Scott, Sr Mary Patrick, played by Maria McNulty and Sr Mary Lazarus, played by Suzanne Garvey. These three ladies worked very well together, and each brought their own individual character to the fore adding variety and comedy to the narrative. Nicole Scott gave us an endearing and introverted Sr Mary Roberts, who later found her true calling, which was not the convent. Watching her realise all the things she had never experienced in her rendition of 'The Life I Never Led' was emotive and honest and the reprise grippingly uplifting. Sr Mary Patrick played by Maria McNulty had great energy and found true fun in this character. Her bubbly and over enthusiastic presence introduced many comical moments. Maria was a key player, contributing greatly to the frontline. Last part of the devout trio was the rapping nun, Sr Mary Lazarus. I have to say this character, played by Suzanne Garvey, had me laughing on many occasions. The rapping was top class and the gruffness in the voice was an undeniable added asset. Very well delivered with featured choreography, getting down like Jay-Z. Suzanne generously embraced this role making it a real audience pleaser. Karen Ronane, doubled up on roles, playing Sr Mary Martin-of Tours and Tina, her Sr Mary Martin was well-delivered and comical, as she wandered the stage talking gibberish. Monsignor O'Hara, this light-hearted and cheerful Irish character was brought to us by Ciaran Kiely. Ciaran embraced this role with a splendid vigour. You often find characters like this can fall between the cracks, but Ciaran Kiely had a bounce in his step and an alertness in his delivery that stood strong with a high emphasis on performance. The culprit of the story was the notorious gangster Curtis, played by David Alexander. David must like the part of the baddie, as I last saw him perform the dentist in 'Little Shop of Horrors', another character who meets an unfortunate demise! David played the smooth criminal with a suave and dispassionate style. Confident and composed in his stylish white suit, he owned the stage, as he gunned down anyone who got in his way showing zero remorse. David's song 'When I Find My Baby' was first-rate and his characterisation of Curtis was strong with excellent delivery and vocal. Eddie Souther, the cop with nervous tendencies, was played by Joff Manning. Joff had a sincere take on this character, and I warmed to him the minute he spoke. His acting was real and honest making his character undeniably believable. Vocal was also to a high standard, and I really enjoyed 'I Could Be That Guy'.

Gearóid Herraghty and Gerard Scott brought the gloriously funny pair of bumbling wannabe gangsters T.J and Pablo to the stage. From the reaction of the audience their facility for comedy was much appreciated. These two hoodlums had very different characteristics but were both equally as humorous in their given roles. Gearóid Herraghty, with a childish take on this character delivered many fine comedic moments and factoring in his tall and broad posture only added to the traditional inane thug look. The characterisation, particularly the facial expressions, mostly of confusion, and body mannerisms were very well explored and the song 'Lady in The Long Black Dress' was highly entertaining. Pablo, T. J's sidekick, was played by Gerard Scott. This, I believe is Gerard's first musical in forty years and he was talked into auditioning by his daughter, Nicole, who played Sr Mary Robert. Well done, Nicole, good move, and I hope this will be the first of many more enjoyable shows for Gerard. The gullible Spanish gangster added so much humour to the scenes, in his frilly shirt with his high-pitched notes and awkwardly, funny moves. He reminded me of Manuel from Fawlty Towers, particularly in the scene with the box of black magic chocolates. Great job, Gerard, keep it up. Sorry to miss Ronan Egan, who was to play the character Joey. Mary Dempsey and Karen Ronane played Micelle and Tina, Deloris's backing singers, both ladies did stellar work especially in ''Take Me to Heaven' and 'Fabulous, Baby' where it's just the two girls and Deloris on stage. Looking the business in glitter dresses and providing good support vocally, with slick and stylish moves. The featured nuns, Clodagh, Emma, Josephine, and June, plus the chorus for this production gave one hundred percent and were clearly enjoying every minute of their stage experience. This exuberance radiated off the stage to an already captivated audience. The sound for this production was supplied by Alan Dunne and was of good quality. The lighting was operated by Indigo Lighting, who gave us some slick, colourful and exciting images. The set was by Stage Wright Design and Construction, some beautiful antique pieces were featured adding to an already well fabricated and detailed set. Lastly, costumes were from Wild Atlantic Way and Wexford Light Opera Society, they were all well-presented and sparkled and shone like the many talented people on 1. A thrilling triumph for Claremorris Musical Society, on the back of a difficult year you managed to bounce back and deliver to your audiences a priceless gift…. Joy.

Thank you for a wonderful night, I couldn't have wished for a better last show to close my AIMS season. I wish you all the very best going forward with future productions. Keep doing what you love and more importantly what makes you happy.

Not a Calamity!

As we start to have an easing of Covid restrictions, it is just fantastic to see societies stage musicals once again for the 2021-2022 season. Fortwilliam Musical Society have taken the plunge, still under many restrictions, in September/October at two theatres, Theatre at the Mill, Newtownabbey and the Belvoir Studio Theatre, Belfast with the ever popular Calamity Jane. I attended the final night at Belvoir, aware that there were restrictions still in place but with a real thrill to see a live show.

The end product shows that this was very much a success, with everyone pulling together in a very difficult time to produce a show (with many Covid restrictions still in place). Many rehearsals must have taken place in very difficult situations. Calamity Jane (A Musical Western) is a stage musical from the Warner Bros film of 1953, based on the historical figure of frontierswoman Calamity Jane or Martha Jane Cannary to give her true name. The show's plot is a fictional account of tomboy Calamity in Deadwood City. To keep the peace, Calamity sets out for Chicago to bring back heart-throb, Adelaide Adams. She mistakes Adelaide's maid, Katie Brown, for the actress and hauls her back to Deadwood. Onstage Katie breaks down and confesses that she is not the famous star. Calamity once more has to restore order and persuades the audience to give Katie a chance. They do, and she wins the heart of every male in town including Calamity's dashing love hope, Lt. Danny Gilmartin. Calamity reluctantly overcomes her jealousy over losing Danny and discovers her true love for Wild Bill.

A very popular show with musical societies, similar in many respects with Annie Get Your Gun, the leading character Calamity Jane, famously played by Doris day in the film, but since played notably by Ginger Rogers, Betty Hutton, Gemma Craven, Toyah Willcox and Jodie Prenger among others, requires a woman of many talents - a strong energetic actor, a funny comedienne, and a singer who can belt out big numbers but also has a voice beautiful enough to do justice to the Oscar award winning 'Secret Love'. The show requires great pace and continuity with a full company of principals, chorus and dancers.

There was certainly a great community feel about this show, with everyone onstage and off pulling their weight. Onstage the enthusiasm flowed out into the audience, who sang along and showed their appreciation.

The director, Kerry Rooney, who also played Wild Bill Hickok, as well as designing the lighting and sound, obviously put in a lot of work into this production of Calamity Jane. Mr Rooney's tight production ensured a great vehicle for his energetic performers. Continuity and pace were good, although at times the band had to ensure musical interludes helped hide any lengthy main scene changes.

Nevertheless, he achieved good character contrasts amongst the principals with fun always to the fore. Likewise with the chorus, who helped highlight the principals with their business and good reactions to the action.

Ciara Bowman has worked successfully with several Belfast societies as Musical Director, and excelled here with band and performers. All the singing from principals and chorus was vigorous, sympathetic and tuneful and Ms Bowman co-ordinated all very ably from her keyboard. The singing from the full company in harmony with 'The Black Hills of Dakota' was beautifully achieved. Although the band consisted of only five instruments, they proved to be very tight and drove the whole show with vigour and panache. It consisted of Keyboards (herself), Violin (Barbara Fitzpatrick), Percussion (Brian Rice), Bass (Thomas Alford) and Guitar (Matt Curran). Mr Curran also doubled up on banjo at the start, to add a little bit of authenticity. They provided a tight combo and helped brighten the scene changing with lovely interludes. All sat to the left of the stage, alongside the audience there. I only really missed the lack of woodwind and brass in the larger numbers like the opening 'Deadwood Stage' and 'The Windy City'. Cheryl O'Dwyer, in her first show as choreographer with the society, did reasonably well with her small group of six dancers, especially I thought in the pictures she created in the little vignette around Adelaide in 'It's Harry I'm Planning to Marry'. I would have liked to have seen more of her work for the Chorus, especially in the bigger numbers like 'The Deadwood Stage','The Windy City' and the Finale, and I felt some movement would have greatly added to 'The Black Hills of Dakota' instead of a line-up across the stage. Moving it subtly, instead of creating simply a line-up would certainly have added extra interest. Much of what I saw, I liked, but there certainly was room for more choreography for the Chorus. Moving on to the solo performances, we had a suitably headlining Calamity Jane (Sophie Patterson), who provided a strong characterisation with high energy and a very pleasant singing voice. Ms Patterson certainly made the character her own, and successfully topped the bill with a voice that was equally successful belting it out, but also showing a more tuneful quality in 'Secret Love'. Perhaps a bit more attention to the comedy in the role was needed, just to point out that side of Calam. If you watch Carol Burnett on YouTube as Calamity in the 1961 made for American tv version, you'll see what I mean.

Wild Bill Hickok was played by director Kerry Rooney, who gave us a very assured performance of Calamity's friend, and husband-to-be.

Always looking comfortable and at ease on the stage, he was the perfect foil for Calam, although perhaps not the acclaimed singer so often seen in this role. Noticeably, as director, he deferred to Danny singing "Higher than a Hawk" rather than sing it himself as directed in the script.

Katie Brown was played by Helena Hendron. A lovely versatile singer and actress, Ms Hendron, played the role of Adelaide's maid, who sees her chance of stardom and goes for it. She was very able for the contrasts of this role - the lowly maid, the saloon star singer/dancer, the love interest for both leading men, yet also a close friend of Calamity Jane. One small point, I thought her nervous singing on her first appearance at the Golden Garter was rather overdone, meaning nothing was right with it, yet, when she resumed perfectly only a few moments later, it was hard to believe her earlier poor effort. Lt. Danny Gilmartin was played by Matthew Jeffrey, who has a very fine trained voice with a lovely tone. Mr Jeffrey created a very believable love interest for both Katie and Calamity as well as showing his comic rivalry with Wild Bill. His fine singing of "Higher Than a Hawk" outshone all other solos. However, he isn't the finished article yet with his acting and this is what he should work on to land more leading men roles. In my opinion, he simply needs to be more comfortable on stage and that will come with time.

Francis Fryer was played by Billy Harvey. I particularly liked Mr Harvey's work when he played dressed as a woman onstage at the saloon. His small but very clever mannerisms made him most successfully pass this test, which was only unsuccessful when one of the men yanked off his wig! This was a good characterisation, and his general movement onstage was always finely observed, especially in his dancing, where he showed himself particularly skilful.

Henry Miller, played by Drew Reid, is very much a link to much of the action, and he showed up very well in this put upon- characterisation of the Golden Garter owner.

Susan Miller was nicely played by Siobhan Morgan, and she played this character, as well as being one of the dancers in the Golden Garter.

Adelaide Adams was played by Orla McCormack. I particularly liked her solo singing in 'It's Harry I'm Planning to Marry' which was one of the musical and visual highlights of the show.

Rattlesnake, by John McConnell, comes forward from time to time to provide moments of comedy, and in this Mr McConnell proved to be well up to the task.

Joe, the bar man by Kevin McReynolds, was constantly seen reacting to the main action and at all times building his character onstage, so that by the end of the show, I felt I knew him.

The Stage Manager was Andy McKnight and he largely worked with three settings - The Golden Garter Saloon, Adelaide's dressing room and Calamity's Shack. The first two worked well, but there was a distinct lack of space in Calamity's place. I realise you had to work in front of the Saloon stage, but if you were to move to either side of that you would have had much more depth and made life much easier for your actors.

The set/scenery team was Brendan McInnes, Seamus Hughes and John McConnell.

There was nothing jaw dropping in the design but it worked well, given it had to work in three different theatres. Maybe a bit more speed in scene changes would have been worthwhile but the Band covered this satisfactorily with very effective interludes of music, especially with the very fine violin playing of Barbara Fitzpatrick.

Drew Reid co-ordinated the Props, and he did a good job with a real assortment of items. I did wonder why there were no glasses on the tables at all in the saloon, but maybe that was because of Covid restrictions!

Lighting is the area where I felt a lot more could have been done to enhance the show. The Lighting was patchy, with characters being caught onstage in dark spots. This was very obvious in Calamity's shack where the lighting was very tight, so that characters in these scenes were having difficulty staying lit. I also felt that atmosphere was lacking in many scenes because of the lack of colours, with no movers and a distinct lack of gels. "The Black Hills of Dakota" was underwhelming, not because of the singing, but because of the 'black spots' and the missing atmosphere that was not created by the lighting.

The Sound, however, was always clear, and most soloists wore radio mikes that were very effective.

The costumes, as stated in the programme, were borrowed from a variety of sources which suggests a variety of styles but in fact were quite well put together and never detracted from the show. Perhaps with one exception - the ladies' dresses to the ball, especially those of Calamity and Katie, which did very little for their appearance! Nevertheless, I still felt the wardrobe team, of Margaret Mehaffey, Ditanya McKinty, Orla McCormack and Janet Hill, did an admirable job.

Front of house was accredited to both the theatre and the society. I was shown to my seat by a very young boy very capably, and there seemed to be no problems in this department.

Kerry Rooney and his team should be justifiably proud of their energetic and fully committed production of Calamity Jane with Fortwilliam Musical Society. The undeniable need for community theatre in Ireland in these troublesome times is self evident in the sheer enjoyment shown by all in this production both on and off stage.

In my opinion this is ingeniously scripted and a testament to the show's longevity. An intimate musical of love and love lost. The story of two young New Yorkers trying desperately to navigate their five year relationship through the successes and struggles of their chosen careers. Cathy relives her story from the tragic heartbreak of the final breakup whereas Jamie relives his version of affairs (literally!) in chronological order meeting in the middle just once for their wedding.

You can't help but be torn between the two characters and feel for both. Who is to blame? It's bittersweet and in the end you might even find yourself hoping they'll pull through. Although on saying that and I'm trying not to be bias writing as a female however you can't avoid noticing how Jamie becomes so self-absorbed and you do feel for Cathy as she tries desperately to convince herself in the pivotal song 'A part of that' that she is still a part of Jamie's achievement. However when Jamie succumbs to the charms of his female fans again you've got to ask yourself would the dedicated and vulnerable Cathy be better off rid of him? The story delves deep into their fractured relationship and highlights how circumstances such as success or failure can completely alter the perspective of life. As we watched the disintegration of their marriage, we still find some fine comic moments particularly in Jamie's 'Schmuel Song' and Cathy's 'Summer in Ohio'. We see the relationship really take its toll on Cathy after a constant string of audition knockbacks instilling a sense of paranoia and low self-esteem. You may even say at times that Cathy becomes quite neurotic, needy and insecure as Jamie's confidence continues to implode!

In every relationship there are two sides to the story! Only you can decide which side is responsible for its demise. Was this couple's relationship doomed from the start? Were they too young? Did Jamie's wild success and Cathy's constant rejection bring their once perfect relationship to breaking point?

I would love a sequel 'The Next Five Years'. Where big time Broadway star Cathy Hiatt meets dried-up down on his luck Jamie Wellerstein on a street in Manhattan!! I so enjoyed the beautiful contrast of storytelling by an extremely believable couple with powerhouse voices expelling a reservoir of sadness. This performance also portrayed honesty, fun and was truly poignant. Thank you.

Director - Cian O'Dowd An artfully staged production of The Last Five Years. Delivered through stringent and challenging times. However, sitting in the Riverbank Arts Centre on July 3rd, the Covid pandemic never once entered my head as I was transported into the lives of Cathy Hiatt and Jamie Wellerstein. This in itself is a triumph to Cian and his team. I felt this production had been given a lot of thought. Cian very obviously aided his actors in truly finding the potency of their story. I felt although Cian kept it real he still managed to deliver a sensory overload and a truly compelling version with fresh intimacy. Cian's direction had what I like to call a strong dramatic spine and his ambitious vision spilled out onto the Riverbank stage. It was a raw and honest production with many moving moments and delicious humour. The pace was spot on as we watched these two characters push boundaries as they slowly destroyed each other. One particularly memorable moment for me was when Jamie sang the line 'I will not fail so you can be comfortable Cathy, I will not lose because you can't win' the deliverance of this line certainly hit a nerve! Well done Cian, in dire times you managed to produce a musical slice of life. A profoundly touching and beautiful piece of theatre.

Musical Director - Keelin Kilduff The singing was flawless. It was well polished and well performed, spirited where it needed to be and somber in turn. The combination of Cathy and Jamie's songs were seamless and 'The Next 10 Minutes' simply beautiful; it was infused with emotion which gave us a genuine portrayal of the characters feelings. The precision of the vocal was stunning and executed with such ease. Both actors provided a beautifully nuanced account of the story through their songs as they soared and belted their way through all 14 musical numbers.

Each of the songs were full-bodied and a faithful version of events.

The excellent work that went in here was very evident.

Choreographer - Cian O'Dowd More musical staging than choreography but well thought through and very well- rehearsed.

What I liked most about this was it didn't seem awkward or overdone, it was natural and seamless. Coming from a choreography background, a pet hate of mine is putting movement in for the sake of it! This didn't happen here every move directed was on point and streamlined effortlessly into the song complementing the lyrics and aiding the overall storytelling. I particularly liked 'Shiska Goddess',' The Schmuel Song' and the crossover of Cathy and Jamie from stage left to stage right and vice versa at the halfway mark of the story, the moment when their life stories changed paths. Very clever. All in all impressive. Well done.

Cathy Hiatt - Keelin Kilduff Keelin portrayed a plethora of emotions in this 90-minute production which I have no doubt left her feeling euphoric and gratified but also most probably drained and exhausted on the floor of her dressing room! It really is an emotional rollercoaster for Cathy and what makes it even more challenging is she performs the narrative in reverse order. It calls for an accomplished and experienced actor to go in cold and drive that first song with the despair and desolation that is required to shape the story, Keelin did this impressively. She left us in no doubt how much she loved Jamie, holding onto that last glimmer of hope right to the bitter end while trying so desperately to convince herself and Jamie that they could still be happy. Singing 'So we'll start again this weekend' and' I think we're going to be ok' in her song' I'm Still Smiling'. The open innocence Keelin brought to the role at times was beautifully convincing and her transition from happiness through frustration to paranoia and final heartbreak was sublime. With perfect pitch Keelin soared through all nine songs and I must comment I particularly liked 'Climbing Uphill'' where you saw a breaking point start to emerge in Cathy's character. Another pivotal point in this production was at the end of 'A part of that 'when she can no longer convince herself of her importance to Jamie and finishes the song actually asking herself the question 'Aren't I'?

It leaves you wonder if Cathy had landed her big break on Broadway would things have turned out differently? Did she give up not only on her career but also in a way on her marriage? We are in no doubt she loved Jamie but was it enough? Did she in fact end up in 'a typical life in a town on the Eastern shore' as she sang in 'I can do better than that'? Keelin gave a richly layered performance of the character Cathy Hiatt's life as we watched her dreams shatter and her life unravel before us.

Jamie Wellerstein - Daniel Ryan From the off, Daniel had a propulsive drive in this production. He never once took his foot off the gas, it started strong and went up from there. Daniel displayed a compelling combination of raw human feeling as he nose -dived into his impulsive marriage to Cathy. This was later followed by a myriad of emotions love, success, self -obsession, guilt and then finally devastating defeat as he gave up and walked away from his marriage.

Daniel's performance was multi-layered. I particularly liked the 'Schmuel Song' which had a real sense of jaunty fun to it! The interpretation of both characters was excellent, the accents spot on, the choreography and use of props very clever and it was smoothly executed. Daniel acted well in quiet moments and used all costumes and props with ease. 'Shiska Godess' was another highlight, excellently acted with great characterisation.

I particularly liked the placing of feet on the table on the appropriate word!! Also the use of the couch throw for the Hebrew slave and the jump on the table for a good strong finish.

Another moment that brought a smile was the tipping of the standing light as if dipping a dance partner in a tango move! Very suave indeed!

'The Last 10 Minutes' was quiet and believable and' If I didn't believe in you' the last spoken "Please" with that look of pure desperation in the eyes was superb.' Nobody needs to know' again vulnerable and desperate on the line "Since I have to be in love with someone" again superb. There are too many points I'd like to mention but summing up, Daniel showed fierce commitment to this role and had a dominant presence on stage. An intensely moving portrayal of Jamie Wellerstein. Piano Accompaniment - Dave McGauran I could have sat and listened to this gentleman play all night. Smooth and sophisticated accompaniment. A standout moment for me was the instrumental break in 'Moving too fast', it reminded me of a Harry Connick Junior track. So chill, I loved it! Tempo and overall interpretation of score excellent. Great job.

Stage Management - Adam Trundle Slick and very well-organised.

The backstage crew tiptoed around the set like ninjas as they meticulously moved the stage furniture and props into place. There was more to manoeuvre than met the eye but then that's the sign of an efficient and well-rehearsed stage crew. What was also very impressive was the accuracy of re- setting a scene for the second time great attention to detail. Well done.

Lighting - Anthony Quinn Subtle yet captivating. Very nice use of the two spots and five hanging lights. Tight on cues and I must mention I particularly liked the full five lights coming on when the wedding rings were put on and again later when Jamie took his off. Very efficient execution overall. Really thought the warm lighting on white quilt in bedroom scene added texture and mood to the song 'Nobody needs to know' Nice balance and intimacy within scenes and strong uniformity which made the show flow with ease.

Overall great job.

Sound - Peter Lee Crystal clear. All cues spot on. Volume levels for mics and piano were perfect. A very professional job from start to finish. Flawless.

Hair and makeup - Natural and suitable to setting Props - Suitable sourced and in keeping with production.

Artwork - Emma Kilduff The artwork was eye-catching and imaginative.

"Who says four chairs and a keyboard can't make a musical?"

This quirky one-act musical with lyrics and music by Jeff Bowen and book by Hunter Bell began its inception in New York in 2004. It premiered at the Lyceum Theatre on Broadway in 2008 and ran for 102 performances. With no orchestra, just a single keyboard, no dancing and no set it was certainly an ambitious task! Centred around the four main characters Jeff, Hunter, Susan and Heidi with Larry on keys, these ambitious Broadway wannabes have only three weeks to write a complete musical for the upcoming Theatre Festival.

Bowen and Bell's autobiographical meta-musical pushes many emotional buttons as we witness the four friends struggle not only with their personal simmering self-doubt but their inner insecurities towards each other. This production provides snappy and brilliantly funny dialogue with lots of in- house jokes and theatre references, rolled in with some superb songs and precisely choreographed musical staging.

Gorey Little Theatre, a fine venue for any performance. As we entered the theatre on the evening of Friday September 10th you could almost immediately sense a feeling of euphoric anticipation in the air. We were generously greeted by the lovely front of house ladies and then by director Stephen Acton. As we settled into our seats, we had the visual of an open stage with four chairs and exquisite mood lighting.

The performance began with a clever and witty voice-over which instructed us to switch off our mobile phones etc. this was subsequently followed by the actors introducing themselves to the audience via a silent walk-through encompassing some highly humorous acting in quiet moments. I found this worked well and was a nice touch as you also immediately identified with each of the characters. Director Stephen Acton's take on this production was fresh and new. It was smartly directed and had an explosive adolescent energy. There was nothing static about this production, it was a truly entertaining 90 minutes of musical theatre. Celebrating the story of so many inspirational people who strive every day to create art, they are the fierce driving force and the shaping element behind countless magnificent productions.

The choreography/musical staging was innovative and exciting to watch, with clever chair-ography and use of props. 'Die Vampire Die' was a personal favourite for me and 'A Way back to When' was beautifully staged as pictures assembled and disintegrated before us and Caoimhe Boyle's voice mesmerised the audience. This show is never going to be an eye- popping spectacle but it's the atmospheric framing that makes it addictive to watch. With multilayered performances Mr Acton ensured the actors delivered a richly nuanced account of the narrative with sublime charm, fresh intimacy and multiple comedic moments.

Laugh out loud for Larry!

Conor McCarthy's unobtrusive presence in the corner of the stage with his keyboard was a real crowd pleaser. Not only had Conor the ambitious task as acting MD, chorus master and one-man orchestra but he also had his own little part, who says men can't multitask! Although on saying that Larry did become loudly intrusive and highly indigent when he was not included in the cast photo shoot and I have to admit this was a real laugh out loud moment for me! Conor also pulled laughs with his many priceless facial expressions and his very dramatic collapse onto the keyboard after the 'Dream Sequence'. Mr McCarthy's work in this production overall was immaculate, the 2- and 4-piece harmonies were stunning and all solo and group work excellent, as was his playing.

Jeff and Hunter, what a double act, played by James Dobbs and Richard O'Toole. The two actors shared snappy dialogue, fabulous song harmonies and portrayed a multifaceted relationship. I have witnessed James on stage many times and always find his performances extremely believable and sincere. Mr Dobbs with his high ability in all three genres makes up what's known as the triple threat, desperately longed for by all production teams. Standout moments in James' performance were 'Two Nobodies in New York', the hilarious dance rehearsal with Heidi beside the piano and the very last scene where he oozes sincerity in 'Nine People's Favourite Thing'. Brilliant work.

His partner in crime was Richard O'Toole. Richard delivered a solid performance with high energy, strong vocals and well- rehearsed choreography. The opening song 'Two Nobodies in New York' was excellent, the harmonies were marvellous and you immediately witnessed the strong relationship and bond between Hunter and Jeff. Another highlight was 'Monkeys and Playbills' this was rapturously funny, as was the scene were Hunter tried to make a pass at Jeff.

Mr O'Toole contributed to a story of losses and gains with many moving moments, all mixed in with some witty pizzazz.

The Girls - Caoimhe Boyle played Heidi Blickenstaff and Maria Forrest played Susan Blackwell. Two very different ladies indeed. Heidi the working Broadway understudy but ultimate Broadway babe, affected, confident and highly ambitious. Susan on the other hand has just kind of given up, she works in an office to pay the bills and has lost that inner spark she once had for the bright lights! The two characters form a fractured relationship but a relationship none the less.

Caoimhe Boyle, well this little lady has pipes! What a wonderful voice, I found myself melting into my seat as Caoimhe sang 'A Way Back to When' it was profoundly beautiful. Ms Boyle delivered many moving moments mixed in with some delicious humour. She embraced the part of Heidi with confidence and feeling while lending great support to her fellow actors.

Maria's take on the part of Susan was fierce. Her character had a dry sense of humour that lent itself beautifully to comedy. She was refreshing to watch and most definitely a dominant presence on stage. Maria delivered full bodied vocals and all her acting and choreography was on point. I particularly liked when Susan had the conversation with the answering machine this was undeniably funny! Maria's show stopping song was 'Die Vampire Die' this for me stole the show. Ms Forrest had a riveting stage presence and certainly put her stamp on this role. The set for this musical is practically non- existent, four chairs used in multiple ways, some stage flats and a few props, but it was the atmospheric lighting of those flats with LED's that gave the story texture and framed the action beautifully.

Eddie O'Brien on lighting provided some lovely use of subtle spots in 'A Way Back to When' and some super dramatic lighting in 'Die Vampire Die'. Over all the lighting was precise and lent itself well to the production.

Sound by Joe Murphy was well managed. Cueing was perfect and balance between singers and piano was good.

Costumes were all in keeping with the era, as was hair and makeup. Props were well researched and may I give a particularly mention to the great props in 'Monkeys and Playbills'.

What a fabulous achievement amid a pandemic. Like the characters Bowen and Bell, you strove to make it possible. Thank you for a great night's entertainment and for having the vision, courage and passion to make it happen.

A production set amidst the trials and tribulations of a pandemic is no easy task but FMT with pure grit and determination seemed to make it happen regardless. A young vibrant and happy company brought us back to a night filled with music, song, dance and laughter, in one word, 'Theatre'. Thank you.

Curtains, with book by Rupert Holmes, music by John Kander and lyrics by Fred Ebb. This production was nominated for eight Tony award nominations in 2007 including best musical and also a Drama Desk Award. First produced in 2006 this comedic musical set in the Colonial Theatre Boston in 1959 rapidly became a real crowd pleaser with high-energy songs and choreography, quirky well written comedy and some beautifully moving moments. As the action unfolds, we find the cast of 'Robbin' Hood of the Old West' the musical in quite a predicament as their leading lady Jessica Cranshaw falls to the ground on her curtain call, she is dead! Immediately we are transported into a murder mystery and as the cast and crew still try to polish the Robbin' Hood production for their Broadway pitch the plot thickens. Lieutenant Frank Cioffi then arrives onto the scene to investigate; he is a huge musical theatre fan and is obsessed with the cast and their production. He manages to solve the crime, re-produce the show and find love along the way! Now that's a result! This is a show within a show infused with playful energy, dazzling costumes and a profusely driven score, all blended with a charming and witty script. In conclusion, a hilarious whodunnit musical that will keep you guessing until the final curtain falls. Director - Sam McElgunn Helmed a solid production. The pacing of the show was good, the cast were clearly enjoying themselves on stage and this in turn was reflected by the great audience reaction.

The production was everything you'd expect: it packed a punch but also delivered freshness and charm. The sets, costumes, hair and make-up were all truthful to the era and the character direction suitably guided.

The production overall had a joyous feel to it and transported us back to the year 1959 in Boston while also shining a light on the old Wild West to boot. Miss McElgunn delivered a faithful version of the script and a production that embraced life, love, quirky vulnerability with some gloriously funny moments thrown into mix.

Musical Director - Moya Sweeney The score was brassy and bright providing some high moments with big dance breaks and ensemble singing but it also delivered some beautifully intimate moments. Favourites had to be 'Show People', 'It's a Business' and 'I Miss the Music'.  23 musical numbers including the overture and reprises, not an easy task in any manner but particularly difficult to achieve in the present climate! Although backing tracks were in use due to the restrictions, after the immediate start this did not reflect on the balance of the performances and production as a whole. All Principal roles and Ensemble singing was tight, well-rehearsed and delivered in strong character with high fine energy, punch and power. Harmonies were excellent in 'In the Same Boat' with Georgia, Nikki and Bambi and also in Act 2 'In the Same Boat - Complete' again some fabulous work with the 3 boys and ensemble.

An uplifting score with catchy songs, addictive earworms and a jovial cast. A job well done.

Choreographer - Aimee Drumm From the off the choreography in this show was slick and well executed. I counted maybe two or three songs that may not have required an amount of choreography but the rest of the musical numbers were really full on! I know from personal experience and being an active choreographer myself going on 35 years now, this can be quite overwhelming! So well done Aimee. The opening number 'Wide Open Spaces' set the show in motion and we saw immediately this chorus had been drilled! Favourites had to be 'In the Same Boat', 'Thataway!' and 'Kansasland', these numbers displayed robust and athletic choreography with some great lifts and solos. All the performers oozed confidence which told me immediately this had been well rehearsed despite covid and zoom conflicts. The execution of the choreography displayed incredible energy as it exploded onto the stage, just how it should be! Great work.

Lieutenant Frank Cioffi - Ryan Moohan What a role to play! This character has to expel talent from every pore, he has to be well able to sing, dance and act. In addition to that he has to have great comic timing, but above all, he has to work vigorously throughout the production because if he falls static at any point so does the momentum of the show. He is integrated so deeply into the plot, and because of this needs a propulsive drive throughout. Ryan Moohan delivered on all fronts and dissolved all doubts in the very first scene that he had prepared himself totally for this character. My first real belly laugh of the night was on Cioffi's first entrance, where he introduced himself to the cast so seriously as the investigating Lieutenant and then proceeded to join into the song 'The Man is Dead', striking the last three finishing poses of the choreography, very funny indeed. Ryan displayed the compelling combination of emotion and exhilaration in 'A Tough Act to Follow' with his love interest Nikki. Here I felt his versatility shone as he magically swept his partner around the stage. This six-minute number requires stamina and discipline and it was obvious Ryan had laid out the groundwork on this one. In conclusion strong vocals, sandwiched between clean well-rehearsed choreography and uplifting dialogue with great comic timing,. A lovely happy ending all delivered with a big dash of comedic charm.

Carmen Bernstein - Brenda Swift The character of Carmen is not exactly subtle to say the least! She brings a powerful resonance and an overwhelming impact to the stage each time she appears. Brenda Swift generously embraced this part and delivered with punch and power never once feeling intimidated by the scale of this gloriously robust role. Swift delivered on all fronts with incredible vocals, solid well executed acting and slick comic timing. I particularly liked Brenda's participation in 'What Kind of Man' and 'It's a Business', this song was a true testament to Miss Swift's multifaceted capabilities.

The confession scene at the end of Act 2 was cleverly gauged and not over acted, as sometimes there is a tendency to oversell this scene, Brenda gave a beautifully nuanced account of this closer. In summing up a sophisticated performance with priceless stage presence and truly hilarious one-liners, for me Swift stole the show.

Nikki Harris - Nadia Stenson I warmed to Nadia from her very first line. The girl next door with a dash of innocent comedic charm and a knack for capturing the moment beautifully. Nadia displayed the true essence of Nikki's character with ease as she floated through her dialogue and songs beautifully.

Perfectly partnered with Cioffi, the couple's comic timing was spot on and of course the highlight for me being 'A Tough Act to Follow'. This number is not one for the faint hearted! It is a marathon of a musical number which is over six minutes long, this number is a test of true showmanship, as following the three-minute dance break you are then expected to finish by singing out the last section. Well, you both certainly rose to the challenge showing fabulous coordination, some lovely partner work and a striking sincerity throughout. I found Nadia's performance refreshing and believable. Suffice to say she totally invested in the part of Nikki Harris and embraced it with meticulous care and compassion. Splendid work. Aaron Fox - Rory Blake Rory lavished us with rich and soaring vocals. The song 'I miss the Music' was infectious and shaped Aaron's character well, while leaving us in absolutely no doubt of his undeniable love for Georgia. Blake and Philips had a natural chemistry and sang and acted well together. The scenes with Cioffi were also well structured and the subject matter convincing. The playing of the piano was spot on and the general carriage and stage movement good. A believable relationship between Aaron and Georgia was evident from the start and this in turn transferred well to the audience. Well done.

Georgia Hendricks - Sarah Philips This character has to be the real deal, the triple threat! Singing, acting and dancing are all a necessary requirement for this role. Sarah did not disappoint on any of the above. A glorious vocal sandwiched with sincere acting and sizzling choreography left us in no doubt that Philips was a well capable young performer. 'Thinking of Him' was beautifully delivered and' Thataway!' was one of the productions highlights. I really liked the multiple shoulder lifts among many other choreography tricks and felt it was performed with confidence and style.

Contributions to 'What kind of Man' and 'In the Same Boat' were also excellent with some marvellous harmonies with Nikki and Bambi in 'In the Same Boat'. Sarah embraced this part with a high emphasis on performance. A full-bodied and captivating interpretation coupled with an infused playful energy.

Christopher Belling - Jonny Cameron One word, Funny!

Fabulous comic timing, facial expressions and body language. Truly one of the productions scene stealers. Cameron's delivery of the witty one-liners was sublime and had us all giggling our way through the production. All the laugh lines landed perfectly and Jonny delivered everything you would expect from this character. The performance was consistent throughout which can often be the problem with a character like this who can rise and fall or even overact. Diction was crystal clear so the audience heard and lapped up the sarcastic and seriously funny one-liners. Because Cameron's performance was so spot on it framed the production with an atmospheric lightness and made for a fun filled and highly entertaining 2 hours. I particularly liked the participation in 'What kind of Man' and 'He Did It'. Vocals and movement were also very secure, well-rehearsed and always held perfectly in character. A gust of giddy good fun. Brilliant work.

Bambi Bernét - Gráinne Kennedy What a great part, again this falls into the triple threat department. 'Kansasland' was another marathon of a musical number from this production but Gráinne's fitness levels are certainly top notch as she energetically displayed.

Off the charts vitality and exuberance are required for this musical number in fact' Girl Power' springs to mind with this character! Kennedy was completely infused with playful energy, even including a spiralling yellow ribbon into her choreography at one point. I really liked the acting in quiet moments and Grainne never once let this slip, one very funny moment was the stretching exercises at the back of the stage during 'He Did It'. The accent was good and the dialogue delivery clear as was the vocal in all ensemble numbers. The interaction with Carmen as Mother and Daughter was spot on and the athletic choreography exhausting to watch! Kennedy to me was the glitter bomb of the show. Take another bow Bambi, you deserve it.

Bobby Pepper - Rhys Hopkins I really liked Bobby from the second he stepped out on stage and smiled I said to myself this guy's got charisma. Rhys had a skip in his step throughout, spinning and stylising his entrances, exits and dance moves with natural ease. Hopkins was visually pleasing to watch as he owned every corner of the stage. The performance was slick and well-polished and he portrayed the cheeky chappie you immediately want to befriend. The dance moves were brave and full of attack as Rhys leaped and spun around the stage in 'Kansasland' barely taking time to draw breath. Vocals were also strong and well-rehearsed.  Hopkins contributions to 'Thinking of him' and 'Kansasland' were solid as were all his ensemble numbers. But it was his acting and the great big smile that stood out for me. I see a bright future for Rhys Hopkins on the stage. Randy Dexter - Odhrán Sweeney We got a glimpse of some great work from Odhrán Sweeney in the musical number 'Kansasland'. His tenor vocal was strong and he delivered with character and confidence. The dance moves were also very well-rehearsed and performed with energy and vigour. 'In the Same Boat' was tight and vocals were impressive as was the musical staging. Sweeney was a strong and reliable chorus member and a shaping element to the production as a whole.

Harv Fermont - Niall Kerr Niall was very much enjoying himself on stage and this became infectious to the audience. His dynamic contribution to the chorus was very noticeable. Niall's opening of Act 2 'The Man is Dead' was excellent and his participation in the trio in 'In the Same Boat' was a highlight. Acting in quiet moments was spot on and support was regularly given in partner choreography. Niall's input in this production was very evident. Well done Niall.

Joanie Harmon - Aoife Cleary Aoife's role was a bit like the glue in this production. She led us in and out of scenes topping and tailing as she went until she unfortunately met her sorry demise! Always ready to move a set or holler out stage cues she moved through the production with poise and purpose. Her support in the ensemble numbers 'The Man is Dead' and 'He Did It' were strongly presented and the dialogue scenes solid and well-rehearsed. I liked Joanie's costume choice the denim dungarees and red bandana really suited the character. A good start for a first performance, well done Aoife, keep it up.

Daryl Grady - Francis Keaney On my notes I had written Daryl Grady - Cool Cat! Francis played a smooth-talking reporter who turns nasty in the end. His introduction to the audience saw the measured and formidable stereo typical rag reporter hold his power of the opening night crit over an already overwrought and distressed cast and crew. Diction and dialogue were well delivered in this scene but it was in the final scene were Keaney really came into his own. Portraying raw human feeling Keaney tapped into the darkness of a desperate love sick man who was snared like a frightened animal. This scene had a propulsive drive and completed the narrative solidly. Good work.

Sidney Bernstein - Andrew Campbell Every show has a baddie, the one the audience love to hate. Well Sidney Bernstein most definitely falls into this category. He likes to push boundaries and is a profound pain of a human. Scene interaction with Carmen and Bambi was convincing, dialogue was clear and well- rehearsed. Andrew helped along the deeply thickening plot until his forcible exit was induced by a rope! Sidney's part may have been short lived but Campbell certainly left an impact with his selfish and unforgiving character.

Jessica Cranshaw - Alison Lapin An over the hill fading Hollywood star with little or no talent but never the less still a flamboyant and demanding Diva. Alison played the opening scene with strident and brassy force, it was cringe worthy to observe as she lost her direction, her dialogue and her deliverance. Unashamedly silly and highly entertaining Lapin hit the nail on the head as she embraced Cranshaw's character and willed us all to join the party that celebrated simple comedy.

Oscar Shapiro - Josiah Johnston Josiah added layers to his role as Oscar Shapiro and this I liked. The costume, shoes and glasses immediately gave the impression of the quirky but likeable character. Acting was excellent, diction and delivery solid and vocals strong. I particularly liked 'What Kind of Man', 'The Woman's Dead' and 'He Did It'. (I loved the striped pjs in this scene).  Johnston was an asset to the front line as his lines fell just right with natural ease and a comical flair.

Ensemble A great team of hard working, energetic and eager to entertain young people who very obviously love being on stage. All musical numbers were very well rehearsed and tight. Singing was spot on with some fabulous harmonies. Moving of sets and use of props was flawless and acting in quiet moments excellent. A real team effort.

Stage Manager - Sonia Norris Solid and secure stage management with slick and beautifully creative lighting. The multipurpose reversible sets were clever and in keeping with the narrative. The Saloon, School House and arrow board in the opening scene were all imperative in setting the Old West scene and then they later cleverly turned to reveal theatre flats.

Set Designer - Sarah McGourty The School and Saloon sets were suitable for the Old West show rehearsal scenes and then similarly they doubled up for the Theatre flats fashionable smothered with old photos, rehearsal schedules, old programmes and such.

Costume Designer - Sean McDermott Bambi's Indian costume in 'Kansasland', Nikki's pretty blue and pink dress with the flowers and Oscar's pin striped pyjamas were the favourites for me. The red and black costumes in 'Thataway' were also on point but basically all costuming throughout was in keeping with both the Wild West and Boston 1959 periods. Lighting The lighting was beautifully creative and I made many comments throughout the production on how slick it was..

Sound The sound was also to a high standard. All dialogue and singing was crystal clear and balanced perfectly.

CURTAINS - A production set amidst the trials and tribulations of a pandemic is no easy task but FMT with pure grit and determination seemed to make it happen regardless. A young vibrant and happy company brought us back to a night filled with music, song, dance and laughter, in one word, 'Theatre'. Thank you.
